One may indeed be entirely without them; probably more than one of you here present is without them in any marked degree; but if you do have them, and have them at all strongly, the probability is that you cannot help regarding them as genuine perceptions of truth, as revelations of a kind of reality which no adverse argument, however unanswerable by you in words, can expel from your belief. The opinion opposed to mysticism in philosophy is sometimes spoken of as rationalism. Rationalism insists that all our beliefs ought ultimately to find for themselves articulate grounds. Such grounds, for rationalism, must consist of four things: definitely statable abstract principles; definite facts of sensation; definite hypotheses based on such facts; and definite inferences logically drawn. Vague impressions of something indefinable have no place in the rationalistic system, which on its positive side is surely a splendid intellectual tendency, for not only are all our philosophies fruits of it, but physical science (amongst other good things) is its result.

Nevertheless, if we look on man’s whole mental life as it exists, on the life of men that lies in them apart from their learning and science, and that they inwardly and privately follow, we have to confess that the part of it of which rationalism can give an account is relatively superficial. It is the part that has the prestige undoubtedly, for it has the loquacity, it can challenge you for proofs, and chop logic, and put you down with words. But it will fail to convince or convert you all the same, if your dumb intuitions are opposed to its conclusions. If you have intuitions at all, they come from a deeper level of your nature than the loquacious level which rationalism inhabits. Your whole subconscious life, your impulses, your faiths, your needs, your divinations, have prepared the premises, of which your consciousness now feels the weight of the result; and something in you absolutely knows that that result must be truer than any logic-chopping rationalistic talk, however clever, that may contradict it. This inferiority of the rationalistic level in founding belief is just as manifest when rationalism argues for religion as when it argues against it. That vast literature of proofs of God’s existence drawn from the order of nature, which a century ago seemed so overwhelmingly convincing, to-day does little more than gather dust in libraries, for the simple reason that our generation has ceased to believe in the kind of God it argued for. Whatever sort of a being God may be, we know to-day that he is nevermore that mere external inventor of “contrivances” intended to make manifest his “glory” in which our great-grandfathers took such satisfaction, though just how we know this we cannot possibly make clear by words either to others or to ourselves. I defy any of you here fully to account for your persuasion that if a God exist he must be a more cosmic and tragic personage than that Being.

The truth is that in the metaphysical and religious sphere, articulate reasons are cogent for us only when our inarticulate feelings of reality have already been impressed in favor of the same conclusion. Then, indeed, our intuitions and our reason work together, and great world-ruling systems, like that of the Buddhist or of the Catholic philosophy, may grow up. Our impulsive belief is here always what sets up the original body of truth, and our articulately verbalized philosophy is but its showy translation into formulas. The unreasoned and immediate assurance is the deep thing in us, the reasoned argument is but a surface exhibition. Instinct leads, intelligence does but follow. If a person feels the presence of a living God after the fashion shown by my quotations, your critical arguments, be they never so superior, will vainly set themselves to change his faith.

Please observe, however, that I do not yet say that it is better that the subconscious and non-rational should thus hold primacy in the religious realm. I confine myself to simply pointing out that they do so hold it as a matter of fact.

sessions.readWhy: James gave these lectures in Edinburgh, Hume's city, and he too was no apologist. He collects first-hand accounts of God's presence and argues that such experiences convince those who have them more than any logic, while declining to say whether that is a good thing. It is the honest answer to Hume, and a challenge to both sides.

think.why: Rudolf Otto's account of the holy and the new psychology of awe sit side by side here, with the fair objection that awe can be felt without God at all.

evidence.why: Keltner and Haidt founded the modern study of awe and traced its roots in religious writing. It shows that awe is a real and widely shared human response; it cannot show whether anything answers to it.

learn.why: Augustine searched outside for what was within all along; it is the most famous description of finding God in Christian writing, and a reply to the hiddenness of the last session.

music.why: Russian Orthodox evening and morning prayer, music written to be prayed through rather than listened to.

look.why: Strozzi paints a man in a monk's robe, his hands together in prayer, elbows on a rock, lit from one side while the rest of the picture falls into deep shadow. Francis is shown not proving anything, but turned towards someone.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, before you sleep, say quietly, 'If you are there, show me', and then do one small, kind thing for someone the next day without telling them.
sessions.reflect: Have you ever had an experience that felt like a presence, or like being known? What did you make of it at the time, and what do you make of it now?

closing.title: What do you think now?
closing.prompt: Having heard the beginning of the universe, fine-tuning, the order of nature, Hume's objections, the multiverse, hiddenness and the experience of presence: is there a God? Write your answer in a few sentences, with the one reason that weighs most with you and the one objection you still find hardest.
closing.practice: Keep asking honestly. Once a week, read one page from someone who sees it the other way, and once a day, pray or pause with the words, 'If you are there, show me.'

title: Who was Jesus?
question: Who did he claim to be, and was he right?
line: A trial with four witnesses: the world he was born into, what he said about himself, what he did, and what the prophets said to expect. Then the case against at full strength, and a verdict.
why: Jesus is the most influential person who has ever lived, and most people have met him only second-hand. This course goes back to the sources, friendly and hostile, and asks the question he asked his own friends: 'Who do you say that I am?' You will read Mark, Matthew, Luke and John beside Daniel, Isaiah, a Jewish psalm that prayed for a warrior Messiah, a pagan wonder-worker, Thomas Paine, D. F. Strauss and the Qur'an. You will hear the case that he was only a good teacher, made into a god by legend, at full strength. And you will see how Jews, Muslims and Christians each answer.
follows: A first-year paper on the figure of Jesus: the historical Jesus in his Jewish setting, the Gospel traditions and their criteria, and the beginnings of Christology, with Jewish and Muslim views.
before: how-to-read-the-bible
outcomes: Explain what historians agree about Jesus, and set him in his world: Herod, Rome, the Jewish groups, the languages, and the date of his birth with the census problem.
Explain what Jesus said about himself, including 'Son of Man' with Daniel 7, the forgiveness of sins and the hearing before the high priest, and say whether he claimed to be divine.
Explain what 'Messiah' meant, using the Psalms of Solomon, and why a suffering Messiah shocked Peter.
Assess the miracle stories as a historian would, with hostile witnesses and other wonder-workers, and say what the Gospels present them as.
Distinguish kinds of prophetic fulfilment, and set the Christian and Jewish readings side by side.
State the 'good teacher' and legend objections at full strength, assess Lewis's trilemma, and give a reasoned verdict, with Jewish, Muslim and Christian views.

sessions.title: The world he was born into
sessions.line: A Galilean Jew, born under Herod in a Roman province where people spoke Aramaic and wrote Greek: meet him first in Mark's first chapter.
sessions.plain: Jesus did not appear out of nowhere. He was a Jew from Galilee, born around 6 to 4 BC under King Herod, in a land ruled by Rome, where people spoke Aramaic, prayed in Hebrew and did business in Greek. Everything he said was heard by people with hopes and fears of their own, above all the hope that God would send a Messiah. This session reads the first chapter of the earliest Gospel, sets beside it Matthew's story of the wise men, and draws the map of his world.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'How to read the Bible' showed you how to read slowly, with the plain sense first, and with others. Now we turn to the person at the centre of the Christian Bible. This journey treats the question like a trial with four witnesses: the world he was born into, what he said about himself, what he did, and what the prophets said to expect. The first witness is his world, because no one can understand a man without knowing where and when he lived.
answers: Did Jesus really exist?
When and where was he born?
What was Judea like under Rome, and who were the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes?
What language did he speak, and why are the Gospels in Greek?
How much of the Christmas story is history?
sessions.finding: Jesus was a Galilean Jew under Roman rule in a Greek-speaking empire, born around 6–4 BC: everything he said must be heard there.

paras: Jesus of Nazareth is the most influential person who has ever lived: about a third of the world's people call themselves his followers, and the West counts its years from his birth. Yet many people know him only second-hand, from Christmas cards, films or arguments. This journey goes back to the sources and asks one question: who did he claim to be, and was he right?

Almost all historians, Christian, Jewish and secular, agree on a short list of facts. He was a Jew from Galilee, in the north of what is now Israel. He was baptised by a preacher called John. He taught about 'the kingdom of God', gathered followers, was known as a healer and was crucified by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate around AD 30. The Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus both mention him; you can read their words in 'What is the Bible?'. Christians say more: that he was the Messiah, the Son of God, and rose from the dead. Muslims honour him as a prophet and the Messiah; most Jews see him as a Jewish teacher, not the Messiah. We will hear all of them.
background.key: Almost all historians agree that Jesus was a Galilean Jew, baptised by John, who taught, healed and was crucified under Pilate around AD 30. Who he was beyond that is the question.

paras: Think of it as a trial. To decide who someone is, a court hears witnesses. We will call four. First, the world he was born into, because words mean what they mean in a place and time. Second, what he said about himself. Third, what he did. Fourth, what the prophets of Israel told people to expect. Then the case against is put at full strength, and the last session gives a verdict.
His death and what his followers said happened three days later belong to the journeys that follow in this hall. This one asks who he claimed to be.

timeline.text: The world he was born into (Mark 1; Matthew 2)
What he said about himself (Mark 2 and 14; Daniel 7)
Who do you say I am? (Mark 8; the Psalms of Solomon)
What he did: miracles (Mark 4; John 6; Philostratus)
Prophecy fulfilled? (Luke 4; Isaiah 61)
The case against: just a good teacher? (Paine; Strauss; John 10)
The verdict (Philippians 2; the Qur'an)

background.key: Who did he claim to be, and was he right? Four witnesses (his world, his words, his deeds, the prophets), the case against, then a verdict.

paras: Jesus's homeland was a strip of land about the size of Wales, between the Mediterranean and the river Jordan. In 63 BC the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem. From 37 BC Rome let a local king, Herod the Great, rule for it. Herod was a brilliant builder and a cruel ruler: he rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem on a vast scale, and he had one of his wives and three of his sons killed. He died in 4 BC, by most scholars' reckoning, and his kingdom was split between three sons. Galilee, where Jesus grew up, went to Herod Antipas. Judea, around Jerusalem, came under a Roman governor from AD 6; Pontius Pilate held the post from AD 26 to 36.

So Jesus was born under a Jewish king who served Rome, grew up under another, and died under a Roman governor. The Jews paid taxes to Rome, lived beside Roman soldiers, and remembered that their land had been promised to them by God.

Herod the Great, king of Judea under Rome
Augustus, the first Roman emperor

Pontius Pilate governs Judea
Jesus's public work, after his baptism by John
The Jewish war against Rome; the Temple is destroyed

background.key: Jesus was born under Herod the Great (d. 4 BC), grew up in Galilee under Herod Antipas, and died under Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea.

paras: The main reading is the whole first chapter of Mark, the shortest Gospel and, most scholars think, the earliest, written around AD 65–75. An early tradition, recorded by the bishop Papias about AD 120 and quoted by Eusebius, says Mark wrote down what the apostle Peter used to preach. Mark has no birth story at all: he starts with the grown man by the river Jordan, and in one breathless chapter shows what kind of man he was and what kind of world he walked into.

The comparison is Matthew's story of the wise men, which answers the question Mark leaves open: where and when was he born? Luke tells the other birth story, the shepherds and the manger (Luke 2:1–20), which you can read in 'Time made holy'. Matthew's opening, with its prophecy of a virgin's son (Matthew 1:22–23), is read in 'The whole story'.
background.key: Mark 1 shows the grown man in his world; Matthew 2 tells where and when he was born, under Herod, in Bethlehem.

before: What does Mark tell you about Jesus in his very first sentence?
Who in the chapter recognises Jesus first, and what do they call him?
In Matthew, who wants to find the child, and why?
sessions.readWhy: Mark's first chapter in three parts: the beginning by the Jordan, the first sabbath in Capernaum, and a day and night of healing. Then Matthew's wise men.

paras: The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
As it is written in the prophets,

“Behold, I send my messenger before your face,
who will prepare your way before you:

the voice of one crying in the wilderness,
‘Make ready the way of the Lord!
Make his paths straight!’ ”
John came baptizing in the wilderness and preaching the baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins.
All the country of Judea and all those of Jerusalem went out to him. They were baptized by him in the Jordan river, confessing their sins.
John was clothed with camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. He ate locusts and wild honey.
He preached, saying, “After me comes he who is mightier than I, the thong of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and loosen.
I baptized you in water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.”
In those days, Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
Immediately coming up from the water, he saw the heavens parting, and the Spirit descending on him like a dove.
A voice came out of the sky, “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
Immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.
He was there in the wilderness forty days tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals; and the angels were serving him.
Now after John was taken into custody, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Good News of God’s Kingdom,
and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.”
Passing along by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, the brother of Simon, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
Jesus said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.”
Immediately they left their nets, and followed him.
Going on a little further from there, he saw James the son of Zebedee, and John, his brother, who were also in the boat mending the nets.
Immediately he called them, and they left their father, Zebedee, in the boat with the hired servants, and went after him.
They went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath day he entered into the synagogue and taught.
They were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes.
Immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out,
saying, “Ha! What do we have to do with you, Jesus, you Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know you who you are: the Holy One of God!”
Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be quiet, and come out of him!”
The unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying with a loud voice, came out of him.
They were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, “What is this? A new teaching? For with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him!”
The report of him went out immediately everywhere into all the region of Galilee and its surrounding area.
Immediately, when they had come out of the synagogue, they came into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.
Now Simon’s wife’s mother lay sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her.
He came and took her by the hand, and raised her up. The fever left her immediately, and she served them.
At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick, and those who were possessed by demons.
All the city was gathered together at the door.
He healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. He didn’t allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.
Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.
Simon and those who were with him searched for him.
They found him and told him, “Everyone is looking for you.”
He said to them, “Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because I came out for this reason.”
He went into their synagogues throughout all Galilee, preaching and casting out demons.
A leper came to him, begging him, kneeling down to him, and saying to him, “If you want to, you can make me clean.”
Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said to him, “I want to. Be made clean.”
When he had said this, immediately the leprosy departed from him, and he was made clean.
He strictly warned him, and immediately sent him out,
and said to him, “See you say nothing to anybody, but go show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them.”

But he went out, and began to proclaim it much, and to spread about the matter, so that Jesus could no more openly enter into a city, but was outside in desert places. People came to him from everywhere.

parts.title: The beginning
parts.context: Mark wrote in Greek, probably in the late 60s AD, perhaps in Rome. He opens not in Bethlehem but in the desert east of Jerusalem, by the river Jordan, where a prophet called John is calling Israel to start again. Jesus, a grown man from the village of Nazareth in Galilee, comes south to be baptised.

commentary.on: The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
commentary.text: Mark's first sentence is his title. 'Good News' translates the Greek euangelion, from which we get 'evangelist'; in the Roman world it was used for announcements about the emperor, such as his birthday. 'Christ' is not a surname: it is Greek for 'anointed', the Hebrew Messiah. Mark tells you his conclusion in his first line. The rest of the book shows how he reached it.

commentary.on: John came baptizing in the wilderness and preaching the baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins.
commentary.text: John the Baptist is known outside the Bible too: Josephus describes him as a good man who urged the Jews to live justly and be baptised, and says Herod Antipas had him killed. Going out to the wilderness and through the Jordan echoed the Exodus: Israel had entered the promised land by crossing this river. John was calling the nation to begin again.

commentary.on: John was clothed with camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist.
commentary.text: This is a costume with a meaning. The prophet Elijah wore 'a leather belt' (2 Kings 1:8), and the last book of the prophets promised that Elijah would return before 'the great and terrible day' of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). Mark's first readers would have caught the hint: the waiting is over.

commentary.on: Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
commentary.text: Nazareth was a small village, perhaps a few hundred people, so obscure that it is never mentioned in the Old Testament or by Josephus. The baptism is one of the facts historians are surest of, for an odd reason: it was embarrassing. Why would the greater man be baptised by the lesser, in a baptism 'for forgiveness of sins'? Matthew later shows John protesting (Matthew 3:14). Early Christians would hardly have invented a story they then had to explain.

commentary.on: You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
commentary.text: The voice combines two Old Testament lines: Psalm 2:7, where God says to Israel's king, 'You are my son', and Isaiah 42:1, about God's chosen servant 'in whom my soul delights'. King and servant: the two ideas this journey will keep meeting.

commentary.on: He was there in the wilderness forty days tempted by Satan.
commentary.text: Forty recalls Israel's forty years in the desert after the Exodus. Mark tells it in two sentences; Matthew and Luke expand it. 'Satan' is Hebrew for 'the accuser' or 'adversary'.

parts.title: The kingdom, and four fishermen
parts.context: John is arrested by Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee. Jesus goes north, to the villages round the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long, busy with fishing boats. Capernaum, a fishing town on its north shore, becomes his base. The synagogue there was a meeting house for prayer and the reading of Scripture on the Sabbath, the seventh day.

commentary.on: The time is fulfilled, and God's Kingdom is at hand!
commentary.text: This is Jesus's message in one line, and 'the kingdom of God' is the phrase he used most. It does not mean a place, or heaven after death. It means God ruling: God at last putting the world right, as the prophets had promised. To people under Rome, 'kingdom' was a political word. That is part of why he was dangerous.

commentary.on: Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.
commentary.text: Teachers in Israel did not usually choose their students; students chose a rabbi. Jesus calls them, and they leave their nets and their father. Simon, whom he will rename Peter, Andrew, James and John become his inner circle. The painting for this session shows this moment.

commentary.on: he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes.
commentary.text: The scribes were the experts in the law of Moses, and they taught by quoting earlier teachers. Jesus does not quote anyone. The people notice that he speaks as if the authority were his own. Hold on to that: it is the first clue to who he thought he was, and the next session follows it.

commentary.on: I know you who you are: the Holy One of God!
commentary.text: In Mark, the first to recognise Jesus are not his friends but the demons. Mark's world, like most of the ancient world, believed in evil spirits that could seize a person. Whatever we make of that, notice the pattern: the spirit knows who Jesus is, and Jesus tells it to be quiet.

commentary.on: What is this? A new teaching? For with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him!
commentary.text: The crowd links his words and his deeds: the same authority is at work in both. Mark keeps asking his reader the crowd's question: what is this, and who is he?

parts.title: At the door, and before dawn
parts.context: The same Sabbath, after the synagogue, Jesus goes to the home of Simon and Andrew. The Sabbath ends at sunset, when people were allowed to carry loads again, so the sick are brought after dark. Then comes a leper: in Jewish law, a person with a skin disease was 'unclean' and had to live apart from others (Leviticus 13:45–46).

commentary.on: At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick
commentary.text: A small detail that shows Mark knows the Jewish world: the townspeople wait for the Sabbath to end before carrying the sick through the streets.

commentary.on: He didn't allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.
commentary.text: Again the command to be silent. Jesus keeps telling people not to say who he is. Scholars call this 'the messianic secret', and a later session, still to come, asks why.

commentary.on: Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.
commentary.text: After the busiest day, he slips away to pray alone. Whatever else he was, he was a man who prayed, and the prayer he taught his friends is this session's words to learn.

commentary.on: Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him
commentary.text: To touch a leper was to become unclean yourself. Jesus touches him before he heals him. One early Greek manuscript and some early Latin versions read 'being angry' instead of 'moved with compassion'; either way, he is not indifferent.

commentary.on: go show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded
commentary.text: Jesus sends the man to keep the law of Moses (Leviticus 14). He is not founding a new religion against Judaism. He is a Jew sending a healed Jew to the Temple's priests, so that he can go home.

paras: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying,
“Where is he who is born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east, and have come to worship him.”
When King Herod heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.
Gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ would be born.
They said to him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is written through the prophet,

‘You Bethlehem, land of Judah,
are in no way least among the princes of Judah:
for out of you shall come a governor,
who shall shepherd my people, Israel.’ ”
Then Herod secretly called the wise men, and learned from them exactly what time the star appeared.
He sent them to Bethlehem, and said, “Go and search diligently for the young child. When you have found him, bring me word, so that I also may come and worship him.”
They, having heard the king, went their way; and behold, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, until it came and stood over where the young child was.
When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.
They came into the house and saw the young child with Mary, his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Opening their treasures, they offered to him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country another way.

parts.title: Where is he who is born King of the Jews?
parts.context: Matthew's Gospel was written in Greek, probably around AD 80–90, for Jewish followers of Jesus. Bethlehem was a small town about six miles south of Jerusalem, the home town of King David a thousand years before. The 'wise men' are in Greek magoi: Persian priests and star-watchers, the word that gives us 'magic'.

commentary.on: in the days of King Herod
commentary.text: Herod died in 4 BC by most scholars' dating, so Jesus was born before then, probably between 6 and 4 BC. That sounds odd: Jesus born 'before Christ'? Our calendar was worked out by a monk, Dionysius Exiguus, in AD 525, and he was a few years out. Luke too places the birth 'in the days of Herod' (Luke 1:5).

commentary.on: Where is he who is born King of the Jews?
commentary.text: The title is a provocation. Herod was 'king of the Jews', appointed by the Roman Senate. Foreign visitors arrive asking for another. The same title will be nailed above Jesus's cross.

commentary.on: When King Herod heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.
commentary.text: Herod was famously suspicious. He executed his wife Mariamne and three of his own sons for plotting against him. A rumour that a new king had been born was the kind of thing that, in his reign, got people killed.

commentary.on: for out of you shall come a governor, who shall shepherd my people, Israel.
commentary.text: The scribes quote Micah 5:2, combined with a line about David from 2 Samuel 5:2. They expect the Messiah to come from David's town, as David's heir: a shepherd-king.

parts.title: Gold, frankincense and myrrh
parts.context: Herod sends the visitors on to Bethlehem. Matthew tells the story with Old Testament echoes: a wicked king, a star, gifts from the nations.

commentary.on: the star, which they saw in the east, went before them
commentary.text: No one knows what the star was, or whether Matthew means a natural sign at all. The astronomer Johannes Kepler suggested in 1606 a rare meeting of the planets Jupiter and Saturn, which happened three times in 7 BC; others suggest a comet or a new star. Many scholars think Matthew is echoing Numbers 24:17: 'A star will come out of Jacob'.

commentary.on: they fell down and worshiped him
commentary.text: The first people in Matthew to worship Jesus are not Jews but foreigners from the east. Matthew's Gospel will end with the risen Jesus sending his followers to 'all the nations' (Matthew 28:19). The whole world is in view from the second chapter.

commentary.on: gold, frankincense, and myrrh
commentary.text: Gifts fit for a king, as Psalm 72:10–15 and Isaiah 60:6 imagine the nations bringing gold and incense to Jerusalem. Later Christians read meanings into each: gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh, a burial spice, for one who would die. Matthew does not say there were three wise men, or that they were kings; that came later.

compare.why: Mark begins with the grown man. Matthew, written about fifteen years later, goes back to the birth and sets it firmly in history: in Bethlehem, under King Herod. Read it beside Mark and ask what each writer wants you to know first.
compare.title: Born in Bethlehem, in the days of Herod

paras: It is worth asking first, because people do. The answer of nearly every historian who studies the ancient world, Christian or not, is yes. The evidence is better than for most people of his time who were not emperors. Paul, writing in the AD 50s, about twenty years after the crucifixion, says he met Jesus's brother James and his friend Peter (Galatians 1:18–19). Four Gospels were written within about forty to seventy years. The Jewish historian Josephus (about AD 93) mentions him twice, once as the brother of 'James', and the Roman historian Tacitus (about AD 116) says he was executed by Pilate.

A small group of writers, sometimes called mythicists, argue that Jesus never existed and was invented from myths. The agnostic scholar Bart Ehrman, no friend of Christian belief, wrote a whole book, Did Jesus Exist? (2012), to answer them. His verdict: the evidence that a Jewish preacher called Jesus lived and was crucified is overwhelming. The real argument is not whether he existed, but who he was. That is the argument this journey is about.
sections.key: Nearly all historians, believers or not, agree that Jesus existed: Paul knew his brother, and Josephus and Tacitus mention him.

sections.h: When was he born? The census problem
paras: Matthew and Luke both say Jesus was born while Herod the Great was king, so before 4 BC. Luke adds that Joseph and Mary went to Bethlehem because of a census ordered by the emperor Augustus 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria' (Luke 2:1–2). Here is a real problem. Josephus says Quirinius became governor of Syria in AD 6 and took a census of Judea then, when it became a Roman province, ten years after Herod's death.

Scholars answer in three ways. Many, such as Raymond Brown, think Luke simply made a mistake, joining the birth to a census he remembered. Some argue that the Greek of Luke 2:2 can be read 'before Quirinius was governor', or that Quirinius held an earlier post in the region. Others point out that Luke is careful elsewhere, and that our knowledge of these years is patchy. There is no evidence of an empire-wide census under Augustus. The fair conclusion is that the date 'about 6–4 BC' is solid, and that Luke's census remains unexplained. 'What is the Bible?' looks at Quirinius as a test of the Bible's accuracy.
sections.key: Jesus was born before Herod died (4 BC). Luke's census under Quirinius, dated by Josephus to AD 6, is a real difficulty that scholars answer in different ways.

paras: Josephus, who knew them first-hand, describes the main Jewish groups of Jesus's time. Each answered differently the question: how should God's people live under foreign rule?

rows: A popular lay movement of teachers; Josephus counts about 6,000
The law of Moses applied to daily life, with the 'traditions of the elders'; the resurrection of the dead
He argues with them most, which suggests he was closest to them
The priestly aristocracy who ran the Temple and dealt with Rome
Only the written law; no resurrection
They lead the hearing against him in the next session
Communities living apart in purity; probably the people of the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran
The Temple was corrupt; God would soon act and send his anointed ones
Never mentioned in the Gospels; like John the Baptist, waiting in the desert
Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the census of AD 6
No king but God; no taxes to Caesar
Jesus is asked about paying taxes to Caesar (Mark 12:13–17)
table.note: Josephus, Jewish War II.8 and Antiquities XVIII.1. The party later called the Zealots led the revolt of AD 66.

sections.key: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and the rebels of the 'fourth philosophy' each answered how to live faithfully under Rome; Jesus has to be heard among them.

paras: 'Messiah' is Hebrew for 'anointed one'; in Greek it is Christos. Israel's kings were anointed with oil when they were crowned, so 'the Lord's anointed' meant the king. After the line of David's kings ended with the Babylonian conquest in 587 BC, the prophets promised that God would one day raise up a new king from David's family, who would rule with justice.

By Jesus's time the hope took many forms, and not every Jew shared it. Some expected a warrior king to drive out the Romans; a later session, still to come, reads a psalm that prays for exactly that. The Dead Sea Scrolls speak of two anointed figures, a king and a priest. Others waited for a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), or for the return of Elijah, or for a heavenly figure whom Daniel had seen 'like a son of man'. When Mark's first line calls Jesus 'Christ', each reader would have heard their own hope in it, and that is exactly the difficulty the rest of this journey works through.
sections.key: 'Messiah' and 'Christ' both mean 'anointed': Israel hoped for a new king from David's line, though the hope took many forms.

paras: Jesus's everyday language was Aramaic, a sister of Hebrew spoken across the Near East. The Gospels keep a few of his Aramaic words: talitha koum, 'little girl, get up' (Mark 5:41), ephphatha, 'be opened' (7:34), and Abba, 'Father' (14:36). Hebrew was the language of Scripture, read aloud in the synagogue. Latin was the language of Roman officials.

But the language that held the eastern empire together was Greek, spread by Alexander the Great's conquests three centuries before. Jews in Egypt had translated their Scriptures into Greek (the Septuagint), and there were Greek-speaking towns a day's walk from Nazareth. So Jesus's words were first spoken in Aramaic and written down in Greek. That is why the New Testament is in Greek, and why 'Christ' is a Greek word for a Hebrew hope. It also means that the Gospels are, from the start, translations: careful readers keep listening for the Aramaic underneath.
sections.key: Jesus spoke Aramaic; Scripture was read in Hebrew; the empire spoke Greek, so the Gospels were written in Greek from the first.

sections.h: The birth stories and the virgin birth
paras: Only Matthew and Luke tell of Jesus's birth, and their stories are very different: Matthew has Joseph's dreams, the wise men, Herod's killing of the boys of Bethlehem and a flight to Egypt; Luke has Mary, the angel Gabriel, the shepherds and the manger. Yet they agree on a core. The Catholic scholar Raymond Brown listed it: Jesus was born in Bethlehem near the end of Herod's reign, to Mary, engaged to Joseph, a descendant of David; an angel gave the name Jesus ('the Lord saves'); Mary conceived before they lived together, not by Joseph; and the family settled in Nazareth.

That last point is the virgin birth: the belief that Mary conceived Jesus by the Holy Spirit, without a human father. Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant Christians hold it, and it is in the creeds. The Qur'an also teaches it. Some modern Protestant scholars treat it as a symbol of who Jesus was rather than a biological fact. Josephus does not mention Herod's killing of the Bethlehem boys; defenders point out that Bethlehem was small and Herod's crimes many, while sceptics see an echo of Pharaoh's killing of the Hebrew boys in Exodus.
sections.key: Matthew and Luke tell very different birth stories but share a core: Bethlehem, Herod, Mary and Joseph, Nazareth, and a conception without a human father.

sections.h: Nazareth, the family and the brothers
paras: Nazareth was a hill village of farmers and craftsmen. Four miles away Herod Antipas was rebuilding Sepphoris as his capital, and some scholars think Joseph and his son may have found work there. Mark calls Jesus a tekton (Mark 6:3): a builder or carpenter, a man who worked with wood and stone. He was not a scribe or a priest, and his neighbours were astonished that he taught at all.
Mark also names his family: 'the brother of James, Joses, Judah, and Simon', and sisters. Christians read this differently, and the difference follows from what they believe about Mary.

rows: Mary remained a virgin all her life; Jerome (c. 383) argued that 'brother' could mean any kinsman, as it does in Genesis 13:8
Joseph's children by an earlier marriage
Mary is ever-virgin; this view is found in the Protevangelium of James (2nd century) and in Epiphanius
Most: Mary and Joseph's later children; some: as the Catholic or Orthodox view
The plain sense of 'brothers', and Matthew 1:25; Luther and Calvin themselves held Mary's perpetual virginity
table.note: All agree that James, 'the Lord's brother', later led the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19).

sections.key: Jesus was a village builder (tekton) with named brothers and sisters; Catholics read them as cousins, Orthodox as Joseph's children, most Protestants as Mary's.

refs: Mark 1:1–45; Matthew 1–2; Luke 1–2; Galatians 1:18–19; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Malachi 4:5; 2 Kings 1:8; Micah 5:2; Numbers 24:17; Leviticus 13–14.

Josephus, Antiquities XVIII.1.1 (Quirinius and Judas the Galilean), XVIII.5.2 (John the Baptist), XVII.2.4 (Pharisees, about 6,000), XVIII.3.3 and XX.9.1 (Jesus); Jewish War II.8.2–14 (the sects). Tacitus, Annals XV.44.
Papias, in Eusebius, Church History III.39.15 (Mark and Peter).

Raymond E. Brown, The Birth of the Messiah (1977; 2nd ed. 1993), especially pp. 34–37 and appendix VII; Bart D. Ehrman, Did Jesus Exist? (2012); E. P. Sanders, The Historical Figure of Jesus (1993); Geza Vermes, The Nativity: History and Legend (2006).
Kepler, De Stella Nova (1606), on the conjunction of 7 BC; the Dead Sea Scrolls, Community Rule (1QS) IX.11 ('the Messiahs of Aaron and Israel').

debate.question: How much of the birth stories is history?

positions.name: History, told as faith
positions.who: Traditional Christian scholarship; Pope Benedict XVI, Jesus of Nazareth: The Infancy Narratives (2012)
positions.view: Matthew and Luke meant to report what happened, from family memory (Luke 2:19 says Mary 'kept all these sayings'). Their differences show independent sources, not invention. Miracles are not ruled out in advance.
positions.evidence: Both independently agree on Bethlehem, Herod, Mary and Joseph, and the virginal conception; Herod's cruelty is well attested by Josephus.

positions.name: A historical core, theologically told
positions.who: Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah (1977); many Catholic and Protestant scholars
positions.view: Some facts lie underneath: the names, Herod's reign, Davidic descent, Nazareth. The evangelists shaped the stories to show who Jesus was, with Old Testament patterns (Moses, David, the star of Jacob). How much more is history cannot be settled.
positions.evidence: The stories are hard to fit together (Matthew's flight to Egypt, Luke's return to Nazareth); the census problem; the heavy use of Old Testament echoes.

positions.name: Legend
positions.who: D. F. Strauss (1835); Geza Vermes, The Nativity (2006)
positions.view: The birth stories grew out of beliefs about the Messiah: he had to be born in David's town, so a story brought him there. They tell us what early Christians believed, not what happened.
positions.evidence: Mark and Paul show no knowledge of them; the census does not fit Josephus; no outside record of the star or the killing of the boys.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus grew up in Nazareth in Galilee, was born around the end of Herod's reign, and that the birth stories were written to say who he was, not only when he arrived.

look.why: Duccio painted this panel between 1308 and 1311 for the great altarpiece of Siena Cathedral. It shows the moment of Mark 1:16–18: two fishermen called from their nets. Look at how small the gesture is, and how much it asks.
points: A man stands on a rocky, tan-coloured outcrop on the left and gestures to two men in a rowing boat, all against a gold background.
He wears a crimson robe under a sea-blue mantle, edged with gold, with a halo around his head; he holds out one hand, palm up, towards the men.
The two men in the wooden boat hold a net heavy with fish over the side.
The man on the left in the boat wears a sky-blue tunic and holds one hand to his chest; the man on the right, with a longer beard, holds the net with both hands and looks up.
The boat floats on a copper-green sea with fish swimming in it; two of them face us with gaping mouths.

music.why: A medieval hymn built from the 'O Antiphons', ancient prayers of longing for the Messiah: 'Emmanuel', 'Root of Jesse', 'Key of David'. It is the sound of the world Jesus was born into: waiting.

think.why: The short answer sets out what historians, believing or not, agree about Jesus, and where faith begins.

learn.why: Mark shows Jesus rising before dawn to pray alone (Mark 1:35). These are the words he taught his friends when they asked him how to pray (Matthew 6:9–13), in the Aramaic world of 'Abba', Father.

check.q: Why are historians especially confident that Jesus was baptised by John?
options: Because all four Gospels describe the dove
Because it was awkward for early Christians, who had to explain why the greater was baptised by the lesser
Because Josephus describes Jesus's baptism
Because John's baptism is recorded on an inscription
check.why: An event that embarrassed the first Christians is unlikely to have been invented by them; Josephus mentions John, not Jesus's baptism.

check.q: Matthew says Jesus was born 'in the days of King Herod'. What follows for the date of his birth?
options: He was born before Herod died in about 4 BC, so probably around 6–4 BC
Nothing, because Herod reigned for a century
He was born in AD 6, at the census of Quirinius
He was born in AD 1, as the calendar says
check.why: Herod died in 4 BC by most reckonings; the calendar of Dionysius Exiguus (525) was a few years out.

check.q: What is the real difficulty with Luke's census 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria'?
options: Rome never held censuses
Josephus dates Quirinius's census of Judea to AD 6, ten years after Herod's death, while Luke places the birth under Herod
Quirinius was a Jewish king, not a Roman governor
Luke does not mention Herod at all
check.why: Luke 1:5 places the birth under Herod; Josephus puts Quirinius's census in AD 6. Scholars still debate how to reconcile them.

check.q: Jesus argues more with the Pharisees than with any other group. What is the best conclusion?
options: The Pharisees were Roman officials
He was a Sadducee
He rejected Judaism altogether
He was in many ways close to them: you argue most with those who share your questions
check.why: Like the Pharisees, he applied the law to daily life and believed in resurrection; the arguments are among neighbours.

check.q: Why are the Gospels written in Greek, when Jesus spoke Aramaic?
options: Because Aramaic had no alphabet
Because Jesus taught only in Greek
Because the Romans banned Aramaic
Because Greek was the shared language of the eastern Roman empire, so his words reached the wider world through it
check.why: After Alexander, Greek was the common language from Egypt to Syria; the Gospels keep a few of his Aramaic words.

check.q: Matthew and Luke tell very different birth stories. Which point do they share?
options: The flight to Egypt
The wise men and the star
Birth in Bethlehem under Herod to Mary, engaged to Joseph, conceived without a human father
The shepherds and the manger
check.why: Raymond Brown's list of agreements: Bethlehem, Herod, Mary and Joseph of David's line, the name Jesus, the virginal conception, Nazareth.

tutorial.question: How much does it matter to understanding Jesus that he was a first-century Galilean Jew under Roman rule?
tutorial.approach: Start with what historians agree on. Then take two or three things from Mark 1 (the kingdom of God, the authority that is not the scribes', the leper sent to the priest) and show what each would have meant to a Jew under Rome. Use the four groups. Then ask: does knowing his world make his claims smaller, or sharper?
strong: Sets out the historians' agreed facts and the date of about 6–4 BC.
Explains Herod, the Roman governors and the census problem fairly.
Uses at least two of the Jewish groups to place Jesus among them.
Explains what 'Messiah' and 'kingdom of God' would have meant to his hearers.
Notes the languages: Aramaic spoken, Greek written.
Draws a conclusion about how context changes the way we hear his words.

reading.author: E. P. Sanders
reading.title: The Historical Figure of Jesus
reading.why: A clear, fair account of what historians can know, by one of the great scholars of first-century Judaism.

reading.author: Raymond E. Brown
reading.title: The Birth of the Messiah
reading.why: The standard commentary on the birth stories of Matthew and Luke.

reading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
reading.title: Did Jesus Exist?
reading.why: An agnostic scholar's answer to those who say Jesus never lived.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Jesus touched the man everyone else kept at arm's length (Mark 1:41). Choose one person who tends to be left out, at work, in your street or in your family, and give them your time: sit with them, ask how they are, and really listen.
sessions.reflect: Reading Mark 1 for yourself, what surprised you about him?
takeaways: Almost all historians agree that Jesus existed: a Galilean Jew, baptised by John, who taught and healed and was crucified under Pilate around AD 30.
He was born around 6–4 BC under Herod the Great, in a land ruled by Rome, among Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and rebels, and spoke Aramaic in a Greek-speaking empire.
Mark begins with his conclusion, 'Jesus Christ, the Son of God', and shows people astonished at an authority that was not the scribes'.

sessions.title: What he said about himself
sessions.line: He forgave sins, which only God could do, and before the high priest he took the title of Daniel's heavenly Son of Man.
sessions.plain: Did Jesus say he was God? Not in those words, in the earliest Gospels. But he did things and said things that, to Jewish ears, meant something very close. He forgave a man's sins, and his critics said only God could do that. He called himself 'the Son of Man', a phrase from the book of Daniel for a figure who comes on the clouds to God's throne. And when the high priest asked him straight out, he said 'I am'. This session reads those two scenes and asks what he meant.
sessions.why: The first session placed Jesus in his world: a Galilean Jew under Rome, among people waiting for God to act. Now we call the second witness: his own words. Mark 1 already showed people amazed that he taught 'with authority'. This session follows that authority to its source, in two scenes from Mark, the first early in his work and the second on the night before he died.
answers: Did Jesus say he was God?
What does 'Son of Man' mean?
Why was forgiving sins so shocking?
Why did the high priest call his answer blasphemy?
How do historians decide what Jesus really said?
sessions.finding: Jesus rarely said 'I am God' in those words, but he forgave sins, called himself the Son of Man of Daniel 7, and spoke with an authority no prophet claimed.

paras: In the first session we met Jesus in Mark's first chapter: baptised by John in the Jordan, calling fishermen, teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum with an authority that was 'not as the scribes', healing the sick and touching a leper. We placed him in his world: Galilee under Herod Antipas, Judea under a Roman governor, a people divided into Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and rebels, many of them hoping for a Messiah.
Now the question sharpens. Prophets in Israel spoke with authority too, but it was borrowed: they said 'Thus says the Lord'. What kind of authority did Jesus claim?
background.key: Mark 1 showed a teacher whose authority astonished people. This session asks where he said that authority came from.

background.h: How the Gospels came to be
paras: Jesus wrote nothing. His sayings were remembered, repeated and taught for some decades before the Gospels were written. Matthew, Mark and Luke are so alike, often word for word, that scholars call them the Synoptic Gospels, from the Greek for 'seen together'. Most think Mark came first, around AD 65–75, and that Matthew and Luke used him, around AD 80–90. John, written around AD 90–100, is very different: long speeches, and Jesus speaking openly of himself as one with the Father.

So historians sift. They ask which sayings are found in more than one independent source, which would have embarrassed the early church, which fit first-century Judaism, and which keep traces of Aramaic. These tests are called the criteria of authenticity. Some scholars now doubt that they work as neatly as was hoped, and prefer to ask what overall picture best explains all the memories. Either way, the two scenes we read today are in the earliest Gospel, and the title they turn on, Son of Man, passes the tests well: it is almost never used of Jesus by anyone but himself.

timeline.text: The crucifixion
Paul's letters, the earliest Christian writings
Mark's Gospel
Matthew and Luke
John's Gospel

background.key: Mark came first, then Matthew and Luke, then John. Historians test sayings by independent sources, embarrassment, fit with Judaism and traces of Aramaic.

paras: The first reading is from early in Mark (2:1–12): a paralysed man is let down through a roof, and Jesus forgives his sins before he heals him. The second (14:53–65) is from the night Jesus was arrested: the high priest asks him directly who he is. Between them they show both halves of his claim: what he did, and what he said when he was asked.

The comparison goes back to the source of the phrase 'Son of Man': a vision in the book of Daniel, written in its final form around 165 BC. Beside it is a passage from a Jewish book called 1 Enoch, from about the time of Jesus, which shows how Jews were already reading Daniel's vision.
background.key: Two scenes from Mark, forgiveness and the hearing before the high priest, then Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' and how 1 Enoch read it.

before: What do the scribes think Jesus is claiming when he forgives the man's sins?
How does Jesus prove that he has 'authority on earth to forgive sins'?
In the hearing, which two Old Testament pictures does Jesus combine in his answer?
sessions.readWhy: Two scenes from Mark: the paralysed man let down through the roof, and the hearing before the high priest.

paras: When he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was in the house.
Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even around the door; and he spoke the word to them.
Four people came, carrying a paralytic to him.
When they could not come near to him for the crowd, they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on.
Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.”
But there were some of the scribes sitting there, and reasoning in their hearts,
“Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you reason these things in your hearts?
Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk?’
But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—
“I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.”
He arose, and immediately took up the mat, and went out in front of them all; so that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!”
They led Jesus away to the high priest. All the chief priests, the elders, and the scribes came together with him.
Peter had followed him from a distance, until he came into the court of the high priest. He was sitting with the officers, and warming himself in the light of the fire.
Now the chief priests and the whole council sought witnesses against Jesus to put him to death, and found none.
For many gave false testimony against him, and their testimony didn’t agree with each other.
Some stood up, and gave false testimony against him, saying,
“We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another made without hands.’ ”
Even so, their testimony didn’t agree.
The high priest stood up in the middle, and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer? What is it which these testify against you?”
But he stayed quiet, and answered nothing. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?”
Jesus said, “I am. You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky.”
The high priest tore his clothes, and said, “What further need have we of witnesses?
You have heard the blasphemy! What do you think?” They all condemned him to be worthy of death.
Some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to beat him with fists, and to tell him, “Prophesy!” The officers struck him with the palms of their hands.

parts.title: Who can forgive sins but God alone?
parts.context: Capernaum, early in Jesus's work. Houses there were built of black basalt stone, with flat roofs of beams, branches and packed mud, reached by an outside stair. The 'scribes' were experts in the law of Moses.

commentary.on: they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat
commentary.text: The four friends dig through a mud roof, which tells you something about how desperate they were and how crowded the house was. Jesus notices 'their faith': trust shown in action.

commentary.on: Son, your sins are forgiven you.
commentary.text: Everyone expects a healing. Instead Jesus says something no one asked for. In Judaism, sins were forgiven by God, through repentance and the sacrifices of the Temple. A priest could declare God's forgiveness after a sacrifice; a prophet could announce it, as Nathan did to David (2 Samuel 12:13). Jesus does it himself, here, in an ordinary house, with no sacrifice.

commentary.on: Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?
commentary.text: The scribes are not stupid or wicked: they have understood exactly. If a man forgives sins done against God, he is acting as God. Either that is blasphemy, or he is who he is acting as. Mark wants you to feel the force of their question.

commentary.on: Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven;' or to say, 'Arise, and take up your bed, and walk?'
commentary.text: Anyone can say 'your sins are forgiven': no one can see whether it worked. A healing can be seen. So Jesus offers the visible deed as evidence for the invisible one.

commentary.on: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
commentary.text: This is the first time in Mark that Jesus calls himself 'the Son of Man', and it comes with a claim to God's own authority 'on earth'. Hold the phrase in mind: the comparison reading shows where it came from.

commentary.on: We never saw anything like this!
commentary.text: The crowd 'glorified God': they see God at work. They do not yet say who Jesus is. That is the question Mark leaves with the reader.

parts.title: Are you the Christ?
parts.context: Jerusalem, at Passover, around AD 30. Jesus has been arrested at night in a garden called Gethsemane. He is taken to the house of the high priest, Caiaphas (Mark does not name him; Matthew does), who led the Temple and the Jewish council, the Sanhedrin, under the Roman governor. 'The Blessed' is a reverent way of saying 'God' without speaking his name.

commentary.on: the chief priests and the whole council sought witnesses against Jesus to put him to death, and found none.
commentary.text: Mark tells it as a trial whose outcome was settled first. Historians debate how formal this hearing was; Jewish law as later written down in the Mishnah forbade capital trials at night, but we do not know how far those rules applied in Jesus's day. What matters here is the question at the centre of it.

commentary.on: I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another made without hands.
commentary.text: The charge is about the Temple. Jesus had caused an uproar there days before, and a threat to the Temple was a threat to the priests, to the peace with Rome, and to the place where God was believed to dwell.

commentary.on: But he stayed quiet, and answered nothing.
commentary.text: His silence echoes Isaiah's suffering servant, who 'didn't open his mouth' before his accusers (Isaiah 53:7). Christians read it that way from the start.

commentary.on: Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?
commentary.text: The high priest asks the question this whole journey asks. 'The Christ' is the Messiah, the anointed king. 'Son of the Blessed', Son of God, was a royal title too: God says to the king in Psalm 2:7, 'You are my son'.

commentary.on: I am. You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky.
commentary.text: In Mark, after keeping it quiet throughout the Gospel, Jesus says it openly, here, when it will cost him his life. He joins two Old Testament texts: Psalm 110:1, where God tells the king to 'sit at my right hand', and Daniel 7:13, where one 'like a son of man' comes 'with the clouds of the sky' to God's throne. He claims to share God's throne. Matthew and Luke give his answer less directly ('You have said it'), and scholars debate which is earlier.

commentary.on: You have heard the blasphemy!
commentary.text: Claiming to be the Messiah was not in itself blasphemy: other men claimed it and were not called blasphemers. What shocked the high priest was the claim to sit beside God. The tearing of clothes was the formal sign of having heard blasphemy. Whether or not every detail is history, Mark's point is clear: Jesus was condemned for who he said he was.

paras:
“I watched until thrones were placed,
and one who was ancient of days sat.
His clothing was white as snow,
and the hair of his head like pure wool.
His throne was fiery flames,
and its wheels burning fire.

A fiery stream issued and came out from before him.
Thousands of thousands ministered to him.
Ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.
The judgment was set.
The books were opened.
“I watched at that time because of the voice of the great words which the horn spoke. I watched even until the animal was slain, and its body destroyed, and it was given to be burned with fire.
As for the rest of the animals, their dominion was taken away; yet their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.
“I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.

Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.

1. And there I saw One, who had a head of days,
And His head was white like wool,
And with Him was another being whose countenance had the appearance of a man,
And his face was full of graciousness, like one of the holy angels.
2. And I asked the angel who went with me and showed me all the hidden things, concerning that Son of Man, who he was, and whence he was, (and) why he went with the Head of Days? 3. And he answered and said unto me:
This is the Son of Man who hath righteousness,
With whom dwelleth righteousness,
And who revealeth all the treasures of that which is hidden,
Because the Lord of Spirits hath chosen him,
And whose lot hath the pre-eminence before the Lord of Spirits in uprightness for ever.

2. And at that hour that Son of Man was named
In the presence of the Lord of Spirits,
And his name before the Head of Days.
3. Yea, before the sun and the signs were created,
Before the stars of the heaven were made,
His name was named before the Lord of Spirits.
4. He shall be a staff to the righteous whereon to stay themselves and not fall,
And he shall be the light of the Gentiles,
And the hope of those who are troubled of heart.
5. All who dwell on earth shall fall down and worship before him,
And will praise and bless and celebrate with song the Lord of Spirits.
6. And for this reason hath he been chosen and hidden before Him,
Before the creation of the world and for evermore.

parts.title: The Ancient of Days and the son of man
parts.context: The book of Daniel is set in the Babylonian exile of the 500s BC; most scholars date its final form to about 165 BC, when the Greek king Antiochus IV was persecuting Jews who kept their law. In chapter 7 Daniel sees four terrible beasts, the empires that have crushed Israel, and then a court in heaven.

commentary.on: one who was ancient of days sat
commentary.text: God, pictured as an old man of infinite age, white-haired, on a throne of fire. The judgement is about to begin.

commentary.on: there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man
commentary.text: In Hebrew and Aramaic, 'son of man' simply means 'a human being'. After four beasts, a human figure. But he comes 'with the clouds', and in the Old Testament it is God who rides on the clouds (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1). So this figure is human in shape and heavenly in standing.

commentary.on: Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him.
commentary.text: He receives the kingdom that the beasts had seized, for ever. Later in the chapter (7:18, 27) the kingdom is given to 'the saints of the Most High', God's faithful people, so many Jewish interpreters read the figure as a symbol of Israel. Others read him as an individual, the Messiah. When Jesus said 'the Son of Man', both readings were in the air.

parts.author: 1 Enoch (the Parables)
parts.title: That Son of Man was named
parts.context: 1 Enoch is a collection of Jewish writings in the name of Enoch, who 'walked with God' (Genesis 5:24). This part, the Parables, survives only in Ethiopic, where it is still Scripture for the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Scholars date it between about 50 BC and AD 70, so around the time of Jesus, though a few date it later. R. H. Charles's translation, 1917. 'The Lord of Spirits' is the writer's name for God; 'Head of Days' is Daniel's 'ancient of days'. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: The writer sees God, the Head of Days, with a second figure who looks like a man. An angel tells him this is the Son of Man, chosen by God, who reveals hidden things. His name was spoken before God before the sun and stars were made. He will be a support to the good and a light to the nations, and everyone on earth will bow down before him.

commentary.on: And with Him was another being whose countenance had the appearance of a man
commentary.text: The writer is reading Daniel 7. The human figure is now beside God himself.

commentary.on: This is the Son of Man who hath righteousness
commentary.text: Here 'the Son of Man' has become a title for one particular person, a heavenly judge and saviour. If the Parables are as early as most scholars think, then some Jews in Jesus's day already spoke of 'the Son of Man' in this way.

commentary.on: Before the stars of the heaven were made, His name was named before the Lord of Spirits.
commentary.text: He exists, at least in God's plan, before creation. That is a very high claim for a figure who is not God.

commentary.on: All who dwell on earth shall fall down and worship before him
commentary.text: The Son of Man receives homage from the whole earth. This shows that Jesus's hearers had words for a figure greater than any prophet. It also shows something the Gospels do not: Enoch's Son of Man never lived on earth, healed a paralysed man in a crowded house, or was condemned to die.

compare.author: 1 Enoch (the Parables)
compare.why: Jesus's favourite name for himself comes from a vision in Daniel. Read the vision, then see how another Jewish book of the time was already reading it: as a heavenly figure beside God.
compare.title: One like a son of man

paras: In Matthew, Mark and Luke, Jesus never says 'I am God' in those words. In Jewish ears the sentence would have sounded like madness or blasphemy, and it would have confused the point: for Jews and for Jesus, God was the one God of Israel, whom he called 'Father' and prayed to. So the plain answer to the question is no.

But that is not the end of it. The earliest Gospel shows him doing and saying things that belonged to God alone: forgiving sins on his own authority, calling himself Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), the day God made holy, and claiming to sit at God's right hand. The scribes in Capernaum and the high priest in Jerusalem drew the conclusion themselves. The New Testament scholar N. T. Wright puts it this way: Jesus did not go about saying 'I am God'; he acted as if he were doing what Israel's God had promised to do in person.
sections.key: In the first three Gospels Jesus never says 'I am God', but he does things that belonged to God alone: forgiving sins, ruling the Sabbath, claiming God's throne.

paras: 'Son of Man' is Jesus's favourite name for himself: it appears more than eighty times in the Gospels, almost always on his lips, and almost never in the rest of the New Testament. That is good evidence that he used it and the church did not invent it. But what did he mean?

Three answers have been given. First, in Aramaic, bar enasha can mean simply 'a human being', or even 'someone like me', a modest way of saying 'I'; the Jewish scholar Geza Vermes argued that this is all it meant. Second, it pointed to Daniel 7, the human figure who receives God's kingdom; the hearing before the high priest makes that link explicit. Third, it was a deliberately puzzling phrase, ordinary and heavenly at once, which let Jesus speak of himself without using the loaded word Messiah. Many scholars think the third answer contains the other two: Jesus used a humble everyday phrase and filled it with Daniel's meaning. Mark's Son of Man is three things: he forgives on earth, he must suffer, and he will come with the clouds.
sections.key: 'Son of Man' could mean 'a human being', or point to Daniel's heavenly figure. Jesus seems to have used the ordinary phrase and filled it with Daniel's meaning.

paras: 'Son of God' did not, in Jesus's world, automatically mean 'divine'. Israel as a people was God's son (Exodus 4:22), and so was the king (Psalm 2:7). Angels were 'sons of God' (Job 1:6). So the title could be royal. In Mark it is spoken by the voice at the baptism, by demons and, at the end, by a Roman centurion. Jesus himself uses 'the Son' only rarely in the first three Gospels, most strikingly in Matthew 11:27: 'no one knows the Son, except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father, except the Son'.

Jesus prayed to God as Abba, the Aramaic word for 'father' (Mark 14:36). The German scholar Joachim Jeremias argued that this was unheard of, a child's 'Daddy'. Later scholars, such as James Barr, showed that it was a grown-up word too, and that Jews did call God Father. But no earlier Jewish prayer is known that addresses God simply as 'Abba', and Paul shows that the first Christians, even Greek-speaking ones, kept the Aramaic word because it was his (Romans 8:15).
sections.key: 'Son of God' could be a royal title; Jesus prayed to God as Abba, 'Father', a word his followers kept in Aramaic because it was his.

paras: Listen to how Jesus talks. The prophets said 'Thus says the Lord'. The rabbis said 'Rabbi so-and-so said'. Jesus begins solemn sayings with 'Amen, I say to you' ('Most certainly I tell you' in the World English Bible). 'Amen' was a word people said at the end of a prayer to agree with it; Jesus puts it at the start, as if his own word guaranteed itself. In the Sermon on the Mount he sets his word beside the law of Moses: 'You have heard that it was said… but I tell you' (Matthew 5:21–22), which 'The Sermon on the Mount' explores.

He also asks for a loyalty that belonged to God. 'Whoever will be ashamed of me and of my words', he says, 'the Son of Man also will be ashamed of him' (Mark 8:38). And: 'Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28), words Jewish wisdom books gave to the voice of God's Wisdom (Sirach 51:23–27). No prophet in Israel spoke like this.
sections.key: Jesus spoke on his own authority ('Amen, I say to you'), set his word beside the law, and asked for a loyalty that belonged to God.

paras: In John's Gospel Jesus speaks of himself constantly: 'I am the bread of life' (6:35), 'I am the light of the world' (8:12), 'I am the good shepherd' (10:11), 'I am the resurrection and the life' (11:25), and most startling, 'before Abraham came into existence, I AM' (8:58), echoing the name God gave himself to Moses at the burning bush, 'I AM WHO I AM' (Exodus 3:14). The crowd picks up stones.

Most scholars think John's speeches are not word-for-word memory but a long meditation on who Jesus was, written by a disciple late in the first century. Others, such as Richard Bauckham, argue that John rests on an eyewitness and preserves real history in its own style. What is striking is that the claims in John are not different in kind from Mark's, only more open: Mark's Jesus forgives sins and claims God's throne; John's says it outright. The question is whether John made explicit what was there from the start, or added what was not.
sections.key: John's 'I am' sayings say openly what Mark shows indirectly; scholars debate whether John unfolded the original claim or added to it.

paras: To be fair to the high priest, we need to know what blasphemy meant. The law of Moses punished anyone who 'blasphemes the name of Yahweh' with stoning (Leviticus 24:16). The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, narrows it: a blasphemer is guilty only if he pronounces the divine name itself (Sanhedrin 7:5). Jesus, in Mark, does not do that; he says 'the Blessed' and 'Power', the reverent substitutes.

So what was the blasphemy? Scholars give different answers. Some, such as Darrell Bock, argue that the later rule was not yet fixed, and that claiming to sit at God's right hand and come on the clouds was itself an attack on God's unique honour. Others think Mark has written the scene in the light of later arguments between church and synagogue, and that Jesus was handed to Pilate mainly as a political danger, after the uproar in the Temple. E. P. Sanders thought the Temple action was the real cause. What the scene shows, on either reading, is how the first Christians understood his death: he was condemned for claiming a place beside God.
sections.key: The Mishnah limits blasphemy to speaking God's name, which Jesus did not; scholars debate whether his claim to God's throne was the charge, or the Temple.

refs: 1 Enoch 46 and 48, tr. R. H. Charles (1917). On the date of the Parables: G. W. E. Nickelsburg and J. C. VanderKam, 1 Enoch 2 (2012).
Geza Vermes, Jesus the Jew (1973), on 'son of man'; Joachim Jeremias, The Prayers of Jesus (1967); James Barr, ''Abba' Isn't 'Daddy'', Journal of Theological Studies 39 (1988).

N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God (1996); Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the God of Israel (2008) and The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple (2007); Larry Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ (2003); Bart D. Ehrman, How Jesus Became God (2014).

On the criteria of authenticity: John P. Meier, A Marginal Jew, vol. 1 (1991), ch. 6; Chris Keith and Anthony Le Donne (eds), Jesus, Criteria, and the Demise of Authenticity (2012). Mishnah, Sanhedrin 4:1 (no capital trials at night).

debate.question: Did his followers see him as divine from the start, or did the belief grow?

positions.name: High from the start
positions.who: Larry Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ (2003); Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the God of Israel (2008)
positions.view: Within a few years of the crucifixion, Jewish followers who believed in one God were praying to Jesus, singing hymns to him and calling him 'Lord', the word their Greek Bible used for God. This was not a slow drift into paganism but an explosion, inside Judaism. Bauckham calls it including Jesus in the identity of the one God.
positions.evidence: Paul's letters of the AD 50s already apply Old Testament texts about God to Jesus (1 Corinthians 8:6); the Aramaic prayer 'Marana tha', 'Our Lord, come!' (1 Corinthians 16:22), from the earliest Aramaic-speaking church.

positions.name: A development
positions.who: Wilhelm Bousset, Kyrios Christos (1913); Bart Ehrman, How Jesus Became God (2014)
positions.view: Jesus saw himself as a prophet of the coming kingdom, perhaps its future king, but not as God. After his death his followers came to believe God had exalted him to heaven; later still, writers like John said he had been divine before his birth. The 'I am' sayings of John reflect that later stage.
positions.evidence: The first three Gospels never have Jesus say he is God; John, the latest Gospel, is the most explicit; Ehrman notes that even Paul may have thought of Christ as a kind of exalted heavenly being, not God himself.

positions.name: Implicit in his own claims
positions.who: N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God (1996); many Catholic and Orthodox scholars
positions.view: The church's later belief unfolds what was implicit in Jesus's own words and actions: forgiving sins, Lord of the Sabbath, the Son of Man on God's throne, his authority over the law. He did not use the later creeds' words, but he acted as God's own return to his people.
positions.evidence: The claims in Mark 2 and 14, which are in the earliest Gospel and fit his Jewish setting; the reaction of opponents, who understood him to claim too much.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus never says 'I am God' in the first three Gospels, that the Son of Man sayings go back to him in some form, and that by the 50s his followers were worshipping him.

look.why: A Netherlandish painter of the later 1500s shows the end of Mark 2:1–12 close up, with the whole story told small in the background. The man who could not walk is carrying the mat that carried him.
points: A man walking hunched over, carrying a large bundle like pillows wrapped in a blanket on his back, nearly fills the painting.
His head is down and his eyes closed or downcast; with muscled forearms raised overhead, he clutches the green cloth tied round the bundle.
He wears a red, waist-length tunic over a long white garment, and strides barefoot across a moss-green rock.
Behind him a path curves to the arched opening of a building, where a couple of dozen tiny figures gather round a person who stands with arm extended over a second person lying on a cloth.
The four corners of that cloth hang from ropes, barely visible, where it was lowered from the roof.

music.why: Bach's chorale, from a cantata of his first year in Leipzig (1723), is sung to a person, not to an idea: 'Jesus, joy of man's desiring'. It is the music of someone who has decided the claims of this session are true.

think.why: What Christians believe: that Jesus is fully human and fully God, the belief the scribes in Capernaum glimpsed and the creeds later set out.

learn.why: One of the sayings in which Jesus speaks with an authority no prophet claimed: 'Come to me… I will give you rest'. Jewish wisdom books gave words like these to the voice of God's Wisdom.

check.q: Why did the scribes in Capernaum call Jesus's words to the paralysed man blasphemy?
options: Because he touched a man who was unclean
Because he claimed to be a priest
Because he healed on the Sabbath
Because only God can forgive sins against God, and Jesus forgave them on his own authority
check.why: 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' A prophet could announce God's forgiveness; Jesus gave it himself.

check.q: Jesus asks, 'Which is easier' to say: 'your sins are forgiven' or 'get up and walk'? What is his argument?
options: That the scribes should heal the man themselves
That neither can really be done
That the visible healing is evidence for the invisible authority to forgive
That healing is more important than forgiveness
check.why: Anyone can claim to forgive; no one can check. The healing can be seen, so he gives it 'that you may know'.

check.q: In his answer to the high priest, Jesus combines Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. What does this combination claim?
options: That he will lead an army against Rome
That the Temple will be rebuilt in three days
That he will share God's throne and come with the clouds, as Daniel's son of man
That he is a prophet like Moses
