check.why: 'Sitting at the right hand of Power' (Psalm 110) and 'coming with the clouds' (Daniel 7): a place beside God himself.

check.q: Why do historians think 'the Son of Man' goes back to Jesus himself rather than the early church?
options: Because it was a common title for the Messiah
Because it is almost always on Jesus's own lips and hardly ever used by the church's writers
Because Paul uses it constantly
Because it appears on an inscription
check.why: If the church had invented it, we would expect the church to use it; it appears in the Gospels, on his lips, and almost nowhere else.

check.q: What does 1 Enoch's Son of Man show about Jesus's world?
options: That some Jews already pictured a heavenly Son of Man beside God, so Jesus's hearers had words for a figure greater than a prophet
That Enoch was the Messiah
That Jews had never heard of such a figure
That Daniel 7 was written after the Gospels
check.why: If the Parables date from around Jesus's time, they show Daniel's figure being read as a heavenly individual; but Enoch's figure never lived on earth or suffered.

check.q: A friend says: 'Jesus never claimed to be God; the church made that up later.' Which reply best fits the evidence of this session?
options: There is no evidence either way
He never used those words in the first three Gospels, but the earliest Gospel shows him forgiving sins and claiming God's throne, and his opponents understood him to be claiming too much
Only John's Gospel is reliable, so the question is settled
He said 'I am God' often in Mark
check.why: The fair reply grants the point about words and shows the claim in deeds and titles, in the earliest source.

tutorial.question: Did Jesus claim to be divine?
tutorial.approach: Begin by granting what is true: he never says 'I am God' in Matthew, Mark or Luke. Then set out the evidence of Mark 2 and 14: forgiveness, Son of Man, the right hand of Power. Use Daniel 7 and 1 Enoch to show what the title could mean. Bring in John's 'I am' sayings and the question of how they relate to Mark. End with the debate: high from the start, a development, or implicit in his own claims?
strong: Distinguishes between explicit statements and implicit claims.
Explains why forgiving sins was a claim to God's authority.
Explains the meanings of 'Son of Man', with Daniel 7.
Explains why the high priest called his answer blasphemy.
Weighs John's 'I am' sayings fairly against Mark.
Uses the scholars' debate (Hurtado or Bauckham; Ehrman; Wright) and reaches a reasoned view.

reading.author: N. T. Wright
reading.title: Jesus and the Victory of God
reading.why: A major historical study of Jesus's aims and self-understanding.

reading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
reading.title: How Jesus Became God
reading.why: An agnostic historian's case that belief in Jesus's divinity developed after his death.

reading.author: Larry W. Hurtado
reading.title: How on Earth Did Jesus Become a God?
reading.why: A short book on the early worship of Jesus, answering the same question the other way.

reading.author: Geza Vermes
reading.title: Jesus the Jew
reading.why: A Jewish historian reads Jesus in his Galilean setting, with a famous chapter on 'son of man'.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the four friends carried a man to Jesus and dug through a roof to get him there. Is there someone you could carry this week: a lift, a meal, a hospital visit, a hard phone call made on their behalf? Do it, without being asked.
sessions.reflect: If someone forgave you for something you had done to another person, what would you think they were claiming?
takeaways: Jesus never says 'I am God' in the first three Gospels, but he forgave sins on his own authority, which his critics saw as claiming God's place.
He called himself 'the Son of Man', an ordinary phrase he filled with Daniel's vision of a human figure who receives God's kingdom.
Before the high priest he claimed to share God's throne, and was condemned for blasphemy: he died for who he said he was.

sessions.title: Who do you say I am?
sessions.line: At the foot of a mountain shrine to Pan and Caesar, Peter calls him the Messiah; Jesus accepts it, and at once says the Messiah must suffer.
sessions.plain: Halfway through Mark's Gospel, Jesus asks his friends what people are saying about him, and then: 'But who do you say that I am?' Peter answers: 'You are the Christ', the Messiah. Jesus does not deny it. But he tells them to keep it quiet, and starts to teach that he must suffer, be rejected and be killed. Peter is horrified. This session asks what 'Messiah' meant to Jews of the time, using a psalm written about seventy years before, and why Jesus's version shocked his own closest friend.
sessions.why: The second session heard Jesus's own words: he forgave sins, called himself the Son of Man, and claimed God's throne before the high priest. But that scene came at the end. Long before it, Mark tells of a turning point in the north, when Jesus asked his friends the question this journey asks. Now we hear what they answered, and what he did with their answer.
answers: What does 'Christ' mean?
What kind of Messiah were people expecting?
Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet about him?
Why did Peter rebuke him, and why did Jesus call Peter 'Satan'?
Did Jesus think he was the Messiah?
sessions.finding: Peter called him the Messiah; Jesus accepted it and at once redefined it as suffering, which no one expected.

paras: We have placed Jesus in his world: a Galilean Jew under Rome, born in Herod's last years, among people with different hopes for what God would do. We have heard his own words: he forgave sins as only God could, called himself by Daniel's title, the Son of Man, and before the high priest answered 'I am' when asked if he was the Christ.

In the first session we saw that 'Christ' is the Greek for 'Messiah', 'anointed one', and that Israel hoped for a new king from David's family. This session asks what such a king was expected to do, and whether Jesus fitted the picture.
background.key: Jesus claimed God's authority and the title Son of Man; now we ask what 'Messiah' meant and whether he took it.

paras: Mark 8 is the hinge of his Gospel. For seven chapters Jesus has healed and taught in Galilee, and people keep asking who he is. In chapter 8 he walks north with his disciples, out of Jewish Galilee, to the villages around Caesarea Philippi, about twenty-five miles north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon.

It was a striking place to ask the question. Here one of the springs of the Jordan rises from a cave that the Greeks had made a shrine to the god Pan; the place is still called Banias. Herod the Great had built a temple of white marble there to the emperor Augustus, and his son Philip had rebuilt the town and named it after Caesar. So Jesus asks who he is in a town named after an emperor whom the empire hailed as son of a god. From here on, Mark's story turns south, towards Jerusalem.

timeline.text: Pompey takes Jerusalem; the Psalms of Solomon are written in the years after
Herod builds a temple to Augustus at Paneas, by the springs of the Jordan
After Herod's death, several men claim to be king; Rome crushes them
Philip the tetrarch rebuilds Paneas as Caesarea Philippi
Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi
Simon bar Kokhba, hailed as Messiah, leads a last revolt against Rome

background.key: At Caesarea Philippi, a town named after Caesar with a shrine to Pan and a temple to Augustus, Jesus asks who he is; then his story turns towards Jerusalem.

paras: The reading is Mark 8:27–33, in two parts: the question and Peter's answer, then Jesus's first teaching that he must suffer, and Peter's protest. It answers directly whether Jesus accepted the title Messiah.

The comparison is the seventeenth of the Psalms of Solomon, a Jewish hymn written some seventy years before, after the Romans had taken Jerusalem. It is the fullest picture we have of the Messiah many Jews were praying for. Read it, and you will understand why Peter could not bear what Jesus said next.
background.key: Mark 8:27–33, the confession and the first prediction of suffering; then the Psalms of Solomon's prayer for a warrior son of David.

before: What do people think Jesus is, according to the disciples? What do those answers have in common?
Why might Jesus tell them to tell no one?
In the psalm, what will the son of David do to the nations and to Jerusalem?
sessions.readWhy: The question at Caesarea Philippi and Peter's answer; then the first teaching that the Son of Man must suffer, and Peter's protest.

paras: Jesus went out, with his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I am?”
They told him, “John the Baptizer, and others say Elijah, but others: one of the prophets.”
He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”
Peter answered, “You are the Christ.”
He commanded them that they should tell no one about him.
He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again.
He spoke to them openly. Peter took him, and began to rebuke him.
But he, turning around, and seeing his disciples, rebuked Peter, and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For you have in mind not the things of God, but the things of men.”

parts.title: But who do you say that I am?
parts.context: Around AD 29, after more than a year of public work in Galilee. Jesus and his twelve closest followers are walking among the villages near Caesarea Philippi.

commentary.on: Who do men say that I am?
commentary.text: Jesus begins with the opinion polls. He knows people are talking. It is the question this whole journey has been asking, and Mark puts it on Jesus's own lips.

commentary.on: John the Baptizer, and others say Elijah, but others: one of the prophets.
commentary.text: Every answer is a prophet. Herod Antipas had wondered if Jesus was John the Baptist come back from the dead (Mark 6:14–16). Elijah was expected to return before the end (Malachi 4:5). The people see a man of God with power; no one in the crowd says Messiah.

commentary.on: But who do you say that I am?
commentary.text: The 'you' is emphatic and plural: you, my friends, who have lived with me. Every reader of Mark is meant to hear the question as addressed to them as well. It is this session's words to learn.

commentary.on: You are the Christ.
commentary.text: Peter says what Mark said in his first line: Christ, Messiah, the anointed king. Jesus does not correct him. In Matthew's longer version (16:16–19) Jesus blesses Peter for it and gives him 'the keys of the Kingdom'.

commentary.on: He commanded them that they should tell no one about him.
commentary.text: Why keep it secret? We have seen Jesus silence demons who knew him. The likeliest reason is in the comparison reading: to most people 'Messiah' meant a king who would fight Rome. Announced in public, the title would mean an uprising, and Jesus did not mean that.

parts.title: The Son of Man must suffer
parts.context: Straight after Peter's answer, Mark says Jesus 'began to teach them' something new. It is the first of three times in Mark that he foretells his death (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34).

commentary.on: the Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed
commentary.text: Peter says Messiah; Jesus answers Son of Man, and fills the title with suffering. 'Must' is the Greek dei: it has to happen; it is part of God's purpose. The elders, chief priests and scribes are the very council we read about in the last session.

commentary.on: and after three days rise again
commentary.text: Mark includes the promise of resurrection, but the disciples do not seem to hear it. What they hear is that their Messiah will be killed. Whether Jesus said these words in this form, or the church sharpened them later, is debated; that he expected to die in Jerusalem is accepted by many historians.

commentary.on: Peter took him, and began to rebuke him.
commentary.text: Peter takes Jesus aside to correct him. It is a shocking reversal: the student rebukes the teacher. But Peter is only saying what everyone believed: the Messiah wins. A crucified Messiah was a contradiction, like a drowned lifeguard.

commentary.on: Get behind me, Satan! For you have in mind not the things of God, but the things of men.
commentary.text: Jesus calls his best friend 'Satan', the adversary who tempted him in the wilderness. The temptation is the same: to be a Messiah of power without the cross. 'The things of men' means the ordinary human way of thinking about greatness. The next verses (8:34) turn it into a call to every follower: 'take up his cross'.

paras: 1 O LORD, thou art our King henceforth and even for evermore, for in thee, O God, our soul exulteth.

23 Behold, O LORD, and raise up unto them their king, the son of David, in the time which thou, O God, knowest, that he may reign over Israel thy servant; 24 And gird him with strength that he may break in pieces them that rule unjustly.

25 Purge Jerusalem from the heathen that trample her down to destroy her, with wisdom and with righteousness. 26 He shall thrust out the sinners from the inheritance, utterly destroy the proud spirit of the sinners, and as potter’s vessels with a rod of iron shall he break in pieces all their substance. 27 He shall destroy the ungodly nations with the word of his mouth, so that at his rebuke the nations may flee before him, and he shall convict the sinners in the thoughts of their hearts.

32 And he shall possess the nations of the heathen to serve him beneath his yoke; and he shall glorify the LORD in a place to be seen of the whole earth; 33 And he shall purge Jerusalem and make it holy, even as it was in the days of old. 34 So that the nations may come from the ends of the earth to see his glory, bringing as gifts her sons that had fainted, 35 And may see the glory of the LORD, wherewith God hath glorified her. And a righteous king and taught of God is he that reigneth over them; 36 And there shall be no iniquity in his days in their midst, for all shall be holy and their king is the Lord Messiah.
37 For he shall not put his trust in horse and rider and bow, nor shall he multiply unto himself gold and silver for war, nor by ships shall he gather confidence for the day of battle.
41 He himself also is pure from sin, so that he may rule a mighty people, and rebuke princes and overthrow sinners by the might of his word.

parts.author: The Psalms of Solomon
parts.translator: H. E. Ryle and M. R. James (1891)
parts.title: Gird him with strength
parts.context: The Psalms of Solomon are eighteen Jewish psalms, not part of the Bible, written in Hebrew and surviving in Greek. They were written in the decades after 63 BC, when the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem and walked into the Temple. Their authors were devout Jews, perhaps Pharisees, who blamed the disaster on the corrupt priest-kings who had ruled before. This translation is by H. E. Ryle and M. R. James, Cambridge, 1891. The verse numbers are theirs. Cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: The psalm begins: God, you are our king for ever. Later it prays: Lord, raise up the son of David, the true king, at the time you choose. Give him strength to break the unjust rulers, to drive the foreigners out of Jerusalem, to smash sinners like pots, and to destroy the godless nations with the word of his mouth.

commentary.on: O LORD, thou art our King henceforth and even for evermore
commentary.text: The psalm opens and closes by calling God the true king. The Messiah will be God's deputy. Hold this together with what follows: the writer is not a warmonger but a man of prayer, who has seen his city taken.

commentary.on: raise up unto them their king, the son of David
commentary.text: This is one of the earliest uses of 'son of David' for the Messiah outside the Bible. The writer believes the priest-kings who had ruled Judea had stolen David's throne. Only God can give it back to its true heir.

commentary.on: that he may break in pieces them that rule unjustly
commentary.text: The Messiah's first task is to break the power of the unjust: the corrupt rulers inside Israel and the Romans outside.

commentary.on: Purge Jerusalem from the heathen that trample her down
commentary.text: 'The heathen' are the Gentiles, the non-Jewish nations, here the Romans. The Messiah's work is to cleanse the holy city of foreign rule. This is the hope Peter grew up with.

commentary.on: as potter's vessels with a rod of iron shall he break in pieces all their substance
commentary.text: The image comes from Psalm 2:9, the royal psalm we met in the last session: 'You shall break them with a rod of iron'. The Messiah is a conqueror.

commentary.on: He shall destroy the ungodly nations with the word of his mouth
commentary.text: But notice: he fights 'with the word of his mouth', an echo of Isaiah 11:4. The psalm mixes war and holiness. Ryle and James noted that it is a Messiah of judgement, not of suffering.

parts.author: The Psalms of Solomon
parts.translator: H. E. Ryle and M. R. James (1891)
parts.title: Their king is the Lord Messiah
parts.context: The second half of the psalm describes the Messiah's reign once he has won. The cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: The nations will serve under his yoke, and come from the ends of the earth to see Jerusalem's glory. He will be a righteous king, taught by God; there will be no wickedness in his days, and he is 'the Lord Messiah'. He will not trust in horses, gold or ships, and he himself will be pure from sin, ruling by the power of his word.

commentary.on: And he shall possess the nations of the heathen to serve him beneath his yoke
commentary.text: Victory reverses history: the nations that ruled Israel now serve Israel's king.

commentary.on: their king is the Lord Messiah
commentary.text: In Greek, christos kyrios, 'Christ the Lord', exactly the words of the angel to the shepherds in Luke 2:11. Ryle and James discussed at length whether the original Hebrew meant 'the Lord's Messiah'. Either way, the Messiah here is a human king, holy and wise, but a man.

commentary.on: For he shall not put his trust in horse and rider and bow
commentary.text: A fair reading must include this. The psalm's king does not rely on armies or money; it echoes the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:16–17. His power is God's.

commentary.on: He himself also is pure from sin
commentary.text: The hoped-for Messiah is sinless and rules by his word. So the gap between this psalm and Jesus is not between violence and peace. It is this: in the psalm, the Messiah wins, purges Jerusalem of the Romans and reigns. In Mark, the Messiah 'must suffer many things… and be killed'.

compare.author: The Psalms of Solomon
compare.translator: H. E. Ryle and M. R. James (1891)
compare.why: This is the Messiah many Jews prayed for: a son of David who would drive the foreigners out of Jerusalem and rule the nations. It was written about seventy years before Peter spoke. Read it, and ask what Peter expected the Messiah to do.
compare.title: Raise up unto them their king, the son of David

paras: 'Christ' is not Jesus's surname. It is a title: the Greek Christos translates the Hebrew Mashiach, 'anointed'. In ancient Israel, oil was poured on the head of a person set apart for a task: kings above all ('the Lord's anointed', 1 Samuel 24:6), but also priests (Leviticus 4:3) and occasionally prophets (1 Kings 19:16). When the line of David's kings ended in 587 BC, the prophets promised a future king from his family: a 'shoot from the stock of Jesse', David's father, on whom God's Spirit would rest (Isaiah 11:1–2).

By the time of Jesus, 'the Messiah' had come to mean that king, though the word was used in more than one way. The first Christians used the title so often that it became almost a name: Paul writes 'Jesus Christ' or 'Christ Jesus' hundreds of times. Each time, he is saying: this crucified man is the king.
sections.key: 'Christ' is a title, the Greek for Messiah, 'anointed': above all, the promised king from David's line.

paras: Jesus was not the only man called king in his century. When Herod died in 4 BC, Josephus tells of three men who claimed the crown: Judas son of Hezekiah in Galilee, Simon, a former slave of Herod, and a shepherd called Athronges. Rome crushed them all. Around AD 45 a man called Theudas led crowds to the Jordan, promising to part it; the Roman governor had him beheaded. Another, called 'the Egyptian', led followers to the Mount of Olives to see Jerusalem's walls fall. The book of Acts mentions both (Acts 5:36; 21:38).

A century after Jesus, the great Rabbi Akiva hailed Simon bar Kosiba as the Messiah and called him Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star', from Numbers 24:17. His revolt (AD 132–135) ended in catastrophe, and Jews were banned from Jerusalem. In every case the pattern was the same: a claim to be the deliverer, a fight with Rome, a death, and the end of the movement. When a Messiah was killed, everyone knew he had not been the Messiah. Bar Kokhba's own followers abandoned the title; later rabbis punned on his name and called him Bar Koziba, 'son of the lie'.
sections.key: Other first- and second-century 'messiahs' fought Rome and were killed, and their movements ended. A dead Messiah was a failed Messiah.

paras: So Peter's rebuke makes sense. As far as we know, no Jewish text before Jesus clearly expected the Messiah to suffer and die. The servant of Isaiah 53, who is 'pierced for our transgressions' (you read it in 'Kings and prophets'), was usually read by Jews as Israel, or as a prophet, not as the Messiah. The later Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah, the Targum, does call the servant 'my servant the Messiah', but it gives the suffering to his enemies. Scholars still argue about a few texts, but none is clear.

Jesus joins two things that had not been joined. He accepts the royal title, and fills it with the servant's suffering, under the name Son of Man. That is why Mark's Gospel turns at this point: from here the road leads to Jerusalem, and Jesus keeps telling his friends what will happen there. It is also one of the strongest reasons historians give for thinking that this teaching goes back to Jesus. A movement trying to make its leader attractive to Jews would not invent a Messiah whom its own leading disciple called a contradiction.
sections.key: No clear Jewish text before Jesus expected a suffering Messiah; Jesus joined the royal title to the servant's suffering, and Peter could not accept it.

paras: Why does Jesus keep telling people to be quiet: the demons in Mark 1, the healed leper, now Peter? In 1901 the German scholar William Wrede gave a famous answer in The Messianic Secret. He argued that Jesus never claimed to be the Messiah in his lifetime; the church came to believe it only after Easter. Mark, he thought, explained the gap by inventing the commands to silence: Jesus was the Messiah all along, but kept it secret.

Wrede's book shaped a century of scholarship, and it rightly showed that Mark is a writer with a purpose, not a simple recorder. But most scholars today think the secrecy fits Jesus's own situation better than Wrede allowed. In a land full of would-be kings and Roman soldiers, the word Messiah in public meant revolution. The Gospel of John says that after a great miracle the crowd wanted 'to take him by force to make him king', and he slipped away (John 6:15). Jesus could accept the title in private and redefine it, but not let a crowd define it for him.
sections.key: Wrede (1901) thought Mark invented the secrecy; most scholars now think Jesus avoided the title in public because to crowds it meant revolt.

paras: In Matthew's version of the scene Jesus answers Peter: 'You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly' (Matthew 16:18). In Greek the name Petros and the word petra, 'rock', sound alike. He gives Peter 'the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven'. Christians have read these words differently, and the difference still divides churches.

cols: Who or what is the rock?
rows: Peter himself, as leader of the apostles
The bishop of Rome, Peter's successor, holds the keys: the papacy
Peter's confession of faith, and Peter as the first among the apostles
Every bishop who keeps Peter's faith sits in Peter's chair; Rome had a primacy of honour, not of rule
Peter's confession, or Christ himself, on whom the confession rests
No office inherits Peter's keys; the keys are the preaching of the gospel and forgiveness
A saying, perhaps shaped by Matthew's church, about Peter's leadership
Shows Peter's standing in early Christianity
table.note: All agree Peter was the leading apostle; Paul calls him Cephas, Aramaic for 'rock' (Galatians 2:9).

sections.key: Matthew's 'on this rock' is read as Peter (Catholic), Peter's faith and office (Orthodox) or the confession of Christ (Protestant).

paras: Peter's answer did not stay a private word on a road in the north. After the crucifixion his followers went on saying it, now about a man the Romans had executed. Paul admits how strange that sounded: 'we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks' (1 Corinthians 1:23). To Jews a crucified Messiah was a contradiction, as it had been to Peter; to Greeks and Romans, worshipping a man executed as a criminal was absurd.

Yet the title stuck so firmly that it became a name. In Antioch, in Syria, around AD 40, outsiders began calling Jesus's followers Christianoi, 'Christ-people' (Acts 11:26); Tacitus uses the same word in Rome a few decades later. Every time someone says 'Christian', they repeat Peter's claim at Caesarea Philippi: that Jesus is the anointed king. Tacitus did not mean it kindly: in Church and Brodribb's translation he calls the movement 'a most mischievous superstition' (Annals XV.44). And they repeat Jesus's redefinition too: that the king's way to his throne was the way of suffering. Mark puts the call that follows straight after it: 'Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me' (Mark 8:34).
sections.key: Within a decade 'Christ' had become a name: Jesus's followers were 'Christians', confessing a crucified Messiah that Paul called a stumbling block.

refs: Mark 6:14–16; 8:27–38; 9:31; 10:33–34; Matthew 16:13–23; John 6:15; Galatians 2:9; 1 Samuel 24:6; Leviticus 4:3; 1 Kings 19:16; Isaiah 11:1–4; 52:13–53:12; Psalm 2:9; Deuteronomy 17:16–17; Numbers 24:17; Luke 2:11; Acts 5:36; 21:38.
Psalms of Solomon 17, ed. and tr. H. E. Ryle and M. R. James, Psalms of the Pharisees, commonly called the Psalms of Solomon (Cambridge, 1891).

Josephus, Antiquities XV.10.3 (the temple to Augustus at Paneas), XVII.10.5–7 (the claimants of 4 BC), XVIII.2.1 (Caesarea Philippi), XX.5.1 (Theudas), XX.8.6 (the Egyptian). Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit 4:5 (Akiva and Bar Kokhba). Targum of Isaiah 52:13.

William Wrede, Das Messiasgeheimnis in den Evangelien (1901; English, The Messianic Secret, 1971); Nils A. Dahl, 'The Crucified Messiah' (1960), in The Crucified Messiah and Other Essays (1974); Rudolf Bultmann, Theology of the New Testament (1948–53); E. P. Sanders, Jesus and Judaism (1985); N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God (1996).

debate.question: Did Jesus think he was the Messiah?

positions.name: No: the church gave him the title
positions.who: William Wrede (1901); Rudolf Bultmann; Geza Vermes
positions.view: Jesus was a prophet or a holy man who announced God's kingdom. The church, convinced after Easter that he was alive and exalted, called him Messiah, and read the title back into his life. The secrecy commands are the seam where the later belief was stitched on.
positions.evidence: Jesus never calls himself 'Messiah' in public in the first three Gospels; the commands to silence; the prophecies of death, which look shaped by hindsight.

positions.name: Yes, and he redefined it
positions.who: N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God (1996); E. P. Sanders, Jesus and Judaism (1985), in a cautious form
positions.view: Jesus believed he was the one through whom God was bringing in his kingdom, and acted the part: he chose twelve, for Israel's twelve tribes; he rode into Jerusalem; he acted in the Temple. But he redefined kingship as service and suffering. Sanders thought Jesus expected to be king in the coming kingdom, even if he avoided the word.
positions.evidence: Peter's confession, which Jesus accepts; the hearing before the high priest; the symbolic acts; the suffering Messiah, which no one would invent.

positions.name: The cross decides it
positions.who: Nils Dahl, 'The Crucified Messiah' (1960); many historians
positions.view: Whatever he said in private, Pilate executed him as 'the King of the Jews' (Mark 15:26), the charge written above the cross. That charge is about as certain as anything in the story. So he must have been seen as a royal claimant in his lifetime, and not denied it; and his followers called him Messiah because he was crucified as one.
positions.evidence: The inscription on the cross in all four Gospels; Roman practice of crucifying rebels; the early church's struggle to explain a crucified Messiah (1 Corinthians 1:23).

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus was executed as a would-be king, that 'Messiah' became his followers' central title for him, and that a suffering Messiah was not what most Jews expected.

look.why: Grifo di Tancredi, a Florentine painter, made this panel of Saint Peter around 1310. Peter holds the keys of Matthew 16:19, given after his answer at Caesarea Philippi. No painting of the moment itself is free in the gallery's open collection, so here is the man who gave the answer.
points: A man with light skin, white hair and a white beard: Saint Peter.
He wears an orange cloth draped over a dark-blue garment with gold embroidery around the shoulder and neckline.
In his left hand he holds two large red keys; in his right, a thin red rod topped with a cross.
There is a faint outline of a halo round his head, which is turned slightly to the right.
The background is gold, inside a red, white and black patterned border.

music.why: An early Irish monastic prayer, sung to a folk melody, that addresses Christ as king and asks him to be first in everything. It is Peter's answer, 'You are the Christ', turned into a prayer.

think.why: Christians say God cannot be found with a telescope but is known above all through Jesus. This depth explains why the question 'who do you say I am?' is, for Christians, a question about God.

learn.why: Jesus's question to his friends, and Peter's answer: the question this whole journey asks, in seven words.

check.q: Every answer the disciples report from the crowd (John the Baptist, Elijah, a prophet) has something in common. What is the best conclusion?
options: The crowd thought he was the Messiah
The crowd thought he was a Roman agent
The crowd thought he was mad
The crowd saw a prophet, a man of God with power, but not the Messiah
check.why: All the crowd's answers are prophets; it is Peter, not the crowd, who says 'the Christ'.

check.q: Why does Jesus probably tell the disciples to tell no one that he is the Messiah?
options: Because the Romans had banned the word
Because in public 'Messiah' meant a king who would fight Rome, and he did not mean that
Because he was ashamed of the title
Because Peter's answer was wrong
check.why: The Psalms of Solomon show what 'Messiah' meant to many: a conqueror. John 6:15 shows a crowd trying to make him king by force.

check.q: Why does Peter rebuke Jesus?
options: Because Jesus wanted to go to Rome
Because Jesus called himself Elijah
Because Jesus said the Son of Man must suffer and be killed, and a killed Messiah was a failed Messiah
Because Jesus refused the title Messiah
check.why: Every known claimant who was killed was taken to have failed. Peter could not fit death into 'Messiah'.

check.q: Comparing the Psalms of Solomon with Mark 8, what is the deepest difference between the two Messiahs?
options: One is violent and the other wholly peaceful in every way
The psalm's Messiah is a priest, not a king
The psalm's Messiah is God, Mark's is only a man
In the psalm the Messiah wins, purges Jerusalem and reigns; in Mark the Messiah must suffer and be killed
check.why: The psalm's king is holy and rules by his word, but he triumphs. Mark's Son of Man is rejected and killed.

check.q: What did William Wrede argue in The Messianic Secret (1901)?
options: That Jesus openly claimed to be the Messiah from the start
That Mark invented the commands to silence to explain why Jesus, whom the church called Messiah, had not claimed the title in his lifetime
That the Messiah was expected to suffer
That Peter was the real Messiah
check.why: Wrede saw the secrecy as Mark's device; most scholars now think it fits Jesus's own setting better.

check.q: Which piece of evidence is usually thought the strongest that Jesus was seen as a royal claimant in his own lifetime?
options: The visit of the wise men
Peter's later sermons in Acts
The Psalms of Solomon
The charge above the cross, 'The King of the Jews'
check.why: Nils Dahl's argument: the Romans crucified him as 'King of the Jews', a charge recorded in all four Gospels.

tutorial.question: Did Jesus think he was the Messiah?
tutorial.approach: Start with what 'Messiah' meant, using the Psalms of Solomon and the other claimants. Then read Mark 8:27–33 closely: the question, the answer, the silence, the prediction, the rebuke. Set out Wrede's view fairly and the replies. End with the charge on the cross and your own judgement.
strong: Explains what 'Messiah' and 'Christ' mean, and the hope for a son of David.
Uses the Psalms of Solomon to show what Peter expected.
Explains the commands to silence and at least two explanations of them.
Explains why a suffering Messiah was a contradiction, and why that suggests the teaching is early.
Uses the charge 'King of the Jews'.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion, granting what is uncertain.

reading.author: Richard Bauckham
reading.title: Jesus: A Very Short Introduction
reading.why: A brief, clear account of Jesus in his Jewish world by a leading New Testament scholar.

reading.author: N. T. Wright
reading.title: Jesus and the Victory of God
reading.why: The case that Jesus saw himself as Messiah and redefined the role.

reading.author: Geza Vermes
reading.title: Jesus the Jew
reading.why: A Jewish historian's case that Jesus was a Galilean holy man, not a self-proclaimed Messiah.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Peter wanted a Messiah who would win; Jesus said greatness meant service. Once this week, at work or at home, take the lowest job in the room (the clearing up, the dull task, the thankless call), and do it well, without mentioning it.
sessions.reflect: If Jesus asked you, 'But who do you say that I am?', what would you honestly answer today?
takeaways: 'Christ' means 'anointed', the promised king from David's line; many Jews prayed for a Messiah who would drive the Romans out, as the Psalms of Solomon show.
At Caesarea Philippi Peter called Jesus the Messiah; Jesus accepted it, told them to keep it quiet, and taught that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed.
A suffering Messiah was a contradiction to Peter, which is one reason historians think the teaching goes back to Jesus; Pilate later crucified him as 'King of the Jews'.

sessions.title: What he did: miracles
sessions.line: A storm stilled and five thousand fed: what the Gospels claim he did, what his enemies said about it, and what a historian can and cannot conclude.
sessions.plain: The Gospels are full of miracles: healings, exorcisms, a storm stilled, crowds fed. Today many people find them the hardest part to believe. But the ancient sources, friendly and hostile, agree that Jesus was known as a man who did astonishing things; his enemies said he did them by magic. This session reads two miracle stories, sets beside them a famous pagan wonder-worker, and asks what the miracles were meant to show, and what a historian can say about them.
sessions.why: We have heard two witnesses: his world, and his words. He claimed God's authority to forgive, took Daniel's title Son of Man, and accepted the title Messiah while saying it meant suffering. The scribes in Capernaum already saw that a claim needs evidence: 'that you may know', he said, and healed the paralysed man. Now we call the third witness: his deeds.
answers: Did Jesus do miracles?
What were the miracles for?
Were there other miracle-workers at the time?
What did his enemies say about his deeds?
Can a historian say that a miracle happened?
sessions.finding: Friends and enemies agreed Jesus did deeds of power; the Gospels present them as signs of the kingdom, not proofs on demand.

paras: Jesus, a Galilean Jew of the first century, claimed an authority that belonged to God, called himself the Son of Man, and accepted Peter's confession that he was the Messiah, while teaching that he must suffer. In Capernaum he offered a healing as evidence of an invisible authority to forgive. That raises the question of this session: what did he actually do, and what does it show?
background.key: Jesus offered his deeds as evidence for his authority. Now we examine the deeds.

paras: About a third of Mark's Gospel is taken up with miracles. They fall into kinds. Most are healings: the blind, the lame, the paralysed, people with skin diseases. Many are exorcisms, the casting out of evil spirits. A few raise the dead. And a few, which scholars call 'nature miracles', show power over the world itself: stilling a storm, walking on water, feeding thousands. The first two kinds are the best attested, in every layer of the sources.

The Gospels have their own words for them. Mark uses dynameis, 'deeds of power'. John uses semeia, 'signs': things that point beyond themselves. Neither Gospel uses a word that means 'a breaking of the laws of nature'; that idea, and the word 'miracle' in its modern sense, came much later. The question the Gospels ask about a miracle is not 'how?' but 'who is this?'
background.key: Healings and exorcisms are the best-attested deeds; the Gospels call them 'deeds of power' and 'signs', and ask what they show about who he is.

paras: The main reading has two parts. Mark 4:35–41 is a nature miracle: Jesus stills a storm on the Sea of Galilee, and his disciples ask 'Who then is this?' John 6:1–15 is the feeding of the five thousand, the only miracle told in all four Gospels, after which the crowd tries to make him king.

The comparison is from a Greek biography of Apollonius of Tyana, a wandering philosopher of the first century who was also said to cast out demons and raise the dead. Later pagans set him up as a rival to Jesus. Reading him shows what the ancient world made of wonder-workers, and what is different about the Gospels.
background.key: A storm stilled (Mark 4) and a crowd fed (John 6); then the pagan wonder-worker Apollonius, for comparison.

before: What question do the disciples ask at the end of the storm, and why is it the right question?
In John 6, what do the crowd conclude, and what do they try to do?
In the story of Apollonius, what does Philostratus himself admit he does not know?
sessions.readWhy: Two stories from two Gospels: a storm on the lake in Mark, and five thousand fed on the hillside in John.

paras: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let’s go over to the other side.”
Leaving the multitude, they took him with them, even as he was, in the boat. Other small boats were also with him.
A big wind storm arose, and the waves beat into the boat, so much that the boat was already filled.
He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion, and they woke him up, and told him, “Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?”
He awoke, and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?”
They were greatly afraid, and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
After these things, Jesus went away to the other side of the sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias.
A great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick.
Jesus went up into the mountain, and he sat there with his disciples.
Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.
Jesus therefore lifting up his eyes, and seeing that a great multitude was coming to him, said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?”
He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.
Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may receive a little.”
One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,
“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?”
Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand.
Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.
When they were filled, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.”
So they gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with broken pieces from the five barley loaves, which were left over by those who had eaten.
When therefore the people saw the sign which Jesus did, they said, “This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.”
Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.

parts.title: Even the wind and the sea obey him
parts.context: The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level, in a basin of hills, and sudden violent winds can still sweep down on it. Most of the disciples were fishermen who knew it well. In the Old Testament the sea is often a picture of chaos, which only God can master.

commentary.on: He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion
commentary.text: Jesus sleeps through the storm, like the prophet Jonah asleep in the ship as the storm rose (Jonah 1:5). In the Psalms, sleep is a sign of trust: 'I laid myself down and slept' (Psalm 3:5).

commentary.on: Teacher, don't you care that we are dying?
commentary.text: The disciples' cry is not polite. Mark keeps it in, though it makes them look bad; Matthew and Luke soften it. That is the kind of detail historians notice: it is not flattering to the leaders of the early church.

commentary.on: He awoke, and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, "Peace! Be still!"
commentary.text: He speaks to the storm as he spoke to the unclean spirit in the synagogue: 'rebuked' is the same word. In Psalm 107, sailors in a storm cry to the Lord, and 'he makes the storm a calm'. In the Old Testament, only God commands the sea.

commentary.on: Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?
commentary.text: Faith here is not believing in miracles. It is trusting the person in the boat.

commentary.on: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
commentary.text: The disciples are 'greatly afraid', more afraid after the calm than in the storm. Their question is the whole point. Any reader who knew the Psalms knew the answer the story implies: the one whom wind and sea obey is God. Mark does not say it; he lets the question hang.

parts.title: Five barley loaves and two fish
parts.context: John's Gospel calls Jesus's miracles 'signs' and tells only seven of them in detail. This is the fourth, on the hills by the Sea of Galilee, near Passover, the spring feast that remembered the Exodus from Egypt.

commentary.on: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.
commentary.text: John sets the scene at Passover on purpose. At the Exodus, God fed Israel in the desert with manna, 'bread from the sky'. Straight after this story, Jesus says: 'I am the bread of life' (John 6:35).

commentary.on: There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?
commentary.text: Barley bread was the food of the poor. There is a clear echo of the prophet Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and had some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Here it is five loaves and five thousand people.

commentary.on: Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed
commentary.text: Taking bread and giving thanks: the words of every Jewish meal, and the words Christians would use of the Last Supper. The early church read this meal and its own meal together.

commentary.on: This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.
commentary.text: Moses had promised that God would raise up 'a prophet like me' (Deuteronomy 18:15). A prophet who fed the people in the wilderness, as in Moses' day, looked like that promise fulfilled.

commentary.on: they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
commentary.text: The crowd draws the political conclusion: a man who can feed an army should lead one. Jesus refuses. The miracle is a sign of the kingdom, not a recruiting drive for a revolt. It is the same refusal we saw at Caesarea Philippi.

paras: But when Tigellinus unrolled the scroll, and did not find upon it the trace of a single word or letter, and his eyes fell on a perfectly blank book, he came to the conclusion that he had to do with a demon; and this is said also subsequently to have been the feeling which Domitian afterwards entertained towards Apollonius.
"And about the demons," said Tigellinus, "and the apparitions of specters, how, O Apollonius, do you exorcise them?"

"In the same way," he answered, "as I should murderers and impious men." This was a sarcastic allusion to Tigellinus himself, for he taught and encouraged in Nero every excess of cruelty and wanton violence.

Here too is a miracle which Apollonius worked: A girl had died just in the hour of her marriage, and the bridegroom was following her bier lamenting as was natural his marriage left unfulfilled, and the whole of Rome was mourning with him, for the maiden belonged to a consular family. Apollonius then witnessing their grief, said: "Put down the bier, for I will stay the tears that you are shedding for this maiden."

And withal he asked what was her name. The crowd accordingly thought that he was about to deliver such an oration as is commonly delivered to grace the funeral as to stir up lamentation; but he did nothing of the kind, but merely touching her and whispering in secret some spell over her, at once woke up the maiden from her seeming death; and the girl spoke out loud, and returned to her father's house, just as Alcestis did when she was brought back to life by Heracles. And the relations of the maiden wanted to present him with the sum of 150,000 sesterces, but he said that he would freely present the money to the young lady by way of dowry.

Now whether he detected some spark of life in her, which those who were nursing her had not noticed -for it is said that although it was raining at the time, a vapor went up from her face- or whether her life was really extinct, and he restored it by the warmth of his touch, is a mysterious problem which neither I myself nor those who were present could decide.

parts.author: Philostratus
parts.work: The Life of Apollonius of Tyana
parts.title: He had to do with a demon
parts.context: Apollonius of Tyana, in what is now central Turkey, was a wandering philosopher of the first century AD, a follower of Pythagoras. Our main source is a long biography by Philostratus, an Athenian writer who lived from about 170 to 247, written at the request of the empress Julia Domna and finished after her death in 217: about 150 years after Apollonius. Here Apollonius has been arrested in Rome under Nero by Tigellinus, commander of the emperor's guard, who has a scroll of charges against him. This is F. C. Conybeare's translation for the Loeb library (1912). The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: When Tigellinus opened the scroll of charges, it was blank, and he decided Apollonius was in league with spirits. He asked him how he cast out demons and ghosts. Apollonius answered with a jibe: the same way he dealt with murderers and wicked men, meaning Tigellinus himself.

commentary.on: he came to the conclusion that he had to do with a demon
commentary.text: In Greek a daimon could be any spirit, good or bad. Apollonius's enemies, like Jesus's, assumed that wonders came from dark powers. Philostratus writes partly to clear his hero of the charge of magic.

commentary.on: how, O Apollonius, do you exorcise them?
commentary.text: Exorcism was common in the ancient world, among pagans and Jews alike. Josephus describes a Jewish exorcist, Eleazar, drawing a demon out through a man's nose with a ring and roots before the emperor Vespasian. So the Gospel exorcisms are not strange in their world; what is distinctive is how Jesus did them, with a word, and what he said they meant.

parts.author: Philostratus
parts.work: The Life of Apollonius of Tyana
parts.title: A girl who had died in the hour of her marriage
parts.context: The most famous story about Apollonius, often compared with Jesus raising Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:21–43) and the widow's son at Nain (Luke 7:11–17).
parts.plain: A young bride from a noble family has died, and all Rome is mourning. Apollonius stops the funeral, touches the girl, whispers a spell, and she wakes and goes home. He refuses a reward. But Philostratus admits that no one could be sure whether she was really dead, or only seemed so.

commentary.on: merely touching her and whispering in secret some spell over her
commentary.text: Apollonius 'whispers a spell'. In Mark, Jesus takes the girl by the hand and says in Aramaic, 'Talitha koum', 'little girl, get up' (Mark 5:41): no spell, no secret formula, a command in her own language.

commentary.on: just as Alcestis did when she was brought back to life by Heracles
commentary.text: Philostratus compares the scene to Greek myth: in Euripides' play Alcestis, the hero Heracles wrestles Death and brings a dead wife back. The pagan writer himself frames his story in the world of legend.

commentary.on: is a mysterious problem which neither I myself nor those who were present could decide
commentary.text: This is the most important line. Writing a century and a half later, Philostratus does not know whether a miracle happened, and says so. The Gospels, written within living memory, make their claims without that hedge. That does not make them true, but it is a real difference of kind.

compare.author: Philostratus
compare.work: The Life of Apollonius of Tyana
compare.why: Apollonius was a first-century philosopher said to have cast out demons and raised a dead girl in Rome. Two centuries later he was set up as a pagan rival to Jesus. Read him and ask how the Gospel stories differ.
compare.title: The wonder-worker of Tyana

paras: The most striking evidence for Jesus's deeds comes from people who did not believe in him. In Mark, scribes from Jerusalem do not deny that he casts out demons; they say he does it 'by the prince of the demons' (Mark 3:22). The Jewish historian Josephus, whose passage you read in 'What is the Bible?', calls Jesus 'a doer of wonderful works'.

The Babylonian Talmud, the great collection of rabbinic teaching completed around AD 500–600, has a short passage (Sanhedrin 43a) saying that a man called Yeshu was hanged on the eve of Passover, and that a herald had announced he was to be stoned for sorcery and for leading Israel astray. Scholars debate whether it refers to Jesus of Nazareth, and it is centuries later and polemical; Peter Schäfer, in Jesus in the Talmud (2007), argues that it is a deliberate counter-story to the Gospels. The Greek philosopher Celsus, around AD 175, also said Jesus had learned magic in Egypt. Hostile witnesses agree on the deeds and dispute their source.
sections.key: His enemies did not deny his deeds; they called them sorcery. Mark 3, Josephus, the Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a) and Celsus agree on that.

paras: Jesus was not the only man of his time said to do wonders. In Jewish tradition, Honi 'the circle-drawer', in the first century BC, drew a circle on the ground in a drought and refused to step out until God sent rain (Mishnah, Taanit 3:8). Hanina ben Dosa, a Galilean holy man of the first century AD, prayed for the sick and knew from how easily his prayer came whether they would live (Mishnah, Berakhot 5:5); the Talmud says he healed the son of Rabban Gamaliel at a distance. The Jewish scholar Geza Vermes argued that Jesus belongs to this world of Galilean charismatic holy men.

Among pagans there were healing shrines of the god Asclepius, and men like Apollonius. In the third century, a Roman governor called Hierocles wrote that Apollonius did greater wonders than Jesus, and so Christians should not call Jesus God; the church historian Eusebius wrote a reply. The comparison is fair. The differences are worth noticing too: Honi and Hanina pray and God answers; Jesus commands. And the Gospels tie his deeds to a claim about the kingdom of God, which no wonder-worker made.
sections.key: Honi, Hanina ben Dosa and Apollonius show that wonder-workers were known; the difference is that Jesus commanded rather than asked, and tied his deeds to the kingdom.

paras: What were the miracles for? The Gospels give one answer again and again: they were signs that God's kingdom was arriving. 'If I by the finger of God cast out demons, then the Kingdom of God has come to you' (Luke 11:20). When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was 'the one who comes', Jesus answered with a list from Isaiah: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, the poor hear good news (Matthew 11:2–5).

Equally striking is what he refused to do. When the Pharisees asked for 'a sign from heaven' to test him, he 'sighed deeply' and said no sign would be given (Mark 8:11–12). In the wilderness he refused to turn stones into bread or throw himself from the Temple. In his home town 'he could do no mighty work there', because of their unbelief (Mark 6:5). The Gospels never present the miracles as proofs on demand, or as tricks to compel belief. They are acts of mercy that also point: to the feeding of Israel in the desert, to God who commands the sea, to a world being put right.
sections.key: The miracles are presented as signs of God's kingdom arriving, and acts of mercy; Jesus refused to perform them as proofs on demand.

paras: A historian works with probabilities and with ordinary causes. So most historians, whatever they believe, say something like this: it is as certain as anything about Jesus that he was known in his lifetime as a healer and exorcist, and that people believed they had seen him do extraordinary things. The Catholic scholar John Meier, in a long and careful study (A Marginal Jew, volume 2, 1994), concluded that the tradition of healings and exorcisms goes back to Jesus himself; the stories are too many, too widespread and too unlike later Christian interests to have been invented.

Whether God acted in those events is a different kind of question. The historian, as historian, cannot answer it either way; it depends on whether one thinks God exists and could act. The philosopher David Hume argued in 1748 that no testimony could ever be strong enough to make a miracle believable; the journey 'Hume and the miracles' in the modern hall answers him at length. Here it is enough to see that the question 'Did miracles happen?' quickly becomes 'Is there a God who could do them?', and that both believers and sceptics bring an answer to the evidence.
sections.key: Historians widely agree that Jesus was known as a healer and exorcist; whether God acted in those deeds is a question history alone cannot settle.

paras: Of all Jesus's deeds, the exorcisms are the most widely attested and the strangest to modern readers. When the scribes said he cast out demons by the prince of demons, he answered with a parable: no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods 'unless he first binds the strong man' (Mark 3:27). The exorcisms, in his own explanation, were a raid on the house of evil: signs that its power was being broken and God's rule was arriving.

How should we read this today? Some modern readers treat the stories as descriptions, in ancient terms, of what we would call epilepsy or mental illness; the boy in Mark 9:17–27, who foams and falls, is often read this way. Anthropologists point out that possession is reported in many cultures today, and that the healing of a person's place in the community was part of what happened. Christian traditions have never stopped praying against evil, and the Catholic and Orthodox churches still have rites of exorcism, used with great caution and with medical advice. What every reading agrees on is that Jesus's contemporaries saw these deeds as conflict, and that he told them what it meant: 'the Kingdom of God has come to you'.
sections.key: Jesus explained his exorcisms as binding 'the strong man': signs that evil's power was breaking; modern readers differ on what the possessions were.

sections.h: Do the churches expect miracles now?
paras: Christians agree that Jesus did deeds of power. They differ about whether such things still happen, and how to tell. The differences are old, and they still shape what a newcomer meets in different churches.

rows: A miracle is normally required before someone is declared a saint; at Lourdes an international medical committee examines claimed cures, and the Church had recognised seventy by 2018
Yes, within the life of the Church
Healings are linked with prayer, the sacraments, holy places and the relics and icons of saints, with little formal investigation
Many held that the age of miracles ended with the apostles
B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles (1918): signs confirmed the first revelation and then ceased
Prayer for healing as part of church life; Craig Keener's Miracles (2011) collects many reports
table.note: All agree that miracles cannot be produced on demand; Jesus himself refused to perform them that way.

sections.key: Catholics investigate rare miracles, Orthodox see them in the Church's life, many Protestants held they had ceased, Pentecostals expect them.

refs: Philostratus, Life of Apollonius IV.44–45, tr. F. C. Conybeare (Loeb, 1912); Eusebius, Against Hierocles. Josephus, Antiquities VIII.2.5 (Eleazar the exorcist), XVIII.3.3.

Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a (the Yeshu passage, omitted from censored editions); Mishnah, Taanit 3:8 (Honi), Berakhot 5:5 (Hanina ben Dosa); Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b; Origen, Against Celsus I.28, I.38.

John P. Meier, A Marginal Jew, vol. 2: Mentor, Message, and Miracles (1994); Graham Twelftree, Jesus the Miracle Worker (1999); Geza Vermes, Jesus the Jew (1973); Peter Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud (2007); Craig Keener, Miracles (2011); David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), section X.

debate.question: The miracle stories: history, legend or signs?

positions.name: Deeds of power that really happened
positions.who: John Meier, A Marginal Jew (1994); Graham Twelftree; Craig Keener, Miracles (2011)
positions.view: The healings and exorcisms are among the best-attested facts about Jesus. If God exists, there is no reason in principle why he could not act. Keener collects many modern eyewitness reports of healings to argue that such claims cannot simply be dismissed.
positions.evidence: Multiple independent sources; hostile witnesses who grant the deeds; details that fit first-century Galilee and embarrassed later Christians.

positions.name: Legend and myth
positions.who: D. F. Strauss (1835); Rudolf Bultmann, 'New Testament and Mythology' (1941)
positions.view: The miracle stories grew as the first Christians told them, modelled on Moses, Elijah and Elisha and on what the Messiah was expected to do. Bultmann held that modern people cannot use electric light and believe in a world of spirits; the stories must be 'demythologised' to find their message.
positions.evidence: The clear Old Testament patterns (Elisha's barley loaves, the Exodus); the growth of the stories between Gospels; the existence of similar tales about Apollonius.

positions.name: Signs whose meaning matters most
positions.who: Augustine, City of God XXI.8; many modern theologians across the traditions
positions.view: Augustine said a miracle is not against nature but against what we know of nature. The Gospels care less about the mechanism than the meaning: the stories are signs of God's kingdom and of who Jesus is. Whether or not each detail is history, they say what the first witnesses saw in him.
positions.evidence: John's word 'signs'; Jesus's refusal of signs on demand; the way every miracle story ends in a question about him.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus was known as a healer and exorcist in his lifetime, and that the Gospels tell the miracles to say who he was.

look.why: No painting for this session: the gallery's open collection has no free painting of the stilling of the storm or the feeding of the five thousand. One painting in the collection shows Christ on the Sea of Galilee, but it appears to show a different story, so we have left it out.

music.why: Horatio Spafford wrote this hymn in 1873, after his four daughters drowned in a shipwreck, as his own ship passed the place where they died. It is the disciples' cry, 'don't you care that we are dying?', answered with trust in the one in the boat, even when no storm was stilled.

think.why: Augustine and Aquinas on why faith and reason cannot truly contradict each other: the background to every argument about miracles.

learn.why: 'Be still, and know that I am God': the psalm in which God, not the sailors, is master of the roaring waters, the God whom the disciples glimpsed in the boat.

check.q: Why do historians attach special weight to the charge that Jesus cast out demons 'by the prince of the demons' (Mark 3:22)?
options: Because it proves the exorcisms were magic
Because Mark invented it to make the scribes look bad
Because the scribes were Roman officials
Because it shows his opponents did not deny his deeds, only disputed their source
check.why: A hostile witness who grants a fact while disputing its meaning is strong evidence for the fact.

check.q: At the end of the storm, the disciples ask 'Who then is this?' Why does the story imply a startling answer?
options: Because only Roman emperors could calm the sea
Because fishermen thought storms were caused by demons
Because Jonah had done the same thing
Because in the Old Testament it is God who rules the sea and stills the storm
check.why: Psalm 107 and other psalms give mastery of the sea to God; Mark lets the reader draw the conclusion.

check.q: After the feeding, the crowd try to make Jesus king by force, and he withdraws. What does this show?
options: That his signs pointed to God's kingdom, not to a political uprising, which he refused
That he did the miracles to win followers for a revolt
That he wanted to be king but feared the Romans
That the crowd did not believe in him
check.why: He refuses the crowd's conclusion, as he refused the warrior-Messiah role at Caesarea Philippi.

check.q: What is the most important difference between Philostratus's story of the girl in Rome and the Gospel accounts?
options: Philostratus, writing 150 years later, admits no one could tell whether she was really dead
Apollonius used Aramaic words
The girl was a Jew
Apollonius charged a large fee
check.why: Philostratus hedges; the Gospels, written within living memory, make their claims without that doubt.

check.q: How did Jesus respond when the Pharisees demanded 'a sign from heaven' (Mark 8:11–12)?
options: He refused: no sign would be given
He asked Peter to do it
He said he needed more faith first
He performed one at once to silence them
check.why: The Gospels never show the miracles as proofs on demand.

check.q: A sceptic says, 'Historians have proved the miracles never happened.' What is the most accurate reply?
options: No ancient source mentions any deeds of Jesus
Miracles are impossible, so the question is closed
Historians agree Jesus was known as a healer and exorcist; whether God acted is a question history alone cannot settle either way
Historians have proved they did happen
check.why: Meier and others show the tradition is early; the question of God's action depends on wider beliefs that both sides bring.

tutorial.question: How far can a historian go in judging the miracle stories of Jesus?
tutorial.approach: Distinguish the kinds of miracle and how well each is attested. Use the hostile witnesses (Mark 3:22, the Talmud, Celsus). Compare Jesus with Honi, Hanina and Apollonius, noting likenesses and differences. Then explain what the Gospels say the miracles were for. End with the limits of history: what it can conclude, and what it cannot.
strong: Distinguishes healings and exorcisms from nature miracles, and judges the evidence for each.
Uses at least two hostile witnesses fairly, including the debate over Sanhedrin 43a.
Compares Jesus with other wonder-workers and names a real difference.
Explains the miracles as 'signs' of the kingdom, and the refusal of signs on demand.
Sees that 'did it happen?' leads to 'is there a God who acts?'
Weighs Strauss or Bultmann against Meier fairly.
