sessions.practice: Live it this week: the miracle began with a boy who offered five barley loaves when they seemed useless. Think of one small thing you could give that seems too little to matter (an hour, a skill, a meal, some money) and give it this week to someone who needs it.
sessions.reflect: Do you find the miracle stories a reason to believe, or a reason to doubt? What would change your mind?
takeaways: Friends and enemies agreed that Jesus did deeds of power; his opponents called it sorcery (Mark 3:22, the Talmud, Celsus).
Other wonder-workers were known, Honi, Hanina and Apollonius among them; Jesus commanded rather than prayed, and tied his deeds to the kingdom of God.
The Gospels present the miracles as signs, not proofs on demand; history can show he was known as a healer, but whether God acted is a further question.

sessions.title: Prophecy fulfilled?
sessions.line: In the synagogue at Nazareth he reads from Isaiah and says, 'Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled.' What did his followers mean by fulfilment, and what do Jews reply?
sessions.plain: The first Christians said again and again that Jesus 'fulfilled the Scriptures': that the Jewish Bible, the Old Testament, pointed to him. Jesus himself began his work in his home town by reading a prophecy of Isaiah and saying it was coming true that day. But what does 'fulfil' mean? Sometimes a prediction, sometimes a pattern repeated, sometimes an echo. And Jews have always answered that the Messiah was to bring peace on earth, which has not come. This session reads the scene at Nazareth and the prophecy itself, and sets the two readings side by side.
sessions.why: We have heard three witnesses: his world, his words and his deeds. He claimed God's authority, accepted the title Messiah while saying it meant suffering, and did deeds that friends and enemies agreed were extraordinary, which he called signs of the kingdom. When John the Baptist asked if he was 'the one who comes', Jesus answered with a list from Isaiah. Now we call the fourth witness: the prophets. Did Israel's Scriptures lead people to expect a man like this?
answers: Did Jesus fulfil the prophecies?
How did Jesus read his own mission?
What did his followers mean by 'fulfilled'?
Why do Jews say he was not the Messiah?
sessions.finding: Jesus read his mission from Isaiah; his followers read the whole Old Testament as pointing to him, and some of their readings are stronger than others.

paras: Three witnesses have spoken. His world: a Galilean Jew under Rome, among people waiting for a Messiah. His words: he forgave sins, called himself the Son of Man, and accepted the title Messiah while teaching that he must suffer. His deeds: healings and exorcisms that even his enemies did not deny, presented as signs of God's kingdom.

Each time, the Gospels point back to Israel's Scriptures: the Son of Man is Daniel's, the feeding echoes Moses and Elisha, the suffering echoes Isaiah's servant. Now we ask about that pattern directly.
background.key: His world, his words and his deeds all point back to Israel's Scriptures. This session examines the claim that he fulfilled them.

background.h: What Christians mean by the Old Testament
paras: Jesus's Bible was the Jewish Scriptures: the Law (the five books of Moses), the Prophets and the Writings, which Jews call the Tanakh, from the first letters of those three parts. Christians call the same books the Old Testament, meaning the 'old covenant', beside the New. Both names are fair from where each stands; this course uses 'the Old Testament' because it is a Christian course, and 'the Jewish Scriptures' when it means what Jesus read.

Jesus grew up hearing these books read in Hebrew in the synagogue, with an Aramaic explanation, and many Jews outside the land read them in Greek, in the translation called the Septuagint. When the Gospels quote the Old Testament, they usually follow the Greek. You read Isaiah 53 in 'Kings and prophets', and Matthew's use of Isaiah 7:14 and Hosea 11:1, with Thomas Paine's attack on it, in 'The whole story'.
background.key: Jesus's Bible was the Jewish Scriptures (the Tanakh); Christians call them the Old Testament. The Gospels often quote the Greek translation, the Septuagint.

paras: The reading is Luke 4:16–21: Jesus, at the start of his public work, reads in the synagogue of his home town and says the prophecy is being fulfilled 'today'. It is the one place in the Gospels where we see him read Scripture aloud, and it answers the question of how he understood his own mission.
The comparison is the prophecy itself, Isaiah 61:1–3, so that you can see exactly what Jesus read, what Luke's version leaves out, and why that matters.
background.key: Luke 4:16–21, Jesus reading Isaiah in Nazareth; then Isaiah 61:1–3 itself, to compare.

before: Which words of the prophecy describe what Jesus has been doing in this journey so far?
Compare Luke's quotation with Isaiah 61. Where does Luke stop?
Why might the people of Nazareth find 'Today' hard to accept?
sessions.readWhy: The scene in the synagogue at Nazareth: the reading, and the sermon of one sentence.

paras: He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and stood up to read.
The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He opened the book, and found the place where it was written,

“The Spirit of the Lord is on me,
because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor.
He has sent me to heal the broken hearted,
to proclaim release to the captives,
recovering of sight to the blind,
to deliver those who are crushed,
and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.”
He closed the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him.
He began to tell them, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

parts.title: The Spirit of the Lord is on me
parts.context: Luke's Gospel, written around AD 80–90 by a companion of Paul, says it is based on 'eyewitnesses' and careful research (Luke 1:1–4). Luke puts this scene at the start of Jesus's work in Galilee, as a kind of manifesto. In a synagogue service, after prayers and a reading from the Law, a member of the congregation could be invited to read from the Prophets and then sit down to explain it.

commentary.on: He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day
commentary.text: 'As was his custom': Jesus was a practising Jew who went to the synagogue every week. The oldest synagogue buildings found in Galilee date from his time, at Magdala and Gamla.

commentary.on: The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him.
commentary.text: The 'book' was a scroll. A complete scroll of Isaiah from about 125 BC was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls in 1947, a thousand years older than any Hebrew copy known before; the text is very close to the one we read.

commentary.on: because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor.
commentary.text: 'Anointed me': in Greek echrisen, from the same root as Christos. The speaker in Isaiah is anointed not with oil but with the Spirit, as a prophet. So Jesus chooses a text about an anointed one whose task is good news for the poor, not victory over the nations. It is the answer to the Psalms of Solomon.

commentary.on: to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed
commentary.text: Luke's quotation follows the Greek Septuagint, which has 'recovering of sight to the blind', and slips in a line from Isaiah 58:6, 'to let the oppressed go free'. Ancient readers often joined related verses like this.

commentary.on: and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.
commentary.text: 'The acceptable year' recalls the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, every fiftieth year, when debts were cancelled, slaves freed and land returned: 'proclaim liberty throughout the land'. Jesus announces God's great year of release.

parts.title: Today
parts.context: Jesus gives the scroll back and sits down, the teacher's position. Luke gives his sermon in a single sentence.

commentary.on: The eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him.
commentary.text: Luke slows the scene down: the rolled scroll, the attendant, the silence, every eye on the carpenter's son.

commentary.on: Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.
commentary.text: Other teachers explained the prophets. Jesus says: it is happening now, here, in me. The verses that follow (Luke 4:22–30) show the town's reaction: amazement, then the question 'Isn't this Joseph's son?', then fury when he reminds them that prophets like Elijah were sent to foreigners. They try to throw him off a cliff.

paras:
The Lord Yahweh’s Spirit is on me,
because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble.
He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted,
to proclaim liberty to the captives
and release to those who are bound,

to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor
and the day of vengeance of our God,
to comfort all who mourn,

to provide for those who mourn in Zion,
to give to them a garland for ashes,
the oil of joy for mourning,
the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness,
that they may be called trees of righteousness,
the planting of Yahweh,
that he may be glorified.

parts.title: Good news to the humble
parts.context: Most scholars think Isaiah 56–66 comes from prophets in the line of Isaiah, writing after the return from Babylon in 538 BC, when Jerusalem was still in ruins and the returning exiles were poor and discouraged. Jewish and Christian tradition reads the whole book as Isaiah's. The speaker is a prophet anointed with God's Spirit.

commentary.on: The Lord Yahweh's Spirit is on me, because Yahweh has anointed me
commentary.text: Yahweh is the personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible; English Bibles often print 'the LORD'. In this course's other passages we write 'the Lord'. Here the anointing is with the Spirit: the prophet is God's messenger.

commentary.on: to proclaim liberty to the captives
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for 'liberty', deror, is the word used for the Jubilee release in Leviticus 25:10. The prophet takes Israel's law of release and makes it a picture of the great restoration God will bring.

commentary.on: to proclaim the year of Yahweh's favor and the day of vengeance of our God
commentary.text: Here is the line Jesus did not finish. He stopped at 'the year of the Lord's favour' and left out 'the day of vengeance'. Christians have long read that pause as meaningful: Jesus brings the favour now, and judgement is left for later. Jews have replied that the prophecy is one whole, and that a Messiah who brings only half of it has not fulfilled it.

commentary.on: to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning
commentary.text: In mourning, people put ashes on their heads. The prophet promises a festival garland instead. A first-century Jewish text from the Dead Sea Scrolls (4Q521) uses these same words of Isaiah about the age to come: God will heal the wounded, give life to the dead and bring good news to the poor, almost the list Jesus sent to John the Baptist (Luke 7:22). Jesus's hearers already read Isaiah 61 as a picture of the messianic age.

compare.why: Here is the prophecy Jesus read, from the last part of Isaiah, written for Jews returning from exile in Babylon. Read it whole, and notice where Jesus stopped.
compare.title: The year of the Lord's favour, and the day of vengeance

paras: When the New Testament says 'that it might be fulfilled', it does not always mean the same thing. It helps to tell three kinds apart.

First, prediction: a prophet foretells something and it happens. Micah's 'Bethlehem', quoted in Matthew 2, is read this way. Second, pattern: something in Israel's story is repeated in a fuller way in Jesus's. Matthew quotes Hosea 11:1, 'I called my son out of Egypt', which in Hosea is about Israel at the Exodus, not a prediction at all; Matthew sees the pattern of Israel's story come round again in one person. Scholars call this typology, from the Greek typos, a model or imprint. Third, echo: the Gospel writers tell stories in words that recall the Old Testament, so that readers hear one in the other, as the feeding echoes Elisha and the storm echoes the Psalms. Luke 4 is something else again: a prophet's description of his calling, which Jesus takes as his own.
sections.key: Fulfilment can mean prediction, pattern (typology) or echo; reading them as if they were all predictions causes confusion.

paras: Some fulfilment claims are strong on any account. The hope for a son of David, a king who would rule with justice, was widespread, and Jesus was hailed, and executed, as one. Isaiah's anointed messenger of good news to the poor is a fair description of what Jesus did, and he chose it himself. The suffering servant of Isaiah 53, 'pierced for our transgressions', fits his death strikingly, whatever the prophet first meant.

Others are weaker as arguments, and fair Christian scholars say so. Hosea 11:1 is not a prediction. Isaiah 7:14, quoted in Matthew 1:23 for the virgin birth, has the Hebrew almah, 'young woman', where the Greek translation has parthenos, 'virgin'; in its setting it gave King Ahaz a sign in his own day. These readings persuade only someone who already believes that Jesus is the key to the whole story. That is how the first Christians read: Luke says the risen Jesus, 'beginning from Moses and from all the prophets', explained 'the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27). Augustine summed it up: the New is hidden in the Old, and the Old made plain in the New.
sections.key: The son of David, Isaiah 61 and Isaiah 53 are strong fits; Hosea 11:1 and Isaiah 7:14 persuade mainly those who already read the Old Testament through Jesus.

paras: Jews have answered the Christian reading for two thousand years, and their answer deserves to be heard in its own words. The most famous statement is by the philosopher and legal scholar Moses Maimonides, in his code of Jewish law, the Mishneh Torah (about 1180). The Messiah, he writes, will be a king from David's line who leads Israel in keeping the law, rebuilds the Temple and gathers the scattered Jews home; if he does not succeed, or is killed, he is not the Messiah. And the prophets promised that in his days the nations would 'beat their swords into plowshares' and 'neither shall they learn war any more' (Isaiah 2:4).

In 1263, at a public debate in Barcelona before King James I of Aragon, the rabbi Nachmanides made the point unforgettably. The prophets promised universal peace, he said; yet from the days of Jesus until now the world has been full of violence and plunder, and Christians are the greatest warriors of all. Jewish readers also point out that Isaiah's servant is named as Israel (Isaiah 49:3), and that Rashi, the great medieval commentator, read Isaiah 53 as the suffering of the Jewish people among the nations.
sections.key: Maimonides: the Messiah will rebuild the Temple, gather the exiles and bring peace; Nachmanides (1263): the world since Jesus has not been at peace.

paras: Christians have answered in two main ways. The first is that the Messiah comes twice. Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho (about AD 155–160), a long and courteous argument with a Jewish teacher, already argued that the prophets speak of two comings: one in humility and suffering, one in glory. Jesus's pause in Nazareth, at 'the year of the Lord's favour', fits this: the kingdom has begun, but is not yet complete.

The second reply is that the kingdom has come in a way no one expected: not by the conquest of Rome, but by the gathering of people from every nation to worship Israel's God. Within three centuries the God of Abraham was worshipped across the Roman world, which the prophets had promised of the messianic age (Isaiah 2:2–3). Jewish readers answer that this is to change the meaning of the promises; Christians answer that Jesus himself changed it, at Caesarea Philippi and in Nazareth. The two readings do not meet on neutral ground. Each reads the same pages with a different key.
sections.key: Christians answer with two comings (Justin Martyr) and a kingdom begun among the nations; Jews answer that the promises were changed. Each reads with a different key.

paras: The Dead Sea Scrolls, found from 1947 in caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea, transformed this debate. They are the library of a Jewish group, probably Essenes, from about 250 BC to AD 68. They show that Jews before Jesus were already reading the prophets as being fulfilled in their own time. Their commentaries, called pesharim, read Habakkuk line by line as about their own community and its 'Teacher of Righteousness'.

Two scrolls bear on Luke 4. One, called 11QMelchizedek, reads Isaiah 61 and the Jubilee of Leviticus 25 together, as Jesus did, and pictures a heavenly figure proclaiming release at the end of days. Another, 4Q521, links Isaiah 61 to healing and raising the dead. So Jesus's way of reading Isaiah was not a Christian invention: it was a Jewish way of reading in his day. What was new was the claim 'Today… in your hearing', and the person making it.
sections.key: The Dead Sea Scrolls show Jews before Jesus reading Isaiah 61 and the Jubilee as fulfilled in the last days; the new thing was 'Today', and who said it.

paras: Luke's scene does not end in triumph. The congregation first 'wondered at the gracious words', then asked, 'Isn't this Joseph's son?' (Luke 4:22). Jesus answered with a proverb, 'no prophet is acceptable in his hometown', and two examples from the books of Kings: Elijah was sent in a famine to a widow of Sidon, and Elisha healed Naaman the Syrian, while many in Israel went without (Luke 4:25–27). Both were foreigners. The town was so angry that it tried to throw him off the hill.

Mark tells the same rejection more briefly (Mark 6:1–6), and admits that 'he could do no mighty work there'. Historians notice this: a story in which Jesus's own town rejects him, and his power seems limited, is not one the early church would have invented. And the reason Luke gives is the point of the whole session. Fulfilment, as Jesus told it, was not a reward for Israel against the nations, as the Psalms of Solomon hoped. It was good news that reached beyond Israel, to the widow of Sidon and the Syrian general. That is the reading many of his hearers found hardest to accept, and the one that carried his message across the Roman world.
sections.key: Nazareth rejected him when he said God's favour reached foreigners like the widow of Sidon and Naaman; fulfilment, for him, went beyond Israel.

refs: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11–12; Nachmanides, Vikuach (the Barcelona Disputation, 1263); Rashi on Isaiah 52:13–53:12; Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 14, 49; Augustine, Questions on the Heptateuch II.73.
Dead Sea Scrolls: 1QIsa(a) (the Great Isaiah Scroll); 11Q13 (11QMelchizedek); 4Q521 (the 'Messianic Apocalypse'); 1QpHab (the Habakkuk commentary).

Richard B. Hays, Echoes of Scripture in the Gospels (2016); Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Zvi Brettler, The Bible With and Without Jesus (2020); John J. Collins, The Scepter and the Star (1995; 2nd ed. 2010).

debate.question: Did Jesus fulfil the prophecies? Christian and Jewish readings side by side

positions.name: Fulfilled: prediction and proof
positions.who: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho (c. 155–160); Blaise Pascal, Pensées (1670); many evangelical writers
positions.view: The prophets foretold the Messiah's birthplace, his line, his suffering and his rejection, and Jesus fitted them as no one else has. The sheer number of fulfilled prophecies is evidence that God was behind both.
positions.evidence: Micah 5:2; Isaiah 53; Psalm 22; Jesus's own reading of Isaiah 61; the spread of Israel's God to the nations.

positions.name: Fulfilled: pattern and echo
positions.who: Richard Hays, Echoes of Scripture in the Gospels (2016); most Catholic, Orthodox and mainstream Protestant scholars
positions.view: The Gospels read the Old Testament backwards, in the light of Jesus, and found in it the shape of his life: the Exodus, the shepherd-king, the servant. This is not proof for outsiders, but it is not arbitrary either: Jesus himself read Israel's story as reaching its climax in him.
positions.evidence: Hosea 11:1 and other non-predictive texts; Luke 24:27; the Jewish reading practices shown in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

positions.name: Not fulfilled
positions.who: Maimonides; Nachmanides at Barcelona (1263); Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Brettler, The Bible With and Without Jesus (2020)
positions.view: The prophecies, read in their own setting, speak of Israel and of a future age of peace, a rebuilt Temple and the gathering of the exiles. These have not happened. Christians changed the meaning of 'Messiah' to fit a man who was crucified. Levine and Brettler argue that both readings are legitimate within their communities, but only one is the passages' first sense.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 2:4; the servant named as Israel (Isaiah 49:3); almah in Isaiah 7:14; history since Jesus.

debate.agree: Both sides agree that the Gospels read the Old Testament through Jesus, that Jesus himself claimed Isaiah 61, and that the world has not yet seen Isaiah's peace.

look.why: No painting for this session: the gallery's open collection has no free painting of Christ in the synagogue at Nazareth or of the prophet Isaiah.

music.why: Handel's Messiah (1741) tells the life of Christ almost entirely in the words of the Old Testament prophets, Isaiah above all, chosen by Charles Jennens. It is the Christian reading of prophecy set to music: listen for 'Comfort ye' and 'He was despised'.

think.why: Justin Martyr, who argued with Trypho that the prophets pointed to Jesus, also taught that 'seeds of the Logos' were scattered in all human wisdom. See how the early church read both Scripture and philosophy as pointing to Christ.

learn.why: Isaiah's promise that 'the word of our God stands forever': the conviction, shared by Jews and Christians, behind every claim that a prophecy is fulfilled.

check.q: Matthew quotes Hosea 11:1, 'I called my son out of Egypt', of the child Jesus. In Hosea the line is about Israel at the Exodus. What kind of fulfilment is this?
options: A prophecy about Moses
A mistake by a copyist
A prediction that came true
A pattern: Israel's story repeated in one person (typology)
check.why: Hosea looks back, not forward; Matthew sees the Exodus pattern come round again in Jesus.

check.q: Jesus stops reading Isaiah 61 before 'the day of vengeance of our God'. How have Christians usually interpreted this?
options: He brought God's favour now and left judgement for later
He lost his place in the scroll
He was afraid of the congregation
He rejected Isaiah's book
check.why: The pause is read as 'now and not yet': the favour begins, judgement waits.

check.q: Why does Jesus's choice of Isaiah 61 matter, compared with the Psalms of Solomon?
options: Because he chooses an anointed one whose task is good news to the poor and release, not conquest of the nations
Because Isaiah 61 is about a warrior king
Because the Psalms of Solomon were not yet written
Because Isaiah 61 mentions Nazareth
check.why: He reads his mission as the Spirit-anointed messenger of release, not the son of David who purges Jerusalem of the Romans.

check.q: What was Nachmanides's main argument at Barcelona in 1263?
options: That Jesus never existed
That the Messiah would be a Greek
That Isaiah was written after Jesus
That the prophets promised universal peace, and the world since Jesus has been full of war
check.why: The test of a Messiah is the messianic age, and it has not come.

check.q: What do the Dead Sea Scrolls 11QMelchizedek and 4Q521 show about Luke 4?
options: That Luke copied the scrolls
That Isaiah 61 was unknown before Jesus
That Jews before Jesus already read Isaiah 61 and the Jubilee as fulfilled at the end of days, so his reading was a Jewish one
That the scrolls mention Jesus by name
check.why: The scrolls show the same way of reading; what was new was 'Today… in your hearing'.

check.q: Which statement about the fulfilment argument is fairest?
options: Only Jewish readings are legitimate
Some fulfilments are strong on any account, others persuade mainly those who already read the Old Testament through Jesus
It has no force at all
It proves Jesus was the Messiah to any open-minded reader
check.why: The son of David, Isaiah 61 and 53 are strong; Hosea 11:1 and Isaiah 7:14 rest on a Christian key.

tutorial.question: Did Jesus fulfil the Old Testament prophecies? Set the Christian and Jewish readings side by side.
tutorial.approach: Begin with Luke 4 and Isaiah 61: what Jesus read, and where he stopped. Explain the three kinds of fulfilment, with an example of each. Then give the Jewish answer at full strength (Maimonides, Nachmanides), and the Christian replies (two comings, the nations). End by saying what the argument can and cannot show.
strong: Reads Luke 4:16–21 closely, including the omitted 'day of vengeance'.
Distinguishes prediction, pattern and echo, with examples.
Judges which fulfilment claims are strong and which weak.
States the Jewish objection in its own terms, citing Maimonides or Nachmanides.
Explains the Christian reply of two comings.
Uses the Dead Sea Scrolls to show how Jews of the time read Isaiah.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Jesus said his good news was for the poor, the captive and the crushed. Find one way this week to bring a piece of good news to someone who is having a hard time: pay off a small debt for them, visit someone housebound, or write to someone in prison through a charity that arranges it.
sessions.reflect: Can you see how someone could read the same pages of Isaiah and come to the opposite conclusion from you? What would it take to move you?
takeaways: In Nazareth Jesus read Isaiah 61, a prophecy of an anointed messenger of good news and release, and said it was fulfilled 'today', stopping before 'the day of vengeance'.
'Fulfilled' can mean prediction, pattern or echo; some Christian readings are strong on any account, others persuade only those who already read the Old Testament through Jesus.
Jews answer that the Messiah was to bring peace, rebuild the Temple and gather the exiles; Christians reply that he comes twice. Each reads the same pages with a different key.

sessions.title: The case against: just a good teacher?
sessions.line: Paine praised a virtuous man and called the rest fable; Strauss explained the Gospels as myth. Is Jesus best seen as a great teacher whose followers turned him into God?
sessions.plain: Many people today admire Jesus as a great moral teacher, like Socrates or the Buddha, and doubt the rest. That view has a long and serious history. Thomas Jefferson cut the miracles out of his Bible with a razor; Thomas Paine called Jesus 'a virtuous and an amiable man' and the story around him 'fable'; the German scholar D. F. Strauss argued that the Gospels' picture of Jesus was largely myth, made from Jewish hopes about the Messiah. C. S. Lewis famously replied that 'just a good teacher' is the one thing Jesus cannot be. This session puts the case against at full strength, and then weighs the reply.
sessions.why: Four witnesses have spoken. Jesus's world was full of hopes for a Messiah; his words claimed an authority that belonged to God; his deeds were called signs of the kingdom; and he read his mission from Isaiah. Taken together, the Gospels present a man who claimed to be far more than a prophet. But what if the Gospels themselves are the problem? Before any verdict, the case against must be heard, in its best advocates' own words.
answers: Was Jesus just a good moral teacher?
Could the Gospels be legend?
What is 'liar, lunatic or Lord', and does it work?
What did Jefferson, Paine and Strauss believe about Jesus?
sessions.finding: 'Just a good teacher' is the hardest view to hold once his claims are heard; but Lewis's trilemma has a fourth option, legend, which has to be answered on the evidence.

paras: We have built a case. Jesus, a Galilean Jew born under Herod, forgave sins and claimed Daniel's title Son of Man, accepted the title Messiah while redefining it as suffering, did deeds that his enemies called sorcery, and read his mission from Isaiah. The Gospels present a man who claimed an authority belonging to God.

But a careful reader will have noticed that almost all of this evidence comes from the Gospels, written by his followers some forty to seventy years after his death. What if they made him into more than he was?
background.key: The case so far rests on the Gospels, written by believers decades later. The objection asks whether they made him more than he was.

background.h: The good teacher in the age of reason
paras: In the 1700s, the Enlightenment, many educated people in Europe and America came to believe in God but not in miracles or revelation. They were called deists. They admired Jesus as a teacher of reason and love, and rejected the church's claims that he was God.

Thomas Jefferson, the author of the American Declaration of Independence, took this to its logical end. Around 1820, in retirement at Monticello, he took two copies each of the New Testament in Greek, Latin, French and English and cut out with a razor the passages he believed were the real words and acts of Jesus, pasting them in columns. He left out the virgin birth, the miracles and the resurrection. His book, The Life and Morals of Jesus of Nazareth, ends with the body laid in the tomb and the stone rolled to the door. Jefferson wrote to John Adams that separating Jesus's genuine teaching from what had been added was like picking diamonds out of a dunghill. The book was printed by order of Congress in 1904.

paras: The reading has two voices. Thomas Paine, in The Age of Reason (1794), gives the 'good teacher' view in its plainest form: a virtuous man, whose followers built a fable around him. D. F. Strauss, in The Life of Jesus Critically Examined (1835), gives the scholarly form: the Gospels are largely 'mythus', stories made from Jewish ideas about the Messiah, wrapped round a historical core. Jefferson's own book could not be used here; we tell its story in our own words.
The comparison is from John's Gospel, the one in which Jesus's claims are plainest: 'I and the Father are one'. The crowd's reaction is the trilemma in a sentence.
background.key: Paine (the good man, the fable) and Strauss (the Gospels as myth) make the case; John 10 shows the claims they have to explain.

before: What does Paine accept about Jesus, and what does he reject?

sessions.readWhy: Paine on the virtuous man and the fable around him; Strauss on how the Gospel stories came to be.

paras: Nothing that is here said can apply, even with the most distant disrespect, to the real character of Jesus Christ. He was a virtuous and an amiable man. The morality that he preached and practiced was of the most benevolent kind; and though similar systems of morality had been preached by Confucius, and by some of the Greek philosophers, many years before, by the Quakers since, and by many good men in all ages, it has not been exceeded by any.

Jesus Christ wrote no account of himself, of his birth, parentage, or anything else. Not a line of what is called the New Testament is of his writing. The history of him is altogether the work of other people; and as to the account given of his resurrection and ascension, it was the necessary counterpart to the story of his birth. His historians, having brought him into the world in a supernatural manner, were obliged to take him out again in the same manner, or the first part of the story must have fallen to the ground.

That such a person as Jesus Christ existed, and that he was crucified, which was the mode of execution at that day, are historical relations strictly within the limits of probability. He preached most excellent morality, and the equality of man; but he preached also against the corruptions and avarice of the Jewish priests, and this brought upon him the hatred and vengeance of the whole order of priest-hood. The accusation which those priests brought against him was that of sedition and conspiracy against the Roman government, to which the Jews were then subject and tributary; and it is not improbable that the Roman government might have some secret apprehension of the effects of his doctrine as well as the Jewish priests; neither is it improbable that Jesus Christ had in contemplation the delivery of the Jewish nation from the bondage of the Romans. Between the two, however, this virtuous reformer and revolutionist lost his life.

It is upon this plain narrative of facts, together with another case I am going to mention, that the Christian mythologists, calling themselves the Christian Church, have erected their fable, which for absurdity and extravagance is not exceeded by anything that is to be found in the mythology of the ancients.

Having thus made an insurrection and a battle in heaven, in which none of the combatants could be either killed or wounded—put Satan into the pit—let him out again—given him a triumph over the whole creation—damned all mankind by the eating of an apple, there Christian mythologists bring the two ends of their fable together. They represent this virtuous and amiable man, Jesus Christ, to be at once both God and man, and also the Son of God, celestially begotten, on purpose to be sacrificed, because they say that Eve in her longing had eaten an apple.

We distinguish by the name evangelical mythus a narrative relating directly or indirectly to Jesus, which may be considered not as the expression of a fact, but as the product of an idea of his earliest followers: such a narrative being mythical in proportion as it exhibits this character. The mythus in this sense of the term meets us, in the Gospel as elsewhere, sometimes in its pure form, constituting the substance of the narrative, and sometimes as an accidental adjunct to the actual history.

The pure mythus in the Gospel will be found to have two sources, which in most cases contributed simultaneously, though in different proportions, to form the mythus. The one source is, as already stated, the Messianic ideas and expectations existing according to their several forms in the Jewish mind before Jesus, and independently of him; the other is that particular impression which was left by the personal character, actions, and fate of Jesus, and which served to modify the Messianic idea in the minds of his people. The account of the Transfiguration, for example, is derived almost exclusively from the former source; the only amplification taken from the latter source being—that they who appeared with Jesus on the Mount spake of his decease. On the other hand, the narrative of the rending of the veil of the temple at the death of Jesus seems to have had its origin in the hostile position which Jesus, and his church after him, sustained in relation to the Jewish temple worship. Here already we have something historical, though consisting merely of certain general features of character, position, etc.; we are thus at once brought upon the ground of the historical mythus.

The historical mythus has for its groundwork a definite individual fact which has been seized upon by religious enthusiasm, and twined around with mythical conceptions culled from the idea of the Christ. This fact is perhaps a saying of Jesus such as that concerning “fishers of men” or the barren fig-tree, which now appear in the Gospels transmuted into marvellous histories: or, it is perhaps a real transaction or event taken from his life; for instance, the mythical traits in the account of the baptism were built upon such a reality. Certain of the miraculous histories may likewise have had some foundation in natural occurrences, which the narrative has either exhibited in a supernatural light, or enriched with miraculous incidents.

All the species of imagery here enumerated may justly be designated as mythi, even according to the modern and precise definition of George, inasmuch as the unhistorical which they embody—whether formed gradually by tradition, or created by an individual author—is in each case the product of an idea. But for those parts of the history which are characterized by indefiniteness and want of connexion, by misconstruction and transformation, by strange combinations and confusion,—the natural results of a long course of oral transmission; or which, on the contrary, are distinguished by highly coloured and pictorial representations, which also seem to point to a traditionary origin;—for these parts the term legendary is certainly the more appropriate.
It is to the various forms of the unhistorical in the Gospels that this enumeration exclusively refers: it does not involve the renunciation of the historical which they may likewise contain.

parts.author: Thomas Paine
parts.work: The Age of Reason, Part I
parts.translator: Original English (1794); Moncure D. Conway's edition (1896)
parts.who: Thomas Paine (1737–1809), the English-born radical whose Common Sense (1776) pushed America towards independence. A deist: he believed in one God but rejected revelation, miracles and the churches.
parts.when: Paris, 1793–94, written as the French Revolution turned to terror; Paine was imprisoned soon after finishing Part I
parts.ref: Thomas Paine, The Age of Reason, Part I, chapter III
parts.title: A virtuous and an amiable man
parts.context: Paine wrote The Age of Reason in Paris in 1793, at the height of the French Revolution, partly to rescue belief in God from the atheism he saw around him; he was arrested by the revolutionary government soon after. In chapter III he turns to Jesus. Conway's edition prints a bracketed editor's note at the end of the last paragraph, which we leave out. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Paine says: I mean no disrespect to Jesus. He was a good and kind man, and his moral teaching has never been bettered, though others taught similar things. He wrote nothing himself; everything we know was written by others. They gave him a miraculous birth, so they had to give him a miraculous departure. That he lived and was crucified is likely. He preached good morals, equality, and against the greed of the priests, who had him accused of rebellion against Rome; perhaps he did hope to free the Jews. He died a good reformer.

commentary.on: He was a virtuous and an amiable man.
commentary.text: This is the 'good teacher' view in seven words. Paine is sincere: he admires Jesus and attacks only what he thinks the church added. Many people today would say exactly this.

commentary.on: it has not been exceeded by any
commentary.text: Paine puts Jesus beside Confucius, the Greek philosophers and the Quakers. Morality, for him, is universal, known by reason; Jesus is its finest teacher, not its source.

commentary.on: Jesus Christ wrote no account of himself
commentary.text: A fair and important point. Like Socrates, Jesus wrote nothing. Everything depends on what his followers remembered and wrote, which is why the reliability of the Gospels matters so much.

commentary.on: His historians, having brought him into the world in a supernatural manner, were obliged to take him out again in the same manner
commentary.text: Here is the legend hypothesis in Paine's sharp form: one miracle needed another to complete the story. Paine thinks the supernatural parts were invented to fit each other.

commentary.on: That such a person as Jesus Christ existed, and that he was crucified, which was the mode of execution at that day, are historical relations strictly within the limits of probability.
commentary.text: Notice what Paine, the fiercest critic of the Bible in his century, does not doubt: that Jesus existed and was crucified.

commentary.on: this virtuous reformer and revolutionist lost his life
commentary.text: Paine's Jesus is a moral reformer and perhaps a would-be liberator of the Jews from Rome, killed by priests and Romans together. He does not ask why a moral reformer forgave sins or claimed God's throne. That is the question the rest of this session presses.

parts.author: Thomas Paine
parts.work: The Age of Reason, Part I
parts.translator: Original English (1794); Moncure D. Conway's edition (1896)
parts.who: Thomas Paine (1737–1809), the English-born radical whose Common Sense (1776) pushed America towards independence. A deist: he believed in one God but rejected revelation, miracles and the churches.
parts.when: Paris, 1793–94, written as the French Revolution turned to terror; Paine was imprisoned soon after finishing Part I
parts.ref: Thomas Paine, The Age of Reason, Part I, chapter IV
parts.title: Their fable
parts.context: In chapter IV Paine turns from Jesus to what he calls the 'Christian mythologists', the church. His tone becomes mocking. Conway's bracketed editor's note in the last paragraph is left out. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Paine says the church built a fable on this plain story, as absurd as any pagan myth. He sums it up with scorn: a war in heaven, Satan let loose, the whole human race damned for eating an apple, and then the good man Jesus made into God and man, born to be sacrificed.

commentary.on: the Christian mythologists, calling themselves the Christian Church, have erected their fable
commentary.text: For Paine, the church's teaching about Jesus is mythology, of the same kind as the Greek stories of Jupiter and the Giants. Strauss, in the next part, will make the same comparison with far more learning and far less scorn.

commentary.on: They represent this virtuous and amiable man, Jesus Christ, to be at once both God and man
commentary.text: Paine states the Christian claim accurately, 'at once both God and man', and rejects it as a contradiction. His argument rests on a choice: keep the good man, discard the God. This session's question is whether that choice is open.

parts.author: D. F. Strauss
parts.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined
parts.ref: D. F. Strauss, The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §15
parts.title: The evangelical mythus
parts.context: David Friedrich Strauss (1808–1874) was a young lecturer at the Protestant seminary in Tübingen when he published his Life of Jesus in 1835, at twenty-seven. It caused a scandal across Europe; he lost his post and never held a university chair. The English translation of 1846 was by Marian Evans, who later wrote novels as George Eliot. In §15 he defines what he means by 'mythus' (myth) in the Gospels. Strauss's footnote numbers are removed. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Strauss says: an 'evangelical mythus' is a story about Jesus that expresses an idea of his first followers rather than a fact. It comes from two sources: the Jewish ideas of the Messiah that existed before Jesus, and the impression Jesus himself made. Sometimes a real saying or event lies underneath, wrapped in miraculous detail; sometimes the story grew in retelling and is better called legend. But he does not deny that the Gospels contain history too.

commentary.on: which may be considered not as the expression of a fact, but as the product of an idea of his earliest followers
commentary.text: This is the heart of Strauss's case. The question is not 'did the evangelists lie?' (Paine's 'fraud'), nor 'did these miracles really have natural causes?' (the rationalists' answer). Strauss offers a third way: the stories are what faith naturally produced. The first Christians believed Jesus was the Messiah, so they told his life as the Messiah's life had to be.

commentary.on: the Messianic ideas and expectations existing according to their several forms in the Jewish mind before Jesus, and independently of him
commentary.text: Here the objection meets this journey head on. In earlier sessions we saw the Gospels echo Daniel, Moses, Elisha, Isaiah and the Psalms. Strauss reads every echo as evidence of invention: the expectations came first, and the stories were made to fit them.

commentary.on: the other is that particular impression which was left by the personal character, actions, and fate of Jesus
commentary.text: Strauss is not a mythicist: he thinks there was a real Jesus who made a powerful impression. But the impression, not the facts, shaped the stories.

commentary.on: This fact is perhaps a saying of Jesus such as that concerning "fishers of men"
commentary.text: An example from the first session: Strauss suggests the saying about 'fishers of men' grew into the miraculous catch of fish in Luke 5. The historical mythus is a real seed, grown into a marvel.

commentary.on: the natural results of a long course of oral transmission
commentary.text: This is the strongest part of the case, and the modern sceptics repeat it: stories passed by word of mouth over decades change, grow and gather detail. If the Gospels are the end of such a process, we cannot simply read off what Jesus said and did.

commentary.on: it does not involve the renunciation of the historical which they may likewise contain
commentary.text: A fair-minded qualification, often forgotten: Strauss does not say everything is myth. The question is how much, and how we can tell.

paras: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem.
It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch.
The Jews therefore came around him and said to him, “How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you don’t believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.
But you don’t believe, because you are not of my sheep, as I told you.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.
I and the Father are one.”
Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him.
Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?”
The Jews answered him, “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.”
Jesus answered them, “Isn’t it written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods?’
If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came (and the Scripture can’t be broken),
do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God?’
If I don’t do the works of my Father, don’t believe me.
But if I do them, though you don’t believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.”
They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand.

parts.title: If you are the Christ, tell us plainly
parts.context: The Feast of the Dedication, Hanukkah, in winter, remembered the rededication of the Temple in 164 BC after the Greek king Antiochus IV had defiled it: a festival of the Maccabees' victory. Jesus is walking in Solomon's porch, a colonnade on the east side of the Temple courts. 'The Jews' in John often means the leaders in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus and his disciples were all Jews.

commentary.on: How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.
commentary.text: The question is the messianic secret seen from the outside. At the feast of a great liberation, people want to know: are you the one?

commentary.on: The works that I do in my Father's name, these testify about me.
commentary.text: Jesus points to his deeds as evidence, as he did in Capernaum. Words and works together.

commentary.on: I and the Father are one.
commentary.text: In Greek, 'one' is neuter: not 'one person' but 'one thing', one in being or in action. Christians have read it as the heart of the doctrine that the Son is God with the Father; others read it as unity of will. The crowd takes it the first way.

parts.title: Because you, being a man, make yourself God
parts.context: Stoning was the punishment for blasphemy in the law of Moses (Leviticus 24:16).

commentary.on: We don't stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.
commentary.text: The crowd states the choice. They do not think he is a good teacher who has been misunderstood; they think he is a man claiming to be God, and therefore a blasphemer. This is the dilemma Lewis made famous, set out in the Gospel itself.

commentary.on: Isn't it written in your law, 'I said, you are gods?'
commentary.text: Jesus answers with Psalm 82:6, where God calls Israel's judges 'gods'. If Scripture can call men 'gods', he asks, why is it blasphemy for the one 'whom the Father sanctified' to say 'I am the Son of God'? It is a rabbi's argument from the lesser to the greater, and it does not withdraw the claim.

commentary.on: believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.
commentary.text: He offers the evidence again: the works. John is the latest Gospel and the most open about Jesus's claims, which is exactly why the sceptic says it cannot be trusted as history. That is the question the lecture now weighs.

compare.why: The 'good teacher' view has to explain what Jesus claimed. Here, in John's Gospel, the claim is open, and the crowd's reaction poses the dilemma: a good man does not say this unless it is true.
compare.title: I and the Father are one

sections.h: The case against, at full strength
paras: Put together, the objection runs like this. Jesus wrote nothing. The Gospels were written by believers, in Greek, forty to seventy years after his death, mostly far from Galilee, by authors who do not name themselves. They were written to persuade (John says so: 'these are written, that you may believe', John 20:31). Between Jesus and the Gospels lie decades of oral retelling, and stories told by word of mouth change. Studies of memory show that even honest eyewitnesses misremember, and that groups reshape shared memories to fit their beliefs.

We can see the stories growing as we read: Mark has no birth story, Matthew and Luke have two that are hard to fit together; Mark's Jesus hints at who he is, John's says it outright. And the Gospels are full of Old Testament patterns, which is exactly what we would expect if, as Strauss argued, the first Christians told his life as the Messiah's life had to be told. So, the sceptic concludes, we can know Jesus was a remarkable Jewish teacher and healer who was crucified. The claims to divinity belong to the legend. This is the view of serious scholars today, of whom Bart Ehrman is the best known.
sections.key: The Gospels are late, anonymous, written to persuade and shaped by oral retelling; the stories visibly grow. So the divine claims may be legend.

paras: The 'good teacher' view has had admirers far beyond the deists. The Russian novelist Leo Tolstoy, after a spiritual crisis in the late 1870s, wrote his own harmony of the Gospels, The Gospel in Brief (1883). Like Jefferson, he left out the miracles and the resurrection. What remained was a teacher of five commandments drawn from the Sermon on the Mount, above all: do not resist evil by force. Tolstoy's Jesus inspired Gandhi; the Russian Orthodox Church excommunicated Tolstoy in 1901. 'The Sermon on the Mount', the next journey in this hall, reads him.

The attraction is obvious. This Jesus asks for a moral life and makes no claims that offend modern reason. He can be admired by people of every faith and none, beside Socrates, the Buddha and Confucius. The question is not whether this is an attractive figure. It is whether it is the figure the sources show.
sections.key: Tolstoy's Jesus (1883), like Jefferson's, is a moral teacher without miracles; the question is whether that is the Jesus the sources show.

paras: In his wartime BBC talks, published as Mere Christianity (1952), C. S. Lewis made the best-known reply. In our own words, his argument in Book 2, chapter 3 goes like this. The one thing we must not say of Jesus is that he was a great moral teacher but not God. A man who said the things Jesus said, who forgave sins committed against other people and spoke as if he were God, would not be a great moral teacher. Either he knew his claims were false, and was a deceiver of the worst kind; or he sincerely believed them and was deluded, like a man who thinks he is a poached egg; or he was telling the truth. Lewis insists that we make the choice, and that calling him merely a great human teacher is not one of the options Jesus left open.

The argument is older than Lewis. The Scottish Hebrew scholar John Duncan put a version of it in the nineteenth century, and its roots are in John 10 itself: 'you, being a man, make yourself God'. It works best against exactly the view Paine and Jefferson held: admire the man, reject his claims. Once his claims are heard, 'just a good teacher' is hard to hold.
sections.key: Lewis (Mere Christianity, 1952): a man who claimed what Jesus claimed is either a deceiver, deluded, or Lord; 'just a good teacher' is not an option.

paras: But critics have pointed out, ever since, that the trilemma has a missing fourth. Lewis assumes we know what Jesus claimed. If the claims themselves are legend, put on his lips by later believers, then Jesus need be neither liar, lunatic nor Lord: he could be a good teacher whose followers made him more. That is exactly Strauss's and Ehrman's case. The philosopher John Hick, editor of The Myth of God Incarnate (1977), added a fifth: Jesus was not deluded but sincerely mistaken, a prophet who expected God to end the world soon, as Albert Schweitzer had argued in 1906; mistaken prophets are not madmen.
So the trilemma, by itself, does not settle the question. It moves it to the evidence. The real issue is whether the claims go back to Jesus. That is a historical question, and it can be argued.
sections.key: The trilemma assumes we know what Jesus claimed; 'legend' and 'sincerely mistaken' are further options, so the question moves to the evidence.

paras: What does the evidence say? First, the claims are not only in John. Forgiveness of sins, the Son of Man on God's throne, the authority over the Sabbath and the law, the 'Amen, I say to you': these are in Mark, the earliest Gospel, and fit the Jewish world of the time, as we saw in the second session. Second, the time is short. Paul's letters, written in the AD 50s, within about twenty-five years, already call Jesus 'Lord' and apply to him texts about God (1 Corinthians 8:6), and keep an Aramaic prayer to him, 'Marana tha', from the first Jewish believers. Larry Hurtado argued that this worship began within a few years, among Jews who would die rather than worship a man.

Third, legends usually need time and distance. The classical historian A. N. Sherwin-White argued in 1963 that even two generations were too short for legend to wipe out the historical core in the sources he knew. Richard Bauckham has argued that the Gospels rest on named eyewitnesses who were still alive. The sceptic replies that belief can grow fast in a movement, and that memory is fragile. Both sides are reasoning about real evidence. But the 'good teacher' who claimed nothing is now the hardest view to defend: he is not in Mark, not in Paul and not in John.
sections.key: The claims are in Mark and Paul as well as John, within twenty to forty years; legend is possible, but a Jesus who claimed nothing is in none of the sources.

sections.h: The face at the bottom of the well
paras: One more warning cuts both ways. In 1906 Albert Schweitzer surveyed more than a century of 'lives of Jesus', from Reimarus to Wrede, Strauss among them, and found that each author had discovered a Jesus remarkably like himself. The liberal Protestants of the 1800s found a liberal Protestant teacher of the fatherhood of God. The Irish Catholic George Tyrrell put it sharply in 1909: their Christ was only the reflection of a liberal Protestant face, seen at the bottom of a deep well.

Jefferson's Jesus is a reasonable Virginian deist; Paine's is a revolutionary; Tolstoy's a Russian pacifist. Each cut away what he could not accept, and what remained looked like him. Schweitzer's own conclusion was that the real Jesus was stranger than any of them: a Jewish prophet who expected God to end the world, and who would not fit modern ideas at all. The warning applies to believers as well, who can make Jesus a comfortable reflection of their own church or politics. The test, for anyone, is whether the picture keeps the parts of the sources that make us uncomfortable, including his claims about himself.
sections.key: Schweitzer (1906) found that each 'life of Jesus' reflected its author; the test of any picture, sceptical or believing, is whether it keeps what makes us uncomfortable.

refs: John 10:22–39; 20:31; Leviticus 24:16; Psalm 82:6; 1 Corinthians 8:6; 16:22; Luke 5:1–11.
