debate.question: Teacher, prophet or Lord?

positions.name: A great moral teacher
positions.who: Thomas Jefferson; Thomas Paine; Leo Tolstoy; many people today
positions.view: Jesus taught the purest morality the world has known: love of God and neighbour, forgiveness, care for the poor. The miracles and the claims to divinity were added by followers who wanted a god, and they obscure the teacher. Keep the teaching; drop the dogma.
positions.evidence: The moral teaching of the Sermon on the Mount, admired across religions; the growth of the stories between Mark and John; Strauss on myth.

positions.name: A prophet, not God
positions.who: Islam (the Qur'an); many Jewish scholars, such as Geza Vermes; Bart Ehrman, Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium (1999)
positions.view: Jesus was a prophet in Israel's line, a holy man who announced God's kingdom and expected God to act soon. Muslims honour him as the Messiah and a great messenger of God, born of a virgin, but not divine. Many Jewish scholars see a Galilean holy man; Ehrman, an apocalyptic prophet who was sincerely mistaken about the end.
positions.evidence: The crowd's verdict, 'one of the prophets' (Mark 8:28); the prophetic shape of his life; his sayings about the kingdom coming soon (Mark 9:1).

positions.name: Lord
positions.who: The Christian churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant; C. S. Lewis; N. T. Wright
positions.view: Jesus claimed an authority belonging to God, and his claims are in the earliest sources. A merely good teacher would not have said what he said. Either he was what he claimed, or he was not good; and the goodness of his life is the one thing everyone admits.
positions.evidence: Mark 2 and 14; John 10; the early worship of Jesus by Jewish monotheists; the trilemma, once the legend option is answered.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus was a Jewish teacher of extraordinary moral power, executed by Rome, and that the question turns on how far the Gospels' account of his claims goes back to him.

look.why: Domenico Fetti painted this Veil of Veronica in Mantua around 1618–22. It shows a legend: a woman who wiped Jesus's face on the way to the cross, and found his image on the cloth. The story is not in the Gospels. It grew up in the Middle Ages, and the name Veronica came to be linked with vera icon, 'true image'. A painting of a legend, for the session about legend: and yet the face it shows is the one every account agrees on, a man who suffered.
points: The head and pale face of a bearded man, crowned with interwoven branches of thorns, floats against a white cloth.
The cloth, hung over a wooden rod, fills the painting; it is frayed along its front edge, where it rests on a wooden surface.
The man faces us and looks down with heavy-lidded brown eyes; his lips are parted and his cheeks slightly sunken.
Blood drips down his pale forehead from the thorns, and a brown spot on one cheek might be a bruise.
A soft brown glow surrounds the head; the background behind the cloth is black.

music.why: The Passion chorale, 'O Sacred Head, Now Wounded', which Bach set five times in the St Matthew Passion. It is sung to the face on Veronica's cloth: not to a good teacher, but to one Christians believe was more.

think.why: The modern debate: what historians agree on, and how the believing N. T. Wright and the agnostic Bart Ehrman read the same evidence.

learn.why: The most famous sentence in John's Gospel, which says in one line what the 'good teacher' view denies: that in Jesus God gave his own Son. Learn it as the claim you are weighing.

check.q: What does Paine accept about Jesus, even as he attacks Christianity?
options: That Jesus was the Messiah
Nothing; he denies Jesus existed
That Jesus rose from the dead
That Jesus existed, was crucified, and was a virtuous man whose moral teaching was unsurpassed
check.why: Paine thinks existence and crucifixion are 'strictly within the limits of probability'; he rejects only the supernatural parts.

check.q: How does Strauss's 'mythus' differ from Paine's 'fraud'?
options: There is no difference
Strauss thinks every Gospel story is true
Strauss thinks the evangelists lied deliberately
Strauss thinks the stories were the natural product of believers' ideas about the Messiah, not deliberate deceit
check.why: For Strauss, myth is what faith naturally produced; for Paine, the supernatural story bore 'every mark of fraud'.

check.q: Lewis's trilemma works best against which view?
options: That Jesus was a Roman agent
That Jesus was a great moral teacher who claimed to be God but was not
That the Gospels are entirely legend
That Jesus never existed
check.why: If he made the claims, 'good teacher but not God' is unstable; the trilemma assumes we know what he claimed.

check.q: What is the strongest objection to Lewis's trilemma?
options: That it assumes Jesus really made the claims; if they are legend, he could be a good teacher after all
That John's Gospel was written first
That Lewis was not a historian
That Jesus was a poached egg
check.why: The 'fourth L', legend, moves the question to the historical evidence.

check.q: Which reply to the legend hypothesis uses the earliest evidence?
options: That Veronica's veil survives
That John's Gospel is the most detailed
That the church councils confirmed it
That Paul's letters of the AD 50s already call Jesus Lord and apply God's texts to him, and Mark shows him forgiving sins and claiming God's throne
check.why: Paul and Mark are the earliest sources, within twenty to forty years; the claims are already there.

check.q: A friend says: 'I admire Jesus as a great moral teacher, but I don't think he was God.' Which response best reflects this session?
options: Only Muslims hold that view
That view is fully proved by the evidence
That view is impossible to hold
It is a serious view with a long history, but it must explain why the earliest sources show him claiming God's authority; the honest alternatives are legend, mistake, or that the claims were true
check.why: The session puts the case against at full strength and shows where the burden then lies.

tutorial.question: Assess Lewis's trilemma: liar, lunatic or Lord?
tutorial.approach: Set out the 'good teacher' view in its strongest form, with Jefferson, Paine and Tolstoy. State the legend hypothesis as Strauss and Ehrman would, granting its real force. Then give Lewis's argument in your own words, and the fourth and fifth options. Finally weigh the evidence that the claims go back to Jesus: Mark, Paul, the time-gap, the eyewitnesses.
strong: States the good-teacher view fairly, with at least two of its advocates.
Explains Strauss's 'mythus' and the case from oral tradition at full strength.
Sets out Lewis's argument accurately, in the student's own words.
Identifies the missing options: legend, and sincere mistake.
Weighs the evidence of Mark and Paul against the legend hypothesis.
Reaches a reasoned judgement on where the burden of proof now lies.

reading.author: C. S. Lewis
reading.title: Mere Christianity
reading.why: The trilemma in Book 2, chapter 3, in Lewis's own conversational style.

reading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
reading.title: Jesus Before the Gospels
reading.why: How memory and oral tradition shaped the stories of Jesus: the case for legend from a leading sceptic.

reading.author: Richard Bauckham
reading.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses
reading.why: The case that the Gospels rest on eyewitness testimony.

reading.author: Albert Schweitzer
reading.title: The Quest of the Historical Jesus
reading.why: The classic history of the search for the 'real' Jesus, from Reimarus to Wrede, including Strauss.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: take one hard saying of Jesus that you would rather leave out of your own 'Jefferson Bible' (perhaps 'love your enemies', or 'do not worry about tomorrow'), and try to live it for one whole day, before deciding whether to cut it.
sessions.reflect: If you had a razor and a Bible, like Jefferson, what would you cut out, and why? What would that tell you about your own picture of Jesus?
takeaways: The 'good teacher' view has a serious history: Jefferson cut out the miracles, Paine praised 'a virtuous and an amiable man', Tolstoy kept only the moral commands.
Strauss argued that the Gospels are largely myth, made from Jewish messianic hopes; the modern legend hypothesis adds what we know of oral tradition and memory.
Lewis's trilemma shows that 'just a good teacher' is hard to hold if he made the claims; the fourth option, legend, must be answered from the earliest evidence, Mark and Paul.

sessions.title: The verdict
sessions.line: The four witnesses and the case against, weighed: a Jewish prophet who claimed an authority belonging to God, and died for it. Was he right?
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict, plainly. Jesus was a real Jew of Galilee, born under Herod, who claimed an authority that belonged to God: he forgave sins, called himself the Son of Man who would sit at God's right hand, accepted the title Messiah and redefined it as suffering, and did deeds even his enemies did not deny. He was executed for it. Whether he was right turns on what happened after his death, which the next journeys in this hall examine. This session reads one of the earliest Christian statements of who he was, a hymn Paul quotes, and sets beside it what the Qur'an says, so that Jewish, Muslim and Christian answers can be seen side by side.
sessions.why: We have called four witnesses (his world, his words, his deeds, the prophets) and heard the case against at full strength: that the Gospels turned a good teacher into a god. The legend option had to be answered from the earliest evidence, and the earliest evidence shows the claims were there from the start. Now we give the verdict, and see how the three faiths that honour Jesus each answer the question this journey asked.
answers: So who was Jesus?
What did the first Christians believe about him?
What do Jews and Muslims say about him?
What did the creeds later say?
What would decide whether he was right?
sessions.finding: The evidence shows a Jewish prophet who claimed an authority belonging to God and died for it; whether he was right turns on what happened next, which is the next journey.

paras: On the evidence of this journey, here is what can fairly be said. Jesus existed: almost no historian doubts it. He was a Galilean Jew, born around 6–4 BC, who lived and taught among Pharisees, priests and rebels under Rome. He claimed an authority that belonged to God: to forgive sins, to rule the Sabbath, to speak on his own word, to sit at God's right hand as Daniel's Son of Man. He accepted the title Messiah and redefined it as suffering. He was known as a healer and exorcist, even by enemies. He read his mission from Isaiah. And he was executed as 'the King of the Jews'.

Was he therefore just a good teacher? That is the one verdict the evidence makes hardest. Was he a legend? The claims are in the earliest sources, within twenty to forty years. What remains open is the question every witness has pointed to: was he right? That cannot be settled by his words alone. It turns on what happened after he died, which is what the next journeys in this hall examine.
background.key: A Galilean Jew who claimed an authority belonging to God, accepted and redefined 'Messiah', and was executed for it. Whether he was right turns on what happened next.

paras: The reading is from Paul's letter to the Philippians, written around AD 55–62. Most scholars think verses 6–11 are a hymn that Paul quotes, perhaps older than the letter itself, which would make it one of the very earliest Christian statements of who Jesus was. It answers our question as the first Christians answered it. John's prologue, 'In the beginning was the Word', is the other great early statement; you read it in 'In the beginning' and 'Psalms and wisdom'.

The comparison is the Qur'an, the holy book of Islam, which honours Jesus, Isa in Arabic, as Messiah, prophet and Word of God, and denies that he is God. Reading it beside Paul shows exactly where two great faiths agree about Jesus and where they part.
background.key: Philippians 2:5–11, an early hymn on who Jesus was; then the Qur'an on Jesus, to see where Christianity and Islam agree and part.

before: According to the hymn, what did Christ do, and what did God do in return?
Which name is given to Jesus in verse 11, and why does it matter?
What does the Qur'an affirm about Jesus, and what does it deny?
sessions.readWhy: An early Christian hymn, quoted by Paul: the way down and the way up.

paras: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

parts.title: He emptied himself
parts.context: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, in northern Greece, where Paul founded a church around AD 49–50. He writes to them from prison, either in Rome around AD 60–62 or perhaps earlier in Ephesus. The church is quarrelling, and Paul urges them to humility; to make his point, he quotes or composes a hymn about Christ.

commentary.on: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus
commentary.text: Paul's purpose is practical: think the way Christ thought. The greatest statement of who Jesus was is given as an example of how to treat each other.

commentary.on: who, existing in the form of God, didn't consider equality with God a thing to be grasped
commentary.text: 'The form of God': in Greek, morphe, the outward reality of a thing. Christ existed in God's form, with 'equality with God', before he was a man. He did not cling to it. Compare Adam, who grasped at being like God (Genesis 3:5). Within about twenty-five years of the crucifixion, this is already being sung.

commentary.on: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
commentary.text: 'Emptied himself' gives theology the word kenosis. What he gave up is debated, but not that he became fully human. 'Servant' (or slave) recalls Isaiah's suffering servant, whom we have met throughout this journey.

commentary.on: he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
commentary.text: The hymn goes down step by step: from God, to a man, to a servant, to death, to the most shameful death the Romans knew, kept for slaves and rebels. This is the Messiah who 'must suffer', the answer to Peter's rebuke.

parts.title: Every knee should bow
parts.context: The second half of the hymn turns upward: God's answer to Christ's humility.

commentary.on: Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name
commentary.text: The name above every name, in Jewish ears, was God's own name. The next verse says what it is.

commentary.on: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow
commentary.text: This is a quotation, and a startling one. In Isaiah 45:23 God says: 'to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath', in a chapter that insists there is no other God. The hymn applies God's words about himself to Jesus. Richard Bauckham calls this the clearest example of early Christians including Jesus in the identity of the one God.

commentary.on: and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
commentary.text: 'Lord' is kyrios, the word the Greek Bible used for God's name. Yet the glory goes 'to God the Father'. Jewish believers in one God are not adding a second God; they are saying that the one God is known in Jesus. Three centuries of argument, leading to the creeds, were spent trying to say this carefully.

paras: O ye people of the Book! overstep not bounds in your religion; and of God, speak only truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, is only an apostle of God, and his Word which he conveyed into Mary, and a Spirit proceeding from himself. Believe therefore in God and his apostles, and say not, "Three:" (there is a Trinity)-Forbear-it will be better for you. God is only one God! Far be it from His glory that He should have a son! His, whatever is in the Heavens, and whatever is in the Earth! And God is a sufficient Guardian.
The Messiah disdaineth not to be a servant of God, nor do the angels who are nigh unto Him.

And when God shall say-"O Jesus, Son of Mary: hast thou said unto mankind- 'Take me and my mother as two Gods, beside God?"' He shall say-"Glory be unto Thee! it is not for me to say that which I know to be not the truth; had I said that, verily thou wouldest have known it: Thou knowest what is in me, but I know not what is in Thee; for Thou well knowest things unseen!

"I spake not to them aught but that which thou didst bid me-'Worship God, my Lord and your Lord;' and I was a witness of their actions while I stayed among them; but since thou hast taken me to Thyself, Thou hast Thyself watched them, and Thou art witness of all things:
"If Thou punish them, they are Thy servants, and if Thou forgive them. . . . Thou, verily, art the Mighty, the Wise!"

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Say not, Three
parts.context: Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed by God to the Prophet Muhammad, through the angel Gabriel, between about AD 610 and 632, in Arabic. Sura 4, 'Women', comes from his years in Medina. Here it addresses 'the people of the Book', Jews and Christians. This is the translation of J. M. Rodwell, an English clergyman (1861), who arranged the suras in the order he thought they were revealed; the verse numbers are the standard ones. His footnote numbers are removed. A Muslim reader would rightly say that a translation is not the Qur'an itself, which is only the Arabic.
parts.plain: The Qur'an tells Jews and Christians not to go too far in their religion. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, is a messenger of God, God's Word given to Mary, and a spirit from God. So believe in God and his messengers, and do not say 'three': God is one, and far above having a son. The Messiah is not too proud to be God's servant.

commentary.on: The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, is only an apostle of God
commentary.text: The Qur'an gives Jesus the title Messiah (al-Masih) eleven times, and no one else. 'Son of Mary' is his usual name in the Qur'an, honouring his virgin birth, which the Qur'an affirms. 'Apostle' here means messenger: one sent by God with a revelation.

commentary.on: and his Word which he conveyed into Mary, and a Spirit proceeding from himself
commentary.text: Remarkable words, close to John's 'the Word became flesh'. In Islamic teaching, Jesus is God's Word because he was created by God's command, 'Be!', as Adam was; not because he is God. Christians and Muslims use the same words and mean different things.

commentary.on: and say not, "Three:" (there is a Trinity)-Forbear-it will be better for you. God is only one God!
commentary.text: The words in brackets are Rodwell's explanation, not the Arabic. The Qur'an rejects the Christian Trinity as a denial of God's oneness, tawhid, the heart of Islam. Christians reply that they too believe in only one God, and that the Trinity is not three gods. This is the deepest point of difference.

commentary.on: The Messiah disdaineth not to be a servant of God
commentary.text: Here the Qur'an and Paul's hymn use the same word: servant. For Paul, Christ in the form of God took the form of a servant. For the Qur'an, Jesus is God's servant and nothing more, and that is his honour.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Hast thou said unto mankind?
parts.context: Sura 5, 'The Table', is from the last years of Muhammad's life. This passage imagines the Day of Judgement, when God questions Jesus. Rodwell's footnote number and his marking of a pause ('. . . .') are as printed, without the number.
parts.plain: On the last day God will ask Jesus whether he told people to worship him and his mother as gods. Jesus will answer: Glory to you; I could never say what I had no right to say. I only told them to worship God, my Lord and theirs. If you punish them, they are your servants; if you forgive them, you are the Mighty, the Wise.

commentary.on: 'Take me and my mother as two Gods, beside God?"'
commentary.text: Christians have never worshipped Mary as God, and Muslim scholars have long discussed what this verse means: perhaps a criticism of excessive devotion to Mary in some Arabian churches. What is clear is the Qur'an's concern: no one may be worshipped beside God.

commentary.on: it is not for me to say that which I know to be not the truth
commentary.text: The Qur'an's Jesus himself denies the claim Christians make about him. For Muslims this is the true Jesus, restored; for Christians, it is a Jesus without the claims of Mark 2 and 14.

commentary.on: 'Worship God, my Lord and your Lord;'
commentary.text: Compare John 20:17, where the risen Jesus says 'my Father and your Father, my God and your God'. Both faiths remember Jesus speaking of God as his God. They read it differently.

compare.author: The Qur'an
compare.why: Islam honours Jesus more than any religion except Christianity: as Messiah, prophet, born of a virgin, the Word of God. And it denies that he is God. Read these verses beside Paul's hymn and see exactly where the two faiths agree and where they part.
compare.title: The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary

paras: Weigh the witnesses one last time. The first, his world, showed us where to stand: a Jew of Galilee in the first century, whose words must be heard as his hearers heard them. The second, his words, showed claims that go beyond any prophet's: forgiveness, the Son of Man, God's throne. The third, his deeds, showed a healer whom friends and enemies alike credited with power. The fourth, the prophets, showed that he read his own mission from Isaiah, and that his followers read the whole of Israel's Scriptures through him, some readings stronger than others.

The case against was strong: the Gospels are late, written by believers, shaped by oral tradition. But the claims are in Mark, the earliest Gospel, and the worship of Jesus is in Paul's letters, within about twenty-five years, and this hymn may be older still. A good teacher who claimed nothing is in none of the sources. The historian can say who he claimed to be, and that he was crucified for it. The historian alone cannot say whether he was right.
sections.key: The claims are early and well attested; 'just a good teacher' is the hardest verdict to hold. Whether the claims were true is not something history alone can settle.

paras: For most of history, Jewish views of Jesus were shaped by Christian persecution of Jews, and were hostile in return. Maimonides, in his code of law (about 1180), wrote that Jesus, who imagined he was the Messiah, caused Israel to be destroyed and the Torah changed; yet, he added in a passage removed by Christian censors, God used Christianity and Islam to spread knowledge of the Torah and the hope of the Messiah through the world, preparing it for the true Messiah to come.

In modern times many Jewish scholars have reclaimed Jesus as a Jew. Joseph Klausner, in Jesus of Nazareth (1922), saw a great Jewish moral teacher. The philosopher Martin Buber wrote that he had found in Jesus a great brother, while denying he was the Messiah. Geza Vermes saw a Galilean holy man; Amy-Jill Levine, an Orthodox Jew who teaches the New Testament, argues in The Misunderstood Jew (2006) that Christians can only understand Jesus by understanding his Judaism. The Jewish answer remains: a Jew, perhaps a great one; not the Messiah, because the messianic age has not come; not God, because God is one.
sections.key: Jews have seen Jesus as a false Messiah (Maimonides) and, in modern times, as a great Jewish teacher (Klausner, Buber, Vermes, Levine); not the Messiah, not God.

paras: Islam gives Jesus, Isa, a place of great honour. The Qur'an calls him the Messiah, a prophet and messenger, God's Word and a spirit from God. It affirms his virgin birth and his miracles, and says he will return before the end. It denies that he is God or the Son of God, rejects the Trinity, and says that he was not crucified but that God raised him to himself (Sura 4:157; 'The last week and the cross', later in this hall, reads that passage).

So Islam agrees with Christianity on more about Jesus than either agrees with Judaism: Messiah, virgin birth, miracles, return. It disagrees on the two things Christians think matter most: that he is God made man, and that he died and rose. For Muslims, the Christian claim about Jesus is a sincere error, an exaggeration of a great prophet; for Christians, the Muslim view keeps the honour and removes the claim.
sections.key: Islam honours Jesus as Messiah, prophet, Word of God and virgin-born, who will return; it denies he is God and that he was crucified.

paras: Christians took four centuries to find words for the faith of Philippians 2. In the early 300s a priest of Alexandria, Arius, taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, not God himself. The Council of Nicaea (325) answered that the Son is 'of one being with the Father', 'true God from true God', words in the Nicene Creed, completed at Constantinople in 381 and still said in churches today. The Council of Chalcedon (451) said that Christ is one person, 'truly God and truly man', in two natures 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'. The journey on the Creed, in the hall of The Great Questions, follows that argument in full.

Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches accept Nicaea and Chalcedon. The Oriental Orthodox churches (the Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian and Syriac) did not accept Chalcedon's wording, preferring to speak of 'one nature of the Word made flesh'; many of them now agree that the difference was mostly one of words.

rows: No: the messianic age has not come

table.note: The Catholic doctrine of the Immaculate Conception (1854) is not held by the Orthodox or by most Protestants; the title Theotokos was agreed at Ephesus in 431.

sections.key: Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451): the Son is 'true God from true God', one person, 'truly God and truly man'. Judaism and Islam deny he is God.

paras: Every witness in this journey has pointed beyond itself. The Son of Man must suffer and 'rise again'. The high priest was told he would 'see the Son of Man… coming with the clouds'. The hymn goes down to the cross and up to the name above every name. Paine saw it too: the story of Jesus's death and what followed is the hinge on which the whole claim turns.

This is the honest place to stop. A man who claimed what Jesus claimed and then died on a Roman cross was, by every standard of his time, a failed Messiah, like Theudas and Bar Kokhba. Yet his movement did not end. His followers, Jews who believed in one God, began within weeks to say that God had raised him from the dead, and to worship him. Whether that claim is true is the question that decides all the others. 'The Sermon on the Mount' comes next, to hear what he taught; then 'The last week and the cross' examines what happened in Jerusalem, and whether he rose.
sections.key: Every witness points to what happened after his death: a crucified Messiah was a failed one, unless God raised him. That question comes next in this hall.

paras: Any verdict about Jesus has to reckon with what was done in his name. For many centuries Christians blamed the Jewish people as a whole for his death, called them 'Christ-killers', and expelled, forcibly converted or killed Jewish communities across Europe: in the Rhineland massacres of 1096, the expulsion from England in 1290 and from Spain in 1492. That history is part of why Maimonides and Nachmanides wrote as they did, and part of why Jesus's own people found it so hard to hear his followers' claims.

In 1965 the Second Vatican Council, in the declaration Nostra Aetate, taught that his death cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against the Jews of today; many Protestant and Orthodox churches have said the same. The Gospels themselves show that Jesus, his mother, his disciples and his first followers were all Jews, and that his trial was led by a few Temple authorities and carried out by Rome. Whatever you conclude about who he was, the evidence of this journey rules out one thing: using him against his own people.
sections.key: Christians long blamed the Jews for his death and persecuted them; in 1965 Nostra Aetate rejected that charge, and the evidence shows Jesus and his first followers were Jews.

refs: Philippians 2:5–11; Isaiah 45:21–23; Genesis 3:5; John 1:1–14; 20:17; Mark 8:31; 14:62.

debate.question: The verdict: where does the case now stand?

positions.name: He was who he claimed to be
positions.who: The Christian churches; N. T. Wright; Richard Bauckham
positions.view: The claims go back to Jesus; a good man does not make them falsely; and his followers' worship of him within a few years, as Jews, is best explained if God vindicated him by raising him from the dead.
positions.evidence: Mark 2 and 14; Philippians 2; the early worship of Jesus; the next journey's evidence about the resurrection.

positions.name: A great prophet, not God
positions.who: Islam; many Jews; Bart Ehrman, as historian
positions.view: Jesus was a Jewish prophet of God's kingdom, honoured rightly; Christians later made him God. Muslims believe God honoured him and raised him to himself; Ehrman thinks he was sincerely mistaken about the end and that the belief in his divinity grew after his death.
positions.evidence: The Qur'an's account; the development from Mark to John; Jesus praying to God as 'my God'.

positions.name: The verdict is still open
positions.who: Many honest enquirers, believing and not
positions.view: History can show what he claimed and that he died for it. Whether he was right cannot be settled by his claims alone. It turns on what happened afterwards, and on whether one thinks God acts in the world.
positions.evidence: The limits of history seen in the session on miracles; the claim of resurrection, which the next journeys weigh.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus was a Jew of Galilee who spoke with extraordinary authority and was crucified, and that his followers believed something had happened after his death that changed everything.

look.why: Grifo di Tancredi painted this Christ Blessing in Florence around 1310. In his book are John's words, 'I am the light of the world' (John 8:12), one of the 'I am' sayings you met in the second session: the claim, held out to the viewer.
points: Shown from the waist up, a man with long, honey-blond hair and beard faces us in front of a gold background.
His right hand is raised, with the index and middle fingers extended up: the gesture of blessing.
His other hand holds an open book with the pages towards us, inscribed in gold letters 'ECO SUM LUX MUNDI', 'I am the light of the world'.
He wears a rose-pink robe under a spruce-blue mantle, both trimmed with gold.
A halo is incised into the gold behind his head, with clusters of five dots in dark red, blue and black.

music.why: Reginald Heber's hymn of 1826, drawn from the worship of heaven in Revelation 4, praises the one God in three persons. It is what Christians sing if the verdict of Philippians 2 is true: every knee bowing, every tongue confessing.

think.why: The great teachers: Athanasius on why God became man, and the Council of Chalcedon's formula, 'truly God and truly human', that the hymn in Philippians set in motion.

learn.why: The hymn you have just read, one of the earliest Christian statements of who Jesus was. Learn it as Paul meant it: as a description of Christ and a pattern for your own humility.

check.q: Why is Philippians 2:10, 'at the name of Jesus every knee should bow', so significant?

Because it is the first mention of Jesus's name
Because it applies to Jesus words that God in Isaiah 45:23 says of himself, in a chapter insisting there is no other God
Because it describes a Roman ceremony
check.why: The hymn takes God's own words about himself and applies them to Jesus, within about twenty-five years of the cross.

That he was crucified and rose
That he is the Messiah, born of a virgin, a worker of miracles, who will return
That he is the Son of God

That he was not born in Galilee
That he did not speak Hebrew
That he never claimed any authority
check.why: Maimonides' tests: a Messiah who did not bring the messianic age was not the Messiah.

options: That he is one person, truly God and truly man, in two natures
That he was God only appearing to be a man
That he was a man adopted by God at his baptism
That he was the first of God's creatures
check.why: Chalcedon: 'truly God and truly man', 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'.

check.q: Why does the verdict of this journey stop short of saying he was right?
options: Because his claims, however early and clear, are vindicated or refuted by what happened after his death, which is a further question
Because the evidence shows he never claimed anything
Because the Qur'an settles it
Because historians have disproved him
check.why: A crucified Messiah was a failed Messiah unless God raised him; that is the question the next journeys weigh.

check.q: The Qur'an calls Jesus God's 'Word', as John's Gospel does. What is the best account of the difference?
options: Only Christians use the term
In Islam the Word means a book; in Christianity a prophet
In Islam he is God's Word because created by God's command, as Adam was; in Christianity the Word 'was God' and became flesh
There is no difference
check.why: The same words carry different meanings: created messenger, or the eternal Word made flesh.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the hymn in Philippians was given as a pattern: 'he humbled himself'. In one disagreement this week, at home or at work, give up your right to win: let the other person have the last word, or take the blame you could have avoided, and notice what happens.
sessions.reflect: Jesus asked, 'But who do you say that I am?' After this journey, what is your answer, and what would you need to know to be sure?
takeaways: On the evidence, Jesus was a Galilean Jew who claimed an authority belonging to God, redefined 'Messiah' as suffering, and was crucified for it; 'just a good teacher' is the hardest view to hold.

Jews see a Jew, perhaps a great teacher, but not the Messiah or God; Muslims honour him as Messiah and prophet but not God; Christians confess him 'truly God and truly man', as the early hymn in Philippians already does.
Whether he was right turns on what happened after his death: the question the next journeys in this hall examine.

closing.title: Who do you say I am?
closing.prompt: Jesus asked his friends, 'But who do you say that I am?' (Mark 8:29). In about 300 words, give your own answer: who was Jesus, on the evidence you have weighed? Use at least two of the four witnesses, and answer the strongest objection to your view, whether it is the legend hypothesis, the Jewish or Muslim answer, or the Christian claim.
closing.practice: Read one Gospel from beginning to end, a chapter a day. Mark takes sixteen days. After each chapter write one line: what did he say or do, and what does it suggest about who he thought he was?
synthesis: This course asked who Jesus claimed to be, and whether he was right. It treated the question like a trial and called four witnesses: the world he was born into, his words, his deeds and the prophets. Then it heard the case against at full strength, and gave a verdict. Here are the short answers to the questions people ask, in order.

Did Jesus exist? Yes. Almost every historian, Christian, Jewish or secular, agrees. Paul met his brother James and his friend Peter; Josephus and Tacitus mention him; the four Gospels were written within about forty to seventy years. The few writers who say he never lived are answered even by agnostic scholars such as Bart Ehrman.

When and where was he born? Before Herod the Great died, in 4 BC, so probably around 6–4 BC: our calendar is a few years out. Matthew and Luke place his birth in Bethlehem, David's town, and agree that he grew up in Nazareth in Galilee. Luke's census under Quirinius, which Josephus dates to AD 6, is a real difficulty that scholars still debate. Both Gospels say Mary conceived him without a human father, which Christians and Muslims believe.

What was his world like? A small land ruled by Rome through Herod's family and then a Roman governor; a people divided into Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and rebels; Aramaic spoken, Hebrew read, Greek written. Many were waiting for a Messiah, an anointed king from David's line, though the hope took many forms. Everything he said must be heard there.

Did he say he was God? Not in those words in the first three Gospels. But in the earliest, Mark, he forgives sins on his own authority, which his critics rightly saw as acting as God; he calls himself Lord of the Sabbath; he speaks on his own word, 'Amen, I say to you'; and before the high priest he claims to sit at God's right hand. He was condemned for blasphemy. In John's Gospel the claims are open: 'I and the Father are one.'

What does 'Son of Man' mean? In Aramaic, simply 'a human being'. But Daniel 7 had seen 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to God's throne to receive an everlasting kingdom, and some Jews of Jesus's day, as 1 Enoch shows, already spoke of a heavenly Son of Man. Jesus used the ordinary phrase and filled it with Daniel's meaning, and with suffering.

What does 'Christ' mean? 'Anointed', the Greek for Messiah. The Psalms of Solomon show what many hoped for: a son of David who would drive the Romans from Jerusalem and rule the nations. At Caesarea Philippi Peter called Jesus the Messiah. Jesus accepted it, told his friends to keep it quiet, because in public the word meant revolt, and taught at once that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed. No one expected that, which is one reason historians think it goes back to him. Pilate crucified him as 'the King of the Jews'.

Did he do miracles? His friends and his enemies agreed that he did astonishing deeds; his enemies said it was sorcery, as Mark, the Talmud and Celsus show. Historians widely accept that he was known as a healer and exorcist. The Gospels present the deeds as signs that God's kingdom was arriving, never as proofs on demand. Whether God acted in them is a question history alone cannot settle, because it depends on whether there is a God who acts.

Did he fulfil prophecy? He read his mission from Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth and said, 'Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled', stopping before 'the day of vengeance'. His followers read the whole Old Testament through him: some readings, the son of David and the suffering servant, are strong on any account; others, such as Hosea's 'out of Egypt', are patterns that persuade only those who already believe. Jews answer, with Maimonides and Nachmanides, that the Messiah was to bring peace, and peace has not come; Christians answer that he comes twice.

Was he just a good teacher? That is the view of Jefferson, Paine and Tolstoy, and of many people today. C. S. Lewis argued that it is the one view that does not work: a man who claimed what Jesus claimed was either a deceiver, deluded, or Lord. Critics rightly add a fourth option, legend: perhaps the claims were put on his lips later, as Strauss argued. But the claims are in Mark, and the worship of Jesus is in Paul's letters within about twenty-five years, among Jews who believed in one God. A good teacher who claimed nothing is in none of the sources.

What do Jews and Muslims think of him? Most Jews see a Jew, perhaps a great teacher, but not the Messiah, because the messianic age has not come, and not God, because God is one. Muslims honour him as the Messiah, a prophet, the Word of God, born of a virgin, who will return; but not God, and not crucified. Christians confess what the early hymn in Philippians already sings: that he was 'in the form of God', emptied himself to the death of the cross, and that every tongue should confess 'Jesus Christ is Lord'. The councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon later said it as 'truly God and truly man'.

So who was he? On the evidence, a Jewish prophet from Galilee who claimed an authority that belonged to God, accepted and remade the title Messiah, and died for it. Whether he was right is the one question his own words cannot settle. A crucified Messiah was, by every standard of his time, a failed Messiah, unless God vindicated him. His followers said within weeks that God had raised him from the dead. That claim decides everything else, and it is where the journeys that follow in this hall go next. Wherever you stand, you have now heard the witnesses for yourself, and the question is yours, as it was Peter's: 'But who do you say that I am?'

next.place: If you can, go to Galilee: Nazareth, Capernaum and the shore of the lake, and Banias at the foot of Mount Hermon, where Peter answered the question. Nearer home, see the Christian and Jewish galleries of a great museum, or simply sit through a sung Creed at a cathedral service and listen to the words 'true God from true God'.

title: Dust that wonders
question: What is a human being?
line: Dust that breathes, a mind that remembers, a creature that wonders what it is: six sessions on the oldest question about ourselves.
why: Machines now talk like us, and neuroscience can describe the brain in astonishing detail, so the old question has come back with force. Over six sessions you will hear the Bible's answer, Plato's, Augustine's and the strongest materialist case, and weigh the science of consciousness honestly. You will come away with a clearer sense of what you are, and why it matters for how you treat the person in front of you.
outcomes: By the end you'll be able to say what Genesis, Plato and Augustine each mean by a human being, and where they agree and differ.
You'll be able to state the strongest materialist view of the mind fairly, and explain what the Libet experiments and the 'hard problem' of consciousness do and do not show.
You'll have practised seeing the people around you, especially the overlooked ones, as more than their usefulness.

sessions.title: Dust and breath
sessions.line: The Bible's first answer: made from the ground, given breath by God, and not meant to be alone.
sessions.why: We start at the beginning, with the two creation stories, because almost every later answer in the West either builds on them or argues against them.

paras: God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
To every animal of the earth, and to every bird of the sky, and to everything that creeps on the earth, in which there is life, I have given every green herb for food;” and it was so.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished.
On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
This is the history of the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that Yahweh God made the earth and the heavens.
No plant of the field was yet in the earth, and no herb of the field had yet sprung up; for Yahweh God had not caused it to rain on the earth. There was not a man to till the ground,
but a mist went up from the earth, and watered the whole surface of the ground.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.

Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
A river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from there it was parted, and became the source of four rivers.
The name of the first is Pishon: it flows through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold;
and the gold of that land is good. Bdellium and onyx stone are also there.
The name of the second river is Gihon. It is the same river that flows through the whole land of Cush.
The name of the third river is Hiddekel. This is the one which flows in front of Assyria. The fourth river is the Euphrates.
Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
Yahweh God commanded the man, saying, “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden;
but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

Out of the ground Yahweh God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name.
The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him.
Yahweh God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep. As the man slept, he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place.
Yahweh God made a woman from the rib which he had taken from the man, and brought her to the man.
The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.”
Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

sessions.readWhy: In a few pages we meet the two great claims: a human being bears God's image, and is shaped from dust with God's own breath. Notice that the first thing called 'not good' is a human being alone.

think.why: The story told plainly, so you can see where these chapters lead next.

listen.why: Peterson and Lennox ask what happens when we try to engineer a 'better' human and forget what a human being is for.

learn.why: Donne's lines carry Genesis 2 into everyday life: we are made for each other.

music.why: Haydn set the whole of Genesis 1 to music, and Part Two of the oratorio reaches the making of man and woman; this chorus is creation praising its maker.

look.why: Thomas Cole paints a baby in a golden boat on a bed of flowers, with a winged angel behind, one hand on the tiller. A life given, not made by itself, and guarded from its first moment.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each day, ask one person a real question about their life and listen to the whole answer without turning the talk back to yourself.
sessions.reflect: Do you think of yourself more as something made, or something you are making? What difference would the other answer make?

sessions.title: The charioteer
sessions.line: Plato's answer: a soul pulled two ways, with reason trying to hold the reins.
sessions.why: Jerusalem gave us dust and breath; Athens gave a different picture. Plato's image of the soul as a driver and two horses shaped how Christians later described the inner life, so we need to know it.

read.author: Plato
read.ref: Socrates' second speech, the soul as a charioteer (246a–248b, 253c–e, shortened)
read.who: Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle (about 428–348 BC).
paras: Of the nature of the soul, though her true form be ever a theme of large and more than mortal discourse, let me speak briefly, and in a figure. And let the figure be composite—a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now the winged horses and the charioteers of the gods are all of them noble and of noble descent, but those of other races are mixed; the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him. I will endeavour to explain to you in what way the mortal differs from the immortal creature. The soul in her totality has the care of inanimate being everywhere, and traverses the whole heaven in divers forms appearing—when perfect and fully winged she soars upward, and orders the whole world; whereas the imperfect soul, losing her wings and drooping in her flight at last settles on the solid ground—there, finding a home, she receives an earthly frame which appears to be self-moved, but is really moved by her power; and this composition of soul and body is called a living and mortal creature. For immortal no such union can be reasonably believed to be; although fancy, not having seen nor surely known the nature of God, may imagine an immortal creature having both a body and also a soul which are united throughout all time. Let that, however, be as God wills, and be spoken of acceptably to him. And now let us ask the reason why the soul loses her wings!

The wing is the corporeal element which is most akin to the divine, and which by nature tends to soar aloft and carry that which gravitates downwards into the upper region, which is the habitation of the gods. The divine is beauty, wisdom, goodness, and the like; and by these the wing of the soul is nourished, and grows apace; but when fed upon evil and foulness and the opposite of good, wastes and falls away. Zeus, the mighty lord, holding the reins of a winged chariot, leads the way in heaven, ordering all and taking care of all; and there follows him the array of gods and demi-gods, marshalled in eleven bands; Hestia alone abides at home in the house of heaven; of the rest they who are reckoned among the princely twelve march in their appointed order. They see many blessed sights in the inner heaven, and there are many ways to and fro, along which the blessed gods are passing, every one doing his own work; he may follow who will and can, for jealousy has no place in the celestial choir. But when they go to banquet and festival, then they move up the steep to the top of the vault of heaven. The chariots of the gods in even poise, obeying the rein, glide rapidly; but the others labour, for the vicious steed goes heavily, weighing down the charioteer to the earth when his steed has not been thoroughly trained:—and this is the hour of agony and extremest conflict for the soul. For the immortals, when they are at the end of their course, go forth and stand upon the outside of heaven, and the revolution of the spheres carries them round, and they behold the things beyond. But of the heaven which is above the heavens, what earthly poet ever did or ever will sing worthily? It is such as I will describe; for I must dare to speak the truth, when truth is my theme. There abides the very being with which true knowledge is concerned; the colourless, formless, intangible essence, visible only to mind, the pilot of the soul. The divine intelligence, being nurtured upon mind and pure knowledge, and the intelligence of every soul which is capable of receiving the food proper to it, rejoices at beholding reality, and once more gazing upon truth, is replenished and made glad, until the revolution of the worlds brings her round again to the same place. In the revolution she beholds justice, and temperance, and knowledge absolute, not in the form of generation or of relation, which men call existence, but knowledge absolute in existence absolute; and beholding the other true existences in like manner, and feasting upon them, she passes down into the interior of the heavens and returns home; and there the charioteer putting up his horses at the stall, gives them ambrosia to eat and nectar to drink.

Such is the life of the gods; but of other souls, that which follows God best and is likest to him lifts the head of the charioteer into the outer world, and is carried round in the revolution, troubled indeed by the steeds, and with difficulty beholding true being; while another only rises and falls, and sees, and again fails to see by reason of the unruliness of the steeds. The rest of the souls are also longing after the upper world and they all follow, but not being strong enough they are carried round below the surface, plunging, treading on one another, each striving to be first; and there is confusion and perspiration and the extremity of effort; and many of them are lamed or have their wings broken through the ill-driving of the charioteers; and all of them after a fruitless toil, not having attained to the mysteries of true being, go away, and feed upon opinion.

As I said at the beginning of this tale, I divided each soul into three—two horses and a charioteer; and one of the horses was good and the other bad: the division may remain, but I have not yet explained in what the goodness or badness of either consists, and to that I will now proceed. The right-hand horse is upright and cleanly made; he has a lofty neck and an aquiline nose; his colour is white, and his eyes dark; he is a lover of honour and modesty and temperance, and the follower of true glory; he needs no touch of the whip, but is guided by word and admonition only. The other is a crooked lumbering animal, put together anyhow; he has a short thick neck; he is flat-faced and of a dark colour, with grey eyes and blood-red complexion; the mate of insolence and pride, shag-eared and deaf, hardly yielding to whip and spur.

sessions.readWhy: This is one of the most famous pictures of the self ever drawn: noble longings and unruly appetites yoked together, and a mind that must drive them. Everyone who has wanted two things at once will recognise it.

think.why: Why the Greek and the Hebrew pictures of a human being, so different, ended up in conversation for two thousand years.

learn.why: Plato again, from the Republic: learning is not stuffing facts in but turning the whole soul towards the light.

music.why: Forty separate voices, each with its own line, held together in one harmony: Plato's hope for a soul whose parts pull together.

look.why: Raphael's knight rides a cream-white horse and drives his lance down at a dragon, while a woman kneels in prayer beyond. Not Plato's chariot, but a rider and his horse working as one against something truly wrong.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: pick one appetite that often drives you, such as the last word in an argument or an unneeded purchase. Each day, take the reins once, and give the time or money you save to someone else.
sessions.reflect: Which of your two horses has been pulling hardest lately, and where is it trying to take you?

sessions.title: The halls of memory
sessions.line: Augustine looks inside and finds a depth he cannot measure.
sessions.why: Plato described the parts of the soul from outside. Augustine, a Christian who had read the Platonists, turns inward and asks what it is like to be a mind at all, which is exactly where modern philosophy of consciousness begins.

read.author: Augustine of Hippo
read.who: Bishop of Hippo in North Africa and the most influential theologian of the Latin West (354–430).
paras: What then do I love, when I love my God? who is He above the head of my soul? By my very soul will I ascend to Him. I will pass beyond that power whereby I am united to my body, and fill its whole frame with life. Nor can I by that power find my God; for so horse and mule that have no understanding might find Him; seeing it is the same power, whereby even their bodies live. But another power there is, not that only whereby I animate, but that too whereby I imbue with sense my flesh, which the Lord hath framed for me: commanding the eye not to hear, and the ear not to see; but the eye, that through it I should see, and the ear, that through it I should hear; and to the other senses severally, what is to each their own peculiar seats and offices; which, being divers, I the one mind, do through them enact. I will pass beyond this power of mine also; for this also have the horse, and mule, for they also perceive through the body.

I will pass then beyond this power of my nature also, rising by degrees unto Him Who made me. And I come to the fields and spacious palaces of my memory, where are the treasures of innumerable images, brought into it from things of all sorts perceived by the senses. There is stored up, whatsoever besides we think, either by enlarging or diminishing, or any other way varying those things which the sense hath come to; and whatever else hath been committed and laid up, which forgetfulness hath not yet swallowed up and buried. When I enter there, I require what I will to be brought forth, and something instantly comes; others must be longer sought after, which are fetched, as it were, out of some inner receptacle; others rush out in troops, and while one thing is desired and required, they start forth, as who should say, "Is it perchance I?" These I drive away with the hand of my heart, from the face of my remembrance; until what I wish for be unveiled, and appear in sight, out of its secret place. Other things come up readily, in unbroken order, as they are called for; those in front making way for the following; and as they make way, they are hidden from sight, ready to come when I will. All which takes place when I repeat a thing by heart.

There are all things preserved distinctly and under general heads, each having entered by its own avenue: as light, and all colours and forms of bodies by the eyes; by the ears all sorts of sounds; all smells by the avenue of the nostrils; all tastes by the mouth; and by the sensation of the whole body, what is hard or soft; hot or cold; or rugged; heavy or light; either outwardly or inwardly to the body. All these doth that great harbour of the memory receive in her numberless secret and inexpressible windings, to be forthcoming, and brought out at need; each entering in by his own gate, and there laid up. Nor yet do the things themselves enter in; only the images of the things perceived are there in readiness, for thought to recall. Which images, how they are formed, who can tell, though it doth plainly appear by which sense each hath been brought in and stored up? For even while I dwell in darkness and silence, in my memory I can produce colours, if I will, and discern betwixt black and white, and what others I will: nor yet do sounds break in and disturb the image drawn in by my eyes, which I am reviewing, though they also are there, lying dormant, and laid up, as it were, apart. For these too I call for, and forthwith they appear. And though my tongue be still, and my throat mute, so can I sing as much as I will; nor do those images of colours, which notwithstanding be there, intrude themselves and interrupt, when another store is called for, which flowed in by the ears. So the other things, piled in and up by the other senses, I recall at my pleasure. Yea, I discern the breath of lilies from violets, though smelling nothing; and I prefer honey to sweet wine, smooth before rugged, at the time neither tasting nor handling, but remembering only.

These things do I within, in that vast court of my memory. For there are present with me, heaven, earth, sea, and whatever I could think on therein, besides what I have forgotten. There also meet I with myself, and recall myself, and when, where, and what I have done, and under what feelings. There be all which I remember, either on my own experience, or other's credit. Out of the same store do I myself with the past continually combine fresh and fresh likenesses of things which I have experienced, or, from what I have experienced, have believed: and thence again infer future actions, events and hopes, and all these again I reflect on, as present. "I will do this or that," say I to myself, in that great receptacle of my mind, stored with the images of things so many and so great, "and this or that will follow." "O that this or that might be!" "God avert this or that!" So speak I to myself: and when I speak, the images of all I speak of are present, out of the same treasury of memory; nor would I speak of any thereof, were the images wanting.

Great is this force of memory, excessive great, O my God; a large and boundless chamber! who ever sounded the bottom thereof? yet is this a power of mine, and belongs unto my nature; nor do I myself comprehend all that I am. Therefore is the mind too strait to contain itself. And where should that be, which it containeth not of itself? Is it without it, and not within? how then doth it not comprehend itself? A wonderful admiration surprises me, amazement seizes me upon this. And men go abroad to admire the heights of mountains, the mighty billows of the sea, the broad tides of rivers, the compass of the ocean, and the circuits of the stars, and pass themselves by; nor wonder that when I spake of all these things, I did not see them with mine eyes, yet could not have spoken of them, unless I then actually saw the mountains, billows, rivers, stars which I had seen, and that ocean which I believe to be, inwardly in my memory, and that, with the same vast spaces between, as if I saw them abroad. Yet did not I by seeing draw them into myself, when with mine eyes I beheld them; nor are they themselves with me, but their images only. And I know by what sense of the body each was impressed upon me.

sessions.readWhy: Augustine passes beyond what he shares with the horse and the mule and comes to memory, where he can sing silently and smell lilies without a flower in the room. 'Nor do I myself comprehend all that I am': sixteen centuries later, that is still true.

think.why: Augustine, Aquinas and Pascal on what makes a human mind more than a mechanism.

evidence.why: Nagel argued that no physical description captures what it is like to be a creature from the inside; Chalmers called this the 'hard problem'. Both are philosophical arguments, not experiments, both are contested, and neither author argues for a soul.

learn.why: From the same book of the Confessions: Augustine searched outside for what was within him all along.

music.why: 'Mirror in the mirror': Pärt's simple lines turn back on themselves, like a mind looking at itself.

look.why: Nicolaes Maes paints an old woman asleep over her book, her head propped on her hand, bright light and deep shadow across her face. Her life is full of memories we cannot see.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: write a short note to someone who gave you a memory you treasure, telling them what you remember and why it has stayed with you.
sessions.reflect: What is one memory you would least want to lose, and what does it tell you about who you are?

sessions.title: The case for the machine
sessions.line: The hardest objection, given its full strength: perhaps we are only what our brains do.
sessions.why: After Augustine's inner palace, we let the sceptic speak. An answer that has only heard one side has not been earned, and the materialist case is strong.

paras: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:

a time to love,
and a time to hate;
a time for war,
and a time for peace.
What profit has he who works in that in which he labors?
I have seen the burden which God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice, and to do good as long as they live.
Also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy good in all his labor, is the gift of God.
I know that whatever God does, it shall be forever. Nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it; and God has done it, that men should fear before him.
That which is has been long ago, and that which is to be has been long ago. God seeks again that which is passed away.
Moreover I saw under the sun, in the place of justice, that wickedness was there; and in the place of righteousness, that wickedness was there.
I said in my heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked; for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.”
I said in my heart, “As for the sons of men, God tests them, so that they may see that they themselves are like animals.

For that which happens to the sons of men happens to animals. Even one thing happens to them. As the one dies, so the other dies. Yes, they have all one breath; and man has no advantage over the animals; for all is vanity.
All go to one place. All are from the dust, and all turn to dust again.
Who knows the spirit of man, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of the animal, whether it goes downward to the earth?”
Therefore I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works; for that is his portion: for who can bring him to see what will be after him?

sessions.readWhy: The Bible itself gives the sceptic a voice: the Teacher looks at death and says humans and animals go to the same place, all from dust, and asks who knows whether the human spirit goes upward. Read it as an honest question, not a trick.

think.why: States the strongest objection from neuroscience plainly, and the Christian reply that hope rests on resurrection, not on a ghost in the machine.

listen.why: A biologist and an archbishop agree that evolution is true and still disagree about what a human being is; listen for the best of Dawkins's case.

evidence.why: Libet found brain activity rising before people felt the urge to move, which many read as the brain deciding first; Frankish argues that consciousness as we picture it is a kind of illusion. Schurger's model then removed the strongest reading of Libet. None of these settles the question: they concern arbitrary wrist movements and contested arguments, not the soul.

learn.why: Hamlet holds both views in one breath: noble in reason, like a god, and yet a 'quintessence of dust'.

music.why: Brahms, never a conventional believer, built his Requiem from the Bible, including 'all flesh is as grass' in its second movement; this movement turns from mortality to longing for God's dwelling.

look.why: Chardin's young man leans on a stone window ledge and blows a large bubble through a long straw while a child watches. The soap bubble was a long-standing image of how brief life is, close to the Teacher's word for 'vanity', which means a breath.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: ask someone who sees the world differently from you what they think a person is, and listen without arguing back. Afterwards write down the best point they made.
sessions.reflect: Put the materialist case in your own words as strongly as you can. Which part of it is hardest for you to answer?

sessions.title: Searched and known
sessions.line: The psalmist's answer: you are not first a puzzle to be solved but someone already known.
sessions.why: The sceptic asked what we are made of. The psalm changes the question: not what am I, but who knows me. That is the Bible's deepest reply to Ecclesiastes.

paras:
Yahweh, you have searched me,
and you know me.

You know my sitting down and my rising up.
You perceive my thoughts from afar.

You search out my path and my lying down,
and are acquainted with all my ways.

For there is not a word on my tongue,
but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.

You hem me in behind and before.
You laid your hand on me.

This knowledge is beyond me.
It’s lofty.
I can’t attain it.

Where could I go from your Spirit?
Or where could I flee from your presence?

If I ascend up into heaven, you are there.
If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, you are there!

If I take the wings of the dawn,
and settle in the uttermost parts of the sea,

even there your hand will lead me,
and your right hand will hold me.

If I say, “Surely the darkness will overwhelm me.
The light around me will be night,”

even the darkness doesn’t hide from you,
but the night shines as the day.
The darkness is like light to you.

For you formed my inmost being.
You knit me together in my mother’s womb.

I will give thanks to you,
for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
Your works are wonderful.
My soul knows that very well.

My frame wasn’t hidden from you,
when I was made in secret,
woven together in the depths of the earth.

Your eyes saw my body.
In your book they were all written,
the days that were ordained for me,
when as yet there were none of them.

How precious to me are your thoughts, God!
How vast is their sum!

If I would count them, they are more in number than the sand.
When I wake up, I am still with you.

If only you, God, would kill the wicked.
Get away from me, you bloodthirsty men!

For they speak against you wickedly.
Your enemies take your name in vain.

Yahweh, don’t I hate those who hate you?
Am I not grieved with those who rise up against you?

I hate them with perfect hatred.
They have become my enemies.

Search me, God, and know my heart.
Try me, and know my thoughts.

See if there is any wicked way in me,
and lead me in the everlasting way.

sessions.readWhy: 'I am fearfully and wonderfully made' comes from here, and so does 'If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, you are there!' The psalm meets the fear of being only dust with the claim that even the grave is not beyond God's knowing.

think.why: Why, in Christian belief, God is not one more thing inside the universe that neuroscience might find or fail to find, but the reason anything exists at all.

learn.why: The psalm's opening lines, worth carrying into any day when you feel unseen.

music.why: Elgar's setting of Newman's poem follows a soul through death into the presence of God; 'Praise to the Holiest' sings of a second Adam who came to the rescue.

look.why: Van Gogh looks straight at us, orange hair against long strokes of blue. A painter searching his own face, as the psalmist knows he is searched.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: write a note to someone telling them one specific good thing you have noticed about them, something they may think nobody sees.
sessions.reflect: Is being completely known by God something you long for, or something you fear? Write a few honest words about why.

sessions.title: What a piece of work
sessions.line: William James finds the greatness of human beings in the people nobody notices.
sessions.why: Having asked what we are, we end with how to see one another. James, a psychologist who never settled the metaphysics, still saw what Genesis and the psalm see: every life has a depth others are blind to.

read.author: William James
read.ref: Talks to Teachers on Psychology: And to Students on Some of Life's Ideals, the third talk to students (shortened)
read.who: American psychologist and philosopher, one of the founders of modern psychology (1842–1910).
paras: Every Jack sees in his own particular Jill charms and perfections to the enchantment of which we stolid onlookers are stone-cold. And which has the superior view of the absolute truth, he or we? Which has the more vital insight into the nature of Jill's existence, as a fact? Is he in excess, being in this matter a maniac? or are we in defect, being victims of a pathological anaesthesia as regards Jill's magical importance? Surely the latter; surely to Jack are the profounder truths revealed; surely poor Jill's palpitating little life-throbs are among the wonders of creation, are worthy of this sympathetic interest; and it is to our shame that the rest of us cannot feel like Jack. For Jack realizes Jill concretely, and we do not. He struggles toward a union with her inner life, divining her feelings, anticipating her desires, understanding her limits as manfully as he can, and yet inadequately, too; for he is also afflicted with some blindness, even here. Whilst we, dead clods that we are, do not even seek after these things, but are contented that that portion of eternal fact named Jill should be for us as if it were not. Jill, who knows her inner life, knows that Jack's way of taking it—so importantly—is the true and serious way; and she responds to the truth in him by taking him truly and seriously, too. May the ancient blindness never wrap its clouds about either of them again! Where would any of us be, were there no one willing to know us as we really are or ready to repay us for our insight by making recognizant return? We ought, all of us, to realize each other in this intense, pathetic, and important way.

With these thoughts in my mind, I was speeding with the train toward Buffalo, when, near that city, the sight of a workman doing something on the dizzy edge of a sky-scaling iron construction brought me to my senses very suddenly. And now I perceived, by a flash of insight, that I had been steeping myself in pure ancestral blindness, and looking at life with the eyes of a remote spectator. Wishing for heroism and the spectacle of human nature on the rack, I had never noticed the great fields of heroism lying round about me, I had failed to see it present and alive. I could only think of it as dead and embalmed, labelled and costumed, as it is in the pages of romance. And yet there it was before me in the daily lives of the laboring classes. Not in clanging fights and desperate marches only is heroism to be looked for, but on every railway bridge and fire-proof building that is going up to-day. On freight-trains, on the decks of vessels, in cattle-yards and mines, on lumber-rafts, among the firemen and the policemen, the demand for courage is incessant; and the supply never fails. There, every day of the year somewhere, is human nature in extremis for you. And wherever a scythe, an axe, a pick, or a shovel is wielded, you have it sweating and aching and with its powers of patient endurance racked to the utmost under the length of hours of the strain.

As I awoke to all this unidealized heroic life around me, the scales seemed to fall from my eyes; and a wave of sympathy greater than anything I had ever before felt with the common life of common men began to fill my soul. It began to seem as if virtue with horny hands and dirty skin were the only virtue genuine and vital enough to take account of. Every other virtue poses; none is absolutely unconscious and simple, and unexpectant of decoration or recognition, like this. These are our soldiers, thought I, these our sustainers, these the very parents of our life.

And there I rested on that day, with a sense of widening of vision, and with what it is surely fair to call an increase of religious insight into life. In God's eyes the differences of social position, of intellect, of culture, of cleanliness, of dress, which different men exhibit, and all the other rarities and exceptions on which they so fantastically pin their pride, must be so small as practically quite to vanish; and all that should remain is the common fact that here we are, a countless multitude of vessels of life, each of us pent in to peculiar difficulties, with which we must severally struggle by using whatever of fortitude and goodness we can summon up. The exercise of the courage, patience, and kindness, must be the significant portion of the whole business; and the distinctions of position can only be a manner of diversifying the phenomenal surface upon which these underground virtues may manifest their effects. At this rate, the deepest human life is everywhere, is eternal. And, if any human attributes exist only in particular individuals, they must belong to the mere trapping and decoration of the surface-show.

Thus are men's lives levelled up as well as levelled down,—levelled up in their common inner meaning, levelled down in their outer gloriousness and show. Yet always, we must confess, this levelling insight tends to be obscured again; and always the ancestral blindness returns and wraps us up, so that we end once more by thinking that creation can be for no other purpose than to develop remarkable situations and conventional distinctions and merits. And then always some new leveller in the shape of a religious prophet has to arise—the Buddha, the Christ, or some Saint Francis, some Rousseau or Tolstoi—to redispel our blindness. Yet, little by little, there comes some stable gain; for the world does get more humane, and the religion of democracy tends toward permanent increase.

sessions.readWhy: From a train window James sees a workman on a high iron frame and realises he has been blind to the heroism all around him. 'In God's eyes', he concludes, the differences we are proud of almost vanish, and courage, patience and kindness are what count.

think.why: The belief underneath James's insight: if every person bears God's image, the weak and the overlooked have the same worth as the powerful.

listen.why: An atheist and a historian ask whether the conviction that every person counts can outlive the faith it came from.

learn.why: Herbert's 'drudgery divine' says in a few lines what James found on the railway: ordinary work, done well and for God, shines.

music.why: Beethoven, by then almost completely deaf, wrote 'From the heart; may it go to the heart' on this Mass: human greatness worked out within human limits.

look.why: Frans Hals paints an older woman in a black dress with a white ruff and lace cuffs, seated in a low wooden chair. The painting's title records her age but not her name, and Hals still gives her his full attention.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: learn the name of one person whose work keeps your days running and usually goes unnoticed, such as a cleaner, a driver or someone on the till. Use it, and thank them for something specific.
sessions.reflect: Whose quiet courage have you been blind to? What would it change to see them as James saw the workman?

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Having heard Genesis, Plato, Augustine, the materialist case, the psalm and William James: what do you now think a human being is? Write your answer in a few sentences, and say what you would still like to understand.
closing.practice: Once a week, do one quiet kindness for someone the world overlooks, and tell no one.

title: Bearing suffering
question: Why is there suffering, and how do we bear it?
line: Six honest sessions on the oldest question: what can be said about pain, and how to carry it.
