paras: God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
To every animal of the earth, and to every bird of the sky, and to everything that creeps on the earth, in which there is life, I have given every green herb for food;” and it was so.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.
Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?”
The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”
The whole earth was of one language and of one speech.
As they traveled from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there.
They said to one another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar.
They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.”
Yahweh came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men built.
Yahweh said, “Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language, and this is what they begin to do. Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do.
Come, let’s go down, and there confuse their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.”
So Yahweh scattered them abroad from there on the surface of all the earth. They stopped building the city.
Therefore its name was called Babel, because there Yahweh confused the language of all the earth. From there, Yahweh scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth.

parts.title: Very good
parts.context: The Bible's first chapter tells of creation in six days, ending with human beings, and a seventh day of rest. Many Christians and Jews read it as a poem or a theological picture rather than a scientific account; 'In the beginning' looks at the debate.

commentary.on: Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness.
commentary.text: The most important sentence about human beings in the Bible. In the ancient world a king set up images of himself to show where he ruled. Genesis says every human being, not only kings, is God's image: his representative on earth. Western ideas of human dignity grew from this verse.

commentary.on: male and female he created them
commentary.text: Both, equally, are made in God's image.

commentary.on: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
commentary.text: Act 1 ends here. The Bible's story begins not with sin but with goodness. Whatever goes wrong next is a spoiling of something good, not the way things were meant to be.

parts.title: Where are you?
parts.context: God has given the first man and woman a garden with one limit: not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A serpent persuades them that God is holding something back. They eat.

commentary.on: the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God
commentary.text: The first result of the break is not punishment but hiding. Trust has gone; fear has come in.

commentary.on: “Where are you?”
commentary.text: God's first words to fallen humanity are a question, not an accusation. Many readers have heard the whole Bible as God's long search for people who hide from him.

commentary.on: The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.
commentary.text: The man blames the woman, and God for giving her to him; the woman blames the serpent. Act 2 is not only disobedience but broken relationships: with God, with each other, and, in the verses that follow, with the earth itself.

parts.title: Babel
parts.context: After the garden come Cain's murder of his brother Abel, spreading violence, the flood, and a new start with Noah. Then this story ends the first part of Genesis.

commentary.on: let’s make a name for ourselves
commentary.text: The builders want fame and security without God. Hold on to the phrase: in the next chapter God promises Abraham, 'I will make your name great.' Babel tries to take what God will give.

commentary.on: So Yahweh scattered them abroad from there on the surface of all the earth.
commentary.text: The first part of the story ends with humanity divided and scattered. The question hanging over the rest of the Bible is how God will gather them again. The New Testament answers at Pentecost, in session 7, still to come, when people from every nation hear one message in their own languages.

paras: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self. The former, in a word, glories in itself, the latter in the Lord. For the one seeks glory from men; but the greatest glory of the other is God, the witness of conscience. The one lifts up its head in its own glory; the other says to its God, "Thou art my glory, and the lifter up of mine head." In the one, the princes and the nations it subdues are ruled by the love of ruling; in the other, the princes and the subjects serve one another in love, the latter obeying, while the former take thought for all. The one delights in its own strength, represented in the persons of its rulers;

the other says to its God, "I will love Thee, O Lord, my strength." And therefore the wise men of the one city, living according to man, have sought for profit to their own bodies or souls, or both, and those who have known God "glorified Him not as God, neither were thankful, but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened; professing themselves to be wise,"--that is, glorying in their own wisdom, and being possessed by pride,--"they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things." For they were either leaders or followers of the people in adoring images, "and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever." But in the other city there is no human wisdom, but only godliness, which offers due worship to the true God, and looks for its reward in the society of the saints, of holy angels as well as holy men, "that God may be all in all."

This race we have distributed into two parts, the one consisting of those who live according to man, the other of those who live according to God. And these we also mystically call the two cities, or the two communities of men, of which the one is predestined to reign eternally with God, and the other to suffer eternal punishment with the devil. This, however, is their end, and of it we are to speak afterwards. At present, as we have said enough about their origin, whether among the angels, whose numbers we know not, or in the two first human beings, it seems suitable to attempt an account of their career, from the time when our two first parents began to propagate the race until all human generation shall cease. For this whole time or world-age, in which the dying give place and those who are born succeed, is the career of these two cities concerning which we treat.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.ref: Augustine, The City of God XIV.28 and XV.1
parts.title: The love of self and the love of God
parts.context: Augustine (354–430) was bishop of Hippo in North Africa. He wrote The City of God between about 413 and 426, after Rome had been sacked by the Goths in 410 and pagans blamed the Christians. It is a history of the world from creation to the end, in twenty-two books. Translated by Marcus Dods (1871). The '…' marks a cut.
parts.plain: Augustine says that all of human history is the story of two cities, made by two loves. One city is built on the love of self, to the point of despising God; the other on the love of God, to the point of forgetting self. The first wants glory and rules others by force; the second serves. Every person belongs to one or the other, and the whole of history, from Adam and Eve to the end, is the story of these two cities.

commentary.on: two cities have been formed by two loves
commentary.text: Augustine's key: the fall was a turning of love, from God to self. Every later act of the Bible's story is a contest between these two loves.

commentary.on: In the one, the princes and the nations it subdues are ruled by the love of ruling
commentary.text: Babel is the first city of the love of self: a tower for 'a name for ourselves'. Augustine sees the same love in every empire, Rome included.

commentary.on: it seems suitable to attempt an account of their career
commentary.text: This is Augustine's plan for the rest of his great book: to follow the two cities through the whole of the Bible's story. This journey does the same, act by act.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.ref: Augustine, The City of God XIV.28 and XV.1
compare.why: Augustine was the first to tell the whole Bible as one story of human history. He begins exactly where Genesis 3 leaves off.
compare.title: Two cities, two loves

paras: Most people know fragments of the Bible: a garden, a flood, a baby in a manger, a cross. Without the whole shape, the pieces make little sense. The Bible itself tells its story again and again in summary: Israel's creed in Deuteronomy 26, the prayer of Nehemiah 9, Stephen's speech in Acts 7, Paul's sermon in Acts 13. You will read some of these retellings in the sessions ahead.

The shape is simple. A good creation; a break; a promise to one family; a rescue and a covenant; a kingdom that fails and a people in exile, waiting; a man who claims to fulfil it all; and a promise that the end will be a new creation. Christians call the whole the drama of salvation.
sections.key: The Bible retells its own story often. Its shape: creation, fall, promise, rescue, kingdom and exile, Jesus, new creation.

sections.h: Made in the image of God
paras: Genesis 1 gave the West one of its foundational ideas: every human being bears God's image, so every human being has dignity, whatever their rank. Ancient kings called themselves the image of a god; Genesis gives that title to everyone. The early Christian writers drew on it against the exposure of infants and gladiator games; medieval lawyers and later campaigners against slavery drew on it too.
sections.key: Every person is God's image: the root of the Western idea of human dignity.

paras: The Bible's explanation of evil is not a theory but a story: human beings, given a good world and one limit, did not trust the one who gave it. Christian tradition calls this the fall. Augustine later developed the idea of 'original sin': that this break affects every human being. Jewish tradition reads Genesis 3 differently, stressing human freedom and the 'evil inclination' that each person must master.

Either way, Genesis 3 to 11 shows the damage spreading: shame, blame, murder (Cain and Abel), violence, and a world so ruined that God sends a flood. The last story, Babel, shows humanity united in pride and then scattered.
sections.key: The fall is a story of broken trust whose damage spreads; Christians speak of original sin, Jews of human freedom and the evil inclination.

paras: Genesis 1 to 11 has close parallels with older Mesopotamian stories: creation epics like the Enuma Elish and flood stories like the Epic of Gilgamesh. Most scholars think these chapters are not history in our sense but Israel's answers to the same questions those stories asked, answered very differently: one God, not many; a good creation, not a battle; human beings as God's image, not the gods' slaves.

Christians differ on how literally to read them, from a young earth to a theological picture. Augustine himself, in his commentary on Genesis, warned Christians not to defend readings of Genesis that contradicted what could be known about the world. 'In the beginning' explores this in depth.
sections.key: Genesis 1–11 answers the questions of older Mesopotamian myths in a new way. Christians differ on how literally to read it.

paras: This journey is a map, not the territory. For acts 1 and 2, the journey 'In the beginning' reads Genesis 1 to 11 in depth, with the Babylonian creation epic, Darwin and the debate about science. Each later session will point you to the journey that goes deeper into its act.
sections.key: Go deeper: 'In the beginning' (Genesis 1–11).

debate.question: What is the Bible's story about?

positions.name: Salvation from sin
positions.who: Augustine; much Western Christian tradition
positions.view: The story is the fall and God's rescue of sinners through Christ; Genesis 3 is the problem and the cross the answer.
positions.evidence: Genesis 3; Romans 5:12–21; the shape of the creeds.

positions.name: God's kingdom over creation
positions.who: Many modern theologians, such as N. T. Wright
positions.view: The story is God restoring his rule over a good creation through a people, Israel, and its Messiah; salvation is part of a bigger picture that ends in a new creation, not an escape from the world.
positions.evidence: Genesis 1–2 and Revelation 21–22 bracket the story; the kingdom of God in Jesus's preaching.

positions.name: God's covenant with Israel
positions.who: Jewish readers of the Tanakh
positions.view: The story is God's covenant with Israel, given the Torah to live by in the land; it is complete without a New Testament.
positions.evidence: The Tanakh's own order ends with Cyrus inviting the exiles home (2 Chronicles 36:23).

debate.agree: All agree that the Bible tells of a good world, a human failure, and a God who does not give up on it.

reading.why: The first great telling of the Bible as one history.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read Genesis 1 to 3 aloud in one sitting. Then notice, once, where you hide or blame instead of answering 'Here I am'.
sessions.reflect: Where in your life do you see 'very good', and where do you see the break?
takeaways: The Bible is a library in two Testaments ('covenants'), read by Christians as one story in seven acts.
It opens with a good world and human beings made in God's image (act 1), and a broken trust whose damage spreads to Babel (act 2).
Augustine read all of history as two cities built by two loves; every later act answers Genesis 3.

sessions.title: A promise to one family
sessions.line: Act 3: after Babel, God calls one man, Abraham, and promises that through his family every family on earth will be blessed.
sessions.plain: After the scattering at Babel, the story narrows suddenly to one man. God tells Abram (later Abraham) to leave his home and promises to make him a great nation, through which all the families of the earth will be blessed. The rest of Genesis follows his family for four generations: Isaac, Jacob (renamed Israel) and Jacob's twelve sons. It ends with Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers, forgiving them in Egypt. This is the promise the rest of the Bible keeps returning to.
sessions.why: Session 1 ended with humanity scattered at Babel. Act 3 is God's answer: not a new flood, but a promise to one family, for the sake of all.
answers: What did God promise Abraham, and for whom?
Who were Isaac, Jacob and Joseph?
Why does the promise matter for the rest of the Bible?
How did Israel itself retell this part of its story?
sessions.finding: God's answer to Babel is a promise to one family, for the sake of every family on earth; Genesis ends with that family in Egypt, held together by forgiveness.

paras: Genesis 12 to 50 follows one family for four generations. Abraham and Sarah leave Haran for Canaan and wait decades for a son, Isaac. Isaac's sons are the twins Esau and Jacob; Jacob cheats his brother, flees, wrestles with God and is renamed Israel. His twelve sons become the twelve tribes of Israel. The favourite, Joseph, is sold into slavery by his brothers, rises to rule Egypt, and saves the family in a famine.

Genesis gives no dates, but if its numbers are added up the story is set around 2000 to 1700 BC. Whether these were real people, and how much of the story is history, is debated; 'Abraham and the promise' sets out the evidence.
background.key: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob (Israel) and his twelve sons, above all Joseph: four generations, from Haran to Canaan to Egypt.

paras: Two passages: the promise at the start (Genesis 12:1–3) and the forgiveness at the end (Genesis 50:15–21). Between them lie forty chapters. The comparison is a prayer from about 450 BC, a thousand years later, in which Israel retells this part of its story.
background.key: The promise and the forgiveness, the two ends of Genesis 12–50; then Israel retelling it.

before: How many times does the word 'bless' appear in Genesis 12:1–3?
What does Joseph say about the evil his brothers did to him?
sessions.readWhy: The beginning and the end of act 3: the promise and the forgiveness.

paras: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.” ’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

parts.title: The promise
parts.context: Abram is living at Haran, in today's south-eastern Turkey, with his father's household. His family worshipped other gods (Joshua 24:2).

commentary.on: Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house
commentary.text: The call costs everything familiar. Faith in the Bible begins as leaving.

commentary.on: I will bless you and make your name great.
commentary.text: At Babel people tried to make a name for themselves. Here God gives a name as a gift.

commentary.on: All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
commentary.text: The heart of act 3. God chooses one family not instead of the world but for the world. Paul quoted this verse as 'the Good News' announced in advance (Galatians 3:8).

parts.title: You meant evil, God meant good
parts.context: Decades earlier Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery. He rose to govern Egypt and saved them from famine. Now their father Jacob has died, and they fear revenge.

commentary.on: Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
commentary.text: The great family of the promise is a story of rivalry, deceit and favouritism. It ends with tears, not triumph.

commentary.on: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive
commentary.text: The key to Genesis, and to much of the Bible: God works through human wrongs without excusing them. Christians later heard in Joseph, betrayed by his own and raised up to save many, a picture of Jesus.

commentary.on: I will provide for you and your little ones.
commentary.text: Act 3 ends with the family safe in Egypt, but far from the promised land. Act 4 begins there, centuries later, with their descendants in slavery.

paras: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.
You are Yahweh, the God who chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, gave him the name of Abraham,

found his heart faithful before you, and made a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite, to give it to his offspring, and have performed your words; for you are righteous.

parts.title: You chose Abram
parts.context: The book of Nehemiah tells of the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls after the return from exile in Babylon. In chapter 9 the people fast and confess, and the Levites lead a long prayer that tells Israel's history from creation to their own day.

commentary.on: You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens
commentary.text: The prayer begins where the Bible begins, with creation. Israel always told its story from the very start.

commentary.on: You are Yahweh, the God who chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, gave him the name of Abraham
commentary.text: Three verbs, all God's: chose, brought out, named. The story of the patriarchs is told as what God did.

commentary.on: and have performed your words; for you are righteous.
commentary.text: The point of retelling: God keeps his promises. The people praying this had just come back from exile; they needed to know it.

compare.why: About 450 BC, after the exile, the people of Jerusalem gathered to confess their sins, and the Levites prayed this prayer, retelling the whole story. Its opening covers acts 1 and 3.
compare.title: Israel tells its own story

paras: The turn at Genesis 12 surprises every first reader. If God cares for the whole world, why choose one man? The Bible's answer is in the promise itself: Abraham is blessed in order to be a blessing to 'all the families of the earth'. The rest of the story keeps both halves together: a particular people, for a universal purpose.

Jews, Christians and Muslims all call Abraham their father. Jews through Isaac and Jacob; Christians through faith, as Paul argued in Romans 4 and Galatians 3; Muslims honour him as Ibrahim, a prophet and ancestor of the Arabs through Ishmael.
sections.key: One family chosen for all families: the particular for the universal. Three faiths call Abraham father.

sections.h: A family, not a set of heroes
paras: Genesis hides nothing. Abraham passes his wife off as his sister to save himself; Sarah mistreats her slave Hagar; Jacob deceives his blind father; Joseph's brothers sell him. God keeps his promise through them, not because of them. This honesty is one of the marks of the Bible: its heroes are seldom heroic.
sections.key: The family of the promise is flawed; God keeps his promise through them.

paras: In Genesis 15 God binds himself to Abraham in a covenant, an ancient form of solemn agreement. The idea runs through the whole Bible: covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, David, and the new covenant promised by Jeremiah. That is why the two parts of the Christian Bible are called Testaments, the Latin word for covenants.
sections.key: Covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel, David, and the new covenant: the thread that gives the Testaments their name.

paras: 'Abraham and the promise' follows the family generation by generation, from the call to Joseph, with the hardest story, the binding of Isaac, at full strength.
sections.key: Go deeper: 'Abraham and the promise' (Genesis 12–50).

refs: Genesis 12–50; Joshua 24:2; Galatians 3:8; Romans 4; Nehemiah 9:6–8.

debate.question: Is it fair that God chose one family?

positions.name: Chosen for others
positions.who: Much Jewish and Christian teaching
positions.view: Election is a calling to serve, not a privilege over others: Abraham is blessed to bless all families.
positions.evidence: Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 49:6, 'a light to the nations'.

positions.name: A scandal of particularity
positions.who: Critics from the Enlightenment on, such as Voltaire
positions.view: A universal God would not reveal himself to one small people in one corner of the world.
positions.evidence: The rest of humanity seems left out for two thousand years.

positions.name: God works through the particular
positions.who: Many modern theologians
positions.view: Love is always particular: God reaches the world as people do, through one family, one place, one person.
positions.evidence: The incarnation: God in one man, in one time and place.

debate.agree: All agree the promise in Genesis 12 is meant to reach beyond Abraham's family.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: think of someone whose wrong against you turned out, in the end, to bring some good. Without excusing the wrong, thank God for the good.

takeaways: After Babel, God calls Abraham and promises that through his family all families on earth will be blessed (act 3).
The family of Isaac, Jacob (Israel) and Joseph is flawed; God keeps his promise through them.
Genesis ends with forgiveness in Egypt: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good'.

sessions.title: Out of slavery, into covenant
sessions.line: Act 4: Abraham's descendants are slaves in Egypt; God hears their cry, brings them out under Moses, and binds himself to them at Sinai.
sessions.plain: Genesis left Abraham's family safe in Egypt. Centuries later their descendants, the Israelites, are slaves there. God hears their cry and sends Moses to lead them out. At Mount Sinai in the desert he makes a covenant with them and gives them his law, including the Ten Commandments. They wander forty years before reaching the edge of the promised land. Israel remembered this as the founding event of its life, and retold it every year at Passover.
sessions.why: Session 2 ended with the family in Egypt. Act 4 is the great rescue: the promise to Abraham's family is kept when they are at their weakest, as slaves.
answers: What happened between Joseph and Moses?
What is the Exodus, and what happened at Sinai?
What did the covenant ask of Israel?
How did Israel retell this story?
sessions.finding: In act 4 God rescues a people of slaves and binds himself to them in covenant; the law begins with grace, 'I brought you out', and Israel told the story every year as its own.

paras: Exodus opens with a new Pharaoh 'who didn't know Joseph', who enslaves the Israelites. Moses, a Hebrew baby saved from Pharaoh's order to drown the boys, grows up in the palace, flees after killing an Egyptian, and meets God at a bush that burns but is not consumed. God sends him back to say to Pharaoh, 'Let my people go.' After ten plagues and the night of Passover, the Israelites leave and cross the sea.

The books from Exodus to Deuteronomy tell what follows: the covenant at Sinai, the law, the golden calf, forty years in the desert, and Moses' death within sight of the land. If it happened as told, many scholars would place it in the 1200s BC, under Ramesses II; whether and how it happened is debated, and 'Exodus and the law' sets out the evidence.
background.key: Slavery, Moses and the burning bush, the plagues and Passover, the sea, Sinai, forty years: Exodus to Deuteronomy.

paras: Three short passages: God hearing the cry of the slaves (Exodus 3), the offer of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 19), and the first words of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20). The comparison is the creed every Israelite farmer was to say when bringing the first fruits of the harvest: the story in seven sentences.
background.key: The cry heard, the covenant offered, the law's first words; then Israel's own creed.

before: In Exodus 3, list the verbs God uses about the slaves. What does he see, hear and know?
In Exodus 19, what will Israel be to God if it keeps the covenant?
How do the Ten Commandments begin, before any command?
sessions.readWhy: Act 4 in three steps: the rescue, the covenant, the law.

paras: Yahweh said, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters, for I know their sorrows.

I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land to a good and large land, to a land flowing with milk and honey; to the place of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.
Now, behold, the cry of the children of Israel has come to me. Moreover I have seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.
Come now therefore, and I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.”
Moses went up to God, and Yahweh called to him out of the mountain, saying, “This is what you shall tell the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel:
‘You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings, and brought you to myself.
Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine;
and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel.”
God spoke all these words, saying,
“I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
“You shall have no other gods before me.

parts.title: I have heard their cry
parts.context: Moses, a fugitive, is keeping sheep in the desert near Mount Sinai (Horeb). A bush is burning and not consumed, and God speaks from it.

commentary.on: I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry
commentary.text: The God of the Bible sees, hears and knows the suffering of slaves. In the ancient world gods were on the side of kings; here God takes the side of the slaves against the king.

commentary.on: I have come down to deliver them
commentary.text: At Babel God 'came down' to scatter; here he comes down to rescue. The same God, the same verb, a different act.

commentary.on: I will send you to Pharaoh
commentary.text: God rescues through a person, as he blessed through a family. Moses' objections follow at once: 'Who am I?'

parts.title: A kingdom of priests
parts.context: Three months after leaving Egypt, the Israelites camp at the foot of Mount Sinai. Moses goes up the mountain.

commentary.on: how I bore you on eagles’ wings, and brought you to myself
commentary.text: The rescue comes first. The covenant is offered to people who have already been saved, not as a test to earn it.

commentary.on: you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine
commentary.text: Again the two halves of Genesis 12: one people chosen, because the whole earth is God's.

commentary.on: you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation
commentary.text: A priest stands between God and others. Israel's calling is to be that for the world. The first letter of Peter later gives these words to the church (1 Peter 2:9).

parts.title: I brought you out
parts.context: God speaks the Ten Commandments from the mountain. They are the heart of the covenant.

commentary.on: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
commentary.text: Before any command, a reminder of grace. The law is the shape of life for people who have been set free, not a ladder to climb to God.

commentary.on: You shall have no other gods before me.
commentary.text: The first commandment is the root of the rest. One God, not many: that conviction runs from here through the whole Bible.

paras: You shall answer and say before Yahweh your God, “My father was a Syrian ready to perish. He went down into Egypt, and lived there, few in number. There he became a great, mighty, and populous nation.
The Egyptians mistreated us, afflicted us, and imposed hard labor on us.
Then we cried to Yahweh, the God of our fathers. Yahweh heard our voice, and saw our affliction, our toil, and our oppression.
Yahweh brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand, with an outstretched arm, with great terror, with signs, and with wonders;
and he has brought us into this place, and has given us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.
Now, behold, I have brought the first of the fruit of the ground, which you, Yahweh, have given me.” You shall set it down before Yahweh your God, and worship before Yahweh your God.

parts.title: The farmer's creed
parts.context: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses' last speeches before Israel enters the land. Here he tells each farmer what to say when bringing the first fruits of the harvest to the sanctuary. 'Syrian' translates 'Aramean': Jacob, who lived in Aram (northern Syria).

commentary.on: My father was a Syrian ready to perish.
commentary.text: Acts 3 and 4 in one breath: Jacob the wanderer, the descent to Egypt, slavery, the cry, the rescue, the land.

commentary.on: The Egyptians mistreated us, afflicted us
commentary.text: Notice 'us'. Generations later, the farmer says that it happened to us, not to our ancestors. Jews still say the same at the Passover meal: in every generation, each person should see themselves as if they came out of Egypt.

commentary.on: Now, behold, I have brought the first of the fruit of the ground
commentary.text: The story ends in thanksgiving. To remember the story is to worship.

compare.why: Deuteronomy commands every Israelite, at harvest, to tell the story in their own words. It is the oldest summary of the Bible's story, and every family was to say it.
compare.title: A wandering Aramean

paras: For Israel the Exodus was what the resurrection is for Christians: the act that showed who God is. The prophets, the psalms and the festivals return to it again and again. Passover retold it every spring. Christians read Jesus's death through it: he died at Passover, and Paul calls him 'our Passover lamb' (1 Corinthians 5:7).
sections.key: The Exodus is Israel's founding event, retold at Passover; Christians read Jesus's death through it.

paras: The order matters: rescue, then covenant, then law. The Ten Commandments begin 'I brought you out'. The law of Moses, with its 613 commandments in later Jewish counting, was Israel's way of living as a freed people: one law for rich and poor, rest for slaves and animals, care for the stranger, 'for you were strangers in Egypt'.

Christians have related to this law in different ways: Jesus summed it up in love of God and neighbour; Paul argued that Gentile believers need not keep the whole law of Moses; the churches have kept its moral teaching, above all the Ten Commandments.
sections.key: Rescue, covenant, law: the commandments begin with grace. Jesus summed up the law in love.

paras: No story has shaped the West's idea of freedom more. Enslaved Africans in America sang 'Go down, Moses'; the American founders proposed a Great Seal showing Pharaoh drowning in the sea; Martin Luther King spoke of seeing the promised land the night before he was killed.
sections.key: The Exodus became the West's story of liberation.

paras: 'Exodus and the law' reads the story from slavery to Sinai in seven sessions, with the law of Hammurabi, Frederick Douglass, and the case that it never happened.
sections.key: Go deeper: 'Exodus and the law'.

refs: Exodus 1–20; Deuteronomy 26:5–10; 1 Corinthians 5:7; 1 Peter 2:9; Mishnah Pesachim 10:5 ('in every generation').

debate.question: Is the law of Moses for Christians?

positions.name: Fulfilled in Christ
positions.who: Paul; most churches
positions.view: The ceremonial and civil laws were for Israel and are fulfilled in Christ; the moral law, summed up in love, remains.
positions.evidence: Galatians 3; Romans 13:8–10; Matthew 5:17.

positions.name: Still binding for Israel
positions.who: Jewish tradition
positions.view: The Torah is the covenant way of life for the Jewish people for ever; non-Jews are bound only by the basic Noahide laws.
positions.evidence: Deuteronomy 29:29; the rabbinic tradition.

positions.name: Only the Ten Commandments
positions.who: Many Protestant catechisms
positions.view: The Ten Commandments are the moral law for everyone; the rest was for ancient Israel.
positions.evidence: The Decalogue's place in catechisms, Luther's and Calvin's included.

debate.agree: All agree that the law begins with grace, 'I brought you out', and that its heart is love of God and neighbour.

sessions.title: Kings, prophets and exile
sessions.line: Act 5: Israel gets a land, kings and a promise to David, loses it all in exile, and the prophets promise a new covenant and a coming king.
sessions.plain: Under Joshua the Israelites settle in Canaan. They are led by judges, then ask for a king. God promises King David that his family will reign for ever. But kings and people turn to other gods and injustice, the kingdom splits, and in 587 BC Babylon destroys Jerusalem and its Temple. In exile the prophets promise a new covenant written on the heart and a king from David's line. Some exiles return, rebuild the Temple, and wait. The Old Testament ends with that waiting.
sessions.why: Session 3 left Israel at the edge of the promised land. Act 5 is the longest: about eight hundred years in the land, from the conquest to the exile and return. It ends in hope, not fulfilment.
answers: What happened between Moses and the exile?
What did God promise David?
Why did the kingdom fall, and what did the prophets promise?
How does the Old Testament end?
Where do the Psalms and wisdom books fit?
sessions.finding: In act 5 Israel gets its land, its kings and a promise to David, loses everything in exile, and is left waiting for a new covenant and a king; the Old Testament ends with the story unfinished.

paras: After Moses' death, Joshua leads the tribes into Canaan. For about two centuries 'judges' lead them in crises. Then they ask for a king: Saul, then David, who makes Jerusalem his capital, then Solomon, who builds the Temple. After Solomon the kingdom splits into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Assyria destroys the north in 722 BC; Babylon destroys Jerusalem in 587 BC and takes its people into exile. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia lets them return; the Temple is rebuilt by 515 BC.

Beside the kings stand the prophets, Elijah, Amos, Isaiah, Jeremiah and others, who call kings and people back to the covenant. And beside the history stand the books of prayer and wisdom: the Psalms, Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes.

background.key: Land, judges, kings (Saul, David, Solomon), division, exile in 587 BC, return; prophets beside the kings, psalms and wisdom beside the history.

paras: Three promises: God's promise to David of a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7), the new covenant promised in exile (Jeremiah 31), and the last words of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles (Malachi 4). The comparison is from Milton's Paradise Lost, where an angel tells Adam this whole act in a few dozen lines.

paras: When your days are fulfilled, and you sleep with your fathers, I will set up your offspring after you, who will proceed out of your body, and I will establish his kingdom.
He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
but my loving kindness will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away before you.
Your house and your kingdom will be made sure forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.” ’ ”

“Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh,
“that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel,
and with the house of Judah:

“But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,”
says Yahweh:
“I will put my law in their inward parts,
and I will write it in their heart.
I will be their God,
and they shall be my people.
Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

parts.title: A house for ever
parts.context: About 1000 BC. David has made Jerusalem his capital and wants to build God a temple. Through the prophet Nathan, God says no: instead God will build David a 'house', a dynasty.

commentary.on: I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
commentary.text: The promise that shapes the rest of the Bible. When David's kingdom fell, Israel's hope became a future king from his line: the Messiah, the 'anointed one'.

commentary.on: I will be his father, and he will be my son.
commentary.text: The king of Israel is called God's son. The New Testament takes up these words for Jesus (Hebrews 1:5).

commentary.on: but my loving kindness will not depart from him
commentary.text: Even when the kings fail, and they will, God's faithful love (Hebrew chesed) stays.

parts.title: A new covenant
parts.context: Jeremiah prophesied in Jerusalem before and during its fall to Babylon in 587 BC. The covenant of Sinai has been broken; the people are going into exile.

commentary.on: I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel
commentary.text: The only place in the Old Testament that speaks of a 'new covenant'. From it the Christian Bible's two halves take their names, old and new.

commentary.on: I will write it in their heart.
commentary.text: The problem with the old covenant was not the law but the human heart. The new covenant changes the heart itself.

commentary.on: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.
commentary.text: Forgiveness is the foundation. Jesus at his last supper: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20).

parts.title: Before the great day
parts.context: Malachi prophesied in Jerusalem about 430 BC, after the return. In Christian Bibles his book closes the Old Testament. (The Jewish Tanakh is ordered differently and ends with 2 Chronicles.)

commentary.on: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
commentary.text: The Christian Old Testament ends looking forward. Jews still set a place for Elijah at the Passover meal; the Gospels see John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14).

commentary.on: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children
commentary.text: The last words are of reconciliation, and of waiting. Then four hundred years of silence before the New Testament opens.

paras:
Mean while they, in their earthly Canaan placed,
Long time shall dwell and prosper, but when sins
National interrupt their publick peace,
Provoking God to raise them enemies;
From whom as oft he saves them penitent
By Judges first, then under Kings; of whom
The second, both for piety renowned
And puissant deeds, a promise shall receive
Irrevocable, that his regal throne
For ever shall endure; the like shall sing
All Prophecy, that of the royal stock
Of David (so I name this king) shall rise
A Son, the Woman's seed to thee foretold,
Foretold to Abraham, as in whom shall trust
All nations; and to kings foretold, of kings
The last; for of his reign shall be no end.

But first, a long succession must ensue;
And his next son, for wealth and wisdom famed,
The clouded ark of God, till then in tents
Wandering, shall in a glorious temple enshrine.
Such follow him, as shall be registered
Part good, part bad; of bad the longer scroll;
Whose foul idolatries, and other faults
Heaped to the popular sum, will so incense
God, as to leave them, and expose their land,
Their city, his temple, and his holy ark,
With all his sacred things, a scorn and prey
To that proud city, whose high walls thou sawest
Left in confusion; Babylon thence called.
There in captivity he lets them dwell
The space of seventy years; then brings them back,
Remembering mercy, and his covenant sworn
To David, stablished as the days of Heaven.

Returned from Babylon by leave of kings
Their lords, whom God disposed, the house of God
They first re-edify; and for a while
In mean estate live moderate; till, grown
In wealth and multitude, factious they grow;
But first among the priests dissention springs,
Men who attend the altar, and should most
Endeavour peace: their strife pollution brings
Upon the temple itself: at last they seise
The scepter, and regard not David's sons;
Then lose it to a stranger, that the true
Anointed King Messiah might be born
Barred of his right; yet at his birth a star,
Unseen before in Heaven, proclaims him come;
And guides the eastern sages, who inquire
His place, to offer incense, myrrh, and gold:
His place of birth a solemn Angel tells
To simple shepherds, keeping watch by night;
They gladly thither haste, and by a quire
Of squadroned Angels hear his carol sung.
A virgin is his mother, but his sire
The power of the Most High: He shall ascend
The throne hereditary, and bound his reign
With Earth's wide bounds, his glory with the Heavens.

parts.author: John Milton
parts.ref: Milton, Paradise Lost, Book XII, lines 315–371
parts.title: Of David (so I name this king)
parts.context: John Milton (1608–1674), blind, dictated Paradise Lost, a retelling of Genesis 1–3 in twelve books of blank verse. In the last book, the archangel Michael tells Adam what will happen after the fall, all the way to Christ. Original English, 1674 edition; 'puissant' means mighty, 'seise' seize.
parts.plain: Michael tells Adam: Israel will live in Canaan, sin, and be rescued by judges and then kings. The second king, David, will receive a promise that his throne will last for ever, and the prophets will sing of a son of David, the seed of the woman promised to Adam and to Abraham. Solomon will build the Temple; later kings will be mostly bad; Babylon will take the people into captivity for seventy years. They will return and rebuild, quarrel, and lose their kingdom to a stranger, so that the true Messiah is born without his throne, and announced by a star and by angels to shepherds.

commentary.on: a promise shall receive
commentary.text: Milton, like the Bible, hangs the whole act on the promise to David.

commentary.on: Part good, part bad; of bad the longer scroll
commentary.text: A fair summary of 1 and 2 Kings in seven words.

commentary.on: Remembering mercy, and his covenant sworn
commentary.text: The return from exile is God keeping his word, not Israel earning it.

commentary.on: the true Anointed King Messiah might be born Barred of his right
commentary.text: Milton's angel sees act 5 ending where act 6 begins: a king from David's line born without a throne.

compare.author: John Milton
compare.ref: Milton, Paradise Lost, Book XII, lines 315–371
compare.why: In the last book of Paradise Lost (1674), Milton has the archangel Michael show Adam the whole future. Here is act 5 in under seventy lines.
compare.title: The angel tells Adam

paras: The history books, Joshua to Kings, were finished during the exile to answer one question: why did it all go wrong? Their answer: kings and people broke the covenant, worshipped other gods and crushed the poor. The prophets had said so, and were mostly ignored.
sections.key: The history books explain the fall of the kingdom: the covenant was broken.

paras: When David's line lost its throne, the promise of 2 Samuel 7 became a hope: God would raise up a son of David, an 'anointed one', Messiah in Hebrew, Christ in Greek, to reign with justice. Isaiah spoke of a child on David's throne whose kingdom would have no end (Isaiah 9:6–7); Jeremiah of a new covenant; Ezekiel of a new heart; Isaiah 40–55 of comfort and of a servant who suffers for others.
sections.key: After the fall, the promise to David became the hope of a Messiah, with a new covenant and a suffering servant.

paras: Act 5 also gave the Bible its prayer book, the Psalms, many credited to David, and its wisdom: Proverbs, Job's protest at suffering, and Ecclesiastes' 'vanity of vanities'. These books step back from the story to ask how to live, pray and suffer within it.
sections.key: The Psalms and the wisdom books: how to pray, live and suffer inside the story.

paras: About four hundred years pass between Malachi and the New Testament. Persia gave way to Alexander the Great in 332 BC, and Greek became the common language of the region; the Jewish Scriptures were translated into Greek (the Septuagint). In 167 BC the Maccabees revolted against a Greek king who desecrated the Temple, and won a century of independence, remembered at Hanukkah. In 63 BC Rome took Jerusalem. By Jesus's day Israel was waiting for God to keep his promises.
sections.key: Persia, Alexander, the Greek Septuagint, the Maccabees, Rome: four hundred years of waiting.

paras: 'Kings and prophets' follows act 5 from the people's demand for a king to the exile and Isaiah's suffering servant, with the hardest question, the conquest of Canaan, at full strength. 'Psalms and wisdom' is still being written.
sections.key: Go deeper: 'Kings and prophets'.

sessions.title: The story's centre
sessions.line: Act 6: a carpenter from Nazareth announces that the time is fulfilled, is crucified, and is seen alive again; he says the whole story was about him.
sessions.plain: Around AD 28, Jesus of Nazareth begins to preach in Galilee: 'The time is fulfilled, and God's Kingdom is at hand.' He heals, teaches, eats with outcasts and gathers twelve disciples, like the twelve tribes. In Jerusalem at Passover he is arrested and crucified by the Romans. Three days later his followers say they have seen him alive. On the road to Emmaus, he explains to two of them that the whole of Scripture, 'Moses and all the prophets', was about him. This is act 6, and Christians believe it is the centre of the story.
sessions.why: Session 4 ended with Israel waiting for a new covenant and a king. Act 6 is the claim that the wait is over.
answers: Who was Jesus, in the Bible's story?
What did he announce?
How did he connect himself to the earlier acts?
How did his first followers retell the whole story?
sessions.finding: In act 6 Jesus announces that the time is fulfilled, dies at Passover and rises; he and his followers read the whole earlier story as pointing to him.

paras: Jesus was born in Bethlehem, probably around 4 BC, and grew up in Nazareth in Galilee, under Roman rule. Four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, written between about AD 65 and 100, tell his life, death and resurrection. Roman and Jewish writers, Tacitus and Josephus among them, confirm that he lived and was crucified under Pontius Pilate; 'What is the Bible?' sets out that evidence.

Each Gospel connects him to the earlier acts. Matthew begins with a family tree from Abraham through David; Luke traces him back to Adam; John begins 'In the beginning', like Genesis. Jesus chose twelve disciples, like the twelve tribes, and gave his last supper at Passover, calling the cup 'the new covenant in my blood'.
background.key: Four Gospels, written AD 65–100, tie Jesus to Adam, Abraham, David, the Exodus and the new covenant.

paras: Jesus's first announcement (Mark 1), and two moments after the resurrection in Luke 24 when he explains the Scriptures. The comparison is a sermon by Paul that retells the whole story from the Exodus to Jesus in one breath.
background.key: The announcement, and the risen Jesus explaining Moses and the prophets; then Paul's retelling.

paras: Now after John was taken into custody, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Good News of God’s Kingdom,
and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.”
He said to them, “Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!
Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
He said to them, “This is what I told you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled.”
Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.
He said to them, “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day,
and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem.
You are witnesses of these things.

parts.title: The time is fulfilled
parts.context: Mark, probably the earliest Gospel, opens with John the Baptist in the desert, as Isaiah and Malachi foretold. After John's arrest, Jesus begins to preach.

commentary.on: The time is fulfilled
commentary.text: The waiting that ended the Old Testament is over. Everything in Jesus's message assumes the earlier acts.

commentary.on: God’s Kingdom is at hand!
commentary.text: The kingdom of God is God's rule over his world, which the prophets promised. Jesus's healings and meals with outcasts show what it looks like.

commentary.on: Repent, and believe in the Good News.
commentary.text: 'Repent' means turn around: the answer to the hiding of Genesis 3.

parts.title: Beginning from Moses
parts.context: Sunday after the crucifixion. Two disciples are walking to Emmaus, sad and confused. A stranger joins them; it is the risen Jesus, though they do not recognise him.

commentary.on: Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?
commentary.text: The disciples expected a king who would win. Jesus says the Scriptures promised a Messiah who would suffer first, as Isaiah's servant does.

commentary.on: Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
commentary.text: This verse is the reason Christians read the Bible as one story. Its claim is that the whole of the Old Testament points to Jesus.

parts.title: The law, the prophets and the psalms
parts.context: Later that evening, in Jerusalem, Jesus appears to the gathered disciples.

commentary.on: all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled
commentary.text: The three parts of Israel's Scriptures: Law, Prophets and Writings (led by the Psalms). All of it, Jesus says, concerns him.

commentary.on: repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations
commentary.text: The promise to Abraham, that all families would be blessed, is about to go to all nations. That is act 7.

paras: Paul stood up, and beckoning with his hand said, “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen.
The God of this people chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they stayed as aliens in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm, he led them out of it.
For a period of about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.
When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land for an inheritance for about four hundred fifty years.
After these things, he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.
Afterward they asked for a king, and God gave to them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also testified, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’
From this man’s offspring, God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise,
before his coming, when John had first preached the baptism of repentance to Israel.
As John was fulfilling his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. But behold, one comes after me, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’
Brothers, children of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation is sent out to you.
For those who dwell in Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they didn’t know him, nor the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him.
Though they found no cause for death, they still asked Pilate to have him killed.
When they had fulfilled all things that were written about him, they took him down from the tree, and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people.
We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers,
that God has fulfilled this to us, their children, in that he raised up Jesus. As it is also written in the second psalm,

‘You are my Son.
Today I have become your father.’

paras: Christians read the Bible with Jesus at its centre: the second Adam who obeys where the first failed (Romans 5); the seed of Abraham in whom the nations are blessed (Galatians 3); the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7); the son of David; the servant who suffers (Isaiah 53); the maker of the new covenant. Each earlier act, on this reading, prepares a part of who he is.

paras: Jesus was crucified by the Romans at Passover, around AD 30. His followers said that God raised him from the dead on the third day, and that they saw him. Christians see in the cross and resurrection the answer to the fall: sin forgiven, death defeated, the first day of a new creation.

sessions.title: The case against: one story or many?
sessions.line: Is the Bible really one story, or many books that Christians later forced together? The objection at full strength.
sessions.plain: Christians read the Bible as one story leading to Jesus. But the Old Testament is the Scriptures of Israel, and Jews have read them for two thousand years without that ending. Critics say Christians took older texts and twisted them: Matthew quotes Hosea's 'Out of Egypt I called my son', which is about Israel, as a prophecy of Jesus; and Isaiah's sign of a child to King Ahaz as a prophecy of the virgin birth. Thomas Paine called this 'forcing' every phrase into meanings it could not have. This session puts the case at full strength, then the best answers.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 5 told the story the way Christians read it. Now, before the last act, we ask whether that reading is fair.
answers: Is the Bible one story, or a library of different voices?
Did the New Testament writers misread the Old Testament?
How do Jews read the same Scriptures?
How have Christians answered?
sessions.finding: The case against is strong on details: some New Testament readings are not what the prophets meant. The answers are that the first Christians read Scripture as a pattern, not a list of predictions, and that the unity of the story is a claim of faith, not something the texts force on any reader.

paras: The Bible was written by dozens of authors over a thousand years, in different languages and genres, often disagreeing. The Jewish Scriptures had their own story and their own ending: the Tanakh closes with Cyrus inviting the exiles home. The New Testament writers, critics say, read Jesus back into texts that were about other things, then called it fulfilment.

The objection is old. Around 150, Justin Martyr wrote a dialogue with a Jewish teacher, Trypho, who told him Christians misread the prophets. Around the same time Marcion, a shipowner turned teacher in Rome, went further: the God of the Old Testament was not the Father of Jesus at all, and Christians should drop the Old Testament. The church rejected Marcion, and kept both Testaments.
background.key: Many authors, one story imposed later? Trypho said Christians misread the prophets; Marcion said drop the Old Testament altogether.

paras: Thomas Paine (1737–1809) wrote Common Sense, which helped spark the American Revolution, and The Age of Reason (1794–1807), which attacked the Bible as a human book. He believed in one God but not in revelation. In the passage you will read, he goes through Isaiah 7:14, the verse Matthew quotes about the virgin birth.
background.key: Paine, author of Common Sense, attacked the Bible in The Age of Reason as a believer in God but not in revelation.

paras: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him,
and called my son out of Egypt.

Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, “Arise and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.”
He arose and took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt,
and was there until the death of Herod; that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, “Out of Egypt I called my son.”
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Now all this has happened that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying,

“Behold, the virgin shall be with child,
and shall give birth to a son.
They shall call his name Immanuel;”
which is, being interpreted, “God with us.”

parts.title: Out of Egypt
parts.context: Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom around 750 BC. Here God remembers the Exodus with tenderness.

commentary.on: When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
commentary.text: The son is Israel, and the calling out of Egypt is the Exodus, in the past. Hosea is not predicting anything.

parts.title: Fulfilled
parts.context: Matthew's Gospel, written around AD 80–90, tells how Joseph took the infant Jesus to Egypt to escape King Herod.

commentary.on: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, “Out of Egypt I called my son.”
commentary.text: Matthew applies Hosea's words about Israel to Jesus. The critic says: that is not what Hosea meant. Matthew's defenders say: he knew that, and meant that Jesus relives Israel's story, as Israel's true son.

parts.title: The sign to Ahaz
parts.context: About 735 BC. King Ahaz of Judah is terrified of an invasion. Isaiah offers him a sign from God; Ahaz refuses, and Isaiah gives one anyway. The Hebrew word translated 'virgin' here, almah, means a young woman; the Greek translation, the Septuagint, used parthenos, 'virgin'.

commentary.on: Behold, the virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
commentary.text: The next verses say that before the child is old enough to know right from wrong, the two invading kings will be gone (Isaiah 7:16). The sign was for Ahaz, in his own time.

parts.title: God with us
parts.context: Matthew tells of Jesus's conception by the Holy Spirit and Joseph's dream.

commentary.on: which is, being interpreted, “God with us.”
commentary.text: Matthew reads the Greek version and hears in 'Immanuel' the meaning of Jesus: God with us. The critic says he took a sign for Ahaz out of its time; his defenders say a prophecy can have a first meaning and a fuller one.

paras: When we see the studied craft of the scripture-makers, in making every part of this romantic book of school-boy's eloquence bend to the monstrous idea of a Son of God, begotten by a ghost on the body of a virgin, there is no imposition we are not justified in suspecting them of. Every phrase and circumstance are marked with the barbarous hand of superstitious torture, and forced into meanings it was impossible they could have. The head of every chapter, and the top of every page, are blazoned with the names of Christ and the Church, that the unwary reader might suck in the error before he began to read.

Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son (Isa. vii. I4), has been interpreted to mean the person called Jesus Christ, and his mother Mary, and has been echoed through christendom for more than a thousand years; and such has been the rage of this opinion, that scarcely a spot in it but has been stained with blood and marked with desolation in consequence of it. Though it is not my intention to enter into controversy on subjects of this kind, but to confine myself to show that the Bible is spurious,--and thus, by taking away the foundation, to overthrow at once the whole structure of superstition raised thereon,--I will however stop a moment to expose the fallacious application of this passage.

Whether Isaiah was playing a trick with Ahaz, king of Judah, to whom this passage is spoken, is no business of mine; I mean only to show the misapplication of the passage, and that it has no more reference to Christ and his mother, than it has to me and my mother. The story is simply this:

The king of Syria and the king of Israel (I have already mentioned that the Jews were split into two nations, one of which was called Judah, the capital of which was Jerusalem, and the other Israel) made war jointly against Ahaz, king of Judah, and marched their armies towards Jerusalem. Ahaz and his people became alarmed, and the account says (Is. vii. 2), Their hearts were moved as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.

In this situation of things, Isaiah addresses himself to Ahaz, and assures him in the name of the Lord (the cant phrase of all the prophets) that these two kings should not succeed against him; and to satisfy Ahaz that this should be the case, tells him to ask a sign. This, the account says, Ahaz declined doing; giving as a reason that he would not tempt the Lord; upon which Isaiah, who is the speaker, says, ver. 14, "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; behold a virgin shall conceive and bear a son;" and the 16th verse says, "And before this child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land which thou abhorrest or dreadest [meaning Syria and the kingdom of Israel] shall be forsaken of both her kings." Here then was the sign, and the time limited for the completion of the assurance or promise; namely, before this child shall know to refuse the evil and choose the good.

parts.author: Thomas Paine
parts.work: The Age of Reason, Part II
parts.ref: Thomas Paine, The Age of Reason, Part II
parts.title: The misapplication of the passage
parts.context: Thomas Paine (1737–1809) published Part II of The Age of Reason in 1795. 'Isa. vii. I4' is printed so in the source, for 7:14. 'Cant' means empty, pious jargon. His language about the virgin birth is deliberately offensive; it is printed as he wrote it, because the case should be heard at full strength.
parts.plain: Paine says the compilers of the Bible bent every phrase to fit the idea of Jesus as the Son of God, and printed Christian headings at the top of every page so that readers would believe before they read. Take Isaiah 7:14: in its own context, Isaiah is reassuring King Ahaz, frightened by two invading kings, that they will not succeed, and the sign is a child who will be born and grow up before they are gone. It has nothing to do with Jesus, Paine says, 'no more reference to Christ and his mother, than it has to me and my mother'.

commentary.on: Every phrase and circumstance are marked with the barbarous hand of superstitious torture, and forced into meanings it was impossible they could have.
commentary.text: The objection in one sentence: Christians have forced the Jewish Scriptures to say what they wanted.

commentary.on: The head of every chapter, and the top of every page, are blazoned with the names of Christ and the Church
commentary.text: Paine means the chapter headings printed in Bibles of his day, such as 'Christ's birth foretold', which told readers what to find before they read.

commentary.on: I mean only to show the misapplication of the passage
commentary.text: Paine's method is a historian's: read the verse in its own time and place. Modern scholars, believing and not, all do the same.

commentary.on: Here then was the sign, and the time limited for the completion of the assurance or promise
commentary.text: This is Paine's strongest point. The sign had a deadline in Ahaz's own lifetime.

compare.work: The Age of Reason, Part II
compare.ref: Thomas Paine, The Age of Reason, Part II
compare.why: Thomas Paine put the case against with all the force of the Enlightenment. Read his argument about Isaiah 7:14.
compare.title: Forced into meanings

paras: Put most sharply: the Old Testament is Israel's library, written over a thousand years by many hands, with its own meanings. The New Testament writers, convinced that Jesus was the Messiah, searched it for proof and found it by taking verses out of context. Matthew's 'fulfilments' are the clearest case. If the unity of the Bible depends on readings like these, it is a unity imposed by Christians, not found in the texts.

Jews add a further point. Their Bible is complete as it is. The Messiah the prophets promised was to bring peace among nations, gather Israel and rebuild the Temple; the world after Jesus did not look like that. To call Israel's Scriptures the 'Old' Testament is to say that they are out of date, which Jews have never accepted.
sections.key: Many hands, verses out of context, a unity imposed later; and for Jews, a Bible complete without the New Testament.

paras: The best answer begins by conceding Paine's point about first meanings. Hosea was not predicting Jesus, and Isaiah's sign was for Ahaz. But Matthew's word 'fulfil' (pleroō) means 'fill up', not only 'come true'. Matthew reads Jesus as reliving Israel's story: out of Egypt, through water, forty days in the desert, up a mountain to teach. The patterns of the earlier acts are filled with a fuller meaning.

Christians have called this typology: earlier people and events as 'types' or patterns of later ones. Augustine put it in a famous phrase: the New is hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New (Questions on the Heptateuch 2.73). It is a reading of faith, from the end of the story back; it does not claim that the first authors foresaw everything.
sections.key: Paine is right about first meanings; 'fulfil' means fill up a pattern. Typology reads backwards from the end, in faith.

paras: Scholars of every kind agree that the Bible contains many voices which sometimes disagree. Some Christian scholars, such as Brevard Childs, argued that the unity lies in the final shape of the canon, the way the books were gathered and ordered, rather than in each author's intention. Others, such as Walter Brueggemann, prefer to hear the Old Testament as a chorus of 'testimony and counter-testimony' without forcing it into one line.

Many Christians now also say plainly that the Hebrew Bible has its own integrity, that Jews read it faithfully without the New Testament, and that 'Old' should mean 'first', not 'obsolete'. The church's rejection of Marcion was a decision to keep the Jewish Scriptures as Scripture, not to replace them.
sections.key: Many voices: unity in the final shape of the canon (Childs), or a chorus (Brueggemann). The Hebrew Bible has its own integrity; the church kept it against Marcion.

paras: If the Bible is only a library, it can still be read with profit, as great literature. If it is one story, it claims to tell the story of the world, and of your life within it. The question cannot be settled by the texts alone; it depends on whether the claim at the centre, that Jesus rose from the dead, is true.
sections.key: Whether the Bible is one story depends, in the end, on its centre: the resurrection.

sessions.title: The church, and the end of the story
sessions.line: Act 7: the Spirit comes, the message goes to every nation, and the Bible ends with a new creation where it began, in a garden with the tree of life.
sessions.plain: Fifty days after the resurrection, at the Jewish feast of Pentecost, the disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit and speak to a crowd from every nation, each hearing in their own language. The church spreads from Jerusalem across the Roman world, as Acts and the letters tell. The Bible ends with Revelation's vision of a new heaven and a new earth: God living with his people, no more death or tears, and the tree of life from Genesis growing again. We live, Christians say, in this seventh act.
sessions.why: Session 6 asked whether the story holds together. The last act is where Christians say it is heading, and the verdict on the whole journey.
answers: What happened at Pentecost, and why does it matter for the story?
How does the Bible end?
How do the end and the beginning match?
So, is the Bible one story, and where are we in it?
sessions.finding: In act 7 the scattering of Babel is reversed at Pentecost, the promise to Abraham goes to every nation, and the story ends where it began, in a garden city where God lives with his people; whether it is one story depends on its centre, the resurrection.

paras: Acts tells how the first followers of Jesus received the Spirit at Pentecost and took the message from Jerusalem to Rome. The letters, mostly by Paul, were written to the first churches between about AD 50 and 100. The last book, Revelation, was written by a Christian called John on the island of Patmos, probably around AD 95, in the language of visions.
Christians believe this act is still going on: the church's mission to every nation, waiting for the end that Revelation describes.
background.key: Acts, the letters and Revelation: the church's mission, which Christians believe is still going on.

paras: Pentecost (Acts 2) and the last two chapters of the Bible (Revelation 21–22). The comparison is the last chapter of Augustine's City of God, where he counts the whole story as seven ages and ends with the eternal Sabbath.
background.key: Pentecost and the new creation; then Augustine's seven ages.

In Revelation 21, what is no more?
