paras: Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place.
Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting.
Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.
Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under the sky.
When this sound was heard, the multitude came together and were bewildered, because everyone heard them speaking in his own language.
They were all amazed and marveled, saying to one another, “Behold, aren’t all these who speak Galileans?
How do we hear, everyone in our own native language?
Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia,
Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, the parts of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes,
Cretans and Arabians: we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!”
I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more.
I saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband.
I heard a loud voice out of heaven saying, “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away.”
He who sits on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” He said, “Write, for these words of God are faithful and true.”
He showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb,

in the middle of its street. On this side of the river and on that was the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruits, yielding its fruit every month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
There will be no curse any more. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will serve him.
They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.
There will be no night, and they need no lamp light or sun light; for the Lord God will illuminate them. They will reign forever and ever.

parts.title: Every one in our own language
parts.context: Pentecost was the Jewish harvest festival fifty days after Passover, when Jerusalem was full of pilgrims from across the world. Jesus had told his disciples to wait there for the Spirit (Acts 1:8).

commentary.on: Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them
commentary.text: Fire on the mountain at Sinai, fire on each person at Pentecost: the new covenant, written on the heart.

commentary.on: everyone heard them speaking in his own language
commentary.text: Babel reversed. At Babel one language was confused and humanity scattered; here many languages hear one message and are gathered. Not one language for all, but every language honoured.

commentary.on: we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!
commentary.text: The promise to Abraham, 'all the families of the earth', begins to come true: Parthians, Egyptians, Romans, Arabs.

parts.title: All things new
parts.context: Revelation was written to churches under Roman pressure, around AD 95. After visions of judgement, it ends with this.

commentary.on: I saw a new heaven and a new earth
commentary.text: The Bible ends not with souls escaping to heaven, but with heaven and earth renewed. Act 7 answers act 1.

commentary.on: God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them
commentary.text: In Eden God walked in the garden; at Sinai he came down on the mountain; in Jesus 'the Word became flesh, and lived among us'. At the end, God lives with his people for ever.

commentary.on: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more
commentary.text: The curse of Genesis 3, pain and death, is undone.

commentary.on: Behold, I am making all things new.
commentary.text: Not all new things, but all things new: the old creation healed, not thrown away.

parts.title: The tree of life
parts.context: The last chapter of the Bible.

commentary.on: the tree of life
commentary.text: The tree of life was last seen in Genesis 3, guarded so that no one could reach it. Now it grows on both sides of the river. The story ends where it began.

commentary.on: The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
commentary.text: The scattered nations of Babel are healed.

commentary.on: They will see his face
commentary.text: In Genesis 3 the man and woman hid from God's presence. At the end they see his face.

paras: There shall be accomplished the words of the psalm, "Be still, and know that I am God." There shall be the great Sabbath which has no evening, which God celebrated among His first works, as it is written, "And God rested on the seventh day from all His works which He had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it; because that in it He had rested from all His work which God began to make." For we shall ourselves be the seventh day, when we shall be filled and replenished with God's blessing and sanctification. There shall we be still, and know that He is God; that He is that which we ourselves aspired to be when we fell away from Him, and listened to the voice of the seducer, "Ye shall be as gods," and so abandoned God, who would have made us as gods, not by deserting Him, but by participating in Him. For without Him what have we accomplished, save to perish in His anger? But when we are restored by Him, and perfected with greater grace, we shall have eternal leisure to see that He is God, for we shall be full of Him when He shall be all in all. For even our good works, when they are understood to be rather His than ours, are imputed to us that we may enjoy this Sabbath rest. For if we attribute them to ourselves, they shall be servile; for it is said of the Sabbath, "Ye shall do no servile work in it." Wherefore also it is said by Ezekiel the prophet, "And I gave them my Sabbaths to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctify them." This knowledge shall be perfected when we shall be perfectly at rest, and shall perfectly know that He is God.

This Sabbath shall appear still more clearly if we count the ages as days, in accordance with the periods of time defined in Scripture, for that period will be found to be the seventh. The first age, as the first day, extends from Adam to the deluge; the second from the deluge to Abraham, equalling the first, not in length of time, but in the number of generations, there being ten in each. From Abraham to the advent of Christ there are, as the evangelist Matthew calculates, three periods, in each of which are fourteen generations,—one period from Abraham to David, a second from David to the captivity, a third from the captivity to the birth of Christ in the flesh. There are thus five ages in all. The sixth is now passing, and cannot be measured by any number of generations, as it has been said, "It is not for you to know the times, which the Father hath put in His own power." After this period God shall rest as on the seventh day, when He shall give us (who shall be the seventh day) rest in Himself. But there is not now space to treat of these ages; suffice it to say that the seventh shall be our Sabbath, which shall be brought to a close, not by an evening, but by the Lord's day, as an eighth and eternal day, consecrated by the resurrection of Christ, and prefiguring the eternal repose not only of the spirit, but also of the body. There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise. This is what shall be in the end without end. For what other end do we propose to ourselves than to attain to the kingdom of which there is no end?

I think I have now, by God's help, discharged my obligation in writing this large work. Let those who think I have said too little, or those who think I have said too much, forgive me; and let those who think I have said just enough join me in giving thanks to God. Amen.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.ref: Augustine, The City of God XXII.30
parts.title: The great Sabbath which has no evening
parts.context: The last chapter of The City of God, finished about 426, after thirteen years' work. Translated by Marcus Dods (1871).
parts.plain: Augustine says the end will be the great Sabbath, God's rest, which we ourselves will share. If the ages of history are counted like the days of creation, there are seven: Adam to the flood, the flood to Abraham, Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to Christ, the present age, and the seventh, our rest in God. Then comes an eighth, eternal day, begun by Christ's resurrection. There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise.

commentary.on: There shall be the great Sabbath which has no evening
commentary.text: Genesis 1 ends each day with 'there was evening'. The seventh day has no evening: Augustine reads it as the endless rest God made us for.

commentary.on: The first age, as the first day, extends from Adam to the deluge
commentary.text: The seven ages are the first Christian map of the whole story, and the ancestor of this journey's seven acts.

commentary.on: There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise.
commentary.text: Augustine's last word on the end of the story, and one of the most famous sentences he wrote.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.ref: Augustine, The City of God XXII.30
compare.why: Augustine ended The City of God by counting the whole story as seven ages, like the days of creation, ending in a Sabbath with no evening.
compare.title: The seventh day

paras: The Bible's last act answers its first ones, point by point. At Babel the nations were scattered; at Pentecost they are gathered, each in its own language. In Genesis 3 humanity hid from God's face; in Revelation 22 they see it. The tree of life, barred in Genesis, grows by the river. Death, which entered in act 2, is no more. Christians call this the new creation.
sections.key: Pentecost reverses Babel; Revelation answers Genesis: the face of God, the tree of life, death no more.

paras: Is the Bible one story? It is many books by many hands, and session 6 showed that some of its links are made from the end, by faith, not found by every reader. Jews read the first part as a complete story of its own. But the shape is not invented from nothing: the Bible tells and retells its own story, in Deuteronomy, Nehemiah, the Psalms and Acts, and its last pages answer its first ones so precisely that the ending seems written with the beginning in mind.

Christians believe the story holds together because of its centre: if Jesus rose from the dead, then the patterns are not coincidence, and the story is the true story of the world. That claim cannot be settled in one journey. But knowing the shape is the first step: without it, the pieces make little sense.
sections.key: Many books, one shape: the Bible retells itself, and its end answers its beginning. Its unity rests on its centre, the resurrection.

sections.h: Where we are in the story
paras: Christians say we live in act 7: after the resurrection, before the end. Tom Wright compared the Christian life to actors who have the script of a play's first acts and its final scene, and must improvise the missing part faithfully. Every other journey in Explore is a part of that improvisation: what Christians have thought, made and done in the seventh act.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Tell the Bible's story in your own words, in about 300 words, in seven acts. Then say whether you think it is one story, and answer the strongest objection.
closing.practice: Over the next month, read one key chapter from each act: Genesis 1 and 3, Genesis 12, Exodus 20, 2 Samuel 7 and Jeremiah 31, Luke 24, Acts 2 and Revelation 21.
synthesis: This journey asked what story the Bible tells. Here is the answer in seven acts.
Act 1, creation: God makes a good world and human beings in his image to care for it. Act 2, the fall: they break trust, hide and blame; violence spreads, and at Babel humanity is scattered.

Act 3, the promise: God calls Abraham and promises that through his family every family on earth will be blessed. The family is flawed; Genesis ends with Joseph forgiving his brothers: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good'.

Act 4, rescue and covenant: God hears the cry of Abraham's descendants, enslaved in Egypt, brings them out under Moses and binds himself to them at Sinai. The law begins with grace: 'I brought you out'. Israel retold this story every year as its own.

Act 5, kingdom and exile: in the land, Israel gets kings and a promise that David's throne will last for ever; it breaks the covenant and goes into exile in 587 BC. The prophets promise a new covenant written on the heart and a king from David's line. The Old Testament ends waiting.

Act 6, Jesus: he announces that the time is fulfilled, dies at Passover, and his followers proclaim him risen. He explains 'all the Scriptures' as pointing to him; his followers tell Israel's story as ending in him.

Act 7, the church and the end: at Pentecost Babel is reversed and the message goes to every nation; the Bible ends with a new heaven and earth, God living with his people, death no more, and the tree of life growing again.

Is it one story? It is many books by many hands, and some of its links are made from the end, in faith; Jews read the first part as complete. But the Bible retells its own story again and again, and its end answers its beginning point by point. Christians believe it holds together because of its centre, the resurrection. Whether or not you share that belief, you now know the shape that every other journey in Explore assumes.

title: What is the Bible?
question: What kind of book is the Bible, where did it come from, and does it hold up?
line: Seven sessions that test the Bible the way you would test any old story: what it is, where both Testaments came from, whether it has been copied faithfully, what archaeology and Roman and Jewish writers say, the strongest case against it, and the verdict.
why: Once you know the Bible's story, the next question is what kind of book it is and whether it deserves a hearing. This journey weighs the evidence the way a historian would: the writers' own claims, the formation of both Testaments and how the churches' Bibles differ, the eyewitness question, archaeology and the Roman and Jewish writers, the manuscripts and the canon. Then it gives the sceptic the floor at full strength, and ends with Augustine on how to read honestly. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year theology paper introducing the study of the Bible: its formation, canon, text and interpretation, with the historical-critical method and its critics.
outcomes: Explain what the Bible is, and exactly how Jewish, Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and views of its authority differ.
Describe how the Old Testament came together and why Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles differ.

State Spinoza's case against the traditional authorship of the Pentateuch at full strength, and say which parts of it are now widely accepted and which conclusions do not follow.
Use Augustine's principles and the four senses to read a passage of Scripture carefully and honestly.

sessions.title: What the Bible is
sessions.line: A library of many books, and why the churches' Bibles differ.
sessions.plain: The Bible is not one book but a library: law, history, poetry, prophecy, letters and biographies, written by many people over more than a thousand years. Jews, Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox Christians do not even agree on exactly which books it contains. Before asking whether it can be trusted, you need to know what it is.
sessions.why: Most arguments about the Bible go wrong at the start, because people treat it as one book of one kind. This session gives you the map: what is in the library, how the churches' Bibles differ, and what the biblical writers themselves claimed.
answers: What exactly is the Bible?
Why are Jewish, Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles different?
How do the churches differ on the Bible's authority?
What did the biblical writers claim for their own work?
before: Each of these writers says something about how their words came to be. What does each one claim?
Does anyone here claim to be a neutral observer?
What is the Bible said to be for?
sessions.readWhy: Four short passages in which biblical writers tell us what they were doing: a letter on the many ways God has spoken, a historian explaining his method, a Gospel writer stating his purpose, and a teacher describing what the Scriptures are for. Before anyone else judges the Bible, hear how it describes itself.

paras: God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways,
has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.
Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us,
even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us,
it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus;
that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.
Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.
But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them.
From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus.
Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

parts.title: God spoke in many ways
parts.context: The opening of the Letter to the Hebrews, written in elegant Greek by an unknown early Christian, probably before AD 70, to Jewish believers tempted to drift back from their new faith. Its first sentence is a summary of the whole Bible.

commentary.on: at many times and in various ways
commentary.text: The writer knows the Scriptures are not one voice from the sky. They came over many centuries, through many people, in many forms: law, story, song, prophecy. Hold on to this phrase; it is the key to this whole session. The Bible is a library, and its variety is not an embarrassment but part of how it says God spoke.

commentary.on: through the prophets
commentary.text: In the Bible a prophet is not mainly a fortune-teller. A prophet is a spokesman, someone who speaks for God to his own generation, often to rebuke kings and call the people back to justice.

commentary.on: has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son
commentary.text: Here is the Christian claim in a sentence. God's speaking reaches its climax not in a book but in a person. That is why Christians read the whole library, Old Testament included, as leading up to Jesus. It also means that, for a Christian, trusting the Bible is in the end about trusting him.

parts.title: A historian's preface
parts.context: The first four verses of Luke's Gospel, written in the later first century by a companion of Paul who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles. In Greek it is one long, polished sentence, in the style of the historians of the day.

commentary.on: many have undertaken to set in order a narrative
commentary.text: Luke is not the first to write about Jesus, and he says so. Written accounts were already circulating. Most scholars think Mark's Gospel was one of them, since Luke uses much of it.

commentary.on: those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us
commentary.text: Luke does not claim to have seen the events himself. He claims something more modest and more checkable: that his sources go back to people who were there from the start. 'Delivered' is a technical word for handing on a tradition carefully. Session 3 tests this claim.

commentary.on: having traced the course of all things accurately from the first
commentary.text: This is the language of research. Luke presents himself as a careful investigator, and in session 5 you will see how his details about rulers and places hold up against archaeology.

commentary.on: that you might know the certainty
commentary.text: His purpose is not entertainment but confidence. Theophilus ('friend of God') has already been taught the faith; Luke wants him to know it rests on solid ground. Notice that the Bible's own writers thought evidence mattered.

parts.title: Written that you may believe
parts.context: Near the end of John's Gospel, probably the last of the four to be written, in the 90s AD. The writer pauses to tell us why he wrote.

commentary.on: many other signs ... which are not written in this book
commentary.text: John admits he has been selective. Every historian selects; the question is whether the selection distorts. John's honesty about it is worth noticing.

commentary.on: these are written, that you may believe
commentary.text: John is open about his purpose: not neutral reporting but testimony meant to persuade. Sceptics sometimes say this makes the Gospels worthless as history. But a witness with a purpose can still be telling the truth; a survivor who writes to warn the world is no less reliable for wanting to warn it. The question is not whether a writer has a point of view, but whether the testimony is true.

parts.title: What the Scriptures are for
parts.context: From a letter to Timothy, Paul's younger colleague, presented as Paul's last letter before his execution in Rome in the mid-60s AD. (Many modern scholars think it was written by a follower in Paul's name; session 6 explains why.)

commentary.on: From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures
commentary.text: Timothy's mother was Jewish and his father Greek (Acts 16:1). He grew up with the Jewish Scriptures, our Old Testament. When this letter says 'Scripture', that is chiefly what it means: the New Testament was still being written.

commentary.on: Every Scripture is God-breathed
commentary.text: One Greek word, theopneustos, found only here. It says the Scriptures come from God as breath comes from a mouth. Christians have understood this in different ways, but most have held that God worked through the human writers, with their own styles and knowledge, rather than dictating to them like a secretary.

commentary.on: profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness
commentary.text: Notice what inspiration is for. Not to answer every question we might ask, about science, say, but to form a person: to teach, to correct and to train in right living. Judge the Bible by what it says it is for.

paras: I resolved then to bend my mind to the holy Scriptures, that I might see what they were. But behold, I see a thing not understood by the proud, nor laid open to children, lowly in access, in its recesses lofty, and veiled with mysteries; and I was not such as could enter into it, or stoop my neck to follow its steps. For not as I now speak, did I feel when I turned to those Scriptures; but they seemed to me unworthy to be compared to the stateliness of Tully: for my swelling pride shrunk from their lowliness, nor could my sharp wit pierce the interior thereof. Yet were they such as would grow up in a little one. But I disdained to be a little one; and, swollen with pride, took myself to be a great one.

parts.title: Unworthy of Cicero?
parts.context: Augustine of Hippo (354–430), later a bishop and the most influential thinker of the Latin West, wrote his Confessions around 397–400 as a prayer to God telling the story of his life. Here he looks back to the age of nineteen, when he was a brilliant young teacher of rhetoric in Carthage.
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: the stateliness of Tully
commentary.text: 'Tully' is Cicero, Marcus Tullius Cicero, the master of Latin prose. Augustine had just been bowled over by Cicero's call to love wisdom. Next to Cicero, the Latin Bible of the day, a rough translation, seemed clumsy and provincial.

commentary.on: lowly in access, in its recesses lofty
commentary.text: This is the older Augustine's verdict, and one of the best descriptions of the Bible ever written. It is simple enough at the door for a child to walk in, and deep enough inside that no scholar reaches the end of it.

commentary.on: I disdained to be a little one
commentary.text: Augustine's problem, he now thinks, was not the Bible's style but his own pride. You need not agree with him. But notice that first impressions of the Bible can mislead, and that he changed his mind after years of reading it. You will meet him again in the last session.

parts.plain: Augustine says: when I was young and proud, I tried reading the Bible, but it seemed plain and clumsy next to the great Roman writer Cicero. I didn't see that it is easy to walk into but very deep inside. I was too proud to become like a child and learn from it.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.why: One of the cleverest men of the fourth century describes his first attempt to read the Bible. He found it crude next to Cicero's polished Latin, and gave up. Many readers today will recognise the feeling.
compare.title: A clever man's first reaction

paras: Our word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, 'the books', a plural. That is the first thing to know. The Bible is a library bound in one cover: in a Protestant Bible, 39 books in the Old Testament and 27 in the New, 66 in all.

These books were written over more than a thousand years by kings, prophets, priests, fishermen, a tax collector, a doctor and a tentmaker, in three languages: Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek. They include law codes, family stories, royal chronicles, love poetry, hymns, proverbs, prophetic visions, four biographies of Jesus and a collection of letters.
sections.key: The Bible is a library of many books, by many writers, in three languages, over more than a thousand years.

sections.h: Read each book as what it is
paras: Because the Bible holds so many kinds of writing, the first rule is to ask what kind you are reading. A psalm is a poem: when it says 'Let the rivers clap their hands' (Psalm 98:8), nobody is meant to look for palms. A proverb is a general truth, not a guarantee. A letter answers questions we have to reconstruct. A history tells what happened, selected and shaped to show what it meant.

Many arguments for and against the Bible go wrong here. Sceptics sometimes read poetry as if it were a science textbook and find it absurd; believers sometimes do the same and end up defending what the writer never claimed.
sections.key: The first rule of reading is to ask what kind of writing you are reading.

paras: The Old Testament is the Bible of Israel, which Jews call the Tanakh, from the initials of its three parts: the Torah (the Law, the five books of Moses), the Nevi'im (the Prophets) and the Ketuvim (the Writings). Jesus and his first followers were Jews, and this was their Bible.

The New Testament was written by Christians in Greek within about seventy years of Jesus' death: four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, letters, and the Revelation to John. 'Testament' means covenant: the old covenant with Israel, and what Christians believe is the new covenant in Jesus, promised by the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31).
sections.key: The Old Testament was Israel's Bible and Jesus' own; the New was written by his followers within about seventy years.

sections.h: Whose Bible? How the canons differ
paras: Here is something many Christians never learn: the churches do not have the same list of books. The differences are all in the Old Testament. Jews and Protestants follow the Hebrew collection. Catholics and the Orthodox also accept books that were in the Greek translation used by the first Christians, the Septuagint, which you will meet in the next session.
The New Testament's 27 books are the same in almost every church. The table shows the main differences.

rows: 24 books: the same text as the Protestant 39, counted differently
39 books, following the Hebrew canon; the extra Greek books are called the Apocrypha and printed separately, if at all
46 books: adds Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach and Baruch, and longer Esther and Daniel (the 'deuterocanonical' books), defined at the Council of Trent in 1546
About 49 books, following the Septuagint: the Catholic additions plus 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh and Psalm 151; lists vary a little between churches
A broader list that also includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees
27, with further books in its broader canon
table.note: The Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (1571) say the Apocrypha may be read 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but not to establish doctrine.

sections.key: Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments include books from the Greek Bible that Jews and Protestants leave out; the New Testament is shared.

sections.h: Who has the last word? How the churches differ on authority
paras: The churches also differ on how the Bible relates to the Church's teaching. All agree that Scripture is inspired. They disagree about who interprets it and whether anything stands beside it.
These differences go back to the Reformation of the sixteenth century, and you will meet them again in Hall VI. For now, it is enough to see them side by side.

rows: Scripture alone (sola scriptura): the Bible judges all church teaching
Every believer may read it, and it is clear on what is needed for salvation
King James Version, New International Version, English Standard Version
Scripture and Tradition together, 'one sacred deposit', interpreted by the Church's teaching office (the Magisterium)
Hebrew text, with Greek for the extra books; Jerome's Latin Vulgate was official for centuries
Every believer should read it; the teaching office gives the authoritative interpretation
Douay–Rheims, Jerusalem Bible, New American Bible
Scripture as the heart of Holy Tradition, read as the Church has always read it, above all by the Fathers and the councils
It is read within the worshipping Church; the liturgy itself is its great commentary
Orthodox Study Bible (with a Septuagint Old Testament)

sections.key: Protestants hold Scripture alone as final; Catholics hold Scripture and Tradition together under the Church's teaching office; the Orthodox read Scripture within Holy Tradition.

paras: Notice what the passages you read claim, and what they do not. Hebrews says God spoke in many ways. Luke claims careful research and sources going back to eyewitnesses. John claims testimony with an open purpose. The letter to Timothy claims that the Scriptures are God-breathed and useful for forming a life. None claims to be a neutral observer, and none claims to answer every question we might put to it.

Most Christians have held that God worked through the human writers rather than dictating to them. That is why Luke can say he researched, why each Gospel sounds like its author, and why the Bible can be studied as human writing without ceasing, for believers, to be the word of God. Muslims believe something different about the Qur'an: that it was dictated word for word.
sections.key: The writers claim research, testimony and inspiration, not neutrality; most Christians believe God worked through their human voices.

refs: Canon lists: Council of Trent, Session IV (8 April 1546); Thirty-Nine Articles (1571), Art. VI; Westminster Confession (1646), ch. 1; Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672).
Dei Verbum, Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation (Second Vatican Council, 1965), §§9–10.
On the Ethiopian canon: R. W. Cowley, 'The Biblical Canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Today', Ostkirchliche Studien 23 (1974).
Languages: Aramaic in Daniel 2:4–7:28, Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26.
On reading by genre: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth (1981).

debate.question: Is the Bible one book or a library?

positions.name: One Word
positions.who: Most of the Christian tradition
positions.view: Behind the many human writers stands one divine author, so the Bible can be read as a single, coherent message, each part interpreting the others.
positions.evidence: The unity of its story from creation to new creation; the way the New Testament reads the Old; Jesus' own reading in Luke 24.

positions.name: Many voices
positions.who: Many modern historians of the Bible
positions.view: The Bible is an anthology of very different writings from different times, which sometimes disagree. Its unity was imposed later by the communities that collected it.
positions.evidence: Differences of language, date, theology and detail between books, such as the four Gospels.

positions.name: Both at once
positions.who: Many theologians today, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant
positions.view: God speaks through real human voices, with all their variety. The diversity is part of the message, and the unity lies in the story they tell together rather than in uniformity.
positions.evidence: The early Church chose to keep four Gospels rather than one harmonised account.

debate.agree: All agree that each book must be read for what it is, and that the Bible has shaped the West more than any other text.

look.why: For most of history people heard the Scriptures read aloud. Carpaccio, around 1505, painted Mary reading a small book alone, which was becoming possible for more people as printing made books cheaper.
points: A woman in a burgundy-red dress with a faint gold halo, reading a small book with a red cover.
One finger kept between the pages, as if she will come back to her place.
Behind a low white wall, a yellow meadow runs down to pale blue water, with hills, a few white buildings and a tower beyond.
At the left edge, a shoulder, an elbow and a foot of someone in midnight blue: a hint that the painting was once part of a larger picture.

music.why: Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil (1915) sets psalms and biblical canticles sung in Orthodox worship: the Bible as most Christians have met it, sung and heard rather than read alone.

think.why: Christians call both the Scriptures and Christ 'the Word'. This depth explains what John meant by it.

learn.why: The Bible's shortest answer to what it is for: light for the next step, not a map of everything.

check.q: A Catholic and a Protestant compare their Bibles. What is the real difference?
options: The Protestant Bible leaves out some of the Psalms
The Catholic Old Testament has seven more books, and longer Esther and Daniel, from the Greek Bible
The Catholic Bible includes Gospels written after AD 300
They have different New Testaments
check.why: Both share the same 27 New Testament books. The difference is the deuterocanonical books of the Septuagint, which Protestants call the Apocrypha.

check.q: A Jewish friend calls her Bible the Tanakh; a Christian friend calls the same books the Old Testament. Why the different names?
options: They are completely different books
Christians believe God made a new covenant in Jesus, so they call the earlier Scriptures the 'old' covenant; Jews do not accept the New Testament
The Torah is only for rabbis
Christians do not read these books
check.why: Same books, different order and different names, because Jews and Christians read them in different lights.

check.q: What does Luke claim in his preface, and what does he not claim?
options: He claims to have seen the events himself
He claims to have researched accounts handed down from eyewitnesses, not to have been one
He claims that God dictated the text to him
He claims to be the first to write about Jesus
check.why: He says 'many' had already written, and that his sources go back to 'eyewitnesses and servants of the word'.

check.q: Why is it a mistake to quote 2 Timothy 3:16 ('Every Scripture is God-breathed') as the New Testament's claim about itself?
options: The verse was added in the Middle Ages
When it was written, 'Scripture' meant chiefly the Jewish Scriptures; the New Testament was still being written
Paul did not believe in inspiration
'God-breathed' only means 'poetic'
check.why: Timothy had known these Scriptures 'from infancy', which can only mean the Jewish Bible.

check.q: Which Old Testament does the Orthodox Church treat as its own?
options: The Hebrew Masoretic text
The Greek Septuagint
Jerome's Latin Vulgate
The King James Version
check.why: The Septuagint was the Bible of the Greek-speaking first Christians, and Orthodox churches still use it.

check.q: On authority, what really separates the Protestant principle from the Catholic one?
options: Protestants reject all tradition; Catholics do not read the Bible
Protestants hold Scripture to be the final judge of all teaching; Catholics hold Scripture and Tradition together, interpreted by the Church's teaching office
Only Catholics believe the Bible is inspired
Protestants accept more books than Catholics
check.why: Both hold Scripture inspired; they differ on whether anything stands beside it and who interprets it.

check.q: A sceptic quotes 'Let the rivers clap their hands' as proof the Bible is unscientific. What is the best reply?
options: The verse is a mistranslation
It is a poem, and mistaking its genre is the sceptic's error
Rivers did once make that sound
The Psalms are not really part of the Bible
check.why: Reading poetry as a science textbook is the commonest mistake about the Bible, made by sceptics and believers alike.

tutorial.question: Is it fair to call the Bible 'a library, not a book'? What follows for how it should be read, and for the differences between the churches?
tutorial.approach: Describe its variety (writers, centuries, languages, kinds of writing). Explain why Christians have nevertheless read it as one story. Use Luke and John to show what the writers claimed. Then explain the differences in canon and authority between Jews, Protestants, Catholics and the Orthodox, and say what they have in common.
strong: Shows the real variety: dates, authors, languages, genres.
Explains the unity Christians find: one story from creation to new creation.
Uses the writers' own claims (Luke's research, John's purpose).
Explains accurately why the canons differ (the Septuagint and the deuterocanonical books).
Explains the difference between sola scriptura, Scripture and Tradition, and Holy Tradition.
Draws practical rules: read by genre; ask what the writer claimed; read the parts in the light of the whole.

reading.author: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart
reading.title: How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth
reading.why: A clear guide to reading each kind of biblical writing.

reading.author: Karen Armstrong
reading.title: The Bible: A Biography
reading.why: A short history of how the Bible was written and read, by a writer outside the churches.

reading.author: John Barton
reading.title: A History of the Bible
reading.why: An Oxford scholar's full account, honest about difficulties, with a good chapter on the canons.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read one whole short book of the Bible in a single sitting (Ruth, Jonah, Mark or Philippians), the way it was meant to be heard, and tell someone what kind of writing it was.
sessions.reflect: What did you assume the Bible was before this session? What, if anything, has changed?
takeaways: The Bible is a library: many writers, three languages, more than a thousand years; each book must be read for what it is.
Jews and Protestants follow the Hebrew canon; Catholics and the Orthodox also accept books from the Greek Bible; the New Testament is shared.
Its writers claim research, testimony and inspiration, not neutrality; whether to trust them is what the rest of the journey weighs.
sessions.finding: The Bible is a library of many books. Christians agree on the New Testament and differ only over a few Old Testament books.

background.h: If you have never read the Bible
paras: That is fine. Most people today haven't, and this journey assumes nothing. You do not need to believe anything to follow it. You only need to be willing to look at the evidence.

The Bible is the sacred book of Christians, and its first and larger part is also the sacred book of Jews. It is not one book but a collection of sixty-six or more books, written over a very long time. Christians divide it into two parts: the Old Testament, written before Jesus, and the New Testament, written by his followers after his death.
background.key: The Bible is a collection of books: the Old Testament before Jesus, the New Testament after him.

paras: The Old Testament opens with God creating the world and human beings, and humans turning away from him. It then follows one family, Abraham's, to whom God promises a land and a blessing for all nations. Abraham's descendants, the Israelites, become slaves in Egypt and are led out by Moses, who receives God's law at Mount Sinai. They settle in Canaan (roughly modern Israel and Palestine), are ruled by kings such as David and Solomon, and are warned by prophets when they turn to injustice and other gods. Their kingdoms are destroyed by the empires of Assyria and Babylon, and many are taken into exile. Some return, rebuild Jerusalem and its Temple, and wait for God to act again.

The New Testament tells of Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher born into that waiting people under Roman rule. He preached, healed, was crucified by the Romans in Jerusalem, and his followers proclaimed that God had raised him from the dead. It then follows the first Christians as the message spread across the Roman Empire, through their letters, and ends with a vision of a renewed creation.
background.key: Creation, Abraham, Moses, the kings and prophets, exile and return; then Jesus, and the first Christians.

background.h: Torah, Hebrew Bible, Old Testament: what's the difference?
paras: These names confuse almost everyone, so here they are simply. The Torah (Hebrew for 'teaching' or 'instruction') is the first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. They tell the story from creation to the death of Moses, and contain the law God gave Israel at Mount Sinai. They are also called the Law of Moses or the Pentateuch ('five scrolls').

The Torah is the heart of Judaism. In every synagogue it is handwritten on a scroll, kept in a cabinet called the ark, and read aloud in portions week by week until the whole of it has been read in a year. Jews live by its commandments, as interpreted over centuries by the rabbis in the Talmud. But the Jewish Bible is bigger than the Torah: it adds the Prophets and the Writings (Psalms, Proverbs and others). Jews call the whole thing the Tanakh, or the Hebrew Bible.

Christians call those very same books the Old Testament. 'Testament' means covenant, a binding agreement between God and people. Christians believe that in Jesus God made the 'new covenant' that the prophet Jeremiah had promised (Jeremiah 31:31), so they call the earlier Scriptures the Old Testament and the writings about Jesus the New Testament. 'Old' means earlier, not out of date: the Old Testament is about three-quarters of the Christian Bible. Jews do not use the name, because they do not accept the New Testament, and many scholars say 'Hebrew Bible' to stay neutral.

So do both honour it? Yes. Jews and Christians both treat these books as God's word: the Psalms are prayed in synagogues and churches every day. The difference is how they read them. Jews read them through the Torah and the rabbis' teaching, and keep the Torah's laws, such as the Sabbath and the food laws. Christians read them through Jesus, who said of the law and the prophets, 'I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill' (Matthew 5:17). The first Christians decided that non-Jewish believers need not keep the Jewish ritual laws (Acts 15), but Christians keep the Torah's moral heart: the Ten Commandments, and the two commands Jesus called the greatest, both quoted from the Torah: love God (Deuteronomy 6:5) and love your neighbour as yourself (Leviticus 19:18).

rows: The first five books, Genesis to Deuteronomy
Jews (and everyone, for these five books)
Torah + Prophets + Writings: the whole Jewish Bible
The same books, in a different order (plus a few more for Catholics and Orthodox)
Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation, about Jesus and his first followers

background.key: The Torah is the first five books; the Tanakh is the whole Jewish Bible; Christians call the same books the Old Testament. Both honour them, reading them in different lights.

paras: Here are the main landmarks, so that every passage in this journey has a place. Dates before about 1000 BC are traditional and debated; later ones are firm. BC means 'before Christ', counting down to the year 1; AD (Anno Domini, 'in the year of the Lord') counts up from it. Many historians write BCE and CE for the same years.

timeline.text: Abraham, by tradition
Moses and the Exodus from Egypt, by a common dating
King David; Solomon builds the Temple in Jerusalem
Assyria destroys the northern kingdom of Israel
Assyria besieges Jerusalem under King Hezekiah
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the Temple; exile
Persia conquers Babylon; exiles begin to return
Ezra reads the Law in Jerusalem
Alexander the Great conquers the region; Greek becomes the common language
Rome takes control
Jesus born, shortly before Herod the Great dies
Jesus crucified under Pontius Pilate
Paul's journeys and letters
The four Gospels written, by most scholars' dating
Rome destroys Jerusalem and the Temple

paras: Imagine your family has an old story, handed down for generations, about something that happened to a great-great-grandparent. How would you decide whether to believe it? You would ask a few simple questions, one after another. This journey asks the same questions of the Bible, one per session.

First, what exactly is it (this session)? Second and third, where did it come from, and were the people who wrote it close to what they describe (sessions 2 and 3)? Fourth, has it been passed down without being changed (session 4)? Fifth, does anything outside the story back it up (session 5)? Sixth, what do the people who doubt it say, at their strongest (session 6)? And last, putting it all together, what should we conclude, and how should we read it (session 7)? At the start of each session you will see the case so far.
background.key: Six checks, as for any old family story: what it is, where it came from, faithful copies, outside evidence, the doubters, the verdict.

background.h: Why we start with these passages
paras: Before asking whether the Bible can be trusted, it is only fair to ask what it claims for itself. So this session begins with four short passages, chosen because in each a biblical writer steps back and tells us what he is doing: one says how God spoke through many voices, one explains how he researched, one says why he wrote, and one says what the Scriptures are for.

They come from the New Testament, written in the first century AD, but they look back on the whole library. Each has a short introduction telling you who wrote it and when, then the text, then a commentary walking you through it. Take them slowly: they are short.
background.key: We start with what the Bible's own writers claim, before testing those claims.

sessions.title: How the Old Testament came together
sessions.line: We cannot watch the books being written. But we can catch them in use, at three moments in history.
sessions.plain: Nobody filmed the Old Testament being written, and its books do not come with dates on them. What historians can do is find moments where we see these books existing and being treated as sacred, and the oldest physical copies. This session follows three such moments, 622 BC, 445 BC and AD 95, and the oldest surviving fragments, to answer a simple question: is the Old Testament we read really the ancient book of ancient Israel, or something put together much later?
sessions.why: Session 1 showed what the Bible is. Before we can trust any part of it, we need to know that it is genuinely old, and that it has not been invented or rewritten since. We begin with the Old Testament, the older and larger half.
answers: Who wrote the Old Testament, and when?
How do we know these books are really ancient, and not invented later?
When did they become a fixed collection, and who decided?
Why do Jewish, Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments differ?
before: In each scene, a book is read aloud. What book, and how do people react?
What does each scene tell you about how old the book already was, and how much authority it had?
In the comparison, what does Josephus say about how many books there were, and how his people treated them?
sessions.readWhy: Two scenes, about 180 years apart, where we can watch the Law of Moses being read aloud to the whole people: first under King Josiah in 622 BC, then under Ezra in about 445 BC. Then, in the comparison, a Jewish historian in AD 95 describes the finished collection. Three snapshots of the Old Testament taking shape.

paras: Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the law in Yahweh’s house.” Hilkiah delivered the book to Shaphan, and he read it.

Shaphan the scribe came to the king, and brought the king word again, and said, “Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house, and have delivered it into the hands of the workmen who have the oversight of Yahweh’s house.”
Shaphan the scribe told the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered a book to me.” Then Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king had heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes.
The king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Achbor the son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying,

“Go inquire of Yahweh for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found; for great is Yahweh’s wrath that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not listened to the words of this book, to do according to all that which is written concerning us.”
The king sent, and they gathered to him all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem.

The king went up to Yahweh’s house, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him, with the priests, the prophets, and all the people, both small and great; and he read in their hearing all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in Yahweh’s house.

The king stood by the pillar, and made a covenant before Yahweh, to walk after Yahweh, and to keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and all his soul, to confirm the words of this covenant that were written in this book; and all the people agreed to the covenant.

All the people gathered themselves together as one man into the wide place that was in front of the water gate; and they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which Yahweh had commanded to Israel.
Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly, both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding, on the first day of the seventh month.

He read from it before the wide place that was in front of the water gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women, and of those who could understand. The ears of all the people were attentive to the book of the law.

Ezra the scribe stood on a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people (for he was above all the people), and when he opened it, all the people stood up.
Then Ezra blessed Yahweh, the great God.
All the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” with the lifting up of their hands. They bowed their heads, and worshiped Yahweh with their faces to the ground.

Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law; and the people stayed in their place.
They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading.

Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people, said to all the people, “Today is holy to Yahweh your God. Don’t mourn, nor weep.” For all the people wept when they heard the words of the law.

Then he said to them, “Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord. Don’t be grieved, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.”
So the Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Hold your peace, for the day is holy. Don’t be grieved.”
All the people went their way to eat, to drink, to send portions, and to celebrate, because they had understood the words that were declared to them.

parts.title: Snapshot 1, 622 BC: a book found in the Temple
parts.context: Jerusalem, 622 BC, in the eighteenth year of King Josiah of Judah. Workmen are repairing the Temple, which Solomon had built about 350 years earlier. During the repairs the high priest finds something. This is the first time the Bible describes a book of God's law being read, and it is about 35 years before the Babylonians destroy the city.

commentary.on: I have found the book of the law in Yahweh's house
commentary.text: A book of the law is found in the Temple. Most scholars, ancient and modern, think it was some form of Deuteronomy, the fifth book of Moses, because what Josiah does next, abolishing worship outside Jerusalem and destroying idols (2 Kings 23), follows Deuteronomy's commands closely.

commentary.on: Shaphan the scribe
commentary.text: Notice the scribe. Writing and reading were specialist skills, and royal scribes kept and copied documents. Shaphan's son and grandson appear in Jeremiah 36, which you will read in session 4, and a clay seal of 'Gemaryahu son of Shaphan' has been found in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: When the king had heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes
commentary.text: The king treats the book as carrying God's authority, and is horrified at how far the nation has strayed from it. So by 622 BC there is a written law, believed to be ancient, with power to judge a king.

commentary.on: our fathers have not listened to the words of this book
commentary.text: Here is the great debate. Josiah and the writer of Kings believe this was an old book that had been neglected and lost. Many modern scholars think Deuteronomy, in the form found, was in fact written not long before, perhaps by reforming priests, and 'found' to give their reforms authority. Others think it preserved much older law. Either way, this scene is a fixed point: a written book of the Law existed and was treated as Scripture by 622 BC.

commentary.on: he read in their hearing all the words of the book of the covenant
commentary.text: The king reads the book to everyone, 'small and great', and the people commit themselves to it. The pattern of a nation ordering its life by a written covenant begins here.

parts.title: Snapshot 2, about 445 BC: the Law read at the Water Gate
parts.context: About 180 years later. In between, Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple (587 BC) and took its leaders into exile; Persia conquered Babylon (539 BC) and let the exiles go home. A small, poor community has rebuilt the Temple and, under Nehemiah, the city walls. Now Ezra, a priest and scribe who has come from Persia, brings out 'the book of the law of Moses'.

commentary.on: they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses
commentary.text: This time the book is not a surprising discovery: everyone knows it, and the people ask for it. Most scholars think 'the book of the law of Moses' here means the Torah, the five books from Genesis to Deuteronomy, in something close to their final form. So by about 445 BC the heart of the Old Testament existed as a finished, recognised book.

commentary.on: both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding
commentary.text: The Law is read to the whole community, women included. A people who had lost their king, their independence and their Temple found their identity in a book. That is why they guarded it so carefully, and why this matters for trust: a community that lives by a text has every reason to preserve it exactly.

commentary.on: all the people stood up
commentary.text: They stand when the book is opened. Jews still stand when the Torah scroll is brought out in the synagogue, and many Christians stand for the Gospel. You are watching a practice that is about 2,500 years old.

commentary.on: they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading
commentary.text: The Levites explain the text, perhaps translating it from Hebrew into Aramaic, which many returned exiles now spoke better. From the start the Bible came with teaching. This verse matters later: in session 6, the sceptic Spinoza uses it to argue that Ezra didn't just read the Law but edited it.

parts.title: From tears to a feast
parts.context: The same morning. Hearing the Law after years of neglect, the people are overcome.

commentary.on: all the people wept when they heard the words of the law
commentary.text: They recognise themselves in the text and are grieved by how far they have strayed, just as Josiah was. Two scenes, 180 years apart, with the same reaction: this book was felt to speak with God's voice.

commentary.on: send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared
commentary.text: The leaders turn grief into a feast, and the feast must include the poor. The verse you will learn by heart.

paras: 8. For we have not an innumerable multitude of books among us, disagreeing from and contradicting one another, [as the Greeks have,] but only twenty-two books, [8] which contain the records of all the past times; which are justly believed to be divine; and of them five belong to Moses, which contain his laws and the traditions of the origin of mankind till his death. This interval of time was little short of three thousand years; but as to the time from the death of Moses till the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, who reigned after Xerxes, the prophets, who were after Moses, wrote down what was done in their times in thirteen books. The remaining four books contain hymns to God, and precepts for the conduct of human life. It is true, our history hath been written since Artaxerxes very particularly, but hath not been esteemed of the like authority with the former by our forefathers, because there hath not been an exact succession of prophets since that time; and how firmly we have given credit to these books of our own nation is evident by what we do; for during so many ages as have already passed, no one has been so bold as either to add any thing to them, to take any thing from them, or to make any change in them;

but it is become natural to all Jews immediately, and from their very birth, to esteem these books to contain Divine doctrines, and to persist in them, and, if occasion be willingly to die for them. For it is no new thing for our captives, many of them in number, and frequently in time, to be seen to endure racks and deaths of all kinds upon the theatres, that they may not be obliged to say one word against our laws and the records that contain them; whereas there are none at all among the Greeks who would undergo the least harm on that account, no, nor in case all the writings that are among them were to be destroyed; for they take them to be such discourses as are framed agreeably to the inclinations of those that write them; and they have justly the same opinion of the ancient writers, since they see some of the present generation bold enough to write about such affairs, wherein they were not present, nor had concern enough to inform themselves about them from those that knew them; examples of which may be had in this late war of ours, where some persons have written histories, and published them, without having been in the places concerned, or having been near them when the actions were done; but these men put a few things together by hearsay, and insolently abuse the world, and call these writings by the name of Histories.

parts.title: Twenty-two books
parts.context: Flavius Josephus (about 37–100) was a Jewish priest and general who fought Rome in the war of 66–70, was captured, changed sides and spent the rest of his life writing history in Rome. Against Apion, written around 95, defends the Jewish people against an Egyptian-Greek writer who had attacked them. Here he contrasts Jewish sacred books with the many conflicting histories of the Greeks.
parts.author: Flavius Josephus

commentary.on: only twenty-two books
commentary.text: Josephus' twenty-two are the same as the thirty-nine of the Protestant Old Testament, counted differently: the twelve minor prophets count as one book, Samuel, Kings and Chronicles as one each, Ezra and Nehemiah together, and so on. He does not include the extra books found in the Greek Bible, which is why Protestants leave them out.

commentary.on: five belong to Moses ... the prophets ... wrote down what was done in their times in thirteen books. The remaining four books contain hymns to God
commentary.text: The three-part shape that Jews still use: the Law (Genesis to Deuteronomy), the Prophets, and the Writings (Psalms, Proverbs and the like). Josephus describes it as something every Jew knew.

commentary.on: the reign of Artaxerxes
commentary.text: Artaxerxes I ruled Persia in the fifth century BC, the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. Josephus says later books exist but lack the same authority, because 'there hath not been an exact succession of prophets since that time'. In other words, he believed the collection closed in Ezra's age, the second snapshot.

commentary.on: no one has been so bold as either to add any thing to them, to take any thing from them
commentary.text: A large claim, and he is arguing a case. But the Dead Sea Scrolls, copied in the centuries just before Josephus, bear out the care with which these books were copied (session 4).

commentary.on: willingly to die for them
commentary.text: This is not exaggeration: in the persecution of 167 BC under the Greek king Antiochus IV, Jews were killed for keeping copies of the Law, as 1 Maccabees records. People do not die for books they think anyone can rewrite.

commentary.on: they see some of the present generation bold enough to write about such affairs, wherein they were not present
commentary.text: Josephus attacks Greek historians who wrote without having been there or asked those who were. Ancient readers already knew the difference between testimony and hearsay. Keep that in mind for session 3.

parts.plain: Josephus says: unlike the Greeks, who have endless history books that contradict each other, we Jews have only twenty-two sacred books: five by Moses, thirteen by the prophets, and four of songs and wise sayings. Books written after the time of Ezra are not equal to them. No one has ever dared to change them, and Jews would rather die than speak against them. The Greeks, by contrast, write histories of things they never saw.

compare.author: Flavius Josephus
compare.why: About 540 years after Ezra, a Jewish historian writing in Rome describes his people's sacred books as a fixed set of twenty-two, the same books as the Protestant Old Testament, and says no one has dared add to them or take from them. It is our clearest ancient witness to the finished collection.
compare.title: Snapshot 3, AD 95: a closed collection

sections.h: Why the origins matter for trust
paras: If the Old Testament had been invented or heavily rewritten late, say by Christians, or by rabbis after Jesus, then whatever it says about ancient Israel would be suspect. If instead its books were already old, treasured and fixed long before Jesus, and copied with great care, then what we read is genuinely what ancient Israel read.

That is what this session tests. It doesn't yet ask whether the events the books describe really happened; that is session 5. It asks a prior question: is the book itself ancient, and has it come down to us intact?
sections.key: Before asking whether the Old Testament is true, we ask whether it is genuinely ancient and intact.

paras: The Old Testament's books mostly do not name their authors. Jewish and Christian tradition assigned them: Moses for the first five books, David for many psalms, Solomon for Proverbs, the prophets for their books, Ezra for Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah. Most modern scholars think the books grew over centuries, through collecting, writing and editing by priests, prophets, royal scribes and their disciples, many unnamed.

Both views agree on something important: the books preserve traditions much older than their final form, and they reached that form before the time of Jesus. Where they differ is in how early, and how much, Moses and the prophets themselves wrote. Session 6 sets out that debate in full.
sections.key: Tradition names authors; most scholars see long growth by many hands. Both agree the books were complete before Jesus.

paras: Because the books carry no dates, historians look for moments where they can be seen in use. This session's readings give three. The table puts them together.

rows: A written book of God's Law, probably a form of Deuteronomy, exists and has authority over the king and the nation
The Law of Moses, probably the whole Torah, is a recognised book read to the entire people
A Jewish writer speaks of 'the law, the prophets and the other books'
Jesus speaks of 'the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms' as Scripture
A closed collection, the same books as the Protestant Old Testament

sections.key: From 622 BC to AD 95 we can watch the Old Testament take shape: first the Law, then the Prophets and Writings, then a closed collection.

paras: Snapshots in texts are one kind of evidence. Physical objects are another. The oldest surviving words of the Bible are on two tiny silver scrolls, found in 1979 in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, dated to around 600 BC, in Josiah's century. Rolled up as amulets, they carry the priestly blessing from Numbers 6:24–26, 'Yahweh bless you, and keep you', in almost the same words as our Bibles.

Then come the Dead Sea Scrolls, found from 1947 in caves near Qumran: about 900 manuscripts copied between about 250 BC and AD 68, including parts of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. They prove that all these books existed, and were being copied as Scripture, before Jesus. Session 5 shows how closely they match the text we read today.
sections.key: Silver amulets from about 600 BC and the Dead Sea Scrolls from before Jesus show the books are genuinely ancient.

paras: No council decided. The Torah was settled first, as the snapshots show; the Prophets were recognised next; the Writings last, with debate about a few books, such as Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, continuing into the first century AD. An old theory said the rabbis fixed the list at a council in Jamnia (Yavneh) around AD 90; most scholars now doubt any such decision was made. The collection was settled by centuries of use in worship and study.
Jesus treated this same collection as the word of God, 'the Scripture can't be broken' (John 10:35), and argued with other teachers about what it meant, never about whether it was Scripture.
sections.key: The collection was settled by long use, not by a council; Jesus treated it as Scripture.

paras: In the third and second centuries BC, Jews in Alexandria translated the Scriptures into Greek. This Septuagint was the Bible of most of the first Christians, and the New Testament usually quotes it. It also included books that were not in the Hebrew collection: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, the Maccabees and others.

Christians disagreed about these books for centuries. At the Reformation Protestants followed the Hebrew list, the one Josephus describes; Catholics, at the Council of Trent in 1546, affirmed the extra books; the Orthodox kept the Septuagint. That is the origin of the different Old Testaments you saw in session 1.
sections.key: The Greek Septuagint's extra books explain why the churches' Old Testaments differ.

paras: The Old Testament was not invented by the Church or by a late council. Its Law can be seen in use by 622 BC, as a finished book by about 445 BC, its three parts by about 130 BC, and a closed collection by AD 95. Its words survive on silver from about 600 BC and on scrolls from before Jesus. It was the Scripture of a people who built their life round it, and who, as Josephus says, would die rather than change it.
This shows the book is ancient and was treasured. It does not yet show that what it says happened, happened. That is the next step, in sessions 3 and 5.
sections.key: The Old Testament is genuinely ancient and was carefully kept; whether its history is true is tested next.

refs: 2 Kings 22–23; Nehemiah 8; the prologue to Sirach (about 130 BC); Luke 24:44; John 10:35; 1 Maccabees 1:56–57.

On Josiah's book and Deuteronomy: W. M. L. de Wette (1805), the classic identification; Ronald Clements, Deuteronomy (1989); for an earlier dating, K. A. Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003).
Josephus, Against Apion I.8 (about AD 95).
Ketef Hinnom: Gabriel Barkay et al., 'The Amulets from Ketef Hinnom: A New Edition and Evaluation', BASOR 334 (2004).
On Jamnia: Jack P. Lewis, 'What Do We Mean by Jabneh?', Journal of Bible and Religion 32 (1964); Lee Martin McDonald, The Formation of the Biblical Canon (2017).
Council of Trent, Session IV (8 April 1546).

debate.question: When was the Old Testament written down?

positions.name: Early
positions.who: Traditional Jewish and Christian views; scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen
positions.view: Much of the Law goes back to Moses, and many books were written close to the events they describe; Josiah's book was a genuinely old law rediscovered.
positions.evidence: The books' own claims; ancient Near Eastern parallels to the Law's forms; the Ketef Hinnom amulets.

positions.name: Late
positions.who: Some 'minimalist' scholars, such as Philip Davies and Niels Peter Lemche
positions.view: Most of the Old Testament was written in the Persian or Greek periods, after the exile, and tells us more about those times than about early Israel.
positions.evidence: The lack of outside evidence for early periods; the post-exile setting of the final editing.

positions.name: Over centuries
positions.who: Most scholars today
positions.view: Written traditions began under the kings, grew through the seventh century (Josiah's reign) and the exile, and were completed in the Persian period; the books preserve older memories within later editions.
positions.evidence: Josiah's book, Ezra's Torah and the long editing visible in the books themselves.

debate.agree: All agree that the Law was recognised Scripture by Ezra's time, that the collection was largely complete before Jesus, and that it was copied with great care.

look.why: For centuries the Scriptures were kept alive in households as well as in synagogues and churches. Rembrandt and his workshop painted this woman in 1637 with a heavy book in her lap.
points: A woman in a black dress with a wide starched white collar and white cuffs.
She sits in a wooden chair against a dark brown background.
Her face is lined; she looks away to our left rather than down.
In her lap, a thick book fastened with metal clasps, her hand resting on it, holding a pair of spectacles.

music.why: Psalm 23 in the Scottish metrical psalter, sung to Crimond: the Old Testament as ordinary people have carried it, by heart and in song.

think.why: Jerusalem is the West's first root. This depth sets it beside Athens.

learn.why: Said to a people weeping over the law they had broken: the reading was meant to end in a feast shared with the poor.

check.q: Why does this session start with scenes of the Law being read, rather than with the writing of the books?
options: Because the books were never written down
Because the books carry no dates, so historians look for datable moments when we can see them existing and in use
Because Ezra wrote the whole Old Testament
Because reading is more important than writing
check.why: Snapshots of use give us latest possible dates for the books' existence and authority.

check.q: What does the scene under King Josiah in 622 BC establish, whatever view one takes of Deuteronomy's origin?
options: That Moses wrote Deuteronomy
That a written book of God's Law existed and had authority over king and people by 622 BC
That the Old Testament was complete
That the book was forged
check.why: Scholars debate whether it was old or recent; all agree on the fixed point.

check.q: Josephus counts twenty-two sacred books; the Protestant Old Testament has thirty-nine. What explains the difference?
options: Josephus had lost seventeen books
They are the same books, counted differently
Protestants added books in the sixteenth century
Josephus left out the Prophets
check.why: The twelve minor prophets count as one book, Samuel, Kings and Chronicles as one each, and so on.

check.q: What is the significance of the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls?
options: They contain the whole Torah
They carry the priestly blessing of Numbers 6 from about 600 BC, the oldest surviving words of the Bible
They prove the Exodus
They were written by Ezra
check.why: Physical evidence that at least part of the Torah's text existed in Josiah's century.

check.q: Why do Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments contain books that Jewish and Protestant ones do not?
options: Medieval popes wrote them
They were in the Greek Septuagint used by the first Christians but not in the Hebrew collection Josephus describes
They were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
Luther removed them from the Hebrew Bible
check.why: Protestants followed the Hebrew list; Catholics and Orthodox kept the Greek.

check.q: What does this session's evidence NOT show?
options: That the Old Testament is ancient
That it was treasured and carefully kept
That the events it describes really happened
That it was largely complete before Jesus
check.why: An ancient, faithfully kept book could still be mistaken; sessions 3 and 5 test the history.

tutorial.question: Is the Old Testament we read today genuinely the ancient book of ancient Israel, or something assembled much later?
tutorial.approach: Explain why the origins matter for trust. Use the three snapshots (Josiah, Ezra, Josephus) and the oldest copies (Ketef Hinnom, the Dead Sea Scrolls). Give the strongest case for late composition. Then say what the evidence establishes, and what it leaves for later sessions.
strong: Explains why origins matter for trust, and distinguishes 'ancient and intact' from 'true'.
Uses 2 Kings 22–23 accurately, including the debate about Deuteronomy.
Uses Nehemiah 8 and Josephus as later snapshots.
Cites the physical evidence: Ketef Hinnom and the Dead Sea Scrolls.
States the late-composition case fairly.
Explains the Septuagint and why the churches' Old Testaments differ.

reading.author: John Barton
reading.title: A History of the Bible
reading.why: Clear chapters on how the Old Testament was formed.

reading.author: Konrad Schmid
reading.title: The Old Testament: A Literary History
reading.why: How scholars now reconstruct the writing of the books, period by period.

reading.author: Lee Martin McDonald
reading.title: The Formation of the Biblical Canon
reading.why: The standard detailed study of how the collection was fixed.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read a psalm aloud with someone else, at a meal or before bed, the way the people listened to Ezra. Ask each other which line stays with you.
sessions.reflect: The people wept when they heard the law, and were told to rejoice. What would make a text bring you to tears, and then to joy?
takeaways: The Old Testament's books carry no dates, so historians trace them through moments of use: Josiah (622 BC), Ezra (about 445 BC) and Josephus (AD 95).
The oldest copies, silver amulets from about 600 BC and the Dead Sea Scrolls, show the books are genuinely ancient and were complete before Jesus.
The collection was settled by long use, not a council; the churches' Old Testaments differ because of the Greek Septuagint's extra books.
sessions.finding: The Old Testament is genuinely ancient: its Law was in use by 622 BC, a finished book by about 445 BC, and the collection was closed by AD 95.

paras: If you pick up a modern book, the first pages tell you who wrote it and when it was printed. The books of the Old Testament have nothing like that. Most do not name their author, and none carries a date. So how can anyone know how old they are, or whether they were made up much later?

Historians do what detectives do. They look for moments in history where we can see these books already existing and being used, and for the oldest physical copies. Each moment tells us: 'by this date, at the latest, this book existed and people treated it as sacred.'
background.key: The books carry no dates, so we look for moments in history where we can see them in use.

paras: Here is the history you need, in brief. Around 1000 BC Israel became a kingdom with Jerusalem as its capital, and King Solomon built a Temple there. After Solomon the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south, around Jerusalem. The Assyrian empire destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC.

Judah survived another 135 years. In 622 BC its king, Josiah, set out to reform the nation's worship; that is our first reading. Then in 587 BC the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and took its leaders into exile in Babylon (in modern Iraq). In 539 BC the Persians conquered Babylon and let the exiles go home. A small community rebuilt Jerusalem, and in about 445 BC the scribe Ezra read them the Law; that is our second reading.

timeline.text: Kingdom under David and Solomon
Northern kingdom destroyed by Assyria
King Josiah: a book of the Law found (reading 1)
Jerusalem destroyed; exile in Babylon
Exiles allowed home by Persia
Ezra reads the Law to the people (reading 2)
Josephus describes the closed collection (comparison)

background.key: Kingdom, Josiah's reform, exile in Babylon, return: our readings sit at two turning points.

paras: The three texts in this session are three snapshots of the Old Testament taking shape. In 622 BC, under King Josiah, a book of God's Law is found and read to the nation: the first time the Bible shows a sacred book being read.
