About 180 years later, around 445 BC, Ezra reads the whole Law of Moses to the people as their recognised Scripture. And in AD 95 the historian Josephus describes a finished collection of sacred books that no one dared to change.

Why does this matter for trust? If these books had been invented late, by Christians or by rabbis after Jesus, we could not rely on them to tell us about ancient Israel. These snapshots, and the oldest copies described in the lecture, show they are genuinely ancient, and were treasured and fixed long before Jesus.
background.key: Three snapshots, 622 BC, 445 BC and AD 95, show the Old Testament is genuinely ancient.

sessions.title: Where the New Testament came from
sessions.line: Who wrote it, how soon after Jesus, and who chose the twenty-seven books.
sessions.plain: The New Testament was written by Jesus' followers within about seventy years of his death. Paul's letters are the earliest; the four Gospels came a little later. This session asks how close they stand to the events, who wrote them, and how the Church came to recognise these twenty-seven books and not others.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed that the Old Testament is genuinely ancient. Now the same question for the New: where did it come from, and were its writers in a position to know?
answers: When were the Gospels and letters written, and by whom?
What is the earliest Christian evidence we have?
What about the differences between the four Gospels?
Who chose the twenty-seven books? Did Constantine?
before: Paul says he 'delivered' what he 'received'. What exactly did he receive, and from whom might he have received it?
Whom does Paul name as witnesses, and why would he mention that most are still alive?
What do the Galatians passage and the end of John add?
sessions.readWhy: Paul's first letter to Corinth, written about AD 53–55, quotes a short summary of the faith which he says he had received earlier, and names witnesses. His letter to Galatia says when he met Peter and James in Jerusalem. Together they are the earliest written evidence about what the first Christians claimed.

paras: Now I declare to you, brothers, the Good News which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand,
by which also you are saved, if you hold firmly the word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep.
Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles,
and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.
But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
Whether then it is I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days.
But of the other apostles I saw no one except James, the Lord’s brother.
Now about the things which I write to you, behold, before God, I’m not lying.
Then I came to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
I was still unknown by face to the assemblies of Judea which were in Christ,
but they only heard: “He who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy.”
So they glorified God in me.
Then after a period of fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me.
I went up by revelation, and I laid before them the Good News which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who were respected, for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain.
This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.
There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.

parts.title: What I also received
parts.context: Paul writes from Ephesus, about AD 53–55, to the church he had founded in Corinth, a busy Greek port. Some there doubt that the dead are raised. Paul reminds them of the message he gave them when he first came, around AD 50.

commentary.on: I delivered to you first of all that which I also received
commentary.text: 'Delivered' and 'received' are the technical words Jewish teachers used for passing on tradition carefully, word for word. Paul is signalling that what follows is not his own composition. He is quoting.

commentary.on: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day
commentary.text: Read verses 3 to 5 aloud and you will hear the rhythm of a formula: four short clauses, each beginning 'that'. Scholars across the spectrum, sceptical ones included, think Paul received it within a few years of the crucifixion, most likely when he visited Peter and James in Jerusalem (the next passage). That makes it perhaps the oldest Christian text we have.

commentary.on: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve
commentary.text: Cephas is Peter's name in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. Its appearance here is a fingerprint of the early, Aramaic-speaking church in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: most of whom remain until now
commentary.text: This is the most remarkable line. Paul is in effect saying: if you doubt me, go and ask them. You do not invite people to check with living witnesses unless you are confident of what they will say.

commentary.on: I persecuted the assembly of God
commentary.text: Paul had been a persecutor of the movement. Whatever we make of his experience, his change of side is one of the best-attested facts of early Christianity, and it cost him dearly.

parts.title: Fifteen days with Peter
parts.context: Paul writes to churches in Galatia (central Turkey), around AD 48–55, to insist that his message is not second-hand. He gives a dated account of his contacts with the leaders in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days
commentary.text: Three years after his conversion, which most date to the early 30s, so this visit is about AD 35–37, within five or six years of the crucifixion. The Greek word for 'visit' (historēsai, from which 'history' comes) can mean to get to know someone and learn from them.

commentary.on: James, the Lord's brother
commentary.text: Paul met Jesus' own brother. James had not followed Jesus in his lifetime (John 7:5) but later led the church in Jerusalem; the creed you just read says the risen Jesus appeared to him. Josephus, the Jewish historian, also mentions 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James' (session 5).

commentary.on: before God, I'm not lying
commentary.text: Paul takes an oath, which tells you that his opponents disputed his account. Ancient readers expected witnesses to swear to what mattered.

commentary.on: I laid before them the Good News which I preach
commentary.text: Fourteen years later he checks his message with the leaders in Jerusalem. The earliest Christians cared that what was taught matched what the first witnesses said.

parts.title: We know that his witness is true
parts.context: The last verses of John's Gospel, probably added by the community that published it in the 90s AD.

commentary.on: This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things
commentary.text: The Gospel claims to rest on the testimony of 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', an eyewitness who is never named. Tradition identifies him with John, son of Zebedee; some scholars think he was another disciple in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: We know that his witness is true
commentary.text: A group speaks here, vouching for the witness. Whether or not you accept their claim, this is how ancient testimony worked: a named community standing behind a named source.

commentary.on: the world itself wouldn't have room for the books
commentary.text: A deliberate exaggeration, a common ancient way of ending a book. It reminds us again that the Gospels are selective portraits, not complete records.

paras: For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
For he received from God the Father honor and glory when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.

parts.title: We were eyewitnesses
parts.context: From the Second Letter of Peter, which presents itself as Peter's farewell. It is the New Testament letter whose authorship is most widely doubted: many scholars, including some conservative ones, date it after Peter's death (session 6 explains pseudonymity). Read it as a statement of what the early Church believed about its own message.

commentary.on: we didn't follow cunningly devised fables
commentary.text: The Greek word is mythos, myth. The writer knows the Greek and Roman myths of gods visiting the earth, and insists the Christian story is a different kind of thing: not a tale about the distant past, but a report about a recent man that people saw and heard.

commentary.on: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty
commentary.text: The writer refers to the Transfiguration (Mark 9:2–8), when three disciples saw Jesus shining on a mountain. The claim is extraordinary, and you may doubt it. But notice its form: not 'it is said' but 'we saw'.

commentary.on: We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him
commentary.text: Whether this letter is by Peter or by a follower writing in his name, it shows that by the end of the first century Christians defended their faith as testimony, not as myth or philosophy. That is why the historical questions in this journey matter to Christianity in a way they would not to a religion of myths.

compare.why: A short passage that insists the Christian message is not myth but eyewitness testimony. Ancient readers knew the difference between a myth and a report, and so did the first Christians.
compare.title: Not cunningly devised fables

paras: Jesus was crucified around AD 30. Paul's letters, the earliest Christian writings we have, date from about AD 48 to the early 60s. Most scholars date Mark's Gospel around 65–70, Matthew and Luke in the 80s, and John in the 90s; some date them earlier. The Gospels were written while people who had known Jesus, or known those who had, were still alive.
How does that compare? The table sets the main sources for Jesus beside the sources for some other famous ancient figures.

rows: Plutarch (about AD 100) and Arrian (2nd century AD), drawing on lost earlier works
Plato and Xenophon, his own pupils
table.note: The point is not that early sources must be true, but that the Gospels are as close to their subject as the sources historians rely on for most of antiquity, and closer than many.

sections.key: The Gospels were written within living memory, closer to Jesus than many ancient biographies are to their subjects.

paras: The most important passage for historians is the one you read first. Paul wrote in the mid-50s, but he is quoting something earlier, with the marks of an oral formula and an Aramaic name for Peter. His visit to Peter and James in Jerusalem, about three years after his conversion, is the likeliest moment he received it.

Scholars across the spectrum date it to within a few years of the crucifixion. Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, put it within three years; Bart Ehrman, an agnostic, agrees it is very early. Whatever one makes of its claim, belief that Jesus had been raised and had appeared to named people was not a legend that grew up over generations. It was there at the start.
sections.key: Paul quotes a summary of the faith that scholars of every view date to within a few years of the crucifixion.

paras: Between Jesus and the written Gospels lie two or three decades of oral tradition: sayings and stories told and retold. How reliable was that stage? In the twentieth century, form critics such as Rudolf Bultmann argued that stories changed freely as communities used them, so that much in the Gospels reflects the early Church more than Jesus.

Other scholars point out that teaching in Jewish and ancient settings was often memorised; that Jesus' sayings are shaped for memory, with parallelism, rhythm and vivid images; and that named people who had known Jesus, Peter, James and John among them, led the communities for decades. Psychologists of memory add a caution on both sides: memory keeps the gist better than the details.
sections.key: Scholars debate whether the oral stage changed the stories freely or kept their substance stable.

paras: The Gospels do not name their authors in the text. The titles 'according to Matthew', 'Mark', 'Luke' and 'John' are attested in the second century, and no rival names were ever attached to them. Around AD 120 Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor, reported that Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down what Peter remembered. Around 180 Irenaeus of Lyons named all four.

Many modern scholars doubt that Matthew and John were written by apostles in their present form, while accepting that they draw on early tradition; others defend the traditional names. Mark and Luke, who were not apostles, are names nobody would invent to give a book authority.
sections.key: The traditional names are attested early and unchallenged; two of them are names nobody would invent.

paras: The Gospels differ. Matthew mentions one angel at the empty tomb, Luke two. Matthew and Luke give different genealogies for Jesus. John places the cleansing of the Temple at the start of Jesus' ministry, the others at the end. Sceptics have long counted these as contradictions.

Historians see them differently. Independent witnesses always differ in detail, and identical accounts suggest copying. Ancient biographers also arranged material by theme rather than strict order, as Plutarch admits. Some differences can be reconciled; some cannot easily be. But none touches the core: that Jesus taught, healed, was crucified under Pilate, and that his followers proclaimed him risen. The early Church had the chance to merge the four into one tidy account (Tatian did so around 170) and chose to keep all four, differences included.
sections.key: The Gospels differ in detail as independent witnesses do; the differences do not touch the core of the story.

paras: How did the Church decide which books belonged in the New Testament? Not by a vote at a single council, but over about three centuries, by recognising books already being read in worship across the churches. The tests, roughly, were apostolic origin (written by an apostle or someone close to one), agreement with the faith handed down, and wide and long use.

The four Gospels and Paul's letters were accepted very early; Irenaeus, around 180, defends the four Gospels against rivals. A few books, such as Hebrews, James, 2 Peter and Revelation, were debated longer. In 367 Athanasius of Alexandria, in his thirty-ninth Festal Letter, listed exactly our twenty-seven books, the first list we have to do so. Councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) in North Africa confirmed the list for the West.
sections.key: The canon was recognised over three centuries from books the churches already read, not chosen by a single decision.

paras: A popular story, repeated by Voltaire and in Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code (2003), says that the Emperor Constantine or the Council of Nicaea in 325 decided which books went into the Bible and suppressed the rest. There is no evidence for this. The Council of Nicaea met to settle the dispute over Arius' teaching about Christ and the date of Easter; none of its surviving decisions mentions the canon.

Constantine did do one thing for the Bible: around 331 he ordered fifty copies of the Scriptures from Eusebius of Caesarea for the churches of his new capital (Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.36). By then the four Gospels and Paul's letters had been read as Scripture for nearly two centuries.
sections.key: Neither Constantine nor the Council of Nicaea chose the books of the Bible; the core was settled long before.

paras: Other early writings were not accepted. Some were respected but late, like the Shepherd of Hermas, which some churches read for a time. Others, such as the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Peter or the Gospel of Judas, were rejected because they taught a different faith, often the 'gnostic' belief that salvation comes through secret knowledge and that the material world is evil. Most date from the second century or later; a few scholars date parts of Thomas earlier.

Marcion, around 140, accepted only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul and rejected the Old Testament altogether. The Church's response, insisting on the Jewish Scriptures and on four Gospels, shaped the canon we have.
sections.key: The 'lost gospels' were mostly later, and were left out because they taught a different faith.

sections.h: What this evidence shows, and what it does not
paras: The evidence shows that the claims about Jesus, including the extraordinary claim that he was raised, were made very early, by people who named witnesses, some of them leaders of the movement. It shows that the Gospels were written within living memory, and that the Church kept four distinct accounts rather than one harmonised story.

It does not, by itself, show that every detail is accurate, or that the miracles happened. And so far all our witnesses are Christians. Two more checks follow: whether the text has been copied faithfully since (session 4), and what evidence from outside the Bible says (session 5).
sections.key: The evidence shows early, named testimony and a canon recognised over time; the next checks are the copies and the outside evidence.

debate.question: How close are the Gospels to the eyewitnesses?

positions.name: Very close
positions.who: Richard Bauckham and others
positions.view: The Gospels were written within living memory and rest on the testimony of named eyewitnesses, such as Peter behind Mark, which the authors signal deliberately.
positions.evidence: 1 Corinthians 15 and Galatians 1; Papias on Mark; the naming of minor characters who could be checked.

positions.name: Shaped by communities
positions.who: Rudolf Bultmann and the form critics; Bart Ehrman in a modern form
positions.view: Stories about Jesus circulated orally for decades and changed as they were retold, so the Gospels show us the faith of the early Church more than the facts about Jesus.
positions.evidence: Differences between the Gospels; studies of how memories change in retelling.

positions.name: Remembered Jesus
positions.who: James D. G. Dunn and many others
positions.view: The tradition was flexible in wording but stable in substance, because communities kept and checked the memory of Jesus together. We meet Jesus as he was remembered, which is how we meet any historical figure.
positions.evidence: The mix of stable core and varied detail in the synoptic Gospels.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus existed, that the Gospels were written in the first century, and that belief in his resurrection goes back to the earliest days.

look.why: Simone Cantarini, in the 1640s, painted the old tradition of Matthew writing his Gospel with an angel's help: the Church's way of saying that inspiration came through a real human author.
points: A balding, grey-bearded man holding open a book with black writing on its pages.
His forehead deeply lined; he looks down at the page.
An angel, seen from behind, with braided blond hair tied with a red bow and snowy white wings.
The angel holds a white feather pen and an inkwell, as if handing the writer his tools.

music.why: Bach set Matthew's account of the Passion word for word in Luther's German. In his hands the Gospel is sung as testimony, by an Evangelist who narrates and a crowd that answers.

think.why: How historians weigh the Gospels as sources.

learn.why: Perhaps the oldest words of Christian faith we have, handed on within a few years of the events they describe.

check.q: Why do historians value 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 even more than the Gospels' dates would suggest?
options: Paul was an eyewitness of the crucifixion
Paul is quoting a formula he received earlier, which takes the evidence back to within a few years of the events
It is the longest account of the resurrection
It was written before the crucifixion
check.why: 'I delivered what I also received': the letter is from the 50s, but the creed is older.

check.q: What is the significance of Paul's remark that 'most' of the five hundred 'remain until now'?
options: It proves the resurrection happened
It invites his readers to check with living witnesses, which a writer confident of his facts would do
It shows the five hundred were all dead
It was added by a later copyist
check.why: It doesn't prove the claim, but it shows Paul expected the witnesses to confirm it.

check.q: Why do historians not count differences between the Gospels as evidence of invention?
options: There are no differences
Independent witnesses always differ in detail, while identical accounts suggest copying
The Church forbade comparing them
One author wrote all four
check.why: And the core events are the same in all four.

check.q: Which statement about the Gospels' authors is most accurate?
options: All four name their authors in the text
The traditional names are attested in the second century and never rivalled, though scholars debate how direct the apostolic link is
The names were first given at the Reformation
No one knew who wrote them until the nineteenth century
check.why: Papias (about 120) and Irenaeus (about 180) give the names; modern scholars disagree about Matthew and John.

check.q: What did the Council of Nicaea (325) decide about the books of the Bible?
options: It chose the four Gospels and burned the rest
Nothing: it dealt with Arius' teaching about Christ and the date of Easter
It added the Book of Revelation
It removed the Apocrypha
check.why: The story that Nicaea chose the canon has no basis in the sources.

check.q: Which best describes how the New Testament canon was formed?
options: An emperor's decree
A gradual recognition, over about three centuries, of books already read across the churches, judged by apostolic origin, faithfulness and wide use
A single vote at Jerusalem in AD 50
The choice of Martin Luther
check.why: Athanasius' list of 367 and the African councils of 393 and 397 recorded a consensus already largely formed.

tutorial.question: Where did the New Testament come from, and were its writers in a position to know?
tutorial.approach: Start with dates, comparing other ancient sources. Use 1 Corinthians 15 and Galatians 1 as your earliest evidence. Set out the case for and against eyewitness testimony, and deal honestly with the differences between the Gospels. Then explain how the twenty-seven books were recognised, and answer the claim that Constantine chose them.
strong: Gives realistic dates and compares other ancient sources.
Explains why 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 is so important and how early it is.
States the form critics' case and the eyewitness reply fairly.
Treats the differences between the Gospels as historians would.
Explains canon as recognition over three centuries, with Athanasius in 367.
Corrects the Nicaea myth and explains why the 'lost gospels' were left out.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: ask an older relative or friend to tell you about an event they witnessed long ago. Notice what stays fixed in their telling and what varies, and thank them for it.
sessions.reflect: Whose testimony do you trust most in your own life, and why?
takeaways: The New Testament was written within living memory; Paul quotes a creed from within a few years of the crucifixion.
The Gospels differ in detail as independent witnesses do; how close they stand to eyewitnesses is debated.
The twenty-seven books were recognised over three centuries; Athanasius first listed them in 367; Constantine and Nicaea did not choose them.
sessions.finding: The New Testament was written within living memory of Jesus, by people who named their witnesses; its books were recognised over time, not picked by an emperor.

background.h: From the Old Testament to the New
paras: Between the last books of the Old Testament and the time of Jesus lie about four centuries. Alexander the Great conquered the region in 332 BC, and Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean. In 63 BC Rome took control. By Jesus' day Judea was ruled by Roman governors and local client kings such as Herod, and many Jews longed for God to free them, perhaps through an anointed king, the 'Messiah' (in Greek, 'Christ').

Jesus was born around 4 BC and crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30. His followers claimed he had been raised from the dead and began to spread the message, first among Jews and then among non-Jews across the Roman Empire.
background.key: Jesus lived under Roman rule, among Jews hoping for a Messiah; his followers spread their message across the Empire.

paras: Paul (also called Saul) was a Jew from Tarsus, in modern Turkey, trained as a strict Pharisee, who at first persecuted the Christians. A few years after Jesus' death he had an experience he describes as seeing the risen Jesus, and he became the movement's most energetic missionary. Between about AD 48 and his execution in Rome in the 60s, he travelled around the eastern Mediterranean founding churches, and wrote them letters.

Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry his name. Scholars agree that at least seven are certainly his, including the two you will read today, 1 Corinthians and Galatians. They are the earliest Christian writings that survive.
background.key: Paul, once a persecutor, became the leading missionary; his letters are the earliest Christian writings.

background.h: Why we read Paul before the Gospels
paras: You might expect a session about the Gospels to start with a Gospel. But the Gospels were written later than Paul's letters, between about AD 65 and 100. If we want to know how close the written record comes to Jesus, the earliest evidence is the place to start.

In 1 Corinthians, Paul quotes a short summary of the faith that he says he had been given, and lists people who saw the risen Jesus. In Galatians he tells us exactly when he met Jesus' closest followers. Then a passage from the end of John's Gospel shows how a Gospel described its own source.
The lecture then asks the other half of the question: how, over the next three centuries, the Church came to recognise these twenty-seven books, and not the 'lost gospels', as its New Testament.
background.key: We start with Paul because his letters are older than the Gospels and take us closest to the events.

sessions.title: Has it been copied faithfully?
sessions.line: No originals survive. So how do we know what was written?
sessions.plain: Before printing, every book was copied by hand, and copies of copies can drift. None of the Bible's original pages survives, and none of any other ancient book. But we have far more, and far older, copies of the Bible than of any other ancient writing, and scholars compare them to work out what was first written. This session shows how that works, what has changed, and what has not.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 and 3 showed where the books came from. But a book written long ago is only useful if what we read today is what was written then. That is the next check.

How many copies are there, and how old?
