In 1849 John Ruskin, in The Seven Lamps of Architecture, called it 'the lamp of sacrifice': the best of what we make should be offered to God not because he needs it but because we owe it, and a gift that costs nothing is not a gift. Wordsworth, standing in King's College Chapel in Cambridge, built by a king for a handful of scholars, put the same thought into two lines: 'Give all thou canst; high Heaven rejects the lore / Of nicely-calculated less or more.'
sections.key: Inner purity comes first, but God should also be honoured with the best we can make.

paras: Look again at the scene in Mark. The bystanders are not wicked; they are right that the poor need help. Jesus does not tell them they are wrong to care. He says that the poor are always with them, and that they can do them good whenever they want to. But this moment, this love poured out for a man about to die, will not come again. The woman, he says, has done 'a good work'.

Perhaps the honest conclusion is that the objection can never be dismissed, only answered case by case. Medieval cathedrals were not only shrines of gold. Their chapters ran schools, hospitals and almshouses, and they were the one splendid place that belonged to everyone, where the poorest could stand in the same light as the king. But they were also built with money raised in ways that were sometimes corrupt, and they sometimes stood in towns where children went hungry.

Bernard's question does not go away by being answered once. It must be asked of every beautiful thing made for God, and of every life that enjoys them: is this beauty serving love of God and neighbour, or competing with it?
sections.key: The objection can never be dismissed once and for all; every beautiful thing must be tested by love of God and neighbour.

refs: Bernard of Clairvaux, Apologia ad Guillelmum (about 1125), chapter XII (sections 28–29); critical Latin text in Sancti Bernardi Opera, vol. 3, ed. J. Leclercq and H. Rochais (1963). The translations here are our own.
Conrad Rudolph, The 'Things of Greater Importance': Bernard of Clairvaux's Apologia and the Medieval Attitude toward Art (1990), with text and translation.
Cistercian statutes on images and glass: the early statutes of the General Chapter (by about 1150), in C. Waddell, Narrative and Legislative Texts from Early Cîteaux (1999).
Suger, De administratione XXXIII (on the altar vessels and his critics), quoting Romans 14:5.
Indulgences and St Peter's: Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517), theses 50 and 86.
Zurich 1524: Lee Palmer Wandel, Voracious Idols and Violent Hands (1995). England: Eamon Duffy, The Stripping of the Altars (1992); The Journal of William Dowsing, ed. Trevor Cooper (2001).
John Ruskin, The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849), chapter 1, 'The Lamp of Sacrifice'.
William Wordsworth, Ecclesiastical Sonnets III.43, 'Inside of King's College Chapel, Cambridge' (1822).

debate.question: Is costly beauty in worship right while people are poor?

positions.name: No: give it to the poor
positions.who: Bernard (for monks), many Reformers, and many Christians and critics today
positions.view: Money spent on gold and glass is money not spent on the hungry, and splendour easily becomes pride, distraction or a way of raising more money. The true temple is the poor person, in whom Christ said he is met (Matthew 25).
positions.evidence: The prophets; Mark 14:5; the abuses of relic-selling and indulgences; the speed with which money is found for buildings.

positions.name: Yes: beauty is an offering, and it belongs to everyone
positions.who: Suger; Ruskin; many who grew up poor in cathedral towns
positions.view: An offering to God is not waste, and splendour in a church is the one splendour the poor are never shut out of. To insist that the poor need only bread is to insult them. Beauty feeds the soul as bread feeds the body.
positions.evidence: Mark 14:6–9; the cathedral as a free and open public space; the long tradition of costly worship in the Temple.

positions.name: It depends on what the beauty serves
positions.who: Augustine; Thomas Aquinas; much modern Christian ethics
positions.view: Things are good when they are used for the love of God and neighbour, and bad when they are loved instead of them. The question is not gold or no gold, but whether the beauty serves love, and whether the poor are being served too.
positions.evidence: Confessions X.34; the cathedral chapters' hospitals, schools and almshouses.

debate.agree: Every side agrees that the poor must never be neglected for the sake of a building, and that beauty can become vanity. They disagree about whether costly beauty can itself be a form of love.

look.why: Outside a carved church door, a bishop in gold stands before a crowd of ordinary people, among them the sick and the troubled. The splendour of the church and the needs of the people are in one picture, which is the question of this session.
points: The bishop in a gold robe and tall white mitre, standing on the church steps, one hand raised.
A man kneeling before him with his hands pressed together.
A line of men, women and children curving through the square.
At the back, two men holding up a third, who lies on the ground staring at a green demon in the air.
The church behind, its arched doorways full of statues and carvings.

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there.' This chant was sung on Maundy Thursday while feet were washed, as Jesus washed his disciples' feet. Duruflé's setting is music that cost little and gives much.

think.why: If every person bears God's image, then the poor person at the cathedral door is holier than the gold on the altar. This is the root of Bernard's objection.

learn.why: Three lines that strip religion back to its bones, and the best test of any beautiful thing made for God.

listen.why: Tom Holland argues that concern for the poor and the weak, Bernard's concern, is one of Christianity's deepest legacies. Listen for whether that legacy needs cathedrals.

check.q: What was Bernard's main target in the Apologia?
options: Parish churches
The rich art and buildings of monasteries such as Cluny
Saint-Denis only
Pagan temples
check.why: He wrote to and about monks, and allowed that bishops serving ordinary people had a different duty.

check.q: What kind of window glass did the Cistercians require?
options: Picture windows in rich colours
Plain glass without crosses or pictures, such as grisaille
No windows at all
Only rose windows
check.why: Their statutes required plain glass. Grisaille, colourless or greyish glass set in patterns, became their art.

check.q: In Mark 14, how much was the ointment said to be worth?
options: Thirty pieces of silver
More than three hundred denarii, about a year's wages
A talent of gold
Two small coins
check.why: A denarius was a day's pay for a labourer, so this was roughly a year's income poured out at once.

check.q: Where does Augustine say the beautiful patterns made by craftsmen come from?
options: From the devil
From human pride
From the Beauty above our souls
From nature alone
check.why: Augustine condemns misuse and excess, not making: the patterns come 'from that Beauty, which is above our souls'.

tutorial.question: 'The church gleams in its walls and goes without in its poor.' Make Bernard's case as strongly as you can, then answer it.
tutorial.approach: Give Bernard the best possible hearing: his arguments about distraction, money and the poor, with the Bible behind him. Do not weaken him by forgetting that he spoke to monks. Then answer with the strongest reply you can find, from Mark, Suger, Ruskin or Augustine. Say where you finally stand, and what it would change in your own life.
strong: States Bernard's three arguments: distraction from prayer, the money motive, and neglect of the poor.
Notes the limits he set: monks, not bishops serving the people.
Shows that the Cistercians chose a different beauty, not ugliness.
Traces the objection into the Reformation and today.
Gives a serious reply: Mark 14, Suger's 'inner purity and outward splendour', Ruskin's sacrifice, or Augustine's test of use.
Reaches a judgement that keeps the poor in view, and applies it beyond medieval churches.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: whenever you spend money on something beautiful, a book, a ticket, flowers, give the same amount, quietly, to someone in need.
sessions.reflect: Where in your own life does beauty sit uneasily beside need? What, if anything, would you change?
takeaways: Bernard's case: costly churches distract, chase money and neglect the poor.
His monks chose a plain beauty of clear glass and proportion.
The best replies (Mark 14, Suger, the icon defenders) still have to be tested against love of God and neighbour.

sessions.title: The sound of stone
sessions.line: A cathedral was built to be heard as much as seen.
sessions.plain: Stone holds a sung note for seconds after the singer stops. For centuries cathedral choirs filled that echo with prayer several times a day, and the music and the buildings grew up together. This session listens to the building.
sessions.why: Bernard's challenge leaves a question: if the beauty of a church is justified, what is it for? The oldest answer is not decoration but worship, and in the cathedrals worship was sung. We go back to the first choir in the Bible, and then into the choir stalls.
before: Notice how many people David appoints, to do what, and with which instruments.
What does David give the singers to do, in a single phrase? It could stand as a job description for every choir since.
The psalm at the end: what does it ask the whole earth to do?

paras: David spoke to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brothers as singers with instruments of music, stringed instruments, harps, and cymbals, sounding aloud and lifting up their voices with joy.
So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers, Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah;
and with them their brothers of the second rank, Zechariah, Ben, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, and Jeiel, the doorkeepers.
So the singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were given cymbals of bronze to sound aloud;
and Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with stringed instruments set to Alamoth;
and Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps tuned to the eight-stringed lyre, to lead.
Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was over the singing. He taught the singers, because he was skillful.
Berechiah and Elkanah were doorkeepers for the ark.
Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, blew the trumpets before God’s ark; and Obed-Edom and Jehiah were doorkeepers for the ark.
So David, the elders of Israel, and the captains over thousands, went to bring the ark of Yahweh’s covenant up out of the house of Obed-Edom with joy.
When God helped the Levites who bore the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.
David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as were all the Levites who bore the ark, the singers, and Chenaniah the choir master with the singers; and David had an ephod of linen on him.
Thus all Israel brought the ark of Yahweh’s covenant up with shouting, with sound of the cornet, with trumpets, and with cymbals, sounding aloud with stringed instruments and harps.
As the ark of Yahweh’s covenant came to David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out at the window, and saw king David dancing and playing; and she despised him in her heart.
They brought in God’s ark, and set it in the middle of the tent that David had pitched for it; and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God.
When David had finished offering the burnt offering and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in Yahweh’s name.
He gave to everyone of Israel, both man and woman, to everyone a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.
He appointed some of the Levites to minister before Yahweh’s ark, and to commemorate, to thank, and to praise Yahweh, the God of Israel:

Asaph the chief, and second to him Zechariah, then Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-Edom, and Jeiel, with stringed instruments and with harps; and Asaph with cymbals, sounding aloud;
with Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets continually, before the ark of the covenant of God.
Then on that day David first ordained to give thanks to Yahweh, by the hand of Asaph and his brothers.

Oh give thanks to Yahweh.
Call on his name.
Make what he has done known among the peoples.

Sing to him.
Sing praises to him.
Tell of all his marvelous works.

Glory in his holy name.
Let the heart of those who seek Yahweh rejoice.

Seek Yahweh and his strength.
Seek his face forever more.

Remember his marvelous works that he has done,
his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth,

you offspring of Israel his servant,
you children of Jacob, his chosen ones.

He is Yahweh our God.
His judgments are in all the earth.

Remember his covenant forever,
the word which he commanded to a thousand generations,

the covenant which he made with Abraham,
his oath to Isaac.

He confirmed it to Jacob for a statute,
and to Israel for an everlasting covenant,

saying, “I will give you the land of Canaan,
The lot of your inheritance,”

when you were but a few men in number,
yes, very few, and foreigners were in it.

They went about from nation to nation,
from one kingdom to another people.

He allowed no man to do them wrong.
Yes, he reproved kings for their sakes,

“Don’t touch my anointed ones!
Do my prophets no harm!”

Sing to Yahweh, all the earth!
Display his salvation from day to day.

Declare his glory among the nations,
and his marvelous works among all the peoples.

For great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised.
He also is to be feared above all gods.

For all the gods of the peoples are idols,
but Yahweh made the heavens.

Honor and majesty are before him.
Strength and gladness are in his place.

Ascribe to Yahweh, you relatives of the peoples,
ascribe to Yahweh glory and strength!

Ascribe to Yahweh the glory due to his name.
Bring an offering, and come before him.
Worship Yahweh in holy array.

Tremble before him, all the earth.
The world also is established that it can’t be moved.

Let the heavens be glad,
and let the earth rejoice!
Let them say among the nations, “Yahweh reigns!”

Let the sea roar, and its fullness!
Let the field exult, and all that is in it!

Then the trees of the forest will sing for joy before Yahweh,
for he comes to judge the earth.

Oh give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good,
for his loving kindness endures forever.

Say, “Save us, God of our salvation!
Gather us together and deliver us from the nations,
to give thanks to your holy name,
to triumph in your praise.”

Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel,
from everlasting even to everlasting.
All the people said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh.

notes.text: The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve at the sanctuary. Here David turns some of them into musicians.
Chenaniah, 'chief of the Levites, was over the singing. He taught the singers': the first choirmaster named in the Bible.
'To commemorate, to thank, and to praise': three verbs that could stand as the job description of every church choir since.
The psalm that follows is put together from parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106. The Chronicler is quoting the hymn book of his own day.

sessions.readWhy: When David brings the ark to Jerusalem he appoints singers and players to praise God every day. The Chronicler, writing centuries later, saw this as the beginning of the Temple's music, and the cathedrals saw their choirs as its heirs.

paras:
Praise Yah!
Praise God in his sanctuary!
Praise him in his heavens for his acts of power!

Praise him for his mighty acts!
Praise him according to his excellent greatness!

Praise him with the sounding of the trumpet!
Praise him with harp and lyre!

Praise him with tambourine and dancing!
Praise him with stringed instruments and flute!

Praise him with loud cymbals!
Praise him with resounding cymbals!

Let everything that has breath praise Yah!
Praise Yah!
compare.why: The last psalm in the Bible's book of songs: everything that has breath, and every instrument, praising God 'in his sanctuary'. It was sung at morning prayer every day in the medieval Church.

paras: Clap your hands in an empty cathedral and the sound goes on and on, rolling round the vaults for several seconds before it fades. In a sitting room it dies almost at once. This lingering is called reverberation, and it changes everything about how a building can be used.

Speech in a great stone church is hard to follow: each syllable runs into the next. But a slow, sung line, one note held and moving gently to the next, is carried and enriched by the echo, which adds a halo of sound around it. It is no accident that the music of the cathedrals was slow, sustained and sung rather than spoken. The building and its music shaped each other for a thousand years.
sections.key: A stone church holds each note for seconds, so its music became slow and sung.

paras: 'Seven times a day, I praise you,' says Psalm 119. The monks took this literally. The Rule of St Benedict, written in the sixth century, sets out the hours of prayer: the night office of Vigils, then Lauds at dawn, Prime, Terce, Sext and None through the day, Vespers in the evening and Compline at bedtime. Benedict arranged that the whole book of 150 psalms be sung every week.

Cathedrals were served by communities of clergy called canons, who kept the same hours. That is why a cathedral has a choir: not only the singers but the part of the building where they sang, between the nave and the high altar, with its rows of carved wooden seats, the choir stalls, facing each other across the aisle so that the psalms could be sung back and forth, verse by verse.
So for most of its history a cathedral was not silent between services. It was a place where, day and night, the psalms went round like a wheel.
sections.key: For centuries the psalms were sung round the clock in the choir: a cathedral was rarely silent.

paras: The music was plainchant: a single melody, sung in unison, without harmony or a regular beat, following the rhythm of the Latin words. A legend said that Pope Gregory the Great received it from the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove singing in his ear, and so it is often called Gregorian chant. In fact it took shape over centuries and was given much of its lasting form in the Frankish kingdom in the eighth and ninth centuries.

For a long time the melodies were learned by ear. Around 1025 an Italian monk, Guido of Arezzo, set out a system of lines, the ancestor of the musical stave, so that singers could read a tune they had never heard. It was one of the most important inventions in the history of music, and it was made to help choirs learn their psalms.
sections.key: Plainchant is a single sung line following the words; Guido's stave was invented to teach it.

sections.h: Notre-Dame and the birth of harmony
paras: In Paris, while the new cathedral of Notre-Dame was rising (it was begun in 1163), its singers began to do something new. Over a long, slow plainchant melody, sung in very long notes, they added one, then two, then three more voices weaving above it. This is called organum. Two musicians of Notre-Dame are known by name: Léonin, and after him Pérotin. In decrees of 1198 and 1199 the bishop of Paris, Odo of Sully, provided for music in three and four parts on the feasts of 1 January and of St Stephen (26 December), and Pérotin's great four-part settings are thought to have been written for exactly these days.

If you listen to Pérotin, you hear sound doing what the new architecture was doing: rising in layers, stretched over a great span, filling a high space. Historians are careful about drawing the parallel too tightly, but the music and the building were made by the same city, for the same church, in the same decades.
sections.key: In Paris, as the cathedral rose, singers began to add voices above the chant: the beginnings of harmony.

paras: At the Reformation, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer reduced the eight daily services to two, in English, for the whole Church of England. His first Book of Common Prayer (1549) combined the old evening offices of Vespers and Compline into one service, Evensong, with its two great canticles, Mary's song, the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), and Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis (Luke 2:29–32). Cranmer wanted music the people could follow; in a letter of 1544 to Henry VIII he asked for music with, as near as may be, one note for each syllable.

Choral evensong, sung daily in English cathedrals and many college chapels, is one of the oldest unbroken musical traditions in the world. Anyone may go in, free, and sit in or near the choir. You need do nothing but listen. It may be the easiest way into a cathedral that exists.
sections.key: Cranmer's Evensong of 1549 is still sung daily, free, in English cathedrals.

paras: Before the singing came the bells, calling the town and the clergy to each hour of prayer. For centuries most people told the time of day not by clocks but by the cathedral's bells.

Organs came into churches slowly. One of the earliest we know of in England was built at Winchester in the late tenth century and described in a Latin poem by the monk Wulfstan: he says it had four hundred pipes and twenty-six bellows, and needed seventy strong men to work it, and that its sound could be heard all over the town. By the late Middle Ages most great churches had organs, which is why the painter of this session's picture, around 1500, imagines one in the church where Clovis was baptised a thousand years before.

And after the singing, silence. Monastic communities kept a 'great silence' after Compline, the last office of the day, until the morning. A cathedral at night, with the echo of the last psalm dying in the vaults, is one of the most silent places on earth. The silence is part of the music.
sections.key: Bells called the hours, organs grew huge, and the silence after Compline is part of the music.

sections.h: A secret in the Sistine Chapel
paras: This session's music was written in the 1630s by Gregorio Allegri for the Pope's choir in the Sistine Chapel, to be sung in Holy Week at Tenebrae, the service of shadows, at which candles are put out one by one until the church is dark. The setting of Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, O God', was said to be so treasured that copying it was forbidden.

In 1770 the fourteen-year-old Mozart, visiting Rome with his father, heard it and wrote it down from memory; his father's letters describe the feat. The famous high C that soars through modern performances is not in Allegri's original. It entered through later copies and nineteenth-century editions, which is a reminder that sacred music, like a cathedral, is something many hands have added to.
sections.key: Allegri's Miserere was written for one chapel and one week; its famous high C was added later.

refs: Psalm 119:164; The Rule of St Benedict, chapters 8–18 (the order of the Office) and 16 ('seven times a day').
Gregorian chant and its Frankish origins: David Hiley, Western Plainchant (1993); Christopher Page, The Christian West and Its Singers (2010).
Guido of Arezzo, Micrologus and the Prologus in Antiphonarium (about 1025–1033).
Pérotin and the decrees of Bishop Odo of Sully (1198, 1199): Craig Wright, Music and Ceremony at Notre Dame of Paris, 500–1550 (1989).
Cranmer's letter to Henry VIII, 7 October 1544; The Book of Common Prayer (1549).
Allegri's Miserere and Mozart: Leopold Mozart's letter of 14 April 1770; on the high C, which appears in later copies and in the version printed in Grove's Dictionary of Music (1880).

debate.question: Does music in church help prayer, or get in its way?

positions.name: A gift that carries prayer
positions.who: Augustine in Milan (Confessions IX.6); Martin Luther; the cathedral tradition
positions.view: Music moves the heart where words alone cannot reach, and lets a whole congregation pray with one voice. Luther said that next to the Word of God, music deserves the highest praise.
positions.evidence: Augustine's tears at the hymns in Milan; the Psalms themselves, which are songs; the experience of countless people moved to prayer by music.

positions.name: A danger to be watched
positions.who: Augustine again (Confessions X.33); Ulrich Zwingli; John Calvin
positions.view: The pleasure of music can take the place of the meaning of the words. Zwingli, himself a fine musician, removed music from worship in Zurich; Calvin allowed only psalms, sung by everyone, in unison.
positions.evidence: Augustine's confession that he was sometimes more moved by the voice than the words; the elaborate church music of the late Middle Ages that few could follow.

positions.name: It depends on the words
positions.who: Thomas Cranmer; the Council of Trent
positions.view: Music should serve the text and let it be heard. Cranmer asked for one note to a syllable. The Council of Trent in the 1560s worried that polyphony was burying the words, and church musicians answered by making them clearer.
positions.evidence: Cranmer's letter of 1544; the Tridentine discussions of church music; the clarity of Palestrina's later masses.

debate.agree: All agree that the words matter, that music should serve worship rather than show, and that it has a unique power over the heart, which is exactly why they argue about it.

look.why: Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptised at Reims around the year 500. The painter imagines the scene a thousand years later, in his own time, and he puts an organ in it: a church is a place of sound as well as sight.
points: The crowned king standing in a stone basin, his hands together in prayer.
The bishop in a gold mitre and a rich cloak, pouring water from a golden bowl.
On a balcony at the right, five men looking down, with a row of organ pipes behind them.
A clergyman holding a large book with metal clasps: the words of the service.
Crowds in the courtyard outside the church door, watching.

music.why: Written for the Sistine Chapel and sung in candlelight in Holy Week, Allegri's Miserere is perhaps the most famous example of music written for a particular building and its echo.

think.why: The hours of prayer were a practice before they were a performance: the same psalms, sung day after day, slowly shaping the singers.

learn.why: Every psalm sung in the Office ended with these words. Choirs have sung them more often than any others.

tutorial.question: Augustine wept at the hymns in Milan, and later worried that he cared more for the voice than for the words. Which Augustine was right?
tutorial.approach: Read the two passages (Confessions IX.6 and X.33, which you may know from the journey 'The sound of faith') or work from the lecture. Set out the case for music as a carrier of prayer and the case for it as a distraction, with one example of each from this session. Then say what you think, using your own experience of music if you have it.
strong: Explains Augustine's two experiences and why they pull different ways.
Uses the history: chant serving the words, Cranmer's one note to a syllable, the Reformers' suspicions.
Notes that the building itself favours slow, sung prayer.
Distinguishes being moved by music from being moved to God by it.
Considers whether the answer differs for different people, as Augustine suggests ('weaker minds').
Reaches a clear conclusion of its own.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: go to choral evensong at a cathedral or college chapel near you. It is free, and you need do nothing but sit and listen. If there is none nearby, listen to one broadcast, and invite someone to listen with you.
sessions.reflect: Has any piece of music ever made you pray, or nearly? What was it doing?
takeaways: Stone holds sound, so cathedral music became slow, sung and continuous through the hours of prayer.

sessions.title: The rose
sessions.line: How to read a whole church, ending at the great round windows.
sessions.plain: Every part of a great church has a name and a purpose: the west door, the nave, the transepts, the choir, the apse, and the great round windows called roses. This last session teaches you to read a whole building from the door to the altar, and ends at the window that gives Rose Window its name.
sessions.why: You have the history, the glass, the objection and the sound. Now put them together by walking through a whole church, as a visitor who can read it. Adams takes us to the west front of Chartres and the three roses, and the session ends by teaching you to read any church you enter.
before: Adams says the architect 'concentrated his whole energy on the rose'. Why, in his view?
Watch for the moment when Adams tells you to stand still and turn your head.
Notice his honesty about what he believes and what he does not.

read.author: Henry Adams
read.who: American historian and writer (1838–1918), who said he came to Chartres to feel Gothic art, not to find religion.
paras: If you want to know what churches were made for, come down here on some great festival of the Virgin, and give yourself up to it; but come alone! That kind of knowledge cannot be taught and can seldom be shared. We are not now seeking religion; indeed, true religion generally comes unsought. We are trying only to feel Gothic art. For us, the world is not a schoolroom or a pulpit, but a stage, and the stage is the highest yet seen on earth. In this church the old Romanesque leaps into the Gothic under our eyes; of a sudden, between the portal and the shrine, the infinite rises into a new expression, always a rare and excellent miracle in thought. The two expressions are nowhere far apart; not further than the Mother from the Son. The new artist drops unwillingly the hand of his father or his grandfather; he looks back, from every corner of his own work, to see whether it goes with the old. He will not part with the western portal or the lancet windows; he holds close to the round columns of the choir; he would have kept the round arch if he could, but the round arch was unable to do the work; it could not rise; so he broke it, lifted the vaulting, threw out flying buttresses, and satisfied the Virgin's wish.

The measured height is the least interest of a church. The architect's business is to make a small building look large, and his failures are in large buildings which he makes to look small. One chief beauty of the Gothic is to exaggerate height, and one of its most curious qualities is its success in imposing an illusion of size. Without leaving the heart of Paris any one can study this illusion in the two great churches of Notre Dame and Saint-Sulpice; for Saint-Sulpice is as lofty as Notre Dame in vaulting, and larger in its other dimensions, besides being, in its style, a fine building; yet its Roman arches show, as if they were of the eleventh century, why the long, clean, unbroken, refined lines of the Gothic, curving to points, and leading the eye with a sort of compulsion to the culminating point above, should have made an architectural triumph that carried all Europe off its feet with delight. The world had seen nothing to approach it except, perhaps, in the dome of Sancta Sophia in Constantinople; and the discovery came at a moment when Europe was making its most united and desperate struggle to attain the kingdom of Heaven.

A single glance shows what trouble the architect had with the old facade and towers, and what temptation to pull them all down. One cannot quite say that he has spoiled his own church in trying to save what he could of the old, but if he did not quite spoil it, he saved it only by the exercise of an amount of intelligence that we shall never learn enough to feel our incapacity to understand. True ignorance approaches the infinite more nearly than any amount of knowledge can do, and, in our case, ignorance is fortified by a certain element of nineteenth-century indifference which refuses to be interested in what it cannot understand; a violent reaction from the thirteenth century which cared little to comprehend anything except the incomprehensible. The architect at Chartres was required by the Virgin to provide more space for her worshippers within the church, without destroying the old portal and fleche which she loved. That this order came directly from the Virgin, may be taken for granted. At Chartres, one sees everywhere the Virgin, and nowhere any rival authority; one sees her give orders, and architects obey them; but very rarely a hesitation as though the architect were deciding for himself. In his western front, the architect has obeyed orders so literally that he has not even taken the trouble to apologize for leaving unfinished the details which, if he had been responsible for them, would have been his anxious care. He has gone to the trouble of moving the heavy doorways forward, so that the chapels in the towers, which were meant to open on a porch, now open into the nave, and the nave itself has, in appearance, two more spans than in the old church; but the work shows blind obedience, as though he were doing his best to please the Virgin without trying to please himself. Probably he could in no case have done much to help the side aisles in their abrupt collision with the solid walls of the two towers, but he might at least have brought the vaulting of his two new bays, in the nave, down to the ground, and finished it. The vaulting is awkward in these two bays, and yet he has taken great trouble to effect what seems at first a small matter. Whether the great rose window was an afterthought or not can never be known, but any one can see with a glass, and better on the architectural plan, that the vaulting of the main church was not high enough to admit the great rose, and that the architect has had to slope his two tower-spans upward. So great is the height that you cannot see this difference of level very plainly even with a glass, but on the plans it seems to amount to several feet; perhaps a metre. The architect has managed to deceive our eyes, in order to enlarge the rose; but you can see as plainly as though he were here to tell you, that, like a great general, he has concentrated his whole energy on the rose, because the Virgin has told him that the rose symbolized herself, and that the light and splendour of her appearance in the west were to redeem all his awkwardnesses.

Of course this idea of the Virgin's interference sounds to you a mere bit of fancy, and that is an account which may be settled between the Virgin and you; but even twentieth-century eyes can see that the rose redeems everything, dominates everything, and gives character to the whole church.

The rose window was not Gothic but Romanesque, and needed a great deal of coaxing to feel at home within the pointed arch. At first, the architects felt the awkwardness so strongly that they avoided it wherever they could. In the beautiful facade of Laon, one of the chief beauties is the setting of the rose under a deep round arch. The western roses of Mantes and Paris are treated in the same way, although a captious critic might complain that their treatment is not so effective or so logical. Rheims boldly imprisoned the roses within the pointed arch; but Amiens, toward 1240, took refuge in the same square exterior setting that was preferred, in 1200, here at Chartres; and in the interior of Amiens the round arch of the rose is the last vault of the nave, seen through a vista of pointed vaults, as it is here. All these are supposed to be among the chief beauties of the Gothic facade, although the Gothic architect, if he had been a man of logic, would have clung to his lines, and put a pointed window in his front, as in fact he did at Coutances. He felt the value of the rose in art, and perhaps still more in religion, for the rose was Mary's emblem. One is fairly sure that the great Chartres rose of the west front was put there to please her, since it was to be always before her eyes, the most conspicuous object she would see from the high altar, and therefore the most carefully considered ornament in the whole church, outside the choir. The mere size proves the importance she gave it. The exterior diameter is nearly forty-four feet (13.36 metres). The nave of Chartres is, next perhaps to the nave of Angers, the widest of all Gothic naves; about fifty-three feet (16.31 metres); and the rose takes every inch it can get of this enormous span. The value of the rose, among architects of the time, was great, since it was the only part of the church that Villard de Honnecourt sketched; and since his time, it has been drawn and redrawn, described and commented by generations of architects till it has become as classic as the Parthenon.

Yet this Chartres rose is solid, serious, sedate, to a degree unusual in its own age; it is even more Romanesque than the pure Romanesque roses. At Beauvais you must stop a moment to look at a Romanesque rose on the transept of the Church of Saint-Etienne; Viollet-le-Duc mentions it, with a drawing (article, "Pignon"), as not earlier than the year 1100, therefore about a century earlier than the rose of Chartres; it is not properly a rose, but a wheel of fortune, with figures climbing up and falling over. Another supposed twelfth-century rose is at Etampes, which goes with that of Laon and Saint-Leu-d'Esserent and Mantes. The rose of Chartres is so much the most serious of them all that Viollet-le-Duc has explained it by its material,—the heavy stone of Bercheres;—but the material was not allowed to affect the great transept roses, and the architect made his material yield to his object wherever he thought it worth while. Standing under the central croisee, you can see all three roses by simply turning your head. That on the north, the Rose de France, was built, or planned, between 1200 and 1210, in the reign of Philip Augustus, since the porch outside, which would be a later construction, was begun by 1212. The Rose de France is the same in diameter as the western rose, but lighter, and built of lighter stone. Opposite the Rose de France stands, on the south front, Pierre Mauclerc's Rose de Dreux, of the same date, with the same motive, but even lighter; more like a rose and less like a wheel. All three roses must have been planned at about the same time, perhaps by the same architect, within the same workshop; yet the western rose stands quite apart, as though it had been especially designed to suit the twelfth-century facade and portal which it rules. Whether this was really the artist's idea is a question that needs the artist to answer; but that this is the effect, needs no expert to prove; it stares one in the face. Within and without, one feels that the twelfth-century spirit is respected and preserved with the same religious feeling which obliged the architect to injure his own work by sparing that of his grandfathers.

Conspicuous, then, in the west front are two feelings:—respect for the twelfth-century work, and passion for the rose fenestration; both subordinated to the demand for light. If it worries you to have to believe that these three things are in fact one; that the architect is listening, like the stone Abraham, for orders from the Virgin, while he caresses and sacrifices his child; that Mary and not her architects built this facade; if the divine intention seems to you a needless impertinence, you can soon get free from it by going to any of the later churches, where you will not be forced to see any work but that of the architect's compasses. According to Viollet-le-Duc, the inspiration ceased about 1250, or, as the Virgin would have dated it, on the death of Blanche of Castile in 1252. The work of Chartres, where her own hand is plainly shown, belongs in feeling, if not in execution, to the last years of the twelfth century (1195-1200). The great western rose which gives the motive for the whole decoration and is repeated in the great roses of the transepts, marks the Virgin's will,—the taste and knowledge of "cele qui la rose est des roses," or, if you prefer the Latin of Adam de Saint-Victor, the hand of her who is "Super rosam rosida."

notes.text: A great festival of the Virgin: for instance the Assumption on 15 August, or her Nativity on 8 September. Adams is honest about himself: he is not seeking religion, he says, only trying to feel Gothic art.

Saint-Sulpice: a large Paris church of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in the classical style, with round arches. Adams uses it to show how Gothic lines make a building look taller than it is.
The 'old facade and towers' survived the fire of 1194: the west front with its three doorways and the two towers. The architect built the new nave behind them.
Villard de Honnecourt was a thirteenth-century craftsman whose sketchbook survives in Paris; among his drawings is the west rose of Chartres.

Adams's dates of 1200 to 1210 for the transept roses are too early: most scholars now date them to the 1220s and 1230s. The north rose, the Rose de France, was given by Blanche of Castile, mother of King Louis IX, and the south by Peter of Dreux, Duke of Brittany (Pierre Mauclerc).

'Cele qui la rose est des roses': Old French, 'she who is the rose of roses', a medieval title of Mary. Adam of Saint-Victor was a twelfth-century poet of the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris; 'super rosam rosida' means 'more rose-like than the rose'.

sessions.readWhy: Adams on the roses of Chartres is Adams at his best: the height of the vault, the struggle of the architect with an old front he would not pull down, and the great west rose that 'redeems everything'.

paras: After these things I looked and saw a door opened in heaven, and the first voice that I heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, was one saying, “Come up here, and I will show you the things which must happen after this.”
Immediately I was in the Spirit. Behold, there was a throne set in heaven, and one sitting on the throne
that looked like a jasper stone and a sardius. There was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald to look at.
Around the throne were twenty-four thrones. On the thrones were twenty-four elders sitting, dressed in white garments, with crowns of gold on their heads.
Out of the throne proceed lightnings, sounds, and thunders. There were seven lamps of fire burning before his throne, which are the seven Spirits of God.
Before the throne was something like a sea of glass, similar to crystal. In the middle of the throne, and around the throne were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind.
The first creature was like a lion, and the second creature like a calf, and the third creature had a face like a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle.

The four living creatures, each one of them having six wings, are full of eyes around and within. They have no rest day and night, saying, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come!”
When the living creatures give glory, honor, and thanks to him who sits on the throne, to him who lives forever and ever,
the twenty-four elders fall down before him who sits on the throne, and worship him who lives forever and ever, and throw their crowns before the throne, saying,
“Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honor, and the power, for you created all things, and because of your desire they existed, and were created!”
compare.why: The south rose of Chartres shows Christ enthroned in the centre, with the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders of this chapter around him in rings of glass. Read it as the programme of a rose window.

paras: Most great churches face east, towards the rising sun, the direction from which Christians expected Christ to return. So you usually enter at the west end, with the sunset behind you, and walk towards the morning. The west front is often carved with the Last Judgement over the central door: you pass under the end of history to come in.

Near the door you will often find the font, where baptisms take place, because baptism is how a Christian enters the Church. Then the nave opens in front of you. The word comes from the Latin navis, a ship, and the old writers loved the image: the Church as an ark carrying its people through the flood. On either side, behind the columns, run the lower aisles.
sections.key: You enter from the west, past the font, into the nave, and walk towards the morning.

paras: Look at the side wall of a Gothic nave and you will usually see three levels. At the bottom is the arcade, the row of great arches opening into the aisles. Above it is a narrow band, often a walkway in the thickness of the wall, called the triforium. At the top is the clerestory, the 'clear storey', the row of high windows that lights the middle of the church. Saenredam's painting in this session shows all three very clearly.

Above them all is the vault, the stone ceiling, with its ribs springing from the columns and meeting at carved keystones called bosses. Round arches and thick walls mean Romanesque; pointed arches, ribs and walls opened into glass mean Gothic. You now know enough to tell them apart in any old church in Europe.
sections.key: Arcade, triforium, clerestory: three storeys, with the vault above. Round arches mean Romanesque, pointed mean Gothic.

paras: Halfway up, the nave is usually crossed by the transepts, two arms reaching out to north and south. Together they turn the plan of the church into a cross. Over the crossing there is often a tower or a lantern letting light down into the centre. Medieval writers saw a body in the plan: the head at the east end, the arms in the transepts, the body in the nave, Christ laid out on the ground like a figure on a tomb. In the thirteenth century Durandus of Mende wrote a whole book explaining every part of the church in this way.

Some churches even bend slightly at the crossing. Guides sometimes say this shows the head of Christ leaning on the cross; it is more often the result of building in stages over many years. The tension between the meaning and the practical explanation is the subject of this session's debate.
sections.key: The transepts make the plan a cross; medieval writers read the body of Christ in it.

paras: Beyond the crossing is the choir, where the clergy sang the hours in their stalls (as you saw in session 5), often separated from the nave by a stone or wooden screen. At the far end stands the high altar, and behind it the apse, the rounded end inherited from the Roman basilica of session 1.

Round the apse runs the ambulatory, the walkway Suger built at Saint-Denis, so that pilgrims could walk round behind the altar to visit the relics without disturbing the services, and out of it open the radiating chapels. In many English cathedrals the chapel at the very east end is a Lady Chapel, dedicated to Mary.
sections.key: Beyond the crossing: the choir, the high altar, the apse and the walkway round it.

paras: Round windows are older than Gothic. Romanesque churches had small round openings, and some had wheel windows with spokes, sometimes carved as a wheel of fortune with figures climbing and falling. The Gothic builders made them vast. At first the stone was simply pierced with openings, which is called plate tracery, as in the west rose of Chartres (about 1215). Soon after, at Reims in the 1210s, masons began to build windows from thin stone bars, bar tracery, and the roses became webs of stone holding acres of glass, as in the transept roses of Notre-Dame in Paris.

The great roses usually show the whole order of things in rings around a centre. At Chartres the west rose shows the Last Judgement, with Christ in the middle; the north rose shows Mary with the Christ child, surrounded by kings and prophets; and the south rose shows Christ enthroned with the creatures and elders of Revelation 4, the passage you have just read. To read a rose, start at the centre and go outwards: from God to the world.

Medieval writers more often called these windows wheels or eyes; the name 'rose' became usual later, and whether it came from the flower of Mary, as Adams believed, is still debated. But at the end of Dante's Paradise, written around 1320, the poet sees all the saints in heaven arranged in the shape of a vast white rose, opening around the light of God. Whatever the window was first called, the image fits.
sections.key: Roses grew from small round windows into great wheels of glass showing the order of heaven, read from the centre out.

sections.h: The church as a clock of light
paras: Because great churches are built on an east–west line, the light moves through them in a regular way every day. In the morning the sun comes through the east windows behind the altar; at midday it pours through the south side; in the late afternoon it strikes the west front and fires the great rose from outside, so that the inside of the west wall glows as the day ends. Some churches mark the sun more precisely: in a few, a beam falls on a particular stone or line on a particular day of the year.
So a cathedral is not only a picture of heaven but a kind of clock: the hours of prayer in its choir, and the hours of the sun in its glass, moving together through the day.
sections.key: Built east to west, a church is also a clock: the light moves through it every day.

paras: You can now read most churches you walk into. Which way does it face, and where is the font? Is it Romanesque or Gothic, or a later imitation? What are the windows about, and what is on the bottom panel? Who are the saints? Saints are known by their emblems: Peter by his keys, Paul by his sword, James by his scallop shell, Catherine by her wheel, John the Baptist by a lamb, John the Evangelist by an eagle.

And what has happened to the building? Clear glass, whitewashed walls and empty niches tell of the Reformation, when many churches were stripped of their images, as in Saenredam's painting, where the windows are clear. Plaques and memorials tell of the parish and its dead; a war memorial, of the families who lost sons. A church is a book with many authors, still being written by the people who pray in it today.
sections.key: Ask which way it faces, where the font is, what style it is, what the windows show, and what has happened to it.

paras: The story did not stop with the Middle Ages. In the nineteenth century the Gothic Revival, championed in England by Augustus Pugin, filled Britain, its empire and America with new churches in the old style, and revived the craft of stained glass. In the twentieth century architects asked the old question in new forms. At Coventry, where the medieval cathedral was destroyed by bombing in 1940, Basil Spence built a new cathedral beside the ruins, consecrated in 1962, with a great baptistery window of abstract coloured glass by John Piper. In Barcelona, Antoni Gaudí's Sagrada Família, begun in 1882, was consecrated in 2010 and is still being built, its forests of columns lit by modern stained glass.
Every one of these buildings is another answer to Solomon's question. None of them contains God. All of them try, in stone and glass, to make a place where people might meet him.
sections.key: Every new church, from Coventry to the Sagrada Família, is another answer to Solomon's question.

refs: Durandus of Mende, Rationale divinorum officiorum (about 1286), Book I; translated as The Symbolism of Churches and Church Ornaments by J. M. Neale and B. Webb (1843).
Plate and bar tracery, Reims: Christopher Wilson, The Gothic Cathedral (1990); Paul Binski, Gothic Wonder (2014).
The Chartres roses and their dates: Painton Cowen, The Rose Window: Splendour and Symbol (2005); Corpus Vitrearum France.
Villard de Honnecourt's portfolio: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS fr. 19093.
Dante, Paradiso XXX–XXXI (the 'candida rosa').
Saints' emblems: Richard Taylor, How to Read a Church (2003).

debate.question: Does a cathedral mean what its builders meant, or what we see in it?

positions.name: Every part has a meaning
positions.who: Durandus of Mende (about 1286); Émile Mâle; many guides today
positions.view: The builders thought symbolically, and the building is a sermon in stone: the plan is a cross, the nave a ship, the windows the Scriptures letting in the light, the roses the order of heaven. To read it is to understand its makers.
positions.evidence: Durandus's book; the clear programmes of the great portals and roses; the dedication rites.

positions.name: Mostly practical
positions.who: Many architectural historians, in the tradition of Viollet-le-Duc's rationalism
positions.view: Most features have practical origins: structure, money, fashion, the availability of stone. The symbolism was often added afterwards by writers like Durandus. A bent axis means building in stages, not a leaning head.
positions.evidence: Building accounts and the physical evidence of construction; the late date of most symbolic commentary.

positions.name: Meanings grow
positions.who: Historians of how buildings are used and received, and Adams himself
positions.view: A church gathers meanings over centuries, from its builders, its worshippers, its destroyers and its visitors. A Reformed church with clear glass means something different from the same church in 1400, and both meanings are real.
positions.evidence: Saenredam's whitewashed interiors; the history of iconoclasm and restoration; Adams's own non-believing love.

debate.agree: All agree that the great churches were built for worship and meant to point beyond themselves, and that reading them well needs both the practical history and the meanings.

look.why: Pieter Saenredam drew this cathedral in 1632 and painted it in 1646, after 's-Hertogenbosch had passed in 1629 to the Protestant Dutch Republic. He measured buildings carefully, so his paintings are among the best records we have of what such churches looked like.
points: Three levels on the wall at the top right: arches at the bottom, a narrow walkway above, and tall windows at the top.
Rose-pink ribs rising between the windows and meeting in the vault of the apse.
The tall windows of the apse, all of clear glass.
The altar with its candlesticks and flowers, and above it a large painting of the Nativity.
Stone statues on the columns, and wooden choir stalls between them.
A single bald man in a white garment, kneeling on the left and facing the altar.

music.why: Every saint in the glass and the stone is in this hymn: 'the saints, who from their labours rest'. Vaughan Williams wrote the tune, Sine Nomine, in 1906.

think.why: The cathedral school of Chartres was a centre of twelfth-century learning, where Plato was studied beside the Bible, and its teacher Bernard of Chartres said that we are dwarfs standing on the shoulders of giants. In the south transept windows the four evangelists are shown sitting on the shoulders of four prophets.

learn.why: 'Like a great ring of pure and endless light': Vaughan never mentions a window, but he describes a rose.

listen.why: John O'Donohue on beauty as something that asks for a fuller way of being alive: a good companion for the end of a journey through the cathedrals.

check.q: What are the three storeys of a Gothic nave wall, from bottom to top?
options: Crypt, nave, roof
Arcade, triforium, clerestory
Aisle, transept, apse
Portal, rose, spire
check.why: The arcade opens into the aisles, the triforium is the narrow middle band, and the clerestory is the row of high windows.

check.q: What turns the plan of most great churches into a cross?
options: The towers
The transepts
The aisles
The crypt
check.why: The transepts reach out north and south at the crossing.

check.q: What does the south rose of Chartres show?
options: The Last Judgement
Christ enthroned with the creatures and elders of Revelation 4
The life of Mary
The months of the year
check.why: The west rose shows the Last Judgement and the north rose Mary; the south shows the heavenly court of Revelation 4.

check.q: In Dante's Paradise, what shape do the saints make?
options: A ladder
A great white rose
A tree
A walled city
check.why: In Paradiso XXX–XXXI the blessed are seated in the petals of a vast white rose around the light of God.

tutorial.question: Choose a church you know, or the one in Saenredam's painting, and read it as this session has taught you. What does the building say, and do you believe it?
tutorial.approach: Walk through it in order: orientation, west front and font, nave and its three storeys, crossing and transepts, choir and east end, windows and saints. Say what each part tells you, using the meanings and the practical history. Then answer the second question honestly: is what the building says true, in your view?
strong: Uses the right names for the parts and describes them in order.
Distinguishes Romanesque from Gothic, or original from later work, with evidence.
Reads at least one window or carving in detail.
Notices what has changed: Reformation, restoration, memorials.
Weighs symbolic and practical explanations, as in the debate.
Answers the personal question with candour.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: take someone with you, a child, a friend or someone new to your area, into a church you can visit, and show them three things you can now read: which way it faces, the font, and one window or carving.
sessions.reflect: If your life were a building, where would the light come in?
takeaways: A church is read from west to east: font, nave, three storeys, crossing, choir, apse.
Rose windows show the order of heaven in rings, read from the centre out.
Buildings gather meanings over time, from their builders, users and destroyers.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Having walked from Solomon's Temple to the roses of Chartres, and heard Bernard's case against it all: can a building lead you to God? Is beauty a way to God, or a substitute for him? And if you could build one thing for God and your neighbour, what would it be?
closing.practice: Make one small place in your home a little set apart, a shelf with a picture or a candle, and spend a few minutes there each day for a month. And each week, do one thing for someone in need, so that the beauty and the poor stay side by side.
synthesis: This journey began with a king who built a house for God and then confessed that heaven itself could not contain him. Everything since has been an attempt to live inside that paradox. If God is everywhere, why build? And if we build, what are we building?

The first Christians answered by not building at all. They were the temple, Paul said: living stones, a community in which God dwelt. When they did build, they borrowed the Roman hall of justice rather than the pagan temple, because they needed room for people, not a house for a statue. And they explained their buildings with the last chapter of the Bible: the church is a picture of the city of God, a city that, in the end, will need no temple at all.

In the twelfth century an abbot near Paris took that picture literally. Suger believed that the mind, slow and bound to the senses, could rise to God through material beauty, and above all through light. Whether or not he had read Dionysius, he built a choir that was a ring of coloured light, and in doing so made possible the Gothic cathedral: a stone skeleton with glass between its bones. At Chartres, a generation later, that idea was carried through to the end, with windows that tell the whole story of salvation in light, to be read from the bottom up and seen from afar.

Then we heard the case against. Bernard of Clairvaux, who chose plain glass and bare walls, asked whether a church that clothes its stones in gold and leaves its children naked has forgotten its Lord. Augustine, centuries before, had confessed the same struggle inside himself: beauty comes from the Beauty above our souls, yet it can hold us instead of leading us on. The question was asked of Jesus himself, when a woman poured out a year's wages of ointment, and his answer was neither a simple yes nor a simple no.

We listened to the building: stone that turns a slow line of chant into something like a halo of sound, choirs singing the psalms seven times a day, organum rising in Paris with the vaults, evensong in English cathedrals to this day. And we learned to read a whole church, from the font at the west door to the rose that, at its best, holds the whole order of heaven in a single wheel of light.

What have we found? Not a single answer. The great churches were built for many reasons: for God, for the saints, for pilgrims and their money, for the glory of bishops and kings and towns. They have been loved and smashed, whitewashed and restored. But they keep doing what Suger hoped. People who believe nothing walk into them and fall silent. Something in the height, the light and the sound reaches the part of us that argument does not.

Along the way you have also learned a craft. You know how a window was made from sand, ash and metal, how to read it from the bottom up and how to look at it at the right time of day. You can name the storeys of a nave, find the font and tell Romanesque from Gothic. You know where the plainchant came from, why it is slow, and where to hear evensong for nothing. These are not small things. They turn a great building from a beautiful blur into something you can read, and a building you can read is one you can return to.

You have also met scholars disagreeing, which is what real learning looks like. Panofsky and Kidson on Suger's theology; Mâle and Kemp on whether windows were read; the symbol-readers and the practical historians on what a building means. None of these arguments is settled, and you are now entitled to a view on each.

Bernard's question remains, and it should. A building can point to God; it cannot replace the God it points to, or the neighbour in whom, Christ said, he is met. The test of any beauty made for God, a cathedral or a single candle, is whether it leads us further into love of God and of the poor, or keeps us admiring the glass. The cathedrals at their best do both: they are the one splendid place that belongs to everyone, and in their light the king and the beggar stand together.

Now it is your turn. You know how these buildings were made, how to read them, why some Christians loved them and others feared them. The question is no longer what the builders believed, but what you do.
exam: 'Gothic architecture is a theology in stone.' Discuss, with reference to Saint-Denis.
How far was Bernard of Clairvaux's Apologia an attack on art itself?
Were medieval stained-glass windows 'the Bible of the poor'?
Why did the first Christians not build temples, and why did they later build basilicas?
'A church is a house for God's people, not for God.' Discuss.
What can the music of Notre-Dame of Paris tell us about its architecture, and what can it not?
Is costly beauty in worship justified while people are poor? Answer with reference to at least two periods.
'The cathedral means what its users make of it.' Discuss, with reference to the Reformation.

next.place: Go to choral evensong in the nearest cathedral. Arrive fifteen minutes early, sit as near the choir as you are allowed, and read the building before the singing begins: which way it faces, its storeys, its windows and its saints.
next.book: Henry Adams, Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres (1904), the whole book, with this journey behind you.

title: In the beginning
question: What does Genesis say about the world and about us?
line: Seven sessions on the Bible's first eleven chapters, read as their oldest interpreters read them: heaven and earth, meaning and matter; the garden at the centre where they meet; the eyes opened and the exile to the edge; and, at the end, the Word made flesh. With the case from science at full strength.
why: There are two ways of seeing the world. One sees only matter: what things are made of. The other, which Genesis shares, sees matter and meaning together, and puts them in order. Read that way, the first pages of the Bible are not a failed science lesson but a map of reality and of the human place in it: the centre we were made for, how we lost it, and how it is restored. This course reads Genesis 1–11 with both eyes open, beside Augustine, Milton and the Babylonian stories, gives the scientific objection its full weight, and ends with John's 'In the beginning was the Word'.
follows: A first-year paper on Genesis 1–11 read through the history of interpretation: patristic and medieval symbolic reading beside modern historical-critical scholarship, with elements of a paper on science and religion.
before: can-i-trust-the-bible
outcomes: Explain what 'the heavens and the earth' and 'formless and empty' mean in Genesis 1, with the merism reading and Augustine's reading of heaven and formless matter.
Explain why Eden is described as the centre of the world and the first sanctuary, using Wenham's evidence and Ezekiel 28.
Read Genesis 3 closely, explain what 'their eyes were opened' means, and set out the Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant and Jewish views of original sin.
Trace the movement from the centre to the edge in Genesis 4–11, and explain the flood as creation undone and renewed, beside Hesiod and Gilgamesh.
State the scientific case against Genesis and the modern sense of being small and off-centre at full strength, with the historians' correction of the Copernican 'demotion' story.
Explain why John's Gospel begins 'In the beginning', what logos meant, and how 'the Word became flesh' answers Genesis.

people.name: Moses
people.line: By tradition the author of Genesis and the rest of the Torah.

people.name: Hesiod
people.line: Greek poet whose Works and Days tells of five declining ages of humanity.

people.name: Ezekiel
people.line: Priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon, who pictured Eden as the holy mountain of God.

people.name: Heraclitus
people.line: Greek philosopher who taught that a logos, a rational order, runs through all things.

people.name: Philo of Alexandria
people.line: Jewish philosopher who used logos for God's instrument in creating the world.

people.name: John the Evangelist
people.line: By tradition the author of the Fourth Gospel, which opens 'In the beginning was the Word'.

people.name: Origen
people.line: Alexandrian scholar who read Genesis for its spiritual sense and asked how there could be days before the sun.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.line: Read 'heaven' in Genesis 1:1 as the spiritual creation and 'earth' as formless matter; gave the West the term 'original sin'.

people.name: Ephrem the Syrian
people.line: Syriac poet whose Hymns on Paradise picture Eden as a great mountain.

people.name: Rashi
people.line: French rabbi whose commentary on the Torah is still the most read in Judaism.

people.name: Nachmanides
people.line: Spanish rabbi who read the tohu of Genesis 1:2 as the first matter, the Greeks' hyle.

people.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
people.line: Astronomer who argued that the earth goes round the sun.

people.name: Galileo Galilei
people.line: Astronomer whose telescope supported Copernicus; condemned by the Inquisition in 1633.

people.name: John Milton
people.line: Poet of Paradise Lost, the great English retelling of the fall.

people.name: Charles Darwin
people.line: Naturalist whose Origin of Species (1859) set out evolution by natural selection.

people.name: Thomas Henry Huxley
people.line: Biologist, 'Darwin's bulldog', inventor of the word 'agnostic'.

people.name: George Smith

sessions.title: Two ways of seeing: heaven and earth
sessions.line: The Bible's first page, read as its oldest interpreters read it.
sessions.plain: The Bible begins: 'In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.' Most of us hear that as outer space and our planet. The oldest Jewish and Christian readers heard something more: two kinds of reality, the meaning of things and the stuff they are made of, both made by God and put in order by his word. This session reads Genesis 1 slowly, that way, and asks what kind of writing it is.
sessions.why: This is the first session. It starts where the Bible starts, with its first sentence, and with a question about how we see the world at all.
answers: What does 'the heavens and the earth' mean?
What does 'formless and empty' mean?
Is Genesis 1 a science lesson?
Was it copied from Babylonian myths?
sessions.finding: Read as the ancient interpreters read it, Genesis 1 is not a description of a planet and outer space: it speaks of two orders, meaning ('heaven') and matter ('earth', formless and empty), which God puts in order by speaking. The modern eye tends to see only the second.

background.h: If you are new to Genesis
paras: Genesis is the first book of the Bible. Its name is Greek for 'origin'; in Hebrew it is called Bereshit, its first word, 'In the beginning'. It is the first of the five books of the Torah, the books of Moses, which you met in What is the Bible?

Genesis has two parts. Chapters 1 to 11 tell the story of everyone: the making of the world, the first man and woman, the first murder, the flood and the tower of Babel. From chapter 12 the story narrows to one family, Abraham's. This course reads those first eleven chapters, which scholars call the 'primeval history'. Most scholars think Genesis reached its final form in the sixth or fifth century BC, when many Israelites lived in exile in Babylon; Jewish and Christian tradition holds that Moses wrote it much earlier. Either way, it was written among peoples who had their own stories of how the world began.
background.key: Genesis 1–11 is the Bible's story of everyone, before it narrows to Abraham's family.

paras: Hold a wedding ring in your hand. You can say what it is made of: a few grams of gold, a metal with atomic number 79. You can also say what it is: a promise, the sign of a marriage. Both are true. A chemist can tell you everything about the first, and nothing about the second.

That is the frame for this whole course. There are two ways of seeing the world. The modern way, at its narrowest, sees only matter: what things are made of and how they work. The ancient way, which Genesis shares, sees two things at once, matter and meaning, and puts them in order: meaning above, matter below. Genesis calls them 'heaven' and 'earth'. Each session reads one step of the story with both eyes open.

background.key: Things have a stuff and a meaning; Genesis calls them earth and heaven, and this course reads it with both in view.

paras: The main reading is the Bible's first page, Genesis 1:1–2:3: seven days, from 'In the beginning' to God's rest. We read it in three parts, with a commentary after each, watching what God does with the 'formless and empty' earth.

The comparison is from Augustine of Hippo, the North African bishop who wrote his Confessions about AD 400. In Book XII he stops on the first two verses of Genesis and asks what 'heaven' and 'earth' are. His answer, a heaven we cannot see and an earth that is matter without form, is the oldest form of the reading this course follows. (In What is the Bible? you read the later chapters of the same book, where Augustine says that Scripture can hold many true meanings at once.)
background.key: Genesis 1 read slowly, then Augustine on what 'heaven' and 'earth' mean.
