sessions.readWhy: The first page of the Bible, read slowly in three parts: the world given its shape, the world filled, and the seventh day.

paras: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness.
God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day.
God said, “Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.”
God made the expanse, and divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse; and it was so.
God called the expanse “sky”. There was evening and there was morning, a second day.
God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered together to one place, and let the dry land appear;” and it was so.
God called the dry land “earth”, and the gathering together of the waters he called “seas”. God saw that it was good.
God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth;” and it was so.
The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
There was evening and there was morning, a third day.
God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years;
and let them be for lights in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth;” and it was so.
God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars.
God set them in the expanse of the sky to give light to the earth,
and to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good.
There was evening and there was morning, a fourth day.
God said, “Let the waters abound with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.”
God created the large sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed, after their kind, and every winged bird after its kind. God saw that it was good.
God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.”
There was evening and there was morning, a fifth day.
God said, “Let the earth produce living creatures after their kind, livestock, creeping things, and animals of the earth after their kind;” and it was so.
God made the animals of the earth after their kind, and the livestock after their kind, and everything that creeps on the ground after its kind. God saw that it was good.

God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
To every animal of the earth, and to every bird of the sky, and to everything that creeps on the earth, in which there is life, I have given every green herb for food;” and it was so.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished.
On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.

parts.title: Days 1 to 3: the world given its shape
parts.context: The opening of Genesis. It was written to be heard: listen for the refrains, repeated like a song. Before anything is described, God is already there, and the earth is a dark, watery waste.

commentary.on: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
commentary.text: The first sentence of the Bible. There is no story of where God came from, no battle and no rival: God is, and everything else is made. 'Heavens' (Hebrew shamayim, always plural) and 'earth' (erets) are the two words this course turns on. Most modern scholars take the pair as a Hebrew way of saying 'everything', as we say 'high and low'. The oldest readers also asked what each half means. Hold both answers for now.

commentary.on: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep
commentary.text: 'Formless and empty' is tohu wa-bohu, a rhyming pair. Tohu elsewhere means a trackless desert or a waste (Deuteronomy 32:10); the two words appear together again only in Jeremiah 4:23, of a land destroyed. So the 'earth' of verse 2 is not yet our planet. It is stuff without shape or purpose: dark, deep, undecided. The next six days answer these two words.

commentary.on: God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
commentary.text: 'Spirit' (ruach) is also 'wind' and 'breath'. God's breath hovers over the waters like a bird over its nest. Before any word is spoken, the formless matter is already held by God.

commentary.on: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
commentary.text: God creates by speaking. Nothing resists him and nothing has to be fought. A word is the plainest thing we know that carries meaning; Genesis says the world comes into being the way a sentence does. 'God said' comes ten times in the chapter.

commentary.on: God divided the light from the darkness. God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”.
commentary.text: Three things happen again and again: God speaks, God divides, God names. Dividing gives the world its order; naming gives each part its identity, what it is and what it is for. To name something, in the Bible, is to give it a meaning. That is the work of 'heaven' on 'earth'.

commentary.on: God made the expanse, and divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse
commentary.text: The 'expanse' (older Bibles say 'firmament') holds the waters apart. Ancient peoples pictured the sky as a dome with waters above it, which is why rain fell when 'the sky's windows opened' (Genesis 7:11). Genesis speaks the picture of its time; its point is that the chaos is now held in its place by God's word. Keep this verse in mind: in session 5 the flood will undo it.

commentary.on: God called the dry land “earth”, and the gathering together of the waters he called “seas”.
commentary.text: The formless 'earth' of verse 2 now has a shape and a name. Matter has received meaning. By the end of day three there are three spaces, like the rooms of a house made ready: day and night, sky and sea, dry land with its plants.

parts.title: Days 4 to 6: the world filled
parts.context: The second half of the week. Each day fills one of the spaces made in the first three.

commentary.on: God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.
commentary.text: The words 'sun' and 'moon' are missing. In Hebrew, as in Babylonian, they were also the names of gods. Genesis refuses to use them. The lights are not gods; they are lamps hung by God to mark days and seasons. They 'rule', but only because they have been given a place.

commentary.on: God created the large sea creatures
commentary.text: The great sea monsters, which Israel's neighbours feared as powers of chaos, are simply creatures God made, and he calls them good. Nothing in the world is a rival to God.

commentary.on: Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness.
commentary.text: The pattern breaks. For the first time God pauses, as if in council: 'Let's make'. Christians have heard the Trinity in the 'us'; Jewish commentators such as Rashi hear God speaking with the angels of his court. Either way, the human being is made with special care, and made to resemble God.

commentary.on: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
commentary.text: Every human being, male and female, bears the image of God. In the ancient world a king set up statues of himself, his 'images', to show who ruled a land. Genesis gives that dignity to everyone. Notice where the human being stands: made last, from the earth like the animals, and yet resembling God. Session 2 will look at that more closely.

commentary.on: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
commentary.text: Seven times the chapter says that what God made is good, and the last time 'very good'. Matter is not evil, and the world is not a battlefield. The earth, given its meaning by God's word, is good.

parts.title: The seventh day
parts.context: The last three verses of the story. They belong with chapter 1, although they are numbered as chapter 2: the chapter numbers were added in the Middle Ages.

commentary.on: he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done
commentary.text: The week ends not with more making but with rest. God is not tired; the work is complete. The Hebrew word for 'rested' is the root of 'Sabbath'. Some scholars note that in the ancient world a god 'rested' in a temple once it was finished and ordered: the world itself is pictured as God's house.

commentary.on: God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy
commentary.text: The first thing in the Bible called holy is a day. The weekly Sabbath, rest for everyone, servants and animals included (Exodus 20:8–11), is rooted here. The seventh day has no 'evening and morning': it is left open, as if the rest goes on.

paras: The lowliness of my tongue confesseth unto Thy Highness, that Thou madest heaven and earth; this heaven which I see, and this earth that I tread upon, whence is this earth that I bear about me; Thou madest it. But where is that heaven of heavens, O Lord, which we hear of in the words of the Psalm. The heaven of heavens are the Lord's; but the earth hath He given to the children of men? Where is that heaven which we see not, to which all this which we see is earth? For this corporeal whole, not being wholly every where, hath in such wise received its portion of beauty in these lower parts, whereof the lowest is this our earth; but to that heaven of heavens, even the heaven of our earth, is but earth: yea both these great bodies, may not absurdly be called earth, to that unknown heaven, which is the Lord's, not the sons' of men.

And now this earth was invisible and without form, and there was I know not what depth of abyss, upon which there was no light, because it had no shape. Therefore didst Thou command it to be written, that darkness was upon the face of the deep; what else than the absence of light? For had there been light, where should it have been but by being over all, aloft, and enlightening? Where then light was not, what was the presence of darkness, but the absence of light? Darkness therefore was upon it, because light was not upon it; as where sound is not, there is silence. And what is it to have silence there, but to have no sound there? Hast not Thou, O Lord, taught his soul, which confesseth unto Thee? Hast not Thou taught me, Lord, that before Thou formedst and diversifiedst this formless matter, there was nothing, neither colour, nor figure, nor body, nor spirit? and yet not altogether nothing; for there was a certain formlessness, without any beauty.

How then should it be called, that it might be in some measure conveyed to those of duller mind, but by some ordinary word? And what, among all parts of the world can be found nearer to an absolute formlessness, than earth and deep? For, occupying the lowest stage, they are less beautiful than the other higher parts are, transparent all and shining. Wherefore then may I not conceive the formlessness of matter (which Thou hadst created without beauty, whereof to make this beautiful world) to be suitably intimated unto men, by the name of earth invisible and without form.

So that when thought seeketh what the sense may conceive under this, and saith to itself, "It is no intellectual form, as life, or justice; because it is the matter of bodies; nor object of sense, because being invisible, and without form, there was in it no object of sight or sense";--while man's thought thus saith to itself, it may endeavour either to know it, by being ignorant of it; or to be ignorant, by knowing it.

But whence had it this degree of being, but from Thee, from Whom are all things, so far forth as they are? But so much the further from Thee, as the unliker Thee; for it is not farness of place. Thou therefore, Lord, Who art not one in one place, and otherwise in another, but the Self-same, and the Self-same, and the Self-same, Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty, didst in the Beginning, which is of Thee, in Thy Wisdom, which was born of Thine own Substance, create something, and that out of nothing. For Thou createdst heaven and earth; not out of Thyself, for so should they have been equal to Thine Only Begotten Son, and thereby to Thee also; whereas no way were it right that aught should be equal to Thee, which was not of Thee. And aught else besides Thee was there not, whereof Thou mightest create them, O God, One Trinity, and Trine Unity; and therefore out of nothing didst Thou create heaven and earth; a great thing, and a small thing; for Thou art Almighty and Good, to make all things good, even the great heaven, and the petty earth. Thou wert, and nothing was there besides, out of which Thou createdst heaven and earth; things of two sorts; one near Thee, the other near to nothing; one to which Thou alone shouldest be superior; the other, to which nothing should be inferior.

But that heaven of heavens was for Thyself, O Lord; but the earth which Thou gavest to the sons of men, to be seen and felt, was not such as we now see and feel. For it was invisible, without form, and there was a deep, upon which there was no light; or, darkness was above the deep, that is, more than in the deep. Because this deep of waters, visible now, hath even in his depths, a light proper for its nature; perceivable in whatever degree unto the fishes, and creeping things in the bottom of it. But that whole deep was almost nothing, because hitherto it was altogether without form; yet there was already that which could be formed. For Thou, Lord, madest the world of a matter without form, which out of nothing, Thou madest next to nothing, thereof to make those great things, which we sons of men wonder at. For very wonderful is this corporeal heaven; of which firmament between water and water, the second day, after the creation of light, Thou saidst, Let it be made, and it was made.

Which firmament Thou calledst heaven; the heaven, that is, to this earth and sea, which Thou madest the third day, by giving a visible figure to the formless matter, which Thou madest before all days. For already hadst Thou made both an heaven, before all days; but that was the heaven of this heaven; because In the beginning Thou hadst made heaven and earth. But this same earth which Thou madest was formless matter, because it was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep, of which invisible earth and without form, of which formlessness, of which almost nothing, Thou mightest make all these things of which this changeable world consists, but subsists not; whose very changeableness appears therein, that times can be observed and numbered in it. For times are made by the alterations of things, while the figures, the matter whereof is the invisible earth aforesaid, are varied and turned.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.title: Where is the heaven of heavens?
parts.context: Augustine speaks to God throughout ('Thou', 'Thy'). He quotes Psalm 115:16 in his Latin Bible: 'The heaven of heavens are the Lord's; but the earth hath He given to the children of men' (the World English Bible has 'The heavens are Yahweh's heavens').
parts.plain: Augustine says: I know you made this sky I see and this earth I walk on, and the body I carry. But the Psalm speaks of a 'heaven of heavens' that belongs to God. Where is that heaven, the one we cannot see? Compared with it, the whole visible universe, sky and earth together, could fairly be called 'earth'.

commentary.on: this heaven which I see, and this earth that I tread upon
commentary.text: Augustine starts with the ordinary meaning: the visible sky and the ground under his feet. He does not deny it. He asks whether it is all the word 'heaven' means.

commentary.on: Where is that heaven which we see not, to which all this which we see is earth?
commentary.text: Here is the step. There is a 'heaven' beyond everything visible, and next to it the whole physical universe, stars included, is 'earth'. Heaven, in this reading, is not higher up in space. It is a different kind of reality: the invisible, the spiritual, what gives the visible world its point.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.title: An earth without form
parts.context: Augustine's Latin Bible, translated from the Greek Septuagint, read Genesis 1:2 as 'the earth was invisible and without form', where the Hebrew has 'formless and empty'. He now asks what this 'earth' is.
parts.plain: Augustine says: before God gave things their shapes and kinds, there was not simply nothing, but there was no colour, shape or body either: a formlessness without beauty. Genesis calls it 'earth' and 'the deep' because those are the lowest, least beautiful things we know, the nearest picture of it. When the mind tries to think of it, it can only know it by not knowing it, because it is neither an idea nor something we could see.

commentary.on: there was nothing, neither colour, nor figure, nor body, nor spirit? and yet not altogether nothing
commentary.text: 'Figure' means shape. Augustine is trying to name something very strange: not nothing, but not yet anything in particular. Philosophers called it 'formless matter': the raw possibility out of which particular things are made.

commentary.on: the formlessness of matter (which Thou hadst created without beauty, whereof to make this beautiful world)
commentary.text: God made the formless matter too, and made it in order to shape it into a beautiful world. Matter is not God's rival or a dark leftover; it is the 'earth' waiting for its meaning.

commentary.on: It is no intellectual form, as life, or justice; because it is the matter of bodies
commentary.text: Here are the two orders plainly. 'Intellectual forms', like life or justice, are meanings: you cannot touch justice. Matter is what bodies are made of. Genesis 1:2's 'earth' is matter before it has any meaning at all, so the mind cannot quite grasp it.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.title: One near you, the other near to nothing
parts.context: Augustine leaves out a long chapter (XII.6) about his years of failing to imagine formless matter, marked '…' in the text. Now he draws his conclusion.
parts.plain: Augustine says: everything that exists comes from you, and the less like you a thing is, the further from you it is, though not in distance. Out of nothing you made two things: a heaven near to you, and an earth near to nothing. That first heaven is not the sky of day two, which is only the heaven of our earth. The earth of verse 2 was formless matter, made before all the days, out of which you shaped everything we see.

commentary.on: so much the further from Thee, as the unliker Thee; for it is not farness of place
commentary.text: This sentence matters for the whole course. 'Near' and 'far' from God are not distances in space. They are a matter of likeness. Hold on to it: when we come to the modern feeling of being far from the centre of the universe, Augustine has already said that the real centre is not a place.

commentary.on: things of two sorts; one near Thee, the other near to nothing
commentary.text: Heaven and earth: one close to God, the other close to nothing. That is Augustine's reading of Genesis 1:1 in seven words. The 'heaven' is the realm of spirit and meaning; the 'earth' is matter, almost nothing until God shapes it.

commentary.on: the heaven of this heaven; because In the beginning Thou hadst made heaven and earth
commentary.text: Augustine notices that Genesis uses the word 'heaven' twice: in verse 1, and again on day two, when God calls the expanse 'sky' (his Latin Bible had 'heaven'). So, he reasons, the first heaven cannot be the sky. It is the 'heaven of this heaven', a heaven above the visible one.

commentary.on: which Thou madest before all days
commentary.text: The heaven and the formless earth come 'before all days'. The days of Genesis, for Augustine, are the shaping of matter into an ordered world. Notice that he is not reading Genesis as a timetable. He is reading it as an account of what the world is, and in what order its parts stand.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.why: Augustine (354–430) was a teacher of rhetoric who became a Christian in 386 and bishop of Hippo, in modern Algeria. In Book XII of his Confessions, written as a long prayer to God, he asks what Genesis 1:1–2 means by 'heaven' and 'earth'. His answer is the oldest form of the reading this course follows.
compare.title: Augustine: the heaven we cannot see

paras: Start with the words. Shamayim, 'heavens', is the sky, where birds fly and rain comes from. It is also where God is said to dwell: 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool' (Isaiah 66:1). Erets, 'earth', is the ground, and also a land or a country. Put together, 'the heavens and the earth' can simply mean 'everything that exists'. That is a merism, a pair of opposites standing for the whole, and most modern commentators read Genesis 1:1 this way.

But the pair is not symmetrical. Heaven is above and earth below; heaven is God's and earth is given to us (Psalm 115:16). The Nicene Creed, agreed in 381 and still said in most churches, calls God 'maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible'. The ancient Church heard two orders in the phrase: the invisible, which gives things their meaning, and the visible, which gives them a body.
sections.key: 'The heavens and the earth' means everything, and also two orders: the invisible above and the visible below.

paras: What is this invisible 'heaven'? Augustine called it a spiritual creation. Today we might put it more plainly: it is meaning. Meaning is what a thing is for, what it is called, what it is. Matter is what it is made of. A modern Orthodox writer, Matthieu Pageau, in The Language of Creation (2018), reads the whole of Genesis this way: heaven as the side of reality that gives unity, identity and purpose; earth as the side that is many, changing and still to be shaped. His brother, the icon carver Jonathan Pageau, has made the reading widely known in talks and on his podcast, The Symbolic World.

Watch Genesis 1 with this in mind. On every day God does the same three things. He speaks, which is meaning. He divides, which gives order. He names, which gives identity. The 'formless and empty' earth receives, day by day, a shape and a purpose. Meaning comes from above; matter receives it from below.
sections.key: Heaven can be read as meaning (what a thing is for) and earth as matter (what it is made of); God's speaking, dividing and naming join them.

paras: Tohu wa-bohu is one of the strangest phrases in the Bible. Tohu is used of a wilderness where travellers lose their way (Deuteronomy 32:10), and of what God did not intend the world to be: 'he didn't create it a waste' (Isaiah 45:18). It describes stuff with no shape, no direction and no purpose yet: the unknown, the merely possible.

Jewish and Christian readers alike saw it as matter before form. Augustine's Latin read 'invisible and without form'. The Spanish rabbi Nachmanides (1194–1270), in his commentary on Genesis, said that tohu is what the Greeks called hyle, the first matter, and bohu the form it later received. Two traditions, independently, read verse 2 the same way: the 'earth' is what things are made from, before God gives them their meaning.
sections.key: Tohu wa-bohu is matter without shape or purpose; Augustine and Nachmanides both read it as formless matter.

paras: The days are arranged with great care. Days one to three answer tohu, 'formless', by dividing: light from dark, waters above from waters below, sea from land. Days four to six answer bohu, 'empty', by filling the spaces just made. Then the seventh day stands apart.

The pattern is a clue to what kind of writing this is. It is not a laboratory report. It is a solemn, ordered account, written to be heard and remembered, that shows what the world is: an order, given by God's word, in which everything has a place and a purpose.

rows: God blesses the day and makes it holy

sections.key: Days one to three give the formless earth its shape; days four to six fill it; day seven is rest.

paras: A modern Old Testament scholar has reached something close to this reading by a different road. John Walton, in The Lost World of Genesis One (2009), argues that ancient people thought something truly existed when it had a function, a place and a purpose in an ordered whole, not merely when it was made of something. Genesis 1, on his reading, is about God giving the world its functions and then 'resting' in it, as a god took up residence in a newly ordered temple. It tells us what the world is for, not what it is made of.

Walton writes as an evangelical scholar of the ancient Near East, not as a symbolic reader, and his case is debated. But notice where it lands. Like Augustine, and like the reading of this course, it says that Genesis 1 is mainly about meaning and order. A world seen only as matter is, by Genesis's own standards, not yet a world.
sections.key: Walton argues that Genesis 1 is about the world's functions and purpose rather than its material origins, which is close to the reading of this course.

paras: Israel lived between Egypt and Mesopotamia, and both had creation stories. The best known is Babylon's Enuma Elish, recited at the New Year festival. In it the first gods are born from mingled waters; the god Marduk kills the sea-goddess Tiamat and makes the sky from half her body; and human beings are made from the blood of a rebel god, to do the gods' labour so that the gods can rest.

Genesis shares the ancient picture of the cosmos: the waters, the dome, the order of making. What it says with that picture is almost the opposite. Most scholars now read Genesis 1 as a deliberate answer to such myths, not a copy of them.

rows: By war and the killing of Tiamat
By God's word, with nothing resisting
To labour so the gods can rest
To bear God's image and care for the world
For the gods, by making humans work
For God, and then for everyone

sections.key: Genesis shares the ancient picture of the cosmos but says the opposite of Babylon about God, the world and humans.

paras: Genesis describes the world as it looked: a flat earth under a dome of sky, with waters above and below. Should that worry us? Christians have long said not. Augustine and John Calvin both taught that Scripture speaks of nature in everyday language, because its aim is to teach about God and ourselves. Calvin, commenting on this chapter in 1554, said that Moses wrote for ordinary people, and that anyone who wants to learn astronomy should look elsewhere.

The Jewish commentator Rashi (1040–1105) made a similar point about verse 1. The verse, he said, does not come to teach the order of creation; it calls out to be interpreted. So the question 'is Genesis 1 science?' has a plain answer: no, and it never claimed to be. Whether it is true is a different question. Session 6 will give the scientific case its full weight.
sections.key: Genesis uses the ancient picture of the world; from Augustine and Rashi to Calvin, readers have said its purpose is not to teach physics.

refs: Genesis 1:1–2:3; 7:11; Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 32:10; Isaiah 45:18; 66:1; Jeremiah 4:23; Psalm 115:16.

Enuma Elish: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Babylonian Legends of the Creation (1921); W. G. Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths (2013). Gerhard Hasel, 'The Polemic Nature of the Genesis Cosmology', Evangelical Quarterly 46 (1974).

debate.question: What do 'the heavens and the earth' mean in Genesis 1:1?

positions.name: Everything: sky and land
positions.who: Most modern commentators, such as Gordon Wenham and Claus Westermann
positions.view: The phrase is a merism, a pair of opposites meaning 'the whole universe'. 'Heavens' is the visible sky and 'earth' the land, as an ancient Israelite saw them. Genesis 1:1 is a heading: God made everything.
positions.evidence: The same pair means 'everything' elsewhere in the Bible; verse 2 goes straight on to describe the earth; the ancient three-storey picture of the world.

positions.name: Two orders: meaning and matter
positions.who: Origen and Augustine; the Nicene Creed's 'visible and invisible'; today Matthieu Pageau, The Language of Creation (2018)
positions.view: The literal sense stands, but 'heaven' is also the invisible order that gives things their meaning, and 'earth' the matter that receives it. Genesis 1 shows God ordering the two by his word.
positions.evidence: Two 'heavens' in the chapter (verse 1 and day two); Psalm 115:16; the formless earth of verse 2; the pattern of speaking, dividing and naming.

positions.name: Chaos and order
positions.who: Jordan Peterson, in his 2017 lecture series on the psychological significance of the biblical stories, the second lecture, 'Genesis 1: Chaos & Order'
positions.view: The 'formless and empty' deep stands for chaos, the unknown and the possible; God's speech stands for the way truthful words bring order out of it. Human beings, made in God's image, take part in that work whenever they speak truly. Peterson offers this as a psychological reading and has been publicly guarded about his own belief.
positions.evidence: Tohu wa-bohu; creation by word; the image of God given to speaking beings; parallels in many cultures' stories of order from chaos.

positions.name: A literal account of origins
positions.who: Young-earth creationists, such as Answers in Genesis; many earlier Christian readers in part, such as Basil of Caesarea (about 378)
positions.view: Genesis 1 describes what God did in six ordinary days, in that order, a few thousand years ago. 'Heavens' is the physical universe, and the account is history.
positions.evidence: The 'evening and morning' of each day; Exodus 20:11 grounds the Sabbath in a six-day creation; the genealogies that follow.

debate.agree: All four agree that one God made everything that exists, freely and by his word, and that the world he made is good.

look.why: Frederic Edwin Church, an American painter fascinated by science and by nature, painted this tropical river in 1877. It is not a picture of Genesis. It is here because it shows what a chemist and a poet would both see: light, water and growing things, matter and its beauty, each in its place.
points: A wide, calm river running away from us between banks of dense tropical forest.
Trees covered in climbing vines, with gnarled, sprawling branches.
Two tiny black birds with cherry-red chests on a curving stem near us, on the left.
A line of white birds flying low over the water, and a small white sun in a hazy sky.
Far off on the river, barely visible, a person rowing a canoe.

music.why: Haydn's oratorio The Creation (1798) sets Genesis 1 to music. It opens with 'The Representation of Chaos', music that wanders without a home key; then, at 'and there was light', choir and orchestra burst out in C major. Formless matter, then a word.

think.why: A first look at how Christians have related faith and science.

learn.why: The first words of the Bible: heaven and earth, the formless deep, the hovering Spirit, and the first word.

listen.why: A psychologist and a mathematician talk about God and the stories of Genesis. Listen for how differently they read the same chapter.

check.q: Augustine says that compared with the 'heaven of heavens', even the visible sky is 'earth'. What does that show about how he reads 'heaven' in Genesis 1:1?
options: He thinks the visible sky is the only heaven Genesis means
He reads it as an invisible, spiritual order, different in kind from anything physical, not as a place further up
He thinks heaven is the highest layer of the sky, above the stars
He thinks Genesis made a mistake about astronomy
check.why: 'For it is not farness of place': nearness to God is likeness, not distance.

check.q: Why does it matter that God names things in Genesis 1 ('God called the light day')?
options: Names were needed so that Adam could learn them
It proves the days were 24 hours long
Naming gives each part its identity and purpose: matter receives meaning by God's word
It shows the writer knew Hebrew grammar
check.why: Speaking, dividing and naming are how God orders the formless earth.

check.q: Most modern commentators read 'the heavens and the earth' as a merism. Which statement fits that reading best?
options: The phrase means 'everything', as 'high and low' does, with heavens as the visible sky
The phrase means God's throne and his footstool and nothing else
The phrase was added by a later editor
The phrase means only the planet Earth
check.why: A merism names two extremes to mean the whole.

check.q: Augustine and the rabbi Nachmanides lived eight hundred years apart. On what do they agree?
options: That there was no God before creation
That Genesis copies Babylonian myth
That the 'earth' of Genesis 1:2 is formless matter, what things are made from before they receive their form
That the days were long geological ages
check.why: Augustine's 'formless matter' and Nachmanides' hyle.

check.q: John Walton argues that Genesis 1 is about functions rather than material origins. How does that relate to the reading of this course?
options: It contradicts it, because Walton denies that God made anything
It lands close to it: both say Genesis 1 is mainly about meaning, order and purpose, though Walton reaches this from ancient Near Eastern texts, not symbolic reading
It has nothing to do with it
It is the same as young-earth creationism
check.why: Different road, similar destination; and Walton's case is debated.

check.q: Genesis does not use the words 'sun' and 'moon'. Which is the best explanation?
options: Hebrew had no words for them
They were added later
The writer did not know what they were
The words were also names of gods, and Genesis makes them lamps placed by God, not powers to be worshipped
check.why: Genesis gives everything a place under God; nothing in the sky is a rival.

tutorial.question: What does Genesis 1 mean by 'the heavens and the earth', and what kind of writing is it?
tutorial.approach: Begin with the Hebrew words and the merism reading. Then set out Augustine's reading of heaven as the invisible order and earth as formless matter, using his own words. Show how God's speaking, dividing and naming order the 'formless and empty' earth. Bring in Walton and the Babylonian background. Finish by saying whether Genesis 1 is science, and what it is if not.
strong: Explains shamayim, erets and the merism fairly.
Quotes Augustine accurately on the heaven of heavens and formless matter.
Explains tohu wa-bohu and the pattern of forming and filling.
Shows God's speaking, dividing and naming as the giving of meaning.
Uses the Babylonian comparison and the ancient picture of the world.
Distinguishes 'not science' from 'not true', and notes that readers have disagreed from the start.

reading.author: John Walton
reading.title: The Lost World of Genesis One
reading.why: A short, clear case that Genesis 1 is about function and purpose.

reading.author: Matthieu Pageau
reading.title: The Language of Creation: Cosmic Symbolism in Genesis
reading.why: A modern Orthodox reading of Genesis as heaven and earth, meaning and matter.

reading.author: Augustine
reading.title: Confessions, Books XI–XIII
reading.why: The oldest great Christian reading of Genesis 1, written as a prayer.

reading.author: Gordon Wenham
reading.title: Genesis 1–15 (Word Biblical Commentary)
reading.why: The standard scholarly commentary, careful and balanced.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, pick one ordinary thing you used that day (a cup, a coat, a key) and say aloud both what it is made of and what it is for, or who it came from. Notice how much of your day you saw with only one eye.
sessions.reflect: In your own life, where have you been seeing only the 'earth' of things, their stuff, and missing their 'heaven', their meaning?
takeaways: 'The heavens and the earth' means everything, and the oldest readers also heard two orders in it: meaning above and matter below.
The 'formless and empty' earth is matter without meaning; God orders it by speaking, dividing and naming, and calls it good.
Genesis 1 is not a science lesson: it answers the myths of its neighbours and shows what the world is and what it is for.

sessions.title: The centre: where heaven and earth meet
sessions.line: A garden on a mountain, four rivers, two trees, and a man made of dust and breath.
sessions.plain: Genesis tells the story of creation a second time, close up: God shaping a man from dust, breathing into him, and planting a garden. Read with care, the garden is more than a park. It is the centre of the world, the place where heaven and earth meet, and the human being stands there as the link between them.
sessions.why: Session 1 found two orders in the world, meaning and matter, put in order by God's word. Now the camera comes down to one place and one creature. Where do the two meet, and what are we?
answers: What is Eden?
Why is there a tree in the middle?
What am I, according to Genesis?
Why are there two creation stories?
sessions.finding: Eden is the centre of the world, the place where heaven and earth meet, and the human being, dust of the ground with God's breath in him, stands there as the link between them.

paras: Session 1 read Genesis 1 with both eyes open. 'Heaven' is the order of meaning, 'earth' the matter that receives it, and God joins them by speaking, dividing and naming. Human beings were made last, from the earth like the animals, yet in God's image.
background.key: Session 1: heaven and earth, meaning and matter, ordered by God's word.

paras: At Genesis 2:4 the style changes. God is now called 'Yahweh God', using his personal name (often printed 'the LORD' in English Bibles). Instead of a cosmic week we are in one place, close up: God shapes a man from the ground like a potter, breathes into him, plants a garden and makes a woman.

Why two accounts? Many scholars think they come from two older sources placed side by side. Others see a deliberate design, a wide view and then a close-up, as a film might show a city and then one house. The editor saw no contradiction. The first account says where human beings stand in the whole order of things; the second says what a human being is.
background.key: Genesis 2 retells creation close up; the two accounts are meant to be read together.

paras: Ancient peoples almost all had a sacred centre: a mountain, a temple or a tree where the world above touched the world below. The Greeks kept a carved stone at Delphi that they called the navel of the world. Babylon's great temple tower was named 'the house of the foundation of heaven and earth'. In the Bible, Jerusalem's Temple came to be that place.
Genesis 2 is the first such centre in the Bible. A river flows out of it to water the world, so it stands high. It has a tree 'in the middle'. God walks there. Read the garden with that in mind.
background.key: Ancient peoples had a sacred centre where heaven met earth; Eden is the Bible's first.

paras: The main reading is the whole of Genesis 2:4–25, in three parts: the man made of dust and breath; the rivers, the work and the one command; and the making of the woman.

The comparison is a few verses from the prophet Ezekiel, written in Babylon in the sixth century BC. They are a lament over the king of Tyre, but they describe Eden in words Genesis does not use: 'the garden of God', on 'the holy mountain of God', guarded by a cherub and full of precious stones. They show how Israel itself pictured Eden: as the first sanctuary, on the mountain where heaven and earth meet.
background.key: Genesis 2 shows the garden and the human being; Ezekiel 28 shows Eden as a holy mountain.

before: What two things is the man made from, and where do they come from?
Where is the tree of life, and where do the rivers go?
What is the man given to do in the garden?
sessions.readWhy: The second creation story, in three parts, with a commentary after each.

paras: This is the history of the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that Yahweh God made the earth and the heavens.
No plant of the field was yet in the earth, and no herb of the field had yet sprung up; for Yahweh God had not caused it to rain on the earth. There was not a man to till the ground,
but a mist went up from the earth, and watered the whole surface of the ground.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.

Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
A river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from there it was parted, and became the source of four rivers.
The name of the first is Pishon: it flows through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold;
and the gold of that land is good. Bdellium and onyx stone are also there.
The name of the second river is Gihon. It is the same river that flows through the whole land of Cush.
The name of the third river is Hiddekel. This is the one which flows in front of Assyria. The fourth river is the Euphrates.
Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
Yahweh God commanded the man, saying, “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden;
but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

Out of the ground Yahweh God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name.
The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him.
Yahweh God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep. As the man slept, he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place.
Yahweh God made a woman from the rib which he had taken from the man, and brought her to the man.
The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.”
Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

parts.title: Dust and breath
parts.context: The second account begins. The ground is bare, and there is no one to work it.

commentary.on: This is the history of the generations of the heavens and of the earth
commentary.text: The new account opens with the same pair as the first: heavens and earth. The phrase 'this is the history of the generations' comes ten times in Genesis, each time opening a new chapter of the story. Notice that here it is 'the earth and the heavens' in the next line: the focus is coming down to the ground.

commentary.on: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground
commentary.text: A pun in Hebrew: the man is adam, made from the adamah, the ground. We might say 'the earthling from the earth'. 'Formed' is a potter's word. The human being is made of the same stuff as the world: earth, matter, from below.

commentary.on: breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul
commentary.text: And then something from above. God breathes his own breath into the man, face to face, and he comes alive. Here is the Bible's picture of a human being: earth and breath together. Matter and meaning meet in us. That is why we can know both what things are made of and what they are for.

commentary.on: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden
commentary.text: Eden probably means 'delight'. The garden is 'eastward', in the direction of sunrise. Remember the word 'east': it will come back each time someone moves away from God.

commentary.on: the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
commentary.text: Two trees, at the centre. A tree is a natural picture of the meeting of heaven and earth: its roots go down into the ground and its branches reach up into the sky. The tree of life stands where the two orders meet, and gives life. The second tree will be the subject of session 3.

parts.title: Four rivers, work and one command
parts.context: The writer pauses to describe the geography of the garden, then gives the man his work. Two of the four rivers are real: the Hiddekel (the Tigris) and the Euphrates of Mesopotamia. The other two are unknown.

commentary.on: A river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from there it was parted, and became the source of four rivers.
commentary.text: Water flows downhill, so Eden is high ground. One river goes out from the centre and divides into four, as if to the four corners of the earth. Life flows from the centre outwards. Later prophets picture a river flowing out of the Temple to heal the land (you will meet that river in Hall V).

commentary.on: where there is gold; and the gold of that land is good. Bdellium and onyx stone are also there.
commentary.text: Why mention gold and precious stones in a garden? Because these are the materials of a sanctuary. Israel's tabernacle, its tent for God, was covered in gold, and the high priest wore two onyx stones on his shoulders (Exodus 28:9–12). The garden is being described like a temple.

commentary.on: The name of the second river is Gihon.
commentary.text: Gihon was also the name of the spring that watered Jerusalem, where King Solomon was anointed (1 Kings 1:33–38). A reader in Jerusalem would hear a link between Eden and the city of the Temple.

commentary.on: put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it
commentary.text: 'Cultivate' (literally 'serve') and 'keep' (guard) are the same two Hebrew verbs used of the Levites, who served and guarded the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7–8). The man is not only a gardener but a priest. His work is to tend the place where heaven and earth meet.

commentary.on: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
commentary.text: Generous permission, 'every tree', and one limit. Freedom in Genesis is life within a good boundary, set by someone who can be trusted. Whether that trust holds is the question of the next session.

parts.title: Not good to be alone
parts.context: For the first time something is 'not good'. Watch how God answers it.

commentary.on: It is not good for the man to be alone.
commentary.text: Everything in chapter 1 was good. The first 'not good' in the Bible is loneliness. The human being is made for others.

commentary.on: I will make him a helper comparable to him.
commentary.text: 'Helper' (ezer) is not a servant's word: it is used of God himself (Psalm 121:2). 'Comparable to him' means 'corresponding to him', a partner face to face.

commentary.on: Whatever the man called every living creature became its name.
commentary.text: In chapter 1 God named the day, the sky and the seas. Now he brings the animals to the man to name. The man shares in God's own work of giving meaning: he sees each creature and says what it is. This is the 'dominion' of chapter 1 in action, rule by understanding.

commentary.on: This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.
commentary.text: The first words a human being speaks in the Bible are a poem of joy at meeting another person. At last, someone like me.

commentary.on: The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
commentary.text: Nothing to hide, from each other or from God. They are looking outwards, at God, at each other and at the world, not at themselves. This last line sets up the next chapter.

paras: “Son of man, take up a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and tell him, ‘The Lord Yahweh says:

“You were the seal of full measure,
full of wisdom,
and perfect in beauty.

You were in Eden,
the garden of God.
Every precious stone adorned you:
ruby, topaz, emerald,
chrysolite, onyx, jasper,
sapphire, turquoise, and beryl.
Gold work of tambourines
and of pipes was in you.
They were prepared in the day that you were created.

You were the anointed cherub who covers.
Then I set you up on the holy mountain of God.
You have walked up and down in the middle of the stones of fire.

You were perfect in your ways from the day that you were created,
until unrighteousness was found in you.

By the abundance of your commerce, your insides were filled with violence,
and you have sinned.
Therefore I have cast you as profane out of God’s mountain.
I have destroyed you, covering cherub,
from the middle of the stones of fire.

parts.title: You were in Eden, the garden of God
parts.context: Ezekiel is mocking the proud king of Tyre, a rich trading city on the coast of modern Lebanon, by comparing him to a glorious being placed in Eden and then thrown out. The poem is about a king; what matters here is the picture of Eden it takes for granted.

commentary.on: You were in Eden, the garden of God.
commentary.text: Genesis says 'a garden eastward, in Eden'. Ezekiel calls it 'the garden of God': God's own place.

commentary.on: Every precious stone adorned you
commentary.text: The stones listed here match stones on the breastpiece of Israel's high priest (Exodus 28:17–20), and in the ancient Greek translation all twelve are there. The figure in Eden is dressed like a priest. Eden is a sanctuary.

commentary.on: You were the anointed cherub who covers.
commentary.text: Cherubim were the winged guardians of holy places. Two golden cherubim covered the ark in the tabernacle (Exodus 25:18–20). In Genesis 3 cherubim will guard the way back into Eden.

commentary.on: Then I set you up on the holy mountain of God.
commentary.text: Here it is plainly: Eden is on 'the holy mountain of God'. In the ancient world the mountain was the meeting place of heaven and earth: Moses met God on Mount Sinai, and the Temple stood on Mount Zion. Ezekiel puts Eden on that mountain, at the top of the world.

commentary.on: Therefore I have cast you as profane out of God’s mountain.
commentary.text: And the figure who was in Eden is thrown out of it, for violence and pride. Ezekiel's poem already tells the shape of the next chapter of Genesis: a fall from the holy centre. Many Christian writers, from Origen on, also read these verses as a picture of the devil's fall.

compare.why: Genesis never calls Eden a mountain or a sanctuary. Ezekiel, a priest and prophet writing among the exiles in Babylon in the sixth century BC, does. Read these verses to see how Israel itself pictured the garden.
compare.title: Eden, the holy mountain of God

paras: Every human culture seems to need a centre: a place where the ordinary world is open to what is above it. The historian of religion Mircea Eliade, in The Sacred and the Profane (1957), called it the 'axis of the world', a pillar, mountain, tree or temple that joins sky, earth and underworld, and around which a people orders its life. The Greeks put a stone at Delphi and called it the navel of the earth. Ezekiel calls the land of Israel 'the middle of the earth' (38:12, literally 'the navel').

Notice what this centre is. It is not the geometric middle of anything. Delphi was not the centre of the earth's surface, and the Temple was not in the middle of the map. A centre in this sense is where heaven and earth meet, where meaning comes down into matter. Genesis 2 puts the first one in Eden.
sections.key: A sacred centre is not a point in space but the place where heaven and earth meet; Genesis 2 puts the first in Eden.

sections.h: The garden as the first sanctuary
paras: In 1986 the Old Testament scholar Gordon Wenham published a short paper, 'Sanctuary Symbolism in the Garden of Eden Story', which changed how many scholars read Genesis 2–3. He showed that the garden is described with the words and objects of Israel's tabernacle and Temple. Others, such as G. K. Beale in The Temple and the Church's Mission (2004), have built on it. The likenesses are too many to be chance.

rows: God 'walking' among his people in the tent (Leviticus 26:12; 2 Samuel 7:6)
The man set to 'serve' and 'keep' it (2:15)
Gold everywhere; onyx on the high priest (Exodus 25; 28:9–12)
Cherubim on the ark and the curtain; the entrance on the east
The tree of life in the middle
The lampstand, shaped like an almond tree (Exodus 25:31–36)

sections.key: Eden is described like Israel's tabernacle and Temple: it is the first sanctuary, the first meeting place of God and humanity.

paras: The river that goes out of Eden and divides into four is a picture of the centre's work. Life does not stay at the centre; it flows out to water the whole world. Two of the rivers are the Tigris and Euphrates, the great rivers of Mesopotamia. The other two, Pishon and Gihon, cannot be found on a map, and people have argued for centuries about where they were.

Perhaps that is the point. Genesis takes rivers its hearers knew and joins them to rivers no one could find. Eden is in the real world, among real rivers, and yet no map can lead you back to it. It is a place, and more than a place. The same pattern, a river flowing out from God's house, returns in the prophets and in the Bible's last chapter.
sections.key: One river from the centre waters the whole world: Eden is among real rivers, yet no map leads back to it.

paras: Why a tree? A tree is the most natural picture there is of the joining of heaven and earth. Its roots go down into the soil, its trunk stands upright like a person, and its branches reach into the sky. Many peoples told of a world tree at the centre of everything: the Norse ash Yggdrasil, described in the Icelandic Prose Edda of Snorri Sturluson (about 1220), holds up the worlds with its roots and branches.

The picture is still alive. In modern fantasy stories a great tree often stands at the heart of a city or a world, and when it withers, the land withers with it: Tolkien's White Tree in the citadel of Gondor is the best-known example. In C. S. Lewis's The Magician's Nephew (1955), a boy is sent to a walled garden on a hill to fetch fruit from the tree at its centre, and is tempted to take one for himself. The writers knew Genesis. The tree at the centre is where life comes from, and where the great test comes.
sections.key: The tree joins the ground to the sky; across cultures and in modern fantasy it marks the centre where life comes from.

paras: Genesis 2:7 says what a human being is in one sentence. We are dust: made of the same stuff as the world, earth from the earth. And we are breath: alive with God's own breath, given face to face. We are made from below and alive from above.

That makes the human being the link between heaven and earth. We are the one creature that can see both the stuff of things and their meaning; we can name the animals, tend the garden, offer the world back to God. Two errors have tempted people ever since: that we are only dust, nothing but chemistry; or that we are really spirits trapped in bodies that do not matter. Genesis rejects both. That is why Christianity has always cared about the body, and why its great hope is not escape from the body but the resurrection of the body.
sections.key: The human being is dust and breath, the link between earth and heaven; Genesis rejects both 'only matter' and 'only spirit'.

paras: Genesis 1 called the human being God's 'image'. In 1979, at Tell Fekheriye in Syria, a farmer found a ninth-century BC statue of a ruler whose inscription calls it his 'image' and 'likeness', the very pair of words in Genesis 1:26. Kings set up such statues to show who ruled a land. Genesis says every person, not only kings, is God's image in the world. Christians have read the image in three ways, which can all be true together.

rows: Reason, freedom and the capacity to know God
Our role as God's representatives, tending the world
Our relationships with God and each other, 'male and female'

sections.key: Like a king's statue, every human being is God's image in the world: in what we are, what we do and whom we are with.

paras: Both accounts insist on man and woman together. The woman is a 'helper comparable to him', a word used of God, and the man greets her with joy as his equal. In a world where women were often treated as property, this was remarkable. A medieval saying, repeated by Peter Lombard in the twelfth century, put it well: the woman was not taken from the man's head to rule him, nor from his feet to be trampled by him, but from his side, to be his partner.

Genesis 2 also founds marriage: a man leaves his parents and the two become 'one flesh'. Jesus quoted it as God's design from the beginning (Mark 10:6–8). The human being at the centre is not a lone individual but a communion.
sections.key: Genesis gives men and women equal dignity and roots marriage in creation: the human at the centre is a communion.

refs: Gordon Wenham, 'Sanctuary Symbolism in the Garden of Eden Story', Proceedings of the Ninth World Congress of Jewish Studies (1986). G. K. Beale, The Temple and the Church's Mission (2004).
Mircea Eliade, The Sacred and the Profane (1957; English 1959).
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning (about 1220), on Yggdrasil.
J. R. R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings (1954–55); C. S. Lewis, The Magician's Nephew (1955).
Tell Fekheriye statue: A. Abou-Assaf, P. Bordreuil and A. R. Millard, La statue de Tell Fekherye (1982). J. Richard Middleton, The Liberating Image (2005).
Peter Lombard, Sentences II.18. Karl Barth, Church Dogmatics III/1 (1945).

debate.question: Is Eden a place, a temple-picture, or both?

positions.name: A real place
positions.who: Many traditional readers; some modern researchers, such as the archaeologist Juris Zarins, who placed it near the head of the Persian Gulf
positions.view: Eden was a real region on earth, where the first humans lived. Genesis gives its rivers so that it can be located, and two of them still flow.
positions.evidence: The Tigris and Euphrates are named; the account reads as history; the genealogies run from Adam onward.

positions.name: A temple-picture
positions.who: Gordon Wenham, G. K. Beale and John Walton, in different ways
positions.view: Eden is described as the first sanctuary, the archetype of the tabernacle and Temple, to show what the world is for: a place where God dwells with humanity. Its geography is symbolic more than mappable.
positions.evidence: The sanctuary vocabulary ('walk', 'serve and keep', gold, onyx, cherubim, the east); Ezekiel 28's 'holy mountain of God'; the unfindable rivers.

positions.name: Both at once
positions.who: Augustine, The Literal Meaning of Genesis VIII; Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on Paradise (fourth century)
positions.view: Paradise was a real place and also a figure of spiritual realities; the two are not rivals. Ephrem pictured Paradise as a great mountain whose slopes are the levels of nearness to God. Origen, by contrast, thought it absurd to imagine God planting a garden like a farmer, and read it chiefly as a figure.
positions.evidence: Augustine's insistence on both senses; Ephrem's mountain; Ezekiel's mountain of God.

debate.agree: All agree that Eden is where God and humanity were at home together, and that the Bible's story is about the way back to that presence.

look.why: Edward Hicks, a Quaker preacher in Pennsylvania, painted dozens of versions of this picture. Its subject is not Eden itself but Isaiah's vision of the world restored to Eden's peace (Isaiah 11), when 'the wolf will live with the lamb' and 'a little child will lead them': creatures and people at peace at the centre.
points: Three small children among a group of animals at rest: a bull, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, sheep, goats, bears and a jaguar.
One child stands with an arm around the tiger's shoulders; another touches the jaguar's nose.
In the distance on the left, a group of Native Americans in feathered headdresses meets a group of men in tricorn hats beside a river.
One of the men holds up a roll of cloth lifted from a chest.
A tree with olive-green, rust-red and yellow leaves at the right edge.

music.why: Bruckner's motet Locus iste (1869) was written for the dedication of a chapel in Linz: 'This place was made by God'. Every sanctuary is a small Eden, a place where heaven and earth meet.

think.why: Dust and breath: are we only matter?

learn.why: One sentence that says what a human being is: dust from below, breath from above.

check.q: Why does it matter that the river flows out of Eden and divides into four?
options: It shows that the garden was in Mesopotamia and nowhere else
It proves that Genesis was written by a geographer
It explains where the flood water came from
It pictures the centre as the source of life for the whole world: water flowing out from a high place to the four corners
check.why: Life flows from the centre outwards; and two of the rivers can't be found.

check.q: Gordon Wenham argued that Eden is described like a sanctuary. Which piece of evidence best supports him?
options: The man is set to 'serve' and 'keep' the garden, the verbs used of the Levites in the tabernacle
Eden means 'delight'
Adam names the animals
There are two trees
check.why: Also: God walking, gold and onyx, cherubim at the east, the tree like the lampstand.

check.q: In what sense is the human being 'the link' between heaven and earth in Genesis 2?
options: Humans were made in heaven and sent to earth
Humans live halfway up the mountain
The man is dust from the ground and alive with God's breath: matter and meaning joined in one creature
Adam was an angel
check.why: Made from below, alive from above.

check.q: Ezekiel 28 puts Eden on 'the holy mountain of God'. Why is that significant?
options: Mountains were where heaven and earth met (Sinai, Zion); Ezekiel pictures Eden as the first holy centre
It means Eden was in Tyre
It shows Ezekiel had visited Eden
It contradicts Genesis, so one of them is wrong
check.why: Genesis implies height (the river flows out); Ezekiel says it.

check.q: In what sense is a sacred 'centre' a centre?
options: It is where heaven and earth meet, wherever it is on the map
It is the capital city
It is the exact geometric middle of the earth
It is the oldest place
check.why: Delphi and Jerusalem were not the middle of any map. Session 6 will come back to this.

check.q: Which statement fits Augustine's view of Paradise best?
options: It was only a symbol and never existed
It was on the moon
It was the same as heaven after death
It was a real place, and also a figure of spiritual truths; the two do not compete
check.why: The Literal Meaning of Genesis VIII; contrast Origen, who doubted a literal garden.

tutorial.question: What is Eden, and what does Genesis 2 say a human being is?
tutorial.approach: Describe Eden as the centre where heaven and earth meet: the high place, the rivers, the tree in the middle. Use Wenham's sanctuary evidence and Ezekiel 28. Then explain the human being as dust and breath, the link between earth and heaven, with the image of God and man and woman. Weigh whether Eden is a place, a picture or both.
strong: Explains the idea of a sacred centre and why it is not a point in space.
Gives specific sanctuary parallels from Wenham and Ezekiel 28.
Explains the four rivers and the tree at the centre.
Explains dust and breath and the two errors it rules out.
Uses the image of God and the equal dignity of man and woman.
Weighs the three views of Eden fairly.

reading.author: Leon Kass
reading.title: The Beginning of Wisdom: Reading Genesis
reading.why: A philosopher reads the garden story slowly, with great insight into human nature.

reading.author: G. K. Beale
reading.title: The Temple and the Church's Mission
reading.why: Eden as the first temple, traced through the whole Bible.

reading.author: Mircea Eliade
reading.title: The Sacred and the Profane
reading.why: The classic study of sacred centres across religions.

reading.author: Gordon Wenham
reading.title: 'Sanctuary Symbolism in the Garden of Eden Story'
reading.why: The short paper that started the modern discussion.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose one place in your home and make it a small centre: a chair by a window, a candle, a picture. Sit there for five minutes each morning and say Genesis 2:7 slowly before the day begins.
sessions.reflect: Where, in your life, have heaven and earth come closest together: a place, a person, a moment?
takeaways: Eden is the centre of the world, the high place where heaven and earth meet, described like Israel's sanctuary.
Its river waters the whole world, and its tree joins the ground to the sky, as world trees do across cultures and in fantasy.
The human being, dust and breath, is the link between earth and heaven, God's image set at the centre to tend it.

sessions.title: The serpent from the edge: eyes opened
sessions.line: A creature from the wild, a tree, and two people who suddenly see themselves.
sessions.plain: If the world was made good, why is it broken? Genesis answers with a story about seeing. A serpent from the wild edge of the world offers knowledge; the man and woman take it, and 'their eyes were opened'. What they see is themselves, exposed, and they hide. This session reads the story closely, beside Milton's great poem, and asks what Christians mean by original sin.
sessions.why: Session 2 placed the man and woman at the centre, where heaven and earth meet, looking outwards at God and each other, 'naked and not ashamed'. Now the centre is lost. How?
answers: What went wrong?
What does 'their eyes were opened' mean?
Was the serpent the devil?
What is original sin, and how do the churches differ about it?
sessions.finding: Genesis tells the fall as a change of seeing: knowledge grasped apart from God makes the man and woman self-conscious, so that they see themselves as exposed objects, hide, and are sent from the centre east, to the edge.

paras: Session 1: heaven and earth, meaning and matter, put in order by God's word. Session 2: Eden is the centre where they meet, and the human being, dust and breath, stands there as the link, tending the garden. They were 'naked, and not ashamed'. Hold that picture: it is about to break.
background.key: Meaning and matter ordered; the human at the centre, unashamed.

paras: If there is a centre, there is also an edge. In the ancient picture the centre is ordered, holy and full of life; the edge is the wild, the desert, the sea, where order fades into chaos. Genesis 2 put the man and woman at the centre. Genesis 3 brings in a creature from the edge.

Notice too how the man and woman are looking. In chapter 2 they look outwards: the man names the animals, greets the woman, tends the garden. They are not looking at themselves at all. Keep that in mind as you read.
background.key: The centre is ordered and holy; the edge is the wild; the man and woman were looking outward.

paras: The main reading is the whole of Genesis 3, in three parts: the temptation and the opened eyes, God's questions, and the consequences and the exile.

The comparison is from Paradise Lost (1667), John Milton's great poem retelling the fall. It is the most famous English telling of the story, and Milton saw more clearly than anyone what 'their eyes were opened' meant.
background.key: Genesis 3 read closely, then Milton's account of the opened eyes.

before: Where does the serpent come from, and what does it promise?
What do the man and woman see when their eyes are opened? What do they do next?
Which direction are they sent, and what guards the way back?
sessions.readWhy: The story of the fall, in three parts, with a commentary after each.

paras: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’ ”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.
Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?”
The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”
Yahweh God said to the serpent,

“Because you have done this,
you are cursed above all livestock,
and above every animal of the field.
You shall go on your belly
and you shall eat dust all the days of your life.

I will put hostility between you and the woman,
and between your offspring and her offspring.
He will bruise your head,
and you will bruise his heel.”
To the woman he said,

“I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth.
You will bear children in pain.
Your desire will be for your husband,
and he will rule over you.”
To Adam he said,

“Because you have listened to your wife’s voice,
and ate from the tree,
about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’
the ground is cursed for your sake.
You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life.

It will yield thorns and thistles to you;
and you will eat the herb of the field.

You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground,
for you were taken out of it.
For you are dust,
and you shall return to dust.”
The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.
Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
Yahweh God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever—”
Therefore Yahweh God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken.
So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.

parts.title: The serpent, the fruit and the opened eyes
parts.context: The same garden, some time after chapter 2. A new character appears.

commentary.on: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made.
commentary.text: The serpent is a creature God made, not a rival god. It is one of the animals 'of the field', the wild beasts outside the garden's order. It moves on the ground, the lowest of creatures. In the ancient world the serpent was a creature of the margins: of the desert, the underworld and the sea. Here the edge comes into the centre. There is also a pun: the couple were 'naked' (arummim), the serpent 'subtle' (arum).

commentary.on: Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?
commentary.text: The first temptation twists God's words. God said 'every tree except one'; the serpent makes it sound like 'no tree'. It makes God seem mean.

commentary.on: your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil
commentary.text: The promise is about seeing. 'Knowing good and evil' may mean knowing everything (a pair of opposites for the whole, like 'heaven and earth'), or deciding for oneself what is good. Either way, it is knowledge taken, not received: grasped apart from the one who gives meaning.

commentary.on: the tree was to be desired to make one wise
commentary.text: Appetite, beauty and the wish to be wise. None of these is bad: the trees of the garden were all 'pleasant to the sight, and good for food'. The wrong is in taking what was refused, in seizing the centre for oneself.

commentary.on: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked.
commentary.text: The serpent was half right. Their eyes were opened. But what they see is not God; it is themselves. For the first time they look at their own bodies as if from outside, as objects among objects, exposed. That is self-consciousness, and its first feeling is shame. The first human invention is a covering.

parts.title: Where are you?
parts.context: Evening in the garden. God comes walking, as if this were his usual time to meet them.

commentary.on: the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden
commentary.text: Before, they looked at God. Now they hide from him, and behind their leaves from each other. Self-consciousness turns the face away.

commentary.on: Where are you?
commentary.text: God's first words after the fall are a question. He knows where they are; the question is for them, an invitation to come out. It is a question about place: you were at the centre; where are you now?

commentary.on: I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.
commentary.text: Fear, nakedness, hiding: the whole new condition in one sentence. Nothing about the man's body has changed. What has changed is how he sees it, and how he imagines being seen.

commentary.on: Who told you that you were naked?
commentary.text: A piercing question. Nakedness is not new; seeing it as exposure is. Knowledge has come, but knowledge cut off from trust leaves them small and afraid.

commentary.on: The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.
commentary.text: The man blames the woman, and by implication God ('whom you gave'). The woman blames the serpent. No one says sorry. The partners of chapter 2 have become separate selves defending themselves.

parts.title: Consequences, and the way east
parts.context: God speaks to each in turn: the serpent, the woman and the man. Then they leave.

commentary.on: You shall go on your belly and you shall eat dust all the days of your life.
commentary.text: The serpent, which came from the low edge, is sent lower still: to the dust.

commentary.on: He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.
commentary.text: Christians since Irenaeus in the second century have called this the 'first gospel': a promise that a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent, though wounded himself. They read it of Christ. Jewish readers take it of the lasting struggle between humanity and evil.

commentary.on: the ground is cursed for your sake
commentary.text: The relationship with the earth is damaged too. The man was taken from the ground and set to tend it with joy; now it yields 'thorns and thistles'. Matter resists.

commentary.on: For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.
commentary.text: The dust and breath of chapter 2 will come apart. These words are still said in many churches on Ash Wednesday as ash is marked on foreheads.

commentary.on: Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
commentary.text: Before they leave, God himself clothes them, better than their leaves. Even in judgement there is care. God covers the exposure they cannot bear.

commentary.on: he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life
commentary.text: They are sent out east, away from the centre. The cherubim are the guardians of the sanctuary, like those on the ark and the Temple curtain. 'The way to the tree of life' is not destroyed, only guarded. The rest of the Bible is the story of the way back.

paras:
Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
Brought Death into the World, and all our woe,
With loss of EDEN, till one greater Man
Restore us, and regain the blissful Seat,
Sing Heav'nly Muse, that on the secret top
Of OREB, or of SINAI, didst inspire
That Shepherd, who first taught the chosen Seed,
In the Beginning how the Heav'ns and Earth
Rose out of CHAOS: Or if SION Hill
Delight thee more, and SILOA'S Brook that flow'd
Fast by the Oracle of God; I thence
Invoke thy aid to my adventrous Song,
That with no middle flight intends to soar
Above th' AONIAN Mount, while it pursues
Things unattempted yet in Prose or Rhime.
And chiefly Thou O Spirit, that dost prefer
Before all Temples th' upright heart and pure,
Instruct me, for Thou know'st; Thou from the first
Wast present, and with mighty wings outspread
Dove-like satst brooding on the vast Abyss
And mad'st it pregnant: What in me is dark
Illumine, what is low raise and support;
That to the highth of this great Argument
I may assert th' Eternal Providence,
And justifie the wayes of God to men.

So saying, her rash hand in evil hour
Forth reaching to the Fruit, she pluck'd, she eat:
Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat
Sighing through all her Works gave signs of woe,
That all was lost.  Back to the Thicket slunk
The guiltie Serpent, and well might, for EVE
Intent now wholly on her taste, naught else
Regarded, such delight till then, as seemd,
In Fruit she never tasted, whether true
Or fansied so, through expectation high
Of knowledg, nor was God-head from her thought.
Greedily she ingorg'd without restraint,
And knew not eating Death: Satiate at length,

Soon as the force of that fallacious Fruit,
That with exhilerating vapour bland
About thir spirits had plaid, and inmost powers
