Made erre, was now exhal'd, and grosser sleep
Bred of unkindly fumes, with conscious dreams
Encumberd, now had left them, up they rose
As from unrest, and each the other viewing,
Soon found thir Eyes how op'nd, and thir minds
How dark'nd; innocence, that as a veile
Had shadow'd them from knowing ill, was gon,
Just confidence, and native righteousness,
And honour from about them, naked left
To guiltie shame hee cover'd, but his Robe
Uncover'd more.  So rose the DANITE strong
HERCULEAN SAMSON from the Harlot-lap
Of PHILISTEAN DALILAH, and wak'd
Shorn of his strength, They destitute and bare
Of all thir vertue: silent, and in face
Confounded long they sate, as struck'n mute,
Till ADAM, though not less then EVE abasht,
At length gave utterance to these words constraind.

O EVE, in evil hour thou didst give care
To that false Worm, of whomsoever taught
To counterfet Mans voice, true in our Fall,
False in our promis'd Rising; since our Eyes
Op'nd we find indeed, and find we know
Both Good and Evil, Good lost and Evil got,
Bad Fruit of Knowledge, if this be to know,
Which leaves us naked thus, of Honour void,
Of Innocence, of Faith, of Puritie,
Our wonted Ornaments now soild and staind,
And in our Faces evident the signes
Of foul concupiscence; whence evil store;
Even shame, the last of evils; of the first
Be sure then.  How shall I behold the face
Henceforth of God or Angel, earst with joy
And rapture so oft beheld? those heav'nly shapes
Will dazle now this earthly, with thir blaze
Insufferably bright.  O might I here
In solitude live savage, in some glad
Obscur'd, where highest Woods impenetrable
To Starr or Sun-light, spread thir umbrage broad,
And brown as Evening: Cover me ye Pines,
Ye Cedars, with innumerable boughs
Hide me, where I may never see them more.
But let us now, as in bad plight, devise
What best may for the present serve to hide
The Parts of each from other, that seem most
To shame obnoxious, and unseemliest seen,
Some Tree whose broad smooth Leaves together sowd,
And girded on our loyns, may cover round
Those middle parts, that this new commer, Shame,
There sit not, and reproach us as unclean.

parts.author: John Milton
parts.ref: Milton, Paradise Lost, Book I, lines 1–26
parts.title: Of man's first disobedience
parts.context: The famous opening of the poem, in which Milton names his subject and asks God's Spirit to help him.
parts.plain: Milton says: I will sing about the first time humans disobeyed God, by eating the forbidden fruit, which brought death and all our sorrow into the world and lost us Eden, until a greater Man, Christ, restores us. I call on the Spirit who inspired Moses and who brooded over the waters at creation, so that I can explain and justify God's ways to human beings.

commentary.on: Of Mans First Disobedience
commentary.text: Milton names the subject in the first line: disobedience, a breach of trust, not sex or knowledge as such.

commentary.on: till one greater Man
commentary.text: From the start Milton looks ahead to Christ, the 'greater Man' who restores what was lost: the way back to the centre.

commentary.on: In the Beginning how the Heav'ns and Earth
commentary.text: Milton quotes Genesis 1:1, and calls Moses 'That Shepherd', following the tradition that Moses wrote Genesis.

commentary.on: Dove-like satst brooding on the vast Abyss
commentary.text: An echo of Genesis 1:2, the Spirit hovering over the waters, pictured as a bird brooding over eggs.

commentary.on: And justifie the wayes of God to men.
commentary.text: Milton's aim: to show that God is just although he allowed the fall. That is this session's question.

parts.author: John Milton
parts.ref: Milton, Paradise Lost, Book IX, lines 780–792
parts.title: She pluck'd, she eat
parts.context: Book IX. Satan, inside the serpent, has persuaded Eve with a long, flattering speech. These lines describe the moment she eats.
parts.plain: Milton says: as she said this, Eve reached out and took the fruit and ate it, and the whole earth felt the wound. The serpent slipped away. Eve was so absorbed in the taste and the hope of becoming wise, even godlike, that she ate greedily, not knowing she was eating death.

commentary.on: she pluck'd, she eat
commentary.text: Two short phrases: the moment that changes everything is over in an instant. 'Eat' is Milton's past tense, pronounced 'et'.

commentary.on: Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat
commentary.text: The whole creation feels it. Heaven and earth were joined in the human being; when the link breaks, the earth suffers too (compare 'the ground is cursed for your sake').

commentary.on: nor was God-head from her thought
commentary.text: Eve is thinking of becoming divine. Milton saw that the heart of the temptation was to take God's place at the centre.

parts.author: John Milton
parts.ref: Milton, Paradise Lost, Book IX, lines 1046–1066
parts.title: Soon found their eyes how opened
parts.context: Adam has eaten too. Drunk on the fruit, they make love and sleep. Now they wake. Milton compares them to Samson, the strong man of Judges 16, who woke in the lap of Delilah to find his strength gone.
parts.plain: Milton says: when the fruit's effect wore off and they woke from a troubled sleep, they looked at each other and found that their eyes were indeed opened, and their minds darkened. Innocence, which had been like a veil keeping them from knowing evil, was gone. They sat silent and ashamed, like Samson after Delilah cut his hair, until Adam forced himself to speak.

commentary.on: each the other viewing, Soon found thir Eyes how op'nd, and thir minds How dark'nd
commentary.text: Milton's great insight. The eyes open and the mind darkens at the same moment. They gain a new kind of seeing, of each other as bodies to be looked at, and lose the light they had.

commentary.on: innocence, that as a veile Had shadow'd them from knowing ill, was gon
commentary.text: A surprising image: innocence was a veil. Before, they did not see themselves as objects; that 'not seeing' protected them. Now the veil is off, and they are exposed.

commentary.on: silent, and in face Confounded long they sate, as struck'n mute
commentary.text: The first effect of self-consciousness is silence. The man who named every creature cannot find words.

parts.author: John Milton
parts.ref: Milton, Paradise Lost, Book IX, lines 1067–1098
parts.title: Cover me, ye pines
parts.context: Adam's first speech after the fall. ('Give care' is a printing error in this edition for 'give ear'.)
parts.plain: Milton says: Adam tells Eve that the serpent's promise came true in one way only: their eyes are opened, and they know good and evil, good lost and evil gained. The knowledge leaves them naked, without honour or innocence. How can he look at God or the angels again? He wishes he could hide in the darkest forest. Then he says they must cover themselves with leaves, so that shame will not sit there and accuse them.

commentary.on: since our Eyes Op'nd we find indeed, and find we know Both Good and Evil, Good lost and Evil got
commentary.text: The serpent's promise kept, bitterly. They do know good and evil now: they know good by losing it.

commentary.on: Bad Fruit of Knowledge, if this be to know, Which leaves us naked thus
commentary.text: 'If this be to know': Milton's Adam sees that knowledge without trust in God is a strange kind of knowing. It leaves them exposed, not wise.

commentary.on: How shall I behold the face Henceforth of God or Angel
commentary.text: Once he looked at God with joy. Now the 'heav'nly shapes' would dazzle 'this earthly'. Heaven and earth, which met in him, are now apart.

commentary.on: Cover me ye Pines, Ye Cedars, with innumerable boughs Hide me
commentary.text: Adam wants to go to the darkest edge of the world, where no sun reaches. This is Genesis 3:8, hiding among the trees, opened out into a whole speech. Exile begins in the heart before it begins on the map.

compare.author: John Milton
compare.ref: Milton, Paradise Lost, Book I, lines 1–26
compare.why: John Milton (1608–1674) wrote Paradise Lost after the English Civil War, blind, dictating it to helpers. It is in blank verse, unrhymed lines of ten syllables, in Milton's own spelling. Read its opening, the moment Eve eats, and the morning after, when Adam and Eve find their eyes opened.
compare.title: Milton: eyes how opened

paras: Genesis calls the serpent simply 'more subtle than any animal of the field'. The 'field' in Hebrew is the open country, the wild beyond cultivated land. The serpent belongs there: low, on the ground, at home in the margins. Elsewhere in the Bible the sea-serpent Leviathan stands for chaos itself, 'the twisted serpent' that God will one day slay (Isaiah 27:1).

Genesis never calls the serpent the devil. Later writers did: the Wisdom of Solomon, about a century before Christ, says that death entered the world 'through the devil's envy' (2:24), and the Book of Revelation calls the devil 'the old serpent' (12:9). Read within this course's frame, the point is clear either way. Disorder does not come from the centre. It comes in from the edge, and it gets in through the human beings who were meant to guard the garden.
sections.key: The serpent is a creature of the wild edge; later writers identified it with the devil; disorder comes in from the margins.

paras: What is 'the knowledge of good and evil'? Three answers are given. It may be knowledge of everything, 'good and evil' being a pair for the whole. It may be moral autonomy: the right to decide for yourself what is good. It may be experience, the knowing that comes from doing.

The great second-century bishop Irenaeus of Lyons suggested that the first humans were like children, meant to grow into wisdom over time, and that the wrong lay in grasping too soon at what God would have given. On every reading the problem is not knowledge itself. It is knowledge taken apart from the one who gives things their meaning: the earth trying to stand without heaven.
sections.key: The fault is not knowledge but knowledge grasped apart from God, the giver of meaning.

paras: 'Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked.' Nothing about their bodies has changed. What has changed is their point of view. Before, they looked outwards, at God, each other and the world. Now they look at themselves, from outside, as one object among others, exposed and vulnerable. That is what we call self-consciousness, and its first fruit is shame.

Thinkers far from the Church have seen the same thing. The French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre, in Being and Nothingness (1943), described shame as the moment I feel myself seen by another and become, in my own eyes, a thing. Jordan Peterson, in his 2017 lecture 'Adam and Eve: Self-Consciousness, Evil, and Death', read Genesis 3 as the dawning of self-consciousness: the awareness of our own nakedness, fragility and death. Genesis tells it more briefly. The opened eyes see the self, and the self wants to hide.
sections.key: 'Their eyes were opened' means self-consciousness: seeing oneself from outside as an exposed object, whose first fruit is shame.

sections.h: From the centre to the edge
paras: The story ends with a journey east. The man and woman are sent out of the garden 'to till the ground from which he was taken': back to the earth, to matter, without the centre. At 'the east of the garden' God places cherubim, the guardians of every later sanctuary, and a turning, flaming sword.

From now on, in Genesis, east is the direction of exile. Cain will go 'east of Eden'; the builders of Babel will move 'from the east'; Lot will choose the eastern plain. Israel's tabernacle and Temple faced east, so that anyone coming to God walked west, back through the guarded door. The way to the tree of life is guarded, not abolished. The Bible's last chapter returns to it, as you saw in The whole story: 'the tree of life' stands in the city, open to all (Revelation 22:2).
sections.key: Exiled east, from centre to edge, the humans leave a way back that is guarded, not destroyed.

sections.h: Original sin: how the traditions differ
paras: The phrase 'original sin' is not in the Bible. It comes from Augustine, around 400, building on Paul: 'sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin' (Romans 5:12). All Christians agree that human beings are not what they were meant to be and that everyone needs God's mercy. They differ about what we inherit from the first sin, and Judaism differs from all of them.

rows: Original sin: the loss of the first holiness and justice, 'contracted, not committed'; washed away in baptism
Human nature wounded, not totally corrupted; still free and capable of good
Ancestral sin: mortality and a tendency to sin, but not Adam's guilt
Nature wounded and darkened; the image of God intact
Every part of human nature affected; we cannot save ourselves
No original sin; each person born innocent and responsible (Ezekiel 18:20)
A good and an evil inclination in everyone, and freedom to choose

sections.key: Catholics speak of inherited loss, the Orthodox of inherited mortality without guilt, Protestants of inherited guilt and corruption; Jews of no inherited sin.

paras: Adam means 'human being' and Eve means 'life'. The story is about all of us. But were they also two individuals? Christians give three main answers. Some hold that they were the first two humans and the sole ancestors of everyone. Some hold that they were real people chosen from among an early human population to stand for all. Others read the story as true of humanity without being about two individuals. Genetics bears on this question, and session 6 will come back to it.

On any of these views, Genesis 3 describes something every person knows from inside: the voice that says God is holding out on us, the sudden self-consciousness, the hiding and the blaming. And it names the hope: God comes looking, asks 'Where are you?', and clothes those who cannot bear to be seen.
sections.key: Adam means 'human': the story is true of everyone, whatever one holds about two historical individuals.

refs: Genesis 3; 4:16; 11:2; 13:11; Isaiah 27:1; Wisdom 2:24; Revelation 12:9; 22:2; Romans 5:12–19; Ezekiel 18:20.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies IV.38 (humans created as children, to grow); V.21.1 (Genesis 3:15 and Christ).
Jean-Paul Sartre, Being and Nothingness (1943), Part III, 'The Look'.
Jordan Peterson, 'Adam and Eve: Self-Consciousness, Evil, and Death', The Psychological Significance of the Biblical Stories, lecture IV (Toronto, 2017).

Augustine, City of God XIII–XIV; Council of Trent, Session V (1546); Catechism of the Catholic Church 396–409; John Meyendorff, Byzantine Theology (1974), ch. 11; Augsburg Confession (1530) Art. II; Westminster Confession (1646) ch. 6.
John Milton, Paradise Lost (1667; 2nd ed. 1674), I.1–26; IX.780–792, 1046–1098.
On Adam and Eve: Hans Madueme and Michael Reeves (eds), Adam, the Fall, and Original Sin (2014); John Walton, The Lost World of Adam and Eve (2015).

debate.question: What do we inherit from Adam?

positions.name: Inherited guilt and corruption
positions.who: Augustine; Lutheran and Reformed Protestants
positions.view: All humanity was 'in Adam'; everyone is born sharing his guilt, with a nature so corrupted that we cannot turn to God without his grace.
positions.evidence: Romans 5:12–19; Psalm 51:5; the universality of sin.

positions.name: Inherited loss
positions.who: Catholic teaching
positions.view: We are born without the first holiness; original sin is 'contracted, not committed', and our nature is wounded but not destroyed.
positions.evidence: Romans 5; the Council of Trent; the practice of infant baptism.

positions.name: Inherited mortality, not guilt
positions.who: Orthodox Christians; and, in a different form, Jewish teaching
positions.view: From Adam we inherit death and a tendency to sin, but each person is guilty only of their own sins.
positions.evidence: Ezekiel 18:20; the Greek reading of Romans 5:12; the Greek Fathers.

debate.agree: All agree that every human being needs God's mercy, and that human nature is not what it was meant to be.

look.why: Hendrick Goltzius, a Dutch engraver turned painter, painted this Fall of Man in 1616. The fruit has already been bitten. Look at where everyone's eyes are, including the serpent's.
points: Adam and Eve recline together under an apple tree, gazing into each other's eyes.
Eve holds up a small green and red apple with a bite taken out of it.
A snake winds round the tree trunk; it has a human face with flushed cheeks and blond hair, just above Eve's head, looking towards us.
A brown and white cat sits near Adam's hip and looks out at us.
Far off in the landscape, tiny animals: an elephant, two camels and others.

music.why: Allegri's setting of Psalm 51, the great psalm of repentance ('Have mercy on me, God'), sung in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week: the answer to 'Where are you?' from someone who has stopped hiding.

think.why: The story of Adam and Eve and what Christians believe about it.

learn.why: God's first words after the fall are a question about where we are, and an invitation to come out of hiding.

check.q: According to the reading in this session, what changes when 'their eyes were opened'?
options: They see the serpent for the first time
They gain perfect knowledge of science
Their bodies change and they become mortal at once
Their point of view: they see themselves from outside, as exposed objects, and feel shame
check.why: Nothing about their bodies has changed: 'Who told you that you were naked?'

check.q: Why does it matter that the serpent is one of the animals 'of the field'?
options: It shows it was a farm animal
The 'field' is the wild beyond the garden: disorder comes in from the edge into the centre
It means it was harmless
It proves it was Satan
check.why: Centre and edge; Genesis itself never names the devil.

check.q: Milton writes that their eyes were opened 'and thir minds How dark'nd'. What is he saying?
options: That the new kind of seeing, of themselves and each other as exposed bodies, came with a loss of the light they had
That they fell asleep
That Milton disliked knowledge
That it was night
check.why: 'Innocence, that as a veile Had shadow'd them from knowing ill, was gon.'

check.q: Irenaeus thought the first humans were like children. What does that suggest the wrong was?
options: Being too young to obey
Eating fruit
Wanting knowledge at all
Grasping too soon, on their own terms, at a wisdom God meant to give over time
check.why: Knowledge is not the problem; grasping it apart from God is.

check.q: Why is it significant that the cherubim are placed 'at the east of the garden'?
options: Cherubim guard sanctuaries, whose entrance faced east: the way back to the centre is guarded, not destroyed
Angels always face east
East was the coldest side
It means the garden was in India
check.why: East becomes the direction of exile; the way to the tree of life remains.

check.q: Which statement best describes the Orthodox view of 'ancestral sin'?
options: Everyone is born guilty of Adam's sin
We inherit mortality and a tendency to sin, but not Adam's guilt
Only Adam's sons inherited sin
There was no fall
check.why: Each person is guilty only of their own sins.

tutorial.question: What does Genesis 3 mean by 'their eyes were opened', and what does it say about why the world is broken?
tutorial.approach: Read the story closely: the serpent from the edge, the promise of opened eyes, the nakedness, the hiding, the questions and the exile east. Explain the opened eyes as self-consciousness, using Milton and one modern thinker. Then set out the traditions on original sin fairly, and the views on Adam and Eve, and say what the story teaches whichever view one takes.
strong: Explains centre and edge, and the serpent as a creature of the margins.
Explains 'their eyes were opened' as self-consciousness and shame, with the text.
Uses Milton's 'eyes how op'nd… minds how dark'nd' accurately.
Traces the exile east and the guarded way back.
Sets out the four traditions on original sin accurately.
Notes the signs of hope: the question, the clothes, Genesis 3:15.

reading.author: Alan Jacobs
reading.title: Original Sin: A Cultural History
reading.why: A lively history of the idea from Augustine to today.

reading.author: C. S. Lewis
reading.title: A Preface to Paradise Lost
reading.why: The classic guide to Milton's poem and its theology.

reading.author: Leon Kass
reading.title: The Beginning of Wisdom: Reading Genesis
reading.why: Superb on shame, self-consciousness and the human condition in Genesis 3.

reading.author: Hans Madueme and Michael Reeves (eds)
reading.title: Adam, the Fall, and Original Sin
reading.why: The case for a historical Adam and the traditional doctrine, with the debates.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice the moments when you become painfully self-conscious, watching yourself as if from outside. Each time, turn your attention outwards to one other person or one thing in front of you, and give it your whole attention for a minute.
sessions.reflect: If God asked you 'Where are you?', how far from the centre would your honest answer be?
takeaways: Genesis 3 tells the fall as a change of seeing: the opened eyes see the self, exposed, and the first fruit is shame.
Disorder comes in from the edge; knowledge grasped apart from God sends the humans east, from the centre to the margin.
The way back is guarded, not destroyed; Christians differ about what we inherit from the first sin.

sessions.title: Further from the centre: Cain
sessions.line: Two brothers, the first city, a song of revenge, and a world filled with violence.
sessions.plain: Outside the garden, the first children grow up, and one kills the other. The murderer goes further east, away from God's presence, and builds the first city. Violence spreads, from one murder to a boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge to a whole world 'filled with violence'. This session follows that movement outwards, beside the Greek poet Hesiod's story of human decline.
sessions.why: Session 3 ended with the man and woman sent east, from the centre to the edge. Now we see what happens further out: why do people hurt each other?
answers: What happens between Cain and Abel, and why?
Am I my brother's keeper?
Why does Cain build a city, and who were the Nephilim?
Did other ancient peoples tell a similar story?
sessions.finding: Away from the centre, violence spreads: Cain goes further east and builds the first city, and violence fills the earth; yet Genesis holds each person responsible, and God still marks and protects the murderer.

paras: Session 1: heaven and earth, meaning and matter, ordered by God's word. Session 2: Eden is the centre where they meet, with the human being as the link. Session 3: knowledge grasped apart from God opened their eyes to their own exposure; they hid, and were sent east, from the centre to the edge. Now the story follows their children, further out.
background.key: Order, the centre, the opened eyes and the exile east.

paras: Adam and Eve have two sons: Cain, a farmer, and Abel, a shepherd. Both bring offerings to God; God accepts Abel's and not Cain's, and Cain kills his brother. God punishes Cain with exile but also protects him. Cain goes to 'the land of Nod, east of Eden' and builds a city. His descendants invent herding, music and metalwork; one of them, Lamech, boasts of killing a man. Chapter 5 lists the generations from Adam to Noah. Chapter 6 opens with a mysterious story about 'God's sons' and 'the Nephilim', and ends with God seeing the earth 'filled with violence'.
Read it as a map. Each step takes humanity further from the centre: from the garden, to the land east of it, to a city of its own making, to a whole earth without peace.
background.key: From one murder to a world filled with violence, each step further from the centre.

paras: The main reading has three parts: Cain and Abel (4:1–16); the first city and Lamech's song (4:17–24); and the world before the flood (6:1–8).

The comparison is from Hesiod's Works and Days, written in Greece around 700 BC. Hesiod tells of five ages of humanity, each worse than the last, ending in an age of iron when 'brother will not be dear to brother'. Read beside Genesis, it shows how both Athens and Jerusalem saw early history as a story of decline, and how differently they explained it.
background.key: Genesis 4–6 beside Hesiod: two ancient accounts of how humans grew violent.

before: What does God say to Cain before the murder? Could Cain have chosen differently?
Where does Cain go, and what does he build?
In the comparison, what does Hesiod blame for the decline of the human race?
sessions.readWhy: The first murder, the first city and its song of revenge, and the world before the flood, in three parts.

paras: The man knew Eve his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Cain, and said, “I have gotten a man with Yahweh’s help.”
Again she gave birth, to Cain’s brother Abel. Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.
As time passed, Cain brought an offering to Yahweh from the fruit of the ground.
Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. Yahweh respected Abel and his offering,
but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell.
Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen?
If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?”
He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”
Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
Now you are cursed because of the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand.
From now on, when you till the ground, it won’t yield its strength to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth.”
Cain said to Yahweh, “My punishment is greater than I can bear.
Behold, you have driven me out today from the surface of the ground. I will be hidden from your face, and I will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth. Whoever finds me will kill me.”
Yahweh said to him, “Therefore whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold.” Yahweh appointed a sign for Cain, so that anyone finding him would not strike him.
Cain left Yahweh’s presence, and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
Cain knew his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Enoch. He built a city, and named the city after the name of his son, Enoch.
Irad was born to Enoch. Irad became the father of Mehujael. Mehujael became the father of Methushael. Methushael became the father of Lamech.
Lamech took two wives: the name of the first one was Adah, and the name of the second one was Zillah.
Adah gave birth to Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.
His brother’s name was Jubal, who was the father of all who handle the harp and pipe.
Zillah also gave birth to Tubal Cain, the forger of every cutting instrument of bronze and iron. Tubal Cain’s sister was Naamah.
Lamech said to his wives,

“Adah and Zillah, hear my voice.
You wives of Lamech, listen to my speech,
for I have slain a man for wounding me,
a young man for bruising me.

If Cain will be avenged seven times,
truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them,
God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives.
Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children with them. Those were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown.
Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
Yahweh was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart.
Yahweh said, “I will destroy man whom I have created from the surface of the ground—man, along with animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky—for I am sorry that I have made them.”
But Noah found favor in Yahweh’s eyes.

parts.title: Cain and Abel
parts.context: The first story outside Eden. Adam and Eve's first two sons grow up, one working the ground, one keeping sheep.

commentary.on: Yahweh respected Abel and his offering, but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering.
commentary.text: Why? Genesis does not say directly. Abel brings 'the firstborn of his flock and of its fat', the best; Cain simply 'an offering'. The letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered 'by faith' (Hebrews 11:4). An offering is matter given a meaning: a gift that says something to God. What matters is the heart behind it.

commentary.on: If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.
commentary.text: The first time the word 'sin' appears in the Bible, it is pictured as a wild animal crouching at the door, a creature of the edge again, waiting to get in. And God says Cain can master it. Before the murder, God warns him and gives him a choice. No one is fated to do wrong.

commentary.on: Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
commentary.text: The word 'brother' comes seven times in this story. The first death in the Bible is not old age but murder.

commentary.on: Am I my brother’s keeper?
commentary.text: Cain answers God with a lie and a shrug. 'Keeper' is the same verb as the man's work in the garden, to 'keep' it. Adam was set to keep the garden; Cain will not keep his brother. The whole Bible answers his question: yes, you are your brother's keeper.

commentary.on: The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
commentary.text: The ground, the adamah from which humanity was made, has received a brother's blood. The earth itself testifies. No murder goes unnoticed by God.

commentary.on: I will be hidden from your face, and I will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth.
commentary.text: Cain describes his own exile: hidden from God's face, with no place to rest. His parents hid among the trees; Cain is hidden from God's presence for good. This is life far from the centre: restless, unsheltered, afraid.

commentary.on: Yahweh appointed a sign for Cain, so that anyone finding him would not strike him.
commentary.text: God punishes Cain, but protects him from revenge. The 'mark of Cain', often imagined as a curse, is a sign of protection. Even at the far edge, God has not let go.

commentary.on: Cain left Yahweh’s presence, and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
commentary.text: 'Nod' means 'wandering'. Cain goes east again, further from the centre than his parents. The direction of exile continues.

parts.title: The first city, and Lamech's song
parts.context: Cain's family grows. Several generations later, Lamech sings a song to his two wives, the first poem in the Bible after Adam's words over Eve.

commentary.on: He built a city, and named the city after the name of his son, Enoch.
commentary.text: The first city in the Bible is built by a murderer in exile, and named after his own son. Far from God's centre, Cain makes a centre of his own, with his family's name on it. Hold this in mind: the builders of Babel will do the same.

commentary.on: the forger of every cutting instrument of bronze and iron
commentary.text: Civilisation advances: herds, music, metalwork. Genesis does not despise these gifts. But the same skill that makes ploughs makes blades, and the next verse shows which way it goes.

commentary.on: for I have slain a man for wounding me
commentary.text: Lamech boasts of killing a man for wounding him: punishment far beyond the injury.

commentary.on: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.
commentary.text: God protected Cain with a sevenfold warning; Lamech turns that mercy into a boast of unlimited revenge. When Peter later asks Jesus how often he must forgive, Jesus answers 'seventy times seven' (Matthew 18:22): Lamech's revenge turned into unlimited forgiveness.

parts.title: A world filled with violence
parts.context: The opening of the flood story. Between Lamech and here comes the list of generations in chapter 5. These verses are among the strangest in the Bible.

commentary.on: God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives.
commentary.text: Who were 'God's sons'? Some ancient Jewish writers, such as the book of 1 Enoch, said they were angels who crossed the boundary between heaven and earth. Augustine said they were the descendants of Seth, Adam's third son, marrying into Cain's line. Others think they were tyrant kings. On the first reading, heaven and earth meet in the wrong way: not ordered, meaning above and matter below, but mixed, by grasping. Whatever they were, the point is boundaries broken and power abused.

commentary.on: The Nephilim were in the earth in those days
commentary.text: The Nephilim, perhaps 'fallen ones', were 'mighty men who were of old, men of renown': legendary heroes, like those in Hesiod. Genesis mentions them briefly and moves on.

commentary.on: every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil
commentary.text: The diagnosis goes deep: not only actions but 'every imagination' of the heart. The disorder that came in from the edge has reached the inside of people.

commentary.on: Yahweh was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart.
commentary.text: God is not a distant force; he grieves. The same word for 'grief' was used of the woman's pain in childbirth (3:16). The God who called the world very good is heartbroken by what it has become.

commentary.on: But Noah found favor in Yahweh’s eyes.
commentary.text: The last line turns the story. Even here, there is one person through whom God will begin again. That is where session 5 will begin.

paras: (ll. 109-120) First of all the deathless gods who dwell on Olympus made a golden race of mortal men who lived in the time of Cronos when he was reigning in heaven. And they lived like gods without sorrow of heart, remote and free from toil and grief: miserable age rested not on them; but with legs and arms never failing they made merry with feasting beyond the reach of all evils. When they died, it was as though they were overcome with sleep, and they had all good things; for the fruitful earth unforced bare them fruit abundantly and without stint. They dwelt in ease and peace upon their lands with many good things, rich in flocks and loved by the blessed gods.

(ll. 140-155) But when earth had covered this generation also--they are called blessed spirits of the underworld by men, and, though they are of second order, yet honour attends them also--Zeus the Father made a third generation of mortal men, a brazen race, sprung from ash-trees; and it was in no way equal to the silver age, but was terrible and strong. They loved the lamentable works of Ares and deeds of violence; they ate no bread, but were hard of heart like adamant, fearful men. Great was their strength and unconquerable the arms which grew from their shoulders on their strong limbs. Their armour was of bronze, and their houses of bronze, and of bronze were their implements: there was no black iron. These were destroyed by their own hands and passed to the dank house of chill Hades, and left no name: terrible though they were, black Death seized them, and they left the bright light of the sun.

(ll. 170-201) Thereafter, would that I were not among the men of the fifth generation, but either had died before or been born afterwards. For now truly is a race of iron, and men never rest from labour and sorrow by day, and from perishing by night; and the gods shall lay sore trouble upon them. But, notwithstanding, even these shall have some good mingled with their evils. And Zeus will destroy this race of mortal men also when they come to have grey hair on the temples at their birth. The father will not agree with his children, nor the children with their father, nor guest with his host, nor comrade with comrade; nor will brother be dear to brother as aforetime. Men will dishonour their parents as they grow quickly old, and will carp at them, chiding them with bitter words, hard-hearted they, not knowing the fear of the gods. They will not repay their aged parents the cost their nurture, for might shall be their right: and one man will sack another's city. There will be no favour for the man who keeps his oath or for the just or for the good; but rather men will praise the evil-doer and his violent dealing. Strength will be right and reverence will cease to be; and the wicked will hurt the worthy man, speaking false words against him, and will swear an oath upon them. Envy, foul-mouthed, delighting in evil, with scowling face, will go along with wretched men one and all. And then Aidos and Nemesis, with their sweet forms wrapped in white robes, will go from the wide-pathed earth and forsake mankind to join the company of the deathless gods: and bitter sorrows will be left for mortal men, and there will be no help against evil.

parts.author: Hesiod
parts.title: Gold, silver, bronze, heroes, iron
parts.context: Hesiod lived in Boeotia, in central Greece. His Works and Days is advice to his idle brother Perses, who had cheated him of his inheritance, mixed with myths about why life is hard. The cuts marked '…' leave out the silver and heroic ages.
parts.plain: Hesiod says: the gods first made a golden race of humans, who lived like gods, without toil, sorrow or old age. Then came worse races: a bronze race who loved war and destroyed themselves. Now we live in the age of iron, full of toil and sorrow, when families fall apart, brothers no longer love each other, children dishonour their parents, might is right, and the wicked are praised. Shame and justice have left the earth.

commentary.on: a golden race of mortal men who lived in the time of Cronos
commentary.text: Like Genesis, Hesiod begins with a lost golden age, without toil. Many peoples remembered, or imagined, a paradise at the beginning.

commentary.on: They loved the lamentable works of Ares and deeds of violence
commentary.text: Ares was the Greek god of war. The bronze race, like the generation before the flood, is filled with violence, and destroys itself 'by their own hands'.

commentary.on: nor will brother be dear to brother as aforetime
commentary.text: The closest echo of Genesis: the age of iron is the age of Cain. Hesiod wrote this, almost certainly, without having heard of Genesis.

commentary.on: might shall be their right
commentary.text: The age of iron is the age of Lamech: strength makes right, and revenge has no limit.

commentary.on: Aidos and Nemesis
commentary.text: Aidos is shame or modesty, the feeling that stops us doing wrong; Nemesis is righteous anger at wrong. Hesiod pictures them as two goddesses leaving the earth for heaven: heaven withdrawing from a world that has lost its meaning.

commentary.on: would that I were not among the men of the fifth generation
commentary.text: The great difference from Genesis: Hesiod's decline is simply fate, the gods making worse races one after another. There is no warning like God's words to Cain, no grief in heaven, and no way back. Genesis explains decline by human choice, and keeps hope open.

compare.author: Hesiod
compare.why: Hesiod, a Greek farmer-poet writing around 700 BC, told of five races of humans, each worse than the one before. His picture of the last age, our own, is strikingly like Genesis 4–6. Read it, and notice both the likeness and the difference.
compare.title: Hesiod's ages of man

paras: Read Genesis 3 to 6 as a map and a pattern appears. At each step humanity moves further from the centre. Adam and Eve are sent out east of the garden. Cain goes further, to Nod, 'east of Eden', 'hidden from your face'. His descendants build a city of their own. By chapter 6 the whole earth is 'filled with violence'.

The movement goes inwards too: from an act, to a habit, to a culture, to 'every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart'. Genesis is not naive about human nature. It sees that wrongdoing grows, passes between generations and becomes part of how a society works. Distance from the centre is not only geography. It is a condition of the heart.
sections.key: Genesis 3–6 shows humanity moving further from the centre, outwards across the land and inwards into the heart.

paras: Cain is 'a fugitive and a wanderer', with no place. So he makes one. He builds a city and names it after his son. A city is a human centre: walls against the wild, a name to last, a place to belong. It is not wicked in itself; the Bible ends with a city, the new Jerusalem. But the first city is built far from God's presence by a man who has lost his own centre and wants to make another.

This is one of Genesis's deepest insights. When people lose the meeting of heaven and earth, they do not stop needing a centre. They build substitutes: a city, a name, a power. The pattern returns at Babel, where people build a city and a tower 'to make a name for ourselves'.
sections.key: Far from God's centre, Cain builds a city and puts his name on it: a human substitute for the lost centre.

paras: Yet Genesis never says anyone had to do wrong. God warns Cain: 'sin crouches at the door… but you are to rule over it.' Cain is free and responsible. When God asks 'Where is Abel, your brother?', Cain must answer.

This is one of the great differences between the Bible and its neighbours. In Hesiod, human decline is fate. In many ancient myths, humans are playthings of quarrelling gods. In Genesis, people choose, and are accountable. Western law, with its idea that every person is responsible for their own acts, owes much to this.
sections.key: Genesis insists that people choose and are accountable; decline is not fate.

paras: Cain's question has echoed through Western history. The Bible's answer, yes, became the root of a whole moral tradition: the Law's care for the stranger, the widow and the orphan; the prophets' demand for justice; Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan, which answers 'Who is my neighbour?'; the hospitals, schools and charities of Christendom.

Even the idea that a murder is a wrong against society, not a private matter between families, grows from 'the voice of your brother's blood cries to me': God himself takes up the cause of the victim.
sections.key: The Bible's answer to Cain, yes, you are your brother's keeper, became a foundation of Western ethics.

paras: The most surprising thing in the story is that God protects Cain. Murder deserves punishment, and Cain is punished; but God sets a limit to it and forbids revenge. Lamech's song shows what happens without such limits: revenge escalates to seventy-sevenfold.

Ancient law codes later limited revenge with 'an eye for an eye', meant as a ceiling, not a demand. Jesus went further: forgive 'seventy times seven'. The mark of Cain says that no one is so far from the centre that God has stopped caring for them. The story of Cain stands at the start of the long path from revenge, to justice, to mercy.
sections.key: God limits Cain's punishment and forbids revenge: even at the far edge, no one is beyond his care.

paras: Who did Cain marry? Genesis does not say, because it is not interested in the question. It mentions later that Adam had 'other sons and daughters' (5:4); an ancient Jewish book, Jubilees, says Cain married his sister. Readers who take Adam and Eve as one couple among a larger early population, or as a picture of all humanity, see other people already present: Cain fears that 'whoever finds me will kill me', and he builds a city.

How did people live so long? Chapter 5 gives the generations from Adam to Noah enormous ages, such as Methuselah's 969 years. Babylonian king lists give their kings before the flood reigns of tens of thousands of years. Some read the numbers literally; many scholars think they are symbolic, marking the great age of the first people and, as they shrink after the flood, the growing distance from Eden.
sections.key: Genesis isn't interested in who Cain married; the long lifespans may be literal or, as many think, symbolic of distance from Eden.

paras: Hesiod and Genesis agree on a great deal: an early paradise, a fall into toil and violence, brothers turning on each other, strength making right. Both became part of how the West understood itself: a civilisation that does not expect human beings to be naturally good.

But they explain it differently. For Hesiod, the gods simply made worse races; there is no reason, no responsibility and no hope beyond enduring. For Genesis, decline comes from human choice; God warns, grieves and protects; and the story is moving towards a new beginning. When the West later combined Greek realism about human nature with biblical hope for its redemption, it drew on both.
sections.key: Hesiod and Genesis both see human decline; Genesis explains it by choice and keeps hope open.

refs: Genesis 4–6; 5:4; 11:4; Hebrews 11:4; Matthew 18:21–22; Luke 10:25–37; Exodus 21:23–25; Revelation 21.
Jubilees 4:1–9 (Cain's wife); 1 Enoch 6–11 (the watchers); Augustine, City of God XV.1 and XV.22–23 (Cain's city; the sons of Seth).
Sumerian King List (reigns before the flood): Thorkild Jacobsen, The Sumerian King List (1939).
Hesiod, Works and Days 106–201, tr. H. G. Evelyn-White (1914); M. L. West, Hesiod: Works and Days (1978).
On Genesis 4–11 as the spread of sin: Gerhard von Rad, Genesis (English 1961); Claus Westermann, Genesis 1–11 (English 1984). On the city: Jacques Ellul, The Meaning of the City (1970).

debate.question: Who were the 'sons of God' in Genesis 6?

positions.name: Angels
positions.who: 1 Enoch; many early Jewish and Christian writers; many scholars today
positions.view: They were heavenly beings who crossed the boundary between heaven and earth, and their offspring were the Nephilim.
positions.evidence: 'Sons of God' means angels elsewhere (Job 1:6); 1 Enoch; Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4.

positions.name: The line of Seth
positions.who: Augustine, John Calvin and many Christian readers
positions.view: They were the godly descendants of Seth who married into Cain's line, so that faith was diluted.
positions.evidence: Genesis 4–5 sets the lines of Cain and Seth side by side; angels do not marry (Matthew 22:30).

positions.name: Tyrant kings
positions.who: Some Jewish commentators and modern scholars
positions.view: They were powerful rulers, 'sons of God' in the royal sense, who took any women they wanted: an abuse of power.
positions.evidence: Ancient kings were called sons of gods; 'they took any that they wanted'.

debate.agree: All agree that the passage describes boundaries broken and power abused, as the world slides towards the flood.

look.why: Benjamin West, an American who became President of the Royal Academy in London, painted the expulsion from Eden in 1791. Look at what he puts in the background: the violence of the world outside the garden, the world Cain will inherit.
points: An angel in a white robe with coral-red fabric raises his arms over a man and a woman being driven away.
The woman, in an animal-skin garment, kneels and looks up, grasping the man's arm; the man covers his face with his hand.
Thistles in the foreground, and a striped serpent lifting its head on the right.
Beyond them, a lion attacks two horses; in the sky an eagle swoops down on a heron.
A spear of light thrusts down from the clouds above the angel.

music.why: 'Dear Lord and Father of mankind, forgive our foolish ways': a hymn from a poem by the Quaker John Greenleaf Whittier, asking for the 'still small voice of calm' in a world of strife.

think.why: If we are our brother's keeper, where does that obligation come from?

learn.why: Cain's shrug, and God's answer: the victim's blood has a voice.

check.q: What does God say to Cain before the murder, and why does it matter?
options: That Cain is cursed already
That sin is crouching at the door but Cain can rule over it, so Cain was free and responsible
That Abel deserves to die
Nothing; Cain acts without warning
check.why: Genesis insists that wrongdoing is a choice, not a fate.

check.q: Why is it significant that Cain builds the first city and names it after his son?
options: It proves that Cain repented
It shows Cain was a skilled architect
Far from God's presence, he makes a centre of his own with his family's name on it, a pattern Babel will repeat
It shows that cities are evil
check.why: A substitute centre; the Bible itself ends with a city, so the city is not bad in itself.

check.q: What is the 'mark of Cain'?
options: A tattoo identifying murderers
A sign of protection so that no one would kill him in revenge
The mark of Satan
A curse that made him evil
check.why: Even at the edge, God has not let go.

check.q: How does Jesus' 'seventy times seven' relate to Lamech's song?
options: It repeats Lamech's boast
It is unrelated
It reverses it: unlimited revenge becomes unlimited forgiveness
It counts Lamech's descendants
check.why: Matthew 18:22 answers Genesis 4:24.

check.q: What is the biggest difference between Hesiod's ages of man and Genesis 4–6?
options: In Hesiod decline is fate; in Genesis it comes from human choice, and God warns, grieves and keeps hope open
Hesiod has no golden age
Hesiod blames women
Genesis has no violence
check.why: Both see decline; only Genesis explains it by responsibility and hope.

check.q: On the reading of 'God's sons' as angels, how does Genesis 6:1–4 fit the frame of heaven and earth?
options: It has nothing to do with heaven and earth
Heaven and earth are mixed by grasping, not ordered: boundaries broken and power abused
It shows that angels are good
Heaven and earth meet properly at last
check.why: Whatever they were, all readings see boundaries crossed.

tutorial.question: Why do people hurt each other, according to Genesis 4–6, and how does its answer compare with Hesiod's?
tutorial.approach: Trace the movement away from the centre, from Eden to Nod to Cain's city to a world filled with violence. Explain what the story says about responsibility, the victim and mercy. Then compare Hesiod: what they share and where they differ.
strong: Traces the movement outward (east, the city) and inward (the heart).
Explains God's warning to Cain and its importance for responsibility.
Explains 'Am I my brother's keeper?' and its legacy.
Notes the mercy shown to Cain, the contrast with Lamech, and Jesus' reversal.
Compares Hesiod accurately, especially fate versus choice.
Deals sensibly with Cain's wife, the Nephilim or the long lifespans.

reading.author: Leon Kass
reading.title: The Beginning of Wisdom: Reading Genesis
reading.why: Superb chapters on Cain and Abel and the rise of the city.

reading.author: Jacques Ellul
reading.title: The Meaning of the City
reading.why: A French thinker reads the Bible's cities from Cain to the new Jerusalem.

reading.author: Robert Alter
reading.title: Genesis: Translation and Commentary
reading.why: A literary translation with notes on the Hebrew.

reading.author: Claus Westermann
reading.title: Genesis 1–11
reading.why: The great critical commentary on the primeval history.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: be your brother's (or sister's, or neighbour's) keeper in one concrete way: check on someone who may be struggling, and do one thing that helps.
sessions.reflect: Where is 'sin crouching at the door' in your own life? What would it mean to rule over it?
takeaways: Genesis 4–6 shows humanity moving further from the centre: east to Nod, into a city of its own making, until violence fills the earth.
God warns Cain before he acts and protects him afterwards: people are free and responsible, and mercy limits revenge.
Hesiod tells a similar story of decline, but as fate; Genesis explains it by choice and keeps hope open.

sessions.title: The waters return
sessions.line: The flood as creation undone, the ark, the rainbow, and the Babylonian flood story found in 1872.
sessions.plain: Genesis says God sent a great flood and saved only Noah, his family and the animals in the ark, then promised never to destroy the earth again. Read with session 1 in mind, the flood is creation running backwards: the waters God divided on the second day pour back, and the world returns to formless matter. Then God orders it again. This session reads the story beside a much older Babylonian flood story, and asks what geology says.
sessions.why: Session 4 ended with the earth 'filled with violence' and God grieving. If humanity has gone so far from the centre, will God give up on the world?
answers: What does the flood story actually say?
Why water?
Was it copied from the Babylonian flood story?
Was there really a worldwide flood?
sessions.finding: The flood is creation undone: the waters above and below that God separated on the second day pour back, and the world returns to formless matter; then God orders it again and binds himself by a promise. Geology finds no worldwide flood, so most readers today take it as a local flood or a theological story.

paras: Sessions 1 to 4: heaven and earth ordered by God's word; Eden the centre where they meet; the eyes opened and the exile east; and humanity moving further out, until the earth is 'filled with violence' and God grieves that he made human beings. But 'Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes'.
background.key: Order, the centre, exile and spreading violence; and one righteous man.

paras: On the second day of Genesis 1, God set an 'expanse' in the middle of the waters, and divided the waters above from the waters below. On the third he gathered the waters below so that dry land appeared. In the ancient picture, the ordered world is a bubble of air and land held safe between two oceans, by God's word.

So when Genesis says that 'all the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the sky's windows opened' (7:11), its hearers knew what that meant. The two oceans God held apart are coming back together. The world is going back to the 'deep' of Genesis 1:2, formless and empty.
background.key: The ordered world sits between waters God divided; the flood lets them come back.

background.h: A discovery at the British Museum
paras: In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught assistant at the British Museum who had started as a banknote engraver, was sorting clay tablets from the ruins of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. He found one that told of a ship resting on a mountain and a dove sent out to find dry land. According to a colleague's later account, he was so excited that he began to undress in the room. On 3 December 1872 he read his translation to the Society of Biblical Archaeology in London, with the Prime Minister, William Gladstone, in the audience.

The tablet was the eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh, a poem about a king who seeks to escape death. In it, an old man named Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamesh how he survived the great flood. An even older Babylonian poem, Atrahasis, from about 1700 BC, tells the same story.
background.key: In 1872 George Smith found the Babylonian flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh, much older than Genesis.

paras: The main reading follows the flood in four parts: God's plan and the ark (6:9–22), the waters (7:17–24), the waters going down and the birds (8:1–12), and the covenant and the rainbow (9:8–17).

The comparison is three passages from Gilgamesh Tablet XI: the warning to build a ship, the storm, and the birds and the sacrifice. Side by side, you will see how much the stories share and how differently they picture God.
background.key: Genesis's flood beside the Gilgamesh flood: shared story, different God.

before: Why does God send the flood, according to Genesis?
Which words in chapter 8 echo Genesis 1?
What promise does God make afterwards, and to whom?
sessions.readWhy: The flood story, in four parts: the ark, the waters, the new creation, and the rainbow.

paras: This is the history of the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God.
Noah became the father of three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.
God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.
God said to Noah, “I will bring an end to all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them and the earth.
Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch.
This is how you shall make it. The length of the ship shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.
You shall make a roof in the ship, and you shall finish it to a cubit upward. You shall set the door of the ship in its side. You shall make it with lower, second, and third levels.
I, even I, will bring the flood of waters on this earth, to destroy all flesh having the breath of life from under the sky. Everything that is in the earth will die.
But I will establish my covenant with you. You shall come into the ship, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you.
Of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ship, to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female.
Of the birds after their kind, of the livestock after their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every sort will come to you, to keep them alive.
Take with you some of all food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself; and it will be for food for you, and for them.”
Thus Noah did. He did all that God commanded him.
The flood was forty days on the earth. The waters increased, and lifted up the ship, and it was lifted up above the earth.
The waters rose, and increased greatly on the earth; and the ship floated on the surface of the waters.
The waters rose very high on the earth. All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered.
The waters rose fifteen cubits higher, and the mountains were covered.
All flesh died that moved on the earth, including birds, livestock, animals, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, and every man.
All on the dry land, in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, died.

Every living thing was destroyed that was on the surface of the ground, including man, livestock, creeping things, and birds of the sky. They were destroyed from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship.
The waters flooded the earth one hundred fifty days.
God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship; and God made a wind to pass over the earth. The waters subsided.
The deep’s fountains and the sky’s windows were also stopped, and the rain from the sky was restrained.
The waters continually receded from the earth. After the end of one hundred fifty days the waters receded.
The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat’s mountains.
The waters receded continually until the tenth month. In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were visible.
At the end of forty days, Noah opened the window of the ship which he had made,
and he sent out a raven. It went back and forth, until the waters were dried up from the earth.
He himself sent out a dove to see if the waters were abated from the surface of the ground,

but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned into the ship to him, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship.
He waited yet another seven days; and again he sent the dove out of the ship.
The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters were abated from the earth.
He waited yet another seven days, and sent out the dove; and she didn’t return to him any more.
God spoke to Noah and to his sons with him, saying,
“As for me, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you,
and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the livestock, and every animal of the earth with you, of all that go out of the ship, even every animal of the earth.
I will establish my covenant with you: All flesh will not be cut off any more by the waters of the flood. There will never again be a flood to destroy the earth.”
God said, “This is the token of the covenant which I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for perpetual generations:
I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth.
When I bring a cloud over the earth, that the rainbow will be seen in the cloud,
I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh, and the waters will no more become a flood to destroy all flesh.
The rainbow will be in the cloud. I will look at it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.”
God said to Noah, “This is the token of the covenant which I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.”

parts.title: Noah and the ark
parts.context: The story begins with Noah, a descendant of Adam's son Seth.

commentary.on: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God.
commentary.text: In a world filled with violence, one man lives rightly. 'Walked with God' is said of only one other person, Enoch (5:24), and it is the same verb as God 'walking' in the garden. Noah still lives near the centre. Genesis does not say he was perfect (chapter 9 shows him drunk), but he trusted God.

commentary.on: the earth was filled with violence
commentary.text: The reason for the flood is stated twice: violence and corruption. Remember this when you read the Babylonian version.

commentary.on: The length of the ship shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.
commentary.text: A cubit is about half a metre. The ark is roughly 140 metres long, 23 wide and 14 high: a long box, built to float, not to sail. It is a small ordered world, carried safely over the chaos.

commentary.on: But I will establish my covenant with you.
commentary.text: The first use of the word 'covenant' in the Bible: a binding promise. Even before the flood, God's purpose is not to end the world but to begin it again.

parts.title: The waters
parts.context: Noah, his family and the animals are in the ark. The waters rise.

commentary.on: All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered.
commentary.text: Even the mountains, the high places where heaven and earth meet, go under. Whether 'the whole sky' means the whole planet, or the whole world the writer knew, is one of the questions readers ask. The lecture comes back to it.

commentary.on: All flesh died that moved on the earth
commentary.text: The creatures of days five and six die. The flood reverses creation step by step: the dry land of day three disappears, and the world goes back to the watery deep of Genesis 1:2.

commentary.on: Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship.
commentary.text: Out of the un-creation a small remnant survives, carried on the waters. The pattern of a faithful few through whom God begins again runs through the whole Bible.

parts.title: God remembered Noah
parts.context: The turning point of the story.

commentary.on: God remembered Noah
commentary.text: The exact centre of the flood story. In the Bible 'remember' does not mean God had forgotten; it means he acts on his promise.

commentary.on: God made a wind to pass over the earth.
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for 'wind', ruach, is the word for 'Spirit' in Genesis 1:2, where 'God's Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters'. As at the beginning, God's breath moves over the deep. The flood is followed by a new creation.

commentary.on: The deep’s fountains and the sky’s windows were also stopped
commentary.text: The waters above and the waters below are shut off again: day two restored. Then dry land appears, as on day three. God is putting the world back in order, dividing the waters once more.

commentary.on: The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat’s mountains.
commentary.text: The ark comes to rest on a mountain, the high place, as Eden was. Ararat is the region of Urartu, in modern eastern Turkey and Armenia, not necessarily the single peak now called Mount Ararat. Many expeditions have searched for the ark; none has found it.

commentary.on: in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf
commentary.text: The dove returns with an olive leaf: life is growing again. The dove with an olive branch became a sign of peace across the Western world.

parts.title: The rainbow
parts.context: Noah has left the ark and offered a sacrifice. Now God speaks.

commentary.on: I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you
commentary.text: The covenant is with 'every living creature': birds, livestock, animals. God binds himself to the whole of the re-made earth.

commentary.on: There will never again be a flood to destroy the earth.
commentary.text: The answer to the question of this session. God will not give up on the world. Whatever he does about evil from now on, it will not be by undoing creation.

commentary.on: I set my rainbow in the cloud
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for rainbow is the word for a warrior's bow. Some scholars suggest a picture of God hanging up his bow in the sky, pointed away from the earth. It also stands between heaven and earth, a sign joining the sky to the ground.

commentary.on: I will remember my covenant
commentary.text: The rainbow is a reminder, Genesis says, for God. The promise does not depend on humans behaving better.

parts.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
parts.title: Build a ship
parts.context: The tablet was copied for the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh in the seventh century BC; the story itself is much older. Shurippak was a real Sumerian city on the Euphrates. Ea (Nin-igi-azag) is the god of wisdom and fresh water; Enlil is the chief of the gods.
parts.plain: Uta-Napishtim says: I will tell you a secret of the gods. In the old city of Shurippak, the great gods decided to send a flood. But the god Ea, who was in their council, warned me secretly, speaking to the reed walls of my house: tear down your house, build a ship, give up your wealth and save your life, and take into the ship the seed of every living thing.

commentary.on: Their hearts induced the great gods to make a wind-storm
commentary.text: No reason is given here for the flood. In the older poem Atrahasis, the gods send it because humans were making too much noise and disturbing their sleep. In Genesis the reason is violence: a moral reason.

commentary.on: Nin-igi-azag, Ea, was with them [in council] and
commentary.text: The gods are divided. Ea betrays the council's plan by whispering to the wall of Uta-Napishtim's reed house. In Genesis there is one God, and he speaks openly to Noah.

commentary.on: Throw down the house, build a ship
commentary.text: The same command as to Noah: build a boat and save life. The likeness is unmistakable.

commentary.on: The breadth and the length thereof shall be the same.
commentary.text: Uta-Napishtim's ship is a cube. Noah's ark is long and low, a shape that would float steadily.

parts.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
parts.title: The storm, and the frightened gods
parts.context: The flood comes. Adad is the storm god, Nergal and En-urta are gods of war and destruction, and the Anunnaki are the gods of the underworld. Ishtar, goddess of love and war, is called 'the Lady of the Gods'.
parts.plain: Uta-Napishtim says: at dawn a black cloud came up and the storm gods brought the flood. Darkness covered everything; the water rose to the mountains and fell on the people like an army. Even the gods were terrified: they fled up to heaven and crouched like dogs. The goddess Ishtar wailed: why did I agree to destroy my own people?

commentary.on: The gods crouched like a dog and cowered by the wall.
commentary.text: The gods who sent the flood lose control of it and cower. In Genesis, God is never frightened; he shuts the door of the ark (7:16), and he 'remembers' Noah. The chaos never escapes his hand.

commentary.on: Did I of myself bring forth my people
commentary.text: Ishtar regrets the flood, as God 'was sorry' in Genesis 6:6. But her regret is over a rash decision of the divine council. God's grief in Genesis is over human violence, and it comes before the flood.

parts.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
parts.title: The birds and the sacrifice
parts.context: After seven days the storm ends. The ship has grounded on Mount Nisir, in the mountains east of the Tigris.
parts.plain: Uta-Napishtim says: after six days and nights the storm stopped; everyone else had turned to mud, and I wept. The ship came to rest on Mount Nisir. On the seventh day I sent out a dove, which came back, then a swallow, which came back, then a raven, which found food and did not return. Then I came out and offered a sacrifice, and the gods smelled it and gathered round like flies.

commentary.on: I brought out a dove and let her go free.
commentary.text: The detail that so excited George Smith: birds sent out to find dry land. A dove and a raven in both stories; a swallow too in Gilgamesh. The likeness is too close to be chance.

commentary.on: The raven flew away, she saw the sinking waters.
commentary.text: In Gilgamesh the raven not returning is the sign. In Genesis the dove's olive leaf is the sign. The stories share the motif and use it differently.

commentary.on: The gods gathered together like flies over him that sacrificed.
commentary.text: After the flood the gods have had no offerings and are hungry; they swarm over the sacrifice. Compare Genesis 8:21: 'Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma', and promises never again to curse the ground. In Babylon the gods need humans to feed them; in Genesis God needs nothing, and answers with a promise.

compare.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
compare.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
compare.why: Three passages from Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, found by George Smith in 1872. The old man Uta-Napishtim tells the hero Gilgamesh how he survived the flood. Watch for the likenesses to Genesis, and then for the differences.
compare.title: The Babylonian flood

paras: The flood in Genesis is not mainly about water. It is about order. In Genesis 1 God divided the waters above from the waters below, gathered the sea so that land appeared, and filled the land with life. In Genesis 7 the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of the sky open: the division of day two is undone, the land of day three goes under, and the creatures of days five and six die. The world returns to the formless deep.

Then the pattern runs forwards. God's wind passes over the waters, as his Spirit hovered at the beginning. The fountains and windows are shut. Dry land appears. The birds go out; the animals come out to be fruitful and multiply; Noah is blessed in the words spoken to Adam (9:1). The flood is a second creation.

rows: Fountains of the deep and windows of the sky opened (7:11), then stopped (8:2)
The waters recede and the ground dries (8:3–14)

sections.key: The flood runs creation backwards to the formless deep, then forwards again: a second creation.

paras: Why should human violence bring back the chaos? Because in Genesis the human being is the link between heaven and earth, set at the centre to tend the world. When that link is broken, and violence 'fills the earth', the earth itself loses its order. The flood is, in a sense, the world becoming outwardly what humanity had already become inwardly: formless, without meaning, drowned.

So the answer to this session's question is no: God will not give up on his world. He grieves, he judges, he saves a remnant, and he binds himself by a promise to every living creature never to undo creation again.
sections.key: When the human link between heaven and earth breaks, the earth loses its order; God answers with a remnant and a promise.

sections.h: The two flood stories side by side
paras: The likenesses between Genesis and Gilgamesh are too many and too specific to be chance. But the differences are just as important, and they are all about God.

rows: No reason given; in Atrahasis, human noise disturbing the gods
A council of gods, one of whom secretly betrays it
One God, who speaks openly to Noah
Raven, then the dove three times, with an olive leaf
God smells the aroma and makes a promise
God makes a covenant with all living things

sections.key: Same outline, opposite pictures of God: a frightened, divided council, or one God who judges, grieves and promises.

paras: How are the stories related? Some think Genesis adapted the Babylonian story, perhaps during the exile, deliberately rewriting it. Some think both go back to a memory of a real, devastating flood in Mesopotamia, told in different ways. Some traditional readers hold that Genesis preserves the true account, and Gilgamesh a distorted one.

Whichever is right, the comparison shows the same pattern as Genesis 1 and Babylon's creation story: Genesis uses the shared stories of the ancient world and transforms what they say about God, about human beings and about why things happen.
sections.key: Genesis may adapt, share or preserve the flood story; either way it transforms what it says about God.

paras: Here science has something to say. Geologists find no evidence of a single flood covering the whole planet in the time of human history: no worldwide layer of flood deposits, and unbroken records in ice layers, tree rings and lake sediments going back far further. That is the conclusion of virtually all geologists, including many Christians.

There is evidence of great local floods. In 1929 the archaeologist Leonard Woolley found a deep layer of flood silt at Ur in southern Iraq, and flood deposits at Shuruppak, Uta-Napishtim's city, date to around 2900 BC. Mesopotamia, a flat plain between two great rivers, was prone to catastrophic floods. Many think the stories remember such a disaster, which to those who lived through it was the whole world.
sections.key: Geology finds no worldwide flood, but great local floods in Mesopotamia, at Ur and Shuruppak, are well attested.

sections.h: Three ways Christians read the flood
paras: Christians read the flood in three main ways today. All three agree on what it teaches about God: that he takes evil seriously, grieves over violence, saves the faithful and binds himself to creation by a promise. Read with this course's frame, they also agree that the flood is about order and chaos, creation undone and renewed.

rows: A worldwide flood a few thousand years ago, which laid down most rock layers
Young-earth creationists; 'flood geology', popularised by The Genesis Flood (1961)
A real, catastrophic flood in Mesopotamia; 'the whole earth' meant the known world
A story using an ancient memory to teach about judgement, grace and covenant
Most biblical scholars; many Catholic, Orthodox and mainline Protestant readers

sections.key: Christians read the flood as global, local or theological; all agree on what it teaches about God.

sections.h: How can a good God send a flood?
paras: Many readers find the flood morally troubling: a God who drowns almost everyone, children included. It is a serious objection, and it should not be brushed aside.

Notice what Genesis itself does with it. It insists the flood was a response to violence, not a whim; that God grieved before he acted; that he saved those who trusted him; and that afterwards he bound himself never to do it again. The story is, in a sense, about God refusing the very thing it describes. Christians add that the Bible's final answer to evil is not a flood but the cross, where God takes judgement on himself.
sections.key: The flood troubles many readers; Genesis presents it as a response to violence that God grieves and promises never to repeat.

debate.question: How are the Genesis and Gilgamesh flood stories related?

positions.name: Genesis adapts Babylon
positions.who: Many biblical scholars
positions.view: The writers of Genesis knew the Mesopotamian flood story and deliberately rewrote it, keeping its outline but transforming its theology.
positions.evidence: Close parallels in order and detail (the birds, the sacrifice); the older dates of Atrahasis and Gilgamesh; Israel's exile in Babylon.

positions.name: A shared memory
positions.who: Some historians and archaeologists
positions.view: Both stories descend independently from a memory of a real catastrophic flood in Mesopotamia, told and retold in different ways.
positions.evidence: Flood deposits at Ur and Shuruppak; flood stories in Sumerian, Akkadian and Hebrew traditions.

positions.name: Genesis preserves the original
positions.who: Some traditional readers
positions.view: The flood happened as Genesis describes, and the Babylonian versions are later, polytheistic distortions of the true account.
positions.evidence: The moral coherence of the Genesis version; belief in its inspiration.

debate.agree: All agree that the stories are related and that Genesis has a strikingly different picture of God.

look.why: J. M. W. Turner painted The Evening of the Deluge around 1843, one of several pictures he made of the flood. It is almost abstract: light, storm and swirling forms, a world dissolving back into formlessness.

Clouds spiralling round the disk, darkening to slate grey, rust brown and wine red at the top.
A flock of birds painted as blue Vs, curving round the sun into the distance.
Below, an arched, copper-brown structure among swirling green and gold forms, forest or waves.
Faint outlines that may be a bear, a crocodile and a giraffe: animals on their way to the ark.

music.why: 'Summer and winter, and springtime and harvest': this hymn echoes God's promise after the flood that 'seed time and harvest… summer and winter… will not cease' (Genesis 8:22).

think.why: The flood raises the oldest question of all: how can a good God allow, or send, suffering?
