background.key: Abram and Sarai, later Abraham and Sarah, around 2000–1800 BC: from Ur to Haran to Canaan.

paras: Genesis does not say who wrote it. Jewish and Christian tradition held that Moses wrote the first five books of the Bible. From the Middle Ages on, careful readers noticed clues pointing to later hands: Genesis 36:31 lists 'the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel', which sounds like someone writing after Israel had kings. Most scholars think Genesis was put together over centuries from older stories and reached its final form around 600 to 400 BC. Many believers accept this and still read it as inspired; others hold to the traditional view. ('What is the Bible?' weighs the evidence; whether Abraham himself existed is in this session's lecture.)

Abraham's world already had cities, writing and stories of its own, and Genesis shares much with it: lists of ancestors, a great flood, customs found in Hammurabi's laws. What is new is the God: one God, not many, who speaks to one man and makes him a promise for the sake of the whole world.
background.key: Tradition says Moses; most scholars say many hands, finished around 600–400 BC. The setting is ancient; the God is new.

paras: The reading has four parts: the family's background, with a verse from Joshua saying they 'served other gods'; the call itself (12:1–9); Abraham at his worst, straight afterwards (12:10–20); and a New Testament view of what he did (Hebrews 11). The comparison is the Jewish and Muslim story of Abraham and the idols, which answers what Genesis leaves out: why did he leave his father's gods?
background.key: The call, Abraham's failure, a New Testament view, and the story of Abraham and the idols.

before: What exactly does God ask Abraham to leave, and what does he promise in return?
Who is the promise for? Look for the word 'all'.
In Egypt, what does Abraham do, and who comes out of the story looking better?
sessions.readWhy: The call of Abraham, the hinge of the whole Bible, read in four parts: his family, the call, his first failure, and how the New Testament saw it.

paras: Now this is the history of the generations of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran became the father of Lot.
Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees, while his father Terah was still alive.
Abram and Nahor married wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, who was also the father of Iscah.
Sarai was barren. She had no child.

Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram’s wife. They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there.
The days of Terah were two hundred five years. Terah died in Haran.
Joshua said to all the people, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, says, ‘Your fathers lived of old time beyond the River, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nahor. They served other gods.
I took your father Abraham from beyond the River, and led him throughout all the land of Canaan, and multiplied his offspring, and gave him Isaac.
Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him. Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.

Abram took Sarai his wife, Lot his brother’s son, all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people whom they had acquired in Haran, and they went to go into the land of Canaan. They entered into the land of Canaan.
Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time, Canaanites were in the land.
Yahweh appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.”
He built an altar there to Yahweh, who had appeared to him.
He left from there to go to the mountain on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to Yahweh and called on Yahweh’s name.
Abram traveled, still going on toward the South.
There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land.
When he had come near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, “See now, I know that you are a beautiful woman to look at.
It will happen, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ They will kill me, but they will save you alive.
Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that my soul may live because of you.”
When Abram had come into Egypt, Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.
The princes of Pharaoh saw her, and praised her to Pharaoh; and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
He dealt well with Abram for her sake. He had sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.
Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
Pharaoh called Abram and said, “What is this that you have done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?
Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her to be my wife? Now therefore, see your wife, take her, and go your way.”
Pharaoh commanded men concerning him, and they escorted him away with his wife and all that he had.
By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went.
By faith, he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise.
For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
By faith, even Sarah herself received power to conceive, and she bore a child when she was past age, since she counted him faithful who had promised.
Therefore as many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as innumerable as the sand which is by the sea shore, were fathered by one man, and him as good as dead.
These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a country of their own.
If indeed they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had enough time to return.
But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

parts.title: A family from Ur
parts.context: The last verses of Genesis 11 introduce Abraham's family. With them we read two verses from the book of Joshua, written about Israel's later history: Joshua, Moses' successor, reminds the people where they came from.

commentary.on: Now this is the history of the generations of Terah.
commentary.text: Genesis is organised by these 'generations' (in Hebrew, toledot): 'this is the history of…'. Each one opens a new chapter of the family story. This one introduces Terah, Abraham's father, and it will run all the way to Abraham's death.

commentary.on: Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees
commentary.text: Ur was one of the oldest and richest cities in the world. Do not confuse Haran, Abraham's brother, with Haran the city where the family later settles: in Hebrew they are spelt differently. 'Of the Chaldees' is a detail worth noticing: the Chaldeans are first mentioned in records of the ninth century BC, so this phrase was probably added by a later writer to tell readers which Ur was meant.

commentary.on: Sarai was barren. She had no child.
commentary.text: Five words, and the whole story hangs on them. Everything God is about to promise depends on children, and Sarai cannot have them. The Bible often begins its greatest stories with an impossibility.

commentary.on: They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there.
commentary.text: The journey starts before God speaks, with Terah, and stalls halfway. Abraham's call in the next chapter is to finish a journey his father did not.

commentary.on: Your fathers lived of old time beyond the River, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nahor. They served other gods.
commentary.text: Genesis never says so, but this verse does: Abraham's family worshipped other gods. 'The River' is the Euphrates. So the call is not only to a new place. It is out of a whole world of gods, into trust in one God. That is the gap the comparison readings fill in.

parts.title: The call
parts.context: The family has settled in Haran. Then God speaks to Abram: the first words God says to him, and the turning point of the whole Bible.

commentary.on: Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house
commentary.text: Three circles, each closer than the last: his country, his clan, his own father's household. In the ancient world these were everything: your safety, your identity, your inheritance, your gods. He is asked to give up all three, for a land God has not yet named: 'the land that I will show you'.

commentary.on: I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great.
commentary.text: Remember Babel, just one chapter earlier, where people said 'let's make a name for ourselves'. Here God says 'I will make your name great'. What the builders tried to seize, God gives as a gift.

commentary.on: You will be a blessing.
commentary.text: The blessing is not only for Abram. He is blessed in order to be a blessing. That is the first answer this journey will find to its question: the family is chosen for the sake of others.

commentary.on: All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
commentary.text: The most important sentence in the passage. The scattered 'families of the earth' from Genesis 10–11 are not forgotten. God chooses one family as the way to reach every family. The New Testament will quote this sentence as the first announcement of the gospel (Galatians 3:8).

commentary.on: So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him.
commentary.text: No argument, no questions, no reply recorded at all. He simply goes. He is seventy-five years old. This is what the Bible will later call faith: trusting God enough to act.

commentary.on: At that time, Canaanites were in the land.
commentary.text: The promised land is not empty. Other peoples live there. The promise will take generations to come true, and Abraham will die owning only a grave (Genesis 23).

commentary.on: There he built an altar to Yahweh and called on Yahweh’s name.
commentary.text: Wherever Abraham stops, he builds an altar: a pile of stones on which to offer sacrifices. He claims no land, but he marks it out for God. Shechem and Bethel will become two of Israel's holiest places.

parts.title: Straight away, a lie
parts.context: Immediately after the call, famine strikes Canaan, and Abram goes down to Egypt, which had the Nile and grain when other lands did not. Genesis tells this story straight after the promise, and it tells a similar one twice more (Genesis 20 and 26).

commentary.on: Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake
commentary.text: The man who has just trusted God with his whole future does not trust God with this. Afraid of being killed for his beautiful wife, he asks her to pretend to be his sister. (She was in fact his half-sister, Genesis 20:12 says; a half-truth is still a lie.) He saves himself by putting her at risk.

commentary.on: the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house
commentary.text: Sarai is taken into the king's household as a wife, and Abram is paid handsomely. It is a shocking story, told without comment. The promised mother of the promised family is lost to a foreign king within a page of the promise.

commentary.on: He had sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.
commentary.text: Notice 'camels': this detail matters for the lecture. Domesticated camels are not found in Canaan's archaeology until the tenth century BC, so many scholars think the storyteller has described Abraham's wealth in the terms of a later age.

commentary.on: Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
commentary.text: God protects Sarai, and so his own promise, when Abram does not. The plagues on Pharaoh look forward to the plagues of Egypt in Exodus, when Abraham's descendants are rescued from another Pharaoh.

commentary.on: What is this that you have done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?
commentary.text: The pagan king behaves more honourably than the man of faith, and rebukes him. Genesis does not hide this. Its heroes are not chosen because they are good. That will be true of every generation of this family.

parts.title: How the New Testament saw it
parts.context: The Letter to the Hebrews, written in the first century AD by an unknown early Christian, has a famous chapter on faith which lists the heroes of Israel's story. This is its section on Abraham and Sarah.

commentary.on: He went out, not knowing where he went.
commentary.text: Hebrews sums up the call in one line. Faith, here, is not believing something without evidence; it is setting out on someone's word without knowing the destination.

commentary.on: dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob
commentary.text: Abraham never builds a house in the promised land. He lives in tents, like a nomad, and so do his son and grandson. He is a resident foreigner in the land he was promised.

commentary.on: For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
commentary.text: Hebrews reads the tents as a sign: Abraham was looking for something more than a piece of land. Compare Babel again: there, people built a city to reach heaven; Abraham waits for a city God builds.

commentary.on: These all died in faith, not having received the promises
commentary.text: An honest line. Abraham died without seeing the promise come true: he had one son of the promise, not a nation, and a grave, not a land. Faith in the Bible often means living towards a promise you will not see fulfilled.

commentary.on: they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one
commentary.text: This is a Christian reading: the earthly land points to a heavenly one. Jewish readers keep the promise of the land itself in view, as you will see in the next session.

paras: When Abraham attained the age of twenty years, his father Terah fell ill. He spoke as follows to his sons Haran and Abraham, "I adjure you by your lives, my sons, sell these two idols for me, for I have not enough money to meet our expenses." Haran executed the wish of his father, but if any one accosted Abraham, to buy an idol from him, and asked him the price, he would answer, "Three manehs," and then question in turn, "How old art thou?" "Thirty years," the reply would be. "Thou art thirty years of age, and yet thou wouldst worship this idol which I made but to-day?" The man would depart and go his way, and another would approach Abraham, and ask, "How much is this idol?" and "Five manehs" would be the reply, and again Abraham would put the question, "How old art thou?"--"Fifty years."--"And dost thou who art fifty years of age bow down before this idol which was made but to-day?" Thereupon the man would depart and go his way. Abraham then took two idols, put a rope about their necks, and, with their faces turned downward, he dragged them along the ground, crying aloud all the time: "Who will buy an idol wherein there is no profit, either unto itself or unto him that buys it in order to worship it? It has a mouth, but it speaketh not; eyes, but it seeth not; feet, but it walketh not; ears, but it heareth not."

Alone with the idols, and while he repeated the words, "The Eternal He is God, the Eternal He is God!" he struck the king's idols from their thrones, and began to belabor them with an axe. With the biggest he started, and with the smallest he ended. He hacked off the feet of one, and the other he beheaded. This one had his eyes struck out, the other had his hands crushed. After all were mutilated, he went away, having first put the axe into the hand of the largest idol.

The feast ended, the king returned, and when he saw all his idols shivered in pieces, he inquired who had perpetrated the mischief. Abraham was named as the one who had been guilty of the outrage, and the king summoned him and questioned him as to his motive for the deed. Abraham replied: "I did not do it; it was the largest of the idols who shattered all the rest. Seest thou not that he still has the axe in his hand? And if thou wilt not believe my words, ask him and he will tell thee."

Of old we gave unto Abraham his direction, for we knew him worthy.
When he said to his Father and to his people, "What are these images to which ye are devoted?"
They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."
He said, "Truly ye and your fathers have been in a plain mistake."
They said, "Hast thou come unto us in earnest? or art thou of those who jest?"
He said, "Nay, your Lord is Lord of the Heavens and of the Earth, who hath created them both; and to this am I one of those who witness:
-And, by God, I will certainly lay a plot against your idols, after ye shall have retired and turned your backs."
So, he broke them all in pieces, except the chief of them, that to it they might return, inquiring.
They said, "Who hath done this to our gods? Verily he is one of the unjust."
They said, "We heard a youth make mention of them: they call him Abraham."
They said, "Then bring him before the people's eyes, that they may witness against him."
They said, "Hast thou done this to our gods, O Abraham?"
He said, "Nay, that their chief hath done it: but ask ye them, if they can speak."
So they turned their thoughts upon themselves, and said, "Ye truly are the impious persons:"
Then became headstrong in their former error and exclaimed,"Thou knowest that these speak not."
He said, "What! do ye then worship, instead of God, that which doth not profit you at all, nor injure you? Fie on you and on that ye worship instead of God! What! do ye not then understand?"
They said: "Burn him, and come to the succour of your gods: if ye will do anything at all."
We said, "O fire! be thou cold, and to Abraham a safety!"

parts.author: Louis Ginzberg
parts.work: The Legends of the Jews, volume I
parts.ref: Legends of the Jews: Abraham and the idols
parts.title: The idol-seller's son
parts.context: Louis Ginzberg (1873–1953), a great Jewish scholar, gathered the stories that rabbis told about the Bible's characters over many centuries, from the Midrash (Jewish commentary in story form) and the Talmud, and retold them in seven volumes (1909–38). This story is first found in Genesis Rabbah 38:13, a Jewish commentary on Genesis from about AD 400–500. In Ginzberg's version Terah makes idols; in the second scene, Abraham is in the palace of King Nimrod, the 'mighty hunter' of Genesis 10, whom legend made Abraham's persecutor. The '…' marks a cut.
parts.plain: The legend says: Abraham's father Terah made and sold idols. When Abraham was sent to sell them, he asked the customers how a grown man could worship something made yesterday, and dragged the idols through the street. Later, left alone with the king's idols, he smashed them all and put the axe in the hand of the biggest. When the king asked who had done it, Abraham said: ask the big idol, he did it.

commentary.on: Thou art thirty years of age, and yet thou wouldst worship this idol which I made but to-day?
commentary.text: The argument is simple, and deep: how can something you made be your god? It is the same argument the Hebrew prophets use (Isaiah 44:9–20).

commentary.on: It has a mouth, but it speaketh not; eyes, but it seeth not
commentary.text: These words come almost exactly from Psalm 115:5–6. The legend puts the psalm's mockery of idols into Abraham's mouth, making him the first to see what the psalm would later say.

commentary.on: having first put the axe into the hand of the largest idol
commentary.text: A joke with a point. Abraham does not argue; he sets a trap. If the idols are gods, the big one could have done it. If they are not, the king must admit it.

commentary.on: ask him and he will tell thee.
commentary.text: The punchline: the king cannot ask the idol, because it cannot speak, and to say so is to admit that it is no god. In the rest of the legend, as in the Qur'an, the king throws Abraham into a furnace and God saves him.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Abraham breaks the idols
parts.context: The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam, revealed, Muslims believe, to the Prophet Muhammad between about AD 610 and 632. It tells many stories of Abraham (Ibrahim in Arabic), whom it calls a prophet and the 'friend of God'. This translation is by J. M. Rodwell, an English clergyman (1861). The one-line breaks follow the verses.
parts.plain: The Qur'an says: God gave Abraham true guidance. Abraham asked his father and his people why they worshipped statues, broke them all except the biggest, and told the people to ask the big one who had done it. They had to admit that the idols could not speak. So they tried to burn him, and God made the fire cool.

commentary.on: They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."
commentary.text: The people's only defence of their gods is custom: it is what our fathers did. Abraham's call is, precisely, to leave his father's house. Both the Jewish and the Islamic stories make him the first person to think the question through.

commentary.on: So, he broke them all in pieces, except the chief of them
commentary.text: The same story as the Jewish legend, almost detail for detail: the idols smashed, the biggest left, the challenge to ask it. The two traditions shared many stories about Abraham, told and retold in the centuries around Muhammad's time.

commentary.on: We said, "O fire! be thou cold, and to Abraham a safety!"
commentary.text: God rescues Abraham from the fire, as in the Jewish legend. In Islam, Abraham is the great example of the hanif: a person who turned from idols to the one God by his own clear sight, before Judaism or Christianity existed (the Qur'an says he 'was neither Jew nor Christian', Sura 3:67).

compare.author: Louis Ginzberg and The Qur'an
compare.work: The Legends of the Jews, volume I
compare.ref: Legends of the Jews: Abraham and the idols
compare.why: Genesis does not say why Abraham left his father's gods. Later Jews and Muslims told a famous story to explain it. Read the Jewish version, from a collection of ancient Jewish legends, and the Qur'an's version, which is remarkably similar.
compare.title: Abraham and the idols

paras: After Babel the question left hanging is: what will God do about the whole world now? Genesis 12 gives a surprising answer. Not a new flood, and not a message to everyone at once, but one man and a promise. Five times in three verses comes the word 'bless'. The story narrows so that the blessing can widen: one family, for the sake of 'all the families of the earth'. Hold on to that pattern. It is the Bible's first answer to the question of this journey.
sections.key: After Babel, God answers the world's problem through one family, blessed in order to bless every family on earth.

paras: There is no archaeological evidence of Abraham himself: no inscription, no grave that can be tested. We should not expect one; nomads leave little behind. So the question is whether the stories fit the world they describe.

In the mid-twentieth century many scholars, led by the American archaeologist William F. Albright, thought they did. Names like Abram and Jacob are found in documents of the early second millennium BC; tablets from Mari, on the Euphrates, describe semi-nomadic herders moving between towns; and customs in the stories, such as a childless wife giving her servant to her husband, appear in ancient laws and contracts. From the 1970s Thomas L. Thompson and John Van Seters argued that the parallels were weak or fitted later periods just as well, and that the stories were written in the first millennium BC. The camels and 'Ur of the Chaldees' point the same way.

Where things stand now: most scholars think the stories as we have them were shaped centuries after the time they describe, and that they cannot be proved or disproved as history. Some, such as the Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen, argue that details fit the early second millennium well. Many think they keep real memories of the family's origins. The honest answer is that we do not know, and that the stories' importance never depended on archaeology: their power is in what they say about God and people.

sections.key: Nothing in archaeology proves or disproves Abraham; most scholars think the stories were shaped later, while some argue they fit an earlier age.

paras: About half the people on earth belong to a religion that calls Abraham its father: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are often called the 'Abrahamic' faiths. In all three he has the same title, the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23; Qur'an 4:125). His traditional tomb, the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron, is holy to Jews and Muslims alike; the Arabic name of Hebron, al-Khalil, means 'the friend'.
But each faith claims him differently, and the differences matter for the whole journey.

rows: Avraham Avinu, 'Abraham our father', the first Jew, who made God known in the world
Being born into, or joining, the people of the covenant, and keeping it
The 'father of all those who believe' (Romans 4:11), Jew and Gentile
Isaac; and Jesus as Abraham's promised offspring (Matthew 1:1; Galatians 3:16)
Ibrahim, a prophet, the hanif who turned from idols; 'neither Jew nor Christian' (Sura 3:67)
Ismail (Ishmael), ancestor of the Arabs and of Muhammad, and Ishaq (Isaac)
Submitting to God as Abraham did; 'Muslim' means 'one who submits'

sections.key: Jews, Christians and Muslims all call Abraham father and 'friend of God', but each claims him through a different son or a different kind of family.

paras: The surprising thing about Abraham is how little Genesis praises him. It never says he was chosen because he was good, wise or devout. God simply calls him. Then, within a page, he lies, endangers his wife, and is scolded by a pagan king. He does it again in Genesis 20. His son Isaac does the same thing in Genesis 26.

This is deliberate, and it is the second clue to the journey's question. If God chose the best family, the story would be about them. Because he chooses an ordinary, flawed family and keeps his promise in spite of them, the story is about him. Genesis gives its own reason later, and it looks forward, not back: God has chosen Abraham 'that he may command his children and his household after him… to do righteousness and justice' (Genesis 18:19, which you will read in session 4).
sections.key: Genesis shows Abraham's failures straight after his call: the family is chosen by grace, not for being good.

paras: What did Abraham actually do? He left. That is the first picture of faith in the Bible: not a feeling, not a theory, but a journey on the strength of a promise. Hebrews calls it going out 'not knowing where he went'.

Ancient people usually belonged to a place and its gods. Abraham's God is not tied to a place: he speaks in Haran, appears at Shechem, rescues in Egypt. This is part of what made Abraham's faith new. The God who calls him is the God of the whole earth, who goes with his people wherever they go.
sections.key: Abraham's faith is first of all action: leaving on the strength of a promise, following a God not tied to any one place.

refs: Genesis 11:27–12:20; Genesis 20; 26:6–11; Joshua 24:2–3; Hebrews 11:8–16; Acts 7:2–4.

Archaeology: W. F. Albright, The Archaeology of Palestine (1949); Thomas L. Thompson, The Historicity of the Patriarchal Narratives (1974); John Van Seters, Abraham in History and Tradition (1975); Kenneth Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003), chapter 7.
Camels: Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, 'The Introduction of Domestic Camels to the Southern Levant', Tel Aviv 40 (2013): 277–285.
Ur and Haran as centres of the moon god Sin: Leonard Woolley, Ur of the Chaldees (1929); Ur was excavated 1922–34.
The idols story: Genesis Rabbah 38:13; Louis Ginzberg, The Legends of the Jews I (1909); Qur'an 21:51–71, 6:74–83, 3:67, 4:125.
Friend of God: Isaiah 41:8; 2 Chronicles 20:7; James 2:23; Qur'an 4:125.

debate.question: How much history is in the Abraham stories?

positions.name: Substantially historical
positions.who: Kenneth Kitchen; many conservative scholars
positions.view: Abraham was a real man of the early second millennium BC, and the stories preserve reliable memories of his life, with some details updated by later scribes.
positions.evidence: Names, customs and ways of life that fit the Middle Bronze Age; the unflattering honesty of the stories, which no one would invent about a national founder.

positions.name: Memories retold
positions.who: Many mainstream scholars
positions.view: There may be real ancestral memories behind the stories, but they were shaped and written down centuries later to speak to Israel's own time, so we cannot recover the history behind them.
positions.evidence: Anachronisms such as camels and the Chaldeans; the stories' focus on later concerns such as the land and neighbouring peoples.

positions.name: Later literature
positions.who: Thomas L. Thompson, John Van Seters
positions.view: The stories were composed in the first millennium BC, perhaps during or after the exile in Babylon, as a founding story for the people; they are not history in any useful sense.
positions.evidence: The weakness of the Bronze Age parallels; the many features that fit the first millennium better.

debate.agree: All agree that there is no direct archaeological evidence of Abraham, and that the stories reached their present form long after the time they describe.

look.why: George Catlin, an American painter who travelled among the native peoples of North America, painted this camp of skin tents between 1855 and 1869. It has nothing to do with Abraham, but it shows the way of life Hebrews describes: a people 'dwelling in tents', moving with their herds, at home in the land without owning it.
points: A camp seen from above, with tents scattered across open land.
Small figures busy among the tents.
Low hills in the background, and a glowing sky at sunrise or sunset.
Green land stretching into the distance, with a river or water on the right.

music.why: 'Precious Lord, take my hand, lead me on': Thomas A. Dorsey's gospel song is the prayer of someone walking a road they cannot see the end of, which is Abraham's road.

think.why: Abraham is the first person in the Bible to be called out alone, by name, from his family and its gods. The idea of the individual person before God starts here.

learn.why: The New Testament's summary of Abraham's faith: going out, not knowing where.

check.q: Genesis tells the story of Abraham lying in Egypt straight after God's promise. What is the best explanation of why?
options: To show from the start that God chose Abraham by grace, not because he was good, and keeps his promise in spite of him
To show that Abraham was punished for lying
To explain why Abraham's descendants later had to go down to Egypt
To show that Abraham's faith was already complete before the covenant
check.why: Abraham is not punished; Pharaoh is. The story shows God protecting his promise when Abraham fails it.

check.q: God says 'I will make your name great'. Which earlier story is this deliberately answering?
options: The creation of Adam
Cain and Abel
The flood
The tower of Babel, where people said 'let's make a name for ourselves'
check.why: What the builders tried to seize, God gives as a gift.

check.q: Why do many scholars think the camels in Genesis 12:16 tell us something about when the story was written?
options: Because camels could not have crossed the desert from Haran to Canaan
Because domestic camels are not found in Canaan's archaeology until the tenth century BC, so the detail may reflect a later age
Because Genesis elsewhere says Abraham travelled only with donkeys
Because the Hebrew word may mean donkeys, so it is a mistranslation
check.why: It may be a later storyteller's updating; it does not by itself show the story is invented.

check.q: What does Joshua 24:2 add to Genesis's account of Abraham?
options: That Abraham's family 'served other gods' beyond the Euphrates
That Abraham smashed his father's idols
That God first called Abraham while he was still in Ur
That Terah refused to leave Ur
check.why: So the call is out of a world of many gods, which is the gap the idol stories fill.

check.q: A Jew, a Christian and a Muslim all call Abraham 'father'. Which statement is accurate?
options: They agree that his heir was Isaac
Muslims, like Jews, claim him chiefly through Isaac
Christians claim him through faith, Jews through the covenant people descended from Isaac and Jacob, and Muslims chiefly through Ishmael and his submission to God
Only Christians call him 'friend of God'
check.why: All three call him 'friend of God'; they differ over the line and the meaning of being his child.

check.q: What is the most accurate summary of the archaeological evidence for Abraham?
options: There is no direct evidence either way; scholars debate how well the stories fit the early second millennium BC
Inscriptions from Ur name him
Tablets from Mari mention Abraham by name
Archaeology has disproved his existence
check.why: Nothing proves or disproves him; the debate is about how well the stories fit their setting.

tutorial.question: Why does the Bible's story turn, at Genesis 12, from the whole world to one man?
tutorial.approach: Start with the problem left at the end of Genesis 1–11 (Babel). Then read the promise of 12:1–3 closely: what is promised, and for whom. Use the story of the lie in Egypt to say what kind of man Abraham is, and what that shows about why he was chosen. Finish with what Jews, Christians and Muslims each make of him.
strong: Connects Genesis 12 with Babel: the scattered nations and the 'name'.
Notices that the blessing is for 'all the families of the earth'.
Uses the lie in Egypt to show that Abraham was chosen by grace, not merit.
Explains what Abraham left behind, including his family's gods (Joshua 24:2).
Is honest about the historical evidence: no proof either way.
Distinguishes how Judaism, Christianity and Islam claim Abraham.

reading.author: Bruce Feiler
reading.title: Abraham: A Journey to the Heart of Three Faiths
reading.why: A journalist's lively journey through Abraham's lands and the three faiths.

reading.author: Jon D. Levenson
reading.title: Inheriting Abraham
reading.why: A leading Jewish scholar on how Judaism, Christianity and Islam each claim Abraham, and why the differences matter.

reading.author: John Van Seters
reading.title: Abraham in History and Tradition
reading.why: The classic argument that the stories are late; read with Kitchen's reply.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do one thing you have been putting off because you cannot see how it will turn out, a conversation, an apology, an offer of help, trusting that it is right even without knowing the outcome.
sessions.reflect: What would you find hardest to leave: your country, your family, or the way your family has always done things?
takeaways: At Genesis 12 the story narrows from all humanity to one family, so that 'all the families of the earth' may be blessed.
Abraham leaves his country, his family and its gods; straight away he fails, and God keeps his promise anyway.
There is no direct evidence of Abraham; Jews, Christians and Muslims all call him father, through different sons and in different ways.

sessions.title: When God makes a promise
sessions.line: Stars, a strange ceremony at sunset, and the sentence that divided the Reformation.
sessions.plain: Years pass and Abram still has no child. God tells him to look at the stars: that is how many descendants he will have. Abram believes him, and Genesis says God 'credited it to him for righteousness'. That one sentence became one of the most argued-over in history. This session reads the two great promises of Genesis 15 and 17, explains the ancient ceremony God performs, and shows how Jews and the different churches understand faith and good works.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed God choosing Abraham by grace and promising a blessing for every family. But a promise is only as good as the one who makes it. Now we ask what binds God to it, and what Abraham has to do.
answers: What is a covenant, and what happens in the strange ceremony of Genesis 15?
What does it mean that Abraham's faith was 'credited to him for righteousness'?
Are we saved by faith or by good works? How do Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox and Jews answer?
Why circumcision, and why does God change Abram's and Sarai's names?
sessions.finding: God binds himself to Abraham by covenant, taking the whole risk of the promise on himself, and Abraham's trust in it, not his merit, is what Genesis calls righteousness; Christians and Jews still debate what that means for faith and works.

paras: In session 1 God called Abram out of Ur and Haran and promised him a land, a great nation, and a blessing for all the families of the earth. Abram went, and almost at once failed. The finding: the family is chosen by grace, for the sake of everyone else.
background.key: Chosen by grace, for everyone's sake.

paras: Between the last session's reading and this one, Genesis tells how Abram and his nephew Lot separate (chapter 13), and how Abram rescues Lot from raiding kings and is blessed by Melchizedek, a mysterious priest-king of Salem, probably Jerusalem (chapter 14). Then comes chapter 15.

By now Abram has lived in Canaan for about ten years. He has wealth and servants, but no son, and he and Sarai are old. The promise of 'a great nation' must look like a joke. So the question of this session is the obvious one: can God's promise be trusted, and what makes it sure?

timeline.text: The call; Abram aged 75
Abram and Lot part; Melchizedek blesses Abram
The stars and the covenant ceremony
Hagar bears Ishmael; Abram aged 86 (session 3)
New names and circumcision; Abraham aged 99
Isaac is born; Abraham aged 100

background.key: Ten years in Canaan, still no son: can the promise be trusted?

paras: A covenant is a binding agreement with promises and obligations, like a treaty or a marriage. Ancient kings made covenants with weaker kings: I will protect you, you will be loyal to me. They were sealed with oaths and ceremonies, and they called down curses on whoever broke them.
In Hebrew you do not 'make' a covenant, you 'cut' one (karat berit). This session shows why.
background.key: A covenant is a binding agreement sealed with an oath; in Hebrew you 'cut' one.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the promise of the stars (15:1–6), the covenant ceremony (15:7–21) and the covenant of circumcision with new names (17:1–14).

The comparison is three short New Testament passages that argue about Genesis 15:6, 'he believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness'. Paul uses it to say we are made right with God by faith; James uses it to say faith without works is dead. Their apparent disagreement split Western Christianity in the sixteenth century. Reading them side by side is the best way to understand that argument.
background.key: The promise, the ceremony and the sign; then Paul and James on what Abraham's faith means.

before: What is Abram's complaint, and how does God answer it?
In the ceremony, who walks between the cut animals, and who doesn't?
In the comparison, do Paul and James really disagree? What does each mean by 'works'?
sessions.readWhy: The two great covenant chapters, in three parts: the stars, the ceremony, and the sign.

paras: After these things Yahweh’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.”
Abram said, “Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless, and he who will inherit my estate is Eliezer of Damascus?”
Abram said, “Behold, you have given no children to me: and, behold, one born in my house is my heir.”
Behold, Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “This man will not be your heir, but he who will come out of your own body will be your heir.”
Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So your offspring will be.”
He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.
He said to Abram, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it.”
He said, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?”
He said to him, “Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.”
He brought him all these, and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other; but he didn’t divide the birds.
The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.
When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. Now terror and great darkness fell on him.
He said to Abram, “Know for sure that your offspring will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them. They will afflict them four hundred years.
I will also judge that nation, whom they will serve. Afterward they will come out with great wealth;
but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried at a good old age.
In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”
It came to pass that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.
In that day Yahweh made a covenant with Abram, saying, “I have given this land to your offspring, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:
the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,
the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,
the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”
When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless.
I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.”
Abram fell on his face. God talked with him, saying,
“As for me, behold, my covenant is with you. You will be the father of a multitude of nations.
Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make nations of you. Kings will come out of you.
I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you.
I will give to you, and to your offspring after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.
This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised.
You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you.
He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring.
He who is born in your house, and he who is bought with your money, must be circumcised. My covenant will be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant.
The uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people. He has broken my covenant.”

parts.title: Count the stars
parts.context: Some time after Abram's rescue of Lot, God speaks to him in a vision. It is the first time in the story that Abram speaks back.

commentary.on: Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.
commentary.text: 'Don't be afraid' is the first thing God says. Abram has just fought kings and refused their spoils (Genesis 14:22–23). God says: I am your protection and your reward. Not the land, not the wealth: God himself.

commentary.on: Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless
commentary.text: Abram answers with an honest complaint. What use is a reward without a son? The heir of his estate will be his steward, Eliezer. The Bible lets its people argue with God; the next session but one is about exactly that.

commentary.on: Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
commentary.text: God answers the complaint not with an explanation but with a sight. Without city lights the desert sky shows thousands of stars. 'So your offspring will be.' One old man, no children, and a promise as big as the sky.

commentary.on: He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.
commentary.text: The most important verse in the chapter. 'Believed' (in Hebrew he'emin, from the same root as 'Amen') means to trust, to rely on, to count something firm. 'Righteousness' means being in the right with God. God counts Abram's trust as putting him right. He has done nothing yet: no law, no circumcision, no sacrifice. He simply trusts the promise. Paul, Luther and the Council of Trent will all argue over this verse.

parts.title: The ceremony at sunset
parts.context: Abram asks for a sign. What follows is an ancient ceremony for making a covenant, strange to us but clear to its first hearers. Jeremiah 34:18 describes the same ceremony: people 'cut the calf in two and passed between its parts'.

commentary.on: Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?
commentary.text: Abram believed about the son; now he asks for assurance about the land. Faith in the Bible is not the absence of questions.

commentary.on: and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other
commentary.text: This is what 'cutting' a covenant meant. The animals were cut in two and the halves laid in two rows. Each party walked between them, saying in effect: may I be cut in pieces like these animals if I break my word. It was a self-curse.

commentary.on: Now terror and great darkness fell on him.
commentary.text: Abram falls into a deep sleep and is overwhelmed. Then God tells him the future: his descendants will be foreigners and slaves for four hundred years, and then will come out with great wealth. This is the story of Exodus, foretold. The promise will be kept, but slowly and through suffering.

commentary.on: for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full
commentary.text: A striking phrase. The land will not be given yet, because its people have not yet sinned enough to lose it. God's gift to Abraham is not a licence to take others' land unjustly; it waits on God's justice towards those people too.

commentary.on: a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces
commentary.text: The climax. Fire and smoke, signs of God's presence (as in the burning bush and the pillar of fire), pass between the pieces. But Abram does not. Only God walks the path of the self-curse. God takes the whole risk of the covenant on himself: may I be torn apart if I fail. Christian readers have seen here a hint of the cross, where God bears the cost of his own promise.

commentary.on: I have given this land to your offspring, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates
commentary.text: The promise of the land, given as already done: 'I have given'. Its borders are ideal rather than surveyed. The promise of the land remains central to Judaism; Christians have usually read it as fulfilled in, or pointing beyond to, a wider inheritance (Romans 4:13 speaks of Abraham inheriting 'the world').

parts.title: New names and a sign
parts.context: Thirteen more years have passed. Ishmael, Abram's son by Sarai's servant Hagar, has been born (you will read that story in session 3). Now God appears again, renews the covenant, and gives it a sign.

commentary.on: I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless.
commentary.text: 'God Almighty' translates El Shaddai, an ancient name of God whose meaning is debated. This time the covenant includes a call on Abram: walk before me, live your whole life in my sight. Genesis 15 was God's promise; Genesis 17 adds the human answer.

commentary.on: Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham
commentary.text: Abram means 'exalted father'; Abraham sounds like 'father of a multitude' (av hamon). In the ancient world a new name meant a new identity, given by a superior. Sarai becomes Sarah (17:15); both forms mean 'princess'. The names announce the promise before there is any child to show for it.

commentary.on: an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you
commentary.text: This is the heart of every covenant in the Bible: 'I will be your God, and you will be my people'. It is about a relationship, not only land and children.

commentary.on: Every male among you shall be circumcised.
commentary.text: Circumcision, the removal of the foreskin, was practised by Egyptians and other neighbours, usually at puberty or marriage. Here it is done to every boy at eight days old, before he can choose anything, as a sign that he belongs to the covenant by God's gift. Jews have kept it ever since as the covenant of Abraham (brit milah). Christians, after a great debate (Acts 15), did not require it of non-Jewish believers, and see baptism as the sign of the new covenant (Colossians 2:11–12). Muslims practise it as a custom of Abraham.

commentary.on: he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner
commentary.text: Even slaves and foreigners in Abraham's household were included in the covenant sign. The family was never only a bloodline.

paras: What then will we say that Abraham, our forefather, has found according to the flesh?
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God.
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”
Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.
But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.
Even as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.”
Know therefore that those who are of faith are children of Abraham.
The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you all the nations will be blessed.”
So then, those who are of faith are blessed with the faithful Abraham.
For you are all children of God, through faith in Christ Jesus.
For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise.
Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?
You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected.
So the Scripture was fulfilled which says, “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness,” and he was called the friend of God.
You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith.

parts.title: Paul: credited, not earned
parts.context: Paul's Letter to the Romans, about AD 57, written to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews (Gentiles). Paul argues that Gentiles do not need to become Jews, by being circumcised and keeping the law of Moses, to belong to God's people. His proof is Abraham.

commentary.on: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God.
commentary.text: 'Justified' means declared or made right with God, the courtroom word for being acquitted. By 'works' Paul means here the deeds that the law of Moses commands. If Abraham earned God's approval, he could boast; but he didn't.

commentary.on: Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.
commentary.text: A wage is earned; a gift is not. Paul's point is that God's acceptance of Abraham was a gift ('grace'), received by trusting, not a wage. That is why it is open to anyone.

commentary.on: believes in him who justifies the ungodly
commentary.text: A startling phrase: God puts right 'the ungodly'. Paul's opponents would have said God justifies the godly. Paul says Abraham was an idol-worshipper's son when God called him.

parts.title: Paul: Abraham's children
parts.context: Paul's Letter to the Galatians, written a few years earlier to churches in what is now Turkey. Teachers had told the Gentile Christians there that they must be circumcised. Paul is furious.

commentary.on: Know therefore that those who are of faith are children of Abraham.
commentary.text: Here is Paul's whole argument in a sentence. Abraham's true family is not defined by blood or by circumcision but by sharing his trust in God. That is how 'all the families of the earth' can be blessed through him.

commentary.on: preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you all the nations will be blessed.”
commentary.text: Paul quotes Genesis 12:3 and calls it the gospel, the 'good news', announced in advance. For him, the promise to Abraham was always meant to reach the Gentiles.

commentary.on: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female
commentary.text: One of the most influential sentences in history. In Abraham's family, the deepest divisions of the ancient world, race, status and sex, no longer decide who belongs. Abraham's household, which included slaves and foreigners, was a first sketch of this.

parts.title: James: faith that works
parts.context: The Letter of James, traditionally by James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the church in Jerusalem, who was killed in AD 62. James writes to Christians whose faith had become talk without action: 'faith, if it has no works, is dead' (2:17).

commentary.on: Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?
commentary.text: James points to the later story of Abraham offering Isaac, which you will read in session 5. For James, Abraham's trust in Genesis 15 was proved, and completed, by what he did.

commentary.on: You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected.
commentary.text: James is not saying works instead of faith. He is saying faith and works belong together, like a body and its breath (2:26). Faith that never acts is not real faith.

commentary.on: You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith.
commentary.text: This sentence seems to contradict Paul directly, and Martin Luther thought it did: in 1522 he called James 'an epistle of straw' compared with Paul's letters. Most interpreters think the two use 'works' and 'faith' differently: Paul is attacking the idea that keeping the law earns God's acceptance; James is attacking a 'faith' that is only words.

compare.why: Genesis 15:6 became the centre of a great argument. Paul uses it to show that we are put right with God by trusting him, not by keeping the law. James, writing to Christians who said they believed but did nothing, uses the same verse to insist that real faith acts. Read all three passages, then the lecture shows how the churches have argued over them.
compare.title: Paul and James on Abraham's faith

paras: The ceremony of Genesis 15 is the key to the whole chapter. In an ancient covenant both parties would walk between the cut animals, calling down death on themselves if they broke faith. Here only God, as fire and smoke, passes through. Abram is asleep.

That means the covenant does not depend on Abram keeping his side. It depends on God. Scholars call this a 'covenant of grant' or a promissory covenant: a king's free gift to a loyal servant, guaranteed by the king's own oath. It is why the promise survives Abraham's failures, and his son's, and his grandson's. It answers the question this session started with: the promise can be trusted because God has bound himself to it.
sections.key: Only God passes between the pieces: he binds himself to the promise, so it does not depend on Abraham's success.

paras: Genesis 15:6 is short, but every word matters. Abram 'believed', or trusted, God's promise when there was no evidence of a son. God 'credited' that trust to him, a bookkeeping word: entered it on his account. As 'righteousness': as being in the right, in a right relationship with God.

Jewish interpreters have read the verse in more than one way. The great medieval commentator Rashi took it as Christians do: God counted Abram's faith as merit. Nachmanides suggested the opposite subject: Abram counted God's promise as an act of God's righteousness. Either way, Judaism has always joined faith to faithfulness: the Mishnah (about AD 200) says that Abraham kept the whole law even before it was given, citing Genesis 26:5.
sections.key: Abram trusted the promise with no evidence, and God counted that trust as putting him right with him.

sections.h: Faith and works: how the traditions answer
paras: In 1517 a German monk, Martin Luther, began the Protestant Reformation, and at its heart was this question: how is a sinner made right with God? Luther's answer, drawn from Paul's reading of Abraham, was 'by faith alone' (sola fide): God counts Christ's righteousness to the one who trusts him, as he counted Abraham's trust; good works follow as the fruit, not the root. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent, in its Decree on Justification of 1547. Trent agreed that justification is God's free gift and that faith is 'the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification'; but it taught that God's grace truly makes a person righteous within, and that this grows through faith working in love and good works.

The argument lasted four centuries. Then, in 1999, the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, agreeing in substance that we are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ, not because of any merit, and that the Holy Spirit renews the heart and calls us to good works. Methodists, Anglicans and Reformed churches later joined it. Differences of emphasis remain.

cols: How we are put right with God
rows: By God's grace, received in faith and baptism, which really makes the person righteous within
Faith working through love; good works done in grace help us grow in justification
Abraham's faith was real and living, and it showed itself in obedience (Trent, Session VI, 1547)
By grace alone, through faith alone: Christ's righteousness counted to the believer
The fruit and evidence of faith, never the ground of acceptance
Abraham was counted righteous before he had done anything (Romans 4)
Salvation is union with God (theosis), a lifelong healing of the whole person, not chiefly a legal verdict
Grace and human freedom work together (synergy); faith and works are inseparable
Abraham's faith and his obedience are one journey towards God
God's covenant with Israel is a gift; repentance and God's mercy restore the relationship
Keeping the commandments is the faithful response to the covenant, not a way to earn it
Abraham trusted and obeyed; he 'kept my commandments' (Genesis 26:5)

sections.key: Protestants say 'faith alone', Catholics 'faith working through love', the Orthodox 'faith and works together towards union with God'; since 1999 Lutherans and Catholics agree that acceptance is by grace through faith.

paras: Since the 1970s many scholars, notably E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, have argued that the Reformation read Paul too much through its own question. They point out that first-century Judaism did not teach that people earn God's favour; it taught that God graciously chose Israel, and that keeping the law was the response. Paul's real argument, they say, was about who belongs to Abraham's family: must non-Jews become Jews, by circumcision and the food laws, to be God's people? His answer was no: Abraham himself was counted righteous before he was circumcised (Romans 4:10–11).

This view, called the New Perspective on Paul, is itself debated; many Protestant scholars think it underplays the human problem of sin that Paul also addresses. But it has helped Christians read Judaism more fairly, and it puts Genesis 12:3 at the centre: the point of Abraham's family is that it should one day include all nations.
sections.key: The 'New Perspective' says Paul's main point was that Gentiles join Abraham's family by faith, without becoming Jews; it is debated.

paras: Genesis 17 adds a sign: circumcision, on the eighth day. It marks the covenant on the body of every male in the household, son or slave, native or foreigner. It comes after Abraham's faith and does not create it; it seals what God has already promised.

The three Abrahamic faiths handle the sign differently. Judaism keeps it as the covenant of Abraham, with the naming of the child. The early Church decided at the Council of Jerusalem (about AD 49, Acts 15) that Gentile believers need not be circumcised, and came to see baptism, given to infants in most churches, as the sign of belonging. Islam keeps circumcision as part of the way of Abraham, though the Qur'an does not command it.
sections.key: Circumcision seals a covenant already given; Judaism keeps it, Christianity replaced it with baptism, Islam keeps it as Abraham's custom.

refs: Genesis 15; 17; 26:5; Jeremiah 34:18–20; Romans 4; Galatians 3; James 2:14–26; Acts 15.

Covenant ritual: Gordon Wenham, Genesis 16–50 and Genesis 1–15 (1987, 1994); Moshe Weinfeld, 'The Covenant of Grant in the Old Testament and in the Ancient Near East', Journal of the American Oriental Society 90 (1970).
