debate.question: After Tolstoy, can anyone honestly pray the Psalms?

positions.name: Tolstoy in chapter VII: no
positions.who: Leo Tolstoy (as he stood in 1879); Arthur Schopenhauer
positions.view: Reason shows that life ends in nothing and so has no meaning. Prayer and enjoyment are ways of not looking. The honest options are to end life or to admit one carries on from weakness.
positions.evidence: A Confession VI–VII; the agreement of Socrates, Schopenhauer, Solomon and the Buddha as Tolstoy read them; Ecclesiastes 1:2; 4:2–3.

positions.name: The modern sceptic: there is no one to pray to
positions.who: J. L. Schellenberg; many secular thinkers
positions.view: We need not despair, as Tolstoy did: human life can have meaning we make ourselves. But the silence of God is evidence that no loving God is there. The Psalms are moving human poetry, not conversation.
positions.evidence: The argument from hiddenness (1993); the many sincere seekers who never find faith; the unanswered endings of Psalms 39 and 88.

positions.name: The psalmist: yes, in the dark
positions.who: The writers of Psalms 13, 39 and 88; Jewish and Christian tradition; e.g. Bonhoeffer, Mother Teresa
positions.view: The Psalms already know everything Tolstoy knew: life is a breath, God is silent. They pray anyway, not because they have answered the argument, but because faith is a relationship that holds on. Praying in the dark is not the denial of the problem but the way through it.
positions.evidence: Psalm 39:7, 'My hope is in you'; Psalm 88:13, 'In the morning, my prayer comes before you'; Jesus praying Psalm 22 on the cross.

debate.agree: All three agree that Tolstoy's question is real, that easy comfort is no answer, and that death and silence must be faced honestly.

look.why: Richard Wilson painted Solitude in the 1760s. It is not a scene from the Bible or from Tolstoy, and it is daylight, not night: a man lies alone at the foot of a broken monument, with a book and a cross beside him. It is here for the stance of Psalm 39: alone, facing the end, with the book still open before him.
points: A broken stone lion stands on a tall, cracked pedestal at the edge of still water; only the back half of its body and one front paw, resting on a ball, remain.
A man lies on the ground, propped on one elbow against the pedestal, a white cloth draped over his head, hiding much of his face.
He looks down at a book propped on a rock; a wooden cross rests against the rock beside him.
Under the dark trees to the left, one robed figure sits reading a book, and an old man with a long white beard and a walking stick stands.
A willow bows over the water; across it is a low arched entrance, perhaps to a grotto, and far away smoke rises from a mountain.

music.why: Henryk Górecki's Symphony of Sorrowful Songs (1976) is three slow laments, one sung from words a young woman wrote on the wall of a Gestapo cell. It does not hurry to comfort: the right sound for the objection.

think.why: The modern debate about whether God exists, including the argument from hiddenness, stated fairly on both sides.

learn.why: The cry Jesus prayed from the cross: the Bible's own words for the silence of God.

check.q: Tolstoy quotes Ecclesiastes 9:7–10 ('eat thy bread with joy') as an example of which 'way out', and why does that matter for this journey?
options: Ignorance; it shows the Preacher was ignorant
Epicureanism; it means the advice session 4 called wisdom, Tolstoy calls looking away from the truth
Weakness; it shows the Preacher had no reasons
Strength; it shows the Preacher recommended suicide
check.why: Tolstoy makes the Preacher's joy a form of distraction; the objection turns the book's answer into part of the problem.

check.q: What is Tolstoy's moral objection to the second way, enjoying what one has?
options: That the Bible forbids wine
That it makes people lazy
That it is only open to the fortunate: for every palace a thousand people build it
That pleasure is always sinful
check.why: 'Not everyone can have a thousand wives and palaces like Solomon': enjoyment as life's answer is a privilege of the few.

check.q: What 'crack' does Tolstoy find in his own reasoning at the end of chapter VII?
options: That his family needed him financially
That Schopenhauer had changed his mind
That reason, which says life is senseless, is itself the fruit of life, so its rejection of life seems self-defeating
That science had disproved God
check.why: 'Reason is life's son... yet reason rejects life itself! I felt that there was something wrong here.'

check.q: Which best states Schellenberg's argument from divine hiddenness?
options: God is hidden because people are sinful, so he must exist
A perfectly loving God would make relationship with himself possible for anyone not resisting; non-resisting unbelievers exist; so there is no such God
Hiddenness proves God is not all-powerful
God is hidden because he does not care
check.why: The argument turns on non-resistant unbelief, people who want to believe and cannot.

check.q: Psalm 39 calls every human life 'a breath' (hevel). What does the psalmist do with that conclusion?
options: He concludes there is no God
He curses his enemies
He turns to God: 'My hope is in you', and keeps praying though no answer is recorded
He decides to enjoy life while he can
check.why: The psalm concedes the premise of the objection and responds with relationship, not argument.

check.q: Which reply to the objection does this session say the Bible itself mainly gives?
options: A stance of holding on to God in prayer through silence, with hope in resurrection and the cross in the background
The claim that suffering is an illusion
A proof that God exists
A proof that life is long
check.why: The Bible concedes much of the premise (hevel, silence) and answers with trust, which the sceptic may call evasion and the believer faith.

tutorial.question: 'The Psalms already knew everything Tolstoy knew.' Do you agree?
tutorial.approach: State Tolstoy's case at full strength, including his treatment of the Preacher as an epicurean. Add the argument from divine silence. Then set Psalms 39 and 88 beside him: what do they concede, and what do they do differently? Decide whether holding on to God in silence is faith or Tolstoy's 'fourth way' of weakness. Be fair to the sceptic.
strong: States the four ways out accurately, with Tolstoy's reasons.
Explains why Tolstoy puts Ecclesiastes 9 under epicureanism, and assesses it.
Presents the argument from hiddenness fairly, with Schellenberg or the psalms' own complaints.
Reads Psalm 39 closely: hevel, 'My hope is in you', 'Don't be silent at my tears'.
Distinguishes an argument from a stance, and asks whether the stance is honest.
Notes Tolstoy's own doubt about his reasoning (reason as 'life's son').

sessions.practice: Live it this week: if a question is troubling you, write it down as a psalmist would, addressed to God, without softening it. Then say it aloud once a day, and add 'My hope is in you' only if you can mean it. If the dark is heavy, tell one person this week.
sessions.reflect: When God, or life, has been silent to you, what have you done: looked away, given up, or held on?
takeaways: Tolstoy's four ways out are the objection at full strength: if death ends everything, the Preacher's joy looks like looking away.
The silence of God is a real problem, argued by philosophers and felt by psalmists and saints.
The Bible concedes much of the premise and answers not with a proof but with a stance: speaking to God in the dark, as Psalms 39 and 88 do.

sessions.title: Love as strong as death
sessions.line: A love poem in the Bible, with no mention of God: why it is there, how Jews and Christians read it, and what it says about the body.
sessions.plain: The Song of Songs is a love poem. Two lovers, a young woman and a young man, long for each other, search for each other in the night, and praise each other's bodies. God is barely mentioned. For two thousand years Jews and Christians have read it both as a celebration of human love and as a picture of the love between God and his people. This session reads its spring song and its climax, 'love is strong as death', and asks why it is in the Bible and what it says about the body.
sessions.why: Session 5 ended in the dark: is life a breath, and is anyone listening? This session answers from a different direction. Against the Preacher's 'all is breath' and Tolstoy's 'the honey no longer tasted sweet', the Song sets one thing that is stronger than death: love.
answers: Why is a love poem in the Bible?
How did Jews and Christians read it?
Is it about sex, or about God?
Does God care about the body?
sessions.finding: The Song of Songs celebrates human love as good in itself, and the tradition read it also as the love between God and his people.

paras: Ecclesiastes said that everything under the sun is hevel, breath, and told us to enjoy 'the wife whom you love' as God's gift (9:9). Tolstoy found that even love of family could not save him from despair. Session 5 left the question open: is there anything that death does not erase?
The Song of Songs, which follows Ecclesiastes in most Bibles, answers with a poem. It is the Bible's only book entirely about the love between a man and a woman.
background.key: Ecclesiastes commended the love of a spouse as a gift; Tolstoy found it not enough. The Song claims love is stronger than death.

paras: The title, 'The Song of songs, which is Solomon's' (1:1), means 'the greatest song'. Its eight short chapters are spoken mostly by the woman, with the man answering and a chorus of 'daughters of Jerusalem'. There is no clear plot. The lovers meet in a garden and a vineyard, are parted, search for each other through the city at night, and are united. The poem is full of the countryside of Israel: gazelles, doves, vines, figs, pomegranates, spices, the mountains of Lebanon.

God's name never appears, unless it is hidden in 8:6, where 'a very flame of Yahweh' may be a Hebrew way of saying 'a mighty flame'. Nobody prays, and nothing is said about the covenant or the law. That is why ancient readers asked whether it belonged in the Bible at all.
background.key: Eight chapters, mostly in the woman's voice: lovers meeting, parted, searching and united. God is named once at most (8:6).

paras: Tradition credits Solomon, because of the title and because he 'spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five' (1 Kings 4:32). The rabbinic tradition you met in session 4 says he wrote it in his youth.

Most scholars think the Song is a collection of love poems, perhaps by several poets, edited after the exile: it uses late Hebrew forms and words borrowed from Persian (pardes, 'orchard', 4:13) and possibly Greek. Some poems may be much older. It closely resembles Egyptian love songs from about 1300 to 1100 BC, found on papyri and pottery, in which lovers also call each other 'brother' and 'sister' (compare 'my sister, my bride', 4:12) and meet in gardens.

Origen's commentary and homilies on the Song
Bernard of Clairvaux preaches 86 sermons on the Song

background.key: Credited to Solomon; most scholars see a collection edited after the exile, like Egyptian love songs of c. 1300–1100 BC.

paras: The main reading has two parts: a spring song (2:8–17), in which the young man comes leaping over the hills to call his beloved out, and the climax of the whole poem (8:6–7), 'love is strong as death'.

The comparison is from the prophet Hosea, who lived about 750 BC, two centuries or more before the Song took its final form. Hosea pictures God as a husband wooing back an unfaithful wife. We read it because it shows where the tradition of reading the Song as God's love for his people came from: the Bible itself had already used the language of marriage for God and Israel.
background.key: The spring song and 'love is strong as death'; then Hosea, whose picture of God as Israel's husband lies behind the allegorical reading.

before: In 2:8–17, what time of year is it, and what does the young man ask the woman to do?
In 8:6–7, what three things is love compared with? Why those?
In Hosea 2, what does God promise to do, and what will Israel call him?
sessions.readWhy: The spring song, and the poem's climax: love as strong as death.

paras:
The voice of my beloved!
Behold, he comes,
leaping on the mountains,
skipping on the hills.

My beloved is like a roe or a young deer.
Behold, he stands behind our wall!
He looks in at the windows.
He glances through the lattice.

My beloved spoke, and said to me,
“Rise up, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.

For behold, the winter is past.
The rain is over and gone.

The flowers appear on the earth.
The time of the singing has come,
and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.

The fig tree ripens her green figs.
The vines are in blossom.
They give out their fragrance.
Arise, my love, my beautiful one,
and come away.”

My dove in the clefts of the rock,
in the hiding places of the mountainside,
let me see your face.
let me hear your voice;
for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.

My beloved is mine, and I am his.
He browses among the lilies.

Until the day is cool, and the shadows flee away,
turn, my beloved,
and be like a roe or a young deer on the mountains of Bether.

Set me as a seal on your heart,
as a seal on your arm;
for love is strong as death.
Jealousy is as cruel as Sheol.
Its flashes are flashes of fire,
a very flame of Yahweh.

Many waters can’t quench love,
neither can floods drown it.
If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love,
he would be utterly scorned.

parts.title: Arise, my love
parts.context: The woman speaks, describing her beloved's arrival and repeating his words to her. It is the end of the rainy winter in Israel, around March, when the hills turn green.

commentary.on: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping on the mountains, skipping on the hills.
commentary.text: The poem begins with a sound and a sight, from the woman's point of view. It is she who speaks most in the Song, and she speaks of desire openly. In the literature of the ancient world, that is rare.

commentary.on: Behold, he stands behind our wall! He looks in at the windows. He glances through the lattice.
commentary.text: He is outside her house, looking in through the lattice, a carved wooden screen over a window. The lovers are close but not yet together: the Song is full of this longing at a threshold.

commentary.on: For behold, the winter is past. The rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth.
commentary.text: Spring is the season of love in poetry everywhere. Here the whole land seems to be in love: flowers, the turtledove, figs ripening, vines in blossom. It is the world of Genesis 1, 'very good', and of Eden, a garden.

commentary.on: My dove in the clefts of the rock
commentary.text: The dove hides in a cleft of the cliff; he wants to see her face and hear her voice. It is tender, not possessive: he calls her out; she is free to come.

commentary.on: Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards
commentary.text: A puzzling line, perhaps a snatch of a song. Small foxes damage vines in blossom. Readers have long taken it as a picture of the small things that spoil love, or of the dangers that threaten it when it is young.

commentary.on: My beloved is mine, and I am his.
commentary.text: The heart of the poem: belonging, both ways. There is no master here, only two people given to each other. The line is engraved on countless wedding rings, often in Hebrew: dodi li va'ani lo.

parts.title: Love is strong as death
parts.context: Near the end of the poem, the woman speaks the Song's one general statement about love. Everything else in the Song is description; this is its conclusion.

commentary.on: Set me as a seal on your heart, as a seal on your arm
commentary.text: A seal was a carved stone, worn on a cord around the neck or as a ring, used to sign documents. It was a person's identity, never parted with. She asks to be that close: on his heart and on his arm, in what he feels and what he does.

commentary.on: for love is strong as death.
commentary.text: Here, at last, is the answer to the Preacher and to Tolstoy: something as strong as death. Not stronger, yet; but its equal. Death never lets go of its own; neither does love.

commentary.on: Jealousy is as cruel as Sheol.
commentary.text: 'Jealousy' here means passionate, exclusive devotion, the word used of God's own 'jealousy' for his people. Sheol, the grave, never gives back what it takes. Love is as relentless.

commentary.on: Its flashes are flashes of fire, a very flame of Yahweh.
commentary.text: The only possible mention of God in the Song. The Hebrew shalhevetyah may mean 'a flame of Yah', or simply 'a mighty flame'. Either way, love is fire, and perhaps a spark of God himself.

commentary.on: Many waters can't quench love, neither can floods drown it.
commentary.text: In the Bible 'many waters' are the forces of chaos God conquered at creation (Psalm 93). Love survives them. Compare Psalm 88, where God's 'waves' overwhelmed the psalmist: here love is what the flood cannot drown.

commentary.on: If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.
commentary.text: And love cannot be bought. In a world where marriages were arranged with money, the Song says the real thing is beyond price.

read.ref: Song of Songs 2:8–17; Song of Songs 8:6–7

paras:
“Therefore behold, I will allure her,
and bring her into the wilderness,
and speak tenderly to her.

I will give her vineyards from there,
and the valley of Achor for a door of hope;
and she will respond there,
as in the days of her youth,
and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.

It will be in that day,” says Yahweh,
“that you will call me ‘my husband,’
and no longer call me ‘my master.’

For I will take away the names of the Baals out of her mouth,
and they will no longer be mentioned by name.

In that day I will make a covenant for them with the animals of the field,
and with the birds of the sky,
and with the creeping things of the ground.
I will break the bow, the sword, and the battle out of the land,
and will make them lie down safely.

I will betroth you to me forever.
Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion.

I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness;
and you shall know Yahweh.

and the earth will respond to the grain, and the new wine, and the oil;
and they will respond to Jezreel.

parts.title: The wilderness honeymoon
parts.context: Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel around 750 to 725 BC. His own wife, Gomer, was unfaithful, and he took her back; he saw in that a picture of Israel, which had turned to other gods, the Baals, and of God, who would not give her up. Here God speaks of winning Israel back.

commentary.on: I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.
commentary.text: God courts Israel like a lover. 'Speak tenderly' is literally 'speak to her heart'. The wilderness is where Israel's love for God began, after the exodus from Egypt: a second honeymoon.

commentary.on: that you will call me 'my husband,' and no longer call me 'my master.'
commentary.text: 'Master' is ba'al in Hebrew, the same word as the name of the Canaanite god. God does not want to be Israel's owner, but its husband. It is the same mutual belonging as the Song's 'I am his'.

commentary.on: I will betroth you to me forever.
commentary.text: Betrothal was a binding promise of marriage. Five gifts are the bride-price: righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion and faithfulness. Jews still say these words each weekday as they wind the strap of the tefillin around their fingers, like a ring.

commentary.on: and I will tell those who were not my people, 'You are my people;' and they will say, 'My God!'
commentary.text: The marriage ends in mutual naming: 'my people', 'my God'. Paul quotes this verse of God's love reaching outsiders (Romans 9:25). With Jeremiah 2:2 and Ezekiel 16, Hosea gave Jews and Christians the language in which they would later read the Song.

compare.why: Long before anyone read the Song as a poem about God, the prophets had described God's love for Israel as a marriage. Read Hosea to see where the allegorical reading came from.
compare.title: I will betroth you to me forever

paras: Read without any interpretation, the Song is a sequence of love poems of great sensuality and delicacy. The lovers describe each other's bodies from head to foot in the style called a wasf, a word Arab poets still use for such praise songs (4:1–7; 5:10–16; 7:1–9). The images can seem strange: her hair 'like a flock of goats', her neck 'like David's tower'. They describe effect, not appearance: the goats streaming down a hillside, the tower's dignity.

Three things stand out. The woman speaks first, most and most boldly. The love is mutual: neither owns the other. And the poem has no shame about the body or desire, though it more than once warns, 'don't stir up, nor awaken love, until it so desires' (2:7; 8:4): love has its time. In the Bible's first love story, Adam and Eve 'were both naked... and were not ashamed' (Genesis 2:25). The Song reads like Eden recovered.

It is also very like its neighbours. Egyptian love songs written down between about 1300 and 1100 BC, on papyri now in London and Dublin and on pottery from the workmen's village at Deir el-Medina, use the same pictures: gardens, gazelles, fragrant oils, the beloved as 'brother' and 'sister', the lover at the door. Israel did not invent love poetry. It kept it, and put it in its Bible.
sections.key: Read plainly, the Song is mutual, frank and unashamed love poetry in the woman's voice, with a warning to wait for love's time: Eden recovered.

paras: Ancient Jewish teachers argued over the Song, as they did over Ecclesiastes. The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records the debate, and Rabbi Akiva's verdict (about AD 100): all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the Holy of Holies. The Holy of Holies was the innermost room of the Temple, where God was present. Akiva also warned that whoever sings the Song in a banqueting house as a drinking song has no share in the world to come (Tosefta Sanhedrin 12:10).

For Akiva the Song was holy because it was about God and Israel. The Targum, the Aramaic paraphrase read in synagogues, turned it into a history of that love, from the exodus to the coming of the Messiah. Today many Jewish communities read the Song on the Sabbath of Passover, the feast of the exodus, when God 'allured' Israel into the wilderness, and some read it every Friday evening as the Sabbath, pictured as a bride, comes in.
sections.key: Rabbi Akiva called the Song 'the Holy of Holies'; the Targum read it as God's love for Israel; Jews read it at Passover.

paras: Christians read the Song in the same way, with the bride as the Church or the individual soul, and the bridegroom as Christ. The New Testament already calls Christ the bridegroom (Mark 2:19; John 3:29) and the Church his bride (Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 21:2). An allegory is a story in which each part stands for something else.

Origen of Alexandria (about 185–253), the greatest Bible scholar of the early church, wrote a ten-volume commentary on the Song around 240, of which part survives in Latin. He reported that Jewish teachers did not let the young read it until they were mature, and advised the same: the Song is for those who have learned to love God above all. Gregory of Nyssa in the East and, in the twelfth century, Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) followed. Bernard, abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Clairvaux, preached 86 sermons on the Song to his monks from 1135 until his death, and reached only the start of chapter 3. In his first sermon he told them that only experience teaches this song: one must love to understand it. In 1578 the Spanish friar John of the Cross, imprisoned in a cell in Toledo, wrote a poem of the soul's search for God modelled on the Song, his Spiritual Canticle.
Medieval readers also applied the Song to Mary. The 'garden locked up' of 4:12 became a picture of her purity, and painters showed her in an enclosed garden, as in this session's painting.
sections.key: Christians read the bride as the Church or soul: Origen (c. 240), Bernard's 86 sermons (1135–53), John of the Cross (1578); the 'garden locked up' became Mary's.

sections.h: The return to the literal sense
paras: A few early readers insisted on the plain meaning. Theodore of Mopsuestia (about 350–428) read the Song as a wedding song of Solomon. In the nineteenth century, scholars began to read it again as human love poetry, and the discovery and translation of the Egyptian love songs, from the 1870s onward, made the case stronger.

Today most scholars, Jewish and Christian, read the Song first as what it appears to be: poetry celebrating the love of a man and a woman. Many Christian theologians say this is itself theological. Human love, sexual love included, is good, made by God; the Bible gives it a book of its own. Pope John Paul II drew on the Song in his talks on 'the theology of the body' (1979–84), and Protestant writers have done the same.

That answers one of this session's questions. Does God care about the body? The Bible begins with God making bodies and calling them 'very good' (Genesis 1:31), and at its centre is a love poem that praises the body without embarrassment. Christianity adds the claim that God himself took a body (the subject of the last session, still to come). Contempt for the body is not biblical.
sections.key: Modern scholars read the Song first as human love poetry. Many theologians say that is the point: the body and love are good, made by God.

paras: A careful reader will notice something. The lovers are not clearly married for most of the poem. He calls her 'my bride' only in chapters 4 and 5. She wishes he were her brother so she could kiss him in public without being despised (8:1). Their meetings are secret, at night, at the window, in the fields. Some modern readers take it as a celebration of love outside any institution.

Jewish and Christian tradition has read it within marriage, and the poem gives reasons. Three times the woman warns the 'daughters of Jerusalem' not to 'stir up, nor awaken love, until it so desires' (2:7; 3:5; 8:4): love has a right time, and must not be forced. The climax asks to be set as a seal, a permanent bond. And love 'strong as death' is not a passing affair. In Jewish weddings, verses from the Song are often sung, and 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine' (6:3) is engraved on rings.
Either way, the Song does not treat desire as shameful or as merely private. It treats it as one of the strongest and most beautiful things in the world, which is exactly why it must be guarded.
sections.key: The lovers are not clearly married, but the Song warns not to awaken love too soon and ends with a lasting seal; tradition read it within marriage.

debate.question: Is the Song a love poem, an allegory, or both?

positions.name: A love poem
positions.who: Theodore of Mopsuestia; most modern scholars, e.g. Marvin Pope, Michael V. Fox, J. Cheryl Exum
positions.view: The Song is what it looks like: poems of human love, close to Egyptian love songs. Allegory was imposed later because readers were embarrassed. Its place in the Bible says that erotic love is God's good gift.
positions.evidence: No mention of God or covenant (except perhaps 8:6); the Egyptian parallels; the frank descriptions of the body; the woman's voice.

positions.name: An allegory of God's love
positions.who: Rabbi Akiva; the Targum; Origen; Bernard of Clairvaux; most Jewish and Christian readers until the 1800s
positions.view: The Song was kept in Scripture because it speaks of the love between God and his people, or Christ and the soul. Its human imagery is the best language we have for that love, as Hosea and Ephesians show.
positions.evidence: Hosea 2, Jeremiah 2:2, Ezekiel 16; Akiva's 'Holy of Holies'; the canonisation debates, which turned on its holiness; Ephesians 5:32.

positions.name: Both, one through the other
positions.who: Many theologians today, e.g. Ellen F. Davis, Robert Jenson; John Paul II
positions.view: Read first as human love, the Song also points beyond itself, because human love at its best is an image of God's. Marriage is a sign of God's covenant, so the literal sense and the spiritual sense are not rivals.
positions.evidence: Ephesians 5:31–32, which quotes Genesis 2:24 and calls it a mystery about Christ and the church; 'love is strong as death... a very flame of Yahweh' (8:6).

debate.agree: All agree that the Song is great poetry, that it honours love and the body, and that it was read for most of history as being also about God.

look.why: Cosmè Tura painted the Virgin Mary in a garden in Ferrara in the 1460s. It is not a picture of the Song's lovers. It is here because medieval readers took the Song's 'locked up garden' (4:12) as a picture of Mary, and painters set her in a garden: the allegorical reading made visible.
points: A woman, Mary, sits facing us on a stone bench with her hands together in prayer over a sleeping baby propped between her knees.
She wears a cherry-red dress under a teal-blue cloak, with a translucent white cloth over her head; both have shiny gold halos.
The baby, in a forest-green robe, rests his chin on his crossed forearms on her knee.
Behind her is a cloud of crimson swirling forms, perhaps blossoms, flanked by leafy dark green bushes bearing round green fruit; tufts of grass grow near her feet.

In the upper corners, inside gold scrolling vines, a winged angel raises two fingers on the left, and a woman in a dark purple robe, one hand on a book on a wooden desk, raises the other on the right.

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there': an old chant sung on Maundy Thursday. It says what the tradition heard in the Song, that true love and God are found together.

think.why: The Song honours the body and the beloved person. What do Christians believe about the dignity of every human being, body and soul?

learn.why: The Song's one statement about love, read at weddings and at funerals: love as strong as death.

check.q: Why did ancient readers question whether the Song belonged in the Bible?
options: It was written in Greek
It was written after Jesus
It contradicts the Ten Commandments
It barely mentions God, and says nothing of covenant, law or prayer, while speaking frankly of desire
check.why: God appears at most in 8:6; the debate in the Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) turned on whether it was holy.

check.q: Rabbi Akiva called the Song 'the Holy of Holies'. What did he mean?
options: That, read as the love of God and Israel, it was the most sacred of the Writings, like the inmost room of the Temple
That it was the oldest book
That it was too dangerous to read
That it should be read only in the Temple
check.why: The Holy of Holies was where God dwelt; Akiva read the Song as about God's love for Israel.

check.q: How does Hosea 2 help explain the allegorical reading of the Song?
options: Hosea was written after the allegorical reading began
Hosea forbade love poetry
Hosea already pictured God as Israel's husband and lover, so reading a love poem as about God followed the Bible's own language
Hosea wrote the Song
check.why: Hosea (c. 750 BC), Jeremiah 2 and Ezekiel 16 use marriage for God and Israel; the allegory grew from that.

check.q: What is the best evidence that the Song was first composed as human love poetry?
options: Its close likeness to Egyptian love songs, its frank descriptions of the body, and its silence about God
The fact that Origen said so
Bernard's sermons
Its use at Passover
check.why: The Egyptian parallels and the poem's own content point to love poetry; the religious uses came later.

check.q: In 8:7 'many waters can't quench love'. Why is this phrase significant in the Bible?
options: It refers to baptism
Water was rare in Israel
'Many waters' are the forces of chaos God mastered at creation; love survives what overwhelms everything else
It is a proverb from Egypt about rivers
check.why: Psalm 93 and other texts use 'many waters' for chaos; compare the waves that overwhelmed the speaker in Psalm 88.

check.q: Why might a theologian say the literal reading of the Song is itself theological?
options: Because a book of Scripture devoted to human love declares that love and the body are good gifts of God
Because it proves Solomon was holy
Because literal readings are always right
Because it removes God from the Bible
check.why: Genesis calls bodies 'very good'; giving love a whole book honours it, which is a claim about God's creation.

tutorial.question: Love poem, allegory, or both? How should the Song of Songs be read?
tutorial.approach: Start with the poem itself: its voices, images and frankness, and the Egyptian parallels. Then set out the allegorical tradition (Akiva, the Targum, Origen, Bernard) and its biblical roots in Hosea. Weigh the modern return to the literal sense. Decide whether the readings must compete, and use 8:6–7 as a test case.

Uses the Egyptian love songs as outside evidence.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: tell someone you love, in a sentence, one specific thing about them you are glad of, as the lovers in the Song do. If you pray, give thanks once a day this week for one person by name.
sessions.reflect: What, in your experience, is as strong as death? Have you ever seen love hold when everything else gave way?
takeaways: The Song of Songs is the Bible's love poem: mutual, frank and unashamed, spoken mostly by the woman, with God named once at most.
Jews and Christians read it also as God's love for his people, a reading rooted in Hosea's picture of God as Israel's husband.
Its place in the Bible says that human love and the body are good; 'love is strong as death' answers the Preacher's 'all is breath'.

sessions.title: Wisdom has a face, and the verdict
sessions.line: The Wisdom that was with God at creation, the Christ through whom all things hold together, and the Psalms as the Church's prayer book, and yours.
sessions.plain: Proverbs pictured Wisdom as a woman who was with God when he made the world. The first Christians said something astonishing: that this Wisdom had become a human being, Jesus of Nazareth. This session reads an early Christian hymn in Paul's letter to the Colossians and the opening of the Letter to the Hebrews beside Proverbs 8 and the Wisdom of Solomon, and shows how Jesus prayed the Psalms and the Church has prayed them ever since. Then it gives the verdict: how, according to these books, do we pray, think and live?
sessions.why: The journey has gone from Israel's prayers (sessions 1 and 2) through its wisdom (3 and 4), the strongest objection (5) and the love poem (6). It began with Psalm 1, the tree by the water. Now it asks where the road leads: in the New Testament, wisdom is no longer only a skill or a personification. It has a face.
answers: What is the verdict: how do we pray, think and live?
How do Christians read the Psalms and Proverbs as about Jesus?
Who is the Wisdom of Proverbs 8, and what is the 'Word' of John 1?
Is reading Christ into the Old Testament fair?
How can I begin to pray the Psalms?
sessions.finding: The New Testament says the Wisdom that was with God at creation became a person; the Psalms became the prayer book of the Church, and they can become yours.

paras: Here is where this journey comes out. How do we pray? The Psalms answer: honestly, about everything, aloud and together, and in the dark as well as the light. How do we think? Proverbs and Ecclesiastes answer: with skill and humility, starting from reverence for God, testing every promise against what we see, and refusing false hopes. How do we live? With joy in ordinary gifts, which are breath and therefore precious; with love, which is as strong as death; and in trust, held on to even through silence.

The Christian claim, which this session examines, is that all of this meets in one person. The Wisdom that Proverbs pictured at God's side, and that Ecclesiastes could not find under the sun, came and lived under the sun. And he prayed the Psalms.
background.key: Pray honestly, about everything, together; think with skill and humility from reverence for God; live with joy, love and trust. Christians say all of this meets in Christ.

paras: Proverbs 8 pictures Wisdom speaking: 'Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work... When he established the heavens, I was there.' You will read it in this session's comparison. Later Jewish writers developed the picture. Ben Sira, writing in Jerusalem around 180 BC, said Wisdom came to dwell in Israel and is the Torah, the law of Moses (Sirach 24). The Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek, probably in Alexandria in the first century BC, called her the breath of God's power and a reflection of his eternal light.

The Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria (about 20 BC to AD 50) spoke of God's Logos, 'Word' or 'Reason', as his firstborn and image, through whom he made the world. If you have taken 'In the beginning', you have read how John's Gospel opens: 'In the beginning was the Word'. The first Christians took up all this language and applied it to Jesus.

timeline.text: Proverbs 1–9, with Wisdom at God's side, probably written
Ben Sira identifies Wisdom with the Torah (Sirach 24)
The Wisdom of Solomon, in Greek, probably in Alexandria
Philo of Alexandria on the Logos
Jesus prays Psalms 22 and 31 on the cross
Paul calls Christ 'the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24)
Colossians and Hebrews written
The Council of Nicaea, after the dispute over Proverbs 8:22

background.key: Proverbs 8, Sirach 24 and the Wisdom of Solomon developed Wisdom at God's side; Philo spoke of the Logos. The first Christians applied it all to Jesus.

paras: Colossians is a letter in Paul's name to the church in Colossae, a small town in what is now western Turkey. If Paul wrote it, he did so from prison around AD 60. Many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name after his death, perhaps AD 70 to 90; others defend Paul's authorship. Either way, the passage we read (1:15–20) is widely thought to be an early Christian hymn, older than the letter, which it quotes.

Hebrews does not name its author. Early Christians guessed Paul, Barnabas, Luke or Apollos; the theologian Origen said only God knows. It was written before about AD 96, when a letter by Clement of Rome echoes it. Its opening, which we also read, uses language very close to the Wisdom of Solomon.
background.key: Colossians, in Paul's name, c. 60 or later, quotes an early hymn; Hebrews, author unknown, before c. 95. Both speak of Christ in the language of Wisdom.

paras: The main reading has two parts: the hymn of Colossians 1:15–20, which says of Christ what Proverbs said of Wisdom, and the opening of Hebrews (1:1–4), which says the Son is 'the radiance of his glory'.

The comparison has two parts: Proverbs 8:22–31, Wisdom at God's side at creation, and the Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–30, where Wisdom is a 'reflection of everlasting light'. Read them side by side with the New Testament to judge for yourself: is this continuity or reinterpretation?
background.key: Colossians 1 and Hebrews 1 on Christ; Proverbs 8 and Wisdom 7 on Wisdom. Continuity or reinterpretation?

before: List what Colossians 1:15–20 says about Christ. Which of these things did Proverbs 8 say about Wisdom?
Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son 'the radiance of his glory'. Where in the comparison do you find a similar phrase?
What does Proverbs 8 say Wisdom was doing while God made the world?
sessions.readWhy: The first Christians say of Christ what Proverbs said of Wisdom.

paras: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him.
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.
He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.
For all the fullness was pleased to dwell in him,
and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross.
God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways,
has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.

His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, who, when he had by himself purified us of our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high,
having become as much better than the angels as the more excellent name he has inherited is better than theirs.

parts.title: The image of the invisible God
parts.context: Early in the letter, after a prayer for the readers. The rhythm and the repeated 'all things' suggest a hymn the church already sang. It has two halves: Christ and creation (15–17), and Christ and the new creation (18–20).

commentary.on: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.
commentary.text: Genesis says humans are made in God's image. Here Christ is the image: the visible likeness of a God no one can see. 'Firstborn' means first in rank and heir, not the first thing made: the next verse says all things were made through him. The Wisdom of Solomon called Wisdom 'an image of his goodness', and Philo called the Logos God's firstborn.

commentary.on: For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things
commentary.text: In Proverbs 8, Wisdom was 'the craftsman by his side' when God made the world. Here the hymn says creation happened 'by him', 'through him' and 'for him'. A Jewish idea about God's wisdom has become a claim about a man crucified only a generation before.

commentary.on: He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.
commentary.text: This is this session's memory piece. 'Held together' is a Greek word Stoic philosophers used for the reason that holds the universe in one. The hymn claims that what holds the cosmos together is not an impersonal law but a person.

commentary.on: the firstborn from the dead
commentary.text: The second half turns from creation to resurrection. Christ is 'firstborn' again, this time from the dead: the first of a new creation. This is the answer the Christian faith gives to the Preacher's 'one event to the righteous and to the wicked': death is not the end of the story.

commentary.on: having made peace through the blood of his cross.
commentary.text: The hymn ends where no Jewish wisdom book would: at a cross. The Wisdom through whom all things were made reconciles all things by dying. Paul calls this 'Christ crucified... the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:23–24): wisdom that looks like folly.

parts.title: The radiance of his glory
parts.context: The first sentence of the Letter to the Hebrews, one long sentence in Greek. It was written to Jewish Christians, and it is full of the language of the Psalms and the wisdom books.

commentary.on: God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways
commentary.text: The writer honours the past: God spoke through the prophets, in many ways. Then something new: he has spoken 'by his Son'. Not a new message from outside the tradition, but its fulfilment.

commentary.on: through whom also he made the worlds.
commentary.text: The same claim as Colossians, and as Proverbs 8 about Wisdom: the Son was God's agent in creation.

commentary.on: His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance
commentary.text: 'Radiance' translates the rare Greek word apaugasma, the brightness that streams from a light. It appears only here in the New Testament, and in the Greek Old Testament only in the Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, which you will read in the comparison. The writer is quoting Wisdom's portrait and saying: this is the Son.

commentary.on: sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high
commentary.text: From Psalm 110:1, 'Sit at my right hand', the psalm the New Testament quotes more than any other. The Psalms, as well as the wisdom books, have become a way of speaking about Jesus.

paras:
“Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work,
before his deeds of old.

I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning,
before the earth existed.

When there were no depths, I was born,
when there were no springs abounding with water.

Before the mountains were settled in place,
before the hills, I was born;

while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields,
nor the beginning of the dust of the world.

When he established the heavens, I was there.
When he set a circle on the surface of the deep,

when he established the clouds above,
when the springs of the deep became strong,

when he gave to the sea its boundary,
that the waters should not violate his commandment,
when he marked out the foundations of the earth,

then I was the craftsman by his side.
I was a delight day by day,
always rejoicing before him,

rejoicing in his whole world.
My delight was with the sons of men.

For there is in her a spirit that is quick to understand, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, freely moving, clear in utterance, unpolluted, distinct, invulnerable, loving what is good, keen, unhindered, beneficent, loving toward man, steadfast, sure, free from care, all-powerful, all-surveying,

and penetrating through all spirits that are quick to understand, pure, most subtle. For wisdom is more mobile than any motion. Yes, she pervades and penetrates all things by reason of her purity. For she is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty. Therefore nothing defiled can find entrance into her.

For she is a reflection of everlasting light, an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. Although she is one, she has power to do all things. Remaining in herself, she renews all things.

From generation to generation passing into holy souls, she makes friends of God and prophets. For God loves nothing as much as one who dwells with wisdom. For she is fairer than the sun, and above all the constellations of the stars. She is better than light. For daylight yields to night, but evil does not prevail against wisdom.

parts.title: I was there
parts.context: Wisdom, the woman who called in the street in Proverbs 1, now speaks of her origins. It is the high point of Proverbs 1–9, probably written after the exile.

commentary.on: Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old.
commentary.text: 'Possessed' translates qanah, which can mean 'acquire', 'possess' or 'create'. The Greek translation said 'created me'. In the fourth century this one word became the centre of the greatest dispute in Christian history, as the lecture explains.

commentary.on: When he established the heavens, I was there.
commentary.text: Wisdom was present at creation, before mountains, springs and fields. The order of the world that Proverbs teaches us to live by was there from the start: the world was made wisely.

commentary.on: then I was the craftsman by his side.
commentary.text: The Hebrew amon can mean 'craftsman' or 'darling child'. Either way Wisdom is beside God in his work. A Jewish teaching (Genesis Rabbah 1:1) read the word as the Torah, God's blueprint: 'God looked into the Torah and created the world'.

commentary.on: I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him, rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.
commentary.text: Creation is joy. Wisdom plays and delights before God, and her delight is in human beings. Christians read the last line as a hint of the incarnation: the Wisdom of God wants to be with us.

parts.author: Wisdom of Solomon
parts.title: A reflection of everlasting light
parts.context: The Wisdom of Solomon was written in Greek, probably by a Jew in Alexandria in the first century BC, in the voice of Solomon. It is in the Bible of Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Protestants place it among the Apocrypha, and it is not in the Jewish Bible. This is the World English Bible translation, from verse 22b; the WEB's two footnote markers in this chapter have been removed.
parts.plain: The writer, speaking as Solomon, praises Wisdom. She is holy, clear, loving and powerful, and she moves through everything. She is like God's breath and his glory streaming out, a mirror of what God does, an image of his goodness. She renews all things and enters holy people, making them friends of God. Night overcomes daylight, but evil never overcomes her.

commentary.on: For she is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty.
commentary.text: Wisdom is more than a quality here: she flows out from God like breath or light. The book draws on the Greek philosophy of Alexandria, where it was written, to describe the God of Israel.

commentary.on: For she is a reflection of everlasting light, an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness.
commentary.text: 'Reflection' is apaugasma, the word Hebrews 1:3 uses of the Son. 'Image' is the word Colossians 1:15 uses of Christ. The New Testament writers knew this passage.

commentary.on: From generation to generation passing into holy souls, she makes friends of God and prophets.
commentary.text: Wisdom is not far off: she enters people and makes them God's friends. Jesus calls his disciples 'friends' (John 15:15).

commentary.on: For daylight yields to night, but evil does not prevail against wisdom.
commentary.text: Compare John's prologue, where the darkness has not overcome the light. It is also a reply to session 5: the silence and darkness are real, but they are not the strongest thing.

compare.author: Wisdom of Solomon
compare.why: Read what Israel's wisdom books said of Wisdom, then decide whether the New Testament continues or reinterprets it.
compare.title: Wisdom at God's side

paras: The first Christians were Jews. When they tried to say who Jesus was, they had the Scriptures to draw on, and one of the richest resources was Wisdom. Jesus himself was remembered as speaking like Wisdom: 'wisdom is justified by her children' (Matthew 11:19), 'one greater than Solomon is here' (Luke 11:31). Paul calls Christ 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24).

Line up the claims. Wisdom was with God before creation; so is the Son. Wisdom was the craftsman of creation; all things were made through him. Wisdom is the image of God's goodness and the radiance of his light; Christ is the image of the invisible God and the radiance of his glory. Wisdom came to dwell among God's people (Sirach 24); John says the Word 'lived among us'. The pattern is too close to be chance.

What is new is a name, a date and a cross. Wisdom in Proverbs is a poetic figure. Jesus was a man from Nazareth who died under Pontius Pilate. The Christian claim is that the order and wisdom built into the universe are not an idea but someone, and that he can be known.
sections.key: The New Testament applies Wisdom's titles to Jesus: before creation, its craftsman, God's image and radiance, dwelling among us. What is new is a person and a cross.

paras: In the 300s, Proverbs 8 caused the greatest quarrel in early Christianity. Arius, a priest of Alexandria (about 256–336), read the Greek of 8:22, 'The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways', as words of the Son. So, he argued, the Son was created: the first and greatest of creatures, but not God in the same sense as the Father. 'There was when he was not' became the slogan of his followers.

Athanasius of Alexandria (about 296–373) replied in his Orations against the Arians that the verse, read as words of Christ, refers to his becoming human, when he was 'created' in a body for our sake; Wisdom herself is eternal. The Council of Nicaea in 325 declared the Son 'of one substance with the Father', 'begotten, not made', words still said in the Nicene Creed.

The episode shows both how seriously Christians took the link between Wisdom and Christ, and how risky it is to build doctrine on a single word of poetry. Most Christians today read Proverbs 8 first as poetry about God's wisdom, and see Christ in it in the light of the New Testament.
sections.key: Arius read Proverbs 8:22 ('created me') as proof the Son was a creature; Athanasius applied it to the incarnation; Nicaea (325) said 'begotten, not made'.

paras: The Gospels show Jesus as a man who knew the Psalms by heart and prayed them. He quoted them in argument (Psalm 110 in Mark 12:36). He sang the Hallel at the Last Supper (Mark 14:26). On the cross he prayed the opening of a lament, Psalm 22: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34). In Luke's Gospel his last words are from Psalm 31:5: 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!' (Luke 23:46). After the resurrection, Luke says, he taught that 'all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled' (Luke 24:44).

So Christians read the Psalms in two directions. They pray them as Jesus did, as their own prayers to God. And they hear in them prayers about Christ: the king of Psalm 2, the sufferer of Psalm 22, the priest-king of Psalm 110. Augustine put it simply: in the Psalms Christ prays for us, prays in us, and is prayed to by us.

Bonhoeffer, writing in 1940, drew the consequence. If Jesus prayed the Psalms, then Christians do not have to make up their own prayers from nothing, or wait to feel like praying. They can pray with him, in words he used, even the laments and the dark ones.
sections.key: Jesus quoted Psalm 110, sang the Hallel, prayed Psalms 22 and 31 on the cross. Christians pray the Psalms with him and hear them as about him.

sections.h: The Psalter today, across the traditions
paras: The Psalms are still the prayer book of Jews and of every Christian tradition, used in different ways. Here they are side by side.

rows: Daily prayer includes Psalms 145–150; the Hallel (113–118) at festivals; a psalm for each day of the week; many recite the whole book in a week or a month
The whole Psalter read every week in twenty sections (kathismata); Psalms 103 (104) and 1 open the all-night vigil
Hebrew in modern Bibles; Greek and Latin in older ones
The Liturgy of the Hours, morning, evening and night prayer, covers the Psalter in four weeks; a psalm is sung at every Mass
The Book of Common Prayer reads the whole Psalter every month at morning and evening prayer, in Coverdale's translation; sung at choral evensong
Apocrypha: read for example of life, not doctrine (Article VI)
Metrical psalms sung by the congregation, from Geneva (1562) and Scotland (1650); some churches sing only psalms
table.note: From Psalm 10 to 147 the Greek and Latin numbers usually run one behind the Hebrew.

sections.key: Jews and every Christian tradition pray the Psalms: Orthodox weekly, Catholics in four weeks, Anglicans monthly, Reformed churches in metre. The Wisdom of Solomon is Scripture for Catholics and Orthodox only.

sections.h: How to begin praying a psalm a day
paras: The Church's experience of three thousand years can be put simply. Begin small: one psalm a day, or part of a long one. Read it aloud, as Psalm 1's 'meditate' means, slowly. Pray the psalm that fits your day if you can, and the one set for the day if you can't: the set psalm will often say what you didn't know you needed to say. Don't skip the dark ones; they are for the day you need them. Don't worry about the lines that don't fit you: someone in the world is praying them today, and you can pray them for that person.

Some simple ways in: the Psalms set in the Book of Common Prayer for each day of the month (Psalm 1 on the morning of the first); the Psalms of the daily office in a prayer app; or straight through, from Psalm 1 to 150, in five months. Colossians, in the verses after this session's hymn, tells the church to teach one another 'with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs' (3:16). James puts it more briefly: 'Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises' (5:13). That is the whole Psalter in two sentences.
sections.key: One psalm a day, aloud and slowly; the dark ones too; the lines that don't fit you are for someone else. 'Is any suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing.'

paras: Christians are not the only heirs of Proverbs 8. For Jewish tradition the Wisdom who was with God at creation is the Torah, God's teaching. Ben Sira says so directly around 180 BC: having let Wisdom praise herself, he adds that all this is the book of God's covenant, the law that Moses commanded (Sirach 24:23). The great collection of rabbinic commentary on Genesis, Genesis Rabbah, opens with Proverbs 8:30: as an architect builds a palace from a plan, so God looked into the Torah and created the world.

This reading is alive in every synagogue. When the Torah scroll is returned to the ark after it has been read, the congregation sings words from Proverbs 3 about Wisdom, applied to the Torah: 'She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her' (3:18; in Hebrew 'she' and 'it' are one word). The tree of Psalm 1 and the tree of life in Eden meet in a scroll carried in procession.

So Jews and Christians both say that the wisdom by which the world was made has been given to God's people. Jews say it is a book; Christians, a person. The resemblance is real, and so is the difference, and honest readers on both sides have learned from each other's reading.
sections.key: Jewish tradition reads Wisdom as the Torah (Sirach 24:23; Genesis Rabbah 1:1) and sings Proverbs 3:18 over the scroll. Jews say a book, Christians a person.

refs: Colossians 1:15–20; 3:16; Hebrews 1:1–4; Proverbs 8:22–31; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–30; Sirach 24; John 1:1–14; 15:15; Matthew 11:19; Luke 11:31; 23:46; 24:44; Mark 12:36; 14:26; 15:34; 1 Corinthians 1:23–24; James 5:13; Psalms 2, 22, 31:5, 110.
Philo of Alexandria, On the Confusion of Tongues 146–147 (the Logos as firstborn and image); Genesis Rabbah 1:1 (the Torah as God's blueprint).
Athanasius, Orations against the Arians II.18–82 (on Proverbs 8:22); the Creed of Nicaea (325) and of Constantinople (381).

Augustine, Expositions of the Psalms, on Psalm 86 (85), 1 (Christ prays for us as our priest, in us as our head, and is prayed to by us as our God); Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible (1940).
James D. G. Dunn, Christology in the Making (1980); Richard Bauckham, Jesus and the God of Israel (2008); The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Articles of Religion, VI.

debate.question: Is reading Christ into the Old Testament fair?

positions.name: No: it takes Israel's books away from Israel
positions.who: Many Jewish scholars and teachers, e.g. Jon Levenson; some historical critics
positions.view: Proverbs 8 is a poem about God's wisdom, and Jewish tradition rightly saw it fulfilled in the Torah (Sirach 24:23; Genesis Rabbah 1:1). The Psalms are Israel's prayers. Reading them as secretly about Jesus ignores what they meant to the people who wrote and prayed them, and has too often been used to say the Jews misread their own Scriptures.
positions.evidence: The plain sense of Proverbs 8 and the Psalms; Sirach 24; the history of Christian anti-Jewish polemic.

positions.name: Yes: they point to him
positions.who: The New Testament writers; the church fathers; much traditional Christian reading, e.g. Augustine
positions.view: Jesus himself said the Psalms spoke of him (Luke 24:44). The Wisdom of the Old Testament was always more than a figure of speech, and the New Testament shows who she was. Reading backwards is how you read any story once you know its ending.
positions.evidence: Luke 24:44; Hebrews 1:3 and Wisdom 7:26; Colossians 1:15–20; the early Christian use of Psalms 2, 22 and 110.

positions.name: Both readings, honestly held
positions.who: Many Christian scholars today, e.g. Richard Bauckham, Richard Hays, and much Jewish–Christian dialogue
positions.view: The texts have their own meaning in Israel, which Christians must respect and learn from Jews. Christians also read them in the light of Jesus, as a second reading, not a replacement. The first Christians did not invent Wisdom Christology from nothing: they found in Jewish thought a ready category for what they believed they had met.
positions.evidence: The Pontifical Biblical Commission, The Jewish People and their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible (2001), which calls the Jewish reading 'possible'; the shared use of Proverbs 8 by Jews (Torah) and Christians (Christ).

debate.agree: All agree that Proverbs 8 and the Psalms had a meaning in Israel before Jesus, and that the New Testament writers drew on them deliberately.

look.why: The Master of Saint Francis painted Saint John the Evangelist around 1272. John's Gospel opens with the Word that was with God and became flesh, the same claim this session reads in Colossians and Hebrews. He holds a scroll: the written word that points to the living Word.
points: A man with white hair and a white beard stands under an arch against a glimmering gold background.
He wears a slate-blue robe over a burgundy-red, ankle-length tunic, and sandals with thin brown straps, on a pine-green floor.
His body faces us but he turns his head to our right, with dark eyes under curving brows.
In one hand he holds a parchment-coloured scroll in front of his chest; his other arm is wrapped in his robe.
A halo is punched and incised into the gold behind his head, decorated with S-shaped spirals and a ring of small flowers.
Writing along the arch reads 'SANCTVS I HANES SSUM'; the arch rests on maroon-red columns with cobalt-blue leafy capitals.

music.why: Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil (1915) sets the Orthodox service of psalms sung through the night, including Psalm 104 and 'Blessed is the man', Psalm 1: the Psalter as the Church still prays it, bringing this journey back to where it began.

think.why: How the Greek idea of the Logos and the Jewish idea of Wisdom met in the Christian claim about Jesus.

learn.why: Perhaps the oldest Christian hymn about creation: what Proverbs said of Wisdom, said of Christ. 'In him all things are held together.'

check.q: Colossians 1:15 calls Christ 'the firstborn of all creation'. Why do most readers think this does not mean he was the first thing created?
options: Because the word is not in the Greek
Because 'firstborn' always means 'youngest'
Because the next verse says all things were created by and through him, so 'firstborn' means first in rank and heir
Because the hymn is a later addition to the letter
check.why: If all things were created through him, he is not one of them; 'firstborn' carries the sense of pre-eminence, as in Psalm 89:27.

check.q: Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son 'the radiance of his glory'. What is the significance of the Greek word used?
options: It is a word from Hebrew poetry
It means 'servant'
It is the word for the sun
It is apaugasma, found in the Greek Old Testament only in Wisdom 7:26, so the writer is applying Wisdom's portrait to the Son
check.why: The rare word links Hebrews directly to the Wisdom of Solomon's description of Wisdom.

check.q: Why did Proverbs 8:22 become central to the Arian controversy?
options: Because it mentions Jesus by name
Because Athanasius wrote it
Because the Greek said Wisdom was 'created', and Arius, reading it as words of the Son, argued the Son was a creature
Because it was missing from some Bibles
check.why: Arius built on the Greek 'created me'; Athanasius applied it to the incarnation; Nicaea answered 'begotten, not made'.

check.q: How did Ben Sira (Sirach 24) and later Jewish tradition interpret the figure of Wisdom?
options: As the Torah, God's law, dwelling in Israel
As the Messiah
As a goddess
As Solomon himself
check.why: Sirach 24:23 identifies Wisdom with the law of Moses; Genesis Rabbah reads the 'craftsman' of Proverbs 8:30 as the Torah, God's blueprint.

check.q: Which of these is the strongest evidence that the first Christians drew deliberately on Jewish wisdom traditions?
options: That Jesus was a carpenter
That the Church later used the Psalms
The close match between what Colossians and Hebrews say of Christ and what Proverbs 8 and Wisdom 7 say of Wisdom, down to rare words
That Philo became a Christian
check.why: The parallels in role (creation), titles (image, radiance) and vocabulary (apaugasma) are too close for chance. Philo never became a Christian.

check.q: A friend says, 'I can't pray the Psalms: half of them don't match how I feel.' Which reply best reflects this journey?
options: Rewrite them to fit your mood
Only pray the happy ones
Then the Psalms aren't for you
Pray them anyway: the dark ones are for the day you need them, and the lines that don't fit you can be prayed for someone who needs them today, as Jesus prayed them
check.why: The Psalms hold every mood (session 1); the Church prays them in common, with Christ, not only as personal expression.

tutorial.question: Wisdom in Proverbs and in the New Testament: continuity or reinterpretation?
tutorial.approach: Set out what Proverbs 8 and the Wisdom of Solomon say about Wisdom, and what Colossians 1 and Hebrews 1 say about Christ, line by line. Explain the Jewish reading of Wisdom as Torah. Consider the Arian dispute over 8:22 as a warning. Then decide: did the first Christians continue Israel's thought, reinterpret it, or both? Be fair to the Jewish reading.
strong: Compares specific phrases: craftsman and 'through him'; image; apaugasma in Wisdom 7:26 and Hebrews 1:3.
Explains that Wisdom in Proverbs is a personification, and what is new in the claim about Jesus.
Gives the Jewish reading (Sirach 24, Genesis Rabbah 1:1) fairly.
Uses the Arian controversy to show the stakes and the risks.
Mentions how Jesus prayed the Psalms (Psalms 22 and 31, Luke 24:44).
Reaches a clear, argued conclusion.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: How do we pray, think and live in God's world? In about 300 words, answer from the Psalms and the wisdom books, using at least three of the texts in this journey, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Pray the Psalms for a month: the psalms the Book of Common Prayer appoints for each day, or five a day so as to finish in thirty days. Read one chapter of Proverbs each day as well, by the date. At the end, read Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs each in one sitting.
synthesis: This journey asked how we pray, think and live in God's world, and followed the Bible's songbook and notebook from Psalm 1 to the Christian claim that Wisdom has a face. Here are the short answers to its questions.

What are the Psalms, and who wrote them? A hundred and fifty songs and prayers in five books, gathered over five centuries or more and shaped from Psalm 1's happy obedience to Psalm 150's praise. The headings name David seventy-three times, and Temple singers such as Asaph and the sons of Korah; most scholars think the headings were added later, and that 'of David' may mean by, for or about him. Hebrew poetry does not rhyme sounds but thoughts: the second line echoes or sharpens the first, which is why the Psalms translate so well. They were sung by Levites in the Temple, in the synagogue, by monks every week and by whole congregations in metre.

Is it all right to be angry with God? Yes: the Bible's songbook is full of complaint. About a third of the psalms are laments, which usually move from complaint to plea to trust. Psalm 88 never turns, and ends in darkness, and Israel kept it. Abraham, Moses, Jeremiah and Jesus on the cross all argued with God. What makes a lament faith is that it is said to God; the opposite of lament is silence. The cursing psalms are rage at injustice handed over to God, read by Augustine against sin, by Lewis as wicked but honest, and by Bonhoeffer as vengeance given up to God.

What is wisdom, and is Proverbs just common sense? Biblical wisdom is a practical skill, like a craftsman's, applied to living well and justly. Much of it Israel shared with its neighbours: Proverbs 22:17–24:22 closely follows the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. But Proverbs sets it all under 'the fear of the Lord', reverence rather than terror, and trains judgement rather than giving rules. Its promises that goodness pays are tendencies, not guarantees, as Psalm 73 shows.

Is Ecclesiastes saying life is meaningless? It says all is hevel, breath: nothing under the sun lasts or can bear the weight of a life's meaning. The good die like the wicked, and everyone is forgotten. Yet seven times the Preacher tells us to eat our bread with joy, for 'God has already accepted your works', and the book ends with the fear of God. It is a cure for false hopes, not a counsel of despair. Tolstoy, at fifty, rich and famous, hid a rope from himself and quoted Ecclesiastes, but heard its question and not its answer.

What if life really is meaningless, and prayer is talking to an empty sky? That is the strongest objection, and the Bible states it itself: Psalm 39 calls every life a breath and asks God to look away; Psalm 88 ends in darkness. Tolstoy's four ways out, ignorance, pleasure, suicide and carrying on from weakness, and the modern argument from divine hiddenness are not easily answered. The Bible does not answer them with a proof. It offers a stance: holding on to God in the dark, with hope in resurrection and, for Christians, a God who entered the silence on the cross.

Why is a love poem in the Bible? Because human love and the body are good, made by God. The Song of Songs is frank, mutual and unashamed, mostly in the woman's voice, and close to Egyptian love songs. Jews and Christians also read it as the love between God and his people, a reading rooted in Hosea's picture of God as Israel's husband: Akiva called it the Holy of Holies, Origen and Bernard the song of Christ and the soul. Its climax answers the Preacher: love is strong as death.

How do Christians read the Psalms and Proverbs as about Jesus? Proverbs 8 pictured Wisdom at God's side at creation; the Wisdom of Solomon called her the reflection of God's eternal light. The New Testament says the same of Christ: the image of the invisible God, through whom all things were made and in whom they hold together, the radiance of God's glory. Jews read Wisdom as the Torah; Christians as a person. And Jesus prayed the Psalms, Psalm 22 and Psalm 31 on the cross, so Christians pray them with him and hear them as about him.

Did Tolstoy really nearly kill himself, and why? He says so: in the late 1870s, at the height of his fame, he hid a cord so as not to hang himself and stopped taking his gun out shooting. The cause was not poverty, illness or loneliness, which he did not suffer, but a question he could not answer: what meaning does my life have that death will not destroy? Science answered every question but that one; the sages, as he read them, said life is an evil. He wrote A Confession to tell the story, and the rest of it tells how he found his way back. If that question ever presses on you as it pressed on him, do what the psalmists did, and say it aloud, to God and to someone near you.

So how do we pray, think and live? Pray honestly, about everything, aloud and with others, in the dark as well as the light: the Psalms give you the words. Think with skill and humility, starting from reverence for God, testing every promise against what you see, and refusing false hopes. Live with joy in ordinary gifts, because they are breath; with love, because it is as strong as death; and with trust, held on to through silence. Can you use the Psalms to pray? Every Jewish and Christian tradition says yes, and has done so for three thousand years.

title: Why the cross?
question: How can one death save?
line: Seven sessions on the oldest puzzle in Christianity: why a man's execution should be good news. One event, five pictures: the Temple, the slave market, the battlefield, the courtroom and the road, then the case against, and a verdict.
why: Christians say that 'Christ died for our sins'. Most people, inside the churches and out, could not say what that means, and many who can find it troubling: why couldn't God simply forgive, and how is it fair for an innocent man to suffer for the guilty? The New Testament does not answer with one theory. It uses at least five pictures, taken from the Temple, the slave market, the battlefield, the law court and the road, and different traditions have made different pictures the key. This journey reads the pictures in the Bible and in the great teachers who explained them, Athanasius, Anselm, Abelard and Calvin among them, hears Thomas Paine's charge that the whole idea is immoral at full strength, and ends with a verdict. It is written at the depth of a university paper in Christian doctrine, for anyone.
follows: A second-year paper in Christian doctrine on the atonement: the biblical images, the patristic, medieval and Reformation theories, and the modern moral critique.
before: the-last-week
outcomes: Explain what 'atonement' means and how the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 16 and the letter to the Hebrews shaped the first Christians' reading of the cross.
Explain what Jesus meant by 'a ransom for many', why some early writers said the ransom was paid to the devil, and why Gregory of Nazianzus rejected the idea.
Explain the 'victory' picture of the cross in Irenaeus and Athanasius, and why it remains central for Orthodox Christians.
Set out Anselm's argument in Why God Became Man step by step, and Abelard's alternative, and assess both.
Explain penal substitution from Romans 3, 2 Corinthians 5 and Calvin, and compare Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox emphases side by side.
State the moral objection to the cross at full strength, from Paine to Girard and modern critics, and weigh the main replies.

people.name: Aaron
people.line: Moses' brother and Israel's first high priest, who in Leviticus 16 performs the rite of the Day of Atonement.

people.name: Jesus of Nazareth
people.line: Jewish teacher crucified under Pontius Pilate; he spoke of giving his life 'as a ransom for many'.

people.name: Paul the Apostle
people.line: Writer of Romans and 2 Corinthians, the earliest Christian writings on what the cross achieved.

people.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
people.line: Bishop in Gaul who taught that Christ 'recapitulated' the human story, undoing Adam's defeat.

people.name: Origen
people.line: Alexandrian scholar, the first to say plainly that the ransom was paid to the devil.

people.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
people.line: Bishop of Alexandria whose On the Incarnation presents the cross as God's rescue of humanity from death.

people.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
people.line: Bishop and theologian who asked to whom the ransom was paid, and answered: to no one.

people.name: Gregory of Nyssa
people.line: Bishop who compared the incarnation to bait hiding a fish-hook, catching the devil.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.line: North African bishop who called the cross the devil's mousetrap and taught that God loved us before he reconciled us.

people.name: Anselm of Canterbury
people.line: Monk of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury whose Why God Became Man (1098) argued that only a God-man could make satisfaction for sin.

people.name: Boso
people.line: Monk of Bec, later its abbot, Anselm's questioner in Why God Became Man.

people.name: Peter Abelard
people.line: Paris teacher who argued that the cross saves by kindling love in us; condemned at Sens in 1141.

people.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
people.line: Cistercian abbot who attacked Abelard's view of the cross.

people.name: Thomas Aquinas
people.line: Dominican theologian who joined satisfaction, sacrifice, merit and love in one account.

people.name: Martin Luther
people.line: German reformer who described the cross as a 'happy exchange' of our sin for Christ's righteousness.

people.name: John Calvin
people.line: French reformer in Geneva whose Institutes set out Christ's death as bearing the penalty in our place.

people.name: Faustus Socinus
people.line: Italian theologian who argued that satisfaction and free forgiveness contradict each other.

people.name: Thomas Paine
people.line: English-born radical whose The Age of Reason (1794) called redemption a 'pecuniary' idea, not moral justice.

people.name: Immanuel Kant
people.line: German philosopher who argued that moral guilt cannot be transferred from one person to another.

people.name: Gustaf Aulén
people.line: Swedish bishop whose Christus Victor (1930) revived the early Church's 'victory' picture.

people.name: René Girard
people.line: French literary theorist who read the cross as the exposure of the scapegoat mechanism.

people.name: John Stott
people.line: Anglican evangelical whose The Cross of Christ (1986) defended substitution as God's self-substitution.

people.name: Fleming Rutledge
people.line: American Episcopal priest whose The Crucifixion (2015) argues for keeping all the biblical pictures.
