debate.question: What did the cross do? Three traditions answer

positions.name: Reformed: he bore our penalty
positions.who: John Calvin; the Westminster Confession (1647); John Stott; J. I. Packer
positions.view: Humanity is guilty before a just God. Christ, God the Son made man, bore the penalty in our place, so that God forgives justly and we are declared righteous by faith alone. Every other picture depends on this one.
positions.evidence: Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; Isaiah 53:5; Calvin, Institutes II.16.5.

positions.name: Catholic: he offered a perfect sacrifice of love
positions.who: Thomas Aquinas; the Council of Trent; the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992)
positions.view: Christ's free obedience and love, offered to the Father on the cross, made superabundant satisfaction for sin and merited grace for us. The cross is a sacrifice, made present in the Mass, and its grace heals and transforms us, not only acquits.
positions.evidence: Hebrews 9:14; Romans 5:19; Ephesians 5:2; Aquinas, Summa III.48; Trent, sixth session, chapter 7.

positions.name: Orthodox: he trampled down death
positions.who: Athanasius; the Orthodox liturgy; modern theologians such as John Behr
positions.view: The cross is God's victory over death and corruption, inseparable from the resurrection. Its goal is not a legal verdict but our healing and our sharing in the life of God. Western talk of satisfying justice is, at best, a secondary picture.
positions.evidence: Hebrews 2:14–15; 1 Corinthians 15:54–57; Athanasius, On the Incarnation 8–9; the Paschal troparion.

debate.agree: All three confess that Christ died 'for us and for our salvation', that God's love is the cause of the cross, and that its benefits are received by faith and sealed in baptism.

look.why: Paolo Veneziano, the leading painter of Venice in his day, made this panel around 1340–1345. Above Christ's head is the plaque reading INRI, the Latin initials of 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews', the charge Pilate had written and fixed to the cross (John 19:19). It is the sentence over the condemned man: the courtroom picture, painted. Armed men stand to one side, and the angels catch his blood as in Daddi's panel in session 1.
points: At the centre, Jesus hangs from nails through his palms and feet, his knees angled to one side and his head tipped down, eyes closed.
A panel at the top of the cross reads 'INRI'.
Three small winged angels catch the red blood from his hands and side in gold bowls; a fourth clasps its hands in prayer.
A woman with long, curly, copper-coloured hair kneels at the foot of the cross, holding his bleeding feet.
To our left, a woman in lapis blue swoons into the arms of two hooded women.
To our right, men in helmets and armoured breastplates stand with a man in a blue robe who prays; one armoured man with a halo points up at Jesus.

music.why: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend's hymn (2001) sings the whole story from the incarnation to the return of Christ, and sings penal substitution plainly. It is also the hymn at the centre of a 2013 dispute about whether to speak of God's wrath at all.

think.why: Luther's question was personal: how can I stand before God? See how that question helped shape the West's belief that every single person counts.

learn.why: The great exchange in one sentence: the verse Luther's 'happy exchange' was built on.

check.q: What is the significance of Romans 3:26, 'that he might himself be just, and the justifier'?
options: God stops being just in order to forgive
Only the just are justified
On the cross God neither pretends sin does not matter nor condemns the sinner: he remains just and puts the guilty right
Justice and justification are the same thing
check.why: The cross 'demonstrates his righteousness' after he had passed over sins, while he justifies those who trust in Jesus.

check.q: Which verse is the best reply to the charge that penal substitution sets an angry Father against an innocent Son?
options: 2 Corinthians 5:19, 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself'
Mark 10:42, on rulers who lord it over others
Leviticus 16:8, on casting lots
Romans 3:23, 'all have sinned'
check.why: The one reconciling is God himself, in Christ: not a third party.

check.q: How does Calvin's view differ from Anselm's?
options: Anselm says God was angry, Calvin that he was not
Calvin denies that Christ died
For Anselm satisfaction is the alternative to punishment; for Calvin Christ makes satisfaction by bearing the punishment
Calvin says the ransom was paid to the devil
check.why: Anselm: 'satisfaction or punishment'. Calvin: Christ 'took the punishment upon himself'.

check.q: Why does Calvin say it matters that Jesus was condemned by Pilate?
options: Because Pilate was a Roman citizen
Because it proves the Gospels are history
Because a formal legal sentence shows Christ bearing the character of a condemned sinner, while the same judge declared him innocent
Because it shows the Jews were not responsible
check.why: Calvin: a death in a riot would not satisfy; 'placed as a criminal at the bar', yet declared innocent, he suffers for others' crimes.

check.q: According to Calvin, what is the relation between God's love and the cross?
options: The cross made God begin to love us
God never loved sinners
Love has nothing to do with the cross
God first loves us, and so reconciles us to himself through the cross
check.why: 'It is because he first loves us, that he afterwards reconciles us to himself.'

check.q: Why did C. H. Dodd and Leon Morris argue over hilasterion?
options: Because it is missing from some manuscripts
Because it is a Latin word
Because whether it means expiation (wiping away sin) or propitiation (turning away wrath) affects whether the cross is aimed at sin or at God's anger
Because it means 'ransom'
check.why: Dodd read 'expiation', Morris 'propitiation'; the debate is about what the cross was directed at.

tutorial.question: What is penal substitution, and is it the heart of the New Testament's teaching on the cross?
tutorial.approach: Define penal substitution with its four claims. Show its roots in Romans 3, 2 Corinthians 5, Galatians 3 and Isaiah 53, and in Calvin. Explain what its defenders say it does not mean. Then compare the Catholic and Orthodox emphases, and decide whether it is the heart of the New Testament, one picture among several, or a misreading.
strong: Defines penal substitution accurately.
Reads Romans 3:25–26 and 2 Corinthians 5:19–21 closely.
Uses Calvin's insistence that God's love comes first.
Distinguishes Calvin from Anselm on satisfaction and punishment.
Sets out the three traditions fairly, side by side.
Notes that Paul combines courtroom, Temple and slave-market pictures in a single sentence.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Calvin wrote that the point of the doctrine is that we need not live 'in trepidation and anxiety'. Name one thing you keep punishing yourself for. Write it down, read 2 Corinthians 5:17 beside it, and then tear the paper up.
sessions.reflect: Is there a difference between God punishing an innocent person and God taking the punishment himself? Does the difference matter to you?
takeaways: The Reformers read the cross through the courtroom: Christ bore the penalty in our place, so that God is 'just, and the justifier'.
Luther called it a 'happy exchange'; Calvin insisted that God's love came first and that Christ was condemned in a real court.
Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox Christians use all the pictures but put a different one first: penalty, sacrifice and satisfaction, or victory and healing.

sessions.title: The case against: can a death save anyone?
sessions.line: A boy on his family's garden steps decides that the sermon he has just heard makes God a murderer. The objection at full strength.
sessions.plain: Many thoughtful people, believers among them, find the whole idea of the cross morally troubling. Thomas Paine put the case in 1794: a debt can be paid by someone else, but a crime cannot, and to punish the innocent for the guilty is not justice but 'indiscriminate revenge'. He remembered deciding, at seven or eight, that a sermon about the cross made God act like a man who killed his son. Others since have added that guilt cannot be transferred, that a God who demands blood is not good, and that the story has been used to tell victims to accept abuse. This session states the objection at full strength, then hears the answers.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 5 set out the five pictures, ending with the strongest form of the courtroom: Christ bore the penalty in our place. Now, with every picture in hand, we can hear the case against them, and above all against that last one. The objection comes here because it is aimed at what you have just learned.
answers: Is it fair for an innocent person to be punished for the guilty?
Is the cross 'divine child abuse'?
Why would God need blood?
Why couldn't God forgive as the father of the prodigal son does?
How do Christians answer, and how strong are the answers?
sessions.finding: The objection is strongest against a crude picture of an angry Father punishing an innocent Son; each tradition answers that Father and Son act as one, freely, out of love, but critics reply that this does not remove the problem of transferred guilt.

paras: Across five sessions the cross has been a sacrifice, a ransom, a victory, a satisfaction and a penalty borne in our place. Each picture had defenders and critics, and some of the criticism came from inside: Gregory of Nazianzus against a ransom to the devil, Abelard against Anselm, Socinus against Calvin.

This session gathers the criticism into one case. It is not a small objection. If it succeeds, it does not only weaken one theory; it suggests that the central symbol of Christianity praises something immoral.
background.key: The criticism has been growing through the journey; gathered together, it charges that the cross praises something immoral.

paras: Thomas Paine (1737–1809) was born in Thetford, Norfolk, the son of a Quaker father and an Anglican mother. He emigrated to America in 1774, and his pamphlet Common Sense (1776) helped persuade the colonists to declare independence. Later his Rights of Man (1791) defended the French Revolution, and he went to France, where he was elected to its parliament and then imprisoned during the Terror.

He wrote the first part of The Age of Reason in Paris in 1793, finishing it, he said, hours before his arrest, and it was published in 1794. Paine was not an atheist. He was a deist: he believed in one God, the creator, known through reason and nature, and he rejected revelation, miracles and the churches. If you took 'Kings and prophets', you read his attack on the wars of Joshua in Part II of the same book.
background.key: Paine (1737–1809), author of Common Sense, wrote The Age of Reason (1794) as a deist: belief in God, rejection of revelation and the churches.

paras: The objection has three strands, and it helps to keep them apart. The first is about justice: guilt belongs to the guilty and cannot be moved to someone else, so punishing the innocent in their place is unjust, however willing the innocent may be. The second is about God's character: a good God would forgive freely, as he tells us to and as the father of the prodigal son does, without needing blood. The third is about effects: the story of a father who sends his son to die has been used to teach that suffering should be accepted, even abuse.

Each strand has serious advocates: Paine, Faustus Socinus and the philosopher Immanuel Kant for the first; many liberal theologians and ordinary believers for the second; feminist and womanist theologians for the third. And the anthropologist René Girard offers a different account of why sacrifice exists at all.
background.key: Three charges: guilt cannot be transferred; a good God would forgive freely; the story has been used to justify abuse. Then Girard's alternative.

paras: The main reading is from The Age of Reason, Part I: Paine's argument that redemption rests on a 'pecuniary', money-based idea of justice, and his memory of the sermon he heard as a child. Read it without looking for a reply.

The comparison has two parts. First, Anselm himself, who let Boso put the same objection in 1098. Then the first letter of Peter, which presents the cross as the example of an innocent sufferer: a passage that critics and defenders both appeal to.
background.key: Paine on the 'pecuniary idea' and the garden steps; then Boso's objection in Anselm, and 1 Peter 2.

before: What is the difference, for Paine, between a debt and a crime?
Why does Paine think the doctrine was invented?
In 1 Peter, what does Christ do when he is wronged? Who does the passage say he is an example for?
sessions.readWhy: The objection in the words of its most famous advocate: redemption as a money idea of justice, and a child's revulsion at the sermon.

paras: The invention of a purgatory, and of the releasing of souls therefrom, by prayers, bought of the church with money; the selling of pardons, dispensations, and indulgences, are revenue laws, without bearing that name or carrying that appearance. But the case nevertheless is, that those things derive their origin from the proxysm of the crucifixion, and the theory deduced therefrom, which was, that one person could stand in the place of another, and could perform meritorious services for him. The probability, therefore, is, that the whole theory or doctrine of what is called the redemption (which is said to have been accomplished by the act of one person in the room of another) was originally fabricated on purpose to bring forward and build all those secondary and pecuniary redemptions upon; and that the passages in the books upon which the idea of theory of redemption is built, have been manufactured and fabricated for that purpose. Why are we to give this church credit, when she tells us that those books are genuine in every part, any more than we give her credit for everything else she has told us; or for the miracles she says she has performed? That she could fabricate writings is certain, because she could write; and the composition of the writings in question, is of that kind that anybody might do it; and that she did fabricate them is not more inconsistent with probability, than that she should tell us, as she has done, that she could and did work miracles.

Since, then, no external evidence can, at this long distance of time, be produced to prove whether the church fabricated the doctrine called redemption or not, (for such evidence, whether for or against, would be subject to the same suspicion of being fabricated,) the case can only be referred to the internal evidence which the thing carries of itself; and this affords a very strong presumption of its being a fabrication. For the internal evidence is, that the theory or doctrine of redemption has for its basis an idea of pecuniary justice, and not that of moral justice.

If I owe a person money, and cannot pay him, and he threatens to put me in prison, another person can take the debt upon himself, and pay it for me. But if I have committed a crime, every circumstance of the case is changed. Moral justice cannot take the innocent for the guilty even if the innocent would offer itself. To suppose justice to do this, is to destroy the principle of its existence, which is the thing itself. It is then no longer justice. It is indiscriminate revenge.

This single reflection will show that the doctrine of redemption is founded on a mere pecuniary idea corresponding to that of a debt which another person might pay; and as this pecuniary idea corresponds again with the system of second redemptions, obtained through the means of money given to the church for pardons, the probability is that the same persons fabricated both the one and the other of those theories; and that, in truth, there is no such thing as redemption; that it is fabulous; and that man stands in the same relative condition with his Maker he ever did stand, since man existed; and that it is his greatest consolation to think so.

From the time I was capable of conceiving an idea, and acting upon it by reflection, I either doubted the truth of the christian system, or thought it to be a strange affair; I scarcely knew which it was: but I well remember, when about seven or eight years of age, hearing a sermon read by a relation of mine, who was a great devotee of the church, upon the subject of what is called Redemption by the death of the Son of God. After the sermon was ended, I went into the garden, and as I was going down the garden steps (for I perfectly recollect the spot) I revolted at the recollection of what I had heard, and thought to myself that it was making God Almighty act like a passionate man, that killed his son, when he could not revenge himself any other way; and as I was sure a man would be hanged that did such a thing, I could not see for what purpose they preached such sermons. This was not one of those kind of thoughts that had any thing in it of childish levity; it was to me a serious reflection, arising from the idea I had that God was too good to do such an action, and also too almighty to be under any necessity of doing it. I believe in the same manner to this moment; and I moreover believe, that any system of religion that has anything in it that shocks the mind of a child, cannot be a true system.

It seems as if parents of the christian profession were ashamed to tell their children any thing about the principles of their religion. They sometimes instruct them in morals, and talk to them of the goodness of what they call Providence; for the Christian mythology has five deities: there is God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Ghost, the God Providence, and the Goddess Nature. But the christian story of God the Father putting his son to death, or employing people to do it, (for that is the plain language of the story,) cannot be told by a parent to a child; and to tell him that it was done to make mankind happier and better, is making the story still worse; as if mankind could be improved by the example of murder; and to tell him that all this is a mystery, is only making an excuse for the incredibility of it.

parts.author: Thomas Paine
parts.work: The Age of Reason, Part I
parts.who: Thomas Paine (1737–1809), English-born radical, author of Common Sense and Rights of Man, a deist
parts.ref: Paine, The Age of Reason, Part I, chapter VIII
parts.title: A pecuniary idea
parts.context: Paine is examining the New Testament. He has argued that the Church built 'a religion of pomp and of revenue' on the story of Jesus. Now he turns to redemption. This is the text of Moncure Conway's edition, from Project Gutenberg.
parts.plain: Paine says: the Church sells pardons and releases from purgatory, which are really taxes, and they all come from one idea, that one person can stand in for another and earn merit for him. Probably the whole doctrine of redemption was made up to support these money-making schemes. We cannot prove it from outside, so look inside the idea. It is based on money justice, not moral justice. If I owe money, someone else can pay it. But if I commit a crime, no one else can take my guilt, even if they offer; that would not be justice but revenge on whoever is nearest. So there is no redemption: we stand before God as we always have, and that should comfort us.

commentary.on: the theory deduced therefrom, which was, that one person could stand in the place of another, and could perform meritorious services for him
commentary.text: Paine traces indulgences back to the idea of substitution. He is right that the Church's 'treasury of merit' depended on the idea that one person's merit could help another. He is writing two and a half centuries after Luther made the same complaint about indulgences from the other side.

commentary.on: was originally fabricated on purpose to bring forward and build all those secondary and pecuniary redemptions upon
commentary.text: This is Paine's historical charge, and it is his weakest. The idea that Christ died 'for our sins' is in Paul's letters of the 50s AD, more than a thousand years before the sale of indulgences. Paine had no access to modern dating of the texts, but even in his day the order was known.

commentary.on: the theory or doctrine of redemption has for its basis an idea of pecuniary justice, and not that of moral justice
commentary.text: This is his strong argument. 'Pecuniary' means to do with money. Paine has Anselm's debt picture and the Reformers' penalty picture in his sights at once.

commentary.on: Moral justice cannot take the innocent for the guilty even if the innocent would offer itself.
commentary.text: Notice 'even if the innocent would offer itself'. Paine anticipates the reply that Christ went willingly, and says it makes no difference: a judge who accepted an innocent volunteer for a murderer's sentence would be corrupt.

commentary.on: It is then no longer justice. It is indiscriminate revenge.
commentary.text: If punishment can fall on anyone, it is no longer about guilt. It is just the satisfying of anger. This is the heart of the moral objection.

commentary.on: man stands in the same relative condition with his Maker he ever did stand, since man existed; and that it is his greatest consolation to think so
commentary.text: Paine's alternative: nothing has gone so wrong between humanity and God that it needs a cross. For him this is good news. It is worth asking whether it is, and whether it fits the world as you find it.

parts.author: Thomas Paine
parts.work: The Age of Reason, Part I
parts.who: Thomas Paine (1737–1809), English-born radical, author of Common Sense and Rights of Man, a deist
parts.ref: Paine, The Age of Reason, Part I, chapter XIII
parts.title: On the garden steps
parts.context: Later in Part I, Paine tells how his doubts began, in a passage that is the most personal in the book.
parts.plain: Paine says: when I was seven or eight, a relative read a sermon about redemption by the death of the Son of God. Going down the garden steps afterwards, I was revolted: it made God act like an angry man who killed his son because he could not take revenge any other way. A man who did that would be hanged. God, I thought, was too good to do it and too powerful to need to. I still believe it, and any religion that shocks the mind of a child cannot be true. Christian parents cannot tell their children the story of a father putting his son to death without making it worse.

commentary.on: I went into the garden, and as I was going down the garden steps (for I perfectly recollect the spot)
commentary.text: The detail of the steps is what makes this passage stay with readers. Paine wants us to see that the objection is not clever but natural: a child sees it at once.

commentary.on: making God Almighty act like a passionate man, that killed his son, when he could not revenge himself any other way
commentary.text: This is the picture Paine rejects: an angry father, a son killed, revenge. It is worth asking which of the five pictures, if any, actually says this. Paine heard it in a sermon, and preachers have often said something like it.

commentary.on: God was too good to do such an action, and also too almighty to be under any necessity of doing it
commentary.text: Two arguments in one line. 'Too good': the moral objection. 'Too almighty to be under any necessity': Anselm's question, why not forgive by will alone? Paine's answer is that an almighty God needs nothing.

commentary.on: any system of religion that has anything in it that shocks the mind of a child, cannot be a true system
commentary.text: A memorable test, and a debatable one. Many true things shock children: death, cruelty, the facts of history. Defenders reply that the cross should shock; the question is whether what shocks is God's cruelty or human cruelty.

commentary.on: as if mankind could be improved by the example of murder
commentary.text: Paine's final charge is about effects: what kind of people does this story make? Feminist critics two centuries later asked the same question.

paras: Boso. Be it so; let nothing be referred to the Divine nature, which is spoken of Christ after the manner of human weakness; but how will it ever be made out a just or reasonable thing that God should treat or suffer to be treated in such a manner, that man whom the Father called his beloved Son in whom he was well pleased, and whom the Son made himself? For what justice is there in his suffering death for the sinner, who was the most just of all men? What man, if he condemned the innocent to free the guilty, would not himself be judged worthy of condemnation? And so the matter seems to return to the same incongruity which is mentioned above. For if he could not save sinners in any other way than by condemning the just, where is his omnipotence? If, however, he could, but did not wish to, how shall we sustain his wisdom and justice?

Anselm. God the Father did not treat that man as you seem to suppose, nor put to death the innocent for the guilty. For the Father did not compel him to suffer death, or even allow him to be slain, against his will, but of his own accord he endured death for the salvation of men.
For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps,
who didn’t sin, “neither was deceit found in his mouth.”
When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds.
For you were going astray like sheep; but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

parts.author: Anselm of Canterbury
parts.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
parts.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
parts.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.8
parts.title: Boso's objection, 1098
parts.context: Early in the dialogue Boso puts the objection plainly, and Anselm gives the first part of his answer. You met the speakers in session 4. The translator is James Gardiner Vose (1854–1855).
parts.plain: Boso asks: how can it be just or reasonable for God to treat, or let be treated in this way, the man he called his beloved Son? What justice is there in the most just of men dying for sinners? Any man who condemned the innocent to free the guilty would himself deserve condemnation. If God could not save sinners any other way, where is his power? If he could but would not, where is his wisdom and justice? Anselm answers: the Father did not do what you suppose. He did not put the innocent to death for the guilty or force him to die. The Son chose to die, of his own accord, to save us.

commentary.on: What man, if he condemned the innocent to free the guilty, would not himself be judged worthy of condemnation?
commentary.text: Seven centuries before Paine, the same charge, put by a monk to his abbot. It shows that the objection is part of the tradition's own conversation, not only an attack from outside.

commentary.on: For if he could not save sinners in any other way than by condemning the just, where is his omnipotence?
commentary.text: Boso even has Paine's second argument: an almighty God should need no such means.

commentary.on: God the Father did not treat that man as you seem to suppose, nor put to death the innocent for the guilty.
commentary.text: Anselm's first answer is to deny the picture. The Father did not condemn the Son. Whatever the cross is, it is not a court sentencing an innocent man.

commentary.on: but of his own accord he endured death for the salvation of men
commentary.text: His second answer is freedom. The Son chose. In the chapters that follow Anselm argues that Christ's obedience was not to an order to die, but to the call to keep justice whatever it cost, and that death came as the result. Critics reply that a volunteer does not make an unjust sentence just, which is Paine's 'even if the innocent would offer itself'.

parts.title: Leaving you an example
parts.context: The first letter of Peter, written to scattered Christian communities in what is now Turkey, probably between AD 60 and 90, addresses household slaves who are being treated unjustly by their masters. It points them to Christ.

commentary.on: Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps
commentary.text: This is the road picture again: Christ as the example, as Abelard taught. But notice the context. It is addressed to slaves suffering injustice. Feminist critics point out exactly this: the cross has been used to tell the powerless to put up with abuse. Defenders reply that the passage praises not submission to evil but refusing to answer evil with evil.

commentary.on: When he was cursed, he didn't curse back. When he suffered, he didn't threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.
commentary.text: The example is specific: not hitting back, and leaving justice to God. It is not 'suffering is good'. It is 'do not become what is hurting you'.

commentary.on: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree
commentary.text: And here, in the same breath, is substitution, in words from Isaiah 53: 'he bore the sins of many'. The writer sees no conflict between the example and the substitute. Christ is more than an example because he did something we could not; he is an example because we can follow how he did it.

commentary.on: You were healed by his wounds.
commentary.text: Isaiah 53:5 again. Healing, not punishment, is the word the writer chooses for the effect of the wounds.

compare.author: Anselm of Canterbury
compare.work: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
compare.ref: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.8
compare.translator: James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra, 1854–1855), reprinted by Open Court (1903)
compare.why: The objection is not new, and it is not only an outsider's. Anselm let his questioner Boso make it in 1098, and the New Testament itself presents the cross as the act of a free and innocent man.
compare.title: Answers from inside

paras: Put as strongly as its best advocates put it, the objection runs like this. Moral guilt belongs to the person who did wrong. It is not a debt that can be paid by a friend; it is a fact about who I am and what I did. To punish an innocent person in my place, even a willing one, does not remove my guilt. It only adds a second wrong. A God who requires such a punishment before he will forgive is less good than an ordinary decent parent, who forgives a repentant child without demanding that anyone suffer.

Worse, the critics say, the story teaches bad lessons. It suggests that violence can be holy, that suffering earns favour, and that those with power may rightly inflict pain on those who obey them. And it is unnecessary: Jesus himself told a story of a son who wasted his inheritance and came home, and of a father who ran to meet him and forgave him with no payment at all (Luke 15:11–24). If God is like that father, why the cross?
sections.key: Guilt is personal and cannot be transferred; a God who needs punishment before forgiving is worse than a decent parent; the story teaches violence; and the prodigal's father forgives freely.

paras: The philosophical form of the objection comes from two thinkers. Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), whom you met in session 5, argued that satisfaction and forgiveness contradict each other. If a creditor is paid in full, he has not forgiven anything. If God forgives, he cannot also require payment. And a single death of limited length cannot equal the eternal death owed by countless sinners.

Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), in Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason (1793), made the point about guilt sharper. In our own words: a debt of money can be paid by anyone, but moral guilt is the most personal thing there is; it cannot be handed to another person as a debt can, and no one else can bear it for me. Kant thought the moral core of the Christian idea could be kept: the old self, turning from evil, as it were 'dies', and the new self bears the suffering of that change. But he denied that one person could carry another's guilt.
sections.key: Socinus: satisfaction and forgiveness contradict each other. Kant: moral guilt is not a transferable debt; no one can bear it for me.

sections.h: The scapegoat, from the other side
paras: The French thinker René Girard (1923–2015) offered a different account, in books such as Violence and the Sacred (1972) and Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World (1978). In our own words: humans want what others want, and this 'mimetic desire' breeds rivalry that threatens to tear communities apart. Again and again, communities have saved themselves by uniting against one victim, the scapegoat, whose death brings peace. Afterwards the victim is often made sacred. Ancient myths, Girard argued, tell these stories from the side of the mob, as if the victim were guilty.

The Gospels, Girard said, tell the same story from the side of the victim, and so expose it. The high priest Caiaphas says the scapegoat's logic aloud: 'it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people' (John 11:50). The cross reveals that the victim was innocent and the mob was wrong. For Girard, at least in his earlier work, the cross saves not because God demanded a sacrifice but because God became the victim to end the sacrificial system. Later he accepted that Christ's death could be called a sacrifice in a different sense: self-giving, not killing.
sections.key: Girard: communities unite by killing a scapegoat; the Gospels tell the story from the victim's side and expose the mechanism. God becomes the victim to end sacrifice.

paras: In 1989 two American theologians, Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker, published an essay asking whether the traditional doctrines of the cross amount to 'divine child abuse': a father who wills the suffering and death of his son. They argued that such a picture had taught women, children and the abused to accept suffering as redemptive and to stay in harmful situations. The womanist theologian Delores Williams, in Sisters in the Wilderness (1993), argued that Black women, forced for centuries to stand in for others, could find no liberation in a saviour who saves by standing in for others; she located salvation in Jesus's life and ministry.

In Britain the phrase became famous in 2003, when the Baptist minister Steve Chalke, in The Lost Message of Jesus, described a crude version of penal substitution as a form of 'cosmic child abuse', and a long argument among evangelicals followed. These critics are not outsiders sneering at faith; most write as Christians who think the story has been told in a way that harms people.
sections.key: Brown and Parker (1989) asked if the cross is 'divine child abuse'; Delores Williams (1993) questioned surrogacy as saving; Steve Chalke's phrase (2003) split British evangelicals.

paras: Christians have answered in five main ways. First, there is no third party. The doctrine of the Trinity means that the Son is not someone else whom God punishes; 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself' (2 Corinthians 5:19). The judge takes the sentence on himself. Second, Jesus was not a child but a free adult: 'No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself' (John 10:18). Third, the love comes first: 'while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us' (Romans 5:8), and even Calvin insisted that the cross is the result of God's love, not its cause.

Fourth, forgiveness is never free for the one who forgives. When someone forgives a serious wrong, they absorb its cost instead of passing it on. The cross, on this view, is what forgiveness costs God. Fifth, substitution in Paul is also union: 'one died for all, therefore all died' (2 Corinthians 5:14). Christ does not stand in for us as a stranger but as the head of a new humanity we are joined to. The Bible itself says that 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father' (Ezekiel 18:20); defenders such as John Stott and Fleming Rutledge argue that the cross is not that, but God bearing our iniquity as one of us.
sections.key: Five replies: no third party (God in Christ); a free adult; love first; forgiveness always costs the forgiver; substitution is also union.

paras: Honesty requires saying what the replies do and do not achieve. They answer the crude picture well: almost no serious Christian theologian has ever taught that an angry Father vented his rage on an unwilling Son, though preachers sometimes have. They answer Paine's historical charge: the doctrine is not a medieval money-making invention.

They answer the moral objection less completely. Socinus and Kant would say that calling the victim God, or a volunteer, does not explain how my guilt can be borne by another. Defenders reply that guilt is not a thing to be moved but a broken relationship to be healed, and that union with Christ is the way it is healed. Whether that is an answer or a change of subject is the question you must decide. And the critics of abuse have changed how the story is told: most Christian teachers today are careful to say that the cross calls people to resist evil, not to accept it, and that God is on the side of victims.
sections.key: The replies defeat the crude picture and Paine's history; whether they answer Socinus and Kant on transferred guilt is still the open question.

refs: Thomas Paine, The Age of Reason, Part I (1794), chapters VIII and XIII (ed. M. D. Conway).
Anselm, Why God Became Man I.8–10; Faustus Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore (1578); Immanuel Kant, Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason (1793), Part Two, Section One.
René Girard, Violence and the Sacred (1972); Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World (1978); I See Satan Fall Like Lightning (1999).

debate.question: Can one person's death take away another's guilt?

positions.name: No: guilt is not transferable
positions.who: Thomas Paine; Faustus Socinus; Immanuel Kant; many modern critics
positions.view: Guilt belongs to the guilty. To punish the innocent in their place, even willingly, is not justice but 'indiscriminate revenge', and a God who required it would be less good than a forgiving parent. Forgiveness should be free.
positions.evidence: The Age of Reason I.8, 13; Ezekiel 18:20; the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15); the moral sense of every child.

positions.name: No, but the cross saves in another way
positions.who: René Girard; Delores Williams; many liberal and some Anabaptist theologians
positions.view: God does not require a victim. Humans do. The cross exposes the violence of the scapegoat mechanism and shows God on the side of the victim; Jesus saves by his life, his non-violence and his resurrection, not by being punished.
positions.evidence: John 11:50; 1 Peter 2:23; Luke 23:34 ('Father, forgive them'); the Gospels' insistence on Jesus's innocence.

positions.name: Yes, because God bears it himself
positions.who: John Stott; Fleming Rutledge; much of the tradition
positions.view: The objection rightly rejects an angry Father punishing a third party, but that is not the doctrine. In Christ, God himself bears the cost of our wrong, as a forgiving person absorbs the cost of a wrong. We are not strangers whose guilt is moved but members of a humanity he has made his own.
positions.evidence: 2 Corinthians 5:14, 19; John 10:18; Romans 5:8; Isaiah 53:5; Anselm I.8.

debate.agree: All sides agree that an angry God punishing an unwilling innocent would be immoral, and that the story must never be used to tell victims to accept abuse.

look.why: Luca Signorelli painted this crowded crucifixion around 1504–1505. It is not a picture of an objection, but it shows what René Girard saw in the story: the many pressing round the one, a bristle of spears, a crowd united against a victim. Look at it with Paine's question and Girard's answer in mind: who, in this picture, is doing the killing?
points: More than two dozen men and women, gathered shoulder to shoulder, nearly fill the scene at the foot of three crosses.
Three men hang from crosses, tied and nailed, blood pouring from their hands and feet; two wear crowns of thorns.
A man on a white horse in the crowd drives a spear into the side of the central man.
Many of the men carry spears, making a bristle of vertical and diagonal lines over the crowd; at least three more are on horseback.
Near the lower left, a woman in a navy-blue robe has fainted and is held up by two kneeling women.
Beyond a spindly tree on the right, two buildings hint at a distant city under a blue sky.

music.why: Gabriel Fauré's Requiem (1888) leaves out almost all of the medieval 'Day of Wrath', and ends 'In Paradisum', with the angels leading the dead to paradise. It is a different picture of God before death: gentle, not angry. Listen to it as a question to this session.

think.why: The objection asks whether God wills suffering. See the modern debate about suffering and God.

learn.why: Paul's answer to whether God is for us or against us: nothing 'will be able to separate us from God's love'.

check.q: What is the core of Paine's moral argument?
options: That the Gospels contradict each other
That God does not exist
That a money debt can be paid by another, but guilt for a crime cannot; to punish the innocent for the guilty is 'indiscriminate revenge', even if the innocent offers
That Jesus never existed
check.why: 'Moral justice cannot take the innocent for the guilty even if the innocent would offer itself.'

check.q: Which part of Paine's case is weakest, and why?
options: His historical claim that redemption was invented to support indulgences, since Paul taught that Christ 'died for our sins' more than a thousand years earlier
His moral argument, because no one has ever agreed with it
His belief in God
His memory of the garden steps
check.why: 1 Corinthians 15:3 and Romans 3 date from the 50s AD; indulgences were sold from the later Middle Ages.

check.q: Why is it significant that Anselm has Boso raise the same objection in 1098?
options: It proves the cross is unjust
It shows the objection was part of the tradition's own debate, and that Anselm denied the Father condemned the innocent or forced him to die
It shows that Anselm agreed with Paine
It shows Boso became a deist
check.why: Anselm: 'the Father did not … put to death the innocent for the guilty'; the Son died 'of his own accord'.

check.q: How does Girard's account differ from Paine's?
options: Girard denies that Jesus died
Paine rejects the cross as unjust; Girard thinks the cross saves by exposing the human habit of uniting against a scapegoat, told from the victim's side
They agree completely
Girard thinks God demanded a victim; Paine does not
check.why: For Girard it is humans, not God, who demand victims; the Gospels expose it (John 11:50).

check.q: Which reply best meets the charge that the cross is 'divine child abuse'?
options: That the critics are not Christians
That suffering is always good for us
That children should obey their fathers
That in the Trinity there is no third party: God himself, in the Son, freely bears the cost, and the Son is a free adult who 'lays down' his life
check.why: 2 Corinthians 5:19 and John 10:18: the answer from the Trinity and from freedom.

check.q: Which objection do the replies answer least completely?
options: Paine's claim that redemption was a medieval invention
The claim that the Gospels mention the cross
Socinus's and Kant's argument that moral guilt cannot be borne by another, even by God
The crude picture of an angry Father and unwilling Son
check.why: Union with Christ and God's self-giving reframe the problem; critics say they do not explain how my guilt is borne by another.

tutorial.question: Is penal substitution morally defensible?
tutorial.approach: State the objection at full strength in its three strands: Paine, Socinus and Kant on transferred guilt; the prodigal's father; the critics of abuse. Then set out Girard's alternative. Weigh the five replies (no third party, freedom, love first, the cost of forgiveness, union). End with what you think is left standing.
strong: States Paine's argument fairly, with 'even if the innocent would offer itself'.
Separates the historical charge from the moral one, and judges each.
Includes Socinus or Kant on non-transferable guilt.
Explains Girard's scapegoat theory accurately.
Takes the abuse critique seriously, with Brown and Parker or Williams.
Weighs at least three replies and says honestly what remains.

reading.author: René Girard
reading.title: I See Satan Fall Like Lightning
reading.why: Girard's clearest short statement of his reading of the cross.

reading.author: Fleming Rutledge
reading.title: The Crucifixion
reading.why: Faces the objections at length and defends keeping substitution among the pictures.

reading.author: Delores S. Williams
reading.title: Sisters in the Wilderness

sessions.practice: Live it this week: 1 Peter's example is not 'accept abuse' but 'don't hit back'. The next time someone is rude or unfair to you this week, do not answer in kind. Say nothing sharp, and later do one small good thing for them. If you are being harmed by someone, the right step is different: tell someone you trust and get help.
sessions.reflect: Paine said any religion that shocks the mind of a child cannot be true. Is that a good test? What shocks you about the cross, and what does the shock tell you?
takeaways: Paine argued that guilt, unlike debt, cannot be paid by another, and that the cross makes God act like a man who killed his son; Socinus and Kant made the same point about guilt philosophically.
Girard read the cross as the exposure of the scapegoat mechanism, and feminist critics warned that the story has been used to justify abuse.
The replies (God in Christ, a free gift, love first, the cost of forgiveness, union with Christ) defeat the crude picture; whether they answer the problem of transferred guilt is for you to judge.

sessions.title: Many pictures, one love: the verdict
sessions.line: A serpent on a pole, a poet's Christ asking 'Was ever grief like mine?', and the five pictures laid side by side.
sessions.plain: The verdict first: no one picture of the cross holds it all, and the New Testament keeps every one of them on purpose. The sacrifice, the ransom, the victory, the courtroom and the road each say something true that the others miss, and together they say one thing: that God took the worst of the world into himself in order to heal it. This session reads John's famous sentence about why God gave his Son, and George Herbert's poem in which Christ speaks from the cross, then lays the five pictures side by side and asks what it means to live under the cross.
sessions.why: Session 6 heard the case against at full strength and asked what is left standing. This last session gives a verdict: not by choosing one picture and discarding the rest, but by seeing why the first Christians needed all of them.
answers: So why the cross?
Which picture is right?
Why does the New Testament use so many images?
What difference does the cross make to how someone lives?
sessions.finding: The New Testament keeps all the pictures because no one picture holds it all; together they say that God took the worst of the world into himself to heal it.

paras: Here is the verdict, in plain words, before the reasons. The cross cannot be explained by one picture, and the New Testament never tries. Each picture answers a different question. Sacrifice answers 'how is what is unclean made clean?' Ransom answers 'how are captives freed?' Victory answers 'how is death defeated?' The courtroom answers 'how can the guilty be put right without justice being mocked?' The road answers 'how does it change the way I live?'

Each picture, pressed on its own until it becomes a machine, goes wrong: a God who needs blood, a devil who gets paid, a creditor, an angry judge, a mere good example. Held together, they correct each other. And at the centre of all of them is one claim: that God was not a spectator of the cross but its subject. 'God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son.'
background.key: Verdict: each picture answers a different question; each goes wrong alone; together they say God himself, out of love, took the worst into himself to heal it.

paras: The journey followed one event through five pictures. Session 1, the Temple: the Day of Atonement and Hebrews' 'offered once'. Session 2, the slave market: a ransom paid to no one. Session 3, the battlefield: Athanasius's God entering death to break it. Session 4, Anselm's debt of honour and Abelard's road of love. Session 5, the Reformers' courtroom. Session 6 heard Paine, Socinus, Kant, Girard and the critics of abuse.

No council of the whole Church has ever made one theory of the atonement binding. The creeds say only that Christ was 'crucified for us', 'for us and for our salvation'. That silence, many theologians think, is wise.
background.key: Five pictures across five sessions, then the objection; the creeds say only 'crucified for us' and no council has defined one theory.

paras: The main reading is John 3:14–17: Jesus's words to Nicodemus, a Jewish teacher who came to him by night. It contains the most famous sentence in the Bible, and it explains the cross not with a theory but with a strange old story about a bronze snake and with the word 'loved'.
The comparison is from George Herbert (1593–1633), an English priest and poet, whose poem 'The Sacrifice' lets Christ speak from the cross. It holds every picture of this journey together in verse.
background.key: John 3:14–17, the cross as God's love; then Herbert's 'The Sacrifice', where Christ speaks from the cross.

before: What story does Jesus compare his being 'lifted up' to? Look it up in Numbers 21 if you can.
According to John 3:17, why did God send his Son?
In Herbert's poem, how many of the five pictures can you find?
sessions.readWhy: The cross explained not by a theory but by love: the sentence many Christians learn first.

paras: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up,
that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.

parts.title: Lifted up
parts.context: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the Jewish council, comes to Jesus at night (John 3:1–2). Jesus tells him he must be 'born again', or 'born from above'. Then he points to a story from Numbers 21: in the wilderness the Israelites were bitten by snakes, and Moses made a bronze snake and set it on a pole, so that 'everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live'.

commentary.on: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up
commentary.text: 'Lifted up' in John means two things at once: lifted up on the cross, and lifted up in glory (12:32). The snake on a pole was the image of the very thing that was killing the people, and looking at it healed them. Gregory of Nazianzus, a few lines after the passage of his Easter sermon you read in session 2, saw it this way: the serpent on the pole is death itself, hung up and killed.

commentary.on: that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life
commentary.text: 'Believe' here means trust, as the Israelites trusted enough to look. 'Eternal life' in John is not only life after death but the life of God's own age, beginning now.

commentary.on: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son
commentary.text: The cause of the cross is stated without any theory: God 'so loved'. And the giver is the Father; the gift is the Son. This is the sentence that answers Paine's angry father: in John the Father does not demand the Son's death to be appeased; he gives the Son because he loves.

commentary.on: For God didn't send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
commentary.text: The purpose is rescue, not condemnation. Whatever the courtroom means, John insists, the judge came to save.

paras: OH all ye, who passe by, whose eyes and minde To worldly things are sharp, but to me blinde; To me, who took eyes that I might you finde: Was ever grief like mine?
I answer nothing, but with patience prove If stonie hearts will melt with gentle love. But who does hawk at eagles with a dove? Was ever grief like mine?
So sits the earths great curse in Adams fall Upon my head: so I remove it all From th’ earth unto my brows, and bear the thrall: Was ever grief like mine?
O all ye who passe by, behold and see; Man stole the fruit, but I must climbe the tree; The tree of life to all, but onely me: Was ever grief like mine?
Lo, here I hang, charg’d with a world of sinne, The greater world o’ th’ two; for that came in By words, but this by sorrow I must win: Was ever grief like mine?
But, O my God, my God! why leav’st thou me, The sonne, in whom thou dost delight to be? My God, my God ------ Never was grief like mine.
Now heal thy self, Physician; now come down. Alas! I did so, when I left my crown And fathers smile for you, to feel his frown: Was ever grief like mine?
In healing not my self, there doth consist All that salvation, which ye now resist; Your safetie in my sicknesse doth subsist: Was ever grief like mine?
But now I die; now all is finished. My wo, mans weal: and now I bow my head. Onely let others say, when I am dead, Never was grief like mine.

parts.author: George Herbert
parts.title: The Sacrifice
parts.context: Herbert (1593–1633) was a brilliant Cambridge scholar and a member of Parliament who gave up a career at court to become the parish priest of Bemerton, near Salisbury. He died at 39. His poems were published after his death by his friend Nicholas Ferrar as The Temple. The spelling is the original of 1633; cuts between stanzas are marked '…'. The web edition prints footnote numbers after two words, which have been removed, and its apostrophes have been restored. The poem's opening echoes Lamentations 1:12, 'Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?'.
parts.plain: Christ speaks from his trial and death to everyone passing by. He answered his accusers with silence, hoping gentle love would melt stony hearts. He takes the curse of Adam's fall onto his own head. Adam stole fruit from a tree, and now Christ must climb a tree, the cross, which is the tree of life for everyone except him. He hangs there loaded with the world's sin. He cries 'My God, my God, why have you left me?' He is mocked, 'Physician, heal yourself', and answers that he did come down, from heaven, and that our safety lies in his not saving himself. Then he dies: 'my woe, man's good'.

commentary.on: OH all ye, who passe by, whose eyes and minde To worldly things are sharp, but to me blinde
commentary.text: Herbert takes the cry of ruined Jerusalem in Lamentations and puts it in Christ's mouth. The reader is the passer-by, sharp-eyed for everything except the one thing that matters.

commentary.on: I answer nothing, but with patience prove If stonie hearts will melt with gentle love.
commentary.text: This is Abelard's road: Christ's silence before his accusers as an appeal of love, hoping to melt hard hearts. Herbert's next line admits the odds: who hunts eagles with a dove?

commentary.on: So sits the earths great curse in Adams fall Upon my head
commentary.text: The crown of thorns becomes the curse of Genesis 3, 'thorns also and thistles'. This is the courtroom and Galatians 3:13: Christ 'having become a curse for us'.

commentary.on: Man stole the fruit, but I must climbe the tree
commentary.text: Irenaeus's recapitulation in seven words. Adam's tree undone by Christ's tree; the theft repaid by the gift. 'The tree of life to all, but onely me': he gives a life he does not keep.

commentary.on: Lo, here I hang, charg’d with a world of sinne
commentary.text: 'Charged' means both loaded and accused. Sacrifice, substitution and courtroom in one word. 'The greater world o' th' two': sin is a world heavier than the created world, which is Anselm's point about the weight of sin.

commentary.on: But, O my God, my God! why leav’st thou me
commentary.text: The one stanza where the refrain breaks. Christ quotes Psalm 22, as in Matthew 27:46, and the line trails off. For once he does not ask 'Was ever grief like mine?' but says 'Never was grief like mine'. Herbert does not explain the cry of dereliction. He lets it stand.

commentary.on: In healing not my self, there doth consist All that salvation, which ye now resist
commentary.text: The mockers say 'heal yourself'. Herbert's answer is the whole journey in two lines: our salvation consists in his not saving himself. The ransom, the victory and the love are all here: he stays on the cross.

commentary.on: My wo, mans weal: and now I bow my head.
commentary.text: 'Weal' means good, as in 'commonweal'. The exchange is stated as simply as possible: his woe, our good. Luther's 'happy exchange' in four words.

compare.author: George Herbert
compare.why: George Herbert's 'The Sacrifice', printed in The Temple in 1633, the year he died, is a poem of 63 stanzas in which Christ speaks from the passion, each stanza ending 'Was ever grief like mine?' Its paradoxes gather the pictures of this journey into a single voice.
compare.title: Was ever grief like mine?

paras: Here are the five pictures of the journey, with the question each answers, its best text, its classic teacher and the way it goes wrong if pressed alone. Read across each row, then down each column.

Notice that the same teachers turn up in more than one row. Athanasius uses victory, sacrifice and debt in one chapter; Paul combines the courtroom, the Temple and the slave market in one sentence (Romans 3:24–25). The pictures were never rivals to the people who first used them.

rows: How is what is unclean made clean?
How can the guilty be put right without mocking justice?
A creditor or an angry judge
How does it change the way I live?
A good example, but no rescue
table.note: Each picture corrects the others: the victory keeps the courtroom from becoming a transaction; the courtroom keeps the road from becoming mere advice; the road keeps the victory personal.

sections.key: Five pictures, five questions; each goes wrong alone, and the first Christians used them together.

paras: Why did the first Christians need so many images? One reason is that the event was unprecedented. When something happens that no one has a word for, people describe it with every word they have. A second is that the problem the cross addresses has many sides. Humans are guilty, but also captive, sick, estranged, mortal and lost. A remedy for one would not be a remedy for all.

The British theologian Colin Gunton, in The Actuality of Atonement (1988), argued that these pictures are not decorations on a plain truth that could be said without them. They are how the truth is told. A metaphor can describe something real: when we say a person was 'crushed' by grief, we are not being vague. In the same way, 'Christ defeated death' and 'Christ bore our sins' are pictures, but they are pictures of something that happened.
sections.key: Many pictures because the event was new and the problem many-sided; Colin Gunton argued that such metaphors tell the truth about something real.

paras: If the pictures have a common centre, it is the one John states and Paul repeats: the cross begins in God's love, and God is its subject, not its audience. 'God so loved the world, that he gave'. 'God commends his own love toward us'. 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself'. Every tradition you have met agrees on this, even Calvin, who insisted that God loved us before he reconciled us.

Gregory of Nazianzus, in the Easter sermon you read in session 2, sums up the whole matter a few paragraphs after his question about the ransom: 'We needed an Incarnate God, a God put to death, that we might live.' Notice the word 'needed'. It is not that God needed blood. It is that we needed God to come as far as death.
sections.key: The common centre: the cross begins in God's love and God is its subject. 'We needed an Incarnate God, a God put to death, that we might live.'

sections.h: The cross in art and song
paras: For most of Christian history, people met these ideas not in books but in pictures and hymns. The earliest crucifixions, from the 400s, show Christ alive and upright on the cross, a king reigning from a tree: the victory picture. From around 1000, especially in the West, artists began to show him dead and suffering, as in the panels in this journey, and by 1500 Matthias Grünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece, painted for a hospital where patients suffered from a disease that ulcerated the skin, showed a Christ covered in sores like theirs.

Hymns carry the pictures too. 'O Sacred Head', the Passion chorale, comes from a medieval Latin poem meditating on Christ's wounded head, translated into German by Paul Gerhardt in 1656 and set by Bach. The African American spiritual 'Were You There', first printed in 1899, asks the listener to stand at the cross: the road picture, sung by people who knew what it was to suffer unjustly.
sections.key: Early art showed Christ reigning from the cross; later art showed him suffering with the sufferers; hymns and spirituals carry the pictures to people who never read the theory.

paras: Any honest verdict must also say that the cross has been a source of terrible harm to Jews. For centuries some Christians called Jews 'Christ-killers', and Good Friday sermons were followed by attacks on Jewish neighbours. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected the charge, and most churches have done the same. The New Testament's own theology points the same way: Christ died for the sins of all, and in Herbert's words the reader, not some other people, is the one passing by.

Jews have their own profound understanding of atonement, without the cross. Since AD 70 Judaism has taught that repentance, prayer and charity restore the sinner to God, as the Yom Kippur liturgy says, and that God's mercy needs no sacrifice to be released. Christians who believe that the cross was God's way do not need to deny that this is a real meeting with the mercy of the same God.
sections.key: The cross has been used against Jews, a charge the churches now reject; Judaism has its own atonement through repentance, prayer and charity.

paras: What difference does the cross make? Christians have answered with their lives as much as their arguments. Because the cross means wrong is serious, it rules out pretending: guilt must be faced, not denied. Because it means wrong is forgiven at cost, it frees people to forgive others at cost: 'forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors' (Matthew 6:12). Because the crucified one is innocent, it puts God on the side of victims and gives the West its instinct to take the victim's part. And because Jesus said the greatest is the servant, it makes self-giving love the measure of greatness.

The cross also became the West's sign of hope in suffering. People who will never read Anselm hang a cross by a hospital bed or wear one at a graveside. For them the meaning is simple: whatever I am going through, God has been there.
sections.key: Living under the cross: facing guilt, forgiving at cost, taking the victim's side, measuring greatness by service, and hope that God has been where we suffer.

sections.h: What the verdict does not settle
paras: A verdict that the pictures belong together does not end every argument. Christians still disagree about whether one of them is the key, as the debate in this session shows, and about how the benefits of the cross reach a person: by faith alone, through the sacraments, or through the whole life of the Church. Those questions are real, they divide churches to this day, and they need a journey of their own.

Nor does it answer the sceptic. Someone who finds Paine or Kant convincing will not be persuaded by a table. Someone who finds Girard convincing will want a cross without any talk of payment at all. What the journey can claim is narrower and still important: that the Christian idea of the cross is not the crude story Paine heard on the garden steps; that it was argued over, with great seriousness, by some of the finest minds in history; and that its centre is not a God who needs blood but a God who, in the words of Gregory of Nazianzus, would rather become 'a God put to death' than leave us to die.
sections.key: The verdict leaves open which picture is key and how the cross reaches us, and it does not refute the sceptic; it shows the idea is not the crude story Paine heard.

debate.question: Should one picture be the key to the others?

positions.name: Yes: substitution is the heart
positions.who: J. I. Packer ('What Did the Cross Achieve?', 1973); John Stott; many evangelicals
positions.view: All the pictures are true, but they rest on one: Christ bearing our sin in our place. Without it, victory has no ground and example has no power. The other pictures describe the results of substitution.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24; Galatians 3:13.

positions.name: Yes: victory is the frame
positions.who: Gustaf Aulén; Orthodox theology; in part N. T. Wright
positions.view: The story the Bible tells is of God defeating the powers that ruin his creation. Sacrifice and substitution are how the victory was won, but the victory is the point, and the resurrection belongs at its centre.
positions.evidence: Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15; 1 Corinthians 15:54–57; the Anastasis icon.

positions.name: No: a kaleidoscope
positions.who: Colin Gunton; Joel Green and Mark Baker; Fleming Rutledge in her own way
positions.view: No one picture rules. Each speaks to a different side of the human problem and to different people and cultures. The New Testament's many images are a gift to be kept, not a puzzle to be reduced.
positions.evidence: Romans 3:24–25, combining three pictures in one sentence; the creeds' silence; Athanasius's mixing of images.

debate.agree: All agree that the pictures are true, that none should be dropped, and that the cross begins in God's love.

look.why: Francesco del Cossa painted this round panel in Ferrara around 1473–1474. It is the simplest form of the scene: Christ, his mother and his friend John, with the charge above his head and a skull at the foot of the cross. Every picture of this journey is in it if you look: the blood of the sacrifice, the charge of the courtroom, the death that is being defeated (the skull and bones beneath), and the two who stayed, the first to walk the road after him.
points: Against a shiny gold background, Jesus hangs from a wooden cross by his outstretched hands, his face tipped down, eyes closed and lips parted.
A plaque at the top of the cross reads 'INRI' in red.
To our left an older woman in an off-white wimple, ocean-blue dress and eggplant-purple cloak stands with her head bowed, gripping her cloak.
To our right a young man in a black tunic and garnet-red cloak looks up at Jesus with narrowed eyes.
Blood drips from the nails in his hands and feet and from the wound in his side, and runs onto a skull at the base of the cross.
The grey stone platform has an arched opening below, with bones protruding from the dark space.

music.why: 'O Sacred Head, Now Wounded' began as a medieval Latin meditation, became Paul Gerhardt's German hymn in 1656, and was set by Bach in the St Matthew Passion. It is sung in Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches alike: many traditions, one song at the cross.

think.why: Everything in this journey depends on who it was that died. See what the great teachers said about who Jesus was.

learn.why: The cross explained in one sentence, without a theory: 'God so loved the world'. If you learned it in 'Who was Jesus?', say it again now with this journey behind it.

check.q: What is the main reason this session gives for keeping all five pictures?
options: Because all theories are equally false
Because each answers a different question and each goes wrong if pressed alone; together they correct each other
Because the New Testament writers could not decide
Because the churches have defined all five as dogma
check.why: Sacrifice, ransom, victory, courtroom and road answer different questions, and each, alone, becomes a caricature.

check.q: Why does Jesus compare his being 'lifted up' to the bronze serpent?
options: Because the image of what was killing the people, lifted on a pole, healed those who looked to it in trust: so the cross heals those who trust
Because snakes were sacred in Israel
Because Nicodemus was a snake-charmer
Because Moses was crucified
check.why: Numbers 21:8–9; John 3:14–15: 'whoever believes in him should not perish'.

check.q: How does John 3:16–17 bear on Paine's picture of 'a passionate man, that killed his son'?
options: It names love as the cause and the Father as the giver of the Son, and says the Son came to save, not to judge
It confirms it
It says the Son was unwilling
It says nothing about the Father
check.why: 'God so loved the world, that he gave'; 'not … to judge the world, but that the world should be saved'.

check.q: In Herbert's 'The Sacrifice', what does 'In healing not my self, there doth consist All that salvation' mean?
options: That doctors cannot heal themselves
That our salvation lies in Christ choosing not to save himself from the cross
That Christ could not heal anyone
That salvation is resisted by Christ
check.why: Answering the taunt 'heal thyself', Christ says our safety depends on his staying on the cross.

check.q: Which line of Herbert's best expresses Irenaeus's idea of recapitulation?
options: 'Man stole the fruit, but I must climbe the tree'
'My dove doth back into my bosome flie'
'Was ever grief like mine?'
'They choose a murderer'
check.why: Adam's tree is undone by Christ's tree: the human story is retold and put right.

check.q: What is Colin Gunton's point about the pictures as metaphors?
options: That the cross is only a metaphor and did not happen
That metaphors are only decoration and can be dropped
That metaphors can describe something real, so the pictures tell the truth about what happened rather than hiding a plainer truth
That only one metaphor is true
check.why: Gunton argued that metaphor is a way of telling the truth, not a way of avoiding it.

tutorial.question: Why does the New Testament use so many images for the death of Christ?
tutorial.approach: Use the table of the five pictures. Give two or three reasons for the variety (an unprecedented event, a many-sided human problem, different audiences). Show how the pictures correct each other, with examples. Use John 3:16 and Herbert to show what holds them together. Then say whether you think one picture should be the key, and why.

Gives reasons for the variety, not just a list.
Shows how each picture, alone, becomes a caricature.
Identifies love, and God as the subject of the cross, as the common centre.
Uses Herbert or Gregory of Nazianzus to show the pictures held together.
Takes a position on whether one picture is the key, and answers an objection.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: 'forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors'. Choose one person who owes you something, an apology, money, a kindness, and let it go this week. Tell them if that would help; if not, tell God.
sessions.reflect: Which of the five pictures speaks most to you, and which least? What does that tell you about the question you bring to the cross?
takeaways: The New Testament keeps the five pictures because each answers a different question and each goes wrong alone.
At the centre of them all is love: God is the subject of the cross, not its audience, and 'so loved the world, that he gave'.
Herbert's 'The Sacrifice' gathers the pictures into one voice: 'In healing not my self, there doth consist All that salvation'.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: How can one death save? In about 300 words, give your own answer. Use at least two of the five pictures, say which you find most convincing and why, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Read one Gospel's account of the last day of Jesus's life slowly this week (Mark 14–15 takes about twenty minutes). Each time someone wrongs him, notice what he does in return. Then think of one wrong done to you that you have been carrying, and take one step towards letting it go.
synthesis: This journey asked how one death could save. The New Testament answers with pictures, and the traditions chose different pictures as the key. Here are the short answers to the questions people ask, in the order the journey took them.

What does 'atonement' mean? It is an English word made from 'at one': the making of peace between God and people, a word William Tyndale put into the English Bible. Its background is Israel's Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), when the high priest carried blood into the Most Holy Place to cleanse the sanctuary and laid the people's sins on a goat that carried them away. Sacrifice in Israel was not a bribe to an angry god. God himself gave it as a way back. The letter to the Hebrews says that Christ is both the priest and the offering, 'offered once to bear the sins of many', and that since his death no more sacrifices are needed. Jews, who lost the Temple in AD 70, have kept the Day of Atonement ever since without sacrifice, through repentance, prayer and charity.

Who was the ransom paid to? Jesus said he came 'to give his life as a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45). A ransom was the price that freed a slave or a prisoner. Some early writers, such as Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, said it was paid to the devil, who had a claim on sinners, and that God tricked him with the bait of Christ's humanity. Gregory of Nazianzus answered that a ransom to the devil was an outrage, and a ransom to the Father made no sense, since the Father did not hold us captive. The word, he thought, means a costly rescue, not a payment to anyone. Most Christians since have agreed.

How do Orthodox Christians see the cross? First of all as a victory. For Irenaeus and Athanasius, death and corruption had taken hold of the human race. God the Son became human, lived our life again and got it right, entered death, and broke it from the inside, so that we can share his life. The Easter icon shows Christ standing on the broken gates of hell, pulling Adam and Eve from their tombs. For the East the incarnation, the cross and the resurrection are one rescue, and salvation means more than being let off: it means being healed and drawn into God's own life.

Why couldn't God just forgive? Anselm of Canterbury, in 1098, said he could not, without making sin not matter. Sin withholds the honour every creature owes God, and justice requires either that it be repaid or that it be punished. No human can repay it, because we owe God everything already; only God could, but only a human ought to. So only one who is both God and man could make satisfaction. Abelard, a generation later, answered that the cross works on us, not on God: it shows a love so great that it wins our love in return. Most theologians since have thought each was half right.

What is penal substitution? It is the view, taught by the Reformers, that on the cross Christ bore the penalty for sin in our place, so that God is 'just, and the justifier' of those who trust him (Romans 3:26), and 'him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf' (2 Corinthians 5:21). Calvin insisted that the Father's love came first: God did not love us because Christ died; Christ died because God loved us. Catholics teach that Christ's death made satisfaction, and is made present in the Mass; the Orthodox speak mainly of victory and healing. All three use all the pictures; they differ over which comes first.

Is it fair for an innocent person to be punished? Thomas Paine said no: a debt can be paid by another, but a crime cannot, and to punish the innocent for the guilty is 'indiscriminate revenge'. Kant said moral guilt cannot be transferred. Socinus said that if a debt is paid, it is not forgiven. These are serious objections, and they hit hardest at a crude picture: an angry Father and an innocent third party. The tradition's reply is that there are not two parties but one: 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself'. The judge takes the sentence on himself; the Son gives his life freely. Whether that answers the objection, or only moves it, is the question the journey left with you.

Is the cross 'divine child abuse'? Some critics, and some victims of abuse, have heard the story that way, and Christians must take the danger seriously: the cross has been used to tell people to accept suffering they should resist. But every main tradition denies that the Father inflicts the cross on an unwilling Son. Jesus is an adult who 'lays down his life' (John 10:18), and the Father and Son act as one. René Girard read the cross as the moment the old cycle of scapegoating was exposed: here, for once, the story is told from the side of the innocent victim.

So why did Jesus have to die? The New Testament does not say God needed blood. It says that the world was in the grip of sin and death, and that God came into it to set it free, at the cost of his own life. The pictures say the same thing from five sides: he is the sacrifice that cleanses, the ransom that frees, the victor who defeats death, the one who stands in our place before the judge, and the example of a love that does not hit back. No one picture holds it all, which is why the New Testament keeps them all.

What does 'Jesus died for our sins' mean, then? In the plainest words: that what is wrong with us and with the world matters to God more than we think; that he did not stand at a distance from it but took it into himself; and that on the cross the worst that humans do met the best that God is, and the best won. John's Gospel puts it in one sentence that many people know by heart: 'God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son.'

Whether you believe it or not, this idea has shaped the West more than most. It lies behind the conviction that guilt is real and must be faced, not denied; that forgiveness is costly; that the innocent victim is the one whose side we must take; and that love may be measured by what it is willing to give up. When people speak of self-sacrifice, or of someone 'taking the blame', or of a scapegoat, they are speaking the language of this journey.

'Is penal substitution morally defensible?'
'Why does the New Testament use so many images for the death of Christ?'
To whom was the ransom paid? Discuss with reference to Mark 10:45, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus.

Does René Girard's account of the scapegoat explain the cross, or explain it away?
How far does Jewish practice of the Day of Atonement since AD 70 challenge the Christian claim that sacrifice was needed?
