reading.title: Paul: A Biography
reading.why: A lively life of Paul, from Tarsus to Rome, by a leading scholar.

reading.author: Krister Stendahl
reading.title: Paul Among Jews and Gentiles
reading.why: Short essays that changed how scholars read Paul's 'conversion'.

reading.author: Alan Segal
reading.title: Paul the Convert
reading.why: A Jewish scholar's study of Paul as a convert in the world of first-century Judaism.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Ananias called his enemy 'Brother Saul'. Think of someone you find it hard to deal with. Once this week, greet them warmly before they have done anything to deserve it.
sessions.reflect: Is there anything you are sure of now that you once fought against? What changed your mind?
takeaways: Stephen, a Greek-speaking believer, was stoned for teaching that God was not confined to the Temple; he died praying to Jesus and forgiving his killers.
The persecution that followed scattered the believers to Judea, Samaria and beyond, and they preached wherever they went.
Saul the zealous Pharisee, stopped on the Damascus road by the risen Jesus, became Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles; Acts and his own letters agree on the core of the story.

sessions.title: To the ends of the earth
sessions.line: A prisoner reaches Rome. A letter sent ahead of him greets more than two dozen friends by name. How a network of households crossed an empire.
sessions.plain: In about twenty-five years Paul and others carried the message from Syria across what is now Turkey and Greece to Rome, the capital of the world. They travelled on Roman roads and ships, spoke the Greek that everyone understood, and began in the Jewish synagogues found in every city. They left behind not buildings but small groups meeting in homes, linked by letters and visitors. This session asks why Christianity spread so fast, and who carried it, including the women Paul greets by name.
sessions.why: Session 2 ended with Saul turned into Paul, sent to the Gentiles. Now we follow him to 'the uttermost parts of the earth' of Acts 1:8, and ask how a movement of Jewish witnesses became a network across the empire.
answers: Why did Christianity spread so fast?
Where did Paul go, and how did he travel?
What was a house church?
Who were the women in the early Church?
How many Christians were there?
sessions.finding: Roman roads, the Greek language and the Jewish synagogues carried the message; Paul's letters built a network of small households across the empire.

paras: After the Damascus road, Paul spent some years in Arabia, Damascus and his home city of Tarsus. Then Barnabas brought him to Antioch in Syria, the third city of the empire, where Greek-speaking believers had begun to welcome non-Jews and where the name 'Christians' was first used (Acts 11:25–26). From Antioch, about AD 46, the church sent Barnabas and Paul out on the first of what are often called Paul's missionary journeys.

The great question of those years was whether non-Jews had to become Jews, by circumcision and keeping the law of Moses, to belong to Jesus's people. A meeting of the apostles in Jerusalem, about AD 49, decided that they did not (Acts 15). That decision opened the door to the Gentile world.
background.key: From Antioch, where non-Jews were first welcomed, Paul set out about AD 46; around 49 the apostles agreed Gentiles need not become Jews.

paras: Acts describes three journeys and a final voyage. They are a convenient way to remember a life of almost constant movement. Paul usually stayed in a city long enough to found a church, sometimes a few weeks, sometimes two or three years, then moved on and kept in touch by letter and by sending co-workers.

timeline.text: First journey: Cyprus and southern Galatia (central Turkey), with Barnabas
The meeting in Jerusalem (Acts 15)
Second journey: across Turkey to Macedonia and Greece: Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth
1 Thessalonians, probably the oldest surviving Christian writing
Third journey: nearly three years in Ephesus; letters to Corinth and Galatia
Romans written from Corinth; Paul arrested in Jerusalem
Two years in prison at Caesarea; appeals to the emperor
Shipwrecked on Malta; two years under house arrest in Rome
Paul executed in Rome under Nero, according to early tradition

background.key: Three journeys and a voyage, AD 46 to 62, from Antioch through Turkey and Greece to Rome.

paras: Paul did not found the church in Rome. When he wrote to it, about AD 57, it already existed, probably begun by Jewish believers who had travelled there. The Roman historian Suetonius records that the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus', very likely a garbled reference to arguments about Christ; Acts mentions the same expulsion (18:2), which is usually dated to AD 49. Among those expelled were Prisca (or Priscilla) and Aquila, a Jewish couple who became Paul's closest friends.
Rome was a city of perhaps a million people, with a Jewish community of tens of thousands, many of them freed slaves and their descendants.
background.key: The church in Rome existed before Paul; Claudius's expulsion of Jews, about AD 49, probably followed arguments about Christ.

paras: The main reading has two parts. The end of Acts (28:16–31) brings Paul to Rome as a prisoner, still preaching: the 'ends of the earth' reached. The end of Romans (16:1–16) is a list of greetings that most readers skip, but historians treasure, because it shows who the first Christians in Rome actually were.

The comparison is from Lucian, a Greek satirist of the second century who disliked Christians. Writing about a con man who exploited them, he describes, without meaning to, how they cared for each other across cities.
background.key: Paul in Rome and his greetings to its Christians; then a pagan satirist's mocking account of how Christians looked after their own.

before: In Acts 28, who does Paul speak to first in Rome, and why?
Count the women in Romans 16. What does Paul say they did?
What does Lucian mock the Christians for, and what does he admire without meaning to?
sessions.readWhy: Paul reaches Rome, and a list of names shows who the church there was.

paras: When we entered into Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard, but Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.

After three days Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews. When they had come together, he said to them, “I, brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the customs of our fathers, still was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
who, when they had examined me, desired to set me free, because there was no cause of death in me.
But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar, not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation.
For this cause therefore I asked to see you and to speak with you. For because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.”
They said to him, “We neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor did any of the brothers come here and report or speak any evil of you.
But we desire to hear from you what you think. For, as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.”

When they had appointed him a day, many people came to him at his lodging. He explained to them, testifying about God’s Kingdom, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening.
Some believed the things which were spoken, and some disbelieved.
When they didn’t agree among themselves, they departed after Paul had spoken one word, “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers,
saying,

‘Go to this people and say,
in hearing, you will hear,
but will in no way understand.
In seeing, you will see,
but will in no way perceive.

For this people’s heart has grown callous.
Their ears are dull of hearing.
Their eyes they have closed.
Lest they should see with their eyes,
hear with their ears,
understand with their heart,
and would turn again,
then I would heal them.’
“Be it known therefore to you, that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen.”
When he had said these words, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves.
Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house and received all who were coming to him,
preaching God’s Kingdom, and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.
I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae,
that you receive her in the Lord, in a way worthy of the saints, and that you assist her in whatever matter she may need from you, for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,
who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles.
Greet the assembly that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first fruits of Achaia to Christ.
Greet Mary, who labored much for us.
Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who were also in Christ before me.
Greet Amplias, my beloved in the Lord.
Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and Stachys, my beloved.
Greet Apelles, the approved in Christ. Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus.
Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet them of the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord.
Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored much in the Lord.
Greet Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.
Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.
Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
Greet one another with a holy kiss. The assemblies of Christ greet you.

parts.title: Paul in Rome
parts.context: About AD 60. Paul has been arrested in Jerusalem after a riot, held for two years at Caesarea and, as a Roman citizen, has appealed to the emperor's court. After a shipwreck on Malta he reaches Rome under guard. These are the last verses of Acts.

commentary.on: Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.
commentary.text: This is house arrest: Paul rents his own lodging, chained to a soldier, waiting for his case to be heard. The word 'we' at the start of the verse is the last of the 'we' passages: the writer seems to have made the voyage with him.

commentary.on: After three days Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews.
commentary.text: As in every city, Paul begins with the synagogue. Rome had many synagogues; inscriptions from the Jewish catacombs name at least eleven. This was Paul's method throughout: the Jewish community, and the non-Jews who attended synagogues as 'God-fearers', were the first to hear.

commentary.on: For because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.
commentary.text: Paul does not say he is in chains for a new religion. He says it is for 'the hope of Israel': the resurrection and the Messiah, promised in Israel's Scriptures. To the end of Acts, the faith is presented as Israel's own story fulfilled.

commentary.on: as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.
commentary.text: Thirty years after the cross, the Roman Jewish leaders know of the movement, and know it is 'spoken against' everywhere. This is the reputation that Roman writers will confirm.

commentary.on: both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening
commentary.text: The method again: an argument from the Scriptures, all day long. The first Christian mission was a mission of reading and explaining texts, which is one reason Christianity became a religion of books.

commentary.on: the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen.
commentary.text: The words are hard, quoting Isaiah's warning that the people would hear and not understand. They have been misused against Jews. Luke's point is not that God has abandoned Israel (Paul himself argued the opposite in Romans 11), but that the message now goes to all peoples.

commentary.on: preaching God's Kingdom, and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.
commentary.text: The last word of Acts in Greek is akolytos, 'unhindered'. The prisoner in chains is free to speak. Luke ends with the message in the capital of the world, and leaves the outcome of Paul's trial untold, perhaps because his readers knew it.

parts.title: Greet one another
parts.context: About AD 57, from Corinth. Paul has written his longest letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he hopes to visit on his way to Spain. He ends with a list of greetings to friends and co-workers already there, many of whom he had met elsewhere, in the cities where they had lived.

commentary.on: I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae
commentary.text: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. 'Servant' translates the Greek diakonos, the word that later meant 'deacon'; many translations now say 'deacon'. Phoebe was almost certainly carrying the letter to Rome, and would have read it aloud or explained it there. The most important letter in Christian history was entrusted to a woman.

commentary.on: for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self.
commentary.text: 'Helper' translates prostatis, which in ordinary Greek means a patron or benefactor: someone of means who protected and supported others. Phoebe was probably a woman of some wealth who used it for the church, and for Paul.

commentary.on: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus
commentary.text: Prisca is named before her husband, as she is in most mentions of them, which was unusual and may mean she was the more prominent. They were tent-makers like Paul, and lived in Rome, Corinth and Ephesus in turn, moving with their trade. Paul calls them not helpers but 'fellow workers'.

commentary.on: Greet the assembly that is in their house.
commentary.text: This is a house church. There were no church buildings for two centuries. Christians met in the homes of members who had enough room, often a workshop with living rooms above, or an apartment. Rome probably had several such groups, which may be why Paul greets people in clusters.

commentary.on: Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who were also in Christ before me.
commentary.text: Junia is a woman's name. Andronicus and Junia were probably a married couple, Jewish believers ('relatives' means fellow Jews) who had followed Jesus before Paul did, had been in prison with him, and were 'notable among the apostles'. Whether that means they were apostles, or well known to the apostles, is debated; most ancient readers, including John Chrysostom in the fourth century, took it to mean that Junia was an apostle.

commentary.on: Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord.
commentary.text: Two women with similar names, perhaps sisters, perhaps freed slaves of the same household: the names mean something like 'Dainty' and 'Delicate'. Paul praises their hard work, 'labour', the same word he uses for his own missionary work.

commentary.on: Greet Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.
commentary.text: A woman who had mothered Paul. Some think this Rufus was the son of Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus's cross; Mark's Gospel, probably written in Rome, names Simon as 'the father of Alexander and Rufus' (Mark 15:21). It is possible, not certain.

commentary.on: Greet one another with a holy kiss.
commentary.text: The kiss of peace, given between believers in worship, men and women, slaves and free. Outsiders misunderstood it, as we will see. It is still exchanged, often as a handshake, in many churches today.

paras: 'It was now that he came across the priests and scribes of the Christians, in Palestine, and picked up their queer creed. I can tell you, he pretty soon convinced them of his superiority; prophet, elder, ruler of the Synagogue--he was everything at once; expounded their books, commented on them, wrote books himself. They took him for a God, accepted his laws, and declared him their president. The Christians, you know, worship a man to this day,--the distinguished personage who introduced their novel rites, and was crucified on that account. Well, the end of it was that Proteus was arrested and thrown into prison. This was the very thing to lend an air to his favourite arts of clap-trap and wonder-working; he was now a made man. The Christians took it all very seriously: he was no sooner in prison, than they began trying every means to get him out again,--but without success. Everything else that could be done for him they most devoutly did. They thought of nothing else. Orphans and ancient widows might be seen hanging about the prison from break of day. Their officials bribed the gaolers to let them sleep inside with him. Elegant dinners were conveyed in; their sacred writings were read;

and our old friend Peregrine (as he was still called in those days) became for them "the modern Socrates." In some of the Asiatic cities, too, the Christian communities put themselves to the expense of sending deputations, with offers of sympathy, assistance, and legal advice. The activity of these people, in dealing with any matter that affects their community, is something extraordinary; they spare no trouble, no expense. Peregrine, all this time, was making quite an income on the strength of his bondage; money came pouring in. You see, these misguided creatures start with the general conviction that they are immortal for all time, which explains the contempt of death and voluntary self-devotion which are so common among them; and then it was impressed on them by their original lawgiver that they are all brothers, from the moment that they are converted, and deny the gods of Greece, and worship the crucified sage, and live after his laws. All this they take quite on trust, with the result that they despise all worldly goods alike, regarding them merely as common property. Now an adroit, unscrupulous fellow, who has seen the world, has only to get among these simple souls, and his fortune is pretty soon made; he plays with them.

parts.author: Lucian of Samosata
parts.translator: H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler (1905)
parts.title: The Christians took it all very seriously
parts.context: Lucian (about AD 125 to after 180) was a Syrian who wrote witty satires in Greek. This piece mocks Peregrinus, a wandering philosopher who burned himself to death at the Olympic Games of AD 165 to win fame. Here Lucian looks back on an episode in Peregrinus's earlier life, when he joined the Christians in Palestine. 'The Synagogue' is the Christian assembly; 'the crucified sage' is Jesus. Translated by the brothers H. W. and F. G. Fowler, Oxford, 1905. The Fowlers use pounds for the sums of money later in the story.
parts.plain: Lucian says: this con man went to Palestine, joined the Christians and quickly became one of their leaders. When he was put in prison, the Christians did everything they could for him. Widows and orphans waited outside from dawn; their leaders bribed the guards to sleep inside; they brought him meals and read their holy books to him; churches in other cities sent people and money to help. They do this, Lucian says, because they believe they are immortal, so they do not fear death; and because their founder taught them they are all brothers. They share everything, and that makes them easy for a clever crook to exploit.

commentary.on: The Christians, you know, worship a man to this day,--the distinguished personage who introduced their novel rites, and was crucified on that account.
commentary.text: A non-Christian witness of the 160s, writing to sneer, confirms the essentials: Christians worship Jesus, he founded their way of life, and he was crucified. Lucian finds this absurd; he does not doubt it.

commentary.on: Orphans and ancient widows might be seen hanging about the prison from break of day.
commentary.text: The people the Church cared for come to care in their turn. Widows and orphans had no protector in the ancient world; in the churches they had a place and a role.

commentary.on: In some of the Asiatic cities, too, the Christian communities put themselves to the expense of sending deputations, with offers of sympathy, assistance, and legal advice.
commentary.text: Here is the network: churches in the province of Asia (western Turkey) send help to a prisoner in Palestine, hundreds of miles away. That is exactly what Paul's letters and visitors had built a century earlier.

commentary.on: The activity of these people, in dealing with any matter that affects their community, is something extraordinary; they spare no trouble, no expense.
commentary.text: The enemy's tribute. Lucian means it as a criticism, a sign of fanaticism. To a historian it is evidence of how strong the bonds were.

commentary.on: it was impressed on them by their original lawgiver that they are all brothers
commentary.text: Lucian's explanation of their behaviour has two parts: they think they are immortal, and they think they are all brothers and sisters. A Christian could hardly have summed it up better.

commentary.on: Now an adroit, unscrupulous fellow, who has seen the world, has only to get among these simple souls, and his fortune is pretty soon made
commentary.text: And here is the sting. Lucian thinks generosity makes them easy to cheat, and he was not wrong: the Didache, a Christian manual of the same period, warns against wandering 'prophets' who ask for money. Openness to strangers was a strength and a risk.

compare.author: Lucian of Samosata
compare.translator: H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler (1905)
compare.why: Lucian of Samosata did not like Christians: he thought them gullible. That makes him a valuable witness. Read what he says they did for a man in prison.
compare.title: A pagan's view

sections.h: Roads, ships and a common language
paras: Christianity was born at a lucky moment for travel. The Roman Empire stretched from Spain to Syria, and for the first time the whole Mediterranean was under one government, at peace. Pirates had been cleared from the sea. Roman roads, such as the Via Egnatia, which ran across northern Greece through Philippi and Thessalonica, made it possible to walk from city to city in safety. Ships carried passengers along the coasts each summer.

Just as important, the eastern half of the empire spoke one language. Since Alexander the Great, the common Greek called koine ('common') was used for trade and government from Egypt to the Black Sea, and was widely spoken in Rome itself. Paul could preach in Greek and be understood almost anywhere he went. He wrote his letters in Greek, and all the books of the New Testament were written in it.

Early Christian writers noticed this. Origen, in the third century, argued that God had united the world under Rome so that the message could travel. Whether or not one sees providence in it, historians agree that the roads, the peace and the language made rapid spread possible.
sections.key: One empire at peace, Roman roads and ships, and the common Greek language made it possible to carry a message across the Mediterranean.

paras: Wherever Paul went, he started at the synagogue. By the first century there were Jewish communities in almost every city of the eastern Mediterranean, and in Rome. Estimates of their size vary widely, from a few per cent of the empire's population to as much as a tenth; scholars disagree.

These communities had already done two things that prepared the way. They had translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, in the version called the Septuagint, so the Bible could be read by anyone who knew Greek. And they had attracted non-Jews, called 'God-fearers' in Acts (13:16, 26), who admired the one God and the Jewish moral law and came to the synagogue without becoming Jews.

These God-fearers were often the first to believe Paul's message, which offered them full membership of God's people without circumcision. Many Jews also believed; many did not, and the arguments that followed drove Paul out of synagogue after synagogue. The relationship between the Church and the synagogue, which began here, is the subject of 'One root, two branches', later in this hall.
sections.key: Synagogues in every city, with the Greek Septuagint and their circle of non-Jewish 'God-fearers', were the bridge by which the message reached the Gentile world.

paras: Paul did not build churches; he gathered households. In the Roman world a household (oikos in Greek) was not just a family. It included slaves, freed slaves, workers and dependants. When a householder became a Christian, the household often did too: Acts speaks of Lydia 'and her household' at Philippi (16:15) and the jailer 'with all his household' (16:33).

The house church met in the largest room of a member's home, perhaps thirty to fifty people. They ate together, prayed, sang, read the Scriptures and Paul's letters, and shared what they had. Several house churches might exist in one city, linked by visitors and letters. The oldest Christian building yet discovered is just such a house, at Dura-Europos on the river Euphrates in Syria, converted for worship around AD 240: a room for meetings and a small room for baptism with painted walls.

This mattered for growth. People joined because someone they knew, a relative, a master, a neighbour, a fellow worker, invited them in. The sociologist Rodney Stark argued that this is how new religious movements usually grow: through networks of personal relationships, one friend at a time.
sections.key: The first churches were households meeting in homes, perhaps thirty to fifty people; the faith spread through networks of family, work and friendship.

paras: Romans 16 greets more than two dozen people. Ten are women: Phoebe, Prisca, Mary, Junia, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, Persis, the mother of Rufus, Julia and the sister of Nereus. Paul describes several of them in the words he uses for his own work: 'fellow workers', those who 'labour in the Lord'. Phoebe is a diakonos and a patron; Junia is 'notable among the apostles'.

Other sources fit this picture. Lydia, a businesswoman who sold purple cloth, hosted the church at Philippi (Acts 16:14–15). Pliny the Younger, as we will see, tortured two Christian slave women who were 'ministers' of the church. Pagan critics such as Celsus mocked Christianity as a religion of women and slaves. Stark argued that women converted in larger numbers than men, partly because the Church forbade practices that harmed them: infanticide of baby girls, forced abortion, divorce at a husband's whim.
How far women led in the early Church is debated, and it touches a live question for the churches today. The table sets out where they stand.

cols: How they read Phoebe and Junia
rows: Priests and bishops are men only; women serve as religious sisters, lay ministers and theologians. Two papal commissions (2016, 2020) studied the ancient women deacons.
Phoebe served the church; Junia was honoured among the apostles; neither shows women as priests.
Priests and bishops are men only. The office of deaconess existed in the East for centuries (for example, Olympias in Constantinople, about 400) and has been revived in a few places.
Phoebe is honoured as a deaconess; Junia as 'equal to the apostles' in the calendar of saints.
Divided. Many churches ordain women (the Church of England has had women priests since 1994 and bishops since 2015); others, often called 'complementarian', keep the pastor's office for men.
Some see Phoebe and Junia as leaders and models for ordained women today; others as valued servants in roles distinct from the elders'.
table.note: All agree that women were among the earliest and most active Christians, and that Paul named them with honour.

sections.key: Ten of the people Paul greets in Romans 16 are women, described as fellow workers; how far women led is debated, and the churches differ today.

paras: No one counted. Historians must estimate from scattered evidence: the size of house churches, a letter from Rome in AD 251 listing the clergy and the 1,500 widows and poor the church supported (preserved by Eusebius), the number of bishops at councils, the proportion of Christian names in Egyptian papyri.

In 1996 the sociologist Rodney Stark made a famous calculation. Start with perhaps 1,000 believers in AD 40. If the movement grew by about 40 per cent each decade, which is close to the growth rate of the Mormons in the twentieth century, it would reach about 7,500 by AD 100, about 200,000 by 200, some six million by 300, about a tenth of the empire, and over thirty million by 350, more than half. Those figures fit the scattered evidence surprisingly well. The historian Keith Hopkins reached similar estimates independently.

The lesson is that no miracle of mass conversion is needed to explain the numbers. Steady growth, sustained over three centuries, was enough. What needs explaining is why the growth was so steady, for so long.

table.note: Stark assumed an empire of about 60 million and growth of 40% a decade. These are models, not counts; other estimates differ, but most put Christians at around a tenth by 300.

sections.key: Stark estimated growth of about 40 per cent a decade, from 1,000 in AD 40 to six million (a tenth of the empire) by 300: steady growth, not sudden mass conversion.

sections.h: Why did it grow? Three answers
paras: Historians have offered many explanations. Three are the best known.

Edward Gibbon, in chapter 15 of The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776), gave five 'secondary causes': the Christians' uncompromising zeal, inherited from the Jews; their teaching of a future life; the miracles claimed for the early Church; their pure and strict morals; and their organisation, which made them a disciplined community within the state. Gibbon said, with famous irony, that the first cause was the truth of the doctrine and the providence of its author, and then explained everything without it.

Rodney Stark, a sociologist, argued that Christianity grew because it offered better lives: networks of friendship, care in plagues, a higher status for women, larger families, and a welcome in cities that were overcrowded, dirty and full of strangers.

Larry Hurtado, a historian of early Christianity, argued in Destroyer of the Gods (2016) that Christianity was a new kind of religion in the Roman world: exclusive (you could worship only one God), open to every people, centred on books and teaching, and demanding a whole way of life. It was odd, he says, and its oddness was its strength. We will meet more of that oddness in the sessions still to come.
sections.key: Gibbon pointed to zeal, belief in a future life, miracles, morals and organisation; Stark to networks and better lives; Hurtado to a new and distinctive kind of religion.

debate.question: Why did Christianity grow so fast?

positions.name: Gibbon: five human causes
positions.who: Edward Gibbon (1737–1794)
positions.view: Allowing, with a wink, for providence, the growth can be explained by five human causes: zeal, belief in an afterlife, claimed miracles, strict morals and tight organisation. Christianity was a disciplined, confident minority in a tired and tolerant pagan world.
positions.evidence: Decline and Fall, ch. 15; the Church's bishops and councils; the zeal of the martyrs.

positions.name: Stark: networks and better lives
positions.who: Rodney Stark (1934–2022), sociologist
positions.view: Christianity grew as new movements grow, through personal networks, and because it made life better for its members, above all in crises: care in plagues, higher status for women, mutual support in crowded cities. People made a rational choice.
positions.evidence: The steady 40% growth model; studies of modern religious movements; ancient accounts of Christian care in epidemics.

positions.name: Hurtado: a distinctive new religion
positions.who: Larry Hurtado (1943–2019), historian
positions.view: Christianity was unlike other religions of the time. It was exclusive, open to all peoples, built on texts, and it demanded a new way of life. What looked odd and anti-social to outsiders gave its members a strong identity and a message worth dying for.
positions.evidence: Pagan complaints that Christians refused other gods; the early Christian love of books; the moral rules of texts such as the Didache.

debate.agree: All agree that Christianity grew steadily for three centuries without state support, and that its communities, not only its ideas, were the key.

look.why: Rembrandt and his workshop painted the apostle Paul about 1657, not on the road but at his desk: the letter-writer whose words held a network of churches together. The sword is Paul's traditional sign, because by tradition he was beheaded in Rome.
points: An older, bearded man sits in a heavy wooden armchair beside a desk in a shadowy room, his head resting in one hand.
In his other hand, which brushes his knee, he holds a quill.
A stack of papers or parchment lies on the desk.
The oversized hilt of a long sword leans against the wall behind the desk.
He wears a brown robe over a rust-red garment; the brightest highlights, on his collar, the quill and the edges of the parchment, are loosely brushed.
The painting is signed on the face of the desktop, near the lower right corner: 'Rembrandt f.'

music.why: 'All creatures of our God and King', from Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Sun, calls every creature to praise: the song of a message meant for every people.

think.why: The message travelled in Greek along Roman roads: see how Greek thought and the faith of Jerusalem met and shaped each other.

learn.why: Written to the church Paul founded in Corinth, the city from which he wrote Romans. It describes the love that held his scattered households together.

check.q: Why did Paul usually begin in the synagogue when he reached a new city?
options: Because the Romans forbade preaching anywhere else
Because there were no other public buildings
Because Jews and 'God-fearers' already knew the Scriptures and the one God, and the message was 'the hope of Israel'
Because the law required travellers to report there
check.why: Synagogues gave him hearers who knew the Septuagint and awaited the Messiah; God-fearers were often first to believe.

check.q: What does the end of Acts suggest Luke most wanted to show?
options: How Paul's trial ended
That Rome had become Christian
That Paul abandoned the Jews entirely
That the message reached the capital of the world and was preached there 'without hindrance'
check.why: Luke ends with Paul preaching unhindered in Rome, the 'ends of the earth' of Acts 1:8, and leaves the trial untold.

check.q: Why do historians value Romans 16, a list of greetings, so highly?
options: Because it shows who the first Roman Christians were: their names, households, status and the prominence of women
Because it contains Paul's main teaching
Because it proves Peter founded the church in Rome
Because it was written by Phoebe
check.why: The names show house churches, slaves and freed slaves, Jews and Gentiles, and ten women.

check.q: What is the most reasonable reading of 'Andronicus and Junia... notable among the apostles'?
options: Junia was an apostle in the same sense as the Twelve, chosen by Jesus during his ministry
Junia was Paul's wife
Junia was a man called Junias
Junia was a woman, and either counted as an apostle or well known to the apostles; most ancient readers took the first view
check.why: Junia is a woman's name; the phrase is debated, but Chrysostom and most early readers took her as an apostle.

check.q: What does Stark's growth model chiefly show?
options: That Christians were a majority by AD 100
That mass conversions explain the numbers
That steady growth of about 40 per cent a decade over three centuries is enough to reach millions, so what needs explaining is the steadiness
That growth stopped during persecution
check.why: From about 1,000 to about six million by 300, without any sudden mass conversion.

check.q: Why is Lucian useful evidence even though he disliked Christians?
options: Because he was secretly a Christian
Because his account is the oldest Christian text
Because he knew Paul personally
Because a hostile witness has no reason to invent their good deeds: he confirms their care for prisoners, their network and their belief that all are brothers
check.why: He reports the care and generosity in order to mock it, which makes the report more credible.

tutorial.question: Why did Christianity spread so fast in its first three centuries?
tutorial.approach: Start with the conditions: roads, peace, the Greek language and the synagogues. Then explain Paul's method: households, letters and co-workers, using Romans 16. Bring in Lucian as a hostile witness. Use Stark's numbers to show what kind of growth needs explaining. Finally compare Gibbon, Stark and Hurtado, and say which you find most convincing and why.
strong: Explains the role of roads, peace, koine Greek and the synagogues.
Explains house churches and personal networks.
Uses Romans 16 as evidence, including the women.
Uses Lucian's account and explains why a hostile witness is valuable.
Uses Stark's growth figures correctly, as estimates.
Weighs at least two of the three explanations fairly.

reading.title: From Paul to Valentinus
reading.why: A detailed study of the Christians of Rome, starting from Romans 16.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Paul held his network together by writing to people by name. Write to, or message, three people this week who have helped you, and tell each one specifically what they did.
sessions.reflect: Who first brought you into a community you belong to? What did they do that made you stay?
takeaways: Roman roads and peace, the common Greek language and Jewish synagogues with their non-Jewish 'God-fearers' carried the message across the empire.
Paul gathered households, not buildings; Romans 16 shows a network of house churches in Rome, with ten women among those he greets.
Steady growth of perhaps 40 per cent a decade could take a thousand believers to six million by AD 300; historians still debate why the growth was so steady.

sessions.title: How they lived
sessions.line: An old manual for new believers, lost for centuries, shows what the first Christians were taught to do: two ways, one of life and one of death.
sessions.plain: In 1873 a Greek scholar in Constantinople found a short book that had been lost for a thousand years: the Didache, 'the Teaching', a manual for new Christians written perhaps within living memory of the apostles. It sets out 'two ways', one of life and one of death, and gives the earliest prayers for the Christian meal. Other evidence shows what the first Christians became known for: refusing to kill unwanted babies, caring for the sick in plagues when others fled, and sharing a meal. This session asks what the first Christians actually did, and why their way of life drew people in.
sessions.why: Session 3 showed how the message travelled. But people did not join a network only because it existed. Lucian mocked Christians for how they lived. This session looks at that way of life from the inside.
answers: What did the early Christians actually do?
What is the Didache?
How did Christians behave in plagues?
Why did their ethics draw people?
sessions.finding: They were known for what they did: caring for the sick, refusing infanticide and the arena, sharing a meal and praying three times a day.

paras: Session 3 followed the message along Roman roads into households across the empire, and heard a pagan satirist mock the Christians for caring so much for one of their own in prison. What were these households taught? What did joining them mean, day by day?
Paul's letters give some answers, but they are letters to particular churches about particular problems. For a picture of ordinary teaching, we have a remarkable document.
background.key: We know how the message travelled; now we ask what life in the households was like.

paras: Its full title is 'The Teaching of the Lord to the Gentiles by the Twelve Apostles'; it is usually called the Didache, Greek for 'teaching'. Early Christian writers mention it, and some thought it nearly belonged in the Bible, but the text itself disappeared. In 1873 Philotheos Bryennios, a Greek Orthodox scholar and later archbishop, found it in a manuscript copied in 1056, in a library in Constantinople. He published it in 1883, and it caused a sensation.

Nobody knows who wrote it. Its title links it to the apostles, but it does not claim to be written by them. Most scholars think it was put together in stages, probably in Syria, between about AD 50 and 120. Some parts may be as old as Paul's letters. It has sixteen short chapters: a moral teaching called 'the two ways' (1–6), instructions on baptism, fasting, prayer and the Christian meal (7–10), rules for visiting teachers and for local leaders (11–15), and a warning about the end (16).

timeline.text: The Didache is written, probably in Syria
A scribe named Leon copies it in a manuscript now in the library of the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem
Philotheos Bryennios finds the manuscript in Constantinople
Bryennios publishes the Didache
J. B. Lightfoot's English translation, used here, is published after his death

background.key: The Didache, 'the Teaching', is an anonymous manual for new Christians, probably from Syria between AD 50 and 120, rediscovered in 1873.

paras: To see why the Didache's teaching stood out, we need to know three things about the Roman world. First, unwanted babies, especially girls and the disabled, were often 'exposed': left outside to die or to be picked up as slaves. It was legal and common. A letter from Egypt of 1 BC, written by a man named Hilarion to his wife, tells her to keep the baby if it is a boy, and to throw it out if it is a girl.

Second, the great public entertainment was the arena, where gladiators fought to the death and condemned criminals were killed by animals before cheering crowds. Third, epidemics swept the cities regularly. The 'Antonine plague' of AD 165 to about 180 and the 'plague of Cyprian' of about 249 to 262 killed large numbers; in such times, those who could fled the cities and left the sick behind.
background.key: Exposure of unwanted babies was legal and common, the arena was the great entertainment, and plagues regularly emptied the cities.

paras: The main reading is from the Didache: the 'way of life' (chapters 1–4), and the prayers for the Christian meal (chapters 9–10). Chapter 7, on baptism, is read in 'What happens at church', later in this hall.

The comparison is Romans 12, Paul's own summary of how his churches should live, written perhaps a generation before the Didache. Reading them side by side shows how consistent the early teaching was.
background.key: The Didache's 'way of life' and its meal prayers; then Paul's Romans 12 for comparison.

before: How many of the Didache's commands do you recognise from the teaching of Jesus?
Which commands would have seemed strangest to an ordinary Roman?
In the meal prayers, what are the believers thankful for?
sessions.readWhy: The oldest surviving manual of Christian life: what new believers were taught to do, and how they gave thanks at their meal.

paras: There are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First of all, thou shalt love the God that made thee; secondly, thy neighbour as thyself. And all things whatsoever thou wouldest not have befal thyself neither do thou unto another. Now of these words the doctrine is this. Bless them that curse you, and pray for your enemies and fast for them that persecute you; for what thank is it, if ye love them that love you? Do not even the Gentiles the same? But do ye love them that hate you, and ye shall not have an enemy. Abstain thou from fleshly and bodily lusts. If any man give thee a blow on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also, and thou shalt be perfect; if a man impress thee to go with him, one mile, go with him twain; if a man take away thy cloak, give him thy coat also; if a man take away from thee that which is thine own, ask it not back, for neither art thou able. To every man that asketh of thee give, and ask not back; for the Father desireth that gifts be given to all from His own bounties. Blessed is he that giveth according to the commandment; for he is guiltless. Woe to him that receiveth; for, if a man receiveth having need, he is guiltless; but he that hath no need shall give satisfaction why and wherefore he received; and being put in confinement he shall be examined concerning the deeds that he hath done, and he shall not come out thence until he hath given back the last farthing. Yea, as touching this also it is said; Let thine alms sweat into thine hands, until thou shalt have learnt to whom to give.

And this is the second commandment of the teaching. Thou shalt do no murder, thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not corrupt boys, thou shalt not commit fornication, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not deal in magic, thou shalt do no sorcery, thou shalt not murder a child by abortion nor kill them when born, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's goods, thou shalt not perjure thyself, thou shalt not bear false witness, thou shalt not speak evil, thou shalt not cherish a grudge, thou shalt not be double-minded nor double-tongued; for the double tongue is a snare of death. Thy word shall not be false or empty, but fulfilled by action. Thou shalt not be avaricious nor a plunderer nor a hypocrite nor ill-tempered nor proud. Thou shalt not entertain an evil design against thy neighbour. Thou shalt not hate any man, but some thou shalt reprove, and for others thou shalt pray, and others thou shalt love more than thy life.

My child, flee from every evil and everything that resembleth it. Be not angry, for anger leadeth to murder, nor jealous nor contentious nor wrathful; for of all these things murders are engendered. My child, be not lustful, for lust leadeth to fornication, neither foul-speaking neither with uplifted eyes; for of all these things adulteries are engendered. My child, be no dealer in omens, since it leads to idolatry, nor an enchanter nor an astrologer nor a magician, neither be willing to look at them; for from all these things idolatry is engendered. My child, be not a liar, since lying leads to theft, neither avaricious neither vainglorious; for from all these things thefts are engendered. My child, be not a murmurer, since it leadeth to blasphemy, neither self-willed neither a thinker of evil thoughts; for from all these things blasphemies are engendered. But be meek, since the meek shall inherit the earth. Be long-suffering and pitiful and guileless and quiet and kindly and always fearing the words which thou hast heard. Thou shalt not exalt thyself, neither shalt thou admit boldness into thy soul. Thy soul shall not cleave together with the lofty, but with the righteous and humble shalt thou walk. The accidents that befal thee thou shalt receive as good, knowing that nothing is done without God.

My child, thou shalt remember him that speaketh unto thee the word of God night and day, and shalt honour him as the Lord; for whencesoever the Lordship speaketh, there is the Lord. Moreover thou shalt seek out day by day the persons of the saints, that thou mayest find rest in their words. Thou shalt not make a schism, but thou shalt pacify them that contend; thou shalt judge righteously, thou shalt not make a difference in a person to reprove him for transgressions. Thou shalt not doubt whether a thing shall be or not be. Be not thou found holding out thy hands to receive, but drawing them in as to giving. If thou hast ought passing through thy hands, thou shalt give a ransom for thy sins. Thou shalt not hesitate to give, neither shalt thou murmur when giving; for thou shalt know who is the good paymaster of thy reward. Thou shalt not turn away from him that is in want, but shalt make thy brother partaker in all things, and shalt not say that anything is thine own.

For if ye are fellow-partakers in that which is imperishable, how much rather in the things which are perishable? Thou shalt not withhold thy hand from thy son or from thy daughter, but from their youth thou shalt teach them the fear of God. Thou shalt not command thy bondservant or thine handmaid in thy bitterness, who trust in the same God as thyself, lest haply they should cease to fear the God who is over both of you; for He cometh, not to call men with respect of persons, but He cometh to those whom the Spirit hath prepared. But ye, servants, shall be subject unto your masters, as to a type of God, in shame and fear. Thou shalt hate all hypocrisy, and everything that is not pleasing to the Lord. Thou shalt never forsake the commandments of the Lord; but shalt keep those things which thou hast received, neither adding to them nor taking away from them. In church thou shalt confess thy transgressions, and shalt not betake thyself to prayer with an evil conscience. This is the way of life.

But as touching the eucharistic thanksgiving give ye thanks thus. First, as regards the cup: We give Thee thanks, O our Father, for the holy vine of Thy son David, which Thou madest known unto us through Thy Son Jesus; Thine is the glory for ever and ever. Then as regards the broken bread: We give Thee thanks, O our Father, for the life and knowledge which Thou didst make known unto us through Thy Son Jesus; Thine is the glory for ever and ever. As this broken bread was scattered upon the mountains and being gathered together became one, so may Thy Church be gathered together from the ends of the earth into Thy kingdom; for Thine is the glory and the power through Jesus Christ for ever and ever. But let no one eat or drink of this eucharistic thanksgiving, but they that have been baptized into the name of the Lord; for concerning this also the Lord hath said: Give not that which is holy to the dogs.

And after ye are satisfied thus give ye thanks: We give Thee thanks, Holy Father, for Thy holy name, which Thou hast made to tabernacle in our hearts, and for the knowledge and faith and immortality, which Thou hast made known unto us through Thy Son Jesus; Thine is the glory for ever and ever. Thou, Almighty Master, didst create all things for Thy name's sake, and didst give food and drink unto men for enjoyment, that they might render thanks to Thee; but didst bestow upon us spiritual food and drink and eternal life through Thy Son. Before all things we give Thee thanks that Thou art powerful; Thine is the glory for ever and ever. Remember, Lord, Thy Church to deliver it from all evil and to perfect it in Thy love; and gather it together from the four winds--even the Church which has been sanctified--into Thy kingdom which Thou hast prepared for it; for Thine is the power and the glory for ever and ever. May grace come and may this world pass away. Hosanna to the God of David. If any man is holy, let him come; if any man is not, let him repent. Maran Atha. Amen. But permit the prophets to offer thanksgiving as much as they desire.

parts.author: Anonymous
parts.work: The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
parts.translator: J. B. Lightfoot, ed. J. R. Harmer (1891)
parts.who: An unknown teacher or teachers in the earliest Church, writing for Gentile converts
parts.when: Probably Syria, between about AD 50 and 120
parts.title: The way of life
parts.context: The opening of the Didache. It is written as a teacher speaks to a pupil ('my child'), for people preparing to be baptised. Its pattern of 'two ways' is Jewish: Moses set before Israel 'life and death' (Deuteronomy 30:19), and the Dead Sea Scrolls describe two spirits, of truth and falsehood. Much of chapter 1 gathers sayings of Jesus from the Sermon on the Mount. Translated by J. B. Lightfoot (1828–1889), Bishop of Durham, published in 1891.
parts.plain: There are two ways of living, the teacher says: one leads to life, the other to death. The way of life is to love God and your neighbour, and not to do to others what you would not want done to you. That means blessing enemies, giving to anyone who asks, and not demanding things back. It also means not murdering, stealing or lying, not using magic, not killing a child before or after birth, not being greedy, proud or angry. Be humble, stay with good people, accept what happens as coming from God, share everything with your fellow believers, teach your children about God, and treat servants kindly.

commentary.on: There are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways.
commentary.text: The first line sets the frame. Christianity was taught first as a way to walk, not a set of ideas to hold. That is why its earliest name was 'the Way'.

commentary.on: First of all, thou shalt love the God that made thee; secondly, thy neighbour as thyself.
commentary.text: These are the two great commandments Jesus gave, from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18 (Mark 12:29–31). Then comes the Golden Rule in its negative form, as the Jewish teacher Hillel had taught it a generation before Jesus.

commentary.on: But do ye love them that hate you, and ye shall not have an enemy.
commentary.text: A lovely addition to Jesus's command to love enemies: if you love those who hate you, you will have no enemies, because an enemy is someone you hate. The Didache turns a hard saying into a promise.

commentary.on: To every man that asketh of thee give, and ask not back
commentary.text: Generosity without conditions, followed at once by a warning to those who receive without need. The teacher knows that open hands attract freeloaders, the problem Lucian mocked.

commentary.on: Let thine alms sweat into thine hands, until thou shalt have learnt to whom to give.
commentary.text: A vivid saying from an unknown source: hold your gift until it sweats in your hand, and think before you give. The Didache balances unconditional giving with good sense.

commentary.on: thou shalt not murder a child by abortion nor kill them when born
commentary.text: Here is the sharpest break with Roman custom. In a list that otherwise follows the Ten Commandments, the Didache adds abortion and infanticide, both legal and common in the Roman world. This is the earliest Christian text to forbid them; Jews had already rejected exposure, and Christians took the rule from them.

commentary.on: thou shalt not deal in magic, thou shalt do no sorcery
commentary.text: Magic was everywhere in the ancient world: curse tablets, love charms, spells for health. Converts had to give it up. In Ephesus, Acts says, new believers burned books of magic worth fifty thousand silver coins (Acts 19:19).

commentary.on: My child, flee from every evil and everything that resembleth it.
commentary.text: Chapter 3 traces how small sins grow into great ones: anger leads to murder, lust to adultery, lying to theft. This is the same insight as Jesus's teaching that anger is the root of murder (Matthew 5:21–22).

commentary.on: Thou shalt not withhold thy hand from thy son or from thy daughter, but from their youth thou shalt teach them the fear of God.
commentary.text: Children, daughters as well as sons, are to be brought up and taught. In a world where daughters could be thrown away, that is a statement of their worth.

commentary.on: Thou shalt not command thy bondservant or thine handmaid in thy bitterness, who trust in the same God as thyself
commentary.text: The Didache does not abolish slavery, and the next line tells slaves to obey. No ancient society abolished it, and this text does not either. But it tells masters that their slaves trust 'the same God', who is over both: the seed of an idea that would one day undo slavery.

commentary.on: In church thou shalt confess thy transgressions, and shalt not betake thyself to prayer with an evil conscience.
commentary.text: Confession of sins in the assembly before prayer. The way of life is not a solitary path; it is walked together, with honesty about failure.

parts.author: Anonymous
parts.work: The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
parts.translator: J. B. Lightfoot, ed. J. R. Harmer (1891)
parts.who: An unknown teacher or teachers in the earliest Church, writing for Gentile converts
parts.when: Probably Syria, between about AD 50 and 120
parts.title: The thanksgiving
parts.context: Chapters 9 and 10 give prayers for the Christian meal, which the Didache calls the 'eucharist', from the Greek for 'thanksgiving'. They are among the oldest Christian prayers outside the New Testament. Chapters 5 to 8, which come between, describe the way of death and give rules on food, baptism, fasting and prayer: the Lord's Prayer is to be said three times a day, and fasts are kept on Wednesdays and Fridays.
parts.plain: Give thanks like this, the teacher says. Over the cup: thank you, Father, for the 'holy vine of David' you made known through Jesus. Over the bread: thank you for the life and knowledge you made known through Jesus. As grain scattered on the hills became one loaf, may your Church be gathered from the ends of the earth into your kingdom. Only the baptised may eat. Afterwards, give thanks for God's name, for knowledge, faith and eternal life, for food and drink, and pray for the Church to be made perfect in love and gathered into God's kingdom. 'Maran Atha': our Lord, come.

commentary.on: for the holy vine of Thy son David, which Thou madest known unto us through Thy Son Jesus
commentary.text: The prayer is thoroughly Jewish in shape: it blesses God over the cup and the bread, as Jewish table prayers do. The 'vine of David' is Israel, God's people, and its promised king. The new believers are thanking God for bringing them into Israel's story.

commentary.on: As this broken bread was scattered upon the mountains and being gathered together became one
commentary.text: One of the most beautiful images of the early Church. Wheat grown on many hillsides becomes one loaf; people from many nations become one Church. It is the network of the last session, seen from inside, as a prayer.

commentary.on: But let no one eat or drink of this eucharistic thanksgiving, but they that have been baptized into the name of the Lord
commentary.text: The meal is for members. That was one reason for suspicion: outsiders could not see what happened at it, and rumours grew, as session 5, still to come, will show.

commentary.on: and didst give food and drink unto men for enjoyment, that they might render thanks to Thee
commentary.text: Food is for enjoyment, and for thanks. There is nothing grim or world-hating in this prayer. Ordinary food and drink are God's gifts, and the 'spiritual food' of the meal is given on top of them.

commentary.on: Remember, Lord, Thy Church to deliver it from all evil and to perfect it in Thy love
commentary.text: The prayer asks not for power or numbers but for the Church to be delivered from evil and 'perfected in love'. That was its idea of success.

commentary.on: May grace come and may this world pass away.
commentary.text: The first Christians lived expecting the end of this age and the coming of God's kingdom. Notice that the expectation did not make them careless about this world: the same document tells them to feed the poor and teach their children.

commentary.on: Maran Atha. Amen.
commentary.text: Maranatha is Aramaic, the language of Jesus: 'Our Lord, come!' Paul uses the same word, untranslated, in a Greek letter (1 Corinthians 16:22). An Aramaic prayer to Jesus as 'Lord', kept in Greek-speaking churches, shows that praying to Jesus began among the first Jewish believers, not later among Greeks.

paras: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.
For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor preferring one another;
not lagging in diligence; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
rejoicing in hope; enduring in troubles; continuing steadfastly in prayer;
contributing to the needs of the saints; given to hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.
Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.
Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
Therefore
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

parts.title: A living sacrifice
parts.context: After eleven chapters on what God has done in Christ, Paul turns to how believers should live. 'Therefore' links the two: the way of life follows from the gift. This is the passage that other journeys in Rose Window point back to.

commentary.on: present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service
commentary.text: In every temple of the empire, animals were sacrificed. Paul says the Christian sacrifice is the believer's own body, the whole of a person's daily life, offered to God. Christians had no altars; their lives were their worship.

commentary.on: Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind
commentary.text: A different way of thinking, producing a different way of living. This is what Hurtado means by Christianity's 'oddness': it asked people to stop fitting in.

commentary.on: so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another
commentary.text: The same idea as the Didache's loaf: many become one. Each person has a different gift, and each is needed. Slaves and masters, men and women, belonged to one body.

commentary.on: contributing to the needs of the saints; given to hospitality
commentary.text: 'Saints' means simply fellow believers. Hospitality, welcoming travellers into your home, held the network together: it is how Phoebe, carrying this letter, would be received in Rome.

commentary.on: Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don't curse.
commentary.text: This echoes Jesus: 'bless those who curse you' (Luke 6:28), the same saying the Didache quotes in its first chapter. Paul does not name Jesus here, but the teaching is his.

commentary.on: associate with the humble
commentary.text: Or 'with lowly people'. In a society obsessed with rank and honour, this was a reversal. Paul's churches mixed people who would never have eaten together anywhere else.

commentary.on: If your enemy is hungry, feed him.
commentary.text: Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21–22. The 'coals of fire' are probably the burning shame that kindness can bring, which may lead an enemy to change.

commentary.on: Don't be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
commentary.text: Paul's whole ethic in eleven words. It is not passive. Evil is to be defeated, but by its opposite.

compare.why: Paul wrote Romans 12 to Christians in Rome about AD 57, perhaps a generation before the Didache took its final form. Compare his teaching with the Didache's 'way of life'.
compare.title: Overcome evil with good

sections.h: A way, not only a belief
paras: The Didache begins not with doctrine but with conduct. That fits everything else we know about the first Christians. Outsiders noticed what they did before they understood what they believed. Pliny, as we will see, found that their oath was not to commit theft, adultery or fraud. Lucian found that they cared for prisoners. Galen, the greatest doctor of the age, was struck by their self-control.

This is not because belief did not matter. The Didache's way of life rests on the two commandments, love of God and neighbour, and on the conviction, which runs through Romans 12, that God's mercy comes first and life is the response. But the early Church expected faith to be visible. A person was taught the way before baptism, and baptised into a community that would hold them to it.

The Church historian Alan Kreider called this 'the patient ferment': Christians did not usually preach in public, but lived in a way that made neighbours ask questions, then taught those who came, slowly, over months or years.
sections.key: The first Christians were taught a way of life before baptism; outsiders noticed their conduct before they understood their beliefs.

paras: The Didache's ban on abortion and infanticide is repeated in almost every early Christian moral text. The Letter of Barnabas says the same; so do the second-century defenders of the faith. Christians did not only refuse to expose their own children. Some took in children others had abandoned.

They were not the first. Jews had long refused to expose infants, and the Roman historian Tacitus thought it one of their odd customs that they reared all their children. A few pagan philosophers agreed: the Stoic teacher Musonius Rufus, in the first century, argued that exposure was wrong. But Christians made it a rule for everyone, slave and free, and their growing numbers made it matter.

The arena was refused for similar reasons. Christian writers such as Tertullian (around 200) told believers not to go to the games, because watching people killed for pleasure corrupted the soul. When gladiatorial games finally ended in the early fifth century, Christian emperors and bishops had pressed against them for a hundred years. The Christian view that every human life mattered, including the unwanted baby and the condemned criminal, came from the conviction that every person is made in the image of God.
sections.key: Christians, following the Jews, refused abortion and infanticide and kept away from the arena, because every human life bore God's image.

paras: The heart of Christian life was a shared meal. Paul calls it 'the Lord's supper' (1 Corinthians 11:20); the Didache calls it the 'eucharist', the thanksgiving. At first it seems to have been a real meal, eaten together in a house, with the bread and cup given special prayers. Later the token meal of bread and wine was separated from the full supper, which was called the agape, the 'love feast'.

Three things about the meal shaped the community. It was shared across social boundaries: slaves and owners ate at one table, which hardly happened anywhere else. It was for members, which bound them together and made outsiders suspicious. And its prayers looked outwards, to the Church being gathered 'from the ends of the earth', and forwards, to the kingdom: 'Maranatha', our Lord, come.

The Didache's meal prayers have no account of the Last Supper, and scholars debate how its meal relates to the Eucharist described by Paul and the Gospels. How the meal developed into the services Christians hold today is the subject of 'What happens at church', later in this hall.
sections.key: The shared meal, the 'eucharist' or thanksgiving, crossed social boundaries, bound the members together and looked forward to God's kingdom.

sections.h: The rhythm of a Christian day
paras: The Didache gives a rhythm as well as a code. Christians fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, not on the Mondays and Thursdays when other pious Jews fasted. They say the Lord's Prayer three times a day (Didache 8), as devout Jews prayed morning, afternoon and evening (Daniel 6:10; Psalm 55:17). Pliny's informants, as we will see, said Christians met before dawn on a fixed day; that day was Sunday, the day of the resurrection, which Christians called 'the Lord's day' (Revelation 1:10).

This rhythm made faith a matter of every day and every week, not only of festivals. It also made Christians recognisable: the household that fasted on Friday and stopped work to pray three times a day was visibly different from its neighbours.

The pattern of daily prayer at fixed hours became the 'offices' of the monasteries and the morning and evening prayer of the churches, and the week with its Sunday became the week of the West. Rose Window's own daily rhythm follows it.
sections.key: The Didache sets a rhythm: the Lord's Prayer three times a day, fasts on Wednesday and Friday, the meeting on the Lord's day.

paras: The clearest test of a way of life is a crisis. Around AD 260, during the plague of Cyprian, Dionysius, the bishop of Alexandria, wrote an Easter letter that the historian Eusebius preserved (Church History VII.22). He describes the Christians of the city: 'They held fast to each other and visited the sick fearlessly, and ministered to them continually.' Many caught the disease and died. 'But with the heathen everything was quite otherwise. They deserted those who began to be sick, and fled from their dearest friends.'

Dionysius was a bishop praising his flock, and he may exaggerate both sides. But other evidence agrees. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in the same plague, urged Christians to care for pagans as well as believers. A century later, the emperor Julian, who wanted to revive the old gods, complained that the Christians supported not only their own poor but pagans too, and that the pagan priests must learn to do the same.

Rodney Stark argued that basic nursing, simply bringing food and water to the sick, could have saved many lives in a plague, and that Christians who survived, and pagans they nursed, would have been drawn closer to the Church. This argument has been criticised as speculative, but it shows how care and growth could have gone together.
sections.key: In the plague of about 260, Dionysius of Alexandria says Christians nursed the sick while others fled; the emperor Julian later admitted they cared for pagans too.

sections.h: Lawrence and the treasures of the Church
paras: By the middle of the third century the church in Rome was large and organised. A letter of AD 251 from its bishop, Cornelius, preserved by Eusebius, says it supported more than fifteen hundred widows and people in need. Deacons managed this care.

One of them, Lawrence, became the most famous martyr of Rome. In August 258 the emperor Valerian ordered the execution of Christian clergy; Bishop Sixtus II was put to death on 6 August, and Lawrence a few days later. A story told by Ambrose of Milan over a century later says that when the authorities demanded the Church's treasures, Lawrence brought them the poor and said these were the Church's treasure. Later legend added that he was roasted on a gridiron; historians think he was more probably beheaded, like Sixtus.

Whether or not the words are his, the story shows what the Church had come to believe about itself: that its wealth was its people, and above all its poor. That conviction, practised in a thousand cities, was one of the things that changed the empire.
sections.key: By 251 the Roman church supported over 1,500 widows and needy people; its deacon Lawrence, martyred in 258, is remembered for calling the poor the Church's treasure.

debate.question: Why did the Christian way of life draw people?

positions.name: Because it worked
positions.who: Rodney Stark; many social historians
positions.view: Christian care gave practical advantages: nursing in plagues, support for widows and orphans, food in famine, a family for strangers in crowded cities. People joined, in part, because Christian communities were better places to survive.
positions.evidence: Dionysius on the plague; the 1,500 widows of Rome; Julian's complaint; Lucian on the care of prisoners.

positions.name: Because it was beautiful and new
positions.who: Larry Hurtado; Alan Kreider; the historian Tom Holland (in Dominion, 2019)
positions.view: The ethic itself was striking: love of enemies, care for the weak, the worth of every baby, the equality of slaves and masters at one table. It rested on a new idea of what a human being is, and people were moved by it before they understood it.
positions.evidence: The Didache and Romans 12; pagan surprise at Christian behaviour; the 'patient ferment' of example.

positions.name: It was less new than it looks
positions.who: Historians of ancient religion and philosophy, such as Robin Lane Fox; some sceptics
positions.view: Much of this ethic was Jewish, and some of it was shared by philosophers such as Musonius Rufus and Seneca. Christian charity was mainly for Christians. And the ideal was not always the practice: Paul's letters and the Didache's warnings show quarrels, freeloaders and failures.
positions.evidence: Jewish refusal of exposure and Jewish charity; Stoic ethics; Paul's rebukes to the Corinthians; the Didache's rules against false prophets.

debate.agree: All agree that early Christians were known for their conduct, especially care for the weak, and that this helped the Church grow; they differ on how new it was and why it drew people.

look.why: An unknown Portuguese painter of the late fifteenth century painted Saint Lawrence, the Roman deacon martyred in 258, with the signs by which he was always recognised. The gridiron comes from the later legend of his death; the deacon's robes from his work for the poor.
points: A figure stands upright, dressed in ornate clergy robes, with a cape draped over one shoulder.
In the right hand he holds a gridiron, the sign of the legend of his death.
In the left hand he holds a book.
His expression is serene, and a halo frames his head.
The background is textured gold and dark green, enclosed by an ornate frame with gold accents.

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there': an ancient chant for the evening when Christians remember the Last Supper, here in Maurice Duruflé's setting. It sums up what the first Christians were known for.

think.why: The Didache's ban on killing infants rested on a new idea of human worth. Trace how the image of God became the modern idea of dignity.

learn.why: Paul's whole ethic in a single line: the way the first Christians answered a hostile world.

check.q: Why does the Didache begin with 'two ways' rather than with a statement of belief?
options: Because it was written for Roman officials
Because Christianity was first taught as a way of life to walk, with belief and conduct joined; it was the 'Way'
Because its author did not believe anything
Because the beliefs were secret
check.why: New believers were taught the way of life before baptism; faith was meant to be visible.

check.q: Which command in the Didache's list broke most sharply with ordinary Roman practice?
options: Thou shalt love the God that made thee
Be meek
Thou shalt not murder a child by abortion nor kill them when born
Thou shalt not steal
check.why: Exposure of infants was legal and common in Rome; Christians, following the Jews, forbade it for everyone.

check.q: What does the Aramaic word 'Maranatha' in a Greek prayer show?
options: That the Didache was written in Aramaic
That Christians did not understand Greek
That Christians in Syria could no longer understand Greek
That praying to Jesus as 'Lord' began among Aramaic-speaking Jewish believers, not later among Greeks
check.why: An untranslated Aramaic prayer, 'Our Lord, come', kept in Greek churches, points back to the earliest Jewish believers; Paul uses it too.

check.q: Why should Dionysius's account of Christians in the plague be read with some caution, and why is it still valuable?
options: He was a pagan, so he was biased against Christians
It was written a thousand years later
He was a bishop praising his own people and may exaggerate, but others, including the hostile emperor Julian, describe Christian care in similar terms
It is a forgery; it has no value
check.why: Partisan sources need checking; here a hostile witness, Julian, confirms the pattern.

check.q: The Didache tells masters not to treat slaves harshly because they 'trust in the same God'. What is the fairest conclusion?
options: The Didache abolished slavery
The Didache accepted slavery, as every ancient society did, but planted an idea of equal standing before God that later helped undo it
The Didache had nothing to say about slaves
The Didache told slaves to rebel
check.why: It tells slaves to obey and masters to be gentle; it does not abolish slavery, but grounds both under 'the God who is over both'.

check.q: How do the Didache and Romans 12 compare?
options: Both teach a way of life rooted in Jesus's teaching: blessing persecutors, generosity, humility and one community of many members
Romans 12 is a copy of the Didache
They contradict each other on the love of enemies
The Didache is about belief and Romans 12 about ritual
check.why: Both echo Jesus's 'bless those who curse you' and picture many becoming one, as one loaf or one body.

tutorial.question: 'They were known for what they did.' What did the first Christians actually do, and why did it draw people?
tutorial.approach: Use the Didache and Romans 12 to describe the way of life: love of God and neighbour, generosity, refusal of infanticide, the meal, the daily rhythm. Explain how each differed from Roman custom. Bring in the evidence of the plague and of Lawrence. Then weigh the three views in the debate, and decide how new the Christian ethic really was.
strong: Describes the 'two ways' and gives specific commands from the Didache.
Explains exposure and the arena, and why Christians refused them.
Describes the meal and the Maranatha prayer, and what they show.
Uses Dionysius and Julian on care in plagues, with appropriate caution.
Notes the Jewish roots and philosophical parallels of the ethic.
Reaches a reasoned view on why the way of life attracted people.
