sessions.practice: Live it this week: the Didache asked Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. For seven days, say it morning, midday and evening, wherever you are, and notice what difference it makes.
sessions.reflect: If someone watched how you lived for a week, without hearing anything you said, what would they conclude you believed?
takeaways: The Didache, a manual for new believers from perhaps AD 50–120, teaches a 'way of life': love of God and neighbour, generosity, and no abortion, infanticide, magic or cruelty.
Christians shared a meal of thanksgiving, prayed three times a day and fasted on Wednesday and Friday; their Aramaic 'Maranatha' shows very early prayer to Jesus as Lord.
In plagues they nursed the sick, and in Rome they supported fifteen hundred widows and poor: even their enemies admitted they cared for others.

sessions.title: What Rome saw
sessions.line: A Roman governor puts Christians on trial, tortures two slave women, and writes to the emperor: what are these people, and what should I do with them?
sessions.plain: Around AD 112, Pliny the Younger, a cultivated Roman senator governing a province in what is now northern Turkey, found himself trying people accused of being Christians. He did not know the law, so he wrote to the emperor Trajan. His letter, and Trajan's reply, are the earliest Roman description of Christians that survives. Pliny found no crime, only 'an absurd and extravagant superstition', and stubbornness; yet he executed those who would not give it up. This session asks what Romans thought of the Christians, and why they were distrusted.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 4 looked at the first Christians mostly from inside: what they believed, how they spread and how they lived. Now we stand outside, with their Roman neighbours and rulers, and ask what they saw.
answers: What did Romans think of the Christians?
Why were Christians suspected and tried?
What were the charges against them?
Did any Romans respect them?
sessions.finding: To Roman officials Christians were a stubborn superstition; to their critics, a threat to the gods and the family; even enemies noticed their discipline.

paras: By the early second century, the networks we followed with Paul had spread through the cities of the eastern empire. In AD 64, after a great fire in Rome, the emperor Nero had blamed the Christians and executed many of them; the historian Tacitus describes it, and if you have taken 'Can I trust the Bible?' you read his account. But there was no general law against Christianity. Persecution was local and occasional: it happened when someone accused a Christian before a governor.

The Christians of session 4 met before dawn, ate a meal no outsider could attend, called each other brother and sister, refused to honour the gods and kept away from the games. To a Roman neighbour, much of that looked strange, secretive and dangerous.
background.key: Nero executed Christians in Rome in AD 64, but there was no general law against them; persecution was local, and began with an accusation.

paras: Roman religion was not mainly about belief. It was about doing the right rites, in the right way, to keep the 'peace of the gods' (pax deorum), on which the safety of the city and the empire depended. You could believe almost anything about the gods, as philosophers did, so long as you joined in the sacrifices. Foreign gods were welcomed; Rome added them to its own.

Christians, like Jews, refused. But Jews were an ancient nation with ancestral customs, which Romans grudgingly respected. Christians were a new group, drawn from every nation, who abandoned their own ancestral gods. To Romans that made them 'atheists', people who denied the gods, and it made their religion a superstitio: an excessive, foreign and irrational cult, as opposed to religio, proper worship. When disaster struck, a famine, a flood, a plague, it was natural to ask whether the gods were angry, and at whom.
background.key: Roman religion was about rites that kept the 'peace of the gods'. Christians, a new group refusing all other gods, were 'atheists' and a superstitio.

paras: Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, Pliny the Younger, was a wealthy lawyer and senator, the nephew of Pliny the Elder, who died in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. He published nine books of elegant letters to friends. The tenth book is his official correspondence with the emperor Trajan while he governed Bithynia and Pontus, on the southern shore of the Black Sea, from about 110 to 112. It shows a conscientious, slightly anxious administrator writing to the emperor about aqueducts, fire brigades and building projects. Letter 96 is about the Christians.
This is the same region to which the first letter of Peter is addressed (1 Peter 1:1), which tells its readers that they will be 'spoken against as evildoers'.

timeline.text: Nero blames the Christians for the fire of Rome
Pliny governs Bithynia and Pontus and writes to Trajan

Lucian mocks the Christians; Galen comments on them
Martyrs of Lyons; Celsus writes his attack, The True Word

Minucius Felix's Octavius, probably

background.key: Pliny, a senator and letter-writer, governed Bithynia and Pontus about 110–112; letter 96 is his report to Trajan on the Christians.

paras: The main reading is Pliny's letter and Trajan's reply, read in full. They answer our question directly, from the side of Roman power.

The comparison is from the Octavius of Minucius Felix, a Christian writer who put the pagan case against Christianity into the mouth of a character, Caecilius, before answering it. It collects what ordinary pagans said about Christians, at its most lurid.
background.key: Pliny and Trajan show what Roman officials thought; Minucius Felix shows what the street said.

before: What does Pliny say the Christians told him they did? Does he find any crime?
Why does he punish them anyway?
What does Trajan forbid Pliny to do?
sessions.readWhy: The earliest Roman account of the Christians: a governor's questions, and an emperor's answer.

paras: IT is my invariable rule, Sir, to refer to you in all matters where I feel doubtful; for who is more capable of removing my scruples, or informing my ignorance? Having never been present at any trials concerning those who profess Christianity, I am unacquainted not only with the nature of their crimes, or the measure of their punishment, but how far it is proper to enter into an examination concerning them. Whether, therefore, any difference is usually made with respect to ages, or no distinction is to be observed between the young and the adult; whether repentance entitles them to a pardon; or if a man has been once a Christian, it avails nothing to desist from his error; whether the very profession of Christianity, unattended with any criminal act, or only the crimes themselves inherent in the profession are punishable; on all these points I am in great doubt. In the meanwhile, the method I have observed towards those who have been brought before me as Christians is this: I asked them whether they were Christians; if they admitted it, I repeated the question twice, and threatened them with punishment;

if they persisted, I ordered them to be at once punished: for I was persuaded, whatever the nature of their opinions might be, a contumacious and inflexible obstinacy certainly deserved correction. There were others also brought before me possessed with the same infatuation, but being Roman citizens, I directed them to be sent to Rome. But this crime spreading (as is usually the case) while it was actually under prosecution, several instances of the same nature occurred. An anonymous information was laid before me containing a charge against several persons, who upon examination denied they were Christians, or had ever been so. They repeated after me an invocation to the gods, and offered religious rites with wine and incense before your statue (which for that purpose I had ordered to be brought, together with those of the gods), and even reviled the name of Christ: whereas there is no forcing, it is said, those who are really Christians into any of these compliances: I thought it proper, therefore, to discharge them. Some among those who were accused by a witness in person at first confessed themselves Christians, but immediately after denied it;

the rest owned indeed that they had been of that number formerly, but had now (some above three, others more, and a few above twenty years ago) renounced that error. They all worshipped your statue and the images of the gods, uttering imprecations at the same time against the name of Christ. They affirmed the whole of their guilt, or their error, was, that they met on a stated day before it was light, and addressed a form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity, binding themselves by a solemn oath, not for the purposes of any wicked design, but never to commit any fraud, theft, or adultery, never to falsify their word, nor deny a trust when they should be called upon to deliver it up; after which it was their custom to separate, and then reassemble, to eat in common a harmless meal. From this custom, however, they desisted after the publication of my edict, by which, according to your commands, I forbade the meeting of any assemblies. After receiving this account, I judged it so much the more necessary to endeavor to extort the real truth, by putting two female slaves to the torture, who were said to officiate' in their religious rites:

but all I could discover was evidence of an absurd and extravagant superstition. I deemed it expedient, therefore, to adjourn all further proceedings, in order to consult you. For it appears to be a matter highly deserving your consideration, more especially as great numbers must be involved in the danger of these prosecutions, which have already extended, and are still likely to extend, to persons of all ranks and ages, and even of both sexes. In fact, this contagious superstition is not confined to the cities only, but has spread its infection among the neighbouring villages and country. Nevertheless, it still seems possible to restrain its progress. The temples, at least, which were once almost deserted, begin now to be frequented; and the sacred rites, after a long intermission, are again revived; while there is a general demand for the victims, which till lately found very few purchasers. From all this it is easy to conjecture what numbers might be reclaimed if a general pardon were granted to those who shall repent of their error.

You have adopted the right course, my dearest Secundtis, in investigating the charges against the Christians who were brought before you. It is not possible to lay down any general rule for all such cases. Do not go out of your way to look for them. If indeed they should be brought before you, and the crime is proved, they must be punished; with the restriction, however, that where the party denies he is a Christian, and shall make it evident that he is not, by invoking our gods, let him (notwithstanding any former suspicion) be pardoned upon his repentance. Anonymous informations ought not to be received in any sort of prosecution. It is introducing a very dangerous precedent, and is quite foreign to the spirit of our age.

parts.author: Pliny the Younger and the emperor Trajan
parts.work: Letters, Book X, 96 and 97 (numbered XCVII and XCVIII in this edition)
parts.translator: William Melmoth (1746), revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet
parts.who: Pliny the Younger (about 61 to about 113), a Roman senator and lawyer, governor of Bithynia and Pontus; and Trajan, emperor from 98 to 117
parts.when: Bithynia (north-west Turkey) and Rome, about AD 112
parts.ref: Pliny, Letters X.96 (XCVII in this edition)
parts.title: Pliny to Trajan
parts.context: About AD 112, in Bithynia. Pliny has been holding trials of people accused of being Christians. Some confessed and were executed; others denied it. An anonymous pamphlet has named many more. He writes to ask the emperor what to do. This is William Melmoth's translation of 1746, revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet. Melmoth's 'who were said to officiate' translates the Latin ministrae, 'ministers', perhaps the women deacons of the church; the stray apostrophe after 'officiate' is in the printed text.
parts.plain: Pliny says: I have never been at a trial of Christians, so I don't know what the crime is or how to punish it. So far I have asked people three times if they are Christians, and executed those who insisted, because such stubbornness deserves punishment anyway; Roman citizens I have sent to Rome. Others, named anonymously, denied it, prayed to the gods, offered incense to your statue and cursed Christ, and I let them go, because real Christians, I am told, will never do that. Former Christians told me that all they ever did was meet before dawn on a fixed day, sing to Christ as to a god, and swear not to steal, commit adultery or break their word, then share an ordinary meal. I tortured two slave women who were their 'ministers' and found nothing but an absurd superstition. But it has spread to every class, age and sex, in villages as well as cities. Now the temples are filling again. Many could be won back if you offered a pardon.

commentary.on: Having never been present at any trials concerning those who profess Christianity, I am unacquainted not only with the nature of their crimes
commentary.text: A senior Roman lawyer does not know what the crime is. There was no law that named it. That is the key to early persecution: it depended on governors, accusers and crowds, not on a statute.

commentary.on: whether the very profession of Christianity, unattended with any criminal act, or only the crimes themselves inherent in the profession are punishable
commentary.text: Pliny's real question: is it a crime simply to be a Christian (the 'name'), or only to do the crimes Christians are rumoured to commit? He has already decided in practice. He has executed people for the name alone.

commentary.on: a contumacious and inflexible obstinacy certainly deserved correction
commentary.text: This is Pliny's reason, and it is very Roman. Whatever they believe, they refused a magistrate's order three times. Defiance of lawful authority was itself a crime. The Christians' steadfastness, which they called faithfulness, Romans called obstinacy.

commentary.on: offered religious rites with wine and incense before your statue
commentary.text: The test was simple. A pinch of incense and a little wine before the image of the emperor and the gods, and a curse on Christ. For a Roman it was a gesture of loyalty, like standing for an anthem. For a Christian it was worshipping a false god and betraying Christ.

commentary.on: there is no forcing, it is said, those who are really Christians into any of these compliances
commentary.text: Pliny has heard that true Christians cannot be made to do it. That reputation had already spread. It is the first Roman testimony to what Christians called martyrdom.

commentary.on: some above three, others more, and a few above twenty years ago
commentary.text: Some had left the church twenty years before, so there were Christians in Bithynia by about AD 90, within sixty years of the cross, in a province Paul never visited.

commentary.on: they met on a stated day before it was light, and addressed a form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity
commentary.text: The 'stated day' was almost certainly Sunday. They met before dawn because many were slaves or workers, with no day off. The Latin says they sang a carmen, a song or chant, to Christ 'as to a god' (quasi deo). Eighty years after the crucifixion, a Roman official reports that Christians worship Jesus as divine.

commentary.on: never to commit any fraud, theft, or adultery, never to falsify their word, nor deny a trust
commentary.text: The 'oath' (sacramentum) sounds like the Didache's way of life: no theft, no adultery, no lying. Pliny, who expected to uncover crimes, found a moral code.

commentary.on: to eat in common a harmless meal
commentary.text: 'Harmless', or 'ordinary': the Latin is cibum promiscuum et innoxium. They insist on it because of the rumours of cannibalism, which the comparison will show. Even this meal they gave up when Pliny banned clubs and societies, which Romans feared as breeding grounds of sedition.

commentary.on: by putting two female slaves to the torture, who were said to officiate' in their religious rites
commentary.text: Under Roman law, slaves' evidence was taken under torture. These two women were leaders of some kind in the church; the Latin word, ministrae, is the feminine of 'minister', perhaps the same office as Phoebe's in Romans 16. We do not know their names or what happened to them.

commentary.on: all I could discover was evidence of an absurd and extravagant superstition
commentary.text: The Latin is superstitio prava et immodica, a depraved and excessive superstition. That is the official verdict: no crime, only a contemptible cult.

commentary.on: to persons of all ranks and ages, and even of both sexes
commentary.text: This is precious evidence for the growth we studied in session 3: in one province, about AD 112, Christians are numerous, in every social class, of every age, men and women, in the countryside as well as the towns.

commentary.on: The temples, at least, which were once almost deserted, begin now to be frequented
commentary.text: The other side of the evidence: the temples had been emptying, and the market for sacrificial animals had collapsed. Christian growth was hurting the local religious economy, which may explain who was making the accusations.

parts.work: Letters, Book X, 96 and 97 (numbered XCVII and XCVIII in this edition)
parts.translator: William Melmoth (1746), revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet
parts.who: Pliny the Younger (about 61 to about 113), a Roman senator and lawyer, governor of Bithynia and Pontus; and Trajan, emperor from 98 to 117
parts.when: Bithynia (north-west Turkey) and Rome, about AD 112
parts.ref: Pliny, Letters X.97 (XCVIII in this edition)
parts.title: Trajan's reply
parts.context: The emperor's short answer, which became, in effect, the policy of the Roman state towards Christians for most of the second century. 'Secundtis' is a misprint in the edition for Secundus, part of Pliny's name.
parts.plain: Trajan replies: you did right. There can be no fixed rule. Do not go looking for Christians. If they are accused and the charge is proved, punish them. But if anyone denies being a Christian and proves it by praying to our gods, pardon him, whatever he did before. Anonymous accusations must never be accepted: that would be a terrible precedent, and not in the spirit of our age.

commentary.on: Do not go out of your way to look for them.
commentary.text: The Christians are not to be hunted. Trajan treats them as a nuisance, not a menace.

commentary.on: If indeed they should be brought before you, and the crime is proved, they must be punished
commentary.text: But if they are accused, they die. Tertullian, about 90 years later, pointed out the contradiction: if Christians are guilty, why not seek them out; if innocent, why punish them? The reply condemns the name, not any deed.

commentary.on: let him (notwithstanding any former suspicion) be pardoned upon his repentance
commentary.text: Anyone can walk free by offering to the gods. The state wanted conformity, not blood. That is why the martyrs' refusal seemed so perverse to Romans, and so heroic to Christians.

commentary.on: Anonymous informations ought not to be received in any sort of prosecution.
commentary.text: A real legal protection. Accusers had to put their name to a charge, and risked punishment if it failed. Trajan's successor Hadrian, about AD 125, said the same.

paras: Therefore, since the consent of all nations concerning the existence of the immortal gods remains established, although their nature or their origin remains uncertain, I suffer nobody swelling with such boldness, and with I know not what irreligious wisdom, who would strive to undermine or weaken this religion, so ancient, so useful, so wholesome, even although he may be Theodorus of Cyrene, or one who is before him, Diagoras the Melian, to whom antiquity applied the surname of Atheist — both of whom, by asseverating that there were no gods, took away all the fear by which humanity is ruled, and all veneration absolutely; yet never will they prevail in this discipline of impiety, under the name and authority of their pretended philosophy.

When the men of Athens both expelled Protagoras of Abdera, and in public assembly burnt his writings, because he disputed deliberately rather than profanely concerning the divinity, why is it not a thing to be lamented, that men (for you will bear with my making use pretty freely of the force of the plea that I have undertaken)— that men, I say, of a reprobate, unlawful, and desperate faction, should rage against the gods? Who, having gathered together from the lowest dregs the more unskilled, and women, credulous and, by the facility of their sex, yielding, establish a herd of a profane conspiracy, which is leagued together by nightly meetings, and solemn fasts and inhuman meats — not by any sacred rite, but by that which requires expiation — a people skulking and shunning the light, silent in public, but garrulous in corners. They despise the temples as dead-houses, they reject the gods, they laugh at sacred things; wretched, they pity, if they are allowed, the priests; half naked themselves, they despise honours and purple robes. Oh, wondrous folly and incredible audacity! They despise present torments, although they fear those which are uncertain and future; and while they fear to die after death, they do not fear to die for the present: so does a deceitful hope soothe their fear with the solace of a revival.

And now, as wickeder things advance more fruitfully, and abandoned manners creep on day by day, those abominable shrines of an impious assembly are maturing themselves throughout the whole world. Assuredly this confederacy ought to be rooted out and execrated. They know one another by secret marks and insignia, and they love one another almost before they know one another. Everywhere also there is mingled among them a certain religion of lust, and they call one another promiscuously brothers and sisters, that even a not unusual debauchery may by the intervention of that sacred name become incestuous: it is thus that their vain and senseless superstition glories in crimes. Nor, concerning these things, would intelligent report speak of things so great and various, and requiring to be prefaced by an apology, unless truth were at the bottom of it. I hear that they adore the head of an ass, that basest of creatures, consecrated by I know not what silly persuasion — a worthy and appropriate religion for such manners.

I know not whether these things are false; certainly suspicion is applicable to secret and nocturnal rites; and he who explains their ceremonies by reference to a man punished by extreme suffering for his wickedness, and to the deadly wood of the cross, appropriates fitting altars for reprobate and wicked men, that they may worship what they deserve. Now the story about the initiation of young novices is as much to be detested as it is well known. An infant covered over with meal, that it may deceive the unwary, is placed before him who is to be stained with their rites: this infant is slain by the young pupil, who has been urged on as if to harmless blows on the surface of the meal, with dark and secret wounds. Thirstily — O horror!— they lick up its blood; eagerly they divide its limbs. By this victim they are pledged together; with this consciousness of wickedness they are covenanted to mutual silence.

Such sacred rites as these are more foul than any sacrileges. And of their banqueting it is well known all men speak of it everywhere; even the speech of our Cirtensian testifies to it. On a solemn day they assemble at the feast, with all their children, sisters, mothers, people of every sex and of every age. There, after much feasting, when the fellowship has grown warm, and the fervour of incestuous lust has grown hot with drunkenness, a dog that has been tied to the chandelier is provoked, by throwing a small piece of offal beyond the length of a line by which he is bound, to rush and spring; and thus the conscious light being overturned and extinguished in the shameless darkness, the connections of abominable lust involve them in the uncertainty of fate. Although not all in fact, yet in consciousness all are alike incestuous, since by the desire of all of them everything is sought for which can happen in the act of each individual.

parts.author: Minucius Felix
parts.translator: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers IV (1885)
parts.title: The case against the Christians
parts.context: The Octavius is a dialogue set on the beach at Ostia, the port of Rome. Minucius Felix, a Christian lawyer, probably from North Africa, describes a debate between his Christian friend Octavius and a pagan friend, Caecilius. Here Caecilius speaks. The date is uncertain, between about AD 160 and 250. 'Our Cirtensian' refers to Fronto of Cirta, tutor of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, who made a speech against Christians. One sentence repeating a crude charge is cut, marked '…'. Translated by R. E. Wallis, 1885.
parts.plain: Caecilius says: every nation agrees that the gods exist, and no one should undermine such an old and useful religion. These Christians are a disgraceful gang of uneducated people and gullible women, meeting at night, skulking in corners. They despise the temples, the gods and honours, and they do not fear death because they hope to rise again. Their cult is spreading everywhere and should be stamped out. They recognise each other by secret signs, love each other before they have even met, and call each other brother and sister, which makes their lust incest. They worship a criminal and his cross. They initiate new members by making them stab a baby hidden in flour, then drink its blood. At their feasts, when the lamps are knocked over, they commit incest in the dark.

commentary.on: who would strive to undermine or weaken this religion, so ancient, so useful, so wholesome
commentary.text: The serious argument comes first. Religion is old, useful and good for society. Whether or not the gods are real, undermining them is dangerous. Many Romans who did not believe the myths still held this view.

commentary.on: from the lowest dregs the more unskilled, and women, credulous and, by the facility of their sex, yielding
commentary.text: The snobbery is typical. Celsus said the same: Christians recruit wool-workers, cobblers and laundry-workers, women and children. It is also, unwillingly, evidence for who joined.

commentary.on: They despise the temples as dead-houses, they reject the gods, they laugh at sacred things
commentary.text: This is the charge of 'atheism'. To Romans, rejecting the gods endangered everyone, because the gods punished cities that neglected them.

commentary.on: while they fear to die after death, they do not fear to die for the present
commentary.text: Caecilius cannot understand it: they fear judgement after death, but not death itself. Lucian said the same. The Christian contempt of death puzzled every pagan observer.

commentary.on: and they love one another almost before they know one another
commentary.text: A complaint that is a compliment. Strangers from another city were treated as family. Notice how the pagan turns it into a sign of conspiracy.

commentary.on: they call one another promiscuously brothers and sisters
commentary.text: Here is the source of the charge of incest. If 'brothers and sisters' married, or exchanged the holy kiss of Romans 16, outsiders could twist it into something obscene.

commentary.on: to a man punished by extreme suffering for his wickedness, and to the deadly wood of the cross
commentary.text: To worship a crucified man was, for a Roman, like worshipping a hanged criminal. The cross was shameful; no Christian art showed it for centuries.

commentary.on: this infant is slain by the young pupil
commentary.text: The charge of cannibalism, which the Greeks called 'Thyestean feasts' after a myth in which a man was fed his own sons. It probably grew from garbled reports of the Eucharist: eating 'the body' and drinking 'the blood'. Notice the irony: Christians were the people who refused to kill infants.

commentary.on: the connections of abominable lust involve them in the uncertainty of fate
commentary.text: And the charge of incest at night-time feasts, the 'Oedipean unions'. These rumours appear again in the account of the martyrs of Lyons in 177, where slaves were tortured into confirming them. Pliny, who investigated, found only a harmless meal.

compare.author: Minucius Felix
compare.translator: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers IV (1885)
compare.why: Pliny wrote as an official. Here is the voice of popular rumour, gathered by a Christian writer who wanted to answer it. Read it to see why ordinary people feared Christians.
compare.title: What the street said

paras: By the second century the accusations against Christians had settled into three, which the Christian writer Athenagoras listed about AD 177: atheism, cannibalism and incest. Each grew from something real, misunderstood.

Atheism came from their refusal to honour any god but their own, and their lack of temples, altars and images. Cannibalism came from the meal of 'body' and 'blood', held privately. Incest came from calling each other brother and sister and greeting each other with a kiss. Add secret meetings before dawn, and the rumours wrote themselves.

The rumours mattered because they made Christians the obvious culprits when things went wrong. Tertullian, writing about 197, said that if the Tiber flooded or the Nile failed to flood, if there was an earthquake or a famine or a plague, the cry went up at once: 'Away with the Christians to the lion!' Persecution came less from emperors than from frightened neighbours.
sections.key: Pagans accused Christians of atheism, cannibalism and incest: twisted versions of their refusal of the gods, their meal and their 'brothers and sisters'.

paras: Pliny and Trajan were not fanatics. They were sensible men who did not want trouble. Their policy (do not hunt Christians, do not accept anonymous charges, but punish the stubborn and pardon anyone who sacrifices) shows what worried them: not belief but disobedience.

To the Roman mind, a citizen who would not perform a simple act of loyalty when a magistrate ordered it was a threat to public order. Pliny's 'inflexible obstinacy' is the key phrase. The great historian of Roman law A. N. Sherwin-White argued that this contumacia, defiance of a magistrate, was what Christians were really punished for.

There were also worries about 'clubs'. Rome feared private associations that could become political. Trajan had refused Pliny permission to form even a fire brigade in Nicomedia, for fear it would turn into a political club. A society that met in secret, across class lines, with its own leaders and funds, looked like exactly that.
sections.key: Officials punished Christians less for belief than for 'obstinacy', refusing a lawful order, and feared them as a secret association.

paras: The historian G. E. M. de Ste. Croix gave a different answer in a famous article of 1963. The heart of it, he argued, was religious. Romans believed that the peace of the gods kept the empire safe. Christians, by refusing to worship, broke that peace and put everyone at risk. That is why mobs blamed them for disasters, and why the great persecutions of the third century, under Decius in 250 and Diocletian in 303, came at times of crisis and demanded that everyone sacrifice.

Pliny's letter supports both views. He punishes obstinacy; but he also notes with relief that the temples are filling again and the sacrifices resuming. For him, public religion and public order were one thing. The Christians' crime was to separate them: to say, as Jesus had, 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mark 12:17). Christians prayed for the emperor, but would not pray to him.
sections.key: De Ste. Croix argued the real issue was religious: refusing the gods broke the 'peace of the gods' on which the empire depended.

paras: Not every pagan sneered. Galen of Pergamum (129 to about 216), the greatest doctor of antiquity and physician to the emperor Marcus Aurelius, mocked Christians for accepting things on faith without proof. Yet in a passage preserved only in an Arabic summary of one of his lost works, he wrote that they sometimes behave like true philosophers: they despise death, they practise self-control in food and drink, some of them, men and women, abstain from sex all their lives, and they pursue justice. He meant it as a grudging compliment: they reach by faith what philosophers reach by reason.

Lucian, as we saw in session 3, mocked their generosity but described it. Pliny found that their oath was to commit no crime. Even Caecilius, in the Octavius, complains that they love one another before they have even met. The hostile witnesses agree on the Christians' discipline, their mutual love and their contempt of death. They differ only on whether these were admirable or ridiculous.
sections.key: Galen, the great doctor, mocked Christians' lack of proof but admired their self-control, contempt of death and justice; hostile witnesses agree on their discipline.

paras: About AD 177 to 180, a Platonist philosopher named Celsus wrote the first full attack on Christianity, The True Word. It is lost, but most of it survives in quotations in the long reply written about seventy years later by the Christian scholar Origen, Against Celsus.

Celsus had read the Gospels and knew his subject. He argued that Jesus was a magician, born of an adulterous union; that the resurrection rested on the word of a hysterical woman; that Christians were rebels against Judaism as the Jews had once rebelled against Egypt; that they recruited the ignorant and refused to give reasons; and, most seriously, that they were tearing the empire apart by refusing to worship its gods or serve in its offices. He ended by urging them to come back and join in public life.

Celsus is the critic Christians most needed to answer, and they did, at length. That argument, between the faith and the best of Greek philosophy, is the subject of 'When Athens met Jerusalem' in Hall IV.
sections.key: Celsus's True Word (about 177–180), preserved by Origen, was the first serious attack on Christianity, charging it with ignorance and disloyalty to the empire.

paras: Christians answered in two ways. The first was writing. From the 120s onwards, a series of 'apologists', from the Greek apologia, a speech for the defence, wrote to emperors and the public: Aristides, Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Tertullian, Minucius Felix. They denied the rumours, explained the meal and the kiss, argued that Christianity was the true philosophy, and insisted that Christians were the emperor's most loyal subjects, praying for him every week. The first letter of Peter had told believers to 'always be ready to give an answer' for their hope, 'with humility and fear' (1 Peter 3:15).

The second was the way they lived and died. The same letter hoped that those who slandered them would be put to shame by their 'good way of life in Christ' (3:16). The Beatitudes had called the persecuted blessed. When the governor ordered incense and the Christian refused, the crowd saw what they believed. Some were disgusted. Some, like the young Justin Martyr in the 130s, were drawn to ask what made people willing to die like that.
sections.key: Christians answered with the 'apologies', written defences addressed to emperors, and with lives and deaths that put the slanders to shame.

refs: Pliny, Letters X.96–97, tr. William Melmoth, rev. F. C. T. Bosanquet (Gutenberg #2811); Latin text in R. A. B. Mynors, Oxford Classical Texts (1963).
Minucius Felix, Octavius 8–9, tr. R. E. Wallis, ANF IV (1885); Athenagoras, Plea for the Christians 3; Eusebius, Church History V.1.14 (the martyrs of Lyons); Martyrdom of Polycarp 9.
Tertullian, Apology 2 and 40; Justin, First Apology 68 (Hadrian's rescript); Justin, Second Apology 12; Mark 12:17; 1 Peter 1:1; 3:15–16.
Galen, in R. Walzer, Galen on Jews and Christians (1949); Origen, Against Celsus I.1, I.28, II.55, III.44, VIII.73–75.

G. E. M. de Ste. Croix, 'Why Were the Early Christians Persecuted?', Past and Present 26 (1963); A. N. Sherwin-White, reply, Past and Present 27 (1964), and The Letters of Pliny: A Historical and Social Commentary (1966).
Robert Wilken, The Christians as the Romans Saw Them (1984).

debate.question: Why did Rome distrust the Christians?

positions.name: For their religion: they angered the gods
positions.who: G. E. M. de Ste. Croix (1963)
positions.view: Romans believed the gods protected the state in return for worship. Christians refused worship and so endangered everyone. That is why crowds blamed them for disasters and why emperors in crisis demanded universal sacrifice.
positions.evidence: Tertullian's 'The Christians to the lion!'; the persecutions of Decius (250) and Diocletian (303); Pliny's relief that the temples were filling.

positions.name: For their disobedience: they defied authority
positions.who: A. N. Sherwin-White (1964)
positions.view: Roman officials did not care much what people believed. What they punished was contumacia: refusing a magistrate's order. Christians were executed for obstinacy, and feared as a secret society.
positions.evidence: Pliny's 'inflexible obstinacy'; Trajan's pardon for anyone who sacrifices; Roman fear of clubs.

positions.name: For their strangeness: rumour and novelty
positions.who: Robert Wilken (1984); many historians
positions.view: Christians were new, secretive and socially odd: they abandoned ancestral customs, met at night and mixed slaves and free, women and men. Distrust grew from the gap between their private life and public suspicion, fed by rumour.
positions.evidence: The charges of cannibalism and incest; Caecilius in the Octavius; Celsus's complaint that they withdrew from public life.

debate.agree: All agree that there was no general law against Christianity before 250, that persecution was local and depended on accusers, and that refusal to honour the gods was at the centre of the conflict.

look.why: Francesco Guardi painted this fanciful view of Rome about 1785. The great round building is the Castel Sant'Angelo, which began as the tomb of the emperor Hadrian, who reigned after Trajan and continued his policy towards Christians. Centuries later it became a fortress of the popes: the painting is here to show the empire that judged the Christians, and what became of it.
points: A large cylindrical reddish-brown fortress stands on the right: the Castel Sant'Angelo.
In the centre a wide blue-green river winds through the city, with people on the bank.
On the left, people walk along a winding tan road that curves round to a stone bridge crossing the river.
In the background are tan buildings with terracotta roofs and a large white building with a blue dome.
The sky is painted in soft blue and peach tones with loose brushstrokes.

music.why: James MacMillan's 'O Radiant Dawn' sets the ancient prayer to Christ as the morning star. Pliny's Christians met 'before it was light' to sing to Christ as to a god.

think.why: Romans thought religion held society together whether or not the gods were real; Christians thought conscience answered to God above the state. Ask what grounds morality.

learn.why: Written to the very region Pliny governed: how to answer suspicion, with a reason and with gentleness. (If you know the Beatitudes, remember the last: 'Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness' sake'.)

check.q: Why does Pliny, an experienced lawyer, not know how to proceed against Christians?
options: Because Christians who were Roman citizens were outside a governor's authority
Because he had never met any
Because there was no law that named being a Christian as a crime, and he had never attended such a trial
Because Trajan had forbidden trials
check.why: Persecution depended on accusers and governors, not on a statute.

check.q: On what ground does Pliny execute those who confess, even before he finds any crime?
options: Treason against Trajan
Cannibalism
Refusing to pay taxes
Their 'inflexible obstinacy' in refusing a magistrate's order three times
check.why: For a Roman, defiance of lawful authority deserved punishment whatever the belief.

check.q: What does Pliny's investigation show about the rumours of cannibalism and incest?
options: That Trajan believed them
That they were true
That he did not investigate
That he found only an oath against crime and 'a harmless meal', and 'an absurd and extravagant superstition'
check.why: Even under torture, he found nothing criminal.

check.q: What contradiction did Tertullian see in Trajan's reply?
options: That Trajan allowed anonymous accusations
That if Christians were guilty they should be sought out, and if innocent they should not be punished; Trajan forbade the search but punished the accused
That Trajan was secretly a Christian
That Trajan pardoned everyone
check.why: The policy punished the name, not any deed.

check.q: Which best explains the charge of cannibalism?
options: It came from Jewish law
Christians really sacrificed children
A twisted version of the meal in which Christians spoke of eating Christ's 'body' and drinking his 'blood', held in private
Christians ate meat offered to idols
check.why: Private meals, 'body' and 'blood': the rumours grew from misunderstood practice.

check.q: Galen and Lucian both disliked Christianity. Why are their remarks about Christian behaviour strong evidence?
options: Because they wrote in Latin
Because they were doctors
Because they were converted later
Because hostile witnesses have no motive to invent their opponents' virtues: they agree on the Christians' self-control, mutual care and contempt of death
check.why: What enemies admit is usually reliable.

tutorial.question: Why did the Romans distrust the Christians, and were they right to?
tutorial.approach: Use Pliny and Trajan to show the officials' view, and Minucius Felix to show popular rumour. Explain Roman religion and the 'peace of the gods'. Weigh the three explanations in the debate. Bring in what hostile witnesses admired. Then ask whether, from a Roman point of view, the Christians really were a threat, and in what sense.
strong: Explains Pliny's procedure and his reason for punishment ('obstinacy').
Explains Trajan's policy and its contradiction.
Explains the three charges and where each came from.
Explains Roman religion as rites for the peace of the gods, and why refusal mattered.
Uses Galen or Lucian as hostile witnesses to Christian conduct.
Reaches a reasoned view on whether Christians threatened the Roman order.

reading.author: Robert Wilken
reading.title: The Christians as the Romans Saw Them
reading.why: Pliny, Galen, Celsus, Porphyry and Julian, explained clearly and fairly.

reading.author: Robin Lane Fox
reading.title: Pagans and Christians
reading.why: A great historian's rich picture of pagan religion and the Christians who rejected it.

reading.author: A. N. Sherwin-White
reading.title: The Letters of Pliny: A Historical and Social Commentary
reading.why: The standard commentary, with a long note on letter 96.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: 1 Peter asks for 'a reason concerning the hope that is in you'. Write down, in no more than five sentences, why you hope what you hope. Keep it where you will see it.
sessions.reflect: Is there a moment when loyalty to a group, an employer or a country would ask you to do something your conscience refuses? What would you do?
takeaways: Pliny, about AD 112, found no crime among Christians, only an oath against wrongdoing, a harmless meal and 'an absurd and extravagant superstition', but executed them for obstinacy.
Popular rumour charged Christians with atheism, cannibalism and incest, twisted versions of their refusal of the gods, their meal and their 'brothers and sisters'.
Hostile witnesses, Pliny, Lucian and Galen, still noticed their discipline, mutual love and contempt of death.

sessions.title: The case against: did Paul invent Christianity?
sessions.line: Paul never met Jesus during his life, quarrelled with Peter, and wrote half the New Testament. Did he turn a Jewish teacher into a god?
sessions.plain: Jesus was a Jewish teacher in Galilee who spoke about the kingdom of God. Paul, who never met him before the crucifixion, wrote about a heavenly Christ whose death and resurrection save the world. Many critics, from the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche to the Jewish scholar Hyam Maccoby, have argued that Paul, not Jesus, was the real founder of Christianity: that he changed a Jewish movement into a new religion. This session states that case at full strength, then weighs the replies.
sessions.why: The first five sessions have told the story largely as Acts and the Church tell it. But the strongest objection to that story strikes at its centre: if Paul invented the faith that spread, then what spread was not the message of the first witnesses. It comes here because the case uses evidence you now have: Paul's conversion, his independence and his mission to the Gentiles.
answers: Did Paul change Jesus's message?
Was Christianity Paul's creation?
Did Paul and Peter disagree?
What did Paul actually receive from those before him?
sessions.finding: Paul handed on what he received within a few years of the cross, and his letters assume Jesus's death, resurrection and teaching; the question is whether he transformed them.

paras: We have followed the first witnesses in Jerusalem, Stephen's death and Paul's conversion, Paul's network across the empire, the way of life taught in the Didache, and what Roman officials saw. Through all of it, Paul has loomed large. Of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament, thirteen bear his name, and Acts gives him more than half its pages.

That is exactly what makes some readers suspicious. The Gospels show Jesus preaching the kingdom of God, healing, telling parables and arguing about the law. Paul's letters say almost nothing about any of that. They speak instead of Christ crucified and risen, of grace and faith, of being 'in Christ'. Was the religion that conquered Rome really Paul's?
background.key: Paul wrote thirteen of the New Testament's twenty-seven books; his letters say little about Jesus's life and much about his death and resurrection.

paras: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900), the German philosopher, made the most violent version in The Antichrist, written in 1888. He admired Jesus as a gentle figure who lived out a way of peace, and blamed Paul for turning this into a religion of guilt, judgement and life after death, built, he said, on resentment and a hunger for power.

William Wrede (1859–1906), a German New Testament scholar, put it calmly in his book Paul (1904): Paul was 'the second founder of Christianity', whose teaching about a divine, pre-existent Christ owed more to Jewish ideas about heavenly beings than to the man from Nazareth. Hyam Maccoby (1924–2004), a British Jewish scholar, went further in The Mythmaker (1986), arguing that Paul invented the Christian religion from a mixture of Judaism and pagan mystery cults, against the wishes of Jesus's own family and followers.
background.key: Nietzsche (1888), Wrede (1904) and Maccoby (1986) argued that Paul, not Jesus, founded Christianity.

paras: Antioch, in Syria, was the city where non-Jewish believers were first welcomed in large numbers and where Paul worked before his journeys. Jewish believers there had begun eating with Gentile believers, though Jewish food laws normally kept them apart. When the apostles in Jerusalem met, about AD 49, they agreed that Gentiles did not need to be circumcised (Acts 15). But the question of whether Jewish believers could eat with them was not settled, and it exploded in Antioch.
Paul tells the story in his letter to the Galatians, which we met in session 2. It is the most important evidence for the case against him, and the most important evidence for the replies.
background.key: In Antioch, Jewish and Gentile believers ate together; after the Jerusalem meeting, about AD 49, a quarrel broke out over it.

paras: The main reading is Galatians 2:3–21, in two parts: Paul's meeting with the 'pillars' of the Jerusalem church, and his public quarrel with Peter at Antioch, which leads into his clearest statement of what he believed. (The first two verses of the chapter are read in 'Can I trust the Bible?'.)
The comparison has two short passages: one in which Paul carefully separates Jesus's commands from his own advice, and one, from the second letter of Peter, about Paul's letters.
background.key: Galatians 2 shows Paul's independence and his clash with Peter; two short passages test whether he freely invented teaching.

before: What did the Jerusalem leaders agree with Paul, and what did they ask of him?
What exactly was the quarrel at Antioch about? Was it about who Jesus was?
In 1 Corinthians 7, why does Paul say 'not I, but the Lord' and then 'I, not the Lord'?
sessions.readWhy: Paul's own account of his relations with Peter and James: the best evidence for the charge that he went his own way, and for the reply.

paras: But not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.
This was because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who stole in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage,
to whom we gave no place in the way of subjection, not for an hour, that the truth of the Good News might continue with you.
But from those who were reputed to be important—whatever they were, it makes no difference to me; God doesn’t show partiality to man—they, I say, who were respected imparted nothing to me,
but to the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Good News for the uncircumcised, even as Peter with the Good News for the circumcised—
for he who worked through Peter in the apostleship with the circumcised also worked through me with the Gentiles—

and when they perceived the grace that was given to me, James and Cephas and John, those who were reputed to be pillars, gave to Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision.
They only asked us to remember the poor—which very thing I was also zealous to do.
But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.
And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.

But when I saw that they didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News, I said to Peter before them all, “If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?
“We, being Jews by nature, and not Gentile sinners,

yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.
But if while we sought to be justified in Christ, we ourselves also were found sinners, is Christ a servant of sin? Certainly not!
For if I build up again those things which I destroyed, I prove myself a law-breaker.
For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.
I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”

parts.title: The pillars
parts.context: About AD 48 to 55, Paul writing to the Galatian churches. He has just told how, fourteen years after his conversion, he went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, a Gentile believer, and set out his message privately before the leaders there.

commentary.on: But not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.
commentary.text: Titus was the test case. If the Jerusalem leaders had insisted he be circumcised, Gentiles would have had to become Jews to belong. They did not insist.

commentary.on: they, I say, who were respected imparted nothing to me
commentary.text: Here is the objection's best evidence. Paul insists the Jerusalem leaders added nothing to his message. His tone is cool: 'whatever they were, it makes no difference to me'. He is not their pupil.

commentary.on: even as Peter with the Good News for the circumcised
commentary.text: But notice what he says next: Peter had the same Good News, for Jews, as Paul had for Gentiles. Paul presents two missions with one message, not two religions.

commentary.on: James and Cephas and John, those who were reputed to be pillars, gave to Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship
commentary.text: Cephas is Peter's name in Aramaic; both mean 'rock'. James is the Lord's brother. The three leaders of the Jerusalem church shake hands with Paul. If Paul had invented a different religion, this is the moment it should have shown, and by his own account they recognised his message as theirs.

commentary.on: They only asked us to remember the poor—which very thing I was also zealous to do.
commentary.text: The one request: help the poor of the Jerusalem church. Paul spent years organising a collection from his Gentile churches for them (Romans 15:25–27), a visible sign that the two branches were one.

parts.title: Paul against Peter
parts.context: Some time after the Jerusalem meeting, perhaps around AD 49 to 50, Peter visits Antioch and at first eats with the Gentile believers. Then people arrive from James in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.
commentary.text: An open quarrel between the two greatest apostles, recorded by one of them. No one inventing a harmonious story of the early Church would have put this in. It is strong evidence that Paul really was independent of Jerusalem, and willing to oppose it.

commentary.on: For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles.
commentary.text: The quarrel is about meals. Peter had been eating with non-Jewish believers. When strict Jewish believers arrived, he withdrew, perhaps to avoid offending them. For Paul, this split the one Church into two tables.

commentary.on: so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy
commentary.text: Even Barnabas, Paul's oldest friend and partner. Acts says that Paul and Barnabas later separated when 'the contention grew so sharp' (15:39). Paul was not an easy colleague.

commentary.on: If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?
commentary.text: Paul's point is consistency. Peter himself had lived freely with Gentiles; now his withdrawal pressures them to adopt Jewish customs to share the table. Notice what the quarrel is not about: neither side disputes who Jesus is, or his death and resurrection.

commentary.on: yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ
commentary.text: Here is Paul's central claim. 'Justified' means put right with God, counted as one of his people. Not by 'works of the law', which here especially means the marks of Jewish identity such as circumcision and food laws, but through faith in Christ. Paul says Peter knows this too: 'even we believed'.

commentary.on: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
commentary.text: This is the verse you learned in session 2. For Paul, belonging to Christ is not a matter of a new rule but of a new life, shared with someone who 'loved me, and gave himself up for me'.

commentary.on: For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!
commentary.text: The whole argument in one sentence. If keeping the law is what makes people right with God, then the cross was unnecessary. Critics say this is Paul's invention; Paul says it is what the cross means.

paras: But to the married I command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife not leave her husband
(but if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or else be reconciled to her husband), and that the husband not leave his wife.
But to the rest I—not the Lord—say, if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she is content to live with him, let him not leave her.
Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you,

as also in all of his letters, speaking in them of these things. In those, there are some things that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unsettled twist, as they also do to the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.

parts.title: Not I, but the Lord
parts.context: About AD 54, Paul writing from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, answering their questions about marriage. (The verses around these, on marriage and singleness, are read in 'Love, friendship and marriage'.)

commentary.on: But to the married I command—not I, but the Lord—
commentary.text: On divorce, Paul has a saying of Jesus (compare Mark 10:9–12), and he cites it as the Lord's command, not his own.

commentary.on: But to the rest I—not the Lord—say
commentary.text: On a new question Jesus never addressed, marriage to an unbeliever, Paul says plainly that this is his own judgement. A man inventing a religion would hardly mark so carefully where Jesus's teaching ends and his begins.

parts.title: Our beloved brother Paul
parts.context: The second letter of Peter presents itself as Peter's. Most scholars think it was written later, perhaps around AD 100 to 130, in Peter's name; some defend Peter's authorship. Either way, it shows how the Church came to see Paul's letters.

commentary.on: even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you
commentary.text: Peter, or a writer in his name, calls Paul 'our beloved brother'. The quarrel at Antioch was remembered as a quarrel within one family.

commentary.on: In those, there are some things that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unsettled twist
commentary.text: An honest admission: Paul is hard, and was being misread already. Notice too that his letters are set beside 'the other Scriptures'. A sceptic will say this is the later Church tidying up an old conflict, which is a fair point; a believer will say the Church recognised Paul as its own.

compare.why: Did Paul feel free to invent? Two short passages: one where Paul himself separates Jesus's commands from his own opinion, and one where another early letter speaks of him.
compare.title: Not I, but the Lord

paras: Here is the objection, as its best advocates would put it. Jesus was a Jew who preached to Jews about the coming kingdom of God. He kept the law, argued about it as rabbis did, and told parables about God's mercy and judgement. He did not found a new religion. After his death, his family and followers in Jerusalem, led by his brother James, remained a Torah-keeping Jewish movement.

Paul never met Jesus. He claimed a private revelation that no one could check, insisted that he learned nothing from those who had known Jesus, and quarrelled with them. His letters barely mention Jesus's teaching, parables or miracles; the phrase 'kingdom of God', the centre of Jesus's preaching, appears only a handful of times. Instead Paul preached a heavenly saviour, pre-existent and divine, who dies and rises, and whose death frees believers from the law. That looks less like the Galilean teacher than like the dying and rising gods of the pagan mystery cults.

It was Paul's version that won, because it was built for the Gentile world. The Jerusalem church disappeared after the Romans destroyed the city in AD 70. On this view, Christianity is Paul's religion about Jesus, not the religion of Jesus.
sections.key: The case: Jesus was a Jewish teacher of the kingdom; Paul, who never knew him, invented a religion of a divine saviour for the Gentiles, and his version won.

paras: The case has three main forms. Nietzsche's (The Antichrist, written 1888, published 1895) is a moral attack. He saw Jesus as a free spirit whose 'glad tidings' were a way of living without resentment, here and now. Paul, he said, turned this inside out: he moved the centre of life from this world to a world beyond, invented the resurrection as a lie to give himself power, and made guilt and judgement the core of the faith.

Wrede's (Paul, 1904) is a historian's. Paul's theology was formed by his Jewish beliefs about a heavenly Messiah before he became a Christian; on the Damascus road he simply identified that figure with Jesus. Hence his lack of interest in Jesus's earthly life: 'the second founder of Christianity' had little need of the first.

Maccoby's (The Mythmaker, 1986) is the most radical. He doubted Paul's claim to have been a trained Pharisee, and drew on a hostile tradition, recorded in the fourth century by Epiphanius, that Paul was a Gentile who became a Jew to marry a priest's daughter. He argued that Paul's ideas of a divine saviour and of a sacred meal of body and blood came from the mystery cults and Gnostic myth, and were alien to Judaism and to Jesus.
sections.key: Nietzsche attacked Paul morally, Wrede historically ('the second founder'), Maccoby most radically: a mythmaker drawing on pagan cults.

paras: The first reply rests on Paul's own words. Twice he uses the technical language of passing on a tradition: 'I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you' (1 Corinthians 11:23), introducing the words of the Last Supper; and 'I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures' (15:3), introducing a summary of the faith with a list of resurrection witnesses. These are the words rabbis used for handing on teaching faithfully.

Most scholars, sceptical and believing, date the summary in 1 Corinthians 15 to within a few years of the crucifixion: Paul probably learned it in Damascus or on his visit to Peter three years after his conversion (Galatians 1:18; you read this if you have taken 'Can I trust the Bible?'). So the core of what Paul preached, Christ's death 'for our sins', his burial, his resurrection on the third day and his appearances, was not Paul's invention. He received it from people who were believers before him.
There is a further point. Paul had persecuted the church because of what it already believed. Whatever made him a persecutor came before him.
sections.key: Paul says he 'received' and 'delivered' the core of the faith, Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection and appearances, a summary most scholars date within a few years of the cross.

paras: The heart of the objection is that Paul turned Jesus into a god. In 1913 the German scholar Wilhelm Bousset argued that worship of Jesus as 'Lord' began only in Greek-speaking churches like Antioch, under pagan influence. The evidence since has gone against him.

First, the Aramaic prayer 'Maranatha', 'Our Lord, come!', appears untranslated in Paul's Greek letter (1 Corinthians 16:22) and in the Didache. Aramaic was the language of the first Jewish believers in Judea, so the prayer to Jesus as Lord must go back to them. Second, the hymn of Philippians 2:6–11, which speaks of Christ 'existing in the form of God' and every knee bowing to him, is widely thought to be older than the letter it is quoted in. Third, Stephen, a Jerusalem believer, prayed to Jesus as he died.

The historian Larry Hurtado concluded, in Lord Jesus Christ (2003), that devotion to Jesus alongside God arose suddenly and very early, among Jewish believers in the first few years, not slowly through pagan influence. Paul inherited it.
sections.key: The Aramaic 'Maranatha', the early hymn of Philippians 2 and Stephen's prayer show that Jesus was worshipped as Lord by Jewish believers before Paul's mission.

paras: It is true that Paul rarely quotes Jesus. But he knows more than he quotes. He cites the Lord's command on divorce, carefully separated from his own advice (1 Corinthians 7:10–12); the Lord's instruction that preachers should be supported (9:14; compare Luke 10:7); the words of the Last Supper (11:23–25). His teaching echoes Jesus's sayings: 'Bless those who persecute you' (Romans 12:14; compare Luke 6:28); the whole law summed up in 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Galatians 5:14; compare Mark 12:31). He knows that Jesus had brothers, that one was James, that Peter was married (1 Corinthians 9:5), and that Jesus was betrayed and crucified.

Why does he not say more? Because his letters were written to churches that had already been taught about Jesus, to deal with particular problems. Scholars such as James Dunn and David Wenham argue that Paul assumes the Jesus tradition rather than repeating it. And the deepest continuity is in practice: Jesus scandalised critics by eating with sinners and outsiders; Paul fought Peter at Antioch so that Gentiles could share the table. Both said God's welcome comes before people deserve it.
sections.key: Paul cites Jesus on divorce, wages and the Last Supper, echoes his teaching on enemies and love, and fought, like Jesus, for an open table.

paras: The replies are strong, but they do not dissolve every difficulty. Paul really did shift the emphasis: from Jesus's message about the kingdom to a message about Jesus himself, crucified and risen. He developed ideas, such as being 'in Christ' and the Church as Christ's body, that go beyond anything in the Gospels. He opened the faith to Gentiles without the law, which some Jewish believers resisted, and the Jewish branch of the movement did fade.

Jewish scholars have read Paul in several ways. Maccoby saw a betrayer. Others, such as Daniel Boyarin (A Radical Jew, 1994) and Paula Fredriksen (Paul: The Pagans' Apostle, 2017), see Paul as a Jew to the end, whose message was for Gentiles and who never imagined a separate religion; on this view, it was later Christians, not Paul, who turned his letters against Judaism. That is a challenge to Christians as well as to Paul's critics.
So the fair question is not whether Paul changed anything, but whether his changes were faithful developments of what he received, as the Church believes, or a new creation, as the critics say.
sections.key: Paul did shift the emphasis to Jesus himself and to the Gentiles; the fair question is whether this was faithful development or a new religion.

sections.h: Peter, Paul and the churches today
paras: The quarrel at Antioch has been argued over ever since, because it touches the authority of Peter. Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians of 386, thought the quarrel was staged for the onlookers' benefit, a pretended dispute to teach the Gentiles. Augustine wrote to him in protest: if Scripture could contain a pious lie here, it could be doubted anywhere. Paul really rebuked Peter, Augustine said, and Peter's humility in accepting it was as admirable as Paul's courage. Jerome eventually came round. At the Reformation the episode was used again: Protestants cited it to show that Peter, and so the pope, could be corrected by Scripture; Catholics replied that Peter erred in conduct, not in teaching. Behind that argument lie two larger questions on which Christians still differ: what office Peter held, and whether it was handed on. The table shows how the traditions see them today.

rows: The rock on whom Christ built the Church (Matthew 16:18), first bishop of Rome; the pope inherits his office of unity and, in defined cases, teaching without error (First Vatican Council, 1870). Antioch shows Peter could err in conduct, not in teaching.
Bishops succeed the apostles by an unbroken laying-on of hands; the bishop of Rome succeeds Peter.
First among the apostles; Rome held a primacy of honour among the ancient churches, but every bishop who keeps the faith shares in Peter's 'chair'.
Bishops succeed the apostles; succession goes with keeping the true faith.
First leader of the apostles, but with no office passed to the bishops of Rome; the 'rock' is often read as Peter's confession of faith. Reformers cited Antioch against papal claims.
Most hold a succession of the apostles' teaching, found in Scripture; Anglicans and some Lutherans also keep bishops in historic succession.
table.note: All honour Peter and Paul together; their shared feast day is 29 June.

sections.key: Augustine and Jerome argued over Antioch; Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants differ on Peter's office and on apostolic succession, and honour Peter and Paul together on 29 June.

refs: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Antichrist §42 (written 1888, published 1895); William Wrede, Paulus (1904; English, Paul, 1907); Wilhelm Bousset, Kyrios Christos (1913); Hyam Maccoby, The Mythmaker: Paul and the Invention of Christianity (1986); Epiphanius, Panarion 30.16.

Larry Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ (2003); James Dunn, The Theology of Paul the Apostle (1998); N. T. Wright, What Saint Paul Really Said (1997); David Wenham, Paul: Follower of Jesus or Founder of Christianity? (1995).
Daniel Boyarin, A Radical Jew: Paul and the Politics of Identity (1994); Paula Fredriksen, Paul: The Pagans' Apostle (2017); E. P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977).
Jerome, Commentary on Galatians (386); Augustine, Letters 28, 40 and 82; First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus (1870).

debate.question: Was Paul the founder of Christianity, its faithful interpreter, or both?

positions.name: The founder
positions.who: Friedrich Nietzsche; William Wrede; Hyam Maccoby
positions.view: Paul created a new religion about a divine saviour, for Gentiles, from Jewish apocalyptic ideas (Wrede) or pagan mystery cults (Maccoby), and it displaced the Jewish movement of Jesus and James. Christianity as we know it is Paul's.
positions.evidence: Paul's claim to independence (Galatians 1–2); his quarrel with Peter; his silence about Jesus's teaching and miracles; the disappearance of the Jerusalem church after AD 70.

positions.name: The faithful interpreter
positions.who: James Dunn; N. T. Wright; David Wenham; Larry Hurtado
positions.view: Paul received the core of the faith from those before him, including the worship of Jesus as Lord, and the Jerusalem leaders recognised his message as theirs. He applied it, brilliantly, to the Gentile world. He was a servant of the tradition, not its inventor.
positions.evidence: 'I received... I delivered' (1 Corinthians 11:23; 15:3); 'Maranatha'; the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:9); his care to separate the Lord's commands from his own (1 Corinthians 7:10–12).

positions.name: A Jew for the Gentiles
positions.who: Krister Stendahl; Daniel Boyarin; Paula Fredriksen
positions.view: Neither founder nor simply interpreter: Paul was a Jew who never left Judaism, sent to bring Gentiles to Israel's God. It was later Christians who read his letters as founding a separate religion, often against the Jews.
positions.evidence: Romans 9–11; Paul's continued Jewish identity (Romans 11:1); the collection for Jerusalem.

debate.agree: All agree that Paul's letters are the earliest Christian writings, that he shaped the faith more than anyone after Jesus, and that he believed he was serving the risen Jesus.

look.why: Michele Giambono, a Venetian painter, painted Saint Peter about 1445–50, holding the keys that Christ promised him (Matthew 16:19). In Galatians he is Cephas, the 'pillar' who shook Paul's hand and whom Paul opposed 'to his face'.
points: A man stands barefoot on a small grassy platform, turned slightly to the left, against a blue background.
He has curly greyish-white hair and a short grey beard, with a golden halo round his head.
He wears a golden robe with intricately patterned hems over a purple garment with gold stripes.
In his right hand he holds a large gold object that looks like a key.
In his left hand he holds a red book.

music.why: Bach's Magnificat sets Mary's song from Luke's Gospel, written by Paul's companion. Its words, 'he has helped his servant Israel... as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham', show the faith Paul preached rooted in Israel's own hope.

think.why: If Paul did not invent Christianity, what can historians say about the Jesus he preached? See where they agree and where faith begins.

learn.why: The tradition Paul 'received' and handed on: the strongest evidence that he did not invent the heart of the faith.

check.q: Which piece of evidence in Galatians 2 best supports the claim that Paul was independent of the Jerusalem apostles?
options: That he took Titus with him
That he says the respected leaders 'imparted nothing to me' and that he opposed Peter 'to his face'
That he wrote in Greek
That James asked him to remember the poor
check.why: Paul insists on his independence and records his public clash with Peter.

check.q: Which piece of evidence in the same chapter best supports the reply that Paul preached the same gospel as Jerusalem?
options: That Peter visited Antioch
That he quarrelled with Barnabas
That Titus was a Greek
That James, Cephas and John gave him 'the right hand of fellowship' after hearing his message
check.why: By his own account, the pillars recognised his message as theirs.

check.q: What was the quarrel at Antioch actually about?
options: Whether Jesus was the Messiah
Whether Paul was a Roman citizen
Whether Jesus rose from the dead
Whether Jewish believers should eat at the same table as Gentile believers
check.why: It was about table fellowship; neither side disputed who Jesus was.

check.q: Why do the words 'I received... I delivered' in 1 Corinthians 15:3 matter for this debate?
options: They show Paul wrote the Gospels
They show Paul learned the whole faith directly from the risen Jesus, with no human source
They are the language of handing on tradition, showing the core of the faith came to Paul from believers before him
They prove the resurrection happened
check.why: Most scholars date the summary to within a few years of the cross; Paul inherited it.

check.q: What does the Aramaic prayer 'Maranatha' suggest about Bousset's theory that Jesus was first worshipped as Lord in Greek churches under pagan influence?
options: It counts against it: an Aramaic prayer to Jesus as Lord must come from the earliest Jewish believers
It shows the Didache was written by Paul
It has nothing to do with it
It confirms it
check.why: Greek-speaking churches kept an untranslated Aramaic prayer: it goes back to Judea.

check.q: Which is the strongest form of the objection that survives the replies?
options: That Paul never mentions the crucifixion
That Paul shifted the emphasis from Jesus's message about the kingdom to a message about Jesus himself, and opened the faith to Gentiles without the law
That Peter and Paul never met
That Paul never existed
check.why: The replies show Paul received the core; whether his development was faithful is the real question.

tutorial.question: Did Paul invent Christianity?
tutorial.approach: State the case at full strength, using Nietzsche, Wrede and Maccoby and the evidence of Galatians 1–2. Then set out the replies: the tradition Paul received, the early worship of Jesus, Paul's knowledge of Jesus's teaching, the right hand of fellowship. Then say where the objection still bites, and bring in the Jewish scholars who see Paul as a Jew for the Gentiles. Conclude with your own judgement: founder, interpreter, or something else?
strong: States the objection fairly and in its strongest form.
Uses Galatians 2 for both sides.
Uses 1 Corinthians 15:3 and 11:23 as evidence of received tradition.
Uses Maranatha or Philippians 2 on early worship of Jesus.
Shows Paul's knowledge of Jesus's teaching, with examples.
Acknowledges what Paul did change, and reaches a reasoned verdict.

reading.why: A careful comparison of Paul's teaching with Jesus's, point by point.

reading.author: Hyam Maccoby
reading.title: The Mythmaker: Paul and the Invention of Christianity
reading.why: The objection at its most radical, by a Jewish scholar.
