sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, name one person you met that day who fits one of the Beatitudes (someone grieving, gentle, making peace) and pray for them by name, or simply wish them well in silence.
sessions.reflect: Who does your world call fortunate? Who would you call blessed?
takeaways: The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) is the first of Matthew's five great speeches, probably gathered from Jesus's teaching on many occasions; Luke has a shorter version on a plain.
Matthew shapes Jesus's story to echo Moses, so the Sermon is heard as a new teaching on a mountain, given in Jesus's own name.
It begins with blessing, not command: the Beatitudes declare God's favour on the poor, the grieving and the gentle, which Augustine read as seven steps to God.

sessions.title: You have heard it said
sessions.line: Jesus says he has come not to abolish the law but to fulfil it, and then presses six commands from the outside of life to the inside.
sessions.plain: Right after the Beatitudes, Jesus says something surprising: he has not come to abolish the Jewish law but to fulfil it, and not a letter of it will pass away. Then he gives six examples, each beginning 'You have heard that it was said... but I tell you'. Do not murder becomes do not even nurse anger; do not commit adultery becomes do not look with lust; keep your oaths becomes do not need oaths at all. This session asks whether Jesus cancelled the Old Testament law, or showed what it was for.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed Matthew framing the Sermon as a new teaching on a mountain, like Sinai. The obvious question follows: what happens to the old law? Here Jesus answers it, and gives the first four of six examples.
answers: Did Jesus abolish the Old Testament law?
What are the six 'antitheses', and what do the first four say?
What did Jesus teach about anger, lust, divorce and oaths?
How do Jewish teachers of the time compare?
sessions.finding: Jesus does not cancel the law but presses it inward: from murder to anger, from adultery to lust, from oaths to plain truth.

paras: Session 1 set the scene: crowds from all over the region, a teacher seated on a mountain, and eight blessings on unlikely people. Matthew shaped the story to echo Moses giving the law at Sinai.

The law in question is the Torah, a Hebrew word meaning 'teaching' or 'instruction'. It refers to the first five books of the Bible (Genesis to Deuteronomy), traditionally written by Moses, and especially the commandments in them: the Ten Commandments, and hundreds more about worship, food, justice, the poor and family life. Jewish tradition counts 613. By Jesus's time, keeping the Torah was what it meant to be a faithful Jew.
background.key: The Torah, 'teaching', is the law of Moses in the first five books of the Bible; keeping it was the mark of a faithful Jew.

background.h: Pharisees, scribes and the arguments about the law
paras: In Jesus's day Jews argued vigorously about how to keep the law. The Pharisees were a popular movement of lay teachers who wanted ordinary Jews to live holy lives in everyday matters, and who kept a body of oral tradition alongside the written law. Scribes were experts who copied and taught the law. Other groups, such as the Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy in Jerusalem, and the Essenes, who probably wrote the Dead Sea Scrolls, had their own views.

The Gospels often show Jesus arguing with Pharisees, and Christians have too often turned 'Pharisee' into a sneer. That is unfair. Many of Jesus's views were close to the Pharisees', and their heirs, the rabbis, shaped Judaism as it is still practised. The arguments in the Sermon are arguments within Judaism, between Jews who all cared deeply about keeping God's law.
background.key: Pharisees, scribes, Sadducees and Essenes argued over how to keep the law; Jesus's debates were arguments within Judaism, not against it.

paras: About two centuries after Jesus, around AD 200, Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered the oral teaching of the rabbis into a book called the Mishnah. One of its tractates, Avot ('Fathers'), collects the sayings of the great teachers, starting with Hillel and Shammai, who taught in Jerusalem a generation before Jesus.

If you have taken 'How to read the Bible', you met Avot's opening saying: 'Make a fence to the Torah'. The idea is to protect a commandment by keeping well back from the line: if you must not work on the Sabbath, stop before sunset in case you misjudge the time. Some scholars have compared Jesus's teaching in this passage to building fences: do not even get angry, and you will never murder. Others think he is doing something deeper. The comparison text lets us test both views.
background.key: The Mishnah (c. AD 200) records the rabbis' sayings, including Avot's 'Make a fence to the Torah': protect a law by keeping well back from the line.

paras: The main reading is Matthew 5:17–37: Jesus's statement on the law, then the first four of six contrasts, often called the 'antitheses' (Greek for 'opposite statements'): murder and anger, adultery and lust, divorce, and oaths. The last two, on retaliation and enemies, are the subject of the next session.

The comparison is from the Mishnah's Avot: two rabbis' sayings, one on anger and one on 'fences'. They show that Jesus's concern with the inner life was shared by other Jewish teachers, and help us see what was distinctive about his.
background.key: Matthew 5:17–37: the law fulfilled and the first four antitheses; then two rabbinic sayings on anger and fences.

before: What does Jesus say will happen to 'one smallest letter' of the law?
In each example, what was 'said', and what does Jesus add?
Why might Jesus put reconciliation with your brother before worship?
sessions.readWhy: Jesus's statement on the law, and four examples of what 'fulfilling' it means.

paras: “Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.
For most certainly, I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not even one smallest letter or one tiny pen stroke shall in any way pass away from the law, until all things are accomplished.

Whoever, therefore, shall break one of these least commandments, and teach others to do so, shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven; but whoever shall do and teach them shall be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven.
For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.
“You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison.
Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there, until you have paid the last penny.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery;’
but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.

If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.

If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off, and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.
“It was also said, ‘Whoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorce,’
but I tell you that whoever puts away his wife, except for the cause of sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress; and whoever marries her when she is put away commits adultery.
“Again you have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not make false vows, but shall perform to the Lord your vows,’
but I tell you, don’t swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God;
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
Neither shall you swear by your head, for you can’t make one hair white or black.
But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.

parts.title: Not to destroy, but to fulfil
parts.context: The Sermon so far: the Beatitudes, and the sayings about salt and light (5:3–16). Now Jesus turns to the question every Jewish listener would ask of a new teacher: what about the law of Moses?

commentary.on: Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets.
commentary.text: Jesus answers a suspicion before anyone voices it. 'The law and the prophets' means the Jewish Scriptures as a whole. Some people evidently thought a teacher who ate with sinners and healed on the Sabbath must be throwing the law away.

commentary.on: I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.
commentary.text: 'Fulfil' (Greek plēroō) means to fill up, complete, bring to its intended goal. Matthew uses it of prophecies coming true. Here it suggests that Jesus brings out the law's full meaning, and in his own life does what it points to. How exactly is the question the rest of the chapter answers.

commentary.on: not even one smallest letter or one tiny pen stroke shall in any way pass away from the law
commentary.text: The 'smallest letter' is the Hebrew yod, a little hook; the 'pen stroke' is a tiny mark that distinguishes one letter from another. This is as strong a statement of the law's permanence as any rabbi made.

commentary.on: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees
commentary.text: The scribes and Pharisees were the most careful law-keepers of the day. Jesus does not ask for less than they did, but more. The examples that follow show what 'more' means: not more rules, but a righteousness that reaches the heart.

parts.title: Anger
parts.context: The first of six contrasts. 'You shall not murder' is the sixth of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:13). 'Will be in danger of the judgement' refers to the local courts.

commentary.on: You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones
commentary.text: Jesus's hearers 'heard' the law read aloud in the synagogue; most could not read. 'The ancient ones' are the generation at Sinai. The formula is not 'Moses was wrong', but 'this is what you were told'.

commentary.on: But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment.
commentary.text: 'But I tell you': no prophet spoke like this. Prophets said 'thus says the Lord'. Jesus speaks on his own authority. The command moves from the act to its root: murder begins in anger nursed against a 'brother'. (The words 'without a cause' are in some ancient manuscripts and not others; the World English Bible keeps them, as Augustine's Bible did.)

commentary.on: Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’
commentary.text: Raca is Aramaic, probably meaning 'empty-head'. Jesus moves from inner anger to contempt spoken aloud. Contempt treats another person as worthless; it is the attitude that makes killing thinkable. 'Gehenna' was the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), which became a picture of final judgement.

commentary.on: First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
commentary.text: An astonishing order of priorities. A man has brought an animal to the Temple, perhaps walking for days from Galilee, and remembers a quarrel: he should leave it at the altar and go and make peace first. Relationships come before religious ritual.

commentary.on: Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way
commentary.text: A practical picture from village life: settle with your opponent on the road to court, before the judge decides. Do not let a quarrel run on; the cost only grows.

parts.title: Lust and divorce
parts.context: 'You shall not commit adultery' is the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14). The law of divorce is in Deuteronomy 24:1–4, which allowed a husband to divorce his wife by giving her a written certificate.

commentary.on: everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart
commentary.text: The tenth commandment had already forbidden coveting your neighbour's wife (Exodus 20:17). Jesus joins the two: adultery starts with a look that treats a woman as something to take. Notice it is the man who is held responsible, not the woman for being seen.

commentary.on: If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out
commentary.text: This is hyperbole, deliberate exaggeration, a common teaching device. Almost no one in the Church has taken it literally; the great third-century scholar Origen, who reportedly took a similar saying (Matthew 19:12) literally, was criticised for it. The point is: deal ruthlessly with whatever leads you into wrong.

commentary.on: whoever puts away his wife, except for the cause of sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress
commentary.text: In Jesus's day a husband could divorce his wife; a wife could not divorce her husband. The schools of Shammai and Hillel argued over the grounds: only unfaithfulness, said Shammai's followers; for almost anything, said Hillel's. Jesus's teaching protected women from being discarded. The exception ('sexual immorality', Greek porneia) appears only in Matthew; Mark 10:11 and Luke 16:18 have none.

parts.title: Oaths
parts.context: The law forbade false oaths and breaking vows to God (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21). People swore by heaven, by earth or by Jerusalem to make their words more binding without, as they thought, invoking God directly.

commentary.on: don’t swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God
commentary.text: Jesus closes the loophole. Swearing by heaven is swearing by God, whose throne it is. You cannot keep God out of your promises.

commentary.on: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’
commentary.text: The point of an oath is to make your word trustworthy. If you are always truthful, you do not need one. An oath implies that, without it, you might lie. Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians have refused to swear oaths in court on the strength of this verse; English law began to let Quakers 'affirm' instead in 1696.

paras: They said three things. Rabbi Eliezer said: "Let the honour of thy associate be dear to thee as thine own"; and "Be not easily provoked, and repent one day before thy death".
Rabbi Akiba said: "Laughter and levity lead to lewdness." He used to say: "The Tradition is a fence to the Torah; vows are a defence to self-control; silence is a defence to wisdom."

parts.author: The rabbis of the Mishnah
parts.work: Mishnah Avot (The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers)
parts.title: Be not easily provoked
parts.context: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus taught around AD 80–120, two generations after Jesus. He was one of five disciples of Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai, who rebuilt Jewish teaching after the Romans destroyed the Temple in AD 70; 'they' are those five. Translated from the Hebrew by W. O. E. Oesterley (1919), whose verse numbers differ from today's standard ones. This text comes from a scanned copy; the translator's footnote markers have been removed.
parts.plain: Rabbi Eliezer gives two pieces of advice. Care about the honour of your friend as much as your own. Do not lose your temper easily, and repent one day before you die: since no one knows when that day will be, repent today.

commentary.on: Let the honour of thy associate be dear to thee as thine own
commentary.text: This is close to 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18), applied to reputation. It is the opposite of saying 'Raca' to your brother.

commentary.on: Be not easily provoked
commentary.text: Like Jesus, the rabbi warns against anger. Jewish teaching shared the concern with the heart: the Ten Commandments themselves end with 'You shall not covet', a command about desire, not action.

commentary.on: repent one day before thy death
commentary.text: The Talmud explains the riddle: since you may die tomorrow, repent today (Shabbat 153a). Compare 'Agree with your adversary quickly': both teachers urge acting now, before it is too late.

parts.work: Mishnah Avot (The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers)
parts.title: A fence to the Torah
parts.context: Rabbi Akiva (c. AD 50–135) was the greatest teacher of his generation; he was put to death by the Romans after the revolt of AD 132–135. 'The Tradition' is the oral teaching passed down alongside the written law. Same translation and editing as above.
parts.plain: Rabbi Akiva says that joking and frivolity lead to sexual looseness. Then he lists protections: the oral tradition protects the written law, making vows helps a person control themselves, and keeping silent protects wisdom.

commentary.on: Laughter and levity lead to lewdness.
commentary.text: A rabbi, like Jesus, sees that wrong acts begin earlier, in attitudes and habits. This is the same insight as 'gazes at a woman to lust after her'.

commentary.on: The Tradition is a fence to the Torah
commentary.text: Here is the 'fence' idea: rules that keep you well back from breaking a commandment. Some Christians have read Jesus's antitheses as fences of this kind: don't be angry, so you never kill.

commentary.on: vows are a defence to self-control
commentary.text: Notice the contrast with Jesus. For Akiva, vows help a person hold to good resolutions. Jesus says not to swear at all, but to be so truthful that 'yes' is enough. He is not adding a fence; he is asking for a heart that needs no fence.

compare.author: The rabbis of the Mishnah
compare.work: Mishnah Avot (The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers)
compare.why: Other Jewish teachers also warned against anger and built 'fences' around the commandments. Read two sayings from the Mishnah and ask: is Jesus building fences too, or doing something else?
compare.title: Fences round the law

paras: Christians have read 'I came not to destroy, but to fulfil' in three main ways. First, Jesus fulfils the law by obeying it perfectly himself. Second, he fulfils it by teaching its full meaning, as the antitheses do. Third, he fulfils it as a prophecy is fulfilled: the law pointed forward to him, and with his coming some parts (sacrifices, food laws) reach their goal and fall away.

Augustine, in the same commentary you met in session 1, combines the first two: Jesus fulfils the law either by adding what was missing or by doing what it commands. The third reading rests on other New Testament passages, such as Mark 7:19, where Mark comments that Jesus 'declared all foods clean', and Paul's letters. Matthew himself is the most Jewish of the Gospels and never says the food laws are over. Scholars still argue about how much of the law Matthew's community kept.
sections.key: 'Fulfil' can mean obey perfectly, reveal the full meaning, or bring to its goal; Matthew stresses that not a letter of the law passes away.

paras: Matthew sets out six contrasts in two groups of three. In each Jesus quotes the law or a common reading of it, and goes further.

In the first, second and fourth, he goes deeper than the law without contradicting it: if you are never angry, you will not murder; if you never look with lust, you will not commit adultery; if you always tell the truth, you need no oath. In the third, fifth and sixth, he seems to set aside something the law allowed: divorce, proportionate revenge, and (as a common reading had it) hatred of enemies. Even there, he does not tell anyone to break a commandment. No command says you must divorce, take an eye for an eye, or hate. Jesus forbids what the law permitted, for the sake of what it was aiming at.

rows: Do not be angry or contemptuous; make peace first
Do not divorce, except for sexual immorality
Do not swear at all; let yes be yes
Do not retaliate; turn the other cheek
Love your neighbour (Leviticus 19:18), and hate your enemy
table.note: The fifth and sixth are the subject of the next session.

sections.key: Six contrasts: three go deeper than the law, three forbid what it permitted; none tells anyone to break a commandment.

sections.h: From the outside to the inside
paras: The common thread is the move from action to heart. Murder starts with anger and contempt; adultery with the look. The law could judge a deed in court; Jesus is concerned with the person who does it.

This was not unheard of. The Hebrew prophets had said God wanted 'a new heart' (Ezekiel 36:26) and promised a covenant in which God says of his law, 'I will write it in their heart' (Jeremiah 31:33). Jewish teachers, as you saw in the Mishnah, warned against anger and the habits that lead to sin. What was distinctive was the authority with which Jesus spoke ('But I tell you'), and how far he pushed the demand: not 'try to control your anger' but treat anger itself as the beginning of murder. At the end of the Sermon, the crowds are astonished because 'he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes' (7:29).
sections.key: Jesus moves from deed to heart, as the prophets and rabbis also did; what was distinctive was his authority and how far he pushed the demand.

paras: For centuries Christian preachers contrasted Jesus's religion of the heart with a supposedly cold Jewish legalism. Modern scholarship has rejected that picture. In 1977 the scholar E. P. Sanders showed in Paul and Palestinian Judaism that the Judaism of Jesus's time was a religion of grace: God chose Israel first, and the law was Israel's grateful response, not a ladder to earn God's favour.

If you took 'Exodus and the law', you read Hillel's famous answer to a Gentile who asked to be taught the whole law standing on one leg, and Rabbi Akiva's death with the Shema on his lips. Hillel taught a generation before Jesus. The Jewish scholar David Flusser (1917–2000) argued that much of the Sermon would have been at home among the more generous Pharisees. A fair reading holds both: Jesus was a Jewish teacher, debating within Judaism, and his followers came to believe that his 'But I tell you' carried an authority no rabbi claimed.
sections.key: The old contrast between Jesus's 'religion of the heart' and Jewish 'legalism' is unfair; Jesus taught within Judaism, though with an authority no rabbi claimed.

paras: Few verses have shaped law and family life as much as Matthew 5:32. Christians agree that Jesus taught that marriage is meant to be for life, and differ on what follows when it fails.

Jewish law, then and now, allows divorce, with a written bill (the get); the Mishnah records the debate between the schools of Shammai and Hillel (Gittin 9:10). Jesus's teaching was stricter than either school.

rows: A valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; remarriage after divorce is not allowed while the spouse lives. A church court may declare that a valid marriage never existed (an annulment).
Marriage is meant to be lifelong, but out of pastoral mercy (oikonomia) the Church may allow a second, and in some cases a third, marriage, with a more penitential service.
Most churches allow divorce, at least for adultery and desertion (Westminster Confession 24.5–6), and many allow remarriage; practice varies widely.
Divorce is permitted by a written bill (get), following Deuteronomy 24; the grounds were debated by Shammai's and Hillel's schools.
table.note: All Christian traditions agree that Jesus taught marriage as a lifelong union.

sections.key: Christians agree Jesus taught lifelong marriage; Catholics forbid remarriage, the Orthodox allow it in mercy, most Protestants allow divorce for adultery or desertion.

paras: The fourth antithesis, on oaths, sounds small, but it has a long history. Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr (c. 150) cited it. In the Reformation, the Anabaptists' Schleitheim Confession (1527) refused all oaths, and Quakers from the 1650s refused to swear in court, which cost many of them prison and fines until Parliament let them 'affirm' instead (1696). Most Christians, from Augustine to the Catholic, Lutheran and Anglican churches, have held that oaths in court are allowed when required for justice, since God himself is said to swear in Scripture (Hebrews 6:13).

Either way, the principle is the same: a person whose word is always true does not need a special guarantee. The idea that a plain 'yes' should be as good as a sworn oath has entered ordinary morality: we still say that someone's word is their bond.
sections.key: Quakers and Anabaptists refused oaths on this verse; most churches allowed them in court. All agree the aim is a word that is always true.

refs: Matthew 5:17–37; 7:29; Mark 7:19; 10:2–12; Luke 16:18; Exodus 20:13–17; 21:24; Leviticus 19:12, 18; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26; Hebrews 6:13.
Augustine, De sermone Domini in monte I.20 (I.8), I.21–25 (I.9).
Mishnah Avot 1:1; 2:10; 3:13, tr. W. O. E. Oesterley, The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (1919); Mishnah Gittin 9:10; Talmud, Shabbat 153a.
E. P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977); David Flusser, Jesus (1968; rev. ed. 1997).
Schleitheim Confession (1527), articles 6–7; Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), 24.5–6; Catechism of the Catholic Church 1614–1615, 1650; Quakers Act 1695 (7 & 8 Will. III c. 34).

debate.question: Is Jesus's teaching stricter than the law, or the law's true meaning?

positions.name: A new and stricter law
positions.who: Some early Christian writers; many modern readers
positions.view: Jesus adds to the law of Moses a higher standard: not only no murder but no anger. The Sermon is a new law for a new people, harder than the old.
positions.evidence: 'But I tell you' six times; 'unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees'; the third, fifth and sixth antitheses forbid what Moses allowed.

positions.name: The law's true meaning
positions.who: Augustine; Thomas Aquinas; John Calvin; most commentators
positions.view: Jesus does not add a new law but strips away shallow readings and shows what the commandments always meant. 'Do not murder' always forbade hatred, as Leviticus 19:17 says: 'You shall not hate your brother in your heart.'
positions.evidence: 'I came not to destroy, but to fulfil'; Leviticus 19:17–18; the prophets' 'new heart'; Calvin's view that Jesus restored the law from the Pharisees' corruptions (Institutes II.8.7).

positions.name: A Jewish teacher's interpretation
positions.who: Jewish scholars such as David Flusser and Amy-Jill Levine
positions.view: Jesus is doing what Jewish teachers did: interpreting the Torah, often strictly, in debate with other schools. Much of what he says has rabbinic parallels; what is new is his personal authority.
positions.evidence: Avot's warnings about anger and fences; the Shammai–Hillel divorce debate; Levine, The Misunderstood Jew (2006).

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus did not tell anyone to break a commandment, and that he moved the law from the deed to the heart.

look.why: There is no painting of Moses with the tablets free in the gallery's collection. Bernard van Orley painted another scene of Jesus and the law, from Luke 2:41–52: at twelve, he sits among the teachers in the Temple in Jerusalem, listening and asking questions. It is the only Gospel story of Jesus between his infancy and his baptism.
points: A young child with shoulder-length, wavy, light brown hair sits barefoot on a low ledge in the centre, in a dark blue gown.
The child gestures with one hand outstretched and the other near his chest.
Older men in turbans, hats and hoods and colourful robes surround him; some hold books or scrolls and seem to be in discussion, most looking towards the child.
Behind the child, a man in pink and a woman in blue with a white cloth over her hair look towards the group; her hands are crossed over her chest.
The scene is set in a structure of thin white columns with gold detailing, blue vaults and small gold cherub-like figures in niches.
Behind them is a pale pink castle with railings and towers.

music.why: Beethoven wrote on the score of his Missa Solemnis: 'From the heart; may it go to the heart.' The words of an old liturgy, sung so that they reach the inside of a person: what Jesus asks of the law.

think.why: Jesus grounds right and wrong in God's law and in the heart. See how Christians answer whether morality needs God.

learn.why: When asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus joined two laws of the Torah: love God, and love your neighbour. It is the key to how he read the law.

check.q: What does Jesus mean by saying he came 'not to destroy, but to fulfil' the law?
options: That only the Ten Commandments still count
That he will write a new law to replace Moses
That the law no longer matters to his followers
That he brings the law to its full meaning and goal; not a letter of it passes away
check.why: 'Fulfil' means to fill up or complete; he immediately insists on the law's permanence and asks for more righteousness, not less.

check.q: In the first antithesis, why does Jesus move from murder to anger and 'Raca'?
options: Because Raca was a legal term for a murderer
Because anger was punishable by death in Jewish law
Because no one in his audience had committed murder
Because murder grows from anger and contempt; God judges the heart as well as the deed
check.why: The command is pressed back to its root: the inner attitude that makes killing thinkable.

check.q: Why does Jesus tell the worshipper to leave his gift at the altar?
options: Because gifts must be offered in secret
Because being reconciled with his brother comes before religious ritual
Because the priest was not ready
Because sacrifices had been abolished
check.why: 'First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.'

check.q: Which statement about the six antitheses is most accurate?
options: They were added to Matthew by a later editor
Three go deeper than a command; three forbid things the law permitted; none tells anyone to break a commandment
They are all about sexual ethics
All six cancel a commandment of Moses
check.why: No law required divorce, revenge or hatred; Jesus forbids what was permitted, for the sake of the law's aim.

check.q: What does the comparison with Rabbi Akiva's saying about vows show?
options: That Akiva and Jesus both cared about inner habits, but Akiva added protections like vows, while Jesus asked for a truthfulness that needs no oath
That Jesus copied Akiva
That vows were forbidden in Judaism
That rabbis never thought about the heart
check.why: Akiva lived after Jesus, so neither copied the other; the contrast shows a fence versus a changed heart.

check.q: Why do most modern scholars reject the old contrast between Jesus's 'religion of the heart' and Jewish 'legalism'?
options: Because Jesus never mentioned the heart
Because the Sermon was written by a rabbi
Because the Pharisees did not exist
Because Jewish sources of the time also stressed the heart and saw the law as a response to God's grace, as E. P. Sanders argued
check.why: The prophets, the rabbis and Sanders's work show that Judaism was not mere rule-keeping; Jesus argued within it.

tutorial.question: Did Jesus abolish the law?
tutorial.approach: Start with Matthew 5:17–20 and the meanings of 'fulfil'. Work through the four antitheses you read, noting which go deeper than the law and which forbid what it allowed. Compare the rabbinic sayings, and be fair to Judaism. End with your own answer, taking account of other New Testament texts such as Mark 7:19.
strong: Explains 5:17–20, including the 'smallest letter' and the higher righteousness.
Distinguishes the three readings of 'fulfil'.
Analyses at least two antitheses in detail.
Uses the Mishnah sayings to show both continuity and difference.
Avoids caricaturing the Pharisees or Judaism.
Notices that other New Testament texts (Mark 7:19, Paul) raise the question differently.

reading.author: Amy-Jill Levine
reading.title: The Misunderstood Jew
reading.why: A Jewish New Testament scholar on reading Jesus fairly within Judaism.

reading.author: David Flusser
reading.title: Jesus
reading.why: A great Jewish scholar's portrait of Jesus as a teacher of the Torah.

reading.author: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison
reading.title: Matthew 1–7 (International Critical Commentary)
reading.why: The standard detailed commentary on the antitheses.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: think of one person you are angry with or have written off. Before Sunday, take one step towards making peace: a message, an apology, or simply praying for them by name.
sessions.reflect: Where in your life do you keep the rule but not its point?
takeaways: Jesus said he came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it: to bring out its full meaning and goal.
His antitheses press the commandments from the deed to the heart: anger, lust, discarded wives and the need for oaths.
Other Jewish teachers shared his concern with the heart; what stood out was his authority, 'But I tell you'.

sessions.title: The other cheek
sessions.line: The two hardest commands in the Sermon: do not hit back, and love your enemies. Tolstoy said they meant exactly what they say.
sessions.plain: Jesus quotes the oldest law of justice, 'an eye for an eye', and then tells his hearers not to retaliate at all: if someone strikes you on the cheek, turn the other one; if a soldier makes you carry his pack a mile, carry it two. Then he goes further: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, because that is what God is like. These are the most admired and the most argued-over words Jesus ever spoke. This session asks what they meant, whether they forbid all force, and how people from Tolstoy to Martin Luther King have tried to live them.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed Jesus pressing the law from the deed to the heart in four examples. The last two of the six contrasts are the hardest, because they seem to ask for something no society could run on. They need a session of their own.
answers: What did 'an eye for an eye' mean, and what does Jesus put in its place?
Does 'turn the other cheek' mean never resisting evil?
Love your enemies: who were the enemies, and what does it mean to love them?
How have Christians lived this: pacifists, just-war thinkers, and nonviolent resisters?
sessions.finding: The hardest teachings, non-retaliation and love of enemies, were meant to be lived, and the Church has argued ever since about how.

paras: In session 2 Jesus said he came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it, and gave four contrasts: anger, lust, divorce and oaths. Each time he moved from what the law forbade in action to what lies behind it in the heart. Now come the fifth and sixth contrasts, on revenge and on enemies.
background.key: After four contrasts on anger, lust, divorce and oaths, Jesus turns to revenge and enemies.

paras: 'An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth' comes from the law of Moses (Exodus 21:23–25; Leviticus 24:19–20; Deuteronomy 19:21). It is often heard today as a licence for revenge. In fact it was a limit on revenge. In a world of blood feuds, where an injury to one man could lead to the killing of his attacker's whole family, the law said: the penalty must fit the injury, and no more. Older law codes, such as Hammurabi's in Babylon around 1750 BC, have similar rules.

It was also a rule for judges, not for private revenge. By the time of the Mishnah, around AD 200, the rabbis taught that it meant paying compensation in money for the injury, not literally taking an eye (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1). Jesus is not attacking a cruel law. He is asking his followers not to claim even what a fair law allowed them.
background.key: 'An eye for an eye' limited revenge to a fair penalty set by judges; the rabbis read it as money compensation. Jesus asks his followers not to claim even that.

paras: Jesus's hearers lived in Galilee, ruled by Herod Antipas under the Roman empire. Most were peasant farmers and fishermen. Taxes were heavy. Roman soldiers could legally force a civilian to carry their baggage for one Roman mile (about 1,500 metres); the Greek word for this, angareuō, is the one Matthew uses when the soldiers 'compelled' Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus's cross (Matthew 27:32). Debts could cost a poor man his land, and even the clothes he slept in.

Enemies were not abstract. They were the occupying soldiers, the tax collectors who worked for Rome and were despised as collaborators, and, for many, the Samaritans, a neighbouring people with a rival temple. Within a generation of Jesus's death, Jews in Judea would rise against Rome, and in AD 70 Jerusalem and its Temple would be destroyed. The Sermon's words about enemies were spoken into a land that would soon be at war.
background.key: Galilee was under Roman rule: heavy taxes, soldiers who could force civilians to carry their packs, collaborators and rivals. War with Rome came in AD 66–70.

paras: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was a Russian count and one of the greatest novelists who ever lived: the author of War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1878). In his fifties he went through a spiritual crisis and came to believe that the heart of Christianity was the Sermon on the Mount, above all 'resist not evil'. He rejected the Russian Orthodox Church, its creeds and its support for the state, and tried to live simply on his estate at Yasnaya Polyana.

His book The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1893) was banned in Russia and published abroad. In its first chapter he describes the letters he received from Quakers and other Americans who had reached the same conclusion before him. The book changed at least one life that changed many others: a young Indian lawyer in South Africa, Mohandas Gandhi, read it in 1894 and later wrote that it overwhelmed him.
background.key: Tolstoy, the novelist, came to see 'resist not evil' as the heart of Christianity; his 1893 book was banned in Russia and deeply shaped Gandhi.

paras: The main reading is Matthew 5:38–48: the fifth contrast, on retaliation, and the sixth, on enemies, ending with 'be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect'.

The comparison sets two great readers side by side. Tolstoy's first chapter quotes American Christians who took Jesus literally and refused all force. Augustine, in the commentary you met in session 1, reads the same verses and argues that love may sometimes punish, as a father corrects a child. Their disagreement is still the Church's disagreement.
background.key: Matthew 5:38–48; then Tolstoy's literal reading set against Augustine's.

before: List the four examples in 5:39–42. What do they have in common?
Why, according to Jesus, should we love our enemies?
What do you think 'perfect' means in the last verse?
sessions.readWhy: The fifth and sixth contrasts: do not retaliate, and love your enemies.

paras: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.’
But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.
If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also.
Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two.
Give to him who asks you, and don’t turn away him who desires to borrow from you.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’
But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,
that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.
For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
If you only greet your friends, what more do you do than others? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.

parts.title: Do not retaliate
parts.context: The fifth contrast. Jesus quotes the law of equal penalty and gives four short examples from everyday life in a village under Roman rule: a blow, a lawsuit, a soldier's demand and a request for money.

commentary.on: ‘An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.’
commentary.text: The law of equal penalty, in Latin the lex talionis. As the background explained, it limited revenge and was applied by judges. Jesus does not deny that it was just. He asks for something beyond justice.

commentary.on: don’t resist him who is evil
commentary.text: The Greek antistēnai means to set oneself against, often in a fight or a lawsuit. It may mean 'do not retaliate against an evil person' rather than 'do nothing about evil'. How far it goes is the whole argument of this session. Jesus himself confronted evil constantly in words; and when struck at his trial, he protested: 'why do you beat me?' (John 18:23).

commentary.on: whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also
commentary.text: A right-handed blow to the right cheek is a backhanded slap: in that culture an insult, the way a master hit a slave, rather than an attack. The disciple is not to answer insult with insult. Some scholars, like Walter Wink, think turning the left cheek also refused to accept the humiliation, as you will see in the lecture.

commentary.on: If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also.
commentary.text: The 'coat' is the tunic worn next to the skin; the 'cloak' is the outer garment, which the poor also used as a blanket. The law said a poor man's cloak taken as a pledge must be returned by sunset (Exodus 22:26–27). A man sued for his tunic who handed over his cloak too would stand nearly naked in court: generosity, and perhaps a protest at a creditor's greed.

commentary.on: Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two.
commentary.text: This is the soldier's right to force a civilian to carry his baggage for a mile. Jesus's hearers hated it. Carrying it a second mile, by choice, turns forced labour into a free gift, and the occupier into a person.

commentary.on: Give to him who asks you, and don’t turn away him who desires to borrow from you.
commentary.text: The last example is about money. In a village where everyone knew everyone, refusing a loan to someone in need was a way of shutting them out. Jesus asks for an open hand.

parts.title: Love your enemies
parts.context: The sixth and last contrast. 'You shall love your neighbour' is from Leviticus 19:18. 'Hate your enemy' is not in the law; it was a common reading of who counted as a neighbour.

commentary.on: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’
commentary.text: The first half is Leviticus 19:18, which Jesus elsewhere calls the second great commandment. The second half is nowhere in the Hebrew Bible, which also says 'love the stranger' (Leviticus 19:34). But it was in the air: one of the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Community Rule, tells its members to 'hate all the sons of darkness'. Jesus rejects that reading.

commentary.on: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you
commentary.text: Love here (Greek agapē) is not a feeling of liking. It is shown in actions: blessing, doing good, praying. You can do all three for someone you cannot yet like. Prayer comes last, and is perhaps the hardest: to ask God's good for someone who is hurting you.

commentary.on: For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.
commentary.text: The reason is not that enemies deserve love, or that loving them will win them over. It is that God is like this. Sun and rain fall on everyone's field. To love enemies is to be 'children of your Father', to share the family likeness.

commentary.on: Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
commentary.text: Tax collectors were despised as collaborators with Rome. Even they love their friends. Love that returns love is ordinary; Jesus asks for love that goes first.

commentary.on: Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.
commentary.text: 'Perfect' (Greek teleios) means complete, whole, mature, not flawless. In context it means loving without limits, as God does: Luke's version says 'Be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful' (Luke 6:36). It echoes Leviticus 19:2: 'You shall be holy; for I, the Lord your God, am holy.'

paras: Among the first responses called forth by my book were some letters from American Quakers. In these letters, expressing their sympathy with my views on the unlawfulness for a Christian of war and the use of force of any kind, the Quakers gave me details of their own so-called sect, which for more than two hundred years has actually professed the teaching of Christ on non-resistance to evil by force, and does not make use of weapons in self-defense. The Quakers sent me also their pamphlets, journals, and books, from which I learnt how they had, years ago, established beyond doubt the duty for a Christian of fulfilling the command of non-resistance to evil by force, and had exposed the error of the Church's teaching in allowing war and capital punishment.

"We believe that the penal code of the old covenant--an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth--has been abrogated by Jesus Christ, and that under the new covenant the forgiveness instead of the punishment of enemies has been enjoined on all his disciples in all cases whatsoever. To extort money from enemies, cast them into prison, exile or execute them, is obviously not to forgive but to take retribution.

"The history of mankind is crowded with evidences proving that physical coercion is not adapted to moral regeneration, and that the sinful dispositions of men can be subdued only by love; that evil can be exterminated only by good; that it is not safe to rely upon the strength of an arm to preserve us from harm; that there is great security in being gentle, long-suffering, and abundant in mercy; that it is only the meek who shall inherit the earth; for those who take up the sword shall perish by the sword.
Q. Then the ancients allowed the resistance of injury by injury?
A. Yes. But Jesus forbids it. The Christian has in no case the right to put to death his neighbor who has done him evil, or to do him injury in return.
Q. May he kill or maim him in self-defense?
A. No.
Q. May he go with a complaint to the judge that he who has wronged him may be punished?
A. No. What he does through others, he is in reality doing himself.
Q. Can he fight in conflict with foreign enemies or disturbers of the peace?

A. Certainly not. He cannot take any part in war or in preparations for war. He cannot make use of a deadly weapon. He cannot oppose injury to injury, whether he is alone or with others, either in person or through other people.
Q. Wherein lies the chief significance of the doctrine of non-resistance?

A. In the fact that it alone allows of the possibility of eradicating evil from one's own heart, and also from one's neighbor's. This doctrine forbids doing that whereby evil has endured for ages and multiplied in the world. He who attacks another and injures him, kindles in the other a feeling of hatred, the root of every evil. To injure another because he has injured us, even with the aim of overcoming evil, is doubling the harm for him and for oneself; it is begetting, or at least setting free and inciting, that evil spirit which we should wish to drive out. Satan can never be driven out by Satan. Error can never be corrected by error, and evil cannot be vanquished by evil.
True non-resistance is the only real resistance to evil. It is crushing the serpent's head. It destroys and in the end extirpates the evil feeling.

56. Hence the Lord goes on to say: You have heard that it has been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: but I say unto you, that you resist not evil; but whosoever shall smite you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if any man will sue you at the law, and take away your coat [tunic, undergarment], let him have your cloak also. And whosoever shall compel you to go a mile, go with him two. Give to him that asks you, and from him that would borrow of you turn not away. It is the lesser righteousness of the Pharisees not to go beyond measure in revenge, that no one should give back more than he has received: and this is a great step. For it is not easy to find any one who, when he has received a blow, wishes merely to return the blow; and who, on hearing one word from a man who reviles him, is content to return only one, and that just an equivalent; but he avenges it more immoderately, either under the disturbing influence of anger, or because he thinks it just, that he who first inflicted injury should suffer more severe injury than he suffered who had not inflicted injury. Such a spirit was in great measure restrained by the law, where it was written, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth; by which expressions a certain measure is intended, so that the vengeance should not exceed the injury. And this is the beginning of peace: but perfect peace is to have no wish at all for such vengeance.

63. Nor are we thus precluded from inflicting such punishment [requital] as avails for correction, and as compassion itself dictates; nor does it stand in the way of that course proposed, where one is prepared to endure more at the hand of him whom he wishes to set right. But no one is fit for inflicting this punishment except the man who, by the greatness of his love, has overcome that hatred wherewith those are wont to be inflamed who wish to avenge themselves. For it is not to be feared that parents would seem to hate a little son when, on committing an offense, he is beaten by them that he may not go on offending. And certainly the perfection of love is set before us by the imitation of God the Father Himself when it is said in what follows: Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which persecute you; and yet it is said of Him by the prophet, For whom the Lord loves He corrects; yea, He scourges every son whom He receives.

The Lord also says, The servant that knows not his Lord's will, and does things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes; but the servant that knows his Lord's will, and does things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with many stripes. No more, therefore, is sought for, except that he should punish to whom, in the natural order of things, the power is given; and that he should punish with the same goodwill which a father has towards his little son, whom by reason of his youth he cannot yet hate. For from this source the most suitable example is drawn, in order that it may be sufficiently manifest that sin can be punished in love rather than be left unpunished; so that one may wish him on whom he inflicts it not to be miserable by means of punishment, but to be happy by means of correction, yet be prepared, if need be, to endure with equanimity more injuries inflicted by him whom he wishes to be corrected, whether he may have the power of putting restraint upon him or not.

parts.author: Leo Tolstoy
parts.work: The Kingdom of God Is Within You, chapter I
parts.ref: Tolstoy, The Kingdom of God Is Within You, chapter I
parts.title: Non-resistance: the Quakers, Garrison and Ballou
parts.context: Tolstoy wrote this book at Yasnaya Polyana, his estate south of Moscow, and finished it in 1893. Chapter I collects the letters and pamphlets he received from Americans who had held his view for decades. The second and third paragraphs are from the Declaration of Sentiments of the Boston Peace Convention of 1838, written by William Lloyd Garrison, the campaigner against slavery. The questions and answers are from a catechism by Adin Ballou (1803–1890), a minister who founded a Christian community at Hopedale, Massachusetts. Translated by Constance Garnett (1894). Cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Tolstoy says that after his book about Christ's teaching appeared, American Quakers wrote to tell him they had taught for two hundred years that Christians must not fight or use force. Garrison's declaration says Jesus abolished the old law of an eye for an eye: Christians must forgive enemies in every case, and only love, not force, can make people good. Ballou's catechism spells it out: a Christian may not kill or injure even in self-defence, may not take a wrongdoer to court to be punished, and may not fight in war. True non-resistance, he says, is the only real way to destroy evil.

commentary.on: which for more than two hundred years has actually professed the teaching of Christ on non-resistance to evil by force
commentary.text: The Quakers, or Society of Friends, began in England in the 1650s with George Fox. Their 'peace testimony' (1660) refused all war. They are one of the 'historic peace churches', with the Mennonites and the Church of the Brethren.

commentary.on: has been abrogated by Jesus Christ
commentary.text: Garrison reads the fifth antithesis as cancelling the law of equal penalty, not just for private revenge but for the state: no prisons, no exile, no execution. That is a much bigger claim than the text makes, and it is the key question: does the Sermon speak to individuals, or to governments too?

commentary.on: the sinful dispositions of men can be subdued only by love; that evil can be exterminated only by good
commentary.text: This echoes Paul: 'Don't be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good' (Romans 12:21). Garrison was no passive man: he spent his life attacking slavery in print. Non-resistance for him meant refusing force, not refusing to fight injustice.

commentary.on: What he does through others, he is in reality doing himself.
commentary.text: Ballou's logic is strict: if I may not strike back, I may not ask a judge or a soldier to strike for me. This is the real challenge of the literal reading. It rules out police, courts, armies and even voting, as his later answers say.

commentary.on: True non-resistance is the only real resistance to evil.
commentary.text: The paradox at the heart of the position. Violence, Ballou says, multiplies evil by kindling hatred; only refusing to return evil for evil can end the cycle. Gandhi and King would turn this into a method of public action.

parts.author: Augustine
parts.work: Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Book I
parts.ref: Augustine, Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount I.56 and I.63 (I.19–20)
parts.title: The beginning of peace, and correction in love
parts.context: From Augustine's commentary, about 394, which you met in session 1. He quotes the verses in his Latin Bible's wording ('resist not evil', 'go with him two'). Translated by William Findlay (1888), as revised for New Advent; the square brackets are the translator's.
parts.plain: Augustine says the old law of an eye for an eye was a great step: it stopped people taking more revenge than they had suffered, and was the beginning of peace. Perfect peace is to want no revenge at all. But this does not stop all punishment. Someone who has the right to punish, like a parent, may punish to correct, out of love, never out of hatred, as God corrects those he loves. And he must be ready to suffer more from the person he is trying to set right.

commentary.on: It is the lesser righteousness of the Pharisees not to go beyond measure in revenge
commentary.text: Augustine is fair to the old law: limiting revenge was 'a great step', because human anger always wants to give back more than it got.

commentary.on: And this is the beginning of peace: but perfect peace is to have no wish at all for such vengeance.
commentary.text: For Augustine the Sermon is about the will: what Jesus forbids is the desire for revenge. That is what makes his reading different from Tolstoy's: the heart must be free of vengeance, but outward action may vary.

commentary.on: Nor are we thus precluded from inflicting such punishment [requital] as avails for correction, and as compassion itself dictates
commentary.text: Here is the crucial move. Punishment that aims at the good of the wrongdoer, and is given by someone with the right to give it, is not revenge. The model is a parent, and behind the parent, God, who 'corrects' those he loves (Proverbs 3:12; Hebrews 12:6).

commentary.on: no one is fit for inflicting this punishment except the man who, by the greatness of his love, has overcome that hatred
commentary.text: A demanding condition: only someone who has stopped hating may punish. Augustine's critics say this gave rulers an easy excuse; his defenders say it set a standard rulers almost never meet.

compare.author: Leo Tolstoy and Augustine
compare.work: The Kingdom of God Is Within You, chapter I
compare.ref: Tolstoy, The Kingdom of God Is Within You, chapter I
compare.why: Two great readers of these verses disagree. Tolstoy quotes Americans who refused all force; Augustine argues that love may punish to correct. Read both and decide which takes Jesus more seriously.
compare.title: Taken literally, or in the heart?

paras: Read closely, the four examples in 5:39–42 are all about personal injuries: an insult, a lawsuit, forced labour, a request for money. None is about defending someone else from attack. Jesus forbids retaliation: answering evil done to me with evil done back.

That leaves open the questions Christians have argued about ever since. May I defend my neighbour, or a child, from violence? May a judge punish? May a state go to war? Jesus does not address them here. He himself drove traders out of the Temple (Matthew 21:12), and rebuked his opponents fiercely. But when his disciple drew a sword to defend him at his arrest, he said: 'Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52).
sections.key: The four examples concern personal injuries; Jesus forbids retaliation. Whether that forbids defending others, courts or war is the open question.

sections.h: A third way? Walter Wink's reading
paras: The American theologian Walter Wink (1935–2012) argued, in Engaging the Powers (1992), that the three examples are not about passive surrender but about creative, nonviolent defiance by people with no power.

In his reading, a backhanded slap on the right cheek was how a superior struck an inferior. Turning the left cheek would force the striker to hit with an open hand or fist, as one hits an equal. Handing over your cloak in court, and standing naked, shamed the creditor who took everything. Carrying a soldier's pack a second mile put him in the wrong, since Roman rules limited the demand to one. Neither fight nor flight, but a 'third way'. Many have found this powerful. Other scholars think it reads too much into the text: Jesus gives no hint of strategy, and the Gospels show him accepting blows at his trial. It is best treated as a possible reading, not a settled one.
sections.key: Walter Wink read the examples as creative nonviolent defiance by the powerless, a 'third way'; others think this reads too much into the text.

paras: For its first three centuries, the Church was mostly against Christians serving as soldiers. Around AD 200 Tertullian wrote that when the Lord disarmed Peter, he disarmed every soldier (On Idolatry 19). Origen, around 248, said Christians fought for the emperor by prayer, not with weapons (Against Celsus VIII.73). There were Christian soldiers, but the leading teachers were uneasy.

After the emperor Constantine became a Christian in 312, most of the Church accepted military service. The peace tradition did not die. In 1527 the Anabaptists' Schleitheim Confession said the sword is 'outside the perfection of Christ'. Mennonites, Quakers from the 1650s, and the Brethren became the 'historic peace churches'. In the nineteenth century Garrison, Ballou and Tolstoy argued that Christians should refuse all force, including the state's.
sections.key: The early Church was mostly against soldiering (Tertullian, Origen); after Constantine most accepted it, but Anabaptists, Quakers and Tolstoy kept the peace tradition.

sections.h: Augustine, the two cities and just war
paras: Augustine gave the Western Church its main alternative. In his Letter 138 (412) he argued that the commands to turn the other cheek concern the inner disposition of the heart rather than outward show: a Christian ruler or soldier may use force to restrain evil and protect the innocent, so long as he acts without hatred and for the sake of peace. War could be just, though always tragic. Thomas Aquinas later set out conditions: lawful authority, a just cause and a right intention (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 40).

Martin Luther, in On Temporal Authority (1523), drew a line between two 'kingdoms': in his own affairs, a Christian should suffer wrong as the Sermon says; but in office, as a judge or prince, he must protect others, and may bear the sword for them. Most Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches hold some version of these views. The hall of The Good Life examines just war in full.

cols: How it reads 'do not resist evil'
rows: Literally: Christians may not kill or use violence, even in war or self-defence
Literally and for everyone: no courts, police, armies or state force
No revenge in the heart; force may be used by lawful authority to protect the innocent (just war)
Two kingdoms: suffer wrong yourself, but protect others in your office
Resist evil actively, but never with violence; accept suffering
table.note: The Orthodox tradition has never fully embraced 'just war' theory; it treats even necessary war as a tragedy requiring repentance.

sections.key: Augustine read the command as forbidding revenge in the heart, not all force; Aquinas set conditions for just war; Luther distinguished two kingdoms.

paras: The love Jesus asks for is agapē: not liking, but willing and doing good. It does not mean pretending an enemy is a friend, or that what they do is acceptable. It means refusing to want their harm, and wanting their good, even while opposing what they do.

There are parallels elsewhere. Proverbs says 'If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat' (25:21). The Stoic philosopher Epictetus said a true Cynic, when beaten, should love the man who beats him (Discourses III.22). The Buddha's Dhammapada says hatred is never ended by hatred, only by love (verse 5). What is distinctive in Jesus is the reason given (God's own love for the unjust), the prayer for persecutors, and that he did it himself: Luke has him pray for those crucifying him, 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34).
sections.key: Agapē is willing and doing good, not liking. There are parallels in Proverbs, Epictetus and the Buddha; distinctive in Jesus are the reason, the prayer and his own example.

paras: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was a Baptist minister who led the American civil rights movement. In his account 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence', in Stride Toward Freedom (1958), he said that during the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955–56 the Sermon on the Mount gave the movement its spirit, and Gandhi gave it its method. When his house was bombed in January 1956, he told the angry crowd outside to put away their weapons and love their enemies.

In his sermon 'Loving Your Enemies', preached in Montgomery in 1957 and published in Strength to Love (1963), he argued that hate multiplies hate, that love is the only force that can turn an enemy into a friend, and that loving enemies does not mean liking them or accepting injustice. For King, non-retaliation was not weakness but the hardest kind of strength: resisting evil openly, accepting suffering, and refusing to hate. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.
sections.key: King took the spirit from the Sermon and the method from Gandhi: active, nonviolent resistance that refuses to hate. He saw love of enemies as strength, not weakness.

refs: Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1; Dead Sea Scrolls, Community Rule (1QS) 1:9–10.

Tertullian, On Idolatry 19; Origen, Against Celsus VIII.73; Augustine, De sermone Domini in monte I.56–68, Letter 138 (to Marcellinus, 412); Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q. 40; Martin Luther, On Temporal Authority (1523); Schleitheim Confession (1527), art. 6.
Leo Tolstoy, The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1893), tr. Constance Garnett (1894), chapter I; Mohandas K. Gandhi, An Autobiography (1927–29), part II, chapter 15.

Walter Wink, Engaging the Powers (1992); Martin Luther King Jr., Stride Toward Freedom (1958), 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence'; Strength to Love (1963), 'Loving Your Enemies'. Epictetus, Discourses III.22; Dhammapada 5.

debate.question: Does 'do not resist evil' forbid all use of force?

positions.name: Yes, for everyone
positions.who: Leo Tolstoy; Adin Ballou; William Lloyd Garrison; the historic peace churches (for their members)
positions.view: Jesus meant what he said. Christians may not kill, injure or use force, and may not ask courts, police or armies to do it for them. Violence only multiplies evil; love alone can end it. The Church betrayed Jesus when it made peace with the sword.
positions.evidence: The plain words of 5:39 and 5:44; Jesus's 'put your sword back' (26:52); his own death without resistance; the early Church's reluctance about soldiering.

positions.name: No: it forbids revenge, not justice
positions.who: Augustine; Thomas Aquinas; Martin Luther; most churches
positions.view: The Sermon governs the heart and personal injuries. It forbids revenge, but love of neighbour may require protecting the innocent. Lawful authority may punish and even fight, without hatred and for the sake of peace.
positions.evidence: The examples are all personal injuries; Romans 13:4 says the ruler 'bears the sword' for justice; John the Baptist did not tell soldiers to leave the army (Luke 3:14).

positions.name: Resist, but never with violence
positions.who: Mohandas Gandhi; Martin Luther King Jr.; Walter Wink
positions.view: Jesus forbids violent resistance, not resistance. The Sermon calls for active, creative, nonviolent opposition to injustice, accepting suffering rather than inflicting it, and seeking to win the opponent over.
positions.evidence: Wink's reading of the cheek, cloak and mile; Jesus's own confrontations; the civil rights movement and the Indian independence movement.

debate.agree: All agree that the Sermon forbids hatred and the desire for revenge, that love must be shown in action, and that Jesus himself refused to use violence for his own cause.

look.why: There is no free painting in the gallery's collection of a scene of mercy to an enemy. This panel by the Florentine painter Bachiacca, around 1512–15, shows Jesus himself at the moment the Sermon describes: struck by men who hate him, and not striking back. The Gospels tell how he was whipped by Roman soldiers before his crucifixion (Matthew 27:26).
points: Jesus stands at the centre, tied by ropes around his upper arms to a freestanding column, his body facing us and his head turned to our right.
He wears only a blue cloth around his hips; a delicate gold ring with red spokes forms his halo.
Two muscular men lean away from him on either side with whips raised, in the same pose, one facing us and one with his back to us.
The man on our left has his mouth wide open and wears a royal-blue cap with lavender and gold ribbons and plumes.
Beyond the arches of the courtyard, grassy hills dotted with trees roll back to hazy blue mountains.

music.why: Thomas A. Dorsey's gospel song was Martin Luther King's favourite. He asked for it to be sung on the evening he was killed, and Mahalia Jackson sang it at his funeral: the prayer of a man who answered hatred with love.

think.why: To love an enemy is to see a person, not a monster. See where the Christian idea of every person's dignity comes from.

learn.why: Luke places the golden rule in the middle of Jesus's words on loving enemies (Luke 6:27–36): treat even your enemy as you would want to be treated.

check.q: What was the original purpose of 'an eye for an eye'?
options: To abolish punishment altogether
To limit revenge to a penalty that fitted the injury, applied by judges
To allow the rich to pay for injuries
To encourage personal revenge
check.why: It stopped blood feuds by setting a fair limit; the rabbis later read it as money compensation.

check.q: What do the four examples in Matthew 5:39–42 have in common?
options: They are all commands to governments
They are all personal injuries or demands made against the disciple himself: an insult, a lawsuit, forced labour, a request for money
They are all about defending other people
They all concern the Temple
check.why: That is why many readers say Jesus forbids retaliation, while leaving open the protection of others.

check.q: Why, according to Jesus, should his followers love their enemies?
options: Because the law of Moses commands it in those words
Because it will always turn them into friends
Because God sends sun and rain on the evil and the good; loving enemies makes us children of our Father
Because enemies deserve love
check.why: The reason is God's character, not the enemy's merit or a guaranteed result.

check.q: What is the key difference between Tolstoy's and Augustine's readings?
options: They agree completely
Augustine was a pacifist and Tolstoy was not
Tolstoy thought the Sermon was not by Jesus
Tolstoy, with Ballou, applies non-resistance to outward action, including courts and armies; Augustine says it forbids the desire for revenge, while lawful authority may punish in love
check.why: 'What he does through others, he is in reality doing himself' (Ballou) against 'punishment ... as compassion itself dictates' (Augustine).

check.q: Which is the strongest objection to Walter Wink's 'third way' reading?
options: The text gives no hint of a strategy of defiance, and Jesus himself accepted blows at his trial
The cheek saying is not in Matthew
Wink was not a Christian
Roman soldiers never forced anyone to carry packs
check.why: Wink's historical points are possible but not certain; critics say he reads tactics into a teaching about not retaliating.

check.q: What did 'perfect' mean in 'be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect'?
options: Never making any mistake
Complete or whole: loving without limits, as God does; Luke has 'be merciful'
Withdrawing from the world
Keeping every rule of the Pharisees
check.why: Teleios means whole or mature; the context is love that includes enemies.

tutorial.question: Does 'turn the other cheek' mean never resisting evil?
tutorial.approach: Read Matthew 5:38–42 closely, with the background on 'an eye for an eye' and life under Rome. Set out Tolstoy's literal reading, Augustine's reading of the heart, and Gandhi and King's nonviolent resistance. Consider Wink's reading and its critics. Then give your own answer and test it on a hard case: someone attacking a child in front of you.
strong: Explains the lex talionis as a limit on revenge.
Notes that the four examples are personal injuries.
States Tolstoy's and Ballou's position fairly, including 'what he does through others'.
States Augustine's position fairly, including the condition of love.
Distinguishes non-resistance from nonviolent resistance.
Tests the answer on a hard case.
