sessions.title: Where to start
sessions.line: A library, not a novel: where to begin, which translation, and how much a day.
sessions.plain: The Bible is not one book but a library, written over about a thousand years, and most people who try to read it from page one give up somewhere in Leviticus. This session asks the practical questions first: where to start, which translation to use, and how much to read. The Bible itself has an answer to the last one, and it is not 'a lot'.
sessions.why: This is the first session of the last journey in the Old Testament hall. You have read the Bible's story and many of its books; now the question is how to keep reading it for the rest of your life. We start with the simplest questions anyone asks.
answers: Where do I start reading the Bible?
Which translation should I use?
How much should I read a day?
Do I need a study Bible?
sessions.finding: The Bible is a library, not a novel: begin with a Gospel, a psalm and Genesis, choose a translation you understand, and read slowly rather than much.

background.h: If you have never opened a Bible
paras: The Bible is a collection of books bound together. Protestant Bibles have 66: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. Catholic Bibles have 73, and Orthodox Bibles a few more, because they include books from the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament that Jews and Protestants leave out (if you took What is the Bible?, you met this there).

The Old Testament is the Jewish Bible, which Jews call the Tanakh, a word made from the first letters of its three parts: Torah (the Law, the five books of Moses), Nevi'im (the Prophets) and Ketuvim (the Writings, such as the Psalms). The New Testament contains four Gospels about Jesus, the Acts of the Apostles, letters, and the book of Revelation.

Every book is divided into chapters and verses, so 'Psalm 119:105' means Psalm 119, verse 105. The chapters were added in the thirteenth century and the verse numbers in the sixteenth, to help people find their place.
background.key: The Bible is a library of 66 to 73 or more books, in two Testaments, with chapter and verse numbers added later to help readers find their way.

paras: This journey asks one question: how do you read a text so that it reads you? It answers with a picture: four rungs of a ladder. First, read it as it was written (its plain sense). Second, read it as one story, in which earlier parts point to later ones. Third, read it with others, as Jews and Christians have always done. Fourth, let it read you, in prayer.

Before the ladder, a first session on the practical questions. After it, a session on the strongest objection, that the Bible can be made to say anything and has been used to justify terrible things. The last session gives a verdict and a practice you can keep for life.

Rung three: reading with others (Augustine, the Jewish Fathers)
The case against: a book that can be made to say anything (Frederick Douglass)
Rung four: let it read you (lectio divina)

background.key: Four rungs: the plain sense, the one story, reading with others, and prayer; then the objection, then the verdict.

paras: The best guide to how to read the Bible is the Bible itself, which has a good deal to say about reading. The main reading gathers four short passages that describe it. A psalm-writer who loves God's law and turns it over all day. Joshua, told to keep 'this book of the law' in his mouth day and night. The command to talk of God's words at home, on the road, at bedtime and on waking. And a synagogue in Greece whose members checked what Paul told them against the Scriptures every day.

You read Psalm 1, 'on his law he meditates day and night', in Psalms and wisdom; here we read the longer psalm that grew from the same idea. Then the comparison turns to translation: the preface the King James translators wrote in 1611, explaining why a Bible in your own language matters.
background.key: The Bible's own words about reading, then the King James translators on why translation matters.

before: What do these passages say people actually did with Scripture: read it, say it, memorise it, discuss it, check it?
How often do they say to do it, and how much at a time?
In the comparison, what pictures do the translators use for what a translation does?
sessions.readWhy: Four short passages in which the Bible describes how it is meant to be read: lovingly, aloud, at home and daily, and with a questioning mind.

paras:
How I love your law!
It is my meditation all day.

Your commandments make me wiser than my enemies,
for your commandments are always with me.

I have more understanding than all my teachers,
for your testimonies are my meditation.

I understand more than the aged,
because I have kept your precepts.

I have kept my feet from every evil way,
that I might observe your word.

I have not turned away from your ordinances,
for you have taught me.

How sweet are your promises to my taste,
more than honey to my mouth!

Through your precepts, I get understanding;
therefore I hate every false way.

Only be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe to do according to all the law which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.

This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.
Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”
Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.
You shall write them on the door posts of your house and on your gates.
The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Many of them therefore believed; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men.

parts.title: How I love your law
parts.context: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible: 176 verses, every one about God's word. It is an acrostic poem: it has 22 sections of eight verses, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every verse in a section begins with that letter. These verses are the section for the letter mem. No one knows who wrote it or when; most scholars place it after the exile, in the fifth or fourth century BC.

commentary.on: How I love your law!
commentary.text: 'Law' translates the Hebrew torah, which means 'teaching' or 'instruction' as much as rules. The psalm uses eight words for God's word (law, testimonies, precepts, commandments, ordinances, promises and others) and rings the changes on them. The first thing it says about reading is not 'study this' but 'I love this'.

commentary.on: It is my meditation all day.
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for meditation here (siach) means musing, talking something over, even complaining aloud. Meditation in the Bible is not emptying the mind. It is turning a text over and over, often under your breath, until it becomes part of you.

commentary.on: I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation.
commentary.text: A bold claim, and a democratic one. You do not need to be a scholar to understand. Someone who lives with the text day after day may see more than an expert who only studies it.

commentary.on: I have kept my feet from every evil way, that I might observe your word.
commentary.text: Reading and living are tied together. The psalmist keeps away from evil so that he can keep the word, and keeps the word so that he can keep away from evil. Understanding grows with obedience.

commentary.on: How sweet are your promises to my taste, more than honey to my mouth!
commentary.text: Reading is described as eating. The Bible does this often: Ezekiel is told to eat a scroll, which tastes as sweet as honey (Ezekiel 3:3). Medieval monks took the picture literally: you take a text in, chew it slowly and taste it. We will meet them again later in this journey.

parts.title: Meditate on it day and night
parts.context: Moses has died, and Joshua is about to lead Israel across the Jordan into the land. Before any battle, God tells him how to lead: by a book.

commentary.on: Don't turn from it to the right hand or to the left
commentary.text: The picture is a road. God's teaching is a path to walk, not a puzzle to solve. Psalm 119 uses the same picture: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet'.

commentary.on: This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth
commentary.text: Notice: from your mouth, not from your eyes. In the ancient world almost all reading was done aloud, even alone. When Philip met the Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza, he 'heard him reading the prophet Isaiah' (Acts 8:30), which you read in Kings and prophets.

commentary.on: you shall meditate on it day and night
commentary.text: The Hebrew word here, hagah, is used of a dove moaning (Isaiah 38:14) and a lion growling over its prey (Isaiah 31:4). To meditate is to murmur the words, low, over and over, the way an animal worries at food. 'Day and night' does not mean reading all day; it means carrying the words with you all day.

commentary.on: that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it
commentary.text: The purpose of reading is doing. That theme will come back at the end of this journey.

commentary.on: for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.
commentary.text: Yahweh is God's personal name in the Hebrew Bible; many English Bibles print it 'the LORD'. The book is not a substitute for God. It is how Joshua stays close to the God who goes with him.

parts.title: When you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way
parts.context: Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses's last speeches before Israel enters the land. These verses, which begin 'Hear, Israel', are called the Shema, from the Hebrew for 'hear'. Jews still say them every morning and evening, and Jesus called the first part the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29–30).

commentary.on: These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart
commentary.text: Before the words are on paper or on a doorpost, they are to be on the heart, which in Hebrew means the mind and will as well as the feelings. The goal is not to own a Bible but to carry its words inside you.

commentary.on: and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
commentary.text: This is the Bible's own reading plan: at home, on the road, at night and in the morning. It is not a plan for scholars in a library but for ordinary families. Little and often, woven into the day.

commentary.on: You shall write them on the door posts of your house and on your gates.
commentary.text: Many Jewish homes still fix a small case called a mezuzah to the doorpost, containing these verses on a tiny scroll. Some Christians keep a verse by the door or on the fridge for the same reason: to meet the words every time you go in or out.

parts.title: Examining the Scriptures daily
parts.context: About AD 50. Paul and Silas have been driven out of Thessalonica, in northern Greece, after preaching that Jesus was the Messiah. They go west to Beroea (modern Veria) and, as usual, start at the synagogue. 'The Scriptures' here means the Jewish Bible, our Old Testament: the New Testament was not yet written.

commentary.on: they received the word with all readiness of mind
commentary.text: The Beroeans were open: they did not reject Paul's message because it was new.

commentary.on: examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
commentary.text: But they were not credulous either. They checked what they heard against the text, every day. The book of Acts calls this 'noble'. Christians ever since have taken it as permission to ask questions: reading the Bible was never meant to switch the mind off.

paras: But how shall men meditate in that, which they cannot understand? How shall they understand that which is kept close in an unknown tongue? as it is written, "Except I know the power of the voice, I shall be to him that speaketh, a Barbarian, and he that speaketh, shall be a Barbarian to me." The Apostle excepteth no tongue; not Hebrew the ancientest, not Greek the most copious, not Latin the finest. Nature taught a natural man to confess, that all of us in those tongues which we do not understand, are plainly deaf; we may turn the deaf ear unto them. The Scythian counted the Athenian, whom he did not understand, barbarous; so the Roman did the Syrian, and the Jew (even S. Jerome himself called the Hebrew tongue barbarous, belike because it was strange to so many) so the Emperor of Constantinople calleth the Latin tongue, barbarous, though Pope Nicolas do storm at it: so the Jews long before Christ called all other nations, Lognazim, which is little better than barbarous.

Therefore as one complaineth, that always in the Senate of Rome, there was one or other that called for an interpreter: so lest the Church be driven to the like exigent, it is necessary to have translations in a readiness. Translation it is that openeth the window, to let in the light; that breaketh the shell, that we may eat the kernel; that putteth aside the curtain, that we may look into the most Holy place; that removeth the cover of the well, that we may come by the water, even as Jacob rolled away the stone from the mouth of the well, by which means the flocks of Laban were watered. Indeed without translation into the vulgar tongue, the unlearned are but like children at Jacob's well (which is deep) without a bucket or something to draw with; or as that person mentioned by Isaiah, to whom when a sealed book was delivered, with this motion, "Read this, I pray thee," he was fain to make this answer, "I cannot, for it is sealed."

parts.author: The King James translators (Miles Smith)
parts.work: The Translators to the Reader, preface to the King James Version
parts.ref: The Translators to the Reader (1611), 'Translation necessary'
parts.title: A window to let in the light
parts.context: The King James Version was made by about fifty scholars in six teams at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge, between 1604 and 1611, at the command of King James I. Their preface, 'The Translators to the Reader', was written by Miles Smith, later Bishop of Gloucester. It is in the English of 1611 and full of learned allusions. Here Smith argues that Scripture is useless to someone who cannot understand its language.
parts.plain: The translators say: how can people meditate on what they cannot understand? Paul himself said that words in an unknown language make the speaker and hearer foreigners to each other, and he made no exception for Hebrew, Greek or Latin. So translations are necessary. A translation is like opening a window, cracking a nutshell, drawing back a curtain or rolling the stone off a well. Without one, ordinary people are like children at a deep well with no bucket.

commentary.on: But how shall men meditate in that, which they cannot understand?
commentary.text: Smith starts where Joshua and the psalm started: meditation. But you cannot turn over words you cannot follow. In 1611 this was a live issue. For a thousand years the Western Church had read the Bible mainly in Latin, which most people did not speak, and in England an unauthorised English Bible had been banned in 1409.

commentary.on: The Apostle excepteth no tongue; not Hebrew the ancientest, not Greek the most copious, not Latin the finest.
commentary.text: The quotation is from 1 Corinthians 14, where Paul tells the church in Corinth that speaking in a language no one understands builds no one up. Smith's point: no language is holy in itself. God's word can be spoken in any tongue, and should be spoken in the hearer's.

commentary.on: Translation it is that openeth the window, to let in the light; that breaketh the shell, that we may eat the kernel
commentary.text: Four pictures in one sentence: a window, a nutshell, a curtain (the curtain of the Temple's most holy place) and the stone over a well (Jacob rolling it away for Rachel's flock, Genesis 29:10). Each says the same thing: the treasure was always there, but it was closed. A translation does not add to the Bible; it opens it.

commentary.on: the unlearned are but like children at Jacob's well (which is deep) without a bucket or something to draw with
commentary.text: The words echo the Samaritan woman's reply to Jesus at the same well: 'you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep' (John 4:11). The 'unlearned' are not stupid; they simply lack the tool.

commentary.on: "I cannot, for it is sealed."
commentary.text: The last picture is from Isaiah 29:11: a sealed book handed to someone who is told to read it. Without translation, the Bible is a sealed book. The translators wanted every English reader to be able to open it. They also said, in the same preface, that no translation is perfect, and that they had revised the good work of earlier translators rather than starting again.

paras: The commonest mistake is to start at Genesis 1 and read straight through. Genesis and the first half of Exodus are gripping. Then come the instructions for the Tabernacle, the whole of Leviticus and the census lists of Numbers, and most readers stop. That is not their fault. You would not read a library from the first shelf to the last.

A better way in is to start with three books at once. A Gospel, because Christians read the whole Bible in the light of Jesus: Mark is the shortest, and can be read in an evening; Luke is the fullest. A psalm a day, because the Psalms are the Bible's prayer book and every mood is in them. And Genesis, because it begins the story that the rest of the Bible continues. After that, Acts, then a short letter such as Philippians, then Exodus.
If you have taken The whole story, you already have a map: the seven acts from creation to new creation. Every book you read finds its place on that map.
sections.key: Don't read the Bible cover to cover first: start with a Gospel, a psalm and Genesis, and use the whole story as your map.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians have read it through
paras: People have always needed a plan, and the oldest plans are communal. In synagogues the Torah is read aloud in weekly portions, so that the five books of Moses are read through every year. The book of Acts already says that Moses is read 'in the synagogues every Sabbath' (Acts 15:21), and Luke shows Jesus standing up in the synagogue at Nazareth to read from Isaiah (Luke 4:16).

Christians kept the habit. In about 155 Justin Martyr described Sunday worship in Rome: the 'memoirs of the apostles' or the writings of the prophets were read 'as long as time permits', and then the leader preached on them. That pattern became the lectionary, a fixed list of readings for each day or Sunday.

In 1549 Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer set the Church of England to read most of the Old Testament once a year and the New Testament three times, with the Psalms every month. In 1842 the Scottish minister Robert Murray M'Cheyne published a calendar of four chapters a day, two for family and two for private reading, which takes you through the Old Testament once and the New Testament and Psalms twice in a year. It is still widely used.
sections.key: From the synagogue's weekly Torah portion to Cranmer's calendar and M'Cheyne's plan, readers have always used a plan, usually shared with others.

paras: The passages you read give a clear answer: not much, but every day, and slowly. Joshua is told to murmur the book day and night. The Shema is talked over at home, on the road, at bedtime and on waking. The Beroeans examined the Scriptures daily. None of them is told to read a great deal at once.

Two ways of reading are both good, and they do different things. Reading widely (several chapters, quickly) gives you the shape of a book and the sweep of the story. Reading deeply (a few verses, slowly, more than once) lets the words sink in. Most people need both: a book of the Bible read through steadily over weeks, and a short passage each day read slowly enough to remember.
A reasonable start is fifteen minutes a day: a psalm, and a chapter of a Gospel. That will take you through all four Gospels and all 150 psalms in about five months.
sections.key: Read a little every day, slowly enough to remember; mix wide reading for the story with deep reading for the words.

paras: Every translation makes choices, and translators describe two broad aims. Formal equivalence ('word for word') keeps as close as possible to the wording and order of the Hebrew and Greek, even if the English is less natural. Dynamic or functional equivalence ('thought for thought'), a term made popular by the linguist Eugene Nida in the 1960s, puts the meaning into natural modern English. A paraphrase goes further, rewriting freely. No translation is purely one or the other.

This journey quotes the World English Bible because it is free of copyright and close to the original. For your own reading, choose one you understand and will actually read. Many readers keep two: one close to the original for study, and one in natural English for reading at length.

sections.h: Do I need a study Bible?
paras: A study Bible is a Bible with notes at the foot of each page, maps, introductions to each book and timelines. It helps a beginner enormously, because the Bible is ancient and its world is strange: who was Herod, where was Samaria, what was a Levite? A good one tells you, on the spot.

Two cautions. First, the notes are not the Bible, and they come from a particular point of view, Catholic, evangelical, Orthodox, Jewish or academic, so it is worth knowing which. Second, notes can stop you looking at the text itself. Read the passage first; then read the notes.

Other helps are simpler. A concordance lists every place a word appears, so you can see how the Bible uses it. A Bible dictionary explains people, places and customs. And the oldest help of all is another person: a friend, a group, a priest or minister, someone to read with. We come back to that in session 4.
sections.key: A study Bible helps a beginner, but read the text first, and know whose notes you are reading.

sections.h: Translation, and the right to read
paras: The comparison reminds us that the right to read the Bible in your own language was hard won. In the fourth century Jerome translated it into the common Latin of his day; that was the Vulgate, the Bible of the Western Church for a thousand years. But as Latin became a learned language, ordinary people lost direct access. In England, John Wycliffe's followers made the first complete English Bible in the 1380s; in 1409 a church council at Oxford forbade new translations without a bishop's approval. William Tyndale translated the New Testament from Greek in 1526, and was executed for heresy near Brussels in 1536.

Catholic translations into English followed (the Douay–Rheims, 1582–1610), and today every church encourages its members to read the Bible in their own language. The Second Vatican Council said in 1965 that 'easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful'.
sections.key: The Bible in ordinary people's language was hard won, by Jerome, Wycliffe, Tyndale and others; today every church urges people to read it.

paras: Two old habits are worth recovering. The first is reading aloud. In the ancient world almost everyone read aloud, even alone, and the Bible was written to be heard: its repetitions, refrains and wordplay work on the ear. Reading aloud slows you down, makes you notice every word, and stops your eyes skimming. Many people who find the Bible hard going on the page find it alive when they read it aloud, or listen to a good recording.

The second is learning by heart. Jewish children learned the Shema as soon as they could speak; monks memorised the whole Psalter; enslaved Christians who were forbidden to read carried whole chapters in memory. A verse you know by heart goes with you, 'when you walk by the way'. That is why each session of this journey gives you a few words to learn. Start with one verse a week.
Neither habit needs any special gift. Both need only the willingness to go slowly, which is the first lesson of every passage you have read in this session.
sections.key: Read aloud to slow down and hear the text; learn a verse a week by heart so that it goes with you.

debate.question: Should you read the Bible straight through, or by a set pattern of readings?

positions.name: Cover to cover
positions.who: Many evangelical teachers; reading plans that run from Genesis to Revelation in a year
positions.view: Read the whole Bible in order, so that you meet every part of it, including the hard and dull parts, and see the story as its editors arranged it.
positions.evidence: The canon has an order for a reason; selective readers skip what challenges them; people who have read the whole Bible know it in a way snippet-readers do not.

positions.name: The Church's pattern
positions.who: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican lectionaries; the synagogue's annual Torah cycle
positions.view: Read what the community reads, a set passage for each day or week, chosen to fit the seasons and set side by side so that each lights up the other.
positions.evidence: The practice goes back to the synagogue and to Justin Martyr; you read with millions of others; the readings are paired (an Old Testament passage with a Gospel).

positions.name: Book by book, slowly
positions.who: Many teachers of lectio divina and of Bible study
positions.view: Take one book at a time and read it slowly, a passage a day, until you know it; depth matters more than coverage.
positions.evidence: Joshua 1:8 and Psalm 119 describe slow, repeated reading; a book read slowly is remembered.

debate.agree: All agree that reading every day matters more than the method, and that reading with others helps.

look.why: Berthe Morisot, one of the founders of Impressionism, painted her mother and her sister at home in Paris in 1869–70. It is not a religious picture. It is here because it shows what most reading is: an ordinary person, in an ordinary room, with a book, giving it her full attention.
points: An older woman in a long black dress, with grey hair under a black veil, sits in a curved chair to the right, looking down at a book with a moss-green cover.
Behind her, a younger woman in a loose cream-white dress sits on a couch, gazing down and into the distance.
A round wooden table to the left holds a glass vase with a violet-purple flower, perhaps a hydrangea, and a slip of paper or an envelope.
The brushstrokes are loose and visible, especially in the furniture and the clothes.
Neither woman speaks; both lips are closed. The room is quiet.

music.why: Anton Bruckner's short motet (1869) sets the words 'This place was made by God'. A good habit needs a place: a chair, a corner, a time of day. Listen to it the first time you sit down to read.

check.q: Why is it usually a mistake for a beginner to start at Genesis 1 and read straight through?
options: Because Genesis was written last and assumes you know the rest
Because the books are printed in the order they were written, so Genesis is the latest
Because the Bible is a library of different kinds of book, and the long sections of law and lists that soon follow stop most readers before they reach the story's centre
Because Christians should begin with the prophets, who come first in time
check.why: It is a library, not a novel. Starting with a Gospel, a psalm and Genesis gives a beginner the centre, the prayer and the story.

check.q: Joshua is told to 'meditate on it day and night'. What does the Hebrew word suggest he was to do?
options: Sit in silence and empty his mind
Leave the reading to the priests
Murmur the words aloud, over and over, carrying them through the day
Read the whole law every day
check.why: Hagah is used of a dove moaning and a lion growling: low, repeated speech.

check.q: Which statement best describes the difference between formal and dynamic equivalence?
options: Dynamic translations are always less accurate
Formal translations keep close to the original wording; dynamic ones put the meaning into natural modern speech
Formal translations add notes; dynamic ones do not
Formal translations are for churches, dynamic ones for scholars
check.why: Both aim at accuracy, by different routes. Neither is automatically more accurate.

check.q: The Beroeans 'examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so'. What does Acts imply about questioning while you read?
options: That only synagogue leaders were entitled to check
That questioning is a sign of unbelief
That only scholars should check
That checking what you are told against the text is noble, not faithless
check.why: Acts calls them 'more noble', and many of them believed.

check.q: In the King James preface, Miles Smith says translation 'openeth the window, to let in the light'. What follows from his argument?
options: That the Hebrew and Greek are unimportant
That the King James Version could never be improved
That a translation adds new meaning to Scripture
That a Bible which cannot be understood cannot be meditated on, so every people should have it in their own language
check.why: The treasure was always there; translation opens it. The same preface admits no translation is perfect.

check.q: What is the main caution about using a study Bible?
options: Study Bibles are forbidden in most churches
Study Bibles always use a less accurate translation
Study Bibles leave out books
The notes are from a particular point of view and can stop you looking at the text itself
check.why: Read the passage first, then the notes, and know whose notes they are.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose a time and a place. Each day, read one psalm and one chapter of Mark's Gospel, aloud and slowly, and stop at the verse that catches you. Write that one verse down.
sessions.reflect: What has stopped you reading the Bible before, and which of those obstacles is real?
takeaways: The Bible is a library, not a novel: begin with a Gospel, a psalm and Genesis, and use the whole story as your map.
The Bible's own picture of reading is little, often, aloud and slow, woven into the day, and joined to doing.
Choose a translation you understand; the right to read the Bible in your own language was hard won.

sessions.title: The plain sense
sessions.line: Rung one: read what the text says, in its own kind of writing.
sessions.plain: People often ask whether they have to take the Bible 'literally'. The oldest Christian answer is yes, in the old sense of 'literal': you must first read what the writer actually meant, and that includes his poetry, his stories and his figures of speech. This session reads Augustine's rules for telling a figure of speech from a plain statement, and a short answer by Thomas Aquinas that clears up what 'literal' means.
sessions.why: Session 1 asked where to start. Now we climb the first rung of the ladder: before anything else, read the text as it was written.
answers: Do I have to take the Bible literally?
How do I know when the Bible is speaking in a figure of speech?
What did a passage mean to its first readers?
Why does it matter what kind of writing a book is?
sessions.finding: The first rule of the whole tradition is to read what the text says in its own kind of writing: poetry as poetry, law as law, letters as letters; 'literal' means what the author meant, which is not the same as 'literalist'.

paras: Today 'literal' usually means 'the words taken at face value, with no figure of speech'. If the Bible says the trees will clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12), a literalist would have to picture trees with hands. Nobody actually reads like that. Everyone knows that some language is figurative.

The older meaning of 'literal' was different. The 'literal sense' (Latin sensus litteralis, the sense of the letter) meant what the writer meant by his words, including his metaphors. The literal sense of 'the trees will clap their hands' is that creation will rejoice. This session is about that older sense, and the rules readers used to find it.
background.key: The literal sense is what the author meant, figures of speech included; literalism is reading every word at face value.

paras: The Bible contains almost every kind of writing the ancient world knew: law codes, family stories, royal chronicles, war songs, love poetry, hymns, proverbs, prophecies, biographies, letters and visions. Each kind works by its own rules. A proverb gives a general truth ('A gentle answer turns away wrath', Proverbs 15:1), not a promise that holds every time. A psalm of lament says how the writer feels, not what God is like. A letter answers questions we have to reconstruct from the replies.
Scholars call these kinds of writing genres. Asking 'what genre is this?' is the first step in reading any book, and the Bible is no exception.
background.key: The Bible has many genres, each with its own rules; asking what kind of writing a passage is comes first.

paras: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was the most influential theologian of the Western Church. As a young man he found the Bible crude beside the Latin classics (you read his account in What is the Bible?). As bishop of Hippo in North Africa he preached on it for over thirty years.

In about 396, soon after becoming bishop, he began On Christian Doctrine, a handbook in four books for people who teach the Bible. Book I is about the purpose of Scripture, which we will read in session 4. Books II and III are about signs: words, and how to tell when they are used plainly and when figuratively. He broke off in the middle of Book III and finished it thirty years later, in 426–427.

paras: The main reading gives Augustine's rules for deciding whether a passage is plain or figurative, and his warning about a trap all readers fall into: assuming that whatever shocks our own culture must be a figure of speech.

The comparison is one short paragraph by Thomas Aquinas (about 1225–1274), the greatest theologian of the Middle Ages, written about 850 years after Augustine. It says exactly what the literal sense includes, and so answers the question 'do I have to take it literally?' in three sentences.
background.key: Augustine gives the rules; Aquinas says what 'literal' means.

before: What test does Augustine give for deciding whether a passage is figurative?
What mistake does he say people make when the Bible says something their own culture disapproves of?

sessions.readWhy: Augustine's rules for telling plain statements from figures of speech, from the handbook he wrote for preachers.

paras: 14. But in addition to the foregoing rule, which guards us against taking a metaphorical form of speech as if it were literal, we must also pay heed to that which tells us not to take a literal form of speech as if it were figurative. In the first place, then, we must show the way to find out whether a phrase is literal or figurative. And the way is certainly as follows: Whatever there is in the word of God that cannot, when taken literally, be referred either to purity of life or soundness of doctrine, you may set down as figurative. Purity of life has reference to the love of God and one's neighbor; soundness of doctrine to the knowledge of God and one's neighbor. Every man, moreover, has hope in his own conscience, so far as he perceives that he has attained to the love and knowledge of God and his neighbor. Now all these matters have been spoken of in the first book.

15. But as men are prone to estimate sins, not by reference to their inherent sinfulness, but rather by reference to their own customs, it frequently happens that a man will think nothing blameable except what the men of his own country and time are accustomed to condemn, and nothing worthy of praise or approval except what is sanctioned by the custom of his companions; and thus it comes to pass, that if Scripture either enjoins what is opposed to the customs of the hearers, or condemns what is not so opposed, and if at the same time the authority of the word has a hold upon their minds, they think that the expression is figurative. Now Scripture enjoins nothing except charity, and condemns nothing except lust, and in that way fashions the lives of men. In the same way, if an erroneous opinion has taken possession of the mind, men think that whatever Scripture asserts contrary to this must be figurative. Now Scripture asserts nothing but the Catholic faith, in regard to things past, future, and present. It is a narrative of the past, a prophecy of the future, and a description of the present. But all these tend to nourish and strengthen charity, and to overcome and root out lust.

22. But when men unacquainted with other modes of life than their own meet with the record of such actions, unless they are restrained by authority, they look upon them as sins, and do not consider that their own customs either in regard to marriage, or feasts, or dress, or the other necessities and adornments of human life, appear sinful to the people of other nations and other times. And, distracted by this endless variety of customs, some who were half asleep (as I may say)— that is, who were neither sunk in the deep sleep of folly, nor were able to awake into the light of wisdom — have thought that there was no such thing as absolute right, but that every nation took its own custom for right; and that, since every nation has a different custom, and right must remain unchangeable, it becomes manifest that there is no such thing as right at all. Such men did not perceive, to take only one example, that the precept, Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them, cannot be altered by any diversity of national customs. And this precept, when it is referred to the love of God, destroys all vices when to the love of one's neighbor, puts an end to all crimes. For no one is willing to defile his own dwelling; he ought not, therefore, to defile the dwelling of God, that is, himself. And no one wishes an injury to be done him by another; he himself, therefore, ought not to do injury to another.

23. The tyranny of lust being thus overthrown, charity reigns through its supremely just laws of love to God for His own sake, and love to one's self and one's neighbor for God's sake. Accordingly, in regard to figurative expressions, a rule such as the following will be observed, to carefully turn over in our minds and meditate upon what we read till an interpretation be found that tends to establish the reign of love. Now, if when taken literally it at once gives a meaning of this kind, the expression is not to be considered figurative.

24. If the sentence is one of command, either forbidding a crime or vice, or enjoining an act of prudence or benevolence, it is not figurative. If, however, it seems to enjoin a crime or vice, or to forbid an act of prudence or benevolence, it is figurative. Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man, says Christ, and drink His blood, you have no life in you. This seems to enjoin a crime or a vice; it is therefore a figure, enjoining that we should have a share [communicandem] in the sufferings of our Lord, and that we should retain a sweet and profitable memory [in memoria] of the fact that His flesh was wounded and crucified for us.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.translator: J. F. Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (1887)
parts.who: Augustine (354–430) was a North African teacher of rhetoric who became a Christian in Milan in 386 and then bishop of Hippo, a port in what is now Algeria, for 34 years. He preached on the Bible several times a week, and he wrote this book to teach preachers how to read it.
parts.when: Hippo, North Africa; Books I–III begun in 396 or 397, the whole finished in 426–427
parts.title: How to tell a figure of speech
parts.context: Book III of Augustine's handbook. In the chapters before this he has warned readers against taking figures of speech literally. Now he turns the warning round: you must also not take plain statements as figures. The numbers (14, 15) are the paragraph numbers of the standard edition.
parts.plain: Augustine says: we must not take figures of speech literally, but we must not take plain statements as figures either. His test is this. If a passage, taken literally, does not lead to a good life (love of God and neighbour) or to true belief, treat it as figurative. He then warns that people judge right and wrong by their own customs, and so they call anything the Bible says against their customs 'figurative'. But Scripture teaches only love, and condemns only selfish desire.

commentary.on: we must also pay heed to that which tells us not to take a literal form of speech as if it were figurative
commentary.text: This is the balance. There are two errors, not one: reading poetry as prose, and reading prose as poetry. Augustine thinks both happen.

commentary.on: Whatever there is in the word of God that cannot, when taken literally, be referred either to purity of life or soundness of doctrine, you may set down as figurative.
commentary.text: His test. Read the passage plainly first. If the plain reading teaches a good way to live or a true belief, keep it. Only if it cannot do either should you look for a figure. Notice the order: plain first.

commentary.on: Purity of life has reference to the love of God and one's neighbor
commentary.text: For Augustine the 'good life' that Scripture teaches comes down to Jesus's two commandments: love God, and love your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22:37–39). This rule will matter for the rest of the journey.

commentary.on: it frequently happens that a man will think nothing blameable except what the men of his own country and time are accustomed to condemn
commentary.text: A sharp observation about human nature. We judge by our own culture's standards and assume they are timeless. Augustine noticed it sixteen centuries before anthropologists made it a science.

commentary.on: they think that the expression is figurative
commentary.text: Here is the trap. When the Bible commands something our culture dislikes, we are tempted to say 'it doesn't really mean that'. Augustine says: be honest. Ask what it means, not what you would like it to mean.

commentary.on: Now Scripture enjoins nothing except charity, and condemns nothing except lust
commentary.text: 'Charity' is the old word for love (Latin caritas). 'Lust' here (Latin cupiditas) is wider than sexual desire: it means desire turned in on itself, wanting things and people for my own sake without reference to God. Augustine's whole reading of the Bible rests on this pair.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.translator: J. F. Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (1887)
parts.who: Augustine (354–430) was a North African teacher of rhetoric who became a Christian in Milan in 386 and then bishop of Hippo, a port in what is now Algeria, for 34 years. He preached on the Bible several times a week, and he wrote this book to teach preachers how to read it.
parts.when: Hippo, North Africa; Books I–III begun in 396 or 397, the whole finished in 426–427
parts.title: Custom, love, and the rule for commands
parts.context: Between the two parts (in chapters 11–13, left out here) Augustine discusses things the patriarchs did, such as having several wives, which were customary in their time. He then turns to a group of readers who drew the opposite conclusion from cultural difference.
parts.plain: Augustine says: some people, noticing that every nation has different customs, decide that there is no real right and wrong at all. They miss that some rules, like 'do to others as you would have them do to you', hold in every culture. So the rule is: turn a passage over in your mind until you find a meaning that builds up love; but if the plain meaning already does that, it is not figurative. And if a command seems to order a crime, it is a figure; Jesus's words 'unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man' are an example.

commentary.on: have thought that there was no such thing as absolute right, but that every nation took its own custom for right
commentary.text: Augustine meets moral relativism, already old in his day: Greek sceptics had argued it. Different customs, they said, prove there is no real right.

commentary.on: Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them, cannot be altered by any diversity of national customs.
commentary.text: His reply: customs differ, but the Golden Rule (Matthew 7:12) holds in every culture. Reading in context does not mean everything is relative.

commentary.on: to carefully turn over in our minds and meditate upon what we read till an interpretation be found that tends to establish the reign of love
commentary.text: This is meditation, as in Joshua and the psalm: turning the words over. The goal is a reading that builds up love. You will see this idea again.

commentary.on: Now, if when taken literally it at once gives a meaning of this kind, the expression is not to be considered figurative.
commentary.text: The plain sense has priority. You only go looking for a figure when the plain meaning fails.

commentary.on: If the sentence is one of command, either forbidding a crime or vice, or enjoining an act of prudence or benevolence, it is not figurative.
commentary.text: A practical rule for commands. 'Do not steal' means do not steal. 'Give to the poor' means give to the poor.

commentary.on: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man, says Christ, and drink His blood, you have no life in you.
commentary.text: Augustine's example, from John 6:53. Taken at face value it commands cannibalism, so it must be a figure. Notice that Catholics and Orthodox, who believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine of the Eucharist, do not read it as cannibalism either; they and Protestants differ on what the figure points to, not on whether it is a figure of flesh-eating.

paras: Reply to Objection 3. The parabolical sense is contained in the literal, for by words things are signified properly and figuratively. Nor is the figure itself, but that which is figured, the literal sense. When Scripture speaks of God's arm, the literal sense is not that God has such a member, but only what is signified by this member, namely operative power. Hence it is plain that nothing false can ever underlie the literal sense of Holy Writ.

parts.author: Thomas Aquinas
parts.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Laurence Shapcote), 2nd revised edition (1920)
parts.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, question 1, article 10, reply to objection 3
parts.title: God's arm
parts.context: The Summa Theologiae ('summary of theology'), written between about 1265 and 1273, is laid out as questions. Each article asks a question, lists objections, gives Aquinas's answer, and then replies to each objection. This is the reply to an objector who says the Bible also has a 'parabolical' sense, the sense of parables and metaphors, besides the four senses we will meet in session 3.
parts.plain: Aquinas says: the meaning of a metaphor is part of the literal sense, because words can be used plainly or figuratively. The literal sense is not the picture itself but what the picture means. When the Bible speaks of God's arm, it does not mean God has an arm; it means God's power to act. So the literal sense of Scripture can never be false.

commentary.on: The parabolical sense is contained in the literal, for by words things are signified properly and figuratively.
commentary.text: This is the key. Metaphor is not a separate, extra meaning that you are free to add. It belongs to the plain sense, because it is what the writer meant.

commentary.on: Nor is the figure itself, but that which is figured, the literal sense.
commentary.text: The 'figure' is the picture (an arm); 'that which is figured' is what the picture stands for (power). The literal sense is the second.

commentary.on: When Scripture speaks of God's arm, the literal sense is not that God has such a member, but only what is signified by this member, namely operative power.
commentary.text: When Exodus says God brought Israel out of Egypt 'with an outstretched arm' (Exodus 6:6), it literally means that God acted with power. A literalist who pictured a giant arm would have misread the literal sense.

commentary.on: Hence it is plain that nothing false can ever underlie the literal sense of Holy Writ.
commentary.text: Aquinas believed Scripture is true. But notice what follows from his definition: you cannot know whether a passage is true until you know what kind of statement it is making. That is why genre comes first.

compare.title: Thomas Aquinas on what 'literal' means

paras: Every great interpreter in the Jewish and Christian traditions agrees on a first rule: start with what the text actually says. The rabbis put it in a maxim: 'a verse never departs from its plain meaning' (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 63a). Augustine said read it plainly first, and look for a figure only when the plain reading fails. Aquinas said all the other meanings rest on the literal. Luther said the Holy Spirit is the simplest writer, whose words have one plain meaning.

They disagreed about much else, as the next sessions will show. But they agreed that you cannot skip this rung. A reading that ignores what the writer meant is not deeper; it is simply someone else's idea.
sections.key: Jewish and Christian interpreters agree that the plain sense, what the writer meant, comes first.

sections.h: Genre: what kind of writing is this?
paras: The plain sense depends on genre. The same words mean different things in different kinds of writing, as 'I could eat a horse' means one thing in a menu and another at the end of a long walk.
So the first question to ask of a passage is what kind of writing it is, and what that kind of writing does.

rows: Sets out rules for a people in a particular time and place
Treating every ancient rule as a direct command for today, or dismissing all of it
Tells what happened, often without comment
Assuming that everything a character does is approved
Expresses feeling and praise in images
Reading images as physics, or a cry of despair as doctrine
Reading a proverb as a guarantee
Calls a people back to God, warns and promises
Treating it only as predictions of our own time
Answers a church's questions and problems
Forgetting we only hear one side of the conversation
Reveals the hidden meaning of history in vivid symbols
Reading the symbols as a coded timetable

sections.key: Ask what genre a passage is and what that genre does; most misreadings come from mistaking one genre for another.

sections.h: What did it mean to them?
paras: The plain sense is what the writer meant to his first readers, so readers need to know something about their world. When Amos condemns those who 'sell the needy for a pair of sandals' (Amos 2:6), it helps to know about debt-slavery in eighth-century Israel. When Paul tells the Corinthians not to eat meat offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8), it helps to know that most meat in a Greek city's market had been sacrificed in a temple.

Ancient readers knew this. Jerome (about 347–420) learned Hebrew from Jewish teachers and moved to Bethlehem to understand the land; he insisted on translating from the 'Hebrew truth' rather than from a translation. Modern study adds archaeology, ancient inscriptions and other texts of the same period. But the aim is the same: to hear the words as the first readers heard them, before asking what they mean for us.
sections.key: The plain sense is what the words meant to their first readers, so knowing their world helps.

paras: In the early Church two great schools of reading grew up, in the two greatest cities of the Greek-speaking East. In Alexandria, in Egypt, teachers such as Clement (about 150–215) and Origen (about 185–253) loved to find hidden, spiritual meanings beneath the words. You will read Origen next.

In Antioch, in Syria, a different school arose in the fourth century. Diodore of Tarsus (died about 390), Theodore of Mopsuestia (about 350–428) and John Chrysostom (about 347–407), the greatest preacher of the early Church, distrusted allegory that floated free of history. They insisted on the historical sense: what happened, what the writer meant, in his own time. Theodore even read most of the Psalms as about the history of Israel rather than as prophecies of Christ, and was later condemned for it (in 553, long after his death).

Most historians now think the two schools were closer than they were once painted. Both read for Christ; both respected the text. But the argument between them, plain sense against hidden sense, has never gone away.
sections.key: Alexandria sought hidden meanings; Antioch insisted on the historical sense; the argument has never gone away.

sections.h: 'Interpret the Scripture like any other book'
paras: In 1860 an Oxford professor of Greek, Benjamin Jowett, published an essay called 'On the Interpretation of Scripture'. Its most famous sentence is: 'Interpret the Scripture like any other book.' He meant: find out what the writer meant, in his own time, using the same tools you would use on Homer or Plato. The essay caused a scandal. Within a few years it was the method of most universities.

This is the historical-critical method: asking who wrote a text, when, from what sources, for whom and why. It has taught us an enormous amount, much of which you met in What is the Bible?. Most churches now use it. The Catholic Church officially welcomed it in 1943 (Divino Afflante Spiritu), and its Pontifical Biblical Commission called it 'indispensable' in 1993.

Its critics say it can stop too soon. If you read the Bible only like any other book, you will never ask whether it is more than any other book. Jowett himself thought the Bible would prove unique if read honestly. Whether he was right is a question the next sessions keep asking.
sections.key: Modern scholarship reads the Bible 'like any other book' to find what its writers meant; its critics say that is the first step, not the last.

paras: Now the question people ask: do I have to take it literally? The tradition's answer is: you must take it in its literal sense, which is what the writer meant. That means reading Genesis 1 in its genre, which you did in In the beginning, and the Song of Songs as love poetry, and Revelation as a book of visions.

Literalism, taking every word at face value regardless of genre, is a modern approach, not an ancient one. Augustine warned in his Literal Meaning of Genesis (about 401–415) that when Christians talk nonsense about nature and claim the Bible's authority for it, they bring the Scriptures into contempt among educated unbelievers.

But the plain sense also binds. Augustine warned just as strongly against calling a passage 'figurative' because we dislike it. Luther put the same point sharply: when the plain words are hard, the reader must not twist them. He compared the Old Testament to the poor swaddling cloths of the manger: plain and humble, but Christ lies in them. The plain sense is not always comfortable.
sections.key: Read for the literal sense, what the writer meant; that rules out both face-value literalism and explaining away what we dislike.

sections.h: Peshat: the plain sense in Jewish reading
paras: Jewish interpreters developed the plain sense with special care. The Hebrew word is peshat, from a root meaning 'to make plain' or 'to spread out'. In eleventh-century France, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), wrote a commentary on the whole Torah that is still printed beside the text in most Jewish Bibles. He said that he had come only to give the plain meaning of Scripture, and the stories of the rabbis that help to explain it. His grandson, Rabbi Samuel ben Meir (Rashbam), went further, and was willing to differ from the rabbis' legal readings where the plain sense required it.

Christian scholars learned from them. In the fourteenth century the Franciscan Nicholas of Lyra drew heavily on Rashi in his commentary on the whole Bible, the most widely used of the late Middle Ages, and Luther used Lyra. So the Reformers' stress on the plain sense owes something, by a long road, to a rabbi in Troyes. The plain sense is common ground between Jews and Christians, even where they read the deeper meanings differently.
sections.key: Jewish scholars such as Rashi developed the plain sense (peshat); through Nicholas of Lyra, Christian readers learned from them.

debate.question: How literally should the Bible be read?

positions.name: Plain reading as far as possible
positions.who: Modern young-earth creationists, such as Henry Morris and Ken Ham; many conservative Protestants
positions.view: Take the Bible at face value unless the text itself signals a figure; this protects its authority from being explained away to suit modern opinion.
positions.evidence: Augustine's own warning against calling unwelcome passages figurative; Exodus 20:11 grounds the Sabbath in six days; the Gospels present themselves as history.

positions.name: The literal sense, read by genre
positions.who: Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin; most Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant scholars today
positions.view: The literal sense is what the writer meant, so it includes figures and depends on genre; Genesis 1 can be literally true without being a scientific account.
positions.evidence: Aquinas on 'God's arm'; Augustine's rules; the many genres of the Bible; Augustine's warning about talking nonsense on nature.

positions.name: Historical criticism
positions.who: Benjamin Jowett and modern critical scholarship
positions.view: Find what the writer meant in his own time, with every tool of history, and do not assume the text is true or unified before you test it.
positions.evidence: What archaeology and ancient texts show about the Bible's world; the gains of two centuries of scholarship.

debate.agree: All agree that you must first find what the writer meant; they disagree on how far genre and history change what that is.

The gallery names the figure as Saint John the Evangelist, by tradition the writer of the fourth Gospel. He is here because the plain sense is the writer's meaning: behind every page is a person who meant something.

He wears a rose-pink robe with a dark olive-green lining over a topaz-blue garment.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each day, before you read your passage, ask one question and write down the answer: what kind of writing is this? Then read it again with that answer in mind.
sessions.reflect: Is there a passage you have always explained away because you dislike what it plainly says?
takeaways: The first rung is the plain sense: what the writer meant, in his own kind of writing.
The old 'literal sense' includes figures of speech (God's 'arm' means his power); literalism, reading every word at face value, is a modern approach.
Augustine's rules bind both ways: read plainly first, and don't call a passage figurative because your culture dislikes it.

sessions.title: One story, four senses
sessions.line: Rung two: why the old writers found Christ everywhere.
sessions.plain: Ancient and medieval Christians believed the Bible was one story with one author behind its many writers, so an event in Exodus could point forward to Christ and to your own life. They read each passage on four levels: what happened, what it shows of Christ, how we should live, and what we hope for. This session reads the man who first set out a method for it, Origen, and the medieval thinker who tied it firmly to the plain sense, Thomas Aquinas.
sessions.why: Session 2 climbed the first rung: read what the writer meant. But Christians have never read the Bible only as separate books. The second rung reads it as one story, in which earlier parts point to later ones.
answers: Why did the old writers find Christ everywhere in the Old Testament?
What are the four senses of Scripture?
Isn't allegory just a way of making a text say what you want?
Do Jews read Scripture on more than one level too?
sessions.finding: Ancient and medieval readers read one text on four levels (what happened, what it shows of Christ, how to live and what to hope for), but the tradition insisted that every higher sense rests on the literal one.

paras: If the Bible is a library, why read it as one story? Because Jesus and the first Christians did. On the road to Emmaus, Luke says, Jesus 'beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27); you read that in What is the Bible? and The whole story.

Paul reads the Old Testament the same way. The rock that gave Israel water in the desert 'was Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:4). Adam is 'a foreshadowing of him who was to come' (Romans 5:14). The Greek word there is typos, a pattern or imprint, from which we get 'type'. And in Galatians 4, which you read in Abraham and the promise, Paul says the story of Hagar and Sarah 'contains an allegory'. So the idea that one part of Scripture can point to another is in the Bible itself.
background.key: Jesus and Paul read the Old Testament as pointing to Christ, so reading the Bible as one story begins in the Bible itself.

paras: Origen was the first Christian to write a full account of how to read the Bible. He was a prodigious scholar: he produced the Hexapla, a huge edition of the Old Testament with the Hebrew and several Greek translations in parallel columns, and he learned from Jewish teachers.

On First Principles, written in Alexandria about 220–230, was the first attempt at a whole Christian theology. Its fourth book is about Scripture. It survives in two forms: a free Latin translation made by Rufinus in 398, and the original Greek of most of Book IV, preserved because two fourth-century bishops, Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus, copied it into an anthology of Origen's writings called the Philocalia. We read the Greek.

Origen was honoured for centuries, but some of his speculations (for example, that souls exist before birth) were condemned in 553, three hundred years after his death. His method of reading outlived the condemnation.

background.key: Origen wrote the first full Christian account of reading Scripture; Book IV of On First Principles survives in Greek.

paras: The main reading gives Origen's theory in his own words: Scripture, like a human being, has body, soul and spirit. Then his most surprising claim, that God put stumbling-blocks into the text on purpose, so that readers would look deeper. Then his insistence that most of the Bible's history really happened.

The comparison is Thomas Aquinas, a thousand years later, answering the question 'can one word of Scripture have several senses?' His answer became the standard account of the four senses in the West, and it ties all of them to the literal sense you studied in session 2.
background.key: Origen gives the theory and its risks; Aquinas gives the standard account and anchors it to the literal sense.
