Why does he think God allowed things into the text that could not have happened?
In the comparison, what does Aquinas say all the senses are 'founded on'?
sessions.readWhy: The first full Christian theory of reading Scripture on more than one level, from Book IV of Origen's On First Principles, with its risks in plain view.

paras: 11. The way, then, as it appears to us, in which we ought to deal with the Scriptures, and extract from them their meaning, is the following, which has been ascertained from the Scriptures themselves. By Solomon in the Proverbs we find some such rule as this enjoined respecting the divine doctrines of Scripture: And portray them in a threefold manner, in counsel and knowledge, to answer words of truth to them who propose them to you. The individual ought, then, to portray the ideas of holy Scripture in a threefold manner upon his own soul; in order that the simple man may be edified by the flesh, as it were, of the Scripture, for so we name the obvious sense; while he who has ascended a certain way (may be edified) by the soul, as it were. The perfect man, again, and he who resembles those spoken of by the apostle, when he says, We speak wisdom among them that are perfect, but not the wisdom of the world, nor of the rulers of this world, who come to nought; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God has ordained before the ages, unto our glory, (may receive edification) from the spiritual law, which has a shadow of good things to come. For as man consists of body, and soul, and spirit, so in the same way does Scripture, which has been arranged to be given by God for the salvation of men.

That the first sense, then, is profitable in this respect, that it is capable of imparting edification, is testified by the multitudes of genuine and simple believers; while of that interpretation which is referred back to the soul, there is an illustration in Paul's first Epistle to the Corinthians. The expression is, You shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain; to which he adds, Does God take care of oxen? Or says He it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this was written: that he that ploughs should plough in hope, and that he who threshes, in hope of partaking. And there are numerous interpretations adapted to the multitude which are in circulation, and which edify those who are unable to understand profounder meanings, and which have somewhat the same character.

15. But since, if the usefulness of the legislation, and the sequence and beauty of the history, were universally evident of itself, we should not believe that any other thing could be understood in the Scriptures save what was obvious, the word of God has arranged that certain stumbling-blocks, as it were, and offenses, and impossibilities, should be introduced into the midst of the law and the history, in order that we may not, through being drawn away in all directions by the merely attractive nature of the language, either altogether fall away from the (true) doctrines, as learning nothing worthy of God, or, by not departing from the letter, come to the knowledge of nothing more divine. And this also we must know, that the principal aim being to announce the spiritual connection in those things that are done, and that ought to be done, where the Word found that things done according to the history could be adapted to these mystical senses, He made use of them, concealing from the multitude the deeper meaning;

but where, in the narrative of the development of super-sensual things, there did not follow the performance of those certain events, which was already indicated by the mystical meaning, the Scripture interwove in the history (the account of) some event that did not take place, sometimes what could not have happened; sometimes what could, but did not. And sometimes a few words are interpolated which are not true in their literal acceptation, and sometimes a larger number. And a similar practice also is to be noticed with regard to the legislation, in which is often to be found what is useful in itself, and appropriate to the times of the legislation; and sometimes also what does not appear to be of utility; and at other times impossibilities are recorded for the sake of the more skilful and inquisitive, in order that they may give themselves to the toil of investigating what is written, and thus attain to a becoming conviction of the manner in which a meaning worthy of God must be sought out in such subjects.

16. It was not only, however, with the (Scriptures composed) before the advent (of Christ) that the Spirit thus dealt; but as being the same Spirit, and (proceeding) from the one God, He did the same thing both with the evangelists and the apostles — as even these do not contain throughout a pure history of events, which are interwoven indeed according to the letter, but which did not actually occur. Nor even do the law and the commandments wholly convey what is agreeable to reason. For who that has understanding will suppose that the first, and second, and third day, and the evening and the morning, existed without a sun, and moon, and stars? And that the first day was, as it were, also without a sky? And who is so foolish as to suppose that God, after the manner of a husbandman, planted a paradise in Eden, towards the east, and placed in it a tree of life, visible and palpable, so that one tasting of the fruit by the bodily teeth obtained life? And again, that one was a partaker of good and evil by masticating what was taken from the tree? And if God is said to walk in the paradise in the evening, and Adam to hide himself under a tree, I do not suppose that anyone doubts that these things figuratively indicate certain mysteries, the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally.

Cain also, when going forth from the presence of God, certainly appears to thoughtful men as likely to lead the reader to inquire what is the presence of God, and what is the meaning of going out from Him. And what need is there to say more, since those who are not altogether blind can collect countless instances of a similar kind recorded as having occurred, but which did not literally take place? Nay, the Gospels themselves are filled with the same kind of narratives; e.g., the devil leading Jesus up into a high mountain, in order to show him from thence the kingdoms of the whole world, and the glory of them. For who is there among those who do not read such accounts carelessly, that would not condemn those who think that with the eye of the body— which requires a lofty height in order that the parts lying (immediately) under and adjacent may be seen — the kingdoms of the Persians, and Scythians, and Indians, and Parthians, were beheld, and the manner in which their princes are glorified among men?

All these statements have been made by us, in order to show that the design of that divine power which gave us the sacred Scriptures is, that we should not receive what is presented by the letter alone (such things being sometimes not true in their literal acceptation, but absurd and impossible), but that certain things have been introduced into the actual history and into the legislation that are useful in their literal sense.

19. But that no one may suppose that we assert respecting the whole that no history is real because a certain one is not; and that no law is to be literally observed, because a certain one, (understood) according to the letter, is absurd or impossible; or that the statements regarding the Saviour are not true in a manner perceptible to the senses; or that no commandment and precept of His ought to be obeyed — we have to answer that, with regard to certain things, it is perfectly clear to us that the historical account is true; as that Abraham was buried in the double cave at Hebron, as also Isaac and Jacob, and the wives of each of them; and that Shechem was given as a portion to Joseph; and that Jerusalem is the metropolis of Judea, in which the temple of God was built by Solomon; and innumerable other statements. For the passages that are true in their historical meaning are much more numerous than those which are interspersed with a purely spiritual signification.

parts.author: Origen
parts.translator: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885), from the Greek
parts.who: Origen (about 185–253) was the greatest scholar of the early Church. Born in Alexandria in Egypt to Christian parents (his father was martyred when he was about seventeen), he ran a school for Christian teaching there, later moved to Caesarea in Palestine, and died after torture in the persecution under the emperor Decius. He wrote commentaries on almost every book of the Bible.
parts.title: Body, soul and spirit
parts.context: Origen has argued that the Scriptures are inspired by God. Now he turns to how to read them, because, he says, misreading them has led people into error. He begins with a verse of Proverbs in the Greek translation he used, which told the reader to write the words 'in a threefold manner' (Proverbs 22:20).
parts.plain: Origen says: Scripture has three levels, as a person has body, soul and spirit. The 'body' is the obvious meaning, which helps simple believers. The 'soul' is a moral meaning for those who have grown a little; Paul gives an example when he says the law about not muzzling an ox was really written about paying those who work for the gospel. The 'spirit' is the deepest meaning, the hidden wisdom of God, for those who are mature.

commentary.on: which has been ascertained from the Scriptures themselves
commentary.text: Origen claims he did not invent his method: he found it in Scripture. His proof text, from Proverbs, depends on the Greek translation, and modern translations read the verse differently. His better evidence is Paul, as you will see.

commentary.on: in order that the simple man may be edified by the flesh, as it were, of the Scripture, for so we name the obvious sense
commentary.text: The first level is the 'flesh' or 'body': the obvious, plain meaning. Origen does not despise it. It feeds most believers, and he says so in the next paragraph.

commentary.on: while he who has ascended a certain way (may be edified) by the soul, as it were.
commentary.text: The second level, the 'soul', is what later writers called the moral sense: what the text teaches about how to live.

commentary.on: For as man consists of body, and soul, and spirit, so in the same way does Scripture
commentary.text: The heart of the theory. A text is like a person: there is more to it than what you see. The third level, 'spirit', is its meaning about Christ and the hidden things of God. This picture shaped Christian reading for over a thousand years.

commentary.on: You shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain; to which he adds, Does God take care of oxen?
commentary.text: Origen's example of the 'soul' sense is Paul's. Deuteronomy 25:4 says not to muzzle an ox while it threshes, so it can eat as it works. Paul applies it to apostles, who have a right to be supported by those they serve (1 Corinthians 9:9–10). Origen's point: the New Testament itself reads the Old for a meaning beyond the first one.

commentary.on: And there are numerous interpretations adapted to the multitude which are in circulation
commentary.text: He admits that many such readings were already in circulation, of uneven quality. The difficulty with a method that looks beneath the surface is that anyone can claim to see something there.

parts.author: Origen
parts.translator: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885), from the Greek
parts.who: Origen (about 185–253) was the greatest scholar of the early Church. Born in Alexandria in Egypt to Christian parents (his father was martyred when he was about seventeen), he ran a school for Christian teaching there, later moved to Caesarea in Palestine, and died after torture in the persecution under the emperor Decius. He wrote commentaries on almost every book of the Bible.
parts.title: Stumbling-blocks on purpose
parts.context: In the paragraphs left out, Origen has argued that the Bible's deepest purpose is to teach about God, Christ and the soul, and that its stories and laws were chosen to carry that teaching. Now comes his boldest claim.
parts.plain: Origen says: if every part of the Bible made perfect sense on the surface, we would never look deeper. So God allowed stumbling-blocks into it: things that are unreasonable or impossible if taken literally, so that readers would be pulled up short and search for a meaning worthy of God. For example, how could there be evening and morning on the first three days, before the sun was made? Did God really plant a garden like a farmer? Could the devil really show Jesus every kingdom of the world from one mountain?

commentary.on: the word of God has arranged that certain stumbling-blocks, as it were, and offenses, and impossibilities, should be introduced into the midst of the law and the history
commentary.text: This is Origen's most famous and most controversial idea. The difficulties in the Bible are not mistakes; they are signposts, put there to stop us reading lazily.

commentary.on: the Scripture interwove in the history (the account of) some event that did not take place
commentary.text: Origen is willing to say that some events in the Bible did not literally happen. That shocks some modern readers, who assume that only modern sceptics say such things. It also worried later Christians, who thought he went too far.

commentary.on: in order that they may give themselves to the toil of investigating what is written
commentary.text: The goal is effort. Reading Scripture is work, and the difficulties are meant to make us do it.

commentary.on: For who that has understanding will suppose that the first, and second, and third day, and the evening and the morning, existed without a sun, and moon, and stars?
commentary.text: You met this question in In the beginning. It was asked in the third century, not invented by modern science.

commentary.on: And who is so foolish as to suppose that God, after the manner of a husbandman, planted a paradise in Eden
commentary.text: A 'husbandman' is a farmer. Origen thinks Genesis 2 is a story whose meaning is spiritual. Augustine, two centuries later, disagreed and argued for a real garden; the debate is old.

commentary.on: the devil leading Jesus up into a high mountain, in order to show him from thence the kingdoms of the whole world
commentary.text: His example from the Gospels (Matthew 4:8). No mountain is high enough to see the whole world, so, he argues, the account is not a plain description of a physical event.

parts.author: Origen
parts.translator: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885), from the Greek
parts.who: Origen (about 185–253) was the greatest scholar of the early Church. Born in Alexandria in Egypt to Christian parents (his father was martyred when he was about seventeen), he ran a school for Christian teaching there, later moved to Caesarea in Palestine, and died after torture in the persecution under the emperor Decius. He wrote commentaries on almost every book of the Bible.
parts.title: But most of it happened
parts.context: Origen has given more examples, from the law of Moses and the Gospels, of commands that cannot be kept literally. Now he guards against being misunderstood.
parts.plain: Origen says: all this is to show that we should not read Scripture by the letter alone. But do not think I deny that its history happened. Abraham really was buried at Hebron, Jerusalem really was the capital of Judea, and Solomon really built the Temple there. The commandments, such as 'do not kill', are to be obeyed literally. And the passages that are historically true are far more numerous than those that are purely spiritual.

commentary.on: that we should not receive what is presented by the letter alone
commentary.text: 'Alone' is the key word. Origen is not against the letter; he is against stopping at it.

commentary.on: with regard to certain things, it is perfectly clear to us that the historical account is true
commentary.text: His examples are deliberately ordinary: a burial place, a city, a building. Origen did not think the Bible was a book of myths.

commentary.on: For the passages that are true in their historical meaning are much more numerous than those which are interspersed with a purely spiritual signification.
commentary.text: A sentence his critics often forget. For Origen, the spiritual sense usually rests on a real history. The difficulty is that he gives the reader the power to decide when it does not, and there his method is open to abuse.

read.author: Origen
read.translator: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885), from the Greek
read.who: Origen (about 185–253) was the greatest scholar of the early Church. Born in Alexandria in Egypt to Christian parents (his father was martyred when he was about seventeen), he ran a school for Christian teaching there, later moved to Caesarea in Palestine, and died after torture in the persecution under the emperor Decius. He wrote commentaries on almost every book of the Bible.

paras: Objection 1. It seems that in Holy Writ a word cannot have several senses, historical or literal, allegorical, tropological or moral, and anagogical. For many different senses in one text produce confusion and deception and destroy all force of argument. Hence no argument, but only fallacies, can be deduced from a multiplicity of propositions. But Holy Writ ought to be able to state the truth without any fallacy. Therefore in it there cannot be several senses to a word.
On the contrary, Gregory says (Moral. xx, 1): "Holy Writ by the manner of its speech transcends every science, because in one and the same sentence, while it describes a fact, it reveals a mystery."

I answer that, The author of Holy Writ is God, in whose power it is to signify His meaning, not by words only (as man also can do), but also by things themselves. So, whereas in every other science things are signified by words, this science has the property, that the things signified by the words have themselves also a signification. Therefore that first signification whereby words signify things belongs to the first sense, the historical or literal. That signification whereby things signified by words have themselves also a signification is called the spiritual sense, which is based on the literal, and presupposes it. Now this spiritual sense has a threefold division. For as the Apostle says (Hebrews 10:1) the Old Law is a figure of the New Law, and Dionysius says (Coel. Hier. i) "the New Law itself is a figure of future glory." Again, in the New Law, whatever our Head has done is a type of what we ought to do. Therefore, so far as the things of the Old Law signify the things of the New Law, there is the allegorical sense; so far as the things done in Christ, or so far as the things which signify Christ, are types of what we ought to do, there is the moral sense. But so far as they signify what relates to eternal glory, there is the anagogical sense. Since the literal sense is that which the author intends, and since the author of Holy Writ is God, Who by one act comprehends all things by His intellect, it is not unfitting, as Augustine says (Confess. xii), if, even according to the literal sense, one word in Holy Writ should have several senses.

Reply to Objection 1. The multiplicity of these senses does not produce equivocation or any other kind of multiplicity, seeing that these senses are not multiplied because one word signifies several things, but because the things signified by the words can be themselves types of other things. Thus in Holy Writ no confusion results, for all the senses are founded on one — the literal — from which alone can any argument be drawn, and not from those intended in allegory, as Augustine says (Epis. 48). Nevertheless, nothing of Holy Scripture perishes on account of this, since nothing necessary to faith is contained under the spiritual sense which is not elsewhere put forward by the Scripture in its literal sense.

parts.author: Thomas Aquinas
parts.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Laurence Shapcote), 2nd revised edition (1920)
parts.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.1.10, objection 1 and 'On the contrary'
parts.title: The objection, and an answer from Gregory
parts.context: Each article of the Summa starts with the strongest objections to Aquinas's own view, stated fairly, then a short quotation on the other side. Here the objector argues that a word with many meanings is useless for argument. Gregory the Great, quoted against him, was Pope from 590 to 604 and wrote a long commentary on Job.
parts.plain: The objection says: if a text can mean several things at once, it will confuse and deceive, and you will never be able to argue from it. But Scripture must state the truth plainly, so it cannot have several senses. Against this, Gregory the Great said that Scripture is unlike any other book: in a single sentence it tells a fact and reveals a mystery.

commentary.on: For many different senses in one text produce confusion and deception and destroy all force of argument.
commentary.text: Aquinas states the objection to Origen's method at full strength. If a text means whatever a clever reader can find in it, it means nothing in particular. This is still the main objection to allegory.

commentary.on: historical or literal, allegorical, tropological or moral, and anagogical
commentary.text: The four senses, named. 'Tropological' (from a Greek word for 'turning') is the moral sense, about how we turn our lives. 'Anagogical' (from a Greek word for 'leading up') is the sense about heaven and the end.

commentary.on: in one and the same sentence, while it describes a fact, it reveals a mystery.
commentary.text: Gregory's answer: the Bible is a book in which facts themselves carry meaning.

parts.author: Thomas Aquinas
parts.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Laurence Shapcote), 2nd revised edition (1920)
parts.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.1.10, answer and reply to objection 1
parts.title: Things that signify
parts.context: Aquinas's own answer, followed by his reply to the first objection.
parts.plain: Aquinas says: human writers can make words mean things, but God, the author of Scripture, can also make the things themselves mean something. The meaning of the words is the literal sense. The meaning of the things is the spiritual sense, which has three parts: allegorical (what the Old Testament shows of Christ), moral (how we should live) and anagogical (what concerns eternal glory). This does not confuse anything, because every sense is founded on the literal one, and only the literal sense can be used to prove a doctrine. Nothing necessary for faith is taught only in a spiritual sense.

commentary.on: The author of Holy Writ is God, in whose power it is to signify His meaning, not by words only (as man also can do), but also by things themselves.
commentary.text: This is the key idea. A human author can only make words mean something. But if God is the author of history as well as of Scripture, then the events themselves (the exodus, the Passover lamb) can point beyond themselves. That is how a real event can have a further meaning without ceasing to be real.

commentary.on: That signification whereby things signified by words have themselves also a signification is called the spiritual sense, which is based on the literal, and presupposes it.
commentary.text: Notice the order: the spiritual sense is 'based on the literal, and presupposes it'. No literal sense, no spiritual sense.

commentary.on: so far as the things of the Old Law signify the things of the New Law, there is the allegorical sense
commentary.text: The allegorical sense is what the Old Testament shows of Christ and the Church: the lamb whose blood saved Israel at Passover points to Christ, whom John the Baptist called 'the Lamb of God' (John 1:29).

commentary.on: as Augustine says (Confess. xii), if, even according to the literal sense, one word in Holy Writ should have several senses.
commentary.text: Aquinas recalls Augustine's Confessions XII, which you read in What is the Bible?: a great text may hold more truth than one reader sees.

commentary.on: for all the senses are founded on one — the literal — from which alone can any argument be drawn
commentary.text: The safeguard. You may find Christ in the story of the exodus, but you may not prove a doctrine from an allegory. Doctrine must rest on the plain sense.

commentary.on: nothing necessary to faith is contained under the spiritual sense which is not elsewhere put forward by the Scripture in its literal sense.
commentary.text: A second safeguard. Allegory can deepen and delight, but it cannot introduce anything new that you must believe. Everything essential is said plainly somewhere.

compare.author: Thomas Aquinas
compare.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.1.10, objection 1 and 'On the contrary'
compare.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (Laurence Shapcote), 2nd revised edition (1920)
compare.why: A thousand years after Origen, the question was still alive: can one word of Scripture mean several things? Aquinas's answer, at the very start of his Summa Theologiae, became the classic account of the four senses, and it ties them all to the literal sense.
compare.title: Thomas Aquinas on the four senses

paras: By the Middle Ages, Origen's three levels had become four. John Cassian, a monk who brought Egyptian monasticism to southern France, gave the classic example in the 420s: Jerusalem. In the medieval schools a rhyme helped students remember the four, attributed to the Dominican Augustine of Dacia (about 1260): Littera gesta docet, quid credas allegoria, / moralis quid agas, quo tendas anagogia. In our translation: 'The letter teaches what happened; the allegory, what to believe; the moral sense, what to do; the anagogy, where you are going.'
Christians still use the scheme. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992) teaches it (paragraphs 115–119), and Orthodox preaching on the feasts is full of it.

rows: What happened? What did the writer mean?
What does this show of Christ and the Church?
The heavenly city, the life to come

sections.key: The four senses ask what happened, what it shows of Christ, how to live and what to hope for; Jerusalem is city, Church, soul and heaven.

paras: A letter traditionally attributed to Dante (though some scholars doubt he wrote it), sent to his patron Can Grande della Scala about 1316, shows the method at work on Psalm 114, 'When Israel went out of Egypt'. Literally, it is about the children of Israel leaving Egypt in the time of Moses. Allegorically, it means our redemption by Christ. Morally, it means the turning of the soul from the misery of sin to grace. Anagogically, it means the soul leaving the slavery of this corruption for the freedom of eternal glory.

This was not a game. Each level answers a different question a reader brings. A historian asks what happened. A believer asks what it has to do with Christ. Someone in trouble asks what to do. Someone facing death asks what to hope for. One story can answer all four, because, as Aquinas said, the events themselves were meant.
The letter goes on to say that Dante's own Divine Comedy is to be read the same way: literally, the state of souls after death; allegorically, how people earn reward or punishment by their choices.
sections.key: Psalm 114's exodus means, on four levels, Israel's escape, our redemption, the soul's conversion and the soul's final freedom.

paras: Scholars often distinguish two kinds of spiritual reading. Typology sees real people and events in the Old Testament as patterns that later events fulfil: Adam and Christ (Romans 5:14), the Passover lamb and the cross, Noah's flood and baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21), the manna and the bread of life (John 6:31–35). Both ends of the pattern are historical. The New Testament does this constantly.

Allegory, in the narrower sense, reads the details of a text as symbols, sometimes with little link to history. An early example: Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, saw in the scarlet cord that Rahab hung from her window in Jericho (Joshua 2:18) a sign of the blood of Christ. Origen read the six water jars at Cana as the purification of a world made in six days.
Typology is generally regarded as sound by Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants alike. Allegory of the freer kind is where readers part company. It can be beautiful, and it can be arbitrary.
sections.key: Typology links real events to real events and is widely accepted; free allegory reads details as symbols, and is where readers part company.

paras: The tradition was not naive about allegory. It set limits. First, the literal sense comes first. Hugh of St Victor, the twelfth-century teacher of Paris, told his students to learn the history before looking for the meaning: history, he said, is the foundation on which the rest of the building stands. Aquinas said all senses are founded on the literal. Second, nothing necessary to faith may rest on allegory alone. Third, a spiritual reading must agree with the faith of the Church, the 'rule of faith' that session 4 will explore. Fourth, it must build up love, as you saw Augustine say.
Within those limits, allegory was a way of praying the whole Bible as one book about Christ. Outside them, it could make the text say anything. Both happened.
sections.key: The tradition limited allegory: literal first, no doctrine from allegory alone, agreement with the faith, and the rule of love.

paras: Jewish interpretation also reads on more than one level. The rabbis distinguished peshat, the plain meaning, from derash, the searching meaning drawn out by midrash (from darash, 'to seek'). Midrash fills the Bible's silences with stories and questions: what was Abraham thinking on the way to Mount Moriah?

By the thirteenth century some Jewish mystics spoke of four levels, summed up in the word PaRDeS, 'orchard' (the word from which 'paradise' comes): peshat (plain), remez (hint), derash (searching) and sod (secret, the mystical sense). Scholars still debate whether the Christian and Jewish four-level schemes influenced each other.

The difference is what the deeper meaning points to. For Christians, the Old Testament points to Christ. For Jews, the Tanakh is read through the rabbis' tradition, and its deeper meanings point to the Torah, to Israel, and to God's ways with the world. Both agree that a holy text has more in it than one reading can find. Neither allows the plain sense to be thrown away.
sections.key: Jews also read on several levels (peshat, remez, derash, sod), but their deeper meanings point to Torah and Israel rather than to Christ.

sections.h: The Reformers, and a modern return
paras: The Reformers of the sixteenth century were suspicious of allegory. Luther, who had used the four senses as a young lecturer, came to dismiss much allegory as empty speculation, and to insist on the plain, grammatical sense. Calvin wrote that the true meaning of Scripture is the natural and obvious one. They had seen allegory used to support teachings they thought had no plain basis in the Bible.

But they did not stop reading the Bible as one story. Luther found Christ throughout the Old Testament and said the whole of Scripture was about him. Calvin read the Old Testament's sacrifices and kings as types of Christ. What they rejected was allegory floating free of the literal sense, which is what Aquinas had also rejected.

In the twentieth century the French Jesuit Henri de Lubac (1896–1991) wrote a vast study, Medieval Exegesis (1959–64), arguing that the four senses were not fanciful but a way of holding history, doctrine, morals and hope together. Many theologians, Protestant and Catholic, now speak of a 'theological interpretation of Scripture' that tries to recover something of it.
sections.key: The Reformers rejected free allegory but kept Christ-centred reading and typology; modern theologians have revisited the four senses.

paras: You do not need to be a medieval monk to use the four senses. They are four questions you can bring to any passage. What happened, or what did the writer mean? What does this have to do with Christ? What does it ask of me? What does it promise? A reader who asks only the first will understand the history and may miss its point. A reader who asks only the third will turn the Bible into a book of tips. Asking all four, in order, keeps a reading both honest and alive.

Take the manna in Exodus 16. Literally: Israel was fed in the desert with bread that came each morning, enough for each day and no more. Allegorically: Jesus calls himself 'the bread of life' and says he is the true bread from heaven (John 6:31–35), and Christians have seen the Lord's Supper in it. Morally: the instruction to gather only enough for today teaches trust and forbids hoarding; Jesus's prayer asks for 'our daily bread'. Anagogically: Revelation promises 'the hidden manna' to those who overcome (Revelation 2:17). Each level depends on the first.
sections.key: The four senses are four questions for any passage, asked in order; the manna shows how each depends on the literal.

debate.question: Is allegory a key that opens the Bible, or a licence to make it say anything?

positions.name: A key
positions.who: Origen; Gregory the Great; Henri de Lubac
positions.view: Because God speaks through events as well as words, the Old Testament really does point to Christ and to the reader's own life. Spiritual reading finds what is there, as the New Testament itself does.
positions.evidence: Paul's readings of the rock, Adam and Hagar; Aquinas's account of 'things that signify'; a thousand years of Christian prayer built on it.

positions.name: A licence
positions.who: The school of Antioch in part; Luther and Calvin; many modern critical scholars
positions.view: Once you leave the plain sense, you can make any text say anything; allegory has been used to support doctrines with no plain basis in Scripture, and it hides the text's own voice.
positions.evidence: The arbitrariness of many patristic allegories (the water jars, the scarlet cord); the objection Aquinas himself states; the Reformers' experience.

positions.name: A key with a lock
positions.who: Aquinas; most Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant theologians today
positions.view: Typology and spiritual reading are legitimate, but only when they rest on the literal sense, agree with the faith, build up love and add nothing necessary to faith.
positions.evidence: Aquinas's reply to objection 1; Hugh of St Victor; the Catechism 115–119.

debate.agree: All agree that the New Testament reads the Old as pointing to Christ, and that a reading which ignores the literal sense is suspect.

look.why: Hans Baldung Grien, a German painter trained in Dürer's workshop, painted this about 1511. It is here because it shows typology at work: John the Baptist points at the child and at a lamb, one thing standing for another, as he says in John's Gospel, 'Behold, the Lamb of God' (John 1:29).
points: Saint Anne, an older woman in a cream-white wimple and a scarlet cloak, sits on a tall wooden throne-like chair, smiling down at the baby Jesus on her lap.
To the right, the young Mary, with long wavy blond hair, holds out a small dark red apple, and the baby grips it.
To the left, Saint John the Baptist kneels, pointing at Jesus with one hand and gesturing down at a white lamb with a halo at his knees with the other.
The halos are inscribed with names: 'S IOHANE', 'S ANNA' and 'MARIA'.
Beyond a black wall with white columns, a landscape with a river, trees and a town on craggy cliffs, under a pale blue sky.

music.why: Palestrina's Mass (published 1567) weaves six voices in many layers, yet the words stay clear: according to a later story, it convinced the Council of Trent that rich music need not drown the text. Many layers, one text, never lost: the ideal of the four senses.

think.why: How the great teachers read the Bible as one Word spoken through many words.

learn.why: The Emmaus disciples, after Jesus opened the Scriptures to them as one story about himself: the experience the four senses were meant to serve.

check.q: Why, according to Aquinas, can a real event in Scripture have a further, spiritual meaning without ceasing to be real?
options: Because the event did not really happen
Because the Church says so
Because God, as author of history as well as of the text, can make things as well as words signify
Because every reader can decide what it means
check.why: Human authors signify by words; God can signify by things. So the exodus can be history and also point to Christ.

check.q: Origen said God allowed 'stumbling-blocks' and impossibilities into Scripture. What did he think they were for?
options: To show that the Bible is unreliable
To hide the truth from Christians
To test whether readers would give up
To stop readers resting on the surface and make them search for a meaning worthy of God
check.why: The difficulties are signposts to deeper reading.

check.q: Which statement would Origen have rejected?
options: Most of the Bible's history is not historically true
Scripture has body, soul and spirit
The plain sense helps simple believers
Some passages cannot be taken literally
check.why: He wrote that the historically true passages are 'much more numerous' than the purely spiritual ones.

check.q: In Cassian's example, what is the moral sense of 'Jerusalem'?
options: The Church
The human soul
The heavenly city
The city in Judea
check.why: Literal: the city; allegorical: the Church; moral: the soul; anagogical: heaven.

check.q: Which of these is typology rather than free allegory?
options: Adam as a pattern of Christ, as in Romans 5:14
Six water jars at Cana as a world made in six days
Each detail of the Tabernacle as a virtue of the soul
Rahab's scarlet cord as the blood of Christ
check.why: Typology links one real person or event to another; both ends are historical, and the link is made in the New Testament itself.

check.q: What is Aquinas's chief safeguard against allegory being used to make Scripture say anything?
options: Allegory may be used only on the Old Testament
Only bishops may use allegory
All the senses are founded on the literal, and no argument for doctrine may be drawn from allegory alone
Allegory must be approved by a council
check.why: Literal first; doctrine from the literal sense only; nothing necessary to faith is only in the spiritual sense.

tutorial.question: 'Allegory lets you make the Bible say anything.' Is that fair to Origen and Aquinas?
tutorial.approach: Set out Origen's body, soul and spirit, and his claim about stumbling-blocks, with his insistence that most of the history is true. Then explain Aquinas's account of the four senses and his safeguards. Distinguish typology from free allegory, with examples. Give the strongest form of the objection, and say whether the safeguards answer it.
strong: Explains Origen's three levels and why he thought difficulties were deliberate.
Notes that Origen insisted most of the history really happened.
Explains Aquinas's distinction between words that signify and things that signify.
States Aquinas's safeguards accurately.
Distinguishes typology from free allegory, with examples from the New Testament and the Fathers.
Gives the objection its due (arbitrariness, the Reformers' experience) and reaches a reasoned view.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: take one short story from Genesis or Exodus that you know (the burning bush, the manna, the crossing of the sea) and write four lines about it: what happened; what it shows of Christ; what it asks of me; what it promises.
sessions.reflect: Which of the four questions do you most often bring to the Bible, and which do you never ask?
takeaways: Reading the Bible as one story begins in the New Testament itself, with Jesus at Emmaus and Paul's types and allegories.
Origen read Scripture as body, soul and spirit; the Middle Ages read it in four senses: literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical.
The tradition limited spiritual reading: it rests on the literal sense, proves no doctrine by itself, and must agree with the faith and build up love.

sessions.title: Reading with others
sessions.line: Rung three: no one reads alone.
sessions.plain: Christians read the same Bible and disagree about what it says. Part of the reason is that everyone reads within a community: Jews with the rabbis, Catholics and Orthodox with the Church's tradition, Protestants with their confessions and preachers. This session reads Augustine's rule that every right reading builds up love, and the Jewish Fathers on a chain of teachers going back to Moses.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 and 3 gave the plain sense and the one story. But who decides when readers disagree? The third rung is the community: reading with others.
answers: Why do Christians disagree about what the Bible says?
What do Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants mean by 'tradition'?
How do Jews read the Bible?
If I can't be sure of the meaning, how do I know I'm reading it rightly?
sessions.finding: No one reads alone: Jews read with the rabbis, Catholics and Orthodox with the Church's tradition, Protestants by Scripture alone but never Scripture in isolation, and Augustine's test for all of them is whether a reading builds up love of God and neighbour.

paras: The Bible itself shows that reading needs help. When Ezra read the Law aloud in Jerusalem, the Levites 'gave the sense, so that they understood the reading' (Nehemiah 8:8), which you read in What is the Bible?. When Philip asked the Ethiopian official whether he understood Isaiah, he replied, 'How can I, unless someone explains it to me?' (Acts 8:31), which you read in Kings and prophets.

Every community that reads Scripture has developed ways of explaining it: preachers and teachers, commentaries, creeds, councils and confessions. That is what 'tradition' means at its simplest: what has been handed on (Latin traditio, 'handing over').
background.key: The Bible itself shows readers needing others to explain it; tradition is what has been handed on.

paras: Jews do not read the Tanakh alone either. Rabbinic Judaism holds that at Sinai God gave Moses two Torahs: the written Torah (the five books) and an oral Torah, the teaching that explains it, handed down by word of mouth. Around AD 200 Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered the oral teaching into the Mishnah. Over the next three centuries rabbis in Babylonia and the land of Israel discussed the Mishnah at enormous length; their discussions became the Talmud.

One tractate of the Mishnah, Avot ('the Fathers'), collects sayings of the early teachers. It begins with a chain: Moses received the Torah and handed it on. Jews still study it, traditionally on Sabbath afternoons in the summer. Study is often done in pairs (chavruta, 'companionship'), arguing over the text together. The printed page of the Talmud puts the text in the middle and centuries of commentary around it: a picture of reading with others.
background.key: Jews read the written Torah with the oral Torah, gathered in the Mishnah and Talmud, and study it together.

paras: The main reading returns to Augustine's handbook, to the end of Book I, where he says what the whole Bible is for. If its purpose is love of God and neighbour, then that purpose becomes a test for every interpretation, whoever proposes it.

The comparison is two sayings from Avot, in the translation of W. O. E. Oesterley, an Anglican scholar of Judaism (1919): the chain of tradition from Moses, and a later teacher's advice to turn the Torah over and over, 'for all things are in it'.
background.key: Augustine gives a test that works across communities; Avot shows how the rabbis saw reading as a chain of teachers.

before: What does Augustine say is 'the fulfillment and the end' of all Scripture?
What does he say about someone who gets the author's meaning wrong but whose reading builds up love?
In the comparison, who received the Torah from whom, and what did they hand on?
sessions.readWhy: The end of Book I of On Christian Doctrine, where Augustine says what the whole Bible is for, and turns it into a test for every reading.

paras: 39. Of all, then, that has been said since we entered upon the discussion about things, this is the sum: that we should clearly understand that the fulfillment and the end of the Law, and of all Holy Scripture, is the love of an object which is to be enjoyed, and the love of an object which can enjoy that other in fellowship with ourselves. For there is no need of a command that each man should love himself. The whole temporal dispensation for our salvation, therefore, was framed by the providence of God that we might know this truth and be able to act upon it; and we ought to use that dispensation, not with such love and delight as if it were a good to rest in, but with a transient feeling rather, such as we have towards the road, or carriages, or other things that are merely means. Perhaps some other comparison can be found that will more suitably express the idea that we are to love the things by which we are borne only for the sake of that towards which we are borne.

40. Whoever, then, thinks that he understands the Holy Scriptures, or any part of them, but puts such an interpretation upon them as does not tend to build up this twofold love of God and our neighbor, does not yet understand them as he ought. If, on the other hand, a man draws a meaning from them that may be used for the building up of love, even though he does not happen upon the precise meaning which the author whom he reads intended to express in that place, his error is not pernicious, and he is wholly clear from the charge of deception.

41. Whoever takes another meaning out of Scripture than the writer intended, goes astray, but not through any falsehood in Scripture. Nevertheless, as I was going to say, if his mistaken interpretation tends to build up love, which is the end of the commandment, he goes astray in much the same way as a man who by mistake quits the high road, but yet reaches through the fields the same place to which the road leads. He is to be corrected, however, and to be shown how much better it is not to quit the straight road, lest, if he get into a habit of going astray, he may sometimes take cross roads, or even go in the wrong direction altogether.

For if he takes up rashly a meaning which the author whom he is reading did not intend, he often falls in with other statements which he cannot harmonize with this meaning. And if he admits that these statements are true and certain, then it follows that the meaning he had put upon the former passage cannot be the true one: and so it comes to pass, one can hardly tell how, that, out of love for his own opinion, he begins to feel more angry with Scripture than he is with himself. And if he should once permit that evil to creep in, it will utterly destroy him. For we walk by faith, not by sight. Now faith will totter if the authority of Scripture begin to shake. And then, if faith totter, love itself will grow cold. For if a man has fallen from faith, he must necessarily also fall from love; for he cannot love what he does not believe to exist. But if he both believes and loves, then through good works, and through diligent attention to the precepts of morality, he comes to hope also that he shall attain the object of his love. And so these are the three things to which all knowledge and all prophecy are subservient: faith, hope, love.

44. And, therefore, if a man fully understands that the end of the commandment is charity, out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned, and is bent upon making all his understanding of Scripture to bear upon these three graces, he may come to the interpretation of these books with an easy mind. For while the apostle says love, he adds out of a pure heart, to provide against anything being loved but that which is worthy of love. And he joins with this a good conscience, in reference to hope; for, if a man has the burden of a bad conscience, he despairs of ever reaching that which he believes in and loves. And in the third place he says: and of faith unfeigned. For if our faith is free from all hypocrisy, then we both abstain from loving what is unworthy of our love, and by living uprightly we are able to indulge the hope that our hope shall not be in vain.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.translator: J. F. Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (1887)
parts.who: Augustine (354–430), bishop of Hippo in North Africa, the most influential theologian of the Western Church. You read his rules for the plain sense in session 2, from Book III of the same handbook.
parts.when: Hippo, North Africa; Book I written in 396 or 397
parts.ref: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine I.35–36 (§§39–40, shortened)
parts.title: The end of all Scripture is love
parts.context: Book I has been about 'things': what we are to enjoy (God, for his own sake) and what we are to use (everything else, as means to God). Now Augustine sums up the whole book.
parts.plain: Augustine says: the purpose of all Scripture is love: love of God, whom we enjoy, and love of our neighbour, who can enjoy God with us. Everything God has done in history was to teach us this. So if someone thinks he understands the Bible, but his reading does not build up love of God and neighbour, he has not understood it yet. And if someone reads a meaning the author did not intend, but it builds up love, his mistake is not harmful, and he is not lying.

commentary.on: the fulfillment and the end of the Law, and of all Holy Scripture, is the love of an object which is to be enjoyed, and the love of an object which can enjoy that other in fellowship with ourselves
commentary.text: Augustine's roundabout phrase means God (the one to be enjoyed) and our neighbour (who can enjoy God with us). He is echoing Paul: 'love is the fulfilment of the law' (Romans 13:10), and Jesus's two great commandments.

commentary.on: with a transient feeling rather, such as we have towards the road, or carriages
commentary.text: The Bible itself, and everything else God gives, is like a road or a vehicle: valued for where it takes us. Augustine does not worship the book; he loves it for where it leads.

commentary.on: but puts such an interpretation upon them as does not tend to build up this twofold love of God and our neighbor, does not yet understand them as he ought
commentary.text: The test. However learned or literal, a reading that leads to hatred or contempt has not yet understood the Bible. This sentence will be important when we come to the strongest objection to this journey's answer.

commentary.on: even though he does not happen upon the precise meaning which the author whom he reads intended to express in that place, his error is not pernicious
commentary.text: A generous and surprising claim: a reader can miss the author's meaning and still read in a way that is good. Augustine is not saying the author's meaning does not matter, as the next part shows.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.translator: J. F. Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (1887)
parts.who: Augustine (354–430), bishop of Hippo in North Africa, the most influential theologian of the Western Church. You read his rules for the plain sense in session 2, from Book III of the same handbook.
parts.when: Hippo, North Africa; Book I written in 396 or 397
parts.title: Leaving the road
parts.context: Augustine has just explained why such a reader is not a liar: lying means intending to deceive, and he does not. Now he warns him.
parts.plain: Augustine says: a reader who takes a meaning the writer did not intend goes astray, though not because Scripture is false. If his reading builds up love, he is like a man who leaves the road by mistake but still reaches the same place across the fields. But he should be corrected, because if he gets into the habit of leaving the road he may end up lost. And a reader who is attached to his own wrong reading may find other passages contradict it, and then get angrier with Scripture than with himself, and lose his faith.

commentary.on: he goes astray in much the same way as a man who by mistake quits the high road, but yet reaches through the fields the same place to which the road leads
commentary.text: Augustine's picture. The 'high road' is the author's meaning. The destination is love. You can sometimes reach it across the fields, but the road is safer.

commentary.on: He is to be corrected, however
commentary.text: So the author's meaning matters after all. A community of readers is needed precisely to correct one another, kindly.

commentary.on: out of love for his own opinion, he begins to feel more angry with Scripture than he is with himself
commentary.text: A sharp piece of psychology. The real danger is not a mistaken reading but pride in it. We would rather the Bible were wrong than we were.

commentary.on: And so these are the three things to which all knowledge and all prophecy are subservient: faith, hope, love.
commentary.text: All knowledge, including biblical scholarship, serves faith, hope and love (1 Corinthians 13:13). Augustine goes on to say love is the greatest, because it alone lasts for ever.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.translator: J. F. Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 2 (1887)
parts.who: Augustine (354–430), bishop of Hippo in North Africa, the most influential theologian of the Western Church. You read his rules for the plain sense in session 2, from Book III of the same handbook.
parts.when: Hippo, North Africa; Book I written in 396 or 397
parts.title: What kind of reader Scripture needs
parts.context: The last paragraph of Book I. Augustine quotes 1 Timothy 1:5: 'the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith'.
parts.plain: Augustine says: if you understand that the aim of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith, and you make all your reading serve those three, you can come to the Bible with an easy mind.

commentary.on: he may come to the interpretation of these books with an easy mind
commentary.text: Augustine's comfort for anxious readers. You do not need to have solved every difficulty. If you read to grow in love, faith and hope, you are on the road.

commentary.on: For while the apostle says love, he adds out of a pure heart, to provide against anything being loved but that which is worthy of love.
commentary.text: Love here is not vague niceness: it is love of the right things, in the right order. Augustine's rule has teeth.

paras: Moses received the Torah from Sinai, and he delivered it to Joshua; and Joshua (delivered it) to the Elders; and the Elders (delivered it) to the Prophets; and the Prophets delivered it to the men of the Great Synagogue. These (men) said three things: "Be deliberate in judgement"; and "Raise up many disciples"; and "Make a fence to the Torah."

Ben Bag-Bag said: "Turn it, and turn it again; and meditate therein; for all things are in it. And look into it; become grey and old in it; and move not away from it; there is no better guide for thee than this."

parts.author: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (Pirke Aboth)
parts.title: Moses received the Torah from Sinai
parts.context: The opening of Avot. The Mishnah was compiled about AD 200, but this saying is older. The 'men of the Great Synagogue' were, by Jewish tradition, the assembly of teachers founded in Ezra's time, after the exile. Words in round brackets are the translator's.
parts.plain: The Fathers say: Moses received the Torah from God at Sinai and handed it to Joshua; Joshua to the elders; the elders to the prophets; and the prophets to the men of the Great Synagogue. They taught three things: be careful in judging, raise up many students, and build a fence around the Torah.

commentary.on: Moses received the Torah from Sinai, and he delivered it to Joshua
commentary.text: 'Torah' here, as Oesterley notes, means the whole of God's teaching, written and oral. The verbs are the language of tradition: 'received' and 'delivered' (handed on). Paul uses the same pair of verbs of the gospel: 'I delivered to you first of all that which I also received' (1 Corinthians 15:3).

commentary.on: and the Prophets delivered it to the men of the Great Synagogue
commentary.text: A chain of living teachers, generation after generation, from Moses to the rabbis. For Jews, reading Torah rightly means reading it within that chain.

commentary.on: "Raise up many disciples"
commentary.text: Reading with others includes teaching others. The tradition survives only if it is handed on.

commentary.on: "Make a fence to the Torah."
commentary.text: A 'fence' is an extra rule that keeps you well away from breaking a commandment, as a fence keeps people back from a cliff edge. The Sermon on the Mount has been compared to this: Jesus forbids anger, not only murder (Matthew 5:21–22).

parts.author: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (Pirke Aboth)
parts.title: Turn it, and turn it again
parts.context: Near the end of the tractate. Editions number the sayings differently: this one is usually cited as Avot 5:22. Ben Bag-Bag is a little-known early teacher; Oesterley thinks the name may be a pseudonym, and notes that one manuscript gives the saying to Hillel. 'It' is the Torah.
parts.plain: Ben Bag-Bag says: turn the Torah over and over, and think about it, because everything is in it. Keep looking into it; grow grey and old in it; never leave it. There is no better guide for you.

commentary.on: Turn it, and turn it again; and meditate therein; for all things are in it.
commentary.text: The Jewish answer to the question 'how much a day?': for a lifetime. Turning a text over is what Augustine called meditating 'till an interpretation be found'. The confidence that 'all things are in it' is close to Gregory's saying, quoted by Aquinas, that Scripture reveals a mystery in every fact.

commentary.on: become grey and old in it
commentary.text: Reading Scripture is not a course you finish. You grow old in it.

commentary.on: And look into it
commentary.text: Oesterley's note on this phrase points to James 1:25, the man who 'looks into the perfect law of freedom'. Jewish and Christian readers share more than they often realise.

compare.author: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (Pirke Aboth)
compare.why: The rabbis also read within a chain of teachers. These two sayings from the Mishnah tractate Avot show how: a line of tradition reaching back to Moses, and a lifetime of turning the text over.
compare.title: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers

paras: Christians who share the same Bible disagree about baptism, the Lord's Supper, church order, the role of women, divorce and much else. Since the Reformation the disagreements have multiplied, and Protestant churches alone now number in the thousands. Critics have long pointed this out: if the Bible is clear, why do its readers not agree?

The question is fair, but it can be overstated. On the main things, the churches agree: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit; Jesus Christ, truly God and truly human, crucified and risen; the double commandment of love. These are the things the early creeds say, and all the large churches accept them. The disagreements, though real, are mostly about what follows.
Still, every community has had to answer the question: when readers disagree, who decides?
sections.key: Christians disagree on much but agree on the core the creeds state; every church has had to say who decides between readings.

paras: The earliest Christian answer was the 'rule of faith' (regula fidei): a short summary of what the apostles taught, handed down in the churches and recited at baptism. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, wrote about 180 that his opponents treated Scripture like a mosaic of a king made by a skilled artist, which they broke up and rearranged into a dog or a fox, claiming it was still the king. The rule of faith, he said, lets you see the true picture.

Later, Vincent of Lérins (434) gave a famous test for true tradition: what has been believed 'everywhere, always, and by all'. The creeds of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) became the standard summary. All the main churches still accept them.
sections.key: The early Church read Scripture by the 'rule of faith', the apostles' teaching in summary, later fixed in the creeds.

sections.h: Scripture and tradition, side by side
paras: The churches agree that Scripture is God's word. They differ on how it relates to tradition and on who may interpret it with authority.

The differences are real, but they are narrower than the sixteenth century's polemics suggested. Catholics after the Second Vatican Council speak of Scripture as 'the soul of sacred theology' and urge every Catholic to read it; many Protestants now speak warmly of the Fathers and the creeds as a 'great tradition' that guides reading. Orthodox theologians often say that the Western argument over 'Scripture or tradition' poses a false choice, because Scripture is itself the heart of the tradition. And Jews and Christians alike hold that the text is received from a community of faith and handed on within one.

rows: Scripture and Tradition 'flow from the same divine wellspring' and are received 'with the same sense of loyalty and reverence'
The bishops in union with the Pope (the Magisterium), which 'is not above the word of God, but serves it'
Council of Trent, Session IV (1546); Dei Verbum 9–10 (1965)
Scripture is the heart of Tradition, read within the life of the Church: the Fathers, the councils and the liturgy
The whole Church, through its bishops in council and its worship
Scripture alone (sola scriptura) is the supreme rule; tradition is respected but can err
Scripture interprets Scripture, read in the church with its confessions
Westminster Confession I.9 (1646): 'The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself'
Scripture 'containeth all things necessary to salvation'; the creeds and the Fathers are honoured guides
Scripture first, with tradition and reason (Richard Hooker)
Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles (1571)
Scripture alone, with suspicion of human tradition
Various confessions, e.g. the Baptist Confession of 1689
The written Torah with the oral Torah, given together
The rabbis, in argument, across the generations
table.note: Simplified; within each tradition there are many views.

sections.key: Catholics read Scripture with Tradition and the Magisterium; the Orthodox within the Church's life; Protestants by Scripture alone; Jews with the oral Torah.

paras: The Reformers' cry was sola scriptura: Scripture alone. At the Diet of Worms in 1521 Luther refused to recant unless he was convinced 'by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason'. The Reformers held that popes and councils can err, and that the Church's teaching must be tested by the Bible.

But sola scriptura never meant reading the Bible in isolation. The Reformers kept the creeds, read the Fathers constantly (Calvin quotes Augustine hundreds of times), wrote confessions and catechisms, and trained preachers. Modern writers draw the distinction with a pair of Latin phrases: the Reformers held to sola scriptura, Scripture as the supreme authority, not nuda scriptura, 'bare Scripture', each person alone with the Bible and nothing else. (The Reformed writer Keith Mathison calls the second 'solo scriptura'.)

Catholics and Orthodox reply that in practice sola scriptura has led to endless division, because there is no final court of appeal. Protestants reply that a final court can also be wrong. The question is still open between them.
sections.key: Sola scriptura meant Scripture as the supreme authority, not each person alone with the Bible; whether it can settle disputes is still debated.

paras: Augustine's test cuts across all these differences. Whatever your church, a reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not yet understood the Bible.

This is not a way of avoiding hard texts. Augustine still thought the author's meaning mattered: the reader who leaves the road should be corrected. And love, for him, meant love of the right things in the right order, which can be demanding. But it means that interpretation is a moral act. You can read the words correctly and still read badly, if you read in order to win, to condemn or to justify yourself.

Jewish tradition says something similar. When a non-Jew asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel, by the Talmud's account, replied: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it' (Shabbat 31a).
sections.key: Augustine's rule makes reading a moral act: a reading that does not build up love has not understood, however correct its words.

paras: What does reading with others look like today? Most simply, hearing the Bible read and preached in church, in a community that has read it for centuries. Many people also read in small groups: a few friends who read a passage aloud, ask what it says, what it means and what it asks of them, and listen to each other. Jews study in pairs, chavruta, arguing over every word.

Reading with others protects against two dangers. One is private eccentricity: the reading only you can see. The other is the echo chamber: a group that only hears what it already thinks. The best protection against both is to read with people who are different from you, including the dead, through their commentaries, and members of other traditions.
sections.key: Read with a church, a group or a partner, and with people different from you, to guard against both eccentricity and echo chambers.

paras: Where do scholars fit? Every tradition needs them. They know the languages, the history and the manuscripts, and they can tell when a favourite reading rests on a mistranslation or a misunderstanding. Jerome and Origen were scholars; so were the rabbis; so were the Reformers, who were university teachers before they were rebels.

But scholars are readers too, with their own communities and assumptions. A scholarly consensus can change, and has, many times. The Catholic Pontifical Biblical Commission, in 1993, put it well: historical study is indispensable, but it is not the whole of interpretation, because the Bible is also the word of God addressed to the Church today. Many Protestant scholars say the same. The best scholars are humble about what their methods can show, and the best churches listen to scholars without handing them the last word.
sections.key: Scholars are indispensable for the languages and history, but they are readers too; neither church nor scholar should have the whole word.

paras: Some disagreements will not be settled in this life. Augustine's advice still helps. Be slow to claim you know exactly what the author meant. Be quick to ask whether a reading is true and builds up love. Correct one another, but gently, as one corrects a traveller who has left the road. And remember that the reader who loves his own opinion more than the truth is in more danger than the reader who is simply mistaken.

In practice this means reading charitably the readings of other traditions, as you would want yours read. A Protestant can learn from the Catholic sense of the Church's long memory; a Catholic from the Protestant hunger for the text itself; both from the Orthodox sense that Scripture is something sung and prayed; all from the Jewish habit of argument for the sake of heaven. Many of the great reconciliations of the last century, such as the joint Lutheran–Catholic statement on justification in 1999, began when Christians read the Bible together again.
sections.key: Some disagreements remain: read other traditions charitably, correct gently, and fear pride in your own reading more than error.

debate.question: When readers disagree, who decides what the Bible means?

positions.name: The Church's teaching office
positions.who: The Catholic Church (Dei Verbum 10)
positions.view: Christ gave the apostles and their successors, the bishops in union with the Pope, the task of interpreting Scripture and Tradition authentically; without that, there is no way to settle disputes.
positions.evidence: Matthew 16:18–19; the Church existed and taught before the New Testament was complete; the multiplication of Protestant churches.

positions.name: The mind of the whole Church
positions.who: Orthodox theologians such as Georges Florovsky
positions.view: The Bible belongs to the Church and is understood within its continuous life: the Fathers, the councils and the liturgy. No single office, and no single reader, owns its meaning.
positions.evidence: The ecumenical councils; Vincent of Lérins's 'everywhere, always, by all'; the Bible read and sung in worship.

positions.name: Scripture interprets Scripture
positions.who: Lutheran and Reformed churches (Westminster Confession I.9)
positions.view: Scripture is clear enough on what is necessary for salvation, and its unclear passages are explained by its clear ones; every church authority can err and must be tested by it.
positions.evidence: The Beroeans testing Paul (Acts 17:11); councils that contradicted each other; the Reformers' experience of the medieval Church.

debate.agree: All agree that the Bible is God's word, that the creeds state its core, and that no one should read it alone or in pride.

Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate, studied and translated the Scriptures in Bethlehem with the help of two Roman women, Paula and her daughter Eustochium, who learned Hebrew to read with him. It is here because it shows Scripture read in company.

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there': an old chant for Maundy Thursday, set by Maurice Duruflé in 1960. Augustine's rule of reading, sung.

think.why: How reason and revelation, the classics and the Bible, have been read together in the Christian tradition.

learn.why: The double commandment on which, Jesus says, the whole law and the prophets hang: Augustine's test for every reading.

check.q: According to Augustine, what should we conclude about a reading that is accurate in its details but leads to contempt for others?
options: That the passage is figurative
That it is correct, because it is accurate
That the reader 'does not yet understand' Scripture as he ought, because its purpose is love
That the reader has found a hidden spiritual sense
check.why: Scripture's end is love of God and neighbour; a reading that does not build it up has missed the point.

check.q: Augustine compares a reader who builds up love while missing the author's meaning to a traveller who leaves the road and reaches the destination across the fields. What does he say should happen to him?
options: He should read only the Psalms
Nothing, since he has arrived
He should be corrected, lest he get into the habit of leaving the road and get lost
He should be praised, since reaching love is all that matters
check.why: The author's meaning still matters, which is one reason reading needs a community.

check.q: What is the best description of sola scriptura as the Reformers held it?
options: Each person reads the Bible alone and decides for themselves
Tradition has equal authority with Scripture
Scripture is the supreme authority, by which tradition is tested, read in the church with creeds and confessions
Only the original languages count
check.why: Sola scriptura, not nuda scriptura.

check.q: What do Jews mean by the 'oral Torah'?
options: A lost book of Moses
The Psalms
Reading the Torah aloud in synagogue
The teaching believed given with the written Torah at Sinai and handed down, later written in the Mishnah and Talmud
check.why: Rabbinic Judaism reads the written Torah with the oral, as Avot 1:1's chain describes.

check.q: Irenaeus compared heretics' use of Scripture to rearranging a mosaic of a king into a dog or a fox. What was his point?
options: That only bishops may arrange the pieces
That Scripture is a work of art
That the same pieces can be made into a false picture, and the rule of faith shows the true one
That Scripture should be read only as a whole book, never in parts

sessions.reflect: Who do you read the Bible with, and whose readings do you never hear?
takeaways: No one reads alone: Jews read with the oral Torah and the rabbis, Catholics with Tradition and the Magisterium, the Orthodox within the Church's life, Protestants by Scripture alone but with creeds and confessions.
The early Church's 'rule of faith', later the creeds, gave the pattern for reading; the churches still share it.
Augustine's rule of love makes reading a moral act: a reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not yet understood.

sessions.title: The case against: a book that can be made to say anything
sessions.line: The Bible quoted to defend the whip, and what that shows.
sessions.plain: The strongest objection to everything in this journey is simple: the Bible can be made to say anything, and it has been used to defend terrible things. In America it was quoted to defend slavery, by men who whipped the people they owned. This session gives that objection its full weight, through the testimony of Frederick Douglass, before asking what can be said in reply.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 to 4 gave three rungs: the plain sense, the one story and reading with others. Now we test them against the hardest case: a whole Christian society that read the Bible with all three and used it to defend slavery.
answers: Hasn't the Bible been used to justify terrible things?
Can't you make the Bible say anything you like?
What about the passages I find shocking?
If the Bible was used to defend slavery, why trust it at all?
sessions.finding: The Bible has been used to defend slavery and conquest, and readers do find what they bring; but the tradition's own rules (read by love, read the whole, read the plain sense) were what exposed those readings, and the enslaved read it best.

paras: The objection has three parts. First, the Bible is so large and so varied that it can be made to support almost anything: you can find a verse for war and a verse for peace. Second, readers find what they bring. Their interests, their class and their culture shape what they see. Third, the record: the Bible has been quoted to defend slavery, the conquest of other peoples, contempt for Jews, apartheid and the subjection of women.

None of this is new. In the Gospels the devil quotes Psalm 91 to Jesus (Matthew 4:6). Shakespeare wrote, in The Merchant of Venice (about 1596), 'The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.' And you met Spinoza in What is the Bible?: in 1670 he accused the theologians of his day of reading their own ideas into Scripture and then claiming God's authority for them.
background.key: The objection: the Bible can be made to say anything, readers find what they bring, and the record shows it used to defend great evils.

paras: The hardest case is American slavery, because it was defended by people who read the Bible constantly and sincerely, and who used the methods of this journey. Pro-slavery preachers pointed out that Abraham owned slaves, that the law of Moses allowed Israelites to buy slaves from the nations around them (Leviticus 25:44–46), that Jesus never condemned slavery, and that Paul told slaves to obey their masters (Ephesians 6:5) and sent the runaway Onesimus back to his master Philemon. Some added the so-called 'curse of Ham' (Genesis 9:25), claiming that Africans were under it.

Abolitionists answered from the Bible too: all human beings are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27); God 'made of one blood all nations' (Acts 17:26, in the King James Version); kidnapping a person to sell him was a capital crime (Exodus 21:16); the Golden Rule; and the whole story of God freeing slaves from Egypt. In 1844–45 the Methodists and Baptists split, north and south, over slavery. In the end the country did not settle the question by the Bible. It settled it by war.
