background.key: American slavery was defended from the Bible by sincere readers, and attacked from it by abolitionists; the question was settled by war.

paras: The main reading is from Frederick Douglass's second autobiography, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855). It has three parts: the old man who taught him to read the Bible's 'spirit'; the 'pious' slaveholder who broke up his Sunday school and quoted Scripture while whipping a disabled woman; and a passage from his great speech of 5 July 1852, which he printed at the end of the book. Douglass is the best witness for both sides of the case: he saw the Bible used as a weapon, and he never stopped reading it.
The comparison is Jesus's parable of the sower: the same seed falling on different ground. It asks whether the problem lies in the seed or in the soil.
background.key: Douglass saw the Bible used as a weapon and read it all his life; the parable of the sower asks whether the fault is in the seed or the soil.

before: Notice how many different readers of the Bible appear in these passages, and how differently they read it.
What does Douglass mean by 'the letter' and 'the spirit'?
In the comparison, what makes the difference between the seed that bears fruit and the seed that does not?
sessions.readWhy: Frederick Douglass's testimony: the same Bible read by an old man of prayer, quoted by a slaveholder with a whip, and invoked against slavery in the name of God.

paras: While thus religiously seeking knowledge, I became acquainted with a good old colored man, named Lawson. A more devout man than he, I never saw. He drove a dray for Mr. James Ramsey, the owner of a rope-walk on Fell's Point, Baltimore. This man not only prayed three time a day, but he prayed as he walked through the streets, at his work--on his dray everywhere. His life was a life of prayer, and his words (when he spoke to his friends,) were about a better world. Uncle Lawson lived near Master Hugh's house; and, becoming deeply attached to the old man, I went often with him to prayer-meeting, and spent much of my leisure time with him on Sunday. The old man could read a little, and I was a great help to him, in making out the hard words, for I was a better reader than he. I could teach him "the letter," but he could teach me "the spirit;" and high, refreshing times we had together, in singing, praying and glorifying God.

Our first Sabbath passed delightfully, and I spent the week after very joyously. I could not go to Baltimore, but I could make a little Baltimore here. At our second meeting, I learned that there was some objection to the existence of the Sabbath school; and, sure enough, we had scarcely got at work--good work, simply teaching a few colored children how to read the gospel of the Son of God--when in rushed a mob, headed by Mr. Wright Fairbanks and Mr. Garrison West--two class-leaders --and Master Thomas; who, armed with sticks and other missiles, drove us off, and commanded us never to meet for such a purpose again. One of this pious crew told me, that as for my part, I wanted to be another Nat Turner; and if I did not look out, I should get as many balls into me, as Nat did into him. Thus ended the infant Sabbath school, in the town of St. Michael's. The reader will not be surprised when I say, that the breaking up of my Sabbath school, by these class-leaders, and professedly holy men, did not serve to strengthen my religious convictions. The cloud over my St. Michael's home grew heavier and blacker than ever.

It was not merely the agency of Master Thomas, in breaking up and destroying my Sabbath school, that shook my confidence in the power of southern religion to make men wiser or better; but I saw in him all the cruelty and meanness, after his conversion, which he had exhibited before he made a profession of religion. His cruelty and meanness were especially displayed in his treatment of my unfortunate cousin, Henny, whose lameness made her a burden to him. I have no extraordinary personal hard usage toward myself to complain of, against him, but I have seen him tie up the lame and maimed woman, and whip her in a manner most brutal, and shocking; and then, with blood-chilling blasphemy, he would quote the passage of scripture, "That servant which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes."

Standing with God and the crushed and bleeding slave on this occasion, I will, in the name of humanity which is outraged, in the name of liberty which is fettered, in the name of the constitution and the bible, which are disregarded and trampled upon, dare to call in question and to denounce, with all the emphasis I can command, everything that serves to perpetuate slavery--the great sin and shame of America! "I will not equivocate; I will not excuse;" I will use the severest language I can command; and yet not one word shall escape me that any man, whose judgment is not blinded by prejudice, or who is not at heart a slaveholder, shall not confess to be right and just.

What, then, remains to be argued? Is it that slavery is not divine; that God did not establish it; that our doctors of divinity are mistaken? There is blasphemy in the thought. That which is inhuman cannot be divine. Who can reason on such a proposition! They that can, may! I cannot. The time for such argument is past.

parts.author: Frederick Douglass
parts.who: Frederick Douglass (about 1818–1895) was born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland. He taught himself to read, became a Christian as a teenager in Baltimore, escaped to the North in 1838, and became the most famous abolitionist speaker in America. You read the Appendix to his first book, the Narrative of 1845, in How we got here.
parts.when: Rochester, New York; the speech given on 5 July 1852, the book published in 1855
parts.ref: Douglass, My Bondage and My Freedom, chapter XII
parts.title: The letter and the spirit
parts.context: About 1831, in Baltimore. Douglass, aged about thirteen, is enslaved in the household of Hugh Auld, a shipbuilder. He has secretly learned to read, and has become a Christian at a Methodist meeting. He has been picking pages of the Bible out of the street gutters and washing them to read.
parts.plain: Douglass says: while I was searching for knowledge, I met an old Black man called Lawson, a carter, the most devout man I ever knew, who prayed all day as he worked. I went with him to prayer meetings and spent Sundays with him. He could only read a little, and I helped him with the hard words. I could teach him the letter, but he could teach me the spirit.

commentary.on: A more devout man than he, I never saw.
commentary.text: Douglass's first teacher in faith was not a minister but an old working man, himself almost certainly enslaved or recently freed. The Bible was not only the slaveholders' book.

commentary.on: This man not only prayed three time a day, but he prayed as he walked through the streets
commentary.text: Lawson's life is the Bible's picture of reading from session 1: the words carried through the day, at work, 'when you walk by the way'.

commentary.on: I could teach him "the letter," but he could teach me "the spirit;"
commentary.text: Douglass borrows Paul's words: 'the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life' (2 Corinthians 3:6). The boy could read better; the old man understood better. It is the rung of the plain sense and the rung of prayer, in two people, needing each other.

parts.author: Frederick Douglass

parts.ref: Douglass, My Bondage and My Freedom, chapter XIV
parts.title: Many stripes
parts.context: About 1833. Douglass has been sent to St Michael's, on Maryland's Eastern Shore, to the household of Thomas Auld, who has recently been converted at a Methodist camp meeting. Douglass and a few others have started a Sunday school to teach other enslaved people to read the Bible. Class-leaders were lay leaders of Methodist groups.
parts.plain: Douglass says: at our second Sunday school meeting, a mob led by two Methodist class-leaders and my master, armed with sticks, broke it up and told us never to meet again; one said I wanted to be another Nat Turner (the leader of a slave revolt in 1831). My master was as cruel after his conversion as before. I saw him tie up and whip my disabled cousin Henny, and quote Scripture as he did it: 'That servant which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.'

commentary.on: simply teaching a few colored children how to read the gospel of the Son of God
commentary.text: Notice what the 'professedly holy men' broke up: a class in Bible reading. In many Southern states it was a crime to teach enslaved people to read. A Bible that slaves could read for themselves was dangerous.

commentary.on: I wanted to be another Nat Turner
commentary.text: Nat Turner, an enslaved preacher in Virginia, led a revolt in 1831 in which about sixty white people were killed; he said he was guided by visions and by Scripture. After it, Southern states tightened their laws against Black literacy and Black preaching.

commentary.on: did not serve to strengthen my religious convictions
commentary.text: Douglass is honest. Christian hypocrisy damaged his faith. The objection of this session is not an outsider's theory; it was his experience.

commentary.on: with blood-chilling blasphemy, he would quote the passage of scripture
commentary.text: The words are Luke 12:47 in the King James Version, from a parable of Jesus about servants waiting for their master's return. The parable is about readiness for the coming of God; it is a warning to the disciples, not an instruction to masters. Thomas Auld took a sentence from a story and turned it into a licence to torture.

commentary.on: shall be beaten with many stripes.
commentary.text: This is exactly the danger the objection describes: a verse, read by its letter, out of its story, by a man with power, against a woman with none. Douglass calls it what Augustine's rule would call it: a reading that does not build up love, and so does not understand.

You read the Appendix to his first book, the Narrative of 1845, in How we got here.
parts.when: Rochester, New York; the speech given on 5 July 1852, the book published in 1855
parts.ref: Douglass, 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?' (5 July 1852), as printed in My Bondage and My Freedom (1855)
parts.title: That which is inhuman cannot be divine
parts.context: Rochester, New York, 5 July 1852. The town's anti-slavery women have invited Douglass to give an Independence Day address. Two years earlier, Congress had passed the Fugitive Slave Act, which required Northerners to help return escaped slaves. The extract printed in the book is shortened.
parts.plain: Douglass says: standing with God and with the slave, in the name of humanity, liberty, the Constitution and the Bible, I will denounce everything that keeps slavery alive. Must I argue that slavery is not of God, and that the clergy who say so are wrong? That would be blasphemy. What is inhuman cannot be divine. The time for that kind of argument is past.

commentary.on: in the name of the constitution and the bible, which are disregarded and trampled upon
commentary.text: Douglass does not throw the Bible away. He claims it. The slaveholders, he says, are the ones trampling on it.

commentary.on: "I will not equivocate; I will not excuse;"
commentary.text: He quotes William Lloyd Garrison, the abolitionist editor, from the first issue of his paper The Liberator (1831).

commentary.on: that our doctors of divinity are mistaken?
commentary.text: 'Doctors of divinity' are learned clergy, many of whom had written defences of slavery from Scripture.

commentary.on: That which is inhuman cannot be divine.
commentary.text: Six words that sum up the reply. Douglass refuses to debate verses with men who use them to justify cruelty. His test is a moral one, very close to Augustine's: a reading that destroys human beings cannot be God's meaning, however many verses it quotes.

paras: On that day Jesus went out of the house, and sat by the seaside.
Great multitudes gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat, and sat, and all the multitude stood on the beach.
He spoke to them many things in parables, saying, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow.
As he sowed, some seeds fell by the roadside, and the birds came and devoured them.
Others fell on rocky ground, where they didn’t have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of earth.
When the sun had risen, they were scorched. Because they had no root, they withered away.
Others fell among thorns. The thorns grew up and choked them.
Others fell on good soil, and yielded fruit: some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.
He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
The disciples came, and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?”
He answered them, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them.
For whoever has, to him will be given, and he will have abundance, but whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he has.
Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they don’t see, and hearing, they don’t hear, neither do they understand.
In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says,

‘By hearing you will hear,
and will in no way understand;
Seeing you will see,
and will in no way perceive:
“But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear.
For most certainly I tell you that many prophets and righteous men desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.
“Hear, then, the parable of the farmer.
When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside.
What was sown on the rocky places, this is he who hears the word, and immediately with joy receives it;
yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he stumbles.
What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful.
What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.”

parts.title: A farmer went out to sow
parts.context: By the Sea of Galilee, about AD 30. Jesus teaches from a boat to a crowd on the shore. In Galilee seed was scattered by hand, often before ploughing, so it fell everywhere: on footpaths, on thin soil over limestone, among thorns.

commentary.on: As he sowed, some seeds fell by the roadside, and the birds came and devoured them.
commentary.text: The seed is the same everywhere. What differs is the ground.

commentary.on: Others fell on good soil, and yielded fruit: some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.
commentary.text: A hundredfold would be an astonishing harvest. The story ends in abundance.

commentary.on: He who has ears to hear, let him hear.
commentary.text: The parable is itself a test of how you listen.

parts.title: Seeing they don't see
parts.context: The disciples ask why Jesus teaches in parables. He quotes Isaiah 6:9–10.

commentary.on: because seeing they don't see, and hearing, they don't hear, neither do they understand.
commentary.text: It is possible to read every word and miss everything. Jesus says the problem is the heart, which 'has grown callous'.

commentary.on: for this people's heart has grown callous
commentary.text: Hearing is a moral act, as Augustine said. A hardened heart can hear the Bible and use it against others.

parts.title: The four soils explained
parts.context: Jesus explains the parable to his disciples.

commentary.on: the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word
commentary.text: Among the things that choke the word is 'the deceitfulness of riches'. The slaveholders' wealth depended on reading the Bible one way. Jesus names the danger.

commentary.on: What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit
commentary.text: The test of a reading is its fruit. Jesus says the same elsewhere: 'By their fruits you will know them' (Matthew 7:20). A reading that bears the fruit of cruelty has fallen on bad ground.

compare.why: Jesus told a story about a farmer whose seed falls on four kinds of ground. It is a story about hearing the word of God, and about why the same word bears fruit in some and not in others.
compare.title: The parable of the sower

paras: Put the objection as its best advocates would. The Bible is a collection of very different writings, from very different times, and it does not speak with one voice. It contains texts that regulate slavery without forbidding it, that command the destruction of whole peoples (which you faced in Kings and prophets), and that place wives under their husbands. Readers have always chosen which texts to stress, and they have usually chosen the ones that suited them.

Modern critics have made the point a theory. The literary critic Stanley Fish argued in Is There a Text in This Class? (1980) that meaning is not simply found in a text but made by 'interpretive communities' that share assumptions. If so, the 'plain sense' is only the sense my community finds plain. The scholar Hector Avalos argued that the Bible's own texts support slavery, and that abolitionists succeeded in spite of them, by reading against their plain sense.

The objection, then, is not that some readers made mistakes. It is that the rules of this journey cannot stop readers making the Bible say what they want, because the rules are themselves applied by interested readers.
sections.key: The objection: the Bible speaks with many voices, readers choose what suits them, and the rules for reading are applied by interested readers.

paras: The historian Mark Noll, in The Civil War as a Theological Crisis (2006), argues that the pro-slavery side often had the better of the argument from individual texts. Read verse by verse, with the 'common-sense' literal method most American Protestants used, the Bible does mention slavery without condemning it. Abolitionists often had to appeal to the Bible's spirit, its larger story and its moral principles. Many Americans found the verses more convincing than the spirit. Noll's conclusion is sobering: a nation that believed the Bible was plain to every reader found it could not agree on what the Bible said, and had no other way to settle the question.

Notice what the pro-slavery readers actually did. They took verses out of their stories (as Thomas Auld did with Luke 12:47). They ignored the plain sense where it went against them: Genesis 9:25 curses Canaan, not Ham, and says nothing about Africa. They passed over texts that judged them: the law of Moses forbade returning a runaway slave (Deuteronomy 23:15–16) and made man-stealing a capital crime (Exodus 21:16). And Paul sent Onesimus back 'no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother' (Philemon 16).
sections.key: Pro-slavery readers had strong individual verses but tore them from their stories, ignored their plain sense where it hurt, and passed over texts that judged them.

paras: Now apply the rungs of this journey. The plain sense: read in context, the curse of Ham is not about Africans, Luke 12:47 is a parable about readiness, and Philemon calls a slave a brother. The whole story: the Bible begins with every human being in God's image and centres on a God who frees slaves from Egypt; read as one story, its regulation of slavery looks like a concession to a hard world, as Jesus said of divorce (Matthew 19:8), not its ideal. Reading with others: the readings of the enslaved themselves, Douglass, Lawson and the makers of the spirituals, who heard Exodus as their story, were the ones the slaveholders refused to hear. And Augustine's rule: a reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not understood.

The early Church already had resources. Gregory of Nyssa, preaching on Ecclesiastes in about 379, attacked slave-owning itself: how much, he asked, did you pay for the image of God? It is one of the first outright condemnations of slavery in any literature. The Quakers of Germantown argued in 1688 from the Golden Rule. Wilberforce's campaign was fuelled by evangelical faith.
sections.key: The plain sense, the whole story, the voices of the enslaved and the rule of love all expose the pro-slavery readings; Gregory of Nyssa saw it in the fourth century.

paras: The reply does not make the objection go away. Three things should be admitted plainly.

First, the Bible does regulate slavery and never explicitly abolishes it. Slavery in ancient Israel and the Roman world differed from the race-based chattel slavery of the Americas, but it was still slavery. Second, Christians held slaves, and defended doing so from Scripture, for most of their history; the rules of good reading were known for centuries before they were applied. Third, readers do bring their interests to the text. Augustine himself warned that people judge by the customs of their own time and place, and the slaveholders proved him right.

What follows is not that the Bible can mean anything, but that reading it well is hard and moral work. It requires reading the whole, reading with those who suffer, and being willing to be judged by the text rather than using it to judge others. Douglass's distinction, in the appendix to his Narrative which you read in How we got here, between 'the Christianity of this land' and 'the Christianity of Christ', is a reading rule: the test of a reading is whether it looks like Christ.
sections.key: The Bible regulates slavery without abolishing it, Christians long defended it, and readers bring their interests; so reading well is hard, moral work.

paras: Slavery is not the only case, and the same pattern recurs. Matthew 27:25 ('May his blood be on us, and on our children') was used for centuries against Jews, though the Second Vatican Council in 1965 rejected the charge that Jews then or now are collectively guilty of Christ's death. Spanish conquerors read the conquest of Canaan as permission for their own conquests. The Dutch Reformed Church in South Africa defended apartheid from the Bible; in 1982 the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared that defence a heresy, and the church itself later repudiated it.

In each case the misreading was eventually challenged by other readers using the same Bible: often its victims, often appealing to its whole story and to Christ. The Bible has been the weapon and also the shield. That does not prove it is true. It does suggest that the problem the objection names is more in the soil than in the seed.
sections.key: The pattern recurs, with antisemitism, conquest and apartheid; each misreading was challenged from the same Bible, often by its victims.

paras: One practical rule follows from this session, and it is the oldest rule of the third rung made sharper: read with those who suffer. The slaveholders could not hear the Bible as Lawson and Douglass heard it, because they never asked how it sounded to the people they owned. Enslaved Christians heard in Exodus a God who takes sides with slaves, and in the cross a God who suffers with them; the spirituals are their commentary.

Augustine's warning about custom cuts here. Every age is blind to its own sins, and assumes its customs are God's will. The surest way to see a passage's demand, rather than our own preferences, is to read it beside people whose experience is unlike ours: the poor, the persecuted, the stranger. The prophets you read in this hall said God judges a society by how it treats the widow, the orphan and the stranger. A reading that does not look right from where they stand should be suspected.
sections.key: Read with those who suffer: the readings of the oppressed expose the blind spots of the powerful, as the prophets' test of the widow and stranger requires.

debate.question: When the Bible is used to oppress, is the problem the book or its readers?

positions.name: The book
positions.who: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, The Woman's Bible (1895–98); Hector Avalos
positions.view: Some biblical texts really do endorse what we now see as oppression; readers who used them were reading them plainly, and those who resisted had to read against the text.
positions.evidence: Leviticus 25:44–46; Ephesians 6:5; the strength of the pro-slavery argument from individual verses, as Noll concedes.

positions.name: The readers
positions.who: Frederick Douglass; Augustine's rule of love; most Christian interpreters
positions.view: The misuse came from reading verses out of their stories and against the whole, in the service of power; read plainly, as one story and by love, the Bible condemned the oppressors.
positions.evidence: Douglass's distinction between 'the Christianity of this land' and 'the Christianity of Christ'; Philemon 16; Genesis 1:27; the readings of the enslaved.

positions.name: The community
positions.who: Reader-response critics such as Stanley Fish
positions.view: Meaning is made by interpretive communities, so the question is not book against reader but which community's reading prevails, and why.
positions.evidence: The same text read in opposite ways by masters and slaves in the same churches.

debate.agree: All agree that the Bible was used to defend slavery, and that the readings of the oppressed must be heard.

look.why: No painting for this session. The preaching and congregation scenes in the National Gallery of Art's open collection are either used by other journeys or have no gallery description, and we do not use a stand-in.

music.why: A spiritual made by enslaved African Americans in the nineteenth century, who heard the same Bible their enslavers misused and found themselves at the foot of the cross. The good soil.

think.why: How Christian conscience, reading the same Bible, fuelled the long fight against slavery.

learn.why: The prophet's summary of what God asks: justice, mercy and humility. A test for any reading that claims God's authority.

check.q: Which statement is the strongest form of the objection in this session?
options: The Bible contains historical errors
The Bible speaks with many voices, readers choose what suits them, and the rules for reading are themselves applied by interested readers
The Bible was written by people with interests of their own
Some readers have made mistakes
check.why: The full objection is that the rules cannot stop readers from making the text say what they want.

check.q: Thomas Auld quoted Luke 12:47 while whipping Henny. What does reading that verse by its plain sense in context show?
options: That it comes from a parable about readiness for God's coming, addressed to disciples, not an instruction to slaveholders
That Luke approved of slavery
That the verse commands masters to whip servants
That it is a mistranslation
check.why: Taken out of its story it becomes a licence; in its story it is a warning to the reader.

check.q: What does Douglass mean by 'I could teach him the letter, but he could teach me the spirit'?
options: That the letter of the Bible is false
That the boy could read the words better, but the old man understood their meaning and lived it
That Lawson could not read at all
That Lawson rejected the Bible
check.why: He echoes 2 Corinthians 3:6: the plain sense and the life of prayer, in two readers who need each other.

check.q: According to Mark Noll, why did the abolitionists find the argument from the Bible hard to win?
options: Because the Bible clearly condemns slavery and no one listened
Because the churches had banned Bible reading
Because they did not read the Bible
Because, read verse by verse with the common literal method, the Bible mentions slavery without condemning it, so they had to appeal to its spirit and larger story
check.why: The pro-slavery case was strong on individual verses; the abolitionist case rested on the whole.

check.q: Which reply to the objection does the parable of the sower best support?
options: The seed is bad
The same word bears fruit or fails according to the ground it falls on, and the test of hearing is its fruit
That the seed itself is sometimes bad
That God deliberately hides the meaning from most hearers
check.why: The problem is in the soil; and 'the deceitfulness of riches' is named as one of the thorns.

check.q: Which of these is something the honest reply should admit?
options: That the objection is entirely false
That the Bible regulates slavery without explicitly abolishing it, and that Christians long defended slavery from it
That the Bible explicitly abolishes slavery
That no Christian ever opposed slavery before 1800
check.why: The reply is stronger for admitting what is true in the objection.

tutorial.question: 'The Bible can be made to say anything.' Assess this claim in the light of the American debate over slavery.
tutorial.approach: State the objection at full strength, including the pro-slavery argument from verses and the modern theory of interpretive communities. Then use Douglass, the parable of the sower and the rules of the earlier sessions to test it. Say clearly what the objection gets right and whether it is finally true.
strong: States the pro-slavery argument fairly, with its texts.
Uses Douglass's testimony accurately, including the Luke 12:47 incident and 'the letter and the spirit'.
Applies the plain sense, the whole story, reading with others and the rule of love to the pro-slavery readings.
Discusses Noll's argument and a modern critic such as Fish or Avalos fairly.
Admits what the objection gets right.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion about whether the Bible can be made to say anything.

reading.author: Frederick Douglass
reading.title: My Bondage and My Freedom
reading.why: Douglass's fullest account of his life, faith and escape.

reading.author: Mark A. Noll
reading.title: The Civil War as a Theological Crisis
reading.why: How the Bible failed to settle the slavery debate in America.

reading.author: Albert J. Raboteau
reading.title: Slave Religion: The 'Invisible Institution' in the Antebellum South
reading.why: How enslaved Christians read the Bible for themselves.

reading.author: Stanley Fish
reading.title: Is There a Text in This Class?
reading.why: The classic case for interpretive communities.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: before you read each day, pray Psalm 119:18 or simply ask: 'Show me where this judges me, not someone else.' Then read, and write down one way the passage challenges you.
sessions.reflect: Which passages do you use to judge others, and which do you avoid because they judge you?
takeaways: The Bible has been used to defend slavery, conquest and contempt, and readers do bring their interests to it: the objection is real.

The pro-slavery readings tore verses from their stories, ignored their plain sense and passed over texts that judged them; the tradition's own rules, and the enslaved readers themselves, exposed them.
Reading well is moral work: the test of a reading is its fruit, as the parable of the sower says, and whether it looks like Christ.

sessions.title: Let it read you
sessions.line: Rung four: lectio divina, the monks' way of reading as prayer.
sessions.plain: Monks in the Middle Ages read the Bible slowly, in four steps: read a passage, chew it over, turn it into prayer, and rest in God. They called it lectio divina, 'divine reading'. This session reads two short monastic texts on reading, explains the four steps, and asks whether they are a method anyone can learn or a gift.
sessions.why: Session 5 ended with a test: whether a reading looks like Christ. The fourth rung asks how a reader becomes the kind of person who reads like that: by letting the text read them.
answers: What is lectio divina?
How do I pray with the Bible?
What if I don't feel anything when I read?
Do Protestants and Jews read like this too?
sessions.finding: The monks read in four steps (reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation) so that the text becomes a conversation with God, and the reader, not only the text, is changed.

paras: Everything so far has been about understanding the text: its plain sense, its place in the one story, its reading in a community. The fourth rung turns the direction round. Instead of the reader examining the text, the reader lets the text examine him. The Letter to the Hebrews says God's word is 'living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword... able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart' (Hebrews 4:12).

The phrase 'divine reading' goes back to Origen, who urged a student, in a letter of about 238, to give himself to the 'divine reading' of Scripture with attention and prayer. In the Rule of Benedict it is lectio divina, a set part of every monk's day.
background.key: The fourth rung turns reading round: the reader lets the text examine him; 'divine reading' goes back to Origen and Benedict.

paras: The classic account of lectio divina is a short letter by Guigo II, ninth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, the mother house of the Carthusian monks in the French Alps (he was prior from about 1174 to 1180, and died about 1188). The Carthusians, founded by Bruno of Cologne in 1084, live largely alone in cells, in silence, and read a great deal.

Guigo wrote to a friend, Brother Gervase, describing a ladder of four rungs, by which monks climb from earth to heaven: reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation. The work is known as The Ladder of Monks (Scala claustralium). No English translation old enough to be out of copyright is available, so we describe it in our own words in the lecture, with its famous images. The readings here are from two other monastic writers.

background.key: Guigo II, a Carthusian prior, described lectio divina as a ladder of four rungs; his work is described here in our own words.

paras: The main reading has two parts. First, the chapter on reading Scripture from The Imitation of Christ, the most widely read devotional book of the late Middle Ages: how to read humbly, for truth rather than cleverness. Second, a short passage from the Rule of Benedict (about 530), which made sacred reading a fixed part of the day. The Rule is given in Ernest Henderson's translation of 1910, which shortens the chapter; the cut is his.
The comparison is the Gospel's picture of the reader as listener: Mary of Bethany, sitting at Jesus's feet, while her sister Martha rushes about.
background.key: Thomas à Kempis on reading humbly, Benedict on fixed hours of reading, and Mary of Bethany as the listener.

before: What does Thomas à Kempis say we should look for in Scripture, and what gets in the way?

sessions.readWhy: Two monastic texts on reading: Thomas à Kempis on reading humbly for truth, and the Rule of Benedict on giving reading fixed hours every day.

paras: It is Truth which we must look for in Holy Writ, not cunning of words. All Scripture ought to be read in the spirit in which it was written. We must rather seek for what is profitable in Scripture, than for what ministereth to subtlety in discourse. Therefore we ought to read books which are devotional and simple, as well as those which are deep and difficult. And let not the weight of the writer be a stumbling-block to thee, whether he be of little or much learning, but let the love of the pure Truth draw thee to read. Ask not, who hath said this or that, but look to what he says.

2. Men pass away, but the truth of the Lord endureth for ever. Without respect of persons God speaketh to us in divers manners. Our own curiosity often hindereth us in the reading of holy writings, when we seek to understand and discuss, where we should pass simply on. If thou wouldst profit by thy reading, read humbly, simply, honestly, and not desiring to win a character for learning. Ask freely, and hear in silence the words of holy men; nor be displeased at the hard sayings of older men than thou, for they are not uttered without cause.

Idleness is the enemy of the soul. And therefore, at fixed times, the brothers ought to be occupied in manual labour; and again, at fixed times, in sacred reading. ... there shall certainly be appointed one or two elders, who shall go round the monastery at the hours in which the brothers are engaged in reading, and see to it that no troublesome brother chance to be found who is open to idleness and trifling, and is not intent on his reading; being not only of no use to himself, but also stirring up others.

parts.author: Thomas à Kempis
parts.who: Thomas à Kempis (about 1380–1471) was a canon of the small Augustinian community of Mount Saint Agnes near Zwolle, in the Netherlands, for seventy years. He belonged to the 'Modern Devotion', a movement of lay people and clergy who sought a simple, inward faith. The Imitation of Christ, usually attributed to him, became the most widely read Christian book after the Bible.
parts.when: Mount Saint Agnes, near Zwolle; written about 1418–1427
parts.ref: Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ I.5
parts.title: Of the reading of Holy Scriptures
parts.context: The Imitation of Christ is four short books of advice for the inner life. Book I gives 'counsels useful for the spiritual life'. Chapter 5 is on reading Scripture. Benham's translation (1874) keeps an older English ('thee', 'hath').
parts.plain: Thomas says: look for truth in Scripture, not fine words. Read it in the spirit in which it was written. Look for what helps you, not for clever points. Read simple books as well as deep ones, and don't worry who wrote them: look at what they say. People pass away, but God's truth lasts. Our curiosity often gets in the way, when we try to analyse and argue where we should simply read on. If you want to benefit, read humbly, simply and honestly, not to look learned. Ask questions freely, and listen in silence to the wise.

commentary.on: It is Truth which we must look for in Holy Writ, not cunning of words.
commentary.text: 'Cunning' here means cleverness or skill. Thomas is not against scholarship, but he knows readers who use the Bible to show off.

commentary.on: All Scripture ought to be read in the spirit in which it was written.
commentary.text: The most quoted sentence in the chapter. The Bible was written to bring people to God, so it should be read with that purpose: prayerfully, and with a will to change.

commentary.on: Ask not, who hath said this or that, but look to what he says.
commentary.text: Don't judge a word by the speaker's reputation. A plain truth from a humble writer is still the truth.

commentary.on: Our own curiosity often hindereth us in the reading of holy writings, when we seek to understand and discuss, where we should pass simply on.
commentary.text: This is the point where lectio differs from study. There is a time to analyse, and a time to let the words work. A reader who stops at every difficulty may never hear what the passage is saying to him.

commentary.on: read humbly, simply, honestly, and not desiring to win a character for learning
commentary.text: Three adverbs that sum up the monks' way. Humbly: ready to be corrected. Simply: without hidden motives. Honestly (Latin fideliter, 'faithfully'): meaning what you pray.

commentary.on: Ask freely, and hear in silence the words of holy men
commentary.text: Lectio is not solitary in the end: it learns from others, the third rung, and it listens.

parts.author: Benedict of Nursia
parts.translator: Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages (1910)
parts.ref: The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 48 (shortened by the translator)
parts.title: At fixed times, in sacred reading
parts.context: Benedict of Nursia (about 480–547) wrote his Rule for the monks of Monte Cassino, south of Rome, about 530. It became the rule of most Western monasteries. Chapter 48 sets out the day: hours for work in the fields and hours for reading. The '...' in the text is the translator's own cut: he omits the timetable.
parts.plain: Benedict says: idleness is the enemy of the soul. So at set times the brothers should do manual work, and at set times sacred reading. One or two senior monks should go round during the reading hours to make sure no one is idling or chatting instead of reading, which harms him and disturbs the others.

commentary.on: Idleness is the enemy of the soul.
commentary.text: The Rule's most famous line. Benedict is not against rest; he is against drift. A day without a shape tends to be wasted.

commentary.on: at fixed times, in sacred reading
commentary.text: In Latin, lectio divina. Benedict's monks spent roughly two to three hours a day in it, more on Sundays and in Lent, when each monk was given a book from the library to read through. Reading was not left to mood. It had its hours, like work and prayer.

commentary.on: and is not intent on his reading
commentary.text: Even monks got distracted. The Rule is realistic: attention needs protecting. A phone left in another room does what Benedict's elders did.

read.ref: Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ I.5

paras: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

parts.title: One thing is needed
parts.context: Jesus is travelling towards Jerusalem with his disciples. John's Gospel says that the sisters Martha and Mary lived at Bethany, just outside Jerusalem, with their brother Lazarus.

commentary.on: who also sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word
commentary.text: To sit at a teacher's feet was the posture of a disciple: Paul says he was brought up 'at the feet of Gamaliel' (Acts 22:3). Mary, a woman, takes the disciple's place, and Jesus defends her. She does nothing but listen.

commentary.on: But Martha was distracted with much serving
commentary.text: Martha is not doing anything wrong: she is serving a guest, as hospitality required. Her problem is distraction. Most readers today know the feeling: the list of things to do that crowds out the one thing.

commentary.on: you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed.
commentary.text: Jesus does not tell Martha off for working. He tells her she is anxious. Lectio divina is a practice against anxiety: one passage, one phrase, slowly.

commentary.on: Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.
commentary.text: What is received in listening is not lost. The monks read Martha and Mary as two ways of life, active and contemplative; most Christians have to live both, and the story says the listening must not be crowded out.

compare.why: The Gospel's picture of the reader as listener. Monks read this story for centuries as the picture of lectio divina: sitting at the Lord's feet and hearing his word.
compare.title: Mary of Bethany: the listener

paras: Guigo describes four steps, each leading to the next. He gives each a definition and an image. In our own words: reading is the careful study of Scripture with the mind's whole attention; meditation is the mind's search for the hidden truth in what it has read; prayer is the heart turning to God, asking for what it has seen to be good; contemplation is the mind lifted to God, tasting the joy of what it longed for.

His most famous image is food. Reading, he says, puts the food whole into the mouth; meditation chews it and breaks it up; prayer draws out its flavour; contemplation is the sweetness itself, which gladdens and refreshes. You will recognise the psalm from session 1: 'How sweet are your promises to my taste, more than honey to my mouth!'

rows: Read a short passage slowly, aloud if you can, until a word or phrase stands out
Putting the food into the mouth
Turn that phrase over: what does it mean, what does it ask, why has it caught you?
Speak to God about it: thanks, confession, a request
Rest quietly in God's presence, without words

sections.key: Reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation: putting food in the mouth, chewing it, tasting it, and enjoying its sweetness.

paras: Guigo shows the ladder at work on one verse: 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matthew 5:8). Reading puts the words in front of you: short, but full of meaning, like a grape put into the mouth. Meditation begins to press it. What is purity of heart? Why is it so precious that it is rewarded with the sight of God? It recalls other verses: 'Who may ascend to Yahweh's mountain? He who has clean hands and a pure heart' (Psalm 24:3–4). It asks how such a heart could be had. And the more the mind turns it over, the more it longs for what it sees.

That longing becomes prayer: the reader, knowing he cannot make his own heart pure, asks God for it. And sometimes, Guigo says, before the prayer is even finished, God comes to meet it, and the soul is refreshed: that is contemplation. He insists it is God's gift, not a technique. The first three rungs are ours to climb; the fourth is given.
sections.key: Guigo's example, Matthew 5:8, moves from reading to longing to prayer, and contemplation comes as a gift.

sections.h: From the desert to the cloister
paras: The roots of lectio go back to the first monks in the Egyptian desert in the third and fourth centuries. They memorised long stretches of Scripture, especially the Psalms, and murmured them as they worked, weaving baskets or ropes; the Greek word for this was meletē, practice or meditation, close to the Hebrew hagah of Joshua 1:8. Athanasius says of Antony that he remembered everything he heard read, 'and afterwards his memory served him for books'.

Benedict made lectio part of the timetable. Medieval monks read aloud, under their breath, which is why the Rule elsewhere asks those who rest after the midday meal not to disturb others with their reading. The twelfth century, Guigo's century, was a high point: Bernard of Clairvaux preached eighty-six sermons on the Song of Songs and only reached the start of chapter 3. The point was never to get through the text, but to get into it.
sections.key: Lectio grew from the desert monks' murmured memorising, through Benedict's timetable, to the twelfth century's slow, deep reading.

sections.h: Other ways of praying the Bible
paras: Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, taught in his Spiritual Exercises (approved 1548) a different method: imaginative contemplation. You picture a Gospel scene as if you were there (he called it 'composition of place'): the road, the crowd, the sounds, and you watch and listen, and speak to Christ at the end.

Protestants developed their own forms. In 1535 Luther wrote A Simple Way to Pray for his barber, Peter Beskendorf, who had asked him how to pray. He suggests taking a commandment or a line of the Lord's Prayer and making of it a garland of four strands: what it teaches, what it gives thanks for, what it calls you to confess, and what it asks you to pray for. Puritan writers taught daily meditation on Scripture; later evangelicals spoke of a 'quiet time' each morning with a Bible and a notebook.

Jews speak of the study of Torah itself as a form of worship. The Mishnah lists the good deeds whose reward has no limit and ends: 'the study of Torah is equal to them all' (Peah 1:1). Torah is studied aloud, often chanted, and argued over in pairs.
sections.key: Ignatius's imaginative contemplation, Luther's four-stranded garland, the Puritan meditation and evangelical quiet time, and Jewish Torah study are other ways of praying Scripture.

paras: Everyone who practises lectio finds that most days nothing dramatic happens. Guigo knew this. Contemplation, he said, is a gift; God comes and goes; the soul must keep climbing the first rungs faithfully and not despair when the fourth is not given. He also warned against the opposite errors: reading without meditating is dry, meditating without reading leads astray, and prayer without meditation is lukewarm.

The reward of faithfulness is usually slow. A phrase read on an ordinary morning comes back months later, in a hospital waiting room or a hard conversation. That is what the Bible means by keeping the words 'on your heart'. Benedict's monks did not read to feel something; they read because it was the hour for reading, and over a lifetime they were changed.

Since the Second Vatican Council lectio divina has been warmly recommended to all Catholics, and Pope Benedict XVI described its steps in Verbum Domini (2010). Many Protestant churches and groups now teach it too. It belongs to no single tradition.
sections.key: Most days nothing dramatic happens: lectio asks for faithfulness, not feelings, and changes readers slowly.

paras: Lectio divina needs very little: a short passage, ten or fifteen minutes, and quiet. Choose the passage in advance, so you do not spend the time deciding. A Gospel story, a psalm or a few verses of a letter all work; long lists and laws are better read in the ordinary way.

Read it once, slowly, aloud if you can. Read it again, and notice which word or phrase catches you; do not choose the cleverest, choose the one that will not let go. Turn it over: repeat it, ask what it means, what it brings to mind, what it asks. Then speak to God about it, as plainly as you would to a friend. Then stop talking, and stay for a minute or two in silence. If your mind wanders, go back to the phrase.

Some people do lectio in a group: one person reads the passage three times, slowly, with a silence after each reading, and each person says only the word or phrase that struck them, then what it seems to ask, then a short prayer. No discussion, no argument: it is listening, together. It is one of the simplest ways for strangers to pray with Scripture.
sections.key: Choose a short passage in advance, read it twice, stop at the phrase that catches you, turn it over, pray, and rest; it can also be done in a group.

debate.question: Is lectio divina a method anyone can learn, or a gift?

positions.name: A method
positions.who: Guigo II for the first three rungs; modern teachers of lectio, such as the Trappist M. Basil Pennington
positions.view: Lectio is a practice with clear steps that anyone can learn and repeat, like any discipline; faithfulness to the method opens a person to God.
positions.evidence: Benedict's fixed hours; Guigo's clear definitions; the experience of many who have learned it in groups.

positions.name: A gift
positions.who: Guigo II on contemplation; Luther; many Reformed teachers
positions.view: Understanding Scripture and meeting God in it come from the Holy Spirit, not from technique; methods can become a way of trying to control God.
positions.evidence: Guigo's insistence that contemplation is given; Luther's stress on the Spirit and the preached word; Jesus's 'to you it is given to know the mysteries' (Matthew 13:11).

positions.name: Study is prayer
positions.who: The rabbinic tradition; many Christian scholars
positions.view: Careful study of the text, arguing over its words, is itself a way of loving God with the mind; there need be no sharp line between understanding and devotion.
positions.evidence: Mishnah Peah 1:1; Jewish chavruta study; Augustine's view that all knowledge serves love.

debate.agree: All agree that reading Scripture should change the reader, and that it needs both effort and openness.

look.why: Giovanni Bellini painted this in Venice in 1505. Jerome, who lived as a monk in Bethlehem, is shown alone at the mouth of a cave, reading. It is here because it shows lectio as the monks practised it: solitude, attention, and a book read slowly.
points: A bearded, balding man with deeply tanned skin, wearing only a strip of robin's-egg-blue cloth, sits on a rock at the mouth of a craggy cave.
He faces left in profile, his head bowed over an open book propped on the rock by his knee.
A lion lies beside him in the lower right corner, its mouth open.
Around him are other animals: a lizard by a rectangular pool, a squirrel on the cave's grassy top, a black bird in a bare tree, and two rabbits touching noses on a low wall.
In the distance, stone buildings, some in ruins, run down a hillside to the water, under a vivid azure sky.

music.why: Gregorio Allegri's setting of Psalm 51 (1630s), sung slowly, verse by verse, in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week: Scripture turned into prayer, which is what lectio teaches.

think.why: What the research and the great teachers say about whether daily practices like slow reading change who we are.

learn.why: A one-line prayer to say before you begin: the wonders are in the text; what you ask for is eyes to see them.

check.q: In Guigo's image, which rung 'chews' the food?
options: Contemplation
Prayer
Reading
Meditation
check.why: Reading puts it in the mouth, meditation chews it, prayer tastes it, contemplation is the sweetness.

check.q: Why does Guigo insist that contemplation is different from the other three rungs?
options: Because it is a technique for emptying the mind
Because it is God's gift, which comes to meet the reader's prayer, rather than something the reader does
Because it is only for monks
Because it requires no reading
check.why: The first three are ours to climb; the fourth is given.

check.q: Thomas à Kempis says our curiosity hinders us 'when we seek to understand and discuss, where we should pass simply on'. What follows for the way lectio differs from study?
options: That only the simple can read Scripture
That we should never ask questions
That there is a time to analyse and a time to let the words work, and lectio is the second
That study is wrong
check.why: He also says 'ask freely': the point is the purpose of the reading, not a ban on thinking.

check.q: Why did Benedict set fixed hours for reading?
options: Because he thought reading less important than work and wanted it limited
Because books were rare
Because 'idleness is the enemy of the soul', and attention left to mood tends to drift
Because books were shared and each monk had only a short turn
check.why: Reading had its hours, like work and prayer, and elders guarded them.

check.q: What is the main difference between Ignatius's imaginative contemplation and Guigo's lectio?

takeaways: Lectio divina climbs four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation; Guigo pictures them as eating.
It grew from the desert monks' murmured memorising and Benedict's fixed hours; Ignatius, Luther, the Puritans and Jewish study offer other ways of praying Scripture.
It asks for faithfulness, not feelings: the first three rungs are climbed, the fourth is given, and readers are changed slowly.

sessions.title: The verdict, and a practice for life
sessions.line: Read it plainly, as one story, with the Church and on your knees.
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict of this journey: read the Bible plainly, as one story, with others and in prayer, and it begins to read you. The last session reads the Bible's own image for this, a mirror, and the story of a young Egyptian who heard one verse read in church and did what it said. Then it gives a daily practice and a plan for a year.
sessions.why: Six sessions have built the ladder and tested it against the strongest objection. Now we put it together, and turn it into a habit.
answers: So how should I read the Bible?
What do I do tomorrow morning?
How do I keep going for a year?
What is the point, if I don't change?
sessions.finding: Read it plainly, as one story, with the Church and on your knees, and then do what it says: that is how a text begins to read you.

paras: The question of this journey was: how do you read a text so that it reads you? The answer has four rungs. Read it as it was written: the plain sense, in its own kind of writing, as the writer meant it. Read it as one story, in which the Old Testament points to Christ, without letting allegory float free of the literal sense. Read it with others: with a community, with the tradition, and with readers unlike yourself. And let it read you, in slow and prayerful reading.

The objection showed that none of these rungs works alone. The slaveholders had the letter without the whole story or the rule of love. The answer was not to throw the Bible away but to read it better, and above all to read it as Lawson did, to be changed by it rather than to control others with it. That is where the last rung ends: in doing.
background.key: Read plainly, as one story, with others and in prayer; the rungs work together, and they end in doing.

paras: The Letter of James is the most practical book in the New Testament. By tradition it was written by James, the brother of Jesus, leader of the church in Jerusalem until his execution in AD 62 (the Jewish historian Josephus records his death). Some scholars think a later writer used his name. It has been called a book of wisdom, like Proverbs, written for Christians.

Antony of Egypt (about 251–356) is counted the father of Christian monks. His life was written soon after his death by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and it spread across the Roman world; Augustine, in his Confessions, says that hearing it helped bring him to faith. Its most famous scene is the moment Antony heard a Gospel read in church.
background.key: James is the New Testament's most practical book; Antony is the reader who heard one verse and did it.

paras: The main reading is James 1:19–27, with its picture of a man who looks in a mirror and forgets what he saw. It is the Bible's own verdict on reading without doing.

The comparison is Athanasius's account of Antony hearing Matthew 19:21 read in church, 'as though the passage had been read on his account', and going out to do it. It shows what it looks like when a text reads someone.
background.key: James's mirror is the verdict; Antony is the example.

before: What is the difference, in James, between a hearer and a doer?
What does the mirror show, and why does the man forget?
In the comparison, what did Antony do when he heard the Gospel, and how quickly?
sessions.readWhy: The Bible's own verdict on reading: James's picture of the mirror, and what it means to be a doer of the word.

paras: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.
Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

parts.title: Receive the implanted word
parts.context: The letter is addressed 'to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion', probably Jewish Christians scattered outside the land of Israel, in the first century AD. Its first chapter is about trials, temptation and the word of God.

commentary.on: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger
commentary.text: The first rule of reading, as of conversation: listen first. Augustine's reader who 'feels more angry with Scripture than he is with himself' broke all three.

commentary.on: receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls
commentary.text: The word is 'implanted', like a seed: the parable of the sower again. It is received with humility, as Thomas à Kempis said.

parts.title: The mirror
parts.context: The centre of the passage.

commentary.on: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
commentary.text: James's verdict. To hear without doing is not neutral; it is self-deception. A person can read the Bible every day and use it to avoid changing.

commentary.on: he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was
commentary.text: Scripture is a mirror: you see yourself in it. The fourth rung of the ladder is exactly this, the text reading you. But a mirror is useless if you walk away and forget.

commentary.on: But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues
commentary.text: 'Looks into' is a strong word in Greek: to stoop and peer closely, the word used of the disciples looking into the empty tomb (John 20:5). 'Continues' means he keeps looking, day after day. 'The law of freedom' is a striking phrase: God's teaching sets people free, as the Exodus story you read in this hall showed.

commentary.on: this man will be blessed in what he does.
commentary.text: The blessing is in the doing. The Bible's first psalm began with the blessed man who meditates on God's law day and night; James finishes the thought: blessed in what he does.

parts.title: Pure religion
parts.context: James gives two tests of real religion.

commentary.on: If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn't bridle his tongue
commentary.text: The first test is speech. A reader who uses Scripture as a weapon in arguments has not yet been read by it.

commentary.on: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world
commentary.text: The second test is care for the most vulnerable. It is the prophets' test, which you met in Kings and prophets, and it is the test Douglass applied to the slaveholders' Christianity.

paras: 2. After the death of his father and mother he was left alone with one little sister: his age was about eighteen or twenty, and on him the care both of home and sister rested. Now it was not six months after the death of his parents, and going according to custom into the Lord's House, he communed with himself and reflected as he walked how the Apostles left all and followed the Saviour; and how they in the Acts sold their possessions and brought and laid them at the Apostles' feet for distribution to the needy, and what and how great a hope was laid up for them in heaven. Pondering over these things he entered the church, and it happened the Gospel was being read, and he heard the Lord saying to the rich man, 'If you would be perfect, go and sell that you have and give to the poor; and come follow Me and you shall have treasure in heaven.' Antony, as though God had put him in mind of the Saints, and the passage had been read on his account, went out immediately from the church, and gave the possessions of his forefathers to the villagers — they were three hundred acres, productive and very fair — that they should be no more a clog upon himself and his sister. And all the rest that was movable he sold, and having got together much money he gave it to the poor, reserving a little however for his sister's sake.

3. And again as he went into the church, hearing the Lord say in the Gospel, 'be not anxious for the morrow,' he could stay no longer, but went out and gave those things also to the poor. Having committed his sister to known and faithful virgins, and put her into a convent to be brought up, he henceforth devoted himself outside his house to discipline, taking heed to himself and training himself with patience. For there were not yet so many monasteries in Egypt, and no monk at all knew of the distant desert; but all who wished to give heed to themselves practised the discipline in solitude near their own village. Now there was then in the next village an old man who had lived the life of a hermit from his youth up. Antony, after he had seen this man, imitated him in piety. And at first he began to abide in places outside the village: then if he heard of a good man anywhere, like the prudent bee, he went forth and sought him, nor turned back to his own palace until he had seen him; and he returned, having got from the good man as it were supplies for his journey in the way of virtue. So dwelling there at first, he confirmed his purpose not to return to the abode of his fathers nor to the remembrance of his kinsfolk; but to keep all his desire and energy for perfecting his discipline. He worked, however, with his hands, having heard, 'he who is idle let him not eat,' and part he spent on bread and part he gave to the needy. And he was constant in prayer, knowing that a man ought to pray in secret unceasingly. For he had given such heed to what was read that none of the things that were written fell from him to the ground, but he remembered all, and afterwards his memory served him for books.

parts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
parts.translator: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
parts.title: As though the passage had been read on his account
parts.context: Egypt, about 270. Antony, born about 251 to a well-off Christian family in a village of Middle Egypt, has lost both parents. He has a younger sister to care for and inherited land. The scene is the village church, where the Gospel is read aloud, as in every service.
parts.plain: Athanasius says: Antony was about eighteen or twenty when his parents died, leaving him to look after his sister and the household. Six months later, walking to church, he was thinking about how the apostles left everything to follow Jesus, and how the first Christians sold their property for the poor. As he went in, the Gospel being read was Jesus's word to the rich young man: 'If you would be perfect, go and sell what you have and give to the poor, and come follow me.' Antony felt it had been read for him. He went straight out, gave his family's land to the villagers, sold everything else and gave the money to the poor, keeping a little for his sister.

commentary.on: he communed with himself and reflected as he walked how the Apostles left all and followed the Saviour
commentary.text: Antony was already meditating on Scripture as he walked, as Deuteronomy said to do: 'when you walk by the way'. The verse that changed him fell on prepared ground.

commentary.on: it happened the Gospel was being read, and he heard the Lord saying to the rich man
commentary.text: He heard it read aloud in church, in the regular reading. Not alone, not by searching: in the community's reading, the third rung.

commentary.on: as though God had put him in mind of the Saints, and the passage had been read on his account
commentary.text: This is what it means for a text to read you. Antony did not think the verse was only about a rich man in Galilee long ago. The plain sense addressed him.

commentary.on: went out immediately from the church, and gave the possessions of his forefathers to the villagers
commentary.text: And he did it. Immediately. James's 'doer of the word'. Antony's response is not the only faithful one; most Christians are not called to give away everything. But it is the clearest picture of reading that ends in doing.

parts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
parts.translator: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
parts.title: His memory served him for books
parts.context: Soon afterwards. Antony begins to live as an ascetic, a person of disciplined prayer and simplicity, near his village. There are as yet no monasteries in the desert.
parts.plain: Athanasius says: another time Antony heard in church 'do not be anxious about tomorrow', and gave away what he had kept. He put his sister in the care of a community of women, and began a life of discipline near his village, learning from an old hermit and from any good person he heard of. He worked with his hands, gave to the poor, and prayed constantly. He listened so carefully to Scripture that he forgot nothing, and his memory served him for books.

commentary.on: hearing the Lord say in the Gospel, 'be not anxious for the morrow,' he could stay no longer
commentary.text: A second verse, a second act. Reading that ends in doing is not one dramatic moment but a habit.

commentary.on: like the prudent bee, he went forth and sought him
commentary.text: Antony learned from others, gathering a little from each, as a bee gathers from many flowers. Even the father of hermits did not read alone.

commentary.on: He worked, however, with his hands
commentary.text: Work and reading, as in Benedict's Rule two centuries later.

commentary.on: afterwards his memory served him for books
commentary.text: Antony probably could not read, or not well; he heard Scripture read aloud. He carried it in memory, as Deuteronomy asked: 'on your heart'. This is why this journey asks you to learn words by heart.

compare.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
compare.translator: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
compare.why: The most famous example in Christian history of a person read by a text: a young man who heard one verse in church and did what it said, that same day.
compare.title: Antony hears the Gospel

paras: Put the four rungs side by side and you can see why each needs the others. The plain sense without the whole story can be used, verse by verse, to defend slavery. The whole story without the plain sense floats off into allegory. Both without a community become private eccentricity; a community without the plain sense becomes an echo chamber. And all three without prayer become an academic exercise, or a weapon.

Together, they make a way of reading that Christians of every tradition, and in large part Jews too, would recognise. The emphasis differs: Protestants stress the plain sense, Catholics and Orthodox the tradition and the liturgy, monks the prayer. But no tradition has given up any of the four.

rows: Where does this fit in the whole, and what does it show of Christ?
Origen's body, soul and spirit; Aquinas's four senses
Verses torn from their story, as the slaveholders did
How have others read it, and who corrects me?
Augustine's rule of love; Avot's chain of teachers
Private eccentricity or an echo chamber
What is it saying to me, and what will I do?
Guigo's ladder; Thomas à Kempis; James's mirror

sections.key: Each rung guards against the failures of the others; every tradition keeps all four, with different emphases.

paras: Here is a daily pattern built from the whole journey. It takes about fifteen minutes. It can be done on a bus or at a kitchen table; it needs a Bible, a notebook and a little quiet.

Begin with a one-line prayer, such as Psalm 119:18: 'Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.' Read the day's passage once, at normal speed, asking only: what kind of writing is this, and what happens? Read it again slowly, aloud if you can, and stop at the phrase that catches you. Turn it over: what does it mean, where else does the Bible say something like it, what does it ask of me? Say one or two sentences to God about it. Sit quietly for a minute. Then write down one thing to do today, however small.

rows: Read the passage through: what kind of writing, what happens?
Read slowly, aloud; stop at the phrase that catches you
Meditate: what it means, where else, what it asks
Speak to God about it; then a minute of silence
Write one thing to do today

sections.key: A fifteen-minute pattern: ask, read, read again, turn it over, pray, and write one thing to do.

paras: A daily pattern needs a plan, or you will spend each morning deciding what to read. Choose one and keep it for a year.

For beginners: one Gospel and one psalm a day. Read Mark, then Luke, then John, then Matthew, a chapter a day, with a psalm each day; then Acts, Genesis and Exodus. That covers the heart of the Bible in about nine months. For those who want the whole Bible: M'Cheyne's four chapters a day, or two of them, which takes two years. For those who want to read with the Church: the daily lectionary of the Catholic Church or the Church of England, which pairs an Old Testament reading, a psalm and a New Testament reading, and is used by millions on the same day.

Whatever plan you choose, keep two kinds of reading going: the daily slow reading, and once in a while a whole book in one sitting, so that you hear it as its first readers did. Mark, Ruth, Jonah, Philippians and James can each be read in under an hour.
sections.key: Choose a plan and keep it for a year: a Gospel and a psalm a day, M'Cheyne's calendar, or the Church's lectionary; and sometimes read a whole book at once.

paras: You will miss days. Everyone does. The Bible's picture of reading is a relationship, not a performance: Mary sitting at Jesus's feet, the Beroeans asking questions, Lawson praying at his work. Augustine said that a reader who aims at love can come to the Bible 'with an easy mind'. If you miss a day, do not try to catch up; simply begin again with today's reading.

Two things help most. A fixed time and place, as Benedict knew: the same chair, the same hour. And another person: a friend, a group or a congregation, who will ask what you are reading and tell you what they are. Reading with others, the third rung, is also the best way to keep going.
sections.key: Missed days are normal: begin again with today, keep a fixed time and place, and read with someone.

sections.h: The Old Testament hall, looking back
paras: This journey closes the first hall, the Old Testament. Look back at what you have read. The whole story gave you the map, seven acts from creation to new creation. What is the Bible? showed you how the library was gathered and handed down, and that it can be trusted as ancient and faithfully copied. In the beginning read Genesis 1–11 beside the myths of Babylon. Abraham and the promise followed one family and its faith. Exodus and the law heard the cry of slaves and the ten words at Sinai. Kings and prophets watched power forget justice and the prophets call it to account. Psalms and wisdom gave the Bible's prayer book and its wisdom.

Now you have the ladder for reading all of it. The next hall begins with Jesus himself, and with the Gospels, where Christians believe the Old Testament's story reaches its centre. Read them plainly, as the end of one story, with others, and on your knees.
sections.key: The Old Testament hall gave the story and its books; this journey gives the way to read them; the next hall turns to Jesus and the Gospels.

paras: This journey has asked you to learn a few words by heart: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet'; 'Every Scripture is God-breathed'; 'Weren't our hearts burning within us?'; the double commandment of love; Micah's 'act justly, love mercy, walk humbly'; 'Open my eyes'; and now 'Be doers of the word'. Together they are a short summary of everything you have read.

Antony's memory 'served him for books'. Most of us will never memorise as the desert monks did, but a handful of verses known by heart change how the Bible works in a life. They come back unbidden in the moments when you need them: in the night, in a hospital, in an argument, at a graveside. Keep adding one a week. In a year you will have fifty, and they will have begun to read you.
sections.key: The verses learned in this journey summarise it; a verse a week, known by heart, lets Scripture go with you.

paras: The hall ends with a short essay: you defend one idea from the Old Testament hall in about 300 words, and answer the strongest objection to it. Here is how to use this journey to write it.

Choose an idea you think is true and important. Find the passage it rests on, and read it by the four rungs: what does it plainly say, in its own kind of writing? Where does it sit in the one story? How have Jews and Christians read it, and is there a reading from someone unlike you that you need to hear? What does it ask of you? Then state the strongest objection fairly, in the terms its best advocate would use, as Aquinas did at the start of every article. Answer it as honestly as you can, admitting what it gets right. That is the method of this whole hall, and of every good argument.
sections.key: To make the case: choose an idea, read its passage by the four rungs, state the strongest objection fairly as Aquinas did, and answer it honestly.
