debate.question: What is lost when the Bible is read only critically, or only devotionally?

positions.name: Only critically
positions.who: The concern of Brevard Childs and of the Pontifical Biblical Commission (1993)
positions.view: Read only as an ancient text to be explained by its history and sources, the Bible's claims on the reader go unheard; you learn a great deal about it and never ask whether it is true or what it asks of you.
positions.evidence: Jowett's hope that honest reading would show the Bible unique; the critique that historical criticism 'stops too soon'.

positions.name: Only devotionally
positions.who: The concern of critical scholars such as James Barr, and of Augustine and Origen before them
positions.view: Read only for personal comfort, the Bible becomes a mirror of the reader's own feelings; its strangeness, its history and its hard sayings are lost, and it can be made to say what we want.
positions.evidence: The slaveholders' use of single verses; Augustine's warning about custom; Origen's insistence that the text is work.

positions.name: Both, in order
positions.who: Augustine, Aquinas, Guigo; most teachers of reading today
positions.view: Study and prayer belong together: the plain sense and the history first, then meditation and prayer, so that understanding feeds devotion and devotion keeps study honest.
positions.evidence: Guigo's warning that prayer without meditation is lukewarm and meditation without reading goes astray; the four rungs of this journey.

debate.agree: All agree that the Bible can be read badly in either way, and that it asks for both mind and heart.

look.why: Martino di Bartolomeo of Siena painted this panel about 1415–20. The main figure is a young deacon saint whom the gallery does not name. Saint Antony appears only small, at the very top, holding a book. He is here because the gallery identifies him, and because he is shown as Athanasius describes him: a man of the book he heard read.
points: A pale-skinned, clean-shaven young man, shown from the hips up against a gold background, holds a palm frond in one hand and a book in the other.
The book has a slate-blue cover and canary-yellow pages.
He wears a red robe edged with gold, with rectangular gold patches on the sleeves, and a white ruffled collar.
In the tip of the panel, tiny in scale, a balding man with a long grey beard, in a muted purple robe under a black cloak, holds a red book in one hand and a crutch in the other: Saint Antony.
Both have halos punched into the gold, under a pointed gilded arch.

music.why: Bach's chorale from a cantata of 1723, his first year in Leipzig, flows on steadily over a gentle triplet melody: a picture of a daily habit, unhurried and joyful.

think.why: James asks for doers of the word: why do Christians think goodness is something God calls us to, not just something we choose?

learn.why: James's verdict on all reading, and the last words of this journey: be doers of the word, and not only hearers.

check.q: Why does each rung of the ladder need the others?
options: Because the four rungs come from four different churches, each holding one

Because each guards against the failures of the others: the plain sense alone can tear verses from their story, the one story alone floats off into allegory, a community alone can become an echo chamber, and all without prayer leave the reader unchanged
Because no single rung is true
Because the churches require all four

check.q: In James's picture, what is the problem with the man who looks in the mirror?

The mirror is distorted
He studies his face too critically
He sees himself and then goes away and forgets: he hears without doing
check.why: Hearing without doing is self-deception.

check.q: What made Antony's hearing of Matthew 19:21 an example of a text 'reading' someone?
options: He took the plain sense as addressed to him, 'as though the passage had been read on his account', and did it at once
He allegorised it
He studied the Greek carefully
He read it alone in the desert
check.why: The plain sense, heard in the community's reading, applied to himself, and done.

check.q: Which daily pattern best reflects the whole journey?
options: Pray, read for the plain sense, read again slowly, meditate, pray, and choose one thing to do
Read only what a commentary says
Read as many chapters as possible
Read only the passages you like
check.why: It climbs all four rungs and ends in doing.

check.q: You miss a week of reading. What does this journey suggest?

Begin again with today's reading, and find a fixed time and someone to read with
Give up, since the habit is broken
Read faster until you are back on schedule
check.why: A relationship, not a performance; Augustine's 'easy mind'.

check.q: What does Antony's 'his memory served him for books' suggest about learning words by heart?
options: That books are unnecessary
That memorising is only for those who cannot read
That Antony was unusual and no one else can do it
That carrying Scripture in memory lets it work on you through the day, as Deuteronomy's 'on your heart' asks
check.why: Memory is how the words go with you, 'when you walk by the way'.

tutorial.question: How should the Bible be read? Give your answer in the form of advice to yourself for the next year.
tutorial.approach: Use the four rungs and the objection. Explain why each rung matters, with one source for each. Describe the daily pattern and the plan you will use, and how you will keep going. End with what 'doing' the word will mean for you.

Shows how the objection of session 5 shapes the answer.
Uses James 1:22–25 or Antony to show reading that ends in doing.
Gives a concrete daily pattern and a year's plan.
Is realistic about missed days and the need for others.
Is personal and specific.

takeaways: Read the Bible plainly, as one story, with others and in prayer; each rung guards against the failures of the others.
James's mirror and Antony's obedience show that reading which reads you ends in doing.
A fifteen-minute daily pattern, a plan for the year, a fixed time and someone to read with will keep you going for life.

closing.title: Your answer, and make the case
closing.prompt: Make the case (the end of the Old Testament hall). Choose one idea you have met in this hall, for example that every human being bears God's image, that God hears the cry of slaves, that power must answer to justice, or that the Bible can be trusted as an ancient witness. In about 300 words, defend it from the passages it rests on, read by the four rungs (the plain sense, the one story, the reading of others, and what it asks of you), and answer the strongest objection to it.
closing.practice: Keep the fifteen-minute pattern for forty days, with a Gospel and a psalm a day. At the end, read back through your notebook and write down the three things the Bible asked you to do that you actually did.
synthesis: This journey asked how to read a text so that it reads you. Its answer is a ladder of four rungs, tested against the strongest objection and ending in a daily practice. Here are the short answers to the questions it set out to answer, in order.

Where do I start? Not at Genesis 1, reading straight through: the Bible is a library, not a novel. Begin with a Gospel (Mark is the shortest), a psalm a day and Genesis; then Acts, a short letter and Exodus. The Bible's own picture of reading is little, often, aloud and slow: Joshua murmuring the book day and night, the Shema talked over at home and on the road, the Beroeans examining the Scriptures daily. Fifteen minutes a day is a good beginning.

Which translation? One you understand and will read. Translations range from formal equivalence, close to the original wording, to dynamic equivalence, which puts the meaning into natural speech. The King James translators said in 1611 that translation opens the window to let in the light, and admitted no translation is perfect. A study Bible helps a beginner; read the text before the notes, and know whose notes they are.

Do I have to take it literally? You must take it in its literal sense, which in the old meaning of the word is what the writer meant, figures of speech included. Aquinas said the literal sense of 'God's arm' is God's power. That depends on genre: poetry as poetry, law as law, letters as letters. Augustine's rules bind both ways: read plainly first and look for a figure only when the plain reading cannot teach love or true belief; and never call a passage figurative merely because your own culture dislikes it. Literalism, taking every word at face value regardless of genre, is a modern approach, not the tradition's.

Why did the old writers find Christ everywhere? Because Jesus and Paul read the Old Testament as one story pointing to him. Origen taught that Scripture, like a person, has body, soul and spirit, and that its difficulties are signposts to deeper reading; but he insisted most of its history happened. The Middle Ages read every passage on four levels: what happened, what it shows of Christ, how to live and what to hope for, with Jerusalem as city, Church, soul and heaven. Aquinas tied them together: God can make things as well as words signify, so a real event can carry a further meaning; but every sense rests on the literal, and no doctrine may be proved from allegory alone. Jews, too, read on several levels, but their deeper meanings point to Torah and Israel. The Reformers rejected free allegory and kept typology.

Why do Christians disagree about what it says, and how do Jews read it? Because the Bible is read within communities, and they differ on who decides. Jews read the written Torah with the oral Torah, handed down from Moses in a chain of teachers and gathered in the Mishnah and Talmud, and they study it together, turning it over 'for all things are in it'. Catholics read Scripture with Tradition and the bishops' teaching office; the Orthodox within the life of the Church, its Fathers, councils and liturgy; Protestants by Scripture alone, but never alone with Scripture, keeping the creeds and confessions. All the large churches share the core the creeds state. And Augustine's rule cuts across them all: a reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not yet understood, however accurate its words.

What about the bits I find shocking, and hasn't the Bible been used to justify terrible things? Yes. In America it was quoted, verse by verse and sincerely, to defend slavery; Frederick Douglass watched a converted slaveholder whip his disabled cousin while quoting Luke 12:47. Readers do find what they bring, and modern critics argue that meaning is made by interpretive communities. The honest reply admits that the Bible regulates slavery without explicitly abolishing it, and that Christians long defended it. But the pro-slavery readings tore verses from their stories, ignored their plain sense and passed over the texts that judged them. The tradition's own rules, the whole story from Genesis 1:27 to Philemon's 'beloved brother', and above all the readings of the enslaved themselves exposed them. Douglass never stopped reading the Bible; he claimed it against his enslavers: 'That which is inhuman cannot be divine.' The parable of the sower puts the problem in the soil, not the seed, and makes fruit the test.

What is lectio divina, and how do I pray with the Bible? It is the monks' slow reading in four steps, as the Carthusian Guigo II described it: reading puts the food in the mouth, meditation chews it, prayer tastes it, and contemplation is its sweetness, which is God's gift rather than our achievement. Benedict gave it fixed hours, because idleness is the enemy of the soul; Thomas à Kempis said to read humbly, simply and honestly, in the spirit in which Scripture was written. Ignatius pictured the Gospel scenes, Luther wove each verse into a garland of instruction, thanks, confession and prayer, and Jews hold the study of Torah itself to be worship. Most days nothing dramatic happens; lectio asks for faithfulness, not feelings.

So how should I read it? Plainly, as one story, with others and on your knees. Each rung guards against the failures of the others. And then do what it says. James's man who looks in the mirror and walks away has heard without being read; Antony, hearing one verse read in church 'as though the passage had been read on his account', went out and did it. A fifteen-minute pattern (ask, read, read again, turn it over, pray, do), a plan for the year, a fixed time and someone to read with will keep you going.

Can a text have more than one true meaning? The tradition says yes, within limits: Augustine thought a great text holds more truth than one reader sees, and Aquinas that God signifies by things as well as words. But it also says no reading is true that contradicts the plain sense or fails to build up love. That balance is the heart of this journey.

One more thing. Notice how much of the West grew from the ways of reading in this journey. Universities began in the cathedral schools where monks and scholars argued over the senses of Scripture, and the very method of the Summa, objections stated fairly before an answer, became the method of disputation and debate. The demand to read what an ancient author actually meant, in his own language and time, which Jerome, the Antiochenes and the Reformers pressed, grew into modern historical scholarship. The conviction that every ploughman and milkmaid should be able to read the Bible for themselves did more than anything else to spread literacy across Protestant Europe and beyond, and drove the translation of the Bible into thousands of languages. And the habit of slow, daily attention to a text, learned in monasteries, is still what every serious reader of anything practises. Whatever you conclude about the Bible, you have learned the way the West learned to read.
exam: 'Interpret the Scripture like any other book' (Jowett). Is this sufficient?
Can a text have more than one true meaning? Discuss with reference to Augustine and Aquinas.
Is allegory a key to Scripture or a licence? Discuss with reference to Origen.
Is sola scriptura coherent?
Compare the relation of Scripture and tradition in Jewish, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant thought.
'The Bible can be made to say anything.' Discuss with reference to the American debate over slavery.
What is lost when the Bible is read only critically, or only devotionally?
Is lectio divina a method or a gift?

title: The last week and the cross
question: What happened in Jerusalem, and did he rise?
line: Seven sessions walking through Jesus's last week as a historian walks through a city: the entry and the Temple, the supper, the trials, the cross, the tomb, the case against the resurrection, and the verdict on Easter.
why: Christianity stands or falls on one week in Jerusalem around AD 30. Everything else in the faith, its worship, its ethics, its hope in the face of death, depends on what happened between Palm Sunday and Easter Day. This journey reads the Gospels' accounts of that week beside the prophets they echo, Roman and Jewish writers who knew Pilate and the cross, and the archaeology, then gives the natural explanations of Easter their full weight before asking what best explains the evidence. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year theology paper on the Passion narratives of the Gospels and the historical question of the resurrection, with elements of a paper on Jesus in his Jewish and Roman setting.
before: sermon-on-the-mount
who-was-jesus
outcomes: Explain the setting of Passover in Roman Jerusalem and read Jesus's entry and Temple action as prophetic signs drawing on Zechariah and Jeremiah.
Set out the dating problem of the Last Supper and the main solutions, and explain what Jesus's words over the bread and cup meant, with the main church traditions side by side.
Explain why Jesus was handed to Pilate and crucified, what Philo and Josephus say about Pilate, and how the charge that 'the Jews' killed Jesus was used and later repudiated.
Describe Roman crucifixion from Cicero, Josephus and archaeology, and explain why a crucified Messiah counts as evidence that the first Christians did not invent their message.
Weigh the evidence for the empty tomb, including the women witnesses, Mark's ending and the differences between the Gospels.

State the natural explanations of the resurrection at full strength, from Strauss to Lüdemann and Ehrman, assess them against the replies of Wright and Allison, and explain Jewish and Muslim views of the cross.

people.name: Jesus of Nazareth
people.line: A Jewish teacher from Galilee, crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate at Passover; his followers proclaimed that God had raised him from the dead.

people.name: Simon Peter
people.line: Leader of the twelve, who denied Jesus three times on the night of his arrest and became the first witness of the resurrection named by Paul.

people.name: Judas Iscariot
people.line: One of the twelve, who led the high priest's men to Jesus at night.

people.name: Mary Magdalene
people.line: A follower from Galilee, at the cross and the burial, and in every Gospel the first to find the tomb empty.

people.name: Thomas
people.line: One of the twelve, who refused to believe without touching the wounds, and then said 'My Lord and my God'.

people.name: Joseph of Arimathea
people.line: A member of the council who asked Pilate for Jesus's body and laid it in a rock tomb.

people.name: Caiaphas
people.line: The high priest who handed Jesus to Pilate; a family ossuary probably his was found in Jerusalem in 1990.

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.line: Roman governor who condemned Jesus to be crucified as 'King of the Jews'; named on a stone found at Caesarea in 1961.

people.name: Paul of Tarsus
people.line: A Pharisee who persecuted the first Christians, then saw the risen Jesus, as he believed; his letters are the earliest Christian writings.

people.name: Cicero
people.line: Roman orator whose speeches against Verres describe the crucifixion of a Roman citizen.

people.name: Philo of Alexandria
people.line: Jewish philosopher who described Pilate's character in his Embassy to Gaius.

people.name: Flavius Josephus
people.line: Jewish priest and historian of the war with Rome, who describes Pilate, Passover crowds and mass crucifixions.

people.name: Celsus
people.line: Greek philosopher, the first known writer against Christianity, who said the appearances were the visions of an excitable woman.

people.name: Hermann Samuel Reimarus
people.line: German scholar, the 'Wolfenbüttel Fragmentist', who argued that the disciples stole the body.

people.name: David Friedrich Strauss
people.line: German theologian whose Life of Jesus (1835) explained the resurrection as visions and legend.

people.name: George Eliot
people.line: The novelist Mary Ann Evans, who translated Strauss into English in 1846.

people.name: Raymond E. Brown
people.line: American Catholic scholar, author of The Death of the Messiah (1994).

people.name: Martin Hengel
people.line: German scholar whose Crucifixion (1977) gathered the ancient evidence on the cross.

people.name: Gerd Lüdemann
people.line: German scholar who argued that the appearances were visions, starting with Peter's grief and guilt.

people.name: Bart D. Ehrman
people.line: American New Testament scholar and agnostic, who accepts that some disciples had visions but doubts the empty tomb.

people.name: N. T. Wright
people.line: British New Testament scholar and former bishop of Durham, whose The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003) argues that only a real resurrection explains the evidence.

people.name: Dale C. Allison Jr.
people.line: American scholar who weighs the case on both sides and concludes that history alone cannot settle it.

glossary.def: Jewish hope, from about 200 BC, that God would soon act to end the present age, judge the world and raise the dead.
The meetings with the risen Jesus that his followers reported, in Jerusalem and in Galilee.
The high priest and the leading priestly families who ran the Temple and dealt with Rome.
An appearance of Christ, such as Paul's on the road to Damascus.
A binding agreement between God and his people; at Sinai sealed with blood, and at the Last Supper renewed in Jesus's blood.
Historians' rule that a story awkward for the people who told it is unlikely to have been invented by them.
Roman execution by nailing or tying a person to a cross to die slowly in public; used for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals.
The feast of the resurrection, the oldest and greatest Christian feast; in most languages called Pascha, from the Hebrew for Passover.
The report that the women, and then Peter, found Jesus's tomb open and his body gone on the Sunday morning.
From the Greek for 'thanksgiving': the meal of bread and wine Jesus commanded at the Last Supper, also called the Mass, Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper.
Roman beating with a whip weighted with bone or metal, often before crucifixion.
Aramaic for 'the place of a skull', the site outside Jerusalem's wall where Jesus was crucified; Calvary in Latin.
The Friday of Holy Week, when Christians remember the crucifixion.
Psalms 113 to 118, sung at the feasts and at the end of the Passover meal.
The view that the disciples' experiences of the risen Jesus were visions produced by their own minds, as in grief.
The week from Palm Sunday to Easter, in which Christians follow Jesus's last days.
Hebrew for 'save us, please', from Psalm 118; shouted as a welcome when Jesus entered Jerusalem.
The Qur'an's name for Jesus, honoured in Islam as a prophet and the Messiah.
The Thursday of Holy Week, remembering the Last Supper; from the Latin mandatum, Jesus's 'new commandment' to love.
Hebrew for 'anointed one' (Greek christos, Christ): the king from David's line whom Israel hoped for.
The Second Vatican Council's declaration of 1965 on other religions, which rejected blaming the Jewish people for Jesus's death.
A stone box into which a family gathered a person's bones a year or so after burial; common in Jerusalem in Jesus's time.
The Sunday before Easter, remembering Jesus's entry into Jerusalem.
Pesach, the Jewish feast remembering the escape from Egypt, with a lamb, unleavened bread and wine.
The title of the Roman governors of Judea from AD 6 to 41, including Pontius Pilate; later governors were called procurators.
A Roman governor's headquarters; in Jerusalem probably Herod's palace, where Pilate stayed at the feasts.
The belief that Christ's body and blood are truly present in the Eucharist, held in different ways by Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and many Anglicans.
In Jewish hope, God raising the dead to bodily life at the end of the age; Christians say it happened to Jesus first.
The seventh day, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, a day of rest on which no work, including burial, could be done.
The Jewish council in Jerusalem, led by the high priest.
A prophet's message acted out in public, such as Jeremiah smashing a jar.
The view that Jesus did not die on the cross but revived in the tomb.
Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share much material and can be 'seen together'.
The house of God in Jerusalem, rebuilt by Herod and destroyed by Rome in AD 70; the only place of sacrifice.
The notice of the charge carried before a condemned man or fixed to his cross; for Jesus, 'The King of the Jews'.
The Catholic teaching that in the Mass the substance of the bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood.
Bread made without yeast, eaten at Passover in memory of the hasty escape from Egypt.

sessions.title: Into the city
sessions.line: A teacher from Galilee rides into Jerusalem on a donkey at Passover, to shouts of 'Hosanna', and the next day overturns the tables in the Temple.
sessions.plain: About the year 30, a Jewish teacher from Galilee called Jesus came to Jerusalem for Passover, the great feast of freedom, when the city was packed with pilgrims and watched by Roman soldiers. He rode in on a donkey while the crowd shouted that David's kingdom was coming, and the next day he drove the traders out of the Temple and quoted the prophets against it. Within a week he was dead. This session asks what he did on those first two days, what it meant, and why no one in power could ignore it.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'Who was Jesus?' asked who he claimed to be: a prophet who spoke with an authority no prophet claimed, who called himself the Son of Man and accepted the title Messiah while redefining it. Now we follow what he did with that claim in the last week of his life, starting on the day he arrived in Jerusalem.
answers: What is Holy Week, and why does it matter so much?
Why did Jesus ride into Jerusalem on a donkey?
What did he do in the Temple, and what did it mean?
Why did the authorities start looking for a way to kill him?
sessions.finding: Jesus entered Jerusalem at Passover as a king on a donkey and attacked the Temple trade: an act no authority could ignore.

paras: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jew from Galilee, the hill country in the north of what is now Israel. For two or three years, probably around AD 28 to 30, he travelled the villages around the Sea of Galilee teaching, healing and gathering followers, among them an inner circle of twelve. If you have taken 'Who was Jesus?', you have read what he said about himself: he forgave sins, spoke of himself as the 'Son of Man' and accepted Peter's confession that he was the Messiah, the anointed king Israel hoped for.

Then, in Mark's Gospel, he turns south towards Jerusalem, and three times on the road he tells his followers that he will be handed over, killed and rise again (Mark 8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34). They do not understand. This journey begins as they reach the city.
background.key: Jesus, a Galilean teacher with twelve close followers, had claimed an authority beyond any prophet's; in Mark he walks to Jerusalem saying he will be killed there.

paras: Christianity stands or falls on what happened in one week in Jerusalem. Christians call it Holy Week: the days from Jesus's entry into the city to the morning his tomb was found empty. The four Gospels spend more time on it than on anything else; Mark gives it six of his sixteen chapters. A German scholar, Martin Kähler, said in 1892 that the Gospels are 'passion narratives with extended introductions'.

So the question of this journey is a historian's question as well as a believer's: what happened in Jerusalem, and did he rise? We will walk through the week as a historian would walk through the city, one place and one day at a time. One session gives the strongest case against the resurrection its full weight. The last gives a verdict.

background.key: What happened in Jerusalem, and did he rise? Seven steps through the week, the case against, then a verdict.

paras: Passover was the feast that remembered Israel's escape from slavery in Egypt, more than a thousand years earlier. (If you have taken 'Exodus and the law', you have read the night of the first Passover in Exodus 12.) Every Jewish man who could was expected to come up to Jerusalem for it, and the city filled with pilgrims from Galilee, Egypt, Babylon and Rome.

By Jesus's time Judea was ruled by Rome. Since AD 6 a Roman governor, called a prefect, had governed it from the port of Caesarea on the coast. The Temple in Jerusalem was run by the high priest and the 'chief priests', the leading priestly families, whom the Romans appointed and could remove. At the big feasts the prefect came up to Jerusalem with extra troops, because a feast of freedom from a foreign empire, held under a foreign empire, could easily turn into a riot. From AD 26 to 36 the prefect was Pontius Pilate.

background.key: Passover remembered freedom from Egypt; under Rome it packed Jerusalem with pilgrims, watched by the prefect's troops and run by Rome's chosen high priests.

background.h: Who wrote Mark, and why we read these passages
paras: Most scholars think Mark is the earliest of the four Gospels, written around AD 65 to 70, about thirty-five years after the events. It does not name its author. The earliest tradition, from Papias, a bishop writing in the early 100s and quoted by the historian Eusebius (Church History 3.39.15), says Mark set down what the apostle Peter used to teach. Matthew and Luke later used Mark as one of their sources. Mark writes fast and plainly, and he is the best place to start on the last week.

The main reading is Mark 11:1–19: the entry into the city, and the next day in the Temple. The comparison is two prophets whose words Jesus acted out: Zechariah, who pictured a king riding a donkey, and Jeremiah, who called the Temple of his own day 'a den of robbers'. Read together, they show what a crowd in Jerusalem would have seen.
background.key: Mark, the earliest Gospel (c. AD 65–70), linked by early tradition to Peter; we read his account of the entry and the Temple, then the two prophets Jesus acted out.

before: What do the crowds shout, and whose kingdom do they say is coming?
What exactly does Jesus do in the Temple, and what does he say?
Who reacts, and how?
sessions.readWhy: Two days in Mark: the king on a donkey, then the fig tree and the Temple.

paras: When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples,
and said to them, “Go your way into the village that is opposite you. Immediately as you enter into it, you will find a young donkey tied, on which no one has sat. Untie him, and bring him.
If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord needs him;’ and immediately he will send him back here.”
They went away, and found a young donkey tied at the door outside in the open street, and they untied him.
Some of those who stood there asked them, “What are you doing, untying the young donkey?”
They said to them just as Jesus had said, and they let them go.
They brought the young donkey to Jesus, and threw their garments on it, and Jesus sat on it.
Many spread their garments on the way, and others were cutting down branches from the trees, and spreading them on the road.
Those who went in front, and those who followed, cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!
Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that is coming in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!”
Jesus entered into the temple in Jerusalem. When he had looked around at everything, it being now evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
The next day, when they had come out from Bethany, he was hungry.
Seeing a fig tree afar off having leaves, he came to see if perhaps he might find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.
Jesus told it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again!” and his disciples heard it.

They came to Jerusalem, and Jesus entered into the temple, and began to throw out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables, and the seats of those who sold the doves.
He would not allow anyone to carry a container through the temple.
He taught, saying to them, “Isn’t it written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations?’ But you have made it a den of robbers!”
The chief priests and the scribes heard it, and sought how they might destroy him. For they feared him, because all the multitude was astonished at his teaching.
When evening came, he went out of the city.

parts.title: The king on a donkey
parts.context: Sunday, five days before Passover, probably in AD 30 or 33. Jesus and his followers have walked up from Jericho, a climb of about a thousand metres. They stop at the villages on the Mount of Olives, the ridge east of Jerusalem from which the whole Temple can be seen across the valley.

commentary.on: When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives
commentary.text: The Mount of Olives mattered. The prophet Zechariah had said that on the day God came to rescue his people, 'His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives' (Zechariah 14:4). Anyone who began a procession here was making a point.

commentary.on: you will find a young donkey tied, on which no one has sat
commentary.text: Jesus has walked all the way from Galilee. Now, for the last two miles, he chooses to ride. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose. It is planned, and it is meant to be seen.

commentary.on: Many spread their garments on the way
commentary.text: When Jehu was proclaimed king of Israel, his officers spread their cloaks under him (2 Kings 9:13). The crowd is treating Jesus as a king arriving.

commentary.on: others were cutting down branches from the trees
commentary.text: Mark says leafy branches; John (12:13) says palm branches, which is why the day is called Palm Sunday. Palms were a sign of national victory: when Simon Maccabeus freed the citadel of Jerusalem in 141 BC, his people entered it with palms (1 Maccabees 13:51).

commentary.on: Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!
commentary.text: 'Hosanna' is Hebrew for 'save us, please'. The words come from Psalm 118, one of the psalms sung by pilgrims at the feasts. On its own it is a pilgrim's greeting. Shouted at one man on a donkey, it becomes a welcome to a deliverer.

commentary.on: Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that is coming
commentary.text: This is the dangerous line. David's kingdom had been gone for six hundred years. To shout that it was coming, in a Roman province, at Passover, was to say that Rome's rule was about to end.

commentary.on: When he had looked around at everything, it being now evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
commentary.text: An odd anticlimax. After the procession, Jesus goes into the Temple, looks around 'at everything', like an inspector, and leaves. Mark is making us wait for the next day.

parts.title: The fig tree and the Temple
parts.context: Monday. Jesus and the twelve are staying at Bethany, a village on the far side of the Mount of Olives, and walk into the city each morning. Mark tells the story of a fig tree on the way in, and finishes it the next morning (11:20–21): the Temple scene is set inside it, like the filling of a sandwich, so that each explains the other.

commentary.on: he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs
commentary.text: It seems unfair to curse a tree for having no fruit out of season. But the prophets used the fig tree as a picture of Israel, and an empty one as a picture of judgement: 'no figs on the fig tree' (Jeremiah 8:13). This is an acted parable, and the Temple is what it is about.

commentary.on: began to throw out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers' tables
commentary.text: This happened in the vast outer court of the Temple, the Court of the Gentiles, open to everyone. Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice and had to pay the Temple tax in one particular silver coin, the shekel of Tyre, so the trade was useful, even necessary. Jesus is not attacking cheating stallholders so much as stopping the whole operation.

commentary.on: the seats of those who sold the doves
commentary.text: Doves were the offering of the poor, who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8). Luke says Jesus's own parents offered two birds when he was a baby (Luke 2:24).

commentary.on: He would not allow anyone to carry a container through the temple.
commentary.text: The Temple platform was enormous, about fourteen hectares. One man could not shut it down for long. Most historians think this was a brief, symbolic act, a sign, not a takeover.

commentary.on: My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations
commentary.text: Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7, a promise that foreigners too would worship in God's house. The trade filled the one court where non-Jews were allowed to pray.

commentary.on: But you have made it a den of robbers!
commentary.text: The second quotation is from Jeremiah 7:11, the prophet's sermon against the Temple of his day, which you will read in the comparison. A robbers' den is not where robbers rob; it is where they hide afterwards. Jeremiah's charge was that people sinned all week and then came to the Temple to feel safe.

commentary.on: The chief priests and the scribes heard it, and sought how they might destroy him.
commentary.text: This is the turning point of Mark's story. Up to now Jesus's opponents have argued with him. From here, the men who ran the Temple want him dead. Many historians, following E. P. Sanders, think this scene was the immediate cause of his death.

paras:
Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion!
Shout, daughter of Jerusalem!
Behold, your King comes to you!
He is righteous, and having salvation;
lowly, and riding on a donkey,
even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, burn incense to Baal, and walk after other gods that you have not known,
then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, ‘We are delivered,’ that you may do all these abominations?
Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it,” says Yahweh.

parts.title: Your King comes to you, riding on a donkey
parts.context: Zechariah prophesied in Jerusalem from 520 BC, after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon and began to rebuild the Temple. Many scholars think chapters 9 to 14 of the book were added later by another prophet. Matthew (21:5) and John (12:15) both quote this passage when they tell of the entry into Jerusalem.

commentary.on: Behold, your King comes to you!
commentary.text: The hope of a king for Jerusalem, from David's line, was alive in Jesus's day. This is the picture of his arrival.

commentary.on: lowly, and riding on a donkey
commentary.text: Not on a war horse. A donkey was the animal of peace and of ordinary people, though kings could ride one: David had his son Solomon ride his own mule to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33). The king of Zechariah's poem comes humbly.

commentary.on: I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem
commentary.text: This king takes the weapons away from his own people. He wins without an army.

commentary.on: he will speak peace to the nations
commentary.text: His rule reaches 'to the ends of the earth', but by peace. A crowd that knew this poem would have seen a claim to be the king, and a strange idea of what the king would do.

parts.title: A den of robbers
parts.context: Jeremiah preached in Jerusalem from about 627 BC until after its fall in 587 BC. This is from his 'Temple sermon', given at the Temple gate around 609 BC. He warned that God would destroy the Temple as he had destroyed the old shrine at Shiloh (7:14). Chapter 26 tells what happened next: the priests and prophets seized him and said, 'You shall surely die!'

commentary.on: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely
commentary.text: Jeremiah lists the Ten Commandments being broken: theft, murder, adultery, false witness, other gods. The problem is not the Temple's rituals but the lives of the people who use it.

commentary.on: and say, 'We are delivered,'
commentary.text: The false comfort Jeremiah attacks: as long as we have the Temple, we are safe, whatever we do.

commentary.on: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?
commentary.text: The line Jesus quoted. By choosing Jeremiah's words, Jesus put himself in Jeremiah's place: a prophet in the Temple court foretelling its destruction. Jeremiah was nearly killed for it. Everyone who knew the story knew what usually happened next.

compare.why: Jesus did not explain his entry or his action in the Temple. He did not need to: the crowds knew their prophets. Read the two passages his actions brought to mind.
compare.title: Two prophets he acted out

paras: How many came to Passover? The Jewish historian Josephus, who was a priest in Jerusalem before its fall, says that one year the high priests counted 256,500 lambs sacrificed, and he reckons ten people to a lamb: 2,700,200 people (Jewish War 6.9.3). No historian believes a number that large. Modern estimates are much lower, though they vary widely; on any of them, the pilgrims outnumbered the people of the city several times over.

Crowds made the Romans nervous. Josephus says that at the feasts a Roman cohort, some hundreds of soldiers, stood on the roofs of the Temple porticoes 'to prevent any innovation which the multitude thus gathered together might make'. Under one governor, Cumanus, around AD 50, a soldier's obscene gesture at Passover set off a riot, and Josephus says ten thousand died in the crush (Jewish War 2.12.1). This was the city Jesus rode into.
sections.key: Passover crowded Jerusalem with pilgrims; Josephus shows Roman soldiers on the Temple roofs and how quickly a feast could turn to a riot.

sections.h: The Temple and the men who ran it
paras: The Temple was the heart of Jewish life: the one place on earth where sacrifice could be offered to God. Herod the Great had rebuilt it on a vast scale from 20/19 BC; its platform still stands, with the Western Wall on one side. Inside were courts, one inside another: the Court of the Gentiles, open to all; the courts of the women and of Israel; the priests' court with the altar; and the sanctuary, where only the high priest entered, once a year. A stone found in 1871, now in Istanbul, warns foreigners that anyone going beyond the barrier will have himself to blame for his death.

The high priest was chosen by Rome. Caiaphas held the office from AD 18 to 36, longer than anyone else under Roman rule, which suggests he worked well with the prefects. In 1990 a family bone-box (an ossuary) inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas' was found in Jerusalem; many scholars think it held his bones. The priestly families were rich, and later Jewish tradition remembered some of them bitterly for violence and greed (Babylonian Talmud, Pesahim 57a).
sections.key: The Temple was the centre of Jewish worship, run by priestly families appointed by Rome; Caiaphas, high priest AD 18–36, may be named on an ossuary found in 1990.

paras: Mark marks the days carefully, and Christians have followed his order ever since. Some details are uncertain: John's Gospel puts Jesus's Temple action at the start of his work (John 2:13–22) rather than the end, and dates the supper and the crucifixion differently, a puzzle the next session takes up. But the outline is shared by all four Gospels.

rows: Debates in the Temple; the warning that it will fall
The anointing at Bethany; Judas goes to the priests
The trials; the crucifixion; the burial
The Sabbath: the body in the tomb
table.note: Mark's markers: 'the next day' (11:12), 'in the morning' (11:20), 'It was now two days before the feast of the Passover' (14:1).

sections.key: All four Gospels share the outline of the week, from Palm Sunday to Easter Day, though John orders some events differently.

paras: Israel's prophets did not only speak. They acted their message out, so that it could not be missed. Jeremiah smashed a clay jar in front of the elders to show that God would smash Jerusalem (Jeremiah 19), and walked about wearing an ox's yoke to show that Babylon would rule (Jeremiah 27). Isaiah went barefoot and stripped for three years as a sign of coming captivity (Isaiah 20). Scholars call these sign-acts.

Read this way, Jesus's two days fit together. The entry acts out Zechariah: the king has come, humbly, to Jerusalem. The Temple action and the fig tree act out Jeremiah: the Temple has failed and will fall. Later that week, in Mark, Jesus says of the Temple's great stones that 'there will not be left here one stone on another' (13:2), and at his trial witnesses accuse him of saying he would destroy it (14:58). The Romans destroyed it forty years later, in AD 70.
sections.key: Prophets acted out their messages; Jesus's entry acts out Zechariah's king, and his Temple action acts out Jeremiah's warning.

paras: To a Roman governor, the meaning was simple. A man from Galilee had been hailed by a Passover crowd as the one bringing David's kingdom, and had disrupted the Temple. Rome had seen such men before and dealt with them by force. In AD 6 Judas the Galilean led a revolt against Roman taxes. Around AD 55, Josephus says, a prophet from Egypt gathered a crowd on the Mount of Olives, promising to take the city; the governor Felix attacked them with his troops (Jewish War 2.13.5).

Yet one fact stands out. When Jesus was arrested, his followers were not hunted down; only he was killed. The historian Paula Fredriksen has argued that this shows the authorities knew he led no armed movement. Whatever his entry meant, the Romans did not treat it as an army. They treated it as a danger in one man, a king without soldiers, which is what Zechariah had described.
sections.key: Rome crushed would-be kings by force; that only Jesus was killed suggests the authorities saw a dangerous claim, not an army.

sections.h: Did it happen as Mark says?
paras: Historians test a story by asking how many independent sources tell it, whether it fits its setting, and whether it explains what came after. The Temple action passes all three tests unusually well. It is told by Mark, followed by Matthew and Luke, and independently by John, though John puts it at the start of Jesus's work rather than the end. It fits what we know of the Temple, its trade and its tensions. And it explains what followed: the priests' hostility, the charge at the trial that Jesus threatened the Temple, and his death within days.

Its details are less certain. John's date is one puzzle; most scholars think Mark's placing is more likely, because it explains the arrest, though some think there were two incidents. The size of the crowd at the entry is another: the Gospels describe excitement, but a large procession might have brought Roman soldiers at once. Many historians think the entry was a smaller event than later tradition imagined, noticed by Jesus's followers and the pilgrims around them, and given its meaning later. On both, the core is secure and the scale debated.
sections.key: The Temple action is told independently by Mark and John and explains Jesus's death; its date and the size of the entry's crowd are debated.

paras: Around AD 381 to 384 a pilgrim named Egeria, probably from Spain or Gaul, wrote down how the Christians of Jerusalem kept the day. In the afternoon they gathered on the Mount of Olives, read the Gospel of the entry, and walked down into the city carrying palm or olive branches, singing 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord', with the children carried on their parents' shoulders. Churches across the world have done the same ever since.

Catholics and Anglicans bless palms and process; many give out small palm crosses. The Orthodox call the day the Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem, and in Russia, where palms do not grow, people carry pussy willow. Protestant churches often sing 'All glory, laud and honour', written by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, around 820. In every tradition the day has a double feeling: a king is welcomed, and the same week ends at a cross.
sections.key: Since at least the 380s Christians have re-enacted the entry with branches; every tradition keeps Palm Sunday as both welcome and warning.

Martin Kähler, The So-Called Historical Jesus and the Historic, Biblical Christ (1892). E. P. Sanders, Jesus and Judaism (1985). Paula Fredriksen, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews (1999).
The Temple warning inscription (found by Charles Clermont-Ganneau, 1871; Istanbul Archaeology Museums). The Caiaphas ossuary (found 1990; Israel Museum). Egeria, Travels 31 (c. 381–384).

debate.question: A prophetic sign or a political act?

positions.name: A sign of the Temple's end
positions.who: E. P. Sanders, Jesus and Judaism (1985); N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God (1996)
positions.view: Jesus was not cleaning up the Temple but acting out its coming destruction, as Jeremiah had, and pointing to a new kind of restoration in himself. This, more than anything he taught, is why the priests wanted him dead.
positions.evidence: The fig tree wrapped round the scene; the quotation of Jeremiah; the prediction that not one stone would be left (13:2); the charge at his trial (14:58).

positions.name: A protest against corruption
positions.who: The traditional reading, 'the cleansing of the Temple'; Craig A. Evans and others
positions.view: Jesus was protesting against the way the Temple was run: its trade and the greed of the high-priestly families, which pushed out the poor and the foreigners who came to pray. He wanted it purified, not abolished.
positions.evidence: 'A den of robbers'; 'a house of prayer for all the nations'; the doves of the poor; later Jewish complaints about the priestly families (Pesahim 57a).

positions.name: A political challenge
positions.who: S. G. F. Brandon, Jesus and the Zealots (1967), in its strong form; Paula Fredriksen (1999), in a different form
positions.view: Brandon argued Jesus was close to the rebels against Rome, and that the Gospels later hid it; very few scholars now agree. Fredriksen argues, more modestly, that what alarmed the authorities was the Passover crowd's belief that he was the coming king.
positions.evidence: 'The kingdom of our father David'; the Passover setting; the Roman charge 'King of the Jews'. Against Brandon: the donkey, not a war horse, and no follower was arrested.

debate.agree: All agree that the entry and the Temple scene were deliberate, public acts at Passover that drew on the prophets, and that they set the city's rulers against him.

look.why: El Greco painted Jesus driving the traders from the Temple several times over his career; this early version is probably from before 1570. It shows the moment of Mark 11:15, and it is also used in 'How we got here'.
points: Jesus stands at the centre, in a dark pink robe with a bright blue cloth over one shoulder, holding a short four-tailed whip high across his body.
To our left, two men with bare torsos and raised arms lean away from him; one bends over and looks back over his shoulder.
Below them a woman rests her hand on a cage holding five white birds.
To our right, a grey-bearded old man sits on the steps with his chin in his hand, looking up at Jesus, his elbow resting on a basket of gold coins.
At his feet two rabbits nose silver spilling from a pouch, and a white lamb lies with its feet tied to a stick.
Columns and arches frame the scene; through the arch above Jesus are blue sky, clouds and distant buildings.

music.why: Theodulf of Orléans's hymn of about 820, in John Mason Neale's translation, has been sung in Palm Sunday processions for centuries.

think.why: Before following the week day by day, see what historians agree on about Jesus, and where faith begins.

learn.why: The prophecy Jesus acted out as he rode into the city: a king who comes in peace.

check.q: Why was the crowd's shout 'Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that is coming' dangerous?
options: Because in a Roman province at Passover it announced that a king of Israel was about to replace Rome's rule
Because it was a quotation from the Psalms
Because David was not a popular king
Because only priests were allowed to say 'Hosanna'
check.why: The words of Psalm 118 were a normal pilgrim greeting; the claim about David's kingdom, at a feast of freedom under Rome, was sedition.

check.q: What is the best explanation of why Jesus chose to ride a donkey for the last two miles?
options: Donkeys were the only animals allowed in the Temple
It showed he was too poor to own a horse
It acted out Zechariah 9:9, a king who comes humbly and in peace
He was tired after the walk from Jericho
check.why: He had walked from Galilee; choosing to ride here was a sign, and the crowds knew Zechariah's poem.

check.q: Why does Mark wrap the story of the fig tree around the Temple scene?
options: To show that Jesus was hungry
So that each explains the other: the barren tree is a picture of the Temple's coming judgement
To show Jesus's power over nature
Because the two events happened in the same place
check.why: Mark's 'sandwich' makes the cursed tree an acted parable of the Temple, as the prophets used the fig tree for Israel.

check.q: Jesus quotes Jeremiah's 'den of robbers'. What does the phrase mean in Jeremiah 7?
options: That the traders were overcharging pilgrims
That people sinned all week and then hid in the Temple, thinking it made them safe
That the priests had stolen the Temple's treasure
That robbers met in the Temple to plan crimes
check.why: A den is where robbers hide afterwards; Jeremiah attacked false security in the Temple, and foretold its fall.

check.q: Why do most historians think the Temple action was a brief, symbolic act rather than a takeover?
options: Because the traders were not really in the Temple
Because the Temple platform was about fourteen hectares and policed by Roman soldiers, so one man could not shut it down for long
Because no Gospel mentions it
Because the Gospels say it lasted a whole day
check.why: The scale of the place and the soldiers on the porticoes make a prolonged takeover impossible; a prophetic sign fits.

check.q: What does the fact that only Jesus, and none of his followers, was killed suggest?
options: That Pilate supported the disciples
That his followers had already fled to Galilee
That the authorities saw a dangerous claim in one man rather than an armed movement
That the Romans did not know he had followers
check.why: Rome usually crushed armed movements wholesale; singling out the leader suggests they did not see an army (Fredriksen's argument).

tutorial.question: Why did the authorities see Jesus's entry into Jerusalem and his action in the Temple as a threat?
tutorial.approach: Start with the setting: Passover, the crowds, the Roman troops and the high priests appointed by Rome. Then take the two acts in turn, with the prophets they drew on (Zechariah 9, Jeremiah 7). Weigh the three readings in the debate. End by asking whether the threat was religious, political, or both, and whether the distinction would have made sense at the time.
strong: Explains Passover as a feast of freedom held under Roman rule, and the role of the prefect and the high priests.
Reads the entry through Zechariah 9:9 and the crowd's shout about David's kingdom.
Reads the Temple action through Jeremiah 7 and the fig tree.
Uses outside evidence: Josephus on Passover crowds and riots, or on other would-be kings.
Weighs 'sign of destruction', 'cleansing' and 'political challenge' fairly.
Notes that in first-century Judea religion and politics could not be separated.

reading.author: Marcus J. Borg and John Dominic Crossan
reading.title: The Last Week
reading.why: A day-by-day reading of Mark's account by two liberal scholars; lively, and open about its own views.

reading.author: E. P. Sanders
reading.title: Jesus and Judaism
reading.why: The classic argument that the Temple action was a sign of destruction and restoration, and the cause of Jesus's death.

reading.author: Paula Fredriksen
reading.title: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews
reading.why: A historian's reconstruction of why Jesus, and only Jesus, was crucified.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Jesus chose a donkey over a war horse. Once each day this week, when you could win an argument or make your point by pressure, choose the humbler way instead: ask a question, give way, or say nothing. Note in a sentence each night what happened.
sessions.reflect: If someone came into the place you feel safest, your work, your home, your church, and overturned the tables, what would they find there?
takeaways: Jesus entered Jerusalem at Passover, when the city was full of pilgrims and Roman troops, riding a donkey as Zechariah's humble king, to shouts that David's kingdom was coming.
The next day he stopped the Temple trade and quoted Jeremiah's 'den of robbers': a prophetic sign that the Temple had failed and would fall.
From that moment, in Mark, the chief priests looked for a way to destroy him.

sessions.title: The last supper
sessions.line: On his last night, Jesus eats the Passover with the twelve, gives them bread and wine as his body and blood, and kneels to wash their feet.
sessions.plain: On the Thursday night of that week, Jesus ate a last meal with his twelve closest followers in a room in Jerusalem. He took bread and said 'This is my body', and took a cup of wine and called it 'my blood of the covenant, poured out for many'. In John's Gospel he also knelt and washed their feet, a slave's job. This session asks what kind of meal it was, what he meant, and why Christians have repeated it every week for two thousand years.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed Jesus provoking the city: a king on a donkey, and an attack on the Temple trade, after which the chief priests wanted him dead. Now, knowing what is coming, he does something extraordinary: he tells his friends what his death will mean, before it happens.
answers: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?
What did Jesus mean by 'this is my body'?
Why did he wash their feet?
Who was Judas, and why did he betray him?
Why do Christians still do this, and why do they disagree about it?
sessions.finding: Jesus gave his death its meaning in advance, at a Passover meal: a new covenant in his blood, and a servant's towel.

paras: After the Temple scene, Mark tells of two more days in which Jesus taught in the Temple courts and argued with priests, scribes and Pharisees, and warned that the Temple would be destroyed. 'Two days before the feast', the chief priests were looking for a way to arrest him quietly, saying 'Not during the feast, because there might be a riot among the people' (Mark 14:1–2). The crowds were the problem: they had to find him at night, away from them.

That evening, at Bethany, a woman poured a jar of costly perfume over his head, and he said she had anointed his body for burial. You read that story in 'Light, stone and glass'. Straight after it, Mark tells us, one of the twelve went to the chief priests.
background.key: The priests wanted to arrest Jesus quietly, away from the Passover crowds; after the anointing at Bethany, Judas went to them.

paras: If you have taken 'Exodus and the law', you know the first Passover: the lamb, the blood on the doorposts, the meal eaten in haste on the night of escape, and God's command, 'This day shall be a memorial for you' (Exodus 12:14). In Jesus's day the lambs were killed in the Temple on the afternoon of the 14th of the month of Nisan, and eaten that night inside the city walls, in households and groups of friends. (A Jewish day begins at sunset, so the meal fell on the 15th.)

The meal had unleavened bread, bitter herbs, wine and the lamb, and ended with the 'Hallel', Psalms 113 to 118, sung together. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law written down around AD 200, describes the order of the meal (Pesahim 10): the cups of wine, the son's questions, the father's explanation of each food. How much of that order goes back to Jesus's time is debated. But the heart of it is old: at Passover, the father explains what the bread and the meal mean.
background.key: Passover lambs were killed in the Temple on 14 Nisan and eaten that night with unleavened bread, wine and psalms; at the meal, the host explained what each food meant.

background.h: Three witnesses: Mark, John and Paul
paras: We have the supper from three independent directions. Mark, the earliest Gospel, gives the betrayal, the meal and the words over the bread and cup. John's Gospel, probably written around AD 90 to 100 and linked by tradition to 'the disciple whom Jesus loved' (John 21:24), has no words over the bread and cup at all; instead he tells of Jesus washing his followers' feet, and gives his long farewell speeches (John 13–17).

The third witness is older than either. Around AD 53 to 55, Paul wrote a letter to the church at Corinth, in Greece, and reminded them of what Jesus did 'on the night in which he was betrayed'. That is the earliest written account of the Last Supper we have, written about twenty-five years after it.

background.key: Mark gives the words over the bread and cup, John the foot-washing, and Paul, writing c. AD 54, the earliest account of all.

paras: The main reading has three parts: Judas's betrayal and the preparations (Mark 14:10–21), the bread and the cup (Mark 14:22–31), and the washing of the feet (John 13:1–17). Luke's account of the supper was read in 'Exodus and the law', and Bach's setting of Matthew's in 'The sound of faith'; what happened next, in the garden of Gethsemane, is read in 'How to pray'.
The comparison is Paul's account, 1 Corinthians 11:23–26. It answers a historian's question directly: was this meal's meaning invented later by the church, or does it go back to Jesus?
background.key: Mark on the betrayal and the bread and cup, John on the foot-washing, then Paul's earlier account.
