What does Jesus say about Peter, and how does Peter answer?
In John, what reason does Jesus give for washing their feet?
sessions.readWhy: The last night in three parts: the betrayal, the bread and the cup, and the towel.

paras: Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went away to the chief priests, that he might deliver him to them.
They, when they heard it, were glad, and promised to give him money. He sought how he might conveniently deliver him.
On the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, his disciples asked him, “Where do you want us to go and prepare that you may eat the Passover?”
He sent two of his disciples, and said to them, “Go into the city, and there you will meet a man carrying a pitcher of water. Follow him,
and wherever he enters in, tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, “Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?” ’
He will himself show you a large upper room furnished and ready. Get ready for us there.”
His disciples went out, and came into the city, and found things as he had said to them, and they prepared the Passover.
When it was evening he came with the twelve.
As they sat and were eating, Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, one of you will betray me—he who eats with me.”
They began to be sorrowful, and to ask him one by one, “Surely not I?” And another said, “Surely not I?”
He answered them, “It is one of the twelve, he who dips with me in the dish.
For the Son of Man goes, even as it is written about him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”
As they were eating, Jesus took bread, and when he had blessed, he broke it, and gave to them, and said, “Take, eat. This is my body.”
He took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave to them. They all drank of it.
He said to them, “This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many.
Most certainly I tell you, I will no more drink of the fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it anew in God’s Kingdom.”
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Jesus said to them, “All of you will be made to stumble because of me tonight, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’
However, after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee.”
But Peter said to him, “Although all will be offended, yet I will not.”
Jesus said to him, “Most certainly I tell you, that you today, even this night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”
But he spoke all the more, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” They all said the same thing.
Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,
Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”
Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.”
Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!”
Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.”
For he knew him who would betray him, therefore he said, “You are not all clean.”
So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.
Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

parts.title: Betrayal and preparation
parts.context: Wednesday and Thursday of Holy Week. The chief priests want to arrest Jesus away from the crowds. On Thursday, the day the Passover lambs are killed, Jesus sends two disciples into the city to prepare the meal.

commentary.on: Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went away to the chief priests, that he might deliver him to them.
commentary.text: Mark gives no motive. Matthew says Judas asked for money and was paid thirty pieces of silver (26:15); Luke and John say Satan entered him (Luke 22:3; John 13:27). What Judas offered was what the priests needed: where Jesus would be at night, away from the crowds.

commentary.on: On the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover
commentary.text: Mark dates this clearly: the day the lambs were killed. On his reckoning the supper that evening is the Passover meal itself. Remember this detail; John dates it differently.

commentary.on: a man carrying a pitcher of water
commentary.text: Fetching water was usually women's work, so a man with a water jar would stand out. It sounds like a sign arranged in advance, so that the place stays secret until the last moment.

commentary.on: a large upper room furnished and ready
commentary.text: Christian tradition places the 'upper room' on Mount Zion, in the south-west of the old city. The building pilgrims visit there now, the Cenacle, dates from the Crusader period, many centuries later.

commentary.on: one of you will betray me—he who eats with me
commentary.text: To eat with someone was to be bound to them. The words echo Psalm 41:9: 'my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.'

commentary.on: It would be better for that man if he had not been born.
commentary.text: Jesus says his death is 'as it is written', part of God's purpose, and also that the man who brings it about is fully responsible. The Bible often holds the two together.

parts.title: This is my body
parts.context: The meal itself, on Thursday night. Jesus is the host; as at every Passover, the host gives thanks over the bread and the wine and says what they mean.

commentary.on: Jesus took bread, and when he had blessed, he broke it, and gave to them
commentary.text: Four verbs: took, blessed, broke, gave. Every Christian Eucharist since has had this shape. At a Jewish meal the blessing over bread was a thanksgiving, praising God as the one who brings bread out of the earth; the Greek word for giving thanks, eucharistein, gave the meal its name, the Eucharist.

commentary.on: Take, eat. This is my body.
commentary.text: At Passover the host would explain the food: this is the bread of affliction our fathers ate in Egypt. Jesus instead says: this is my body. In Aramaic, the language he spoke, the sentence would probably have had no word for 'is' at all. What exactly he meant has divided Christians for five hundred years; the lecture sets the views side by side.

commentary.on: This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many.
commentary.text: Three echoes in one sentence. At Sinai, Moses sealed the covenant by sprinkling blood and saying 'Look, this is the blood of the covenant' (Exodus 24:8). Jeremiah promised a 'new covenant' written on the heart (31:31). And 'for many' recalls the servant in Isaiah who 'bore the sins of many' (53:12), read in 'Kings and prophets'. Jesus is saying his death will do what the sacrifices at Sinai did: bind God and his people together.

commentary.on: I will no more drink of the fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it anew in God's Kingdom.
commentary.text: A vow, and a hope. He expects to die, and he expects God's kingdom to come after his death: the prophets pictured it as a great feast (Isaiah 25:6).

commentary.on: When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
commentary.text: Almost certainly the Hallel psalms that closed the Passover meal. Psalm 118 is among them, with the line the crowds shouted on Sunday: 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'

commentary.on: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.
commentary.text: Zechariah again (13:7). The prophet who gave the king on a donkey also gave the shepherd struck down.

commentary.on: after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee.
commentary.text: Keep this promise in mind. It will come back.

commentary.on: before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.
commentary.text: Peter, the leader of the twelve, swears loyalty and will break his word within hours (14:66–72). Would the first Christians have invented a story that shamed their own leader? Historians think not, which is one reason they trust it.

parts.title: The servant's towel
parts.context: John's account of the same evening. John does not say it is the Passover meal; he says it is 'before the feast of the Passover'. In place of the words over the bread and cup, he tells of something Jesus did before the meal was over.

commentary.on: Now before the feast of the Passover
commentary.text: John's timing differs from Mark's: for John the Passover lambs are killed the next afternoon, while Jesus is on the cross. The lecture asks why.

commentary.on: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
commentary.text: 'To the end' (Greek eis telos) means both to the end of his life and to the uttermost. On the cross, in John, his last word is 'It is finished' (19:30), from the same root.

commentary.on: knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands
commentary.text: Notice the logic. Because he knows he holds all power, he gets up and takes a towel. In John, power is shown by service.

commentary.on: laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
commentary.text: Guests' feet were dusty from sandals and roads. Washing them was the job of a slave, or of a devoted wife or pupil. A teacher washing his pupils' feet turned the order of the ancient world upside down.

commentary.on: You will never wash my feet!
commentary.text: Peter's protest is about rank: a master should not kneel to a follower. It is the same mistake he made when Jesus spoke of suffering (Mark 8:32).

commentary.on: If I don't wash you, you have no part with me.
commentary.text: The washing points beyond itself, to the death that will make them clean. To belong to Jesus is to let him serve you first.

commentary.on: you also ought to wash one another's feet.
commentary.text: Later the same night, in John, Jesus gives a 'new commandment': love one another (13:34). In Latin 'commandment' is mandatum, which is why this Thursday is called Maundy Thursday. Popes, bishops and many ministers still wash feet on this night.

commentary.on: If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
commentary.text: Knowing is not enough. The session's practice takes this at its word.

paras: For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread.
When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”
In the same way he also took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

parts.title: On the night in which he was betrayed
parts.context: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53 to 55, to a church he had founded in Corinth. Its shared meals had gone wrong: the rich ate and drank first and the poor went hungry (11:21–22). To correct them, Paul reminds them what the meal is.

commentary.on: For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you
commentary.text: 'Received' and 'delivered' were the words Jewish teachers used for handing on a tradition faithfully, word for word. Paul is not composing; he is passing on what he was taught, probably within a few years of the crucifixion. The same pair of words opens his list of Easter witnesses (15:3), which you met in 'What is the Bible?'.

commentary.on: the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread
commentary.text: Paul, who never mentions many events of Jesus's life, knows these: it was at night, and it was the night of the betrayal.

commentary.on: This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.
commentary.text: Paul and Luke have the command 'Do this in memory of me'; Mark does not. The word for memory, anamnesis, is the word the Greek Bible used for Passover as a 'memorial'. To remember, in this sense, is not just to recall but to make the past event present, as every Passover makes the Exodus present.

commentary.on: This cup is the new covenant in my blood.
commentary.text: Paul's wording differs slightly from Mark's 'my blood of the covenant'. Scholars think the words reached Mark and Paul by two separate routes, which makes them stronger evidence: two lines of tradition, both going back before AD 50, both with Jesus giving the bread and cup a meaning tied to his death.

commentary.on: you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.
commentary.text: The meal itself is a kind of preaching, and it looks forward as well as back.

compare.why: Did the church invent the meaning of the supper later? Paul's account, written about twenty-five years after the night itself and before any Gospel, answers that question.
compare.title: The earliest account

paras: Mark, Matthew and Luke say the supper was the Passover meal: Jesus ate it on the evening of the day the lambs were killed, and was crucified the next day, the feast itself. John says the supper was 'before the feast'; the next morning the priests would not enter Pilate's headquarters 'that they might ... eat the Passover' (18:28), and Jesus was condemned on 'the Preparation Day of the Passover' (19:14), the day the lambs were killed.

So the two accounts agree on the day of the week, a Friday, the day before the Sabbath, and on a supper the night before. They disagree on how that Friday fits the feast. In Mark it is Passover day. In John it is the day before, and Jesus dies in the afternoon as the lambs are being killed in the Temple.

rows: Friday, the first day of the feast
Friday, 'the Preparation Day', as the lambs were killed
A Friday, the day before the Sabbath
A Friday, the day before the Sabbath
table.note: In both, the Sabbath begins at sunset on the Friday.

sections.key: Both accounts put the supper on Thursday night and the death on Friday; Mark makes the supper the Passover meal, John puts the death at the hour the lambs were killed.

paras: Scholars have proposed four main answers. First, Mark is right and John has moved the date for a theological reason: John calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God' (1:29) and quotes the Passover law 'a bone of him will not be broken' (19:36; Exodus 12:46), so he has Jesus die with the lambs. Joachim Jeremias, in The Eucharistic Words of Jesus (1935; English 1966), argued at length that the supper had all the marks of a Passover: at night, in Jerusalem, reclining, with wine, with words of explanation, ending with a hymn.

Second, John is right, and the supper was a farewell meal the night before Passover, which the other Gospels later made into a Passover. Raymond Brown and John P. Meier leaned this way: it is hard to believe the high priests held a trial and an execution on the feast day itself.

Third, different groups kept different calendars. Annie Jaubert (1957) pointed to the solar calendar used by the community at Qumran, and Colin Humphreys (2011) to an older Jewish calendar; on these views Jesus ate a Passover earlier in the week. Fourth, astronomy: in 1983 Humphreys and W. G. Waddington calculated that 14 Nisan fell on a Friday in AD 30 and AD 33, which fits John's date and gives the two likeliest years for the crucifixion.
sections.key: John moved the date for theology; Mark made a farewell meal a Passover; there were two calendars: each answer has scholars behind it, and astronomy fits John's Friday in AD 30 or 33.

paras: Whichever date is right, the meal was soaked in Passover. And Passover was about a covenant: God freed a people from slavery and bound them to himself at Sinai, sealed with blood (Exodus 24:8). Jeremiah promised a new covenant, with the law written on the heart and sins forgiven (31:31–34), which you read in 'Exodus and the law'.

At the supper Jesus took the two central symbols of the meal and gave them a new meaning. The bread is his body. The cup is the covenant in his blood, poured out for many. He was saying that his coming death would be a new Exodus and a new Sinai: a liberation, and a binding of God and people. Paul could later write simply, 'Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed in our place' (1 Corinthians 5:7).

For the historian this matters. The words over the bread and cup reached Mark and Paul by separate routes, both early. It is very hard to explain them as an idea the church invented after Easter. Jesus seems to have known he would die, and to have said in advance what his death would mean.
sections.key: Jesus turned the Passover bread and cup into signs of his own death as a new covenant; the early, independent accounts make it likely the words are his.

paras: Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve. 'Iscariot' may mean 'man of Kerioth', a town in Judea, which would make him the only one of the twelve not from Galilee; no one is sure. John says he kept the group's money and stole from it (12:6). Why he betrayed Jesus, the Gospels do not agree: for money (Matthew), because Satan entered him (Luke, John). Modern writers have guessed that he was disappointed in a Messiah who would not fight, or wanted to force his hand. These are guesses; the sources are silent. What the sources do agree on is the horror of it: Judas was one of the twelve, chosen by Jesus, who dipped in the same dish. Christians have never been able to say that betrayal came only from outside.

His death is told twice, differently. In Matthew (27:3–10) he throws the money back into the Temple and hangs himself, and the priests buy a potter's field with it. In Acts (1:18–19) he buys a field himself and falls headlong. Both remember a 'field of blood' in Jerusalem linked to Judas. A text called the Gospel of Judas, written in the 100s and known to the bishop Irenaeus around 180, was rediscovered in a Coptic copy and published in 2006; it makes Judas the hero. Scholars agree it tells us about a second-century sect, not about Judas.
sections.key: Judas was one of the twelve; the Gospels give different motives and two accounts of his death; the second-century Gospel of Judas is not evidence for what he did.

sections.h: This is my body: how the churches understand it
paras: Every main tradition keeps the supper, and calls it by different names: the Mass, the Divine Liturgy, the Eucharist, Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper. All agree that Jesus commanded it and that in it believers meet him. They disagree about how the bread and wine relate to his body and blood. At Marburg in 1529, Martin Luther and Ulrich Zwingli agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles and split on this one; Luther is said to have chalked 'This is my body', in Latin, on the table.

cols: What happens to the bread and wine
rows: Their substance becomes the body and blood of Christ, though they still look and taste like bread and wine ('transubstantiation'); the Mass makes present the one sacrifice of the cross
Fourth Lateran Council (1215); Council of Trent (1551)
A real change into the body and blood, by the Holy Spirit, called down in a prayer (the epiclesis); a mystery not to be defined
The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
Christ's body and blood are truly present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine
Augsburg Confession, Article 10 (1530); Formula of Concord (1577)
Christ is truly present and received; a range of views on how; transubstantiation rejected
Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 28 (1571); Book of Common Prayer
Christ is truly given, spiritually, by the Spirit, to those who receive in faith
A memorial and an act of obedience: 'is' means 'represents' (an 'ordinance', not a sacrament)
table.note: Many churches have moved closer in recent decades; the Anglican–Roman Catholic International Commission agreed a statement on the Eucharist in 1971.

sections.key: All the churches keep the supper; Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Anglicans affirm a real presence in different ways, the Reformed a spiritual presence, and many free churches a memorial.

sections.h: From an upper room to the whole world
paras: The first Christians met to 'break bread' in their homes from the start (Acts 2:46). By about AD 155, the philosopher Justin Martyr, writing to the emperor in Rome, could describe how Christians gathered every Sunday, read from the writings of the apostles and prophets, prayed, and shared bread and wine over which thanks had been given. He explained that Christians did not receive it as ordinary food and drink, but as the flesh and blood of Jesus (First Apology 65–67).

The foot-washing has its own history. In many churches the priest or bishop washes the feet of twelve people on Maundy Thursday; in 2013 Pope Francis washed the feet of young prisoners in Rome, including women and Muslims. Some Christian groups, such as the Mennonites and the Brethren, keep foot-washing as a regular practice. English monarchs once washed the feet of poor people on this day; today the King gives specially minted 'Maundy money' to older people chosen for their service to church and community.
sections.key: Christians have shared the bread and cup since the first weeks, every Sunday by the 150s; the foot-washing survives on Maundy Thursday and in some churches every time they meet.

refs: Mishnah, Pesahim 10. Justin Martyr, First Apology 65–67 (c. 155). Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.31.1 (on the Gospel of Judas).

Colin J. Humphreys, The Mystery of the Last Supper (2011). Raymond E. Brown, The Death of the Messiah (1994). Brant Pitre, Jesus and the Last Supper (2015).

debate.question: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?

positions.name: Yes: a Passover meal
positions.who: Joachim Jeremias (1935); Brant Pitre (2015); many scholars
positions.view: Mark is right. The meal had all the marks of a Passover: held at night inside Jerusalem, reclining, with wine, words of explanation over the food, and a closing hymn. John changed the date to make a theological point about the Lamb of God.
positions.evidence: Mark 14:12–16; the hymn (14:26); Paul's 'Christ our Passover' (1 Corinthians 5:7); John's interest in Jesus as the lamb (1:29; 19:36).

positions.name: No: a farewell meal the night before
positions.who: Raymond E. Brown (1994); John P. Meier; others
positions.view: John is right. Jesus died as the lambs were killed; the supper was a solemn farewell meal in the shadow of Passover, which the other Gospels later made into the Passover itself. A trial and execution on the feast day is very unlikely.
positions.evidence: John 18:28 and 19:14; the priests' 'Not during the feast' (Mark 14:2); no lamb is mentioned in any account of the supper.

positions.name: Both: two calendars
positions.who: Annie Jaubert (1957); Colin Humphreys (2011)
positions.view: Jesus followed a different calendar from the Temple's and ate the Passover earlier in the week, so Mark's meal was a Passover and John's date for the official feast is also right. This also gives more time for the arrest and trials.
positions.evidence: The Qumran community's solar calendar; an early Christian tradition that the supper was on the Tuesday evening (the Didascalia, 3rd century).

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus shared a last meal with the twelve in Jerusalem at Passover time, that Judas betrayed him that night, and that he gave the bread and cup a meaning tied to his death.

look.why: Garofalo, a painter from Ferrara in northern Italy, painted this around 1520 to 1525. It shows the moment of John 13:5: Jesus on his knees with the basin, among the twelve.
points: Twelve people sit and stand along a curved white stone bench; a thirteenth, Jesus, kneels at the centre.
Jesus, seen in profile, has blond shoulder-length ringlets and a pointed beard, and wears a red, gold-trimmed robe over a white garment.
He holds the lower leg of a seated man with short curly white hair and washes his foot in a gold-coloured basin; the man looks down at him, one hand flat against his chest, as if to protest.

A faint gold halo circles every head but one: a man near the lower right, who looks out at us and points towards Jesus. A pouch is tucked into the band round his orange robe. (John 12:6 says Judas kept the common purse, and painters often marked him this way.)
Behind the group rises a white stone building with columns.

music.why: 'Hail, true body': Mozart's short motet of 1791, written for the feast of Corpus Christi, on the body given at the supper and on the cross.

think.why: A teacher kneeling to wash his pupils' feet turned the ancient order of rank upside down. See how the belief that every person has dignity grew in the West.

learn.why: The oldest written words of the Last Supper, said at every Eucharist. They take up the Passover command you may know from Exodus: 'This day shall be a memorial for you.'

check.q: Why does Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11 matter so much to historians?
options: Because Paul was present at the supper
Because it is the only account that mentions bread
Because it agrees with John's date for the supper
Because it is the earliest written account, and uses the language of handing on a fixed tradition, so the words go back before AD 50
check.why: Paul was not there; but writing c. AD 54 he passes on what he 'received', a tradition independent of Mark.

check.q: What do Mark and John agree on about the timing?
options: That the supper was on Thursday night and the crucifixion on Friday, the day before the Sabbath
That the supper was on Tuesday
That Jesus died on the feast day itself
That the supper was the Passover meal
check.why: They disagree about how the Friday relates to Passover, not about the day of the week.

check.q: In John's account, what is the point of 'knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands' just before Jesus takes a towel?
options: That he knew Judas would betray him
That his supreme power is shown in doing a slave's work
That he was about to perform a miracle
That the disciples' feet were very dirty
check.why: John links the two on purpose: because he holds all things, he serves.

check.q: When Jesus says 'This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many', which earlier texts is he drawing on?
options: Roman laws about contracts
The Psalms of David only
The creation story and the flood
Moses sealing the covenant with blood at Sinai, Jeremiah's new covenant and the servant who bore the sins of many
check.why: Exodus 24:8, Jeremiah 31:31 and Isaiah 53:12 all sound in the sentence.

check.q: Which statement best describes how the churches differ about the bread and wine?
options: Protestants reject the Last Supper as unhistorical
They agree Christ commanded it, but differ on how he is present: a change of substance, a mystery, 'in, with and under', a spiritual gift, or a memorial
All churches teach transubstantiation
Only Catholics celebrate the Eucharist
check.why: The disagreement is about the manner of Christ's presence, not about keeping the meal.

check.q: Why do historians think the story of Peter's boast and denial is probably true?
options: Because Peter wrote it down himself
Because it shames the leader of the early church, which the first Christians are unlikely to have invented
Because a rooster was found at the site
Because it appears only in John
check.why: Stories embarrassing to the people who told them are less likely to be invented.

tutorial.question: What did Jesus mean by 'This is my body'? Answer as a historian first, then set out how the churches have answered.
tutorial.approach: Begin with the setting: a Passover, or a meal in Passover's shadow, where the host explained the food. Use Mark and Paul as early, independent witnesses, and the echoes of Exodus 24, Jeremiah 31 and Isaiah 53. Say what a historian can conclude about what Jesus intended. Then set the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and memorial views side by side, and say which best fits the evidence you have described, and why.
strong: Explains the Passover setting and the dating problem fairly.
Uses Paul (c. AD 54) and Mark as independent early witnesses.
Connects 'covenant', 'blood' and 'for many' to Exodus, Jeremiah and Isaiah.
Draws a careful historical conclusion: Jesus gave his coming death a meaning in advance.
Sets out at least three church traditions accurately, without caricature.
Distinguishes what history can show from what faith or doctrine adds.

reading.title: Jesus and the Last Supper
reading.why: A Catholic scholar's full case that the supper was a Passover meal with a new meaning.

reading.author: Colin J. Humphreys
reading.title: The Mystery of the Last Supper
reading.why: A physicist's attempt to solve the dating problem with astronomy and old calendars.

reading.why: The classic study of the words over the bread and cup and their Passover setting (German 1935).

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do one piece of unseen, humble service each day for someone in your home or at work, a job usually left to someone else, without mentioning it. At the end of the week, write down what it was like to do it, and what it was like not to be thanked.
sessions.reflect: Peter would rather wash himself than be washed. Is it harder for you to serve, or to let someone serve you?
takeaways: Jesus's last meal was held at Passover time; Mark makes it the Passover meal, John dates his death to the hour the lambs were killed, and scholars still debate which is right.
Over the bread and cup Jesus said what his death would mean: his body, and a new covenant in his blood for many; Paul's account, c. AD 54, shows these words go back very early.
In John he washed his followers' feet: power shown as service, and an example to follow.

sessions.title: On trial
sessions.line: Before dawn on Friday the high priests hand Jesus to the Roman governor. Pilate asks if he is a king, has him flogged, and gives the crowd a choice.
sessions.plain: Early on the Friday morning, the high priests brought Jesus, bound, to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, because only Rome could put a man to death. Pilate questioned him about one thing, whether he claimed to be 'King of the Jews', had him flogged and mocked, and in the end handed him over to be crucified. For centuries Christians blamed 'the Jews' for his death, with terrible results. This session asks why he was killed, who was responsible, and what the evidence outside the Gospels says about Pilate.
sessions.why: Session 2 ended on Thursday night with the supper, where Jesus said what his death would mean. Later that night he was arrested in a garden on the Mount of Olives and questioned by the high priest. Now the case goes to the one man who could order an execution.
answers: Why did they kill Jesus?
Why did the high priests need Pilate?
What was Pilate really like?
Who was responsible for Jesus's death: the Romans, the Jewish leaders, or 'the Jews'?
How was the charge against 'the Jews' used, and what do the churches say now?
sessions.finding: The high priests handed him to Pilate as a threat to order, and Rome crucified him as 'King of the Jews'; the Gospels' 'the Jews' has a terrible later history.

paras: After the supper, Jesus went with his followers to Gethsemane, an olive garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives, and prayed in anguish; that prayer is read in 'How to pray'. Judas arrived with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests and identified him with a kiss. His followers ran away (Mark 14:43–50).

That night he was taken to the high priest's house. In 'Who was Jesus?' you read Mark's account of the hearing: witnesses who could not agree, the charge that he had threatened the Temple, and his answer when the high priest asked if he was the Messiah: 'I am', and they would see the Son of Man coming with the clouds (Mark 14:53–65). The high priest called it blasphemy. Outside, in the courtyard, Peter swore three times that he did not know him.
background.key: Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane after Judas's kiss, questioned at night by the high priest, and accused of blasphemy; Peter denied him.

paras: Judea had two kinds of authority. The Jewish council, the Sanhedrin, led by the high priest, judged matters of Jewish law and ran the Temple. The Roman governor kept order and alone held the power of life and death. In John, the priests say so: 'It is illegal for us to put anyone to death' (18:31). A later Jewish source, the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin 1:1), remembers that the right to judge capital cases was taken from Israel forty years before the Temple fell.

There is supporting evidence. In AD 62, between two Roman governors, the high priest Ananus had James, the brother of Jesus, stoned; Josephus says the new governor was told, and Ananus was removed from office for acting without permission (Antiquities 20.9.1). The one exception Rome allowed was the Temple itself: a foreigner who entered its inner courts could be killed. Crucifixion was never a Jewish punishment. If Jesus died on a cross, Rome killed him.
background.key: The Jewish council judged religious law; only the Roman governor could execute, and crucifixion was a Roman punishment.

paras: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36. He was a Roman of the equestrian class, the rank below senators, with a small army of auxiliary soldiers, a few thousand men, mostly recruited from the non-Jewish cities of the region. In 1961 Italian archaeologists working in the theatre at Caesarea found a stone reused in a later building; its Latin inscription names '[Pon]tius Pilatus', '[Praef]ectus Iuda[eae]', prefect of Judea, dedicating a building in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It is the only inscription from his lifetime that names him.

Josephus tells several stories about him. He sent troops into Jerusalem by night carrying standards with the emperor's image, and backed down only when a crowd at Caesarea lay down and bared their necks rather than accept it. He took money from the Temple treasury to build an aqueduct, and had protesters clubbed by soldiers in disguise. In 36 he attacked a crowd of Samaritans, and the governor of Syria sent him to Rome to answer for it (Antiquities 18.3.1–2; 18.4.1–2; Jewish War 2.9.2–4). Luke mentions Galileans 'whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices' (13:1).

timeline.text: Caiaphas becomes high priest

background.key: Pilate, prefect AD 26–36, is named on a stone found at Caesarea; Josephus remembers him as provocative and violent, though able to back down.

paras: The main reading is John's account of the trial before Pilate (John 18:28–19:16), the fullest in the Gospels. John knows the places, the governor's headquarters and a stone pavement called Gabbatha, and he tells the story as a drama that moves between Pilate inside with Jesus and the priests outside. Mark's shorter account is part of the next session's reading.

The comparison answers a historian's question about the Gospels' Pilate, who seems to want to let Jesus go: is that believable, or have Christians whitewashed Rome? Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer who lived at the same time, tells a story about Pilate that shows what kind of man he was, and what he was afraid of.
background.key: John's full account of the Roman trial, then Philo's portrait of Pilate to test it.

paras: They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. It was early, and they themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.
Pilate therefore went out to them, and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man weren’t an evildoer, we wouldn’t have delivered him up to you.”
Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law.”
Therefore the Jews said to him, “It is illegal for us to put anyone to death,”
that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
Pilate therefore entered again into the Praetorium, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”
Jesus answered him, “Do you say this by yourself, or did others tell you about me?”
Pilate answered, “I’m not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests delivered you to me. What have you done?”
Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.”
Pilate therefore said to him, “Are you a king then?”

Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?”
When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him.
But you have a custom, that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Therefore, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
Then they all shouted again, saying, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
So Pilate then took Jesus, and flogged him.
The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment.
They kept saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and they kept slapping him.
Then Pilate went out again, and said to them, “Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.”
Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, “Behold, the man!”
When therefore the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted, saying, “Crucify! Crucify!”
Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves, and crucify him, for I find no basis for a charge against him.”
The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”
When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid.
He entered into the Praetorium again, and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.
Pilate therefore said to him, “Aren’t you speaking to me? Don’t you know that I have power to release you and have power to crucify you?”
Jesus answered, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.”
At this, Pilate was seeking to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying, “If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend! Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!”
When Pilate therefore heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called “The Pavement”, but in Hebrew, “Gabbatha.”
Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold, your King!”
They cried out, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!”
Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?”
The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar!”
So then he delivered him to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus and led him away.

parts.title: Are you the King of the Jews?
parts.context: Early on Friday morning. The high priest's men bring Jesus to the Praetorium, the governor's headquarters. At the feasts Pilate probably stayed in Herod's old palace on the west side of the city. John has the trial move in and out: the priests stay outside, Pilate goes in to Jesus and out to them.

commentary.on: They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. It was early
commentary.text: Roman officials began their working day at first light. Handing Jesus over early meant the matter could be finished, and the body buried, before the Sabbath began at sunset.

commentary.on: they themselves didn't enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover
commentary.text: Entering a Gentile's house would make them ritually unclean for the feast. John lets the irony speak: they are careful about purity while handing over an innocent man. It also shows John's dating: the Passover meal is still to come.

commentary.on: If this man weren't an evildoer, we wouldn't have delivered him up to you.
commentary.text: They give no charge. 'Delivered up' runs right through the Passion story: Judas hands Jesus to the priests, the priests to Pilate, Pilate to the soldiers.

commentary.on: It is illegal for us to put anyone to death
commentary.text: The legal heart of the matter: the council can judge, but only Rome can kill.

commentary.on: Are you the King of the Jews?
commentary.text: In all four Gospels this is the first thing Pilate says to Jesus. Rome did not care about blasphemy. It cared about kings. A man who claimed to be king of a Roman province was guilty of treason, and the penalty for a non-citizen was the cross.

commentary.on: My Kingdom is not of this world.
commentary.text: Not 'not in this world' but 'not from this world': its authority does not come from armies. His proof is that his servants do not fight. In John, Peter drew a sword at the arrest, and Jesus told him to put it away (18:10–11).

commentary.on: What is truth?
commentary.text: Pilate's famous question. He does not wait for an answer; he goes straight out to the priests. Francis Bacon opened his essay 'Of Truth' (1625) with this scene: the governor who asked about truth and did not stay to hear.

commentary.on: I find no basis for a charge against him.
commentary.text: Pilate says this three times in John (18:38; 19:4; 19:6). The Gospel writers are keen to show that Rome's own judge found Jesus innocent.

commentary.on: Not this man, but Barabbas!
commentary.text: The custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover is not recorded anywhere outside the Gospels, and historians debate it. Barabbas means 'son of the father' in Aramaic. Some old manuscripts of Matthew call him 'Jesus Barabbas' (27:16–17): the crowd chooses between two men called Jesus.

commentary.on: Now Barabbas was a robber.
commentary.text: The Greek word, lēstēs, means a bandit, and is the word Josephus uses for armed rebels. Mark says Barabbas was in prison with insurgents who had committed murder (15:7). The crowd chooses the man who fought Rome over the man who would not.

parts.title: Behold, the man!
parts.context: Still Friday morning. Pilate tries one more way out: perhaps if the crowd sees Jesus beaten and humiliated, they will be satisfied.

commentary.on: So Pilate then took Jesus, and flogged him.
commentary.text: Roman flogging was done with a whip of leather thongs weighted with bone or metal. It could kill. In Mark it comes just before the crucifixion; in John, Pilate seems to use it to win sympathy.

commentary.on: The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment.
commentary.text: A crown, royal purple, and a mocking salute: the soldiers play at crowning a king. They were probably auxiliaries recruited from the non-Jewish cities nearby, men with little love for Jews or their hopes.

commentary.on: Behold, the man!
commentary.text: In Latin, Ecce homo, the title of countless paintings. Pilate perhaps means: look at him, bleeding and ridiculous; is this a threat to anyone? John's readers hear more: here is what a human being looks like, and what human beings do to goodness.

commentary.on: he made himself the Son of God.
commentary.text: Now the religious charge comes out. The law of Leviticus (24:16) punished blasphemy with death. Pilate, John says, 'was more afraid': Romans had their own stories of divine men, and of judges who wronged them.

commentary.on: You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above.
commentary.text: Pilate boasts of his power; Jesus says it is borrowed, from God. Then he grades the guilt: 'he who delivered me to you has greater sin'. Even here, John does not make everyone equally responsible.

commentary.on: If you release this man, you aren't Caesar's friend!
commentary.text: This is what breaks Pilate. 'Friend of Caesar' may have been an honorary title for loyal officials. The threat is that they will report him to Tiberius for letting a would-be king go: exactly the threat you will see in the comparison, in a story about Pilate from another source.

commentary.on: Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour.
commentary.text: Noon on the day the Passover lambs were killed. Mark says Jesus was crucified at 'the third hour', nine in the morning (15:25). One of the two has the time wrong, or both are rounding; the ancients reckoned the day in rough quarters.

commentary.on: Shall I crucify your King?
commentary.text: Pilate turns the taunt on the priests: he mocks Jesus, and he mocks their hopes for a king.

commentary.on: We have no king but Caesar!
commentary.text: An astonishing sentence from the chief priests, whose own prayers called God the only king. Notice who says it: not 'the Jews' as a people, but the Temple's leaders, who held office at Rome's pleasure.

commentary.on: So then he delivered him to them to be crucified.
commentary.text: 'To them' is ambiguous; in fact, as John himself goes on to say, Roman soldiers did the crucifying (19:23). The sentence was Pilate's.

paras: (299) "Moreover, I have it in my power to relate one act of ambition on his part, though I suffered an infinite number of evils when he was alive; but nevertheless the truth is considered dear, and much to be honoured by you. Pilate was one of the emperor's lieutenants, having been appointed governor of Judaea. He, not more with the object of doing honour to Tiberius than with that of vexing the multitude, dedicated some gilt shields in the palace of Herod, in the holy city; which had no form nor any other forbidden thing represented on them except some necessary inscription, which mentioned these two facts, the name of the person who had placed them there, and the person in whose honour they were so placed there.

(300) But when the multitude heard what had been done, and when the circumstance became notorious, then the people, putting forward the four sons of the king, who were in no respect inferior to the kings themselves, in fortune or in rank, and his other descendants, and those magistrates who were among them at the time, entreated him to alter and to rectify the innovation which he had committed in respect of the shields; and not to make any alteration in their national customs, which had hitherto been preserved without any interruption, without being in the least degree changed by any king of emperor. (301) "But when he steadfastly refused this petition (for he was a man of a very inflexible disposition, and very merciless as well as very obstinate), they cried out: 'Do not cause a sedition; do not make war upon us; do not destroy the peace which exists. The honour of the emperor is not identical with dishonour to the ancient laws; let it not be to you a pretence for heaping insult on our nation. Tiberius is not desirous that any of our laws or customs shall be destroyed. And if you yourself say that he is, show us either some command from him, or some letter, or something of the kind, that we, who have been sent to you as ambassadors, may cease to trouble you, and may address our supplications to your master.'

(302) "But this last sentence exasperated him in the greatest possible degree, as he feared least they might in reality go on an embassy to the emperor, and might impeach him with respect to other particulars of his government, in respect of his corruption, and his acts of insolence, and his rapine, and his habit of insulting people, and his cruelty, and his continual murders of people untried and uncondemned, and his never ending, and gratuitous, and most grievous inhumanity. (303) Therefore, being exceedingly angry, and being at all times a man of most ferocious passions, he was in great perplexity, neither venturing to take down what he had once set up, nor wishing to do any thing which could be acceptable to his subjects, and at the same time being sufficiently acquainted with the firmness of Tiberius on these points. And those who were in power in our nation, seeing this, and perceiving that he was inclined to change his mind as to what he had done, but that he was not willing to be thought to do so, wrote a most supplicatory letter to Tiberius.

(304) And he, when he had read it, what did he say of Pilate, and what threats did he utter against him! But it is beside our purpose at present to relate to you how very angry he was, although he was not very liable to sudden anger; since the facts speak for themselves; (305) for immediately, without putting any thing off till the next day, he wrote a letter, reproaching and reviling him in the most bitter manner for his act of unprecedented audacity and wickedness, and commanding him immediately to take down the shields and to convey them away from the metropolis of Judaea to Caesarea, on the sea which had been named Caesarea Augusta, after his grandfather, in order that they might be set up in the temple of Augustus. And accordingly, they were set up in that edifice. And in this way he provided for two matters: both for the honour due to the emperor, and for the preservation of the ancient customs of the city.

parts.author: Philo of Alexandria
parts.ref: Philo, On the Embassy to Gaius 299–305
parts.title: The golden shields
parts.context: Philo (c. 20 BC – c. AD 50) was a Jewish philosopher in Alexandria, in Egypt. In AD 39–40 he led a Jewish embassy to the emperor Gaius, known as Caligula, who wanted his statue set up in the Temple at Jerusalem. Here Philo quotes, or composes, a letter to Gaius from Herod Agrippa I, Herod the Great's grandson, reminding him how the previous emperor, Tiberius, had dealt with Pilate. The story probably dates from about AD 31. The numbers in brackets are the modern section numbers. Translated by C. D. Yonge (1855); the source prints 'least' for 'lest' and 'king of emperor' for 'king or emperor'.
parts.plain: Pilate set up some gilded shields in Herod's palace in Jerusalem, inscribed with Tiberius's name: more to annoy the Jews than to honour the emperor. The Jewish leaders, with four of Herod's sons, begged him to take them down; he refused, being stubborn and cruel. When they threatened to complain to Tiberius, he was frightened, because they might report all his other crimes too. They wrote; Tiberius was furious and ordered the shields moved to Caesarea.

commentary.on: Pilate was one of the emperor's lieutenants, having been appointed governor of Judaea.
commentary.text: One of only two writers of Pilate's own time to describe him; the other is Josephus, who was born just after he left.

commentary.on: not more with the object of doing honour to Tiberius than with that of vexing the multitude
commentary.text: Philo's verdict on Pilate's motive: he enjoyed provoking his subjects. The shields carried no images, only an inscription, but in the holy city even that felt like a claim of ownership.

commentary.on: putting forward the four sons of the king
commentary.text: Sons of Herod the Great. One of them was probably Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, to whom Luke says Pilate sent Jesus during the trial (Luke 23:7–12).

commentary.on: for he was a man of a very inflexible disposition, and very merciless as well as very obstinate
commentary.text: This is the Pilate of Josephus too. Philo has his own reasons to paint him black: he is writing to show a mad emperor that insulting the Jews' laws displeases Rome.

commentary.on: as he feared least they might in reality go on an embassy to the emperor
commentary.text: Here is the key. The hard, cruel governor had one fear: being reported to Tiberius.

commentary.on: his continual murders of people untried and uncondemned
commentary.text: A sweeping charge. Whether or not every word is fair, this is not a man who would lose sleep over crucifying one more Galilean.

commentary.on: neither venturing to take down what he had once set up, nor wishing to do any thing which could be acceptable to his subjects
commentary.text: Stubborn, but trapped. Compare John 19:12: 'If you release this man, you aren't Caesar's friend!' In both stories, Pilate's subjects know how to move him: threaten to go over his head.

commentary.on: commanding him immediately to take down the shields
commentary.text: Tiberius sides with the Jews against his own governor. Rome's policy was to keep the peace and respect local religion; Pilate kept pushing it.

compare.author: Philo of Alexandria
compare.ref: Philo, On the Embassy to Gaius 299–305
compare.why: The Gospels' Pilate hesitates and is pushed into a decision by a threat to report him to the emperor. Is that believable? Read a story about Pilate from a Jewish writer of the same generation, who had no interest in Jesus at all.
compare.title: Pilate in a Jewish writer's eyes

paras: Put the sources together and a likely story emerges. Jesus came to Jerusalem at Passover, was hailed by crowds as the one bringing David's kingdom, and acted against the Temple. The high priests, responsible to Rome for order, had reasons of their own to fear him: his threat to the Temple, his claims, and the danger that crowds would riot and bring Roman troops down on everyone. John gives Caiaphas the words: 'it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish' (11:50).

So they arrested him at night, examined him, and handed him to Pilate on a charge Rome would understand: he claimed to be king. Pilate, who had killed men for less, had him crucified, with the charge written above him. Two writers outside the Bible agree on this outline. Tacitus, around AD 116, says Christ was executed by Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius (Annals 15.44, read in 'What is the Bible?'). Josephus, in a passage scholars think has been added to by later Christian copyists but has a genuine core, says Pilate condemned him to the cross after he was accused by the leading men of the Jews (Antiquities 18.3.3).
sections.key: The Temple authorities feared him and handed him over as a would-be king; Pilate crucified him; Tacitus and Josephus confirm the outline.

paras: In all four Gospels Pilate seems to believe Jesus innocent and to give way only under pressure. Many scholars think this is partly apologetic: Christians, writing in the Roman empire after AD 70, wanted to show that Rome's own judge had found their founder innocent, and so shifted the blame towards the Jewish leaders. Paul Winter (On the Trial of Jesus, 1961) and John Dominic Crossan (Who Killed Jesus?, 1995) argued this strongly.

Others reply that the Gospels' Pilate is not a good man: he flogs an innocent prisoner, lets soldiers mock him, taunts the priests and crucifies a man he thinks innocent to protect his own position. That fits Philo's portrait well: arrogant, provocative, cruel, and afraid of being reported. The historian Helen Bond (Pontius Pilate in History and Interpretation, 1998) concluded that each Gospel shapes Pilate for its own purposes, but that the historical Pilate was probably a fairly ordinary Roman governor, for whom executing a troublemaker at the request of the local elite was routine.
sections.key: The Gospels may soften Pilate's guilt, but their Pilate is still cruel and self-serving, and fits Philo's portrait of a governor afraid of being reported.

paras: All four Gospels say Pilate offered to release a prisoner for the feast, and the crowd chose Barabbas. No other ancient source mentions such a custom in Judea, and some historians think the story was shaped to show the people choosing a rebel over the prince of peace. Others point to a rule in the Mishnah that a Passover lamb may be killed for a person whose release from prison has been promised (Pesahim 8:6), which may hint at releases at the feast, and to Roman governors elsewhere who pardoned prisoners to please a crowd.

Whatever the custom, Barabbas himself is probably historical: an insurgent, Mark says, held with others who had committed murder 'in the insurrection', as if his readers knew which one. The Gospels make the choice a parable without needing to invent it. The crowd that chose him was not the crowd of pilgrims who had shouted 'Hosanna' five days earlier: it was the people gathered at the governor's gate at dawn, stirred up, Mark says, by the chief priests (15:11).
sections.key: The Passover pardon is not recorded outside the Gospels and is debated; Barabbas, an insurgent, is probably historical, and the dawn crowd was not the Palm Sunday crowd.

paras: John's Gospel uses the phrase 'the Jews' about seventy times, often for Jesus's opponents. Yet Jesus, his mother, all twelve disciples, the women at the cross and Joseph of Arimathea were Jews; so were the crowds that welcomed him, and the 'great multitude' of people and women Luke says mourned him on the way to the cross (Luke 23:27). In the trial scenes John means a small group: the chief priests and their officers, and a crowd at Pilate's gate, not a nation.

Many scholars think the word has a hard edge in John because of when it was written. By the 90s, followers of Jesus were being put out of some synagogues; John mentions it (9:22). The quarrel of John's day, between two groups of Jews, coloured how he told the story of Jesus. Some modern translations render the word as 'the Judeans' or 'the Jewish authorities' where that is what it means. Others keep 'the Jews' and explain it, as here.
sections.key: In the trial, John's 'the Jews' means the Temple authorities and a crowd, not the Jewish people; the hard edge reflects a later quarrel.

sections.h: 'His blood be on us': a terrible history
paras: Matthew alone tells that Pilate washed his hands, saying 'I am innocent of the blood of this righteous person', and 'all the people answered, "May his blood be on us, and on our children!"' (27:24–25). Many scholars think Matthew meant the generation that saw Jerusalem destroyed in AD 70. But Christians read it as a curse on all Jews for ever.

The consequences were dreadful. Around 170, Melito, bishop of Sardis, preached that Israel had murdered God. In 386–387 John Chrysostom preached sermons against the Jews in Antioch. In medieval Europe, Holy Week was a dangerous time for Jews, when sermons on the Passion could end in violence; the charge of 'deicide', killing God, was repeated for centuries. On Good Friday the Catholic liturgy prayed for the 'perfidious' Jews until Pope John XXIII removed the word in 1959. Luther, in On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), urged that synagogues be burned. The Nazis quoted him. The journey 'One root, two branches', later in this hall, takes up how Jews and Christians have faced this history.
sections.key: Matthew 27:25 was read for centuries as a curse on all Jews, fuelling the charge of deicide, persecution and worse.

sections.h: Who killed Jesus? What the churches say now
paras: After the Holocaust the churches looked again. Christian teaching had always also said that every sinner shares the guilt of the cross. The Catechism of the Council of Trent (1566) said so plainly, and Lutheran hymns put it in the believer's mouth: in Johann Heermann's 'Ah, holy Jesus' (1630) the singer confesses that he crucified Christ, and Bach set a similar confession in his St Matthew Passion.

rows: Antisemitism is a sin against God and man

Nostra Aetate: what happened in his passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today'; Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed
Second Vatican Council, 1965; Catechism of the Catholic Church 597–598 (1992)
Lutheran World Federation, 1984; Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, 1994
No single statement; some Orthodox scholars have asked that hostile lines in the Holy Week hymns be revised

Dabru Emet, 'Speak the truth', signed by over 170 rabbis and scholars, answered the churches: Christians worship the God of Israel, and Nazism was not a Christian phenomenon, though it drew on Christian anti-Judaism

sections.key: Since 1945 the churches have rejected blaming the Jewish people; Nostra Aetate (1965) is the landmark, and Jewish scholars answered in Dabru Emet (2000).

paras: A careful historian can say three things with confidence. First, Jesus was executed by the Roman governor, by a Roman method, on a Roman charge of claiming to be a king. Second, he was handed over by the Temple's leadership, a small group of men whose power depended on Rome and who saw him as a threat. Third, the Jewish people as a whole were not involved: most had never heard of him, many who had followed him, and his first followers were Jews.

The Gospels add a further claim that history cannot test. In Mark, Jesus walks to Jerusalem saying he must be handed over; in John he says 'No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself' (10:18). On that view, the answer to 'who killed Jesus?' is not only Caiaphas and Pilate, but no one, and everyone: he gave his life, and every human being is among those he gave it for. That is the believer's answer. It is not a historian's, and it must never again be an excuse to blame a people.
sections.key: History shows Rome executed Jesus at the instigation of the Temple leadership, not the Jewish people; Christians add that he gave his life, for all.
