debate.question: Who was responsible for the death of Jesus?

positions.name: Rome
positions.who: Paul Winter (1961); John Dominic Crossan (1995); many historians
positions.view: Pilate alone had the power to execute, the method was Roman and the charge, 'King of the Jews', was political. The Gospels, written for readers in the Roman empire, shifted the blame onto Jewish leaders to make Christians look harmless to Rome.
positions.evidence: John 18:31; the cross and the titulus; Philo and Josephus on Pilate's brutality; Tacitus names only Pilate.

positions.name: The Temple leaders and Rome together
positions.who: Raymond E. Brown (1994); E. P. Sanders (1985); Helen Bond (1998)
positions.view: A small group of priests, fearing for the Temple and for order, handed Jesus over; Pilate, for whom such executions were routine, condemned him. Responsibility was shared by a handful of powerful men, not by any people.
positions.evidence: John 11:50; Mark 14:1–2; Josephus, Antiquities 18.3.3, 'accused by the leading men'; the fate of James in AD 62.

positions.name: All of us
positions.who: The Catechism of the Council of Trent (1566); Lutheran hymns and Bach's St Matthew Passion; Nostra Aetate (1965)
positions.view: The theological answer: the cross shows what all human beings do to goodness, and Christ died for all, so every sinner shares the guilt, Christians first. Jesus also chose his death. This view rules out blaming any one people.
positions.evidence: John 10:18; Mark 10:45; the chorales in which the singer confesses 'I crucified thee'.

debate.agree: All agree that Rome carried out the execution, that a few Temple leaders handed him over, and that blaming the Jewish people, then or now, is false and has done terrible harm.

look.why: The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of Jesus before Pilate or of 'Behold, the man' that is free to use here, so this session has none rather than a stand-in. Picture instead what John describes: a stone pavement called Gabbatha, a judge's seat, a beaten man in a purple cloak, and a governor asking 'Shall I crucify your King?'

music.why: Bach's St Matthew Passion (1727) sets the trial with the crowd's cry for Barabbas, and answers it with chorales in which the congregation confesses that it is they, not the Jews, who should suffer.

think.why: Collective guilt blames a whole people for what a few did. See where the West's belief that each person answers for themselves came from.

learn.why: The psalm of a righteous man surrounded and mocked by his enemies, which Jesus will pray from the cross. Learn its first line now.

listen.why: A historian and an atheist discuss how the crucifixion shocked the Roman world, and whether Western values still rest on it.

check.q: Why did the high priests need to take Jesus to Pilate?
options: Because the council did not meet at Passover
Because Pilate was the high priest's superior in the Temple
Because Jesus was a Roman citizen
Because only the Roman governor could order an execution, and crucifixion was a Roman punishment
check.why: John 18:31, the Jerusalem Talmud and the fate of the high priest Ananus in AD 62 all point to Rome's monopoly on capital punishment.

check.q: Why is Pilate's question 'Are you the King of the Jews?' the key to the trial?
options: Because Jesus had already been crowned
Because a claim to be king of a Roman province was treason, which Rome punished with the cross
Because Pilate wanted to become king himself
Because blasphemy was a crime in Roman law
check.why: Rome cared about kings, not Jewish law; the titulus on the cross gave the political charge.

check.q: How does Philo's story of the golden shields help us judge the Gospels' account?
options: It mentions Jesus by name
It shows a stubborn, cruel Pilate who could be moved by the threat of being reported to the emperor, as in John 19:12
It shows that Pilate never came to Jerusalem
It proves Pilate was a kind and fair governor
check.why: Philo's Pilate is hard and provocative, and fears an embassy to Tiberius: the same pressure the priests use in John.

check.q: When John's trial scene says 'the Jews', what does it mostly refer to?
options: The Roman soldiers
The whole Jewish people of every age
The chief priests, their officers and a crowd at Pilate's gate
Jesus's own disciples
check.why: Jesus and his followers were Jews; in the trial the phrase means the Temple authorities and their supporters.

check.q: Which statement best describes the Catholic Church's teaching since Nostra Aetate (1965)?
options: That the Jews of Jesus's day and of today bear collective guilt for his death
That his death cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against Jews today
That the Gospels' accounts of the trial are fiction
That Pilate alone was guilty
check.why: Nostra Aetate 4 rejected collective guilt; the Catechism adds that all sinners share responsibility.

check.q: A friend says, 'The Gospels just invented a reluctant Pilate to please Rome.' What is the strongest reply?
options: That the Gospels' Pilate is still cruel and self-serving, and his fear of being reported matches Philo's independent portrait, so the picture is at least partly historical
That no historians think the Gospels shaped Pilate at all
That Pilate later became a Christian
That Tacitus describes Pilate as merciful
check.why: Many scholars do think the Gospels shaped Pilate; but the core picture fits Philo, so it is not pure invention.

tutorial.question: Who was responsible for the death of Jesus?
tutorial.approach: Separate the historical question from the theological one. For the history, set out the two courts, the evidence about Pilate in Philo and Josephus, and what Tacitus and Josephus say about Jesus's execution. Weigh the argument that the Gospels shifted blame from Rome. Then explain how Matthew 27:25 and John's 'the Jews' were later used, and what the churches have said since 1945. End with the theological answer, and say why it rules out collective blame.
strong: Explains why only Rome could execute, with evidence (John 18:31; James in AD 62).
Uses Philo and Josephus to assess the Gospels' portrait of Pilate.
Distinguishes the Temple leadership from the Jewish people.
Explains the later use of Matthew 27:25 and the charge of deicide honestly.
Cites Nostra Aetate and at least one Protestant or Jewish response.
Keeps the historical and theological answers distinct.

reading.author: Helen K. Bond
reading.title: Pontius Pilate in History and Interpretation
reading.why: The best study of the historical Pilate and how each Gospel portrays him.

reading.author: John Dominic Crossan
reading.title: Who Killed Jesus?
reading.why: A sceptical scholar's case that the Gospels' trial stories are shaped by later polemic.

reading.author: Raymond E. Brown
reading.title: The Death of the Messiah
reading.why: The standard detailed commentary on the arrest and trials.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice each time you hear, or say, a sentence that blames a whole group for what some of its members did ('they always...', 'those people...'). Each time, say or write a fairer sentence about the particular people involved. Keep a count for the week.
sessions.reflect: Pilate knew what was right and did what was safe. Where are you most tempted to do the same?
takeaways: Only Rome could execute; the high priests handed Jesus to Pilate as a would-be king, and Pilate crucified him on that charge.
Philo and Josephus show a Pilate who was provocative and cruel but afraid of being reported to the emperor, much like the Gospels' Pilate under pressure.
The Gospels' 'the Jews' and Matthew 27:25 were used for centuries to blame the Jewish people, with terrible results; since 1945 the churches have rejected collective guilt.

sessions.title: The cross
sessions.line: Jesus is crucified as 'King of the Jews' between two rebels, cries out the first line of a psalm, and dies within six hours.
sessions.plain: On the Friday, Roman soldiers nailed Jesus to a cross outside the city wall, under a notice that read 'The King of the Jews'. Crucifixion was the most shameful death the Romans had, kept for slaves and rebels, and meant to be seen. He died in the afternoon, much sooner than most, and a member of the council buried him before the Sabbath began. This session asks what crucifixion really was, what the Gospels say happened, and why the first Christians proclaimed a crucified Messiah when it was the last thing anyone would invent.
sessions.why: Session 3 followed the trial to its end: Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified as King of the Jews. Now we follow the soldiers out of the city to the place of execution.
answers: What was crucifixion really like, and what was it for?
Why did Jesus die so quickly?
What were his last words, and why do the Gospels differ?
Why would anyone preach a crucified Messiah?
sessions.finding: Crucifixion was Rome's most shameful death, meant for slaves and rebels; that the first Christians proclaimed a crucified Messiah is itself evidence they did not invent it.

paras: Jesus has been arrested at night, examined by the high priest and handed to Pontius Pilate on the charge of claiming to be king. Pilate, under pressure and with no great scruple, has had him flogged and sentenced to the cross. It is the morning of the Friday before the Sabbath, at Passover.
background.key: Pilate has sentenced Jesus to crucifixion on Friday morning, before the Sabbath, at Passover.

paras: The Romans did not invent crucifixion; the Persians and Carthaginians used it before them. But Rome made it a system. It was the 'slaves' punishment', also used for rebels, bandits and deserters, and very rarely for Roman citizens, which is why Cicero's speech in the comparison is so angry. After the slave revolt of Spartacus in 71 BC, Crassus crucified six thousand of the rebels along the Appian Way from Capua to Rome. In 4 BC, near Jerusalem, the governor of Syria, Varus, crucified about two thousand Jewish rebels (Josephus, Jewish War 2.5.2).

For Jews the cross carried an extra horror. The law said that the body of an executed man hung on a tree must be buried the same day, 'for he who is hanged is accursed of God' (Deuteronomy 21:23). By Jesus's time this was applied to the crucified. A crucified man was not only dead; he looked cursed.
background.key: Rome used the cross for slaves and rebels, in thousands; Jewish law saw anyone hanged on a tree as accursed.

background.h: Who wrote Luke, and why we read these passages
paras: The main reading is the whole of Mark 15, from the morning hearing to the burial, and a passage from Luke 23. Luke wrote around AD 80 to 90; tradition names him as a doctor and a companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14). At the start of his Gospel he says he used earlier accounts and eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4, read in 'What is the Bible?'). He used Mark, and he had other sources too: the conversation with the two criminals and Jesus's last prayer are found only in Luke.

The comparison is two passages from outside the Bible: Cicero, the greatest Roman orator, on the crucifixion of a Roman citizen, and Josephus, who watched the Romans crucify hundreds of Jews a day outside Jerusalem in AD 70. They show what the word 'cross' meant to a Roman and to a Jew.
background.key: Mark 15 whole and Luke's account of the death; then a Roman and a Jewish witness to what crucifixion was.

before: Count the people who mock Jesus. What do they say?
What does Jesus say from the cross in Mark, and what in Luke?
Who is watching at the end, and who buries him?
sessions.readWhy: The day of the crucifixion in four parts: handed over, Golgotha, the death and burial, and Luke's account of the last hours.

paras: Immediately in the morning the chief priests, with the elders and scribes, and the whole council, held a consultation, bound Jesus, carried him away, and delivered him up to Pilate.
Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”
He answered, “So you say.”
The chief priests accused him of many things.
Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer? See how many things they testify against you!”
But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate marveled.
Now at the feast he used to release to them one prisoner, whom they asked of him.
There was one called Barabbas, bound with his fellow insurgents, men who in the insurrection had committed murder.
The multitude, crying aloud, began to ask him to do as he always did for them.
Pilate answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
For he perceived that for envy the chief priests had delivered him up.
But the chief priests stirred up the multitude, that he should release Barabbas to them instead.
Pilate again asked them, “What then should I do to him whom you call the King of the Jews?”
They cried out again, “Crucify him!”
Pilate said to them, “Why, what evil has he done?”
But they cried out exceedingly, “Crucify him!”
Pilate, wishing to please the multitude, released Barabbas to them, and handed over Jesus, when he had flogged him, to be crucified.
The soldiers led him away within the court, which is the Praetorium; and they called together the whole cohort.
They clothed him with purple, and weaving a crown of thorns, they put it on him.
They began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!”
They struck his head with a reed, and spat on him, and bowing their knees, did homage to him.
When they had mocked him, they took the purple off him, and put his own garments on him. They led him out to crucify him.
They compelled one passing by, coming from the country, Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to go with them, that he might bear his cross.
They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.”
They offered him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he didn’t take it.
Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them, casting lots on them, what each should take.
It was the third hour, and they crucified him.
The superscription of his accusation was written over him, “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
With him they crucified two robbers; one on his right hand, and one on his left.
The Scripture was fulfilled, which says, “He was counted with transgressors.”
Those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads, and saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple, and build it in three days,
save yourself, and come down from the cross!”
Likewise, also the chief priests mocking among themselves with the scribes said, “He saved others. He can’t save himself.
Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him.” Those who were crucified with him also insulted him.
When the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.
At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Some of those who stood by, when they heard it, said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.”
One ran, and filling a sponge full of vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”
Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and gave up the spirit.
The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.
When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
There were also women watching from afar, among whom were both Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome;
who, when he was in Galilee, followed him and served him; and many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
When evening had now come, because it was the Preparation Day, that is, the day before the Sabbath,
Joseph of Arimathaea, a prominent council member who also himself was looking for God’s Kingdom, came. He boldly went in to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body.
Pilate marveled if he were already dead; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had been dead long.
When he found out from the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph.
He bought a linen cloth, and taking him down, wound him in the linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb which had been cut out of a rock. He rolled a stone against the door of the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary, the mother of Joses, saw where he was laid.
One of the criminals who was hanged insulted him, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!”
But the other answered, and rebuking him said, “Don’t you even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation?
And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward for our deeds, but this man has done nothing wrong.”
He said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.”
Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”
It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.
The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn in two.
Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” Having said this, he breathed his last.
When the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying, “Certainly this was a righteous man.”
All the multitudes that came together to see this, when they saw the things that were done, returned home beating their breasts.
All his acquaintances and the women who followed with him from Galilee stood at a distance, watching these things.

parts.title: Handed over
parts.context: Friday morning. Mark tells the trial before Pilate briefly; you read John's longer account in the last session. Notice what Mark adds: the soldiers' mockery inside the governor's headquarters.

commentary.on: held a consultation, bound Jesus, carried him away, and delivered him up to Pilate
commentary.text: Mark's 'delivered up' again. Bound, Jesus is now a prisoner of Rome.

commentary.on: So you say.
commentary.text: Neither yes nor no. Jesus does not deny being king, but he will not accept Pilate's meaning of the word.

commentary.on: For he perceived that for envy the chief priests had delivered him up.
commentary.text: Mark's judgement on the priests' motive: rivalry for the people's loyalty, not concern for the law.

commentary.on: released Barabbas to them, and handed over Jesus, when he had flogged him, to be crucified.
commentary.text: Flogging was the usual first stage of crucifixion. It weakened the victim, sometimes fatally, and may be one reason Jesus died so soon.

commentary.on: they called together the whole cohort
commentary.text: A cohort was several hundred soldiers. The whole unit gathers to watch the mockery: a game at the prisoner's expense, as Josephus describes in the comparison.

commentary.on: Hail, King of the Jews!
commentary.text: A parody of the salute to the emperor, 'Hail, Caesar'. The soldiers are mocking not only Jesus but any Jew who hoped for a king.

parts.title: Golgotha
parts.context: The soldiers lead Jesus out of the city to the place of execution, just outside the wall, by a road where passers-by would see. The condemned usually carried the crossbeam themselves.

commentary.on: Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus
commentary.text: Cyrene was a city in what is now Libya, with a large Jewish community. Mark names Simon's sons, as if his readers knew them. It looks like a witness's family memory, kept because people could check it.

commentary.on: the place called Golgotha
commentary.text: Calvary, in Latin. The site was outside the city wall then; the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built over it from 326, is inside the walls today because the city later grew.

commentary.on: They offered him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he didn't take it.
commentary.text: A drugged drink to dull pain (compare Proverbs 31:6). He refuses it.

commentary.on: they parted his garments among them, casting lots on them
commentary.text: The crucified were usually stripped. Mark does not say so, but the words echo Psalm 22:18, 'They divide my garments among them'; John quotes it (19:24).

commentary.on: It was the third hour, and they crucified him.
commentary.text: About nine in the morning. John has the sentence still being passed at noon (19:14).

commentary.on: THE KING OF THE JEWS.
commentary.text: The titulus, the notice of the charge. It is in all four Gospels, in slightly different words, and almost no historian doubts it. It was Rome's warning to anyone else who claimed to be king. To Mark's readers it was true.

commentary.on: With him they crucified two robbers
commentary.text: The same word as for Barabbas: bandits or rebels. Jesus dies in the place of an insurgent, between two more.

commentary.on: He was counted with transgressors.
commentary.text: This verse, Mark 15:28, is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts and was probably added later from Luke 22:37; the World English Bible includes it. The words are from Isaiah 53:12, the suffering servant.

commentary.on: He saved others. He can't save himself.
commentary.text: Mockery that is truer than the mockers know: in Mark's story, he will not save himself precisely so that he can save others (10:45).

parts.title: My God, my God
parts.context: From noon to three in the afternoon. Mark's account of the death is short and stark.

commentary.on: there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour
commentary.text: Not an eclipse: Passover fell at full moon, when an eclipse of the sun is impossible. Mark presents it as a sign; the prophet Amos had spoken of God making 'the sun to go down at noon' on a day of judgement (8:9).

commentary.on: Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?
commentary.text: Mark keeps the Aramaic, Jesus's own language: the first line of Psalm 22. It is a cry of abandonment from the Messiah to his God, so hard that Luke and John leave it out. But the psalm it begins ends in trust and in praise among 'the great assembly' (22:25). Jews often named a psalm by its first line.

commentary.on: Behold, he is calling Elijah.
commentary.text: 'Eloi' sounds like 'Elijah', who in Jewish belief came to help the righteous in trouble.

commentary.on: filling a sponge full of vinegar
commentary.text: Sour wine, the cheap drink of soldiers and labourers. Psalm 69:21: 'In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.'

commentary.on: Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and gave up the spirit.
commentary.text: After about six hours. The crucified often took a day or more to die, and a loud cry at the end is not what exhaustion usually produces. Mark tells it simply.

commentary.on: The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.
commentary.text: The curtain that closed off the holiest place of the Temple, where only the high priest went. 'From the top' means God tore it. The story that began with Jesus in the Temple court ends with the Temple's inner curtain split open.

commentary.on: Truly this man was the Son of God!
commentary.text: Mark's Gospel opens with 'the Son of God' (1:1), and the first human being to say it out loud is a Roman officer, the man in charge of the execution, watching him die.

commentary.on: There were also women watching from afar
commentary.text: The men have fled. The women from Galilee stay. Remember their names: they will be needed as witnesses.

commentary.on: Joseph of Arimathaea, a prominent council member
commentary.text: A member of the council that handed Jesus over now asks for his body. It is an odd detail for Christians to invent, and Joseph is otherwise unknown.

commentary.on: Pilate marveled if he were already dead
commentary.text: Pilate is surprised it was so quick, and checks with the centurion. Mark records the official confirmation of the death.

commentary.on: laid him in a tomb which had been cut out of a rock. He rolled a stone against the door of the tomb.
commentary.text: Wealthy families in Jerusalem cut tombs into the rock: a chamber with shelves or niches for bodies, closed with a large stone. The burial had to be quick: the Sabbath began at sunset, and the law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight.

commentary.on: Mary Magdalene and Mary, the mother of Joses, saw where he was laid.
commentary.text: Mark notes exactly who saw the tomb. They know which one it is.

parts.title: Into your hands
parts.context: Luke's account of the last hours, from his own sources as well as Mark. Luke has three sayings of Jesus from the cross that are not in Mark.

commentary.on: If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!
commentary.text: The third time in Luke that someone says 'save yourself': the rulers, the soldiers, and now a dying criminal.

commentary.on: this man has done nothing wrong.
commentary.text: Luke presses Jesus's innocence: Pilate says it three times, Herod finds nothing, now a criminal says it, and soon the centurion.

commentary.on: Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.
commentary.text: The only person in the whole Passion who speaks to Jesus as a king and means it is a condemned man on the next cross.

commentary.on: today you will be with me in Paradise.
commentary.text: 'Paradise', from a Persian word for a walled garden, was the Jewish picture of the place where the righteous dead wait for God.

commentary.on: The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn in two.
commentary.text: Luke puts the torn curtain before the death, Mark after it. Small differences like this are typical of independent tellings.

commentary.on: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!
commentary.text: Psalm 31:5, the evening prayer of a devout Jew going to sleep. Mark's Jesus cries out the first line of Psalm 22; Luke's dies with a line of trust from Psalm 31. Both are prayers from the psalms; each Gospel chose one.

commentary.on: Certainly this was a righteous man.
commentary.text: In Luke, the centurion says 'righteous', or 'innocent': the word Luke has been building towards.

commentary.on: the women who followed with him from Galilee stood at a distance, watching these things.
commentary.text: Luke too ends with the watching women.

paras: Then he orders the man to be most violently scourged on all sides. In the middle of the forum of Messana a Roman citizen, O judges, was beaten with rods; while in the mean time no groan was heard, no other expression was heard from that wretched man, amid all his pain, and between the sound of the blows, except these words, “I am a citizen of Rome.” He fancied that by this one statement of his citizenship he could ward off all blows, and remove all torture from his person. He not only did not succeed in averting by his entreaties the violence of the rods, but as he kept on repeating his entreaties and the assertion of his citizenship, a cross—a cross I say—was got ready for that miserable man, who had never witnessed such a stretch of power.

O the sweet name of liberty! O the admirable privileges of our citizenship! O Porcian law! O Sempronian laws! O power of the tribunes, bitterly regretted by, and at last restored to the Roman people! Have all our rights fallen so far, that in a province of the Roman people,—in a town of our confederate allies,—a Roman citizen should be bound in the forum, and beaten with rods by a man who only had the fasces and the axes through the kindness of the Roman people? What shall I say? When fire, and red-hot plates and other instruments of torture were employed? It the bitter entreaties and the miserable cries of that man had no power to restrain you, were you not moved even by the weeping and loud groans of the Roman citizens who were present at that time? Did you dare to drag any one to the cross who said that he was a Roman citizen? I was unwilling, O judges, to press this point so strongly at the former pleading; I was unwilling to do so. For you saw how the feelings of the multitude were excited against him with indignation, and hatred, and fear of their common danger. I, at that time, fixed a limit to my oration, and checked the eagerness of Caius Numitorius a Roman knight, a man of the highest character, one of my witnesses. And I rejoiced that Glabrio had acted (and he had acted most wisely) as he did in dismissing that witness immediately, in the middle of the discussion. In fact he was afraid that the Roman people might seem to have inflicted that punishment on Verres by tumultuary violence, which he was anxious he should only suffer according to the laws and by your judicial sentence.

When I have made all these points, which I undertake to prove, abundantly plain to your most intimate friends, then I will also turn my attention to that which is granted me by you. I will say that I am content with that. For what—what, I say—did you yourself lately say, when in an agitated state you escaped from the outcry and violence of the Roman people? Why, that he had only cried out that he was a Roman citizen because he was seeking some respite, but that he was a spy. My witnesses are unimpeachable. For what else does Caius Numitorius say? what else do Marcus and Publius Cottius say, most noble men of the district of Tauromenium? what else does Marcus Lucceius say, who had a great business as a money-changer at Rhegium? what else do all the others ray? For as yet witnesses have only been produced by me of this class, not men who say that they were acquainted with Gavius, but men who say that they saw him at the time that he was being dragged to the cross, while crying out that he was a Roman citizen. And you, O Verres, say the same thing. You confess that he did cry out that he was a Roman citizen; but that the name of citizenship did not avail with you even as much as to cause the least hesitation in your mind, or even any brief respite from a most cruel and ignominious punishment.

But why need I say more about Gavius? as if you were hostile to Gavius, and not rather an enemy to the name and class of citizens, and to all their rights. You were not, I say, an enemy to the individual, but to the common cause of liberty. For what was your object in ordering the Mamertines, when, according to their regular custom and usage, they had erected the cross behind the city in the Pompeian road, to place it where it looked towards the strait; and in adding, what you can by no means deny, what you said openly in the hearing of every one, that you chose that place in order that the man who said that he was a Roman citizen, might be able from his cross to behold Italy and to look towards his own home? And accordingly, O judges, that cross, for the first time since the foundation of Messana, was erected in that place. A spot commanding a view of Italy was picked out by that man, for the express purpose that the wretched man who was dying in agony and torture might see that the rights of liberty and of slavery were only separated by a very narrow strait, and that Italy might behold her son murdered by the most miserable and most painful punishment appropriate to slaves alone.

It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen; to scourge him is a wickedness; to put him to death is almost parricide. What shall I say of crucifying him? So guilty an action cannot by any possibility be adequately expressed by any name bad enough for it. Yet with all this that man was not content. “Let him behold his country,” said he; “let him die within sight of laws and liberty.” It was not Gavius, it was not one individual, I know not whom,—it was not one Roman citizen,—it was the common cause of freedom and citizenship that you exposed to that torture and nailed on that cross. But now consider the audacity of the man. Do not you think that he was indignant that be could not erect that cross for Roman citizens in the forum, in the comitium, in the very rostra? For the place in his province which was the most like those places in celebrity, and the nearest to them in point of distance, he did select. He chose that monument of his wickedness and audacity to be in the sight of Italy, in the very vestibule of Sicily, within sight of all passers-by as they sailed to and fro.

So now Titus's banks were advanced a great way, notwithstanding his soldiers had been very much distressed from the wall. He then sent a party of horsemen, and ordered they should lay ambushes for those that went out into the valleys to gather food. Some of these were indeed fighting men, who were not contented with what they got by rapine; but the greater part of them were poor people, who were deterred from deserting by the concern they were under for their own relations; for they could not hope to escape away, together with their wives and children, without the knowledge of the seditious; nor could they think of leaving these relations to be slain by the robbers on their account; nay, the severity of the famine made them bold in thus going out; so nothing remained but that, when they were concealed from the robbers, they should be taken by the enemy; and when they were going to be taken, they were forced to defend themselves for fear of being punished;

as after they had fought, they thought it too late to make any supplications for mercy; so they were first whipped, and then tormented with all sorts of tortures, before they died, and were then crucified before the wall of the city. This miserable procedure made Titus greatly to pity them, while they caught every day five hundred Jews; nay, some days they caught more: yet it did not appear to be safe for him to let those that were taken by force go their way, and to set a guard over so many he saw would be to make such as great deal them useless to him. The main reason why he did not forbid that cruelty was this, that he hoped the Jews might perhaps yield at that sight, out of fear lest they might themselves afterwards be liable to the same cruel treatment. So the soldiers, out of the wrath and hatred they bore the Jews, nailed those they caught, one after one way, and another after another, to the crosses, by way of jest, when their multitude was so great, that room was wanting for the crosses, and crosses wanting for the bodies.

parts.author: Cicero
parts.translator: C. D. Yonge (Bohn's Classical Library; 1903 printing)
parts.title: 'I am a citizen of Rome'
parts.context: In 70 BC Cicero (106–43 BC) prosecuted Gaius Verres, governor of Sicily from 73 to 71 BC, for plundering his province. This comes from the second part of the case, which Cicero published as a speech after Verres fled into exile. Publius Gavius, a Roman citizen from Cosa in Italy, had escaped from Verres's stone quarries at Syracuse; at Messana (Messina), on the strait facing Italy, he was seized, flogged in the forum and crucified. Translated by C. D. Yonge (Bohn's Classical Library, 1903 printing). Cuts are marked '…'; the source's own misprints ('It the bitter', 'relations,,', 'ray' for 'say', 'be' for 'he') are left as printed.
parts.plain: Cicero says: a Roman citizen was beaten with rods in the middle of the forum, saying nothing but 'I am a citizen of Rome', and a cross was got ready for him. Cicero cries out at the laws that should have protected him. Verres admitted the man said he was a citizen, and crucified him anyway. To bind a citizen is a crime, to flog him wicked, to kill him nearly murdering your own father; there is no word bad enough for crucifying him. Verres even had the cross set up facing Italy, so that the man could see his homeland as he died.

commentary.on: In the middle of the forum of Messana a Roman citizen, O judges, was beaten with rods
commentary.text: Flogging first, as with Jesus. The forum was the city's public square: the point was to be seen.

commentary.on: I am a citizen of Rome.
commentary.text: In Latin, civis Romanus sum: the words that should have saved him. Paul used his citizenship in the same way to stop a flogging (Acts 22:25). Christian tradition says Paul, a citizen, was beheaded in Rome, while Peter, who was not, was crucified.

commentary.on: a cross—a cross I say—was got ready for that miserable man
commentary.text: Cicero repeats the word as if it were too dreadful to say once. Romans of his class thought the cross unspeakable.

commentary.on: a most cruel and ignominious punishment
commentary.text: In Latin, crudelissimum taeterrimumque supplicium: more literally, 'the cruellest and most disgusting penalty'. This is the Roman verdict on the cross by the most famous voice in Rome.

commentary.on: the most miserable and most painful punishment appropriate to slaves alone
commentary.text: The cross was for slaves. To crucify Gavius was to treat a free citizen as a slave: that, more than the pain, is what outrages Cicero.

commentary.on: It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen; to scourge him is a wickedness; to put him to death is almost parricide. What shall I say of crucifying him?
commentary.text: A ladder of horror with the cross at the top, beyond words. Now imagine Cicero's audience hearing that a crucified Jew from Galilee was the Son of God.

commentary.on: within sight of all passers-by as they sailed to and fro
commentary.text: Crosses were set up beside roads and harbours, where most people would see them. Golgotha too was by a road outside the gate (John 19:20).

parts.author: Josephus
parts.title: Five hundred a day
parts.context: Josephus (AD 37 – c. 100) was a Jewish priest and commander who surrendered to the Romans in the war of AD 66–70 and served the general Titus as an interpreter during the siege of Jerusalem. He wrote this in Rome in the 70s. In the summer of AD 70 the city was starving; people crept out at night to look for food. Translated by William Whiston (1737). The section number and a footnote marker have been removed.
parts.plain: Josephus says: Titus's soldiers caught the poor people who came out of the starving city to find food. They were whipped and tortured, then crucified in front of the walls, five hundred a day or more. Titus pitied them but allowed it, hoping the sight would frighten the city into surrender. The soldiers, full of hatred, nailed them up in different positions as a joke, until there was no room left for crosses, and not enough crosses for the bodies.

commentary.on: they were first whipped, and then tormented with all sorts of tortures, before they died, and were then crucified before the wall of the city
commentary.text: The same order as in Mark: flogging, mockery or torture, then the cross, in public.

commentary.on: he hoped the Jews might perhaps yield at that sight
commentary.text: The purpose of crucifixion was terror. It was a message to everyone watching.

commentary.on: nailed those they caught, one after one way, and another after another, to the crosses, by way of jest
commentary.text: There was no fixed method: soldiers improvised, and made a game of it, as the cohort did with Jesus. This is why the Gospels say little about the details: their first readers knew.

commentary.on: room was wanting for the crosses, and crosses wanting for the bodies.
commentary.text: Forty years after Jesus, outside the same walls. To a Jew who had seen this, the cross meant Rome's power to crush the hope of Israel.

compare.author: Cicero and Josephus
compare.translator: C. D. Yonge (Bohn's Classical Library; 1903 printing)
compare.why: Today the cross is jewellery and church decoration. To read the Gospels as their first readers did, hear two ancient witnesses: a Roman, outraged that a citizen was crucified, and a Jew who watched it done to his own people by the hundred.
compare.title: What 'cross' meant

paras: The German scholar Martin Hengel gathered the ancient evidence in Crucifixion (1977). Three things stand out. The cross was meant to hurt for as long as possible: victims could live for hours or days. It was meant to shame: the victim was stripped, mocked and displayed, and the body was often left for birds and dogs. And it was meant to be seen: crosses stood by roads, gates and harbours as a warning.

The method varied, as Josephus shows. Usually the victim was flogged, carried the crossbeam to the place of execution, and was fixed to it by nails or ropes through or around the wrists or forearms, then lifted onto an upright post. The feet might be nailed. Death came slowly, from exhaustion, shock, loss of blood and the difficulty of breathing while hanging. The Roman philosopher Seneca, in a letter written in the 60s AD (Letter 101), wondered at a man who would rather cling to life on a cross, wasting away in pain drop by drop, than die at once.
sections.key: The cross was designed for long pain, total shame and public warning; methods varied, and death came slowly.

paras: Thousands were crucified around Jerusalem, yet only one victim has been found there. In 1968, building work at Giv'at ha-Mivtar, in north Jerusalem, uncovered a family tomb with bone boxes. One ossuary was inscribed 'Yehohanan son of Hagakol'. Inside was the right heel bone of a young man in his twenties with an iron nail, about 11.5 centimetres long, still driven through it, bent at the tip and with a fragment of olive wood beneath the head. It seems the nail hit a knot and could not be pulled out, so it was buried with him.

A re-examination by Joseph Zias and Eliezer Sekeles (1985) concluded that his arms were probably tied rather than nailed, and his legs placed either side of the upright. A second heel bone with a nail hole, from Gavello in northern Italy, was published in 2018. Why so few? Nails were valuable and were pulled out and reused, and most bodies were never buried at all. Yehohanan shows something else that matters later: a crucified Jew could be taken down and buried in a family tomb.
sections.key: The heel bone of Yehohanan (found 1968) is the only crucifixion victim found near Jerusalem; it shows the nails, and that the crucified could be buried.

paras: Mark says Jesus was crucified at nine and died at three, about six hours, and that Pilate was surprised he was already dead. John says the soldiers broke the legs of the two others to hasten their deaths before the Sabbath, found Jesus dead already, and pierced his side with a spear, and 'blood and water' came out (19:31–34). Breaking the legs meant the victim could no longer push up to breathe.

Doctors have offered many explanations: the severe flogging and loss of blood (W. D. Edwards and colleagues, Journal of the American Medical Association, 1986), shock, heart failure, or suffocation, which the French surgeon Pierre Barbet argued for in the 1950s but later experiments have disputed. The Gospels hint at weakness: Simon had to carry the cross. The honest answer is that no one knows exactly how he died. What all the sources agree on is that he did: the Roman soldiers, whose job it was, were sure, and so was the governor's officer.
sections.key: Jesus died after about six hours, probably weakened by the flogging; the exact cause is debated, but the sources agree he was certainly dead.

paras: No Gospel gives all of Jesus's words from the cross. Put together, there are seven, and Christians have meditated on them for centuries: in the 'Three Hours' service on Good Friday, begun by a Jesuit, Alonso Messia, in Lima in Peru, and in Haydn's Seven Last Words, written for Cádiz Cathedral in 1787. The differences are not so much contradictions as choices: Mark gives only the cry of abandonment, Luke the forgiveness and trust, John the care and the completion.

rows: 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing.'
Luke 23:34 (missing from some of the oldest manuscripts)
'Today you will be with me in Paradise.'
A promise to a dying criminal
Care for his mother, entrusted to the beloved disciple
'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'
Abandonment, in the words of Psalm 22
'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!'
Trust, in the words of Psalm 31
table.note: The traditional order runs from Luke's forgiveness to Luke's last prayer.

sections.key: Seven sayings across the Gospels, from the cry of abandonment to the prayer of trust; each Gospel chose what to tell.

paras: Historians ask of any ancient story: would the people who told it have made this up? A detail that embarrassed them is less likely to be invention. John P. Meier, in A Marginal Jew (1991), called this the 'criterion of embarrassment'. The Passion is full of such details: the leader denies him, the rest run away, the Messiah cries that God has forsaken him, his own council's member has to bury him, and women, not men, are the faithful witnesses.

Above all, the cross itself. Jews expected a Messiah who would defeat Rome, not be crucified by it; Deuteronomy said the hanged were cursed. Greeks and Romans thought worship of a crucified man was madness: a graffito scratched on a wall on the Palatine Hill in Rome, probably around AD 200, shows a man with a donkey's head on a cross and the words 'Alexamenos worships [his] god'. Paul admits it: 'we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks' (1 Corinthians 1:23). No one founding a new movement would have chosen this message. The first Christians proclaimed it because it had happened.
sections.key: A crucified Messiah was a scandal to Jews and folly to Greeks; no one would have invented it, which is why historians count the crucifixion as certain.

sections.h: From a sign of shame to the sign of a faith
paras: For three centuries Christians rarely pictured the cross. Their early art used the fish, the anchor, the shepherd. The earliest surviving carvings of the crucifixion, on the wooden doors of Santa Sabina in Rome and an ivory now in the British Museum, date from around 420 to 430, a century after the emperor Constantine abolished crucifixion as a punishment.

Yet from the beginning they spoke of it. Paul wrote, about AD 50, that Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us' (Galatians 3:13): the curse of Deuteronomy turned inside out. The historian Tom Holland, in Dominion (2019), argues that this reversal, a tortured victim worshipped as God, slowly changed the values of the West, until the suffering of the weak came to matter more than the glory of the strong. How one death could save is the question of the next journey in this hall, 'Why the cross?'.
sections.key: Christians did not picture the cross for centuries, but proclaimed it from the start; it turned the ancient world's idea of glory upside down.

paras: Mark's account of the cross is full of named people: Simon of Cyrene, 'the father of Alexander and Rufus'; Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome; Joseph of Arimathea. Mark rarely names minor characters, and when he does, the scholar Richard Bauckham has argued (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006), it may be because they were known in the early church as the sources of the story, people whom readers could ask.

Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome around AD 57, greets 'Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother' (Romans 16:13); some think this is Simon's son, though the name was common. Sceptics reply that names can be added to make a story sound true. But the women's names matter in another way: they will be needed in the next session, as the witnesses of where he was buried and of what they found.
sections.key: Mark names people who could be asked: Simon and his sons, the women, Joseph; scholars debate whether these point to eyewitness sources.

refs: Mark 1:1; 10:45; 15:1–47; Luke 1:1–4; 23:26–49; John 19:17–37; Matthew 27:46; Psalms 22; 31:5; 69:21; Proverbs 31:6; Amos 8:9; Isaiah 53:12; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Galatians 3:13; 1 Corinthians 1:23; Acts 22:25; Colossians 4:14.

Sekeles, Israel Exploration Journal 35 (1985). E. Gualdi-Russo and others, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2018), on the Gavello find.
W. D. Edwards, W. J. Gabel and F. E. Hosmer, 'On the Physical Death of Jesus Christ', JAMA 255 (1986). Pierre Barbet, A Doctor at Calvary (1950; English 1953).

debate.question: Why did it matter that it was a cross?

positions.name: A scandal no one would invent
positions.who: Martin Hengel (1977); John P. Meier (1991); also sceptical historians such as Bart Ehrman
positions.view: The crucifixion is one of the surest facts of ancient history precisely because it was the worst possible start for a movement claiming a Messiah. Whatever else the first Christians believed, they did not make this up.
positions.evidence: Tacitus and Josephus; the titulus; Paul's 'stumbling block'; the Alexamenos graffito; the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23.

positions.name: A defeat turned into a theology
positions.who: D. F. Strauss (1835); Gerd Lüdemann; many sceptical scholars
positions.view: The disciples, shattered by the cross, searched their Scriptures and found a suffering Messiah in Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22. The theology of the cross was their way of coping with a disaster; it shows how badly they needed it to mean something, not that it did.
positions.evidence: Luke 24:26 'Didn't the Christ have to suffer?'; the Passion stories' many echoes of the Psalms; studies of how groups reinterpret failed hopes, such as Leon Festinger's When Prophecy Fails (1956).

positions.name: The meaning was there before the cross
positions.who: N. T. Wright; most Christian traditions
positions.view: Jesus himself went to Jerusalem expecting to die and said at the supper what his death would mean. The first Christians did not invent a meaning afterwards; they remembered one.
positions.evidence: Mark 8:31; 10:45; the words over the bread and cup, early and independently attested (Mark 14; 1 Corinthians 11).

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus was crucified under Pilate, that the cross was a death of utter shame, and that the first Christians proclaimed it openly anyway.

look.why: A Netherlandish painter known only as the Master of the Starck Triptych painted this altarpiece around 1480 to 1490. It shows the moment of Mark 15:24–25, 'they crucified him': the cross being hauled upright, with the people of a northern European town of the painter's day looking on.
points: Three panels make one scene: the cross at the centre, the mourning women to our left, horsemen to our right.
Two men push the T-shaped cross up from behind with poles while three men pull it upright with two ropes, and others drive its base into a hole in the ground.
Jesus, naked but for a white cloth, is nailed by his hands and by a single nail through both feet; blood trickles from the nails and a ring of thorns is on his forehead. He looks down at the crowd.
Skulls and bones lie on the ground around the cross, and two more crosses and some rope lie nearby: the place of a skull, and two more executions to come.
In the left panel Mary, in azure blue, looks down with her fingers interlaced; a woman in emerald green holds a cloth bearing Jesus's face.
In the right panel a man in armour on horseback gestures up at Jesus; near the corner sits a bald man with his hands tied behind his back.

music.why: The African American spiritual asks the question this session asks: were you there when they crucified my Lord? It was sung by people who knew what it was to be bought, beaten and displayed.

think.why: Christians say God himself suffered on the cross. See what that claim means for the hardest question.

learn.why: Jesus's last words in Luke, and the night prayer of Jews and Christians ever since.

check.q: Why does Cicero call the crucifixion of Gavius so shocking?
options: Because crucifixion was illegal in Sicily
Because Gavius was innocent of any crime
Because the cross was a punishment for slaves, and inflicting it on a Roman citizen treated a free man as a slave
Because Verres crucified him at night
check.why: The cross was the 'slaves' punishment'; citizens were exempt, which is what makes Cicero's case.

check.q: What does the heel bone of Yehohanan add to the discussion of Jesus's burial?
options: It was found in Jesus's tomb
It proves Jesus was buried in a rock tomb
It shows that at least one crucified Jew near Jerusalem was taken down and buried in a family tomb
It shows that the Romans never nailed the feet
check.why: Some scholars doubt the crucified were ever buried; Yehohanan shows it could happen, though it does not prove it did for Jesus.

check.q: Mark records Jesus's cry 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'. Why do historians think it probably goes back to the event?
options: Because it is embarrassing: a Messiah crying that God has abandoned him, which Luke and John leave out
Because all four Gospels record it
Because it is not from the Psalms
Because it is in Aramaic
check.why: The criterion of embarrassment: the later Gospels drop it, suggesting it was awkward to tell.

check.q: What is the best explanation of why the four Gospels give different last words?
options: Some Gospels are forgeries
Jesus said nothing from the cross
Each writer selected from the sayings and traditions he had, to bring out a different side of the death: abandonment, forgiveness, trust, completion
The words were added in the Middle Ages
check.why: The sayings complement more than contradict; each Gospel chose what to tell, though critics note Luke may have replaced Mark's cry.

check.q: Why does the crucifixion count, for historians, as one of the most certain facts about Jesus?
options: Because Jesus's tomb has been found
Because it is attested by Christian and non-Christian sources, and a crucified Messiah was so shameful that no one would have invented it
Because the Romans kept records of every crucifixion
Because a relic of the cross survives
check.why: Tacitus and Josephus confirm it, and the criterion of embarrassment makes invention very unlikely.

check.q: Josephus says the soldiers crucified people 'one after one way, and another after another'. What follows for reading the Gospels?
options: That Jesus was not crucified by Romans
That crucifixion was rare in Judea
That the Gospels must be wrong about the nails
That there was no single method, and the Gospels' first readers knew the horrors so well that the writers did not need to describe them
check.why: The method varied, and the readers knew; the Gospels' restraint is not ignorance.

tutorial.question: Why did the first Christians proclaim a crucified Messiah?
tutorial.approach: Begin with what crucifixion meant to Romans (Cicero) and to Jews (Josephus; Deuteronomy 21:23), and what kind of Messiah Jews expected. Show from Paul, the Alexamenos graffito and the criterion of embarrassment why the message was a liability. Then weigh three explanations: they could not deny a public fact; they reinterpreted a disaster (Strauss, Lüdemann); Jesus had already given the death a meaning (the supper). Say which you find strongest and why.
strong: Describes crucifixion as shameful and servile, with ancient evidence.
Explains why a crucified Messiah was a contradiction for Jews and folly for Greeks.
Uses the criterion of embarrassment accurately.
States the 'reinterpreted disaster' view fairly.
Connects the cross back to the words at the supper.
Recognises that why they proclaimed it depends partly on what happened next.

reading.author: Martin Hengel
reading.title: Crucifixion in the Ancient World and the Folly of the Message of the Cross
reading.why: Short, vivid and fully sourced.

reading.author: Fleming Rutledge
reading.title: The Crucifixion: Understanding the Death of Jesus Christ
reading.why: A theologian on why the cross, and not some other death, matters.

reading.author: John Granger Cook
reading.title: Crucifixion in the Mediterranean World
reading.why: The full ancient and archaeological evidence.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Jesus prayed for those who executed him. Choose one person who has wronged you, and each day this week pray or wish for one specific good thing for them, by name. You do not have to feel it.
sessions.reflect: The cross was meant to say: this is what happens to people who threaten us. What did it come to say instead?
takeaways: Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels, designed for long pain, shame and public warning; Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting penalty.
Mark tells the death starkly: mocked as king, crucified between rebels, a cry from Psalm 22, death within six hours, burial by a council member while the women watched.
A crucified Messiah was a scandal to Jews and folly to Greeks; no one would have invented it, which is why the crucifixion is one of the surest facts of ancient history.

sessions.title: The empty tomb
sessions.line: On Sunday morning the women who watched the burial come back with spices, and find the stone rolled away and the body gone.
sessions.plain: Early on the Sunday after the crucifixion, a few women who had followed Jesus from Galilee went to his tomb to finish anointing his body, and found it open and empty. The four Gospels all tell this, though they differ in the details: how many women, how many angels, what happened next. Jesus's opponents did not deny the tomb was empty; they said the disciples had stolen the body. This session asks whether the empty tomb is history or legend, and why the accounts differ.
sessions.why: Session 4 ended on Friday evening: Jesus dead, certified by a Roman officer, and laid in a rock tomb by Joseph of Arimathea while two of the women watched where he was laid. The Sabbath followed. Now it is Sunday.
answers: Was the tomb really empty?
Why do the four Gospels' accounts differ?
Why does Mark's Gospel end so suddenly?
Why does it matter that women found it?
What did Jesus's opponents say had happened?
sessions.finding: The earliest accounts agree that women found the tomb empty, an unlikely detail to invent; they differ in the details as independent witnesses do.

paras: Jesus died on the Friday afternoon. Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, asked Pilate for the body, wrapped it in linen and laid it in a tomb cut into the rock, and rolled a stone across the entrance; Mary Magdalene and another Mary saw where. Then the Sabbath began at sunset, and no work, including the work of burial, could be done until it ended at sunset on Saturday. Matthew adds that the chief priests asked Pilate for a guard on the tomb, in case the disciples stole the body (27:62–66).
The disciples had scattered. Peter had denied him. As far as anyone in Jerusalem could see, the movement was finished.
background.key: Jesus was buried on Friday in a rock tomb that the women saw; the Sabbath followed, and the disciples had scattered.

paras: Families in Jerusalem who could afford it cut tombs into the soft limestone of the hills around the city. A low doorway, closed by a stone, led to a chamber with benches or long niches where bodies were laid, washed, anointed with spices and wrapped in cloth. About a year later, when only the bones remained, they were gathered into an ossuary, a stone box, like those of Caiaphas and Yehohanan. Hundreds of such tombs have been found.

Since the 300s, Christians have honoured the tomb inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The emperor Constantine had a pagan temple cleared from the site in 326; his biographer Eusebius says a rock tomb was found beneath it (Life of Constantine 3.25–28). When the shrine over it was restored in 2016, the original limestone burial bench was exposed for the first time in centuries, and mortar from the site was dated to the mid-300s, the time of Constantine's builders. Whether it is the very tomb cannot be proved; it is in the right kind of place, a former quarry just outside the wall of Jesus's day, with other first-century tombs nearby. The 'Garden Tomb', proposed in 1883, is loved by many Protestant pilgrims, but archaeologists date it centuries earlier.
background.key: Jews laid their dead in rock-cut tombs and later gathered the bones; the Holy Sepulchre has been honoured as Jesus's tomb since 326, and is in the right kind of place.

paras: Some scholars, notably John Dominic Crossan and Bart Ehrman, doubt the burial story. Romans often left the crucified on the cross to rot or be eaten, as part of the punishment; perhaps Jesus's body went into a common grave, and the story of Joseph grew later.

Others reply that Judea was different. The law required the hanged to be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:23). Josephus says the Jews 'took down those that were condemned and crucified, and buried them before the going down of the sun' (Jewish War 4.5.2), and Philo says Roman governors sometimes gave the bodies of the crucified to their families at festivals (Against Flaccus 83). Yehohanan was buried in a family tomb. And Paul's summary of what he received, written within about twenty-five years, says Christ died, 'that he was buried', and that he was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Most scholars think the burial by Joseph is historical.
background.key: Some doubt Jesus was buried, since Romans often left bodies; Jewish law and practice, Josephus, Yehohanan and Paul's early summary suggest he was.

paras: The main reading is the two earliest accounts of the discovery: Mark 16:1–8, the oldest, and Luke 24:1–12. John's account, the fullest, comes in the last session, with what followed. The comparison is Matthew's report of the first explanation offered by Jesus's opponents: the disciples stole the body. It answers a historian's question: what did the other side say?
background.key: Mark and Luke on the discovery; then Matthew on the first counter-explanation.

before: What do the women expect to find, and what do they bring?
What does the messenger tell them to do?
How do the men react when the women tell them?
sessions.readWhy: The two earliest accounts of Sunday morning.

paras: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, bought spices, that they might come and anoint him.
Very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb when the sun had risen.
They were saying among themselves, “Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?”
for it was very big. Looking up, they saw that the stone was rolled back.
Entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were amazed.
He said to them, “Don’t be amazed. You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen. He is not here. Behold, the place where they laid him!
But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.’ ”
They went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.
But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they and some others came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away from the tomb.
They entered in, and didn’t find the Lord Jesus’ body.
While they were greatly perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling clothing.
Becoming terrified, they bowed their faces down to the earth.
They said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?
He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee,
saying that the Son of Man must be delivered up into the hands of sinful men and be crucified, and the third day rise again?”
They remembered his words,
returned from the tomb, and told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
Now they were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James. The other women with them told these things to the apostles.
These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn’t believe them.
But Peter got up and ran to the tomb. Stooping and looking in, he saw the strips of linen lying by themselves, and he departed to his home, wondering what had happened.

parts.title: He is not here
parts.context: Sunday morning. The oldest and shortest account, written about thirty-five years later. In the oldest manuscripts, Mark's Gospel ends with verse 8.

commentary.on: When the Sabbath was past
commentary.text: Saturday evening. The shops could open again, and the women bought spices to finish what the hurried burial on Friday had not done.

commentary.on: Very early on the first day of the week
commentary.text: Sunday. This is why Christians, nearly all of them Jews at first, began to meet on the first day of the week, not the Sabbath, and called it 'the Lord's day' (Revelation 1:10).

commentary.on: Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?
commentary.text: They are expecting a corpse. No one in this story is waiting for a resurrection.

commentary.on: they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe
commentary.text: Mark does not call him an angel, though his white robe and his message mark him as one; Matthew does call him so (28:2–5).

commentary.on: He has risen. He is not here. Behold, the place where they laid him!
commentary.text: The message in three short sentences, and an empty place to look at. The empty tomb does not explain itself; the messenger has to say what it means.

commentary.on: tell his disciples and Peter
commentary.text: Peter is singled out: the one who denied him three times is the first to be sent for.

commentary.on: He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.
commentary.text: The promise Jesus made on the way to Gethsemane (14:28).

commentary.on: They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.
commentary.text: And there, in the oldest manuscripts, Mark stops, in Greek on the little word 'for'. No appearance of Jesus, no joy, only fear and silence. The lecture asks why.

parts.title: Why do you seek the living among the dead?
parts.context: Luke, writing about fifteen or twenty years after Mark, follows Mark's outline but adds names and details from his own sources, and in Luke the meetings with the risen Jesus all happen in and near Jerusalem.

commentary.on: they and some others came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared
commentary.text: 'They' are the women from Galilee who watched the burial (23:55–56).

commentary.on: They entered in, and didn't find the Lord Jesus' body.
commentary.text: Luke says plainly what Mark implies. They went in; the body was not there.

commentary.on: two men stood by them in dazzling clothing
commentary.text: Mark has one young man, Luke two men, Matthew one angel, John two angels. The number differs; the messenger and the message do not.

commentary.on: Why do you seek the living among the dead?
commentary.text: The line this session asks you to learn. It turns the question round: the women have come to the wrong place.

commentary.on: Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee
commentary.text: In Mark, Galilee is where they will see him. In Luke, Galilee becomes a memory of what he said. Luke keeps the whole story in Jerusalem, where his second book, Acts, begins.

commentary.on: Now they were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James.
commentary.text: Named witnesses. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas (8:3): a woman people could have asked.

commentary.on: These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn't believe them.
commentary.text: The Greek word means idle chatter. The apostles do not believe the women. It is not a flattering story about the church's future leaders.

commentary.on: But Peter got up and ran to the tomb.
commentary.text: This verse is missing from a few manuscripts but present in the oldest ones; most scholars accept it. John tells the same visit in more detail.

commentary.on: he saw the strips of linen lying by themselves
commentary.text: The grave clothes were left behind. Someone stealing a body would hardly have stopped to unwrap it.

paras: Now while they were going, behold, some of the guards came into the city, and told the chief priests all the things that had happened.
When they were assembled with the elders, and had taken counsel, they gave a large amount of silver to the soldiers,
saying, “Say that his disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept.
If this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and make you free of worry.”
So they took the money and did as they were told. This saying was spread abroad among the Jews, and continues until today.

parts.title: His disciples came by night
parts.context: Matthew wrote around AD 80 to 90, using Mark. Only he tells of a guard at the tomb (27:62–66), who saw an angel roll back the stone and 'became like dead men' (28:4). This is what happened next, in his account.

commentary.on: some of the guards came into the city, and told the chief priests all the things that had happened.
commentary.text: The guards report to the priests, who had asked for them.

commentary.on: Say that his disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept.
commentary.text: This is the counter-explanation. Notice what it assumes: the tomb was empty. The argument was never about whether the body was there, but about where it had gone. (Notice too the weak point Christians soon pointed out: how could sleeping men know who took it?)

commentary.on: If this comes to the governor's ears, we will persuade him and make you free of worry.
commentary.text: Sleeping on watch could cost a Roman soldier his life. The priests promise to protect them.

commentary.on: This saying was spread abroad among the Jews, and continues until today.
commentary.text: Matthew says the story was still told in his own day. Around AD 160, Justin Martyr says the same: Jewish teachers were sending word that the disciples had stolen the body (Dialogue with Trypho 108). Many scholars doubt Matthew's guard story, which only he tells; but the counter-claim itself, told by opponents, is strong evidence that both sides agreed the tomb was empty.

compare.why: What did Jesus's opponents say? Matthew reports the first explanation offered by the other side, and it tells us something both sides agreed on.
compare.title: The other side's story

paras: The two oldest complete Greek Bibles, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both from the 300s, end Mark at 16:8: 'for they were afraid'. The historian Eusebius and the scholar Jerome both said that most of the Greek copies they knew ended there. Later manuscripts add a 'longer ending' (16:9–20), with appearances, a commission and the ascension, which the World English Bible prints; its style and vocabulary are unlike Mark's, and it seems to summarise the other Gospels. Irenaeus quotes it around 180, so it is old, but most scholars think it was added in the 100s. Some manuscripts have a different, shorter ending instead.

Did Mark mean to stop at verse 8? Some think the last page was lost. Many now think he ended there on purpose: the promise has been made twice, 'you will see him', and the reader is left to finish the story, to go to Galilee, to stop being afraid. Either way, the earliest Gospel tells the empty tomb without any appearance of Jesus at all.
sections.key: The oldest manuscripts end Mark at 16:8, with the women afraid; the longer ending was added in the 100s; Mark may have meant to stop there.

paras: In every Gospel the first people at the empty tomb are women, and Mary Magdalene is always among them. That matters, because in the ancient world women's testimony counted for little. Josephus says that in Jewish courts women were not accepted as witnesses (Antiquities 4.8.15), and the Mishnah agrees for many cases (Shevuot 4:1). The pagan critic Celsus, around 175, mocked the resurrection as resting on the word of a hysterical woman (in Origen, Against Celsus 2.55). Paul's own list of witnesses, a summary for public argument, leaves the women out.

If someone had invented the story to persuade, would they have made women the discoverers, and men the ones who did not believe? Most historians think not: this is the criterion of embarrassment again. Sceptics reply that this shows the women were real followers, not that the tomb was empty; and that Mark's 'they said nothing to anyone' may explain why no one had heard the story before he wrote it down.
sections.key: Women's testimony was little valued, yet all four Gospels make women the first witnesses: an unlikely detail to invent.

paras: Read the four accounts together and the differences are plain. Read them again and so is what they share.

rows: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, Salome
Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James and others
Very early, when the sun had risen
An angel, who rolls the stone away
They run to tell; Jesus meets them
They tell the eleven, who do not believe
She runs to Peter and the beloved disciple
table.note: All four agree: the first day of the week, early; women led by Mary Magdalene; the stone moved; the body gone; a messenger.

sections.key: The accounts differ on numbers, times and places, and agree on the core: early on Sunday, women led by Mary Magdalene found the stone moved and the body gone.

paras: Are the differences a problem? Historians are used to independent witnesses who agree on the main event and disagree on details. Survivors of the Titanic gave conflicting accounts of whether the ship broke in two before it sank; no one doubts that it sank. If all four Gospels matched word for word, we would suspect copying. The Gospels do depend on each other in part, Matthew and Luke on Mark, yet each also tells what the others do not.

Sceptics answer that some differences are more than details, and they have a point. Where did the disciples see Jesus: in Galilee, as Mark and Matthew say, or in Jerusalem, as Luke and John 20 say? Strauss, whose argument comes in the next session, thought that question was the key to the whole thing. And the accounts become fuller and more physical in the later Gospels, which can be read as a story growing in the telling. Both sides agree on what the differences cannot do: they cannot by themselves prove the core true or false.
sections.key: Differences in detail are typical of independent witnesses; but the Galilee–Jerusalem difference and the growth of the stories are real questions for the sceptic.

sections.h: Outside evidence: what it shows, and where it is silent
paras: No Roman or Jewish document of the time mentions the tomb. What we do have is indirect. Jesus's opponents, in Matthew and in Justin, never said the body was still there; they said it had been stolen. A medieval Jewish counter-gospel, the Toledot Yeshu, has a gardener move it. And there is no sign that anyone ever venerated a tomb containing Jesus's body, though Jews in his day did honour the tombs of prophets and holy men (Matthew 23:29).

Two finds are sometimes claimed as evidence, and both fail. The 'Nazareth inscription', a Greek decree threatening death for anyone who disturbs a tomb, bought in Nazareth in 1878, was once linked to the empty tomb; a study of its marble published in 2020 (Kyle Harper and colleagues) found it came from the Greek island of Kos, so it probably has nothing to do with Galilee. A tomb found at Talpiot in Jerusalem in 1980, with ossuaries bearing common names including Yeshua and Maria, was presented in a 2007 documentary as the family tomb of Jesus; most archaeologists, including its excavator, Amos Kloner, rejected the claim. The empty tomb rests on the Gospels and on the opponents' own response.
sections.key: No document of the time mentions the tomb; the opponents' 'they stole him' implies it was empty; the Nazareth inscription and the Talpiot tomb are not evidence.

paras: One piece of evidence is hiding in plain sight. The first Christians were Jews, for whom the seventh day, the Sabbath, was the holy day given at creation and commanded at Sinai. Yet within a few years they were meeting on the first day of the week. Paul tells the Corinthians to set money aside 'on the first day of every week' (1 Corinthians 16:2), around AD 54; Acts describes the church at Troas gathering 'on the first day of the week' to break bread (20:7); Revelation calls it 'the Lord's day' (1:10). By around 110, the Roman governor Pliny reports to the emperor that Christians met before dawn on a set day of the week (Letters 10.96).

Changing the holy day was a large step for Jews, and the early sources give only one reason for it: it was the day the tomb was found empty and the Lord was seen. This does not prove what happened that morning. It does show that the first Christians dated their faith to a particular day, two days after the crucifixion, and not to a slow dawning of belief over months.
sections.key: Jewish followers of Jesus began worshipping on Sunday within a few years, because it was the day of the empty tomb: their faith was dated to a particular morning.

sections.h: What an empty tomb cannot prove
paras: Even if the tomb was empty, that alone would not show that Jesus rose. A body can be stolen, moved, or lost. In John, Mary Magdalene's first thought is exactly that: 'They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb' (20:2). The empty tomb was not what convinced the first Christians; in Mark and Luke it produces fear and disbelief. What convinced them, they said, was that they saw him.

So the empty tomb is one half of the evidence. The other half is the claim that he appeared, to individuals and to groups, which Paul lists in 1 Corinthians 15, read in 'What is the Bible?'. The question of this journey turns on both, and the natural explanations try to account for both. They deserve to be heard at full strength, before any verdict.
sections.key: An empty tomb alone proves nothing; the first Christians pointed to the appearances as well, and the natural explanations must account for both.

refs: Josephus, Jewish War 4.5.2; Antiquities 4.8.15. Philo, Against Flaccus 83. Mishnah, Shevuot 4:1. Origen, Against Celsus 2.55. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 108. Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.25–28. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.10.5.
Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century). Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament (2nd ed. 1994), on Mark 16:9–20 and Luke 24:12.

A. Moropoulou and others, reports on the restoration of the Edicule of the Holy Sepulchre (2016–2017). Kyle Harper and others, 'Nazareth Inscription', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 30 (2020). Amos Kloner, 'A Tomb with Inscribed Ossuaries in East Talpiyot', 'Atiqot 29 (1996).
