debate.question: The empty tomb: history or legend?

positions.name: History
positions.who: N. T. Wright (2003); Dale Allison (2021), cautiously; most scholars, on some counts
positions.view: The tomb was found empty. The disciples proclaimed the resurrection in Jerusalem, where the tomb could be checked; their opponents said the body was stolen, not that it was there; and no one inventing the story would have made women its witnesses.
positions.evidence: Mark 16 and the other Gospels independently; 'he was buried' in Paul's early summary; Matthew 28:11–15 and Justin; the women.

positions.name: Legend
positions.who: Rudolf Bultmann; Gerd Lüdemann; Bart Ehrman (2014)
positions.view: The empty tomb story appears first in Mark, about forty years later. Paul never mentions it. Belief in the resurrection came from visions, and the story of an empty tomb grew afterwards to explain and defend it; Mark's 'they said nothing to anyone' covers its late arrival.
positions.evidence: Paul's silence about the tomb; Roman practice of leaving bodies; the growth of detail from Mark to John.

positions.name: Probably empty, but it settles little
positions.who: Dale C. Allison Jr.; many historians
positions.view: On balance the tomb was probably empty. But an empty tomb has many possible explanations, and the historian cannot get from it to a resurrection. What matters is how it fits with the appearances.
positions.evidence: John 20:2, where Mary assumes the body was taken; the variety of possible natural causes.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus's followers proclaimed his resurrection in Jerusalem within weeks or months, that Mary Magdalene is named in every account, and that an empty tomb alone would not prove a resurrection.

look.why: The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of the women at the tomb that is free to use here, so this session has none rather than a stand-in. The scene most painted is the one no Gospel describes: Christ stepping out of the tomb. The Gospels give only the aftermath: a rolled stone, folded linen, and frightened women.

music.why: Charles Wesley's Easter hymn of 1739 sets the women's news to rolling alleluias: 'Christ the Lord is risen today'.

think.why: Read the modern debate over what historians can say about Jesus, including the resurrection, with the strongest objections stated fairly.

learn.why: What the women heard at the empty tomb: the Easter message in two short sentences.

check.q: Matthew reports that the priests told the guards to say 'his disciples came by night, and stole him away'. Why do historians think this matters, even if they doubt the guard story?
options: Because Pilate confirmed it
Because it proves the disciples stole the body
Because the opponents' own explanation assumes the tomb was empty
Because the guards were Christians
check.why: Both sides argued about where the body had gone, not whether it was there.

check.q: Why does it matter that all four Gospels make women the first witnesses?
options: Because women were the only disciples
Because the women were related to Pilate
Because Paul names them first in his list
Because women's testimony carried little weight then, so it is an unlikely detail to invent
check.why: Josephus, the Mishnah and Celsus show how little women's testimony counted; Paul's list leaves them out.

check.q: What is the best description of how the four accounts relate?
options: They agree in every detail, which proves they are true
They contradict each other on everything, so nothing can be known
They differ on numbers, times and places but agree on the core: early on Sunday, women led by Mary Magdalene found the stone moved and the body gone
Only Mark mentions the empty tomb
check.why: Differences in detail with agreement on the core is the usual pattern of independent testimony.

check.q: The oldest manuscripts of Mark end at 16:8. What follows?
options: That the whole of Mark is unreliable
That the World English Bible is mistranslated
That the earliest Gospel tells the empty tomb and the promise of seeing Jesus, but no appearance; the longer ending was added later
That Mark did not believe in the resurrection
check.why: Mark promises the appearances (14:28; 16:7) but does not narrate them; 16:9–20 is a later addition.

check.q: A friend says: 'The tomb was empty, so Jesus rose.' What is the strongest reply?
options: That the tomb was certainly not empty
That Paul invented the tomb
That no one has ever found a first-century tomb
That an empty tomb has several possible explanations; the first Christians pointed to the appearances as well, and the case depends on both
check.why: Even Mary first thought the body had been taken (John 20:2); the empty tomb alone is not enough.

check.q: Why do most archaeologists reject the claim that the Talpiot tomb is Jesus's family tomb?
options: Because it is a medieval tomb
Because the names on its ossuaries were very common in Jerusalem at the time, and its excavator rejected the identification
Because it was found in Galilee
Because it contained no ossuaries
check.why: Yeshua and Maria were among the commonest names; Amos Kloner and most specialists rejected the claim.

tutorial.question: Is the empty tomb historical?
tutorial.approach: Set out first what must be true for the story to be possible: was Jesus buried, and in a known tomb? Then weigh the evidence for: the women, the Jerusalem setting, the opponents' counter-claim, Paul's 'he was buried'. Then the evidence against: Paul's silence, Mark's late date and his ending, the growth of the stories, Roman practice. Use the table of differences. Conclude, and say what your conclusion does and does not show about the resurrection.
strong: Addresses the burial question with evidence on both sides (Deuteronomy 21, Josephus, Yehohanan; Crossan and Ehrman).
Uses the women witnesses and the criterion of embarrassment accurately.
Uses Matthew 28:11–15 and Justin as evidence from opponents.
Explains Mark's ending and the manuscript evidence.
Handles the differences between the Gospels fairly.
Recognises that an empty tomb alone does not prove a resurrection.

reading.why: On Joanna, Mary Magdalene and the women as named witnesses.

reading.author: Bart D. Ehrman

reading.why: The case for doubting the burial and the empty tomb, from an agnostic historian.

reading.why: A full, fair weighing of the tomb and the appearances.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the women went to the tomb to do the last kind thing they could for someone they loved. This week, do one thing for someone who is grieving or forgotten: visit, write, or ring them, and listen more than you speak.
sessions.reflect: The women went expecting a body. What do you go looking for in the wrong place?
takeaways: Jesus was probably buried by Joseph of Arimathea in a rock tomb the women saw; some scholars doubt it, but Jewish law and practice and Paul's early summary support it.
All four Gospels say women led by Mary Magdalene found the tomb empty early on Sunday; the opponents' own claim that the body was stolen assumes it was empty.
The accounts differ in detail as independent witnesses do, and Mark ends with fear and silence; an empty tomb alone would not prove a resurrection.

sessions.title: The case against: did he rise?
sessions.line: Hallucinations, a stolen body, a man who did not die, a legend that grew: the natural explanations of Easter, at full strength.
sessions.plain: The first Christians said that God raised Jesus from the dead. For two hundred years, critics have offered other explanations: Jesus did not really die, the body was stolen or moved, the disciples saw visions produced by grief, or the story grew as a legend. Behind them all stands a deeper objection: that no historian can ever conclude that a miracle happened. This session gives the strongest of these views their full weight, in the words of the man who first set them out in full, before any reply.
sessions.why: Five sessions have followed the week: the entry and the Temple, the supper, the trial, the cross and the empty tomb. You have seen the evidence the first Christians pointed to. Now the strongest objection gets its turn: everything in that evidence, its critics say, can be explained without a resurrection.
answers: Could Jesus have survived the cross?
Could the body have been stolen or moved?
Could the disciples have seen hallucinations?
Could the story have grown as a legend?
Can a historian ever say that a miracle happened?
sessions.finding: Each natural explanation explains part of the evidence; the question is which explains all of it best, and the answer depends on whether you allow that God could act.

paras: Here is what the earlier sessions found. Jesus came to Jerusalem at Passover and acted as a king and a prophet against the Temple. At a last supper he gave his coming death a meaning. The high priests handed him to Pilate, who crucified him as King of the Jews. He died, probably within six hours, and was buried. On the Sunday, women found the tomb empty, and his opponents said the body had been stolen.

The other half of the evidence is the appearances. In 'What is the Bible?' you read Paul's list, which he says he 'received' and handed on: Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas (Peter), then to the twelve, then to more than five hundred at once, then to James, then to all the apostles, and last to Paul himself (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Paul wrote that around AD 54; most scholars think he received the list within a few years of the crucifixion, perhaps when he visited Peter in Jerusalem about AD 35 (Galatians 1:18).
background.key: The case so far: death, burial, an empty tomb, and Paul's early list of appearances to individuals and groups, received within a few years.

paras: Historians who disagree about the resurrection agree on more than you might think. Bart Ehrman, an agnostic, and N. T. Wright, a former bishop, both accept that Jesus died by crucifixion; that soon afterwards some of his followers, and at least one opponent, Paul, sincerely believed they had seen him alive; that they proclaimed this in Jerusalem within weeks or months; and that they were willing to suffer for it. Most also accept the burial and, more cautiously, the empty tomb.

So the question is not whether something happened to the disciples. It is what. Any explanation has to account for the death, the empty tomb if it is accepted, the appearances to individuals and groups, the change in the disciples, and the conversion of an enemy. The natural explanations each try.
background.key: Sceptics and believers mostly agree on the facts: the death, the sincere experiences, the early proclamation; they disagree on what caused the experiences.

paras: David Friedrich Strauss (1808–1874) was a young lecturer at the Protestant seminary at Tübingen, in Germany, when he published The Life of Jesus Critically Examined in 1835. He argued that the Gospels are largely 'myth': not lies, but the early church's faith in Jesus told as if it were history, drawing on the Old Testament and Jewish hopes. The book caused a scandal and cost him his post. In 1846 it was translated into English by Mary Ann Evans, later famous as the novelist George Eliot.

Strauss took on two older explanations: the rationalists' 'swoon', which said Jesus did not die, and the claim of Hermann Samuel Reimarus, published by Gotthold Lessing in 1778, that the disciples stole the body. He rejected both and argued instead for visions. His argument is still, in essentials, the one modern sceptics make.
background.key: Strauss's Life of Jesus (1835; tr. George Eliot, 1846) rejected the swoon and the theft and explained Easter by visions: still the sceptics' main case.

paras: The main reading is short: Paul's own statement of what is at stake, 1 Corinthians 15:12–20. Paul does not treat the resurrection as a pious metaphor. He says that if it did not happen, the faith is empty and he is a liar.

The comparison is the heart of this session: Strauss's own argument against the resurrection, in George Eliot's translation, in five parts. It is long and dense, so each part is introduced in plain words first. A later hall of Rose Window, The Modern World, gives a journey of its own to David Hume's argument against miracles; here it is summarised in the lecture.
background.key: Paul says everything depends on the resurrection; Strauss makes the strongest case that it can be explained without one.

before: What does Paul say follows if Christ has not been raised?
In Strauss, which explanations does he reject, and why?
What does Strauss think the disciples really experienced, and where?
sessions.readWhy: Paul's statement of what is at stake.

paras: Now if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?
But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised.
If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith also is in vain.
Yes, we are also found false witnesses of God, because we testified about God that he raised up Christ, whom he didn’t raise up, if it is so that the dead are not raised.
For if the dead aren’t raised, neither has Christ been raised.
If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins.
Then they also who are fallen asleep in Christ have perished.
If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable.
But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep.

parts.title: If Christ has not been raised
parts.context: Paul, writing to Corinth around AD 54, has just listed the witnesses to the risen Christ. Some Christians in Corinth, Greeks by birth, say there is no resurrection of the dead. Greeks could believe in an immortal soul, but a body raised from death seemed absurd to them; at Athens, Luke says, some laughed at Paul when he mentioned it (Acts 17:32).

commentary.on: how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?
commentary.text: The Corinthians probably did not deny life after death. They denied that the body would rise. Paul insists that the two cannot be separated: if bodies are never raised, Christ's was not.

commentary.on: If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith also is in vain.
commentary.text: Paul makes his faith depend on something that either happened or did not. He does not say: believe it anyway, it is a beautiful idea.

commentary.on: we are also found false witnesses of God
commentary.text: Paul knows the charge that would be made, and accepts the terms: if it did not happen, he is lying about God.

commentary.on: your faith is vain; you are still in your sins.
commentary.text: For Paul, the cross without the resurrection would be one more execution. It is the rising that shows the death was not the end.

commentary.on: If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable.
commentary.text: Paul had been flogged, stoned, shipwrecked and imprisoned for this message (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). If it is false, he says, he has thrown his life away.

commentary.on: He became the first fruits of those who are asleep.
commentary.text: The 'first fruits' was the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God the day after the Sabbath at Passover time (Leviticus 23:10–11), as a promise of the rest. For Paul, Jesus's resurrection is the first sheaf of the resurrection of all the dead.

paras: Hence the cultivated intellect of the present day has very decidedly stated the following dilemma: either Jesus was not really dead, or he did not really rise again.

Rationalism has principally given its adhesion to the former opinion. The short time that Jesus hung on the cross, together with the otherwise ascertained tardiness of death by crucifixion, and the uncertain nature and effects of the wound from the spear, appeared to render the reality of the death doubtful. That the agents in the crucifixion, as well as the disciples themselves, entertained no such doubt, would be explained not only by the general difficulty of distinguishing deep swoons and the rigidity of syncope from real death, but also from the low state of medical science in that age; while at least one example of the restoration of a crucified person appeared to render conceivable a resuscitation in the case of Jesus also. This example is found in Josephus, who informs us that of three crucified acquaintances whose release he begged from Titus, two died after being taken down from the cross, but one survived. How long these people had hung on the cross Josephus does not mention;

but from the manner in which he connects them with his expedition to Thekoah, by stating that he saw them on his return from thence, they must probably have been crucified during this expedition, and as this, from the trifling distance of the above place from Jerusalem, might possibly be achieved in a day, they had in all probability not hung on the cross more than a day, and perhaps a yet shorter time. These three persons, then, can scarcely have hung much longer than Jesus, who, according to Mark, was on the cross from nine in the morning till towards six in the evening, and they were apparently taken down while they still showed signs of life; yet with the most careful medical tendance only one survived. Truly it is difficult to perceive how it can hence be shown probable that Jesus, who when taken from the cross showed all the signs of death, should have come to life entirely of himself, without the application of medical skill.

Notwithstanding all these improbabilities, which are against the opinion that Jesus came to life after a merely apparent death by the operation of natural causes, this nevertheless remains so far possible, that if we had secure evidence of the resuscitation of Jesus, we might, on the strength of such certainty as to the result, supply the omissions in the narrative, and approve the opinion above presented,—with the rejection, however, of all precise conjectures. Secure evidence of the resurrection of Jesus, would be the attestation of it in a decided and accordant manner by impartial witnesses. But the impartiality of the alleged witnesses for the resurrection of Jesus, is the very point which the opponents of Christianity, from Celsus down to the Wolfenbüttel Fragmentist, have invariably called in question. Jesus showed himself to his adherents only: why not also to his enemies, that they too might be convinced, and that by their testimony posterity might be precluded from every conjecture of a designed fraud on the part of his disciples? I cannot certainly attach much weight to the replies by which apologists have sought to repel this objection, from that of Origen, who says: Christ avoided the judge who condemned him, and his enemies, that they might not be smitten with blindness; to the opinions of the modern theologians, who by their vacillation between the assertion that by such an appearance the enemies of Jesus would have been compelled to believe, and the opposite one, that they would not have believed even on such evidence,—mutually confute one another. Nevertheless, it can still be urged in reply to that objection, that the adherents of Jesus, from their hopelessness, which is both unanimously attested by the narratives, and is in perfect accordance with the nature of the case, here rise to the rank of impartial witnesses.

If they had expected a resurrection of Jesus and we had then been called upon to believe it on their testimony alone: there would certainly be a possibility and perhaps also a probability, if not of an intentional deception, yet of an involuntary self-delusion on their part; but this possibility vanishes in proportion as the disciples of Jesus lost all hope after his death. Now even if it be denied that any one of the gospels proceeded immediately from a disciple of Jesus, it is still certain from the epistles of Paul and the Acts that the Apostles themselves had the conviction that they had seen the risen Jesus. We might then rest satisfied with the evangelical testimonies in favour of the resurrection, were but these testimonies in the first place sufficiently precise, and in the second, in agreement with themselves and with each other. But in fact the testimony of Paul, which is intrinsically consistent and is otherwise most important, is so general and vague, that taken by itself, it does not carry us beyond the subjective fact, that the disciples were convinced of the resurrection of Jesus; while the more fully detailed narratives of the gospels, in which the resurrection of Jesus appears as an objective fact, are, from the contradictions of which they are convicted, incapable of being used as evidence, and in general their account of the life of Jesus after his resurrection is not one which has connexion and unity, presenting a clear historical idea of the subject, but a fragmentary compilation, which presents a series of visions, rather than a continuous history.

If we compare with this account of the resurrection of Jesus, the precise and internally consistent attestation of his death: we must incline to the other side of the dilemma above stated, and be induced to doubt the reality of the resurrection rather than that of the death. Hence Celsus chose this alternative, deriving the alleged appearance of Jesus after the resurrection, from the self-delusion of the disciples, especially the women, either dreaming or waking; or from what appeared to him still more probable, intentional deception: and more modern writers, as, for example, the Wolfenbüttel Fragmentist, have adopted the accusation of the Jews in Matthew, namely, that the disciples stole the body of Jesus, and afterwards fabricated, with slender agreement, stories of his resurrection and subsequent appearances. This suspicion is repelled by the remark of Origen, that a spontaneous falsehood on the part of the disciples could not possibly have animated them to so unflinching an announcement of the resurrection of Jesus amid the greatest perils; and it is a just argument of modern apologists that the astonishing revolution from the deep depression and utter hopelessness of the disciples at the death of Jesus, to the strong faith and enthusiasm with which they proclaimed him as the Messiah on the succeeding Pentecost, would be inexplicable unless in the interim something extraordinarily encouraging had taken place—something, in fact, which had convinced them of his resurrection. But that this cause of conviction was precisely a real appearance of the risen Jesus—that, indeed it was necessarily an external event at all—is by no means proved.

If we chose to remain on supranatural ground, we might with Spinoza suppose that a vision was produced by miraculous means in the minds of the disciples, the object of which was to make evident to them, in a manner accordant with their powers of comprehension and the ideas of their age, that Jesus by his virtuous life had risen from spiritual death, and that to those who followed his example he would grant a similar resurrection. With one foot at least on the same ground stands the supposition of Weisse, that the departed spirit of Jesus really acted on the disciples whom he had left behind; in connexion with which he refers to the apparitions of spirits, the impossibility of which remains unproved. In order to escape from the magic circle of the supernatural, others have searched for natural external causes which might induce the belief that Jesus had risen and had been seen after his resurrection. The first impetus to this opinion, it has been conjectured, was given by the circumstance that on the second morning after the burial his grave was found empty, the linen clothes which lay in it being taken first for angels and then for an appearance of the risen Jesus himself: but if the body of Jesus was not reanimated, how are we to suppose that it came out of the grave? Here it would be necessary to recur to the supposition of a theft: unless the intimation of John, that Jesus on account of haste was laid in a strange grave, were thought available for the conjecture that perhaps the owner of the grave caused the corpse to be removed: which however the disciples must subsequently have learned, and which in any case has too frail a foundation in the solitary statement of the fourth gospel.

Far more fruitful is the appeal to the passage of Paul (1 Cor. xv. 5 ff.), as the most appropriate starting point in this inquiry, and the key to the comprehension of all the appearances of Jesus after his resurrection. When Paul there places the Christophany which occurred to himself in the same series with the appearances of Jesus in the days after his resurrection: this authorizes us, so far as nothing else stands in the way of such an inference, to conclude that, for aught the Apostle knew, those earlier appearances were of the same nature with the one experienced by himself. Now with respect to the latter as narrated to us in the Acts (ix. 1 ff., xxii. 3 ff., xxvi. 12 ff.), it is no longer possible, after the analysis of Eichhorn and Ammon, to retain it as an external, objective appearance of the real Christ; even Neander does not positively dare to maintain more than an internal influence of Christ on the mind of Paul, only appending in a very beseeching manner the supposition of an external appearance;

and even that internal influence he himself renders superfluous by detailing the causes which might in a natural manner produce such a revolution in the disposition of the man thus: the favourable impression of Christianity, of the doctrine, life and conduct of its adherents, which he had here and there received, especially on the occasion of the martyrdom of Stephen, threw his mind into a state of excitement and conflict, which he might indeed for a time forcibly repress, perhaps even by redoubled zeal against the new sect, but which must at last find vent in a decisive spiritual crisis, concerning which it need not surprise us that in an oriental it took the form of a Christophany. If according to this we have in the Apostle Paul an example, that strong impressions from the infant Christian community might carry an ardent mind that had long striven against it, to a pitch of exaltation which issued in a Christophany, and a total change of sentiment:

surely the impression of the sublime personality of Jesus would suffice to inspire into his immediate disciples, struggling with the doubts concerning his messiahship which his death had excited in them, the experience of similar visions. They who think it necessary and desirable in relation to the Christophany of Paul to call in the aid of external natural phenomena, as thunder and lightning, may also seek to facilitate the explanation of the appearances of the risen Jesus which his immediate disciples believed themselves to have previously had, by the supposition of similar incidents. Only it must be observed that, as Eichhorn’s explanation of the event in the life of Paul proved a failure from his maintaining as historical every single detail in the New Testament narrative, as the blindness of Paul and his cure, the vision of Ananias, and so on, which he could only transform into natural occurrences by a very strained interpretation:

so it would inevitably render impossible the psychological explanation of the appearances of Jesus, to acknowledge as historical all the evangelical narratives concerning them, especially those of the tests which Thomas applied by touching the wounds of Jesus, and which Jesus himself afforded by taking material nourishment; and indeed these narratives, from the contradiction which they are shown to present, have not the slightest claim to such a character. The two first gospels, and our chief informant in this matter, the Apostle Paul, tell us nothing of such tests, and it is quite natural that the Christophanies which, in the actual experience of the women and Apostles, may have floated before them as visions of much the same character as that which Paul had on the way to Damascus, when once received into tradition, should by reason of the apologetic effort to cut off all doubts as to their reality, be continually more and more consolidated so that the mute appearances became speaking ones, the ghostlike form was exchanged for one that ate, and the merely visible body was made palpable also.

Meanwhile, if the body of Jesus was interred in a known place, and could there (so far as we are not at liberty to suppose a theft, or an accidental removal) be sought for and exhibited: it is difficult to conceive how the disciples in Jerusalem itself, and not quite two days after the interment, could believe and declare that Jesus was risen, without refuting themselves, or meeting with refutation from their adversaries, (to whom however they appear to have made the first disclosure as to the resurrection of their Messiah at Pentecost,) by ocular demonstration at the grave. Now it is here that the narrative of the first gospel, which has been unjustly placed below the others, presents an explanatory and satisfactory indication. According to this gospel also the risen Jesus does indeed appear in Jerusalem, but only to the women, and so entirely as a mere preparation for a succeeding interview, nay, so superfluously, that we have already questioned the truth of this appearance, and pronounced it to be a later modification of the legend of the angelic appearance, which Matthew nevertheless also included in his narrative.

The sole important appearance of Jesus after the resurrection occurs, according to Matthew, in Galilee, whither an angel, and Jesus himself on the last evening of his life and on the morning of the resurrection, most urgently directed his disciples, and where the fourth gospel also, in its appendix, places an appearance of the resuscitated Jesus. That the disciples, dispersed by their alarm, at the execution of their Messiah, should return to their home in Galilee, where they had no need, as in the metropolis of Judea, the seat of the enemies of their crucified Christ, to shut the doors for fear of the Jews, was natural. Here was the place where they gradually began to breathe freely, and where their faith in Jesus, which had been temporarily depressed, might once more expand with its former vigour. But here also, where no body lay in the grave to contradict bold suppositions, might gradually be formed the idea of the resurrection of Jesus; and when this conviction had so elevated the courage and enthusiasm of his adherents that they ventured to proclaim it in the metropolis, it was no longer possible by the sight of the body of Jesus either to convict themselves, or to be convicted by others.

parts.author: D. F. Strauss
parts.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §140
parts.translator: George Eliot (1846; 1902 printing of the fourth edition)
parts.title: Not dead, or not risen?
parts.context: From §140 of Strauss's Life of Jesus, 'Debates concerning the reality of the death and resurrection of Jesus', in George Eliot's translation (first published 1846; this is the 1902 printing of the fourth edition). Before this, Strauss has argued that a dead body cannot be brought back to life without a miracle that breaks the laws of nature. Footnote numbers have been removed. Strauss refers to Josephus, Life 75, where Josephus begged Titus to release three crucified friends.
parts.plain: Strauss says: modern educated people face a choice. Either Jesus was not really dead, or he did not really rise. The rationalists chose the first: Jesus hung on the cross only a short time, people often took a deep faint for death, and Josephus knew a man who survived crucifixion. But Strauss rejects this. Of Josephus's three friends, taken down alive and nursed with every care, two died anyway. It is hard to believe that Jesus, who showed every sign of death, came back to life by himself, with no doctor at all.

commentary.on: either Jesus was not really dead, or he did not really rise again.
commentary.text: Strauss's dilemma. Notice his starting point: a real resurrection is ruled out from the beginning, because it would need a miracle.

commentary.on: The short time that Jesus hung on the cross
commentary.text: The swoon theory's best evidence: Pilate himself was surprised (Mark 15:44). It was argued by the rationalist scholar H. E. G. Paulus (1828), and had been put forward by others before him.

commentary.on: of three crucified acquaintances whose release he begged from Titus, two died after being taken down from the cross, but one survived
commentary.text: A real case of survival, from Josephus. The swoon theory is not absurd on its face.

commentary.on: Truly it is difficult to perceive how it can hence be shown probable that Jesus, who when taken from the cross showed all the signs of death, should have come to life entirely of himself
commentary.text: Strauss, no believer, demolishes the swoon himself. Even with nursing, two of Josephus's three friends died; Jesus had none, a spear wound in John, and a sealed tomb.

parts.author: D. F. Strauss
parts.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §140
parts.translator: George Eliot (1846; 1902 printing of the fourth edition)
parts.title: Witnesses who were not neutral
parts.context: Strauss has dismissed further versions of the swoon (a plot with a drug, or secret helpers) as fantasies with no basis in the sources. Now he asks what kind of evidence would prove a resurrection, and whether we have it. Celsus was a pagan critic of the 170s; 'the Wolfenbüttel Fragmentist' is Reimarus.
parts.plain: Strauss says: we could accept the resurrection if impartial witnesses agreed about it. But Jesus appeared only to his followers, never to his enemies. In their favour, the disciples had lost all hope at his death, so they were not expecting it; and Paul's letters show the apostles really were convinced they had seen him. But Paul's account is too vague to show more than that they were convinced, and the Gospels' fuller accounts contradict each other. They read like a series of visions, not a history.

commentary.on: Jesus showed himself to his adherents only: why not also to his enemies
commentary.text: The oldest objection, already made by Celsus in the second century. (Christians would reply that Paul and James were not followers when they saw him; the lecture returns to this.)

commentary.on: the adherents of Jesus, from their hopelessness ... here rise to the rank of impartial witnesses
commentary.text: Strauss is fair. He concedes the believers' strongest point: the disciples were not expecting a resurrection, so they were not simply seeing what they hoped to see.

commentary.on: it is still certain from the epistles of Paul and the Acts that the Apostles themselves had the conviction that they had seen the risen Jesus
commentary.text: Strauss accepts what almost every historian now accepts: the disciples sincerely believed they had seen him. He is not calling them liars.

commentary.on: a series of visions, rather than a continuous history
commentary.text: His diagnosis: the Easter stories are disconnected glimpses, the kind of thing visions produce, not the connected narrative of an event.

parts.author: D. F. Strauss
parts.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §140
parts.translator: George Eliot (1846; 1902 printing of the fourth edition)
parts.title: Not fraud, but something
parts.context: Strauss now turns to the other side of his dilemma: that Jesus really died and did not rise. Origen (c. 185–254) was the great Christian scholar of Alexandria; 'Pentecost' is the feast seven weeks after Passover, when Acts says the apostles first preached in public.
parts.plain: Strauss says: if the death is better attested than the resurrection, we should doubt the resurrection. Celsus and Reimarus said the disciples deceived themselves or stole the body. But Origen was right that liars could not have preached so fearlessly in the face of death, and modern defenders are right that something extraordinary must have turned the disciples from despair to bold faith. Strauss agrees. But he denies that the something had to be a real appearance, or anything outside their minds at all.

commentary.on: deriving the alleged appearance of Jesus after the resurrection, from the self-delusion of the disciples, especially the women
commentary.text: Celsus's explanation. Strauss's own phrase 'especially the women' shows the prejudice that made women's testimony suspect, in his century as in the first.

commentary.on: the disciples stole the body of Jesus
commentary.text: Reimarus revived the charge in Matthew 28. Strauss takes it seriously only to set it aside.

commentary.on: a spontaneous falsehood on the part of the disciples could not possibly have animated them to so unflinching an announcement
commentary.text: Strauss agrees with Origen: people do not suffer and die for what they know to be a lie. This is why almost no modern scholar holds the fraud theory.

commentary.on: the astonishing revolution from the deep depression and utter hopelessness of the disciples
commentary.text: Strauss grants the whole of what Christians call the transformation of the disciples. Something happened.

commentary.on: But that this cause of conviction was precisely a real appearance of the risen Jesus—that, indeed it was necessarily an external event at all—is by no means proved.
commentary.text: The pivot of the whole argument. The 'something' may have happened inside the disciples' minds.

parts.author: D. F. Strauss
parts.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §140
parts.translator: George Eliot (1846; 1902 printing of the fourth edition)
parts.title: Paul's vision as the key
parts.context: Strauss now gives his own explanation. He starts from Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 15, where Paul places his own experience on the road to Damascus in the same series as the earlier appearances, and from the accounts of Paul's conversion in Acts 9, 22 and 26. Eichhorn, Ammon and Neander were German scholars of Strauss's day. 'Christophany' means an appearance of Christ.
parts.plain: Strauss says: Paul puts his own vision in the same list as the other appearances, so they were probably the same kind of thing. Even believing scholars now explain Paul's experience mainly as something inside his mind, brought on by an inner struggle after he had seen Christians die for their faith. If an inner crisis could produce a vision of Christ in Paul, the powerful memory of Jesus could have produced similar visions in his grieving disciples. Over time the stories hardened: the silent appearances began to speak, then to eat, then to be touched.

commentary.on: When Paul there places the Christophany which occurred to himself in the same series with the appearances of Jesus
commentary.text: This is Strauss's strongest card, and modern sceptics still play it. Paul's experience came some years later and, in Acts, involved a light and a voice. If the earlier appearances were like Paul's, they may have been visions.

commentary.on: those earlier appearances were of the same nature with the one experienced by himself
commentary.text: Christians reply that Paul himself distinguished his experience as the 'last' and 'untimely' one (15:8), and that he speaks of a body raised, not a vision.

commentary.on: concerning which it need not surprise us that in an oriental it took the form of a Christophany
commentary.text: Strauss's phrase 'an oriental' reflects the prejudice of his time, as if Jews were especially prone to visions. The argument does not need it.

commentary.on: the mute appearances became speaking ones, the ghostlike form was exchanged for one that ate, and the merely visible body was made palpable also
commentary.text: The legend argument: in Paul, Jesus 'appeared'; in Luke he eats fish (24:42–43); in John, Thomas is invited to touch him. Strauss reads this as a story growing more solid to answer doubters.

parts.author: D. F. Strauss
parts.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §140
parts.translator: George Eliot (1846; 1902 printing of the fourth edition)
parts.title: Far from the tomb
parts.context: Strauss has argued that the disciples, searching their Scriptures for a suffering Messiah, came to believe that Jesus lived in glory, and that some saw him in visions. Now he faces the obvious problem: if the body was in a known tomb, why did no one produce it?
parts.plain: Strauss says: if the body lay in a known tomb in Jerusalem, it is hard to see how the disciples could proclaim the resurrection there two days later without being refuted. His answer: Matthew is right that the appearances happened in Galilee. The disciples fled home; there, far from the tomb, the belief grew over time. By the time they came back to Jerusalem to preach it, it was too late for anyone to show them the body.

commentary.on: it is difficult to conceive how the disciples in Jerusalem itself, and not quite two days after the interment, could believe and declare that Jesus was risen
commentary.text: Strauss sees the problem clearly, and states it more sharply than many believers do.

commentary.on: But here also, where no body lay in the grave to contradict bold suppositions, might gradually be formed the idea of the resurrection of Jesus
commentary.text: His solution: distance and time. The belief formed in Galilee, a hundred kilometres away, over months.

commentary.on: it was no longer possible by the sight of the body of Jesus either to convict themselves, or to be convicted by others
commentary.text: By then the body would have decayed beyond recognition. Critics of Strauss reply that Paul's list and Acts place the first proclamation in Jerusalem, and that Strauss has to call Acts 'historically worthless' on this point to make his theory work.

compare.author: D. F. Strauss
compare.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §140
compare.translator: George Eliot (1846; 1902 printing of the fourth edition)
compare.why: Strauss set out the natural explanations of Easter more fully and more fairly than anyone before him, and rejected the weaker ones himself. Read his argument as he made it.
compare.title: The case against, by its first great advocate

paras: The swoon theory says Jesus fainted on the cross, was taken down alive, revived in the cool of the tomb and appeared to his disciples. It was argued by Karl Venturini (1800) and H. E. G. Paulus (1828), and has returned in popular books ever since, such as Hugh Schonfield's The Passover Plot (1965). Its strongest points are real: Jesus died unusually quickly, and Josephus knew a man who survived crucifixion.

Almost no scholar holds it today, believer or sceptic, and Strauss gave the reason. In A New Life of Jesus (1864) he added a famous argument: a man half dead, who had crept out of a tomb and needed nursing, could never have convinced his followers that he had conquered death. At most he would have left them pitying him. The Roman executioners, whose trade was killing, and the centurion who confirmed the death to Pilate, are against it too.
sections.key: The swoon theory has some evidence, but a half-dead man would never have been hailed as conqueror of death; Strauss himself rejected it.

paras: Explanations of the empty tomb alone come in three kinds. The disciples stole the body, as the priests said in Matthew and Reimarus argued in the 1700s. Someone else moved it: the Jewish scholar Joseph Klausner suggested in 1922 that Joseph of Arimathea may have moved it to another grave. Or the women went to the wrong tomb in the half-light, as Kirsopp Lake proposed in 1907.

Each explains how a tomb could be empty without a miracle, and each is possible. Their weakness is that they explain only half the evidence. A moved body does not explain why Peter, James and Paul believed they saw Jesus alive. Theft by the disciples makes them liars, and, as Origen and Strauss agreed, liars do not suffer for what they know to be false. The wrong tomb ignores the women who, in Mark, saw where he was laid; and anyone could have gone to the right one.
sections.key: Theft, reburial and the wrong tomb can explain an empty tomb, but not the appearances; theft makes the disciples liars who died for a lie.

sections.h: Visions: the hallucination hypothesis at full strength
paras: This is the strongest natural explanation, and the one most sceptical scholars hold. Gerd Lüdemann (The Resurrection of Jesus, 1994) argued that Peter, crushed by grief and guilt at his denial, had a vision of Jesus forgiving him; others, in the same state, had visions too, and the experience spread through the group. Paul, he argued, was troubled by persecuting Christians, and his conversion vision resolved it. Michael Goulder compared such experiences to other 'conversion visions' in religious history.

The evidence for it is serious. Experiences of the dead are common after bereavement. In a study of 293 widowed people in mid-Wales, published in the British Medical Journal in 1971, W. Dewi Rees found that nearly half had sensed, seen or heard their dead husband or wife, often for years. Group experiences are known too: crowds have reported seeing the Virgin Mary, for example at Knock in Ireland in 1879. The disciples were grieving, guilty, together, and steeped in Scripture that spoke of the righteous being vindicated. Visions explain why they were sincere, why the appearances came to individuals and groups, and why the stories vary. Dale Allison, who is not a sceptic, has documented how closely bereavement experiences match parts of the Easter stories (Resurrecting Jesus, 2005).
sections.key: The vision theory explains the disciples' sincerity and the appearances by grief, guilt and group experience, and bereavement studies show such experiences are common.

paras: The legend view adds time. The Gospels were written forty to seventy years after the events, by people who were not eyewitnesses, from stories passed on by word of mouth. Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) argues that stories change as they are retold, and that the Easter stories show it happening: Paul's list gives no details at all; Mark has no appearance; Matthew one in Galilee; Luke and John a body that eats fish and can be touched. The empty tomb itself, Ehrman suggests, may have entered the story only later.

In its strongest form the legend view is joined to the vision view: some disciples really had experiences of Jesus after his death; the stories about those experiences then grew, as Strauss said, more physical and more detailed, to answer doubters. Rudolf Bultmann, the most influential New Testament scholar of the twentieth century, put it as a believer: what rose at Easter was the disciples' faith; the resurrection is not an event of past history that a historian could check.
sections.key: The legend view says the Easter stories grew in the retelling, from Paul's bare list to John's touchable body, on top of real visions.

sections.h: The deepest objection: can a historian say God acted?
paras: Behind every natural explanation lies a principle. In 1748 the Scottish philosopher David Hume argued that we should believe a report of a miracle only if the falsehood of the report would be more miraculous than the event, and that this is never the case: it is always more likely that witnesses were mistaken or deceived than that the laws of nature were broken (An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, section 10). Later, the German theologian Ernst Troeltsch (1898) argued that historians must judge the past by analogy with what happens now, and dead men do not rise now.

On this view, even if every natural explanation is weak, a historian must still prefer it to a miracle, because a miracle is by definition the least likely explanation of anything. This is the real heart of the case against. It does not claim to know what happened in Jerusalem. It claims that, whatever happened, the answer cannot be that God raised Jesus. A later hall, The Modern World, gives Hume's argument a journey of its own.
sections.key: Hume and Troeltsch argue that a natural explanation, however weak, must always be preferred to a miracle: this, not any one theory, is the core of the case against.

paras: N. T. Wright (The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003) replies that visions of the dead were well known in the ancient world, and people had words for them: a ghost, an angel, a spirit (Acts 12:15). 'Resurrection' meant something else: a body raised from the grave at the end of time. Grieving Jews who saw visions of their dead teacher would have said he was with God, not that he was raised, unless the tomb was empty too. Only the two together, an empty tomb and appearances, explain why they used the word. Critics, including Allison and Ehrman, reply that Wright underrates how varied Jewish ideas were, and how much a vision could mean.

Others point to what the vision theory leaves over: appearances to groups, including five hundred at once; to James, Jesus's brother, who had not followed him (Mark 3:21) and became a leader of the church; and to Paul, an enemy with no grief to resolve. Allison, weighing all this, concludes that the tomb was probably empty and the disciples saw something, but that history cannot settle what. Which explanation is best depends on a prior question: is there a God who could raise the dead? If not, a natural explanation must be right, however strained. If so, the resurrection becomes a live option. That question cannot be settled by this evidence alone.
sections.key: Wright argues that only an empty tomb plus appearances explains the word 'resurrection'; Allison concludes history cannot settle it; the answer turns on whether God could act.

refs: 1 Corinthians 15:3–20; Galatians 1:18; 2 Corinthians 11:23–27; Acts 9; 12:15; 17:32; 22; 26; Mark 3:21; 15:44; Luke 24:36–43; John 20:24–29; Leviticus 23:10–11.

D. F. Strauss, The Life of Jesus Critically Examined §140, tr. George Eliot (1846; 1902 printing); A New Life of Jesus (1864; English 1865). Josephus, Life 75. Origen, Against Celsus 2.55–56. H. S. Reimarus, 'On the Aim of Jesus and His Disciples', published by G. E. Lessing (1778).

David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), section 10. Ernst Troeltsch, 'On Historical and Dogmatic Method in Theology' (1898). Rudolf Bultmann, 'New Testament and Mythology' (1941).

K. Lake, The Historical Evidence for the Resurrection of Jesus Christ (1907). J. Klausner, Jesus of Nazareth (1922; English 1925). H. J. Schonfield, The Passover Plot (1965). Gerd Lüdemann, The Resurrection of Jesus (1994). Michael Goulder, 'The Baseless Fabric of a Vision', in G. D'Costa (ed.), Resurrection Reconsidered (1996).

W. Dewi Rees, 'The Hallucinations of Widowhood', British Medical Journal 4 (1971). N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003). Dale C. Allison Jr., Resurrecting Jesus (2005). Bart D. Ehrman, How Jesus Became God (2014).

debate.question: What best explains the Easter experiences?

positions.name: Visions and a growing legend
positions.who: D. F. Strauss (1835); Gerd Lüdemann (1994); Bart Ehrman (2014)
positions.view: Jesus died and stayed dead. Grieving, guilt-stricken disciples, and later Paul, had vivid experiences of him, as bereaved people often do; the stories grew more physical in the retelling, and the empty tomb was added or explained later. No miracle is needed, and historians should never assume one.
positions.evidence: Paul's own vision in the same list; bereavement studies (Rees, 1971); the growth from Mark to John; Hume's principle.

positions.name: God raised Jesus
positions.who: N. T. Wright (2003); Richard Swinburne, The Resurrection of God Incarnate (2003); most Christian traditions
positions.view: Only an empty tomb together with real appearances explains why Jews, who had words for visions and ghosts, said 'resurrection'; why groups, a sceptical brother and an enemy saw him; and why the movement began in Jerusalem. Hume's principle simply rules out the answer in advance.
positions.evidence: 1 Corinthians 15:3–8; the empty tomb and the opponents' reply; James and Paul; Sunday worship from the start.

positions.name: History cannot settle it
positions.who: Dale C. Allison Jr. (2005, 2021); Geza Vermes, The Resurrection (2008)
positions.view: The tomb was probably empty and the disciples saw something they could not explain otherwise. But the evidence is fragmentary, visions are real and strange, and what a person concludes depends on their beliefs about God and the world before they start.
positions.evidence: The strengths and gaps on both sides; the honest limits of historical method.

debate.agree: All agree that the disciples sincerely believed they had seen Jesus alive, that fraud and the swoon do not explain it, and that the answer depends partly on whether one allows that God could act.

look.why: The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of Thomas touching the wounds, or of another appearance, that is free to use here, so this session has none rather than a stand-in. Strauss would say that is fitting: the appearances, as he read them, were things seen by a few and painted afterwards by everyone.

music.why: Mozart was writing this mass for the dead when he died in 1791, and left it unfinished: music that stands at the edge of the question whether death is the end.

think.why: Whether you can believe a resurrection depends on whether there is a God who could act. Read the modern debate about God, with the objections stated fairly.

learn.why: The words Paul 'received' within a few years of the crucifixion: the evidence that every natural explanation has to explain.

listen.why: An agnostic New Testament scholar sets out to an atheist philosopher what historians can and cannot say about the resurrection.

check.q: Why did Strauss himself reject the swoon theory?
options: Because he believed Jesus rose from the dead
Because even Josephus's friends, taken down alive and nursed, mostly died, and a half-dead man could not have convinced anyone he had conquered death
Because Paulus had not read Josephus
Because the Gospels say Jesus was on the cross for three days
check.why: Strauss, a sceptic, argued against the swoon from Josephus and, later, from the effect a half-dead Jesus would have had.

check.q: Which point in favour of the disciples' sincerity does Strauss concede?
options: That Jesus appeared to his enemies
That they were trained historians
That they wrote the Gospels themselves
That their hopelessness after the death meant they were not expecting a resurrection, and that they really were convinced they had seen him
check.why: He grants that they 'rise to the rank of impartial witnesses' through their hopelessness, and that their conviction is certain.

check.q: What is Strauss's strongest card for the vision theory?
options: That Jesus never predicted his death
That Mary Magdalene was a known visionary
That the tomb was never found
That Paul places his own experience, later and visionary in kind, in the same list as the other appearances
check.why: 1 Corinthians 15:8: if the earlier appearances were like Paul's, they may have been visions.

check.q: Which part of the evidence does the theft or wrong-tomb theory fail to explain?
options: The crucifixion
The burial
The empty tomb
The appearances to Peter, James, the five hundred and Paul
check.why: It explains an empty tomb, not why people believed they saw Jesus alive.

check.q: What is the force of Hume's principle in this debate?
options: It shows that visions are impossible
It says that, whatever the evidence, a natural explanation must always be preferred to a miracle
It proves the disciples were lying
It shows that the tomb was not empty
check.why: Hume's argument is about the weight of testimony to any miracle, not about the details of this case.

check.q: N. T. Wright argues that visions alone would not have led the disciples to say 'resurrection'. Why?
options: Because Jews had other words for seeing the dead (ghost, angel, spirit); 'resurrection' meant a body raised from the grave, so they would only have used it if the tomb was empty too
Because the disciples spoke only Greek
Because Jews did not believe in visions
Because Paul forbade the word
check.why: Wright's case is that the empty tomb and the appearances together are needed to explain the language; critics say he underrates the variety of Jewish ideas.

tutorial.question: Assess the hallucination hypothesis.
tutorial.approach: State the hypothesis at full strength first, in Strauss's and Lüdemann's terms, with its best evidence: Paul's list, bereavement experiences, group visions, the growth of the stories. Then test it against each part of the evidence: the empty tomb, the group appearances, James and Paul, the word 'resurrection', the Jerusalem proclamation. Bring in Wright's reply and Allison's middle view. End by saying how far your answer depends on Hume's principle, and whether that principle is a conclusion from the evidence or an assumption brought to it.
strong: States the hypothesis fairly, in its advocates' own terms.
Uses Strauss's text, including what he concedes.
Uses outside evidence on bereavement experiences accurately.
Tests the hypothesis against the empty tomb, the group appearances and the conversions of James and Paul.
Represents Wright and Allison accurately.
Sees that the verdict depends partly on prior beliefs about God and miracles, and says so.

reading.author: Gerd Lüdemann
reading.title: What Really Happened to Jesus
reading.why: A short popular version of the vision hypothesis by its leading advocate.

reading.author: Dale C. Allison Jr.
reading.title: Resurrecting Jesus
reading.why: The long final chapter is the fairest assessment of the visions argument in print.

reading.author: N. T. Wright
reading.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God
reading.why: The fullest historical case for the resurrection, with the alternatives examined.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose one belief you hold strongly, about faith, politics or anything else. Write down the best case against it, as its best advocate would put it, until you think they would accept your summary. Then write two sentences on what, if anything, it changes.
sessions.reflect: Strauss gave up his career for what he thought true. What would you give up for what you think true?
takeaways: The swoon and the fraud theories fail, as Strauss himself argued; theft or reburial can explain an empty tomb but not the appearances.
The strongest natural explanation is visions, born of grief and guilt, with stories that grew in the retelling; bereavement studies show such experiences are common.
Behind them all is Hume's principle that a miracle is never the best explanation; whether that is right depends on whether God could act, which this evidence alone cannot settle.

sessions.title: My Lord and my God: the verdict
sessions.line: In John, Mary Magdalene meets him in the garden, and Thomas, who would not believe without touching the wounds, says 'My Lord and my God'.
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict first. Something happened after Jesus's death that turned his frightened followers into witnesses ready to die for the claim that he was alive; Christians say it was the resurrection, sceptics say it was visions and legend, and the evidence fits the first more naturally than the second if you allow that God could act. This session reads John's account of Easter Day and of Thomas, sets the Jewish and Muslim views of the cross and resurrection beside the Christian, and asks what Easter is about.
sessions.why: Session 6 gave the natural explanations their full weight and found that each explains part of the evidence, and that the choice between them and the resurrection turns on whether God could act. Now, the verdict, and the story of the man who would not believe without evidence.
answers: So did he rise?
What is Easter about, and how is it kept?
What do Jews say about the resurrection of Jesus?
What do Muslims say about the cross?
sessions.finding: Something happened that turned frightened followers into witnesses ready to die; Christians say it was the resurrection, and this journey has set out why and what else it might be.

paras: What happened in Jerusalem? Jesus came to the city at Passover as a king without an army, acted against the Temple, gave his death a meaning at a last supper, was handed over by the high priests and crucified by Pilate as King of the Jews. On all this, historians largely agree.

Did he rise? History can say this much. He was buried; the tomb was very probably found empty; his followers, and at least one enemy, sincerely believed they had seen him alive, alone and in groups; and they proclaimed it in Jerusalem, soon, at the cost of their lives. The natural explanations each account for part of that. The resurrection accounts for all of it, if God exists and can act. Whether he does is not a question this evidence can settle on its own, but the evidence is not neutral either: it is the kind of evidence that would exist if the first Christians were right.
background.key: The verdict: the evidence is best explained by the resurrection if God can act; the natural explanations each explain part; the choice turns on God.

paras: The idea of resurrection did not begin with Christians. Most of the Hebrew Bible says little about life after death. Then, around 165 BC, during a persecution by the Greek king Antiochus IV, the book of Daniel promised: 'Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt' (12:2). In 2 Maccabees 7, written about the same time, a mother and her seven sons die under torture rather than break God's law, confident that God will give them back their bodies.

By Jesus's time the Pharisees believed in the resurrection of the dead; the Sadducees, the priestly party, did not (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). Martha speaks for the Pharisees' hope in John: 'I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day' (11:24), read in 'Death and hope'. What no one expected was that one man would be raised in the middle of history, ahead of everyone else. That is what the first Christians claimed.

timeline.text: Daniel 12 promises the dead will awake
2 Maccabees 7: the mother and her seven sons
The first Easter
Paul: Christ the 'first fruits' of the dead
John's Gospel
The Qur'an, by Muslim belief, is revealed to Muhammad

background.key: Jews hoped for the resurrection of all the dead at the end of time; no one expected one man to be raised first.

paras: The main reading is John 20:1–29: Easter Day in John, in three parts, ending with Thomas. John's Gospel was written last, around AD 90 to 100; its closing words, which you read in 'What is the Bible?', say it was written 'that you may believe'. John is open about wanting a response.

The comparison is from the Qur'an, the holy book of Islam, which honours Jesus as a prophet and the Messiah, but says that he was not crucified. It is the one great tradition that denies the event every other source on this journey has assumed.
background.key: John's Easter Day and Thomas; then the Qur'an's denial of the crucifixion.

before: What does Mary Magdalene think has happened, and when does she recognise Jesus?
What does Thomas ask for, and what does he say?
Who, according to Jesus, is blessed?
sessions.readWhy: Easter Day in John in three parts: the tomb, the garden, and Thomas.

paras: Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb.
Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”
Therefore Peter and the other disciple went out, and they went toward the tomb.
They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first.
Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in.
Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying,
and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.
So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed.
For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
So the disciples went away again to their own homes.
But Mary was standing outside at the tomb weeping. So as she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.
They asked her, “Woman, why are you weeping?”
She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.”
When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn’t know that it was Jesus.
Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?”
She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.”
She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!”
Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ ”
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.

When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle, and said to them, “Peace be to you.”
When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord.
Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”
When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit!
If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained.”
But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.
The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!”
But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.”

parts.title: He saw and believed
parts.context: Sunday, before dawn. In John, Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb alone, or with others ('we', 20:2), finds it open, and runs for Peter and 'the other disciple whom Jesus loved', the figure John's Gospel claims as its source (21:24).

commentary.on: They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don't know where they have laid him!
commentary.text: Mary's first explanation is the natural one: someone has moved the body. The first person to suggest the theft theory in the Gospels is the first witness.

commentary.on: The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first.
commentary.text: A small, human detail, the kind a witness remembers, or a writer adds to sound like one; historians argue which.

commentary.on: the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself
commentary.text: The grave clothes are left neatly. Thieves would not unwrap a body, still less fold the cloth. Compare Lazarus, who came out of his tomb still bound (11:44): Jesus has left his behind.

commentary.on: he saw and believed.
commentary.text: The beloved disciple believes from the empty tomb alone, before any appearance.

commentary.on: For as yet they didn't know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
commentary.text: An honest admission. They had not read it in their Scriptures beforehand; they found the Scriptures afterwards. This tells against the idea that they talked themselves into it from the Bible first.

parts.title: Mary
parts.context: The two men go home. Mary stays at the tomb, weeping.

commentary.on: she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn't know that it was Jesus.
commentary.text: In several Easter stories he is not recognised at first: on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:16), read in 'What is the Bible?', and by the lake (John 21:4). Sceptics see visions; believers see a body changed. Either way, it is not what an inventor would write.

commentary.on: She, supposing him to be the gardener
commentary.text: John has said the tomb was in a garden (19:41). Later Jewish polemic, in the Toledot Yeshu, made a gardener the man who moved the body.

commentary.on: Mary.
commentary.text: One word, her name, and she knows him.

commentary.on: Don't hold me, for I haven't yet ascended to my Father
commentary.text: Often known by its Latin, Noli me tangere. She is not to cling to him as if things were as they were; something new has begun.

commentary.on: Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord
commentary.text: In John the first witness of the risen Jesus, and the first to announce it, is a woman. Early Christian writers called her 'the apostle to the apostles'.

parts.title: My Lord and my God
parts.context: That evening, and a week later, in Jerusalem, behind locked doors.

commentary.on: when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews
commentary.text: Frightened men, hiding. Whatever happened next changed that: within weeks, Acts says, they were preaching in the Temple courts.

commentary.on: he showed them his hands and his side.
commentary.text: The risen Jesus is the crucified one, wounds and all. Christianity's hope is not that the cross is undone, but that it is transformed.

commentary.on: As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.
commentary.text: Easter in John is not only an event but a sending. This is the beginning of the church's mission.

commentary.on: Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.
commentary.text: Thomas asks for the evidence a sceptic would ask for, and more: not to see, but to touch. 'Doubting Thomas' has become a name for anyone who wants proof.

commentary.on: Reach here your finger, and see my hands.
commentary.text: Jesus offers exactly what Thomas asked. John does not say he took it.

commentary.on: My Lord and my God!
commentary.text: The highest confession in the Gospels, from the man who doubted most. John's Gospel began 'the Word was God' (1:1); it ends its Easter story with a disciple saying it to Jesus's face. In the Greek Bible, 'Lord' was the word for God's own name.

commentary.on: Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.
commentary.text: Spoken to every later reader, including you. John knows we cannot touch the wounds. He has given us, instead, the witnesses.

paras: And for their unbelief,-and for their having spoken against Mary a grievous calumny,-

And for their saying, "Verily we have slain the Messiah, Jesus the son of Mary, an Apostle of God." Yet they slew him not, and they crucified him not, but they had only his likeness. And they who differed about him were in doubt concerning him: No sure knowledge had they about him, but followed only an opinion, and they did not really slay him, but God took him up to Himself. And God is Mighty, Wise!
There shall not be one of the people of the Book but shall believe in Him before his death, and in the day of resurrection, He will be a witness against them.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: They slew him not
parts.context: Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed by God to the Prophet Muhammad in Arabic between 610 and 632. Sura 4, 'Women', comes from his years in Medina, where he was in conflict with some of the city's Jewish tribes; these verses answer a boast that 'we have slain the Messiah'. The translation is by J. M. Rodwell (1861), an English clergyman; Muslims hold that no translation is the Qur'an itself, and readers have criticised parts of Rodwell's. A footnote number has been removed. Rodwell joins verses 157 and 158 in one paragraph.
parts.plain: The Qur'an says: some of the Jews claimed they had killed Jesus, son of Mary, the Messiah and God's messenger. But they did not kill him or crucify him; it was only made to appear so to them. Those who argued about it were in doubt and had no real knowledge. God raised Jesus up to himself. Every one of the People of the Book will believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.

commentary.on: And for their unbelief,-and for their having spoken against Mary a grievous calumny,-
commentary.text: The verses are part of a list of charges against some of the Jews of the Prophet's time, including a slander against Mary, whom the Qur'an honours as a virgin mother. They are polemical; they are not a license for hatred of Jews, and modern Muslim scholars reject that reading.

commentary.on: Verily we have slain the Messiah, Jesus the son of Mary, an Apostle of God
commentary.text: The Qur'an calls Jesus (Isa) 'the Messiah', al-Masih, and an apostle, a messenger of God: one of the greatest prophets, but not God's Son.

commentary.on: Yet they slew him not, and they crucified him not, but they had only his likeness.
commentary.text: The key words in Arabic, shubbiha lahum, mean 'it was made to seem so to them'. Most classical commentators, such as al-Tabari (died 923), understood that someone else was made to look like Jesus and was crucified in his place: Judas, Simon of Cyrene or a volunteer disciple, in different accounts.

commentary.on: No sure knowledge had they about him, but followed only an opinion
commentary.text: The Qur'an presents the crucifixion as a matter of mistaken opinion, not fact.

commentary.on: but God took him up to Himself.
commentary.text: Most Muslims believe Jesus was raised bodily to heaven without dying, and will return before the end of the world. For them, there was no death, and so no resurrection on the third day.

commentary.on: There shall not be one of the people of the Book but shall believe in Him before his death
commentary.text: 'People of the Book' means Jews and Christians. Whose death is meant, Jesus's (after his return) or each believer's, is debated among Muslim commentators.

compare.author: The Qur'an
compare.why: Every source on this journey, Christian, Jewish and Roman, assumes that Jesus was crucified. Islam, which honours Jesus as a prophet and the Messiah, denies it. Read the verses, and how Muslims understand them.
compare.title: The Qur'an on the cross

paras: Put the sessions together and three kinds of claim emerge. Some are as certain as ancient history gets: that Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate at Passover, on a charge of claiming to be King of the Jews, and that within a short time his followers were proclaiming that God had raised him. Some are probable, and most scholars accept them: the burial, the empty tomb, the appearances to Peter, the twelve, James and Paul. And one is the question itself: what caused it all?

The natural explanations are serious. Visions after bereavement are common; stories grow; people believe what they need to. But each struggles with something: the swoon with the soldiers, theft with the disciples' suffering, visions with the empty tomb, the groups, James and Paul, and the word 'resurrection'. The resurrection explains everything, but only if there is a God who raises the dead. A sceptic and a believer can look at the same evidence and both act reasonably, if they start from different places. What no one can reasonably say is that nothing happened.
sections.key: The crucifixion and the early proclamation are certain, the tomb and appearances probable; the resurrection explains all of it if God can act.

paras: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all speak of Jesus, and differ at exactly the point this journey has studied.

rows: A Jewish teacher, not the Messiah: the Messiah would bring peace, gather the exiles and rebuild the Temple
The Messiah and the Son of God
A great prophet and the Messiah, born of the Virgin Mary, but not divine
No: it was made to appear so; God raised him to himself
No; Jews hope for the resurrection of all the dead at the end
Yes, on the third day, the first fruits of all the dead
He did not die, so he did not rise; he will return
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11–12
table.note: Each tradition has a range of views; this is the mainstream of each.

sections.key: Jews accept the crucifixion but not the resurrection; Christians affirm both; most Muslims deny the crucifixion and so the need for a resurrection.

paras: Jews have never accepted that Jesus rose or that he was the Messiah. The main reason is simple: the Messiah, in Jewish hope, would bring peace to the world, gather the exiles and rebuild the Temple, and the world is plainly not yet redeemed. Maimonides set this out in the twelfth century. At the same time, belief in the resurrection of the dead remained central to Judaism: it is the last of Maimonides' thirteen principles, and the daily prayer, the Amidah, praises God 'who revives the dead'.

Some modern Jewish scholars have studied the Easter evidence closely. The most surprising was Pinchas Lapide (1922–1997), an Orthodox Jewish scholar, who concluded in The Resurrection of Jesus (1977; English 1983) that Jesus's resurrection may have been a real event, worked by God for the sake of the Gentiles, without making Jesus the Messiah of Israel. Others, like Geza Vermes (2008), found the evidence inconclusive. Jewish readers today often see Jesus as a Jewish teacher reclaimed for his own people, a reminder that Easter began as a Jewish claim made by Jews.
sections.key: Judaism rejects Jesus's resurrection and messiahship but keeps the hope of the resurrection of all the dead; Pinchas Lapide thought Jesus's resurrection may have been real.

paras: Muslims honour Jesus more than any other religion apart from Christianity: he is born of a virgin, works miracles, is called the Messiah and the Word of God, and will return at the end. But most Muslims believe he was not crucified. God, they say, would not let his prophet be shamed and killed by his enemies; someone else died in his place, and Jesus was taken up alive.

There are other Muslim readings. Some modern scholars, such as Mahmoud Ayoub (1980), have argued that the verse denies that the Jews had the power to kill Jesus, since God alone gives life and death, rather than denying that he died. The Ahmadiyya movement, founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad in the 1880s, taught that Jesus survived the cross and died much later in Kashmir: a swoon theory, held for religious reasons.
