Historians working by ordinary historical methods treat the crucifixion as certain, because Roman, Jewish and Christian sources attest it within a century; Muslims answer that the Qur'an is revelation, not historical reconstruction. This journey has set out the evidence; a Muslim reader will weigh it by a different authority.
sections.key: Most Muslims believe Jesus was not crucified but raised alive to God; some modern Muslim scholars read the verse differently; historians treat the crucifixion as certain.

sections.h: Easter: what it is and how it is kept
paras: Easter is the oldest Christian feast and the greatest. In most languages it is called Pascha, from the Hebrew Pesach, Passover; the English 'Easter' may come, as the monk Bede said in 725, from an old English spring goddess, Eostre, though some doubt it. Every Sunday is a little Easter, which is why Christians worship on the first day of the week.

Its date caused an early quarrel. Churches in Asia Minor kept it on the 14th of Nisan, whatever the day of the week; Rome kept it on the Sunday after, and around 190 Pope Victor tried to excommunicate the Asian churches for it. The Council of Nicaea in 325 agreed that all should keep the same Sunday, calculated independently of the Jewish calendar; the rule became the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox. Because the Orthodox churches still use the older Julian calendar for it, their Easter often falls a week or more after the Western one.

The night before, many churches keep the Easter Vigil: a new fire is lit in the dark, a great candle carried in, the ancient hymn called the Exsultet sung, and new Christians baptised. At midnight the Orthodox greet each other, 'Christ is risen!', and answer, 'Truly he is risen!'. Moravian Christians in Herrnhut, in Germany, began the Protestant custom of sunrise services in their graveyard in 1732.
sections.key: Easter, Pascha, is the oldest feast, kept since Nicaea (325) on a shared Sunday, though East and West calculate it differently; the Vigil, the Orthodox greeting and sunrise services mark it.

paras: Paul was clear: if Christ has not been raised, faith is in vain. Christians have never treated Easter as a happy ending added to a sad story. It is the claim that the cross, the Roman empire's most shameful death, was not the end of the man it killed, and so that death itself is not the end. The first Christians drew conclusions at once. They faced death without the old terror: the martyrs of the next centuries went to the beasts singing. They cared for the bodies of the poor and the dead, because bodies would be raised. They called Sunday the eighth day, the first day of a new creation. And every year, from Palm Sunday to Easter, they told the story of the week, as you have just walked it.

This journey cannot make anyone believe. It has tried to show what happened, what the first witnesses said, and what the best arguments are on both sides. Thomas asked for evidence and was offered it. John says that the rest of us, who cannot touch the wounds, are 'blessed' if we believe. That is an invitation, not a proof. The question it leaves is the one Jesus asked Peter on the road: who do you say I am?
sections.key: Easter is the claim that death is not the end; it changed how the first Christians lived and died. The journey ends with the evidence and an invitation, not a proof.

refs: The Qur'an, Sura 4:156–159, tr. J. M. Rodwell (1861); also 3:55; 19:33. Al-Tabari, Commentary on the Qur'an, on 4:157. Mahmoud Ayoub, 'Towards an Islamic Christology II: The Death of Jesus, Reality or Delusion', The Muslim World 70 (1980). Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, Jesus in India (1899).

Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10 (the thirteen principles); Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11–12. Pinchas Lapide, The Resurrection of Jesus: A Jewish Perspective (1977; English 1983). Geza Vermes, The Resurrection (2008).
Eusebius, Church History 5.23–25 (the Easter controversy). The Council of Nicaea (325). Bede, The Reckoning of Time 15 (725).
N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003). Dale C. Allison Jr., The Resurrection of Jesus (2021).

debate.question: The verdict: what happened at Easter?

positions.name: He rose
positions.who: N. T. Wright; Richard Swinburne; the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches
positions.view: God raised Jesus bodily from the dead on the third day. It is the best explanation of the empty tomb, the appearances, the transformation of the disciples and the birth of the church, and it fits who Jesus claimed to be.
positions.evidence: The case built across this journey: 1 Corinthians 15; the women; the opponents' reply; James and Paul; Sunday worship.

positions.name: He did not rise
positions.who: Gerd Lüdemann; Bart Ehrman; Judaism and Islam for different reasons
positions.view: Jesus died and did not rise. Sceptics explain the belief by visions and legend; Jews say the world is not yet redeemed, so he was not the Messiah; most Muslims say he was not crucified at all.
positions.evidence: Bereavement visions; the growth of the stories; Hume's principle; Qur'an 4:157.

positions.name: History can only go so far
positions.who: Dale C. Allison Jr.; Geza Vermes; Pinchas Lapide, in his own way
positions.view: The historian can show that something extraordinary happened to the disciples, and probably that the tomb was empty. Whether God raised Jesus is a question history raises but cannot answer; each person must answer it.
positions.evidence: The real strength and the real gaps of the evidence on both sides.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus was crucified under Pilate, except most Muslims, and that his followers sincerely proclaimed his resurrection; the disagreement is about the cause.

look.why: Benvenuto di Giovanni of Siena painted this in about 1491. It shows what no Gospel describes: the moment of rising itself. The painter imagines Matthew's guards fallen around the tomb and Christ standing over them, wounds and all, with the banner of victory over death.
points: Jesus stands in front of a doorway set into a rocky cave, on a chest-shaped stone tomb, with a gold halo and long reddish-blond hair.
A lavender cloth drapes over one shoulder and around his hips; his right hand is raised with two fingers lifted, in blessing.
He holds a tall staff with a white banner bearing a red cross.
A white stone slab lies across the ground in front of the tomb, and six soldiers in brightly coloured armour lie sprawled under and around it; one props himself on an elbow and looks up at him.
Behind, rivers zigzag through rocks and mountains to a distant town under a sky deepening from pale yellow to deep blue.

music.why: Part Two of Handel's Messiah (1741) tells the Passion and the rising, and ends with the Hallelujah chorus; audiences have stood for it since the eighteenth century.

think.why: If Jesus rose, what does it mean for everyone else? See what Christians believe about death and resurrection.

learn.why: John Donne's sonnet answers death with Easter: 'Death, thou shalt die.'

check.q: Mary Magdalene's first words in John 20 are 'They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb'. What follows?
options: That John did not believe in the resurrection
That she had stolen the body
That the tomb was not empty
That the first witness assumed a natural explanation, and that the empty tomb on its own did not produce belief
check.why: She thinks the body was moved; she believes only when she meets him.

check.q: John says 'as yet they didn't know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead'. Why does this matter for the debate in the last session?
options: It proves that Strauss was right
It shows the disciples could not read
It shows John had no Old Testament
It tells against the view that they talked themselves into a resurrection from Scripture beforehand
check.why: In John's account the Scriptures were understood afterwards, not before.

check.q: Why is Thomas's 'My Lord and my God' the climax of John's Gospel?
options: Because it is the last verse of the Bible
Because Thomas was the most important apostle

States openly the assumptions about God and miracles that the verdict depends on.
Represents Jewish and Muslim views accurately and fairly.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What happened in Jerusalem, and did he rise? In about 300 words, give your own verdict. Use at least three pieces of evidence from the journey, say plainly what your answer assumes about God, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Over the next Holy Week, or in any seven days, read one Gospel's account of the last week at the pace of the events: Mark 11 on the first day, Mark 12 and 13 over the next two, Mark 14 on the Thursday, Mark 15 on the Friday, nothing on the Saturday, and Mark 16 early on the Sunday morning. Each day, write one sentence about what you would have seen if you had been there.
synthesis: This journey asked what happened in Jerusalem in one week around AD 30, and whether Jesus rose from the dead. It walked through the week as a historian walks through a city, one place and one day at a time. Here are the short answers to its questions.

What is Holy Week, and what happened on Palm Sunday? Holy Week is the week from Jesus's entry into Jerusalem to the morning his tomb was found empty; the Gospels spend more time on it than on anything else. Jesus came to the city at Passover, the feast of freedom from Egypt, held under Roman rule, with the city full of pilgrims and Roman soldiers on the Temple roofs. He rode the last two miles on a donkey, acting out Zechariah's humble king, while the crowd shouted that David's kingdom was coming. The next day he overturned the traders' tables in the Temple and quoted Jeremiah's 'den of robbers': a prophet's sign that the Temple had failed and would fall. From then on, in Mark, the chief priests looked for a way to destroy him.

Was the Last Supper a Passover meal, and what did 'this is my body' mean? Mark says it was the Passover meal; John says Jesus died the next afternoon, as the Passover lambs were being killed. Scholars still argue which is right, or whether two calendars were in use; astronomy puts the likeliest dates in AD 30 or 33. Either way, the meal was steeped in Passover, and Jesus used it to say what his death would mean: his body given, and a new covenant in his blood, poured out for many. Paul's account, written around AD 54 and handed on as fixed tradition, shows that these words go back very early. In John, Jesus also knelt to wash his followers' feet, showing power as service. The churches have kept the meal ever since and still disagree about how Christ is present in it, from the Catholic and Orthodox belief in a real change to the memorial of many free churches.

Why did they kill him, and who was responsible? Only Rome could put a man to death, and crucifixion was a Roman punishment. The high priests, whose power depended on Rome and who feared his threat to the Temple and the crowds' hopes, arrested him at night and handed him to Pontius Pilate on the one charge Rome cared about: he claimed to be king. Philo and Josephus show a Pilate who was provocative and cruel but afraid of being reported to the emperor, much like the governor in the Gospels who gives way when told he will be no friend of Caesar. Tacitus and Josephus confirm the outline. The Jewish people were not responsible: Jesus and all his first followers were Jews. Yet for centuries Christians blamed 'the Jews', reading Matthew's 'his blood be on us' as a curse, with terrible results. Since 1945, and above all in Nostra Aetate in 1965, the churches have rejected that, and taught instead what their hymns had long said: every sinner shares the guilt.

What was crucifixion really like? It was the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels, designed for long pain, total shame and public warning. Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting penalty, unthinkable for a citizen; Josephus watched the Romans crucify five hundred Jews a day outside Jerusalem in AD 70. The heel bone of Yehohanan, found in 1968, still has the nail in it. Jesus died after about six hours, probably weakened by the flogging, and the Roman officer confirmed it. His words from the cross differ from Gospel to Gospel, from the cry of Psalm 22 to the trust of Psalm 31. That the first Christians proclaimed a crucified Messiah, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Greeks, is the strongest reason historians count the crucifixion as certain: no one would have invented it.

Was the tomb empty, and why do the accounts differ? Jesus was probably buried by Joseph of Arimathea in a rock tomb that the women saw, though some scholars doubt it. All four Gospels say women led by Mary Magdalene found it empty early on the Sunday, an unlikely detail to invent when women's testimony counted for little. Jesus's opponents said the disciples had stolen the body, which assumes the tomb was empty. The accounts differ on the number of women and angels, the time and where Jesus was seen, as independent witnesses do; Mark's Gospel ends, in the oldest manuscripts, with the women afraid and silent. And an empty tomb, on its own, proves nothing: Mary's first thought was that someone had moved him.

Could it have been hallucinations, a stolen body, a swoon, a legend? The swoon fails, as Strauss himself argued: a half-dead man could never have seemed the conqueror of death. Theft makes the disciples liars who suffered for what they knew to be false. The strongest natural explanation is visions, born of grief and guilt, of the kind many bereaved people have, with stories that grew more physical in the retelling. It explains the disciples' sincerity and the appearances. It struggles with the empty tomb, the group appearances, James and Paul, who were not grieving followers, and the choice of the word 'resurrection'. Behind every natural explanation lies Hume's principle: that a miracle can never be the best explanation of anything.

So did he rise? History can show that something extraordinary happened: that frightened men who had run away became, within weeks, witnesses ready to die for the claim that they had seen him alive, and that they made it first in the city where he was buried. The resurrection explains all of the evidence, if there is a God who can raise the dead. The natural explanations each explain part of it, and they must be right if there is not. That is why honest people, looking at the same evidence, reach different verdicts. Jews accept the crucifixion but not the resurrection; most Muslims believe Jesus was not crucified at all, but taken up alive to God; Christians say he died and rose, and keep Easter, Pascha, as their oldest and greatest feast.

One more thing. Count how much of the West comes from this week. The cross, once the sign of the empire's power to crush the weak, became the sign on churches, flags and graves. The idea that the victim, not the executioner, is the one to honour; that a ruler's power is borrowed from above; that a teacher should kneel to wash his pupils' feet; that a meal of bread and wine can bind strangers into one people; that every person, not one people, answers for the wrong done to the innocent; that death is not the end. When people in the West stand for the Hallelujah chorus, keep Good Friday, or say of someone who forgave their killers that they died like Christ, they are, knowingly or not, remembering one week in Jerusalem.

Thomas asked for evidence and was offered it. This journey has tried to give you the evidence, and the best case against it, as fairly as it can. The last word in John's Easter story is not a proof but a blessing on those who believe without seeing. Whether you accept it is your answer to write.

title: One root, two branches
question: How did Christianity grow out of Judaism, and why did they part?
line: Seven sessions on Paul's picture of one olive tree: Jesus the Jew, a Jewish church in the Temple, the Gentiles grafted in, the Temple's fall and the slow parting, the contempt that grew from it, the Church keeping Israel's Scriptures, and the verdict, 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable'.
why: Every Christian prays to the God of Abraham, sings the Psalms of Israel and follows a Jewish teacher. Yet for most of history Christians treated Jews as enemies, with terrible results. This course follows the story from the inside: how a Jewish movement became a mostly Gentile Church, why the two communities drew apart after the Temple fell, how family arguments in the New Testament were turned into a teaching of contempt, and how Jews and Christians are learning, since 1945, to speak as two branches of one root. It reads the Gospels, Acts and Romans beside Josephus, Ignatius, Eusebius, Irenaeus and Justin, and gives the case against the New Testament its full weight.
follows: A first-year paper on Christian origins and the 'parting of the ways' between Judaism and Christianity, with elements of a paper on Jewish–Christian relations after the Holocaust.
before: first-christians
outcomes: Explain, from Luke 2 and the Judaism of the Second Temple period, in what ways Jesus was a Jew, and describe the Pharisees fairly.
Describe the Jerusalem church under James and explain, from Acts 21 and Hegesippus, why it can be called a Jewish sect.
Set out the arguments over Gentile believers in Acts 10 and 15, and trace the shift from 'need not' to 'must not' in Ignatius.
Explain how the fall of the Temple in 70 and the Bar Kokhba revolt reshaped both communities, and weigh Dunn, Boyarin and Neusner on when the ways parted.
State Jules Isaac's charge of a 'teaching of contempt' at full strength, and assess whether the fault lies in the texts of Matthew 27 and John 8 or in their readers.
Explain why the Church rejected Marcion, define supersessionism, and interpret Paul's olive tree in Romans 11 with the main readings of 'all Israel will be saved'.

sessions.title: Jesus the Jew
sessions.line: A baby circumcised on the eighth day, a family at the Temple, a boy at Passover asking the teachers questions: where Christianity's story begins.
sessions.plain: Jesus was a Jew. He was circumcised as a baby, taken to the Temple in Jerusalem, brought up keeping the Jewish festivals, and as a man he prayed Israel's prayers and taught in its synagogues. For most of history Christians half forgot this, and it mattered terribly that they did. This session goes back to the beginning, to see what kind of Jew Jesus was and what the Judaism of his day was like.
sessions.why: This is the first session. To ask how Christianity grew out of Judaism and why the two parted, we have to start where both stories start: with a Jewish family in the land of Israel, in the time of the Second Temple, keeping the law of Moses.
answers: Was Jesus Jewish?
What was Judaism like in Jesus's day?
Who were the Pharisees, really?
What prayers did Jesus pray?
sessions.finding: Jesus was a Jew who kept the festivals, prayed the Shema and taught in synagogues; his quarrels were family quarrels inside the Judaism of his day.

paras: Today Judaism and Christianity are two religions. They have different holy days, different buildings, different leaders and different answers to the question 'who was Jesus?'. Yet they share a great deal: the God of Abraham, the Ten Commandments, the Psalms, the prophets. How did that happen? How did one grow out of the other, and why did they part?

Paul, one of the first Christian writers and a Jew himself, gave a picture for it. In his letter to the Romans he described God's people as an olive tree. Israel is the tree, with its root in Abraham. Non-Jews who come to believe in Jesus are like branches of a wild olive, grafted in. We will use that picture all the way through: the root, the branches, the grafting, and the branches that were broken off.
One session gives the case against at full strength: that the New Testament itself planted the seed of centuries of Christian contempt for Jews. The last session gives a verdict.

background.key: How did Christianity grow out of Judaism, and why did they part? Paul's picture of one olive tree, with branches grafted in, frames the whole journey.

background.h: Who were the Jews in Jesus's day?
paras: The Jews were the descendants of the people of Israel, whose story fills the Old Testament: Abraham, Moses, the kings and the prophets. In 587 BC the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and took many Jews into exile. After about fifty years the Persians let them return, and a second Temple was built on the same hill and finished in 515 BC. That is why historians call the six centuries from then until AD 70 the 'Second Temple period'.

In Jesus's time the Jews lived under the Roman empire. Rome had taken control in 63 BC. Herod the Great, a king who ruled for Rome, rebuilt the Temple on a huge scale from about 20 BC. Many Jews also lived outside the land, in Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor (modern Turkey) and Rome itself: this is the 'diaspora', the scattering. Jews everywhere shared four things: one God, the Torah (the law of Moses), the Temple in Jerusalem, and the hope that God would one day set his people free.

background.key: Jesus lived late in the 'Second Temple period' (515 BC–AD 70), when Jews under Rome shared one God, the Torah, the Temple and a hope of freedom.

background.h: Who wrote Luke, and why read it here?
paras: The Gospel of Luke does not name its author. From the second century, Christian tradition credited it to Luke, a doctor and a companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14). The same writer wrote the Acts of the Apostles, which we will also read. Most scholars date the Gospel to about AD 80–90; some argue for the 60s. Luke was probably a non-Jew who knew the Jewish Scriptures well, and he wrote in good Greek for readers across the Roman world.

Luke is the right place to start because he takes such care to show Jesus inside Israel's life. His Gospel opens in the Temple, with a priest offering incense (Luke 1:9), and closes in the Temple, with the disciples praising God there (Luke 24:53). Chapter 2, our reading, is the only place in the New Testament that tells us anything about Jesus between his birth and the age of thirty.
background.key: Luke, by tradition Paul's companion, wrote around AD 80–90. His Gospel begins and ends in the Temple, and only he tells of Jesus's childhood.

paras: The main reading is Luke 2:21–52, in three parts: Jesus circumcised and presented at the Temple, the old man Simeon and the prophetess Anna, and the boy Jesus at Passover. The question is simple: what kind of upbringing did Jesus have? Luke's answer is: a fully Jewish one.

The comparison is from the Shema, the prayer Jews have said every morning and evening for more than two thousand years. Its first line, 'Hear, Israel: the Lord is our God; the Lord is one', is the one Jesus called the first commandment (Mark 12:29). We read its third paragraph, from Numbers 15, about the tassels Jesus wore.
background.key: Luke 2 shows Jesus's Jewish upbringing; the Shema is the prayer he grew up saying, and its third paragraph commands the tassels he wore.

before: Count how many times Luke mentions 'the law'. Why might he stress it?
What do Simeon and Anna hope for?
Where is the boy Jesus found, and what is he doing?
sessions.readWhy: Luke's account of Jesus's childhood: circumcised, presented in the Temple, welcomed by two old people waiting for God's promise, and at Passover in Jerusalem at twelve.

paras: When eight days were fulfilled for the circumcision of the child, his name was called Jesus, which was given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
When the days of their purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him up to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord
(as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”),
and to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, “A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.”
Behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, looking for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was on him.
It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.
He came in the Spirit into the temple. When the parents brought in the child, Jesus, that they might do concerning him according to the custom of the law,
then he received him into his arms, and blessed God, and said,

“Now you are releasing your servant, Master,
according to your word, in peace;
for my eyes have seen your salvation,
which you have prepared before the face of all peoples;

a light for revelation to the nations,
and the glory of your people Israel.”
Joseph and his mother were marveling at the things which were spoken concerning him,
and Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary, his mother, “Behold, this child is set for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which is spoken against.
Yes, a sword will pierce through your own soul, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”
There was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher (she was of a great age, having lived with a husband seven years from her virginity,
and she had been a widow for about eighty-four years), who didn’t depart from the temple, worshiping with fastings and petitions night and day.
Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of him to all those who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem.
When they had accomplished all things that were according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth.
The child was growing, and was becoming strong in spirit, being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.
His parents went every year to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover.
When he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast,
and when they had fulfilled the days, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. Joseph and his mother didn’t know it,
but supposing him to be in the company, they went a day’s journey, and they looked for him among their relatives and acquaintances.
When they didn’t find him, they returned to Jerusalem, looking for him.
After three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them, and asking them questions.
All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
When they saw him, they were astonished, and his mother said to him, “Son, why have you treated us this way? Behold, your father and I were anxiously looking for you.”
He said to them, “Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?”
They didn’t understand the saying which he spoke to them.
And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

parts.title: The eighth day
parts.context: Bethlehem and Jerusalem, about 6–4 BC. Mary and Joseph's son has just been born in Bethlehem, a few miles south of Jerusalem. Luke now tells what every Jewish family did after a son's birth.

commentary.on: When eight days were fulfilled for the circumcision of the child
commentary.text: Circumcision, cutting away the foreskin, was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, commanded on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). Jewish boys are still circumcised on the eighth day, at a ceremony called the brit milah, 'the covenant of circumcision'. Jesus received the mark of Israel's covenant in his own body.

commentary.on: his name was called Jesus
commentary.text: Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, a short form of Joshua, meaning 'the Lord saves'. It was a common Jewish name. So were the names of his family: his mother Miriam (Mary), his father Yosef (Joseph), and his brothers Jacob (James), Joseph, Judah (Judas) and Simon (Mark 6:3).

commentary.on: When the days of their purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled
commentary.text: Leviticus 12 tells a mother to wait forty days after a son's birth and then bring an offering to the Temple. Luke uses the phrase 'the law' five times in this short chapter. He wants no reader to miss it: this family did everything the law asked.

commentary.on: A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.
commentary.text: The law asked for a lamb, but allowed two birds 'if she cannot afford a lamb' (Leviticus 12:8). It is a quiet detail: Jesus's family were poor.

parts.title: Simeon and Anna
parts.context: The Temple courts in Jerusalem, forty days after the birth. The Temple was the centre of Jewish worship, where sacrifices were offered every day. Two old people who spend their lives there recognise the child.

commentary.on: looking for the consolation of Israel
commentary.text: Simeon is waiting for God to keep his promises to his people. 'Consolation' echoes Isaiah 40:1: 'Comfort, comfort my people.' Many Jews of the time lived with this longing for God to act.

commentary.on: a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel
commentary.text: Simeon's song holds both halves of this journey in one line: light for 'the nations' (the non-Jews, the Gentiles), and glory for Israel. Neither is set against the other. The song, called the Nunc Dimittis from its first words in Latin, is still sung every evening in Anglican cathedrals at Evensong.

commentary.on: this child is set for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which is spoken against
commentary.text: The first hint of division. Jesus will divide opinion among his own people, some rising, some falling. Luke knows, as he writes, that most Jews did not follow Jesus; he places that sorrow right at the start.

commentary.on: There was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher
commentary.text: Anna is named with her father and her tribe, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. She fasts and prays in the Temple 'night and day'. A woman prophet, honoured in the Temple, is the second witness. In Jewish law two witnesses establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15).

parts.title: At Passover, aged twelve
parts.context: Nazareth, a village in Galilee in the north, and Jerusalem, about AD 6–8. Passover was the spring festival remembering the escape from Egypt, and the law asked men to go up to the Temple for it each year (Deuteronomy 16:16).

commentary.on: His parents went every year to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover.
commentary.text: A journey of about 80 miles on foot, perhaps four days each way, in a large group of relatives and neighbours. This was a family that took the festivals seriously.

commentary.on: sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them, and asking them questions
commentary.text: Jewish learning has always worked by questions and answers, and still does in the yeshiva, the house of study, where students argue over the text in pairs. The boy Jesus is not lecturing the teachers; he is learning the Jewish way, by asking.

commentary.on: Didn't you know that I must be in my Father's house?
commentary.text: Jesus's first recorded words call the Temple his Father's house. Whatever Christians later said about Jesus, Luke shows him at home in the centre of Jewish worship.

commentary.on: He was subject to them
commentary.text: He goes home and obeys his parents, as the fifth commandment asks. Then Luke is silent for eighteen years. Jesus grew up as a village Jew in Galilee, probably working, as Mark says, as a builder (Mark 6:3).

paras: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,

“Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes on the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue.

It shall be to you for a fringe, that you may see it, and remember all Yahweh’s commandments, and do them; and that you don’t follow your own heart and your own eyes, after which you used to play the prostitute;
so that you may remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God.
I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to be your God: I am Yahweh your God.”

parts.title: The third paragraph of the Shema
parts.context: Numbers, the fourth book of the Torah, follows Israel through the wilderness after the escape from Egypt. The Shema, named from its first Hebrew word, 'Hear', joins three passages: Deuteronomy 6:4–9 ('Hear, Israel: the Lord is our God; the Lord is one'), Deuteronomy 11:13–21, and these verses. Josephus, a Jewish writer of the first century, says Jews remembered God's gifts in prayer twice a day, at rising and at going to sleep (Antiquities IV.8.13); the Mishnah, written down about AD 200, begins with rules for saying the Shema morning and evening, and names these three paragraphs (Berakhot 2:2).

commentary.on: they should make themselves fringes on the borders of their garments throughout their generations
commentary.text: The fringes, in Hebrew tzitzit, are tassels tied at the four corners of a garment. Observant Jewish men still wear them, on the prayer shawl (the tallit) and often on a small garment under their shirts. When a sick woman touched 'the fringe' of Jesus's cloak (Matthew 9:20), the Greek word is the one the Greek Bible uses here. Jesus dressed as a law-keeping Jew.

commentary.on: a cord of blue
commentary.text: A thread dyed blue, the colour of the sky and of the priests' robes. The dye came from a sea snail and was costly; after the Roman period the art was lost, and most Jews wore white tassels only. Some have revived the blue in recent decades.

commentary.on: that you may see it, and remember all Yahweh's commandments, and do them
commentary.text: The tassels are a reminder worn on the body: seeing leads to remembering, and remembering to doing. This is the shape of Jewish faith Jesus grew up in. It is not first a set of beliefs but a life of remembered commandments.

commentary.on: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to be your God
commentary.text: The paragraph ends with the exodus, the story Passover retells, the festival Luke shows the boy Jesus keeping. The WEB prints God's name as Yahweh; Jews do not pronounce it, and say 'Adonai', 'Lord', instead. Twice a day, the Shema joined the oneness of God, love for him, and the memory of freedom.

compare.why: The Shema is the prayer Jesus grew up with, said morning and evening by Jews then and now. It has three paragraphs. You read the first, Deuteronomy 6:4–9, in 'How to read the Bible'; here is the third, which Jews say with it, about the tassels on a Jew's clothes. The Gospels say Jesus wore them.
compare.title: Hear, Israel: the tassels

paras: Every Gospel takes it for granted that Jesus was a Jew. He was born to a Jewish mother, circumcised, named Yeshua, raised in a Jewish village. Luke says he went to the synagogue at Nazareth on the Sabbath 'as his custom was' and stood up to read from the prophet Isaiah (Luke 4:16). Matthew and Luke mention the 'fringe' of his cloak (Matthew 9:20; Luke 8:44): probably the tassels the law told Israelites to wear (Numbers 15:38–39). He kept Passover in Jerusalem. He spoke Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in the land, and read Hebrew.

His teaching is full of the Jewish Scriptures. Asked for the first commandment, he quoted the Shema; for the second, Leviticus. His parables use the pictures of Israel's prophets: the vineyard, the shepherd, the wedding feast. He chose twelve disciples, the number of Israel's tribes. When he first sent them out, Matthew says he told them to go 'rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Matthew 10:6).
sections.key: Jesus was born, raised and lived as a Jew: circumcised, at synagogue on the Sabbath, wearing the tassels, keeping Passover, teaching from Israel's Scriptures.

paras: Judaism in Jesus's day was not one tidy system. Josephus, writing in the 90s, describes several 'schools' (Antiquities XVIII.1.2–6). The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, centred on the Temple; they accepted only the written Torah and did not believe in resurrection. The Pharisees were popular lay teachers who kept an 'oral law' alongside the written one and believed in the resurrection. The Essenes lived apart in strict communities; most scholars link them with the Dead Sea Scrolls, found in caves near Qumran from 1947. Josephus adds a 'fourth philosophy' of rebels who would accept no master but God.

These groups argued fiercely. The scrolls call their opponents 'seekers of smooth things' and their own members 'sons of light'. What they shared was more basic: one God, the covenant with Abraham, the Torah, the Temple, the land, and the hope of redemption. Scholars sometimes speak of 'Second Temple Judaisms', plural. Jesus and his followers were one more voice in a lively family argument.
sections.key: First-century Judaism held Sadducees, Pharisees, Essenes and rebels, who argued fiercely but shared one God, the Torah, the Temple and the hope of redemption.

paras: In English 'Pharisee' has come to mean a hypocrite. That is unfair to history. The Pharisees were respected teachers who tried to make holiness part of everyday life, not just the Temple's. Josephus says the ordinary people trusted them (Antiquities XVIII.1.3). Paul was proud to have been one (Philippians 3:5). In Acts, the Pharisee Gamaliel defends the apostles in the council (Acts 5:34–39), and in Luke some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him (Luke 13:31).

Jesus argued with Pharisees because he was close to them: they cared about the same things, the Sabbath, purity, prayer, the meaning of the law. The rabbis who came after them argued the same way among themselves. The schools of Hillel and Shammai, two teachers a generation before Jesus, disagreed about divorce (Mishnah, Gittin 9:10) in terms that echo Jesus's own debate in Matthew 19. When Hillel was asked to sum up the Torah, the Talmud says he answered: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour' (Shabbat 31a). In 1977 E. P. Sanders showed in Paul and Palestinian Judaism that the old Christian picture of Pharisees as cold legalists, earning salvation by rules, does not fit their own writings. For them the law was a gift within God's covenant of grace.
sections.key: The Pharisees were respected teachers of everyday holiness. Jesus argued with them because he was close to them; the old picture of them as cold legalists is false.

paras: Besides the Shema, the great prayer of Judaism is the Amidah, 'the standing prayer', also called the Eighteen Blessings. Jews say it standing, three times a day. Its first blessing praises 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob', the God of the fathers. The second praises God's power, who sustains the living and gives life to the dead. The third praises his holiness. Its wording was fixed after AD 70, but many of its blessings are older, and some form of it was probably known in Jesus's day.

Jesus's own prayer, the Lord's Prayer, has the shape of Jewish prayer. 'Hallowed be your name' echoes the Kaddish, a Jewish prayer that begins 'Magnified and sanctified be his great name'; 'your kingdom come' echoes its hope that God will establish his kingdom soon. Jews call God 'our Father' in the Amidah and in the old prayer Avinu Malkenu, 'Our Father, our King'. When Christians pray the Lord's Prayer, they pray as Jews have long prayed.
sections.key: Jews pray the Amidah three times a day to the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The Lord's Prayer has the shape of Jewish prayer, echoing the Kaddish.

paras: For much of Christian history Jesus was pictured as anything but Jewish. Medieval and Renaissance painters dressed him like a European, while 'the Jews' around him were often drawn as villains. In the twentieth century both Jewish and Christian scholars set out to recover the real man.

In 1922 the Jewish historian Joseph Klausner published Jesus of Nazareth in Hebrew, the first full study of Jesus by a Jewish scholar in modern times: he saw Jesus as a great Jewish moral teacher. Geza Vermes, born in Hungary to a Jewish family, a Catholic priest for a time, and later a Jewish scholar at Oxford, wrote Jesus the Jew (1973), which placed Jesus among the Galilean holy men of his day. The American New Testament scholar Amy-Jill Levine, an Orthodox Jew by upbringing and a teacher of Christian ministers, argues in The Misunderstood Jew (2006) that Christians cannot understand Jesus at all without understanding the Judaism he lived in, and that they often misread it. Christian scholars such as E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) and N. T. Wright reached the same starting point. There is no serious debate left about whether Jesus was a Jew. The debate is about what kind.
sections.key: Christian art long forgot that Jesus was Jewish; Klausner, Vermes, Levine and Christian scholars such as Sanders recovered him. The debate now is what kind of Jew he was.

refs: Josephus, Antiquities IV.8.13 (prayer twice a day); XVIII.1.2–6 (the schools). Mishnah, Berakhot 1 (the Shema), Gittin 9:10 (Hillel and Shammai on divorce). Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (Hillel's summary).

Joseph Klausner, Jesus of Nazareth (Hebrew 1922; English 1925). Geza Vermes, Jesus the Jew (1973). E. P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) and Jesus and Judaism (1985). Amy-Jill Levine, The Misunderstood Jew (2006). All summarised in our own words.
On the Amidah and the Kaddish: Lawrence Hoffman (ed.), My People's Prayer Book (1997–2017); Ismar Elbogen, Jewish Liturgy: A Comprehensive History (German 1913; English 1993).

debate.question: What kind of Jew was Jesus?

positions.name: A Jewish holy man and teacher
positions.who: Geza Vermes; Joseph Klausner, in part
positions.view: Jesus belonged to the world of Galilean charismatic holy men, healers and wise teachers, such as Honi the Circle-Drawer and Hanina ben Dosa, remembered in the Mishnah and Talmud. He did not mean to found a new religion. The Church later turned a Jewish teacher into a divine saviour.
positions.evidence: His healings, his intimate prayer to God as Father, his Galilean setting, and the parallels in rabbinic stories of holy men.

positions.name: A Jewish prophet who claimed more
positions.who: N. T. Wright; E. P. Sanders, in part; most Christian scholars
positions.view: Jesus was thoroughly Jewish, but he acted as if he spoke and acted for Israel's God: he chose twelve to stand for Israel renewed, forgave sins, spoke of the Temple's end, said 'but I tell you'. His claims were made in Jewish terms, and they were controversial among Jews from the start.
positions.evidence: The Twelve; the action in the Temple; sayings such as Mark 2:5–10 and Matthew 5:21–22; the charge brought against him.

positions.name: A Jew whose teaching led away from Judaism
positions.who: Joseph Klausner; some later Jewish scholars
positions.view: Jesus was a great Jewish moralist, but some of his teaching, such as setting aside food laws and an ethic so extreme it could not govern a nation, held seeds that Judaism could not accept, and these grew into a separate faith.
positions.evidence: Mark 7:19 ('making all foods clean', Mark's comment); 'turn the other cheek'; the gathering of followers around himself.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus was a Jew, steeped in Israel's Scriptures, prayers and festivals, and that he cannot be understood apart from the Judaism of his day.

look.why: Rembrandt painted Luke 2:21, the circumcision of Jesus on the eighth day, in 1661. He lived for twenty years in Amsterdam's Jewish quarter, on the street now called the Jodenbreestraat, 'Jewish Broad Street'.
points: The space is almost entirely in shadow; light falls on a bearded man kneeling in front of a woman cradling an infant.
The man, woman and baby are small, at the bottom centre, reaching less than halfway up the picture.
The kneeling man wears a long, pale yellow robe and holds an instrument like a stylus; the baby, wrapped in white with gold fabric over his head and shoulders, looks towards him.
The woman, in a muted red dress and a pale grey turban, looks down at the child on her lap.
To the left, about a dozen people look on; at the front a bearded man in a brown turban writes in an open book slung over his forearm.
Behind the woman a ladder leans against a platform, perhaps a loft, and draped fabric makes a canopy over her.

music.why: Lauridsen's motet sets an old Christmas text marvelling that animals saw the newborn Lord lying in a manger: the scene just before today's reading, when the child is eight days old and not yet named.

think.why: What Christians believe about the man Luke shows growing up in a Jewish home.

learn.why: The Shema: the prayer Jesus grew up saying morning and evening, and the commandment he called first.

check.q: Why does Luke mention 'the law' so often in chapter 2?
options: To explain Roman law to his readers
To show that Jesus's family ignored it
Because Luke was a lawyer
To show that the family did everything the law of Moses asked: Jesus grew up inside Israel's covenant
check.why: Circumcision, purification, the offering and Passover: Luke stresses that this was a law-keeping Jewish family.

check.q: What does the offering of 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons' tell us?
options: That birds were sacred in Galilee
That the family was priestly
That they had come from Egypt
That the family could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8)
check.why: The law allowed two birds instead of a lamb for those who could not afford one.

check.q: Simeon calls the child 'a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel'. What follows for this journey?
options: That Jesus came only for Israel
That from the start Luke sees Jesus as glory for Israel and light for the Gentiles together, not one against the other
That Israel had already rejected him
That Jesus came only for the Gentiles
check.why: Both halves stand side by side, which is the question the journey follows.

check.q: Which is the fairest description of the Pharisees in Jesus's day?
options: Hypocrites who cared only for outward show
The priestly aristocracy who ran the Temple and denied resurrection
A group of rebels against Rome
Respected lay teachers of everyday holiness who believed in the resurrection, with whom Jesus argued because he was close to them
check.why: The second option describes the Sadducees; the first is a later Christian caricature.

check.q: Why do scholars sometimes speak of 'Second Temple Judaisms', in the plural?
options: Because there were two Temples at once
Because Jews then held many views and argued fiercely, while sharing one God, the Torah and the Temple
Because the Romans counted Jews in two groups
Because Judaism had split into two religions
check.why: Sadducees, Pharisees, Essenes and others differed, within a shared core.

check.q: The Lord's Prayer begins 'Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come'. What does that show?
options: That it was written by later Gentile Christians
That it is a translation of the Shema
That Jesus invented a new kind of prayer
That it has the shape of Jewish prayer, echoing the Kaddish's hope that God's name be sanctified and his kingdom come
check.why: The Kaddish begins 'Magnified and sanctified be his great name' and prays for God's kingdom.

tutorial.question: 'Jesus was not a Christian; he was a Jew.' What does this mean, and why does it matter?
tutorial.approach: Use Luke 2 to show Jesus's upbringing, and the lecture to describe the Judaism of his day. Say what 'Jewish' meant then: one God, Torah, Temple, festivals, prayer. Then explain why Christians forgot it, and what changes when they remember.
strong: Uses details from Luke 2: circumcision, the Temple, Passover.
Describes the variety of Second Temple Judaism fairly, including the Pharisees.
Mentions the Shema and the Jewish shape of Jesus's prayer.
Notes that the debate now is what kind of Jew Jesus was, with at least two views.
Explains why forgetting Jesus's Jewishness mattered for how Christians treated Jews.

reading.author: Amy-Jill Levine
reading.title: The Misunderstood Jew
reading.why: A Jewish New Testament scholar on how Christians misread Jesus's Judaism, and how to read better.

reading.author: Geza Vermes
reading.title: Jesus the Jew
reading.why: The classic book that placed Jesus among the Galilean holy men of his time.

reading.author: E. P. Sanders
reading.title: Jesus and Judaism
reading.why: A landmark study of what Jesus did and how it fitted the Judaism of his day.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: say the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5) when you wake and before you sleep, as Jesus did. Notice what it is like to begin and end the day with 'Hear'.
sessions.reflect: If Jesus was a Jew who prayed Israel's prayers, what does that change in how you picture him?
takeaways: Luke shows Jesus circumcised on the eighth day, presented in the Temple and at Passover in Jerusalem: a fully Jewish upbringing.
Judaism in his day was varied, Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, but shared one God, the Torah, the Temple and the hope of redemption; the Pharisees were respected teachers, not hypocrites.
Jesus prayed the Shema and taught in synagogues; his arguments were family arguments inside Judaism.

sessions.title: A Jewish sect
sessions.line: For a generation after Easter, the followers of Jesus in Jerusalem were Jews who prayed in the Temple, kept the law, and were led by Jesus's brother James.
sessions.plain: After Jesus died and his followers said he had risen, they did not leave Judaism. They went on praying in the Temple every day and keeping the law of Moses. Their leader in Jerusalem was James, Jesus's brother, so devout that even other Jews called him 'the Just'. This session looks at that first church, and at the moment when the apostle Paul, accused of turning Jews away from the law, went into the Temple to show he had not.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed that Jesus was a Jew. The next question is what happened to his followers after his death. Did they start a new religion? The evidence says that, at first, they did not: they were a movement inside Judaism.
answers: Were the first Christians Jews?
Who was James, the brother of Jesus?
What did the first followers of Jesus call themselves?
Did Paul stop keeping the Jewish law?
sessions.finding: For a generation the Jerusalem church under James was a Jewish movement that worshipped in the Temple and kept the law; believing in Jesus did not, at first, mean leaving Judaism.

paras: Jesus was crucified by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate in Jerusalem, around AD 30–33. His followers said that God had raised him from the dead and that he had appeared to them. Within weeks, at the Jewish festival of Pentecost (Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks), they were proclaiming in Jerusalem that he was the Messiah, the anointed king Israel had hoped for. Luke tells this in the Acts of the Apostles, his second book.

All the first believers were Jews: the twelve apostles, Jesus's mother Mary, his brothers, and the thousands Acts says joined them in Jerusalem. The question this session asks is what they did next. Did they think of themselves as a new religion? Or as Jews who had found Israel's Messiah?
background.key: After the crucifixion (c. AD 30–33), Jesus's Jewish followers proclaimed him Israel's Messiah in Jerusalem. All the first believers were Jews.

paras: The Gospels name four 'brothers' of Jesus: James, Joses (Joseph), Judas and Simon (Mark 6:3). James did not follow Jesus during his life (John 7:5), but Paul lists him among those to whom the risen Jesus appeared (1 Corinthians 15:7). By the 40s he was leading the church in Jerusalem. Paul calls him one of the three 'pillars' there, with Peter and John (Galatians 2:9).

He is not the same person as James the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, whom Herod Agrippa I beheaded around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). Christians call our James 'James the Just' or 'James the brother of the Lord'. The Letter of James in the New Testament is traditionally credited to him; scholars debate whether he wrote it.
background.key: James, a 'brother of the Lord', led the Jerusalem church from the 40s; Paul calls him a 'pillar'. He is not James son of Zebedee, killed c. 44.

paras: The reading from Acts is set in Jerusalem in about AD 57. Paul, a Jew from Tarsus and a former Pharisee, has spent nearly twenty years taking the message about Jesus to cities around the eastern Mediterranean, where many non-Jews have believed. He now arrives in Jerusalem with a collection of money from his churches for the poor believers there (Romans 15:25–27). Rumours about him have gone ahead.

timeline.text: The crucifixion; Pentecost
Paul, a persecutor, becomes a follower of Jesus
James son of Zebedee killed; Peter leaves Jerusalem; James the Lord's brother leads
The meeting of apostles in Jerusalem
Paul's last visit to Jerusalem; his arrest in the Temple
James the Just is killed in Jerusalem
The Jewish revolt against Rome begins

background.key: Acts 21 is set in Jerusalem around AD 57, when Paul brings a collection for the poor and meets James amid rumours that he has abandoned the law.

paras: Luke's first picture of the church comes just after Pentecost: the believers 'continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home' (Acts 2:46). You read that chapter in 'The whole story'. In Greek Luke says they kept to 'the prayers', with the article: most likely the set Jewish prayers, for in the next chapter Peter and John go up to the Temple 'at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour' (Acts 3:1), three in the afternoon. The believers built no sanctuary of their own.

The main reading is Paul's meeting with James in Jerusalem nearly thirty years later (Acts 21:17–26). It shows that the church was still inside Jewish worship a generation on, and it shows the first strain.

The comparison is the oldest account of James's life and death outside the New Testament, by Hegesippus, a Christian writer of the second century, preserved by Eusebius in his Church History. It shows how James was remembered: as a Jew of extraordinary devotion to the Temple.
background.key: From Acts 2 to Acts 21 the church stayed inside Temple worship; Hegesippus, preserved by Eusebius, remembers James as a devout Jew.

before: Who welcomes Paul in Jerusalem, and how do they react to his news?
What were the thousands of Jewish believers 'zealous for', according to James?
What does James ask Paul to do, and why?
sessions.readWhy: A snapshot of the Jerusalem church a generation after Easter, when its leader James asks Paul to prove in the Temple that he still keeps the law.

paras: When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly.
The day following, Paul went in with us to James; and all the elders were present.
When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry.
They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
They have been informed about you, that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children and not to walk after the customs.
What then? The assembly must certainly meet, for they will hear that you have come.
Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow.

Take them and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses for them, that they may shave their heads. Then all will know that there is no truth in the things that they have been informed about you, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law.

But concerning the Gentiles who believe, we have written our decision that they should observe no such thing, except that they should keep themselves from food offered to idols, from blood, from strangled things, and from sexual immorality.”

Then Paul took the men, and the next day purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them.

parts.title: Paul meets James
parts.context: Jerusalem, about AD 57. Paul arrives with companions from his Gentile churches, including Luke himself, as the 'we' shows. The next day they go to James and the elders who lead the church.

commentary.on: he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry. They, when they heard it, glorified God.
commentary.text: James and the elders welcome the news of non-Jews believing. There is no quarrel over whether Gentiles can belong; that was settled earlier, as we will see in the next session. The worry is about something else.

commentary.on: how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law
commentary.text: This is the key sentence. A generation after Easter, there are 'thousands', literally 'tens of thousands', of Jewish believers in Jesus, and they are all keen to keep the law of Moses. Believing in Jesus had not made them stop being Jews.

commentary.on: you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children
commentary.text: The rumour: that Paul tells Jews living abroad to give up circumcision and the customs. Paul's letters show he told Gentiles not to be circumcised (Galatians 5:2), but he never says Jews should stop. He describes himself as living 'as a Jew' among Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

commentary.on: We have four men who have taken a vow.
commentary.text: Probably a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), a special time of dedication to God that ended with shaving the head and offering sacrifices in the Temple. Paying for poorer men's offerings was a recognised act of piety.

commentary.on: that you yourself also walk keeping the law
commentary.text: James's proposal is a public sign that Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, is still a law-keeping Jew. Paul agrees.

commentary.on: Then Paul took the men, and the next day purified himself and went with them into the temple
commentary.text: Paul, the great apostle of grace, goes into the Temple to take part in its sacrifices nearly thirty years after the resurrection. Whatever the parting of the ways was, it had not yet happened here. (A few days later, Acts goes on, Jews from Asia saw Paul in the Temple, accused him of bringing a Gentile into the inner courts, and he was arrested.)

paras: 3. The manner of James' death has been already indicated by the above-quoted words of Clement, who records that he was thrown from the pinnacle of the temple, and was beaten to death with a club. But Hegesippus, who lived immediately after the apostles, gives the most accurate account in the fifth book of his Memoirs. He writes as follows:

4. James, the brother of the Lord, succeeded to the government of the Church in conjunction with the apostles. He has been called the Just by all from the time of our Saviour to the present day; for there were many that bore the name of James.
5. He was holy from his mother's womb; and he drank no wine nor strong drink, nor did he eat flesh. No razor came upon his head; he did not anoint himself with oil, and he did not use the bath.

6. He alone was permitted to enter into the holy place; for he wore not woolen but linen garments. And he was in the habit of entering alone into the temple, and was frequently found upon his knees begging forgiveness for the people, so that his knees became hard like those of a camel, in consequence of his constantly bending them in his worship of God, and asking forgiveness for the people.

7. Because of his exceeding great justice he was called the Just, and Oblias, which signifies in Greek, 'Bulwark of the people' and 'Justice,' in accordance with what the prophets declare concerning him.

10. Therefore when many even of the rulers believed, there was a commotion among the Jews and Scribes and Pharisees, who said that there was danger that the whole people would be looking for Jesus as the Christ. Coming therefore in a body to James they said, 'We entreat you, restrain the people; for they are gone astray in regard to Jesus, as if he were the Christ. We entreat you to persuade all that have come to the feast of the Passover concerning Jesus; for we all have confidence in you. For we bear you witness, as do all the people, that you are just, and do not respect persons.

11. Therefore, persuade the multitude not to be led astray concerning Jesus. For the whole people, and all of us also, have confidence in you. Stand therefore upon the pinnacle of the temple, that from that high position you may be clearly seen, and that your words may be readily heard by all the people. For all the tribes, with the Gentiles also, have come together on account of the Passover.'

12. The aforesaid Scribes and Pharisees therefore placed James upon the pinnacle of the temple, and cried out to him and said: 'You just one, in whom we ought all to have confidence, forasmuch as the people are led astray after Jesus, the crucified one, declare to us, what is the gate of Jesus.'

13. And he answered with a loud voice, 'Why do you ask me concerning Jesus, the Son of Man? He himself sits in heaven at the right hand of the great Power, and is about to come upon the clouds of heaven.'

14. And when many were fully convinced and gloried in the testimony of James, and said, 'Hosanna to the Son of David,' these same Scribes and Pharisees said again to one another, 'We have done badly in supplying such testimony to Jesus. But let us go up and throw him down, in order that they may be afraid to believe him.'

15. And they cried out, saying, 'Oh! Oh! The just man is also in error.' And they fulfilled the Scripture written in Isaiah, 'Let us take away the just man, because he is troublesome to us: therefore they shall eat the fruit of their doings.'

16. So they went up and threw down the just man, and said to each other, 'Let us stone James the Just.' And they began to stone him, for he was not killed by the fall; but he turned and knelt down and said, 'I entreat you, Lord God our Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.'

17. And while they were thus stoning him one of the priests of the sons of Rechab, the son of the Rechabites, who are mentioned by Jeremiah the prophet, cried out, saying, 'Stop. What are you doing? The just one prays for you.'

18. And one of them, who was a fuller, took the club with which he beat out clothes and struck the just man on the head. And thus he suffered martyrdom. And they buried him on the spot, by the temple, and his monument still remains by the temple. He became a true witness, both to Jews and Greeks, that Jesus is the Christ. And immediately Vespasian besieged them.

parts.author: Eusebius, quoting Hegesippus
parts.translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (1890), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1
parts.ref: Eusebius, Church History II.23.3–7, quoting Hegesippus
parts.title: A man of the Temple
parts.context: Eusebius (c. 260–339), bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, wrote the first history of the Church, finishing it in the 320s. Here he quotes Hegesippus, who wrote around 170–180, about a century after James's death. 'Oblias' is a word scholars have not securely explained. Translated by A. C. McGiffert (1890). The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Hegesippus says James led the church with the apostles and was called 'the Just' by everyone. He lived like a Nazirite, set apart for God: no wine, no meat, no razor. He prayed so often in the Temple, on his knees, asking forgiveness for the people, that his knees became as hard as a camel's.

commentary.on: He has been called the Just by all from the time of our Saviour to the present day
commentary.text: 'The Just' means the righteous one, the one who keeps God's law faithfully. It was a title of honour among Jews, and Hegesippus says everyone used it.

commentary.on: he drank no wine nor strong drink, nor did he eat flesh. No razor came upon his head
commentary.text: This is the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, kept for life, like Samson's or Samuel's. Hegesippus remembers James as more strict than most Jews, not less. Some details, such as his entering 'the holy place', where only priests went, are probably legend; scholars treat Hegesippus with care.

commentary.on: his knees became hard like those of a camel
commentary.text: The most famous detail about James: years of kneeling in prayer in the Temple, 'asking forgiveness for the people'. The leader of the Jerusalem church is remembered as an intercessor for Israel.

parts.author: Eusebius, quoting Hegesippus
parts.translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (1890), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1
parts.ref: Eusebius, Church History II.23.10–18, quoting Hegesippus
parts.title: The death of James
parts.context: Hegesippus goes on to tell how James was killed, at Passover. His account is dramatic and in places hard to believe: it puts James on the 'pinnacle', the high corner, of the Temple. The Jewish historian Josephus gives a shorter and earlier account (Antiquities XX.9.1), which you met in 'Who was Jesus?' if you took it. Translated by A. C. McGiffert (1890).
parts.plain: The leaders, worried that people were coming to believe Jesus was the Messiah, ask James, whom everyone trusts, to calm the crowds from the top of the Temple at Passover. Instead he declares that Jesus is the Son of Man, seated in heaven. They throw him down and stone him. Dying, he prays that God will forgive them. A priest cries out for them to stop, and a laundryman kills him with a club. Hegesippus says the siege of Jerusalem followed at once.

commentary.on: for we all have confidence in you. For we bear you witness, as do all the people, that you are just
commentary.text: Even in a hostile story, James's opponents trust him. He is a respected figure among Jews in Jerusalem, not an outsider.

commentary.on: He himself sits in heaven at the right hand of the great Power, and is about to come upon the clouds of heaven.
commentary.text: James's words echo Jesus's own at his trial (Mark 14:62) and Daniel 7:13. The faith of the Jerusalem church was Jewish in its words: the Son of Man, the right hand of Power, the clouds.

commentary.on: I entreat you, Lord God our Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
commentary.text: James dies like Jesus in Luke 23:34 and like Stephen in Acts 7:60, praying for those who kill him.

commentary.on: one of the priests of the sons of Rechab
commentary.text: A priest cries out to save him. Hegesippus blames 'the Scribes and Pharisees', but Josephus says it was the high priest Ananus, a Sadducee, who had James stoned while Rome had no governor in Judea, and that the most fair-minded and law-observant men of Jerusalem protested to the king and to the new Roman governor, who removed Ananus from office. Many scholars think those protesters were Pharisees. Josephus's account is older and more sober; on this point it should be preferred.

commentary.on: He became a true witness, both to Jews and Greeks, that Jesus is the Christ. And immediately Vespasian besieged them.
commentary.text: James's death is dated by Josephus to AD 62. The Roman general Vespasian's war began four years later. Hegesippus, like other Christians, saw the war as a judgement following James's death. Keep that idea in mind: what Christians made of Jerusalem's fall becomes one of the hardest parts of this story.

compare.author: Eusebius, quoting Hegesippus
compare.ref: Eusebius, Church History II.23.3–7, quoting Hegesippus
compare.translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (1890), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1
compare.why: Outside the New Testament, the fullest memory of James comes from Hegesippus, a second-century Christian whose Memoirs are lost except where Eusebius quoted them. It shows James remembered as a Jew of the Temple.
compare.title: James the Just

sections.h: The Way, the Nazarenes, the Christians
paras: The first believers had no word for 'Christianity'. Acts says they called their movement 'the Way' (Acts 9:2; 24:14). Paul's accuser before the Roman governor calls him a ringleader of 'the sect of the Nazarenes' (Acts 24:5): followers of the man from Nazareth. The Greek word for 'sect', hairesis, is the same one Acts uses for the Pharisees and Sadducees (Acts 5:17; 15:5). To outsiders, the believers were one more Jewish party.

The name 'Christians', from Christos, the Greek for Messiah, was first used in Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26), probably by outsiders, where many non-Jews had joined. In Hebrew, Christians are still called Notzrim, Nazarenes, the name of the first Jerusalem church.
sections.key: The first believers called their movement 'the Way'; outsiders called them a Jewish 'sect' of Nazarenes. 'Christians' was first used at Antioch.

paras: For its first years the church was entirely Jewish, and it was Jewish in two ways. Acts 6:1 speaks of 'Hebrews', Jews from the land who spoke Aramaic, and 'Hellenists', Jews from abroad who spoke Greek. Stephen, the first martyr, was a Hellenist. After his death, Acts says, the believers were scattered, apart from the apostles (Acts 8:1), and some Hellenists began to speak to non-Jews in Antioch (Acts 11:19–20). The Aramaic-speaking church stayed in Jerusalem, worshipped in the Temple, and kept the law.

Its faith was in Jewish terms. Jesus was the Messiah, the Son of Man, the prophet like Moses. Its oldest prayer, preserved in Aramaic in Paul's Greek letter, was Maranatha, 'Our Lord, come!' (1 Corinthians 16:22). Paul's collection from his Gentile churches for 'the poor among the saints at Jerusalem' (Romans 15:26) was his way of honouring this mother church. He wrote that the Gentiles owed it a debt, because they had come to share in its spiritual blessings (Romans 15:27).
sections.key: The first church was Jewish, both Aramaic- and Greek-speaking; its faith was in Jewish words like Maranatha, and Paul honoured it with his collection.

paras: James is one of the most important and least known figures of early Christianity. He led the Jerusalem church for nearly twenty years. He gave the deciding speech at the meeting about the Gentiles (Acts 15:13–21). Paul visited him (Galatians 1:19; 2:9), and when 'certain people came from James' to Antioch, even Peter changed his behaviour (Galatians 2:12); if you took 'The first Christians', you read that story there.

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing about AD 93, says the high priest Ananus took advantage of a gap between Roman governors in 62 to have 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James' stoned, and that law-observant Jews protested. After James, Eusebius says, another relative of Jesus, Simeon son of Clopas, led the church (Church History III.11). The family of Jesus, Jews of Galilee, led the mother church for two generations.
sections.key: James led the Jerusalem church for about twenty years and was stoned in 62 (Josephus). Jesus's relatives led it for two generations.

sections.h: Did Paul stop keeping the law?
paras: The rumour in Acts 21 was that Paul taught Jews to abandon Moses. His letters show a more complicated man. He fought hard against requiring circumcision of Gentiles (Galatians 5:2–6), and he wrote that 'Christ is the fulfilment of the law' (Romans 10:4). But he never tells Jewish believers to stop circumcising their sons. He calls himself 'a Hebrew of Hebrews' (Philippians 3:5), says that to the Jews he 'became as a Jew' (1 Corinthians 9:20), and in Acts he keeps a vow (Acts 18:18) and hurries to reach Jerusalem for Pentecost (Acts 20:16).

Scholars read this in different ways. The traditional Protestant reading, from Luther, sees Paul setting the law aside for everyone as a way to God, and keeping Jewish customs only as a courtesy. The 'new perspective' of E. P. Sanders and James Dunn, from the late 1970s, argued that Paul's quarrel was not with Jewish legalism but with the law as a wall keeping Gentiles out. More recently the 'Paul within Judaism' scholars, such as Mark Nanos and Paula Fredriksen, argue that Paul lived and died a law-observant Jew, and that his harsh words about the law were meant for Gentiles who wanted to be circumcised. Acts 21 is one of their strongest pieces of evidence.
sections.key: Paul opposed circumcising Gentiles but never told Jews to stop; scholars read him as setting the law aside (Luther), opening it to Gentiles (Sanders, Dunn), or staying a law-keeping Jew ('Paul within Judaism').

sections.h: What did 'brother' mean? The traditions side by side
paras: Christians have long disagreed about what the New Testament means when it calls James the Lord's 'brother'. The answer depends on what each tradition teaches about Mary. All three views are ancient, and each draws on the fact that Hebrew and Aramaic used 'brother' broadly, for a cousin or kinsman too (Genesis 13:8).

rows: A son of Joseph by an earlier marriage: Jesus's step-brother
The Protevangelium of James (2nd century); Epiphanius (4th century)
A cousin or close relative of Jesus
Jerome, Against Helvidius (383); often identified with James son of Alphaeus
A son of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus
Helvidius (4th century); the plain sense of Mark 6:3 and Matthew 1:25, as they read it
table.note: Luther and Calvin both held that Mary remained a virgin; the 'younger brother' view became common among Protestants later.

sections.key: Orthodox say James was Joseph's son by an earlier marriage; Catholics, a cousin; most Protestants, a younger son of Mary and Joseph.

sections.h: What happened to the Jewish church?
paras: When the war with Rome began in 66, Eusebius says the Jerusalem believers, warned by a revelation, fled across the Jordan to Pella (Church History III.5.3). Some scholars doubt the story; others think it is an old memory. After the second Jewish revolt, in 135, Jews were banned from Jerusalem, and the church there was led for the first time by a non-Jew, Mark (Eusebius IV.6.4).

Jewish believers in Jesus who kept the law did not vanish. Second- to fourth-century writers mention groups called Ebionites ('the poor') and Nazarenes. Irenaeus says the Ebionites used only Matthew's Gospel, rejected Paul and were circumcised (Against Heresies I.26.2). Epiphanius, around 375, describes Nazarenes in Syria who believed in Jesus and kept the law (Panarion 29). By then the Gentile Church called them heretics, and Jewish teachers called them minim, sectarians. The first Christians had become a group neither side would own.
sections.key: The Jerusalem church may have fled to Pella in 66; after 135 its leaders were Gentiles. Law-keeping Jewish believers survived as Ebionites and Nazarenes, rejected by both sides.

debate.question: Was James's Jewish church the true heir of Jesus?

positions.name: Yes: Paul changed the movement
positions.who: F. C. Baur (1831); Hyam Maccoby (1986); Robert Eisenman (1997)
positions.view: The original followers of Jesus were law-keeping Jews led by his family. Paul, who never knew Jesus, created a different, Gentile religion, and Acts smooths over a deep conflict between the two parties.
positions.evidence: The quarrel at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14); the rumours about Paul in Acts 21; the Ebionites' rejection of Paul; the loss of the Jewish church after 70.

positions.name: No: one gospel, two missions
positions.who: Richard Bauckham; most scholars
positions.view: James, Peter and Paul disagreed about practice, but they shared one faith and recognised each other. They shook hands on a division of labour: Peter to the Jews, Paul to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9).
positions.evidence: The handshake of Galatians 2:9; the agreement of Acts 15; Paul's collection for Jerusalem; James's welcome of Paul in Acts 21.

positions.name: Unity with diversity from the start
positions.who: James D. G. Dunn
positions.view: There was never one uniform early church. Jewish and Gentile believers held one core, Jesus as Messiah and Lord, with different practices. The tragedy came later, when each side made its practice the test of faith.
positions.evidence: The variety within the New Testament itself: Matthew and James beside Paul's letters; the Hebrews and Hellenists of Acts 6.

debate.agree: All agree that the first church was Jewish, that James led it, and that the relation between law-keeping Jewish believers and Paul's Gentile churches was the great question of the first generation.

look.why: An Italian painter of about 1272 painted 'Saint James Minor', James 'the Less'. Western tradition joined James the son of Alphaeus, one of the Twelve, with James the Lord's brother, and the inscription on the arch seems to call him 'the Just'. That joining is a tradition, not a certainty, and Protestant and Orthodox Christians usually keep them apart.

music.why: 'This place was made by God': Bruckner's motet for the dedication of a chapel. The first church still worshipped in the Temple, the place Jews believed God had chosen.

think.why: James prayed daily in the Temple until his knees were hard. Does steady practice shape who we are?

learn.why: The first church in one sentence: Jews who believed in Jesus, praying in the Temple every day and sharing bread at home.
