sessions.practice: Live it this week: the first church kept fixed hours of prayer. Choose one fixed time each day, as they prayed at the ninth hour, and stop for two minutes to pray for your own people: your family, your town, your country.
sessions.reflect: James is remembered for kneeling for his people. Who do you pray for, and who prays for you?
takeaways: The first believers in Jesus were Jews who prayed in the Temple daily and kept the law; outsiders saw them as a Jewish 'sect', the Nazarenes.
James, the Lord's brother, led the Jerusalem church for about twenty years; he was remembered as 'the Just' and stoned in 62.
Even Paul worshipped in the Temple around 57; law-keeping Jewish believers survived for centuries, but were later rejected by both Church and synagogue.

sessions.title: The Gentile question
sessions.line: A Roman officer has a vision, Peter has a dream about unclean food, and the first great Christian argument begins: must non-Jews become Jews?
sessions.plain: The first Christians were Jews. Then non-Jews, Gentiles, began to believe in Jesus too. Did they have to become Jews first, being circumcised and keeping the Jewish food laws? This was the first great argument in the Church. Peter's visit to a Roman officer called Cornelius, and a meeting of the apostles in Jerusalem, gave the answer: no. This session follows how they decided, and what it cost.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed a Jewish church inside Judaism. Now the question that would change everything: what to do with non-Jews who believed. The answer decided whether the movement would stay a Jewish sect or become something new.
answers: Why did Christians stop keeping the Jewish law?
Who was Cornelius, and why does his story matter?
What did the apostles decide in Jerusalem, and why?
Did Jews expect non-Jews to keep the law?
sessions.finding: The first great Christian argument was whether Gentiles must become Jews to belong to Israel's Messiah; Peter's vision and the meeting at Jerusalem said no, and within two generations many Gentile Christians had stopped keeping Jewish customs altogether.

paras: The church in Jerusalem was made of Jews who kept the law. But the message about Jesus spread. After the death of Stephen, believers scattered to Samaria and the coast, and as far as Antioch in Syria (Acts 8–11). Along the way they met non-Jews who wanted to join them.

In Jewish law, a non-Jew who wanted to become part of Israel could convert. A man would be circumcised; all converts were immersed in water and took on the commandments, including the food laws and the Sabbath. Was that what Gentile believers in Jesus had to do? Or could they belong as Gentiles? Nobody had asked the question before, because no Jewish movement had ever drawn so many Gentiles while claiming the Messiah had come.
background.key: As the message spread beyond Jerusalem, non-Jews wanted to join. Must they convert to Judaism, with circumcision and the food laws, first?

paras: In many cities of the Roman empire there were non-Jews who admired Judaism, attended the synagogue, prayed to Israel's God and gave to the poor, without being circumcised. Acts calls them those who 'fear God' or 'worship God' (Acts 10:2; 13:16; 16:14). Josephus mentions Gentiles who sent gifts to the Temple (Antiquities XIV.7.2), and a stone inscription from Aphrodisias in Turkey lists Jewish donors and, separately, a group of theosebeis, 'God-fearers'; scholars date it between the 3rd and 5th centuries.
Cornelius, a Roman officer, was one. God-fearers were the bridge across which the gospel walked into the Gentile world. They knew the Scriptures, they prayed to the one God, and they were not Jews.
background.key: 'God-fearers' were Gentiles who worshipped Israel's God in the synagogue without converting. Cornelius was one; they were the bridge to the Gentile world.

paras: To modern readers, arguments about food and circumcision can seem small. They were not. These were the marks that kept Jews distinct from the nations around them. About two centuries earlier, a Greek king, Antiochus IV, had banned circumcision and forced Jews to eat pork; mothers who circumcised their sons were killed, and many Jews 'chose to die rather than to be defiled with food' (1 Maccabees 1:60–63, a book in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament). The festival of Hanukkah remembers the revolt that followed.

So when Gentile believers were told they need not be circumcised, and Jewish believers began to eat with them, some faithful Jews, including believers in Jesus, saw it as giving up what their ancestors had died for.
background.key: Circumcision and the food laws were the marks of Jewish identity, for which Jews had died under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC. Setting them aside was no small thing.

paras: The main reading has three parts: Cornelius's vision and Peter's dream (Acts 10:1–23), Peter in Cornelius's house (Acts 10:24–48), and the meeting of the apostles in Jerusalem about AD 49 (Acts 15:1–29). They tell how the Church decided its first great question.

The comparison is from Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, writing around AD 110. It shows how far the Gentile church had moved within two generations: Ignatius tells Christians that they no longer keep the Sabbath and that it is 'absurd' to follow Christ and live as a Jew.
background.key: Cornelius and the Jerusalem meeting (c. 49) settled the question; Ignatius (c. 110) shows how far the Gentile church had moved two generations later.

sessions.readWhy: Luke's account of how the Gentile question was settled: by a vision, a visit, and a meeting.

paras: Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment,
a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God.
At about the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him, and saying to him, “Cornelius!”
He, fastening his eyes on him, and being frightened, said, “What is it, Lord?”
He said to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God.
Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is also called Peter.
He is staying with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the seaside.
When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually.
Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
Now on the next day as they were on their journey, and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon.
He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth,
in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky.
A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!”
But Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”
A voice came to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.”
This was done three times, and immediately the vessel was received up into heaven.
Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate,
and called and asked whether Simon, who was also called Peter, was lodging there.
While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men seek you.
But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.”
Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?”

They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.”
So he called them in and provided a place to stay. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.
When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him.
But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.”
As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together.

He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean.
Therefore I also came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?”
Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing,
and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God.
Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He is staying in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’
Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”
Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism;
but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.
The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all—
you yourselves know what happened, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached;
even Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree.
God raised him up the third day, and gave him to be revealed,
not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead.
All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”
While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word.
They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles.
For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God.
Then Peter answered,
“Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.”
He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.
Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.”

Therefore when Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with them, they appointed Paul and Barnabas, and some others of them, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
They, being sent on their way by the assembly, passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They caused great joy to all the brothers.
When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported everything that God had done with them.
But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter.

When there had been much discussion, Peter rose up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Good News and believe.
God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us.
He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”
All the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them.
After they were silent, James answered, “Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has reported how God first visited the nations to take out of them a people for his name.
This agrees with the words of the prophets. As it is written,

‘After these things I will return.
I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen.
I will again build its ruins.
I will set it up
“All of God’s works are known to him from eternity.
Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God,
but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.
For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men out of their company, and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers.
They wrote these things by their hand:
“The apostles, the elders, and the brothers, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings.
Because we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the law,’ to whom we gave no commandment;
it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose out men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things:
that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, from which if you keep yourselves, it will be well with you. Farewell.”

parts.title: Two visions
parts.context: Caesarea and Joppa, on the coast of Judea, in the late 30s. Caesarea was the Roman capital of the province, a mostly Gentile city built by Herod. Joppa (modern Jaffa) was a Jewish port about 30 miles south, where Peter was staying.

commentary.on: a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment, a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house
commentary.text: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers of the occupying army. Yet Luke presents him as a God-fearer, generous to the Jewish poor and praying at the Jewish hours: 'the ninth hour' is the hour of the Temple's afternoon prayer.

commentary.on: He is staying with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the seaside.
commentary.text: A small detail: tanners worked with dead animals, which made them ritually impure, and the work smelled. Peter is already staying somewhere strict Jews might avoid.

commentary.on: Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.
commentary.text: Peter has kept the food laws of Leviticus 11 all his life, as Jesus's other disciples did. Even after years with Jesus, eating unclean animals is unthinkable to him. That tells us Jesus had not taught his followers to stop keeping kosher.

commentary.on: What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.
commentary.text: The voice repeats it three times. The vision is about food, but Peter soon sees it is about people: Jews avoided eating with Gentiles because of food, so the food laws and the separation of peoples went together.

parts.title: In Cornelius's house
parts.context: Caesarea, the next day. Peter, with six Jewish believers from Joppa (Acts 11:12), enters a Gentile's house. Cornelius has gathered his family and friends.

commentary.on: You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation
commentary.text: Peter states the custom of strict Jews of his day: not to share a home or a table with Gentiles. The Torah itself does not forbid it, but it was widely kept to avoid impure food and idolatry. Peter is crossing a line.

commentary.on: Truly I perceive that God doesn't show favoritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.
commentary.text: The turning point of Acts. Peter, a Galilean fisherman and devout Jew, says that God accepts people from every nation. The idea has Jewish roots: 'the Lord your God... is not partial' (Deuteronomy 10:17). What is new is drawing the conclusion that Gentiles may join God's people as Gentiles.

commentary.on: the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles
commentary.text: The Jewish believers are 'amazed'. God has acted before anyone decided anything: the Gentiles receive the same Spirit the Jewish believers received at Pentecost.

commentary.on: Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water?
commentary.text: Baptism, immersion in water, was already part of conversion to Judaism. Peter baptises them, but no one mentions circumcision. That silence is the beginning of the great argument.

parts.title: The meeting in Jerusalem
parts.context: Antioch and Jerusalem, about AD 49. Antioch, the third city of the empire, now has a large church of Jews and Gentiles together. Believers from Judea arrive and tell the Gentiles they must be circumcised. Paul and Barnabas go up to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders.

commentary.on: Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can't be saved.
commentary.text: The other side's case was strong. God's covenant with Abraham required circumcision 'for ever' (Genesis 17:13). Jesus was circumcised. If Gentiles were joining Israel's Messiah, why not join Israel in the way the Torah laid down?

commentary.on: But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up
commentary.text: Some Pharisees had become believers in Jesus and stayed Pharisees. The argument was not between Christians and Jews but between Jewish believers.

commentary.on: why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
commentary.text: Peter calls the full law a 'yoke'. Jews also spoke of 'the yoke of the commandments', but as a joy to carry. Peter's point is that Gentiles have received the Spirit without it, so it cannot be required of them.

commentary.on: I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen.
commentary.text: James quotes Amos 9:11–12 in its Greek form: when God restores David's kingdom, the nations will seek him too. For James the Gentiles' coming is a sign that Israel's restoration has begun, not that Israel is being replaced.

commentary.on: that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood
commentary.text: Four rules. Most scholars link them with the laws for 'the stranger who lives among you' in Leviticus 17–18: no sacrifices to idols, no eating blood or meat not properly drained, no forbidden unions. Gentiles are asked to keep what the Torah asked of Gentiles living among Israel, so that Jewish and Gentile believers can eat together.

commentary.on: For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.
commentary.text: A hard verse. It probably means: Jewish believers will still hear and keep Moses in the synagogue every Sabbath, so the rules for Gentiles will not threaten the law. The council assumes Jewish believers go on keeping it.

commentary.on: For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us
commentary.text: The decision is presented as discernment, the Spirit and the apostles together. Later Church councils would look back to this as their model.

paras: Be not deceived with strange doctrines, nor with old fables, which are unprofitable. For if we still live according to the Jewish law, we acknowledge that we have not received grace. For the divinest prophets lived according to Christ Jesus. On this account also they were persecuted, being inspired by His grace to fully convince the unbelieving that there is one God, who has manifested Himself by Jesus Christ His Son, who is His eternal Word, not proceeding forth from silence, and who in all things pleased Him that sent Him.

If, therefore, those who were brought up in the ancient order of things have come to the possession of a new hope, no longer observing the Sabbath, but living in the observance of the Lord's Day, on which also our life has sprung up again by Him and by His death — whom some deny, by which mystery we have obtained faith, and therefore endure, that we may be found the disciples of Jesus Christ, our only Master — how shall we be able to live apart from Him, whose disciples the prophets themselves in the Spirit did wait for Him as their Teacher? And therefore He whom they rightly waited for, having come, raised them from the dead.

Let us not, therefore, be insensible to His kindness. For were He to reward us according to our works, we should cease to be. Therefore, having become His disciples, let us learn to live according to the principles of Christianity. For whosoever is called by any other name besides this, is not of God. Lay aside, therefore, the evil, the old, the sour leaven, and be changed into the new leaven, which is Jesus Christ. Be salted in Him, lest any one among you should be corrupted, since by your savour you shall be convicted. It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize. For Christianity did not embrace Judaism, but Judaism Christianity, that so every tongue which believes might be gathered together to God.

parts.author: Ignatius of Antioch
parts.translator: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (1867; Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)
parts.title: Beware of Judaizing
parts.context: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch. Around AD 110, under arrest and being taken to Rome to be killed in the arena, he wrote seven letters to churches along the way. This one went to Magnesia, a city in western Turkey, where some Christians seem to have been drawn to Jewish customs. The chapter headings are the translators'. Translated by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (1867).
parts.plain: Ignatius says: if we still live by the Jewish law, we have not received grace. Even the prophets lived 'according to Christ' and waited for him. People brought up in the old ways have now come to a new hope: they no longer keep the Sabbath but the Lord's Day, the day of the resurrection. So it makes no sense to follow Christ and live like a Jew. Christianity did not come into Judaism; Judaism came into Christianity.

commentary.on: For if we still live according to the Jewish law, we acknowledge that we have not received grace.
commentary.text: This goes far beyond the Jerusalem council, which left Jewish believers to keep the law. Ignatius treats keeping the law as a sign that one has not received grace at all. In two generations the question has turned round: not 'must Gentiles become Jews?' but 'may Christians live as Jews?'

commentary.on: For the divinest prophets lived according to Christ Jesus.
commentary.text: Ignatius claims Israel's prophets for the Church: they were already disciples of Christ, waiting for him. Here is an early form of an idea that will matter later in this journey: that the Jewish Scriptures belong to the Church.

commentary.on: no longer observing the Sabbath, but living in the observance of the Lord's Day
commentary.text: One of the earliest clear signs that Christians kept Sunday, 'the Lord's Day', the day of the resurrection, instead of the Sabbath, Saturday. The calendar, more than anything, marked the two communities apart.

commentary.on: It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize.
commentary.text: 'Judaize' means to live like a Jew, to adopt Jewish customs. That Ignatius has to warn against it shows that some Gentile Christians found the synagogue attractive. Similar warnings run on for centuries, which tells us the line between the communities was not as clear on the ground as bishops wished.

commentary.on: For Christianity did not embrace Judaism, but Judaism Christianity
commentary.text: This is one of the first uses of the word 'Christianity' (Christianismos) set against 'Judaism' (Ioudaismos). For Ignatius they are now two things, and Judaism has been taken up into the newer one. Paul's picture was the opposite: the Gentiles grafted into Israel's tree.

compare.author: Ignatius of Antioch
compare.translator: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (1867; Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)
compare.why: Two generations later, Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, the same city where the Gentile question began, tells another church how Christians should live. See how far the Gentile church has moved.
compare.title: No longer keeping the Sabbath

paras: Ancient Judaism did not teach that only Jews could be saved. The rabbis later taught that God gave Noah, and so all humanity, seven basic laws: not to worship idols, not to curse God, not to murder, not to commit sexual immorality, not to steal, not to eat flesh torn from a living animal, and to set up courts of justice (Tosefta, Avodah Zarah 8:4; Talmud, Sanhedrin 56a). A Gentile who kept them was righteous. Rabbi Joshua, in the generation after the Temple's fall, said 'the righteous of the nations have a share in the world to come' (Tosefta, Sanhedrin 13:2).

The written collections of these 'Noahide laws' come from after the New Testament, so we cannot be sure how they were understood in Peter's day. But the idea that Gentiles should keep a few basic laws, without becoming Jews, was clearly in the air, and the four rules of Acts 15 look like a version of it. Judaism had a place for righteous Gentiles. What it did not have was Gentiles counted as members of God's people without converting.
sections.key: Judaism held that Gentiles who kept the basic 'Noahide laws' were righteous. What was new in Acts was Gentiles belonging to God's people without converting.

sections.h: How a Gentile became a Jew
paras: A Gentile who wanted to join Israel fully could become a proselyte, a convert. Later rabbinic sources describe three steps for a man: circumcision, immersion in water, and an offering in the Temple while it stood; a woman was immersed (Babylonian Talmud, Keritot 9a; Yevamot 46a–47b). The convert took on the whole Torah and became, the rabbis said, like a newborn child, a full member of the people. Josephus tells of the royal house of Adiabene, in what is now northern Iraq, who converted in the 40s; Queen Helena even sent food to Jerusalem in a famine (Antiquities XX.2–5).

Did Jews go out looking for converts? Jesus speaks of Pharisees who 'travel around by sea and land to make one proselyte' (Matthew 23:15). But Scot McKnight (A Light among the Gentiles, 1991) and Martin Goodman (Mission and Conversion, 1994) argued that Judaism welcomed converts without organised missions, and that the God-fearers were far more common than full converts. That is the background to Acts 15. The Jerusalem believers were not inventing a way for Gentiles to approach Israel's God; that already existed. They were deciding that Gentiles who believed in the Messiah were not God-fearers on the edge but full members, without the convert's three steps.
sections.key: A convert to Judaism was circumcised, immersed and offered sacrifice, becoming a full member; God-fearers stayed on the edge. Acts 15 made believing Gentiles full members without conversion.

paras: Acts gives three reasons for not requiring Gentiles to be circumcised. First, experience: God had given them the Holy Spirit already, as uncircumcised Gentiles (Acts 15:8). Second, grace: 'we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are' (15:11). Third, Scripture: the prophets foretold that the nations would seek the Lord when David's house was restored (15:16–17).

Paul, in his letter to the Galatians, adds a fourth, the sharpest: if Gentiles must be circumcised to belong, then Christ's death is not enough (Galatians 2:21; 5:2–4). For Paul, the Messiah had come, and in him Jew and Gentile were one people: 'There is neither Jew nor Greek' (Galatians 3:28). He did not mean that the difference vanished; he went on calling himself a Jew. He meant that neither had to become the other to belong.
sections.key: The apostles gave four reasons: the Spirit already given, grace, the prophets, and (Paul) that requiring circumcision would make Christ's death not enough.

paras: The Jerusalem council decided that Gentile believers need not keep the whole law. It did not decide that Jewish believers must stop. Acts 21, which we read in the previous session, shows Jewish believers still keeping it years later. But in the generations that followed, as Gentiles became the great majority, the ground shifted.

By about 110, Ignatius treats Jewish practice as incompatible with grace. The Letter of Barnabas, written perhaps in the 130s, argues that the Jews had always misunderstood their own law, which was meant to be read spiritually. By the 4th century, Church councils forbade Christians to keep the Sabbath or celebrate Jewish festivals (Council of Laodicea, canons 29 and 37–38). What began as freedom for Gentiles became a rule against Jewish practice, even for Jews who believed in Jesus.
sections.key: Jerusalem said Gentiles need not keep the law; within a century Gentile Christians were saying no one in the Church should. Freedom for Gentiles became a ban on Jewish practice.

sections.h: How the churches kept the decree
paras: The Jerusalem letter's four rules were kept for centuries, but differently in different churches.

rows: Long kept the ban on eating blood and strangled meat
Council in Trullo (692), canon 67, repeated the rule
Still keeps some Old Testament food laws, avoiding pork, and long honoured both Saturday and Sunday
One of the oldest churches, in close contact with Judaism
Treated the food rules as for their own time; the decree's lasting point is the council's authority
Augustine, Against Faustus 32.13, saw the food rules as a passing measure
Reads Acts 15 as the charter of salvation by grace, not law
Luther and Calvin, commentaries on Galatians and Acts
Many Jewish believers in Jesus keep the Sabbath and kosher food as Jews, while not requiring them of Gentiles
Close to the council's own picture
table.note: The decree was meant to let Jews and Gentiles share one table; how long its rules bind has always been debated.

sections.key: Orthodox and Ethiopian churches kept parts of the decree's food rules; Catholics and Protestants saw them as temporary, stressing the council's authority or grace.

sections.h: A Jewish argument about the Messiah
paras: It is worth seeing the argument as the first Jewish believers saw it. They did not think they were leaving Israel. They thought the age the prophets promised had arrived, when 'many nations shall join themselves to the Lord' (Zechariah 2:11) and come to Zion. In that age, many Jews expected, the nations would turn to Israel's God as nations, not as converts.

The scholar Paula Fredriksen argues in Paul: The Pagans' Apostle (2017) that this end-time hope explains the decision: Gentiles had to give up their gods, but not become Jews. Seen this way, the Gentile mission was a Jewish idea. It was its huge success, and the failure of most Jews to accept that the Messiah had come, that made the movement more and more Gentile.
sections.key: The first believers saw Gentiles coming in as the prophets' promise for the end of the age: nations turning to Israel's God as nations. The Gentile mission began as a Jewish hope.

refs: Josephus, Antiquities XIV.7.2; XX.2–5 (Adiabene). Babylonian Talmud, Keritot 9a; Yevamot 46a–47b. Matthew 23:15. Tannenbaum, Jews and Godfearers at Aphrodisias, 1987; redated by A. Chaniotis, 2002).
Tosefta, Avodah Zarah 8:4 and Sanhedrin 13:2; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 56a.

debate.question: What did the Jerusalem council really decide?

positions.name: Freedom from the law
positions.who: Augustine; Luther; much traditional Protestant reading
positions.view: The council recognised that salvation comes by grace through faith, not by keeping the law, which had been a temporary guardian until Christ (Galatians 3:24). The four rules were a passing courtesy for mixed churches.
positions.evidence: Peter's speech on grace (15:10–11); Paul's letters; the later practice of the whole Church.

positions.name: A law for Gentiles, not the end of the law
positions.who: Paula Fredriksen; Mark Nanos; the 'Paul within Judaism' scholars; many Jewish scholars
positions.view: The council left Jews keeping the Torah and gave Gentiles the Torah's own rules for Gentiles. Jews stayed Jews, Gentiles stayed Gentiles, together in one community. Later Christians misread this as abolishing the law for everyone.
positions.evidence: The parallel with Leviticus 17–18; James's remark on Moses read every Sabbath (15:21); Acts 21:20–26.

positions.name: The Church deciding under the Spirit
positions.who: Catholic and Orthodox tradition
positions.view: Whatever the details, the council shows how the Church decides: apostles and elders gathered, Scripture and experience weighed, and a decision that 'seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us'. It is the model for every later council.
positions.evidence: Acts 15:6, 22, 28; the councils of Nicaea (325) and after, which cited it.

debate.agree: All agree that the council refused to require circumcision of Gentile believers, and that this decision opened the movement to the Gentile world.

look.why: No painting of Peter and Cornelius, or of Peter's vision, is in the gallery's open collection. Marco Zoppo painted Peter himself, about 1468: the Galilean fisherman who kept the food laws all his life and then went into a Gentile's house. The keys come from Jesus's words to him in Matthew 16:19.

music.why: Francis of Assisi's hymn calls every creature to praise one God. The Gentile question was answered by the conviction that 'in every nation' people who fear God are welcome.

think.why: 'God doesn't show favouritism.' See how that conviction shaped the Christian idea that every human being has equal worth.

learn.why: Peter's words in a Gentile's house, the moment the door opened to the nations.

check.q: What does Peter's reply in the vision, 'I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean', tell us about Jesus's first followers?
options: That Peter was not Jewish
That Jesus had told them to stop keeping the food laws
That years after following Jesus, Peter still kept the Jewish food laws
That the food laws only applied in Galilee
check.why: Peter had kept kosher all his life; the vision is a shock to him.

check.q: Why was the vision about food also about people?
options: Because Jews avoided eating with Gentiles largely because of food, so the food laws kept the peoples apart
Because Peter was hungry
Because Cornelius was a cook
Because the animals stood for the Roman legions
check.why: Peter draws the conclusion himself: 'I shouldn't call any man unholy or unclean.'

check.q: Which argument for requiring circumcision of Gentile believers was the strongest?
options: That it was a Roman law
That Gentiles were not allowed in synagogues
That Peter had commanded it
That God's covenant with Abraham commanded circumcision for ever, and Jesus himself was circumcised
check.why: Genesis 17:13 calls it 'an everlasting covenant'; the case was rooted in Scripture.

check.q: The four rules of Acts 15 most likely come from:
options: The Torah's laws for Gentiles living among Israel, in Leviticus 17–18
Jesus's Sermon on the Mount
Roman law
Greek philosophy
check.why: Idols, blood, strangled meat and sexual immorality match Leviticus 17–18.

check.q: What is the main difference between the Jerusalem council and Ignatius about sixty years later?
options: Ignatius required circumcision
The council said Gentiles need not keep the law; Ignatius says living by the Jewish law is a sign of not having received grace
The council banned Sunday worship
There is no difference
check.why: 'Need not' for Gentiles had become 'must not' for Christians.

check.q: Which statement about ancient Jewish views of Gentiles is most accurate?
options: Jews had no view of Gentiles
Jews taught that all Gentiles were damned
Rabbinic tradition held that Gentiles who kept the basic Noahide laws were righteous; what was new in Acts was Gentiles belonging to God's people without converting
Jews required every Gentile to convert
check.why: 'The righteous of the nations have a share in the world to come' (Tosefta, Sanhedrin 13:2).

tutorial.question: Why did the first Christians decide that Gentiles need not become Jews, and was it the right decision?
tutorial.approach: Set out both sides fairly, using Acts 10 and 15: the case for circumcision from Genesis 17 and the case against from the Spirit, grace and the prophets. Explain what Judaism already thought about righteous Gentiles. Then show how the decision changed over the next century (Ignatius). Weigh what was gained and what was lost.
strong: States the case for circumcision at full strength.
Gives the council's reasons: the Spirit, grace, Amos 9.
Explains the four rules and their link with Leviticus 17–18.
Mentions the Noahide laws and the God-fearers.
Shows the shift from 'need not' to 'must not' in Ignatius.
Notes what was lost: a church of Jews and Gentiles keeping their own ways together.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Peter crossed a line to eat in a stranger's house. Share a meal or a coffee with someone from a different background, faith or culture from your own, and listen more than you speak.
sessions.reflect: Who are the people you would find it hardest to sit at a table with? What would it take?
takeaways: The first great Christian argument was whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law; Peter's visit to Cornelius and the Jerusalem council (c. 49) said no.
The council's four rules echo the Torah's laws for Gentiles among Israel; Judaism already honoured righteous Gentiles, but not as members of God's people without conversion.
Within sixty years Ignatius was telling Christians not to keep the Sabbath at all: freedom for Gentiles had become a line between two communities.

sessions.title: The Temple falls
sessions.line: August, AD 70: Roman soldiers set fire to the Temple in Jerusalem. Two communities lose their centre, and each rebuilds itself in a different way.
sessions.plain: In AD 70 the Roman army destroyed Jerusalem and burned its Temple, the one place on earth where Jews offered sacrifice to God. Both Jews and the followers of Jesus had to find a way to live without it. Jews rebuilt their faith around the Torah, prayer and the teachers who became the rabbis; Christians rebuilt theirs around Christ. This session reads an eyewitness account of the fire and asks how two groups who shared so much began to walk apart.
sessions.why: Session 3 showed the Church opening its doors to Gentiles while Jewish believers still kept the law. Now comes the event that changed the ground under everyone's feet. While the Temple stood, Jewish believers in Jesus still had a place in Israel's worship, as Acts 21 showed. When it fell, Judaism and the Church each had to answer the question 'where is God now?', and they gave different answers.
answers: What happened to the Temple, and why does it matter so much?
How did Judaism survive without the Temple?
When did Christianity and Judaism separate?
Did Jews curse Christians in their prayers?
sessions.finding: Rome's destruction of the Temple in AD 70, and the crushing of a second revolt in 135, forced both communities to rebuild: rabbinic Judaism around the Torah, prayer and the sages, the Church around Christ; and on that new ground they drew apart, slowly and unevenly.

paras: Three sessions have shown a family story. Jesus was a Jew. His first followers were Jews who worshipped in the Temple, led by his brother James. Gentiles were welcomed without becoming Jews, and within two generations some Gentile Christians, like Ignatius, were saying that Christians should not keep Jewish customs at all.

Through all of it the Temple stood in Jerusalem. It was the house of God for every Jew, including Jews who believed in Jesus. Pilgrims came from across the world at the festivals. Even Jews who never visited paid a yearly Temple tax of two drachmas. Then, in four years of war, it was gone.
background.key: Until 70 the Temple was the centre for every Jew, including Jewish believers in Jesus. In four years of war it was destroyed.

paras: Roman rule in Judea had grown harsh and corrupt. In 66 the governor Gessius Florus took money from the Temple treasury; riots followed, and the Temple's priests stopped offering the daily sacrifice for the emperor. That was open revolt. A Roman army from Syria was beaten back, and the general Vespasian was sent with three legions. He conquered Galilee in 67. Then the emperor Nero died, Rome fell into civil war, and in 69 Vespasian himself became emperor. He left his son Titus to finish the war.

Inside Jerusalem, rival rebel leaders, John of Gischala and Simon bar Giora, fought each other as well as Rome. Titus besieged the city from the spring of 70. Famine set in. In late summer the Romans broke into the Temple courts, and the Temple burned. The last rebels held out at the desert fortress of Masada until 73 or 74.

timeline.text: Revolt breaks out in Jerusalem
Vespasian conquers Galilee; Josephus surrenders at Jotapata
Nero dies; civil war; Vespasian becomes emperor
Titus besieges Jerusalem; the Temple burns in August
Masada falls
Josephus writes The Jewish War in Rome
The Arch of Titus is set up in Rome, showing the Temple's lampstand carried in triumph
The second revolt, under Simon bar Kosiba (Bar Kokhba)

background.key: The revolt began in 66; Vespasian, then his son Titus, crushed it. Jerusalem was besieged in 70, and the Temple burned in August.

paras: Josephus was born in Jerusalem in 37 to a priestly family. At the start of the war he commanded the Jewish forces in Galilee. Besieged at Jotapata in 67, he surrendered to Vespasian and, by his own account, foretold that Vespasian would become emperor. When that came true he was freed, took the family name Flavius, and spent the siege of Jerusalem at Titus's side, calling on the defenders to give up. He wrote The Jewish War in Rome in the 70s, under the emperor's patronage.

So he is an eyewitness, but not a neutral one. He wants to clear the Romans, and above all Titus, of blame; he blames a small group of rebels, whom he calls 'the seditious' and 'robbers', for the disaster; and he wants to show that his people's God was not defeated but had used Rome to punish sin. Read him as you would read any memoir by a man who changed sides: vivid, informed and self-justifying. The translation is William Whiston's, of 1737, in old but readable English.
background.key: Josephus, a priest and rebel general who went over to Rome, saw the Temple burn. He is an eyewitness with motives: to clear Titus and to blame the rebels.

paras: The main reading is Josephus's account of the night the Temple burned (Jewish War VI.4.5–8 and VI.5.1, 3). It is the only eyewitness account of the event that decided the future of both Judaism and Christianity.

The comparison is two verses from Mark's Gospel, in which Jesus, leaving the Temple, says that not one stone will be left on another. Christians remembered those words when the Temple fell, and they read the disaster through them.
background.key: Josephus is the only eyewitness of the Temple's fall; Mark 13 shows how Christians remembered Jesus's words about it.

before: Who, according to Josephus, set the Temple on fire, and who tried to stop it?
How does Josephus explain why it happened?
What did the man called Jesus son of Ananus cry out, and what happened to him?
sessions.readWhy: An eyewitness account of the burning of the Temple in AD 70, the event that forced Jews and Christians alike to rebuild their faith without it.

paras: 5. So Titus retired into the tower of Antonia, and resolved to storm the temple the next day, early in the morning, with his whole army, and to encamp round about the holy house. But as for that house, God had, for certain, long ago doomed it to the fire; and now that fatal day was come, according to the revolution of ages; it was the tenth day of the month Lous, [Ab,] upon which it was formerly burnt by the king of Babylon; although these flames took their rise from the Jews themselves, and were occasioned by them; for upon Titus's retiring, the seditious lay still for a little while, and then attacked the Romans again, when those that guarded the holy house fought with those that quenched the fire that was burning the inner [court of the] temple; but these Romans put the Jews to flight, and proceeded as far as the holy house itself. At which time one of the soldiers, without staying for any orders, and without any concern or dread upon him at so great an undertaking, and being hurried on by a certain divine fury, snatched somewhat out of the materials that were on fire, and being lifted up by another soldier, he set fire to a golden window, through which there was a passage to the rooms that were round about the holy house, on the north side of it. As the flames went upward, the Jews made a great clamor, such as so mighty an affliction required, and ran together to prevent it; and now they spared not their lives any longer, nor suffered any thing to restrain their force, since that holy house was perishing, for whose sake it was that they kept such a guard about it.

6. And now a certain person came running to Titus, and told him of this fire, as he was resting himself in his tent after the last battle; whereupon he rose up in great haste, and, as he was, ran to the holy house, in order to have a stop put to the fire; after him followed all his commanders, and after them followed the several legions, in great astonishment; so there was a great clamor and tumult raised, as was natural upon the disorderly motion of so great an army. Then did Caesar, both by calling to the soldiers that were fighting, with a loud voice, and by giving a signal to them with his right hand, order them to quench the fire. But they did not hear what he said, though he spake so loud, having their ears already dimmed by a greater noise another way; nor did they attend to the signal he made with his hand neither, as still some of them were distracted with fighting, and others with passion. But as for the legions that came running thither, neither any persuasions nor any threatenings could restrain their violence, but each one's own passion was his commander at this time;

and as they were crowding into the temple together, many of them were trampled on by one another, while a great number fell among the ruins of the cloisters, which were still hot and smoking, and were destroyed in the same miserable way with those whom they had conquered; and when they were come near the holy house, they made as if they did not so much as hear Caesar's orders to the contrary; but they encouraged those that were before them to set it on fire. As for the seditious, they were in too great distress already to afford their assistance [towards quenching the fire]; they were every where slain, and every where beaten; and as for a great part of the people, they were weak and without arms, and had their throats cut wherever they were caught. Now round about the altar lay dead bodies heaped one upon another, as at the steps going up to it ran a great quantity of their blood, whither also the dead bodies that were slain above [on the altar] fell down.

7. And now, since Caesar was no way able to restrain the enthusiastic fury of the soldiers, and the fire proceeded on more and more, he went into the holy place of the temple, with his commanders, and saw it, with what was in it, which he found to be far superior to what the relations of foreigners contained, and not inferior to what we ourselves boasted of and believed about it. But as the flame had not as yet reached to its inward parts, but was still consuming the rooms that were about the holy house, and Titus supposing what the fact was, that the house itself might yet be saved, he came in haste and endeavored to persuade the soldiers to quench the fire, and gave order to Liberalius the centurion, and one of those spearmen that were about him, to beat the soldiers that were refractory with their staves, and to restrain them; yet were their passions too hard for the regards they had for Caesar, and the dread they had of him who forbade them, as was their hatred of the Jews, and a certain vehement inclination to fight them, too hard for them also. Moreover, the hope of plunder induced many to go on, as having this opinion, that all the places within were full of money, and as seeing that all round about it was made of gold. And besides, one of those that went into the place prevented Caesar, when he ran so hastily out to restrain the soldiers, and threw the fire upon the hinges of the gate, in the dark; whereby the flame burst out from within the holy house itself immediately, when the commanders retired, and Caesar with them, and when nobody any longer forbade those that were without to set fire to it. And thus was the holy house burnt down, without Caesar's approbation.

8. Now although any one would justly lament the destruction of such a work as this was, since it was the most admirable of all the works that we have seen or heard of, both for its curious structure and its magnitude, and also for the vast wealth bestowed upon it, as well as for the glorious reputation it had for its holiness; yet might such a one comfort himself with this thought, that it was fate that decreed it so to be, which is inevitable, both as to living creatures, and as to works and places also. However, one cannot but wonder at the accuracy of this period thereto relating; for the same month and day were now observed, as I said before, wherein the holy house was burnt formerly by the Babylonians. Now the number of years that passed from its first foundation, which was laid by king Solomon, till this its destruction, which happened in the second year of the reign of Vespasian, are collected to be one thousand one hundred and thirty, besides seven months and fifteen days; and from the second building of it, which was done by Haggai, in the second year of Cyrus the king, till its destruction under Vespasian, there were six hundred and thirty-nine years and forty-five days.

1. While the holy house was on fire, every thing was plundered that came to hand, and ten thousand of those that were caught were slain; nor was there a commiseration of any age, or any reverence of gravity, but children, and old men, and profane persons, and priests were all slain in the same manner; so that this war went round all sorts of men, and brought them to destruction, and as well those that made supplication for their lives, as those that defended themselves by fighting. The flame was also carried a long way, and made an echo, together with the groans of those that were slain; and because this hill was high, and the works at the temple were very great, one would have thought the whole city had been on fire. Nor can one imagine any thing either greater or more terrible than this noise; for there was at once a shout of the Roman legions, who were marching all together, and a sad clamor of the seditious, who were now surrounded with fire and sword. The people also that were left above were beaten back upon the enemy, and under a great consternation, and made sad moans at the calamity they were under; the multitude also that was in the city joined in this outcry with those that were upon the hill. And besides, many of those that were worn away by the famine, and their mouths almost closed, when they saw the fire of the holy house, they exerted their utmost strength, and brake out into groans and outcries again:

Perea did also return the echo, as well as the mountains round about [the city,] and augmented the force of the entire noise. Yet was the misery itself more terrible than this disorder; for one would have thought that the hill itself, on which the temple stood, was seething hot, as full of fire on every part of it, that the blood was larger in quantity than the fire, and those that were slain more in number than those that slew them; for the ground did no where appear visible, for the dead bodies that lay on it; but the soldiers went over heaps of those bodies, as they ran upon such as fled from them. And now it was that the multitude of the robbers were thrust out [of the inner court of the temple by the Romans,] and had much ado to get into the outward court, and from thence into the city, while the remainder of the populace fled into the cloister of that outer court. As for the priests, some of them plucked up from the holy house the spikes that were upon it, with their bases, which were made of lead, and shot them at the Romans instead of darts. But then as they gained nothing by so doing, and as the fire burst out upon them, they retired to the wall that was eight cubits broad, and there they tarried; yet did two of these of eminence among them, who might have saved themselves by going over to the Romans, or have borne up with courage, and taken their fortune with the others, throw themselves into the fire, and were burnt together with the holy house; their names were Meirus the son of Belgas, and Joseph the son of Daleus.

3. Thus were the miserable people persuaded by these deceivers, and such as belied God himself; while they did not attend nor give credit to the signs that were so evident, and did so plainly foretell their future desolation, but, like men infatuated, without either eyes to see or minds to consider, did not regard the denunciations that God made to them. Thus there was a star resembling a sword, which stood over the city, and a comet, that continued a whole year. Thus also before the Jews' rebellion, and before those commotions which preceded the war, when the people were come in great crowds to the feast of unleavened bread, on the eighth day of the month Xanthicus, [Nisan,] and at the ninth hour of the night, so great a light shone round the altar and the holy house, that it appeared to be bright day time; which lasted for half an hour. This light seemed to be a good sign to the unskillful, but was so interpreted by the sacred scribes, as to portend those events that followed immediately upon it. At the same festival also, a heifer, as she was led by the high priest to be sacrificed, brought forth a lamb in the midst of the temple.

Moreover, the eastern gate of the inner [court of the] temple, which was of brass, and vastly heavy, and had been with difficulty shut by twenty men, and rested upon a basis armed with iron, and had bolts fastened very deep into the firm floor, which was there made of one entire stone, was seen to be opened of its own accord about the sixth hour of the night. Now those that kept watch in the temple came hereupon running to the captain of the temple, and told him of it; who then came up thither, and not without great difficulty was able to shut the gate again. This also appeared to the vulgar to be a very happy prodigy, as if God did thereby open them the gate of happiness. But the men of learning understood it, that the security of their holy house was dissolved of its own accord, and that the gate was opened for the advantage of their enemies. So these publicly declared that the signal foreshowed the desolation that was coming upon them. Besides these, a few days after that feast, on the one and twentieth day of the month Artemisius, [Jyar,] a certain prodigious and incredible phenomenon appeared: I suppose the account of it would seem to be a fable, were it not related by those that saw it, and were not the events that followed it of so considerable a nature as to deserve such signals; for, before sun-setting, chariots and troops of soldiers in their armor were seen running about among the clouds, and surrounding of cities.

Moreover, at that feast which we call Pentecost, as the priests were going by night into the inner [court of the temple,] as their custom was, to perform their sacred ministrations, they said that, in the first place, they felt a quaking, and heard a great noise, and after that they heard a sound as of a great multitude, saying, "Let us remove hence." But, what is still more terrible, there was one Jesus, the son of Ananus, a plebeian and a husbandman, who, four years before the war began, and at a time when the city was in very great peace and prosperity, came to that feast whereon it is our custom for every one to make tabernacles to God in the temple, began on a sudden to cry aloud, "A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and the holy house, a voice against the bridegrooms and the brides, and a voice against this whole people!" This was his cry, as he went about by day and by night, in all the lanes of the city. However, certain of the most eminent among the populace had great indignation at this dire cry of his, and took up the man, and gave him a great number of severe stripes; yet did not he either say any thing for himself, or any thing peculiar to those that chastised him, but still went on with the same words which he cried before. Hereupon our rulers, supposing, as the case proved to be, that this was a sort of divine fury in the man, brought him to the Roman procurator, where he was whipped till his bones were laid bare;

yet he did not make any supplication for himself, nor shed any tears, but turning his voice to the most lamentable tone possible, at every stroke of the whip his answer was, "Woe, woe to Jerusalem!" And when Albinus [for he was then our procurator] asked him, Who he was? and whence he came? and why he uttered such words? he made no manner of reply to what he said, but still did not leave off his melancholy ditty, till Albinus took him to be a madman, and dismissed him. Now, during all the time that passed before the war began, this man did not go near any of the citizens, nor was seen by them while he said so; but he every day uttered these lamentable words, as if it were his premeditated vow, "Woe, woe to Jerusalem!" Nor did he give ill words to any of those that beat him every day, nor good words to those that gave him food; but this was his reply to all men, and indeed no other than a melancholy presage of what was to come. This cry of his was the loudest at the festivals; and he continued this ditty for seven years and five months, without growing hoarse, or being tired therewith, until the very time that he saw his presage in earnest fulfilled in our siege, when it ceased; for as he was going round upon the wall, he cried out with his utmost force, "Woe, woe to the city again, and to the people, and to the holy house!" And just as he added at the last, "Woe, woe to myself also!" there came a stone out of one of the engines, and smote him, and killed him immediately; and as he was uttering the very same presages he gave up the ghost.

parts.author: Flavius Josephus
parts.title: The holy house burns
parts.context: Jerusalem, August 70. The Romans have taken the Antonia, the fortress at the north-west corner of the Temple, and fought their way into the outer courts. 'The holy house' is Whiston's phrase for the sanctuary itself, the inner building with the Holy of Holies. 'Caesar' here means Titus, the emperor's son. Whiston's footnote number has been removed; the words in square brackets are his.
parts.plain: Titus plans to attack the Temple the next morning. But the defenders attack first, the Romans chase them back, and a soldier, without orders, throws a burning brand through a golden window. Titus runs to stop the fire, but his soldiers, wild with fighting, hatred and the hope of loot, will not listen. Titus sees the inside of the sanctuary before the fire reaches it. Then someone sets the gates alight and the house burns. Josephus says it burned on the same day of the year as Solomon's Temple was burned by Babylon.

commentary.on: God had, for certain, long ago doomed it to the fire
commentary.text: Josephus begins with his explanation before he tells the story: God himself had decided the Temple's end. For a Jew this was the only bearable way to see it. If God had allowed it, then God was not defeated; Israel had sinned and been punished, as when Babylon burned the first Temple. The prophets had said the same in their day (Jeremiah 7:12–14).

commentary.on: it was the tenth day of the month Lous, [Ab,] upon which it was formerly burnt by the king of Babylon
commentary.text: Lous is the Macedonian month name; Ab (Av) is the Hebrew. Jews still mourn both Temples on one day, Tisha b'Av, the ninth of Av, with fasting and the reading of Lamentations. The rabbis dated the burning to the ninth (Mishnah, Ta'anit 4:6); Josephus says the tenth. Either way, the second ruin was felt as a repetition of the first.

commentary.on: he set fire to a golden window
commentary.text: Josephus insists the fire was not planned: one soldier, 'without staying for any orders', acting from 'a certain divine fury'. Notice how he holds two things together, an accident and the hand of God.

commentary.on: order them to quench the fire
commentary.text: Titus tries to save the Temple. This is Josephus's central claim, and historians doubt it. A Christian writer of about 400, Sulpicius Severus, says that Titus held a council and decided to destroy the Temple, so as to root out the religion of both Jews and Christians (Chronicle II.30). Many scholars think Severus took this from a lost part of the Roman historian Tacitus. Josephus, writing for Titus's family, had every reason to tell it the other way.

commentary.on: as was their hatred of the Jews, and a certain vehement inclination to fight them
commentary.text: Josephus names the soldiers' hatred plainly. Many of the troops were recruited in Syria and the coast, where Jews and their Gentile neighbours had been killing each other since 66.

commentary.on: And thus was the holy house burnt down, without Caesar's approbation.
commentary.text: 'Approbation' means approval. The sentence is Josephus's verdict, and his defence of his patron.

commentary.on: it was fate that decreed it so to be
commentary.text: Josephus writes for Greek and Roman readers, so he uses their word, 'fate'. He then counts the years from Solomon. His numbers are his own and do not match modern dates, but the point is plain: an age of more than a thousand years of sacrifice had ended.

parts.author: Flavius Josephus
parts.title: The slaughter
parts.context: The same night. Josephus describes what followed in the Temple courts. It is hard reading; it is meant to be. Whiston's footnote numbers have been removed.
parts.plain: While the Temple burns, the soldiers loot and kill everyone they catch, children, old people and priests alike. The noise of the fire, the legions and the dying echoes off the hills. The ground cannot be seen for the bodies. Some priests fight on from the wall; two throw themselves into the fire and die with the Temple.

commentary.on: children, and old men, and profane persons, and priests were all slain in the same manner
commentary.text: No one was spared. Josephus elsewhere claims that 1,100,000 people died in the siege and 97,000 were taken captive (Jewish War VI.9.3). Historians think the first number is far too high, since Jerusalem could not have held so many even at Passover, but no one doubts that the loss of life was immense.

commentary.on: the blood was larger in quantity than the fire
commentary.text: Josephus writes like a tragedian here, with sound, echo and image. He wants his Roman readers to feel what their victory cost.

commentary.on: throw themselves into the fire, and were burnt together with the holy house
commentary.text: Two priests choose to die with the Temple rather than live without it. For them there was no Judaism imaginable without the house of God. The great question after 70 was whether they were right.

parts.author: Flavius Josephus
parts.title: Signs, and a voice of woe
parts.context: Josephus steps back to tell of the warnings God had given, which the people ignored because false prophets promised them rescue. He ends with a man called Jesus son of Ananus, a common name; he is not Jesus of Nazareth. The festivals named are Passover ('the feast of unleavened bread'), Pentecost and Tabernacles ('make tabernacles to God'). Whiston's footnote numbers have been removed.
parts.plain: Josephus says there were many signs: a star like a sword, a light round the altar at night, a heavy gate opening by itself, armies seen in the clouds, a voice in the Temple saying 'Let us remove hence'. Then a farmer called Jesus son of Ananus began, four years before the war, to cry 'woe to Jerusalem' day and night. The leaders beat him and handed him to the Roman governor, who had him flogged to the bone; he never answered. He kept crying for seven years, until a stone from a Roman catapult killed him on the wall.

commentary.on: Thus were the miserable people persuaded by these deceivers
commentary.text: Just before this, Josephus says a false prophet had told the people to go up to the Temple to receive 'signs of deliverance', and six thousand died in the fire there. Josephus blames the prophets of rescue, not God.

commentary.on: was seen to be opened of its own accord about the sixth hour of the night
commentary.text: The gate opening by itself was read two ways: 'the vulgar', ordinary people, saw it as God opening the gate of happiness; 'the men of learning' saw the Temple's protection dissolving. The Roman historian Tacitus reports the same portents, including the voice saying the gods were leaving (Histories V.13). The rabbis remembered a similar sign forty years before the destruction: the Temple doors opening by themselves (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 39b).

commentary.on: there was one Jesus, the son of Ananus, a plebeian and a husbandman
commentary.text: A 'plebeian and a husbandman' is a common man and a farmer. Listen to what happens to him: he speaks against the Temple at a festival, the leaders beat him, they hand him to the Roman governor, he is flogged, and he gives no answer. Many scholars have noticed how closely this follows the story of Jesus of Nazareth thirty years earlier. It shows that a prophet who spoke against the Temple could expect exactly that treatment, and it makes the Gospels' account of Jesus's arrest more believable, not less.

commentary.on: brought him to the Roman procurator, where he was whipped till his bones were laid bare
commentary.text: The procurator, the Roman governor, was Albinus, who ruled Judea from 62 to 64. That dates the start of the cries to 62, the year James the brother of Jesus was killed.

commentary.on: until the very time that he saw his presage in earnest fulfilled in our siege
commentary.text: A 'presage' is a warning of what is to come. 'Our siege': Josephus writes as a Jew who lost his city, even though he watched from the Roman lines.

read.author: Flavius Josephus

paras: As he went out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Teacher, see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings!”
Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone on another, which will not be thrown down.”

parts.title: Leaving the Temple
parts.context: Jerusalem, a few days before Jesus's death, about AD 30–33. Jesus has been teaching in the Temple courts. Mark's Gospel is usually dated about 65–75: some scholars think just before the Temple fell, others just after. That question matters, because if Mark wrote after 70, sceptics say the prophecy was written after the event.

commentary.on: Teacher, see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings!
commentary.text: Herod's Temple was one of the wonders of the Roman world. Some of the stones still in place in its retaining walls, the Western Wall among them, are more than ten metres long and weigh hundreds of tonnes. A disciple from Galilee is amazed, as any visitor would be.

commentary.on: There will not be left here one stone on another, which will not be thrown down.
commentary.text: Jesus stands in a line of Jewish prophets who warned that the Temple could fall, from Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:14; 26:6) to Jesus son of Ananus, whom you have just met. It was a prophet's warning, not a Gentile's sneer. Archaeologists excavating at the south-west corner of the Temple Mount since 1968 have found great Herodian stones lying where they fell onto the first-century street below, pushed down by Roman soldiers. The Western Wall itself was part of the platform's retaining wall, not of the Temple building, which is why it still stands.

compare.why: Mark's Gospel remembers Jesus foretelling the Temple's destruction. When it happened, Christians read the event through these words, and that reading would shape how they saw the Jews who did not follow Jesus.
compare.title: Not one stone on another

paras: It is hard to overstate what the Temple meant. For a thousand years, with one break, Israel had believed that God had chosen one place to put his name (Deuteronomy 12:5). There the priests offered the daily sacrifices; there, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest entered the Holy of Holies to seek forgiveness for the whole people. The Torah's laws of purity, offerings and festivals assumed a Temple.

Now it was gone, and Rome made sure the loss was felt. Titus carried the Temple's golden lampstand and table through Rome in triumph; the Arch of Titus, which still stands in the Forum, shows them. Vespasian turned the Temple tax that every Jew paid into a tax for the temple of Jupiter in Rome, the fiscus Judaicus (Josephus, Jewish War VII.6.6). Jews everywhere were now paying for a pagan god's house because their own had been destroyed.
sections.key: The Temple was where God had put his name and sins were atoned for. Rome paraded its treasures in triumph and turned the Temple tax into a tax for Jupiter.

sections.h: Judaism rebuilt: Yavneh and the sages
paras: The Judaism that survived was led by the heirs of the Pharisees. A famous story in the Talmud (Gittin 56a–b) tells how Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai was smuggled out of besieged Jerusalem in a coffin, met Vespasian, and asked for one thing: 'Give me Yavneh and its sages.' Yavneh (Jamnia) was a small town near the coast. Whether or not the story is history, Yavneh became the place where teachers gathered to rebuild.

Their answer to 'where is God now?' was the Torah, prayer and acts of love. Another old story (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4) tells of Yohanan walking past the ruins with a pupil, who wept that the place of atonement was gone. Yohanan replied that they had another atonement just as good, deeds of loving-kindness, and quoted Hosea 6:6: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' Prayer three times a day took the place of the daily sacrifices. Study of the Torah became the holiest act. Over the next centuries the sages, now called rabbis ('my teacher'), wrote down their oral law in the Mishnah (about 200) and its commentaries, the Talmuds (about 400 and 500–600). This rabbinic Judaism is the ancestor of almost all Judaism today.
sections.key: The heirs of the Pharisees rebuilt Judaism at Yavneh around the Torah, prayer and loving-kindness: rabbinic Judaism, the ancestor of Judaism today.

sections.h: The Church rebuilt: Christ as the Temple
paras: Christians answered the same question differently. They already spoke of Jesus himself as the Temple: John's Gospel says that when Jesus said 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up', 'he spoke of the temple of his body' (John 2:19–21). Paul told the Corinthians that they, the community, were God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). The Letter to the Hebrews presents Christ as the great high priest who offered himself once for all, so that no more sacrifices are needed (Hebrews 9:11–12; 10:11–12).

Strikingly, Jesus too had quoted Hosea 6:6, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice' (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). Both communities reached for the same verse. But where the rabbis built a life of Torah around the Temple's absence, the Church built a life of worship around Christ's presence: baptism, the Lord's Supper, Sunday. The two answers were each complete. That is why, after 70, it became harder and harder to belong to both.
sections.key: Christians saw Christ as the true Temple and sacrifice; the rabbis turned to Torah and prayer. Both quoted Hosea 6:6, but each answer was complete, so belonging to both grew harder.

paras: The Amidah, the standing prayer you met in session 1, came to have a blessing (strictly, a curse) against the minim, 'heretics' or 'sectarians'. The Talmud says that Samuel the Lesser composed it at Yavneh in the time of Rabban Gamaliel II, about 80–100 (Berakhot 28b–29a). Copies found in the Cairo Genizah, a storeroom of old manuscripts, and published by Solomon Schechter in 1898, name the notzrim, the Nazarenes, beside the minim. John's Gospel three times speaks of believers being 'put out of the synagogue' (John 9:22; 12:42; 16:2), and Justin Martyr, about 160, accused the Jews of cursing Christians in their synagogues (Dialogue with Trypho 16).

For a long time scholars put these together: the curse was written at Yavneh to drive Jewish Christians out. In 1981 Reuven Kimelman questioned this. The early evidence, he argued, aims at Jewish sectarians of every kind, not at Christians as such; the word notzrim was probably added later; and there was no single decree that everyone obeyed. Most scholars now think the 'Birkat ha-Minim' was part of a slow drawing of lines, not one decisive expulsion. Both sides were drawing them.
sections.key: The Amidah came to include a curse on 'sectarians', later naming Nazarenes. Scholars now see it as one step in a slow drawing of lines on both sides, not one expulsion.

paras: Sixty years after Titus, Judea rose again. The leader was Simon bar Kosiba, whose letters were found in caves by the Dead Sea in 1960–61. Rabbi Akiva, the greatest teacher of his day, is remembered as calling him Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star', after the messianic prophecy 'a star will come out of Jacob' (Numbers 24:17; Jerusalem Talmud, Ta'anit 4:5). Jewish believers in Jesus could not follow a second messiah. Justin Martyr, writing soon after, says Bar Kokhba had Christians punished if they would not deny Jesus.

The emperor Hadrian crushed the revolt at terrible cost. He rebuilt Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina, banned Jews from entering it, and renamed the province Syria Palaestina. From now on, as session 2 showed, the church in Jerusalem was led by Gentiles. Akiva himself was executed, dying, the Talmud says, with the Shema on his lips (Berakhot 61b). After 135 there was no Jewish Jerusalem for anyone to share, and the two communities, each mourning, each sure of its own reading of what had happened, faced each other across a wider gap.
sections.key: In 132–135 many Jews followed Bar Kokhba as messiah; Jewish Christians could not. Hadrian banned Jews from Jerusalem, and the gap between the communities widened.

paras: By the second century the two communities looked like this. Both claimed the same God, the same Scriptures and the same ancestors. Each read the loss of the Temple through its own centre.

rows: The Torah, studied and kept; the home and the synagogue
Christ, the true Temple; the gathered community
Prayer three times a day; deeds of loving-kindness
Christ's sacrifice once for all; the Lord's Supper
The oral law: Mishnah (c. 200), Talmuds (c. 400 and 500–600)
The Gospels and apostles' letters: the New Testament
Punishment for Israel's sins, and a call to return; the exile will end
The fulfilment of Jesus's warning; for many, a judgement on those who rejected him
table.note: Each was a complete way of living with God after the Temple. Neither needed the other, and that is part of why they parted.

sections.key: Rabbinic Judaism put Torah, prayer and the sages where the Temple had been; the Church put Christ there. Each was complete without the other.
