debate.question: When did Judaism and Christianity part?

positions.name: Early, after the two wars
positions.who: James D. G. Dunn, The Partings of the Ways (1991); many historians
positions.view: There were several partings, not one, but the decisive ones came with the two revolts. After 70 the Temple, which Jewish believers still shared, was gone; after 135 Jewish believers could not follow Bar Kokhba, and Jerusalem was closed to Jews. By the mid-second century the two were clearly separate bodies.
positions.evidence: Ignatius's 'Christianity' against 'Judaism' (c. 110); the Birkat ha-Minim; Justin's Dialogue with a Jew as an outsider (c. 160); Gentile bishops in Jerusalem after 135.

positions.name: Late, and never cleanly
positions.who: Daniel Boyarin, Border Lines (2004); the essays in The Ways That Never Parted (2003, ed. Adam Becker and Annette Yoshiko Reed)
positions.view: On the ground, the line stayed blurred for centuries. Christians went on visiting synagogues and keeping Jewish feasts; Jewish believers in Jesus kept the law; rabbis and bishops both worked hard to draw a border that ordinary people kept crossing. The border was finally fixed in the fourth century, when the Church became the empire's religion and defined 'heresy'.
positions.evidence: John Chrysostom's sermons (386–387) against Christians who went to synagogue; the Council of Laodicea's bans; the Nazarenes Epiphanius met (c. 375); shared stories and methods in rabbinic and Christian texts.

positions.name: Different from the start
positions.who: Jacob Neusner, Jews and Christians: The Myth of a Common Tradition (1991)
positions.view: To speak of a 'parting' assumes a shared road. Rabbinic Judaism and Christianity are two different religions that each made a new whole from Israel's Scriptures, asking different questions and giving different answers. They were never in one conversation, so they did not so much part as grow up separately.
positions.evidence: The rabbis' focus on the holiness of Israel's life under the Torah; the Church's focus on salvation in Christ; how little each tradition engages the other's real questions.

debate.agree: All agree that the fall of the Temple in 70 and the crushing of the second revolt in 135 changed both communities for ever, and that the separation was a process, not a single day.

look.why: No painting of the destruction of Jerusalem is in the gallery's open collection. Picture instead the Arch of Titus in the Roman Forum, where the Temple's lampstand is still carried in stone.

music.why: Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, O God', one of the psalms of Israel's worship, which both Jews and Christians went on praying after the Temple fell. It ends: 'Build the walls of Jerusalem. Then you will delight in the sacrifices.'

think.why: Josephus, today's eyewitness, is also one of the few writers outside the New Testament to mention Jesus. See what historians make of him.

learn.why: Israel's lament for the first Temple, by the rivers of Babylon. Jews have sung it for both.

check.q: Josephus says Titus tried to save the Temple. Why do historians treat this claim with caution?
options: Because Josephus wrote under the patronage of Titus's family, and another ancient source, Sulpicius Severus, possibly drawing on Tacitus, says Titus chose to destroy it
Because the Temple was never burned
Because Josephus was not in Jerusalem at the time
Because Josephus hated the Romans
check.why: Josephus was an eyewitness, but he had every reason to clear his patron.

check.q: Why does the story of Jesus son of Ananus matter for the study of Jesus of Nazareth?
options: Because it shows that a prophet who spoke against the Temple could be beaten by the leaders and handed to the Roman governor, making the Gospel account more believable
Because they were the same person
Because Josephus says he was a Christian
Because he founded the church in Jerusalem
check.why: The parallel shows how Jerusalem's authorities dealt with prophets against the Temple, thirty years after Jesus.

check.q: What was the rabbis' main answer to the loss of the Temple?
options: To move it to Yavneh
To accept Jesus as the true Temple
To rebuild it at once
Study and keeping of the Torah, prayer in place of sacrifice, and deeds of loving-kindness
check.why: Yohanan ben Zakkai's reply, quoting Hosea 6:6, sums it up.

check.q: Both the rabbis and Jesus quoted Hosea 6:6, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice'. Why, then, did their answers to the Temple's fall pull the communities apart?
options: Because they quoted different translations
Because each built a complete way of living with God around a different centre, Torah or Christ, so neither needed the other
Because Hosea was a Christian prophet
Because the rabbis rejected Hosea
check.why: Shared texts, different centres: each answer was whole in itself.

check.q: What do most scholars now think about the Birkat ha-Minim, the curse on 'sectarians'?
options: That it was one part of a slow drawing of lines, aimed at Jewish sectarians in general, with 'Nazarenes' probably added later
That it never existed
That it was written by Christians
That it was a decree, obeyed everywhere, that expelled all Christians from synagogues in about 85
check.why: Kimelman's 1981 study changed the consensus away from a single expulsion.

check.q: Why did the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135) widen the gap between the communities?
options: Because it rebuilt the Temple
Because Jewish believers in Jesus could not follow a second messiah, and afterwards Jews were banned from Jerusalem
Because Christians led it
Because Bar Kokhba became a Christian
check.why: Rabbi Akiva hailed Bar Kokhba as 'son of the star'; Justin says Christians who refused to deny Jesus were punished.

tutorial.question: 'The fall of the Temple did more to separate Judaism and Christianity than anything Jesus or Paul said.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Use Josephus to describe what was lost, and the lecture to show how each community rebuilt. Weigh the Temple's fall against the earlier questions of the Gentiles and the law, and against the Bar Kokhba revolt. Use the scholars' debate to say when you think the ways parted, and why.
strong: Describes what the Temple meant and what its loss meant, using Josephus.
Explains Yavneh and the rabbis' answer, and the Church's answer in Christ.
Weighs the Temple's fall against the Gentile question and against 135.
Treats the Birkat ha-Minim with care, noting Kimelman's case.
Engages at least two positions in the debate (Dunn, Boyarin, Neusner).
Notices that Josephus is a partial witness.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the rabbis said that when the Temple fell, deeds of loving-kindness took the place of sacrifice. Each day this week do one hidden act of kindness for someone who cannot repay it, and tell no one.
sessions.reflect: When something you built your life around is taken away, what do you rebuild around?
takeaways: Rome burned the Temple in AD 70; Josephus, an eyewitness with his own motives, saw it as God's judgement carried out by Rome.
Rabbinic Judaism rebuilt around the Torah, prayer and loving-kindness; the Church around Christ as the true Temple. Each answer was complete, so belonging to both grew harder.
The ways parted slowly, through the two wars, the drawing of lines on both sides and, later, the power of a Christian empire; scholars still debate when.

sessions.title: The case against: did the New Testament teach contempt?
sessions.line: 'May his blood be on us, and on our children.' 'You are of your father, the devil.' Words from a family quarrel, and the centuries of contempt and killing that grew from them.
sessions.plain: Some words in the New Testament about 'the Jews' are harsh. For centuries Christians used them to blame all Jews for Jesus's death, to call them cursed, and to justify hatred, expulsion and murder. That history ends in the Holocaust, in Christian Europe. This session lets the case against the New Testament speak at full strength, before asking whether the fault lies in the text or in its readers.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 4 have shown a family story: Jesus the Jew, a Jewish church, the Gentiles welcomed, and the slow parting after the Temple fell. The parting left two communities, one of which became the religion of an empire. Now we must face what the stronger branch did to the other, and the strongest charge against the Christian story: that the poison was there in its own Scriptures from the start.
answers: Is the New Testament anti-Semitic?
Did Christians blame the Jews for killing Jesus?
What is 'the teaching of contempt'?
Has the Church repented of it?
sessions.finding: Some New Testament words, torn from their family quarrel, became the root of centuries of Christian contempt and violence towards Jews, which helped prepare the ground for the Holocaust; the churches have repented of that teaching, but the question whether the texts themselves are to blame remains open.

background.h: The story so far, and where it went
paras: The first Christians were a small Jewish movement, arguing with other Jews about whether Jesus was the Messiah. Their arguments were sharp, as family arguments are. But within three centuries the Church had become the religion of the Roman empire, and the Jews a small minority within it. Words written by a persecuted minority about its own family were now read aloud by the powerful about the powerless.

This session does something the others have not. It states the case against, at full strength, in the words of those who have pressed it hardest: the French Jewish historian Jules Isaac, whose wife and daughter were murdered at Auschwitz, and Christian and Jewish scholars after him. A reply comes only at the end, and it is a partial one.
background.key: Words of a small Jewish movement in a family quarrel became, once the Church held power, words of the strong about the weak.

paras: 'Anti-Semitism' is a word coined in Germany around 1879 for hatred of Jews as a race. Scholars often call the older Christian hostility 'anti-Judaism': contempt for Jews because of their religion, and the claim that God had rejected them. The two are different, but, as we will see, the first grew in ground the second had prepared.

The main readings are two of the passages most used against Jews. In Matthew 27:24–26 the crowd before Pilate cries 'May his blood be on us, and on our children!' In John 8:31–47 Jesus tells a group of Jews, 'You are of your father, the devil.'
background.key: 'Anti-Judaism' is religious contempt; 'antisemitism', a word of about 1879, is racial hatred. The first prepared the ground for the second.

paras: These two passages are the heart of the charge. Matthew's 'his blood be on us' was read for centuries as a curse the Jews called down on all their descendants. John's 'your father, the devil' was preached for centuries as a description of every Jew, and Nazi propaganda revived the picture. If the New Testament teaches contempt, it is here.

The comparison is from Eusebius, the first great historian of the Church, writing as the empire was becoming Christian, about 313–325. He reads the sufferings of the Jews, ending in the fall of Jerusalem, as 'divine vengeance' for what they did to Christ. It is the harsh reading in its early, learned form.
background.key: Matthew 27:25 and John 8:44 are the texts most used against Jews; Eusebius shows the early Christian reading of Jewish suffering as divine vengeance.

before: Who exactly says 'May his blood be on us'? How many people could have been there?
In John 8, to whom is Jesus speaking at the start? Who is the argument with?
What does Eusebius think caused the Jews' misfortunes?
sessions.readWhy: The two New Testament passages most used to teach contempt for Jews, read closely, so that the charge against them can be weighed fairly.

paras: So when Pilate saw that nothing was being gained, but rather that a disturbance was starting, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous person. You see to it.”
All the people answered, “May his blood be on us, and on our children!”
Then he released to them Barabbas, but Jesus he flogged and delivered to be crucified.
Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”
They answered him, “We are Abraham’s offspring, and have never been in bondage to anyone. How do you say, ‘You will be made free’?”
Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin.
A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever.
If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
I know that you are Abraham’s offspring, yet you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you.
I say the things which I have seen with my Father; and you also do the things which you have seen with your father.”
They answered him, “Our father is Abraham.”
Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.
But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham didn’t do this.
You do the works of your father.”
They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father, God.”
Therefore Jesus said to them, “If God were your father, you would love me, for I came out and have come from God. For I haven’t come of myself, but he sent me.
Why don’t you understand my speech? Because you can’t hear my word.

You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies.
But because I tell the truth, you don’t believe me.
Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?
He who is of God hears the words of God. For this cause you don’t hear, because you are not of God.”

parts.title: 'His blood be on us'
parts.context: Jerusalem, about AD 30–33, the morning of Jesus's death. Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, has offered to release a prisoner for the festival. The crowd asks for Barabbas. Matthew wrote his Gospel probably about 80–90, after the fall of Jerusalem, most likely for a community of Jewish believers in Jesus in bitter conflict with the synagogue leaders of their town. Only Matthew has these words.

commentary.on: he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude
commentary.text: A Jewish gesture: the law tells the elders of a town to wash their hands over a heifer and say 'our hands have not shed this blood' (Deuteronomy 21:6–7). Matthew shows Pilate trying to put the blame elsewhere. Yet it was Pilate who had the power, and crucifixion was a Roman punishment. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of the time, called Pilate cruel and stubborn, and Josephus tells of his violence against crowds.

commentary.on: I am innocent of the blood of this righteous person. You see to it.
commentary.text: The words echo what the chief priests said to Judas a few verses earlier: 'What is that to us? You see to it' (Matthew 27:4). Matthew is building a theme of guilt passed from hand to hand.

commentary.on: May his blood be on us, and on our children!
commentary.text: The most terrible verse in Christian history. 'All the people', the crowd in Pilate's courtyard, perhaps a few hundred, say it. For Matthew, writing after 70, 'our children' probably meant the next generation, who saw Jerusalem fall, which he read as the consequence. But from the fourth century these words were read as a curse on every Jew in every age. They were preached each Holy Week, and Holy Week was for centuries a time of danger for Jews in Christian towns. The charge built on them, that the Jews were 'Christ-killers', is called the charge of deicide, 'killing God'.

commentary.on: Then he released to them Barabbas, but Jesus he flogged and delivered to be crucified.
commentary.text: Pilate gives the order. The Creed, said in churches every week, names him, not the Jews: 'crucified under Pontius Pilate'. Christian teaching has always held that Christ died for the sins of all, and in 1566 the Catechism of the Council of Trent said that sinners of every age, Christians most of all, bear the guilt of his death. That teaching was too often forgotten in the street.

parts.title: 'Your father, the devil'
parts.context: The Temple courts in Jerusalem, at the autumn festival of Tabernacles. John's Gospel, usually dated about 90–100, was probably written for a community that had been put out of the synagogue (John 9:22). It uses the phrase 'the Jews' about seventy times, far more than the other Gospels, often for Jesus's opponents among the Jerusalem leaders, though Jesus and all his disciples are Jews too.

commentary.on: Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him
commentary.text: Notice who the argument is with: Jews who had believed in Jesus. This is a quarrel inside the movement, between Jesus and some of his own followers, over who he really is. It is not Christians against Jews, for in the story there are no Christians who are not Jews.

commentary.on: We are Abraham's offspring
commentary.text: Both sides argue about the same thing: who are Abraham's true children? It is a family argument about the family's inheritance. John the Baptist had said the same to his hearers: 'Don't think to yourselves, "We have Abraham for our father"' (Matthew 3:9).

commentary.on: If you were Abraham's children, you would do the works of Abraham.
commentary.text: Being a child, in this way of speaking, means acting like your father. The prophets used the same logic: Isaiah called his own people 'rulers of Sodom' (Isaiah 1:10). This is the language of insiders calling their own back.

commentary.on: You are of your father, the devil
commentary.text: The harshest words in the Gospels. In the setting of ancient argument they are polemic: the Dead Sea Scrolls call fellow Jews 'sons of darkness', and Greek philosophers insulted their rivals in much the same way. But polemic copied into Scripture and read in every church for nineteen centuries does not stay polemic. Medieval preachers and artists linked Jews with the devil, horns and all, and Nazi propaganda revived the picture in its own way. This is the verse Jules Isaac most wanted Christians to face.

commentary.on: For this cause you don't hear, because you are not of God.
commentary.text: The argument ends with a verdict on those who will not hear. In John's Gospel the same Jesus says 'salvation is from the Jews' (John 4:22). Both sayings are in one book. The question of this session is which one Christians chose to hear, and why.

paras: 3. Innumerable other terrible and almost indescribable calamities which came upon the Jews in Alexandria during the reign of the same emperor, are recorded by the same author in a second work, to which he gave the title, On the Virtues. With him agrees also Josephus, who likewise indicates that the misfortunes of the whole nation began with the time of Pilate, and with their daring crimes against the Saviour.

5. Comparing these things with the writings of the evangelists, you will see that it was not long before there came upon them the penalty for the exclamation which they had uttered under the same Pilate, when they cried out that they had no other king than Cæsar.

8. In addition to these the same author records many other tumults which were stirred up in Jerusalem itself, and shows that from that time seditions and wars and mischievous plots followed each other in quick succession, and never ceased in the city and in all Judea until finally the siege of Vespasian overwhelmed them. Thus the divine vengeance overtook the Jews for the crimes which they dared to commit against Christ.

parts.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
parts.translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (1890), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1
parts.title: The penalty
parts.context: Eusebius (c. 260–339) was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a few days' walk from Jerusalem. He finished his Church History in the 320s, soon after the emperor Constantine had made Christianity legal. Here he draws on Philo of Alexandria ('the same author'), a Jewish writer of the time of Christ, and on Josephus, to list the disasters that fell on the Jews under the emperor Gaius (37–41) and after. Translated by A. C. McGiffert (1890). The cuts are marked '…'; New Advent's inserted Bible reference has been removed.
parts.plain: Eusebius says that the Jews' misfortunes began under Pilate, when they committed crimes against Jesus, and that Josephus agrees. When they told Pilate that they had no king but Caesar, they brought a penalty on themselves. From then on there were riots, wars and plots in Jerusalem until Vespasian's siege destroyed them. That, he says, was God's vengeance on the Jews for what they did to Christ.

commentary.on: the misfortunes of the whole nation began with the time of Pilate, and with their daring crimes against the Saviour
commentary.text: 'The whole nation': not the Temple leaders, not a crowd, but a people. This is the step Matthew did not take and later readers did. Notice too that Eusebius says 'Josephus agrees'. Josephus says nothing of the kind about Jesus; he blamed the rebels. Eusebius has read a Jewish witness to say what a Christian wanted to hear.

commentary.on: it was not long before there came upon them the penalty for the exclamation
commentary.text: The 'exclamation' is the cry 'We have no king but Caesar' (John 19:15). Eusebius links a saying from the Gospels to events forty years later as cause and penalty. The method is the same one used for Matthew 27:25.

commentary.on: Thus the divine vengeance overtook the Jews for the crimes which they dared to commit against Christ.
commentary.text: Here is the theology in one sentence. Jews themselves read the fall of Jerusalem as a judgement on Israel's sins, as Josephus did, and as the prophets read the fall of the first Temple. The difference is that a prophet's warning, spoken in love from inside, has become an outsider's verdict, spoken in triumph. Within sixty years of Eusebius, Christian emperors were passing laws against Jews, and preachers like John Chrysostom were preaching against them.

compare.why: Eusebius, writing as the empire was becoming Christian, gives the reading that shaped the next fifteen centuries: the Jews' sufferings were God's punishment for what they did to Christ. It is the first of Jules Isaac's three 'themes of contempt'.
compare.title: Divine vengeance

paras: Jules Isaac (1877–1963) was a French historian, a Jew, and the author of the history textbooks generations of French schoolchildren learned from. In 1943 his wife Laure and his daughter Juliette were arrested by the Gestapo and murdered at Auschwitz. In hiding, he began to study the Gospels and how the Church had taught them. In Jesus and Israel (1948) and The Teaching of Contempt (1962) he made a charge that changed the Church.

His case, in our own words, was this. For many centuries Christian preaching, catechisms and art had taught three things about the Jews. First, that their scattering among the nations was God's punishment for the death of Jesus. Second, that the Judaism of Jesus's day was dead and corrupt, so that he came to a people who had lost the faith. Third, that the Jews were a people of 'deicide', guilty for ever of killing God. This 'teaching of contempt', he argued, was not a fringe error but mainstream Christian teaching, and it made Christians ready to believe the worst of Jews, and so prepared the way for what happened in his own day.
sections.key: Jules Isaac, whose wife and daughter were murdered at Auschwitz, named three Christian 'themes of contempt': dispersion as punishment, Judaism as corrupt, and the Jews as 'deicide'.

paras: The record supports him. About 170, Melito, bishop of Sardis, preached a Passover sermon accusing Israel of murdering God, the first clear charge of deicide (On Pascha 96). In 386–387 John Chrysostom, the greatest preacher of the Greek church, preached eight sermons in Antioch against Christians who went to the synagogue, calling it a brothel and a den of thieves. In 1096 crusading bands passing through the Rhineland massacred the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, though some bishops tried to protect them; the hall on the Middle Ages comes back to this. In 1144 at Norwich the 'blood libel' began, the lie that Jews murdered Christian children, and spread across Europe.

In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council required Jews to wear distinctive dress (canon 68). Jews were expelled from England in 1290, from France more than once, and from Spain in 1492. Martin Luther, who in 1523 had written kindly in That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew, wrote in 1543 On the Jews and Their Lies, urging princes to burn synagogues and Jewish schools, destroy Jewish homes, take away their prayer books and forbid rabbis to teach. None of this needed racial theory. It needed only the conviction that the Jews were enemies of God.
sections.key: From Melito's deicide charge (c. 170) and Chrysostom's sermons (386) to the Rhineland massacres (1096), the blood libel, expulsions and Luther's 1543 tract, contempt became violence.

paras: Between 1941 and 1945 Nazi Germany and its helpers murdered about six million Jews. Nazism was not Christian: its antisemitism was racial, it despised Christian morality, and many of its leaders hoped to be rid of the churches. Some Christians risked their lives to hide Jews; Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, honours many of them as 'Righteous Among the Nations'.

But the historian Raul Hilberg, in The Destruction of the European Jews (1961), set out a table showing that many Nazi laws had Church precedents: the ban on marriage between Christians and Jews (Synod of Elvira, about 306), the ban on Jews holding public office (Synod of Clermont, 535), the badge (Fourth Lateran Council, 1215), the compulsory ghetto (Synod of Breslau, 1267). On the night of 9–10 November 1938, Kristallnacht, synagogues burned across Germany. The tenth was Luther's birthday. Martin Sasse, a Lutheran bishop in Thuringia, rushed out a pamphlet of Luther's words on the Jews to celebrate. Most Christians in Germany were silent. The ground had been prepared.
sections.key: Nazism was racial, not Christian, and some Christians hid Jews; but many Nazi measures had Church precedents, and most Christians were silent.

sections.h: Is the fault in the text itself?
paras: The hardest form of the charge is not about bad readers. It is that the texts themselves teach contempt. Rosemary Radford Ruether, a Catholic theologian, argued in Faith and Fratricide (1974) that anti-Judaism was 'the left hand of Christology': that to say Jesus is the Messiah, as the Church said it, was already to say that the Jews who refused him were blind and rejected. If that is right, then repairing the readings is not enough; the claim itself is the problem.

Others point to the shape of the Passion stories. Across the four Gospels, written one after another, the Roman governor becomes steadily more reluctant and the Jewish crowd steadily more guilty: Matthew adds the hand-washing and the cry; John speaks simply of 'the Jews'. Some historians think this was written for Roman readers, by a movement wanting to show Rome it was harmless. And Paul, in his earliest letter, wrote of the Jews 'who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets' (1 Thessalonians 2:14–15). Jewish critics ask a simple question: if a text has been used to kill for sixteen centuries, can it be called innocent?
sections.key: The strongest form of the charge: the texts themselves, not just their readers, teach contempt; to claim Jesus as Messiah already implies the rejection of Jews who refuse him (Ruether).

sections.h: Repentance: the churches side by side
paras: After the Holocaust the churches began to change. In 1947 Christians and Jews meeting at Seelisberg in Switzerland, Jules Isaac among them, drew up ten points for Christian teaching. In 1960 Isaac met Pope John XXIII. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued Nostra Aetate. Its fourth section, in our own words, says that the Church received the Old Testament through the Jewish people and is fed by that root; that what happened in Christ's Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against Jews today; that Jews must not be presented as rejected or accursed by God; and that the Church deplores hatred, persecution and displays of antisemitism against Jews at any time and by anyone.

rows: No collective guilt for Jesus's death; Jews not rejected or accursed; antisemitism deplored

debate.question: Is the problem the text, or its readers?

positions.name: The text itself
positions.who: Rosemary Radford Ruether, Faith and Fratricide (1974); Samuel Sandmel, Anti-Semitism in the New Testament? (1978); many Jewish critics
positions.view: Contempt is woven into the New Testament's central claims and into the shape of its Passion stories. Better reading cannot remove it: the Church must say plainly that some of its Scripture is wrong about the Jews, and rethink how it speaks of Christ as the fulfilment of Israel.
positions.evidence: Matthew 27:25; John 8:44; 1 Thessalonians 2:14–16; the growing blame of 'the Jews' from Mark to John.

positions.name: The readers
positions.who: Luke Timothy Johnson (1989); much Catholic and Protestant scholarship since Nostra Aetate
positions.view: These are the words of Jews arguing with Jews, in the normal harsh style of ancient polemic, the same style the prophets and the Dead Sea Scrolls used about fellow Jews. They became poison when Gentile readers, holding power, heard them as words about another people. The fault lies with those readers.
positions.evidence: John 8:31 (the argument is with believing Jews); John 4:22; the polemic of Qumran and the prophets; Romans 9–11.

positions.name: Both: text and power together
positions.who: Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Brettler, The Jewish Annotated New Testament (2011); James Carroll, Constantine's Sword (2001)
positions.view: The texts contain words that can be, and were, read against Jews; and their meaning changed when a minority's polemic became an empire's teaching. So Christians must both read the texts in their first setting and teach them with care, explaining in sermons and classrooms what these words did and did not mean.
positions.evidence: The change after Constantine; Eusebius's 'divine vengeance'; the Holy Week preaching of the Middle Ages; the churches' later statements.

debate.agree: All agree that these texts were used for centuries to justify contempt and violence towards Jews, that this was a grave evil, and that Christians must read and teach them differently.

look.why: No painting is shown for this session. Many old paintings of the Passion picture Jewish figures in caricature, and the spec for this journey forbids that. Sit with the readings and the history instead.

music.why: Górecki's Symphony of Sorrowful Songs (1976) is a lament of mothers and children. Its second movement sets a prayer an eighteen-year-old girl wrote on the wall of a Gestapo cell in 1944. It is not about the Jews alone, but it is the sound of Europe's grief for what was done there.

think.why: After the Holocaust the world wrote down the dignity of every human being. See how that modern idea grew from, and was betrayed by, Christian Europe.

learn.why: A Jewish prophet's summary of what God asks of everyone: justice, mercy and a humble walk. It judges every contempt.

Use the churches' statements to say what has changed, and end with your own judgement.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: listen for how you, and the people around you, speak about groups you belong to and groups you don't. Each time you catch a contemptuous word about a whole people, stop, and say instead one true and particular thing about a person you know from that group.
sessions.reflect: Is there a group of people you were taught, without anyone quite saying it, to think less of?
takeaways: Matthew 27:25 and John 8:44 come from Jewish arguments with Jews; read later by a powerful Gentile Church, they became a 'teaching of contempt': dispersion as punishment, Judaism as dead, the Jews as 'deicide'.
Contempt became violence, from Chrysostom and the Rhineland massacres to Luther's 1543 tract, and prepared the ground on which the Holocaust was built.
Since 1945 the churches have repented, from Nostra Aetate to the Lutheran repudiation of Luther; whether the fault lies only in the readers or also in the texts remains the hardest question.

sessions.title: Why keep the Old Testament?
sessions.line: A rich shipowner from the Black Sea offers the Church a new Bible without the Jewish Scriptures and a kinder God without the God of Israel. The Church refuses.
sessions.plain: Around AD 140 a Christian called Marcion taught that the God of the Old Testament, the God of the Jews, was a lesser and harsher god than the Father of Jesus. He threw out the Jewish Scriptures and kept only one Gospel and ten letters of Paul, cut to fit. The Church said no: the God of Israel and the Father of Jesus are one God, and the Jewish Scriptures are Christian Scripture too. This session reads the bishop who answered Marcion, and asks what it means for Christians to keep a Bible that is also the Jews' Bible.
sessions.why: Session 5 showed how Christians came to treat Jews with contempt. You might expect the Church to have dropped the Jewish Scriptures too. One man proposed exactly that, and the Church's refusal is one of the most important decisions it ever made. It bound Christians, for good, to the God of Israel, and so, whether they liked it or not, to the Jews.
answers: Why do Christians keep the Old Testament?
Who was Marcion?
Is the God of the Old Testament a different God?
Did the Church replace Israel?
sessions.finding: Marcion cut the Jewish Scriptures out and split the God of Israel from the Father of Jesus; the Church refused, insisting that one God made the world, gave the law and sent Christ, and so kept Israel's Scriptures at the heart of its own Bible, though it often read them against the Jews.

paras: By the middle of the second century the Church was mostly Gentile. The Temple had fallen, the ways were parting, and some Christians were already reading the sufferings of the Jews as God's punishment. Many Gentile Christians knew little of Judaism, and the Jewish Scriptures could seem a strange book: laws about sacrifices they did not offer, food they did not keep, and wars they did not fight.

So a question was in the air. If the Church was not Jewish, why read the Jews' Bible? And if the God of the law commanded wars and punished, while Jesus taught love of enemies, were they really the same God?
background.key: By the mid-second century the Church was mostly Gentile, and some asked: why keep the Jews' Bible, and is its God the Father of Jesus?

paras: Marcion came from Sinope, a port in Pontus on the Black Sea coast of what is now Turkey. Tertullian, who wrote five books against him, says he was a shipowner, and that when he came to Rome around 140 he gave the church there a large gift of 200,000 sesterces. Tertullian's reckoning puts his break with the Roman church in 144; the money was handed back.

Marcion taught that there were two gods. The god of the Jewish Scriptures made the world and gave the law; he was just but harsh, a god of rules and punishments. Jesus revealed another, the good Father, unknown until then, who came to rescue people from the world's maker. Marcion wrote a book called Antitheses, 'Oppositions', setting sayings of the law beside sayings of Jesus to show they could not come from one God. He made his own Bible: one Gospel, a shortened Luke, and ten letters of Paul, cut to remove what tied Jesus to the God of Israel. His churches spread widely and lasted for centuries, especially in Syria.

background.key: Marcion, a shipowner from Pontus, came to Rome around 140 and broke with the church in 144. He taught two gods and made a Bible without the Jewish Scriptures.

paras: Irenaeus grew up in Smyrna (modern İzmir) in Asia Minor, where as a boy he heard Polycarp, a bishop who had known John the apostle. He moved to Gaul, and around 177 became bishop of Lyon, after the church there had been persecuted. About 180 he wrote a long work in Greek, usually called Against Heresies, attacking the many teachers, Marcion among them, who said the world's maker was not the true God. It survives mainly in an early Latin translation. The English is by Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (1885).

Irenaeus is the first writer to set out a full Christian Bible of two parts, and the first to insist that there are exactly four Gospels (Against Heresies III.11.8). His great idea is that one God works through all of history, from Adam through Abraham and Moses to Christ, in one plan.
background.key: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, who as a boy heard Polycarp, wrote Against Heresies about 180: one God, one plan, from Adam to Christ.

paras: The main reading has three parts from Irenaeus: his description of Marcion (I.27), his answer that the apostles preached one God who gave both the law and the gospel (III.12.11–12), and his argument from the apostles' own Jewish practice (III.12.15), which takes us back to Peter, Cornelius and James.

The comparison is from Justin Martyr, a Gentile philosopher who became a Christian, writing about 155. He explains why the Church reads the Jewish prophets: they foretold Christ. His words show the other side of keeping the Old Testament: keeping it, but saying the Jews could not understand it.
background.key: Irenaeus answers Marcion: one God gave law and gospel. Justin shows the Church claiming the prophets, and saying the Jews could not read them.
