sessions.readWhy: The bishop who answered Marcion: why the Church refused to cut the Jewish Scriptures out of its Bible, or to cut the God of Israel off from the Father of Jesus.

paras: 1. Cerdo was one who took his system from the followers of Simon, and came to live at Rome in the time of Hyginus, who held the ninth place in the episcopal succession from the apostles downwards. He taught that the God proclaimed by the law and the prophets was not the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the former was known, but the latter unknown; while the one also was righteous, but the other benevolent.

2. Marcion of Pontus succeeded him, and developed his doctrine. In so doing, he advanced the most daring blasphemy against Him who is proclaimed as God by the law and the prophets, declaring Him to be the author of evils, to take delight in war, to be infirm of purpose, and even to be contrary to Himself. But Jesus being derived from that father who is above the God that made the world, and coming into Judæa in the times of Pontius Pilate the governor, who was the procurator of Tiberius Cæsar, was manifested in the form of a man to those who were in Judæa, abolishing the prophets and the law, and all the works of that God who made the world, whom also he calls Cosmocrator. Besides this, he mutilates the Gospel which is according to Luke, removing all that is written respecting the generation of the Lord, and setting aside a great deal of the teaching of the Lord, in which the Lord is recorded as most dearly confessing that the Maker of this universe is His Father. He likewise persuaded his disciples that he himself was more worthy of credit than are those apostles who have handed down the Gospel to us, furnishing them not with the Gospel, but merely a fragment of it. In like manner, too, he dismembered the Epistles of Paul, removing all that is said by the apostle respecting that God who made the world, to the effect that He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also those passages from the prophetical writings which the apostle quotes, in order to teach us that they announced beforehand the coming of the Lord.

11. And that the whole range of the doctrine of the apostles proclaimed one and the same God, who removed Abraham, who made to him the promise of inheritance, who in due season gave to him the covenant of circumcision, who called his descendants out of Egypt, preserved outwardly by circumcision— for he gave it as a sign, that they might not be like the Egyptians — that He was the Maker of all things, that He was the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that He was the God of glory — they who wish may learn from the very words and acts of the apostles, and may contemplate the fact that this God is one, above whom is no other. But even if there were another god above Him, we should say, upon [instituting] a comparison of the quantity [of the work done by each], that the latter is superior to the former. For by deeds the better man appears, as I have already remarked;

and, inasmuch as these men have no works of their father to adduce, the latter is shown to be God alone. But if any one, doting about questions, do imagine that what the apostles have declared about God should be allegorized, let him consider my previous statements, in which I set forth one God as the Founder and Maker of all things, and destroyed and laid bare their allegations; and he shall find them agreeable to the doctrine of the apostles, and so to maintain what they used to teach, and were persuaded of, that there is one God, the Maker of all things. And when he shall have divested his mind of such error, and of that blasphemy against God which it implies, he will of himself find reason to acknowledge that both the Mosaic law and the grace of the new covenant, as both fitted for the times [at which they were given], were bestowed by one and the same God for the benefit of the human race.

12. For all those who are of a perverse mind, having been set against the Mosaic legislation, judging it to be dissimilar and contrary to the doctrine of the Gospel, have not applied themselves to investigate the causes of the difference of each covenant. Since, therefore, they have been deserted by the paternal love, and puffed up by Satan, being brought over to the doctrine of Simon Magus, they have apostatized in their opinions from Him who is God, and imagined that they have themselves discovered more than the apostles, by finding out another god; and [maintained] that the apostles preached the Gospel still somewhat under the influence of Jewish opinions, but that they themselves are purer [in doctrine], and more intelligent, than the apostles. Wherefore also Marcion and his followers have betaken themselves to mutilating the Scriptures, not acknowledging some books at all; and, curtailing the Gospel according to Luke and the Epistles of Paul, they assert that these are alone authentic, which they have themselves thus shortened. In another work, however, I shall, God granting [me strength], refute them out of these which they still retain.

But all the rest, inflated with the false name of knowledge, do certainly recognise the Scriptures; but they pervert the interpretations, as I have shown in the first book. And, indeed, the followers of Marcion do directly blaspheme the Creator, alleging him to be the creator of evils, [but] holding a more tolerable theory as to his origin, [and] maintaining that there are two beings, gods by nature, differing from each other — the one being good, but the other evil. Those from Valentinus, however, while they employ names of a more honourable kind, and set forth that He who is Creator is both Father, and Lord, and God, do [nevertheless] render their theory or sect more blasphemous, by maintaining that He was not produced from any one of those Æons within the Pleroma, but from that defect which had been expelled beyond the Pleroma. Ignorance of the Scriptures and of the dispensation of God has brought all these things upon them. And in the course of this work I shall touch upon the cause of the difference of the covenants on the one hand, and, on the other hand, of their unity and harmony.

15. Neither [in that case] would they have had such a tenor with regard to the first covenant, as not even to have been willing to eat with the Gentiles. For even Peter, although he had been sent to instruct them, and had been constrained by a vision to that effect, spoke nevertheless with not a little hesitation, saying to them: You know how it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company with, or to come unto, one of another nation; but God has shown me that I should not call any man common or unclean. Therefore came I without gainsaying; indicating by these words, that he would not have come to them unless he had been commanded. Neither, for a like reason, would he have given them baptism so readily, had he not heard them prophesying when the Holy Ghost rested upon them. And therefore did he exclaim, Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, who have received the Holy Ghost as well as we? He persuaded, at the same time, those that were with him, and pointed out that, unless the Holy Ghost had rested upon them, there might have been some one who would have raised objections to their baptism.

And the apostles who were with James allowed the Gentiles to act freely, yielding us up to the Spirit of God. But they themselves, while knowing the same God, continued in the ancient observances; so that even Peter, fearing also lest he might incur their reproof, although formerly eating with the Gentiles, because of the vision, and of the Spirit who had rested upon them, yet, when certain persons came from James, withdrew himself, and did not eat with them. And Paul said that Barnabas likewise did the same thing. Thus did the apostles, whom the Lord made witnesses of every action and of every doctrine — for upon all occasions do we find Peter, and James, and John present with Him — scrupulously act according to the dispensation of the Mosaic law, showing that it was from one and the same God; which they certainly never would have done, as I have already said, if they had learned from the Lord [that there existed] another Father besides Him who appointed the dispensation of the law.

parts.author: Irenaeus of Lyon
parts.translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)
parts.title: Cerdo and Marcion
parts.context: Lyon, about 180. In Book I Irenaeus describes, one by one, the teachers he opposes. Cerdo was a Syrian teacher in Rome in the 130s; Hyginus was bishop of Rome around 138–142. 'Simon' is Simon Magus, the magician of Acts 8, whom Irenaeus treats as the father of all such teachers. Translated by Roberts and Rambaut (1885).
parts.plain: Irenaeus says a teacher called Cerdo taught that the God of the law and the prophets was not the Father of Jesus: the first was known and just, the second unknown and kind. Marcion took this further. He called the God of the Old Testament the author of evil, a lover of war, changeable and self-contradictory. He taught that Jesus came from a higher Father to abolish the law and the prophets. He cut down Luke's Gospel and Paul's letters, removing everything that linked Jesus to the God who made the world.

commentary.on: He taught that the God proclaimed by the law and the prophets was not the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
commentary.text: This is the whole question in one sentence. 'The law and the prophets' was the Jewish name for the Scriptures (Matthew 7:12). To separate their God from Jesus's Father was to separate Christianity from Israel at the root.

commentary.on: the one also was righteous, but the other benevolent
commentary.text: 'Righteous' here means strictly just, giving each what they deserve; 'benevolent' means kind and loving. The contrast is still common: 'the angry God of the Old Testament and the loving God of the New'. Hearing it here, you are hearing Cerdo and Marcion.

commentary.on: declaring Him to be the author of evils, to take delight in war, to be infirm of purpose, and even to be contrary to Himself
commentary.text: Marcion read the Scriptures closely and found real problems: God hardening Pharaoh's heart, commanding wars of conquest, regretting that he made humanity (Genesis 6:6), 'I create calamity' (Isaiah 45:7). These passages still trouble readers. Marcion's answer was that they describe a lesser god. 'Infirm of purpose' means changeable.

commentary.on: abolishing the prophets and the law
commentary.text: Compare Jesus in Matthew 5:17: 'Don't think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn't come to destroy, but to fulfil.' Marcion had no Matthew in his Bible.

commentary.on: removing all that is written respecting the generation of the Lord
commentary.text: Marcion's Luke began with Jesus appearing, already grown, at Capernaum. He removed the birth stories, and with them the passage you read in session 1: the circumcision on the eighth day, the Temple, Simeon and Anna, Passover at twelve. Marcion's Jesus was not a Jew.

commentary.on: he dismembered the Epistles of Paul
commentary.text: Marcion loved Paul, whom he took as the one true apostle of grace against the law. But he cut out Paul's quotations from the prophets and his passages about Abraham. Tertullian says his version of Romans lacked much of chapters 9–11. A Paul without Israel needed a great deal of cutting.

parts.author: Irenaeus of Lyon
parts.translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)
parts.title: One God, two covenants
parts.context: In Book III Irenaeus answers from the apostles' own words. He has just gone through the speeches in Acts, to show that Peter, Stephen and Paul all preached the God of Abraham and Moses. Words in square brackets are the translators'; a New Advent Bible reference has been removed. 'Valentinus' was another teacher in Rome; 'the Pleroma' and 'Æons' are terms from his system for the heavenly world.
parts.plain: Irenaeus says the apostles preached one God: the God who called Abraham, gave him circumcision, brought Israel out of Egypt, made all things and is the Father of Jesus. The law of Moses and the grace of the new covenant were both given by this one God, each suited to its time. Marcion's followers think they understand more than the apostles, and that the apostles were still half Jewish in their thinking; so they cut the Scriptures down. Irenaeus promises to explain both why the covenants differ and how they belong together.

commentary.on: proclaimed one and the same God, who removed Abraham
commentary.text: 'Removed' means moved Abraham from his homeland (Genesis 12:1). Irenaeus lists God's acts in Israel's story, Abraham, circumcision, the exodus, and says they are the acts of the Father of Jesus. The God of the Church has a history, and it is Israel's history.

commentary.on: both the Mosaic law and the grace of the new covenant, as both fitted for the times [at which they were given], were bestowed by one and the same God for the benefit of the human race
commentary.text: This is Irenaeus's answer to Marcion's 'antitheses'. Law and gospel are different, but the difference is one of time, not of gods: one God teaching humanity step by step, as a parent teaches a growing child. Irenaeus elsewhere says Christ 'recapitulated', summed up and renewed, the whole of human history in himself (III.18.1).

commentary.on: that the apostles preached the Gospel still somewhat under the influence of Jewish opinions
commentary.text: Marcion's claim, as Irenaeus reports it, was that the apostles were too Jewish and had misunderstood Jesus. It is a striking charge: Marcion saw clearly that the apostles were Jews, and thought that was the problem. Irenaeus thought it was the guarantee.

commentary.on: Wherefore also Marcion and his followers have betaken themselves to mutilating the Scriptures
commentary.text: Irenaeus's point is that Marcion had to cut the texts to make them fit. A Bible that has to be cut to support a teaching is evidence against the teaching.

commentary.on: the cause of the difference of the covenants on the one hand, and, on the other hand, of their unity and harmony
commentary.text: Here is the Church's position in one phrase: the covenants are different, and they are one. Holding both halves together has never been easy, and when Christians stressed the difference alone they slid towards contempt for the first covenant and its people.

parts.author: Irenaeus of Lyon
parts.translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)
parts.title: The apostles kept the law
parts.context: Irenaeus now argues from what the apostles did. He retells Peter's visit to Cornelius (Acts 10) and the quarrel at Antioch, when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles after 'certain persons came from James' (Galatians 2:12). The cut is marked '…'; New Advent's Bible references have been removed.
parts.plain: If the apostles had believed in another god, they would not have been so careful to keep the law of Moses. Peter only went to Cornelius because a vision made him, and only baptised the Gentiles because the Spirit came on them. The apostles with James let the Gentiles go free, but they themselves kept the old customs; even Peter drew back from eating with Gentiles when James's people came. So the apostles, who knew Jesus best, kept the law, which proves that the law came from the same God as the gospel.

commentary.on: For even Peter, although he had been sent to instruct them, and had been constrained by a vision
commentary.text: You read this story in session 3. Irenaeus uses Peter's reluctance as evidence: a man who had to be 'constrained by a vision' to enter a Gentile's house had not been taught by Jesus that the law was the work of a lesser god.

commentary.on: But they themselves, while knowing the same God, continued in the ancient observances
commentary.text: Irenaeus, writing about 180, still knows and says plainly what session 2 showed: the apostles in Jerusalem went on keeping the law. He does not treat it as a weakness. For him their Jewish practice proves the unity of God.

commentary.on: scrupulously act according to the dispensation of the Mosaic law, showing that it was from one and the same God
commentary.text: 'Dispensation' means an ordered arrangement, a stage in God's plan. Irenaeus's argument cuts two ways. It defends the Jewish Scriptures against Marcion. But it also places the law in a stage that has passed, which later Christians would turn into the claim that the Church had replaced Israel.

read.author: Irenaeus of Lyon
read.translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)

paras: There were, then, among the Jews certain men who were prophets of God, through whom the prophetic Spirit published beforehand things that were to come to pass, ere ever they happened. And their prophecies, as they were spoken and when they were uttered, the kings who happened to be reigning among the Jews at the several times carefully preserved in their possession, when they had been arranged in books by the prophets themselves in their own Hebrew language. And when Ptolemy king of Egypt formed a library, and endeavoured to collect the writings of all men, he heard also of these prophets, and sent to Herod, who was at that time king of the Jews, requesting that the books of the prophets be sent to him. And Herod the king did indeed send them, written, as they were, in the foresaid Hebrew language. And when their contents were found to be unintelligible to the Egyptians, he again sent and requested that men be commissioned to translate them into the Greek language. And when this was done, the books remained with the Egyptians, where they are until now. They are also in the possession of all Jews throughout the world;

but they, though they read, do not understand what is said, but count us foes and enemies; and, like yourselves, they kill and punish us whenever they have the power, as you can well believe. For in the Jewish war which lately raged, Barchochebas, the leader of the revolt of the Jews, gave orders that Christians alone should be led to cruel punishments, unless they would deny Jesus Christ and utter blasphemy. In these books, then, of the prophets we found Jesus our Christ foretold as coming, born of a virgin, growing up to man's estate, and healing every disease and every sickness, and raising the dead, and being hated, and unrecognised, and crucified, and dying, and rising again, and ascending into heaven, and being, and being called, the Son of God. We find it also predicted that certain persons should be sent by Him into every nation to publish these things, and that rather among the Gentiles [than among the Jews] men should believe in Him. And He was predicted before He appeared, first 5000 years before, and again 3000, then 2000, then 1000, and yet again 800; for in the succession of generations prophets after prophets arose.

parts.author: Justin Martyr
parts.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)
parts.title: The Hebrew prophets
parts.context: Rome, about 155. Justin, born about 100 at Flavia Neapolis (modern Nablus) in Samaria, was a Gentile who studied philosophy and became a Christian. He addressed his First Apology, a defence of Christians, to the emperor Antoninus Pius. He was executed in Rome about 165. Translated by Marcus Dods and George Reith (1885).
parts.plain: Justin says God sent prophets among the Jews, whose books were kept by the Jewish kings in Hebrew. A king of Egypt asked for them for his library, and had them translated into Greek. All Jews have these books, but, he says, they read them without understanding, and treat Christians as enemies: in the recent war their leader Bar Kokhba punished Christians who would not deny Jesus. In these books, Justin says, Christians find Jesus foretold: his birth, healings, death, rising, and the spread of faith among the Gentiles.

commentary.on: There were, then, among the Jews certain men who were prophets of God
commentary.text: Justin starts from common ground. He does not deny that the prophets were Jews or that their God was the true God. Unlike Marcion, whom he also attacked (First Apology 26), Justin needs the Jewish Scriptures: they are his main evidence that Christianity is not a new invention.

commentary.on: And when Ptolemy king of Egypt formed a library
commentary.text: Justin is retelling the story of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Jewish Scriptures made in Alexandria from about 280 BC. But he has his kings wrong: Ptolemy II reigned about 285–246 BC, and Herod the Great, to whom Justin says he wrote, about 37–4 BC. The older Letter of Aristeas says Ptolemy wrote to the high priest Eleazar. The early Church read the Old Testament mostly in this Greek version, which is why Christians and Jews sometimes quote different wording.

commentary.on: They are also in the possession of all Jews throughout the world; but they, though they read, do not understand what is said
commentary.text: Here is the turn. The books belong to the Jews, Justin admits, but only Christians understand them. This claim, that the Jews are blind to the meaning of their own Scriptures, became standard. Medieval cathedrals carved it in stone as two women: the Church, crowned, and the Synagogue, blindfolded, as at Strasbourg.

commentary.on: Barchochebas, the leader of the revolt of the Jews, gave orders that Christians alone should be led to cruel punishments
commentary.text: Justin is writing about twenty years after the Bar Kokhba war of 132–135, which you met in session 4. His report is one of the earliest pieces of evidence that the revolt was a breaking point: Jewish believers in Jesus could not accept Bar Kokhba as messiah, and they suffered for it.

commentary.on: In these books, then, of the prophets we found Jesus our Christ foretold
commentary.text: This is why the Church kept the Old Testament: it read the whole of it as pointing to Christ, as the Gospels do (Luke 24:27). Jews have always read the same books differently, as the story of God's covenant with Israel lived out in the Torah. Both readings are ancient, and both are serious.

commentary.on: rather among the Gentiles [than among the Jews] men should believe in Him
commentary.text: By Justin's day this was simply a fact: the Church was mostly Gentile. Justin reads it as foretold. Paul, as we will read in the final session, had felt the same fact as 'great sorrow and unceasing pain'.

compare.author: Justin Martyr
compare.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, 1885)
compare.why: Justin Martyr, writing about 155, explains to the emperor why Christians read the Jewish prophets. He keeps the Old Testament, as Irenaeus will; but in the same breath he says that the Jews read it without understanding. This is how the Church kept the Jews' Scriptures while turning them against the Jews.
compare.title: Who owns the prophets?

paras: Marcion was not a fool, and his question has never gone away. He noticed things in the Jewish Scriptures that trouble readers still: the conquest of Canaan, God's anger, laws that seem harsh. He noticed that Paul set grace against the law. He thought Jesus's love of enemies could not come from the same God who ordered Israel's wars. So he made a clean solution: two gods, two books, no contradiction.

He was also, so far as we know, the first Christian to draw up a fixed list of books, a 'canon' (from the Greek for a measuring rod). The great German historian Adolf von Harnack argued in 1921 that Marcion forced the Church to define its own New Testament. Most scholars now think the Church was already reading the four Gospels and Paul, and that Marcion sped up a process rather than starting it. Either way, he made the Church say clearly what its Bible was.
sections.key: Marcion saw real difficulties in the Jewish Scriptures and solved them with two gods and a cut-down Bible. He was the first to fix a list of books.

paras: The Church's answer, given by Justin, Irenaeus and Tertullian, had four parts. First, there is one God, maker of heaven and earth, and he is the Father of Jesus; to say otherwise splits creation from salvation and makes the world the work of an enemy. Second, Jesus and the apostles were Jews who prayed to the God of Israel and read his Scriptures as God's word; to cut them out is to cut out Jesus himself, as Marcion's shortened Luke showed. Third, the Scriptures make one story: the God who called Abraham keeps his promises in Christ. Fourth, the hard passages are real, but they belong to a God teaching people over time, not to a second god.

The decision shaped everything. The creeds begin with 'one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth'. About 170 Melito of Sardis gave the first Christian list of 'the books of the old covenant' (Eusebius, Church History IV.26.14), and the name 'Old Testament' was born. Christians did not keep the Jewish Scriptures as a historical appendix. They made them more than half their Bible.
sections.key: The Church said: one God made the world and sent Christ; Jesus and the apostles were Jews; the Scriptures are one story. So it kept the Jewish Scriptures as most of its Bible.

paras: Justin also wrote the first surviving Christian book addressed to a Jew, the Dialogue with Trypho, about 160. Its text is not among this journey's set texts, so here it is in our own words. Justin begins by telling how he went from one school of philosophy to another, until an old man by the sea told him to read the Hebrew prophets, who had seen the truth before the philosophers (chapters 1–8). Trypho, a Jew who says he has fled the recent war, listens politely and replies that Justin would have done better to stay with Plato than trust in a man.

Over two days they argue, mostly about Scripture: whether the prophets foretold a suffering Messiah, whether the law still binds, whether Gentiles can be God's people. Justin can be harsh: he says the Jews' sufferings in the war were deserved (chapter 16) and that the law was given because of their hardness of heart. Yet the two part as friends, and Trypho says he has enjoyed the conversation. The Dialogue shows both things at once: Christians and Jews still talking, and the Church claiming the Jewish Scriptures for itself.
sections.key: Justin's Dialogue with Trypho (c. 160) is the first Christian book addressed to a Jew: a courteous argument over the same Scriptures, with harsh claims on Justin's side.

paras: Keeping the Jewish Scriptures did not mean keeping them in the same form. Jews and Christians, and Christians among themselves, came to arrange them differently. You met the history of the canon in 'What is the Bible?'; here is how the arrangements compare.

rows: 24 books in three parts: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets), Ketuvim (Writings); in Hebrew
With Chronicles: the call to return to Jerusalem and build the Temple
46 books: the Hebrew books plus Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and longer Esther and Daniel, from the Greek Bible
With Malachi: Elijah will come before the day of the Lord
The Catholic books plus others from the Greek Bible, such as 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh and Psalm 151
With the prophets, in the Greek order
39 books: the same contents as the Hebrew Bible, in the Christian order
table.note: The order matters. The Jewish Bible ends looking back to Jerusalem; the Christian Old Testament ends looking forward to one who will come.

sections.key: Jews and Christians keep the same Hebrew books, but arranged differently; Catholics and Orthodox add books from the Greek Bible. The Christian order ends looking forward.

paras: Marcion's churches died out, but his idea did not. In 1921 Harnack, the most famous church historian of his day, argued in our own words that the Church had been right to keep the Old Testament in the second century, that the Reformers could not have dropped it in the sixteenth, but that for Protestants still to treat it as Scripture in the twentieth was a sign of paralysis. He meant it as liberal religion, not hatred. Others took it further.

In November 1933, at a rally of the 'German Christians', the pro-Nazi movement in the Protestant church, held in the Berlin Sportpalast, a speaker demanded that the Church be freed from the Old Testament and its 'Jewish' morality; the crowd cheered. In 1939 an 'Institute for the Study and Elimination of Jewish Influence on German Church Life' was founded at Eisenach, and it published a New Testament with Jewish names and Old Testament quotations removed. Cutting out the Jewish Scriptures and cutting off the Jews had gone together. The Confessing Church, the Protestants who resisted, held on to the Old Testament as God's word.
sections.key: Harnack (1921) said Protestants should drop the Old Testament; the pro-Nazi 'German Christians' tried to, and an institute 'de-Judaised' the New Testament. Marcion's idea and contempt for Jews travelled together.

sections.h: Keeping the book, replacing the people?
paras: Here is the irony. The Church refused to throw out Israel's Scriptures, but it often read them as if Israel itself had been thrown out. This view is called supersessionism, from the Latin for 'to sit on top of', or replacement theology: the Church has taken Israel's place as God's people, and the Jews' covenant is over.

The theologian R. Kendall Soulen, in The God of Israel and Christian Theology (1996), distinguishes three forms. In 'economic' supersessionism, Israel's role was always meant to end when Christ came, as scaffolding is taken down when a building is finished. In 'punitive' supersessionism, God rejected Israel as punishment for rejecting Christ, as Eusebius thought. In 'structural' supersessionism, Christians tell the Bible's story, creation, fall, Christ, end, in a way that leaves Israel out of the middle altogether. Critics say all three betray Paul and the God who keeps promises. Defenders of a careful 'fulfilment' view reply that some claim of newness is built into Christian faith itself: the Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the first covenant as 'old' (Hebrews 8:13). How to say that Christ fulfils Israel's hope without saying that Israel is finished is the question of the final session.
sections.key: The Church kept Israel's book but often taught that it had replaced Israel's people: supersessionism, in economic, punitive and structural forms (Soulen, 1996).

refs: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.27.1–2; III.11.8; III.12.11–15; III.18.1, tr. Roberts and Rambaut (1885). Justin Martyr, First Apology 26, 31, tr. Dods and Reith (1885); Dialogue with Trypho 1–8, 16, 142 (summarised in our own words). Tertullian, Against Marcion I.19; Prescription against Heretics 30. Eusebius, Church History IV.26.14 (Melito's list). The Letter of Aristeas.
Genesis 6:6; 12:1; Isaiah 45:7; Matthew 5:17; 7:12; Luke 24:27; Galatians 2:12; Hebrews 8:13.

Adolf von Harnack, Marcion: Das Evangelium vom fremden Gott (1921; English, Marcion: The Gospel of the Alien God, 1990). Susannah Heschel, The Aryan Jesus: Christian Theologians and the Bible in Nazi Germany (2008). R. Kendall Soulen, The God of Israel and Christian Theology (1996). Judith Lieu, Marcion and the Making of a Heretic (2015). John Barton, Holy Writings, Sacred Text (1997). Summarised in our own words.

debate.question: When Christians kept the Jewish Scriptures, did they keep them, or take them?

positions.name: Kept: one story of one God
positions.who: Irenaeus; the creeds; Brevard Childs, Biblical Theology of the Old and New Testaments (1992); most Christian traditions
positions.view: The Church kept the Scriptures it had always had, the Bible of Jesus and the apostles. Reading them as pointing to Christ is not theft but faithfulness to how Jesus himself read them. Without them Christianity would be a different religion, as Marcion's was.
positions.evidence: Luke 24:27; the apostles' preaching in Acts; Irenaeus's case that Marcion had to cut the texts.

positions.name: Taken: a different book under the same cover
positions.who: Jon D. Levenson, The Hebrew Bible, the Old Testament, and Historical Criticism (1993); many Jewish scholars
positions.view: The 'Old Testament' is not simply the Hebrew Bible. Christians rearranged it, read it through the New Testament, and for centuries told the Jews they could not understand their own book. Jews read the same texts through the oral Torah and the rabbis. Neither tradition reads the text 'plainly', and Christians should not pretend their reading is the obvious one.
positions.evidence: The different order and endings; Justin's 'they do not understand'; the blindfolded Synagogue of medieval art.

positions.name: Two readings of one book, both serious
positions.who: Pontifical Biblical Commission, The Jewish People and Their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible (2001)
positions.view: Christians read the Scriptures in the light of Christ, and believe that light is true. But they can and should grant that the Jewish reading, which grew from the same texts in the same way, is a possible one, and they can learn from it.
positions.evidence: The shared origins of Jewish and Christian reading in Second Temple Judaism; the commission's own argument, summarised in our own words.

debate.agree: All agree that the Church's refusal to follow Marcion tied Christianity for ever to the God and Scriptures of Israel, and that the way Christians read those Scriptures shaped how they treated Jews.

look.why: No free painting of the Old Testament prophets is left in the gallery's open collection; the ones there are used elsewhere in Rose Window. Hold in mind instead Marcion's shortened Luke, which began with no birth, no circumcision and no Temple.

music.why: Mendelssohn, grandson of the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn and baptised a Lutheran as a child, set the story of Elijah, a prophet honoured by Jews and Christians alike, for a Christian audience in Birmingham in 1846. The Old Testament sung by one who belonged to both.

think.why: Marcion solved the problem of evil by splitting God in two. See how the great teachers answered it without that.

learn.why: The new covenant, promised in the Old Testament to 'the house of Israel': the one God writing his law on the heart.

check.q: Why did Marcion have to cut down Luke's Gospel and Paul's letters?
options: Because the bishop of Rome ordered it
Because they were too long to copy
Because, as written, they tie Jesus and Paul to the God of Israel and his Scriptures, which his two-god teaching could not allow
Because they were written in Hebrew
check.why: Irenaeus's point: a teaching that needs the texts cut to fit is suspect.

check.q: How does Irenaeus explain the difference between the law of Moses and the new covenant?
options: They come from two different gods
One God gave both, each suited to its time, teaching humanity step by step
The law was given only to Gentiles
The law was a mistake that God corrected
check.why: 'Both fitted for the times… bestowed by one and the same God.'

check.q: What is Irenaeus's argument from the apostles' practice in III.12.15?
options: That James was a follower of Marcion
That the apostles kept the law of Moses, which they would not have done had Jesus taught that it came from a lesser god
That the apostles gave up the law at once
That Peter refused to visit Cornelius
check.why: He uses Peter's reluctance and the Jerusalem church's observance as evidence for one God.

check.q: Justin says the Jews 'though they read, do not understand' their Scriptures. How does this differ from Marcion's view?
options: Marcion praised the Jews' reading
It is the same view
Justin rejects the prophets
Justin keeps the Jewish Scriptures as true and God-given but claims that only Christians understand them; Marcion rejected them as the work of a lesser god
check.why: Both views harmed Jews in different ways: Marcion by cutting their God off, Justin by claiming their book.

check.q: Which of these is an example of what Soulen calls 'punitive' supersessionism?
options: Saying God's gifts to Israel are irrevocable
Saying that God rejected Israel as a punishment for rejecting Christ, as Eusebius did
Saying that Israel's role was always meant to end when Christ came
Telling the Bible's story without mentioning Israel
check.why: Economic is the second option, structural the first; the fourth is Paul's view, against supersessionism.

check.q: Why is the history of the 'German Christians' and the Eisenach institute relevant to Marcion?
options: Because they were Marcion's direct descendants
Because it shows that removing the Jewish Scriptures from Christianity and contempt for Jews have travelled together
Because they defended the Old Testament
Because they wrote the Septuagint
check.why: In 1933 and 1939 the call to drop the Old Testament was part of a programme against the Jews; the Confessing Church held on to it.

tutorial.question: 'Marcion was more honest than the Church: if Christians think the Jews' covenant is over, they should give the Jews back their Bible.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: State Marcion's view and its appeal fairly. Give Irenaeus's answer from the one God and from the apostles' practice. Then face the charge with Justin and with supersessionism: did the Church keep the book while rejecting the people? End with what it would mean to keep the Old Testament without replacing Israel.
strong: States Marcion's two gods and cut-down Bible accurately, from Irenaeus I.27.
Gives Irenaeus's case: one God, two covenants fitted to their times, and the apostles' practice.
Uses Justin to show how the Church claimed the prophets while denying Jews understood them.
Explains supersessionism with at least two of Soulen's forms.
Uses the modern history (Harnack; the German Christians) with care.
Reaches a reasoned judgement on whether keeping the book requires replacing the people.

reading.author: Judith Lieu
reading.title: Marcion and the Making of a Heretic
reading.why: The best modern study of Marcion and what his opponents made of him.

reading.author: R. Kendall Soulen
reading.title: The God of Israel and Christian Theology
reading.why: The classic analysis of supersessionism and how to move beyond it.

reading.author: Susannah Heschel
reading.title: The Aryan Jesus
reading.why: How Nazi-era theologians tried to remove the Jewishness from Jesus and the Bible.

reading.author: John Barton
reading.title: A History of the Bible
reading.why: How Jews and Christians came to have the Bibles they have.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each day read one chapter of the Old Testament you have never read before, and note one thing it shows you about God that the New Testament takes for granted.
sessions.reflect: Have you ever thought of 'the God of the Old Testament' as a different God from the God of Jesus? What would change if they are one?
takeaways: Marcion (in Rome c. 140–144) taught that the God of the Jewish Scriptures was a lesser god and made a Bible without them; the Church refused.
Irenaeus answered that one God gave both law and gospel, each fitted to its time, and that the apostles themselves kept the law; so the Jewish Scriptures became most of the Christian Bible.
Yet the Church often kept the book while teaching that it had replaced the people: Justin's 'they do not understand', and supersessionism in its several forms.

sessions.title: One olive tree: the verdict
sessions.line: Paul, a Jew writing to Gentile Christians in Rome, refuses to say that God has rejected Israel: 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable'.
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict. Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, was asked the question this whole journey has followed: if most Jews did not accept Jesus, has God rejected them? His answer, in Romans 9–11, is no. Israel is the olive tree; Gentile believers are wild branches grafted in, who must not boast, because the root supports them. Today, after centuries of contempt, Jews and Christians are learning to read the same Scriptures as two branches of one root, still disagreeing about Jesus, but no longer as enemies.
sessions.why: The journey has followed one tree. Session 1 found its root in Jesus the Jew; sessions 2 and 3 the first Jewish church and the grafting in of Gentiles; session 4 the Temple's fall and the parting; session 5 the contempt that grew from it; session 6 the Church keeping Israel's Scriptures but often rejecting Israel. Now we return to the picture we began with, in the words of the one who drew it, and ask what it means for Jews and Christians today.
answers: Has God rejected the Jews?
Why don't Jews believe Jesus was the Messiah?
What do Jews and Christians think of each other today?
Who are Messianic Jews?
sessions.finding: Paul refused to say that God had rejected Israel: 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable'. Gentile Christians are wild branches grafted into Israel's tree and must not boast; and today, after centuries of contempt, Jews and Christians are learning to read the same Scriptures as two branches of one root, while still disagreeing about Jesus.

paras: Christianity grew out of Judaism. Jesus was a Jew; his first followers were Jews; the first great argument was about letting Gentiles in. The ways parted slowly, above all after the Temple fell in 70 and the second revolt failed in 135, as each community rebuilt itself around a different centre: the Torah, or Christ. In the centuries that followed, the stronger branch taught contempt for the other, and that contempt helped prepare the ground for the Holocaust.

Yet the oldest Christian answer to the question 'has God rejected Israel?' is the one Paul gave, before the Temple fell and before any of this happened: no. He wrote it in the letter that Christians have read more closely than any other. This session reads it.
background.key: Christianity grew from Judaism, parted slowly, and turned to contempt; but Paul's own answer to 'has God rejected Israel?' was no.

background.h: Paul and his letter to Rome
paras: Paul wrote to the Christians in Rome in about 57, from Corinth, just before the journey to Jerusalem where James met him, as you read in session 2. He had never been to Rome. The church there had Jewish and Gentile members, and it may have had a hard history: the Roman writer Suetonius says the emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome, about 49, because of disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus' (Claudius 25.4), which many scholars take to be a garbled reference to arguments about Christ. If Jewish believers were later allowed back, they may have found Gentile believers in charge, and some Gentiles inclined to look down on them.

Chapters 9–11 are Paul's answer to the question his message raised: if Jesus is Israel's Messiah, why have most of Israel not believed, and what does that say about God's faithfulness? He was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin (Romans 11:1), and the question was personal.

timeline.text: Claudius expels Jews from Rome; the Jerusalem meeting
Paul writes to the Romans from Corinth
Paul visits James in Jerusalem and is arrested in the Temple
Paul dies in Rome, by tradition under Nero
Nostra Aetate quotes Romans 11:28–29
Dabru Emet: a Jewish statement on Christians and Christianity
The Vatican's 'The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable'; an Orthodox rabbis' statement on Christianity

background.key: Paul wrote Romans about 57, to a mixed church where some Gentiles may have looked down on Jews. Chapters 9–11 ask whether God has been faithful to Israel.

paras: Paul's picture comes from farming. An olive tree lives for centuries, and its root and trunk can go on producing new growth long after branches have died. Farmers improve trees by grafting: cutting a branch from one tree and setting it into a slit in another, where it grows as part of the new tree.

Normally a farmer grafts a good, cultivated branch onto wild stock. Paul describes the opposite, wild branches grafted into a cultivated tree, and he knows it: he calls it 'contrary to nature' (Romans 11:24). The Roman writer on farming Columella mentions grafting a wild olive slip into an old tree to give it new life (On Agriculture V.9.16), so Paul may have known that practice too. Either way, the point is the same: the Gentile branch did nothing to deserve its place, and it lives from a root that is not its own.
background.key: Farmers graft cultivated branches onto wild stock; Paul pictures wild branches grafted into a cultivated tree, 'contrary to nature'. The grafted branch lives from a root not its own.

paras: The main reading has three parts: Paul's grief for his people (Romans 9:1–5), the olive tree (Romans 11:11–24), and his conclusion that 'all Israel will be saved' because God's gifts and calling cannot be taken back (Romans 11:25–36).

The comparison is from the prophet Zechariah, about 520 BC: a picture of the nations coming to Israel's God, holding on to the garment of a Jew. It shows the hope the first Jewish believers had, and that Jews and Christians still share.
background.key: Romans 9 and 11 give Paul's verdict on Israel; Zechariah 8 shows the shared hope of the nations coming to Israel's God.

before: What does Paul list as belonging to Israel in Romans 9:4–5? Is it in the past or the present tense?
In the olive tree, who is the root, who are the natural branches, and who are the wild ones? What warning does Paul give the wild branches?
What does Paul say about Israel's future, and why?
sessions.readWhy: Paul's own answer to the question of this journey: Israel is the olive tree, the Gentiles are grafted in, and God has not taken back his gifts and calling.

paras: I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit
that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart.
For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers’ sake, my relatives according to the flesh
who are Israelites; whose is the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service, and the promises;
of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ as concerning the flesh, who is over all, God, blessed forever. Amen.
I ask then, did they stumble that they might fall? May it never be! But by their fall salvation has come to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy.
Now if their fall is the riches of the world, and their loss the riches of the Gentiles; how much more their fullness?
For I speak to you who are Gentiles. Since then as I am an apostle to Gentiles, I glorify my ministry;
if by any means I may provoke to jealousy those who are my flesh, and may save some of them.
For if the rejection of them is the reconciling of the world, what would their acceptance be, but life from the dead?
If the first fruit is holy, so is the lump. If the root is holy, so are the branches.
But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became partaker with them of the root and of the richness of the olive tree,
don’t boast over the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you.
You will say then, “Branches were broken off, that I might be grafted in.”
True; by their unbelief they were broken off, and you stand by your faith. Don’t be conceited, but fear;
for if God didn’t spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.
See then the goodness and severity of God. Toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off.
They also, if they don’t continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.

For if you were cut out of that which is by nature a wild olive tree, and were grafted contrary to nature into a good olive tree, how much more will these, which are the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree?

For I don’t desire you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you won’t be wise in your own conceits, that a partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in,
and so all Israel will be saved. Even as it is written,

“There will come out of Zion the Deliverer,
and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.

This is my covenant with them,
when I will take away their sins.”
Concerning the Good News, they are enemies for your sake. But concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers’ sake.
For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
For as you in time past were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy by their disobedience,
even so these also have now been disobedient, that by the mercy shown to you they may also obtain mercy.
For God has bound all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all.
Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out!

“For who has known the mind of the Lord?
Or who has been his counselor?”

“Or who has first given to him,
and it will be repaid to him again?”
For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.

parts.title: Great sorrow
parts.context: Corinth, about AD 57. Paul has just finished Romans 8, with its great ending: nothing 'will be able to separate us from the love of God' (8:39). At once he turns to the grief that makes that promise a question: what about his own people?

commentary.on: I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart
commentary.text: Paul does not begin with an argument but with grief. He is not looking at 'the Jews' from outside. They are his family, and their not believing in the Messiah is a wound he carries.

commentary.on: For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers' sake
commentary.text: An astonishing wish: to be cut off himself if it would save them. It echoes Moses after the golden calf, asking God to blot him out of the book rather than destroy Israel (Exodus 32:32). Compare this with Eusebius's 'divine vengeance'.

commentary.on: whose is the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service, and the promises
commentary.text: 'Whose is': present tense. Paul does not say these gifts were Israel's; he says they are. Israel is God's adopted son (Exodus 4:22); the glory is God's presence; the 'service' is the worship of the Temple, still standing as he wrote. Nothing in the list has been transferred to the Church.

commentary.on: from whom is Christ as concerning the flesh
commentary.text: The Messiah himself is listed as one of Israel's gifts. Jesus belongs to Israel before he belongs to anyone else. Session 1 began here.

commentary.on: who is over all, God, blessed forever. Amen.
commentary.text: The Greek has no punctuation, and scholars still argue whether Paul calls Christ 'God over all' or ends with a separate praise of God. Either way, Paul ends his list of Israel's gifts by blessing God, as a Jew would.

parts.title: The olive tree
parts.context: Paul has argued in Romans 9–10 that God has always chosen by grace, and that most of Israel has, for now, not accepted the Messiah. In 11:1 he asks, 'Did God reject his people?' and answers, 'May it never be!' Now he speaks directly to the Gentile believers in Rome.

commentary.on: did they stumble that they might fall? May it never be!
commentary.text: A stumble is not a fall. Paul allows that Israel has stumbled, but denies that it has fallen for good. 'May it never be!' is his strongest denial, the same he used in 11:1.

commentary.on: to provoke them to jealousy
commentary.text: Paul borrows from Deuteronomy 32:21, where God says he will make Israel jealous with 'those who are not a people'. In Paul's picture, the Gentiles' faith is meant to make Israel long for what is theirs, not to replace them. Centuries of contempt have made Christians the least enviable witnesses imaginable.

commentary.on: For I speak to you who are Gentiles.
commentary.text: The warning that follows is addressed to Gentile Christians, not to Jews. The danger Paul sees in Rome is Gentile pride.

commentary.on: If the root is holy, so are the branches.
commentary.text: The root is probably Israel's patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and God's promises to them (11:28). Its holiness passes to the whole tree.

commentary.on: you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became partaker with them of the root and of the richness of the olive tree
commentary.text: 'Among them': the Gentile branches are grafted in among the natural branches that remain, the Jewish believers such as Paul, James and Peter. They share the root 'with them'. This is the frame of this journey: one tree, Jewish and Gentile branches together.

commentary.on: it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you
commentary.text: Perhaps the most important sentence a Gentile Christian can hear about the Jews. The Church does not carry Israel; Israel's root carries the Church. Every sermon that treated Judaism as dead forgot this sentence.

commentary.on: Don't be conceited, but fear
commentary.text: Paul foresees exactly the danger that came true: Gentile Christians boasting over the 'broken branches'. His remedy is humility, and the warning that God can cut off wild branches too.

commentary.on: God is able to graft them in again
commentary.text: The broken branches are not firewood. They remain 'natural branches' of 'their own olive tree' (11:24), and God can restore them.

parts.title: All Israel will be saved
parts.context: Paul reaches his conclusion, which he calls a 'mystery': something hidden that God has now made known. He ends not with an argument but with a hymn of praise.

commentary.on: so that you won't be wise in your own conceits
commentary.text: Again the warning is to the Gentiles. Paul tells them this mystery precisely so that they will not think themselves wiser than Israel.

commentary.on: a partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in
commentary.text: 'Partial' and 'until': the hardening is neither total nor permanent. Paul sees it as part of God's plan, making room for the Gentiles.

commentary.on: and so all Israel will be saved
commentary.text: Christians read these words in three main ways. Many, from the early Church to most modern scholars, take 'all Israel' to mean the Jewish people as a whole, who will turn to the Messiah at the end. Calvin and some others read 'Israel' as the whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together. Some modern theologians, such as Krister Stendahl, noticed that Paul does not name Christ in these verses, and suggested that God will save Israel in God's own way. All three agree that Israel has a future.

commentary.on: Concerning the Good News, they are enemies for your sake. But concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers' sake.
commentary.text: 'Enemies' here means opponents of the message, for now. 'Election' means God's choosing. Paul holds both at once: in the argument about Jesus, opponents; in God's choice, beloved. Christians later remembered the first half and forgot the second.

commentary.on: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
commentary.text: The heart of the verdict. 'Irrevocable' means cannot be taken back. God does not change his mind about Israel. In 1965 Nostra Aetate quoted these verses, and in 2015 the Vatican took this sentence as the title of a document on Jews and Christians.

commentary.on: For God has bound all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all.
commentary.text: Paul's argument ends with both peoples on the same level: all have disobeyed, all receive mercy. There is no room left for boasting.

commentary.on: Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God!
commentary.text: Paul gives up explaining and praises. The question of Israel and the Church, he admits, goes beyond what he can see. The hymn draws on Isaiah 40:13 and Job 41:11, Israel's own Scriptures.

paras: Yahweh of Armies says: “Many peoples, and the inhabitants of many cities will yet come;
and the inhabitants of one shall go to another, saying, ‘Let’s go speedily to entreat the favor of Yahweh, and to seek Yahweh of Armies. I will go also.’
Yes, many peoples and strong nations will come to seek Yahweh of Armies in Jerusalem, and to entreat the favor of Yahweh.”

Yahweh of Armies says: “In those days, ten men will take hold, out of all the languages of the nations, they will take hold of the skirt of him who is a Jew, saying, ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.’ ”

parts.title: Many peoples will come
parts.context: Jerusalem, about 520–518 BC. The Jews have come back from exile in Babylon and are rebuilding the Temple. The prophet Zechariah promises that the ruined city will one day draw the whole world.

commentary.on: many peoples and strong nations will come to seek Yahweh of Armies in Jerusalem
commentary.text: The nations come to Israel's God, in Israel's city. This is the end-time hope you met in session 3, which the first Jewish believers saw coming true in the Gentiles who joined them.

commentary.on: they will take hold of the skirt of him who is a Jew
commentary.text: 'Skirt' translates the Hebrew kanaf, the corner of a garment: where, as you read in session 1, the tassels were worn (Numbers 15:38). The nations hold on to the very place where a Jew wears the reminder of God's commandments. They are not told to tear the garment off.

commentary.on: We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.
commentary.text: The Gentiles come because God is with the Jews. In this picture there is no rivalry: the nations' faith depends on Israel's. It is Paul's olive tree in a prophet's words.

compare.why: A prophet's picture of the nations coming to Israel's God, not instead of the Jews but holding on to them. It was the hope behind the Gentile mission, and it is a hope Jews and Christians still share.
compare.title: Holding the edge of a Jew's garment

sections.h: Paul's answer, and what the Church forgot
paras: Romans 9–11 gives a clear verdict. Most of Israel has not, for now, accepted Jesus as Messiah. Paul grieves over it. But God has not rejected his people: their gifts and calling stand; the Gentiles are grafted into their tree, not planted in its place; and in the end God will have mercy on all.

The Church kept Romans in its Bible and read it constantly. Augustine took from these chapters a teaching that the Jews should be preserved, not killed, as witnesses to the Scriptures (City of God XVIII.46), a teaching that saved Jewish lives in the Middle Ages even as it kept Jews humiliated. But on the whole, the warning to Gentiles not to boast was the part most forgotten. Only after the Holocaust did Christians return to these chapters as a judgement on themselves. Nostra Aetate's account of the Jews is built on them.
sections.key: Paul's verdict: God has not rejected Israel. The Church kept the text but forgot its warning to Gentiles not to boast, until after the Holocaust.

paras: A fair course must say why most Jews, then and now, have not accepted Jesus as the Messiah. In Jewish tradition, the Messiah is a human king of David's line who will bring the exiles home, rebuild the Temple, bring all nations to worship the one God and establish peace: 'nation shall not lift up sword against nation' (Isaiah 2:4). Maimonides, the great Jewish thinker of the twelfth century, wrote that someone who claims to be the Messiah and does not do these things is not the Messiah (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11–12). Jesus died, the Temple fell, and the world is not at peace.

Jews also hear in the Christian worship of Jesus as God a breach of the Shema, 'the Lord is one', and they hold that the Torah, given for ever, was never meant to be set aside. Christians answer that the Messiah came first to suffer, as they read Isaiah 53, and will come again to finish the work; that the kingdom has begun but is not complete. Each side's answer makes sense from inside its own reading of the Scriptures. Interestingly, Maimonides also wrote that Christianity and Islam, by spreading knowledge of the Torah and the commandments across the world, were preparing the way for the true Messiah (Laws of Kings 11:4, in the uncensored text).
sections.key: Jews expect a Messiah who brings the exiles home, rebuilds the Temple and brings world peace; Jesus did not. Christians answer: two comings. Maimonides saw Christianity as preparing the world.

paras: Since 1965 relations have changed more than in the previous eighteen centuries. In 1986 Pope John Paul II became the first pope known to have visited a synagogue since Peter, in Rome, and called the Jews Christians' 'elder brothers'. In 2000 he prayed at the Western Wall in Jerusalem, leaving a note asking God's forgiveness for Christians' treatment of Jews. In 2015 the Vatican's Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews published 'The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable', which, in our own words, says the Church neither runs nor supports any institutional mission aimed specifically at Jews, while Christians still bear witness to their faith.

Jews have answered. In 2000 more than two hundred rabbis and Jewish scholars signed Dabru Emet ('Speak the truth'). In eight short statements, in our own words: Jews and Christians worship the same God; they seek authority from the same book; Christians can respect the Jewish people's tie to the land of Israel; both accept the moral principles of the Torah; Nazism was not a Christian phenomenon; the difference between them will not be settled until God redeems the world; the new relationship will not weaken Jewish practice; and both must work together for justice and peace. In 2015 a group of Orthodox rabbis went further, saying that Christianity was not an accident or an error but part of God's purpose for the nations. Not all Jews agree: Jon Levenson criticised Dabru Emet for blurring real differences, and the great Orthodox thinker Joseph Soloveitchik had warned in 1964 against theological dialogue, while welcoming cooperation on shared moral concerns.
sections.key: Since 1965: John Paul II at the Rome synagogue (1986) and the Western Wall (2000); the Vatican's 2015 document. Jews answered with Dabru Emet (2000) and a 2015 Orthodox statement; some Jews remain cautious.

paras: There are Jews today who believe that Jesus, whom they call Yeshua, is the Messiah, and who go on keeping Jewish practice: the Sabbath, the festivals, often the food laws. They call themselves Messianic Jews. Hebrew Christian groups existed in the nineteenth century, and the modern movement grew strongly from the 1960s and 1970s, especially in the United States and Israel.

Opinion about them divides sharply. Some Christians see in them a return of the church of James, the natural branches back on the tree, keeping the law as the Jerusalem council assumed Jewish believers would. Almost all Jewish bodies, Orthodox, Conservative and Reform, regard Messianic Judaism as a form of Christianity, not of Judaism; in 1989 Israel's Supreme Court ruled that Messianic Jews could not claim citizenship as Jews under the Law of Return. Many Jews see Messianic congregations as a mission aimed at them, after centuries in which conversion was forced. A fair account must hold both views, and listen to Messianic Jews describe themselves too.
sections.key: Messianic Jews believe Jesus is the Messiah and keep Jewish practice. Some Christians see the church of James restored; almost all Jewish bodies see them as Christians, not Jews.

sections.h: What each says of the other
paras: The traditions do not speak with one voice, but their main positions can be set side by side.

cols: What it says of the other
rows: God's covenant with the Jews has never been revoked; Christians and Jews share a great spiritual heritage; no institutional mission aimed at Jews
Nostra Aetate 4 (1965); John Paul II, Mainz (1980); The Gifts and the Calling (2015)
Honours the Old Testament saints in its calendar; dialogue with Jewish bodies since 1977; less formal teaching on Judaism today
Some Holy Week texts still debated
Repudiate Luther's anti-Jewish writings and replacement teaching; many say the Church is grafted into Israel's covenant
Condemn antisemitism; most hold that the gospel is for Jews as for all, shared with respect; many strongly support the state of Israel
Christianity is not Judaism; some see it as part of God's plan for the nations; caution about theological dialogue
Generally open to dialogue and joint work; firm that Jesus was not the Messiah and that Jews need not become Christians
table.note: Each tradition has internal debate; these are main positions, not the view of every member. A Jewish and a Christian reviewer should check this table.

sections.key: Christian churches now mostly affirm God's unrevoked covenant with the Jews; Jews range from cautious Orthodox to open Reform; all still differ about Jesus.

sections.h: Should Christians seek to convert Jews?
paras: This is the most sensitive question between the two communities, and Christians are divided on it. Some, following the German Jewish philosopher Franz Rosenzweig (The Star of Redemption, 1921), hold a 'two covenant' view: the Jews are already with the Father, and Christianity is God's way of bringing the nations to him. Others, including the Catholic Church since 2015, hold that Christ is the one saviour of all, but that God's covenant with the Jews stands, so the Church should not target Jews for mission, and leaves the 'how' of Romans 11:26 to God. Many evangelicals, citing Paul's 'to the Jew first' (Romans 1:16), hold that it would be unloving not to share the gospel with Jews, while condemning any pressure or deceit.

Jews, for their part, remember forced baptisms, disputations they were made to lose, and missions to Jews that followed hard on persecution, and many hear any mission to them as a continuation of the attempt to end Judaism. Paul's own picture asks Christians to hold two things: that Christ is Israel's Messiah, and that Israel is the tree they are grafted into. How to hold both, with love and without boasting, is the question this journey leaves you with.
sections.key: Christians differ: a 'two covenant' view (Rosenzweig), no targeted mission (Catholic, 2015), or respectful witness to all (many evangelicals). Jews remember forced conversions.

debate.question: What does 'all Israel will be saved' mean for Jews and Christians today?

positions.name: Israel will turn to Christ at the end
positions.who: Many Church Fathers; much Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical teaching; most modern commentators on Romans
positions.view: Paul means the Jewish people as a whole, who will come to faith in Jesus as Messiah when God's purpose for the Gentiles is complete. Until then Israel remains beloved and must never be despised, and Christians bear witness with humility.
positions.evidence: Romans 11:23 ('if they don't continue in their unbelief'); 11:26–27, quoting Isaiah 59:20 on the Deliverer from Zion.

positions.name: 'Israel' is the whole people of God
positions.who: John Calvin; N. T. Wright
positions.view: Paul has redefined Israel around the Messiah: 'all Israel' is the one family of Jews and Gentiles who believe. This is not replacement, Wright insists, because Jews remain welcome on the same terms, but it denies a separate future for the Jewish people as such.
positions.evidence: Romans 9:6 ('they are not all Israel, that are of Israel'); Galatians 6:16 ('the Israel of God').

positions.name: God will save Israel in God's own way
positions.who: Krister Stendahl (1976); some 'two covenant' theologians; Franz Rosenzweig, from the Jewish side
positions.view: Paul leaves the 'how' to God: he does not name Christ in 11:25–32, and ends in praise of God's unsearchable ways. Christians should not make the Jews' salvation depend on becoming Christians, or treat Judaism as a failed Christianity.
positions.evidence: The absence of Christ's name in 11:25–32; 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable'; the hymn of 11:33–36.

debate.agree: All agree that Paul denies that God has rejected Israel, that Gentile Christians must not boast, and that the Jewish people remain beloved of God.

look.why: Vincent van Gogh painted a series of olive groves in 1889, at Saint-Rémy in the south of France. This is a cultivated orchard at harvest, not a picture of grafting; it is here for Paul's tree, with its old trunks still bearing fruit.
points: Three women stand on or next to a ladder, picking olives in an orchard.
Women, trees, ground and sky are all painted with long, parallel brushstrokes that curve and swirl over the canvas.
One woman stands on the ladder facing us; another leans against it, facing away, her hair covered in a cloth; the third stands at the foot of the ladder, turning away.
The trees' gnarled trunks are outlined in dark brown, with leaves made of short strokes of pine and light green and touches of silvery blue.
The sky, above a horizon about a third of the way up, is ivory, pale mint green and a little shell pink.
In places the strokes are spaced so far apart that bare canvas shows through, especially in the ground.

music.why: A Christian Advent hymn, built from ancient antiphons, that prays in Israel's voice for the coming of Emmanuel, 'God with us', and the ransom of captive Israel: a hope Christians learned from Jews.

think.why: The West grew from two roots, and one of them is Jerusalem: the Hebrew Scriptures that Jews and Christians share.

learn.why: Paul's last word on his own people: God does not take back his gifts or his calling.

check.q: In Romans 9:4, Paul says Israel's is 'the adoption, the glory, the covenants…'. What is the significance of the present tense?
options: It shows the gifts belong to the Gentiles
Paul says these gifts still belong to Israel, not that they once did and have passed to the Church
It shows Paul was writing before the exile
None; Greek has no tenses
check.why: 'Whose is': nothing in the list is transferred.

check.q: To whom is the warning 'don't boast over the branches' addressed, and why does that matter?
options: To the apostle Peter
To the Roman emperor
To Jews who did not believe
To Gentile Christians in Rome, who were in danger of looking down on Jews: exactly the danger that later came true
check.why: 'For I speak to you who are Gentiles.' Paul foresaw Gentile pride.

check.q: Paul says the wild branches were grafted in 'contrary to nature'. What point does this make?
options: That the tree was diseased
That Paul knew nothing about farming
That the Gentile branches did nothing to earn their place and live from a root that is not their own
That grafting is forbidden in the Torah
check.why: Normally the good branch goes onto the wild stock; here the reverse, as pure gift.

check.q: Which is the fairest summary of why most Jews do not accept Jesus as Messiah?
options: Because the rabbis did not know of him
Because they have not read their Scriptures
Because Jesus was not Jewish
Because the Messiah of Jewish hope brings the exiles home, rebuilds the Temple and brings world peace, which did not happen; and worship of Jesus as God seems to them to breach the Shema
check.why: Maimonides' criteria and the Shema state the Jewish case in its own terms.

takeaways: Paul refused to say God had rejected Israel: Israel's gifts and calling stand, Gentile believers are wild branches grafted into its tree, and they must not boast.

Hard questions remain, about mission, Messianic Jews and what 'all Israel will be saved' means, but the old teaching of contempt has no place in Paul's picture.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: How did Christianity grow out of Judaism, and why did they part? In about 300 words, give your answer, using the picture of the olive tree if it helps you. Say what you think Christians should believe and say about Jews today, and answer the strongest objection: that the New Testament itself taught contempt.
closing.practice: Read Romans 9–11 in one sitting, aloud if you can. Then, this week, find out where the nearest synagogue is, and whether it welcomes visitors; or read the story of one Jewish community in your own country before and after 1945.
synthesis: This course asked how Christianity grew out of Judaism, and why the two parted. It followed Paul's picture of one olive tree: Israel the tree, its root in Abraham, Gentile believers grafted in, and branches broken off. Here are the short answers, in order.

Was Jesus Jewish? Yes, entirely. Luke shows him circumcised on the eighth day, presented in the Temple, at Passover in Jerusalem at twelve, asking the teachers questions. He prayed the Shema, wore the tassels the Torah commands, taught in synagogues and chose twelve to stand for Israel's tribes. The Judaism of his day was varied and argumentative, Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and rebels, but shared one God, the Torah, the Temple and a hope of redemption. The Pharisees were not hypocrites but respected teachers of everyday holiness, and Jesus argued with them because he was close to them. His quarrels were family quarrels. There is no debate left among scholars about whether he was a Jew, only about what kind.

Were the first Christians Jews? Yes. For a generation the church in Jerusalem was a Jewish movement, which outsiders called a 'sect' of Nazarenes, as they called the Pharisees a sect. Its leader was Jesus's brother James, remembered as 'the Just' and as a man of the Temple, his knees hard from praying for his people. Around 57 tens of thousands of Jewish believers were 'all zealous for the law', and Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, went into the Temple to show that he still kept it. Law-keeping Jewish believers survived for centuries, as Ebionites and Nazarenes, until neither Church nor synagogue would own them.

Why did Christians stop keeping the Jewish law? Because of the first great Christian argument: must Gentiles become Jews to belong to Israel's Messiah? Peter's vision and his visit to the Roman officer Cornelius, and the meeting in Jerusalem around 49, said no. Gentiles were asked to keep only the Torah's rules for strangers living among Israel. Judaism already held that righteous Gentiles had a share in the world to come; what was new was Gentiles belonging to God's people without converting. The council said Gentiles need not keep the law. Within sixty years Ignatius was saying Christians must not: 'need not' had become 'must not', and the calendar, Sabbath or Sunday, marked the communities apart.

When did Christianity and Judaism separate? Slowly. The decisive blows were Roman. In 70 Titus's soldiers burned the Temple, as Josephus, an eyewitness with his own motives, describes. Both communities had to answer the question 'where is God now?'. The heirs of the Pharisees rebuilt Judaism at Yavneh around the Torah, prayer and deeds of loving-kindness; the Church rebuilt itself around Christ as the true Temple and sacrifice. Each answer was complete, so belonging to both grew harder. Lines were drawn on both sides, among them the Birkat ha-Minim, and in 132–135 Jewish believers could not follow Bar Kokhba as messiah. Scholars still debate whether the ways had parted by the mid-second century (Dunn), only in the fourth century under a Christian empire (Boyarin), or whether they were never one road (Neusner).

Is the New Testament anti-Semitic? This was the objection, and it was given at full strength. Matthew's 'His blood be on us, and on our children' and John's 'You are of your father, the devil' were words of Jews arguing with Jews, in the harsh style of ancient polemic. But read by a powerful Gentile Church about a powerless minority, they became what Jules Isaac called 'the teaching of contempt': the Jews scattered as punishment, Judaism dead, the Jews guilty of deicide. Eusebius called the Jews' sufferings 'divine vengeance'. Contempt became violence: Chrysostom's sermons, the Rhineland massacres of 1096, the blood libel, expulsions, Luther's 1543 tract. Nazism was racial and not Christian, but it was built on ground the churches had prepared, and many of its laws had Church precedents. Since 1945, and above all since Nostra Aetate in 1965, the churches have repented of that teaching. Whether the fault lies only with the readers, or also in the texts and in the Christian claim itself, as Rosemary Radford Ruether argued, is still the hardest question in this course, and a fair answer must keep both possibilities in view.

Why do Christians keep the Old Testament? Because the Church refused Marcion. Around 140 he taught that the God of the Jewish Scriptures was a lesser, harsher god, and made a Bible without them. Irenaeus answered that one God made the world, called Abraham, gave the law and sent Christ, the two covenants fitted to their times; and that the apostles themselves kept the law. So the Jewish Scriptures became most of the Christian Bible, and Christianity was bound for good to the God of Israel. Yet the Church often kept the book while claiming that the Jews could not read it and that it had replaced them. Marcion's idea returned in the twentieth century with the pro-Nazi 'German Christians', and contempt for the Old Testament and contempt for Jews travelled together.

Has God rejected the Jews? Paul's answer was no. Israel's are 'the adoption, the glory, the covenants', present tense; the Gentiles are wild branches grafted in 'contrary to nature'; 'it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you'; and 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable'. Why don't Jews believe Jesus was the Messiah? Because the Messiah of Jewish hope brings the exiles home, rebuilds the Temple and brings peace to the world, which has not happened, and because the worship of Jesus as God seems to them to breach the Shema. Christians answer that the Messiah comes twice. What do Jews and Christians think of each other today? More warmly than in eighteen centuries: Nostra Aetate, the Lutheran repudiation of Luther, John Paul II at the Western Wall, Dabru Emet, an Orthodox rabbis' statement that Christianity is part of God's purpose for the nations. They still disagree about Jesus, about mission, and about what 'all Israel will be saved' means, and Messianic Jews remain a point of tension.

So the verdict is this. Christianity is a branch grafted into a Jewish tree. It did not grow against Judaism but out of it, and parted from it slowly, under the weight of Roman wars and of its own success among the Gentiles. The worst of the story came when the grafted branch forgot Paul's warning and boasted over the natural branches. The best of it is the slow return, since 1945, to his picture: two communities that read the same Scriptures, pray to the same God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and wait, in different ways, for the same redemption.
