title: What happens at church
question: Why do Christians baptise and break bread?
line: Seven sessions that walk through a church service part by part, the day, the water, the word and the table, find where each came from, hear the case that it is all empty ritual, face the Reformation's quarrel over the bread, and end with what to expect if you go.
why: Most people in the West have never been to a church service, or have been only to weddings and funerals. Yet the service itself is one of the oldest things in Western life: by about AD 155 a Christian philosopher in Rome could describe a Sunday gathering with readings, a sermon, prayers, bread and wine and a collection for the poor, much as it happens today. This journey reads Paul, Justin Martyr, the Didache, Cyril of Jerusalem, Ambrose, Luther, the Book of Common Prayer, the Quaker Robert Barclay and Voltaire, sets the traditions side by side, gives the objection to ritual its full strength, and ends with a plain guide to going for the first time. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year theology paper in liturgy and sacraments: the origins of Christian worship, baptism and the Eucharist in the early Church, the Reformation controversies, and comparative liturgy.
before: one-root-two-branches
outcomes: Explain why Christians meet on Sunday, and set out the order of service described by Justin Martyr in about AD 155.
Explain what baptism means in Romans 6, how it was done in the early Church, and the case for infant and for believer's baptism.
Explain where the readings, sermon, psalms, hymns and creed come from, and what the Book of Common Prayer did.
Explain what Paul and Justin say about the Lord's Supper, Dix's four actions, and how six traditions celebrate it and who may receive.
State the objection to ritual at full strength, from the prophets to the Quakers and the Enlightenment, and assess the replies.
Distinguish transubstantiation, sacramental union, spiritual presence, memorial and the Orthodox view, and explain why the Marburg Colloquy failed.

people.name: Paul
people.line: Apostle whose letters give the oldest teaching on baptism (Romans 6) and the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 10–11).

people.line: Roman governor of Bithynia whose letter of about 112 describes Christians meeting before dawn on a fixed day.

people.name: Justin Martyr

glossary.def: Greek for love: the 'love feast', a shared meal of the early Christians, held separately from the Eucharist after about AD 150.
Hebrew for 'so be it' or 'it is true'; the people's answer to a prayer, which makes it theirs.
'Rebaptiser': the name given to the radical Reformers who, from 1525, baptised only believers.
Greek for remembering: in the Eucharist, a remembering of Christ's death and resurrection that makes them present.
Washing with or plunging into water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit: the way into the Church.
Baptism only of those old enough to profess faith themselves, usually by full immersion, as among Baptists.
A note in the 1552 Prayer Book, restored in 1662, explaining that kneeling at Communion did not mean adoring the bread.
The Church of England's service book, first written by Thomas Cranmer in 1549 and revised in 1552 and 1662.
A 'learner': someone being taught the faith before baptism.
In the Orthodox Church, anointing with holy oil straight after baptism, giving the Holy Spirit; it matches confirmation in the West.
From the Greek koinonia, sharing: the receiving of the bread and wine, and a name for the whole service.
The fellowship of all Christians, living and dead, in Christ.
In Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches, a rite in which a baptised person affirms their faith and, usually through a bishop, receives the Spirit's strengthening.
From the Latin credo, 'I believe': a short summary of the faith said together, such as the Apostles' or Nicene Creed.
'The Teaching': a short early Christian handbook, probably of AD 50–120, rediscovered in 1873.
The sending out at the end of a service; the Latin dismissal gave the Mass its name.
The Orthodox name for the Eucharist and its service.
Greek for 'calling upon': the prayer asking the Holy Spirit to come on the bread and wine and on the people.
Greek for 'thanksgiving': the oldest name for the service of bread and wine.
Evening Prayer in the Anglican tradition, often sung by a choir; a service of psalms, readings and prayers without Communion.
Latin for 'by the work done': the Catholic teaching that a sacrament's power comes from Christ, not the minister's holiness, though it bears fruit only with faith.
The basin or pool used for baptism, often by the door of a church.
Originally a Greek actor in a mask: someone whose outward religion hides a different heart.
A list of Bible readings set for each Sunday or day, so that the Bible is heard in order over time.
From the Greek for a public work: the set form of a church's worship, or worship itself.
The Christian name for Sunday, the day of the resurrection.
The Catholic (and some Anglican) name for the Eucharist, from the Latin words of dismissal.
A remembering; for Zwingli and many evangelicals, the Lord's Supper is chiefly a memorial of Christ's death.
The practice of inviting all who believe in or love Christ to receive, not only members of one church.
A rite Christ ordered his followers to keep; the word many Protestants prefer to 'sacrament'.
A member of the Religious Society of Friends, founded by George Fox in the 1650s, who worship in silence without outward sacraments.
The belief that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist, not only remembered; churches differ on how.
An instruction in a service book saying what to do, once printed in red (Latin ruber).
The seventh day, Saturday, the day of rest in the Ten Commandments, kept by Jews from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset.
A visible sign of an invisible grace (Augustine): above all baptism and the Eucharist.
The Lutheran teaching that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain.
'Holy, holy, holy': the angels' song from Isaiah 6, sung in the eucharistic prayer.
A talk explaining and applying the readings; also called a homily.
A Jewish house of prayer and study, where the Law and the prophets are read every Sabbath.
The Catholic teaching that the substance of the bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood, while their appearances remain.

sessions.title: The first day of the week
sessions.line: Why Christians meet on Sunday, and the oldest description of what they do when they meet.
sessions.plain: Walk into almost any church on a Sunday morning and something is happening that has happened every week for nearly two thousand years. This session asks why it happens on Sunday, and what the first Christians actually did when they met. The answer comes from a philosopher called Justin, who wrote it down for the Roman emperor in about AD 155: readings, a sermon, prayers, bread and wine, and a collection for the poor. You will find the same shape in a cathedral, a village church and a modern hall today.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'The first Christians' showed you a small movement spreading through the Roman empire, and 'The last week and the cross' followed Jesus to his last supper, his death and the empty tomb. Now we ask what his followers did next, week after week, and why. Before we can understand baptism, the readings or the bread and wine, we need the day and the shape that hold them all together.

sessions.finding: Christians gathered on Sunday because it was the day of the resurrection, and by about AD 155 their gathering already had the shape it has today: readings, a sermon, prayers, bread and wine given with thanks, and gifts for the poor.

background.h: If you have never been to church
paras: This journey assumes nothing. If you have never been inside a church for a service, you are like most people in Britain and much of Europe today. A service can look strange from outside: people stand up and sit down, say words together, sing, and sometimes queue to receive a piece of bread. This journey walks through it part by part and asks where each part came from and what it means.

We will use one simple frame all the way through. Imagine walking into a service and noticing, in order, the day, the water, the word, the table and the sending. Each session takes one of them, finds the oldest evidence for it, and shows how Christians of different traditions do it now. Then we hear the strongest case against the whole business of ritual, face the bitterest argument Christians have had about it, and end with a practical verdict: what to expect if you go.

paras: Jesus of Nazareth was crucified in Jerusalem in about AD 30, under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. His followers said that on the third day, a Sunday, his tomb was found empty and he appeared to them alive. Within a few decades there were groups of his followers in cities across the eastern Mediterranean and in Rome itself. They were mostly ordinary people, meeting in houses, with no church buildings for two centuries.

Jesus himself was a Jew, and so were his first followers. Jews kept the Sabbath, the seventh day, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, as the Ten Commandments required: you may have read Exodus 20 in 'Exodus and the law'. So why do Christians meet on the first day instead? That is the first question of this journey.
background.key: Jesus died in about AD 30 and his followers said he rose on a Sunday. They met in houses for two centuries. Jews kept the Sabbath on Saturday.

paras: Justin was born in about AD 100 in Flavia Neapolis, the modern Nablus, in Samaria. He went looking for the truth among the philosophers, Stoic, Aristotelian, Pythagorean and Platonist, and then became a Christian, keeping his philosopher's cloak. He taught in Rome, and in about AD 165 he was beheaded there with several of his students for refusing to sacrifice to the gods. That is why he is called Justin Martyr.

In about AD 155 he wrote a defence of Christianity, an 'apology', addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius. Christians were suspected of secret crimes, even of eating human flesh, because people heard rumours about 'body' and 'blood'. Justin answered by describing exactly what Christians did. That is why we have, from so early, a plain account of a Christian service, written for outsiders.
background.key: Justin, a philosopher who became a Christian, wrote to the emperor in about AD 155 to describe what Christians really did. He was executed in Rome in about 165.

paras: The main reading is two chapters of Justin's First Apology. Chapter 65 tells what happens when a new Christian is brought into the gathering for the first time; chapter 67 describes an ordinary Sunday. Together they are the oldest full description of a Christian service that we have.

The comparison has two shorter texts from even earlier: a scene from the Acts of the Apostles, in which Paul talks all night at a Sunday gathering, and a chapter of the Didache, a short handbook for Christian communities written perhaps fifty years before Justin, on what to do 'on the Lord's own day'.
background.key: Justin's two chapters give the oldest full order of service; Acts 20 and the Didache show the same Sunday gathering even earlier.

before: Make a list of everything Justin says happens, in order. How many of the parts can you find in a service today?
What reasons does Justin give for meeting on Sunday?

sessions.readWhy: The oldest full description of a Christian service, written by a Christian for the Roman emperor in about AD 155.

paras: But we, after we have thus washed him who has been convinced and has assented to our teaching, bring him to the place where those who are called brethren are assembled, in order that we may offer hearty prayers in common for ourselves and for the baptized [illuminated] person, and for all others in every place, that we may be counted worthy, now that we have learned the truth, by our works also to be found good citizens and keepers of the commandments, so that we may be saved with an everlasting salvation. Having ended the prayers, we salute one another with a kiss. There is then brought to the president of the brethren bread and a cup of wine mixed with water; and he taking them, gives praise and glory to the Father of the universe, through the name of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, and offers thanks at considerable length for our being counted worthy to receive these things at His hands. And when he has concluded the prayers and thanksgivings, all the people present express their assent by saying Amen. This word Amen answers in the Hebrew language to γένοιτο [so be it]. And when the president has given thanks, and all the people have expressed their assent, those who are called by us deacons give to each of those present to partake of the bread and wine mixed with water over which the thanksgiving was pronounced, and to those who are absent they carry away a portion.

And we afterwards continually remind each other of these things. And the wealthy among us help the needy; and we always keep together; and for all things wherewith we are supplied, we bless the Maker of all through His Son Jesus Christ, and through the Holy Ghost. And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things. Then we all rise together and pray, and, as we before said, when our prayer is ended, bread and wine and water are brought, and the president in like manner offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability, and the people assent, saying Amen; and there is a distribution to each, and a participation of that over which thanks have been given, and to those who are absent a portion is sent by the deacons.

And they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit; and what is collected is deposited with the president, who succours the orphans and widows and those who, through sickness or any other cause, are in want, and those who are in bonds and the strangers sojourning among us, and in a word takes care of all who are in need. But Sunday is the day on which we all hold our common assembly, because it is the first day on which God, having wrought a change in the darkness and matter, made the world; and Jesus Christ our Saviour on the same day rose from the dead. For He was crucified on the day before that of Saturn (Saturday); and on the day after that of Saturn, which is the day of the Sun, having appeared to His apostles and disciples, He taught them these things, which we have submitted to you also for your consideration.

parts.author: Justin Martyr
parts.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers I (1885)
parts.who: Justin Martyr (c. 100–165), a philosopher from Samaria who became a Christian and taught in Rome, where he was executed
parts.title: The newcomer brought to the brethren
parts.context: Justin has just described baptism (you will read his account in the next session). Now he tells what happens next: the newly baptised person is brought to the assembled community for the first time. 'Brethren' means brothers and sisters, the Christians' name for one another. The 'president' is the person who leads, later called the bishop or priest. Words in square brackets were added by the Victorian translators.
parts.plain: After someone has been baptised, we take them to the place where the others are gathered. We all pray together for ourselves, the new Christian and everyone everywhere. We greet one another with a kiss. Then bread and a cup of wine mixed with water are brought to the leader, who gives thanks to God at length; everyone says 'Amen'. Then the deacons give the bread and wine to everyone present, and take some to those who could not come.

commentary.on: bring him to the place where those who are called brethren are assembled
commentary.text: Christianity is not something you do alone. The first thing that happens after baptism is that you are brought into a room full of people. Justin calls them 'brethren': a family, not an audience.

commentary.on: for all others in every place
commentary.text: The prayers are not only for those present. Christians prayed for the whole world, including, as other early writers say, the emperor who persecuted them. Most services today still have 'intercessions', prayers for the Church, the world, the sick and the dead.

commentary.on: we salute one another with a kiss
commentary.text: The 'kiss of peace' is mentioned in Paul's letters ('Greet one another with a holy kiss', Romans 16:16). Today it is usually a handshake, and it is called 'the Peace': people turn to those near them and say 'Peace be with you'. If you go to a service, this is the moment strangers will offer you their hand.

commentary.on: bread and a cup of wine mixed with water
commentary.text: In the ancient world wine was usually drunk mixed with water. Catholic and Orthodox priests, and some Anglicans, still add a little water to the wine. The bread and cup are brought to the president: this later became the 'offertory', when the gifts are carried to the altar.

commentary.on: offers thanks at considerable length
commentary.text: The prayer over the bread and wine is a long thanksgiving. The Greek for 'thanksgiving' is eucharistia, which is why the service is called the Eucharist. In Justin's day the president prayed in his own words; set prayers came later.

commentary.on: all the people present express their assent by saying Amen
commentary.text: 'Amen' is a Hebrew word meaning 'so be it' or 'it is true'. Justin explains it for his Roman reader. The people's 'Amen' makes the president's prayer theirs. It is still the one word every congregation says.

commentary.on: to those who are absent they carry away a portion
commentary.text: The deacons, the community's helpers, take the bread and wine to the sick and to those in prison. Churches still do this: a minister takes Communion to people at home or in hospital.

parts.author: Justin Martyr
parts.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers I (1885)
parts.who: Justin Martyr (c. 100–165), a philosopher from Samaria who became a Christian and taught in Rome, where he was executed
parts.title: On the day called Sunday
parts.context: Chapter 67 describes the ordinary weekly gathering, and gives Justin's reasons for holding it on Sunday. 'The memoirs of the apostles' is Justin's name for the Gospels; 'the writings of the prophets' means the Jewish Scriptures, our Old Testament. Saturn's day is Saturday and the day of the Sun is Sunday: the Romans named the days after the planets.
parts.plain: We keep reminding each other of these things, and the rich help the poor. On Sunday everyone from the town and the countryside gathers in one place. The Gospels or the prophets are read for as long as there is time. Then the leader preaches, urging us to live by what was read. We stand and pray. Then bread, wine and water are brought; the leader gives thanks, and the people say 'Amen'. Everyone receives, and the deacons take some to those who are absent. Those who can afford it give money, which the leader uses for orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers. We meet on Sunday because it is the day God began creation, and the day Jesus rose from the dead.

commentary.on: the wealthy among us help the needy
commentary.text: Before Justin describes the service, he describes the community: rich and poor together, with the rich helping. Worship and care for the poor go together from the start.

commentary.on: all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place
commentary.text: Town and country, rich and poor, slave and free gather in one place. In a society divided by rank, this was unusual.

commentary.on: the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits
commentary.text: First, readings from the Bible. Notice 'as long as time permits': there was no fixed length. Many of those present could not read, and owned no books; this was how they learned the Scriptures.

commentary.on: the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things
commentary.text: Then a sermon. Its purpose is practical: to urge people to imitate what they have heard. The pattern of reading followed by explanation came from the Jewish synagogue.

commentary.on: Then we all rise together and pray
commentary.text: Christians prayed standing, as Jews did, often with hands raised. Kneeling to pray became common later.

commentary.on: bread and wine and water are brought, and the president in like manner offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability
commentary.text: Then the meal: the thanksgiving over bread and wine, and the people's Amen. 'According to his ability' confirms that the prayer was not yet fixed in a book.

commentary.on: what is collected is deposited with the president
commentary.text: The collection began here, and it was for the needy: orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners and 'strangers sojourning among us', that is, travellers and migrants. When a plate or bag is passed round in a church today, this is its ancestor.

commentary.on: it is the first day on which God, having wrought a change in the darkness and matter, made the world
commentary.text: Justin gives two reasons for Sunday. The first: it is the first day of creation, when God said 'Let there be light' (Genesis 1:3).

commentary.on: Jesus Christ our Saviour on the same day rose from the dead
commentary.text: The second, and decisive, reason: it is the day of the resurrection. Every Sunday is a small Easter. Justin even fixes the dates for his Roman reader: crucified on Friday, the day before Saturn's day, risen on Sunday, the Sun's day.

read.author: Justin Martyr
read.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers I (1885)
read.who: Justin Martyr (c. 100–165), a philosopher from Samaria who became a Christian and taught in Rome, where he was executed

paras: On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and continued his speech until midnight.
There were many lights in the upper room where we were gathered together.

A certain young man named Eutychus sat in the window, weighed down with deep sleep. As Paul spoke still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he fell down from the third floor and was taken up dead.
Paul went down and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”
When he had gone up, and had broken bread and eaten, and had talked with them a long while, even until break of day, he departed.
They brought the boy in alive, and were greatly comforted.

And on the Lord's own day gather yourselves together and break bread and give thanks, first confessing your transgressions, that your sacrifice may be pure. And let no man, having his dispute with his fellow, join your assembly until they have been reconciled, that your sacrifice may not be defiled; for this sacrifice it is that was spoken of by the Lord; In every place and at every time offer Me a pure sacrifice; for I am a great king, saith the Lord and My name is wonderful among the nations.

parts.title: A sermon until midnight
parts.context: Acts, written by Luke in the later first century, tells the story of the first Christians. Here Paul, on his last journey to Jerusalem in about AD 57, stops at Troas on the north-west coast of modern Turkey. Luke writes 'we': he was there. A Jewish day ran from sunset to sunset, so this gathering may have been on Saturday night or Sunday night; scholars disagree.

commentary.on: On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread
commentary.text: This is the earliest clear mention of Christians meeting on the first day of the week, and of why they met: 'to break bread'. The phrase is Luke's name for the shared meal Jesus had commanded.

commentary.on: continued his speech until midnight
commentary.text: Teaching came with the meal. Paul was leaving the next day, so he talked for a long time. Anyone who has sat through a long sermon will sympathise with what happens next.

commentary.on: There were many lights in the upper room
commentary.text: They met in an upper room of a house, at night, by lamplight. Lamps were hot and smoky, which may explain why the young man fell asleep.

commentary.on: When he had gone up, and had broken bread and eaten
commentary.text: After the crisis, they return upstairs, break bread, and Paul talks until dawn. The order of the gathering survives even a fall from the third floor.

parts.author: Anonymous
parts.work: The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
parts.translator: J. B. Lightfoot, ed. J. R. Harmer (1891)
parts.who: An unknown teacher or teachers in the earliest Church, writing for Gentile converts
parts.when: Probably Syria, between about AD 50 and 120
parts.title: On the Lord's own day
parts.context: The Didache, 'the Teaching', is a short handbook for Christian communities, lost for centuries and found in 1873 in a library in Constantinople. Most scholars date it between about AD 50 and 120, probably in Syria. You read its prayers over the bread and cup in 'The first Christians'; here is its rule for Sunday. The verse numbers and brackets of the website have been removed.
parts.plain: On the Lord's day, gather together, break bread and give thanks, but first confess your sins, so that your offering is pure. Anyone who has a quarrel with someone must not join the gathering until they have made peace. This is the pure offering the prophet Malachi spoke of.

commentary.on: on the Lord's own day gather yourselves together and break bread and give thanks
commentary.text: 'The Lord's day' is the Christian name for Sunday; it appears in Revelation 1:10, and it survives in the Greek, Italian and Spanish words for Sunday (kyriake, domenica, domingo). Three verbs give the shape: gather, break bread, give thanks.

commentary.on: first confessing your transgressions
commentary.text: Confession comes before the meal. Most services still begin with a prayer of confession, said together, and a declaration of forgiveness.

commentary.on: let no man, having his dispute with his fellow, join your assembly until they have been reconciled
commentary.text: An echo of Jesus: 'first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift' (Matthew 5:24). Worship is not allowed to cover over a quarrel. This is where the Peace comes from.

commentary.on: In every place and at every time offer Me a pure sacrifice
commentary.text: The Didache quotes Malachi 1:11, a prophet's promise that God would be worshipped among the nations. The first Christians saw their simple meal of thanksgiving as that 'pure offering'. Calling it a 'sacrifice' will matter later in this journey, when Christians argue over what it means.

compare.author: Anonymous
compare.why: Two shorter texts, both older than Justin, show the same Sunday gathering for the breaking of bread: one tells a story, the other gives instructions.
compare.title: Before Justin: Troas and the Didache

paras: The Sabbath is the seventh day, Saturday. The Ten Commandments tell Israel to rest on it because God rested after creation (Exodus 20:8–11). For Jews it is still the heart of the week, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, a 'palace in time', as the Jewish thinker Abraham Joshua Heschel called it in 1951.

The first Christians were Jews, and many went on keeping the Sabbath. But from the start they also met on the first day, the day after the Sabbath, because that was the day of the resurrection. Paul asks the Corinthians to set money aside 'on the first day of every week' (1 Corinthians 16:2); Acts describes a gathering 'on the first day of the week'; Revelation calls it 'the Lord's day'. As the Church became mostly Gentile, Sunday replaced the Sabbath: in about AD 110 Ignatius of Antioch spoke of Christians no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's day (you read him in 'One root, two branches').
sections.key: Jews keep the Sabbath on Saturday. The first Christians also met on the first day, the day of the resurrection, and Sunday gradually took the Sabbath's place.

paras: Early Christian writers gave Sunday a rich meaning. It was the first day, when God made light. It was the day of the resurrection, when the new creation began. And it was sometimes called 'the eighth day': the day after the seven days of the old week, a sign of a new age beyond ordinary time. That is one reason many ancient baptisteries are eight-sided.

Sunday was not a holiday in the Roman empire. Christians met before dawn or in the evening, around their work. In AD 321 the emperor Constantine, the first Christian emperor, made 'the venerable day of the Sun' a day of rest for courts and town workers, though farmers could still work (the law survives in the Code of Justinian, 3.12.2). From then on, the Christian day of worship slowly became the West's day off: the 'weekend' grew out of it.
sections.key: Sunday was the first day of creation, the day of the resurrection and the 'eighth day' of the new creation; Constantine made it a day of rest in AD 321.

paras: Justin was not the first outsider-facing account. In about AD 112 Pliny the Younger, the Roman governor of Bithynia in northern Turkey, wrote to the emperor Trajan about the Christians he was interrogating. You read his letter in 'The first Christians'. He reported that they met on a fixed day before dawn, sang a hymn to Christ 'as to a god', bound themselves by an oath not to steal or commit adultery, and later met again to eat ordinary, harmless food.

Put Pliny and Justin side by side and you have two witnesses, one hostile and one friendly, forty years apart, describing the same things: a fixed weekly day, early meeting, song or prayer to Christ, a moral commitment and a shared meal. Pliny thought it was a 'depraved and excessive superstition'; Justin thought it was the truth. Both agree on what happened.
sections.key: Pliny, a hostile Roman governor (c. 112), and Justin (c. 155) describe the same weekly gathering: a fixed day, song or prayer to Christ, a moral life and a shared meal.

paras: Here is Justin's order, set out as a list. Nearly every Christian service today can be laid over it.

The great Anglican liturgist Gregory Dix (1901–1952) argued in The Shape of the Liturgy (1945) that this two-part pattern, the word and then the meal, is the backbone of Christian worship everywhere. Later scholars, such as Paul Bradshaw, warn that early worship was more varied than Dix thought: different cities did things differently, and we have only a few texts. But Justin's account is real evidence from Rome in the 150s, and its shape is unmistakable.

rows: Gathering on Sunday in one place
The gathering, often with a hymn
The Gospels or the prophets read
Deacons give to all and take to the absent
A collection for widows, orphans, the sick, prisoners and strangers
table.note: The order of Justin's chapter 67, with the kiss from chapter 65.

sections.key: Justin's order, word then meal, matches the shape of most services today; scholars debate how uniform early worship was.

paras: If every Sunday is a small Easter, Easter itself is the great Sunday. In the second century churches disagreed about its date. Christians in the province of Asia, in western Turkey, kept it on the fourteenth day of the Jewish month Nisan, the date of Passover, whatever day of the week it fell on; they were called 'Quartodecimans', the 'fourteenth' people. Rome and most other churches kept it on the Sunday after. In about 155 Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, visited Rome and failed to persuade its bishop Anicetus, but they shared the Eucharist and parted in peace, as the historian Eusebius records.

The Council of Nicaea in 325 settled that all should keep Easter on a Sunday. That is why Easter moves: it falls on the Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. Eastern and Western churches still often keep it on different Sundays, because the Orthodox calculate it with the older Julian calendar. Around Easter grew the whole Christian year: the forty days of Lent before it, the fifty days to Pentecost after it. All of it begins with one Sunday.
sections.key: Easter is the great Sunday; Nicaea (325) fixed it on a Sunday, and the Christian year grew around it.

paras: If you walk into a Catholic Mass, an Orthodox Divine Liturgy, an Anglican or Lutheran Eucharist, you will find Justin's pattern, with more words and more ceremony added over the centuries. In many Protestant churches, Reformed, Baptist, Methodist and Pentecostal, the second half, the meal, is held monthly or quarterly rather than weekly, so a typical Sunday has the first half: hymns, readings, a sermon and prayers. Quakers keep neither readings nor sermon fixed, and meet in silence; you will hear their case later in the journey.

So the differences between churches are real, but they are variations on one theme. Knowing Justin's chapter 67 is like knowing the plan of a house: whatever the furniture, you can find your way around.
sections.key: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran services keep both halves every Sunday; many Protestant churches keep the word weekly and the meal less often.

paras: The English word 'service' is revealing. It translates the Latin servitium and the Greek leitourgia, 'liturgy', which in Athens meant a public work done for the city at a citizen's own expense, such as paying for a warship or a festival chorus. In Greek Bibles it was used for the priests' work in the Temple. Christians used it for their worship: a public work, done by the people together, for God and for the world.

Justin's account shows what that work includes. It is praise and thanks to God. It is learning: the readings and the sermon. It is prayer for everyone. It is a meal that binds the community together. And it is practical charity: the collection for the poor. The Russian Orthodox theologian Alexander Schmemann, in For the Life of the World (1963), argued that the service is not an escape from ordinary life but its meaning: the Church gathers to offer the world to God in thanks, and is sent back into it. We will test that claim through the journey.
sections.key: 'Liturgy' meant a public work. The service is praise, learning, prayer, a shared meal and charity, done together.

debate.question: Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath?

positions.name: Sunday is the Lord's day, not the Sabbath
positions.who: Ignatius of Antioch, Justin; the Catholic and Orthodox Churches; Luther; most churches today
positions.view: The Sabbath was a sign for Israel, fulfilled in Christ. Christians meet on Sunday to celebrate the resurrection; rest is good, but the day is a feast, not a law.
positions.evidence: The first Christians met 'on the first day of the week' (Acts 20:7); Paul warns against judging people over 'a Sabbath day' (Colossians 2:16); Justin gives the resurrection as the reason for Sunday.

positions.name: Sunday is the Christian Sabbath
positions.who: The English and Scottish Puritans; the Westminster Confession (1646), chapter 21
positions.view: The fourth commandment still binds, but since the resurrection the day has moved to Sunday. The whole day should be kept holy, free of work and amusement.
positions.evidence: The commandment is part of the moral law given at creation (Genesis 2:3); the 'Lord's day' replaced the seventh. This view shaped the quiet British and American Sunday for three centuries.

positions.name: The Sabbath is still Saturday
positions.who: Seventh-day Adventists; Seventh Day Baptists; Messianic Jews
positions.view: God blessed the seventh day, and no text in the New Testament moves it. Christians should rest and worship on Saturday, as Jesus and the apostles did.
positions.evidence: Jesus kept the Sabbath (Luke 4:16); the commandment says 'the seventh day'; the change to Sunday came through later Church custom.

debate.agree: All three agree that one day in seven belongs to God and to rest, and that Christians gather weekly because of the resurrection; they differ on whether the commandment moved, and on how strictly to keep the day.

look.why: No painting of an early Christian gathering is in the National Gallery's open collection. This painting shows instead the reason for the day: Christ risen from the tomb, the event Justin gives for meeting on Sunday. (The painting also appears in 'Who was Jesus?' and other journeys.)
points: A man draped in a white cloth, Christ, steps towards us onto a ledge.
He holds a red staff with a long white banner bearing a red cross.
His raised right hand is held palm out to show it has been pierced, and there is a gash over his ribs.
His bare foot rests on a low wall or the side of a casket in front of him.
His whole body is surrounded by radiating lines within a glowing golden halo, with celestial blue in the corners.

music.why: Charles Wesley's Easter hymn. Every Sunday, Justin says, is the day of the resurrection, and many churches sing Easter hymns not only at Easter.

think.why: What the research says about people who meet every week, and what it cannot show.

learn.why: The psalm the first Christians read as a song of the resurrection, still sung on Easter Day and on Sundays: every Sunday is the day the Lord has made.

check.q: What is the main reason Justin gives for meeting on Sunday?
options: The Jews met on the same day
It was the day Jesus rose from the dead, and the first day of creation
It was the only day slaves were free
The emperor had made it a day of rest
check.why: Justin gives creation and, decisively, the resurrection. Constantine's Sunday law came over 150 years later.

check.q: Why does Justin describe the Christian service in such detail?
options: Because the emperor had asked for a liturgy book
To answer suspicion and rumour by showing outsiders exactly what Christians did
To train new priests
To persuade Jews to join
check.why: The First Apology is a defence addressed to the emperor; plain description was Justin's answer to rumours of secret crimes.

check.q: Which of these is NOT in Justin's account of a Sunday?
options: Readings from the Gospels or the prophets
A set prayer read from a book
A sermon urging people to live by the readings
A collection for widows, orphans and prisoners
check.why: The president prays 'according to his ability': in Justin's time the thanksgiving was not yet a fixed text.

check.q: What does the Didache require before someone joins the Sunday assembly?
options: That they can read
That they have been a Christian for three years
That they bring bread and wine
That they have made peace with anyone they have quarrelled with
check.why: No one with a dispute may join 'until they have been reconciled', echoing Matthew 5:24.

check.q: Pliny and Justin describe the same gatherings. Why does that matter to a historian?
options: Because a hostile witness and a friendly one, forty years apart, agree on the facts while disagreeing about their meaning
Because Justin was a Roman governor
Because Pliny copied Justin
Because both were Christians
check.why: Independent witnesses with opposite sympathies, agreeing on what happened, make the account far more secure.

check.q: Which best describes how most services today relate to Justin's?
options: Only the collection survives
Only the Orthodox keep any of it
They keep his two-part shape, word then meal, though some churches hold the meal less often
They are completely different
check.why: The word and the table are still the two halves; many Protestant churches hold the meal monthly or quarterly.

tutorial.question: Why do Christians gather on Sunday, and what did the earliest gatherings do?
tutorial.approach: Start with the Sabbath and why the first Christians, though Jews, also met on the first day. Use Acts 20, the Didache 14, Pliny and Justin as evidence, in date order. Then set out Justin's order and compare it with a service you know or can find described. End with what the word 'liturgy' suggests a service is for.
strong: Explains the Sabbath and the reasons for Sunday: creation and, above all, the resurrection.
Uses the evidence in order: Acts 20, the Didache, Pliny, Justin.
Sets out Justin's order: readings, sermon, prayers, kiss, bread and wine with thanksgiving, Amen, distribution, collection.
Notes Pliny's value as a hostile witness.
Mentions the debate over how uniform early worship was (Dix and Bradshaw).
Connects worship with care for the poor.

reading.why: A clear, up-to-date account of how the first Christians worshipped, with the evidence.

reading.author: Abraham Joshua Heschel
reading.title: The Sabbath
reading.why: A short, beautiful Jewish book on holy time, to understand what Sunday grew out of.
