reading.why: The standard scholarly warning against tidy accounts of early worship.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: keep one part of Sunday different. Set aside an hour, the same hour, for something you would not do on a working day: a walk with someone, a meal shared, or simply sitting in a church while a service is on, at the back.
sessions.reflect: What, if anything, makes one day of your week different from the others? What would you want it to be for?
takeaways: Christians meet on Sunday because it was the day of the resurrection, and the first day of creation; Sunday gradually took the Sabbath's place.
Justin's First Apology (about AD 155) gives the oldest full order of service: readings, sermon, prayers, the kiss, bread and wine with thanksgiving and Amen, Communion and a collection for the poor.
Acts 20, the Didache and the hostile witness Pliny show the same weekly gathering even earlier; most services today keep its two-part shape.

sessions.title: Water
sessions.line: Baptism: why Christians go under the water, once, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and why they argue about babies.
sessions.plain: Baptism is how a person becomes a Christian: they are washed with water, or plunged into it, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Paul says it is like being buried with Christ and rising with him to a new life. This session reads Paul and Jesus's command, then three ancient accounts of how it was done, and asks the question that still divides churches: should babies be baptised, or only believers who can choose?
sessions.why: Session 1 showed the Sunday gathering, and Justin began it with a newcomer 'after we have thus washed him'. Baptism is the door into that room. Before we can understand the word or the table, we need to know how someone comes in, and what Christians think happens at the door.
answers: What is baptism, and where did it come from?
What does it mean, according to the Bible?
How was it done in the early Church?
Why do some churches baptise babies, and others only adults?
Do I have to be baptised to be a Christian?
sessions.finding: Baptism is the door into the Church: a washing once for all, in water and in the name of the Trinity, which Paul calls dying and rising with Christ; Christians agree on that, and differ over whether it is for infants as well as believers.

paras: Washing as a sign of becoming clean is very old. The Law of Moses required ritual washings after certain kinds of uncleanness (Leviticus 15). By the time of Jesus, Jews used stone-lined pools for ritual immersion; archaeologists have found hundreds from the first century, many around the Temple in Jerusalem. The Hebrew word is mikveh. Later Jewish sources describe Gentiles who converted to Judaism being immersed; how early that practice began is debated.

Then came John the Baptist, a prophet in the wilderness by the Jordan in about AD 28. He called people to repent and be baptised as a sign that they were turning their lives around, ready for God's coming judgement. Jesus himself came to be baptised by John. The Gospels say that as he came up out of the water the Spirit came down on him like a dove, and a voice said, 'You are my beloved Son' (Mark 1:9–11).
background.key: Jews used ritual washing and immersion pools; John the Baptist called for a once-only baptism of repentance, and baptised Jesus in the Jordan.

background.h: From John's baptism to the Church's
paras: After the resurrection, the first Christians baptised new believers from the very first day. Peter, preaching at Pentecost in Jerusalem, says: 'Repent, and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit' (Acts 2:38). Acts goes on to describe baptisms of individuals, such as an Ethiopian official on a desert road, and of whole households, such as a Roman jailer's 'and all his household' (Acts 16:33).

Christian baptism kept John's sign of washing and repentance, but added two things: it was done in the name of Jesus, or of the Father, Son and Spirit, and it brought a person into the community of his followers. You could be baptised by John and remain where you were; after Christian baptism you belonged to the Church.
background.key: From the first day, the Church baptised new believers, individuals and whole households, in the name of Jesus, as the way into the community.

paras: Paul wrote his letter to the Romans in about AD 57, from Corinth, to a church he had not yet visited. It is his fullest statement of what he believed. In chapter 6 he answers an objection: if God forgives freely, why not go on sinning? His answer is baptism.

Matthew's Gospel was written in the later first century, most scholars think between AD 70 and 90. It ends with the risen Jesus on a mountain in Galilee, sending his followers out to make disciples and baptise them. Some scholars think the threefold name was the wording of baptism in Matthew's own church, put on Jesus's lips; others accept it as his command. Either way, it is the formula used ever since.
background.key: Romans (about AD 57) explains what baptism means; Matthew (about AD 70–90) gives the command and the threefold name.

before: What picture does Paul use for going under the water, and for coming up?
What three things does Jesus command in Matthew 28?
In the comparison texts, notice what has to happen before the baptism itself.
sessions.readWhy: Paul's explanation of what baptism means, and the risen Jesus's command to baptise.

paras: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?
Or don’t you know that all we who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection;
knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.
For he who has died has been freed from sin.
But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him;
knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over him!
For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God.
Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had sent them.
When they saw him, they bowed down to him, but some doubted.
Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.
Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.

parts.title: Buried and raised with him
parts.context: Paul has spent five chapters arguing that God accepts people not because they keep the law perfectly but freely, by grace, through faith in Christ. Now he imagines an objection: then why not keep sinning, so that there is more grace? He answers by reminding the Romans of their baptism.

commentary.on: Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? May it never be!
commentary.text: Paul's objector has a point: if forgiveness is free, why change? Paul's answer is not a rule but a reminder of who they now are. Baptism is his argument.

commentary.on: all we who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death
commentary.text: The Greek baptizo means to dip or plunge. Paul takes the picture literally: to be plunged into Christ is to be plunged into his death. He assumes all his readers have been baptised; there were no unbaptised Christians.

commentary.on: We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death
commentary.text: Going under the water is like being buried. Early baptisms were usually by immersion, so the picture was vivid: you went down into the water as into a grave. Your old life, Paul says, is dead and buried.

commentary.on: so we also might walk in newness of life
commentary.text: Coming up out of the water is like rising from the dead. 'Walk' is a Jewish way of speaking about how you live day by day. Baptism happens once; the new life it begins is lived every day after.

commentary.on: our old man was crucified with him
commentary.text: 'The old man' means the old self, the person you were before. Paul uses the same picture elsewhere: 'put off the old man' and 'put on the new' (Ephesians 4:22–24), which is why the newly baptised were later dressed in white.

commentary.on: Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
commentary.text: 'Consider yourselves': Paul asks them to live from what baptism says about them. Martin Luther, when tempted to despair, is said to have written on his desk 'I am baptised'. Baptism was not a feeling but a fact he could hold on to.

parts.title: Go and make disciples
parts.context: The last words of Matthew's Gospel. After the resurrection, the eleven remaining disciples (Judas is dead) go to Galilee, the region in the north where Jesus had first called them, and meet him on a mountain.

commentary.on: When they saw him, they bowed down to him, but some doubted.
commentary.text: An honest detail: even at the end, some doubted. The Church was founded by people with mixed faith, and Matthew does not hide it.

commentary.on: Go and make disciples of all nations
commentary.text: The command is to make 'disciples', learners and followers, not just converts. And it is for 'all nations': no longer only Israel. This is the charter of a world-wide faith.

commentary.on: baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
commentary.text: One name, three persons. This is the formula of Christian baptism in almost every church today: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches recognise a baptism done with water and these words. It is also one of the roots of the doctrine of the Trinity.

commentary.on: teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you
commentary.text: Baptism is not the end but the beginning: teaching follows. That is why, as we will see, the early Church taught people both before baptism and after it.

commentary.on: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.
commentary.text: Matthew's Gospel began with the name 'Immanuel', 'God with us' (Matthew 1:23); it ends with the same promise. Christians believe this presence is what they meet in the water, the word and the bread.

paras: But concerning baptism, thus shall ye baptize. Having first recited all these things, baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit in living (running) water. But if thou hast not living water, then baptize in other water; and if thou art not able in cold, then in warm. But if thou hast neither, then pour water on the head thrice in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. But before the baptism let him that baptizeth and him that is baptized fast, and any others also who are able; and thou shalt order him that is baptized to fast a day or two before.

I will also relate the manner in which we dedicated ourselves to God when we had been made new through Christ; lest, if we omit this, we seem to be unfair in the explanation we are making. As many as are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and undertake to be able to live accordingly, are instructed to pray and to entreat God with fasting, for the remission of their sins that are past, we praying and fasting with them. Then they are brought by us where there is water, and are regenerated in the same manner in which we were ourselves regenerated. For, in the name of God, the Father and Lord of the universe, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they then receive the washing with water. For Christ also said, Unless you be born again, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.

And for this [rite] we have learned from the apostles this reason. Since at our birth we were born without our own knowledge or choice, by our parents coming together, and were brought up in bad habits and wicked training; in order that we may not remain the children of necessity and of ignorance, but may become the children of choice and knowledge, and may obtain in the water the remission of sins formerly committed, there is pronounced over him who chooses to be born again, and has repented of his sins, the name of God the Father and Lord of the universe; he who leads to the laver the person that is to be washed calling him by this name alone. For no one can utter the name of the ineffable God; and if any one dare to say that there is a name, he raves with a hopeless madness. And this washing is called illumination, because they who learn these things are illuminated in their understandings. And in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and in the name of the Holy Ghost, who through the prophets foretold all things about Jesus, he who is illuminated is washed.

4. But nevertheless you are bidden to say, with arm outstretched towards him as though he were present, I renounce you, Satan. I wish also to say wherefore ye stand facing to the West; for it is necessary. Since the West is the region of sensible darkness, and he being darkness has his dominion also in darkness, therefore, looking with a symbolic meaning towards the West, you renounce that dark and gloomy potentate. What then did each of you stand up and say? I renounce you, Satan,— you wicked and most cruel tyrant! Meaning, I fear your might no longer; for that Christ has overthrown, having partaken with me of flesh and blood, that through these He might by death destroy death, that I might not be made subject to bondage forever. I renounce you,— you crafty and most subtle serpent. I renounce you,— plotter as you are, who under the guise of friendship contrived all disobedience, and work apostasy in our first parents. I renounce you, Satan,— the artificer and abettor of all wickedness.

9. When therefore you renounce Satan, utterly breaking all your covenant with him, that ancient league with hell, there is opened to you the paradise of God, which He planted towards the East, whence for his transgression our first father was banished; and a symbol of this was your turning from West to East, the place of light. Then you were told to say, I believe in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Ghost, and in one Baptism of repentance. Of which things we spoke to you at length in the former Lectures, as God's grace allowed us.

2. As soon, then, as you entered, you put off your tunic; and this was an image of putting off the old man with his deeds. Having stripped yourselves, you were naked; in this also imitating Christ, who was stripped naked on the Cross, and by His nakedness put off from Himself the principalities and powers, and openly triumphed over them on the tree. For since the adverse powers made their lair in your members, you may no longer wear that old garment; I do not at all mean this visible one, but the old man, which waxes corrupt in the lusts of deceit. May the soul which has once put him off, never again put him on, but say with the Spouse of Christ in the Song of Songs, I have put off my garment, how shall I put it on? O wondrous thing! You were naked in the sight of all, and were not ashamed; for truly ye bore the likeness of the first-formed Adam, who was naked in the garden, and was not ashamed.

3. Then, when you were stripped, you were anointed with exorcised oil, from the very hairs of your head to your feet, and were made partakers of the good olive-tree, Jesus Christ. For you were cut off from the wild olive-tree, and grafted into the good one, and were made to share the fatness of the true olive-tree. The exorcised oil therefore was a symbol of the participation of the fatness of Christ, being a charm to drive away every trace of hostile influence. For as the breathing of the saints, and the invocation of the Name of God, like fiercest flame, scorch and drive out evil spirits, so also this exorcised oil receives such virtue by the invocation of God and by prayer, as not only to burn and cleanse away the traces of sins, but also to chase away all the invisible powers of the evil one.

4. After these things, you were led to the holy pool of Divine Baptism, as Christ was carried from the Cross to the Sepulchre which is before our eyes. And each of you was asked, whether he believed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, and you made that saving confession, and descended three times into the water, and ascended again; here also hinting by a symbol at the three days burial of Christ. For as our Saviour passed three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, so you also in your first ascent out of the water, represented the first day of Christ in the earth, and by your descent, the night; for as he who is in the night, no longer sees, but he who is in the day, remains in the light, so in the descent, as in the night, you saw nothing, but in ascending again you were as in the day. And at the self-same moment you were both dying and being born; and that Water of salvation was at once your grave and your mother. And what Solomon spoke of others will suit you also; for he said, in that case, There is a time to bear and a time to die; but to you, in the reverse order, there was a time to die and a time to be born; and one and the same time effected both of these, and your birth went hand in hand with your death.

5. O strange and inconceivable thing! We did not really die, we were not really buried, we were not really crucified and raised again; but our imitation was in a figure, and our salvation in reality. Christ was actually crucified, and actually buried, and truly rose again; and all these things He has freely bestowed upon us, that we, sharing His sufferings by imitation, might gain salvation in reality. O surpassing loving-kindness! Christ received nails in His undefiled hands and feet, and suffered anguish; while on me without pain or toil by the fellowship of His suffering He freely bestows salvation.

parts.author: Anonymous
parts.work: The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
parts.translator: J. B. Lightfoot, ed. J. R. Harmer (1891)
parts.who: An unknown teacher or teachers in the earliest Church, writing for Gentile converts
parts.when: Probably Syria, between about AD 50 and 120
parts.title: Living water
parts.context: The Didache's instructions on baptism, written perhaps between AD 50 and 120. 'All these things' means the moral teaching of the Didache's first six chapters, which you read some of in 'The first Christians': the candidate was taught first. 'Living water' means running water, as in a river or spring.
parts.plain: This is how to baptise. First teach all of this. Then baptise in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in running water. If there is none, use other water, cold if possible, warm if not. If you have neither, pour water three times on the head, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Before the baptism, the one baptising and the one being baptised should fast, with others if they can.

commentary.on: Having first recited all these things
commentary.text: Teaching comes before baptism. The candidate learns the way of life first, and then is baptised. This is the beginning of what became the 'catechumenate', a period of instruction.

commentary.on: baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit in living (running) water
commentary.text: The same words as Matthew 28, within a few decades of the Gospel. Running water was best, like the Jordan where Jesus was baptised.

commentary.on: then pour water on the head thrice
commentary.text: This is the earliest evidence that pouring was allowed when immersion was not possible. It matters for later arguments: churches that baptise by pouring, as most do, can point to the Didache; churches that insist on immersion point to its first preference.

commentary.on: before the baptism let him that baptizeth and him that is baptized fast
commentary.text: Fasting prepares body and mind. The whole community could join in. This is one root of Lent, the forty days before Easter, when in later centuries candidates prepared for baptism.

parts.author: Justin Martyr
parts.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers I (1885)
parts.who: Justin Martyr (c. 100–165), a philosopher from Samaria who became a Christian and taught in Rome, where he was executed
parts.title: Born again by choice
parts.context: Justin's account of baptism, from the chapter just before the Sunday gathering you read in session 1. The cut is marked '…'. 'Regenerated' means born again. 'Laver' means a basin or pool for washing.
parts.plain: Those who believe our teaching and promise to live by it are taught to pray and fast for forgiveness, and we pray and fast with them. Then we take them to water and they are born again, washed in the name of the Father, of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit. We were born the first time without choosing it, into bad habits; in baptism we are born again by our own choice and knowledge. That is why it is called 'illumination': the mind is lit up.

commentary.on: As many as are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and undertake to be able to live accordingly
commentary.text: Justin describes adults who choose: they believe, and they promise to live a new life. Baptist and other believer-baptising churches often quote this passage.

commentary.on: we praying and fasting with them
commentary.text: The whole community prepares with the candidate. Baptism is not a private ceremony.

commentary.on: Unless you be born again, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven
commentary.text: Justin quotes Jesus's words to Nicodemus in John 3:3–5, in a slightly different form from our Gospel text. 'Born again' first meant baptism.

commentary.on: may become the children of choice and knowledge
commentary.text: A philosopher's point. Our first birth happened to us without our choice; the second is chosen. To a Greek reader this was baptism as freedom: no longer 'children of necessity'.

commentary.on: this washing is called illumination
commentary.text: The newly baptised were called 'the enlightened', and Eastern Christians still call baptism 'illumination'. It is why candles are given at baptisms in many churches today.

parts.author: Cyril of Jerusalem
parts.translator: E. H. Gifford, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, VII (1894)
parts.who: Cyril (c. 313–386), bishop of Jerusalem, or possibly his successor John
parts.ref: Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Lecture 1.4 and 1.9
parts.title: Facing west, then east
parts.context: About two hundred years after Justin, in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, built by Constantine over the place where Jesus was believed to have been buried and raised. In the week after Easter, the bishop explained to the newly baptised what had happened to them on Easter night: these talks are called 'mystagogical', leading into the mysteries. The manuscripts credit them to Cyril (bishop 350–386); some scholars think they are by his successor John. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Before you were baptised, you stood facing west, the direction of darkness, stretched out your arm and said, 'I renounce you, Satan', as if he were in front of you. You were saying: I am no longer afraid of you, because Christ has broken your power. Then you turned east, towards the light and the garden of paradise, and said what you believe: in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and in one baptism of repentance.

commentary.on: with arm outstretched towards him as though he were present, I renounce you, Satan
commentary.text: Baptism began with a dramatic refusal. Candidates turned their backs on evil out loud. Many baptism services today still ask, 'Do you reject the devil and all rebellion against God?' or 'Do you turn away from sin?'

commentary.on: ye stand facing to the West
commentary.text: West is where the sun goes down: darkness. Churches were built facing east, towards the sunrise and the expected return of Christ, which is why most old churches still point east.

commentary.on: I fear your might no longer
commentary.text: Cyril explains the renunciation as freedom from fear. Echoing Hebrews 2:14–15, he says Christ shared our flesh and blood to destroy the one who held the power of death.

commentary.on: a symbol of this was your turning from West to East, the place of light
commentary.text: The candidate physically turns round. 'Conversion' means turning, and here it is acted out with the whole body.

commentary.on: I believe in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Ghost, and in one Baptism of repentance
commentary.text: After the renunciation comes the profession of faith. These short statements of belief, said at baptism, grew into the creeds, such as the Apostles' Creed.

parts.author: Cyril of Jerusalem
parts.translator: E. H. Gifford, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, VII (1894)
parts.who: Cyril (c. 313–386), bishop of Jerusalem, or possibly his successor John
parts.title: Your grave and your mother
parts.context: The second lecture, given the next day, explains what happened at the pool. Candidates were baptised naked, men and women separately, with women assisted by women. 'Exorcised oil' is olive oil prayed over to drive away evil. The 'Sepulchre which is before our eyes' is the tomb of Jesus, inside the church where Cyril was speaking.
parts.plain: When you went in, you took off your tunic: a sign of putting off your old self, as Christ was stripped on the cross. You were anointed all over with oil, a sign of being grafted into Christ, the true olive tree. Then you were led to the pool, as Christ was carried to the tomb. You were asked if you believed in the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, said yes, and went down into the water three times and came up three times, like Christ's three days in the tomb. In that moment you died and were born: the water was your grave and your mother. We did not really die; we imitated his death in a sign. But our salvation is real.

commentary.on: you put off your tunic; and this was an image of putting off the old man with his deeds
commentary.text: Paul's picture of the 'old man' in Romans 6 becomes a physical act. You strip off your old clothes, go through the water, and come out to be dressed in white.

commentary.on: you were anointed with exorcised oil
commentary.text: Oil was used in the ancient world for athletes and the sick. Anointing at baptism survives in the Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican and Lutheran services.

commentary.on: descended three times into the water, and ascended again
commentary.text: Three immersions, one for each person of the Trinity, and for Christ's three days in the tomb. The Orthodox Church still baptises by threefold immersion, babies included.

commentary.on: that Water of salvation was at once your grave and your mother
commentary.text: One of the great sentences of early Christianity. The water is both tomb and womb: you die in it and are born from it. This is Romans 6 turned into poetry.

commentary.on: our imitation was in a figure, and our salvation in reality
commentary.text: Cyril is careful. The candidates did not literally die. The rite is a figure, a sign. But what it signifies, Christ's death and resurrection and their share in it, is real. This distinction between sign and reality will matter a great deal when Christians later argue about the bread and wine.

compare.author: Anonymous and Justin Martyr and Cyril of Jerusalem
compare.work: The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles
compare.translator: J. B. Lightfoot, ed. J. R. Harmer (1891)
compare.why: Paul tells us what baptism means; these three texts tell us how it was done, from a first-century handbook to a fourth-century bishop speaking to the newly baptised in Jerusalem.
compare.title: How it was done: three ancient witnesses

paras: The New Testament piles up pictures for baptism. It is a washing: 'be baptized, and wash away your sins' (Acts 22:16). It is a burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6). It is a new birth, 'of water and Spirit' (John 3:5). It is putting on Christ like a garment (Galatians 3:27). It is the way into one body: 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free' (1 Corinthians 12:13). The Church's later teaching gathers these up: in baptism, sins are forgiven, the Spirit is given, and a person is joined to Christ and to his people.

Christians call baptism a 'sacrament' (from the Latin sacramentum, a soldier's oath, used to translate the Greek mysterion, 'mystery'). Augustine of Hippo (354–430) gave the classic definition: a visible sign of an invisible grace. Some Protestant churches prefer the word 'ordinance', something Christ ordered his followers to do, to avoid any suggestion that the water itself does anything.
sections.key: Baptism is washing, burial and rising, new birth, putting on Christ and joining one body; Christians call it a sacrament (a visible sign of invisible grace) or an ordinance.

paras: Baptism is done once. A Christian may fall away and come back, but is not baptised again: Paul speaks of 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism' (Ephesians 4:5), and the Nicene Creed, as finalised in 381, confesses 'one baptism for the remission of sins'. In the third and fourth centuries a bitter dispute arose over people baptised by heretics or by clergy who had lapsed under persecution. The Church of Rome, and later Augustine against the Donatists of North Africa, held that baptism with water in the name of the Trinity is valid whoever performs it, because it is Christ who baptises.

That principle has ecumenical consequences today. The Catholic Church recognises the baptism of Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and Baptists, if water and the threefold name were used. The World Council of Churches' document Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (Lima, 1982) asked all churches to avoid anything that looks like rebaptism. Practice in the Orthodox churches varies: some receive other Christians by chrismation, anointing, and some, especially on Mount Athos and in parts of the Greek and Russian churches, rebaptise.
sections.key: Baptism is once for all; since Augustine the Western Church has held that any baptism with water and the threefold name is valid, and most churches recognise each other's.

sections.h: Becoming a Christian in the early Church
paras: By about AD 200, joining the Church took time. A document called the Apostolic Tradition, traditionally ascribed to Hippolytus of Rome (about 215, though its date and authorship are now much debated), describes a period of instruction that could last three years. Candidates, called 'catechumens' (learners), heard the readings and sermon but left before the meal. Their way of life was examined. Some trades were forbidden: a gladiator, for instance, had to give up his work.

Baptism was normally at Easter, at the night vigil, so that candidates died and rose with Christ on the very night of the resurrection. Afterwards, in Easter week, the bishop explained what they had experienced, as Cyril does. A pilgrim called Egeria, probably from Spain or Gaul, saw this in Jerusalem in about 381–384 and described in her travel diary how the newly baptised applauded the bishop's explanations so loudly they could be heard outside the church.
sections.key: By about 200, candidates (catechumens) were taught, sometimes for years, baptised at the Easter vigil, and taught again afterwards.

paras: The oldest known church building, a house converted for worship at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates in Syria, before the town was destroyed in 256, has a room with a basin under a canopy, painted with the Good Shepherd and Adam and Eve. It is now reconstructed at the Yale University Art Gallery. After Constantine, great baptisteries were built beside cathedrals, often eight-sided for the 'eighth day' of resurrection. An inscription attributed to Ambrose of Milan explained the eight sides in just this way.

Some early fonts had steps going down on one side and up on the other: down into death, up into life. Many were shaped like a cross or a tomb. Later, as most candidates were babies, fonts became raised basins near the church door, which is where you will usually find one in an old English church: at the entrance, because baptism is the way in. Many Baptist churches have a pool under the floor at the front, opened for baptisms.
sections.key: From the house church at Dura-Europos (before 256) to octagonal baptisteries and fonts by the door, the building shows that baptism is the way in.

paras: The Didache prefers running water and allows pouring. Ancient art and fonts suggest that many early baptisms had the candidate standing in shallow water while water was poured over the head, a mixture of the two. Full immersion is the practice of the Orthodox churches, babies included, and of Baptists, Pentecostals and many evangelicals. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and the Reformed usually pour water on the head, three times or once; some sprinkle.

Does the amount of water matter? The churches that pour say the sign is washing, and a little water signifies it truly, as the Didache allows. The churches that immerse say Paul's picture of burial needs a real going-under, and that baptizo means to plunge. Both agree that the water must be real and the name must be the Trinity's.
sections.key: Orthodox and Baptists immerse; Catholics, Anglicans and most Protestants pour or sprinkle. All agree on real water and the threefold name.

paras: The New Testament describes the baptism of believers, and of whole 'households' (Acts 16:33; 1 Corinthians 1:16), which may or may not have included children. The first clear mentions of infant baptism come around AD 200. Tertullian of Carthage, in On Baptism 18 (about 200), advised delay: let children come when they can know Christ. Origen (about 185–254) said the Church had received from the apostles the custom of baptising infants. In 253 a council at Carthage under Cyprian ruled that babies need not wait until the eighth day. Augustine's teaching on original sin made infant baptism urgent, and it became the norm.

In January 1525 in Zurich, a group of the Reformer Zwingli's former followers, led by Conrad Grebel, baptised one another as adults. They were called Anabaptists, 'rebaptisers', and were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike; Felix Manz was drowned in the river Limmat in 1527. The Baptists, beginning with John Smyth's congregation of English exiles in Amsterdam in 1609, took up believer's baptism and are now among the largest Protestant families in the world.
sections.key: Infant baptism is clearly attested from about 200 and became the norm; Anabaptists (1525) and Baptists (1609) returned to the baptism of believers only.

paras: Here is how baptism is done in the main traditions today. If you attend a service with a baptism, this is what you will see.

rows: Chrismation (anointing) and first Communion straight away, even for babies
Confirmation and first Communion later (usually around age 7 to 16); adults receive all three at once, often at Easter
Confirmation by a bishop later; many now admit children to Communion before
Infants of believers and adult converts
Profession of faith or confirmation later
Believers only, who can profess faith
Membership of the church; babies are presented and blessed instead
They hold that the inward baptism of the Spirit is what matters
table.note: Practices vary within each tradition; this is the usual pattern.

sections.key: Orthodox, Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Reformed and Methodists baptise infants; Baptists and Pentecostals baptise believers by immersion; Quakers and the Salvation Army do not baptise with water.

refs: Romans 6:1–11; Matthew 28:16–20; Mark 1:9–11; John 3:3–5; Acts 2:38; 8:26–39; 16:33; 22:16; 1 Corinthians 1:16; 12:13; Galatians 3:27; Ephesians 4:5, 22–24.
Didache 7, tr. Lightfoot (1891); Justin, First Apology 61; Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Lectures 1–2, tr. Gifford, NPNF II.7 (1894).

Apostolic Tradition 15–21 (ed. Bradshaw, Johnson and Phillips, Hermeneia 2002); Egeria, Travels 46–47; Tertullian, On Baptism 18; Origen, Commentary on Romans 5.9; Cyprian, Letter 64 (58 in some editions).
Augustine, On Baptism, against the Donatists; Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381); World Council of Churches, Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (Faith and Order Paper 111, 1982).
Everett Ferguson, Baptism in the Early Church (2009); Carl H. Kraeling, The Christian Building (Dura-Europos, 1967).
On the Anabaptists: the first baptisms in Zurich, 21 January 1525; Felix Manz, executed 5 January 1527; John Smyth's congregation, Amsterdam, 1609.

debate.question: Should babies be baptised, or only believers?

positions.name: Infants, as members of the covenant
positions.who: Origen; Augustine; the Catholic and Orthodox Churches; Luther, Calvin and Cranmer; Anglicans, Lutherans, Reformed and Methodists
positions.view: Baptism is God's gift before it is our response. As Jewish boys were circumcised as babies into God's covenant, so Christian children are baptised into the Church and raised in faith, which they later make their own. Grace comes first.
positions.evidence: Household baptisms (Acts 16:33); 'the promise is to you, and to your children' (Acts 2:39); Jesus: 'Allow the little children to come to me' (Mark 10:14); Origen's claim of an apostolic custom; baptism replacing circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12).

positions.name: Believers only
positions.who: Tertullian (who advised delay); the Anabaptists; Baptists, Pentecostals, Churches of Christ and many evangelicals
positions.view: Baptism is a sign of faith and repentance, and a baby can have neither. Every baptism in the New Testament follows belief. Infant baptism risks making people think they are Christians because something was done to them, whatever they believe.
positions.evidence: 'Repent, and be baptized' (Acts 2:38); Justin's candidates who are 'persuaded and believe'; 'buried with him in baptism… through faith' (Colossians 2:12); no clear case of an infant baptism in the New Testament.

positions.name: Both, side by side
positions.who: Many modern ecumenical theologians; the Lima document (1982); some Methodist, Reformed and united churches
positions.view: Both practices honour real parts of the truth: God's grace before we respond, and the need for personal faith. Churches can recognise each other's baptisms, offer infant baptism with later confirmation, or dedication with later believer's baptism.
positions.evidence: The early Church clearly had adult converts and, at least from about 200, infants; Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry calls the two 'equivalent alternatives' when each is followed by growth in faith within the community.

debate.agree: All agree that baptism is with water, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, once, into Christ's death and resurrection, and that it must lead to a life of faith.

look.why: Giovanni Baronzio, a painter from Rimini, made this panel in about 1335. It shows Jesus's baptism by John in the Jordan, the baptism that Christians believe gives theirs its meaning.
points: Jesus stands hip-deep in a stylised river, his hands together in prayer, his head tipped to one side.
The water is painted slate blue with regular, white, curving lines to suggest it flowing.
On a rocky bank to our left a bearded man in a brown, fur-like garment under a white robe, John the Baptist, touches Jesus's head with his right hand and holds a staff in the other.
On the other side, two winged angels stand facing Jesus with their hands together in prayer; one has a patterned cloth draped over its arm.
In a blue half-circle with gold starbursts at the top, a smaller bearded figure in a white robe hovers over the scene, lifting his right hand towards Jesus and holding a book with a crimson cover.
Everything is set against a gleaming gold background, with a gold border.

music.why: A medieval Italian prayer to the Holy Spirit. Peter promised the Spirit to all who were baptised (Acts 2:38), and in the Gospels the Spirit came down on Jesus as he rose from the water.

think.why: Baptism rehearses a death and a resurrection. See what Christians believe about the real ones.

learn.why: Paul's one sentence on what baptism means: buried with Christ, raised to walk in newness of life.

check.q: In Romans 6, why does Paul bring up baptism?
options: To argue for infant baptism
To describe Jesus's baptism by John
To explain how to baptise
To answer the objection that free grace means we may as well go on sinning
check.why: His answer to 'shall we continue in sin?' is that the baptised have died to the old life and been raised to a new one.

check.q: What does the Didache allow when there is no running water at all?
options: The baptism must be postponed
Pouring water three times on the head in the threefold name
Baptism with oil instead
Baptism in the name of Jesus only
check.why: It prefers running water, then other water, then pouring three times: the earliest evidence that pouring was accepted.

check.q: Cyril says the candidates 'did not really die'. Why does he say this?
options: Because some had been raised from the dead
To argue against immersion
To admit that baptism means nothing
To distinguish the sign, an imitation of Christ's death, from the reality it gives, salvation
check.why: 'Our imitation was in a figure, and our salvation in reality': the rite is a sign, but what it signifies is real.

check.q: Why did Augustine and the Western Church refuse to rebaptise people baptised by heretics?
options: Because they held that Christ is the one who baptises, so a baptism with water and the threefold name is valid whoever performs it
Because the emperor forbade it
Because water was scarce
Because heretics' baptisms were better
check.why: Validity rests on Christ, not the minister's worthiness; that is why most churches recognise one another's baptisms today.

check.q: Which of these is the strongest evidence for the believers-only view?
options: The baptism of Jesus as an adult
Household baptisms in Acts
Every baptism described in the New Testament follows a hearing of the gospel and faith
Origen's statement about an apostolic custom
check.why: Household baptisms and Origen support infant baptism; Jesus's baptism was John's, not Christian baptism. The pattern of faith first is the Baptist case.

check.q: A Catholic and a Baptist disagree about infant baptism. What do they agree on?
options: That baptism is optional
That baptism should use water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, once, into Christ's death and resurrection
Whether confirmation is needed
That babies should be immersed
check.why: The water, the threefold name, once only and the meaning are shared; who and how are disputed.

tutorial.question: Should churches baptise babies?
tutorial.approach: Begin with what baptism means in Romans 6 and Matthew 28, and how it was done in the Didache, Justin and Cyril. Then set out the evidence for infant baptism (households, Origen, the covenant) and against (faith first, Tertullian's advice). Explain how Augustine and the Anabaptists changed the debate. Give your own view, and say what the other side gets right.
strong: Explains Paul's picture of burial and resurrection, and the threefold name.
Uses the ancient sources: teaching and fasting first (Didache, Justin), the renunciation and immersion (Cyril).
Weighs the household baptisms and Origen against the pattern of faith first and Tertullian.
Explains the role of Augustine and original sin, and of the Anabaptists in 1525.
Notes what both sides agree on, and the ecumenical recognition of baptism.
Reaches a reasoned view and states the best objection to it fairly.

reading.author: Rowan Williams
reading.title: Being Christian: Baptism, Bible, Eucharist, Prayer
reading.why: Four short chapters by a former Archbishop of Canterbury; the first is on baptism.

reading.author: Everett Ferguson
reading.title: Baptism in the Early Church
reading.why: The fullest survey of the evidence for baptism in the first five centuries.

reading.author: World Council of Churches
reading.title: Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry
reading.why: The short Lima text in which most churches set out what they agree on.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: find out where and when you were baptised, if you were, and who was there. If you were not, find the font in a church near you, usually by the door, and stand beside it for a minute. Either way, each morning this week, as you wash your face, say one line: 'buried with him, raised to newness of life.'
sessions.reflect: Paul says the baptised should 'consider' themselves dead to the old life. What in your old life would you most want to leave in the water?
takeaways: Baptism grew out of Jewish washings and John's baptism of repentance; from the first day the Church baptised new believers in Jesus's name, as the way into the community.
Paul calls it being buried and raised with Christ; the Didache, Justin and Cyril show teaching and fasting first, the renunciation, immersion or pouring in the threefold name, and teaching after.
All churches agree on water, the threefold name and once only; they differ over infants or believers, and immersion or pouring.

sessions.title: The word
sessions.line: Readings, psalms, a sermon and a creed: the half of the service the Church inherited from the synagogue.
sessions.plain: The first half of almost every Christian service is words: readings from the Bible, psalms and hymns, a sermon and a creed. This session shows where that came from: the Jewish synagogue, where Scripture was read aloud every Sabbath and someone explained it. It reads the New Testament's own instructions for reading aloud, and then the opening of Morning Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer, the English service book that shaped how millions of people heard the Bible for four hundred years.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed how someone comes in through baptism; Justin's Sunday began with readings 'as long as time permits' and a sermon. The early Church taught before baptism and after it, and the readings were how most Christians, who could not read, met the Scriptures at all. Now we look at that first half of the service: what is read, why, and why Christians sing and say what they believe.
answers: Why are there readings and a sermon in church?
How do churches choose what to read each week?
Why do Christians sing hymns and psalms?
What is the creed, and why is it said?
What is the Book of Common Prayer?
sessions.finding: From the synagogue the Church kept readings, psalms and a sermon, and added the apostles' letters and the creed: the service teaches as well as prays, and most Christians learned their Bible by hearing it there.

paras: A synagogue (from the Greek for 'gathering') is a Jewish house of prayer and study. By the time of Jesus there were synagogues in towns across Galilee and Judea and throughout the Jewish communities of the Roman empire. The Temple in Jerusalem was the one place of sacrifice; the synagogue was the local place where the Law was read and taught every Sabbath.

The pattern was simple. The Torah, the five books of Moses, was read aloud in order, and then a passage from the prophets. Then someone might explain it or preach. Luke's Gospel tells how Jesus, at Nazareth, stood up to read from the scroll of Isaiah and then sat down to teach (Luke 4:16–21). Long before, Ezra had read the Law to the people of Jerusalem while the Levites 'gave the sense': you read that passage, Nehemiah 8, in 'What is the Bible?'.
background.key: The synagogue was the local Jewish house of prayer and study, where the Law and the prophets were read every Sabbath and then explained.

paras: The first Christians, like Paul, preached in synagogues wherever they went. When they met on their own, they kept the synagogue's habit of reading and explaining Scripture. At first 'Scripture' meant the Jewish Bible, in its Greek translation. Then the apostles' letters were read aloud too, and the memoirs of Jesus, the Gospels, which is exactly what Justin describes in Rome in about 155.

That public reading is how the New Testament came to be. When the Church later drew up its list of books, its 'canon', one of the main tests was which writings had been read in the churches from the beginning.
background.key: The Church kept the synagogue's reading and explanation, adding the apostles' letters and the Gospels; public reading helped decide which books entered the New Testament.

paras: The main reading is five short passages. One shows a synagogue service, with Paul invited to speak after the readings. Four are instructions from Paul's letters about reading aloud, singing and teaching. Together they show the word half of worship being born.

The comparison jumps fifteen centuries, to the Book of Common Prayer. In 1549 Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, gave the Church of England services in English instead of Latin, with set readings so that the whole Bible would be heard. Its Morning Prayer, revised in 1662, was said daily in cathedrals and colleges and on Sundays in parish churches for centuries, and choirs still sing it.
background.key: Five short New Testament passages show the word in early worship; Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer shows it fifteen centuries on.

before: In Acts 13, what happens before anyone speaks?
What three things does Paul tell Timothy to pay attention to?
In the Prayer Book, who says which lines? Why do you think it is written as a dialogue?
sessions.readWhy: A synagogue service, and Paul's instructions for reading, singing and teaching when Christians meet.

paras: But they, passing on from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia. They went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and sat down.
After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak.”
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.
Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father, through him.
When this letter has been read among you, cause it to be read also in the assembly of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
I solemnly command you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers.
Until I come, pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching.

parts.title: After the reading of the law and the prophets
parts.context: On his first missionary journey, in about AD 47, Paul and his companion Barnabas reach Antioch in Pisidia, in central Turkey (not the great Antioch in Syria). They go to the synagogue on the Sabbath. Luke goes on to give Paul's sermon in full.

commentary.on: They went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and sat down.
commentary.text: Paul, a Jew trained as a Pharisee, begins in the synagogue. Visitors sat with everyone else; the readers stood.

commentary.on: After the reading of the law and the prophets
commentary.text: Two readings: one from the Torah, one from the prophets. This is the order Christians kept, and why many services still have an Old Testament reading before the New.

commentary.on: if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak
commentary.text: Then a 'word of exhortation', a sermon. The leaders invite a visiting teacher. Reading followed by explanation: this is the oldest part of Christian worship, and it is Jewish.

parts.title: Let this letter be read
parts.context: Four short passages from letters written to Christian communities in the AD 50s and 60s. 1 Thessalonians, of about AD 50, is probably the oldest book of the New Testament. Colossians and 1 Timothy carry Paul's name; many scholars think they were written by his followers after his death, others defend Paul's authorship.

commentary.on: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly
commentary.text: 'The word of Christ' is his teaching, and the message about him. It is meant to live in a community, not just in books. In a world with few books, it 'dwelt' in people by being heard, sung and remembered.

commentary.on: teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs
commentary.text: Singing is a way of teaching. The psalms were Israel's hymn book; 'hymns and spiritual songs' were probably new Christian songs. Some may survive inside the New Testament, such as the hymn to Christ in Philippians 2:6–11.

commentary.on: giving thanks to God the Father, through him
commentary.text: Thanksgiving again, the word that gives the Eucharist its name. Everything, 'in word or in deed', is to be done in thanks.

commentary.on: When this letter has been read among you, cause it to be read also in the assembly of the Laodiceans
commentary.text: Letters were written to be read aloud to the gathered church, and then passed on to the next town. This is how the apostles' writings became Scripture: they were read in worship, again and again, in more and more places.

commentary.on: I solemnly command you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers
commentary.text: Paul insists everyone hears it, not just the leaders. Public reading was for the whole community, most of whom could not read for themselves.

commentary.on: pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching
commentary.text: Three tasks for a church leader: public reading of Scripture, exhortation (the sermon), and teaching. It is the synagogue's pattern, now in a Christian church.

paras: Then likewise he shall say, O Lord, open thou our lips.
Answer. And our mouth shall show forth thy praise.
Priest. O God, make speed to save us.
Answer. O Lord, make haste to help us.
Here all standing up, the Priest shall say, Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost;
Answer. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.
Priest. Praise ye the Lord.
Answer. The Lord's Name be praised.

Then shall be said or sung this Psalm following; Except on Easter Day, upon which another Anthem is appointed; and on the nineteenth day of every month it is not to be read here, but in the ordinary course of the Psalms. Venite, exultemus Domino. Psalm xcv. COME, let us sing unto the Lord : let us heartily rejoice in the strength of our salvation. Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving : and show ourselves glad in him with Psalms. For the Lord is a great God : and a great King above all gods. In his hand are all the corners of the earth : and the strength of the hills is his also. The sea is his, and he made it : and his hands prepared the dry land. O come, let us worship and fall down : and kneel before the Lord our Maker. For he is the Lord our God : and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand.

Then shall be read distinctly with an audible voice the First Lesson, taken out of the Old Testament, as is appointed in the Calendar, except there be proper Lessons assigned for that day : He that readeth so standing and turning himself, as he may best be heard of all such as are present. And after that, shall be said or sung, in English, the Hymn called Te Deum Laudamus, daily throughout the Year.
Note, That before every Lesson the Minister shall say, Here beginneth such a Chapter, or Verse of such a Chapter, of such a Book : And after every Lesson, Here endeth the First, or the Second Lesson.
Then shall be sung or said the Apostle's Creed, by the Minister and the people standing : Except only such days as the Creed of Saint Athanasius is appointed to be read.

parts.author: The Book of Common Prayer (1662)
parts.translator: Original English (Thomas Cranmer's text of 1549 and 1552, revised in 1662); transcribed from a twentieth-century printing
parts.who: Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556), Archbishop of Canterbury, and the revisers of 1662
parts.ref: The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer: the opening responses and the Venite
parts.title: O Lord, open thou our lips
parts.context: After the opening confession and absolution, Morning Prayer begins in earnest with a dialogue between the priest and the people, mostly lines from the psalms, and then Psalm 95, called the Venite from its first word in Latin, 'O come'. The words in italics in the printed book, which tell the minister what to do, are called 'rubrics' because they were once printed in red. Spelling is that of a twentieth-century printing; the colons mark where the two halves of a choir alternate.
parts.plain: The priest says, 'Lord, open our lips', and the people answer, 'and our mouths will praise you'. They ask God to hurry to help them. Everyone stands for 'Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit', and the people complete it. Then all say or sing Psalm 95: come, let us sing to the Lord, our rock and our maker; let us kneel before him, because we are his people, the sheep he looks after.

commentary.on: O Lord, open thou our lips.
commentary.text: From Psalm 51:15. These are the first words monks had said every night for a thousand years at the start of their prayers, and Cranmer kept them. Before we speak to God, we ask God to give us the words.

commentary.on: Answer. And our mouth shall show forth thy praise.
commentary.text: The service is a conversation. The people have their own lines, printed for them, so worship is not something done by the priest alone. This was one of the Reformation's aims: common prayer, said by everyone, in their own language.

commentary.on: Here all standing up, the Priest shall say, Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost;
commentary.text: The Gloria Patri, 'Glory be to the Father', ends almost every psalm in Christian worship. It turns each Jewish psalm into a Christian prayer to the Trinity. Everyone stands for it.

commentary.on: COME, let us sing unto the Lord : let us heartily rejoice in the strength of our salvation.
commentary.text: This is Psalm 95 in Miles Coverdale's translation of 1535, which the Prayer Book kept for the psalms even after the King James Bible of 1611. It is why the Prayer Book psalms sound different from other English Bibles. You can learn its first lines, in the World English Bible, in this session.

commentary.on: O come, let us worship and fall down : and kneel before the Lord our Maker.
commentary.text: The psalm tells the body what to do: sing, come in, kneel. Worship is not only an idea in the head. That is why services involve standing, sitting and kneeling.

parts.author: The Book of Common Prayer (1662)
parts.translator: Original English (Thomas Cranmer's text of 1549 and 1552, revised in 1662); transcribed from a twentieth-century printing
parts.who: Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556), Archbishop of Canterbury, and the revisers of 1662
parts.ref: The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer: the lessons and the creed
parts.title: Here beginneth
parts.context: After the psalms appointed for the day come two readings, called 'lessons', one from the Old Testament and one from the New, each followed by a canticle, a song from Scripture or the early Church. The 'Calendar' at the front of the Prayer Book set the chapters for every day of the year. Then the Apostles' Creed.
parts.plain: The first reading, from the Old Testament, is read clearly and loudly, from the passage set in the calendar, by a reader who stands and turns so that everyone can hear. Then the hymn 'We praise thee, O God' (the Te Deum) is sung or said. Before each reading the minister announces where it is from, and after it says that it has ended. Then everyone stands to say the Apostles' Creed.

commentary.on: Then shall be read distinctly with an audible voice the First Lesson, taken out of the Old Testament, as is appointed in the Calendar
commentary.text: The readings are not the minister's choice. A calendar sets them, so that the whole Bible is heard in order. Cranmer's preface of 1549 complained that the old Latin services had broken up the Bible into fragments; his scheme read most of the Old Testament once a year and the New Testament three times.

commentary.on: He that readeth so standing and turning himself, as he may best be heard of all such as are present.
commentary.text: The point is to be heard. Cranmer wanted ordinary people to hear the Bible read in English in their own parish church, every day if they could.

commentary.on: the Hymn called Te Deum Laudamus
commentary.text: The Te Deum ('We praise thee, O God') is a Latin hymn of the fourth or fifth century, sung after the first reading. The response to hearing God's word is praise.

commentary.on: Here beginneth such a Chapter, or Verse of such a Chapter, of such a Book
commentary.text: Generations of English speakers knew these words. Every reading has a frame: where it begins and where it ends.

commentary.on: Then shall be sung or said the Apostle's Creed, by the Minister and the people standing
commentary.text: After the readings, everyone stands to say what they believe. The creed sums up the story the readings tell. The Apostles' Creed grew from the questions asked at baptism in Rome, the same kind of questions Cyril's candidates answered.

compare.author: The Book of Common Prayer (1662)
compare.ref: The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer: the opening responses and the Venite
compare.translator: Original English (Thomas Cranmer's text of 1549 and 1552, revised in 1662); transcribed from a twentieth-century printing
compare.why: Cranmer's Morning Prayer shows the word half of worship fully grown: a dialogue of short responses, a psalm sung by all, set readings from both Testaments, and the creed. Notice how much of it is Scripture.
compare.title: Fifteen centuries on: the Prayer Book

paras: A 'lectionary' is a list of readings for each day or Sunday. Jews read the whole Torah in a yearly cycle, a portion each Sabbath, with a passage from the prophets beside it. Churches developed their own schemes, built around the Christian year: the readings of Advent prepare for Christmas, those of Lent for Easter.

Today most churches that use a lectionary follow one of two closely related schemes. The Catholic Church's Lectionary for Mass of 1969 reads through the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke over three years, with John at the great seasons, plus an Old Testament reading, a psalm and an epistle each Sunday. The Revised Common Lectionary (1992), based on it, is used by many Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and Reformed churches. On any given Sunday, Christians in different churches around the world often hear the same passages. Many evangelical and Pentecostal churches instead preach through a book of the Bible over several weeks.
sections.key: Lectionaries set the readings so the whole Bible is heard over time; many churches share one three-year cycle, and others preach through a book.

sections.h: The word in a world without books
paras: It is hard now to imagine how few people in the ancient world could read. The historian William Harris, in Ancient Literacy (1989), estimated that in the Roman empire perhaps no more than one person in ten could read well, and books, copied by hand, were expensive. For almost all early Christians, the Bible was something heard, not read. That is why the readings were long, 'as long as time permits', and why so much of the service is Scripture, said or sung.

Christians were early adopters of a new technology: the codex, a book with pages, instead of the scroll. Almost all early Christian manuscripts are codices, which were cheaper, held more and made it easy to find a passage. Through the Middle Ages most people still learned the Bible by ear and by eye: from the readings, the psalms, the plays performed on feast days, and the windows and wall paintings of their churches. Only with printing and the Reformation did large numbers of ordinary Christians read the Bible for themselves, and even then most first met it in church.
sections.key: Few in the ancient world could read; for most Christians, until printing, the Bible was heard in worship, sung and seen in church.

paras: The sermon, or 'homily' (Greek for a conversation or talk), explains the readings and applies them. Many early sermons survive. John Chrysostom, preacher at Antioch and then bishop of Constantinople (died 407), was called 'golden-mouthed' for his; Augustine preached thousands in his small cathedral at Hippo in North Africa, and congregations sometimes applauded.

The Reformation put the sermon at the centre. For Luther and Calvin, God speaks through the preaching of his word, and in Reformed churches the pulpit, not the altar, became the focus of the building. Puritan sermons could last an hour, timed by an hourglass on the pulpit. Today a Catholic homily may be ten minutes and an evangelical sermon forty; either way, it is the part where someone tries to show what these ancient texts mean for the people in front of them, this week.
sections.key: The sermon explains and applies the readings; the Reformation made preaching central, and its length still varies widely between traditions.

paras: The psalms are the prayer book of Israel, and the Church sang them from the beginning: Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26), most likely from the psalms of the Passover. Monks sang all 150 psalms every week; Cranmer's Prayer Book has the whole psalter said or sung every month. Calvin's Geneva, and later Scotland, sang only psalms, translated into rhyming verse so a congregation could sing them to simple tunes: Crimond is one.

Christians also wrote new songs. Pliny reported Christians singing to Christ. Ambrose of Milan wrote hymns in the 380s that are still sung; you may have read in 'The sound of faith' how they moved Augustine to tears. Luther wrote hymns so that ordinary people could sing the faith in German. In England, Isaac Watts (1674–1748) and Charles Wesley (1707–1788), who wrote over six thousand hymns, taught congregations to sing their theology. A hymn teaches by repetition: people remember what they sing far longer than what they hear.
sections.key: The Church sang the psalms from the start and wrote new hymns, from Ambrose to Luther, Watts and Wesley; singing teaches by heart.

paras: A creed (from the Latin credo, 'I believe') is a short summary of the faith said together. Creeds grew out of baptism: the candidate was asked 'Do you believe in God the Father?', 'in Christ Jesus?', 'in the Holy Spirit?', and answered 'I believe.' The Apostles' Creed, said at baptism and at Morning and Evening Prayer in the West, grew from the questions used in Rome. The Nicene Creed, agreed at the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), is said at the Eucharist in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches.

Saying a creed in church is not a test of each person's certainty that morning. It is the Church saying together what it believes, and inviting each person to make it their own. The creeds have a journey of their own later on the path, which looks at what each line means and why it was fought over.
sections.key: Creeds grew from the questions at baptism; the Apostles' Creed is said at morning and evening prayer, the Nicene Creed at the Eucharist.

paras: Before the Reformation, services in the West were in Latin, which most people did not understand, and were said in several different books. Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury under Henry VIII and Edward VI, produced the first Book of Common Prayer in 1549, in English, in one volume, for everyone. 'Common' meant shared: priest and people, and every parish in the land, saying the same words. He revised it more radically in 1552. Under the Catholic Queen Mary he was burned at the stake in Oxford in 1556.

After the Civil War, when Parliament had banned the Prayer Book (1645), it was restored with small revisions in 1662. That book remained the official prayer book of the Church of England, and was taken across the world wherever Anglicans went. Its phrases passed into everyday English: 'till death us do part', 'ashes to ashes', 'read, mark, learn and inwardly digest'. Many cathedrals still sing its Evensong every day.
sections.key: Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1552, 1662) put the services in English, for all; it shaped English worship and the English language.

paras: Every Christian tradition has a service of the word; what differs is its shape, its place and its weight.

debate.question: Set prayers or free prayer?

positions.name: Set words, shared by all
positions.who: The Orthodox and Catholic Churches; Cranmer and the Anglican tradition; Lutherans
positions.view: Fixed prayers protect worship from the minister's moods and opinions, let everyone join in, and join each congregation to the whole Church across the world and the centuries. When you cannot pray, the words carry you.
positions.evidence: Jews prayed set prayers and psalms; Jesus gave his disciples a set prayer, the Lord's Prayer (Luke 11:2–4); the Didache gives set prayers; the Prayer Book's phrases have been prayed by millions.

positions.name: Free prayer, led by the Spirit
positions.who: The Puritans and the Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645); Baptists, many evangelicals and Pentecostals
positions.view: Set forms can become rote, said without meaning. The minister and people should pray from the heart, as the Spirit gives them words, and the sermon should open the Bible freshly.
positions.evidence: Justin's president prays 'according to his ability'; 'when you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching' (1 Corinthians 14:26); Jesus warned against 'vain repetitions' (Matthew 6:7, in older translations).

positions.name: A fixed shape, with room inside
positions.who: Most churches today, including modern Anglican and Catholic services and many Free Churches
positions.view: Keep a common structure and some shared words, such as the Lord's Prayer and the creed, but allow free intercessions, local hymns and fresh preaching.
positions.evidence: Justin's own service: a fixed order (readings, sermon, prayers, meal) with words freely chosen; Common Worship (2000) in the Church of England offers many options within one shape.

debate.agree: All agree that worship should be in a language people understand, that Scripture must be read and explained, and that words, set or free, must come from the heart.

look.why: Rembrandt and his workshop painted the apostle Paul at his desk in about 1657. Paul's letters were written to be read aloud when the churches met; you read his instruction that this be done. (This painting also appears in 'The first Christians'.)
points: An older, bearded man, Paul, sits at a desk in a shadowy room, his head resting in one hand.
He holds a quill in his other hand, which brushes his knee.
The desk to our right has a stack of papers or parchment.
The oversized hilt of a long sword leans against the wall behind the desk.
His brown robe is loosely painted with golden-brown highlights; brushstrokes are visible in the brightest highlights on his collar, the quill and the edges of the parchment.
The artist signed the painting on the face of the desk, near the lower right: 'Rembrandt f.'

music.why: Psalm 23 in the Scottish metrical psalter, sung to the tune Crimond: the word of Scripture turned into verse so that a whole congregation could sing it, as Calvin and the Scottish Reformers wanted.

think.why: Why Christians speak of Christ himself as 'the Word', and why words matter so much in their worship.

learn.why: The Venite, the psalm you read in the Prayer Book: sung at the start of morning prayer in monasteries and parish churches for fifteen hundred years.

check.q: Where does the pattern of reading Scripture followed by a sermon come from?

The Jewish synagogue, where the Law and the prophets were read and then explained

check.q: Why does Paul insist that his letter be read 'to all the holy brothers'?

Because public reading was how the whole community, most of whom could not read, heard it
Because it was secret

check.why: Letters were written to be read aloud to the gathered church and passed on to others.

check.q: How did public reading in worship help shape the New Testament?
options: Only books read in synagogues were accepted
Writings read in the churches from the beginning were among those accepted into the canon
It did not; the books were chosen by an emperor

check.why: Long use in worship was one of the main tests for which books were Scripture.

check.q: What was the main purpose of the Prayer Book's calendar of lessons?
options: To replace the sermon
To let each minister choose favourite passages
That the whole Bible would be read in order and heard by the people in English
To shorten the services
check.why: Cranmer's scheme read most of the Old Testament once a year and the New Testament three times, in English.

check.q: Where did the creeds come from?

From the Reformation
From Roman legal oaths
From the questions asked at baptism, and later from Church councils
check.why: Baptismal questions ('Do you believe in God the Father…?') grew into the Apostles' Creed; Nicaea and Constantinople gave the Nicene Creed.

check.q: A Puritan objects that set prayers become rote. What is the best reply from the tradition of set prayer?
options: Free prayer is forbidden in the Bible
Set prayers are older, so they must be right
Shared words let everyone join in, guard against the minister's whims, and carry people when they cannot find words; but they must be prayed from the heart
Nobody really means what they pray anyway
check.why: This answers the objection on its own terms while granting its point about the heart.

tutorial.question: What does the 'word' half of a Christian service do, and where did it come from?
tutorial.approach: Trace the line from the synagogue (Acts 13; Luke 4) through Paul's letters read aloud to Justin's Sunday readings and sermon. Then explain lectionaries, psalms and hymns, and the creed. Use the Prayer Book as a case study of how a church organised the word. End by weighing set and free prayer.
strong: Explains the synagogue's reading of the law and the prophets and the sermon after it.
Shows how the apostles' letters were read aloud and became Scripture.
Explains what a lectionary is and why churches use one.
Explains why singing and the creed are part of the word, with examples (Ambrose, Watts, Wesley; baptismal questions).
Uses the Book of Common Prayer as evidence, with dates.
Weighs set and free prayer fairly.
