sessions.practice: Live it this week: read the Gospel set for next Sunday (search 'Revised Common Lectionary' and the date) aloud, once a day, slowly, as if to a room of people. On Sunday, if you can, go and hear it read in church, or listen to a choral Evensong broadcast.
sessions.reflect: Which words do you know by heart because you heard them over and over: a song, a saying, a prayer? What have they done to you?
takeaways: From the synagogue the Church kept the reading of Scripture and a sermon; Paul's letters were written to be read aloud, and public reading helped make the New Testament.
Lectionaries set the readings so the whole Bible is heard; psalms and hymns teach by singing; creeds grew from the questions at baptism.
Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer (1549–1662) put worship in English for everyone, with set readings, psalms and the creed.

sessions.title: The table
sessions.line: At the heart of most Christian worship is a meal: bread and wine, taken with thanks, as Jesus commanded.
sessions.plain: At the centre of most Christian worship is a meal: a little bread and wine, over which the minister gives thanks, and which the people eat and drink. It is called the Eucharist, the Mass, the Lord's Supper, Holy Communion or the Divine Liturgy. This session reads what Paul told a quarrelling church in Corinth about it, and what Justin told the emperor, and then sets out how the different churches celebrate it today, and who may receive.
sessions.why: Session 3 covered the first half of the service, the word. Justin's Sunday then moves to the table: bread and wine brought, a long thanksgiving, the people's Amen, and the bread and wine shared. 'The last week and the cross' read the account of the Last Supper itself; now we see what the first churches did with Jesus's command 'do this in memory of me', and what they thought they were doing.
answers: What is Communion, and why do Christians do it?
Why does it have so many names?
What happens during it, step by step?
Why do some churches have it every week and others rarely?
Who may receive it, and what should a visitor do?
sessions.finding: At the heart of most Christian worship is a meal: thanksgiving (eucharistia) over bread and wine, as Jesus commanded, which makes many people one body; from the first, it was meant to be shared by rich and poor alike.

background.h: The story so far: the Last Supper
paras: On the night before he died, Jesus ate a final meal with his disciples in Jerusalem, at the time of Passover, the Jewish feast remembering the escape from slavery in Egypt. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said 'This is my body'; after supper he took a cup and called it 'the new covenant in my blood'. 'Do this', he said, 'in memory of me'. You read Paul's account of it, 1 Corinthians 11:23–26, in 'The last week and the cross', and you can learn it by heart in this session.

On the evening of the resurrection, Luke says, two disciples recognised the risen Jesus at Emmaus when he 'took the bread and gave thanks' and broke it (Luke 24:30). After Pentecost, the first believers 'continued steadfastly in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer' (Acts 2:42). The Didache, which you read in 'The first Christians', gives the earliest prayers over the cup and the broken bread: 'as this broken bread was scattered upon the mountains and being gathered together became one'.
background.key: Jesus took bread and wine at his last supper and said 'do this in memory of me'; the first Christians broke bread together from the beginning.

paras: Corinth was a rich, mixed port city in Greece, rebuilt by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony. Paul founded a church there in about AD 50, and wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus in about AD 54. The church met in the houses of its wealthier members, probably several dozen people at a time. The Lord's Supper was still part of a full evening meal.

That caused trouble. Archaeologists have excavated Roman villas in and near Corinth; the dining room in a house of that size seated perhaps nine to twelve on couches, with the rest in the courtyard. Scholars such as Gerd Theissen and Jerome Murphy-O'Connor have argued that the host's friends ate first and best, inside, while poorer members, slaves and labourers who arrived late from work, got what was left. Paul is furious.
background.key: In Corinth the Lord's Supper was part of a full meal in rich members' houses, and the rich ate before the poor arrived; Paul wrote in about AD 54 to stop it.

paras: The main reading is from 1 Corinthians: two verses from chapter 10 on what the bread and cup are, and Paul's rebuke from chapter 11, on either side of the account of the Last Supper you have already read. It is the oldest discussion of the Eucharist we have, and it is about the poor.
The comparison is the chapter of Justin you have not yet read, chapter 66, written about a century later: what Christians called this food, who could receive it, and what they believed it was.
background.key: 1 Corinthians 10 and 11 give the oldest discussion of the Lord's Supper; Justin's chapter 66 tells what Christians a century later believed it was.

before: What does Paul say the bread and cup are a 'sharing' in?
What exactly is going wrong at Corinth?
In Justin, who may receive, and why is this 'not common bread'?
sessions.readWhy: The oldest discussion of the Lord's Supper: what it is, and how the Corinthians were getting it wrong.

paras: The cup of blessing which we bless, isn’t it a sharing of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, isn’t it a sharing of the body of Christ?
Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread.
But in giving you this command, I don’t praise you, that you come together not for the better but for the worse.
For first of all, when you come together in the assembly, I hear that divisions exist among you, and I partly believe it.
For there also must be factions among you, that those who are approved may be revealed among you.
When therefore you assemble yourselves together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.
For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken.

What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly and put them to shame who don’t have enough? What shall I tell you? Shall I praise you? In this I don’t praise you.
Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way unworthy of the Lord will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread, and drink of the cup.
For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment to himself if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body.
For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep.
For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn’t be judged.
But when we are judged, we are punished by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world.
Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
But if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, lest your coming together be for judgment. The rest I will set in order whenever I come.

parts.title: One loaf, one body
parts.context: Paul is warning the Corinthians not to eat in pagan temples, where meat was offered to idols. To make his point he reminds them what they do at the Lord's table.

commentary.on: The cup of blessing which we bless
commentary.text: 'The cup of blessing' was the Jewish name for a cup of wine over which thanks was said at the end of a festive meal, as at Passover. Paul, a Jew, uses the term for the Christian cup.

commentary.on: isn’t it a sharing of the blood of Christ?
commentary.text: The Greek word is koinonia: sharing, fellowship, communion. This is where the name 'Holy Communion' comes from. Those who drink share in Christ himself.

commentary.on: Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body
commentary.text: The single loaf makes a single people. Communion is not only with Christ but with one another: you cannot share the one bread and treat each other as strangers. That is the point Paul is about to press home.

parts.title: Not the Lord's supper
parts.context: A few paragraphs later, Paul turns to the Corinthians' gatherings. After these verses he repeats the words of the Last Supper (11:23–26), which you read in 'The last week and the cross'.

commentary.on: I hear that divisions exist among you
commentary.text: The church is split, and the split shows at the meal. Paul has already rebuked them for forming parties around leaders (1 Corinthians 1:12).

commentary.on: it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat
commentary.text: A shocking sentence. They are performing the ceremony, but Paul says it is not the Lord's Supper at all. A meal that humiliates the poor is not his meal, whatever words are said over it.

commentary.on: For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken.
commentary.text: The better-off eat their own food, and drink too much, before others arrive; the poor go hungry. The meal reproduces the class system of Roman society instead of overturning it.

commentary.on: put them to shame who don’t have enough
commentary.text: Paul's charge is shaming the poor. In a culture of honour and shame, that was a public wound. Remember Justin's collection for widows and orphans: from the start, the table and care for the poor belong together.

parts.title: Discerning the body
parts.context: Having repeated Jesus's words over the bread and the cup, Paul draws the consequences.

commentary.on: whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way unworthy of the Lord will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord
commentary.text: To treat the meal carelessly is to sin against Christ himself. This verse is one reason many churches ask people to prepare before receiving, and why some people, unsure, stay in their seats.

commentary.on: But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread
commentary.text: Self-examination comes before receiving. This is why most services have a confession before Communion. Notice: examine yourself, and then eat. The point is to come, not to stay away.

commentary.on: if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body
commentary.text: What is 'the Lord's body' here? Some readers say: the bread, recognised as Christ's body. Others say: the church, the body of believers, which the Corinthians were despising. Paul has just called the church 'one body' (10:17), and the problem was the poor. Both readings may be meant.

commentary.on: when you come together to eat, wait for one another
commentary.text: The practical remedy is simple: wait. Eat together, all at once, rich and poor. Later the full meal and the bread and wine were separated, partly for this reason.

paras: And this food is called among us Εὐχαριστία [the Eucharist], of which no one is allowed to partake but the man who believes that the things which we teach are true, and who has been washed with the washing that is for the remission of sins, and unto regeneration, and who is so living as Christ has enjoined. For not as common bread and common drink do we receive these; but in like manner as Jesus Christ our Saviour, having been made flesh by the Word of God, had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so likewise have we been taught that the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word, and from which our blood and flesh by transmutation are nourished, is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh. For the apostles, in the memoirs composed by them, which are called Gospels, have thus delivered unto us what was enjoined upon them; that Jesus took bread, and when He had given thanks, said, This do in remembrance of Me, this is My body; and that, after the same manner, having taken the cup and given thanks, He said, This is My blood; and gave it to them alone. Which the wicked devils have imitated in the mysteries of Mithras, commanding the same thing to be done. For, that bread and a cup of water are placed with certain incantations in the mystic rites of one who is being initiated, you either know or can learn.

parts.author: Justin Martyr
parts.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers I (1885)
parts.who: Justin Martyr (c. 100–165), a philosopher from Samaria who became a Christian and taught in Rome, where he was executed
parts.title: This food is called among us the Eucharist
parts.context: The chapter between the two you read in session 1. Justin has described the bread and wine being given out; now he explains them. Mithras was a Persian god whose mystery cult was popular with Roman soldiers; Justin claims its ritual meal is a demonic imitation. The Greek words were printed by the translators; square brackets are theirs.
parts.plain: We call this food the Eucharist. Only those may receive it who believe our teaching, have been baptised, and live as Christ taught. We do not receive it as ordinary bread and drink. Just as Jesus, by God's Word, became flesh and blood for us, so the food over which thanks has been given by his word is the flesh and blood of Jesus. The Gospels tell us he took bread, gave thanks and said, 'This is my body', and the cup, 'This is my blood'. The followers of Mithras copy this, with bread and a cup of water.

commentary.on: this food is called among us
commentary.text: Eucharistia, 'thanksgiving', is already the name of the food itself in Justin's day, and the oldest name for the whole service.

commentary.on: no one is allowed to partake but the man who believes that the things which we teach are true, and who has been washed
commentary.text: Three conditions: belief, baptism and a Christian life. From the earliest times Communion was for the baptised. That is the root of today's question of who may receive.

commentary.on: For not as common bread and common drink do we receive these
commentary.text: Justin is clear that this is not an ordinary meal. Something has happened to the bread and wine through the prayer of thanksgiving.

commentary.on: is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh
commentary.text: As God's Word became flesh in Jesus, so the blessed bread and wine are his flesh and blood. Justin does not explain how. This plain sentence, from about 155, is quoted by Catholics and Orthodox as evidence that the early Church believed in Christ's real presence; Protestants reply that Justin's language is sacramental and does not settle how.

commentary.on: the memoirs composed by them, which are called Gospels
commentary.text: This is the earliest passage outside the New Testament where the books about Jesus are called 'Gospels'.

commentary.on: Which the wicked devils have imitated in the mysteries of Mithras
commentary.text: Justin knows his reader may think the Christian meal looks like other cults' rituals. His answer, typical of his time, is that the demons copied it. Modern historians note that our evidence for the Mithraic meal is later than Justin, and the influence, if any, is debated.

compare.author: Justin Martyr
compare.translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers I (1885)
compare.why: Justin, writing in Rome in about 155, tells the emperor what Christians call this food, who may receive it, and what they believe it is. It is the earliest statement outside the New Testament of what the bread and wine are.
compare.title: A century later: not common bread

paras: The names tell you which church you are in, and which part of the meal it stresses. 'Eucharist', from the Greek for thanksgiving, is the oldest, used by the Didache and Justin, and now by Catholics, Orthodox and many Anglicans. 'The Lord's Supper' is Paul's phrase (1 Corinthians 11:20), preferred by many Protestants. 'Holy Communion' comes from koinonia, sharing (1 Corinthians 10:16), and is common among Anglicans and Methodists.

'The Mass' comes from the last words of the old Latin service, Ite, missa est, 'Go, it is the dismissal', and is used by Catholics and some Anglicans. The Orthodox call the whole service 'the Divine Liturgy'. Brethren and some Baptists say 'the breaking of bread', from Acts. All of them mean the same act: bread and wine, taken with thanks, as Jesus commanded.
sections.key: Eucharist (thanksgiving), Lord's Supper, Holy Communion (sharing), Mass (dismissal), Divine Liturgy and the breaking of bread all name one meal.

paras: At first the Lord's Supper was part of a real evening meal, as at Corinth. By Justin's time in Rome, about a century later, the bread and cup were taken on Sunday morning after the readings, without a full meal. A separate shared meal, the 'love feast' or agape, continued for some centuries.

Why the change? Scholars give several reasons: the abuses Paul attacked; the size of congregations; and Roman laws against private clubs holding evening dinners, which may be why Pliny's Christians gave up their meal after his edict. The bread and wine became the centre of their own service. Some churches have revived the full meal: Moravians keep a 'lovefeast', and some Anglican and Baptist churches share 'agape meals' on Maundy Thursday.
sections.key: The Lord's Supper began within a full meal; by about 150 the bread and cup stood on their own, and the 'love feast' was held separately.

paras: Gregory Dix noticed that at the Last Supper Jesus does seven things: took bread, gave thanks, broke it, gave it; and after supper took the cup, gave thanks, gave it. When the meal dropped out, the two sets merged into four actions that every Eucharist still has. The bread and wine are taken (the offertory). Thanks is given over them (the eucharistic prayer). The bread is broken (the fraction). They are given to the people (Communion).

Watch any Eucharist, from a pope's Mass to a Baptist communion service, and you will see these four. Dix's history has been criticised as too tidy, but his four actions remain the best simple key to what is going on.
sections.key: Dix's key: every Eucharist takes, gives thanks, breaks and gives, the four actions of the Last Supper without the meal.

paras: The prayer over the bread and wine, the part Justin says the president made 'at considerable length', grew into the eucharistic prayer. Its main parts are shared by nearly all traditions. It opens with a dialogue: 'Lift up your hearts', and the people's reply. It gives thanks for creation and salvation, and joins the angels' song from Isaiah 6:3: 'Holy, holy, holy'. It repeats Jesus's words at the Last Supper. It remembers his death and resurrection (Greek anamnesis, remembering). In most traditions it asks the Holy Spirit to come on the gifts and on the people (Greek epiclesis, calling upon). It ends with praise, and the people say 'Amen', as in Justin.
When people kneel or bow during this prayer, it is because they believe something holy is happening. What exactly is happening is the question of a later session, still to come.
sections.key: The eucharistic prayer: the dialogue, thanksgiving, 'Holy, holy, holy', Jesus's words, remembering, calling on the Spirit, and the people's Amen.

paras: The Didache calls the Sunday meal a 'sacrifice', quoting Malachi's 'pure offering'. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross: not a new sacrifice, nor a repetition, but the same offering, now available to the Church. That is why their churches have an altar.

The Reformers objected strongly. The Letter to the Hebrews says Christ was offered 'once' (Hebrews 9:28), and they feared that calling the Mass a sacrifice suggested the cross was not enough, especially when Masses were paid for on behalf of the dead. Cranmer's Prayer Book spoke instead of a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving, and of offering ourselves; the altar became a 'table'. Since the 1970s, ecumenical dialogues between Catholics and Anglicans and Lutherans have found more agreement than the sixteenth century did, using the idea of remembrance (anamnesis) that makes a past event present.
sections.key: Catholics and Orthodox see the Eucharist as making present Christ's one sacrifice; the Reformers called it a sacrifice of praise only; modern dialogues have narrowed the gap.

paras: What is on the table varies too. The Orthodox use ordinary leavened bread, a loaf stamped with a seal, which is cut and placed in the wine. The Latin West came to use unleavened bread, like the bread of Passover, which became the thin round wafer called the 'host' (from the Latin hostia, a sacrificial offering). The difference was one of the complaints exchanged when the Eastern and Western churches split in 1054. Many Protestant churches use an ordinary loaf, broken in front of everyone, to show Paul's 'one loaf'.

In the medieval West, ordinary people usually received only the bread; the cup was for the priest. The Reformers restored the cup to everyone, and since the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) Catholics may receive both. Many Methodist, Baptist and other churches use unfermented grape juice instead of wine, a practice that began in the temperance movement of the nineteenth century, when the Methodist Thomas Welch developed a way to keep grape juice from fermenting in 1869. Small individual cups became common in the same era.
sections.key: The Orthodox use leavened bread, Catholics a wafer, many Protestants a loaf; the cup was restored to all at the Reformation; many churches use grape juice.

paras: How the meal is held differs widely. If you go to a service, here is roughly what to expect.

rows: Leavened bread in the wine, given on a spoon; after fasting and preparation
A thin wafer on the tongue or in the hand, sometimes the cup too
Most churches weekly (the 1662 Prayer Book required at least three times a year)
Kneeling or standing at a rail; wafer or bread, and the cup
At a rail or standing; wafer and cup
Often seated, bread and small cups passed along the pews
Often seated; bread and small cups of wine or grape juice
table.note: Quakers and the Salvation Army do not celebrate an outward Communion; you will hear why in the next session.

sections.key: Orthodox, Catholics, many Anglicans and Lutherans hold the meal weekly; Reformed and many evangelical churches less often; how people receive differs too.

paras: From Justin onwards, Communion was for the baptised. Churches still differ on who may come. The Orthodox Church gives Communion only to Orthodox Christians who have prepared. The Catholic Church asks that only Catholics receive, with limited exceptions (Code of Canon Law, canon 844). The Church of England welcomes baptised members of other Trinitarian churches in good standing. Methodists and many other Protestant churches invite all who love Christ or wish to follow him; some Baptist and Brethren churches allow only baptised believers, or only their members.

For a visitor, the simple rule is this: you never have to receive. In Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican churches you may go forward with your arms crossed over your chest to receive a blessing instead, or simply stay in your seat. Nobody minds, and many people do it.
sections.key: Orthodox and Catholics generally limit Communion to their own members; Anglicans welcome baptised Christians; many Protestant churches invite all who love Christ. A visitor may always stay seated or ask for a blessing.

refs: 1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 11:17–34; 11:20; Luke 24:30; Acts 2:42; Mark 14:22–26; Isaiah 6:3; Malachi 1:11; Hebrews 9:28.
Didache 9–10, 14; Justin, First Apology 65–67; Pliny, Letters X.96.
Gregory Dix, The Shape of the Liturgy (1945), chapter 4; Paul F. Bradshaw and Maxwell E. Johnson, The Eucharistic Liturgies (2012).
Gerd Theissen, The Social Setting of Pauline Christianity (1982); Jerome Murphy-O'Connor, St. Paul's Corinth (3rd ed., 2002).

Catechism of the Catholic Church 1362–1367; Code of Canon Law (1983), canon 844; Church of England, Canon B 15A; Anglican-Roman Catholic International Commission, Eucharistic Doctrine (Windsor, 1971).
The Book of Common Prayer (1662), rubrics at the end of the Holy Communion; Calvin, Institutes IV.17.43–46. On bread and cup: Council of Trent, Session XXI (1562); Sacrosanctum Concilium 55 (1963).

debate.question: Who should be welcome at the table?

positions.name: Only those in full communion with the Church
positions.who: The Orthodox Church; the Catholic Church (with exceptions); some Lutheran churches
positions.view: To receive Communion is to say 'Amen' to the faith and fellowship of the church that gives it. Sharing it before churches are united in belief papers over real divisions. It is the sign of unity, so it should follow unity, not replace it.
positions.evidence: Justin: only those who believe, are baptised and live as Christ taught; Paul's warning against receiving 'in an unworthy way' (1 Corinthians 11:27); the early Church's practice of excommunication.

positions.name: All baptised believers
positions.who: The Church of England and most Anglicans; many Lutheran and Reformed churches
positions.view: Baptism makes a person a member of the one Church of Christ, whatever their denomination. All the baptised who believe should be welcome, even before churches are fully united.
positions.evidence: 'One Lord, one faith, one baptism' (Ephesians 4:5); the Didache and Justin limit the meal to the baptised, not to one church; Canon B 15A of the Church of England.

positions.name: An open table
positions.who: John Wesley and Methodists; many United, Baptist and Free churches
positions.view: Christ welcomed sinners and outsiders to eat with him. The table is a means of grace for anyone who wants to follow him; Wesley called it a 'converting ordinance', where people might first come to faith.
positions.evidence: Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Mark 2:15–17); at the Last Supper he gave the bread to Judas; Wesley's Journal, 27–28 June 1740.

debate.agree: All agree that the table is Christ's, that it is a sign of the Church's unity, that people should come with repentance and faith, and that the divisions between churches here are a wound.

look.why: William Blake painted the Last Supper in 1799, in tempera on canvas. It shows the meal that every Eucharist remembers. (The painting also appears in the daily stories.)
points: Thirteen people surround a long, rectangular dining table against a nearly black background.
At the centre a radiating gold starburst surrounds the head and shoulders of Jesus, who looks towards us and holds his hands up, palms facing out.
Jesus and the figure beside him on our right recline, as people did at ancient feasts; the second figure, in teal blue, turns to look at him.
Most of the others look towards Jesus, while two bend low to the table in prayer.
In the lower right, a man in brick red turns his back on the table as he counts or touches coins in a sack: Judas.
The table is set with goblets and plates of food; Blake signed his initials in the lower left: 'WB inv.'

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there': the chant sung on Maundy Thursday, the night of the Last Supper. Paul's quarrel with Corinth is exactly this: without love for the poor, it is not the Lord's Supper.

think.why: Paul refused to let the rich and poor eat apart. Why Christians came to believe every person has the same worth.

learn.why: You may have learned these words in 'The last week and the cross'. They are said at every Eucharist, Mass and Holy Communion; say them again this week, knowing now the quarrel at Corinth that they answered.

check.q: Why does Paul say 'it is not the Lord's supper that you eat'?
options: Because they had used the wrong words
Because they used water instead of wine
Because the rich were eating first and humiliating the poor, so the meal contradicted what it meant
Because they met on the wrong day
check.why: Divisions and shaming 'those who don't have enough' made it not the Lord's meal, whatever was said over it.

check.q: What does Paul's word koinonia (1 Corinthians 10:16) add to our understanding of the meal?
options: That it is private
That it is only symbolic
That it is a sacrifice for the dead
That it is a sharing in Christ and, through the one loaf, with one another
check.why: 'We, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf': communion with Christ and with each other.

check.q: 'Discern the Lord's body' (11:29) has two main interpretations. Which pair is right?
options: The bread as Christ's body; the church as Christ's body
Jesus's physical body; Paul's body
The church in Rome; the church in Corinth
The bread; the wine
check.why: Some read it as recognising Christ in the bread, others as recognising the church, especially its poor, as his body; the context supports both.

check.q: According to Justin, who may receive the Eucharist?
options: Only the clergy
Anyone present
Those who believe the teaching, have been baptised and live as Christ taught
Only those who have fasted for three days
check.why: Justin's three conditions: belief, baptism and a Christian life.

check.q: Which best explains why the bread and cup came to be separated from a full meal?
options: Constantine banned meals
There was no wine in Rome
Jesus commanded it
Abuses like those at Corinth, growing congregations and Roman suspicion of evening club dinners
check.why: Scholars give these reasons; by about 150 the bread and cup stood on their own, with a separate 'love feast'.

check.q: A visitor who is not a member of the church is unsure whether to receive. What is the best advice?
options: Ask the person next to you to receive for you
Never go to a service with Communion
Follow the church's own invitation; if in doubt, stay seated or go forward with arms crossed for a blessing
Always receive, to be polite
check.why: Churches differ on who may receive; no visitor is ever obliged to, and a blessing is usually offered.

tutorial.question: What did the first Christians think they were doing when they broke bread?
tutorial.approach: Start with the Last Supper and Jesus's command. Use 1 Corinthians 10 and 11 to show what Paul thought the meal was (a sharing in Christ, one body) and what it required (no shaming of the poor). Then use Justin 65–67 for what Christians did and believed a century later. End with how far today's churches keep that pattern, and where they differ.
strong: Explains the Last Supper and the command 'do this in memory of me'.
Uses koinonia and 'one loaf, one body' from 1 Corinthians 10.
Explains the abuse at Corinth and Paul's response, including the two readings of 'discerning the body'.
Uses Justin 66: 'not common bread', only for the baptised, the flesh and blood of Jesus.
Explains the four actions and the eucharistic prayer.
Sets out the differences between traditions fairly, including who may receive.

reading.author: Alexander Schmemann
reading.title: For the Life of the World
reading.why: A short Orthodox classic on the Eucharist as the meaning of all of life.

reading.author: Gregory Dix
reading.title: The Shape of the Liturgy
reading.why: The great Anglican history of the Eucharist, source of the 'four actions'.

reading.author: Gerd Theissen
reading.title: The Social Setting of Pauline Christianity
reading.why: The study that showed the Corinthian quarrel was about rich and poor.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: share one meal with someone you would not normally eat with, and wait until everyone is served before you begin. Before you eat, give thanks aloud, even in a sentence.
sessions.reflect: Paul says a meal that shames the poor is not the Lord's Supper, whatever words are said. Where in your life could ritual be covering over something that is wrong?
takeaways: At the Last Supper Jesus took bread and wine, gave thanks and said 'do this in memory of me'; the first Christians broke bread together from the beginning.
Paul calls the bread and cup a sharing (koinonia) in Christ that makes many one body, and says a meal that shames the poor is not the Lord's Supper.

By Justin's time it was a separate act of thanksgiving (eucharistia), for the baptised, received as 'not common bread'; churches still keep its four actions, but differ on how often, how and who may receive.

sessions.title: The case against: empty ritual?
sessions.line: Prophets, Reformers, Quakers and the Enlightenment all asked the same question: does God want ceremonies at all?
sessions.plain: Many thoughtful people, inside the Church and outside it, have said that ritual is the enemy of real religion. The Hebrew prophets said God hated festivals held by people who cheated the poor. Jesus quoted them. The Reformers said the Mass had become a show. The Quakers gave up sermons, sacraments and set prayers altogether and met in silence. Enlightenment thinkers said ceremonies were superstition, and many people today say they are spiritual but not religious. This session gives that case its full strength, then hears the reply.
sessions.why: The first four sessions built up a picture of Christian worship: the day, the water, the word and the table. A fair reader should now ask whether all this is necessary, or even good. Paul has already shown, at Corinth, that a ceremony can contradict its own meaning. This session asks whether that is the exception or the rule.
answers: Isn't ritual just going through the motions?
Didn't the prophets and Jesus attack religious ceremony?
Why do Quakers worship in silence, without sacraments?
Can't I be spiritual without going to church?
What is the best defence of ritual?
sessions.finding: The prophets, Jesus, the Reformers and the Quakers all attacked worship without justice or faith, and the Quakers did without outward ritual altogether; the best defence of liturgy is that it is not a substitute for love but a training in it, keeping people faithful when feelings fail.

paras: The objection to ritual is not modern. In the 700s BC the prophet Amos told Israel that God hated their feasts and wanted justice to roll down like waters: you read him in 'Kings and prophets'. Isaiah, in the same century, said the people honoured God with their lips while their hearts were far away. Jesus quoted Isaiah against religious leaders of his own day.

In the sixteenth century the Protestant Reformers turned the same charge on the medieval Church: Masses paid for and said in a language few understood, relics, pilgrimages and indulgences. In the seventeenth century the Quakers went further and gave up all outward sacraments. In the eighteenth, writers of the Enlightenment, the movement that put human reason at the centre, treated ceremonies as superstition. Each wave said it was recovering something truer.
background.key: The prophets, Jesus, the Reformers, the Quakers and the Enlightenment all, in different ways, accused ritual of replacing real religion.

paras: The Religious Society of Friends began in England in the 1650s, in the turmoil after the Civil War, around George Fox (1624–1691). Fox taught that every person could know Christ directly, by an 'inward light', without priests, churches ('steeple-houses', he called them) or ceremonies. Friends were mocked as 'Quakers' because they trembled in worship. They refused oaths, refused to take off their hats to their social superiors, and called everyone 'thou'. Thousands were imprisoned.

Robert Barclay (1648–1690), a Scottish laird from Ury near Aberdeen, educated in Paris, became their great theologian. His Apology for the True Christian Divinity, published in Latin in 1676 and in English in 1678, set out Quaker belief in fifteen 'propositions' and was addressed to King Charles II. Proposition XI is on worship. The Apology is still read by Quakers today.
background.key: The Quakers began in England in the 1650s around George Fox; Robert Barclay's Apology (1676, English 1678) is their classic defence.

paras: The main reading puts the objection in the Bible's own words: Isaiah's charge against worship from the lips, and Jesus quoting it. Then, from the Letter to the Hebrews, a passage that answers it by telling Christians not to stop meeting.

The comparison gives the objection three more voices, in date order: Luther in 1520, attacking worship that is formal and superficial; Barclay in 1678, on why Quakers wait in silence; and Voltaire in 1733, telling the story of his conversation with an English Quaker who had never been baptised.
background.key: Isaiah and Jesus put the objection; Hebrews replies; Luther, Barclay and Voltaire press the objection further.

before: What exactly is Isaiah's complaint: that the people worship, or how they worship?
Barclay says Quakers do meet together. So what is he against?
Is Voltaire's Quaker against baptism, or against something else?
sessions.readWhy: The objection to empty worship in the Bible's own words, and the Bible's reply.

paras: The Lord said, “Because this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught;

therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”
You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, saying,

And in vain do they worship me,
teaching as doctrine rules made by men.’ ”
Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus,
by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh,
and having a great priest over God’s house,
let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and having our body washed with pure water,
let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful.
Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.

parts.title: With their lips
parts.context: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the late 700s BC. The city was busy with worship at the Temple while its leaders made alliances and ignored the poor. 'The Lord said' introduces God's verdict.

commentary.on: this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me
commentary.text: This is the objection in a sentence. The words are right; the heart is absent. Notice that Isaiah does not condemn speaking or worship as such, but the gap between mouth and heart.

commentary.on: their fear of me is a commandment of men which has been taught
commentary.text: Their religion has become a set of human rules, learned by rote. Reverence has turned into routine.

commentary.on: the wisdom of their wise men will perish
commentary.text: God will act in a way the experts cannot manage or predict. Religion that is all technique, the prophet warns, will be shown up.

parts.title: In vain do they worship me
parts.context: Religious teachers from Jerusalem have criticised Jesus's disciples for not washing their hands before eating, a matter of ritual purity. Jesus answers with a case of their own: a tradition that let people avoid supporting their parents by declaring their money 'a gift devoted to God'. Then he quotes Isaiah.

commentary.on: You hypocrites!
commentary.text: A 'hypocrite' was originally an actor in the Greek theatre, someone who wore a mask. Jesus's charge is that religion has become a performance.

commentary.on: These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.
commentary.text: Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13 in its Greek form. Seven centuries apart, prophet and teacher make the same charge.

commentary.on: teaching as doctrine rules made by men
commentary.text: The danger is not tradition itself (Jesus went to synagogue and Temple, and gave his disciples a prayer and a meal) but human rules that let people avoid God's commandment, here the duty to care for parents.

parts.title: Not forsaking our own assembling together
parts.context: Hebrews is an anonymous sermon-letter of the later first century, written to Christians, probably of Jewish background, who were tempted to drift away under pressure. The writer has argued that Christ has opened the way to God once for all. Now he draws the practical conclusion.

commentary.on: let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith
commentary.text: The answer to Isaiah's charge: draw near, but with a true heart. Hebrews keeps both the outward act and the inward truth.

commentary.on: having our body washed with pure water
commentary.text: A reference to baptism. Body and heart are both mentioned: the outward washing and the inward cleansing belong together.

commentary.on: Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works
commentary.text: A striking word: 'provoke', stir up. Meeting together is for each other's sake, to spur one another on.

commentary.on: not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is
commentary.text: Already in the first century 'some' had stopped coming. The writer's reply is not that meeting is a rule to obey but that people need one another to keep going. Barclay quotes this very phrase in the comparison.

paras: The first works of this Commandment are plain and outward, which we commonly call worship, such as going to mass, praying, and hearing a sermon on holy days. So understood there are very few works in this Commandment; and these, if they are not done in assurance of and with faith in God's favor, are nothing, as was said above. Hence it would also be a good thing if there were fewer saint's days, since in our times the works done on them are for the greater part worse than those of the work days, what with loafing, gluttony, and drunkenness, gambling and other evil deeds; and then, the mass and the sermon are listened to without edification, the prayer is spoken without faith. It almost happens that men think it is sufficient that we look on at the mass with our eyes, hear the preaching with our ears, and say the prayers with our mouths. It is all so formal and superficial! We do not think that we might receive something out of the mass into our hearts, learn and remember something out of the preaching, seek, desire and expect something in our prayer. Although in this matter the bishops and priests, or they to whom the work of preaching is entrusted, are most at fault, because they do not preach the Gospel, and do not teach the people how they ought to look on at mass, hear preaching and pray. Therefore, we will briefly explain these three works.

§. III. Secondly, Albeit I say, that this Worship is neither limited to Times, Places nor Persons; yet I would not be understood, as if I intended the putting away of all set Times and Places to worship: God forbid I should think of such an Opinion. Nay, we are none of those that forsake the Assembling of ourselves together; but have even certain Times and Places, in which we carefully meet together (nor can we be driven therefrom by the Threats and Persecutions of Men) to wait upon God, and worship him. To meet together we think necessary for the People of God; because, so long as we are clothed with this outward Tabernacle, there is a Necessity to the entertaining of a joint and visible Fellowship, and bearing of an outward Testimony for God, and seeing of the Faces of one another, that we concur with our Persons as well as Spirits: To be accompanied with that inward Love and Unity of Spirit, doth greatly tend to encourage and refresh the Saints.

But the Limitation we condemn is, that whereas the Spirit of God should be the immediate Actor, Mover, Persuader and Influencer of Man in the particular Acts of Worship, when the Saints are met together, this Spirit is limited in its Operations, by setting up a particular Man or Men to preach and pray in Man’s Will; and all the rest are excluded from so much as believing that they are to wait for God’s Spirit to move them in such Things: And so they neglecting that in themselves which should quicken them, and not waiting to feel the pure Breathings of God’s Spirit, so as to obey them, are led merely to depend upon the Preacher, and hear what he will say.

I myself, in Part, am a true Witness, who not by Strength of Arguments, or by a particular Disquisition of each Doctrine, and Convincement of my Understanding thereby, came to receive and bear Witness of the Truth, but by being secretly reached by this Life; for when I came into the silent Assemblies of God’s People, I felt a secret Power among them, which touched my Heart, and as I gave Way unto it, I found the Evil weakening in me, and the Good raised up, and so I became thus knit and united unto them, hungering more and more after the Increase of this Power and Life, whereby I might feel myself perfectly redeemed. And indeed this is the surest Way to become a Christian, to whom afterwards the Knowledge and Understanding of Principles will not be wanting, but will grow up so much as is needful, as the natural Fruit of this good Root, and such a Knowledge will not be barren nor unfruitful. After this Manner we desire therefore all that come among us to be proselyted, knowing that though Thousands should be convinced in their Understanding of all the Truths we maintain, yet if they were not sensible of this inward Life, and their Souls not changed from Unrighteousness to Righteousness, they could add nothing to us.

§. XXVII. But Lastly, The great Advantage of this true Worship of God, which we profess and practise, is, that it consisteth not in Man’s Wisdom, Arts or Industry; neither needeth the Glory, Pomp, Riches, nor Splendor of this World to beautify it, as being of a spiritual and heavenly Nature; and therefore too simple and contemptible to the natural Mind and Will of Man, that hath no Delight to abide in it, because he finds no Room there for his Imaginations and Inventions, and hath not the Opportunity to gratify his outward and carnal Senses: So that this Form being observed, is not likely to be long kept pure without the Power; for it is of itself so naked without it, that it hath nothing in it to invite and tempt Men to dote upon it, further than it is accompanied with the Power. Whereas the Worship of our Adversaries, being performed in their own Wills, is self-pleasing, as in which they can largely exercise their natural Parts and Invention: And so (as to most of them) having somewhat of an outward and worldly Splendor, delectable to the carnal and worldly Senses, they can pleasantly continue it, and satisfy themselves, though without the Spirit and Power; which they make no Ways essential to the Performance of their Worship, and therefore neither wait for, nor expect it.

"My dear sir," said I, "were you ever baptised?" "I never was," replied the Quaker, "nor any of my brethren." "Zounds!" say I to him, "you are not Christians, then." "Friend," replies the old man in a soft tone of voice, "swear not; we are Christians, and endeavour to be good Christians, but we are not of opinion that the sprinkling water on a child's head makes him a Christian." "Heavens!" say I, shocked at his impiety, "you have then forgot that Christ was baptised by St. John." "Friend," replies the mild Quaker once again, "swear not; Christ indeed was baptised by John, but He himself never baptised anyone. We are the disciples of Christ, not of John." I pitied very much the sincerity of my worthy Quaker, and was absolutely for forcing him to get himself christened. "Were that all," replied he very gravely, "we would submit cheerfully to baptism, purely in compliance with thy weakness, for we don't condemn any person who uses it; but then we think that those who profess a religion of so holy, so spiritual a nature as that of Christ, ought to abstain to the utmost of their power from the Jewish ceremonies." "O unaccountable!" say I: "what! baptism a Jewish ceremony?" "Yes, my friend," says he, "so truly Jewish, that a great many Jews use the baptism of John to this day.

Look into ancient authors, and thou wilt find that John only revived this practice; and that it had been used by the Hebrews, long before his time, in like manner as the Mahometans imitated the Ishmaelites in their pilgrimages to Mecca. Jesus indeed submitted to the baptism of John, as He had suffered Himself to be circumcised; but circumcision and the washing with water ought to be abolished by the baptism of Christ, that baptism of the Spirit, that ablution of the soul, which is the salvation of mankind. Thus the forerunner said, 'I indeed baptise you with water unto repentance; but He that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptise you with the Holy Ghost and with fire.' Likewise Paul, the great apostle of the Gentiles, writes as follows to the Corinthians, 'Christ sent me not to baptise, but to preach the Gospel;' and indeed Paul never baptised but two persons with water, and that very much against his inclinations. He circumcised his disciple Timothy, and the other disciples likewise circumcised all who were willing to submit to that carnal ordinance. But art thou circumcised?" added he. "I have not the honour to be so," say I. "Well, friend," continues the Quaker, "thou art a Christian without being circumcised, and I am one without being baptised."

"Well," said I to him, "what sort of a communion have you?" "We have none like that thou hintest at among us," replied he. "How! no communion?" said I. "Only that spiritual one," replied he, "of hearts." He then began again to throw out his texts of Scripture; and preached a most eloquent sermon against that ordinance. He harangued in a tone as though he had been inspired, to prove that the sacraments were merely of human invention, and that the word "sacrament" was not once mentioned in the Gospel.

parts.author: Martin Luther
parts.translator: J. M. Reu, Works of Martin Luther I (Philadelphia, 1915)
parts.ref: Luther, A Treatise on Good Works (1520), on the Third Commandment
parts.title: So formal and superficial
parts.context: Martin Luther (1483–1546), a German friar and professor, began the Reformation in 1517. In 1520 he wrote this treatise for ordinary readers, arguing that faith is the first and greatest 'good work'. Here he discusses the commandment to keep the holy day. This is J. M. Reu's English translation of 1915.
parts.plain: The outward works of this commandment are going to Mass, praying and hearing sermons on holy days. Without faith they are worth nothing. In fact there are too many holy days, since people spend them idling, drinking and gambling, and they watch the Mass, hear the sermon and say the prayers without taking anything in. People think it is enough to look, listen and say the words. It is all formal and superficial. The bishops and priests are most to blame, because they do not preach the gospel or teach people how to take part.

commentary.on: if they are not done in assurance of and with faith in God's favor, are nothing
commentary.text: Luther's principle: an act of worship without faith is worth nothing before God. This is Isaiah's 'heart far from me' in Reformation terms.

commentary.on: men think it is sufficient that we look on at the mass with our eyes, hear the preaching with our ears, and say the prayers with our mouths
commentary.text: Eyes, ears and mouth, but not the heart. Medieval people often watched the Mass rather than took part; most received Communion only once a year, at Easter.

commentary.on: It is all so formal and superficial!
commentary.text: Luther did not abolish the Mass. He reformed it, in German, with preaching and Communion for the people. His complaint is against empty form, not form itself.

parts.author: Robert Barclay
parts.work: An Apology for the True Christian Divinity, Proposition XI
parts.translator: Original English (1678); Gutenberg text of a later edition
parts.ref: Barclay, Apology (1678), Proposition XI, sections III, VII and XXVII
parts.title: The silent assemblies
parts.context: Barclay's Proposition XI argues that true worship is 'in the Spirit', and cannot be tied to set times, words or persons. Here he answers the charge that Quakers abandon meeting altogether, describes his own experience of a silent meeting, and closes with the advantage of such worship. Sidenotes and footnote markers in the Gutenberg text have been removed; the capitals and spelling are the edition's. Cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: We do not do away with meetings: we meet at set times and places, even when persecuted, because people need to see each other and worship together. What we condemn is limiting the Spirit by appointing one man to preach and pray by his own will, while everyone else simply waits for what he will say. I came to the truth not by argument, but because in the silent meetings I felt a hidden power that touched my heart, weakened the evil in me and raised the good. That is the surest way to become a Christian. The great advantage of this worship is that it needs no human skill, wealth or splendour. It is so plain that no one would keep it up without the real power of God; whereas worship full of human invention and outward splendour pleases people, so they continue it even without the Spirit.

commentary.on: we are none of those that forsake the Assembling of ourselves together
commentary.text: Barclay echoes Hebrews 10:25. Quakers met faithfully, and paid for it: Barclay himself was imprisoned in Aberdeen for attending meetings. The Quaker objection is not to gathering but to what usually happens when people gather.

commentary.on: by setting up a particular Man or Men to preach and pray in Man’s Will
commentary.text: Here is the heart of the charge. In most churches one person does the speaking and praying, from a book or a prepared text, at a fixed time. Barclay calls this 'limiting' the Spirit: it trains the congregation to depend on the preacher instead of waiting on God themselves.

commentary.on: when I came into the silent Assemblies of God’s People, I felt a secret Power among them
commentary.text: Barclay's own testimony. He was not argued into faith; he was 'secretly reached' in silence. This is the strongest form of the Quaker case: experience, not theory.

commentary.on: though Thousands should be convinced in their Understanding of all the Truths we maintain, yet if they were not sensible of this inward Life
commentary.text: Right belief, like right ritual, is not enough. What matters is a changed life, 'from Unrighteousness to Righteousness'.

commentary.on: it is of itself so naked without it, that it hath nothing in it to invite and tempt Men to dote upon it
commentary.text: A sharp argument. Silent worship is self-correcting: without the Spirit it is just people sitting in silence, and nobody would keep it up. Splendid worship, with music and ceremony, can carry on for centuries with no spiritual life at all, because people enjoy it for its own sake.

parts.author: Voltaire
parts.translator: The English translation of 1733 (usually credited to John Lockman), ed. Henry Morley (1894)
parts.ref: Voltaire, Letters on England (1733), Letter I
parts.title: Were you ever baptised?
parts.context: Voltaire (1694–1778), the most famous writer of the French Enlightenment, lived in England in 1726–1728. His Letters on England praised English freedom to shame France; the first four are about Quakers. The English translation was published in 1733, before the French. Here he describes visiting an old Quaker near London. The narrator plays a conventional Catholic; the wit is aimed at the narrator as much as the Quaker. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: I asked the Quaker whether he had been baptised. He said no, nor had any of his brethren. 'Then you are not Christians!' I said. He answered gently: we are Christians, but we do not think that sprinkling water on a child's head makes someone a Christian. Christ was baptised by John, but never baptised anyone himself. We think followers of so spiritual a religion should leave Jewish ceremonies behind; what matters is the baptism of the Spirit. Paul said Christ did not send him to baptise. You are a Christian without being circumcised; I am one without being baptised. Then I asked about communion. 'Only the spiritual communion of hearts', he said, and preached that the sacraments were human inventions, and that the word 'sacrament' is not in the Gospel.

commentary.on: we are not of opinion that the sprinkling water on a child's head makes him a Christian
commentary.text: The Quaker's sharpest point, and one many people today would share: how can a ceremony done to a baby, who knows nothing about it, make anyone a Christian?

commentary.on: Christ indeed was baptised by John, but He himself never baptised anyone
commentary.text: He appeals to John 4:2, which says Jesus himself did not baptise, his disciples did. It is a clever use of Scripture; a reply would point to Matthew 28:19.

commentary.on: that baptism of the Spirit, that ablution of the soul
commentary.text: The Quaker does not reject baptism; he spiritualises it. The real thing, he says, is inward; the outward water was a Jewish ceremony that Christ came to end, like circumcision.

commentary.on: Only that spiritual one," replied he, "of hearts.
commentary.text: And the same with Communion: the true communion is inward, of hearts, with no bread and wine.

commentary.on: the sacraments were merely of human invention
commentary.text: This is the Enlightenment's favourite form of the objection: ceremonies are human inventions, the work of priests. Voltaire, a deist who believed in a creator but not in revelation or the Church, enjoyed seeing devout Christians make that case against other Christians.

compare.author: Martin Luther and Robert Barclay and Voltaire
compare.ref: Luther, A Treatise on Good Works (1520), on the Third Commandment
compare.translator: J. M. Reu, Works of Martin Luther I (Philadelphia, 1915)
compare.why: Three voices, a Reformer, a Quaker and an Enlightenment wit, each pressing the charge further than the last: worship done without faith, worship controlled by a preacher, and the sacraments themselves as human inventions.
compare.title: The objection pressed: Luther, Barclay and Voltaire

paras: Put together, the case against ritual has four strands. First, hypocrisy: ritual lets people feel religious while living unjustly, as Amos, Isaiah and Jesus said, and as Paul found at Corinth. Second, magic: it tempts people to think that saying the right words or receiving the right object guarantees God's favour, whatever their hearts, so that religion becomes a technique for managing God. Third, control: liturgy puts power in the hands of a priest or preacher who alone may speak and act, while the people watch; Barclay calls this limiting the Spirit. Fourth, irrelevance: the forms of worship are human inventions, and a reasonable person can love God and neighbour without them.

Each strand has real evidence behind it. The late medieval Church sold indulgences and paid for thousands of Masses for the dead. Church attendance has often been a mark of respectability rather than faith. And there are many deeply good people who never go to church. The objection does not need to deny that worship can be beautiful; it says that beauty is beside the point, or worse, a distraction.
sections.key: The objection has four strands: hypocrisy, magic, control and irrelevance; each has real historical evidence.

paras: The philosophers of the Enlightenment gave the objection its classic modern form. David Hume, in The Natural History of Religion (1757), argued that superstitious religion pleases its followers with frivolous observances rather than virtue. Immanuel Kant, in Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason (1793), argued that the only true service of God is a good moral life; everything else that people do to win God's favour, ceremonies, observances, confessions, he called a 'counterfeit service' and religious illusion. Kant did not deny that churches could help moral life, but he thought their rituals were at best scaffolding, to be taken down.

Voltaire went further in his satire, treating priests and their rites as tools of power. In the century after him, many of the educated in Europe kept Christian ethics while drifting away from Christian worship. The Victorian poet Matthew Arnold heard the 'melancholy, long, withdrawing roar' of the sea of faith in 'Dover Beach' (1867).
sections.key: Hume called ceremonies frivolous observances; Kant called them 'counterfeit service', holding that only a moral life truly serves God.

paras: Today the objection is usually put more gently. Surveys by the Pew Research Center in 2017 found that about a quarter of American adults described themselves as 'spiritual but not religious', and similar numbers are found in Britain and Europe. People who say this often pray, meditate, feel awe in nature or music, and believe in something beyond themselves, but find churches cold, judgemental or simply irrelevant.

Their objection is rarely to God. It is to institutions, to being told what to believe, and to rituals that seem to belong to someone else. In that sense they are heirs of George Fox and Barclay as much as of Voltaire: the real thing, they say, is inward, personal and free. Any defence of Christian worship has to take that seriously, and admit how often churches have deserved it.
sections.key: About a quarter of American adults call themselves 'spiritual but not religious' (Pew, 2017): heirs of the Quaker and Enlightenment case, objecting to institutions more than to God.

sections.h: Reply one: the prophets were not against worship
paras: The first reply is that the prophets attacked worship without justice, not worship itself. Isaiah received his calling during worship in the Temple, seeing the angels cry 'Holy, holy, holy' (Isaiah 6). Jesus kept the Sabbath, went to the synagogue 'as his custom was' (Luke 4:16), taught his disciples a set prayer and gave them a meal to repeat. He criticised the religion of his day from inside it.

The Reformers, too, reformed worship rather than abolishing it: Luther wanted people to receive Communion with faith, Calvin wanted it weekly, and Cranmer wanted the whole Bible read aloud in English. The charge of hypocrisy is a charge against people, not against prayer. The cure for bad worship, on this view, is good worship, offered with the heart.
sections.key: The prophets, Jesus and the Reformers attacked worship without justice or faith; they kept and reformed worship rather than abolishing it.

sections.h: Reply two: not magic but promise
paras: The second reply addresses magic. Magic tries to control a power by technique. Christian teaching, at its best, has always said the opposite: in the sacraments God gives, freely, what he has promised, and people receive it by faith. Augustine called a sacrament a visible word, a promise you can see and touch. The Catholic Council of Trent (1547) taught that the sacraments work ex opere operato, 'by the work done', meaning that their power comes from Christ and not from the priest's holiness; but it also taught that they bear fruit only in those who receive them without putting an obstacle in the way, that is, with faith and repentance.

Luther made the same point in his own way: the Mass is Christ's testament, a promise, and a promise is received by trusting it. The sacraments are not ways of getting God to do something; they are the ways God has chosen to give himself to people who have bodies and need signs. Cyril's 'our imitation was in a figure, and our salvation in reality' says the same.
sections.key: Christian teaching says sacraments are not techniques but God's promises, which bear fruit when received by faith, as Augustine, Trent and Luther all held.

paras: The third and most modern reply concerns habit. Aristotle argued in the Nicomachean Ethics that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones: virtue is formed by practice. The philosopher James K. A. Smith, in Desiring the Kingdom (2009) and You Are What You Love (2016), argues that worship works the same way. We are shaped less by what we think than by what we repeatedly do and love. The world has its own liturgies, the shopping centre and the screen, that train our desires every day. Christian worship is a counter-training: confessing, listening, giving thanks, sharing bread with strangers, being sent out to serve.

On this view the objection gets things backwards. Feelings come and go; a liturgy carries you through the weeks when you feel nothing. It is precisely when you do not mean it yet that the words do their work, teaching your heart to mean them. Rowan Williams makes a similar point: you do not wait to be a good pianist before practising scales.
sections.key: Following Aristotle on habit, James K. A. Smith argues that worship forms what we love; liturgy carries people when feelings fail.

sections.h: Reply four: we cannot do it alone
paras: The last reply is from Hebrews: 'not forsaking our own assembling together'. A purely inward faith, without others, is hard to sustain and easy to bend to suit oneself. Gathering puts us next to people we did not choose, under words we did not write, before a God we do not control. Barclay agreed: Quakers met, often at great cost, because people need to see one another's faces.

There is some outside evidence. Large long-term studies, such as Tyler VanderWeele's work on the Nurses' Health Study (2016), found that people who attend religious services regularly have lower death rates, less depression and stronger social ties than those who never attend, while private spirituality alone shows much weaker links. These studies are observational and cannot prove cause, and healthier people may find it easier to go. But they suggest that what the 'spiritual but not religious' may be missing is precisely the gathering. And the Quakers are a reminder that the gathering need not be elaborate. Silence, too, can be a liturgy.
sections.key: Faith alone is hard to sustain; research finds regular attendance, not private spirituality, linked to better health and community, though it cannot prove cause.

David Hume, The Natural History of Religion (1757), section XIV; Immanuel Kant, Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason (1793), Part IV; Matthew Arnold, 'Dover Beach' (1867).

Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1; James K. A. Smith, Desiring the Kingdom (2009) and You Are What You Love (2016).
