debate.question: Is ritual a help or a hindrance to real faith?

positions.name: A hindrance: worship in the Spirit, without forms
positions.who: George Fox, Robert Barclay and the Quakers; in a different key, Kant and many 'spiritual but not religious'
positions.view: God is spirit and is met inwardly. Set words, sacraments and appointed preachers quench the Spirit, breed hypocrisy and make people dependent on outward things. Silence and a just life are the truest worship.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 29:13 and Jesus's use of it; John 4:24, 'God is spirit'; Barclay's experience in silent meetings; the long record of corrupt or empty ceremony.

positions.name: A help: God gives himself through signs
positions.who: The Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran traditions; Augustine, Cyril, Cranmer
positions.view: Humans are bodies as well as souls. Christ commanded the water and the meal, and promised to be present in them. Rites done with faith do not replace love; they are where it is received and renewed.
positions.evidence: Matthew 28:19 and 1 Corinthians 11:24; Jesus's own practice of synagogue, prayer and meal; Cyril's 'figure' and 'reality'; two thousand years of saints formed by liturgy.

positions.name: A training: practice forms the heart
positions.who: Aristotle on habit; James K. A. Smith; Rowan Williams; many evangelical and Reformed writers
positions.view: Whatever its theology, ritual forms us. Everyone has liturgies; the question is which ones. Worship trains our loves when we would otherwise drift, and the danger of emptiness is met not by abolishing forms but by entering them honestly.
positions.evidence: Nicomachean Ethics II.1; Hebrews 10:24–25, 'provoke one another to love'; research linking regular attendance with community and wellbeing.

debate.agree: All agree that worship without justice, faith or love is worthless, that God looks at the heart, and that Christians need one another; the Quakers themselves meet faithfully.

look.why: No painting of a Quaker meeting is in the National Gallery's open collection. This portrait of an unnamed Quaker, attributed to the Swedish painter Adolph-Ulrich Wertmüller, was painted in 1795, when he was working in Philadelphia, the city William Penn founded as a Quaker colony. It shows the plain dress Friends were known for, not their worship.
points: A man is shown in a three-quarter view, from the upper body up, looking at us.
He has a round face with gentle features, fair skin, and white hair styled in eighteenth-century fashion.
He wears a dark coat with gold buttons, a light waistcoat and a white cravat with ruffled edges.
The background is plain and dark: there is nothing else in the picture.

music.why: The words come from a poem by the American Quaker John Greenleaf Whittier (1872), which asks God to forgive our 'foolish ways' and to speak in stillness; set as a hymn, it is now sung in the very churches whose noisy worship he gently criticised.

think.why: What the research says about habits and practice, and the honest objections.

learn.why: Paul's chapter on love begins by saying that without love, eloquence, knowledge and even faith are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1–3): the test every ritual must pass.

check.q: What exactly does Isaiah 29:13 condemn?
options: All worship
Worship in the Temple rather than at home
Singing
The gap between honouring God with the lips and a heart far from him
check.why: The complaint is the gap between mouth and heart, not worship itself.

check.q: Barclay insists Quakers do meet together. What, then, is his objection to other churches' worship?
options: That they appoint particular people to preach and pray by human will, so that the rest depend on the preacher instead of waiting on the Spirit
That they meet on Sundays
That their buildings are too small
That they read the Bible
check.why: He condemns 'the Limitation': setting up a man to preach and pray 'in Man's Will'.

check.q: What is Barclay's argument that silent worship is self-correcting?
options: It is cheaper
It was commanded by Christ
It is shorter
Without the Spirit's power it is so bare that nobody would keep it up, whereas splendid worship can continue without the Spirit because people enjoy it
check.why: Plain worship has nothing to 'tempt Men to dote upon it' without the power.

check.q: How does the Council of Trent's teaching differ from magic?
options: It holds that their power is Christ's, not the minister's, but that they bear fruit only in those who receive them without obstacle, with faith and repentance
It leaves everything to the priest's holiness
It teaches that the right words always work, whatever the heart
It denies that sacraments do anything
check.why: Ex opere operato concerns where the power comes from; it is not a guarantee regardless of the recipient.

check.q: Which reply best answers the charge that people often go to church without meaning it?
options: Going without meaning it is better than meaning it
Practice forms the heart: as Aristotle said of virtue, doing comes before feeling, and liturgy can teach people to mean what they say
Only priests need to mean it
Nobody ever means it, so it does not matter
check.why: The formation argument (Aristotle, Smith) treats ritual as training, not pretending.

check.q: What do the research studies on attendance show, and not show?
options: That church makes people immortal
That private spirituality is linked to better health than attendance
Nothing at all
That regular attenders have lower death rates and stronger social ties, though as observational studies they cannot prove cause
check.why: The links are with regular shared attendance; the studies cannot rule out other causes.

tutorial.question: 'Ritual is the enemy of real religion.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: State the case at full strength first: the prophets and Jesus, Luther, Barclay, Voltaire, Kant and the 'spiritual but not religious'. Then weigh the replies: the prophets reformed worship rather than abolished it; sacraments as promise, not magic; liturgy as formation; the need to gather. Give the Quakers their due. Reach a view.
strong: Separates the four strands of the objection: hypocrisy, magic, control and irrelevance.
Uses Isaiah 29, Matthew 15 and Hebrews 10 accurately.
Represents Barclay fairly: Quakers meet, and his case rests on the Spirit and experience.
Explains the Enlightenment version (Kant's 'counterfeit service').
Gives the replies: reform not abolition; promise not magic; formation; community.
Reaches a reasoned view and concedes what the objection gets right.

reading.author: James K. A. Smith
reading.title: You Are What You Love
reading.why: A readable case that worship forms our desires, for good or ill.

reading.author: Rex Ambler
reading.title: Truth of the Heart: An Anthology of George Fox
reading.why: Fox's own words, put into modern English, for the Quaker case.

reading.author: Linda Woodhead and Paul Heelas
reading.title: The Spiritual Revolution
reading.why: A study in Kendal of the move from congregations to 'spirituality'.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: go to two different kinds of gathering if you can, one with set words (a choral Evensong or a Mass) and one silent (a Quaker meeting for worship, usually on Sunday morning, open to anyone). Sit through each to the end. Afterwards, write down what each did to you.
sessions.reflect: Is there anything you do regularly, without always meaning it, that has nonetheless shaped you for the better?
takeaways: The objection to ritual runs from Isaiah and Jesus through Luther, the Quakers and the Enlightenment to the 'spiritual but not religious': worship can be hypocrisy, magic, control or irrelevance.
Barclay's Quakers met faithfully but in silence, without sacraments or appointed preachers, so as not to limit the Spirit; Voltaire's Quaker called the sacraments human inventions.
The replies: the prophets reformed worship rather than abolishing it; sacraments are promise, not magic; liturgy trains love when feelings fail; and faith needs a gathering.

sessions.title: Is it really his body?
sessions.line: The Reformation's sharpest quarrel: what the bread and wine are, and five answers side by side.
sessions.plain: When Jesus said 'This is my body', what did he mean? For a thousand years almost all Christians said the bread and wine truly became his body and blood, without arguing much about how. Then the medieval Church defined it, and the Reformers split over it, so bitterly that they could not unite even against their common enemies. This session reads a bishop of the fourth century who believed the bread was changed, Jesus's own words about eating his flesh, and Luther on the promise in the bread, then sets out five views fairly.
sessions.why: Session 4 showed the meal at the heart of worship, and Justin saying it was 'not common bread'. Session 5 asked whether any of it was more than empty ritual. Now we face the question that those two raise together: if the meal is not empty, what is it? This is where Christians disagree most deeply, and you need to know why, and what each side is protecting.
answers: Is the bread really Jesus's body?
What is transubstantiation?
What did the Reformers believe instead?
Why did it matter so much?
What do the Orthodox say?
sessions.finding: The Reformation's sharpest quarrel was over what the bread is: changed in its substance (Catholic), Christ truly present in, with and under it (Lutheran), received spiritually by faith (Reformed and Anglican), or a memorial (Zwingli); the Orthodox affirm a real change and decline to define how.

paras: The first Christians spoke of the Eucharist with great realism. Ignatius of Antioch, about AD 110, called it 'the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ'; Justin said it was 'the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh'. They also used the language of sign and figure: Tertullian called the bread 'the figure of his body', and Augustine said 'what you see is bread', while what faith receives is Christ's body. For the early Church, sign and reality were not opposites: a sacrament was a sign that truly gave what it signified.

Disputes came later. In the ninth century two monks of the same abbey, Corbie in France, disagreed over whether Christ's body in the sacrament was the same as his historical body. In the eleventh, Berengar of Tours was made to recant his view that the presence was only symbolic. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council used the word 'transubstantiated' for the change in the bread and wine.
background.key: The early Church spoke of the Eucharist as truly Christ's body and also as a sign; disputes began in the ninth century, and in 1215 the Church used the word 'transubstantiation'.

paras: Ambrose was the Roman governor of northern Italy, based in Milan, when in 374 the city's Christians, quarrelling over a new bishop, demanded him for the post. He was not yet even baptised. Within a week he was baptised and made bishop. He became one of the great figures of the Western Church: he wrote hymns, stood up to emperors, and in 387 baptised Augustine.

On the Mysteries is a set of talks to the newly baptised, given in Easter week like Cyril's, probably in the 380s or 390s. It explains baptism and then the Eucharist. Ambrose is the clearest early witness to the belief that the words of Christ change the bread and wine, and he was quoted for centuries by every side of the later argument.
background.key: Ambrose, governor turned bishop of Milan in 374, baptised Augustine; his talks to the newly baptised, about 390, say Christ's words change the bread and wine.

paras: The main reading is Ambrose's argument that the bread becomes Christ's body: from the manna in the desert, from the power of blessing, from creation and from the Virgin Birth.

The comparison has two texts. First, the words of Jesus in John 6 that every side of the debate has appealed to: 'unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man'. Then Luther, in 1520, on what the Mass is: Christ's testament, with his own body and blood 'under the bread and wine' as its seal.
background.key: Ambrose argues for a change; John 6 gives Jesus's words about eating his flesh; Luther explains the Mass as Christ's testament.

before: How many different arguments does Ambrose use? Which seems strongest to you?
In John 6, how do the listeners take Jesus's words, and does he soften them?
For Luther, what is the most important thing about the Mass?
sessions.readWhy: The clearest early witness to the belief that the bread is changed, in a bishop's talk to the newly baptised.

paras: 47. We have proved the sacraments of the Church to be the more ancient, now recognize that they are superior. In very truth it is a marvellous thing that God rained manna on the fathers, and fed them with daily food from heaven; so that it is said, So man ate angels' food. But yet all those who ate that food died in the wilderness, but that food which you receive, that living Bread which came down from heaven, furnishes the substance of eternal life; and whosoever shall eat of this Bread shall never die, and it is the Body of Christ.

48. Now consider whether the bread of angels be more excellent or the Flesh of Christ, which is indeed the body of life. That manna came from heaven, this is above the heavens; that was of heaven, this is of the Lord of the heavens; that was liable to corruption, if kept a second day, this is far from all corruption, for whosoever shall taste it holily shall not be able to feel corruption. For them water flowed from the rock, for you Blood flowed from Christ; water satisfied them for a time, the Blood satiates you for eternity. The Jew drinks and thirsts again, you after drinking will be beyond the power of thirsting; that was in a shadow, this is in truth.

50. Perhaps you will say, I see something else, how is it that you assert that I receive the Body of Christ? And this is the point which remains for us to prove. And what evidence shall we make use of? Let us prove that this is not what nature made, but what the blessing consecrated, and the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing nature itself is changed.

52. We observe, then, that grace has more power than nature, and yet so far we have only spoken of the grace of a prophet's blessing. But if the blessing of man had such power as to change nature, what are we to say of that divine consecration where the very words of the Lord and Saviour operate? For that sacrament which you receive is made what it is by the word of Christ. But if the word of Elijah had such power as to bring down fire from heaven, shall not the word of Christ have power to change the nature of the elements? You read concerning the making of the whole world: He spoke and they were made, He commanded and they were created. Shall not the word of Christ, which was able to make out of nothing that which was not, be able to change things which already are into what they were not? For it is not less to give a new nature to things than to change them.

53. But why make use of arguments? Let us use the examples He gives, and by the example of the Incarnation prove the truth of the mystery. Did the course of nature proceed as usual when the Lord Jesus was born of Mary? If we look to the usual course, a woman ordinarily conceives after connection with a man. And this body which we make is that which was born of the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in the Body of Christ, seeing that the Lord Jesus Himself was born of a Virgin, not according to nature? It is the true Flesh of Christ which crucified and buried, this is then truly the Sacrament of His Body.

54. The Lord Jesus Himself proclaims: This is My Body. Before the blessing of the heavenly words another nature is spoken of, after the consecration the Body is signified. He Himself speaks of His Blood. Before the consecration it has another name, after it is called Blood. And you say, Amen, that is, It is true. Let the heart within confess what the mouth utters, let the soul feel what the voice speaks.

parts.author: Ambrose of Milan
parts.translator: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, X (1896)
parts.who: Ambrose (c. 339–397), Roman governor turned bishop of Milan, who baptised Augustine
parts.title: Not what nature made, but what the blessing consecrated
parts.context: Ambrose has explained baptism, and is now speaking to the newly baptised about the Eucharist they received for the first time at Easter. He has just argued that Christian sacraments are older than the Jewish ones, because Melchizedek offered bread and wine before Moses (Genesis 14:18). Now he argues they are superior. Cuts, where he gives more Old Testament examples, are marked '…'. New Advent's inserted Scripture references have been removed.
parts.plain: God fed Israel with manna in the desert, but they died. The bread you receive is the living bread from heaven, the body of Christ, and whoever eats it will never die. You may say: I see something else; how can it be Christ's body? I will prove it is not what nature made but what the blessing made, because blessing can change nature itself. Prophets' words changed nature, as Moses' rod became a snake. If Elijah's word brought down fire, can Christ's word not change bread and wine? He made the world from nothing by his word; he can change what already exists. And if he was born of a virgin, against nature, why expect nature's order here? Christ himself says 'This is my body'. Before the blessing it is called bread; after, it is called his body. And you say 'Amen', which means 'It is true'.

commentary.on: that living Bread which came down from heaven, furnishes the substance of eternal life
commentary.text: Ambrose begins with John 6, which you will read in the comparison: the manna fed the body for a time; the bread of life gives eternal life. The comparison between manna and Eucharist runs through early Christian preaching.

commentary.on: that was in a shadow, this is in truth
commentary.text: A key idea for the early Church: the Old Testament events were 'shadows' or types, and the Christian sacraments are the reality they pointed to.

commentary.on: Perhaps you will say, I see something else
commentary.text: Ambrose takes the obvious objection head on. The newly baptised can see it looks and tastes like bread. He does not deny it; he argues it is no longer only bread.

commentary.on: this is not what nature made, but what the blessing consecrated
commentary.text: The heart of the argument: the blessing, or consecration, changes what the thing is. 'Consecrate' means make holy, set apart for God.

commentary.on: shall not the word of Christ have power to change the nature of the elements?
commentary.text: An argument from the greater to the lesser. If a prophet's word could work wonders, Christ's word, the word that made the world, can change bread and wine. 'Elements' is the technical word for the bread and wine.

commentary.on: For it is not less to give a new nature to things than to change them.
commentary.text: If God can create from nothing, changing something is no harder. Note that Ambrose says 'change the nature': later Catholic theology would speak of the substance changing while the appearance stays.

commentary.on: And this body which we make is that which was born of the Virgin.
commentary.text: A bold sentence. The body in the sacrament is the same body that was born of Mary. Catholics and Orthodox read Ambrose as clear evidence for a real change; some Protestant scholars point out that elsewhere he also speaks of 'likeness' and 'figure'.

commentary.on: And you say, Amen, that is, It is true.
commentary.text: As in Justin, the people's Amen. The newly baptised said it when they received: the minister said 'the body of Christ', and they answered 'Amen'. Most churches still do this.

commentary.on: Let the heart within confess what the mouth utters
commentary.text: Ambrose ends where the last session did: the mouth must not say what the heart does not believe. Even the strongest believer in a real change insists on faith.

read.author: Ambrose of Milan
read.translator: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, X (1896)
read.who: Ambrose (c. 339–397), Roman governor turned bishop of Milan, who baptised Augustine

paras: I am the bread of life.
Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and they died.
This is the bread which comes down out of heaven, that anyone may eat of it and not die.
I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Yes, the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”
The Jews therefore contended with one another, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”
Jesus therefore said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves.
He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.
For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.
He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him.
As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father; so he who feeds on me, he will also live because of me.
This is the bread which came down out of heaven—not as our fathers ate the manna, and died. He who eats this bread will live forever.”

II. In the mass it is necessary that we attend with our a hearts also; and we do attend, when we exercise faith in our hearts. Here we must repeat the words of Christ, when He institutes the mass and says, "Take and eat, this is My Body, which is given for you"; in like manner over the cup, "Take and drink ye all of it: this is a new, everlasting Testament in My Blood, which is shed for you and for many for the remission of sins. This shall ye do, as oft as ye do it, in remembrance of Me." In these words Christ has made for Himself a memorial or anniversary, to be daily observed in all Christendom, and has added to it a glorious, rich, great testament, in which no interest, money or temporal possessions are bequeathed and distributed, but the forgiveness of all sins, grace and mercy unto eternal life, that all who come to this memorial shall have the same testament; and then He died, whereby this testament has become permanent and irrevocable. In proof and evidence of which, instead of letter and seal, He has left with us His own Body and Blood under the bread and wine.

Here there is need that a man practise the first works of this Commandment right well, that he doubt not that what Christ has said is true, and consider the testament sure, so that he make not Christ a liar. For if you are present at mass and do not consider nor believe that here Christ through His testament has bequeathed and given you forgiveness of all your sins, what else is it, than as if you said: "I do not know or do not believe that it is true that forgiveness of my sins is here bequeathed and given me"? Oh, how many masses there are in the world at present! but how few who hear them with such faith and benefit! Most grievously is God provoked to anger thereby. For this reason also no one shall or can reap any benefit from the mass except he be in trouble of soul and long for divine mercy, and desire to be rid of his sins; or, if he have an evil intention, he must be changed during the mass, and come to have a desire for this testament. For this reason in olden times no open sinner was allowed to be present at the mass.

parts.title: Unless you eat my flesh
parts.context: The day after feeding five thousand people with five loaves, Jesus teaches in the synagogue at Capernaum, by the Sea of Galilee. The crowd has asked for a sign like the manna Moses gave. John's Gospel, written in the late first century, does not describe the Last Supper's bread and cup; many readers think this chapter is where John teaches about the Eucharist.

commentary.on: I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and they died.
commentary.text: The comparison Ambrose used. The manna kept people alive for a day; Jesus offers life that does not end.

commentary.on: the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh
commentary.text: The bread is his flesh, given 'for the life of the world': a pointer to his death on the cross.

commentary.on: How can this man give us his flesh to eat?
commentary.text: His hearers take him literally, and are shocked. Jews were forbidden to drink blood (Leviticus 17:10–14).

commentary.on: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves
commentary.text: Jesus does not soften it; he makes it stronger. Catholics, Orthodox and Lutherans see here the real eating of Christ in the sacrament. Zwingli and many Protestants read it as eating by faith: later in the chapter Jesus says 'the flesh profits nothing; the words that I speak to you are spirit' (John 6:63).

commentary.on: For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.
commentary.text: 'Indeed' means 'truly', 'really'. This verse is the root of the phrase 'real presence'.

commentary.on: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him.
commentary.text: On every reading, the point is union: to eat is to live in Christ and to have him live in you. That much all Christians affirm.

parts.author: Martin Luther
parts.translator: J. M. Reu, Works of Martin Luther I (Philadelphia, 1915)
parts.ref: Luther, A Treatise on Good Works (1520): the Mass
parts.title: Under the bread and wine
parts.context: Later in the same section of the treatise you read in session 5, Luther explains how to take part in the Mass with the heart. A 'testament' is a will, the document in which someone leaves their goods to their heirs. (The Gutenberg text has a misprint in its first line, 'our a hearts', kept here as printed.)
parts.plain: At Mass we must take part with our hearts, by faith. Christ said, 'Take and eat, this is my body, given for you', and over the cup, 'this is the new testament in my blood, shed for you for the forgiveness of sins; do this in remembrance of me'. With these words Christ made a memorial and a will. What he leaves us is not money but the forgiveness of all our sins, grace and mercy. Then he died, so the will cannot be changed. As its seal he left us his own body and blood under the bread and wine. So we must trust that what he said is true. If you go to Mass without believing that Christ is giving you forgiveness there, what are you doing?

commentary.on: In these words Christ has made for Himself a memorial or anniversary
commentary.text: Luther keeps the idea of memorial, but a memorial with a gift attached.

commentary.on: a glorious, rich, great testament
commentary.text: This is Luther's key idea. The Mass is not something we offer to God, a sacrifice, but something God gives us: a testament, a promise of forgiveness. That turned the medieval emphasis around.

commentary.on: He has left with us His own Body and Blood under the bread and wine
commentary.text: Luther never doubted that Christ's body and blood were truly present. He rejected transubstantiation as a philosopher's theory, but held to the presence 'under' the bread and wine. At Marburg in 1529 he would refuse to give an inch on this.

commentary.on: that he doubt not that what Christ has said is true
commentary.text: For Luther the issue is trust. Christ said 'This is my body'; to doubt it is to 'make Christ a liar'.

commentary.on: how few who hear them with such faith and benefit!
commentary.text: Luther's complaint from the previous session returns: many Masses, little faith. His remedy is not fewer sacraments but more faith in them.

compare.author: Martin Luther
compare.why: John 6 is the passage every side appeals to, and Luther's 1520 treatise shows how a Reformer who still believed Christ's body was truly present moved the emphasis from the change in the bread to the promise it carries.
compare.title: Jesus's words, and Luther's testament

paras: In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council taught that in the Eucharist the bread and wine are 'transubstantiated' into Christ's body and blood. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) explained the idea with the philosophy of Aristotle. Everything has a 'substance', what it is, and 'accidents', how it appears: colour, taste, weight. In the Eucharist, Aquinas said, the whole substance of the bread becomes the substance of Christ's body, while the accidents of bread remain (Summa Theologiae III, questions 75–77). So it looks and tastes like bread, and is Christ.

Catholics do not claim this can be seen or tested; it is a mystery of faith. It explains Catholic practice: the consecrated bread, the 'host', is kept in a tabernacle, a lamp burns beside it, people genuflect to it, and on the feast of Corpus Christi, established in the thirteenth century, it is carried in procession. The Council of Trent reaffirmed transubstantiation in 1551, against the Reformers.
sections.key: Lateran IV (1215) and Aquinas taught that the bread's substance becomes Christ's body while its appearances remain; Trent reaffirmed it in 1551.

paras: Luther rejected transubstantiation in The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520) as an unnecessary theory borrowed from Aristotle. But he held as firmly as any Catholic that Christ's body and blood are truly present. The bread remains bread, he said, and Christ's body is there too, as fire fills red-hot iron. Lutherans later spoke of the body present 'in, with and under' the bread, and call it a 'sacramental union'. (The label 'consubstantiation' is often used, but most Lutherans reject it.)

Luther's ground was the plain words: 'This is my body'. How Christ's risen body, which the creed says is at the right hand of the Father, could be present on many altars at once, he answered by saying that the right hand of God is everywhere, and Christ's humanity shares in his divine presence.
sections.key: Luther rejected transubstantiation but held that Christ's body is truly present in, with and under the bread: a 'sacramental union'.

paras: Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), the Reformer of Zurich, read 'This is my body' as 'This signifies my body', as when Jesus says 'I am the vine'. His key text was John 6:63: 'the flesh profits nothing'. Christ's risen body is in heaven, he argued, and cannot be in many places at once. The supper is a memorial of his death and a pledge of our faith, in which the congregation, by eating together, declares itself his body.

Zwingli's view is often called 'merely symbolic', which is unfair to him: for Zwingli, Christ was truly present to the faith of the believers, by his Spirit, even if not in the bread. Many Baptist and evangelical churches today hold a view close to his, calling the Lord's Supper an 'ordinance' and a remembrance.
sections.key: Zwingli read 'is' as 'signifies': Christ's body is in heaven, and the supper is a memorial and pledge, with Christ present to faith.

paras: The Protestant princes needed unity against the Catholic emperor. In October 1529 Philip of Hesse brought Luther and Zwingli together at his castle in Marburg. They agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles: the Trinity, Christ, faith, baptism and more. On the fifteenth, the Lord's Supper, they could not agree. The story is told that Luther chalked the words 'This is my body' on the table and kept pointing to them. When it was over he refused Zwingli's offered hand, saying, in one report, that they were of a different spirit.

The failure at Marburg meant that the Protestant Reformation split permanently into Lutheran and Reformed churches. Two years later Zwingli was killed at the battle of Kappel, fighting for Zurich against the Catholic cantons.
sections.key: At Marburg in 1529 Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen articles and split on the fifteenth, the Lord's Supper; the Lutheran and Reformed churches went separate ways.

sections.h: Calvin and Cranmer: a spiritual feeding
paras: John Calvin (1509–1564) of Geneva took a middle way. Against Zwingli he insisted that in the supper we truly receive Christ's body and blood, not just a reminder; against Luther and Rome he held that Christ's body stays in heaven. The Holy Spirit, he said, lifts believers up to feed on Christ there, so that the presence is real but spiritual, received by faith (Institutes IV.17). The bread is a true sign that gives what it signifies, to those who believe.

Thomas Cranmer's Prayer Book of 1552 was close to this view. Its words at the giving of the bread told people to take and eat in remembrance, and to feed on Christ in their hearts by faith. It added a note, later called the 'Black Rubric', explaining that kneeling to receive did not mean adoring the bread, since Christ's natural body was in heaven. The Rubric was dropped under Elizabeth I and restored in 1662 with one change of wording, which now denied a 'corporal' presence rather than a 'real and essential' one. Anglicans have held a range of views ever since, from close to Calvin to close to Rome.
sections.key: Calvin taught a real but spiritual presence, received by faith through the Spirit; Cranmer's Prayer Book and its 'Black Rubric' (1552, revised 1662) took a similar line.

sections.h: The Orthodox: a mystery, not a theory
paras: The Orthodox Church believes that the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood: its liturgy prays for the Holy Spirit to come and change them, and Orthodox writers speak of a 'change' (Greek metabole). But it has generally refused to say how. Transubstantiation appears in some Orthodox statements from the seventeenth century, but many Orthodox theologians regard it as one Western attempt to explain a mystery best left unexplained.

For the Orthodox, the moment of change is not only Christ's words but the prayer to the Spirit, the epiclesis. The Orthodox theologian Alexander Schmemann argued that the whole service, not one moment in it, is the 'sacrament of the Kingdom': the Church is taken up into the presence of God, and the bread and wine with it.
sections.key: The Orthodox affirm a real change through the Spirit's coming but decline to define how; for Schmemann the whole liturgy is the sacrament.

paras: Here are the main answers to the question 'What is the bread?', as each tradition would put it.

rows: Its substance becomes Christ's body; the appearances of bread remain
'This is my body'; Ambrose's change; Aquinas's substance and accidents
Truly changed into Christ's body by the Spirit; how is not defined
The epiclesis; 'my flesh is food indeed' (John 6:55)
Bread still, and Christ's body truly present in, with and under it
The plain words 'This is my body'
Bread still; by the Spirit, believers truly feed on Christ, who is in heaven
John 6:63; Christ's ascension; 'a sharing of the body' (1 Corinthians 10:16)
Bread, a sign that recalls Christ's death; Christ present to faith
'Do this in memory of me'; 'the flesh profits nothing'
table.note: Each tradition contains a range of views; this is the classic position of each.

sections.key: Five classic answers: transubstantiation, an undefined mystery of change, sacramental union, spiritual real presence and memorial.

sections.h: Why it mattered, and where things stand
paras: It can look like hair-splitting. It was not. If Christ is bodily present, the bread may be adored and the Mass offered as a sacrifice; if he is not, adoring it is idolatry. People were burned for these differences: the Protestant John Frith in 1533 and Cranmer himself in 1556, Catholics under Elizabeth I and Protestants under Mary. Each side thought the other was either despising Christ or worshipping bread.

Since the twentieth century, the gap has narrowed. Lutherans and Reformed churches in Europe reached agreement in the Leuenberg Agreement of 1973. Catholic and Anglican theologians, in the Windsor statement of 1971, agreed that Christ's presence is real and the Eucharist a memorial in the biblical sense, which makes the past present. Real differences remain, above all on whether Christians of divided churches may share Communion. But nearly all agree that Christ gives himself in the meal, and that it is to be received with faith.
sections.key: The quarrel cost lives, because worship and idolatry were at stake; modern agreements (Windsor 1971, Leuenberg 1973) have narrowed it, though sharing Communion remains divided.

refs: John 6:22–71; 1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23–29; Genesis 14:18; Leviticus 17:10–14.
Ambrose, On the Mysteries 47–54, tr. de Romestin, NPNF II.10 (1896); Ignatius, To the Smyrnaeans 7; Justin, First Apology 66; Tertullian, Against Marcion IV.40; Augustine, Sermon 272.
Fourth Lateran Council (1215), canon 1; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae III, qq. 75–77; Council of Trent, Session XIII (1551).
Luther, A Treatise on Good Works (1520), tr. Reu; The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520); on Marburg, the Marburg Articles (October 1529) and Hermann Sasse, This Is My Body (1959).
Zwingli, On the Lord's Supper (1526); Calvin, Institutes IV.17 (1559); The Book of Common Prayer (1552 and 1662), the declaration on kneeling.
Alexander Schmemann, The Eucharist: Sacrament of the Kingdom (1988); ARCIC, Eucharistic Doctrine (Windsor, 1971); the Leuenberg Agreement (1973).

debate.question: What happens to the bread?

positions.name: It is changed
positions.who: Ambrose; the Catholic Church (Lateran IV, Aquinas, Trent); the Orthodox Churches
positions.view: Christ's words, and the Spirit's coming, change the bread and wine into his body and blood. It still looks like bread, but it is Christ, to be received with awe and even adored.
positions.evidence: 'This is my body'; John 6:53–55; Justin's 'not common bread'; Ambrose's 'not what nature made, but what the blessing consecrated'; the unbroken early tradition of realist language.

positions.name: Christ is truly given, but the bread is not changed
positions.who: Luther and the Lutherans (sacramental union); Calvin, the Reformed and many Anglicans (spiritual presence)
positions.view: The bread remains bread, but Christ's body and blood are truly received in the supper, whether present in, with and under the bread (Luther) or by the Spirit lifting believers to Christ (Calvin). The change is in what God gives, not in the substance of the bread.
positions.evidence: 'A sharing of the body of Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:16); Paul still calls it 'bread' after the blessing (1 Corinthians 11:26–28); Augustine's sign and reality; Luther's testament.

positions.name: It is a memorial
positions.who: Zwingli; many Baptists, evangelicals and Pentecostals
positions.view: 'This is my body' means 'this signifies my body', as 'I am the door' is a figure. Christ's body is in heaven. The supper is a memorial of his death and a public pledge of faith, in which Christ is present to the believers by his Spirit.
positions.evidence: 'Do this in memory of me' (1 Corinthians 11:24); 'the flesh profits nothing' (John 6:63); Jesus's other 'I am' sayings; the ascension.

debate.agree: All agree that Christ instituted the meal, that it proclaims his death until he comes, that he meets his people in it, and that it must be received with faith and love.

look.why: There is no painting of a Eucharist in the gallery's open collection. Bachiacca's Gathering of Manna (1540s) shows instead the bread from heaven that both Jesus in John 6 and Ambrose contrast with the bread of life: 'your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and they died'. (The painting also appears in 'Exodus and the law'.)
points: About fifty men, women and children, with a giraffe, an ox and other animals, gather in groups across a hilly landscape.
They wear robes in carnation pink, honey orange, sky blue, ruby red, leaf green and golden brown.
In the lower left, eight men and women gather behind a man who points to the right with a stick.
Others sit on the ground or on rocks, stand at barrel-sized urns, or bend to the ground.
A porcupine, a white rabbit, a black bear, a cow and cheetah-like animals are spaced along the foreground.
In the distance a path leads to buildings by a jagged coastline, under craggy blue mountains and a cloudy sky.

music.why: 'Hail, true body, born of the Virgin Mary': a medieval hymn to Christ's presence in the Eucharist, set by Mozart months before his death. Its words make Ambrose's point, that this is the body born of the Virgin.

think.why: Ambrose argues from the incarnation: if God could become flesh, he can give his flesh. See what Christians believe about who Jesus was.

learn.why: Jesus's first 'I am' saying in John's Gospel. Christians who disagree about what the bread is can all say these words together.

check.q: What is Ambrose's main reason for saying the bread is no longer only bread?
options: That the manna was the same
That the blessing, by Christ's word, changes what nature made
That it tastes different
That the priest is holy
check.why: 'Not what nature made, but what the blessing consecrated': Christ's word can change the nature of the elements.

check.q: In Aquinas's account of transubstantiation, what changes and what stays?
options: The bread becomes a symbol only
The substance of bread becomes Christ's body; the appearances of bread remain
Nothing changes
The appearances change; the substance stays
check.why: Substance (what it is) changes; accidents (how it appears) remain.

check.q: Why did Luther reject transubstantiation?
options: Because Zwingli persuaded him
Because he thought Christ was absent
Because he thought it an unnecessary philosophical theory, while still holding Christ's body truly present with the bread
Because the Bible forbids bread
check.why: Luther held the real presence firmly, but not Aristotle's explanation of it.

check.q: Which text was Zwingli's key support?
options: 'The flesh profits nothing; the words that I speak to you are spirit' (John 6:63)
'My flesh is food indeed'
'This is my body'
'The cup of blessing'
check.why: He read John 6 spiritually, with verse 63 as the key, and 'is' as 'signifies'.

check.q: How did Calvin's view differ from both Luther's and Zwingli's?
options: He held a real feeding on Christ's body, by the Spirit lifting believers to heaven, without Christ's body being in the bread
He thought the supper unnecessary
He accepted transubstantiation
He denied any presence
check.why: Real against Zwingli; spiritual, and Christ in heaven, against Luther and Rome.

check.q: Why did a difference over the bread matter enough to divide churches and cost lives?
options: It did not matter to anyone
Because kings preferred one view
Because if Christ is bodily present the bread may be adored, and if not, adoring it is idolatry: worship itself was at stake
Because bread was scarce
check.why: Each side thought the other was either despising Christ or worshipping a created thing.

tutorial.question: 'This is my body.' Assess the main interpretations.
tutorial.approach: Begin with the texts: the words of institution, 1 Corinthians 10–11, John 6. Show the early Church's realist and sign language (Justin, Ambrose, Augustine). Explain transubstantiation, Luther's sacramental union, Zwingli's memorial, Calvin's spiritual presence and the Orthodox view, with Marburg as the turning point. Say what each is protecting, and where modern agreement has been reached.
strong: Uses the biblical texts accurately, including John 6:53–55 and 6:63.
Shows that the early Church used both realist and sign language.
Explains transubstantiation with substance and accidents.
Distinguishes Luther, Zwingli and Calvin clearly, with the Marburg Colloquy.
Gives the Orthodox view and the Anglican range, including the Black Rubric.
Explains why it mattered (adoration, sacrifice) and notes modern agreements.

reading.author: Alexander Schmemann
reading.title: The Eucharist: Sacrament of the Kingdom
reading.why: The Orthodox understanding, from inside the liturgy.

reading.author: Diarmaid MacCulloch
reading.title: Reformation: Europe's House Divided
reading.why: The best one-volume history, with Marburg and the Eucharistic quarrels at its heart.

reading.author: Hermann Sasse
reading.title: This Is My Body
reading.why: A Lutheran account of the Marburg Colloquy and what was at stake.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: before each meal, before you eat, say one sentence of thanks aloud and name one person whose work put it on your table. At the end of the week, read John 6 in one sitting.
sessions.reflect: What would it change for you if Christ were truly present in a piece of bread, and what if he were not?
takeaways: The early Church spoke of the Eucharist as truly Christ's body (Justin, Ambrose) and also as a sign; Lateran IV (1215) and Aquinas defined transubstantiation.
The Reformers split: Luther held Christ's body truly present with the bread, Zwingli saw a memorial, Calvin and Cranmer a real but spiritual feeding; Marburg (1529) failed to unite them.
The Orthodox affirm a real change without defining how; modern agreements have narrowed the divide, but sharing Communion remains a wound.

sessions.title: Going for the first time
sessions.line: The verdict: every service has the same bones, and knowing them, you can walk into any church.
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict of this journey. However different they look, nearly all Christian services have the same bones: people gather, they hear the word, they share the table or pray, and they are sent out. Knowing that, you can walk into any church and find your way. This session reads the passage in Hebrews that tells Christians what they are really walking into, the end of the Prayer Book's Morning Prayer, and then gives a plain, practical guide to going for the first time.
sessions.why: The journey has walked through a service part by part: the day, the water, the word and the table. It heard the strongest case that all of it is empty ritual, and faced the question that divided the Reformers. Now it can answer its own question, why Christians baptise and break bread, and the question most readers really have: what should I do if I go?
answers: What do all Christian services have in common?
Why are services so different in different churches?
What should I expect if I go, and what should I do?
Why do Christians think it matters?
sessions.finding: Every service, however different, has the same bones: gathering, word, table or prayer, and sending; knowing them, you can walk into any church, and Christians believe that what you walk into is more than a building full of people.

paras: Why do Christians baptise and break bread? Because Jesus commanded both, and because they believe that in the water and the meal he gives himself. Baptism is the door, once for all: dying and rising with Christ. The meal is the table, week after week: thanksgiving, sharing in Christ, many made one body. Around them are the day (Sunday, the resurrection), the word (Scripture read and explained, psalms, hymns and the creed) and the prayers. All of it was in place by Justin's time, about 155.

Christians disagree, sometimes bitterly, about who should be baptised, what the bread is, and who may receive. The objection that it is all empty ritual is old and serious, and the Church has often deserved it. But the best answer is not to abandon the gathering; it is to enter it honestly, with justice and faith. That is the verdict. The rest of this session is about what it looks like on an ordinary Sunday.
background.key: Christians baptise and break bread because Jesus commanded it and they believe he gives himself in them; the forms are ancient, the disagreements real, and the answer to empty ritual is honest worship.

paras: If the bones are the same, why do services feel so different? Partly because of history: the Orthodox liturgy grew in the Greek-speaking East, the Mass in the Latin West, and Protestant services from the Reformers' reforms. Partly because of theology: a church that believes Christ is bodily present will kneel, bow and use beautiful vessels; a church that stresses the word will give the sermon the most time. And partly because of culture: a Pentecostal service in Lagos, a Lutheran one in Hamburg and choral Evensong in an English cathedral are each at home in their place.

You will meet all of these in the practical guide that follows. None of them is hard to attend. Most churches are used to visitors, and most people in any congregation once walked in for the first time themselves.
background.key: Services differ because of history (East and West, Reformation), theology (presence and word) and culture, but the bones are shared.

paras: The main reading is from the Letter to the Hebrews, which you met in session 5. It tells Christians what they come to when they gather: not only a room of people but 'the heavenly Jerusalem', angels and the saints. It is the reason Christians give for why worship matters.
The comparison is the end of Morning Prayer in the Book of Common Prayer: a prayer and a blessing that send people out. Every service ends with a sending.
background.key: Hebrews 12 says what Christians believe they come to; the end of Morning Prayer shows how a service sends them out.

before: Hebrews contrasts two mountains. What is each like?
Who, according to Hebrews, is present when Christians gather?
In the Prayer Book, what does the Prayer of St Chrysostom ask for?
sessions.readWhy: What Christians believe they come to when they gather for worship.

paras: For you have not come to a mountain that might be touched, and that burned with fire, and to blackness, darkness, storm,
the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which those who heard it begged that not one more word should be spoken to them,
for they could not stand that which was commanded, “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned”.
So fearful was the appearance that Moses said, “I am terrified and trembling.”
But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable multitudes of angels,
to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of just men made perfect,
to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel.
See that you don’t refuse him who speaks. For if they didn’t escape when they refused him who warned on the earth, how much more will we not escape who turn away from him who warns from heaven,
whose voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised, saying, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth, but also the heavens.”
This phrase, “Yet once more” signifies the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, that those things which are not shaken may remain.
Therefore, receiving a Kingdom that can’t be shaken, let’s have grace, through which we serve God acceptably, with reverence and awe,
for our God is a consuming fire.

parts.title: You have come to Mount Zion
parts.context: Near the end of the Letter to the Hebrews, the writer contrasts two gatherings. The first is Israel at Mount Sinai, where God gave the law amid fire and darkness (Exodus 19–20). The second is the Christian assembly. Zion is the hill of Jerusalem where the Temple stood, and here stands for the city of God.

commentary.on: For you have not come to a mountain that might be touched, and that burned with fire
commentary.text: Sinai was terrifying: fire, darkness, a trumpet, a voice the people begged not to hear again. Holiness there meant distance.

commentary.on: But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem
commentary.text: 'You have come': not 'you will come one day'. When Christians gather, the writer says, they already join the worship of heaven. This is the deepest Christian reason for going to church.

commentary.on: to innumerable multitudes of angels, to the festal gathering
commentary.text: A 'festal gathering' is a festival crowd. Worship on earth joins a feast in heaven. That is why the eucharistic prayer joins the angels' 'Holy, holy, holy'.

commentary.on: to the spirits of just men made perfect
commentary.text: The faithful who have died are part of the gathering too. Christians call this 'the communion of saints': a small congregation on a wet Sunday is, in faith, part of a crowd beyond counting.

commentary.on: to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant
commentary.text: At the centre is Jesus, the 'new covenant' of the Last Supper's cup. Every service, of every tradition, is gathered round him.

commentary.on: let’s have grace, through which we serve God acceptably, with reverence and awe
commentary.text: 'Serve' is the word behind 'service'. Worship should have both joy, a festival, and awe, 'for our God is a consuming fire'. A good service holds both.

paras: A Prayer of St. Chrysostom. ALMIGHTY God, who hast given us grace at this time with one accord to make our common supplications unto thee; and dost promise, that when two or three are gathered together in thy Name thou wilt grant their requests; Fulfil now, O Lord, the desires and petitions of thy servants, as may be most expedient for them; granting us in this world knowledge of thy truth, and in the world to come life everlasting. Amen.
THE grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost, be with us all evermore. Amen.

parts.author: The Book of Common Prayer (1662)
parts.translator: Original English (Thomas Cranmer's text of 1549 and 1552, revised in 1662); transcribed from a twentieth-century printing
parts.who: Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556), Archbishop of Canterbury, and the revisers of 1662
parts.ref: The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer: the Prayer of St Chrysostom and the Grace
parts.title: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ
parts.context: The last two prayers of Morning Prayer, after the prayers for the monarch, the clergy and people. Cranmer translated the Prayer of St Chrysostom from the Greek Orthodox liturgy; it is named after John Chrysostom, though its author is unknown. The Grace is Paul's blessing at the end of 2 Corinthians (13:14). The capitals at the start of each prayer are the printed book's large initial letters.
parts.plain: Almighty God, you have let us pray together with one mind, and you promise that when two or three gather in your name you will hear them. Answer our prayers as is best for us: give us knowledge of your truth in this world, and eternal life in the next. Then all say together: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with us all for ever.

commentary.on: who hast given us grace at this time with one accord to make our common supplications unto thee
commentary.text: 'With one accord' and 'common': the prayer thanks God for the very fact of praying together. Cranmer's whole book was about common prayer.

commentary.on: when two or three are gathered together in thy Name thou wilt grant their requests
commentary.text: Jesus's promise in Matthew 18:19–20. However few turn up, the prayer says, it is enough.

commentary.on: as may be most expedient for them
commentary.text: A wise clause: not 'give us whatever we ask', but what is best for us. It is a lesson in how to pray.

commentary.on: granting us in this world knowledge of thy truth, and in the world to come life everlasting
commentary.text: Two requests that sum up what worship is for: truth now, life for ever.

commentary.on: THE grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost, be with us all evermore.
commentary.text: The Grace is often said at the end of services and meetings, with people looking at one another. 'Fellowship' translates koinonia, the same word as 'communion' in 1 Corinthians 10:16. The service ends where the table began: in sharing.

compare.author: The Book of Common Prayer (1662)
compare.ref: The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer: the Prayer of St Chrysostom and the Grace
compare.translator: Original English (Thomas Cranmer's text of 1549 and 1552, revised in 1662); transcribed from a twentieth-century printing
compare.why: Every service ends by sending people back into the world. The Prayer Book ends Morning Prayer with a prayer from the Greek liturgy and Paul's blessing.
compare.title: Sent out: the end of Morning Prayer

paras: Strip away the differences and almost every Christian service has four parts. First, the gathering: people arrive, often with a hymn, a greeting and a prayer of confession. Second, the word: readings from the Bible, a psalm or hymn, a sermon, and often the creed. Third, the table or the prayers: on a Communion Sunday, the bread and wine with the great thanksgiving; otherwise, prayers for the world and the Lord's Prayer. Fourth, the sending: a blessing and a dismissal, often with a final hymn.

These are Justin's parts, give or take: gathering, readings, sermon, prayers, the kiss of peace, bread and wine, thanksgiving, Amen, Communion and a collection. If you know the four bones, you will not be lost anywhere. A Catholic Mass, a Baptist morning service and choral Evensong all follow them, though Evensong, a service of the word and prayers without Communion, has no table.
sections.key: Four bones: gathering, word, table or prayers, sending. They are Justin's parts, and you will find them in almost every service.

paras: Look up the church's website for the time of its main Sunday service, and what kind it is: Mass, Eucharist, Holy Communion, morning worship or Divine Liturgy. Choral Evensong, at many cathedrals on most days of the week, is an easy first visit: you can sit and listen, and nothing is asked of you. Arrive about ten minutes early. Wear what you would wear to meet a friend for coffee; in Orthodox churches people dress a little more modestly, and some women cover their heads.

Take whatever you are handed at the door: a booklet, a hymn book, a sheet. It usually contains everything you need, with the people's words in bold. Sit anywhere that is free; a few rows from the back lets you watch what others do. Nobody expects a visitor to know what to do, and nobody will single you out. Going alone is fine: most first-timers do.
sections.key: Check the time and kind of service, arrive ten minutes early, take the booklet, sit near the back and watch; going alone is fine.

paras: The simple rule is: stand to sing and to hear the Gospel, sit to listen, and stand or kneel to pray. Follow the people around you, or stay seated; nobody minds. In Catholic and Orthodox churches people may cross themselves, bow or light candles; you do not have to. At the Peace, people turn to those near them, shake hands and say 'Peace be with you'; you can say it back, or just smile.

When the collection is taken, a plate or bag is passed along the rows. You do not have to give; just pass it on. In an Orthodox church the service may be long and many people stand throughout, coming and going quietly: that is normal. In a Pentecostal church people may raise their hands, call out or pray aloud together: that is normal too.
sections.key: Stand to sing, sit to listen, stand or kneel to pray; join the Peace if you like; you never have to give, cross yourself or bow.

paras: This is the moment visitors worry about most. Every church handles it differently. In Orthodox and Catholic churches, only members of that church are asked to receive. In most Anglican churches, baptised Christians who receive in their own church are welcome. In many Protestant churches, all who love Christ are invited. The minister or the booklet will usually say.

If you are not sure, you have two good options. Stay in your seat while others go forward; many people do. Or, in Catholic, Anglican and many other churches, go forward with your arms crossed over your chest, and the priest will say a blessing over you instead. In an Orthodox church, at the very end, people go forward to receive a piece of blessed bread, the antidoron; visitors are often offered it too. Nobody will be offended either way.
sections.key: Follow the church's invitation; if unsure, stay seated, or go forward with arms crossed for a blessing.

paras: Every service ends with a blessing and a dismissal. The old Latin Mass ended with Ite, missa est, 'Go, it is the dismissal', which gave the Mass its name. The Orthodox liturgy ends with the call to go forth in peace. Modern services often end with a charge to go out and love and serve the Lord. The point is the same: worship is not an escape from the world, but a gathering that sends people back into it, fed.

That is Schmemann's argument, and Justin's practice: the collection for widows, orphans, prisoners and strangers was part of the service. Many churches end with tea or coffee. Stay if you can: that is where people say hello, and where you can ask anything you like. Afterwards, ask yourself the question the journey has been building to: would you go back?
sections.key: Every service ends with a blessing and a sending out into the world; stay for coffee if you can.

paras: If you have never been, some services are easier first visits than others. Choral Evensong, sung in cathedrals and some parish churches, asks nothing of you: a choir sings psalms and canticles, two readings are read, prayers are said, and it is over in about forty-five minutes. A Sunday Eucharist or Mass, about an hour, shows you the whole shape, word and table. An evangelical or Pentecostal morning service will have more singing, a longer sermon and usually a warm welcome at the door.

An Orthodox Divine Liturgy is longer, almost entirely sung, often in a language other than English, and full of icons, candles and incense; you may stand at the back and come and go. A Quaker meeting for worship is an hour, mostly silent, with anyone free to stand and speak briefly if moved to. Each shows you the same bones from a different angle. You may find, as many do, that the one that suits you is not the one you expected.
sections.key: Evensong asks nothing of you; a Eucharist shows the whole shape; evangelical, Orthodox and Quaker services show the same bones from other angles.

paras: The Christian answer is Hebrews 12: 'you have come to Mount Zion'. When Christians gather, however few and however ordinary, they believe they join the worship of heaven, with the angels and the saints, around Jesus. The meal is a foretaste of a feast; the word is God speaking now; the water is a death and a birth. Rowan Williams, in Being Christian (2014), argues that baptism, the Bible, the Eucharist and prayer are simply the four things that make a Christian life: practices you live into, not ideas you first have to master.

You do not have to believe all of that to go. Many people first go out of curiosity, grief, love of music or a sense that something is missing. The Church has always had room at the back for the curious. Justin wrote his description for people outside; this journey has tried to do the same.
sections.key: Christians go because they believe they join the worship of heaven, around Christ; you do not have to believe that to go and see.

refs: Hebrews 12:18–29; Exodus 19–20; Matthew 18:19–20; 2 Corinthians 13:14; 1 Corinthians 10:16.
The Book of Common Prayer (1662), Morning Prayer; Justin, First Apology 65–67.
The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, the dismissal (in Isabel Hapgood's Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic Church, 1906).
Alexander Schmemann, For the Life of the World (1963); Rowan Williams, Being Christian (2014).
Rose Window's Sunday guide (content/sunday.json, draft) for the practical advice, which this session follows.

debate.question: Does it matter which church you go to?

positions.name: Yes: truth and unity matter
positions.who: The Catholic and Orthodox Churches
positions.view: Christ founded one Church, with the apostles' teaching and sacraments handed down through bishops. Other churches have much that is true and holy, but the fullness of the faith and the sacraments is found in one communion, and the divisions are a wound to be healed, not a menu to choose from.
positions.evidence: Jesus's prayer 'that they may all be one' (John 17:21); the creed's 'one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church'; Ignatius's and Irenaeus's appeal to bishops in apostolic succession.

positions.name: Go where the word is preached and the sacraments rightly given
positions.who: Luther, Calvin and the Reformation confessions (Augsburg Confession, article VII, 1530)
positions.view: The true Church is wherever the gospel is faithfully taught and the sacraments rightly given. The denomination matters less than whether Christ is preached there and the life of the congregation follows him.
positions.evidence: Augsburg Confession VII; Calvin, Institutes IV.1.9; Acts 2:42, teaching and fellowship, breaking of bread and prayer.

positions.name: The bones are shared: start anywhere
positions.who: Ecumenical Christians; the World Council of Churches; many evangelicals and Anglicans
positions.view: All Christians share one baptism, one Bible and the Lord's Supper, and most share the creeds. Start where you can understand and are welcomed; the rest can be worked out later.
positions.evidence: Ephesians 4:4–6; the mutual recognition of baptism; the shared shape of worship from Justin to today.

debate.agree: All agree that Christ calls his followers to gather, that baptism, the word and the meal are his gifts, and that a first visit anywhere is better than none.

look.why: There is no painting of a congregation in the gallery's open collection. Titian and his workshop painted Saint John the Evangelist on Patmos in about 1553–1555, looking up to a vision of heaven. It shows not a service but what Hebrews says lies behind every service: heaven open, and the worshipper looking up. (The painting also appears in 'The whole story'.)
points: From far below, we look up at an older man, Saint John, half crouching on a rocky ledge with his arms raised and palms facing up.
He turns his head back to look up at the clouds; he has a short, curly white beard.
He wears a light, rose-pink tunic with crimson drapery billowing around him.
Beside him on the ledge are a book with a scarlet cover and a brown eagle with slightly lifted wings.
In silvery-grey clouds above, a second man with a long white beard, in a plum-purple robe, raises his right hand, with six winged children among the clouds.
An aqua-coloured sky fills most of the painting behind the saint.

music.why: 'This place was made by God': Bruckner's short motet for the consecration of a chapel in Linz Cathedral. It is what Hebrews says about every gathering of Christians, in a few minutes of music.

think.why: Hebrews asks for 'reverence and awe'. What awe does to us, and what the cathedral builders knew.

learn.why: The blessing God gave Aaron's priests to say over the people, still said at the end of services in synagogues and churches alike: the sending, in Scripture's own words.

check.q: What are the four 'bones' of almost every Christian service?
options: Gathering, word, table or prayers, sending
Confession, creed, Communion, blessing
Hymn, sermon, collection, coffee
Procession, readings, incense, dismissal
check.why: The other lists name parts found in some services; the four bones are found in nearly all.

check.q: According to Hebrews 12, what do Christians come to when they gather?
options: A future reward only
A building and a preacher
The heavenly Jerusalem, angels, the saints and Jesus
Mount Sinai, with fire and darkness
check.why: 'You have come to Mount Zion': worship on earth joins the worship of heaven, now.

check.q: Why do services in different traditions look so different, if the bones are the same?
options: Because of history, theology (for example, belief about Christ's presence) and local culture
Because they worship different gods
Because the Bible requires different services in each country
Because some have no readings
check.why: East and West, the Reformation, beliefs about the presence and the word, and culture all shape the same bones differently.

check.q: A friend is going to a Catholic Mass for the first time and is not Catholic. What is the best advice for Communion?
options: Receive anyway, to fit in
Leave before Communion
Stay in your seat, or go forward with arms crossed for a blessing
Ask to receive twice
check.why: The Catholic Church asks that only Catholics receive; a blessing or staying seated is always welcome.

check.q: Why does every service end with a sending?
options: Because the sermon is over
To clear the building
Because worship is meant to send people back into the world, fed, to love and serve
Because the collection must be counted
check.why: From Justin's collection for the poor to 'Go, it is the dismissal', worship faces outwards.

check.q: What is the journey's verdict on why Christians baptise and break bread?
options: Because Jesus commanded both and Christians believe he gives himself in them; the forms are ancient and shared, though disputed in detail
Because the Reformers required it
Because it is traditional, and nothing more
Because Constantine made it law
check.why: Command, belief in Christ's self-giving, and an ancient shared shape, with real disagreements over infants, presence and who may receive.

tutorial.question: Write a guide for a friend going to church for the first time: what will happen, and why?
tutorial.approach: Use the four bones as your structure, and for each part say where it came from (Justin, the synagogue, the Didache, Paul) and what it means. Include practical advice: arriving, posture, the Peace, the collection, Communion. Explain why services differ. End with what Christians believe they are doing, using Hebrews 12.
strong: Uses the four bones: gathering, word, table or prayers, sending.
Traces each part to its source, with dates.
Gives accurate, kind practical advice, including on Communion for visitors.
Explains differences between traditions fairly.
Uses Hebrews 12 for what Christians believe happens.
Is honest that the visitor need not believe anything to go.

reading.why: Short and clear: the four practices that make a Christian life.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: go to one service. Choose a time on a church's website, or a choral Evensong at a cathedral. Go alone or take someone. Sit near the back, take the booklet, and stay for coffee if there is any. Afterwards, write one line: would you go back?
sessions.reflect: If Hebrews is right that a gathering of Christians is part of the worship of heaven, what would you expect to notice? What did you notice?
takeaways: Every service, however different, has four bones: gathering, word, table or prayers, and sending.
Hebrews 12 says that when Christians gather they come to the heavenly Jerusalem, with angels and saints around Jesus; every service ends by sending people out.
A visitor can go anywhere: arrive early, take the booklet, follow others or stay seated, and at Communion follow the church's invitation or ask for a blessing.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Why do Christians baptise and break bread? In about 300 words, answer from what you have read in this journey, using at least three of its sources, and answer the strongest objection to your view: that it is all empty ritual.
closing.practice: Over the next month, go to three different services: one Eucharist or Mass, one service of the word (such as choral Evensong or an evangelical morning service), and, if you can, a Quaker meeting or an Orthodox Divine Liturgy. Each time, notice the four bones, and write one line afterwards: would you go back?
synthesis: This journey asked why Christians baptise and break bread, and walked into a service part by part to find out. Here are the short answers to its questions.

Why Sunday? Because Jesus rose on the first day of the week. The first Christians, who were Jews, kept meeting on that day as well as, and then instead of, the Sabbath. Paul's collection 'on the first day of every week', the all-night gathering at Troas, the Didache's 'Lord's own day' and Pliny's report of Christians meeting before dawn on a fixed day all show it within a century of the resurrection. Justin gave the reasons in about 155: the first day of creation, and the day Christ rose.

What happens at a service, and is it really that old? Justin described it for the emperor: readings from the Gospels and the prophets, a sermon urging people to live by them, prayers for everyone, the kiss of peace, bread and wine brought, a long thanksgiving, the people's Amen, the bread and wine shared and taken to the absent, and a collection for widows, orphans, the sick, prisoners and strangers. Almost every service today keeps that shape, with the word first and then the table.

What is baptism? It is the door. Jesus told his disciples to make disciples of all nations, 'baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit'. Paul explained it as being buried with Christ and raised to newness of life. The Didache, Justin and Cyril show teaching and fasting first, the renunciation of evil, the turn to the light, going down into the water three times, and coming up: 'at once your grave and your mother'. It is done once, and nearly all churches recognise one another's baptisms.

Why do some churches baptise babies? Because they see baptism as God's gift before it is our response, received like the promise to Israel's children, and attested from about AD 200. Others, from Tertullian's advice to the Anabaptists of 1525 and the Baptists, baptise only believers, because every baptism in the New Testament follows faith. Both agree on the water, the threefold name and the life of faith that must follow.

Why the readings, hymns and creed? Because the Church inherited the synagogue's reading of the law and the prophets and the 'word of exhortation' after it, and added the apostles' letters and the Gospels, which became the New Testament partly by being read aloud. The psalms and hymns teach by singing; the creeds grew from the questions asked at baptism. Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer put all this in English, for everyone, with the whole Bible read in order.

What is Communion? It is the meal Jesus gave his disciples on the night before he died: bread and wine, taken with thanks, as he commanded. Paul calls it a 'sharing' in Christ that makes many one body, and says a meal that shames the poor is not the Lord's Supper at all. Justin calls it 'not common bread', for the baptised. It has five names and is held in six main ways, weekly or less often, at a rail or in the pews. Churches differ on who may receive; a visitor may always stay seated or ask for a blessing.

Isn't it all empty ritual? That is the strongest objection, and it is old: Isaiah and Jesus accused worship from the lips while the heart was far away; Luther attacked worship that was formal and superficial; the Quakers gave up sacraments and appointed preachers to wait in silence; Voltaire's Quaker called the sacraments human inventions and Kant called them counterfeit service; many today are spiritual but not religious. The replies are that the prophets reformed worship rather than abolishing it; that sacraments are promises received by faith, not magic; that liturgy trains love when feelings fail, as Aristotle said virtue is formed by practice; and that faith needs a gathering. The Quakers themselves never stopped meeting.

Is the bread really his body? Here Christians divide. The early Church spoke realistically, and Ambrose said the blessing changes what nature made. Catholics call the change transubstantiation; the Orthodox affirm a change without defining it; Lutherans say Christ's body is truly present in, with and under the bread; Calvin and many Anglicans speak of a real but spiritual feeding by faith; Zwingli and many evangelicals of a memorial. The quarrel split the Reformation at Marburg in 1529 and cost lives, because worship and idolatry were at stake. Modern dialogues have narrowed it.

One more thing. Notice how much of the West grew from these few practices. The weekend began as the Lord's day. The collection for widows, orphans, prisoners and strangers became the hospitals, schools and charities of Christendom. The idea that rich and poor eat at one table, and kneel at one rail, was a quiet revolution in societies built on rank. The Prayer Book's phrases are in the English language; the psalms, hymns and Masses of the Church are much of the West's music. Even the quarrel over the bread taught Europe, slowly and at terrible cost, that people who disagree about the deepest things must find a way to live together. When the Peace is passed between strangers on a Sunday morning, something very old is still happening.

So what should I do if I go? Know the four bones: gathering, word, table or prayers, and sending. Arrive early, take the booklet, sit near the back, stand to sing, sit to listen, stand or kneel to pray, and at Communion follow the church's invitation, or stay seated, or go forward for a blessing. Stay for coffee. Christians believe that what you walk into is more than a building full of people: 'you have come to Mount Zion', to the worship of heaven around Jesus. You do not have to believe that to go and see. Justin wrote for outsiders; the door has been open ever since.
exam: Why did the first Christians meet on Sunday? Discuss with reference to the New Testament, the Didache, Pliny and Justin.
How far does Justin's First Apology 65–67 describe the shape of Christian worship today?
Infant or believer's baptism? Assess the arguments.
What does Romans 6 teach about baptism, and how did Cyril of Jerusalem develop it?
'It is not the Lord's supper that you eat.' What does 1 Corinthians 11 show about the meaning of the Eucharist?
What is the real presence? Compare the Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and Zwinglian views.
Why did the Marburg Colloquy fail, and did it matter?
'Ritual is the enemy of real religion.' Discuss, with reference to Barclay and at least one defender of liturgy.
