title: Homer and the heroes
question: What did the Greeks think a great life was?
line: Seven sessions on the Iliad and the Odyssey: Achilles' anger, his choice of glory, the death of Hector, Priam in the tent, Odysseus' refusal of immortality, the case against Homer's gods and glory, and the hero beside the saint.
why: For a thousand years, to be educated in the Greek world was to know Homer. His two poems gave the West its first pictures of a great life: Achilles, who chooses a short life and a glory that never dies, and Odysseus, who refuses to become a god so that he can go home to his wife. This journey follows the Iliad from its first quarrel to its last scene of mercy between enemies, then the Odyssey's long way home, gives the case against Homer's gods and glory at full strength, from Achilles' own ghost and from Plato, and ends by setting the hero beside the Christian saint. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year classics paper on Homeric epic: the Iliad and the Odyssey in translation, with the Homeric question, the archaeology of Troy, the heroic code (timē, kleos, aretē), the gods, and the reception of Homer by Plato and the early Christians.
before: end-of-the-story
outcomes: Explain who Homer was, how the poems were composed in an oral tradition (Parry and Lord), and what archaeology and the Hittite records say about Troy.
Explain timē, kleos and aretē, and why Achilles' quarrel with Agamemnon and his refusal of the gifts in Book IX matter.
Read the death of Hector and the meeting of Priam and Achilles closely, explain the ring between Iliad I and XXIV, and assess Simone Weil's reading of the poem.
Explain Odysseus' refusal of Calypso, nostos and mētis, and the part Penelope plays.
State the case against Homer's gods and glory at full strength, from Odyssey XI, Xenophanes and Plato's Republic, with Nietzsche's opposite objection.
Compare the Homeric hero with the Christian saint, and explain how Christians such as Augustine read Homer.

people.name: Homer
people.line: The name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey; by tradition a blind singer from Ionia.

people.name: Achilles
people.line: Son of Peleus and the sea goddess Thetis, greatest of the Greek warriors at Troy; the hero of the Iliad.

people.name: Agamemnon
people.line: King of Mycenae and commander of the Greeks; his quarrel with Achilles begins the Iliad.

people.name: Hector
people.line: Eldest son of Priam, defender of Troy, husband of Andromache; killed by Achilles.

people.name: Andromache
people.line: Hector's wife, whose family Achilles had killed; her laments are among the great speeches of the Iliad.

people.name: Priam
people.line: Old king of Troy, who goes to Achilles' hut to ransom his son's body.

people.name: Patroclus
people.line: Achilles' dearest friend, killed by Hector while wearing Achilles' armour.

people.name: Odysseus (Ulysses)
people.line: King of Ithaca, the cleverest of the Greeks; the hero of the Odyssey, ten years on his way home.

people.name: Penelope
people.line: Odysseus' wife, who held off the suitors for years by cunning and tests her husband on his return.

people.name: Calypso
people.line: The nymph who kept Odysseus on her island for seven years and offered him immortality.

people.name: Xenophanes of Colophon
people.line: Poet-philosopher who first attacked Homer's gods as human vices projected onto heaven.

people.name: Plato
people.line: Athenian philosopher whose Republic criticised Homer's gods and heroes and banished the poets from the ideal city.

people.name: Aristotle
people.line: Plato's pupil, whose Poetics praised the unity of Homer's plots and defended poetry.

people.name: Jeremiah
people.line: Prophet in Jerusalem: 'let him who glories glory in this, that he... knows me'.

people.name: Paul
people.line: Christian apostle who wrote to the Greeks of Corinth that God's power is made perfect in weakness.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.line: North African bishop whose Confessions remember learning Homer and Virgil at school.

people.name: Samuel Butler
people.line: English novelist who translated the Iliad (1898) and the Odyssey (1900) into plain prose; the translation read here.

people.name: Benjamin Jowett
people.line: Master of Balliol College, Oxford, whose translation of Plato (1871) is read here.

people.name: Heinrich Schliemann
people.line: German businessman and excavator who dug at Hisarlik from 1871 in search of Troy.

people.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
people.line: German philosopher who praised the Homeric world's morality of strength against Christianity.

people.name: Milman Parry
people.line: American scholar who showed that Homer's formulas belong to oral composition.

people.name: Albert Lord
people.line: Parry's assistant, whose The Singer of Tales (1960) set out the oral theory.

people.name: Simone Weil
people.line: French philosopher whose essay 'The Iliad, or the Poem of Force' (1940) is the most famous modern reading of Homer.

people.name: Manfred Korfmann
people.line: German archaeologist who excavated Troy from 1988 and found its lower town.

people.name: Jasper Griffin
people.line: Oxford classicist, author of Homer on Life and Death (1980).

people.name: Bernard Knox
people.line: Classicist whose introductions to Robert Fagles's translations are classic short essays on Homer.

people.name: Jonathan Shay
people.line: Psychiatrist who compared Achilles with combat veterans in Achilles in Vietnam (1994).

people.name: Emily Wilson
people.line: Classicist whose verse translations of the Odyssey (2017) and the Iliad (2023) are widely read.

Reading a story as a picture of something else, as ancient readers read Homer's gods as forces of nature or virtues.
Excellence or virtue: being outstanding at what you are; for Homer's heroes, skill in word and deed.

The god of the dead, and the dim underworld where all the dead go as shadows.

Wrath: the first word of the Iliad, a deep and lasting anger.

The Greek civilisation of the late Bronze Age (c. 1600–1100 BC), named after Mycenae.
Homecoming, especially the return of the heroes from Troy; the root of 'nostalgia'.
A minor goddess of nature, of springs, trees or islands, like Calypso.

The twelve chief Greek gods, ruled by Zeus from Mount Olympus.

A payment to recover a captive or a body, as Chryses and Priam bring.
A professional reciter of Homer in classical Greece.
A pattern in which a work ends by echoing its beginning, as Iliad XXIV echoes Iliad I.

The young nobles who occupied Odysseus' palace demanding to marry Penelope.
Begging mercy by kneeling and clasping someone's knees; protected by Zeus.
A defence of God's goodness in the face of evil.

sessions.title: Sing, goddess, the wrath
sessions.line: The first words of European literature: a priest is insulted, a god sends a plague, and two kings quarrel over a captive girl. Homer's subject is anger, and what it costs.
sessions.plain: The Iliad is a long poem about a few weeks near the end of a ten-year war between the Greeks and the city of Troy. Its first word is 'anger': the anger of Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior, when his commander Agamemnon takes away the prize he had won. Everything that happens in the poem flows from that quarrel. This session reads the opening, asks who Homer was and whether the war really happened, and introduces the idea that ruled the whole Greek world of heroes: honour.
sessions.why: This is the first session, and the first journey in the hall of Athens. You have read the story of Jerusalem in the Bible's own books. The West has a second root, Greece, and the Greeks' first and greatest book was Homer. Before we can ask what the Greeks thought a great life was, we need to meet their heroes where they first meet us: in a quarrel.
answers: Who was Homer, and how were his poems made?
What is the Iliad about?
Did the Trojan War really happen?
What did the Greeks mean by honour?
sessions.finding: The Iliad opens on one man's wounded honour, and the whole war turns on it: Homer's subject is not the fall of Troy but what anger costs.

paras: If you have walked the first two halls, you know the story of Israel and of Jesus, as the Bible tells it. But the West grew from two roots. Beside Jerusalem stands Athens: the Greeks, who gave the West its philosophy, its drama, its history-writing, its science and its idea of the citizen. Every one of those things began with boys learning Homer by heart. For more than a thousand years, to be educated in the Greek world meant to know the Iliad and the Odyssey. Plato, who argued with Homer all his life, called him the poet who had educated Greece.

So this journey asks the question Homer's poems answer: what did the Greeks think a great life was? The two poems give two answers, through two heroes. Achilles, in the Iliad, chooses a short life and a glory that will never die. Odysseus, in the Odyssey, refuses to become a god so that he can go home to his wife. We will follow the Iliad from its first quarrel to its last scene of mercy, then the Odyssey's long way home, hear the case against Homer's world at full strength, and end by setting the hero beside the Christian saint.

background.key: What did the Greeks think a great life was? Two poems give two answers: Achilles' glory and Odysseus' homecoming.

background.h: The story of Troy, from the beginning
paras: The Greeks told the whole story like this. At the wedding of Peleus, a mortal king, and Thetis, a sea goddess, three goddesses quarrelled over which was the most beautiful: Hera, Athena and Aphrodite. Paris, a prince of Troy, was made the judge. He chose Aphrodite, who had promised him the most beautiful woman in the world: Helen, wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta. Paris carried Helen off to Troy, a rich city near the straits that lead from the Aegean Sea to the Black Sea.

Menelaus' brother Agamemnon, king of Mycenae and the most powerful of the Greek kings, gathered an army from all over Greece and sailed against Troy. Among them were the wise old Nestor, the giant Ajax, the cunning Odysseus and the greatest fighter of all, Achilles, the son of Peleus and Thetis. The Trojans were led by their old king Priam and his eldest son, Hector. The siege lasted ten years.

The Iliad covers only a few weeks of the tenth year. It ends before Achilles dies and before Troy falls. The wooden horse, the most famous part of the story, is not in the Iliad at all: it is mentioned in the Odyssey and told in full by later poets, above all the Roman Virgil.
background.key: Paris took Helen to Troy; Agamemnon led the Greeks to get her back; the siege lasted ten years. The Iliad tells a few weeks of the last year.

paras: We do not know. The Greeks said he was a blind poet from Ionia, the Greek coast of what is now western Turkey; several cities, among them Smyrna and the island of Chios, claimed him. The historian Herodotus, writing around 430 BC, thought Homer had lived about four hundred years before him (Histories II.53). Most scholars today think the poems reached something like their present form between about 750 and 650 BC, the Iliad a little before the Odyssey, and that they grew out of a long tradition of poets who sang without writing.

The poems are huge. The Iliad has about 15,700 lines of Greek verse, the Odyssey about 12,100, each later divided into twenty-four books. They are in hexameter, a long six-beat line, and were performed aloud by singers and, later, by professional reciters called rhapsodes. We read them here in the prose translation of Samuel Butler (1835–1902), the novelist who wrote Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh: plain, clear English, published in 1898 and 1900.

background.h: Reading Butler: a word on names
paras: One thing will puzzle you at first. Butler, like most English writers of his time, calls the gods by their Roman names: Zeus is 'Jove', Athena is 'Minerva', Hermes is 'Mercury'. He also calls Odysseus 'Ulysses', the Roman form. And the Greeks have three names, all meaning the same people: Achaeans, Argives and Danaans. Keep this table to hand.

God of the sea and of earthquakes
Goddess of love; she favours Troy

table.note: Butler, like most English writers of his day, used the Roman names for the gods and for Odysseus. Apollo, Hades and the heroes keep their Greek names.

background.key: Butler uses Roman names: Jove for Zeus, Minerva for Athena, Ulysses for Odysseus. Achaeans, Argives and Danaans all mean the Greeks.

paras: The main reading is the opening of the Iliad: the first lines, which name the poem's subject, then the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, to the moment Achilles swears to stop fighting. It answers the question of what the Iliad is about, because Homer tells us, in his first word.
The comparison is the first ten lines of the Odyssey, the other poem. Set the two openings side by side and you will see at once that they are about two different kinds of hero.

sessions.readWhy: The opening of the Iliad: the first lines, the insult to Apollo's priest, and the quarrel that sets the whole poem in motion.

paras: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled from the day on which the son of Atreus, king of men, and great Achilles, first fell out with one another.

And which of the gods was it that set them on to quarrel? It was the son of Jove and Leto; for he was angry with the king and sent a pestilence upon the host to plague the people, because the son of Atreus had dishonoured Chryses his priest. Now Chryses had come to the ships of the Achaeans to free his daughter, and had brought with him a great ransom: moreover he bore in his hand the sceptre of Apollo wreathed with a suppliant’s wreath, and he besought the Achaeans, but most of all the two sons of Atreus, who were their chiefs.

“Sons of Atreus,” he cried, “and all other Achaeans, may the gods who dwell in Olympus grant you to sack the city of Priam, and to reach your homes in safety; but free my daughter, and accept a ransom for her, in reverence to Apollo, son of Jove.”

On this the rest of the Achaeans with one voice were for respecting the priest and taking the ransom that he offered; but not so Agamemnon, who spoke fiercely to him and sent him roughly away. “Old man,” said he, “let me not find you tarrying about our ships, nor yet coming hereafter. Your sceptre of the god and your wreath shall profit you nothing. I will not free her. She shall grow old in my house at Argos far from her own home, busying herself with her loom and visiting my couch; so go, and do not provoke me or it shall be the worse for you.”

The old man feared him and obeyed. Not a word he spoke, but went by the shore of the sounding sea and prayed apart to King Apollo whom lovely Leto had borne. “Hear me,” he cried, “O god of the silver bow, that protectest Chryse and holy Cilla and rulest Tenedos with thy might, hear me oh thou of Sminthe. If I have ever decked your temple with garlands, or burned your thigh-bones in fat of bulls or goats, grant my prayer, and let your arrows avenge these my tears upon the Danaans.”

Thus did he pray, and Apollo heard his prayer. He came down furious from the summits of Olympus, with his bow and his quiver upon his shoulder, and the arrows rattled on his back with the rage that trembled within him. He sat himself down away from the ships with a face as dark as night, and his silver bow rang death as he shot his arrow in the midst of them. First he smote their mules and their hounds, but presently he aimed his shafts at the people themselves, and all day long the pyres of the dead were burning.

With these words he sat down, and Agamemnon rose in anger. His heart was black with rage, and his eyes flashed fire as he scowled on Calchas and said, “Seer of evil, you never yet prophesied smooth things concerning me, but have ever loved to foretell that which was evil. You have brought me neither comfort nor performance; and now you come seeing among Danaans, and saying that Apollo has plagued us because I would not take a ransom for this girl, the daughter of Chryses. I have set my heart on keeping her in my own house, for I love her better even than my own wife Clytemnestra, whose peer she is alike in form and feature, in understanding and accomplishments. Still I will give her up if I must, for I would have the people live, not die; but you must find me a prize instead, or I alone among the Argives shall be without one. This is not well; for you behold, all of you, that my prize is to go elsewhither.”

And Achilles answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, covetous beyond all mankind, how shall the Achaeans find you another prize? We have no common store from which to take one. Those we took from the cities have been awarded; we cannot disallow the awards that have been made already. Give this girl, therefore, to the god, and if ever Jove grants us to sack the city of Troy we will requite you three and fourfold.”

Then Agamemnon said, “Achilles, valiant though you be, you shall not thus outwit me. You shall not overreach and you shall not persuade me. Are you to keep your own prize, while I sit tamely under my loss and give up the girl at your bidding? Let the Achaeans find me a prize in fair exchange to my liking, or I will come and take your own, or that of Ajax or of Ulysses; and he to whomsoever I may come shall rue my coming. But of this we will take thought hereafter; for the present, let us draw a ship into the sea, and find a crew for her expressly; let us put a hecatomb on board, and let us send Chryseis also; further, let some chief man among us be in command, either Ajax, or Idomeneus, or yourself, son of Peleus, mighty warrior that you are, that we may offer sacrifice and appease the anger of the god.”

Achilles scowled at him and answered, “You are steeped in insolence and lust of gain. With what heart can any of the Achaeans do your bidding, either on foray or in open fighting? I came not warring here for any ill the Trojans had done me. I have no quarrel with them. They have not raided my cattle nor my horses, nor cut down my harvests on the rich plains of Phthia; for between me and them there is a great space, both mountain and sounding sea. We have followed you, Sir Insolence! for your pleasure, not ours—to gain satisfaction from the Trojans for your shameless self and for Menelaus. You forget this, and threaten to rob me of the prize for which I have toiled, and which the sons of the Achaeans have given me. Never when the Achaeans sack any rich city of the Trojans do I receive so good a prize as you do, though it is my hands that do the better part of the fighting. When the sharing comes, your share is far the largest, and I, forsooth, must go back to my ships, take what I can get and be thankful, when my labour of fighting is done. Now, therefore, I shall go back to Phthia; it will be much better for me to return home with my ships, for I will not stay here dishonoured to gather gold and substance for you.”

And Agamemnon answered, “Fly if you will, I shall make you no prayers to stay you. I have others here who will do me honour, and above all Jove, the lord of counsel. There is no king here so hateful to me as you are, for you are ever quarrelsome and ill-affected. What though you be brave? Was it not heaven that made you so? Go home, then, with your ships and comrades to lord it over the Myrmidons. I care neither for you nor for your anger; and thus will I do: since Phoebus Apollo is taking Chryseis from me, I shall send her with my ship and my followers, but I shall come to your tent and take your own prize Briseis, that you may learn how much stronger I am than you are, and that another may fear to set himself up as equal or comparable with me.”

The son of Peleus was furious, and his heart within his shaggy breast was divided whether to draw his sword, push the others aside, and kill the son of Atreus, or to restrain himself and check his anger. While he was thus in two minds, and was drawing his mighty sword from its scabbard, Minerva came down from heaven (for Juno had sent her in the love she bore to them both), and seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair, visible to him alone, for of the others no man could see her. Achilles turned in amaze, and by the fire that flashed from her eyes at once knew that she was Minerva. “Why are you here,” said he, “daughter of aegis-bearing Jove? To see the pride of Agamemnon, son of Atreus? Let me tell you—and it shall surely be—he shall pay for this insolence with his life.”

And Minerva said, “I come from heaven, if you will hear me, to bid you stay your anger. Juno has sent me, who cares for both of you alike. Cease, then, this brawling, and do not draw your sword; rail at him if you will, and your railing will not be vain, for I tell you—and it shall surely be—that you shall hereafter receive gifts three times as splendid by reason of this present insult. Hold, therefore, and obey.”
“Goddess,” answered Achilles, “however angry a man may be, he must do as you two command him. This will be best, for the gods ever hear the prayers of him who has obeyed them.”

He stayed his hand on the silver hilt of his sword, and thrust it back into the scabbard as Minerva bade him. Then she went back to Olympus among the other gods, and to the house of aegis-bearing Jove.

But the son of Peleus again began railing at the son of Atreus, for he was still in a rage. “Wine-bibber,” he cried, “with the face of a dog and the heart of a hind, you never dare to go out with the host in fight, nor yet with our chosen men in ambuscade. You shun this as you do death itself. You had rather go round and rob his prizes from any man who contradicts you. You devour your people, for you are king over a feeble folk; otherwise, son of Atreus, henceforward you would insult no man. Therefore I say, and swear it with a great oath—nay, by this my sceptre which shalt sprout neither leaf nor shoot, nor bud anew from the day on which it left its parent stem upon the mountains—for the axe stripped it of leaf and bark, and now the sons of the Achaeans bear it as judges and guardians of the decrees of heaven—so surely and solemnly do I swear that hereafter they shall look fondly for Achilles and shall not find him. In the day of your distress, when your men fall dying by the murderous hand of Hector, you shall not know how to help them, and shall rend your heart with rage for the hour when you offered insult to the bravest of the Achaeans.”

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The anger, and the priest
parts.context: The first lines of the poem. The Greek army is camped on the beach before Troy, in the tenth year of the war. Its kings have shared out the women and treasure taken from raids on nearby towns. Agamemnon's share includes Chryseis, the daughter of Chryses, a priest of the god Apollo. 'The son of Atreus' is Agamemnon; 'the son of Jove and Leto' is Apollo.
parts.plain: The poet asks the goddess, the Muse, to sing of Achilles' anger, which killed many Greeks. It began with a quarrel. An old priest came to buy back his captive daughter, but Agamemnon insulted him and sent him away. The priest prayed to his god Apollo, who shot arrows of plague into the Greek camp for nine days.

commentary.on: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus
commentary.text: The first word of the Greek poem is menin, 'anger' or 'wrath'. It is an unusual word: elsewhere Homer uses it mostly of the gods, for a deep, lasting rage. The poet does not announce a war or a victory. He announces one man's anger. The 'goddess' is the Muse, the goddess of poetry: the singer claims that the song comes to him from outside, from someone who knows.

commentary.on: Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures
commentary.text: Notice what is sent where. The souls go down to Hades, the world of the dead; but 'the heroes', the men themselves, are left as food for dogs and birds. For Homer the real person is the living body. The soul that survives is a shadow. Hold on to this: it explains why the treatment of dead bodies matters so much in this poem.

commentary.on: for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled
commentary.text: 'Jove' is Zeus, the king of the gods. Behind the human quarrel stands a divine plan. Homer never explains it fully, but he wants us to know that the suffering is not random: it is part of an order we do not see.

commentary.on: because the son of Atreus had dishonoured Chryses his priest
commentary.text: The chain of disaster begins with dishonour. Agamemnon refuses a father's ransom and insults a priest. In Homer's world, to dishonour someone is to deny them what they are owed. The rest of the poem will be one long chain of dishonour and revenge.

commentary.on: and had brought with him a great ransom
commentary.text: A father comes alone to the enemy camp with a great ransom, to beg for his child. Remember this scene. The Iliad is built with care, and it will end with another old father doing the same.

commentary.on: She shall grow old in my house at Argos far from her own home, busying herself with her loom and visiting my couch
commentary.text: Homer does not hide what war meant for women. The prizes the kings quarrel over are captured women, made slaves, to work and to share their master's bed. The poem never questions slavery, but it lets us hear exactly what it is.

commentary.on: let your arrows avenge these my tears upon the Danaans
commentary.text: The priest's prayer is a bargain: I have honoured you with temples and sacrifices, now honour me. Greek religion was largely this: gifts to the gods in return for their favour. Apollo answers because his own honour has been insulted in his priest. Notice that the whole army suffers for one king's insult.

commentary.on: and all day long the pyres of the dead were burning
commentary.text: Within fifty lines of the poem's start, the dead are being burned in heaps. Before a single Trojan has been fought, the Greeks are dying, and the cause is their own king's pride.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The quarrel
parts.context: On the tenth day of the plague, Achilles calls an assembly. The prophet Calchas reveals that Apollo is angry because Agamemnon would not release the priest's daughter (this part is cut, marked '…'). Now Agamemnon stands up, furious.
parts.plain: Agamemnon agrees to give the girl back, but demands another prize so that he is not left without one. Achilles calls him greedy and says the Greeks have nothing left to give. Agamemnon says he will take someone else's prize instead. Achilles says he came to Troy for Agamemnon's sake, not his own, does most of the fighting and gets the smallest share, and threatens to go home. Agamemnon says he will take Achilles' own prize, the girl Briseis, to show who is stronger.

commentary.on: Still I will give her up if I must, for I would have the people live, not die; but you must find me a prize instead, or I alone among the Argives shall be without one.
commentary.text: This is the key to the whole quarrel. Agamemnon will give up the girl, but not the honour she stands for. The Greek word for such a prize is geras, a gift of honour: a visible share of the spoils that shows a man's rank. To be left without one, as commander, is to be shamed in front of everyone.

commentary.on: Most noble son of Atreus, covetous beyond all mankind
commentary.text: Achilles' politeness lasts four words. He is right that there is no common store: everything has been shared out. Taking a prize back from someone would be an insult to him.

commentary.on: I came not warring here for any ill the Trojans had done me. I have no quarrel with them.
commentary.text: A startling thing for a warrior to say in the middle of a war. Achilles is fighting for honour and for loyalty to Agamemnon, not because Troy has wronged him. Once that honour is withheld, he sees no reason to fight at all.

commentary.on: Never when the Achaeans sack any rich city of the Trojans do I receive so good a prize as you do, though it is my hands that do the better part of the fighting.
commentary.text: Here is the clash at the heart of the Iliad: rank against merit. Agamemnon is the greatest king; Achilles is the greatest warrior. Who deserves the most honour, the one with the most power or the one who does the most?

commentary.on: that you may learn how much stronger I am than you are
commentary.text: Agamemnon says it plainly. Taking Briseis is not about wanting a woman. It is about showing everyone who is in charge. Honour, in this world, is something you can take from another man.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The goddess and the oath
parts.context: Achilles must decide what to do. 'Minerva' is Athena, goddess of wisdom and war, who favours the Greeks; 'Juno' is Hera, queen of the gods. The sceptre Achilles holds is the staff passed to whoever is speaking in the assembly.
parts.plain: Achilles starts to draw his sword to kill Agamemnon. Athena, whom only he can see, pulls him back by the hair and tells him not to kill, but to insult Agamemnon as much as he likes: he will be repaid three times over. Achilles obeys, puts his sword away, then curses Agamemnon and swears that the Greeks will one day long for him when Hector is killing them.

commentary.on: seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair, visible to him alone
commentary.text: This is how Homer's gods often work: from inside and outside at once. Athena is a real goddess who grabs Achilles' hair; she is also, we might say, his own second thought. Scholars call this 'double motivation': a decision is fully the man's own and fully the god's.

commentary.on: rail at him if you will
commentary.text: Look at what wisdom advises. Not forgiveness, not peace: only 'don't kill him, insult him instead, and you will get more gifts later'. Athena restrains the sword, not the anger. Honour is still the only measure.

commentary.on: by this my sceptre which shalt sprout neither leaf nor shoot
commentary.text: Achilles swears by the staff in his hand: as surely as this dead wood will never grow leaves again, so surely will I keep my word. The image is cut off, dry and final, like his anger.

commentary.on: they shall look fondly for Achilles and shall not find him
commentary.text: His revenge is to be missed. He will not fight, and the Greeks will die until they understand what he was worth. He is willing to let his own side be killed to restore his honour. That is the anger the poem promised in its first line.

read.author: Homer
read.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
read.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC

paras: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, too, about all these things, oh daughter of Jove, from whatsoever source you may know them.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero
parts.context: The opening of the Odyssey, which tells how Odysseus took ten years to get home from Troy to his island kingdom of Ithaca. 'Ulysses' is Butler's name for him. The cattle of the Sun were sacred animals that his starving men ate, against his warning, near the end of their voyage.
parts.plain: The poet asks the Muse to tell of a clever man who wandered for years after the fall of Troy, saw many peoples, and suffered at sea trying to get himself and his men home. He could not save them: they died because they foolishly ate the Sun god's cattle.

commentary.on: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero
commentary.text: The Iliad's first word is 'anger'. The Odyssey's is andra, 'a man'. Butler's 'ingenious' translates polytropos, 'of many turns': a man who is versatile, resourceful, much-travelled, and slippery. The poem does not even give his name for twenty lines.

commentary.on: Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted
commentary.text: Achilles' greatness is in his strength. This hero's greatness is in his mind: his curiosity, his knowledge of other peoples, his ability to survive. It is a different picture of what makes a man great.

commentary.on: but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly
commentary.text: The Iliad blamed one man's anger for many deaths. The Odyssey begins by saying the men died through their own folly. A few lines later Zeus himself complains that mortals blame the gods for troubles they bring on themselves. From its first lines this poem is interested in human responsibility.

compare.author: Homer
compare.why: The Odyssey, the second poem under Homer's name, opens in a completely different way. Read its first lines beside the Iliad's.
compare.title: The other hero

paras: The Iliad is not the story of the Trojan War. It is the story of Achilles' anger, from its beginning to its end, set in the war. Its plot is simple. Agamemnon takes Achilles' prize; Achilles refuses to fight; his mother Thetis persuades Zeus to let the Trojans win until the Greeks honour her son again (Book I). The Greeks are driven back to their ships. Agamemnon sends envoys to offer Achilles enormous gifts; he refuses (Book IX). His dearest friend Patroclus goes into battle in Achilles' armour and is killed by Hector (Book XVI). Achilles' anger turns from Agamemnon to Hector; he returns to the fight (Book XIX), kills Hector and mistreats his body (Book XXII). Hector's father Priam comes to ransom the body, and Achilles gives it back (Book XXIV).

So the poem's shape is the shape of one man's anger: wounded, stubborn, turned to grief, turned to savage revenge, and finally, unexpectedly, laid to rest. The first line promised a poem about what anger costs. Homer keeps the promise.

rows: The quarrel: Agamemnon takes Briseis; Achilles withdraws
The war without Achilles; the Trojans gain the upper hand
The embassy: Achilles refuses Agamemnon's gifts
Patroclus fights in Achilles' armour and is killed by Hector
Achilles' grief; he is reconciled with Agamemnon and returns
Achilles kills Hector and drags his body
Priam ransoms Hector's body; Hector's funeral
table.note: The Iliad covers about fifty days of the tenth year of the war.

sections.key: The Iliad tells the story of Achilles' anger from its beginning in a quarrel to its end in the return of Hector's body.

paras: To understand the quarrel you need one Greek word: timē, usually translated 'honour'. It does not mean an inner sense of integrity. It means the worth that other people give you, made visible: your seat at the feast, your share of the meat, your portion of the spoils, the respect paid to your word. Timē comes from a root meaning 'price' or 'value'. A man's honour is, quite literally, what he is worth in the eyes of his community.

That is why Agamemnon cannot simply give up his prize, and why Achilles cannot simply let his go. The girl is a geras, a gift of honour. To take it away is to say, in front of the whole army, 'you are worth less than you thought'. Achilles' anger is not jealousy over a woman. It is the rage of a man publicly made smaller.

This is sometimes called a 'shame culture': a world where what matters most is how others see you. The phrase can be unfair, since Homer's heroes also have consciences. But it captures something true. In the Iliad, a man without honour is almost a man without a self.
sections.key: Timē, honour, is the worth others give you, made visible in shares and prizes. Taking Achilles' prize is a public statement that he is worth less.

paras: How could anyone compose a poem of fifteen thousand lines without writing? In the 1920s a young American scholar, Milman Parry (1902–1935), noticed how Homer's language is built from ready-made phrases that fit the metre: 'rosy-fingered Dawn', 'swift-footed Achilles', 'the wine-dark sea'. Each hero has several, of different lengths, to fill different parts of the line. Parry argued, in his doctoral work in Paris (1928), that this was the language of poets who composed as they sang.

To test the idea, Parry went to Yugoslavia in 1933 and 1935 with his assistant Albert Lord, and recorded singers who could still perform long heroic songs without writing. The greatest of them, Avdo Međedović, dictated and sang a single epic of over twelve thousand lines. Such singers did not memorise a fixed text; they rebuilt the song each time from formulas and familiar scenes. Lord set out the theory in The Singer of Tales (1960). Most scholars now accept that Homer stands at the end of a tradition like this, though they disagree about how the poems came to be written down.
sections.key: Milman Parry and Albert Lord showed that Homer's repeated phrases are the tools of poets who composed as they sang, without writing.

paras: For centuries many people thought Troy was a legend. In 1871 the German businessman Heinrich Schliemann, following the Englishman Frank Calvert, began digging at Hisarlik, a mound in north-west Turkey near the Dardanelles. He found not one city but many, built on top of one another: archaeologists now count nine main levels, from about 3000 BC to Roman times. Schliemann dug so fast that he destroyed much of what he was looking for, and the treasure he called 'Priam's' turned out to be about a thousand years too early.

Later digs did better. In the 1930s Carl Blegen identified a city of about 1180 BC destroyed by fire as Homer's Troy. From 1988 Manfred Korfmann found evidence of a large lower town around the citadel, which made Troy far bigger than had been thought; the historian Frank Kolb argued that he had overstated the evidence, and the dispute was fierce. Meanwhile documents of the Hittite empire, the great power of Anatolia, mention a kingdom called Wilusa, which matches the Greek name for Troy, Ilios, and a people called the Ahhiyawa, very likely Homer's Achaeans. One treaty, of about 1280 BC, is with a king of Wilusa called Alaksandu, a name close to Alexandros, Paris's other name.

So there was a real, rich city at Troy, destroyed more than once in the late Bronze Age, and Greeks were active in the region. Whether there was a single war fought over a queen called Helen, no evidence can show.
sections.key: Troy was real: a large city at Hisarlik destroyed around 1200 BC, probably the Wilusa of Hittite records. A war over Helen cannot be proved.

paras: The poems were composed some five hundred years after the world they describe. Did anything survive that long? Some things did. In 1952 Michael Ventris deciphered Linear B, the script of the Greek palaces of about 1400–1200 BC, and showed it was an early form of Greek. Its clay tablets name men called Achilles and Hector, though not these heroes. Homer describes a helmet covered with boars' tusks (Iliad X), and such helmets have been found in tombs of exactly that period, long before Homer's time. Some formulas seem to be just as old.

But the poems also mix in later things: iron tools, the burning of the dead, the way cities are run. Homer's world is not a photograph of any one age. It is a memory, reshaped by generations of singers into a heroic past, grander than the present. That is why the Greeks of Homer's day could look at it as we look at it: as the time when men were greater.
sections.key: The poems keep genuine memories of the Bronze Age, like the boar's-tusk helmet, mixed with later things: a heroic past remembered and reshaped.

paras: No translation carries everything. Homer's Greek is in long, rolling hexameters, full of repeated phrases and sound effects; any English version must choose what to keep. George Chapman (1598–1616) made Homer an Elizabethan, in rhyming fourteen-syllable lines. Alexander Pope (1715–26) made him an elegant Augustan in rhyming couplets: you will meet Pope's Odyssey later in this journey, in the memory piece about the dog Argus. Samuel Butler, whom we read, chose plain prose, because he wanted Homer to sound like a story told by a sensible man rather than a monument.

Modern verse translations are closer to the Greek line by line: Richmond Lattimore's (1951), Robert Fagles's (1990, 1996) and Emily Wilson's (2017, 2023), the first by a woman into English. They are still in copyright, so we read Butler here and point you to them. A good habit: when a passage moves you, read it in a second translation, and notice what changes.
sections.key: Every translation chooses: Chapman and Pope rhymed, Butler chose plain prose, and modern versions (Lattimore, Fagles, Wilson) follow the Greek line by line.

refs: Homer, Iliad I.1–244 (Butler 1898); Odyssey I.1–43, esp. 32–34 (Zeus on human folly).
Herodotus, Histories II.53 (Homer and Hesiod four hundred years before his time); Plato, Republic X.606e (Homer the educator of Greece).
Milman Parry, L'Épithète traditionnelle dans Homère (Paris, 1928); Albert B. Lord, The Singer of Tales (1960); on Avdo Međedović, Lord's edition of The Wedding of Smailagić Meho (1974).

Carl Blegen, Troy and the Trojans (1963); Manfred Korfmann, excavations at Troy 1988–2005; Frank Kolb, 'Troy VI: A Trading Center and Commercial City?', American Journal of Archaeology 108 (2004); Trevor Bryce, The Trojans and Their Neighbours (2006) on Wilusa, Ahhiyawa and the Alaksandu treaty.
Michael Ventris and John Chadwick, Documents in Mycenaean Greek (1956); on the boar's-tusk helmet, Iliad X.261–265.
On timē and 'shame culture': E. R. Dodds, The Greeks and the Irrational (1951), ch. 2; Bernard Williams, Shame and Necessity (1993).

debate.question: One poet or many?

positions.name: Many poets: the poems were stitched together
positions.who: Friedrich August Wolf, Prolegomena to Homer (1795), and the 'Analysts' of the 19th century
positions.view: Writing came late to Greece, so no single poet could have composed such long poems. They are collections of shorter songs by different singers, joined and edited later, perhaps in Athens in the 500s BC. The contradictions in the text, such as heroes killed in one book who fight again in another, show the joins.
positions.evidence: An ancient tradition that the Athenian ruler Peisistratus had the poems collected (Cicero, On the Orator III.137); inconsistencies in the plot; differences of language between parts.

positions.name: One poet: the design is too good to be an accident
positions.who: Aristotle (Poetics 8 and 23); the 'Unitarians'; most literary critics today
positions.view: The Iliad is shaped around one action, Achilles' anger, with echoes running from the first book to the last, like the two fathers bringing ransom. Aristotle praised Homer above all poets for this unity. Only a single great mind could have made it.
positions.evidence: The ring between Book I and Book XXIV; the careful build-up to Patroclus's death; the consistent characters of Achilles and Hector.

positions.name: A tradition, with a master at the end
positions.who: Milman Parry and Albert Lord; Gregory Nagy (Homeric Questions, 1996) and others in different forms
positions.view: The poems were made by generations of oral singers. Some think one outstanding singer gave them their final shape, perhaps by dictating to someone who could write; others think the text slowly fixed itself over centuries of performance. Either way, 'Homer' names a tradition as much as a person.
positions.evidence: The formulaic language; the evidence of living oral poets in the Balkans; the long period before a standard text existed.

debate.agree: All agree that the poems draw on a long tradition of oral song, and that the Iliad as we have it is built with remarkable design around a single story.

look.why: The Iliad begins by asking 'the goddess', the Muse, to sing. Simon Vouet and his studio painted two of the nine Muses around 1634. The gallery's title names them: Urania, the Muse of astronomy, and Calliope, the Muse of epic poetry, Homer's Muse.
points: Two women in jewel-coloured robes, blue, pink and yellow, sit on the ground at the foot of a stone building.
The woman on the left wears a sky-blue diadem lined with six silver stars and leans her elbow on a silver sphere: the stars and the globe of Urania, Muse of the heavens.
The woman beside her holds a book in her lap. On the edges of its pages is written the partial word 'odiss': the Odyssey.
Three winged putti, small child-like angels with blue wings, flutter nearby holding up three crowns of leaves.
Behind them rises a pale stone building with two columns; to the right, green hills and far-off ice-blue mountains.

music.why: There is no music from Homer's world that we can play. Vaughan Williams's Fantasia, slow and vast, opens on a grave single theme that grows and grows: a fitting overture to a poem that begins with one man's anger and spreads to a whole war.

think.why: This journey opens the hall of Athens. See in brief how the West grew from two roots, the Greeks and the Bible, and why both matter.

learn.why: The first sentence of European literature. Learn it, and you have the subject of the whole Iliad in your head.

check.q: Why does Agamemnon insist on being given another prize when he returns the priest's daughter?
options: Because a prize is a visible sign of honour, and a commander left without one is shamed before the army
Because he wants to start a quarrel so that Achilles will go home
Because the prophet Calchas told him the gods demanded it
Because he loves Chryseis more than his wife and cannot bear to be alone
check.why: He says he will give her up 'if I must', but not be 'without one': the geras shows his rank. The first option is something he says, but it is not why he demands a replacement.

check.q: Achilles says, 'I came not warring here for any ill the Trojans had done me.' What follows from this for his decision to stop fighting?
options: He was secretly on the Trojans' side all along
He wants to fight the Trojans on his own, without Agamemnon
Since he fights for honour and loyalty, not for any wrong done to him, once his honour is denied he has no reason left to fight
He is afraid of dying and is looking for an excuse
check.why: His reason for fighting was the honour the Greeks gave him. Take that away and nothing is left. The third option is a common misreading: Achilles is not a coward.

check.q: What does Athena advise Achilles to do instead of killing Agamemnon?
options: Insult him as much as he likes, because he will later be repaid with gifts three times as great
Go home to Phthia at once
Forgive him and make peace for the army's sake
Challenge him to single combat before the army
check.why: 'Rail at him if you will': the goddess of wisdom restrains the sword, not the anger, and promises more honour. Forgiveness is not on offer.

check.q: What did Milman Parry's study of Homer's repeated phrases, such as 'swift-footed Achilles', suggest?
options: That the poems were copied by many scribes who added their own phrases
That Homer was a careless poet who repeated himself
That Homer wrote the poems in Athens in the 500s BC
That the poems were composed by singers who built their verses from ready-made formulas as they performed
check.why: The formulas fit the metre and let a singer compose aloud; Parry and Lord tested this on living singers in Yugoslavia.

check.q: Which statement best sums up what archaeology says about the Trojan War?
options: Schliemann proved that the war happened exactly as Homer describes
The Hittite records describe Achilles killing Hector
A large city at Hisarlik was destroyed around 1200 BC and is probably the Wilusa of Hittite texts, but a war over Helen cannot be proved
Troy never existed; the story is pure invention
check.why: The city was real and important, and the Hittite evidence fits, but archaeology cannot confirm the story of the war itself.

check.q: Compare the first words of the two poems. What does the difference suggest?
options: That Homer preferred Odysseus to Achilles
That the Odyssey is a comedy and the Iliad a tragedy
That they were written in different languages
That the Iliad is about a hero's anger and its cost, and the Odyssey about a resourceful man trying to get home
check.why: 'Anger' against 'a man... of many turns': two subjects and two kinds of hero. The last option goes beyond anything the openings show.

tutorial.question: 'The Iliad is not about the Trojan War; it is about the anger of Achilles.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Start with the first line and what it names. Explain the quarrel in Book I through the idea of timē, honour as a visible share, and say why both men think they are in the right. Then use the outline of the poem to show how the anger shapes the whole plot. Finally ask what is lost if we read it only as a war story, and what is lost if we forget the war.
strong: Notes that the first word of the poem is 'anger' (mēnis) and that the poem ends before Troy falls.
Explains timē and the geras, and why taking Briseis is a public dishonour.
Sees that both Agamemnon and Achilles have a case: rank against merit.
Traces the anger's course through the poem: withdrawal, Patroclus, Hector, Priam.
Notices the echo between Chryses' ransom in Book I and Priam's in Book XXIV.
Recognises that the war is the setting that gives the anger its cost: the dead Greeks.

reading.author: Homer, tr. Richmond Lattimore
reading.title: The Iliad of Homer
reading.why: A faithful line-by-line verse translation, still widely used in universities.

reading.author: Jasper Griffin
reading.title: Homer
reading.why: A short, wise introduction in the Past Masters series.

reading.author: Albert B. Lord
reading.title: The Singer of Tales
reading.why: The classic account of oral composition, from Homer to the singers of the Balkans.

reading.author: Michael Wood
reading.title: In Search of the Trojan War
reading.why: A readable history of the search for Troy, revised as the digs went on.

reading.author: Trevor Bryce
reading.title: The Trojans and Their Neighbours
reading.why: What the Hittite records and archaeology say about Troy and Wilusa.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice the next time you feel slighted, when someone takes credit, interrupts or overlooks you. Before you answer, name the feeling to yourself in Homer's word, 'anger', and ask what it will cost the people around you if you act on it.
sessions.reflect: Where in your own life do you measure your worth by what others give you? What would it be like to be free of that?
takeaways: The Iliad's first word is 'anger': the poem follows Achilles' wrath from a quarrel over honour to its end, and counts its cost.
In Homer's world honour, timē, is the worth others give you, made visible in prizes; to take a man's prize is to make him smaller.
The poems come from a long tradition of singers who composed without writing; Troy was a real city, but the war over Helen cannot be proved.

sessions.title: The man who will not fight
sessions.line: The Greeks are losing. Agamemnon offers Achilles everything to come back, and Achilles says no: he has learned that life is worth more than all the treasure in the world. Beside him, Hector says goodbye to his wife and son.
sessions.plain: Without Achilles, the Greeks are being beaten. Agamemnon sends three friends to offer him enormous gifts if he will fight again. Achilles refuses, and in doing so he says something no hero had said before: that a man's life cannot be bought back, and that his mother has told him he must choose between a short life with undying glory and a long life with none. On the other side, the Trojan prince Hector goes back to the battle knowing his wife and child will suffer if he dies. This session asks what the Greeks meant by glory, and whether it is worth a life.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed that the Iliad turns on honour: Achilles' anger began when his prize was taken. Now Agamemnon offers to give back far more honour than he took. If honour were all that mattered, Achilles would accept. His refusal shows that something else is at stake: the value of life itself, and the choice between glory and a long, quiet life.
answers: Who was Achilles?
What did the Greeks mean by glory (kleos)?
Why does Achilles refuse Agamemnon's gifts?
What is the warrior's code, and what does it cost the people at home?
sessions.finding: Achilles chooses a short life with undying glory over a long, quiet one, and Homer makes us feel both the grandeur of the choice and its waste, above all for the women and children it leaves behind.

paras: In session 1 Achilles withdrew from the fighting after Agamemnon took his prize, the captive woman Briseis. His mother, the sea goddess Thetis, went to Zeus and begged him to give the Trojans victory until the Greeks honoured her son again. Zeus agreed.

Books II to VIII tell of the war without Achilles. There are duels and battles, and slowly the Trojans, led by Hector, drive the Greeks back towards their ships on the beach. The Greeks build a wall and a ditch to protect the ships. At the end of Book VIII the Trojans camp on the open plain, their watch-fires burning, ready to attack in the morning.

Book IX opens at night, with Agamemnon in despair. The old counsellor Nestor tells him he must make peace with Achilles. Agamemnon agrees and lists his offer: Briseis returned, untouched; seven tripods, ten talents of gold, twenty cauldrons, twelve prize horses, seven skilled women; one of his daughters in marriage, with seven cities as a dowry (IX.121–156). Three envoys go to Achilles' hut: Odysseus, the most persuasive; Ajax, the strongest fighter after Achilles; and Phoenix, the old man who brought Achilles up. They find him playing the lyre and singing of 'the glorious deeds of men' (IX.189). Odysseus repeats the offer. Our reading is Achilles' answer.
background.key: Zeus lets the Trojans win; the Greeks are driven back to their ships; Agamemnon offers Achilles vast gifts through three envoys.

paras: Achilles is the son of Peleus, a mortal king of Phthia in northern Greece, and Thetis, a goddess of the sea. He leads the Myrmidons, the men of Phthia. He is the fastest runner, the strongest fighter and the most beautiful of the Greeks, and the most passionate: in grief, anger, love and pity he feels more than anyone else. His closest friend is Patroclus, who grew up with him.

From the start of the poem we are told that Achilles will die young. Thetis says so in Book I. The famous story that she dipped him in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, except for the heel she held him by, is not in Homer at all; it first appears in the Roman poet Statius, around AD 95. Homer's Achilles is not invulnerable. He is simply doomed, and he knows it.
background.key: Achilles: son of a mortal king and a sea goddess, the greatest of the Greeks, fated to die young. The story of his heel is not in Homer.

paras: Hector is the eldest son of Priam, king of Troy, and his queen Hecuba. He leads the Trojan army and is the city's chief defender. He is married to Andromache, whose father and brothers Achilles killed when he sacked her city, and they have a baby son, Astyanax, whose name means 'lord of the city'.

Achilles fights for honour and glory; Hector fights for his city, his parents, his wife and his child. Many readers have thought him the most sympathetic person in the poem. The comparison passage comes from Book VI, earlier in the poem than the main reading, when Hector briefly returns to Troy during the fighting. We read it second because it shows what the hero's code looks like from home.
background.key: Hector, Priam's eldest son, defends Troy and his family. The comparison, from Book VI, shows the warrior's choice from the side of those he leaves.

paras: The main reading is Achilles' great speech to Odysseus in Book IX, one of the longest speeches in the poem. It answers the question 'what is glory worth?', because in it the greatest hero of the poem weighs glory against life aloud.

The comparison is the farewell of Hector and Andromache in Book VI, perhaps the most famous scene in Homer. It answers the same question from the other side of the wall: what does the hero's glory cost his family?
background.key: Achilles weighs glory against life; Hector and Andromache show what glory costs at home.

before: What reasons does Achilles give for refusing the gifts? List them.
What are the 'two ways' in which Achilles may meet his end?
In the comparison, what does Andromache ask Hector to do, and what does he answer?
sessions.readWhy: Achilles' answer to Agamemnon's envoys: why he will not take the gifts, and the choice of two fates.

paras: Achilles answered, “Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, I should give you formal notice plainly and in all fixity of purpose that there be no more of this cajoling, from whatsoever quarter it may come. Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart; therefore I will say what I mean. I will be appeased neither by Agamemnon son of Atreus nor by any other of the Danaans, for I see that I have no thanks for all my fighting. He that fights fares no better than he that does not; coward and hero are held in equal honour, and death deals like measure to him who works and him who is idle. I have taken nothing by all my hardships—with my life ever in my hand; as a bird when she has found a morsel takes it to her nestlings, and herself fares hardly, even so many a long night have I been wakeful, and many a bloody battle have I waged by day against those who were fighting for their women. With my ships I have taken twelve cities, and eleven round about Troy have I stormed with my men by land; I took great store of wealth from every one of them, but I gave all up to Agamemnon son of Atreus. He stayed where he was by his ships, yet of what came to him he gave little, and kept much himself.

“Nevertheless he did distribute some meeds of honour among the chieftains and kings, and these have them still; from me alone of the Achaeans did he take the woman in whom I delighted—let him keep her and sleep with her. Why, pray, must the Argives needs fight the Trojans? What made the son of Atreus gather the host and bring them? Was it not for the sake of Helen? Are the sons of Atreus the only men in the world who love their wives? Any man of common right feeling will love and cherish her who is his own, as I this woman, with my whole heart, though she was but a fruitling of my spear. Agamemnon has taken her from me; he has played me false; I know him; let him tempt me no further, for he shall not move me. Let him look to you, Ulysses, and to the other princes to save his ships from burning. He has done much without me already. He has built a wall; he has dug a trench deep and wide all round it, and he has planted it within with stakes; but even so he stays not the murderous might of Hector.

So long as I fought the Achaeans Hector suffered not the battle range far from the city walls; he would come to the Scaean gates and to the oak tree, but no further. Once he stayed to meet me and hardly did he escape my onset: now, however, since I am in no mood to fight him, I will to-morrow offer sacrifice to Jove and to all the gods; I will draw my ships into the water and then victual them duly; to-morrow morning, if you care to look, you will see my ships on the Hellespont, and my men rowing out to sea with might and main. If great Neptune vouchsafes me a fair passage, in three days I shall be in Phthia. I have much there that I left behind me when I came here to my sorrow, and I shall bring back still further store of gold, of red copper, of fair women, and of iron, my share of the spoils that we have taken; but one prize, he who gave has insolently taken away. Tell him all as I now bid you, and tell him in public that the Achaeans may hate him and beware of him should he think that he can yet dupe others for his effrontery never fails him.

“As for me, hound that he is, he dares not look me in the face. I will take no counsel with him, and will undertake nothing in common with him. He has wronged me and deceived me enough, he shall not cozen me further; let him go his own way, for Jove has robbed him of his reason. I loathe his presents, and for himself care not one straw. He may offer me ten or even twenty times what he has now done, nay—not though it be all that he has in the world, both now or ever shall have; he may promise me the wealth of Orchomenus or of Egyptian Thebes, which is the richest city in the whole world, for it has a hundred gates through each of which two hundred men may drive at once with their chariots and horses; he may offer me gifts as the sands of the sea or the dust of the plain in multitude, but even so he shall not move me till I have been revenged in full for the bitter wrong he has done me. I will not marry his daughter;

she may be fair as Venus, and skilful as Minerva, but I will have none of her: let another take her, who may be a good match for her and who rules a larger kingdom. If the gods spare me to return home, Peleus will find me a wife; there are Achaean women in Hellas and Phthia, daughters of kings that have cities under them; of these I can take whom I will and marry her. Many a time was I minded when at home in Phthia to woo and wed a woman who would make me a suitable wife, and to enjoy the riches of my old father Peleus. My life is more to me than all the wealth of Ilius while it was yet at peace before the Achaeans went there, or than all the treasure that lies on the stone floor of Apollo’s temple beneath the cliffs of Pytho. Cattle and sheep are to be had for harrying, and a man buy both tripods and horses if he wants them, but when his life has once left him it can neither be bought nor harried back again.

“My mother Thetis tells me that there are two ways in which I may meet my end. If I stay here and fight, I shall not return alive but my name will live for ever: whereas if I go home my name will die, but it will be long ere death shall take me. To the rest of you, then, I say, ‘Go home, for you will not take Ilius.’ Jove has held his hand over her to protect her, and her people have taken heart. Go, therefore, as in duty bound, and tell the princes of the Achaeans the message that I have sent them; tell them to find some other plan for the saving of their ships and people, for so long as my displeasure lasts the one that they have now hit upon may not be. As for Phoenix, let him sleep here that he may sail with me in the morning if he so will. But I will not take him by force.”

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: No more cajoling
parts.context: Achilles' hut by the ships, at night. Odysseus ('Ulysses') has just listed Agamemnon's gifts and begged Achilles to save the Greeks. Achilles answers him. 'The son of Atreus' is Agamemnon; 'Phthia' is Achilles' home.
parts.plain: Achilles says he will speak plainly. He has fought and suffered for years and taken many cities, but Agamemnon kept most of the spoils and took the one prize Achilles loved. Brave men and cowards end up with the same honour and the same death. He will sail home tomorrow. He tells Odysseus to let Agamemnon defend the ships himself.

commentary.on: Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart
commentary.text: Achilles speaks to Odysseus, the master of clever words, and opens by attacking clever words. Some readers think he is hinting at Odysseus himself, who repeated the gifts but left out Agamemnon's closing demand that Achilles yield to him as the greater king (IX.158–161). Achilles values one thing above tact: saying what you mean.

commentary.on: He that fights fares no better than he that does not; coward and hero are held in equal honour, and death deals like measure to him who works and him who is idle.
commentary.text: This is the most important sentence in the speech. The whole heroic code rests on a bargain: risk your life, and you will be honoured more than others. Achilles says the bargain is broken. Worse, it was always hollow, because death comes to the brave and the idle alike. He has begun to question the world he was made for.

commentary.on: as a bird when she has found a morsel takes it to her nestlings, and herself fares hardly
commentary.text: A tender image from the hardest of men: he has been like a mother bird, going hungry so that others can eat. It tells you how he sees himself: not as a killer, but as the one who has given everything for the others.

commentary.on: Are the sons of Atreus the only men in the world who love their wives?
commentary.text: A sharp point. The whole war is being fought because one man, Menelaus, lost his wife. Now his brother has taken the woman Achilles says he loved. Achilles turns the reason for the war against the men who lead it. Yet Briseis was 'a fruitling of my spear', a captive: the love is real, but so is the slavery.

commentary.on: to-morrow morning, if you care to look, you will see my ships on the Hellespont
commentary.text: The Hellespont is the strait beside Troy, today's Dardanelles. Achilles is not bluffing: he is planning to go home. The greatest warrior in the world is about to walk away from the war.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The two fates
parts.context: Achilles goes on. Orchomenus and Egyptian Thebes were the richest cities the Greeks knew of; Pytho is Delphi, where Apollo's temple held great treasures. 'Ilius' is Troy.
parts.plain: No gift, however vast, will move him: not all the wealth of the richest cities in the world. He will not marry Agamemnon's daughter. Life cannot be bought back once it is lost. His mother has told him he has two possible fates: stay and die young with undying fame, or go home and live long without it. He will go home, and he advises the others to do the same.

commentary.on: he may offer me gifts as the sands of the sea or the dust of the plain in multitude, but even so he shall not move me
commentary.text: Odysseus had offered a long list of gifts. Achilles answers that no list could ever be long enough. Honour, in this world, was measured in gifts. He has stepped outside the measure.

commentary.on: My life is more to me than all the wealth of Ilius
commentary.text: In a poem about warriors who are praised for throwing their lives away, this is an astonishing line. Achilles has discovered that his own life is worth more than anything that can be given in exchange for it.

commentary.on: when his life has once left him it can neither be bought nor harried back again
commentary.text: 'Harried' means taken in a raid. Cattle, tripods and horses can be won, lost and won again. A life cannot. This is the insight that sets Achilles apart: the one thing that cannot be replaced is the one thing the code asks you to spend.

commentary.on: If I stay here and fight, I shall not return alive but my name will live for ever: whereas if I go home my name will die, but it will be long ere death shall take me.
commentary.text: Here is the famous choice. The Greek for 'my name will live for ever' is kleos aphthiton, 'glory that never perishes', one of the oldest phrases in Greek poetry; scholars have found the same phrase in the ancient poetry of India. Kleos means 'what is heard': the fame that lives in songs after you die. Achilles must choose between kleos and a long life. At this moment, he chooses life.

commentary.on: Go home, for you will not take Ilius.
commentary.text: He even tells the others to give up. Yet he does not leave. By the end of Book IX he says he will stay by his ships until Hector reaches them. Homer lets us see a man pulled two ways, and the choice is not finally made here.
