paras: Hector hurried from the house when she had done speaking, and went down the streets by the same way that he had come. When he had gone through the city and had reached the Scaean gates through which he would go out on to the plain, his wife came running towards him, Andromache, daughter of great Eetion who ruled in Thebe under the wooded slopes of Mt. Placus, and was king of the Cilicians. His daughter had married Hector, and now came to meet him with a nurse who carried his little child in her bosom—a mere babe. Hector’s darling son, and lovely as a star. Hector had named him Scamandrius, but the people called him Astyanax, for his father stood alone as chief guardian of Ilius. Hector smiled as he looked upon the boy, but he did not speak, and Andromache stood by him weeping and taking his hand in her own. “Dear husband,” said she, “your valour will bring you to destruction; think on your infant son, and on my hapless self who ere long shall be your widow—for the Achaeans will set upon you in a body and kill you. It would be better for me, should I lose you, to lie dead and buried, for I shall have nothing left to comfort me when you are gone, save only sorrow.

I have neither father nor mother now. Achilles slew my father when he sacked Thebe the goodly city of the Cilicians. He slew him, but did not for very shame despoil him; when he had burned him in his wondrous armour, he raised a barrow over his ashes and the mountain nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Jove, planted a grove of elms about his tomb. I had seven brothers in my father’s house, but on the same day they all went within the house of Hades. Achilles killed them as they were with their sheep and cattle. My mother—her who had been queen of all the land under Mt. Placus—he brought hither with the spoil, and freed her for a great sum, but the archer-queen Diana took her in the house of your father. Nay—Hector—you who to me are father, mother, brother, and dear husband—have mercy upon me; stay here upon this wall; make not your child fatherless, and your wife a widow; as for the host, place them near the fig-tree, where the city can be best scaled, and the wall is weakest. Thrice have the bravest of them come thither and assailed it, under the two Ajaxes, Idomeneus, the sons of Atreus, and the brave son of Tydeus, either of their own bidding, or because some soothsayer had told them.”

And Hector answered, “Wife, I too have thought upon all this, but with what face should I look upon the Trojans, men or women, if I shirked battle like a coward? I cannot do so: I know nothing save to fight bravely in the forefront of the Trojan host and win renown alike for my father and myself. Well do I know that the day will surely come when mighty Ilius shall be destroyed with Priam and Priam’s people, but I grieve for none of these—not even for Hecuba, nor King Priam, nor for my brothers many and brave who may fall in the dust before their foes—for none of these do I grieve as for yourself when the day shall come on which some one of the Achaeans shall rob you for ever of your freedom, and bear you weeping away. It may be that you will have to ply the loom in Argos at the bidding of a mistress, or to fetch water from the springs Messeis or Hypereia, treated brutally by some cruel task-master; then will one say who sees you weeping, ‘She was wife to Hector, the bravest warrior among the Trojans during the war before Ilius.’ On this your tears will break forth anew for him who would have put away the day of captivity from you. May I lie dead under the barrow that is heaped over my body ere I hear your cry as they carry you into bondage.”

He stretched his arms towards his child, but the boy cried and nestled in his nurse’s bosom, scared at the sight of his father’s armour, and at the horse-hair plume that nodded fiercely from his helmet. His father and mother laughed to see him, but Hector took the helmet from his head and laid it all gleaming upon the ground. Then he took his darling child, kissed him, and dandled him in his arms, praying over him the while to Jove and to all the gods. “Jove,” he cried, “grant that this my child may be even as myself, chief among the Trojans; let him be not less excellent in strength, and let him rule Ilius with his might. Then may one say of him as he comes from battle, ‘The son is far better than the father.’ May he bring back the blood-stained spoils of him whom he has laid low, and let his mother’s heart be glad.”

With this he laid the child again in the arms of his wife, who took him to her own soft bosom, smiling through her tears. As her husband watched her his heart yearned towards her and he caressed her fondly, saying, “My own wife, do not take these things too bitterly to heart. No one can hurry me down to Hades before my time, but if a man’s hour is come, be he brave or be he coward, there is no escape for him when he has once been born. Go, then, within the house, and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your distaff, and the ordering of your servants; for war is man’s matter, and mine above all others of them that have been born in Ilius.”

He took his plumed helmet from the ground, and his wife went back again to her house, weeping bitterly and often looking back towards him. When she reached her home she found her maidens within, and bade them all join in her lament; so they mourned Hector in his own house though he was yet alive, for they deemed that they should never see him return safe from battle, and from the furious hands of the Achaeans.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Andromache's plea
parts.context: Earlier in the poem, in the middle of the fighting, Hector has come back into Troy to ask the women to pray. He is on his way back to the battle when his wife Andromache meets him at the Scaean gates, the main gate of the city, with a nurse carrying their baby. Thebe, her home, was a town near Troy that Achilles sacked.
parts.plain: Andromache begs Hector not to go back to the front. Achilles killed her father and her seven brothers; her mother is dead too. Hector is now everything to her: father, mother, brother and husband. She asks him to stay on the wall and guard the weak point in the defences.

commentary.on: your valour will bring you to destruction; think on your infant son, and on my hapless self who ere long shall be your widow
commentary.text: Andromache sees the hero's courage from the other side: not as glory but as the thing that will destroy her family. Homer gives her the first word, and the stronger case.

commentary.on: Achilles slew my father when he sacked Thebe the goodly city of the Cilicians. He slew him, but did not for very shame despoil him
commentary.text: Notice that even Andromache honours Achilles for one thing: he did not strip her father's body of its armour, but burned and buried him with honour. Keep this in mind. It shows what Achilles once was, and what he will cease to be when he meets Hector.

commentary.on: you who to me are father, mother, brother, and dear husband
commentary.text: War has taken every other person she loved. All of them are now in Hector. It is one of the most moving lines in ancient poetry, and it makes his decision almost unbearable.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Hector's answer
parts.context: Hector answers. Argos is in Greece; Messeis and Hypereia were famous springs there, where slave women would fetch water.
parts.plain: Hector says he would be ashamed before the Trojans if he hid from battle. He knows Troy will fall, and what grieves him most is the thought of Andromache taken as a slave. He reaches for his son, who is frightened by his helmet; they laugh, he takes it off, kisses the boy and prays that he will be a greater warrior than his father. Then he sends Andromache home to her loom, saying that no one dies before his time, and goes back to the fighting.

commentary.on: with what face should I look upon the Trojans, men or women, if I shirked battle like a coward?
commentary.text: Hector's reason is shame, the Greek aidōs: the respect he owes others and the dread of losing theirs. He fights not for himself, as Achilles does, but because his whole city is watching. The code holds him even when he knows it will kill him.

commentary.on: Well do I know that the day will surely come when mighty Ilius shall be destroyed
commentary.text: Hector knows Troy will fall. He fights anyway. This is courage without hope of victory, and it is part of why so many readers love him.

commentary.on: the boy cried and nestled in his nurse's bosom, scared at the sight of his father's armour
commentary.text: The baby does not know his father in his war gear. It is a tiny moment of comedy, and a terrible one: the helmet that makes Hector a hero makes him a stranger to his son. He has to take it off to hold him.

commentary.on: The son is far better than the father.
commentary.text: Hector prays that his son will be a greater warrior and bring home 'blood-stained spoils'. Even in his tenderest moment he can only imagine greatness as killing. Homer does not comment. He simply lets us hear it, knowing, as his first audience knew, that the boy will be thrown from the walls when Troy falls.

commentary.on: if a man's hour is come, be he brave or be he coward, there is no escape for him when he has once been born
commentary.text: Hector's comfort to his wife is fate: no one dies before his time. It is the same truth Achilles turned against the code ('death deals like measure'). Hector draws the opposite conclusion: since death is certain, meet it bravely.

commentary.on: so they mourned Hector in his own house though he was yet alive
commentary.text: The women begin the lament for Hector while he is still alive. The poem will make us wait many books for his death, but here, at home, it has already happened.

compare.author: Homer
compare.why: Achilles weighs his own life against glory. Hector, on the walls of Troy, has to weigh his wife's and his son's. Read the farewell from Book VI.
compare.title: Hector and Andromache

sections.h: Kleos: the glory that is heard
paras: The Greek word kleos comes from the verb kluein, 'to hear'. Glory is what is said about you, and above all what is sung. When the envoys arrive in Book IX, they find Achilles singing to the lyre 'the glorious deeds of men', klea andrōn (IX.189). The hero is listening to the kind of song that will one day be sung about him.

That is why kleos matters so much to men who have no hope of heaven. Homer's dead go down to Hades as shadows, without strength or mind. What survives of a man, in any way worth having, is his name in the mouths of the living. The poet, who keeps that name alive, is the one who gives a hero his only immortality. The phrase Achilles uses, kleos aphthiton, 'unperishing glory', is so old that a close match is found in the Rig Veda, the most ancient poetry of India: a sign that the idea goes back to a common ancestor of the Greek and Indian peoples, thousands of years before Homer.
sections.key: Kleos, from 'to hear', is the glory sung about a hero after death: in a world without heaven, it was the only immortality.

paras: The clearest statement of the heroic code in the Iliad is made not by Achilles but by Sarpedon, a Trojan ally, in Book XII (310–328). In our own words: Why are we two honoured above everyone at home, with the best seats, the best meat and the best land? Because we fight in the front line. If we could escape old age and death by staying out of the battle, I would not fight, nor send you to fight. But since death in ten thousand forms stands over us anyway, let us go forward, and either win glory or give it to another.

That is the bargain: honour now and glory after death, in return for the risk of your life. It is a bargain made because death is certain. It does not deny death; it tries to make death mean something. Hector lives by it. Achilles, in Book IX, is the first to say that the bargain does not add up.
sections.key: Sarpedon states the code: we are honoured because we fight in front, and since death is certain, we may as well win glory.

paras: Achilles' speech is unlike anything else in the poem. He says that the brave and the coward receive the same honour and the same death; that no gift can match the value of a life; that life cannot be raided back. The classical scholar Adam Parry argued in a famous essay (1956) that Achilles is trying to say something his language has no words for. Every word he has, honour, prize, glory, comes from the system he now rejects. So he uses them in strange ways, and even contradicts himself.

It matters that the poem gives these thoughts to its greatest hero. Homer is not a simple praiser of war. Through Achilles he lets the warrior culture question itself from within. Yet Achilles does not, in the end, choose the long life. He stays. And when the poem returns to the choice, it will be grief, not argument, that decides it.
sections.key: Achilles questions the whole heroic code from within, using its own words against it; Homer gives the doubt to his greatest hero.

paras: The Greeks had one word for what made anything good at being what it is: aretē, usually translated 'virtue' or 'excellence'. A knife's aretē is to cut well, a horse's to run well. A hero's aretē was to be, in the words Phoenix uses of Achilles' upbringing in this same book, both a good speaker in council and a doer of deeds in battle (IX.443).

Notice what is missing. Homeric aretē is mostly about strength, courage, skill and success, not about kindness, humility or mercy. A man could be excellent and cruel at once. When later Greek philosophers, above all Socrates and Plato, asked what aretē really is, they began to turn it inward, towards justice and wisdom of the soul. The Christian idea of virtue, which put love and humility at the centre, turned it further still. But the word began here, on the battlefield.
sections.key: Aretē, excellence, meant for Homer's heroes skill in word and deed, strength and success, not yet kindness or humility.

paras: Hector lives by the same code, but for different reasons. Achilles fights for his own honour; Hector fights for Troy. What drives him is aidōs, a word that means both shame and respect: the sense of what others expect of you, and the dread of failing them. He cannot face 'the Trojans, men or women' if he hides.

The American scholar James Redfield called the Iliad, for this reason, a tragedy of Hector (Nature and Culture in the Iliad, 1975). Hector is a man of the city, a husband and father, who must leave everything he loves to defend it, and whose very sense of duty will destroy it. Many readers have found him the moral centre of the poem. Yet Homer does not make him a saint. He can be rash and boastful, and in Book XXII his shame will keep him outside the walls when he should have gone in.
sections.key: Hector fights for city and family, driven by aidōs, shame and respect: a different, more social greatness, which also leads to ruin.

paras: The heroes' honour is counted in women: Chryseis, Briseis, the seven women of Lesbos in Agamemnon's offer. They are captives, slaves taken when their cities fell and their men were killed. Andromache's father and brothers were killed by Achilles; Hector imagines her fetching water as a slave in Greece. Homer never says this system is wrong.

Yet Homer gives these women voices, and some of the poem's most powerful speeches. It is Andromache who states the cost of Hector's courage, and the women who lead the laments for the dead. Modern writers have taken up the side the poem leaves half-told: Pat Barker's novel The Silence of the Girls (2018) retells the Iliad through Briseis. Homer's world is not ours, and it is honest to say so. But he saw more than his heroes did.
sections.key: Homer's heroes count honour in captive women and never question it, but the poem gives the women's grief some of its strongest words.

paras: In the same book as Hector's farewell, a Greek and a Trojan meet between the armies. Diomedes asks the young Lycian Glaucus who he is. Glaucus answers with the most famous simile in Homer, which you will learn this session: men come and go like the leaves of the forest; the wind sheds one year's leaves, and in spring the trees put out new ones (VI.146–149). Then the two discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends, refuse to fight, and exchange armour.

The leaves explain the whole heroic code. If a human life is one season's leaf, then the only thing that can outlast it is kleos, the name that is sung. Achilles' choice of glory and Hector's fear of shame are both answers to that brevity. The Bible uses the same picture, 'all flesh is like grass' (Isaiah 40:6), and then adds what Homer does not: 'the word of our God stands forever' (Isaiah 40:8).
sections.key: Glaucus compares human generations to leaves: since a life is so brief, only the name that is sung can outlast it.

refs: Homer, Iliad IX.121–161 (the offer), 186–189 (Achilles sings klea andrōn), 307–429 (Achilles' answer), 443 (Phoenix), 650–655 (Achilles will stay until Hector reaches the ships); VI.390–502; XII.310–328 (Sarpedon). Tr. Samuel Butler (1898).
Statius, Achilleid I (the dipping in the Styx), c. AD 95.
Adam Parry, 'The Language of Achilles', Transactions of the American Philological Association 87 (1956).
On kleos aphthiton and the Rig Veda (śrávas ákṣitam): Gregory Nagy, The Best of the Achaeans (1979); M. L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth (2007).
James Redfield, Nature and Culture in the Iliad: The Tragedy of Hector (1975); Pat Barker, The Silence of the Girls (2018).

debate.question: Is Achilles right to refuse the gifts?

positions.name: Yes: he sees through the code
positions.who: Adam Parry (1956); many modern readers
positions.view: Achilles has grasped that honour measured in gifts is hollow and that nothing can be exchanged for a life. His refusal is the moment of insight in the poem, the first time a hero sees the world his culture has built from outside.
positions.evidence: 'Coward and hero are held in equal honour'; 'my life is more to me than all the wealth of Ilius'; life 'can neither be bought nor harried back'.

positions.name: No: his pride kills his friends
positions.who: Phoenix and Ajax in Book IX itself; many ancient readers
positions.view: Achilles is right to be angry but wrong to refuse a generous offer. Phoenix warns him with the story of Meleager, a hero who refused to fight until too late and got no gifts at all, and of the Prayers who follow Ruin (IX.502–605). Ajax calls him pitiless. His refusal leads straight to the death of Patroclus.
positions.evidence: Agamemnon offers more than he took; Ajax calls him savage and pitiless towards his friends (IX.628–632); Patroclus dies because Achilles stays out.

positions.name: Both: Homer shows the greatness and the waste
positions.who: Jasper Griffin, Homer on Life and Death (1980); Seth Schein, The Mortal Hero (1984)
positions.view: Homer does not take sides. Achilles' refusal is both a true insight and a terrible error, as tragic heroes' choices often are. The poem makes us admire him and fear for him at once.
positions.evidence: Achilles himself wavers: he will sail tomorrow, then he will stay until Hector reaches the ships; the poem's later books punish and vindicate him.

debate.agree: All agree that Achilles' speech is the deepest questioning of the heroic code in the poem, and that its consequences, beginning with Patroclus's death, are disastrous.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art in Washington holds no painting of Achilles, of the embassy, or of Hector and Andromache, and we will not use a picture of another story in their place.

music.why: Fauré wrote a requiem without terror, music of rest and consolation. Hear it as a lament for the long life Achilles may give up, and for the family Hector leaves on the walls.

think.why: Achilles chooses between a long life and a name that outlives him, because Homer's dead are only shadows. See in brief what Christians came to hope for instead.

learn.why: In the same book as Hector's farewell, a young warrior describes human generations as leaves that fall and grow again: the Iliad's clearest picture of why glory mattered to men so short-lived.

check.q: Agamemnon offers to return Briseis and give far more besides. Why is Achilles' refusal so surprising, given what session 1 showed about honour?
options: Because Agamemnon has apologised in person
Because the gods have ordered him to accept
Because if honour were measured only in gifts, an offer this large should restore it, so his refusal shows he now values something else
Because Achilles had said he did not love Briseis
check.why: The gifts more than repay the insult. Refusing them means Achilles has moved beyond the measure of honour-as-gifts. Agamemnon never apologises in person: he sends envoys.

check.q: What is the force of Achilles' line that 'coward and hero are held in equal honour, and death deals like measure' to both?
options: He is saying that the warrior's bargain, risk your life for more honour, is broken, because all men end the same way
He is admitting that he is afraid
He is threatening to kill the cowards in the army
He is boasting that he is braver than anyone
check.why: The code promises that courage earns more honour; Achilles says it doesn't, and that death levels everyone anyway.

check.q: What does 'kleos' mean, and why did it matter so much to Homer's heroes?
options: Excellence in battle; it made them hard to kill
Honour shown by gifts while alive; it made them rich
The glory that is heard, sung after death; since the dead are only shadows, it was the only lasting life
The favour of the gods; it protected them in battle
check.why: Kleos comes from 'to hear'. In Homer's Hades the dead have no strength or mind, so fame in song was the only immortality worth having. The first option describes timē, not kleos.

check.q: Hector and Achilles both live by the heroic code. What is the main difference in why they fight?
options: Hector is a coward forced to fight; Achilles loves battle
Achilles fights for his own honour and glory; Hector fights for his city and family, out of shame before the Trojans
There is no difference: both fight because the gods command it
Hector fights for gold, Achilles for love
check.why: Hector's motive is aidōs, shame and respect before 'the Trojans, men or women'. Achilles fights for timē and kleos.

check.q: Hector prays that his son will be 'far better than the father' and bring home blood-stained spoils. What does this moment show?
options: That Hector secretly wants his son to avoid war
That even in his tenderest moment, Hector can only picture greatness as success in killing
That Hector expects to win the war
That Andromache agrees with Hector's choice
check.why: The prayer is loving and terrible at once. Homeric aretē is excellence in battle; the poem lets us hear its limits without comment.

check.q: Andromache says Hector is 'father, mother, brother, and dear husband' to her. What is the best reading of this line in the argument of the session?
options: It shows that Andromache's family is still alive in Thebe
It shows the full cost of the hero's choice: war has already taken everyone else she loved, and his glory will take the last
It is a formula Homer uses of all wives
She is exaggerating to manipulate him
check.why: Achilles killed her father and brothers; her mother is dead. The line makes us feel what the code costs those at home. Her family is not alive: she has just said so.

tutorial.question: 'Achilles' refusal in Book IX is the moment the Iliad questions its own values.' Do you agree?
tutorial.approach: Set out the heroic code, using Sarpedon's speech and the idea of timē. Then go through Achilles' answer and show which parts of the code he rejects. Weigh Phoenix's and Ajax's case against him. Bring in Hector and Andromache to show the code from the side of the family. Conclude: does the poem side with the code, with Achilles' doubt, or with neither?
strong: Explains timē, kleos and the warrior's bargain, with Sarpedon's speech.
Quotes and explains 'coward and hero are held in equal honour' and the line about life not being bought back.
Explains the choice of two fates and the phrase kleos aphthiton.
Gives a fair hearing to the case that Achilles is wrong, using Phoenix and Ajax.
Uses the farewell of Hector and Andromache to show what the code costs others.
Notes that Achilles wavers, and does not in fact leave.

reading.author: James Redfield

reading.author: Gregory Nagy
reading.title: The Best of the Achaeans
reading.why: Kleos and the idea of the hero in early Greek poetry.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: think of one person whose life is quietly paid for by your ambitions: a partner, a child, a colleague who covers for you. Ask them this week what your work or plans cost them, and listen without defending yourself.
sessions.reflect: If you had Achilles' choice, a short life remembered for ever or a long life soon forgotten, which would you choose, and why?
takeaways: Kleos, glory, is what is sung of a hero after death: in a world where the dead are shadows, it was the only immortality.
Achilles refuses Agamemnon's gifts because he has seen that a life cannot be exchanged for anything; he questions the heroic code from within.
Hector lives by the same code for his city and family, and his farewell to Andromache shows what the hero's glory costs those he loves.

sessions.title: The death of Hector
sessions.line: Achilles returns to the war to avenge his friend, kills Hector before the walls of Troy, and drags his body in the dust while Hector's parents and wife watch. Homer does not look away.
sessions.plain: Achilles' friend Patroclus has been killed by Hector. Achilles' anger turns from Agamemnon to Hector, and he comes back to the battle like a force of nature. He chases Hector round the walls of Troy, the gods tip the balance, and Achilles kills him. Then he does something terrible: he refuses Hector's dying plea, mutilates his body and drags it behind his chariot in front of his family. This session asks what glory does to the man who wins it, and why Homer makes us see it so clearly.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed Achilles questioning the heroic code and choosing, for a moment, a long life. Then his friend died because he stayed out of the fighting. Now he has chosen glory and an early death after all. This session shows what that choice looks like at the very height of a hero's success, and asks what it has made of him.
answers: Why does Achilles go back to the war?
How does Hector die, and what part do the gods play?
Why does Achilles mistreat Hector's body, and why was that so shocking?
Is the Iliad for war or against it?
sessions.finding: At the height of his glory Achilles is at his most inhuman: Homer shows what force does to the one who uses it and to the one it strikes, and makes us pity both sides.

paras: After Achilles refused the gifts in session 2, the war went worse for the Greeks. Their best fighters, Agamemnon, Odysseus and Diomedes, were wounded, and Hector broke through the wall and set fire to one of the ships. Achilles' friend Patroclus, weeping, begged to be allowed to fight in Achilles' armour, so that the Trojans would think Achilles had returned. Achilles agreed, but told him only to drive them from the ships.

Patroclus went too far. He drove the Trojans back to the walls of Troy and killed many, including Sarpedon, a son of Zeus. Then the god Apollo struck him from behind, a Trojan wounded him, and Hector killed him with a spear and stripped off Achilles' armour (Book XVI).

When Achilles heard, he poured ashes over his head and lay in the dust. His mother Thetis warned him that if he killed Hector, his own death would follow soon after. He answered that he would die gladly, since he had failed his friend (Book XVIII). The smith god Hephaestus made him new armour, and a great shield painted with the whole world at peace and at war. Achilles was reconciled with Agamemnon, refused all food, and went back into battle, killing so many Trojans that the river of Troy rose up against him (Books XIX–XXI).
background.key: Patroclus, fighting in Achilles' armour, is killed by Hector. Achilles, told that his own death will follow Hector's, returns to the war to avenge him.

paras: The Trojans fled inside their city. Only Hector stayed outside, by the Scaean gates. From the wall his father Priam and his mother Hecuba begged him to come in. He stayed, because he had led his men into disaster against advice and was ashamed to face them (XXII.99–110). When Achilles came at him, Hector's nerve broke, and he ran. Achilles chased him three times round the walls, while the gods watched as if at a race.

Then Zeus held up his golden scales with the two men's deaths in them, and Hector's sank down towards Hades (XXII.209–213). Apollo, who had protected Hector, left him. Athena took the form of Hector's brother Deiphobus and told him that the two of them together would stand and fight. That is where our reading begins.

timeline.text: Patroclus is killed by Hector
Achilles' grief; Thetis warns him his death will follow Hector's
Achilles is reconciled with Agamemnon and returns
Achilles' rampage; the river fights him
Hector waits outside the walls; the chase; the duel

background.key: Hector stays outside Troy out of shame, runs, and is chased round the walls; Zeus's scales doom him and Athena tricks him into fighting.

paras: The main reading is the duel and its aftermath, from Hector's offer of a pact to Achilles dragging his body away. It answers the question of what glory does to the man who wins it, because this is Achilles' greatest victory and the poem shows exactly what he does with it.

The comparison is the next scene in the same book: Troy, watching from the walls. Priam, then Andromache, who did not yet know. It answers the question from the side of the victim's family, and it is where Homer's pity is clearest. A modern thinker, Simone Weil, read these scenes as the heart of the poem; you will meet her reading in the lecture.
background.key: The duel and the dragging of the body; then Troy watching from the walls: glory from the winner's side and the losers'.

before: What does Hector ask Achilles to agree to before they fight, and why does Achilles refuse?
When Hector realises he has been tricked, what does he decide to do?
What does Achilles do to the body, and how do the other Greeks behave?
sessions.readWhy: The duel of Achilles and Hector, Hector's death, and what Achilles does to his body.

paras: Thus did Minerva inveigle him by her cunning, and when the two were now close to one another great Hector was first to speak. “I will no longer fly you, son of Peleus,” said he, “as I have been doing hitherto. Three times have I fled round the mighty city of Priam, without daring to withstand you, but now, let me either slay or be slain, for I am in the mind to face you. Let us, then, give pledges to one another by our gods, who are the fittest witnesses and guardians of all covenants; let it be agreed between us that if Jove vouchsafes me the longer stay and I take your life, I am not to treat your dead body in any unseemly fashion, but when I have stripped you of your armour, I am to give up your body to the Achaeans. And do you likewise.”

Achilles glared at him and answered, “Fool, prate not to me about covenants. There can be no covenants between men and lions, wolves and lambs can never be of one mind, but hate each other out and out all through. Therefore there can be no understanding between you and me, nor may there be any covenants between us, till one or other shall fall and glut grim Mars with his life’s blood. Put forth all your strength; you have need now to prove yourself indeed a bold soldier and man of war. You have no more chance, and Pallas Minerva will forthwith vanquish you by my spear: you shall now pay me in full for the grief you have caused me on account of my comrades whom you have killed in battle.”

He poised his spear as he spoke and hurled it. Hector saw it coming and avoided it; he watched it and crouched down so that it flew over his head and stuck in the ground beyond; Minerva then snatched it up and gave it back to Achilles without Hector’s seeing her; Hector thereon said to the son of Peleus, “You have missed your aim, Achilles, peer of the gods, and Jove has not yet revealed to you the hour of my doom, though you made sure that he had done so. You were a false-tongued liar when you deemed that I should forget my valour and quail before you. You shall not drive your spear into the back of a runaway—drive it, should heaven so grant you power, drive it into me as I make straight towards you; and now for your own part avoid my spear if you can—would that you might receive the whole of it into your body; if you were once dead the Trojans would find the war an easier matter, for it is you who have harmed them most.”

He poised his spear as he spoke and hurled it. His aim was true for he hit the middle of Achilles’ shield, but the spear rebounded from it, and did not pierce it. Hector was angry when he saw that the weapon had sped from his hand in vain, and stood there in dismay for he had no second spear. With a loud cry he called Deiphobus and asked him for one, but there was no man; then he saw the truth and said to himself, “Alas! the gods have lured me on to my destruction. I deemed that the hero Deiphobus was by my side, but he is within the wall, and Minerva has inveigled me; death is now indeed exceedingly near at hand and there is no way out of it—for so Jove and his son Apollo the far-darter have willed it, though heretofore they have been ever ready to protect me. My doom has come upon me; let me not then die ingloriously and without a struggle, but let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter.”

As he spoke he drew the keen blade that hung so great and strong by his side, and gathering himself together be sprang on Achilles like a soaring eagle which swoops down from the clouds on to some lamb or timid hare—even so did Hector brandish his sword and spring upon Achilles. Achilles mad with rage darted towards him, with his wondrous shield before his breast, and his gleaming helmet, made with four layers of metal, nodding fiercely forward. The thick tresses of gold with which Vulcan had crested the helmet floated round it, and as the evening star that shines brighter than all others through the stillness of night, even such was the gleam of the spear which Achilles poised in his right hand, fraught with the death of noble Hector. He eyed his fair flesh over and over to see where he could best wound it, but all was protected by the goodly armour of which Hector had spoiled Patroclus after he had slain him, save only the throat where the collar-bones divide the neck from the shoulders, and this is a most deadly place: here then did Achilles strike him as he was coming on towards him, and the point of his spear went right through the fleshy part of the neck, but it did not sever his windpipe so that he could still speak. Hector fell headlong, and Achilles vaunted over him saying, “Hector, you deemed that you should come off scatheless when you were spoiling Patroclus, and recked not of myself who was not with him. Fool that you were: for I, his comrade, mightier far than he, was still left behind him at the ships, and now I have laid you low. The Achaeans shall give him all due funeral rites, while dogs and vultures shall work their will upon yourself.”

Then Hector said, as the life ebbed out of him, “I pray you by your life and knees, and by your parents, let not dogs devour me at the ships of the Achaeans, but accept the rich treasure of gold and bronze which my father and mother will offer you, and send my body home, that the Trojans and their wives may give me my dues of fire when I am dead.”

Achilles glared at him and answered, “Dog, talk not to me neither of knees nor parents; would that I could be as sure of being able to cut your flesh into pieces and eat it raw, for the ill you have done me, as I am that nothing shall save you from the dogs—it shall not be, though they bring ten or twenty-fold ransom and weigh it out for me on the spot, with promise of yet more hereafter. Though Priam son of Dardanus should bid them offer me your weight in gold, even so your mother shall never lay you out and make lament over the son she bore, but dogs and vultures shall eat you utterly up.”

Hector with his dying breath then said, “I know you what you are, and was sure that I should not move you, for your heart is hard as iron; look to it that I bring not heaven’s anger upon you on the day when Paris and Phoebus Apollo, valiant though you be, shall slay you at the Scaean gates.”

When he had thus said the shrouds of death enfolded him, whereon his soul went out of him and flew down to the house of Hades, lamenting its sad fate that it should enjoy youth and strength no longer. But Achilles said, speaking to the dead body, “Die; for my part I will accept my fate whensoever Jove and the other gods see fit to send it.”

As he spoke he drew his spear from the body and set it on one side; then he stripped the blood-stained armour from Hector’s shoulders while the other Achaeans came running up to view his wondrous strength and beauty; and no one came near him without giving him a fresh wound. Then would one turn to his neighbour and say, “It is easier to handle Hector now than when he was flinging fire on to our ships”—and as he spoke he would thrust his spear into him anew.

On this he treated the body of Hector with contumely: he pierced the sinews at the back of both his feet from heel to ancle and passed thongs of ox-hide through the slits he had made: thus he made the body fast to his chariot, letting the head trail upon the ground. Then when he had put the goodly armour on the chariot and had himself mounted, he lashed his horses on and they flew forward nothing loth. The dust rose from Hector as he was being dragged along, his dark hair flew all abroad, and his head once so comely was laid low on earth, for Jove had now delivered him into the hands of his foes to do him outrage in his own land.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: No covenants between men and lions
parts.context: Outside the Scaean gates of Troy. Hector, thinking his brother Deiphobus is beside him, turns to face Achilles. 'Minerva' and 'Pallas Minerva' are Athena; 'Mars' is Ares, the god of war; 'Jove' is Zeus.
parts.plain: Hector offers a pact: whoever wins will strip the other's armour but give back his body for burial. Achilles refuses: there can be no agreements between them, any more than between lions and men. Achilles throws his spear and misses; Athena secretly gives it back. Hector throws and hits Achilles' shield, but it bounces off. He turns to Deiphobus for another spear, and no one is there. He understands that the gods have tricked him and that he will die, and he resolves to die fighting.

commentary.on: I am not to treat your dead body in any unseemly fashion, but when I have stripped you of your armour, I am to give up your body to the Achaeans. And do you likewise.
commentary.text: Hector's last proposal is about bodies. The armour belonged to the winner by custom; the body belonged to the family, for burial. Hector asks Achilles to keep the decencies of war. He is trying to set a limit on what force may do.

commentary.on: There can be no covenants between men and lions, wolves and lambs can never be of one mind
commentary.text: Achilles refuses, and his image tells us where he now stands. Agreements are for human beings; he speaks as a beast to its prey. Throughout these books Homer compares Achilles to lions, fire and floods. His grief has taken him outside the human community.

commentary.on: Minerva then snatched it up and gave it back to Achilles without Hector's seeing her
commentary.text: The goddess cheats. Achilles would almost certainly have won anyway, but the gods make sure of it. Homer's gods take sides like fans, and the side they take is not always the better man.

commentary.on: With a loud cry he called Deiphobus and asked him for one, but there was no man
commentary.text: 'There was no man.' Hector turns for help and finds himself completely alone. It is one of the loneliest moments in literature: abandoned by his brother, by his city, by the gods.

commentary.on: let me not then die ingloriously and without a struggle, but let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter
commentary.text: Hector's answer to certain death is the heroic code at its finest. He cannot live; he can still choose how he dies, and be remembered. This is kleos, the glory that is heard, which you met in session 2. Here it is not vanity. It is the only freedom left to him.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The death of Hector
parts.context: The two men close. Hector is wearing the armour he stripped from Patroclus, which was Achilles' own. 'Vulcan' is Hephaestus, the smith god who made Achilles' new armour. Paris and 'Phoebus Apollo' are named as the future killers of Achilles.
parts.plain: Hector charges with his sword. Achilles looks for a gap in the armour, his own old armour, and spears Hector through the neck. Dying, Hector begs him to accept a ransom from his parents and give his body back for burial. Achilles says he wishes he could eat Hector's flesh raw, and that dogs and birds will devour him. Hector, dying, warns him that Paris and Apollo will kill him at the Scaean gates. Achilles answers that he will accept his death whenever it comes.

commentary.on: all was protected by the goodly armour of which Hector had spoiled Patroclus after he had slain him
commentary.text: Achilles is looking for a way to kill a man wearing his own armour. It is as if he were fighting himself, and in a sense he is: Hector killed Patroclus, and Achilles, by staying out, let him die.

commentary.on: let not dogs devour me at the ships of the Achaeans, but accept the rich treasure of gold and bronze which my father and mother will offer you, and send my body home
commentary.text: Hector's dying plea is not for his life but for his body. To lie unburied, eaten by animals, was to the Greeks the worst fate a person could suffer, because the dead could not rest and the family could not mourn. He offers ransom: the same thing Chryses offered in Book I.

commentary.on: would that I could be as sure of being able to cut your flesh into pieces and eat it raw
commentary.text: This is the most savage line in the poem. Achilles, who in session 2 said a life could not be bought back, now refuses even a body to be bought back. He wishes he were a cannibal, a beast. Homer has shown us the greatest of heroes at the moment of his greatest victory, and it is not glorious. It is horrifying.

commentary.on: I know you what you are, and was sure that I should not move you, for your heart is hard as iron
commentary.text: Hector names what Achilles has become: iron, unmovable. Keep the word. When Priam comes to Achilles' tent, Achilles will say that Priam himself must have a heart of iron to dare it.

commentary.on: Die; for my part I will accept my fate whensoever Jove and the other gods see fit to send it.
commentary.text: Achilles knows Hector's prophecy is true: his own death is near. He accepts it. He has chosen the short life and the undying name. But look at the price: the triumph of the code has made him something less than human.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The body in the dust
parts.context: Hector is dead. The other Greeks run up. A short passage where Achilles speaks to the army is cut (marked '…'). 'Ancle' is Butler's spelling of ankle; 'contumely' means insulting contempt.
parts.plain: Achilles strips the armour. The other Greeks gather to stare at Hector's beauty, and every one of them stabs the corpse, joking that he is easier to handle now. Achilles pierces Hector's ankles, ties him to his chariot by the feet, and drags him through the dust with his head trailing on the ground.

commentary.on: the other Achaeans came running up to view his wondrous strength and beauty; and no one came near him without giving him a fresh wound
commentary.text: They admire his beauty and stab him in the same breath. It is not only Achilles: the whole army joins in. Homer shows how ordinary men, safe in a crowd, behave towards an enemy who can no longer hurt them.

commentary.on: It is easier to handle Hector now than when he was flinging fire on to our ships
commentary.text: The joke of the soldier who never dared face him alive. Homer gives it no comment, and needs none.

commentary.on: he pierced the sinews at the back of both his feet from heel to ancle and passed thongs of ox-hide through the slits he had made
commentary.text: Achilles treats the body as a thing: an object to be tied, dragged and spoiled. The poet describes it with flat, exact detail, which makes it worse.

commentary.on: his head once so comely was laid low on earth, for Jove had now delivered him into the hands of his foes to do him outrage in his own land
commentary.text: 'Once so comely': the poet remembers what Hector was, and grieves. 'In his own land': this happens before his own city, in front of his family. And Zeus has allowed it. Homer's gods do not always stop evil. Sometimes they hand a man over to it.

read.author: Homer
read.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
read.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC

paras: Thus was the head of Hector being dishonoured in the dust. His mother tore her hair, and flung her veil from her with a loud cry as she looked upon her son. His father made piteous moan, and throughout the city the people fell to weeping and wailing. It was as though the whole of frowning Ilius was being smirched with fire. Hardly could the people hold Priam back in his hot haste to rush without the gates of the city. He grovelled in the mire and besought them, calling each one of them by his name. “Let be, my friends,” he cried, “and for all your sorrow, suffer me to go single-handed to the ships of the Achaeans. Let me beseech this cruel and terrible man, if maybe he will respect the feeling of his fellow-men, and have compassion on my old age. His own father is even such another as myself—Peleus, who bred him and reared him to be the bane of us Trojans, and of myself more than of all others. Many a son of mine has he slain in the flower of his youth, and yet, grieve for these as I may, I do so for one—Hector—more than for them all, and the bitterness of my sorrow will bring me down to the house of Hades. Would that he had died in my arms, for so both his ill-starred mother who bore him, and myself, should have had the comfort of weeping and mourning over him.”

Hector’s wife had as yet heard nothing, for no one had come to tell her that her husband had remained without the gates. She was at her loom in an inner part of the house, weaving a double purple web, and embroidering it with many flowers. She told her maids to set a large tripod on the fire, so as to have a warm bath ready for Hector when he came out of battle; poor woman, she knew not that he was now beyond the reach of baths, and that Minerva had laid him low by the hands of Achilles. She heard the cry coming as from the wall, and trembled in every limb; the shuttle fell from her hands, and again she spoke to her waiting-women. “Two of you,” she said, “come with me that I may learn what it is that has befallen; I heard the voice of my husband’s honoured mother; my own heart beats as though it would come into my mouth and my limbs refuse to carry me; some great misfortune for Priam’s children must be at hand. May I never live to hear it, but I greatly fear that Achilles has cut off the retreat of brave Hector and has chased him on to the plain where he was single-handed; I fear he may have put an end to the reckless daring which possessed my husband, who would never remain with the body of his men, but would dash on far in front, foremost of them all in valour.”

Her heart beat fast, and as she spoke she flew from the house like a maniac, with her waiting-women following after. When she reached the battlements and the crowd of people, she stood looking out upon the wall, and saw Hector being borne away in front of the city—the horses dragging him without heed or care over the ground towards the ships of the Achaeans. Her eyes were then shrouded as with the darkness of night and she fell fainting backwards. She tore the attiring from her head and flung it from her, the frontlet and net with its plaited band, and the veil which golden Venus had given her on the day when Hector took her with him from the house of Eetion, after having given countless gifts of wooing for her sake. Her husband’s sisters and the wives of his brothers crowded round her and supported her, for she was fain to die in her distraction; when she again presently breathed and came to herself, she sobbed and made lament among the Trojans saying, “Woe is me, O Hector; woe, indeed, that to share a common lot we were born, you at Troy in the house of Priam, and I at Thebes under the wooded mountain of Placus in the house of Eetion who brought me up when I was a child—ill-starred sire of an ill-starred daughter—would that he had never begotten me. You are now going into the house of Hades under the secret places of the earth, and you leave me a sorrowing widow in your house. The child, of whom you and I are the unhappy parents, is as yet a mere infant. Now that you are gone, O Hector, you can do nothing for him nor he for you.

Even though he escape the horrors of this woeful war with the Achaeans, yet shall his life henceforth be one of labour and sorrow, for others will seize his lands. The day that robs a child of his parents severs him from his own kind; his head is bowed, his cheeks are wet with tears, and he will go about destitute among the friends of his father, plucking one by the cloak and another by the shirt. Some one or other of these may so far pity him as to hold the cup for a moment towards him and let him moisten his lips, but he must not drink enough to wet the roof of his mouth; then one whose parents are alive will drive him from the table with blows and angry words. ‘Out with you,’ he will say, ‘you have no father here,’ and the child will go crying back to his widowed mother—he, Astyanax, who erewhile would sit upon his father’s knees, and have none but the daintiest and choicest morsels set before him. When he had played till he was tired and went to sleep, he would lie in a bed, in the arms of his nurse, on a soft couch, knowing neither want nor care, whereas now that he has lost his father his lot will be full of hardship—he, whom the Trojans name Astyanax, because you, O Hector, were the only defence of their gates and battlements. The wriggling writhing worms will now eat you at the ships, far from your parents, when the dogs have glutted themselves upon you. You will lie naked, although in your house you have fine and goodly raiment made by hands of women. This will I now burn; it is of no use to you, for you can never again wear it, and thus you will have respect shown you by the Trojans both men and women.”
In such wise did she cry aloud amid her tears, and the women joined in her lament.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Priam in the dirt
parts.context: The walls of Troy, moments later. Hector's mother Hecuba and father Priam have watched everything. 'Ilius' is Troy; Peleus is Achilles' father.
parts.plain: Hector's mother tears her hair; his father groans; the whole city weeps. The people hold Priam back from running out of the gates. He rolls in the dirt and begs to be allowed to go alone to Achilles, to beg him for pity, since Achilles too has an old father. He grieves for Hector more than for all his other dead sons.

commentary.on: It was as though the whole of frowning Ilius was being smirched with fire.
commentary.text: Troy has not fallen yet, but the poet says it is as if it were already burning. Hector was the city's defence. His death is Troy's death, seen in advance.

commentary.on: He grovelled in the mire and besought them, calling each one of them by his name.
commentary.text: The king of Troy rolls in the mud. Grief strips away rank. Plato thought this line unworthy of a king, and wanted it struck out of the poem.

commentary.on: His own father is even such another as myself—Peleus
commentary.text: Priam already sees the one thing that might move Achilles: that he too has an old father. The thought he has here, in despair, is the thought that will end the poem.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Andromache
parts.context: After Hecuba's lament (cut, '…'), the poet turns to Hector's wife, who has heard nothing. The 'double purple web' is a cloth she is weaving. Eetion was her father, killed by Achilles. 'Venus' is Aphrodite.
parts.plain: Andromache is at her loom, telling her maids to heat a bath for Hector when he comes back. She hears the cry, runs to the wall, and sees him being dragged away. She faints. When she comes round, she laments: their son is now an orphan and will be pushed away from other men's tables; Hector will be eaten by worms and dogs, naked; she will burn the clothes she made for him.

commentary.on: She told her maids to set a large tripod on the fire, so as to have a warm bath ready for Hector when he came out of battle
commentary.text: The bath is the most heartbreaking detail in the poem. While her husband is being dragged in the dust, Andromache is getting ready to look after him. The ordinary care of a home, set against the war.

commentary.on: poor woman, she knew not that he was now beyond the reach of baths
commentary.text: Homer speaks in his own voice, which he rarely does: 'poor woman'. The poet's pity is for the losers here as much as the winners.

commentary.on: the veil which golden Venus had given her on the day when Hector took her with him from the house of Eetion
commentary.text: She tears off her wedding veil. The day of her marriage and the day of her husband's death are joined in one gesture.

commentary.on: you have no father here
commentary.text: Andromache imagines her son as an orphan, driven from the table by other children. The war is not only about heroes dying well. It is about a small boy left with no one.

commentary.on: This will I now burn; it is of no use to you, for you can never again wear it
commentary.text: She cannot bury him, so she will burn the clothes she wove for him, the only funeral she can give. The poem has shown us glory in the main reading. Here it shows us what glory leaves behind.

compare.author: Homer
compare.why: The main reading showed Achilles' victory from the battlefield. Homer then turns the camera round. Read the same moment from the walls of Troy: his father, and his wife.
compare.title: Troy on the walls

sections.h: Simone Weil: the poem of force
paras: In 1940, as German armies overran France, a young French philosopher, Simone Weil (1909–1943), wrote an essay called 'The Iliad, or the Poem of Force'. It was published in Marseille in the winter of 1940–41, under an anagram of her name. It has become the most famous modern reading of Homer.

Weil's argument, in our own words, is that the real hero of the Iliad is force: the power that turns a human being into a thing. It does so most obviously by killing, which turns a man into a corpse. But it also does it to the living: to the suppliant who kneels and waits, to the captive woman, to the man who has a sword at his throat. And it does it to the one who uses force. The victor is made a thing too, blind and drunk with his power, until the force he serves turns on him in his turn. No one in the Iliad, Weil saw, really possesses force; it passes through them.

What made the poem great, for Weil, was that Homer saw this without hatred and without self-deception, and spread his pity equally over Greeks and Trojans. She thought this 'bitterness' and fairness were found nowhere else in literature until the Gospels.
sections.key: Simone Weil (1940) read the Iliad as a poem about force, which turns both victim and victor into things, and praised Homer's equal pity for both sides.

paras: Weil's reading rests on something you can see on almost every page. When a minor warrior dies, Homer often stops for a moment to tell us who he was: where he grew up, who his parents were, what he will never do now. A young Trojan called Simoeisius, named after the river beside which his mother bore him, falls like a poplar cut down for a chariot wheel, and never repays his parents for bringing him up (Iliad IV.473–489). These short obituaries give each death its weight.

The British scholar Jasper Griffin (Homer on Life and Death, 1980) showed how carefully Homer does this, and how often he sets the moment of death against a memory of peace: a home, a wife, a field. In the comparison, the warm bath that Andromache prepares is the most famous example. The poet stands back from the fighting, sees the whole, and mourns.
sections.key: Homer gives even minor warriors brief life stories as they die, setting each death against a memory of peace: the source of his pity.

paras: In this book the gods behave in ways that disturb modern readers. They watch the chase round the walls 'as at a race' for a prize. Zeus pities Hector and wonders aloud whether to save him; Athena tells him not to, and he gives way at once (XXII.167–185). Then Zeus weighs the two men's deaths in his scales, and Hector's is the heavier. Apollo leaves him. Athena, disguised as his brother, lures him to his death and hands Achilles back his spear.

What are we to make of this? Homer's gods are not moral judges. They are immensely powerful persons, with favourites and grudges, who live for ever and so can never risk what mortals risk. The scholar Griffin put it sharply: the gods watch human suffering as spectators, and their ease makes human courage both more glorious and more tragic. Hector stands his ground knowing that heaven has abandoned him. Whether such gods deserve worship is a question the Greeks themselves would raise, and this journey will raise it too, in the case against still to come.
sections.key: Homer's gods watch the duel like spectators, take sides and cheat; they are powerful, not good. Their ease makes human courage more tragic.

paras: Why does what Achilles does to the body matter so much? For the Greeks, as for the Hebrews, the dead had a right to burial. Without it, they believed, the dead could not rest, and the living could not mourn. Hector's plea is the most natural thing in the world to Homer's audience, and Achilles' refusal the most terrible.

The poem goes further. For twelve days after Patroclus's funeral, Achilles drags Hector's body round his friend's tomb at every dawn (XXIV.14–18). The gods keep the body from harm. In Book XXIV Apollo condemns him before the other gods: Achilles has destroyed pity and has no shame, and he outrages the senseless earth (XXIV.39–54). The great Athenian tragedy Antigone, by Sophocles (about 441 BC), is built on the same belief: a sister defies the king to bury her brother, because the gods' unwritten law demands it.
sections.key: Burial was a sacred right; refusing it was an outrage. Apollo condemns Achilles for destroying pity, and the gods protect Hector's body.

paras: One of the most striking modern readings of these books comes not from a classicist but from an American psychiatrist. Jonathan Shay treated veterans of the Vietnam War, and in Achilles in Vietnam (1994) he compared their stories with the Iliad. He found two things in both. First, a betrayal of 'what's right' by a commander: Agamemnon taking Achilles' prize. Second, the death of a close comrade. Together, these produced in many soldiers what they themselves called going 'berserk': a state in which a man feels dead already, godlike and beast-like at once, refuses food and rest, and does things he cannot later explain.

Shay's point was that Homer had described, with clinical accuracy, what war does to the mind. Achilles fasting, killing without limit, mutilating the dead, is not a monster from a legend. He is a recognisable human being in the grip of grief and rage. That is part of why the poem still speaks to soldiers, and to anyone who has been wronged and has lost someone.
sections.key: Jonathan Shay (1994) found in Achilles' betrayal, grief and rage the same pattern as in Vietnam veterans who went 'berserk': Homer saw what war does to the mind.

paras: Not everyone accepts Weil's reading. The Iliad also loves battle. It describes fighting with relish and great technical detail; it gives each great warrior an aristeia, a run of glorious success; it uses the word kudos for the glory of victory, the god-given rush of triumph. The Greeks who learned it at school were not taught pacifism: Alexander the Great, by Plutarch's account, carried a copy on campaign and slept with it under his pillow beside a dagger (Life of Alexander 8).

The fairest answer is probably that Homer sees war whole: its terrible attraction and its terrible cost, the courage it calls out and the cruelty it releases. The scholar Bernard Knox, introducing a popular translation (1990), wrote of the poem's double vision. The Iliad does not tell us whether to be for or against war. It shows us what war is, and lets us weep. Which of these readings convinces you is the question of the debate that follows.
sections.key: The Iliad also celebrates battle and was read by soldiers like Alexander; most readers think it sees war whole, its glory and its cost.

refs: Homer, Iliad IV.473–489 (Simoeisius); XVI (Patroclus); XVIII.88–126 (Achilles' choice to die); XXII.99–110, 158–185, 209–213, 247–515; XXIII.175–176; XXIV.14–18, 39–54. Tr. Samuel Butler (1898).

Jonathan Shay, Achilles in Vietnam: Combat Trauma and the Undoing of Character (1994).
Bernard Knox, introduction to The Iliad, tr. Robert Fagles (1990); Plutarch, Life of Alexander 8; Sophocles, Antigone 450–457.
Charles Segal, The Theme of the Mutilation of the Corpse in the Iliad (1971).

debate.question: Is the Iliad for war or against it?

positions.name: Against: the poem of force
positions.who: Simone Weil (1940); many readers since the World Wars
positions.view: The Iliad shows force turning everyone it touches into a thing, victor and victim alike. Its pity for both sides and its unflinching detail make it the greatest poem against war ever written, whatever its singers intended.
positions.evidence: Hector's body dragged in the dust; Andromache's bath; the obituaries of the minor dead; Achilles' wish to eat raw flesh.

positions.name: For: the poem of glory
positions.who: Ancient readers from Alexander the Great on; the military education of Greece and Rome
positions.view: The Iliad celebrates the warrior. It is full of the joy of battle and the beauty of courage, and it makes undying glory the highest prize. Reading it as anti-war imposes modern feelings on an ancient poem.
positions.evidence: The aristeiai of the great heroes; the language of kudos and kleos; Hector's 'some great thing that shall be told among men'; Alexander's copy under his pillow.

positions.name: Neither: it sees war whole
positions.who: Jasper Griffin (1980); Bernard Knox (1990); Seth Schein (1984)
positions.view: Homer sees both the glory and the horror, and does not resolve them. That double vision, not a message for or against, is what makes the poem tragic and true.
positions.evidence: Hector's courage and his terror in the same book; Achilles both magnificent and monstrous; the poet's pity and his relish side by side.

debate.agree: All agree that Homer shows the cruelty of war with unusual honesty and gives pity to both sides, and that Achilles at his triumph is a figure of horror as well as greatness.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art in Washington has no painting of Achilles, Hector or the walls of Troy.

music.why: Mozart's Requiem holds terror and tenderness together, the Day of Wrath beside the tearful Lacrimosa. It fits a book in which Homer shows both the violence and the grief, and pities everyone in it.

think.why: Achilles treats Hector's body as a thing. See in brief where the West's conviction that every human being has a dignity no one may take away came from.

learn.why: Hector's words when he knows the gods have abandoned him: the heroic code at its noblest, courage when nothing is left but how you meet the end.

check.q: Hector asks Achilles to agree that the winner will return the loser's body. Why does Achilles' refusal matter so much?
options: Because Hector wanted to keep Achilles' armour
Because burial was a sacred right, and refusing it shows that Achilles has stepped outside the shared decencies that make men human
Because it breaks a law that Agamemnon had made
Because it means the duel is unfair
check.why: His image of 'men and lions' says it: agreements are for humans, and he now speaks as a beast. The armour was the winner's by custom anyway.

check.q: What does Hector decide when he realises Athena has tricked him?
options: To run back into the city
To beg Achilles for mercy
To curse the gods and refuse to fight
To die fighting and do some great thing that will be remembered
check.why: 'Let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter': kleos is the only freedom left him.

check.q: Achilles in session 2 said a life 'can neither be bought nor harried back'. How does his treatment of Hector contrast with that insight?
options: Having once seen the value of life, he now refuses even to let a dead man's body be ransomed, and wishes to eat it: grief has made him less than human
He now accepts the ransom he refused earlier
He decides to go home after killing Hector
It doesn't: he is consistent in valuing life above gifts
check.why: The man who saw the worth of a life now denies the dead any worth at all. The poem shows how far grief and rage have taken him.

check.q: According to Simone Weil, what does force do in the Iliad?
options: It makes the strong noble and the weak contemptible
It shows which side the gods favour
It turns both its victims and those who wield it into things
It brings justice in the end
check.why: Weil's central claim is that force reifies everyone, the victor too. The first option is the view she was attacking.

check.q: What is the best objection to Weil's reading?
options: That Weil did not read Greek
That Homer never describes violence
That the poem also celebrates the glory and joy of battle, and its ancient readers took it as a model of the warrior's greatness
That the Trojans deserved to lose
check.why: The aristeiai, the language of kudos and Alexander's copy all show a poem that loves the warrior too. Weil did read Greek; the other options are false or beside the point.

check.q: Why does Homer show Andromache preparing a bath for Hector at the moment he is being dragged in the dust?
options: Because a bath was part of Trojan funeral rites
To show that she does not love him
To set the ordinary care of home against the war, so that we feel what glory destroys
To show that the gods had hidden the news from her deliberately
check.why: 'Poor woman, she knew not that he was now beyond the reach of baths': the contrast between peace and war is the source of Homer's pity.

tutorial.question: 'At the height of his glory, Achilles is at his most inhuman.' How does Book XXII show this, and what does it suggest about the heroic code?
tutorial.approach: Walk through the duel and its aftermath, picking out the images of beasts and iron, the refusal of the body and the wish to eat it. Compare the Greeks stabbing the corpse. Then turn to the walls of Troy and Homer's pity. Use Weil's reading and its critics, and Shay's comparison with veterans. Ask whether the poem condemns Achilles, the code, war itself, or none of these.
strong: Explains why Hector's plea for his body mattered so much to Greeks.
Uses 'men and lions' and 'hard as iron' to show Achilles outside the human community.
Notes that the whole army joins in mutilating the corpse.
Uses the comparison passage: Priam in the dirt, Andromache's bath.
Sets out Weil's reading fairly and gives the best objection to it.
Brings in the gods' part: the scales, Athena's trick, Apollo's condemnation.

reading.why: A short essay, the most influential modern reading of the poem.
