sessions.practice: Live it this week: when you hear or read of someone you dislike, or a public enemy, being humiliated, notice whether you enjoy it. Once this week, refuse to join in: say one fair or kind thing about that person instead, aloud or in writing.
sessions.reflect: Have you ever wanted to hurt someone who had hurt someone you loved? What did that feeling make of you?
takeaways: Achilles kills Hector and refuses his body to his family: at the height of his glory, grief and rage have made him less than human.
Homer shows the cruelty of the victor and the grief of the defeated with equal pity; Simone Weil read the poem as the poem of force.
The gods take sides, cheat and watch like spectators: Homer's heaven is powerful but not good, which makes human courage more tragic.

sessions.title: Priam in the tent
sessions.line: An old king crosses the enemy lines at night, kneels before the man who killed his son and kisses his hands. The two enemies weep together, eat together, and the Iliad ends not with victory but with a funeral.
sessions.plain: After Hector's death, Achilles cannot stop grieving or stop mistreating the body. Then the gods intervene. Priam, Hector's old father, goes alone through the Greek camp at night to Achilles' hut, with a ransom, to beg for his son's body. He kneels and kisses the hands that killed his son, and asks Achilles to think of his own father. Achilles weeps, raises him up, gives back the body, and the two men eat together. This session asks why the greatest war poem of the West ends with mercy between enemies, and what kind of mercy it is.
sessions.why: Session 3 left Achilles at his most inhuman, dragging Hector's body in the dust. The Iliad began with an old father turned away when he came to ransom his child. Now the poem returns to the same scene. What happens in Achilles' hut answers the anger that the poem began with.
answers: Why does Priam go to Achilles, and why does Achilles give way?
What were supplication and guest-friendship (xenia)?
Why does the Iliad end with a funeral and not the fall of Troy?
How is this mercy like, and unlike, forgiveness in the Bible?
sessions.finding: The Iliad ends not with victory but with two enemies weeping together: mercy, born of a shared mortality, is the poem's last word, though it is a truce and not yet forgiveness.

paras: After killing Hector, Achilles held a great funeral for Patroclus (Book XXIII). He sacrificed twelve young Trojan prisoners on the pyre, an act the poet calls evil in a single phrase (XXIII.176), and then held funeral games, where he was a generous and courteous host. But he still could not sleep. Every dawn he tied Hector's body to his chariot and dragged it three times round Patroclus's tomb. This went on for twelve days. Apollo kept the body from decay and harm.

At last the gods met. Apollo accused Achilles of destroying pity and shame, the feelings that make human beings human (XXIV.39–54). Zeus agreed that it must stop. He sent Thetis to tell her son that he must accept a ransom for the body, and Achilles agreed at once. He sent the messenger goddess Iris to tell Priam to go to Achilles' hut with gifts. Priam's wife Hecuba begged him not to go: Achilles was a savage, and would kill him. Priam went anyway, with one old herald, Idaeus, and a waggon full of treasure. On the way the god Hermes ('Mercury' in Butler) met him, disguised as a young Greek, and led him unseen through the camp.
background.key: Achilles drags Hector's body for twelve days. The gods intervene; Thetis tells Achilles to accept a ransom; Priam crosses the camp at night, guided by Hermes.

paras: To understand the scene you need two Greek customs. The first is supplication. A suppliant was someone who threw himself on another's mercy by kneeling, clasping their knees and touching their chin or hands. It was a ritual act with religious force: Zeus was believed to protect suppliants, and to reject one was a serious wrong. Chryses came to the Greeks as a suppliant in Book I, with a priest's wreath, and was turned away.

The second is xenia, guest-friendship: the sacred bond between host and guest. A host must welcome a stranger, feed him before asking his business, give him a bed and send him safely on his way. Guest and host were bound to each other, and even their descendants were. Zeus Xenios, 'Zeus of strangers', watched over it. In Book VI two warriors on opposite sides, Glaucus and Diomedes, discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends, and refuse to fight each other. The war itself began with a breach of xenia: Paris was Menelaus's guest when he took Helen. Priam comes to Achilles as both suppliant and guest.

rows: Kneeling to clasp someone's knees and beg mercy; to reject a suppliant was a sin
The bond of host and guest: welcome, food, a bed and safe conduct, binding for generations
A payment to recover a captive or a body; accepting it ended the claim of the captor
None in particular: a human custom
Washing, anointing, lament and burning or burial; owed to every dead person

background.key: Supplication (begging mercy on one's knees) and xenia (the sacred bond of host and guest) were protected by Zeus. Priam comes as both.

paras: The main reading is the meeting of Priam and Achilles in Book XXIV, from Priam's entrance to the moment they lie down to sleep. It answers the question of why the poem ends as it does, because here Achilles' anger, which the poem began with, finally ends.
The comparison is the last lines of the Iliad: Helen's lament for Hector, and his funeral. It answers the question of how the poem chooses to end, and what it leaves out.
background.key: The meeting of Priam and Achilles, where the anger ends; then the last lines of the poem, Hector's funeral.

before: What does Priam do when he first comes into the hut, and what does he ask Achilles to think of?
What does Achilles say about the two urns on the floor of Zeus's palace?
Achilles is gentle, then suddenly stern. What does that tell you about him?
sessions.readWhy: Priam ransoms Hector's body from Achilles: the meeting where the Iliad's anger ends.

paras: With these words Mercury went back to high Olympus. Priam sprang from his chariot to the ground, leaving Idaeus where he was, in charge of the mules and horses. The old man went straight into the house where Achilles, loved of the gods, was sitting. There he found him with his men seated at a distance from him: only two, the hero Automedon, and Alcimus of the race of Mars, were busy in attendance about his person, for he had but just done eating and drinking, and the table was still there. King Priam entered without their seeing him, and going right up to Achilles he clasped his knees and kissed the dread murderous hands that had slain so many of his sons.

As when some cruel spite has befallen a man that he should have killed some one in his own country, and must fly to a great man’s protection in a land of strangers, and all marvel who see him, even so did Achilles marvel as he beheld Priam. The others looked one to another and marvelled also, but Priam besought Achilles saying, “Think of your father, O Achilles like unto the gods, who is such even as I am, on the sad threshold of old age. It may be that those who dwell near him harass him, and there is none to keep war and ruin from him. Yet when he hears of you being still alive, he is glad, and his days are full of hope that he shall see his dear son come home to him from Troy; but I, wretched man that I am, had the bravest in all Troy for my sons, and there is not one of them left. I had fifty sons when the Achaeans came here; nineteen of them were from a single womb, and the others were borne to me by the women of my household. The greater part of them has fierce Mars laid low, and Hector, him who was alone left, him who was the guardian of the city and ourselves, him have you lately slain; therefore I am now come to the ships of the Achaeans to ransom his body from you with a great ransom. Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me, who am the more pitiable, for I have steeled myself as no man yet has ever steeled himself before me, and have raised to my lips the hand of him who slew my son.”

Thus spoke Priam, and the heart of Achilles yearned as he bethought him of his father. He took the old man’s hand and moved him gently away. The two wept bitterly—Priam, as he lay at Achilles’ feet, weeping for Hector, and Achilles now for his father and now for Patroclus, till the house was filled with their lamentation. But when Achilles was now sated with grief and had unburthened the bitterness of his sorrow, he left his seat and raised the old man by the hand, in pity for his white hair and beard; then he said, “Unhappy man, you have indeed been greatly daring; how could you venture to come alone to the ships of the Achaeans, and enter the presence of him who has slain so many of your brave sons? You must have iron courage: sit now upon this seat, and for all our grief we will hide our sorrows in our hearts, for weeping will not avail us. The immortals know no care, yet the lot they spin for man is full of sorrow; on the floor of Jove’s palace there stand two urns, the one filled with evil gifts, and the other with good ones. He for whom Jove the lord of thunder mixes the gifts he sends, will meet now with good and now with evil fortune;

but he to whom Jove sends none but evil gifts will be pointed at by the finger of scorn, the hand of famine will pursue him to the ends of the world, and he will go up and down the face of the earth, respected neither by gods nor men. Even so did it befall Peleus; the gods endowed him with all good things from his birth upwards, for he reigned over the Myrmidons excelling all men in prosperity and wealth, and mortal though he was they gave him a goddess for his bride. But even on him too did heaven send misfortune, for there is no race of royal children born to him in his house, save one son who is doomed to die all untimely; nor may I take care of him now that he is growing old, for I must stay here at Troy to be the bane of you and your children. And you too, O Priam, I have heard that you were aforetime happy. They say that in wealth and plenitude of offspring you surpassed all that is in Lesbos, the realm of Makar to the northward, Phrygia that is more inland, and those that dwell upon the great Hellespont; but from the day when the dwellers in heaven sent this evil upon you, war and slaughter have been about your city continually. Bear up against it, and let there be some intervals in your sorrow. Mourn as you may for your brave son, you will take nothing by it. You cannot raise him from the dead, ere you do so yet another sorrow shall befall you.”

And Priam answered, “O king, bid me not be seated, while Hector is still lying uncared for in your tents, but accept the great ransom which I have brought you, and give him to me at once that I may look upon him. May you prosper with the ransom and reach your own land in safety, seeing that you have suffered me to live and to look upon the light of the sun.”

Achilles looked at him sternly and said, “Vex me, sir, no longer; I am of myself minded to give up the body of Hector. My mother, daughter of the old man of the sea, came to me from Jove to bid me deliver it to you. Moreover I know well, O Priam, and you cannot hide it, that some god has brought you to the ships of the Achaeans, for else, no man however strong and in his prime would dare to come to our host; he could neither pass our guard unseen, nor draw the bolt of my gates thus easily; therefore, provoke me no further, lest I sin against the word of Jove, and suffer you not, suppliant though you are, within my tents.”

The old man feared him and obeyed. Then the son of Peleus sprang like a lion through the door of his house, not alone, but with him went his two squires Automedon and Alcimus who were closer to him than any others of his comrades now that Patroclus was no more. These unyoked the horses and mules, and bade Priam’s herald and attendant be seated within the house. They lifted the ransom for Hector’s body from the waggon, but they left two mantles and a goodly shirt, that Achilles might wrap the body in them when he gave it to be taken home. Then he called to his servants and ordered them to wash the body and anoint it, but he first took it to a place where Priam should not see it, lest if he did so, he should break out in the bitterness of his grief, and enrage Achilles, who might then kill him and sin against the word of Jove. When the servants had washed the body and anointed it, and had wrapped it in a fair shirt and mantle, Achilles himself lifted it on to a bier, and he and his men then laid it on the waggon. He cried aloud as he did so and called on the name of his dear comrade, “Be not angry with me, Patroclus,” he said, “if you hear even in the house of Hades that I have given Hector to his father for a ransom. It has been no unworthy one, and I will share it equitably with you.”

Achilles then went back into the tent and took his place on the richly inlaid seat from which he had risen, by the wall that was at right angles to the one against which Priam was sitting. “Sir,” he said, “your son is now laid upon his bier and is ransomed according to desire; you shall look upon him when you take him away at daybreak; for the present let us prepare our supper. Even lovely Niobe had to think about eating, though her twelve children—six daughters and six lusty sons—had been all slain in her house. Apollo killed the sons with arrows from his silver bow, to punish Niobe, and Diana slew the daughters, because Niobe had vaunted herself against Leto; she said Leto had borne two children only, whereas she had herself borne many—whereon the two killed the many. Nine days did they lie weltering, and there was none to bury them, for the son of Saturn turned the people into stone; but on the tenth day the gods in heaven themselves buried them, and Niobe then took food, being worn out with weeping. They say that somewhere among the rocks on the mountain pastures of Sipylus, where the nymphs live that haunt the river Achelous, there, they say, she lives in stone and still nurses the sorrows sent upon her by the hand of heaven. Therefore, noble sir, let us two now take food; you can weep for your dear son hereafter as you are bearing him back to Ilius—and many a tear will he cost you.”

With this Achilles sprang from his seat and killed a sheep of silvery whiteness, which his followers skinned and made ready all in due order. They cut the meat carefully up into smaller pieces, spitted them, and drew them off again when they were well roasted. Automedon brought bread in fair baskets and served it round the table, while Achilles dealt out the meat, and they laid their hands on the good things that were before them. As soon as they had had enough to eat and drink, Priam, descendant of Dardanus, marvelled at the strength and beauty of Achilles for he was as a god to see, and Achilles marvelled at Priam as he listened to him and looked upon his noble presence. When they had gazed their fill Priam spoke first. “And now, O king,” he said, “take me to my couch that we may lie down and enjoy the blessed boon of sleep. Never once have my eyes been closed from the day your hands took the life of my son; I have grovelled without ceasing in the mire of my stable-yard, making moan and brooding over my countless sorrows. Now, moreover, I have eaten bread and drunk wine; hitherto I have tasted nothing.”

As he spoke Achilles told his men and the women servants to set beds in the room that was in the gatehouse, and make them with good red rugs, and spread coverlets on the top of them with woollen cloaks for Priam and Idaeus to wear. So the maids went out carrying a torch and got the two beds ready in all haste. Then Achilles said laughingly to Priam, “Dear sir, you shall lie outside, lest some counsellor of those who in due course keep coming to advise with me should see you here in the darkness of the flying night, and tell it to Agamemnon. This might cause delay in the delivery of the body. And now tell me and tell me true, for how many days would you celebrate the funeral rites of noble Hector? Tell me, that I may hold aloof from war and restrain the host.”

And Priam answered, “Since, then, you suffer me to bury my noble son with all due rites, do thus, Achilles, and I shall be grateful. You know how we are pent up within our city; it is far for us to fetch wood from the mountain, and the people live in fear. Nine days, therefore, will we mourn Hector in my house; on the tenth day we will bury him and there shall be a public feast in his honour; on the eleventh we will build a mound over his ashes, and on the twelfth, if there be need, we will fight.”
And Achilles answered, “All, King Priam, shall be as you have said. I will stay our fighting for as long a time as you have named.”

As he spoke he laid his hand on the old man’s right wrist, in token that he should have no fear; thus then did Priam and his attendant sleep there in the forecourt, full of thought, while Achilles lay in an inner room of the house, with fair Briseis by his side.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The hand of him who slew my son
parts.context: Night, in Achilles' hut in the Greek camp. Hermes ('Mercury') has guided Priam there and left. Achilles has just finished eating with two companions. Priam has fifty sons, nineteen by his queen Hecuba; most are dead.
parts.plain: Priam walks in unseen, kneels, clasps Achilles' knees and kisses his hands. Everyone is astonished. Priam asks Achilles to think of his own father, Peleus, old and alone, who at least can hope to see his son again. Priam has lost almost all his sons, Hector last. He asks Achilles to fear the gods and pity him, who has done what no man has ever done: kissed the hand that killed his son.

commentary.on: he clasped his knees and kissed the dread murderous hands that had slain so many of his sons
commentary.text: The gesture of the suppliant, taken to its extreme. 'Murderous' translates androphonous, 'man-slaying': the same words Homer used of Achilles' hands when he laid them on the chest of the dead Patroclus (XVIII.317). Priam kisses the hands that killed his children. The whole poem has been building to this act.

commentary.on: As when some cruel spite has befallen a man that he should have killed some one in his own country, and must fly to a great man's protection in a land of strangers
commentary.text: The simile turns things upside down. Priam is the victim, yet Homer compares him to a murderer seeking refuge. It is as if Priam, by coming, has done something as shocking as a killing: he has broken all the rules of how an enemy behaves.

commentary.on: Think of your father, O Achilles like unto the gods, who is such even as I am, on the sad threshold of old age.
commentary.text: Priam's first word is 'think of your father'. He does not argue about the war or offer the ransom first. He asks Achilles to see in him someone he loves. This is the thought Priam had in despair on the walls of Troy in session 3, and now he dares to say it.

commentary.on: and have raised to my lips the hand of him who slew my son
commentary.text: The heart of the poem. These words are in By heart as 'The hand of him who slew my son'. Priam has humbled himself further than any king, any father, any man. That is what gives his plea its power.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The two urns
parts.context: Achilles answers. Peleus was his father, who married the goddess Thetis; Lesbos and Phrygia were lands near Troy that Priam's kingdom once rivalled. 'The old man of the sea' is Thetis's father.
parts.plain: Achilles is moved. He weeps for his father and for Patroclus while Priam weeps for Hector. Then he raises Priam up and says that the gods give men a mixture of good and evil from two urns, or only evil, but never only good. Peleus had everything, but has one son who will die young far from him; Priam was rich, and now has war. Weeping will not bring Hector back. When Priam presses him, Achilles flares up: he has decided to give the body, because his mother told him to, and Priam must not provoke him.

commentary.on: The two wept bitterly—Priam, as he lay at Achilles' feet, weeping for Hector, and Achilles now for his father and now for Patroclus
commentary.text: Two enemies weep in the same room, each for his own dead. They do not weep for the same person; they weep for the same reason. This is the moment the anger that began the poem finally breaks.

commentary.on: in pity for his white hair and beard
commentary.text: The word Homer uses is oiktirōn, pitying. Apollo said Achilles had destroyed pity. Here it returns, through the sight of an old man's white hair.

commentary.on: You must have iron courage
commentary.text: Hector told Achilles his heart was iron. Now Achilles says the same of Priam. The two men have recognised each other's strength.

commentary.on: on the floor of Jove's palace there stand two urns, the one filled with evil gifts, and the other with good ones
commentary.text: Achilles' consolation is a picture of human life. Zeus gives some people a mixture of good and evil, and some only evil. No one gets only good. It is a bleak comfort, but a shared one: Achilles and Priam are both in this condition, and so is everyone.

commentary.on: save one son who is doomed to die all untimely; nor may I take care of him now that he is growing old
commentary.text: Achilles speaks of himself in the third person, as Peleus's son who will die young. He knows that Peleus will be left as Priam is: an old man whose son is dead. He is looking at his own father's future.

commentary.on: lest I sin against the word of Jove, and suffer you not, suppliant though you are, within my tents
commentary.text: The mercy is fragile. A moment after weeping together, Achilles threatens Priam. His anger is still there, held down. Homer does not give us a softened Achilles, but a dangerous man choosing, with effort, not to kill.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Let us two now take food
parts.context: Achilles goes out to prepare the body. Niobe was a mother in legend who boasted that she had more children than the goddess Leto, so Leto's children, Apollo and Artemis ('Diana'), killed all twelve of hers.
parts.plain: Achilles has the body washed and wrapped, out of Priam's sight in case the old man's grief makes Achilles lose his temper. He lays it on the waggon himself and asks the dead Patroclus not to be angry. Then he tells Priam the story of Niobe, who ate even after all her children were killed, and asks him to eat. They share a meal and look at each other in wonder. Priam says he has not slept or eaten since Hector died.

commentary.on: he first took it to a place where Priam should not see it, lest if he did so, he should break out in the bitterness of his grief, and enrage Achilles, who might then kill him
commentary.text: An extraordinary moment of self-knowledge. Achilles knows his own temper, and arranges things so that he will not be tested beyond what he can bear. Mercy, here, includes knowing your own weakness.

commentary.on: Achilles himself lifted it on to a bier
commentary.text: The man who dragged the body through the dust now lifts it himself, washed and wrapped. The same hands Priam kissed now care for his son.

commentary.on: Be not angry with me, Patroclus
commentary.text: Achilles still feels he owes his dead friend revenge. He apologises to the ghost. Even in mercy he has not forgotten love.

commentary.on: Even lovely Niobe had to think about eating
commentary.text: Achilles, who refused all food after Patroclus died, now tells a grieving father to eat. To eat is to choose to go on living. The meal is the sign that both men are returning to the human world.

commentary.on: Priam, descendant of Dardanus, marvelled at the strength and beauty of Achilles for he was as a god to see, and Achilles marvelled at Priam
commentary.text: Enemies, after the meal, simply look at each other and wonder. Each sees the other's greatness. For a moment there is no war in the hut, only two human beings.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: A truce for the funeral
parts.context: Achilles has beds made for Priam and his herald on the porch. Briseis, the captive woman taken from Achilles in Book I and returned with Agamemnon's gifts, is with him.
parts.plain: Achilles puts Priam to sleep outside, so that no Greek will see him and tell Agamemnon. He asks how many days Priam needs for the funeral. Priam asks for eleven days of mourning and burial, and on the twelfth they will fight again. Achilles promises, and takes Priam's wrist so that he will not be afraid.

commentary.on: lest some counsellor of those who in due course keep coming to advise with me should see you here
commentary.text: Achilles protects his guest from his own side. He is now Priam's host, bound by xenia to keep him safe.

commentary.on: on the twelfth, if there be need, we will fight
commentary.text: The truce has an end date. The war is not over. Troy will still fall, Hector's son will still die, Achilles will still be killed. The mercy in this hut changes nothing in the history of the war. It changes everything in the meaning of the poem.

commentary.on: he laid his hand on the old man's right wrist, in token that he should have no fear
commentary.text: The last gesture between them is a hand on a wrist. The hand Priam kissed, the hand that killed Hector, now gives a promise of safety.

commentary.on: with fair Briseis by his side
commentary.text: The woman over whom the whole quarrel began is back. The anger of Book I has come full circle. Homer names her, and says nothing more.

read.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC

paras: Bitterly did she weep the while, and the women joined in her lament. Hecuba in her turn took up the strains of woe. “Hector,” she cried, “dearest to me of all my children. So long as you were alive the gods loved you well, and even in death they have not been utterly unmindful of you; for when Achilles took any other of my sons, he would sell him beyond the seas, to Samos Imbrus or rugged Lemnos; and when he had slain you too with his sword, many a time did he drag you round the sepulchre of his comrade—though this could not give him life—yet here you lie all fresh as dew, and comely as one whom Apollo has slain with his painless shafts.”

Thus did she too speak through her tears with bitter moan, and then Helen for a third time took up the strain of lamentation. “Hector,” said she, “dearest of all my brothers-in-law—for I am wife to Alexandrus who brought me hither to Troy—would that I had died ere he did so—twenty years are come and gone since I left my home and came from over the sea, but I have never heard one word of insult or unkindness from you. When another would chide with me, as it might be one of your brothers or sisters or of your brothers’ wives, or my mother-in-law—for Priam was as kind to me as though he were my own father—you would rebuke and check them with words of gentleness and goodwill. Therefore my tears flow both for you and for my unhappy self, for there is no one else in Troy who is kind to me, but all shrink and shudder as they go by me.”

She wept as she spoke and the vast crowd that was gathered round her joined in her lament. Then King Priam spoke to them saying, “Bring wood, O Trojans, to the city, and fear no cunning ambush of the Argives, for Achilles when he dismissed me from the ships gave me his word that they should not attack us until the morning of the twelfth day.”

Forthwith they yoked their oxen and mules and gathered together before the city. Nine days long did they bring in great heaps of wood, and on the morning of the tenth day with many tears they took brave Hector forth, laid his dead body upon the summit of the pile, and set the fire thereto. Then when the child of morning, rosy-fingered dawn, appeared on the eleventh day, the people again assembled, round the pyre of mighty Hector. When they were got together, they first quenched the fire with wine wherever it was burning, and then his brothers and comrades with many a bitter tear gathered his white bones, wrapped them in soft robes of purple, and laid them in a golden urn, which they placed in a grave and covered over with large stones set close together. Then they built a barrow hurriedly over it keeping guard on every side lest the Achaeans should attack them before they had finished. When they had heaped up the barrow they went back again into the city, and being well assembled they held high feast in the house of Priam their king.
Thus, then, did they celebrate the funeral of Hector tamer of horses.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Hecuba and Helen
parts.context: Priam has brought the body home. In Troy, the women lead the laments: first Andromache (her lament ends as this passage begins), then Hecuba, then Helen, the woman the war was fought over. 'Alexandrus' is Paris. Samos, Imbrus and Lemnos are islands where Achilles sold captured Trojans as slaves.
parts.plain: Hecuba finishes her lament: Achilles dragged Hector round Patroclus's tomb, but the gods have kept his body fresh. Then Helen speaks: in twenty years at Troy, Hector never said an unkind word to her, and stopped others when they did. Now she has no friend left in Troy. Priam tells the people to bring wood, since Achilles has promised them a truce.

commentary.on: yet here you lie all fresh as dew, and comely as one whom Apollo has slain with his painless shafts
commentary.text: Hecuba takes comfort that her son's body was not destroyed. The gods' protection of Hector is the only kindness heaven has shown Troy in the poem, and it is enough for a mother.

commentary.on: I have never heard one word of insult or unkindness from you
commentary.text: The last private voice in the Iliad is Helen's, praising Hector not for his courage but for his kindness. Of all the things that could be said of the greatest Trojan, the poem ends with this: he was gentle to a woman everyone else blamed.

commentary.on: Achilles when he dismissed me from the ships gave me his word
commentary.text: Priam trusts Achilles' word, and he is right to. The killer of his son has become a man whose promise can be relied on.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The funeral of Hector
parts.context: The last lines of the poem.
parts.plain: For nine days the Trojans gather wood. On the tenth they burn Hector's body; on the eleventh they gather his bones into a golden urn, bury it and raise a mound, and hold a feast in Priam's house. The poem ends: 'Thus, then, did they celebrate the funeral of Hector tamer of horses.'

commentary.on: gathered his white bones, wrapped them in soft robes of purple, and laid them in a golden urn
commentary.text: Everything Hector asked for as he died is given: his body home, fire, his family's mourning. The very rite Achilles swore to deny him is the last thing the poem describes.

commentary.on: keeping guard on every side lest the Achaeans should attack them
commentary.text: Even at the funeral, the war is waiting outside. Homer does not let us forget it.

commentary.on: Thus, then, did they celebrate the funeral of Hector tamer of horses.
commentary.text: The last line of the Iliad is about the burial of the enemy. The poem that began with Achilles' anger ends with the name of the man he killed, honoured. Not the Greeks' victory, not the fall of Troy: a funeral. That choice is the poem's judgement on everything that came before.

compare.author: Homer
compare.why: The Iliad could have ended with the fall of Troy, or the death of Achilles. Read how it does end.
compare.title: How the Iliad ends

paras: The Iliad is built in a ring. Its last book answers its first, scene for scene. In Book I an old father came to the Greek camp with a ransom for his child and was turned away; the result was a plague and nine days of death. In Book XXIV an old father comes with a ransom for his child and is received; the result is nine days of mourning and a burial. In Book I Thetis went to Zeus to ask for her son's honour; in Book XXIV Zeus sends Thetis to her son. In Book I Achilles' anger began with Briseis; in Book XXIV it ends with Briseis beside him. The scholar Cedric Whitman (Homer and the Heroic Tradition, 1958) showed how carefully this ring is made.

What the ring says is that the poem's subject was never the war. It was the anger, and the anger is now over. By ending with Hector's funeral, Homer makes the last word not the triumph of the Greeks but the honour paid to their greatest enemy.

rows: Chryses comes to the Greek ships with a ransom for his daughter
Priam comes to the Greek ships with a ransom for his son
Nine days of plague and burning pyres
Nine days of gathering wood for Hector's pyre
Thetis goes to Zeus for her son's honour
Zeus sends Thetis to her son
The quarrel over Briseis begins the anger
Briseis beside Achilles as the anger ends
table.note: The pattern is called ring composition: a work ends by echoing its beginning.

sections.key: Book XXIV mirrors Book I: a father with a ransom, refused then received. The anger that began the poem ends, and the last word is an enemy's funeral.

paras: Why does Achilles give way? Partly because the gods tell him to: Thetis brought Zeus's command before Priam arrived, and Achilles reminds Priam of it sharply. But Homer shows something more. What moves Achilles to tears is Priam's appeal to his father. Seeing Priam, he sees Peleus, who will soon lose his only son as Priam has lost Hector. He sees his own death.

The mercy in the hut comes from that recognition: we are both sons and fathers, and we will both die. The parable of the two urns puts it into words. No one, not even the son of a goddess, gets only good things from Zeus. What joins Achilles and Priam is not forgiveness or a common cause, but a common condition. The Greek word for it is pity, eleos, the feeling Aristotle would later say tragedy is meant to arouse (Poetics 6).
sections.key: Achilles' pity is born when he sees his own father, and his own death, in Priam: mercy from a shared mortal condition, not from forgiveness.

paras: Look at what Achilles does after the weeping. He prepares the body himself. He kills a sheep with his own hands and serves the meat. He makes up beds. He protects his guest from Agamemnon. He grants a truce and takes Priam's wrist. Every one of these is a duty of xenia, the sacred bond between host and guest that you met in the background. The man who would not make a covenant with Hector because 'there can be no covenants between men and lions' now makes one with Hector's father.

The meal matters most. Achilles has refused food since Patroclus died; Priam has not eaten since Hector died. In eating together, the two men return to ordinary human life, which needs bread, wine and sleep. The story of Niobe, who ate even after losing twelve children, says the same thing: grief must make room for life. It is a very human mercy, made of small, concrete acts.
sections.key: Achilles becomes Priam's host, doing every duty of xenia; the shared meal marks their return to human life from grief.

paras: It would be easy to sentimentalise this scene. Homer does not. Achilles threatens Priam even after they have wept together. He hides the body so that he will not lose his temper. The truce is for eleven days; on the twelfth, Priam says, 'we will fight'. The poem's audience knew what came next: Achilles killed by Paris and Apollo, Troy burned, Priam killed at his own altar by Achilles' son, Hector's baby son thrown from the walls.

So the mercy changes nothing in the war. It is one night. And yet the poem ends there, not with the sack of Troy. Homer chose to make that one night the end of his story. That choice is a judgement: that what matters most in the whole war is the moment two enemies recognised each other as human.
sections.key: The mercy is a truce of eleven days, and the audience knew Troy would fall; yet Homer chose that night, not the sack, to end his poem.

paras: If you have taken 'Abraham and the promise', you read the end of Genesis, where Joseph, ruler in Egypt, meets the brothers who sold him into slavery. They beg forgiveness; 'Joseph wept when they spoke to him' (Genesis 50:17). Here too are tears between an injured man and those who wronged him.

But the differences are deep. Joseph forgives a wrong: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good' (Genesis 50:20). He sees a providence that brings good out of evil, and the family is reconciled for good. Achilles and Priam forgive nothing. Nothing is asked and nothing is given: Priam does not say Achilles was right, and Achilles does not repent. They share grief across a war that will go on. Homer's mercy is pity between fellow sufferers under indifferent gods. The Bible's is forgiveness under a God who means good. Jesus would go further still: 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44), not only in a moment of shared grief, but as a way of life.
sections.key: Joseph forgives and is reconciled under a providence; Achilles and Priam share grief and forgive nothing. Pity under the gods; forgiveness under God.

paras: Readers in every century have found this the greatest scene in Homer. It is the source of one of the West's deepest instincts: that an enemy is still a human being, that the dead must be honoured on both sides, that mercy is greater than victory. The rules of war that later ages tried to write down, from the medieval truce of God to the Geneva Conventions on the treatment of the dead and wounded, express the same conviction, though they owe more to Christian teaching than to Homer.

It is worth seeing how much is there already, eight centuries before Christ: a king who humbles himself, a killer who weeps, a body returned with care. And how much is not yet there: forgiveness, repentance, love for an enemy as a command. The Iliad reaches the edge of something it cannot name.
sections.key: The scene gave the West its instinct that an enemy is human and mercy greater than victory, though forgiveness and love of enemies lie beyond it.

paras: Priam does not cross the Greek camp alone. Zeus sends Hermes, the guide of travellers and of the dead, who meets the old man at night disguised as a young Greek, puts the sentries to sleep, opens the gates and brings him to Achilles' door (XXIV.334–467). Then Hermes reveals who he is and leaves, saying that it would not be right for a god to be seen favouring a mortal so openly.

So the gods, who in Book XXII handed Hector over to his enemy, here make mercy possible. They do not do the merciful thing themselves. They open the way, and leave the two men to do it. That is typical of Homer: the gods set the scene, but the great human moments, Priam's kiss and Achilles' tears, belong to the humans alone. Plato, as this journey will show, wanted gods who are simply good. Homer's are sometimes kind and sometimes cruel, and never as kind as Priam.
sections.key: Hermes guides Priam through the camp and leaves; the gods open the way to mercy, but the merciful acts are human.

refs: Homer, Iliad I.12–52, 348–427, 493–530; VI.119–236 (Glaucus and Diomedes); XXIII.175–176; XXIV.14–140, 468–804. Tr. Samuel Butler (1898).
Cedric Whitman, Homer and the Heroic Tradition (1958), on ring composition.
Aristotle, Poetics 6 (pity and fear).
Genesis 50:15–21; Matthew 5:44 (World English Bible).
Kevin Crotty, The Poetics of Supplication: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey (1994); John Gould, 'Hiketeia', Journal of Hellenic Studies 93 (1973), on supplication.
The later fall of Troy: Virgil, Aeneid II (Priam's death, Neoptolemus); Euripides, The Trojan Women (Astyanax).

debate.question: What changes Achilles?

positions.name: The gods' command
positions.who: A close reading of the plot; some scholars stress the divine frame
positions.view: Achilles gives back the body because Zeus commands it through Thetis, and Achilles has always obeyed the gods (as with Athena in Book I). The tears are real, but the decision was made before Priam arrived. Homer's world is one where the gods decide.
positions.evidence: Thetis's message (XXIV.126–137); Achilles: 'I am of myself minded... My mother... came to me from Jove'; his warning not to make him 'sin against the word of Jove'.

positions.name: Pity: he sees his father in Priam
positions.who: Jasper Griffin; Simone Weil; most readers
positions.view: The command gives Achilles permission, but what transforms him is Priam's appeal. In the old man he sees Peleus, and his own death. Pity, born of shared mortality, is what makes him human again.
positions.evidence: 'Think of your father'; Achilles weeps 'now for his father and now for Patroclus'; the parable of the two urns; the care he takes with the body.

positions.name: The power of ritual
positions.who: Kevin Crotty (1994); John Gould (1973)
positions.view: Supplication and xenia are rituals with their own force. By kneeling and kissing his hands, Priam puts Achilles under obligations that even he cannot ignore. The rituals give both men a way back from grief into a shared human order.
positions.evidence: The suppliant's gestures; the shared meal; the beds; the truce sealed by a hand on the wrist.

debate.agree: All agree that the scene ends the anger the poem began with, and that the gods' command, Priam's appeal and the customs of supplication and hospitality all play a part.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art in Washington has no painting of Priam and Achilles, and no other scene from the Iliad.

music.why: Brahms's German Requiem is comfort for the living, not a prayer for the dead. It opens 'Blessed are they that mourn': fitting for a scene in which two mourners comfort each other.

think.why: Achilles' two urns are a Greek answer to suffering: no one escapes it, and it comes from the gods. Read what Christians believe about suffering, and see where the answers differ.

learn.why: Priam's plea and Achilles' answer: the moment the Iliad's anger ends, and the West's first great scene of mercy between enemies.

check.q: Priam's first words to Achilles are 'Think of your father'. Why is this the most powerful thing he could say?
options: Because Achilles hated his father
Because it reminds Achilles that his father had ordered him to show mercy
Because Peleus was Priam's old friend
Because it makes Achilles see in Priam his own father, who will soon lose his son as Priam has, and so his own death
check.why: Achilles weeps 'now for his father': he sees Peleus's future in Priam. Peleus was not Priam's friend; the other options are not in the text.

check.q: How does the scene in Book XXIV answer the scene in Book I?
options: In both an old father comes with a ransom for his child: in Book I he is refused and disaster follows; in Book XXIV he is received and the anger ends
Both show Achilles winning a duel
Both end with a plague
In both, Agamemnon is humiliated
check.why: The ring composition: Chryses refused, Priam received. The poem returns to its first scene to end its first subject, the anger.

check.q: What is the point of Achilles' parable of the two urns?
options: That Priam should have prayed more to Zeus
That good people are rewarded and bad people punished
That Achilles will soon receive only good gifts
That Zeus gives some men a mixture of good and evil and some only evil, but none only good, so suffering is the common lot of all
check.why: It is a bleak but shared consolation: Achilles and Priam are in the same condition. The first option is the view the parable denies.

check.q: Why does Achilles have Hector's body prepared out of Priam's sight?
options: So that he could keep some of the ransom secretly
So that Priam's grief at the sight will not provoke Achilles' own temper and lead him to kill his guest
Because the body was too damaged to be seen
Because Greek custom forbade a father to see his son's body
check.why: Homer says so: lest Priam break out in grief and enrage Achilles. The gods had kept the body unharmed, so the first option is wrong.

check.q: Which statement best describes how the mercy in Achilles' hut differs from Joseph's forgiveness in Genesis 50?
options: They are the same: both are forgiveness of a wrong
Joseph forgives a wrong and is reconciled under a God who brings good from evil; Achilles and Priam forgive nothing but share grief, and the war goes on
Joseph's mercy is temporary, Achilles' is permanent
Achilles repents and Priam forgives him
check.why: No forgiveness is asked or given in the hut; it is a truce of eleven days. Joseph says 'God meant it for good', and the family is reconciled.

check.q: The Iliad ends with the funeral of Hector, not the fall of Troy. What does that choice suggest?
options: That Homer did not know how the war ended
That the Trojans won the war
That the poem's subject was Achilles' anger, now ended, and that its final judgement honours the human dignity of the enemy over the victory
That Homer wanted to write a sequel
check.why: The audience knew Troy fell. Ending with Hector honoured makes recognition of the enemy's humanity the poem's last word.

tutorial.question: Why does the Iliad end with Priam?
tutorial.approach: Begin with the ring composition between Books I and XXIV. Then read the scene closely: the supplication, the appeal to Peleus, the weeping, the two urns, the meal, the truce. Weigh the three explanations of what changes Achilles. Then ask what kind of mercy this is, comparing Joseph in Genesis 50. Conclude with what the ending says about the poem as a whole.
strong: Explains the ring between Book I and Book XXIV, with at least three parallels.
Explains supplication and xenia and shows them at work in the scene.
Analyses 'think of your father' and the two urns.
Weighs the gods' command against Achilles' own pity.
Notes the limits: the truce, the threat, the fall of Troy to come.
Compares the scene fairly with Joseph's forgiveness and with Jesus' command to love enemies.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: think of someone you are at odds with. Before you next speak to them, take two minutes to imagine what they have lost or are afraid of, as Achilles saw Peleus in Priam. Then begin the conversation with one sincere question about their life, not about the dispute.
sessions.reflect: Is there someone you would find it hardest to sit and eat with? What would it take for you to see them as Achilles saw Priam?
takeaways: Priam kisses the hands that killed his son and asks Achilles to think of his father; seeing his own father and his own death in Priam, Achilles weeps and gives back the body.
The scene mirrors Book I, ends the anger the poem began with, and closes with the enemy's funeral: mercy is the Iliad's last word.
It is pity from a shared mortality, with a truce and not a peace: forgiveness and love of enemies, as Genesis and the Gospels teach them, lie beyond it.

sessions.title: The long way home
sessions.line: On an enchanted island a goddess offers Odysseus eternal life if he will stay with her. He sits on the shore and weeps for home, for an ageing wife on a rocky island. Twenty years on, she tests him with a secret only the two of them share.
sessions.plain: The Odyssey tells how Odysseus, the cleverest of the Greeks, took ten years to get home from Troy. When we meet him he has lost all his men and is held on an island by the goddess Calypso, who loves him and offers to make him immortal. He refuses: he wants to go home to his wife Penelope, though he admits she is not as beautiful as a goddess. When at last he gets home, Penelope, who has waited twenty years, tests him before she believes it is really him. This session asks what kind of hero chooses home over immortality, and what the Odyssey thinks a good life is.
sessions.why: The Iliad ended in session 4 with mercy in Achilles' hut, but its hero had chosen a short life and undying glory. Homer's second poem tells of a hero who makes the opposite choice. Having seen what glory costs, we now see what it means to choose a mortal life, a home and a faithful love.
answers: What is the Odyssey about?
Why does Odysseus refuse to become immortal?
What did the Greeks admire in Odysseus: cunning, endurance, or something else?
Who is Penelope, and why is she his equal?
sessions.finding: Odysseus refuses an immortal goddess to go home to an ageing wife: the Odyssey's hero chooses a mortal, faithful life, and finds his match in a woman as clever and as faithful as he is.

paras: When Troy fell, by the trick of the wooden horse that Odysseus devised, the Greek kings sailed home. Many never arrived. Odysseus, king of the small rocky island of Ithaca off the west coast of Greece, spent ten years at sea. On the way he blinded the one-eyed giant Polyphemus, a son of the sea god Poseidon, who cursed him; he escaped the witch Circe, went down to the land of the dead, sailed past the Sirens, and lost his last men when they ate the sacred cattle of the Sun. Alone, he was washed up on the island of Ogygia, where the goddess Calypso kept him for seven years (Odyssey VII.259).

At home, his wife Penelope has waited for twenty years. More than a hundred young nobles, the suitors, have moved into the palace, eating and drinking her husband's wealth and demanding that she marry one of them. She has held them off by cunning: she said she would choose when she had finished weaving a shroud for Odysseus's father, and for three years she unpicked by night what she wove by day (II.93–110). Their son Telemachus, a baby when Odysseus left, is now a young man.
background.key: Odysseus spends ten years getting home, the last seven held by Calypso. At home Penelope holds off the suitors by cunning, and Telemachus has grown up.

paras: The Odyssey does not tell the story in order. It opens in the tenth year of the wanderings, with Telemachus at home (Books I–IV). Then it turns to Odysseus on Calypso's island (Book V), our main reading. He reaches the land of the Phaeacians, a people of perfect hosts, and tells them his adventures in a long flashback (Books IX–XII). They sail him home to Ithaca (Book XIII). There, disguised by Athena as an old beggar, he tests who is loyal, kills the suitors and is reunited with Penelope (Books XIV–XXIII).

rows: Ithaca and the suitors; Telemachus goes to look for news of his father
The gods order Calypso to release Odysseus; he builds a raft
The Phaeacians: the princess Nausicaa, the court of King Alcinous
Odysseus tells his adventures: the Cyclops, Circe, the dead, the Sirens, the cattle of the Sun
Home on Ithaca, disguised; Telemachus returns; father and son meet
The beggar in his own palace; the dog Argus; the contest of the bow
The killing of the suitors; Penelope and the bed; peace on Ithaca

background.key: The Odyssey begins near the end, tells the adventures as a flashback, and gives half its length to the return to Ithaca.

paras: The main reading is Book V, where the gods order Calypso to let Odysseus go and she offers him immortality one last time. It answers the question of what this hero values, because he is offered the one thing no mortal can have and turns it down.
The comparison is from near the end, Book XXIII: Penelope's test. It answers the question of what he goes home to, and shows that she is as clever as he is.
background.key: Calypso's offer of immortality, refused; then Penelope's test of the bed, which shows what he has come home for.

before: What is Odysseus doing when Hermes arrives on the island?
What does Calypso offer him, and what does she say about Penelope?
In the comparison, how does Penelope test whether the stranger really is her husband?
sessions.readWhy: Calypso is ordered to release Odysseus; he is offered immortality and chooses to go home.

paras: And now, as Dawn rose from her couch beside Tithonus—harbinger of light alike to mortals and immortals—the gods met in council and with them, Jove the lord of thunder, who is their king. Thereon Minerva began to tell them of the many sufferings of Ulysses, for she pitied him away there in the house of the nymph Calypso.

“Father Jove,” said she, “and all you other gods that live in everlasting bliss, I hope there may never be such a thing as a kind and well-disposed ruler any more, nor one who will govern equitably. I hope they will be all henceforth cruel and unjust, for there is not one of his subjects but has forgotten Ulysses, who ruled them as though he were their father. There he is, lying in great pain in an island where dwells the nymph Calypso, who will not let him go; and he cannot get back to his own country, for he can find neither ships nor sailors to take him over the sea. Furthermore, wicked people are now trying to murder his only son Telemachus, who is coming home from Pylos and Lacedaemon, where he has been to see if he can get news of his father.”

“What, my dear, are you talking about?” replied her father, “did you not send him there yourself, because you thought it would help Ulysses to get home and punish the suitors? Besides, you are perfectly able to protect Telemachus, and to see him safely home again, while the suitors have to come hurry-skurrying back without having killed him.”

When he had thus spoken, he said to his son Mercury, “Mercury, you are our messenger, go therefore and tell Calypso we have decreed that poor Ulysses is to return home. He is to be convoyed neither by gods nor men, but after a perilous voyage of twenty days upon a raft he is to reach fertile Scheria, the land of the Phaeacians, who are near of kin to the gods, and will honour him as though he were one of ourselves. They will send him in a ship to his own country, and will give him more bronze and gold and raiment than he would have brought back from Troy, if he had had all his prize money and had got home without disaster. This is how we have settled that he shall return to his country and his friends.”

Thus he spoke, and Mercury, guide and guardian, slayer of Argus, did as he was told. Forthwith he bound on his glittering golden sandals with which he could fly like the wind over land and sea. He took the wand with which he seals men’s eyes in sleep or wakes them just as he pleases, and flew holding it in his hand over Pieria; then he swooped down through the firmament till he reached the level of the sea, whose waves he skimmed like a cormorant that flies fishing every hole and corner of the ocean, and drenching its thick plumage in the spray. He flew and flew over many a weary wave, but when at last he got to the island which was his journey’s end, he left the sea and went on by land till he came to the cave where the nymph Calypso lived.

He found her at home. There was a large fire burning on the hearth, and one could smell from far the fragrant reek of burning cedar and sandal wood. As for herself, she was busy at her loom, shooting her golden shuttle through the warp and singing beautifully. Round her cave there was a thick wood of alder, poplar, and sweet smelling cypress trees, wherein all kinds of great birds had built their nests—owls, hawks, and chattering sea-crows that occupy their business in the waters. A vine loaded with grapes was trained and grew luxuriantly about the mouth of the cave; there were also four running rills of water in channels cut pretty close together, and turned hither and thither so as to irrigate the beds of violets and luscious herbage over which they flowed. Even a god could not help being charmed with such a lovely spot, so Mercury stood still and looked at it; but when he had admired it sufficiently he went inside the cave.

Calypso knew him at once—for the gods all know each other, no matter how far they live from one another—but Ulysses was not within; he was on the sea-shore as usual, looking out upon the barren ocean with tears in his eyes, groaning and breaking his heart for sorrow. Calypso gave Mercury a seat and said: “Why have you come to see me, Mercury—honoured, and ever welcome—for you do not visit me often? Say what you want; I will do it for you at once if I can, and if it can be done at all; but come inside, and let me set refreshment before you.”
As she spoke she drew a table loaded with ambrosia beside him and mixed him some red nectar, so Mercury ate and drank till he had had enough, and then said:

“We are speaking god and goddess to one another, and you ask me why I have come here, and I will tell you truly as you would have me do. Jove sent me; it was no doing of mine; who could possibly want to come all this way over the sea where there are no cities full of people to offer me sacrifices or choice hecatombs? Nevertheless I had to come, for none of us other gods can cross Jove, nor transgress his orders. He says that you have here the most ill-starred of all those who fought nine years before the city of King Priam and sailed home in the tenth year after having sacked it. On their way home they sinned against Minerva, who raised both wind and waves against them, so that all his brave companions perished, and he alone was carried hither by wind and tide. Jove says that you are to let this man go at once, for it is decreed that he shall not perish here, far from his own people, but shall return to his house and country and see his friends again.”

Calypso trembled with rage when she heard this, “You gods,” she exclaimed, “ought to be ashamed of yourselves. You are always jealous and hate seeing a goddess take a fancy to a mortal man, and live with him in open matrimony. So when rosy-fingered Dawn made love to Orion, you precious gods were all of you furious till Diana went and killed him in Ortygia. So again when Ceres fell in love with Iasion, and yielded to him in a thrice-ploughed fallow field, Jove came to hear of it before so very long and killed Iasion with his thunderbolts. And now you are angry with me too because I have a man here. I found the poor creature sitting all alone astride of a keel, for Jove had struck his ship with lightning and sunk it in mid ocean, so that all his crew were drowned, while he himself was driven by wind and waves on to my island. I got fond of him and cherished him, and had set my heart on making him immortal, so that he should never grow old all his days; still I cannot cross Jove, nor bring his counsels to nothing; therefore, if he insists upon it, let the man go beyond the seas again; but I cannot send him anywhere myself for I have neither ships nor men who can take him. Nevertheless I will readily give him such advice, in all good faith, as will be likely to bring him safely to his own country.”
“Then send him away,” said Mercury, “or Jove will be angry with you and punish you”.

On this he took his leave, and Calypso went out to look for Ulysses, for she had heard Jove’s message. She found him sitting upon the beach with his eyes ever filled with tears, and dying of sheer home sickness; for he had got tired of Calypso, and though he was forced to sleep with her in the cave by night, it was she, not he, that would have it so. As for the day time, he spent it on the rocks and on the sea shore, weeping, crying aloud for his despair, and always looking out upon the sea. Calypso then went close up to him said:

“My poor fellow, you shall not stay here grieving and fretting your life out any longer. I am going to send you away of my own free will; so go, cut some beams of wood, and make yourself a large raft with an upper deck that it may carry you safely over the sea. I will put bread, wine, and water on board to save you from starving. I will also give you clothes, and will send you a fair wind to take you home, if the gods in heaven so will it—for they know more about these things, and can settle them better than I can.”

Ulysses shuddered as he heard her. “Now goddess,” he answered, “there is something behind all this; you cannot be really meaning to help me home when you bid me do such a dreadful thing as put to sea on a raft. Not even a well found ship with a fair wind could venture on such a distant voyage: nothing that you can say or do shall make me go on board a raft unless you first solemnly swear that you mean me no mischief.”

Calypso smiled at this and caressed him with her hand: “You know a great deal,” said she, “but you are quite wrong here. May heaven above and earth below be my witnesses, with the waters of the river Styx—and this is the most solemn oath which a blessed god can take—that I mean you no sort of harm, and am only advising you to do exactly what I should do myself in your place. I am dealing with you quite straightforwardly; my heart is not made of iron, and I am very sorry for you.”

When she had thus spoken she led the way rapidly before him, and Ulysses followed in her steps; so the pair, goddess and man, went on and on till they came to Calypso’s cave, where Ulysses took the seat that Mercury had just left. Calypso set meat and drink before him of the food that mortals eat; but her maids brought ambrosia and nectar for herself, and they laid their hands on the good things that were before them. When they had satisfied themselves with meat and drink, Calypso spoke, saying:

“Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, so you would start home to your own land at once? Good luck go with you, but if you could only know how much suffering is in store for you before you get back to your own country, you would stay where you are, keep house along with me, and let me make you immortal, no matter how anxious you may be to see this wife of yours, of whom you are thinking all the time day after day; yet I flatter myself that I am no whit less tall or well-looking than she is, for it is not to be expected that a mortal woman should compare in beauty with an immortal.”

“Goddess,” replied Ulysses, “do not be angry with me about this. I am quite aware that my wife Penelope is nothing like so tall or so beautiful as yourself. She is only a woman, whereas you are an immortal. Nevertheless, I want to get home, and can think of nothing else. If some god wrecks me when I am on the sea, I will bear it and make the best of it. I have had infinite trouble both by land and sea already, so let this go with the rest.”
Presently the sun set and it became dark, whereon the pair retired into the inner part of the cave and went to bed.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The gods decide
parts.context: Mount Olympus, the home of the gods. Athena ('Minerva'), who loves Odysseus, complains to Zeus ('Jove'). Hermes ('Mercury') is the gods' messenger; 'slayer of Argus' is one of his titles (not the dog of that name). Scheria is the land of the Phaeacians.
parts.plain: Athena tells the gods that Odysseus, a just and fatherly king, has been forgotten: he is stuck on Calypso's island and the suitors are plotting to kill his son. Zeus agrees that he must go home and sends Hermes to tell Calypso. Hermes flies over the sea like a seabird to her island.

commentary.on: there is not one of his subjects but has forgotten Ulysses, who ruled them as though he were their father
commentary.text: Athena's case for Odysseus is not only that he is clever. It is that he was a good king, who ruled like a father. The Odyssey cares about justice in a way the Iliad rarely does: the good are rescued, the wicked punished.

commentary.on: He is to be convoyed neither by gods nor men, but after a perilous voyage of twenty days upon a raft
commentary.text: Even rescued, Odysseus must save himself: on a raft, with his own strength and wits. The gods help those who keep going.

commentary.on: whose waves he skimmed like a cormorant that flies fishing every hole and corner of the ocean
commentary.text: Homer's similes, here a seabird diving for fish, bring the ordinary world into the world of the gods. The audience knew cormorants. They had never seen a god fly.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Calypso's island
parts.context: Ogygia, Calypso's island, far out in the sea. Calypso is a nymph, a minor goddess, who lives in a cave. Her name means something like 'she who hides'. Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the gods. Dawn, Orion, Ceres (Demeter) and Iasion are figures from older stories of goddesses who loved mortal men.
parts.plain: Calypso's cave is beautiful: a fire of cedar, vines, springs and meadows of violets. Hermes admires it. Odysseus is not there: he is on the shore, weeping and looking out to sea. Hermes gives Calypso Zeus's order. She is furious: the male gods always punish goddesses who love mortals. She saved Odysseus from the sea and wanted to make him immortal. But she cannot defy Zeus.

commentary.on: Even a god could not help being charmed with such a lovely spot
commentary.text: Calypso's island is paradise: warmth, fragrance, birds, water, flowers. Homer makes it as attractive as he can, so that we feel what Odysseus is giving up.

commentary.on: he was on the sea-shore as usual, looking out upon the barren ocean with tears in his eyes
commentary.text: The first time the poem shows us its hero, he is weeping on a beach. In paradise, he is homesick. Butler's 'barren' translates a word for the sea that cannot be harvested: the place of no home.

commentary.on: You are always jealous and hate seeing a goddess take a fancy to a mortal man
commentary.text: Calypso has a point. Zeus has loved many mortal women; the goddesses who loved mortal men were punished. Homer lets a goddess accuse the gods of a double standard.

commentary.on: had set my heart on making him immortal, so that he should never grow old all his days
commentary.text: Here is the offer: to be young and alive for ever. It is the thing every hero in the Iliad longed for and could not have. Sarpedon said he would not fight if he could escape death. Achilles fought because he could not.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: I want to get home
parts.context: Calypso goes to tell Odysseus he may leave. The river Styx, in the underworld, was the most solemn oath of the gods. The scene ends with the two going to bed for the last time: the poem is frank that he has been her lover, unwillingly.
parts.plain: Calypso finds Odysseus weeping and tells him to build a raft; she will help him. He suspects a trick and makes her swear she means no harm. She laughs, swears, and gives him supper. Then she tries once more: if he knew what suffering lies ahead, he would stay and become immortal; and surely she is more beautiful than his wife. He answers that he knows Penelope cannot compare with her, but he wants to go home, whatever it costs.

commentary.on: for he had got tired of Calypso, and though he was forced to sleep with her in the cave by night, it was she, not he, that would have it so
commentary.text: The poem is honest: Odysseus is a prisoner, and a goddess's love is not freely returned. Paradise without freedom is a prison.

commentary.on: nothing that you can say or do shall make me go on board a raft unless you first solemnly swear that you mean me no mischief
commentary.text: Even when he is offered what he longs for, Odysseus suspects a trap. His caution has kept him alive. It is mētis, the practical cunning that is his great quality.

commentary.on: but you are quite wrong here
commentary.text: Calypso smiles at him. She knows him well: always clever, always suspicious. The two have a real, if unequal, intimacy.

commentary.on: keep house along with me, and let me make you immortal, no matter how anxious you may be to see this wife of yours
commentary.text: The final offer: immortality, and a goddess. And a sting: you are thinking about her all the time. Calypso knows she has already lost.

commentary.on: I am quite aware that my wife Penelope is nothing like so tall or so beautiful as yourself. She is only a woman, whereas you are an immortal. Nevertheless, I want to get home, and can think of nothing else.
commentary.text: This is the centre of the Odyssey. Odysseus does not pretend that Penelope is a goddess. He admits that what he is choosing is less, by every outward measure: a mortal, ageing woman on a rocky island. He chooses it anyway, because it is his. The word 'nevertheless' carries a whole idea of love: not for the best, but for the one.

commentary.on: If some god wrecks me when I am on the sea, I will bear it and make the best of it.
commentary.text: Odysseus' other great quality: endurance. One of his titles in Greek is polytlas, 'much-enduring'. He chooses suffering and home over ease and exile. Two days later, the sea god will wreck his raft.

paras: This was what they said, but they did not know what it was that had been happening. The upper servant Eurynome washed and anointed Ulysses in his own house and gave him a shirt and cloak, while Minerva made him look taller and stronger than before; she also made the hair grow thick on the top of his head, and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms; she glorified him about the head and shoulders just as a skilful workman who has studied art of all kinds under Vulcan or Minerva—and his work is full of beauty—enriches a piece of silver plate by gilding it. He came from the bath looking like one of the immortals, and sat down opposite his wife on the seat he had left. “My dear,” said he, “heaven has endowed you with a heart more unyielding than woman ever yet had. No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he had come back to her after twenty years of absence, and after having gone through so much. But come, nurse, get a bed ready for me; I will sleep alone, for this woman has a heart as hard as iron.”

“My dear,” answered Penelope, “I have no wish to set myself up, nor to depreciate you; but I am not struck by your appearance, for I very well remember what kind of a man you were when you set sail from Ithaca. Nevertheless, Euryclea, take his bed outside the bed chamber that he himself built. Bring the bed outside this room, and put bedding upon it with fleeces, good coverlets, and blankets.”

She said this to try him, but Ulysses was very angry and said, “Wife, I am much displeased at what you have just been saying. Who has been taking my bed from the place in which I left it? He must have found it a hard task, no matter how skilled a workman he was, unless some god came and helped him to shift it. There is no man living, however strong and in his prime, who could move it from its place, for it is a marvellous curiosity which I made with my very own hands. There was a young olive growing within the precincts of the house, in full vigour, and about as thick as a bearing-post. I built my room round this with strong walls of stone and a roof to cover them, and I made the doors strong and well-fitting. Then I cut off the top boughs of the olive tree and left the stump standing. This I dressed roughly from the root upwards and then worked with carpenter’s tools well and skilfully, straightening my work by drawing a line on the wood, and making it into a bed-prop. I then bored a hole down the middle, and made it the centre-post of my bed, at which I worked till I had finished it, inlaying it with gold and silver; after this I stretched a hide of crimson leather from one side of it to the other. So you see I know all about it, and I desire to learn whether it is still there, or whether any one has been removing it by cutting down the olive tree at its roots.”

When she heard the sure proofs Ulysses now gave her, she fairly broke down. She flew weeping to his side, flung her arms about his neck, and kissed him. “Do not be angry with me Ulysses,” she cried, “you, who are the wisest of mankind. We have suffered, both of us. Heaven has denied us the happiness of spending our youth, and of growing old, together; do not then be aggrieved or take it amiss that I did not embrace you thus as soon as I saw you. I have been shuddering all the time through fear that someone might come here and deceive me with a lying story; for there are many very wicked people going about. Jove’s daughter Helen would never have yielded herself to a man from a foreign country, if she had known that the sons of Achaeans would come after her and bring her back. Heaven put it in her heart to do wrong, and she gave no thought to that sin, which has been the source of all our sorrows. Now, however, that you have convinced me by showing that you know all about our bed (which no human being has ever seen but you and I and a single maidservant, the daughter of Actor, who was given me by my father on my marriage, and who keeps the doors of our room) hard of belief though I have been I can mistrust no longer.”

Then Ulysses in his turn melted, and wept as he clasped his dear and faithful wife to his bosom. As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming towards the shore, when Neptune has wrecked their ship with the fury of his winds and waves; a few alone reach the land, and these, covered with brine, are thankful when they find themselves on firm ground and out of danger—even so was her husband welcome to her as she looked upon him, and she could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck. Indeed they would have gone on indulging their sorrow till rosy-fingered morn appeared, had not Minerva determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west, while she would not suffer Dawn to leave Oceanus, nor to yoke the two steeds Lampus and Phaethon that bear her onward to break the day upon mankind.
