parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Penelope's test
parts.context: The palace on Ithaca. Odysseus has killed the suitors, and the old nurse has told Penelope that the beggar was her husband. She does not believe it. Eurynome and Euryclea are servants. Athena ('Minerva') makes Odysseus look young again.
parts.plain: Odysseus, bathed and handsome, sits opposite Penelope and complains that she is hard-hearted. He asks for a bed to sleep alone. Penelope tells the nurse to move the bed he built out of their bedroom. Odysseus explodes: no one could move that bed, because he built it round a living olive tree, with the trunk as one of its posts. He describes exactly how he made it.

commentary.on: this woman has a heart as hard as iron
commentary.text: The phrase Hector used of Achilles, and Achilles of Priam. Here it is a husband's frustration with a wife who will not believe him. But Penelope's 'iron' is not cruelty. It is the caution that kept her faithful for twenty years.

commentary.on: take his bed outside the bed chamber that he himself built
commentary.text: Her test is a trick worthy of Odysseus himself. She speaks as if the bed could be moved. Only the real Odysseus would know that it cannot.

commentary.on: I built my room round this with strong walls of stone and a roof to cover them
commentary.text: The bed is the heart of the house, and the house was built round it. It is rooted in the earth, a living tree. It is the poem's image of their marriage: made by his own hands, unmovable, known only to the two of them.

commentary.on: or whether any one has been removing it by cutting down the olive tree at its roots
commentary.text: Odysseus' anger gives him away. The man who can lie about everything cannot hide his fear that the marriage, the rooted thing, has been cut. Penelope has outwitted the cleverest man in Greece.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Like land to a swimmer
parts.context: Penelope's response. Helen, whose story began the war, is mentioned as the wife who was not faithful.
parts.plain: Penelope breaks down and throws her arms round him. She explains that she was afraid of being deceived by a stranger. Now she believes. Odysseus weeps and holds her. She is as glad of him as shipwrecked sailors are of the shore. Athena holds back the dawn to give them a longer night.

commentary.on: We have suffered, both of us. Heaven has denied us the happiness of spending our youth, and of growing old, together
commentary.text: The Odyssey's great theme in one sentence. The war took twenty years from both of them. What they have now is not youth but the rest of a mortal life together.

commentary.on: I have been shuddering all the time through fear that someone might come here and deceive me with a lying story
commentary.text: Penelope's caution mirrors his. Odysseus tested everyone in disguise; she tested him. The poem calls such a marriage homophrosynē elsewhere (VI.183): being of one mind.

commentary.on: As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming towards the shore, when Neptune has wrecked their ship
commentary.text: The simile describes Odysseus's own experience, the shipwreck after leaving Calypso. But it is applied to Penelope. She too has been at sea for twenty years. The two survivors reach land in each other.

commentary.on: had not Minerva determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west
commentary.text: The goddess stops the sun for a married couple. In the Iliad the gods fought over heroes on a battlefield. Here a goddess's greatest gift is a longer night for husband and wife.

compare.author: Homer
compare.why: Odysseus refused a goddess for a mortal wife. Twenty years on, home at last, he finds that she will not simply take him back. Read how Penelope tests him.
compare.title: The bed

paras: The Greeks had a word, nostos, for the return home from war, and a whole group of poems, now lost, about the homecomings of the heroes from Troy. Most were stories of disaster. Agamemnon got home and was murdered in his bath by his wife and her lover. Ajax the Lesser drowned. Menelaus wandered for years. The Odyssey alludes to them all, as a dark background to its own story of a homecoming that succeeds. Our English word 'nostalgia' was made from it in 1688, by a Swiss medical student, for the sickness of homesickness: nostos plus algos, pain.

So the Odyssey's question is the opposite of the Iliad's. The Iliad asks what is worth dying for. The Odyssey asks what is worth living for, and answers: home. Not a place only, but a household, a wife, a son, an old father, a dog, a bed, servants who stayed loyal, a land you can kiss.
sections.key: Nostos, homecoming, was the subject of many Greek poems, most of them tragic. The Odyssey asks what is worth living for, and answers: home.

paras: Odysseus is the only hero in Greek poetry who is offered immortality and turns it down. Why? The French classicist Jean-Pierre Vernant, in an essay called 'The Refusal of Odysseus', suggested an answer in our own words: to stay with Calypso would be to vanish. Her name means 'she who hides'. On her island, out of all stories, Odysseus would live for ever but be nobody: no past, no future, no name in anyone's song. To be human, for the Odyssey, is to be mortal, with a particular past, particular loves and a place in the world.

Set this beside Achilles. Achilles could have had a long life and chose a short one, for undying glory. Odysseus could have had an undying life and chose a mortal one, for love and home. Both refuse the long, empty life. Both choose a human life with meaning. But they place the meaning differently: Achilles in what is sung of him after death, Odysseus in the people he lives among.
sections.key: Odysseus refuses immortality because it would make him nobody; he chooses a mortal life with a name, a past and people he loves.

paras: If Achilles' excellence is strength, Odysseus's is mētis: practical intelligence, cunning, the ability to find a way out. He devised the wooden horse. He escaped the Cyclops by telling him his name was 'Nobody', so that when the blinded giant called for help, he shouted 'Nobody is killing me!' (IX.366–414). He has himself tied to the mast to hear the Sirens without dying. Again and again he survives by lying, disguising himself, waiting.

His other quality is endurance. Homer calls him 'much-enduring' and 'much-suffering'. He loses everything: his ships, his men, twenty years of his life. He goes on. Mētis and endurance together make a new kind of heroism, one that suits not the battlefield but ordinary life, where most of our problems cannot be solved by force. That is part of why later ages loved him: from Tennyson's old Ulysses, still setting out, to James Joyce's Ulysses (1922), which turned a day in the life of an ordinary Dublin man into an Odyssey.
sections.key: Odysseus' excellence is mētis, cunning, and endurance: a heroism for ordinary life, where force rarely solves anything.

paras: Penelope is not a prize waiting to be won. She is as clever as her husband. She invented the trick of the weaving and kept a hundred suitors waiting for three years. When the beggar comes, she half-recognises him and sets up the contest of the bow (XIX–XXI), which only Odysseus can win. And she tests him with the bed, and wins. The poem calls her 'circumspect' or 'wise' again and again.

In Book VI Odysseus wishes the young princess Nausicaa a husband and a home and, best of all, homophrosynē: a man and woman 'of one mind' in their home, a grief to their enemies and a joy to their friends (VI.180–185). That is what he and Penelope have. Samuel Butler, our translator, was so struck by the women of the poem that he argued in The Authoress of the Odyssey (1897) that it was written by a young woman in Sicily. Few scholars agree, but his question was a good one: why does this poem take its women so seriously?
sections.key: Penelope matches Odysseus in cunning and faithfulness; their marriage is homophrosynē, being of one mind. Butler even thought a woman wrote the poem.

paras: The Odyssey is a poem about hospitality. Every place Odysseus comes to is a test of xenia, the bond between host and guest that you met in session 4. The Phaeacians are perfect hosts: they feed him, honour him and sail him home with gifts. The Cyclops is the worst host imaginable: he eats his guests. The suitors are the worst guests: they eat their absent host's wealth and abuse the beggar at his door, not knowing he is the master of the house.

This gives the Odyssey a moral world clearer than the Iliad's. At its beginning Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for troubles they bring on themselves by their own wickedness (I.32–43). The suitors are warned, and ignore the warnings. When Odysseus kills them, the poem presents it as justice, the punishment of those who broke the laws of Zeus of strangers. In the Odyssey, unlike the Iliad, the gods seem to care how people behave.
sections.key: The Odyssey tests everyone by xenia: perfect hosts, a cannibal host, guests who devour their host. Its gods punish the wicked, as the Iliad's rarely do.

sections.h: The dark side of the homecoming
paras: The homecoming is not gentle. Odysseus and his son kill all the suitors in the hall, more than a hundred young men, though some beg for mercy (Book XXII). Then Telemachus hangs twelve slave women who had slept with the suitors, and the disloyal goatherd is mutilated (XXII.465–477). Homer presents this as just punishment. Many modern readers find it horrifying, and Margaret Atwood retold the story from the side of the hanged maids in The Penelopiad (2005).

It is right to see this clearly. The Odyssey's justice is real but harsh, and its mercy is narrow. The household is restored by a massacre. Only in the last book does Athena stop the killing, when the suitors' families come for revenge, and impose a peace (XXIV.528–548). The Odyssey reaches a world of home and order. It does not reach a world of forgiveness. Keep this in mind for the case against Homer, which comes next.
sections.key: The homecoming ends in a massacre of the suitors and the hanging of twelve slave women: the Odyssey's justice is real but harsh, and its mercy narrow.

paras: Odysseus does not come home only to Penelope. The Odyssey takes great care over the people who kept faith while he was away: the swineherd Eumaeus, a slave who shares his little food with a beggar he does not recognise (XIV); the old nurse Euryclea, who knows him by a scar on his leg as she washes his feet (XIX.386–475); his old father Laertes, digging in his orchard in rags (XXIV); and the dog Argus, who knows him at once, wags his tail and dies (XVII.290–327).

These are among the poem's most loved scenes, and they say something new. Greatness in the Odyssey is not only in kings and goddesses. It is in the loyalty of a pig-keeper and the memory of a dog. A home is made of such faithfulness, and the poem honours it as warmly as any deed at Troy.
sections.key: The Odyssey honours the faithful household, the swineherd, the nurse, the old father and the dog: greatness in loyalty, not only in kings.

refs: Homer, Odyssey I.32–43; II.93–110; V.1–227; VI.180–185; VII.259; IX.366–414; XXII; XXIII.153–240; XXIV.528–548. Tr. Samuel Butler (1900).

debate.question: Is Odysseus a hero or a con man?

positions.name: A hero of intelligence
positions.who: The Odyssey itself and Athena; Tennyson; many modern readers
positions.view: Odysseus shows that wit, patience and endurance are as heroic as strength. He keeps his men alive as long as he can, refuses a goddess for his wife, and restores justice to his home. He is the model of a mind that will not give up.
positions.evidence: His refusal of Calypso; the Cyclops escape; Athena's love for him; Zeus calling him the wisest of mortals (I.65–67).

positions.name: A liar and manipulator
positions.who: Sophocles (Philoctetes, 409 BC); Euripides; Virgil (Aeneid II, 'cruel Ulysses'); Dante (Inferno XXVI)
positions.view: Later Greeks and Romans saw the darker side of mētis: Odysseus lies, tricks and betrays, and loses all his men. Dante put him in hell among the fraudulent counsellors for the trick of the wooden horse and for leading his men to their deaths.
positions.evidence: His lying tales; the death of all his crew; the massacre of the suitors and the maids; his tricking of Philoctetes in Sophocles' play.

positions.name: Neither: a human being
positions.who: Many recent scholars
positions.view: The Odyssey shows a man whose gifts can be used well or badly. His cunning saves his life and also costs his men theirs. The poem lets us admire and doubt him, and that complexity is why he has lasted.
positions.evidence: The opening's admission that 'he could not save his men'; the poem's mixture of tenderness and cruelty.

debate.agree: All agree that Odysseus is a new kind of hero, whose greatness is in his mind and his endurance rather than in strength, and that his cunning has a dark side.

look.why: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres painted this study of Ulysses, the Roman name for Odysseus, in 1827. It is not a scene from the poem but a portrait of the hero himself.
points: The man's upper body and face are seen from below, in profile, facing the right side of the painting.
He has a long, straight nose, a thick dark beard and curly dark hair.
A yellow helmet sits tipped upward on top of his head.
He wears a warm reddish-orange garment, and his left hand, in shadow, is clenched against his chest.
The background is a muted blend of yellows and greens; the signature 'Ingres' is in the lower right corner.

music.why: John Tavener's Song for Athene was written in memory of a young woman named Athene, and sets words of rest and homecoming from the Orthodox funeral service over a single held note. Hear it as music of arrival, after a long voyage.

think.why: Odysseus chooses not the most beautiful but his own: this particular wife, this home. See in brief how the West came to believe that each single person counts.

learn.why: When Odysseus comes home disguised, the first to know him is his old dog, who has waited twenty years. Note that this piece is in Alexander Pope's verse translation (1726), not Butler's prose.

check.q: Why does Homer make Calypso's island so beautiful?
options: Because the gods wanted to reward him
Because it is where Odysseus was born
To show that Calypso is wicked
So that we feel what Odysseus is giving up when he chooses home
check.why: Paradise makes the choice real: he is turning down ease, beauty and immortality. Calypso is not shown as wicked; she is honest and even kind.

check.q: Odysseus admits that Penelope is less beautiful than Calypso. What does this admission add to his choice?
options: It shows he is lying to Calypso to escape
It shows he does not love Penelope
It shows that he chooses Penelope not because she is the best by any outward measure, but because she is his: love for the one, not the best
It shows that he is afraid of Calypso
check.why: 'Nevertheless, I want to get home': he admits the comparison and chooses anyway. That is what makes the choice an act of love.

check.q: How does Odysseus' choice compare with Achilles' choice in session 2?
options: Both choose to go home
Both choose glory over life
Achilles chooses a short life for undying glory; Odysseus chooses a mortal life over an undying one, for love and home: both refuse an empty life, but place meaning differently
Achilles chooses immortality and Odysseus refuses it
check.why: The two heroes face mirror-image choices. Achilles was never offered immortality, so the last option is wrong.

check.q: Why is Penelope's test of the bed so clever?
options: Because she has asked the nurse to watch his face
Because only the real Odysseus would know that the bed cannot be moved, being built round a living olive tree, and his anger proves it
Because she knows the bed is broken
Because Athena told her what to say
check.why: The bed's secret is known only to the two of them and one servant. Odysseus' outburst gives him away.

check.q: What makes the Odyssey's moral world different from the Iliad's?
options: In the Odyssey everyone is forgiven
The Iliad's gods punish the wicked and the Odyssey's do not
The Odyssey has no gods in it
In the Odyssey the gods seem to care how people behave, and the breakers of hospitality are punished
check.why: Zeus's complaint in Book I, the suitors' warnings and their punishment show a world of justice. But it is not a world of forgiveness: the suitors and maids are killed.

check.q: Which is the best objection to reading the Odyssey as a simple story of love and home?
options: That the homecoming is achieved by a massacre of the suitors and the hanging of twelve slave women, presented as justice
That Penelope marries one of the suitors
That Odysseus never really reaches Ithaca
That Calypso is the real heroine
check.why: Book XXII is brutal. The home is restored, but by a justice that is harsh and a mercy that is narrow.

tutorial.question: 'Glory or home?' Compare the choices of Achilles and Odysseus.
tutorial.approach: Set out Achilles' two fates (Iliad IX) and Calypso's offer (Odyssey V). Explain kleos and nostos. Ask what each hero gains and loses by his choice, and what each thinks gives a life meaning. Use Penelope to show what Odysseus' choice is for. Do not forget the dark side of both poems. End with your own view: which is the better life, and is there a third answer neither poem gives?
strong: Explains the two fates and kleos aphthiton accurately.
Explains Calypso's offer and why refusing immortality is unique.
Uses 'nevertheless, I want to get home' to show the nature of Odysseus' love.
Explains nostos, mētis and Penelope's equal cleverness.
Notes that both heroes reject a long, empty life, but place meaning differently.
Acknowledges the massacre in Book XXII and the limits of the Odyssey's justice.

reading.title: The Odyssey
reading.why: A clear, fast modern verse translation, the first into English by a woman; read it beside Butler.

reading.why: How the Odyssey has been retold, from antiquity to film.

reading.title: Disguise and Recognition in the Odyssey
reading.why: On the poem's tests and recognitions, Penelope's above all.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do one ordinary, faithful thing for the people you live with that no one will notice or praise: mend something, cook a meal they love, write a note. Do it as Odysseus chose Penelope: not because it is glorious, but because they are yours.
sessions.reflect: What, for you, is home? What would you refuse, even immortality, to keep it?
takeaways: Odysseus refuses Calypso's offer of immortality to go home to a mortal, ageing wife: 'nevertheless, I want to get home'.
His greatness is mētis and endurance, and Penelope is his equal in both; their marriage is homophrosynē, being of one mind.
The Odyssey's world has more justice than the Iliad's, but its homecoming ends in a massacre: home and order, not yet forgiveness.

sessions.title: The case against: were the gods any good, and is glory worth it?
sessions.line: Among the dead, Achilles says he would rather be a poor man's servant than king of all the ghosts. Three centuries later Plato says Homer's gods are liars and his heroes poor models, and wants the poems censored. The case against Homer's world, at full strength.
sessions.plain: This journey has admired Homer: the honesty of the Iliad, the mercy in Achilles' hut, Odysseus' faithful choice. Now hear the case against. It comes first from Homer himself: in the Odyssey, the ghost of Achilles says that glory is worthless beside life. Then from the Greek philosophers, above all Plato, who said that Homer's gods lie, cheat and quarrel, that his heroes weep and despair, and that the poems should not be taught to the young. Put at its strongest, the charge is this: Homer's world has courage and pity, but its gods are not good and its glory is hollow.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 5 followed both poems to their endings and found greatness in them: honour, glory, mercy, home. Before we can say what Homer gave the West, we have to face the strongest reasons to think his picture of greatness is wrong. The objection comes here, after you have read enough Homer to weigh it.
answers: Was glory worth it, by the heroes' own account?
Were the Greek gods good?
Why did Plato want to censor Homer?
What is the strongest case against Homer's idea of a great life?
sessions.finding: Homer's own Achilles repudiates glory among the dead, and Plato charged that Homer's gods are neither good nor truthful; the strongest charge is that Homer's world has courage and pity but no goodness at the top and no mercy beyond the tent.

paras: The Iliad opened with Achilles' anger over his honour (session 1). Achilles weighed glory against a long life and doubted the code (session 2). At the height of his glory he was at his most inhuman, dragging Hector's body (session 3). The poem ended with mercy between enemies, a truce and not yet forgiveness (session 4). In the Odyssey, Odysseus refused immortality to go home, and found home restored by a harsh justice (session 5).

Through all of it, the gods have been there: Athena pulling Achilles' hair, Zeus weighing deaths, Athena tricking Hector, Calypso protesting, Athena stopping the dawn. And through all of it, the heroes have lived by one belief: that death is the end of anything worth having, and glory is all that survives it. This session asks whether either the gods or the glory deserve the place Homer gives them.
background.key: The journey has found honour, glory, mercy and home in Homer. Behind them stand the gods and the belief that only glory survives death: now both are tested.

paras: In Book XI of the Odyssey, Odysseus, on Circe's instructions, sails to the edge of the world and calls up the dead. He digs a pit and pours in the blood of sacrificed sheep; the ghosts come up and must drink before they can speak. He meets the prophet Tiresias, and the ghost of his own mother, who died of grief while he was away: three times he tries to hold her, and three times she slips through his arms like a shadow (XI.204–208). He meets Agamemnon, murdered by his wife on his return. Then come Achilles and his friends.

Homer's Hades is not heaven or hell. It is a dim, joyless place where all the dead go, good and bad alike, as shadows without strength or understanding. This is the background to the whole heroic code: if this is what waits for everyone, glory in the memory of the living is the only kind of survival worth having.
background.key: In Odyssey XI Odysseus calls up the dead with blood. Homer's Hades is a dim place where all go as shadows, which is why glory mattered so much.

paras: The first known critic of Homer's gods was Xenophanes of Colophon (about 570–475 BC), a wandering poet-philosopher. Next came Heraclitus of Ephesus (about 500 BC). The greatest was Plato (about 428–348 BC), an Athenian aristocrat, pupil of Socrates, who founded the Academy, the first school of philosophy. His Republic, written around 375 BC, is a long conversation in which Socrates and two young men, Glaucon and Adeimantus (Plato's own brothers), design an ideal city in order to discover what justice is.

In Books II and III they ask how the city's guardians should be educated. In Greece, education meant Homer. So Socrates goes through the poems and asks which stories are fit to be taught. His answer is the most famous attack on Homer ever written. You will read it in Benjamin Jowett's translation (1871), the classic Victorian English Plato.

background.key: Xenophanes, Heraclitus and above all Plato's Republic (c. 375 BC) attacked Homer's gods and heroes as unfit to educate the young.

paras: The main reading is Achilles' ghost in Odyssey XI, and the silent ghost of Ajax. It answers the question 'was glory worth it?' in the words of the greatest hero himself. The comparison is Plato's charge from Republic II and III: that Homer's gods are made the authors of evil, and his heroes taught to fear death and weep. It answers the question 'were the gods any good?'. The objection is given here without reply. The replies come in the debate.
background.key: Achilles' ghost judges glory; Plato judges the gods. The case is stated before any reply.

before: What does Odysseus say to comfort Achilles, and how does Achilles answer?
What does Achilles ask about, and what makes him happy at the end?
List Plato's charges against Homer. Which do you find strongest?
sessions.readWhy: Achilles' ghost says what glory is worth among the dead, and Ajax's ghost will not speak.

paras: “As we two sat weeping and talking thus sadly with one another the ghost of Achilles came up to us with Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax who was the finest and goodliest man of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus. The fleet descendant of Aeacus knew me and spoke piteously, saying, ‘Ulysses, noble son of Laertes, what deed of daring will you undertake next, that you venture down to the house of Hades among us silly dead, who are but the ghosts of them that can labour no more?’

“And I said, ‘Achilles, son of Peleus, foremost champion of the Achaeans, I came to consult Teiresias, and see if he could advise me about my return home to Ithaca, for I have never yet been able to get near the Achaean land, nor to set foot in my own country, but have been in trouble all the time. As for you, Achilles, no one was ever yet so fortunate as you have been, nor ever will be, for you were adored by all us Argives as long as you were alive, and now that you are here you are a great prince among the dead. Do not, therefore, take it so much to heart even if you are dead.’

“‘Say not a word,’ he answered, ‘in death’s favour; I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man’s house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead. But give me news about my son; is he gone to the wars and will he be a great soldier, or is this not so? Tell me also if you have heard anything about my father Peleus—does he still rule among the Myrmidons, or do they show him no respect throughout Hellas and Phthia now that he is old and his limbs fail him? Could I but stand by his side, in the light of day, with the same strength that I had when I killed the bravest of our foes upon the plain of Troy—could I but be as I then was and go even for a short time to my father’s house, any one who tried to do him violence or supersede him would soon rue it.’

“‘I have heard nothing,’ I answered, ‘of Peleus, but I can tell you all about your son Neoptolemus, for I took him in my own ship from Scyros with the Achaeans. In our councils of war before Troy he was always first to speak, and his judgement was unerring. Nestor and I were the only two who could surpass him; and when it came to fighting on the plain of Troy, he would never remain with the body of his men, but would dash on far in front, foremost of them all in valour. Many a man did he kill in battle—I cannot name every single one of those whom he slew while fighting on the side of the Argives, but will only say how he killed that valiant hero Eurypylus son of Telephus, who was the handsomest man I ever saw except Memnon; many others also of the Ceteians fell around him by reason of a woman’s bribes. Moreover, when all the bravest of the Argives went inside the horse that Epeus had made, and it was left to me to settle when we should either open the door of our ambuscade, or close it, though all the other leaders and chief men among the Danaans were drying their eyes and quaking in every limb, I never once saw him turn pale nor wipe a tear from his cheek; he was all the time urging me to break out from the horse—grasping the handle of his sword and his bronze-shod spear, and breathing fury against the foe. Yet when we had sacked the city of Priam he got his handsome share of the prize money and went on board (such is the fortune of war) without a wound upon him, neither from a thrown spear nor in close combat, for the rage of Mars is a matter of great chance.’
“When I had told him this, the ghost of Achilles strode off across a meadow full of asphodel, exulting over what I had said concerning the prowess of his son.

“The ghosts of other dead men stood near me and told me each his own melancholy tale; but that of Ajax son of Telamon alone held aloof—still angry with me for having won the cause in our dispute about the armour of Achilles. Thetis had offered it as a prize, but the Trojan prisoners and Minerva were the judges. Would that I had never gained the day in such a contest, for it cost the life of Ajax, who was foremost of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus, alike in stature and prowess.

“When I saw him I tried to pacify him and said, ‘Ajax, will you not forget and forgive even in death, but must the judgement about that hateful armour still rankle with you? It cost us Argives dear enough to lose such a tower of strength as you were to us. We mourned you as much as we mourned Achilles son of Peleus himself, nor can the blame be laid on anything but on the spite which Jove bore against the Danaans, for it was this that made him counsel your destruction—come hither, therefore, bring your proud spirit into subjection, and hear what I can tell you.’

“He would not answer, but turned away to Erebus and to the other ghosts; nevertheless, I should have made him talk to me in spite of his being so angry, or I should have gone on talking to him, only that there were still others among the dead whom I desired to see.

parts.author: Homer

parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: Better a servant above ground
parts.context: Odysseus is telling his story to the Phaeacians. At the edge of the world, among the dead, he has just spoken with Agamemnon's ghost. 'The son of Peleus' and 'descendant of Aeacus' are Achilles; Patroclus, Antilochus and Ajax were his friends. Neoptolemus is Achilles' son, who fought at Troy after his father's death. Mars is Ares, god of war.
parts.plain: Achilles' ghost asks Odysseus why he has dared to come among the dead. Odysseus says he came for advice, and tells Achilles he should not grieve: he was honoured like a god in life and is a great prince among the dead. Achilles answers that he would rather be a poor man's paid servant on earth than king of all the dead. He asks about his son and his father. Odysseus tells him his son was a brave fighter at Troy, and Achilles strides away across the meadow, happy.

commentary.on: among us silly dead, who are but the ghosts of them that can labour no more
commentary.text: 'Silly' here means senseless, without mind. The greatest hero of all now speaks of himself as one of the witless dead. This is Homer's Hades: not punishment, just emptiness.

commentary.on: no one was ever yet so fortunate as you have been, nor ever will be, for you were adored by all us Argives as long as you were alive, and now that you are here you are a great prince among the dead
commentary.text: Odysseus offers the heroic code's consolation: you had honour in life and you have rank in death. It is exactly the bargain Achilles chose in the Iliad, and exactly what he made his choice for.

commentary.on: I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead
commentary.text: Achilles rejects it utterly. A 'paid servant' in a poor man's house was close to the lowest thing a free man could be, a landless labourer. Achilles, who chose glory over a long life, now says he would take the lowest life on earth over all the glory in Hades. This is the strongest objection to the heroic code ever written, and Homer wrote it.

commentary.on: could I but be as I then was and go even for a short time to my father's house, any one who tried to do him violence or supersede him would soon rue it
commentary.text: Look at what he still wants: to protect his father. In death, what Achilles longs for is not glory but the chance to care for the old man he left. The Iliad's last book, where he saw Peleus in Priam, is not far away.

commentary.on: exulting over what I had said concerning the prowess of his son
commentary.text: And yet. When he hears his son is a great warrior, Achilles strides off happy. The code is not quite dead in him. Glory is worthless for himself, but he still rejoices in it for his son. Homer gives us both, and lets us decide which is the last word.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The silence of Ajax
parts.context: Ajax, son of Telamon, was the greatest Greek warrior after Achilles. After Achilles' death, Odysseus and Ajax competed for his armour, and the judges gave it to Odysseus. Ajax, shamed, killed himself. Erebus is the darkness of the underworld.
parts.plain: All the other ghosts tell their stories, but Ajax keeps away, still angry about the contest for Achilles' armour. Odysseus wishes he had never won it, and begs Ajax to forgive him, even in death. Ajax turns away without a word into the darkness.

commentary.on: still angry with me for having won the cause in our dispute about the armour of Achilles
commentary.text: Ajax died for honour. He lost a prize, the armour, and could not bear the shame. It is the Iliad's quarrel over a prize again, and this time it ended in suicide.

commentary.on: Would that I had never gained the day in such a contest, for it cost the life of Ajax
commentary.text: Odysseus, now, sees what honour cost: a friend's life for a suit of armour. He has learned something the code cannot teach.

commentary.on: will you not forget and forgive even in death
commentary.text: The word 'forgive' appears here, at the edge of the world. Odysseus asks for it. It is the nearest the poems come to the idea.

commentary.on: He would not answer, but turned away to Erebus and to the other ghosts
commentary.text: Ajax refuses. His silence is one of the most famous moments in ancient literature: honour wounded beyond healing, even after death. In Homer's world, forgiveness can be asked for, but there is nothing to make it happen.

read.author: Homer
read.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
read.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC

paras: Those, I said, which are narrated by Homer and Hesiod, and the rest of the poets, who have ever been the great story-tellers of mankind.
But which stories do you mean, he said; and what fault do you find with them?
A fault which is most serious, I said; the fault of telling a lie, and, what is more, a bad lie.
But when is this fault committed?
Whenever an erroneous representation is made of the nature of gods and heroes,—as when a painter paints a portrait not having the shadow of a likeness to the original.
Yes, he said, that sort of thing is certainly very blameable; but what are the stories which you mean?

First of all, I said, there was that greatest of all lies in high places, which the poet told about Uranus, and which was a bad lie too,—I mean what Hesiod says that Uranus did, and how Cronus retaliated on him. The doings of Cronus, and the sufferings which in turn his son inflicted upon him, even if they were true, ought certainly not to be lightly told to young and thoughtless persons; if possible, they had better be buried in silence. But if there is an absolute necessity for their mention, a chosen few might hear them in a mystery, and they should sacrifice not a common (Eleusinian) pig, but some huge and unprocurable victim; and then the number of the hearers will be very few indeed.
Why, yes, said he, those stories are extremely objectionable.

Yes, Adeimantus, they are stories not to be repeated in our State; the young man should not be told that in committing the worst of crimes he is far from doing anything outrageous; and that even if he chastises his father when he does wrong, in whatever manner, he will only be following the example of the first and greatest among the gods.
I entirely agree with you, he said; in my opinion those stories are quite unfit to be repeated.

Neither, if we mean our future guardians to regard the habit of quarrelling among themselves as of all things the basest, should any word be said to them of the wars in heaven, and of the plots and fightings of the gods against one another, for they are not true. No, we shall never mention the battles of the giants, or let them be embroidered on garments; and we shall be silent about the innumerable other quarrels of gods and heroes with their friends and relatives. If they would only believe us we would tell them that quarrelling is unholy, and that never up to this time has there been any quarrel between citizens; this is what old men and old women should begin by telling children; and when they grow up, the poets also should be told to compose for them in a similar spirit. But the narrative of Hephaestus binding Here his mother, or how on another occasion Zeus sent him flying for taking her part when she was being beaten, and all the battles of the gods in Homer—these tales must not be admitted into our State, whether they are supposed to have an allegorical meaning or not. For a young person cannot judge what is allegorical and what is literal; anything that he receives into his mind at that age is likely to become indelible and unalterable; and therefore it is most important that the tales which the young first hear should be models of virtuous thoughts.

Then God, if he be good, is not the author of all things, as the many assert, but he is the cause of a few things only, and not of most things that occur to men. For few are the goods of human life, and many are the evils, and the good is to be attributed to God alone; of the evils the causes are to be sought elsewhere, and not in him.
That appears to me to be most true, he said.
Then we must not listen to Homer or to any other poet who is guilty of the folly of saying that two casks
‘Lie at the threshold of Zeus, full of lots, one of good, the other of evil lots,’
and that he to whom Zeus gives a mixture of the two
‘Sometimes meets with evil fortune, at other times with good;’
but that he to whom is given the cup of unmingled ill,
‘Him wild hunger drives o’er the beauteous earth.’
And again—
‘Zeus, who is the dispenser of good and evil to us.’

And if any one asserts that the violation of oaths and treaties, which was really the work of Pandarus, was brought about by Athene and Zeus, or that the strife and contention of the gods was instigated by Themis and Zeus, he shall not have our approval; neither will we allow our young men to hear the words of Aeschylus, that
‘God plants guilt among men when he desires utterly to destroy a house.’

And if a poet writes of the sufferings of Niobe—the subject of the tragedy in which these iambic verses occur—or of the house of Pelops, or of the Trojan war or on any similar theme, either we must not permit him to say that these are the works of God, or if they are of God, he must devise some explanation of them such as we are seeking; he must say that God did what was just and right, and they were the better for being punished; but that those who are punished are miserable, and that God is the author of their misery—the poet is not to be permitted to say; though he may say that the wicked are miserable because they require to be punished, and are benefited by receiving punishment from God; but that God being good is the author of evil to any one is to be strenuously denied, and not to be said or sung or heard in verse or prose by any one whether old or young in any well-ordered commonwealth. Such a fiction is suicidal, ruinous, impious.
I agree with you, he replied, and am ready to give my assent to the law.

Such then, I said, are our principles of theology—some tales are to be told, and others are not to be told to our disciples from their youth upwards, if we mean them to honour the gods and their parents, and to value friendship with one another.
Yes; and I think that our principles are right, he said.

But if they are to be courageous, must they not learn other lessons besides these, and lessons of such a kind as will take away the fear of death? Can any man be courageous who has the fear of death in him?
Certainly not, he said.
And can he be fearless of death, or will he choose death in battle rather than defeat and slavery, who believes the world below to be real and terrible?
Impossible.

Then we must assume a control over the narrators of this class of tales as well as over the others, and beg them not simply to revile but rather to commend the world below, intimating to them that their descriptions are untrue, and will do harm to our future warriors.
That will be our duty, he said.
Then, I said, we shall have to obliterate many obnoxious passages, beginning with the verses,
‘I would rather be a serf on the land of a poor and portionless man than rule over all the dead who have come to nought.’
We must also expunge the verse, which tells us how Pluto feared,
‘Lest the mansions grim and squalid which the gods abhor should be seen both of mortals and immortals.’
And again:—
‘O heavens! verily in the house of Hades there is soul and ghostly form but no mind at all!’
Again of Tiresias:—
‘(To him even after death did Persephone grant mind,) that he alone should be wise; but the other souls are flitting shades.’
Again:—
‘The soul flying from the limbs had gone to Hades, lamenting her fate, leaving manhood and youth.’
Again:—
‘And the soul, with shrilling cry, passed like smoke beneath the earth.’
And,—

‘As bats in hollow of mystic cavern, whenever any of them has dropped out of the string and falls from the rock, fly shrilling and cling to one another, so did they with shrilling cry hold together as they moved.’

And we must beg Homer and the other poets not to be angry if we strike out these and similar passages, not because they are unpoetical, or unattractive to the popular ear, but because the greater the poetical charm of them, the less are they meet for the ears of boys and men who are meant to be free, and who should fear slavery more than death.

Then we will once more entreat Homer and the other poets not to depict Achilles, who is the son of a goddess, first lying on his side, then on his back, and then on his face; then starting up and sailing in a frenzy along the shores of the barren sea; now taking the sooty ashes in both his hands and pouring them over his head, or weeping and wailing in the various modes which Homer has delineated. Nor should he describe Priam the kinsman of the gods as praying and beseeching,
‘Rolling in the dirt, calling each man loudly by his name.’
Still more earnestly will we beg of him at all events not to introduce the gods lamenting and saying,
‘Alas! my misery! Alas! that I bore the bravest to my sorrow.’
But if he must introduce the gods, at any rate let him not dare so completely to misrepresent the greatest of the gods, as to make him say—
‘O heavens! with my eyes verily I behold a dear friend of mine chased round and round the city, and my heart is sorrowful.’
Or again:—
Woe is me that I am fated to have Sarpedon, dearest of men to me, subdued at the hands of Patroclus the son of Menoetius.’

For if, my sweet Adeimantus, our youth seriously listen to such unworthy representations of the gods, instead of laughing at them as they ought, hardly will any of them deem that he himself, being but a man, can be dishonoured by similar actions; neither will he rebuke any inclination which may arise in his mind to say and do the like. And instead of having any shame or self-control, he will be always whining and lamenting on slight occasions.
Yes, he said, that is most true.
Yes, I replied; but that surely is what ought not to be, as the argument has just proved to us; and by that proof we must abide until it is disproved by a better.
It ought not to be.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates
parts.title: A bad lie about the gods
parts.context: Socrates (the 'I' speaking) and Adeimantus are discussing which stories should be told to the children who will become the guardians of their ideal city. Uranus and Cronus are gods in Hesiod's account of the beginning, who mutilated and overthrew their fathers. Hephaestus and Here (Hera) are the smith god and the queen of the gods.
parts.plain: Socrates says the greatest fault of Homer, Hesiod and the other poets is to tell lies, and bad lies, about the gods and heroes: like a painter whose portrait looks nothing like its subject. Stories of gods attacking their fathers, fighting and plotting against one another should not be told to the young, even as allegories, because the young cannot tell allegory from fact, and what they hear first stays with them for life.

commentary.on: Whenever an erroneous representation is made of the nature of gods and heroes
commentary.text: Plato's charge is not that the stories are untrue history. It is that they are untrue to what the divine is. If the gods are truly gods, they cannot be what Homer shows.

commentary.on: he will only be following the example of the first and greatest among the gods
commentary.text: The danger is imitation. Children learn by copying. If the greatest god punished his father, a young man may think he can too. Myths are not harmless entertainment; they shape character.

commentary.on: and all the battles of the gods in Homer—these tales must not be admitted into our State, whether they are supposed to have an allegorical meaning or not
commentary.text: Plato knows the defence that the stories are allegories, symbols of deeper truths, and rejects it for the young. 'Our State' is the ideal city of the dialogue. This is a call for censorship, made openly.

commentary.on: anything that he receives into his mind at that age is likely to become indelible and unalterable
commentary.text: The heart of Plato's concern: early stories become part of who we are. Modern psychologists and every parent would agree with the premise, whatever they think of the conclusion.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates
parts.title: God is not the author of evil
parts.context: After a cut ('…'), Socrates states the first principle of a true theology. The 'two casks' are the two urns of Zeus that Achilles described to Priam in Iliad XXIV; Plato quotes the passage. Pandarus broke a truce in Iliad IV at Athena's prompting; Niobe and the house of Pelops were subjects of tragedies.
parts.plain: Since God is good, he is the cause only of good things, not of evil. So we must not believe Homer when he says that Zeus hands out good and evil from two jars, or that the gods caused men to break oaths. If a poet tells of suffering, he must either not say God caused it, or say it was just punishment that did the sufferers good. To say a good God causes evil is impious.

commentary.on: Then God, if he be good, is not the author of all things
commentary.text: This is the first rule of Plato's theology, and one of the most important sentences in the history of religion: God is good, and so cannot be the cause of evil. Notice the singular, 'God'. Plato is moving beyond Homer's many quarrelling gods towards one perfectly good divine being.

commentary.on: Lie at the threshold of Zeus, full of lots, one of good, the other of evil lots
commentary.text: Plato quotes Achilles' consolation to Priam, the parable of the two urns that you read in session 4, and condemns it. The very words that brought two enemies together are, for Plato, a lie about God.

commentary.on: the violation of oaths and treaties, which was really the work of Pandarus, was brought about by Athene and Zeus
commentary.text: In Iliad IV the gods arrange for a Trojan to break a sworn truce, so that the war will continue. Plato says this cannot be true: a god who causes oath-breaking is no god.

commentary.on: but that God being good is the author of evil to any one is to be strenuously denied
commentary.text: Plato's alternative: if God punishes, it is for the good of the punished. This is an early form of what later Christians would call theodicy, the defence of God's goodness in the face of evil.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates
parts.title: Do not fear the world below
parts.context: Book III continues. The guardians must be brave, so they must not fear death. Socrates quotes, in verse, several of Homer's lines about Hades. The first is Achilles' words to Odysseus in the passage you have just read, in a different translation.
parts.plain: Brave men must not fear death. But Homer describes the world of the dead as horrible, so we must cut out such passages: Achilles saying he would rather be a serf than rule the dead; Hades as a mindless place; souls flying off like smoke, or squeaking like bats. Not because they are bad poetry, but because the better the poetry, the more harm it does to men who should fear slavery more than death.

commentary.on: Can any man be courageous who has the fear of death in him?
commentary.text: Plato's argument is practical: a society needs brave defenders, and fear of death makes cowards. Homer's bleak Hades undermines the very courage his heroes display.

commentary.on: I would rather be a serf on the land of a poor and portionless man than rule over all the dead who have come to nought.
commentary.text: The first line Plato wants to strike out is the one you have just read in Butler. He understood its power exactly. It says that nothing, not even glory, outweighs life, and so it makes men afraid to die.

commentary.on: not because they are unpoetical, or unattractive to the popular ear, but because the greater the poetical charm of them, the less are they meet for the ears of boys and men who are meant to be free
commentary.text: A remarkable admission. Plato loved Homer, and says so elsewhere. He is not attacking bad poetry but great poetry, because great poetry shapes the soul most powerfully. The better Homer is, the more dangerous.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates
parts.title: Heroes must not weep
parts.context: After another cut, Socrates turns to the heroes' grief. He describes Achilles' mourning for Patroclus in Iliad XVIII and XXIV, and quotes Priam rolling in the dirt (Iliad XXII, which you read in session 3), Thetis lamenting, and Zeus grieving for Hector and for his son Sarpedon.
parts.plain: Homer should not show Achilles, a goddess's son, rolling about and pouring ashes on his head, or Priam begging in the dirt, or the gods weeping. Above all he should not show Zeus himself lamenting. If the young hear such things without laughing at them, they will think it fine for them to whine and lament at every small trouble.

commentary.on: Rolling in the dirt, calling each man loudly by his name.
commentary.text: Plato quotes the line about Priam on the walls of Troy, from the comparison in session 3. What Homer offered as the truth of grief, Plato sees as an unworthy example.

commentary.on: O heavens! with my eyes verily I behold a dear friend of mine chased round and round the city, and my heart is sorrowful.
commentary.text: Zeus's words as he watches Achilles chase Hector round Troy. Plato's objection is double: a god should not grieve, and if he grieves, he should act. A Zeus who pities Hector and lets him die anyway is neither happy nor good.

commentary.on: he will be always whining and lamenting on slight occasions
commentary.text: Here Plato's case is at its weakest for many modern readers, and its most revealing. He wants heroes who do not weep. Homer's greatness, and much of what moved you in sessions 3 and 4, lies in the weeping.

compare.author: Plato
compare.why: Achilles' ghost doubted glory. Plato, writing about three centuries later, went further and put Homer's gods and heroes on trial. Read the charges in his own words.
compare.title: Plato's charge

sections.h: The charge from Homer's own mouth
paras: The strongest witness against the heroic code is Achilles. In the Iliad he chose a short life and undying glory. In the Odyssey, dead, he says he would rather be a poor man's labourer than king of all the dead. The scholar Jasper Griffin and many others have read this as the Odyssey's deliberate answer to the Iliad: the poet of homecoming judging the poet of glory, and finding glory wanting.

Think through what follows. If glory is worthless to the one who has it, then the whole bargain of the code collapses: risk your life, and you will be remembered. Remembered by whom, and for what, if you are a mindless shadow? Ajax's silence completes the picture. He died for honour, and in death he is still trapped in his wounded pride, unable to forgive. Homer's world offers the dead neither peace nor reconciliation. The best it can offer is a name, and Achilles has just told us what a name is worth.
sections.key: Achilles' ghost repudiates the glory he chose; Ajax remains trapped in wounded honour. The code's promise, a name that survives, is empty to those who have it.

sections.h: Xenophanes: gods made in our image
paras: The philosophical attack on Homer began two centuries before Plato. Xenophanes of Colophon complained, in our own words, that Homer and Hesiod had attributed to the gods everything that is shameful among humans: theft, adultery and deceiving one another (fragment B11). He went further. Ethiopians, he said, make their gods dark-skinned and snub-nosed, and Thracians make theirs blue-eyed and red-haired; and if oxen and horses had hands, they would draw gods that looked like oxen and horses (B15–16). The gods of the poets, in other words, are human beings projected onto the sky.

Against them, Xenophanes proposed one god, greatest among gods and men, unlike mortals in body or thought, who moves all things by the power of his mind without moving (B23–26). His contemporary Heraclitus said that Homer deserved to be thrown out of the poetry contests and beaten (B42). The Greeks' own thinkers, in other words, saw early that Homer's gods could not be the true divine.
sections.key: Xenophanes (c. 570–475 BC) said Homer's gods were human vices projected onto the sky, and proposed one god unlike us. Heraclitus wanted Homer flogged.

paras: Plato built these complaints into a system. In the Republic, Books II and III, he lays down rules for any true account of the divine. God is good, so he causes only good (379b–c). God is unchanging, so he does not disguise himself as strangers, as Homer's gods constantly do (381d). God is truthful, so he does not deceive, as Zeus does when he sends Agamemnon a lying dream (383a). And the poets must not make men fear death or admire heroes who weep and rage.

In Book X Plato goes further still. He argues that poetry as such is an imitation of an imitation, far from truth, and that it feeds the emotions that reason should govern. Homer, 'the first of the tragedians', must be banished from the ideal city, though Plato admits his own love for him since childhood (595b, 607a). He calls this 'the ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry' (607b), and invites anyone to defend poetry if they can. It is the first great argument in the West about whether art can be dangerous, and whether truth or beauty should rule.
sections.key: Plato's rules: God is good, unchanging and truthful; Homer's gods are none of these. In Republic X he banishes Homer, while admitting he loves him.

paras: Put the case together and it is formidable. Homer's world has courage, honour, loyalty, endurance and moments of piercing pity. But at the top of it are gods who are not good: they cheat, take sides, punish the innocent and watch human suffering like a game. Their favour goes to the strong and the clever, not the just. Zeus gives evil from his urn, and Achilles can only tell Priam to bear it.

And the mercy is narrow. It happens once, in a tent, for one night, between two men who have both lost everything. It is a truce. The war resumes; Troy is burned; its women are enslaved; Hector's son is thrown from the walls. In the Odyssey, the hero's homecoming ends with a massacre and twelve women hanged. Glory, the highest good Homer knows, needs victims: there is no kleos without someone to kill. At its strongest, the charge is this: Homer saw the human condition with terrible clarity, and offered no remedy for it. His world has pity but no goodness at its source, and no hope beyond the grave.
sections.key: The full charge: Homer's gods are powerful but not good, his mercy is a one-night truce, his glory needs victims, and he offers no hope beyond the grave.

sections.h: The objection from the other side: Nietzsche
paras: There is a second objection, aimed not at Homer but at those who criticise him. The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900), who began his career as a professor of Greek, admired the Homeric world precisely for what Plato and Christianity disliked. In an early essay, 'Homer's Contest' (1872), and later in On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), he argued, in our own words, that the Homeric nobles lived by a healthy morality of strength, pride, competition and self-affirmation, in which 'good' meant noble and powerful.

Then, Nietzsche said, came a revolt of the weak, which reached its height in Christianity. It turned the values upside down: humility, meekness and pity became 'good', and pride and strength 'evil'. On this view the Christian reading of Homer is not an improvement but a loss: the replacement of a brave, tragic acceptance of life with a morality of resentment. If you have taken 'The Sermon on the Mount', you met a version of this charge there. Here it means that the case against Homer can be turned round into a case for him, and against the saint.
sections.key: Nietzsche praised the Homeric world's morality of strength and pride, and called Christianity's elevation of humility and pity a revolt of the weak: the case turned round.

sections.h: What the case does not prove
paras: An objection at full strength should also be weighed honestly. The critics' best points stand: Homer's gods are not good, and his heroes' hope ends at the grave. But some of Plato's charges cut against what readers have valued most. He wanted heroes who never weep and a Zeus who never grieves. Most readers since have thought Homer's tears truer than Plato's calm, and Aristotle, Plato's own pupil, answered him in the Poetics: poetry may show things as they are said to be, or as they ought to be, and its pity and fear can purify rather than corrupt (Poetics 6, 25).

So the objection leaves us with a real question rather than a verdict. If Homer's gods are not good, and his glory is hollow, what did his poems actually give the West that was worth keeping? That question is for the next and last session, which is still to come.
sections.key: The critics are right that Homer's gods are not good and his hope ends at the grave; but Aristotle defended poetry's truth, and Homer's tears have convinced more readers than Plato's calm.

refs: Homer, Odyssey XI.204–208, 465–567 (Butler 1900); Iliad II.1–34 (Agamemnon's dream), IV.68–104 (Pandarus), XXIV.527–533 (the two urns).
Plato, Republic II.377d–383c; III.386a–388e; X.595b, 606e–608a. Tr. Benjamin Jowett (1871; 3rd ed. 1888).

Xenophanes, fragments B11, B15, B16, B23–26 (Diels–Kranz); Heraclitus, fragment B42. In J. H. Lesher, Xenophanes of Colophon (1992); G. S. Kirk, J. E. Raven and M. Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers (2nd ed., 1983).
Aristotle, Poetics 6 (catharsis) and 25 (answers to critics of Homer).
Friedrich Nietzsche, 'Homer's Contest' (1872); On the Genealogy of Morality, First Essay (1887).
Jasper Griffin, Homer on Life and Death (1980); Christopher Janaway, Images of Excellence: Plato's Critique of the Arts (1995).

debate.question: Should Homer be taught?

positions.name: No, or only in part: censor it
positions.who: Plato, Republic II, III and X
positions.view: Stories shape character, especially in the young. Homer's gods are liars and evildoers and his heroes are bad examples, and the greater his art the more harm he does. A just city would keep only the passages that show the gods as good and the heroes as brave and self-controlled.
positions.evidence: The two urns; Pandarus' broken oath; Achilles' lament among the dead; Priam in the dirt; Zeus weeping for Hector.

positions.name: Yes: read it for its hidden meaning
positions.who: Theagenes of Rhegium (c. 525 BC); the Stoics; the Neoplatonist Porphyry (3rd century AD)
positions.view: Homer's stories are allegories. The battles of the gods are the conflicts of the elements or of virtues and vices; Athena is wisdom; the cave of the nymphs on Ithaca is the cosmos. Read rightly, Homer teaches truth.
positions.evidence: Porphyry's essay On the Cave of the Nymphs, on Odyssey XIII; the Stoic readings of the gods as forces of nature.

positions.name: Yes: take the honey, leave the poison
positions.who: Aristotle (Poetics); later, Christian teachers such as Basil of Caesarea (4th century), whom you will meet in Hall IV
positions.view: Poetry shows human life as it is, and its pity and fear can purify the soul. A wise reader admires what is noble, such as courage, endurance and mercy, and passes over what is base, as a bee takes honey from flowers and leaves the rest.
positions.evidence: Aristotle's answers to Homer's critics (Poetics 25); the long tradition of teaching Homer in Christian schools from late antiquity on.

debate.agree: All three agree that Homer is the most powerful educator the Greeks had, that stories shape the soul, and that some of what he says about the gods cannot be true of the divine as such.

look.why: Giovanni Bellini painted The Feast of the Gods in 1514, and Titian later repainted its landscape. Its story comes from the Roman poet Ovid, not from Homer. It is here because it shows the gods of Greek and Roman myth as the poets imagined them, and as Plato objected to them: feasting, drinking and taking their ease.
points: Six women, eight men, two satyrs and one child gather in pairs and trios in a loose row across the width of the painting.
The two satyrs have men's torsos and furry goat's legs.
The men wear loose robes in white, blue, green, coral and pink; the women wear long dresses, most of them slipping from one shoulder.
On the rocky ground in front lie a wooden bucket, a glass goblet, a pitchfork, a blue and white dish of grapes and fruit, and an overturned cup.
Craggy cliffs rise on the left and a grove of dark green trees on the right, under a vivid blue sky.
A slip of paper on the bucket bears Bellini's signature and the date 1514.

music.why: Allegri's Miserere sets Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, O God', a prayer to a God who is good and who forgives. It sounds the note that this session finds missing at the top of Homer's world.

think.why: Plato said the gods must be good to be gods; Nietzsche said strength, not goodness, is the old and healthy morality. Read the modern debate on whether morality needs God.

learn.why: Achilles' verdict on glory, from among the dead: the objection to the heroic code in Homer's own words.

check.q: Odysseus tells Achilles' ghost that he was honoured in life and is a prince among the dead. Why does Achilles' answer matter so much for this journey?
options: Because the greatest hero, who chose glory over a long life, now says glory is worth less than the lowest life on earth, so the code is judged by its own champion
Because it proves that the Odyssey was written by a different poet
Because Achilles is lying to Odysseus out of jealousy
Because it shows that Achilles was a coward all along
check.why: Odysseus offers the code's consolation and Achilles rejects it. The objection comes from inside Homer, which makes it stronger.

check.q: Achilles strides away happy when he hears his son is a great warrior. What is the best reading of this?
options: It shows that Achilles has changed his mind again and now values glory for himself
It shows that the dead feel nothing
It is a mistake in the text
It shows that the code is not quite dead in him: glory is worthless to the dead man, but he still rejoices in it for his son
check.why: Homer gives both: the repudiation and the lingering pride. The answer does not say he wants glory for himself, and the dead in Homer do feel grief and joy, faintly.

check.q: What is Plato's first principle about God in Republic II?
options: That there are many gods, all equal
That the gods do not exist
That God is the author of all things, good and evil alike
That God is good, and therefore the cause only of good things, not of evil
check.why: 'God, if he be good, is not the author of all things.' The first option is the view he rejects, and Homer's two urns express it.

check.q: Why does Plato reject the defence that Homer's stories of the gods are allegories?
options: Because he thinks allegory is always false
Because the young cannot tell what is allegorical from what is literal, and what they hear first becomes part of them
Because Homer said himself that they were literal
Because allegories were illegal in Athens
check.why: Republic 378d: 'a young person cannot judge what is allegorical and what is literal'. He objects to their effect on the young, not to allegory as such.

check.q: Plato wants to strike out the passages about weeping heroes and grieving gods. Which is the best objection to this part of his case?
options: That Plato did not know Homer well
That the weeping is where much of Homer's truth and power lie: the mercy in Achilles' hut comes from shared tears, and Aristotle argued that pity can purify the soul
That Homer's heroes never weep
That gods cannot feel anything
check.why: This is where Plato's case is weakest. Priam and Achilles weep together; Aristotle answered Plato in the Poetics. Plato knew Homer very well.

check.q: Nietzsche's objection runs the opposite way to Plato's. What does it claim?
options: That Plato was right to censor Homer
That the Homeric nobles' morality of strength and pride was healthy, and that Christianity's elevation of humility and pity was a revolt of the weak
That Homer's gods were too good
That Homer was a Christian before Christ
check.why: For Nietzsche the Homeric world is the standard, and the saint is the decline. It turns the case against Homer into a case against Christianity.

tutorial.question: 'Homer's world has courage but no mercy beyond the tent.' Is this fair?
tutorial.approach: State the case against at full strength, using Achilles' ghost, Ajax's silence, Xenophanes and Plato. Then test it against what you have read: the mercy of Iliad XXIV, Homer's pity for both sides, the justice of the Odyssey. Consider Nietzsche's opposite objection. Decide which parts of the charge stand, and which do not.
strong: Uses Achilles' words among the dead and explains why they come from Homer himself.
Explains Ajax's silence as honour beyond healing.
Sets out Xenophanes' and Plato's charges accurately, with Plato's principle that God is good.
Assesses the mercy in Iliad XXIV: real, but a one-night truce.
Weighs Plato's weakest point, the objection to weeping, against Aristotle's reply.
Considers Nietzsche's counter-charge fairly.
