sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice one story you take in, a film, a series, a game or the news, and ask Plato's question of it: what does this teach me to admire? Write down one sentence of answer, and decide whether you want to be shaped by it.
sessions.reflect: Plato wanted only good gods and heroes who never weep. Homer gave weeping heroes and gods who are not good. Which is nearer the truth about the world you know?
takeaways: Among the dead, Achilles says he would rather be a poor man's servant than king of the dead: the code is judged by its greatest hero.
Xenophanes and Plato charged that Homer's gods are human vices writ large; Plato's first rule was that God is good, and so not the author of evil.
The full charge is that Homer's world has courage and pity but no goodness at its source and no mercy beyond a one-night truce; Nietzsche turned it into a charge against Christianity.

sessions.title: Hero and saint: the verdict
sessions.line: Odysseus wakes on his own island and does not know it; the goddess who loves him laughs at his lies. Augustine remembers weeping for a heroine at school. The verdict: what Homer gave the West, and what Christianity kept and turned upside down.
sessions.plain: This last session gives the journey's answer. Homer gave the West its first picture of a great life: courage, honour, endurance, loyalty to home, and a glimpse of pity even for an enemy. The case against it is real: its gods are not good, and its glory ends at the grave. When Christianity met Homer, it did not throw him out. It kept the courage and the pity, and turned glory upside down: the greatest became the one who serves. We read Odysseus coming home, Augustine on learning Homer at school, and the prophet Jeremiah and Paul on what is worth glorying in.
sessions.why: Session 6 put the case against Homer's world at full strength: gods who are not good, a glory Achilles himself rejected, mercy that lasts one night. That left a question: what did Homer give the West that was worth keeping, and what did the West do with it? This session answers, setting the hero beside the saint.
answers: So what did the Greeks think a great life was?
Why is Homer still read?
How did Christians read Homer?
How is a Homeric hero different from a Christian saint?
sessions.finding: Homer gave the West its first picture of greatness, courage, honour and home, and its first glimpse of pity; Christianity kept the courage and the pity and turned glory upside down, so that the greatest became the one who serves.

paras: Here is the answer to this journey's question, before the evidence for it. The Greeks of Homer thought a great life was one of aretē, excellence, shown in courage and skill; of timē, the honour others give you; and of kleos, the glory that outlives you in song. The Iliad tests that idea to breaking point and finds, in its last book, something greater: pity between enemies who share a mortal lot. The Odyssey offers a second picture: a great life is a faithful, enduring, clever life, lived among the people you love, at home.

Homer's own poems, and the philosophers after him, exposed its limits: gods who are not good, glory that the dead despise, a mercy that is a truce. Christianity, when it met this world, kept its courage, its honesty, its pity and its love of home, and turned its idea of glory upside down. The rest of this session shows how.
background.key: Homer: greatness is excellence, honour and glory, deepened by pity and the love of home. Christianity kept courage and pity and turned glory upside down.

paras: The Iliad began with anger over honour (session 1). Achilles weighed glory against a long life (session 2), and at his triumph became inhuman (session 3). The poem ended in mercy between enemies, a truce and not forgiveness (session 4). Odysseus refused immortality for home (session 5). Homer's own Achilles, and then Plato, judged the code and the gods and found them wanting (session 6).
background.key: Anger, the choice of glory, its inhuman triumph, mercy in the tent, the choice of home, and the case against: six steps to a verdict.

background.h: Odysseus home, and Augustine at school
paras: The main reading returns to the Odyssey. The Phaeacians have sailed Odysseus home while he slept and left him on the shore of Ithaca with their gifts. Athena has wrapped the island in mist, so he does not recognise it. It is the moment the whole poem has been moving towards, and Homer turns it into a game of wits between the hero and his goddess. Some ancient readers made this passage the centre of their allegories: the Neoplatonist Porphyry wrote a whole essay on the cave of the nymphs it mentions.

The comparison is from Augustine of Hippo (354–430). Born in Thagaste in North Africa, he was educated in the Roman schools in Latin literature, became a famous teacher of rhetoric in Carthage, Rome and Milan, and became a Christian in 386. He was bishop of Hippo, on the coast of modern Algeria, for over thirty years. Around 397–400 he wrote the Confessions, the story of his life addressed as a prayer to God. In Book I he remembers his schooldays, where boys learned Virgil, the Roman Homer, and Homer himself in Greek.
background.key: Odysseus wakes on Ithaca in Athena's mist; Augustine, educated on Virgil and Homer, looks back on his schooling as a Christian bishop.

paras: The main reading, Odysseus' homecoming and his meeting with Athena, answers the question of what Homer's gods love in a man, and so what his world finally admires. The comparison has three short parts. Augustine answers the question of how a Christian who loved the classics judged them. Then two passages from the Bible, Jeremiah 9:23–24 and 2 Corinthians 12:9–10, answer the question of what Scripture thinks is worth glorying in, the very word at the heart of Homer.
background.key: Odysseus and Athena show what Homer's gods admire; Augustine, Jeremiah and Paul show how the Bible's idea of glory differs.

before: Odysseus has just reached home. What does he do when the 'shepherd' tells him where he is?
What does Athena admire in Odysseus? Is it his goodness?
In the comparison, what does Augustine say he wept for, and what should he have wept for instead?
sessions.readWhy: Odysseus wakes on Ithaca, lies to the goddess in disguise, and is welcomed by her laughter; then kisses his own soil.

paras: “Alas,” he exclaimed, “among what manner of people am I fallen? Are they savage and uncivilised or hospitable and humane? Where shall I put all this treasure, and which way shall I go? I wish I had staid over there with the Phaeacians; or I could have gone to some other great chief who would have been good to me and given me an escort. As it is I do not know where to put my treasure, and I cannot leave it here for fear somebody else should get hold of it. In good truth the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians have not been dealing fairly by me, and have left me in the wrong country; they said they would take me back to Ithaca and they have not done so: may Jove the protector of suppliants chastise them, for he watches over everybody and punishes those who do wrong. Still, I suppose I must count my goods and see if the crew have gone off with any of them.”

He counted his goodly coppers and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes, but there was nothing missing; still he kept grieving about not being in his own country, and wandered up and down by the shore of the sounding sea bewailing his hard fate. Then Minerva came up to him disguised as a young shepherd of delicate and princely mien, with a good cloak folded double about her shoulders; she had sandals on her comely feet and held a javelin in her hand. Ulysses was glad when he saw her, and went straight up to her.

“My friend,” said he, “you are the first person whom I have met with in this country; I salute you, therefore, and beg you to be well disposed towards me. Protect these my goods, and myself too, for I embrace your knees and pray to you as though you were a god. Tell me, then, and tell me truly, what land and country is this? Who are its inhabitants? Am I on an island, or is this the sea board of some continent?”

Minerva answered, “Stranger, you must be very simple, or must have come from somewhere a long way off, not to know what country this is. It is a very celebrated place, and everybody knows it East and West. It is rugged and not a good driving country, but it is by no means a bad island for what there is of it. It grows any quantity of corn and also wine, for it is watered both by rain and dew; it breeds cattle also and goats; all kinds of timber grow here, and there are watering places where the water never runs dry; so, sir, the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy, which I understand to be a long way off from this Achaean country.”

Ulysses was glad at finding himself, as Minerva told him, in his own country, and he began to answer, but he did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart.

“I heard of Ithaca,” said he, “when I was in Crete beyond the seas, and now it seems I have reached it with all these treasures. I have left as much more behind me for my children, but am flying because I killed Orsilochus son of Idomeneus, the fleetest runner in Crete. I killed him because he wanted to rob me of the spoils I had got from Troy with so much trouble and danger both on the field of battle and by the waves of the weary sea; he said I had not served his father loyally at Troy as vassal, but had set myself up as an independent ruler, so I lay in wait for him with one of my followers by the road side, and speared him as he was coming into town from the country. It was a very dark night and nobody saw us; it was not known, therefore, that I had killed him, but as soon as I had done so I went to a ship and besought the owners, who were Phoenicians, to take me on board and set me in Pylos or in Elis where the Epeans rule, giving them as much spoil as satisfied them. They meant no guile, but the wind drove them off their course, and we sailed on till we came hither by night. It was all we could do to get inside the harbour, and none of us said a word about supper though we wanted it badly, but we all went on shore and lay down just as we were. I was very tired and fell asleep directly, so they took my goods out of the ship, and placed them beside me where I was lying upon the sand. Then they sailed away to Sidonia, and I was left here in great distress of mind.”

Such was his story, but Minerva smiled and caressed him with her hand. Then she took the form of a woman, fair, stately, and wise, “He must be indeed a shifty lying fellow,” said she, “who could surpass you in all manner of craft even though you had a god for your antagonist. Dare devil that you are, full of guile, unwearying in deceit, can you not drop your tricks and your instinctive falsehood, even now that you are in your own country again? We will say no more, however, about this, for we can both of us deceive upon occasion—you are the most accomplished counsellor and orator among all mankind, while I for diplomacy and subtlety have no equal among the gods. Did you not know Jove’s daughter Minerva—me, who have been ever with you, who kept watch over you in all your troubles, and who made the Phaeacians take so great a liking to you? And now, again, I am come here to talk things over with you, and help you to hide the treasure I made the Phaeacians give you; I want to tell you about the troubles that await you in your own house; you have got to face them, but tell no one, neither man nor woman, that you have come home again. Bear everything, and put up with every man’s insolence, without a word.”

And Ulysses answered, “A man, goddess, may know a great deal, but you are so constantly changing your appearance that when he meets you it is a hard matter for him to know whether it is you or not. This much, however, I know exceedingly well; you were very kind to me as long as we Achaeans were fighting before Troy, but from the day on which we went on board ship after having sacked the city of Priam, and heaven dispersed us—from that day, Minerva, I saw no more of you, and cannot ever remember your coming to my ship to help me in a difficulty; I had to wander on sick and sorry till the gods delivered me from evil and I reached the city of the Phaeacians, where you encouraged me and took me into the town. And now, I beseech you in your father’s name, tell me the truth, for I do not believe I am really back in Ithaca. I am in some other country and you are mocking me and deceiving me in all you have been saying. Tell me then truly, have I really got back to my own country?”

“You are always taking something of that sort in your head,” replied Minerva, “and that is why I cannot desert you in your afflictions; you are so plausible, shrewd and shifty. Any one but yourself on returning from so long a voyage would at once have gone home to see his wife and children, but you do not seem to care about asking after them or hearing any news about them till you have exploited your wife, who remains at home vainly grieving for you, and having no peace night or day for the tears she sheds on your behalf. As for my not coming near you, I was never uneasy about you, for I was certain you would get back safely though you would lose all your men, and I did not wish to quarrel with my uncle Neptune, who never forgave you for having blinded his son. I will now, however, point out to you the lie of the land, and you will then perhaps believe me. This is the haven of the old merman Phorcys, and here is the olive tree that grows at the head of it; [near it is the cave sacred to the Naiads; here too is the overarching cavern in which you have offered many an acceptable hecatomb to the nymphs, and this is the wooded mountain Neritum.”

As she spoke the goddess dispersed the mist and the land appeared. Then Ulysses rejoiced at finding himself again in his own land, and kissed the bounteous soil; he lifted up his hands and prayed to the nymphs, saying, “Naiad nymphs, daughters of Jove, I made sure that I was never again to see you, now therefore I greet you with all loving salutations, and I will bring you offerings as in the old days, if Jove’s redoubtable daughter will grant me life, and bring my son to manhood.”

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: A lying tale on his own shore
parts.context: Ithaca, at dawn. The Phaeacians have left Odysseus asleep on the beach with all their gifts. Athena ('Minerva') has hidden the island in mist. Idomeneus was a king of Crete; the Phoenicians were the great traders of the Mediterranean; Pylos and Elis are on the Greek mainland.
parts.plain: Odysseus wakes and does not know where he is. He fears he has been abandoned, counts his treasure, and weeps. Athena comes to him disguised as a young shepherd. He asks where he is, and she tells him: Ithaca. He is overjoyed, but instead of telling the truth he invents a long lie: that he is a Cretan on the run after killing a man.

commentary.on: among what manner of people am I fallen? Are they savage and uncivilised or hospitable and humane?
commentary.text: Odysseus asks the question he has asked on every shore of his voyage: will these people honour strangers? It is the Odyssey's test of a civilisation. Now he asks it of his own home, without knowing.

commentary.on: Still, I suppose I must count my goods and see if the crew have gone off with any of them.
commentary.text: The first thing the hero does at home is count his treasure. Homer's heroes care about their goods; gifts are honour made visible, as you saw in session 1. It is also a little comic.

commentary.on: the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy
commentary.text: Athena teases him. The name he has longed for through twenty years is the last word of her speech in the Greek. She holds it back to the end.

commentary.on: he did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart
commentary.text: At the moment of homecoming, his reflex is to lie. It has kept him alive among Cyclopes and suitors; now it is part of him. Homer calls it instinctive: mētis has become his nature.

commentary.on: I killed him because he wanted to rob me of the spoils I had got from Troy
commentary.text: The lie he invents is a story of honour and spoils: a quarrel over a prize, ending in murder. It is the Iliad's world, told as a lie. He presents himself as a dangerous man, a sensible thing to do on a strange shore.

parts.author: Homer
parts.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
parts.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC
parts.title: The goddess and the liar
parts.context: Athena reveals herself. Neptune (Poseidon) is angry with Odysseus for blinding his son, the Cyclops. Phorcys is an old sea god; the Naiads are water nymphs; Neritum is the island's mountain. Butler prints a square bracket ('[near it') where he thought the Greek text was doubtful; it is kept here as he printed it.
parts.plain: Athena smiles and strokes him, and takes the form of a woman. She says it would take a master trickster to outdo him, and that they are a pair: he the best liar among men, she the cleverest among gods. She tells him he must bear insults silently at home. He reproaches her for abandoning him on his voyage; she says she never doubted he would get home. She clears the mist, and he sees Ithaca, kisses the ground and prays to the nymphs.

commentary.on: Minerva smiled and caressed him with her hand
commentary.text: The goddess's response to a lie is affection. She is delighted. Calypso smiled at him in the same way in session 5. Homer's divine women love Odysseus for his cleverness.

commentary.on: for we can both of us deceive upon occasion—you are the most accomplished counsellor and orator among all mankind, while I for diplomacy and subtlety have no equal among the gods
commentary.text: This is the heart of the session. What does the goddess of wisdom love in her favourite? Not his goodness, his justice or his humility, but that he is the best deceiver among men, as she is among gods. Homer's heaven rewards excellence, and here excellence is cunning. Plato would say: a god who boasts of deceiving is no god.

commentary.on: Bear everything, and put up with every man's insolence, without a word.
commentary.text: And yet the next thing she asks of him is humility: to bear insults in silence, disguised as a beggar in his own house. In the Odyssey, the hero must become the lowest before he can be restored. It is a hint of something the saint would take much further.

commentary.on: from that day, Minerva, I saw no more of you, and cannot ever remember your coming to my ship to help me in a difficulty
commentary.text: Odysseus speaks for every believer who has felt abandoned: where were you? Athena's answer is not love but confidence: 'I was certain you would get back safely though you would lose all your men'. She did not want to quarrel with her uncle Poseidon. The gods' friendship is real, but it has its politics.

commentary.on: Then Ulysses rejoiced at finding himself again in his own land, and kissed the bounteous soil
commentary.text: The homecoming at last: the hero kisses the ground. Of all the moments in Homer, this is perhaps the simplest and most human. The great life, in the Odyssey, ends here: on your own earth, among your own people, with the gods' blessing.

read.author: Homer
read.who: Homer, the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
read.when: Ionia (the west coast of modern Turkey), probably the late 700s or 600s BC

paras: But why did I so much hate the Greek, which I studied as a boy? I do not yet fully know. For the Latin I loved; not what my first masters, but what the so-called grammarians taught me. For those first lessons, reading, writing and arithmetic, I thought as great a burden and penalty as any Greek. And yet whence was this too, but from the sin and vanity of this life, because I was flesh, and a breath that passeth away and cometh not again? For those first lessons were better certainly, because more certain; by them I obtained, and still retain, the power of reading what I find written, and myself writing what I will; whereas in the others, I was forced to learn the wanderings of one Aeneas, forgetful of my own, and to weep for dead Dido, because she killed herself for love; the while, with dry eyes, I endured my miserable self dying among these things, far from Thee, O God my life.

For what more miserable than a miserable being who commiserates not himself; weeping the death of Dido for love to Aeneas, but weeping not his own death for want of love to Thee, O God. Thou light of my heart, Thou bread of my inmost soul, Thou Power who givest vigour to my mind, who quickenest my thoughts, I loved Thee not. I committed fornication against Thee, and all around me thus fornicating there echoed "Well done! well done!" for the friendship of this world is fornication against Thee; and "Well done! well done!" echoes on till one is ashamed not to be thus a man. And for all this I wept not, I who wept for Dido slain, and "seeking by the sword a stroke and wound extreme," myself seeking the while a worse extreme, the extremest and lowest of Thy creatures, having forsaken Thee, earth passing into the earth. And if forbid to read all this, I was grieved that I might not read what grieved me. Madness like this is thought a higher and a richer learning, than that by which I learned to read and write.

Why then did I hate the Greek classics, which have the like tales? For Homer also curiously wove the like fictions, and is most sweetly-vain, yet was he bitter to my boyish taste. And so I suppose would Virgil be to Grecian children, when forced to learn him as I was Homer. Difficulty, in truth, the difficulty of a foreign tongue, dashed, as it were, with gall all the sweetness of Grecian fable. For not one word of it did I understand, and to make me understand I was urged vehemently with cruel threats and punishments. Time was also (as an infant) I knew no Latin; but this I learned without fear or suffering, by mere observation, amid the caresses of my nursery and jests of friends, smiling and sportively encouraging me. This I learned without any pressure of punishment to urge me on, for my heart urged me to give birth to its conceptions, which I could only do by learning words not of those who taught, but of those who talked with me; in whose ears also I gave birth to the thoughts, whatever I conceived. No doubt, then, that a free curiosity has more force in our learning these things, than a frightful enforcement. Only this enforcement restrains the rovings of that freedom, through Thy laws, O my God, Thy laws, from the master's cane to the martyr's trials, being able to temper for us a wholesome bitter, recalling us to Thyself from that deadly pleasure which lures us from Thee.

But woe is thee, thou torrent of human custom! Who shall stand against thee? how long shalt thou not be dried up? how long roll the sons of Eve into that huge and hideous ocean, which even they scarcely overpass who climb the cross? Did not I read in thee of Jove the thunderer and the adulterer? both, doubtless, he could not be; but so the feigned thunder might countenance and pander to real adultery. And now which of our gowned masters lends a sober ear to one who from their own school cries out, "These were Homer's fictions, transferring things human to the gods; would he had brought down things divine to us!" Yet more truly had he said, "These are indeed his fictions; but attributing a divine nature to wicked men, that crimes might be no longer crimes, and whoso commits them might seem to imitate not abandoned men, but the celestial gods."
Yahweh says,

“Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom.
Don’t let the mighty man glory in his might.
Don’t let the rich man glory in his riches.

But let him who glories glory in this,
that he has understanding, and knows me,
that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness in the earth,
for I delight in these things,” says Yahweh.
He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.
Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.who: Augustine (354–430), teacher of rhetoric, then bishop of Hippo in North Africa
parts.title: Weeping for Dido
parts.context: Augustine, now a bishop, remembers his schooldays in North Africa around 365–370. Aeneas and Dido are the hero and the queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid, the Roman epic modelled on Homer; Dido killed herself when Aeneas left her. Augustine speaks to God throughout. 'Fornication' is his strong word for loving the world in God's place. Pusey's text has no chapter numbers; the cuts are marked '…'. The last sentence's quotation ('These were Homer's fictions…') is from the Roman orator Cicero.
parts.plain: Augustine asks why he hated learning Greek as a boy but loved Latin poetry. He learned to weep for Dido, who died for love, while not weeping for himself, dying without God's love. He found Homer bitter only because he was forced to learn him in a foreign language, under the cane; a free curiosity teaches better than fear. And he complains that the schools taught stories of Jupiter the thunderer and adulterer, so that crimes would seem divine.

commentary.on: I was forced to learn the wanderings of one Aeneas, forgetful of my own
commentary.text: Augustine's great insight about the epics. He studied a hero's wanderings and forgot that he was a wanderer too: a soul far from its true home. The Christian reading of the Odyssey, the soul's journey home to God, is in this one phrase.

commentary.on: weeping the death of Dido for love to Aeneas, but weeping not his own death for want of love to Thee, O God
commentary.text: Augustine does not say the poems are worthless. He says they moved him deeply, to tears, but for the wrong things. The pity Homer and Virgil awakened was real; it was aimed at a story, while his own life was going wrong.

commentary.on: For Homer also curiously wove the like fictions, and is most sweetly-vain
commentary.text: Augustine's verdict on Homer in four words: 'most sweetly-vain'. Sweet, because the poetry is beautiful; vain, because its stories are empty fictions. He loved and distrusted the classics at once, as Plato had.

commentary.on: No doubt, then, that a free curiosity has more force in our learning these things, than a frightful enforcement.
commentary.text: An aside that every teacher should know. Augustine hated Homer only because he was beaten into learning him. Love of learning, he says, teaches better than fear.

commentary.on: Did not I read in thee of Jove the thunderer and the adulterer? both, doubtless, he could not be
commentary.text: Augustine repeats Plato's charge, in a Christian voice: the supreme god of the poets cannot be both the just judge who thunders and an adulterer. Stories that make the gods immoral make immorality seem divine.

parts.title: Let him who glories
parts.context: Jeremiah was a prophet in Jerusalem about 627–580 BC, a century or so after Homer, in the years before Babylon destroyed the city. Here God speaks through him about what a person may rightly boast of. 'Yahweh' is the personal name of Israel's God.

commentary.on: Don’t let the mighty man glory in his might.
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for 'glory' here means to boast, to praise oneself. Jeremiah names the three things every ancient hero gloried in: wisdom, strength and riches: Odysseus' cunning, Achilles' might, the treasure of the spoils. All three are set aside.

commentary.on: But let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me
commentary.text: The only glory left is knowing God. Glory is moved from what you are and do to whom you know.

commentary.on: that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness in the earth, for I delight in these things
commentary.text: And this God is defined by goodness: loving kindness, justice and righteousness. It is exactly what Plato said a true god must be, and what Homer's gods are not. Athena delights in deception; the God of Jeremiah delights in kindness.

parts.title: When I am weak, then am I strong
parts.context: Paul, the early Christian missionary, writing to the church in Corinth, a Greek city, in the mid-50s AD. Rivals there had boasted of their credentials and visions, and Paul answers with a mock boast. He has prayed to be freed of some suffering he calls 'a thorn in the flesh', and Christ has answered him.

commentary.on: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.
commentary.text: Here the Homeric order is turned upside down. In Homer, power is shown in strength and victory. Here God's power is shown in weakness: in Christ crucified, and in a suffering apostle. Paul writes this to Greeks, who knew their Homer.

commentary.on: Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses
commentary.text: Paul uses the very word, glory, and attaches it to the opposite of what a hero boasts of. A Homeric hero would never boast of weakness, injury or persecution. Paul does.

commentary.on: For when I am weak, then am I strong.
commentary.text: Five words that sum up the change. The saint's greatness is not the hero's. It does not deny courage: Paul's life was full of danger. But it locates strength in dependence on God rather than in oneself, and glory in service rather than in fame.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.why: Homer's word for the highest good was glory. Read how a Christian who had learned Homer at school judged it, and two passages of the Bible that redefine glory itself.
compare.title: What is worth glorying in?

paras: The main reading shows, very clearly, what Homer's gods admire. Athena, the goddess of wisdom, loves Odysseus not because he is good, but because he is the best liar and schemer among men, as she is among gods. She delights in his deceit. That is not a flaw in the story; it is the Homeric idea of excellence. Aretē is being outstanding at what you do, and the gods love the outstanding: the strongest, the cleverest, the most beautiful.

Notice what follows. In such a world, there is no reason for the gods to love the weak, the poor or the plain, except as they happen to favour someone. Priam is pitied, but Troy is destroyed. The suitors are punished, but so are the maids. Compare Jeremiah: the God of Israel delights in loving kindness, justice and righteousness. The difference between the two heavens is the difference between two ideas of greatness.
sections.key: Athena loves Odysseus for his cunning, not his goodness: Homer's gods love excellence. Jeremiah's God delights in kindness and justice.

paras: For the Greeks Homer was the schoolbook: boys learned him by heart, and Plato called him the educator of Greece. Alexander the Great, by Plutarch's account, slept with the Iliad under his pillow. The scholars of Alexandria in the 200s and 100s BC edited the text we read and divided each poem into twenty-four books. In the Greek East, in Byzantium, Homer was never lost: the 12th-century bishop Eustathius of Thessalonica wrote a vast commentary on both poems.

In the Latin West Homer was almost forgotten for a thousand years. Dante, around 1310, put him first among the poets in Limbo (Inferno IV), but could not read him. Petrarch was given a Greek manuscript of Homer in 1354 and wept that he could not read it. The first printed Greek Homer came out in Florence in 1488. Then the translations came: George Chapman's (1598–1616), which inspired Keats's sonnet 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer' (1816), Alexander Pope's (1715–26), and many more. Homer has been read for nearly three thousand years because he saw human beings whole: their rage and their tenderness, their courage and their grief, under a sky that does not care.
sections.key: Homer was the Greeks' schoolbook, never lost in Byzantium, rediscovered in the West after 1354, and read for nearly three thousand years for his whole view of human life.

paras: The first Christians lived in a world where everyone educated had learned Homer. They had to decide what to do with him. Some, like the Latin writer Tertullian (around 200), asked what Athens had to do with Jerusalem. Jerome (around 347–420) described, in a letter of 384, a dream in which he was accused before Christ's judgement seat of being 'a Ciceronian, not a Christian' for loving the classics too much (Letter 22.30). Augustine, as you have read, wept for Dido and called Homer 'sweetly-vain'.

But most did not throw the classics away. Clement of Alexandria (around 200) read Odysseus tied to the mast as he sailed past the Sirens as a picture of the Christian bound to the cross, sailing safely past the world's temptations (Exhortation to the Greeks 12). Basil of Caesarea, in the 4th century, wrote an address to young men on how to read the Greek poets, which you will meet in Hall IV. The pattern that won was Augustine's and Basil's: read the classics, admire their beauty, take what is true and good, and judge the rest by Christ. That is why Homer was still taught in Christian schools in every century after.
sections.key: Some Christians feared the classics (Tertullian, Jerome's dream); most kept them, reading Odysseus at the mast as the Christian at the cross and taking what was true and good.

paras: Put the Homeric hero beside the Christian saint and the differences are plain. Both are brave. Both endure. Both can be moved by pity. But they differ about almost everything else: where a person's worth comes from, what to do with enemies, what death is, and what glory means. The table sets them side by side. It is a picture of two ideals, not of how every Greek or every Christian actually lived.

Read it row by row, and notice that the differences are not between bravery and cowardice. The martyrs who died in the arena were as brave as Hector. The difference is in what the courage is for, where a person's worth comes from, and what lies beyond death. Hold the two columns in mind for the rest of this hall, and the halls after it: much of the story of the West is the attempt to combine them.

rows: Holiness: love of God and neighbour
God, who made and loves every person
Kleos: your name sung after death
God's glory; 'your names are written in heaven' (Luke 10:20)
Where God's power is made perfect (2 Corinthians 12:9)
To be killed, or pitied for a night
To be loved and prayed for (Matthew 5:44)
The end of all that matters; a shadow life in Hades
Not the end; the hope of resurrection
One God, perfectly good, who became a servant
table.note: Homer's two poems already point towards some saintly qualities: pity in Iliad XXIV, faithfulness and endurance in the Odyssey.

sections.key: Hero and saint share courage, endurance and pity, but differ on worth, glory, weakness, enemies, death and God.

paras: It is easy to stress only the contrast. Christianity kept a great deal of Homer. It kept courage: the martyrs were praised as athletes and soldiers, and Paul told Christians to put on armour (Ephesians 6). It kept endurance: Odysseus, 'much-enduring', became a figure of the Christian life as a voyage home through trials, as Augustine saw when he wrote of 'my own' wanderings. It kept pity: Weil thought the Gospels were the last and greatest expression of the Greek genius for seeing the suffering of others.

It kept the love of a particular home and a particular person, which the Odyssey had shown in Penelope and the bed. And it kept Homer's honesty about suffering. The Psalms and Job weep as frankly as Achilles. What it did not keep was the idea that glory belongs to the strong, and that the divine is merely powerful.
sections.key: Christianity kept Homer's courage, endurance, pity, love of home and honesty about suffering.

paras: What Christianity changed was glory itself. In Homer, glory goes to the one who kills. In the Gospels, the one called 'the Lord of glory' is killed. Paul's hymn in Philippians 2 says that Christ, though in the form of God, did not consider equality with God 'a thing to be grasped' but 'emptied himself, taking the form of a servant' and was obedient 'to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross'. Achilles grasps glory with both hands. Christ lets it go.

And the comparison passages put the turn in two sentences. Jeremiah: let no one glory in wisdom, strength or riches, but in knowing a God of kindness and justice. Paul: I will glory in my weaknesses, for when I am weak, then am I strong. Homer's Achilles, among the dead, said glory was worth less than a servant's life on earth. Christianity agreed that the hero's glory was hollow, and then said something Homer never imagined: that the true glory is a servant's. The West has lived with both ideals ever since, the hero and the saint, and much of its history is the argument between them.
sections.key: In Homer glory goes to the killer; in the Gospels the Lord of glory is killed. Christ 'emptied himself, taking the form of a servant': glory became a servant's.

refs: Homer, Odyssey XIII.187–360 (Butler 1900); Porphyry, On the Cave of the Nymphs (3rd century AD).

Jeremiah 9:23–24; 2 Corinthians 12:9–10; Philippians 2:6–8; Luke 10:20; Matthew 5:44; Ephesians 6:10–17; 1 Corinthians 2:8 (World English Bible).
Plutarch, Life of Alexander 8; Dante, Inferno IV.86–88; Petrarch, letter to Nicholas Sigeros (1354); the Florence editio princeps of Homer (1488).
George Chapman, Homer (1598–1616); Alexander Pope, Iliad (1715–20) and Odyssey (1725–26); John Keats, 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer' (1816).

debate.question: Did Christianity improve on Homer, or betray him?

positions.name: It fulfilled him
positions.who: Augustine; Simone Weil; many Christian humanists
positions.view: Homer saw the human condition truly but had no remedy. His pity for both sides and his sense that glory is hollow reach towards something only the Gospel supplies: a God who is good, who suffers with us, and who makes the servant great. Christianity keeps what was best in Homer and completes it.
positions.evidence: Achilles among the dead; Priam and Achilles weeping; Weil's view of the Gospels as heir of the Iliad; Philippians 2.

positions.name: It betrayed him
positions.who: Friedrich Nietzsche; some modern humanists
positions.view: Homer's world faced death and suffering bravely without consolation, and honoured strength, pride and excellence. Christianity replaced that tragic courage with a morality of humility and pity, born of weakness, and offered comforts that are not true.
positions.evidence: Hector's 'some great thing'; the Homeric love of excellence; Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morality (1887).

positions.name: Two ideals in tension
positions.who: Many historians of the West; the poet John Milton (Paradise Lost IX, 1667)
positions.view: The West inherited both the hero and the saint and never fully reconciled them. Its literature, from the medieval knight to Milton, who said he preferred to sing the 'better fortitude' of patience and martyrdom to the wars of epic, keeps trying to join courage and humility, glory and service.
positions.evidence: Chivalry, which tried to make warriors Christian; Milton's opening to Book IX; the enduring popularity of both Homer and the Gospels.

debate.agree: All agree that Christianity changed the meaning of glory decisively, and that the West carries both ideals, the Homeric and the Christian, to this day.

look.why: Claude Lorrain painted The Judgment of Paris in 1645–46. It shows where, in the Greek story, the Trojan war began: a young man choosing between three goddesses. The gallery's description names no figures, but the peacock, the winged child and the helmet and lance are the traditional signs of Hera, Aphrodite with Cupid, and Athena. It is here because this whole journey has been about choices of what makes a life great.
points: The figures are small, in the lower left of a vast landscape.
A young man in red drapery, Paris, sits on a rock with a long staff and points at three women.
The woman in the centre, in coral red and lapis blue, stands beside a peacock with its tail fanned open, and points upward.
A second woman holds a white cloth around her; beside her stands a winged child holding an arrow, with a quiver on his back.
The third sits on a yellow-draped rock, touching her sandal, with a long lance under the cloth and a metal helmet with a red feather beside the rock.
Six sheep graze in the foreground; a waterfall and tall trees fill the left; water winds towards hazy purple mountains under a blue sky.

music.why: 'For All the Saints' is a hymn to those who 'from their labours rest': a company of the faithful remembered not for their glory but for their faith. Hear it as the saint's answer to the hero's kleos.

think.why: This journey began with Athens and Jerusalem in brief. Now read the great teachers who held the two together, and how they judged what to keep from the Greeks.

learn.why: The first lines of the Odyssey: the man of many turns, trying to bring himself and his friends home. Augustine read his own life as such a voyage.

check.q: What does Athena admire most in Odysseus, according to the main reading?
options: That he is the most accomplished deceiver and counsellor among men, as she is among gods
His piety towards the nymphs
His justice as a king
His faithfulness to Penelope
check.why: 'We can both of us deceive upon occasion': she loves his cunning. Athena praised his fatherly rule in Book V, but that is not what she admires here.

check.q: Augustine says he wept for Dido but not for himself. What is his point about the classics?
options: That they move us deeply, but can direct our pity at stories while our own lives go wrong
That boys should not be taught to read
That Virgil was a better poet than Homer
That the poems are worthless and should not be read
check.why: He does not call the poems worthless: they moved him to tears. His complaint is that the tears were for the wrong thing.

check.q: Jeremiah 9:23–24 sets aside glorying in wisdom, might and riches. Why is this so pointed after reading Homer?
options: Because Jeremiah was against all learning
Because those are exactly the things Homer's heroes gloried in, Odysseus' cunning, Achilles' might, the spoils, and Jeremiah puts glory instead in knowing a God of kindness and justice
Because Israel had no warriors
Because Jeremiah had read Homer
check.why: Jeremiah did not know Homer; but his three boasts match the hero's three. And his God delights in kindness, not cunning.

check.q: What does Paul mean by 'when I am weak, then am I strong'?
options: That strength is an illusion
That Christians should avoid danger
That God's power is shown in weakness and dependence on him, so that glory lies in service rather than self
That weakness is good in itself
check.why: Paul's life was full of courage and danger; he does not praise weakness for its own sake but says God's power is 'made perfect in weakness'.

check.q: Which of these did Christianity keep from Homer, according to the lecture?
options: The belief that death is the end
The belief that glory belongs to the strongest
Courage, endurance, pity, love of home and honesty about suffering
The worship of the Olympian gods
check.why: These were kept and transformed. The other three are what it rejected.

check.q: What is the best summary of the journey's verdict?
options: Christianity copied Homer exactly
Homer was simply wrong and should be forgotten
Homer gave the West its first picture of greatness, courage, honour and home, with a glimpse of pity; Christianity kept the courage and pity and turned glory upside down
The Greeks thought a great life was a long and comfortable one
check.why: This is the finding. The last option is precisely what Achilles rejected in the Iliad.

tutorial.question: How is a Homeric hero different from a Christian saint?
tutorial.approach: Define the hero from the poems: aretē, timē, kleos, mētis, and the choices of Achilles and Odysseus. Define the saint from the comparison texts and Philippians 2. Use the table, but go beyond it: show what they share as well as how they differ. Bring in Augustine's double attitude and Nietzsche's objection. End with your own judgement: can a person be both?
strong: Defines aretē, timē and kleos accurately, with examples from both poems.
Uses Athena's love of Odysseus' cunning to show what Homer's gods admire.
Uses Jeremiah 9 and 2 Corinthians 12 to show glory redefined.
Notes what the two ideals share: courage, endurance, pity.
Explains Augustine's love and distrust of the classics.
Engages Nietzsche's view that the change was a loss.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do one piece of real service for someone that no one will praise: the task at work or at home that everyone avoids. Do it well, as Odysseus did his work, and quietly, as a servant does, and notice how it feels to do something great without kleos.
sessions.reflect: Whose life do you most admire: someone strong and brilliant, or someone faithful and kind? What does your answer say about which ideal you live by?
takeaways: For Homer's Greeks a great life was excellence, honour and glory, deepened in the Iliad by pity and in the Odyssey by faithful love of home.
Homer's gods love excellence, even cunning, not goodness; the critics, from Plato to Augustine, saw this clearly.
Christianity kept Homer's courage, endurance and pity, and turned glory upside down: 'when I am weak, then am I strong'; the greatest is the servant.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What did the Greeks think a great life was? In about 300 words, answer from Homer's two poems, using at least three passages you have read, and say whether you think they were right. Then answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Read the whole of Iliad XXIV over the next week, a few pages a night, in Butler or a modern translation, and then Odyssey XXIII. Before each reading, ask: what is this person choosing, and what does it cost?
synthesis: This journey asked what the Greeks thought a great life was, and found two answers in Homer's two poems, a case against both, and a third answer that came later. Here are the short answers to its questions, in order.

Who was Homer? We do not know. The Greeks said a blind poet from Ionia; most scholars think the poems took shape between about 750 and 650 BC, at the end of a long tradition of singers who composed without writing, as Milman Parry and Albert Lord showed. Did the Trojan War happen? There was a real and rich city at Hisarlik, destroyed more than once around 1200 BC, probably the Wilusa of Hittite records, and Greeks were active nearby. A war over Helen cannot be proved.

What is the Iliad about? Not the fall of Troy, but the anger of Achilles: its first word. Agamemnon takes Achilles' prize, and with it his timē, the honour others give him. Achilles withdraws and lets the Greeks die. In Book IX he refuses gifts worth far more than he lost, because he has seen that a life cannot be bought back, and he weighs the two fates: a short life with kleos, the glory that is sung, or a long one without it. Hector, defending his city, lives by the same code for his wife and child.

What did glory cost? When Patroclus dies, Achilles chooses glory and death. At the height of his triumph he kills Hector, refuses his dying plea, wishes to eat his flesh and drags his body in the dust before his family. Homer does not look away, and pities both sides: Andromache heating a bath for a husband already dead. Simone Weil called it the poem of force, which turns victor and victim alike into things.

Why does the Iliad end with Priam? Because the anger the poem began with ends there. An old father comes with a ransom, as one came in Book I; this time he is received. Priam kisses the hands that killed his son and asks Achilles to think of his father. Seeing Peleus, and his own death, in Priam, Achilles weeps, gives back the body, eats with his enemy and grants a truce. The poem ends with Hector's funeral. It is mercy born of shared mortality, under gods who give evil from their urns: a truce, not yet forgiveness.

What is the Odyssey about? A different hero and a different choice. Odysseus, much-enduring and full of mētis, is offered immortality by a goddess and refuses it, because Penelope, 'only a woman', is his. Home, nostos, a faithful marriage of one mind, is the Odyssey's great life. Its world has more justice than the Iliad's, but its homecoming ends in a massacre.

Were the Greek gods good? No. They take sides, cheat and watch human suffering like a game; Athena loves Odysseus for his lying. Xenophanes said they were human vices written on the sky, and Plato laid down that God, being good, cannot be the author of evil, and wanted Homer censored. And glory? Achilles himself, among the dead, says he would rather be a poor man's servant than king of the dead. At full strength the charge is that Homer's world has courage and pity, but no goodness at its source and no mercy beyond a night in a tent. Nietzsche answered from the other side that Homer's proud, tragic world was healthier than the Christian one that judged it.

Why is Homer still read? Because he saw human beings whole: rage and tenderness, courage and grief, under a sky that does not care. He was the Greeks' schoolbook, never lost in Byzantium, rediscovered in the West after Petrarch, and translated in every age since.

How is a hero different from a saint? Both are brave, both endure, both can pity. But the hero's worth is the honour others give him, his glory is his name in song, his enemies are to be killed, and death ends everything. The saint's worth comes from God, glory belongs to God, enemies are to be loved, and death is not the end. When Christianity met Homer it kept his courage, his endurance, his pity and his honesty about suffering, and turned glory upside down. 'Let him who glories glory in this, that he... knows me' (Jeremiah); 'when I am weak, then am I strong' (Paul); Christ 'emptied himself, taking the form of a servant'.

So the West has lived with two ideals of greatness ever since, the hero and the saint, and much of its history is the argument between them. Homer gave it the first, and with it the first glimpse of what lay beyond: an old king on his knees and a killer in tears, two enemies who for one night saw each other as human. Whatever you conclude, you cannot understand the West without that night, or, perhaps, yourself.

title: Democracy and its dangers
question: Who should rule, and how?
line: Seven sessions on the world's first democracy: Solon's laws, the assembly and the lot, Pericles the first citizen, the Mytilene debate, Plato's case against, Aristotle's answer, and what Jerusalem added.
why: Most of us take democracy for granted, and many fear for it. The Athenians invented it, ran it for nearly two centuries and argued about it more sharply than anyone since. This journey treats Athens as a laboratory: how democracy was built, how it worked at its best, how it went wrong, how Plato and Aristotle judged it, and what the Bible added. It reads Plutarch, Aristotle, Thucydides, Plato, Lord Acton and the Mayflower Compact beside the law of Moses and the Proverbs, gives the case against democracy at full strength, and ends with a verdict. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year paper in ancient political thought and Athenian history, with elements of a paper on the history of political ideas from antiquity to the American founding.
before: tragedy
outcomes: Explain the crisis Solon faced, what he did about debt and the poor, and why he refused to become tyrant, comparing the jubilee of Leviticus 25.
Describe how Athenian democracy worked (assembly, council, lot, courts, ostracism), who was excluded, and assess whether it was a democracy.
Explain Thucydides' judgement of Pericles as 'first citizen' and of his successors, and the place of empire in Athens' greatness.
Analyse the Mytilene debate and the trial of the Arginusae generals as evidence of democracy's dangers, and the remedies the Athenians and later democracies found.
State Plato's case against democracy at full strength, with its modern versions, and assess Aristotle's answer: the wisdom of the many, the middle class and the rule of law.
Explain what the Bible and Christianity added to the Greek inheritance, using Acton and the Mayflower Compact, and weigh the objections.

people.name: Draco
people.line: First to write down the laws of Athens; his punishments were notoriously harsh.

people.name: Solon
people.line: Poet and lawgiver; archon in 594 BC; cancelled debts, banned debt-slavery and gave the poor a voice, then left Athens for ten years.

people.name: Peisistratus
people.line: Seized power with a bodyguard voted by the assembly; ruled as tyrant, followed by his sons.

people.name: Cleisthenes
people.line: Nobleman who gave power to the people and reorganised Athens into ten tribes.

people.name: Themistocles
people.line: Built the fleet that won at Salamis (480 BC); later ostracised.

people.name: Pericles
people.line: Elected general every year from 443 BC; led Athens at its height; died in the plague.

people.name: Cleon
people.line: The most powerful popular leader after Pericles; proposed the massacre at Mytilene.

people.name: Diodotus
people.line: Known only for his speech against the massacre at Mytilene.

people.name: Thucydides
people.line: Athenian general and historian of the Peloponnesian War.

people.name: Socrates
people.line: Philosopher; refused to put an illegal motion in 406 BC; condemned to death by an Athenian jury.

people.name: Plato
people.line: Socrates' pupil; argued in the Republic that democracy breeds disorder and tyranny.

people.name: Aristotle
people.line: Plato's pupil; argued for the wisdom of the many, the middle class and the rule of law.

people.name: Plutarch
people.line: Greek biographer whose Lives tell the stories of Solon, Themistocles, Pericles and Alcibiades.

people.name: Thomas Aquinas
people.line: Theologian who saw in Deuteronomy 1 a model of mixed government.

people.name: John Calvin
people.line: Reformer who preferred aristocracy mixed with democracy.

people.name: James Madison

glossary.def: One of the nine chief magistrates of Athens, chosen yearly; by lot from 487 BC.
The council of former archons, named after the hill where it met; stripped of most political power in 462/1 BC.
Greek for 'rule of the best': for Aristotle, rule by a few for the common good.
In Greek ekklesia: the meeting of all adult male citizens, which decided war, peace, laws and policy by show of hands.
In Greek boule: fifty citizens from each tribe, chosen by lot for a year, who prepared business for the assembly.
A solemn agreement with promises on both sides, made before God; used by the Puritans to found churches and governments.
The alliance of Greek cities led by Athens against Persia from 478 BC, which became an Athenian empire.
Greek for 'leader of the people'; came to mean a leader who wins power by flattering the crowd and stirring its fear and anger.
A village or district of Attica, about 140 in all; the basic unit of citizenship after Cleisthenes.
From demos, 'the people', and kratos, 'power': rule by the people. For Aristotle, the corrupt form of rule by the many, in the interest of the poor.
The people: the whole body of citizens, and sometimes the common people as against the rich.
Rule over other peoples; Athens' empire was its former allies, who paid tribute.
Rule by the knowledgeable: a modern proposal, made by Jason Brennan, to weight political power towards those with more political knowledge.
The 'charge of illegality': an Athenian lawsuit to annul a decree that broke the laws, and punish its proposer.
'Sixth-parters': poor Athenian farmers before Solon who handed a sixth of their crop to the rich.
The Bible's teaching that every human being is made in God's likeness (Genesis 1:27), the ground of equal human worth.
In Israel's law, every fiftieth year, when land returned to its families and Israelite debt-slaves went free (Leviticus 25).
Government whose power is bounded by something outside itself: a constitution, rights, or a higher law.
Choosing by random draw; the Athenians used it for most offices and juries, as the most democratic method.
A free foreigner living in Athens, who paid a special tax and served in the forces but had no political rights.
For Aristotle, the citizens between the very rich and the very poor, whose strength makes a city stable.
A government that combines rule by one, few and many, so that no class rules alone.
Greek for 'rule of the few': for Aristotle, rule by the rich in their own interest.
A yearly vote, from 487 to about 417 BC, by which the Athenians could exile one man for ten years without disgrace or loss of property.
A broken piece of pottery, used as a ballot in an ostracism; plural ostraka.
In Plato's Republic, the ruler trained for decades to know the good, who alone should govern.
A Greek city-state: a city with its surrounding countryside, governing itself; the root of 'politics'.
Aristotle's name (politeia) for the good form of rule by the many: a mixture of oligarchy and democracy.
A tenth of the Athenian year, when the fifty councillors of one tribe served as the standing committee of the state.
Government by known laws that bind rulers as well as ruled, rather than by the will of a person or crowd.
'The shaking-off of burdens': Solon's cancellation of debts and ban on enslaving Athenians for debt.
A general: one of ten elected each year in Athens, and the most powerful office in Pericles' time.
The poorest class of free Athenian citizens; under Solon they could attend the assembly and sit on juries, and they rowed the fleet.
The oligarchs installed by Sparta in 404 BC, who ruled Athens by terror for eight months.
In Greek, a ruler who held sole power without a lawful title; later, any ruler who rules for himself and by force.
Tocqueville's phrase for oppression by the majority of those who lose the vote, from which there is no appeal.

sessions.title: Solon: law instead of strife
sessions.line: Athens on the edge of civil war, the poor sold as slaves for their debts, and a poet who could have made himself tyrant and gave the city laws instead.
sessions.plain: Around 594 BC Athens was close to civil war. A few rich families owned most of the land, and poor farmers who could not pay their debts were sold as slaves, some of them abroad. Both sides asked one man, Solon, a poet and a respected citizen, to make new laws. He cancelled the debts, made it illegal to enslave an Athenian for debt, and gave the poorest citizens a place in the assembly and the law courts. His friends begged him to make himself king. He refused, and left Athens for ten years so that the laws, not he, would rule.
sessions.why: This is the first session. 'Kings and prophets' asked what happens when power forgets justice, in Israel. This journey asks the same question of the Greeks, who gave the world the word democracy. Before we can judge democracy, we need to see where it came from: not from a theory, but from a crisis of debt and slavery, and from one man who refused power.
answers: Did the Greeks invent democracy?
What was wrong in Athens before democracy?
What did Solon actually do?
Why did he refuse to make himself king?
sessions.finding: Athens' road to democracy began with a lawgiver who refused to become tyrant, freed the poor from slavery for debt and gave every citizen, however poor, a voice in the assembly and the courts.

paras: Every society has to answer one question: who should rule, and how? A king? The rich? The wise? Everyone? Today most people in the West would say 'the people', and would call any other answer dangerous. But the first people to try government by the people, the Athenians, argued about it fiercely, and their greatest thinkers thought it a mistake.

This journey treats Athens as a laboratory. We will see how democracy was built, how it worked at its best, how it went wrong, how Plato and Aristotle judged it, and what the Bible added. One session gives the case against democracy at full strength, in Plato's own words. The last session gives a verdict.

background.key: Who should rule, and how? We follow the first democracy from its birth to its judges, hear the case against, then give a verdict.

paras: Ancient Greece was not one country but hundreds of small, fiercely independent city-states. The Greek word is polis, from which we get 'politics'. Athens was one of the largest: a city with its surrounding countryside, called Attica, about the size of an English county.

In the 600s BC Athens was ruled by a few noble families. Each year they chose nine magistrates, called archons, from among themselves; former archons sat for life on a council called the Areopagus, after the hill where it met. Around 632 BC a nobleman named Kylon tried to seize power as a 'tyrant', a sole ruler who took power outside the law, and failed. Around 621 BC a lawgiver named Draco wrote down the laws for the first time. They were so harsh that we still call severe rules 'draconian'.

Writing the laws down did not solve the deeper problem: debt. Poor farmers borrowed from rich neighbours, often pledging their own bodies as security. If they could not pay, they became slaves. That is where our reading begins.

timeline.text: Kylon tries to make himself tyrant of Athens, and fails
