Peisistratus seizes power as tyrant, in Solon's old age
Death of Solon

background.key: Athens was a city-state ruled by a few noble families, with harsh written laws and a crisis of debt that turned poor citizens into slaves.

paras: Solon was a poet as well as a statesman, and he defended his laws in verse. His poems are lost except for fragments quoted by later writers. The two most important are the ones we read in this journey.

Aristotle, the philosopher, or a student working under him, wrote The Athenian Constitution in the 320s BC, about 270 years after Solon. It was lost for over a thousand years, until a papyrus copy was found in Egypt and published by the British scholar Frederic Kenyon in 1891. Plutarch, a Greek priest and biographer, wrote his Life of Solon around AD 100, about 700 years after Solon, using older books, including Aristotle's. Both quote Solon's own poems, which is the best evidence we have. Historians trust the outline of the story, and argue about many details.
background.key: We know Solon through his own poems, quoted by Aristotle (320s BC) and Plutarch (about AD 100); the outline is trusted, many details are debated.

paras: The main reading is from Plutarch's Life of Solon, in five parts: the crisis of debt; the offer of absolute power and Solon's refusal; the cancelling of debts; the share he gave to the poor; and his departure from Athens.

The comparison is from the Bible: the law of the jubilee in Leviticus 25, where every fiftieth year land returned to its families and debt-slaves went free. Athens and Israel, at about the same time, faced the same problem, and answered it in different ways.
background.key: Plutarch on Solon's crisis, refusal and reforms; then Israel's law of the jubilee.

before: What exactly was wrong in Athens, according to Plutarch?
Why did Solon's friends think he was a fool to refuse power?
What did Solon give the poorest citizens, and what did he not give them?
sessions.readWhy: Five passages from Plutarch's Life of Solon: the crisis, the refusal, the cancelling of debts, the share for the poor, and the departure.

paras: XIII. When the troubles about Kylon were over, and the accursed men cast out of the country, the Athenians relapsed into their old dispute about the constitution. The state was divided into as many factions as there were parts of the country, for the Diakrii, or mountaineers, favoured democracy; the Pedioei, oligarchy; while those who dwelt along the seashore, called Parali, preferred a constitution midway between these two forms, and thus prevented either of the other parties from carrying their point. Moreover, the state was on the verge of revolution, because of the excessive poverty of some citizens, and the enormous wealth of others, and it appeared that the only means of putting an end to these disorders was by establishing an absolute despotism. The whole people were in debt to a few wealthy men; they either cultivated their farms, in which case they were obliged to pay one-sixth of the profit to their creditors, and were called Hektemori, or servants, or else they had raised loans upon personal security, and had become the slaves of their creditors, who either employed them at home, or sold them to foreigners. Many were even compelled to sell their own children, which was not illegal, and to leave the country because of the harshness of their creditors.

The greater part, and those of most spirit, combined together, and encouraged one another not to suffer such oppression any longer, but to choose some trustworthy person to protect their interests, to set free all enslaved debtors, redistribute the land, and, in a word, entirely remodel the constitution.

XIV. In this position of affairs, the most sensible men in Athens perceived that Solon was a person who shared the vices of neither faction, as he took no part in the oppressive conduct of the wealthy, and yet had sufficient fortune to save him from the straits to which the poor were reduced. In consequence of this, they begged him to come forward and end their disputes. But Phanias of Lesbos says that Solon deceived both parties, in order to save the state, promising the poor a redistribution of lands, and the rich a confirmation of their securities. However, Solon himself tells us that it was with reluctance that he interfered, as he was threatened by the avarice of the one party, and the desperation of the other. He was chosen archon next after Philombrotus, to act as an arbitrator and lawgiver at once, because the rich had confidence in him as a man of easy fortune, and the poor trusted him as a good man. It is said also that a saying which he had let fall some time before, that "equality does not breed strife," was much circulated at the time, and pleased both parties, because the rich thought it meant that property should be distributed according to merit and desert, while the poor thought it meant according to rule and measure. Both parties were now elate with hope, and their leaders urged Solon to seize the supreme power in the state, of which he was practically possessed, and make himself king. Many even of the more moderate class of politicians, who saw how weary and difficult a task it would be to reform the state by debates and legislative measures, were quite willing that so wise and honest a man should undertake the sole management of affairs. It is even said that Solon received an oracle as follows:

"Take thou the helm, the vessel guide,
Athens will rally to thy side."

His intimate friends were loudest in their reproaches, pointing out that it was merely the name of despot from which he shrunk, and that in his case his virtues would lead men to regard him as a legitimate hereditary sovereign; instancing also Tunnondas, who in former times had been chosen by the Euboeans, and, at the present time, Pittakus, who had been chosen king of Mitylene. But nothing could shake Solon's determination. He told his friends that monarchy is indeed a pleasant place, but there is no way out of it; and he inserted the following verses in answer to Phokus, in one of his poems:

"But if I spared
My country, and with dread tyrannic sway,
Forbore to stain and to pollute my glory;
I feel no shame at this; nay rather thus,
I think that I excel mankind."

Being afterwards asked whether he had composed the best possible laws for the Athenians, he answered, "The best that they would endure." And the habit of Athenians of later times, who soften down harsh words by using politer equivalents, calling harlots "mistresses," taxes "contributions," garrisons of cities "protectors," and the common prison "the house," was, it seems, first invented by Solon, who devised the name of "relief from burdens" for his measure to abolish all debts.
This was his first measure; namely, to put an end to all existing debts and obligations, and to forbid any one in future to lend money upon security of the person of the debtor.

XVIII. In the next place, Solon, who wished to leave all magistracies as he found them, in the hands of the wealthy classes, but to give the people a share in the rest of the constitution, from which they were then excluded, took a census of the wealth of the citizens, and made a first class of those who had an annual income of not less than five hundred medimni of dry or liquid produce; these he called Pentakosiomedimni. The next class were the Hippeis, or knights, consisting of those who were able to keep a horse, or who had an income of three hundred medimni. The third class were the Zeugitae, whose property qualification was two hundred medimni of dry or liquid produce; and the last class were the Thetes, whom Solon did not permit to be magistrates, but whose only political privilege was the right of attending the public assemblies and sitting as jurymen in the law courts. This privilege was at first insignificant, but afterwards became of infinite importance, because most disputes were settled before a jury. Even in those cases which he allowed the magistrates to settle, he provided a final appeal to the people.

Solon moreover is said to have purposely worded his laws vaguely and with several interpretations, in order to increase the powers of these juries, because persons who could not settle their disputes by the letter of the law were obliged to have recourse to juries of the people, and to refer all disputes to them, as being to a certain extent above the laws. He himself notices this in the following verses:

"I gave the people all the strength they needed,
Yet kept the power of the nobles strong;
Thus each from other's violence I shielded,
Not letting either do the other wrong."

Thinking that the weakness of the populace required still further protection, he permitted any man to prosecute on behalf of any other who might be ill-treated. Thus if a man were struck or injured, any one else who was able and willing might prosecute on his behalf, and the lawgiver by this means endeavoured to make the whole body of citizens act together and feel as one. A saying of his is recorded which quite agrees with the spirit of this law. Being asked, what he thought was the best managed city? "That," he answered, "in which those who are not wronged espouse the cause of those who are, and punish their oppressors."

When Solon had passed all his laws, as people came to him every day to praise or blame, or advise him to add or take away from what he had written, while innumerable people wanted to ask questions, and discuss points, and kept bidding him explain what was the object of this or that regulation, he, feeling that he could not do all this, and that, if he did not, his motives would be misunderstood; wishing, moreover, to escape from troubles and the criticism and fault-finding of his countrymen [for, as he himself writes, it is "Hard in great measures every one to please"], made his private commercial business an excuse for leaving the country, and set sail after having obtained from the Athenians leave of absence for ten years. In this time he thought they would become used to his laws.

parts.author: Plutarch
parts.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
parts.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100
parts.title: A city in debt
parts.context: Plutarch is describing Athens just before 594 BC. The 'troubles about Kylon' were the aftermath of a failed attempt at tyranny about forty years earlier. The three factions he names are regional parties: the hill country, the plain and the coast. This is the translation by Aubrey Stewart and George Long (1880), who spell Greek names closely to the Greek, so Kylon for Cylon and Drakon for Draco.
parts.plain: Athens was split into parties, and the gap between rich and poor was so great that people thought only a dictator could end it. The poor were all in debt to a few rich men. Some farmed land and paid a sixth of the crop to their creditors. Others had borrowed on the security of their own bodies, and had become slaves, kept at home or sold abroad. Some sold their own children. The poor began to organise, wanting a leader who would free the slaves and share out the land.

commentary.on: the excessive poverty of some citizens, and the enormous wealth of others
commentary.text: Plutarch's diagnosis is simple: the danger to the city was inequality. Notice what he says people thought was the only cure: 'absolute despotism'. When a society is split, the first answer that occurs to people is a strong man.

commentary.on: pay one-sixth of the profit to their creditors, and were called Hektemori
commentary.text: Hektemoroi means 'sixth-parters'. Historians still argue about exactly what they were: tenants, debtors or serfs. What is clear is that they were not free farmers on their own land.

commentary.on: had raised loans upon personal security, and had become the slaves of their creditors
commentary.text: This is debt bondage: you pledge your own body, and if you cannot pay, your creditor owns you. It was common across the ancient world, in Mesopotamia and Israel as well as Greece. A citizen of Athens could become a slave in his own city.

commentary.on: Many were even compelled to sell their own children, which was not illegal
commentary.text: The phrase 'which was not illegal' is the sting. The law protected the creditor, not the child.

commentary.on: set free all enslaved debtors, redistribute the land, and, in a word, entirely remodel the constitution
commentary.text: The poor wanted two things: freedom for the enslaved, and a new share-out of the land. Solon would give them the first and refuse the second, and that choice shaped everything that followed.

parts.author: Plutarch
parts.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
parts.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100
parts.title: The offer of a crown
parts.context: Both sides now ask Solon to settle the crisis. Plutarch tells how he was chosen archon, the chief magistrate, with full power to make new laws, and how everyone, even his friends, urged him to keep that power for himself. The verses are Solon's own, from his poems, in Stewart and Long's rendering.
parts.plain: Sensible Athenians saw that Solon belonged to neither side: he had money, but he had not joined in oppressing the poor. Both sides trusted him. His friends urged him to take power for good and make himself king, saying it was only the word 'tyrant' that frightened him. Solon refused, and wrote a poem saying he was prouder of sparing his country than he would have been of ruling it.

commentary.on: the rich had confidence in him as a man of easy fortune, and the poor trusted him as a good man
commentary.text: Solon was trusted by both sides for different reasons. The rich trusted his money; the poor trusted his character. This is the first example in this journey of something we will meet again: a free people needs leaders trusted across its divisions.

commentary.on: equality does not breed strife
commentary.text: A saying both sides could read their own way: the rich heard 'equality by merit', the poor 'equality by measure'. The argument about what kind of equality a city owes its citizens never ended, and Aristotle will take it up in session 6, still to come.

commentary.on: urged Solon to seize the supreme power in the state, of which he was practically possessed, and make himself king
commentary.text: This is the turning point. In many Greek cities of the 600s and 500s BC, a crisis like this produced a tyrant. In Greek, 'tyrant' did not always mean a cruel ruler; it meant someone who held sole power without a lawful title. Some tyrants were popular. Solon could have been one.

commentary.on: Take thou the helm, the vessel guide
commentary.text: The image of the city as a ship and its ruler as the helmsman is very old in Greek poetry. Plato will use it against democracy in session 5, still to come.

commentary.on: it was merely the name of despot from which he shrunk
commentary.text: His friends' argument is still heard today: a good man with unlimited power would do more good than a slow, quarrelling assembly. Solon's refusal is a judgement about power itself, not only about himself.

commentary.on: Forbore to stain and to pollute my glory
commentary.text: Solon's own words. He thinks of tyranny as a stain. His glory is to have had the power and not used it for himself.

parts.author: Plutarch
parts.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
parts.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100
parts.title: The shaking-off of burdens
parts.context: Solon is now lawgiver. Plutarch turns to his first and most famous law. The cut is marked '…'; what follows it in Plutarch is a dispute among ancient writers about whether Solon cancelled the debts entirely or only lowered the interest.
parts.plain: Asked whether he had given Athens the best laws, Solon answered: the best they would accept. His first law cancelled all existing debts and forbade anyone, ever again, to lend money on the security of a person's body. He gave it a gentle name: the 'relief from burdens'.

commentary.on: The best that they would endure.
commentary.text: One of the wisest things any lawgiver has said. Solon did not impose a perfect plan. He asked what this people, divided as it was, could actually live with. That is the difference between a lawgiver and a utopian.

commentary.on: relief from burdens
commentary.text: In Greek, seisachtheia, 'the shaking-off of burdens'. Plutarch notes, with a smile, that Solon invented the habit of giving a hard measure a soft name.

commentary.on: to forbid any one in future to lend money upon security of the person of the debtor
commentary.text: This is the heart of it. From now on no Athenian citizen could be made a slave for debt. Whatever else changed in Athens over the next three centuries, this law stood. It is one of the first laws in history to make a citizen's freedom something no contract could sell.

parts.author: Plutarch
parts.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
parts.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100
parts.title: A voice for the poor
parts.context: Having freed the slaves, Solon reorganised the constitution. Plutarch describes the four property classes he set up and the rights he gave to the poorest. A medimnus was a measure of grain, about fifty litres.
parts.plain: Solon divided the citizens into four classes by income, not by birth. Only the richer classes could hold office. The poorest, the thetes, could attend the assembly and sit on juries, and anyone could appeal a magistrate's decision to a jury of the people. Solon also allowed any citizen to take a case to court on behalf of someone who had been wronged. Asked which city was best run, he said: the one where those who are not wronged take up the cause of those who are.

commentary.on: took a census of the wealth of the citizens
commentary.text: This was a quiet revolution. Before Solon, office went by birth: you had to be from a noble family. Now it went by wealth, which could be earned. A rich commoner could rise. It was not democracy, but it broke the nobles' monopoly.

commentary.on: the right of attending the public assemblies and sitting as jurymen in the law courts
commentary.text: The thetes, the poorest free men, could not hold office, but they could vote and judge. Plutarch saw that this small right grew into the greatest power in Athens, because in the end the courts decided everything.

commentary.on: he provided a final appeal to the people
commentary.text: The right of appeal meant that a magistrate's decision was not final: a citizen could take it to a court of ordinary citizens. Power had to answer to the people.

commentary.on: he permitted any man to prosecute on behalf of any other who might be ill-treated
commentary.text: In most ancient law only the victim, or his family, could bring a case. Solon let anyone do it. A slave-owner's neighbour, a stranger in the street, could take up the cause of someone too weak to do it himself. The law was meant to make citizens responsible for each other.

commentary.on: in which those who are not wronged espouse the cause of those who are, and punish their oppressors
commentary.text: This saying is the best summary of Solon's ideal. A good city is not one where everyone looks after himself, but one where people stand up for others. It is very close to the Bible's 'defend the fatherless, plead for the widow' (Isaiah 1:17).

parts.author: Plutarch
parts.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
parts.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100
parts.title: The lawgiver leaves
parts.context: The laws are written on wooden tablets and set up in public, and the council and magistrates swear to keep them for a hundred years. Then Solon does something very few lawgivers have done.
parts.plain: Once the laws were passed, people came to Solon every day to praise them, criticise them or ask what they meant. He could not satisfy them all, and did not want to be accused of bending the laws. So he left Athens for ten years, hoping that in that time they would get used to the laws.

commentary.on: Hard in great measures every one to please
commentary.text: A line of Solon's own poetry. Every reformer knows it.

commentary.on: set sail after having obtained from the Athenians leave of absence for ten years
commentary.text: Solon removed himself so that the laws, not their author, would rule. If he had stayed, every dispute would have come back to him, and he would have become the tyrant he refused to be. It is a principle the West later called the rule of law: government by known laws, not by the will of a person.

commentary.on: In this time he thought they would become used to his laws.
commentary.text: Laws work only when they become habits. Solon knew that a constitution needs time and loyalty, not only good drafting. Within a generation a tyrant, Peisistratus, had taken power anyway, and under the tyrants Solon's laws fell into disuse.

read.author: Plutarch
read.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
read.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100

paras: “ ‘You shall count off seven Sabbaths of years, seven times seven years; and there shall be to you the days of seven Sabbaths of years, even forty-nine years.
Then you shall sound the loud trumpet on the tenth day of the seventh month. On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land.

You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.
That fiftieth year shall be a jubilee to you. In it you shall not sow, neither reap that which grows of itself, nor gather from the undressed vines.
For it is a jubilee; it shall be holy to you. You shall eat of its increase out of the field.
“ ‘In this Year of Jubilee each of you shall return to his property.
“ ‘If you sell anything to your neighbor, or buy from your neighbor, you shall not wrong one another.
According to the number of years after the Jubilee you shall buy from your neighbor. According to the number of years of the crops he shall sell to you.
According to the length of the years you shall increase its price, and according to the shortness of the years you shall diminish its price; for he is selling the number of the crops to you.
You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God; for I am Yahweh your God.

parts.title: The year of jubilee
parts.context: Leviticus is the third book of the Torah, the law of Moses. Chapter 25 sets out the sabbath year, when the land rests every seventh year, and the jubilee, every fiftieth year. When it was written, and how far the jubilee was ever kept, are debated; many scholars date the chapter's final form to the 500s BC, close to Solon's time. The rest of the chapter adds that Israelites who had sold themselves into service for debt went free in the jubilee (25:39–41).

commentary.on: proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants
commentary.text: These words were cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia in 1752–53, in the King James wording. Abolitionists later adopted the bell as their symbol. The liberty meant here is very concrete: release from debt and slavery, and the return of land.

commentary.on: each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family
commentary.text: Unlike Solon, Israel's law did give land back. Every family's ancestral land returned to it in the fiftieth year, so that no family could be permanently landless. The poor of Athens asked Solon for exactly this, and he refused.

commentary.on: According to the number of years after the Jubilee you shall buy from your neighbor
commentary.text: Land was not really sold, only leased until the jubilee. Its price depended on how many harvests were left. A few verses later God gives the reason: 'the land is mine; for you are strangers and live as foreigners with me' (25:23).

commentary.on: You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God
commentary.text: Here is the deepest difference. Solon appealed to justice and to the gods, but his laws were his own. The jubilee is grounded in God: the land and the people belong to him, so no one can own another Israelite for ever.

compare.why: At about the same time as Solon, Israel's law dealt with the same crisis of debt, land and slavery in a different way: not one great cancellation, but a release built into the calendar every fifty years.
compare.title: Liberty throughout the land

paras: Athens in the 590s BC was not unusual. All over the ancient world, small farmers borrowed seed and food in bad years, and if the harvest failed again they lost their land and then their freedom. In Mesopotamia, kings issued decrees, called misharum, cancelling debts and freeing debt-slaves when a new king came to the throne. In Israel the law limited debt-slavery to six years (Exodus 21:2) and set out the jubilee.

What made Athens dangerous was that the crisis was political as well as economic. The poor were citizens, they could fight, and they were organising. Elsewhere in Greece, crises like this had brought tyrants to power: Cypselus at Corinth, Theagenes at Megara. Solon's poems speak of the 'pillars' planted in the earth: these were probably marker-stones showing that land was pledged against a debt. When he says he uprooted them and made the black earth free, he is speaking literally.
sections.key: Debt-slavery was common in the ancient world; in Athens it threatened civil war and tyranny, as it had in other Greek cities.

paras: Solon's first law, the seisachtheia, did two things: it cancelled existing debts secured on land and persons, and it forbade loans on the security of the body for the future. Those sold abroad were brought home where possible. Ancient writers disagreed about how far the cancellation went, as Plutarch shows; most historians accept that the ban on debt-slavery itself is certain, because Solon boasts of it in his poems.

The historian Moses Finley made a sharp point about what followed. Once Athenians could no longer be enslaved by other Athenians, the rich needed labour from somewhere else, and over the next century Athens came to depend more and more on slaves bought from outside, Thracians, Scythians and others. Freedom for citizens and slavery for foreigners grew up together. It is one of the hard facts of the first democracy, and we will meet it again in the next session, still to come.
sections.key: Solon cancelled debts and banned debt-slavery for citizens for ever; but as citizen freedom grew, Athens came to rely on slaves bought abroad.

paras: Solon's second great change was to the constitution. He kept the old offices but changed who could hold them. Four classes were defined by the yearly harvest of their land: the 'five-hundred-measure men', the 'horsemen', the 'yoke-men' (those who could keep a pair of oxen) and the thetes, the labourers. Only the top classes could be archons; the thetes could attend the assembly and sit in the law courts.

Two other rights mattered more than they seemed. A citizen could appeal against a magistrate to a court of the people, and anyone could prosecute on behalf of someone wronged. Aristotle, as we will see in the next session, called these, with the ban on debt-slavery, the three most democratic things Solon did. The power of ordinary people grew from there, through the courts, until it was the power of the whole city.
sections.key: Solon replaced birth with wealth as the test for office, and gave the poorest citizens the assembly, the courts, the right of appeal and the right to defend others.

sections.h: Why he would not be tyrant
paras: The most remarkable thing about Solon is what he did not do. He had the trust of both sides and the power of a dictator. His friends told him it was only the name that frightened him. Plutarch reports his answer: tyranny is a pleasant place, but there is no way out of it. Once you rule by force, you must go on ruling by force, or be destroyed.

Solon also refused the poor's demand to share out the land again. In one of his poems he says he stood 'with his shield outstretched' over both sides, letting neither win unjustly. It satisfied no one, and he left. Then, in his old age, in 561 BC, his kinsman Peisistratus made himself tyrant after all, and the old man is said to have warned the Athenians in vain. A good constitution, it turned out, needs more than a good lawgiver. It needs citizens who will defend it. That is the problem this whole journey will keep returning to.
sections.key: Solon refused both tyranny and a new share-out of land, satisfying neither side; a generation later a tyrant took power anyway.

sections.h: Good order, in Solon's own words
paras: One of Solon's longest surviving poems, quoted by the orator Demosthenes, is about the city's good order, eunomia. Its argument, in our own words, is this: Athens will not be destroyed by the gods, who protect it, but by its own citizens, who are greedy and will not keep their hands off public and sacred property. Injustice brings slavery and civil war into every house; a lawless city is a sick city. But good order makes everything fit and wise, straightens crooked judgements and calms the pride of the powerful.

This is a new kind of thought. The city's fate is not simply in the hands of the gods; it is the citizens' own responsibility, and law is the remedy. That idea, that a people can choose order or disorder by how it governs itself, is the seed of everything that follows. Solon's own lines about the freed land, in Kenyon's translation, are this session's words to learn.
sections.key: Solon taught that a city is ruined not by the gods but by its citizens' injustice, and saved by good order under law.

paras: Not quite, and not with Solon. People had governed themselves in small ways long before: councils of elders in Israel and Mesopotamia, assemblies in Phoenician cities, the clan meetings of many peoples. The historian Thorkild Jacobsen argued in 1943 for a 'primitive democracy' in early Mesopotamia. And Solon's Athens was not yet a democracy: the offices stayed with the rich.

What the Greeks did invent was the idea and the word. Demokratia, from demos, 'the people', and kratos, 'power', first appears in the 400s BC. Athens was the first known state to make the whole body of its citizens, rich and poor, the final authority, to keep it that way for most of two centuries, and to argue openly about whether it was right. Solon laid the foundation; the building, as we will see in the next session, came later.
sections.key: Self-government in small forms is older than Greece; the Greeks invented the word demokratia and the first state in which the whole citizen body was sovereign.

sections.h: Solon and the jubilee side by side
paras: Athens and Israel faced the same crisis, and it is worth setting their answers side by side. Both ended slavery for debt among their own people, and both kept slavery for outsiders: Leviticus 25 allows Israelites to buy slaves from the nations around them (25:44–46), as Athens bought Thracians. Both put limits on the creditor. But they differ in three ways.

First, Solon acted once; the jubilee is a rhythm, built into the calendar, so that inequality is undone again every fifty years instead of waiting for the next crisis. Second, Solon refused to return land; the jubilee returns it, so that no family is landless for ever. Third, Solon's authority was his own and the people's consent; the jubilee rests on God's ownership: 'the land is mine' (25:23). Historians debate whether the jubilee was ever fully kept. Its ideal outlived it: the Liberty Bell, the abolitionists, and in the year 2000 the Jubilee campaign for the cancellation of poor countries' debts all took their words from this chapter.
sections.key: Both Solon and the jubilee ended debt-slavery among citizens; the jubilee made release a regular rhythm, returned land, and rested on God's ownership of the land.

refs: Plutarch, Life of Solon 13–18, 25, tr. A. Stewart and G. Long (1880); Aristotle, The Athenian Constitution 2–12, tr. F. G. Kenyon (1891).

Solon's poems: fragments 4 (Eunomia, quoted by Demosthenes, On the False Embassy 254–255) and 36 (quoted in The Athenian Constitution 12), numbered as in M. L. West, Iambi et Elegi Graeci (2nd edn, 1989–92).

debate.question: Was Solon the founder of democracy?

positions.name: Yes: he planted the seed
positions.who: The Athenian orators of the 300s BC; Lord Acton (1877)
positions.view: Solon gave the poor the assembly, the courts and the right of appeal, and made every citizen's freedom inviolable. Everything later democracy did grew from those rights. The Athenians themselves honoured him as the father of their laws.
positions.evidence: The Athenian Constitution 9 calls his reforms 'democratic'; the 4th-century orators cite 'the laws of Solon' for the whole democratic code.

positions.name: No: he was a moderate aristocrat
positions.who: Most modern historians, such as P. J. Rhodes
positions.view: Solon kept office in the hands of the rich and refused to share out the land. He was a mediator who wanted to save the existing order, not overturn it. Democracy proper began with Cleisthenes in 508/7 BC.
positions.evidence: The property classes; his own poems, which say he protected the rich as well as the poor; Herodotus (6.131) credits Cleisthenes with establishing democracy.

positions.name: He made it possible, not inevitable
positions.who: Many recent historians, such as Paul Cartledge
positions.view: Solon did not intend democracy, but by ending debt-slavery and giving the poor courts and appeal, he created citizens who could later claim power. Democracy needed his foundation and a later revolution.
positions.evidence: The tyranny of Peisistratus came after Solon, yet many of his laws survived it and were built on by Cleisthenes.

debate.agree: All agree that Solon ended debt-slavery for Athenians, gave the poorest citizens a voice, and refused to make himself tyrant.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art has no painting of Solon or of any Greek lawgiver, and we will not use a stand-in.

music.why: John Newton, a former slave-ship captain, wrote it after his conversion. It is a song about release that the singer did not earn: the same longing for freedom from bondage that drove the poor of Athens, and Israel's jubilee.

think.why: Solon freed Athenians from slavery for debt, but not the slaves Athens bought abroad. See the long story of how slavery was finally challenged.

learn.why: Solon's own words, written to defend his laws: he set the enslaved free, and gave equal laws to good and bad alike. Among the oldest words in Western political thought.

check.q: According to Plutarch, why did many Athenians think 'absolute despotism' was the only cure for their troubles?
options: Because the gap between rich and poor was so great that the city was on the verge of revolution
Because Draco's laws had been forgotten
Because Athens had just lost a war with Persia
Because Solon had demanded it
check.why: Plutarch says the state was on the verge of revolution because of 'the excessive poverty of some citizens, and the enormous wealth of others'.

check.q: Solon refused to share out the land again. What does this tell us about him?
options: He was secretly on the side of the rich
He did not care about the poor
He was following the law of the jubilee
He tried to protect both sides, freeing the enslaved without taking the land of the rich, and satisfied neither
check.why: He cancelled debts and banned debt-slavery, but refused redistribution; both sides were disappointed, which is why he left.

check.q: Which of Solon's laws lasted longest and mattered most for later democracy?
options: The four property classes
The ban on enslaving an Athenian for debt, with the right of appeal and of prosecuting for others
The rule that laws should last a hundred years
The repeal of Draco's murder laws
check.why: The property classes faded; the ban on debt-slavery, appeal to the courts and the right of anyone to prosecute for the wronged were the roots of popular power.

check.q: Why did Solon leave Athens for ten years?
options: He was afraid of Peisistratus
To fight in Egypt
He had been ostracised
So that the laws, not their author, would rule, and the people would get used to them
check.why: He did not want to be asked to change or explain every law; by leaving he let the laws stand on their own.

check.q: What is the biggest difference between Solon's reform and the jubilee of Leviticus 25?
options: The jubilee was a single cancellation, Solon's a recurring one
Solon freed foreign slaves too, while the jubilee freed only Israelites
The jubilee cancelled debts but Solon did not
Solon's was one great cancellation by a lawgiver; the jubilee built a regular release of land and debt-slaves into the calendar, grounded in God's ownership of the land
check.why: Solon acted once, by his own authority, and refused to return land; the jubilee returned land every fifty years because 'the land is mine', says God.

check.q: Why is it misleading to say simply that Solon 'invented democracy'?
options: Because offices stayed with the rich: he gave the poor a voice and rights, but the city was not yet ruled by the whole people
Because the Athenians themselves never credited him with anything democratic
Because the poor got the land redistribution they asked for, not political rights
Because he abolished the assembly and ruled through the Areopagus
check.why: Solon's Athens was a mixed order run by the wealthy; the people became sovereign only later, under Cleisthenes and after.

tutorial.question: Why did Solon refuse to become tyrant, and was he right?
tutorial.approach: Set out the crisis Solon faced and the case his friends made for taking power. Then give his reasons, from Plutarch and his own verses. Weigh what followed: within a generation Peisistratus made himself tyrant, and Solon's laws fell into disuse. Did his refusal fail, or did it succeed in the long run?
strong: Describes the debt crisis and the danger of civil war accurately.
States the friends' argument fairly: a good man with power might do more good than a divided assembly.
Uses Solon's own words, 'the best that they would endure' and his verses on sparing his country.
Explains why leaving Athens served the rule of law.
Considers the tyranny of Peisistratus and what it shows about laws and citizens.
Compares Solon's answer with the jubilee.

takeaways: Athens' first step towards democracy came from a crisis of debt, in which poor citizens were enslaved by their creditors.
Solon cancelled debts, banned debt-slavery and gave the poorest citizens the assembly, the courts and the right to defend others, but kept office for the rich.
He refused to make himself tyrant and left Athens so that the laws, not he, would rule; Israel's jubilee met the same crisis by returning land every fifty years.

sessions.title: How it worked
sessions.line: A revolution against a Spartan king, ten new tribes, an assembly of thousands on a hillside, offices filled by lottery, juries of hundreds, and a vote to send a man away.
sessions.plain: After Solon came a family of tyrants, and after them, in 508 BC, a revolution. A nobleman named Cleisthenes gave power to the people, and when a Spartan king tried to stop it, the people rose and drove him out. The democracy that followed was direct: citizens did not elect representatives but came to the assembly and voted themselves, and most officials were chosen by drawing lots. Juries of hundreds decided cases, and once a year the people could vote to exile anyone who seemed too powerful. But only adult male citizens could take part: women, foreigners and slaves, most of the people living in Athens, could not.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed how Solon freed the poor from slavery for debt and gave them a voice, but left power with the rich. A tyranny came after him anyway. This session shows how the Athenians finally made the people sovereign, and how their democracy actually worked, day by day. We need the machinery before we can judge it.
answers: How did Athenian democracy work?
Who could vote, and who could not?
Why did they choose officials by lottery?
What was ostracism?
Was it really a democracy if women and slaves were excluded?
sessions.finding: Athenian democracy was direct: the citizens themselves decided in the assembly, officials and the council were chosen by lot, juries of hundreds judged, and ostracism guarded against tyranny; but only adult male citizens, a small part of the population, could take part.

paras: In session 1, Solon cancelled debts, banned the enslaving of Athenians for debt and gave the poorest citizens a voice in the assembly and the courts. But he kept office for the rich, and he refused to make himself tyrant.

Others were less scrupulous. In 561 BC his kinsman Peisistratus seized power. He was driven out twice and came back twice, and ruled until his death in 527 BC, by most accounts mildly; he kept Solon's laws but made sure his friends held office. His sons Hippias and Hipparchus succeeded him. In 514 BC Hipparchus was murdered by two Athenians, Harmodius and Aristogeiton, later honoured as 'tyrant-slayers'. Hippias grew harsh, and in 510 BC the Spartans, the great military power of Greece, drove him out. Our reading begins with the struggle for power that followed.

background.key: After Solon, Athens had tyrants for half a century; when they fell in 510 BC, a struggle for power led to the revolution of 508/7 BC.

paras: Before we look at the machinery, we should be clear about who could use it. Only adult male citizens could vote, speak in the assembly, sit on juries or hold office. From 451 BC a citizen had to have an Athenian father and an Athenian mother. Estimates vary, but in the 300s BC there were perhaps 30,000 adult male citizens, and perhaps twice that before the great war with Sparta began in 431 BC.
The whole population of Attica was much larger, perhaps 250,000 or more. Most of it could not take part.

rows: Adult men with Athenian parents, rich and poor alike
Wives, daughters and mothers of citizens
None; they passed on citizenship, and had religious roles, but could not vote or speak in the assembly
Free foreigners living in Athens, many of them traders and craftsmen
None; they paid a special tax and served in the army and navy
Bought or captured people, many from Thrace and the Black Sea; perhaps tens of thousands
table.note: All numbers are estimates; ancient writers rarely counted women, children or slaves.

paras: The Athenian Constitution, which you met in session 1, has two halves. The first tells the history of the constitution from the earliest times to 403 BC. The second, from chapter 42, describes 'the present state of the constitution', in the 320s BC: how citizens were registered, how the council worked, how juries were chosen. It is the nearest thing we have to an official handbook of Athenian democracy, written by or for a philosopher who was himself not a citizen of Athens, but a metic from the north of Greece.
background.key: The Athenian Constitution tells the history of the democracy, then describes how it worked in the 320s BC: our best handbook.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the revolution of 508/7 BC and Cleisthenes' new tribes; the law of ostracism and how it was first used; and a description of citizenship, the council and the assembly in Aristotle's own day.

The comparison is from Plutarch's Lives: two stories of ostracism in action, one against Athens' greatest hero, one against a man nobody thought worth exiling. Together they show the best and worst of the most unusual vote in history.
background.key: Aristotle on the revolution, ostracism and the working democracy; then Plutarch on two ostracisms.
