paras: After the overthrow of the tyranny, the rival leaders in the state were Isagoras son of Tisander, a partisan of the tyrants, and Cleisthenes, who belonged to the family of the Alcmeonidae. Cleisthenes, being beaten in the political clubs, called in the people by giving the franchise to the masses. Thereupon Isagoras, finding himself left inferior in power, invited Cleomenes, who was united to him by ties of hospitality, to return to Athens, and persuaded him to 'drive out the pollution', a plea derived from the fact that the Alcmeonidae were suppposed to be under the curse of pollution. On this Cleisthenes retired from the country, and Cleomenes, entering Attica with a small force, expelled, as polluted, seven hundred Athenian families. Having effected this, he next attempted to dissolve the Council, and to set up Isagoras and three hundred of his partisans as the supreme power in the state. The Council, however, resisted, the populace flocked together, and Cleomenes and Isagoras, with their adherents, took refuge in the Acropolis. Here the people sat down and besieged them for two days; and on the third they agreed to let Cleomenes and all his followers depart, while they summoned Cleisthenes and the other exiles back to Athens. When the people had thus obtained the command of affairs, Cleisthenes was their chief and popular leader. And this was natural; for the Alcmeonidae were perhaps the chief cause of the expulsion of the tyrants, and for the greater part of their rule were at perpetual war with them. But even earlier than the attempts of the Alcmeonidae, one Cedon made an attack on the tyrants; when there came another popular drinking song, addressed to him:

Pour a health yet again, boy, to Cedon; forget not this duty to do,
If a health is an honour befitting the name of a good man and true.

The people, therefore, had good reason to place confidence in Cleisthenes. Accordingly, now that he was the popular leader, three years after the expulsion of the tyrants, in the archonship of Isagoras, his first step was to distribute the whole population into ten tribes in place of the existing four, with the object of intermixing the members of the different tribes, and so securing that more persons might have a share in the franchise. From this arose the saying 'Do not look at the tribes', addressed to those who wished to scrutinize the lists of the old families. Next he made the Council to consist of five hundred members instead of four hundred, each tribe now contributing fifty, whereas formerly each had sent a hundred. The reason why he did not organize the people into twelve tribes was that he might not have to use the existing division into trittyes; for the four tribes had twelve trittyes, so that he would not have achieved his object of redistributing the population in fresh combinations. Further, he divided the country into thirty groups of demes, ten from the districts about the city, ten from the coast, and ten from the interior.

These he called trittyes; and he assigned three of them by lot to each tribe, in such a way that each should have one portion in each of these three localities. All who lived in any given deme he declared fellow-demesmen, to the end that the new citizens might not be exposed by the habitual use of family names, but that men might be officially described by the names of their demes; and accordingly it is by the names of their demes that the Athenians speak of one another. He also instituted Demarchs, who had the same duties as the previously existing Naucrari,--the demes being made to take the place of the naucraries. He gave names to the demes, some from the localities to which they belonged, some from the persons who founded them, since some of the areas no longer corresponded to localities possessing names. On the other hand he allowed every one to retain his family and clan and religious rites according to ancestral custom. The names given to the tribes were the ten which the Pythia appointed out of the hundred selected national heroes.

By these reforms the constitution became much more democratic than that of Solon. The laws of Solon had been obliterated by disuse during the period of the tyranny, while Cleisthenes substituted new ones with the object of securing the goodwill of the masses. Among these was the law concerning ostracism. Four years after the establishment of this system, in the archonship of Hermocreon, they first imposed upon the Council of Five Hundred the oath which they take to the present day. Next they began to elect the generals by tribes, one from each tribe, while the Polemarch was the commander of the whole army. Then, eleven years later, in the archonship of Phaenippus they won the battle of Marathon; and two years after this victory, when the people had now gained self-confidence, they for the first time made use of the law of ostracism. This had originally been passed as a precaution against men in high office, because Pisistratus took advantage of his position as a popular leader and general to make himself tyrant; and the first person ostracized was one of his relatives, Hipparchus son of Charmus, of the deme of Collytus, the very person on whose account especially Cleisthenes had enacted the law, as he wished to get rid of him. Hitherto, however, he had escaped; for the Athenians, with the usual leniency of the democracy, allowed all the partisans of the tyrants, who had not joined in their evil deeds in the time of the troubles to remain in the city; and the chief and leader of these was Hipparchus. Then in the very next year, in the archonship of Telesinus, they for the first time since the tyranny elected, tribe by tribe, the nine Archons by lot out of the five hundred candidates selected by the demes, all the earlier ones having been elected by vote;

and in the same year Megacles son of Hippocrates, of the deme of Alopece, was ostracized. Thus for three years they continued to ostracize the friends of the tyrants, on whose account the law had been passed; but in the following year they began to remove others as well, including any one who seemed to be more powerful than was expedient. The first person unconnected with the tyrants who was ostracized was Xanthippus son of Ariphron. Two years later, in the archonship of Nicodemus, the mines of Maroneia were discovered, and the state made a profit of a hundred talents from the working of them. Some persons advised the people to make a distribution of the money among themselves, but this was prevented by Themistocles. He refused to say on what he proposed to spend the money, but he bade them lend it to the hundred richest men in Athens, one talent to each, and then, if the manner in which it was employed pleased the people, the expenditure should be charged to the state, but otherwise the state should receive the sum back from those to whom it was lent. On these terms he received the money and with it he had a hundred triremes built, each of the hundred individuals building one; and it was with these ships that they fought the battle of Salamis against the barbarians. About this time Aristides the son of Lysimachus was ostracized. Three years later, however, in the archonship of Hypsichides, all the ostracized persons were recalled, on account of the advance of the army of Xerxes; and it was laid down for the future that persons under sentence of ostracism must live between Geraestus and Scyllaeum, on pain of losing their civic rights irrevocably.

The present state of the constitution is as follows. The franchise is open to all who are of citizen birth by both parents. They are enrolled among the demesmen at the age of eighteen. On the occasion of their enrollment the demesmen give their votes on oath, first whether the candidates appear to be of the age prescribed by the law (if not, they are dismissed back into the ranks of the boys), and secondly whether the candidate is free born and of such parentage as the laws require. Then if they decide that he is not a free man, he appeals to the law-courts, and the demesmen appoint five of their own number to act as accusers; if the court decides that he has no right to be enrolled, he is sold by the state as a slave, but if he wins his case he has a right to be enrolled among the demesmen without further question. After this the Council examines those who have been enrolled, and if it comes to the conclusion that any of them is less than eighteen years of age, it fines the demesmen who enrolled him. When the youths (Ephebi) have passed this examination, their fathers meet by their tribes, and appoint on oath three of their fellow tribesmen, over forty years of age, who, in their opinion, are the best and most suitable persons to have charge of the youths; and of these the Assembly elects one from each tribe as guardian, together with a director, chosen from the general body of Athenians, to control the while. Under the charge of these persons the youths first of all make the circuit of the temples;

then they proceed to Piraeus, and some of them garrison Munichia and some the south shore. The Assembly also elects two trainers, with subordinate instructors, who teach them to fight in heavy armour, to use the bow and javelin, and to discharge a catapult. The guardians receive from the state a drachma apiece for their keep, and the youths four obols apiece. Each guardian receives the allowance for all the members of his tribe and buys the necessary provisions for the common stock (they mess together by tribes), and generally superintends everything. In this way they spend the first year. The next year, after giving a public display of their military evolutions, on the occasion when the Assembly meets in the theatre, they receive a shield and spear from the state; after which they patrol the country and spend their time in the forts. For these two years they are on garrison duty, and wear the military cloak, and during this time they are exempt from all taxes. They also can neither bring an action at law, nor have one brought against them, in order that they may have no excuse for requiring leave of absence; though exception is made in cases of actions concerning inheritances and wards of state, or of any sacrificial ceremony connected with the family. When the two years have elapsed they thereupon take their position among the other citizens. Such is the manner of the enrollment of the citizens and the training of the youths.

All the magistrates that are concerned with the ordinary routine of administration are elected by lot, except the Military Treasurer, the Commissioners of the Theoric fund, and the Superintendent of Springs. These are elected by vote, and hold office from one Panathenaic festival to the next. All military officers are also elected by vote.

The Council of Five Hundred is elected by lot, fifty from each tribe. Each tribe holds the office of Prytanes in turn, the order being determined by lot; the first four serve for thirty-six days each, the last six for thirty-five, since the reckoning is by lunar years. The Prytanes for the time being, in the first place, mess together in the Tholus, and receive a sum of money from the state for their maintenance; and, secondly, they convene the meetings of the Council and the Assembly. The Council they convene every day, unless it is a holiday, the Assembly four times in each prytany. It is also their duty to draw up the programme of the business of the Council and to decide what subjects are to be dealt with on each particular day, and where the sitting is to be held. They also draw up the programme for the meetings of the Assembly. One of these in each prytany is called the 'sovereign' Assembly; in this the people have to ratify the continuance of the magistrates in office, if they are performing their duties properly, and to consider the supply of corn and the defence of the country.

On this day, too, impeachments are introduced by those who wish to do so, the lists of property confiscated by the state are read, and also applications for inheritances and wards of state, so that nothing may pass unclaimed without the cognizance of any person concerned. In the sixth prytany, in addition to the business already stated, the question is put to the vote whether it is desirable to hold a vote of ostracism or not; and complaints against professional accusers, whether Athenian or aliens domiciled in Athens, are received, to the number of not more than three of either class, together with cases in which an individual has made some promise to the people and has not performed it. Another Assembly in each prytany is assigned to the hearing of petitions, and at this meeting any one is free, on depositing the petitioner's olive-branch, to speak to the people concerning any matter, public or private. The two remaining meetings are devoted to all other subjects, and the laws require them to deal with three questions connected with religion, three connected with heralds and embassies, and three on secular subjects. Sometimes questions are brought forward without a preliminary vote of the Assembly to take them into consideration.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC) or a student working under him, in his school at Athens, the Lyceum
parts.title: The people take power
parts.context: Hippias the tyrant has been driven out (510 BC). Two noblemen compete for power: Isagoras, backed by Sparta, and Cleisthenes, of the powerful Alcmeonid family. Cleomenes was one of Sparta's two kings. The 'pollution' was an old curse on Cleisthenes' family for a killing in the time of Kylon, whom you met in session 1. The 'political clubs' were the dining-societies through which nobles organised their supporters.
parts.plain: Beaten by his rival among the nobles, Cleisthenes turned to the people and offered them power. His rival called in the Spartan king, who expelled hundreds of families and tried to dissolve the council. The council refused, the people gathered, and they besieged the Spartans on the Acropolis until they left. Cleisthenes came back as the people's leader and reorganised Athens into ten new tribes, each mixing people from the city, the coast and the inland country, so that the old family loyalties were broken up.

commentary.on: called in the people by giving the franchise to the masses
commentary.text: Cleisthenes was a nobleman playing politics, and he lost among the nobles. So he did something new: he appealed to the whole people. Whatever his motives, the people took him at his word.

commentary.on: The Council, however, resisted, the populace flocked together
commentary.text: This is the moment democracy was born, and it was not a lawgiver's gift. When a foreign king tried to hand Athens to three hundred oligarchs, the council said no and ordinary Athenians, without a leader (Cleisthenes was in exile), besieged the Spartans until they gave up. The historian Josiah Ober calls it the 'Athenian Revolution'.

commentary.on: distribute the whole population into ten tribes in place of the existing four
commentary.text: The old four tribes were based on kinship, and noble families dominated them. Cleisthenes' ten new tribes were artificial, each made of three pieces from different parts of Attica. A tribe now brought together fishermen, farmers and townsmen who had never met. It was a deliberate break-up of local power.

commentary.on: Do not look at the tribes
commentary.text: A saying aimed at snobs checking family pedigrees. Under the new system your descent did not decide your standing.

commentary.on: officially described by the names of their demes
commentary.text: A deme was a village or district, about 140 in all. Citizens were now named by their deme rather than their father: 'Pericles of Cholargos', not only 'Pericles son of Xanthippus'. Your political identity came from where you belonged, not from whose son you were.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC) or a student working under him, in his school at Athens, the Lyceum
parts.title: Ostracism
parts.context: The next twenty-five years, which included the Persian invasions. Marathon (490 BC) was the battle where Athens defeated a Persian army; Salamis (480 BC), the sea battle that saved Greece from the Persian king Xerxes. An archonship is a year, named after that year's chief archon.
parts.plain: Cleisthenes' reforms made Athens much more democratic. Among his laws was ostracism: once a year the people could vote to send one man into exile for ten years. It was meant to stop anyone becoming a tyrant, and was first used in 487 BC against a relative of the old tyrants. Soon it was used against anyone thought too powerful. In the same years the archons began to be chosen by lot, and when a rich vein of silver was found, Themistocles persuaded the people to build a fleet instead of sharing out the money; that fleet won the battle of Salamis.

commentary.on: a precaution against men in high office, because Pisistratus took advantage of his position as a popular leader and general to make himself tyrant
commentary.text: Ostracism was designed against a specific danger: the popular leader who becomes a tyrant. Athens had seen it happen. Plato will describe exactly this path in session 5, still to come.

commentary.on: with the usual leniency of the democracy
commentary.text: An interesting remark. The writer, no friend of extreme democracy, still notes that the Athenians let the tyrants' supporters stay. Ostracism was a mild weapon: exile for ten years, with property kept and no disgrace attached.

commentary.on: any one who seemed to be more powerful than was expedient
commentary.text: Here is the danger in ostracism. It began as a guard against tyranny and became a way of removing anyone who stood out. Xanthippus, the first victim 'unconnected with the tyrants', was the father of Pericles.

commentary.on: elected, tribe by tribe, the nine Archons by lot out of the five hundred candidates selected by the demes
commentary.text: From 487 BC the archons, the old chief magistrates, were chosen by lot from a shortlist. Once office went to the lucky rather than the eminent, it lost its prestige, and real leadership moved to the ten generals, who were still elected.

commentary.on: it was with these ships that they fought the battle of Salamis against the barbarians
commentary.text: This matters for democracy. The fleet was rowed by the poorest citizens, the thetes. Having saved Greece at Salamis, they had a strong claim to power, and the democracy grew more radical as Athens became a sea power.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC) or a student working under him, in his school at Athens, the Lyceum
parts.title: The democracy at work
parts.context: Here the book jumps to its own time, the 320s BC, and describes the working constitution. Ephebi ('youths') were young citizens doing two years' military training. The Council of Five Hundred prepared business for the assembly; its members from one tribe at a time, the prytanes, served as a standing committee for a tenth of the year, called a prytany.
parts.plain: Citizenship was for those with two Athenian parents, checked by the deme at eighteen, with a jury deciding disputed cases. Young citizens did two years' military training. Most officials were chosen by lot; military officers and a few financial officers were elected. The Council of Five Hundred was chosen by lot, fifty from each tribe; each tribe's fifty took turns to run the council and the assembly. The assembly met four times in each prytany: once to review officials and debate food and defence, once for petitions from any citizen, and twice for other business.

commentary.on: The franchise is open to all who are of citizen birth by both parents
commentary.text: Since Pericles' law of 451/0 BC, both parents had to be Athenian. It made citizenship a privilege of birth again, and shut out the children of Athenian men and foreign women.

commentary.on: he is sold by the state as a slave
commentary.text: A hard sentence: a man who falsely claimed citizenship and lost his appeal was sold. Athenian freedom had a sharp edge for those outside it.

commentary.on: All the magistrates that are concerned with the ordinary routine of administration are elected by lot
commentary.text: To us, choosing officials by lottery sounds mad. To the Athenians it was the most democratic method of all. An election favours the rich, the famous and the good speakers; a lottery gives every citizen an equal chance. Aristotle says in the Politics that choosing by lot is thought democratic, and choosing by election oligarchic (IV.9).

commentary.on: All military officers are also elected by vote
commentary.text: But not for everything. Generals, and officials who handled large sums, were elected, because skill mattered too much to leave to chance. The Athenians knew exactly where expertise counted.

commentary.on: The Council of Five Hundred is elected by lot, fifty from each tribe
commentary.text: The council was the engine of the democracy, chosen by lot for a year at a time; a man could serve only twice in his life. Over a lifetime a large share of citizens served at least once, and for one day, by lot, one of them was chairman of the whole state.

commentary.on: the question is put to the vote whether it is desirable to hold a vote of ostracism or not
commentary.text: Ostracism was a two-step process. First the assembly voted whether to hold one at all; then, two months later, citizens scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery. If at least 6,000 votes were cast (on the usual ancient account), the man with most votes left the city.

commentary.on: any one is free, on depositing the petitioner's olive-branch, to speak to the people concerning any matter, public or private
commentary.text: Any citizen could address the people. The Greeks had words for this: isegoria, the equal right to speak, and parrhesia, frankness. The herald opened each debate by asking who wished to speak.

read.author: Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC) or a student working under him, in his school at Athens, the Lyceum

paras: XXII. As the Athenians, through his unpopularity, eagerly listened to any story to his discredit, he was obliged to weary them by constantly repeating the tale of his own exploits to them. In answer to those who were angry with him, he would ask, "Are you weary of always receiving benefits from the same hand?" He also vexed the people by building the Temple of Artemis of Good Counsel, as he called her, hinting that he had taken good counsel for the Greeks. This temple he placed close to his own house in Melite, at the place where at the present day the public executioner casts out the bodies of executed criminals, and the clothes and ropes of men who have hanged themselves. Even in our own times a small statue of Themistokles used to stand in the Temple of Artemis of Good Counsel; and he seems to have been a hero not only in mind, but in appearance. The Athenians made use of ostracism to banish him, in order to reduce his extravagant pretensions, as they always were wont to do in the case of men whom they thought over powerful and unfit for living in the equality of a democracy. For ostracism implied no censure, but was intended as a vent for envious feelings, which were satisfied by seeing the object of their hatred thus humbled.

There was at Athens one Hyperbolus, of the township of Peirithois, whom Thucydides mentions as a worthless man, and one who was constantly ridiculed by the comic dramatists. From his utter disregard of what was said of him, and his carelessness for his honour, which, though it was mere shameless impudence and apathy, was thought by some to show firmness and true courage, he was pleasing to no party, but frequently made use of by the people when they wished to have a scurrilous attack made upon those in power. At this time he was about to resort to the proceeding called ostracism, by which from time to time the Athenians force into exile those citizens who are remarkable for influence and power, rather because they envy them than because they fear them.

But as it was clear that one of the three, Nikias, Phaeax, and Alkibiades, would be ostracised, Alkibiades combined their several parties, arranged matters with Nikias, and turned the ostracism against Hyperbolus himself. Some say that it was not Nikias but Phaeax with whom Alkibiades joined interest, and that with the assistance of his political party he managed to expel Hyperbolus, who never expected any such treatment; for before that time this punishment had never been extended to low persons of no reputation, as Plato, the comic dramatist, says in the lines where he mentions Hyperbolus:

"Full worthy to be punished though he be,
Yet ostracism's not for such as he."

parts.author: Plutarch
parts.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
parts.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100
parts.title: The man who saved Greece
parts.context: Themistocles built the fleet and won the battle of Salamis in 480 BC. Within a decade, about 471 BC, the Athenians ostracised him. Plutarch, writing nearly six hundred years later, explains why.
parts.plain: Themistocles kept reminding the Athenians of his great deeds, and they grew tired of him. He built a temple near his house to 'Artemis of Good Counsel', as if to say his advice had saved Greece. So they ostracised him, as they did with anyone who seemed too great for a democracy. Plutarch says ostracism was not a punishment but a release for envy.

commentary.on: Are you weary of always receiving benefits from the same hand?
commentary.text: A great man's complaint about a free people: they are ungrateful. It is also a sign of why he was dangerous. A man who thinks the city owes him everything is halfway to thinking it should obey him.

commentary.on: men whom they thought over powerful and unfit for living in the equality of a democracy
commentary.text: This is the logic of ostracism. Democracy depends on rough equality among citizens; a man too great unbalances it. Aristotle compared it to cutting down the tallest ears of corn.

commentary.on: For ostracism implied no censure, but was intended as a vent for envious feelings
commentary.text: Plutarch's judgement is double-edged. Ostracism was not a criminal sentence, which made it mild. But it could be used against the best men simply because they were the best.

parts.author: Plutarch
parts.who: Plutarch (about AD 46 to after 119), a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans
parts.when: Chaeronea, in central Greece, about AD 100
parts.title: The last ostracism
parts.context: About 417 BC. Alcibiades and Nicias were the two leading politicians of Athens, bitter rivals. Hyperbolus was a lamp-maker turned popular speaker, who hoped an ostracism would remove one of them. Plato here is not the philosopher but a comic playwright of the same name.
parts.plain: Hyperbolus, a man mocked by everyone, called for an ostracism, expecting Nicias or Alcibiades to go. Instead the two rivals combined their supporters and voted Hyperbolus out. Everyone thought it absurd to use ostracism on so small a man, and it was never used again.

commentary.on: frequently made use of by the people when they wished to have a scurrilous attack made upon those in power
commentary.text: Hyperbolus was one of the 'demagogues', the popular speakers who led the assembly after Pericles. You will meet more of them in sessions 3 and 4, still to come.

commentary.on: Alkibiades combined their several parties, arranged matters with Nikias, and turned the ostracism against Hyperbolus himself
commentary.text: The safeguard had become a game. Two powerful men, who should each have feared it, organised their followers to use it on a third. A device meant to protect the people was captured by the very people it was meant to restrain.

commentary.on: Yet ostracism's not for such as he.
commentary.text: After this, the Athenians never held another ostracism. They used prosecutions in the courts instead, which, as we will see, were not always gentler.

compare.author: Plutarch
compare.why: Aristotle gives the law. Plutarch shows what it did in practice: once against the hero who saved Greece, and once, the last time it was ever used, against a man nobody thought worth exiling.
compare.title: Ostracism in action

paras: Older histories gave the credit for democracy to Cleisthenes, as if a wise nobleman had handed the people a constitution. Josiah Ober has argued that the key moment was the uprising of 508/7 BC: when Cleomenes and Isagoras tried to install an oligarchy, the council refused and the people besieged them on the Acropolis, with no leader at all. Cleisthenes' reforms, on this view, gave lasting form to a power the people had already shown.

Either way, the result was a new idea: that the people as a whole, the demos, could govern. Herodotus, writing a generation later, said that Athens, freed from tyrants, became the first power in Greece, because free men work for themselves while slaves of a tyrant hold back.
sections.key: Democracy began in a popular uprising in 508/7 BC, given lasting form by Cleisthenes' reforms.

paras: The heart of the democracy was the assembly, the ekklesia, open to every adult male citizen. It met about forty times a year, on the Pnyx, a hillside west of the Acropolis, where several thousand men could sit; some business required a quorum of 6,000. It decided war and peace, treaties, laws (from the late 400s through a special board), taxes and honours. Anyone could propose a motion and anyone could speak. Votes were taken by a show of hands.

This was direct democracy. There were no parties and no representatives: the citizens voted on the questions themselves. From about 400 BC, citizens were paid a small sum to attend, so that the poor could afford to come. The Greek word ekklesia, 'those called out', was later taken by the first Christians as their word for the church.
sections.key: The assembly of all male citizens met about forty times a year on the Pnyx and decided everything directly, by show of hands.

paras: Most of the roughly seven hundred officials of Athens, and the Council of Five Hundred, were chosen by lot from volunteers. To prevent cheating, the Athenians later used an allotment machine, the kleroterion: a stone slab with rows of slots for citizens' name tokens, and a tube down which coloured balls were dropped to choose rows at random. Fragments survive in the Agora Museum in Athens.

Why the lot? Because the Athenians thought elections favoured the few: they favour the rich, the famous and the persuasive. The lot treats every citizen as equally fit. Office was held for one year, usually only once, and every official was examined before and audited after. The exceptions prove the rule: generals and some financial officers were elected, and could be re-elected, because their work needed skill. Pericles was elected general fifteen years running.
sections.key: Most officials and the council were chosen by lot, because election favours the few; generals and financial officers, whose work needed skill, were elected.

paras: Every year 6,000 citizens over thirty were enrolled as jurors. Panels of 201, 501 or more, chosen by lot on the morning of the trial so that no one could be bribed in advance, heard cases and voted by secret ballot, with bronze tokens. There were no professional judges and no lawyers: each side spoke for itself, timed by a water-clock. From the 450s BC jurors were paid, on Pericles' proposal, so that poor men could serve.

The courts were where Solon's right of appeal had grown into the people's power. They tried officials, reviewed laws and settled private disputes. They were also, as Aristotle said, where the people were 'master of the constitution'. In 399 BC a jury of 501 citizens tried a philosopher named Socrates. We will come to that in session 5, still to come.
sections.key: Huge juries of ordinary citizens, chosen by lot on the day and paid for their time, decided cases and controlled officials.

paras: Ostracism is one place where archaeology meets the texts. More than ten thousand ostraka, the broken pieces of pottery on which votes were scratched, have been found in Athens, many in a single dump in the Kerameikos district excavated in the 1960s. Many carry famous names: Megacles, Aristides, Pericles, Themistocles. Some add insults.

One find raises a question. In a well on the north slope of the Acropolis, the archaeologist Oscar Broneer found 190 ostraka against Themistocles in the 1930s, written by only a handful of hands. They were probably prepared in advance and handed out to voters, perhaps to men who could not write. Was this organised campaigning, or fraud? Historians disagree. The ostraka also show something the texts do not: many ordinary Athenians could write a name, even if badly spelled.
sections.key: Over ten thousand ostraka confirm the texts; a batch of 190 against Themistocles, in a few hands, shows votes being organised.

paras: Here is the hard question. If most people living in Athens could not vote, was it a democracy at all? Critics say no: it was a club of male citizens, living off the labour of slaves and of an empire of allied cities who paid tribute. Women had no political voice. Metics who lived there for generations never became citizens. Slaves were property.

Defenders reply that for its members it was the most democratic state there has ever been: poor citizens had exactly the same vote as rich ones, could speak in the assembly, sit on juries and hold office by lot. No modern democracy gives an ordinary citizen that much direct power. Both things are true. Athens took a great step by including the poor, and stopped short of including everyone. Some Athenians imagined going further: in Aristophanes' comedy Women in Assembly (about 391 BC), the women take over the assembly; it was written as a joke.

rows: Adult male citizens with two Athenian parents
Almost all adult citizens, women and men
Directly, by the citizens in assembly
Mostly by lot, for one year
By election, or appointment of professionals
Citizen juries of hundreds, no professional judges
Professional judges, with small juries for some cases
Little: the assembly's will was final
Constitutions, courts and bills of rights limit the majority
table.note: The comparison is simplified; modern democracies differ widely among themselves.

sections.key: For its citizens Athens was more democratic than any modern state; but it excluded women, foreigners and slaves, and rested partly on slavery and empire.

paras: Aristotle later defined a citizen as someone who shares in judging and in holding office (Politics III.1), and a good citizen as one who knows how both to rule and to be ruled. Athens tried to make that literal. With hundreds of offices filled by lot each year, five hundred councillors who could serve only twice, and six thousand jurors, a large share of citizens held some public office at some point in their lives. Mogens Hansen has estimated that most citizens over thirty served at least once on the council.

This had a cost and a benefit. The cost was amateurism: officials served for a year and went home, and real expertise sat with the elected generals and with the clerks, many of them public slaves. The benefit was a citizen body that knew from experience how its government worked. When Pericles said, in the funeral oration you read in 'How we got here', that Athenians who took no part in public life were thought not quiet but useless, he was describing a city in which taking turns to govern was simply part of being a citizen.
sections.key: Athens made citizenship mean ruling and being ruled in turn: through the lot, most citizens held office at some point, at the cost of amateurism and the gain of experience.

refs: Aristotle, The Athenian Constitution 20–22, 42–43, 63–69 (the courts), tr. F. G. Kenyon (1891); Aristotle, Politics IV.9 (1294b, election and the lot).
Herodotus 5.66–78 (Cleisthenes and Cleomenes; 5.78 on freedom); 6.131.
Plutarch, Life of Themistocles 22; Life of Aristides 7; Life of Alcibiades 13.

Josiah Ober, 'The Athenian Revolution of 508/7 BCE', in The Athenian Revolution (1996); Mogens Herman Hansen, The Athenian Democracy in the Age of Demosthenes (1991), on numbers, the assembly and the courts.

O. Broneer, 'Excavations on the North Slope of the Acropolis, 1937', Hesperia 7 (1938), on the Themistocles ostraka; S. Brenne, Ostrakismos und Prominenz in Athen (2001); Aristophanes, Ecclesiazusae (about 391 BC).
M. I. Finley, Democracy Ancient and Modern (1973).

debate.question: Was Athens a real democracy?

positions.name: Yes: the most democratic state there has been
positions.who: Mogens Hansen; Josiah Ober
positions.view: Among its citizens, Athens achieved a degree of self-government no modern state has matched: the poor ruled alongside the rich, directly, and power was spread by lot. It was not perfect, but it was real, and it worked for nearly two centuries.
positions.evidence: The assembly of all citizens; the lot; pay for office; the survival of the democracy from 508 to 322 BC, with two short oligarchic interruptions.

positions.name: No: a privileged men's club
positions.who: Many modern critics of Athens; in part M. I. Finley
positions.view: A state in which most residents had no voice, and which depended on slaves and on tribute from subject cities, cannot be called rule by the people. Calling it the birth of democracy flatters it.
positions.evidence: The exclusion of women, metics and slaves; the citizenship law of 451 BC; the tribute of the Athenian empire.

positions.name: Judge it by its time
positions.who: Paul Cartledge, among others
positions.view: Every society before the modern age excluded women and accepted slavery. What was new at Athens was the inclusion of the poor. It was a democracy in its own terms, and different from ours; both the achievement and the exclusions should be seen clearly.
positions.evidence: No other ancient state gave its poorest free men equal political power; Greek critics of democracy objected precisely to that.

debate.agree: All agree that Athens gave political power to poor citizens on equal terms with the rich, and excluded women, foreigners and slaves.

look.why: Sanford Robinson Gifford painted the Acropolis of Athens in 1880. The temples on it were built by the democracy in its greatest years; the assembly met on the Pnyx, a hill a short walk to the west. The painting shows the hill as Gifford saw it: in ruins, in soft pink light.
points: A wide, brightly lit field scattered with broken pieces of stone, framed left and right by crumbling stone temples.
On the left, a temple on a low rise with a row of at least nine columns; several are broken, and the roof is missing.
Fragments of pediments and wheel-like sections of columns tumble across the field.
Two small figures in the centre, inspecting the fragments: one in an orange suit and bowler hat kneels to write or sketch; the other wears a white pleated tunic and red cap.
On the right, columns carved as six identical robed women, and beyond, a plain, a blue sea and distant mountains under a pink haze.

music.why: Vaughan Williams's Fantasia takes a simple hymn tune by Thomas Tallis and lets it pass between a large string orchestra, a smaller one and a quartet, answering one another. Listen for many voices taking turns to lead a single theme.

think.why: Athens counted every male citizen equally, but not everyone was a citizen. See how the West came to believe that every single person counts.

learn.why: You learned Pericles' words over the Athenian dead in 'How we got here'. Say them again now that you know the democracy those citizen-soldiers voted in and died for.

check.q: Why did Cleisthenes mix the population into ten new tribes, each with parts from the city, the coast and the inland country?
options: Because the Delphic oracle ordered ten tribes
To prepare for war with Persia
To make tax collection easier
To break up the local and family loyalties through which noble families controlled their followers
check.why: Mixing districts into artificial tribes broke the old networks of kinship and patronage, so 'more persons might have a share in the franchise'.

check.q: Why did the Athenians choose most officials by lot rather than by election?
options: Elections were too slow for a large city
Lots made sure the most experienced men were chosen
Elections favour the rich, famous and persuasive; the lot gives every citizen an equal chance
Officials had no real power
check.why: Aristotle says the lot is thought democratic and election oligarchic; equality of chance was the point.

check.q: The generals were elected, not chosen by lot. What does this show?
options: That war was thought too sacred for the lot
That the people did not trust the generals
That the Athenians knew some jobs needed skill and experience too much to leave to chance
That Athens was secretly an aristocracy
check.why: Where expertise mattered most, war and large sums of money, the Athenians used election.

check.q: Ostracism was designed against which danger?
options: A popular leader becoming a tyrant, as Peisistratus had
Corrupt judges
Rich men refusing to pay taxes
Foreign spies
check.why: The law was passed 'as a precaution against men in high office, because Pisistratus took advantage of his position as a popular leader... to make himself tyrant'.

check.q: What does the last ostracism, of Hyperbolus, suggest about the institution?
options: That Hyperbolus was planning a tyranny
That a safeguard against the powerful could be captured and used by the powerful against a weaker man
That the Athenians had stopped voting
That it worked perfectly
check.why: Nicias and Alcibiades combined their followers to turn it on Hyperbolus; it was never used again.

check.q: Which is the fairest reply to 'Athens was not a democracy because women and slaves could not vote'?
options: Women and metics could vote in the council, though not in the assembly
It is true that most residents were excluded; what was new was that poor male citizens had equal power with the rich, and both facts should be held together
Exclusions do not matter, because the assembly decided for everyone
Athens was not a democracy at all, since only the rich held power
check.why: The exclusions were real and large; the inclusion of the poor was also real and without precedent.

tutorial.question: Was Athens a democracy?
tutorial.approach: Describe the main institutions (assembly, council, lot, courts, ostracism) with evidence from the reading. Then set out who was excluded and why. Compare Athens with a modern democracy on two or three points. Decide what you think the word 'democracy' should require.
strong: Describes the assembly, lot, council, courts and ostracism accurately, with references.
Explains why the Athenians preferred the lot for most offices and election for generals.
Gives the exclusions honestly: women, metics, slaves, and the citizenship law of 451 BC.
Uses the archaeological evidence of the ostraka.
Compares Athenian direct democracy with modern representative democracy.
Reaches a clear, argued judgement.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Athens trusted ordinary citizens with real decisions. Find one decision in your street, workplace, church or club where people affected have no say, and ask one of them what they think before you act.
sessions.reflect: If you were chosen by lot tomorrow to help run your town for a year, would you feel able to do it? What would you need?
takeaways: Athenian democracy began with the revolution of 508/7 BC and Cleisthenes' ten tribes, which broke up the power of noble families.
It was direct: citizens decided in the assembly, most officials and the council were chosen by lot, juries of hundreds judged, and ostracism guarded against tyranny.
Only adult male citizens, a small part of the population, could take part; women, metics and slaves were excluded.

sessions.title: At its best: the first citizen
sessions.line: A plague, a war going badly, an angry people, and a leader who tells them they are wrong. Thucydides on what made Pericles great, and what happened without him.
sessions.plain: In 430 BC Athens was at war with Sparta, its farms burned, its people crowded inside the walls and dying of plague. They turned on Pericles, the statesman who had led them into the war, and fined him. He answered them in the assembly without flattery, and within months they elected him again. The historian Thucydides, who lived through it, judged that Athens was at its best when Pericles led it, because he could lead the people instead of following them: 'what was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen'. After Pericles died, his successors competed for the crowd's favour, and Athens made blunder after blunder until it lost the war.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed the machinery of democracy: assembly, lot, courts and ostracism. But machinery does not run itself. Thucydides, who knew the democracy from inside, thought what mattered most was leadership. This session asks what kind of leader a democracy needs, and what happens when it does not have one.
answers: What made Pericles a great leader?
Was Athens under Pericles really a democracy?
What went wrong after Pericles died?
What does a democracy need from its leaders?
sessions.finding: Thucydides judged that Athens was at its best under Pericles, who could tell the people what they did not want to hear, so that 'what was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen'; without such leaders, private ambition and the whims of the crowd ruined it.

paras: In session 1, Solon ended debt-slavery and gave the poor a voice. In session 2, the revolution of 508/7 BC made the people sovereign, through the assembly, the lot and the courts. Then came the Persian invasions, which Athens and Sparta together drove back (490 and 480–479 BC).

After the Persian wars Athens led a league of Greek cities against Persia, with a common treasury on the island of Delos. Gradually the league became an Athenian empire: in 454 BC the treasury moved to Athens, and allies who tried to leave were forced back. The tribute paid for the fleet, rowed by poor citizens, and for the temples on the Acropolis. Sparta and its allies watched Athens' power grow with alarm. In 431 BC war broke out: the Peloponnesian War, which lasted, with a break, until 404 BC.

timeline.text: The Delian League is founded under Athenian leadership
Ephialtes, with the young Pericles, strips the Areopagus of its powers
The league treasury is moved to Athens
The Parthenon is built
Pericles is elected general every year
War with Sparta begins; Pericles' funeral oration
Plague in Athens; Pericles is fined, then re-elected
Pericles dies of the plague
The Sicilian expedition ends in disaster
Athens surrenders to Sparta

background.key: Athens turned its league against Persia into an empire; war with Sparta came in 431 BC and lasted, with a break, until Athens surrendered in 404 BC.

paras: Pericles (about 495–429 BC) came from the old nobility: his mother was a niece of Cleisthenes. Yet he made his career as the leader of the people. He helped strip the old council of the Areopagus of its political powers in 462/1 BC, introduced pay for jurors so that the poor could serve, proposed the law of 451/0 BC limiting citizenship to those with two Athenian parents, and directed the building of the Parthenon. From 443 BC he was elected one of the ten generals every year until his death.

He was famous for his calm and his oratory; comic poets nicknamed him 'the Olympian', like Zeus. He held no office above any other general. His power came entirely from persuasion and re-election. In 'How we got here' you read his funeral oration of 431 BC, the most famous praise of democracy ever spoken. Here we read what happened a year later.
background.key: Pericles, an aristocrat who led the people, held no special office: his power came from persuasion and from being re-elected general fifteen years running.

paras: Thucydides, son of Olorus, was an Athenian who caught the plague and survived. In 424 BC, as a general, he failed to save the city of Amphipolis from the Spartans and was exiled for twenty years, which gave him time and access to both sides. He set out to write the history of the war from its start, promising accuracy rather than entertainment.

He was not neutral. He admired Pericles and despised Cleon, the popular leader who may have been behind his exile. Our main passage, II.65, looks back from the end of the war, after 404 BC: it is a verdict written with hindsight. Historians take it seriously and question it.
background.key: Thucydides was an exiled Athenian general who wrote the war's history; he admired Pericles, disliked his successors, and wrote II.65 after the war was lost.

paras: The main reading has two parts: the opening of Pericles' last speech, in 430 BC, where he answers the people's anger; and Thucydides' verdict on Pericles and his successors.

The comparison is from the book of Proverbs, Israel's collection of wisdom for kings and ordinary people. It asks the same question from another tradition: what does the character of a ruler do to a people?
background.key: Pericles answers an angry people; Thucydides judges him; then Proverbs on rulers.

before: What four qualities does Pericles claim for himself?
What, according to Thucydides, did Pericles do that his successors did not?
Why does Thucydides say Athens lost the war in the end?
sessions.readWhy: Pericles' answer to an angry assembly, and Thucydides' verdict on him and on the leaders who came after.

paras: “I was not unprepared for the indignation of which I have been the object, as I know its causes; and I have called an assembly for the purpose of reminding you upon certain points, and of protesting against your being unreasonably irritated with me, or cowed by your sufferings. I am of opinion that national greatness is more for the advantage of private citizens, than any individual well-being coupled with public humiliation. A man may be personally ever so well off, and yet if his country be ruined he must be ruined with it; whereas a flourishing commonwealth always affords chances of salvation to unfortunate individuals. Since then a state can support the misfortunes of private citizens, while they cannot support hers, it is surely the duty of every one to be forward in her defence, and not like you to be so confounded with your domestic afflictions as to give up all thoughts of the common safety, and to blame me for having counselled war and yourselves for having voted it. And yet if you are angry with me, it is with one who, as I believe, is second to no man either in knowledge of the proper policy, or in the ability to expound it, and who is moreover not only a patriot but an honest one. A man possessing that knowledge without that faculty of exposition might as well have no idea at all on the matter: if he had both these gifts, but no love for his country, he would be but a cold advocate for her interests; while were his patriotism not proof against bribery, everything would go for a price. So that if you thought that I was even moderately distinguished for these qualities when you took my advice and went to war, there is certainly no reason now why I should be charged with having done wrong.

Such were the arguments by which Pericles tried to cure the Athenians of their anger against him and to divert their thoughts from their immediate afflictions. As a community he succeeded in convincing them; they not only gave up all idea of sending to Lacedaemon, but applied themselves with increased energy to the war; still as private individuals they could not help smarting under their sufferings, the common people having been deprived of the little that they were possessed, while the higher orders had lost fine properties with costly establishments and buildings in the country, and, worst of all, had war instead of peace. In fact, the public feeling against him did not subside until he had been fined. Not long afterwards, however, according to the way of the multitude, they again elected him general and committed all their affairs to his hands, having now become less sensitive to their private and domestic afflictions, and understanding that he was the best man of all for the public necessities.

For as long as he was at the head of the state during the peace, he pursued a moderate and conservative policy; and in his time its greatness was at its height. When the war broke out, here also he seems to have rightly gauged the power of his country. He outlived its commencement two years and six months, and the correctness of his previsions respecting it became better known by his death. He told them to wait quietly, to pay attention to their marine, to attempt no new conquests, and to expose the city to no hazards during the war, and doing this, promised them a favourable result. What they did was the very contrary, allowing private ambitions and private interests, in matters apparently quite foreign to the war, to lead them into projects unjust both to themselves and to their allies—projects whose success would only conduce to the honour and advantage of private persons, and whose failure entailed certain disaster on the country in the war. The causes of this are not far to seek.

Pericles indeed, by his rank, ability, and known integrity, was enabled to exercise an independent control over the multitude—in short, to lead them instead of being led by them; for as he never sought power by improper means, he was never compelled to flatter them, but, on the contrary, enjoyed so high an estimation that he could afford to anger them by contradiction. Whenever he saw them unseasonably and insolently elated, he would with a word reduce them to alarm; on the other hand, if they fell victims to a panic, he could at once restore them to confidence. In short, what was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen. With his successors it was different. More on a level with one another, and each grasping at supremacy, they ended by committing even the conduct of state affairs to the whims of the multitude. This, as might have been expected in a great and sovereign state, produced a host of blunders, and amongst them the Sicilian expedition;

though this failed not so much through a miscalculation of the power of those against whom it was sent, as through a fault in the senders in not taking the best measures afterwards to assist those who had gone out, but choosing rather to occupy themselves with private cabals for the leadership of the commons, by which they not only paralysed operations in the field, but also first introduced civil discord at home. Yet after losing most of their fleet besides other forces in Sicily, and with faction already dominant in the city, they could still for three years make head against their original adversaries, joined not only by the Sicilians, but also by their own allies nearly all in revolt, and at last by the King’s son, Cyrus, who furnished the funds for the Peloponnesian navy. Nor did they finally succumb till they fell the victims of their own intestine disorders. So superfluously abundant were the resources from which the genius of Pericles foresaw an easy triumph in the war over the unaided forces of the Peloponnesians.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through
parts.when: Athens and exile, written between 431 and about 400 BC
parts.title: A leader answers his critics
parts.context: Summer 430 BC. A Spartan army has ravaged the farms of Attica for the second year running, while the Athenians shelter behind their walls on Pericles' advice. Plague has broken out in the crowded city. The people blame Pericles and have sent envoys to Sparta to ask for peace, which Sparta refused. Pericles, as general, calls an assembly. Thucydides, as was usual for ancient historians, writes the speech in his own words, keeping as closely as he could to what was actually said.
parts.plain: Pericles says: I expected your anger. But a man cannot prosper if his country is ruined, and a strong country can rescue its unlucky citizens. So it is your duty to defend it instead of giving up because of your private troubles, and blaming me for a war you yourselves voted for. You are angry with someone who knows what policy is needed, can explain it, loves his country and cannot be bribed. If you thought I had those qualities when you took my advice, you should not blame me now.

commentary.on: I was not unprepared for the indignation of which I have been the object
commentary.text: Pericles begins by admitting the people are angry with him, and refusing to apologise. A demagogue would have flattered them. He scolds them.

commentary.on: A man may be personally ever so well off, and yet if his country be ruined he must be ruined with it
commentary.text: His argument is about the common good. Private suffering is real, but the city is what keeps every private life safe. This is the heart of ancient civic thought: you are a citizen before you are a private person.

commentary.on: to blame me for having counselled war and yourselves for having voted it
commentary.text: A sharp reminder of how democracy works. The assembly voted for the war. In a democracy the people cannot simply blame their leaders for decisions they made themselves.

commentary.on: second to no man either in knowledge of the proper policy, or in the ability to expound it, and who is moreover not only a patriot but an honest one
commentary.text: Pericles lists four qualities: knowledge, the power to explain it, love of country and honesty. Each without the others is useless, he goes on: knowledge without words is silent, words without patriotism are cold, and patriotism that can be bribed sells everything. It is still one of the best short descriptions of what a democracy needs in a leader.

commentary.on: everything would go for a price
commentary.text: Corruption is the end of all public life. A leader who can be bought turns the city into a market.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through
parts.when: Athens and exile, written between 431 and about 400 BC
parts.title: The first citizen and his successors
parts.context: Thucydides now steps back from the story and gives his own judgement. The passage looks ahead to the end of the war: it mentions the Sicilian expedition of 415–413 BC, the help Persia's prince Cyrus gave Sparta, and Athens' final defeat in 404 BC. So it was written, or revised, after the war was over.
parts.plain: The Athenians fined Pericles but soon re-elected him. Thucydides explains why he was the right leader: in peace his policy was moderate, and in war he judged Athens' strength correctly, telling them to defend, keep the fleet strong and not try to conquer more. Because he never sought power by improper means, he did not need to flatter the people; he could calm them when they were overconfident and encourage them when they panicked. So Athens was in name a democracy but in fact ruled by its first citizen. His successors, more equal to one another and each wanting to be first, handed policy to the whims of the crowd. Private ambition led to blunders like the Sicilian expedition, and in the end Athens fell through its own quarrels.

commentary.on: according to the way of the multitude, they again elected him general and committed all their affairs to his hands
commentary.text: 'The way of the multitude': quick to anger, quick to forgive. Thucydides is not contemptuous here. The people punished their leader, then saw they needed him. A democracy can correct itself.

commentary.on: to attempt no new conquests, and to expose the city to no hazards during the war
commentary.text: Pericles' strategy was patience: stay behind the walls, use the navy, wait for Sparta to tire. It was not glamorous, and it was hard to sell to people watching their farms burn.

commentary.on: allowing private ambitions and private interests
commentary.text: Thucydides' diagnosis of decline: leaders who served themselves rather than the city. It is the same thing Aristotle would call the mark of a corrupt constitution: rule for one's own good, not the common good.

commentary.on: to lead them instead of being led by them
commentary.text: The key phrase. A democratic leader can either follow public feeling or shape it. Pericles shaped it.

commentary.on: he could afford to anger them by contradiction
commentary.text: Because his power did not depend on flattery, he could tell the people unwelcome truths. The freedom to disagree with your own voters is, for Thucydides, the mark of a real leader.

commentary.on: what was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen
commentary.text: The most famous sentence on Pericles. It is praise, but it is also a puzzle. Was Athens at its best when it was least a democracy? Some readers think Thucydides is saying democracy works only when it is not really democracy. Others think he means a democracy needs leaders whom the people freely trust.

commentary.on: they ended by committing even the conduct of state affairs to the whims of the multitude
commentary.text: After Pericles, leaders competed for the crowd's favour. Each promised more. The assembly, no longer led, followed its passions. The next session, still to come, shows one such day.

commentary.on: Nor did they finally succumb till they fell the victims of their own intestine disorders
commentary.text: 'Intestine' means internal. Athens was not beaten mainly by Sparta, Thucydides says, but by its own divisions. It is a warning he meant for every free people.

read.author: Thucydides
read.who: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through
read.when: Athens and exile, written between 431 and about 400 BC

paras:
When the righteous thrive, the people rejoice;
but when the wicked rule, the people groan.

The king by justice makes the land stable,
but he who takes bribes tears it down.

If a ruler listens to lies,
all of his officials are wicked.

The king who fairly judges the poor,
his throne shall be established forever.

Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint;
but one who keeps the law is blessed.

parts.title: A ruler and his people
parts.context: Proverbs is a collection of short sayings, many credited to King Solomon (about 970–930 BC). Chapters 25–29 are introduced as proverbs of Solomon copied by the men of King Hezekiah of Judah, around 700 BC (Proverbs 25:1). Many were sayings for those who served at court: advice for rulers and those around them.

commentary.on: When the righteous thrive, the people rejoice; but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
commentary.text: The same insight as Thucydides: the character of those in power is felt by everyone. 'The righteous' are those who live by God's justice, not simply the clever.

commentary.on: he who takes bribes tears it down
commentary.text: Pericles' fourth quality, honesty, is here too. A ruler who can be bought destroys the land he rules.

commentary.on: If a ruler listens to lies, all of his officials are wicked.
commentary.text: A shrewd observation about power: courtiers say what the ruler wants to hear. In a democracy the people are the ruler, and the flatterers are the demagogues.

commentary.on: The king who fairly judges the poor, his throne shall be established forever.
commentary.text: Here Proverbs goes beyond Thucydides. The test of a ruler is not only good strategy, but justice to the poor.

commentary.on: Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint
commentary.text: Older English Bibles put it: 'Where there is no vision, the people perish.' The Hebrew means prophetic vision or revelation: without a word from God, a people 'runs wild'. Thucydides blamed the loss of a great leader; Proverbs blames the loss of a guiding word above any leader.

compare.why: Thucydides thought a city's fortune depended on its leaders' character. Israel's book of Proverbs says the same, in a few lines, and adds something Thucydides does not: the ruler is answerable to God.
compare.title: When the righteous rule

paras: Thucydides' praise of Pericles rests on one idea: a democratic leader must be able to say no to the people. Pericles could do so because his power came from trust, not favours. He was rich, but famously incorruptible; Plutarch says he never added a drachma to the fortune his father left him.

Notice that Thucydides does not say Pericles overrode the democracy. He held the same office as nine other generals, was elected every year, and could be fined and was. Every decision was still voted by the assembly. What he had was authority: the people listened to him. That is why the sentence about 'government by the first citizen' is so interesting. Thucydides found the best democracy to be one guided by a single trusted voice.
sections.key: Pericles held no special office; his authority came from trust and incorruptibility, which let him tell the people unwelcome truths.

paras: The Athens Pericles led was rich and powerful, and part of the reason was its empire. Some 150 or more allied cities paid tribute; the money built the fleet and paid for the Parthenon. Pericles was frank about it. In his last speech, which we have just read in part, he tells the Athenians: 'what you hold is, to speak somewhat plainly, a tyranny; to take it perhaps was wrong, but to let it go is unsafe' (II.63).

This is the uncomfortable truth about Athens' greatest years. The most democratic city in Greece was a tyrant to other Greeks. Democracy at home and domination abroad went together: the poor citizens who rowed the fleet were the empire's greatest supporters, because it paid them. It is a pattern that later democracies with empires, Britain and others, would repeat.
sections.key: Pericles' Athens was funded by an empire over other Greek cities, which Pericles himself called a tyranny: democracy at home, domination abroad.

paras: Not everyone admired him. Plutarch reports the charge, made by his opponents and by later writers, that Pericles bought the people's support with public money: pay for jurors, festivals, and building work for the poor. In Plato's dialogue Gorgias (about 380 BC), Socrates argues that Pericles did not make the Athenians better at all; by introducing pay he made them, Socrates says, idle, cowardly, talkative and greedy, and the proof is that they turned on him at the end.

So there are two very different Pericles in our sources. For Thucydides he is the leader who held the democracy together. For Plato he is the first of the flatterers, who fed the people instead of teaching them. Both views will matter when we come to Plato's own case against democracy in session 5, still to come.
sections.key: Plutarch reports that critics said Pericles bought the people with public pay; Plato's Socrates said he made them worse, not better.

paras: In 430 BC plague struck the crowded city. Thucydides, who caught it and survived, describes how it killed perhaps a quarter or more of the population and how people stopped caring for law or religion. Pericles himself died of it in 429 BC, after two of his sons.

The leaders who followed him were of a new kind. Cleon, a rich owner of a tannery, was the first great popular speaker who was not from the old families. Comic poets and Thucydides mocked him. The Greeks called such men demagogues, 'leaders of the people'. At first the word was neutral; by the end of the century it meant a man who wins the crowd by flattery and fear. Cleon, Hyperbolus and, in his own way, the brilliant and reckless Alcibiades all competed for the people's favour, and the people, Thucydides says, were no longer led.
sections.key: Pericles died of the plague in 429 BC; his successors, the 'demagogues', competed for the crowd's favour rather than leading it.

paras: Historians take Thucydides' verdict seriously, but not on trust. He wrote it after the war was lost, and with strong personal feelings: Cleon may have been behind his own exile. Some scholars argue that Pericles' cautious strategy was itself failing by 430 BC, and that the plague, which no leader could have prevented, did more damage than any demagogue. Others point out that Athens fought on for twenty-five years after Pericles' death and nearly won.

The Sicilian expedition, which Thucydides calls the greatest blunder, was voted by an enthusiastic assembly in 415 BC, against the warnings of the cautious general Nicias. Its destruction in 413 BC was the turning point of the war. Even so, Thucydides himself notes that Athens held out for years afterwards, and fell finally through its own internal quarrels, including two oligarchic coups, in 411 and 404 BC.
sections.key: Thucydides wrote with hindsight and bias; scholars debate whether Pericles' strategy was wise, but agree the Sicilian disaster and internal strife were decisive.

paras: Thucydides' question is still ours. Should a leader in a democracy follow public opinion, or try to lead it? Modern democracies answered with representation: we elect people to use their own judgement, not simply to repeat our views. The Irish-born statesman Edmund Burke told his voters in Bristol in 1774, in effect, that he owed them his judgement, not his obedience; he lost his seat six years later.

There is a danger on the other side. A people that waits for a great leader can end up with a tyrant: the protector who becomes a wolf, as Plato will put it in session 5, still to come. Proverbs offers a third thing. It agrees that rulers make or break a people, but it does not trust any ruler without a law and a God above him. 'The king who fairly judges the poor' is a king under judgement himself.
sections.key: Thucydides asks whether democracies need leaders who lead rather than follow; Proverbs adds that every ruler is under a law above him.

sections.h: The funeral oration and the realism
paras: You read Pericles' funeral oration of 431 BC in 'How we got here': Athens as 'the school of Hellas', a city where power is in the hands of the many, where everyone is equal before the law, and where advancement goes by merit, not class. It is the most famous praise of democracy ever spoken. It is worth reading it again beside the speech in this session.

A year apart, the two speeches show two faces of the same man. In 431 BC Pericles praises freedom, openness and generosity. In 430 BC, facing a plague and an angry people, he speaks of empire as a tyranny that cannot safely be let go, and of the city's greatness as the reason private suffering must be borne. Thucydides set them close together on purpose. Democracy's highest ideals and its harder realities came from the same mouth, in the same war. Any honest judgement of Athens has to keep both in view.
sections.key: Read together, the funeral oration and the speech of 430 BC show Athens' democratic ideals and its imperial realism coming from the same leader in the same war.

refs: Thucydides II.59–65, especially II.60, 63 and 65; I.22 (speeches); V.26 (his exile), tr. R. Crawley (1874).
Plutarch, Life of Pericles 9, 15–16, 38; Plato, Gorgias 515c–516d.
Proverbs 25:1; 29.
Simon Hornblower, A Commentary on Thucydides, vol. I (1991), on II.65; Donald Kagan, Pericles of Athens and the Birth of Democracy (1991); Russell Meiggs, The Athenian Empire (1972).
Edmund Burke, Speech to the Electors of Bristol (3 November 1774).

debate.question: Was Athens at its best when it was least a democracy?

positions.name: Yes: democracy needs a guiding hand
positions.who: Thucydides, on one reading; many later admirers of Pericles
positions.view: The people as a whole are moved by passion. They do best when one wise, incorruptible man has their trust and guides them. Athens flourished under Pericles and fell when no such man remained.
positions.evidence: II.65: 'government by the first citizen'; the blunders after his death, above all Sicily.

positions.name: No: Pericles was democracy working
positions.who: Many modern historians, such as Josiah Ober
positions.view: Pericles held no special power. He was elected, fined and re-elected; every decision was the assembly's. His authority was democratic: the people chose to trust him. A democracy that listens to good advice is still a democracy.
positions.evidence: His annual re-election; the fine of 430 BC; the assembly's control of every decision.

positions.name: Neither: he was the first flatterer
positions.who: Plato's Socrates in the Gorgias
positions.view: Pericles was no better than his successors. He made the people dependent on public pay and pleasure, and did not make them wiser or juster; the proof is that they turned on him.
positions.evidence: Pay for jurors and building work; the people's anger in 430 BC.

debate.agree: All agree that a democracy's health depends on the character of those it trusts, and that flattery of the people is a danger.

look.why: There is no painting of Pericles at the National Gallery of Art. This is a portrait of a modern 'first citizen': George Washington, painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1795, while he was President. Washington, like Solon, chose to give power up: he resigned his army command in 1783 and declined a third term as President in 1796. The painting itself shows only the man.
points: An older man shown from the chest up, his body angled to our right, turning his face to look at us.
He wears a high-collared black coat and a cream-white ruffled collar.
Grey eyes under pale grey eyebrows, a hooked nose, flushed cheeks and lips set in a line.
White hair flaring out at the sides, tied at the nape of the neck with a ribbon.
A deep wine-red background, painted with light brushstrokes, deepening to black at the upper corners.

music.why: Brahms chose his own words from the Bible, among them 'all flesh is as grass': the greatest leaders pass, like Pericles in the plague. It is music of comfort for a people in mourning.

think.why: Thucydides and Proverbs ask the same question about rulers from Athens and from Jerusalem. See how the two roots of the West meet.

learn.why: One line that says what Thucydides took a whole history to show: a people feels the character of those who rule it.

check.q: Pericles lists four qualities he claims to have. What is his point in listing them together?
options: That he is the richest man in Athens
That the people should never have voted for war
That each is useless without the others: knowledge needs words, words need love of country, and love of country must be proof against bribery
That only aristocrats should lead
check.why: He explains how each quality fails without the next; it is a description of the whole leader.

check.q: Why, according to Thucydides, could Pericles 'afford to anger them by contradiction'?
options: Because he never sought power by improper means and so never needed to flatter them
Because his opponents had all been ostracised
Because the people feared his wealth
Because as general he could overrule the assembly
check.why: His power rested on trust and integrity, not on favours, so he could tell the people unwelcome truths.

check.q: What does Thucydides mean by 'what was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen'?
options: The constitution stayed democratic, but in practice the people followed one trusted leader
Pericles had ended the use of the lot
Pericles held a special office above the other generals
The council of the Areopagus governed through Pericles
check.why: Every decision was still the assembly's; what changed was who guided it.

check.q: Which is the strongest reason to be cautious about Thucydides' verdict in II.65?
options: He relied only on Spartan informants
He was too young to remember Pericles
He wrote it with hindsight after the war was lost, and disliked Pericles' successors, one of whom may have caused his exile
He disliked Pericles and wanted to belittle him
check.why: Hindsight and personal feeling both shaped the passage, which is why historians test it against other evidence.

check.q: Pericles called the Athenian empire 'a tyranny'. Why does this matter for judging Athenian democracy?
options: It shows Pericles was secretly opposed to the democracy
It shows Athens had a king
It shows the most democratic city in Greece ruled other Greeks by force, and its democracy was funded partly by that empire
It shows Pericles opposed the empire
check.why: Tribute from allies paid for the fleet and the buildings; democracy at home and domination abroad went together.

check.q: What does Proverbs 29 add to Thucydides' view of leadership?
options: That only kings should rule
That leaders should be chosen by lot
That a ruler's justice to the poor is a test of his rule, and that a people needs a guiding word from God above any leader
That the people should always obey
check.why: Proverbs makes justice to the poor the test and looks to revelation, not only to a great man, to restrain a people.

tutorial.question: 'Nominally a democracy, in fact government by the first citizen.' What does Thucydides' judgement of Pericles tell us about what democracy needs?
tutorial.approach: Explain what Pericles did and why Thucydides admired him, using II.60 and II.65. Set out the critics' view, from Plutarch and Plato's Gorgias. Consider the empire. Then ask what a democracy needs from its leaders, and whether it should rely on them at all, using Proverbs 29.
strong: Explains the four qualities of II.60 and the 'lead instead of being led' of II.65.
Shows that Pericles held no special office and was fined and re-elected.
Gives the critics' case fairly: pay, flattery, the Gorgias.
Deals honestly with the empire, using II.63.
Weighs Thucydides' hindsight and bias.
Uses Proverbs 29 to compare a different source of restraint.
