sessions.practice: Live it this week: Pericles could tell the people what they did not want to hear because he never flattered them. Once this week, when someone asks your opinion, give your honest view kindly instead of the one they want, and notice what it costs you.
sessions.reflect: Whom do you trust to tell you hard truths? And who trusts you to tell them?
takeaways: Pericles held no special office; his authority came from knowledge, eloquence, love of country and incorruptibility, which let him lead the people instead of following them.
Thucydides judged that Athens was best under its 'first citizen' and fell when his successors competed for the crowd's favour; he wrote with hindsight and bias.
Pericles' Athens was funded by an empire he called a tyranny; Proverbs adds that every ruler is judged by his justice to the poor.

sessions.title: The crowd decides
sessions.line: One day the Athenians vote to kill every man in a rebel city. The next day they are sorry. A second debate, two speeches, a vote almost equal, and a ship racing to arrive in time.
sessions.plain: In 427 BC the city of Mytilene, on the island of Lesbos, rebelled against Athens and was crushed. In a fury the Athenian assembly voted to kill all its men and enslave its women and children, and sent a ship to carry out the order. The next morning many regretted it, and the assembly met again. Cleon argued that changing their minds was weakness; Diodotus argued that mass killing was against Athens' own interest. Diodotus won by a hair, and a second ship rowed day and night to arrive just in time. This session asks what happens when the people's passion becomes law, and what can restrain it.
sessions.why: Session 3 showed Athens at its best, led by Pericles, and Thucydides' warning that after him the people were no longer led. This session shows what that meant, on one day in the assembly, two years after Pericles' death. It is the clearest picture we have of democracy's great danger: a whole people deciding in anger.
answers: What is a demagogue?
What happened at Mytilene?
Can a democracy restrain its own passions?
What does the Bible say about following the crowd?
sessions.finding: In the Mytilene debate the assembly voted in anger to kill a whole city's men, then repented overnight and reversed itself by a hair: democracy's great danger is passion without restraint, and it can be corrected only by deliberation, second thoughts and principles above the vote.

paras: In session 2 we saw how the Athenian assembly worked: thousands of citizens deciding directly, by show of hands. In session 3 Thucydides judged that under Pericles the people were led, and after his death, in 429 BC, they were not. Their new leaders, he said, gave policy over to the whims of the crowd.

Athens was now two years further into the war with Sparta, still suffering from the plague. Its empire was restless. In 428 BC Mytilene, the chief city of the island of Lesbos, rebelled. Mytilene was one of the few allies still free to keep its own fleet and government; it was ruled by an oligarchy, a council of the rich, and it hoped for help from Sparta.

timeline.text: Pericles dies
Mytilene revolts; Athens besieges it
Mytilene surrenders; the two debates in the Athenian assembly
Aristophanes mocks Cleon in his comedy The Knights
Cleon is killed in battle at Amphipolis
Athens destroys the island of Melos, killing its men
After the sea victory at Arginusae, the assembly condemns its generals
After the restoration of democracy, new limits on the assembly's power to change laws

background.key: Two years after Pericles' death, Mytilene, an ally with its own fleet, revolted; in 427 BC it surrendered and Athens had to decide its fate.

paras: Cleon, son of Cleaenetus, was the most powerful popular leader in Athens after Pericles. His family's wealth came from a tannery, not old land, and he spoke in a new, aggressive style; Aristotle's school says he was the first to shout and abuse people from the speaker's platform (Athenian Constitution 28). Thucydides calls him 'the most violent man at Athens'. He was not a fool: he was a successful general at Pylos in 425 BC, and he died fighting at Amphipolis in 422 BC.
Diodotus, son of Eucrates, is known only from this debate. He had argued against the massacre the day before.
background.key: Cleon was the leading popular speaker after Pericles, forceful and aggressive; Diodotus is known only from this debate.

paras: This is one of the most famous debates in history, and one of the few times we can watch a democracy change its mind. The reading has four parts: the first decree and the morning after; Cleon's speech; Diodotus' speech; and the vote and the race of the two ships. Thucydides writes the speeches in his own words, true to what was said as far as he could be (I.22).
The comparison is a short passage of Israel's law: 'You shall not follow a crowd to do evil.' The Bible names the danger the Athenians nearly fell into, and gives a different reason for avoiding it.
background.key: Four parts: the decree, Cleon, Diodotus, the race of the ships; then the Bible's law against following a crowd to do evil.

before: What does Cleon say is wrong with the Athenians as an audience?
On what grounds does Diodotus oppose the massacre: justice, mercy or interest?
What saved Mytilene in the end?
sessions.readWhy: The first decree, the speeches of Cleon and Diodotus at the second debate, and the race of the two ships.

paras: Upon the arrival of the prisoners with Salaethus, the Athenians at once put the latter to death, although he offered, among other things, to procure the withdrawal of the Peloponnesians from Plataea, which was still under siege; and after deliberating as to what they should do with the former, in the fury of the moment determined to put to death not only the prisoners at Athens, but the whole adult male population of Mitylene, and to make slaves of the women and children. It was remarked that Mitylene had revolted without being, like the rest, subjected to the empire; and what above all swelled the wrath of the Athenians was the fact of the Peloponnesian fleet having ventured over to Ionia to her support, a fact which was held to argue a long meditated rebellion. They accordingly sent a galley to communicate the decree to Paches, commanding him to lose no time in dispatching the Mitylenians. The morrow brought repentance with it and reflection on the horrid cruelty of a decree, which condemned a whole city to the fate merited only by the guilty. This was no sooner perceived by the Mitylenian ambassadors at Athens and their Athenian supporters, than they moved the authorities to put the question again to the vote; which they the more easily consented to do, as they themselves plainly saw that most of the citizens wished some one to give them an opportunity for reconsidering the matter. An assembly was therefore at once called, and after much expression of opinion upon both sides, Cleon, son of Cleaenetus, the same who had carried the former motion of putting the Mitylenians to death, the most violent man at Athens, and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons, came forward again and spoke as follows:

“I have often before now been convinced that a democracy is incapable of empire, and never more so than by your present change of mind in the matter of Mitylene. Fears or plots being unknown to you in your daily relations with each other, you feel just the same with regard to your allies, and never reflect that the mistakes into which you may be led by listening to their appeals, or by giving way to your own compassion, are full of danger to yourselves, and bring you no thanks for your weakness from your allies; entirely forgetting that your empire is a despotism and your subjects disaffected conspirators, whose obedience is ensured not by your suicidal concessions, but by the superiority given you by your own strength and not their loyalty. The most alarming feature in the case is the constant change of measures with which we appear to be threatened, and our seeming ignorance of the fact that bad laws which are never changed are better for a city than good ones that have no authority; that unlearned loyalty is more serviceable than quick-witted insubordination; and that ordinary men usually manage public affairs better than their more gifted fellows. The latter are always wanting to appear wiser than the laws, and to overrule every proposition brought forward, thinking that they cannot show their wit in more important matters, and by such behaviour too often ruin their country; while those who mistrust their own cleverness are content to be less learned than the laws, and less able to pick holes in the speech of a good speaker; and being fair judges rather than rival athletes, generally conduct affairs successfully. These we ought to imitate, instead of being led on by cleverness and intellectual rivalry to advise your people against our real opinions.

“For myself, I adhere to my former opinion, and wonder at those who have proposed to reopen the case of the Mitylenians, and who are thus causing a delay which is all in favour of the guilty, by making the sufferer proceed against the offender with the edge of his anger blunted; although where vengeance follows most closely upon the wrong, it best equals it and most amply requites it. I wonder also who will be the man who will maintain the contrary, and will pretend to show that the crimes of the Mitylenians are of service to us, and our misfortunes injurious to the allies. Such a man must plainly either have such confidence in his rhetoric as to adventure to prove that what has been once for all decided is still undetermined, or be bribed to try to delude us by elaborate sophisms. In such contests the state gives the rewards to others, and takes the dangers for herself. The persons to blame are you who are so foolish as to institute these contests;

who go to see an oration as you would to see a sight, take your facts on hearsay, judge of the practicability of a project by the wit of its advocates, and trust for the truth as to past events not to the fact which you saw more than to the clever strictures which you heard; the easy victims of new-fangled arguments, unwilling to follow received conclusions; slaves to every new paradox, despisers of the commonplace; the first wish of every man being that he could speak himself, the next to rival those who can speak by seeming to be quite up with their ideas by applauding every hit almost before it is made, and by being as quick in catching an argument as you are slow in foreseeing its consequences; asking, if I may so say, for something different from the conditions under which we live, and yet comprehending inadequately those very conditions; very slaves to the pleasure of the ear, and more like the audience of a rhetorician than the council of a city.

“No hope, therefore, that rhetoric may instil or money purchase, of the mercy due to human infirmity must be held out to the Mitylenians. Their offence was not involuntary, but of malice and deliberate; and mercy is only for unwilling offenders. I therefore, now as before, persist against your reversing your first decision, or giving way to the three failings most fatal to empire—pity, sentiment, and indulgence. Compassion is due to those who can reciprocate the feeling, not to those who will never pity us in return, but are our natural and necessary foes: the orators who charm us with sentiment may find other less important arenas for their talents, in the place of one where the city pays a heavy penalty for a momentary pleasure, themselves receiving fine acknowledgments for their fine phrases; while indulgence should be shown towards those who will be our friends in future, instead of towards men who will remain just what they were, and as much our enemies as before. To sum up shortly, I say that if you follow my advice you will do what is just towards the Mitylenians, and at the same time expedient; while by a different decision you will not oblige them so much as pass sentence upon yourselves. For if they were right in rebelling, you must be wrong in ruling.

However, if, right or wrong, you determine to rule, you must carry out your principle and punish the Mitylenians as your interest requires; or else you must give up your empire and cultivate honesty without danger. Make up your minds, therefore, to give them like for like; and do not let the victims who escaped the plot be more insensible than the conspirators who hatched it; but reflect what they would have done if victorious over you, especially they were the aggressors. It is they who wrong their neighbour without a cause, that pursue their victim to the death, on account of the danger which they foresee in letting their enemy survive; since the object of a wanton wrong is more dangerous, if he escape, than an enemy who has not this to complain of. Do not, therefore, be traitors to yourselves, but recall as nearly as possible the moment of suffering and the supreme importance which you then attached to their reduction; and now pay them back in their turn, without yielding to present weakness or forgetting the peril that once hung over you. Punish them as they deserve, and teach your other allies by a striking example that the penalty of rebellion is death. Let them once understand this and you will not have so often to neglect your enemies while you are fighting with your own confederates.”

Such were the words of Cleon. After him Diodotus, son of Eucrates, who had also in the previous assembly spoken most strongly against putting the Mitylenians to death, came forward and spoke as follows:

“I do not blame the persons who have reopened the case of the Mitylenians, nor do I approve the protests which we have heard against important questions being frequently debated. I think the two things most opposed to good counsel are haste and passion; haste usually goes hand in hand with folly, passion with coarseness and narrowness of mind. As for the argument that speech ought not to be the exponent of action, the man who uses it must be either senseless or interested: senseless if he believes it possible to treat of the uncertain future through any other medium; interested if, wishing to carry a disgraceful measure and doubting his ability to speak well in a bad cause, he thinks to frighten opponents and hearers by well-aimed calumny. What is still more intolerable is to accuse a speaker of making a display in order to be paid for it. If ignorance only were imputed, an unsuccessful speaker might retire with a reputation for honesty, if not for wisdom; while the charge of dishonesty makes him suspected, if successful, and thought, if defeated, not only a fool but a rogue. The city is no gainer by such a system, since fear deprives it of its advisers; although in truth, if our speakers are to make such assertions, it would be better for the country if they could not speak at all, as we should then make fewer blunders. The good citizen ought to triumph not by frightening his opponents but by beating them fairly in argument; and a wise city, without over-distinguishing its best advisers, will nevertheless not deprive them of their due, and, far from punishing an unlucky counsellor, will not even regard him as disgraced. In this way successful orators would be least tempted to sacrifice their convictions to popularity, in the hope of still higher honours, and unsuccessful speakers to resort to the same popular arts in order to win over the multitude.

“However, I have not come forward either to oppose or to accuse in the matter of Mitylene; indeed, the question before us as sensible men is not their guilt, but our interests. Though I prove them ever so guilty, I shall not, therefore, advise their death, unless it be expedient; nor though they should have claims to indulgence, shall I recommend it, unless it be dearly for the good of the country. I consider that we are deliberating for the future more than for the present; and where Cleon is so positive as to the useful deterrent effects that will follow from making rebellion capital, I, who consider the interests of the future quite as much as he, as positively maintain the contrary. And I require you not to reject my useful considerations for his specious ones: his speech may have the attraction of seeming the more just in your present temper against Mitylene; but we are not in a court of justice, but in a political assembly; and the question is not justice, but how to make the Mitylenians useful to Athens.

“Now of course communities have enacted the penalty of death for many offences far lighter than this: still hope leads men to venture, and no one ever yet put himself in peril without the inward conviction that he would succeed in his design. Again, was there ever city rebelling that did not believe that it possessed either in itself or in its alliances resources adequate to the enterprise? All, states and individuals, are alike prone to err, and there is no law that will prevent them; or why should men have exhausted the list of punishments in search of enactments to protect them from evildoers? It is probable that in early times the penalties for the greatest offences were less severe, and that, as these were disregarded, the penalty of death has been by degrees in most cases arrived at, which is itself disregarded in like manner. Either then some means of terror more terrible than this must be discovered, or it must be owned that this restraint is useless;

and that as long as poverty gives men the courage of necessity, or plenty fills them with the ambition which belongs to insolence and pride, and the other conditions of life remain each under the thraldom of some fatal and master passion, so long will the impulse never be wanting to drive men into danger. Hope also and cupidity, the one leading and the other following, the one conceiving the attempt, the other suggesting the facility of succeeding, cause the widest ruin, and, although invisible agents, are far stronger than the dangers that are seen. Fortune, too, powerfully helps the delusion and, by the unexpected aid that she sometimes lends, tempts men to venture with inferior means; and this is especially the case with communities, because the stakes played for are the highest, freedom or empire, and, when all are acting together, each man irrationally magnifies his own capacity. In fine, it is impossible to prevent, and only great simplicity can hope to prevent, human nature doing what it has once set its mind upon, by force of law or by any other deterrent force whatsoever.

“We must not, therefore, commit ourselves to a false policy through a belief in the efficacy of the punishment of death, or exclude rebels from the hope of repentance and an early atonement of their error. Consider a moment. At present, if a city that has already revolted perceive that it cannot succeed, it will come to terms while it is still able to refund expenses, and pay tribute afterwards. In the other case, what city, think you, would not prepare better than is now done, and hold out to the last against its besiegers, if it is all one whether it surrender late or soon? And how can it be otherwise than hurtful to us to be put to the expense of a siege, because surrender is out of the question; and if we take the city, to receive a ruined town from which we can no longer draw the revenue which forms our real strength against the enemy? We must not, therefore, sit as strict judges of the offenders to our own prejudice, but rather see how by moderate chastisements we may be enabled to benefit in future by the revenue-producing powers of our dependencies; and we must make up our minds to look for our protection not to legal terrors but to careful administration. At present we do exactly the opposite. When a free community, held in subjection by force, rises, as is only natural, and asserts its independence, it is no sooner reduced than we fancy ourselves obliged to punish it severely; although the right course with freemen is not to chastise them rigorously when they do rise, but rigorously to watch them before they rise, and to prevent their ever entertaining the idea, and, the insurrection suppressed, to make as few responsible for it as possible.

“Only consider what a blunder you would commit in doing as Cleon recommends. As things are at present, in all the cities the people is your friend, and either does not revolt with the oligarchy, or, if forced to do so, becomes at once the enemy of the insurgents; so that in the war with the hostile city you have the masses on your side. But if you butcher the people of Mitylene, who had nothing to do with the revolt, and who, as soon as they got arms, of their own motion surrendered the town, first you will commit the crime of killing your benefactors; and next you will play directly into the hands of the higher classes, who when they induce their cities to rise, will immediately have the people on their side, through your having announced in advance the same punishment for those who are guilty and for those who are not. On the contrary, even if they were guilty, you ought to seem not to notice it, in order to avoid alienating the only class still friendly to us. In short, I consider it far more useful for the preservation of our empire voluntarily to put up with injustice, than to put to death, however justly, those whom it is our interest to keep alive. As for Cleon’s idea that in punishment the claims of justice and expediency can both be satisfied, facts do not confirm the possibility of such a combination.

Such were the words of Diodotus. The two opinions thus expressed were the ones that most directly contradicted each other; and the Athenians, notwithstanding their change of feeling, now proceeded to a division, in which the show of hands was almost equal, although the motion of Diodotus carried the day. Another galley was at once sent off in haste, for fear that the first might reach Lesbos in the interval, and the city be found destroyed; the first ship having about a day and a night’s start. Wine and barley-cakes were provided for the vessel by the Mitylenian ambassadors, and great promises made if they arrived in time; which caused the men to use such diligence upon the voyage that they took their meals of barley-cakes kneaded with oil and wine as they rowed, and only slept by turns while the others were at the oar. Luckily they met with no contrary wind, and the first ship making no haste upon so horrid an errand, while the second pressed on in the manner described, the first arrived so little before them, that Paches had only just had time to read the decree, and to prepare to execute the sentence, when the second put into port and prevented the massacre. The danger of Mitylene had indeed been great.
The other party whom Paches had sent off as the prime movers in the rebellion, were upon Cleon’s motion put to death by the Athenians, the number being rather more than a thousand.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through
parts.when: Athens and exile, written between 431 and about 400 BC
parts.title: The decree and the morning after
parts.context: Summer 427 BC. The Athenian general Paches has taken Mytilene and sent the leaders of the revolt, with Salaethus, the Spartan officer who had come to help them, to Athens. A galley is a warship rowed by oarsmen.
parts.plain: The Athenians killed the Spartan at once. Then, in their fury, they voted to kill not only the prisoners but every adult man in Mytilene, and to enslave the women and children. They sent a ship with the order. The next day they began to regret 'the horrid cruelty' of condemning a whole city for the guilt of a few. The Mytilenian envoys and their friends persuaded the officials to call a new assembly. Cleon, who had proposed the massacre, spoke again.

commentary.on: in the fury of the moment determined to put to death not only the prisoners at Athens, but the whole adult male population of Mitylene
commentary.text: 'The fury of the moment.' A whole people decided, in a single meeting, to wipe out a city. There was no court, no appeal and no upper house: the assembly's vote was final.

commentary.on: The morrow brought repentance with it and reflection on the horrid cruelty of a decree, which condemned a whole city to the fate merited only by the guilty
commentary.text: Overnight the mood changed. The moral point is plain to the Athenians themselves: the innocent were to die with the guilty. Thucydides does not say who changed their minds. It was the people's own conscience.

commentary.on: most of the citizens wished some one to give them an opportunity for reconsidering the matter
commentary.text: A democracy can repent, but it needs someone to give it the chance. The second assembly was itself unusual: reopening a decision was controversial, as Cleon is about to say.

commentary.on: the most violent man at Athens, and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons
commentary.text: Thucydides' introduction of Cleon is not neutral. 'The commons' means the ordinary people. Cleon's power came from them.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through
parts.when: Athens and exile, written between 431 and about 400 BC
parts.title: Cleon: do not change your minds
parts.context: Cleon speaks first. The cut, marked '…', leaves out his argument that Mytilene's revolt was worse than others' because it was free and well treated.
parts.plain: Cleon says: a democracy cannot run an empire, and your change of mind proves it. Your empire is a tyranny over unwilling subjects, held by strength, not their goodwill. Bad laws that stay fixed are better than good laws that keep changing. You go to the assembly like an audience at a show, enjoying clever speeches instead of deciding. Do not give way to pity, sentiment or indulgence. Punish them as they deserve, and teach your allies that the penalty of rebellion is death.

commentary.on: I have often before now been convinced that a democracy is incapable of empire
commentary.text: A remarkable opening from the people's own champion. Cleon attacks democracy itself: its habits of trust and debate make it soft. He uses the people's anger against their own institutions.

commentary.on: your empire is a despotism and your subjects disaffected conspirators
commentary.text: He repeats Pericles' word for the empire, a tyranny, but draws a harsher conclusion. If you rule by force, you must be feared.

commentary.on: bad laws which are never changed are better for a city than good ones that have no authority
commentary.text: This is a real argument, and not a stupid one. Laws that change with every mood are no laws at all. But Cleon is using it to stop the people reconsidering a massacre they voted in anger.

commentary.on: who go to see an oration as you would to see a sight
commentary.text: Cleon's portrait of the Athenian assembly is brilliant and bitter: people who love clever speeches, who are 'slaves to every new paradox', who judge a policy by the wit of its speaker. It is exactly the criticism Plato would later make, from the opposite side.

commentary.on: very slaves to the pleasure of the ear, and more like the audience of a rhetorician than the council of a city
commentary.text: The irony is that Cleon is himself the most skilful manipulator of the crowd in Athens. A demagogue attacking the people's love of speeches is still giving a speech.

commentary.on: pity, sentiment, and indulgence
commentary.text: Cleon names the 'three failings most fatal to empire'. Every one of them is a virtue in ordinary life. His argument requires the people to stop feeling what they felt that morning.

commentary.on: For if they were right in rebelling, you must be wrong in ruling.
commentary.text: The sharpest sentence in the speech. Either Athens' empire is just and rebellion deserves death, or the empire is unjust and Athens should give it up. Cleon forces the choice.

commentary.on: teach your other allies by a striking example that the penalty of rebellion is death
commentary.text: The argument is deterrence: kill them all, and no one else will rebel.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through
parts.when: Athens and exile, written between 431 and about 400 BC
parts.title: Diodotus: think of the future
parts.context: Diodotus replies. The cut, marked '…', leaves out a passage on how suspicion of speakers' motives forces even good advisers to lie.
parts.plain: Diodotus says: haste and passion are the enemies of good advice, and debate is not weakness. The question is not whether Mytilene is guilty but what is in Athens' interest. The death penalty does not deter: people rebel because they hope to succeed. If rebels know they will die anyway, they will fight to the last, and you will win only a ruined city. In most cities the common people are on your side; at Mytilene they surrendered the city. Kill them, and you will drive the people everywhere into the arms of the oligarchs. Try the guilty calmly, and spare the rest.

commentary.on: I think the two things most opposed to good counsel are haste and passion
commentary.text: Diodotus defends the second debate itself. Changing your mind after thinking is not weakness; deciding in haste and anger is the real danger. It is the best defence of deliberation in Greek literature.

commentary.on: The good citizen ought to triumph not by frightening his opponents but by beating them fairly in argument
commentary.text: A reply to Cleon's hint that anyone who argued for mercy had been bribed. A democracy dies when speakers win by accusing opponents rather than answering them.

commentary.on: the question before us as sensible men is not their guilt, but our interests
commentary.text: Here is the surprise. Diodotus does not argue for mercy. He accepts Cleon's ground, Athenian interest, and beats him on it. Many readers think he chose this argument because it was the only one the assembly would accept.

commentary.on: we are not in a court of justice, but in a political assembly
commentary.text: An important distinction: a court asks what someone deserves; an assembly asks what is wise. Cleon had mixed the two.

commentary.on: it is impossible to prevent, and only great simplicity can hope to prevent, human nature doing what it has once set its mind upon, by force of law or by any other deterrent force whatsoever
commentary.text: Diodotus' argument against deterrence: hope and desire are stronger than fear. Harsher punishments have never stopped crime. It is one of the earliest arguments of its kind, and it is still made today.

commentary.on: the right course with freemen is not to chastise them rigorously when they do rise, but rigorously to watch them before they rise
commentary.text: Prevention, not revenge. He calls the Mytilenians 'freemen', a quiet reminder that their revolt was a bid for freedom.

commentary.on: if you butcher the people of Mitylene, who had nothing to do with the revolt
commentary.text: The common people of Mytilene had been given arms by the oligarchs and had at once surrendered the city to Athens. To kill them would be to kill friends.

commentary.on: it far more useful for the preservation of our empire voluntarily to put up with injustice
commentary.text: Diodotus says it is in Athens' interest to tolerate some injustice rather than kill those whom it needs alive. He never says the massacre would be wrong. He shows it would be stupid.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (about 460 to about 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through
parts.when: Athens and exile, written between 431 and about 400 BC
parts.title: The race of the two ships
parts.context: The vote, and what followed. Lesbos is about 350 kilometres from Athens by sea. Paches was the Athenian general at Mytilene.
parts.plain: The vote was almost equal, but Diodotus won. A second ship was sent at once. The Mytilenian envoys promised the rowers great rewards, and they rowed day and night, eating as they rowed and sleeping in turns. The first ship, on its 'horrid errand', went slowly. The second arrived just as Paches was reading the decree, in time to stop the massacre. But the thousand or so men Paches had sent to Athens as leaders of the revolt were put to death on Cleon's motion.

commentary.on: the show of hands was almost equal, although the motion of Diodotus carried the day
commentary.text: Almost equal. Thousands of men would live or die by a handful of votes in a crowd. That is both the glory and the terror of direct democracy.

commentary.on: they took their meals of barley-cakes kneaded with oil and wine as they rowed, and only slept by turns
commentary.text: The rowers were themselves poor Athenian citizens. Some of those who had voted for death the day before may have been among those who rowed to undo it.

commentary.on: the first ship making no haste upon so horrid an errand
commentary.text: A small, human detail: the crew carrying the death sentence did not hurry. Thucydides lets it speak for itself.

commentary.on: The danger of Mitylene had indeed been great.
commentary.text: Thucydides' only comment, typically understated.

commentary.on: were upon Cleon's motion put to death by the Athenians, the number being rather more than a thousand
commentary.text: Mercy was partial. More than a thousand men, judged guilty, were killed without individual trial. Some scholars think the number has been miscopied in the manuscripts and was much smaller; others accept it. Either way, the story does not end in pure mercy.

paras: “You shall not spread a false report. Don’t join your hand with the wicked to be a malicious witness.
“You shall not follow a crowd to do evil. You shall not testify in court to side with a multitude to pervert justice.
You shall not favor a poor man in his cause.
“If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again.
If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him. You shall surely help him with it.
“You shall not deny justice to your poor people in their lawsuits.
“Keep far from a false charge, and don’t kill the innocent and righteous; for I will not justify the wicked.
“You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds those who have sight and perverts the words of the righteous.

parts.title: You shall not follow a crowd to do evil
parts.context: These verses are from the 'book of the covenant' (Exodus 20:22–23:33), the oldest law code in the Bible, given at Mount Sinai in the story of Exodus. Most of it concerns courts and justice in village life. In 'Exodus and the law' you read the verse that follows these, about the foreigner.

commentary.on: You shall not follow a crowd to do evil.
commentary.text: This is the precise danger of Mytilene: thousands of men voting for a massacre because everyone around them was angry. The law makes each person responsible for his own judgement, even inside a crowd.

commentary.on: You shall not testify in court to side with a multitude to pervert justice.
commentary.text: In a court, the majority is not a reason. The truth is. The Athenians had no such principle in their assembly; Diodotus had to argue from interest instead.

commentary.on: You shall not favor a poor man in his cause.
commentary.text: Justice must not bend either way: not to the crowd, and not even to the poor out of sympathy. It is a hard, even-handed law.

commentary.on: If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again.
commentary.text: A remarkable command: help your enemy. Cleon said compassion is due only to those who can return it. Israel's law says you owe decency even to the man who hates you.

commentary.on: don’t kill the innocent and righteous; for I will not justify the wicked
commentary.text: Here is the reason Diodotus never gave: killing the innocent is wrong, whatever it gains, because God will judge it.

compare.why: The Athenian assembly nearly did evil because the crowd demanded it. Israel's law forbids exactly that, and gives a reason the Athenians never gave: justice for the innocent and the poor is commanded by God.
compare.title: Not following a crowd

paras: Cleon's speech is often read as simple brutality, but it is a serious argument, and it should be stated at its strongest. An empire held by force, he says, can survive only if rebellion is punished without mercy; the alternative is endless revolts, each costing Athenian lives and money. A city that changes its mind every day has no law at all. And the assembly is too easily moved by clever speakers and by its own feelings, so it should stick to its first decision.

Some modern 'realists' in international politics, who think states act on power rather than morals, have found Cleon's logic clear-eyed. His speech also contains a real criticism of democratic assemblies that later writers repeated: they treat politics as entertainment, and are swayed by whoever speaks best.
sections.key: Cleon argued for deterrence, consistency and firmness, and attacked the assembly for being moved by speeches and feelings.

paras: Diodotus wins on Cleon's own ground. He does not ask the Athenians to be kind; he asks them to be sensible. Punishment does not deter people driven by hope; mass killing makes every future rebel fight to the end; and in a war between democracy and oligarchy across Greece, killing the common people of Mytilene would drive the common people everywhere to the other side.

Why did he not argue that the massacre was simply wrong? Many readers, such as Clifford Orwin in The Humanity of Thucydides (1994), think Diodotus was a humane man who knew the assembly would not listen to a moral argument after Cleon had mocked pity as weakness. So he dressed mercy as self-interest. If so, the debate shows something troubling: in that assembly, on that day, justice had to be disguised to be heard.
sections.key: Diodotus argued from Athenian interest, not justice: punishment does not deter, and killing friends is folly; perhaps he disguised mercy as interest.

paras: In the end three things saved Mytilene. First, conscience: the morning after, ordinary Athenians felt the horror of what they had voted. Second, deliberation: the officials allowed a second debate, and Diodotus was allowed to speak. Third, sheer luck: the wind was calm and the second ship arrived in time.

None of these was built into the system. The assembly could have refused to meet again; Diodotus could have lost by a few hands; the wind could have turned. Athens had no court that could overrule the assembly, no second chamber, no written rights. The people's will that day was the highest law there was. This is the problem that will run through the rest of this journey: what restrains a sovereign people?
sections.key: Mytilene was saved by conscience, deliberation and luck; nothing in Athens' constitution could have stopped the first decree.

paras: A demagogue, in Greek demagogos, was simply a 'leader of the people'. By the end of the 400s the word had come to mean a leader who wins power by flattering the crowd, stirring up its fear and anger, and attacking his opponents as traitors. Cleon was the model. In Aristophanes' comedy The Knights (424 BC), he appears as a slave who fawns on his old master, 'Demos', the people, while robbing him.

Notice the demagogue's methods in Cleon's speech: he tells the people they are being fooled by clever speakers, suggests that his opponents have been bribed, and urges them to act on their first anger before it cools. Those three moves, contempt for debate, suspicion of opponents and urgency, are still the demagogue's tools. Aristotle later observed that demagogues arise where the laws are not supreme, and the people rule by decree (Politics IV.4).
sections.key: A demagogue wins the crowd by flattery, fear and attacks on opponents; Cleon was the model, and Aristotle said demagogues flourish where laws are not supreme.

sections.h: Arginusae: when there was no second ship
paras: Twenty years later there was no second debate in time. In 406 BC the Athenian fleet won a great sea battle at the Arginusae islands, but a storm prevented the rescue of the crews of sunken ships, and many drowned. The assembly, enraged, tried the eight generals together, in one vote, which was against Athenian law: each accused had the right to be tried separately. When some objected, the crowd shouted that it was monstrous to stop the people doing whatever they wished.

One of the presiding committee that day, chosen by lot, was a citizen named Socrates. According to both Xenophon and Plato, he refused to put the illegal motion to the vote. He was overruled. The six generals who had returned to Athens were executed, including Pericles' son. Xenophon says the Athenians soon repented and prosecuted those who had misled them. This time repentance came too late.
sections.key: In 406 BC the assembly illegally condemned the generals of Arginusae; Socrates refused to put the motion, was overruled, and the people repented too late.

paras: The Athenians learned from their mistakes. From about 415 BC a citizen could bring a 'charge of illegality' (graphe paranomon) against anyone who proposed a decree contrary to the laws, and a jury could annul it. After the democracy was restored in 403 BC, laws were separated from decrees: the assembly could no longer change the laws by a simple vote; changes went to a special board of lawmakers. In effect, the Athenians began to put limits on their own sovereignty.

Later democracies went further. James Madison, defending the American Constitution in The Federalist (1788), argued that in every large assembly passion overcomes reason, and that even if every Athenian had been a Socrates, their assembly would still have behaved like a mob. His remedy was representation, a senate, courts and a written constitution: ways of giving the people a second ship. Israel's law offered another restraint, in the conscience of each person: you shall not follow a crowd to do evil.
sections.key: Athens added the charge of illegality and separated laws from decrees; Madison's answer was representation, a senate, courts and a constitution; Exodus puts the restraint in each conscience.

sections.h: Melos: when no one spoke for mercy
paras: Mytilene was not the end of the story. In 416 BC Athens demanded that the small neutral island of Melos join its empire. Thucydides gives the negotiations as a dialogue in which the Athenians refuse to talk of justice at all: right, they say, is a question only between equals, and 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must' (V.89). When Melos refused, Athens took it, killed the men and enslaved the women and children. This time Thucydides records no second debate.

The journey 'The first historians', later in this hall, reads the Melian dialogue in full. Here it is enough to notice the line from Mytilene to Melos. At Mytilene, Diodotus already had to argue from interest, not justice, to be heard. Eleven years later no one in the story argues for mercy at all. A democracy that learns to speak only the language of interest may in the end forget any other.
sections.key: At Melos in 416 BC Athens killed the men of a neutral island after refusing even to discuss justice: the end of the road that began when mercy had to be argued as interest.

refs: Thucydides III.36–50; I.22, tr. R. Crawley (1874).
Xenophon, Hellenica I.7 (Arginusae); Plato, Apology 32b–c; Aristotle, The Athenian Constitution 28, 34; Aristotle, Politics IV.4 (1292a).
Aristophanes, Knights (424 BC).

James Madison, The Federalist 55 (1788).

debate.question: Cleon or Diodotus?

positions.name: Cleon: be firm
positions.who: Cleon; some modern 'realists' in international relations
positions.view: An empire held by force must punish rebellion without mercy, or it invites more. Changing decisions on a whim destroys the authority of law. The assembly should distrust its own feelings and clever speakers.
positions.evidence: His speech; the many revolts Athens later faced; the principle that stable laws matter more than perfect ones.

positions.name: Diodotus: be prudent
positions.who: Diodotus; Thucydides, by the space and care he gives the speech, on many readings
positions.view: Punishment does not deter people driven by hope; mass killing makes rebels fight to the end and turns friends into enemies. The wise course is to punish the guilty and spare the rest, for Athens' own sake.
positions.evidence: His speech; the common people of Mytilene, who surrendered the city; the later history of Athens' alliances.

positions.name: Neither: it was simply wrong
positions.who: The Athenians' own 'repentance' the morning after; Israel's law in Exodus 23; Christian and many modern readers
positions.view: Both speakers argued only from Athenian interest. But killing the innocent with the guilty is wrong whatever it gains or loses. The true restraint on a crowd is not a better calculation but a law of justice above the crowd.
positions.evidence: 'The horrid cruelty of a decree, which condemned a whole city to the fate merited only by the guilty'; Exodus 23:2, 7.

debate.agree: All agree that the first decree was made in anger and in haste, and that a second, calmer debate was what saved Mytilene.

look.why: There is no painting of the Athenian assembly at the National Gallery of Art. This is a crowd of voters in a modern democracy: an election day in Catonsville, Maryland, painted by Alfred Jacob Miller around 1860. It shows what Thucydides could only describe: a crowd arguing, reading, laughing and deciding together.
points: Twelve people, standing and on horseback, talk and gesture in a tight group around a wagon outside a house; all appear to be men.
On the far left a rider in an olive-green jacket, with a curving horn on his back, raises a whip.
A rider in a red shirt on a white horse smiles as he reads a paper braced against the horse's mane.
A man in a gold-coloured coat with a red sash holds up a paper; nearby, two men smile at each other as they talk.
Four men stand or sit on the wagon above the crowd, and beyond a low fence, in a yard, at least three brown-skinned people stand together.

music.why: In Bach's Passion the crowd sings too: asked whom to release, it shouts for Barabbas, and asked what to do with Jesus, it cries 'crucify him'. Listen to those short, violent choruses: a crowd deciding in anger.

think.why: Diodotus argued from interest; the Athenians' own consciences and Exodus argued from right and wrong. See whether morality needs something above us.

learn.why: The law that names the danger of Mytilene: each person is answerable for his own vote, even in a crowd.

check.q: What is the strongest part of Cleon's argument?
options: That the Mytilenians had been badly treated by Athens
That mercy would win Athens the loyalty of its allies
That laws which change with every mood lose their authority, so a city should not reopen decisions lightly
That Diodotus had been bribed
check.why: Stability of law is a real value; Cleon uses it to block reconsideration of a decision made in anger.

check.q: Why does Diodotus say the question is 'not their guilt, but our interests'?
options: Because the law forbade discussing guilt
Because he thinks justice has no place in politics at all
Because he thinks the Mytilenians were innocent
Because he believes an assembly deciding policy should ask what is wise for the future, not act as a court deciding what is deserved
check.why: 'We are not in a court of justice, but in a political assembly': he shifts the question to future consequences.

check.q: Diodotus argues that the death penalty will not deter rebellion. What is his reason?
options: Athens could not afford executions
Rebels do not know the law
The Mytilenians were brave
Hope and desire drive people to take risks whatever the punishment, and rebels facing certain death will fight to the end
check.why: He says no law or deterrent can stop human nature once it has set its mind on something; harsher penalties only make surrender pointless.

check.q: What does the Mytilene debate show about the Athenian constitution?
options: That there was no institution above the assembly: only conscience, a second debate and luck saved the city
That the courts could overrule the assembly
That Athens had a written bill of rights
That the generals made all decisions
check.why: The assembly's vote was final; nothing in the system could have stopped the first decree being carried out.

check.q: Which of these is a demagogue's tactic that Cleon uses?
options: Suggesting that those who argue the other side have been bribed, and urging action before anger cools
Proposing a careful inquiry
Refusing to speak
Asking for a secret ballot
check.why: He hints his opponents are bribed and says vengeance is best 'where it follows most closely upon the wrong'.

check.q: What does Exodus 23 give as a reason not to follow the crowd that neither Cleon nor Diodotus gives?
options: That killing the innocent is wrong because God will not justify the wicked, whatever it gains
That only priests can judge
That the poor should always win
That crowds are usually wrong
check.why: Both speakers argue from Athenian interest; Exodus grounds justice in God's judgement.

tutorial.question: What does the Mytilene debate teach about the dangers of democracy, and the remedies?
tutorial.approach: Tell the story briefly. Set out Cleon's and Diodotus' arguments at their strongest. Ask what actually saved Mytilene. Use Arginusae as a contrast. Then consider remedies: the Athenians' own reforms, Madison's, and the individual conscience of Exodus 23.
strong: Narrates the two decrees accurately, with the 'fury of the moment' and the 'repentance' of the morrow.
States Cleon's case fairly, including stability of law and deterrence.
Explains why Diodotus argued from interest, not justice, and what that implies.
Uses Arginusae as a case where there was no second chance.
Discusses at least two remedies: the graphe paranomon, separation of laws and decrees, Madison's institutions.
Uses Exodus 23:2 to show a different kind of restraint.
