sessions.practice: Live it this week: Diodotus said the enemies of good counsel are haste and passion. Next time you are angry enough to send a message, post a comment or make a decision, wait a night first, as the Athenians did, and then decide again.
sessions.reflect: When have you gone along with a group in something you later regretted? What would have helped you stand apart?
takeaways: In 427 BC the Athenian assembly voted in anger to kill all the men of Mytilene, repented overnight, and reversed the decree by a handful of votes.
Cleon argued for firmness and deterrence; Diodotus won by arguing from Athenian interest, perhaps disguising mercy as self-interest.
Nothing in Athens could overrule the assembly; the remedies came later: the charge of illegality, fixed laws, Madison's institutions, and the conscience Exodus 23 demands.

sessions.title: The case against: Plato
sessions.line: A philosopher who watched his city kill his teacher argues that democracy's love of freedom breeds disorder, and that disorder ends in tyranny.
sessions.plain: Plato grew up in Athens during the war, saw the democracy make terrible decisions, and in 399 BC saw a jury of his fellow citizens condemn his teacher Socrates to death. In his Republic he argues that democracy is the second-worst kind of government. Ruling, he says, is a skill like steering a ship, and a crowd that thinks anyone can steer will throw the real navigator overboard. Democracy loves freedom above everything, and treats every desire as equal, until no one respects any authority at all; then the people look for a champion against the rich, and the champion becomes a tyrant. This session gives that case in Plato's own words, at full strength.
sessions.why: Session 4 showed the Athenian assembly voting in anger to kill a whole city, and nearly doing it. Arginusae showed it did not always repent in time. Plato drew the conclusion that Thucydides only hinted at: the problem is not bad leaders but democracy itself. Before we can defend democracy, we have to face the strongest case against it.
answers: Why did Plato hate democracy?
What is the ship of state?
Does too much freedom lead to tyranny?
Should the wise rule instead of the many?
sessions.finding: Plato argued that ruling is a skill most people lack, that democracy's love of freedom treats every desire and every person as equal until all authority dissolves, and that the people then raise up a protector who becomes a tyrant: on this view rule should belong to those who know.

paras: In sessions 1 to 3 we saw how Athens built its democracy and how it worked at its best. In session 4 we saw its danger: an assembly that could vote a massacre in anger, and a constitution with nothing above the assembly to stop it. We also met a citizen named Socrates, who in 406 BC refused to put an illegal motion to the vote.

The war with Sparta ended in 404 BC with Athens' surrender. Sparta installed a group of oligarchs, the Thirty, who ruled by terror for eight months and killed perhaps 1,500 Athenians before the democrats drove them out in 403 BC. The restored democracy passed an amnesty forbidding prosecution for what had happened. Four years later, in 399 BC, three citizens prosecuted Socrates for impiety and for corrupting the young. A jury of 501 found him guilty, by about 280 votes to 220, and sentenced him to death by drinking hemlock.

timeline.text: Plato is born in Athens
Socrates opposes the illegal trial of the generals
The Thirty Tyrants, among them Plato's relatives Critias and Charmides
Democracy restored, with an amnesty
Trial and death of Socrates
Plato founds the Academy in Athens
The Republic
Death of Plato

background.key: After defeat, the Thirty Tyrants' terror and the democracy's return, an Athenian jury condemned Socrates to death in 399 BC.

paras: Plato came from one of the old families of Athens. Two of his relatives, Critias and Charmides, were leaders of the Thirty. As a young man he was drawn to Socrates, who spent his life questioning his fellow citizens about justice, courage and the good, and showing them they did not know what they thought they knew. A letter that has come down under Plato's name, the Seventh Letter (its authenticity is debated), says he hoped to go into politics, was disgusted first by the Thirty and then by the democracy that killed Socrates, and concluded that cities would have no rest from evils until philosophers ruled.

So Plato was not a neutral observer. He had seen tyranny from his own family and democracy from the jury that killed his teacher. That does not make his arguments wrong. It explains why he made them so sharply.
background.key: Plato, from an aristocratic family linked to the Thirty, turned against both oligarchy and democracy after the death of Socrates.

paras: The Republic is a long dialogue, a conversation written as a play, in which Socrates and his friends ask what justice is. To find out, they imagine an ideal city ruled by philosopher-kings, men and women trained for decades to know the good. (The ideal city itself is explored in the journey 'Plato', later in this hall.)

In Book VIII Socrates describes how the ideal city would decay, step by step, through four worse forms: timocracy, the rule of honour, like Sparta; oligarchy, the rule of the rich; democracy; and tyranny, the worst. Each form, he says, is destroyed by too much of the very thing it values. Democracy comes fourth of five: better only than tyranny, which it produces.

rows: Rulers mistake the right times for breeding, and lesser rulers arise
Love of honour turns into love of money
Greed makes many poor, who rise up
The worst state, and the most miserable ruler
table.note: Republic VIII–IX, in outline.

background.key: In Republic VIII Plato traces the decline of the ideal city through timocracy, oligarchy and democracy to tyranny, each destroyed by excess of what it values.

paras: The main reading follows Plato's case in five steps: democracy as the 'fairest' of states; the democratic man; too much freedom; the protector who becomes a tyrant; and the end, slavery. The speaker is Socrates; his partner in conversation is Plato's brother Adeimantus. Short replies like 'True' and 'Clearly' are his.
The comparison is from Book VI: the parable of the ship of state, Plato's most famous image of what is wrong with government by the people.
background.key: Five steps from Republic VIII, then the ship of state from Book VI.

before: Why does Socrates call democracy 'the fairest of States', and is he being sincere?
What does the democratic man do with his desires?
How exactly does a protector of the people become a tyrant?
sessions.readWhy: Plato's case against democracy in five steps, from 'the fairest of States' to 'the harshest and bitterest form of slavery'.

paras: And then democracy comes into being after the poor have conquered their opponents, slaughtering some and banishing some, while to the remainder they give an equal share of freedom and power; and this is the form of government in which the magistrates are commonly elected by lot.
Yes, he said, that is the nature of democracy, whether the revolution has been effected by arms, or whether fear has caused the opposite party to withdraw.
And now what is their manner of life, and what sort of a government have they? for as the government is, such will be the man.
Clearly, he said.
In the first place, are they not free; and is not the city full of freedom and frankness—a man may say and do what he likes?
’Tis said so, he replied.
And where freedom is, the individual is clearly able to order for himself his own life as he pleases?
Clearly.
Then in this kind of State there will be the greatest variety of human natures?
There will.

This, then, seems likely to be the fairest of States, being like an embroidered robe which is spangled with every sort of flower. And just as women and children think a variety of colours to be of all things most charming, so there are many men to whom this State, which is spangled with the manners and characters of mankind, will appear to be the fairest of States.
Yes.
Yes, my good Sir, and there will be no better in which to look for a government.
Why?

Because of the liberty which reigns there—they have a complete assortment of constitutions; and he who has a mind to establish a State, as we have been doing, must go to a democracy as he would to a bazaar at which they sell them, and pick out the one that suits him; then, when he has made his choice, he may found his State.
He will be sure to have patterns enough.

And there being no necessity, I said, for you to govern in this State, even if you have the capacity, or to be governed, unless you like, or go to war when the rest go to war, or to be at peace when others are at peace, unless you are so disposed—there being no necessity also, because some law forbids you to hold office or be a dicast, that you should not hold office or be a dicast, if you have a fancy—is not this a way of life which for the moment is supremely delightful?
For the moment, yes.

And is not their humanity to the condemned in some cases quite charming? Have you not observed how, in a democracy, many persons, although they have been sentenced to death or exile, just stay where they are and walk about the world—the gentleman parades like a hero, and nobody sees or cares?
Yes, he replied, many and many a one.

See too, I said, the forgiving spirit of democracy, and the ‘don’t care’ about trifles, and the disregard which she shows of all the fine principles which we solemnly laid down at the foundation of the city—as when we said that, except in the case of some rarely gifted nature, there never will be a good man who has not from his childhood been used to play amid things of beauty and make of them a joy and a study—how grandly does she trample all these fine notions of ours under her feet, never giving a thought to the pursuits which make a statesman, and promoting to honour any one who professes to be the people’s friend.
Yes, she is of a noble spirit.
These and other kindred characteristics are proper to democracy, which is a charming form of government, full of variety and disorder, and dispensing a sort of equality to equals and unequals alike.
We know her well.

Yes, I said, he lives from day to day indulging the appetite of the hour; and sometimes he is lapped in drink and strains of the flute; then he becomes a water-drinker, and tries to get thin; then he takes a turn at gymnastics; sometimes idling and neglecting everything, then once more living the life of a philosopher; often he is busy with politics, and starts to his feet and says and does whatever comes into his head; and, if he is emulous of any one who is a warrior, off he is in that direction, or of men of business, once more in that. His life has neither law nor order; and this distracted existence he terms joy and bliss and freedom; and so he goes on.
Yes, he replied, he is all liberty and equality.

Yes, I said; his life is motley and manifold and an epitome of the lives of many;—he answers to the State which we described as fair and spangled. And many a man and many a woman will take him for their pattern, and many a constitution and many an example of manners is contained in him.
Just so.
Last of all comes the most beautiful of all, man and State alike, tyranny and the tyrant; these we have now to consider.
Quite true, he said.
Say then, my friend, In what manner does tyranny arise?—that it has a democratic origin is evident.
Clearly.
And does not tyranny spring from democracy in the same manner as democracy from oligarchy—I mean, after a sort?
How?
The good which oligarchy proposed to itself and the means by which it was maintained was excess of wealth—am I not right?
Yes.
And the insatiable desire of wealth and the neglect of all other things for the sake of money-getting was also the ruin of oligarchy?
True.
And democracy has her own good, of which the insatiable desire brings her to dissolution?
What good?
Freedom, I replied; which, as they tell you in a democracy, is the glory of the State—and that therefore in a democracy alone will the freeman of nature deign to dwell.
Yes; the saying is in every body’s mouth.
I was going to observe, that the insatiable desire of this and the neglect of other things introduces the change in democracy, which occasions a demand for tyranny.
How so?

When a democracy which is thirsting for freedom has evil cup-bearers presiding over the feast, and has drunk too deeply of the strong wine of freedom, then, unless her rulers are very amenable and give a plentiful draught, she calls them to account and punishes them, and says that they are cursed oligarchs.
Yes, he replied, a very common occurrence.

Yes, I said; and loyal citizens are insultingly termed by her slaves who hug their chains and men of naught; she would have subjects who are like rulers, and rulers who are like subjects: these are men after her own heart, whom she praises and honours both in private and public. Now, in such a State, can liberty have any limit?
Certainly not.
By degrees the anarchy finds a way into private houses, and ends by getting among the animals and infecting them.
How do you mean?

I mean that the father grows accustomed to descend to the level of his sons and to fear them, and the son is on a level with his father, he having no respect or reverence for either of his parents; and this is his freedom, and the metic is equal with the citizen and the citizen with the metic, and the stranger is quite as good as either.
Yes, he said, that is the way.

And these are not the only evils, I said—there are several lesser ones: In such a state of society the master fears and flatters his scholars, and the scholars despise their masters and tutors; young and old are all alike; and the young man is on a level with the old, and is ready to compete with him in word or deed; and old men condescend to the young and are full of pleasantry and gaiety; they are loth to be thought morose and authoritative, and therefore they adopt the manners of the young.
Quite true, he said.

The last extreme of popular liberty is when the slave bought with money, whether male or female, is just as free as his or her purchaser; nor must I forget to tell of the liberty and equality of the two sexes in relation to each other.
Why not, as Aeschylus says, utter the word which rises to our lips?

That is what I am doing, I replied; and I must add that no one who does not know would believe, how much greater is the liberty which the animals who are under the dominion of man have in a democracy than in any other State: for truly, the she-dogs, as the proverb says, are as good as their she-mistresses, and the horses and asses have a way of marching along with all the rights and dignities of freemen; and they will run at any body who comes in their way if he does not leave the road clear for them: and all things are just ready to burst with liberty.
When I take a country walk, he said, I often experience what you describe. You and I have dreamed the same thing.

And above all, I said, and as the result of all, see how sensitive the citizens become; they chafe impatiently at the least touch of authority, and at length, as you know, they cease to care even for the laws, written or unwritten; they will have no one over them.
Yes, he said, I know it too well.
Such, my friend, I said, is the fair and glorious beginning out of which springs tyranny.
Glorious indeed, he said. But what is the next step?

The ruin of oligarchy is the ruin of democracy; the same disease magnified and intensified by liberty overmasters democracy—the truth being that the excessive increase of anything often causes a reaction in the opposite direction; and this is the case not only in the seasons and in vegetable and animal life, but above all in forms of government.
True.
The excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery.
Yes, the natural order.
And so tyranny naturally arises out of democracy, and the most aggravated form of tyranny and slavery out of the most extreme form of liberty?
As we might expect.
The people have always some champion whom they set over them and nurse into greatness.
Yes, that is their way.
This and no other is the root from which a tyrant springs; when he first appears above ground he is a protector.
Yes, that is quite clear.
How then does a protector begin to change into a tyrant? Clearly when he does what the man is said to do in the tale of the Arcadian temple of Lycaean Zeus.
What tale?
The tale is that he who has tasted the entrails of a single human victim minced up with the entrails of other victims is destined to become a wolf. Did you never hear it?
Oh, yes.

And the protector of the people is like him; having a mob entirely at his disposal, he is not restrained from shedding the blood of kinsmen; by the favourite method of false accusation he brings them into court and murders them, making the life of man to disappear, and with unholy tongue and lips tasting the blood of his fellow citizens; some he kills and others he banishes, at the same time hinting at the abolition of debts and partition of lands: and after this, what will be his destiny? Must he not either perish at the hands of his enemies, or from being a man become a wolf—that is, a tyrant?
Inevitably.
This, I said, is he who begins to make a party against the rich?
The same.
After a while he is driven out, but comes back, in spite of his enemies, a tyrant full grown.
That is clear.
And if they are unable to expel him, or to get him condemned to death by a public accusation, they conspire to assassinate him.
Yes, he said, that is their usual way.
Then comes the famous request for a body-guard, which is the device of all those who have got thus far in their tyrannical career—‘Let not the people’s friend,’ as they say, ‘be lost to them.’
Exactly.
The people readily assent; all their fears are for him—they have none for themselves.
Very true.
And when a man who is wealthy and is also accused of being an enemy of the people sees this, then, my friend, as the oracle said to Croesus,
‘By pebbly Hermus’ shore he flees and rests not, and is not ashamed to be a coward.’
And quite right too, said he, for if he were, he would never be ashamed again.
But if he is caught he dies.
Of course.

And he, the protector of whom we spoke, is to be seen, not ‘larding the plain’ with his bulk, but himself the overthrower of many, standing up in the chariot of State with the reins in his hand, no longer protector, but tyrant absolute.
No doubt, he said.

Then he is a parricide, and a cruel guardian of an aged parent; and this is real tyranny, about which there can be no longer a mistake: as the saying is, the people who would escape the smoke which is the slavery of freemen, has fallen into the fire which is the tyranny of slaves. Thus liberty, getting out of all order and reason, passes into the harshest and bitterest form of slavery.
True, he said.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The fairest of states
parts.context: Socrates has just described how oligarchy, the rule of the rich, makes many citizens poor, until the poor rise up. A dicast was a juror. Jowett's translation dates from 1871; its English can be old-fashioned ('a man may say and do what he likes'), but it is close to the Greek.
parts.plain: Democracy comes when the poor win and give everyone an equal share of freedom and power, with officials chosen by lot. Everyone is free to say and do what he likes and to live as he pleases, so there is endless variety, like a robe embroidered with flowers. No one has to rule, obey, fight or keep the peace unless he wants to. Even condemned men walk about freely. Democracy ignores the training a statesman needs and honours anyone who says he is the people's friend. It is charming, varied and disorderly, and gives equality to equals and unequals alike.

commentary.on: this is the form of government in which the magistrates are commonly elected by lot
commentary.text: Plato picks out the lot, which we met in session 2, as the mark of democracy. To him it is absurd: it assumes anyone is fit to rule.

commentary.on: is not the city full of freedom and frankness—a man may say and do what he likes?
commentary.text: Freedom (eleutheria) and frankness (parrhesia) were the Athenians' proudest words. Plato does not deny democracy has them. His argument is that they are the problem.

commentary.on: like an embroidered robe which is spangled with every sort of flower
commentary.text: Socrates' praise is ironic. Variety is attractive, he says, as bright colours are to children. But variety is not the same as goodness.

commentary.on: go to a democracy as he would to a bazaar at which they sell them
commentary.text: A wonderful joke: democracy is a shop selling every kind of constitution, because it tolerates every way of life. Defenders of democracy would later make this its glory: pluralism.

commentary.on: the gentleman parades like a hero, and nobody sees or cares
commentary.text: A dig at Athenian laxness. Some of those condemned did not leave. Plato may be thinking bitterly of the one condemned man who did stay to die: Socrates.

commentary.on: promoting to honour any one who professes to be the people’s friend
commentary.text: Here is the core charge. Democracy does not ask whether a leader knows how to rule; it asks whether he says he loves the people. That is the opening for the demagogue.

commentary.on: dispensing a sort of equality to equals and unequals alike
commentary.text: The key phrase. For Plato people are not equal in wisdom or virtue. Treating them as equal in power is not justice but a kind of blindness.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The democratic man
parts.context: For Plato, every kind of city has a matching kind of person, because a city is its citizens writ large. Socrates now describes the man shaped by democracy. Just before this passage he says this man refuses to rank his pleasures: 'one is as good as another'.
parts.plain: The democratic man lives for whatever he feels like today: drinking one day, dieting the next, sport, idleness, philosophy, politics, business. He follows each desire in turn. His life has no law or order, and he calls this freedom and happiness. He is the city in miniature, and many people admire him.

commentary.on: he lives from day to day indulging the appetite of the hour
commentary.text: A portrait that many readers find uncomfortably modern. Every desire gets its turn; none is ruled by any idea of what is good.

commentary.on: His life has neither law nor order; and this distracted existence he terms joy and bliss and freedom
commentary.text: The charge is not that he is wicked, but that he has no centre. For Plato freedom without order is not freedom at all, but being pushed around by your appetites.

commentary.on: he is all liberty and equality
commentary.text: Liberty and equality: the watchwords of later democracy, here used as an accusation. If all desires are equal, none can be ruled.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Too much freedom
parts.context: Now Socrates turns to the last step, the change from democracy to tyranny. Metics, you will remember from session 2, were resident foreigners. The bema was the speaker's platform in the assembly.
parts.plain: Oligarchy was ruined by its love of money; democracy is ruined by its love of freedom. A people drunk on freedom calls its rulers oligarchs if they restrain it. Soon no authority is respected: fathers fear their sons, teachers flatter their pupils, the young and old are on a level, slaves and even animals behave as if free. In the end people resent the slightest control and ignore the laws. Too much of anything turns into its opposite: too much freedom turns into slavery, and tyranny grows out of democracy.

commentary.on: And democracy has her own good, of which the insatiable desire brings her to dissolution?
commentary.text: This is the pattern of Book VIII. Each constitution dies of its own virtue taken to excess. Democracy's virtue is freedom.

commentary.on: has drunk too deeply of the strong wine of freedom
commentary.text: Freedom as wine: good in measure, ruinous in excess. Leaders who try to set limits are called enemies of the people.

commentary.on: she would have subjects who are like rulers, and rulers who are like subjects
commentary.text: In a democracy everyone wants to rule and no one wants to be ruled. Authority itself becomes suspect.

commentary.on: the father grows accustomed to descend to the level of his sons and to fear them
commentary.text: Plato's picture moves from the city into the home and the school. The loss of authority is not only political; it runs through every relationship.

commentary.on: the master fears and flatters his scholars, and the scholars despise their masters and tutors
commentary.text: Readers in every age have recognised their own society in this sentence. That may be a sign of its insight, or of how easily every generation thinks the young are disrespectful.

commentary.on: The last extreme of popular liberty is when the slave bought with money, whether male or female, is just as free as his or her purchaser
commentary.text: Notice what Plato counts as a symptom of decline: slaves behaving like free people, and women like men. Here his case rests on assumptions almost no one now shares. A fair reading must say so.

commentary.on: they cease to care even for the laws, written or unwritten; they will have no one over them
commentary.text: This is the heart of the argument, and the hardest to dismiss. A people that will accept no authority above itself, not even law, has nothing to stop it. Mytilene and Arginusae are the evidence.

commentary.on: The excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery.
commentary.text: The most famous sentence of the book, and this session's words to learn. Extreme freedom produces its opposite, because people who have dissolved every authority will in the end accept any master who promises order.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The protector becomes a wolf
parts.context: Socrates has described three classes in a democracy: the 'drones' (idle, ambitious speakers), the rich, and the working people. The drones take from the rich to give a little to the people, and the rich, accused of plotting, begin to plot in earnest. The Arcadian tale is a legend that whoever ate human flesh at a sacrifice to Zeus would turn into a wolf.
parts.plain: The people always set up a champion and make him great; that is where a tyrant comes from. At first he is their protector. Then, with a mob behind him, he begins to bring false charges, kill and exile his opponents, and promise to cancel debts and share out land. Like the man in the legend who tasted human flesh, he becomes a wolf. When his enemies try to kill him, he asks for a bodyguard, and the people gladly give it, fearing for him and not for themselves. Then he stands in the chariot of state, no longer a protector but a tyrant.

commentary.on: The people have always some champion whom they set over them and nurse into greatness.
commentary.text: The Greek word is prostates, 'one who stands in front': a champion or protector of the people. Plato's claim is that tyranny does not come from outside democracy. The people make it themselves.

commentary.on: when he first appears above ground he is a protector
commentary.text: Every tyrant begins as a defender of the people against someone: the rich, the elites, the foreigners.

commentary.on: by the favourite method of false accusation he brings them into court and murders them
commentary.text: The courts, democracy's proudest institution, become the tyrant's weapon. Plato's readers would have thought of Socrates.

commentary.on: hinting at the abolition of debts and partition of lands
commentary.text: The very things the poor asked of Solon in session 1. Solon gave the first and refused the second; Plato's protector promises both.

commentary.on: Then comes the famous request for a body-guard
commentary.text: 'Famous', because every Athenian knew the story. Herodotus (1.59) tells how Peisistratus wounded himself and his mules, drove into the market-place claiming his enemies had attacked him, and persuaded the assembly to give him a bodyguard. With it he seized the Acropolis and made himself tyrant. Plato is describing Athens' own history.

commentary.on: The people readily assent; all their fears are for him—they have none for themselves.
commentary.text: This is the moment democracy gives itself away: the people fear for their champion, not for their freedom.

commentary.on: no longer protector, but tyrant absolute
commentary.text: The champion of the people now drives the chariot of state. The ship image, which we are about to read, says the same thing differently.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Out of the smoke into the fire
parts.context: The end of Book VIII. Socrates has compared the people to a father who has raised a son, the tyrant, and now cannot control him.
parts.plain: When the people try to throw out the tyrant they have raised, they find he is stronger than they are. Trying to escape the 'smoke' of being ruled by free men, they have fallen into the 'fire' of being ruled by a tyrant's slaves. Liberty without order and reason becomes the worst slavery.

commentary.on: the people who would escape the smoke which is the slavery of freemen, has fallen into the fire which is the tyranny of slaves
commentary.text: Our phrase 'out of the frying pan into the fire' has an ancient cousin here. The people wanted to be free of all masters, even the mild rule of fellow citizens, and got the harshest master of all.

commentary.on: Thus liberty, getting out of all order and reason, passes into the harshest and bitterest form of slavery.
commentary.text: Plato's conclusion. Notice what he says, and what he does not. He does not say freedom is bad. He says freedom 'out of all order and reason' destroys itself. Any defence of democracy has to say what supplies that order and reason.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy

paras: I perceive, I said, that you are vastly amused at having plunged me into such a hopeless discussion; but now hear the parable, and then you will be still more amused at the meagreness of my imagination: for the manner in which the best men are treated in their own States is so grievous that no single thing on earth is comparable to it; and therefore, if I am to plead their cause, I must have recourse to fiction, and put together a figure made up of many things, like the fabulous unions of goats and stags which are found in pictures. Imagine then a fleet or a ship in which there is a captain who is taller and stronger than any of the crew, but he is a little deaf and has a similar infirmity in sight, and his knowledge of navigation is not much better. The sailors are quarrelling with one another about the steering—every one is of opinion that he has a right to steer, though he has never learned the art of navigation and cannot tell who taught him or when he learned, and will further assert that it cannot be taught, and they are ready to cut in pieces any one who says the contrary. They throng about the captain, begging and praying him to commit the helm to them;

and if at any time they do not prevail, but others are preferred to them, they kill the others or throw them overboard, and having first chained up the noble captain’s senses with drink or some narcotic drug, they mutiny and take possession of the ship and make free with the stores; thus, eating and drinking, they proceed on their voyage in such manner as might be expected of them. Him who is their partisan and cleverly aids them in their plot for getting the ship out of the captain’s hands into their own whether by force or persuasion, they compliment with the name of sailor, pilot, able seaman, and abuse the other sort of man, whom they call a good-for-nothing; but that the true pilot must pay attention to the year and seasons and sky and stars and winds, and whatever else belongs to his art, if he intends to be really qualified for the command of a ship, and that he must and will be the steerer, whether other people like or not—the possibility of this union of authority with the steerer’s art has never seriously entered into their thoughts or been made part of their calling. Now in vessels which are in a state of mutiny and by sailors who are mutineers, how will the true pilot be regarded? Will he not be called by them a prater, a star-gazer, a good-for-nothing?
Of course, said Adeimantus.
Then you will hardly need, I said, to hear the interpretation of the figure, which describes the true philosopher in his relation to the State; for you understand already.
Certainly.

Then suppose you now take this parable to the gentleman who is surprised at finding that philosophers have no honour in their cities; explain it to him and try to convince him that their having honour would be far more extraordinary.
I will.

Say to him, that, in deeming the best votaries of philosophy to be useless to the rest of the world, he is right; but also tell him to attribute their uselessness to the fault of those who will not use them, and not to themselves. The pilot should not humbly beg the sailors to be commanded by him—that is not the order of nature; neither are ‘the wise to go to the doors of the rich’—the ingenious author of this saying told a lie—but the truth is, that, when a man is ill, whether he be rich or poor, to the physician he must go, and he who wants to be governed, to him who is able to govern. The ruler who is good for anything ought not to beg his subjects to be ruled by him; although the present governors of mankind are of a different stamp; they may be justly compared to the mutinous sailors, and the true helmsmen to those who are called by them good-for-nothings and star-gazers.
Precisely so, he said.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Who should steer?
parts.context: Adeimantus has objected that philosophers are obviously useless in politics, so how can Socrates say they should rule? Socrates answers with a parable. The 'captain' is the people: big and strong, but half deaf and half blind. The sailors are the politicians. The 'true pilot' is the philosopher.
parts.plain: Imagine a ship whose owner is strong but deaf, short-sighted and ignorant of navigation. The sailors quarrel over who should steer; none has learned how, and they say it cannot be taught. They drug the owner, seize the ship and feast on its stores, and they praise whoever helps them as a fine seaman. The man who has actually studied the stars, winds and seasons, they call a useless star-gazer. That, says Socrates, is how cities treat philosophers. The sick should go to the doctor; those who need governing should go to one who knows how.

commentary.on: a captain who is taller and stronger than any of the crew, but he is a little deaf and has a similar infirmity in sight
commentary.text: The captain, or ship-owner, is the demos: the people, who own the city and are powerful but poorly informed. Plato is not cruel to him; he is simply not a navigator.

commentary.on: every one is of opinion that he has a right to steer, though he has never learned the art of navigation
commentary.text: This is the heart of Plato's objection. In democracy everyone claims the right to rule, and no one is asked to show that he knows how.

commentary.on: will further assert that it cannot be taught
commentary.text: Plato's sharpest point. Democrats, he says, must deny that ruling is a skill at all, because if it were, the skilled should do it.

commentary.on: the true pilot must pay attention to the year and seasons and sky and stars and winds
commentary.text: Ruling, like navigation, needs real knowledge. The image of the city as a ship, which Solon's oracle used in session 1, now becomes an argument for rule by experts.

commentary.on: Will he not be called by them a prater, a star-gazer, a good-for-nothing?
commentary.text: In a democracy, the one who knows is mocked. Aristophanes had mocked Socrates in exactly these terms in his comedy The Clouds (423 BC).

commentary.on: when a man is ill, whether he be rich or poor, to the physician he must go, and he who wants to be governed, to him who is able to govern
commentary.text: The doctor is Plato's other favourite comparison. No one would choose a surgeon by lot or by show of hands. Why choose a government that way?

compare.author: Plato
compare.why: In Book VI Plato gives his case in one image. It is the most famous argument ever made against government by the people, and it answers the question directly: who should steer?
compare.title: The ship of state

paras: Plato's case is philosophical, but it grew out of experience. He was a boy during the plague, a young man during Mytilene's aftermath, Arginusae and the Sicilian disaster. He saw the oligarchs of 404 BC, including his own relatives, murder their fellow citizens. And he saw the restored democracy, which had shown real restraint in passing an amnesty, put the best man he knew to death.

The trial of Socrates is the heart of it. Socrates was charged with not believing in the city's gods, bringing in new ones, and corrupting the young. Many historians think politics lay behind the charges: Socrates had been the teacher of Critias, the leader of the Thirty, and of Alcibiades, who betrayed Athens to Sparta. The amnesty meant he could not be charged with that directly. For Plato, the verdict proved that the many cannot tell a philosopher from a sophist, or a friend of the city from its enemy.
sections.key: Plato's case grew from experience, above all the democracy's execution of Socrates in 399 BC, which he took as proof that the many cannot judge.

paras: Plato's first argument is about knowledge. In every other field we go to experts: doctors, pilots, builders. Ruling a city, deciding war and peace, justice and law, is harder than any of these. So it too must be a skill, a techne, and the people who should do it are those who have it. Democracy assumes, absurdly, that everyone is equally qualified.

Plato knew the democratic reply. In his dialogue Protagoras, the sophist Protagoras tells a myth: when Zeus gave out skills, he gave medicine to a few, but a sense of justice and shame to everyone, because no city could survive otherwise. That is why Athenians listen only to experts on building ships, but let anyone speak on how the city should be run. Plato did not accept the answer. Notice, though, that the defence of democracy and the attack on it were both written down by the same man.
sections.key: Plato argued that ruling is a skill like medicine or navigation, so experts should rule; he also recorded Protagoras' reply that everyone shares a sense of justice.

paras: Plato's second argument is about the soul. A democracy values freedom above everything else, and so it cannot say that one way of life is better than another. The democratic man, who follows every desire in turn and calls it freedom, is its natural product. And a society of such people cannot recognise wisdom, because recognising wisdom means admitting that some views and some lives are better than others.

This is the part of Plato's case that has worn best. Writers as different as Alexis de Tocqueville, in Democracy in America (1835–40), and the American philosopher Allan Bloom, in The Closing of the American Mind (1987), took it up in their own words. Their worry was not tyranny by force, but a soft drift in which people stop asking what is good and ask only what they want.
sections.key: Plato argued that democracy, valuing freedom above all, cannot rank desires or ways of life, and so cannot recognise wisdom.

paras: Plato's third argument is about history. Democracies dissolve authority until people feel unprotected; the rich and the poor turn on each other; and the people find a champion who promises to defend them. Given a bodyguard, he becomes a tyrant. Plato had good examples. Peisistratus became tyrant of Athens exactly this way, as Herodotus tells. Dionysius I of Syracuse, whose court Plato visited, rose as a popular general and was given a bodyguard by the assembly.

The pattern has repeated itself. Rome's republic ended when a series of popular generals, the last of them Julius Caesar, won the people's support against the senate. Political scientists such as Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt, in How Democracies Die (2018), have described how modern democracies can end not in a coup but through leaders who are elected and then, step by step, capture the courts, silence critics and change the rules. Plato would not have been surprised.
sections.key: Plato argued that democracies produce tyrants through popular champions; Peisistratus and Dionysius fit his pattern, and modern scholars describe elected leaders dismantling democracy.

paras: Plato's argument is not only ancient. Economists and philosophers have revived it with modern evidence. Bryan Caplan's The Myth of the Rational Voter (2007) argued that voters hold systematic, predictable errors about economics, and vote for policies that harm them, because a single vote costs nothing to cast badly.

The philosopher Jason Brennan, in Against Democracy (2016), sorts citizens into three types: those who know little and care little; those who care passionately but treat politics like supporting a sports team, ignoring evidence that goes against their side; and the rare few who reason carefully. Since most voters are of the first two kinds, he argues, we have no right to impose their decisions on everyone. He proposes 'epistocracy', rule by the knowledgeable: for example, giving extra votes to those who pass a test of basic political knowledge, or letting an expert council veto ignorant laws. Brennan does not want philosopher-kings, but his argument is Plato's ship, with modern surveys of voters' knowledge as the evidence.
sections.key: Caplan and Brennan renew Plato's case with evidence that most voters are uninformed or partisan; Brennan proposes 'epistocracy', rule weighted towards the knowledgeable.

paras: Plato's case is strong, and it should be left standing for a moment before anyone replies. Any defence of democracy has to answer three charges. First, competence: if most people do not know enough to rule well, why should they rule? Second, character: if a free society cannot say that some lives are better than others, what stops it drifting into disorder? Third, tyranny: if democracies breed demagogues, and demagogues become tyrants, what stops the slide?

The Athenians' own history gives Plato some of his best evidence: Mytilene, Arginusae, the death of Socrates. It also gives some evidence against him: the second debate at Mytilene, the amnesty of 403 BC, the restored democracy that lasted for another eighty years. The next two sessions, still to come, give the two great answers: Aristotle's, from Athens, and the Bible's, from Jerusalem.
sections.key: Any defence of democracy must answer Plato's three charges: competence, character and the slide into tyranny.

paras: In 1945 the Austrian-born philosopher Karl Popper, who had fled the Nazis, published The Open Society and Its Enemies. Its first volume accused Plato of designing a closed, totalitarian state: rule by a caste that claims to know the good, censorship of poets, lies told to the people 'for their own good', and the individual sacrificed to the city. Popper thought Plato's question, 'Who should rule?', was itself the mistake. The right question was how to arrange institutions so that bad rulers can be removed without bloodshed.

Plato's defenders reply that the Republic is an ideal to think with, not a blueprint, and that Plato himself, in his later dialogue the Laws, turned to a government ruled by law and mixing monarchy with democracy. The debate over Plato is part of the journey 'Plato', later in this hall. For this journey Popper matters because he gives the most influential modern answer to the ship of state: we do not need a perfect pilot, only a crew that can replace a bad one.
sections.key: Popper accused Plato of designing a closed society and replied that the real question is how to remove bad rulers peacefully; Plato's defenders note the Republic is an ideal, and his Laws turned to rule by law.

debate.question: Should the wise rule?

positions.name: Yes: rule belongs to those who know
positions.who: Plato, Republic VI–VIII
positions.view: Ruling is a skill, the hardest of all. A city should be governed by those who know the good, trained for it over a lifetime, as a ship is steered by a navigator. Democracy hands the helm to whoever flatters the crew.
positions.evidence: The ship of state; the doctor; the death of Socrates; the history of tyrants like Peisistratus.

positions.name: Partly: weight power towards knowledge
positions.who: Jason Brennan, Against Democracy (2016)
positions.view: We cannot find philosopher-kings, but we can stop ignorant majorities from imposing bad laws on everyone, for instance by giving more votes to those who show basic knowledge, or by an expert veto.
positions.evidence: Surveys showing widespread ignorance of basic political facts; research on partisan bias.

positions.name: No: the question is how to remove rulers
positions.who: Karl Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945)
positions.view: 'Who should rule?' is the wrong question, because no one can be trusted with power. The right question is how to arrange things so that bad rulers can be removed without bloodshed. Democracy's virtue is not that the people are wise, but that they can sack their rulers.
positions.evidence: The record of rulers who claimed special knowledge; the peaceful change of government in democracies.

debate.agree: All agree that ruling needs knowledge and that unchecked power, whether of a crowd or of one man, is dangerous.

music.why: Beethoven headed the last movement of this Mass with a prayer for inner and outer peace, and let the sounds of war break in before the prayer returns. Plato thought the order of a city and the order of a soul were one problem; so, in its way, does this music.

think.why: Plato's longing for rule by the wise shaped Christian thinkers too. See how the great teachers joined Athens to Jerusalem.

learn.why: Plato's warning in a single sentence. Learn it not because it is the last word, but because every defender of freedom has to answer it.

check.q: Why does Plato think democracy's freedom is its downfall rather than its strength?
options: Because freedom made Athens too rich
Because free speech let foreigners spread Spartan ideas
Because free citizens refuse to fight in wars
Because a democracy values freedom so highly that it treats every desire and every person as equal and will accept no authority, not even law, until it falls to a tyrant
check.why: Each constitution in Book VIII dies of excess of its own good; democracy's is freedom 'out of all order and reason'.

check.q: In the ship of state, who does the deaf and short-sighted captain stand for?
options: The people, the demos: strong and the rightful owner, but not a navigator
The tyrant
Pericles
The philosopher
check.why: The owner is the people; the quarrelling sailors are politicians; the true pilot is the philosopher.

check.q: Why does Plato say democrats must claim that the art of navigation 'cannot be taught'?
options: Because sailors are uneducated
Because Athens had no schools
Because Plato thought navigation was more important than politics
Because if ruling were a teachable skill, it would follow that those with the skill should rule, not everyone
check.why: Admitting ruling is a skill would undercut the claim that every citizen is equally fit.

check.q: How does a 'protector of the people' become a tyrant, according to Plato?
options: He is appointed by Sparta
He inherits the throne
He wins a war abroad
He champions the people against the rich, uses false accusations and violence against opponents, then asks for a bodyguard which the people gladly give
check.why: Plato describes exactly the path Peisistratus took, as Herodotus tells it.

check.q: Which part of Plato's case rests on assumptions most people now reject?
options: That the people can be flattered
That knowledge matters in government
That tyrants are dangerous
That slaves acting free and women equal to men are signs of decline
check.why: Plato lists the freedom of slaves and the equality of the sexes among the symptoms; a fair reader notes this.

check.q: What is Karl Popper's main reply to Plato?
options: That the people are naturally wiser than philosophers, so they should steer
That the people are wiser than philosophers
That 'who should rule?' is the wrong question; the right one is how bad rulers can be removed without bloodshed
That rulers should be chosen by lot, as in Athens
check.why: Popper shifts the question from finding the best rulers to limiting and removing any rulers.

tutorial.question: Assess Plato's critique of democracy.
tutorial.approach: Set out Plato's three charges, competence, character and the slide into tyranny, in his own words. Give the evidence from Athens' history that supports them. Then state the modern versions (Brennan, Levitsky and Ziblatt). Only then begin to weigh them: which is strongest, and what would a defender of democracy have to show?
strong: States the ship of state and the craft argument accurately.
Explains the democratic man and the dissolution of authority.
Explains the protector who becomes a tyrant, with Peisistratus as evidence.
Links the critique to Plato's experience, especially the death of Socrates, without dismissing it for that reason.
Notes where Plato's assumptions (slaves, women) are unacceptable today.
Brings in a modern version and a modern reply such as Popper's.

takeaways: Plato, who saw the democracy put Socrates to death, argued that ruling is a skill most people lack, as steering a ship is.
He argued that democracy's love of freedom treats every desire and person as equal until all authority, even law, dissolves.
He argued that the people then raise up a protector who becomes a tyrant, as Peisistratus did; modern critics such as Brennan renew the case.

sessions.title: Aristotle: the many, the middle and the law
sessions.line: Plato's greatest student disagrees with him: a crowd may judge better than one wise man, the law should rule, and the safest city is one where most people are neither rich nor poor.
sessions.plain: Aristotle studied under Plato for twenty years, then collected the constitutions of 158 Greek cities to see what actually worked. He did not think democracy was best, but he took its case seriously. A crowd, he said, can be wiser than a few experts, as a meal to which many contribute is better than one man's dinner, and those who live in a house can judge it better than the builder. Power should belong to laws, not to men. And the most stable city has a large middle class, people who are neither too rich to obey nor too poor to rule. His answer to Plato is not 'the people are always right', but a mixed constitution under law.
sessions.why: Session 5 set out Plato's case: ruling is a skill, democracy dissolves authority, and it breeds tyrants. This session gives the first great answer, from inside the Greek world itself. Aristotle accepts much of Plato's worry, and turns it into a design for government that later republics, from Rome to America, studied.
answers: What did Aristotle think was the best government?
Can a crowd be wiser than experts?
Why did Aristotle think the middle class mattered?
What is a mixed constitution?
sessions.finding: Aristotle answered Plato that the many, gathered together and under law, can judge better than the few, and that the most stable constitution mixes rule by the few and the many and rests on a large middle class: not pure democracy, but government under law.

paras: Plato argued, in session 5, that democracy hands the ship to sailors who cannot steer, that its love of freedom dissolves all authority, and that it ends in tyranny. His three charges were competence, character and tyranny. Aristotle, his student, replies to all three.
background.key: Aristotle replies to Plato's three charges: competence, character and tyranny.

paras: Aristotle was born in 384 BC at Stagira in northern Greece, the son of a doctor at the Macedonian court. At seventeen he went to Athens and studied in Plato's Academy for twenty years, until Plato's death. Later he tutored the young Alexander the Great. In 335 BC he returned to Athens and founded his own school, the Lyceum. He lived there as a metic, a resident foreigner, so he could never vote in the assembly he wrote about.

Where Plato began with an ideal, Aristotle began with evidence. His students collected the constitutions of 158 Greek cities; The Athenian Constitution, which you read in sessions 1 and 2, is the only one that survives. The Politics, probably put together from his lecture notes, is the fruit of that research. When Alexander died in 323 BC, anti-Macedonian feeling rose in Athens, and Aristotle left the city. He died the next year.

background.key: Aristotle, Plato's student and a resident foreigner in Athens, studied 158 constitutions and wrote the Politics from evidence rather than an ideal.

paras: You met Aristotle's map of constitutions in 'Kings and prophets'. He asks two questions: how many rule, and in whose interest? Rule by one, few or many can each be good, if it serves the common good, or corrupt, if it serves only the rulers. Democracy, for Aristotle, is the corrupt form of rule by the many: the poor ruling in their own interest. Its good form he calls politeia, 'constitution', usually translated 'polity'. Our translator, William Ellis, calls it simply 'a state' or 'a free state'.

table.note: Politics III.7. In Book IV Aristotle describes polity as a mixture of oligarchy and democracy.

background.key: Aristotle sorts governments by how many rule and whether they serve the common good; his 'polity' is the good form of rule by the many.

paras: The main reading has two parts: Politics III.11, where Aristotle asks whether the many should hold supreme power and gives his famous argument for the wisdom of the crowd; and IV.11, where he argues that the best practical constitution rests on the middle class.

The comparison is from Deuteronomy: Moses asks the tribes to choose wise men from among themselves, whom he then appoints as judges. Christian thinkers later read it as a picture of the mixed government Aristotle described.
background.key: Politics III.11 on the wisdom of the many, IV.11 on the middle class; then Deuteronomy 1 on judges chosen by the tribes.
