paras: Other particulars we will consider separately; but it seems proper to prove, that the supreme power ought to be lodged with the many, rather than with those of the better sort, who are few; and also to explain what doubts (and probably just ones) may arise: now, though not one individual of the many may himself be fit for the supreme power, yet when these many are joined together, it does not follow but they may be better qualified for it than those; and this not separately, but as a collective body; as the public suppers exceed those which are given at one person's private expense: for, as they are many, each person brings in his share of virtue and wisdom; and thus, coming together, they are like one man made up of a multitude, with many feet, many hands, and many intelligences: thus is it with respect to the manners and understandings of the multitude taken together; for which reason the public are the best judges of music and poetry; for some understand one part, some another, and all collectively the whole; and in this particular men of consequence differ from each of the many; as they say those who are beautiful do from those who are not so, and as fine pictures excel any natural objects, by collecting the several beautiful parts which were dispersed among different originals into one, although the separate parts, as the eye or any other, might be handsomer than in the picture.

But if this distinction is to be made between every people and every general assembly, and some few men of consequence, it may be doubtful whether it is true; nay, it is clear enough that, with respect to a few, it is not; since the same conclusion might be applied even to brutes: and indeed wherein do some men differ from brutes? Not but that nothing prevents what I have said being true of the people in some states. The doubt then which we have lately proposed, with all its consequences, may be settled in this manner; it is necessary that the freemen who compose the bulk of the people should have absolute power in some things; but as they are neither men of property, nor act uniformly upon principles of virtue, it is not safe to trust them with the first offices in the state, both on account of their iniquity and their ignorance; from the one of which they will do what is wrong, from the other they will mistake: and yet it is dangerous to allow them no power or share in the government; for when there are many poor people who are incapable of acquiring the honours of their country, the state must necessarily have many enemies in it; let them then be permitted to vote in the public assemblies and to determine causes; for which reason Socrates, and some other legislators, gave them the power of electing the officers of the state, and also of inquiring into their conduct when they came out of office, and only prevented their being magistrates by themselves; for the multitude when they are collected together have all of them sufficient understanding for these purposes, and, mixing among those of higher rank, are serviceable to the city, as some things, which alone are improper for food, when mixed with others make the whole more wholesome than a few of them would be.

But there is a difficulty attending this form of government, for it seems, that the person who himself was capable of curing any one who was then sick, must be the best judge whom to employ as a physician; but such a one must be himself a physician; and the same holds true in every other practice and art: and as a physician ought to give an account of his practice to a physician, so ought it to be in other arts: those whose business is physic may be divided into three sorts, the first of these is he who makes up the medicines; the second prescribes, and is to the other as the architect is to the mason; the third is he who understands the science, but never practises it: now these three distinctions may be found in those who understand all other arts; nor have we less opinion of their judgment who are only instructed in the principles of the art than of those who practise it: and with respect to elections the same method of proceeding seems right; for to elect a proper person in any science is the business of those who are skilful therein; as in geometry, of geometricians; in steering, of steersmen: but if some individuals should know something of particular arts and works, they do not know more than the professors of them: so that even upon this principle neither the election of magistrates, nor the censure of their conduct, should be entrusted to the many.

But probably all that has been here said may not be right; for, to resume the argument I lately used, if the people are not very brutal indeed, although we allow that each individual knows less of these affairs than those who have given particular attention to them, yet when they come together they will know them better, or at least not worse; besides, in some particular arts it is not the workman only who is the best judge; namely, in those the works of which are understood by those who do not profess them: thus he who builds a house is not the only judge of it, for the master of the family who inhabits it is a better; thus also a steersman is a better judge of a tiller than he who made it; and he who gives an entertainment than the cook. What has been said seems a sufficient solution of this difficulty; but there is another that follows: for it seems absurd that the power of the state should be lodged with those who are but of indifferent morals, instead of those who are of excellent characters.

Now the power of election and censure are of the utmost consequence, and this, as has been said, in some states they entrust to the people; for the general assembly is the supreme court of all, and they have a voice in this, and deliberate in all public affairs, and try all causes, without any objection to the meanness of their circumstances, and at any age: but their treasurers, generals, and other great officers of state are taken from men of great fortune and worth. This difficulty also may be solved upon the same principle; and here too they may be right, for the power is not in the man who is member of the assembly, or council, but the assembly itself, and the council, and the people, of which each individual of the whole community are the parts, I mean as senator, adviser, or judge; for which reason it is very right, that the many should have the greatest powers in their own hands; for the people, the council, and the judges are composed of them, and the property of all these collectively is more than the property of any person or a few who fill the great offices of the state: and thus I determine these points.

The first question that we stated shows plainly, that the supreme power should be lodged in laws duly made and that the magistrate or magistrates, either one or more, should be authorised to determine those cases which the laws cannot particularly speak to, as it is impossible for them, in general language, to explain themselves upon everything that may arise: but what these laws are which are established upon the best foundations has not been yet explained, but still remains a matter of some question: but the laws of every state will necessarily be like every state, either trifling or excellent, just or unjust; for it is evident, that the laws must be framed correspondent to the constitution of the government; and, if so, it is plain, that a well-formed government will have good laws, a bad one, bad ones.

We proceed now to inquire what form of government and what manner of life is best for communities in general, not adapting it to that superior virtue which is above the reach of the vulgar, or that education which every advantage of nature and fortune only can furnish, nor to those imaginary plans which may be formed at pleasure; but to that mode of life which the greater part of mankind can attain to, and that government which most cities may establish: for as to those aristocracies which we have now mentioned, they are either too perfect for a state to support, or one so nearly alike to that state we now going to inquire into, that we shall treat of them both as one.

The opinions which we form upon these subjects must depend upon one common principle: for if what I have said in my treatise on Morals is true, a happy life must arise from an uninterrupted course of virtue; and if virtue consists in a certain medium, the middle life must certainly be the happiest; which medium is attainable by every one. The boundaries of virtue and vice in the state must also necessarily be the same as in a private person; for the form of government is the life of the city. In every city the people are divided into three sorts; the very rich, the very poor, and those who are between them. If this is universally admitted, that the mean is best, it is evident that even in point of fortune mediocrity is to be preferred; for that state is most submissive to reason; for those who are very handsome, or very strong, or very noble, or very rich; or, on the contrary; those who are very poor, or very weak, or very mean, with difficulty obey it; for the one are capricious and greatly flagitious, the other rascally and mean, the crimes of each arising from their different excesses: nor will they go through the different offices of the state; which is detrimental to it: besides, those who excel in strength, in riches, or friends, or the like, neither know how nor are willing to submit to command: and this begins at home when they are boys; for there they are brought up too delicately to be accustomed to obey their preceptors: as for the very poor, their general and excessive want of what the rich enjoy reduces them to a state too mean: so that the one know not how to command, but to be commanded as slaves, the others know not how to submit to any command, nor to command themselves but with despotic power.

A city composed of such men must therefore consist of slaves and masters, not freemen; where one party must hate, and the other despise, where there could be no possibility of friendship or political community: for community supposes affection; for we do not even on the road associate with our enemies. It is also the genius of a city to be composed as much as possible of equals; which will be most so when the inhabitants are in the middle state: from whence it follows, that that city must be best framed which is composed of those whom we say are naturally its proper members. It is men of this station also who will be best assured of safety and protection; for they will neither covet what belongs to others, as the poor do; nor will others covet what is theirs, as the poor do what belongs to the rich; and thus, without plotting against any one, or having any one plot against them, they will live free from danger: for which reason Phocylides wisely wishes for the middle state, as being most productive of happiness. It is plain, then, that the most perfect political community must be amongst those who are in the middle rank, and those states are best instituted wherein these are a larger and more respectable part, if possible, than both the other; or, if that cannot be, at least than either of them separate; so that being thrown into the balance it may prevent either scale from preponderating.

It is therefore the greatest happiness which the citizens can enjoy to possess a moderate and convenient fortune; for when some possess too much, and others nothing at all, the government must either be in the hands of the meanest rabble or else a pure oligarchy; or, from the excesses of both, a tyranny; for this arises from a headstrong democracy or an oligarchy, but very seldom when the members of the community are nearly on an equality with each other. We will assign a reason for this when we come to treat of the alterations which different states are likely to undergo. The middle state is therefore best, as being least liable to those seditions and insurrections which disturb the community; and for the same reason extensive governments are least liable to these inconveniences; for there those in a middle state are very numerous, whereas in small ones it is easy to pass to the two extremes, so as hardly to have any in a medium remaining, but the one half rich, the other poor: and from the same principle it is that democracies are more firmly established and of longer continuance than oligarchies; but even in those when there is a want of a proper number of men of middling fortune, the poor extend their power too far, abuses arise, and the government is soon at an end.

We ought to consider as a proof of what I now advance, that the best lawgivers themselves were those in the middle rank of life, amongst whom was Solon, as is evident from his poems, and Lycurgus, for he was not a king, and Charondas, and indeed most others. What has been said will show us why of so many free states some have changed to democracies, others to oligarchies: for whenever the number of those in the middle state has been too small, those who were the more numerous, whether the rich or the poor, always overpowered them and assumed to themselves the administration of public affairs; from hence arose either a democracy or an oligarchy. Moreover, when in consequence of their disputes and quarrels with each other, either the rich get the better of the poor, or the poor of the rich, neither of them will establish a free state; but, as the record of their victory, one which inclines to their own principles, and form either a democracy or an oligarchy.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato's pupil, who taught at his own school in Athens, the Lyceum
parts.title: The wisdom of the many
parts.context: Aristotle has been asking who should hold supreme power: the many, the rich, the good, one best man, or a tyrant? Every answer has difficulties. Now he gives the case for the many. William Ellis's translation (1776) is old and sometimes loose; 'the supreme power' means sovereignty, 'magistrates' means officials. Page numbers from the standard Greek edition, printed in brackets in this edition, have been removed. The chapter is given whole.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: none of the many may be fit to rule alone, but together they may be better judges than the few best, as a dinner to which many contribute beats one man's. Each brings a share of wisdom, and together they are like one person with many eyes and hands. This is not true of every crowd. The many should not hold the highest offices, because they lack the knowledge and virtue; but to give them no power at all would fill the city with enemies. So let them elect officials and audit them afterwards. Some object that only an expert can judge an expert, as only doctors can judge doctors. But the user of a thing often judges it better than its maker: the family who live in a house, the steersman who uses a rudder, the guest who eats the dinner. In any case, the supreme power should belong to laws, rightly made, with officials deciding only what laws cannot cover.

commentary.on: when these many are joined together, it does not follow but they may be better qualified for it than those; and this not separately, but as a collective body
commentary.text: This is Aristotle's great argument, sometimes called the 'summation' argument, or the doctrine of the wisdom of the multitude. Individually the many are not wise; collectively they may be wiser than any expert. It is the first statement in history of what is now called 'collective intelligence'.

commentary.on: as the public suppers exceed those which are given at one person's private expense
commentary.text: A potluck dinner: each brings one dish, and the meal is richer than any one host could provide. Each citizen sees something the others miss.

commentary.on: they are like one man made up of a multitude, with many feet, many hands, and many intelligences
commentary.text: The crowd, for Aristotle, can be one body with many eyes. Plato's crowd was a deaf and short-sighted ship-owner; Aristotle's sees more because it has more eyes.

commentary.on: it is clear enough that, with respect to a few, it is not; since the same conclusion might be applied even to brutes
commentary.text: Aristotle is careful. The argument does not hold for every crowd; a mob of brutes pooling their brutishness is no wiser. It depends on what each person brings.

commentary.on: it is not safe to trust them with the first offices in the state, both on account of their iniquity and their ignorance
commentary.text: Aristotle grants Plato's point about competence for the highest offices. He is no simple democrat.

commentary.on: when there are many poor people who are incapable of acquiring the honours of their country, the state must necessarily have many enemies in it
commentary.text: His second argument is practical. A city that shuts out the many makes enemies of them. Including them is a matter of safety as well as justice.

commentary.on: for which reason Socrates, and some other legislators, gave them the power of electing the officers of the state, and also of inquiring into their conduct when they came out of office
commentary.text: Ellis prints 'Socrates' here, but Aristotle's Greek names Solon, the lawgiver of session 1, who gave the people the right to elect officials and hold them to account. Aristotle's answer to Plato is Solon's: the many choose and audit; they need not steer.

commentary.on: thus he who builds a house is not the only judge of it, for the master of the family who inhabits it is a better
commentary.text: The direct reply to Plato's craft argument. You do not need to be a navigator to know whether you have arrived, or a builder to know whether the roof leaks. Government is judged by those who live under it.

commentary.on: the supreme power should be lodged in laws duly made
commentary.text: This is the most important sentence for the rest of the journey. Above both the many and the officials, Aristotle puts the law. It is his answer to the assembly at Mytilene and to the crowd at Arginusae, which thought it monstrous to be prevented from doing whatever it wished.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato's pupil, who taught at his own school in Athens, the Lyceum
parts.title: The middle way
parts.context: In Book IV Aristotle turns from the ideal to the practical: what constitution is best for most cities and most people, as they actually are? 'Mediocrity' here means moderation, the middle position, not poor quality. Phocylides was a Greek poet of the 500s BC. The 'treatise on Morals' is Aristotle's Ethics, which defines virtue as a mean between extremes.
parts.plain: If virtue is a middle path, the best life for a city is too. Every city has the very rich, the very poor and those in between. The very rich will not obey, and the very poor do not know how to command; a city of such people is a city of masters and slaves, full of hatred and contempt. The middle class covet nothing of others' and no one covets theirs, so they are the safest citizens. The best city has a large middle class, larger than either extreme, so that it can tip the balance. Where some have far too much and others nothing, the result is extreme democracy, oligarchy or tyranny. The best lawgivers, like Solon, came from the middle rank.

commentary.on: not adapting it to that superior virtue which is above the reach of the vulgar
commentary.text: A quiet rebuke to Plato. Aristotle will not design a city for philosophers. He asks what works for ordinary people.

commentary.on: if virtue consists in a certain medium, the middle life must certainly be the happiest
commentary.text: Aristotle's ethics, applied to politics. Courage is the mean between cowardice and rashness; the stable city is the mean between plutocracy and mob rule.

commentary.on: the one know not how to command, but to be commanded as slaves, the others know not how to submit to any command
commentary.text: Extreme inequality corrupts both ends: the rich never learn to obey and the poor never learn to rule. Neither can be a citizen in the full sense, which for Aristotle means ruling and being ruled in turn.

commentary.on: A city composed of such men must therefore consist of slaves and masters, not freemen; where one party must hate, and the other despise
commentary.text: Hatred from below and contempt from above: Aristotle's diagnosis of a divided society. 'Community supposes affection', he goes on. A city needs a kind of friendship among citizens.

commentary.on: so that being thrown into the balance it may prevent either scale from preponderating
commentary.text: The middle class as a balance weight, stopping either rich or poor from taking over. It is the same picture as Solon's poem of standing with his shield over both parties.

commentary.on: for this arises from a headstrong democracy or an oligarchy, but very seldom when the members of the community are nearly on an equality with each other
commentary.text: Aristotle's answer to Plato's third charge. Tyranny comes from extreme inequality and the class war it breeds, not from democracy as such. Narrow the gap, and the protector has no one to protect.

commentary.on: the best lawgivers themselves were those in the middle rank of life, amongst whom was Solon
commentary.text: The journey comes full circle. Aristotle's model statesman is the man we began with, who would favour neither rich nor poor.

read.author: Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato's pupil, who taught at his own school in Athens, the Lyceum

paras: I spoke to you at that time, saying, “I am not able to bear you myself alone.
Yahweh your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as the stars of the sky for multitude.
Yahweh, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you, as he has promised you!
How can I myself alone bear your problems, your burdens, and your strife?
Take wise men of understanding who are respected among your tribes, and I will make them heads over you.”
You answered me, and said, “The thing which you have spoken is good to do.”

So I took the heads of your tribes, wise and respected men, and made them heads over you, captains of thousands, captains of hundreds, captains of fifties, captains of tens, and officers, according to your tribes.
I commanded your judges at that time, saying, “Hear cases between your brothers and judge righteously between a man and his brother, and the foreigner who is living with him.

You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”
I commanded you at that time all the things which you should do.

parts.title: Choosing judges
parts.context: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses' last speeches to Israel before it enters the promised land. Here he recalls how, in the wilderness, he could no longer judge the people's disputes alone. The same story is told in Exodus 18, where his father-in-law Jethro gives him the advice.

commentary.on: How can I myself alone bear your problems, your burdens, and your strife?
commentary.text: Even Moses, who spoke with God, could not govern alone. One man's rule, however good, is not enough for a people.

commentary.on: Take wise men of understanding who are respected among your tribes, and I will make them heads over you.
commentary.text: The people choose, and the leader appoints. Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae (I–II, q. 105, a. 1, about 1270), read this as the best form of government: one ruler, with others governing under him, all chosen from and by the whole people. He called it a mixture of kingship, aristocracy and democracy, and said God himself had instituted it.

commentary.on: You answered me, and said, “The thing which you have spoken is good to do.”
commentary.text: A small detail: the people consent. Government here is something they agree to, not only something done to them.

commentary.on: captains of thousands, captains of hundreds, captains of fifties, captains of tens
commentary.text: Authority is spread out, layer by layer, close to the people, like Cleisthenes' demes and tribes.

commentary.on: You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike.
commentary.text: Equality before the law, small and great alike, is commanded. Aristotle wanted the law supreme; Deuteronomy wants the law to treat everyone the same.

commentary.on: You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s.
commentary.text: Here is what Aristotle does not have. The judges answer not only to the people or the law, but to God. Neither the crowd nor the powerful should frighten them, because justice is not theirs to give away.

compare.why: Aristotle wanted the many to choose and the able to govern, under law. Deuteronomy describes something similar in Israel's founding story, and medieval Christian thinkers read it as a model of mixed government.
compare.title: Wise men from your tribes

paras: Aristotle's argument in III.11 has had a remarkable modern life. In 1785 the French mathematician the Marquis de Condorcet proved what is now called the jury theorem: if each voter is a little more likely than not to be right on a yes-or-no question, then the larger the group, the more likely the majority is to be right. Political theorists such as Jeremy Waldron and Hélène Landemore, in Democratic Reason (2013), have built on Aristotle's idea that a diverse group can outperform a small group of experts, because each member brings different knowledge.

Aristotle's conditions matter, though. The argument works only if people think for themselves, bring something to the table and are not 'brutes'. Condorcet's theorem works only if each voter is more likely right than wrong, and voters are independent. A crowd swept by one passion, like the assembly at Mytilene, is not many eyes but one.
sections.key: Aristotle's 'wisdom of the many' anticipates Condorcet's jury theorem and modern work on collective intelligence, but only for groups who think independently and bring real knowledge.

paras: Aristotle's reply to the ship of state is subtle. He agrees that the highest offices need skill and character. But he divides the work. The people need not steer; they can choose the steersman, judge where the ship has got to, and hold the crew to account. The user of a house judges it better than the builder.

This division, with experts doing the work and the people choosing and judging them, is the basic shape of modern representative democracy. It is also, as Aristotle says, Solon's arrangement: the poor elect and audit, the able serve. It answers Plato's charge of competence not by denying that knowledge matters, but by giving knowledge and consent different jobs.
sections.key: Aristotle gives the people the jobs of choosing and judging officials, and leaves the skilled work to the able: the shape of modern representative government.

paras: The last paragraph of III.11 is short and decisive: supreme power should lie with laws rightly made. A few chapters later (III.16) Aristotle goes further, in a line that Christian and modern readers would quote for centuries: to let the law rule is to let God and reason rule, while to let a man rule adds a wild beast, because desire and passion warp even the best rulers.

This is his answer to Plato's charge of tyranny, and to the danger we saw at Mytilene and Arginusae. The problem was never only who ruled, but that the ruler, the people in the assembly, could do anything at all. A government of laws, not men, limits every ruler, including the many. The Athenians had begun to learn it after 403 BC, when they separated fixed laws from the decrees of the assembly.
sections.key: Aristotle put supreme power in the law, not in any person or crowd: law is reason without passion, and limits every ruler.

paras: Aristotle's answer to Plato's charge about character is the middle class. Plato feared that democracy breeds disorder. Aristotle says the real cause of disorder is extreme inequality, which turns a city into masters and slaves, hatred and contempt. Where most people are neither very rich nor very poor, they neither plot nor are plotted against, and the city is stable.

This idea has had a long life. Historians and political scientists have often argued that stable democracies rest on a broad middle class, and that democracies with very unequal wealth are more prone to demagogues and coups. The idea is debated; but it is Aristotle's, and it gives a democrat something to work for besides votes: a society where most people have enough to be independent.
sections.key: Aristotle saw extreme inequality as the cause of disorder and tyranny, and a large middle class as the foundation of stable government.

paras: Aristotle's practical ideal, polity, is a mixture. It takes something from oligarchy (some offices need property or skill; some officials are elected) and something from democracy (all citizens vote, sit on juries and hold some offices by lot). No class rules alone. The idea is older than Aristotle, and it became the great model of the West.

The Greek historian Polybius, in the 100s BC, explained Rome's success by its mixture of consuls (like kings), senate (like an aristocracy) and popular assemblies, each checking the others. Cicero, Aquinas and the Renaissance republicans of Florence and Venice took up the idea. Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws (1748) turned it into the separation of powers. John Adams and James Madison built it into the American Constitution: a president, a senate and a house, with courts above them all, under a written constitution.
sections.key: The mixed constitution, no class ruling alone, passed from Aristotle through Polybius, Cicero, Aquinas and Montesquieu into the American Constitution.

paras: Aristotle's answer to Plato is strong, but it has limits. His citizens were the same small group as Athens': free men born of citizens. In Book I of the Politics he argued that some people are slaves by nature and that women are naturally ruled by men. His 'many' were not everyone.

And his foundation for the rule of law is reason and nature. That is a great deal. But it leaves a question he could not fully answer: why should the many, or the law, respect a person who is not a citizen, not rational enough, not useful? Deuteronomy points to another foundation: judgement 'is God's', and the small and the great must be heard alike. The next session, still to come, follows that thread.
sections.key: Aristotle's many were still free male citizens, and he defended natural slavery; Deuteronomy points to a different foundation for equal justice.

sections.h: Aristotle on democracy at its worst
paras: Aristotle did not defend every democracy. In Politics IV.4 he distinguishes several kinds. In the best, the law rules, offices have modest property qualifications, and the farmers who make up most citizens have little time for meetings, so the assembly meets rarely. In the worst, the people rule by decree rather than by law, and 'the people become a monarch', one ruler made of many. That, he says, is where demagogues arise, flattering the people as courtiers flatter a tyrant, and such a democracy is no constitution at all, because where the laws do not rule there is no constitution.

This is very close to Plato's picture, and to what happened at Arginusae. The difference is the conclusion. Plato thought democracy as such slides into tyranny. Aristotle thought it does so when law gives way to decree, and that a democracy under law, resting on a broad and busy middle class, can last. His remedy is not to take power from the many, but to bind them, like everyone else, to the law.
sections.key: Aristotle agreed that democracy ruled by decree becomes a many-headed tyrant with demagogues as its courtiers, but held that democracy under law can last.

refs: Aristotle, Politics III.7, 11, 16; IV.4, 8–9, 11; I.4–6, 13, tr. W. Ellis (1776); Bekker numbers 1281a–1282b, 1295a–1296b.
Polybius VI.3–18; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II, q. 105, a. 1; Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws XI.6 (1748); The Federalist 47–51 (1788).
Deuteronomy 1:9–18; Exodus 18:13–26.

Condorcet, Essai sur l'application de l'analyse à la probabilité des décisions (1785); Jeremy Waldron, 'The Wisdom of the Multitude', Political Theory 23 (1995); Hélène Landemore, Democratic Reason (2013); Josiah Ober, Democracy and Knowledge (2008).
Richard Kraut, Aristotle: Political Philosophy (2002).

debate.question: Can the many be wiser than the few?

positions.name: Yes, together and under law
positions.who: Aristotle, Politics III.11; Condorcet; Hélène Landemore
positions.view: Each citizen sees part of the truth; pooled, their judgement can beat any small group of experts, especially on what affects their own lives. Diversity of views is a strength.
positions.evidence: The public supper; the user of the house; Condorcet's jury theorem; studies of group problem-solving.

positions.name: No: ignorance does not add up to wisdom
positions.who: Plato; Jason Brennan
positions.view: Pooling ignorance gives you more ignorance. Voters' errors are not random but systematic, so they do not cancel out; a crowd led by one passion is no wiser than one fool.
positions.evidence: Mytilene; Arginusae; surveys of voter knowledge and bias.

positions.name: Only under conditions
positions.who: Aristotle himself, read carefully; James Madison
positions.view: The many are wise only when they deliberate, are independent, are not split into rich and poor, and act under law. The task of a constitution is to create those conditions.
positions.evidence: Aristotle's warning about 'brutes'; IV.11 on the middle class; the American separation of powers.

debate.agree: All agree that a crowd swept by a single passion is not wise, and that law and institutions matter as much as numbers.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art has no painting of Aristotle or of a Greek school of philosophy, and we will not use a stand-in.

music.why: In Byrd's Mass for Four Voices no single part carries the tune while the others accompany it: four voices, each independent, make one harmony. Byrd, a Catholic in Protestant England, wrote it for secret Masses: harmony among the many, under a law above them.

think.why: Aristotle's many were still a select few. See how the great teachers came to say that every single person counts.

learn.why: Equal justice for small and great, and judges who fear no one, because judgement belongs to God: the foundation Aristotle's rule of law lacked.

check.q: What is the point of Aristotle's 'public supper' comparison?
options: That food is a political issue
That many people, each contributing something, can together produce a better judgement than one expert alone
That democracies should feed the poor
That the rich should pay for public dinners
check.why: Each brings a share of 'virtue and wisdom', and together they are like one man with many eyes and hands.

check.q: How does the example of the house answer Plato's ship of state?
options: It shows the people should build their own houses
It shows builders should rule
It shows that those who live with the results can judge a thing well without having the skill to make it, so the people can judge and choose rulers without being expert rulers
It shows that houses are more important than ships
check.why: The family judges the house better than the builder; the steersman judges the rudder better than its maker.

check.q: Which powers does Aristotle give the many in III.11?
options: Electing officials, auditing them afterwards, and judging in the assembly and courts, but not the highest offices
All the highest offices
Only the right to petition
None at all
check.why: He follows Solon: the many elect and inquire into officials' conduct, but are not trusted with the first offices.

check.q: Why does Aristotle think a large middle class makes a city stable?
options: Because the middle class is always virtuous
Because the very rich will not obey and the very poor cannot rule, while those in the middle neither covet others' goods nor are coveted, and can balance the extremes
Because the middle class was the largest class in Athens
Because the middle class pays most tax
check.why: Extreme inequality makes masters and slaves, hatred and contempt; the middle prevents 'either scale from preponderating'.

check.q: What is Aristotle's answer to Plato's fear that democracy breeds tyranny?
options: That tyranny comes from extreme inequality and class war, and is rare where citizens are nearly equal; and that law, not any person, should be supreme
That tyranny is good
That the people should be kept out of power altogether
That the people never choose tyrants
check.why: IV.11: tyranny 'arises from a headstrong democracy or an oligarchy, but very seldom' among near-equals; III.11: supreme power in laws.

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 1:17 add to Aristotle's rule of law?
options: That laws should change often
That only priests can judge
That judges must hear small and great alike and fear no one, because judgement belongs to God
That the many should judge everything
check.why: Equal justice is commanded, and grounded in God rather than in reason or the city alone.

tutorial.question: How well does Aristotle answer Plato's case against democracy?
tutorial.approach: Restate Plato's three charges from session 5. Then take Aristotle's answers in turn: the wisdom of the many and the division between choosing and steering (competence); the middle class (character and stability); and the rule of law (tyranny). Weigh each. End with what Aristotle's answer leaves out.
strong: Restates Plato's three charges accurately.
Explains the summation argument and its conditions, including Aristotle's own warning about 'brutes'.
Explains the house example as a reply to the ship of state.
Explains the middle class argument and its link to tyranny.
Explains the supremacy of law and why it answers Mytilene and Arginusae.
Notes the limits: natural slavery, women, citizenship.

takeaways: Aristotle argued that the many, pooling their judgement and acting under law, can be wiser than the few, and should choose and audit officials while the able serve.
He argued that extreme inequality breeds disorder and tyranny, and that a large middle class and a mixed constitution make a city stable.
He put supreme power in the law; Deuteronomy adds equal justice for small and great, grounded in God.

sessions.title: What Jerusalem added: the verdict
sessions.line: A Victorian historian looks back at Athens and finds its glory and its failure; a carpenter's son tells the powerful where their power ends; and a shipload of exiles makes a covenant to govern themselves.
sessions.plain: The verdict first. Athens gave the West the idea that a people can govern itself: citizens deciding together, under law, with power spread out and rulers held to account. But Athens also showed that a sovereign people can become a tyrant, because nothing stood above its will. What Jerusalem added was that something does: a God above every ruler, before whom every person, slave or free, man or woman, has equal worth. Modern democracy needs both: Athens' machinery of self-government, and Jerusalem's limits on all power and its belief in the worth of every person.
sessions.why: Session 5 gave Plato's case against democracy, and session 6 Aristotle's answer: the wisdom of the many, the middle class and the rule of law. But Aristotle's many were still a few, and his law rested on reason and nature alone. This last session asks what the Bible added, and gives the journey's answer to its question: who should rule, and how?
answers: What did the Bible add to democracy?
Why did Athens' democracy fail?
How did democracy reach the modern world?
Does democracy need Christianity?
sessions.finding: Athens gave the West self-government under law; Jerusalem gave it the equal worth of every person and a God above every ruler, which set limits even on the people; modern democracy has needed both.

paras: Who should rule, and how? This journey's answer is this. No one should rule without limit: not one man, not the wise, not even the people. The many should govern themselves, choosing and judging their rulers, as Solon and Aristotle taught. But their power must be held under law, and the law itself under something higher: the equal worth of every human being, which no majority can vote away.

The first half of that answer comes from Athens. The second half, in the form the West received it, comes from Jerusalem. This session shows how they came together, and is honest about the objections.
background.key: No one should rule without limit, not even the people: self-government under law (Athens), and law under the equal worth of every person (Jerusalem).

paras: Solon freed the poor and gave them a voice (session 1). Cleisthenes and the people made Athens a democracy, run by the assembly, the lot and the courts, for male citizens only (session 2). Pericles showed what a trusted leader could do, and Athens under him ruled an empire (session 3). At Mytilene the assembly nearly committed a massacre, and at Arginusae it condemned its own generals illegally (session 4). Plato argued that democracy breeds disorder and tyranny (session 5); Aristotle answered with the wisdom of the many, the middle class and the rule of law (session 6).

What became of Athens? Its democracy survived the defeat by Sparta and lasted until 322 BC, when Macedon ended it. For the next two thousand years almost no one in the West wanted to imitate it. 'Democracy' was a word of abuse, meaning mob rule. When it returned, in England, America and France, it came back changed, by a tradition that Athens never knew.

Paul: 'neither slave nor free... neither male nor female' (Galatians 3:28)

background.key: Athens' democracy ended in 322 BC; when democracy returned to the West, centuries later, it had been reshaped by Christianity.

paras: You have met much of the Bible's political teaching already. In 'Kings and prophets', the king had to copy out God's law and not think himself 'above his brothers' (Deuteronomy 17:20), and prophets told kings to their faces that they had sinned. In 'How we got here' you read Paul's letter to the Galatians: 'There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28). Behind both lies the first chapter of the Bible: every human being, male and female, is made 'in God's image' (Genesis 1:27).

None of this is a theory of democracy. The Bible describes kings, judges, elders and apostles, not assemblies voting. But it says two things Athens never said: every person has the same worth before God, whatever their class or sex, and every ruler is under a law he did not make. Jesus adds a third: that the state's power has a boundary. 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mark 12:17). When the apostles were ordered to stop preaching, Peter answered: 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29).
background.key: The Bible teaches the equal worth of every person (Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28), the ruler under God's law (Deuteronomy 17) and limits to the state's power (Mark 12:17; Acts 5:29).

paras: John Dalberg-Acton (1834–1902) was an English Catholic historian, a friend and adviser of the Liberal prime minister Gladstone, and later Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge. He planned all his life to write a history of liberty, and never finished it. He is best remembered for a line in a letter of 1887 to the historian Mandell Creighton: that power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.

In 1877 he gave two lectures to a local institute at Bridgnorth in Shropshire: 'The History of Freedom in Antiquity' and 'The History of Freedom in Christianity'. Our reading comes from the first. Acton writes in long Victorian sentences, but his judgement is sharp, and he admired Athens as much as he criticised it.
background.key: Acton (1834–1902), Catholic historian of liberty, gave 'The History of Freedom in Antiquity' as a lecture at Bridgnorth in 1877.

paras: The main reading has three parts from Acton's lecture: his praise of Solon; his verdict on why the Athenian democracy failed; and his argument that Christ's words about Caesar did what no Greek could do, putting a limit on every government.

The comparison is the Mayflower Compact of 1620, in which a shipload of English Puritans, about to land in America, bound themselves 'in the Presence of God and one another' to make their own laws. It is a small document that shows the two traditions meeting.
background.key: Acton on Solon, on Athens' failure and on Christ's limit on power; then the Mayflower Compact.

before: What, according to Acton, did Solon's 'slender' concession to the poor start?
Why does Acton say it is worse to be oppressed by a majority than by a minority?
What did Christ's words about Caesar do that Socrates and the Stoics could not?

paras: From this universal degradation the world was rescued by the most gifted of the nations. Athens, which like other cities was distracted and oppressed by a privileged class, avoided violence and appointed Solon to revise its laws. It was the happiest choice that history records. Solon was not only the wisest man to be found in Athens, but the most profound political genius of antiquity; and the easy, bloodless, and pacific revolution by which he accomplished the deliverance of his country was the first step in a career which our age glories in pursuing, and instituted a power which has done more than anything, except revealed religion, for the regeneration of society. The upper class had possessed the right of making and administering the laws, and he left them in possession, only transferring to wealth what had been the privilege of birth. To the rich, who alone had the means of sustaining the burden of public service in taxation and war, Solon gave a share of power proportioned to the demands made on their resources.

The poorest classes were exempt from direct taxes, but were excluded from office. Solon gave them a voice in electing magistrates from the classes above them, and the right of calling them to account. This concession, apparently so slender, was the beginning of a mighty change. It introduced the idea that a man ought to have a voice in selecting those to whose rectitude and wisdom he is compelled to trust his fortune, his family, and his life. And this idea completely inverted the notion of human authority, for it inaugurated the reign of moral influence where all political power had depended on moral force. Government by consent superseded government by compulsion, and the pyramid which had stood on a point was made to stand upon its base. By making every citizen the guardian of his own interest Solon admitted the element of Democracy into the State. The greatest glory of a ruler, he said, is to create a popular government. Believing that no man can be entirely trusted, he subjected all who exercised power to the vigilant control of those for whom they acted.

The only resource against political disorders that had been known till then was the concentration of power. Solon undertook to effect the same object by the distribution of power. He gave to the common people as much influence as he thought them able to employ, that the State might be exempt from arbitrary government. It is the essence of Democracy, he said, to obey no master but the law. Solon recognised the principle that political forms are not final or inviolable, and must adapt themselves to facts; and he provided so well for the revision of his constitution, without breach of continuity or loss of stability, that for centuries after his death the Attic orators attributed to him, and quoted by his name, the whole structure of Athenian law. The direction of its growth was determined by the fundamental doctrine of Solon, that political power ought to be commensurate with public service. In the Persian war the services of the Democracy eclipsed those of the Patrician orders, for the fleet that swept the Asiatics from the Egean Sea was manned by the poorer Athenians. That class, whose valour had saved the State and had preserved European civilisation, had gained a title to increase of influence and privilege. The offices of State, which had been a monopoly of the rich, were thrown open to the poor, and in order to make sure that they should obtain their share, all but the highest commands were distributed by lot.

It was a momentous step in the progress of nations when the principle that every interest should have the right and the means of asserting itself was adopted by the Athenian Constitution. But for those who were beaten in the vote there was no redress. The law did not check the triumph of majorities or rescue the minority from the dire penalty of having been outnumbered. When the overwhelming influence of Pericles was removed, the conflict between classes raged without restraint, and the slaughter that befell the higher ranks in the Peloponnesian war gave an irresistible preponderance to the lower. The restless and inquiring spirit of the Athenians was prompt to unfold the reason of every institution and the consequences of every principle, and their Constitution ran its course from infancy to decrepitude with unexampled speed.

Two men's lives span the interval from the first admission of popular influence, under Solon, to the downfall of the State. Their history furnishes the classic example of the peril of Democracy under conditions singularly favourable. For the Athenians were not only brave and patriotic and capable of generous sacrifice, but they were the most religious of the Greeks. They venerated the Constitution which had given them prosperity, and equality, and freedom, and never questioned the fundamental laws which regulated the enormous power of the Assembly. They tolerated considerable variety of opinion and great licence of speech; and their humanity towards their slaves roused the indignation even of the most intelligent partisan of aristocracy. Thus they became the only people of antiquity that grew great by democratic institutions. But the possession of unlimited power, which corrodes the conscience, hardens the heart, and confounds the understanding of monarchs, exercised its demoralising influence on the illustrious democracy of Athens. It is bad to be oppressed by a minority, but it is worse to be oppressed by a majority. For there is a reserve of latent power in the masses which, if it is called into play, the minority can seldom resist. But from the absolute will of an entire people there is no appeal, no redemption, no refuge but treason. The humblest and most numerous class of the Athenians united the legislative, the judicial, and, in part, the executive power. The philosophy that was then in the ascendant taught them that there is no law superior to that of the State--the lawgiver is above the law.

It followed that the sovereign people had a right to do whatever was within its power, and was bound by no rule of right or wrong but its own judgment of expediency. On a memorable occasion the assembled Athenians declared it monstrous that they should be prevented from doing whatever they chose. No force that existed could restrain them; and they resolved that no duty should restrain them, and that they would be bound by no laws that were not of their own making. In this way the emancipated people of Athens became a tyrant; and their Government, the pioneer of European freedom, stands condemned with a terrible unanimity by all the wisest of the ancients. They ruined their city by attempting to conduct war by debate in the marketplace. Like the French Republic, they put their unsuccessful commanders to death. They treated their dependencies with such injustice that they lost their maritime Empire. They plundered the rich until the rich conspired with the public enemy, and they crowned their guilt by the martyrdom of Socrates.

When the absolute sway of numbers had endured for near a quarter of a century, nothing but bare existence was left for the State to lose; and the Athenians, wearied and despondent, confessed the true cause of their ruin. They understood that for liberty, justice, and equal laws, it is as necessary that Democracy should restrain itself as it had been that it should restrain the Oligarchy. They resolved to take their stand once more upon the ancient ways, and to restore the order of things which had subsisted when the monopoly of power had been taken from the rich and had not been acquired by the poor. After a first restoration had failed, which is only memorable because Thucydides, whose judgment in politics is never at fault, pronounced it the best Government Athens had enjoyed, the attempt was renewed with more experience and greater singleness of purpose. The hostile parties were reconciled, and proclaimed an amnesty, the first in history.

They resolved to govern by concurrence. The laws, which had the sanction of tradition, were reduced to a code; and no act of the sovereign assembly was valid with which they might be found to disagree. Between the sacred lines of the Constitution which were to remain inviolate, and the decrees which met from time to time the needs and notions of the day, a broad distinction was drawn; and the fabric of a law which had been the work of generations was made independent of momentary variations in the popular will. The repentance of the Athenians came too late to save the Republic. But the lesson of their experience endures for all times, for it teaches that government by the whole people, being the government of the most numerous and most powerful class, is an evil of the same nature as unmixed monarchy, and requires, for nearly the same reasons, institutions that shall protect it against itself, and shall uphold the permanent reign of law against arbitrary revolutions of opinion.

After the fourth century the declarations against slavery are earnest and continual. And in a theological but yet pregnant sense, divines of the second century insist on liberty, and divines of the fourth century on equality. There was one essential and inevitable transformation in politics. Popular governments had existed, and also mixed and federal governments, but there had been no limited government, no State the circumference of whose authority had been defined by a force external to its own. That was the great problem which philosophy had raised, and which no statesmanship had been able to solve. Those who proclaimed the assistance of a higher authority had indeed drawn a metaphysical barrier before the governments, but they had not known how to make it real. All that Socrates could effect by way of protest against the tyranny of the reformed democracy was to die for his convictions. The Stoics could only advise the wise man to hold aloof from politics, keeping the unwritten law in his heart.

But when Christ said: "Render unto Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's, and unto God the things that are God's," those words, spoken on His last visit to the Temple, three days before His death, gave to the civil power, under the protection of conscience, a sacredness it had never enjoyed, and bounds it had never acknowledged; and they were the repudiation of absolutism and the inauguration of freedom. For our Lord not only delivered the precept, but created the force to execute it. To maintain the necessary immunity in one supreme sphere, to reduce all political authority within defined limits, ceased to be an aspiration of patient reasoners, and was made the perpetual charge and care of the most energetic institution and the most universal association in the world. The new law, the new spirit, the new authority, gave to liberty a meaning and a value it had not possessed in the philosophy or in the constitution of Greece or Rome before the knowledge of the truth that makes us free.

parts.author: Lord Acton
parts.work: The History of Freedom in Antiquity
parts.who: John Dalberg-Acton, Lord Acton (1834–1902), English Catholic historian, later Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge
parts.when: An address given at Bridgnorth, Shropshire, 26 February 1877; printed in The History of Freedom and Other Essays (1907)
parts.ref: Acton, 'The History of Freedom in Antiquity' (1877), on Solon
parts.title: The pyramid on its base
parts.context: Acton has just described the ancient empires of the East, where rulers held absolute power. Now he turns to Athens. He is speaking in 1877, in a confident Victorian voice; 'our race' and 'the most gifted of the nations' are his phrases, not ours.
parts.plain: Acton says Solon was the greatest political genius of antiquity. He let the rich keep office but gave the poor a vote in choosing officials and the right to call them to account. That small change introduced a revolutionary idea: people should have a say in choosing those they must trust with their lives. It replaced government by force with government by consent. Solon spread power instead of concentrating it, and taught that democracy means obeying no master but the law.

commentary.on: It was the happiest choice that history records.
commentary.text: Acton's praise of Solon is the highest he gives anyone. It confirms the finding of session 1: democracy began with a man who refused to be tyrant.

commentary.on: It introduced the idea that a man ought to have a voice in selecting those to whose rectitude and wisdom he is compelled to trust his fortune, his family, and his life.
commentary.text: This is the core of democratic consent, put better than almost anyone has put it. If others will decide your fate, you should help choose them.

commentary.on: Government by consent superseded government by compulsion, and the pyramid which had stood on a point was made to stand upon its base.
commentary.text: A memorable image. In the ancient empires, all power came down from one man at the top: a pyramid balanced on its point. Solon turned it over, so that power rested on the whole people.

commentary.on: Believing that no man can be entirely trusted, he subjected all who exercised power to the vigilant control of those for whom they acted.
commentary.text: Acton's own conviction, which he finds in Solon: no one can be trusted with unchecked power.

commentary.on: It is the essence of Democracy, he said, to obey no master but the law.
commentary.text: The rule of law again, which Aristotle put above every ruler in session 6.

parts.author: Lord Acton
parts.work: The History of Freedom in Antiquity
parts.who: John Dalberg-Acton, Lord Acton (1834–1902), English Catholic historian, later Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge
parts.when: An address given at Bridgnorth, Shropshire, 26 February 1877; printed in The History of Freedom and Other Essays (1907)
parts.ref: Acton, 'The History of Freedom in Antiquity' (1877), on Athens
parts.title: When the people became a tyrant
parts.context: Acton has praised Pericles' idea of a constitution that protects every interest. Now he explains why the democracy failed after Pericles. 'Two men's lives' means two long lifetimes, from Solon to the end. The 'memorable occasion' is the trial of the Arginusae generals in 406 BC, which you met in session 4. The 'first restoration' is the government of 411 BC that Thucydides praised.
parts.plain: Athens gave every interest a voice, but gave no protection to those who lost the vote. After Pericles, class war broke out. The Athenians were brave, patriotic and religious, but unlimited power corrupted them as it corrupts kings. It is bad to be oppressed by a minority but worse by a majority, because there is no appeal. The people believed no law stood above the state, so they did whatever they wanted: they ran wars by debate, executed their generals, abused their allies, plundered the rich, and killed Socrates. At last they learned that democracy must restrain itself, made an amnesty, and put fixed laws beyond the reach of the assembly. It came too late. The lesson is that rule by the whole people needs institutions to protect it from itself.

commentary.on: But for those who were beaten in the vote there was no redress.
commentary.text: The heart of Acton's criticism. Athens protected the right to vote, but not the rights of those who lost. There was nothing a minority could appeal to.

commentary.on: It is bad to be oppressed by a minority, but it is worse to be oppressed by a majority.
commentary.text: Why worse? Because a tyrant can be resisted by the many; a majority can be resisted by no one. This is what Tocqueville, a few decades before Acton, called 'the tyranny of the majority'.

commentary.on: The philosophy that was then in the ascendant taught them that there is no law superior to that of the State--the lawgiver is above the law.
commentary.text: This is the root of the failure, for Acton. The Athenians had no idea of a law above their own law. Whatever the assembly decided was right.

commentary.on: On a memorable occasion the assembled Athenians declared it monstrous that they should be prevented from doing whatever they chose.
commentary.text: The trial of the Arginusae generals, where the crowd shouted down those who objected to an illegal motion, Socrates among them.

commentary.on: and they crowned their guilt by the martyrdom of Socrates
commentary.text: Acton calls Socrates' death a martyrdom: a death for truth. He accepts Plato's charge on the facts, though not his conclusion.

commentary.on: it is as necessary that Democracy should restrain itself as it had been that it should restrain the Oligarchy
commentary.text: The lesson the Athenians learned too late, and the lesson of this journey: the people too must be limited.

commentary.on: requires, for nearly the same reasons, institutions that shall protect it against itself
commentary.text: Acton's verdict: pure democracy is like pure monarchy, power without limit, and needs the same remedies: constitutions, courts and laws the majority cannot simply change.

parts.author: Lord Acton
parts.work: The History of Freedom in Antiquity
parts.who: John Dalberg-Acton, Lord Acton (1834–1902), English Catholic historian, later Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge
parts.when: An address given at Bridgnorth, Shropshire, 26 February 1877; printed in The History of Freedom and Other Essays (1907)
parts.ref: Acton, 'The History of Freedom in Antiquity' (1877), on Christianity
parts.title: Render to Caesar
parts.context: The end of the lecture. Acton has described the Stoics, who taught a law of nature above human laws, and Rome's fall into despotism. He has admitted that the early Christians were slow to challenge the state, and that some taught passive obedience. Then he turns to Christ's answer about paying taxes to Caesar (Mark 12:13–17).
parts.plain: Acton says the early Christians mostly kept out of politics, but they insisted on liberty and, later, on equality, and spoke out against slavery. Their great change was this: there had been popular governments before, but never a limited government, one whose power was bounded by something outside itself. Socrates could only die in protest; the Stoics could only keep the unwritten law in their hearts. When Christ said 'Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's', he gave the state a sacredness and a boundary it had never had, and founded a Church that would defend that boundary for ever.

commentary.on: divines of the second century insist on liberty, and divines of the fourth century on equality
commentary.text: 'Divines' are theologians. Acton is careful not to overclaim: Christians did not invent political liberty, and for a long time did not apply their beliefs to politics.

commentary.on: there had been no limited government, no State the circumference of whose authority had been defined by a force external to its own
commentary.text: This is Acton's central claim. Athens had popular government, Rome mixed government, but neither had a government whose authority stopped somewhere, at a line drawn by something other than itself.

commentary.on: All that Socrates could effect by way of protest against the tyranny of the reformed democracy was to die for his convictions.
commentary.text: Socrates was the greatest individual protest against unlimited democracy, but he had nothing behind him except his own conscience.

commentary.on: gave to the civil power, under the protection of conscience, a sacredness it had never enjoyed, and bounds it had never acknowledged
commentary.text: Two things at once. The state is given real authority: Caesar is owed his due. And it is given a limit: some things are God's, and the state may not take them. The WEB translates Christ's words: 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mark 12:17).

commentary.on: For our Lord not only delivered the precept, but created the force to execute it.
commentary.text: Acton means the Church: an institution independent of the state, spread across every nation, that could tell emperors no, as Ambrose told Theodosius.

commentary.on: before the knowledge of the truth that makes us free
commentary.text: Acton ends by quoting Jesus in John 8:32: 'you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.' Freedom, for him, rests finally on truth that no state can vote on.

paras: IN THE NAME OF GOD, AMEN. We, whose names are underwritten, the Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, King, Defender of the Faith, &c. Having undertaken for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honour of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the first Colony in the northern Parts of Virginia; Do by these Presents, solemnly and mutually, in the Presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick, for our better Ordering and Preservation, and Furtherance of the Ends aforesaid: And by Virtue hereof do enact, constitute, and frame, such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions, and Officers, from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general Good of the Colony; unto which we promise all due Submission and Obedience. IN WITNESS whereof we have hereunto subscribed our names at Cape-Cod the eleventh of November, in the Reign of our Sovereign Lord King James, of England, France, and Ireland, the eighteenth, and of Scotland the fifty-fourth, Anno Domini; 1620.

parts.author: The passengers of the Mayflower
parts.title: A civil body politic
parts.context: In 1620 about a hundred English passengers, many of them Puritan Separatists who had left the Church of England, sailed for Virginia in the Mayflower. Storms drove them far north, to Cape Cod, outside the territory their charter covered. Some threatened to do as they pleased once ashore. So, before landing, forty-one men signed this agreement. They founded Plymouth Colony. The text is from William Bradford's history of the colony, as printed by Yale's Avalon Project; the spelling is old ('Politick' for politic).
parts.plain: We, loyal subjects of King James, have sailed to plant a colony for God's glory, the Christian faith and our country. Before God and each other, we solemnly agree to join together as one civil body, to make just and equal laws and choose officers for the good of the colony, and we promise to obey them. Signed at Cape Cod, 11 November 1620.

commentary.on: the Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James
commentary.text: This is not a declaration of independence. The signers are loyal subjects of a king. But in a place where his government could not reach, they create their own.

commentary.on: solemnly and mutually, in the Presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick
commentary.text: 'Covenant' is the key word. The Puritans formed their churches by covenant, a solemn agreement before God, on the model of God's covenants with Israel. Here they use the same form for a government. Authority comes from the consent of the governed, made sacred by being made before God.

commentary.on: such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions, and Officers
commentary.text: 'Just and equal laws': the phrase joins Solon's 'equal laws' and Deuteronomy's 'small and great alike'. The laws will be made by the community, not handed down by the king.

commentary.on: for the general Good of the Colony; unto which we promise all due Submission and Obedience
commentary.text: Aristotle's test of a good constitution was rule for the common good. Here the common good is named as the purpose of the laws, and the signers promise to obey them, even those who disagree.

compare.author: The passengers of the Mayflower
compare.why: Acton's argument can sound abstract. The Mayflower Compact shows the two traditions meeting in one paragraph: a people choosing to govern itself by just and equal laws, by a covenant made before God.
compare.title: In the presence of God and one another

paras: Begin with what the West owes Athens, because it is a great deal. The idea that the people can govern themselves; the word democracy; the assembly where anyone may speak; officials held to account; the jury of citizens; the rule of law, praised by Solon and made supreme by Aristotle; and the first great arguments for and against it all, in Thucydides, Plato and Aristotle. Every later democracy has looked back to Athens, sometimes as a model and often as a warning.

Athens also showed what could go wrong. Its people were sovereign, and there was nothing above them. They could vote a massacre, condemn their generals together, and execute a philosopher. Acton's diagnosis is precise: Athens protected the vote but not those who lost it, because it knew no law higher than its own.
sections.key: Athens gave the West self-government, the jury, accountability and the rule of law, and showed that a people with nothing above it can become a tyrant.

paras: The first thing the Bible added was a new view of the person. In Athens, worth depended on status: citizen or foreigner, free or slave, man or woman. Aristotle thought some people were slaves by nature. The Bible says every human being is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and Paul that in Christ there is 'neither slave nor free... neither male nor female' (Galatians 3:28).

The historian Larry Siedentop, in Inventing the Individual (2014), and Tom Holland, in Dominion (2019), have argued, in different ways, that this belief in the equal moral worth of every individual is the deepest root of Western liberalism, and that it came from Christianity, not Greece. The German philosopher Jürgen Habermas, who does not write as a believer, has said something similar: that the West's ideas of equal freedom and human rights are heirs of the Jewish ethic of justice and the Christian ethic of love. Democracy for everyone, not only for male citizens, needs a reason to count everyone. This is one.
sections.key: The Bible taught the equal worth of every person, in God's image; Siedentop, Holland and Habermas argue this is a root of the West's belief in equal rights.

sections.h: What Jerusalem gave: a limit on power
paras: The second thing was a limit on every ruler. Israel's king was under God's law and the prophets' rebuke. Jesus' answer about Caesar gave the state its due and set a boundary to it. Peter told the authorities that he must obey God rather than men. Acton's point is that the Church made this boundary an institution: a body independent of the state, which could and sometimes did tell emperors no, as Bishop Ambrose did in 390, when he refused the emperor Theodosius communion until he did penance for a massacre at Thessalonica.

Over centuries, the struggle between Church and state, popes and emperors, bishops and kings, kept either from absolute power. Magna Carta in 1215 began with the freedom of the English Church. This is not democracy. But it is the soil democracy later grew in: the conviction that there are things no government, not even an elected one, may do.
sections.key: Christ's 'render to Caesar' and the Church's independence set a boundary on the state's power, the soil in which limited government grew.

paras: Christians have never agreed on one form of government. The main traditions differ, and the differences matter.

rows: Earthly cities are founded on love of self; without justice, kingdoms are great robberies (IV.4). Christians use the earthly peace, but their true city is God's. No political form is final.
Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II, q. 105, a. 1 (c. 1270)
The best government is mixed: one ruler of virtue, others under him, all chosen from and by the people, as in Deuteronomy 1. Law that is unjust is not true law.
The 'symphony' of Church and emperor (Justinian, Novel 6, 535)
Church and state work in harmony, each with its own sphere; the emperor protects the faith and the Church prays and counsels. Historically closer to monarchy.
Calvin preferred aristocracy mixed with democracy, because kings rarely restrain themselves; lesser magistrates may resist a tyrant. His heirs shaped Dutch, Scottish and American republicanism.
The Church values democracy, which lets citizens choose and replace rulers; but authentic democracy needs the rule of law and a true idea of the person, or it slides into hidden tyranny.
table.note: In outline. Each tradition holds a range of views; Anabaptists and later Baptists added a strong separation of church and state.

sections.key: Christians have held many views of government, from Augustine's caution to Aquinas' mixed government, Calvin's republicanism and modern Catholic support for democracy under law.

sections.h: From Athens to Westminster and Philadelphia
paras: When democracy returned, it came through these channels. Puritans who formed churches by covenant formed governments the same way, as at Plymouth in 1620. In 1647, in the Putney Debates, soldiers of Cromwell's army argued that every Englishman, however poor, had as much right to choose his government as the greatest; their spokesman Colonel Thomas Rainsborough put it that the poorest man in England had a life to live as much as the greatest. The American Declaration of Independence (1776) grounded rights in all men being 'created equal'. The Constitution of 1787 built in Aristotle's mixed government and the rule of law.

Alexis de Tocqueville, a French Catholic aristocrat who toured America in 1831–32, thought religion essential to the American experiment. 'Religion in America takes no direct part in the government of society,' he wrote, 'but it must nevertheless be regarded as the foremost of the political institutions of that country.' It did not make laws, he said, but it restrained what Americans would even conceive of doing. In 1863 Lincoln, at Gettysburg, called the war a test of whether a nation 'conceived in Liberty' could long endure, and hoped for 'a new birth of freedom' under God.
sections.key: Covenant churches, the Putney Debates, the Declaration and the Constitution carried democracy back into the West; Tocqueville called religion America's foremost political institution.

paras: This verdict has strong critics, and they deserve a fair hearing. For most of its history the Church supported kings, not democracy. Paul told Christians to be subject to the governing authorities (Romans 13:1), and kings used the verse to claim a divine right to rule. Many modern democrats, from Thomas Paine to the French revolutionaries of 1789, were hostile to the Church, and many of the steps to democracy, such as votes for all and freedom of religion, were won against churchmen as much as with them. Historians such as Steven Pinker, in Enlightenment Now (2018), credit reason, science and humanism, not faith.

There are fair replies. Acton himself admits the Church was slow; the seed took centuries to grow. The secular champions of equal rights often argued from premises, such as the equal worth of every person, that had come to them through Christianity, as Holland and Habermas argue. And the Greek inheritance is real and essential: without Athens there would be no word for democracy and no tools for running one. The fairest conclusion is that modern democracy has two parents, and has needed both.
sections.key: Critics note that churches long backed kings and many democrats were secular; the reply is that Christianity's seed grew slowly, and modern democracy has two parents.

paras: So, who should rule, and how? Not one man, however wise: Solon refused, and the protector becomes a wolf. Not only the wise: Plato's case is strong, but no one can be trusted with power without account. The many, then, choosing and judging their rulers, as Aristotle argued, in a mixed government under law.

But that is not enough, as Athens showed. The many must themselves be under a law they did not make, and that law must protect every person, because every person, citizen or foreigner, rich or poor, man or woman, bears the image of God. The Athenians gave the West the machinery of freedom. Jerusalem gave it a reason to extend freedom to everyone, and a limit that keeps freedom from becoming tyranny. Lincoln put the hope of both in a single phrase: government of the people, by the people, for the people.
sections.key: The many should rule, choosing and judging their rulers under law; and the law itself should be under the equal worth of every person, which no majority may override.

refs: Lord Acton, 'The History of Freedom in Antiquity' and 'The History of Freedom in Christianity' (1877), in The History of Freedom and Other Essays (1907); letter to Mandell Creighton, 5 April 1887.
