debate.question: What does democracy owe to Christianity?

positions.name: A great deal
positions.who: Alexis de Tocqueville; Lord Acton; Larry Siedentop; Tom Holland
positions.view: Democracy for everyone rests on the belief that every person has equal worth, and limited government on the belief that some things belong to God, not Caesar. Both came to the West through Christianity, and free societies have relied on the habits of restraint it formed.
positions.evidence: Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28; Mark 12:17; covenant churches and the Mayflower Compact; Tocqueville's observations of America.

positions.name: Little: it came from Athens and the Enlightenment
positions.who: Many secular historians; Steven Pinker
positions.view: Democracy was invented by pagan Greeks and revived by Enlightenment thinkers, often against the churches, which for centuries backed kings and divine right. Equal rights came from reason and humanism.
positions.evidence: Athens; Romans 13 used for divine right; the anticlerical French Revolution; Paine.

positions.name: Both, and neither guarantees it
positions.who: Jürgen Habermas, as a secular philosopher; many historians
positions.view: Modern democracy combines Greek institutions with Jewish and Christian ideas of equal dignity and limits on power. Whether it can keep those ideas without the faith that gave them is an open question.
positions.evidence: The two inheritances traced in this journey; the debate over whether secular societies live on 'borrowed' moral capital.

debate.agree: All agree that Athens gave the word and the first institutions, and that modern democracy's belief in the equal rights of every person is not found in Athens.

look.why: John Singleton Copley, an American painter working in London, painted the collapse of William Pitt, Earl of Chatham, in the House of Lords on 7 April 1778, during a debate on the war with America; he died a month later. The gallery's description does not name him; the title does. It is a picture of a parliament: power shared, argued over and held to account.
points: A large gathering of men in elaborate robes, with curled white hair, in a grand hall.
Light streams from a round window near the top left, falling on a group to the right of centre.
In that group one man appears to have fainted, and the others support his head and limbs.
The other men in the room look to the right, towards this group.
A high curved ceiling with recessed areas, draping fabric near the top right and a tapestry below the window on the left, all in pale yellow, brown, cream, white and grey.

music.why: Handel's anthem sets the anointing of King Solomon (1 Kings 1) and has been sung at every British coronation since 1727. In Britain the anointed monarch reigns under God and Parliament: Jerusalem's king under the law, joined to Athens' government by consent.

think.why: Where do equal rights come from? See the modern debate about dignity, God and the foundations of human rights.

learn.why: Lincoln joined the two traditions in one speech: a nation 'conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal', and government of the people, by the people, for the people.

listen.why: An atheist and a historian discuss whether the West's values, equality among them, came from Christianity. Listen for whether they think those values can survive without the faith.

check.q: What, according to Acton, was the root of Athenian democracy's failure?
options: Its leaders were foreigners
It allowed women to vote
It recognised no law above the state, so the majority could do whatever it chose and those who lost the vote had no redress
It was too small
check.why: 'There is no law superior to that of the State'; 'for those who were beaten in the vote there was no redress'.

check.q: Why does Acton say it is worse to be oppressed by a majority than by a minority?
options: Because there is no one left to resist or appeal to: from the will of an entire people there is no refuge
Because majorities are always crueller than minorities
Because a majority can be outvoted at the next election
Because the Athenians had no written laws at all
check.why: A minority's oppression can be resisted by the many; 'from the absolute will of an entire people there is no appeal'.

check.q: What did Christ's words about Caesar do, in Acton's view, that Socrates and the Stoics could not?
options: Teach that taxes to Rome should be refused
Give the state real authority and also a boundary set from outside it, with a Church to defend that boundary
Teach that the wise man should keep out of politics
Give the people the right to vote on religion
check.why: They gave civil power 'a sacredness it had never enjoyed, and bounds it had never acknowledged', and Christ 'created the force to execute it'.

check.q: Why is the word 'covenant' important in the Mayflower Compact?
options: It shows the signers forming a government by mutual consent, made solemn before God, on the model of their covenant churches
It means a business contract
It was a legal requirement
It means they were leaving the king's authority
check.why: They 'covenant and combine' themselves 'in the Presence of God and one another' into a body politic.

check.q: Which is the strongest objection to the claim that democracy owes much to Christianity?
options: Tocqueville denied religion mattered in America
The early Christians demanded votes for slaves and women
The Bible says nothing at all about rulers or law
For centuries the churches supported kings and divine right, and many modern democratic gains were won by secular thinkers, sometimes against churchmen
check.why: This is the critics' best evidence; the reply is that the seed grew slowly and secular arguments often rested on Christian premises.

check.q: What is this journey's verdict on 'Who should rule, and how?'
options: The wise alone
The many, choosing and judging their rulers under law, with the law itself protecting the equal worth of every person
One good king
Whoever wins the most votes, without limit
check.why: Self-government under law from Athens; equal worth and limits on all power from Jerusalem.

tutorial.question: What does democracy owe to Christianity?
tutorial.approach: Set out what Athens gave, with examples from earlier sessions. Then what the Bible added: equal worth (Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28), the ruler under law (Deuteronomy 17), limits on the state (Mark 12:17). Use Acton and the Mayflower Compact. State the objections at full strength. Reach your own judgement.
strong: Gives Athens full credit for the word, the institutions and the arguments.
Explains Acton's diagnosis of Athens' failure: no law above the state, no redress for the defeated.
Explains the biblical ideas of equal worth and limited power, with references.
Uses the Mayflower Compact as evidence of the traditions meeting.
States the objections fairly: divine right, Romans 13, secular democrats.
Reaches a clear, argued answer.

takeaways: Athens gave the West self-government, accountability and the rule of law, but failed because it knew no law above the people's will.
Jerusalem added the equal worth of every person and a God above every ruler, which set limits even on the people; Acton saw this in Christ's words about Caesar.
Modern democracy has two parents: Greek institutions and biblical convictions, joined in covenants like the Mayflower Compact and in Lincoln's 'government of the people'.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Who should rule, and how? In about 300 words, give your own answer, using at least three episodes or texts from this journey (for example Solon, Mytilene, Plato's ship, Aristotle's public supper, Acton or the Mayflower Compact), and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Over the next two weeks, read the whole of Thucydides' Book II and the Mytilene chapters of Book III, a few chapters a day. Then, once, go to a public meeting where decisions are made, a council meeting, a court gallery or a parish meeting, and watch self-government at work.
synthesis: This journey asked who should rule, and how, by following the first democracy from its birth to its judges. Here are the short answers to its questions.

Did the Greeks invent democracy? They invented the word and the first state in which the whole body of citizens was sovereign. People had governed themselves in small ways before, in councils of elders and assemblies; but Athens, from 508/7 BC to 322 BC, was the first to make rich and poor citizens equal in power and to argue openly about whether that was right.

How did it begin? With a crisis of debt in which poor Athenians were enslaved by their creditors. Solon, chosen to settle it in 594 BC, cancelled the debts, banned debt-slavery for ever, and gave the poorest citizens the assembly, the courts, the right of appeal and the right to take up the cause of the wronged. He refused to make himself tyrant and left Athens so the laws would rule. Israel's law met the same crisis with the jubilee, returning land and freeing debt-slaves every fifty years, because the land and the people belong to God.

How did it work? After a revolution against a Spartan king in 508/7 BC, Cleisthenes reorganised Athens into ten tribes. The assembly of all male citizens decided everything directly; most officials and the council were chosen by lot, because election favours the few; juries of hundreds judged; ostracism exiled anyone who seemed a danger. Only adult male citizens took part, perhaps a fifth of the adult population; women, metics and slaves did not. For its members it was the most democratic state there has been; it also rested partly on slavery and empire.

What did it look like at its best? Under Pericles, Thucydides said, Athens was nominally a democracy but in fact governed by its first citizen: a leader with knowledge, eloquence, love of country and honesty, who could tell the people what they did not want to hear. After him, leaders competed for the crowd's favour. The 'demagogues' flattered the people, stirred their anger and accused opponents of treason. Pericles' Athens was also an empire over other Greeks, which he himself called a tyranny.

What went wrong? At Mytilene in 427 BC the assembly voted in anger to kill every man in a rebel city, repented overnight and reversed the decree by a handful of votes; a second ship arrived just in time. At Arginusae in 406 BC it condemned its generals illegally, shouting down Socrates and others who objected, and repented too late. In 399 BC a jury condemned Socrates to death. The danger was passion without restraint, and a constitution with nothing above the people's will.

Why did Plato hate democracy? Because, he argued, ruling is a skill like navigation, and democracy gives the helm to whoever flatters the crew; because it values freedom so highly that it treats every desire and every person as equal and dissolves all authority, even law; and because a people that will have no master at last raises a protector who becomes a tyrant, as Peisistratus had. Modern critics such as Jason Brennan renew the case with evidence of voters' ignorance and bias. It is a strong case, and any defence of democracy has to answer it.

What did Aristotle think? That the many, each bringing a share of wisdom, can judge better together than the few, as a shared dinner beats one man's and the family who live in a house judge it better than the builder; that the people should choose and audit officials while the able serve; that supreme power belongs to laws, not men; and that the most stable city has a large middle class and a mixed constitution. That idea passed through Polybius, Aquinas and Montesquieu into the American Constitution. But Aristotle's many were still free male citizens, and he defended natural slavery.

What did the Bible add? Two things Athens never had. First, the equal worth of every human being, made in God's image, slave or free, man or woman. Second, a God above every ruler: the king under the law, the judge who fears no one 'for the judgment is God's', and Christ's words, 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's', which, as Acton argued, gave the state both authority and a boundary. When democracy returned to the West, it came through covenants like the Mayflower Compact, made 'in the Presence of God and one another'. Critics rightly note that the churches long supported kings, and that many democrats were secular; the fairest judgement is that modern democracy has two parents.

So who should rule, and how? Not one man, however good; not the wise alone; not the people without limit. The many should govern themselves, choosing and judging their rulers in a mixed government under law; and the law itself should protect every person, because every person has a worth no majority can vote away. Athens gave the West the machinery of freedom. Jerusalem gave it a reason to include everyone, and a limit that keeps a free people from becoming a tyrant. Lincoln joined the two when he hoped that government of the people, by the people, for the people would not perish from the earth.
exam: Was Athens a democracy?
Why did Solon refuse to become tyrant, and what did his refusal achieve?
'Nominally a democracy, in fact government by the first citizen.' Discuss Thucydides' judgement of Pericles.
What does the Mytilene debate reveal about the strengths and weaknesses of direct democracy?
Assess Plato's critique of democracy.
Can the many be wiser than the few? Discuss with reference to Aristotle, Politics III.11.
Why did Aristotle think the middle class mattered?
What does democracy owe to Christianity?

title: The end of the story
question: Where is history going?
line: Seven sessions on the Bible's hope for the end: the prophets' new heavens and new earth, the unveiling of apocalypse, Jesus's command to watch, Paul's hope for the dead, the charge that it all failed, Revelation's great multitude and its thousand years, and a verdict.
why: Every Sunday Christians say that Christ 'shall come again' and that they look for 'the life of the world to come'. Few people know what that means, and many imagine street-corner prophets, the rapture and souls on clouds. The Bible's own hope is stranger and more earthy: it ends with a city, not a cloud. This journey reads that hope in four stages, the prophets, apocalyptic, Jesus and Paul, sets beside it 1 Enoch, Plato, Augustine and Hopkins, faces the charge, made by David Strauss and Albert Schweitzer, that Jesus expected the end within a generation and was wrong, and ends the hall by asking you to make the case. It is written at the depth of a university course, for anyone.
follows: A second-year theology paper on biblical eschatology and apocalyptic, with elements of papers on the historical Jesus and the history of Christian doctrine.

the-last-week
outcomes: Explain how Israel's hope grew after the exile from national restoration to a new creation and the resurrection of the dead, with Isaiah 65, Ezekiel 37 and Daniel 12.
Define apocalypse, explain how Revelation's symbols and numbers work, and compare Revelation 1 with 1 Enoch 1.
Read Mark 13 in three ways (AD 70, the end, or both) and explain why Jesus told his followers to watch, not to calculate.
Explain Paul's hope of resurrection and new creation, contrast it with Plato's immortal soul, and assess the rapture.
State Strauss's, Schweitzer's and Russell's objection from failed prophecy at full strength and assess the main replies.
Explain the three views of the millennium, with Augustine's argument, and how Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching on the end differ.

sessions.title: New heavens and a new earth
sessions.line: Israel's prophets did not dream of escaping the world. They promised that God would remake it: dry bones raised, the wolf feeding with the lamb.
sessions.plain: Every story needs an ending, and the Bible's is not what most people expect. It does not end with souls floating up to a heaven in the clouds. It ends with a renewed world, and that hope begins with Israel's prophets. Writing after their nation had been destroyed, they promised that God would make 'new heavens and a new earth', and that he could even raise a valley of dry bones to life. This session reads those promises and asks where the hope of resurrection came from.
sessions.why: This is the first session. The journeys of this hall have followed Jesus, his death and resurrection, the first Christians and their worship, which ends every Sunday with the creed's 'he will come again'. Now we ask where all of it is going. Christians did not invent their hope from nothing: they inherited it from Israel's prophets, so that is where we begin.
answers: What does the Bible mean by 'the end'?
Did the Old Testament believe in heaven, or in something else?
What did the prophets hope for after the exile?
Where did the idea of the resurrection of the dead come from?
sessions.finding: The prophets hoped not to escape the world but for its renewal: a new creation where people live long and the wolf feeds with the lamb, and, by the end of the Old Testament, the dead raised to share it.

paras: If you have walked this hall so far, you have met Jesus in Mark's Gospel, read his teaching on the mountain, followed his last week to the cross and the empty tomb, asked why his death mattered, watched the first Christians spread across the Roman world, and seen what they did when they met on Sundays. Every one of those services, then and now, looks forward. Paul told the Corinthians that each time they shared the bread and cup they proclaimed the Lord's death 'until he comes' (1 Corinthians 11:26). The creeds end the same way: 'he shall come again with glory to judge both the quick and the dead', in the words of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer, 'and the life of the world to come'.
So this hall cannot end without a question. Christianity is a story that claims to be going somewhere. Where?
background.key: Christian worship and the creeds look forward to Christ's coming and 'the life of the world to come'; this journey asks what that means.

paras: The study of 'the last things' is called eschatology, from the Greek eschatos, 'last'. It covers death, judgement, heaven, hell, the return of Christ and the end of the world. It is also where Christians have argued most and where outsiders have laughed most: think of street preachers with placards and best-selling novels about the rapture.

This journey reads the Bible's hope in four stages: the prophets' promise of a new creation, the strange writing called apocalyptic, Jesus's warnings about the end, and Paul's hope for the dead. Then it faces the sharpest objection, that Jesus expected the end within a generation and was wrong, looks at how Christians have read the book of Revelation and its 'thousand years', and ends with a verdict.

background.key: Eschatology means 'the study of the last things'. We read the Bible's hope in four stages, face the objection, read Revelation's millennium, then give a verdict.

paras: The book of Isaiah is named after a prophet who worked in Jerusalem around 740 to 700 BC. Most scholars think the book grew over two centuries: chapters 1 to 39 come largely from Isaiah's time; chapters 40 to 55 from an unnamed prophet among the exiles in Babylon; and chapters 56 to 66, where our first reading comes from, from prophets in Jerusalem after the return from exile, around 530 to 500 BC. Many traditional Jewish and Christian readers hold that Isaiah himself wrote the whole book, foreseeing the exile. Either way, chapter 65 speaks to people living among ruins.

Ezekiel was a priest taken from Jerusalem to Babylon with the first group of exiles in 597 BC. His book is dated precisely, year by year, and most scholars think much of it comes from him. His vision of the valley of bones belongs to the years after 587 BC, when news reached the exiles that Jerusalem and its Temple had been burned.
background.key: Isaiah 65 probably comes from prophets in Jerusalem after the exile (c. 530–500 BC); Ezekiel was a priest in exile in Babylon from 597 BC.

paras: In 587 BC the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and took its leading families into exile. To Israel it seemed that everything God had promised, the land, the king from David's line and the Temple, was gone. In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus conquered Babylon and let the exiles go home, but they returned to a small, poor province. The prophets of this period had to say what God's promises meant now. Their answer was bigger than the old hopes: not a repaired kingdom but a remade world.

paras: The main reading has two parts. Isaiah 65 is the Bible's first promise of 'new heavens and a new earth', the words the book of Revelation will take up at the very end of the Bible. Ezekiel 37 is the most famous picture of God raising the dead, though Ezekiel uses it as a picture of a nation coming back to life.

The comparison is Daniel 12, the first place in the Hebrew Bible where the resurrection of individual dead people is promised in plain words. Together they show the hope growing: from a nation restored to a creation renewed and the dead raised.

paras:
I will rejoice in Jerusalem,
and delight in my people;
and the voice of weeping and the voice of crying
will be heard in her no more.

They will build houses and inhabit them.
They will plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

They will not build and another inhabit.
They will not plant and another eat:
for the days of my people will be like the days of a tree,
and my chosen will long enjoy the work of their hands.

They will not labor in vain
nor give birth for calamity;
for they are the offspring of Yahweh’s blessed
and their descendants with them.

It will happen that before they call, I will answer;
and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.

The wolf and the lamb will feed together.
The lion will eat straw like the ox.
Dust will be the serpent’s food.
They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain,”
says Yahweh.
Yahweh’s hand was on me, and he brought me out in Yahweh’s Spirit, and set me down in the middle of the valley; and it was full of bones.
He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry.
He said to me, “Son of man, can these bones live?”
I answered, “Lord Yahweh, you know.”
Again he said to me, “Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, ‘You dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word.
The Lord Yahweh says to these bones: “Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live.
I will lay sinews on you, and will bring up flesh on you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you will live. Then you will know that I am Yahweh.” ’ ”
So I prophesied as I was commanded. As I prophesied, there was a noise, and behold, there was an earthquake. Then the bones came together, bone to its bone.
I saw, and, behold, there were sinews on them, and flesh came up, and skin covered them above; but there was no breath in them.
Then he said to me, “Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and tell the wind, ‘The Lord Yahweh says: “Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live.” ’ ”
So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.
Then he said to me, “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost. We are completely cut off.’
Therefore prophesy, and tell them, ‘The Lord Yahweh says: “Behold, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people; and I will bring you into the land of Israel.
You will know that I am Yahweh, when I have opened your graves, and caused you to come up out of your graves, my people.
I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live. Then I will place you in your own land; and you will know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it,” says Yahweh.’ ”

parts.title: New heavens and a new earth
parts.context: Probably Jerusalem, around 530 to 500 BC. The exiles have come home to a ruined city and a hard life. The chapter begins with God's complaint against his unfaithful people, then turns, in these verses, to what he will do.

commentary.on: For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth
commentary.text: 'Heavens and earth' is the Bible's way of saying 'everything', as in its first verse: 'In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.' The same verb, 'create', is used. The promise is not a better corner of the world but a second creation. Notice what it is not: it is not a promise that people will leave the earth for heaven.

commentary.on: the former things will not be remembered
commentary.text: The past will not haunt the future. People who had seen their city burned and their children killed are promised a world where the memory no longer wounds.

commentary.on: I create Jerusalem to be a delight
commentary.text: The new creation has a city at its centre, a real place with real people. God says he will 'rejoice in Jerusalem': the joy is his as well as theirs.

commentary.on: No more will there be an infant who only lives a few days
commentary.text: In the ancient world perhaps a third of children died before the age of five. The first gift of the new creation is that babies live and old people reach the end of their days. This is not yet a promise that death will end: a man who dies at a hundred is 'a child'. The prophet stretches ordinary life as far as he can imagine it.

commentary.on: They will build houses and inhabit them.
commentary.text: Everyday, earthly things: houses, vineyards, harvests. The curse of exile and war was that others took what you made. Now the work of your hands is yours. The new creation is full of human work, not idle.

commentary.on: before they call, I will answer
commentary.text: The deepest promise is not long life but closeness to God: prayer answered before it is spoken.

commentary.on: The wolf and the lamb will feed together.
commentary.text: These words echo Isaiah 11:6–9, an older prophecy about a king from David's line, where 'the wolf will live with the lamb'. Even animals will stop killing. The violence that runs through nature is not part of God's final plan.

commentary.on: They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain
commentary.text: The holy mountain is Zion, where the Temple stood. In the end the whole renewed world becomes like a temple, a place where nothing harms anything.

parts.title: Can these bones live?
parts.context: Babylon, after 587 BC. Ezekiel is among the exiles. The news has come that Jerusalem has fallen. The exiles say their hope is dead. Ezekiel describes a vision.

commentary.on: set me down in the middle of the valley; and it was full of bones
commentary.text: A battlefield after the vultures have gone. The bones have not been buried: in Israel that was the worst fate, a sign of being forgotten by God and man.

commentary.on: Son of man, can these bones live?
commentary.text: 'Son of man' here simply means 'human being': God addresses Ezekiel as a mortal. The question is put to someone who knows the answer is no. Ezekiel's reply, 'you know', is the honest answer of a man who will not say no to God and cannot say yes.

commentary.on: I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live.
commentary.text: In Hebrew one word, ruach, means breath, wind and spirit. The scene echoes Genesis 2:7, where God breathes into the first man. Raising the dead is creation again.

commentary.on: the bones came together, bone to its bone
commentary.text: It happens in two stages: first bodies, then breath. Without God's breath the bodies are only better-assembled corpses. The African-American spiritual 'Dem Bones' ('the toe bone connected to the foot bone') was made from this verse.

commentary.on: these bones are the whole house of Israel
commentary.text: God explains the vision himself. The bones are the nation, which says 'our hope is lost'. Ezekiel is not yet teaching that dead individuals will rise; he is promising that a dead people will live again.

commentary.on: I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people
commentary.text: Yet the picture he chose is the raising of the dead. Once Israel could imagine God doing this to a nation, it was a short step to believe he could do it to people. Later Jewish and Christian readers took the passage in both senses at once.

commentary.on: I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live.
commentary.text: The vision ends with God's own Spirit living in his people, and the land restored. The hope is still earthly: graves opened, a people home.

paras: “At that time Michael will stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there will be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time. At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.
Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse. Those who turn many to righteousness will shine as the stars forever and ever.

parts.title: Some to everlasting life
parts.context: The book of Daniel tells of a Jewish wise man at the court of Babylon in the 500s BC. Most scholars think its visions were written down in their final form during the persecution under the Greek king Antiochus IV, between 167 and 164 BC, when Jews were being killed for keeping their law; many traditional readers hold that Daniel wrote it himself. These are the last words of its final vision. (If you took 'Who was Jesus?', you read its chapter 7, the vision of 'one like a son of man'.)

commentary.on: there will be a time of trouble, such as never was
commentary.text: The promise is given in the middle of persecution. The question was urgent: what about the faithful who had already been killed for keeping God's law? If God's justice only works in this life, they had lost.

commentary.on: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake
commentary.text: This is the clearest statement in the Hebrew Bible that dead individuals will rise. 'Sleep' for death will be used by Jesus and Paul. Notice: they sleep 'in the dust of the earth' and wake from it. It is the body that rises, not a soul that escapes.

commentary.on: some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt
commentary.text: The resurrection is for judgement: justice at last for the martyrs and for their persecutors. Here, for the first time in the Bible, we meet the phrase 'everlasting life'.

commentary.on: Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse.
commentary.text: The 'expanse' is the sky, as in Genesis 1. The wise, who taught others to stay faithful, will shine like stars. A persecuted people is promised that the faithful dead are not forgotten.

compare.why: Ezekiel used the raising of the dead as a picture. Daniel, centuries later, promised it plainly. Read the first verses in the Hebrew Bible that say individual dead people will rise.
compare.title: Those who sleep in the dust

paras: In English, 'the end' can mean the finish or the goal. The Bible means both, but mostly the second. The Greek word telos means the end a thing is for: the end of an acorn is an oak. When the Bible speaks of the end of the world, it is asking what the world is for.

Its answer is surprising. Popular pictures of heaven, with harps and clouds, come mostly from later art and piety. The Bible itself begins with God creating 'the heavens and the earth' and ends, in Revelation 21, with 'a new heaven and a new earth' and a city coming down from God to earth. The story does not end with people leaving the world but with God coming to live in it. You may have read those final chapters already in 'The whole story' or 'Light, stone and glass'.
That hope did not begin with Christianity. It began with Israel's prophets, and it began in disaster.
sections.key: The Bible's 'end' is the world's goal, and the Bible ends with a renewed heaven and earth, not with souls leaving the world.

paras: For most of the Old Testament, hope means this life: land, children, a long life, peace, a king from David's line and God's presence in the Temple. The dead go down to Sheol, a shadowy place under the earth where, as one psalm asks, 'In Sheol, who shall give you thanks?' (Psalm 6:5). There is almost no talk of heaven as a destination for the dead.

Then, in 587 BC, the land, the king and the Temple were lost. The prophets of the exile did not say the promises were false. They said God would keep them in a greater way than anyone had imagined. The unnamed prophet of Isaiah 40–55 promised a new exodus across the desert. The prophets after the return promised a new creation. Ezekiel saw the nation raised from its grave. Hope moved from repair to renewal: not the old world patched up, but the old world made new.
sections.key: Old Testament hope was for this life; after the exile of 587 BC, the prophets enlarged it into a hope for a renewed world.

sections.h: From a nation raised to the dead raised
paras: When did Israel come to believe that the dead would rise? There are hints early: 'Yahweh kills and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol and brings up' (1 Samuel 2:6). Isaiah 26:19 promises, 'Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise.' But the clearest text is Daniel 12, from the persecution of the 160s BC.

The reason is moral. Under Antiochus IV, faithful Jews were tortured and killed precisely for being faithful. Second Maccabees, a Jewish history written in Greek in the next century (part of the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament), tells of a mother and her seven sons who were executed one by one; the second son tells the king that the King of the universe will raise up those who die for his laws. If God is just, death cannot be the end for them.

By Jesus's time most Jews, led by the Pharisees, believed in the resurrection of the dead at the end of history. The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied it (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). In Judaism it remains a central belief: the last of Maimonides' thirteen principles of faith (1168) is the resurrection of the dead.
sections.key: Belief in the resurrection grew from the question of justice for the martyrs: clearest in Daniel 12 (160s BC), held by the Pharisees, denied by the Sadducees.

paras: Notice what kind of hope this is. It is not the Greek idea, which you may meet in Plato, that the soul is immortal by nature and is released from the body at death. It is the belief that God, who made bodies, will remake them. The dead 'sleep in the dust of the earth' and 'awake'.

That is why resurrection and new creation belong together. A raised body needs a world to live in. Isaiah's houses, vineyards and peaceable animals are where Daniel's raised dead will live. The early Christians would put the two together at once.

There is a real question here, which scholars debate. Some, such as the historians of religion who first studied ancient Persia, have suggested that Israel learned the hope of resurrection from Persian Zoroastrianism, which also taught a final resurrection and judgement, during the two centuries of Persian rule. Others point out that the Persian texts are hard to date and that the roots of the idea are already in Israel's own faith in a God who 'kills and makes alive'. The evidence does not settle it.
sections.key: Resurrection is not the soul's escape but God remaking bodies, so it goes with a new creation; whether Persian ideas influenced it is debated.

sections.h: A golden age behind, or ahead?
paras: If you took 'In the beginning', you read Hesiod's myth of the ages in his Works and Days (about 700 BC): first a golden race who lived like gods, then silver, bronze, heroes, and now iron, the worst of all. For the Greek poet the best was behind us, and history ran downhill.

Israel's prophets reversed the direction. Their best was ahead. Eden is not simply lost; the peaceable kingdom is coming. Even the Roman poet Virgil, in his Fourth Eclogue (about 40 BC), imagined the golden age returning with the birth of a child; medieval Christians read that poem as a prophecy of Christ, which is one reason Dante chose Virgil as his guide.

Many historians argue that this forward-looking hope, carried by Christianity, shaped the West's sense that history has a direction: a story with a meaning, not an endless cycle. Modern ideas of progress, some say, are a secular version of it. Whether or not that is so, the shape of the Bible's hope is clear: forward, and earthly.
sections.key: Hesiod's best age was in the past; the prophets' was in the future. That forward-looking hope helped give the West its sense of history as a story.

sections.h: A hope Jews and Christians share
paras: The hope in this session is not only Christian. It is still said every day in synagogues. The second blessing of the Amidah, the central Jewish prayer, praises God who 'gives life to the dead' (in Hebrew, mechayeh hametim), and the Mishnah, the first written collection of Jewish law (about AD 200), says that whoever denies the resurrection of the dead has no share in the world to come (Sanhedrin 10:1). Jewish tradition speaks of the 'world to come' (olam ha-ba) and of the days of the Messiah, when Isaiah's peace will come to the earth.

Christians and Jews read the same prophets and share the same hope: a renewed world, the dead raised, God's justice done. Where they part is over Jesus. Christians claim that the resurrection Daniel promised for the end has already begun in one man. Jews, for the most part, reply that the world is plainly not yet redeemed: the wolf does not yet feed with the lamb. Both are reading Isaiah 65. That disagreement runs through the rest of this journey, and it is a fair one.
sections.key: Jews still pray daily to God who 'gives life to the dead'; Jews and Christians share the prophets' hope and part over whether it has begun in Jesus.

refs: Isaiah 11:6–9; 26:19; 65:17–25; Ezekiel 37:1–14; Daniel 12:1–3; 1 Samuel 2:6; Psalm 6:5; Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8; 1 Corinthians 11:26; Revelation 21:1–5.
2 Maccabees 7 (the mother and her seven sons). Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10 (the thirteen principles, 1168).
Hesiod, Works and Days 109–201; Virgil, Eclogue 4.

John Day, 'The Development of Belief in Life after Death in Ancient Israel', in After the Exile, ed. Barton and Reimer (1996); Jon D. Levenson, Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel (2006); N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003), chapters 3–4; J. Richard Middleton, A New Heaven and a New Earth (2014).
On Persian influence: Mary Boyce, Zoroastrians (1979), argues for it; Levenson (2006) argues for roots within Israel.

debate.question: Is the Old Testament's hope about this world or another?

positions.name: This world, renewed
positions.who: Jon D. Levenson; N. T. Wright; J. Richard Middleton; the Jewish tradition of the resurrection
positions.view: The prophets' hope is for God to renew his creation and raise his people bodily within it. Heaven in the sense of a place for disembodied souls is not the Old Testament's goal at all.
positions.evidence: 'New heavens and a new earth' with houses and vineyards (Isaiah 65); graves opened and the people brought home (Ezekiel 37); the dead waking from 'the dust of the earth' (Daniel 12).

positions.name: Earthly pictures of a heavenly hope
positions.who: Origen (c. 185–254) and many readers after him; much traditional Christian devotion
positions.view: The earthly images are pictures. The vineyards and the holy mountain point to a spiritual fulfilment in heaven, as the earthly Jerusalem points to the heavenly one (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22).
positions.evidence: The prophets' language is poetic; the New Testament speaks of a Jerusalem 'above'; the life to come is beyond our imagining (1 Corinthians 2:9).

positions.name: A hope that grew
positions.who: Most historical scholars
positions.view: The hope developed over centuries: first national restoration, then a renewed world, and only late, under persecution, the resurrection of individuals. Each stage answered a crisis.
positions.evidence: Psalm 6:5 knows no praise in Sheol; Ezekiel 37 is explained as the nation; Daniel 12 is the first plain promise of individual resurrection.

debate.agree: All agree that the prophets' hope was God's doing, not human progress, and that it looked forward, not back.

look.why: Edward Hicks, a Quaker preacher in Pennsylvania, painted more than sixty versions of the Peaceable Kingdom, the prophecy that 'the wolf and the lamb will feed together'. You may have seen this one in 'In the beginning'; it is here because it is the very scene Isaiah 65:25 promises. In the background he set William Penn making his treaty with the Lenape people: for Hicks, the prophecy could begin to come true in human history.
points: Three small children with blond hair sit and stand among a group of animals on a grassy spit of land to the right.
The largest animal is a caramel-brown bull standing next to a pale golden lion; around them, at rest, are a tiger, a wolf, sheep, goats, cows, bears and a jaguar.
One child stands over the lion's back with an arm around the tiger's shoulders; another touches the jaguar's nose.
In the distance on the left, eight indigenous people in feathered headdresses gather with eight men in tricorn hats and long coats; one of the men holds up a roll of cloth lifted from a chest.
A river runs into the distance under a sky that deepens from shell pink at the horizon to light blue.

music.why: Haydn's Creation (1798) sings the world as God made it, and good. The prophets' hope is for that same world renewed, not abandoned.

think.why: What Christians believe about death and the resurrection, in short.

learn.why: The Bible's first promise of a new creation, taken up in its last chapters.

check.q: Why does Isaiah 65 promise that 'the child will die one hundred years old'?
options: Because the prophet believed that in the new creation death would be abolished entirely
Because Israel's law required people to live a hundred years
Because he stretched ordinary life as far as he could imagine it: babies survive and the old reach full age
Because he was describing life in heaven after death
check.why: Isaiah 65 still includes death; its promise is long, full, earthly life. Death's abolition comes later in the Bible's hope (Isaiah 25; Revelation 21).

check.q: What do the dry bones in Ezekiel 37 stand for, according to the passage itself?
options: The soldiers of Babylon
The individual dead of Israel, who will rise at the end of time
The souls of the righteous in heaven
The whole house of Israel, which says its hope is lost
check.why: God explains it: 'these bones are the whole house of Israel'. The vision is about a nation restored, though it uses the picture of resurrection.

check.q: Why is Daniel 12 important for the history of belief in resurrection?
options: It is the clearest promise in the Hebrew Bible that individual dead people will rise, some to everlasting life
It denies the resurrection
It is the first book of the Bible
It describes the soul leaving the body at death
check.why: 'Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake': the first plain promise of individual resurrection.

check.q: What crisis best explains why the hope of resurrection became clear in the 160s BC?
options: The persecution under Antiochus IV, when the faithful were killed for being faithful
The birth of Jesus
The Persian conquest of Babylon
The building of the second Temple
check.why: If the martyrs had died for God's law, justice required that death not be the end for them.

check.q: How does the prophets' hope differ from the Greek idea of the immortal soul?
options: The prophets hoped for God to raise bodies and renew the world; the Greek idea is of a soul released from the body
The prophets believed in reincarnation
It does not: both say the soul escapes the body
The Greeks believed in a new heaven and a new earth
check.why: The dead 'awake' from the dust; resurrection is God remaking bodies, and it needs a renewed world.

check.q: Which group in Jesus's time denied the resurrection of the dead?
options: The Christians
The Sadducees
The Pharisees
The followers of Daniel
check.why: Mark 12:18 and Acts 23:8: the Sadducees, the priestly party, denied it; the Pharisees affirmed it.

tutorial.question: Did the Old Testament hope for heaven?
tutorial.approach: Define what you mean by 'heaven'. Then set out the evidence: Sheol in the Psalms, the new creation of Isaiah 65, Ezekiel's bones and Daniel's resurrection. Ask how the hope changed after the exile and under persecution. Compare it with the Greek idea of the immortal soul, and end with what Christians inherited.
strong: Distinguishes heaven as a destination for souls from the hope of a renewed creation.
Uses Isaiah 65 to show the earthly, embodied character of the hope.
Explains that Ezekiel 37 is about a nation, but uses the picture of resurrection.
Identifies Daniel 12 as the first plain promise of individual resurrection and explains its setting.
Notes the debate about how the hope developed, and possible Persian influence.
Contrasts the Greek immortal soul with bodily resurrection.

reading.author: N. T. Wright
reading.title: Surprised by Hope
reading.why: A readable case that the Bible's hope is new creation and resurrection, not 'going to heaven'.

reading.author: J. Richard Middleton
reading.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
reading.why: The hope of a renewed creation traced from Genesis to Revelation.

reading.author: Jon D. Levenson
reading.title: Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel
reading.why: A Jewish scholar argues that resurrection grew from within Israel's own faith.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Isaiah's new creation is full of ordinary work: houses built, vineyards planted. Each day, do one small piece of work slowly and well, as if it were going to last, and offer it to God when you finish.
sessions.reflect: When you imagine the end of the world, or heaven, what do you see? Where did that picture come from?
takeaways: The Bible's 'end' is the world's goal, and its hope is a renewed creation, not souls leaving the world.
After the exile, Isaiah promised 'new heavens and a new earth' and Ezekiel saw a dead nation raised.
Daniel 12, written under persecution, gave the first plain promise that the dead will rise, the hope Jesus and Paul inherited.

sessions.title: Apocalypse
sessions.line: A prisoner on an island sees a vision. 'Apocalypse' does not mean disaster. It means unveiling: the curtain pulled back on who really rules the world.
sessions.plain: Today 'apocalypse' means disaster: bombs, plagues, zombies. In Greek it means something quite different: an unveiling, the curtain pulled back. Apocalypses were a kind of Jewish and Christian writing, full of strange beasts, numbers and visions, written mostly for people under pressure, to show them who really rules history. This session reads the opening vision of the book of Revelation, set beside the older Book of Enoch, and learns how to read their symbols.
sessions.why: The first session ended with the prophets' hope and Daniel's promise that the dead will rise, given to a persecuted people. Daniel is the first full apocalypse in the Bible. Before we can read what Jesus and Paul said about the end, we need to understand the kind of writing in which so much of that hope was expressed.
answers: What does 'apocalypse' actually mean?
Who wrote the book of Revelation, and why?
Is Revelation about now? Is it a code for the future?
How should its symbols and numbers be read?
sessions.finding: 'Apocalypse' means unveiling: a kind of writing for persecuted people, full of symbols, which pulls back the curtain to show who really rules history. Revelation is first a letter to seven real churches, centred on the risen Christ.

paras: In the first session we read the prophets' hope: a new heaven and earth, the dead raised. We ended with Daniel, written under the persecution of Antiochus IV, promising that the faithful dead would wake.

Daniel belongs to a new kind of writing that flourished among Jews from about 250 BC to AD 150, and then among Christians: the apocalypse. Two of them stand in our Bibles, Daniel in the Old Testament and Revelation in the New. Many more were written that did not become Scripture. Without knowing how these books work, it is easy to misread them badly, and many have.
background.key: Daniel is the first biblical apocalypse; Revelation is the second. Apocalypses were written from about 250 BC on.

paras: The Greek word apokalypsis means 'uncovering' or 'revelation'. It is the first word of the book of Revelation: 'This is the Revelation of Jesus Christ' (1:1). Scholars use the word for a whole type of writing. In 1979 a group led by the American scholar John J. Collins gave a definition that most still use: in an apocalypse a heavenly being reveals to a human being a hidden world, both a heaven above and a future ahead, usually in visions.

Apocalypses share some features: a seer who is shown things, often by an angel; strange creatures standing for empires; numbers with meanings; a cosmic battle between good and evil; and a final judgement. Their purpose is usually comfort and courage. They tell people who feel powerless that the empire which seems to rule the world is not the last word.
background.key: An apocalypse is a vision in which a heavenly being unveils the hidden world above and the future ahead, usually to give courage to people under pressure.

paras: The writer calls himself John (1:9), a 'brother' of the churches he writes to, exiled on Patmos, a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea off the coast of what is now Turkey. Christian tradition from the second century, beginning with Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, identified him with John the apostle, Jesus's disciple. In the third century Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, noticed that its Greek is very different from the Gospel of John's and argued that it was another John. Most scholars today agree it was a Christian prophet named John, whether or not he was the apostle.

Irenaeus, writing around 180, says the vision was seen near the end of the reign of the emperor Domitian, that is, around AD 95 (Against Heresies V.30.3). Most scholars accept a date in the 90s; some argue for the late 60s, under Nero, before the Temple fell.

timeline.text: The earliest parts of 1 Enoch
Daniel's visions in their final form
Nero blames the Christians for the fire of Rome; many are killed
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and its Temple
The emperor Domitian
John's vision on Patmos (Irenaeus's date)
Irenaeus on the date and author of Revelation

background.key: Revelation was written by a Christian prophet named John, exiled on Patmos, most likely around AD 95; whether he was the apostle is debated.

paras: The main reading is Revelation 1:9–20, John's first vision: the risen Christ standing among seven lamp stands, holding seven stars. It shows how the whole book works: a real place and a real situation, then a vision full of symbols, then an explanation.

The comparison is the opening of 1 Enoch, an older Jewish apocalypse that the first Christians knew well. The Letter of Jude in the New Testament quotes it. Reading it shows that Revelation is part of a living tradition, and also what is new in it.
background.key: Revelation 1:9–20 shows how the book works; 1 Enoch 1, quoted in Jude, shows the tradition John belonged to.

before: Where is John, and why? What does he share with the people he writes to?
Make a list of the images in the vision. Which of them does the passage explain?
What does the figure in the vision say about himself?
sessions.readWhy: John's first vision: the risen Christ among the lamp stands, the key to the whole book.

paras: I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus, was on the isle that is called Patmos because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ.
I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice, like a trumpet
saying, “What you see, write in a book and send to the seven assemblies: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and to Laodicea.”
I turned to see the voice that spoke with me. Having turned, I saw seven golden lamp stands.
And among the lamp stands was one like a son of man, clothed with a robe reaching down to his feet, and with a golden sash around his chest.
His head and his hair were white as white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire.
His feet were like burnished brass, as if it had been refined in a furnace. His voice was like the voice of many waters.
He had seven stars in his right hand. Out of his mouth proceeded a sharp two-edged sword. His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.
When I saw him, I fell at his feet like a dead man.
He laid his right hand on me, saying, “Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last,
and the Living one. I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades.
Write therefore the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which will happen hereafter.

The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lamp stands is this: The seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies. The seven lamp stands are seven assemblies.

parts.title: One like a son of man
parts.context: The island of Patmos, probably around AD 95. John writes to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey), each a few days' journey apart on a circular road. Some of their members face hostility for refusing to honour the emperor and the gods of their cities.

commentary.on: I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus
commentary.text: John does not write as a superior. He shares three things with his readers: suffering, a kingdom, and endurance. That combination is the whole book's message: the kingdom is already theirs, but it is lived out under pressure, and it calls for endurance.

commentary.on: was on the isle that is called Patmos because of God's Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ
commentary.text: Most likely he was banished there for his preaching. Roman governors used islands as places of exile. So the book is written by a prisoner to people under pressure, about the power that seemed to be crushing them.

commentary.on: I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day
commentary.text: 'The Lord's day' is Sunday, the day of the resurrection, when the churches met. It is one of the earliest uses of the phrase in Christian writing. The vision comes during worship, and the book was meant to be read aloud in worship (1:3).

commentary.on: write in a book and send to the seven assemblies
commentary.text: These are seven real churches in seven real cities. Chapters 2 and 3 contain a letter to each. Whatever else Revelation is, it is first a letter to people in the first century, about their situation. That rules out any reading that makes it mean nothing to them.

commentary.on: one like a son of man
commentary.text: These words come from Daniel 7:13, where 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds to God and receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus called himself 'the Son of Man'. John sees him already in glory.

commentary.on: His head and his hair were white as white wool, like snow.
commentary.text: In Daniel 7:9 it is God, 'the Ancient of Days', whose hair is 'like pure wool'. John gives the risen Jesus the features of God himself. This is how apocalypse says what a creed would later say in words.

commentary.on: Out of his mouth proceeded a sharp two-edged sword.
commentary.text: Not a picture to draw literally. The sword is his word, which judges (Hebrews 4:12; Isaiah 49:2). The only weapon Christ uses in Revelation is what he says.

commentary.on: I fell at his feet like a dead man.
commentary.text: Every seer in the Bible reacts to the vision of God like this: Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel. The holy is terrifying before it is comforting.

commentary.on: I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever.
commentary.text: This is the centre of the vision. The one who rules history is not the emperor but a man the empire executed, who is alive. He holds 'the keys of Death and of Hades': death itself is locked and unlocked by him.

commentary.on: The seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies. The seven lamp stands are seven assemblies.
commentary.text: Revelation explains its own symbols here, and teaches us how to read the rest. Seven is the number of completeness (the seven days of creation): seven churches stand for the whole Church. And the risen Christ walks among them, not far away.

paras: I. 1. The words of the blessing of Enoch, wherewith he blessed the elect and righteous, who will be living in the day of tribulation, when all the wicked and godless are to be removed. 2. And he took up his parable and said—Enoch a righteous man, whose eyes were opened by God, saw the vision of the Holy One in the heavens, which the angels showed me, and from them I heard everything, and from them I understood as I saw, but not for this generation, but for a remote one which is for to come. 3. Concerning the elect I said, and took up my parable concerning them:
The Holy Great One will come forth from His dwelling,

4. And the eternal God will tread upon the earth, (even) on Mount Sinai,
[And appear from His camp]
And appear in the strength of His might from the heaven of heavens.

5. And all shall be smitten with fear,
And the Watchers shall quake,
And great fear and trembling shall seize them unto the ends of the earth.

6. And the high mountains shall be shaken,
And the high hills shall be made low,
And shall melt like wax before the flame

7. And the earth shall be wholly rent in sunder,
And all that is upon the earth shall perish,
And there shall be a judgement upon all (men).

8. But with the righteous He will make peace,
And will protect the elect,
And mercy shall be upon them.

And they shall all belong to God,
And they shall be prospered,
And they shall all be blessed.

And He will help them all,
And light shall appear unto them,
And He will make peace with them.

9. And behold! He cometh with ten thousands of His holy ones
To execute judgement upon all,
And to destroy all the ungodly:

And to convict all flesh
Of all the works of their ungodliness which they have ungodly committed,
And of all the hard things which ungodly sinners have spoken against Him.

parts.author: 1 Enoch
parts.title: The words of the blessing of Enoch
parts.context: 1 Enoch is a collection of five books written in the name of Enoch, the man who 'walked with God' in Genesis 5:24. This opening comes from the oldest part, the Book of the Watchers (chapters 1–36), which most scholars date to the 200s BC. Fragments in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls; the whole book survives in Ge'ez, the ancient language of Ethiopia, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it as Scripture. (If you took 'Who was Jesus?', you read another part of 1 Enoch there, its Son of Man; this is its opening.) This is R. H. Charles's translation (1917). Charles marked words he thought had been added or needed supplying with special brackets; we have removed those marks and kept his words, and kept his square brackets and verse numbers. 'The Watchers' are fallen angels.
parts.plain: Enoch, a righteous man, says that God showed him a vision for a far future generation. God will come down from heaven onto Mount Sinai. The whole earth will shake, the mountains will melt, and everything will be judged. But God will make peace with the righteous, protect them, and give them light. He will come with countless holy ones to judge the wicked for what they have done and said against him.

commentary.on: who will be living in the day of tribulation
commentary.text: Like Daniel and Revelation, Enoch is written for people facing 'tribulation'. The message is for those who suffer: God has not forgotten.

commentary.on: but not for this generation, but for a remote one which is for to come
commentary.text: A typical apocalyptic device. The book is written in the name of a hero of long ago, who 'foresees' the readers' own time. Scholars call such books pseudepigrapha, writings under an assumed name. Revelation does not do this: John writes in his own name, to his own time.

commentary.on: The Holy Great One will come forth from His dwelling
commentary.text: The old Jewish hope was that God himself would come to put things right. In Revelation the one who comes is the risen Jesus, with God's own features.

commentary.on: And the high mountains shall be shaken
commentary.text: The language of earthquake and melting mountains is borrowed from older poetry about God's appearing (Micah 1:3–4; Psalm 97:5). It is the language of awe, not a geological forecast. Apocalypses use the strongest images they can find to say that God's coming changes everything.

commentary.on: But with the righteous He will make peace
commentary.text: Judgement in apocalyptic is good news for the faithful: it means injustice will not last. 'Light shall appear unto them.'

commentary.on: And behold! He cometh with ten thousands of His holy ones
commentary.text: This is the verse the Letter of Jude quotes (Jude 14–15), calling it the prophecy of 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam'. The early Church knew and valued this book; most churches later left it out of their Bibles, but the Ethiopian Church kept it.

compare.author: 1 Enoch
compare.why: The first Christians knew this older Jewish apocalypse well; the New Testament Letter of Jude quotes its ninth verse (Jude 14–15). Read it to see the tradition John belonged to, and what is new in his vision.
compare.title: The Holy Great One will come forth

paras: Apocalypses usually come from people who feel history is out of their hands. Daniel was finished under a king who banned the Jewish law. Revelation was written under an empire that demanded honour for the emperor. The visions answer a question the powerless always ask: who is really in charge?

Their answer is to pull back the curtain. Behind the empire's display, God is on his throne, and the empire is shown for what it is: a beast. That is why apocalypse is often called 'resistance literature'. It does not organise a revolt; it refuses to let the powerful define reality. The American theologian Richard Bauckham has argued that Revelation's chief aim is to purge its readers' imagination of the empire's picture of the world and replace it with God's.

The genre has a dark side too. A writing that sees history as a battle between good and evil can make its readers sure they are the good, and its enemies wholly evil. Readers of every age have had to watch for that.
sections.key: Apocalypses were written for the powerless to show who really rules history; they unmask empires, though their sharp divisions can be misused.

paras: Revelation is written in pictures, and most of them come from the Old Testament: scholars count hundreds of allusions, though hardly any direct quotations. A reader who knows Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah and Exodus finds keys everywhere. The beasts of chapter 13 come from Daniel 7's four beasts, which Daniel himself explains as empires.

Numbers carry meaning. Seven means completeness. Twelve means God's people (twelve tribes, twelve apostles). A thousand means a great, full number. Three and a half (sometimes 'a time, times and half a time', or 42 months, or 1,260 days) is half of seven, a limited time of trouble that will not last.

The most famous number, 666 (13:18), is called 'the number of a man'. In Hebrew and Greek, letters doubled as numbers. Many scholars think it spells 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters; some early manuscripts read 616, which is what the Latin form of the name gives. If so, John was pointing at the emperor who had killed Christians in Rome in AD 64.
sections.key: Revelation's images come from the Old Testament and its numbers carry meanings: seven is completeness, and 666 most likely stands for Nero.

rows: Mainly the first century: Rome, Nero, the persecution of the churches
Many modern scholars; some Catholic and Reformed writers
The whole history of the Church, chapter by chapter, from John to the end
Many Protestant Reformers and their heirs, who often saw the papacy in the beast
Mostly events still to come just before Christ returns
Many evangelicals, especially dispensationalists (see session 4, still to come); some early Fathers
Timeless truths: the battle of good and evil in every age
Many readers since Augustine and Tyconius in the 300s
table.note: Many careful readers combine them: written to the first century, true of every age, and pointing to a real end.

paras: Christians have read Revelation in four main ways. They are worth knowing, because almost every argument about the book is an argument between them.
sections.key: Revelation has been read as about the first century, the whole of Church history, the last days or every age; many combine them.

paras: Patmos is a small island, about twelve kilometres long, in the eastern Aegean. Visitors today are shown a cave, the Cave of the Apocalypse, where tradition says John received the vision, and above it the monastery of St John the Theologian, founded in 1088. Both are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

We know almost nothing else about John's exile. The early Christian writer Tertullian (about 200) says the apostle John was banished to an island after surviving an attempt on his life in Rome; how much of that is legend is uncertain. What the text itself says is enough: he was there 'because of God's Word and the testimony of Jesus', and he was 'in the Spirit on the Lord's day'. A man cut off from his churches on a Sunday sees the risen Christ walking among them.
sections.key: Patmos, a small Aegean island, keeps a cave and a monastery (1088) in John's memory; we know little of his exile beyond what he says.

paras: Set beside 1 Enoch, Revelation looks familiar: a seer, a vision of God's coming, judgement on the wicked and peace for the righteous. Three things are new.

First, the name. Enoch is a hero of long ago 'foreseeing' a later age. John writes in his own name to his own churches. Second, the centre. In Enoch, God comes forth with his holy ones. In Revelation the central figure is a crucified man alive for ever, and the victory has already been won: 'I was dead, and behold, I am alive.' Later in the book the conquering Lion of Judah turns out to be 'a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain' (5:5–6). The world is not saved by a greater violence but by a death.
Third, the hope is not escape. The book ends with the holy city coming down to earth. Apocalypse, for John, is not about leaving the world but about seeing it as it really is, and as it will be.
sections.key: Unlike Enoch, Revelation is written in John's own name, centres on the crucified and risen Christ, and hopes for a renewed earth, not escape.

sections.h: Why Enoch is not in most Bibles
paras: If the Letter of Jude quotes 1 Enoch as prophecy, why is Enoch not in most Bibles? Its story is a good example of how the canon, the list of books the Church accepted as Scripture, was formed.

Enoch was widely read by Jews before Jesus: at least eleven Aramaic manuscripts were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran. Some early Christians valued it highly; around AD 200 Tertullian argued that it should be accepted, partly because Jude quotes it (On the Apparel of Women I.3). But it was never part of the Jewish Bible, and most churches, East and West, left it out, judging it not to be ancient prophecy but a later book in Enoch's name. Only the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and the Eritrean Church, kept it, which is why it survives complete only in Ge'ez.

Quoting a book is not the same as treating it as Scripture: Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). For our purposes, Enoch matters as a window on the world of thought in which Daniel, Jesus and Revelation were heard.
sections.key: 1 Enoch was widely read and quoted by Jude, but most churches left it out of the canon; only the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches kept it.

sections.h: The book the Church hesitated over
paras: Revelation itself was slow to be accepted everywhere. In the West it was received early. In the East, doubts about its authorship and its use by enthusiasts made many hesitate. Around 325 Eusebius listed it both among the accepted books and, 'if it seem proper', among the disputed ones (Church History III.25). Cyril of Jerusalem left it out of his list of books in the 350s. To this day it is not read aloud in the Eastern Orthodox Divine Liturgy, though the Orthodox accept it as Scripture.

At the Reformation, Martin Luther wrote in his preface of 1522 that he could not find Christ clearly taught in it and did not count it among the chief books; in a later preface (1530) he was kinder, reading it as a picture of the Church's history. Calvin wrote commentaries on almost every New Testament book except Revelation.
That hesitation is worth knowing. The Church has always known that Revelation is easy to misread. It kept the book, and has warned its readers to read it carefully.
sections.key: The Eastern Church hesitated over Revelation, it is still not read in the Orthodox liturgy, and Luther doubted it in 1522: the Church kept it while warning against misreading it.

refs: Revelation 1:1–20; 2–3; 5:5–6; 13:18; Daniel 7:1–14; Jude 14–15; Genesis 5:24; Micah 1:3–4; Psalm 97:5.

debate.question: Is Revelation about the past, the future, or every age?

positions.name: The first century
positions.who: Many historical scholars; preterist readers
positions.view: Revelation was written to seven churches about Rome. The beast is the empire, 666 is Nero, Babylon is Rome on its seven hills (17:9). Its truth for us comes through what it meant then.
positions.evidence: The letters to real churches (chs 2–3); 'the things which must happen soon' (1:1); 666 as Nero; Rome's seven hills.

positions.name: The last days
positions.who: Many evangelical and dispensationalist readers; Hal Lindsey, The Late Great Planet Earth (1970)
positions.view: Most of the book, from chapter 4, describes events still to come before Christ returns: a great tribulation, an Antichrist, a final battle.
positions.evidence: 'The things which will happen hereafter' (1:19); events of cosmic scale that did not happen in the first century; the second coming in chapter 19.

positions.name: Every age, and the end
positions.who: Augustine; Richard Bauckham; many Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant scholars
positions.view: Revelation unveils the pattern of every age: empires that make themselves gods, the Church called to faithful witness, the Lamb who conquers by dying. It speaks first to the first century, but its beasts reappear in every age, and it points to a real end.
positions.evidence: The symbols are drawn from the Old Testament, not coded predictions; seven churches stand for the whole Church; the book's call is to endure (1:9; 13:10).

debate.agree: All agree that the book centres on the risen Christ, and that it was meant to give courage to Christians under pressure.

look.why: Titian and his workshop painted John on Patmos in about 1553–55 for a ceiling in Venice, which is why we look up at him from below. You may have seen it in 'The whole story'; it is used again here because it is exactly this moment: John on his island, turning to the vision.
points: We look up from far below at an older man, Saint John, half crouching on a rocky ledge, both hands raised with palms up.
He turns his head back to gaze up at the clouds; he has a short, curly white beard and wears a rose-pink tunic with crimson drapery billowing round him.
On the ledge beside him lie a book with a scarlet-red cover and a brown eagle, its wings slightly lifted and its mouth open.
Above, in a bank of silvery grey clouds lit with pale yellow, a man with a long white beard in a plum-purple robe raises his right hand.
Six winged, nude young children nestle near him or flutter among the clouds.

music.why: Olivier Messiaen wrote his Quartet for the End of Time in a German prisoner-of-war camp, inspired by the angel of Revelation 10, and it was first played there in January 1941: an apocalypse written, like John's, by a prisoner.

think.why: Apocalypse is a way of speaking about suffering: what Christians believe about it, in short.

learn.why: God's name at the opening of Revelation: the beginning and the end of the story.

check.q: What does the Greek word apokalypsis mean?
options: Destruction
The end of the world
Judgement
Unveiling or revelation
check.why: It means 'uncovering': the curtain pulled back on the hidden world and the future.

check.q: Why does it matter that Revelation is addressed to seven real churches?
options: Because there were only seven churches in the world
Because the number seven predicts the date of the end
Because any reading that makes it meaningless to its first readers is unlikely to be right
Because it proves the apostle John wrote it
check.why: It is first a letter to people in the first century, about their situation; seven also stands for the whole Church.

check.q: In Revelation 1, the risen Jesus has hair 'white as white wool'. What is John saying?
options: That Jesus was old when he died
That Jesus is an angel
Nothing: it is decoration
That he is giving Jesus the features of God, the Ancient of Days of Daniel 7
check.why: In Daniel 7:9 it is God whose hair is like pure wool. Apocalypse says in pictures what the creeds later say in words.

check.q: Which is the best explanation of the number 666 in Revelation 13?
options: It has no meaning
Many scholars think it spells 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters, and some manuscripts read 616, the Latin form
It stands for the year the world will end
It is a code for a world leader in our own time
check.why: Letters doubled as numbers; Nero had killed Christians in Rome in AD 64.

check.q: What is the main difference between 1 Enoch 1 and Revelation 1?
options: Revelation does not mention the coming of God
Enoch is written in the name of a hero of long ago; John writes in his own name, and his centre is a crucified man alive for ever
Enoch is about judgement and Revelation is not
Enoch was written after Revelation
check.why: Enoch is pseudepigraphal and centres on God's coming; Revelation is signed by John and centres on Christ's death and life.

check.q: Which reading of Revelation holds that it is mostly about events still to come just before Christ returns?
options: Preterist
Futurist
Idealist
Historicist
check.why: Futurists read most of chapters 4–22 as still to come; preterists read it as about the first century.

tutorial.question: How should the book of Revelation be read?
tutorial.approach: Start with what kind of writing it is: an apocalypse, a prophecy and a letter. Explain how its symbols work, using Revelation 1 and 666 as examples. Set out the four main readings and judge their strengths and weaknesses. End with what you think the book was for, then and now.

Uses the letters to seven real churches to anchor the book in the first century.
Shows how Revelation's images come from the Old Testament, with an example.
Sets out preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist readings fairly.
Compares Revelation with 1 Enoch to show what is distinctive.
Explains the centrality of the slain and risen Christ.

reading.title: The Theology of the Book of Revelation
