sessions.practice: Live it this week: apocalypse pulls back the curtain on who really rules. Each evening, look at one news story that frightened or angered you and write one line: what would it look like if God, not this power, had the last word?
sessions.reflect: Who or what seems to rule your world? What would it mean to see it 'unveiled'?
takeaways: 'Apocalypse' means unveiling: a kind of writing, like Daniel and 1 Enoch, that shows the powerless who really rules history.
Revelation is a letter from a prisoner named John to seven real churches, written in Old Testament symbols and numbers.
Its centre is the crucified and risen Christ, who holds the keys of death, and its hope is not escape but a renewed world.

sessions.title: Stay awake
sessions.line: Jesus's disciples admire the Temple's great stones. He tells them every stone will fall, and that the Son of Man will come. Then he tells them not to calculate, but to watch.
sessions.plain: A few days before his death, Jesus's disciples admired the huge stones of the Temple in Jerusalem. He told them it would be torn down, and then gave his longest speech about the future: wars, persecution, false messiahs, the sun darkened, and 'the Son of Man coming in clouds'. Forty years later the Romans destroyed the Temple. But is the speech about that, about the end of the world, or both? And what did Jesus want his followers to do about it? His answer is one word, repeated four times: watch.
sessions.why: The last session taught us how apocalyptic writing works: images drawn from the Old Testament, cosmic language for historical events, and hope for people under pressure. Now we can read the one long apocalyptic speech of Jesus himself, in Mark 13, and see what he said about the end and what he refused to say.
answers: Did Jesus predict the destruction of the Temple?
What is the Second Coming?
Is Mark 13 about AD 70, the end of the world, or both?
Did Jesus tell us when the end would come?
sessions.finding: Jesus warned of the Temple's fall and of a coming of the Son of Man, but he refused to give a date: he told his followers to watch, not to calculate.

paras: In the first session the prophets promised a new creation and Daniel promised the resurrection. In the second we learned to read apocalypse: a curtain pulled back, in pictures taken from the Old Testament, to give courage to people under pressure.

Now we come to Jesus. His message began with the words 'The time is fulfilled, and God's Kingdom is at hand!' (Mark 1:15). The 'Kingdom of God' meant God's rule finally coming on earth, as the prophets had promised. In Mark 13, a few days before his death, he speaks about how that will come.
background.key: Jesus announced that God's kingdom was at hand; in Mark 13 he speaks of how it will come.

background.h: Where we are in the story
paras: It is the last week of Jesus's life, in Jerusalem, at Passover, around AD 30. If you have taken 'The last week', you followed his entry into the city and his action in the Temple courts, overturning the tables of the money-changers (Mark 11). Mark 12 is a series of arguments with the Temple's leaders.

The Temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. King Herod the Great had begun rebuilding it in about 20 BC, on a vast platform; some of its stones weighed hundreds of tonnes, and parts of the platform's western wall still stand. It was the centre of Jewish life, the place where heaven and earth met. To say it would be destroyed was close to blasphemy. At Jesus's trial witnesses claimed he had said he would destroy it (Mark 14:58).
background.key: Around AD 30, in his last week, Jesus has confronted the Temple; Herod's Temple was huge, and to foretell its fall was shocking.

paras: In AD 66 the Jews of Judea revolted against Rome. After four years of war, the Roman general Titus besieged Jerusalem, and in August AD 70 the Temple was burned and the city destroyed. The Jewish historian Josephus, who watched the siege from the Roman side, describes famine, mass crucifixions and the Temple in flames; if you have taken 'One root, two branches', you read his account there. The Arch of Titus in Rome, still standing, shows Roman soldiers carrying off the great lampstand from the Temple.

The early Christian historian Eusebius, writing around 325, says the Christians of Jerusalem left the city before the war, after a warning, and settled in Pella across the Jordan (Church History III.5.3). Historians debate how reliable that report is.

Jesus's last week in Jerusalem; Mark 13
Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians
The Jewish revolt against Rome begins
Most scholars date Mark's Gospel to these years
Titus destroys Jerusalem and the Temple
The Arch of Titus is set up in Rome

background.key: In AD 70, after a four-year revolt, Rome destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple; Mark was written around those years.

paras: The main reading is the whole of Mark 13, Jesus's speech on the Mount of Olives, often called 'the little apocalypse'. We read it in three parts: the warnings, the 'abomination' and the coming of the Son of Man, and the call to watch.

The comparison is the parable of the ten bridesmaids in Matthew 25, which Matthew places just after his version of the same speech. It shows what 'watch' means in a story, and it is the parable behind Bach's cantata in this session's music.
background.key: Mark 13 in three parts, then Matthew 25's parable of the bridesmaids, which shows what watching means.

before: What two things do the disciples ask in verse 4? Does Jesus answer both?
Find every time Jesus says 'watch' or 'be careful'. What does he seem most worried about?
Does Jesus say when the end will come? Compare verses 30 and 32.
sessions.readWhy: Jesus's longest speech about the future, read in three parts: warnings, the coming of the Son of Man, and the call to watch.

paras: As he went out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Teacher, see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings!”
Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone on another, which will not be thrown down.”
As he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked him privately,
“Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign that these things are all about to be fulfilled?”
Jesus, answering, began to tell them, “Be careful that no one leads you astray.
For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and will lead many astray.
“When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, don’t be troubled. For those must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places. There will be famines and troubles. These things are the beginning of birth pains.
But watch yourselves, for they will deliver you up to councils. You will be beaten in synagogues. You will stand before rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them.
The Good News must first be preached to all the nations.

When they lead you away and deliver you up, don’t be anxious beforehand, or premeditate what you will say, but say whatever will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.
“Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child. Children will rise up against parents, and cause them to be put to death.
You will be hated by all men for my name’s sake, but he who endures to the end will be saved.
But when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing where it ought not” (let the reader understand), “then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains,
and let him who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter in, to take anything out of his house.
Let him who is in the field not return back to take his cloak.
But woe to those who are with child and to those who nurse babies in those days!
Pray that your flight won’t be in the winter.
For in those days there will be oppression, such as there has not been the like from the beginning of the creation which God created until now, and never will be.
Unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the chosen ones, whom he picked out, he shortened the days.
Then if anyone tells you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or, ‘Look, there!’ don’t believe it.
For there will arise false christs and false prophets, and will show signs and wonders, that they may lead astray, if possible, even the chosen ones.
But you watch.
“Behold, I have told you all things beforehand.
But in those days, after that oppression, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light,
the stars will be falling from the sky, and the powers that are in the heavens will be shaken.
Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.
Then he will send out his angels, and will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of the sky.
“Now from the fig tree, learn this parable. When the branch has now become tender, and produces its leaves, you know that the summer is near;
even so you also, when you see these things coming to pass, know that it is near, at the doors.
Most certainly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things happen.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
Watch, keep alert, and pray; for you don’t know when the time is.
“It is like a man, traveling to another country, having left his house, and given authority to his servants, and to each one his work, and also commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch.
Watch therefore, for you don’t know when the lord of the house is coming, whether at evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning;
lest coming suddenly he might find you sleeping.
What I tell you, I tell all: Watch.”

parts.title: Not one stone on another
parts.context: Jerusalem, around AD 30, a few days before Jesus's death. He leaves the Temple and crosses the Kidron valley to the Mount of Olives, which looks straight across at the Temple. Four of his first disciples ask him privately what he meant.

commentary.on: Teacher, see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings!
commentary.text: The disciples are country men from Galilee, and the Temple was built to impress. Some of its stones were over ten metres long.

commentary.on: There will not be left here one stone on another
commentary.text: A plain prediction of total destruction. Forty years later it happened. Sceptical scholars argue that Mark wrote after AD 70 and put the prophecy into Jesus's mouth; others point out that prophets had foretold the Temple's fall before (Micah 3:12; Jeremiah 26), and that a Jewish prophet called Jesus son of Ananias did the same in the 60s, according to Josephus (Jewish War VI.5.3). It is not hard to believe Jesus said it.

commentary.on: Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign
commentary.text: Two questions: when, and what sign? The rest of the speech is Jesus's answer, and it is not quite the answer they wanted.

commentary.on: Be careful that no one leads you astray.
commentary.text: The first words of the answer are not a timetable but a warning. The greatest danger is not the catastrophe but being deceived by those who claim to know.

commentary.on: When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, don't be troubled. For those must happen, but the end is not yet.
commentary.text: This verse alone should have stopped many confident predictions. Wars and earthquakes are not signs that the end is here. They are 'the beginning of birth pains': the world groaning, as it always has, towards something new.

commentary.on: The Good News must first be preached to all the nations.
commentary.text: Before the end, the message goes to every nation. History has a task to complete. This one verse turns the waiting into mission.

commentary.on: he who endures to the end will be saved
commentary.text: Not escaping suffering but enduring it. Jesus promises persecution, arrests and betrayal within families, and asks for faithfulness.

parts.title: The abomination, and the coming of the Son of Man
parts.context: Jesus now moves to the crisis itself, using phrases from Daniel and the prophets that his hearers would have recognised.

commentary.on: when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet
commentary.text: In Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11) the 'abomination' was the pagan altar Antiochus IV set up in the Temple in 167 BC, an object so horrifying that it empties the holy place. Jesus warns of something like it again. Mark's aside, 'let the reader understand', suggests that his first readers could see it coming.

commentary.on: then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains
commentary.text: Very practical, local advice: Judea, housetops, fields, winter. This is about a real war in a real country, not the end of the universe. It fits the Roman siege of Jerusalem.

commentary.on: Look, here is the Christ!
commentary.text: Josephus describes many would-be deliverers in the years before AD 70. Jesus's followers are not to be taken in by anyone who claims to be him.

commentary.on: the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light
commentary.text: This is the language of the prophets for the fall of empires: Isaiah used it of Babylon (13:10) and of Edom (34:4). Cosmic language for an earth-shaking event in history, as the last session taught us. It may also point beyond history, to the end.

commentary.on: Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.
commentary.text: Daniel 7:13 again: 'one like a son of man' coming 'with the clouds of the sky'. In Daniel he comes to God, to receive the kingdom. Christians have mostly read this verse as Jesus's return to earth, the Second Coming. Some scholars, such as N. T. Wright, read it as his vindication: the fall of the Temple would show that God had given him the kingdom. The verse is at the centre of the debate.

commentary.on: he will send out his angels, and will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds
commentary.text: The end is a gathering, not a scattering. The prophets promised that God would gather his scattered people (Isaiah 43:5–6). Here the gathering is from the whole earth.

parts.title: Watch
parts.context: Jesus ends with two short parables, a saying about timing and a command.

commentary.on: When the branch has now become tender, and produces its leaves, you know that the summer is near
commentary.text: The fig tree in Israel loses its leaves in winter; when they come back, summer is close. Signs can be read, but only roughly: you know the season, not the day.

commentary.on: this generation will not pass away until all these things happen
commentary.text: The hardest verse in the chapter. 'This generation' usually means the people then alive. If 'all these things' includes the coming of the Son of Man and the end of the world, Jesus seems to have been wrong. If it means the fall of the Temple, it came true within forty years. The fifth session of this journey, still to come, faces this objection at full strength.

commentary.on: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
commentary.text: An astonishing claim. In Isaiah 40:8 it is 'the word of our God' that 'stands forever'. Jesus says it of his own words.

commentary.on: But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
commentary.text: Here Jesus refuses to set a date and says that he himself does not know it. Every person in history who has set a date for the end has had to ignore this verse. It also puzzled the Church Fathers, the great Christian teachers of the first centuries: how could the Son not know? Many answered that he did not know it in his human nature.

commentary.on: Watch, keep alert, and pray; for you don't know when the time is.
commentary.text: This is the point of the whole speech. The disciples asked 'when?'; Jesus answers 'watch'. Not calculation but readiness.

commentary.on: given authority to his servants, and to each one his work
commentary.text: Watching is not staring at the sky. The servants have work to do while the master is away. Waiting for the end, in Jesus's picture, means being faithful in your work now.

commentary.on: What I tell you, I tell all: Watch.
commentary.text: The last word of Jesus's teaching in Mark before the passion begins. It is said to four disciples on a hillside and, Mark insists, to all his readers.

paras: “Then the Kingdom of Heaven will be like ten virgins, who took their lamps, and went out to meet the bridegroom.
Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
Those who were foolish, when they took their lamps, took no oil with them,
but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
Now while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept.
But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’
Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’
But the wise answered, saying, ‘What if there isn’t enough for us and you? You go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’
While they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.
Afterward the other virgins also came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’
But he answered, ‘Most certainly I tell you, I don’t know you.’
Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming.

parts.title: The bridegroom is coming
parts.context: In a village wedding of Jesus's time, the bridegroom came at night to the bride's home and led a procession, with lamps, to his own family's house for the feast. Young women of the village went out to meet him. The 'virgins' are bridesmaids.

commentary.on: Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
commentary.text: The two groups look the same from outside. All have lamps, all are waiting, all fall asleep. The difference only shows when the moment comes.

commentary.on: while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept
commentary.text: The parable expects a delay. Matthew was writing when the first generation of Christians was dying; the parable tells them not to be surprised that the bridegroom is late.

commentary.on: Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.
commentary.text: Readiness cannot be borrowed at the last minute. Many interpreters have taken the oil as the good works or the faith that only a life can build up.

commentary.on: those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut
commentary.text: The end in this story is a wedding feast, the prophets' picture of joy (Isaiah 25:6). Being shut out is the tragedy. The parable is a warning, but what is being missed is a party.

commentary.on: Watch therefore, for you don't know the day nor the hour
commentary.text: The same word as Mark 13: watch. The parable makes it concrete: keep your lamp filled.

compare.why: Matthew sets this parable just after his version of the same speech. It shows what 'watch' means in a story: not knowing the hour, but being ready for it.
compare.title: The wise and foolish bridesmaids

paras: The New Testament's most common word for Christ's return is parousia, Greek for 'presence' or 'arrival'. It was used for the visit of an emperor or governor to a city, when citizens went out to meet him. Christians took it for the coming of Christ in glory, which they also called 'the day of the Lord'.

All the historic creeds teach it. The Apostles' Creed says 'from thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead', 'quick' meaning living. The Nicene Creed adds 'with glory' and 'whose kingdom shall have no end'. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches all affirm it. What they mean by it, and how much detail they claim to know, varies a great deal.

At its simplest, the Second Coming means this: the story will not just stop or fade away. The one who came in weakness, and was crucified, will be seen as he really is, and everything will be put right in his presence.
sections.key: The parousia, Christ's coming in glory, is in all the creeds; at its simplest it means the story ends with Christ seen as he is and all put right.

rows: Mostly the last days and Christ's return
The cosmic language; the coming of the Son of Man
The local details: Judea, housetops, winter; and 'this generation'
Mostly the fall of Jerusalem; the 'coming' is Jesus's vindication
The disciples' question is about the Temple; it came true within a generation
Seems to empty the Second Coming from a key text
The fall of the Temple as a near event and a picture of the final end
Prophets often saw a near crisis and the final day together
Hard to tell where one ends and the other begins
table.note: Most readers, ancient and modern, take some form of the third view.

paras: Mark 13 is one of the most argued-over chapters in the Bible. There are three main readings.
sections.key: Mark 13 has been read as about the end of the world, about AD 70, or both; most take some form of 'both'.

paras: Why might a prophet speak of two events as one? A common illustration is a range of mountains seen from far away: two peaks look side by side, though miles of valley lie between them. Old Testament prophets often spoke of a coming disaster, such as the fall of Babylon, in the language of the end of all things.

Read that way, Mark 13 answers the disciples' question about the Temple, and uses its fall as a window on the end. The near event shows what the final one will be like: sudden, judging, and a gathering of God's people. Many Church Fathers read it so, and so do many modern scholars.
Sceptics reply that this is a convenient way to save a failed prediction. That objection is real, and it deserves its own session.
sections.key: Prophets often saw a near crisis and the final end together; read so, the Temple's fall is a window on the end, though sceptics call this convenient.

paras: Mark 13:32 is remarkable. It is not the kind of saying the early Church would invent: it says Jesus did not know something. Matthew keeps it (24:36); Luke leaves it out. Arius, in the fourth century, used it to argue that the Son was less than the Father. Athanasius replied that Christ, being truly human, did not know it in his human mind, though he knew it as God (Against the Arians III.42–46).

Whatever we make of that, the saying cuts off every attempt to set a date. William Miller, an American Baptist preacher, worked out from Daniel that Christ would return in 1843, then on 22 October 1844. Thousands sold their farms; when nothing happened, it became known as the Great Disappointment. Many others have set dates since, and every one has passed.
Jesus's own teaching was the opposite: the end is certain, its date is unknown, and so the right response is not calculation but faithfulness.
sections.key: Jesus said not even the Son knew the day; every date-setter, like William Miller in 1844, has had to ignore it.

paras: 'Watch' in Mark 13 is the opposite of sleep, not the opposite of work. The servants in the last parable each have their work. Paul tells the Thessalonians, who had stopped working because they thought the end was near, that anyone who will not work should not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

So the Church has understood watching as a way of living. The monks kept vigils at night, praying the psalms before dawn. Advent, the four weeks before Christmas, begins each year with the readings of Mark 13 and the parables of watching: the Church year starts by looking to the end. In 1780, when a sudden darkness fell over New England and members of the Connecticut legislature thought the Day of Judgement had come and wanted to adjourn, Abraham Davenport is said to have replied that if it was, he wished to be found doing his duty, and asked for candles.
That is what Jesus asked: not to know the hour, but to be found doing your work.
sections.key: Watching means faithful work and prayer, not sky-gazing: Advent begins with Mark 13, and Davenport asked for candles to keep working.

sections.h: Prophecy and the date of the Gospels
paras: Mark 13 matters to an argument about when the Gospels were written. If Jesus could not have foretold the Temple's fall, then any Gospel that contains the prediction must have been written after AD 70. Many scholars date Mark to around 70 for this and other reasons.

Others reply that the reasoning assumes what it sets out to prove, and point to a detail. Mark's version is vague: 'the abomination of desolation', a phrase from Daniel, and flight to the mountains. Luke's version, which most scholars date after 70, is far more specific: 'when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies' (Luke 21:20), and 'they will fall by the edge of the sword, and will be led captive into all the nations' (21:24). If Mark had known how the siege went, they ask, why did he not say so? And Mark's warning to pray that the flight would not be in winter fits poorly with what happened: the Temple fell in August.
The evidence does not settle the date. But it does show that Mark 13 reads more like a warning given before the event than a description written after it.
sections.key: Some date Mark after AD 70 because of the prediction; others note Mark is vaguer than Luke 21, which suggests a warning given before the event.

paras: Jesus's warning against people who say 'I am he' was not abstract. Josephus describes several leaders in the decades after Jesus who gathered followers with promises of deliverance. A man called Theudas led a crowd to the Jordan around AD 45, promising to part the river; the Roman governor's cavalry killed him (Antiquities 20.5.1; compare Acts 5:36). A man known as 'the Egyptian' led a crowd to the Mount of Olives around AD 55, promising that the walls of Jerusalem would fall at his command; the governor Felix attacked them (Antiquities 20.8.6; Jewish War II.13.5; compare Acts 21:38). During the siege itself, Josephus says, a false prophet led people into the Temple courts to await signs of deliverance, and they died in the flames (Jewish War VI.5.2).

Against all of them, Jesus's advice is the same: do not believe it, and do not run after them. It is the advice that every later generation, offered a leader who claims to know when the end will come, has needed to hear.
sections.key: Josephus records would-be deliverers, such as Theudas and 'the Egyptian', before AD 70; Jesus's warning was concrete, and remains needed.

refs: Josephus, Jewish War VI.5.3 (Jesus son of Ananias); VI.4–5 (the burning of the Temple). Eusebius, Church History III.5.3 (the flight to Pella). Athanasius, Against the Arians III.42–46.
N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God (1996), chapter 8; R. T. France, The Gospel of Mark (NIGTC, 2002); Adela Yarbro Collins, Mark (Hermeneia, 2007); Dale C. Allison, Constructing Jesus (2010).

On William Miller: David L. Rowe, God's Strange Work: William Miller and the End of the World (2008). On Davenport and the Dark Day of 19 May 1780: Timothy Dwight's account, retold in John Greenleaf Whittier's poem 'Abraham Davenport'.

debate.question: Is Mark 13 about AD 70 or the end of the world?

positions.name: Mainly AD 70
positions.who: N. T. Wright; R. T. France (on 13:24–31); many preterist readers
positions.view: The disciples asked about the Temple, and Jesus answered. The cosmic language is the prophets' way of describing the fall of a power, and the 'coming of the Son of Man' is Daniel's picture of his vindication. 'This generation' then means exactly what it says. The real end is spoken of only from verse 32.
positions.evidence: The local details (Judea, housetops, winter); Isaiah 13:10 used of Babylon; Daniel 7:13 where the Son of Man comes to God; the Temple fell within forty years.

positions.name: Mainly the end
positions.who: Many traditional readers; many modern scholars, such as Dale Allison and Adela Yarbro Collins
positions.view: The speech moves from the war to the final coming of the Son of Man to gather the elect from the ends of the earth. That did not happen in AD 70. Jesus, like other Jewish prophets of his day, expected the end soon after the Temple's fall.
positions.evidence: Angels gathering the elect from the whole earth (13:27); Paul and the earliest Christians expected Christ's return from heaven (1 Thessalonians 4:16); Matthew joins the Temple's fall and 'the end of the age' (24:3).

positions.name: Both, seen together
positions.who: Many Church Fathers; many Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant commentators
positions.view: Like the prophets, Jesus saw the near judgement on Jerusalem and the final judgement together. The first came true within a generation; the second is still awaited, and the first is its pledge.
positions.evidence: The prophets' foreshortening; the shift at verse 32 from 'these things' to 'that day'; the command to watch, which covers both.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus foretold the fall of the Temple, refused to give a date for the end, and commanded his followers to watch.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of the wise and foolish bridesmaids, of the fall of the Temple or of the coming of the Son of Man that is free to use here, and we do not use a stand-in.

music.why: 'Sleepers, wake!': Bach's cantata of 1731 on the parable of the wise and foolish bridesmaids, built on Philipp Nicolai's hymn of 1599. Listen for the watchmen's call and the bridegroom's arrival.

think.why: What Christians believe about who Jesus is, including the one who will come again.

learn.why: The point of Jesus's whole speech about the end, in one line.

check.q: The disciples ask 'when?' What is the main point of Jesus's answer?
options: He says the end will never come
He warns them not to be deceived, refuses to give the date, and tells them to watch
He gives them a precise timetable of signs
He tells them to flee Jerusalem at once
check.why: 'No one knows... Watch': the answer to 'when?' is readiness, not calculation.

check.q: Why do many scholars think verses 14–20 are about a real war in Judea?
options: Because of the local, practical details: Judea, the mountains, housetops, fields and winter
Because they are in poetry
Because they mention Rome by name
Because they quote Josephus
check.why: Advice to flee to the mountains before winter fits the siege of Jerusalem, not the end of the universe.

check.q: Why does 'the sun will be darkened' not have to mean a literal astronomical event?
options: Because Jesus said it was a parable
Because the prophets used such language for the fall of empires, as Isaiah did of Babylon
Because eclipses did not happen in the ancient world
Because the sun is mentioned only once in the Bible
check.why: Isaiah 13:10 uses it of Babylon's fall: cosmic language for earth-shaking events in history.

check.q: In Daniel 7:13, where does 'one like a son of man' come 'with the clouds'?
options: To Jerusalem, to destroy the Temple
To God, the Ancient of Days, to receive a kingdom
To Babylon
Down to earth
check.why: That is why some scholars read Mark 13:26 as vindication rather than return; most Christians have read it as the Second Coming.

check.q: What does Mark 13:32 ('not even the Son') rule out?
options: Belief that Jesus was human
Any attempt to calculate the date of the end
Belief in the Second Coming
The fall of the Temple
check.why: If the Son did not know the day, no one can calculate it; William Miller's 1844 prediction ignored this.

check.q: According to the parable of the servants (13:34) and the bridesmaids, what does 'watching' involve?
options: Sleeping until the bridegroom comes
Studying the signs to set a date
Leaving work to wait for the end
Being faithful in the work you have been given, ready at any time
check.why: Each servant has his work; the wise have oil in their lamps. Watching is a way of living now.

tutorial.question: Did Jesus predict the end of the world?
tutorial.approach: Read Mark 13 carefully. Set out what Jesus clearly predicted (the fall of the Temple), what is disputed (the coming of the Son of Man and 'this generation'), and what he refused to predict (the day). Weigh the three readings, using Daniel and the prophets. End with what he asked his followers to do.
strong: Distinguishes the two questions in 13:4 and the fall of the Temple from the final end.
Uses the local details of 13:14–20 and AD 70 as evidence.
Explains the background of Daniel 7:13 and prophetic cosmic language.
Weighs the AD 70, end-of-the-world and 'both' readings fairly.
Gives due weight to 13:32 and the command to watch.
Recognises that 13:30 is a real difficulty.

reading.author: Tom Wright
reading.title: Mark for Everyone
reading.why: A short, clear commentary for ordinary readers.

reading.author: R. T. France
reading.title: The Gospel of Mark (NIGTC)
reading.why: A careful commentary that reads most of Mark 13 as about AD 70.

reading.author: Adela Yarbro Collins
reading.title: Mark (Hermeneia)
reading.why: A major commentary that reads Mark 13 as apocalyptic prophecy of the end.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Jesus's servants each have their work while the master is away. Choose one task you have been putting off that someone is relying on you for, and do it this week as if he might come back today.
sessions.reflect: If you knew the world would end next year, what would you stop doing, and what would you keep doing? What does your answer say about your life now?
takeaways: In Mark 13 Jesus foretold the fall of the Temple, which happened in AD 70, and the coming of the Son of Man in Daniel's words.
The speech can be read as about AD 70, the end, or both; 'this generation' is its hardest verse.
Jesus refused to give a date ('not even the Son' knows) and told his followers to watch: to be found faithful in their work.

sessions.title: The hope of the dead
sessions.line: A young church grieves its first dead. Paul writes the earliest Christian letter we have: they are asleep, they will rise, and the whole creation is waiting with them.
sessions.plain: Within twenty years of Jesus's death, Christians in the Greek city of Thessalonica were burying their first members, and they were afraid the dead had missed out. Paul wrote to comfort them: the dead will rise when Christ comes. In later letters he says what happens in between, and that the whole of creation, not only humans, is waiting to be set free. This session asks what Paul hoped for, what the 'rapture' is, and whether Christians hope for heaven or for something larger.
sessions.why: The last session read Jesus's warnings: the Temple would fall, the Son of Man would come, and no one knows the hour. The first Christians lived with that hope, and very soon they had to ask what it meant for those who died before the end. Paul's answers, written within a generation of Jesus, are the earliest Christian teaching on death that we have.
answers: What happens to Christians when they die?
What is the rapture?
Do Christians hope for heaven or for a new creation?
What will happen to the world itself?
sessions.finding: Paul's hope is resurrection with Christ and the renewal of the whole creation, not a soul floating free; 'heaven' is where the dead wait with Christ, not the end of the story.

paras: The prophets promised a new creation and the resurrection of the dead. Apocalyptic writing unveiled God's rule behind the empires. Jesus warned of the Temple's fall and the coming of the Son of Man, and told his followers to watch.

Then something happened that changed the hope. His followers said that Jesus himself had been raised from the dead, three days after his crucifixion. If you have taken 'The last week', you weighed the evidence for that claim. For our question, what matters is this: Jews had expected the resurrection of all the righteous at the end of history. The first Christians said it had begun early, with one man. Paul calls him 'the first fruits' (1 Corinthians 15:20): the first sheaf of a harvest still to come.
background.key: The first Christians believed the resurrection expected at the end had begun with Jesus, 'the first fruits' of the harvest.

paras: Paul was a Jew from Tarsus, in what is now southern Turkey, a Pharisee by training and so a believer in the resurrection of the dead. He persecuted the first Christians until, around AD 33, he became convinced that he had seen the risen Jesus. He spent the next thirty years founding churches around the eastern Mediterranean and writing them letters, thirteen of which are in the New Testament (scholars agree he wrote at least seven of them, including all three we read here). He was executed in Rome, probably in the mid-60s.
If you have taken 'The first Christians', you followed his journeys. Here we read him on one subject: what Christians hope for when they die.
background.key: Paul, a Pharisee from Tarsus who believed in the resurrection, became a Christian around AD 33 and wrote letters to his churches until his death in Rome in the 60s.

paras: Thessalonica (modern Thessaloniki, in northern Greece) was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia. Paul founded a church there around AD 49 or 50, but had to leave after a few weeks. A few months later he wrote 1 Thessalonians from Corinth, which makes it most likely the oldest Christian writing that survives.

2 Corinthians was written around AD 55 or 56, to the church in Corinth, after Paul had faced what he calls a deadly danger in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Romans was written around AD 57, from Corinth, to a church he had not yet visited.

timeline.text: Jesus's crucifixion and resurrection
Paul's conversion
Paul founds the church at Thessalonica
1 Thessalonians, probably the oldest Christian writing that survives
2 Corinthians
Romans
Paul executed in Rome

background.key: 1 Thessalonians (c. AD 50) is probably the oldest Christian writing; 2 Corinthians (c. 55) and Romans (c. 57) follow.

paras: The main reading has three parts, from three letters. In 1 Thessalonians Paul answers a grieving church: what about our dead? In 2 Corinthians, after nearly dying himself, he says what happens to a Christian at death. In Romans he widens the view to the whole creation. (Paul's great chapter on the resurrection body, 1 Corinthians 15, you may have read in 'Death and hope' or 'The last week'.)
The comparison is from Plato, the Greek philosopher whose idea of the immortal soul shaped how many Christians later pictured heaven. Setting him beside Paul shows how different the two hopes are.
background.key: Three letters: the dead will rise (1 Thessalonians), what happens at death (2 Corinthians), the whole creation set free (Romans); then Plato on the soul.

before: What were the Thessalonians afraid of? What does Paul tell them to do with his words?
In 2 Corinthians 5, does Paul want to be 'unclothed', free of a body, or 'clothed'?
In Romans 8, who else is groaning and waiting, besides Christians?
sessions.readWhy: Paul on the hope of the dead, in three letters: they will rise, they are with the Lord, and creation itself will be set free.

paras: But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will in no way precede those who have fallen asleep.
For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and with God’s trumpet. The dead in Christ will rise first,
then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord forever.
Therefore comfort one another with these words.
But concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need that anything be written to you.
For you yourselves know well that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night.
For when they are saying, “Peace and safety,” then sudden destruction will come on them, like birth pains on a pregnant woman. Then they will in no way escape.
But you, brothers, aren’t in darkness, that the day should overtake you like a thief.
You are all children of light and children of the day. We don’t belong to the night, nor to darkness,
so then let’s not sleep, as the rest do, but let’s watch and be sober.
For those who sleep, sleep in the night; and those who are drunk are drunk in the night.
But since we belong to the day, let’s be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet, the hope of salvation.
For God didn’t appoint us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,
who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him.
Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.
For we know that if the earthly house of our tent is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens.
For most certainly in this we groan, longing to be clothed with our habitation which is from heaven,
if indeed being clothed, we will not be found naked.
For indeed we who are in this tent do groan, being burdened, not that we desire to be unclothed, but that we desire to be clothed, that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
Now he who made us for this very thing is God, who also gave to us the down payment of the Spirit.
Therefore we are always confident and know that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord;
for we walk by faith, not by sight.
We are courageous, I say, and are willing rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord.
Therefore also we make it our aim, whether at home or absent, to be well pleasing to him.
For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ that each one may receive the things in the body according to what he has done, whether good or bad.
For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.
For the creation waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed.
For the creation was subjected to vanity, not of its own will, but because of him who subjected it, in hope
that the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.
For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now.
Not only so, but ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body.
For we were saved in hope, but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for that which he sees?
But if we hope for that which we don’t see, we wait for it with patience.

parts.title: Those who have fallen asleep
parts.context: Corinth, around AD 50. Timothy has just come back from Thessalonica with news: the young church is holding firm, but some of its members have died, and the others are afraid that the dead will miss the coming of the Lord.

commentary.on: concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don't grieve like the rest, who have no hope
commentary.text: Paul does not say 'don't grieve'. He says don't grieve 'like the rest'. Ancient tombstones often say the opposite of hope; one common Latin epitaph read, in effect, 'I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care.' Christian grief is real grief, with hope in it. 'Asleep' was the Christians' word for their dead, which is why their burial grounds came to be called cemeteries, from the Greek for 'sleeping place'.

commentary.on: For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
commentary.text: The whole argument rests on one fact. If Jesus rose, those who belong to him will rise. The resurrection of Jesus is not only something that happened to him; it is the pattern for everyone united to him.

commentary.on: we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord
commentary.text: Paul writes 'we': he seems to expect to be alive when Christ comes. Later letters show him facing the likelihood of his own death first (2 Corinthians 5; Philippians 1:21–23). This 'we' is part of the evidence in the next session's objection, still to come.

commentary.on: For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and with God's trumpet.
commentary.text: This is apocalyptic language, the kind we learned to read in the second session: a shout, an archangel, a trumpet, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). Whatever else it is, it is not quiet or secret. The whole world hears it.

commentary.on: will be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air
commentary.text: 'Caught up' in the Latin Bible is rapiemur, from which comes the English word 'rapture'. The word for 'meet' (apantēsis) was used when the citizens of a city went out to meet a visiting emperor and escorted him back into the city. Read that way, Christians do not go up to stay in the sky; they go out to greet their king and come back with him to the renewed earth.

commentary.on: So we will be with the Lord forever. Therefore comfort one another with these words.
commentary.text: The goal is not a place but a person: 'with the Lord'. And the purpose of this teaching is pastoral. Paul is not drawing a timetable; he is comforting the bereaved.

parts.title: Like a thief in the night
parts.context: Paul turns from the dead to the living: when will it happen, and how should they live meanwhile?

commentary.on: the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night
commentary.text: Jesus's own picture (Matthew 24:43). Paul, like Jesus, refuses to give a date. No burglar sends a letter in advance.

commentary.on: For when they are saying, “Peace and safety,” then sudden destruction will come on them
commentary.text: 'Peace and security' was a slogan of Roman propaganda: the empire claimed to bring peace. Paul warns that the world's promises of security are not the last word.

commentary.on: You are all children of light and children of the day.
commentary.text: The 'day' is already dawning for those who belong to Christ. Christians live now as people of the morning, before the sun is fully up.

commentary.on: putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet, the hope of salvation
commentary.text: Faith, love and hope: the three virtues Paul names together (1 Corinthians 13:13). Hope is a helmet: it protects the head, the place of thoughts, from despair.

commentary.on: whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him
commentary.text: Alive or dead at his coming, it makes no difference: either way Christians 'live together with him'. That is the answer to the Thessalonians' fear.

parts.title: At home with the Lord
parts.context: Around AD 55–56. Paul has recently thought he was going to die (1:8–9). He writes about what happens if he dies before Christ comes.

commentary.on: if the earthly house of our tent is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands
commentary.text: Paul was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3). The present body is a tent, temporary; the resurrection body is a building, permanent, made by God.

commentary.on: not that we desire to be unclothed, but that we desire to be clothed, that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life
commentary.text: Here is the difference between Paul and Plato in one sentence. Paul does not want to be 'unclothed', a soul without a body. He wants to be 'further clothed', with a new body that swallows mortality up. Being bodiless is not the goal; it is something to be got through.

commentary.on: the down payment of the Spirit
commentary.text: A down payment is part of the price, paid now, guaranteeing the rest. The Spirit in Christians now is the first instalment of the life to come.

commentary.on: willing rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord
commentary.text: This is the text behind the Christian belief that the dead are 'with Christ' straight away, before the resurrection (compare Philippians 1:23). Theologians call this time between death and resurrection the 'intermediate state'. It is real, and it is good, but it is not the end.

commentary.on: For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ
commentary.text: Hope and judgement go together. The 'judgement seat' (Greek bēma) was the raised platform in a Roman city where a magistrate gave judgement; Paul had stood before one in Corinth (Acts 18:12). What people do with their bodies matters, because bodies are not thrown away.

parts.title: The whole creation groans
parts.context: Corinth, around AD 57. Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, whom he has not yet met, setting out his whole message. In chapter 8 he describes life in the Spirit, and then, in these verses, widens the view to the whole universe.

commentary.on: the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed
commentary.text: Paul does not deny suffering; he has had plenty. He weighs it against what is coming, and the scales are not close.

commentary.on: For the creation waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed.
commentary.text: Not only humans wait. The whole created world is waiting, as on tiptoe, for what will happen to God's people. Its future is bound up with ours.

commentary.on: the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay
commentary.text: Decay, death and waste are a kind of slavery for the world, and the world itself will be set free from it. This is the prophets' new creation again. God does not throw away the world he made; he rescues it.

commentary.on: the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now
commentary.text: Birth pains, as in Jesus's words in Mark 13:8. The world's suffering is real, but it is labour, not death throes. Something is being born.

commentary.on: waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body
commentary.text: The redemption of the body, not redemption from the body. Paul's hope is the resurrection, in a renewed creation.

commentary.on: For we were saved in hope, but hope that is seen is not hope.
commentary.text: Christian hope is not optimism, the belief that things will get better by themselves. It is waiting with patience for something not yet seen, because of something already done.

paras: But when returning into herself she reflects, then she passes into the other world, the region of purity, and eternity, and immortality, and unchangeableness, which are her kindred, and with them she ever lives, when she is by herself and is not let or hindered; then she ceases from her erring ways, and being in communion with the unchanging is unchanging. And this state of the soul is called wisdom?
That is well and truly said, Socrates, he replied.
And to which class is the soul more nearly alike and akin, as far as may be inferred from this argument, as well as from the preceding one?
I think, Socrates, that, in the opinion of every one who follows the argument, the soul will be infinitely more like the unchangeable--even the most stupid person will not deny that.
And the body is more like the changing?
Yes.

Yet once more consider the matter in another light: When the soul and the body are united, then nature orders the soul to rule and govern, and the body to obey and serve. Now which of these two functions is akin to the divine? and which to the mortal? Does not the divine appear to you to be that which naturally orders and rules, and the mortal to be that which is subject and servant?
True.
And which does the soul resemble?
The soul resembles the divine, and the body the mortal--there can be no doubt of that, Socrates.

Then reflect, Cebes: of all which has been said is not this the conclusion?--that the soul is in the very likeness of the divine, and immortal, and intellectual, and uniform, and indissoluble, and unchangeable; and that the body is in the very likeness of the human, and mortal, and unintellectual, and multiform, and dissoluble, and changeable. Can this, my dear Cebes, be denied?
It cannot.
But if it be true, then is not the body liable to speedy dissolution? and is not the soul almost or altogether indissoluble?
Certainly.

And do you further observe, that after a man is dead, the body, or visible part of him, which is lying in the visible world, and is called a corpse, and would naturally be dissolved and decomposed and dissipated, is not dissolved or decomposed at once, but may remain for a for some time, nay even for a long time, if the constitution be sound at the time of death, and the season of the year favourable? For the body when shrunk and embalmed, as the manner is in Egypt, may remain almost entire through infinite ages; and even in decay, there are still some portions, such as the bones and ligaments, which are practically indestructible:--Do you agree?
Yes.

And is it likely that the soul, which is invisible, in passing to the place of the true Hades, which like her is invisible, and pure, and noble, and on her way to the good and wise God, whither, if God will, my soul is also soon to go,--that the soul, I repeat, if this be her nature and origin, will be blown away and destroyed immediately on quitting the body, as the many say? That can never be, my dear Simmias and Cebes. The truth rather is, that the soul which is pure at departing and draws after her no bodily taint, having never voluntarily during life had connection with the body, which she is ever avoiding, herself gathered into herself;--and making such abstraction her perpetual study--which means that she has been a true disciple of philosophy; and therefore has in fact been always engaged in the practice of dying? For is not philosophy the practice of death?--
Certainly--

That soul, I say, herself invisible, departs to the invisible world--to the divine and immortal and rational: thither arriving, she is secure of bliss and is released from the error and folly of men, their fears and wild passions and all other human ills, and for ever dwells, as they say of the initiated, in company with the gods. Is not this true, Cebes?
Yes, said Cebes, beyond a doubt.

parts.author: Plato
parts.title: Akin to the divine
parts.context: Athens, 399 BC. Socrates has been condemned to death and will drink poison at sunset. Plato (about 428–348 BC), his pupil, wrote this dialogue some years later, imagining his last conversation with his friends Simmias and Cebes about whether the soul survives death. This is Benjamin Jowett's translation (first published 1871). We have removed one cross-reference Jowett added to the text, '(compare Apol.)'.
parts.plain: Socrates argues that the soul is like the unseen, unchanging and divine, while the body is like the visible, changing and mortal. When the soul turns away from the senses and thinks by itself, it is at home among eternal things. So the body falls apart after death, but the soul does not. A pure soul, one that has kept itself apart from the body all its life, which is what philosophy trains it to do, goes at death to the invisible world, to be with the gods for ever.

commentary.on: then she passes into the other world, the region of purity, and eternity, and immortality, and unchangeableness, which are her kindred
commentary.text: For Plato the soul belongs by nature to 'the other world' of eternal, unchanging things. It is immortal because of what it is, not because of what God does. That is the first difference from the Bible, where life after death is God's gift.

commentary.on: The soul resembles the divine, and the body the mortal
commentary.text: The body is the lower partner, meant to obey. Christians would agree that the body should not rule; but they believed that God made the body and called it good, and that the Son of God took one.

commentary.on: the body, or visible part of him, which is lying in the visible world, and is called a corpse
commentary.text: Plato's picture: the body is left behind to decay, while the real person goes elsewhere. Paul's picture: the body is 'sown' and will be raised, transformed (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

commentary.on: having never voluntarily during life had connection with the body, which she is ever avoiding
commentary.text: For Plato, the good life is a long training to get away from the body. 'Is not philosophy the practice of death?' This shaped Christian monks and mystics deeply, and often helpfully, in their discipline. But it is not Paul's hope, which is 'not that we desire to be unclothed'.

commentary.on: That soul, I say, herself invisible, departs to the invisible world
commentary.text: Here is the hope of the soul set free: invisible, bodiless, among the gods. Many Christian hymns and paintings of heaven, with souls rising to the clouds, owe more to this passage than to Paul. The early Church Fathers kept the soul's survival but insisted, against Greek philosophers, on the resurrection of the body.

compare.author: Plato
compare.why: Plato's picture of the soul set free from the body shaped how many later Christians imagined heaven. Set it beside Paul's 'clothed, not unclothed' and see how different the two hopes are. (If you took 'Death and hope', you read the end of the same dialogue, Socrates' death; this is an earlier passage.)
compare.title: The soul departs to the invisible world

paras: The first Christian teaching on death that we have is a letter of comfort. The Thessalonians were not asking an abstract question. People they loved had died, and they feared those people had missed the coming of the Lord.

Paul's answer rests on one thing, the resurrection of Jesus. Because he rose, those who belong to him will rise. And because the dead will rise first, they have lost nothing. Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say the dead are already enjoying everything, or that grief is wrong. He says they are 'asleep', which assumes they will wake, and that Christians grieve differently, not less.

That pattern has shaped Christian funerals ever since. The 1662 Book of Common Prayer commits the body to the ground 'in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life'. It is a hope about the body, spoken over the body.
sections.key: Paul's first teaching on death comforts the grieving: because Jesus rose, the dead in Christ will rise; Christians grieve with hope, not less.

paras: Many people have heard that Christians believe in 'the rapture': one day believers will vanish, leaving cars without drivers, while the rest of the world suffers seven years of tribulation before Christ returns. This idea was popularised by the Left Behind novels (1995–2007), which sold tens of millions of copies.

It is a recent idea. It was developed in the 1830s by John Nelson Darby, a former Anglican priest who became a leader of the Plymouth Brethren, as part of a system called dispensationalism, which divides history into ages and keeps God's plans for Israel and for the Church separate. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) spread it across America.

Most Christian traditions, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and many evangelicals, reject a secret rapture before the end. Their reasons come from the text. 1 Thessalonians 4 is loud, not secret: a shout, a trumpet. It describes the resurrection and Christ's single coming, not a separate earlier one. And the word 'meet' suggests going out to welcome a king who is arriving, not leaving with him for somewhere else.
sections.key: The secret rapture comes from Darby in the 1830s and the Left Behind novels; most traditions reject it, because 1 Thessalonians 4 describes one, public coming.

paras: If the dead rise only at the end, where are they now? Paul's answer is short: 'absent from the body and at home with the Lord' (2 Corinthians 5:8); 'to depart and be with Christ, which is far better' (Philippians 1:23). Jesus tells the thief on the cross, 'today you will be with me in Paradise' (Luke 23:43). Theologians call this the intermediate state.
The traditions describe it differently, and the differences matter to many people at the graveside.

rows: The soul is judged at once; those who die in God's friendship but are not yet wholly purified are cleansed in purgatory before entering heaven
Yes: the Church prays and offers the Mass for the dead
The soul goes to a foretaste of joy or sorrow, awaiting the resurrection; purgatory as Catholics define it is not taught
Yes: memorial services for the departed are central
The believer goes straight to be with Christ, awaiting the resurrection; purgatory is rejected
Generally no, though some Anglicans and Lutherans do
'Soul sleep': the dead are unconscious until the resurrection (Seventh-day Adventists; at times Luther's own language)
table.note: All agree that the intermediate state is not the end: the resurrection is still to come.

sections.key: At death the faithful are 'with Christ' while they await the resurrection; Catholics add purgatory, Orthodox pray for the dead, most Protestants reject both.

paras: Romans 8 makes the hope as wide as the universe. The creation 'groans' and will be 'delivered from the bondage of decay'. That is the prophets' new creation, now tied to the resurrection of Christ: what happened to his body will happen to the world.

The early Church took this seriously. Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around 180, argued against those who despised matter that God would not annihilate his creation; only its present form would pass away, and the renewed earth would be the home of the raised (Against Heresies V.32–36). Thomas Aquinas, in the 1200s, held that the world would be renewed, not destroyed.

In recent decades this has become one of the roots of Christian care for the environment. If God means to rescue the material world, it is not a stage set to be thrown away when the play is over. It matters what we do with it.
sections.key: Romans 8 says the whole creation will be set free from decay; Irenaeus and Aquinas taught renewal, not destruction, and many now draw an ethic of care from it.

paras: So do Christians hope to go to heaven? Yes, and no. The New Testament does speak of heaven: treasure 'in heaven' (Matthew 6:20), 'our citizenship is in heaven' (Philippians 3:20). But 'heaven' in the Bible is God's dimension of reality, where his will is done, not mainly a place where souls go for ever. Philippians 3:20 goes on: from heaven 'we also wait for a Savior', who will transform our bodies.

The English scholar and bishop N. T. Wright puts it in a phrase: the Christian hope is not life after death but 'life after life after death'. First the dead are with Christ; then they are raised, in a renewed world. The final picture of the Bible is not people going up but the holy city 'coming down out of heaven from God' (Revelation 21:2).

C. S. Lewis imagined this differently, but to the same effect, in The Great Divorce (1945): visitors from hell find heaven so solid that its grass hurts their feet. Heaven, for Lewis, is not less real than earth but more. Both reject the picture of the soul as a wisp that floats away.
sections.key: Biblical 'heaven' is God's realm, where the dead wait with Christ; the final hope is resurrection in a renewed world, 'life after life after death'.

paras: If the dead are raised, with what body? Paul answers at length in 1 Corinthians 15, which you may have read in 'Death and hope'. In short: the raised body is the same person, but transformed, as a plant is the same life as the seed but far greater (15:36–44). It is 'imperishable', 'glorious', 'powerful' and, in Paul's word, 'spiritual', which means not made of spirit but wholly alive with God's Spirit.

The Gospels' accounts of the risen Jesus point the same way. He can be touched and he eats fish (Luke 24:39–43), yet he appears in a locked room (John 20:19) and is not at first recognised. His body bears the marks of the nails (John 20:27). That last detail mattered to the Church Fathers: the new creation does not erase the history of the old one but heals it. Augustine thought the martyrs' wounds would be seen in glory, not as disfigurements but as marks of honour (City of God XXII.19).
None of this is a description we can picture. It is a way of saying that the person who rises is really you, and really new.
sections.key: The raised body is the same person transformed, like seed and plant; the risen Jesus could be touched yet passed locked doors, and still bore his wounds.

refs: 1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:11; 2 Corinthians 1:8–9; 5:1–10; Romans 8:18–25; 1 Corinthians 15:20, 42–44; Philippians 1:21–23; 3:20–21; Luke 23:43; Matthew 6:20; 24:43; Revelation 21:2; Acts 18:3, 12.
Plato, Phaedo 79d–81a, tr. Benjamin Jowett. Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.32–36; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, Supplement q. 91.

The Book of Common Prayer (1662), The Order for the Burial of the Dead. Catechism of the Catholic Church 1030–1032 (purgatory). Council of Florence (1439) and Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563), on purgatory.

On apantēsis: Erik Peterson, 'Die Einholung des Kyrios', Zeitschrift für systematische Theologie 7 (1930); F. F. Bruce, 1 and 2 Thessalonians (1982). On the rapture: Timothy P. Weber, On the Road to Armageddon (2004); Barbara R. Rossing, The Rapture Exposed (2004).
N. T. Wright, Surprised by Hope (2008); C. S. Lewis, The Great Divorce (1945); Douglas J. Moo, 'Nature in the New Creation', Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 49 (2006).

debate.question: Will the world be renewed or replaced?

positions.name: Renewed
positions.who: Irenaeus; Thomas Aquinas; N. T. Wright; Jürgen Moltmann; most Catholic and Orthodox theology
positions.view: God will set the present creation free from decay and transform it, as he transformed Jesus's body without discarding it. The new creation is this creation healed.
positions.evidence: Romans 8:21; the risen Jesus's body bore the wounds (John 20:27); 'I am making all things new', not 'all new things' (Revelation 21:5).

positions.name: Replaced
positions.who: Some Lutheran theologians of the 1600s, such as Johann Gerhard; some evangelicals
positions.view: The present world will be destroyed by fire and a new one created. Our hope is not in this world, which is passing away.
positions.evidence: 'The earth and the works that are in it will be burned up' (2 Peter 3:10); 'the first heaven and the first earth have passed away' (Revelation 21:1).

positions.name: Transformed beyond telling
positions.who: Many biblical scholars, including Richard Bauckham
positions.view: Both kinds of language are pictures. Fire purifies as well as destroys; the old order passes but what God made is not lost. We cannot describe the result, only trust that it is this world made new.
positions.evidence: The oldest manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10 read 'will be found' or 'laid bare', not 'burned up'; Paul's seed and plant (1 Corinthians 15:37).

debate.agree: All agree that the end is God's act, that it includes the resurrection of the body, and that suffering and decay will not have the last word.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of the general resurrection or the Last Judgement that is free to use here, and its paintings of Christ's own resurrection are already used by other journeys for that subject. We do not use a stand-in.

music.why: Brahms chose his own texts for A German Requiem (1868): 'Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted', and Paul's 'we shall all be changed'. It is a requiem written to comfort the living, as Paul wrote to the Thessalonians.

think.why: The modern debate about death, the soul and resurrection, including Wright and the objection from neuroscience.

learn.why: The end of the same chapter of Romans: neither death nor anything else can separate us from God's love. You may know it already from 'Why the cross?' or 'Death and hope'.

check.q: What were the Thessalonians afraid of?
options: That Christ would never come
That they would be raptured
That the Romans would destroy their city
That their members who had died would miss the coming of the Lord
check.why: Paul writes so that they do not grieve 'like the rest': the dead in Christ will rise first.

check.q: What does the Greek word for 'meet' in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 suggest about the 'rapture'?
options: That the meeting will be secret
That, as citizens went out to welcome a visiting ruler and escort him back, believers go out to meet Christ and return with him
That Christians will leave earth for ever
That only the living will meet him
check.why: Apantēsis was used of welcoming a dignitary into a city, which fits a public coming to earth.

check.q: Why do most Christian traditions reject a secret rapture before the end?
options: Because the Left Behind novels are fiction
Because Paul did not believe in Christ's return
Because 1 Thessalonians 4 describes a single, loud, public coming with the resurrection, not a secret one before it
Because the word 'rapture' is not in the English Bible
check.why: A shout, a trumpet, the dead rising: the passage is about one public coming. The secret rapture comes from Darby in the 1830s.

check.q: In 2 Corinthians 5:4, what does Paul long for?
options: To stay alive until the end
To be 'unclothed', free of any body
To be 'clothed', so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life
To be reincarnated
check.why: Not unclothed but further clothed: the hope is a new body, not bodilessness, which is where he differs from Plato.

check.q: What is the main difference between Plato's hope in the Phaedo and Paul's?
options: Paul believed the soul is immortal and the body is evil
Plato's soul is immortal by nature and escapes the body; Paul hopes for God to raise and transform the body in a renewed creation
They are the same
Plato believed in life after death and Paul did not
check.why: Plato: 'herself invisible, departs to the invisible world'. Paul: 'the redemption of our body'.

check.q: According to Romans 8, what will happen to creation itself?
options: It will be abandoned when believers go to heaven
It will be destroyed and forgotten
Nothing: Paul only speaks of humans
It will be delivered from the bondage of decay into freedom
check.why: 'The creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay': the world shares the future of God's children.

tutorial.question: Heaven or new creation: what do Christians hope for?
tutorial.approach: Define the terms. Use 1 Thessalonians 4, 2 Corinthians 5 and Romans 8 to set out Paul's hope, and compare it with Plato's in the Phaedo. Explain the intermediate state and how the traditions differ. Assess the rapture. Conclude with what you think the final hope is, and why it matters for how people live.
strong: Distinguishes the intermediate state ('with Christ') from the final resurrection.
Uses 2 Corinthians 5:4 to show that Paul's hope is embodied, against Plato's immortal soul.
Explains Romans 8's hope for the whole creation.
Explains the origin of the rapture idea and the reasons most traditions reject it.
Sets out Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant differences fairly.
Draws out a consequence for life now: the body, grief or the care of creation.

reading.why: Heaven, resurrection and new creation for the general reader.

reading.why: A short imaginative tale of heaven as more real than earth.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Paul says, 'comfort one another with these words.' Think of one person you know who is grieving, however long ago their loss. This week, get in touch: a card, a call or a visit. You need not say anything wise. Just let them know you remember.
sessions.reflect: What picture of life after death did you grow up with? How does Paul's 'clothed, not unclothed' change it?
takeaways: Paul's earliest teaching on death is comfort: because Jesus rose, the dead in Christ will rise; Christians grieve with hope.
Between death and resurrection the faithful are 'with the Lord'; the secret rapture is a nineteenth-century idea that most traditions reject.
Paul hopes not for a soul set free, as Plato did, but for the body raised and the whole creation freed from decay.

sessions.title: The case against: failed prophecy?
sessions.line: The sharpest objection of all: Jesus said the end would come within a generation, and it did not. David Strauss and Albert Schweitzer said so, and Schweitzer still followed him.
sessions.plain: Some of Jesus's sayings seem to promise that the end would come very soon: before his disciples finished a journey, before some of his hearers died, within 'this generation'. Two thousand years later, the world goes on. In 1835 the German scholar David Friedrich Strauss argued that Jesus's speech about the end joins the fall of Jerusalem to the end of the world. In 1906 Albert Schweitzer went further: Jesus really did expect the end in his own lifetime, and was wrong. Bertrand Russell later made it a reason not to be a Christian. This session gives the objection its full force, and then hears the replies.
sessions.why: The last four sessions have built up the Bible's hope: new creation, apocalyptic unveiling, Jesus's warnings, Paul's resurrection hope. Now we must ask the hardest question. Paul wrote 'we who are alive'; Jesus said 'this generation will not pass away'. If they expected the end within their lifetimes and it did not come, is the whole hope a mistake?
answers: Did Jesus think the world would end soon?
If he did, was he wrong, and what would follow?
How have Christians answered?
Why didn't the first Christians give up?
sessions.finding: Strauss and Schweitzer argued that Jesus expected the end within a generation and was wrong; Christians answer that the sayings point to AD 70 and the resurrection, that the kingdom has 'already' come but 'not yet' in full, or admit a genuine puzzle that does not undo the hope.

paras: We have read the prophets' new creation, John's apocalypse, Jesus's speech on the Mount of Olives and Paul's letters. One thread runs through the New Testament: the end is near. 'God's Kingdom is at hand' (Mark 1:15). 'This generation will not pass away until all these things happen' (Mark 13:30). 'We who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord' (1 Thessalonians 4:15). 'The Lord is at hand' (Philippians 4:5). 'Behold, I come quickly' (Revelation 22:12).
Every session so far has noticed this and set it aside. Now we face it.
background.key: Again and again the New Testament says the end is near; this session faces what that means.

background.h: The quest of the historical Jesus
paras: In the 1700s and 1800s scholars in Germany, Britain and France tried to write a life of Jesus as a historian would, setting aside the Church's doctrines. This movement is called the quest of the historical Jesus. It began with Hermann Samuel Reimarus (1694–1768), a Hamburg teacher whose secret writings, published after his death by Gotthold Lessing between 1774 and 1778, argued that Jesus was a failed political messiah and that his disciples invented the resurrection after their hopes collapsed.

Most of the 'lives of Jesus' that followed made him a wise teacher of timeless morality, someone a nineteenth-century liberal could admire. In 1892 Johannes Weiss argued that this was false: Jesus's message of the kingdom was apocalyptic through and through. Albert Schweitzer pressed the point further.
background.key: From Reimarus (published 1774–78) on, scholars sought the 'historical Jesus'; most made him a moral teacher until Weiss (1892) and Schweitzer said he was an apocalyptic prophet.

paras: Strauss (1808–1874) was a young lecturer at Tübingen, in southern Germany, when he published his Life of Jesus Critically Examined in 1835–36. He argued that much of the Gospels is 'myth': not lies, but the early Church's faith told as history. The book caused a scandal; he lost his post and never held a university chair again. If you took 'The last week', you read his argument against the resurrection there.

In 1846 the book was translated into English by Mary Ann Evans, who later wrote novels as George Eliot. Her translation made Strauss the most discussed critic of the Gospels in Victorian Britain. On the end of the world his argument is simple and has never gone away: read the speech on the Mount of Olives as it stands, and it says the end will come soon after the Temple falls.
background.key: Strauss (1808–1874) argued in 1835 that much of the Gospels is the early Church's faith told as history; George Eliot translated him in 1846.

paras: Seventy years after Strauss, the objection was made even more forcefully. Albert Schweitzer (1875–1965) was born in Alsace, then part of Germany. By thirty he was a lecturer in theology at Strasbourg, a famous organist and an authority on Bach. In 1906 he published a history of the whole quest, translated into English in 1910 as The Quest of the Historical Jesus. His book is still in copyright, so we tell his argument in our own words in the lecture.

Then he did something remarkable. He trained as a doctor and in 1913 went to Lambaréné, in what is now Gabon, in west-central Africa, where he founded a hospital and worked for most of the rest of his life. He received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952. He never stopped calling himself a follower of Jesus. That matters: the strongest form of this objection comes not from an enemy of Christianity but from a man who gave his life to following the Jesus he believed was mistaken.

paras: The main reading is from Strauss's section on Jesus's speeches about his second coming. In the first part he states what the Gospels say. In the second he argues that 'this generation' can only mean the people alive at the time. In the third he takes apart the most popular way of saving the prediction, and gives his own explanation. Schweitzer's sharper version of the same case comes in the lecture.
The comparison sets the sayings on which the objection rests beside 2 Peter 3, the New Testament's own answer to people who were already asking 'Where is the promise of his coming?'
