before: What does Strauss say the Gospels claim Jesus predicted?
Why does Strauss think 'generation' cannot mean the Jewish nation or the Church?
What is the 'perpetual coming', and why does Strauss reject it?
sessions.readWhy: The objection in its classic nineteenth-century form: Strauss's argument that Jesus's speech joins the fall of Jerusalem to the end of the world, within 'this generation'.

paras: Not only did Jesus, according to the evangelical accounts, predict that he should return to life three days after his death; but also that at a later period, in the midst of the calamities which would issue in the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem, he should come in the clouds of heaven, to close the present period of the world, and by a general judgment, open the future age (Matt. xxiv. and xxv.; Mark. xiii.; Luke xvii. 22–37, xxi. 5–36).

But the very possibility of interpreting γενεὰ in the above manner vanishes, when it is considered, that in connexion with a verb of time, and without anything to imply a special application, γενεὰ cannot have any other than its original sense: i.e. generation, age; that in a passage aiming to determine the signs of the Messiah’s advent, it would be very unsuitable to introduce a declaration which, instead of giving any information concerning the arrival of that catastrophe, should rather treat of the duration of the Jewish nation, or of the Christian community, of which nothing had previously been said; that, moreover, already at v. 33, in the words ὑμεῖς ὅταν ἴδητε πάντα ταῦτα, γινώσκετε κ.τ.λ., Ye, when ye shall SEE all these things, know, etc., it is presupposed that the parties addressed would witness the approach of the event in question; and lastly, that in another passage (Matt. xvi. 28 parall.) the certainty of living to see the coming of the Son of man is asserted not simply of this generation, γενεὰ αὕτη, but of some standing here, τινες τῶν ὧδε ἑστηκότων, whereby it is shown in the most decisive manner, that in the present passage also, Jesus intended by the above expression the race of his cotemporaries, who were not to have become extinct before that catastrophe should occur.

Thus it is impossible to evade the acknowledgment, that in this discourse, if we do not mutilate it to suit our own views, Jesus at first speaks of the destruction of Jerusalem, and farther on and until the close, of his return at the end of all things, and that he places the two events in immediate connexion. There remains, therefore, but one expedient for vindicating the correctness of his announcement, namely, on the one hand, to assign the coming of which he speaks to the future, but, on the other hand, to bring it at the same time into the present—instead of a merely future, to make it a perpetual coming. The whole history of the world, it is said, since the first appearance of Christ, is an invisible return on his part, a spiritual judgment which he holds over mankind. Of this, the destruction of Jerusalem (in our passage until v. 28) is only the first act; in immediate succession (εὐθέως, v. 29 ff.) comes the revolution effected among mankind by the publication of the gospel; a revolution which is to be carried on in a series of acts and epochs, until the end of all things, when the judgment gradually effected in the history of the world, will be made known by an all-comprehending, final revelation.

But the famous utterance of the poet, spoken from the inmost depth of modern conviction, is ill-adapted to become the key of a discourse, which more than any other has its root in the point of view proper to the ancient world. To regard the judgment of the world, the coming of Christ, as something successive, is a mode of conception in the most direct opposition to that of the New Testament. The very expressions by which it designates that catastrophe, as that day or the last day, ἐκείνη or ἐσχάτη ἡμέρα, show that it is to be thought of as momentary; the συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος, end of the age (v. 3), concerning the signs of which the apostles inquire, and which Jesus elsewhere (Matt. xiii. 39) represents under the image of the harvest, can only be the final close of the course of the world, not something which is gradually effected during this course; when Jesus compares his coming to lightning (xxiv. 27), and to the entrance of the thief in the night (v. 43), he represents it as one sudden event, and not as a series of events. If we consider in addition to this the extravagant figures, which it is not less necessary to suppose on this interpretation, than on the above-mentioned reference of the 24th chapter to the destruction of Jerusalem, it will appear necessary to abstain from this expedient, as from all the previous ones.

Thus the last attempt to discover in the discourse before us the immense interval which, looking from our position in the present day, is fixed between the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of all things, having failed; we are taught practically that that interval lies only in our own conception, which we are not justified in introducing into the text. And when we consider that we owe our idea of that interval only to the experience of many centuries, which have elapsed since the destruction of Jerusalem: it cannot be difficult to us to imagine how the author of this discourse, who had not had this experience, might entertain the belief that shortly after the fall of the Jewish sanctuary, the world itself, of which, in the Jewish idea, that sanctuary was the centre, would also come to an end, and the Messiah appear in judgment.

parts.author: David Friedrich Strauss
parts.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, section 115
parts.who: David Friedrich Strauss (1808–1874), a German theologian and pupil of the philosopher Hegel, whose Life of Jesus (1835) cost him his academic career.

parts.title: This generation
parts.context: From section 115, 'The discourses of Jesus on his second advent: criticism of the different interpretations'. Strauss uses Matthew 24–25, which most scholars think is Matthew's expanded version of Mark 13; his verse numbers are Matthew's (24:34 is the same saying as Mark 13:30). 'Advent' means coming. The Greek word genea means 'generation'; the Greek phrases mean 'when you see all these things' and 'some of those standing here'. We have removed the footnote numbers. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Strauss begins by saying what the Gospels report: Jesus predicted that, amid the disasters that would destroy the Temple, he would come on the clouds to end the present age and judge the world. Then he deals with a common escape. Some interpreters say that 'this generation' means the Jewish people, or the Church, which would still exist whenever the end came. Strauss says no: the word means the people alive then. Jesus told his hearers they would 'see' these things, and elsewhere said that 'some standing here' would live to see the Son of Man come.

commentary.on: he should come in the clouds of heaven, to close the present period of the world, and by a general judgment, open the future age
commentary.text: Strauss states the Gospels' claim plainly and fairly: not a vague hope, but a coming in the clouds, the end of the age and a judgement, linked to the fall of the Temple.

commentary.on: γενεὰ cannot have any other than its original sense: i.e. generation, age
commentary.text: This is the heart of the argument. Some defenders had said that genea could mean 'race' or 'nation', so that Jesus meant only that the Jewish people would survive until the end. Strauss replies that, used with a verb of time, it means a generation: people living at the same time.

commentary.on: of which nothing had previously been said
commentary.text: A good point of method. The speech is about the signs of the end. A sudden remark about how long the Jewish nation or the Church will last would not fit the question being answered.

commentary.on: it is presupposed that the parties addressed would witness the approach of the event in question
commentary.text: 'When you see all these things': the hearers are expected to be there.

commentary.on: the certainty of living to see the coming of the Son of man is asserted not simply of this generation
commentary.text: Strauss brings in Matthew 16:28, the saying you will meet in the comparison: 'some standing here' will not die before they see it. That, he says, settles what 'this generation' means.

commentary.on: the race of his cotemporaries, who were not to have become extinct before that catastrophe should occur
commentary.text: 'Cotemporaries' is the old spelling of 'contemporaries'. The conclusion: Jesus told people then alive that they would see the end.

parts.title: The interval lies only in our own conception
parts.context: Further on in the same section. Strauss has shown, to his own satisfaction, that each attempt to split the speech into a part about AD 70 and a part about the far future fails. Now he takes on the last and most sophisticated defence. 'The famous utterance of the poet' is Friedrich Schiller's line 'the history of the world is the judgement of the world' (1786); the translator's note names it.
parts.plain: Strauss admits there is one remaining way to save the prediction: say that Christ's 'coming' is going on all through history, a spiritual judgement of which the fall of Jerusalem was only the first act, and the end the last. But that, he says, is a modern idea, not the New Testament's. The New Testament calls the end 'that day' and compares it to lightning and to a thief in the night: one sudden event, not a long process. So we must accept it. The long gap we imagine between the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the world is not in the text. The writer, who had not lived through the centuries since, believed that soon after the Temple fell the world itself would end.

commentary.on: Jesus at first speaks of the destruction of Jerusalem, and farther on and until the close, of his return at the end of all things, and that he places the two events in immediate connexion
commentary.text: The objection in a sentence. The speech joins the near event and the final one, without a break.

commentary.on: instead of a merely future, to make it a perpetual coming
commentary.text: This is a version of the 'already and not yet' reply you will meet in the lecture: Christ's coming is spread across history, judging the world from within, and completed at the end. Strauss sets it out fairly before rejecting it.

commentary.on: a discourse, which more than any other has its root in the point of view proper to the ancient world
commentary.text: Strauss's charge is that the 'perpetual coming' reads a modern philosophy of history back into an ancient Jewish text.

commentary.on: he represents it as one sudden event, and not as a series of events
commentary.text: The strongest part of his case: lightning, a thief in the night, 'that day'. The New Testament pictures the end as an event, not a process. Defenders reply that the New Testament also speaks of the kingdom already present, which Strauss does not discuss here.

commentary.on: that interval lies only in our own conception, which we are not justified in introducing into the text
commentary.text: We know that centuries have passed since AD 70, so we look for a gap in the speech. The first hearers did not know that, and the text has no gap.

commentary.on: the world itself, of which, in the Jewish idea, that sanctuary was the centre, would also come to an end
commentary.text: Strauss's own explanation. For Jews the Temple was the centre of the world, where heaven met earth. If it fell, surely the world would fall with it. Notice that he speaks of 'the author of this discourse': he is not sure how much of it goes back to Jesus himself.

paras: But when they persecute you in this city, flee into the next, for most certainly I tell you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel until the Son of Man has come.
He said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, there are some standing here who will in no way taste death until they see God’s Kingdom come with power.”
Most certainly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things happen.
knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come, walking after their own lusts
and saying, “Where is the promise of his coming? For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.”
For this they willfully forget that there were heavens from of old, and an earth formed out of water and amid water by the word of God,
by which means the world that existed then, being overflowed with water, perished.
But the heavens that exist now and the earth, by the same word have been stored up for fire, being reserved against the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.
But don’t forget this one thing, beloved, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.

parts.title: The 'soon' sayings
parts.context: Three sayings of Jesus: to the twelve as he sends them out (Matthew 10), to the crowd just before the transfiguration (Mark 9), and on the Mount of Olives (Mark 13). These are the texts Schweitzer, Russell and others point to.

commentary.on: you will not have gone through the cities of Israel until the Son of Man has come
commentary.text: Schweitzer's key text. Some read it as a promise that the mission to Israel will not be finished before the end, which would still be true; others as a prediction about weeks.

commentary.on: there are some standing here who will in no way taste death until they see God's Kingdom come with power
commentary.text: In all three Gospels this saying comes just before the transfiguration, when three disciples see Jesus shining with glory (Mark 9:2–8). Many early readers, such as John Chrysostom, took the transfiguration as its fulfilment. Others point to the resurrection or Pentecost. Sceptics think the arrangement was made to rescue the saying.

commentary.on: this generation will not pass away until all these things happen
commentary.text: Bertrand Russell's text, and C. S. Lewis's. Lewis called it, in a 1952 essay, 'the most embarrassing verse in the Bible', and then noted that the very next sentences say no one knows the day, not even the Son. The evangelists put both side by side and saw no contradiction.

parts.title: One day is with the Lord as a thousand years
parts.context: 2 Peter is a letter in the name of the apostle Peter. Many scholars think it was written after his death, perhaps around AD 100 or later, by a follower; others defend Peter's authorship before his death in the 60s. Either way, by then some were mocking the Christian hope because the first generation had died.

commentary.on: Where is the promise of his coming? For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were
commentary.text: The objection is already here, in the New Testament itself. 'The fathers' are probably the first generation of Christians. The mockers' argument is Schweitzer's and Russell's in a sentence: nothing has changed.

commentary.on: one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day
commentary.text: Taken from Psalm 90:4. God does not measure time as we do. Critics call this a way of making any prediction unfalsifiable. Defenders say it is simply true that 'soon' in the prophets means 'next on God's calendar', not 'within a lifetime'.

commentary.on: The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
commentary.text: The heart of the answer. The delay is not failure but mercy: time given for people to turn. That reverses the objection. Every day the world goes on is, on this view, a day of grace.

commentary.on: the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night
commentary.text: The writer does not give up the hope. He restates Jesus's and Paul's words: it will come, unannounced.

commentary.on: the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up
commentary.text: The oldest Greek manuscripts read not 'burned up' but 'will be found' or 'laid bare': exposed to God's judgement. Translations differ; the WEB follows the later reading.

compare.why: First the sayings the objection rests on. Then 2 Peter 3, which shows that Christians were already facing the question in the first or second century, and how one of them answered.
compare.title: Where is the promise of his coming?

paras: Here is the case, put as strongly as its best advocates put it. Jesus's central message was that God's kingdom was about to arrive, ending history as we know it. He said so repeatedly, with timing: before the disciples finished their mission (Matthew 10:23), before some of his hearers died (Mark 9:1), within 'this generation' (Mark 13:30). He told the high priest at his trial that he would see the Son of Man 'coming with the clouds of the sky' (Mark 14:62). Paul expected to be alive at the end (1 Thessalonians 4:15). Revelation says 'I come quickly'.

It did not happen. Every generation of those hearers died. Two thousand years later, the world continues. If Jesus was wrong about the very thing he was most sure of, and which he made central to his message, why trust him about anything else, about God, forgiveness or his own identity?

Notice how hard this objection is to dodge. It is not based on a few odd verses. It is based on the most solid conclusion of historical scholarship about Jesus: that he was a Jewish prophet who announced the coming kingdom of God. Most historians, Christian and not, accept that.
sections.key: The objection: Jesus announced the end within a generation, Paul expected it in his lifetime, and it did not come; if Jesus was wrong about that, why trust him?

paras: Strauss doubted how much of the speech went back to Jesus. Schweitzer, writing seventy years later, made the objection sharper by taking it all as history. In the last chapters of The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906) he argued, in summary, as follows.

When Jesus sent the twelve out to preach, he told them they would not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man came (Matthew 10:23). Schweitzer insisted that the saying be read as it stands, without softening. It did not come true: the disciples came back and nothing happened. That, for Schweitzer, was the turning point of Jesus's life. Having failed to bring in the end by their mission, he resolved to bring it by his own suffering and death.

Schweitzer put it in a famous picture. Jesus, sure that he was the coming Son of Man, 'lays hold of the wheel of the world' to turn it one last time and end history. It will not move, so he throws himself on it; it turns and crushes him, and rolls on, with his broken body still hanging on it. Schweitzer thought the whole later history of Christianity was the long work of coming to terms with the end that did not come.

Yet he did not think faith was finished. The gentle moral teacher of the nineteenth-century 'lives', he said, had never existed; the real Jesus is a stranger from his own time. But his words still set people free, and he still calls them to follow him without a name or a title, as he called the fishermen. Schweitzer answered that call himself, as a doctor in Africa.
sections.key: Schweitzer (1906) argued that Jesus expected the end before his disciples returned, then threw himself on 'the wheel of the world' and was crushed; yet he still called people to follow him.

paras: On 6 March 1927 the philosopher Bertrand Russell gave a lecture at Battersea Town Hall in London, later published as 'Why I Am Not a Christian'. Russell was willing to grant that Jesus taught much that was good. But he argued that Jesus could not be the wisest of men, because he plainly believed that his second coming would happen within the lifetime of many who were listening to him. Russell quoted Matthew 10:23 and 16:28 (the parallel of Mark 9:1), and noted that Jesus's first followers believed it too, and that it lay behind some of his moral teaching.

Russell then added objections of other kinds: Jesus's teaching on hell, which Russell thought cruel, and what he called vindictive passages. Those belong to other journeys. Here what matters is his central point, made in our own words: a man who was mistaken about the timing of the end of the world was not infallibly wise.
Russell's lecture became one of the most widely read statements of modern unbelief. Its strength is its simplicity: it needs no theory of the Gospels, only the sayings as they stand.
sections.key: Russell (1927) argued that Jesus believed he would return within his hearers' lifetimes, and so cannot have been the wisest of men.

paras: The first reply says the sayings have been misread. 'The Son of Man coming' comes from Daniel 7:13, where the human figure comes to God, not to earth, to receive the kingdom. On this reading, the 'coming' Jesus promised within a generation was his vindication: his resurrection, his exaltation and, as a public sign, the fall of the Temple he had condemned, in AD 70. That came true within forty years. N. T. Wright has argued this at length in Jesus and the Victory of God (1996).

Matthew 10:23 can then be read as promising that the mission to Israel would not be completed before that judgement came. Mark 9:1 is followed at once by the transfiguration, which Mark seems to present as a glimpse of the kingdom 'with power'.

The strength of this reply is that it takes Jewish language seriously. Its weakness is that it seems to some to empty out what the first Christians plainly also believed: Paul's Lord who 'will descend from heaven'. Wright himself affirms the Second Coming, but finds it taught elsewhere.
sections.key: The first reply: the 'coming' within a generation was Jesus's vindication, shown in the resurrection and the fall of the Temple in AD 70.

sections.h: Second reply: already and not yet
paras: The second reply is the one most theologians give. Jesus taught that the kingdom was both future and already present: 'if I by God's finger cast out demons, then God's Kingdom has come to you' (Luke 11:20). In 1935 the Welsh scholar C. H. Dodd went so far as to call Jesus's teaching 'realised eschatology': the end had arrived in Jesus. Most scholars thought that went too far, and settled on a balance: the kingdom has been 'inaugurated' but not yet 'consummated'.

The Swiss theologian Oscar Cullmann, in Christ and Time (1946), compared it to the Second World War. D-Day, in June 1944, decided the war; V-Day, in May 1945, ended it. The fighting between was real, but the outcome was settled. For Cullmann, the cross and resurrection are D-Day; Christ's return is V-Day. The first Christians, on this view, were not wrong that the decisive event had happened; the end had begun.
On this reading the nearness of the end is a matter of its certainty and its decisiveness, not a calendar. Critics reply that this is wise theology but may not be what Jesus himself meant.
sections.key: The second reply: the kingdom came 'already' in Jesus's work, death and resurrection, and is 'not yet' complete; like D-Day before V-Day (Cullmann).

paras: Some Christian scholars do not think either reply fully answers the problem. Dale Allison, an American New Testament scholar and an Episcopalian, has argued in Jesus of Nazareth: Millenarian Prophet (1998) and later books that Jesus probably did expect the end soon, as Schweitzer said. Allison does not conclude that Christianity is false. He argues that prophets often spoke of God's future as near because of its urgency, that the prophets of Israel were often 'wrong' about timing and were still kept as Scripture, and that what matters is whether God raised Jesus and will finish what he began.

C. S. Lewis took a similar line in 1952. He admitted the difficulty in the plainest words. Then he argued that the same speech says the Son does not know the day; that if Jesus was truly human, he could be ignorant of things, as all humans are; and that the doctrine was never given to tell us when, but to keep us ready.
The agnostic scholar Bart Ehrman, in Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium (1999), agrees with Allison's history and draws the opposite conclusion: Jesus was a prophet who was wrong.
sections.key: The third reply: Jesus may have spoken of the end as near and been ignorant of its timing (Allison; Lewis), which does not settle whether God raised him.

sections.h: Why the first Christians did not give up
paras: One historical fact cuts across the debate. Movements built on a failed prediction usually collapse or reinvent themselves dramatically; William Miller's followers split after 1844. The first Christians lost their whole first generation without the end coming, and the movement grew. 2 Peter shows them facing the question openly, inside their own Scriptures.

Why? Christians answer: because their hope never rested only on a date. It rested on what they said had already happened, the resurrection of Jesus, which they took as the first instalment of the end. If he had been raised, the end had begun, however long the rest took. If he had not, Paul himself said, their faith was useless (1 Corinthians 15:17).

So the objection in the end comes back to the question of the resurrection, which you may have weighed in 'The last week'. Schweitzer's wheel crushes Jesus. The Christian claim is that three days later he got up.
sections.key: The first Christians survived the delay because their hope rested on the resurrection as the end begun; so the objection finally turns on whether Jesus rose.

debate.question: Was Jesus wrong about the end?

positions.name: Yes, he was mistaken
positions.who: Albert Schweitzer; Bertrand Russell; Bart Ehrman; in a qualified form, Dale Allison
positions.view: Jesus expected the kingdom to come, and history to end, within his generation. It did not. Christians should admit it. For Russell and Ehrman, that counts against his authority; for Schweitzer and Allison, it does not end faith but changes it.
positions.evidence: Matthew 10:23; Mark 9:1; 13:30; 14:62; Paul's 'we who are alive'; the mockers of 2 Peter 3.

positions.name: No, the sayings were fulfilled
positions.who: N. T. Wright; R. T. France; many Church Fathers on Mark 9:1
positions.view: The 'coming' within a generation was the Son of Man's vindication before God, seen in the resurrection and in the fall of the Temple in AD 70; Mark 9:1 points to the transfiguration. Jesus also spoke of a final day whose date no one knows.
positions.evidence: Daniel 7:13 (coming to God); the Temple fell within forty years; the transfiguration follows Mark 9:1 at once; Mark 13:32.

positions.name: Already, and not yet
positions.who: C. H. Dodd (in part); Oscar Cullmann; George Eldon Ladd; most Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant theology
positions.view: The kingdom truly arrived in Jesus's work, death, resurrection and the gift of the Spirit; that is why its nearness could be announced. Its completion awaits his return, whose date is unknown. The delay is God's patience.
positions.evidence: Luke 11:20; 1 Corinthians 15:20 (first fruits); 2 Peter 3:9; the parables of delay (Matthew 25:5).

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus proclaimed the coming kingdom of God at the heart of his message, and that the 'soon' sayings are real and must be faced, not explained away.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of the Last Judgement or of the Second Coming that is free to use here, and we do not use a stand-in.

music.why: Mozart died in 1791 with his Requiem unfinished. Its 'Dies irae', the day of wrath, sets the medieval poem on the Last Judgement: the day of the Lord taken with full seriousness, by a man facing his own end.

think.why: The modern debate about the historical Jesus, including the arguments over his resurrection.

learn.why: 'The word of our God stands forever': the line Jesus echoed when he said, 'my words will not pass away'. You may know it already from 'Who was Jesus?'.

check.q: Why is Schweitzer's objection harder to dismiss than a few odd verses?
options: Because Paul agreed with it
Because it rests on the most widely accepted historical conclusion about Jesus, that he proclaimed the coming kingdom of God
Because Schweitzer was a famous organist
Because no Christian has ever answered it
check.why: Most historians accept that Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet; the objection grows from that consensus.

check.q: What does Schweitzer's image of the wheel of the world claim about the cross?
options: That Jesus was a political rebel
That the cross brought history to an end
That Jesus threw himself on history to force the end, and was crushed when it did not come
That Jesus died by accident
check.why: In Schweitzer's picture Jesus tried to force history to its end by his death, and it crushed him and rolled on.

check.q: What is the point of the 'AD 70 and vindication' reply?
options: That the 'coming of the Son of Man' within a generation draws on Daniel 7, where he comes to God, and was fulfilled in his vindication and the Temple's fall
That Jesus was wrong but it does not matter
That Mark 13 was written after AD 70
That Jesus never mentioned the end
check.why: Daniel's Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom; the Temple fell within forty years.

check.q: What does Cullmann's D-Day and V-Day comparison illustrate?
options: That history has no direction
That Christians should fight wars
That the Second Coming happened in 1944
That the decisive victory has been won in Jesus's death and resurrection, though its completion is still awaited
check.why: The 'already and not yet': the outcome is settled, the end not yet reached.

check.q: How does 2 Peter 3:9 reverse the mockers' objection?
options: By setting a new date
By saying the delay is not failure but God's patience, giving time for repentance
By denying that Christ will come
By saying the mockers will be raptured
check.why: 'He is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish': every day of delay is a day of mercy.

check.q: Why, on the Christian view, did the first Christians survive the delay when other movements built on predictions collapsed?
options: Because the end did come in AD 70
Because the Romans protected them
Because they forgot the predictions
Because their hope rested on the resurrection, which they took as the end already begun
check.why: Paul: if Christ is not raised, faith is futile. The objection finally turns on the resurrection.

tutorial.question: 'Jesus expected the end of the world within a generation, and he was wrong.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: State the objection at full strength, using Schweitzer and Russell and the key sayings. Then weigh the three main replies: vindication and AD 70, already and not yet, and the honest puzzle. Use 2 Peter 3 to show that the first Christians faced the question. Decide what you think, and what follows for faith if the objection is right.
strong: States the objection fairly, citing Matthew 10:23, Mark 9:1 and 13:30.
Explains Strauss's argument on 'this generation' and Schweitzer's reconstruction and image of the wheel.
Presents Russell's argument in his own terms.
Weighs the AD 70, 'already and not yet' and honest-puzzle replies.
Uses 2 Peter 3 and Mark 13:32 as evidence that the delay was faced early.
Connects the question to the resurrection.

reading.author: C. S. Lewis
reading.title: The World's Last Night and Other Essays
reading.why: Lewis's title essay faces the 'embarrassing verse' directly.

reading.author: Albert Schweitzer
reading.title: The Quest of the Historical Jesus
reading.why: The classic itself; the last two chapters can be read on their own.

reading.author: Dale C. Allison
reading.title: Jesus of Nazareth: Millenarian Prophet
reading.why: The strongest modern case that Jesus expected the end soon, by a Christian scholar.

reading.author: N. T. Wright
reading.title: Jesus and the Victory of God
reading.why: The strongest case that the 'coming' sayings point to Jesus's vindication and AD 70.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: 2 Peter calls the delay God's patience. Think of someone whose slowness to change frustrates you. This week, practise patience with them once on purpose, and give them the time you would want to be given.
sessions.reflect: If you found that someone you admire was mistaken about something they were sure of, would you stop trusting them? What would it depend on?
takeaways: Schweitzer and Russell argued that Jesus expected the end within a generation and was wrong; the sayings are real, and most historians accept that he proclaimed the coming kingdom.
Christians reply that the 'coming' was his vindication and the fall of the Temple, that the kingdom has come 'already' but 'not yet', or that his human ignorance of the date does not undo the hope.
2 Peter shows the first Christians facing the delay openly; their hope survived because it rested on the resurrection.

sessions.title: A great multitude
sessions.line: John hears a number, a hundred and forty-four thousand, and turns to see a crowd no one can count, from every nation, before the Lamb. Then: what is the thousand years?
sessions.plain: In the middle of Revelation's visions of disaster, John sees something else: a crowd too big to count, from every nation and language, dressed in white and singing before God's throne. Their suffering is over, and God wipes away every tear. This is where the whole book is going: not destruction but worship, and the healing of the nations. This session reads that vision, and then the strangest idea in Revelation, the 'thousand years', which Christians have read in three main ways, and some in ways that did great harm.
sessions.why: The last session faced the objection that the end never came and heard the replies, above all that the end began with the resurrection. Revelation was written for a Church living in that long 'meanwhile'. Now we ask what it says the end is for, and how Christians have read its most disputed chapter, on the thousand years.
answers: What is heaven like, according to the Bible?
Who are the 144,000?
What is the millennium, and what do the different views mean?
How do Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants differ on the end, and why have end-times movements done harm?
sessions.finding: Revelation's goal is worship by every nation and the healing of the nations; its 'thousand years' has been read in three main ways, and Augustine's reading, that it is the age of the Church now, became the main view of most churches.

paras: We have read the prophets' new creation, the unveiling of apocalypse, Jesus's command to watch, Paul's hope of resurrection, and the hard question of the delay. The answer to that question that runs through the New Testament is 'already and not yet': the end began with the resurrection, and its completion is still to come.

Revelation, which we first opened in the second session, was written to seven churches living in that meantime, under pressure from Rome. Chapters 6 to 19 are its central visions: seals broken, trumpets blown, bowls poured out, beasts rising from sea and land, and the fall of 'Babylon', a code name for Rome. They are frightening, and they are what most people mean by 'apocalyptic'. But they are interrupted, again and again, by scenes of worship.
background.key: Revelation was written for the Church in the 'meantime'; its frightening central visions are interrupted by scenes of worship.

paras: Revelation 6 tells of six seals broken on a scroll: war, famine, death, martyrs crying 'how long?', and the sky rolled up. The question at the end of chapter 6 is 'who is able to stand?' Chapter 7 answers it, before the seventh seal is opened.

It does so in two scenes. First John hears the number of those 'sealed', marked as God's, from the twelve tribes of Israel: 144,000, twelve thousand from each tribe (7:4–8). Then he looks, and sees our passage. This is the same pattern as chapter 5, where John hears of 'the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah' and turns to see 'a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain'. What he hears is explained by what he sees.
background.key: Revelation 7 answers 'who can stand?': John hears 144,000 from Israel's tribes, then sees a multitude no one can count.

paras: Augustine (354–430) was born in North Africa, taught rhetoric in Rome and Milan, became a Christian in 386 and was bishop of Hippo, on the coast of modern Algeria, from 395 until his death. After the Goths sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed the Christians for the disaster, and Augustine answered with The City of God, written between 413 and 426. It tells the history of two 'cities', one built on love of God and one on love of self, mixed together until the end.
Book XX, written in the 420s, is about the last judgement. In it Augustine gave the reading of Revelation 20 that became the Western Church's standard view for a thousand years.

timeline.text: Revelation written
Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, teaches an earthly thousand-year kingdom
Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 80–81, defends the millennium
Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.32–36
Tyconius, a North African, reads Revelation as about the Church in every age
The Goths sack Rome

The Anabaptist 'kingdom' at Münster
Darby's dispensationalism
William Miller's 'Great Disappointment'

background.key: Augustine (354–430), bishop of Hippo, wrote The City of God after the sack of Rome; Book XX gave the West its standard reading of the millennium.

paras: The main reading is Revelation 7:9–17, the great multitude: the clearest picture in the Bible of where the story is going, and the reading for All Saints' Day, 1 November, in many churches.

The comparison is Augustine on Revelation 20, the 'thousand years'. Revelation's goal is plain; its timetable is not. Augustine shows how one of the greatest minds of the early Church read the hardest chapter, and why most churches followed him.
background.key: Revelation 7's multitude shows the goal; Augustine on Revelation 20 shows how the Church came to read the thousand years.

before: Who is in the crowd John sees? Count the words he uses for where they come from.
What are they doing? What do they say?
What has happened to them before, and what will never happen again?
sessions.readWhy: The great multitude before the throne: the goal of the whole story, worship by every nation and every tear wiped away.

paras: After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude, which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.
They cried with a loud voice, saying, “Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”
All the angels were standing around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell on their faces before his throne, and worshiped God,
saying, “Amen! Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might, be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”
One of the elders answered, saying to me, “These who are arrayed in the white robes, who are they, and where did they come from?”
I told him, “My lord, you know.”
He said to me, “These are those who came out of the great suffering.They washed their robes, and made them white in the Lamb’s blood.
Therefore they are before the throne of God, they serve him day and night in his temple. He who sits on the throne will spread his tabernacle over them.
They will never be hungry or thirsty any more. The sun won’t beat on them, nor any heat;
for the Lamb who is in the middle of the throne shepherds them and leads them to springs of life-giving waters. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

parts.title: From every nation
parts.context: After the six seals of chapter 6 and the sealing of the 144,000 (7:1–8), John looks, and sees the scene in heaven change.

commentary.on: a great multitude, which no man could count
commentary.text: John has just heard a number, 144,000, twelve times twelve times a thousand: the complete people of God, built on Israel's twelve tribes. Now he sees them, and they cannot be counted. Most interpreters think the two are the same people, heard and seen, as the Lion was seen as a Lamb: God's Israel, made limitless. God had promised Abraham descendants like the stars, which no one could count (Genesis 15:5).

commentary.on: out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages
commentary.text: Four words for human difference, and all of them are kept. The crowd does not become one nation or speak one language. At Babel, languages divided people (Genesis 11); here they are all present before God. Christianity today is the most widely spread faith in the world, and this verse is often read as its charter.

commentary.on: dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands
commentary.text: White for victory and purity; palms for celebration. At the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles, worshippers carried palm branches and remembered God's care in the wilderness. Palms also greeted Jesus entering Jerusalem (John 12:13).

commentary.on: Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!
commentary.text: Salvation is not their achievement but God's gift, and they say so. The Lamb, the crucified Jesus, is praised with God, on the throne. In Revelation only God is worshipped: when John tries to worship an angel, he is told to stop (19:10). The book is saying who Jesus is.

commentary.on: Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might, be to our God forever and ever!
commentary.text: Seven words of praise: complete praise. This is what the end is for. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647) begins with the same idea: the chief end of man is to glorify God and enjoy him for ever.

parts.title: Every tear wiped away
parts.context: One of the twenty-four elders around the throne, who stand for God's people in heaven (4:4), asks John a question, then answers it.

commentary.on: These who are arrayed in the white robes, who are they, and where did they come from?
commentary.text: A teacher's question. John's reply, 'My lord, you know', is the same as Ezekiel's in the valley of bones: the human does not know, and waits to be told.

commentary.on: These are those who came out of the great suffering.
commentary.text: They have come through suffering, not around it. For John's first readers this was a promise: those who die faithful under Rome have not lost. Some readers take 'the great suffering' (often 'the great tribulation') as a specific time at the end; others as the suffering of the faithful in every age.

commentary.on: They washed their robes, and made them white in the Lamb's blood.
commentary.text: A deliberate paradox: blood that makes things white. Christ's death cleanses them. Their victory is his, given to them.

commentary.on: He who sits on the throne will spread his tabernacle over them.
commentary.text: The tabernacle was the tent where God was present among Israel in the wilderness. God himself shelters them. This is the hope of Revelation 21:3, 'God's dwelling is with people', already in view.

commentary.on: They will never be hungry or thirsty any more. The sun won't beat on them, nor any heat
commentary.text: Words from Isaiah 49:10, the prophet's promise to the returning exiles. Hunger, thirst and heat are the sufferings of refugees on the road, and of the poor. The end is their reversal.

commentary.on: the Lamb who is in the middle of the throne shepherds them
commentary.text: The Lamb becomes the shepherd: the one who was sacrificed now leads the flock. Psalm 23 is close: he leads them to water.

commentary.on: And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
commentary.text: From Isaiah 25:8. Not 'there will be no tears' but God wiping each one away, as a parent does. Suffering is remembered, and comforted, by God himself. The same words come again at the Bible's end (Revelation 21:4).

paras: The evangelist John has spoken of these two resurrections in the book which is called the Apocalypse, but in such a way that some Christians do not understand the first of the two, and so construe the passage into ridiculous fancies. For the Apostle John says in the foresaid book, "And I saw an angel come down from heaven.... Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power; but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with Him a thousand years." Those who, on the strength of this passage, have suspected that the first resurrection is future and bodily, have been moved, among other things, specially by the number of a thousand years, as if it were a fit thing that the saints should thus enjoy a kind of Sabbath-rest during that period, a holy leisure after the labours of the six thousand years since man was created, and was on account of his great sin dismissed from the blessedness of paradise into the woes of this mortal life, so that thus, as it is written, "One day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day," there should follow on the completion of six thousand years, as of six days, a kind of seventh-day Sabbath in the succeeding thousand years;

and that it is for this purpose the saints rise, viz. to celebrate this Sabbath. And this opinion would not be objectionable, if it were believed that the joys of the saints in that Sabbath shall be spiritual, and consequent on the presence of God; for I myself, too, once held this opinion. But, as they assert that those who then rise again shall enjoy the leisure of immoderate carnal banquets, furnished with an amount of meat and drink such as not only to shock the feeling of the temperate, but even to surpass the measure of credulity itself, such assertions can be believed only by the carnal. They who do believe them are called by the spiritual Chiliasts, which we may literally reproduce by the name Millenarians. It were a tedious process to refute these opinions point by point: we prefer proceeding to show how that passage of Scripture should be understood.

The Lord Jesus Christ Himself says, "No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man,"--meaning by the strong man the devil, because he had power to take captive the human race; and meaning by his goods which he was to take, those who had been held by the devil in divers sins and iniquities, but were to become believers in Himself. It was then for the binding of this strong one that the apostle saw in the Apocalypse "an angel coming down from heaven, having the key of the abyss, and a chain in his hand. And he laid hold," he says, "on the dragon, that old serpent, which is called the devil and Satan, and bound him a thousand years,"--that is, bridled and restrained his power so that he could not seduce and gain possession of those who were to be freed. Now the thousand years may be understood in two ways, so far as occurs to me: either because these things happen in the sixth thousand of years or sixth millennium (the latter part of which is now passing), as if during the sixth day, which is to be followed by a Sabbath which has no evening, the endless rest of the saints, so that, speaking of a part under the name of the whole, he calls the last part of the millennium--the part, that is, which had yet to expire before the end of the world--a thousand years; or he used the thousand years as an equivalent for the whole duration of this world, employing the number of perfection to mark the fulness of time.

But while the devil is bound, the saints reign with Christ during the same thousand years, understood in the same way, that is, of the time of His first coming. For, leaving out of account that kingdom concerning which He shall say in the end, "Come, ye blessed of my Father, take possession of the kingdom prepared for you," the Church could not now be called His kingdom or the kingdom of heaven unless His saints were even now reigning with Him, though in another and far different way; for to His saints He says, "Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the world." Certainly it is in this present time that the scribe well instructed in the kingdom of God, and of whom we have already spoken, brings forth from his treasure things new and old. And from the Church those reapers shall gather out the tares which He suffered to grow with the wheat till the harvest, as He explains in the words, "The harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels. As therefore the tares are gathered together and burned with fire, so shall it be in the end of the world. The Son of man shall send His angels, and they shall gather out of His kingdom all offences." Can He mean out of that kingdom in which are no offences? Then it must be out of His present kingdom, the Church, that they are gathered. So He says, "He that breaketh one of the least of these commandments, and teacheth men so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven:

but he that doeth and teacheth thus shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." He speaks of both as being in the kingdom of heaven, both the man who does not perform the commandments which He teaches,--for "to break" means not to keep, not to perform,--and the man who does and teaches as He did; but the one He calls least, the other great. And He immediately adds, "For I say unto you, that except your righteousness exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees,"--that is, the righteousness of those who break what they teach; for of the scribes and Pharisees He elsewhere says, "For they say and do not;"--unless, therefore, your righteousness exceed theirs, that is, so that you do not break but rather do what you teach, "ye shall not enter the kingdom of heaven." We must understand in one sense the kingdom of heaven in which exist together both he who breaks what he teaches and he who does it, the one being least, the other great, and in another sense the kingdom of heaven into which only he who does what he teaches shall enter. Consequently, where both classes exist, it is the Church as it now is, but where only the one shall exist, it is the Church as it is destined to be when no wicked person shall be in her. Therefore the Church even now is the kingdom of Christ, and the kingdom of heaven.

It is then of this kingdom militant, in which conflict with the enemy is still maintained, and war carried on with warring lusts, or government laid upon them as they yield, until we come to that most peaceful kingdom in which we shall reign without an enemy, and it is of this first resurrection in the present life, that the Apocalypse speaks in the words just quoted.

"And the souls," says John, "of those who were slain for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God,"--understanding what he afterwards says, "reigned with Christ a thousand years,"--that is, the souls of the martyrs not yet restored to their bodies. For the souls of the pious dead are not separated from the Church, which even now is the kingdom of Christ; otherwise there would be no remembrance made of them at the altar of God in the partaking of the body of Christ, nor would it do any good in danger to run to His baptism, that we might not pass from this life without it; nor to reconciliation, if by penitence or a bad conscience any one may be severed from His body. For why are these things practised, if not because the faithful, even though dead, are His members? Therefore, while these thousand years run on, their souls reign with Him, though not as yet in conjunction with their bodies.

parts.author: Augustine
parts.work: The City of God, Book XX
parts.ref: Augustine, The City of God XX.7
parts.title: Ridiculous fancies
parts.context: From Book XX, chapter 7, written in the 420s. Augustine is discussing Revelation 20, where John sees an angel bind Satan for 'a thousand years' and the martyrs rise and 'reign with Christ' for that time, before the final judgement. This is Marcus Dods's translation (1871). We have removed the footnote numbers. 'Chiliasts' comes from the Greek for a thousand; 'Millenarians' from the Latin. 'Carnal' means fleshly, worldly. 'Spoil his goods' means 'plunder his possessions'. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Some Christians, Augustine says, take Revelation's 'first resurrection' to mean that the saints will rise bodily before the end and reign on earth for a thousand years, a great Sabbath rest after six thousand years of history. He once held that view himself, and it would be harmless if the joys were spiritual. But some imagine huge feasts, and he will not accept that. Instead, he reads it through Jesus's saying about binding the strong man. Christ has already bound Satan, so that he cannot hold the nations captive. The 'thousand years' is either the last part of history or, more likely, a symbol for the whole time of the Church, the full number standing for 'all the time there is'.

commentary.on: some Christians do not understand the first of the two, and so construe the passage into ridiculous fancies
commentary.text: Augustine is blunt. But notice who he is arguing against: other Christians. Many respected teachers before him, Papias, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and Tertullian among them, had expected a literal thousand-year kingdom on earth after Christ's return.

commentary.on: a kind of Sabbath-rest during that period, a holy leisure after the labours of the six thousand years since man was created
commentary.text: The popular scheme: history is a week of six thousand-year 'days' (because 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years', 2 Peter 3:8, which we read in the last session), followed by a thousand-year Sabbath. It was neat, and it invited people to work out dates.

commentary.on: for I myself, too, once held this opinion
commentary.text: An honest admission. Augustine changed his mind, and says so in the middle of arguing against the view he used to hold.

commentary.on: such assertions can be believed only by the carnal
commentary.text: What Augustine rejects most is not hope but a hope of 'immoderate carnal banquets', heaven as endless eating and drinking. His objection is to a hope that is merely an indulgence.

commentary.on: No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man
commentary.text: The key move. Jesus said this of his own work, driving out demons (Mark 3:27). So Satan's binding has already happened, in Christ's ministry, death and resurrection. Augustine reads Revelation by the Gospels.

commentary.on: bridled and restrained his power so that he could not seduce and gain possession of those who were to be freed
commentary.text: Satan is not idle, but he is restrained: he cannot stop the nations hearing the gospel. On this reading, the spread of the Church through the world is itself the sign that the strong man is bound.

commentary.on: employing the number of perfection to mark the fulness of time
commentary.text: Augustine's second, preferred explanation: a thousand (ten times ten times ten) is a symbol for completeness, so 'a thousand years' means the whole time until the end. This is the way of reading numbers we learned in the second session.

parts.author: Augustine
parts.work: The City of God, Book XX
parts.ref: Augustine, The City of God XX.9
parts.title: The Church even now is the kingdom
parts.context: From Book XX, chapter 9. Augustine explains who 'reigns with Christ' during the thousand years. 'The kingdom militant' means the Church still fighting its battle on earth. The cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: If Satan is bound now, then the saints reign with Christ now. Augustine argues that the Church can already be called Christ's kingdom, though it is a mixed kingdom, with weeds among the wheat until the harvest at the end. The 'first resurrection' is not a bodily one but the new life of those who turn to Christ in this life. And the souls of the faithful dead, the martyrs above all, already reign with him too, not yet with their bodies, because the dead still belong to the Church.

commentary.on: the saints reign with Christ during the same thousand years, understood in the same way, that is, of the time of His first coming
commentary.text: The millennium began with Christ's first coming. We are living in it. That is the view now called amillennialism: not 'no millennium' but a millennium that is symbolic and present.

commentary.on: the Church as it now is, but where only the one shall exist, it is the Church as it is destined to be when no wicked person shall be in her
commentary.text: Augustine does not idealise the Church. It is full of people who 'say and do not'. It is a kingdom, but a mixed one; the pure kingdom comes only at the end. This guarded later readers against claiming that any church, or any state, was already God's perfect kingdom.

commentary.on: it is of this first resurrection in the present life, that the Apocalypse speaks
commentary.text: The 'first resurrection' is spiritual: rising from the death of sin to new life now (compare Colossians 3:1, which he quotes). The second, the resurrection of the body, comes at the end.

commentary.on: the souls of the martyrs not yet restored to their bodies
commentary.text: The martyrs who 'reign with Christ' are the faithful dead, with Christ now, as Paul said, while they await the resurrection. Augustine holds together the intermediate state and the final hope.

commentary.on: For the souls of the pious dead are not separated from the Church
commentary.text: The dead are still members of Christ's body: that is why the Church remembers them at the Eucharist. Catholic and Orthodox prayer for the dead, and the feast of All Saints, rest on this conviction.

compare.author: Augustine
compare.work: The City of God, Book XX
compare.ref: Augustine, The City of God XX.7
compare.why: Revelation 20:1–6 says Satan will be bound for a thousand years while the martyrs reign with Christ. Many early Christians took this as a future earthly kingdom. Augustine, who once believed it, argued that the thousand years is the age of the Church, now. Read his argument; most churches came to follow it.
compare.title: The thousand years is now

paras: Read straight through, Revelation can feel like a catalogue of catastrophes. But its structure keeps pointing elsewhere. After every cycle of judgement comes worship: chapters 4–5, 7, 11:15–19, 15, 19. The catastrophes are what the world's own violence and idolatry lead to; the worship is where God is leading it.

The goal is described twice. In chapter 7, a multitude from every nation before the throne. In chapters 21–22, which you may have read in 'The whole story' or 'Light, stone and glass', a city where 'the nations will walk in its light' and a tree whose leaves are 'for the healing of the nations' (22:2). Not the nations destroyed, but healed.

The theologian Richard Bauckham has argued that the book's real question is not 'when?' but 'who is Lord?', and that its hope is the conversion of the nations, not their annihilation. Not every reader agrees: the book's judgements are real and severe. But even its harshest scenes are written so that, as 14:6 says, the eternal Good News might reach 'every nation, tribe, language, and people'.
sections.key: Revelation's judgements are interrupted by worship; its goal is a multitude from every nation and 'the healing of the nations'.

paras: Few numbers in the Bible have been argued over more. Jehovah's Witnesses teach that 144,000 faithful Christians will reign with Christ in heaven, while others live for ever on a renewed earth. Some dispensationalists take it as Jewish believers in a future tribulation. Others, ancient and modern, take it as a symbol.

The text itself gives clues. The number is 12 × 12 × 1,000: the twelve tribes, multiplied and made complete. It is heard, not seen, and what John then sees is a crowd 'which no man could count' from every nation, the same pattern as the Lion who turns out to be a Lamb. And in chapter 14 the 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion as 'first fruits' of humanity (14:4). Most scholars therefore read them as the whole people of God, described in the language of Israel: the promise to Abraham, of descendants beyond counting, fulfilled.
sections.key: The 144,000 (12 × 12 × 1,000) are best read as God's whole people in Israel's language; John hears the number and then sees a countless multitude.

paras: Revelation's worship scenes have a political edge. In the cities of Asia, the province John writes to, the emperors were honoured with temples, statues and festivals: the 'imperial cult'. Pergamum, one of the seven cities, had built one of the first temples to Rome and Augustus, in 29 BC; John calls the city the place 'where Satan's throne is' (2:13). To refuse to honour the emperor could cost a trader his guild and a citizen his safety.

So when the multitude cries 'Salvation be to our God', it is saying what Rome claimed for itself. Coins and inscriptions called the emperor 'saviour' and 'lord'. Chapters 13 and 17–18 show Rome as a beast and as 'Babylon the great', a city drunk on the blood of the saints, whose merchants grow rich on a trade whose list of goods ends with 'people's bodies and souls' (18:13).

That is why Revelation has been loved by Christians under persecution, from the early martyrs to churches under twentieth-century dictatorships. Worship, in this book, is a decision about who is Lord.
sections.key: In the province of the imperial cult, the multitude's 'Salvation be to our God' contradicts Rome's claims; Revelation's worship is a decision about who is Lord.

sections.h: All Saints and the communion of saints
paras: Revelation 7 is read in many Western churches on All Saints' Day, 1 November. The feast grew from early commemorations of all the martyrs. In the 730s Pope Gregory III dedicated a chapel in St Peter's in Rome to all the saints on 1 November, and in the 830s the feast was kept across the Frankish empire. The next day, All Souls (2 November), remembers all the faithful dead. The Orthodox keep All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost. Many Protestant churches keep it too, as a day to remember the whole Church, living and dead.

Behind the feast is a line of the Apostles' Creed: 'I believe in the communion of saints'. Augustine's chapter in this session's comparison explains it: the faithful dead are not separated from the Church. Catholics and Orthodox ask the saints to pray for them, as one asks a friend. Most Protestants do not, but still believe that the living and the dead belong to one body in Christ. Revelation 7 is the picture: a single crowd, too large to count, in one act of worship.
sections.key: All Saints (1 November) grew from feasts of the martyrs; behind it is the creed's 'communion of saints': the living and the faithful dead are one Church.

paras: Revelation 20:1–6 is the only passage in the Bible that mentions a thousand-year reign. Christians have read it in three main ways, named by when Christ returns in relation to it.

rows: A future reign of Christ on earth
Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian; many evangelicals today, including dispensationalists
A symbol of the present age of the Church, with Christ reigning from heaven and Satan restrained
At its end, once for all
Tyconius, Augustine; most Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed teaching
A future golden age on earth brought about by the spread of the gospel
Daniel Whitby (1703); Jonathan Edwards; many nineteenth-century British and American Protestants
table.note: All three affirm Christ's return, the resurrection and the final judgement. They differ on the order of events and on how much good to expect from history before the end.

sections.key: Premillennialists expect Christ's return before an earthly thousand years, amillennialists read it as the present Church age, postmillennialists as a coming golden age.

paras: Beyond the millennium, the churches share a core and differ on details. All teach Christ's return, the resurrection of the dead, the judgement and the life of the world to come; all of them are in the creeds.

rows: Purgatory; the Church's 'final trial' before Christ's return; rejects even modified millenarianism (Catechism 676)
Hell is real; the Church hopes and prays for all, and declares no one damned
Prayer for the departed; strong emphasis on the transfiguration of the whole creation (theosis); no defined purgatory
Some Fathers, like Gregory of Nyssa, hoped all would be restored; this has been allowed as a hope but not a teaching
No purgatory; the Augsburg Confession (1530, art. XVII) rejects an earthly kingdom of the godly before the resurrection
Traditionally a double outcome, heaven or hell; some modern theologians, like Karl Barth, left the question open
Often premillennial, sometimes dispensationalist, with a rapture; others amillennial
Mostly a double outcome; a minority hold 'conditional immortality', that the lost cease to exist
table.note: Universal salvation, the belief that all will finally be saved, goes back to Origen (c. 185–254); a form of it was condemned in the anathemas associated with the Council of Constantinople in 553, yet the hope has had defenders in every age, including Julian of Norwich.

sections.key: All churches share the creeds' hope; they differ on purgatory, the millennium and whether all may finally be saved.

paras: End-times belief has done real harm when people have claimed to know the date, or to be God's instruments for bringing the end. In 1534–35 radical Anabaptists seized the German city of Münster, declared it the New Jerusalem, practised polygamy and executed opponents, until the city was retaken and its leaders killed. In 1844 William Miller's followers sold their farms for a coming that did not come. In 1993 the siege at the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, whose leader David Koresh taught that he could open the seals of Revelation, ended in a fire in which seventy-six people died, about twenty-five of them children. Some recent end-times teaching has also shaped politics, by treating wars in the Middle East as the fulfilment of prophecy.

There is another side. Hope for the end has often been a source of courage and of reform. Postmillennial Christians in the nineteenth century worked against slavery and for schools and missions, believing God's kingdom would spread. The enslaved sang of a Jordan to cross and a home over there. The difference, Augustine might say, is between those who claim to know the timetable and those who keep the hope and do their work.
sections.key: End-times movements have done harm when they set dates or claimed to bring the end, as at Münster and Waco; the same hope has also fuelled courage and reform.

refs: Augustine, The City of God XX.7–9, tr. Marcus Dods (1871). Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 80–81; Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.32–36; Eusebius, Church History III.39 (Papias).
Catechism of the Catholic Church 668–682, 1020–1060 (676 on millenarianism); the Augsburg Confession (1530), article XVII; the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647), question 1.
Richard Bauckham, The Theology of the Book of Revelation (1993); Robert G. Clouse (ed.), The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views (1977); Brian E. Daley, The Hope of the Early Church (1991).
On Münster: R. Po-chia Hsia (ed.), The German People and the Reformation (1988); Norman Cohn, The Pursuit of the Millennium (1957). On Waco: James D. Tabor and Eugene V. Gallagher, Why Waco? (1995).

debate.question: What is the thousand years?

positions.name: A future kingdom on earth
positions.who: Papias; Justin Martyr; Irenaeus; many evangelicals today
positions.view: After Christ returns, the faithful will be raised and reign with him on a renewed earth for a long age before the final judgement. God's promises to the earth and to Israel will be fulfilled in history, not only beyond it.
positions.evidence: Revelation 20:4–6 speaks of a 'first resurrection' and a reign; Isaiah 65's long-lived earthly kingdom; the earliest Christian writers read it so.

positions.name: The age of the Church, now
positions.who: Tyconius; Augustine; most Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed teaching
positions.view: Revelation's numbers are symbols. Satan was bound by Christ's victory (Mark 3:27); the saints, living and dead, reign with Christ now; Christ will come once, at the end, for the resurrection and judgement.
positions.evidence: Revelation 20 is a vision full of symbols; the strong man bound; the rest of the New Testament speaks of one coming and one resurrection of all (John 5:28–29).

positions.name: A golden age before the end
positions.who: Jonathan Edwards; many nineteenth-century Protestants
positions.view: The gospel will spread until most of the world is Christian and a long age of peace and justice follows, after which Christ returns.
positions.evidence: The parables of the mustard seed and the leaven (Matthew 13:31–33); 'the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh' (Isaiah 11:9); the spread of the Church.

debate.agree: All agree that Christ will return, the dead will be raised and judged, and that God's kingdom will have no end; and the creeds bind none of them to a millennial view.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of the great multitude, the Adoration of the Lamb or All Saints that is free to use here, and we do not use a stand-in.

music.why: William Walsham How's hymn (1864), sung to Ralph Vaughan Williams's tune 'Sine Nomine' (1906), is the great multitude in song: 'from earth's wide bounds, from ocean's farthest coast'. It is sung on All Saints' Day, when Revelation 7 is read.

think.why: What Christians believe about the worth of every human being, of every nation and language.

learn.why: The promise of Revelation 7:17, given again at the Bible's end: God will wipe away every tear.

check.q: What is the best reading of the relation between the 144,000 (7:4) and the great multitude (7:9)?
options: The 144,000 are the only people who will be saved
They are two quite different groups, Jews and Gentiles, with different destinies
They are the same people, heard as Israel's complete number and seen as a multitude from every nation, as the Lion is seen as a Lamb
The multitude are angels
check.why: John hears, then sees, as in chapter 5; 12 × 12 × 1,000 is the complete people of God, made limitless.

check.q: Why does it matter that the multitude comes from 'every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages'?
options: Because languages will be abolished
Because only some nations are included
Because in the end everyone will speak Greek
Because the end keeps human differences and brings them all before God, reversing Babel's division
check.why: Four words for difference, all present: unity without uniformity.

check.q: What is Augustine's key argument that the thousand years is now?
options: That the martyrs will reign on earth after Christ returns
That Revelation is not Scripture
That Christ has already bound Satan, as Jesus said of the strong man, so the saints reign with him in the Church now
That the world will end in the year 1000
check.why: He reads Revelation 20 by Mark 3:27: the binding happened in Christ's first coming.

check.q: Which view expects Christ to return before an earthly thousand-year reign?
options: Amillennial
Postmillennial
Preterist
Premillennial
check.why: 'Pre': Christ returns first, then reigns a thousand years on earth.

check.q: Why, on Augustine's view, is the Church a 'mixed' kingdom?
options: Because it is ruled by both Rome and Constantinople
Because it has both Jews and Gentiles
Because the wheat and the weeds grow together until the harvest; only at the end will no wicked person be in her
Because it includes angels
check.why: He refuses to call any present church God's perfect kingdom.

check.q: What do the disasters at Münster (1534–35) and Waco (1993) have in common?
options: Leaders claimed special knowledge of the end and cast their communities as God's instruments for it
Both followed Augustine
Both were amillennial
Both were caused by the rapture
check.why: Claiming to know the timetable, or to bring the end, has repeatedly done harm.

tutorial.question: Is Revelation a book of destruction or of hope?
tutorial.approach: Set the frightening visions beside the scenes of worship, especially Revelation 7. Ask what the book says its goal is. Explain the three views of the millennium and Augustine's argument. Weigh the harm done by some end-times movements. Decide whether the book itself, read well, encourages or restrains them.
strong: Notes the structure: judgement interrupted by worship.
Reads Revelation 7 closely: every nation, suffering ended, tears wiped away.
Explains the 144,000 and the 'heard and seen' pattern.
Sets out pre-, a- and postmillennialism fairly, with Augustine's reasons.
Uses at least one historical example of harm and one of hope.
Shows how traditions differ on the end, side by side.
