sessions.practice: Live it this week: the multitude comes from every nation and language. This week, learn the name and something of the story of one person near you from a country or culture other than your own: a neighbour, a colleague, the person who serves you coffee.
sessions.reflect: Revelation says the end is for worship. What would it mean for your life now to be aimed at that?
takeaways: Revelation 7 shows the goal of the story: a multitude from every nation before God, their suffering ended and every tear wiped away.
The thousand years of Revelation 20 has been read as a future earthly reign, the present age of the Church (Augustine) or a coming golden age.
The churches share the creeds' hope and differ on purgatory, the millennium and hope for all; date-setting movements have done real harm.

sessions.title: The verdict, and making the case
sessions.line: The Bible ends with a feast, a city and one word: 'Come.' Is this the truest story ever told, or the greatest wish? And what will you say?
sessions.plain: We have followed the Bible's hope from the prophets to Revelation. Now for the verdict. The Bible's story ends not with escape but with a renewed creation where God lives with people, death is swallowed up and every tear is wiped away. Its last words are a prayer: 'Come, Lord Jesus.' Critics say this is the greatest wish ever dreamed. Believers say it is the truest story. This session weighs both, and then, at the end of this hall, asks you to make the case.
sessions.why: The last session showed where Revelation says the story is going: worship by every nation, every tear wiped away, and how Christians have read the thousand years. Now we gather everything: the prophets, apocalypse, Jesus's warnings, Paul's hope, the objection and the replies. This is the last journey of the hall on Jesus and the New Testament, so it ends with your own case.
answers: So what does the Bible say about the end of the world?
Is the Christian hope just wishful thinking?
What difference does it make to how people live now?
How do I make the case for what I have learned in this hall?
sessions.finding: The Bible's story ends in a renewed creation where God lives with people; it is either the truest story or the greatest wish, and this hall has given you what you need to decide.

paras: Here is the verdict of this journey, in plain words. The Bible's hope is not that souls will escape to heaven but that God will renew the whole creation, raise the dead and live among his people. It began with Israel's prophets after the exile, was expressed in apocalyptic visions for people under pressure, was announced by Jesus as the kingdom of God, and was tied by Paul to Jesus's resurrection as its first instalment. Its timing is unknown, and that has been a real difficulty from the first generation, but Christians have held that the end has 'already' begun. Its goal is worship by every nation and the healing of the world.

Whether it is true depends on two things this hall has looked at: whether Jesus was raised from the dead, and whether the God of Israel exists and keeps his promises. Neither can be settled by this journey alone. What can be settled is what the hope actually is, and that it is very different from its popular caricature.
background.key: The verdict: the Bible hopes for a renewed creation, the dead raised and God with his people, begun in Jesus's resurrection; its truth turns on the resurrection and on God.

background.h: The story so far, in this hall
paras: This is the last journey of the hall on Jesus and the New Testament. It began by meeting Jesus first-hand and weighing the evidence for him outside the Bible; it read his teaching on the mountain, followed his last week, asked why his death mattered, watched the first Christians spread and, in this hall's later journeys, asked how Christianity grew from Judaism and what Christians do when they meet. This journey has asked where all of that is going.
So the end of this journey is also a moment to look back. The hall's question, in the end, is simple: is the story of Jesus true, and is it yours?
background.key: This journey closes the hall on Jesus and the New Testament, whose question is: is this story true, and is it mine?

paras: Romans 8, which you read in the fourth session, showed the whole creation waiting. Revelation 21 and 22, the city coming down and the river of life, you may have read in 'The whole story' or 'Light, stone and glass'. Here we read two passages not yet read: Isaiah 25, the prophet's feast on the mountain where death is swallowed up, which Revelation quotes; and the very last words of the Bible, which end with an invitation and a prayer.

The comparison is the end of a great Victorian poem, 'The Wreck of the Deutschland' by Gerard Manley Hopkins, written after a shipwreck in which five nuns drowned, which ends by praying for Christ to come again to England.
background.key: Isaiah 25's feast, where death is swallowed up, and the Bible's last words; then the end of Hopkins's 'Wreck of the Deutschland'.

before: In Isaiah 25, who is invited to the feast, and what is destroyed?
In Revelation 22, who says 'Come', and to whom?
Is the Bible's ending a threat, an invitation, or both?
sessions.readWhy: The feast where death is swallowed up, and the last words of the Bible: an invitation, and a prayer.

paras: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of choice meat, a feast of choice wines, of choice meat full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations.
He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.
It shall be said in that day, “Behold, this is our God! We have waited for him, and he will save us! This is Yahweh! We have waited for him. We will be glad and rejoice in his salvation!”
“Behold, I come quickly. My reward is with me, to repay to each man according to his work.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.
Blessed are those who do his commandments, that they may have the right to the tree of life, and may enter in by the gates into the city.
Outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you for the assemblies. I am the root and the offspring of David, the Bright and Morning Star.”
The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” He who hears, let him say, “Come!” He who is thirsty, let him come. He who desires, let him take the water of life freely.
He who testifies these things says, “Yes, I come quickly.”
Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen.

parts.title: A feast for all peoples
parts.context: Isaiah 24–27 is sometimes called the 'Isaiah apocalypse', because it speaks of judgement on the whole earth and of God's final reign. Scholars debate its date, from Isaiah's own time to after the exile. Here the prophet pictures the end as a banquet on Mount Zion.

commentary.on: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of choice meat
commentary.text: 'All peoples', not only Israel. The end is a party, with the best food and the best wine. Jesus's parables of the wedding feast, and the Eucharist itself, which you may have met in 'What happens at church', look forward to this table.

commentary.on: the veil that is spread over all nations
commentary.text: The veil may be a mourning veil, or the blindness that keeps the nations from knowing God. Either way, God takes it away. This is 'apocalypse' in its first meaning: unveiling.

commentary.on: He has swallowed up death forever!
commentary.text: Death, which swallows everyone, is itself swallowed. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 15:54, 'Death is swallowed up in victory.' Isaiah 65's new creation still had death at a hundred; here it is gone.

commentary.on: The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces.
commentary.text: The words Revelation takes up twice (7:17; 21:4). Notice: 'all faces'. The hope is as wide as humanity.

commentary.on: Behold, this is our God! We have waited for him, and he will save us!
commentary.text: The end is not first a place or an event but recognition: 'this is our God'. The waiting, which has run through this whole journey, turns out to have been worth it.

parts.title: Come
parts.context: The last verses of the Bible, after the vision of the holy city. Jesus speaks, then the Spirit and the Church, then John. (Verses 18–19, a warning not to add to or take from the book, are left out here; you may have read them in 'Can I trust the Bible?'.)

commentary.on: Behold, I come quickly.
commentary.text: The 'soon' saying again, which the fifth session faced. Revelation does not hide it. It repeats it three times in its last chapter.

commentary.on: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.
commentary.text: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. In Revelation 1:8 God says this of himself; here Jesus says it. The one who began the story will end it. The 'end' of the world is a person.

commentary.on: Blessed are those who do his commandments, that they may have the right to the tree of life
commentary.text: The tree of life was in Eden (Genesis 2:9), and humans were barred from it (3:24). Now the way back is open. The Bible ends where it began, in a garden, but the garden is now a city.

commentary.on: Outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
commentary.text: The ending is not sentimental. Some things have no place in the new creation: cruelty, violence, the lie. Christians have argued about who, if anyone, will finally be outside. The text's point is that evil will not be part of the end.

commentary.on: I am the root and the offspring of David, the Bright and Morning Star.
commentary.text: Both David's ancestor and his descendant. The morning star is the last star seen before dawn, the sign that the night is nearly over.

commentary.on: The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” He who hears, let him say, “Come!” He who is thirsty, let him come.
commentary.text: Two invitations in one. The Church (the bride) and the Spirit say 'Come' to Christ, praying for his return. And they say 'Come' to anyone who is thirsty. The Bible's last appeal is not a threat but an offer: 'let him take the water of life freely.'

commentary.on: Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus.
commentary.text: The Bible ends with a prayer. Paul preserves the earliest form in Aramaic, Maranatha, 'Our Lord, come!' (1 Corinthians 16:22), one of the oldest Christian prayers we have. The whole hope of this journey is gathered into it.

commentary.on: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen.
commentary.text: And the last word of all is grace. The story ends, as it continues for its readers now, with a gift.

paras:
Now burn, new born to the world,
Doubled-naturèd name,
The heaven-flung, heart-fleshed, maiden-furled
Miracle-in-Mary-of-flame,
Mid-numbered He in three of the thunder-throne!
Not a dooms-day dazzle in his coming nor dark as he came;
Kind, but royally reclaiming his own;
A released shower, let flash to the shire, not a lightning of fire
hard-hurled.

Dame, at our door
Drowned, and among our shoals,
Remember us in the roads, the heaven-haven of the
Reward:
Our King back, oh, upon English souls!
Let him easter in us, be a dayspring to the dimness of us,
be a crimson-cresseted east,
More brightening her, rare-dear Britain, as his reign rolls,
Pride, rose, prince, hero of us, high-priest,
Our hearts' charity's hearth's fire, our thoughts' chivalry's throng's
Lord.

parts.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
parts.translator: Original English (written 1875–76; first published 1918, ed. Robert Bridges)
parts.ref: Hopkins, 'The Wreck of the Deutschland', stanzas 34–35
parts.title: Our King back
parts.context: Gerard Manley Hopkins (1844–1889) was an English Jesuit priest and poet. He wrote this poem in 1875–76, but it was refused by the Jesuit journal The Month and published only in 1918, when his friend Robert Bridges edited his poems. The ship Deutschland ran aground on the Kentish Knock, a sandbank in the mouth of the Thames, on 6 December 1875. Hopkins's language is compressed and strange on purpose: read it aloud, slowly.
parts.plain: Stanza 34: Hopkins prays to Christ, born of Mary, one of the three persons of God. He asks that Christ come, not in a terrifying doomsday flash, nor as hidden as when he was born, but kindly, reclaiming his own, like a gentle shower rather than a bolt of lightning. Stanza 35: he turns to the drowned nun, 'at our door', and asks her to pray for England: that Christ, England's King, would come back to English souls; that he would rise in them like Easter, like a sunrise, and reign over their hearts and thoughts.

commentary.on: Doubled-naturèd name
commentary.text: Christ is both God and man, two natures in one person: the creed's teaching packed into three words.

commentary.on: Not a dooms-day dazzle in his coming nor dark as he came
commentary.text: The second coming, Hopkins says, need not be the terror of doomsday paintings; nor will it be as hidden as the first coming, in a stable. He asks for something between: real, visible, but kind.

commentary.on: Kind, but royally reclaiming his own
commentary.text: This is the whole hope in one line. Christ comes as a king, and what he claims is his own: the world he made and the people he loves. Reclaiming, not destroying.

commentary.on: A released shower, let flash to the shire, not a lightning of fire
commentary.text: Rain on the farmland of England, not fire from the sky. Hopkins chooses an image of renewal over one of destruction.

commentary.on: Let him easter in us, be a dayspring to the dimness of us
commentary.text: Hopkins makes 'Easter' a verb. The coming of Christ is resurrection happening in people now, a 'dayspring', the old word for dawn. This is 'already and not yet' in poetry: the end begins in us.

commentary.on: Our hearts' charity's hearth's fire
commentary.text: The poem ends with Christ as the fire at the centre of the home of love. The great, cosmic hope comes down to a hearth. That is where the Christian hope is lived, between the first coming and the last.

compare.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
compare.ref: Hopkins, 'The Wreck of the Deutschland', stanzas 34–35
compare.translator: Original English (written 1875–76; first published 1918, ed. Robert Bridges)
compare.why: Hopkins wrote 'The Wreck of the Deutschland' after five Franciscan nuns, exiled from Germany, drowned in a shipwreck off the English coast in December 1875. One of them was reported to have cried out, 'O Christ, Christ, come quickly.' The poem's last two stanzas turn her cry into a prayer for the coming of Christ.
compare.title: Let him easter in us

paras: Here is what this journey has found, stage by stage.

rows: Not escape but a new creation; a dead nation raised; then the dead themselves
An unveiling for the powerless: the risen Christ, not the empire, holds the keys
The Temple will fall, the Son of Man will come; no one knows the day: watch
Resurrection with Christ, the first fruits; the dead with the Lord; the whole creation freed
Was Jesus wrong about the timing? Vindication, 'already and not yet', or an honest puzzle
Worship by every nation, every tear wiped away; the millennium read three ways
table.note: Each stage needs the one before it: the prophets' hope, given voice in apocalypse, announced by Jesus, anchored by Paul in the resurrection, tested by the delay, and pictured in Revelation's end.

sections.key: The Bible's hope runs from the prophets' new creation through apocalypse, Jesus and Paul, is tested by the delay, and ends in Revelation's renewed world.

paras: The strongest general objection to all of this is older than Schweitzer. In The Essence of Christianity (1841) the German philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach argued that religion projects human wishes onto the sky: we want to live for ever and to see justice, so we imagine a God who will give us both. Sigmund Freud, in The Future of an Illusion (1927), called religious belief an illusion in his technical sense: a belief held because we wish it were true, whether or not it is.

Friedrich Nietzsche added a moral charge. Christians, he argued in Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–85), despise this world and this body for the sake of an imagined 'beyond', and so betray life. He urged his readers to remain faithful to the earth.

These objections deserve to be taken seriously. Hope can be a drug. People have used heaven to make the poor accept their lot, as Karl Marx charged when he called religion 'the opium of the people' (1844).
sections.key: Feuerbach (1841) and Freud (1927) called the Christian hope a projection of wishes; Nietzsche said it betrays the earth; Marx called it an opiate.

paras: First, the charge of escapism does not fit the Bible's actual hope. Nietzsche's target is a soul fleeing the body for a heaven in the clouds, which is closer to Plato than to Paul. The Bible's end is a renewed earth, raised bodies, houses and vineyards, a city with its gates open: about as faithful to the earth as a hope can be.

Second, the argument from wishing cuts both ways. That we wish something is true does not make it false; we wish for water, and water exists. And a person may as easily wish there were no God and no judgement. The Bible's hope includes judgement, which few people simply wish for: it says that what we do with our lives will be revealed. C. S. Lewis made a version of this point: our desires do not prove their objects exist, but a deep desire nothing in this world can satisfy is at least a clue.

Third, the history. The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann, in Theology of Hope (1964), argued that Christian hope, rightly understood, is not an opiate but a protest: it refuses to accept the world as it is, because it knows what the world is meant to be. Hospitals, the abolition of slavery and the care of the dying owe much to people who believed that God would make all things new and acted accordingly.
sections.key: Replies: the Bible's hope is earthly, not escapist; wishing does not make a belief false; and hope has driven protest and reform, not only passivity (Moltmann).

paras: If the Bible's hope is true, it changes how people live now. If the body will be raised, the body matters: what we do with it, and with the bodies of others. If creation will be renewed, the world is not a stage set to be thrown away. If there is a judgement, injustice will not have the last word, and neither will our own excuses. If no one knows the day, the right response is not anxiety or calculation but faithful work, as Abraham Davenport called for candles.

And if the end is a feast for all peoples, with every tear wiped away, then grief is real but not final. The Book of Common Prayer's burial service commits the body to the ground 'in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life'. That is a strong claim to make over a grave. It is the claim this whole journey has examined.
sections.key: If the hope is true, bodies, the world, justice and grief all matter differently now; the burial service's 'sure and certain hope' is the claim this journey has tested.

paras: The Christian hope is not the only account of where history is going. It helps to set it beside others, as their own holders describe them.

rows: Towards the days of the Messiah and the world to come

Towards the Last Day, one of the six articles of faith

Round and round: the Stoic world-cycles, or rebirth in Hindu and Buddhist thought
Release from the cycle, or acceptance of it
Upwards, by human effort, through science, reason and reform
A better world for future generations; for Marx, a classless society
Towards the 'heat death' of the universe, when no useful energy is left

table.note: Jews and Muslims, like Christians, expect a resurrection and a judgement; they differ over Jesus. Some modern ideas of progress began as secular versions of the biblical hope.

sections.key: Judaism and Islam also expect resurrection and judgement; others see history as a cycle, as progress, or as ending in cosmic cold.

paras: This is the last journey of the hall on Jesus and the New Testament. Every hall ends with the same task: to make the case. You choose one idea you have met in this hall and defend it in about 300 words, using the texts it rests on, and you answer the strongest objection to it.

You might choose the claim that Jesus really lived and was crucified under Pontius Pilate; that he rose from the dead; that his death was 'for us'; that the Sermon on the Mount is the best way to live; that the first Christians' faith spread because of what they had seen; or that the Bible's hope is a renewed creation, not escape. Choose the one you find most convincing, or most important.

A good case does three things. It states the claim plainly. It gives the evidence, quoting the texts you have read. And it answers the objection at its strongest, not at its weakest, as this hall has tried to do in every journey. You may decide at the end that you are not persuaded. That is allowed. The aim is not agreement but honest thought: to know what you believe about this story, and why.

debate.question: Is the Christian hope the truest story or the greatest wish?

positions.name: The greatest wish
positions.who: Ludwig Feuerbach; Sigmund Freud; Bertrand Russell
positions.view: Human beings fear death and long for justice, so they imagine a God who will give them life and right every wrong. The hope tells us much about human desire and nothing about the world.
positions.evidence: Hope of life after death is found in many cultures; it matches our wishes exactly; the predicted end has not come.

positions.name: The truest story
positions.who: The New Testament writers; Augustine; N. T. Wright; Jürgen Moltmann
positions.view: The hope rests on an event, the resurrection of Jesus, not on a wish. If he was raised, the end has begun, and the world's story is going where the prophets said. The hope fits our deepest longings because we were made for it.
positions.evidence: The resurrection as first fruits (1 Corinthians 15:20); the early Christians' survival of the delay; the hope's earthy, unsentimental character, including judgement.

positions.name: A hope to live by, whether or not it can be proved
positions.who: Albert Schweitzer; many modern believers and seekers
positions.view: The details of the end are beyond our knowing. What matters is to follow Jesus now, in the toils and conflicts of life, and to find out in that way who he is.
positions.evidence: Schweitzer's closing picture of Jesus calling people to follow him, unnamed, as he called the fishermen; Jesus's own refusal to give the date; 'hope that is seen is not hope' (Romans 8:24).

debate.agree: All agree that the hope stands or falls with what one thinks of Jesus, and that it shapes how people face death.

check.q: Which reply best answers Nietzsche's charge that Christian hope betrays the earth?

check.q: Why does the argument that the hope is 'just a wish' not settle the question?
options: Because no one wishes to live for ever

Because Freud was a believer
Because the Bible says so
check.why: A wish is no evidence either way; the truth of the hope turns on the resurrection and on God.

options: That Easter should be celebrated more often

That the nuns were not really drowned
check.why: Hopkins makes Easter a verb: the end begins in us, a 'dayspring' to our dimness.

takeaways: The Bible's story ends not in escape but in a renewed creation, death swallowed up and God living with people.
Critics call it the greatest wish; believers answer that it rests on the resurrection, is earthy rather than escapist, and has driven reform.
The Bible's last words are an invitation and a prayer, 'Come', and this hall ends by asking you to make your own case.

closing.title: Your answer, and make the case
closing.prompt: Make the case (the end of the hall on Jesus and the New Testament). Choose one idea you have met in this hall, for example that Jesus really lived and was crucified, that he rose from the dead, that his death was 'for us', that the Sermon on the Mount is the best way to live, or that the Bible's hope is a renewed creation, not escape. In about 300 words, defend it from the texts it rests on and answer the strongest objection to it. Then add a few lines: where is history going, in your view, and what difference does your answer make?
closing.practice: Read the book of Revelation in one sitting, aloud if you can, as its first hearers did (it takes about seventy minutes). Before you start, read Revelation 1:3. Afterwards, write down the one image that stayed with you, and why.
synthesis: This journey asked where history is going, and read the Bible's answer in four stages, tested it against the hardest objection, and ended with its last words. Here are the short answers to the questions it set out to answer, in order.

What does the Bible say about the end of the world? That it will not simply stop, or be thrown away, but be renewed. The Bible begins with God creating 'the heavens and the earth' and ends with 'a new heaven and a new earth', and a city coming down from God to live among people. 'The end' in the Bible is the world's goal, not only its finish. That hope began with Israel's prophets after the disaster of 587 BC: Isaiah 65 promised a new creation full of houses, vineyards and long lives, where the wolf and the lamb feed together; Ezekiel saw a valley of dry bones breathe again, a nation raised from its grave. Under persecution in the 160s BC, Daniel promised plainly that 'those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake'. Unlike the Greek hope of an immortal soul, this was a hope for God to raise bodies and renew the world.

Is Revelation about now? Revelation is an apocalypse, an 'unveiling', a kind of writing for people under pressure that pulls back the curtain to show who really rules. It was written by a prisoner named John on Patmos, most likely around AD 95, to seven real churches in what is now Turkey, in pictures taken from the Old Testament: seven for completeness, a thousand for fullness, 666 most likely for Nero. It has been read as about the first century, the whole history of the Church, the last days, or every age; the best readings begin with what it meant to its first hearers and find its pattern repeated in every age. Its centre is not a timetable but a person: a crucified man alive for ever, who holds the keys of death. Set beside the older Book of Enoch, it is signed in John's own name and centred on the Lamb who conquers by dying.

What is the Second Coming, and did Jesus say when? The parousia, Christ's coming in glory, is in all the creeds: the story will end with him seen as he is and everything put right. In Mark 13 Jesus foretold the fall of the Temple, which Rome destroyed in AD 70, and the coming of the Son of Man in Daniel's words. Christians have read the speech as about AD 70, about the end, or about both, the near judgement a window on the final one. But on the date Jesus was clear: 'no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son'. His answer to 'when?' was 'watch': be found faithful in your work, like servants whose master may return at any time, or bridesmaids with oil in their lamps.

What is heaven like, and what is the rapture? Paul's earliest letter was written to comfort a church burying its first dead: because Jesus rose, those who belong to him will rise; Christians grieve, but with hope. Between death and resurrection the faithful are 'at home with the Lord'; that is what the New Testament usually means by going to heaven, and the traditions describe it differently, with purgatory in Catholic teaching and prayer for the dead in Catholic and Orthodox practice. But it is not the end: Paul longs to be 'clothed', not 'unclothed', and says the whole creation will be freed from decay. As N. T. Wright puts it, the hope is 'life after life after death'. The secret rapture, in which believers vanish before the end, was developed by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s; most traditions reject it, because 1 Thessalonians 4 describes one loud, public coming, and its 'meeting' is going out to welcome a king who is arriving.

Did Jesus think the world would end soon? This is the hardest question, and the journey gave it full weight. Albert Schweitzer argued in 1906 that Jesus expected the end before his disciples returned from their mission, then threw himself on 'the wheel of the world' to force it, and was crushed. Bertrand Russell argued in 1927 that a man so mistaken could not be the wisest of men. The sayings are real, and most historians accept that Jesus proclaimed the coming kingdom. Christians reply in three ways: that the 'coming' within a generation was the Son of Man's vindication, seen in the resurrection and the Temple's fall; that the kingdom came 'already' in Jesus and is 'not yet' complete, like D-Day before V-Day; or, honestly, that Jesus in his humanity did not know the date and spoke of the end as near because it was certain. The New Testament itself faces the mockers in 2 Peter: the delay is God's patience. The first Christians survived the delay because their hope rested on the resurrection, so in the end the objection turns on whether Jesus rose. Schweitzer himself kept following the Jesus he thought mistaken, and spent his life as a doctor in Africa.

What is the millennium? Revelation's goal is a multitude from every nation, language and people before God's throne, their suffering ended and every tear wiped away, and 'the healing of the nations'. Its thousand years (Revelation 20) has been read three ways: a future reign on earth after Christ returns (premillennial: Justin, Irenaeus, many evangelicals); the present age of the Church, with Satan bound by Christ's victory and the saints reigning with him now (amillennial: Augustine, and most Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed teaching); or a golden age before Christ returns (postmillennial: Jonathan Edwards). The creeds bind none of them. Where Christians have claimed to know the timetable or to bring the end, as at Münster in 1535 or Waco in 1993, the results have been disastrous; where they have kept the hope and done their work, it has often fuelled courage and reform.

Why are Christians so interested in the end? Because the end tells you what the story means. The Bible's story ends with a feast for all peoples where death is swallowed up, an invitation to anyone who is thirsty, and a prayer: 'Come, Lord Jesus.' Feuerbach and Freud called this the greatest wish; Nietzsche said it betrays the earth. The replies are that the Bible's hope is about as earthy as a hope can be; that wishing does not make a belief false, and this one includes a judgement nobody simply wishes for; and that hope, as Moltmann argued, has been a protest against the world as it is. Whether it is the truest story depends on what you make of Jesus and his resurrection, which is the question this whole hall has asked.

One more thing. Notice how much of the West grew from this hope. The sense that history is a story going somewhere, rather than an endless cycle, owes much to the prophets and to Augustine's two cities, and many historians see modern ideas of progress as its secular child. The Christian refusal to treat the body as a prison, and the hope that it will be raised, stand behind the burial of the dead with honour, the building of hospitals, and the conviction that the bodies of the poor and the sick matter. The belief that every nation and language will stand before God shaped the translation of the Bible into thousands of languages. The warning that no ruler is final, and that empires are beasts when they make themselves gods, gave courage to many who resisted tyranny. And the music of the end, from the Dies irae to Messiah and Messiaen's quartet in a prison camp, is among the greatest the West has made. Whatever you conclude, you have learned where the West's sense of an ending came from.

title: Tragedy
question: Can suffering teach us?
line: Seven sessions in the theatre of Dionysus: Aeschylus on learning through suffering and on justice replacing revenge, Sophocles on Oedipus and Antigone, Euripides' dark case against the gods, and Aristotle on why we watch, ending at the cross.
why: Everyone suffers, and everyone wonders whether it means anything. The Greeks asked the question in public, every spring, in front of the whole city, and the plays they wrote are still performed. This journey spends a day at the theatre with the three great tragedians: Aeschylus, who said that Zeus has made suffering a teacher and showed a city learning to judge instead of avenge; Sophocles, who asked whether a good man can be guilty of what he did not know, and whether conscience can stand against the state; and Euripides, who asked whether the gods are just at all. Aristotle then asks why we watch, and we ask what Christianity made of tragedy, and whether the cross is one. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year classics paper on Greek tragedy (Aeschylus' Oresteia, Sophocles' Oedipus the King and Antigone, Euripides' Bacchae, Aristotle's Poetics), with elements of papers on tragedy and Christian theology.
before: homer
outcomes: Describe the City Dionysia, the competition, masks, actors and chorus, and explain why a whole city watched tragedies.
Explain Aeschylus' 'learning through suffering' (pathei mathos), the dilemma at Aulis, and how the Oresteia ends with a court replacing revenge, compared with Israel's cities of refuge.
Argue whether Oedipus is guilty, using Aristotle's hamartia correctly and distinguishing guilt in the deed from guilt in the will.
State both Creon's and Antigone's cases at full strength, explain the 'unwritten laws' and Hegel's reading, and trace the idea to natural law and Acts 5:29.
State the objection from the Bacchae and Herodotus' 'jealousy of the gods' at full strength, with Dodds' and Nietzsche's readings, and assess the Christian reply.
Explain Aristotle's definition of tragedy and the three readings of catharsis, and argue whether there can be Christian tragedy.

sessions.title: The theatre of Dionysus
sessions.line: A spring morning in Athens, a hillside full of citizens, masked actors and a singing chorus: how tragedy began, and why a whole city came to watch.
sessions.plain: Every spring, the people of Athens gave several days to a festival for the god Dionysus. On the slope below the Acropolis, thousands of citizens sat from dawn to watch plays about kings, gods and terrible choices. These were the first tragedies, and the West has never stopped writing them. This session asks what a Greek tragedy was, who wrote them, and why a city would choose to spend its holiday watching suffering.
sessions.why: This is the first session. If you have taken 'Homer and the heroes', you met Achilles, Hector and Odysseus, and a world where a great life meant glory and courage. Tragedy took the same myths and asked harder questions of them, in front of the whole city. Before we can ask whether suffering teaches, we need to see the place where the Greeks asked it.
answers: What is a Greek tragedy?
Why did a whole city spend its festival watching sad plays?
Who were the three great tragic playwrights, and when did they live?
What did a chorus do, and why did the actors wear masks?
sessions.finding: Tragedy was a civic and religious festival in which a whole city watched its own myths and asked its hardest questions: about the gods, justice and what a human being is.

paras: If you have taken 'Homer and the heroes', you know the stories the Greeks told about themselves: the war at Troy, the anger of Achilles, the long voyage home of Odysseus. Those poems were recited, not acted. By about 500 BC something new had begun in Athens: the stories were acted out, by masked performers, before an audience, with a chorus singing and dancing between the scenes.

Tragedy did not invent new stories. Almost every surviving tragedy takes its plot from the old myths: the house of Atreus, the family of Oedipus at Thebes, the heroes of the Trojan war. A later writer, Athenaeus (about AD 200), reports that Aeschylus called his plays 'slices from the great banquets of Homer'. The audience usually knew how the story ended. What they did not know was how the playwright would make them feel it, and what questions he would ask.
background.key: Tragedy took Homer's myths and acted them out before the city; the audience knew the stories, but not the questions the playwright would ask.

paras: Everyone suffers. The question is whether suffering can teach us anything, or whether it is simply pain. The Greek tragedians asked this more sharply than anyone before them, and their answers still shape how the West thinks about grief, guilt and justice.

We will follow the question through one long day at the theatre. First, the place itself. Then Aeschylus, who said that we learn by suffering, and who showed revenge turning into justice. Then Sophocles, who asked whether a good person can be destroyed by what he cannot know, or by what she must do. Then Euripides, who asked whether the gods are just at all: that is the strongest objection, and it gets a session of its own. Last, Aristotle asks why we watch, and we ask what Christianity made of tragedy.

background.key: Can suffering teach us? We spend a day at the theatre with Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, hear the case against, then let Aristotle ask why we watch.

paras: Hundreds of tragedies were written in Athens, but only thirty-two survive complete, by three men. Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC) fought the Persians at Marathon in 490 BC; seven plays survive under his name. Sophocles (about 496–406 BC) lived through Athens' whole golden age and is said to have written over a hundred and twenty plays; seven survive. Euripides (about 480–406 BC), the youngest and most disturbing, left eighteen or nineteen.

All three worked in the same century, the fifth before Christ. It was the century in which Athens beat the Persian empire, built the Parthenon, invented democracy and then fought a ruinous war with Sparta (431–404 BC), which it lost. Tragedy rose and fell with the city: it was born with Athenian freedom, and its greatest age ended with Athens' defeat.
