background.key: Only thirty-two tragedies survive, by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, all written in fifth-century Athens, the century of the Persian wars, democracy and the war with Sparta.

paras: The main reading has two short parts. The first is the opening of the oldest trilogy we have, Aeschylus' Agamemnon (458 BC): a lonely watchman on a palace roof at night, waiting for a signal fire. It shows how a tragedy began, with one actor speaking to the whole theatre. The second is a song of the chorus from Sophocles' Antigone, the 'ode to man', perhaps the most famous chorus in Greek: a hymn to human greatness that ends with a warning.

The comparison is from Aristotle, writing about a century later. He asks where tragedy came from and why we enjoy watching painful things at all, and gives the earliest history of the theatre we have.
background.key: Aeschylus' watchman shows how a play opened; Sophocles' ode to man shows what a chorus sang; Aristotle explains where tragedy came from.

before: What does the watchman want, and what does he hint at but refuse to say?
In the ode to man, list what human beings have mastered. What is the one thing they cannot master?
According to Aristotle, why do we enjoy looking at pictures of things that would upset us in real life?
sessions.readWhy: Two openings: a play beginning with one actor at night, and a chorus singing of human greatness and its limit.

paras: A Watchman

I pray the gods to quit me of my toils,
To close the watch I keep, this livelong year;
For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest,
Propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof
Of Atreus’ race, too long, too well I know
The starry conclave of the midnight sky,
Too well, the splendours of the firmament,
The lords of light, whose kingly aspect shows—
What time they set or climb the sky in turn—
The year’s divisions, bringing frost or fire.

And now, as ever, am I set to mark
When shall stream up the glow of signal-flame,
The bale-fire bright, and tell its Trojan tale—
Troy town is ta’en: such issue holds in hope
She in whose woman’s breast beats heart of man.

Thus upon mine unrestful couch I lie,
Bathed with the dews of night, unvisited
By dreams—ah me!—for in the place of sleep
Stands Fear as my familiar, and repels
The soft repose that would mine eyelids seal.
And if at whiles, for the lost balm of sleep,
I medicine my soul with melody
Of trill or song—anon to tears I turn,
Wailing the woe that broods upon this home,
Not now by honour guided as of old.

But now at last fair fall the welcome hour
That sets me free, whene’er the thick night glow
With beacon-fire of hope deferred no more.
All hail!
[A beacon-light is seen reddening the distant sky.]

Fire of the night, that brings my spirit day,
Shedding on Argos light, and dance, and song,
Greetings to fortune, hail!

Let my loud summons ring within the ears
Of Agamemnon’s queen, that she anon
Start from her couch and with a shrill voice cry
A joyous welcome to the beacon-blaze,
For Ilion’s fall; such fiery message gleams
From yon high flame; and I, before the rest,
Will foot the lightsome measure of our joy;
For I can say, My master’s dice fell fair—
Behold! the triple sice, the lucky flame!
Now be my lot to clasp, in loyal love,
The hand of him restored, who rules our home:
Home—but I say no more: upon my tongue
Treads hard the ox o’ the adage.
Had it voice,
The home itself might soothliest tell its tale;
I, of set will, speak words the wise may learn,
To others, nought remember nor discern.

CHORUS.
(Str. 1)
Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man;
Over the surging sea, with a whitening south wind wan,
Through the foam of the firth, man makes his perilous way;
And the eldest of deities Earth that knows not toil nor decay
Ever he furrows and scores, as his team, year in year out,
With breed of the yoked horse, the ploughshare turneth about.

(Ant. 1)
The light-witted birds of the air, the beasts of the weald and the wood
He traps with his woven snare, and the brood of the briny flood.
Master of cunning he: the savage bull, and the hart
Who roams the mountain free, are tamed by his infinite art;
And the shaggy rough-maned steed is broken to bear the bit.

(Str. 2)
Speech and the wind-swift speed of counsel and civic wit,
He hath learnt for himself all these; and the arrowy rain to fly
And the nipping airs that freeze, ’neath the open winter sky.
He hath provision for all: fell plague he hath learnt to endure;
Safe whate’er may befall: yet for death he hath found no cure.

(Ant. 2)
Passing the wildest flight thought are the cunning and skill,
That guide man now to the light, but now to counsels of ill.
If he honors the laws of the land, and reveres the Gods of the State
Proudly his city shall stand; but a cityless outcast I rate
Whoso bold in his pride from the path of right doth depart;
Ne’er may I sit by his side, or share the thoughts of his heart.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: A watchman on the roof
parts.who: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC), Athenian playwright and soldier
parts.when: Athens, the City Dionysia of 458 BC
parts.context: The first lines of the Oresteia, the only complete trilogy that survives. The scene is the palace of King Agamemnon at Argos (Morshead says Mycenae). Agamemnon has been away for ten years fighting at Troy. His wife Clytemnestra has posted a watchman on the roof to look for a chain of beacon fires that will announce the city's fall. The play was first performed in daylight, in the open air: the 'night' is in the words. Translated in verse by E. D. A. Morshead (1881).
parts.plain: A servant lies on the palace roof, as he has every night for a year, watching the stars and waiting for a fire on the horizon that will mean Troy has fallen. He cannot sleep for fear, and he weeps for the house, which is 'not now by honour guided'. Then the fire appears. He is overjoyed and will wake the queen. But something is wrong in this house, and he will not say what.

commentary.on: I pray the gods to quit me of my toils,
commentary.text: The oldest surviving trilogy begins with a prayer and a complaint from a nobody. Tragedy is about kings, but it often lets ordinary people speak first. The audience, thousands of them on the hillside, are put in his place: waiting in the dark.

commentary.on: For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest,
commentary.text: He compares himself to a dog. It is homely, a little comic, and very human. Greek tragedy is not all grand speeches; it mixes the high and the low.

commentary.on: She in whose woman’s breast beats heart of man.
commentary.text: The first hint of danger. The queen, Clytemnestra, has a 'heart of man': in the Greek, a mind that plans like a man's. The audience knows the myth. She is waiting for her husband to come home so that she can kill him.

commentary.on: Stands Fear as my familiar, and repels
commentary.text: Fear stands beside his bed instead of sleep. Fear is one of the two feelings Aristotle will later say tragedy is made to stir; the other is pity.

commentary.on: Not now by honour guided as of old.
commentary.text: Something has gone wrong in the house while the king was away. The watchman knows more than he says.

commentary.on: Fire of the night, that brings my spirit day,
commentary.text: The beacon blazes. In the theatre there was no fire, only an actor pointing at the sky. Greek staging was simple; the words did the work.

commentary.on: Treads hard the ox o’ the adage.
commentary.text: A proverb: 'an ox stands on my tongue', meaning 'I must keep silent'. The watchman stops himself. The house itself, he says, could tell the tale if it had a voice.

commentary.on: I, of set will, speak words the wise may learn,
commentary.text: The last line is addressed to the audience as much as to anyone: those who know will understand. Every Greek tragedy plays on this. The audience knows the end; the characters do not.

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: Many wonders
parts.who: Sophocles (about 496–406 BC), Athenian playwright
parts.context: A choral song from Antigone, first performed about 441 BC. A chorus of fifteen old men of Thebes sang and danced it in the orchestra, the round dancing floor in front of the stage. They have just heard that someone has defied the king's order and given a forbidden burial to a traitor's body. They do not yet know who did it. Their song moves from wonder to warning. The labels 'Str.' and 'Ant.' (strophe and antistrophe) mark verses danced in one direction and then the other. Translated by F. Storr (1912).
parts.plain: The chorus sings that nothing in the world is more wonderful, or more terrible, than human beings. We cross the sea, plough the earth, tame animals, and have taught ourselves speech, thought and the arts of living together in cities. We have a remedy for almost everything, except death. And our cleverness can lead to good or to evil: a person who keeps the laws and honours the gods makes a city great, and one who breaks them is an outcast.

commentary.on: Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man;
commentary.text: The Greek word translated 'wonders' is deina. It means wonderful and terrible at once: awesome, uncanny, dangerous. The whole song turns on that double meaning. Human beings are the most amazing and the most frightening thing in the world.

commentary.on: Through the foam of the firth, man makes his perilous way;
commentary.text: The list of human achievements begins with sailing and farming: mastering the sea and the earth. The Greeks were a seafaring and farming people, and these were the oldest arts they knew.

commentary.on: Speech and the wind-swift speed of counsel and civic wit,
commentary.text: Then the higher arts: language, thought, and 'civic wit', the skill of living together in a city under law. For a Greek, the city (polis) was the height of human achievement. The audience in the theatre were that city.

commentary.on: Safe whate’er may befall: yet for death he hath found no cure.
commentary.text: The turn. After all the triumphs, one limit remains. It is a very old thought: compare the psalmist's 'what is man, that you think of him?' in Psalm 8, which you may have read in 'Human dignity' or 'In the beginning'. The Hebrew poet wonders that God cares for such a small creature; the Greek chorus wonders at our power and then names its limit.

commentary.on: That guide man now to the light, but now to counsels of ill.
commentary.text: Cleverness is neutral. The same skill can lead to light or to evil. This is the warning at the heart of tragedy, and of much of Western thought since: knowledge is not the same as goodness.

commentary.on: If he honors the laws of the land, and reveres the Gods of the State
commentary.text: The chorus sides with law and the gods of the city. But notice the irony, which the audience will feel later: the person who broke the king's order is Antigone, who will claim she obeyed a higher law. Which laws, and which gods? That question is session 5, still to come.

read.author: Aeschylus and Sophocles
read.who: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC), Athenian playwright and soldier
read.when: Athens, the City Dionysia of 458 BC

paras: Poetry in general seems to have sprung from two causes, each of them lying deep in our nature. First, the instinct of imitation is implanted in man from childhood, one difference between him and other animals being that he is the most imitative of living creatures, and through imitation learns his earliest lessons; and no less universal is the pleasure felt in things imitated. We have evidence of this in the facts of experience. Objects which in themselves we view with pain, we delight to contemplate when reproduced with minute fidelity: such as the forms of the most ignoble animals and of dead bodies. The cause of this again is, that to learn gives the liveliest pleasure, not only to philosophers but to men in general; whose capacity, however, of learning is more limited. Thus the reason why men enjoy seeing a likeness is, that in contemplating it they find themselves learning or inferring, and saying perhaps, 'Ah, that is he.' For if you happen not to have seen the original, the pleasure will be due not to the imitation as such, but to the execution, the colouring, or some such other cause.

Whether Tragedy has as yet perfected its proper types or not; and whether it is to be judged in itself, or in relation also to the audience,--this raises another question. Be that as it may, Tragedy--as also Comedy--was at first mere improvisation. The one originated with the authors of the Dithyramb, the other with those of the phallic songs, which are still in use in many of our cities. Tragedy advanced by slow degrees; each new element that showed itself was in turn developed. Having passed through many changes, it found its natural form, and there it stopped.

Aeschylus first introduced a second actor; he diminished the importance of the Chorus, and assigned the leading part to the dialogue. Sophocles raised the number of actors to three, and added scene-painting. Moreover, it was not till late that the short plot was discarded for one of greater compass, and the grotesque diction of the earlier satyric form for the stately manner of Tragedy. The iambic measure then replaced the trochaic tetrameter, which was originally employed when the poetry was of the Satyric order, and had greater affinities with dancing. Once dialogue had come in, Nature herself discovered the appropriate measure. For the iambic is, of all measures, the most colloquial: we see it in the fact that conversational speech runs into iambic lines more frequently than into any other kind of verse; rarely into hexameters, and only when we drop the colloquial intonation. The additions to the number of 'episodes' or acts, and the other accessories of which tradition; tells, must be taken as already described; for to discuss them in detail would, doubtless, be a large undertaking.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: The pleasure of imitation
parts.context: Aristotle (384–322 BC) studied under Plato in Athens and later taught there himself. His Poetics, probably lecture notes from about 335 BC, is the first book of literary criticism in the West. Here he explains why people make poetry and drama at all, and sketches the history of tragedy. Translated by S. H. Butcher (1895). The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Aristotle says we are natural imitators, and we enjoy imitations, even of things that are painful to see in real life, such as corpses, because looking at them teaches us something. Tragedy began with improvised songs for Dionysus, called dithyrambs. Aeschylus added a second actor and gave the speaking more weight than the singing; Sophocles added a third actor and painted scenery. Then tragedy found its proper form and stopped changing.

commentary.on: Objects which in themselves we view with pain, we delight to contemplate when reproduced with minute fidelity
commentary.text: Here is Aristotle's first answer to the puzzle of this session: why would anyone enjoy watching suffering? Because an imitation is not the thing itself. We can look at it steadily, and we learn from it. Hold on to this. Aristotle's fuller answer, catharsis, is the subject of session 7, still to come.

commentary.on: to learn gives the liveliest pleasure, not only to philosophers but to men in general
commentary.text: For Aristotle, the pleasure of drama is a pleasure of understanding. That already half-answers the journey's question: if we enjoy tragedy because we learn from it, then suffering, at least suffering shown, can teach.

commentary.on: The one originated with the authors of the Dithyramb
commentary.text: A dithyramb was a hymn to Dionysus sung and danced by a chorus. Aristotle thinks tragedy grew out of it when the leader of the chorus began to speak alone. Scholars still debate how this happened; Aristotle is our oldest witness, writing a century and a half after the event.

commentary.on: Aeschylus first introduced a second actor; he diminished the importance of the Chorus, and assigned the leading part to the dialogue.
commentary.text: With two actors, characters can argue. That is the birth of drama as we know it: conflict between people on a stage, not just a story told by one voice.

commentary.on: Sophocles raised the number of actors to three, and added scene-painting.
commentary.text: Three actors, never more, played every speaking part by changing masks. A whole tragedy, with kings, queens, messengers and gods, was acted by three men and a chorus.

compare.author: Aristotle
compare.why: Aristotle, writing about a century after these plays, gives the oldest account of how tragedy began and why we enjoy watching painful things at all.
compare.title: Where tragedy came from

paras: Tragedy was not entertainment in our sense. It was part of a religious festival, the City Dionysia, held every spring in Athens in honour of Dionysus, the god of wine, of ecstasy and of the theatre. The festival opened with a procession bringing the god's statue into his theatre on the south slope of the Acropolis, with sacrifices and singing. Only then did the plays begin.

The plays were a competition. Each year an official chose three playwrights. Each presented three tragedies and a short comic 'satyr play', on one day, from early morning. A wealthy citizen paid for each playwright's chorus as a public duty; this was called the choregia. At the end, judges chosen by lot awarded first, second and third prizes. Aeschylus won first prize thirteen times, Sophocles perhaps eighteen or more; Euripides, the greatest of them in the eyes of many later readers, won only four times in his life.
sections.key: Tragedy was a religious competition at the City Dionysia: three playwrights, each with three tragedies and a satyr play, judged by citizens.

sections.h: The whole city in the audience
paras: The theatre of Dionysus held many thousands: estimates for the fifth century range from about six thousand to more than fifteen thousand. In a city of perhaps thirty to fifty thousand adult male citizens, that was a large part of the people. Before the plays, the city held ceremonies of its own: the tribute of its allies was displayed, and young men whose fathers had died in battle, raised at public expense, paraded in armour.

So the audience watched as citizens. The same people who sat in the theatre also sat in the Assembly, which voted on war and peace, and on the juries of the law courts. The plays put before them questions they faced as a democracy: who should rule, whether law can replace revenge, what a city owes the dead and the gods. Whether women attended is debated; the evidence is thin either way.
sections.key: The audience was the citizen body of a democracy, watching its own myths and its own questions.

paras: All the actors were men, and all wore masks of linen or wood covering the whole head. A mask let one actor play several parts, including women and gods, and it made faces readable from the back rows. Most scenes have only two speakers, and never more than three.

The chorus, twelve and later fifteen men, sang and danced in the orchestra, the round floor in front of the stage building. They usually play a group, such as the old men of Thebes or the women of a city, and they react to what happens: they fear, mourn, warn and pray. A tragedy alternates between spoken scenes (episodes) and choral songs (odes). The chorus is a little like the audience on stage: it is ordinary, often wrong, and always present.
sections.key: Masked male actors, never more than three, spoke the scenes; a chorus of twelve to fifteen sang and danced between them.

paras: The Greek word tragoidia probably means 'goat-song'. Nobody is sure why: perhaps a goat was the prize, or was sacrificed. A Greek tragedy was not defined by an unhappy ending. Several end in reconciliation, as the Oresteia does. What they share is seriousness: great people from the old myths, under great pressure, making choices that matter, often between two goods or two evils.

Our word 'tragic' now often means only 'very sad'. The Greek idea is sharper. A tragedy shows a person of real stature brought low, usually by something that is partly their own doing and partly not. It forces the audience to ask why: the gods, fate, human error, the clash of duties. It gives no easy answer, and it does not let you look away.
sections.key: A Greek tragedy is a serious play about great figures under pressure; it need not end unhappily, but it always asks why people suffer.

paras: The ode to man shows what the tragedians thought about human beings. We are deina: wonderful and terrible. We have conquered the sea, the earth and the animals, and taught ourselves speech and law. Everything yields to us except death. And the same skill that builds a city can destroy it.

This double view runs through the whole tradition. The Bible says human beings are made 'a little lower than the angels' (Psalm 8:5) and also that 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jeremiah 17:9). Pascal would call man 'a thinking reed'. The Greek theatre gave the West its first great public image of it: a human being, magnificent and fragile, under the open sky, in front of everyone.
sections.key: Tragedy sees human beings as deina, wonderful and terrible at once: masters of everything except death and themselves.

sections.h: Did it matter that it was religious?
paras: It is easy to treat Greek tragedy as literature that happened to be performed at a festival. That misses something. The plays were offered to a god, in his sanctuary, with his priest in the front row. They are full of prayers, oracles, curses and sacrifices, and their deepest questions are religious: are the gods just? Can a polluted person be made clean? What do we owe the dead?

Yet the Greeks had no creed and no scripture, and their gods were not good in the way the God of the Bible is said to be good. That left the tragedians free to ask questions a priest could not. The Christian West inherited both things from Athens: the habit of asking the hardest questions in public, and an art that takes suffering seriously enough to look at it.
sections.key: Tragedy was worship as well as art; because Greek religion had no creed, its poets could put the gods themselves on trial.

refs: Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1–39; Sophocles, Antigone 332–375; Aristotle, Poetics IV (1448b–1449a).
Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 8.347e (Aeschylus' 'slices from the banquets of Homer').
On the festival: A. W. Pickard-Cambridge, The Dramatic Festivals of Athens (1953; 2nd ed. 1968); Simon Goldhill, 'The Great Dionysia and Civic Ideology', Journal of Hellenic Studies 107 (1987).
Victory counts: the ancient Lives of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides and the Suda; see Oliver Taplin, Greek Tragedy in Action (1978); Edith Hall, Greek Tragedy: Suffering under the Sun (2010).
Psalm 8:4–5; Jeremiah 17:9; Pascal, Pensées (the thinking reed).

debate.question: Was Greek tragedy a religious ritual or a civic event?

positions.name: A ritual for Dionysus
positions.who: Walter Burkert, 'Greek Tragedy and Sacrificial Ritual' (1966); Richard Seaford, Reciprocity and Ritual (1994)
positions.view: Tragedy grew out of the worship of Dionysus and kept the shape of ritual: sacrifice, lament and the death of a victim. Its power comes from that religious core.
positions.evidence: The festival setting, the priest of Dionysus in the front row, the dithyramb origin in Aristotle, and the many sacrifices and ritual deaths in the plays.

positions.name: A festival of the city
positions.who: Simon Goldhill, 'The Great Dionysia and Civic Ideology' (1987); John J. Winkler and Froma Zeitlin (eds.), Nothing to Do with Dionysos? (1990)
positions.view: Tragedy was an institution of the democracy. Its ceremonies displayed the city's power, and its plays questioned the city's values in front of its citizens.
positions.evidence: The display of allied tribute and the parade of war orphans before the plays; the plays' constant concern with law, rule and the city.

positions.name: Both, inseparably
positions.who: Many recent scholars, including Christiane Sourvinou-Inwood, Tragedy and Athenian Religion (2003)
positions.view: In Athens religion and politics were not separate. Worshipping the city's gods and asking the city's questions were one act.
positions.evidence: The same citizens were worshippers, voters and jurors; the plays mix prayer and politics in every scene.

debate.agree: All agree that tragedy was performed before the whole citizen body at a festival of Dionysus, and that it asked the city's deepest questions in public.

look.why: Few paintings show a Greek theatre. Louise-Joséphine Sarazin de Belmont painted the ancient theatre at Taormina in Sicily in 1828. The theatre there was first built by Greeks and later rebuilt by the Romans, which is why the gallery calls it 'The Roman Theater'. The theatre of Dionysus in Athens would have looked out over the city in the same way: an open hillside, a curving wall, the sky.
points: A curving stone wall set into the earth runs in a shallow U from the left edge of the painting towards us and off to the right.
Two tiny men in long brown robes, with bald heads ringed with hair, stand on the grass and speak to a young boy, who holds a hand to his head.
Beyond the wall, honey-brown stone ruins sit in a shallow valley between a rust-brown cliff on the left and a steep steel-grey mountain on the right.
Buildings cluster along a cliff above a coastline of ice-blue water.
In the distance, smoke pours from a snow-tipped mountain under a pale blue sky.

music.why: Vaughan Williams wrote this music to fill a great building with sound, as a chorus once filled an open-air theatre: an old tune, sung again and again in a vast space.

think.why: The ode to man asks what a human being is: wonderful and terrible. See what Christians have said about human greatness and its limits.

learn.why: The most famous chorus in Greek, on human greatness and the one thing we cannot master.

check.q: Why does the session call the audience of a tragedy 'the city'?
options: Because the actors were elected by the citizens
Because thousands of citizens, the same people who voted in the Assembly and sat on juries, watched together at a public festival
Because the plays were always set in Athens
Because only the city's officials were allowed in
check.why: The theatre held a large part of the citizen body, who watched as citizens; most plays were set elsewhere, in Thebes or Argos.

check.q: The Greek word deina in the ode to man means both 'wonderful' and 'terrible'. What does that double meaning suggest about the chorus's view of human beings?
options: That the same human powers which build cities can also destroy them
That the chorus could not decide which word to use
That humans are wonderful and the gods are terrible
That only clever people are dangerous
check.why: The ode ends by saying cleverness leads 'now to the light, but now to counsels of ill'.

check.q: According to Aristotle, why do people enjoy imitations of painful things, such as corpses?
options: Because the imitation teaches them something, and learning gives pleasure
Because they are cruel by nature
Because the colours are beautiful
Because the gods command it
check.why: 'To learn gives the liveliest pleasure'; colour and execution are only a secondary pleasure, when you have not seen the original.

check.q: What did Aeschylus' second actor make possible?
options: Dialogue and conflict between characters on stage
Scene-painting
The satyr play
Women's parts
check.why: With two actors, characters can argue; Aristotle says Aeschylus 'assigned the leading part to the dialogue'. Scene-painting came with Sophocles.

check.q: Which of these is true of a Greek tragedy?
options: It was performed indoors at night
It usually retold an old myth, and could end in reconciliation
It always ended with the hero's death
It was always a new story invented by the playwright
check.why: The plots came from myth, and the Oresteia ends in reconciliation; the plays were performed in daylight, in the open air.

check.q: Why does the watchman stop himself ('an ox stands on my tongue')?
options: He knows something is wrong in the house but dares not say it
He wants the queen to tell the news herself
He is about to fall asleep
He has forgotten the story
check.why: He hints that the house is 'not now by honour guided' and says the house itself could tell the tale; the audience knows the queen plans murder.

tutorial.question: Why would a city spend its great festival watching tragedies?
tutorial.approach: Describe the City Dionysia: its religious setting, the competition, the audience. Then use the ode to man and Aristotle's account of the pleasure of imitation to suggest what the citizens gained. Weigh the religious and the civic explanations. End with whether anything in our own society plays the same part.
strong: Describes the festival accurately: Dionysus, the competition, three tragedies and a satyr play, the citizen audience.
Explains the role of masks, actors and chorus.
Uses the ode to man to show the questions tragedy asked about human beings.
Uses Aristotle's point that we learn from imitations of painful things.
Weighs the religious and civic explanations fairly.
Draws a thoughtful comparison with today (theatre, film, public mourning).

reading.author: Edith Hall
reading.title: Greek Tragedy: Suffering under the Sun
reading.why: A lively, wide-ranging introduction to the plays and their world.

reading.author: Oliver Taplin
reading.title: Greek Tragedy in Action
reading.why: How the plays worked on stage: entrances, masks, silences.

reading.author: A. W. Pickard-Cambridge
reading.title: The Dramatic Festivals of Athens
reading.why: The standard collection of the evidence for the festivals.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: watch, read or listen to one serious drama (a play, a film, or a tragedy on the radio) with someone else, and afterwards talk for ten minutes about what it asked you. Tragedy was meant to be shared, not consumed alone.
sessions.reflect: When did you last see something sad that made you understand more, not less? What did it teach you?
takeaways: Tragedy was a religious and civic festival: three playwrights, masked actors and a chorus, watched by the citizen body of Athens.
Its plots came from the old myths; its power lay in the questions it asked about gods, justice and human beings.
The ode to man calls us deina, wonderful and terrible, and Aristotle says we enjoy tragedy because imitations of pain teach us.

sessions.title: Learning through suffering
sessions.line: A king kills his daughter so that his fleet can sail, and an old chorus sings that Zeus has made a law: we learn by suffering.
sessions.plain: Aeschylus' Agamemnon begins with old men remembering how their king sacrificed his own daughter, Iphigenia, ten years earlier, to get a wind for the war against Troy. In the middle of that memory they sing a hymn to Zeus, which says that the god has laid down a law: wisdom comes through suffering, even to those who do not want it. This session asks what that famous idea means, whether it is comfort or warning, and how the New Testament says something strikingly similar.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed the place: a festival where a whole city watched its myths. Now we hear the first great answer to the journey's question. Aeschylus is the oldest of the three playwrights, and his answer is the most hopeful: suffering is not meaningless, because Zeus has made it a teacher.
answers: What does 'learning through suffering' mean?
Why did Agamemnon sacrifice his daughter, and was he to blame?
Is suffering a punishment, a lesson, or both?
Does the Bible say anything like it?
sessions.finding: Aeschylus taught that Zeus has laid down a law that we learn by suffering, and that wisdom comes even to the unwilling; but in his play the lesson comes too late for those who suffer it.

paras: In session 1 we met the watchman on the roof of Agamemnon's palace, waiting for the fire that would announce the fall of Troy. Now the chorus enters: old men of the city, too old to have gone to war ten years before. While they wait for news, they remember how the war began.

The myth runs like this. Paris, a prince of Troy, took Helen, the wife of the Greek king Menelaus. Menelaus' brother Agamemnon, the most powerful king in Greece, led a great fleet to win her back. The fleet gathered at Aulis, on the coast opposite the island of Euboea. There the winds stopped, and the army began to starve. The prophet Calchas declared that the goddess Artemis was angry, and that only one thing would release the winds: Agamemnon must sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia.
background.key: The chorus of old men remembers Aulis: the fleet stranded, and the prophet's demand that Agamemnon sacrifice his daughter.

background.h: The curse on the house of Atreus
paras: Agamemnon's family was cursed long before Aulis. His father Atreus had quarrelled with his own brother Thyestes and, in revenge, killed Thyestes' children and served them to him at a feast. Thyestes cursed the house. The one son he had left, Aegisthus, grew up wanting revenge.

So the Oresteia is the story of a family in which every killing calls for another. Agamemnon kills his daughter; his wife Clytemnestra, with Aegisthus as her lover, will kill Agamemnon when he returns; their son Orestes will kill his mother. Aeschylus asks whether this chain can ever be broken. That question belongs to session 3, still to come. Here, the chorus asks something more personal: what can anyone learn from such suffering?

timeline.text: Atreus kills his brother's children; Thyestes curses the house
At Aulis, Agamemnon sacrifices Iphigenia; the fleet sails for Troy
Troy falls; Agamemnon returns and Clytemnestra kills him
Their son Orestes returns and kills his mother
Orestes, pursued by the Furies, is tried at Athens

background.key: The house of Atreus is cursed: every killing calls for another, from Thyestes' feast to Iphigenia, Agamemnon and Clytemnestra.

paras: Aeschylus was born about 525 BC at Eleusis, near Athens. He fought against the Persians at Marathon in 490 BC, where his brother was killed, and probably at Salamis ten years later. His epitaph, which he is said to have written himself, mentions only that he fought at Marathon, not his plays.

He wrote between seventy and ninety plays, by ancient reports; seven survive under his name. The Oresteia (Agamemnon, The Libation-Bearers and The Eumenides) won first prize in 458 BC, two years before his death in Sicily. Its language is dense, majestic and hard, even for Greeks: in Aristophanes' comedy The Frogs (405 BC), the god Dionysus goes down to the underworld and judges a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides, and Aeschylus' long, thundering words are part of the joke.
background.key: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC) fought at Marathon and wrote the Oresteia, the only complete trilogy we have, in 458 BC.

paras: The main reading has three parts, all sung by the chorus of Agamemnon. First, the hymn to Zeus, with the famous words about learning through suffering. Second, the chorus's memory of Aulis: Agamemnon's choice and the death of Iphigenia. Third, a few lines from near the end of the play, after Agamemnon has been killed, where the chorus states the law of the house: the doer must suffer.

The comparison is from the New Testament letter to the Hebrews, which uses the same Greek play on words about Jesus: he 'learned obedience by the things which he suffered'. Read the two side by side and ask whether they mean the same thing.
background.key: The hymn to Zeus, the sacrifice at Aulis, the law of the house; then Hebrews on Jesus learning through suffering.

before: In the hymn, what has Zeus 'ruled' or laid down for human beings?
At Aulis, what two evils is Agamemnon caught between? What does he choose, and how does the chorus describe the moment he chooses?
Does the chorus think suffering is a punishment, a lesson, or both?
sessions.readWhy: The first and most hopeful answer to the journey's question, set beside the worst thing a father can do.

paras:
Zeus—if to The Unknown
That name of many names seem good—
Zeus, upon Thee I call.
Thro’ the mind’s every road
I passed, but vain are all,
Save that which names thee Zeus, the Highest One,
Were it but mine to cast away the load,
The weary load, that weighs my spirit down.

He that was Lord of old,
In full-blown pride of place and valour bold,
Hath fallen and is gone, even as an old tale told!
And he that next held sway,
By stronger grasp o’erthrown
Hath pass’d away!
And whoso now shall bid the triumph-chant arise
To Zeus, and Zeus alone,
He shall be found the truly wise.
’Tis Zeus alone who shows the perfect way
Of knowledge: He hath ruled,
Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled.

In visions of the night, like dropping rain,
Descend the many memories of pain
Before the spirit’s sight: through tears and dole
Comes wisdom o’er the unwilling soul—
A boon, I wot, of all Divinity,
That holds its sacred throne in strength, above the sky!

And then the elder chief, at whose command
The fleet of Greece was manned,
Cast on the seer no word of hate,
But veered before the sudden breath of Fate—

Ah, weary while! for, ere they put forth sail,
Did every store, each minish’d vessel, fail,
While all the Achaean host
At Aulis anchored lay,
Looking across to Chalics and the coast
Where refluent waters welter, rock, and sway;
And rife with ill delay
From northern Strymon blew the thwarting blast—
Mother of famine fell,
That holds men wand’ring still
Far from the haven where they fain would be!—
And pitiless did waste
Each ship and cable, rotting on the sea,
And, doubling with delay each weary hour,
Withered with hope deferred th’ Achaeans’ warlike flower.

But when, for bitter storm, a deadlier relief,
And heavier with ill to either chief,
Pleading the ire of Artemis, the seer avowed,
The two Atridae smote their sceptres on the plain,
And, striving hard, could not their tears restrain!
And then the elder monarch spake aloud—
Ill lot were mine, to disobey!
And ill, to smite my child, my household’s love and pride!
To stain with virgin blood a father’s hands, and slay
My daughter, by the altar’s side!
’Twixt woe and woe I dwell—
I dare not like a recreant fly,
And leave the league of ships, and fail each true ally;
For rightfully they crave, with eager fiery mind,
The virgin’s blood, shed forth to lull the adverse wind—
God send the deed be well!

Thus on his neck he took
Fate’s hard compelling yoke;
Then, in the counter-gale of will abhorr’d, accursed,
To recklessness his shifting spirit veered—
Alas! that Frenzy, first of ills and worst,
With evil craft men’s souls to sin hath ever stirred!

And so he steeled his heart—ah, well-a-day—
Aiding a war for one false woman’s sake,
His child to slay,
And with her spilt blood make
An offering, to speed the ships upon their way!

Lusting for war, the bloody arbiters
Closed heart and ears, and would nor hear nor heed
The girl-voice plead,
Pity me, Father! nor her prayers,
Nor tender, virgin years.

So, when the chant of sacrifice was done,
Her father bade the youthful priestly train
Raise her, like some poor kid, above the altar-stone,
From where amid her robes she lay
Sunk all in swoon away—
Bade them, as with the bit that mutely tames the steed,
Her fair lips’ speech refrain,
Lest she should speak a curse on Atreus’ home and seed,

So, trailing on the earth her robe of saffron dye,
With one last piteous dart from her beseeching eye
Those that should smite she smote—
Fair, silent, as a pictur’d form, but fain
To plead, Is all forgot?
How oft those halls of old,
Wherein my sire high feast did hold,
Rang to the virginal soft strain,
When I, a stainless child,
Sang from pure lips and undefiled,
Sang of my sire, and all
His honoured life, and how on him should fall
Heaven’s highest gift and gain!
And then—but I beheld not, nor can tell,
What further fate befel:
But this is sure, that Calchas’ boding strain
Can ne’er be void or vain.
This wage from Justice’ hand do sufferers earn,
The future to discern:
And yet—farewell, O secret of To-morrow!
Fore-knowledge is fore-sorrow.
Clear with the clear beams of the morrow’s sun,
The future presseth on.
Now, let the house’s tale, how dark soe’er,
Find yet an issue fair!—
So prays the loyal, solitary band
That guards the Apian land.

CHORUS
Lo! sin by sin and sorrow dogg’d by sorrow—
And who the end can know?
The slayer of to-day shall die to-morrow—
The wage of wrong is woe.
While Time shall be, while Zeus in heaven is lord,
His law is fixed and stern;
On him that wrought shall vengeance be outpoured—
The tides of doom return.
The children of the curse abide within
These halls of high estate—
And none can wrench from off the home of sin
The clinging grasp of fate.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: The hymn to Zeus
parts.who: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC), Athenian playwright and soldier
parts.when: Athens, the City Dionysia of 458 BC
parts.context: The chorus of old men of Argos are in the middle of telling the story of Aulis. Before they reach the worst of it, they break off and pray to Zeus, the king of the gods. This short hymn is the most quoted passage in Aeschylus. Morshead's verse is old-fashioned; read it slowly, and use the plain words below.
parts.plain: Zeus, whoever you are, if that is the name you like: I have thought about everything, and only Zeus can lift the weight from my mind. The old gods who ruled before him have fallen. Whoever praises Zeus is truly wise, because Zeus has set human beings on the road to understanding by this law: we learn by suffering. Even in sleep, the memory of pain drips on the heart, and wisdom comes to us against our will. This is the grace of the gods who rule from heaven, though it comes with force.

commentary.on: Zeus—if to The Unknown
commentary.text: The prayer begins with uncertainty. 'Zeus, whoever he is': the chorus is not sure of God's true name or nature. This humility before the unknown divine is one of the things early Christians admired in the Greeks; Paul in Athens would speak of an altar 'to an unknown god' (Acts 17:23).

commentary.on: He that was Lord of old,
commentary.text: In Greek myth, Zeus overthrew his father Cronos, who had overthrown his father Ouranos. Even the gods have a history of violence. But the chorus sees in Zeus's victory something final: the last ruler, whose rule is wisdom.

commentary.on: Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled.
commentary.text: This is the heart of it. In Greek it is two words: pathei mathos, 'by suffering, learning'. Zeus has made it a law. The two words sound alike in Greek (pathos, suffering; mathos, learning), and the Greeks had long used the pair in proverbs. Aeschylus turns a proverb into a theology: suffering is not random; it is part of the way the world is ruled.

commentary.on: Descend the many memories of pain
commentary.text: Suffering teaches through memory. Even asleep, the pain drips on the heart 'like dropping rain'. This is not a quick lesson but a slow one, the kind grief teaches over years.

commentary.on: Comes wisdom o’er the unwilling soul—
commentary.text: We do not choose the lesson. Wisdom comes 'to the unwilling'. That is honest: nobody wants to learn this way.

commentary.on: A boon, I wot, of all Divinity,
commentary.text: 'A boon': in Greek, a charis, a grace or favour, from gods who sit on their thrones 'in strength'. The Greek is often translated 'a violent grace'. Robert Kennedy, announcing the murder of Martin Luther King to a crowd in Indianapolis on 4 April 1968, quoted this passage in Edith Hamilton's translation, ending with 'the awful grace of God'. A grace, but an awful one.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: The sacrifice at Aulis
parts.context: The chorus returns to the story. The Greek fleet is stranded at Aulis by contrary winds, the army starving. The prophet Calchas has said that Artemis demands the sacrifice of Agamemnon's daughter Iphigenia. Agamemnon is 'the elder chief'; his brother Menelaus is the other of 'the two Atridae' (sons of Atreus). Some readers will find this passage hard to read. It is meant to be.
parts.plain: The fleet waits for weeks; ships rot, men starve. When the prophet names the price, both kings weep. Agamemnon says that either choice is terrible: to kill his child, or to desert his army and allies. Then he 'puts on the yoke of necessity' and his mind turns reckless. He has his daughter gagged so that she cannot curse the house, and lifted onto the altar like a young goat. Her eyes plead with each man. The chorus cannot bring itself to describe the killing. They only say that justice makes those who suffer learn, and that knowing the future early is only grieving early.

commentary.on: Pleading the ire of Artemis, the seer avowed,
commentary.text: Why is Artemis angry? Aeschylus is vague, perhaps deliberately. Earlier in the song, two eagles tear a pregnant hare, an omen of the Greeks destroying Troy and its unborn children, and Artemis, who protects the young, hates the omen. The gods' reasons are not fully clear to the people who must obey them.

commentary.on: Ill lot were mine, to disobey!
commentary.text: Agamemnon's dilemma in his own words: disobey the gods and desert the army, or 'smite my child'. Both are wrong. This is what makes the scene tragic and not simply wicked: a man caught between two duties.

commentary.on: Fate’s hard compelling yoke;
commentary.text: In Greek, 'he put on the harness of necessity'. Notice the paradox. It is necessity, yet he 'put it on'. He chose it. Ever since, readers have argued whether Agamemnon was forced or guilty. Aeschylus seems to say: both.

commentary.on: To recklessness his shifting spirit veered—
commentary.text: The chorus does not blame the choice alone; it blames what happened inside him once he made it. His mind 'veered' to daring everything. A man who must do a terrible thing should do it with horror. Agamemnon begins to do it with zeal.

commentary.on: Aiding a war for one false woman’s sake,
commentary.text: The chorus also judges the cause. A whole war, and a daughter's life, for Helen. Aeschylus does not let the audience forget the cost of glory, which Homer's heroes counted so highly.

commentary.on: Pity me, Father!
commentary.text: The only words of Iphigenia we hear, and they are a memory of her pleading. Then she is gagged 'lest she should speak a curse'. The silencing of the victim is part of the horror.

commentary.on: Raise her, like some poor kid, above the altar-stone,
commentary.text: She is lifted 'like a young goat'. The ritual of animal sacrifice, which the audience had just watched at the festival's opening, is turned on a human child. Tragedy uses the city's own rituals to make it see.

commentary.on: And then—but I beheld not, nor can tell,
commentary.text: The chorus refuses to describe the death. Greek tragedy almost never shows killing on stage; it reports it, or falls silent. The silence is louder than a description.

commentary.on: This wage from Justice’ hand do sufferers earn,
commentary.text: The law of the hymn again, now spoken by Justice (Dike): those who suffer are given to learn. But who learns here? Not Iphigenia, who is dead. This is the hard edge of Aeschylus' idea: the lesson often comes to others, or too late.

commentary.on: Fore-knowledge is fore-sorrow.
commentary.text: A bitter little proverb. Knowing what is coming does not help; it only means grieving sooner. The chorus can see the end of this house, and it does not comfort them.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: The doer must suffer
parts.context: Near the end of the play. Agamemnon has come home from Troy and Clytemnestra has killed him in his bath. She claims she has avenged Iphigenia. The chorus answers with the old law of the house.
parts.plain: Wrong answers wrong, and no one can see where it ends. Whoever kills will be killed. As long as Zeus rules, his law stands: the one who does wrong must suffer. The curse is fixed to this house and no one can pull it off.

commentary.on: The slayer of to-day shall die to-morrow—
commentary.text: This is the logic of revenge, stated as law: every killer becomes the next victim. Clytemnestra has just killed for her daughter; she too will be killed.

commentary.on: On him that wrought shall vengeance be outpoured—
commentary.text: In Greek, pathein ton erxanta: 'the doer must suffer'. The same verb as pathei mathos. So in Aeschylus suffering is both punishment (the doer must suffer) and teaching (by suffering, learning). The question is whether anyone ever learns enough to stop the cycle.

commentary.on: The clinging grasp of fate.
commentary.text: The chorus ends in despair: the curse is 'glued' to the house. If suffering teaches, here it has not yet taught. Aeschylus will need a third play, and a new idea, to answer this.

read.author: Aeschylus
read.who: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC), Athenian playwright and soldier
read.when: Athens, the City Dionysia of 458 BC

paras: He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear,
though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.
Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation,
It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children, for what son is there whom his father doesn’t discipline?
But if you are without discipline, of which all have been made partakers, then you are illegitimate, and not children.
Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh to chasten us, and we paid them respect. Shall we not much rather be in subjection to the Father of spirits, and live?
For they indeed, for a few days, punished us as seemed good to them; but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness.
All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

parts.title: Learned by suffering
parts.context: Hebrews is an early Christian sermon in letter form, written in polished Greek before or soon after AD 70 by an unknown author. It presents Jesus as the great high priest. Here the writer speaks of Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane before his death.

commentary.on: with strong crying and tears
commentary.text: Jesus is not shown as calm. He cries out and weeps, like the chorus with its 'tears and dole'. Christianity did not begin by denying the pain of suffering.

commentary.on: yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered
commentary.text: In Greek: emathen aph' hōn epathen, 'he learned from what he suffered'. It is the same pair of words Aeschylus used, and the same old proverb. A reader who knew Greek literature would have heard the echo at once.

commentary.on: Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation
commentary.text: Here the two ideas part. In Aeschylus, the sufferer learns, often too late, and the cycle goes on. In Hebrews, the sufferer is God's Son, who does not need to learn from his own wrongdoing, and his suffering becomes salvation for others. The lesson is not kept by the one who suffers; it is given away.

parts.title: A father's training
parts.context: Later in the same letter, the writer turns to his readers, who are facing hardship and persecution, and tells them how to see it.

commentary.on: God deals with you as with children
commentary.text: Suffering is pictured as a father's discipline. It is a striking contrast with Aulis, where a father destroys his child for a war. Here the father trains the child for its own good.

commentary.on: but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness
commentary.text: Human fathers discipline 'as seemed good to them'; God's purpose is to share his own holiness. Suffering has an aim, and the aim is the sufferer's good.

commentary.on: All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous
commentary.text: The writer does not pretend it feels good. Like Aeschylus, he admits the lesson comes against our will.

commentary.on: yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it
commentary.text: 'Trained' is the Greek word for exercise in the gymnasium. Suffering can form a person, like training forms an athlete. But notice the condition: 'to those who have been trained by it'. Not all suffering teaches; it depends on what it is and how it is borne.

compare.why: The letter to the Hebrews, written in Greek in the first century, uses the same old play on words, pathein and mathein, about Jesus himself. Then it speaks of suffering as a father's training. Is this Aeschylus' idea, or a different one?
compare.title: He learned obedience by what he suffered

paras: The two Greek words pathei mathos, 'by suffering, learning', are among the most quoted in ancient literature. They were not new. Herodotus has the defeated king Croesus say 'my sufferings have been my lessons', and a proverb said that fools learn by suffering. Aeschylus took the folk saying and made it a law of Zeus.

That is a large claim. It says the world is not random. The supreme god rules it, and he has arranged it so that pain leads to understanding. Suffering is not only something that happens to us; it is part of a moral order. In this, Aeschylus is closer to the Hebrew prophets than to Homer, whose gods quarrel and play favourites.
sections.key: Aeschylus turned a proverb into a theology: Zeus has made suffering the road to wisdom.

paras: Aeschylus uses the same Greek verb, paschein, 'to suffer', in two ways. 'By suffering, learning' (line 177) makes suffering a teacher. 'The doer must suffer' (line 1564) makes it a punishment. Both are laws of Zeus.

The two ideas fit together. If you do wrong, you will suffer; and if you suffer, you may learn not to do wrong. But in the Agamemnon the second half rarely happens. Agamemnon does not learn; Clytemnestra does not learn. The house learns nothing for a generation. That is why the chorus is both hopeful and despairing: they believe in the law, and they see it grinding on without anyone learning from it.
sections.key: In Aeschylus suffering is both punishment ('the doer must suffer') and teacher ('by suffering, learning'); the tragedy is that the lesson comes late.

paras: Readers have argued about Aulis for two and a half thousand years. Agamemnon seems to have no good choice. If he refuses, the army starves, the gods' will is defied and Troy goes unpunished. If he obeys, he kills his child. Philosophers call this a tragic dilemma: a situation where every option involves a real wrong.

Aeschylus does not let him off. The chorus blames not only the choice but the way he made it: his mind 'veered' to recklessness; he 'steeled his heart'; he had his daughter gagged. The American philosopher Martha Nussbaum, in The Fragility of Goodness (1986), argued that this is the point. A good person forced to do wrong should feel the full horror of it, and Agamemnon does not. Even when we cannot avoid doing wrong, how we do it still matters.
sections.key: Aulis is a tragic dilemma with no clean choice; Aeschylus blames Agamemnon less for choosing than for choosing with a hardened heart.

paras: The hardest question about pathei mathos is: who learns? Iphigenia learns nothing; she dies. The lesson seems to go to the survivors and the onlookers: the chorus, and above all the audience. That is one reason the Greeks watched tragedy. They could learn from suffering without having to suffer it themselves.

Robert Kennedy understood this. On the night Martin Luther King was murdered in April 1968, he told a mainly Black crowd in Indianapolis the news, spoke of his own brother's murder five years earlier, and quoted Aeschylus. His point was that grief could lead either to bitterness and revenge or to wisdom and compassion, and he asked the crowd to choose the second. Indianapolis stayed calm that night while many American cities burned. Two months later Kennedy himself was shot.
sections.key: Suffering may teach the onlookers more than the sufferer; Robert Kennedy used Aeschylus in 1968 to turn grief away from revenge.

paras: The letter to the Hebrews says that Jesus 'learned obedience by the things which he suffered'. The writer uses the same old pair of words, and probably knew the proverb. So there is a real echo between Athens and Jerusalem. Both say suffering can teach, both admit it comes against our will, and both see a purpose above it.

The differences matter as much. In Aeschylus, the one who learns is usually the one who did wrong, and the lesson comes too late to save anyone. In Hebrews, the one who suffers is innocent, and his suffering becomes salvation for others. And Hebrews pictures God as a father training his children, the opposite of Agamemnon sacrificing his. The Christian claim is not that suffering is good, but that God can bring good out of it, and that he does not stand outside it.

rows: Mostly the guilty, and their families
Jesus, the innocent Son; and believers
The survivors and onlookers, often too late
The sufferer, and those who are 'trained by it'
Zeus, who rules by force; a 'violent grace'
A Father who trains his children for their good
The cycle of revenge goes on, until a new answer is found
table.note: The same Greek words, two different pictures of what suffering is for.

sections.key: Hebrews uses Aeschylus' words but changes the picture: the innocent suffers for others, and God is a father, not a force.

paras: Modern psychologists have studied what they call post-traumatic growth: some people report that after a serious loss or trauma they value life more, feel closer to others or find a new sense of purpose. Others do not; many are simply harmed, and some research suggests such reports partly reflect how people wish to see themselves. Suffering does not automatically make anyone wiser.

That is close to what the Agamemnon shows. Suffering can teach, but it does not have to. It teaches those who remember it honestly ('the many memories of pain'), who do not harden their hearts, and who do not pass it on as revenge. The rest of this journey asks what helps that happen: a court, a conscience, an audience, and perhaps a god who suffers too.
sections.key: Suffering can teach but often does not; it teaches those who remember honestly and refuse revenge.

debate.question: What does 'learning through suffering' really mean?

positions.name: A just order: Zeus punishes and teaches
positions.who: Hugh Lloyd-Jones, The Justice of Zeus (1971); most traditional readers
positions.view: Aeschylus believed in a moral universe. Zeus punishes wrongdoing through suffering and through it brings people, and in the end cities, to wisdom. The trilogy shows the lesson finally learned.
positions.evidence: The hymn calls suffering a law of Zeus and a 'grace'; 'the doer must suffer'; the trilogy ends with justice established in Athens.

positions.name: A bitter truth: the lesson comes too late
positions.who: Many modern readers; Martha Nussbaum, The Fragility of Goodness (1986)
positions.view: The hymn is not comfort. It admits that the only wisdom available is learned through loss, usually too late, and often by people other than those who suffer. Life can force us into wrongs we cannot avoid.
positions.evidence: Iphigenia dies and learns nothing; Agamemnon learns nothing; 'fore-knowledge is fore-sorrow'; the chorus ends Agamemnon in despair.

positions.name: A hint of something greater
positions.who: Christian readers from the early Church to today; compare Hebrews 5:8
positions.view: Aeschylus saw truly that suffering has a place in God's ordering of the world, but could not see how the cycle of guilt ends. The New Testament takes up his words and answers his question: the innocent suffers for the guilty.
positions.evidence: The same Greek words in Hebrews 5:8; Hebrews 12's father who trains rather than destroys.

debate.agree: All agree that Aeschylus made suffering part of a divine order, and that in his play the lesson is learned, if at all, against the will and at terrible cost.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art has no painting of Iphigenia at Aulis or of the house of Atreus, and a stand-in would only pretend.

music.why: Brahms chose his words for comfort that comes through grief, not instead of it: 'Blessed are they that mourn.' It is the hope of the hymn to Zeus, without the violence.

think.why: What Christians believe about suffering: why it happens, and what God does with it. Compare it with Aeschylus' law of Zeus.

learn.why: The hymn to Zeus: wisdom through suffering, which comes even to the unwilling. Robert Kennedy quoted these lines on the night Martin Luther King was killed.

check.q: In the hymn to Zeus, what is the 'law' that Zeus has laid down?
options: That human beings learn wisdom by suffering, even against their will
That kings must obey prophets
That the old gods must be honoured
That every war must have a sacrifice
check.why: 'Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled'; wisdom comes 'o'er the unwilling soul'.

check.q: What makes Aulis a tragic dilemma rather than a simple crime?
options: Agamemnon did not know Iphigenia was his daughter
The prophet lied
Both choices were wrong: kill his child, or desert his army and defy the gods
Iphigenia volunteered to die
check.why: Agamemnon himself says 'Ill lot were mine, to disobey! And ill, to smite my child'. The not-knowing is Oedipus' situation, not his.

check.q: The chorus blames Agamemnon. For what, above all?
options: For not consulting Clytemnestra
For the way his mind turned reckless and hard once he chose
For going to war at all
For disobeying the prophet
check.why: 'To recklessness his shifting spirit veered'; 'so he steeled his heart'.

check.q: Aeschylus uses the verb 'to suffer' in two laws: 'by suffering, learning' and 'the doer must suffer'. What follows?
options: That only the innocent suffer
That suffering is both punishment for wrong and a possible teacher
That the two laws contradict each other, so Aeschylus was confused
That suffering is only ever a punishment
check.why: Suffering punishes the doer and may teach him or others; the tragedy is that the lesson comes late.

check.q: What is the most important difference between Aeschylus and Hebrews 5:7–9?
options: In Hebrews the one who suffers is innocent, and his suffering becomes salvation for others
Hebrews says suffering teaches nothing
Hebrews denies that suffering hurts
Aeschylus writes in Greek and Hebrews in Hebrew
check.why: Both use the same Greek words, but in Hebrews the innocent Son 'became ... the author of eternal salvation'.

check.q: Which is the best reply to someone who says 'suffering always makes people wiser'?
options: Agree: Aeschylus proves it
Agree: Hebrews says all suffering is discipline
Disagree: the Agamemnon itself shows suffering that teaches no one, and modern research finds growth in some people, not all
Disagree: the Greeks thought suffering was meaningless
check.why: Iphigenia, Agamemnon and Clytemnestra learn nothing; Hebrews says the fruit comes 'to those who have been trained by it'.

tutorial.question: 'Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled.' Is this comfort or warning?
tutorial.approach: Explain the hymn to Zeus and the phrase pathei mathos. Use Aulis and the end of the play to ask who actually learns. Compare Hebrews 5 and 12. Take a view, and answer the strongest case on the other side.
strong: Explains pathei mathos and its place as a law of Zeus.
Uses Aulis to show the dilemma and the chorus's judgement of Agamemnon.
Notes the two uses of 'suffer': punishment and lesson.
Asks honestly who learns, and when.
Compares Hebrews, noting both the shared words and the different picture.
Reaches a clear view and answers the other side.

reading.why: The classic argument that the Greeks, from Homer to the tragedians, believed in divine justice.

reading.author: Martha C. Nussbaum

reading.author: Edith Hamilton
