sessions.practice: Live it this week: write down one hard thing from your past that taught you something. Then think of one person going through something hard now, and do one small thing for them this week, without offering them a lesson.
sessions.reflect: Has suffering taught you anything? Or has it mostly been something to survive? Can both be true?
takeaways: Aeschylus made the proverb pathei mathos a law of Zeus: we learn by suffering, even against our will.
At Aulis, Agamemnon faced a tragic dilemma, and the chorus blames him for hardening his heart; in his house, suffering punishes but rarely teaches in time.
Hebrews uses the same words of Jesus, but in its picture the innocent suffers for others, and God is a father who trains, not a force that crushes.

sessions.title: From revenge to justice
sessions.line: A son who killed his mother, goddesses of vengeance at his heels, and a court of citizens on a hill in Athens: the end of the Oresteia.
sessions.plain: The Oresteia ends in Athens. Orestes has killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge his father, and the Furies, ancient goddesses of blood-vengeance, are hunting him. Instead of another killing, the goddess Athena founds a court: twelve citizens hear both sides, vote, and decide. Then she persuades the Furies to accept the verdict and become guardians of the city. This session asks how law replaced revenge, and whether the new justice came at anyone's cost.
sessions.why: Session 2 ended in despair: in the house of Atreus 'the doer must suffer', and every killing called for another. Suffering punished, but nobody learned in time. Now Aeschylus gives his answer. The cycle of revenge is broken not by one more act of vengeance but by a court, a vote and persuasion. This is the lesson the whole trilogy has been learning.
answers: How does the Oresteia end?
Who were the Furies, and what did they stand for?
How did a court replace revenge, and why did it matter?
Was the new justice fair to everyone?
sessions.finding: The Oresteia ends with the Furies tamed and a court founded: the West's first great drama of law replacing vendetta, in which a city learns, through generations of suffering, to judge instead of avenge.

paras: In session 2, Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter at Aulis, sailed to Troy and, ten years later, came home to be killed in his bath by his wife Clytemnestra. In the second play, The Libation-Bearers, their son Orestes returns from exile. The god Apollo, through his oracle at Delphi, commands him to avenge his father. Orestes kills Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus. As he stands over the bodies, he sees the Furies coming for him, and runs.

The third play, The Eumenides, opens at Apollo's temple in Delphi, where Orestes has fled for purification. The Furies sleep around him. Apollo sends him on to Athens, to the goddess Athena. There, on the Acropolis, he clasps her ancient statue and asks for judgement. The Furies follow him, singing that they will drink his blood.
background.key: Orestes has avenged his father by killing his mother, on Apollo's orders; pursued by the Furies, he comes to Athens for judgement.

paras: The Furies, in Greek the Erinyes, were among the oldest powers in Greek religion, older than Zeus. They were daughters of Night. Their work was to punish crimes against kin, above all the shedding of family blood, and they did it by hunting the killer until he went mad or died. In Aeschylus they are hideous: black, snake-haired, dripping from the eyes. When the play was first performed, a later story claimed, their appearance terrified the audience.

They are not simply evil. They stand for something real: the conviction that blood cries out, that a murder cannot just be forgotten, that someone must answer for it. Without them, there is no justice at all. The question of the play is whether that old, terrible justice can be kept and changed, rather than simply abolished.
background.key: The Furies were ancient goddesses who hunted those who shed kindred blood: vengeance, but also the demand that murder be answered.

background.h: The Areopagus and the year 458 BC
paras: The court Athena founds is real. The Areopagus, the 'Hill of Ares', is a bare rock just north-west of the Acropolis, where an ancient council of former magistrates met. In 462/461 BC, four years before the Oresteia, the democratic leader Ephialtes stripped it of most of its political powers, leaving it chiefly as a court for murder trials. Ephialtes was assassinated soon after. Athens was bitterly divided.

So when Aeschylus showed Athena founding the Areopagus as a murder court for all time, his audience could hardly miss the politics. Scholars still argue whether he was supporting the reform, warning against going further, or simply calling for peace between the factions. The play's last part is full of prayers that Athens never fall into civil war. Five centuries later, the apostle Paul would speak about the unknown god on the same hill (Acts 17:22).

timeline.text: Draco's law on homicide in Athens distinguishes deliberate from unintended killing
Ephialtes' reforms leave the Areopagus chiefly a murder court; Ephialtes is murdered
Aeschylus' Oresteia wins first prize
Athens republishes Draco's homicide law on stone; part of the inscription survives
Paul speaks at the Areopagus (Acts 17)

background.key: The Areopagus was a real murder court in Athens; Aeschylus wrote just after reforms that had divided the city.

paras: The main reading has five short parts from the trial at the end of The Eumenides. The Furies cross-examine Orestes; Athena founds the court; the votes are counted; the Furies rage at the verdict; and Athena, instead of crushing them, persuades them.

The comparison is from Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah. Ancient Israel faced the same problem: how to stop the 'avenger of blood' from turning every death into a feud. Its answer was the cities of refuge.
background.key: Five scenes from the trial; then Israel's cities of refuge, another ancient answer to blood-vengeance.

before: What arguments do the Furies and Apollo use? Which do you find stronger?
What does Athena say the court will give the city, and what must the citizens never banish?
Why does Athena persuade the Furies instead of defeating them?
sessions.readWhy: The end of the Oresteia: a court instead of a killing, and persuasion instead of force.

paras:
ATHENA (to the Chorus)
’Tis I announce the cause—first speech be yours;
For rightfully shall they whose plaint is tried
Tell the tale first and set the matter clear.

CHORUS
Though we be many, brief shall be our tale.
(To Orestes) Answer thou, setting word to match with word;
And first avow—hast thou thy mother slain?

ORESTES
I slew her. I deny no word hereof.

CHORUS
Three falls decide the wrestle—this is one.

ORESTES
Thou vauntest thee—but o’er no final fall.

CHORUS
Yet must thou tell the manner of thy deed.

ORESTES
Drawn sword in hand, I gashed her neck. ’Tis told.

CHORUS
But by whose word, whose craft, wert thou impelled?

ORESTES
By oracles of him who here attests me.

CHORUS
The prophet-god bade thee thy mother slay?

ORESTES
Yea, and thro’ him less ill I fared, till now.

CHORUS
If the vote grip thee, thou shalt change that word.

ORESTES
Strong is my hope; my buried sire shall aid.

CHORUS
Go to now, trust the dead, a matricide!

ORESTES
Yea, for in her combined two stains of sin.

CHORUS
How? speak this clearly to the judges’ mind.

ORESTES
Slaying her husband, she did slay my sire.

CHORUS
Therefore thou livest; death assoils her deed.

ORESTES
Then while she lived why didst thou hunt her not?

CHORUS
She was not kin by blood to him she slew.

ORESTES
And I, am I by blood my mother’s kin?

CHORUS
O cursed with murder’s guilt, how else wert thou
The burden of her womb? Dost thou forswear
Thy mother’s kinship, closest bond of love?

ORESTES
It is thine hour, Apollo—speak the law,
Averring if this deed were justly done;
For done it is, and clear and undenied.
But if to thee this murder’s cause seem right
Or wrongful, speak—that I to these may tell.

ATHENA
O men of Athens, ye who first do judge
The law of bloodshed, hear me now ordain.
Here to all time for Aegeus’ Attic host
Shall stand this council-court of judges sworn,
Here the tribunal, set on Ares’ Hill
Where camped of old the tented Amazons,
What time in hate of Theseus they assailed
Athens, and set against her citadel
A counterwork of new sky-pointing towers,
And there to Ares held their sacrifice,
Where now the rock hath name, even Ares’ Hill.
And hence shall Reverence and her kinsman Fear
Pass to each free man’s heart, by day and night
Enjoining, Thou shalt do no unjust thing,
So long as law stands as it stood of old
Unmarred by civic change. Look you, the spring
Is pure; but foul it once with influx vile
And muddy clay, and none can drink thereof.
Therefore, O citizens, I bid ye bow
In awe to this command, Let no man live
Uncurbed by law nor curbed by tyranny;
Nor banish ye the monarchy of Awe
Beyond the walls; untouched by fear divine,
No man doth justice in the world of men.
Therefore in purity and holy dread
Stand and revere; so shall ye have and hold
A saving bulwark of the state and land,
Such as no man hath ever elsewhere known,
Nor in far Scythia, nor in Pelops’ realm.
Thus I ordain it now, a council-court
Pure and unsullied by the lust of gain,
Sacred and swift to vengeance, wakeful ever
To champion men who sleep, the country’s guard.
Thus have I spoken, thus to mine own clan
Commended it for ever. Ye who judge,
Arise, take each his vote, mete out the right,
Your oath revering. Lo, my word is said.

ATHENA
Mine is the right to add the final vote,
And I award it to Orestes’ cause.
For me no mother bore within her womb,
And, save for wedlock evermore eschewed,
I vouch myself the champion of the man,
Not of the woman, yea, with all my soul,—
In heart, as birth, a father’s child alone.
Thus will I not too heinously regard
A woman’s death who did her husband slay,
The guardian of her home; and if the votes
Equal do fall, Orestes shall prevail.
Ye of the judges who are named thereto,
Swiftly shake forth the lots from either urn.
[Two judges come forward, one to each urn.

ORESTES
O bright Apollo, what shall be the end?

CHORUS
O Night, dark mother mine, dost mark these things?

OSESTES
Now shall my doom be life, or strangling cords.

CHORUS
And mine, lost honour or a wider sway.

APOLLO
O stranger judges, sum aright the count
Of votes cast forth, and, parting them, take heed
Ye err not in decision. The default
Of one vote only bringeth ruin deep,
One, cast aright, doth stablish house and home.

ATHENA
Behold, this man is free from guilt of blood,
For half the votes condemn him, half set free!

CHORUS
Woe on you, younger gods! the ancient right
Ye have o’erridden, rent it from my hands.

I am dishonoured of you, thrust to scorn!
But heavily my wrath
Shall on this land fling forth the drops that blast and burn
Venom of vengeance, that shall work such scathe
As I have suffered; where that dew shall fall,
Shall leafless blight arise,
Wasting Earth’s offspring,—Justice, hear my call!—
And thorough all the land in deadly wise
Shall scatter venom, to exude again
In pestilence on men.
What cry avails me now, what deed of blood,
Unto this land what dark despite?
Alack, alack, forlorn
Are we, a bitter injury have borne!
Alack, O sisters, O dishonoured brood
Of mother Night!

ATHENA
Nay, bow ye to my words, chafe not nor moan:
Ye are not worsted nor disgraced; behold,
With balanced vote the cause had issue fair,
Nor in the end did aught dishonour thee.
But thus the will of Zeus shone clearly forth,
And his own prophet-god avouched the same,
Orestes slew: his slaying is atoned.
Therefore I pray you, not upon this land
Shoot forth the dart of vengeance; be appeased,
Nor blast the land with blight, nor loose thereon
Drops of eternal venom, direful darts
Wasting and marring nature’s seed of growth.

For I, the queen of Athens’ sacred right,
Do pledge to you a holy sanctuary
Deep in the heart of this my land, made just
By your indwelling presence, while ye sit
Hard by your sacred shrines that gleam with oil
Of sacrifice, and by this folk adored.

ATHENA
I will not weary of soft words to thee,
That never mayst thou say, Behold me spurned,
An elder by a younger deity,
And from this land rejected and forlorn,
Unhonoured by the men who dwell therein.
But, if Persuasion’s grace be sacred to thee,
Soft in the soothing accents of my tongue,
Tarry, I pray thee; yet, if go thou wilt,
Not rightfully wilt thou on this my town
Sway down the scale that beareth wrath and teen
Or wasting plague upon this folk. ’Tis thine,
If so thou wilt, inheritress to be
Of this my land, its utmost grace to win.

CHORUS
O queen, what refuge dost thou promise me?

ATHENA
Refuge untouched by bale: take thou my boon.

CHORUS
What, if I take it, shall mine honour be?

ATHENA
No house shall prosper without grace of thine.

CHORUS
Canst thou achieve and grant such power to me?

ATHENA
Yea, for my hand shall bless thy worshippers.

CHORUS
And wilt thou pledge me this for time eterne?

ATHENA
Yea: none can bid me pledge beyond my power.

CHORUS
Lo, I desist from wrath, appeased by thee.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: The cross-examination
parts.who: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC), Athenian playwright and soldier
parts.when: Athens, the City Dionysia of 458 BC
parts.context: Athena has agreed to try the case and has chosen jurors from among the citizens. Apollo has come to speak for Orestes. The Furies, who are the chorus, are the prosecution. The rapid one-line exchanges are called stichomythia: verbal sword-play. Translated by E. D. A. Morshead (1881).
parts.plain: Athena tells the Furies to speak first, as the accusers. They ask Orestes whether he killed his mother; he admits it, and says Apollo ordered it. They ask why he deserves to live. He asks why they never hunted his mother, who killed her husband. They answer that she was not related to him by blood. He asks if he is related to her by blood, and they are shocked: how else could she have carried him? Then Orestes asks Apollo to speak.

commentary.on: For rightfully shall they whose plaint is tried
commentary.text: A simple rule that is new in this story: the accuser speaks first, and then the accused answers. Nobody in the house of Atreus has been given a hearing before. Procedure itself is the beginning of justice.

commentary.on: I slew her. I deny no word hereof.
commentary.text: Orestes does not deny the deed. The question is not whether he did it, but whether he is guilty. That distinction, between the act and the guilt, is what courts exist to judge.

commentary.on: By oracles of him who here attests me.
commentary.text: His defence is that a god commanded it. Divine command, or the higher duty to avenge his father, against the duty owed to his mother: the old clash of obligations again.

commentary.on: She was not kin by blood to him she slew.
commentary.text: The Furies' reasoning: they punish the shedding of kindred blood. A wife is not blood kin to her husband, so Clytemnestra's crime was not theirs to punish. It shows how narrow the old justice was: it protected blood, not persons.

commentary.on: And I, am I by blood my mother’s kin?
commentary.text: Orestes' reply seems absurd, and it prepares Apollo's notorious argument (in the lines that follow, not printed here) that the mother is only the 'nurse' of the father's seed, not truly a parent. Modern readers find this hard to stomach, and so, probably, did some ancient ones.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: Athena founds the court
parts.context: Both sides have spoken. Before the vote, Athena speaks to the jurors, and through them to the Athenians in the theatre, who were sitting a few hundred yards from the real Hill of Ares.
parts.plain: Athena declares that this court will sit on the Hill of Ares for ever. Reverence and Fear will keep citizens from wrongdoing day and night, as long as the law is kept pure. Let no one live without law, nor under a tyrant; and do not throw fear out of the city altogether, because no one does justice who fears nothing. Keep this court honourable, incorruptible and watchful, and it will protect the land as no other people's court has.

commentary.on: O men of Athens, ye who first do judge
commentary.text: This is a founding myth. The first trial for bloodshed is held here, and every later one descends from it. Aeschylus is telling his audience where their own justice came from: from a goddess, and from a terrible family history.

commentary.on: And hence shall Reverence and her kinsman Fear
commentary.text: Athena does not abolish the Furies' fear; she moves it. Fear of the court and of doing wrong now restrains citizens, instead of fear of a blood feud. Law needs some of the old dread to work.

commentary.on:
Let no man live
Uncurbed by law nor curbed by tyranny;
commentary.text: The most quoted lines of the speech, and among the most important in Greek political thought: neither anarchy nor despotism. Athena says the same thing the Furies will say later: the middle way is best.

commentary.on:
untouched by fear divine,
No man doth justice in the world of men.
commentary.text: A religious point as well as a legal one. Justice needs something sacred behind it, something feared and revered; a merely human arrangement will not hold.

commentary.on: Pure and unsullied by the lust of gain,
commentary.text: Incorruptible: the court must not take bribes. Compare the prophets of Israel, who attacked judges who 'take bribes' (Amos 5:12). Athens and Jerusalem agreed that a bought court is no court.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: The votes are counted
parts.context: The jurors have voted by dropping pebbles into two urns. Athena announces that she will cast the deciding vote, and that a tie means acquittal. The speaker named 'OSESTES' is a misprint in this edition for Orestes.
parts.plain: Athena says she will vote for Orestes, because she, born from Zeus without a mother, sides with the father, and she will not count a woman who killed her husband as worse. If the votes are equal, Orestes goes free. The votes are counted, and they are equal. Orestes is acquitted.

commentary.on: Mine is the right to add the final vote,
commentary.text: Athena does not decide the case alone; the citizens do. Her vote only breaks a tie, and the rule she lays down, that an equal vote acquits, became the custom of Athenian courts. The defendant gets the benefit of the doubt.

commentary.on: I vouch myself the champion of the man,
commentary.text: Her reason is uncomfortable: she was born from Zeus' head, with no mother, and so she favours the father. The play's justice is not neutral between men and women, and modern critics have rightly pointed this out.

commentary.on:
The default
Of one vote only bringeth ruin deep,
commentary.text: Apollo reminds the jurors how fine the line is: one vote destroys or saves a house. Every juror carries a terrible weight. That is what it means to replace private revenge with public judgement.

commentary.on: For half the votes condemn him, half set free!
commentary.text: A tie. Aeschylus could have made the jury unanimous; instead the citizens are split, as the case deserved. Justice is not a clear answer from heaven; it is a fair decision made by people in the face of real doubt.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: The Furies' rage
parts.context: Orestes has gone home free. The Furies are left humiliated. They threaten to poison the land of Athens with blight and plague. Athena answers.
parts.plain: The Furies cry that the young gods have trampled the ancient law and dishonoured them. They will drip poison on the land: no leaf, no child, only plague. Athena tells them they have not been disgraced: the vote was equal, and Zeus' will was clear. Instead of revenge, she offers them a home in Athens, an underground shrine, and honour from the people.

commentary.on: Woe on you, younger gods! the ancient right
commentary.text: The Furies speak for the old order, and their grief is real. Something has been lost: the certainty that blood will always be repaid. The new court is fairer, but it can let a killer walk free.

commentary.on: Shall on this land fling forth the drops that blast and burn
commentary.text: Their threat is to turn their anger on the whole city: crops, births, health. Unanswered grievance poisons a community. Every society that ends a feud has to deal with the losers' rage.

commentary.on: Ye are not worsted nor disgraced; behold,
commentary.text: Athena's first move is to speak to their honour. She does not say they were wrong; she says they were not shamed. The equal vote means their case was strong.

commentary.on: Do pledge to you a holy sanctuary
commentary.text: Her second move is an offer: a place in the city. The old justice is not to be destroyed but given a home, under the law.

parts.author: Aeschylus
parts.title: Persuasion
parts.context: The Furies have repeated their curse twice. Athena has answered them each time. Now, at last, she appeals to Persuasion (Peitho), whom the Greeks also worshipped as a goddess.
parts.plain: Athena says she will never tire of speaking gently to them, so that they cannot say they were driven out. If they honour Persuasion, they will stay; they can be honoured partners in the land. They ask what honour they will have; she says no house will prosper without them. They ask if she can promise it for ever; she says yes. They give up their anger.

commentary.on: I will not weary of soft words to thee,
commentary.text: Athena has power: she mentions that she alone knows where Zeus' thunderbolts are kept. She chooses not to use it. The founding of the city's justice ends with persuasion, not force.

commentary.on: But, if Persuasion’s grace be sacred to thee,
commentary.text: Persuasion, the art of speech that changes minds, was at the heart of Athenian democracy: in the Assembly, the courts and the theatre. Aeschylus makes it the power that completes justice.

commentary.on: No house shall prosper without grace of thine.
commentary.text: The Furies' power is not abolished but given a new purpose: they will bless the households that keep justice. The old terror becomes a guardian. In Greek they are later called Eumenides, 'the Kindly Ones', which gives the play its title.

commentary.on: Lo, I desist from wrath, appeased by thee.
commentary.text: The end of a cycle that began with Thyestes' feast. Generations of killing end not with victory but with a court, a vote and a reconciliation. This is the lesson the house of Atreus learned by suffering.

read.author: Aeschylus
read.who: Aeschylus (about 525–456 BC), Athenian playwright and soldier
read.when: Athens, the City Dionysia of 458 BC

paras: When Yahweh your God cuts off the nations whose land Yahweh your God gives you, and you succeed them and dwell in their cities and in their houses,
you shall set apart three cities for yourselves in the middle of your land, which Yahweh your God gives you to possess.
You shall prepare the way, and divide the borders of your land which Yahweh your God causes you to inherit into three parts, that every man slayer may flee there.
This is the case of the man slayer who shall flee there and live: Whoever kills his neighbor unintentionally, and didn’t hate him in time past—

as when a man goes into the forest with his neighbor to chop wood and his hand swings the ax to cut down the tree, and the head slips from the handle and hits his neighbor so that he dies—he shall flee to one of these cities and live.

Otherwise, the avenger of blood might pursue the man slayer while hot anger is in his heart and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him mortally, even though he was not worthy of death, because he didn’t hate him in time past.
Therefore I command you to set apart three cities for yourselves.
If Yahweh your God enlarges your border, as he has sworn to your fathers, and gives you all the land which he promised to give to your fathers;

and if you keep all this commandment to do it, which I command you today, to love Yahweh your God, and to walk ever in his ways, then you shall add three cities more for yourselves, in addition to these three.
This is so that innocent blood will not be shed in the middle of your land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance, leaving blood guilt on you.
But if any man hates his neighbor, lies in wait for him, rises up against him, strikes him mortally so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities;
then the elders of his city shall send and bring him there, and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die.
Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall purge the innocent blood from Israel that it may go well with you.

parts.title: The avenger of blood
parts.context: Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses' last speeches before Israel enters the land. Most scholars date its final form to the seventh century BC, about two hundred years before Aeschylus. Numbers 35 and Joshua 20 give the same law, and name six cities.

commentary.on: that every man slayer may flee there
commentary.text: The law assumes the old custom: a killing is answered by the 'avenger of blood' (in Hebrew, go'el ha-dam), the nearest male relative. Deuteronomy does not abolish him; like Athena, it limits him.

commentary.on: Whoever kills his neighbor unintentionally, and didn’t hate him in time past
commentary.text: The key distinction: intention. A man whose axe-head flies off and kills his friend is not a murderer. Athens drew the same line in Draco's homicide law of about 621 BC. Both cultures saw that justice must look at the heart, not only the deed, a question session 4, still to come, will press hard.

commentary.on: while hot anger is in his heart
commentary.text: The law understands vengeance psychologically. The avenger is not wicked; he is grieving and angry, and anger cannot judge. Distance, time and a place of safety give justice room to work.

commentary.on: the elders of his city shall send and bring him there
commentary.text: The deliberate murderer is not protected. The elders, a public authority, hand him over. So the private avenger remains, but under public judgement: in Israel the elders, in Athens the court.

commentary.on: Your eye shall not pity him
commentary.text: Here Israel and Aeschylus differ. In Deuteronomy, a murderer must still die, so that 'innocent blood' does not defile the land. In the Eumenides, Orestes is acquitted. Both aim to end the feud; they weigh mercy and justice differently.

compare.why: Israel faced the same problem as Athens: in a world without police, a killing was avenged by the victim's family, and an accident could start a feud. Deuteronomy's answer is read here.
compare.title: Cities of refuge

paras: In most societies before the modern state, there were no police and no public prosecutors. If someone killed your brother, it fell to your family to answer. Vengeance was not lawlessness; it was the law. It kept people from killing lightly, because they knew someone would come for them.

But revenge has no natural end. Each killing creates a new victim and a new avenger. Feuds in Iceland, Albania, the Scottish Highlands and many other places have run for generations. The house of Atreus is the Greek picture of it: the doer must suffer, and the sufferer becomes the next doer. Aeschylus' question is how a people escapes this without simply ceasing to care about murder.
sections.key: Revenge was the old law; it deterred killing but could never end, as the house of Atreus shows.

paras: Athena's court changes four things. Judgement passes from the victim's family to neutral citizens under oath. Both sides are heard. The question becomes not only 'who did it?' but 'is he guilty?', so that motive, command and circumstance matter. And the decision is final: once the court has spoken, the feud is over.

This is the idea behind every criminal court in the West. The Crown or the State, not the victim's family, prosecutes. Juries of citizens decide. In English law the presumption of innocence and the rule that doubt favours the accused have long roots; Athena's rule that a tie acquits is one of the oldest recorded forms of the idea. The Oresteia is the first great drama of the change from vendetta to law.

rows: Is the accused guilty, given why he acted?
table.note: Athena's court in the Eumenides, as against the law of the house of Atreus.

sections.key: The court moves judgement from the family to impartial citizens, hears both sides, asks about guilt, and ends the feud.

paras: The most surprising thing in the Eumenides is that the Furies are not defeated. Athena could have banished them. Instead she spends some two hundred lines persuading them, and they end as honoured guardians of Athens, carried in torchlit procession to a shrine beneath the Areopagus.

Aeschylus seems to be saying that a just order must find a place for the passion for retribution. People who have lost someone to murder do want the killer punished, and that wish is not wicked. If the law ignores it, it will return as vigilante violence. The law must take up the victims' anger, give it a fair form, and so turn it from a curse on the city into a guard of it. Modern debates about victims' rights and restorative justice still turn on this.
sections.key: The Furies are not destroyed but persuaded and honoured: law must take up the demand for retribution, not deny it.

paras: The trial is not fair to everyone. Apollo argues that a mother is not truly her child's parent, only the soil in which the father's seed grows. Athena votes for Orestes because she 'favours the male'. Clytemnestra's murder of her husband is treated as worse than Orestes' murder of his mother.

The classicist Froma Zeitlin, in an influential essay of 1978, argued that the Oresteia founds the city's order by putting women in their place: the female powers, Clytemnestra and the Furies, are defeated or tamed, and male, Olympian reason rules. Others reply that the Furies, who are female, end with real honour and power, and that the play shows the cost of its settlement openly. Either way, a careful reader should notice that even a founding act of justice can carry the prejudices of its time.
sections.key: The verdict rests partly on Apollo's claim that only the father is a parent; critics such as Froma Zeitlin argue the new order is built on silencing the female.

paras: Israel's cities of refuge solved the same problem a different way. The avenger of blood remained, but an accidental killer could flee to a city and be protected, while the elders handed over a deliberate murderer. Like Athena's court, it took judgement out of the hands of the angry and gave it to a public authority. Like Draco's law in Athens, it turned on intention.

Both peoples believed justice was sacred. In Aeschylus, the court is founded by a goddess and needs 'fear divine'. In Deuteronomy, the law comes from God, and innocent blood defiles his land. The Hebrew prophets went further: 'let justice roll on like rivers' (Amos 5:24). The West's courts grew from both roots: Greek procedure, juries and persuasion; Hebrew law under God, equal for rich and poor.
sections.key: Athens and Israel both put public judgement in place of private vengeance, turned on intention, and held justice to be sacred.

sections.h: Did the Greeks learn by suffering?
paras: Read as a whole, the Oresteia answers the hymn of session 2. The house of Atreus suffered for three generations. The lesson it finally learned was not private wisdom but a public institution: a court, and the habit of persuasion. In Aeschylus, then, the deepest learning through suffering belongs not to one person but to a city.

That is a hopeful idea, and the West has taken it seriously. The rule of law, juries, appeals and the slow replacement of feuds by courts are among its great achievements. But it leaves a question for the sessions ahead: what about the person who suffers through no fault of their own, and learns only that the world is not just? Sophocles will ask it.
sections.key: The Oresteia's lesson by suffering is a public one: a city learns to judge instead of avenge.

debate.question: What does the end of the Oresteia celebrate?

positions.name: The triumph of law
positions.who: Most readers from Hegel to the present; H. D. F. Kitto, Greek Tragedy (1939)
positions.view: The trilogy shows humanity's passage from blood-feud to civic justice. The court on the Areopagus is the answer to the curse of the house, and the reconciliation of the Furies shows that law can include the old passions.
positions.evidence: Athena's founding speech; the equal vote and acquittal; the Furies renamed and honoured in the closing procession.

positions.name: An order built on exclusion
positions.who: Froma Zeitlin (1978); many feminist critics since
positions.view: The new order rests on Apollo's denial that mothers are parents and on the defeat of female powers. The play's 'justice' is patriarchy made sacred.
positions.evidence: Apollo's argument about the father's seed; Athena's vote 'for the male'; Clytemnestra's crime counted worse than matricide.

positions.name: A plea for peace in a divided city
positions.who: E. R. Dodds, 'Morals and Politics in the Oresteia' (1960); Christopher Pelling
positions.view: Written just after Ephialtes' reforms and his murder, the play asks Athens to keep its courts, avoid tyranny and anarchy, and never fall into civil war.
positions.evidence: 'Let no man live uncurbed by law nor curbed by tyranny'; the Furies' blessings against civil strife in the closing scenes.

debate.agree: All agree that the trilogy ends by replacing an endless chain of vengeance with a court of citizens, and that persuasion, not force, completes the change.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art has no painting of Orestes, the Furies or the Areopagus, and a stand-in would only pretend.

music.why: Beethoven's Mass ends with 'Dona nobis pacem', a prayer for peace in which the sounds of war break in and are answered. The Oresteia ends the same way: a long feud brought to peace, with its violence remembered.

think.why: Athena says that without 'fear divine' no one does justice. Is that true? See what Christians and their critics have said.

learn.why: Israel's prophetic cry for justice, which Athens' courts and Israel's law both served in their own ways.

check.q: Why does the court break the cycle of revenge where the house of Atreus could not?
options: Because Apollo was stronger than the Furies
Because judgement passes to impartial citizens who hear both sides, and their verdict ends the matter
Because Athena executed the Furies
Because Orestes was innocent
check.why: Procedure, impartial judges and a final verdict end the feud; the Furies are persuaded, not killed.

check.q: The Furies say they did not pursue Clytemnestra because she was 'not kin by blood' to her husband. What does that show about the old justice?
options: That husbands had no rights
That it protected blood relationships, not persons as such
That it was more merciful than the court
That the Furies were bribed
check.why: Their law punished the shedding of kindred blood; a murdered husband fell outside it.

check.q: Why does Athena persuade the Furies instead of banishing them?
options: Because a just order must give the demand for retribution an honoured place, or it will poison the city
Because she is too weak to banish them
Because the jurors voted that way
Because Zeus forbids her to use the thunderbolt
check.why: She says she knows where the thunderbolts are, but chooses persuasion; the Furies become guardians.

check.q: What do Athena's court and Israel's cities of refuge have most in common?
options: Both acquit every killer
Both abolished the death penalty
Both were founded by a goddess
Both put a public authority between the killer and the avenger, and both distinguish intended from unintended killing
check.why: The elders or the court judge; Deuteronomy protects the unintentional killer, as Draco's law did in Athens.

check.q: Which is the strongest criticism of the trial's fairness?
options: Orestes did not admit the deed
The Furies spoke first
The verdict depends partly on Apollo's claim that a mother is not truly a parent, and Athena's preference for the male
The jury was too large
check.why: Apollo's argument and Athena's stated reason are the basis of Froma Zeitlin's critique.

check.q: In what sense does the Oresteia answer 'learning through suffering'?
options: The suffering of three generations leads a city to found a court and the habit of persuasion
Clytemnestra repents before she dies
Zeus explains why Iphigenia had to die
Orestes becomes a philosopher
check.why: In Aeschylus the deepest lesson is public: an institution, not a private insight.

tutorial.question: 'Let no man live uncurbed by law nor curbed by tyranny.' What does the Oresteia teach about justice?
tutorial.approach: Trace the change from the law of the house ('the doer must suffer') to Athena's court. Explain what the court changes, why the Furies are persuaded and not destroyed, and what the verdict costs. Compare Deuteronomy 19. End with what the West inherited.
strong: Explains the cycle of revenge in the house of Atreus.
Explains what Athena's court changes: impartial judges, both sides heard, guilt, a final verdict.
Interprets the persuasion of the Furies.
Faces the critique of Apollo's argument and Athena's vote.
Compares the cities of refuge and the role of intention.
Connects the play to later Western law.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: think of a grudge you hold, large or small. Instead of rehearsing it, write down the strongest case the other person could make, as Athena let both sides speak. Then decide one fair thing to do about it.
sessions.reflect: Where in your life do you want revenge rather than justice? What would it take to move from one to the other?
takeaways: The Oresteia ends with Athena founding a court on the Areopagus: citizens hear both sides and give a final verdict, ending the cycle of revenge.
The Furies are persuaded and honoured, not destroyed: law must take up the demand for retribution.
Israel's cities of refuge answered the same problem; both cultures turned on intention and held justice sacred, though Aeschylus' verdict also carries the prejudices of its time.

sessions.title: Oedipus: guilty or innocent?
sessions.line: A king sets out to find a murderer and discovers it is himself: Sophocles' Oedipus, and what it means to be guilty of what you did not know you did.
sessions.plain: Oedipus is the king of Thebes, famous for his intelligence. A plague strikes the city, and the god Apollo says it will end only when the killer of the old king, Laius, is found. Oedipus investigates, and learns that he himself killed Laius, who was his father, and then married the widow, who was his mother. He did not know. This session asks whether he was guilty, what Aristotle meant by the 'tragic flaw', and what the play says about knowing and seeing.
sessions.why: Session 3 ended with a court that asks not only who did the deed but whether the doer is guilty. Aeschylus' world was one of curses and clear commands. Now Sophocles sets a harder case: a man who did terrible things without knowing it. If guilt lies in the will, Oedipus is innocent. If it lies in the deed, he is the worst of men. Which is it?
answers: Is Oedipus to blame for what he did?
What is a 'tragic flaw', and is it the right translation?
Why does Oedipus blind himself?
What did Freud make of Oedipus, and was he right?
sessions.finding: Oedipus did terrible things without knowing; Sophocles makes us ask whether guilt lies in what we do or in what we will, and shows that the clearest-sighted man can be blind to himself.

paras: In session 3, a court in Athens learned to ask whether a killer was guilty, and why he acted. Orestes knew exactly what he was doing: he killed his mother on a god's orders. Now we move from Aeschylus to Sophocles, a generation younger, and from Argos to Thebes, a city in central Greece with its own cursed royal house.

The myth was well known. An oracle told Laius, king of Thebes, that his son would kill him. When a son was born, Laius had his ankles pinned and gave him to a shepherd to leave on Mount Cithaeron to die. The shepherd took pity and passed the baby to a shepherd from Corinth, and the childless king and queen of Corinth raised him as their own. They called him Oedipus, which may mean 'swollen foot'.
background.key: Laius, warned that his son would kill him, had the baby exposed; he was saved and raised in Corinth as Oedipus.

background.h: What Oedipus did before the play begins
paras: As a young man, Oedipus heard a rumour that he was not his parents' son. He went to Delphi, and the oracle told him he would kill his father and marry his mother. Horrified, he fled from Corinth so that it could never happen. At a place where three roads meet, an old man in a carriage tried to force him off the road and struck him; Oedipus killed him and his attendants. It was Laius.

Oedipus came to Thebes, which was being terrorised by the Sphinx, a monster with a woman's face that killed everyone who could not answer her riddle. Oedipus answered it, the Sphinx died, and the grateful city made him king. He married the widowed queen, Jocasta, and had four children. Years later, when the play opens, a plague is destroying Thebes.

timeline.text: Laius is told his son will kill him
Exposed on Mount Cithaeron; saved and raised in Corinth
The oracle at Delphi; flight from Corinth; the killing at the three roads
Answers the Sphinx's riddle; becomes king and marries Jocasta
Plague; the investigation; the discovery in a single day

background.key: Fleeing the oracle, Oedipus killed a stranger at a crossroads, saved Thebes from the Sphinx and married its queen, all without knowing who they were.

paras: Sophocles was born about 496 BC at Colonus, just outside Athens, to a wealthy family. He was handsome, musical and much loved; ancient writers call him the most fortunate of men. He served Athens as a treasurer and was elected one of its ten generals in 441/440 BC, alongside Pericles. He is said to have written over a hundred and twenty plays and won more victories than any other tragedian; he never came last.

Oedipus the King was probably first performed in the 420s BC, perhaps soon after the great plague that struck Athens in 430–426 BC and killed Pericles. The audience watching a play that opens with a plague-stricken city begging its brilliant leader for help would have known that feeling. Aristotle thought it the most perfect tragedy ever written.
background.key: Sophocles (about 496–406 BC), general and playwright; Oedipus the King dates from the 420s BC, perhaps after Athens' own plague.

paras: The main reading has five parts. The opening of the play: the plague, the people's plea, the oracle. The moment of discovery and the chorus's song. Oedipus' first words after blinding himself. His defence of what he did. And, from the play Sophocles wrote at the end of his life, Oedipus at Colonus, the old Oedipus arguing that he is innocent.
The comparison is Aristotle's Poetics, chapter 13, where he uses Oedipus to explain what a tragic hero should be, and uses the word hamartia, which English has often translated 'tragic flaw'.
background.key: The plague, the discovery, the blinding, and Oedipus' two verdicts on himself; then Aristotle on hamartia.

before: In the opening scene, what kind of king is Oedipus? List his good qualities.
After he blinds himself, who does Oedipus say is responsible: Apollo, himself, or both?
In Oedipus at Colonus, what is his argument that he cannot 'with justice' be blamed? Do you agree?
sessions.readWhy: The most perfect tragedy, said Aristotle: a good king who investigates a crime and finds himself.

paras:
OEDIPUS.
My children, latest born to Cadmus old,
Why sit ye here as suppliants, in your hands
Branches of olive filleted with wool?
What means this reek of incense everywhere,
And everywhere laments and litanies?
Children, it were not meet that I should learn
From others, and am hither come, myself,
I Oedipus, your world-renowned king.
Ho! aged sire, whose venerable locks
Proclaim thee spokesman of this company,
Explain your mood and purport. Is it dread
Of ill that moves you or a boon ye crave?
My zeal in your behalf ye cannot doubt;
Ruthless indeed were I and obdurate
If such petitioners as you I spurned.

PRIEST.
Yea, Oedipus, my sovereign lord and king,
Thou seest how both extremes of age besiege
Thy palace altars—fledglings hardly winged,
and greybeards bowed with years; priests, as am I
of Zeus, and these the flower of our youth.
Meanwhile, the common folk, with wreathed boughs
Crowd our two market-places, or before
Both shrines of Pallas congregate, or where
Ismenus gives his oracles by fire.
For, as thou seest thyself, our ship of State,
Sore buffeted, can no more lift her head,
Foundered beneath a weltering surge of blood.
A blight is on our harvest in the ear,
A blight upon the grazing flocks and herds,
A blight on wives in travail; and withal
Armed with his blazing torch the God of Plague
Hath swooped upon our city emptying
The house of Cadmus, and the murky realm
Of Pluto is full fed with groans and tears.
Therefore, O King, here at thy hearth we sit,
I and these children;

not as deeming thee
A new divinity, but the first of men;
First in the common accidents of life,
And first in visitations of the Gods.
Art thou not he who coming to the town
of Cadmus freed us from the tax we paid
To the fell songstress? Nor hadst thou received
Prompting from us or been by others schooled;
No, by a god inspired (so all men deem,
And testify) didst thou renew our life.
And now, O Oedipus, our peerless king,
All we thy votaries beseech thee, find
Some succor, whether by a voice from heaven
Whispered, or haply known by human wit.
Tried counselors, methinks, are aptest found
To furnish for the future pregnant rede.
Upraise, O chief of men, upraise our State!
Look to thy laurels! for thy zeal of yore
Our country’s savior thou art justly hailed:
O never may we thus record thy reign:—
“He raised us up only to cast us down.”
Uplift us, build our city on a rock.
Thy happy star ascendant brought us luck,
O let it not decline! If thou wouldst rule
This land, as now thou reignest, better sure
To rule a peopled than a desert realm.
Nor battlements nor galleys aught avail,
If men to man and guards to guard them tail.

OEDIPUS.
Ah! my poor children, known, ah, known too well,
The quest that brings you hither and your need.
Ye sicken all, well wot I, yet my pain,
How great soever yours, outtops it all.
Your sorrow touches each man severally,
Him and none other, but I grieve at once
Both for the general and myself and you.
Therefore ye rouse no sluggard from day-dreams.
Many, my children, are the tears I’ve wept,
And threaded many a maze of weary thought.
Thus pondering one clue of hope I caught,
And tracked it up; I have sent Menoeceus’ son,
Creon, my consort’s brother, to inquire
Of Pythian Phoebus at his Delphic shrine,
How I might save the State by act or word.
And now I reckon up the tale of days
Since he set forth, and marvel how he fares.
’Tis strange, this endless tarrying, passing strange.
But when he comes, then I were base indeed,
If I perform not all the god declares.

PRIEST.
Thy words are well timed; even as thou speakest
That shouting tells me Creon is at hand.

OEDIPUS.
O King Apollo! may his joyous looks
Be presage of the joyous news he brings!

PRIEST.
As I surmise, ’tis welcome; else his head
Had scarce been crowned with berry-laden bays.

OEDIPUS.
We soon shall know; he’s now in earshot range.
[Enter CREON]
My royal cousin, say, Menoeceus’ child,
What message hast thou brought us from the god?

CREON.
Good news, for e’en intolerable ills,
Finding right issue, tend to naught but good.

OEDIPUS.
How runs the oracle? thus far thy words
Give me no ground for confidence or fear.

CREON.
If thou wouldst hear my message publicly,
I’ll tell thee straight, or with thee pass within.

OEDIPUS.
Speak before all; the burden that I bear
Is more for these my subjects than myself.

CREON.
Let me report then all the god declared.
King Phoebus bids us straitly extirpate
A fell pollution that infests the land,
And no more harbor an inveterate sore.

OEDIPUS.
What expiation means he? What’s amiss?

CREON.
Banishment, or the shedding blood for blood.
This stain of blood makes shipwreck of our state.

OEDIPUS.
Whom can he mean, the miscreant thus denounced?

CREON.
Before thou didst assume the helm of State,
The sovereign of this land was Laius.

OEDIPUS.
I heard as much, but never saw the man.

CREON.
He fell; and now the god’s command is plain:
Punish his takers-off, whoe’er they be.

OEDIPUS.
Where are they? Where in the wide world to find
The far, faint traces of a bygone crime?

OEDIPUS.
Was he within his palace, or afield,
Or traveling, when Laius met his fate?

CREON.
Abroad; he started, so he told us, bound
For Delphi, but he never thence returned.

OEDIPUS.
Came there no news, no fellow-traveler
To give some clue that might be followed up?

CREON.
But one escape, who flying for dear life,
Could tell of all he saw but one thing sure.

OEDIPUS.
And what was that? One clue might lead us far,
With but a spark of hope to guide our quest.

CREON.
Robbers, he told us, not one bandit but
A troop of knaves, attacked and murdered him.

OEDIPUS.
Did any bandit dare so bold a stroke,
Unless indeed he were suborned from Thebes?

CREON.
So ’twas surmised, but none was found to avenge
His murder mid the trouble that ensued.

OEDIPUS.
What trouble can have hindered a full quest,
When royalty had fallen thus miserably?

CREON.
The riddling Sphinx compelled us to let slide
The dim past and attend to instant needs.

OEDIPUS.
Well, I will start afresh and once again
Make dark things clear. Right worthy the concern
Of Phoebus, worthy thine too, for the dead;
I also, as is meet, will lend my aid
To avenge this wrong to Thebes and to the god.
Not for some far-off kinsman, but myself,
Shall I expel this poison in the blood;
For whoso slew that king might have a mind
To strike me too with his assassin hand.
Therefore in righting him I serve myself.
Up, children, haste ye, quit these altar stairs,
Take hence your suppliant wands, go summon hither
The Theban commons. With the god’s good help
Success is sure; ’tis ruin if we fail.
[Exeunt OEDIPUS and CREON]

PRIEST.
Come, children, let us hence; these gracious words
Forestall the very purpose of our suit.
And may the god who sent this oracle
Save us withal and rid us of this pest.
[Exeunt PRIEST and SUPPLIANTS]

OEDIPUS.
Ah me! ah me! all brought to pass, all true!
O light, may I behold thee nevermore!
I stand a wretch, in birth, in wedlock cursed,
A parricide, incestuously, triply cursed!
[Exit OEDIPUS]

CHORUS.
(Str. 1)
Races of mortal man
Whose life is but a span,
I count ye but the shadow of a shade!
For he who most doth know
Of bliss, hath but the show;
A moment, and the visions pale and fade.
Thy fall, O Oedipus, thy piteous fall
Warns me none born of women blest to call.

(Ant. 1)
For he of marksmen best,
O Zeus, outshot the rest,
And won the prize supreme of wealth and power.
By him the vulture maid
Was quelled, her witchery laid;
He rose our savior and the land’s strong tower.
We hailed thee king and from that day adored
Of mighty Thebes the universal lord.

(Str. 2)
O heavy hand of fate!
Who now more desolate,
Whose tale more sad than thine, whose lot more dire?
O Oedipus, discrowned head,
Thy cradle was thy marriage bed;
One harborage sufficed for son and sire.
How could the soil thy father eared so long
Endure to bear in silence such a wrong?

(Ant. 2)
All-seeing Time hath caught
Guilt, and to justice brought
The son and sire commingled in one bed.
O child of Laius’ ill-starred race
Would I had ne’er beheld thy face;
I raise for thee a dirge as o’er the dead.
Yet, sooth to say, through thee I drew new breath,
And now through thee I feel a second death.
[Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]

OEDIPUS.
(Str. 2)
Apollo, friend, Apollo, he it was
That brought these ills to pass;
But the right hand that dealt the blow
Was mine, none other. How,
How, could I longer see when sight
Brought no delight?

OEDIPUS.
What’s done was well done. Thou canst never shake
My firm belief. A truce to argument.
For, had I sight, I know not with what eyes
I could have met my father in the shades,
Or my poor mother, since against the twain
I sinned, a sin no gallows could atone.
Aye, but, ye say, the sight of children joys
A parent’s eyes. What, born as mine were born?
No, such a sight could never bring me joy;
Nor this fair city with its battlements,
Its temples and the statues of its gods,
Sights from which I, now wretchedst of all,
Once ranked the foremost Theban in all Thebes,
By my own sentence am cut off, condemned
By my own proclamation ’gainst the wretch,
The miscreant by heaven itself declared
Unclean—and of the race of Laius.
Thus branded as a felon by myself,
How had I dared to look you in the face?

OEDIPUS.
O shameless railer, think’st thou this abuse
Defames my grey hairs rather than thine own?
Murder and incest, deeds of horror, all
Thou blurtest forth against me, all I have borne,
No willing sinner; so it pleased the gods
Wrath haply with my sinful race of old,
Since thou could’st find no sin in me myself
For which in retribution I was doomed
To trespass thus against myself and mine.
Answer me now, if by some oracle
My sire was destined to a bloody end
By a son’s hand, can this reflect on me,
Me then unborn, begotten by no sire,
Conceived in no mother’s womb? And if
When born to misery, as born I was,
I met my sire, not knowing whom I met
or what I did, and slew him, how canst thou
With justice blame the all-unconscious hand?
And for my mother, wretch, art not ashamed,
Seeing she was thy sister, to extort
From me the story of her marriage, such
A marriage as I straightway will proclaim.
For I will speak; thy lewd and impious speech
Has broken all the bonds of reticence.
She was, ah woe is me! she was my mother;
I knew it not, nor she; and she my mother
Bare children to the son whom she had borne,
A birth of shame. But this at least I know
Wittingly thou aspersest her and me;
But I unwitting wed, unwilling speak.
Nay neither in this marriage or this deed
Which thou art ever casting in my teeth—
A murdered sire—shall I be held to blame.

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: A city in plague
parts.who: Sophocles (about 496–406 BC), Athenian playwright and general
parts.context: The opening scene. Before the palace at Thebes, citizens sit at the altars as suppliants, holding olive branches wound with wool, the sign of people begging for help. A priest of Zeus speaks for them. Creon, Jocasta's brother, has been sent to Delphi to ask Apollo what to do. Storr's verse translation (Loeb, 1912) is used; a footnote number has been removed from the priest's speech.
parts.plain: Oedipus comes out and asks his people why they are weeping and praying. The priest tells him: the crops, the herds and the women in childbirth are dying, and plague is emptying the city. They come to him not as a god but as the best of men, who once saved them from the Sphinx. Oedipus says he grieves for them more than for himself and has already sent Creon to Delphi. Creon returns: Apollo says the killer of the old king Laius is in the city and must be driven out. Oedipus vows to find him, saying he does it for himself as well, since the killer might strike him too.

commentary.on: I Oedipus, your world-renowned king.
commentary.text: His first words about himself. He is proud, and he has reason to be. Every word of this scene will be turned inside out by the end of the day: the famous king will be the most wretched of men.

commentary.on: A blight is on our harvest in the ear,
commentary.text: The plague strikes fields, flocks and births: the whole life of the city. For the Greeks, an unpunished killing caused pollution (miasma), a kind of spiritual contagion that infected a community. The audience, who had lived through the plague of 430 BC, would have felt this.

commentary.on: A new divinity, but the first of men;
commentary.text: The priest is careful: Oedipus is not a god, but the best of men. Sophocles sets up his hero as the very height of human ability, the man of the ode to man in session 1, with his 'counsel and civic wit'.

commentary.on: Your sorrow touches each man severally,
commentary.text: Oedipus is a good king. He feels his people's pain, has already acted, and will not rest. Whatever his faults, he is not a tyrant who cares only for himself.

commentary.on: Banishment, or the shedding blood for blood.
commentary.text: Apollo's oracle, as Creon reports it. The pollution must be driven out: the killer exiled or killed. Oedipus does not know he is pronouncing his own sentence.

commentary.on: In this land, said the god; “who seeks shall find;
commentary.text: The play is a detective story, perhaps the first. Oedipus is the investigator, and his greatest gift, his relentless intelligence, is what will destroy him. He will seek, and he will find.

commentary.on:
Well, I will start afresh and once again
Make dark things clear.
commentary.text: He promises to bring the dark into the light. The whole play is built on this image: light and darkness, sight and blindness. By the end he will see everything and choose never to see again.

commentary.on: Therefore in righting him I serve myself.
commentary.text: Terrible irony: the killer he hunts is himself. The audience knows; Oedipus does not. Greek tragedy lives on this gap between what the audience knows and what the hero knows.

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: All brought to pass
parts.context: Many hours of the play later. Teiresias the blind prophet has told Oedipus he is the killer, and Oedipus has accused him of plotting with Creon. A messenger from Corinth has revealed that Oedipus was adopted. Jocasta has realised the truth and run into the palace. Now the old shepherd who once saved the baby has been forced to confess. Oedipus understands.
parts.plain: Oedipus cries out that everything has come true, and wishes never to see the light again. He rushes into the palace. The chorus sings that human happiness is only a shadow: Oedipus, the greatest of men, who saved the city, has fallen further than anyone. Time, which sees all, has found him out. They wish they had never seen him, and yet he once gave them life.

commentary.on: Ah me! ah me! all brought to pass, all true!
commentary.text: The moment of recognition. Aristotle called it anagnorisis, the change from ignorance to knowledge, and said the best tragedies combine it with peripeteia, the reversal of fortune. Here they happen in the same instant.

commentary.on: O light, may I behold thee nevermore!
commentary.text: He has spent the whole play seeking light. Now that he sees, he wants darkness. Knowing the truth about yourself can be unbearable.

commentary.on: I count ye but the shadow of a shade!
commentary.text: The chorus draws the general lesson. If even Oedipus can fall, all human happiness is a shadow. It is the dark side of the ode to man: we master everything except our own fate.

commentary.on: Warns me none born of women blest to call.
commentary.text: An old Greek saying: call no one happy until they are dead. You cannot judge a life until you see its end.

commentary.on:
All-seeing Time hath caught
Guilt, and to justice brought
commentary.text: The chorus speaks of guilt and justice. The deeds are found out. But the chorus does not say Oedipus deserved it. Is this justice, or only exposure? The play leaves it open.

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: But the hand was mine
parts.context: A messenger has told how Jocasta hanged herself, and how Oedipus, finding her, tore the gold pins from her dress and drove them into his eyes. Now he comes out, blind, and the chorus asks him what god drove him to it.
parts.plain: Oedipus says Apollo brought these sufferings about, but the hand that struck his eyes was his own. Why should he see, when there is nothing good left to see?

commentary.on:
Apollo, friend, Apollo, he it was
That brought these ills to pass;
commentary.text: Oedipus names the god. Apollo's oracles foretold everything; in some sense the god brought it about.

commentary.on:
But the right hand that dealt the blow
Was mine, none other.
commentary.text: And yet he claims the blinding as his own act. These lines hold the whole problem together: the gods determined what happened, and Oedipus is still responsible for what he does. Sophocles does not choose between fate and freedom; he shows a man who suffers both.

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: What's done was well done
parts.context: The chorus has said he would be better dead than blind. Oedipus answers.
parts.plain: Oedipus says he was right to blind himself. How could he look at his father and mother in the world of the dead, or at his children, or at the city and its temples? He has condemned himself by his own proclamation, the curse he laid on Laius' killer at the start of the play.

commentary.on: What’s done was well done.
commentary.text: Oedipus does not plead ignorance here. He judges himself as harshly as anyone could. Whatever the law might say, he feels the deed as his.

commentary.on: I sinned, a sin no gallows could atone.
commentary.text: He speaks of sin. The Greeks thought that killing a parent and marrying a mother polluted a person whether or not they knew, as touching a corpse made one unclean. Guilt, for Oedipus here, is not only a matter of intention; it is a stain on what he is.

commentary.on:
By my own sentence am cut off, condemned
By my own proclamation
commentary.text: At the start he proclaimed exile for the killer. He keeps his word. The just king judges himself by his own law.

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: The all-unconscious hand
parts.context: Sophocles returned to Oedipus at the very end of his life, in Oedipus at Colonus, first staged after his death in 401 BC. The blind Oedipus, now old, has wandered for years with his daughter Antigone and has reached Colonus, near Athens, Sophocles' own birthplace. Creon has come to drag him back to Thebes and has publicly called him a parricide and the husband of his mother. Oedipus replies.
parts.plain: Oedipus says he committed murder and incest against his will: the gods willed it, perhaps angry with his family. He could not be blamed for an oracle spoken before he was born. He killed a man who attacked him, not knowing he was his father. He married a woman not knowing she was his mother, and she did not know either. Anyone attacked on the road would defend himself without asking whether the attacker was his father. So he will not be held to blame.

commentary.on: No willing sinner; so it pleased the gods
commentary.text: The old Oedipus has had years to think. His verdict now is different: he sinned, but not willingly. The fault, if anyone's, is the gods'.

commentary.on: With justice blame the all-unconscious hand?
commentary.text: This is the heart of his defence. Can you justly blame a hand that did not know what it did? It is the same distinction Deuteronomy drew between the man who kills 'unintentionally' and the murderer.

commentary.on: I knew it not, nor she;
commentary.text: Neither of them knew. If guilt lies in the will, there is no guilt here at all.

commentary.on: shall I be held to blame.
commentary.text: So Sophocles gives us two answers from the same man. The young Oedipus, in the first shock of discovery, condemns himself. The old Oedipus, after long suffering, declares himself innocent. Has he learned something, or only found a defence? The play leaves that with the audience.

read.author: Sophocles
read.who: Sophocles (about 496–406 BC), Athenian playwright and general

paras: A perfect tragedy should, as we have seen, be arranged not on the simple but on the complex plan. It should, moreover, imitate actions which excite pity and fear, this being the distinctive mark of tragic imitation. It follows plainly, in the first place, that the change, of fortune presented must not be the spectacle of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity: for this moves neither pity nor fear; it merely shocks us. Nor, again, that of a bad man passing from adversity to prosperity: for nothing can be more alien to the spirit of Tragedy; it possesses no single tragic quality; it neither satisfies the moral sense nor calls forth pity or fear. Nor, again, should the downfall of the utter villain be exhibited. A plot of this kind would, doubtless, satisfy the moral sense, but it would inspire neither pity nor fear; for pity is aroused by unmerited misfortune, fear by the misfortune of a man like ourselves. Such an event, therefore, will be neither pitiful nor terrible. There remains, then, the character between these two extremes,--that of a man who is not eminently good and just,-yet whose misfortune is brought about not by vice or depravity, but by some error or frailty. He must be one who is highly renowned and prosperous,--a personage like Oedipus, Thyestes, or other illustrious men of such families.

A well constructed plot should, therefore, be single in its issue, rather than double as some maintain. The change of fortune should be not from bad to good, but, reversely, from good to bad. It should come about as the result not of vice, but of some great error or frailty, in a character either such as we have described, or better rather than worse. The practice of the stage bears out our view. At first the poets recounted any legend that came in their way. Now, the best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses, on the fortunes of Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes, Meleager, Thyestes, Telephus, and those others who have done or suffered something terrible. A tragedy, then, to be perfect according to the rules of art should be of this construction. Hence they are in error who censure Euripides just because he follows this principle in his plays, many of which end unhappily. It is, as we have said, the right ending. The best proof is that on the stage and in dramatic competition, such plays, if well worked out, are the most tragic in effect; and Euripides, faulty though he may be in the general management of his subject, yet is felt to be the most tragic of the poets.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: What makes a tragic hero
parts.context: Aristotle has defined tragedy (in chapter 6, which session 7, still to come, reads) as stirring pity and fear. Now he asks what kind of story stirs them best. Translated by S. H. Butcher (1895).
parts.plain: A good man falling into misfortune only shocks us. A bad man rising is not tragic at all, and a villain falling satisfies our sense of justice but moves neither pity nor fear. The best tragic hero is between: not outstandingly good, a man like us, who falls not because of wickedness but because of some great error. Oedipus is the example. The best plays end unhappily, which is why Euripides, criticised for it, is 'the most tragic of the poets'.

commentary.on: pity is aroused by unmerited misfortune, fear by the misfortune of a man like ourselves
commentary.text: Aristotle's definitions. We pity those who suffer more than they deserve; we fear for those who are like us. So the hero must not deserve his fate, and must be close enough to us that we feel it could happen to us.

commentary.on: whose misfortune is brought about not by vice or depravity, but by some error or frailty
commentary.text: The Greek word Butcher translates 'error or frailty' is hamartia. It comes from a verb meaning 'to miss the mark', as an archer misses. English critics later called it the 'tragic flaw', as if it meant a fault of character such as pride. Many scholars now think Aristotle meant something closer to a mistake: an act done in ignorance, like Oedipus killing a stranger who was his father.

commentary.on: a personage like Oedipus, Thyestes, or other illustrious men of such families
commentary.text: Oedipus is Aristotle's prime example. So for Aristotle, Oedipus is not a wicked man punished: he is a good man who made a terrible mistake. That is what makes his fall pitiable.

commentary.on: Euripides, faulty though he may be in the general management of his subject, yet is felt to be the most tragic of the poets
commentary.text: A glimpse ahead. Euripides' plays end in disaster more often than the others', and Aristotle defends him for it. Session 6, still to come, asks what such endings say about the gods.

compare.author: Aristotle
compare.why: Aristotle uses Oedipus as his model of the perfect tragic hero, and in doing so coins the idea English calls the 'tragic flaw'. Read what he actually says.
compare.title: Not by vice, but by some error

paras: Oedipus the King takes place in a single day, in front of a single palace, and has one plot: the search for a killer. Oedipus calls witnesses one by one: Creon, then Teiresias the blind prophet, then Jocasta, then a messenger from Corinth, then the old shepherd. Each brings him closer to the truth, and each time he could stop. Jocasta begs him to stop. He refuses.

That is what makes the play so gripping, and so modern. Oedipus is not crushed by an external force; he destroys himself by insisting on the truth. His virtues, his intelligence, courage and care for his city, are exactly what bring him down. The play asks whether it is better to know, even when knowing destroys you. Oedipus' answer is yes.
sections.key: The play is an investigation in which Oedipus' own virtues, intelligence and love of truth, uncover his ruin.

paras: Generations of students have been taught that a tragic hero has a 'tragic flaw', usually pride, and that his fall is the punishment for it. On this reading Oedipus is hot-tempered and arrogant: he kills a man in a road-rage, insults Teiresias and accuses Creon of treason.

Most scholars now think this misreads both Aristotle and Sophocles. Aristotle's word hamartia means missing the mark: an error, often made in ignorance. He chose Oedipus as his example precisely because Oedipus is not wicked. The British classicist E. R. Dodds, in a famous essay of 1966, 'On Misunderstanding the Oedipus Rex', argued that Oedipus is not punished for any flaw at all; his temper is real, but it is not why he suffers. What destroys him is what he did not know.
sections.key: Hamartia means an error or mistake, not necessarily a flaw of character; Oedipus suffers for what he did not know, not for pride.

paras: Is Oedipus guilty? It depends where you think guilt lies. If guilt is in the deed, he is guilty of the worst crimes a Greek could imagine. If it is in the will, he is innocent: he fled Corinth precisely to avoid them. The old Oedipus at Colonus argues the second; the young Oedipus, blinded, feels the first.

Greek religion leaned towards the deed. A killing polluted the killer whether or not he meant it, and even the accidental killer had to be purified. Greek law, from Draco, leaned towards the will. Israel's law did the same with the cities of refuge. Christianity would put the will at the centre: Jesus taught that sin begins in the heart (Mark 7:21–23), and Augustine and Aquinas defined sin by consent. Sophocles holds both views in one play. He knew that we feel responsible for what we did even when we did not mean it, as anyone who has caused an accident knows.
sections.key: If guilt is in the deed, Oedipus is guilty; if in the will, innocent. Sophocles shows both, and that we feel the deed even when we did not will it.

paras: Did the gods make Oedipus do it? The oracles foretold it, but foretelling is not forcing. Nothing in the play says Apollo made Oedipus kill Laius; Oedipus chose to fight at the crossroads and chose to marry Jocasta. What was fated was the outcome; what was free was each step he took to escape it, and every step led him into it.

Oedipus' own words hold both together: 'Apollo ... brought these ills to pass; but the right hand that dealt the blow was mine'. Christians have wrestled with the same knot in a different form: how God can know the future and humans still be free. Boethius, writing in prison in AD 524, argued that God sees all time at once, as we see a man walking without making him walk. Sophocles offered no theory. He showed a man who is fully responsible and fully a victim, and asked us to pity and fear him.
sections.key: The oracles foretell but do not force; Oedipus is both responsible for his acts and a victim of what he could not know.

paras: The play is built on sight. Oedipus, who sees, is blind to the truth; Teiresias, who is blind, sees it. Oedipus solved the Sphinx's riddle (what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon and three in the evening? a human being) but did not know what kind of human being he was. When at last he sees, he puts out his eyes.

Bernard Knox, in Oedipus at Thebes (1957), read Oedipus as the image of fifth-century Athens itself: brilliant, confident, sure that human intelligence could master everything, and blind to its limits. That links the play to the ode to man: man masters everything except death and himself. The Christian tradition has its own version: 'If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves' (1 John 1:8). Self-knowledge, the oldest Greek command ('Know thyself', carved at Delphi), turns out to be the hardest knowledge of all.
sections.key: The seeing king is blind to himself and the blind prophet sees; self-knowledge, 'Know thyself', is the hardest knowledge.

paras: In The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), Sigmund Freud argued that the play moves us because it fulfils a wish buried in every child: to possess the mother and remove the father. He called this the Oedipus complex, and the name has stuck in everyday speech.

Freud's reading tells us more about Freud than about Sophocles. Oedipus has no such desire: he flees Corinth precisely to avoid killing the man he thinks is his father, and he marries Jocasta as a stranger, for political reasons. The horror of the play is that he did what he did not want. Yet Freud saw something real: the play is about what we do not know about ourselves, and the dreadful possibility that our lives are shaped by forces we never chose. Many modern scholars, from Dodds to Vernant, discuss Freud only to set him aside.
sections.key: Freud read the play as a buried wish; but Oedipus wanted the opposite of what he did, and the play is about ignorance, not desire.
