debate.question: Is Oedipus guilty?

positions.name: Yes: his flaws brought him down
positions.who: The traditional 'tragic flaw' reading, common in schools and older criticism
positions.view: Oedipus is proud, quick to anger and suspicious. He killed a man in a rage, insulted the prophet and accused Creon. His fall shows the punishment of pride (hubris).
positions.evidence: The killing at the crossroads; his rage at Teiresias and Creon; the chorus's ode on the tyrant who is born of hubris (lines 872–910).

positions.name: No: he is a good man destroyed by what he could not know
positions.who: E. R. Dodds (1966); Aristotle, Poetics XIII; the old Oedipus himself at Colonus
positions.view: Oedipus did everything he could to avoid his fate and acted in ignorance. He is pitiable, not punished. The play shows that the world is not arranged to reward the good.
positions.evidence: He fled Corinth to avoid the oracle; Aristotle's choice of him as the hero who falls 'not by vice'; 'With justice blame the all-unconscious hand?'

positions.name: The wrong question: the play is about knowing
positions.who: Bernard Knox, Oedipus at Thebes (1957); J.-P. Vernant (1970)
positions.view: Sophocles is not trying a case. He shows the greatness and the limits of human intelligence: a man who can answer any riddle but his own. The question is not 'guilty or innocent?' but 'what can a human being know?'
positions.evidence: The imagery of sight and blindness; the Sphinx's riddle, whose answer is 'man'; Teiresias the blind seer.

debate.agree: All agree that Oedipus acted without knowing the truth, that he condemned himself, and that Sophocles leaves the audience to weigh guilt, fate and knowledge for themselves.

look.why: Henry Fuseli painted the blind Oedipus in 1786, but not from this play. The scene comes from Oedipus at Colonus, which you read at the end of the reading: the old Oedipus, exiled and blind, curses his son Polynices, who has come to ask for his help. In the play his daughters Antigone and Ismene are with him. The painting shows what the Oedipus story became: an old man whose suffering has made him terrible.
points: Four people are locked together by dramatic gestures against a dark background, almost filling the nearly square canvas.
An old man with white hair and beard, in a short-sleeved brown garment, sits right of centre with both arms stretched straight out; his head juts forward and his bulging eyes appear white.
He points with his left hand at a younger dark-haired man in a golden yellow tunic, who kneels with his head thrown back and raises a hand as if to shield his face.
A woman with long blond hair leans her forehead on the old man's knee in the lower right corner.
A second woman, with long curly brown hair, stands behind the two men with her arms spread wide, looking at the old man with her lips parted.

music.why: Allegri set Psalm 51, a king's confession of sin: 'my sin is constantly before me'. Oedipus, blinded, judges himself as harshly as David did, though he sinned without knowing.

think.why: Is a person responsible for what they did not choose? See how Christianity came to put the will and conscience at the centre of who we are.

learn.why: Oedipus did not know who he was. The psalmist prays to the one who knows us better than we know ourselves: an existing piece, as no new one is planned for this session.

check.q: Why does the opening scene stress what a good king Oedipus is?
options: Because Sophocles admired monarchy
To show that he is a god
So that his fall is more pitiable and the irony sharper: the best of men is the polluted killer
To show that the gods reward good kings
check.why: The priest calls him 'the first of men'; Aristotle says we pity those who do not deserve their misfortune.

check.q: What did Aristotle most probably mean by hamartia?
options: A wicked character
Pride, which the gods punish
An error or mistake, often made in ignorance
A curse inherited from one's ancestors
check.why: The word means 'missing the mark'; Aristotle says the hero falls 'not by vice or depravity, but by some error'.

check.q: The young Oedipus says 'I sinned'; the old Oedipus says he cannot justly be blamed. Which distinction explains the difference?
options: Between gods and men
Between guilt in the deed and guilt in the will
Between Thebes and Athens
Between youth and old age only
check.why: The blinded Oedipus feels the pollution of the deed; at Colonus he argues from his ignorance, 'the all-unconscious hand'.

check.q: Do the oracles force Oedipus to do what he does?
options: Yes: Oedipus says the gods blinded him
Yes: Apollo controls his hands
No: there are no oracles in the play
No: they foretell the outcome, but each step, including the flight from Corinth meant to avoid it, is his own choice
check.why: Oedipus says Apollo brought it about, 'but the right hand that dealt the blow was mine'.

check.q: What is the best reply to Freud's reading of the play?
options: Oedipus wanted to marry his mother
Oedipus fled to avoid what he did, so the play is about ignorance rather than hidden desire, though it does show how little we know ourselves
Freud was right in every detail
Freud never read Sophocles
check.why: Oedipus' horror is that he did what he did not want; Freud still saw that the play is about what we do not know about ourselves.

check.q: How does the play's imagery of sight connect with the ode to man in session 1?
options: Both praise the gods of Thebes
Both are about the sea
Both show human beings mastering everything except themselves and their fate
Both are sung by Teiresias
check.why: The man who solved the Sphinx's riddle does not know who he is, as the ode said man masters all but death.

tutorial.question: Is Oedipus guilty?
tutorial.approach: Set out the case for guilt (the deeds, his temper, his own self-condemnation) and for innocence (his ignorance, his flight from Corinth, his defence at Colonus). Use Aristotle on hamartia. Then ask whether 'guilty or innocent?' is the right question, and say what the play shows about knowledge and responsibility.
strong: Tells the story accurately, including what happened before the play.
Distinguishes guilt in the deed from guilt in the will, with Greek pollution and law.
Explains hamartia correctly and criticises the 'tragic flaw' reading.
Uses both the young Oedipus' and the old Oedipus' verdicts.
Discusses fate and freedom with Oedipus' own words.
Reaches a view and answers the strongest objection.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: think of one thing you did that hurt someone, though you did not mean it. Without excusing or punishing yourself, say sorry to them, or, if you cannot, write down what you would say.
sessions.reflect: Are you responsible for harm you did without knowing? What would you want someone to say to you if you were?
takeaways: Oedipus investigates a killing and discovers he killed his father and married his mother without knowing; his virtues lead to his ruin.
Aristotle's hamartia means an error, often in ignorance, not a 'tragic flaw' of character; Oedipus is a good man who made a terrible mistake.
Sophocles shows guilt in the deed and in the will, fate and freedom, together, and that the clearest-sighted man can be blind to himself.

sessions.title: Antigone: God's law or the king's?
sessions.line: A king forbids anyone to bury a traitor; his sister buries him, and tells the king that his law cannot override the unwritten laws of heaven.
sessions.plain: After Oedipus, his two sons kill each other fighting for Thebes. The new king, Creon, decrees that one brother be buried with honour and the other, who attacked the city, be left for the dogs. Their sister Antigone buries him anyway, and when she is caught she tells Creon that no human decree can override the 'unwritten laws' of the gods. This session asks who was right, and why Antigone has become the West's first great case of conscience against the state.
sessions.why: Session 4 asked whether a person is guilty for what they did not know. Antigone knows exactly what she is doing. Here suffering comes not from ignorance but from a clear choice between two laws. Aeschylus showed a city learning to judge; Sophocles now asks what happens when the city's ruler judges wrongly, and a citizen must choose whom to obey.
answers: What is Antigone about?
What are the 'unwritten laws', and where do they come from?
Did Creon have a case?
Why has Antigone mattered so much since?
sessions.finding: Antigone defies the king to bury her brother by 'the unwritten laws of Heaven': the West's first great case of conscience against the state, in which both sides have a real claim.

paras: In session 4, Oedipus discovered who he was and blinded himself. The myth goes on. His two sons, Eteocles and Polynices, agreed to rule Thebes in turn, but Eteocles refused to give up the throne. Polynices raised an army in Argos and attacked his own city. The brothers killed each other in single combat at one of the seven gates.

Their uncle Creon, Jocasta's brother, became king. Antigone was written before Oedipus the King, probably about 441 BC, but its story comes after: it opens on the morning after the battle. Creon has decreed that Eteocles, who defended the city, will be buried with honour, and that Polynices, the traitor, will be left unburied on the plain.
background.key: Oedipus' sons killed each other in the war for Thebes; the new king Creon forbids the burial of Polynices, who attacked the city.

paras: For the Greeks, leaving a body unburied was one of the worst things one could do. The dead needed burial rites, at least a sprinkling of dust, to pass to the underworld; an unburied body was an offence to the gods below and a pollution to the living. Families, and above all the women of the family, had the duty of mourning and burying their dead. In Homer, even Achilles at last gives back Hector's body to his father.

Denying burial to traitors did happen in Athens: traitors could be refused burial in Attic soil. So Creon's decree was harsh but not unheard of. What makes it extreme is that he leaves the body for the dogs and birds in sight of the city, and threatens death to anyone who buries it, even his own nieces.
background.key: Burial was a sacred duty, especially of the family's women; refusing it to traitors was known, but Creon's decree is extreme.

background.h: Hegel, Anouilh and the modern Antigone
paras: No Greek play has meant more to modern Europe. The philosopher G. W. F. Hegel (1770–1831) called it one of the most sublime works of art ever made and built part of his philosophy on it. In Nazi-occupied Paris in 1944, Jean Anouilh's Antigone was staged with the censor's approval, and audiences took it as a play about resistance. Bertolt Brecht set his version (1948) in Berlin at the end of the war. In 2004 the Irish poet Seamus Heaney wrote The Burial at Thebes, with the war in Iraq in mind.

The scholar George Steiner, in Antigones (1984), traced how almost every generation in Europe has rewritten the play to argue about its own conflicts: family and state, women and men, the living and the dead, conscience and law.
background.key: Hegel, Anouilh in occupied Paris, Brecht and Heaney all remade Antigone; George Steiner traced its versions in Antigones (1984).

paras: The main reading has two parts. First, Creon's speech to the elders explaining his decree, his case at full strength: loyalty to the city above friends and family. Second, the confrontation: Antigone, caught in the act, admits it, and defends herself by the unwritten laws; then the two argue line against line.

The comparison is from the Acts of the Apostles. Peter and the apostles, ordered by the high priest's council to stop preaching about Jesus, answer: 'We must obey God rather than men.' It is the Bible's own Antigone moment.
background.key: Creon's case, then Antigone's defence; then Peter before the council, 'We must obey God rather than men'.

before: What is Creon's principle? Write it in one sentence. Is it a good one?
What does Antigone say about the laws she obeyed? Where do they come from?
In the quick exchange at the end, which line do you find most powerful, and why?
sessions.readWhy: The clash of conscience and the state in its first and greatest form, with both sides heard.

paras:
CREON.
Elders, the gods have righted one again
Our storm-tossed ship of state, now safe in port.
But you by special summons I convened
As my most trusted councilors; first, because
I knew you loyal to Laius of old;
Again, when Oedipus restored our State,
Both while he ruled and when his rule was o’er,
Ye still were constant to the royal line.
Now that his two sons perished in one day,
Brother by brother murderously slain,
By right of kinship to the Princes dead,
I claim and hold the throne and sovereignty.
Yet ’tis no easy matter to discern
The temper of a man, his mind and will,
Till he be proved by exercise of power;
And in my case, if one who reigns supreme
Swerve from the highest policy, tongue-tied
By fear of consequence, that man I hold,
And ever held, the basest of the base.
And I contemn the man who sets his friend
Before his country.

For myself, I call
To witness Zeus, whose eyes are everywhere,
If I perceive some mischievous design
To sap the State, I will not hold my tongue;
Nor would I reckon as my private friend
A public foe, well knowing that the State
Is the good ship that holds our fortunes all:
Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck.
Such is the policy by which I seek
To serve the Commons and conformably
I have proclaimed an edict as concerns
The sons of Oedipus; Eteocles
Who in his country’s battle fought and fell,
The foremost champion—duly bury him
With all observances and ceremonies
That are the guerdon of the heroic dead.
But for the miscreant exile who returned
Minded in flames and ashes to blot out
His father’s city and his father’s gods,
And glut his vengeance with his kinsmen’s blood,
Or drag them captive at his chariot wheels—
For Polyneices ’tis ordained that none
Shall give him burial or make mourn for him,
But leave his corpse unburied, to be meat
For dogs and carrion crows, a ghastly sight.
So am I purposed; never by my will
Shall miscreants take precedence of true men,
But all good patriots, alive or dead,
Shall be by me preferred and honored.

CREON.
Speak, girl, with head bent low and downcast eyes,
Does thou plead guilty or deny the deed?

ANTIGONE.
Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.

CREON (to GUARD)
Sirrah, begone whither thou wilt, and thank
Thy luck that thou hast ’scaped a heavy charge.
(To ANTIGONE)
Now answer this plain question, yes or no,
Wast thou acquainted with the interdict?

ANTIGONE.
I knew, all knew; how should I fail to know?

CREON.
And yet wert bold enough to break the law?

ANTIGONE.
Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus,
And she who sits enthroned with gods below,
Justice, enacted not these human laws.
Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man,
Could’st by a breath annul and override
The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
They were not born today nor yesterday;
They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang.
I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown,
To disobey these laws and so provoke
The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die,
E’en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death
Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain.
For death is gain to him whose life, like mine,
Is full of misery. Thus my lot appears
Not sad, but blissful; for had I endured
To leave my mother’s son unburied there,
I should have grieved with reason, but not now.
And if in this thou judgest me a fool,
Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.

CHORUS.
A stubborn daughter of a stubborn sire,
This ill-starred maiden kicks against the pricks.

CREON.
Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills
Are soonest bended, as the hardest iron,
O’er-heated in the fire to brittleness,
Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through.
A snaffle curbs the fieriest steed, and he
Who in subjection lives must needs be meek.
But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled,
First overstepped the established law, and then—
A second and worse act of insolence—
She boasts and glories in her wickedness.
Now if she thus can flout authority
Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
But though she be my sister’s child or nearer
Of kin than all who worship at my hearth,
Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape
The utmost penalty, for both I hold,
As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt.
Bring forth the older; even now I saw her
Within the palace, frenzied and distraught.
The workings of the mind discover oft
Dark deeds in darkness schemed, before the act.
More hateful still the miscreant who seeks
When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.

ANTIGONE.
Would’st thou do more than slay thy prisoner?

CREON.
Not I, thy life is mine, and that’s enough.

ANTIGONE.
Why dally then? To me no word of thine
Is pleasant: God forbid it e’er should please;
Nor am I more acceptable to thee.
And yet how otherwise had I achieved
A name so glorious as by burying
A brother? so my townsmen all would say,
Where they not gagged by terror, Manifold
A king’s prerogatives, and not the least
That all his acts and all his words are law.

CREON.
Of all these Thebans none so deems but thou.

ANTIGONE.
These think as I, but bate their breath to thee.

CREON.
Hast thou no shame to differ from all these?

ANTIGONE.
To reverence kith and kin can bring no shame.

CREON.
Was his dead foeman not thy kinsman too?

ANTIGONE.
One mother bare them and the self-same sire.

CREON.
Why cast a slur on one by honoring one?

ANTIGONE.
The dead man will not bear thee out in this.

CREON.
Surely, if good and evil fare alive.

ANTIGONE.
The slain man was no villain but a brother.

CREON.
The patriot perished by the outlaw’s brand.

ANTIGONE.
Nathless the realms below these rites require.

CREON.
Not that the base should fare as do the brave.

ANTIGONE.
Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?

CREON.
Not even death can make a foe a friend.

ANTIGONE.
My nature is for mutual love, not hate.

CREON.
Die then, and love the dead if thou must;
No woman shall be the master while I live.
[Enter ISMENE]

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: Creon's case
parts.who: Sophocles (about 496–406 BC), Athenian playwright and general
parts.context: The morning after the battle. The chorus of Theban elders has sung a hymn of victory. Creon, the new king, enters and explains his first decree. Read it fairly: Athens' own leaders spoke like this in the Assembly. Translated by F. Storr (1912).
parts.plain: Creon says the gods have saved the city like a ship in a storm. He is king now by right of kinship. A ruler shows his worth only when he holds power, and the worst ruler is one who keeps silent from fear, or puts a friend before his country. The state is the ship that carries all of us; without it there are no friendships. So he decrees: Eteocles, who died for the city, will be buried with honour; Polynices, who came to burn it, will lie unburied for the dogs and birds. Patriots, alive or dead, will be honoured above traitors.

commentary.on: Our storm-tossed ship of state, now safe in port.
commentary.text: The 'ship of state' is an old Greek image, and Creon's case rests on it. A city that has just survived civil war is fragile. Order is a matter of life and death.

commentary.on: Till he be proved by exercise of power;
commentary.text: A shrewd line, and true: power reveals character. Creon says it of himself. The play will prove it, though not as he hopes.

commentary.on:
And I contemn the man who sets his friend
Before his country.
commentary.text: This is Creon's principle: loyalty to the city comes before loyalty to family and friends. Pericles, the leading Athenian of Sophocles' day, said something similar. It is the voice of the public servant, and it is not foolish.

commentary.on: Is the good ship that holds our fortunes all:
commentary.text: Without the city, nothing else is safe, including friendship. Hobbes would say much the same two thousand years later: without a sovereign, life is 'nasty, brutish, and short'.

commentary.on:
For Polyneices ’tis ordained that none
Shall give him burial or make mourn for him,
commentary.text: Here Creon goes too far. Punishing a traitor is one thing; denying the dead their rites is an offence against the gods below. He has extended the state's power into a realm that is not his.

parts.author: Sophocles
parts.title: The unwritten laws
parts.context: Some hours later. A guard has caught Antigone sprinkling dust on her brother's body and pouring offerings. He brings her before Creon. She is Creon's niece, and engaged to his son Haemon. The speech beginning 'Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus' is the most famous in the play. A few misprints in this edition ('Does thou', 'Where they not') are kept as printed.
parts.plain: Creon asks if she knew of his order. She did; everyone did. Then why break it? Because his order did not come from Zeus or from Justice, and no mortal can override the unwritten, everlasting laws of heaven. She knew she would die anyway; dying for this is gain. Creon says stubborn wills break soonest; he will not let a girl defy him, and will punish her and her sister. They argue: she says the dead require these rites and her nature is to share love, not hate; he says an enemy stays an enemy even in death, and no woman will rule him.

commentary.on: Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.
commentary.text: Like Orestes before the court, Antigone does not deny the deed. Her defence is not ignorance, as with Oedipus, but a higher law.

commentary.on: Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus,
commentary.text: Creon's decree, she says, has no divine authority. Zeus did not make it, nor Justice who lives with the gods below. A command is not law just because a king gives it.

commentary.on: The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
commentary.text: The heart of the play. Some laws are not written by any state: they are older, unchanging, and binding on rulers. This is the seed of the Western idea of natural law, and of the conviction that a state can command what is wrong. Aristotle quoted these lines in his Rhetoric (I.13) as the example of a law 'common to all'.

commentary.on: They were not born today nor yesterday;
commentary.text: The unwritten laws are eternal: 'no one knows when they first appeared'. Antigone does not claim to have invented them, or to be following her own feelings. She claims they bind everyone, Creon included.

commentary.on: I knew that I must die,
commentary.text: She has counted the cost. Conscience, in her case, is not a convenient excuse; it costs her life.

commentary.on: A stubborn daughter of a stubborn sire,
commentary.text: The chorus sees Oedipus in her: 'fierce child of a fierce father'. The old men respect the king and are not sure she is right. Neither, at first, is the audience.

commentary.on:
Now if she thus can flout authority
Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
commentary.text: Creon's anger shows another motive: wounded pride, and a man's fear of being defied by a woman. His public principle is becoming personal.

commentary.on: These think as I, but bate their breath to thee.
commentary.text: Antigone claims the citizens agree with her but are afraid. Later in the play Haemon tells his father the same thing. A ruler surrounded by fear does not hear the truth.

commentary.on: Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?
commentary.text: Perhaps the gods below judge differently from the city. It is the question of a higher court beyond the state's.

commentary.on: My nature is for mutual love, not hate.
commentary.text: In Greek: 'I was born to join in loving, not in hating'. It is one of the most beautiful lines in Greek drama, and many Christian readers have heard in it something close to the gospel.

commentary.on: No woman shall be the master while I live.
commentary.text: Creon's last word here. He has moved from the good of the city to his own will. By the end of the play he will lose his son and his wife to suicide, and be left saying he is 'no more than nothing'. Too late, he learns by suffering.

read.author: Sophocles
read.who: Sophocles (about 496–406 BC), Athenian playwright and general

paras: When they had brought them, they set them before the council. The high priest questioned them,
saying, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us.”
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree.
God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins.
We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

parts.title: Before the council
parts.context: The Acts of the Apostles, by the author of Luke's Gospel, tells the story of the first Christians. Peter and John have already been forbidden to teach in Jesus' name (Acts 4:18–20). They have gone on teaching, been arrested, and now stand before the council (the Sanhedrin), led by the high priest.

commentary.on: Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name?
commentary.text: Like Creon, the high priest speaks for public order. The council feared unrest and Roman reprisals. They had a case.

commentary.on: We must obey God rather than men.
commentary.text: Peter's answer is Antigone's, in one sentence: when a human command contradicts God's, God must be obeyed. In Greek the verb is peitharchein, 'to obey a ruler'. Peter recognises the council's authority in general, but not over this.

commentary.on: The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree.
commentary.text: Notice the difference from Antigone. She appeals to unwritten, everlasting laws known to all. Peter appeals to a particular act of God, raising Jesus, which he has witnessed. Christianity would hold both: a natural law written on the heart (Romans 2:14–15), and a revelation in history.

commentary.on: We are his witnesses of these things
commentary.text: The Greek word for 'witnesses' is martyres, from which 'martyr' comes. Most of the apostles, by tradition, died for this witness, as Antigone died for hers.

compare.why: About AD 30, in Jerusalem, the apostles were ordered by the city's highest council to stop teaching about Jesus. Their answer, given in Acts, is the Bible's own statement of what Antigone claimed.
compare.title: We must obey God rather than men

paras: It is easy to make Creon a villain, and the end of the play condemns him. But Sophocles gives him a real case. Thebes has just survived a civil war in which a prince led a foreign army against his own city. A new ruler must show that treason will not be honoured. If the traitor and the defender are buried alike, what does loyalty mean?

Creon also speaks for law itself. A decree publicly made must be obeyed, or there is no city. 'Anarchy', he says later in the play, 'is the worst of evils'. Every state faces citizens who claim that their conscience exempts them. If every individual decides which laws to obey, can there be law at all? That is the strongest form of Creon's case, and it has never gone away.
sections.key: Creon speaks for a city just saved from civil war, for loyalty and for the rule of law itself; his case is real.

paras: Antigone does not say 'I follow my feelings'. She says there are laws above the king's: 'immutable unwritten laws', not made today or yesterday, binding on everyone. The king's decree conflicts with them, so it is not truly law.

This is one of the founding ideas of the West. Aristotle cited Antigone's words as the example of law 'according to nature'. The Stoics and Cicero developed the idea of a natural law common to all humanity. Paul spoke of a law written on the heart (Romans 2:15). Aquinas wrote that a human law contrary to the natural law 'is no longer a law but a perversion of law'. Martin Luther King quoted Aquinas in his Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) to defend breaking unjust laws. The line from Antigone to King runs through this idea.
sections.key: Antigone appeals to unwritten laws above the state: the root of natural law, from Aristotle and Cicero to Aquinas and Martin Luther King.

paras: The most influential reading of the play is Hegel's. In his lectures on aesthetics, Hegel argued that tragedy at its greatest is not a conflict of right and wrong but of right and right. Antigone stands for the family and the gods of the dead; Creon stands for the state and its law. Both are genuine ethical powers. Each is wrong only in being one-sided, in refusing to recognise the other.

On this reading, the tragedy is that both are destroyed: Antigone dies, and Creon loses his son and wife. The truth lies in a reconciliation neither can see. Many critics think Hegel was too even-handed: the play's gods side clearly with Antigone, since the prophet Teiresias later tells Creon he has offended them. But Hegel made later readers take Creon's case seriously, and his idea of tragedy as the collision of two goods has shaped tragic theory ever since.
sections.key: Hegel read Antigone as a collision of two rights, family and state, each wrong only in being one-sided.

paras: The Christian tradition gave Antigone's claim a name, conscience, and a long history of struggle. The early martyrs refused to offer incense to the emperor. Bishop Ambrose of Milan barred the emperor Theodosius from church in 390 until he did penance for a massacre. Thomas More went to the block in 1535 saying he died 'the king's good servant, but God's first'.

But Christianity also kept Creon's truth. Paul told the Romans that rulers are 'servants of God' and must be obeyed (Romans 13:1–7). The tradition's answer has been that the state has real authority, given by God and limited by God. Ordinarily we obey; when the state commands what God forbids, we must refuse, openly, and accept the penalty, as Antigone did. That is the difference between civil disobedience and rebellion.

rows: The gods and the family's dead
God, who gives the state its authority
The unwritten laws above any decree
Human law binds unless it contradicts God's law
Obey God, openly, and accept the penalty
table.note: The Christian answer keeps both Creon's respect for authority and Antigone's limit on it.

sections.key: Christianity named Antigone's claim conscience and kept Creon's truth too: authority is real but limited by God.

paras: In the twentieth century Antigone came to stand for resistance to tyranny. Anouilh's version played in occupied Paris in 1944; audiences heard in it the choice between collaboration and resistance. In Germany, the students of the White Rose, executed in 1943 for distributing leaflets against Hitler, have often been compared to her. Women's movements read her as a woman who would not be silenced by a man's law.

Simone Weil, the French philosopher, wrote an essay on the play for factory workers in 1936, describing Antigone as someone who, alone and without support, chose love over the city's orders. Weil gave special weight to Antigone's line that she was born to share in love, not in hate. Whatever one makes of Creon, it is Antigone the West remembers.
sections.key: Modern Europe made Antigone a figure of resistance, from occupied Paris to the White Rose; Simone Weil read her as love choosing against the city.

paras: Does Antigone's suffering teach anyone? Not her: she dies, walled up in a tomb, where she hangs herself. Creon learns, but too late: Teiresias warns him, he relents, and he arrives to find Antigone dead and his son Haemon killing himself over her body; his wife Eurydice kills herself on hearing the news. The play ends with the chorus saying that wisdom is the chief part of happiness, and that the proud learn it, in old age, by suffering.

So Sophocles repeats Aeschylus' law, but darker. The lesson comes, as in the Agamemnon, too late to save anyone. And both Antigone and Creon are 'stubborn'. Sophocles seems to admire her and to fear what such certainty can do. The play leaves us with two questions: whether we would have had Antigone's courage, and whether we would know when our certainty was Creon's.
sections.key: Creon learns by suffering, too late; Sophocles admires Antigone's courage while showing what unbending certainty costs.

debate.question: Antigone or Creon?

positions.name: Antigone is right
positions.who: Most readers ancient and modern; Aristotle's Rhetoric; Simone Weil; the resistance readings
positions.view: Some laws are above any state. Creon's decree violated them, and Antigone was right to disobey openly and accept death. The gods of the play agree: Teiresias condemns Creon.
positions.evidence: 'The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven'; Teiresias' warning; Creon's ruin; 'My nature is for mutual love, not hate'.

positions.name: Creon has the stronger case, or at least a real one
positions.who: Some modern political readers; Creon's own speeches
positions.view: After a civil war, the city's survival depends on law and loyalty. A citizen who decides for herself which laws to keep threatens all order. Antigone is admirable but also proud and uncompromising.
positions.evidence: The ship of state speech; 'anarchy is the worst of evils'; the chorus calling Antigone 'stubborn' and 'self-willed'.

positions.name: Both are right, and both are wrong
positions.who: G. W. F. Hegel, Lectures on Aesthetics; many critics after him
positions.view: The play is a collision of two genuine goods, the family and its gods against the state and its law. Each is destroyed by refusing to see the other's claim.
positions.evidence: Both are called stubborn; both are destroyed; the play's last words praise wisdom over pride.

debate.agree: All agree that the play gives both sides real arguments, that Creon learns his error too late, and that Antigone's appeal to unwritten laws has shaped Western ideas of conscience and law.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art has no painting of Antigone or of the burial of a brother, and a stand-in would only pretend.

music.why: Fauré's Requiem is music for burying the dead with love and without terror: the rite Antigone gave her brother at the cost of her life.

think.why: Antigone appealed to laws no state wrote. Where could such laws come from? See the great teachers on natural law and conscience.

learn.why: Peter's answer to the council, the Bible's own Antigone moment, and the motto of conscience ever since.

check.q: What is the strongest form of Creon's case?
options: That women should never bury the dead
That a city just saved from civil war cannot survive if traitors are honoured like defenders and citizens choose which laws to obey
That the gods ordered him
That Polynices was ugly
check.why: The ship of state and 'anarchy is the worst of evils'; his misogyny is a weakness, not his case.

check.q: What does Antigone claim about the laws she obeyed?
options: That they were her own feelings
That the people of Thebes had voted for them
That Creon had secretly approved them
That they are unwritten, everlasting laws of the gods, binding even on kings
check.why: 'The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday'.

check.q: How does Peter's answer in Acts 5 differ from Antigone's?
options: There is no difference
Peter denies that the council has any authority at all
Peter says he will stop teaching
Peter appeals to a particular act of God he has witnessed, the raising of Jesus, as well as to God's authority
check.why: Antigone appeals to unwritten laws known to all; Peter adds 'The God of our fathers raised up Jesus ... We are his witnesses'.

check.q: What is Hegel's reading of the play?
options: It shows that the gods do not exist
Antigone is simply right and Creon simply wrong
It is a collision of two rights, family and state, each wrong in being one-sided
It is about the evils of monarchy
check.why: Hegel saw tragedy as right against right; critics reply that the play's gods side with Antigone.

check.q: How has the Christian tradition kept both Creon's truth and Antigone's?
options: By forbidding all burial customs
By saying the state's authority is real but limited by God: ordinarily obey, and when it commands what God forbids, refuse openly and accept the penalty
By saying the state has no authority
By saying conscience must always obey the state
check.why: Romans 13 and Acts 5:29 together; More's 'the king's good servant, but God's first'.

check.q: Who in the play learns by suffering, and when?
options: The guard
Antigone, before she dies
Creon, but too late to save Antigone, his son or his wife
No one, because the play has no lesson
check.why: Creon relents after Teiresias' warning and arrives too late; the chorus ends saying the proud learn wisdom by suffering in old age.

tutorial.question: Antigone or Creon?
tutorial.approach: State Creon's case at full strength, then Antigone's. Explain the idea of unwritten laws and its later history. Discuss Hegel's view. Compare Acts 5:29 and Romans 13. Take a side, or argue Hegel's view, and answer the strongest objection.
strong: States Creon's case fairly: civil war, loyalty, the rule of law.
Explains Antigone's appeal to the unwritten laws and why burial mattered.
Explains Hegel's reading and its critics.
Uses Acts 5:29 and Romans 13 to show the Christian position.
Traces the idea's influence: natural law, conscience, civil disobedience.
Reaches a view and answers the other side.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: find one small rule at work or home that you follow without thinking. Ask whether it serves people well. If it does, keep it gladly; if it does not, raise it openly and kindly with whoever can change it.
sessions.reflect: Is there anything you would refuse to do even if the law commanded it? How would you know your conscience was right, and not just stubborn?
takeaways: Creon forbids the burial of the traitor Polynices; Antigone buries him and defends herself by 'the immutable unwritten laws of Heaven'.
Both have real claims: Creon the city's order after civil war, Antigone the laws above any state; Hegel read it as two rights in collision.
Antigone's claim became natural law and conscience in the West, from Aristotle to Acts 5:29 and Martin Luther King; Creon learns by suffering, too late.

sessions.title: The case against: are the gods just?
sessions.line: A god comes to his own city in human form, is rejected by its king, and makes the king's mother tear her son apart. Euripides' last and darkest play.
sessions.plain: In Euripides' Bacchae, the god Dionysus comes to Thebes disguised as a man, to make the city worship him. The young king Pentheus refuses and tries to stop the god's rites. Dionysus drives the women of Thebes mad, and Pentheus' own mother, Agave, tears him to pieces, thinking he is a lion. When she comes to her senses and her father asks the god for mercy, Dionysus answers that they learned too late. Herodotus, writing in the same years, says the same of the divine in plain prose: it is jealous of human greatness. This session gives the strongest objection to everything so far: perhaps the gods are not just, and suffering teaches nothing except that the powerful will have their way.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 to 5 built a hopeful case. Aeschylus said Zeus has made suffering a teacher and showed a city learning justice; Sophocles showed a good man destroyed by ignorance, and a woman dying for the gods' unwritten laws, but in both plays the gods were on the side of right. Euripides, the youngest of the three, asks whether that is true. This is the objection at full strength, and it must be heard before any verdict.
answers: Are the gods of tragedy just?
What happens in the Bacchae, and what does it show?
What did the Greeks mean by the jealousy of the gods?
What did Nietzsche think tragedy was, and why did he blame Euripides?
What do Christians say God does with suffering, and is it an answer?
sessions.finding: Euripides' Bacchae shows a god who destroys a family for refusing him honour, and Herodotus' 'jealousy of the gods' says the divine strikes greatness, not wickedness: tragedy's darkest answer is that the divine may be power without justice, and that suffering teaches only submission.

paras: The case so far has been that suffering can teach. In Aeschylus it taught a city to judge instead of avenge. In Sophocles, Oedipus learned the truth about himself and Creon learned his error, both too late, but the gods stood behind the moral order: Apollo's oracles were true, and the unwritten laws Antigone obeyed were the gods' own.

Now the objection. Suppose the gods are not good. Suppose they are simply powerful, and punish not wickedness but disrespect. Then 'learning through suffering' means only learning to bow. Euripides put this possibility on the Athenian stage more boldly than anyone, and in the Bacchae he did it with the god of the theatre himself.
background.key: So far the gods stood behind the moral order; the objection is that they may be power without justice.

paras: Euripides was born about 480 BC and lived through the whole of Athens' greatest age and its long war with Sparta. Ancient stories say he was a recluse who wrote in a cave on the island of Salamis and owned the largest private library in Athens. He was associated with the new thinkers of his day, the Sophists, who questioned traditional beliefs. Aristophanes mocked him for bringing everyday people, clever arguments and doubt about the gods onto the stage.

He was popular, much quoted and much parodied, but he won first prize only four times in his life. Near the end he left Athens for the court of King Archelaus in Macedonia, where he died in 406 BC. The Bacchae was found among his papers and staged in Athens after his death, probably in 405 BC, by his son. It won first prize. Athens surrendered to Sparta the next year.

timeline.text: Euripides is born
Medea; the war with Sparta begins
Hippolytus, in which Aphrodite destroys a young man for refusing her
Euripides leaves for Macedonia
Euripides dies in Macedonia; Sophocles dies in Athens
The Bacchae staged after his death; Aristophanes' Frogs
Athens surrenders to Sparta

background.key: Euripides (about 480–406 BC), the questioner of the gods, won only four prizes in life; the Bacchae was staged after his death and won.

paras: Dionysus was the son of Zeus and Semele, a daughter of Kadmos, the old founder of Thebes. He was the god of wine, of ecstasy and of the theatre itself; his women followers, the maenads or Bacchae, danced on the mountains at night in fawnskins, carrying the thyrsos, an ivy-topped staff. The Romans called him Bacchus. In the Bacchae the god of tragedy appears in a tragedy, and the play asks what kind of god he is.

The play opens with Dionysus alone, disguised as a young man from the east. Semele's sisters, he says, denied that Zeus was his father, so he has driven all the women of Thebes mad and sent them to the mountain. Thebes must learn, whether it wants to or not, that he is a god. The young king, his cousin Pentheus, refuses: he jails the stranger, who walks free, and is lured by him to spy on the women, dressed as one of them. On the mountain the god sets him in a pine tree and calls on the maenads to punish him. They tear the tree down. His mother Agave, possessed, does not know him; he pulls off his headdress and begs her for pity, and she and her sisters tear him apart.

Agave comes home carrying his head on her staff, proud of the 'lion' she has caught. Her father Kadmos, in one of the most moving scenes in Greek drama, brings her slowly back to her senses with questions, until she sees what she holds. Then the god appears in his own form and pronounces exile on the whole family. Kadmos begs for mercy and admits their fault. The god replies, in effect, that they learned too late, and that he had been insulted. Kadmos makes his protest: a god ought not to be as angry as a mortal. Dionysus answers only that Zeus approved it long ago. The play ends there, with the question unanswered.
background.key: Dionysus drives Thebes mad because it denied him; Agave kills her son Pentheus in ecstasy; Kadmos protests that a god should not rage like a mortal, and the god answers only with Zeus' approval.

paras: We cannot yet quote the Bacchae: no English translation of it out of copyright was available to us in a form we could use, so the play is told above in our own words. Instead the main reading gives the same idea in the words of Herodotus, the first Greek historian, who wrote in the same generation as Euripides. Two short passages state what the Greeks called the jealousy of the gods: the ring of Polycrates, and a Persian's warning to his king. If you have taken 'Bearing suffering', you have read Job, the Bible's own great argument with God over innocent suffering; here we hear the Greek one.
The comparison is from the prophet Hosea, where Israel's God speaks of a people who have rejected him and asks: 'How can I give you up?' It answers Kadmos' protest directly.
background.key: The Bacchae told in our own words; Herodotus on the jealousy of the gods; then Hosea, where God refuses to act in wrath.

before: In the story of Polycrates, what has he done to deserve ruin? What does Amasis advise, and why does it fail?
According to Artabanus, why does God strike the tallest trees? Is that justice?
Kadmos protests that a god ought not to be as angry as a mortal. Is he right? Does the god answer him?
sessions.readWhy: The objection at full strength: the Greek belief, shared by poet and historian, that the gods resent human greatness and punish it regardless of desert.

paras: 40. Now Amasis, as may be supposed, did not fail to perceive that Polycrates was very greatly fortunate, and it was to him an object of concern; and as much more good fortune yet continued to come to Polycrates, he wrote upon a paper these words and sent them to Samos: "Amasis to Polycrates thus saith:—It is a pleasant thing indeed to hear that one who is a friend and guest is faring well; yet to me thy great good fortune is not pleasing, since I know that the Divinity is jealous; and I think that I desire, both for myself and for those about whom I have care, that in some of our affairs we should be prosperous and in others should fail, and thus go through life alternately faring well and ill, rather than that we should be prosperous in all things: for never yet did I hear tell of any one who was prosperous in all things and did not come to an utterly evil end at the last. Now therefore do thou follow my counsel and act as I shall say with respect to thy prosperous fortunes. Take thought and consider, and that which thou findest to be the most valued by thee, and for the loss of which thou wilt most be vexed in thy soul, that take and cast away in such a manner that it shall never again come to the sight of men; and if in future from that time forward good fortune does not befall thee in alternation with calamities, apply remedies in the manner by me suggested."

41. Polycrates, having read this and having perceived by reflection that Amasis suggested to him good counsel, sought to find which one of his treasures he would be most afflicted in his soul to lose; and seeking he found this which I shall say:—he had a signet which he used to wear, enchased in gold and made of an emerald stone; and it was the work of Theodoros the son of Telecles of Samos. Seeing then that he thought it good to cast this away, he did thus:—he manned a fifty-oared galley with sailors and went on board of it himself; and then he bade them put out into the deep sea. And when he had got to a distance from the island, he took off the signet-ring, and in the sight of all who were with him in the ship he threw it into the sea. Thus having done he sailed home; and when he came to his house he mourned for his loss.

42. But on the fifth or sixth day after these things it happened to him as follows:—a fisherman having caught a large and beautiful fish, thought it right that this should be given as a gift to Polycrates. He bore it therefore to the door of the palace and said that he desired to come into the presence of Polycrates, and when he had obtained this he gave him the fish, saying: "O king, having taken this fish I did not think fit to bear it to the market, although I am one who lives by the labour of his hands; but it seemed to me that it was worthy of thee and of thy monarchy: therefore I bring it and present it to thee." He then, being pleased at the words spoken, answered thus: "Thou didst exceedingly well, and double thanks are due to thee, for thy words and also for thy gift; and we invite thee to come to dinner." The fisherman then, thinking this a great thing, went away to this house; and the servants as they were cutting up the fish found in its belly the signet-ring of Polycrates. Then as soon as they had seen it and taken it up, they bore it rejoicing to Polycrates, and giving him the signet-ring they told him in what manner it had been found: and he perceiving that the matter was of God, wrote upon paper all that he had done and all that had happened to him, and having written he despatched it to Egypt.

43. Then Amasis, when he had read the paper which had come from Polycrates, perceived that it was impossible for man to rescue man from the event which was to come to pass, and that Polycrates was destined not to have a good end, being prosperous in all things, seeing that he found again even that which he cast away. Therefore he sent an envoy to him in Samos and said that he broke off the guest-friendship; and this he did lest when a fearful and great mishap befell Polycrates, he might himself be grieved in his soul as for a man who was his guest.

Thou seest how God strikes with thunderbolts the creatures which stand above the rest and suffers them not to make a proud show; while those which are small do not provoke him to jealousy: thou seest also how he hurls his darts ever at those buildings which are the highest and those trees likewise; for God is wont to cut short all those things which stand out above the rest. Thus also a numerous army is destroyed by one of few men in some such manner as this, namely when God having become jealous of them casts upon them panic or thundering from heaven, then they are destroyed utterly and not as their worth deserves; for God suffers not any other to have high thoughts save only himself.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.title: The ring of Polycrates
parts.who: Herodotus (about 484–425 BC), the first Greek historian, from Halicarnassus
parts.when: Written in Athens and elsewhere, about 440–425 BC, in the years of the tragedians
parts.context: Herodotus, whom you may meet in 'The first historians', wrote in the same decades as Sophocles and Euripides, and knew Sophocles personally by ancient report. This story, set about 525 BC, is about Polycrates, tyrant of the island of Samos, whose luck never failed, and his ally Amasis, king of Egypt. It is the plainest statement in Greek prose of what the Greeks called phthonos theon, 'the jealousy of the gods'. Translated by G. C. Macaulay (1890); his note numbers have been removed. The numbers 40 to 43 are Herodotus' chapter numbers.
parts.plain: Amasis writes to Polycrates: your good fortune frightens me, because the divine is jealous. I have never heard of anyone who was lucky in everything who did not come to a terrible end. Throw away the thing you value most, so that you suffer a little loss. Polycrates throws his precious emerald ring into the sea. A few days later a fisherman brings him a fine fish, and the ring is found inside it. When Amasis hears this, he sees that no one can save Polycrates from what is coming, and breaks off their friendship so that he will not have to grieve for him.

commentary.on: yet to me thy great good fortune is not pleasing, since I know that the Divinity is jealous
commentary.text: Here is the objection in its oldest Greek form. The divine does not punish wickedness; it resents greatness. Polycrates has done nothing to deserve ruin except succeed.

commentary.on: never yet did I hear tell of any one who was prosperous in all things and did not come to an utterly evil end at the last
commentary.text: Amasis states it as a law of experience. It is the dark twin of Aeschylus' hymn: not 'by suffering, learning', but 'after success, ruin'.

commentary.on: that take and cast away in such a manner that it shall never again come to the sight of men
commentary.text: His remedy is a kind of sacrifice: lose something on purpose, so that the gods will be satisfied. Notice there is no question of becoming better, only of seeming smaller.

commentary.on: found in its belly the signet-ring of Polycrates
commentary.text: The ring returns. The gods have refused his offering. A modern reader might call it luck; Herodotus says Polycrates saw 'that the matter was of God'.

commentary.on: perceived that it was impossible for man to rescue man from the event which was to come to pass
commentary.text: There is nothing to be done. Herodotus later tells the end (III.120–125): Polycrates was lured to the mainland by a Persian governor and put to a horrible death. The story teaches no virtue; it teaches only that greatness is dangerous.

commentary.on: he broke off the guest-friendship
commentary.text: The coldest detail of all. Amasis abandons his friend to spare himself grief. If the gods are like this, the wise thing is not to love too much what they may destroy.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.title: God suffers no one to think high thoughts
parts.context: In 480 BC Xerxes, king of Persia, is planning to invade Greece. His uncle Artabanus advises him not to. This is the heart of his warning. Herodotus wrote it for Greek readers who knew how the invasion ended: in defeat at Salamis, the battle Aeschylus fought in.
parts.plain: Artabanus says: God strikes with lightning the animals, houses and trees that stand out above the rest, and leaves the small ones alone. A great army can be destroyed by a small one when God, out of jealousy, sends panic or thunder on it; they die not as they deserve. God allows no one but himself to think high thoughts.

commentary.on: Thou seest how God strikes with thunderbolts the creatures which stand above the rest
commentary.text: The image is of lightning hitting the tallest tree. Height itself attracts the blow. It is the same idea as Amasis', now in the mouth of a Persian, which shows Herodotus thought it was wisdom common to all peoples.

commentary.on: then they are destroyed utterly and not as their worth deserves
commentary.text: This is the sting of the objection: the destruction is 'not as their worth deserves'. Divine action is not justice.

commentary.on: for God suffers not any other to have high thoughts save only himself
commentary.text: The god's motive is jealousy for his own greatness. Hold this line beside the Bacchae, retold in the background, where a god destroys a royal house because he was not honoured. It is the same picture of the divine, drawn by a historian and a poet in the same generation.

read.author: Herodotus
read.who: Herodotus (about 484–425 BC), the first Greek historian, from Halicarnassus
read.when: Written in Athens and elsewhere, about 440–425 BC, in the years of the tragedians

paras:
The sword will fall on their cities,
and will destroy the bars of their gates,
and will put an end to their plans.

My people are determined to turn from me.
Though they call to the Most High,
he certainly won’t exalt them.

“How can I give you up, Ephraim?
How can I hand you over, Israel?
How can I make you like Admah?
How can I make you like Zeboiim?
My heart is turned within me,
my compassion is aroused.

I will not execute the fierceness of my anger.
I will not return to destroy Ephraim:
for I am God, and not man; the Holy One among you;
and I will not come in wrath.

parts.title: I am God, and not man
parts.context: Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel (called Ephraim here, after its leading tribe) in the decades before it fell to Assyria in 722 BC. He pictures God as a parent whose child has turned away. The speaker is God.

commentary.on: Yet I taught Ephraim to walk. I took them by his arms
commentary.text: God as a parent teaching a toddler to walk. The picture is the opposite of Dionysus, who came to Thebes to be honoured: this God came to care for a child who did not even know he was being healed.

commentary.on: because they refused to repent
commentary.text: Israel's rejection is real, and it will have consequences: Assyria will come. The prophet does not pretend that turning from God costs nothing.

commentary.on: How can I give you up, Ephraim?
commentary.text: This is the turn. Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). God has every right, by the logic of offended honour, to do the same. Instead he asks how he can bear to.

commentary.on: I will not execute the fierceness of my anger.
commentary.text: Exactly what Dionysus does, God here refuses to do.

commentary.on: for I am God, and not man
commentary.text: Here is the answer to Kadmos. Kadmos said gods should not be like mortals in their anger. Hosea's God agrees: because he is God and not a man, he will not act in wrath. Holiness, in Hosea, means a love greater than wounded pride, not a power greater than ours.

compare.why: Hosea was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century BC. In this chapter God speaks of a people who have rejected him, as Thebes rejected Dionysus, and faces the same choice. Read it beside Kadmos' protest. (Verse 1 is read in 'The whole story'.)
compare.title: How can I give you up?

paras: The objection can be put simply. The hopeful case of this journey depends on a just order behind suffering: Zeus who makes suffering a teacher, gods who uphold the unwritten laws. But the gods of Greek myth are not reliably just. They are jealous, proud and violent, and they punish the innocent with the guilty. If that is what the divine is like, then suffering teaches nothing except that the strong will be obeyed.

And the objection does not depend on Greek religion. Look at the world: earthquakes, plagues, children who die. Whatever rules it, the critic says, does not seem to care about desert. The Bacchae is the West's most powerful picture of that possibility, written by a great poet at the end of his life, in exile, while his city was losing a war.
sections.key: If the divine is power without justice, suffering teaches only submission; the Bacchae is the West's strongest picture of that possibility.

paras: Euripides returned to this theme again and again. In Hippolytus (428 BC), the goddess Aphrodite destroys a young man because he will not worship her. In Heracles, the goddess Hera drives the hero mad so that he kills his own wife and children. In the Trojan Women (415 BC), staged a few months after Athens destroyed the island of Melos and enslaved its people, the gods plan the Greeks' destruction after they have helped them destroy Troy.

His characters often say what the audience may have thought. In a lost play, a character said that if gods do anything shameful, they are not gods. The rationalist critic A. W. Verrall (1910) thought the Bacchae was an attack on religion. That is probably too simple: Euripides wrote the play with deep feeling for the god's beauty and power. But no one has written more searchingly about divine power that does not answer to justice.
sections.key: Euripides repeatedly showed gods destroying those who slighted them, and let his characters ask whether such gods deserve the name.

paras: The great modern commentary on the Bacchae is by E. R. Dodds (1944). Dodds argued that the play is neither an attack on religion nor a defence of it. Dionysus is not a moral being at all; he is a force of nature, the power of the irrational in us: ecstasy, intoxication, the crowd, the release of everything civilisation holds down. That power is beautiful and terrible. Deny it, as Pentheus does, and it will come back as madness.

On this reading the play is a warning, not a theology. Its lesson is psychological: what we refuse to acknowledge in ourselves can destroy us. Dodds wrote in the 1940s, having watched Europe give itself to mass movements. He saw in the Bacchae a picture of what happens when the irrational is first despised and then unleashed. Even so, his reading leaves the objection standing: a force that tears apart a son by his mother's hands is not good, whatever else it is.
sections.key: E. R. Dodds read Dionysus as the irrational power in nature and in us, beautiful and terrible, which destroys those who deny it.

sections.h: Nietzsche and the death of tragedy
paras: The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, in The Birth of Tragedy (1872), gave a quite different account. Greek tragedy, he said, was born from two powers: the Apollonian, of order, form and dream, and the Dionysian, of ecstasy and dissolution. The tragic chorus let the audience feel, beneath every individual's destruction, the indestructible life of the whole. Tragedy did not justify suffering morally; it affirmed life in spite of it, as an aesthetic, not a moral, phenomenon.

Nietzsche blamed Euripides, under the influence of Socrates, for killing tragedy by making it rational, argumentative and moral. Most scholars reject his history. But his challenge goes to the heart of this journey. He thought the search for a moral meaning in suffering, whether Aeschylus' Zeus or the Christian God, was a failure of nerve. The strong, he said, can accept a world without justice and still say yes to it.
sections.key: Nietzsche said tragedy affirms life beyond morality, not by justifying suffering; he blamed Euripides and Socrates for killing it with reason.

paras: The philosopher Bernard Williams, in Shame and Necessity (1993), argued that the Greek tragedians saw something modern moral philosophy and Christianity have tried to deny: that the world is not necessarily shaped to fit our sense of justice. Sometimes there is no answer. That is the objection at its most sober.

The Christian reply does not deny that the world is full of undeserved suffering. It denies that God is like Dionysus. Hosea's God refuses to act in wrath 'for I am God, and not man'. And the Gospels tell a story eerily like the Bacchae's: a divine son comes in human form to his own city, is rejected by its rulers and is killed. But the roles are reversed. In Thebes, the god destroys those who reject him. In Jerusalem, the rejected one is destroyed, and prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34). This verse is missing from some early manuscripts, though most scholars think it records an early tradition.

rows: A son of Zeus, in human form
The Son of God, made flesh
Rejected by Pentheus, king of his mother's city
Rejected by the rulers of Jerusalem
Destroys the king through his own mother
Too late: you should have learned in time
'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing'
table.note: The French thinker René Girard argued in Violence and the Sacred (1972) and later books that the Bacchae shows a crowd killing a victim in the god's name, and the Gospels expose such killing from the victim's side.

sections.key: The Christian answer is not that suffering is just, but that God is unlike Dionysus: in the Gospels the rejected God suffers and forgives.

sections.h: Does the answer meet the objection?
paras: Not entirely, and it should not be presented as if it did. The Christian God, critics reply, is still said to rule a world where the innocent suffer, and Christian history has had its own Pentheuses, people destroyed in God's name. Job's friends defended God's justice, and God rebuked them. If you have taken 'Bearing suffering', you will remember that Job's own answer was not an explanation.

What Christianity offers is different from a theory. It says that God has entered the tragedy rather than staging it from outside; that he is on the side of Pentheus' mother and Iphigenia, not of the god who uses them; and that the last word is not 'too late'. Whether that is true is the question the closing session, still to come, takes up. But it is a real answer to Kadmos, who said gods should not be like mortals in their anger. Christians agree with Kadmos.
sections.key: The Christian reply does not explain suffering away; it claims God entered the tragedy and sided with its victims. Whether that is true remains to be weighed.
