debate.question: Are the gods of tragedy just?

positions.name: No: the divine is power without justice
positions.who: Euripides' characters (Kadmos, protesting that a god should not rage like a mortal); Herodotus' Amasis and Artabanus; A. W. Verrall (1910); Bernard Williams, Shame and Necessity (1993)
positions.view: The gods destroy the innocent with the guilty and punish disrespect, not wrong. The tragedians saw, more honestly than later moralists, that the world is not shaped to our sense of justice.
positions.evidence: Dionysus destroys Pentheus through his mother; Aphrodite destroys Hippolytus; the god's answer that he was insulted; Iphigenia and Pentheus both beg for pity in vain.

positions.name: Neither: the play shows a power to be respected, not judged
positions.who: E. R. Dodds, Bacchae commentary (1944); Friedrich Nietzsche, The Birth of Tragedy (1872), in his own way
positions.view: Dionysus is the irrational force in nature and the soul, beyond good and evil. To ask whether he is just is a category mistake; the play warns of what happens when we deny such powers, or affirms life in the face of them.
positions.evidence: The beauty of the choral odes to the god; Pentheus' rigidity and hidden desire to see the rites; the messenger's closing advice that sound mind and reverence are best.

positions.name: The Christian answer: God suffers rather than inflicts
positions.who: Hosea 11; the Gospels; René Girard (1972 and after); Christian theologians from Irenaeus to Rowan Williams
positions.view: Kadmos was right that a god should not be like mortals in anger. The God of Israel refuses to act in wrath, and in Christ enters the tragedy as its victim and forgives. Suffering is not justified by this, but it is not the last word.
positions.evidence: 'I am God, and not man ... I will not come in wrath'; 'Father, forgive them'; the parallel and reversal of the Bacchae and the Passion.

debate.agree: All agree that the Bacchae shows a god who punishes disrespect with terrible suffering, and that Kadmos' protest, that gods should be better than us, is never answered in the play.

look.why: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo painted Bacchus, as the Romans called Dionysus, in about 1743–45. It shows a gentler story of the same god: in the myth, he found Ariadne abandoned on the island of Naxos and married her, and set her crown among the stars. It is here to show the god's other face, wine, joy and abundance, which the Bacchae never lets us forget. The god who blesses and the god who destroys are the same god.
points: Bacchus sits astride a wine barrel at the centre, crowned with grapevines and leaves, a claret-purple cloth across his lap and a staff topped with vines across his leg.
With one hand he lifts a delicate gold circlet lined with tiny bright stars over Ariadne, and smiles down at her.
Ariadne reclines beside the barrel, stems of wheat in her blond hair, looking away from him, up and to the left.
Six putti surround them: one drinks from a rope-wrapped bottle, one holds a tray, one stands on a cheetah lying in front of the barrel.
In the background a satyr, with goat's legs and horns, walks beside a donkey ridden by a child; the scene is framed by painted stone ornament.

music.why: Górecki's Symphony of Sorrowful Songs is three laments, one of them by a mother for her lost son. It gives the grief of Agave and Kadmos a voice, and answers nothing.

think.why: The strongest modern objections from suffering, stated fairly, and the main replies. Read them beside Kadmos' protest.

learn.why: The Bible's own cry of protest to God, which Jesus prayed on the cross. Faith, too, can say 'why?'.

check.q: In the Bacchae Dionysus says Thebes must learn, willing or not, that he is a god. How does this change Aeschylus' idea of learning through suffering?
options: It means the city will learn nothing
It shows that Dionysus is Zeus
The lesson is now only that the god must be honoured: learning becomes submission to power
It makes the lesson justice
check.why: Aeschylus' wisdom 'o'er the unwilling soul' becomes learning that Dionysus is a god.

check.q: Why is Agave's suffering the strongest part of the objection?
options: Because the god acted through her, possessed, so the punishment falls on someone who did not know what she did
Because she was the most wicked character
Because she killed a lion
Because she refused to worship Dionysus at the start
check.why: She was possessed by the god; like Oedipus she acted in ignorance, but here a god caused it.

check.q: Kadmos protests that a god ought not to be as angry as a mortal. What follows if he is right?
options: That Pentheus was innocent
That a being who punishes from wounded honour is not worthy of worship, however powerful
That Dionysus is not a god
That anger is always wrong
check.why: He judges the god by a moral standard; if the god is above it, 'divine' means only 'powerful'.

check.q: What was E. R. Dodds' reading of the play?
options: A political allegory of Athens and Sparta
A picture of the irrational power in nature and the soul, which destroys those who deny it
An attack on all religion
A defence of Christian morality
check.why: Dodds read Dionysus as the force of the irrational, beyond good and evil; that is different from Verrall's anti-religious reading.

check.q: How does Hosea 11 answer Kadmos?
options: It says Israel deserved destruction
It agrees that God is not like man in anger: 'I am God, and not man ... I will not come in wrath'
It says God never punishes
It says the gods of Greece are false
check.why: The consequences of rejection are real (Assyria), but God refuses 'the fierceness of my anger'.

check.q: Which is the fairest statement of how far the Christian reply meets the objection?
options: It agrees with Nietzsche
It does not explain suffering, but claims God entered the tragedy as its victim and forgives, which answers Kadmos' protest about divine anger
It explains why every innocent suffers
It meets it completely, so there is nothing left to discuss
check.why: The session says the Christian answer is 'different from a theory' and should not be presented as meeting the objection entirely.

tutorial.question: Is the Bacchae an argument against the gods?
tutorial.approach: Set out what Dionysus does and why, and what Herodotus meant by the jealousy of the gods. Weigh three readings: Euripides as sceptic, Dodds' force of nature, Nietzsche's affirmation. Then state the Christian reply, with Hosea and the Gospels, and judge how far it meets Kadmos' protest. Be honest about what it does not explain.
strong: Tells the story accurately and quotes the prologue and the last exchange.
States the objection at full strength, with Euripides' other plays.
Explains Dodds' and Nietzsche's readings fairly.
Uses Hosea 11 and the Gospels' parallel and reversal.
Says honestly what the Christian reply does not explain.
Reaches a view.

reading.author: E. R. Dodds
reading.title: The Greeks and the Irrational
reading.why: The classic study of the irrational in Greek religion and thought.

reading.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
reading.title: The Birth of Tragedy
reading.why: The most influential philosophy of tragedy since Aristotle, read critically.

reading.author: Bernard Williams
reading.title: Shame and Necessity
reading.why: A philosopher's case that the Greeks saw the world more truly than their moralist successors.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: when you feel wronged or slighted, notice whether your anger is about justice or about honour. Before you respond, wait one night, and ask what a good person, not an offended one, would do.
sessions.reflect: Have you ever felt that the world, or God, was unjust? What did you do with that feeling? Is Kadmos' protest one you have made?
takeaways: In the Bacchae Dionysus destroys Pentheus through his own mother for refusing him honour; 'learning through suffering' becomes learning who is in charge.
Kadmos' protest, that a god should not be as angry as a mortal, is never answered in the play: the objection that the divine may be power without justice.
Dodds and Nietzsche read the god as a force beyond morality; Christians agree with Kadmos, and point to Hosea's God and the Gospels' God who suffers and forgives.

sessions.title: Why we watch: the verdict
sessions.line: Aristotle explains why we watch suffering on stage; Christians ask whether the cross is a tragedy; and we give our answer to the journey's question.
sessions.plain: Our verdict: suffering can teach, but it does not teach by itself. The Greek plays show it teaching when it is faced honestly and shared, in a court, a conscience or a theatre; they also show it teaching too late, or teaching only fear. Aristotle said we watch tragedy to feel pity and fear rightly and be cleansed by them. Christians said the cross is the one story that begins as tragedy and does not end as one, and yet the West kept writing tragedies, from Shakespeare on. This session gives the verdict and asks whether there can be a Christian tragedy.
sessions.why: Session 6 gave the objection at full strength: perhaps the divine is power without justice, and suffering teaches only submission. Now we weigh the whole case. Aristotle, who watched these plays a century later, asks why anyone would want to see such things, and his answer brings together everything we have read. Then we ask what happened to tragedy when the West became Christian.
answers: Why did the Greeks watch sad plays?
What is catharsis?
Why did Christianity have no tragedies, or did it?
Is the cross a tragedy?
So can suffering teach us?
sessions.finding: Aristotle said tragedy purifies pity and fear; Christians said the cross is not finally a tragedy because it ends in resurrection; yet the West kept tragedy alive, because suffering faced truthfully still teaches, and the resurrection did not erase the wounds.

paras: Here is our verdict, before the evidence for it. Can suffering teach us? Yes, but not automatically, and not always the person who suffers. In Aeschylus it taught a city to judge instead of avenge. In Sophocles it taught Oedipus the truth about himself and Creon his error, too late. In Euripides it taught only that a god must be obeyed. Suffering teaches when it is faced honestly, shared with others, and set within some order of justice and love. Without that, it only wounds.

Two more claims complete the verdict. Aristotle was right that watching tragedy is a way of learning from suffering without having to suffer it: it trains pity and fear. And Christianity did not abolish tragedy. It claimed that God himself entered it, and that it is not the last word; but the risen Christ still carries his wounds.
background.key: Suffering can teach, but only when faced honestly, shared and set within justice and love; tragedy trains pity and fear; Christianity changed the ending but kept the wounds.

paras: We have spent a long day in the theatre of Dionysus. Session 1 showed the festival: a city watching its myths. Session 2 heard Aeschylus' hymn: Zeus has made suffering a teacher. Session 3 watched the Oresteia end with a court. Session 4 asked whether Oedipus was guilty of what he did not know. Session 5 watched Antigone defy a king for the unwritten laws. Session 6 heard Euripides' objection: a god who destroys for honour.

Aristotle was born in 384 BC, twenty-two years after Euripides and Sophocles died. He never saw these plays new, but he read them and saw them revived, and he wrote the first theory of what tragedy is and does. His Poetics has been the starting point for every theory since.
background.key: Six sessions, from the festival to the objection; Aristotle, a century later, wrote the first theory of tragedy.

paras: When the Roman empire became Christian, the theatres slowly closed. Church writers such as Tertullian (about AD 200) and Augustine (Confessions III.2) attacked the stage for its immorality and for making people enjoy grief without doing anything about it. For a thousand years, Europe wrote no tragedies of the Greek kind. A Byzantine play, Christus Patiens ('Christ Suffering'), retold the Passion in lines borrowed from Euripides, including the lost lament of Agave from the Bacchae; it was once credited to Gregory of Nazianzus in the fourth century, but its date and author are uncertain.

The medieval Church had its own drama, the mystery plays, which staged the whole Bible story from Creation to Judgement, with the Passion at the centre. Then, in the sixteenth century, tragedy was reborn in a Christian culture: Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, Shakespeare's Hamlet, Othello, King Lear and Macbeth. Whether these are Christian tragedies, or tragedies written by Christians in spite of their faith, is the question of this session's comparison.
background.key: The Church closed the theatres and wrote no Greek-style tragedy for a thousand years; tragedy was reborn in Christian England with Marlowe and Shakespeare.

paras: The main reading is from Aristotle's Poetics: his definition of tragedy in chapter 6, with its famous word katharsis, and chapter 14, on how the best tragedies stir pity and fear, with Oedipus again his example.

The comparison is from A. C. Bradley's Shakespearean Tragedy (1904), the most influential book on Shakespeare ever written. Bradley asks what power rules the tragic world, and says the answer cannot be given in religious language. It is the sharpest statement of the question: can there be a Christian tragedy?
background.key: Aristotle's definition and theory of pity and fear; then Bradley on tragedy as 'a painful mystery'.

before: Write down Aristotle's definition of tragedy in your own words. Which part is hardest to understand?
Why does Aristotle think the best tragic deeds happen between people 'near or dear to one another'? Think of the plays you have read.
Bradley says Shakespeare 'was not attempting to justify the ways of God to men'. What does he think tragedy shows instead?
sessions.readWhy: The first theory of why we watch, from the man who knew these plays best.

paras: Tragedy, then, is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions. By 'language embellished,' I mean language into which rhythm, 'harmony,' and song enter. By 'the several kinds in separate parts,' I mean, that some parts are rendered through the medium of verse alone, others again with the aid of song.

Again, Tragedy is the imitation of an action; and an action implies personal agents, who necessarily possess certain distinctive qualities both of character and thought; for it is by these that we qualify actions themselves, and these--thought and character--are the two natural causes from which actions spring, and on actions again all success or failure depends. Hence, the Plot is the imitation of the action: for by plot I here mean the arrangement of the incidents. By Character I mean that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents. Thought is required wherever a statement is proved, or, it may be, a general truth enunciated. Every Tragedy, therefore, must have six parts, which parts determine its quality--namely, Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song. Two of the parts constitute the medium of imitation, one the manner, and three the objects of imitation. And these complete the list. These elements have been employed, we may say, by the poets to a man; in fact, every play contains Spectacular elements as well as Character, Plot, Diction, Song, and Thought.

But most important of all is the structure of the incidents. For Tragedy is an imitation, not of men, but of an action and of life, and life consists in action, and its end is a mode of action, not a quality. Now character determines men's qualities, but it is by their actions that they are happy or the reverse. Dramatic action, therefore, is not with a view to the representation of character: character comes in as subsidiary to the actions. Hence the incidents and the plot are the end of a tragedy; and the end is the chief thing of all. Again, without action there cannot be a tragedy; there may be without character. The tragedies of most of our modern poets fail in the rendering of character; and of poets in general this is often true. It is the same in painting; and here lies the difference between Zeuxis and Polygnotus. Polygnotus delineates character well: the style of Zeuxis is devoid of ethical quality. Again, if you string together a set of speeches expressive of character, and well finished in point of diction and thought, you will not produce the essential tragic effect nearly so well as with a play which, however deficient in these respects, yet has a plot and artistically constructed incidents. Besides which, the most powerful elements of emotional: interest in Tragedy Peripeteia or Reversal of the Situation, and Recognition scenes--are parts of the plot. A further proof is, that novices in the art attain to finish: of diction and precision of portraiture before they can construct the plot. It is the same with almost all the early poets.

The Plot, then, is the first principle, and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy: Character holds the second place. A similar fact is seen in painting. The most beautiful colours, laid on confusedly, will not give as much pleasure as the chalk outline of a portrait. Thus Tragedy is the imitation of an action, and of the agents mainly with a view to the action.

The Spectacle has, indeed, an emotional attraction of its own, but, of all the parts, it is the least artistic, and connected least with the art of poetry. For the power of Tragedy, we may be sure, is felt even apart from representation and actors. Besides, the production of spectacular effects depends more on the art of the stage machinist than on that of the poet.

Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way, and indicates a superior poet. For the plot ought to be so constructed that, even without the aid of the eye, he who hears the tale told will thrill with horror and melt to pity at what takes place. This is the impression we should receive from hearing the story of the Oedipus. But to produce this effect by the mere spectacle is a less artistic method, and dependent on extraneous aids. Those who employ spectacular means to create a sense not of the terrible but only of the monstrous, are strangers to the purpose of Tragedy; for we must not demand of Tragedy any and every kind of pleasure, but only that which is proper to it. And since the pleasure which the poet should afford is that which comes from pity and fear through imitation, it is evident that this quality must be impressed upon the incidents.

Actions capable of this effect must happen between persons who are either friends or enemies or indifferent to one another. If an enemy kills an enemy, there is nothing to excite pity either in the act or the intention,--except so far as the suffering in itself is pitiful. So again with indifferent persons. But when the tragic incident occurs between those who are near or dear to one another--if, for example, a brother kills, or intends to kill, a brother, a son his father, a mother her son, a son his mother, or any other deed of the kind is done--these are the situations to be looked for by the poet. He may not indeed destroy the framework of the received legends--the fact, for instance, that Clytemnestra was slain by Orestes and Eriphyle by Alcmaeon but he ought to show invention of his own, and skilfully handle the traditional material. Let us explain more clearly what is meant by skilful handling.

The action may be done consciously and with knowledge of the persons, in the manner of the older poets. It is thus too that Euripides makes Medea slay her children. Or, again, the deed of horror may be done, but done in ignorance, and the tie of kinship or friendship be discovered afterwards. The Oedipus of Sophocles is an example. Here, indeed, the incident is outside the drama proper; but cases occur where it falls within the action of the play: one may cite the Alcmaeon of Astydamas, or Telegonus in the Wounded Odysseus. Again, there is a third case,--<to be about to act with knowledge of the persons and then not to act. The fourth case is> when some one is about to do an irreparable deed through ignorance, and makes the discovery before it is done. These are the only possible ways. For the deed must either be done or not done,--and that wittingly or unwittingly. But of all these ways, to be about to act knowing the persons, and then not to act, is the worst. It is shocking without being tragic, for no disaster follows.

It is, therefore, never, or very rarely, found in poetry. One instance, however, is in the Antigone, where Haemon threatens to kill Creon. The next and better way is that the deed should be perpetrated. Still better, that it should be perpetrated in ignorance, and the discovery made afterwards. There is then nothing to shock us, while the discovery produces a startling effect. The last case is the best, as when in the Cresphontes Merope is about to slay her son, but, recognising who he is, spares his life. So in the Iphigenia, the sister recognises the brother just in time. Again in the Helle, the son recognises the mother when on the point of giving her up. This, then, is why a few families only, as has been already observed, furnish the subjects of tragedy. It was not art, but happy chance, that led the poets in search of subjects to impress the tragic quality upon their plots. They are compelled, therefore, to have recourse to those houses whose history contains moving incidents like these.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: What tragedy is
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.context: Aristotle wrote the Poetics probably as lecture notes for his school, the Lyceum, in Athens around 335 BC. Chapter 6 gives his definition of tragedy and sets out its six parts. Butcher's translation (1895) is careful and close. The cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Tragedy is an imitation of a serious, complete action of some size, in beautiful language, acted out rather than told, which through pity and fear brings about the katharsis, the purging or purifying, of those feelings. Its six parts are plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle. Plot matters most: tragedy imitates action, and life is action, not character. Reversal and recognition, the most moving things in tragedy, are parts of the plot. Spectacle matters least: tragedy works even when you only read it.

commentary.on: Tragedy, then, is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude
commentary.text: The most famous definition in literary history. 'Imitation' (mimesis) means representation: the play shows an action, as a painting shows a face. 'Serious' separates it from comedy. 'Complete' means it has a beginning, middle and end. 'Of a certain magnitude' means big enough to matter and small enough to grasp.

commentary.on: in the form of action, not of narrative
commentary.text: Tragedy is acted, not told. We see people choosing and suffering before our eyes, which is why it moves us more than a report.

commentary.on: through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions
commentary.text: The Greek is katharsis. Aristotle never explains it in the Poetics, and scholars have argued about it for five hundred years. It can mean purgation, as a medicine purges the body; purification, as a ritual cleanses; or clarification, as muddy water clears. The lecture sets out the three readings.

commentary.on: For Tragedy is an imitation, not of men, but of an action and of life
commentary.text: Aristotle puts action above character. We are what we do. A tragedy is not a study of a personality but of a deed and its consequences: Agamemnon at Aulis, Oedipus at the crossroads, Antigone at her brother's body.

commentary.on: Peripeteia or Reversal of the Situation, and Recognition scenes
commentary.text: Reversal and recognition, which you saw in Oedipus ('all brought to pass, all true!') and in Agave, when she sees what she holds. These are the moments when suffering turns into knowledge.

commentary.on: The Plot, then, is the first principle, and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy
commentary.text: The soul (psyche) of a tragedy is its plot: the order of events, what leads to what. A tragedy teaches by showing how actions bring their consequences.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: Pity and fear
parts.context: Chapter 14 asks how the poet should stir pity and fear, and which tragic situations do it best. Aristotle names many plays, some now lost. The cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Pity and fear should come from the story itself, so that even someone who only hears the plot of Oedipus shudders and pities. Shock and spectacle are a lesser art. The most moving deeds happen between people who are close: a brother kills a brother, a son a mother. The poet must keep the old stories but handle them well. A terrible deed can be done knowingly, as Medea kills her children; in ignorance and then discovered, as in Oedipus; or nearly done in ignorance and stopped by recognition just in time, which Aristotle thinks best.

commentary.on: he who hears the tale told will thrill with horror and melt to pity at what takes place
commentary.text: Fear and pity, Aristotle's two tragic emotions. You do not need to see the play: the story itself does the work. Oedipus is his example, as in chapter 13.

commentary.on: the pleasure which the poet should afford is that which comes from pity and fear through imitation
commentary.text: A strange phrase: pleasure from pity and fear. The pleasure is not in the suffering but in the imitation and what we learn from it, as Aristotle said in chapter 4, which you read in session 1.

commentary.on: But when the tragic incident occurs between those who are near or dear to one another
commentary.text: Agamemnon and his daughter; Clytemnestra and her husband; Orestes and his mother; Oedipus and his parents; Antigone and her brother; Agave and her son. Every play in this journey turns on a wound within a family. Tragedy shows that the deepest suffering comes from those we love.

commentary.on: Still better, that it should be perpetrated in ignorance, and the discovery made afterwards.
commentary.text: Oedipus' case. The deed done without knowing, then recognised: the most tragic, because the person is innocent in will and yet the deed is real.

commentary.on: The last case is the best, as when in the Cresphontes Merope is about to slay her son, but, recognising who he is, spares his life.
commentary.text: Surprisingly, Aristotle thinks the best plot is one where the terrible deed is prevented at the last moment by recognition. Perhaps the most hopeful line in the Poetics: knowledge, in time, can save. It is the opposite of the Bacchae, where Pentheus pulls off his headband to be recognised, and is not.

read.author: Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great

paras: Hence, in the first place, a Shakespearean tragedy is never, like some miscalled tragedies, depressing. No one ever closes the book with the feeling that man is a poor mean creature. He may be wretched and he may be awful, but he is not small. His lot may be heart-rending and mysterious, but it is not contemptible. The most confirmed of cynics ceases to be a cynic while he reads these plays. And with this greatness of the tragic hero (which is not always confined to him) is connected, secondly, what I venture to describe as the centre of the tragic impression. This central feeling is the impression of waste. With Shakespeare, at any rate, the pity and fear which are stirred by the tragic story seem to unite with, and even to merge in, a profound sense of sadness and mystery, which is due to this impression of waste. 'What a piece of work is man,' we cry; 'so much more beautiful and so much more terrible than we knew! Why should he be so if this beauty and greatness only tortures itself and throws itself away?' We seem to have before us a type of the mystery of the whole world, the tragic fact which extends far beyond the limits of tragedy. Everywhere, from the crushed rocks beneath our feet to the soul of man, we see power, intelligence, life and glory, which astound us and seem to call for our worship. And everywhere we see them perishing, devouring one another and destroying themselves, often with dreadful pain, as though they came into being for no other end. Tragedy is the typical form of this mystery, because that greatness of soul which it exhibits oppressed, conflicting and destroyed, is the highest existence in our view. It forces the mystery upon us, and it makes us realise so vividly the worth of that which is wasted that we cannot possibly seek comfort in the reflection that all is vanity.

It will be agreed, however, first, that this question must not be answered in 'religious' language. For although this or that dramatis persona may speak of gods or of God, of evil spirits or of Satan, of heaven and of hell, and although the poet may show us ghosts from another world, these ideas do not materially influence his representation of life, nor are they used to throw light on the mystery of its tragedy. The Elizabethan drama was almost wholly secular; and while Shakespeare was writing he practically confined his view to the world of non-theological observation and thought, so that he represents it substantially in one and the same way whether the period of the story is pre-Christian or Christian. He looked at this 'secular' world most intently and seriously; and he painted it, we cannot but conclude, with entire fidelity, without the wish to enforce an opinion of his own, and, in essentials, without regard to anyone's hopes, fears, or beliefs. His greatness is largely due to this fidelity in a mind of extraordinary power; and if, as a private person, he had a religious faith, his tragic view can hardly have been in contradiction with this faith, but must have been included in it, and supplemented, not abolished, by additional ideas.

Thus we are left at last with an idea showing two sides or aspects which we can neither separate nor reconcile. The whole or order against which the individual part shows itself powerless seems to be animated by a passion for perfection: we cannot otherwise explain its behaviour towards evil. Yet it appears to engender this evil within itself, and in its effort to overcome and expel it it is agonised with pain, and driven to mutilate its own substance and to lose not only evil but priceless good. That this idea, though very different from the idea of a blank fate, is no solution of the riddle of life is obvious; but why should we expect it to be such a solution? Shakespeare was not attempting to justify the ways of God to men, or to show the universe as a Divine Comedy. He was writing tragedy, and tragedy would not be tragedy if it were not a painful mystery. Nor can he be said even to point distinctly, like some writers of tragedy, in any direction where a solution might lie. We find a few references to gods or God, to the influence of the stars, to another life: some of them certainly, all of them perhaps, merely dramatic--appropriate to the person from whose lips they fall. A ghost comes from Purgatory to impart a secret out of the reach of its hearer--who presently meditates on the question whether the sleep of death is dreamless.

Accidents once or twice remind us strangely of the words, 'There's a divinity that shapes our ends.' More important are other impressions. Sometimes from the very furnace of affliction a conviction seems borne to us that somehow, if we could see it, this agony counts as nothing against the heroism and love which appear in it and thrill our hearts. Sometimes we are driven to cry out that these mighty or heavenly spirits who perish are too great for the little space in which they move, and that they vanish not into nothingness but into freedom. Sometimes from these sources and from others comes a presentiment, formless but haunting and even profound, that all the fury of conflict, with its waste and woe, is less than half the truth, even an illusion, 'such stuff as dreams are made on.' But these faint and scattered intimations that the tragic world, being but a fragment of a whole beyond our vision, must needs be a contradiction and no ultimate truth, avail nothing to interpret the mystery. We remain confronted with the inexplicable fact, or the no less inexplicable appearance, of a world travailing for perfection, but bringing to birth, together with glorious good, an evil which it is able to overcome only by self-torture and self-waste. And this fact or appearance is tragedy.

parts.author: A. C. Bradley

parts.title: Waste, and a world travailing
parts.who: A. C. Bradley (1851–1935), Oxford professor of poetry
parts.context: Bradley gave these lectures at Oxford and published them in 1904. Lecture I, 'The Substance of Shakespearean Tragedy', asks what Shakespeare's tragedies have in common and what they tell us about the world. Footnote numbers have been removed. The cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Bradley says Shakespeare's tragedies never make us think human beings are small: their heroes are great, and their fall gives an impression of 'waste'. We see power and goodness everywhere destroying themselves. The power ruling the tragic world cannot be described in religious terms, because Shakespeare's drama is secular. It is not a just moral order, or we would not feel the mystery so deeply, and not a blind fate, or we would despair. It is a world that seems to long for perfection, yet produces evil that it can drive out only by destroying good. That, he says, is tragedy: a painful mystery.

commentary.on: No one ever closes the book with the feeling that man is a poor mean creature.
commentary.text: The ode to man again: human beings are deina, wonderful and terrible. Tragedy shows our greatness even in our fall. This is why it is not simply depressing.

commentary.on: This central feeling is the impression of waste.
commentary.text: Bradley's key word. What we feel at the end of King Lear is not that justice has been done but that something precious has been thrown away. Iphigenia, Antigone, Pentheus: the Greek plays leave the same feeling.

commentary.on: this question must not be answered in 'religious' language
commentary.text: Bradley's challenge. Characters in Shakespeare speak of God and heaven, but the plays do not explain their suffering by religion. Shakespeare painted the world as it is, 'without regard to anyone's hopes, fears, or beliefs'.

commentary.on: his tragic view can hardly have been in contradiction with this faith, but must have been included in it, and supplemented, not abolished, by additional ideas.
commentary.text: But notice what Bradley does not say. He does not say tragedy and faith are enemies. If Shakespeare had a faith, his tragic view was included in it and 'supplemented, not abolished'. That is close to the Christian position this session defends.

commentary.on: Shakespeare was not attempting to justify the ways of God to men, or to show the universe as a Divine Comedy.
commentary.text: Two famous allusions. Milton's Paradise Lost aimed 'to justify the ways of God to men'. Dante called his poem a Comedy, because it moves from hell to paradise: a story with a happy ending. Tragedy, says Bradley, does neither.

commentary.on: tragedy would not be tragedy if it were not a painful mystery
commentary.text: If we could explain suffering completely, it would not be tragic. Tragedy keeps the mystery open.

commentary.on: a world travailing for perfection, but bringing to birth, together with glorious good, an evil which it is able to overcome only by self-torture and self-waste
commentary.text: 'Travailing' means labouring in childbirth. Bradley may be echoing Paul: 'the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now' (Romans 8:22). For Paul the labour ends in birth, the glory of the children of God; for Bradley, in the tragic world, the end is not shown. That is the difference between tragedy and the gospel, and it is very small and very great.

compare.title: A painful mystery

paras: Aristotle says tragedy 'through pity and fear' brings about the katharsis of such emotions, and never explains the word. Three main readings have been proposed. Purgation: tragedy works like a medicine, releasing pent-up emotion so we feel better afterwards. The German scholar Jacob Bernays argued this in 1857. Purification: tragedy refines our emotions, teaching us to feel pity and fear for the right things in the right way, as Aristotle's Ethics says virtue requires. Clarification: tragedy makes things clear; through pity and fear we understand something about human life.

The three are not exclusive. A good tragedy releases feeling, educates it and illuminates it. What they share is that tragedy does something good to us. That is Aristotle's answer to his teacher Plato, who wanted to ban the tragic poets from his ideal city because they stirred up grief and fed the irrational part of the soul (Republic X). Aristotle replies that tragedy trains the emotions rather than inflaming them.

rows: Releasing pent-up emotion, like a medicine
Refining feeling, so we pity and fear rightly
Many readers since the Renaissance; linked to Aristotle's Ethics
Making things clear; learning through feeling
Leon Golden and others in the twentieth century
table.note: Aristotle's Politics VIII.7 uses katharsis of music and promises an explanation in the Poetics that does not survive.

sections.key: Catharsis may mean purgation, purification or clarification; all say tragedy does us good, Aristotle's reply to Plato's ban on the poets.

paras: So why did the Greeks watch sad plays? Put Aristotle together with what we have read. Because imitations of painful things teach us, and learning is a pleasure (Poetics 4). Because tragedy shows us people like ourselves suffering more than they deserve, and so trains our pity, and shows us what could happen to us, and so trains our fear (Poetics 13). Because it shows how actions bring their consequences, and so teaches us about life, which is action (Poetics 6).

And because they watched together. Tragedy was a festival of the whole city. The citizens who would vote on war wept together for Hecuba and Agave. That is learning through suffering in its most practical form: a people rehearsing grief, guilt and justice in public, so that they might meet them better in their own lives. Robert Kennedy's use of Aeschylus in 1968 is a late example of what Athens did every spring.
sections.key: We watch tragedy to learn from imitated suffering, to train pity and fear, to see how deeds bring consequences, and to grieve and think together.

sections.h: Why the Christians closed the theatres
paras: Early Christians distrusted the theatre. Tertullian, in On the Spectacles (about AD 200), condemned it as idolatrous and immoral. Augustine, who loved the theatre as a young man in Carthage, wrote in his Confessions (III.2) that he had enjoyed weeping for invented sorrows while doing nothing for real ones, and called that a sickness. The Roman theatres of his day showed little Greek tragedy and much obscenity and violence, which partly explains the hostility.

But there was a deeper reason. Christians believed the world's story was not a tragedy. It began in goodness, fell, was redeemed by Christ, and would end in a new creation. Dante called his great poem a Comedy for this reason. George Steiner, in The Death of Tragedy (1961), argued that Christianity is, at bottom, anti-tragic: where there is redemption and final justice, there can be no absolute tragedy. In his view, real tragedy needs a world without hope of repair.
sections.key: Tertullian and Augustine attacked the theatre; and since the Christian story ends in redemption, George Steiner argued Christianity is 'anti-tragic'.

paras: By Aristotle's standards, the Passion has the shape of a tragedy. A man of great stature, innocent, is destroyed. There is a reversal: the one hailed with palms on Sunday is crucified on Friday. There is recognition: the centurion says 'Truly this was the Son of God' (Matthew 27:54). The deepest suffering comes from those near and dear: Judas betrays him, Peter denies him. And the cry from the cross, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?', is as dark as anything in Greek.

But it does not end there. On the third day, the Gospels say, he rose. Dorothy L. Sayers, the detective novelist and translator of Dante, wrote in 1938 that the Christian story is the greatest drama ever staged, and that it is the dogma, the claim that God himself suffered, that makes it so. Christians have said, then, that the cross is the tragedy to end tragedies: everything tragic is in it, and it ends in resurrection.
sections.key: The Passion has the shape of tragedy, reversal, recognition, betrayal by friends, the cry of abandonment, but Christians say it ends in resurrection.

paras: If the cross ends in resurrection, is there any room left for tragedy in Christian faith? Steiner said no. Bradley, in the comparison, said Shakespeare's tragedies cannot be explained in religious language, and yet a tragic view could be 'included' in a faith, 'supplemented, not abolished'.

Many Christian thinkers have taken Bradley's side. The theologian Donald MacKinnon (1913–1994) argued that Christians who rush past Good Friday to Easter falsify both. The former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams, in The Tragic Imagination (2016), argued that tragedy, by making us look at suffering without explaining it away, is something faith needs, not something it abolishes. And there is a detail in the Gospels: the risen Christ still bears his wounds, and invites Thomas to touch them (John 20:27). The resurrection does not erase the suffering; it transforms it. On this view, Christian tragedy is possible because the Christian hope is not that suffering never happened, but that it will not have the last word.

sections.key: Steiner said Christianity is anti-tragic; Bradley, MacKinnon and Rowan Williams argue tragedy can live inside faith, because the risen Christ keeps his wounds.

paras: The Greek plays give three answers. Aeschylus: yes, by Zeus's law, and a whole city can learn. Sophocles: yes, but usually too late, and the deepest knowledge, of oneself, is the most painful. Euripides: perhaps it teaches only that power must be obeyed. Aristotle adds that we can learn from suffering by watching it, if we feel pity and fear rightly.

The Christian answer takes up all three. With Aeschylus, it believes suffering can be part of a good God's purpose (Hebrews 12). With Sophocles, it knows that self-knowledge is costly and conscience can demand everything. With Euripides' Kadmos, it insists that God must be better than us, not angrier, and claims that he is: that in Christ God suffered rather than inflicted. That does not explain every pain. But it changes the question from 'what does suffering teach?' to 'who suffers with us?', and that is the question the West has asked ever since, at the foot of the cross and in the theatre.
sections.key: Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides give three answers; the Christian answer takes up all three and adds a God who suffers with us.

debate.question: Can there be a Christian tragedy?

positions.name: No: Christianity is anti-tragic
positions.who: George Steiner, The Death of Tragedy (1961); in another way, Nietzsche
positions.view: Real tragedy needs irreparable loss in a world without final justice. Christianity promises redemption, judgement and resurrection, so its stories, however sad, end as comedies in Dante's sense.
positions.evidence: Dante's Divine Comedy; the Church's closing of the theatres; the Passion ending in Easter.

positions.name: Yes: tragedy lives inside faith
positions.who: A. C. Bradley (1904); Donald MacKinnon; Rowan Williams, The Tragic Imagination (2016)
positions.view: Faith does not abolish tragic loss but includes it. Good Friday is real; the risen Christ keeps his wounds; Christians, too, must look at suffering without explaining it away.
positions.evidence: Shakespeare's tragedies written in a Christian culture; John 20:27; Bradley's 'supplemented, not abolished'.

positions.name: The cross as the tragedy to end tragedies
positions.who: Dorothy L. Sayers, 'The Greatest Drama Ever Staged' (1938); the Christus Patiens; the mystery plays
positions.view: The Passion has every element of tragedy, raised to its height, because the sufferer is God. It is the tragic story that becomes, through resurrection, the opposite.
positions.evidence: The reversal from Palm Sunday to Good Friday; the cry of abandonment; the centurion's recognition; the empty tomb.

debate.agree: All agree that the Christian story does not end in tragedy, and that the cross contains everything tragic; they differ on whether tragedy keeps a place inside faith.

look.why: Moretto da Brescia painted this Pietà, the dead Christ held by mourners, in the 1520s. In paintings of this subject the mourners are usually Mary his mother, John and Mary Magdalene, though the gallery's description does not name them. It is the moment between the cross and the empty tomb: the point at which the Christian story looks most like a Greek tragedy, and the session asks whether it is one.
points: Two women and a man support the grey, lifeless body of Jesus along a stone ledge; blood trickles from a gash over his right ribs and from holes in his feet.
To the left, a woman in a navy-blue cloak over a white veil holds her face close to his, her brows deeply furrowed and her mouth wide open.
On his other side, a clean-shaven man in emerald green and vivid red holds Jesus' arm with both hands, his eyes squinting with tears.
A fourth figure, a woman in rose pink with long auburn hair falling over her face, sits on the ground with her arms wrapped tightly around his crossed ankles.
A lidded white jar sits on the ground; behind, a rocky outcrop with a cave-like opening, a winding path between green hills, and white clouds in a blue sky.

music.why: Bach's St Matthew Passion is the greatest Christian setting of the story that has the shape of tragedy: the chorus of mourners, the betrayals, the death. It ends at the tomb, in grief, and yet it was written to be sung on Good Friday by people who knew what came on the third day.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: go to see a serious play or a choral work, or attend a service on a day that remembers suffering (a funeral, a Good Friday, a memorial). Notice what it does to your pity and fear. Then do one thing for someone who is suffering now.

takeaways: Aristotle defined tragedy as an imitation of serious action that, through pity and fear, brings katharsis: purging, purifying or clarifying our emotions; we watch to learn and to feel rightly.
The Passion has the shape of tragedy but ends in resurrection; Steiner called Christianity anti-tragic, while Bradley, MacKinnon and Rowan Williams argue tragedy can live inside faith.
Suffering can teach, when faced honestly, shared and set within justice and love; the Christian claim is that God himself entered the tragedy and keeps its wounds.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Can suffering teach us? In about 300 words, give your answer, using at least three of the plays in this journey and Aristotle, and answer the strongest objection to your view, Kadmos' protest that the gods may be power without justice.
closing.practice: Read one whole Greek tragedy this month, in a modern translation: Antigone or Oedipus the King takes about two hours. If you can, see one performed, live or filmed. Then read the Passion in one of the Gospels (Mark 14–16 takes half an hour) and notice what is the same and what is not.
synthesis: This journey asked whether suffering can teach us, and spent a day in the theatre of Dionysus to find out. Here are the short answers to its questions.

What is a Greek tragedy? A serious play on a story from myth, performed with masks, three actors and a singing chorus, at the City Dionysia, a spring festival of the god Dionysus in Athens. Three playwrights competed each year, each with three tragedies and a satyr play, before many thousands of citizens. Only thirty-two tragedies survive, by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, all from the fifth century BC. A tragedy need not end unhappily; it always asks why people suffer.

Why did the Greeks watch sad plays? Aristotle gave the first answer: we enjoy imitations of painful things because they teach us, and learning is pleasure. Tragedy stirs pity for those who suffer more than they deserve, and fear for people like ourselves, and through them it brings catharsis: a purging, purifying or clarifying of those feelings. And the Greeks watched together, as a city: the same people who voted on war and sat on juries rehearsed grief, guilt and justice in public every spring.

What does 'learning through suffering' mean? Aeschylus' chorus sings that Zeus has made it a law: pathei mathos, by suffering, learning; wisdom comes even to the unwilling, a 'violent grace'. But the same play says 'the doer must suffer', and at Aulis and in the house of Atreus the lesson comes too late for anyone to be saved by it. Robert Kennedy quoted the hymn on the night Martin Luther King was killed, to ask a grieving crowd to choose wisdom over revenge. The letter to the Hebrews uses the same Greek words of Jesus, who 'learned obedience by the things which he suffered', but in its picture the innocent suffers for others, and God is a father who trains, not a force that crushes.

Can revenge become justice? The Oresteia says yes. After three generations of killing, Athena founds a court on the Areopagus: citizens hear both sides and vote, a tie acquits, and the verdict is final. The Furies, goddesses of blood-vengeance, are not destroyed but persuaded, and become guardians of the city. Israel's cities of refuge answered the same problem; both looked at intention, and both held justice to be sacred. The verdict also carries its time's prejudice, in Apollo's claim that only the father is truly a parent. But the West's courts descend from this idea: in Aeschylus, the deepest learning through suffering is a public institution.

Is Oedipus to blame? He killed his father and married his mother without knowing, after fleeing the oracle to avoid exactly that. If guilt lies in the deed, he is guilty; if in the will, innocent. Sophocles shows both: the young Oedipus blinds himself and says 'I sinned'; the old Oedipus at Colonus asks how anyone can blame 'the all-unconscious hand'. Aristotle's hamartia means an error, not a 'tragic flaw' of character: Oedipus is a good man who made a terrible mistake. Freud read the play as a buried wish; the play is about ignorance, and about how the clearest-sighted man can be blind to himself.

What is Antigone about? A king, Creon, forbids the burial of a traitor after a civil war; his niece Antigone buries her brother and tells him that his decree cannot override 'the immutable unwritten laws of Heaven'. Both have real claims: Creon the city's order and the rule of law, Antigone the laws above any state. Hegel called it two rights in collision. Antigone's claim became natural law and conscience in the West: Aristotle cited it, Peter said 'We must obey God rather than men', Aquinas said an unjust law is no law, and Martin Luther King quoted Aquinas from a Birmingham jail. Creon learns by suffering, too late.

Are the gods just? Euripides' Bacchae gives the darkest answer. Dionysus comes to Thebes in human form, is rejected by the king, and makes the king's mother tear him apart. When old Kadmos protests that a god should not be as angry as a mortal, the god answers only that he was insulted and Zeus approved. If the divine is power without justice, suffering teaches only submission. Dodds read the god as the irrational force we deny at our peril; Nietzsche said tragedy affirms life beyond morality. The Christian reply is not a theory of suffering: it agrees with Kadmos, points to Hosea's God, who will not act in wrath 'for I am God, and not man', and to the Gospels, where the rejected Son of God is killed and forgives.

Is the cross a tragedy? It has the shape of one: reversal, recognition, betrayal by friends, the cry 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' But Christians say it ends in resurrection. George Steiner argued that Christianity is therefore anti-tragic; Bradley, MacKinnon and Rowan Williams reply that tragedy can live inside faith, 'supplemented, not abolished', because the risen Christ still carries his wounds. The West kept tragedy alive, from Shakespeare on, in a Christian culture.

So can suffering teach us? Yes, but not by itself. It teaches when it is faced honestly, shared with others, and set within some order of justice and love; then it can make a court out of a feud, a conscience out of a grief, and pity out of fear. Without that, it only wounds, or teaches, as in the Bacchae, that the strong will be obeyed. The Christian claim is that the order of justice and love is real, and that its author did not stand outside the tragedy but entered it. Whether that is true is the question every other hall in this cathedral will help you weigh.

title: The first historians
question: How did history begin, and what does power do?
line: Seven sessions with the two men who invented history: Herodotus, who asked why the Greeks and Persians fought and listened to everyone, and Thucydides, who asked what power does to people and trusted only what he could check. From Croesus on the pyre to Thermopylae, the plague and Melos, where the strong do what they can.
why: Every time you ask 'how do we know?' or 'what really caused it?', you are using a habit of mind that began with two Greeks in the fifth century BC. Herodotus invented history as an inquiry, fair to the enemy and alert to pride. Thucydides made it strict, and used it to show, more clearly than anyone before or since, what power does to those who hold it. This journey reads them at length, tests them against archaeology, gives the case that history is only power its full weight at Melos, and sets them beside the Bible, which saw what they did not: a direction in history, and a God who sees the weak. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year classics paper on Greek historiography (Herodotus and Thucydides in translation), with elements of a paper on ancient and biblical history writing and an introduction to political realism.
before: democracy
outcomes: Explain what Herodotus meant by historia, why he began with the legends of who started the quarrel, and how he gathered and reported his sources.
Retell the story of Solon and Croesus, explain hybris and nemesis, and weigh whether the meeting happened.
Explain Demaratus' 'Law as a master', the battles of the Persian Wars and the evidence for and against Herodotus' reliability.

Describe the plague of Athens and what it did to religion and law, and compare Dionysius of Alexandria's account of Christians in a later plague.
State the Athenians' case at Melos at full strength, assess the Melians' replies and Isaiah's answer, and compare Greek and biblical history.

sessions.title: Why did they fight?
sessions.line: A Greek from the edge of the Persian Empire sets out to keep great deeds from being forgotten, and to find out why Greeks and Persians went to war.
sessions.plain: About 2,450 years ago a Greek called Herodotus wrote a long book about a war between the Greeks and the Persian Empire. He did something new: instead of singing about gods and heroes, he asked questions, listened to people on both sides, and tried to find the real causes. His word for this was historia, 'inquiry', and it gave us our word 'history'. This session reads his first page and asks what it means to look for the causes of things.
sessions.why: This is the first session. If you have taken 'Democracy and its dangers', you have seen Athens govern itself and, in the end, fail. This journey goes back to the two men who first wrote down how Athens rose and fell, and asks what they invented: a way of finding out what really happened, and why. Before we can judge whether history can be trusted, or what it teaches, we need to see where it began.
answers: Who was the first historian?
What does 'history' mean, and where does the word come from?
What were the Persian Wars, and why did Herodotus write about them?
How did Herodotus gather his information?
sessions.finding: Herodotus set out to keep great deeds from being forgotten and to find their causes: history began as an inquiry (historia), listening to both sides.

paras: Imagine the Greek world in about 500 BC. There is no country called Greece. There are hundreds of small independent cities, each with its own laws and its own gods' festivals, scattered round the Aegean Sea from mainland Greece to the coast of what is now Turkey. Their people call themselves Hellenes. Athens and Sparta are the strongest.

To the east lies something much bigger: the Persian Empire, the largest the world had yet seen. In fifty years its kings had conquered everything from Egypt to the borders of India, including the Greek cities on the Turkish coast. In 490 BC and again in 480 BC the Persian kings sent armies against mainland Greece itself. Against all expectation, a handful of Greek cities beat them. These are the Persian Wars, and they are the subject of the first history book.
background.key: Around 500 BC the Greeks lived in hundreds of small cities; the vast Persian Empire invaded Greece in 490 and 480 BC and was beaten.

paras: This journey asks two questions: how did history begin, and what does power do? We follow the two men who invented history writing in the West. Herodotus asked why the Greeks and Persians fought, and listened to everyone. Thucydides, a generation later, asked what power does to people, and trusted only what he could check.

The sessions go in order. First Herodotus: the causes of the war, the story of a king who thought he was the happiest man alive, and the meaning of the battle of Thermopylae. Then Thucydides: his method, the plague that broke Athens, and the hardest passage of all, when Athens tells a small island that the strong do what they can. The last session gives a verdict, comparing Greek history with the Bible's.

background.key: How did history begin, and what does power do? Three sessions on Herodotus, three on Thucydides, then a verdict.

paras: Herodotus was born around 484 BC in Halicarnassus, a Greek city on the south-west coast of what is now Turkey (today's Bodrum). When he was born, his city was ruled by the Persian Empire: he grew up on the border between the two worlds he would write about. He seems to have been exiled after a quarrel with the local ruler, and he travelled widely: to Egypt, to Babylon or near it, to the Black Sea, to Athens, and finally to Thurii, a new Greek colony in southern Italy, where he probably died around 425 BC.

His book, which we call the Histories, is very long: about a quarter of a million words in English translation, divided by later editors into nine 'books'. He probably read parts of it aloud to audiences before it was written down as a whole. The Roman orator Cicero, four centuries later, called him 'the father of history' (On the Laws I.5), and in the same sentence noted his 'countless stories'.
background.key: Herodotus (c. 484–c. 425 BC) grew up in a Greek city under Persian rule, travelled widely, and wrote the Histories; Cicero called him 'the father of history'.

paras: The main reading is the very first page of the Histories: one sentence saying why Herodotus wrote, and five short chapters in which he reports what the Persians and the Phoenicians said about how the quarrel between Asia and Europe began. Then, in one sentence, he puts their stories aside and starts from what he himself knows.

The comparison is the first four verses of Luke's Gospel, written about five hundred years later by a Greek-speaking Christian. Luke also begins by saying why he is writing and how he found out. Reading the two openings side by side shows what it meant, in the ancient world, to promise your reader the truth.
background.key: Herodotus' opening sentence and his first five chapters on the causes of the war; then Luke's preface, which makes a similar promise.

before: What two things does Herodotus say he wants to do in his first sentence?
