Where does Herodotus decide to begin his own account, and why?
sessions.readWhy: The first page of the first history book: why Herodotus wrote, the stories others told about the start of the quarrel, and where he chose to begin.

paras: This is the Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos, to the end that neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time, nor the works great and marvellous, which have been produced some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians, may lose their renown; and especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another.

1. Those of the Persians who have knowledge of history declare that the Phenicians first began the quarrel. These, they say, came from that which is called the Erythraian Sea to this of ours; and having settled in the land where they continue even now to dwell, set themselves forthwith to make long voyages by sea. And conveying merchandise of Egypt and of Assyria they arrived at other places and also at Argos; now Argos was at that time in all points the first of the States within that land which is now called Hellas;—the Phenicians arrived then at this land of Argos, and began to dispose of their ship's cargo: and on the fifth or sixth day after they had arrived, when their goods had been almost all sold, there came down to the sea a great company of women, and among them the daughter of the king; and her name, as the Hellenes also agree, was Io the daughter of Inachos. These standing near to the stern of the ship were buying of the wares such as pleased them most, when of a sudden the Phenicians, passing the word from one to another, made a rush upon them; and the greater part of the women escaped by flight, but Io and certain others were carried off. So they put them on board their ship, and forthwith departed, sailing away to Egypt.

2. In this manner the Persians report that Io came to Egypt, not agreeing therein with the Hellenes, and this they say was the first beginning of wrongs. Then after this, they say, certain Hellenes (but the name of the people they are not able to report) put in to the city of Tyre in Phenicia and carried off the king's daughter Europa;—these would doubtless be Cretans;—and so they were quits for the former injury. After this however the Hellenes, they say, were the authors of the second wrong; for they sailed in to Aia of Colchis and to the river Phasis with a ship of war, and from thence, after they had done the other business for which they came, they carried off the king's daughter Medea: and the king of Colchis sent a herald to the land of Hellas and demanded satisfaction for the rape and to have his daughter back; but they answered that, as the Barbarians had given them no satisfaction for the rape of Io the Argive, so neither would they give satisfaction to the Barbarians for this.

3. In the next generation after this, they say, Alexander the son of Priam, having heard of these things, desired to get a wife for himself by violence from Hellas, being fully assured that he would not be compelled to give any satisfaction for this wrong, inasmuch as the Hellenes gave none for theirs. So he carried off Helen, and the Hellenes resolved to send messengers first and to demand her back with satisfaction for the rape; and when they put forth this demand, the others alleged to them the rape of Medea, saying that the Hellenes were now desiring satisfaction to be given to them by others, though they had given none themselves nor had surrendered the person when demand was made.

4. Up to this point, they say, nothing more happened than the carrying away of women on both sides; but after this the Hellenes were very greatly to blame; for they set the first example of war, making an expedition into Asia before the Barbarians made any into Europe. Now they say that in their judgment, though it is an act of wrong to carry away women by force, it is a folly to set one's heart on taking vengeance for their rape, and the wise course is to pay no regard when they have been carried away; for it is evident that they would never be carried away if they were not themselves willing to go. And the Persians say that they, namely the people of Asia, when their women were carried away by force, had made it a matter of no account, but the Hellenes on account of a woman of Lacedemon gathered together a great armament, and then came to Asia and destroyed the dominion of Priam; and that from this time forward they had always considered the Hellenic race to be their enemy: for Asia and the Barbarian races which dwell there the Persians claim as belonging to them; but Europe and the Hellenic race they consider to be parted off from them.

5. The Persians for their part say that things happened thus; and they conclude that the beginning of their quarrel with the Hellenes was on account of the taking of Ilion: but as regards Io the Phenicians do not agree with the Persians in telling the tale thus; for they deny that they carried her off to Egypt by violent means, and they say on the other hand that when they were in Argos she was intimate with the master of their ship, and perceiving that she was with child, she was ashamed to confess it to her parents, and therefore sailed away with the Phenicians of her own will, for fear of being found out. These are the tales told by the Persians and the Phenicians severally: and concerning these things I am not going to say that they happened thus or thus, but when I have pointed to the man who first within my own knowledge began to commit wrong against the Hellenes, I shall go forward further with the story, giving an account of the cities of men, small as well as great: for those which in old times were great have for the most part become small, while those that were in my own time great used in former times to be small: so then, since I know that human prosperity never continues steadfast, I shall make mention of both indifferently.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: So that great deeds are not forgotten
parts.context: This is the opening sentence of the whole Histories, written in the 430s or 420s BC. In Greek it begins with Herodotus' own name and his city, like a signature. Macaulay translated it in 1890; the footnote numbers in his edition have been removed. 'Hellenes' means Greeks; 'Barbarians' means everyone who did not speak Greek, and here it is not an insult: it simply means foreigners, above all the Persians.
parts.plain: Herodotus says: this book is the result of my inquiry. I wrote it so that what people have done will not be forgotten, and so that the great things done by both Greeks and foreigners will keep their fame. Above all, I want to record why they went to war with each other.

commentary.on: This is the Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos
commentary.text: The Greek word Macaulay translates 'Inquiry' is historia. It meant asking questions and finding out: the same word was used by the first Greek scientists, who inquired into nature. Herodotus' title page gave the word its new meaning. Every time we say 'history', we are using his word for asking.

commentary.on: neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time
commentary.text: The first purpose is memory. Before Herodotus, the Greeks kept the memory of great deeds in poetry: Homer's Iliad sang of the Trojan War so that the heroes' fame would never die. Herodotus takes over the poet's task, but in prose, and about people who had lived within living memory.

commentary.on: some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians
commentary.text: This is remarkable for a Greek writing after a war against Persia. He promises to record the great works of the enemy as well as his own side. Later in the book he praises Persian courage and customs so warmly that the Greek writer Plutarch, five centuries later, accused him of being a 'friend of barbarians'.

commentary.on: especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another
commentary.text: The second purpose is the new one: causes. Not just what happened, but why. The Greek word is aitia, which also meant 'blame' or 'responsibility'. Asking 'why did they fight?' turns out to mean asking 'who was in the wrong?'

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: What the Persians say
parts.context: Herodotus now reports what 'the Persians who have knowledge of history' say about how the quarrel began. These are old legends, in which kings' daughters are carried off by sailors: Io from Argos in Greece, Europa from Tyre in Phoenicia (modern Lebanon), Medea from Colchis on the Black Sea. The Phoenicians were the great traders and sailors of the ancient Mediterranean. 'Rape' here, in Macaulay's old sense, means abduction: carrying a woman off by force.
parts.plain: The Persians say the trouble began when Phoenician traders kidnapped Io, a Greek king's daughter, and took her to Egypt. Then some Greeks kidnapped Europa from Phoenicia, so the score was even. Then the Greeks went further and took Medea from Colchis, and refused to give her back.

commentary.on: Those of the Persians who have knowledge of history declare that the Phenicians first began the quarrel.
commentary.text: Notice who is speaking. Herodotus does not start with his own view, or with the Greek view. He starts by reporting what the enemy's experts say. From the first line, history means listening to the other side.

commentary.on: In this manner the Persians report that Io came to Egypt, not agreeing therein with the Hellenes
commentary.text: Already there are two versions. The Greeks told the story of Io differently: in Greek myth she was loved by Zeus and turned into a cow. Herodotus says nothing about gods. He tells a human, almost political version: traders, kidnapping, revenge.

commentary.on: and this they say was the first beginning of wrongs
commentary.text: This is the question Herodotus will keep asking: who did wrong first? It is the question of every quarrel, between children or between nations, and it is rarely easy to answer.

commentary.on: and so they were quits for the former injury
commentary.text: The Persians imagine history as a ledger of wrongs, each one paid back. Herodotus tells it with a straight face, but the tit-for-tat begins to look absurd, as it is meant to.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: I know who began it
parts.context: The tale reaches the Trojan War. Alexander, son of King Priam of Troy, is better known as Paris; he carried off Helen, the wife of a king of Sparta ('Lacedemon'), and the Greeks sailed to Asia and destroyed Troy ('Ilion'). Then Herodotus stops reporting other people's stories and tells us where he will begin his own. The man he has in mind is Croesus, king of Lydia in western Turkey, who conquered the Greek cities of the coast in the 550s BC.
parts.plain: The Persians say that until the Trojan War there were only kidnappings on both sides, but then the Greeks started a real war over one woman, Helen, and destroyed Troy. The Phoenicians tell the story of Io differently. Herodotus says he will not decide between these legends. He will begin with the first man he knows for certain did wrong to the Greeks, and tell the story of cities great and small, because human success never lasts.

commentary.on: the Hellenes on account of a woman of Lacedemon gathered together a great armament, and then came to Asia and destroyed the dominion of Priam
commentary.text: In the Persian telling, the Greeks are the aggressors: they were the first to turn a quarrel over women into an invasion of another continent. A Greek audience, proud of the Trojan War, would have been startled to hear it told from the other side.

commentary.on: Europe and the Hellenic race they consider to be parted off from them
commentary.text: Here is the oldest statement of an idea that has shaped the world ever since: that Asia and Europe, East and West, are two worlds. Herodotus puts it in Persian mouths. Whether that division is real, or something people make up and then fight over, is a question this journey will return to.

commentary.on: concerning these things I am not going to say that they happened thus or thus
commentary.text: This is the turning point of the opening, and perhaps the moment history begins. Herodotus refuses to judge between the legends. He cannot check them, so he will not build on them.

commentary.on: when I have pointed to the man who first within my own knowledge began to commit wrong against the Hellenes
commentary.text: 'Within my own knowledge' is the key phrase. Herodotus will start where evidence starts: with Croesus, a real king whose gifts to the temple at Delphi Herodotus could still see in his own day. History, for him, begins where myth runs out.

commentary.on: since I know that human prosperity never continues steadfast
commentary.text: This short phrase states the theme of the whole book. Great cities become small and small ones great. Fortune turns. The next session follows this idea in the story of Croesus himself.

read.author: Herodotus
read.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.

paras: Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us,
even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us,
it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus;
that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.

parts.title: An orderly account
parts.context: Luke wrote his Gospel, and its sequel the Acts of the Apostles, around AD 80–90, in good literary Greek. Tradition, from the second century, names him as a companion of Paul and a doctor. These four verses, one long sentence in Greek, are addressed to a patron called Theophilus.

commentary.on: Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative
commentary.text: Like Herodotus, Luke begins by placing himself among other accounts. He does not claim to be the first; he claims to be careful.

commentary.on: even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses
commentary.text: Luke's source is eyewitnesses, as Herodotus' was people who had been there. The Greek word is autoptai, 'those who saw for themselves'. Herodotus used the same idea, autopsy, for what he had seen with his own eyes.

commentary.on: having traced the course of all things accurately from the first
commentary.text: Luke promises accuracy and order. Some scholars (Loveday Alexander, 1993) think his preface is closer to the prefaces of Greek technical and medical writers than to historians; either way, it is the language of someone who has checked.

commentary.on: that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed
commentary.text: Here the two writers part. Herodotus wanted great deeds remembered and their causes found. Luke wants his reader to be sure of something he already believes, because, for Luke, what happened in history is the ground of faith.

compare.why: Five centuries later, Luke opened his Gospel with a preface in the style of a Greek writer. If you have taken 'First Christians', you met it there in passing; here we read it beside Herodotus. Compare what each man promises his reader, and how each says he found out.
compare.title: Another historian's promise

paras: Every people remembers its past, but not every people writes history. The kings of Egypt, Assyria and Persia carved lists of their victories on stone. The Babylonians kept chronicles, year by year, of kings and battles. Israel's scribes wrote a long account of their kings, from David to the fall of Jerusalem, which you can read in the books of Samuel and Kings. The Greeks had Homer, whose Iliad kept alive the memory of a war at Troy, perhaps five hundred years earlier, in poetry full of gods.

What none of these did, as far as we know, was to set out, as a private person, to inquire: to travel, ask questions of strangers and enemies, compare their answers, and explain what caused a great event. That is what Herodotus claims to do on his first page, and it is why the Greek word historia, 'inquiry', became our word for the study of the past.
sections.key: Older peoples kept king lists, chronicles and epic poems; Herodotus was the first we know of to make an inquiry into the causes of a great event.

paras: Not quite. Herodotus had predecessors, and he mentions one: Hecataeus of Miletus (c. 550–476 BC), who wrote a description of the known world and a book of family trees of the heroes, which began, 'I write what seems to me to be true, for the stories of the Greeks are many and absurd.' Only fragments survive. There were other early prose writers, whom later scholars call logographers, 'prose-writers'.

There is also the question of Israel. Some scholars, such as Baruch Halpern in The First Historians (1988), argue that the writers of Samuel and Kings were real historians, working from sources and explaining causes, centuries before Herodotus. Others reply that their aim was different: to show the hand of God in their nation's story, not to inquire. We will return to this in the last session. What is clear is that Herodotus is the first whose whole work survives, the first to call it an inquiry, and the one Western history writing looked back to.
sections.key: Hecataeus came before Herodotus, and some argue Israel's historians did too; Herodotus is the first whose whole inquiry survives.

paras: The empire Herodotus wrote about was founded by Cyrus the Great, who around 550 BC united the Medes and Persians of what is now Iran. In about 547 BC he conquered Croesus' kingdom of Lydia, and with it the Greek cities of the Turkish coast; in 539 BC he took Babylon and let the Jewish exiles go home (Ezra 1). His successors added Egypt and lands as far as the Indus.

At its height under Darius I (reigned 522–486 BC) it stretched about 3,000 miles, with royal roads, a postal system and a tolerant policy towards local religions. Its kings called themselves 'King of Kings'. The Greek cities, by comparison, were tiny: Athens had perhaps 30,000 adult male citizens. When the Greek cities of Ionia, on the Turkish coast, rebelled against Persia in 499 BC and Athens sent ships to help them, Darius resolved to punish Athens. That was the beginning of the Persian Wars.

sections.key: The Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus c. 550 BC, was the largest yet seen; after Athens helped the Ionian revolt, Persia invaded Greece in 490 and 480 BC.

paras: Herodotus had almost no documents. He gathered his history by talking to people: priests in Egypt, guides at temples, old men in Athens and Sparta, Persians who had served the king. He says again and again whose story he is telling: 'the Persians say', 'the Corinthians say', 'this is what the priests told me'. He separates three kinds of knowledge: what he saw himself, what he heard, and what he concluded by reasoning.

He also looked at things. He measured the pyramids, described the dedications of Croesus he had seen at Delphi, and copied inscriptions. Some of what he reports is wrong, and some is fantastic, like the gold-digging ants of India. But he often tells us when he does not believe a story, and sometimes he gives two or three versions and lets us choose. This habit, naming sources and weighing them, is the root of every footnote in every history book since.
sections.key: Herodotus worked mainly from oral sources, named them, separated what he saw from what he heard, and often gave more than one version.

paras: The first five chapters can seem strange: why tell legends only to say you will not judge them? Scholars think Herodotus is doing two things. First, he is showing that he knows the old way of explaining the war, by myth and revenge, and setting it aside. The Persians' story is a tit-for-tat that never ends; the Greeks' own story, of Troy, is poetry. Neither can be checked.

Second, he is making a point about causes. Everyone has a version in which the other side began it. Instead of arguing about the distant past, he will start 'within my own knowledge', with a real king and real events that he can investigate. The move from myth to evidence, from 'they say' to 'I know', happens on the first page. It is a small step, but the whole discipline of history comes through that door.
sections.key: Herodotus reports the legends of who started it, then sets them aside to begin from what he can know: the move from myth to evidence.

paras: Herodotus gives two reasons for writing, and they are still the two reasons for studying the past. The first is memory: so that what people have done will not be forgotten. A people that forgets what happened to it can be told anything. The second is understanding: so that we know why things happened, and who was responsible.

Both are moral tasks. To remember is to do justice to the dead, including the enemy's dead. To ask for causes is to ask who bears the blame. Herodotus does both with unusual fairness, giving the Persians' view first and praising their great deeds alongside the Greeks'. Christians would later add a third reason, which Luke states: that history matters because God has acted in it. Herodotus does not say that, but he does believe the gods watch over human affairs, as the next session shows.
sections.key: History has two purposes for Herodotus, memory and understanding of causes; both are moral tasks, which he carries out with fairness to both sides.

paras: Herodotus is long, and he wanders. He breaks off the story of the war to describe the customs of the Egyptians, the Scythians or the Babylonians for a whole book at a time. Readers who expect a straight narrative find this frustrating. But the wanderings are part of the inquiry: to understand why the Persians and Greeks fought, he thought, you must know who they and their neighbours were, what they believed and how they lived.

Three habits will help you read him. First, notice who is speaking: Herodotus himself, or 'the Persians say'. Second, notice when he gives his own judgement, often in a short sentence at the end of a story. Third, notice the patterns he finds: wealth and pride, warnings ignored, fortune turning. In the next session we follow one of those patterns through the most famous story in his first book.
sections.key: Herodotus' digressions are part of his inquiry; read him by noticing who is speaking, when he judges, and what patterns he finds.

debate.question: Was Herodotus the first historian?

positions.name: Yes: he invented the inquiry
positions.who: Cicero; most classical scholars, such as Arnaldo Momigliano (The Classical Foundations of Modern Historiography, 1990)
positions.view: Herodotus was the first to set out, as a private inquirer, to explain a great event by its causes, collecting and weighing evidence from both sides, and to call it historia. Every later Western historian descends from him.
positions.evidence: His first sentence; his constant naming of sources; the fact that later Greek and Roman historians, from Thucydides to Cicero, treated him as the beginning.

positions.name: No: he had predecessors
positions.who: Scholars of the early Greek prose writers; Baruch Halpern (The First Historians, 1988)
positions.view: Hecataeus and other Greek prose writers had already begun criticising myth and describing peoples, and Israel's historians in Samuel and Kings had written a connected, source-based account of their nation centuries earlier.
positions.evidence: The fragment of Hecataeus calling the Greek stories 'many and absurd'; Kings' citations of 'the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel'.

positions.name: Both: the first of a kind
positions.who: Many modern historians of historiography, such as John Marincola
positions.view: There were many ways of keeping the past before Herodotus; his was new in combining inquiry, prose, a great war, fairness to the enemy and a search for causes. 'First historian' is true if we mean the first historian of this Greek kind.
positions.evidence: The differences between Herodotus and Babylonian chronicles or Israelite history: one inquires, one records, one interprets.

debate.agree: All agree that Herodotus is the first whose whole work survives, and that his idea of history as inquiry shaped every later Western historian.

check.q: Why does Herodotus begin by reporting what the Persians say, rather than the Greeks?
options: Because he had no Greek sources
Because he was Persian himself
Because the Persians had written records and the Greeks had none
Because his method is to listen to both sides, and he deliberately starts with the enemy's view
check.why: He promises to record the deeds of 'Hellenes and Barbarians' alike and begins with the Persians' account; fairness to the other side is part of his method. He was a Greek, though from a city under Persian rule.

check.q: What is the best explanation of why Herodotus refuses to decide between the legends of Io, Europa, Medea and Helen?
options: He could not check them, so he chose to begin from a man he knew of for certain
He did not know the stories well
He thought the gods had caused all of it
He believed all of them were true
check.why: 'I am not going to say that they happened thus or thus' ... 'the man who first within my own knowledge': he starts where evidence starts.

check.q: The Greek word aitia, which Herodotus uses for the 'causes' of the war, also meant 'blame'. What follows for his history?
options: That he wrote only about the Persians' guilt
That he did not believe in causes
That asking why the war happened also means asking who was responsible
That he blamed the gods for everything
check.why: Looking for causes in human affairs is also looking for responsibility, which makes history a moral inquiry.

check.q: Which of these is the strongest reason to doubt that Herodotus was the very first historian?
options: His book is very long
He lived in Persian territory
Cicero called him 'the father of history'
Hecataeus had already written in prose criticising Greek myths, and some scholars argue Israel's historians wrote connected, source-based history earlier
check.why: Cicero's title supports the claim; Hecataeus and the books of Kings are the real challenges.

check.q: How does Luke's preface differ from Herodotus' in its purpose?
options: Luke writes in poetry
Luke does not mention eyewitnesses
Luke claims to be the first to write about his subject
Luke writes so that his reader may be certain of what he was taught; Herodotus writes so that deeds are remembered and their causes known
check.why: Both claim careful inquiry, but Luke writes to ground faith; Herodotus to preserve memory and find causes. Luke says 'many' wrote before him.

check.q: Why did the Persian Wars begin, according to the outline in the lecture?
options: The Greeks invaded Persia to free Babylon
The Persians wanted revenge for Troy
After Athens helped the Ionian Greeks rebel against Persia in 499 BC, Darius resolved to punish Athens
Croesus asked Persia for help
check.why: The legends of Troy are what the Persians 'say'; the historical trigger was the Ionian revolt and Athens' part in it.

tutorial.question: What did Herodotus invent?
tutorial.approach: Start with his first sentence: what two purposes does he give? Then show, from chapters 1 to 5, what he does with the legends and where he chooses to begin. Weigh the claims of Hecataeus and of Israel's historians. Compare Luke's preface. End by saying, in a sentence, what was new.

Notes his fairness to non-Greeks.
Weighs the case for Hecataeus or Israel's historians as earlier.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: ask one older person in your family, or a neighbour, to tell you about one thing they lived through. Listen without correcting, then write down what they said, in their words, before you forget it.
sessions.reflect: When you tell the story of a quarrel you were part of, do you begin with the other person's version? What would change if you did?
takeaways: Herodotus wrote so that great deeds would not be forgotten and their causes would be known; his word historia, 'inquiry', became 'history'.
He began by reporting the enemy's version of who started the quarrel, then set the legends aside to start from what he could know.
He had predecessors, but his was the first surviving inquiry into the causes of a great event, fair to both sides.

sessions.title: Call no man happy
sessions.line: The richest king alive asks a wise man who is the happiest person in the world, and does not like the answer. Years later, on a burning pyre, he remembers it.
sessions.plain: Croesus, king of Lydia, was so rich that 'as rich as Croesus' is still a saying. He showed his treasure to Solon, a wise lawgiver from Athens, and asked who was the happiest man in the world, expecting to hear his own name. Solon named ordinary people who had lived well and died well, and told him: call no one happy until you see how his life ends. Croesus sent him away, lost his son, his kingdom and his freedom, and remembered Solon's words on the pyre. This session asks what Herodotus thought history teaches about wealth, pride and fortune.
sessions.why: The first session ended with Herodotus beginning from 'the man who first within my own knowledge' wronged the Greeks: Croesus. It also ended with his theme, that 'human prosperity never continues steadfast'. Now we see that theme as a story. Herodotus did not only record what happened; he looked for a pattern in it.
answers: Who were Croesus and Solon?
What does 'call no man happy until he is dead' mean?
What are hybris and nemesis?
Did Herodotus think the gods control history?
Did the meeting of Solon and Croesus really happen?
sessions.finding: Herodotus found a pattern in history: Solon told the richest king alive to call no man happy until he is dead, and Croesus learned it on the pyre. Pride goes before a fall.

paras: In the last session Herodotus set aside the old legends and chose to begin with Croesus, king of Lydia, the first foreign ruler to conquer Greek cities. Lydia was a rich kingdom in what is now western Turkey, with its capital at Sardis. It had gold in its rivers, and the Lydians are said to have been the first to strike coins of gold and silver (Herodotus I.94).

Croesus reigned from about 560 to 546 BC. He conquered the Greek cities of the coast, but he also admired the Greeks: he sent huge gifts of gold to the temple of Apollo at Delphi, the most famous oracle in Greece, where Herodotus himself saw some of them a century later.
background.key: Croesus ruled the rich kingdom of Lydia (c. 560–546 BC), conquered the Greek cities of the coast and sent gold to Delphi.

paras: Solon was an Athenian statesman and poet. In about 594 BC, when Athens was close to civil war between rich and poor, the Athenians gave him power to write new laws. He cancelled debts that had made poor farmers into slaves, and gave every citizen some share in government. Later Athenians saw him as a founder of their democracy.

Herodotus says that Solon then left Athens for ten years so that he would not be pressed to change his laws, and travelled to Egypt and to Sardis. Solon was famous as one of the 'Seven Sages', the wise men of early Greece. Some of his poems survive, and they share the thought Herodotus gives him: that no one should trust in wealth, because the gods bring down the proud.
background.key: Solon was Athens' great lawgiver (c. 594 BC), a poet and one of the Seven Sages; his surviving poems warn against trusting wealth.

paras: The story moves across about twenty years and from Athens to Sardis. Croesus attacked Cyrus, the new king of Persia, after the oracle at Delphi told him that if he crossed the river Halys he would destroy a great empire. He did: his own. In about 547 BC Cyrus took Sardis, and Croesus was captured.

timeline.text: Solon writes new laws for Athens
Croesus becomes king of Lydia
Cyrus founds the Persian Empire
Cyrus takes Sardis and captures Croesus
The poet Bacchylides tells of Croesus on the pyre, saved by Apollo
Herodotus tells the story in the Histories

background.key: Croesus attacked Persia on the strength of an oracle and lost his kingdom to Cyrus in about 547 BC.

paras: The main reading has two scenes. In the first (I.28–33), Croesus at the height of his power shows Solon his treasury and asks who is the happiest of men. In the second (I.86–88), years later, he stands bound on a pyre and remembers the answer.

The comparison is a parable of Jesus about a rich man who plans bigger barns and dies that night (Luke 12:16–21). It answers the same question, what makes a life go well, from a different direction. If you have taken 'Psalms and wisdom', you have read Ecclesiastes 9, which says that 'time and chance happen to them all'; this parable takes the thought further.
background.key: Solon and Croesus in the treasury, then Croesus on the pyre; compared with Jesus' parable of the rich fool.

before: What does Croesus expect Solon to say, and why?
Why does Solon rank Tellos, Cleobis and Biton above a king?
What makes Cyrus change his mind on the pyre?
sessions.readWhy: Two scenes: Croesus at the height of his power, and Croesus on the pyre. Together they are Herodotus' clearest lesson about fortune and pride.

paras: 28. As time went on, when nearly all those dwelling on this side the river Halys had been subdued, (for except the Kilikians and Lykians Croesus subdued and kept under his rule all the nations, that is to say Lydians, Phrygians, Mysians, Mariandynoi, Chalybians, Paphlagonians, Thracians both Thynian and Bithynian, Carians, Ionians, Dorians, Aiolians, and Pamphylians),

29, when these, I say, had been subdued, and while he was still adding to his Lydian dominions, there came to Sardis, then at the height of its wealth, all the wise men of the Hellas who chanced to be alive at that time, brought thither severally by various occasions; and of them one was Solon the Athenian, who after he had made laws for the Athenians at their bidding, left his native country for ten years and sailed away saying that he desired to visit various lands, in order that he might not be compelled to repeal any of the laws which he had proposed. For of themselves the Athenians were not competent to do this, having bound themselves by solemn oaths to submit for ten years to the laws which Solon should propose for them.

30. So Solon, having left his native country for this reason and for the sake of seeing various lands, came to Amasis in Egypt, and also to Croesus at Sardis. Having there arrived he was entertained as a guest by Croesus in the king's palace; and afterwards, on the third or fourth day, at the bidding of Croesus his servants led Solon round to see his treasuries; and they showed him all things, how great and magnificent they were: and after he had looked upon them all and examined them as he had occasion, Croesus asked him as follows: "Athenian guest, much report of thee has come to us, both in regard to thy wisdom and thy wanderings, how that in thy search for wisdom thou hast traversed many lands to see them; now therefore a desire has come upon me to ask thee whether thou hast seen any whom thou deemest to be of all men the most happy." This he asked supposing that he himself was the happiest of men; but Solon, using no flattery but the truth only, said: "Yes, O king, Tellos the Athenian." And Croesus, marvelling at that which he said, asked him earnestly: "In what respect dost thou judge Tellos to be the most happy?" And he said: "Tellos, in the first place, living while his native State was prosperous, had sons fair and good and saw from all of them children begotten and living to grow up; and secondly he had what with us is accounted wealth, and after his life a most glorious end: for when a battle was fought by the Athenians at Eleusis against the neighbouring people, he brought up supports and routed the foe and there died by a most fair death; and the Athenians buried him publicly where he fell, and honoured him greatly."

31. So when Solon had moved Croesus to inquire further by the story of Tellos, recounting how many points of happiness he had, the king asked again whom he had seen proper to be placed next after this man, supposing that he himself would certainly obtain at least the second place; but he replied: "Cleobis and Biton: for these, who were of Argos by race, possessed a sufficiency of wealth and, in addition to this, strength of body such as I shall tell. Both equally had won prizes in the games, and moreover the following tale is told of them:—There was a feast of Hera among the Argives and it was by all means necessary that their mother should be borne in a car to the temple. But since their oxen were not brought up in time from the field, the young men, barred from all else by lack of time, submitted themselves to the yoke and drew the wain, their mother being borne by them upon it; and so they brought it on for five-and-forty furlongs, and came to the temple.

Then after they had done this and had been seen by the assembled crowd, there came to their life a most excellent ending; and in this the deity declared that it was better for man to die than to continue to live. For the Argive men were standing round and extolling the strength of the young men, while the Argive women were extolling the mother to whose lot it had fallen to have such sons; and the mother being exceedingly rejoiced both by the deed itself and by the report made of it, took her stand in front of the image of the goddess and prayed that she would give to Cleobis and Biton her sons, who had honoured her greatly, that gift which is best for man to receive: and after this prayer, when they had sacrificed and feasted, the young men lay down to sleep within the temple itself, and never rose again, but were held bound in this last end. And the Argives made statues in the likeness of them and dedicated them as offerings at Delphi, thinking that they had proved themselves most excellent."

32. Thus Solon assigned the second place in respect of happiness to these: and Croesus was moved to anger and said: "Athenian guest, hast thou then so cast aside our prosperous state as worth nothing, that thou dost prefer to us even men of private station?" And he said: "Croesus, thou art inquiring about human fortunes of one who well knows that the Deity is altogether envious and apt to disturb our lot. For in the course of long time a man may see many things which he would not desire to see, and suffer also many things which he would not desire to suffer. The limit of life for a man I lay down at seventy years: and these seventy years give twenty-five thousand and two hundred days, not reckoning for any intercalated month. Then if every other one of these years shall be made longer by one month, that the seasons may be caused to come round at the due time of the year, the intercalated months will be in number five-and-thirty besides the seventy years; and of these months the days will be one thousand and fifty. Of all these days, being in number twenty-six thousand two hundred and fifty, which go to the seventy years, one day produces nothing at all which resembles what another brings with it. Thus then, O Croesus, man is altogether a creature of accident. As for thee, I perceive that thou art both great in wealth and king of many men, but that of which thou didst ask me I cannot call thee yet, until I learn that thou hast brought thy life to a fair ending: for the very rich man is not at all to be accounted more happy than he who has but his subsistence from day to day, unless also the fortune go with him of ending his life well in possession of all things fair.

For many very wealthy men are not happy, while many who have but a moderate living are fortunate; and in truth the very rich man who is not happy has two advantages only as compared with the poor man who is fortunate, whereas this latter has many as compared with the rich man who is not happy. The rich man is able better to fulfil his desire, and also to endure a great calamity if it fall upon him; whereas the other has advantage over him in these things which follow:—he is not indeed able equally with the rich man to endure a calamity or to fulfil his desire, but these his good fortune keeps away from him, while he is sound of limb, free from disease, untouched by suffering, the father of fair children and himself of comely form; and if in addition to this he shall end his life well, he is worthy to be called that which thou seekest, namely a happy man;

but before he comes to his end it is well to hold back and not to call him yet happy but only fortunate. Now to possess all these things together is impossible for one who is mere man, just as no single land suffices to supply all things for itself, but one thing it has and another it lacks, and the land that has the greatest number of things is the best: so also in the case of a man, no single person is complete in himself, for one thing he has and another he lacks; but whosoever of men continues to the end in possession of the greatest number of these things and then has a gracious ending of his life, he is by me accounted worthy, O king, to receive this name. But we must of every thing examine the end and how it will turn out at the last, for to many God shows but a glimpse of happiness and then plucks them up by the roots and overturns them."

33. Thus saying he refused to gratify Croesus, who sent him away from his presence holding him in no esteem, and thinking him utterly senseless in that he passed over present good things and bade men look to the end of every matter.

86. The Persians then had obtained possession of Sardis and had taken Croesus himself prisoner, after he had reigned fourteen years and had been besieged fourteen days, having fulfilled the oracle in that he had brought to an end his own great empire. So the Persians having taken him brought him into the presence of Cyrus: and he piled up a great pyre and caused Croesus to go up upon it bound in fetters, and along with him twice seven sons of Lydians, whether it was that he meant to dedicate this offering as first-fruits of his victory to some god, or whether he desired to fulfil a vow, or else had heard that Croesus was a god-fearing man and so caused him to go up on the pyre because he wished to know if any one of the divine powers would save him, so that he should not be burnt alive. He, they say, did this; but to Croesus as he stood upon the pyre there came, although he was in such evil case, a memory of the saying of Solon, how he had said with divine inspiration that no one of the living might be called happy. And when this thought came into his mind, they say that he sighed deeply and groaned aloud, having been for long silent, and three times he uttered the name of Solon. Hearing this, Cyrus bade the interpreters ask Croesus who was this person on whom he called; and they came near and asked. And Croesus for a time, it is said, kept silence when he was asked this, but afterwards being pressed he said:

"One whom more than much wealth I should have desired to have speech with all monarchs." Then, since his words were of doubtful import, they asked again of that which he said; and as they were urgent with him and gave him no peace, he told how once Solon an Athenian had come, and having inspected all his wealth had made light of it, with such and such words; and how all had turned out for him according as Solon had said, not speaking at all especially with a view to Croesus himself, but with a view to the whole human race and especially those who seem to themselves to be happy men. And while Croesus related these things, already the pyre was lighted and the edges of it round about were burning. Then they say that Cyrus, hearing from the interpreters what Croesus had said, changed his purpose and considered that he himself also was but a man, and that he was delivering another man, who had been not inferior to himself in felicity, alive to the fire; and moreover he feared the requital, and reflected that there was nothing of that which men possessed which was secure; therefore, they say, he ordered them to extinguish as quickly as possible the fire that was burning, and to bring down Croesus and those who were with him from the pyre; and they using endeavours were not able now to get the mastery of the flames.

87. Then it is related by the Lydians that Croesus, having learned how Cyrus had changed his mind, and seeing that every one was trying to put out the fire but that they were no longer able to check it, cried aloud entreating Apollo that if any gift had ever been given by him which had been acceptable to the god, he would come to his aid and rescue him from the evil which was now upon him. So he with tears entreated the god, and suddenly, they say, after clear sky and calm weather clouds gathered and a storm burst, and it rained with a very violent shower, and the pyre was extinguished. Then Cyrus, having perceived that Croesus was a lover of the gods and a good man, caused him to be brought down from the pyre and asked him as follows: "Croesus, tell me who of all men was it who persuaded thee to march upon my land and so to become an enemy to me instead of a friend?" and he said: "O king, I did this to thy felicity and to my own misfortune, and the causer of this was the god of the Hellenes, who incited me to march with my army. For no one is so senseless as to choose of his own will war rather peace, since in peace the sons bury their fathers, but in war the fathers bury their sons. But it was pleasing, I suppose, to the divine powers that these things should come to pass thus."

88. So he spoke, and Cyrus loosed his bonds and caused him to sit near himself and paid to him much regard, and he marvelled both himself and all who were about him at the sight of Croesus. And Croesus wrapt in thought was silent; but after a time, turning round and seeing the Persians plundering the city of the Lydians, he said: "O king, must I say to thee that which I chance to have in my thought, or must I keep silent in this my present fortune?" Then Cyrus bade him say boldly whatsoever he desired; and he asked him saying: "What is the business that this great multitude of men is doing with so much eagerness?" and he said: "They are plundering thy city and carrying away thy wealth." And Croesus answered: "Neither is it my city that they are plundering nor my wealth which they are carrying away; for I have no longer any property in these things: but it is thy wealth that they are carrying and driving away."

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: The happiest man
parts.context: Croesus is at the height of his power: he has conquered almost all of western Turkey. Wise men from all over Greece visit his court at Sardis, among them Solon of Athens. The numbering of the chapters (28, 29, 30) comes from later editors; chapter 28 runs into 29 mid-sentence. Footnote numbers in Macaulay's edition have been removed.
parts.plain: When Croesus had conquered nearly everyone, wise men came to Sardis, among them Solon, who was travelling for ten years after giving Athens its laws. Croesus showed him his treasure and asked who was the happiest man he had ever seen, expecting to hear his own name. Solon named Tellos, an ordinary Athenian who had good sons and grandchildren, enough to live on, and died bravely in battle for his city.

commentary.on: then at the height of its wealth
commentary.text: Herodotus sets the scene with a warning: this is the top of the wheel. Readers who knew the end, and every Greek did, would feel the drop coming.

commentary.on: in order that he might not be compelled to repeal any of the laws which he had proposed
commentary.text: Solon is a man who gave up power on purpose. He made laws and then left, so that no one could make him change them, and so that he would not rule. He is the opposite of a king who wants more.

commentary.on: This he asked supposing that he himself was the happiest of men
commentary.text: The Greek word translated 'happy' is olbios: blessed, prosperous, fortunate. Croesus thinks happiness is something you can show in a treasury. His question is really a request for praise.

commentary.on: Solon, using no flattery but the truth only
commentary.text: Telling the truth to power is dangerous. Here a citizen of a small city tells the richest man in the world what he does not want to hear. The scene is a Greek cousin of Nathan telling King David, 'You are the man' (2 Samuel 12), which you may have read in 'Kings and prophets'.

commentary.on: living while his native State was prosperous, had sons fair and good and saw from all of them children begotten and living to grow up
commentary.text: Tellos' happiness is a whole life seen from the end: a city at peace, children and grandchildren who lived (in a world where many children died), enough to live on, and a death that his city honoured. None of it can be locked in a treasury.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: Look to the end
parts.context: Croesus asks who is second, sure that it will be him. Solon tells the story of Cleobis and Biton, two young men of Argos who pulled their mother's cart to the festival of the goddess Hera when the oxen were late, and then died peacefully in the temple. Then Croesus loses his temper, and Solon explains himself. 'Furlongs' are Greek stades, about 200 metres each.
parts.plain: Solon names two brothers who pulled their mother to the temple in a cart, were praised by everyone, and died in their sleep that night, as if the goddess had given them the best gift there is. Croesus is angry. Solon explains: life is long and full of chance; God often brings down the prosperous; so no one should be called happy until he has ended his life well. You must look at the end of everything.

commentary.on: in this the deity declared that it was better for man to die than to continue to live
commentary.text: This is a dark thought, and it runs through Greek poetry: since life is so uncertain, a good death at the height of honour may be the best gift of the gods. Herodotus reports it without comment.

commentary.on: the Deity is altogether envious and apt to disturb our lot
commentary.text: Here is the theology of the story. The Greek word for 'envious' is phthonos: the gods resent human greatness and bring it low. It is not the God of the Bible, who is described as 'merciful and gracious' (Psalm 103:8). But it shares one thought with the Bible: no one is master of his own fate.

commentary.on: Thus then, O Croesus, man is altogether a creature of accident
commentary.text: Solon counts the days of a seventy-year life, 26,250 of them, and says no two are alike. Any one of them can bring disaster. It is a vivid way to say that a life cannot be judged until it is over.

commentary.on: but before he comes to his end it is well to hold back and not to call him yet happy but only fortunate
commentary.text: This is the famous saying, usually remembered as 'call no man happy until he is dead'. Solon distinguishes being lucky, which can change tomorrow, from being happy, which describes a whole life. Aristotle discussed the saying a century later (Nicomachean Ethics I.10).

commentary.on: for to many God shows but a glimpse of happiness and then plucks them up by the roots and overturns them
commentary.text: The last line of Solon's speech is a prophecy of what will happen to Croesus himself, as every reader knew.

commentary.on: bade men look to the end of every matter
commentary.text: Croesus thinks Solon is a fool for ignoring the good things in front of him. Herodotus' readers know who the fool is.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: On the pyre
parts.context: Years have passed. Croesus' son has been killed in a hunting accident. Trusting an oracle, Croesus has attacked Cyrus of Persia and lost. Sardis has fallen after a siege of fourteen days, and Croesus is a prisoner. Cyrus builds a pyre, a great heap of wood for burning, and puts him on it in chains with fourteen Lydian boys.
parts.plain: Cyrus puts Croesus on a pyre to burn. Croesus suddenly remembers Solon and calls his name three times. When he explains, Cyrus realises that he too is only a man, fears the same fate, and orders the fire put out, but it is too late. Croesus prays to Apollo, a storm puts out the fire, and Cyrus takes him as an adviser. Watching the Persians loot Sardis, Croesus points out that it is no longer his city they are robbing, but Cyrus' own.

commentary.on: there came, although he was in such evil case, a memory of the saying of Solon
commentary.text: The whole story turns on memory. Croesus did not listen when he was prosperous; he remembers when he has lost everything. This is the 'end' Solon told him to look to.

commentary.on: not speaking at all especially with a view to Croesus himself, but with a view to the whole human race
commentary.text: Herodotus makes the lesson universal. Solon's words were not a personal insult but a truth about all human beings, 'especially those who seem to themselves to be happy men'.

commentary.on: considered that he himself also was but a man
commentary.text: This is the turning point. The conqueror sees himself in the conquered. The lesson passes from Solon to Croesus to Cyrus, the most powerful man in the world: you too are mortal, and your fortune can turn.

commentary.on: in peace the sons bury their fathers, but in war the fathers bury their sons
commentary.text: One of the most quoted lines in Herodotus. War reverses the natural order of life. Croesus, who started a war on the strength of an oracle he misunderstood, says it from bitter experience: his own son was already dead.

commentary.on: it is thy wealth that they are carrying and driving away
commentary.text: Croesus' first piece of advice as Cyrus' counsellor: the looters are stealing from their own king. The man who once boasted of his treasury now teaches that what we own changes hands in a day.

read.author: Herodotus
read.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.

paras: One of the multitude said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?”
He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”
He spoke a parable to them, saying, “The ground of a certain rich man produced abundantly.
He reasoned within himself, saying, ‘What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?’
He said, ‘This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.
I will tell my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.” ’
“But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’
So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”

parts.title: The rich fool
parts.context: Jesus is teaching a crowd in Galilee, around AD 30. A man asks him to settle a quarrel over an inheritance, and Jesus answers with a story. Only Luke's Gospel records it.

commentary.on: for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses
commentary.text: This is Solon's point in one line. Croesus thought his life consisted in his treasury.

commentary.on: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
commentary.text: The rich man, like Croesus, thinks he can see far into the future. Solon would have told him that any one of his days could bring disaster.

commentary.on: You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you.
commentary.text: The end comes suddenly, as Solon warned. But notice who speaks: not envious gods who resent human greatness, but God, who judges how a man has lived.

commentary.on: So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.
commentary.text: Here Jesus goes beyond Solon. Solon says: wait to see whether your fortune holds to the end. Jesus says: there is another kind of wealth, being 'rich toward God', which no turn of fortune can take away.

compare.why: Jesus told a parable about a rich man who thought his wealth made him secure. Compare his answer to Croesus' question, what makes a life go well, with Solon's.
compare.title: Tonight your soul is required of you

paras: The story of Croesus is told in Book I of the Histories in about seventy chapters, and Herodotus shapes it like a tragedy. A great man at the height of his fortune is warned; he does not listen; he makes a terrible mistake; and he comes to understanding only through suffering. Between the two scenes we have read, Croesus loses his son Atys in a hunting accident, misreads the oracle at Delphi ('if you cross the Halys you will destroy a great empire') and attacks Persia.

Athenian tragedy, performed at the festivals of Dionysus in the same years, used the same shape. The poet Aeschylus' Persians (472 BC), the oldest surviving tragedy, shows Xerxes' defeat in exactly these terms. If you have taken 'Tragedy', you will recognise it. Herodotus is writing history, but he is writing it with a tragedian's eye for the pattern of a life.
sections.key: Herodotus shapes Croesus' story like a tragedy: warning, pride, a fatal mistake, suffering, understanding.

paras: Two Greek words name the pattern. Hybris (often spelled hubris) means violent pride: arrogance that oversteps the limits set for human beings, often by insulting others. Nemesis is the retribution that follows, sometimes pictured as a goddess. Croesus' hybris is mild compared with others in Herodotus: he simply thinks himself the happiest of men. Herodotus says that after Solon left 'a great retribution from God came upon Croesus, probably because he judged himself to be the happiest of all men' (I.34).

The same pattern runs through the whole book. Kings who try to go beyond the limits of nature, like Xerxes, who bridged the sea between Asia and Europe and had it whipped when a storm broke his bridge (VII.35), are brought down. Christians later called the first of the deadly sins 'pride', and the Bible says, 'Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall' (Proverbs 16:18). The thought is shared; the reasons, as we will see, are not.
sections.key: Hybris is violent pride that oversteps human limits; nemesis is the retribution that follows. Herodotus finds this pattern again and again.

paras: Herodotus believes in the gods and in oracles. Dreams come true in his book; omens warn; Apollo sends a storm to put out the pyre. Yet he is not sure exactly how the gods act. Solon calls the divine 'envious'. Elsewhere, Herodotus speaks of a divine forethought that keeps the balance of nature (III.108). And many of his explanations are entirely human: ambition, revenge, fear, misunderstanding.

Most scholars think Herodotus held both at once. Human beings choose freely and are responsible; but the world has a moral order, and those who overstep it fall. The god does not force Croesus to attack Persia. He misreads an oracle that was true, because he wanted it to mean what he wished. When Croesus complains, Delphi replies that he was paying for a crime of his ancestor Gyges, five generations back, which even a god could not undo, and that he should have asked which empire was meant: 'let him pronounce himself to be the cause of that which followed' (I.91). Fate and responsibility stand side by side. Herodotus was, in this sense, the first historian to ask the question every later historian has faced: are events caused by human choices, by impersonal forces, or by providence?
sections.key: Herodotus believed both in human responsibility and in a divine order that brings down the proud; Croesus' fall is his own fault, through an oracle he misread.

paras: Here is a problem. Solon's laws are usually dated to about 594 BC, and Herodotus says he travelled for ten years afterwards. Croesus became king around 560 BC. If those dates are right, Solon could hardly have visited Croesus as king. Plutarch, writing his Life of Solon around AD 100, knew this objection, and kept the story anyway, because, he said, it was so famous and so fitting to Solon's character (Life of Solon 27).

The pyre is also uncertain. A Babylonian record, the Nabonidus Chronicle, says that in 547 BC Cyrus marched to a land whose name is damaged (many read it as Lydia), and 'killed its king'. The poet Bacchylides, in an ode of 468 BC, says Croesus climbed the pyre of his own will and Apollo carried him away to a land beyond the north wind. An Athenian vase of about 500–490 BC, now in the Louvre, shows Croesus enthroned on his pyre, pouring an offering, as if it were a sacrifice. So within fifty years there were several versions. Herodotus tells the one he heard 'from the Lydians'.
sections.key: The meeting of Solon and Croesus is chronologically very hard; the pyre story existed in several versions within fifty years, and Croesus may have died in 547 BC.

paras: If the story may not have happened, why is it the centrepiece of Book I? Because for Herodotus, history is not only a record of events but a search for what they mean. The fall of Croesus was real: Sardis did fall to Cyrus around 547 BC, and the Greek cities of Ionia passed under Persian rule. That is the first link in the chain that led to the Persian Wars. The story of Solon tells his readers how to understand the chain: as a lesson about the limits of power and wealth.

This is both the strength and the weakness of Herodotus. He gives us the meaning of events in stories we remember for life. But he sometimes lets a good story outrun the evidence. The next historian in this journey, Thucydides, will reject exactly this, and we will need to ask whether he was right.
sections.key: Herodotus uses a story that may not be literally true to give the meaning of a real event, the fall of Lydia: his strength and his weakness.

paras: Solon's answer and Jesus' answer agree about a great deal. Wealth does not make a life good. No one controls the future. Death comes suddenly. The rich fool, like Croesus, makes plans as if he owned tomorrow.

But the differences are deep, and they will matter for the rest of this journey. Solon's divine is envious and brings down anyone who rises too high, good or bad. His advice is caution: wait and see. Jesus' God is not jealous of human happiness; he judges what we do with what we have. His advice is not to wait but to become 'rich toward God' now, by generosity and trust, which, in the verses that follow (Luke 12:22–34), means giving to the poor. For Solon, the end of a life reveals whether it was happy. For Jesus, the end is a meeting with God.

rows: A whole life that ends well: family, enough, an honoured death
Look to the end; don't boast
table.note: Herodotus, Histories I.32; Luke 12:13–34.

sections.key: Solon and Jesus agree that wealth does not make a life good and that death is sudden; they differ on who God is and what to do about it.

paras: A century after Herodotus, Aristotle took up Solon's saying in his Nicomachean Ethics (I.10). Must we really wait until a man is dead to call him happy? That seems absurd, he says, if happiness is an activity, something we do. Aristotle's answer is that happiness lies mainly in living well, in acting with virtue, and a good person will bear misfortune nobly and never do anything hateful or mean. So he will never become truly miserable.

Yet Aristotle admits Solon has a point. Great disasters, like those of King Priam of Troy, who lost his sons and his city in old age, can spoil a happy life. No one, he says, calls a man happy who ends like Priam. So the question Croesus asked runs through Greek philosophy: how much of a good life is in our hands, and how much is fortune's? If you take 'Aristotle', later in this hall, you will meet his full answer.
sections.key: Aristotle argued that happiness lies mainly in virtuous activity, which misfortune cannot wholly destroy, though disasters like Priam's can mar a life.

debate.question: Is the story of Solon and Croesus history or a moral tale?

positions.name: A moral tale
positions.who: Many modern scholars; Plutarch already knew the chronological objection
positions.view: Solon could not have met Croesus as king; the scene was invented, or grew in the telling, to dramatise Greek wisdom about fortune. Herodotus uses it as a parable, and we should read it as one.
positions.evidence: The dates of Solon's laws (c. 594 BC) and of Croesus' reign (c. 560–546 BC); the speeches' resemblance to Solon's poems; the several versions of the pyre.

positions.name: A real event, shaped
positions.who: Some historians who allow for doubt about early Greek dates
positions.view: Early Greek dates are uncertain; Solon may have travelled later, or met Croesus before he was king. Herodotus heard the story from Lydian and Greek sources and shaped it, but did not invent it.
positions.evidence: The uncertainty of Solon's dates in ancient sources; Herodotus' explicit naming of 'the Lydians' as his source for the pyre.

positions.name: It doesn't matter as much as we think
positions.who: Scholars who read Herodotus as a thinker, such as John Gould and Rosalind Thomas
positions.view: Herodotus' readers cared about what events meant as much as what happened. The fall of Lydia was real; the story tells us how Greeks understood it. To ask only 'did it happen?' is to miss half of what history is for.
positions.evidence: Herodotus' habit of giving more than one version; the way he links the story to his theme in I.5.

debate.agree: All agree that Sardis fell to Cyrus around 547 BC and that the story, true or not, states Herodotus' view of how history works.

look.why: No painting in the gallery shows Croesus or Solon. This is a 'vanitas' still life by François van Daellen, about 1650: a Dutch kind of painting whose name comes from Ecclesiastes ('vanity of vanities'), made to remind its owner that wealth and learning end in death. It says what Solon said.
points: A human skull rests in profile, facing left, on two small leather-bound books and papers, near the bottom centre.
A large thighbone is propped up behind the skull on a taller book.
On a box to the right stands a brass candlestick. The candle has just been snuffed out: the end of the wick still glows red and a wisp of smoke rises.
The objects lie on a brick-red marble tabletop veined with grey and white, with black cloth hanging off the right side.
Light comes in through a window with small leaded panes on the left; the rest of the room is in deep black shadow.

music.why: A hymn written in 1847 by Henry Francis Lyte, a dying vicar in Devon, about the end of life, when the brightness of the day fades: Solon's 'look to the end', answered with trust.

think.why: Solon and Jesus give two answers to 'who is happy?'. See where Athens and Jerusalem agree and where they part.

learn.why: The sentence that ends the rich fool's plans: a short answer to anyone who thinks he owns tomorrow.

check.q: Why does Solon rank Tellos, an ordinary Athenian, above Croesus?
options: Because Solon disliked kings on principle
Because Tellos had won the Olympic games
Because a life can only be judged as a whole, and Tellos' life ended well: children who lived, enough to live on, an honoured death
Because Tellos was richer than Croesus
check.why: Solon judges a whole life from its end. Tellos had 'what with us is accounted wealth', not great riches.

check.q: Croesus misread the oracle 'if you cross the Halys you will destroy a great empire'. What does Herodotus suggest by this?
options: That oracles always lie
That the oracle was true but Croesus heard what he wanted, so the fault was his own
That Herodotus did not believe in oracles
That the gods forced Croesus to attack
check.why: He did destroy a great empire, his own. Delphi later tells him he should have asked which empire was meant, 'let him pronounce himself to be the cause' (I.91), though it also blames an ancestor's crime.

check.q: Which best describes hybris as Herodotus uses it?
options: Any kind of sin
Bad luck
The anger of the gods
Pride that oversteps the limits set for human beings, which brings retribution
check.why: Hybris is the overstepping; nemesis is the retribution. They are two halves of one pattern.

check.q: What is the strongest evidence that the meeting of Solon and Croesus may not have happened?
options: Solon's laws date to about 594 BC and Croesus became king about 560 BC, which makes a visit to Croesus as king very hard
Croesus could not speak Greek
Solon never left Athens
Herodotus says he invented it
check.why: The chronology is the problem; Plutarch knew it and kept the story because it fitted Solon's character.

check.q: What makes Cyrus change his mind on the pyre?
options: Apollo appears to him in a dream
Croesus offers him gold
His soldiers refuse to light the fire
He realises he too is only a man, and fears that his own fortune could turn
check.why: 'He considered that he himself also was but a man ... and moreover he feared the requital'. The storm comes after.

check.q: Where do Solon and Jesus most deeply differ?
options: Jesus thinks death is far away
Solon thinks wealth makes a life good
Solon's divine is envious of human greatness and his advice is caution; Jesus' God judges how we use what we have and his advice is to be 'rich toward God'
They do not differ at all
check.why: Both say wealth is no security and death is sudden; they differ on who God is and what follows.

tutorial.question: 'Call no man happy until he is dead.' Is Solon right?
tutorial.approach: Explain what Solon means, using Tellos and Cleobis and Biton. Show how Croesus' story illustrates it, and what part the gods play. Say whether the story is history or parable, and whether that matters. Compare Jesus' parable. Then give your own view: can a life be called good before it ends?
strong: Explains Solon's distinction between 'fortunate' and 'happy' (a whole life).
Uses the details of Tellos, Cleobis and Biton accurately.
Explains hybris and nemesis and the role of the oracle.
Notes the chronological problem and what follows from it.
Compares the rich fool fairly, including the difference about God.
Reaches a reasoned view of its own.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, name one thing you own or have achieved that you are proud of, and then one person you could give some of it to: time, money or praise. Give it to one of them before the week is out.
sessions.reflect: What would you want someone to say about your life if they could only judge it from the end?
takeaways: Solon told Croesus that no one should be called happy until his life has ended well, because fortune can turn on any day.
Herodotus saw a pattern in history, hybris and nemesis: pride that oversteps human limits is brought down, and the fault is our own.
The meeting may not have happened as told, but Herodotus uses it to give the meaning of a real event; Jesus' rich fool agrees about wealth but differs about God.

sessions.title: Free men and a king
sessions.line: The King of Kings weeps over his vast army, asks an exiled Spartan whether the Greeks will dare to fight, and is told: their master is the law. Then three hundred Spartans hold the pass.
sessions.plain: In 480 BC Xerxes, king of Persia, led the largest army the world had seen into Greece. Herodotus tells how, before the battle, Xerxes asked a Greek exile at his court whether the Greeks would really fight. The answer was that they would, because they were free men who obeyed the law more than Persians feared their king. A few days later, at the narrow pass of Thermopylae, the Spartan king Leonidas and his men fought to the last. This session asks what Herodotus thought the war was about, and how far we can trust him.
sessions.why: The last session showed Herodotus finding a pattern in history: pride before a fall, in the story of Croesus. Now that pattern meets its greatest example, the Persian king who tried to conquer Europe. But Herodotus adds something new: he sees the war as a contest between two ways of living, under a master or under the law. And because his story has become a legend, we must ask how much of it is true.
answers: What happened at Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis?
Why did the Greeks win against such odds?
What did Herodotus mean by free men under law?
Why is Herodotus called the 'father of lies', and is it fair?
Is the story of 'East against West' true?
sessions.finding: Herodotus made freedom the meaning of the war: at Thermopylae the Greeks fought as free men whose master was the law, not as slaves driven by a king. Archaeology confirms much of his account, though not his numbers.

paras: Croesus' fall, about 547 BC, put the Greek cities of the Turkish coast under Persian rule. In 499 BC they rebelled, and Athens sent twenty ships to help them. The revolt was crushed. King Darius sent an army to punish Athens, and in 490 BC, at Marathon, 26 miles from the city, the Athenians and their small neighbour Plataea beat it. Herodotus says 6,400 Persians died and 192 Athenians (VI.117).

Darius died before he could try again. His son Xerxes spent four years preparing. In 480 BC he crossed from Asia into Europe over the Hellespont, the narrow strait by modern Gallipoli, on two bridges of boats, with an army and fleet drawn from every nation of the empire. Many Greek cities submitted. About thirty, led by Sparta and Athens, decided to fight.
background.key: After Athens helped the Ionian revolt, Persia was beaten at Marathon (490 BC); in 480 BC Xerxes invaded with a vast army, and about thirty Greek cities resisted.

background.h: Who are the people in this reading?
paras: Xerxes (reigned 486–465 BC) was the King of Kings, ruler of perhaps a quarter of the world's people. Artabanus was his uncle, who had warned him against the invasion. Demaratus had been one of Sparta's two kings until he was deposed in about 491 BC, after a quarrel with his fellow king; he fled to Persia, and now marched with Xerxes as an adviser.

Sparta was the strongest military power in Greece. Its citizens trained for war from the age of seven, and lived under strict laws said to come from an ancient lawgiver, Lycurgus. Their land was farmed by helots, a whole population of Greeks held in serfdom. Leonidas was one of Sparta's kings in 480 BC.
background.key: Xerxes, the Persian king; Artabanus, his cautious uncle; Demaratus, a deposed Spartan king at his court; and Sparta, a city of soldiers whose land was worked by serfs.

paras: Thermopylae, the 'hot gates', named after its hot springs, was a narrow pass between mountains and the sea in central Greece, the only good road south. There a small Greek force could hold back a huge army. At sea, the Greek fleet waited nearby at Artemisium.
