background.key: In 480 BC Xerxes crossed into Europe, broke through at Thermopylae and burned Athens, then lost at Salamis; in 479 BC the invasion ended.

paras: The main reading has two scenes from Book VII. At Abydos, on the Asian shore of the Hellespont, Xerxes looks over his army, calls himself happy, and weeps. Then, in Thrace, he asks Demaratus whether the Greeks will really fight. Demaratus' answer is Herodotus' clearest statement of what the war meant.
The comparison is Herodotus' account of the last day at Thermopylae, and the epitaphs on the Spartans' graves. It shows whether Demaratus was right.
background.key: Xerxes weeping at Abydos and his conversation with Demaratus; then the last stand at Thermopylae.

before: Why does Xerxes weep, and what does Artabanus reply? Does it remind you of Solon?
What two things does Demaratus say the Greeks have instead of wealth?
Why does Xerxes think free men will not fight, and what is Demaratus' answer?
sessions.readWhy: Two scenes before the battle: the King of Kings weeps over his army, and an exiled Spartan tells him what free men will do.

paras: 44. When Xerxes had come into the midst of Abydos, he had a desire to see all the army; and there had been made purposely for him beforehand upon a hill in this place a raised seat of white stone, which the people of Abydos had built at the command of the king given beforehand. There he took his seat, and looking down upon the shore he gazed both upon the land-army and the ships; and gazing upon them he had a longing to see a contest take place between the ships; and when it had taken place and the Phenicians of Sidon were victorious, he was delighted both with the contest and with the whole armament.
45. And seeing all the Hellespont covered over with the ships, and all the shores and the plains of Abydos full of men, then Xerxes pronounced himself a happy man, and after that he fell to weeping.

46. Artabanos his uncle therefore perceiving him,--the same who at first boldly declared his opinion advising Xerxes not to march against Hellas,--this man, I say, having observed that Xerxes wept, asked as follows: "O king, how far different from one another are the things which thou hast done now and a short while before now! for having pronounced thyself a happy man, thou art now shedding tears." He said: "Yea, for after I had reckoned up, it came into my mind to feel pity at the thought how brief was the whole life of man, seeing that of these multitudes not one will be alive when a hundred years have gone by." He then made answer and said: "To another evil more pitiful than this we are made subject in the course of our life; for in the period of life, short as it is, no man, either of these here or of others, is made by nature so happy, that there will not come to him many times, and not once only, the desire to be dead rather than to live; for misfortunes falling upon us and diseases disturbing our happiness make the time of life, though short indeed, seem long: thus, since life is full of trouble, death has become the most acceptable refuge for man; and God, having given him to taste of the sweetness of life, is discovered in this matter to be full of jealousy."

101. Now when he had sailed through these and had disembarked from his ship, he sent for Demaratos the son of Ariston, who was marching with him against Hellas; and having called him he asked as follows: "Demaratos, now it is my pleasure to ask thee somewhat which I desire to know. Thou art not only a Hellene, but also, as I am informed both by thee and by the other Hellenes who come to speech with me, of a city which is neither the least nor the feeblest of Hellas. Now therefore declare to me this, namely whether the Hellenes will endure to raise hands against me: for, as I suppose, even if all the Hellenes and the remaining nations who dwell towards the West should be gathered together, they are not strong enough in fight to endure my attack, supposing them to be my enemies. I desire however to be informed also of thy opinion, what thou sayest about these matters." He inquired thus, and the other made answer and said: "O king, shall I utter the truth in speaking to thee, or that which will give pleasure?" and he bade him utter the truth, saying that he should suffer nothing unpleasant in consequence of this, any more than he suffered before.

102. When Demaratos heard this, he spoke as follows: "O king, since thou biddest me by all means utter the truth, and so speak as one who shall not be afterwards convicted by thee of having spoken falsely, I say this:--with Hellas poverty is ever an inbred growth, while valour is one that has been brought in, being acquired by intelligence and the force of law; and of it Hellas makes use ever to avert from herself not only poverty but also servitude to a master. Now I commend all the Hellenes who are settled in those Dorian lands, but this which I am about to say has regard not to all, but to the Lacedemonians alone: of these I say, first that it is not possible that they will ever accept thy terms, which carry with them servitude for Hellas; and next I say that they will stand against thee in fight, even if all the other Hellenes shall be of thy party: and as for numbers, ask now how many they are, that they are able to do this; for whether it chances that a thousand of them have come out into the field, these will fight with thee, or if there be less than this, or again if there be more."

103. Xerxes hearing this laughed, and said: "Demaratos, what a speech is this which thou hast uttered, saying that a thousand men will fight with this vast army! Come tell me this:--thou sayest that thou wert thyself king of these men; wilt thou therefore consent forthwith to fight with ten men? and yet if your State is such throughout as thou dost describe it, thou their king ought by your laws to stand in array against double as many as another man; that is to say, if each of them is a match for ten men of my army, I expect of thee that thou shouldest be a match for twenty. Thus would be confirmed the report which is made by thee: but if ye, who boast thus greatly are such men and in size so great only as the Hellenes who come commonly to speech with me, thyself included, then beware lest this which has been spoken prove but an empty vaunt. For come, let me examine it by all that is probable:

how could a thousand or ten thousand or even fifty thousand, at least if they were all equally free and were not ruled by one man, stand against so great an army? since, as thou knowest, we shall be more than a thousand coming about each one of them, supposing them to be in number five thousand. If indeed they were ruled by one man after our fashion, they might perhaps from fear of him become braver than it was their nature to be, or they might go compelled by the lash to fight with greater numbers, being themselves fewer in number; but if left at liberty, they would do neither of these things: and I for my part suppose that, even if equally matched in numbers, the Hellenes would hardly dare to fight with the Persians taken alone. With us however this of which thou speakest is found in single men, not indeed often, but rarely; for there are Persians of my spearmen who will consent to fight with three men of the Hellenes at once: but thou hast had no experience of these things and therefore thou speakest very much at random."

104. To this Demaratos replied: "O king, from the first I was sure that if I uttered the truth I should not speak that which was pleasing to thee; since however thou didst compel me to speak the very truth, I told thee of the matters which concern the Spartans. And yet how I am at this present time attached to them by affection thou knowest better than any; seeing that first they took away from me the rank and privileges which came to me from my fathers, and then also they have caused me to be without native land and an exile; but thy father took me up and gave me livelihood and a house to dwell in. Surely it is not to be supposed likely that the prudent man will thrust aside friendliness which is offered to him, but rather that he will accept it with full contentment. And I do not profess that I am able to fight either with ten men or with two, nay, if I had my will, I would not even fight with one;

but if there were necessity or if the cause which urged me to the combat were a great one, I would fight most willingly with one of these men who says that he is a match for three of the Hellenes. So also the Lacedemonians are not inferior to any men when fighting one by one, and they are the best of all men when fighting in a body: for though free, yet they are not free in all things, for over them is set Law as a master, whom they fear much more even than thy people fear thee. It is certain at least that they do whatsoever that master commands; and he commands ever the same thing, that is to say, he bids them not flee out of battle from any multitude of men, but stay in their post and win the victory or lose their life. But if when I say these things I seem to thee to be speaking at random, of other things for the future I prefer to be silent; and at this time I spake only because I was compelled. May it come to pass however according to thy mind, O king."

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: The king weeps
parts.context: Spring 480 BC. Xerxes has marched across Asia and reached Abydos, on the Asian side of the Hellespont, where his engineers have built two bridges of boats into Europe. The people of Abydos have built him a throne of white marble on a hill. Below him are his army and fleet. Footnote numbers in Macaulay's edition have been removed.
parts.plain: Xerxes sits on a marble throne and watches his army and fleet fill the shore and the sea. He calls himself happy, and then weeps. His uncle Artabanus asks why. Xerxes says that in a hundred years not one of all these men will be alive. Artabanus answers that there is something worse: life is so full of trouble that every man has wished at some time to be dead, and the divine is jealous of us.

commentary.on: then Xerxes pronounced himself a happy man, and after that he fell to weeping
commentary.text: Herodotus' readers would have heard Croesus behind these words. The greatest king on earth calls himself happy at the height of his power, exactly as Croesus did in the treasury. We know what follows.

commentary.on: how brief was the whole life of man, seeing that of these multitudes not one will be alive when a hundred years have gone by
commentary.text: It is a moving moment, and it makes Xerxes human. He is not a monster. He sees, for a moment, what Solon saw: that no power lasts. But he does not change course.

commentary.on: God, having given him to taste of the sweetness of life, is discovered in this matter to be full of jealousy
commentary.text: Artabanus repeats Solon's theology of the 'envious' divine. In Herodotus, the wise warners all say the same thing, and the great kings never listen.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: Will they fight?
parts.context: Xerxes has crossed into Europe and reviewed his forces at Doriscus in Thrace (north-eastern Greece). He sends for Demaratus, the exiled king of Sparta who has lived at the Persian court for about ten years. 'Hellas' is Greece; 'Lacedemonians' are the Spartans.
parts.plain: Xerxes asks Demaratus whether the Greeks will dare to fight him, when even all the peoples of the West together could not stand against his army. Demaratus asks whether he wants the truth or flattery. Told to speak the truth, he says: Greece has always been poor, but it has courage, learned through wisdom and law. The Spartans will never accept slavery, and they will fight however few they are.

commentary.on: O king, shall I utter the truth in speaking to thee, or that which will give pleasure?
commentary.text: The same question Solon faced in Croesus' treasury. In Herodotus, the man who tells a king the truth is always worth listening to.

commentary.on: with Hellas poverty is ever an inbred growth, while valour is one that has been brought in, being acquired by intelligence and the force of law
commentary.text: Here is Herodotus' explanation of how the Greeks could win. They were poor, but their courage was learned, made by good sense and by law. Courage is not something a people is born with; it is something its laws and customs teach.

commentary.on: it is not possible that they will ever accept thy terms, which carry with them servitude for Hellas
commentary.text: For Demaratus, as for Herodotus, the war is about freedom. To accept Xerxes' terms, earth and water as a sign of submission, would be to become the king's slaves.

commentary.on: whether it chances that a thousand of them have come out into the field, these will fight with thee
commentary.text: Numbers do not matter. This is the prediction that Thermopylae will test.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: Law as a master
parts.context: Xerxes laughs at Demaratus and argues back. His argument is the core of the scene: how can men who are free, with no one to command them, stand against an army driven by one man's will?
parts.plain: Xerxes laughs. How can a few thousand free men, with no one ruling them, fight so huge an army? Under one master they might fight from fear, or under the whip; free, they will do neither. Demaratus answers: the Spartans are free, but not free in everything, because they have a master, the law, whom they fear more than Persians fear their king. The law commands them never to run, but to stand and win or die.

commentary.on: at least if they were all equally free and were not ruled by one man
commentary.text: Xerxes speaks for a whole view of power. Men fight only if someone makes them. Freedom means no one is in charge, so free men will run. To an absolute ruler, it is obvious.

commentary.on: they might go compelled by the lash to fight with greater numbers
commentary.text: Herodotus will show Persian officers doing exactly this at Thermopylae itself (VII.223), in the comparison reading. Whether it was common practice or a Greek picture of the enemy, we cannot check.

commentary.on: for though free, yet they are not free in all things, for over them is set Law as a master
commentary.text: This sentence is the heart of the session. Freedom, for Demaratus, is not having no master. It is having the right master: a law that everyone, king included, obeys. The Greek word is nomos, law or custom. The Persians obey a man; the Greeks obey a law.

commentary.on: whom they fear much more even than thy people fear thee
commentary.text: Fear has not disappeared. It has changed its object. The Spartans fear disgrace before the law more than death. Xerxes' soldiers fear Xerxes.

commentary.on: he bids them not flee out of battle from any multitude of men, but stay in their post and win the victory or lose their life
commentary.text: The law gives one command, and Thermopylae will show them keeping it.

read.author: Herodotus
read.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.

paras: 223. Xerxes meanwhile, having made libations at sunrise, stayed for some time, until about the hour when the market fills, and then made an advance upon them; for thus it had been enjoined by Epialtes, seeing that the descent of the mountain is shorter and the space to be passed over much less than the going round and the ascent. The Barbarians accordingly with Xerxes were advancing to the attack; and the Hellenes with Leonidas, feeling that they were going forth to death, now advanced out much further than at first into the broader part of the defile; for when the fence of the wall was being guarded, they on the former days fought retiring before the enemy into the narrow part of the pass; but now they engaged with them outside the narrows, and very many of the Barbarians fell: for behind them the leaders of the divisions with scourges in their hands were striking each man, ever urging them on to the front. Many of them then were driven into the sea and perished, and many more still were trodden down while yet alive by one another, and there was no reckoning of the number that perished: for knowing the death which was about to come upon them by reason of those who were going round the mountain, they displayed upon the Barbarians all the strength which they had, to its greatest extent, disregarding danger and acting as if possessed by a spirit of recklessness.

224. Now by this time the spears of the greater number of them were broken, so it chanced, in this combat, and they were slaying the Persians with their swords; and in this fighting fell Leonidas, having proved himself a very good man, and others also of the Spartans with him, men of note, of whose names I was informed as of men who had proved themselves worthy, and indeed I was told also the names of all the three hundred. Moreover of the Persians there fell here, besides many others of note, especially two sons of Dareios, Abrocomes and Hyperanthes, born to Dareios of Phratagune the daughter of Artanes: now Artanes was the brother of king Dareios and the son of Hystaspes, the son of Arsames; and he in giving his daughter in marriage to Dareios gave also with her all his substance, because she was his only child.

225. Two brothers of Xerxes, I say, fell here fighting; and meanwhile over the body of Leonidas there arose a great struggle between the Persians and the Lacedemonians, until the Hellenes by valour dragged this away from the enemy and turned their opponents to flight four times. This conflict continued until those who had gone with Epialtes came up; and when the Hellenes learnt that these had come, from that moment the nature of the combat was changed; for they retired backwards to the narrow part of the way, and having passed by the wall they went and placed themselves upon the hillock, all in a body together except only the Thebans: now this hillock is in the entrance, where now the stone lion is placed for Leonidas. On this spot while defending themselves with daggers, that is those who still had them left, and also with hands and with teeth, they were overwhelmed by the missiles of the Barbarians, some of these having followed directly after them and destroyed the fence of the wall, while others had come round and stood about them on all sides.

226. Such were the proofs of valour given by the Lacedemonians and Thespians; yet the Spartan Dienekes is said to have proved himself the best man of all, the same who, as they report, uttered this saying before they engaged battle with the Medes:--being informed by one of the men of Trachis that when the Barbarians discharged their arrows they obscured the light of the sun by the multitude of the arrows, so great was the number of their host, he was not dismayed by this, but making small account of the number of the Medes, he said that their guest from Trachis brought them very good news, for if the Medes obscured the light of the sun, the battle against them would be in the shade and not in the sun.
228. The men were buried where they fell; and for these, as well as for those who were slain before being sent away by Leonidas, there is an inscription which runs thus:
"Here once, facing in fight three hundred myriads of foemen, Thousands four did contend, men of the Peloponnese."
This is the inscription for the whole body; and for the Spartans separately there is this:
"Stranger, report this word, we pray, to the Spartans, that lying Here in this spot we remain, faithfully keeping their laws."

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: The last day
parts.context: For two days the Greeks held the pass. Then a local man, Ephialtes ('Epialtes' in Macaulay), showed the Persians a mountain path round behind them. Leonidas sent most of the Greek army away and stayed with his 300 Spartans, about 700 men of Thespiae and 400 Thebans. Herodotus says the Thebans were kept against their will and later surrendered. The 'Medes' are the Persians.
parts.plain: On the last morning the Greeks, knowing they would die, advanced into the open and killed many Persians, whose officers drove them on with whips. Leonidas fell; the Spartans fought over his body and drove the Persians back four times. When the Persians who had come round the mountain arrived, the Greeks withdrew to a small hill and fought with daggers, hands and teeth until they were overwhelmed.

commentary.on: the leaders of the divisions with scourges in their hands were striking each man, ever urging them on to the front
commentary.text: Herodotus makes Xerxes' words come true in the opposite way. The Persians are driven 'by the lash'; the Greeks go forward of their own will.

commentary.on: of whose names I was informed as of men who had proved themselves worthy, and indeed I was told also the names of all the three hundred
commentary.text: This is Herodotus the historian at work: he went and found out the names. In his day, a list of the 300 was kept at Sparta, and the Greek traveller Pausanias saw it there in the second century AD (Description of Greece III.14.1).

commentary.on: they were overwhelmed by the missiles of the Barbarians
commentary.text: In 1939 the Greek archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos excavated the little hill, Kolonos, and found many Persian bronze arrowheads, as the account would lead us to expect.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: Tell the Spartans
parts.context: Herodotus records the sayings and the graves. The epitaphs were in verse; the one for the Spartans is often attributed to the poet Simonides, though Herodotus names him only for the seer Megistias. A 'myriad' is ten thousand, so 'three hundred myriads' is three million. Chapter 227, on the bravest men, has been left out; the cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: The Spartan Dienekes, told that the Persian arrows would hide the sun, said: good, then we shall fight in the shade. The dead were buried where they fell. One stone honoured all the Peloponnesians who fought. Another, for the Spartans, asked a passer-by to tell Sparta that they lay there, obedient to its laws.

commentary.on: the battle against them would be in the shade and not in the sun
commentary.text: A Spartan joke in the face of death. 'Laconic', meaning short and dry, comes from Laconia, the Spartans' country.

commentary.on: Here once, facing in fight three hundred myriads of foemen
commentary.text: Three million is a poet's number, and it matches Herodotus' own impossible figure for Xerxes' forces, over five million men with their attendants (VII.186). Modern historians think the army may have been between about 100,000 and 300,000 men: still overwhelming.

commentary.on: Stranger, report this word, we pray, to the Spartans, that lying Here in this spot we remain, faithfully keeping their laws.
commentary.text: The most famous epitaph in the world. Notice what it says: not 'we died for glory', nor 'we died for Sparta', but 'faithfully keeping their laws'. It is Demaratus' answer carved in stone. Their master was the law, and they obeyed it.

compare.author: Herodotus
compare.why: Was Demaratus right? Read Herodotus' account of the last day at Thermopylae, and the words carved on the graves.
compare.title: The last stand

paras: The war of 480–479 BC turned on three battles. At Thermopylae the Greeks held the pass for three days and lost; the Persians marched south and burned Athens, whose people had fled to the island of Salamis. Then, in September 480 BC, the Athenian leader Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow strait between Salamis and the mainland, where its numbers were useless. The Greek ships, most of them Athenian, destroyed it while Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore. He went home.

The next summer, at Plataea, a Greek army under the Spartan regent Pausanias destroyed the Persian land army that Xerxes had left behind, and on the same day, Herodotus says, a Greek force beat the Persians at Mycale on the Turkish coast. The invasion was over. Thermopylae was a defeat, but it became the symbol of the whole war.

rows: Athenians and Plataeans beat Darius' army
Leonidas holds the pass, then is destroyed
The Greek fleet destroys the Persian fleet in a narrow strait
A Greek army destroys the Persian land army
table.note: Herodotus VI–IX.

sections.key: Thermopylae was lost, Athens burned; Salamis (480 BC) and Plataea (479 BC) won the war.

paras: Why did the Greeks win? Herodotus gives practical reasons: the narrow places at Thermopylae and Salamis, Themistocles' cunning, the Greek heavy infantry. But his deepest explanation is the one Demaratus gives. Free men fight for themselves; slaves fight because they are driven. Earlier, he says the same of Athens: once freed from its tyrants, it became the first of cities, 'when they were kept down they were wilfully slack, because they were working for a master, whereas when they had been set free each one was eager to achieve something for himself' (V.78).

This is a new idea of freedom. It is not doing whatever you want. It is living under a law that you and your fellow citizens share, and that binds the powerful too. The Greeks called it isonomia, 'equality under the law'. It is close to what Israel's law said of its king, who must not think himself 'above his brothers' (Deuteronomy 17:20), which you may have read in 'Kings and prophets'. Two ancient peoples, in different ways, had come to the same thought: no one should be above the law.
sections.key: Herodotus' deepest explanation is freedom: men who obey a shared law, not a master, fight for themselves. The Greeks called it isonomia, equality under law.

paras: We must be honest about the limits of this freedom. Sparta's citizens were a few thousand men. Its land was worked by helots, Greeks held as serfs, whom the Spartans each year formally declared war on, so that killing them would not be a crime (Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 28). Athens, the city of democracy, had tens of thousands of slaves. Women had no vote anywhere. 'Free Greeks against slave Persians' was a proud simplification.

The historian Paul Cartledge, in Thermopylae (2006), argues that the battle really was a turning point in the history of freedom, and also that Sparta was, in its own way, one of the least free societies in Greece. Both are true. The Greeks had found an idea larger than their own practice. It would take more than two thousand years, and much help from the Christian conviction that every person bears God's image, before the West began to apply it to everyone.
sections.key: Greek freedom was for citizen men only: Sparta rested on serfs and Athens on slaves. The idea was larger than the practice.

paras: Herodotus was attacked even in antiquity. Thucydides, as we will see in the next session, quietly criticised writers who prefer a good story to the truth. Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court around 400 BC, said Herodotus lied about Persia. Plutarch wrote a whole essay, On the Malice of Herodotus, accusing him of bias. Later readers turned Cicero's compliment around and called him 'the father of lies'.

In 1971 the German scholar Detlev Fehling went further: he argued that Herodotus invented most of his sources, and that his 'the Egyptians say' is a literary device. Others, such as W. Kendrick Pritchett in The Liar School of Herodotus (1993), replied that where Herodotus can be checked, he is usually describing real places and real reports. Most scholars now take a middle view: Herodotus reports honestly what he was told, and often says so; what he was told was sometimes wrong.
sections.key: Critics from Ctesias to Fehling have called Herodotus a liar; most scholars now think he honestly reports what he was told, which was sometimes wrong.

paras: Where we can test Herodotus, he often does well. The burial mound of the Athenians at Marathon still stands. At Thermopylae, Marinatos found the arrowheads on the hill. The bronze Serpent Column, which the Greeks dedicated at Delphi after Plataea (Herodotus IX.81), now stands in the Hippodrome in Istanbul, and lists the cities that fought, much as Herodotus does. Darius' own inscription at Behistun in Iran names the six nobles who helped him seize the throne; five of the names match Herodotus' list (III.70). Herodotus' description of Scythian royal burials (IV.71–72) matches tombs excavated on the steppe.

Where he fails, it is usually with numbers, distant lands and the inner thoughts of kings. Five million people could not have crossed the Hellespont or been fed. The speeches of Xerxes and Demaratus are not recordings: Herodotus was a child in 480 BC and was not in Thrace. They are what he believed such men would have said, shaped to show what the war meant.
sections.key: Archaeology confirms much of Herodotus (Marathon, Thermopylae, the Serpent Column, Behistun); his numbers and his speeches are not to be taken literally.

paras: Herodotus' story has been used ever since as the founding myth of 'the West' against 'the East'. The philosopher John Stuart Mill wrote in 1846 that the battle of Marathon was more important to English history than the battle of Hastings. In the 20th century, the critic Edward Said (Orientalism, 1978) argued that this picture of a free, rational West and a despotic, luxurious East had long served to justify Western empires.

Historians of Persia, such as Pierre Briant, have shown how much the Greeks missed: an empire that tolerated local religions, let the Jews rebuild their Temple, and governed vast lands with roads and law. Yet Herodotus himself is not the problem. He admires Persian courage, honesty and customs, tells us Persian boys are taught 'in three things only, in riding, in shooting, and in speaking the truth' (I.136), and lets Persians state the case against the Greeks on his first page. The simplification belongs to his later readers more than to him.
sections.key: Herodotus became the founding story of 'West against East'; critics like Said and historians like Briant show what it missed, but Herodotus himself was fairer to Persia than his later readers.

paras: One more comparison. If you have taken 'Exodus and the law', you have read how Israel, a people of slaves, crossed the sea while Pharaoh's army was drowned (Exodus 14). The two stories have been told side by side for centuries: a small people, a great empire, the sea, and freedom.

The differences are as important as the likeness. In Herodotus, the Greeks free themselves, by courage, law and clever tactics; the gods help, but men win. In Exodus, the people do nothing but walk: 'Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still' (Exodus 14:14). And the freedom Israel receives is not mainly freedom from a foreign king but freedom to serve God under his law. Both stories put freedom under law. They disagree about whose law, and who sets people free.
sections.key: Exodus and Thermopylae both tell of a small people's freedom against an empire; in Herodotus men free themselves, in Exodus God does.

debate.question: Did the Persian Wars save the West?

positions.name: Yes: freedom survived
positions.who: J. S. Mill (1846); Tom Holland (Persian Fire, 2005); Paul Cartledge, with qualifications
positions.view: Had Persia won, Athens would have become a province, and the democracy, drama, philosophy and history that grew there in the next century might never have happened. The idea of citizens living under a law they share survived because a few cities fought.
positions.evidence: Athens' great age came after 479 BC; Herodotus V.78 on what freedom did for Athens; the Persians' practice of installing tyrants in Greek cities.

positions.name: No: a myth of East and West
positions.who: Edward Said (Orientalism, 1978); historians of Persia such as Pierre Briant
positions.view: Persia was a tolerant, well-governed empire, and Greek cities under it kept much of their life. The story of free West and slavish East was a Greek self-image, later used to justify Western domination. 'The West' did not exist in 480 BC.
positions.evidence: Persian tolerance of local religions (the Cyrus Cylinder; Ezra 1); Greek cities that chose Persia; the later uses of Herodotus by European empires.

positions.name: Both: a real turning point, badly remembered
positions.who: Many historians, including Cartledge
positions.view: The Greek victory did matter: it let a rare kind of self-governing city survive. But the freedom it protected was for a few, and the 'clash of civilisations' was largely invented by later readers, not by Herodotus.
positions.evidence: Herodotus' own fairness to Persia; the helots and slaves of the Greek cities; the long afterlife of the story.

debate.agree: All agree that the Greeks won against heavy odds, that their victory let Athens flourish, and that Herodotus told it as a story of freedom under law.

look.why: No painting for this session: the gallery's open collection has no work showing Thermopylae, Xerxes or any battle of the Persian Wars, and we use no stand-in that pretends to be the subject.

music.why: A requiem without terror, ending with angels leading the dead into paradise. Listen to it as music for the dead at Thermopylae, who 'remain' where they fell.

think.why: Herodotus' free men under law are one root of the Western idea of the free person. See how the Bible added the rest.

learn.why: Two lines on a grave that say what freedom under law costs: the most famous epitaph ever written.

check.q: Why does Xerxes think free men will not fight?
options: Because the Greeks are too poor to buy weapons
Because the gods favour Persia
Because the Spartans had already surrendered
Because, in his view, men fight only when one master compels them by fear or the whip, and free men have no master
check.why: 'If they were all equally free and were not ruled by one man' ... 'compelled by the lash'. For an absolute ruler, freedom means no one is in charge.

check.q: What is the best summary of Demaratus' reply?
options: The Spartans are free but have a master, the law, which they fear more than Persians fear their king
The Spartans fear Xerxes more than their own king
The Spartans have no master at all
The Spartans are better armed
check.why: 'Though free, yet they are not free in all things, for over them is set Law as a master.' Freedom is obeying a shared law, not having no master.

check.q: Why does the Spartan epitaph matter for Herodotus' argument?
options: It says the Spartans died 'faithfully keeping their laws', which is Demaratus' claim carved in stone
It proves the army was three million strong
It was written by Xerxes
It shows the Spartans died for glory alone
check.why: The epitaph names obedience to law as the reason they stayed, exactly as Demaratus said.

check.q: Which is the fairest judgement on Herodotus' reliability?
options: Everything he says is confirmed by archaeology
He was reliable about Persia but not about Greece
He invented all his sources
Much of his account is confirmed by archaeology, but his numbers are impossible and his speeches are not records of what was said
check.why: Marathon, Thermopylae, the Serpent Column and Behistun confirm him; five million men and verbatim speeches do not survive scrutiny.

check.q: What is the strongest objection to calling the war 'free men against slaves'?
options: The Persians had no army
Sparta rested on helot serfs and Athens on slaves, and only citizen men had political freedom
The Greeks lost the war
Herodotus disliked the Greeks
check.why: Greek freedom was real but narrow; the idea was larger than the practice.

check.q: How does Exodus 14 differ most from Herodotus' account of the Greek victory?
options: In Exodus the people are freed by God while they 'stand still'; in Herodotus men free themselves by courage and law
There is no difference
In Exodus the people fight a great battle
In Exodus there is no empire
check.why: 'Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still.' In Herodotus, men win.

tutorial.question: 'Over them is set Law as a master.' What did Herodotus think the Persian Wars were about, and was he right?
tutorial.approach: Explain Xerxes' view of power and Demaratus' answer. Use Thermopylae and its epitaph. Then weigh the evidence for his account and the objections: the numbers, the speeches, the helots and slaves, the myth of East and West. End with your own view of what the war decided.
strong: Explains freedom under law (nomos, isonomia) as Demaratus states it.
Uses the Thermopylae account and epitaph as evidence for Herodotus' view.
Weighs Herodotus' reliability with specific evidence for and against.
Faces the limits of Greek freedom honestly.
Discusses the 'East and West' critique fairly.
Compares or contrasts Exodus 14 or Deuteronomy 17.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose one rule you have made for yourself (about money, food, speech or time) and keep it every day this week, especially when no one would know if you broke it. Notice what it does to you to obey a law you chose.

takeaways: Xerxes believed men fight only when a master drives them; Demaratus answered that the Spartans' master was the law.
Thermopylae and its epitaph made freedom under law the meaning of the war; archaeology confirms much of Herodotus' account, though not his numbers or his speeches.
Greek freedom was for citizen men only, and the 'East against West' story is a later simplification; Herodotus himself was fair to Persia.

sessions.title: A possession for ever
sessions.line: A disgraced Athenian general sets out to write the history of the war he is living through, and to tell the exact truth, so that it will be useful for ever.
sessions.plain: Thucydides was an Athenian who fought in the great war between Athens and Sparta that began in 431 BC, and was exiled for losing a town. He used his exile to write its history. He wanted to do better than Herodotus and the poets: to test every report, to trust only what he or careful witnesses had seen, and to write something that would still be useful when the war was long forgotten. This session reads his own account of his method and asks what it means to tell the truth about the past.
sessions.why: The first three sessions followed Herodotus, who listened to everyone and gave the meaning of events in stories, some of them too good to be true. Now the second founder of history answers him. Thucydides lived through the war he describes, and he set out to find the exact truth. To judge what he later says about power, we first need to know how he worked and how far to trust him.
answers: Who was Thucydides?
What was the Peloponnesian War?
How was Thucydides' method different from Herodotus'?
Did he make up the speeches?
What is the 'Thucydides Trap'?
sessions.finding: Thucydides wanted the exact truth, tested against witnesses who disagreed, so that his work would be 'a possession for all time'; he also wrote speeches of what was 'demanded', and said so.

paras: After the Persians were driven out in 479 BC, the Greek cities split into two camps. Athens, with the strongest fleet, led a league of island and coastal cities, which it slowly turned into an empire: its 'allies' paid it tribute, and those who tried to leave were crushed. Sparta, with the strongest army, led the cities of the Peloponnese, the southern peninsula of Greece. Athens grew rich and confident: this was the age of the Parthenon, of the plays of Sophocles and of the statesman Pericles.

In 431 BC the two camps went to war. The war lasted, with a break, for twenty-seven years, until Athens surrendered in 404 BC. It is called the Peloponnesian War, and its history was written by a man who fought in it.
background.key: After 479 BC Athens built a naval empire and Sparta led the Peloponnese; in 431 BC they went to war for twenty-seven years.

paras: Thucydides, son of Olorus, was born an Athenian citizen around 460 BC, from a wealthy family with links to the gold mines of Thrace in northern Greece. He caught the great plague of 430 BC and survived (II.48). In 424 BC he was one of Athens' ten generals; he failed to save the city of Amphipolis from the Spartan general Brasidas, and the Athenians exiled him. He spent twenty years away, which, he says, let him talk to both sides (V.26).

He began writing, he tells us, as soon as the war broke out, because he expected it to be the greatest war ever (I.1). He died around 400 BC, and his book stops in mid-sentence in 411 BC, seven years before the end. If you have taken 'How we got here' or 'Democracy and its dangers', you have already read his account of Pericles' funeral speech and of the Athenian assembly.
background.key: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, wrote the history of the war as it happened; it breaks off in 411 BC.

paras: Thucydides wrote only a generation after Herodotus. He almost certainly knew Herodotus' work, though he never names him. His history is in eight books, divided by later editors, and covers the war year by year, summer and winter.

paras: The main reading is the four chapters (I.20–23) in which Thucydides explains how he worked: why most people get the past wrong, how he wrote the speeches and the narrative, why his book will be useful, and what he thinks really caused the war.
The comparison is two short statements by Herodotus about his own method. Read together, they show how the two founders of history disagreed, and what each of them got right.
background.key: Thucydides' account of his method (I.20–23), then two sentences in which Herodotus describes his.

before: What does Thucydides say most people do with stories about the past?
How does he say he wrote the speeches? How does he say he wrote the narrative?

sessions.readWhy: Thucydides' own account of how to find the truth about the past, and why it matters.

paras: Having now given the result of my inquiries into early times, I grant that there will be a difficulty in believing every particular detail. The way that most men deal with traditions, even traditions of their own country, is to receive them all alike as they are delivered, without applying any critical test whatever. The general Athenian public fancy that Hipparchus was tyrant when he fell by the hands of Harmodius and Aristogiton, not knowing that Hippias, the eldest of the sons of Pisistratus, was really supreme, and that Hipparchus and Thessalus were his brothers; and that Harmodius and Aristogiton suspecting, on the very day, nay at the very moment fixed on for the deed, that information had been conveyed to Hippias by their accomplices, concluded that he had been warned, and did not attack him, yet, not liking to be apprehended and risk their lives for nothing, fell upon Hipparchus near the temple of the daughters of Leos, and slew him as he was arranging the Panathenaic procession.

There are many other unfounded ideas current among the rest of the Hellenes, even on matters of contemporary history, which have not been obscured by time. For instance, there is the notion that the Lacedaemonian kings have two votes each, the fact being that they have only one; and that there is a company of Pitane, there being simply no such thing. So little pains do the vulgar take in the investigation of truth, accepting readily the first story that comes to hand. On the whole, however, the conclusions I have drawn from the proofs quoted may, I believe, safely be relied on. Assuredly they will not be disturbed either by the lays of a poet displaying the exaggeration of his craft, or by the compositions of the chroniclers that are attractive at truth’s expense; the subjects they treat of being out of the reach of evidence, and time having robbed most of them of historical value by enthroning them in the region of legend. Turning from these, we can rest satisfied with having proceeded upon the clearest data, and having arrived at conclusions as exact as can be expected in matters of such antiquity. To come to this war: despite the known disposition of the actors in a struggle to overrate its importance, and when it is over to return to their admiration of earlier events, yet an examination of the facts will show that it was much greater than the wars which preceded it.

With reference to the speeches in this history, some were delivered before the war began, others while it was going on; some I heard myself, others I got from various quarters; it was in all cases difficult to carry them word for word in one’s memory, so my habit has been to make the speakers say what was in my opinion demanded of them by the various occasions, of course adhering as closely as possible to the general sense of what they really said. And with reference to the narrative of events, far from permitting myself to derive it from the first source that came to hand, I did not even trust my own impressions, but it rests partly on what I saw myself, partly on what others saw for me, the accuracy of the report being always tried by the most severe and detailed tests possible. My conclusions have cost me some labour from the want of coincidence between accounts of the same occurrences by different eye-witnesses, arising sometimes from imperfect memory, sometimes from undue partiality for one side or the other. The absence of romance in my history will, I fear, detract somewhat from its interest; but if it be judged useful by those inquirers who desire an exact knowledge of the past as an aid to the interpretation of the future, which in the course of human things must resemble if it does not reflect it, I shall be content. In fine, I have written my work, not as an essay which is to win the applause of the moment, but as a possession for all time.

The Median War, the greatest achievement of past times, yet found a speedy decision in two actions by sea and two by land. The Peloponnesian War was prolonged to an immense length, and, long as it was, it was short without parallel for the misfortunes that it brought upon Hellas. Never had so many cities been taken and laid desolate, here by the barbarians, here by the parties contending (the old inhabitants being sometimes removed to make room for others); never was there so much banishing and blood-shedding, now on the field of battle, now in the strife of faction. Old stories of occurrences handed down by tradition, but scantily confirmed by experience, suddenly ceased to be incredible; there were earthquakes of unparalleled extent and violence; eclipses of the sun occurred with a frequency unrecorded in previous history; there were great droughts in sundry places and consequent famines, and that most calamitous and awfully fatal visitation, the plague. All this came upon them with the late war, which was begun by the Athenians and Peloponnesians by the dissolution of the thirty years’ truce made after the conquest of Euboea. To the question why they broke the treaty, I answer by placing first an account of their grounds of complaint and points of difference, that no one may ever have to ask the immediate cause which plunged the Hellenes into a war of such magnitude. The real cause I consider to be the one which was formally most kept out of sight. The growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm which this inspired in Lacedaemon, made war inevitable. Still it is well to give the grounds alleged by either side which led to the dissolution of the treaty and the breaking out of the war.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Most people do not check
parts.context: Thucydides has just written a short history of early Greece, reasoning from what evidence there was. Now he explains why the common stories cannot be trusted. Hipparchus and Hippias were sons of Pisistratus, a tyrant of Athens; in 514 BC two young men, Harmodius and Aristogiton, killed Hipparchus, and Athenians honoured them with statues as the killers of the tyrant. Thucydides says they got the story wrong. 'Lacedaemonian' means Spartan. This is Richard Crawley's translation of 1874.
parts.plain: Thucydides says: most people accept the stories they are told, even about their own city, without testing them. The Athenians think Harmodius and Aristogiton killed the tyrant, but the tyrant was actually his brother Hippias. Other Greeks believe false things even about the present. Poets exaggerate and storytellers prefer to please their audience. I have gone by the clearest evidence, and this war, when you look at the facts, was the greatest ever.

commentary.on: The way that most men deal with traditions, even traditions of their own country, is to receive them all alike as they are delivered, without applying any critical test whatever.
commentary.text: This sentence is the beginning of critical history. Do not believe a story because it is old, or because it is your own people's. Test it.

commentary.on: The general Athenian public fancy that Hipparchus was tyrant when he fell by the hands of Harmodius and Aristogiton
commentary.text: He chooses a hard example: Athens' favourite story about its own freedom. The statues of the 'tyrant-slayers' stood in the market place. Thucydides says, in effect, your heroes killed the wrong man, for a private quarrel. It takes courage to correct a nation's myth.

commentary.on: So little pains do the vulgar take in the investigation of truth, accepting readily the first story that comes to hand.
commentary.text: 'The vulgar' means ordinary people, not rude people. The fault he names is laziness: taking the first story you hear. In an age of instant news, it has not gone away.

commentary.on: the compositions of the chroniclers that are attractive at truth’s expense
commentary.text: Many scholars think he has Herodotus partly in mind: writers who tell a good story for an audience, at the cost of the truth. He never names him.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: A possession for all time
parts.context: These are the most famous paragraphs Thucydides wrote, and among the most discussed in all ancient literature. He explains how he wrote the speeches, which fill about a quarter of his book, and the narrative of events. Then he says why the war was so terrible, and what really caused it. The 'Median War' is the Persian War of Herodotus; the 'thirty years' truce' was a peace made between Athens and Sparta in 446/5 BC.
parts.plain: For the speeches, Thucydides says, I could not remember the exact words, so I have made the speakers say what the occasion required, keeping as close as possible to what they actually said. For the events, I did not trust the first report, or even my own impressions; I checked every account as strictly as I could, and found that eyewitnesses disagreed. My history has no romance, but it will be useful to anyone who wants to understand the past and so the future, because human nature does not change. It is not written to please for a moment but as a possession for all time. The war was greater and more terrible than any before. Its real cause was Athens' growing power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

commentary.on: so my habit has been to make the speakers say what was in my opinion demanded of them by the various occasions, of course adhering as closely as possible to the general sense of what they really said
commentary.text: An honest confession. The speeches are not recordings. Thucydides wrote them, keeping to 'the general sense' of what was said. Scholars have argued ever since about how much of each speech is the speaker and how much is Thucydides.

commentary.on: I did not even trust my own impressions
commentary.text: This is stricter than Herodotus, who was happy to write 'I saw'. Thucydides distrusts even himself. Memory and first impressions, as modern psychology has confirmed, are often wrong.

commentary.on: My conclusions have cost me some labour from the want of coincidence between accounts of the same occurrences by different eye-witnesses, arising sometimes from imperfect memory, sometimes from undue partiality for one side or the other.
commentary.text: He names the two great dangers in any witness: a bad memory and bias. Every judge, journalist and historian still works with these two.

commentary.on: The absence of romance in my history will, I fear, detract somewhat from its interest
commentary.text: The Greek word is to muthodes, 'the story-like', from mythos. Thucydides gives up the pleasure of Herodotus' tales for the sake of the truth, and knows it will cost him readers.

commentary.on: the interpretation of the future, which in the course of human things must resemble if it does not reflect it
commentary.text: Why study the past? Because human nature stays the same, so similar things will happen again. Thucydides' history is meant to be a tool for understanding.

commentary.on: not as an essay which is to win the applause of the moment, but as a possession for all time
commentary.text: The famous phrase. Herodotus probably read his work aloud to audiences who applauded. Thucydides writes for readers far in the future, and he was right: politicians and generals still read him.

commentary.on: The growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm which this inspired in Lacedaemon, made war inevitable.
commentary.text: The first distinction in history between the stated reasons for a war and its 'real cause'. In 2017 the political scientist Graham Allison called the danger of a rising power frightening an established one 'the Thucydides Trap'.

I however am bound to report that which is reported, though I am not bound altogether to believe it; and let this saying be considered to hold good as regards every narrative in the history

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: I write what is told
parts.context: Book II is about Egypt, which Herodotus visited. He has just told an Egyptian story about a king who went down alive to the underworld and played dice with the goddess Demeter. The footnote number in Macaulay's edition has been removed.
parts.plain: Anyone may believe these Egyptian stories who finds them believable. Throughout my history, I write what the people in each place told me.

commentary.on: any man may accept them to whom such things appear credible
commentary.text: Herodotus passes the judgement to his reader. He does not say the story is true; he says this is what the Egyptians say.

commentary.on: I write by hearsay that which is reported by the people in each place
commentary.text: This is his method in one sentence: report faithfully what each people says about itself. It is a method of recording, more than of testing.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.who: Herodotus of Halicarnassus (c. 484–c. 425 BC), a Greek from what is now Bodrum in Turkey, who travelled the eastern Mediterranean collecting stories.
parts.title: Bound to report, not bound to believe
parts.context: Herodotus is discussing an accusation that the city of Argos had betrayed Greece to Persia. He gives several versions and then states a rule for his whole book. The sentence continues with another version of the story, left out here.
parts.plain: I must report what is said, but I do not have to believe all of it, and this rule applies to everything in my history.

commentary.on: I however am bound to report that which is reported, though I am not bound altogether to believe it
commentary.text: This is fairer to Herodotus than his critics allow. He does not claim everything he reports is true. He keeps the reports, as evidence of what people said, and keeps his own judgement separate.

commentary.on: let this saying be considered to hold good as regards every narrative in the history
commentary.text: A reader who remembers this rule will read Herodotus very differently from one who takes every story as his own claim. The two historians disagree less about honesty than about what a history should contain.

compare.author: Herodotus
compare.why: Herodotus also explained how he worked, in passing. Read his two sentences, and compare them with Thucydides'.
compare.title: Herodotus on his own method

paras: Thucydides' war had three stages. In the first (431–421 BC), Sparta invaded Attica, the country round Athens, every summer, and Pericles' strategy was to bring the people inside the city walls and fight by sea. Plague struck the crowded city in 430 BC. The fighting ended in a peace named after the Athenian general Nicias (421 BC).

In the second, Athens tried to extend its power: it destroyed the neutral island of Melos (416 BC) and sent a vast fleet to conquer Sicily (415–413 BC), which ended in disaster. In the third, Sparta, now with Persian money, fought on until it destroyed the last Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BC. Athens surrendered in 404 BC; its walls were pulled down to the music of flute girls, Xenophon says, and a group of pro-Spartan oligarchs, the 'Thirty Tyrants', took over for a year.

rows: Spartan invasions; plague; Pericles dies; Peace of Nicias
Melos destroyed; the Sicilian expedition fails
Sparta builds a fleet with Persian money; Athens surrenders
table.note: Thucydides covers 431–411 BC; Xenophon's Hellenica continues to 404 BC and beyond.

sections.key: The war ran from 431 to 404 BC in three stages: Spartan invasions and plague, Athenian overreach at Melos and Sicily, and final defeat.

paras: Thucydides' method is close to what a modern historian, a journalist or a judge tries to do. He relies on eyewitnesses, including himself; he cross-examines them; he knows they disagree because memory fails and people take sides. He prefers the 'clearest data'. He uses documents where he has them, and copies some treaties word for word (for example, the treaty of 421 BC in V.18–19). He dates events precisely, by summers and winters, rather than by the years of local officials, which differed from city to city.

He also leaves the gods out. In Herodotus, oracles and dreams explain events. Thucydides mentions oracles only to show how people twisted them to fit what had happened, as we will see in the next session. His causes are human: fear, honour and interest (I.76). This is why he is often called the first scientific historian. It is also why some readers find him cold.
sections.key: Thucydides relied on cross-examined eyewitnesses and documents, dated precisely, and left the gods out of his explanations: the first 'scientific' historian.

paras: About a quarter of Thucydides' history is speeches: debates in the Athenian assembly, generals before battle, envoys arguing. They are among the greatest things in Greek, and they all sound like Thucydides: dense, abstract, full of argument. He tells us he wrote them himself, keeping to 'the general sense' of what was said.

How much of each is real? Scholars disagree. Some, like the Cambridge scholar F. M. Cornford in Thucydides Mythistoricus (1907), argued that Thucydides shaped his whole history like a tragedy, and that the speeches carry his own ideas. Others think he kept close to real arguments, where he heard them or had good reports. The honest answer is that the speeches are Thucydides' reconstruction: the best evidence we have of the arguments people made, and also his analysis of what was at stake. We should read them as both.
sections.key: The speeches are Thucydides' reconstruction of what was said: evidence of the arguments, and also his own analysis.

paras: Thucydides was a participant, an exile and a man with opinions. He admired Pericles and despised Cleon, the popular leader who followed him; Cleon may have been behind his exile. He hardly mentions economics, women or religion. He leaves out events we know from inscriptions, such as the sharp rise in the tribute Athens demanded from its allies in 425 BC.

Virginia Hunter, in Thucydides the Artful Reporter (1973), argued that he arranges facts so skilfully that we accept his judgements without noticing. Simon Hornblower, whose commentary on Thucydides (1991–2008) is the standard one in English, finds him generally accurate but always shaping. That is the lesson of this session for every reader of history: the most careful historian is still choosing, and the more persuasive he is, the more we must ask what he left out.
sections.key: Thucydides is generally accurate but partisan and selective; the most careful historian still chooses, and we must ask what he left out.

paras: Thucydides distinguishes the 'grounds alleged by either side' (a quarrel over Corcyra, a siege at Potidaea, a trade ban on Megara) from the 'real cause', which was 'the growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm which this inspired in Lacedaemon'. This is the first known distinction between the occasion of an event and its underlying cause, and every modern historian uses it.

It also gives the second theme of this journey: what power does. In Thucydides, power grows by its own logic, and fear grows with it, until war seems inevitable. The American political scientist Graham Allison, in Destined for War (2017), studied sixteen cases in the last five hundred years when a rising power challenged a ruling one, and found that twelve ended in war. Critics say Thucydides himself thought choices mattered: the war was 'inevitable' only once both sides chose to see it that way. That argument is still being had about our own century.
sections.key: Thucydides separated the stated reasons for the war from its real cause, Athens' growth and Sparta's fear; Allison's 'Thucydides Trap' applies this to today.

paras: Thucydides wrote 'a possession for all time' because he believed human nature does not change. Read the later chapters of his book and you meet propaganda, party hatred, the excuses of the powerful and the fear of the weak, and you will recognise them. The English philosopher Thomas Hobbes made the first English translation from the Greek in 1629, because he believed Thucydides taught what happens when people trust their passions in politics.

There is a Christian reason to value him too. Christianity rests on claims about real events: a man crucified under Pontius Pilate, an empty tomb. It needs a way of testing what witnesses say. When Luke promised 'certainty', he was using the kind of language Thucydides had made respectable. The habit of asking 'how do we know?' is not the enemy of faith; it is what lets faith be more than a story.
sections.key: Thucydides believed human nature does not change, so the past can help us understand the future; his way of testing witnesses also matters for a faith that rests on events.

paras: Thucydides never finished. His eighth book has no speeches in direct form, as if it were still a draft, and it stops in the middle of a sentence in the autumn of 411 BC, seven years before the war ended. In Book V he writes what scholars call a 'second preface' (V.26), saying he lived through the whole war, 'being of an age to comprehend events', and intends to write it to the end, which tells us he survived until at least 404 BC.

Others took up where he stopped. Xenophon, an Athenian who had known Socrates, began his Hellenica with the words 'After this', continuing directly from Thucydides' last events. That a great history could be continued by someone else, as if history were a shared task, was itself something new. From then on, Greek historians saw themselves as links in a chain, each correcting and carrying on from the last.
sections.key: Thucydides' history breaks off in 411 BC; Xenophon continued it, and history became a shared task carried on from writer to writer.

debate.question: Can we trust Thucydides?

positions.name: Yes: the most careful historian of antiquity
positions.who: Most historians of Greece; Donald Kagan, who built his four-volume history of the war on him
positions.view: Thucydides was a participant who cross-examined witnesses, dated events precisely, copied documents and left the gods out. Where he can be checked against inscriptions, he usually holds up. We would know almost nothing of the war without him.
positions.evidence: His own method (I.22); treaties copied verbatim; agreement with surviving inscriptions on many points.

positions.name: Only with care: an artful persuader
positions.who: F. M. Cornford (1907); Virginia Hunter (1973)
positions.view: Thucydides shaped his history like a tragedy and arranged his facts to lead the reader to his own judgements. The speeches are his. His silence about some things (the tribute rise of 425 BC, his own failure at Amphipolis) shows a partisan at work.
positions.evidence: The tragic shape of the Melos and Sicily books; the uniform style of the speeches; omissions revealed by inscriptions.

positions.name: Both: accurate and shaping
positions.who: Simon Hornblower; most modern commentators
positions.view: Thucydides is usually right about what happened and always shaping how we see it. Read him as a great historian and a great writer at once, and check him where we can.
positions.evidence: Hornblower's commentary, which tests him chapter by chapter.

debate.agree: All agree that Thucydides is our main source for the war, that the speeches are his reconstructions, and that he set a new standard for testing evidence.

look.why: No painting in the gallery shows Thucydides. This portrait by Giovanni Battista Moroni, about 1575, long known as 'Titian's Schoolmaster', shows a learned man in the act of reading: a scholar who has stopped to look up and think, as Thucydides asks his readers to do.
points: A man in a loose, ink-black garment with a white collar leans back in a wooden chair, shown from the knees up.
His body faces left, but he turns his head to look at us from the corners of his light hazel-brown eyes, one eyebrow slightly cocked.
He has a close-trimmed silvery-grey beard, lined cheeks and a black, three-pointed cap.
With one hand he marks his place in a closed book with a sand-brown cover, about the size of a thick paperback.
His other arm stretches along the arm of the chair, its hand curled round a carved terminal; he wears a gold ring with a dark blue stone on his little finger.
Behind him is a crimson-red chair lining with fringes, against a brown background that lightens to tan around his head.

music.why: Bach assembled it at the end of his life from music he had written over decades, and it was not performed complete while he lived: a work written, like Thucydides', not for the applause of the moment.

think.why: Historians test the Gospels with the questions Thucydides asked: who saw it, who wrote it down, who disagreed. See how the modern debate about Jesus works.

learn.why: Thucydides' own reason for writing, and a good test for anything we make: is it for the applause of the moment, or for good?

check.q: Why does Thucydides choose the story of Harmodius and Aristogiton as his example?
options: Because it shows that even a nation's favourite story about its own past can be wrong, if no one tests it
Because it was the cause of the war
Because it was a Spartan story
Because he was related to them
check.why: Athenians honoured them as the tyrant-slayers; Thucydides shows they killed the tyrant's brother. Testing applies to your own people's stories too.

check.q: What does Thucydides admit about the speeches in his history?
options: That they are word-for-word records
That he invented them freely with no basis
That he made the speakers say what the occasion demanded, keeping as close as possible to the general sense of what was said
That they were written by the speakers themselves
check.why: He could not remember the exact words, so he reconstructed them, keeping to 'the general sense'.

check.q: Why does Thucydides think his history will be useful?
options: Because it entertains
Because it flatters Athens
Because it proves the gods favour Sparta
Because human nature does not change, so the past will help people understand what is likely to happen again
check.why: 'An aid to the interpretation of the future, which in the course of human things must resemble if it does not reflect it.'

check.q: What is the best reply to the charge that Herodotus simply believed whatever he was told?
options: He wrote only about events he saw himself
He used written documents only
He never travelled, so he could not have been told anything
He says he is bound to report what is said but not bound to believe it, and often gives several versions
check.why: VII.152 is his rule for the whole book; he records reports as reports.

check.q: Thucydides says the 'real cause' of the war was Athens' growing power and Sparta's fear. Why was this distinction important?
options: Because it separated the stated reasons for a war from its underlying cause, a distinction historians still use
Because it showed the war was an accident
Because it blamed the gods
Because it proved Sparta was innocent
check.why: Corcyra, Potidaea and Megara were the occasions; the shift in power was the cause.

check.q: Which is the strongest reason to read Thucydides critically, even though he is careful?
options: He had no eyewitnesses
He believed in oracles
He wrote centuries after the war
He was a participant with strong views, who chose what to include and wrote the speeches himself, and inscriptions show things he left out
check.why: Care and bias can live together; the tribute rise of 425 BC is one omission.

tutorial.question: Herodotus or Thucydides: which was the better historian?
tutorial.approach: Set out each man's method in his own words (I.22; II.123; VII.152). Give the strengths of each: Herodotus' breadth and fairness to many voices, Thucydides' testing and precision. Give the weaknesses of each: Herodotus' credulity and numbers, Thucydides' speeches and selectivity. Decide what 'better' means, and answer.
strong: Quotes or explains Thucydides' account of the speeches and of the narrative accurately.
Gives Herodotus' rule ('bound to report ... not bound to believe') fairly.
Weighs strengths and weaknesses of each with examples.
Explains the 'real cause' and why it mattered.
Notes that even Thucydides shapes and selects.
Defines what makes a historian good before deciding.
