sessions.practice: Live it this week: the next time you hear a story that makes you angry (in the news, at work, in the family), before you repeat it, find one other account of the same event. Notice whether the two agree.
sessions.reflect: Which story about your own family, town or country have you never tested, because you wanted it to be true?
takeaways: Thucydides set out to find the exact truth, testing eyewitnesses who disagreed through bad memory or bias, and to write 'a possession for all time'.
He admits he reconstructed the speeches, and he separated the stated reasons for the war from its real cause: Athens' growth and Sparta's fear.
Herodotus recorded what he was told without claiming to believe it all; Thucydides tested; both chose and shaped, and we must read both critically.

sessions.title: The plague
sessions.line: In the second year of the war a plague breaks out in crowded Athens. Thucydides, who caught it, describes the symptoms, and then something worse: how fast law and religion collapsed.
sessions.plain: In 430 BC, with the whole population of the countryside crowded inside the walls of Athens, a terrible disease broke out. Thucydides caught it and survived, and he described it so that it could be recognised if it ever came again. He also described what it did to people: they stopped caring for the sick, stopped burying the dead properly, and stopped fearing the gods or the law. This session asks what a catastrophe reveals about a civilisation, and compares how Christians in a later plague behaved.
sessions.why: The last session showed Thucydides' method: test every report, trust only what can be checked, and write for the future because human nature does not change. Now we see that method at work on the worst thing he witnessed. His account of the plague is the first great case study in what happens to people when the order of their world breaks down, and it is a test of his claim that human nature does not change.
answers: What was the plague of Athens?
What did Thucydides see happen to the Athenians?
Do we know what disease it was?
How did Christians behave in later plagues, and why?
sessions.finding: When plague struck Athens, law and religion collapsed within months: Thucydides recorded how quickly a civilisation can forget itself. In a later plague, Christians were remembered for staying with the sick.

paras: In the last session we saw how the war began in 431 BC, with Athens' growing power and Sparta's fear. Pericles, Athens' leading statesman, had a plan. Athens could not beat Sparta's army on land, but it ruled the sea. So the people of Attica, the countryside around Athens, were brought inside the walls that joined the city to its port, Piraeus, while the Spartans burned their farms. Athens would live on food brought by sea.

At the end of the first year, Pericles gave the funeral speech for the war dead that you may have read in 'How we got here', praising Athens as 'the school of Hellas'. Thucydides places the plague immediately after it. The contrast is deliberate: the city at its most glorious, and then the city broken.
background.key: Pericles brought the people of Attica inside the walls of Athens; in 430 BC, straight after his funeral speech, plague broke out in the crowded city.

paras: The plague lasted, with a pause, from 430 to 426 BC. Pericles himself died of it in 429 BC. Thucydides later says that 4,400 heavy infantry and 300 cavalry died, besides 'a number of the multitude that was never ascertained' (III.87). Modern historians often estimate that a quarter to a third of the people in Athens died.

timeline.text: War begins; Attica moved inside the walls; Pericles' funeral speech
The plague breaks out in Piraeus and the city
Pericles dies of the plague
The plague returns
The 'plague of Cyprian' across the Roman Empire
Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, writes his Easter letter
A mass grave of the plague years is found in the Kerameikos cemetery, Athens

background.key: The plague lasted from 430 to 426 BC, killed Pericles and perhaps a quarter to a third of the people of Athens.

paras: The main reading is Thucydides' whole account of the plague (II.47–54): how it came, its symptoms, how people died, and what it did to their morals and their religion.

The comparison is a letter written about 690 years later by Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria in Egypt, during another great epidemic. It was preserved by Eusebius, the first historian of the Church. If you have taken 'First Christians', you met it there in a sentence; here we read it whole, beside Thucydides, because it describes the same kind of catastrophe and a different response to it.
background.key: Thucydides' account of the plague, then a bishop's account of how Christians behaved in a plague 690 years later.

before: Why does Thucydides describe the symptoms in such detail?
Who died most, according to him, and why?
What happened to religion and to law in the plague, and why does Thucydides say it happened?
sessions.readWhy: Thucydides' account of the plague: the clearest picture in ancient history of a society coming apart.

paras: Such was the funeral that took place during this winter, with which the first year of the war came to an end. In the first days of summer the Lacedaemonians and their allies, with two-thirds of their forces as before, invaded Attica, under the command of Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, King of Lacedaemon, and sat down and laid waste the country. Not many days after their arrival in Attica the plague first began to show itself among the Athenians. It was said that it had broken out in many places previously in the neighbourhood of Lemnos and elsewhere; but a pestilence of such extent and mortality was nowhere remembered. Neither were the physicians at first of any service, ignorant as they were of the proper way to treat it, but they died themselves the most thickly, as they visited the sick most often; nor did any human art succeed any better. Supplications in the temples, divinations, and so forth were found equally futile, till the overwhelming nature of the disaster at last put a stop to them altogether.

It first began, it is said, in the parts of Ethiopia above Egypt, and thence descended into Egypt and Libya and into most of the King’s country. Suddenly falling upon Athens, it first attacked the population in Piraeus—which was the occasion of their saying that the Peloponnesians had poisoned the reservoirs, there being as yet no wells there—and afterwards appeared in the upper city, when the deaths became much more frequent. All speculation as to its origin and its causes, if causes can be found adequate to produce so great a disturbance, I leave to other writers, whether lay or professional; for myself, I shall simply set down its nature, and explain the symptoms by which perhaps it may be recognized by the student, if it should ever break out again. This I can the better do, as I had the disease myself, and watched its operation in the case of others.

That year then is admitted to have been otherwise unprecedentedly free from sickness; and such few cases as occurred all determined in this. As a rule, however, there was no ostensible cause; but people in good health were all of a sudden attacked by violent heats in the head, and redness and inflammation in the eyes, the inward parts, such as the throat or tongue, becoming bloody and emitting an unnatural and fetid breath. These symptoms were followed by sneezing and hoarseness, after which the pain soon reached the chest, and produced a hard cough. When it fixed in the stomach, it upset it; and discharges of bile of every kind named by physicians ensued, accompanied by very great distress. In most cases also an ineffectual retching followed, producing violent spasms, which in some cases ceased soon after, in others much later. Externally the body was not very hot to the touch, nor pale in its appearance, but reddish, livid, and breaking out into small pustules and ulcers. But internally it burned so that the patient could not bear to have on him clothing or linen even of the very lightest description; or indeed to be otherwise than stark naked. What they would have liked best would have been to throw themselves into cold water;

as indeed was done by some of the neglected sick, who plunged into the rain-tanks in their agonies of unquenchable thirst; though it made no difference whether they drank little or much. Besides this, the miserable feeling of not being able to rest or sleep never ceased to torment them. The body meanwhile did not waste away so long as the distemper was at its height, but held out to a marvel against its ravages; so that when they succumbed, as in most cases, on the seventh or eighth day to the internal inflammation, they had still some strength in them. But if they passed this stage, and the disease descended further into the bowels, inducing a violent ulceration there accompanied by severe diarrhoea, this brought on a weakness which was generally fatal. For the disorder first settled in the head, ran its course from thence through the whole of the body, and, even where it did not prove mortal, it still left its mark on the extremities; for it settled in the privy parts, the fingers and the toes, and many escaped with the loss of these, some too with that of their eyes. Others again were seized with an entire loss of memory on their first recovery, and did not know either themselves or their friends.

But while the nature of the distemper was such as to baffle all description, and its attacks almost too grievous for human nature to endure, it was still in the following circumstance that its difference from all ordinary disorders was most clearly shown. All the birds and beasts that prey upon human bodies, either abstained from touching them (though there were many lying unburied), or died after tasting them. In proof of this, it was noticed that birds of this kind actually disappeared; they were not about the bodies, or indeed to be seen at all. But of course the effects which I have mentioned could best be studied in a domestic animal like the dog.

Such then, if we pass over the varieties of particular cases which were many and peculiar, were the general features of the distemper. Meanwhile the town enjoyed an immunity from all the ordinary disorders; or if any case occurred, it ended in this. Some died in neglect, others in the midst of every attention. No remedy was found that could be used as a specific; for what did good in one case, did harm in another. Strong and weak constitutions proved equally incapable of resistance, all alike being swept away, although dieted with the utmost precaution. By far the most terrible feature in the malady was the dejection which ensued when any one felt himself sickening, for the despair into which they instantly fell took away their power of resistance, and left them a much easier prey to the disorder; besides which, there was the awful spectacle of men dying like sheep, through having caught the infection in nursing each other. This caused the greatest mortality.

On the one hand, if they were afraid to visit each other, they perished from neglect; indeed many houses were emptied of their inmates for want of a nurse: on the other, if they ventured to do so, death was the consequence. This was especially the case with such as made any pretensions to goodness: honour made them unsparing of themselves in their attendance in their friends’ houses, where even the members of the family were at last worn out by the moans of the dying, and succumbed to the force of the disaster. Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the dying found most compassion. These knew what it was from experience, and had now no fear for themselves; for the same man was never attacked twice—never at least fatally. And such persons not only received the congratulations of others, but themselves also, in the elation of the moment, half entertained the vain hope that they were for the future safe from any disease whatsoever.

An aggravation of the existing calamity was the influx from the country into the city, and this was especially felt by the new arrivals. As there were no houses to receive them, they had to be lodged at the hot season of the year in stifling cabins, where the mortality raged without restraint. The bodies of dying men lay one upon another, and half-dead creatures reeled about the streets and gathered round all the fountains in their longing for water. The sacred places also in which they had quartered themselves were full of corpses of persons that had died there, just as they were; for as the disaster passed all bounds, men, not knowing what was to become of them, became utterly careless of everything, whether sacred or profane. All the burial rites before in use were entirely upset, and they buried the bodies as best they could. Many from want of the proper appliances, through so many of their friends having died already, had recourse to the most shameless sepultures: sometimes getting the start of those who had raised a pile, they threw their own dead body upon the stranger’s pyre and ignited it; sometimes they tossed the corpse which they were carrying on the top of another that was burning, and so went off.

Nor was this the only form of lawless extravagance which owed its origin to the plague. Men now coolly ventured on what they had formerly done in a corner, and not just as they pleased, seeing the rapid transitions produced by persons in prosperity suddenly dying and those who before had nothing succeeding to their property. So they resolved to spend quickly and enjoy themselves, regarding their lives and riches as alike things of a day. Perseverance in what men called honour was popular with none, it was so uncertain whether they would be spared to attain the object; but it was settled that present enjoyment, and all that contributed to it, was both honourable and useful. Fear of gods or law of man there was none to restrain them. As for the first, they judged it to be just the same whether they worshipped them or not, as they saw all alike perishing; and for the last, no one expected to live to be brought to trial for his offences, but each felt that a far severer sentence had been already passed upon them all and hung ever over their heads, and before this fell it was only reasonable to enjoy life a little.

Such was the nature of the calamity, and heavily did it weigh on the Athenians; death raging within the city and devastation without. Among other things which they remembered in their distress was, very naturally, the following verse which the old men said had long ago been uttered:
A Dorian war shall come and with it death.

So a dispute arose as to whether dearth and not death had not been the word in the verse; but at the present juncture, it was of course decided in favour of the latter; for the people made their recollection fit in with their sufferings. I fancy, however, that if another Dorian war should ever afterwards come upon us, and a dearth should happen to accompany it, the verse will probably be read accordingly. The oracle also which had been given to the Lacedaemonians was now remembered by those who knew of it. When the god was asked whether they should go to war, he answered that if they put their might into it, victory would be theirs, and that he would himself be with them. With this oracle events were supposed to tally. For the plague broke out as soon as the Peloponnesians invaded Attica, and never entering Peloponnese (not at least to an extent worth noticing), committed its worst ravages at Athens, and next to Athens, at the most populous of the other towns. Such was the history of the plague.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: It began in Piraeus
parts.context: Summer 430 BC, the second year of the war. The Spartan king Archidamus has invaded Attica again and is laying waste the farms. Inside the walls the city is packed with refugees. 'The King's country' is the Persian Empire.
parts.plain: Soon after the Spartans invaded, the plague broke out. No one remembered anything like it. Doctors were no use and died fastest; prayers and oracles were no use either. It seems to have come from Africa through Egypt and the Persian Empire, and it began in the port of Piraeus. Thucydides says he will not guess at the cause, but will describe the disease so it can be recognised again, because he had it himself and watched others.

commentary.on: Neither were the physicians at first of any service, ignorant as they were of the proper way to treat it, but they died themselves the most thickly, as they visited the sick most often
commentary.text: The first detail Thucydides gives is that those who cared for the sick died first. It will matter at the end of this session.

commentary.on: Supplications in the temples, divinations, and so forth were found equally futile
commentary.text: Neither medicine nor religion could help. Thucydides reports this flatly. He does not say the gods sent the plague, as Homer did at the start of the Iliad; he says prayer did not work.

commentary.on: which was the occasion of their saying that the Peloponnesians had poisoned the reservoirs
commentary.text: In every epidemic people look for someone to blame. In the Black Death of 1348 it was the Jews; in Athens, the enemy. Thucydides records the rumour without believing it.

commentary.on: All speculation as to its origin and its causes, if causes can be found adequate to produce so great a disturbance, I leave to other writers
commentary.text: This is the method of the last session. He will not guess. He will describe what he knows.

commentary.on: This I can the better do, as I had the disease myself, and watched its operation in the case of others.
commentary.text: The historian as eyewitness and patient. Thucydides writes like the Greek doctors of his day, the school of Hippocrates, whose case notes describe symptoms day by day so that others can recognise a disease.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Dying like sheep
parts.context: Thucydides now describes the disease. It is the most detailed account of an epidemic to survive from the ancient world, and doctors still argue over it. Some of it is hard to read.
parts.plain: People in good health were suddenly struck with burning in the head, red eyes, a bleeding throat, then coughing, vomiting and terrible thirst. They burned inside so that they could not bear clothes. Most died on the seventh or eighth day; those who survived often lost fingers, toes or eyes, or their memory. Even the birds and dogs that ate the dead died. Worst of all was despair, and the infection spreading through those who nursed each other. Those who had recovered were the kindest to the sick, because they could not catch it again.

commentary.on: people in good health were all of a sudden attacked by violent heats in the head, and redness and inflammation in the eyes
commentary.text: Thucydides gives the symptoms in the order they came, from the head downwards, like a doctor's notes. This is why historians of medicine take his account seriously.

commentary.on: plunged into the rain-tanks in their agonies of unquenchable thirst
commentary.text: A detail that brings the horror close: the sick throwing themselves into the water tanks.

commentary.on: By far the most terrible feature in the malady was the dejection which ensued when any one felt himself sickening
commentary.text: Thucydides notices the mind as well as the body. Despair took away the will to live, and killed people faster.

commentary.on: there was the awful spectacle of men dying like sheep, through having caught the infection in nursing each other
commentary.text: Here is the dilemma of every plague. If you stay away, the sick die of neglect. If you nurse them, you may die too. Many houses were emptied 'for want of a nurse'.

commentary.on: This was especially the case with such as made any pretensions to goodness
commentary.text: The best people died first, because their sense of honour made them visit their friends. Thucydides says this without comment, but it is bitter: in the plague, virtue was a death sentence.

commentary.on: Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the dying found most compassion.
commentary.text: One of the first recorded observations of immunity: 'the same man was never attacked twice'. And with it, a human truth. Those who knew suffering from inside were the most compassionate.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Fear of gods or law of man there was none
parts.context: Now Thucydides turns from the disease to what it did to the city. The refugees from the countryside were living in stifling huts. A 'pyre' is a pile of wood for burning a body; the Greeks thought proper burial a sacred duty, and to leave a body unburied was among the worst of crimes, as in Sophocles' Antigone.
parts.plain: The refugees died in huts and in the temples where they camped; bodies lay in heaps. People stopped caring about anything sacred. Burial customs collapsed; people threw their dead on other families' pyres. Then morality went. Seeing the rich die and the poor inherit, people spent fast and lived for pleasure. No one cared about honour, because they might not live to see the reward. No fear of gods or law held them back, because good and bad died alike, and no one expected to live long enough to be tried.

commentary.on: men, not knowing what was to become of them, became utterly careless of everything, whether sacred or profane
commentary.text: This is the turning point of the account. The disease breaks bodies; the fear breaks the moral order.

commentary.on: they threw their own dead body upon the stranger’s pyre and ignited it
commentary.text: For a Greek, this was shocking: the duty to bury one's own dead properly was among the oldest laws there were.

commentary.on: regarding their lives and riches as alike things of a day
commentary.text: If life is short and uncertain, why not take what you can now? It is Solon's insight, that no one controls tomorrow, turned upside down: not 'look to the end' but 'eat, drink, for tomorrow we die' (the phrase Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:32).

commentary.on: Fear of gods or law of man there was none to restrain them.
commentary.text: This is the sentence Thucydides wants us to remember. Two things held Athenian society together: religion and law. Both failed in a few months.

commentary.on: they judged it to be just the same whether they worshipped them or not, as they saw all alike perishing
commentary.text: The Athenians' religion promised that the gods reward the pious. When the pious and the impious died alike, faith in the gods collapsed. Whether a different faith could survive such a test is the question of the comparison.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Dearth or death?
parts.context: Thucydides ends with what people remembered. A 'Dorian war' is a war with the Dorians, the Greek people to whom Sparta belonged. 'Dearth' means famine; in Greek the two words, loimos (plague) and limos (famine), differ by one letter.
parts.plain: The old men remembered a verse that said a Dorian war would bring death. Some said the word had been 'dearth', famine, but in a plague everyone agreed it was 'death'. Thucydides drily remarks that people make their memories fit their sufferings, and that in a future war with a famine, they will remember it the other way. They also recalled that Apollo had promised Sparta his help, and the plague never really reached the Peloponnese.

commentary.on: for the people made their recollection fit in with their sufferings
commentary.text: This is Thucydides at his sharpest. Oracles do not predict events; people remember oracles to fit events. It is the same lesson as the tyrant-slayers in the last session: memory bends to what we want, or fear.

commentary.on: if another Dorian war should ever afterwards come upon us, and a dearth should happen to accompany it, the verse will probably be read accordingly
commentary.text: A historian's joke, and a serious point: prophecy that can be read two ways proves nothing.

commentary.on: With this oracle events were supposed to tally.
commentary.text: Thucydides does not say the gods sent the plague to help Sparta. He says people 'supposed' it. That one word is the whole difference between him and Herodotus.

read.author: Thucydides
read.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
read.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC

paras: To other men the present might not seem to be a suitable time for a festival. Nor indeed is this or any other time suitable for them; neither sorrowful times, nor even such as might be thought especially cheerful. Now, indeed, everything is tears and every one is mourning, and wailings resound daily through the city because of the multitude of the dead and dying.
For as it was written of the firstborn of the Egyptians, so now 'there has arisen a great cry, for there is not a house where there is not one dead.' And would that this were all!

But after both we and they had enjoyed a very brief season of rest this pestilence assailed us; to them more dreadful than any dread, and more intolerable than any other calamity; and, as one of their own writers has said, the only thing which prevails over all hope. But to us this was not so, but no less than the other things was it an exercise and probation. For it did not keep aloof even from us, but the heathen it assailed more severely.

The most of our brethren were unsparing in their exceeding love and brotherly kindness. They held fast to each other and visited the sick fearlessly, and ministered to them continually, serving them in Christ. And they died with them most joyfully, taking the affliction of others, and drawing the sickness from their neighbors to themselves and willingly receiving their pains. And many who cared for the sick and gave strength to others died themselves having transferred to themselves their death. And the popular saying which always seems a mere expression of courtesy, they then made real in action, taking their departure as the others' 'offscouring.'

Truly the best of our brethren departed from life in this manner, including some presbyters and deacons and those of the people who had the highest reputation; so that this form of death, through the great piety and strong faith it exhibited, seemed to lack nothing of martyrdom.

And they took the bodies of the saints in their open hands and in their bosoms, and closed their eyes and their mouths; and they bore them away on their shoulders and laid them out; and they clung to them and embraced them; and they prepared them suitably with washings and garments. And after a little they received like treatment themselves, for the survivors were continually following those who had gone before them.

But with the heathen everything was quite otherwise. They deserted those who began to be sick, and fled from their dearest friends. And they cast them out into the streets when they were half dead, and left the dead like refuse, unburied. They shunned any participation or fellowship with death; which yet, with all their precautions, it was not easy for them to escape.

parts.author: Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius
parts.ref: Dionysius of Alexandria, Festal Letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.22.2–3, 6
parts.title: Everything is tears
parts.context: Dionysius was bishop of Alexandria, the great city of Roman Egypt, from about 248 to 264. Around 260, after persecution, civil war and famine, a great epidemic struck, part of what is called the 'plague of Cyprian' (249–262), after a bishop of Carthage who described it. Each year the bishop wrote a 'festal letter' before Easter, 'the feast'. Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), the first historian of the Church, copied this one into his Church History. This is A. C. McGiffert's translation (1890); New Advent's section numbers and inserted Bible reference have been removed, and the cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Dionysius says: this hardly seems a time for a festival. The city is full of weeping, and there is not a house without its dead, as in Egypt in the time of Moses. The Christians kept Easter even in persecution, in deserts and prisons. Now the plague has come, more terrible to the pagans than anything; to the Christians it is a test, and it struck the pagans harder.

commentary.on: wailings resound daily through the city because of the multitude of the dead and dying
commentary.text: Alexandria, like Athens, is a great city in an epidemic. The scene is the same.

commentary.on: there has arisen a great cry, for there is not a house where there is not one dead
commentary.text: Dionysius quotes Exodus 12:30, the night of the death of the firstborn in Egypt. A Christian bishop reads a plague through the Bible's story, as a Greek historian read it through medicine.

commentary.on: But to us this was not so, but no less than the other things was it an exercise and probation.
commentary.text: The difference begins here. For the Athenians, the plague destroyed their reason for believing: the gods did not reward the pious. For Dionysius, suffering is not a sign that God has failed but a test of faith. Christians had never been promised safety; their Lord had been crucified.

parts.author: Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius
parts.ref: Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Church History VII.22.7–10
parts.title: They visited the sick fearlessly
parts.context: Dionysius now describes what the Christians of Alexandria did. 'Presbyters and deacons' are clergy. 'Offscouring' means filth scraped off: a phrase from 1 Corinthians 4:13, which ordinary people in Alexandria used as a polite way of saying 'your humble servant'. 'The heathen' means pagans.
parts.plain: Most of our people, he says, showed boundless love. They stayed together, visited the sick without fear, nursed them, and caught the disease and died with them. Many of the best, including clergy, died this way, and it was as good as martyrdom. They washed and buried the dead with their own hands. The pagans did the opposite: they pushed away the sick, even their dearest, threw them into the street half dead, and left bodies unburied.

commentary.on: They held fast to each other and visited the sick fearlessly, and ministered to them continually, serving them in Christ.
commentary.text: This is the exact opposite of Thucydides' Athens, where 'they were afraid to visit each other' and houses emptied 'for want of a nurse'. The Christians faced the same dilemma and chose to nurse.

commentary.on: And many who cared for the sick and gave strength to others died themselves having transferred to themselves their death.
commentary.text: Just as in Athens, those who nursed died. Dionysius does not pretend otherwise. What has changed is not the danger but the reason for facing it.

commentary.on: seemed to lack nothing of martyrdom
commentary.text: For a Christian of the 200s, martyrdom, dying for Christ, was the highest honour. Dionysius gives the same honour to dying while nursing the sick. Love of neighbour counts as witness to Christ.

commentary.on: they prepared them suitably with washings and garments
commentary.text: Where Athenians threw their dead on strangers' pyres, Christians washed and dressed theirs. Burial, the oldest duty, was kept.

commentary.on: They deserted those who began to be sick, and fled from their dearest friends.
commentary.text: A bishop praising his own people may exaggerate the pagans' failings. But notice that his description of the pagans is almost exactly Thucydides' description of the Athenians. Fear in a plague does this to anyone, unless something stronger holds them.

compare.author: Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius
compare.ref: Dionysius of Alexandria, Festal Letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.22.2–3, 6
compare.why: Around AD 260, during an epidemic across the Roman Empire, a bishop wrote to his people. Compare how he says Christians and their neighbours behaved with what Thucydides saw in Athens.
compare.title: In a later plague

paras: For two centuries doctors have tried to name the disease from Thucydides' description. Suggestions include smallpox, typhus, measles, bubonic plague and a viral haemorrhagic fever like Ebola. Each fits some symptoms and not others. Thucydides was describing what he saw, not what we would test for, and diseases can change over 2,400 years.

In 1994–95, during building work for the Athens metro, archaeologists found a mass grave in the Kerameikos, the ancient cemetery of Athens, with about 150 bodies thrown in without care, dated to the years of the plague. In 2006 a Greek team led by Manolis Papagrigorakis reported DNA from the teeth matching typhoid fever. Other scientists, such as Beth Shapiro and her colleagues, replied the same year that the DNA evidence was not conclusive and might be contamination. The honest answer is that we do not know. What the grave does show is Thucydides' 'shameless sepultures': bodies dumped in haste, as he said.
sections.key: The disease is still unidentified; a mass grave of the plague years, found in 1994–95, confirms hasty burial, and its DNA suggested typhoid, though that is disputed.

paras: The deepest thing in Thucydides' account is not the medicine but the morals. In a few months, the Athenians, whom Pericles had just praised for their reverence for law and custom, abandoned the sick, threw away the burial rites, spent for pleasure and stopped fearing gods or law. Thucydides says why: when good and bad died alike, there seemed no point in being good; when no one expected to live to be tried, there was no point in obeying the law.

This is a hard lesson. It suggests that Athenian goodness rested on two supports: the belief that the gods reward the pious, and the fear of punishment. Take them away and goodness goes. Thucydides will show the same thing again, in the civil war at Corcyra (III.82), where 'words had to change their ordinary meaning'. For him, civilisation is a thin crust over human nature, and catastrophe breaks it.
sections.key: Athenian goodness rested on belief in divine reward and fear of punishment; when the plague removed both, it collapsed. For Thucydides, civilisation is a thin crust.

paras: Thucydides admired Pericles, and he places the plague straight after the funeral speech, in which Pericles praised the Athenians for their courage, their generosity and their respect for the law, including 'that code which, although unwritten, yet cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace' (II.37). Within a year, that unwritten code was broken everywhere.

The contrast does not mean Pericles was wrong about Athens. It means that ideals need something to hold them up when fear arrives. Pericles himself died of the plague in 429 BC, after trying to steady the people in a speech that admitted the plague was 'the only point indeed at which our calculation has been at fault' (II.64). If you have taken 'Democracy and its dangers', you have seen what happened to Athens without him.
sections.key: Thucydides puts the plague straight after Pericles' praise of Athens' unwritten laws; within a year they were broken. Ideals need something to hold them when fear comes.

paras: Dionysius was a bishop praising his own people, and he may exaggerate both their courage and their neighbours' cowardice. But other evidence agrees. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in the same epidemic, told his people in On Mortality to care for pagans as well as their own. A century later the emperor Julian, who wanted to bring back the old gods, complained in a letter to a pagan high priest that the Christians, whom he called 'Galileans', fed not only their own poor but pagans too, while the pagans neglected their own (Letter to Arsacius, 362).

The sociologist Rodney Stark, in The Rise of Christianity (1996), argued that this care made a measurable difference. Simple nursing, food and water, can greatly reduce deaths in an epidemic. Christians who nursed each other would have survived in larger numbers, and pagans nursed by Christians would have had reason to join them. Stark's numbers are estimates and some historians doubt them, but the pattern Dionysius describes appears in sources hostile to Christians as well as friendly.
sections.key: Cyprian and the hostile emperor Julian confirm that Christians cared for the sick, including pagans; Rodney Stark argues it helped Christianity grow.

paras: Christians in Alexandria faced the same disease and the same dilemma as the Athenians. Why did many respond differently? Dionysius gives his reasons. First, they did not expect God to keep them safe in return for worship, so the plague did not destroy their faith; it was 'an exercise and probation'. Second, they believed death was not the end: the dead were 'perfected' and the martyrs 'feasting in heaven'. Third, they had a command: love your neighbour, which Jesus had illustrated with a man who stopped for a stranger left half dead by the road (Luke 10:30–37).

Thucydides' Athenians had religion and law, both of which depended on reward and punishment in this life. Dionysius' Christians had a love that did not depend on reward, and a hope beyond death. That is not a proof that Christianity is true. But it is evidence for a claim this journey will return to: what people believe about God and death changes how they behave when the crust breaks.
sections.key: Dionysius gives three reasons: Christians expected no safety in return for worship, hoped beyond death, and were commanded to love their neighbour.

paras: Christians have often prayed Psalm 91 in epidemics: 'You shall not be afraid ... of the pestilence that walks in darkness ... A thousand may fall at your side ... but it will not come near you' (91:5–7). Read alone, it might sound like a promise of safety for the faithful, exactly the promise that failed the Athenians. Dionysius' letter shows Christians did not read it that way: they knew that many of their best had died.

In 1527, when plague came to Wittenberg, Martin Luther wrote a letter on whether a Christian may flee. He said yes, unless your duty to your neighbour keeps you: pastors, doctors, officials and anyone caring for the sick must stay. Fear is natural; abandoning those who need you is not. The psalm's promise, in this reading, is that God is with you in the danger, not that the danger will pass you by. Catholic and Orthodox writers in later plagues, such as Charles Borromeo in Milan in 1576, said much the same.
sections.key: Psalm 91 was read in plagues not as a promise of safety but of God's presence; Luther (1527) and Borromeo (1576) told Christians with duties to the sick to stay.

paras: Thucydides wrote his account so that the disease could be recognised if it came again. In a sense, his account of what plague does to people has been recognised in every epidemic since. When plague struck Constantinople in AD 542, the historian Procopius described it in words that deliberately imitate Thucydides. Accounts of the Black Death in 1348, of cholera in the 1800s and of the influenza of 1918 tell of the same things: the sick abandoned, rumours of poisoned water, the dead buried in haste, some people living for pleasure and others giving their lives to nurse strangers.

That is Thucydides' strongest evidence for his claim that human nature does not change. It is also the strongest evidence that it can be transformed: in every one of those epidemics, as in Alexandria, there were people who stayed. Which of the two is the deeper truth about us is a question this journey now faces head on.
sections.key: Later epidemics, from Procopius' Constantinople to 1918, repeat Thucydides' picture, and also Dionysius': the sick abandoned, and the few who stayed.

refs: Thucydides, History II.34–54, 64; III.82, 87, tr. Richard Crawley (1874).
Eusebius, Church History VII.22, tr. A. C. McGiffert (NPNF II.1, 1890); Cyprian, On Mortality (De mortalitate), c. 252; Julian, Letter to Arsacius (Letter 22, 362).

Rodney Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996), ch. 4; Martin Luther, Whether One May Flee from a Deadly Plague (1527).
1 Corinthians 4:13; 15:32; Exodus 12:30; Psalm 91; Luke 10:30–37.

debate.question: What does the plague show about morality?

positions.name: Morality is a thin crust
positions.who: Thucydides; many modern realists and some evolutionary psychologists
positions.view: Human goodness depends on order, reward and the fear of punishment. Remove them, as the plague did, and people revert to self-interest. Civilisation is a fragile achievement, held up by institutions, not by human nature.
positions.evidence: Athens in II.52–53; Corcyra in III.82; the desertion of the sick in many later epidemics.

positions.name: It depends what people believe
positions.who: Dionysius of Alexandria; Christian writers from Cyprian to Luther
positions.view: The Athenians' goodness collapsed because it rested on the hope of reward in this life. A love that does not depend on reward, and a hope beyond death, can hold when everything else fails. The Christians of Alexandria show it.
positions.evidence: Dionysius' letter; Julian's complaint that Christians fed pagans too; Luther's and Borromeo's advice to stay with the sick.

positions.name: It was practical, not only moral
positions.who: Rodney Stark; social historians
positions.view: Christian communities were networks of mutual obligation, and nursing saves lives. Their behaviour in plagues can be explained by social bonds and good results, whatever their beliefs. Belief helped by making the bonds strong.
positions.evidence: Stark's estimates of reduced mortality with basic care; the growth of Christianity after the epidemics of the 160s and 250s.

debate.agree: All agree that the plague of Athens broke both religion and law, and that in later plagues many Christians cared for the sick at the cost of their lives.

look.why: No painting in the gallery shows the plague of Athens. This is a quiet sickroom painted by Gwen John between about 1915 and 1925: a woman recovering. It is the other side of Thucydides' 'those who had recovered', and of every patient whom someone stayed to nurse.
points: A woman sits in a chair, her legs covered by her long, dark blue dress.
She has pale skin and long, dark, straight hair, and looks down at something in her hands that could be a light grey sheet of paper.
A teacup and teapot stand on a table beside her, in the bottom right corner.
Her wooden chair seems to have a cloth or blanket over its back, though the details are hard to make out.
The background is a textured beige with spots of light orange; the paint is laid on in short, thick strokes or dots, and in places the bare canvas shows through.

music.why: The Mass for the dead that Mozart left unfinished when he died in 1791: a requiem for all who die in a plague, and its 'Lacrimosa', a day of weeping, is the sound of a city like Athens or Alexandria in mourning.

think.why: The plague broke the Athenians' faith because they expected the gods to protect the pious. See what Christians believe about suffering instead.

learn.why: The opening of the psalm Christians have prayed in every plague, read not as a promise of safety but of shelter.

check.q: Why does Thucydides describe the symptoms of the plague in such detail?
options: Because he blamed the Spartans
Because he was a doctor by profession
So that it could be recognised if it broke out again, as he says, having had it himself
To frighten his readers
check.why: 'I shall simply set down its nature, and explain the symptoms by which perhaps it may be recognized by the student, if it should ever break out again.' He was a general, not a doctor.

check.q: Why, according to Thucydides, did the Athenians stop fearing the gods?
options: Because they saw the pious and the impious dying alike, so worship seemed to make no difference
Because the temples had been closed by law
Because the Spartans had destroyed the temples
Because philosophers had proved the gods did not exist
check.why: 'They judged it to be just the same whether they worshipped them or not, as they saw all alike perishing.'

check.q: What does Thucydides' remark about 'dearth' and 'death' show?
options: That he did not know Greek well
That the Spartans caused the famine
That the oracle had correctly predicted the plague
That people make their memories of prophecies fit what has happened
check.why: 'The people made their recollection fit in with their sufferings.' An oracle that can be read two ways proves nothing.

check.q: What does the Kerameikos mass grave, found in 1994–95, best support?
options: Thucydides' account of hasty, careless burials in the plague years; the DNA identification of typhoid is disputed
That Thucydides invented the plague
That the disease was certainly typhoid
That the plague killed no one important
check.why: The grave confirms the 'shameless sepultures'; Papagrigorakis's typhoid claim was challenged the same year.

check.q: Dionysius was a bishop praising his own flock. What is the best reason to think his account is not simply propaganda?
options: Eusebius was a pagan
He admits Christians did not die
He was an eyewitness, so he cannot have exaggerated
Other sources, including the hostile emperor Julian a century later, say similar things about Christian care
check.why: He may exaggerate, but Cyprian and especially Julian, who wanted Christianity to fail, confirm the pattern.

check.q: Which best explains, from Dionysius' letter, why the Christians' behaviour held when the Athenians' collapsed?
options: Christians had better doctors
Christians were immune to the disease
Their faith did not promise them safety, they hoped beyond death, and they were commanded to love their neighbour
The plague of Cyprian was milder
check.why: To them the plague was 'an exercise and probation', the dead were 'perfected', and nursing was 'serving them in Christ'. Many Christians died too.

tutorial.question: 'Fear of gods or law of man there was none to restrain them.' What does Thucydides' account of the plague show about what holds a society together?
tutorial.approach: Explain what the plague did, first to bodies and then to morals, and Thucydides' reasons. Show how the account follows Pericles' funeral speech. Then use Dionysius' letter to test Thucydides' claim that human nature does not change: is Christian behaviour in the plague an exception, and if so, why? Weigh the evidence fairly.
strong: Describes Thucydides' method in the plague narrative (eyewitness, symptoms for recognition).
Explains why religion and law collapsed, using II.52–53.
Notes the placement after the funeral speech.
Uses Dionysius accurately, with caution about his bias and the confirming evidence.
Mentions the modern evidence: the Kerameikos grave and the dispute over the disease.
Reaches a reasoned view about what holds a society together.
