sessions.practice: Live it this week: visit, call or write to one person who is ill or housebound, and stay longer than is comfortable. Ask what would actually help, and do it.
sessions.reflect: If everything you rely on were taken away for a month, what would still make you good to other people?
takeaways: Thucydides described the plague of 430 BC as an eyewitness and patient, and showed how fast religion and law collapsed when good and bad died alike.
The disease is still unidentified; a mass grave of the plague years confirms the hasty burials he describes.
In a later plague, Dionysius describes Christians nursing the sick and burying the dead at the cost of their lives, for reasons that did not depend on safety; hostile witnesses agree.

sessions.title: The case against: the strong do what they can
sessions.line: Athens sends an army to a small neutral island and tells its leaders, in a private meeting, that justice is only for equals. The islanders appeal to justice, the gods and hope. Then the Athenians kill the men and sell the women and children.
sessions.plain: In 416 BC Athens wanted the island of Melos, which had stayed out of the war. Before attacking, the Athenian envoys met the island's leaders, and Thucydides gives their conversation as a dialogue. The Athenians say plainly that justice only matters between equals: 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must'. The Melians appeal to fairness, to the gods and to hope. They refuse to surrender, and they are destroyed. This session states, at full strength, the hardest objection to everything this journey has suggested: that history is only the story of power.
sessions.why: The last session showed that when catastrophe struck Athens, its religion and law collapsed, and that people behaved well in a later plague for reasons that did not depend on reward. Now Thucydides goes further. At Melos, Athens is not breaking down in panic. It is calm, and it gives reasons for doing whatever it likes. If the strong are right, then justice, the gods and the hopes of the weak are illusions. We must hear that case at its strongest before we can answer it.
answers: What is the Melian dialogue?
Is might right?
What is political realism?
Who wins the Melian dialogue?
What did the Bible's prophets say about empires?
sessions.finding: At Melos, Athens told a small neutral island that justice exists only between equals and that hope and the gods are no defence; Thucydides gives power's case at full strength, and then shows its result, and lets the reader judge.

paras: In 421 BC Athens and Sparta made peace, but it did not hold. Athens, its empire intact, looked for ways to extend its power. Most of the islands of the Aegean Sea were already its subject allies, paying tribute. Melos, a small island in the south-western Aegean, was not.

The Melians were Dorians, settled from Sparta, Thucydides says, 'seven hundred years' before. They had stayed neutral at the start of the war. In 426 BC the Athenian general Nicias had ravaged their land without taking the city (III.91). An Athenian inscription of 425 BC listing what each ally must pay assesses Melos at fifteen talents, a large sum, though there is no sign it was ever paid. After the attacks, Thucydides says, the Melians 'assumed an attitude of open hostility'.
background.key: Melos, a Dorian island settled from Sparta, had stayed out of Athens' empire; Athens had attacked it in 426 BC and assessed it for tribute in 425 BC.

paras: In the summer of 416 BC, Athens sent thirty-eight ships and over 3,000 soldiers. Before attacking, the generals sent envoys to talk. The Melian leaders met them privately, not before the people. Thucydides writes the meeting as a dialogue, the only one in his history, with speakers named only 'Athenians' and 'Melians'. No one else recorded it, and Thucydides was in exile; this is his reconstruction of what he believed was said, by his own rule of what the occasion 'demanded'.

The Melians refused to give in. The Athenians besieged the city through the winter. When it fell, by treachery inside, they killed every grown man they captured, sold the women and children as slaves, and sent 500 Athenian settlers to live on the island.

timeline.text: Nicias ravages Melos
Athens assesses Melos for tribute
The Peace of Nicias
The Athenians land; the dialogue
Melos falls; the men are killed, the women and children enslaved
Euripides' The Trojan Women; the Sicilian expedition sails

background.key: In 416 BC Athens besieged Melos; when it fell, the men were killed and the women and children sold. The dialogue is Thucydides' reconstruction.

paras: So far this journey has suggested that history has a moral shape: that pride goes before a fall, that free people under law are stronger than slaves, that a love that does not depend on reward can hold when everything else breaks. The Athenians at Melos say the opposite. There is no moral order. Justice is a word the weak use. The gods, if they exist, are on the side of the strong. History is the story of power, and nothing else.

This is not a straw man. It has been held by serious thinkers in every age: in Thucydides' own time by the sophists Thrasymachus and Callicles, whom Plato set out to refute; later by Machiavelli and Hobbes; in our own time by many students of international politics. Read it as its defenders would want it read: not as cynicism but as honesty.
background.key: The Athenians argue there is no moral order in history, only power; this view has been held seriously from Thrasymachus to modern realists.

paras: The main reading is the whole Melian dialogue and its end (V.84–116), in five parts: the setting; the Athenians' first principle; whether neutrality is possible; the appeal to hope and the gods; the end of Melos.
The comparison is from the prophet Isaiah, about three hundred years earlier, speaking of Assyria, the superpower of his day, which boasted, like Athens, 'By the strength of my hand I have done it'.
background.key: The whole Melian dialogue in five parts; then Isaiah on the boast of Assyria.

before: What do the Athenians refuse to talk about, and why?
What does 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must' actually claim?
What three things do the Melians trust in, and what do the Athenians say about each?
sessions.readWhy: The Melian dialogue: the strongest statement in ancient literature of the case that power, not justice, rules history.

paras: The next summer Alcibiades sailed with twenty ships to Argos and seized the suspected persons still left of the Lacedaemonian faction to the number of three hundred, whom the Athenians forthwith lodged in the neighbouring islands of their empire. The Athenians also made an expedition against the isle of Melos with thirty ships of their own, six Chian, and two Lesbian vessels, sixteen hundred heavy infantry, three hundred archers, and twenty mounted archers from Athens, and about fifteen hundred heavy infantry from the allies and the islanders. The Melians are a colony of Lacedaemon that would not submit to the Athenians like the other islanders, and at first remained neutral and took no part in the struggle, but afterwards upon the Athenians using violence and plundering their territory, assumed an attitude of open hostility. Cleomedes, son of Lycomedes, and Tisias, son of Tisimachus, the generals, encamping in their territory with the above armament, before doing any harm to their land, sent envoys to negotiate. These the Melians did not bring before the people, but bade them state the object of their mission to the magistrates and the few; upon which the Athenian envoys spoke as follows:

Athenians. Since the negotiations are not to go on before the people, in order that we may not be able to speak straight on without interruption, and deceive the ears of the multitude by seductive arguments which would pass without refutation (for we know that this is the meaning of our being brought before the few), what if you who sit there were to pursue a method more cautious still? Make no set speech yourselves, but take us up at whatever you do not like, and settle that before going any farther. And first tell us if this proposition of ours suits you.
The Melian commissioners answered:

Melians. To the fairness of quietly instructing each other as you propose there is nothing to object; but your military preparations are too far advanced to agree with what you say, as we see you are come to be judges in your own cause, and that all we can reasonably expect from this negotiation is war, if we prove to have right on our side and refuse to submit, and in the contrary case, slavery.

Athenians. If you have met to reason about presentiments of the future, or for anything else than to consult for the safety of your state upon the facts that you see before you, we will give over; otherwise we will go on.

Melians. It is natural and excusable for men in our position to turn more ways than one both in thought and utterance. However, the question in this conference is, as you say, the safety of our country; and the discussion, if you please, can proceed in the way which you propose.

Athenians. For ourselves, we shall not trouble you with specious pretences—either of how we have a right to our empire because we overthrew the Mede, or are now attacking you because of wrong that you have done us—and make a long speech which would not be believed; and in return we hope that you, instead of thinking to influence us by saying that you did not join the Lacedaemonians, although their colonists, or that you have done us no wrong, will aim at what is feasible, holding in view the real sentiments of us both; since you know as well as we do that right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

Melians. As we think, at any rate, it is expedient—we speak as we are obliged, since you enjoin us to let right alone and talk only of interest—that you should not destroy what is our common protection, the privilege of being allowed in danger to invoke what is fair and right, and even to profit by arguments not strictly valid if they can be got to pass current. And you are as much interested in this as any, as your fall would be a signal for the heaviest vengeance and an example for the world to meditate upon.

Athenians. The end of our empire, if end it should, does not frighten us: a rival empire like Lacedaemon, even if Lacedaemon was our real antagonist, is not so terrible to the vanquished as subjects who by themselves attack and overpower their rulers. This, however, is a risk that we are content to take. We will now proceed to show you that we are come here in the interest of our empire, and that we shall say what we are now going to say, for the preservation of your country; as we would fain exercise that empire over you without trouble, and see you preserved for the good of us both.
Melians. And how, pray, could it turn out as good for us to serve as for you to rule?
Athenians. Because you would have the advantage of submitting before suffering the worst, and we should gain by not destroying you.
Melians. So that you would not consent to our being neutral, friends instead of enemies, but allies of neither side.
Athenians. No; for your hostility cannot so much hurt us as your friendship will be an argument to our subjects of our weakness, and your enmity of our power.
Melians. Is that your subjects’ idea of equity, to put those who have nothing to do with you in the same category with peoples that are most of them your own colonists, and some conquered rebels?

Athenians. As far as right goes they think one has as much of it as the other, and that if any maintain their independence it is because they are strong, and that if we do not molest them it is because we are afraid; so that besides extending our empire we should gain in security by your subjection; the fact that you are islanders and weaker than others rendering it all the more important that you should not succeed in baffling the masters of the sea.

Melians. But do you consider that there is no security in the policy which we indicate? For here again if you debar us from talking about justice and invite us to obey your interest, we also must explain ours, and try to persuade you, if the two happen to coincide. How can you avoid making enemies of all existing neutrals who shall look at case from it that one day or another you will attack them? And what is this but to make greater the enemies that you have already, and to force others to become so who would otherwise have never thought of it?

Athenians. Why, the fact is that continentals generally give us but little alarm; the liberty which they enjoy will long prevent their taking precautions against us; it is rather islanders like yourselves, outside our empire, and subjects smarting under the yoke, who would be the most likely to take a rash step and lead themselves and us into obvious danger.

Melians. Well then, if you risk so much to retain your empire, and your subjects to get rid of it, it were surely great baseness and cowardice in us who are still free not to try everything that can be tried, before submitting to your yoke.

Athenians. Not if you are well advised, the contest not being an equal one, with honour as the prize and shame as the penalty, but a question of self-preservation and of not resisting those who are far stronger than you are.

Melians. But we know that the fortune of war is sometimes more impartial than the disproportion of numbers might lead one to suppose; to submit is to give ourselves over to despair, while action still preserves for us a hope that we may stand erect.

Athenians. Hope, danger’s comforter, may be indulged in by those who have abundant resources, if not without loss at all events without ruin; but its nature is to be extravagant, and those who go so far as to put their all upon the venture see it in its true colours only when they are ruined; but so long as the discovery would enable them to guard against it, it is never found wanting. Let not this be the case with you, who are weak and hang on a single turn of the scale; nor be like the vulgar, who, abandoning such security as human means may still afford, when visible hopes fail them in extremity, turn to invisible, to prophecies and oracles, and other such inventions that delude men with hopes to their destruction.

Melians. You may be sure that we are as well aware as you of the difficulty of contending against your power and fortune, unless the terms be equal. But we trust that the gods may grant us fortune as good as yours, since we are just men fighting against unjust, and that what we want in power will be made up by the alliance of the Lacedaemonians, who are bound, if only for very shame, to come to the aid of their kindred. Our confidence, therefore, after all is not so utterly irrational.

Athenians. When you speak of the favour of the gods, we may as fairly hope for that as yourselves; neither our pretensions nor our conduct being in any way contrary to what men believe of the gods, or practise among themselves. Of the gods we believe, and of men we know, that by a necessary law of their nature they rule wherever they can. And it is not as if we were the first to make this law, or to act upon it when made: we found it existing before us, and shall leave it to exist for ever after us; all we do is to make use of it, knowing that you and everybody else, having the same power as we have, would do the same as we do. Thus, as far as the gods are concerned, we have no fear and no reason to fear that we shall be at a disadvantage. But when we come to your notion about the Lacedaemonians, which leads you to believe that shame will make them help you, here we bless your simplicity but do not envy your folly. The Lacedaemonians, when their own interests or their country’s laws are in question, are the worthiest men alive; of their conduct towards others much might be said, but no clearer idea of it could be given than by shortly saying that of all the men we know they are most conspicuous in considering what is agreeable honourable, and what is expedient just. Such a way of thinking does not promise much for the safety which you now unreasonably count upon.

Melians. But it is for this very reason that we now trust to their respect for expediency to prevent them from betraying the Melians, their colonists, and thereby losing the confidence of their friends in Hellas and helping their enemies.

Athenians. Then you do not adopt the view that expediency goes with security, while justice and honour cannot be followed without danger; and danger the Lacedaemonians generally court as little as possible.

Melians. But we believe that they would be more likely to face even danger for our sake, and with more confidence than for others, as our nearness to Peloponnese makes it easier for them to act, and our common blood ensures our fidelity.

Athenians. Yes, but what an intending ally trusts to is not the goodwill of those who ask his aid, but a decided superiority of power for action; and the Lacedaemonians look to this even more than others. At least, such is their distrust of their home resources that it is only with numerous allies that they attack a neighbour; now is it likely that while we are masters of the sea they will cross over to an island?

Melians. But they would have others to send. The Cretan Sea is a wide one, and it is more difficult for those who command it to intercept others, than for those who wish to elude them to do so safely. And should the Lacedaemonians miscarry in this, they would fall upon your land, and upon those left of your allies whom Brasidas did not reach; and instead of places which are not yours, you will have to fight for your own country and your own confederacy.

Athenians. Some diversion of the kind you speak of you may one day experience, only to learn, as others have done, that the Athenians never once yet withdrew from a siege for fear of any. But we are struck by the fact that, after saying you would consult for the safety of your country, in all this discussion you have mentioned nothing which men might trust in and think to be saved by. Your strongest arguments depend upon hope and the future, and your actual resources are too scanty, as compared with those arrayed against you, for you to come out victorious. You will therefore show great blindness of judgment, unless, after allowing us to retire, you can find some counsel more prudent than this. You will surely not be caught by that idea of disgrace, which in dangers that are disgraceful, and at the same time too plain to be mistaken, proves so fatal to mankind;

since in too many cases the very men that have their eyes perfectly open to what they are rushing into, let the thing called disgrace, by the mere influence of a seductive name, lead them on to a point at which they become so enslaved by the phrase as in fact to fall wilfully into hopeless disaster, and incur disgrace more disgraceful as the companion of error, than when it comes as the result of misfortune. This, if you are well advised, you will guard against; and you will not think it dishonourable to submit to the greatest city in Hellas, when it makes you the moderate offer of becoming its tributary ally, without ceasing to enjoy the country that belongs to you; nor when you have the choice given you between war and security, will you be so blinded as to choose the worse. And it is certain that those who do not yield to their equals, who keep terms with their superiors, and are moderate towards their inferiors, on the whole succeed best. Think over the matter, therefore, after our withdrawal, and reflect once and again that it is for your country that you are consulting, that you have not more than one, and that upon this one deliberation depends its prosperity or ruin.

The Athenians now withdrew from the conference; and the Melians, left to themselves, came to a decision corresponding with what they had maintained in the discussion, and answered: “Our resolution, Athenians, is the same as it was at first. We will not in a moment deprive of freedom a city that has been inhabited these seven hundred years; but we put our trust in the fortune by which the gods have preserved it until now, and in the help of men, that is, of the Lacedaemonians; and so we will try and save ourselves. Meanwhile we invite you to allow us to be friends to you and foes to neither party, and to retire from our country after making such a treaty as shall seem fit to us both.”

Such was the answer of the Melians. The Athenians now departing from the conference said: “Well, you alone, as it seems to us, judging from these resolutions, regard what is future as more certain than what is before your eyes, and what is out of sight, in your eagerness, as already coming to pass; and as you have staked most on, and trusted most in, the Lacedaemonians, your fortune, and your hopes, so will you be most completely deceived.”

The Athenian envoys now returned to the army; and the Melians showing no signs of yielding, the generals at once betook themselves to hostilities, and drew a line of circumvallation round the Melians, dividing the work among the different states. Subsequently the Athenians returned with most of their army, leaving behind them a certain number of their own citizens and of the allies to keep guard by land and sea. The force thus left stayed on and besieged the place.

About the same time the Argives invaded the territory of Phlius and lost eighty men cut off in an ambush by the Phliasians and Argive exiles. Meanwhile the Athenians at Pylos took so much plunder from the Lacedaemonians that the latter, although they still refrained from breaking off the treaty and going to war with Athens, yet proclaimed that any of their people that chose might plunder the Athenians. The Corinthians also commenced hostilities with the Athenians for private quarrels of their own; but the rest of the Peloponnesians stayed quiet. Meanwhile the Melians attacked by night and took the part of the Athenian lines over against the market, and killed some of the men, and brought in corn and all else that they could find useful to them, and so returned and kept quiet, while the Athenians took measures to keep better guard in future.

Summer was now over. The next winter the Lacedaemonians intended to invade the Argive territory, but arriving at the frontier found the sacrifices for crossing unfavourable, and went back again. This intention of theirs gave the Argives suspicions of certain of their fellow citizens, some of whom they arrested; others, however, escaped them. About the same time the Melians again took another part of the Athenian lines which were but feebly garrisoned. Reinforcements afterwards arriving from Athens in consequence, under the command of Philocrates, son of Demeas, the siege was now pressed vigorously; and some treachery taking place inside, the Melians surrendered at discretion to the Athenians, who put to death all the grown men whom they took, and sold the women and children for slaves, and subsequently sent out five hundred colonists and inhabited the place themselves.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Not before the people
parts.context: Summer 416 BC. The reading opens with a sentence on another raid that summer, by Alcibiades, an ambitious young Athenian general. Then the Athenian generals Cleomedes and Tisias land on Melos. 'Lacedaemon' is Sparta. 'The few' are the island's ruling council; the Melians, like many small states, were governed by an oligarchy, a council of leading families.
parts.plain: Athens sends a large force to Melos. The Melian leaders will not let the Athenian envoys speak to the people, only to the council. The Athenians suggest a dialogue instead of speeches. The Melians agree, but point out that the Athenian army is already here: if they win the argument they will get war, and if they lose it, slavery. The Athenians say: talk about your safety, or we stop now.

commentary.on: These the Melians did not bring before the people
commentary.text: A detail with a sting. The Athenians come from a democracy; the Melian rulers will not let their own people hear. Each side may have its reasons: the Athenians suspect the council fears its people will give in.

commentary.on: you are come to be judges in your own cause
commentary.text: The Melians name the problem at once. This is not a negotiation between equals. One side has an army on the beach. A judge in his own cause is no judge at all.

commentary.on: all we can reasonably expect from this negotiation is war, if we prove to have right on our side and refuse to submit, and in the contrary case, slavery
commentary.text: The choice is set out with complete clarity: be right and die, or be wrong and be enslaved.

commentary.on: or for anything else than to consult for the safety of your state upon the facts that you see before you
commentary.text: The Athenians set the rules: only facts, only safety. No talk of the future, of hopes, of rights.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Right is only between equals
parts.context: This is the most famous passage in Thucydides. The Athenians refuse to justify their empire with fine words (that they earned it by beating the Persians, the 'Mede') and ask the Melians not to plead that they have done nothing wrong. Then they state their principle.
parts.plain: The Athenians say: we will not pretend we have a right to our empire, or that you have wronged us, and you should not plead that you have done us no harm. Let us both be realistic. You know as well as we do that justice only comes into question between equals in power; otherwise, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. The Melians answer: then it is in your interest too to keep fairness alive, because one day you may fall and need it. The Athenians reply that they are willing to take that risk.

commentary.on: we shall not trouble you with specious pretences
commentary.text: This is what makes the Athenians frightening and, in a strange way, admirable. They do not lie. Every empire has claimed to be bringing order, civilisation or freedom. The Athenians say: we want your island because we can take it.

commentary.on: right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must
commentary.text: Here is the sentence. Notice exactly what it says. It does not say that might makes right. It says that questions of right only arise between parties who are equal enough to make each other listen. Between the strong and the weak there are no rights, only outcomes. That is the claim this session must weigh.

commentary.on: that you should not destroy what is our common protection, the privilege of being allowed in danger to invoke what is fair and right
commentary.text: The Melians' first reply is clever. They do not argue from justice, since that has been ruled out. They argue from Athens' interest: one day you too may be weak, and you will want fairness to exist.

commentary.on: your fall would be a signal for the heaviest vengeance and an example for the world to meditate upon
commentary.text: Thucydides' readers knew Athens did fall, in 404 BC, and that its enemies proposed doing to Athens exactly what Athens did to Melos (Xenophon, Hellenica II.2.19–20). The Melians' warning is a prophecy.

commentary.on: This, however, is a risk that we are content to take.
commentary.text: The Athenians answer coolly. Power accepts risk; that is what power is.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: No room for neutrals
parts.context: The argument turns to whether Melos could stay neutral. The 'subjects' are the islands already in Athens' empire; 'continentals' are cities on the mainland, out of reach of Athens' fleet.
parts.plain: Why would it be good for us to serve you? Because you would avoid the worst, and we would gain by not destroying you. Can we not stay neutral? No: your friendship would make us look weak to our subjects, your hatred would make us look strong. You will make enemies of every other neutral. We are not afraid of mainland cities, only of islands like you. Then surely we would be cowards not to fight for our freedom? Not if you are sensible: this is not a contest of honour but of survival, against a far stronger power.

commentary.on: And how, pray, could it turn out as good for us to serve as for you to rule?
commentary.text: A simple question that every subject people has asked. The Athenians' answer is only that submission is better than destruction.

commentary.on: your hostility cannot so much hurt us as your friendship will be an argument to our subjects of our weakness, and your enmity of our power
commentary.text: The logic of empire. Melos is no threat. But an empire depends on looking strong. If a small island can stay free, others will ask why they cannot. So Melos must be crushed not for what it has done but for what it shows.

commentary.on: if any maintain their independence it is because they are strong, and that if we do not molest them it is because we are afraid
commentary.text: In this world, every act of restraint is read as weakness. It is the reasoning of every arms race and every gang.

commentary.on: it were surely great baseness and cowardice in us who are still free not to try everything that can be tried, before submitting to your yoke
commentary.text: The Melians speak the language of Thermopylae: free men do not surrender. Herodotus' Greeks said it to Persia. Now Greeks hear it from Greeks.

commentary.on: the contest not being an equal one, with honour as the prize and shame as the penalty, but a question of self-preservation
commentary.text: The Athenians' reply is the hardest sentence for anyone who loves the story of Thermopylae. Honour is for equals. When you cannot win, the wise course is to survive.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Hope, the gods and Sparta
parts.context: The Melians now turn to the three things they trust: hope, the gods and their kinsmen the Spartans. 'Brasidas' was the Spartan general who had taken several of Athens' allies in the north, including Amphipolis, which Thucydides himself had failed to save.
parts.plain: The Melians: the fortunes of war are sometimes even, and while we fight there is hope. The Athenians: hope is a luxury for those who can afford to lose; the weak who stake everything on it see what it is only when they are ruined; do not turn to oracles. The Melians: the gods will help us, because we are just and you are not, and Sparta will help its kin. The Athenians: we expect the gods' favour as much as you, because gods and men alike rule wherever they can, by a law of nature that we did not make; and Sparta only helps when it is safe. You have offered nothing but hope. Do not be destroyed by the word 'disgrace'. Submit to the greatest city in Greece; it is no shame.

commentary.on: Hope, danger’s comforter, may be indulged in by those who have abundant resources
commentary.text: The Athenians' speech on hope is one of the bleakest passages in Greek. Hope, they say, is for the rich; the poor who live on it are destroyed by it.

commentary.on: turn to invisible, to prophecies and oracles, and other such inventions that delude men with hopes to their destruction
commentary.text: The voice is very close to Thucydides' own, which mocked the oracle about 'dearth' and 'death' in the plague. Some readers think this is why the Athenians' case is so strong: Thucydides half agreed with it.

commentary.on: since we are just men fighting against unjust
commentary.text: The Melians' appeal to the gods rests on an old Greek belief, the one that failed the Athenians in the plague: the gods help the just.

commentary.on: Of the gods we believe, and of men we know, that by a necessary law of their nature they rule wherever they can.
commentary.text: This is the Athenians' deepest claim. It is not that they are wicked; it is that ruling is what all beings do, gods and men alike. They did not make this law; they found it, and anyone in their place would act the same. If that is true, there is no one to appeal to.

commentary.on: of all the men we know they are most conspicuous in considering what is agreeable honourable, and what is expedient just
commentary.text: The Athenians are cynical about everyone. The Spartans, they say, call 'just' whatever suits them. They were right: no Spartan help came.

commentary.on: you have mentioned nothing which men might trust in and think to be saved by
commentary.text: From the Athenians' point of view, the Melians have offered nothing real: only hope, gods and allies who will not come.

commentary.on: those who do not yield to their equals, who keep terms with their superiors, and are moderate towards their inferiors, on the whole succeed best
commentary.text: The Athenians end with a rule of prudence that sounds almost reasonable. Within months they will break the third part of it themselves.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: The end of Melos
parts.context: The envoys leave so the Melians can decide. The Melian answer is the last word spoken by Melos in history. Thucydides interleaves the siege with other events of the year; 'circumvallation' means a wall built round a city to besiege it.
parts.plain: The Melians answer: we will not give up in a moment the freedom of a city seven hundred years old. We trust in the fortune of the gods and in the Spartans. We offer to be your friends and enemies to neither side. The Athenians reply that the Melians alone think the future more certain than what is in front of them, and will be the most completely deceived. The siege goes on through the winter. The Melians fight back twice, but at last, betrayed from within, they surrender. The Athenians kill all the grown men, sell the women and children as slaves, and settle the island themselves.

commentary.on: We will not in a moment deprive of freedom a city that has been inhabited these seven hundred years
commentary.text: The Melians' last word is about time. A city is not just its present strength; it is seven centuries of people. They will not end it in a day.

commentary.on: you alone, as it seems to us, judging from these resolutions, regard what is future as more certain than what is before your eyes
commentary.text: The Athenians' last word is about sight. Trust what you can see. It is, in a way, Thucydides' own method: the clearest data, not romance. That is what makes the dialogue so uncomfortable.

commentary.on: the Melians surrendered at discretion to the Athenians, who put to death all the grown men whom they took, and sold the women and children for slaves
commentary.text: Thucydides tells it in one flat sentence, without comment. That is his comment. He has given the Athenians every argument; now he shows what the arguments were for.

paras: Alas Assyrian, the rod of my anger, the staff in whose hand is my indignation!
I will send him against a profane nation, and against the people who anger me I will give him a command to take the plunder and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets.
However he doesn’t mean so, neither does his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off not a few nations.
For he says, “Aren’t all of my princes kings?
Isn’t Calno like Carchemish? Isn’t Hamath like Arpad? Isn’t Samaria like Damascus?”
As my hand has found the kingdoms of the idols, whose engraved images exceeded those of Jerusalem and of Samaria;
shall I not, as I have done to Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols?

Therefore it will happen that when the Lord has performed his whole work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the willful proud heart of the king of Assyria, and the insolence of his arrogant looks.

For he has said, “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I have understanding. I have removed the boundaries of the peoples, and have robbed their treasures. Like a valiant man I have brought down their rulers.

My hand has found the riches of the peoples like a nest, and like one gathers eggs that are abandoned, I have gathered all the earth. There was no one who moved their wing, or that opened their mouth, or chirped.”

Should an ax brag against him who chops with it? Should a saw exalt itself above him who saws with it? As if a rod should lift those who lift it up, or as if a staff should lift up someone who is not wood.

parts.title: Assyria, the rod of my anger
parts.context: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC, while Assyria conquered one small kingdom after another: Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Damascus and Samaria, all named here. In 701 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem itself. The prophet speaks for God.

commentary.on: Alas Assyrian, the rod of my anger
commentary.text: Isaiah agrees with the Athenians about one thing: Assyria is strong, and the small nations will fall to it. He even says God is using it to punish his own people's injustice. He does not deny power.

commentary.on: However he doesn’t mean so, neither does his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy
commentary.text: But the empire does not know what it is for. It thinks it is acting for itself, 'to destroy'. For Isaiah, every empire is inside a story larger than its own.

commentary.on: By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom
commentary.text: This is Assyria's version of 'the strong do what they can'. There is no one above me; I did it myself.

commentary.on: I will punish the fruit of the willful proud heart of the king of Assyria
commentary.text: Here Isaiah and the Athenians part completely. For the Athenians, there is no one to punish the strong. For Isaiah, there is: the God who judges the nations. Hybris meets not envious gods but justice.

commentary.on: Should an ax brag against him who chops with it?
commentary.text: One of the great images of the Bible. An empire is a tool, an axe or a saw. It has no reason to boast. Assyria fell to Babylon in 612 BC, little more than a century after it destroyed Samaria.

compare.why: About 300 years before Melos, Assyria was the superpower of the ancient Near East. It destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC. Isaiah, a prophet in Jerusalem, answered its boast. Compare his view of power with the Athenians'.
compare.title: The axe that boasts

paras: Let us state the Athenian case as its best defenders would. First: in relations between peoples, there is no court, no police and no judge. Each must look after itself. Second: in that condition, justice can only exist between those strong enough to make each other keep agreements. Between the strong and the weak, there are only interests and outcomes. Third: this is not wickedness but nature. 'Of the gods we believe, and of men we know' that all rule where they can. Anyone in Athens' place would do the same.

Fourth: honesty is better than hypocrisy. The Athenians refuse 'specious pretences'. Every empire claims to be bringing peace or freedom; Athens at least tells the truth. Fifth: hope and the gods are dangerous. They led the Melians to destruction when submission would have saved their lives. The kindest thing to say to the weak is: do not fight a battle you cannot win. On this view, history is the record of power, and morality is what the powerful allow.
sections.key: The Athenian case: there is no judge between peoples; justice exists only between equals; ruling is nature, not wickedness; honesty beats hypocrisy; hope destroys the weak.

paras: The Athenians' view was not peculiar to Athens. In Plato's Republic, written perhaps thirty years later, the sophist Thrasymachus says that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger' (Republic I, 338c). In the Gorgias, Callicles argues that nature itself shows it is just for the stronger and better to have more than the weaker (483d), and points to Xerxes as an example. Plato wrote those dialogues to answer them, and if you take 'Plato' later in this hall you will see how.

In the Renaissance, Niccolò Machiavelli's The Prince (1513) told rulers that a prince who wants to survive must learn to do wrong when necessity demands it (ch. 15). Thomas Hobbes, who translated Thucydides into English in 1629, argued in Leviathan (1651) that without a common power to keep them in awe, people are in a war of all against all, where 'The notions of Right and Wrong, Justice and Injustice have there no place' (ch. 13). Melos was his example before he had a theory.
sections.key: Thrasymachus and Callicles in Plato, Machiavelli and Hobbes all argued versions of the Athenian case: justice is the interest of the stronger, or does not exist without a power to enforce it.

paras: In the 20th century, the Athenians' view became a school of thought in the study of international relations, called realism. Hans Morgenthau's Politics Among Nations (1948) argued that states always pursue power, and statesmen must think in terms of interest, not moral ideals. Kenneth Waltz's Theory of International Politics (1979) said that because there is no world government, states must arm and ally to survive, whatever they believe. Students of international relations in many universities still read the Melian dialogue in their first term.

Realists are not usually cynics. Many argue that realism prevents wars: that crusades for justice abroad cause more suffering than a sober balance of power. Morgenthau opposed the Vietnam War on realist grounds. Their challenge to everyone else is serious: if you think justice should rule between nations, who will enforce it, and at what cost?
sections.key: Modern realism (Morgenthau 1948, Waltz 1979) holds that states pursue power because there is no world government; many realists argue this prevents wars.

paras: Now the Melians, at their strongest. First: fairness is a 'common protection' even for the strong, because fortunes change; an empire that abolishes justice will have none when it falls. They were right about that: when Athens lost in 404 BC, Corinth and Thebes proposed to destroy it as Athens destroyed Melos, and Sparta refused (Xenophon, Hellenica II.2.19–20).

Second: freedom is worth dying for. A city of seven hundred years is not just its population today. Third: hope and the gods. The Athenians call hope a luxury, and in this case they were right, because no help came. But the Melians' reply raises a question the Athenians cannot answer. If 'ruling wherever they can' is the law of nature for gods and men, why did Herodotus' free Greeks at Thermopylae, and the Melians themselves, choose to die rather than submit? Something in human beings refuses the law the Athenians found, and that refusal is as much a fact of history as power.
sections.key: The Melians argued that fairness protects the strong when they fall, that freedom is worth dying for, and that hope and the gods are real; the first proved true in 404 BC.

paras: Thucydides never tells us who won. He gives the Athenians the better arguments and the Melians the last word, and then reports the massacre in one flat sentence. Readers have taken him both ways. Hobbes and many realists think he agreed with the Athenians: he describes the world as it is. Others, such as the French scholar Jacqueline de Romilly in Thucydides and Athenian Imperialism (1947), think he shows imperial reasoning leading to its own ruin.

The best evidence is where he put it. The very next chapter begins Book VI: the same winter, the Athenians decide to conquer Sicily, an island much bigger than Melos, 'ignorant of its size' (VI.1). That expedition, as the next session shows, ended in disaster. Many readers think Thucydides placed Melos there deliberately, like a scene before the fall in a tragedy. In spring 415 BC, Euripides staged The Trojan Women in Athens, about the women of a conquered city waiting to be carried off as slaves. Some think it was a response to Melos; we cannot be sure.
sections.key: Thucydides does not say who won, but he places Melos straight before the decision to invade Sicily, as if before a fall; Euripides' Trojan Women followed within months.

paras: Isaiah gives a third answer, different from both the Athenians and the Melians. He agrees with the Athenians that the strong win: Assyria will take Samaria and threaten Jerusalem. He does not tell the weak that their gods will save them. But he denies the Athenians' central claim: that there is no one above the strong. 'Should an ax brag against him who chops with it?' Empires are instruments in a larger history, and they are judged by the God who 'will judge between the nations' (Isaiah 2:4).

This is why the Bible's history is so full of the weak: widows, orphans, strangers, slaves in Egypt, a small nation between empires. The prophets insist that the God of history sees those whom the strong do not count. If that is true, then the Melians were not wrong to appeal to justice, even though they were wrong about Sparta. If it is false, the Athenians win. Whether it is true is not a question Thucydides can answer, and it is the question the last session takes up.
sections.key: Isaiah agrees the strong win but denies there is no one above them: empires are tools, judged by God, who sees the weak whom the strong do not count.

paras: The Greeks themselves did not forget Melos. About forty years later, the Athenian orator Isocrates, praising Athens' old empire in his Panegyricus (around 380 BC), felt he had to answer the charge that Athens had treated Melos harshly, and argued that it had only punished those who made war on it (Panegyricus 100–102). Its enemies used Melos against it; its defenders had to explain it away.

Melos became a byword for what power does when no one can stop it. The very fact that Athens' defenders needed excuses is evidence against the Athenians' claim. If justice were only a word the weak use, no one would have needed to justify what happened. The strong, too, want to be thought just. That is a small point, but it is where every answer to the Athenians begins.
sections.key: Athens' defenders, like Isocrates, felt bound to excuse Melos: even the strong want to be thought just, which is where every answer to the Athenians begins.

refs: Thucydides, History III.91; V.84–116; VI.1, tr. Richard Crawley (1874); Inscriptiones Graecae I³ 71 (the assessment of 425 BC, listing Melos).
Xenophon, Hellenica II.2.19–20; Euripides, The Trojan Women (415 BC).

debate.question: Who wins the Melian dialogue?

positions.name: The Athenians
positions.who: Thomas Hobbes; Hans Morgenthau and the realist school; many readers who see Thucydides as a clear-eyed analyst
positions.view: The Athenians tell the truth about how the world works. The Melians' appeals to justice, the gods and hope were empty, as events proved. Their leaders' refusal to face facts cost their people their lives. Sober recognition of power is the beginning of wisdom in politics.
positions.evidence: No Spartan help came; Melos fell exactly as the Athenians said; the realists' long record of explaining wars.

positions.name: The Melians
positions.who: Jacqueline de Romilly; many readers who see Thucydides' history as a tragedy of Athenian pride
positions.view: The Athenians win the argument and lose everything. Their reasoning leads straight to Sicily and to the destruction of their own empire. The Melians were right that fairness is a 'common protection' and that Athens' fall would be terrible. Thucydides shows hybris and nemesis without gods.
positions.evidence: The placing of Melos straight before the Sicilian expedition (VI.1); the end of Athens in 404 BC; Xenophon on the proposal to destroy Athens.

positions.name: The prophets
positions.who: Isaiah; the Hebrew prophets; Augustine and the Christian tradition
positions.view: Both sides share a mistake: they think the only powers are human or the Greek gods who 'rule wherever they can'. The prophets say the strong are instruments of a God who judges them and who sees the weak. Power wins for a time; it does not have the last word.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 10:5–15; Assyria's fall in 612 BC; the Bible's long attention to the weak.

debate.agree: All agree that the Athenians' arguments are powerful, that the Melians' hopes in Sparta were mistaken, and that Thucydides lets the reader decide.

look.why: Nothing survives of the city the Athenians destroyed, and the gallery has no painting of Melos. This is a ruined ancient city painted in 1819 by the French artist Achille-Etna Michallon: the Forum of Pompeii, destroyed by a volcano, not by an army. It is here for what Melos became: a place where a people had been.
points: Ancient ruins of reddish-brown stone fill the painting.
In front of the broken walls stand lines of tan and grey columns and free-standing arches.
The brown ground is littered with cream-coloured stones.
Behind, rolling grey hills and distant mountains lie under a blue sky with fluffy white clouds.

music.why: The 'Symphony of Sorrowful Songs': three laments, of mothers for children and of a child for her mother, including a prayer an 18-year-old girl wrote on the wall of a Gestapo cell. Music for the women and children of Melos.

think.why: The Athenians say there is no justice without power to enforce it. See the modern debate: does morality need God?

learn.why: Isaiah's vision of a judge between the nations and an end of war: the prophets' answer to 'the strong do what they can'.

check.q: What exactly does 'right ... is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must' claim?
options: That the gods favour the weak
That the weak should always fight
That questions of justice only arise between parties strong enough to make each other listen; between strong and weak there are only outcomes
That whatever the strong do is morally right
check.why: It is not 'might makes right' but 'right only exists between equals'. The difference matters for the debate.

check.q: Why do the Athenians say they cannot let Melos stay neutral?
options: Because Melos had attacked Athens
Because a free Melos would look like Athenian weakness to their subjects, and its subjection would show Athenian power
Because Sparta had asked them to
Because Melos was rich in silver
check.why: 'Your friendship will be an argument to our subjects of our weakness, and your enmity of our power.' Melos must fall for what it shows.

check.q: What is the Melians' best argument, judged by later events?
options: That the fortunes of war are even
That fairness is a 'common protection', and Athens' own fall would bring terrible vengeance
That the gods would save them
That Sparta would come to help them
check.why: No Spartans came and the gods did not save them; but when Athens fell in 404 BC, its enemies proposed to destroy it as it destroyed Melos.

check.q: How do the Athenians use the gods in their argument?
options: They say the gods have commanded them to take Melos
They say the gods do not exist
They say gods and men alike rule wherever they can, by a law of nature, so the gods are no more on Melos' side than theirs
They refuse to mention the gods
check.why: 'Of the gods we believe, and of men we know, that by a necessary law of their nature they rule wherever they can.'

check.q: What is the strongest evidence that Thucydides did not simply agree with the Athenians?
options: He was exiled by Athens
He places Melos straight before Athens' decision to invade Sicily, which ended in disaster, as if before a fall
He gives the Melians more words than the Athenians
He says so in the dialogue
check.why: He never states his view; the placing (VI.1 follows V.116) is the clue many readers follow. His exile is a fact but not evidence of his view.

check.q: How does Isaiah's answer differ from both the Athenians' and the Melians'?
options: He says Assyria is righteous
He says the weak always win
He says the gods are envious
He agrees the strong win for a time, but says there is a God above them who uses and judges empires and sees the weak
check.why: 'Should an ax brag against him who chops with it?' He denies the Athenians' claim that there is no one above the strong, without promising the weak a rescue.

tutorial.question: 'The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.' Is the Athenians' view of history true?
tutorial.approach: State the Athenian case at full strength, as a realist would. Give the Melians' replies and how events tested them. Ask what Thucydides himself thought, using where he placed the dialogue. Then bring in Isaiah's answer. End with your own view, and the strongest objection to it.
strong: States the Athenian case fairly and precisely, including 'right only between equals' and the law of nature.
Shows why the case has persuaded serious thinkers (Hobbes, the realists).
Gives the Melians' replies and tests them against later events.
Uses the placing of Melos before Sicily as evidence for Thucydides' view.
Explains Isaiah's answer and how it differs from both sides.
Reaches its own view and answers the strongest objection.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice one situation where you have more power than someone else (at work, as a customer, in the family) and you could simply get your way. This once, ask what would be fair if you were equals, and do that.
sessions.reflect: When have you told yourself that something was 'just how the world works', to avoid asking whether it was right?
takeaways: At Melos the Athenians argued, with brutal honesty, that justice exists only between equals and that ruling where they can is a law of nature for gods and men.
The Melians appealed to fairness, freedom, hope and the gods; they were destroyed, but their warning about Athens' own fall came true.
Thucydides does not say who won; Isaiah answers that empires are tools judged by a God who sees the weak.

sessions.title: What history teaches: the verdict
sessions.line: The greatest Athenian army ever sent out is destroyed in Sicily, and Thucydides calls it most glorious to the victors and most calamitous to the conquered. Augustine asks what kingdoms are without justice. Then the verdict.
sessions.plain: Here is the verdict first. The Greeks taught the West to investigate the past, test witnesses and see how power corrupts those who hold it. The Bible added two things the Greek historians did not have: that history has a direction, and that the weak are seen by God. This session reads Thucydides' account of the end of the Athenian army in Sicily, two years after Melos, and Augustine's famous question about kingdoms without justice, and then puts Greek and biblical history side by side.
sessions.why: The last session stated the objection at full strength: that history is only the story of power, and the strong do what they can. Now we see what happened to the Athenians who said it, and hear the answer of a Christian writing as another empire fell. Then we can say what the first historians taught, and what they did not.
answers: What happened in Sicily?
Does history punish the proud?
What is the difference between Greek and biblical history?
What did Augustine mean by 'kingdoms without justice'?
So what does history teach?
sessions.finding: The Greeks taught the West to investigate and to see how power corrupts; the Bible added that history has a direction and that the weak are seen by God. Neither alone is enough.

paras: Herodotus invented history as an inquiry: listen to both sides, find the causes, remember the great deeds of friend and enemy. He found a moral pattern in events, pride before a fall. Thucydides made the inquiry strict: test every witness, trust only what can be checked, and write for the future. He found that power has its own logic, that catastrophe strips away religion and law, and that the strong do what they can.

Both were right about a great deal. But neither could say why the weak should matter, or where history is going. The Bible, written by a small people who were usually the weak, says both: history is going somewhere, under a God who judges the strong and sees the weak. The West inherited the method from Athens and the hope from Jerusalem. That is the verdict; the rest of this session is the evidence.
background.key: The Greeks gave the West the method of history and a clear view of power; the Bible gave it a direction and a concern for the weak.

paras: The same winter that Melos fell, 416–415 BC, the Athenian assembly voted to send a great fleet to conquer Sicily, the large, rich island south of Italy, home to many Greek cities led by Syracuse. Nicias, the cautious general who had made the peace of 421 BC, argued against it; the brilliant young Alcibiades argued for it. The assembly chose Alcibiades, and then made both men generals.

In 415 BC the fleet sailed: 134 warships and over 5,000 heavy infantry, the greatest force a Greek city had ever sent out. Alcibiades was soon recalled to face trial and fled to Sparta. Syracuse held out. In 413 BC Athens sent a second fleet under Demosthenes. Both fleets were trapped in the harbour of Syracuse and destroyed. The army, about 40,000 men with its servants, tried to retreat overland.

timeline.text: Melos destroyed
The fleet sails for Sicily; Alcibiades flees to Sparta
The Spartan general Gylippus reaches Syracuse
A second fleet arrives; both are destroyed in the harbour
The retreat; the massacre at the Assinarus; the quarries
Athens surrenders to Sparta
The Goths sack Rome
Augustine writes The City of God

background.key: In 415 BC Athens sent its greatest force ever to conquer Sicily; by 413 BC both fleets were destroyed and the army retreated overland.

paras: The main reading is the end of Thucydides' Book VII: the last day of the retreat, the slaughter at the river Assinarus, the deaths of Nicias and Demosthenes, the prisoners in the stone quarries, and Thucydides' own verdict.

The comparison is a short chapter from Augustine's The City of God, written after the Goths sacked Rome in AD 410. Augustine asks the Athenians' question from the other side: if a kingdom has no justice, what is the difference between it and a gang of robbers?
background.key: The destruction of the Athenian army in Sicily, then Augustine on kingdoms without justice.

before: What is happening to the Athenians at the river, and why do they keep drinking?
What does Thucydides say about Nicias, and why is it surprising?
How does Thucydides sum up the Sicilian expedition in his last paragraph?
sessions.readWhy: The end of the expedition that followed Melos: Thucydides' account of the destruction of the Athenian army in Sicily.

paras: As soon as it was day Nicias put his army in motion, pressed, as before, by the Syracusans and their allies, pelted from every side by their missiles, and struck down by their javelins. The Athenians pushed on for the Assinarus, impelled by the attacks made upon them from every side by a numerous cavalry and the swarm of other arms, fancying that they should breathe more freely if once across the river, and driven on also by their exhaustion and craving for water. Once there they rushed in, and all order was at an end, each man wanting to cross first, and the attacks of the enemy making it difficult to cross at all; forced to huddle together, they fell against and trod down one another, some dying immediately upon the javelins, others getting entangled together and stumbling over the articles of baggage, without being able to rise again. Meanwhile the opposite bank, which was steep, was lined by the Syracusans, who showered missiles down upon the Athenians, most of them drinking greedily and heaped together in disorder in the hollow bed of the river. The Peloponnesians also came down and butchered them, especially those in the water, which was thus immediately spoiled, but which they went on drinking just the same, mud and all, bloody as it was, most even fighting to have it.

At last, when many dead now lay piled one upon another in the stream, and part of the army had been destroyed at the river, and the few that escaped from thence cut off by the cavalry, Nicias surrendered himself to Gylippus, whom he trusted more than he did the Syracusans, and told him and the Lacedaemonians to do what they liked with him, but to stop the slaughter of the soldiers. Gylippus, after this, immediately gave orders to make prisoners; upon which the rest were brought together alive, except a large number secreted by the soldiery, and a party was sent in pursuit of the three hundred who had got through the guard during the night, and who were now taken with the rest. The number of the enemy collected as public property was not considerable; but that secreted was very large, and all Sicily was filled with them, no convention having been made in their case as for those taken with Demosthenes. Besides this, a large portion were killed outright, the carnage being very great, and not exceeded by any in this Sicilian war. In the numerous other encounters upon the march, not a few also had fallen. Nevertheless many escaped, some at the moment, others served as slaves, and then ran away subsequently. These found refuge at Catana.

The Syracusans and their allies now mustered and took up the spoils and as many prisoners as they could, and went back to the city. The rest of their Athenian and allied captives were deposited in the quarries, this seeming the safest way of keeping them; but Nicias and Demosthenes were butchered, against the will of Gylippus, who thought that it would be the crown of his triumph if he could take the enemy’s generals to Lacedaemon. One of them, as it happened, Demosthenes, was one of her greatest enemies, on account of the affair of the island and of Pylos; while the other, Nicias, was for the same reasons one of her greatest friends, owing to his exertions to procure the release of the prisoners by persuading the Athenians to make peace. For these reasons the Lacedaemonians felt kindly towards him; and it was in this that Nicias himself mainly confided when he surrendered to Gylippus. But some of the Syracusans who had been in correspondence with him were afraid, it was said, of his being put to the torture and troubling their success by his revelations; others, especially the Corinthians, of his escaping, as he was wealthy, by means of bribes, and living to do them further mischief; and these persuaded the allies and put him to death. This or the like was the cause of the death of a man who, of all the Hellenes in my time, least deserved such a fate, seeing that the whole course of his life had been regulated with strict attention to virtue.

The prisoners in the quarries were at first hardly treated by the Syracusans. Crowded in a narrow hole, without any roof to cover them, the heat of the sun and the stifling closeness of the air tormented them during the day, and then the nights, which came on autumnal and chilly, made them ill by the violence of the change; besides, as they had to do everything in the same place for want of room, and the bodies of those who died of their wounds or from the variation in the temperature, or from similar causes, were left heaped together one upon another, intolerable stenches arose; while hunger and thirst never ceased to afflict them, each man during eight months having only half a pint of water and a pint of corn given him daily. In short, no single suffering to be apprehended by men thrust into such a place was spared them. For some seventy days they thus lived all together, after which all, except the Athenians and any Siceliots or Italiots who had joined in the expedition, were sold. The total number of prisoners taken it would be difficult to state exactly, but it could not have been less than seven thousand.

This was the greatest Hellenic achievement of any in this war, or, in my opinion, in Hellenic history; at once most glorious to the victors, and most calamitous to the conquered. They were beaten at all points and altogether; all that they suffered was great; they were destroyed, as the saying is, with a total destruction, their fleet, their army, everything was destroyed, and few out of many returned home. Such were the events in Sicily.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: At the river
parts.context: September 413 BC. After eight days of retreat, starving and attacked on every side by Syracusan cavalry and javelin-throwers, the Athenian army under Nicias reaches the river Assinarus in south-eastern Sicily. Demosthenes, with the other half of the army, has already surrendered. Gylippus is the Spartan general who organised Syracuse's defence; 'the Peloponnesians' are his Spartan and allied troops.
parts.plain: At dawn Nicias marches on towards the river, under constant attack. The Athenians rush into the water, desperate to drink, and all order breaks down. They trample one another and are killed in the riverbed by missiles from the steep bank, and the enemy come down and butcher them in the water, which they go on drinking though it is full of mud and blood. At last Nicias surrenders to Gylippus and begs him to stop the slaughter. Many are killed, many taken and hidden as private slaves.

commentary.on: driven on also by their exhaustion and craving for water
commentary.text: The army that sailed out to conquer an island is now driven by thirst. Thucydides makes us feel the reversal in the body.

commentary.on: which they went on drinking just the same, mud and all, bloody as it was, most even fighting to have it
commentary.text: One of the most terrible sentences in ancient history. The citizens of the 'school of Hellas' fight each other for bloody water.

commentary.on: told him and the Lacedaemonians to do what they liked with him, but to stop the slaughter of the soldiers
commentary.text: Nicias, who had argued against the expedition, gives himself up to save his men. The strong now do what they can, and the Athenians suffer what they must.

commentary.on: all Sicily was filled with them
commentary.text: Athenian soldiers were sold across the island as slaves, as the women and children of Melos had been sold two years before. Thucydides does not draw the comparison. He does not need to.

parts.author: Thucydides
parts.who: Thucydides (c. 460–c. 400 BC), an Athenian general exiled in 424 BC, who wrote the history of the war he lived through.
parts.when: Written in exile and in Athens, c. 424–400 BC
parts.title: Most calamitous to the conquered
parts.context: The prisoners are taken to Syracuse. The 'quarries' are the great stone quarries outside the city, still visible today, deep pits with sheer sides. The 'affair of the island and of Pylos' was an Athenian victory of 425 BC, led by Demosthenes, in which Spartan soldiers were captured; Nicias had later arranged their release. 'Siceliots or Italiots' are Greeks of Sicily and Italy.
parts.plain: The prisoners are put in the quarries. Nicias and Demosthenes are killed, against Gylippus' wishes. Thucydides says Nicias, of all the Greeks of his time, least deserved such an end, because he lived his whole life by virtue. In the quarries, 7,000 or more men are crowded without shelter, burned by day and chilled by night, given a little water and grain, among the bodies of the dead, for seventy days; then most are sold. Thucydides calls it the greatest event of the war, perhaps of Greek history: most glorious to the victors, most calamitous to the conquered. Few out of many came home.

commentary.on: This or the like was the cause of the death of a man who, of all the Hellenes in my time, least deserved such a fate, seeing that the whole course of his life had been regulated with strict attention to virtue
commentary.text: A rare personal judgement from Thucydides, and a troubling one. Nicias was pious and careful; Thucydides elsewhere shows him delaying the retreat because of an eclipse of the moon (VII.50). If history rewarded virtue, Nicias would have lived. Thucydides' world has no such justice.

commentary.on: Crowded in a narrow hole, without any roof to cover them
commentary.text: The quarries of Syracuse can still be visited. Plutarch, five centuries later, says some prisoners were freed because they could recite the choruses of Euripides, whom the Sicilians loved (Life of Nicias 29).

commentary.on: In short, no single suffering to be apprehended by men thrust into such a place was spared them.
commentary.text: Thucydides, who described the plague, describes this with the same exactness. He gives us suffering as it is, without consolation.

commentary.on: at once most glorious to the victors, and most calamitous to the conquered
commentary.text: Thucydides' verdict holds both sides at once. The victors are glorious; the conquered are destroyed. He does not say it was just. He says it was great.

commentary.on: few out of many returned home
commentary.text: The last words of the book on Sicily. The greatest force a Greek city ever sent out is gone. Thucydides does not mention Melos, two years before. Many readers cannot help remembering it.
