paras: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms? The band itself is made up of men; it is ruled by the authority of a prince, it is knit together by the pact of the confederacy; the booty is divided by the law agreed on. If, by the admittance of abandoned men, this evil increases to such a degree that it holds places, fixes abodes, takes possession of cities, and subdues peoples, it assumes the more plainly the name of a kingdom, because the reality is now manifestly conferred on it, not by the removal of covetousness, but by the addition of impunity. Indeed, that was an apt and true reply which was given to Alexander the Great by a pirate who had been seized. For when that king had asked the man what he meant by keeping hostile possession of the sea, he answered with bold pride, What you mean by seizing the whole earth; but because I do it with a petty ship, I am called a robber, while you who does it with a great fleet are styled emperor.

parts.author: Augustine
parts.ref: Augustine, The City of God IV.4
parts.title: Great robberies
parts.context: In AD 410 the Goths sacked Rome, the first time in eight centuries the city had fallen to a foreign enemy. Pagans said Rome had fallen because it had abandoned its old gods for Christ. Augustine (354–430), bishop of Hippo in North Africa, answered in The City of God, written between 413 and 426. In Book IV he asks whether Rome's empire was really a gift of the gods, and whether great empires are as admirable as they seem. The story of the pirate comes from Cicero's Republic (III.24), which is mostly lost. This is Marcus Dods' translation (1871).
parts.plain: Augustine says: take away justice, and a kingdom is just a big gang of robbers, and a gang of robbers is a small kingdom. A gang has a leader, an agreement and rules for sharing the loot. If it grows big enough to take cities and rule peoples, it is called a kingdom, not because it has stopped being greedy but because it can no longer be punished. A captured pirate told Alexander the Great: you and I do the same thing; because I do it with one ship I am called a robber, and because you do it with a great fleet you are called an emperor.

commentary.on: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?
commentary.text: Augustine accepts the Athenians' description of power, and turns it into an accusation. Yes, empires take what they can. That is exactly what robbers do. Without justice, the only difference is size.

commentary.on: the booty is divided by the law agreed on
commentary.text: Even a gang has laws and loyalty. So having laws is not the same as having justice. Augustine is asking a harder question: are the laws just?

commentary.on: not by the removal of covetousness, but by the addition of impunity
commentary.text: This is the heart of it. A gang becomes a 'kingdom' not when it stops being greedy but when no one can punish it. That is the Athenians at Melos exactly: 'the strong do what they can'. Augustine's word for their condition is impunity.

commentary.on: because I do it with a petty ship, I am called a robber, while you who does it with a great fleet are styled emperor
commentary.text: The pirate's answer is the Melians' answer, with the courage of a man who has nothing to lose. Augustine, a bishop of the Roman Empire, lets a pirate have the last word over Alexander the Great. In the Bible's view of history, the voice of the weak can judge the strong.

compare.author: Augustine
compare.ref: Augustine, The City of God IV.4
compare.why: Eight hundred years later, another empire was falling. Read Augustine's answer to the question the Athenians raised at Melos: what is power without justice?
compare.title: Kingdoms without justice

paras: Thucydides places Melos at the end of Book V and the vote to invade Sicily at the start of Book VI, in the same winter. He shows the Athenians, 'ignorant of its size' (VI.1), sending out their greatest fleet on the strength of hope, the very thing they had told the Melians was a luxury of the strong. In the debate before the expedition, Nicias warns that Athens should not reach for a new empire before securing the one it has (VI.10). He is overruled.

Then, two years later, he gives us the end: the army fighting for bloody water, sold as slaves 'all over Sicily', the quarries, 'few out of many returned home'. The Athenians had said at Melos that the weak suffer what they must. Now they are the weak. Thucydides never says this is a punishment. There are no gods in his account to punish anyone. But he shows hybris and nemesis as clearly as Herodotus did, as the working out of human choices: the pride of power led to the overreach that destroyed it.
sections.key: Thucydides places Melos straight before Sicily; the Athenians who scorned hope sailed on hope, and became the weak who suffer what they must. Hybris and nemesis without gods.

paras: So does history punish the proud? Herodotus thought so: the divine brings down those who overstep human limits. Thucydides shows something like it without the gods: overreaching power provokes resistance, ruins its own judgement and falls. Athens surrendered in 404 BC. Five years later, in 399 BC, the restored democracy put Socrates to death, which you will meet in 'Socrates', later in this hall.

But Thucydides also shows that history does not reward virtue. Nicias, the most virtuous, died in the quarry; the Melians, who were in the right, were destroyed. History may bring down the proud, but it does not lift up the humble. If there is justice in history, it is not visible in the history itself. That is the limit of the Greek historians, and it is where the Bible's account of history begins.
sections.key: In both historians the proud fall, but the virtuous are not rewarded: Nicias and the Melians perished. Justice, if it exists, is not visible within history itself.

paras: Augustine wrote The City of God because Rome's fall seemed to many to prove what the Athenians said: power is everything, and when the gods stop protecting you, you fall. Augustine agreed that earthly power runs on the 'lust for domination' (libido dominandi). He described Rome's glory, as Thucydides described Athens', as greatness without justice. His pirate says what the Melians said.

But he added something no Greek historian had. All of human history, he said, is the story of two 'cities' mixed together: the earthly city, built on love of self even to contempt of God, and the city of God, built on love of God even to contempt of self (XIV.28). Empires rise and fall; the city of God is a pilgrim through them, heading for an end that God has set. History is not a circle of rising and falling powers, but a story with a beginning, a centre in Christ and an end.
sections.key: Augustine agreed that earthly power runs on the lust for domination, but saw history as two cities mixed together, moving to an end that God has set.

sections.h: Greek and biblical history side by side
paras: If you have taken 'Kings and prophets', you have read 2 Kings 25: Babylon burns Jerusalem, kills the king's sons before his eyes, blinds him and takes him away. It is the Bible's own Sicily. But notice how differently the two traditions tell their disasters. Israel's historians blame their own nation: Jerusalem fell, they say, because its kings and people did evil. No Greek city wrote its own history as a confession. Here are the main differences, side by side.

The table is a simplification, and scholars warn against making it too neat. Arnaldo Momigliano showed that Greek historians did not all think history went in circles, and that the Hebrews had no single 'linear' view. But the broad contrast holds.

rows: Testimony: what the community remembers, and the prophets interpret
Human choices, fortune, power; for Herodotus, the gods too
Human choices, under a God who acts in history
Human nature is the same, so things recur
From creation to a promised end
Often the weak: slaves, exiles, a small people
Often our own side: Israel's kings and people
table.note: Herodotus I.0, I.5; Thucydides I.22; 2 Kings 17:7–23 and 25; Deuteronomy 26:5–9. See Momigliano (1990) and Yerushalmi (1982).

sections.key: The Greeks inquired, explained by human nature and looked at the great; the Bible remembered, saw a direction under God, blamed its own side and looked at the weak.

paras: Scholars still argue about this. Some, following Momigliano, say the Greeks invented history as a discipline: inquiry, criticism of sources, explanation by causes. Others, like Baruch Halpern in The First Historians (1988), argue that the authors of Samuel and Kings were historians in the full sense, using sources and reasoning about causes, and that they wrote before Herodotus. The Jewish historian Yosef Hayim Yerushalmi, in Zakhor (1982), said something subtler: the Bible commands Israel to remember ('zakhor'), and memory of what God has done, not curiosity about the past, was its reason for writing.

Perhaps both are true. The Greeks gave us the method: how to find out what happened. The Bible gave us a reason to care: because what happens in history matters to God, and because the forgotten are not forgotten by him. Christian historians from Eusebius and Bede onwards used both, and so, knowingly or not, does every historian who checks the sources and tells the story of the defeated.
sections.key: The Greeks gave history its method; the Bible gave it a reason to remember and to care for the forgotten. Christian historians used both.

paras: The line from Herodotus and Thucydides runs through the Greek historian Polybius, the Romans Livy and Tacitus, Eusebius, the first Church historian, and Bede, who in 731 wrote the history of the English Church and carefully named his sources. In 1824 the German historian Leopold von Ranke said the historian's task was to show the past 'as it actually was', which is Thucydides' ambition in a modern phrase.

Modern history keeps both of Herodotus' purposes, memory and causes, and Thucydides' method of testing. It has also learned to tell the story of those whom the great historians left out: slaves, women, the poor, the conquered, the people of Melos. That last habit does not come from Athens. It comes from a tradition that said God 'has put down princes from their thrones, and has exalted the lowly' (Luke 1:52).
sections.key: From Polybius to Ranke, history kept the Greeks' purposes and method; its modern care for the defeated and forgotten owes more to the Bible.

sections.h: What the first historians leave us
paras: Gather up what we have seen. From Herodotus: listen to both sides; name your sources; distinguish what you saw from what you heard; remember the deeds of the enemy as well as your own; look for causes; beware pride. From Thucydides: test every story, even your nation's favourite; distrust your own impressions; separate the reasons people give from the real cause; watch what fear and power do; write for the long run, not the applause of the moment.

These are not only rules for historians. They are rules for anyone who reads the news, judges a quarrel, sits on a jury or tries to understand their own family's past. And from Isaiah, Dionysius and Augustine, one more: when you have found out what happened, ask who suffered, and remember them. The first historians taught the West to ask 'how do we know?' The Bible taught it to ask 'who has been forgotten?'
sections.key: Herodotus and Thucydides left rules for anyone who weighs evidence; the Bible added: ask who suffered, and remember them.

refs: Thucydides, History VI.1, 10; VII.50, 84–87, tr. Richard Crawley (1874); Plutarch, Life of Nicias 29.
Augustine, The City of God IV.4; XIV.28, tr. Marcus Dods (1871); Cicero, Republic III.24 (the pirate).
2 Kings 17:7–23; 25; Deuteronomy 26:5–9; Luke 1:52.

Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People (731), Preface; Leopold von Ranke, Histories of the Latin and Germanic Peoples (1824), Preface.

debate.question: Did the Greeks or the Hebrews invent history?

positions.name: The Greeks
positions.who: Arnaldo Momigliano; most classical scholars
positions.view: History as a discipline, a critical inquiry into the causes of events using tested evidence, began with Herodotus and Thucydides. Israel's writers recorded and interpreted their past, but they did not question their sources or explain events by human causes alone.
positions.evidence: Thucydides I.20–22; Herodotus VII.152; the anonymous, sacred character of the biblical histories.

positions.name: The Hebrews
positions.who: Baruch Halpern (The First Historians, 1988); John Van Seters (In Search of History, 1983, who compared Herodotus and the Deuteronomistic history)
positions.view: The authors of Samuel and Kings wrote a connected, source-based account of their nation's past, centuries before Herodotus, and reasoned about causes, including human ones. They were historians, even if they also saw God's hand.
positions.evidence: The books' citations of royal chronicles; their unflattering honesty about Israel's kings; their date.

positions.name: Both, differently
positions.who: Yosef Hayim Yerushalmi (Zakhor, 1982); many historians of historiography
positions.view: Greece invented history as inquiry; Israel invented history as meaning, a story with a direction that a people is commanded to remember. The West inherited both, and needs both.
positions.evidence: 'Remember' (zakhor) in Deuteronomy; the Greek historians' secular method; Christian historians from Eusebius on, who combined them.

debate.agree: All agree that Western history writing has two roots, Greek inquiry and biblical memory, and that each saw what the other did not.

look.why: The gallery has no painting of the Athenian disaster at Syracuse. This oil sketch of 1842 by Jean-Charles-Joseph Rémond shows ruins on a hill above Messina, in north-eastern Sicily, over a hundred miles from where the Athenian army was destroyed: the island that swallowed an empire's pride, centuries later, with a living city below.

On the left, large green cacti and succulents grow on sandy, rocky ground beside the ruins of a sand-coloured structure.

Below on the right, white and tan buildings packed closely together stretch down to a blue sea.

music.why: Not a prayer for the dead but comfort for the living, from the words 'Blessed are they that mourn': the Bible's answer to Thucydides' 'most calamitous to the conquered', that the mourners are seen.

think.why: Why should the weak matter, if the strong do what they can? See how the great teachers grounded human dignity.

learn.why: Augustine's question in two sentences: the best short answer ever given to 'the strong do what they can'.

check.q: Why do many readers think Thucydides' account of Sicily is linked to Melos, though he never says so?
options: Because Thucydides says the gods punished Athens
Because the same generals led both
Because he places the vote for Sicily straight after Melos, and the Athenians who told the weak to suffer what they must become the weak, sold as slaves across the island
Because the Melians fought in Sicily
check.why: The placing and the reversal tell the story; Thucydides gives no divine explanation.

check.q: What does Thucydides' judgement on Nicias show about his view of history?
options: That Nicias deserved his fate
That the gods protect the pious
That virtue is always rewarded
That history does not reward virtue: the most virtuous Greek of his time died in disgrace
check.why: 'Of all the Hellenes in my time, least deserved such a fate.' The proud may fall, but the good are not lifted up.

check.q: According to Augustine, what makes a band of robbers into a 'kingdom'?
options: The removal of greed
Its laws for sharing the loot
Justice
Impunity: it becomes large enough that no one can punish it
check.why: 'Not by the removal of covetousness, but by the addition of impunity.' Even a gang has laws; that is not justice.

check.q: Which of these is the clearest difference between Greek and biblical history writing?
options: Israel's historians often blamed their own nation for its disasters, where Greek historians did not write their city's history as a confession
The Greeks wrote about wars and the Bible did not
The Greeks did not believe in causes
The Bible has no dates
check.why: 2 Kings 17 and 25 blame Israel's kings and people. Both traditions wrote about wars and causes.

check.q: Why does Momigliano warn against a neat contrast of 'Greek cyclical' and 'Hebrew linear' history?
options: Because the Hebrews had no history
Because Thucydides was Jewish
Because both are completely cyclical
Because Greek historians did not all think history went in circles and the Hebrews had no single view; the broad contrast holds only roughly
check.why: Thucydides thought human nature recurs, not that history literally repeats; the contrast is real but rough.

check.q: What is the best statement of this journey's verdict?
options: The Bible invented history and the Greeks copied it
The Greeks gave the West the method of history and a clear view of power; the Bible gave it a direction and a reason to see the weak; neither alone is enough
History is only the story of power
The Greeks were right and the Bible wrong
check.why: Each tradition saw what the other did not; the West inherited both.

tutorial.question: Compare Greek and biblical history. What did each see that the other missed?
tutorial.approach: Use Thucydides on Sicily and Melos, Herodotus on Croesus, and 2 Kings 25 or Isaiah 10. Set out the differences: method, causes, direction, heroes, blame, purpose. Bring in Augustine's 'great robberies'. Then answer: does the West need both, and why?
strong: Uses specific passages from both Greek historians.
Uses at least one biblical history and one prophet accurately.
Sets out the differences clearly, with the caution that the contrast is rough.
Explains Augustine's argument and how it answers Melos.
Gives credit to each tradition for what it saw.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion of its own.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: find out the history of one group in your own town or family whose story is usually left out (the workers who built a building, a family that left, the people who were there before). Write down three facts about them and tell one other person.
sessions.reflect: Whose suffering in history, or in your own life, would you rather not look at? What would it mean to see it as God sees it?
takeaways: Two years after Melos, the Athenian army was destroyed in Sicily; Thucydides shows pride leading to ruin without gods, and that history does not reward virtue.
Augustine answered the Athenians: without justice, kingdoms are great robberies, made kingdoms only by impunity.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: How did history begin, and what does power do? In about 300 words, answer from Herodotus and Thucydides, using at least three passages from this journey, and answer the strongest objection to your view: the Athenians' claim at Melos that the strong do what they can.
closing.practice: Read Herodotus Book I and Thucydides Book I over the next two weeks, a few chapters a day, then the Melian dialogue again. Each time you read the news this fortnight, ask Thucydides' two questions: who saw it, and what is the real cause?
synthesis: This journey asked how history began and what power does, following the two Greeks who invented history writing in the West. Here are the short answers to its questions, in order.

Who was the first historian? Herodotus of Halicarnassus, writing around 430 BC, is the first whose whole inquiry survives. He had predecessors, like Hecataeus, and some scholars argue that Israel's historians, in Samuel and Kings, came first. But it was Herodotus who called his work historia, inquiry, and set out to keep great deeds from being forgotten and to find their causes. He began by reporting what the enemy said about who started the quarrel, then set the legends aside and began 'within my own knowledge'. History began as listening to both sides.

Why is Herodotus called the father of history, and of lies? Because he gathered and named his sources, separated what he saw from what he heard, and was fair to Persia; and because he also told stories too good to be true, like Solon's visit to Croesus, which the dates make very hard, and gave impossible numbers. He warned us himself: he was bound to report what was said, not bound to believe it. Where he can be tested, at Marathon, Thermopylae, Behistun and the Serpent Column, he usually holds up. His speeches and numbers do not.

What did he think history teaches? That 'human prosperity never continues steadfast'. Solon told the richest king alive to call no man happy until he had ended well; Croesus remembered it on the pyre, and Cyrus saw that he too was a man. Pride oversteps and is brought down: hybris and nemesis. Jesus' parable of the rich fool agrees that wealth is no security, but says God is not envious of us; he asks us to be rich toward him.

What were the Persian Wars? The invasions of 490 and 480–479 BC, beaten at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea. Herodotus made freedom their meaning: Demaratus told Xerxes that the Spartans were free but had a master, the law, and the epitaph at Thermopylae says they died 'faithfully keeping their laws'. That freedom was for citizen men only, resting on helots and slaves, and the later story of West against East is a simplification Herodotus himself did not make.

How did Thucydides do it differently? He tested. Most people, he said, accept stories without any critical test, even about their own city. He cross-examined eyewitnesses who disagreed through bad memory or bias, admitted that he wrote the speeches to give the general sense, left the gods out, and separated the stated reasons for the war from its real cause: Athens' growing power and Sparta's fear. He wrote, he said, 'a possession for all time', because human nature does not change. He was careful and also partisan, and the most persuasive historian is the one we must check most.

What did he learn from the plague? That a civilisation can forget itself in months. When the pious and the impious died alike and no one expected to live to be tried, 'fear of gods or law of man there was none'. In a later plague, Dionysius of Alexandria described Christians who stayed with the sick and buried the dead, because their faith had never promised them safety, they hoped beyond death and they were commanded to love their neighbour. Hostile witnesses agree.

Is might right? At Melos the Athenians said that justice exists only between equals, that gods and men alike rule wherever they can, and that hope is a luxury of the strong. Their case has persuaded serious thinkers from Hobbes to modern realists, and the Melians who trusted justice, the gods and Sparta were destroyed. But the Athenians who scorned hope then sailed on it to Sicily, where their army fought for bloody water and was sold into slavery. Thucydides shows pride and ruin without gods, and he also shows that history does not reward virtue: Nicias, the most virtuous, died in disgrace.

How is Greek history different from the Bible's? The Greeks inquired; the Bible remembered. The Greeks explained by human nature and looked at the great; the Bible saw history moving under God from creation to a promised end, blamed its own people for their disasters and looked at the weak. Isaiah told the empire that boasted 'by the strength of my hand' that an axe does not brag against the one who swings it. Augustine said that without justice, kingdoms are only great robberies, made kingdoms by impunity.

How do we know ancient history is true? The same way Thucydides did: by testing witnesses against each other and against what can be dug up, and by holding our conclusions as firmly as the evidence allows and no more. That method is the Greeks' gift. The conviction that the forgotten matter, which is why modern historians tell the story of the Melians and not only of Athens, is the Bible's. The West took the method from Athens and the hope from Jerusalem, and it needs both.

One last thought. Herodotus wrote so that great deeds would not be forgotten; Thucydides so that we would understand what is likely to happen again. Both wanted the past to change how we live. That is why this journey ends each session with something to do. The first historians would ask you to test what you hear before you repeat it, to listen to the other side first, to distrust your own pride, and to notice how you use whatever power you have. The prophets would add: and do not forget the people of Melos.

title: Number and nature
question: How did the Greeks begin to explain the world?
line: Seven sessions on the Greek wager that the world can be understood by reason: Thales's water, Pythagoras's numbers, Euclid's proofs, Archimedes' machines and Hippocrates' oath; then the charge that Christianity killed Greek science, at full strength; and, at the end, whether science needs God.
why: Around 600 BC a few Greeks began to explain the world without stories of the gods: by natural causes, by number, by proof and by measurement. Everything we call science grew from that wager. This course follows it from Miletus to Alexandria, reading the oldest accounts of the first philosophers, Plato on geometry, Polybius and Cicero on Archimedes, and the Hippocratic doctors in their own words. Then it faces the hardest charge, that the Church burned the Library and murdered Hypatia, and asks what the evidence shows. It ends with the question people ask today: has science outgrown God, or does it still rest on an order that only a Creator explains?
follows: A first-year paper in the history of ancient science and philosophy: the Presocratics, Pythagoreanism, Euclid and the axiomatic method, Hellenistic mathematics and astronomy, Hippocratic medicine, the reception of Greek science in late antiquity, with elements of a paper on science and religion.
before: first-historians
outcomes: Explain what was new in the Ionian philosophers' natural explanations, and how we know about them from late sources.
Explain the Pythagorean musical ratios and the discovery of irrational lengths, and compare the Pythagorean view of number with Wisdom of Solomon 11:20.
Describe Euclid's axiomatic method with examples from Elements I, and explain what non-Euclidean geometry did and did not overturn.
Explain how Archimedes joined mathematics to the physical world, how the Greeks knew the earth was round, and how Eratosthenes measured it.
Analyse On the Sacred Disease and the Hippocratic Oath clause by clause, and explain the Christian origin of the hospital.
Assess the claim that Christianity killed Greek science, using Gibbon, Socrates Scholasticus and modern historians, and weigh Whitehead's argument that belief in a Creator helped modern science.

people.name: Thales of Miletus
people.line: Called the first philosopher; said everything comes from water and was said to have foretold an eclipse.

people.name: Anaximander
people.line: Thales's successor in Miletus; the boundless, the earth floating free, the first map.

people.name: Anaximenes
people.line: Third of the Milesians; everything is air, thickened or thinned.

people.name: Pythagoras
people.line: Founder of a brotherhood in Croton that saw number as the key to the world and taught the soul's rebirth.

people.name: Heraclitus
people.line: Philosopher of Ephesus: fire, flux and the logos.

people.name: Xenophanes
people.line: Poet-philosopher who mocked gods made in human shape, and Pythagoras.

people.name: Hippocrates of Cos
people.line: The most famous Greek doctor; about sixty medical works bear his name.

people.name: Plato
people.line: Athenian philosopher; on geometry in the Republic, and the making of the world in the Timaeus.

people.name: Aristotle
people.line: Plato's pupil; our best early witness to the first philosophers, and gave evidence the earth is round.

people.name: Euclid
people.line: Alexandrian mathematician whose Elements built geometry from axioms.

people.name: Archimedes
people.line: Mathematician and engineer of Syracuse: the lever, floating bodies, pi, the Sand-Reckoner.

people.name: Eratosthenes
people.line: Librarian of Alexandria who measured the earth's circumference.

people.name: Polybius
people.line: Greek historian of Rome who described Archimedes' defence of Syracuse.

people.name: Cicero
people.line: Roman statesman who found Archimedes' tomb and described his sphere.

people.name: Galen
people.line: The great physician of the Roman Empire, whose medicine ruled for 1,400 years.

people.name: Diogenes Laertius
people.line: Collector of the lives and opinions of the philosophers.

people.name: Basil of Caesarea
people.line: Bishop who built one of the first Christian hospitals, around 370.

people.name: Hypatia
people.line: Mathematician and Platonist of Alexandria, murdered by a Christian mob.

people.name: Socrates Scholasticus
people.line: Christian historian of Constantinople; the earliest account of Hypatia's death.

people.name: John Philoponus
people.line: Christian philosopher of Alexandria who criticised Aristotle's physics.

people.name: Edward Gibbon
people.line: Historian of Rome's decline and fall, and sharp critic of the Church.

people.name: A. N. Whitehead
people.line: Mathematician and philosopher who argued that modern science grew from belief in a rational God.

people.name: David C. Lindberg
people.line: Historian of science; author of The Beginnings of Western Science.

people.name: Carl Sagan

The upward push of a liquid on a body in it, equal (Archimedes showed) to the weight of liquid displaced.
The Greek-speaking, Christian Eastern Roman Empire, centred on Constantinople, which lasted until 1453.
A doctor's duty to keep secret what is learned about a patient; promised in the Hippocratic Oath.
The view, popularised by Draper (1874) and White (1896), that religion and science have always been at war.
Being able to have been otherwise; a world freely created is contingent, so its laws must be discovered by looking.
In Latin, creatio ex nihilo: the Jewish, Christian and Muslim teaching that God made everything, matter included, without any pre-existing material.
Greek for 'craftsman': the maker of the world in Plato's Timaeus, who orders a pre-existing chaos after an eternal pattern.
'Of the second canon': books such as the Wisdom of Solomon that are in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but in the Protestant Apocrypha.
A disorder of the brain causing seizures; the Greeks' 'sacred disease'.
The age of Greek kingdoms after Alexander the Great, from 323 BC to the Roman conquest of Egypt in 30 BC.
Greek harmonia: a fitting together, then a musical scale; for the Pythagoreans, the right proportion in music, soul and world.
About sixty Greek medical works, by many authors of the late 400s BC onwards, gathered under the name of Hippocrates.
The four body fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance, Greek doctors thought, meant health.
In Plato, a starting point 'placed under' an argument and assumed; today, a proposal to be tested.
The Greek cities on the west coast of modern Turkey, such as Miletus and Ephesus, where natural philosophy began.
A number that cannot be written as a ratio of whole numbers, such as the square root of 2, the diagonal of a unit square.
The regular patterns that natural events follow; the phrase, common from the 1600s, has a legal and theological origin.
The great library founded by the Ptolemies around 300 BC; it declined under Rome and was probably lost by AD 272.
Plato's term (eikos mythos) for an account of the changing physical world: probable, never as certain as geometry.
Greek for word, reason or account: Heraclitus's rational order of the world; for Christians, the Word through whom all things were made.
Greek for 'unit' or 'one': in Pythagorean teaching, the first principle from which numbers and all things come.
The Pythagorean idea that the heavenly bodies make a harmony by their motions.
The old name for the study of nature, from Thales to Newton; what we now call science.
The late form of Plato's philosophy taught from Plotinus (3rd century AD) onwards; Hypatia's school.
Consistent geometries in which Euclid's parallel postulate does not hold, discovered around 1830.
A manuscript whose writing was scraped off so the parchment could be reused, like the Archimedes Palimpsest.
Euclid's fifth postulate: roughly, that through a point beside a line only one line can be drawn that never meets it.
In Euclid, a starting point specific to geometry that the reader is asked to grant.
The Greek philosophers before Socrates (died 399 BC), known only from fragments and later reports.
In Euclid, a statement proved from the starting points and earlier propositions.
The 'four ways' of medieval education: arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy.
The great temple of the god Serapis in Alexandria, with a daughter library; destroyed in 391.
A Greek unit of length, about 160–185 metres; its exact value in Eratosthenes' measurement is uncertain.
The Pythagorean triangle of ten dots in rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4, sacred to the school.
The translation of Greek science into Arabic (800s, Baghdad) and then from Arabic and Greek into Latin (1100s).
The passing of a soul into another body after death, taught by Pythagoras.

sessions.title: Everything is water
sessions.line: Around 600 BC, in a Greek trading city on the coast of what is now Turkey, a few men began to explain the world without telling stories about gods.
sessions.plain: Before about 600 BC, if you asked why there was thunder, or what the world was made of, the answer was a story about gods. Then, in the Greek city of Miletus, a man called Thales said that everything comes from water. He was wrong, but the way he was wrong changed the world: he gave a natural answer that anyone could test and argue with. This session meets Thales and the thinkers who argued with him, and asks what was really new about what they did.
sessions.why: This is the first session. The journeys before it in this hall followed the Greeks through their poems, their plays, their politics and their first histories. Now we turn to the oldest Greek question of all: what is the world made of, and how does it work? Everything later in this journey, numbers, proofs, machines, medicine, starts here, with a handful of men in one city who decided to look for causes in nature itself.
answers: Who was the first philosopher?
What did Thales actually say, and how do we know?
What was new about it, compared with the old myths?
Why did this happen in Greece, and in Ionia in particular?
Is it a different kind of answer from Genesis, or a rival one?
sessions.finding: Around 600 BC, in Ionia, Thales and his successors began to explain the world by natural causes rather than myths, and to argue openly with each other about which explanation was right.

paras: Every culture has asked what the world is made of and why it behaves as it does. The Greeks were the first we know of to make a habit of answering by reason: by looking for natural causes, giving arguments, measuring, proving, and arguing with each other in public. That habit is the root of what we call science and philosophy.

This journey asks how they began, and follows one simple frame: the Greek wager that the world can be understood by reason. We start with the first natural explanations, then number, then proof, then measurement, then medicine. One session puts the strongest charge against the Christian story: that Christianity killed Greek science. The last session asks whether science needs God at all.

The case against: did Christianity kill Greek science?
Does science need God? The verdict

background.key: The journey follows the Greek wager that the world can be understood by reason, from the first natural explanations to the question whether science needs God.

paras: Ionia was a strip of Greek cities on the west coast of what is now Turkey, facing the Aegean Sea. The greatest of them was Miletus, a busy port with colonies all round the Black Sea and trading links with Egypt, with the kingdom of Lydia inland, and through it with Babylon. Lydia had just begun to strike the first coins, around 600 BC.

This was a world of ships, money and strangers. Merchants met people with other gods and other customs. The Greeks had recently taken up the alphabet from the Phoenicians, which made writing easy to learn. And there was no single priesthood in charge of what people should think about the world. Many historians think these things together made room for a new kind of question.

timeline.text: Homer and Hesiod: the world explained by the gods
Thales born in Miletus (the traditional date)
A total eclipse of the sun in Asia Minor, which Thales was said to have foretold
Anaximander of Miletus
Anaximenes of Miletus
Heraclitus of Ephesus
The Persians destroy Miletus
Aristotle writes the first history of these thinkers, in his Metaphysics
Diogenes Laertius collects their lives

background.key: Miletus, a rich Greek port on the coast of modern Turkey around 600 BC, open to Egypt, Lydia and Babylon, was where it began.

background.h: How do we know anything about them?
paras: Here is the first surprise. Not one complete book by any of these early thinkers survives. Thales may never have written anything. What we have are fragments: a sentence quoted by a later writer, a summary of someone's opinions, a story. Scholars call these thinkers the Presocratics, because they came before Socrates (died 399 BC).

Our best early witness is Aristotle (384–322 BC), who wrote about 230 years after Thales. Our fullest is Diogenes Laertius, who wrote about 800 years after him, around AD 230, in a book called Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers. Diogenes was a collector, not a critic: he copied from many older books, often naming them, and he mixes good evidence with gossip. So we read him the way a historian reads an old family story: with interest, and with care.
background.key: No book by the first philosophers survives; we know them from later writers, chiefly Aristotle (about 230 years later) and Diogenes Laertius (about 800 years later).

paras: The main reading is Diogenes Laertius on Thales and on three thinkers who followed him: Anaximander and Anaximenes, also of Miletus, and Heraclitus of nearby Ephesus. Then a short passage from Herodotus, the first Greek historian, who wrote about 150 years after Thales and tells the most famous story about him: the eclipse.
The comparison is the opening of Genesis, which you read in 'In the beginning'. It also starts with water. Setting them side by side shows what kind of answer each one is giving.
background.key: We read Diogenes on Thales and his successors, Herodotus on the eclipse, and then the first verses of Genesis for comparison.

before: How many times does Diogenes say 'as some say' or name another writer? What does that tell you about his evidence?
Which of Thales's ideas could someone check for themselves?
Do Anaximander and Heraclitus agree with Thales?
sessions.readWhy: Diogenes Laertius on Thales and his successors, and Herodotus on the eclipse: the oldest stories about the first natural philosophers.

paras: After having been immersed in state affairs he applied himself to speculations in natural philosophy; though, as some people state, he left no writings behind him. For the book on Naval Astronomy, which is attributed to him is said in reality to be the work of Phocus the Samian.

According to others he wrote two books, and no more, about the solstice and the equinox; thinking that everything else was easily to be comprehended. According to other statements, he is said to have been the first who studied astronomy, and who foretold the eclipses and motions of the sun, as Eudemus relates in his history of the discoveries made in astronomy; on which account Xenophanes and Herodotus praise him greatly; and Heraclitus and Democritus confirm this statement.

Some again (one of whom is Chœrilus the poet) say that he was the first person who affirmed that the souls of men were immortal; and he was the first person, too, who discovered the path of the sun from one end of the ecliptic to the other: and who, as one account tells us, defined the magnitude of the sun as being seven hundred and twenty times as great as that of the moon. He was also the first person who called the last day of the month the thirtieth. And likewise the first to converse about natural philosophy, as some say. But Aristotle and Hippias say that he attributed souls also to lifeless things, forming his conjecture from the nature of the magnet, and of amber. And Pamphile relates that he, having learnt geometry from the Egyptians, was the first person to describe a right-angled triangle in a circle, and that he sacrificed an ox in honour of his discovery.

He asserted water to be the principle of all things, and that the world had life, and was full of dæmons: they say, too, that he was the original definer of the seasons of the year, and that it was he who divided the year into three hundred and sixty-five days. And he never had any teacher except during the time that he went to Egypt, and associated with the priests. Hieronymus also says that he measured the Pyramids: watching their shadow, and calculating when they were of the same size as that was. He lived with Thrasybulus the tyrant of Miletus, as we are informed by Minyas.

It is said that once he was led out of his house by an old woman for the purpose of observing the stars, and he fell into a ditch and bewailed himself, on which the old woman said to him—“Do you, O Thales, who cannot see what is under your feet, think that you shall understand what is in heaven?”

And the following are quoted as sayings of his:—“God is the most ancient of all things, for he had no birth: the world is the most beautiful of things, for it is the work of God: place is the greatest of things, for it contains all things: intellect is the swiftest of things, for it runs through everything: necessity is the strongest of things, for it rules everything: time is the wisest of things, for it finds out everything.”

He used to assert that the principle and primary element of all things was the Infinity, giving no exact definition as to whether he meant air or water, or anything else. And he said that the parts were susceptible of change, but that the whole was unchangeable; and that the earth lay in the middle, being placed there as a sort of centre, of a spherical shape. The moon, he said, had a borrowed light, and borrowed it from the sun; and the sun he affirmed to be not less than the earth, and the purest possible fire.

He also was the first discoverer of the gnomon; and he placed some in Lacedæmon on the sun-dials there, as Phavorinus says in his Universal History, and they showed the solstices and the equinoxes; he also made clocks. He was the first person, too, who drew a map of the earth and sea, and he also made a globe; and he published a concise statement of whatever opinions he embraced or entertained; and this treatise was met with by Apollodorus, the Athenian.

Anaximenes, the son of Eurystratus, a Milesian, was a pupil of Anaximander; but some say that he was also a pupil of Parmenides. He said that the principles of everything were the air, and the Infinite; and that the stars moved not under the earth, but around the earth.

He was above all men of a lofty and arrogant spirit, as is plain from his writings, in which he says, “Abundant learning does not form the mind; for if it did, it would have instructed Hesiod, and Pythagoras, and likewise Xenophanes, and Hecatæus. For the only piece of real wisdom is to know that idea, which by itself will govern everything on every occasion.”

In particulars, his doctrines are of this kind. That fire is an element, and that it is by the changes of fire that all things exist; being engendered sometimes by rarity, some times by density. But he explains nothing clearly. He also says, that everything is produced by contrariety, and that everything flows on like a river; that the universe is finite, and that there is one world, and that that is produced from fire, and that the whole world is in its turn again consumed by fire at certain periods, and that all this happens according to fate. That of the contraries, that which leads to production is called war and contest, and that which leads to the conflagration is called harmony and peace; that change is the road leading upward, and the road leading downward; and that the whole world exists according to it.

After this, seeing that Alyattes would not give up the Scythians when Kyaxares demanded them, there had arisen war between the Lydians and the Medes lasting five years; in which years the Medes often discomfited the Lydians and the Lydians often discomfited the Medes (and among others they fought also a battle by night): and as they still carried on the war with equally balanced fortune, in the sixth year a battle took place in which it happened, when the fight had begun, that suddenly the day became night. And this change of the day Thales the Milesian had foretold to the Ionians laying down as a limit this very year in which the change took place. The Lydians however and the Medes, when they saw that it had become night instead of day, ceased from their fighting and were much more eager both of them that peace should be made between them.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
parts.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
parts.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250
parts.title: Thales of Miletus
parts.context: Diogenes Laertius gathered these stories about AD 230 from older books, most of them now lost. Thales lived in Miletus about 624–546 BC. This is C. D. Yonge's translation of 1853; Yonge numbered the sections himself, and his numbers are left out here. Cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Thales was a statesman who turned to the study of nature. People said he studied the stars, foretold an eclipse, measured the pyramids by their shadows, and learned geometry in Egypt. He taught that water is the beginning of all things, and that even a magnet has a kind of soul. There is a famous joke about him falling into a ditch while looking at the stars. And he is said to have spoken of God as the oldest of all things, and of the world as God's beautiful work.

commentary.on: he applied himself to speculations in natural philosophy
commentary.text: 'Natural philosophy' was the old name for what we call science: the love of wisdom (philosophia) about nature (in Greek, physis, from which we get 'physics'). The phrase stayed in use until the 1800s; Newton's great book of 1687 was called The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy.

commentary.on: as some people state, he left no writings behind him
commentary.text: Notice how careful Diogenes is to say where each story comes from: 'some people state', 'according to others', 'as Eudemus relates'. Eudemus was a pupil of Aristotle who wrote a history of astronomy around 320 BC, now lost. Diogenes is passing on a chain of reports.

commentary.on: foretold the eclipses and motions of the sun
commentary.text: This is the most famous claim about Thales, and the Herodotus passage below tells the story. How he could have done it is a real puzzle, which the lecture takes up.

commentary.on: having learnt geometry from the Egyptians, was the first person to describe a right-angled triangle in a circle
commentary.text: The Greeks themselves said they learned from Egypt and Babylon. What is credited to Thales is not measuring but proving: that any triangle drawn in a semicircle has a right angle. Whether he really proved it we cannot know; later Greeks believed he was the first to treat geometry as a matter of general proofs.

commentary.on: he attributed souls also to lifeless things, forming his conjecture from the nature of the magnet, and of amber
commentary.text: Aristotle reports this too (On the Soul I.2). A magnet moves iron; amber, rubbed, picks up straw. Thales reasoned from something he could see to a general conclusion: what moves other things must have a kind of life. It is a wrong conclusion, but it is an argument from evidence.

commentary.on: He asserted water to be the principle of all things
commentary.text: Here is the famous claim. 'Principle' translates the Greek arche: the beginning, the source, what everything comes from and is made of. Aristotle guessed at Thales's reasons: all living things are fed by moisture, and seeds are moist. Water can be solid, liquid and vapour. It was a reasonable guess.

commentary.on: and that the world had life, and was full of dæmons
commentary.text: A 'dæmon' (daimon) in Greek was a spirit or divine power, not necessarily evil. So Thales did not banish the divine. He found it inside nature, rather than in gods who stood outside it and acted on whims.

commentary.on: he measured the Pyramids: watching their shadow, and calculating when they were of the same size as that was
commentary.text: A lovely method: wait until your own shadow is as long as you are tall; at that moment the pyramid's shadow is as long as the pyramid is high. You need no ladder, only a principle that holds for every shape: similar triangles.

commentary.on: Do you, O Thales, who cannot see what is under your feet, think that you shall understand what is in heaven?
commentary.text: Plato tells a version of this joke too (Theaetetus 174a), with a Thracian servant girl laughing. It has been told against scientists and philosophers ever since. Aristotle tells the opposite story: that Thales foresaw a good olive harvest from the stars, hired all the olive presses cheaply, and made a fortune, to show that philosophers could be rich if they wanted to (Politics I.11).

commentary.on: God is the most ancient of all things, for he had no birth: the world is the most beautiful of things, for it is the work of God
commentary.text: These sayings are almost certainly later inventions put in Thales's mouth. But they show something true about how the Greeks remembered him: not as an atheist, but as a man who looked for order in a world he thought beautiful.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
parts.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
parts.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250
parts.title: Anaximander: the boundless
parts.context: Anaximander was Thales's younger fellow citizen, about 610–546 BC. He is the first Greek known to have written a book in prose about nature. One sentence of it survives, quoted a thousand years later.
parts.plain: Anaximander said the source of everything was not water but something without limits, 'the Infinite'. The earth sits in the middle of everything. The moon shines with light borrowed from the sun. He made sundials, drew the first map of the world, and made a model of the heavens.

commentary.on: the principle and primary element of all things was the Infinity
commentary.text: The Greek word is apeiron: the boundless, the unlimited. Anaximander saw a problem in Thales: if everything were water, how could fire exist? Water puts fire out. So the source must be something deeper than any of the things we see. Notice what has happened. A pupil has disagreed with his teacher, and given a reason. That is the beginning of a tradition of criticism.

commentary.on: the earth lay in the middle, being placed there as a sort of centre
commentary.text: Aristotle tells us Anaximander's reason (On the Heavens II.13): the earth stays where it is because it is the same distance from everything, so it has no reason to fall one way rather than another. The earth needs no turtle or giant to hold it up. The physicist Carlo Rovelli has called this one of the greatest leaps in the history of thought. (Diogenes says Anaximander thought the earth was a sphere; other ancient reports say he pictured it as a short drum, and most scholars think they are right.)

commentary.on: The moon, he said, had a borrowed light
commentary.text: True, and an observation anyone can check against the moon's phases. Some scholars think this was first said a little later, by Parmenides or Anaxagoras; Diogenes may be crediting Anaximander with more than he did.

commentary.on: He was the first person, too, who drew a map of the earth and sea
commentary.text: To draw a map, you have to imagine looking down on the world from above, from no particular place. That is the scientist's point of view: the world as it is, not as it looks from my village.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
parts.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
parts.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250
parts.title: Anaximenes: air
parts.context: Anaximenes, about 585–525 BC, was the third of the thinkers of Miletus.
parts.plain: Anaximenes said everything comes from air. He also said the stars go round the earth, not underneath it.

commentary.on: He said that the principles of everything were the air, and the Infinite
commentary.text: Anaximenes went back to a single stuff we can see, air, but with a new idea, reported by later writers: air becomes fire when it thins out and becomes wind, cloud, water, earth and stone as it is packed tighter. For the first time, differences of kind are explained by differences of amount. That is the idea behind all later physics.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
parts.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
parts.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250
parts.title: Heraclitus: fire and flux
parts.context: Heraclitus lived in Ephesus, up the coast from Miletus, about 535–475 BC. He wrote a book of short, riddling sayings, of which about a hundred survive. Diogenes found him arrogant, and says so.
parts.plain: Heraclitus scorned learning without understanding, even in famous men like Pythagoras. He taught that everything comes from fire and returns to fire, that all things flow like a river, and that the world holds together by the tension of opposites, according to a single rule.

commentary.on: Abundant learning does not form the mind
commentary.text: A swipe at Pythagoras, the subject of the next session, still to come. Heraclitus is the first of many philosophers to say that knowing many facts is not the same as understanding.

commentary.on: to know that idea, which by itself will govern everything on every occasion
commentary.text: Yonge's 'idea' stands for Heraclitus's own word, which other fragments give as logos: word, reason, account. Heraclitus believed a single rational order steers everything. Christians later noticed the word: John's Gospel begins 'In the beginning was the Word (logos)'.

commentary.on: everything flows on like a river
commentary.text: The famous saying 'you cannot step into the same river twice' is Plato's summary of Heraclitus (Cratylus 402a). The world is not made of fixed things but of steady processes, like a flame that keeps its shape while its fuel changes.

commentary.on: that which leads to production is called war and contest
commentary.text: Heraclitus saw opposites, hot and cold, day and night, life and death, as needing each other. Strife is not the enemy of order; it is how order is kept. Not every philosopher agreed. That they argued at all is the point.

parts.author: Herodotus
parts.title: The day became night
parts.who: The Greek historian from Halicarnassus who wrote the first great prose history, of the wars between Greeks and Persians.
parts.when: Asia Minor and Athens, about 430 BC
parts.context: Herodotus wrote about 150 years after Thales. He is describing a war between the Lydians, Thales's neighbours inland, and the Medes, from what is now Iran. This is G. C. Macaulay's translation of 1890; two footnote numbers are removed.
parts.plain: In the sixth year of a war between the Lydians and the Medes, in the middle of a battle, the day suddenly turned to night. Thales had told the Ionians it would happen in that year. Both armies stopped fighting and made peace.

commentary.on: suddenly the day became night
commentary.text: A total eclipse of the sun. Modern astronomers can calculate past eclipses exactly, and there was a total eclipse over Asia Minor on 28 May 585 BC. Most historians identify the battle with it, which makes this one of the earliest exactly dated events in Greek history.

commentary.on: Thales the Milesian had foretold to the Ionians laying down as a limit this very year
commentary.text: Note the careful words: not the day or the hour, but the year. Babylonian astronomers had kept records of eclipses for centuries and knew they recur in cycles. Thales may have learned of such a cycle. Some modern scholars doubt he could have predicted a solar eclipse at all, since whether it is seen depends on where you stand; others think a lucky prediction of a year is possible. Either way, the Greeks remembered him as the man who showed that even the most terrifying events in the sky follow a pattern.

commentary.on: ceased from their fighting and were much more eager both of them that peace should be made between them
commentary.text: To the soldiers, the eclipse was an omen from the gods. To Thales, if the story is true, it was a regular event that could be known in advance. The same event, two ways of seeing it: that is the shift this session is about.

read.author: Diogenes Laertius and Herodotus
read.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
read.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
read.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250

paras: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.

parts.title: The deep
parts.context: The first verses of the Bible, probably given their final form in the 500s BC, the same century as Thales, though from a very different world: the small kingdom of Judah and its exiles in Babylon.

commentary.on: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
commentary.text: Genesis does not say what the world is made of. It says who made it, and that it had a beginning. Thales asks: from what? Genesis asks: from whom, and for what? They are not obviously answering the same question.

commentary.on: The earth was formless and empty.
commentary.text: Before God speaks, the world is without form. Like the Greeks, Genesis pictures order coming out of a formless state. Unlike them, it says the order comes from a word spoken by someone.

commentary.on: God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
commentary.text: Here are the waters, before anything else is named. Many ancient peoples, the Babylonians and the Egyptians among them, pictured the world rising out of primeval water. Thales may have inherited that picture and turned it into a theory. Genesis keeps the picture but takes the gods out of the water: the deep is not a goddess to be defeated, as in the Babylonian Enuma Elish, but simply part of what God made. In different ways, both Genesis and Thales took the gods out of nature.

compare.why: Genesis also begins with water. You read it in 'In the beginning'; here are just its first two verses, to set beside Thales and ask what kind of answer each one gives.
compare.title: In the beginning, the waters

paras: The old Greek account of the world was Hesiod's Theogony, written around 700 BC: Chaos, then Earth, then Sky, gods born from gods, a war in heaven. Thunder was Zeus's anger. Earthquakes were Poseidon shaking the ground. Disease was Apollo's arrows.

Thales and his successors did something different. They explained the world by things inside it: water, air, fire, the boundless. They did not deny the divine; Thales said the world was 'full of gods'. But they stopped explaining events by the will of persons who might do anything. They looked for what happens always or for the most part.

Historians used to call this the move 'from myth to reason', or the 'Greek miracle', a phrase made popular by the French writer Ernest Renan in the 1880s. Today most prefer a gentler story. The Greeks borrowed heavily from Babylon and Egypt, and myth did not vanish: Plato himself told myths. But something real did change: the explanations became open to argument.
sections.key: Earlier Greeks explained the world by the gods' will; Thales and his successors explained it by natural things, without denying the divine.

paras: Aristotle wrote the first history of philosophy in Book I of his Metaphysics, about 350 BC. He says that most of the first philosophers looked only for the material cause of things, what they are made of, and that Thales, 'the founder of this kind of philosophy', said it was water. He guesses at Thales's reasons: all things are nourished by moisture, heat itself comes from moisture, and the seeds of everything are moist.

Aristotle also adds a warning that we should keep. He is guessing. Thales left no book, and Aristotle knew him only from reports. Much of what we 'know' about the first philosophers is Aristotle's reconstruction, made to fit Aristotle's own scheme of four causes. (We have no English translation of the Metaphysics old enough to quote here, so this paragraph is in our own words.)
sections.key: Aristotle, our best early witness, called Thales the founder of natural philosophy, but admitted he was reconstructing Thales's reasons.

paras: The philosopher Karl Popper argued in 1958 that the great Ionian invention was not any one theory but a tradition of criticism. Thales taught Anaximander, and Anaximander disagreed with him. Anaximenes disagreed with both. Heraclitus mocked them all. In most ancient schools of wisdom, a pupil's duty was to hand on the master's teaching unchanged. In Miletus the pupil's duty seems to have been to improve it.

This matters more than whether water or air is the answer. A theory that can be argued with can be improved. A theory that cannot be questioned can only be repeated. Science, as later centuries came to practise it, is that tradition of criticism, joined to measurement and experiment.
sections.key: The deepest Ionian invention may have been a tradition of criticism: pupils were free to disagree with their teachers and give reasons.

paras: Of all the Milesians, Anaximander was the boldest. He said the earth floats unsupported in the middle of everything. He said the first living things arose in moisture, and that human beings must once have come from other creatures, since a human baby could not survive alone (reported by later writers). He drew a map of the known world. He wrote one sentence that survives, quoted by Simplicius in the AD 500s: things perish into what they came from 'according to necessity', paying penalty to each other for their injustice 'according to the ordering of time'.

That sentence is a picture of nature as a court of law, with rules everything must keep. The physicist Carlo Rovelli, in a short book on Anaximander (2011), argues that this was the first real scientific revolution: the earth set free in space, and nature governed by laws rather than whims.
sections.key: Anaximander set the earth floating free in space and pictured nature as governed by laws, a step Carlo Rovelli calls the first scientific revolution.

paras: Heraclitus of Ephesus said the world is an ever-living fire, always changing, held together by a logos, a rational order. Change is not the enemy of order; it is how order works.

About a generation later, Parmenides of Elea, a Greek city in southern Italy, argued the opposite. Reason shows, he said, that what is cannot come from what is not, so real change is impossible; the senses deceive us. It sounds absurd, but it forced every later thinker to ask how reason and the senses fit together. The answer of the atomists Leucippus and Democritus, in the 400s BC, was that the world is made of tiny unchanging pieces moving in empty space, and that every change is a rearrangement. Here, 2,400 years early, is the idea of the atom.

Xenophanes of Colophon, another Ionian, turned the new criticism on the gods themselves: if oxen and horses had hands, he said, they would draw gods that looked like oxen and horses. God, he argued, must be one, and nothing like us.
sections.key: Heraclitus saw a world of flux held by a logos; Parmenides denied change; the atomists answered with atoms; Xenophanes criticised gods made in human shape.

paras: No one knows for certain. Historians usually point to several things together. The Ionian cities were rich trading ports in touch with Egypt and Babylon, whose astronomers and surveyors had piled up knowledge for a thousand years. The Greeks had an easy alphabet, so writing was not the secret of a priestly class. There was no single religious authority with a fixed account of the world to defend. And Greek cities argued in public: in assemblies, in law courts, in the market. A habit of argument about laws may have become a habit of argument about nature.

The historian David Lindberg, in The Beginnings of Western Science (1992), adds a caution. The Babylonians had better astronomical data than the Greeks for centuries. What the Greeks added was not data but a demand for explanation: a picture of how the whole works, which others could test.
sections.key: Trade with older civilisations, an easy alphabet, no single priesthood and a culture of public argument probably all helped; the Greeks added a demand for explanation.

paras: Does this mean the Greeks replaced religion with science? Not quite. Thales thought the world was full of gods. Heraclitus spoke of a divine logos. Xenophanes argued for one God. What they rejected was the idea that nature is pushed about by arbitrary divine wills.

Here the Greeks and the Bible are closer than they look. Genesis also takes the gods out of nature: the sun and moon are not deities but 'lights' set in the sky. Both say the world has an order. They differ on where it comes from. For the Greeks, order was in nature itself, eternal. For Genesis, order was given by a Creator who made the world from outside it. Later sessions will show why that difference mattered, still to come.
sections.key: The Greeks and Genesis both took the gods out of nature; they differed on whether its order was eternal or given by a Creator.

debate.question: Was the Ionian beginning a 'Greek miracle', or a step in a longer story?

positions.name: A genuine break
positions.who: John Burnet (Early Greek Philosophy, 1892); Karl Popper; Carlo Rovelli
positions.view: Something new began in Miletus: a search for natural causes for the whole world, carried on by open criticism. Babylon and Egypt had lists and techniques, not explanations of the whole that anyone could argue with.
positions.evidence: The Milesians each corrected the last; Anaximander's free-floating earth; the absence of anything like it in older surviving texts.

positions.name: A borrowing and a continuation
positions.who: Martin West (Early Greek Philosophy and the Orient, 1971); historians of Babylonian astronomy
positions.view: The Greeks themselves said they learned from Egypt and Babylon. Water at the origin, eclipse cycles and much geometry were older. The 'miracle' story flatters the Greeks and forgets their teachers.
positions.evidence: Babylonian eclipse records from the 700s BC; Mesopotamian creation stories beginning in water; Greek reports of Thales studying in Egypt.

positions.name: Myth and reason together
positions.who: F. M. Cornford (From Religion to Philosophy, 1912); G. E. R. Lloyd
positions.view: The first philosophers kept much of the mythical picture, a world born from a first state, ruled by justice and strife, but argued for it. What changed was not the content so much as the habit of giving reasons in public.
positions.evidence: Anaximander's fragment speaks of justice and penalty; Thales said the world was full of gods; Plato still told myths.

debate.agree: All agree that by 500 BC the Greeks were arguing openly about the nature of the whole world, and that this habit, whatever its sources, is one root of Western science.

look.why: There is no painting of Thales at the National Gallery. This is a Renaissance scholar, painted by Sebastiano del Piombo about 1520: a picture of the tradition the Ionians began, two thousand years later. Anaximander, Diogenes tells us, was the first to draw a map and make a globe.
points: A bearded man with shoulder-length dark brown hair, parted in the middle, looks straight at us.
He wears a dark robe over a white shirt with a high collar, against an emerald-green curtain.
On a shelf covered with green, beside his shoulder, stands a globe.
Next to it are an open book with pages of text, a stack of closed books, and a quill resting in an inkwell.
He holds a folded piece of yellowish paper or cloth in one hand.

music.why: Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Sun (1225) calls the sun his brother and water and fire his sister and brother: the same elements the Ionians studied, praised now as creatures, not gods.

think.why: The Ionians began the Greek search for the order of things; see how Athens and Jerusalem, reason and revelation, came together in the West.

check.q: Why do historians treat the stories in Diogenes Laertius with caution?
options: Because he was hostile to philosophers
Because Thales's own books contradict him
Because he wrote in Latin, not Greek
Because he wrote about 800 years after Thales and mixed good sources with gossip, often passing on reports at second or third hand
check.why: Diogenes was a collector; Thales left no books to check him against, and Diogenes himself says 'some say' again and again.

check.q: What was most new about Thales's claim that everything comes from water?
options: That it denied the existence of anything divine
That water is important for life
That it gave a natural explanation of the whole world, which others could argue with and improve
That it was correct
check.why: The claim was wrong, and Thales still thought the world 'full of dæmons'; what was new was a natural explanation open to criticism.

check.q: Anaximander rejected water as the source of everything. What does that show?
options: That Anaximander was more religious than Thales
That Thales was not really a philosopher
That the Milesians had no common method
That a pupil could disagree with his teacher and give a reason, the beginning of a tradition of criticism
check.why: Popper's point: the pupil improves on the master, and says why.

check.q: Herodotus says Thales foretold the eclipse to within a year. What is the most likely explanation, if the story is true?
options: Herodotus invented the eclipse
He received it from an oracle
He calculated the moon's orbit exactly with Greek geometry
He drew on knowledge that eclipses recur in cycles, which Babylonian astronomers had recorded
check.why: Babylonian records reached back centuries; Greek geometry could not yet calculate eclipses. The eclipse itself is real: 28 May 585 BC.

check.q: How does Genesis 1:1–2 differ from Thales's account?
options: Genesis says who made the world and that it had a beginning; Thales says what it is made of
Genesis denies that there was water at the beginning
There is no real difference
Genesis says the world was made of water; Thales says it was made by God
check.why: Thales asks 'from what?'; Genesis asks 'from whom, and for what?' Both take the gods out of nature.

check.q: Which of these best explains why natural philosophy began in Ionia rather than Babylon, which had better astronomical records?
options: Babylon had no interest in the sky
The Ionians were cleverer
The Persians forbade Babylonian science
Ionian cities combined trade with older civilisations, an easy alphabet, no single priesthood and a culture of public argument, and asked for explanations of the whole
check.why: Lindberg: the Greeks added not data but a demand for explanation, in a culture of open argument.

tutorial.question: Was Thales the first scientist?
tutorial.approach: Say first what we know about Thales, and how we know it. Then decide what you mean by 'scientist': someone who looks for natural causes, who argues, who measures, who tests? Weigh the evidence for each in Thales and his successors, and compare what Babylon and Egypt had already done. End with your own judgement.
strong: Notes that our evidence is late and second-hand (Aristotle, Diogenes, Herodotus).
Explains the water claim and why it was a natural, not mythical, explanation.
Uses the eclipse and the pyramids as examples, with their limits.
Discusses the tradition of criticism among the Milesians.
Weighs the debt to Babylon and Egypt fairly.
Distinguishes natural philosophy from modern experimental science.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice one thing you would normally explain with a shrug or a superstition (a run of bad luck, a mood, a breakdown). Ask what its natural cause might be, and check one guess. Then thank God for a world orderly enough to be understood.
sessions.reflect: When you meet an explanation you disagree with, do you argue with it, or simply repeat your own? What would the Milesians do?
takeaways: Around 600 BC in Miletus, Thales said everything comes from water: a natural explanation of the whole world, open to argument.
His successors Anaximander, Anaximenes and Heraclitus each corrected the last, beginning a tradition of criticism.
We know them only from later writers; and like Genesis, they took the gods out of nature, though they saw its order as eternal rather than given.

sessions.title: All is number
sessions.line: A teacher from Samos found that musical harmony is a matter of simple ratios, and his followers concluded that number is the secret of everything.
sessions.plain: Pluck a string, then pluck one exactly half as long: you hear the same note, an octave higher. Pythagoras, or his followers, discovered that the sounds we find beautiful match simple ratios of whole numbers. From this they leapt to a great idea: the whole world is built on number, and number is divine. This session asks who Pythagoras was, what his school really found, and why the Bible's Wisdom of Solomon says God made all things 'by measure, number, and weight'.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed the Ionians looking for the stuff the world is made of: water, air, fire. Pythagoras looked for something else: not the stuff but the pattern. If the Ionians asked 'what is it made of?', the Pythagoreans asked 'what is its shape and proportion?' That question would turn out to be the more powerful one.
answers: Who was Pythagoras, and can we trust what is said about him?
Did Pythagoras discover Pythagoras's theorem?
What does music have to do with mathematics?
What is the 'music of the spheres'?
What did the Bible say about an ordered, measured world?
sessions.finding: Pythagoras's school discovered that music, and they believed the whole world, follow mathematical ratios, and they saw number as divine; the Bible's Wisdom of Solomon says the same order comes from a Creator who loves what he made.

paras: In the last session we met the first natural philosophers of Miletus, around 600 BC: Thales, who said everything comes from water, and his successors, who argued with him. They looked for the one stuff behind everything.

Pythagoras was born on Samos, an island just off the Ionian coast, around 570 BC, a generation after Thales. Around 530 BC he left, perhaps to escape the tyrant Polycrates, and settled in Croton, a Greek city in the toe of Italy. There he founded something between a school, a religious brotherhood and a political party. Its members shared property, kept rules of diet and silence, and believed the soul is reborn in other bodies. After riots in which their meeting houses were burned, the brotherhood spread through southern Italy and Greece.

Pythagoras born on Samos
Pythagoras settles in Croton, southern Italy
Pythagoras dies, probably at Metapontum
Riots against the Pythagoreans in southern Italy
