Kepler's Harmonies of the World revives the music of the spheres

background.key: Pythagoras, born on Samos about 570 BC, founded a brotherhood in Croton, southern Italy, that was part school, part religious order.

paras: Pythagoras wrote nothing, and his followers credited their discoveries to him for centuries. Within a few generations he had become a legend: a man with a golden thigh, who could be in two places at once, who remembered his past lives. The great scholar Walter Burkert (Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism, 1962) argued that the real Pythagoras was a religious teacher of the soul's rebirth rather than a mathematician, and that the mathematics came from his later followers.

So when we say 'Pythagoras discovered', we usually mean 'the Pythagoreans, between about 530 and 400 BC, came to believe'. The earliest witnesses are good and hostile: Xenophanes, who mocked him for hearing a friend's soul in a dog, and Heraclitus, who called him a collector of other people's learning.
background.key: Pythagoras left no writings and quickly became a legend; 'Pythagoras discovered' usually means 'his school came to believe'.

background.h: What is the Wisdom of Solomon?
paras: The comparison in this session comes from a book many readers will not know. The Wisdom of Solomon was written in Greek, probably by a Jewish teacher in Alexandria in Egypt, in the century or so before Jesus. It speaks in the voice of King Solomon, but it is much later than him.

Christians disagree about its status, and it helps to see how. Catholics and Orthodox include it in the Old Testament; they call it 'deuterocanonical', a second layer of the canon. Protestants place it in the Apocrypha, books worth reading but not used to establish doctrine (as the Church of England's Article VI says). Jews do not include it in the Hebrew Bible. Whatever its status, it is a fascinating meeting of Greek and Jewish thought.

cols: Status of the Wisdom of Solomon
rows: Part of the Old Testament (deuterocanonical), confirmed at the Council of Trent, 1546
Part of the Old Testament, as in the Greek Septuagint
In the Apocrypha: read 'for example of life', not for doctrine (Church of England, Article VI)
Not part of the Hebrew Bible
table.note: The World English Bible translates it in its ecumenical edition.

background.key: The Wisdom of Solomon is a Greek-Jewish book from Alexandria, in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament and the Protestant Apocrypha.

paras: The main reading is from Diogenes Laertius's life of Pythagoras, the fullest ancient account we have, written about 750 years after him. It mixes three kinds of report: the man, his rules for living, and the teachings later found in Pythagorean books. Read it asking which parts sound like history and which like legend.

The comparison is from the Wisdom of Solomon, chapter 11, which says God 'arranged all things by measure, number, and weight'. It is the Bible's closest approach to the Pythagorean idea, and it adds something the Pythagoreans did not say.
background.key: We read Diogenes on Pythagoras and his school, then Wisdom 11, where God orders all things by measure, number and weight.

before: What did Pythagoras discover about music, according to Diogenes?
Which teachings are about mathematics, and which about how to live?
In Wisdom 11, why does God order things by measure, and what does he do instead of destroying?
sessions.readWhy: Diogenes Laertius on Pythagoras: the man, his discoveries, and the teaching that number is the beginning of all things.

paras: And Sosicrates, in his Successions, relates that he, having being asked by Leon, the tyrant of the Phliasians, who he was, replied, “A philosopher.” And adds, that he used to compare life to a festival. “And as some people came to a festival to contend for the prizes, and others for the purposes of traffic, and the best as spectators; so also in life, the men of slavish dispositions,” said he, “are born hunters after glory and covetousness, but philosophers are seekers after truth.”

He was the first person, as Timæus says, who asserted that the property of friends is common, and that friendship is equality. And his disciples used to put all their possessions together into one store, and use them in common; and for five years they kept silence, doing nothing but listen to discourses, and never once seeing Pythagoras, until they were approved; after that time they were admitted into his house, and allowed to see him. They also abstained from the use of cypress coffins, because the sceptre of Jupiter was made of that wood, as Hermippus tells us in the second book of his account of Pythagoras.

It was Pythagoras also who carried geometry to perfection, after Mœris had first found out the principles of the elements of that science, as Aristiclides tells us in the second book of his History of Alexander; and the part of the science to which Pythagoras applied himself above all others was arithmetic. He also discovered the numerical relation of sounds on a single string: he also studied medicine. And Apollodorus, the logician, records of him, that he sacrificed a hecatomb, when he had discovered that the square of the hypothenuse of a right-angled triangle is equal to the squares of the sides containing the right angle.
He was also the first person who introduced measures and weights among the Greeks; as Aristoxenus the musician informs us.

That the monad was the beginning of everything. From the monad proceeds an indefinite duad, which is subordinate to the monad as to its cause. That from the monad and the indefinite duad proceed numbers. And from numbers signs. And from these last, lines of which plane figures consist. And from plane figures are derived solid bodies. And from solid bodies sensible bodies, of which last there are four elements; fire, water, earth, and air. And that the world, which is endued with life, and intellect, and which is of a spherical figure, having the earth, which is also spherical, and inhabited all over in its centre, results from a combination of these elements, and derives its motion from them; and also that there are antipodes, and that what is below, as respects us, is above in respect of them.

They also say, that the most important privilege in man is, the being able to persuade his soul to either good or bad. And that men are happy when they have a good soul; yet, that they are never quiet, and that they never retain the same mind long. Also, that an oath is justice; and that on that account, Jupiter is called Jupiter of Oaths (Ὅρκιος). Also, that virtue is harmony, and health, and universal good, and God; on which account everything owes its existence and consistency to harmony. Also, that friendship is a harmonious equality.

Another of his doctrines was, that of all solid figures the sphere was the most beautiful; and of all plane figures, the circle. That old age and all diminution were similar, and also increase and youth were identical. That health was the permanence of form, and disease the destruction of it.
And respecting his having been different people at different times, Xenophanes adds his evidence in an elegiac poem which commences thus:—

They say that once, as passing by he saw
A dog severely beaten, he did pity him,
And spoke as follows to the man who beat him:—
“Stop now, and beat him not; since in his body,
Abides the soul of a dear friend of mine,
Whose voice I recognized as he was crying.”

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
parts.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
parts.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250
parts.title: The man and his discoveries
parts.context: Diogenes wrote about AD 230, drawing on writers from Aristoxenus (about 330 BC), who knew late Pythagoreans, to much later gossip. This is C. D. Yonge's translation of 1853, with his section numbers left out. Cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Pythagoras called himself a 'philosopher', a lover of wisdom, and said life is like a festival where the best people come not to win or to trade but to watch. His followers shared their property and kept silence for five years. He is said to have perfected geometry and arithmetic, discovered that musical notes follow number on a single string, and found the rule about the sides of a right-angled triangle. He also brought measures and weights to the Greeks.

commentary.on: replied, “A philosopher.”
commentary.text: The story goes back to Heraclides of Pontus, a pupil of Plato, and Cicero tells it too (Tusculan Disputations V.3). Philosophos means 'lover of wisdom'. Whether or not Pythagoras coined it, the word stuck: not a wise man, which only God is, but someone who loves wisdom and seeks it.

commentary.on: the best as spectators
commentary.text: The Greek for 'spectator' is theoros, from which we get 'theory'. A theory, first of all, is a way of looking. For the Pythagoreans, the highest life was to look at the order of the world and understand it.

commentary.on: the property of friends is common, and that friendship is equality
commentary.text: The brotherhood was a way of life, not only a school. Plato admired it (Republic X.600b), and early Christian monks were later compared to it. Notice that equality appears here as a kind of proportion: friends are equal as numbers are.

commentary.on: the part of the science to which Pythagoras applied himself above all others was arithmetic
commentary.text: Greek 'arithmetic' was not sums but the study of number itself: odd and even, square and triangular numbers. The Pythagoreans pictured numbers as patterns of dots. Three dots make a triangle; four make a square. The 'tetractys', ten dots in rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4, was so sacred that they swore oaths by it.

commentary.on: He also discovered the numerical relation of sounds on a single string
commentary.text: This is the heart of the session. Stop a string at half its length and it sounds an octave higher: a ratio of 2:1. Stop it at two-thirds and you hear a fifth (3:2); at three-quarters, a fourth (4:3). The notes that sound most harmonious are made from the smallest whole numbers, 1, 2, 3, 4: the numbers of the tetractys. For the first time, something we feel, beauty in sound, turned out to be governed by number.

commentary.on: he sacrificed a hecatomb, when he had discovered that the square of the hypothenuse
commentary.text: A hecatomb is a sacrifice of a hundred oxen, which sits oddly with reports that Pythagoras refused to kill animals; Diogenes himself notes the contradiction a little later. The rule itself was known in Babylon more than a thousand years earlier. What the Greeks would add, as the next session shows, still to come, is a proof that it holds for every right-angled triangle.

commentary.on: He was also the first person who introduced measures and weights among the Greeks
commentary.text: Whether or not it is true, it is telling that the Greeks connected Pythagoras with measures and weights: the tools of trade and of science alike. Hold on to those words for the comparison.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
parts.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
parts.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250
parts.ref: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VIII.25, 32–35 (the Pythagorean teaching)
parts.title: From the monad to the world
parts.context: Diogenes now reports what one Alexander Polyhistor (1st century BC) found in 'Pythagorean notebooks'. Most scholars date this teaching much later than Pythagoras, to Platonists of the 200s or 100s BC who wrote in his name; Diogenes says Aristotle gives a similar account.
parts.plain: Everything begins from the One (the 'monad'). From the One comes the Two, and from them the numbers; from numbers come points, lines, surfaces and solid bodies, and so the four elements and the whole round world, with people living all round the round earth. Virtue, health and God are a kind of harmony. The sphere and the circle are the most beautiful shapes.

commentary.on: That the monad was the beginning of everything.
commentary.text: 'Monad' means 'unit' or 'one'. Here is the boldest Pythagorean idea: not water or air, but number is the arche, the beginning. Aristotle reports the older Pythagoreans thought 'the elements of numbers were the elements of all things' (Metaphysics I.5), though he found it hard to see how a number could be a thing.

commentary.on: And from numbers signs. And from these last, lines of which plane figures consist.
commentary.text: 'Signs' means points. One point, then two make a line, three a plane, four a solid: the tetractys again. Geometry is built up out of number.

commentary.on: having the earth, which is also spherical, and inhabited all over in its centre
commentary.text: A round earth, with 'antipodes': people on the other side whose 'down' is our 'up'. The idea of a spherical earth may well have begun among the Pythagoreans, though by Aristotle's time it rested on evidence.

commentary.on: virtue is harmony, and health, and universal good, and God
commentary.text: 'Harmony' in Greek (harmonia) meant first a joining or fitting together, as a carpenter joins wood, then a musical scale. For the Pythagoreans a good soul, a healthy body and a well-ordered world are all tuned, like a lyre. This idea, that goodness is a kind of right proportion, ran through Plato and Aristotle into the whole of Western ethics.

commentary.on: of all solid figures the sphere was the most beautiful; and of all plane figures, the circle
commentary.text: This aesthetic judgement shaped astronomy for two thousand years: the heavens must move in perfect circles. Only in 1609 did Kepler show, from careful measurement, that the planets move in ellipses. The Pythagorean faith that nature is mathematical was right; their guess about which mathematics was not.

parts.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers

parts.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250

parts.title: The friend in the dog
parts.context: Xenophanes of Colophon, a poet and thinker who lived at the same time as Pythagoras, is our earliest witness. He is making fun of Pythagoras's belief that souls are reborn in other bodies, including animals.
parts.plain: Xenophanes tells how Pythagoras saw a dog being beaten and told the man to stop, because he recognised the voice of a dead friend in the dog's cries.

commentary.on: Abides the soul of a dear friend of mine
commentary.text: This is the oldest surviving mention of Pythagoras by anyone, and it is a joke. But it tells us the real Pythagoras taught the transmigration of souls: the soul is immortal and passes into other bodies. This is why his followers would not eat meat. Mathematics and mysticism were not separate in his school. Both were ways of purifying the soul by bringing it into tune with the order of the world.

read.author: Diogenes Laertius
read.work: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
read.who: A Greek writer of the third century AD who collected stories and opinions of the philosophers from older books, many now lost.
read.when: Probably the eastern Roman Empire, about AD 220–250

paras:
17 For your all-powerful hand
that created the world out of formless matter
didn’t lack means to send upon them a multitude of bears, fierce lions,

18 or newly-created and unknown wild beasts, full of rage,
either breathing out a blast of fiery breath,
or belching out smoke,
or flashing dreadful sparks from their eyes;

19 which had power not only to consume them by their violence,
but to destroy them even by the terror of their sight.

21 For to be greatly strong is yours at all times.
Who could withstand the might of your arm?

22 Because the whole world before you is as a grain in a balance,
and as a drop of dew that comes down upon the earth in the morning.

23 But you have mercy on all men, because you have power to do all things,
and you overlook the sins of men to the end that they may repent.

25 How would anything have endured unless you had willed it?
Or that which was not called by you, how would it have been preserved?

26 But you spare all things, because they are yours,
O Sovereign Lord, you who love the living.

parts.author: Wisdom of Solomon
parts.title: You arranged all things
parts.who: An unnamed Jewish teacher, writing in Greek in the voice of King Solomon.
parts.context: Chapters 11–19 of the Wisdom of Solomon retell the Exodus as a lesson: the plagues on Egypt fitted the Egyptians' own sins. Here the writer pauses to say God could have destroyed them in an instant, but did not. This is the World English Bible's translation, from its ecumenical edition.
parts.plain: God made the world out of formless matter and could have destroyed the wicked with a single breath. But he arranged everything by measure, number and weight. The whole world is like a grain on a scale before him. Yet he is merciful to all, because he loves everything he has made; he would not have made anything he hated.

commentary.on: that created the world out of formless matter
commentary.text: A striking phrase. It uses the language of Greek philosophy, where a craftsman shapes formless matter, as Plato's Timaeus pictured it. Later Jewish and Christian teachers went further and said God made even the matter, out of nothing (2 Maccabees 7:28 already says God did not make the world from things that existed).

commentary.on: but you arranged all things by measure, number, and weight.
commentary.text: The key verse. Measure, number and weight are the very tools Diogenes says Pythagoras brought to the Greeks. But here they are not the source of the world; they are how a Creator made it. For Christian readers this verse became a charter for studying nature: Augustine returned to it again and again, and medieval scholars quoted it to defend mathematics and astronomy.

commentary.on: Because the whole world before you is as a grain in a balance
commentary.text: The image comes from Isaiah 40:15, where nations are 'like a drop in a bucket'. The God who measures the world is far greater than it.

commentary.on: For you love all things that are,
commentary.text: Here is what the Pythagoreans did not say. Their cosmos was harmonious and divine, but it did not love. In Wisdom, the order of the world comes from someone, and the reason for it is love. Measure and mercy belong together.

commentary.on: For you never would have formed anything if you hated it.
commentary.text: The world is ordered because it is wanted. A Christian scientist could take this verse to mean: the world is worth studying, because it is both rational and good.

compare.author: Wisdom of Solomon
compare.why: The Bible's closest parallel to the Pythagorean idea, written in Greek by a Jewish teacher who knew Greek philosophy. Read what it says God does with his ordered power.
compare.title: Measure, number and weight

paras: The discovery the Pythagoreans valued most was musical. The later story, told by Nicomachus around AD 100 and passed to the Middle Ages by Boethius, says Pythagoras heard blacksmiths' hammers ringing in harmony and found their weights were in simple ratios. As physics, the hammer story is wrong: hammer weights do not work that way. But the string does. An instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, the monochord, shows it to anyone.

Halve the string and it sounds an octave higher (2:1). Two-thirds gives the fifth (3:2), three-quarters the fourth (4:3). Archytas of Tarentum, a Pythagorean friend of Plato, worked out the mathematics of musical scales around 380 BC. This was the first law of nature ever stated in numbers: a fact about the world, something we hear and feel, that turned out to be exactly mathematical.
sections.key: The octave (2:1), fifth (3:2) and fourth (4:3) on a string were perhaps the first law of nature ever stated in numbers.

paras: The rule that in a right-angled triangle the square on the longest side equals the squares on the other two is far older than Pythagoras. A Babylonian tablet of about 1800 BC, now at Columbia University and known as Plimpton 322, lists sets of whole numbers that fit it, such as 3, 4 and 5. Another Babylonian tablet, YBC 7289 at Yale, gives the diagonal of a square to six decimal places. Indian builders of altars, in the Sulba Sutras of perhaps 800–500 BC, also knew the rule.

What we cannot find before the Greeks is a proof: an argument showing that it must be true for every right-angled triangle, not just the ones measured. Whether Pythagoras himself proved it, no one knows. The first proof that survives is in Euclid, about 300 BC, which is where we go next.

rows: Lists of number triples fitting the rule (Plimpton 322)
The rule, used for laying out altars (Sulba Sutras)
Credited with the theorem; whether they proved it is unknown
table.note: Dates for the Sulba Sutras are uncertain.

sections.key: The rule was known in Babylon a thousand years before Pythagoras; the Greek contribution was proof, first surviving in Euclid.

paras: If all is number, every length should be a ratio of whole numbers. Then someone in the school found it was not so. The diagonal of a square cannot be measured as any exact fraction of its side: in our terms, the square root of 2 is irrational. Aristotle mentions the proof, which uses odd and even numbers (Prior Analytics I.23).

Later legend said the man who revealed this, Hippasus of Metapontum, was drowned at sea by the gods, or by his brothers. That is a legend. But the discovery was real and deep. It showed that the world of geometry is larger than the world of whole numbers, and that reasoning can overturn what a whole school believed. The Greeks responded by building a theory of proportion that worked for any lengths, which Euclid recorded.
sections.key: The discovery that the diagonal of a square is not a ratio of whole numbers shook the Pythagorean faith that all is number, and showed reason correcting belief.

paras: If music is number and the heavens are number, the heavens must make music. The Pythagoreans said the sun, moon and planets, moving at different speeds, sound notes in a cosmic harmony we cannot hear because it has sounded since our birth. Aristotle reported the idea and rejected it (On the Heavens II.9). Plato put it into the myth at the end of his Republic, with a siren singing on each circle of the heavens.

The idea lasted two thousand years. Boethius, around AD 520, divided music into three: the music of the world (musica mundana), the harmony of soul and body (musica humana), and the music we play. Shakespeare's Lorenzo says in The Merchant of Venice that there is not the smallest star 'but in his motion like an angel sings'. And in 1619 the astronomer Johannes Kepler, in his Harmonies of the World, published his third law of planetary motion, an exact numerical relation, in a book about the harmonies he believed God had built into the solar system.
sections.key: The music of the spheres, the harmony of the heavens, ran from the Pythagoreans through Plato and Boethius to Kepler, who found a real planetary law while looking for it.

paras: Archytas called arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy 'sisters', and Plato repeats the word in the Republic. All four study number: number in itself, number in space, number in time, and number in space and time together. In the Middle Ages these became the quadrivium, the 'four ways', taught in every cathedral school and university after the grammar, logic and rhetoric of the trivium.

So when a student at Oxford or Paris in 1300 studied music, it meant the mathematics of harmony, not playing the lute. This is one of the clearest lines from Pythagoras's Croton to the classrooms of Christian Europe.
sections.key: Arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy, the Pythagorean 'sisters', became the medieval quadrivium of the universities.

paras: In one sense, astonishingly so. In 1623 Galileo wrote that the book of nature is written in the language of mathematics, its letters triangles, circles and other figures (The Assayer; our own words). Newton's law of gravity, Maxwell's equations for electricity and light (1865), and the equations of quantum physics all describe nature in numbers and ratios far more exact than the Pythagoreans dreamed. Particles behave in ways first predicted by mathematics, sometimes decades before anyone could detect them.

In another sense, no. Number is not a thing, and the world is not made of numbers in the way a wall is made of bricks. What modern science found is that the world's behaviour can be described by mathematics, not that mathematics is what the world is made of. Some physicists, such as Max Tegmark, do argue that reality simply is a mathematical structure; most do not. The puzzle of why mathematics fits the world so well is one this journey will return to at its end, still to come.
sections.key: Modern physics vindicates the Pythagorean faith that nature is described by mathematics, though not the belief that things are made of numbers.

paras: The Pythagoreans did not see mathematics as a cold tool. It was a religious path. Studying the harmony of the world tuned the soul, purified it, and brought it closer to the divine. Number was itself divine.

Jewish and Christian readers took much of this and changed one thing. In the Wisdom of Solomon, number is not God; it is how God made the world. God measures; he is not the measure. That change kept the reverence and the confidence that nature is mathematical, but put them under a God who loves what he makes. Augustine, writing on the six days of creation, asked how measure, number and weight could be in God before anything existed to be measured, and answered that God is himself the measure without measure, the number without number, the weight without weight (The Literal Meaning of Genesis IV.3–4; our own words).
sections.key: For the Pythagoreans number was divine; for the Wisdom of Solomon and Augustine, number is how a loving God made the world.

debate.question: Was Pythagoras a mathematician or a mystic?

positions.name: Mainly a religious teacher
positions.who: Walter Burkert; Carl Huffman (in part)
positions.view: The earliest witnesses (Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Herodotus) speak of the soul's rebirth and wide learning, not proofs. The mathematics belongs to later Pythagoreans like Philolaus and Archytas, and the rest was credited to the founder.
positions.evidence: No early source credits Pythagoras with a proof; the theorem was known long before; the legends grow over time.

positions.name: A founder of mathematical science
positions.who: The ancient tradition (Aristoxenus, Proclus); some modern historians such as Leonid Zhmud
positions.view: The school's distinctive work in number, harmony and astronomy must have started somewhere, and the simplest explanation is its founder. The musical ratios are the kind of discovery one person makes.
positions.evidence: Aristoxenus, who knew late Pythagoreans, says he honoured the study of number above all; the consistent link between the school and the musical ratios.

positions.name: Both at once
positions.who: Many historians of ancient thought
positions.view: For the Pythagoreans there was no line between mysticism and mathematics. Studying the order of the world was how the soul was purified. To ask which he was is to impose a modern division.
positions.evidence: Number is called divine; harmony describes soul, body and cosmos; the rules of life and the mathematics come from the same school.

debate.agree: All agree that the Pythagorean school, whatever its founder did, taught that the world is ordered by number, and that this idea shaped Plato, medieval learning and modern science.

look.why: There is no portrait of Pythagoras at the National Gallery. This is François Boucher's Allegory of Music (1764), a figure of Music herself, not of the Greeks. It is here for the lyre: the strings on which, the ancients said, the Pythagoreans first heard number.
points: A woman in flowing pastel robes sits on a bank of clouds, leaning back on one elbow.
With one hand she props a lyre against her knee and points to it with the other.
A winged child-like putto reaches forward to strum the lyre's strings.
Another putto hovers above, holding up a ring of laurel leaves in one hand and a flute in the other.
Two white doves with spread wings support an open book of sheet music under her elbow.
A gold horn wrapped in laurel lies at the bottom of the picture.

music.why: Tallis's motet of about 1570 weaves forty separate voices, in eight choirs of five, into one harmony: a cathedral built of proportion and number.

learn.why: The Bible's sentence about an ordered world, joined to the reason it exists: measure and love together.

think.why: The Pythagoreans felt that the order of the world was holy. Read on wonder as a way to God.

check.q: What does the musical discovery on a single string show, and why did it matter so much to the Pythagoreans?
options: That the octave was invented by Pythagoras
That the sounds we find harmonious match simple whole-number ratios, so beauty itself seemed governed by number
That music is only a matter of taste
That strings make louder sounds when shorter
check.why: Octave 2:1, fifth 3:2, fourth 4:3: something felt turned out to be exactly mathematical, the seed of 'all is number'.

check.q: The 'Pythagorean' rule was known in Babylon around 1800 BC. What, then, was new in Greek mathematics?
options: Proof: showing that the rule must hold for every right-angled triangle
Nothing; the Greeks copied Babylon
The use of whole numbers
Writing numbers down
check.why: Babylon had lists of cases; the Greeks sought general proofs, first surviving in Euclid.

check.q: Why was the discovery that the diagonal of a square cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers a 'scandal'?
options: Because it was discovered by an outsider
Because it contradicted the school's belief that all things are whole numbers and their ratios
Because squares were sacred
Because it was used in magic
check.why: If all is number, every length should be a ratio; the diagonal is not. Reason overturned a school's belief.

check.q: Xenophanes's joke about the dog is our oldest evidence about Pythagoras. What does it tell us?
options: That the real Pythagoras taught that souls are reborn in other bodies, so religion and mathematics went together in his school
That Xenophanes was a Pythagorean
That Pythagoras loved animals
That Pythagoras was a mathematician
check.why: The earliest witness speaks of transmigration, not proofs, which is why Burkert thought him mainly a religious teacher.

check.q: What is the most important difference between the Pythagorean view of number and Wisdom of Solomon 11?
options: Wisdom denies that the world is ordered
There is no difference
For the Pythagoreans number itself is divine; in Wisdom, God orders the world by number, and does so out of love
Wisdom says the world is made of water
check.why: 'You arranged all things by measure, number, and weight… For you love all things that are.' God measures; he is not the measure.

check.q: Why might the music of the spheres, an idea now known to be false, still have helped science?
options: It was the reason for the round earth
It kept alive the belief that the heavens follow exact numerical laws, and Kepler found his third law while looking for such harmonies
It explained eclipses
It was proved by Aristotle
check.why: A wrong picture with the right faith, that nature is mathematical, led Kepler to a real law in 1619.

tutorial.question: 'All is number.' What did the Pythagoreans mean, and were they right?
tutorial.approach: Explain what we know of Pythagoras and why the evidence is difficult. Then set out the school's discoveries (musical ratios, the theorem, the irrational) and the leap from them to 'all is number'. Weigh it against modern science, which describes the world in mathematics, and against Wisdom 11, which puts number under a Creator. End with your own view.
strong: Distinguishes the legendary Pythagoras from the work of his school.
Explains the musical ratios clearly and why they were persuasive.
Notes the Babylonian evidence and the Greek contribution of proof.
Uses the irrational diagonal as a case of reason correcting belief.
Compares number as divine with number as God's way of making.
Connects the idea to modern mathematical physics, with care.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: find something ordered by number in your ordinary day (the beats of a piece of music, the spiral of a sunflower or pine cone, the proportions of a building) and look at it slowly for five minutes. Then read Wisdom 11:20–24 and give thanks that the order is loved.
sessions.reflect: Do you think the world is beautiful because it is ordered, or ordered because someone wanted it to be beautiful?
takeaways: The Pythagoreans found that musical harmony follows simple ratios, and concluded that all things are number, and that number is divine.
The theorem was known in Babylon long before; the Greek gift was proof, and the irrational diagonal showed reason correcting belief.
The Wisdom of Solomon says God 'arranged all things by measure, number, and weight', and adds that he loves what he made.

sessions.title: Proof
sessions.line: In Alexandria around 300 BC, Euclid built the whole of geometry from a handful of starting points, and gave the West its model of certain knowledge.
sessions.plain: How can you know something for certain, not just for now or for most cases, but always? The Greek answer was proof: start from a few things everyone accepts, and reason step by step until the conclusion cannot be denied. Euclid's Elements did this for all of geometry, and for two thousand years it was the model of what knowledge should look like. This session asks what a proof is, why Plato thought geometry lifted the mind to eternal truth, and what happened when one of Euclid's starting points turned out to be optional.
sessions.why: Session 2 ended with a puzzle. The Pythagoreans found that the diagonal of a square is not a ratio of whole numbers, and a whole school's belief gave way, not to new measurements, but to an argument. That is the power this session studies: proof, reasoning that forces agreement. Babylon knew the 'Pythagorean' rule from examples; the Greeks wanted to show it must be true.
answers: What did Euclid prove, and how?
What are axioms, and why start from them?
Why did Plato think geometry was more than a practical skill?
Why did Lincoln, Descartes and Newton all study Euclid?
What is non-Euclidean geometry, and did it overthrow Euclid?
sessions.finding: Euclid built all of geometry from a few definitions, postulates and common notions, and his method of proof became the model of certain knowledge for two thousand years, until the discovery that his starting points could be chosen otherwise.

paras: We have met the Ionians, who looked for natural causes, and the Pythagoreans, who found number at the heart of things, and discovered that some lengths cannot be measured by whole numbers. In the 400s and 300s BC Greek mathematicians worked hard on the problems this raised: Hippocrates of Chios (not the doctor) wrote the first 'Elements' around 430 BC, now lost; Eudoxus of Cnidus, a friend of Plato, built a theory of proportion that worked for any lengths at all.

Then, around 300 BC, in the new Greek city of Alexandria in Egypt, Euclid gathered the work of two centuries into one book. Its success was so complete that the older books were no longer copied, and they are lost.

background.key: Euclid, around 300 BC in Alexandria, gathered two centuries of Greek geometry into the Elements, which replaced every book before it.

paras: Almost nothing is known about him. Proclus, a philosopher writing in Athens about 750 years later, says he lived under the first King Ptolemy, who ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great, and tells a story that the king asked whether there was a shorter way to learn geometry than the Elements, and Euclid replied that there is no royal road to geometry. The same story is told of others, so it may be a legend.
Alexandria was the boom town of the Greek world: a royal capital with a 'Museum', a house of the Muses where scholars were paid to study, and the famous Library. Euclid probably taught there.
background.key: Almost nothing is known of Euclid except that he worked in Alexandria around 300 BC, probably at the royal Museum.

paras: The Elements has thirteen 'books' (we would say chapters): plane geometry, proportion, the theory of numbers, irrational lengths, and solid geometry, ending with the five regular solids. Book I begins with three lists, given here in our own words, since we have no old enough English translation to quote.

Definitions (23 of them): for example, a point is what has no parts; a line is length without breadth; a circle is a figure whose edge is everywhere the same distance from its centre. Postulates (5), things we are asked to grant: a straight line can be drawn between any two points; it can be extended; a circle can be drawn with any centre and radius; all right angles are equal; and the fifth, the parallel postulate, which says, roughly, that through a point beside a line you can draw only one line that never meets it. Common notions (5), truths about any quantities: things equal to the same thing are equal to each other; if equals are added to equals, the results are equal; the whole is greater than the part.

From these, Book I proves 48 propositions. The first: how to build a triangle with three equal sides on a given line, with two circles. The 47th: in a right-angled triangle, the square on the longest side equals the squares on the other two. That is the first surviving proof of Pythagoras's theorem.
background.key: Book I starts from 23 definitions, 5 postulates and 5 common notions, and proves 48 propositions, among them the first surviving proof of Pythagoras's theorem (I.47).

paras: Since we cannot quote Euclid in an old enough translation, the main reading is Plato, writing about seventy years before him, on what geometers do. In the Republic Plato describes their method exactly: they begin from things they assume, their 'hypotheses', and reason down to a conclusion. Then he says why it matters: geometry is knowledge of what is eternal, and it 'will draw the soul towards truth'.

The comparison is from René Descartes, who in 1637 tried to rebuild all of human knowledge on the model of the geometers' 'long chains of simple and easy reasonings'. It shows how far Euclid's method travelled.
background.key: Plato describes the geometers' method and why it matters; Descartes, two thousand years later, tries to rebuild all knowledge on it.

before: What do geometers 'assume', according to Plato, and do they prove those assumptions?
When a geometer draws a square, what is he really thinking about?
What does Descartes think the geometers have that other sciences lack?
sessions.readWhy: Plato on the geometers: they start from hypotheses and reason step by step, and their subject is eternal truth.

paras: Thus:—There are two subdivisions, in the lower of which the soul uses the figures given by the former division as images; the enquiry can only be hypothetical, and instead of going upwards to a principle descends to the other end; in the higher of the two, the soul passes out of hypotheses, and goes up to a principle which is above hypotheses, making no use of images as in the former case, but proceeding only in and through the ideas themselves.
I do not quite understand your meaning, he said.

Then I will try again; you will understand me better when I have made some preliminary remarks. You are aware that students of geometry, arithmetic, and the kindred sciences assume the odd and the even and the figures and three kinds of angles and the like in their several branches of science; these are their hypotheses, which they and every body are supposed to know, and therefore they do not deign to give any account of them either to themselves or others; but they begin with them, and go on until they arrive at last, and in a consistent manner, at their conclusion?
Yes, he said, I know.

And do you not know also that although they make use of the visible forms and reason about them, they are thinking not of these, but of the ideals which they resemble; not of the figures which they draw, but of the absolute square and the absolute diameter, and so on—the forms which they draw or make, and which have shadows and reflections in water of their own, are converted by them into images, but they are really seeking to behold the things themselves, which can only be seen with the eye of the mind?
That is true.

And of this kind I spoke as the intelligible, although in the search after it the soul is compelled to use hypotheses; not ascending to a first principle, because she is unable to rise above the region of hypothesis, but employing the objects of which the shadows below are resemblances in their turn as images, they having in relation to the shadows and reflections of them a greater distinctness, and therefore a higher value.
I understand, he said, that you are speaking of the province of geometry and the sister arts.

And when I speak of the other division of the intelligible, you will understand me to speak of that other sort of knowledge which reason herself attains by the power of dialectic, using the hypotheses not as first principles, but only as hypotheses—that is to say, as steps and points of departure into a world which is above hypotheses, in order that she may soar beyond them to the first principle of the whole; and clinging to this and then to that which depends on this, by successive steps she descends again without the aid of any sensible object, from ideas, through ideas, and in ideas she ends.

I understand you, he replied; not perfectly, for you seem to me to be describing a task which is really tremendous; but, at any rate, I understand you to say that knowledge and being, which the science of dialectic contemplates, are clearer than the notions of the arts, as they are termed, which proceed from hypotheses only: these are also contemplated by the understanding, and not by the senses: yet, because they start from hypotheses and do not ascend to a principle, those who contemplate them appear to you not to exercise the higher reason upon them, although when a first principle is added to them they are cognizable by the higher reason. And the habit which is concerned with geometry and the cognate sciences I suppose that you would term understanding and not reason, as being intermediate between opinion and reason.

You have quite conceived my meaning, I said; and now, corresponding to these four divisions, let there be four faculties in the soul—reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, faith (or conviction) to the third, and perception of shadows to the last—and let there be a scale of them, and let us suppose that the several faculties have clearness in the same degree that their objects have truth.

Yes, I said, but for that purpose a very little of either geometry or calculation will be enough; the question relates rather to the greater and more advanced part of geometry—whether that tends in any degree to make more easy the vision of the idea of good; and thither, as I was saying, all things tend which compel the soul to turn her gaze towards that place, where is the full perfection of being, which she ought, by all means, to behold.
True, he said.
Then if geometry compels us to view being, it concerns us; if becoming only, it does not concern us?
Yes, that is what we assert.
Yet anybody who has the least acquaintance with geometry will not deny that such a conception of the science is in flat contradiction to the ordinary language of geometricians.
How so?

They have in view practice only, and are always speaking, in a narrow and ridiculous manner, of squaring and extending and applying and the like—they confuse the necessities of geometry with those of daily life; whereas knowledge is the real object of the whole science.
Certainly, he said.
Then must not a further admission be made?
What admission?
That the knowledge at which geometry aims is knowledge of the eternal, and not of aught perishing and transient.
That, he replied, may be readily allowed, and is true.
Then, my noble friend, geometry will draw the soul towards truth, and create the spirit of philosophy, and raise up that which is now unhappily allowed to fall down.
Nothing will be more likely to have such an effect.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: The Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy, the first school of higher learning in the West.
parts.title: What geometers do
parts.context: Plato's Republic is a long conversation, written about 375 BC, in which Socrates talks with Plato's brothers about justice and education. Here Socrates is describing the 'divided line', four levels of knowing, from shadows up to the highest understanding. 'He' is Plato's brother Glaucon. This is Benjamin Jowett's translation.
parts.plain: Socrates says there are two kinds of thinking about things the mind alone can grasp. Geometers use drawings, but they are not thinking about the drawings; they are thinking about the perfect square and the perfect diagonal, which can only be seen by the mind. They begin from assumptions, like odd and even and the kinds of angles, which they do not prove, and reason from them to a conclusion. Philosophy, Socrates says, goes further: it questions even the assumptions, and climbs to a first principle above them.

commentary.on: students of geometry, arithmetic, and the kindred sciences assume the odd and the even and the figures and three kinds of angles
commentary.text: Here, seventy years before Euclid, is the method of the Elements: you begin from certain assumptions. The three kinds of angles are acute, right and obtuse. Plato's word is 'hypotheses', things 'placed under' an argument as its foundation.

commentary.on: they do not deign to give any account of them either to themselves or others; but they begin with them, and go on until they arrive at last, and in a consistent manner, at their conclusion
commentary.text: This is exactly what a proof is: from accepted starting points, by steps that each follow from the last, to a conclusion that cannot be denied without denying the starting points. Notice 'in a consistent manner': every step must agree with every other.

commentary.on: they are thinking not of these, but of the ideals which they resemble; not of the figures which they draw, but of the absolute square and the absolute diameter
commentary.text: A drawn line is never perfectly straight and has some width. Yet geometry is about lines with no width at all. Plato concluded that geometry is about things no eye has seen: perfect forms, grasped by the mind. 'Diameter' here means the diagonal of the square, the very line the Pythagoreans found they could not measure by whole numbers.

commentary.on: which can only be seen with the eye of the mind
commentary.text: For Plato this was the great lesson of mathematics: there are truths more certain than anything we see, and the mind can reach them. It is one reason mathematics stood at the centre of his school.

commentary.on: using the hypotheses not as first principles, but only as hypotheses
commentary.text: Plato's criticism of the geometers. They take their starting points on trust. A philosopher should ask why those starting points are true. Two thousand years later, mathematicians did exactly that, with surprising results, as the lecture explains.

commentary.on: the habit which is concerned with geometry and the cognate sciences I suppose that you would term understanding and not reason
commentary.text: Plato ranks geometry high, above opinion and belief, but just below the highest knowledge. It is a training for the mind on its way to the Good.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: The Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy, the first school of higher learning in the West.
parts.title: Geometry draws the soul towards truth
parts.context: A little later Socrates and Glaucon discuss what the future rulers of their ideal city should study. They have agreed on arithmetic. Now they turn to geometry.
parts.plain: Glaucon says geometry is useful in war, for laying out camps. Socrates says a little will do for that. The real value of geometry is that it is about what always is, not what comes and goes. Geometers talk as if they were doing practical jobs, 'squaring' and 'applying', but really they are seeking knowledge of the eternal. So geometry draws the soul towards truth.

commentary.on: a very little of either geometry or calculation will be enough
commentary.text: The Egyptians and Babylonians used geometry to measure fields and build pyramids. Plato does not despise that, but says it is not the point.

commentary.on: they confuse the necessities of geometry with those of daily life
commentary.text: Geometers' words were taken from practical life: 'squaring' a figure, 'applying' one area to another. Plato thinks the words hide what geometry really is: not doing but knowing.

commentary.on: That the knowledge at which geometry aims is knowledge of the eternal, and not of aught perishing and transient.
commentary.text: The key sentence. A triangle drawn in sand is gone with the tide, but the truth that its angles add up to two right angles is the same in every age and every place. Plato saw in this a glimpse of eternity.

commentary.on: geometry will draw the soul towards truth, and create the spirit of philosophy
commentary.text: Later tradition said that over the door of Plato's Academy was written 'Let no one ignorant of geometry enter'. The earliest source for that is about 800 years later, so it is probably a legend; but it fits this passage exactly.

read.author: Plato
read.who: The Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy, the first school of higher learning in the West.

paras: The first was never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such; that is to say, carefully to avoid precipitancy and prejudice, and to comprise nothing more in my judgement than what was presented to my mind so clearly and distinctly as to exclude all ground of doubt.
The second, to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.

The third, to conduct my thoughts in such order that, by commencing with objects the simplest and easiest to know, I might ascend by little and little, and, as it were, step by step, to the knowledge of the more complex; assigning in thought a certain order even to those objects which in their own nature do not stand in a relation of antecedence and sequence.
And the last, in every case to make enumerations so complete, and reviews so general, that I might be assured that nothing was omitted.

The long chains of simple and easy reasonings by means of which geometers are accustomed to reach the conclusions of their most difficult demonstrations, had led me to imagine that all things, to the knowledge of which man is competent, are mutually connected in the same way, and that there is nothing so far removed from us as to be beyond our reach, or so hidden that we cannot discover it, provided only we abstain from accepting the false for the true, and always preserve in our thoughts the order necessary for the deduction of one truth from another. And I had little difficulty in determining the objects with which it was necessary to commence, for I was already persuaded that it must be with the simplest and easiest to know, and, considering that of all those who have hitherto sought truth in the sciences, the mathematicians alone have been able to find any demonstrations, that is, any certain and evident reasons, I did not doubt but that such must have been the rule of their investigations.

parts.author: René Descartes
parts.ref: Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part II
parts.title: Four rules from geometry
parts.who: French philosopher and mathematician, inventor of coordinate geometry.
parts.context: René Descartes (1596–1650) published his Discourse on Method in 1637 as the preface to his works on geometry, optics and weather. Here he sets out the four rules he chose for his thinking. This is John Veitch's translation of 1850; one word printed in italics in the source ('last') is given plainly.
parts.plain: Descartes gives himself four rules: accept nothing as true unless it is so clear you cannot doubt it; split every problem into small parts; go in order, from the simplest to the hardest; and check that nothing has been left out. He says the geometers' long chains of simple steps made him hope that everything we can know is connected in the same way, and that only mathematicians had ever found real proofs.

commentary.on: never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such
commentary.text: Descartes wants for all knowledge the certainty of a proof in geometry. This rule led him, a few pages later, to doubt everything he could and look for one thing beyond doubt.

commentary.on: by commencing with objects the simplest and easiest to know, I might ascend by little and little, and, as it were, step by step
commentary.text: This is Euclid's order: from definitions, to the simplest propositions, to the hardest, each built on the ones before. Proposition 47 depends on many of the 46 before it.

commentary.on: The long chains of simple and easy reasonings by means of which geometers are accustomed to reach the conclusions of their most difficult demonstrations
commentary.text: Here is the hope Euclid gave the West: no single step is hard, yet together they reach truths nobody could see at a glance. 'Demonstration' was the technical word for a proof.

commentary.on: the mathematicians alone have been able to find any demonstrations, that is, any certain and evident reasons
commentary.text: Descartes thought every other field, from medicine to philosophy, was a matter of opinion and dispute. Only geometry had settled its questions. His hope that the same method would settle everything was magnificent, and, most later philosophers think, too optimistic: most of life cannot be reduced to a few self-evident axioms.

compare.author: René Descartes
compare.ref: Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part II
compare.why: Two thousand years after Euclid, a French philosopher tried to rebuild all human knowledge on the geometers' method. Read why he trusted it.
compare.title: Long chains of reasoning

paras: A proof is an argument that leaves no room for doubt, given its starting points. Measure a thousand right-angled triangles and you have strong evidence for Pythagoras's rule; but the thousand-and-first might fail. Prove it from the axioms, and it cannot fail for any triangle that satisfies them.

That is the difference between Babylonian and Greek mathematics. The Babylonians had rules that worked, with worked examples. The Greeks asked why the rules worked, and answered with arguments that hold always and everywhere. Aristotle, in his Posterior Analytics, described the ideal of such knowledge: we know something scientifically when we know its cause and that it cannot be otherwise, by demonstration from first principles that are themselves not demonstrated (our own words).
sections.key: A proof shows that a conclusion must follow from its starting points, for every case: the Greek step beyond Babylonian rules.

sections.h: Starting points: why you cannot prove everything
paras: If every claim needs a proof, the proofs would go back for ever. So every chain of reasoning has to start somewhere. Euclid's starting points come in three kinds. Definitions say what words mean. Common notions are true of any quantity: the whole is greater than the part. Postulates are specific to geometry: a straight line can be drawn between two points; a circle can be drawn with any centre.

Later writers called these 'axioms', from a Greek word meaning 'what is thought worthy'. The idea is that they are so simple that any rational person will grant them. Then everything else must be granted too. The power of the method is that a whole world of truths, hundreds of propositions in thirteen books, rests openly on a page of starting points anyone can inspect.
sections.key: Every proof needs starting points; Euclid set his out openly, as definitions, postulates and common notions, so anyone could inspect them.

paras: Proposition 1: to build an equilateral triangle on a given straight line. Put the point of a compass on one end of the line, and draw a circle through the other end. Do the same from the other end. Where the circles cross, join that point to both ends. Every side is a radius of one of the circles, so all three sides are equal. It is a child's construction, and a perfect proof.

Proposition 47 is Pythagoras's theorem. Euclid draws a square on each side of the right-angled triangle and drops a line from the right angle across the biggest square, splitting it into two rectangles. Then he shows, with pairs of equal triangles, that each rectangle equals one of the smaller squares. Students called the figure 'the windmill' or 'the bride's chair'. It uses earlier propositions about triangles and parallel lines, and so, ultimately, every postulate, including the fifth.
sections.key: Proposition 1 builds an equilateral triangle with two circles; Proposition 47 proves Pythagoras's theorem by cutting the largest square into two pieces equal to the smaller squares.

paras: Ptolemy's astronomy and Archimedes' physics were written in Euclid's style. The Elements was translated into Arabic in Baghdad around 800, and into Latin from the Arabic by the English scholar Adelard of Bath in the 1120s. It was printed in Venice in 1482, and has often been called the most widely printed book after the Bible, though no one has counted exactly.

Isaac Newton set out his Principia (1687) like Euclid, with definitions, axioms or laws, and propositions. The Dutch philosopher Spinoza wrote his Ethics (1677) 'in geometrical order'. And Abraham Lincoln, in a short autobiography of 1860, wrote that after his term in Congress he studied and nearly mastered the six books of Euclid. A minister, J. P. Gulliver, later recalled Lincoln telling him why: as a young lawyer he kept meeting the word 'demonstrate', realised he did not know what it meant, and went home to study Euclid until he did (our own words).
sections.key: Euclid passed through Arabic and Latin into print, and his method shaped Newton's Principia, Spinoza's Ethics and Lincoln's way of arguing.

sections.h: The trouble with the fifth postulate
paras: The first four postulates are short and obvious. The fifth is long and less obvious, and Euclid himself avoided using it for his first 28 propositions. For two thousand years mathematicians tried to prove it from the other four: Proclus in Athens; Ibn al-Haytham in Cairo and Omar Khayyam in Persia around 1000–1100; Nasir al-Din al-Tusi in the 1200s; the Jesuit Girolamo Saccheri in 1733. All failed.

Then, around 1830, the Russian Nikolai Lobachevsky and the Hungarian János Bolyai, independently, tried something bold. They assumed the fifth postulate was false and reasoned on. No contradiction came. They had found a new, consistent geometry in which many parallels pass through one point. Gauss had seen it too but kept quiet. In 1854 Bernhard Riemann described still other geometries, on curved surfaces.
sections.key: Two thousand years of attempts to prove the parallel postulate failed; around 1830 Lobachevsky and Bolyai showed that geometries without it are consistent.

paras: Non-Euclidean geometry was a shock. Kant had argued that Euclid's geometry was built into the way the human mind sees space. Now it seemed geometry's starting points could be chosen, and which geometry fits the real world became a question for physics, not pure reason. Einstein's general theory of relativity (1915) describes space and time as curved, and the Euclidean picture as a very good approximation for everyday scales.

But notice what survived. Euclid's proofs are still valid: if the postulates hold, the conclusions follow. What changed was the belief that the postulates are certainly true of the world. In 1899 David Hilbert rebuilt geometry on a fuller set of axioms, filling small gaps (Euclid's first proof assumes, without saying so, that his two circles meet). In 1931 Kurt Gödel showed that any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. Proof remained the gold standard of certainty; but it became clear that certainty rests on starting points we must choose or trust.
sections.key: Euclid's proofs still hold, but non-Euclidean geometry, relativity and Gödel showed that certainty depends on starting points that must be chosen or trusted.

paras: The method of starting points and proofs spread far beyond mathematics. The American Declaration of Independence (1776) opens with truths held to be 'self-evident', and many readers have heard Euclid in that language. Lincoln, the Euclid student, called the Declaration's principle of equality the 'axiom' of a free society, and argued from it as a geometer argues from a postulate.

There is a lesson here for any argument about God or goodness. No argument proves everything. Every argument starts from something taken as given. The honest question is not 'can you prove it from nothing?' but 'are your starting points worthy of trust, and do your conclusions really follow?' That was Plato's challenge to the geometers, and it is a fair challenge to everyone.
sections.key: The language of self-evident axioms passed into politics; and every argument, like every proof, rests on starting points that must be trusted.

debate.question: What did non-Euclidean geometry show about certainty?

positions.name: Certainty was an illusion
positions.who: Many empiricists, from Hermann von Helmholtz (1870s) to the logical positivists
positions.view: Euclid's geometry was taken for necessary truth about space for two thousand years and turned out to be one choice among several. If even geometry is not certain about the world, nothing is. Knowledge of the world comes from experience, and is always open to revision.
positions.evidence: Consistent non-Euclidean geometries; general relativity's curved space-time, confirmed by the 1919 eclipse observations.

positions.name: Certainty moved, it did not vanish
positions.who: David Hilbert; most working mathematicians
positions.view: Proof gives certainty about what follows from what. Euclid's theorems follow from his axioms as surely as ever. What we learned is to separate pure mathematics, which is certain, from the question which mathematics describes the world, which is physics.
positions.evidence: Hilbert's axioms (1899); Euclid's proofs remain valid; mathematics has no known contradiction at its core.

positions.name: Reason rests on trust
positions.who: Plato's challenge, revived by Gödel and by many philosophers of religion
positions.view: Every proof rests on starting points that cannot themselves be proved within the system. Reason does not create its own foundations; it must trust them. That is not a defeat of reason but its condition, and it applies to science, ethics and faith alike.
positions.evidence: Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931); the regress of proofs; Plato's demand to examine the hypotheses.

debate.agree: All agree that Euclid's proofs are valid from his axioms, and that after 1830 no one could treat those axioms as beyond question for the physical world.

look.why: No painting for this session: the National Gallery has no painting of Euclid or of a geometer at work that is free to use. Try instead to do Proposition 1 yourself with a compass and a ruler.

music.why: The recording begins with the first Kyrie, a five-part fugue: Bach builds a vast structure from one short theme by strict rules, step by step, like a proof in sound.

think.why: Plato saw in geometry a glimpse of eternal reason. Read how Christians came to speak of Christ as the Logos, the reason behind the world.

options: Because proofs would have to go back for ever; every chain of reasoning has to start from something accepted without proof
Because geometry is based on measurement
Because Euclid forgot to prove some
Because some are too difficult
check.why: Hence definitions, postulates and common notions: the starting points of the Elements.

check.q: In Plato's account, what are geometers really thinking about when they draw a square?
options: Fields and buildings
Numbers only
The perfect square, which can only be seen with the mind
The drawing in front of them
check.why: 'Not of the figures which they draw, but of the absolute square and the absolute diameter'.

check.q: What is Plato's criticism of the geometers, even though he praises them?
options: That they are too practical
That they do not use numbers
That they draw badly
That they take their starting points (hypotheses) on trust instead of examining them
check.why: They use hypotheses 'as first principles' and do not ascend to a principle above them; philosophy must question them.

check.q: Why did Descartes take geometry as his model for all knowledge?

Because the Church required it

Because it was the oldest science

That it is false
That a consistent geometry can be built without it, so it is independent of the others
That it can be proved from the other four
check.why: Assuming it false led to no contradiction: a new, consistent geometry.

check.q: After non-Euclidean geometry, which statement is most accurate?
options: Geometry is no longer certain at all
Euclid's geometry is useless
Euclid's proofs are now invalid

check.why: The proofs stand; the question which geometry fits the world became one for physics.

Then set out what non-Euclidean geometry and Gödel changed. End with what you think proof can and cannot give us outside mathematics.
