sessions.practice: Live it this week: with a compass (or a pin and string) and a ruler, do Euclid's first proposition: build an equilateral triangle on a line. Then, in one argument you have this week, ask honestly what your starting points are, and whether the other person shares them.
sessions.reflect: What do you take as given, without proof, in how you live? Are those starting points worthy of trust?
takeaways: Euclid built all of geometry from a page of definitions, postulates and common notions, by proofs that hold for every case.
Plato saw geometry as knowledge of the eternal, while asking geometers to examine their starting points; Descartes tried to rebuild all knowledge on their method.
Non-Euclidean geometry left Euclid's proofs standing but showed that certainty depends on starting points we must choose or trust.

sessions.title: Give me a place to stand
sessions.line: Archimedes of Syracuse measured the circle, weighed the floating world, counted the grains of sand that would fill the universe, and held off a Roman army with his machines.
sessions.plain: Archimedes, who lived in Sicily in the 200s BC, was the greatest mathematician of the ancient world, and he did something new with mathematics: he used it to understand and move real things. He worked out the law of the lever, how things float, and the size of numbers big enough to count the sand in the universe. When the Romans attacked his city, his machines kept them out for months. This session asks how mathematics was joined to the physical world, how the Greeks knew the earth was round and even measured it, and why, with such genius, they never had an industrial revolution.
sessions.why: Session 3 showed Euclid's method of proof: certain knowledge, built step by step from starting points. But Plato had said geometry was about eternal things, not the world of 'practice'. Archimedes took Euclid's method and turned it on levers, floating bodies, the sky and war. This is where mathematics meets the physical world.
answers: Who was Archimedes, and what did he discover?
What does 'give me a place to stand' mean?
Did the Greeks know the earth was round, and how did they measure it?
What was the Antikythera mechanism?
Why didn't the Greeks have an industrial revolution?
sessions.finding: Archimedes measured, calculated and built, joining mathematics to the physical world; and the Greeks of his age measured the size of the round earth and built machines to model the heavens.

paras: We have followed the Greek wager that the world can be understood by reason: the Ionians' natural causes, the Pythagoreans' numbers, and Euclid's proofs. After Alexander the Great died in 323 BC, his empire split into kingdoms ruled by Greek dynasties: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Syria and Mesopotamia. Historians call the next three centuries the Hellenistic age. Its kings paid for science as a mark of prestige, and Alexandria's Museum and Library became the centre of learning.

Archimedes was born around 287 BC in Syracuse, the greatest Greek city in Sicily, ruled then by King Hiero II, who may have been his relative. His father Phidias was an astronomer. He seems to have studied in Alexandria, and all his life he sent his discoveries in letters to mathematicians there.

timeline.text: Death of Alexander the Great; the Hellenistic age begins
Aristarchus of Samos, who proposed that the earth goes round the sun
Archimedes born in Syracuse
Eratosthenes, librarian at Alexandria, who measured the earth
The Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage
The Roman siege of Syracuse; Archimedes killed when the city falls
Polybius writes his Histories
The Antikythera mechanism is made (dates debated)
Cicero finds Archimedes' tomb
Cicero writes On the Commonwealth
J. L. Heiberg identifies lost works of Archimedes in a prayer book (the Archimedes Palimpsest)

background.key: Archimedes (c. 287–212 BC) lived in Syracuse in the Hellenistic age, when kings paid for science and Alexandria was its centre.

paras: About a dozen of his works survive, all in Euclid's style of definitions, postulates and proofs. In On the Equilibrium of Planes he proves the law of the lever: weights balance at distances in inverse proportion to their sizes. In On Floating Bodies he states the principle that a body in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. In Measurement of a Circle he shows that the ratio we call pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7. In On the Sphere and Cylinder he proves that a sphere has two-thirds of the volume and surface of the cylinder that just encloses it, the result he was proudest of.

And in The Sand-Reckoner, a short letter to Gelon, son of King Hiero, he does something playful and deep. Some people say, he writes, that the grains of sand are past counting. He sets out to show that a number can be named bigger than the grains of sand needed to fill the whole universe. To do it he invents a way of naming very large numbers, and estimates the size of the universe, reporting along the way that Aristarchus of Samos had proposed that the earth goes round the sun. His answer, in our notation, is fewer than 10 to the power of 63 grains. (We have no English translation of Archimedes old enough to quote here, so this is in our own words.)
background.key: Archimedes proved the law of the lever and the principle of floating bodies, bounded pi, and in the Sand-Reckoner named a number larger than the grains of sand needed to fill the universe.

paras: Archimedes' own works are technical, and we have no old enough translation to quote. So we read him as the ancient world saw him. Polybius, a Greek historian born about twenty years before Archimedes died, tells how his machines held off the Roman army at Syracuse. Then Cicero, the Roman statesman, describes the bronze model of the heavens that Archimedes built, taken to Rome as plunder.
The comparison is Cicero again, telling how, as a young official in Sicily in 75 BC, he found Archimedes' forgotten tomb under the brambles. It is a story about how easily knowledge is lost.
background.key: We read Polybius on Archimedes' machines and Cicero on his model of the heavens, then Cicero's discovery of his forgotten tomb.

before: What does Polybius say one man can achieve against an army?
What could Archimedes' globe show that an ordinary globe could not?
Why did the people of Syracuse not know where Archimedes was buried?
sessions.readWhy: Polybius on Archimedes at war, and Cicero on his model of the heavens: mathematics turned into machines.

paras: When Epicydes and Hippocrates had occupied Syracuse, and had alienated the rest of the citizens with themselves from the friendship of Rome, the Romans who had already been informed of the murder of Hieronymus, tyrant of Syracuse, appointed Appius Claudius as Propraetor to command a land force, while Marcus Claudius Marcellus commanded the fleet. These officers took up a position not far from Syracuse, and determined to assault the town from the land at Hexapylus, and by sea at what was called Stoa Scytice in Achradina, where the wall has its foundation close down to the sea. Having prepared their wicker pent-houses, and darts, and other siege material, they felt confident that, with so many hands employed, they would in five days get their works in such an advanced state as to give them the advantage over the enemy. But in this they did not take into account the abilities of Archimedes; nor calculate on the truth that, in certain circumstances, the genius of one man is more effective than any numbers whatever. However they now learnt it by experience. The city was strong from the fact of its encircling wall lying along a chain of hills with overhanging brows, the ascent of which was no easy task, even with no one to hinder it, except at certain definite points. Taking advantage of this, Archimedes had constructed such defences both in the town, and at the places where an attack might be made by sea, that the garrison would have everything at hand which they might require at any moment, and be ready to meet without delay whatever the enemy might attempt against them.

With such contrivances and preparations were the Romans intending to assault the towers. But Archimedes had constructed catapults to suit every range; and as the ships sailing up were still at a considerable distance, he so wounded the enemy with stones and darts, from the tighter wound and longer engines, as to harass and perplex them to the last degree; and when these began to carry over their heads, he used smaller engines graduated according to the range required from time to time, and by this means caused so much confusion among them as to altogether check their advance and attack; and finally Marcellus was reduced in despair to bringing up his ships under cover of night. But when they had come close to land, and so too near to be hit by the catapults, they found that Archimedes had prepared another contrivance against the soldiers who fought from the decks. He had pierced the wall as high as a man’s stature with numerous loop-holes, which, on the outside, were about as big as the palm of the hand.

Inside the wall he stationed archers and cross-bows, or scorpions, and by the volleys discharged through these he made the marines useless. By these means he not only baffled the enemy, whether at a distance or close at hand, but also killed the greater number of them. As often, too, as they tried to work their Sambucae, he had engines ready all along the walls, not visible at other times, but which suddenly reared themselves above the wall from inside, when the moment for their use had come, and stretched their beams far over the battlements, some of them carrying stones weighing as much as ten talents, and others great masses of lead. So whenever the Sambucae were approaching, these beams swung round on their pivot the required distance, and by means of a rope running through a pulley dropped the stone upon the Sambucae, with the result that it not only smashed the machine itself to pieces, but put the ship also and all on board into the most serious danger.

Other machines which he invented were directed against storming parties, who, advancing under the protection of pent-houses, were secured by them from being hurt by missiles shot through the walls. Against these he either shot stones big enough to drive the marines from the prow; or let down an iron hand swung on a chain, by which the man who guided the crane, having fastened on some part of the prow where he could get a hold, pressed down the lever of the machine inside the wall; and when he had thus lifted the prow and made the vessel rest upright on its stern, he fastened the lever of his machine so that it could not be moved; and then suddenly slackened the hand and chain by means of a rope and pulley. The result was that many of the vessels heeled over and fell on their sides: some completely capsized; while the greater number, by their prows coming down suddenly from a height, dipped low in the sea, shipped a great quantity of water, and became a scene of the utmost confusion. Though reduced almost to despair by these baffling inventions of Archimedes, and though he saw that all his attempts were repulsed by the garrison with mockery on their part and loss to himself, Marcellus could not yet refrain from making a joke at his own expense, saying that “Archimedes was using his ships to ladle out the sea-water, but that his 'harps’ not having been invited to the party were buffeted and turned out with disgrace.” Such was the end of the attempt at storming Syracuse by sea.

Nor was Appius Claudius more successful. He, too, was compelled by similar difficulties to desist from the attempt; for while his men were still at a considerable distance from the wall, they began falling by the stones and shots from the engines and catapults. The volleys of missiles, indeed, were extraordinarily rapid and sharp, for their construction had been provided for by all the liberality of a Hiero, and had been planned and engineered by the skill of an Archimedes. Moreover, when they did at length get near the walls, they were prevented from making an assault by the unceasing fire through the loop-holes, which I mentioned before; or if they tried to carry the place under cover of pent-houses, they were killed by the stones and beams let down upon their heads. The garrison also did them no little damage with those hands at the end of their engines; for they used to lift the men, armour, and all, into the air, and then throw them down. At last Appius retired into the camp, and summoning the Tribunes to a council of war, decided to try every possible means of taking Syracuse except a storm. And this decision they carried out; for during the eight months of siege which followed, though there was no stratagem or measure of daring which they did not attempt, they never again ventured to attempt a storm. So true it is that one man and one intellect, properly qualified for the particular undertaking, is a host in itself and of extraordinary efficacy. In this instance, at any rate, we find the Romans confident that their forces by land and sea would enable them to become masters of the town, if only one old man could be got rid of; while as long as he remained there, they did not venture even to think of making the attempt, at least by any method which made it possible for Archimedes to oppose them.

I am not about to bring you anything new, or anything which has been thought over or discovered by me myself. But I recollect that Caius Sulpicius Gallus, who was a man of profound learning, as you are aware, when this same thing was reported to have taken place in his time, while he was staying in the house of Marcus Marcellus, who had been his colleague in the consulship, asked to see a celestial globe which Marcellus's grandfather had saved after the capture of Syracuse from that magnificent and opulent city, without bringing to his own home any other memorial out of so great a booty; which I had often heard mentioned on account of the great fame of Archimedes; but its appearance, however, did not seem to me particularly striking. For that other is more elegant in form, and more generally known, which was made by the same Archimedes, and deposited by the same Marcellus in the Temple of Virtue at Rome. But as soon as Gallus had begun to explain, in a most scientific manner, the principle of this machine, I felt that the Sicilian geometrician must have possessed a genius superior to anything we usually conceive to belong to our nature.

For Gallus assured us that that other solid and compact globe was a very ancient invention, and that the first model had been originally made by Thales of Miletus. That afterward Eudoxus of Cnidus, a disciple of Plato, had traced on its surface the stars that appear in the sky, and that many years subsequently, borrowing from Eudoxus this beautiful design and representation, Aratus had illustrated it in his verses, not by any science of astronomy, but by the ornament of poetic description. He added that the figure of the globe, which displayed the motions of the sun and moon, and the five planets, or wandering stars, could not be represented by the primitive solid globe; and that in this the invention of Archimedes was admirable, because he had calculated how a single revolution should maintain unequal and diversified progressions in dissimilar motions. In fact, when Gallus moved this globe, we observed that the moon succeeded the sun by as many turns of the wheel in the machine as days in the heavens. From whence it resulted that the progress of the sun was marked as in the heavens, and that the moon touched the point where she is obscured by the earth's shadow at the instant the sun appears opposite.

parts.author: Polybius
parts.who: A Greek statesman taken to Rome as a hostage, who became the historian of Rome's rise to world power.
parts.title: One old man against Rome
parts.context: In 214 BC, during Rome's great war with Carthage, Syracuse went over to the Carthaginian side. Rome sent the general Marcus Claudius Marcellus to take it, by land and by sea. Polybius wrote this about sixty years later, from earlier accounts. This is Evelyn Shuckburgh's translation of 1889; his section numbers and two footnote numbers are left out, and the description of the Romans' ship-borne ladders (VIII.6) is cut.
parts.plain: The Romans expected to take Syracuse in five days. They forgot Archimedes. He had built catapults for every range, holes in the walls for archers, cranes that dropped huge stones on the Roman ships, and an iron hand that lifted a ship by its bow and dropped it. Marcellus joked about it, but gave up the assault. Polybius's lesson: one mind, properly prepared, can be worth an army.

commentary.on: they did not take into account the abilities of Archimedes
commentary.text: Archimedes was about seventy. He had spent his life on pure mathematics; now he turned it to defending his city.

commentary.on: the genius of one man is more effective than any numbers whatever
commentary.text: Polybius writes as a soldier and statesman, not a scientist. What impresses him is the practical power of knowledge.

commentary.on: Archimedes had constructed catapults to suit every range
commentary.text: Every catapult was a problem in the mathematics of levers, tension and trajectories. Archimedes 'graduated' them by range: a system, not a single trick. That is applied mathematics.

commentary.on: let down an iron hand swung on a chain
commentary.text: The famous 'claw of Archimedes': a crane that hooked a ship's prow, lifted it with a lever, and let it drop. Later writers added that he set the Roman fleet on fire with mirrors; Polybius, the earliest source, says nothing of mirrors, and most historians doubt it.

commentary.on: Archimedes was using his ships to ladle out the sea-water
commentary.text: Marcellus's grim joke. A sambuca was a ship-borne siege ladder shaped like a harp; 'not invited to the party' means thrown out of the feast in disgrace.

commentary.on: if only one old man could be got rid of
commentary.text: The siege became a blockade. In 212 BC the city was betrayed and fell. Plutarch and Livy say Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier, against Marcellus's orders, while he was absorbed in a diagram.

parts.author: Cicero
parts.work: On the Commonwealth and Tusculan Disputations
parts.translator: C. D. Yonge (1853), revising Francis Barham (1841)
parts.title: A machine of the heavens
parts.who: The Roman statesman, orator and philosopher, who brought Greek philosophy into Latin.
parts.context: Cicero's On the Commonwealth is a dialogue set in 129 BC. One speaker, Philus, remembers seeing a globe of the heavens that Marcellus took from Syracuse as his only plunder. This is C. D. Yonge's revision of Francis Barham's translation; a footnote number and a gap in the manuscript at the end are left out.
parts.plain: Marcellus took two globes from Syracuse. One was a solid star globe, an old invention going back to Thales. The other, made by Archimedes, was a machine: turning it showed the motions of the sun, the moon and the five planets, all from one movement, and even showed eclipses at the right time. The speaker felt that its maker had a genius beyond ordinary human nature.

commentary.on: without bringing to his own home any other memorial out of so great a booty
commentary.text: Of all the riches of Syracuse, Marcellus kept only this. Rome was beginning to value Greek learning, even as it conquered the Greeks.

commentary.on: the first model had been originally made by Thales of Miletus
commentary.text: Thales again, from the first session: the Greeks remembered him as the father of astronomy. Eudoxus, a friend of Plato, drew the constellations on such a globe.

commentary.on: he had calculated how a single revolution should maintain unequal and diversified progressions in dissimilar motions
commentary.text: This is the marvel: one turning motion drives many different speeds, the sun's year, the moon's month, each planet's cycle. That needs gears in carefully calculated ratios. A machine built on number reproduces the motions of the heavens.

commentary.on: the moon touched the point where she is obscured by the earth's shadow at the instant the sun appears opposite
commentary.text: It showed eclipses of the moon, when sun, earth and moon line up. Until 1901, many scholars thought Cicero must be exaggerating. Then sponge divers found the Antikythera mechanism, as the lecture explains.

read.author: Polybius and Cicero
read.who: A Greek statesman taken to Rome as a hostage, who became the historian of Rome's rise to world power.

paras: I will present you with an humble and obscure mathematician of the same city, called Archimedes, who lived many years after; whose tomb, overgrown with shrubs and briers, I in my quæstorship discovered, when the Syracusans knew nothing of it, and even denied that there was any such thing remaining; for I remembered some verses, which I had been informed were engraved on his monument, and these set forth that on the top of the tomb there was placed a sphere with a cylinder. When I had carefully examined all the monuments (for there are a great many tombs at the gate Achradinæ), I observed a small column standing out a little above the briers, with the figure of a sphere and a cylinder upon it; whereupon I immediately said to the Syracusans--for there were some of their principal men with me there--that I imagined that was what I was inquiring for. Several men, being sent in with scythes, cleared the way, and made an opening for us.

When we could get at it, and were come near to the front of the pedestal, I found the inscription, though the latter parts of all the verses were effaced almost half away. Thus one of the noblest cities of Greece, and one which at one time likewise had been very celebrated for learning, had known nothing of the monument of its greatest genius, if it had not been discovered to them by a native of Arpinum. But to return to the subject from which I have been digressing. Who is there in the least degree acquainted with the Muses, that is, with liberal knowledge, or that deals at all in learning, who would not choose to be this mathematician rather than that tyrant? If we look into their methods of living and their employments, we shall find the mind of the one strengthened and improved with tracing the deductions of reason, amused with his own ingenuity, which is the one most delicious food of the mind; the thoughts of the other engaged in continual murders and injuries, in constant fears by night and by day.

parts.author: Cicero
parts.work: On the Commonwealth and Tusculan Disputations
parts.translator: C. D. Yonge (1853), revising Francis Barham (1841)
parts.title: A sphere and a cylinder
parts.who: The Roman statesman, orator and philosopher.
parts.when: His villa at Tusculum, near Rome, 45 BC
parts.context: In 75 BC Cicero served as quaestor, a junior financial officer, in Sicily. Thirty years later, in a book on whether virtue is enough for happiness, he contrasts the cruel tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse with the 'humble' mathematician of the same city, and remembers finding his grave. This is Yonge's translation.
parts.plain: Cicero says that when he was in Sicily the people of Syracuse did not know where Archimedes was buried and even denied the tomb existed. Cicero remembered that it had a sphere and a cylinder on it. Searching among the tombs at one of the city gates, he saw a small column with that shape above the brambles. Men with scythes cleared the way, and he found the half-worn verses. So a Roman from a country town had to show the Greeks where their greatest genius lay. Who, Cicero asks, would not rather be that mathematician than the tyrant?

commentary.on: an humble and obscure mathematician
commentary.text: Cicero is being ironic: humble in rank, beside a king. But it is true that Archimedes had no power, only knowledge.

commentary.on: on the top of the tomb there was placed a sphere with a cylinder
commentary.text: Plutarch says Archimedes asked for this: his proof that a sphere is two-thirds of its enclosing cylinder, carved on his grave. Of all he did, it was the pure mathematics he wanted remembered, not the machines.

commentary.on: the Syracusans knew nothing of it, and even denied that there was any such thing remaining
commentary.text: Within 140 years his own city had forgotten him. Knowledge is not kept by itself; someone has to care enough to keep it. Hold that thought.

commentary.on: Several men, being sent in with scythes, cleared the way
commentary.text: A picture of recovering lost learning: someone remembers, someone searches, someone clears the brambles. Much of Archimedes' work came down to us the same way, through a few copies that survived by chance.

commentary.on: the mind of the one strengthened and improved with tracing the deductions of reason
commentary.text: Cicero's real point: the life of the mind, 'tracing the deductions of reason', is happier than the life of power. It is the Pythagorean and Platonic view of the first sessions, in a Roman voice.

compare.author: Cicero
compare.work: On the Commonwealth and Tusculan Disputations
compare.translator: C. D. Yonge (1853), revising Francis Barham (1841)
compare.why: A story about how quickly even the greatest knowledge can be forgotten, and found again.
compare.title: The forgotten tomb

sections.h: The lever and the place to stand
paras: Archimedes proved the law of the lever as Euclid proved theorems: from postulates such as 'equal weights at equal distances balance'. The result is that a small weight far from the pivot can balance a large weight near it. In principle, any weight can be moved by any force, given a long enough lever.

Later writers put a famous saying in his mouth. Pappus of Alexandria, around AD 320, reports it as 'give me a place to stand and I will move the earth'. Plutarch, around AD 100, tells a gentler version: Archimedes wrote to King Hiero that any weight could be moved by a given force, and boasted that with another world to stand on he could move this one; challenged, he hauled a loaded ship onto land single-handed with a system of pulleys. We cannot know his exact words. But the saying captures his achievement: mathematics gives a fixed point from which the physical world can be moved.
sections.key: Archimedes proved the law of the lever from postulates; 'give me a place to stand and I will move the earth' is a later report that sums up his joining of mathematics to the world.

paras: The best known story is the least certain. The Roman architect Vitruvius, writing around 25 BC, says King Hiero suspected a goldsmith of mixing silver into a gold crown, and asked Archimedes to find out without damaging it. In the bath, noticing the water rise as he got in, Archimedes saw the answer, and ran home naked shouting 'Eureka!', 'I have found it!'

The story comes two centuries after Archimedes, and the method Vitruvius describes, measuring the overflow, would have been too crude for a small crown. Historians think Archimedes more likely used his own principle of buoyancy with a balance: hang the crown and an equal weight of pure gold from a balance in water, and if the crown is less dense, the balance tips. Either way, the story shows what the ancient world admired: a real problem, solved by an idea.
sections.key: The 'Eureka' story comes from Vitruvius two centuries later and is probably embellished; Archimedes' real principle of buoyancy would have solved the crown problem better.

paras: Did the Greeks know the earth was round? Yes. The idea may go back to the Pythagoreans, but by about 350 BC Aristotle gave evidence for it (On the Heavens II.14). In an eclipse of the moon, the earth's shadow on the moon is always curved. Travelling north or south, you see different stars: some stars visible in Egypt and Cyprus cannot be seen further north. And all heavy things fall towards a centre, which would make a sphere. (These are in our own words.)

From then on, every educated Greek, Roman and medieval European knew the earth was a sphere. The idea that medieval people thought it flat is a modern myth, as later sessions will show, still to come.
sections.key: By 350 BC Aristotle gave evidence that the earth is round: its curved shadow in lunar eclipses, the changing stars, and heavy things falling to a centre.

paras: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, a friend of Archimedes and head of the Library of Alexandria, did something more daring around 240 BC: he measured the earth. Our account comes from Cleomedes, a later Greek writer on astronomy (in our own words).

At Syene, far up the Nile (modern Aswan), at noon on midsummer's day, the sun stood directly overhead: it lit the bottom of wells and upright posts cast no shadow. At the same moment in Alexandria, further north, an upright pointer cast a short shadow, showing the sun was one fiftieth of a full circle away from overhead. Assuming the sun is so far away that its rays arrive parallel, the distance from Syene to Alexandria must be one fiftieth of the earth's circumference. That distance was reckoned at 5,000 stades, so the whole earth was 250,000 stades round.

How accurate was it? It depends on the length of his stade, which is uncertain. On the likeliest values he was within about two to fifteen per cent of the true figure of 40,000 kilometres. With a stick, a shadow, a known distance and Euclid's geometry of parallel lines, a man in Egypt measured the planet.
sections.key: Around 240 BC Eratosthenes compared noon shadows at Syene and Alexandria and, with Euclid's geometry, measured the earth's circumference, probably within a few per cent.

paras: In 1900–1901 sponge divers off the Greek island of Antikythera brought up statues from a Roman-era shipwreck, and with them a lump of corroded bronze. It turned out to contain gearwheels. The historian of science Derek de Solla Price studied it with X-rays and published Gears from the Greeks in 1974. Since 2005, an international team using high-resolution scanning has shown what it did.

Turning a handle drove some thirty surviving gears. Dials showed the positions of the sun and moon, the phase of the moon, a calendar, the dates of the Olympic Games, and the cycles in which eclipses repeat; reconstructions suggest it also showed the planets. It was made, most scholars think, between about 150 and 60 BC. Nothing so complex is known again until the astronomical clocks of medieval Europe. Cicero was not exaggerating about Archimedes' sphere: the Greeks really did build mathematical models of the heavens in bronze.
sections.key: The Antikythera mechanism, found in 1901 and made around 150–60 BC, is a geared bronze calculator of the heavens: proof that machines like Archimedes' sphere were real.

paras: If the Greeks could build the Antikythera mechanism, and Hero of Alexandria, in the first century AD, described a little steam-driven spinning globe, why did they never build steam engines and factories? Historians give several answers, and the honest answer is probably all of them together.

There was slavery: with cheap human labour, there was little reason to save it with machines. There was an attitude: Plutarch says Archimedes himself thought mechanical work ignoble and wrote only about pure theory, though Plutarch may be projecting his own Platonism. The economic historian Moses Finley (The Ancient Economy, 1973) argued that ancient society lacked the markets, credit and drive for profit that would reward invention. Others point out that the Romans did spread watermills and other machines widely, so the picture of a society blind to technology is too simple. And science itself had not yet joined theory to systematic experiment. Archimedes' level of mathematics was rarely matched for over a thousand years.
sections.key: Slavery, a low view of manual work, the shape of the ancient economy and the lack of systematic experiment probably all held the Greeks back from industrialising.

paras: Cicero had to clear brambles to find Archimedes' tomb. His books had a narrower escape. In the 900s a scribe in Constantinople copied several of his works, including The Method, in which Archimedes explains how he found results by imagining figures balanced on a lever before proving them. In 1229 a priest scraped the parchment and wrote a prayer book over it. In 1906 the Danish scholar J. L. Heiberg noticed the faint mathematics underneath. After vanishing again, the book was sold in 1998, and between 1999 and 2008 a team at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore used X-rays and ultraviolet light to read it.

So the same Christian scribes who copied Archimedes also scraped him off to write prayers. Which of those facts matters more is exactly the question the next session but one, still to come, will press.
sections.key: Archimedes' Method survived only in a 10th-century copy overwritten with prayers in 1229 and recovered between 1906 and 2008.

Cicero, On the Commonwealth I.14 (I.21–22) and Tusculan Disputations V.23 (V.64–66), tr. C. D. Yonge (Bohn/Harper).

Archimedes, The Sand-Reckoner; On the Equilibrium of Planes I; On Floating Bodies I; Measurement of a Circle 3; On the Sphere and Cylinder I.34 (standard English: T. L. Heath, The Works of Archimedes, 1897).
Pappus, Collection VIII.11; Vitruvius, On Architecture IX, preface 9–12.
Aristotle, On the Heavens II.14, 297b23–298a20. Cleomedes, On the Heavens I.7.
Derek de Solla Price, Gears from the Greeks (1974); T. Freeth and others, 'Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism', Nature 444 (2006).
M. I. Finley, The Ancient Economy (1973). Reviel Netz and William Noel, The Archimedes Codex (2007).

debate.question: Why did Greek science not lead to a scientific and industrial revolution?

positions.name: Society held it back
positions.who: M. I. Finley; Benjamin Farrington (Greek Science, 1944–49)
positions.view: Slavery made labour cheap; the elite despised manual work; there was no market economy hungry for productivity. Science stayed a gentleman's contemplation, and inventions stayed toys and weapons.
positions.evidence: Hero's steam toy; Plutarch on Archimedes scorning mechanics; the scale of ancient slavery.

positions.name: The ideas were not ready
positions.who: Historians of science such as David Lindberg and H. Floris Cohen
positions.view: What was missing was not money but method: the habit of systematic experiment, and the conviction that the whole of nature, not just the heavens, follows exact mathematical laws. That came together only in the 1600s.
positions.evidence: Greek physics remained Aristotle's qualitative physics; Archimedes' mathematical physics had few followers; experiment was occasional.

positions.name: It did not stop: it was handed on
positions.who: Historians of Byzantine, Islamic and medieval science
positions.view: Greek science did not end but passed through Byzantium, the Islamic world and medieval Europe, each adding to it, until the 1600s built on all of them. The question 'why not then?' assumes a single line that history does not follow.
positions.evidence: Arabic translations of Euclid, Archimedes and Ptolemy; medieval improvements in optics and mechanics; Galileo's study of Archimedes.

debate.agree: All agree that Greek mathematics and machines reached a level not matched for many centuries, and that Archimedes' works were among the foundations of the scientific revolution.

look.why: No painting for this session: the National Gallery has no painting of Archimedes, of Syracuse or of an ancient astronomer that is free to use.

music.why: A hymn about the steady, dependable order of seasons and the heavens, read as the faithfulness of God: the same regularity Archimedes built into his bronze sphere.

think.why: Archimedes showed that the world can be measured and modelled. Read how believers and sceptics have thought about what that means.

check.q: What was most new about Archimedes compared with Euclid?
options: He used proofs
He rejected Plato
He was the first to study circles
He used Euclid's method of proof on physical things: levers, floating bodies, the heavens
check.why: Mathematics joined to the physical world: the law of the lever and the principle of buoyancy, proved from postulates.

check.q: Why do historians doubt that Archimedes burned the Roman fleet with mirrors?
options: Because Archimedes was dead
Because Cicero denies it
Because Polybius, the earliest source, says nothing about it; the story appears only in much later writers
Because mirrors had not been invented
check.why: Polybius describes catapults, loop-holes, cranes and the iron hand, but no mirrors.

check.q: Which of these was not part of Aristotle's evidence that the earth is round?
options: Heavy things falling towards a centre
Different stars visible as you travel north or south
Photographs from high mountains
The earth's curved shadow on the moon in eclipses
check.why: The first, second and fourth are Aristotle's arguments; the third is, of course, modern.

check.q: What did Eratosthenes need to measure the earth?
options: A telescope
The angle of the noon sun at two places a known distance apart, and the assumption that the sun's rays arrive parallel
The speed of light
A ship that sailed round it
check.why: One fiftieth of a circle between Syene and Alexandria, 5,000 stades apart, gave 250,000 stades.

check.q: Why does the Antikythera mechanism matter for reading Cicero?
options: It shows that geared machines modelling the heavens really existed, so Cicero's description of Archimedes' sphere is credible
It was made by Archimedes
It proves Cicero owned one
It shows that the Greeks had clocks
check.why: Before 1901 many scholars doubted such machines; the mechanism showed the Greeks could build them.

check.q: What is the strongest point of the story of Cicero finding the tomb, for this journey's question?
options: That Cicero was a good detective
That knowledge is not kept automatically: within 140 years Archimedes' own city had forgotten him
That Archimedes wanted machines on his tomb
That Romans were cleverer than Greeks
check.why: Knowledge survives only when someone cares to keep it: a point that matters when we ask who lost and who saved Greek science.

tutorial.question: 'Give me a place to stand and I will move the earth.' What did Archimedes add to Greek science, and why did it not lead further?
tutorial.approach: Set out what Archimedes proved, and how he used Euclid's method on physical problems. Use Polybius and Cicero to show how the ancient world saw him. Explain how the Greeks knew and measured the round earth, and what the Antikythera mechanism shows. Then weigh the explanations for why there was no ancient industrial revolution.
strong: Explains the law of the lever and buoyancy as proofs from postulates.
Uses Polybius critically (earliest source; no mirrors).
Describes Archimedes' sphere and the Antikythera mechanism accurately.
Explains Aristotle's evidence and Eratosthenes' method.
Weighs slavery, attitudes, economy and method fairly.
Notes how Archimedes' works survived.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do Eratosthenes' experiment in miniature. At noon on a sunny day, stand a stick upright and measure its height and its shadow. Notice that a stick and a shadow already tell you the angle of the sun. Then think of one skill you have that could help someone else this week, and use it for them.
sessions.reflect: Cicero asks whether you would rather be the mathematician or the tyrant. What do you really want your life's 'tomb' to say?
takeaways: Archimedes used Euclid's method on the physical world: the lever, floating bodies, the heavens, and machines that held off Rome.
The Greeks knew the earth was round (Aristotle's evidence), Eratosthenes measured it, and the Antikythera mechanism shows they modelled the heavens in bronze.
Their knowledge was fragile: Syracuse forgot Archimedes' tomb, and slavery, attitudes and method kept Greek science from going further.

sessions.title: First, do no harm
sessions.line: Greek doctors refused to blame the gods for disease, and bound themselves by an oath to the good of the patient.
sessions.plain: In ancient Greece, a person who fell in a fit was thought to be seized by a god, and was treated with charms and purifications. A Greek doctor of the 400s BC wrote that this 'sacred disease', epilepsy, has a natural cause in the brain like any other illness. The same school produced an oath in which doctors swore to work only for the good of the sick. This session asks what Greek medicine got right and wrong, what the Oath really says, and how Christians took it further by building the first hospitals for everyone.
sessions.why: Session 4 showed mathematics joined to the physical world in Archimedes' machines. Medicine joined reason to the most personal part of the world: the human body in pain. It brought the Ionian search for natural causes to bear on sickness, and asked a new question that mathematics never asked: what do we owe the person in front of us?
answers: Who was Hippocrates?
What did Greek doctors think caused disease?
What is the Hippocratic Oath, and do doctors still take it?
What does the Oath say about abortion and euthanasia?
Where did hospitals come from?
sessions.finding: Hippocratic medicine refused to blame the gods for disease and bound doctors by an oath to the patient's good; Christians extended that care to every sick stranger and built the first public hospitals.

paras: So far this journey has followed the Greek wager that the world can be understood by reason: the first natural causes in Ionia, number, proof and measurement. Now we go back a little in time, to the 400s BC, the age of Socrates and the Athenian democracy, and to the island of Cos, just off the coast near Ionia.

Before the Greek doctors, sickness was widely seen as sent by gods or spirits. In Homer's Iliad a plague is Apollo's arrows. Sick Greeks went to temples of Asclepius, the god of healing, slept there and hoped for a healing dream. Wandering healers sold charms and purifications. There were also skilled practical doctors, in Egypt and Babylon as well as Greece, who set bones and treated wounds. What changed in the 400s was a theory: that every disease has a natural cause, which can be studied.

background.key: In the 400s BC, when sickness was widely blamed on gods, the doctors of Cos began to treat every disease as having a natural cause.

paras: Hippocrates of Cos lived about 460–370 BC. Plato mentions him twice as a famous doctor who taught for a fee. That is almost all we know for certain. About sixty medical works survive under his name, the 'Hippocratic Corpus', but they were written by many authors over more than a century and gathered later, probably in Alexandria. Scholars cannot say which, if any, Hippocrates wrote himself.

Most of these doctors explained health as a balance of the body's fluids, or 'humours': later fixed at four, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Disease was imbalance; treatment was diet, rest, exercise and drugs to restore balance. The theory was wrong, but it was natural, and it led them to observe patients closely, record case histories and predict how illnesses would go. Their writing is full of careful description.
background.key: Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BC) was a real doctor of Cos, but the sixty 'Hippocratic' works were written by many authors; most explained disease by an imbalance of humours.

paras: The main reading has two parts. First, On the Sacred Disease, by an unknown Hippocratic author of the late 400s BC: the clearest ancient argument that a disease thought divine has a natural cause. Second, the Oath, the most famous text in the history of medicine.

The comparison is the parable of the Good Samaritan, from Luke's Gospel, written by a man Paul calls 'the beloved physician'. It asks a question the Oath does not: who is the neighbour I must care for?
background.key: We read On the Sacred Disease and the Oath, then the Good Samaritan, on who must be cared for.

sessions.readWhy: On the Sacred Disease, the first great argument that a 'divine' disease has a natural cause, and the doctor's Oath.

paras: It is thus with regard to the disease called Sacred: it appears to me to be nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause from the originates like other affections. Men regard its nature and cause as divine from ignorance and wonder, because it is not at all like to other diseases. And this notion of its divinity is kept up by their inability to comprehend it, and the simplicity of the mode by which it is cured, for men are freed from it by purifications and incantations. But if it is reckoned divine because it is wonderful, instead of one there are many diseases which would be sacred; for, as I will show, there are others no less wonderful and prodigious, which nobody imagines to be sacred. The quotidian, tertian, and quartan fevers, seem to me no less sacred and divine in their origin than this disease, although they are not reckoned so wonderful. And I see men become mad and demented from no manifest cause, and at the same time doing many things out of place; and I have known many persons in sleep groaning and crying out, some in a state of suffocation, some jumping up and fleeing out of doors, and deprived of their reason until they awaken, and afterward becoming well and rational as before, although they be pale and weak; and this will happen not once but frequently. And there are many and various things of the like kind, which it would be tedious to state particularly.

Thus, they who try to cure these maladies in this way, appear to me neither to reckon them sacred nor divine. For when they are removed by such purifications, and this method of cure, what is to prevent them from being brought upon men and induced by other devices similar to these? So that the cause is no longer divine, but human. For whoever is able, by purifications conjurations, to drive away such an affection, will be able, by other practices, to excite it; and, according to this view, its divine nature is entirely done away with. By such sayings and doings, they profess to be possessed of superior knowledge, and deceive mankind by enjoining lustrations and purifications upon them, while their discourse turns upon the divinity and the godhead. And yet it would appear to me that their discourse savors not of piety, as they suppose, but rather of impiety, and as if there were no gods, and that what they hold to be holy and divine, were impious and unholy. This I will now explain.

But this disease seems to me to be no more divine than others; but it has its nature such as other diseases have, and a cause whence it originates, and its nature and cause are divine only just as much as all others are, and it is curable no less than the others, unless when, the from of time, it is confirmed, and has became stronger than the remedies applied. Its origin is hereditary, like that of other diseases.

Men ought to know that from nothing else but the brain come joys, delights, laughter and sports, and sorrows, griefs, despondency, and lamentations. And by this, in an especial manner, we acquire wisdom and knowledge, and see and hear, and know what are foul and what are fair, what are bad and what are good, what are sweet, and what unsavory; some we discriminate by habit, and some we perceive by their utility. By this we distinguish objects of relish and disrelish, according to the seasons; and the same things do not always please us. And by the same organ we become mad and delirious, and fears and terrors assail us, some by night, and some by day, and dreams and untimely wanderings, and cares that are not suitable, and ignorance of present circumstances, desuetude, and unskilfulness. All these things we endure from the brain, when it is not healthy, but is more hot, more cold, more moist, or more dry than natural, or when it suffers any other preternatural and unusual affection. And we become mad from its humidity. For when it is more moist than natural, it is necessarily put into motion, and the affection being moved, neither the sight nor hearing can be at rest, and the tongue speaks in accordance with the sight and hearing.

And the disease called the Sacred arises from causes as the others, namely, those things which enter and quit the body, such as cold, the sun, and the winds, which are ever changing and are never at rest. And these things are divine, so that there is no necessity for making a distinction, and holding this disease to be more divine than the others, but all are divine, and all human. And each has its own peculiar nature and power, and none is of an ambiguous nature, or irremediable. And the most of them are curable by the same means as those by which any other thing is food to one, and injurious to another. Thus, then, the physician should understand and distinguish the season of each, so that at one time he may attend to the nourishment and increase, and at another to abstraction and diminution. And in this disease as in all others, he must strive not to feed the disease, but endeavor to wear it out by administering whatever is most opposed to each disease, and not that which favors and is allied to it. For by that which is allied to it, it gains vigor and increase, but it wears out and disappears under the use of that which is opposed to it. But whoever is acquainted with such a change in men, and can render a man humid and dry, hot and cold by regimen, could also cure this disease, if he recognizes the proper season for administering his remedies, without minding purifications, spells, and all other illiberal practices of a like kind.

I SWEAR by Apollo the physician, and Aesculapius, and Health, and All-heal, and all the gods and goddesses, that, according to my ability and judgment, I will keep this Oath and this stipulation- to reckon him who taught me this Art equally dear to me as my parents, to share my substance with him, and relieve his necessities if required; to look upon his offspring in the same footing as my own brothers, and to teach them this art, if they shall wish to learn it, without fee or stipulation; and that by precept, lecture, and every other mode of instruction, I will impart a knowledge of the Art to my own sons, and those of my teachers, and to disciples bound by a stipulation and oath according to the law of medicine, but to none others.

I will follow that system of regimen which, according to my ability and judgment, I consider for the benefit of my patients, and abstain from whatever is deleterious and mischievous. I will give no deadly medicine to any one if asked, nor suggest any such counsel; and in like manner I will not give to a woman a pessary to produce abortion.
With purity and with holiness I will pass my life and practice my Art. I will not cut persons laboring under the stone, but will leave this to be done by men who are practitioners of this work.

Into whatever houses I enter, I will go into them for the benefit of the sick, and will abstain from every voluntary act of mischief and corruption; and, further from the seduction of females or males, of freemen and slaves. Whatever, in connection with my professional practice or not, in connection with it, I see or hear, in the life of men, which ought not to be spoken of abroad, I will not divulge, as reckoning that all such should be kept secret.

While I continue to keep this Oath unviolated, may it be granted to me to enjoy life and the practice of the art, respected by all men, in all times! But should I trespass and violate this Oath, may the reverse be my lot!

parts.title: No more divine than other diseases
parts.context: The 'sacred disease' is epilepsy. The author, an unknown doctor of the late 400s BC, writes against the healers who treated it with charms. This is Francis Adams's translation of 1849, as given by the Internet Classics Archive; the archive's text has two garbled phrases ('from the originates', 'the from of time'), kept as they are and noted for the reviewer. Cuts are marked '…'.
parts.plain: Epilepsy, the author says, is no more divine than any other disease; it has a natural cause. People call it sacred because they do not understand it. The charm-sellers who claim to cure it by purifications are actually impious: if men can drive a disease away by magic, it is not divine but human. It is inherited like other diseases. Everything we feel and think, joy and grief, wisdom and madness, comes from the brain. And all diseases are equally divine and equally human: they come from nature, and can be treated.

commentary.on: it appears to me to be nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases
commentary.text: The thesis, stated at once. Epilepsy is frightening: a person falls, shakes and foams at the mouth. It looked like possession. The author says: it is a disease like others.

commentary.on: Men regard its nature and cause as divine from ignorance and wonder
commentary.text: A diagnosis of the diagnosis. 'Divine' was being used to mean 'not understood'. This is the Ionian move from the first session, now applied to the body.

commentary.on: their discourse savors not of piety, as they suppose, but rather of impiety
commentary.text: A surprising twist. The author does not attack religion; he attacks magic as bad religion. If a charm-seller can command a god's disease, he is claiming power over the gods. True reverence, he implies, does not treat gods as tools.

commentary.on: its nature and cause are divine only just as much as all others are
commentary.text: Not 'nothing is divine' but 'nothing is more divine than anything else'. The whole of nature is divine in the sense that it is ordered, and none of it is a special intervention to be bought off.

commentary.on: Its origin is hereditary, like that of other diseases.
commentary.text: Some epilepsies do run in families, as modern genetics confirms. The author's reason, that seed comes from all parts of the body, is wrong; the observation is right.

commentary.on: Men ought to know that from nothing else but the brain come joys, delights, laughter and sports, and sorrows, griefs, despondency, and lamentations.
commentary.text: One of the great sentences in the history of science. Many Greeks, Aristotle among them, placed thought in the heart. This author says the brain is the seat of all experience, and of madness too. He explains it by phlegm and moisture, which is wrong; but the brain is the right organ.

commentary.on: but all are divine, and all human
commentary.text: The conclusion. Every disease is part of the natural order, which the author calls divine, and every disease is a matter for human study and care. This is close to what Christians later said: nature is God's work and runs by its own causes, so medicine is not a lack of faith.

commentary.on: without minding purifications, spells, and all other illiberal practices of a like kind
commentary.text: The treatment is by regimen, diet and season: natural means for a natural cause. 'Illiberal' meant unworthy of a free, educated person.

parts.author: Hippocrates (the Hippocratic writers)
parts.work: On the Sacred Disease and The Oath
parts.who: The Greek physician Hippocrates of Cos and the doctors of his school, whose writings were gathered under his name.
parts.title: The Oath
parts.context: The Oath's date is unknown: perhaps the late 400s or the 300s BC. It may have been sworn only by a particular group of doctors; it was not a law. This is Francis Adams's translation (1849). It is one paragraph in the source; here it is shown in five pieces, split only where sentences end.
parts.plain: The doctor swears by the gods of healing to treat his teacher as a parent and to teach the art only to those bound by the oath. He will treat the sick for their benefit and never harm them. He will give no deadly drug, even if asked, and will not help a woman to an abortion. He will live a pure life, leave surgery for the stone to specialists, enter houses only for the good of the sick, never seduce anyone in the household, free or slave, and keep secret what he learns. If he keeps the oath, may he be honoured; if he breaks it, may the opposite happen.

commentary.on: I SWEAR by Apollo the physician, and Aesculapius, and Health, and All-heal
commentary.text: The Oath is religious: sworn by Apollo, his son Asclepius (Aesculapius) and Asclepius's daughters Hygieia ('Health', from which 'hygiene') and Panacea ('All-heal'). Naturalistic medicine and piety were not enemies. Medieval Christian copies replaced the gods with God; one Byzantine manuscript writes the Oath in the shape of a cross.

commentary.on: to reckon him who taught me this Art equally dear to me as my parents
commentary.text: Medicine was a family guild. Much of the Oath protects the teacher and the secrets of the craft.

commentary.on: I will follow that system of regimen which, according to my ability and judgment, I consider for the benefit of my patients, and abstain from whatever is deleterious and mischievous
commentary.text: The heart of the Oath. The famous phrase 'First, do no harm' is not in it; it is a later Latin summary (primum non nocere). But the idea is here, and in another Hippocratic work, Epidemics I.11: 'to help, or at least to do no harm' (our own words).

commentary.on: I will give no deadly medicine to any one if asked, nor suggest any such counsel
commentary.text: A refusal to help anyone die, even at their request. Greek and Roman society widely accepted suicide and the exposure of unwanted babies, so this was a minority position. Some scholars, following Ludwig Edelstein (1943), think the Oath came from a Pythagorean circle, which opposed suicide.

commentary.on: I will not give to a woman a pessary to produce abortion
commentary.text: A pessary is a medicine inserted into the body. Scholars still debate whether the clause forbade all abortion or only this method, since other Hippocratic texts mention ways to end pregnancy. Both this clause and the one before are argued over in medicine today; the journey Hard cases takes those questions up.

commentary.on: Into whatever houses I enter, I will go into them for the benefit of the sick
commentary.text: Doctors visited patients at home. The patient's household, wife, children, slaves, was vulnerable, and the Oath binds the doctor to their good.

commentary.on: of freemen and slaves
commentary.text: A striking phrase. In a slave society the Oath protects slaves too from the doctor's abuse. It does not abolish slavery, but it sets a line no patient's status removes.

commentary.on: I will not divulge, as reckoning that all such should be kept secret
commentary.text: Medical confidentiality, still the rule today: what a doctor learns in the home of the sick belongs to the patient.

paras: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place, and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.”
Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

parts.title: The Good Samaritan
parts.context: A lawyer has asked Jesus what the law means by 'love your neighbour', and then, 'Who is my neighbour?' Jesus answers with a story. Luke, who tells it, was by tradition a doctor (Colossians 4:14), writing around AD 80–90. The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops about a thousand metres through desert, and was notorious for robbers. Jews and Samaritans were bitter enemies.

commentary.on: leaving him half dead
commentary.text: The man is anonymous: not described by nation, class or religion. He is simply a wounded human being.

commentary.on: When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
commentary.text: A priest and then a Levite, temple officials, pass by. Perhaps they feared ritual impurity from touching a body. The parable does not say why; it only shows that the respectable religious professionals did nothing.

commentary.on: But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
commentary.text: The hero is the enemy, the outsider. The Greek word for 'moved with compassion' is used elsewhere in the Gospels for Jesus himself.

commentary.on: bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine
commentary.text: This is first aid as Greek doctors practised it: wine to clean the wound, oil to soothe it, bandages. Hippocratic writings on wounds use wine the same way. The Samaritan does what a doctor would do.

commentary.on: brought him to an inn, and took care of him
commentary.text: He does not stop at first aid. He takes the man somewhere he can recover, stays the night and pays for his continued care: two denarii were about two days' wages. Here is the idea of a hospital in a sentence.

commentary.on: Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?
commentary.text: Jesus turns the question round. The lawyer asked whom he must love; Jesus asks who acted as a neighbour. The Oath bound a doctor to the patients he chose to treat. The parable says: anyone in need, even an enemy, is your neighbour, and you must stop for them.

compare.why: The Oath binds a doctor to his patient. Jesus's parable asks a wider question: who is the person I am bound to care for? It became the founding story of Christian medicine.
compare.title: Who is my neighbour?

sections.h: What the Hippocratics got right, and wrong
paras: They got the method right: look for natural causes, observe closely, record what happens, predict the course of illness, and treat with the gentlest effective means. Their case histories in the Epidemics describe patients day by day, including those who died. They saw that climate, water and way of life affect health (Airs, Waters, Places).

They got most of the theory wrong. The four humours did not exist as they imagined. They could not see inside the body, did not know that blood circulates or that germs cause infection, and many of their remedies, bleeding and purging, did harm. But a wrong theory honestly tested can be corrected. A cause that is said to be the gods' secret cannot.
sections.key: The Hippocratics' method, natural causes, observation and records, was right even where their theory of humours was wrong.

paras: The greatest doctor of the ancient world came five centuries later. Galen of Pergamum (AD 129–about 216) trained in Alexandria, treated gladiators, and became physician to the emperor Marcus Aurelius in Rome. He dissected and experimented on animals, showed that arteries carry blood, not air, and that the nerves from the brain control the voice. He wrote so much that his works fill some twenty volumes.

Galen thought the body showed the purpose and skill of a creator, and praised its design in terms Christians and Muslims later loved. His authority was so great that for fourteen hundred years, in Byzantium, the Islamic world and Latin Europe, medicine largely meant Galen. In 1543 Andreas Vesalius, dissecting human bodies in Padua, showed that some of Galen's anatomy came from apes and oxen, not people. Even then, Vesalius's method was Galen's own: look and see.
sections.key: Galen (129–c. 216) joined Hippocratic medicine to anatomy and experiment, and dominated medicine until Vesalius corrected him in 1543.

paras: The Oath has two halves. The first is a contract with the teacher: honour him like a parent, support him, teach his sons without fee. The second is a set of promises about patients: treat for their benefit; never harm; no deadly drug; no abortive pessary; purity of life; no surgery beyond one's skill; no abuse of the household; confidentiality.

It was not universal. Many ancient doctors ignored it, and Roman law allowed much it forbids. But it stated an ideal that outlived its gods: the doctor's skill exists for the patient's good, and the patient's weakness must never become the doctor's opportunity.

Treat for the patient's benefit; avoid harm
Give no poison even if asked
Contested: assisted dying is legal in some countries
Contested: most modern oaths leave it out

sections.key: The Oath binds the doctor to the teacher and, above all, to the patient's good; some clauses are universal today, others fiercely contested.

paras: Few take the original. In 1948, after the trials of Nazi doctors who had experimented on prisoners, the World Medical Association drew up the Declaration of Geneva, a modern oath: the health of my patient will be my first consideration; I will respect the secrets confided in me; I will not use my medical knowledge to violate human rights. It was last revised in 2017. Many medical schools use it or their own pledge.

The two clauses most often dropped are those against the deadly drug and against abortion. That is where modern medicine and the ancient Oath most disagree, and where the deepest moral arguments in medicine now lie. This journey does not settle them: it only notes that the oldest code of medical ethics drew a line there, in a pagan society that did not.
sections.key: Most doctors now swear modern oaths such as the Declaration of Geneva (1948); the clauses on the deadly drug and abortion are those most often dropped.

sections.h: From the Oath to the hospital
paras: The Oath bound a doctor to his own patients, who could usually pay. The ancient world had healing temples, and Roman army hospitals for soldiers and estate infirmaries for slaves. It did not have public hospitals where any sick stranger, especially the poor, could be cared for free.

Christians built them. Already in the plague of the 250s, Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote that Christians nursed the sick, pagans as well as their own, while others fled (quoted by Eusebius, Church History VII.22). Around 369–372 Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (in modern Turkey), built a great complex outside his city, with doctors, nurses, lodgings for travellers and a place for lepers. His friend Gregory of Nazianzus called it a new city outside the city. Around 390 a Roman noblewoman, Fabiola, founded a hospital in Rome and nursed patients herself (Jerome, Letter 77). The emperor Julian, who tried to restore paganism in the 360s, complained in a letter that the 'Galileans' supported not only their own poor but pagans too.
sections.key: The ancient world had healing temples and military infirmaries; Christians in the 300s, such as Basil of Caesarea and Fabiola, built the first hospitals for any sick stranger.

paras: There was a limit to Hippocratic care. A Hippocratic treatise called The Art says the doctor should refuse to treat those who are overmastered by their disease, since medicine cannot help them (our own words). There was a practical reason: a doctor who took on hopeless cases risked his reputation and his fees, and Greek doctors were craftsmen competing for clients. Prognosis, foretelling how an illness would go, helped a doctor know which cases to take.

This is where the Christian difference shows most sharply. The first Christian hospitals took in exactly those Greek medicine sent away: lepers, the dying, the destitute. Basil's foundation had a place for lepers, and he is said to have kissed them. The care was not always medical cure; often it was food, shelter, washing and company to the end. The modern hospice movement, begun by the Christian doctor Cicely Saunders at St Christopher's in London in 1967, stands in that line.
sections.key: Hippocratic doctors were advised to refuse incurable cases; Christian hospitals took in lepers and the dying, a line that runs to the modern hospice.

paras: Did Christians reject Greek medicine as a lack of trust in God? Some individuals did. But the main tradition embraced it. Basil himself wrote that medicine is a gift of God, and that to refuse it out of pride is as wrong as to trust it alone (Longer Rules 55, our own words). The deuterocanonical book of Sirach, chapter 38, already told Jews to honour the physician, for the Lord created him.

The historian Gary Ferngren, in Medicine and Health Care in Early Christianity (2009), argues that early Christians usually used doctors and drugs like everyone else, and that their great addition was not a new theory but a new reach: care for the poor, the stranger and the incurable, who had no claim on anyone. The Hippocratic author said all diseases are 'divine and human'. Christians agreed, and added: and every sick person is my neighbour.
sections.key: The main Christian tradition embraced Greek medicine as God's gift; its great addition, Ferngren argues, was care for the poor, the stranger and the incurable.

debate.question: Did the Christians invent the hospital?

positions.name: Yes: the hospital is a Christian creation
positions.who: Timothy Miller; Gary Ferngren; many historians of medicine
positions.view: Healing temples, army hospitals and slave infirmaries served gods, soldiers or owners' property. The institution that takes in any sick stranger, especially the poor, for free, begins with Christian foundations like Basil's in the 300s, inspired by the command to love the neighbour.
positions.evidence: Basil's Basileias (c. 370); Fabiola in Rome (c. 390); Julian's complaint about Christian charity; no earlier public civilian hospital known.

positions.name: No: it grew from older roots
positions.who: Some classicists and historians of Roman medicine
positions.view: The Romans had valetudinaria for soldiers and slaves; the Asclepian temples housed the sick; Jewish communities cared for the poor and sick. Christians combined and widened existing practices rather than inventing from nothing.
positions.evidence: Excavated Roman military hospitals such as at Vetera on the Rhine; the guest-houses of Asclepian sanctuaries; Jewish charity for the sick.

positions.name: A new purpose for old forms
positions.who: Vivian Nutton and others
positions.view: The buildings and the medicine were Greek and Roman; what was new was who they were for and why. The Christian hospital joined Greek medicine to a theology in which the sick poor are Christ himself (Matthew 25:36).
positions.evidence: Christian hospitals employed Galenic doctors; their founding texts cite the Gospel; the poor and lepers were central.

debate.agree: All agree that public hospitals caring for any sick stranger spread across the Roman world in the 300s and 400s through Christian bishops and benefactors, using Greek medicine.

look.why: No painting for this session: the National Gallery has no painting of a Greek physician, or of the Good Samaritan, that is free to use.

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there': the old chant sung at the washing of feet, the hymn of every Christian hospital's reason for being.

learn.why: The heart of the doctor's oath, worth carrying into any house where people trust you with themselves.

think.why: The Oath protected 'freemen and slaves'; the Samaritan stopped for a stranger. Read where the idea that every person has equal worth came from.

sessions.title: The case against: did Christianity kill Greek science?
sessions.line: A temple and its library destroyed in Alexandria, a woman philosopher murdered by a Christian mob: the strongest case that the Church ended ancient science, and what historians now say.
sessions.plain: Many people have learned a simple story: the Greeks were rational and scientific, then Christianity came, burned the great Library of Alexandria, murdered the philosopher Hypatia, and plunged Europe into a thousand years of darkness until the Renaissance. This session states that case at full strength, in the words of its most famous historian, Edward Gibbon, and its later champions. Then it looks at what really happened in Alexandria, and at what historians of science now say about who lost, and who kept, the learning of the Greeks.
sessions.why: The first five sessions followed the Greek wager on reason from Thales to Hippocrates, and kept meeting hints that knowledge is fragile: Archimedes' forgotten tomb, his works scraped off for a prayer book. Now we must face the hardest question for a Christian telling of this story. If Christianity is good news for reason, why is it so often blamed for killing it? The charge deserves its full weight before any reply.
answers: Did Christians burn the Library of Alexandria?
Who was Hypatia, and why was she killed?
Did Christianity stop Greek science?
Did people in the Middle Ages think the earth was flat?
Who preserved Greek science?
sessions.finding: The popular story says Christians burned the library and ended science; the evidence shows real Christian violence in Alexandria, but historians find that Greek science was already declining, that the great Library had largely gone before 391, and that monks, Byzantine and Muslim scholars and medieval universities preserved and extended Greek science.

paras: We have seen Greek natural philosophy begin in Ionia around 600 BC, grow through Pythagoras, Euclid and Archimedes, and reach medicine with the Hippocratic doctors. Its centre in the Hellenistic age was Alexandria, with its Museum and Library, founded around 300 BC by the first two Ptolemies.

Then Rome conquered the Greek world, and in the AD 300s the Roman Empire became Christian. Constantine favoured the Church from 312; by 380 the emperor Theodosius made Christianity the official religion, and in 391–392 he banned pagan sacrifice. Temples were closed, and some were destroyed, often by monks and crowds. This is the setting of the charge.

background.key: Alexandria was the centre of Greek science; in the 300s the empire became Christian, temples were closed, and in 391 the Serapeum was destroyed.

background.h: The charge, in its own words
paras: The case has a long history. Edward Gibbon (1737–1794), the great historian of Rome's fall, blamed Christianity, with barbarism, for the ruin of the ancient world, and described the destruction of the Serapeum with cold contempt. In 1874 the American scientist John William Draper published a History of the Conflict between Religion and Science, and in 1896 Andrew Dickson White, founding president of Cornell University, published A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom. Their 'conflict thesis' said religion and science have always been at war, and religion has always lost.

In 1980 the astronomer Carl Sagan, in his television series Cosmos, told millions that the Library of Alexandria was the brain of the ancient world, that Hypatia was its last light, murdered by Christians, and that its destruction was followed by a thousand years of darkness. More recently, the historian Charles Freeman (The Closing of the Western Mind, 2002) and the journalist Catherine Nixey (The Darkening Age, 2017) have argued that Christianity's demand for faith and its war on paganism closed down open inquiry.
background.key: Gibbon, then Draper (1874) and White (1896), then Sagan (1980), Freeman and Nixey made the case that Christianity ended ancient science.

paras: The main reading is Gibbon himself: his account of the Serapeum in 391, the strongest classic statement of the charge. Then a second, shorter passage from much later in his book, where Gibbon turns to the most famous story of all, that the Arabs burned the Library in 642, and says what he thinks of it.
The comparison is the oldest account of Hypatia's death, by Socrates Scholasticus, a Christian historian writing about twenty-five years later. It is a Christian witness against Christians.
background.key: We read Gibbon on the Serapeum and on the library legends, then the earliest, Christian account of Hypatia's murder.
