paras: In this wide and various prospect of devastation, the spectator may distinguish the ruins of the temple of Serapis, at Alexandria. Serapis does not appear to have been one of the native gods, or monsters, who sprung from the fruitful soil of superstitious Egypt. The first of the Ptolemies had been commanded, by a dream, to import the mysterious stranger from the coast of Pontus, where he had been long adored by the inhabitants of Sinope; but his attributes and his reign were so imperfectly understood, that it became a subject of dispute, whether he represented the bright orb of day, or the gloomy monarch of the subterraneous regions. The Egyptians, who were obstinately devoted to the religion of their fathers, refused to admit this foreign deity within the walls of their cities. But the obsequious priests, who were seduced by the liberality of the Ptolemies, submitted, without resistance, to the power of the god of Pontus: an honorable and domestic genealogy was provided; and this fortunate usurper was introduced into the throne and bed of Osiris, the husband of Isis, and the celestial monarch of Egypt.

Alexandria, which claimed his peculiar protection, gloried in the name of the city of Serapis. His temple, which rivalled the pride and magnificence of the Capitol, was erected on the spacious summit of an artificial mount, raised one hundred steps above the level of the adjacent parts of the city; and the interior cavity was strongly supported by arches, and distributed into vaults and subterraneous apartments. The consecrated buildings were surrounded by a quadrangular portico; the stately halls, and exquisite statues, displayed the triumph of the arts; and the treasures of ancient learning were preserved in the famous Alexandrian library, which had arisen with new splendor from its ashes. After the edicts of Theodosius had severely prohibited the sacrifices of the Pagans, they were still tolerated in the city and temple of Serapis; and this singular indulgence was imprudently ascribed to the superstitious terrors of the Christians themselves; as if they had feared to abolish those ancient rites, which could alone secure the inundations of the Nile, the harvests of Egypt, and the subsistence of Constantinople.

At that time the archiepiscopal throne of Alexandria was filled by Theophilus, the perpetual enemy of peace and virtue; a bold, bad man, whose hands were alternately polluted with gold and with blood. His pious indignation was excited by the honors of Serapis; and the insults which he offered to an ancient temple of Bacchus, convinced the Pagans that he meditated a more important and dangerous enterprise. In the tumultuous capital of Egypt, the slightest provocation was sufficient to inflame a civil war. The votaries of Serapis, whose strength and numbers were much inferior to those of their antagonists, rose in arms at the instigation of the philosopher Olympius, who exhorted them to die in the defence of the altars of the gods. These Pagan fanatics fortified themselves in the temple, or rather fortress, of Serapis; repelled the besiegers by daring sallies, and a resolute defence; and, by the inhuman cruelties which they exercised on their Christian prisoners, obtained the last consolation of despair. The efforts of the prudent magistrate were usefully exerted for the establishment of a truce, till the answer of Theodosius should determine the fate of Serapis. The two parties assembled, without arms, in the principal square; and the Imperial rescript was publicly read.

But when a sentence of destruction against the idols of Alexandria was pronounced, the Christians set up a shout of joy and exultation, whilst the unfortunate Pagans, whose fury had given way to consternation, retired with hasty and silent steps, and eluded, by their flight or obscurity, the resentment of their enemies. Theophilus proceeded to demolish the temple of Serapis, without any other difficulties, than those which he found in the weight and solidity of the materials: but these obstacles proved so insuperable, that he was obliged to leave the foundations; and to content himself with reducing the edifice itself to a heap of rubbish, a part of which was soon afterwards cleared away, to make room for a church, erected in honor of the Christian martyrs. The valuable library of Alexandria was pillaged or destroyed; and near twenty years afterwards, the appearance of the empty shelves excited the regret and indignation of every spectator, whose mind was not totally darkened by religious prejudice. The compositions of ancient genius, so many of which have irretrievably perished, might surely have been excepted from the wreck of idolatry, for the amusement and instruction of succeeding ages; and either the zeal or the avarice of the archbishop, might have been satiated with the rich spoils, which were the reward of his victory.

The colossal statue of Serapis was involved in the ruin of his temple and religion. A great number of plates of different metals, artificially joined together, composed the majestic figure of the deity, who touched on either side the walls of the sanctuary. The aspect of Serapis, his sitting posture, and the sceptre, which he bore in his left hand, were extremely similar to the ordinary representations of Jupiter. He was distinguished from Jupiter by the basket, or bushel, which was placed on his head; and by the emblematic monster which he held in his right hand; the head and body of a serpent branching into three tails, which were again terminated by the triple heads of a dog, a lion, and a wolf. It was confidently affirmed, that if any impious hand should dare to violate the majesty of the god, the heavens and the earth would instantly return to their original chaos. An intrepid soldier, animated by zeal, and armed with a weighty battle-axe, ascended the ladder; and even the Christian multitude expected, with some anxiety, the event of the combat. He aimed a vigorous stroke against the cheek of Serapis; the cheek fell to the ground; the thunder was still silent, and both the heavens and the earth continued to preserve their accustomed order and tranquillity.

The victorious soldier repeated his blows: the huge idol was overthrown, and broken in pieces; and the limbs of Serapis were ignominiously dragged through the streets of Alexandria. His mangled carcass was burnt in the Amphitheatre, amidst the shouts of the populace; and many persons attributed their conversion to this discovery of the impotence of their tutelar deity. The popular modes of religion, that propose any visible and material objects of worship, have the advantage of adapting and familiarizing themselves to the senses of mankind: but this advantage is counterbalanced by the various and inevitable accidents to which the faith of the idolater is exposed. It is scarcely possible, that, in every disposition of mind, he should preserve his implicit reverence for the idols, or the relics, which the naked eye, and the profane hand, are unable to distinguish from the most common productions of art or nature; and if, in the hour of danger, their secret and miraculous virtue does not operate for their own preservation, he scorns the vain apologies of his priests, and justly derides the object, and the folly, of his superstitious attachment.

I should deceive the expectation of the reader, if I passed in silence the fate of the Alexandrian library, as it is described by the learned Abulpharagius. The spirit of Amrou was more curious and liberal than that of his brethren, and in his leisure hours, the Arabian chief was pleased with the conversation of John, the last disciple of Ammonius, and who derived the surname of Philoponus from his laborious studies of grammar and philosophy. Emboldened by this familiar intercourse, Philoponus presumed to solicit a gift, inestimable in his opinion, contemptible in that of the Barbarians—the royal library, which alone, among the spoils of Alexandria, had not been appropriated by the visit and the seal of the conqueror.

Amrou was inclined to gratify the wish of the grammarian, but his rigid integrity refused to alienate the minutest object without the consent of the caliph; and the well-known answer of Omar was inspired by the ignorance of a fanatic. “If these writings of the Greeks agree with the book of God, they are useless, and need not be preserved: if they disagree, they are pernicious, and ought to be destroyed.” The sentence was executed with blind obedience: the volumes of paper or parchment were distributed to the four thousand baths of the city; and such was their incredible multitude, that six months were barely sufficient for the consumption of this precious fuel. Since the Dynasties of Abulpharagius have been given to the world in a Latin version, the tale has been repeatedly transcribed; and every scholar, with pious indignation, has deplored the irreparable shipwreck of the learning, the arts, and the genius, of antiquity. For my own part, I am strongly tempted to deny both the fact and the consequences. The fact is indeed marvellous. “Read and wonder!” says the historian himself: and the solitary report of a stranger who wrote at the end of six hundred years on the confines of Media, is overbalanced by the silence of two annalist of a more early date, both Christians, both natives of Egypt, and the most ancient of whom, the patriarch Eutychius, has amply described the conquest of Alexandria. The rigid sentence of Omar is repugnant to the sound and orthodox precept of the Mahometan casuists they expressly declare, that the religious books of the Jews and Christians, which are acquired by the right of war, should never be committed to the flames;

and that the works of profane science, historians or poets, physicians or philosophers, may be lawfully applied to the use of the faithful. A more destructive zeal may perhaps be attributed to the first successors of Mahomet; yet in this instance, the conflagration would have speedily expired in the deficiency of materials. I should not recapitulate the disasters of the Alexandrian library, the involuntary flame that was kindled by Caesar in his own defence, or the mischievous bigotry of the Christians, who studied to destroy the monuments of idolatry. But if we gradually descend from the age of the Antonines to that of Theodosius, we shall learn from a chain of contemporary witnesses, that the royal palace and the temple of Serapis no longer contained the four, or the seven, hundred thousand volumes, which had been assembled by the curiosity and magnificence of the Ptolemies. Perhaps the church and seat of the patriarchs might be enriched with a repository of books; but if the ponderous mass of Arian and Monophysite controversy were indeed consumed in the public baths, a philosopher may allow, with a smile, that it was ultimately devoted to the benefit of mankind. I sincerely regret the more valuable libraries which have been involved in the ruin of the Roman empire; but when I seriously compute the lapse of ages, the waste of ignorance, and the calamities of war, our treasures, rather than our losses, are the objects of my surprise.

parts.author: Edward Gibbon
parts.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
parts.who: The English historian whose six-volume history of Rome's fall made him the most famous historian of the Enlightenment, and a sharp critic of the Church.
parts.ref: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. XXVIII (1781)
parts.title: The fall of Serapis
parts.context: Chapter XXVIII describes the end of paganism under Theodosius. Gibbon had read the ancient Christian historians who described the Serapeum's fall (Rufinus, Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret) and the pagan Eunapius. The text is from the edition with notes by H. H. Milman; Gibbon's and Milman's footnote numbers are left out. A cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: The Serapeum was Alexandria's great temple of the god Serapis, on a raised hill, with halls, statues and a famous library. When the bishop, Theophilus, whom Gibbon calls a bold, bad man, insulted pagan worship, pagans fortified the temple and killed Christian prisoners. The emperor ordered the idols destroyed. The temple was pulled down and a church built in its place. Gibbon says the library was plundered or destroyed, and that twenty years later its empty shelves shocked visitors. A soldier struck the giant statue of Serapis; the heavens did not fall; and many pagans lost their faith.

commentary.on: the treasures of ancient learning were preserved in the famous Alexandrian library, which had arisen with new splendor from its ashes
commentary.text: Gibbon's key claim. Note what he concedes in passing: the original library had already burned, in his footnote, 'in Caesar's Alexandrian war'. What stood in the Serapeum was a daughter library, the one founded later beside the temple.

commentary.on: a bold, bad man, whose hands were alternately polluted with gold and with blood
commentary.text: Gibbon at his most brilliant and least neutral. Theophilus was indeed a ruthless church politician; he later engineered the exile of John Chrysostom. But the sentence is written to make the reader despise him, and the Church with him.

commentary.on: by the inhuman cruelties which they exercised on their Christian prisoners
commentary.text: Gibbon is fair enough to record that the violence was not one-sided: pagans led by the philosopher Olympius held the temple and tortured Christians. The ancient sources agree.

commentary.on: The valuable library of Alexandria was pillaged or destroyed
commentary.text: The centre of the charge. Gibbon's evidence, given in his footnote, is the Christian writer Orosius, who around 416 said he had seen empty book-chests in temples, emptied, he was told, by men of his own side in his own day. Gibbon adds that Orosius 'seems to blush'. Notice that none of the ancient accounts of 391 says that books were burned; and some scholars think that by 391 the Serapeum held few books, since the pagan historian Ammianus, writing around 390, speaks of its libraries in the past tense.

commentary.on: The compositions of ancient genius, so many of which have irretrievably perished, might surely have been excepted from the wreck of idolatry
commentary.text: The heart of Gibbon's lament, and it is fair as far as it goes. Christian zeal against idols did not stop to save what was valuable in pagan temples.

commentary.on: the thunder was still silent, and both the heavens and the earth continued to preserve their accustomed order and tranquillity
commentary.text: Gibbon's irony cuts both ways. The pagans believed the world would collapse if Serapis were struck; nature carried on by its own order. Gibbon mocks the pagans' superstition here as freely as he mocks Christian zeal elsewhere.

parts.author: Edward Gibbon
parts.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
parts.who: The English historian whose six-volume history of Rome's fall made him the most famous historian of the Enlightenment, and a sharp critic of the Church.
parts.ref: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. LI (1788)
parts.title: Our treasures, rather than our losses
parts.context: Seven years later, in his account of the Arab conquest of Egypt (641–642), Gibbon reaches the most famous library story of all: that the caliph Omar ordered the books burned to heat the public baths. Footnote numbers are left out.
parts.plain: Gibbon tells the story of the Arab general Amr, the scholar John Philoponus, and Caliph Omar's order: if the Greek books agree with the Qur'an they are useless, and if they disagree they are wicked, so burn them. Then Gibbon says he does not believe it. The story first appears six hundred years later; earlier Christian writers in Egypt say nothing of it; Muslim law forbade burning such books; and the great collections had long gone before the Arabs came. Considering how much time, ignorance and war destroy, he says, what surprises him is how much has survived.

commentary.on: John, the last disciple of Ammonius, and who derived the surname of Philoponus from his laborious studies
commentary.text: John Philoponus ('lover of work') was a Christian philosopher of Alexandria. He had died about seventy years before the Arabs arrived, so he could not have asked Amr for the books: one sign that the story is legend. We meet him again in the lecture.

commentary.on: For my own part, I am strongly tempted to deny both the fact and the consequences.
commentary.text: The great critic of the Church refuses a story that would have suited him, because the evidence is bad. That is a historian's honesty, and it is worth applying to every library legend, including the one he told about 391.

commentary.on: the solitary report of a stranger who wrote at the end of six hundred years
commentary.text: Gibbon's test: how early is the source, and is it alone? The same test, applied to the claim that Christians destroyed the Library, finds that no ancient source says so.

commentary.on: the mischievous bigotry of the Christians, who studied to destroy the monuments of idolatry
commentary.text: Gibbon keeps his charge against the Christians, but now as one cause among many.

commentary.on: our treasures, rather than our losses, are the objects of my surprise
commentary.text: Gibbon's own conclusion: given the 'lapse of ages, the waste of ignorance, and the calamities of war', the surprise is how much survived. That raises a question this session must answer: who kept it?

paras: There was a woman at Alexandria named Hypatia, daughter of the philosopher Theon, who made such attainments in literature and science, as to far surpass all the philosophers of her own time. Having succeeded to the school of Plato and Plotinus, she explained the principles of philosophy to her auditors, many of whom came from a distance to receive her instructions. On account of the self-possession and ease of manner, which she had acquired in consequence of the cultivation of her mind, she not unfrequently appeared in public in presence of the magistrates. Neither did she feel abashed in coming to an assembly of men. For all men on account of her extraordinary dignity and virtue admired her the more. Yet even she fell a victim to the political jealousy which at that time prevailed. For as she had frequent interviews with Orestes, it was calumniously reported among the Christian populace, that it was she who prevented Orestes from being reconciled to the bishop. Some of them therefore, hurried away by a fierce and bigoted zeal, whose ringleader was a reader named Peter, waylaid her returning home, and dragging her from her carriage, they took her to the church called Cæsareum, where they completely stripped her, and then murdered her with tiles. After tearing her body in pieces, they took her mangled limbs to a place called Cinaron, and there burnt them. This affair brought not the least opprobrium, not only upon Cyril, but also upon the whole Alexandrian church. And surely nothing can be farther from the spirit of Christianity than the allowance of massacres, fights, and transactions of that sort. This happened in the month of March during Lent, in the fourth year of Cyril's episcopate, under the tenth consulate of Honorius, and the sixth of Theodosius.

parts.author: Socrates Scholasticus
parts.title: Of Hypatia the female philosopher
parts.who: A Christian lawyer of Constantinople who continued Eusebius's history of the Church.
parts.context: In 415 Alexandria was torn by a feud between its new bishop, Cyril (Theophilus's nephew), and the imperial prefect, Orestes, with riots between Christians, Jews and pagans. Socrates wrote about twenty-five years later. This is A. C. Zenos's translation (1890), in the New Advent edition; an HTML letter-code in the source ('Cæsareum') is printed as the letter.
parts.plain: Hypatia, daughter of the mathematician Theon, was the leading philosopher in Alexandria, teaching Plato's philosophy to students from far away and respected even by magistrates. Because she often met the prefect Orestes, Christians spread the rumour that she was stopping him making peace with the bishop. A mob led by a church reader called Peter dragged her from her carriage into a church, stripped her, killed her with roof tiles, tore her body apart and burned it. Socrates says this brought great shame on Cyril and the church of Alexandria, and that nothing could be further from the spirit of Christianity.

commentary.on: who made such attainments in literature and science, as to far surpass all the philosophers of her own time
commentary.text: Hypatia (born perhaps 355–370, died 415) taught mathematics, astronomy and Platonic philosophy. Later sources say she edited her father's commentaries on Ptolemy and wrote on Diophantus and Apollonius. One of her pupils, Synesius, became a Christian bishop and wrote her warm letters; she taught Christians and pagans alike.

commentary.on: Yet even she fell a victim to the political jealousy which at that time prevailed.
commentary.text: Socrates's diagnosis is politics, not science. Hypatia was killed as an ally of the prefect in a power struggle with the bishop, not for her mathematics or for being a woman. That does not make it less terrible; it changes what it shows.

commentary.on: hurried away by a fierce and bigoted zeal, whose ringleader was a reader named Peter
commentary.text: A reader was a minor church office. The murderers were Christians acting in the name of their faith. Whether Cyril ordered or encouraged it is disputed; the sources do not say he did, and later hostile and friendly writers disagree.

commentary.on: they took her to the church called Cæsareum, where they completely stripped her, and then murdered her with tiles
commentary.text: The murder took place in a church. The detail is deliberate: Socrates does not spare his own side.

commentary.on: And surely nothing can be farther from the spirit of Christianity than the allowance of massacres, fights, and transactions of that sort.
commentary.text: The earliest witness judges the killing by Christianity's own standard and condemns it. The charge against the Church in Alexandria is real, and a Christian historian made it first.

compare.author: Socrates Scholasticus
compare.why: The oldest account of the most famous victim of Christian violence in Alexandria, written by a Christian. Read what he blames, and what he thinks of it.
compare.title: The death of Hypatia

paras: Put the charge as strongly as its best advocates would. In the 300s the Roman state became Christian and turned on the old religions. Temples, which housed libraries and statues as well as altars, were closed and many destroyed; the Serapeum was the most famous. Philosophers were harassed; Hypatia was butchered in a church. The Church taught that faith comes before reason: Paul asked, 'Hasn't God made foolish the wisdom of this world?' (1 Corinthians 1:20), and Tertullian, around 200, asked what Athens has to do with Jerusalem (Prescription against Heretics 7, our own words). Some Christian writers, such as Lactantius around 310, mocked the idea of a round earth with people on the underside.

And the outcome, the case goes on, speaks for itself. After about 400, original Greek science almost stops. Western Europe forgets most of it. For centuries the most learned men are monks studying Scripture, not nature. Only when the Renaissance and the scientific revolution threw off the Church's authority did inquiry revive, and even then the Church condemned Galileo. In the words of Freeman's title, the Western mind was closed. This is the conflict thesis, and much of it rests on real events.
sections.key: The charge: a Christian state destroyed temples and their libraries, a mob killed Hypatia, faith was put above reason, and Greek science stopped for a thousand years.

paras: Now the replies, beginning with the facts. The great Library of the Ptolemies stood in the palace quarter. Ancient writers say that books were burned in Julius Caesar's fighting in 48 BC; Seneca gives 40,000 books, others more. The Library seems to have declined under Roman rule, losing royal patronage. In AD 272 the emperor Aurelian's war destroyed much of the palace quarter, and after that we hear nothing of the great Library. The daughter library in the Serapeum survived longer, but by 391 it may have held little: no account of 391 mentions books.

So the main Library died slowly, of neglect, war and fire, mostly before Christianity was legal. The Christian destruction of the Serapeum was real, and may have destroyed books; Orosius's empty shelves suggest losses. But the picture of monks torching the brain of the ancient world in one night is not what the sources say. The Arab story of 642 is, as Gibbon saw, a legend first told six centuries later.
sections.key: The great Library declined and was probably destroyed by 272, before Christianity was legal; the Serapeum's destruction in 391 was real, but no source says its books were burned.

paras: Hypatia's murder was a real atrocity by Christians. It should be said plainly. But what does it show? The earliest source places it in a political feud between bishop and prefect. Hypatia was not the last scientist of antiquity: mathematics and philosophy continued in Alexandria for two more centuries, taught by pagans and Christians, and the Neoplatonist school in Athens continued until around 529.

Modern retellings, from the Victorian novel Hypatia (1853) by the clergyman Charles Kingsley to Sagan's Cosmos and the film Agora (2009), have made her a symbol of science martyred by faith. The historian Maria Dzielska, in Hypatia of Alexandria (1995), traces how the legend grew and argues that the real woman was a respected teacher, loyal to Plato, caught in city politics. Her death shows what religious zeal and mob violence can do. It does not show that Christianity ended science.
sections.key: Hypatia's murder was a Christian atrocity rooted in politics; it did not end ancient science, which continued in Alexandria for two centuries.

paras: The historian David Lindberg, whose Beginnings of Western Science is the standard account, points out that original Greek science peaked in the 200s BC, the age of Archimedes, Eratosthenes and Aristarchus, and slowed long before Christianity. Under Rome there were great names, Ptolemy and Galen in the 100s AD, but fewer of them. Patronage moved to other things; Latin readers wanted handbooks, not research; the crises of the 200s AD, war, plague and inflation, hit every kind of learning.

In a much-cited essay in Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion (2009), edited by Ronald Numbers, Lindberg called the idea that Christianity caused the decline of ancient science a myth. He did not say the early Church was a friend of research. He said its attitude was mixed, and mostly that of a 'handmaiden': Greek learning was valued where it served faith, as Augustine argued (On Christian Teaching II.40), not for its own sake. That was no worse, he argued, than the attitude of the Roman elite in general.
sections.key: Lindberg and Numbers: Greek science peaked in the 200s BC and declined under Rome; the Church treated it as a 'handmaiden', which neither killed nor greatly fostered it.

paras: Gibbon was surprised by how much survived. It survived because people copied it, by hand, for a thousand years. In the Greek-speaking Christian empire of Byzantium, scholars kept copying Euclid, Archimedes, Ptolemy and Galen; the oldest complete manuscript of Euclid, now in Oxford, was copied in Constantinople in 888. In the Latin West, Boethius (about 480–524) translated and wrote handbooks on arithmetic, music and geometry, and Cassiodorus founded a monastery around 550 where copying books was part of the monks' work.

In the 800s, in Baghdad, the Abbasid caliphs paid for Greek books to be translated into Arabic. Many translators were Syriac-speaking Christians, the most famous, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Nestorian Christian who translated Galen. Muslim scholars such as al-Khwarizmi, Ibn al-Haytham and Ibn Sina took the work much further. In the 1100s, in Toledo and Sicily, Christian scholars translated the Arabic and Greek into Latin. The new universities of Bologna, Paris and Oxford, founded around 1100–1200, made Aristotle, Euclid and Ptolemy the core of the syllabus for every student.
sections.key: Greek science survived because Byzantine copyists, Latin monks, Christian and Muslim translators in Baghdad, and the medieval universities kept and extended it.

sections.h: John Philoponus and the flat-earth myth
paras: The best answer to the charge may be a single Christian of Alexandria. John Philoponus (about 490–570), a century after Hypatia, criticised Aristotle's physics. He argued that a thrown object keeps moving because of a force given to it, not because the air pushes it, and that heavy and light bodies dropped together fall at almost the same speed, which a simple test shows. He argued, against the pagan philosophers, that the world had a beginning. Galileo cited him a thousand years later.

And the flat earth? A few Christian writers, Lactantius and the merchant Cosmas around 550, did reject a round earth. But nearly every educated Christian accepted it. Bede, the English monk, explained around 725 that the earth is a globe; John of Sacrobosco's On the Sphere (about 1230) taught it in every university. The story that medieval people believed in a flat earth was spread in the 1800s, not least by Washington Irving's romantic life of Columbus (1828) and by Draper and White. The historian Jeffrey Burton Russell exposed it in Inventing the Flat Earth (1991).
sections.key: John Philoponus, a Christian of Alexandria, improved on Aristotle's physics; and the idea that medieval Christians thought the earth flat is a 19th-century myth.

paras: The honest verdict is mixed, and should be said so. Christian zeal destroyed temples and some of what was in them; a Christian mob murdered a philosopher; some Christian writers despised pagan learning and a few despised the round earth; later, the Church tried Galileo. The conflict thesis is wrong as a general law, but there were real conflicts, and Christians should not pretend otherwise.

What the evidence does not support is the grand story: that Christianity burned the Library, ended Greek science and caused a thousand years of darkness. The Library was lost mainly before Christian rule; Greek science was already declining; and the people who kept it alive for a thousand years were mostly Christian monks, scholars and translators, with Muslim and Jewish scholars beside them. Historians of science today, believers and unbelievers alike, almost all reject the simple conflict story. The historian John Hedley Brooke's summary is that the relationship has been one of complexity: sometimes conflict, often cooperation, usually something in between.
sections.key: Real Christian violence and hostility happened; but the grand story that Christianity burned the Library and ended Greek science is rejected by almost all historians of science.

debate.question: Did Christianity kill Greek science?

positions.name: Yes: it closed the Western mind
positions.who: Edward Gibbon; J. W. Draper; A. D. White; Carl Sagan; Charles Freeman; Catherine Nixey
positions.view: A Christian state destroyed pagan temples and their learning; Christian teachers put faith above reason and authority above inquiry; original science stopped and was not revived until Europe began to escape the Church's grip.
positions.evidence: The Serapeum (391); Hypatia (415); Paul and Tertullian on worldly wisdom; Lactantius on the round earth; the long gap between Ptolemy and Copernicus.

positions.name: No: the decline had other causes, and Christians preserved it
positions.who: David Lindberg; Ronald Numbers; Edward Grant; James Hannam
positions.view: Greek science peaked centuries before Christianity and declined under Rome for economic and cultural reasons. The Library was largely lost before 391. Christian scholars in Byzantium and the West, with Muslim and Jewish scholars, copied, translated and extended Greek science, and the medieval universities made it the core of education.
positions.evidence: No source says Christians burned the Library; the Library's earlier destructions; John Philoponus; the Byzantine manuscripts; the Arabic and Latin translation movements; the universities.

positions.name: Complexity: neither war nor harmony
positions.who: John Hedley Brooke; Peter Harrison
positions.view: Religion and science have related in many ways at different times: conflict, cooperation, indifference. Ask about particular people and events, not 'Christianity' and 'science' as armies. The very idea of two opposed camps is a 19th-century invention.
positions.evidence: Real conflicts (Hypatia, Galileo) beside deep cooperation (monastic copying, clerical scientists); the late origin of the words 'science' and 'religion' in their modern senses.

debate.agree: All agree that the Serapeum was destroyed by Christians in 391 and that Hypatia was murdered by a Christian mob in 415, and that the story of the Arab burning in 642 is unreliable.

look.why: Saint Jerome (about 347–420), who translated the Bible into Latin, loved the pagan classics so much that he dreamed he stood before Christ's judgement seat and was accused of following Cicero rather than Christ (Letter 22.30). He lived through the years of the Serapeum and Hypatia. El Greco painted him about 1610–1614.
points: An elderly man with short white hair and a frost-white beard kneels at the opening of a rocky cave.
His body is long and sinewy, nearly nude except for a light cloth across his hips.
One arm lies along an open book, resting against his hip or on a rock.
With the other hand he grips a rock, held away from his body.
He lifts his face towards rays of yellow and white light in a turquoise sky at the upper left.
The inside of the cave is swallowed in darkness.

music.why: Its own legend is a parable for this session: the story that this Mass saved polyphony from a Church ban is mostly myth, but the music, and the Church's long care for it, are real.

think.why: 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?' Read how the Church argued over pagan learning, and why it mostly chose to keep it.

check.q: What is the strongest evidence for the claim that Christians destroyed books in 391?
options: Orosius's report, around 416, of empty book-chests in temples, emptied by Christians in his own day
Several eyewitnesses describe books being burned
Socrates Scholasticus says Hypatia's books were burned
The Arab historians say so
check.why: Gibbon's footnote rests on Orosius; no account of 391 itself mentions books.

check.q: Why does Gibbon reject the story that the Arabs burned the Library in 642?
options: Because the story first appears six hundred years later, earlier Egyptian Christian writers are silent, and the great collections had already gone
Because he blamed the Christians instead
Because John Philoponus denied it
Because he admired Islam
check.why: Gibbon applies a historian's test: late, solitary sources and silence in earlier ones.

check.q: According to Socrates Scholasticus, why was Hypatia killed?
options: For teaching that the earth goes round the sun
Because she was a woman who taught
Because she refused to be baptised
Because of political jealousy: Christians believed she was stopping the prefect making peace with the bishop
check.why: 'She fell a victim to the political jealousy which at that time prevailed'.

check.q: Which fact most weakens the claim that Christians destroyed the great Library of Alexandria?
options: The great Library seems to have been lost by about 272, after Caesar's fire and Aurelian's war, before Christianity was legal
Hypatia was a Christian
Christians loved books
The Library never existed
check.why: The main Library declined and was destroyed before 312; only the Serapeum's daughter library fell in 391.

check.q: Which reply to the charge is strongest, according to Lindberg?
options: Hypatia was not a scientist
Christians never harmed pagans
Greek science had peaked in the 200s BC and was declining under Rome, and Christian scholars later preserved and extended it
Science began only in the 1600s
check.why: The decline began earlier and had other causes; Christians copied, translated and built universities.

check.q: Which statement is the fairest overall verdict?
options: Christianity had nothing to do with any loss
Muslims, not Christians, were responsible
There was real Christian violence and hostility, but the grand story of Christians burning the Library and ending science is not supported; Christians were also chief preservers
Christianity killed Greek science
check.why: Real conflicts, but not the grand narrative: Brooke's 'complexity'.

tutorial.question: 'Christianity killed Greek science.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: State the case at full strength first, with Gibbon's account and the later conflict thesis. Then examine the evidence for the Library and for Hypatia, using the earliest sources. Then weigh the wider question: when and why Greek science declined, and who preserved it. End with a verdict that admits what is true in the charge.
strong: States the charge fairly and strongly, with real events.
Distinguishes the great Library from the Serapeum, with dates.
Uses Socrates Scholasticus as the earliest, Christian, source on Hypatia.
Applies Gibbon's own test of sources to the library legends.
Gives evidence for the earlier decline and for preservation (Byzantium, Baghdad, monasteries, universities, Philoponus).
Reaches a balanced verdict that does not deny real Christian violence.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: next time you hear a story that makes the other side look very bad (in politics, in religion, at work), apply Gibbon's test before you repeat it: how early is the source, and is it alone? And if it is true, say so.
sessions.reflect: Where do you find it hardest to admit that people on your own side did wrong?
takeaways: The charge is real in part: Christians destroyed the Serapeum in 391 and a Christian mob murdered Hypatia in 415.
But the great Library was lost mostly before Christian rule, no source says Christians burned it, and Greek science was already declining.
Christian copyists, translators and universities, with Muslim and Jewish scholars, preserved and extended Greek science; most historians reject the simple conflict story.

sessions.title: Does science need God? The verdict
sessions.line: Plato pictured a good craftsman ordering the world after an eternal pattern; Christians said a rational Creator made it freely. Did that belief help modern science to be born?
sessions.plain: Science works only if the world is orderly and our minds can grasp that order. Why should either be true? The Greeks trusted that the world is rational; Plato's Timaeus said a good maker shaped it after an eternal pattern. Christians added that a rational God made the world freely, out of nothing, so its laws had to be discovered by looking, not deduced from the armchair. This session reads the Timaeus, recalls Psalm 19, weighs the famous argument that belief in a Creator helped give birth to modern science, and gives the journey's verdict.
sessions.why: Session 6 answered the charge that Christianity killed Greek science: the real violence was admitted, but the evidence showed decline from other causes and long preservation by Christians and others. That clears the ground for the last question, the one people actually ask today: does science need God, or has it outgrown him? To answer, we go back to the deepest Greek account of why the world is orderly at all.
answers: Why is the world orderly enough for science?
What did Plato think about the making of the world?
Did belief in a Creator help science to begin?
Does science need God now?
What is the journey's verdict?
sessions.finding: Greek reason trusted the world to be orderly; the biblical belief in a rational, free Creator gave later science a reason to expect laws and to test them; science does not prove God, but it rests on an order that belief in God explains.

paras: Here is where this journey ends, so that you can test it as you read. The Greeks made the great wager that the world can be understood by reason, and won it: natural causes, number, proof, measurement and medicine are all theirs. Christianity did not kill that inheritance; Christians, with others, kept and extended it. And the biblical belief that the world was made by a rational and free Creator gave the scientists of the 1600s a reason to expect laws of nature, and a reason to find them by experiment. Science does not need God to do its daily work. But it needs an orderly, intelligible world and minds fit to know it, and it cannot explain where those come from.
That is a conclusion to weigh, not to swallow. This session gives the case for it and the best objections.
background.key: The verdict: the Greeks won the wager on reason; Christians preserved it; belief in a rational, free Creator helped modern science; science relies on an order it cannot itself explain.

paras: The journey has run from Thales's water to Pythagoras's numbers, Euclid's proofs, Archimedes' machines, Hippocrates' natural causes, and then the charge against the Church in Alexandria. Through all of it ran a question the Greeks rarely asked out loud: why should the world make sense at all?

Plato faced it near the end of his life, around 360 BC, in the Timaeus. It is his only dialogue about the physical world, and for a thousand years it was the only work of Plato most of the Latin West could read, in a partial Latin translation by Calcidius from the 300s. In Raphael's School of Athens (1509–1511), Plato carries it under his arm.

background.key: Plato's Timaeus (c. 360 BC) asked why the world is orderly, and shaped the Western picture of creation for a thousand years.

paras: The main reading is the opening of Timaeus's speech: the distinction between what always is and what is always becoming; the maker who looks to an eternal pattern; and the reason he made the world: because he was good, and wished all things to be like himself.

The comparison has two short parts. First, the opening of Psalm 19, which you read in full in 'Is there a God?': the heavens declare the glory of God. Then Cicero, who saw in Archimedes' sphere a picture of Plato's God making the world.
background.key: We read Plato's account of the making of the world, then Psalm 19 recalled and Cicero on Archimedes' sphere as an image of the Maker.

before: What two kinds of things does Timaeus distinguish, and which can be known by reason?
Why, according to Timaeus, did the maker make the world?
Why does Timaeus say his account can only be 'probable'?
sessions.readWhy: Plato's Timaeus: the world made by a good maker after an eternal pattern, and why we can understand it.

paras: TIMAEUS: All men, Socrates, who have any degree of right feeling, at the beginning of every enterprise, whether small or great, always call upon God. And we, too, who are going to discourse of the nature of the universe, how created or how existing without creation, if we be not altogether out of our wits, must invoke the aid of Gods and Goddesses and pray that our words may be acceptable to them and consistent with themselves. Let this, then, be our invocation of the Gods, to which I add an exhortation of myself to speak in such manner as will be most intelligible to you, and will most accord with my own intent.

First then, in my judgment, we must make a distinction and ask, What is that which always is and has no becoming; and what is that which is always becoming and never is? That which is apprehended by intelligence and reason is always in the same state; but that which is conceived by opinion with the help of sensation and without reason, is always in a process of becoming and perishing and never really is. Now everything that becomes or is created must of necessity be created by some cause, for without a cause nothing can be created. The work of the creator, whenever he looks to the unchangeable and fashions the form and nature of his work after an unchangeable pattern, must necessarily be made fair and perfect; but when he looks to the created only, and uses a created pattern, it is not fair or perfect. Was the heaven then or the world, whether called by this or by any other more appropriate name—assuming the name, I am asking a question which has to be asked at the beginning of an enquiry about anything—was the world, I say, always in existence and without beginning? or created, and had it a beginning? Created, I reply, being visible and tangible and having a body, and therefore sensible; and all sensible things are apprehended by opinion and sense and are in a process of creation and created. Now that which is created must, as we affirm, of necessity be created by a cause. But the father and maker of all this universe is past finding out; and even if we found him, to tell of him to all men would be impossible. And there is still a question to be asked about him:

Which of the patterns had the artificer in view when he made the world—the pattern of the unchangeable, or of that which is created? If the world be indeed fair and the artificer good, it is manifest that he must have looked to that which is eternal; but if what cannot be said without blasphemy is true, then to the created pattern. Every one will see that he must have looked to the eternal; for the world is the fairest of creations and he is the best of causes. And having been created in this way, the world has been framed in the likeness of that which is apprehended by reason and mind and is unchangeable, and must therefore of necessity, if this is admitted, be a copy of something. Now it is all-important that the beginning of everything should be according to nature. And in speaking of the copy and the original we may assume that words are akin to the matter which they describe; when they relate to the lasting and permanent and intelligible, they ought to be lasting and unalterable, and, as far as their nature allows, irrefutable and immovable—nothing less. But when they express only the copy or likeness and not the eternal things themselves, they need only be likely and analogous to the real words. As being is to becoming, so is truth to belief. If then, Socrates, amid the many opinions about the gods and the generation of the universe, we are not able to give notions which are altogether and in every respect exact and consistent with one another, do not be surprised. Enough, if we adduce probabilities as likely as any others; for we must remember that I who am the speaker, and you who are the judges, are only mortal men, and we ought to accept the tale which is probable and enquire no further.
SOCRATES: Excellent, Timaeus; and we will do precisely as you bid us. The prelude is charming, and is already accepted by us—may we beg of you to proceed to the strain?

TIMAEUS: Let me tell you then why the creator made this world of generation. He was good, and the good can never have any jealousy of anything. And being free from jealousy, he desired that all things should be as like himself as they could be. This is in the truest sense the origin of creation and of the world, as we shall do well in believing on the testimony of wise men: God desired that all things should be good and nothing bad, so far as this was attainable. Wherefore also finding the whole visible sphere not at rest, but moving in an irregular and disorderly fashion, out of disorder he brought order, considering that this was in every way better than the other. Now the deeds of the best could never be or have been other than the fairest; and the creator, reflecting on the things which are by nature visible, found that no unintelligent creature taken as a whole was fairer than the intelligent taken as a whole; and that intelligence could not be present in anything which was devoid of soul. For which reason, when he was framing the universe, he put intelligence in soul, and soul in body, that he might be the creator of a work which was by nature fairest and best. Wherefore, using the language of probability, we may say that the world became a living creature truly endowed with soul and intelligence by the providence of God.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: The Athenian philosopher, writing near the end of his life.
parts.title: Why the maker made the world
parts.context: The Timaeus is set the day after the conversation of the Republic. Timaeus of Locri, an astronomer from southern Italy (perhaps Plato's invention), is asked to tell the story of the universe from its beginning to the making of human beings. This is Benjamin Jowett's translation.
parts.plain: Timaeus prays first. Then he says there are two kinds of things: what always is and never changes, known by reason, and what is always changing, known by the senses. The world can be seen and touched, so it came to be, and everything that comes to be has a cause. Its maker looked to an eternal pattern, since the world is beautiful and he is good. An account of such a world can only be likely, not exact, because we are mortal. The maker was good and without envy, and wanted everything to be as like himself as possible; so he brought order out of disorder, and made the world a living thing with soul and intelligence.

commentary.on: at the beginning of every enterprise, whether small or great, always call upon God
commentary.text: Plato's account of nature begins with prayer. For him there was no conflict between the study of the world and reverence for the divine.

commentary.on: What is that which always is and has no becoming; and what is that which is always becoming and never is?
commentary.text: Plato's great distinction, which you met in the divided line of session 3. The world we see changes; the patterns it follows do not. Science lives on exactly this: changing things, unchanging laws.

commentary.on: Now everything that becomes or is created must of necessity be created by some cause
commentary.text: The principle of causality, which the Ionians assumed, stated outright. Notice that Plato applies it to the world as a whole: if the world came to be, something made it.

commentary.on: But the father and maker of all this universe is past finding out
commentary.text: Plato's maker, the Demiurge ('craftsman'), is hard to know and harder to tell of. Christians loved this sentence and quoted it often.

commentary.on: If the world be indeed fair and the artificer good, it is manifest that he must have looked to that which is eternal
commentary.text: Because the world is beautiful, its maker must have used a perfect pattern. That is why the world is intelligible: it is a copy of what reason can grasp.

commentary.on: we ought to accept the tale which is probable and enquire no further
commentary.text: A striking humility. Physics, for Plato, gives a 'likely story' (in Greek, eikos mythos), never the certainty of geometry, because its subject is changing things known through the senses. Modern scientists would agree that scientific theories are always open to revision.

commentary.on: He was good, and the good can never have any jealousy of anything.
commentary.text: Here is the reason for the world. In Greek myth the gods were often envious of humans; Herodotus has a sage say the divine is jealous. Plato's maker is good, so not jealous: he wants to share his goodness. Christians heard in this an echo of their own faith.

commentary.on: out of disorder he brought order
commentary.text: Plato's maker does not create from nothing; he orders a chaos that is already there. That is the great difference from Christian teaching, which said God made even the raw material, out of nothing, as the lecture explains.

commentary.on: the world became a living creature truly endowed with soul and intelligence by the providence of God
commentary.text: For Plato the world is itself a divine, living thing with a soul. Christians denied this: the world is not God or divine, but made by God and distinct from him. That distinction will matter.

read.author: Plato
read.who: The Athenian philosopher, writing near the end of his life.

paras:
The heavens declare the glory of God.
The expanse shows his handiwork.

Day after day they pour out speech,
and night after night they display knowledge.

There is no speech nor language,
where their voice is not heard.

Their voice has gone out through all the earth,
their words to the end of the world.
In them he has set a tent for the sun,

For we have provided great entertainments for the ears by inventing and modulating the variety and nature of sounds; we have learned to survey the stars, not only those that are fixed, but also those which are improperly called wandering; and the man who has acquainted himself with all their revolutions and motions is fairly considered to have a soul resembling the soul of that Being who has created those stars in the heavens: for when Archimedes described in a sphere the motions of the moon, sun, and five planets, he did the very same thing as Plato's God, in his Timæus, who made the world, causing one revolution to adjust motions differing as much as possible in their slowness and velocity. Now, allowing that what we see in the world could not be effected without a God, Archimedes could not have imitated the same motions in his sphere without a divine soul.

parts.title: The heavens declare
parts.context: Psalm 19 is a Hebrew hymn traditionally credited to King David. Its first half praises God in the sky; its second half praises God's law. You read it in full in 'Is there a God?'. Here are its first four verses.

commentary.on: The heavens declare the glory of God.
commentary.text: Unlike the Timaeus, the psalm does not say the heavens are divine. They declare someone else's glory. The sky is creation, not a god.

commentary.on: night after night they display knowledge
commentary.text: The heavens teach. The psalmist did not do astronomy, but he believed the sky is meant to be understood. The astronomer Johannes Kepler loved this psalm; he wrote that astronomers are priests of God in the book of nature (our own words).

commentary.on: There is no speech nor language,
commentary.text: A wordless speech heard everywhere: an order anyone, of any people, can read. That is what science needs.

parts.author: Cicero
parts.title: Archimedes and Plato's God
parts.who: The Roman statesman and philosopher.
parts.context: Cicero is arguing that the human soul is divine in origin, because of what it can do. He has just praised the inventors of language and the first astronomers. This is Yonge's translation.
parts.plain: We have learned to trace the paths of the stars and planets, Cicero says, and someone who understands them has a soul like the soul of the maker of the stars. When Archimedes built a sphere showing the motions of the sun, moon and planets, he did what Plato's God did in the Timaeus. And if the world could not be made without a God, Archimedes could not have imitated it without a divine soul.

commentary.on: he did the very same thing as Plato's God, in his Timæus, who made the world
commentary.text: To understand the order of the world is, in a small way, to think the maker's thoughts. Cicero puts session 4 and this session together: the mind that models the heavens resembles the Mind that made them.

commentary.on: Archimedes could not have imitated the same motions in his sphere without a divine soul
commentary.text: An argument from the fit between mind and world: our minds can grasp and copy the order of nature because they are akin to its source. Christians would later say: because we are made in the image of the God who made the world.

compare.author: Cicero
compare.why: Two short recollections. First, the psalm you read in 'Is there a God?', which sings the same order of the heavens as an act of praise. Then Cicero, who saw in Archimedes' sphere of session 4 a picture of Plato's maker.
compare.title: The heavens declare, and the sphere

sections.h: The question science cannot ask itself
paras: Every scientific experiment assumes two things it cannot prove by experiment. First, that nature is orderly: the same causes, in the same conditions, give the same effects, today and tomorrow, here and in a distant galaxy. Second, that the human mind can grasp that order, often in mathematics that was worked out for its own beauty long before anyone found it in nature.

Einstein said the most incomprehensible thing about the world is that it is comprehensible (our own words, from his essay 'Physics and Reality', 1936). The physicist Eugene Wigner wrote in 1960 of 'the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences'. Neither was a Christian. Both saw that science rests on a fit between the world and the mind which science itself does not explain.
sections.key: Science assumes, but cannot prove by experiment, that nature is orderly and that our minds can grasp its order; Einstein and Wigner both marvelled at this.

sections.h: Plato's answer and the Christian answer
paras: The Greek answer, in the Timaeus, is that the world is a copy of an eternal rational pattern, made by a good maker, and so reason can know it. The Bible, read by the early Christians who knew Plato, gave an answer close to it in some ways and different in three.

Justin Martyr, around 150, thought Plato must have learned from Moses (First Apology 59–60, our own words). Augustine thought the Platonists had seen much of the truth. But the differences mattered for science.

rows: It was already there: the maker orders a pre-existing chaos
God made it out of nothing (creatio ex nihilo)
Yes: a living creature with a world-soul
No: it is God's creation, good but not God
Did the maker have to make it this way?
He copied the best pattern; little room for choice
God made it freely; it could have been otherwise
The maker was good and not envious
God is love, and made the world out of goodness
Yes, as a copy of what reason grasps, but only as a 'likely story'
Yes, because our minds are made in the image of its Maker
table.note: Christian teaching here is the common teaching of Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants; Jews and Muslims share the first three answers.

sections.key: Christians shared Plato's rational maker but taught creation from nothing, a world that is not divine, and a Creator who chose freely.

paras: In 1925 the mathematician and philosopher Alfred North Whitehead, then at Harvard, gave the Lowell Lectures, published as Science and the Modern World. He was not an orthodox Christian. But he argued that modern science could only have arisen where people had an instinctive conviction that every detail of nature is ordered and can be understood (in our own words). Where did Europe get that conviction?

His answer was the Middle Ages: the long medieval insistence that God is rational, personal and in charge of every detail of creation. A mind formed by that belief expected to find order in the smallest event. Asian cultures, he suggested, more often pictured the source of things as impersonal or arbitrary, and so had less reason to expect exact laws. The historian Joseph Needham, the great Western scholar of Chinese science, reached a related conclusion: Chinese thought lacked the idea of a divine lawgiver, and so the idea of 'laws of nature' (our own words).
sections.key: Whitehead (1925) argued that modern science grew from the medieval conviction that a rational God orders every detail of nature.

paras: A second argument adds something Whitehead did not stress. If the world copied a necessary pattern, as in Plato, you might hope to work out how it must be by pure reason. But if God made it freely, he could have made it otherwise, and the only way to find out what he actually did is to look. The philosopher Michael Foster argued this in a series of articles in the journal Mind (1934–1936), and the historian Peter Harrison has developed it.

This is exactly the mood of the scientists of the 1600s. Robert Boyle, Isaac Newton and many others were devout, and they spoke of discovering the 'laws' God had given to nature, a word with a legal and theological ring. They thought a philosopher could not dictate to God how the world must be, so they tested and measured. Kepler gave up the perfect circles of Plato and the Pythagoreans when Tycho Brahe's measurements of Mars would not fit, and found the ellipse. Belief in a free Creator did not replace Greek reason; it disciplined it with observation.
sections.key: Because Christians believed God created freely, the world's laws had to be found by observation and experiment, not deduced: the attitude of Boyle, Newton and Kepler.

paras: A sentence often credited to Kepler says that the scientist is 'thinking God's thoughts after him'. It is not found in those words in his writings; it seems to be a later summary. But it is a fair summary. In letters and books Kepler wrote that God made the world by number and measure, that he gave human beings minds able to grasp them, and that astronomers, studying the book of nature, serve God like priests (our own words). His third law appeared in a book about the harmony of the world, which the Pythagoreans of session 2 would have recognised.

Newton ended the second edition of his Principia (1713) with a General Scholium arguing, in our own words, that so beautiful a system of sun, planets and comets could only come from the design of an intelligent and powerful Being. Not every scientist of the age was orthodox, and Newton himself was not; but almost all of them saw nature as a work of mind. The Greek trust in order and the biblical faith in a Creator had joined in their work.
sections.key: Kepler and Newton saw their discoveries as reading the order a rational Creator had built into the world: the Greek trust in order joined to biblical faith.

paras: The objections are serious. First, correlation is not cause. Modern science arose in Christian Europe, but also amid printing, trade, new instruments, universities and rivalry between states; belief may have been a passenger, not a driver. Second, the same God was believed in for a thousand years before the scientific revolution, and in the Islamic world, whose science flourished and then declined; so belief in a Creator is not enough. Third, the Greeks made their great discoveries without the biblical God, which shows that trust in order does not need him.

Fourth, and deepest, today's science works perfectly well without mentioning God. A believing and an unbelieving chemist do the same experiments. And some argue that the world's order may simply be a brute fact, needing no explanation, or that minds like ours were shaped by evolution to grasp the parts of nature that matter for survival. On this view, science has outgrown its religious cradle, whatever it owed to it.
sections.key: Objections: correlation is not cause; the same belief did not produce science elsewhere; the Greeks did without it; and science today works without God.

paras: What can fairly be said? The strong claim, that only Christian belief could have produced science, is not proved; the Greeks show that trust in order can come from elsewhere, and history has many causes. The weaker claim is well supported: many of the founders of modern science were moved by belief in a rational, free Creator, and said so; and that belief gave them reasons both to expect laws and to test for them. Most historians of science accept this much.

And the deepest question remains open in a way that matters. Science explains things by laws. It cannot, by its own method, explain why there are laws, or why our minds can know them. 'It is a brute fact' is a possible answer; but it is not a scientific discovery, and many find it a strange place for reason to stop. The Greek wager was that the world makes sense. The Christian answer is that it makes sense because it was made by Sense, the Logos, 'through whom all things were made'. That does not prove God. It says that the belief which helped science begin still offers the best account of why science works.
sections.key: The strong claim (only Christianity could produce science) is unproved; the weaker claim (belief in a rational, free Creator helped) is well supported; why the world is intelligible remains a question science cannot answer alone.

debate.question: Did belief in a Creator help modern science to be born?

positions.name: Yes: it supplied the conviction of order and the need to test
positions.who: A. N. Whitehead; M. B. Foster; Stanley Jaki; Peter Harrison (in part)
positions.view: Belief in a rational God gave Europe the expectation that every detail of nature follows law; belief that he created freely meant the laws had to be discovered by experiment. The founders of modern science said they were reading God's book of nature.
positions.evidence: Kepler, Boyle and Newton's own words; the language of 'laws of nature'; Needham on the lack of a divine lawgiver in Chinese thought; the medieval universities.

positions.name: No: science grew from other roots
positions.who: Many secular historians and philosophers; Bertrand Russell in his day
positions.view: Science rose in the 1600s through instruments, printing, trade, Greek texts recovered and the revolt against authority, often against the Church. Religious language was the idiom of the time, not the engine. Science needs no God now.
positions.evidence: Greek science without the biblical God; the Galileo affair; the same theology in other times and places without a scientific revolution; modern science's methodological naturalism.

positions.name: A partial cause, and an open question
positions.who: John Hedley Brooke; many historians of science
positions.view: Religious belief was one important cause among several: it motivated, justified and shaped early modern science, without being sufficient. Whether the intelligibility of nature points to God is a philosophical question that history cannot settle.
positions.evidence: The varied religious motives of early scientists; the many social and technical causes; the continuing debate over why mathematics fits the world.

debate.agree: All agree that many founders of modern science were devout, and that science depends on an orderly, intelligible world which science itself does not explain.

takeaways: Plato's Timaeus said a good maker ordered the world after an eternal pattern, so reason can know it, though physics is only a 'likely story'.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: How did the Greeks begin to explain the world, and does that explanation need God? In about 300 words, make your case: say what you think was the Greeks' greatest step, whether Christianity helped or hindered it, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Over the next week, do one small piece of Greek science with your own hands: measure a tree by its shadow as Thales measured the pyramids, build Euclid's equilateral triangle with a compass, or find the octave on a guitar string at half its length. Each time, ask: why does this work? Then read Psalm 19 and Wisdom 11:20–26 aloud.
synthesis: This course asked how the Greeks began to explain the world. It followed one wager, that the world can be understood by reason, from a harbour town in Ionia to the libraries of Alexandria, and then asked two hard questions: did Christianity kill that inheritance, and does science need God? Here are the short answers, in order.

Who was the first philosopher? By the Greeks' own account, Thales of Miletus, around 600 BC. He said everything comes from water. He was wrong, but he gave a natural explanation of the whole world, open to argument, and his successors argued: Anaximander set the earth floating free in space, Anaximenes explained differences of kind by thickening and thinning, Heraclitus saw a world of flux held by a logos. We know them only from later writers, Aristotle and Diogenes Laertius, and we read those writers with care. Why Greece? Trade with older civilisations, an easy alphabet, no single priesthood, and a culture of public argument. Babylon had better data; the Greeks asked for explanations.

Who was Pythagoras? A teacher from Samos who founded a brotherhood in southern Italy around 530 BC, taught the soul's rebirth, and became a legend. His school found that musical harmony follows simple ratios of whole numbers, and leapt to the idea that all is number, and that number is divine. The theorem that bears his name was known in Babylon a thousand years earlier; the Greek gift was proof. The discovery that the diagonal of a square is not a ratio of whole numbers showed reason overturning a school's belief. The Wisdom of Solomon said something close and different: God 'arranged all things by measure, number, and weight', and loves all that he made.

What did Euclid prove? All of geometry, from a page of starting points: definitions, postulates and common notions. Plato had described the method seventy years earlier and said geometry 'will draw the soul towards truth', while asking geometers to examine their assumptions. For two thousand years the Elements was the model of certain knowledge, for Descartes, Newton and Lincoln alike. When mathematicians around 1830 found consistent geometries without Euclid's fifth postulate, his proofs still stood; what fell was the belief that his starting points were beyond question. Every argument, it turned out, rests on starting points that must be trusted.

What did Archimedes discover? The law of the lever, the principle of buoyancy, close bounds for pi, the volume of the sphere, and a way of naming numbers larger than the sand that would fill the universe. He joined mathematics to the physical world, and his machines held off Rome at Syracuse. Did the Greeks know the earth was round? Yes: Aristotle gave the evidence, Eratosthenes measured it to within a few per cent, and the Antikythera mechanism shows they modelled the heavens in bronze. Why no industrial revolution? Slavery, a low view of manual work, the ancient economy and the lack of systematic experiment, probably together. And knowledge was fragile: Syracuse forgot Archimedes' tomb.

What is the Hippocratic Oath? A doctor's promise, from the late 400s or 300s BC, to treat the sick for their benefit, to give no deadly drug even if asked, to give no pessary for abortion, to protect everyone in the household, free or slave, and to keep secrets. The same school argued in On the Sacred Disease that epilepsy has a natural cause in the brain, since all diseases are 'divine, and all human'. Christians took up Greek medicine, and widened its reach: the Good Samaritan stopped for a stranger, and in the 300s bishops like Basil built the first hospitals for anyone in need, including the incurable whom Greek doctors were advised to refuse.

Did Christianity stop Greek science? The charge is partly true. Christians destroyed the Serapeum in 391, and a Christian mob murdered Hypatia in 415; some Christian writers despised pagan learning. But the great Library had been lost mainly before Christianity was legal, and no ancient source says Christians burned it. The story that the Arabs burned it in 642 is a late legend, as Gibbon himself saw. Greek science had peaked in the 200s BC and declined under Rome for other reasons. And the people who kept it alive for a thousand years were mostly Christian copyists in Byzantium and the Latin monasteries, Christian and Muslim translators in Baghdad, and the medieval universities. The medieval flat earth is a 19th-century myth. Historians of science, believers or not, almost all reject the simple conflict story, while admitting real conflicts.

Does science need God? Science, to work at all, must trust that nature is orderly and that our minds can grasp it. The Greeks trusted it; Plato's Timaeus explained it by a good maker who ordered the world after an eternal pattern. Christians added creation from nothing, a world that is not divine, and a Creator who chose freely, so that the laws of nature had to be found by looking. Whitehead argued that modern science grew from this conviction, and Kepler, Boyle and Newton spoke of reading God's book of nature. The strong claim, that only Christianity could have produced science, is unproved. The weaker claim, that belief in a rational, free Creator helped, is well supported. And the deepest question remains: why is the world intelligible at all?

So the Greek wager was won. The world can be understood by reason, far better than Thales dreamed. Jerusalem did not cancel Athens; in the long run it gave Greek reason a home, a discipline and a reason to expect that nature's order is real, freely given and worth discovering. A believer and an unbeliever can do the same experiment. But only one of them has an answer to why the experiment works. Whatever you conclude, you cannot understand Western science without both: the Greeks who trusted that the world makes sense, and the faith that said it was made by the Word through whom all things were made.

title: Socrates
question: What is the examined life?
line: Seven sessions on the trial and death of Socrates in 399 BC: the man and his witnesses, the oracle, the method, the defence, the prison, the case against him, and the last day.
why: Socrates wrote nothing, held no office and was put to death by his own city, yet almost every Western idea of what it means to think for yourself goes back to him: to ask what words mean, to follow the argument wherever it leads, to obey conscience before the crowd, and to care for the soul more than for money or reputation. This journey follows his trial step by step in the words of Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, beside Paul, Daniel and the early Christians who called him a Christian before Christ. It gives the prosecution its full say, and asks whether the examined life is worth dying for. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year philosophy paper on Socrates and the early dialogues of Plato (Apology, Crito, Meno, Phaedo), with elements of a classics paper on Athens in the late fifth century BC and of a theology paper on early Christian readings of Greek philosophy.
before: number-and-nature
outcomes: Explain who Socrates was, what we know of him and from whom, and why the 'Socratic problem' arises.
Explain the story of the oracle and what Socrates meant by not thinking he knew what he did not know.
Describe the Socratic method of questioning step by step, and the theory of recollection in the Meno.
Explain the charges against Socrates, his defence, the vote and why he would not stop philosophising.
Set out the argument of the Laws in the Crito and assess whether Socrates was right not to escape.
State the case against Socrates at full strength, and compare Socrates' death with the death of Jesus as the Church Fathers did.

sessions.title: The gadfly of Athens
sessions.line: A stonemason's son who wrote nothing, talked to everyone, and was put to death by his city. Who was he, and how do we know?
sessions.plain: Socrates lived in Athens about 2,400 years ago. He wrote no books, held no office and charged no fees; he spent his life in the streets and the market place asking people what they meant by justice, courage and goodness. In 399 BC his fellow citizens put him on trial and sentenced him to death. Everything we know about him comes from other people, and they disagree. This session meets the man and his three main witnesses: a friend who was a soldier, a pupil who was a genius, and a comic playwright who laughed at him.
sessions.why: This is the first session. The journey asks what the examined life is, and tests the answer the hardest way: Socrates' own life ended in a trial and a cup of poison. Before we can follow the trial, we need to know who he was, what Athens was like, and how much we can trust what we are told about him.
answers: Who was Socrates?
How do we know anything about him, if he wrote nothing?
Why didn't he write anything down?
What was Athens like in his lifetime?
sessions.finding: Socrates was a stonemason's son who wrote nothing and spent his life questioning people in public; we know him through three very different witnesses, and the trial of 399 BC is where their pictures meet.

paras: In the spring of 399 BC a jury of about five hundred Athenians, chosen by lot, heard a case brought against a man of seventy. The charge was impiety: not believing in the city's gods, bringing in new ones, and corrupting the young. The jury found him guilty and sentenced him to death. About a month later, in prison, surrounded by his friends, he drank a cup of poison and died.

This journey follows that story in order: the man, his mission, his method, his defence, his refusal to escape, the case against him, and his last day. At each step it asks what he was doing and why it cost him his life. The question that runs through it is the one he made famous: what is the examined life, and is it worth dying for?
