The defence: obey God rather than you (Apology; Daniel 3)
Why he did not run: the Laws speak (Crito; Romans 13)
The case against: was Socrates a danger? (Clouds; Xenophon; Mill)
Practising death: the last day, and the verdict (Phaedo; Justin Martyr)

background.key: In 399 BC Athens tried and executed Socrates. We follow the man, his mission, his method, his defence, his prison, the case against him and his death, asking what the examined life is.

paras: Socrates was born in about 470 BC, ten years after the Greeks beat the Persian invasion at Salamis. He grew up in Athens' golden age. The city was a democracy: every male citizen could speak and vote in the Assembly, and juries and many officials were chosen by lot. Its navy ruled an empire of island cities; under Pericles it built the Parthenon, whose columns Socrates watched go up as a young man. Tragedy, comedy, history and philosophy flourished.

Then it went wrong. From 431 to 404 BC Athens fought Sparta in the Peloponnesian War. Plague killed perhaps a quarter of the city. An expedition to Sicily ended in disaster in 413 BC. In 404 BC Athens surrendered, and Sparta put in a junta of thirty oligarchs, the 'Thirty Tyrants', who killed about 1,500 citizens before the democrats drove them out in 403 BC. The restored democracy declared an amnesty for crimes committed under the Thirty. Four years later it put Socrates on trial. If you have taken Democracy and its dangers, you have already seen this city at its best and worst.

timeline.text: Socrates born in the district of Alopece, Athens
The Parthenon is built
War with Sparta begins
Socrates serves as an infantryman at Potidaea, Delium and Amphipolis
Aristophanes' comedy The Clouds mocks him
On the Council, he refuses an illegal vote against the generals
Defeat; the Thirty Tyrants; the democracy restored, with an amnesty
Trial and death of Socrates

background.key: Socrates lived through Athens' golden age, a long war, a plague, defeat, a reign of terror and a restored democracy that tried him in 399 BC.

paras: His father, Sophroniscus, was a stonemason or sculptor; his mother, Phaenarete, was a midwife. He married Xanthippe and had three sons. He served as a heavy infantryman, a hoplite, in three campaigns and was remembered for his courage: Plato has the young general Alcibiades say that Socrates saved his life at Potidaea and stayed calm in the rout at Delium.

He was famously ugly, with a snub nose and bulging eyes, and famously poor. He went barefoot in winter, took no money for teaching and had no fixed school. Every day he went where the people were, to the market place (the agora), the gymnasiums and the workshops, and asked questions. The Roman writer Cicero summed him up three centuries later: he was the first to bring philosophy 'down from the heavens' and place it in cities, to examine 'life and morals, and good and evil' (Tusculan Disputations V.4, tr. C. D. Yonge).
background.key: A stonemason's son and a midwife's, a brave soldier, poor, ugly and barefoot, Socrates turned philosophy from the stars to how we should live.

paras: Socrates wrote nothing, so we must go to the people who knew him. The main reading is from Xenophon's Memorabilia, 'Recollections'. Xenophon was a soldier who knew Socrates as a young man, and he wrote this book to answer the charges that killed his teacher. Its first chapter tells us what the charges were, and what Socrates actually did all day.

The comparison is the oldest picture of Socrates we have, written while he was alive: the comic poet Aristophanes' play The Clouds of 423 BC. It shows a very different man, hanging in a basket in the sky. Between them, the two passages answer this session's question: who was he, and why did people misunderstand him?
background.key: Xenophon, a soldier-friend, describes the real Socrates and the charges; Aristophanes' comedy shows the caricature Athens laughed at, 24 years before the trial.

before: What two charges does Xenophon say were brought against Socrates?
What kinds of questions did Socrates ask, according to Xenophon, and which ones did he refuse to waste time on?
In the comedy, what is Socrates doing when we first meet him? Why would that be funny, or alarming, to an Athenian audience?
sessions.readWhy: Xenophon's first chapter: the charges, Socrates' religion, his day in the market place and his questions about how to live.

paras: I have often wondered by what arguments those who indicted Socrates could have persuaded the Athenians that his life was justly forfeit to the state. The indictment was to this effect: "Socrates is guilty of crime in refusing to recognise the gods acknowledged by the state, and importing strange divinities of his own; he is further guilty of corrupting the young."

In the first place, what evidence did they produce that Socrates refused to recognise the gods acknowledged by the state? Was it that he did not sacrifice? or that he dispensed with divination? On the contrary, he was often to be seen engaged in sacrifice, at home or at the common altars of the state. Nor was his dependence on divination less manifest. Indeed that saying of his, "A divinity gives me a sign," was on everybody's lips. So much so that, if I am not mistaken, it lay at the root of the imputation that he imported novel divinities; though there was no greater novelty in his case than in that of other believers in oracular help, who commonly rely on omens of all sorts: the flight or cry of birds, the utterances of man, chance meetings, or a victim's entrails. Even according to the popular conception, it is not the mere fowl, it is not the chance individual one meets, who knows what things are profitable for a man, but it is the gods who vouchsafe by such instruments to signify the same. This was also the tenet of Socrates.

Only, whereas men ordinarily speak of being turned aside, or urged onwards by birds, or other creatures encountered on the path, Socrates suited his language to his conviction. "The divinity," said he, "gives me a sign." Further, he would constantly advise his associates to do this, or beware of doing that, upon the authority of this same divine voice; and, as a matter of fact, those who listened to his warnings prospered, whilst he who turned a deaf ear to them repented afterwards. Yet, it will be readily conceded, he would hardly desire to present himself to his everyday companions in the character of either knave or fool. Whereas he would have appeared to be both, supposing the God-given revelations had but revealed his own proneness to deception. It is plain he would not have ventured on forecast at all, but for his belief that the words he spoke would in fact be verified. Then on whom, or what, was the assurance rooted, if not upon God? And if he had faith in the gods, how could he fail to recognise them?

But his mode of dealing with his intimates has another aspect. As regards the ordinary necessities of life, his advice was, "Act as you believe these things may best be done." But in the case of those darker problems, the issues of which are incalculable, he directed his friends to consult the oracle, whether the business should be undertaken or not. "No one," he would say, "who wishes to manage a house or city with success: no one aspiring to guide the helm of state aright, can afford to dipense with aid from above. Doubtless, skill in carpentering, building, smithying, farming, of the art of governing men, together with the theory of these processes, and the sciences of arithmetic, economy, strategy, are affairs of study, and within the grasp of human intelligence. Yet there is a side even of these, and that not the least important, which the gods reserve to themselves, the bearing of which is hidden from mortal vision. Thus, let a man sow a field or plant a farm never so well, yet he cannot foretell who will gather in the fruits: another may build him a house of fairest proportion, yet he knows not who will inhabit it. Neither can a general foresee whether it will profit him to conduct a campaign, nor a politician be certain whether his leadership will turn to evil or good.

Nor can the man who weds a fair wife, looking forward to joy, know whether through her he shall not reap sorrow. Neither can he who has built up a powerful connection in the state know whether he shall not by means of it be cast out of his city. To suppose that all these matters lay within the scope of human judgment, to the exclusion of the preternatural, was preternatural folly. Nor was it less extravagant to go and consult the will of Heaven on any questions which it is given to us to decide by dint of learning. As though a man should inquire, "Am I to choose an expert driver as my coachman, or one who has never handled the reins?" "Shall I appoint a mariner to be skipper of my vessel, or a landsman?" And so with respect to all we may know by numbering, weighing, and measuring. To seek advice from Heaven on such points was a sort of profanity. "Our duty is plain," he would observe; "where we are permitted to work through our natural faculties, there let us by all means apply them. But in things which are hidden, let us seek to gain knowledge from above, by divination; for the gods," he added, "grant signs to those to whom they will be gracious."

Again, Socrates ever lived in the public eye; at early morning he was to be seen betaking himself to one of the promenades, or wrestling-grounds; at noon he would appear with the gathering crowds in the market-place; and as day declined, wherever the largest throng might be encountered, there was he to be found, talking for the most part, while any one who chose might stop and listen. Yet no one ever heard him say, or saw him do anything impious or irreverent. Indeed, in contrast to others he set his face against all discussion of such high matters as the nature of the Universe; how the "kosmos," as the savants phrase it, came into being; or by what forces the celestial phenomena arise. To trouble one's brain about such matters was, he argued, to play the fool. He would ask first: Did these investigators feel their knowledge of things human so complete that they betook themselves to these lofty speculations? Or did they maintain that they were playing their proper parts in thus neglecting the affairs of man to speculate on the concerns of God? He was astonished they did not see how far these problems lay beyond mortal ken;

since even those who pride themselves most on their discussion of these points differ from each other, as madmen do. For just as some madmen, he said, have no apprehension of what is truly terrible, others fear where no fear is; some are ready to say and do anything in public without the slightest symptom of shame; others think they ought not so much as to set foot among their fellow-men; some honour neither temple, nor altar, nor aught else sacred to the name of God; others bow down to stocks and stones and worship the very beasts:--so is it with those thinkers whose minds are cumbered with cares concerning the Universal Nature. One sect has discovered that Being is one and indivisible. Another that it is infinite in number. If one proclaims that all things are in a continual flux, another replies that nothing can possibly be moved at any time. The theory of the universe as a process of birth and death is met by the counter theory, that nothing ever could be born or ever will die.

But the questioning of Socrates on the merits of these speculators sometimes took another form. The student of human learning expects, he said, to make something of his studies for the benefit of himself or others, as he likes. Do these explorers into the divine operations hope that when they have discovered by what forces the various phenomena occur, they will create winds and waters at will and fruitful seasons? Will they manipulate these and the like to suit their needs? or has no such notion perhaps ever entered their heads, and will they be content simply to know how such things come into existence? But if this was his mode of describing those who meddle with such matters as these, he himself never wearied of discussing human topics. What is piety? what is impiety? What is the beautiful? what the ugly? What the noble? what the base? What are meant by just and unjust? what by sobriety and madness? what by courage and cowardice? What is a state? what is a statesman? what is a ruler over men? what is a ruling character? and other like problems, the knowledge of which, as he put it, conferred a patent of nobility on the possessor, whereas those who lacked the knowledge might deservedly be stigmatised as slaves.

Now, in so far as the opinions of Socrates were unknown to the world at large, it is not surprising that the court should draw false conclusions respecting them; but that facts patent to all should have been ignored is indeed astonishing.

At one time Socrates was a member of the Council, he had taken the senatorial oath, and sworn "as a member of that house to act in conformity with the laws." It was thus he chanced to be President of the Popular Assembly, when that body was seized with a desire to put the nine generals, Thrasyllus, Erasinides, and the rest, to death by a single inclusive vote. Whereupon, in spite of the bitter resentment of the people, and the menaces of several influential citizens, he refused to put the question, esteeming it of greater importance faithfully to abide by the oath which he had taken, than to gratify the people wrongfully, or to screen himself from the menaces of the mighty. The fact being, that with regard to the care bestowed by the gods upon men, his belief differed widely from that of the multitude. Whereas most people seem to imagine that the gods know in part, and are ignorant in part, Socrates believed firmly that the gods know all things--both the things that are said and the things that are done, and the things that are counselled in the silent chambers of the heart. Moreover, they are present everywhere, and bestow signs upon man concerning all the things of man.

I can, therefore, but repeat my former words. It is a marvel to me how the Athenians came to be persuaded that Socrates fell short of sober-mindedness as touching the gods. A man who never ventured one impious word or deed against the gods we worship, but whose whole language concerning them, and his every act, closely coincided, word for word, and deed for deed, with all we deem distinctive of devoutest piety.

parts.author: Xenophon
parts.who: Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), Athenian soldier, historian and friend of Socrates in his youth
parts.when: Written in exile in the Peloponnese, probably in the 380s or 370s BC
parts.title: The charges, and the sign
parts.context: Xenophon was away in Asia as a mercenary soldier when Socrates was tried, and was later exiled from Athens. Years afterwards he wrote four books of 'recollections' to defend his teacher. He opens by quoting the charge and then takes it apart. Dakyns's translation was published in 1897; his footnote numbers have been removed.
parts.plain: Xenophon says: I cannot understand how the Athenians were persuaded to kill Socrates. The charge was that he did not recognise the city's gods, brought in new ones and corrupted the young. But he sacrificed in public and at home, and he trusted divination. He spoke of 'a divinity' that gave him signs, and that is probably why people said he brought in new gods. But other people trust birds and omens in just the same way; he simply named the source.

commentary.on: I have often wondered by what arguments those who indicted Socrates could have persuaded the Athenians that his life was justly forfeit to the state.
commentary.text: Xenophon writes as a defence lawyer, after the event. That makes him a witness with a purpose: he wants to show that Socrates was a normal, pious Athenian. Keep that in mind; it helps and it limits him.

commentary.on: Socrates is guilty of crime in refusing to recognise the gods acknowledged by the state, and importing strange divinities of his own; he is further guilty of corrupting the young.
commentary.text: This is the charge, almost word for word as it appears in Plato and in a later writer who saw the court records. Notice that it has three parts: not recognising the city's gods, bringing in new ones, and corrupting the young. In Athens religion was public business. The gods protected the city; neglect them, and the city might suffer.

commentary.on: he was often to be seen engaged in sacrifice, at home or at the common altars of the state
commentary.text: Greek religion was mostly about practice, not belief: you showed piety by sacrificing, keeping the festivals and consulting oracles. Xenophon answers the charge on those terms: Socrates did all of it.

commentary.on: "A divinity gives me a sign," was on everybody's lips.
commentary.text: Socrates' famous 'sign' or 'voice', in Greek his daimonion, 'divine something'. Session 4, still to come, looks at it closely. Xenophon thinks it is the real root of the charge of 'new gods': Socrates spoke as if a god talked to him personally.

parts.author: Xenophon
parts.who: Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), Athenian soldier, historian and friend of Socrates in his youth
parts.when: Written in exile in the Peloponnese, probably in the 380s or 370s BC
parts.title: What we can know, and what we cannot
parts.context: Xenophon now describes what Socrates told his friends about decisions. It shows a man who trusted human reason a great deal, but not completely.
parts.plain: Socrates said: use your own skill and learning for everything you can learn, like building, farming or choosing a good driver. But no one can know how things will turn out: who will live in the house you build, or whether your marriage will bring joy. For those things, ask the gods. It is foolish to think human judgement covers everything, and irreverent to ask the gods what you could find out for yourself.

commentary.on: Act as you believe these things may best be done.
commentary.text: For ordinary matters, Socrates says: think it through and decide. He did not want people running to the gods to avoid thinking.

commentary.on: Yet there is a side even of these, and that not the least important, which the gods reserve to themselves, the bearing of which is hidden from mortal vision.
commentary.text: Here is the limit. However skilled we are, we cannot see how our lives will turn out. This humility about the reach of human knowledge will matter in the next session, which is about the oracle: Socrates thought the wise man is the one who knows where his knowledge ends.

commentary.on: To seek advice from Heaven on such points was a sort of profanity.
commentary.text: A balance worth noticing: it is irreverent to ask God to do your thinking for you. Christians have said something similar ever since: pray as if everything depends on God, and work as if everything depends on you.

parts.author: Xenophon
parts.who: Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), Athenian soldier, historian and friend of Socrates in his youth
parts.when: Written in exile in the Peloponnese, probably in the 380s or 370s BC
parts.title: In the market place
parts.context: Now Xenophon describes Socrates' day, and the kinds of questions he asked. The 'savants' are the natural philosophers of the time, who argued about what the universe was made of.
parts.plain: Socrates was always in public: the walks and gymnasiums in the morning, the market at noon, wherever the crowds were in the evening. He would not argue about how the universe began; the experts disagreed like madmen, and could not even control the winds they studied. Instead he talked about human things: what is holy, what is just, what is courage, what is a city, what makes a good ruler.

commentary.on: at noon he would appear with the gathering crowds in the market-place
commentary.text: The agora was the heart of Athens: shops, law courts, temples and government buildings around an open square. Socrates did his philosophy there, in public, with anyone. That matters for the trial: everyone had seen him, and many had been embarrassed by him.

commentary.on: he set his face against all discussion of such high matters as the nature of the Universe
commentary.text: This is the opposite of the man in the comedy you will read next, who studies the sky. Xenophon is insisting that the popular picture was wrong.

commentary.on: One sect has discovered that Being is one and indivisible. Another that it is infinite in number.
commentary.text: Socrates' complaint about the early Greek thinkers: Parmenides said all is one, others said there are infinitely many atoms; Heraclitus said everything flows, Zeno that nothing moves. If the experts contradict each other so wildly, he asks, have they really understood?

commentary.on: What is piety? what is impiety? What is the beautiful? what the ugly?
commentary.text: These are Socrates' questions, and they are the subject of this whole journey. Notice their form: 'What is…?' He wanted to know what justice or courage is, not just examples of it. Questions like these are where Western moral philosophy begins.

parts.author: Xenophon
parts.who: Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), Athenian soldier, historian and friend of Socrates in his youth
parts.when: Written in exile in the Peloponnese, probably in the 380s or 370s BC
parts.title: The facts everyone knew
parts.context: Xenophon ends the chapter with an event every Athenian juror would remember. In 406 BC the Athenian navy won a sea battle at Arginusae, but a storm stopped the generals rescuing the survivors. The Assembly, in fury, wanted to condemn the generals all together in one vote, which was against the law: each man had a right to his own trial. Socrates was on the presiding committee that day. (Xenophon writes 'nine generals'; there were eight, as his own history of the war says.)
parts.plain: Xenophon says: people might misunderstand his private views, but his public acts were known to all. When he presided over the Assembly, he refused to put an illegal vote, whatever the crowd and the powerful threatened, because he had sworn to keep the law. He believed the gods know everything, even our silent thoughts. How could such a man be called impious?

commentary.on: he refused to put the question, esteeming it of greater importance faithfully to abide by the oath which he had taken
commentary.text: This is the first glimpse of something we will see again and again: Socrates standing alone against a crowd because he thinks it is wrong. The generals were executed anyway; the Athenians later regretted it.

commentary.on: the things that are counselled in the silent chambers of the heart
commentary.text: A striking belief for a Greek of his time: the gods see not only what we do but what we think. Many Athenians thought the gods were like powerful people, who knew some things and not others. This is one reason later Christians felt that Socrates was reaching towards something they recognised.

commentary.on: with all we deem distinctive of devoutest piety
commentary.text: Xenophon's verdict: Socrates was the most pious of men. The question for the rest of the journey is whether this is the whole truth. Plato's Socrates, as we will see, was a more unsettling figure.

paras: Come, who is this man who is in the basket?
Dis. Himself.
Strep. Who's "Himself"?
Dis. Socrates.
Strep. O Socrates! Come, you sir, call upon him loudly for me.
Dis. Nay, rather, call him yourself; for I have no leisure.
[Exit Disciple.]
Strep. Socrates! My little Socrates!
Socrates. Why callest thou me, thou creature of a day?
Strep. First tell me, I beseech you, what are you doing.
Soc. I am walking in the air, and speculating about the sun.
Strep. And so you look down upon the gods from your basket, and not from the earth?

Soc. For I should not have rightly discovered things celestial if I had not suspended the intellect, and mixed the thought in a subtle form with its kindred air. But if, being on the ground, I speculated from below on things above, I should never have discovered them. For the earth forcibly attracts to itself the meditative moisture. Water-cresses also suffer the very same thing.
Strep. What do you say? Does meditation attract the moisture to the water-cresses? Come then, my little Socrates, descend to me, that you may teach me those things, for the sake of which I have come.
[Socrates lowers himself and gets out of the basket.]
Soc. And for what did you come?
Strep. Wishing to learn to speak; for by reason of usury, and most ill-natured creditors, I am pillaged and plundered, and have my goods seized for debt.
Soc. How did you get in debt without observing it?

Strep. A horse-disease consumed me--terrible at eating. But teach me the other one of your two causes, that which pays nothing; and I will swear by the gods, I will pay down to you whatever reward you exact of me.
Soc. By what gods will you swear? For, in the first place, gods are not a current coin with us.
Strep. By what do you swear? By iron money, as in Byzantium?
Soc. Do you wish to know clearly celestial matters, what they rightly are?
Strep. Yes, by Jupiter, if it be possible!

parts.author: Aristophanes
parts.title: The man in the basket
parts.context: The Clouds was first staged at the festival of Dionysus in Athens in 423 BC and came third of three. An old farmer, Strepsiades, is drowning in debts run up by his horse-mad son. He hears that at Socrates' 'thinking-shop' you can learn to win any argument, right or wrong, so he goes to enrol. A student shows him in, and he looks up. W. J. Hickie's prose translation (1853) calls Zeus 'Jupiter', as Victorian translators often did. 'Dis.' is a disciple.
parts.plain: The farmer sees a man hanging in a basket in the air. It is Socrates, who says grandly that he is 'walking in the air' and thinking about the sun, because thought works better up high. The farmer says he wants to learn the clever argument that gets you out of paying debts, and offers to swear by the gods to pay his fees. Socrates replies that 'gods are not a current coin' here: in this school, the old gods count for nothing.

commentary.on: Come, who is this man who is in the basket?
commentary.text: The audience sees Socrates swung above the stage by the theatre's crane, the machine normally used for gods. It is a joke with an edge: the philosopher sets himself above the gods.

commentary.on: I am walking in the air, and speculating about the sun.
commentary.text: The Socrates of the comedy is a natural philosopher, studying the sky. In Plato's account of the trial, Socrates quotes this very line and says it was the start of the prejudice against him. Xenophon, as you have just read, says he never talked about such things.

commentary.on: Wishing to learn to speak; for by reason of usury, and most ill-natured creditors, I am pillaged and plundered
commentary.text: Strepsiades wants a trick for escaping his debts. The play lumps Socrates together with the 'sophists', travelling teachers who charged high fees to teach young men to argue in the courts and the Assembly. Socrates, unlike them, took no money.

commentary.on: By what gods will you swear? For, in the first place, gods are not a current coin with us.
commentary.text: The sharpest line in the scene. In Athens you swore by the gods in every contract and court case; an oath held society together. A school where the gods are 'not current' attacks the city's foundations. This is exactly the charge brought against Socrates 24 years later.

compare.author: Aristophanes
compare.why: The oldest portrait of Socrates was drawn while he was alive, by the greatest comic poet of Athens, and it is a cartoon. Read how Aristophanes introduced him to an audience of thousands in 423 BC, when Socrates was about forty-six.
compare.title: The comic Socrates

paras: Socrates is the most famous person in Western history who wrote nothing. Like Jesus, and like the Buddha, he is known only through others. For Socrates there are three main witnesses: Aristophanes, who mocked him in his lifetime; Xenophon, a soldier who knew him in his youth and wrote about him decades later; and Plato, his most brilliant pupil, who wrote about thirty dialogues in which Socrates is the main speaker. Aristotle, who came to Athens fifteen years after Socrates died, adds a few remarks at second hand.

The witnesses do not agree. Aristophanes' Socrates studies the sky and runs a school; Xenophon's is a practical, pious adviser; Plato's is an endlessly searching questioner who, in the later dialogues, sets out grand theories about the soul and the ideal city. Which is the real one? Scholars call this 'the Socratic problem', and it has no final solution.
sections.key: Socrates wrote nothing; we know him through Aristophanes, Xenophon and Plato, who disagree. This is 'the Socratic problem'.

paras: Most scholars today proceed roughly like this. Aristophanes wrote comedy, so his portrait is a caricature, though caricatures exaggerate real features: Socrates really did look odd, talk endlessly and make people uneasy. Xenophon was honest but not a philosopher, and he was writing a defence, so he may have made Socrates more ordinary than he was. Plato understood him best, but was a great philosopher in his own right and put his own ideas into his teacher's mouth.

Many scholars, following the American philosopher Gregory Vlastos (1907–1991), think Plato's early dialogues, such as the Apology, Crito and Euthyphro, are the nearest we have to the historical Socrates, and the later ones, like the Republic, are mostly Plato's own. Others, like Charles Kahn, doubt that we can separate them so neatly. On one thing all the witnesses agree: the public facts. He questioned people, he was put on trial, and he died. That is where this journey stands.
sections.key: Most scholars treat Plato's early dialogues as closest to the historical Socrates, Xenophon as honest but plainer, and Aristophanes as caricature; all agree on the public facts.

paras: It helps to set the witnesses out together. Each knew Socrates differently, wrote at a different time and wanted something different. None is simply wrong; each is partial.

Notice especially the dates. Aristophanes wrote while Socrates was alive and in mid-career, and his audience knew the man; the joke had to be recognisable. Plato and Xenophon wrote after the execution, when Socrates had become a cause: the man their city had wrongly killed. Their portraits are coloured by grief and by the need to clear his name. The truth about Socrates is somewhere in the overlap.

rows: Comedy: to make Athens laugh and win the prize
A sky-gazing, godless sophist running a school for cheats
Defence: to show the charges were false
Yes, closely, for about ten years
Philosophy: to show what thinking well looks like
A searching questioner who knows he does not know, and later a great theorist
table.note: Aristotle, who never met Socrates, adds that he asked 'What is…?' questions about the virtues and looked for general definitions (Metaphysics XIII.4).

sections.key: Aristophanes mocked a living man; Xenophon and Plato defended a dead one. Each portrait is partial; the truth lies in the overlap.

paras: Why would a man so devoted to ideas leave no books? Plato gives one answer in his dialogue Phaedrus (274c–277a). Socrates tells a story about the Egyptian god who invented writing. The king of the gods replies that writing will make people forgetful, and give them the look of wisdom without the reality. A written text, Socrates adds, is like a painting: ask it a question and it says the same thing over and over. It cannot answer back, explain itself or defend itself.

For Socrates, philosophy was a living conversation between two people, adjusted to who they were and what they thought. You cannot examine a book, and a book cannot examine you. There is an irony here, which Plato surely felt: we only have Socrates' case against writing because Plato wrote it down.
sections.key: In the Phaedrus, Socrates says writing cannot answer questions; philosophy was a living conversation, which is why he wrote nothing.

paras: Greek thinkers before Socrates, from Thales of Miletus (about 585 BC) onwards, mostly asked what the world is made of: water, air, fire, numbers, atoms. They are often called the Presocratics, which shows how much Socrates changed. He turned philosophy to the question of how a human being should live. 'What is justice? What is courage? What is a good life?'

At the same time, Athens was full of sophists, 'experts in wisdom': clever travelling teachers, such as Protagoras and Gorgias, who charged high fees to teach the art of persuasion. Some taught that right and wrong are only human customs. To most Athenians Socrates looked like one of them: he argued with everyone and young men followed him about. But he took no fees, claimed to know nothing, and wanted the truth, not victory. The confusion between Socrates and the sophists is one of the keys to his trial.
sections.key: Socrates turned philosophy from the stars to how to live; Athenians confused him with the sophists, paid teachers of persuasion, which helped condemn him.

sections.h: The war, the Thirty and the amnesty
paras: The years before the trial were the worst in Athens' history. Defeat by Sparta in 404 BC was followed by the Thirty Tyrants. Their leader, Critias, had been one of Socrates' companions; so, years before, had Alcibiades, the brilliant, treacherous general who had defected to Sparta. Plato tells us that the Thirty once ordered Socrates and four others to arrest an innocent man, Leon of Salamis, for execution; the four went, and Socrates went home (Apology 32c–d). He might have died for it, he says, if the Thirty had not fallen.

When democracy returned in 403 BC, the citizens swore an amnesty: no one could be prosecuted for what had happened under the Thirty. It was a remarkable act of reconciliation. But it meant that if anyone wanted to blame Socrates for the men he had taught, they could not say so in a charge. Many historians think this is why the charge was about religion. The case against Socrates, made in its strongest form, is the subject of session 6, which comes later.
sections.key: Critias and Alcibiades, once his companions, had harmed Athens; the amnesty of 403 BC barred political charges, which may be why the charge was impiety.

paras: At his trial, as Plato tells it, Socrates gave himself a picture that has stuck. Athens was like a great, noble horse, slow because of its size; he was a gadfly, a stinging fly, sent by God to keep it awake (Apology 30e). A gadfly is irritating. It is also, he claimed, a gift.

That is the tension this journey explores. Was Socrates the conscience of Athens, as Plato and Xenophon thought, or a corrosive influence on a city that had just survived war and terror, as many of his fellow citizens believed? Did his examined life make people better, or only more clever? We will listen to his own defence first, and then to the prosecution.

One warning before we start. It is easy to read this story as heroes and villains, because the heroes wrote it. The jurors were ordinary citizens, farmers, potters and sailors, many of whom had lost sons in the war and fought to restore their democracy. They deserve to be understood too.
sections.key: Socrates called himself a gadfly sent by God to wake Athens; whether he was its conscience or its danger is the question of this journey.

debate.question: Which witness gives us the real Socrates?

positions.name: Plato's early dialogues
positions.who: Gregory Vlastos; Terence Irwin; many philosophers
positions.view: Plato knew Socrates best and had the mind to understand him. His early dialogues show a distinctive philosopher who claims no knowledge, questions others and asks 'What is…?' about the virtues; the big theories of the later dialogues are Plato's own.
positions.evidence: Aristotle distinguishes Socrates, who asked about definitions and the virtues, from Plato, who made the forms separate (Metaphysics I.6, XIII.4); the early dialogues end without answers, as a Socratic conversation would.

positions.name: Xenophon deserves more trust
positions.who: Some historians, such as Louis-André Dorion; earlier, many nineteenth-century readers
positions.view: Xenophon was not a philosophical genius, so he had less reason to improve on his teacher. His practical, pious, friendly Socrates may be closer to the man Athenians actually met.
positions.evidence: Xenophon reports conversations on running a household, friendship and generalship that ring true to life; he agrees with Plato on the trial, the sign and the refusal at Arginusae.

positions.name: We cannot know; read them as literature
positions.who: Charles Kahn; many classicists
positions.view: Every Socratic writer, and there were many, shaped Socrates to his own purposes. We have portraits, not photographs. Better to read each witness for what he shows, and to rely only on what they agree on.
positions.evidence: Plato's Socrates changes from dialogue to dialogue; other followers, such as Antisthenes and Aeschines of Sphettus, wrote Socratic dialogues now mostly lost.

debate.agree: All agree that Socrates questioned people in public, took no fees, claimed no wisdom, spoke of a divine sign, served bravely in war and was condemned to death in 399 BC.

look.why: There is no painting of Socrates in the National Gallery of Art's open collection. The best-known painting of him, Jacques-Louis David's The Death of Socrates (1787), is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

music.why: Philosophy means 'love of wisdom'. Hildegard of Bingen's chant 'O virtus Sapientiae', 'O power of Wisdom', is a single line of melody addressed to Wisdom herself, written by a twelfth-century abbess. Listen to how one voice, unaccompanied, can carry a whole thought: the way Socrates did philosophy, one voice at a time.

think.why: Socrates is one of the two roots of the West, beside the Bible. See how Athens and Jerusalem together made us.

learn.why: The most famous words Socrates ever spoke, to the jury that was about to condemn him: why he would not stop asking questions, even to save his life.

check.q: Why do historians find it hard to say what Socrates really believed?
options: His books were burned after his trial
He wrote in a dialect of Greek no one can now read
He wrote nothing, and our three main witnesses give different pictures for their own purposes
He changed his views every year
check.why: This is the Socratic problem: Aristophanes, Xenophon and Plato disagree, and each has a purpose (comedy, defence, philosophy).

check.q: Xenophon replies to the charge of impiety mainly by pointing to:
options: Socrates' public practice: sacrifice, divination and keeping his oath
Socrates' arguments for the existence of one God
Socrates' attacks on Homer's gods
The oracle's verdict that he was wisest
check.why: Greek piety was about practice. Xenophon shows that Socrates sacrificed, consulted oracles and kept his oath at Arginusae.

check.q: What does Xenophon think lay behind the charge of 'new divinities'?
options: Socrates taught that the sun was a stone
Socrates said 'a divinity gives me a sign', as if a god spoke to him personally
Socrates worshipped Egyptian gods
Socrates refused to attend the festivals
check.why: His daimonion, the divine sign, was 'on everybody's lips' and probably fed the charge.

check.q: The joke 'gods are not a current coin with us' would have alarmed an Athenian audience most because:
options: Coins showed the faces of the gods
Socrates was known to be very rich
Athens was short of money in 423 BC
Oaths sworn by the gods held contracts, courts and the city together
check.why: A school where the gods don't count undermines oaths, and so the city's whole system of trust. The trial's charge grew from this fear.

check.q: Which statement best explains why Socrates wrote nothing, according to Plato's Phaedrus?
options: He could not write
A written text cannot answer questions or defend itself; philosophy is a living conversation
He wanted his pupils to become famous instead
Writing was forbidden to philosophers in Athens
check.why: Socrates compares writing to a painting that can't reply when questioned.

check.q: Why do many historians think the charge against Socrates was framed as religious rather than political?
options: Because religious trials were quicker
Because Socrates had never been involved in politics
Because the amnesty of 403 BC barred prosecutions for what happened under the Thirty
Because Athens had no political crimes
check.why: Critias and Alcibiades could not be named in a charge without breaking the amnesty; impiety and corrupting the young could stand in for the real grievance.

tutorial.question: How far can we know the historical Socrates?
tutorial.approach: Set out the three witnesses and what each gains or loses from his purpose: comedy, defence, philosophy. Use the two readings to compare Xenophon and Aristophanes on one point, such as studying the heavens or the gods. Then say what all the witnesses agree on, and how much we can build on that.
strong: Names the three witnesses and their purposes.
Compares Xenophon's and Aristophanes' pictures on a specific point, using the texts.
Explains the Socratic problem and at least one scholarly approach (Vlastos; Kahn).
Notes that caricature exaggerates real features.
Identifies the agreed facts: questioning, no fees, the sign, war service, Arginusae, the trial.
Reaches a balanced conclusion about how much we can know.

reading.author: Bettany Hughes
reading.title: The Hemlock Cup: Socrates, Athens and the Search for the Good Life
reading.why: A vivid portrait of Socrates' Athens by a historian who walks its streets.

reading.author: Xenophon
reading.title: Memorabilia (Recollections of Socrates)
reading.why: Read all of Book I: Socrates as his friend remembered him.

reading.author: Gregory Vlastos
reading.title: Socrates: Ironist and Moral Philosopher
reading.why: The most influential modern attempt to recover the historical Socrates from Plato's early dialogues.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Socrates spent his days asking people what they meant. Once a day this week, when someone (or you) uses a big word like 'fair', 'respect' or 'freedom', ask, kindly and with real curiosity: 'What do you mean by that?' Listen to the whole answer.
sessions.reflect: Who has been a gadfly in your life, someone whose questions annoyed you but woke you up? Did you thank them?
takeaways: Socrates (c. 470–399 BC), a stonemason's son, wrote nothing and spent his life questioning Athenians in public about how to live.
We know him through Aristophanes' caricature, Xenophon's defence and Plato's dialogues: the 'Socratic problem'.
He lived through war, plague, defeat and the Thirty Tyrants; after the amnesty of 403 BC, he was charged with impiety and corrupting the young.

sessions.title: I know that I do not know
sessions.line: A friend asks the oracle at Delphi whether anyone is wiser than Socrates. The answer sends him out to question the whole city.
sessions.plain: At his trial Socrates told a strange story. A friend had gone to the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, the most sacred place in Greece, and asked whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The priestess answered: no one. Socrates was baffled, because he knew he was not wise. So he went to test the oracle, questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen, and found that they thought they knew things they did not. He concluded that his only wisdom was knowing that he did not know. This session reads his account and asks what that kind of wisdom is, and why it made him so many enemies.
sessions.why: Session 1 met the man and his witnesses, and saw how Athens confused him with the sophists. Now we hear Socrates explain himself, at the trial, in Plato's account: where his mission came from and what it was.
answers: What did the oracle at Delphi say about Socrates?
What did he mean by 'I know that I know nothing'?
What does 'know thyself' mean?
Why did his questioning make him so many enemies?
Did Socrates believe in God?
sessions.finding: The oracle called Socrates the wisest man; he concluded that his wisdom was knowing he did not know, and set out to test everyone who claimed to know, which made him wiser and hated.

paras: In session 1 we met Socrates through his friend Xenophon and his mocker Aristophanes, and saw the charge against him: not recognising the city's gods, bringing in new ones, and corrupting the young. We also saw why many Athenians had come to distrust him: he looked like a sophist, his companions had included Critias and Alcibiades, and the city had just come through war and terror.

Now we go to court. The trial took place in the spring of 399 BC before a jury of about five hundred citizens. There were no lawyers and no judge in our sense: the prosecutors spoke, the defendant spoke, and the jury voted at once, without discussion. The whole trial took one day.
background.key: We have met the man and the charge; now the trial of 399 BC, a single day before a jury of about five hundred.

paras: Delphi sits on the side of Mount Parnassus, about a hundred miles north-west of Athens. The Greeks thought it the centre of the world. There, in the temple of Apollo, god of light, music and prophecy, a priestess called the Pythia sat on a tripod and gave the god's answers to anyone who came with a question: cities asking whether to go to war or found a colony, private people asking about marriage or debts. The answers were famous for being riddles.

Carved at the entrance to the temple were short sayings attributed to the Seven Sages, the wise men of early Greece. The most famous was 'Know thyself', in Greek gnōthi seauton. It meant, first of all: know that you are a mortal, not a god; know your limits. Socrates made it the motto of his life (Plato quotes it in Phaedrus 229e and elsewhere). This session is about what happened when the god of Delphi spoke about him.
background.key: Delphi was Greece's holiest oracle, where Apollo's priestess answered questions in riddles; its motto was 'Know thyself': know your limits.

paras: Plato was about twenty-eight at the time of the trial and was present in court; he names himself among Socrates' friends there (Apology 34a, 38b). Some years later he wrote the Apology. The title does not mean saying sorry: Greek apologia means a speech for the defence. It is written as Socrates' own words to the jury, in three parts: his main defence, his proposal for a penalty after he was found guilty, and his last words after the death sentence.

Is it what Socrates really said? We cannot be sure. Ancient writers often composed speeches for real people. But hundreds of the people who had been there were still alive when Plato wrote, and most scholars think it gives the substance of Socrates' defence, in Plato's words.
background.key: The Apology (Greek 'defence') is Plato's account of Socrates' speech, written by a pupil who was there; most scholars think it keeps its substance.

paras: The main reading is the opening of the defence (Apology 17a–24b). Socrates explains that his real enemies are not his three prosecutors but years of rumour, and then tells the story of the oracle that is the key to his whole life.

The comparison comes from the other root of the West. About 450 years later, the apostle Paul wrote to the Christians of Corinth, a Greek city, about 'the wisdom of the wise' and the 'foolishness of God'. Paul and Socrates both say that human wisdom is worth little. Reading them side by side shows where they agree and where they part.
background.key: Socrates' story of the oracle (Apology 17a–24b), then Paul on the wisdom of the world and the foolishness of God (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

before: Socrates says he fears his old accusers more than the new ones. Why?
What exactly did the oracle say, and why did Socrates not simply believe it?
Which three groups of people did Socrates question, and what did he find in each?
sessions.readWhy: Socrates' own account of where his questioning came from: the rumours, the oracle, and his search through Athens.

paras: How you, O Athenians, have been affected by my accusers, I cannot tell; but I know that they almost made me forget who I was—so persuasively did they speak; and yet they have hardly uttered a word of truth. But of the many falsehoods told by them, there was one which quite amazed me;—I mean when they said that you should be upon your guard and not allow yourselves to be deceived by the force of my eloquence. To say this, when they were certain to be detected as soon as I opened my lips and proved myself to be anything but a great speaker, did indeed appear to me most shameless—unless by the force of eloquence they mean the force of truth; for if such is their meaning, I admit that I am eloquent. But in how different a way from theirs! Well, as I was saying, they have scarcely spoken the truth at all; but from me you shall hear the whole truth: not, however, delivered after their manner in a set oration duly ornamented with words and phrases. No, by heaven! but I shall use the words and arguments which occur to me at the moment;

for I am confident in the justice of my cause: at my time of life I ought not to be appearing before you, O men of Athens, in the character of a juvenile orator—let no one expect it of me. And I must beg of you to grant me a favour:—If I defend myself in my accustomed manner, and you hear me using the words which I have been in the habit of using in the agora, at the tables of the money-changers, or anywhere else, I would ask you not to be surprised, and not to interrupt me on this account. For I am more than seventy years of age, and appearing now for the first time in a court of law, I am quite a stranger to the language of the place; and therefore I would have you regard me as if I were really a stranger, whom you would excuse if he spoke in his native tongue, and after the fashion of his country:—Am I making an unfair request of you? Never mind the manner, which may or may not be good; but think only of the truth of my words, and give heed to that: let the speaker speak truly and the judge decide justly.

And first, I have to reply to the older charges and to my first accusers, and then I will go on to the later ones. For of old I have had many accusers, who have accused me falsely to you during many years; and I am more afraid of them than of Anytus and his associates, who are dangerous, too, in their own way. But far more dangerous are the others, who began when you were children, and took possession of your minds with their falsehoods, telling of one Socrates, a wise man, who speculated about the heaven above, and searched into the earth beneath, and made the worse appear the better cause. The disseminators of this tale are the accusers whom I dread; for their hearers are apt to fancy that such enquirers do not believe in the existence of the gods. And they are many, and their charges against me are of ancient date, and they were made by them in the days when you were more impressible than you are now—in childhood, or it may have been in youth—and the cause when heard went by default, for there was none to answer. And hardest of all, I do not know and cannot tell the names of my accusers; unless in the chance case of a Comic poet. All who from envy and malice have persuaded you—some of them having first convinced themselves—all this class of men are most difficult to deal with; for I cannot have them up here, and cross-examine them, and therefore I must simply fight with shadows in my own defence, and argue when there is no one who answers. I will ask you then to assume with me, as I was saying, that my opponents are of two kinds; one recent, the other ancient: and I hope that you will see the propriety of my answering the latter first, for these accusations you heard long before the others, and much oftener.

Well, then, I must make my defence, and endeavour to clear away in a short time, a slander which has lasted a long time. May I succeed, if to succeed be for my good and yours, or likely to avail me in my cause! The task is not an easy one; I quite understand the nature of it. And so leaving the event with God, in obedience to the law I will now make my defence.

I will begin at the beginning, and ask what is the accusation which has given rise to the slander of me, and in fact has encouraged Meletus to proof this charge against me. Well, what do the slanderers say? They shall be my prosecutors, and I will sum up their words in an affidavit: “Socrates is an evil-doer, and a curious person, who searches into things under the earth and in heaven, and he makes the worse appear the better cause; and he teaches the aforesaid doctrines to others.” Such is the nature of the accusation: it is just what you have yourselves seen in the comedy of Aristophanes, who has introduced a man whom he calls Socrates, going about and saying that he walks in air, and talking a deal of nonsense concerning matters of which I do not pretend to know either much or little—not that I mean to speak disparagingly of any one who is a student of natural philosophy. I should be very sorry if Meletus could bring so grave a charge against me. But the simple truth is, O Athenians, that I have nothing to do with physical speculations. Very many of those here present are witnesses to the truth of this, and to them I appeal. Speak then, you who have heard me, and tell your neighbours whether any of you have ever known me hold forth in few words or in many upon such matters...You hear their answer. And from what they say of this part of the charge you will be able to judge of the truth of the rest.

As little foundation is there for the report that I am a teacher, and take money; this accusation has no more truth in it than the other. Although, if a man were really able to instruct mankind, to receive money for giving instruction would, in my opinion, be an honour to him. There is Gorgias of Leontium, and Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis, who go the round of the cities, and are able to persuade the young men to leave their own citizens by whom they might be taught for nothing, and come to them whom they not only pay, but are thankful if they may be allowed to pay them. There is at this time a Parian philosopher residing in Athens, of whom I have heard; and I came to hear of him in this way:—I came across a man who has spent a world of money on the Sophists, Callias, the son of Hipponicus, and knowing that he had sons, I asked him:

“Callias,” I said, “if your two sons were foals or calves, there would be no difficulty in finding some one to put over them; we should hire a trainer of horses, or a farmer probably, who would improve and perfect them in their own proper virtue and excellence; but as they are human beings, whom are you thinking of placing over them? Is there any one who understands human and political virtue? You must have thought about the matter, for you have sons; is there any one?” “There is,” he said. “Who is he?” said I; “and of what country? and what does he charge?” “Evenus the Parian,” he replied; “he is the man, and his charge is five minæ.” Happy is Evenus, I said to myself, if he really has this wisdom, and teaches at such a moderate charge. Had I the same, I should have been very proud and conceited; but the truth is that I have no knowledge of the kind.

I dare say, Athenians, that some one among you will reply, “Yes, Socrates, but what is the origin of these accusations which are brought against you; there must have been something strange which you have been doing? All these rumours and this talk about you would never have arisen if you had been like other men: tell us, then, what is the cause of them, for we should be sorry to judge hastily of you.” Now I regard this as a fair challenge, and I will endeavour to explain to you the reason why I am called wise and have such an evil fame. Please to attend then. And although some of you may think that I am joking, I declare that I will tell you the entire truth. Men of Athens, this reputation of mine has come of a certain sort of wisdom which I possess. If you ask me what kind of wisdom, I reply, wisdom such as may perhaps be attained by man, for to that extent I am inclined to believe that I am wise; whereas the persons of whom I was speaking have a superhuman wisdom which I may fail to describe, because I have it not myself;

and he who says that I have, speaks falsely, and is taking away my character. And here, O men of Athens, I must beg you not to interrupt me, even if I seem to say something extravagant. For the word which I will speak is not mine. I will refer you to a witness who is worthy of credit; that witness shall be the God of Delphi—he will tell you about my wisdom, if I have any, and of what sort it is. You must have known Chaerephon; he was early a friend of mine, and also a friend of yours, for he shared in the recent exile of the people, and returned with you. Well, Chaerephon, as you know, was very impetuous in all his doings, and he went to Delphi and boldly asked the oracle to tell him whether—as I was saying, I must beg you not to interrupt—he asked the oracle to tell him whether anyone was wiser than I was, and the Pythian prophetess answered, that there was no man wiser. Chaerephon is dead himself; but his brother, who is in court, will confirm the truth of what I am saying.

Why do I mention this? Because I am going to explain to you why I have such an evil name. When I heard the answer, I said to myself, What can the god mean? and what is the interpretation of his riddle? for I know that I have no wisdom, small or great. What then can he mean when he says that I am the wisest of men? And yet he is a god, and cannot lie; that would be against his nature. After long consideration, I thought of a method of trying the question. I reflected that if I could only find a man wiser than myself, then I might go to the god with a refutation in my hand. I should say to him, “Here is a man who is wiser than I am; but you said that I was the wisest.” Accordingly I went to one who had the reputation of wisdom, and observed him—his name I need not mention; he was a politician whom I selected for examination—and the result was as follows:

When I began to talk with him, I could not help thinking that he was not really wise, although he was thought wise by many, and still wiser by himself; and thereupon I tried to explain to him that he thought himself wise, but was not really wise; and the consequence was that he hated me, and his enmity was shared by several who were present and heard me. So I left him, saying to myself, as I went away: Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know. In this latter particular, then, I seem to have slightly the advantage of him. Then I went to another who had still higher pretensions to wisdom, and my conclusion was exactly the same. Whereupon I made another enemy of him, and of many others besides him.

Then I went to one man after another, being not unconscious of the enmity which I provoked, and I lamented and feared this: but necessity was laid upon me,—the word of God, I thought, ought to be considered first. And I said to myself, Go I must to all who appear to know, and find out the meaning of the oracle. And I swear to you, Athenians, by the dog I swear!—for I must tell you the truth—the result of my mission was just this: I found that the men most in repute were all but the most foolish; and that others less esteemed were really wiser and better. I will tell you the tale of my wanderings and of the “Herculean” labours, as I may call them, which I endured only to find at last the oracle irrefutable. After the politicians, I went to the poets; tragic, dithyrambic, and all sorts. And there, I said to myself, you will be instantly detected; now you will find out that you are more ignorant than they are.

Accordingly, I took them some of the most elaborate passages in their own writings, and asked what was the meaning of them—thinking that they would teach me something. Will you believe me? I am almost ashamed to confess the truth, but I must say that there is hardly a person present who would not have talked better about their poetry than they did themselves. Then I knew that not by wisdom do poets write poetry, but by a sort of genius and inspiration; they are like diviners or soothsayers who also say many fine things, but do not understand the meaning of them. The poets appeared to me to be much in the same case; and I further observed that upon the strength of their poetry they believed themselves to be the wisest of men in other things in which they were not wise. So I departed, conceiving myself to be superior to them for the same reason that I was superior to the politicians.

At last I went to the artisans. I was conscious that I knew nothing at all, as I may say, and I was sure that they knew many fine things; and here I was not mistaken, for they did know many things of which I was ignorant, and in this they certainly were wiser than I was. But I observed that even the good artisans fell into the same error as the poets;—because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters, and this defect in them overshadowed their wisdom; and therefore I asked myself on behalf of the oracle, whether I would like to be as I was, neither having their knowledge nor their ignorance, or like them in both; and I made answer to myself and to the oracle that I was better off as I was.

This inquisition has led to my having many enemies of the worst and most dangerous kind, and has given occasion also to many calumnies. And I am called wise, for my hearers always imagine that I myself possess the wisdom which I find wanting in others: but the truth is, O men of Athens, that God only is wise; and by his answer he intends to show that the wisdom of men is worth little or nothing; he is not speaking of Socrates, he is only using my name by way of illustration, as if he said, He, O men, is the wisest, who, like Socrates, knows that his wisdom is in truth worth nothing. And so I go about the world, obedient to the god, and search and make enquiry into the wisdom of any one, whether citizen or stranger, who appears to be wise; and if he is not wise, then in vindication of the oracle I show him that he is not wise; and my occupation quite absorbs me, and I have no time to give either to any public matter of interest or to any concern of my own, but I am in utter poverty by reason of my devotion to the god.

There is another thing:—young men of the richer classes, who have not much to do, come about me of their own accord; they like to hear the pretenders examined, and they often imitate me, and proceed to examine others; there are plenty of persons, as they quickly discover, who think that they know something, but really know little or nothing; and then those who are examined by them instead of being angry with themselves are angry with me: This confounded Socrates, they say; this villainous misleader of youth!—and then if somebody asks them, Why, what evil does he practise or teach? they do not know, and cannot tell; but in order that they may not appear to be at a loss, they repeat the ready-made charges which are used against all philosophers about teaching things up in the clouds and under the earth, and having no gods, and making the worse appear the better cause; for they do not like to confess that their pretence of knowledge has been detected—which is the truth;

and as they are numerous and ambitious and energetic, and are drawn up in battle array and have persuasive tongues, they have filled your ears with their loud and inveterate calumnies. And this is the reason why my three accusers, Meletus and Anytus and Lycon, have set upon me; Meletus, who has a quarrel with me on behalf of the poets; Anytus, on behalf of the craftsmen and politicians; Lycon, on behalf of the rhetoricians: and as I said at the beginning, I cannot expect to get rid of such a mass of calumny all in a moment. And this, O men of Athens, is the truth and the whole truth; I have concealed nothing, I have dissembled nothing. And yet, I know that my plainness of speech makes them hate me, and what is their hatred but a proof that I am speaking the truth?—Hence has arisen the prejudice against me; and this is the reason of it, as you will find out either in this or in any future enquiry.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was in court that day
parts.when: Athens, written some years after the trial of 399 BC
parts.title: The truth, plainly spoken
parts.context: The prosecutors have just finished. Their speeches are lost; we only know them from Socrates' reply. The jury sits on benches in a court near the agora; the spectators include Socrates' friends. 'Anytus and his associates' are the prosecutors: Meletus, a young poet, who brought the charge; Anytus, a leading democratic politician; and Lycon, an orator. Benjamin Jowett, the Oxford scholar who translated all of Plato, published this version in 1871; one note of his giving another possible translation has been removed.
parts.plain: Socrates says: my accusers warned you that I am a clever speaker. That is the biggest lie of all, unless they mean that I speak the truth. I will talk as I always talk in the market place. I am seventy and have never been in court before. My real problem is older: for years people have told you a story about 'a wise man' who studies the sky and the earth and makes the weaker argument the stronger. Those rumours are harder to fight than these three men, because I cannot cross-examine them.

commentary.on: unless by the force of eloquence they mean the force of truth; for if such is their meaning, I admit that I am eloquent
commentary.text: The first line of the defence already shows the Socratic method at work: he takes the prosecutors' word, 'eloquence', and turns it round. The only power he admits to is the power of truth.

commentary.on: let the speaker speak truly and the judge decide justly
commentary.text: Socrates asks the jury to do its proper job. In Athenian courts defendants usually wept, brought their children and flattered the jury. Socrates refuses all that, and the jury will notice.

commentary.on: telling of one Socrates, a wise man, who speculated about the heaven above, and searched into the earth beneath, and made the worse appear the better cause
commentary.text: Here are the 'old charges': the picture from The Clouds that you read in session 1. 'Making the worse appear the better cause' was what sophists were accused of: winning arguments for the wrong side.

commentary.on: unless in the chance case of a Comic poet
commentary.text: A clear reference to Aristophanes. Socrates suggests that comedy, repeated over a generation, did more harm than any prosecutor.

commentary.on: I must simply fight with shadows in my own defence, and argue when there is no one who answers
commentary.text: For a man whose whole method was question and answer, the worst enemy is a rumour, because a rumour cannot be questioned.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was in court that day
parts.when: Athens, written some years after the trial of 399 BC
parts.title: Not a scientist, not a sophist
parts.context: Socrates deals with the two parts of the old slander: that he studies nature, and that he teaches for money. Gorgias, Prodicus and Hippias were famous sophists; Evenus of Paros, mentioned here, was a minor one who charged five minae, a large sum.
parts.plain: Socrates says: you have all seen Aristophanes' comedy, but none of you has ever heard me talk about the heavens. Nor am I a paid teacher. I would be proud to have the sophists' skill, but I do not have it.

commentary.on: it is just what you have yourselves seen in the comedy of Aristophanes
commentary.text: Socrates names the comedy you have read. He treats the jury as witnesses: you know me; have you ever heard me talk about the sky?

commentary.on: the truth is that I have no knowledge of the kind
commentary.text: His irony is gentle but real. He says he would be proud to teach virtue, if he knew how. The whole defence rests on this claim not to know.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was in court that day
parts.when: Athens, written some years after the trial of 399 BC
parts.title: The oracle
parts.context: Now Socrates answers the obvious question: if you are so ordinary, why do people say these things about you? His answer is a story. Chaerephon was an excitable friend of Socrates, mocked in The Clouds too; he had gone into exile with the democrats under the Thirty, so the jury would know him as one of their own. 'By the dog' was Socrates' favourite mild oath.
parts.plain: Socrates says: my friend Chaerephon asked the oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than me, and the priestess said no. I was puzzled, because I know I am not wise, and a god cannot lie. So I tested it. I questioned a politician who was thought wise: he was not, but thought he was. So I was a little wiser: I do not think I know what I do not know. The poets could not explain their own poems. The craftsmen knew their crafts, but thought this made them experts on everything. Each time I made enemies.

commentary.on: he asked the oracle to tell him whether anyone was wiser than I was, and the Pythian prophetess answered, that there was no man wiser
commentary.text: Notice that Chaerephon's question already assumes Socrates was known for something before the oracle. And the answer is negative: not 'Socrates is wise', but 'no one is wiser'. That leaves room for Socrates' own reading of it.

commentary.on: for I know that I have no wisdom, small or great
commentary.text: This is the start of the famous paradox. Socrates does not doubt the god; he doubts his own understanding of the god's words. He treats the oracle as a riddle to be solved, which is how Greeks treated oracles.

commentary.on: I neither know nor think that I know
commentary.text: Here is the original of 'I know that I know nothing'. Socrates never says exactly that in Plato. What he says is narrower and more precise: I do not think I know what I do not know. The difference matters. He is not claiming to know nothing at all; he knows, for instance, that doing wrong is evil. He claims to know the limits of his knowledge.

commentary.on: I found that the men most in repute were all but the most foolish; and that others less esteemed were really wiser and better
commentary.text: A dangerous thing to say to a jury of ordinary citizens about their leaders, and a democratic thing too: reputation is not wisdom.

commentary.on: not by wisdom do poets write poetry, but by a sort of genius and inspiration
commentary.text: The poets, Homer's heirs, were the teachers of Greece. Socrates finds that they cannot explain what they have written. Inspiration is not understanding.

commentary.on: they did know many things of which I was ignorant, and in this they certainly were wiser than I was
commentary.text: Socrates respects real skill. The craftsmen's fault is not ignorance but overreach: being good at one thing, they thought they were wise about everything. It is a very modern fault too: think of experts speaking outside their field.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was in court that day
parts.when: Athens, written some years after the trial of 399 BC
parts.title: Why they hate me
parts.context: Socrates draws his conclusions about the oracle, and explains how his questioning turned into a prosecution.
parts.plain: Socrates says: these examinations made me many enemies, and people assume I have the wisdom I find missing in others. But only God is wise. The oracle meant that human wisdom is worth little, and that the wisest man is the one who knows it. So I go on questioning, as a service to the god, and I am poor because of it. Rich young men follow me and imitate me, and the people they embarrass blame me, and repeat the old slanders. That is why Meletus, Anytus and Lycon have come after me.

commentary.on: God only is wise; and by his answer he intends to show that the wisdom of men is worth little or nothing
commentary.text: The heart of the passage. Socrates' 'human wisdom' is to know that real wisdom belongs to God. Jowett writes 'God' with a capital; the Greek says 'the god', meaning Apollo, though Socrates often speaks of the divine as if it were one.

commentary.on: He, O men, is the wisest, who, like Socrates, knows that his wisdom is in truth worth nothing
commentary.text: This is what 'know thyself' meant to Socrates: know that you are not wise. It is a kind of humility. Christians would later see in it something like the first of the Beatitudes, 'Blessed are the poor in spirit'.

commentary.on: I am in utter poverty by reason of my devotion to the god
commentary.text: Socrates presents his questioning as a religious duty. That is his answer to the charge of impiety: far from despising the gods, he has given his life to a god's command.

commentary.on: they often imitate me, and proceed to examine others
commentary.text: Here, Socrates admits, is the grain of truth in the charge of 'corrupting the young'. Young men learned to make their elders look foolish. The fathers did not like it.

commentary.on: what is their hatred but a proof that I am speaking the truth?
commentary.text: A bold claim, and not quite a sound argument: people can be hated for many reasons. But it shows how Socrates understood himself. Exposing pretended knowledge makes people angry, because it wounds their pride.
