read.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was in court that day
read.when: Athens, written some years after the trial of 399 BC

paras: For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
For it is written,

“I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.
I will bring the discernment of the discerning to nothing.”
Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the lawyer of this world? Hasn’t God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
For seeing that in the wisdom of God, the world through its wisdom didn’t know God, it was God’s good pleasure through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe.
For Jews ask for signs, Greeks seek after wisdom,
but we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks,
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God;
because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

parts.title: The foolishness of God
parts.context: Paul, a Jewish teacher who became a follower of Jesus, had founded the church in Corinth a few years earlier. Now it was split into factions, some boasting of clever leaders and eloquent speech. Paul reminds them what the Christian message is: the 'word of the cross', the news that the Messiah, God's chosen king, was crucified like a criminal.

commentary.on: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.
commentary.text: Paul quotes the prophet Isaiah (29:14). Like Socrates' oracle, God shows that the reputed wise are not wise.

commentary.on: Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the lawyer of this world?
commentary.text: Paul's three 'wise men' are like Socrates' politicians, poets and craftsmen: the respected experts of his world, Greek philosophers and Jewish scholars.

commentary.on: the world through its wisdom didn’t know God
commentary.text: Here Paul goes further than Socrates. Socrates thought careful questioning could at least clear away false wisdom and point towards the truth. Paul says human wisdom, by itself, did not find God at all; God had to come to us.

commentary.on: Greeks seek after wisdom
commentary.text: Paul may be thinking of exactly the tradition Socrates began. The Greeks love philosophy; to them a crucified saviour sounds absurd.

commentary.on: because the foolishness of God is wiser than men
commentary.text: The deepest link with Socrates. Both say that what looks foolish may be wise, and that real wisdom belongs to God. The difference is in what God reveals: for Socrates, our ignorance; for Paul, a crucified Christ.

compare.why: About AD 54, Paul wrote to the Christians of Corinth, a Greek city where people prized philosophy and fine speaking. Like Socrates, he says that God has shown human wisdom to be worth little. Read what he puts in its place.
compare.title: The wisdom of the wise

paras: Did the oracle really say it? Some scholars have doubted it: Xenophon tells the story differently (in his Apology, the oracle says no one is more free, just or sensible), and Plato may have shaped it. But Chaerephon was a real person whose brother was in court to confirm it, and most historians accept that some such answer was given.

What matters more is what Socrates did with it. A Greek who received an oracle was expected to interpret it, often wrongly: the famous case was King Croesus, told that if he attacked Persia a great empire would fall, which it did, his own. Socrates did not take the oracle as praise. He took it as a puzzle, and solved it by an experiment: if he could find someone wiser, he would have a 'refutation'. His whole mission began as an attempt to test a god.
sections.key: Socrates treated the oracle as a riddle and tested it by questioning others: his mission began as an experiment.

paras: The phrase 'I know that I know nothing' is not in Plato. It comes from later summaries, especially in Latin (scio me nihil scire). What the Apology says is more careful: 'I neither know nor think that I know' (21d). Elsewhere Socrates says he does know some things: that it is wrong to disobey a better, whether God or man (29b), and that it is worse to do wrong than to suffer it.

Philosophers distinguish two readings. On one, Socrates is ironic: he knows a good deal and pretends not to, to draw people out. On the other, which most scholars now prefer, he is sincere: he has no expert, certain knowledge of what virtue is, the kind that could be taught like a craft, but he has many well-tested beliefs. His 'ignorance' is not emptiness. It is the honesty of someone who will not claim more than he has.
sections.key: Socrates says 'I neither know nor think that I know'; he means he lacks certain, expert knowledge of virtue, not that he knows nothing at all.

paras: Before Socrates, 'Know thyself' meant: remember you are mortal. Do not act like a god. Socrates kept that meaning and added another: examine what is in you, your beliefs, your motives, your claims to know. In Plato's Alcibiades I (whose authorship is debated) Socrates compares the soul to an eye, which can only see itself reflected in another eye; we come to know ourselves through honest conversation with others.

This inward turn is one of Socrates' great legacies. Augustine, the North African bishop of the fourth and fifth centuries, wrote that he had become 'a great question' to himself, and that God is found by going inward. The daily examination of conscience, the 'examen' in Christian practice, is a descendant of the Socratic habit. So, in a different way, is modern psychology's interest in what we do not know about ourselves.

There is a modern finding that fits Socrates' craftsmen uncomfortably well. In 1999 the psychologists Justin Kruger and David Dunning reported that people who did worst on tests of grammar and logic tended to overestimate their scores the most: lacking the skill also meant lacking the means to see the lack. Later researchers have argued about how large and how general the effect is, and some think much of it is a statistical artefact. But the old point survives the dispute: we are poor judges of the edges of our own knowledge, and other people's questions are one of the few ways we find them.
sections.key: Socrates turned 'Know thyself' from 'remember you are mortal' into the examination of one's own beliefs, a habit later taken up by Christian practice.

paras: Imagine being questioned in public by Socrates. You say what courage is; he asks two or three innocent questions; within minutes you have contradicted yourself in front of your friends, and a crowd of young men are smiling. Plato shows people leaving these conversations furious: in the Meno, the politician Anytus, later one of the prosecutors, warns Socrates to be careful (94e).

Socrates says the politicians, poets and craftsmen hated him. Notice who those groups are: the three prosecutors represented them (23e–24a). His questioning attacked the reputations on which public life rested. In a city that had just suffered defeat and tyranny, and was trying to rebuild trust, a man who showed that its leaders did not know what justice was could look less like a gadfly and more like a danger.
sections.key: Socratic questioning humiliated reputed experts in public; the prosecutors spoke for the groups he had embarrassed.

paras: People often ask this, and the honest answer is: yes, though not quite in the way his city did. Socrates took part in the city's worship; he obeyed an oracle; he spoke constantly of 'the god' and of a divine sign. Xenophon reports him arguing that the human body, with its eyelids to guard the eyes and teeth shaped to cut and grind, shows the work of a wise maker who cares for us (Memorabilia I.4): one of the first arguments from design in Western thought.

But his gods were not Homer's. In Plato's Euthyphro, set on the steps of the court that same spring, he says he finds it hard to believe stories of gods quarrelling and doing wrong (6a). For Socrates, a god must be good and wise, and cannot lie (Apology 21b). That is a real change. The gods of the poets were powerful, jealous and often unjust; Socrates' divine is wholly good. Some Athenians may have heard this as atheism. Later Christians heard it as a step towards the one God.
sections.key: Socrates worshipped, obeyed the oracle and argued that the world shows a caring maker; but he held that the divine must be wholly good, unlike Homer's gods.

paras: Socrates and Paul agree that the world's reputed wisdom is hollow and that true wisdom belongs to God. Both were mocked as fools and both thought the mockery was itself a sign. Early Christian writers noticed the likeness: Justin Martyr, in the second century, said Socrates had known part of the truth.

But the differences are sharp. Socrates' wisdom is achieved by human effort: careful questioning, the honest admission of ignorance. Paul's wisdom is given: it comes as news, 'the word of the cross', and it is received by faith. Socrates hopes that reason, cleared of pretence, will lead towards the good. Paul thinks human reason, left to itself, 'didn't know God', and that God came to find us in a form no philosopher would have chosen: a crucified man. Christians have argued ever since about how far these two can be combined. That argument will return when the journey reaches its verdict.
sections.key: Socrates and Paul both say human wisdom is hollow and wisdom is God's; for Socrates it is reached by questioning, for Paul it is given in the cross.

Herodotus, Histories I.53 (Croesus and the oracle).
Pausanias, Description of Greece X.24.1 (the sayings at Delphi).
Augustine, Confessions IV.4.9 ('a great question to myself').
1 Corinthians 1:18–25; Isaiah 29:14; Matthew 5:3.

Justin Kruger and David Dunning, 'Unskilled and Unaware of It', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 77 (1999), 1121–1134; for the critique, e.g. Nuhfer et al., Numeracy 9 (2016).

debate.question: Was Socrates' claim not to know sincere?

positions.name: Irony: he knew more than he said
positions.who: Thrasymachus in Plato's Republic (I.337a); many ancient readers, including Cicero and Quintilian
positions.view: Socrates' 'ignorance' was a pose, his famous irony (eirōneia), meant to draw people out and then trap them. A man who argued so brilliantly plainly knew a great deal.
positions.evidence: In the Republic, Thrasymachus complains of Socrates' 'customary irony'; Socrates often leads people step by step to conclusions he seems to have in view.

positions.name: Sincere: no certain knowledge of virtue
positions.who: Gregory Vlastos; most modern scholars
positions.view: Socrates means it. He lacks the certain, expert knowledge of what virtue is, but holds many beliefs that have survived every test. His disavowal is honest about the difference.
positions.evidence: He says he knows some things (Apology 29b); he never claims to have found a definition of a virtue; he risks his life on his beliefs.

positions.name: A religious humility
positions.who: Many Christian readers, from Justin Martyr to Søren Kierkegaard
positions.view: Socrates' ignorance is the right posture of a human being before God: only God is wise. It prepares the ground for revelation without claiming to be revelation.
positions.evidence: 'God only is wise' (23a); his questioning as service to the god; Kierkegaard's lifelong admiration for Socratic ignorance.

debate.agree: All agree that Socrates claimed no expert wisdom and that this claim, sincere or not, was the engine of his questioning.

look.why: The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of Delphi, its oracle or a sibyl.

music.why: Arvo Pärt's 'Spiegel im Spiegel' means 'mirror in the mirror': a piano and a violin repeating a few simple notes, each reflecting the other. Listen to it as a picture of 'Know thyself': looking at yourself honestly, and seeing yourself reflected in another.

think.why: Plato said philosophy begins in wonder. Knowing that you do not know is where wonder starts.

learn.why: The real words behind 'I know that I know nothing': the one advantage Socrates claimed over the politician.

check.q: Why does Socrates say he fears his 'old accusers' more than Meletus, Anytus and Lycon?
options: They have bribed the jury
They are the real prosecutors in disguise
They have spread rumours for years, since the jurors were young, and a rumour cannot be cross-examined
They are richer and more powerful
check.why: Old prejudice, much of it from comedy, is harder to fight than three men in court, because it cannot answer questions.

check.q: How did Socrates respond when he heard the oracle's answer?
options: He asked the oracle again
He was puzzled and set out to test it by finding someone wiser
He accepted it gladly and began to teach for fees
He rejected it as a lie
check.why: He treated it as a riddle, and tried to refute it by questioning those reputed wise.

check.q: What, precisely, was Socrates' advantage over the politician?
options: He knew everything the politician knew, and more
He knew nothing at all
He did not think he knew what he did not know
He was better at public speaking
check.why: 'I neither know nor think that I know' (21d): his wisdom was not thinking he knew what he didn't.

check.q: What was wrong with the craftsmen, according to Socrates?
options: Because they were good at their crafts, they thought they were wise about everything else
They charged too much
They knew nothing about their crafts
They refused to speak to him
check.why: He grants that they had real knowledge; their error was overreaching from it.

check.q: Which statement best captures the difference between Socrates and Paul on wisdom?
options: Paul admires the Greek philosophers; Socrates despised them
Socrates trusts human wisdom; Paul trusts it more
There is no real difference
Both say human wisdom is hollow, but for Socrates the remedy is honest questioning, for Paul it is God's self-revelation in the cross
check.why: They agree on the diagnosis but not the cure: reason cleared of pretence, or the 'word of the cross' received by faith.

check.q: Socrates says rich young men imitated him and examined others. Why does this matter for the trial?
options: It shows the young men were his prosecutors
It gives some ground for the charge of 'corrupting the young', as their elders saw it
It proves he was innocent
It shows he was paid
check.why: Young men learning to humiliate their elders is the grain of truth the prosecution could build on.

tutorial.question: What did Socrates mean by his wisdom, and was it really wisdom?
tutorial.approach: Explain the oracle and how Socrates interpreted it. Distinguish 'I know nothing' from what he actually says at 21d. Weigh whether knowing your ignorance is a kind of knowledge. Compare Paul's view in 1 Corinthians 1, and end with what you think: is Socratic ignorance the beginning of wisdom, or a polite name for scepticism?
strong: Tells the oracle story accurately and shows how Socrates turned it into a test.
Quotes or closely paraphrases 21d, not the popular misquotation.
Notes that Socrates claims to know some things (29b).
Discusses irony versus sincerity.
Compares Paul's 'foolishness of God' fairly, noting agreement and difference.
Reaches a reasoned view.
