sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, write down one thing you said today as if you were sure of it. Then ask: do I really know this, or do I only think I know it? What would it take to find out?
sessions.reflect: Where in your life are you most like the craftsmen: good at one thing, and inclined to think that makes you wise about everything?
takeaways: The oracle at Delphi said no one was wiser than Socrates; he tested it by questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen.
He concluded that his wisdom was not thinking he knew what he did not know (Apology 21d): the real meaning of 'I know that I know nothing'.
Socrates and Paul agree that human wisdom is hollow and wisdom is God's; they differ on how we reach it.

sessions.title: The method
sessions.line: Socrates draws a square in the sand, asks a slave boy a few questions, and claims the boy already knew the answer.
sessions.plain: Socrates did not lecture. He asked questions, and his questions usually showed people that they did not know what they thought they knew. Then, sometimes, they helped people find out. This session reads the most famous example: in Plato's Meno, Socrates takes a boy who has never studied geometry and, by questions alone, leads him to solve a hard problem. Plato draws a startling conclusion: learning is really remembering. We ask how the method works, what it does to people, and whether the conclusion follows.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed what Socrates found when he questioned the politicians, poets and craftsmen: false confidence. Now we look at the questioning itself, step by step, and at what Socrates thought it could do for someone willing to be questioned.
answers: What is the Socratic method?
Why did Socrates' questions make people feel stunned, like a 'torpedo fish'?
What happens in the famous scene with the slave boy?
Is learning really remembering?
sessions.finding: Socratic questioning (the elenchus) shows people they do not know what they think they know, and the Meno suggests that learning is drawing out what is already within: being shown your ignorance is the first step to knowledge.

paras: We have met Socrates and his witnesses (session 1), and heard him tell the jury how an oracle sent him to question everyone who claimed to be wise (session 2). He found that most people thought they knew what they did not. Here we step back from the trial to watch him at work.

Plato wrote dozens of Socratic conversations. Many of the early ones have the same shape: someone confident is asked 'What is courage?' or 'What is piety?', gives an answer, and after a few questions finds he has contradicted himself. The conversation ends in puzzlement. Scholars call this questioning the elenchus, a Greek word for testing or cross-examination.
background.key: Socrates' typical conversation tests a confident answer to 'What is…?' until it collapses: the elenchus.

paras: Meno was a rich, handsome young aristocrat from Thessaly in northern Greece, visiting Athens about 402 BC, three years before the trial. He had studied with the famous sophist Gorgias and was proud of his speeches about virtue. Xenophon, who later served with him as a mercenary in Persia, describes him as greedy, treacherous and ruthless (Anabasis II.6.21–29). Plato's readers knew how Meno turned out. Every time he asks about virtue, there is irony in the air.

The dialogue opens with Meno's question: can virtue be taught? Socrates replies that he does not even know what virtue is. Meno tries three definitions, and Socrates shows each one fails. Our reading begins at that point, when Meno, stunned, loses his temper. Later in the same dialogue, the politician Anytus, who would be one of Socrates' prosecutors, walks in, and warns Socrates that it is easy to do people harm in Athens (94e).
background.key: Meno, a proud young aristocrat later known for treachery, asks whether virtue can be taught; Anytus, the future prosecutor, appears in the same dialogue.

paras: The main reading (Meno 80a–86c) is the clearest picture of the Socratic method we have. It shows both sides of it: what it feels like to be refuted, and how questioning can lead someone, step by step, to a truth he did not know he could reach. It also contains Plato's theory of recollection, the boldest answer ever given to the question of how learning is possible.

The comparison is two short proverbs from the Bible, from the collection of wisdom traditionally linked with King Solomon. They say something close to Socrates: that the understanding in a person's heart is like deep water, and needs someone to draw it out.
background.key: The slave-boy scene shows the method at work and Plato's theory of recollection; two proverbs speak of drawing understanding out of the heart.

before: What does Meno compare Socrates to, and why?
Watch the boy's answers: when is he confident, when is he puzzled, and which state does Socrates think is better?
Does Socrates really teach the boy nothing? Look at how the questions are put.
sessions.readWhy: The most famous demonstration of the Socratic method: a boy, a square, and a theory of how anyone can learn anything.

paras: MENO: O Socrates, I used to be told, before I knew you, that you were always doubting yourself and making others doubt; and now you are casting your spells over me, and I am simply getting bewitched and enchanted, and am at my wits' end. And if I may venture to make a jest upon you, you seem to me both in your appearance and in your power over others to be very like the flat torpedo fish, who torpifies those who come near him and touch him, as you have now torpified me, I think. For my soul and my tongue are really torpid, and I do not know how to answer you; and though I have been delivered of an infinite variety of speeches about virtue before now, and to many persons--and very good ones they were, as I thought--at this moment I cannot even say what virtue is. And I think that you are very wise in not voyaging and going away from home, for if you did in other places as you do in Athens, you would be cast into prison as a magician.
SOCRATES: You are a rogue, Meno, and had all but caught me.
MENO: What do you mean, Socrates?
SOCRATES: I can tell why you made a simile about me.
MENO: Why?

SOCRATES: In order that I might make another simile about you. For I know that all pretty young gentlemen like to have pretty similes made about them--as well they may--but I shall not return the compliment. As to my being a torpedo, if the torpedo is torpid as well as the cause of torpidity in others, then indeed I am a torpedo, but not otherwise; for I perplex others, not because I am clear, but because I am utterly perplexed myself. And now I know not what virtue is, and you seem to be in the same case, although you did once perhaps know before you touched me. However, I have no objection to join with you in the enquiry.

MENO: And how will you enquire, Socrates, into that which you do not know? What will you put forth as the subject of enquiry? And if you find what you want, how will you ever know that this is the thing which you did not know?

SOCRATES: I know, Meno, what you mean; but just see what a tiresome dispute you are introducing. You argue that a man cannot enquire either about that which he knows, or about that which he does not know; for if he knows, he has no need to enquire; and if not, he cannot; for he does not know the very subject about which he is to enquire.
MENO: Well, Socrates, and is not the argument sound?
SOCRATES: I think not.
MENO: Why not?
SOCRATES: I will tell you why: I have heard from certain wise men and women who spoke of things divine that--
MENO: What did they say?
SOCRATES: They spoke of a glorious truth, as I conceive.
MENO: What was it? and who were they?

SOCRATES: Some of them were priests and priestesses, who had studied how they might be able to give a reason of their profession: there have been poets also, who spoke of these things by inspiration, like Pindar, and many others who were inspired. And they say--mark, now, and see whether their words are true--they say that the soul of man is immortal, and at one time has an end, which is termed dying, and at another time is born again, but is never destroyed. And the moral is, that a man ought to live always in perfect holiness. 'For in the ninth year Persephone sends the souls of those from whom she has received the penalty of ancient crime back again from beneath into the light of the sun above, and these are they who become noble kings and mighty men and great in wisdom and are called saintly heroes in after ages.' The soul, then, as being immortal, and having been born again many times, and having seen all things that exist, whether in this world or in the world below, has knowledge of them all; and it is no wonder that she should be able to call to remembrance all that she ever knew about virtue, and about everything; for as all nature is akin, and the soul has learned all things; there is no difficulty in her eliciting or as men say learning, out of a single recollection all the rest, if a man is strenuous and does not faint; for all enquiry and all learning is but recollection. And therefore we ought not to listen to this sophistical argument about the impossibility of enquiry: for it will make us idle; and is sweet only to the sluggard; but the other saying will make us active and inquisitive. In that confiding, I will gladly enquire with you into the nature of virtue.
MENO: Yes, Socrates; but what do you mean by saying that we do not learn, and that what we call learning is only a process of recollection? Can you teach me how this is?

SOCRATES: I told you, Meno, just now that you were a rogue, and now you ask whether I can teach you, when I am saying that there is no teaching, but only recollection; and thus you imagine that you will involve me in a contradiction.
MENO: Indeed, Socrates, I protest that I had no such intention. I only asked the question from habit; but if you can prove to me that what you say is true, I wish that you would.
SOCRATES: It will be no easy matter, but I will try to please you to the utmost of my power. Suppose that you call one of your numerous attendants, that I may demonstrate on him.
MENO: Certainly. Come hither, boy.
SOCRATES: He is Greek, and speaks Greek, does he not?
MENO: Yes, indeed; he was born in the house.
SOCRATES: Attend now to the questions which I ask him, and observe whether he learns of me or only remembers.
MENO: I will.
SOCRATES: Tell me, boy, do you know that a figure like this is a square?
BOY: I do.
SOCRATES: And you know that a square figure has these four lines equal?
BOY: Certainly.
SOCRATES: And these lines which I have drawn through the middle of the square are also equal?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: A square may be of any size?
BOY: Certainly.

SOCRATES: And if one side of the figure be of two feet, and the other side be of two feet, how much will the whole be? Let me explain: if in one direction the space was of two feet, and in the other direction of one foot, the whole would be of two feet taken once?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: But since this side is also of two feet, there are twice two feet?
BOY: There are.
SOCRATES: Then the square is of twice two feet?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And how many are twice two feet? count and tell me.
BOY: Four, Socrates.
SOCRATES: And might there not be another square twice as large as this, and having like this the lines equal?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And of how many feet will that be?
BOY: Of eight feet.
SOCRATES: And now try and tell me the length of the line which forms the side of that double square: this is two feet--what will that be?
BOY: Clearly, Socrates, it will be double.

SOCRATES: Do you observe, Meno, that I am not teaching the boy anything, but only asking him questions; and now he fancies that he knows how long a line is necessary in order to produce a figure of eight square feet; does he not?
MENO: Yes.
SOCRATES: And does he really know?
MENO: Certainly not.
SOCRATES: He only guesses that because the square is double, the line is double.
MENO: True.

SOCRATES: Observe him while he recalls the steps in regular order. (To the Boy:) Tell me, boy, do you assert that a double space comes from a double line? Remember that I am not speaking of an oblong, but of a figure equal every way, and twice the size of this--that is to say of eight feet; and I want to know whether you still say that a double square comes from double line?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: But does not this line become doubled if we add another such line here?
BOY: Certainly.
SOCRATES: And four such lines will make a space containing eight feet?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: Let us describe such a figure: Would you not say that this is the figure of eight feet?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And are there not these four divisions in the figure, each of which is equal to the figure of four feet?
BOY: True.
SOCRATES: And is not that four times four?
BOY: Certainly.
SOCRATES: And four times is not double?
BOY: No, indeed.
SOCRATES: But how much?
BOY: Four times as much.
SOCRATES: Therefore the double line, boy, has given a space, not twice, but four times as much.
BOY: True.
SOCRATES: Four times four are sixteen--are they not?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: What line would give you a space of eight feet, as this gives one of sixteen feet;--do you see?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And the space of four feet is made from this half line?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: Good; and is not a space of eight feet twice the size of this, and half the size of the other?
BOY: Certainly.
SOCRATES: Such a space, then, will be made out of a line greater than this one, and less than that one?
BOY: Yes; I think so.
SOCRATES: Very good; I like to hear you say what you think. And now tell me, is not this a line of two feet and that of four?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: Then the line which forms the side of eight feet ought to be more than this line of two feet, and less than the other of four feet?
BOY: It ought.
SOCRATES: Try and see if you can tell me how much it will be.
BOY: Three feet.

SOCRATES: Then if we add a half to this line of two, that will be the line of three. Here are two and there is one; and on the other side, here are two also and there is one: and that makes the figure of which you speak?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: But if there are three feet this way and three feet that way, the whole space will be three times three feet?
BOY: That is evident.
SOCRATES: And how much are three times three feet?
BOY: Nine.
SOCRATES: And how much is the double of four?
BOY: Eight.
SOCRATES: Then the figure of eight is not made out of a line of three?
BOY: No.
SOCRATES: But from what line?--tell me exactly; and if you would rather not reckon, try and show me the line.
BOY: Indeed, Socrates, I do not know.

SOCRATES: Do you see, Meno, what advances he has made in his power of recollection? He did not know at first, and he does not know now, what is the side of a figure of eight feet: but then he thought that he knew, and answered confidently as if he knew, and had no difficulty; now he has a difficulty, and neither knows nor fancies that he knows.
MENO: True.
SOCRATES: Is he not better off in knowing his ignorance?
MENO: I think that he is.
SOCRATES: If we have made him doubt, and given him the 'torpedo's shock,' have we done him any harm?
MENO: I think not.

SOCRATES: We have certainly, as would seem, assisted him in some degree to the discovery of the truth; and now he will wish to remedy his ignorance, but then he would have been ready to tell all the world again and again that the double space should have a double side.
MENO: True.

SOCRATES: But do you suppose that he would ever have enquired into or learned what he fancied that he knew, though he was really ignorant of it, until he had fallen into perplexity under the idea that he did not know, and had desired to know?
MENO: I think not, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Then he was the better for the torpedo's touch?
MENO: I think so.

SOCRATES: Mark now the farther development. I shall only ask him, and not teach him, and he shall share the enquiry with me: and do you watch and see if you find me telling or explaining anything to him, instead of eliciting his opinion. Tell me, boy, is not this a square of four feet which I have drawn?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And now I add another square equal to the former one?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And a third, which is equal to either of them?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: Suppose that we fill up the vacant corner?
BOY: Very good.
SOCRATES: Here, then, there are four equal spaces?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And how many times larger is this space than this other?
BOY: Four times.
SOCRATES: But it ought to have been twice only, as you will remember.
BOY: True.
SOCRATES: And does not this line, reaching from corner to corner, bisect each of these spaces?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And are there not here four equal lines which contain this space?
BOY: There are.
SOCRATES: Look and see how much this space is.
BOY: I do not understand.
SOCRATES: Has not each interior line cut off half of the four spaces?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And how many spaces are there in this section?
BOY: Four.
SOCRATES: And how many in this?
BOY: Two.
SOCRATES: And four is how many times two?
BOY: Twice.
SOCRATES: And this space is of how many feet?
BOY: Of eight feet.
SOCRATES: And from what line do you get this figure?
BOY: From this.
SOCRATES: That is, from the line which extends from corner to corner of the figure of four feet?
BOY: Yes.
SOCRATES: And that is the line which the learned call the diagonal. And if this is the proper name, then you, Meno's slave, are prepared to affirm that the double space is the square of the diagonal?
BOY: Certainly, Socrates.
SOCRATES: What do you say of him, Meno? Were not all these answers given out of his own head?
MENO: Yes, they were all his own.
SOCRATES: And yet, as we were just now saying, he did not know?
MENO: True.
SOCRATES: But still he had in him those notions of his--had he not?
MENO: Yes.
SOCRATES: Then he who does not know may still have true notions of that which he does not know?
MENO: He has.

SOCRATES: And at present these notions have just been stirred up in him, as in a dream; but if he were frequently asked the same questions, in different forms, he would know as well as any one at last?
MENO: I dare say.
SOCRATES: Without any one teaching him he will recover his knowledge for himself, if he is only asked questions?
MENO: Yes.
SOCRATES: And this spontaneous recovery of knowledge in him is recollection?
MENO: True.
SOCRATES: And this knowledge which he now has must he not either have acquired or always possessed?
MENO: Yes.

SOCRATES: But if he always possessed this knowledge he would always have known; or if he has acquired the knowledge he could not have acquired it in this life, unless he has been taught geometry; for he may be made to do the same with all geometry and every other branch of knowledge. Now, has any one ever taught him all this? You must know about him, if, as you say, he was born and bred in your house.
MENO: And I am certain that no one ever did teach him.
SOCRATES: And yet he has the knowledge?
MENO: The fact, Socrates, is undeniable.
SOCRATES: But if he did not acquire the knowledge in this life, then he must have had and learned it at some other time?
MENO: Clearly he must.
SOCRATES: Which must have been the time when he was not a man?
MENO: Yes.

SOCRATES: And if there have been always true thoughts in him, both at the time when he was and was not a man, which only need to be awakened into knowledge by putting questions to him, his soul must have always possessed this knowledge, for he always either was or was not a man?
MENO: Obviously.

SOCRATES: And if the truth of all things always existed in the soul, then the soul is immortal. Wherefore be of good cheer, and try to recollect what you do not know, or rather what you do not remember.
MENO: I feel, somehow, that I like what you are saying.

SOCRATES: And I, Meno, like what I am saying. Some things I have said of which I am not altogether confident. But that we shall be better and braver and less helpless if we think that we ought to enquire, than we should have been if we indulged in the idle fancy that there was no knowing and no use in seeking to know what we do not know;--that is a theme upon which I am ready to fight, in word and deed, to the utmost of my power.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s BC; the conversation is set about 402 BC
parts.title: The torpedo fish and the paradox
parts.context: Socrates has just shown that Meno's third definition of virtue is circular. Meno, who has made many fine speeches about virtue, finds he cannot say what it is. Jowett's translation is from 1871; one cross-reference he inserted has been removed. Persephone, mentioned near the end, was the queen of the underworld in Greek myth.
parts.plain: Meno says: you are like the torpedo fish, which numbs anyone who touches it; I can't think or speak. Socrates answers: I numb others only because I am numb myself; I don't know what virtue is either, but let us look together. Meno objects: how can you look for something when you don't know what it is? And if you found it, how would you know? Socrates answers with an old teaching of priests and poets: the soul is immortal and has seen everything before, so learning is really remembering.

commentary.on: very like the flat torpedo fish, who torpifies those who come near him and touch him
commentary.text: The torpedo is the electric ray, a fish that stuns its prey with a shock. Meno's picture is a good description of being refuted by Socrates: you were sure, and now you cannot say anything. Many people felt this and resented it.

commentary.on: if you did in other places as you do in Athens, you would be cast into prison as a magician
commentary.text: A dark joke, with the trial three years away. Plato's readers knew that Athens itself would do worse than imprison him.

commentary.on: I perplex others, not because I am clear, but because I am utterly perplexed myself
commentary.text: Socrates is not a teacher who knows the answer and hides it. He claims to be searching too. That is why he says 'enquire with you': philosophy, for him, is done together.

commentary.on: You argue that a man cannot enquire either about that which he knows, or about that which he does not know
commentary.text: This is 'Meno's paradox', and it is a real puzzle. If I know something, I need not search for it. If I don't know it at all, I won't know what to look for, or recognise it when I find it. So how is learning possible?

commentary.on: for all enquiry and all learning is but recollection
commentary.text: Plato's answer, put in Socrates' mouth. The soul has lived before and knows everything; learning is recovering what we have forgotten. Socrates presents it as an old religious teaching, not his own proof.

commentary.on: for it will make us idle; and is sweet only to the sluggard
commentary.text: Notice the reason Socrates gives for preferring this teaching: it makes people search. Whatever we think of the theory, the practical point is Socratic: never let a clever argument talk you out of trying to learn.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s BC; the conversation is set about 402 BC
parts.title: The boy and the square
parts.context: Socrates now offers to show that learning is recollection. He asks Meno to call one of his household slaves, a boy who speaks Greek but has never been taught geometry. Socrates draws in the sand. The problem: a square has sides of two feet, so its area is four square feet. How long must the side be of a square twice as big, eight square feet? It helps to draw it as you read.
parts.plain: Socrates asks simple questions. The boy agrees about the first square (four square feet) and that a double square would be eight. Then, confidently, he says the side must be double: four feet. Socrates shows him that a four-foot side gives sixteen square feet, four times as big. The boy tries three feet: that gives nine. Now he is stuck, and says, 'I do not know.'

commentary.on: observe whether he learns of me or only remembers
commentary.text: Socrates sets up the test. Meno is to watch and decide whether Socrates is telling the boy anything.

commentary.on: Clearly, Socrates, it will be double.
commentary.text: The obvious answer, and wrong. Double the side and you get four times the area. The boy is in exactly the state of the politicians and craftsmen of session 2: confident and mistaken.

commentary.on: I am not teaching the boy anything, but only asking him questions
commentary.text: Is that true? The questions are leading: 'And is not that four times four?' Critics have often said that Socrates does the thinking and the boy just agrees. Socrates' reply would be that the boy must see for himself that each answer is right. No one can see it for him.

commentary.on: Indeed, Socrates, I do not know.
commentary.text: The turning point. This is aporia, 'no way through': honest puzzlement. In most of Plato's early dialogues, the conversation ends here. In this one, it goes further.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s BC; the conversation is set about 402 BC
parts.title: The good of being stunned
parts.context: Socrates turns to Meno to explain what has happened. This short exchange is his defence of the method.
parts.plain: Socrates asks: is the boy better off now that he knows he doesn't know? Has the numbing shock done him any harm? Before, he would have told everyone the wrong answer. Now he wants to find the right one. He would never have started looking while he thought he already knew.

commentary.on: now he has a difficulty, and neither knows nor fancies that he knows
commentary.text: Almost the same words as Socrates used of himself in the Apology: 'I neither know nor think that I know.' The boy has reached Socratic wisdom about this one problem.

commentary.on: Is he not better off in knowing his ignorance?
commentary.text: This is the whole defence of the elenchus in one line. Being refuted hurts, but it is the necessary first step to learning. You cannot fill a cup that is already full.

commentary.on: If we have made him doubt, and given him the 'torpedo's shock,' have we done him any harm?
commentary.text: Socrates takes Meno's insult and turns it into a compliment. The shock that stunned Meno is exactly what makes learning possible.

commentary.on: until he had fallen into perplexity under the idea that he did not know, and had desired to know
commentary.text: Notice the two steps: perplexity, then desire. Socratic teaching is less about giving answers than about making people want them.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s BC; the conversation is set about 402 BC
parts.title: The diagonal, and the soul
parts.context: Now Socrates draws four squares together, making a big square of sixteen, and draws a line from corner to corner across each small square. 'The learned call it the diagonal.' The diagonals make a tilted square in the middle. Each diagonal cuts its small square in half, so the tilted square has four halves of four: eight square feet. The answer is: build the new square on the diagonal of the old one.
parts.plain: By more questions, the boy sees that the square on the diagonal is twice the original. Socrates says: he worked it out himself; no one taught him geometry; so the knowledge must have been in him already, from before he was born. Therefore the soul is immortal. Then he adds: I would not swear to every detail of this, but I would fight for one thing: we are better and braver if we believe we should search for what we do not know.

commentary.on: And that is the line which the learned call the diagonal.
commentary.text: The boy has discovered a special case of what we call Pythagoras' theorem: the square on the diagonal of a square is twice the original. The length of that diagonal, the square root of eight, cannot be written as any fraction, which shocked Greek mathematicians. If you have taken Number and nature, you have met them.

commentary.on: Were not all these answers given out of his own head?
commentary.text: This is the claim the whole demonstration rests on. Every step was the boy's own 'yes', reached by seeing that it was so.

commentary.on: these notions have just been stirred up in him, as in a dream
commentary.text: One round of questions is not yet knowledge. True belief becomes knowledge, Socrates suggests, when it is tested again and again in different forms, until it is secure.

commentary.on: And if the truth of all things always existed in the soul, then the soul is immortal.
commentary.text: Plato's big conclusion, and the most disputed step. Does the boy's success show that he knew geometry before birth? Or only that human minds can see mathematical truths when they are put in the right order? We return to this in the lecture.

commentary.on: Some things I have said of which I am not altogether confident.
commentary.text: Typically Socratic: he holds the theory lightly. What he will not give up is the practical conclusion that follows.

commentary.on: we shall be better and braver and less helpless if we think that we ought to enquire
commentary.text: This is the heart of the examined life. Whatever the truth about the soul, we must keep searching, because the alternative is to give up on truth and become 'idle'.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
read.when: Athens, probably the 380s BC; the conversation is set about 402 BC

paras:
Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water,
but a man of understanding will draw it out.

The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp,
searching all his innermost parts.

parts.title: A man of understanding will draw it out
parts.context: Proverbs is a collection of short sayings, gathered in Israel over several centuries and traditionally linked with King Solomon (about 970–930 BC). Chapters 10 to 22 are mostly two-line proverbs. These two come from the same chapter. 'Yahweh' is the name of Israel's God, written 'the LORD' in most English Bibles.

commentary.on: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water,
commentary.text: 'Counsel' here means purpose, understanding, the plans and wisdom deep in a person. Like water in a deep well, it is there but out of reach.

commentary.on: but a man of understanding will draw it out.
commentary.text: The image is of drawing water with a bucket and rope. The wise person does not pour wisdom in; he draws out what is already there. It is the same picture as Socrates' questions to the boy. Socrates' mother was a midwife, and he called his own work a kind of midwifery: helping others give birth to what was in them (Theaetetus 150b–c).

commentary.on: The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp,
commentary.text: Here the Bible says where the light inside us comes from. The human spirit is a lamp lit by God, which searches our 'innermost parts'. Socrates thought the truth was in the soul because it had seen everything before birth. The Bible says the light within is God's gift. Augustine would join the two pictures: the truth we 'remember' is the light of God shining in the mind.

compare.why: The book of Proverbs, from Israel's wisdom tradition, has two sayings close to Socrates' picture of teaching as drawing out. Read them beside the slave boy.
compare.title: Deep water in the heart

paras: Gregory Vlastos described the Socratic elenchus in a famous article (1983) as a regular pattern. First, the other person states something he believes, often a definition: 'Courage is endurance of the soul.' Second, Socrates gets him to agree to further statements: 'Is courage always a fine thing? Is foolish endurance fine?' Third, Socrates shows that these further beliefs contradict the first one: some endurance is foolish, so it is not fine, so it cannot be courage. Fourth, Socrates concludes that the first claim was false, or at least that the person's beliefs do not hang together.

Notice what the method needs: the person must say what he really thinks, and must be honest when he agrees. Socrates insisted on this ('say what you believe'). It is not a debating trick to win; it is a test of a person's own beliefs against each other. That is why it was personal. To be refuted by Socrates was to be shown that your own mind was in disorder.
sections.key: The elenchus: you state a belief, agree to other beliefs, and are shown they contradict it; it tests a person's own beliefs for consistency.

sections.h: What the method can and cannot do
paras: The elenchus has a limit, which philosophers have long noticed. It can show that a set of beliefs is inconsistent; it cannot, on its own, show which belief is false. If my beliefs A, B and C contradict each other, I might give up A, as Socrates wants, or I might give up B. Vlastos called this 'the problem of the elenchus'.

Socrates seems to have trusted that some beliefs, such as 'it is worse to do wrong than to suffer it', always survive the test, because everyone, deep down, believes them, even those who say otherwise. In the Gorgias he tells a cynical politician that his own other beliefs commit him to this, whether he admits it or not. That is a remarkable faith: that buried in every human being is a knowledge of the good, waiting to be drawn out. The Meno gives that faith a theory.
sections.key: Questioning reveals contradictions but cannot alone say which belief to drop; Socrates trusted that some moral truths are buried in everyone.

paras: Plato's theory of recollection (anamnēsis) says the soul existed before birth and knew all things; birth made it forget; learning is remembering. The slave-boy scene is offered as evidence. In the Phaedo, written later, Plato connects it with his theory of forms: we recognise that two sticks are 'nearly equal' only because we already know what Equality itself is, which nothing in this world perfectly shows us.

Most philosophers today reject the idea of a previous life. But the problem Plato was wrestling with is real and still discussed: how do we know things that experience alone cannot teach, such as that the square on the diagonal is double the square, always and everywhere? Some answers since: the mind has innate ideas (Descartes, Leibniz); the mind has built-in forms by which it orders experience (Kant); human beings have inherited capacities for language and number (some modern cognitive science). The Meno started that conversation.
sections.key: Recollection says learning is remembering what the soul knew before birth; the real problem it addresses, how we know necessary truths, is still debated.

paras: Christians admired the Meno and could not accept its theory, because the Church did not teach that souls live before birth. Augustine of Hippo (354–430) gave a different answer. In his dialogue The Teacher (De Magistro, 389), written with his teenage son Adeodatus, he argues that words never really teach us anything. A teacher's words prompt us to look; but we see that a thing is true by consulting the truth that 'presides over the mind within', which is Christ, the Wisdom of God. In The Trinity (XII.15.24) he discusses the Meno directly: the boy answered rightly not because he remembered a past life, but because the light of eternal reason is present to every mind.
This is Proverbs 20:27 turned into philosophy: the human spirit is the Lord's lamp. Medieval thinkers called it illumination. It kept Socrates' method and replaced Plato's explanation.
sections.key: Augustine kept the Socratic method but said we see truth by an inner light from God, Christ the inner teacher, not by memory of a past life.

paras: The Socratic method is everywhere in modern education. American law schools have used it since the 1870s, when Christopher Columbus Langdell at Harvard began cross-examining students on cases instead of lecturing. Oxford and Cambridge tutorials are Socratic in spirit: a student reads an essay, and the tutor asks questions until its weaknesses show. Cognitive therapy, developed by Aaron Beck in the 1960s, uses 'Socratic questioning' to help patients test their own anxious beliefs.

Research on learning suggests why it works. Being asked to retrieve and explain what we think, rather than just hearing it, makes it stick and shows us our gaps. But the method can also go wrong: questions can humiliate, and clever questioning can be used to win, not to learn. Socrates' own conversations show both. The difference lies in whether the questioner is himself looking for the truth.
sections.key: Law schools, tutorials and cognitive therapy use Socratic questioning; it helps people see their gaps, but can humiliate if the questioner is not seeking the truth.

paras: The Meno began with Meno's question, and it ends without a clear answer. If virtue were knowledge, it could be taught, like geometry. But where are its teachers? The sophists charge fees and disagree; great men like Pericles failed to make their own sons good. So perhaps good men are good by a kind of 'right opinion' given by the gods, not by knowledge they could pass on (99e–100b).

Behind this is one of Socrates' most famous ideas: that virtue is a kind of knowledge, and that no one does wrong willingly. If you really knew what was good for you, you would do it; wrongdoing is a kind of ignorance. Christians would later disagree: Paul says 'the good which I desire, I don't do' (Romans 7:19). We can know the good and still not do it. That disagreement, between a Greek faith in knowledge and a biblical account of the divided will, is one of the great conversations of the West.
sections.key: The Meno asks whether virtue can be taught; Socrates held that virtue is knowledge and no one does wrong willingly, which Paul's divided will disputes.

sections.h: What the method did to Athens
paras: The Meno has a sting in its tail. Soon after the slave-boy scene, Anytus joins the conversation. Socrates asks whether great Athenian statesmen like Pericles taught their sons virtue; apparently not, since the sons were mediocre. Anytus hears an insult to Athens' heroes and warns him: 'Socrates, I think that you are too ready to speak evil of men', and advises him to be careful, since in Athens 'it is easier to do men harm than to do them good' (94e, tr. Jowett).

Here are the two faces of the method side by side. For a boy with no reputation to lose, questioning is a gift: he ends wiser and glad. For a proud politician, the same questions are an attack on everything he honours. When Socrates questioned the city's received beliefs about its heroes and its gods, many citizens felt what Meno felt: numbed, and then angry. The trial was, in part, Athens' answer to the torpedo fish.
sections.key: For the boy, questioning was a gift; for Anytus, an insult to Athens' heroes. The future prosecutor appears in the Meno, warning Socrates.

refs: Plato, Meno 80a–86c, 94e, tr. B. Jowett (1871); Gorgias 474b, 482b; Theaetetus 150b–c; Phaedo 72e–77a.
Xenophon, Anabasis II.6.21–29 (Meno's character).
Gregory Vlastos, 'The Socratic Elenchus', Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy 1 (1983), 27–58.
Augustine, De Magistro (389), esp. 11.38; De Trinitate XII.15.24.
Proverbs 20:5, 27.

On Langdell and the case method: Bruce A. Kimball, The Inception of Modern Professional Education (2009). On Socratic questioning in therapy: Aaron T. Beck, Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders (1976).

debate.question: Did the slave boy learn, or remember, or was he led?

positions.name: Recollection
positions.who: Plato, Meno and Phaedo; later Platonists
positions.view: The boy reached a truth no one had taught him and no experience showed him. The knowledge must have been in his soul already, from before birth.
positions.evidence: Every answer came 'out of his own head' (85b); the truth is necessary and universal, not learned from examples.

positions.name: Illumination, not memory
positions.who: Augustine; Bonaventure; much medieval Christian thought
positions.view: The boy saw the truth because the light of God's eternal reason is present to every mind, not because he lived before. The method is right; the explanation is wrong.
positions.evidence: Augustine, The Trinity XII.15.24: anyone, rightly questioned, can answer about geometry, though not everyone can have been a geometer in a past life.

positions.name: He was led
positions.who: Many modern critics
positions.view: Socrates' questions do the work. Each one invites 'yes', and the drawing in the sand does the rest. The scene shows good teaching, not hidden knowledge.
positions.evidence: Questions like 'And is not that four times four?' (82e–83b); Socrates chooses the figure and adds the diagonals himself.

debate.agree: All agree that the boy came to see a necessary truth for himself, and that seeing it required first admitting that he did not know.

look.why: This double portrait, attributed to the Venetian painter Giorgione, shows a boy, Giovanni Borgherini, with his tutor, in the early sixteenth century. It is not Socrates and the slave boy. It is here because it shows what the Meno is about: a teacher and a pupil, and the instruments of learning between them. The Latin inscription reads, roughly, 'Talent is worth nothing unless deeds follow.'
points: Two figures are shown from the chest up against a black background.
On the left a boy or young man with curly brown hair and a floppy blue hat looks out at us.
Along the bottom edge, the boy grips a paint brush, a quill pen, a flute and a compass in his fist: the tools of the arts and of learning.
The older man on the right, in a honey-yellow tunic, leans towards the boy, holds up an armillary sphere (a model of the heavens made of interlocking bands) and points to it.
A white scroll curls around the sphere's handle, inscribed 'NON VALET. INGENIVM. NISI FACTA VALEBVNT.'

music.why: This old Irish prayer, translated in 1905 and 1912, asks God to be the light within: 'Be Thou my Wisdom, and Thou my true Word'. It is Augustine's answer to the Meno set to a folk tune: the truth we find inside is lit by Someone else.

think.why: If the mind can see necessary truths that no experience shows, what is a mind? Plato's question, asked again today.

learn.why: A proverb about what Socrates did all his life: drawing out the understanding hidden in a person.

check.q: What is Meno's paradox?
options: That Socrates is both wise and ignorant
That virtue is both teachable and not teachable
That you cannot search for what you know, since you have it, nor for what you don't know, since you wouldn't recognise it
That the soul is both mortal and immortal
check.why: Meno argues that enquiry is impossible either way; recollection is Socrates' answer.

check.q: At what point does Socrates say the boy is better off than at the start?
options: Only when he finds the diagonal
When he first says the side should be double
When he says 'Three feet'
When he admits 'I do not know', and wants to find out
check.why: Knowing his ignorance, the boy now wants to search: 'Is he not better off in knowing his ignorance?'

check.q: Which is the strongest objection to Socrates' claim that he taught the boy nothing?
options: The answer was wrong
The boy was too young to understand
Socrates' questions were leading and he chose the diagram, so he guided each step
The boy was a slave and therefore could not learn
check.why: Critics point out that questions like 'And is not that four times four?' do much of the work.

check.q: What can the elenchus, by itself, not do?
options: Show that someone's beliefs contradict each other
Be used in a conversation
Tell us which of the contradictory beliefs is the false one
Make someone feel puzzled
check.why: It reveals inconsistency; it cannot alone decide which belief to give up. Vlastos called this the problem of the elenchus.

check.q: How did Augustine change the Meno's explanation?
options: He kept recollection of a past life
He denied the boy could know geometry
He said the boy saw the truth by the light of God's eternal reason present to every mind
He said geometry is learned only from teachers
check.why: Illumination replaced recollection: Christ as the inner teacher (The Teacher; The Trinity XII.15.24).

check.q: Why does the appearance of Anytus in the Meno matter for understanding the trial?
options: He was the slave boy's owner
He shows how proud public men took Socratic questioning of Athens' heroes as an insult; he later prosecuted Socrates
He defends Socrates
He was Meno's teacher
check.why: Anytus warns Socrates about speaking ill of men (94e); three years later he helped bring the charge.

tutorial.question: Does the slave-boy scene show that learning is recollection?
tutorial.approach: Describe the scene's steps, especially the moment of 'I do not know'. Set out Plato's argument from it, then the objections (leading questions; other explanations of how we know necessary truths). Compare Augustine's illumination. End with your view of what the scene really shows about teaching and learning.
strong: Describes the geometry problem and the boy's mistakes accurately.
Explains Meno's paradox and how recollection answers it.
Weighs the 'leading questions' objection fairly.
Notes that the underlying problem (knowledge of necessary truths) remains real.
Explains Augustine's alternative.
Draws a clear conclusion about what the method achieves.

reading.author: Plato
reading.title: Meno
reading.why: Short and lively; read it with a pencil and draw the squares.

reading.author: Ward Farnsworth
reading.title: The Socratic Method: A Practitioner's Handbook
reading.why: How to use Socratic questioning in your own thinking and conversations.

reading.author: Gregory Vlastos
reading.title: Socratic Studies
reading.why: Includes 'The Socratic Elenchus', the classic analysis of the method.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: in one conversation where you would normally give advice, ask three questions instead and let the other person find their own answer. Afterwards, note what they found that you would not have told them.
sessions.reflect: When were you last 'numbed' by a question you could not answer? Did you turn away from it, or did it make you want to know?
takeaways: The elenchus tests a person's beliefs against each other until they see that they do not know what they thought they knew.
In the Meno, a boy who admits 'I do not know' goes on to find, by questions, that the square on the diagonal is double: Plato concludes that learning is recollection.
Augustine kept the method but replaced recollection with an inner light from God; the questioning that helped the boy insulted proud men like Anytus.

sessions.title: The defence
sessions.line: Charged with impiety and corrupting the young, Socrates tells the jury he will obey God rather than them.
sessions.plain: Now we return to the court. Socrates had dealt with the old rumours; now he faced the real charge, and the real danger of death. He did not beg, weep or promise to change. Instead he told the jury that God had posted him, like a soldier, to examine himself and others, and that he would not leave his post even to save his life. Athens was a sleepy horse and he was the gadfly God had sent to sting it awake. This session reads the heart of his defence and asks what he was willing to die for, and why the jury voted as it did.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 and 3 showed where Socrates' questioning came from and how it worked. Now we see the cost. The method that stunned Meno and angered Anytus is on trial, and Socrates must say whether he will give it up to live.
answers: What exactly was Socrates charged with?
Why did he refuse to stop philosophising, even to save his life?
What was his 'divine sign', and why did he stay out of politics?
How did the jury vote, and what penalty did he propose?
sessions.finding: On trial for impiety and corrupting the young, Socrates refused to stop philosophising or beg for mercy: he would obey God rather than Athens, and the jury condemned him.

paras: We have met Socrates (session 1), heard his account of the oracle and his mission (session 2), and watched his method at work (session 3). We saw that his questioning helped some and humiliated others, and that one of the humiliated, Anytus, was among his prosecutors.

In the part of the speech we skipped (Apology 24b–28a), Socrates cross-examines his young accuser Meletus in front of the jury. He gets him to say that everyone in Athens improves the young except Socrates, and that Socrates believes in no gods at all, though the charge says he brings in new ones. It is brilliant, and it makes Meletus look foolish. It may not have made the jury like Socrates any better.
background.key: After the oracle story, Socrates humiliated his accuser Meletus in cross-examination (24b–28a), a brilliant but perhaps costly performance.

paras: Any citizen could bring a charge of impiety (a graphē asebeias) by lodging it with the official in charge of religion, the 'king archon', at his office in the agora. The case was then heard by a jury of citizens over thirty, chosen by lot that morning: for this trial, about five hundred. Each side had the same time, measured by a water clock. There was no judge to explain the law and no deliberation: the jurors voted at once by secret ballot.

If the defendant was found guilty and the law fixed no penalty, there was a second stage. The prosecutor proposed a penalty, the defendant proposed another, and the jury had to choose one of the two. Meletus proposed death. Socrates would have been expected to propose exile, which the jury would probably have accepted.

timeline.text: Meletus lodges the charge with the king archon
The trial: speeches, the first vote (guilty), the penalty, the second vote (death)
The sacred ship leaves for Delos; no executions until it returns
The ship returns; Socrates dies

background.key: Any citizen could prosecute impiety; a jury of about five hundred voted at once; after a guilty verdict, each side proposed a penalty and the jury chose.

paras: The main reading begins with the charge itself, in the words a later writer copied from the official record. Then comes the centre of Socrates' defence (Apology 28b–32a): why he will not abandon his mission, the gadfly, and the divine sign that kept him out of politics.

The comparison is from the book of Daniel: three young Jews in Babylon who refuse a king's command to worship his golden statue, even under threat of a furnace. It is one of the Bible's great stories of obeying God rather than human power. If you have taken Tragedy, you have met the same idea in Antigone and in the apostles' words, 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29).
background.key: The charge as recorded, Socrates' refusal to stop (Apology 28b–32a), and Daniel's three young men who would not bow.

before: What comparison does Socrates draw between himself and a soldier?
What does Socrates say he would do if the jury offered to free him on condition that he stopped philosophising?
What does his divine sign do, and what does it never do?
sessions.readWhy: The charge itself, and the heart of Socrates' defence: why he would rather die than stop.

paras: But the sworn informations, on which the trial proceeded, were drawn up in this fashion; for they are preserved to this day, says Phavorinus, in the temple of Cybele:—“Meletus, the son of Meletus, of Pithus, impeaches Socrates, the son of Sophroniscus, of Alopece: Socrates is guilty, inasmuch as he does not believe in the Gods whom the city worships, but introduces other strange deities; he is also guilty, inasmuch as he corrupts the young men, and the punishment he has incurred is death.”

Some one will say: And are you not ashamed, Socrates, of a course of life which is likely to bring you to an untimely end? To him I may fairly answer: There you are mistaken: a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong—acting the part of a good man or of a bad. Whereas, upon your view, the heroes who fell at Troy were not good for much, and the son of Thetis above all, who altogether despised danger in comparison with disgrace; and when he was so eager to slay Hector, his goddess mother said to him, that if he avenged his companion Patroclus, and slew Hector, he would die himself—“Fate,” she said, in these or the like words, “waits for you next after Hector;” he, receiving this warning, utterly despised danger and death, and instead of fearing them, feared rather to live in dishonour, and not to avenge his friend. “Let me die forthwith,” he replies, “and be avenged of my enemy, rather than abide here by the beaked ships, a laughing-stock and a burden of the earth.” Had Achilles any thought of death and danger? For wherever a man’s place is, whether the place which he has chosen or that in which he has been placed by a commander, there he ought to remain in the hour of danger; he should not think of death or of anything but of disgrace. And this, O men of Athens, is a true saying.

Strange, indeed, would be my conduct, O men of Athens, if I who, when I was ordered by the generals whom you chose to command me at Potidaea and Amphipolis and Delium, remained where they placed me, like any other man, facing death—if now, when, as I conceive and imagine, God orders me to fulfil the philosopher’s mission of searching into myself and other men, I were to desert my post through fear of death, or any other fear; that would indeed be strange, and I might justly be arraigned in court for denying the existence of the gods, if I disobeyed the oracle because I was afraid of death, fancying that I was wise when I was not wise. For the fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being a pretence of knowing the unknown; and no one knows whether death, which men in their fear apprehend to be the greatest evil, may not be the greatest good.

Is not this ignorance of a disgraceful sort, the ignorance which is the conceit that a man knows what he does not know? And in this respect only I believe myself to differ from men in general, and may perhaps claim to be wiser than they are:—that whereas I know but little of the world below, I do not suppose that I know: but I do know that injustice and disobedience to a better, whether God or man, is evil and dishonourable, and I will never fear or avoid a possible good rather than a certain evil. And therefore if you let me go now, and are not convinced by Anytus, who said that since I had been prosecuted I must be put to death; (or if not that I ought never to have been prosecuted at all); and that if I escape now, your sons will all be utterly ruined by listening to my words—if you say to me, Socrates, this time we will not mind Anytus, and you shall be let off, but upon one condition, that you are not to enquire and speculate in this way any more, and that if you are caught doing so again you shall die;—if this was the condition on which you let me go, I should reply:

Men of Athens, I honour and love you; but I shall obey God rather than you, and while I have life and strength I shall never cease from the practice and teaching of philosophy, exhorting any one whom I meet and saying to him after my manner: You, my friend,—a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens,—are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard or heed at all? And if the person with whom I am arguing, says: Yes, but I do care; then I do not leave him or let him go at once; but I proceed to interrogate and examine and cross-examine him, and if I think that he has no virtue in him, but only says that he has, I reproach him with undervaluing the greater, and overvaluing the less. And I shall repeat the same words to every one whom I meet, young and old, citizen and alien, but especially to the citizens, inasmuch as they are my brethren.

For know that this is the command of God; and I believe that no greater good has ever happened in the state than my service to the God. For I do nothing but go about persuading you all, old and young alike, not to take thought for your persons or your properties, but first and chiefly to care about the greatest improvement of the soul. I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue comes money and every other good of man, public as well as private. This is my teaching, and if this is the doctrine which corrupts the youth, I am a mischievous person. But if any one says that this is not my teaching, he is speaking an untruth. Wherefore, O men of Athens, I say to you, do as Anytus bids or not as Anytus bids, and either acquit me or not; but whichever you do, understand that I shall never alter my ways, not even if I have to die many times.

Men of Athens, do not interrupt, but hear me; there was an understanding between us that you should hear me to the end: I have something more to say, at which you may be inclined to cry out; but I believe that to hear me will be good for you, and therefore I beg that you will not cry out. I would have you know, that if you kill such an one as I am, you will injure yourselves more than you will injure me. Nothing will injure me, not Meletus nor yet Anytus—they cannot, for a bad man is not permitted to injure a better than himself. I do not deny that Anytus may, perhaps, kill him, or drive him into exile, or deprive him of civil rights; and he may imagine, and others may imagine, that he is inflicting a great injury upon him: but there I do not agree. For the evil of doing as he is doing—the evil of unjustly taking away the life of another—is greater far.

And now, Athenians, I am not going to argue for my own sake, as you may think, but for yours, that you may not sin against the God by condemning me, who am his gift to you. For if you kill me you will not easily find a successor to me, who, if I may use such a ludicrous figure of speech, am a sort of gadfly, given to the state by God; and the state is a great and noble steed who is tardy in his motions owing to his very size, and requires to be stirred into life. I am that gadfly which God has attached to the state, and all day long and in all places am always fastening upon you, arousing and persuading and reproaching you. You will not easily find another like me, and therefore I would advise you to spare me. I dare say that you may feel out of temper (like a person who is suddenly awakened from sleep), and you think that you might easily strike me dead as Anytus advises, and then you would sleep on for the remainder of your lives, unless God in his care of you sent you another gadfly.

When I say that I am given to you by God, the proof of my mission is this:—if I had been like other men, I should not have neglected all my own concerns or patiently seen the neglect of them during all these years, and have been doing yours, coming to you individually like a father or elder brother, exhorting you to regard virtue; such conduct, I say, would be unlike human nature. If I had gained anything, or if my exhortations had been paid, there would have been some sense in my doing so; but now, as you will perceive, not even the impudence of my accusers dares to say that I have ever exacted or sought pay of any one; of that they have no witness. And I have a sufficient witness to the truth of what I say—my poverty.

Some one may wonder why I go about in private giving advice and busying myself with the concerns of others, but do not venture to come forward in public and advise the state. I will tell you why. You have heard me speak at sundry times and in divers places of an oracle or sign which comes to me, and is the divinity which Meletus ridicules in the indictment. This sign, which is a kind of voice, first began to come to me when I was a child; it always forbids but never commands me to do anything which I am going to do. This is what deters me from being a politician. And rightly, as I think. For I am certain, O men of Athens, that if I had engaged in politics, I should have perished long ago, and done no good either to you or to myself. And do not be offended at my telling you the truth: for the truth is, that no man who goes to war with you or any other multitude, honestly striving against the many lawless and unrighteous deeds which are done in a state, will save his life; he who will fight for the right, if he would live even for a brief space, must have a private station and not a public one.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.who: Diogenes Laertius (3rd century AD), quoting the court record; then Plato (about 428–348 BC), who was in court
parts.title: The indictment
parts.context: Diogenes Laertius wrote his Lives of the Philosophers in the third century AD, six hundred years after the trial, from many older books. Here he quotes Favorinus, a scholar of the second century AD, who said the sworn charge was still kept in the Metroon, the temple of the Mother of the Gods in the Athenian agora, which also served as the city's record office. Yonge (1853) calls her Cybele.
parts.plain: The charge: Meletus accuses Socrates of not believing in the gods the city worships, of bringing in other new divinities, and of corrupting the young. The penalty asked: death.

commentary.on: they are preserved to this day, says Phavorinus, in the temple of Cybele
commentary.text: This is as near as we get to a document from the trial. The wording matches Plato (24b) and Xenophon almost exactly, which makes it likely that all three reflect the real charge.

commentary.on: he does not believe in the Gods whom the city worships, but introduces other strange deities
commentary.text: Two religious charges. 'Believe in' (nomizein) can also mean 'recognise' or 'honour by custom': the charge may be about practice as much as belief. The 'strange deities' were probably his divine sign.

commentary.on: he corrupts the young men, and the punishment he has incurred is death
commentary.text: The third charge, and probably the real one. It was vague enough to cover the influence of Socrates on young men like Critias and Alcibiades without naming them.

parts.author: Plato
parts.title: I shall obey God rather than you
parts.context: Socrates has finished with Meletus. Now he faces the real question every juror is asking: why not just stop, and live? Achilles, 'the son of Thetis', was the hero of Homer's Iliad, who chose to avenge his friend Patroclus knowing it meant his own death. Potidaea, Amphipolis and Delium were battles of the war with Sparta in which Socrates served. Jowett's translation, 1871.
parts.plain: Socrates says: a good man does not count the risk of death, only whether he is doing right. Achilles chose death rather than disgrace. I stood my ground in battle where the generals placed me; how can I desert the post where God has placed me, to examine myself and others? To fear death is to think you know what you don't: death may be the greatest good. If you offered to free me on condition that I stopped philosophising, I would say: I love you, but I will obey God rather than you. I will go on asking every citizen: are you not ashamed to care for money and reputation and not for your soul?

commentary.on: he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong
commentary.text: This sentence is the moral core of Socrates' life. The only question is whether an act is right; consequences, even death, do not enter into it. Moral philosophers would later call this a refusal to let calculation override duty.

commentary.on: when, as I conceive and imagine, God orders me to fulfil the philosopher’s mission of searching into myself and other men, I were to desert my post
commentary.text: Socrates uses the soldier's code, which every juror respected. You do not leave your post in battle. He applies it to his mission: God has posted him to question. Abandoning philosophy would be desertion.

commentary.on: For the fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being a pretence of knowing the unknown
commentary.text: Socratic ignorance turned on death itself. We fear death as if we knew it was the worst thing. But we do not know what it is. So fearing it is another case of thinking we know what we do not.

commentary.on: but I do know that injustice and disobedience to a better, whether God or man, is evil and dishonourable
commentary.text: Here Socrates says plainly that he does know something. His 'ignorance' is not total: he is certain that doing wrong is evil.

commentary.on: Men of Athens, I honour and love you; but I shall obey God rather than you
commentary.text: The most famous words of the defence. Socrates does not despise the city; he loves it. But there is a higher authority. About 430 years later, Peter and the apostles would say almost the same words to the council in Jerusalem (Acts 5:29).

commentary.on: are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul
commentary.text: This is what Socratic questioning was for: the care of the soul. The Greek psychē meant life, self and mind. Socrates' message was that your soul, what kind of person you are, matters more than anything you have.

commentary.on: I shall never alter my ways, not even if I have to die many times
commentary.text: A juror might have heard this as courage, or as defiance of the court. It left them no middle way: acquit him and let him carry on, or condemn him.

parts.author: Plato
parts.title: The gadfly
parts.context: The jury has started shouting, as Athenian juries did. Socrates asks them to let him finish.
parts.plain: Socrates says: if you kill me you harm yourselves more than me, because doing injustice is worse than suffering it. I am God's gift to you, a gadfly on a great, lazy horse, waking you up. Kill me, and you will sleep on, unless God sends another. The proof that I am sent by God: I have neglected my own affairs for years and taken no money.

commentary.on: a bad man is not permitted to injure a better than himself
commentary.text: A startling claim. They can kill him, but they cannot harm him, because the only real harm is to become worse, and that only a person can do to himself. This idea runs through Stoic philosophy and into Christian thought: 'Don't be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul' (Matthew 10:28).

commentary.on: am a sort of gadfly, given to the state by God
commentary.text: The image that gives this journey's first session its title. A gadfly stings horses and cattle. It is annoying; it also keeps them moving. Socrates claims that the irritation he causes is a gift.

commentary.on: then you would sleep on for the remainder of your lives, unless God in his care of you sent you another gadfly
commentary.text: A warning that sounds like prophecy. Plato, writing later, knew that Socrates' pupils would carry on his questioning after his death.

commentary.on: my poverty
commentary.text: His last witness. Unlike the sophists, he took no fees. Poverty is his evidence that he served the god, not himself.

parts.author: Plato
parts.title: The sign
parts.context: If he cares so much for Athens, someone might ask, why did he not go into politics? Socrates explains by his divine sign, the daimonion in the charge.
parts.plain: Socrates says: you have often heard me speak of a sign, a kind of voice, that has come to me since childhood. It always holds me back and never pushes me on. It held me back from politics, and rightly, because an honest man who opposes the many will not survive long in public life. Anyone who really fights for justice must keep to private life.

commentary.on: This sign, which is a kind of voice, first began to come to me when I was a child; it always forbids but never commands me to do anything which I am going to do.
commentary.text: Plato's description of the daimonion. It was not a set of teachings and not a god with a name. It was a warning, like an inner check, that stopped him from doing something. Xenophon says it also gave positive advice; Plato insists it only forbade. Christian readers have compared it to conscience.

commentary.on: if I had engaged in politics, I should have perished long ago
commentary.text: A bitter remark in a democratic court. Socrates says honest opposition to the many is fatal in public life. The jury could hear it as a criticism of democracy itself.

commentary.on: he who will fight for the right, if he would live even for a brief space, must have a private station and not a public one
commentary.text: Socrates' politics was one person at a time. He thought he served the city best by improving its citizens one by one, not by speeches in the Assembly. Some see this as wisdom; others, as a refusal to share the burden of governing.

read.author: Diogenes Laertius and Plato
read.who: Diogenes Laertius (3rd century AD), quoting the court record; then Plato (about 428–348 BC), who was in court

paras: Then Nebuchadnezzar in rage and fury commanded that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought. Then these men were brought before the king.
Nebuchadnezzar answered them, “Is it on purpose, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you don’t serve my god, nor worship the golden image which I have set up?

Now if you are ready whenever you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe, and all kinds of music to fall down and worship the image which I have made, good; but if you don’t worship, you shall be cast the same hour into the middle of a burning fiery furnace. Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?”
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered the king, “Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter.
If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.
But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.”

parts.title: Three men before the king
parts.context: The book of Daniel is set in the 500s BC, when Jews had been taken into exile in Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar, its king, had set up a golden image and ordered everyone to bow down at the sound of music. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, Jewish officials at his court, refused. Many scholars think the book reached its present form in the 160s BC, when a Greek king, Antiochus IV, was forcing Jews to give up their faith, so it may have been written for people facing exactly this choice.

commentary.on: Who is that god that will deliver you out of my hands?
commentary.text: The king's question is the real issue: who has the final authority, the state or God? Athens asked Socrates the same question in a gentler voice.

commentary.on: we have no need to answer you in this matter.
commentary.text: Like Socrates, they do not plead or bargain. Their minds are made up.

commentary.on: But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods
commentary.text: 'But if not' is the heart of it. They trust that God can save them, but their obedience does not depend on being saved. Socrates said the same: whether or not death is evil, he will not leave his post. The difference is the object of obedience: for the three, the God of Israel who has spoken in the law; for Socrates, a god who sent him to question, and a voice within.

compare.why: In the book of Daniel, three young Jews are ordered by the king of Babylon to worship his golden statue or be thrown into a furnace. Read their answer beside Socrates': two of the oldest stories of a person who would rather die than disobey God.
compare.title: But if not

sections.h: The charges, and what lay behind them
paras: The charge had three parts: not recognising the city's gods, introducing new divinities, and corrupting the young. Ancient and modern historians have asked whether it meant what it said. In Athens religion and politics were not separate. The gods protected the city; impiety put everyone at risk. Only a few years earlier, in 415 BC, the city had been in panic over the mutilation of the Herms, sacred statues in the streets, and the mocking of the Mysteries, crimes for which Alcibiades himself was condemned.

Many historians think the deeper motive was political. Socrates had taught Critias and Alcibiades, and had criticised the democracy's habit of choosing officials by lot. Fifty years later the orator Aeschines told an Athenian jury, as if it were common knowledge: 'you put to death Socrates the sophist, because he was shown to have educated Critias' (Against Timarchus 173). Because of the amnesty, that could not be the charge. But it may well have been in the jurors' minds.
sections.key: The charge was religious; many historians, citing Aeschines, think the real grievance was political: Critias, Alcibiades and Socrates' criticism of democracy.

paras: The jury found Socrates guilty. Plato has him say that if only thirty votes had gone the other way he would have been acquitted (36a): with about five hundred jurors, that suggests roughly 280 against 220. It was close.

Then came the penalty. Meletus asked for death. Socrates, invited to propose an alternative, said that what he really deserved for his services was free meals for life in the Prytaneum, the honour Athens gave to Olympic victors (36d). He then offered a fine of one mina, about a hundred days' wages for a skilled worker, raised to thirty minae when his friends, including Plato, offered to guarantee it (38b). He refused to propose exile: he would only go on questioning wherever he went, and 'the unexamined life is not worth living' (38a). The jury chose death by a larger margin than it had found him guilty; Diogenes Laertius says by eighty more votes.

Think of who those jurors were. Jury pay, three obols a day, attracted many older and poorer citizens. Many had fought to restore the democracy against the Thirty; some had lost relatives to them. They had just heard a man whose friends had included Critias propose a public honour for himself. Some who voted to acquit him on the charge then voted for death, which tells us how much the penalty speech cost him.
sections.key: Guilty by about 280 to 220; Socrates proposed free meals as his 'penalty', then a fine; the jury chose death by a larger margin.

sections.h: Why didn't he try harder to win?
paras: Socrates could almost certainly have saved himself. Xenophon says he deliberately did not try, partly because he thought it was time to die, at seventy, before old age took his mind (Xenophon, Apology 1–9). Plato's Socrates says he would not stoop to tears or bring his children to plead, because it would shame the city and dishonour justice (34b–35d).

Was his defence arrogance or integrity? Readers have always divided. To some, the proposal of free meals was provocation that cost him his life. To others, it was the only honest answer: if he truly believed his questioning was a service to Athens, he could not propose a punishment for it without lying. The examined life, here, meant refusing to say anything he did not believe, even to a court that held his life.
sections.key: Socrates refused to plead or weep and proposed a reward, not a penalty: arrogance to some, integrity to others.

paras: The daimonion puzzled ancient writers as much as modern ones. Plutarch wrote a whole dialogue, On the Sign of Socrates, suggesting that it was a direct communication from a higher mind. Some modern writers have tried medical explanations; most scholars think it is wiser simply to describe what Socrates says about it.

What he says is modest. It is a voice that has come since childhood; it only ever holds him back; and on the day of his trial, he tells the jury after the verdict, it did not oppose him once, which he takes as a sign that what was happening to him was good (40a–c). Notice what the sign is not: it gives him no doctrine and does not replace argument. Socrates still reasons everything out. When he was condemned, he did not appeal to the sign to prove he was right; he appealed to argument, and to the jury's own consciences. Christian writers often compared it to conscience, the inner voice that warns; others saw it as a real, if partial, contact with God.
sections.key: Socrates' sign was an inner voice from childhood that only held him back; it never replaced argument, and many compared it to conscience.

paras: 'I shall obey God rather than you' became one of the founding sentences of the West. It says that there is an authority above the city, and that a person may have a duty to refuse the state's command. Greek tragedy had imagined it: Sophocles' Antigone defied King Creon to bury her brother by the 'unwritten laws' of the gods (about 441 BC). Socrates lived it in a law court.

The Bible says it too: the three young men before Nebuchadnezzar, the midwives who would not kill the Hebrew boys in Egypt (Exodus 1), Peter before the council in Jerusalem. The early Christian martyrs, refusing to sacrifice to the emperor, stood in both traditions at once. Later, conscientious objectors, dissidents under totalitarian regimes and campaigners for civil rights would appeal to the same principle. Its danger is plain: anyone can claim God's authority for anything. Socrates' answer was to submit every conviction to questioning, and to harm no one in its name.
sections.key: Socrates' 'obey God rather than you', like Antigone, Daniel and Peter, founded the Western idea that a higher authority can limit the state's command.

paras: One more thing about the defence: Socrates was not an outsider. He fought for Athens in three campaigns; he served on its Council; he says he hardly ever left the city. He calls the Athenians 'my brethren' and says he speaks to them because he loves them. His refusal at Arginusae (406 BC) and his refusal to arrest Leon of Salamis under the Thirty (404 BC) were acts of obedience to law against the city's own leaders: once against the democracy, once against the oligarchs.

That makes his defiance in court more interesting, not less. He was not a rebel against law; he was a man who thought the city's laws, and its gods, deserved a better obedience than the city itself was giving. Whether a citizen who thinks so may also break the law to save himself is the question of the next session.
sections.key: Socrates was a loyal citizen who had defied both democrats and oligarchs for the sake of law; his defiance in court came from loyalty, not rebellion.
