debate.question: Was Socrates guilty as charged?

positions.name: Guilty, by Athenian standards
positions.who: Some classicists, such as Mogens Hansen; in his way, I. F. Stone
positions.view: Athens had a public religion and a right to protect it. A man who claimed a private divine voice above the city's oracles and gods, and whose pupils despised the democracy, did break its norms, even if he sacrificed.
positions.evidence: The daimonion as a personal god; Socrates' criticisms of the lot and of the many; the careers of Critias and Alcibiades.

positions.name: Innocent: the charges were a pretext
positions.who: Plato; Xenophon; most modern scholars, e.g. Thomas Brickhouse and Nicholas Smith
positions.view: Socrates honoured the gods and was devoted to a god's command. The charges dressed up resentment and political suspicion that the amnesty forbade the prosecutors to name.
positions.evidence: His sacrifices and obedience to Delphi; Meletus's confusion under cross-examination; Aeschines' remark about Critias.

positions.name: Innocent of impiety, but a real threat
positions.who: Hegel; some modern historians
positions.view: Socrates was no atheist, but his questioning put the individual's reason above the city's customs. The jury sensed, rightly, that this would change Athens. That is not a crime, but it is a real conflict.
positions.evidence: His appeal to his own sign and to 'God' over the jury; his wish to examine every inherited belief.

debate.agree: All agree that the vote was close, that Socrates could probably have saved himself, and that he chose not to compromise his mission.

look.why: The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of Socrates before his judges, and none of the three young men in the furnace.

music.why: A hymn from a poem by the Quaker John Greenleaf Whittier (1872), who believed in the 'inner light' and prayed to hear 'the still small voice of calm'. Quakers refused oaths and war for conscience's sake and suffered for it. Listen to it as a prayer for the kind of inner voice Socrates trusted.

think.why: Where did the idea come from that one person's conscience can stand against the state? Socrates is one of its roots.

learn.why: Socrates' last words to the jury after the death sentence: no evil can happen to a good man, and 'which is better God only knows'.

check.q: Why does Socrates compare himself to a soldier at his post?
options: Because soldiers were exempt from trial
Because, as he held his ground in battle where the generals placed him, he must hold the post God gave him, to question, even at the risk of death
Because he wanted to be a general
Because he was still in the army
check.why: Deserting philosophy through fear of death would be like deserting in battle.

check.q: Why does Socrates say fearing death is a kind of false wisdom?
options: Because death is certainly good
Because the gods have told him what happens after death
Because brave men never die
Because it treats death as the worst evil when we do not know what death is
check.why: It is 'a pretence of knowing the unknown': Socratic ignorance applied to death.

check.q: What would Socrates do if acquitted on condition that he stopped philosophising?
options: Refuse: 'I shall obey God rather than you', and carry on
Accept and retire
Ask for time to consider
Leave Athens
check.why: He would never cease from the practice and teaching of philosophy.

check.q: What did Socrates' divine sign do, according to Plato?
options: It told him to enter politics
It told him what to teach
It predicted the future
It held him back from things, and never urged him on
check.why: 'It always forbids but never commands'; it held him back from politics.

check.q: Many historians think the charge of 'corrupting the young' carried a political grievance. Which evidence best supports this?
options: Socrates was poor
The jury was chosen by lot
Socrates fought at Delium
Aeschines told a jury in 345 BC that Athens executed Socrates because he had educated Critias
check.why: Aeschines' remark suggests that Athenians remembered the trial as about Critias, whom the amnesty prevented them from naming.

check.q: What is the deepest likeness between Socrates and the three young men in Daniel 3?
options: Both put obedience to God above the command of the state, whatever the outcome ('But if not')
Both were Athenians
Both escaped unharmed
Both refused a command to worship a statue
check.why: Neither made obedience depend on being saved.

tutorial.question: Was Socrates' defence an act of integrity or of arrogance?
tutorial.approach: Summarise the defence (the post, the fear of death, 'I shall obey God rather than you', the gadfly, the sign). Then look at the penalty stage: free meals, the fine, the refusal of exile. Weigh the case that he provoked the jury against the case that he could not honestly say anything else. Use Daniel 3 as a comparison.
strong: Accurately states the charges and the structure of an Athenian trial.
Uses the soldier's post and 'obey God rather than you' precisely.
Discusses the penalty proposal and the second vote.
Gives the arrogance reading fairly.
Gives the integrity reading fairly, linking it to the examined life.
Uses the comparison with Daniel to sharpen the argument.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Socrates asked every citizen whether they cared more for money and reputation than for the soul. Once this week, before a choice that involves money or how others see you, ask: what would this do to the kind of person I am? Then choose.
sessions.reflect: Is there anything you would refuse to stop doing even if your whole community told you to? How do you know it is God, or conscience, and not just pride?
takeaways: Socrates was charged with not recognising the city's gods, introducing new divinities and corrupting the young; many think the real grievance was political.
He refused to stop philosophising: like a soldier at his post, he would 'obey God rather than you', and called himself Athens' gadfly.
Found guilty by about 280 to 220, he proposed free meals, then a fine, and the jury chose death by a larger margin.

sessions.title: Why he did not run
sessions.line: In prison, his oldest friend has bribed the guard and arranged an escape. Socrates asks one question: would it be just?
sessions.plain: After the trial Socrates waited in prison for about a month, because no one could be executed while a sacred ship was away on its yearly voyage to the island of Delos. His rich friend Crito came before dawn with news that the ship was nearly home, and a plan: the guards were bribed, friends abroad would welcome him; he only had to walk out. Socrates refused. In Plato's Crito he imagines the Laws of Athens themselves coming to question him. This session asks why he stayed, and whether he was right.
sessions.why: Session 4 ended with Socrates condemned. He had told the jury he would obey God rather than them. Now a way out is offered, and the question is turned round: if he would disobey the city to keep philosophising, why not disobey it to save his life?
answers: Why didn't Socrates escape from prison?
What did the Laws of Athens say to him?
How can he obey the city here, after defying it in court?
Is there a duty to obey unjust laws or verdicts?
sessions.finding: In prison, offered escape, Socrates refused to return wrong for wrong, and let the Laws of Athens argue that a citizen who has accepted their protection all his life must persuade them or obey: he died rather than break the agreement.

paras: Socrates has been found guilty and sentenced to death (session 4). His defence was built on one principle: do what is right, and do not count the risk of death. He told the jury that if they freed him on condition that he stopped philosophising, he would refuse.

But the execution could not happen at once. Every year Athens sent a ship to the sacred island of Delos to honour Apollo, remembering how the hero Theseus had saved the city's young people from the Minotaur. While the ship was away, the city had to be kept pure: no executions. The ship had sailed the day before the trial. Socrates spent about a month in prison, in chains by night, talking with his friends by day.
background.key: Condemned, Socrates waited about a month in prison while the sacred ship was away at Delos, talking with his friends.

paras: Crito was Socrates' age, from the same district of Athens, and his friend for life: a wealthy, practical man with a son, Critobulus, among Socrates' companions. In the opening of the dialogue, which comes just before our reading, he arrives before dawn and finds Socrates peacefully asleep. The ship has been seen off Cape Sunium; it will be in tomorrow. The escape is arranged. Simmias and Cebes, two young men from Thebes, have brought money; friends in Thessaly will protect him.

Crito gives four reasons to go: people will say his friends let him die to save money; he owes it to his children; staying is doing what his enemies want; it is cowardly. Socrates answers: we have always agreed to be guided by reason, not by fear or by what the many think. Let us think it through.
background.key: Crito, his oldest friend, had arranged the escape and pleaded with him: for his reputation, his children and his friends' honour.

paras: The main reading is the rest of the Crito (47a–54e): Socrates' principles, and the famous speech of the Laws. It is one of the first sustained arguments in history about why a citizen should obey the law, and it is still discussed in every course on political philosophy.

The comparison is Paul's teaching on obedience to the government in his letter to the Christians of Rome (Romans 13:1–7), written about AD 57 to people living under the emperor Nero. Paul and the Laws of Athens both say the citizen owes obedience. They give different reasons.
background.key: The Crito's argument for obeying the law (47a–54e), beside Paul on the governing authorities (Romans 13:1–7).

before: What principle does Socrates insist on before he will even discuss escaping?
List the reasons the Laws give why Socrates owes them obedience.
What does 'persuade or obey' mean, and does Socrates think he has had a fair chance to persuade?
sessions.readWhy: Socrates' reasons for staying: his principles, and the speech he imagines the Laws of Athens making to him.

paras: SOCRATES: The good are to be regarded, and not the bad?
CRITO: Yes.
SOCRATES: And the opinions of the wise are good, and the opinions of the unwise are evil?
CRITO: Certainly.

SOCRATES: And what was said about another matter? Is the pupil who devotes himself to the practice of gymnastics supposed to attend to the praise and blame and opinion of every man, or of one man only--his physician or trainer, whoever he may be?
CRITO: Of one man only.
SOCRATES: And he ought to fear the censure and welcome the praise of that one only, and not of the many?
CRITO: Clearly so.
SOCRATES: And he ought to act and train, and eat and drink in the way which seems good to his single master who has understanding, rather than according to the opinion of all other men put together?
CRITO: True.
SOCRATES: And if he disobeys and disregards the opinion and approval of the one, and regards the opinion of the many who have no understanding, will he not suffer evil?
CRITO: Certainly he will.
SOCRATES: And what will the evil be, whither tending and what affecting, in the disobedient person?
CRITO: Clearly, affecting the body; that is what is destroyed by the evil.

SOCRATES: Very good; and is not this true, Crito, of other things which we need not separately enumerate? In questions of just and unjust, fair and foul, good and evil, which are the subjects of our present consultation, ought we to follow the opinion of the many and to fear them; or the opinion of the one man who has understanding? ought we not to fear and reverence him more than all the rest of the world: and if we desert him shall we not destroy and injure that principle in us which may be assumed to be improved by justice and deteriorated by injustice;--there is such a principle?
CRITO: Certainly there is, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Take a parallel instance:--if, acting under the advice of those who have no understanding, we destroy that which is improved by health and is deteriorated by disease, would life be worth having? And that which has been destroyed is--the body?
CRITO: Yes.
SOCRATES: Could we live, having an evil and corrupted body?
CRITO: Certainly not.

SOCRATES: And will life be worth having, if that higher part of man be destroyed, which is improved by justice and depraved by injustice? Do we suppose that principle, whatever it may be in man, which has to do with justice and injustice, to be inferior to the body?
CRITO: Certainly not.
SOCRATES: More honourable than the body?
CRITO: Far more.

SOCRATES: Then, my friend, we must not regard what the many say of us: but what he, the one man who has understanding of just and unjust, will say, and what the truth will say. And therefore you begin in error when you advise that we should regard the opinion of the many about just and unjust, good and evil, honorable and dishonorable.--'Well,' some one will say, 'but the many can kill us.'
CRITO: Yes, Socrates; that will clearly be the answer.

SOCRATES: And it is true; but still I find with surprise that the old argument is unshaken as ever. And I should like to know whether I may say the same of another proposition--that not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued?
CRITO: Yes, that also remains unshaken.
SOCRATES: And a good life is equivalent to a just and honorable one--that holds also?
CRITO: Yes, it does.

SOCRATES: From these premisses I proceed to argue the question whether I ought or ought not to try and escape without the consent of the Athenians: and if I am clearly right in escaping, then I will make the attempt; but if not, I will abstain. The other considerations which you mention, of money and loss of character and the duty of educating one's children, are, I fear, only the doctrines of the multitude, who would be as ready to restore people to life, if they were able, as they are to put them to death--and with as little reason. But now, since the argument has thus far prevailed, the only question which remains to be considered is, whether we shall do rightly either in escaping or in suffering others to aid in our escape and paying them in money and thanks, or whether in reality we shall not do rightly; and if the latter, then death or any other calamity which may ensue on my remaining here must not be allowed to enter into the calculation.
CRITO: I think that you are right, Socrates; how then shall we proceed?

SOCRATES: Let us consider the matter together, and do you either refute me if you can, and I will be convinced; or else cease, my dear friend, from repeating to me that I ought to escape against the wishes of the Athenians: for I highly value your attempts to persuade me to do so, but I may not be persuaded against my own better judgment. And now please to consider my first position, and try how you can best answer me.
CRITO: I will.

SOCRATES: Are we to say that we are never intentionally to do wrong, or that in one way we ought and in another way we ought not to do wrong, or is doing wrong always evil and dishonorable, as I was just now saying, and as has been already acknowledged by us? Are all our former admissions which were made within a few days to be thrown away? And have we, at our age, been earnestly discoursing with one another all our life long only to discover that we are no better than children? Or, in spite of the opinion of the many, and in spite of consequences whether better or worse, shall we insist on the truth of what was then said, that injustice is always an evil and dishonour to him who acts unjustly? Shall we say so or not?
CRITO: Yes.
SOCRATES: Then we must do no wrong?
CRITO: Certainly not.
SOCRATES: Nor when injured injure in return, as the many imagine; for we must injure no one at all?
CRITO: Clearly not.
SOCRATES: Again, Crito, may we do evil?
CRITO: Surely not, Socrates.
SOCRATES: And what of doing evil in return for evil, which is the morality of the many--is that just or not?
CRITO: Not just.
SOCRATES: For doing evil to another is the same as injuring him?
CRITO: Very true.

SOCRATES: Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to any one, whatever evil we may have suffered from him. But I would have you consider, Crito, whether you really mean what you are saying. For this opinion has never been held, and never will be held, by any considerable number of persons; and those who are agreed and those who are not agreed upon this point have no common ground, and can only despise one another when they see how widely they differ. Tell me, then, whether you agree with and assent to my first principle, that neither injury nor retaliation nor warding off evil by evil is ever right. And shall that be the premiss of our argument? Or do you decline and dissent from this? For so I have ever thought, and continue to think; but, if you are of another opinion, let me hear what you have to say. If, however, you remain of the same mind as formerly, I will proceed to the next step.
CRITO: You may proceed, for I have not changed my mind.
SOCRATES: Then I will go on to the next point, which may be put in the form of a question:--Ought a man to do what he admits to be right, or ought he to betray the right?
CRITO: He ought to do what he thinks right.

SOCRATES: But if this is true, what is the application? In leaving the prison against the will of the Athenians, do I wrong any? or rather do I not wrong those whom I ought least to wrong? Do I not desert the principles which were acknowledged by us to be just--what do you say?
CRITO: I cannot tell, Socrates, for I do not know.

SOCRATES: Then consider the matter in this way:--Imagine that I am about to play truant (you may call the proceeding by any name which you like), and the laws and the government come and interrogate me: 'Tell us, Socrates,' they say; 'what are you about? are you not going by an act of yours to overturn us--the laws, and the whole state, as far as in you lies? Do you imagine that a state can subsist and not be overthrown, in which the decisions of law have no power, but are set aside and trampled upon by individuals?' What will be our answer, Crito, to these and the like words? Any one, and especially a rhetorician, will have a good deal to say on behalf of the law which requires a sentence to be carried out. He will argue that this law should not be set aside; and shall we reply, 'Yes; but the state has injured us and given an unjust sentence.' Suppose I say that?
CRITO: Very good, Socrates.

SOCRATES: 'And was that our agreement with you?' the law would answer; 'or were you to abide by the sentence of the state?' And if I were to express my astonishment at their words, the law would probably add: 'Answer, Socrates, instead of opening your eyes--you are in the habit of asking and answering questions. Tell us,--What complaint have you to make against us which justifies you in attempting to destroy us and the state? In the first place did we not bring you into existence? Your father married your mother by our aid and begat you. Say whether you have any objection to urge against those of us who regulate marriage?' None, I should reply. 'Or against those of us who after birth regulate the nurture and education of children, in which you also were trained? Were not the laws, which have the charge of education, right in commanding your father to train you in music and gymnastic?' Right, I should reply. 'Well then, since you were brought into the world and nurtured and educated by us, can you deny in the first place that you are our child and slave, as your fathers were before you? And if this is true you are not on equal terms with us; nor can you think that you have a right to do to us what we are doing to you.

Would you have any right to strike or revile or do any other evil to your father or your master, if you had one, because you have been struck or reviled by him, or received some other evil at his hands?--you would not say this? And because we think right to destroy you, do you think that you have any right to destroy us in return, and your country as far as in you lies? Will you, O professor of true virtue, pretend that you are justified in this? Has a philosopher like you failed to discover that our country is more to be valued and higher and holier far than mother or father or any ancestor, and more to be regarded in the eyes of the gods and of men of understanding? also to be soothed, and gently and reverently entreated when angry, even more than a father, and either to be persuaded, or if not persuaded, to be obeyed? And when we are punished by her, whether with imprisonment or stripes, the punishment is to be endured in silence; and if she lead us to wounds or death in battle, thither we follow as is right; neither may any one yield or retreat or leave his rank, but whether in battle or in a court of law, or in any other place, he must do what his city and his country order him; or he must change their view of what is just: and if he may do no violence to his father or mother, much less may he do violence to his country.' What answer shall we make to this, Crito? Do the laws speak truly, or do they not?
CRITO: I think that they do.

SOCRATES: Then the laws will say: 'Consider, Socrates, if we are speaking truly that in your present attempt you are going to do us an injury. For, having brought you into the world, and nurtured and educated you, and given you and every other citizen a share in every good which we had to give, we further proclaim to any Athenian by the liberty which we allow him, that if he does not like us when he has become of age and has seen the ways of the city, and made our acquaintance, he may go where he pleases and take his goods with him. None of us laws will forbid him or interfere with him. Any one who does not like us and the city, and who wants to emigrate to a colony or to any other city, may go where he likes, retaining his property. But he who has experience of the manner in which we order justice and administer the state, and still remains, has entered into an implied contract that he will do as we command him. And he who disobeys us is, as we maintain, thrice wrong: first, because in disobeying us he is disobeying his parents; secondly, because we are the authors of his education; thirdly, because he has made an agreement with us that he will duly obey our commands; and he neither obeys them nor convinces us that our commands are unjust; and we do not rudely impose them, but give him the alternative of obeying or convincing us;--that is what we offer, and he does neither.

'These are the sort of accusations to which, as we were saying, you, Socrates, will be exposed if you accomplish your intentions; you, above all other Athenians.' Suppose now I ask, why I rather than anybody else? they will justly retort upon me that I above all other men have acknowledged the agreement. 'There is clear proof,' they will say, 'Socrates, that we and the city were not displeasing to you. Of all Athenians you have been the most constant resident in the city, which, as you never leave, you may be supposed to love. For you never went out of the city either to see the games, except once when you went to the Isthmus, or to any other place unless when you were on military service; nor did you travel as other men do. Nor had you any curiosity to know other states or their laws: your affections did not go beyond us and our state; we were your especial favourites, and you acquiesced in our government of you; and here in this city you begat your children, which is a proof of your satisfaction. Moreover, you might in the course of the trial, if you had liked, have fixed the penalty at banishment; the state which refuses to let you go now would have let you go then. But you pretended that you preferred death to exile, and that you were not unwilling to die. And now you have forgotten these fine sentiments, and pay no respect to us the laws, of whom you are the destroyer; and are doing what only a miserable slave would do, running away and turning your back upon the compacts and agreements which you made as a citizen. And first of all answer this very question: Are we right in saying that you agreed to be governed according to us in deed, and not in word only? Is that true or not?' How shall we answer, Crito? Must we not assent?
CRITO: We cannot help it, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Then will they not say: 'You, Socrates, are breaking the covenants and agreements which you made with us at your leisure, not in any haste or under any compulsion or deception, but after you have had seventy years to think of them, during which time you were at liberty to leave the city, if we were not to your mind, or if our covenants appeared to you to be unfair. You had your choice, and might have gone either to Lacedaemon or Crete, both which states are often praised by you for their good government, or to some other Hellenic or foreign state. Whereas you, above all other Athenians, seemed to be so fond of the state, or, in other words, of us her laws (and who would care about a state which has no laws?), that you never stirred out of her; the halt, the blind, the maimed, were not more stationary in her than you were. And now you run away and forsake your agreements. Not so, Socrates, if you will take our advice; do not make yourself ridiculous by escaping out of the city.

'For just consider, if you transgress and err in this sort of way, what good will you do either to yourself or to your friends? That your friends will be driven into exile and deprived of citizenship, or will lose their property, is tolerably certain; and you yourself, if you fly to one of the neighbouring cities, as, for example, Thebes or Megara, both of which are well governed, will come to them as an enemy, Socrates, and their government will be against you, and all patriotic citizens will cast an evil eye upon you as a subverter of the laws, and you will confirm in the minds of the judges the justice of their own condemnation of you. For he who is a corrupter of the laws is more than likely to be a corrupter of the young and foolish portion of mankind. Will you then flee from well-ordered cities and virtuous men? and is existence worth having on these terms? Or will you go to them without shame, and talk to them, Socrates? And what will you say to them? What you say here about virtue and justice and institutions and laws being the best things among men? Would that be decent of you? Surely not. But if you go away from well-governed states to Crito's friends in Thessaly, where there is great disorder and licence, they will be charmed to hear the tale of your escape from prison, set off with ludicrous particulars of the manner in which you were wrapped in a goatskin or some other disguise, and metamorphosed as the manner is of runaways;

but will there be no one to remind you that in your old age you were not ashamed to violate the most sacred laws from a miserable desire of a little more life? Perhaps not, if you keep them in a good temper; but if they are out of temper you will hear many degrading things; you will live, but how?--as the flatterer of all men, and the servant of all men; and doing what?--eating and drinking in Thessaly, having gone abroad in order that you may get a dinner. And where will be your fine sentiments about justice and virtue? Say that you wish to live for the sake of your children--you want to bring them up and educate them--will you take them into Thessaly and deprive them of Athenian citizenship? Is this the benefit which you will confer upon them? Or are you under the impression that they will be better cared for and educated here if you are still alive, although absent from them; for your friends will take care of them? Do you fancy that if you are an inhabitant of Thessaly they will take care of them, and if you are an inhabitant of the other world that they will not take care of them? Nay; but if they who call themselves friends are good for anything, they will--to be sure they will.

'Listen, then, Socrates, to us who have brought you up. Think not of life and children first, and of justice afterwards, but of justice first, that you may be justified before the princes of the world below. For neither will you nor any that belong to you be happier or holier or juster in this life, or happier in another, if you do as Crito bids. Now you depart in innocence, a sufferer and not a doer of evil; a victim, not of the laws, but of men. But if you go forth, returning evil for evil, and injury for injury, breaking the covenants and agreements which you have made with us, and wronging those whom you ought least of all to wrong, that is to say, yourself, your friends, your country, and us, we shall be angry with you while you live, and our brethren, the laws in the world below, will receive you as an enemy; for they will know that you have done your best to destroy us. Listen, then, to us and not to Crito.'

This, dear Crito, is the voice which I seem to hear murmuring in my ears, like the sound of the flute in the ears of the mystic; that voice, I say, is humming in my ears, and prevents me from hearing any other. And I know that anything more which you may say will be vain. Yet speak, if you have anything to say.
CRITO: I have nothing to say, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Leave me then, Crito, to fulfil the will of God, and to follow whither he leads.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens; the conversation is set in the prison, two or three days before Socrates' death in 399 BC
parts.title: Whose opinion counts?
parts.context: Socrates has asked Crito whether they were right, before the trial, to say that some people's opinions should be respected and others' not. Jowett's translation, 1871; two cross-references he inserted have been removed.
parts.plain: Socrates says: an athlete listens to his trainer, not to the crowd, or his body is ruined. In the same way, about right and wrong we should listen to the one who understands, and to the truth, not to the many; otherwise we ruin the part of us that justice improves and injustice destroys, which is worth far more than the body. 'But the many can kill us', someone will say. True. But what matters is not living, but living well, and living well means living justly.

commentary.on: Is the pupil who devotes himself to the practice of gymnastics supposed to attend to the praise and blame and opinion of every man, or of one man only
commentary.text: A typical Socratic analogy from ordinary life. You do not take medical advice from a crowd. Why take moral advice from one?

commentary.on: that principle in us which may be assumed to be improved by justice and deteriorated by injustice
commentary.text: Socrates calls it only 'that principle in us', but he means the soul. As the body is ruined by bad training, the soul is ruined by injustice. This is the same 'care of the soul' he preached to the jury.

commentary.on: 'Well,' some one will say, 'but the many can kill us.'
commentary.text: Socrates states the obvious objection, which is Crito's real fear. He does not deny it. He denies that it changes the question.

commentary.on: that not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued
commentary.text: The key principle of the whole dialogue. The aim is not survival but a good life, which means a just one. Everything Socrates decides follows from this.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens; the conversation is set in the prison, two or three days before Socrates' death in 399 BC
parts.title: Never return wrong for wrong
parts.context: Now Socrates turns to the actual question. Before he discusses the escape, he gets Crito to agree to a principle.
parts.plain: Socrates says: forget money, reputation and children; the only question is whether escaping would be just. We agreed long ago that it is never right to do wrong, not even in return for wrong: not to injure anyone, whatever they have done to us. Very few people believe this, and those who do and those who don't can hardly talk to each other. Do you still agree? Crito does. Then, says Socrates: would escaping against the city's will wrong anyone?

commentary.on: are, I fear, only the doctrines of the multitude, who would be as ready to restore people to life, if they were able, as they are to put them to death--and with as little reason
commentary.text: A sharp line about the crowd that condemned him: as thoughtless in killing as they would be in reviving. Socrates will not let their opinion decide his act.

commentary.on: have we, at our age, been earnestly discoursing with one another all our life long only to discover that we are no better than children?
commentary.text: Socrates appeals to their whole lives. If the principles they argued for for seventy years collapse at the first real test, their talk was childish. The examined life must be lived, not just discussed.

commentary.on: Nor when injured injure in return, as the many imagine; for we must injure no one at all?
commentary.text: This is a revolution in Greek ethics. Ordinary Greek morality said: help your friends and harm your enemies. Socrates says: harm no one, ever, even in return. It is the nearest thing in pagan philosophy to Jesus' 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44) and Paul's 'Repay no one evil for evil' (Romans 12:17).

commentary.on: For this opinion has never been held, and never will be held, by any considerable number of persons
commentary.text: Socrates knows how unusual this is. He even admits that people who disagree about it 'can only despise one another'. Some disagreements go to the root.

commentary.on: In leaving the prison against the will of the Athenians, do I wrong any?
commentary.text: Now the principle is applied. If escaping wrongs someone, Socrates cannot do it, whatever the city has done to him.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens; the conversation is set in the prison, two or three days before Socrates' death in 399 BC
parts.title: The Laws speak
parts.context: Crito cannot answer. So Socrates imagines the Laws of Athens, and 'the government', the city itself, appearing in the prison as he is about to slip out, and questioning him, as he had questioned so many. It is the most famous passage in the dialogue.
parts.plain: The Laws say: if you escape, you are trying to destroy us, for a city cannot survive if its court verdicts can be ignored by anyone. You say the verdict was unjust? But did you agree to abide by our verdicts? We brought you into being: your parents married under our laws; we educated you. You are like our child. You may not strike your father because he struck you; still less your country. You must persuade her, or obey her. And any Athenian who dislikes us may leave with his goods; whoever stays has agreed, by staying, to do what we command, or to persuade us that we are wrong.

commentary.on: Do you imagine that a state can subsist and not be overthrown, in which the decisions of law have no power, but are set aside and trampled upon by individuals?
commentary.text: The Laws' first argument: if every citizen ignored the verdicts he disliked, there would be no law at all. This is the argument from consequences, still used today against breaking the law even for good reasons.

commentary.on: 'Yes; but the state has injured us and given an unjust sentence.'
commentary.text: The obvious reply, and Socrates puts it himself. Notice that neither Socrates nor the Laws deny that the verdict was unjust. The question is whether an unjust verdict releases him.

commentary.on: can you deny in the first place that you are our child and slave, as your fathers were before you?
commentary.text: The Laws' second argument: they are like parents. In Greek thought, a child owes parents a debt he can never repay. 'Slave' here is Jowett's word for one who owes service; modern readers find it the hardest part of the speech.

commentary.on: either to be persuaded, or if not persuaded, to be obeyed
commentary.text: The key phrase: 'persuade or obey'. The Laws do not demand silent obedience. A citizen may argue, petition, plead in court. If he fails to persuade, he must obey. Scholars have argued for two thousand years about how this fits with Socrates' defiance in the Apology.

commentary.on: he who has experience of the manner in which we order justice and administer the state, and still remains, has entered into an implied contract that he will do as we command him
commentary.text: The third argument: agreement. By choosing to stay in Athens as an adult, when he was free to leave, Socrates agreed to its laws. This is the first known form of what later philosophers called tacit consent, the root of social contract theory.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
parts.when: Athens; the conversation is set in the prison, two or three days before Socrates' death in 399 BC
parts.title: Seventy years, and the voice
parts.context: The Laws press their case home, and Socrates gives Crito his answer. Lacedaemon is Sparta. 'The princes of the world below' are the judges of the dead in Greek religion.
parts.plain: The Laws say: you had seventy years to leave, and you hardly ever left the city; you could have asked for exile at your trial and you chose death. Now you would run away like a slave, in disguise, and make yourself ridiculous. Put justice first, not life or children. You go now as a victim of men, not of the laws; if you return evil for evil, our brothers the laws of the underworld will receive you as an enemy. Socrates says: Crito, this is the voice I hear, like flutes in the ears of worshippers. Let me follow where God leads.

commentary.on: after you have had seventy years to think of them
commentary.text: This is what makes the agreement argument strong in Socrates' case. He was not a young man with no choice. He had a lifetime, and he chose Athens, even praising Sparta and Crete without moving there.

commentary.on: Think not of life and children first, and of justice afterwards, but of justice first
commentary.text: This answers Crito's appeal to the children. Socrates' friends will care for them. A father who escaped would teach his sons that justice gives way when life is at stake.

commentary.on: a victim, not of the laws, but of men
commentary.text: A precise and important distinction. The Laws are just; the men who applied them in his case were not. If he stays, he dies wronged. If he runs, he becomes a wrongdoer.

commentary.on: like the sound of the flute in the ears of the mystic
commentary.text: The 'mystic' is someone being initiated into a sacred rite, where music filled the ears. The argument has become, for Socrates, a kind of call that drowns out every other voice.

commentary.on: Leave me then, Crito, to fulfil the will of God, and to follow whither he leads.
commentary.text: The last words of the dialogue. Socrates ends, as in the Apology, with God. For him, obeying the Laws here and obeying God are the same act.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil
read.when: Athens; the conversation is set in the prison, two or three days before Socrates' death in 399 BC

paras: Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God.
Therefore he who resists the authority withstands the ordinance of God; and those who withstand will receive to themselves judgment.
For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Do you desire to have no fear of the authority? Do that which is good, and you will have praise from the authority,
for he is a servant of God to you for good. But if you do that which is evil, be afraid, for he doesn’t bear the sword in vain; for he is a servant of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil.
Therefore you need to be in subjection, not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake.
For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are servants of God’s service, continually doing this very thing.
Therefore give everyone what you owe: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honor, then honor.

parts.title: Be in subjection
parts.context: Paul's letter to the Romans is his longest and most systematic. Just before this passage he has told them 'Repay no one evil for evil' and 'overcome evil with good' (12:17, 21); if you have taken First Christians, you read that chapter there. The emperor was Nero, though his persecution of Christians was still some years off.

commentary.on: for there is no authority except from God
commentary.text: Paul's reason for obedience is not a contract or a debt to one's parents, as in the Crito, but God's appointment. Government, even a pagan one, exists by God's will to restrain evil.

commentary.on: For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil.
commentary.text: Paul describes government as it is meant to be. Christians have argued ever since about what follows when it is not: when rulers become a terror to the good, as Rome later was to Paul.

commentary.on: not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake
commentary.text: Like Socrates, Paul makes obedience a matter of conscience, not just fear of punishment. Both reject the view that you may break any law you can get away with.

commentary.on: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honor, then honor.
commentary.text: Paul's obedience is concrete and limited: pay what you owe. It does not say to obey a command to sin; elsewhere the apostles refuse exactly that (Acts 5:29). Socrates also obeyed the Laws only where obeying did no wrong: he would accept death, but not stop doing what God commanded.

compare.why: About AD 57, Paul wrote to the Christians in Rome, the capital of an empire that would later put him to death. Read his reasons for obeying the state beside the Laws of Athens.
compare.title: The governing authorities

sections.h: The puzzle: the Apology and the Crito
paras: Readers have long noticed a tension. In the Apology, Socrates says that if the city ordered him to stop philosophising, he would disobey: 'I shall obey God rather than you.' In the Crito, the Laws say a citizen must 'persuade or obey'. Is Socrates a rebel or a loyalist?

The best-known answers say the two are consistent. First, the cases differ. In the Apology, the hypothetical order would require him to do wrong: to abandon the mission God gave him. In the Crito, obeying requires him only to suffer wrong: to accept an unjust death. Socrates' rule is never to do wrong; it is not never to suffer it. Second, even in the Apology Socrates does not hide or flee; he disobeys openly, in court, and accepts the penalty. Richard Kraut's influential study Socrates and the State (1984) argues that 'persuade or obey' leaves room for this: a citizen may refuse an unjust command if he openly tries to persuade the city and accepts what follows.
sections.key: Socrates would refuse to do wrong at the city's command, but would suffer wrong rather than escape; his disobedience was open and accepted its penalty.

sections.h: Three arguments for obeying the law
paras: The Laws give three kinds of reason, which philosophers still use. The first is from consequences: if individuals can set aside court verdicts when they think them unjust, law collapses. The second is from gratitude, or the debt to one's 'parents': the city gave you birth, nurture and education. The third is from agreement: by staying when you could leave, you have agreed to obey or persuade.

Each has critics. The first proves too much: one escape would not destroy Athens. The second makes the citizen too much like a child or slave, and modern readers dislike it most. The third has had the longest career. John Locke, in his Second Treatise of Government (1689), argued that anyone who enjoys a country's protection gives 'tacit consent' to its laws (§119). David Hume replied in his essay 'Of the Original Contract' (1748) that a poor peasant who knows no foreign language and lives on daily wages cannot really leave, so his staying is no more consent than a man carried aboard a ship asleep consents to the captain. Socrates, rich in years if not in money, and free to go to Sparta or Crete, is the strongest possible case for the argument.

rows: A city cannot survive if verdicts are ignored
One disobedience does not destroy a state
The laws are your parents and educators
Citizens are not children; benefits do not create unlimited debts
You stayed for seventy years when free to leave
Locke's tacit consent; the social contract
Hume: most people cannot really leave

sections.key: The Laws argue from consequences, gratitude and agreement; the agreement argument became the social contract, and Hume asked whether staying is really consent.

paras: Underneath the speech of the Laws is the principle Socrates sets first: never do wrong, not even in return. Greek morality, from Homer onwards, praised the man who helped friends and harmed enemies. Socrates breaks with it completely. Whatever the city has done to him, he may not harm it in return.

Christians noticed. Jesus told his followers to love their enemies and turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38–44); Paul, 'Repay no one evil for evil' (Romans 12:17). The Crito was read in the early Church as a pagan witness to the same truth. There is a difference worth seeing. Socrates' reason is the good of his own soul: doing wrong harms the doer. The Christian reason adds love for the enemy, who is also God's child, and trust that God, not we, will judge: 'Vengeance belongs to me' (Romans 12:19).
sections.key: Socrates broke with 'harm your enemies': never return wrong for wrong. Christians saw in it an echo of Jesus' teaching, while giving it a further reason, love.

paras: Paul and Plato's Laws agree that citizens owe obedience for conscience's sake. They differ on why. For the Laws of Athens, the city is a kind of parent, and the citizen has agreed. For Paul, all authority comes from God and is accountable to him. That gives Paul's obedience a ceiling: the state is God's servant, not God. When the apostles were ordered to stop preaching, they refused (Acts 5:29), as Socrates refused to stop philosophising.

Romans 13 has been used, in Christian history, to demand obedience to tyrants, and resisted for the same reason. John Calvin, for example, taught that God's command comes first and that lesser magistrates may restrain a tyrant (Institutes IV.20.31–32); many since have argued that a ruler who becomes 'a terror to the good' has stepped outside the authority Paul describes. The Crito and Romans 13 together frame a question every citizen faces: when does the duty to obey end?
sections.key: The Laws ground obedience in birth and agreement; Paul grounds it in God, which both strengthens it and limits it.

paras: Later thinkers took from Socrates a model of how to disobey. Henry David Thoreau went to jail in 1846 rather than pay a tax that supported slavery and war, and wrote 'Civil Disobedience' (1849). The essay's most famous line says that under a government that imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison. Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. developed the idea: break an unjust law openly, non-violently, and accept the penalty, so as to persuade the community that it is wrong. King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (1963) names Socrates as an example; you will meet him again in Hall VII of the cathedral.

Notice how this model combines the Apology and the Crito. It disobeys, like the Apology, but it does not flee, like the Crito. It respects law in general while refusing one unjust law. Some scholars think this reads modern ideas back into Socrates, who never campaigned to change a law. But it shows how fruitful his choice in prison has been.
sections.key: Thoreau, Gandhi and King disobeyed openly and accepted the penalty, combining Socrates' defiance in the Apology with his refusal to flee in the Crito.

paras: Plato wants us to see the Crito as an argument. But other motives may have been present. Socrates was seventy; Xenophon says he thought it a good time to die. An escape would have proved his accusers right: that philosophy makes men despise the law. It would have meant life in Thessaly, where, the Laws say, there is 'great disorder and licence', as a fugitive and a figure of fun. And his death, as he surely knew, would make his life's argument unanswerable in a way that no speech could.

None of this makes his reasons less real. It does remind us that the examined life is lived by whole people, not by arguments alone. Plato himself tells us, in the Phaedo, that Socrates spent his last month composing verses and a hymn to Apollo, in case a recurring dream had been telling him to make music of the ordinary kind (60e–61b): a man still examining himself to the end. What Socrates did in prison was consistent with everything he had said: that the only question is whether an act is just, and that a good man cannot be harmed.
sections.key: Age, the danger of proving his accusers right and the power of a consistent death may also have weighed; his choice was of a piece with his whole life.

debate.question: Was Socrates right not to escape?

positions.name: Yes: he had agreed, and justice forbade it
positions.who: Plato's Laws; Richard Kraut; many classical and Christian readers
positions.view: Socrates had freely accepted Athens' laws for seventy years and had his chance to persuade the court. To escape would be to wrong the city in return for wrong. His death taught more than any escape could.
positions.evidence: The 'persuade or obey' principle; his refusal of exile at the trial; the principle of never returning wrong for wrong.

positions.name: No: an unjust verdict does not bind
positions.who: Crito in the dialogue; A. D. Woozley; many modern philosophers
positions.view: The Laws' arguments are weaker than they look. One escape would not destroy Athens; citizens are not the city's children or slaves; staying is not consent. An innocent man may avoid an unjust death, and he had duties to his sons.
positions.evidence: Crito's arguments (45c–46a); Hume's critique of tacit consent; the Laws' own admission that he was a victim 'of men'.

positions.name: Right for him, not a rule for all
positions.who: Many readers since Thoreau and King
positions.view: Socrates' choice fits his unique position: a seventy-year-old who had chosen Athens, argued his case in full, and whose whole mission would be discredited by flight. It shows how to disobey with integrity, openly and accepting the penalty, rather than a duty to obey every verdict.
positions.evidence: The Apology's defiance and the Crito's obedience together; the later tradition of civil disobedience.

debate.agree: All agree that Socrates acted consistently with his principles, and that the Crito raises the question every citizen must answer: when, if ever, may I break the law?

look.why: The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of Socrates in prison.

music.why: Olivier Messiaen composed this quartet as a prisoner of war in Stalag VIII-A in 1940–41, and first performed it there, in the cold, to fellow prisoners and guards. It is music written in captivity that refuses to be captive: listen for the long, slow cello song, 'Praise to the eternity of Jesus'.

think.why: Socrates could stay calm in prison because he had practised his principles all his life. Do the habits we keep shape who we become?

learn.why: The principle Socrates set before every other argument in the prison: never return wrong for wrong.

check.q: What is the first principle Socrates insists on before discussing the escape?
options: That death is the greatest evil
That a man must care for his children first
That the many are always wrong
That it is never right to do wrong, even in return for a wrong
check.why: 'Neither injury nor retaliation nor warding off evil by evil is ever right' (49c–d). Everything else follows.

check.q: Which of the Laws' arguments is about consent?
options: A city cannot survive if verdicts are ignored
You stayed seventy years when free to leave, and so agreed to persuade or obey
We gave you birth and education
The laws of the underworld will receive you as an enemy
check.why: This is the 'implied contract': tacit consent by remaining.

check.q: How can Socrates defy the city in the Apology and obey it in the Crito?
options: He only obeyed because the guards were watching
The Apology is by Xenophon, not Plato
He refuses to do wrong at the city's command, but will suffer wrong; and his defiance is open, accepting the penalty
He changed his mind in prison
check.why: Doing wrong and suffering wrong are different; open disobedience that accepts the penalty is consistent with 'persuade or obey'.

check.q: What is Hume's objection to the argument from consent?
options: Consent is always written
Socrates had never lived in Athens
Governments never benefit their citizens
Most people cannot realistically leave their country, so staying is not true consent
check.why: Hume's peasant, like a man carried aboard ship asleep, has no real choice.

check.q: How do Paul's reasons for obedience in Romans 13 differ from the Laws' in the Crito?
options: Paul says Christians need not pay taxes
Paul says the state is a parent
There is no difference
Paul grounds authority in God's appointment, which also sets it a limit; the Laws ground it in birth, education and agreement
check.why: 'There is no authority except from God': a stronger and a more limited claim than the Laws'.

check.q: The phrase 'a victim, not of the laws, but of men' means:
options: The Thirty Tyrants condemned him
Socrates was not really condemned
The laws themselves are good; the men who applied them unjustly are to blame, and escaping would make him a wrongdoer against the laws
The laws of Athens were unjust
check.why: If he stays, he is wronged by men; if he flees, he wrongs the laws.

tutorial.question: Should Socrates have escaped?
tutorial.approach: Give Crito's case first, at full strength. Then set out the Laws' three arguments and Socrates' principle of not returning wrong for wrong. Test each argument (Hume on consent; the parent analogy). Address the Apology–Crito tension. Bring in Romans 13 or the later tradition of civil disobedience, and give your verdict.
strong: States Crito's arguments fairly.
Identifies the three arguments of the Laws.
Explains 'persuade or obey' and the principle of not returning wrong.
Uses at least one serious objection (Hume, or the parent analogy).
Resolves or honestly leaves open the tension with the Apology.
Reaches a clear, argued verdict.

reading.why: Fifteen pages; read it aloud with a friend taking Crito's part.

reading.title: Socrates and the State
