sessions.practice: Live it this week: Socrates would not return wrong for wrong. The next time someone wrongs you this week, even in a small way, refuse to pay it back: no cutting remark, no cold shoulder. If something needs to be said, say it openly and calmly, once.
sessions.reflect: What do you owe to the country, family or community that raised you? Is there anything they could ask of you that you would refuse?
takeaways: Offered escape by Crito, Socrates asked only whether it would be just, beginning from the principle that one must never return wrong for wrong.
The Laws argued from consequences, from their care for him as parents, and from his seventy years' agreement: persuade or obey.
His open defiance in court and his refusal to flee together became a model for later civil disobedience; Paul grounds obedience in God, which also limits it.

sessions.title: The case against: was Socrates a danger?
sessions.line: Athens had its reasons. This session gives the prosecution the floor: the comic poet, the accuser, the historians and a philosopher who thought Socrates was a disease.
sessions.plain: So far we have heard Socrates' side, told by his friends. But five hundred ordinary Athenians found him guilty, and they were not all fools or villains. His companions had included a traitor and a tyrant. He mocked the democracy and its choice of officials by lot. His questions dissolved the beliefs that held the city together and, critics say, put nothing in their place. This session states the case against Socrates as strongly as its best advocates have made it, from Aristophanes and the ancient prosecutor to the journalist I. F. Stone and the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche. Only then do we ask what can be said in reply.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 to 5 followed the trial through Socrates' own words: his mission, his method, his defence and his refusal to escape. Every one of those texts was written by an admirer. A fair verdict needs the other side, and now we have the tools to weigh it.
answers: Why was Socrates really put to death?
What did Socrates have to do with Alcibiades and Critias?
Was Socrates against democracy?
What did Nietzsche have against Socrates?
sessions.finding: Athens had real reasons: his companions included the traitor Alcibiades and the tyrant Critias, he scorned democratic equality, and his questioning dissolved the city's beliefs without replacing them; the charge deserves a hearing, though it does not justify his death.

paras: We have followed Socrates through his trial and into prison. His friends' accounts show a man of integrity: obedient to a divine mission, poor, brave, unwilling to do wrong even to save his life. That picture has shaped the West. But it comes almost entirely from Plato and Xenophon, both devoted followers writing to clear his name.

The prosecution's speeches are lost. What we know of their case comes from hints in the defence, from a pamphlet called The Accusation of Socrates written a few years after the trial by a teacher of rhetoric named Polycrates (also lost, but answered by Xenophon), and from what later Athenians said. Historians have reconstructed it carefully. Here it is.
background.key: Our sources are Socrates' admirers; the prosecution's case must be pieced together from hints, from Polycrates' lost pamphlet and from Xenophon's reply to it.

paras: Alcibiades (about 450–404 BC) was the most brilliant young man of his generation: rich, beautiful, a ward of Pericles, and Socrates' close companion, who served beside him at Potidaea. In 415 BC he persuaded Athens to send a vast expedition to conquer Sicily. Accused of mocking the sacred Mysteries, he fled to Sparta and advised it how to beat Athens. He switched sides twice more. The Sicilian disaster cost Athens perhaps forty thousand men.

Critias (about 460–403 BC), a poet, thinker and relative of Plato, was another of Socrates' companions. In 404 BC he became the leader of the Thirty Tyrants, who executed about 1,500 Athenians, seized property and disarmed the citizens. He was killed fighting the democrats in 403 BC. Charmides, Plato's uncle and another companion of Socrates, died with him. To many Athenians at the trial, these were the young men Socrates had 'corrupted'.

timeline.text: Alcibiades leads the Sicilian expedition; accused of impiety, he defects to Sparta
The Sicilian expedition destroyed
A first oligarchic coup, the Four Hundred, briefly overthrows the democracy
Critias leads the Thirty Tyrants
The last oligarchs, at Eleusis, are crushed
Trial of Socrates
Polycrates' pamphlet, The Accusation of Socrates

background.key: Alcibiades betrayed Athens to Sparta; Critias led the Thirty Tyrants. Both had been Socrates' companions, and many jurors had suffered from them.

paras: The main reading has two parts. First, the end of Aristophanes' The Clouds: the old farmer, ruined by what Socrates' school taught his son, burns the 'thinking-shop' down. It shows what many Athenians feared from Socrates a generation before the trial. Second, two charges from 'the accuser', almost certainly Polycrates, as Xenophon reports them: that Socrates taught the young to despise the laws, and that he was the teacher of Critias and Alcibiades.

The comparison is from John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859), the most famous modern defence of free speech. Mill grants something important to the prosecution: the jurors were very likely honest men doing what they thought right. That is exactly why the case is so troubling.
background.key: The burning of the thinking-shop in The Clouds, the accuser's charges in Xenophon, and Mill on the honesty of Socrates' judges.

before: In The Clouds, what has the son learned at Socrates' school, and what does it lead him to do?
What two charges does 'the accuser' bring in Xenophon? How strong are they?
Mill says the jurors 'honestly found him guilty'. If so, what went wrong?
sessions.readWhy: The prosecution's case in the oldest words we have: the comic poet's warning and the accuser's charges.

paras: Strep. Ah me! it is severe, O Clouds! But it is just; for I ought not to have withheld the money which I borrowed. Now, therefore, come with me, my dearest son, that you may destroy the blackguard Chaerephon and Socrates, who deceived you and me.
Phid. I will not injure my teachers.
Strep. Yes, yes, reverence Paternal Jove.
Phid. "Paternal Jove" quoth'a! How antiquated you are! Why, is there any Jove?
Strep. There is.
Phid. There is not, no; for Vortex reigns having expelled Jupiter.
Strep. He has not expelled him; but I fancied this, on account of this Vortex here. Ah me, unhappy man! When I even took you who are of earthenware for a god.
Phid. Here rave and babble to yourself.
[Exit Phidippides]

Strep. Ah me, what madness! How mad, then, I was when I ejected the gods on account of Socrates! But O dear Hermes, by no means be wroth with me, nor destroy me; but pardon me, since I have gone crazy through prating. And become my adviser, whether I shall bring an action and prosecute them, or whatever you think. You advise me rightly, not permitting me to get up a lawsuit, but as soon as possible to set fire to the house of the prating fellows. Come hither, come hither, Xanthias! Come forth with a ladder and with a mattock and then mount upon the thinking-shop and dig down the roof, if you love your master, until you tumble the house upon them.
[Xanthias mounts upon the roof]
But let some one bring me a lighted torch and I'll make some of them this day suffer punishment, even if they be ever so much impostors.
1st Dis. (from within) Hollo! Hollo!
Strep. It is your business, O torch, to send forth abundant flame.
[Mounts upon the roof]
1st Dis. What are you doing, fellow?
Strep. What am I doing? Why, what else, than chopping logic with the beams of your house?
[Sets the house on fire]
2nd Dis. (from within) You will destroy us! You will destroy us!
Strep. For I also wish this very thing; unless my mattock deceive my hopes, or I should somehow fall first and break my neck.
Soc. (from within). Hollo you! What are you doing, pray, you fellow on the roof?
Strep. I am walking on air, and speculating about the sun.
Soc. Ah me, unhappy! I shall be suffocated, wretched man!
Chaer. And I, miserable man, shall be burnt to death!

Strep. For what has come into your heads that you acted insolently toward the gods, and pried into the seat of the moon? Chase, pelt, smite them, for many reasons, but especially because you know that they offended against the gods!

But, says the accuser, by all that's sacred! did not Socrates cause his associates to despise the established laws when he dwelt on the folly of appointing state officers by ballot? a principle which, he said, no one would care to apply in selecting a pilot or a flute-player or in any similar case, where a mistake would be far less disastrous than in matters political. Words like these, according to the accuser, tended to incite the young to contemn the established constitution, rendering them violent and headstrong. But for myself I think that those who cultivate wisdom and believe themselves able to instruct their fellow-citizens as to their interests are least likely to become partisans of violence. They are too well aware that to violence attach enmities and dangers, whereas results as good may be obtained by persuasion safely and amicably. For the victim of violence hates with vindictiveness as one from whom something precious has been stolen, while the willing subject of persuasion is ready to kiss the hand which has done him a service. Hence compulsion is not the method of him who makes wisdom his study, but of him who wields power untempered by reflection. Once more: the man who ventures on violence needs the support of many to fight his battles, while he whose strength lies in persuasiveness triumphs single-handed, for he is conscious of a cunning to compel consent unaided. And what has such a one to do with the spilling of blood? since how ridiculous it were to do men to death rather than turn to account the trusty service of the living.

But, the accuser answers, the two men who wrought the greatest evils to the state at any time--to wit, Critias and Alcibiades--were both companions of Socrates--Critias the oligarch, and Alcibiades the democrat. Where would you find a more arrant thief, savage, and murderer than the one? where such a portent of insolence, incontinence, and high-handedness as the other? For my part, in so far as these two wrought evil to the state, I have no desire to appear as the apologist of either. I confine myself to explaining what this intimacy of theirs with Socrates really was.

parts.author: Aristophanes
parts.who: Aristophanes (about 446–386 BC), the great comic poet of Athens; then Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), reporting the prosecution's case
parts.when: Athens, 423 BC (revised about 418–416 BC); Xenophon writing in the 380s–370s BC
parts.title: The thinking-shop burns
parts.context: The end of the play. The farmer Strepsiades sent his son Phidippides to Socrates' school to learn the argument that wins bad cases, to cheat his creditors. The son learned it too well: he has just beaten his father, and proved by argument that a son may beat his father, and his mother too. The Chorus of Clouds, whom Socrates worshipped as new gods, now reveal that they lead the wicked on to ruin so that they learn to fear the gods. 'Vortex' is the swirling force some natural philosophers said ruled the universe; Strepsiades has a cup, a 'vortex' in Greek, in front of his house. Hermes was the god whose statues stood at Athenian doors. Hickie, 1853, writes 'Jove' and 'Jupiter' for Zeus.
parts.plain: The father admits he was wrong to cheat his creditors and calls his son to take revenge on Socrates. The son refuses: there is no Zeus any more, only Vortex. The father, ashamed that he threw away the gods for Socrates, asks the god Hermes for advice and decides not to sue but to burn the school. He climbs on the roof with a torch. Socrates, inside, cries out that he is choking. The father mocks him with his own words, 'I am walking on air', and shouts that they insulted the gods.

commentary.on: Phid. I will not injure my teachers.
commentary.text: The son has learned loyalty to his teachers and contempt for his father. For the audience this was the nightmare: a clever education that turns the young against the family and the gods.

commentary.on: There is not, no; for Vortex reigns having expelled Jupiter.
commentary.text: The joke is on natural philosophy, which explained thunder and rain by physical forces instead of Zeus. Socrates was lumped with these thinkers, wrongly, as he insisted in court. But the fear was real: if the gods are explained away, what holds people to their oaths?

commentary.on: How mad, then, I was when I ejected the gods on account of Socrates!
commentary.text: The play's verdict, in the mouth of a foolish old man who has learned his lesson. Some twenty-four years later, a jury of men like him would decide Socrates' fate.

commentary.on: You advise me rightly, not permitting me to get up a lawsuit, but as soon as possible to set fire to the house
commentary.text: A comic ending of mob justice. Modern readers find it chilling. Aristophanes cannot have meant it as a call to violence; but in Plato's Apology Socrates blames the comedy for the prejudice that killed him.

commentary.on: I am walking on air, and speculating about the sun.
commentary.text: The farmer repeats Socrates' own first words in the play, now from the burning roof. The circle closes: the man who looked down on the gods is brought down.

commentary.on: For what has come into your heads that you acted insolently toward the gods, and pried into the seat of the moon?
commentary.text: The last charge of the play is impiety: insolence to the gods. It is, almost exactly, the charge of 399 BC.

parts.author: Xenophon
parts.title: The accuser's charges
parts.context: In the second chapter of his Memorabilia, Xenophon quotes and answers the charges of 'the accuser'. Most scholars think this is Polycrates, whose Accusation of Socrates appeared about 393 BC, six years after the trial, and probably drew on what was said in court. Choosing officials 'by ballot' means by lot: most Athenian officials were picked at random from volunteers, a central democratic practice. Read the charges first; Xenophon's replies follow each one, and the lecture weighs them.
parts.plain: The accuser says: Socrates taught his followers to despise the laws, by mocking the choice of officials by lot; nobody would choose a ship's pilot or a flute-player that way. That made the young violent and contemptuous of the constitution. And the two men who did Athens the greatest harm, Critias the oligarch and Alcibiades the democrat, were both his companions. Xenophon replies that wise men use persuasion, not violence, and that he will explain what the two men's friendship with Socrates really was.

commentary.on: did not Socrates cause his associates to despise the established laws when he dwelt on the folly of appointing state officers by ballot?
commentary.text: This charge is about democracy itself. Choosing by lot expressed the democratic belief that any citizen was fit to serve. Socrates thought ruling was a skill, like steering a ship, which needs knowledge. To democrats this was not a neutral opinion; it was the argument the oligarchs had used to justify their coups.

commentary.on: Words like these, according to the accuser, tended to incite the young to contemn the established constitution, rendering them violent and headstrong.
commentary.text: The heart of 'corrupting the young'. The accuser does not say Socrates taught violence. He says Socrates taught contempt for democratic equality, and that contempt in clever, rich young men turned violent.

commentary.on: But for myself I think that those who cultivate wisdom and believe themselves able to instruct their fellow-citizens as to their interests are least likely to become partisans of violence.
commentary.text: Here Xenophon's reply begins. Hold it for now: the point of this session is to hear the charge first.

commentary.on: the two men who wrought the greatest evils to the state at any time--to wit, Critias and Alcibiades--were both companions of Socrates
commentary.text: The strongest single point for the prosecution. Critias, 'the oligarch', led a reign of terror; Alcibiades, 'the democrat', betrayed the city in war. One from each side: Socrates' influence seemed dangerous whatever party a young man belonged to.

commentary.on: Where would you find a more arrant thief, savage, and murderer than the one?
commentary.text: Xenophon does not defend them at all. He concedes the facts and contests only their connection with Socrates.

read.author: Aristophanes and Xenophon
read.who: Aristophanes (about 446–386 BC), the great comic poet of Athens; then Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), reporting the prosecution's case
read.when: Athens, 423 BC (revised about 418–416 BC); Xenophon writing in the 380s–370s BC

paras: Mankind can hardly be too often reminded that there was once a man named Socrates, between whom and the legal authorities and public opinion of his time, there took place a memorable collision. Born in an age and country abounding in individual greatness, this man has been handed down to us by those who best knew both him and the age, as the most virtuous man in it; while we know him as the head and prototype of all subsequent teachers of virtue, the source equally of the lofty inspiration of Plato and the judicious utilitarianism of Aristotle, "i maëstri di color che sanno," the two headsprings of ethical as of all other philosophy. This acknowledged master of all the eminent thinkers who have since lived--whose fame, still growing after more than two thousand years, all but outweighs the whole remainder of the names which make his native city illustrious--was put to death by his countrymen, after a judicial conviction, for impiety and immorality. Impiety, in denying the gods recognised by the State; indeed his accuser asserted (see the "Apologia") that he believed in no gods at all. Immorality, in being, by his doctrines and instructions, a "corruptor of youth." Of these charges the tribunal, there is every ground for believing, honestly found him guilty, and condemned the man who probably of all then born had deserved best of mankind, to be put to death as a criminal.

To pass from this to the only other instance of judicial iniquity, the mention of which, after the condemnation of Socrates, would not be an anticlimax: the event which took place on Calvary rather more than eighteen hundred years ago. The man who left on the memory of those who witnessed his life and conversation, such an impression of his moral grandeur, that eighteen subsequent centuries have done homage to him as the Almighty in person, was ignominiously put to death, as what? As a blasphemer. Men did not merely mistake their benefactor; they mistook him for the exact contrary of what he was, and treated him as that prodigy of impiety, which they themselves are now held to be, for their treatment of him. The feelings with which mankind now regard these lamentable transactions, especially the later of the two, render them extremely unjust in their judgment of the unhappy actors. These were, to all appearance, not bad men--not worse than men commonly are, but rather the contrary;

men who possessed in a full, or somewhat more than a full measure, the religious, moral, and patriotic feelings of their time and people: the very kind of men who, in all times, our own included, have every chance of passing through life blameless and respected. The high-priest who rent his garments when the words were pronounced, which, according to all the ideas of his country, constituted the blackest guilt, was in all probability quite as sincere in his horror and indignation, as the generality of respectable and pious men now are in the religious and moral sentiments they profess; and most of those who now shudder at his conduct, if they had lived in his time, and been born Jews, would have acted precisely as he did. Orthodox Christians who are tempted to think that those who stoned to death the first martyrs must have been worse men than they themselves are, ought to remember that one of those persecutors was Saint Paul.

parts.author: John Stuart Mill
parts.title: A memorable collision
parts.context: Mill is arguing that no society should silence an opinion because it is sure the opinion is false and harmful, since history shows how wrong such certainty can be. He chooses the most famous examples he can. 'I maestri di color che sanno', 'the masters of those who know', is Dante's description of Aristotle; Mill applies it to Plato and Aristotle together. 'Cotemporaries' is an old spelling. Gutenberg's marks for italics have been removed.
parts.plain: Mill says: remember that Athens put to death, after a fair trial, the man who was the best of them all and the teacher of all later philosophy, for impiety and immorality. The jurors very probably believed honestly that he was guilty. The same is true of those who condemned Jesus as a blasphemer: they were not bad men, but ordinary, respectable, religious, patriotic people of their time, the kind we would think blameless today. That is the point. Good people, sure they are right, can do the greatest wrong.

commentary.on: there took place a memorable collision
commentary.text: Mill's word is well chosen: a collision is not a crime by one side. Two forces met: the city's settled beliefs, and a man who questioned them.

commentary.on: Of these charges the tribunal, there is every ground for believing, honestly found him guilty
commentary.text: This is Mill's great concession, and it strengthens the case against Socrates as a case: the jury was not corrupt. By the standards of Athens, he really was impious and a danger to the young.

commentary.on: These were, to all appearance, not bad men--not worse than men commonly are, but rather the contrary
commentary.text: Mill turns from Socrates to Jesus. His point is uncomfortable for every age: the people who condemned the best men were respectable and sincere, and we would very likely have done the same.

commentary.on: one of those persecutors was Saint Paul
commentary.text: Paul, whose words you have read beside Socrates in this journey, began as a persecutor of Christians, 'in all good conscience' as he said later (Acts 23:1). Mill's moral: sincerity is no guarantee of being right, so we should never silence dissent merely because we are sure.

compare.author: John Stuart Mill
compare.why: John Stuart Mill was the great English liberal philosopher of the nineteenth century. In On Liberty (1859) he begins his case for free speech with the trial of Socrates, and then the trial of Jesus. Read how much he concedes to the prosecution.
compare.title: Honest judges

paras: Put the case against Socrates as the prosecution might have, in its strongest form. First, his companions. Alcibiades betrayed Athens; Critias and Charmides led the Thirty, who killed about 1,500 citizens. A teacher who spent years with such men cannot simply wash his hands of them. Fifty years later Athenians still remembered the trial this way: the orator Aeschines told a jury, 'you put to death Socrates the sophist, because he was shown to have educated Critias' (Against Timarchus 173).

Second, his politics. Socrates mocked the lot and the Assembly; he held that ruling, like medicine, belongs to experts; he admired Sparta and Crete, the very cities the oligarchs held up as models. Third, his religion. He spoke of a private divine voice that overruled the city's customs, and claimed God's authority for his questioning. Fourth, his effect. He took the city's shared beliefs about justice, piety and courage, showed they did not hold together, and offered no replacement but more questions. In a city that had just survived defeat, terror and civil war, that was not a harmless hobby.
sections.key: The prosecution's case: his companions (Alcibiades, Critias), his contempt for democracy, his private religion, and questioning that dissolved shared beliefs.

sections.h: I. F. Stone: the political trial
paras: In 1988 the American radical journalist I. F. Stone, a lifelong champion of free speech, published The Trial of Socrates, after teaching himself ancient Greek in his seventies to write it. His aim was not to defend the verdict but to understand it. His case, in summary, is this.

Socrates was, in Stone's view, a consistent enemy of democracy: he taught that the many are ignorant and that the city should be ruled by 'the one who knows'. Athens had suffered three oligarchic seizures of power in twelve years, in 411, 404 and, in a last attempt from Eleusis, 401 BC. The jurors had every reason to fear a man whose teaching had formed the leaders of the second. Yet Stone also argues that Socrates could have won. Athens prided itself on free speech, parrhēsia; had Socrates appealed to it, he might have been acquitted. Instead, in Stone's reading, he provoked the jury, as if he wanted to die and to shame the democracy. Stone concludes that Athens betrayed its own principles, but that Socrates helped it to.
sections.key: I. F. Stone (1988) argued that Socrates was an enemy of democracy feared after three oligarchic coups, who could have appealed to free speech but provoked the jury instead.

paras: The German philosopher G. W. F. Hegel (1770–1831), in his Lectures on the History of Philosophy, gave the most profound version of the objection. He called Socrates' fate truly tragic, in the sense of Greek tragedy: not good against evil, but right against right.

On one side stood the ethical life of the Greek city: its customs, gods and laws, which people lived by without needing to justify them. On the other stood a new principle, which Socrates introduced: that the individual must test everything by his own reason and conscience, and accept only what survives the test. Socrates' inner voice, Hegel says, was the first form of this principle. Athens was right that the principle would destroy the old city; it did. Socrates was right that the principle was true and must come. The Athenians condemned him justly by their own law, and then repented, because they recognised that the principle was already in them. Hegel thought the modern world was born from this collision.
sections.key: Hegel saw a tragedy of two rights: the city's inherited ethical life against the individual's right to test everything by reason; both were justified.

paras: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) brought a different, deeper charge. In The Birth of Tragedy (1872) he blamed Socrates for killing the spirit of Greek tragedy, with its acceptance of life's dark and irrational depths, and replacing it with 'theoretical man', who believes reason can understand and even correct everything.

In 'The Problem of Socrates', in Twilight of the Idols (1889), he went further. Socrates, he says, was a sign of decline. His famous ugliness and low birth, his irony and his endless arguments were the weapons of a man who had no other way to win: dialectic as revenge on the noble and the strong. He made reason a tyrant over the instincts, as if a healthy person needed reasons for everything. And his last words, asking for a cock to be offered to Asclepius, the god of healing, show what he really thought: that life is a long illness, and death the cure. Socrates wanted to die, Nietzsche says; Athens only gave him what he asked. On this view Socrates did not corrupt the young; he corrupted life itself, and Christianity, 'Platonism for the people', spread the disease.
sections.key: Nietzsche charged Socrates with making reason a tyrant over instinct and treating life as an illness, a decline Christianity later spread.

sections.h: What can be said in reply
paras: The replies begin with the facts. Critias turned against Socrates: Xenophon says the Thirty forbade him to teach the young, and Plato that Socrates refused their order to arrest Leon of Salamis. Alcibiades' own speech in Plato's Symposium shows a man who admired Socrates and failed to follow him. A teacher is not responsible for every pupil, as Xenophon argues; and Socrates had democratic friends too, such as Chaerephon. He obeyed the laws of the democracy all his life and died rather than break them.

On politics, scholars such as Gregory Vlastos and Richard Kraut point out that Socrates criticised every regime, defied the democracy at Arginusae and the oligarchy over Leon, and chose to live in democratic Athens. On religion, his piety was real. Against Nietzsche, many answer that Socrates' last words are more naturally read as gratitude, or as care for a small debt, and that his reason was never a tyrant: it served his love of the good. And the deepest reply is Mill's: even if the jurors were sincere, a city that kills its questioners loses the only means it has of correcting its own mistakes.
sections.key: Critias turned on Socrates; he criticised all regimes and obeyed democratic law; his piety was real; Mill: killing questioners destroys a city's means of correcting itself.

paras: Even after the replies, something in the objection stands. Socratic questioning really can dissolve. It can leave clever young people without the beliefs they were raised in and without anything to replace them, proud of their doubts and contemptuous of those who still believe. Plato knew this: in the Republic (VII.537e–539d) he warns that young people who taste argument too early become like puppies, tearing at everything, and end by believing nothing. Many parents and teachers have watched it happen.

So the objection leaves a real question for the verdict: is the examined life enough by itself? Socrates claimed only to know that he did not know. Is that a foundation, or only a clearing of the ground? Hegel thought Athens' faith could not survive it. Nietzsche thought nothing should replace it but a stronger will. The early Christians, as we will see in the last session, gave a third answer.
sections.key: Socratic questioning can dissolve beliefs without replacing them, as Plato himself warned; whether the examined life is enough by itself remains the open question.

debate.question: Was Athens right to fear Socrates?

positions.name: The prosecution: yes
positions.who: Anytus and Polycrates (as reported by Xenophon); I. F. Stone (1988), in part
positions.view: Socrates taught contempt for democratic equality to rich young men, two of whom did Athens enormous harm, and dissolved the city's religious and moral beliefs. After war, terror and three coups, the city was entitled to defend itself, even if the verdict was harsh.
positions.evidence: Critias and Alcibiades; his mockery of the lot; Aeschines' remark; the fear of oligarchic coups in 411, 404 and 401 BC.

positions.name: Plato and Xenophon: no
positions.who: Plato; Xenophon; Gregory Vlastos and most modern scholars
positions.view: Socrates was the best citizen Athens had: brave, law-abiding, just, and critical of every regime. Critias and Alcibiades became bad when they left him. The city killed the conscience it needed.
positions.evidence: Arginusae and Leon of Salamis; the Thirty's ban on his teaching; his obedience to the laws even to death.

positions.name: Nietzsche: yes, but for the wrong reason
positions.who: Friedrich Nietzsche
positions.view: The danger was not to democracy but to life. Socrates replaced the instincts and tragic wisdom of the Greeks with the tyranny of reason, and taught people to treat life as a sickness to be cured. The jury did not understand the real charge.
positions.evidence: The 'problem of Socrates' in Twilight of the Idols; his last words about Asclepius; the decline of tragedy.

debate.agree: All agree that Socrates was not an ordinary citizen, that his questioning changed Athens, and that the trial was about more than the words of the charge.

look.why: The National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of Alcibiades, Critias or a Greek symposium. Paintings of Socrates' companions, such as Jean-Baptiste Regnault's Socrates Dragging Alcibiades from the Embrace of Sensual Pleasure (1791), are in other museums.

music.why: Ralph Vaughan Williams, who called himself an agnostic, spent years editing The English Hymnal (1906), and here takes a hymn tune that Thomas Tallis wrote for the Archbishop of Canterbury's psalter in 1567 and builds from it something vast and new. It is a picture of the other way to treat an inherited tradition: not to dissolve it, but to question it, love it and make it sing again.

think.why: If questioning dissolves inherited morality, what can ground it? The modern form of the objection to Socrates.

check.q: Which was the prosecution's strongest piece of evidence for 'corrupting the young'?
options: Socrates charged high fees
Two of his companions, Critias and Alcibiades, had done Athens great harm
Socrates was poor
Socrates studied the stars
check.why: Xenophon himself concedes their crimes; even he can only argue about their link to Socrates.

check.q: Why would Socrates' criticism of choosing officials by lot sound dangerous to a democratic jury in 399 BC?
options: Because the lot was a religious ritual
Because it echoed the oligarchs' argument that ruling needs experts, used to justify coups in 411 and 404 BC
Because Socrates had lost a lottery
Because the lot was a recent invention
check.why: The argument that the many are unfit to rule was the oligarchs' case, and the city had just survived their terror.

check.q: What does Mill concede to the prosecution?
options: That Socrates' philosophy was false
That the jurors very probably honestly believed him guilty
That Socrates was guilty of treason
That free speech is dangerous
check.why: Mill thinks the tribunal 'honestly found him guilty': which is why sincerity cannot justify silencing anyone.

check.q: Hegel called Socrates' death tragic because:
options: Socrates was innocent and the jury wicked
Tragedy was popular in Athens
It was a collision of two rights: the city's inherited ethical life and the individual's right to test everything by reason
Socrates died young
check.why: For Hegel, both Athens and Socrates were justified: right against right.

check.q: How did Nietzsche read Socrates' last words about a cock for Asclepius?
options: As a joke
As proof he believed in the gods
As a debt Crito forgot to pay
As a sign that he thought life was an illness and death its cure
check.why: Asclepius was the god of healing: Nietzsche took the offering as thanks for being cured of life.

check.q: Which reply best answers the charge that Socrates made Critias a tyrant?
options: Critias was a democrat
Critias, once in power, banned Socrates from teaching and Socrates defied the Thirty's order to arrest Leon
Socrates never met Critias
Critias was never in Athens
check.why: Their later conflict suggests Critias abandoned Socrates' influence rather than followed it.

tutorial.question: 'Why was Socrates executed?' State the case for the prosecution at full strength, then decide how far it succeeds.
tutorial.approach: Begin with the prosecution in its strongest form: Alcibiades and Critias, Socrates' contempt for the lot, his private religion, the dissolving effect of his questioning, and the fear of coups. Use Stone, Hegel and Nietzsche. Then give the replies and judge which parts of the case stand and which fall.
strong: States the prosecution's case without caricature.
Uses the evidence of Alcibiades, Critias and Aeschines accurately.
Explains Stone's political reading, including the amnesty and the coups.
Explains Hegel's 'two rights' and Nietzsche's deeper charge in its own terms.
Gives the replies (the Thirty's ban, Leon, Arginusae, Mill).
Concludes with a clear judgement on what remains of the objection.

reading.author: I. F. Stone
reading.title: The Trial of Socrates
reading.why: The prosecution's case, passionately argued by a lover of free speech.

reading.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
reading.title: Twilight of the Idols
reading.why: Read 'The Problem of Socrates': ten short sections that changed how many moderns see him.

reading.author: Gregory Vlastos
reading.title: 'The Historical Socrates and Athenian Democracy', Political Theory 11
reading.why: The scholarly reply: Socrates as a critic of every regime, not an oligarch.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose one person whose views you think are dangerous. Write down their case as they would put it, so well that they would agree with your summary. Only then write your reply.
sessions.reflect: Have your questions ever dissolved something in someone else, or in you, without putting anything better in its place? What would it take to build as well as to question?
takeaways: The prosecution had real grounds: Alcibiades and Critias, Socrates' contempt for choosing by lot, his private religion, and questioning that dissolved shared beliefs.
Stone read the trial as political; Hegel as a tragic collision of two rights; Nietzsche as a verdict on a man who treated life as a disease.
Replies show Socrates defied the Thirty and obeyed democratic law; but the question whether questioning alone can build a life remains.

sessions.title: Practising death: the verdict
sessions.line: On his last day Socrates tells his friends that philosophy is practice for dying, and drinks the poison. What should we make of him?
sessions.plain: The verdict: Socrates was not guilty of impiety, and Athens was wrong to kill him, though it was not wrong to find him unsettling. His examined life, honest about ignorance, ruled by conscience and caring for the soul above everything, was worth living and worth dying for. But it was not complete in itself, and the early Christians who loved him said so. This session reads his last conversation in Plato's Phaedo, where he calls philosophy 'the practice of dying', and Justin Martyr's comparison of Socrates with Christ, and then draws the journey together.
sessions.why: Session 6 gave the prosecution its full say and left a question standing: is the examined life enough by itself? Now we go to the prison on the last day to see how Socrates answered it with his own death, and to hear how the first Christian philosophers judged him.
answers: How did Socrates face death, and what did he believe about the soul?
What did he mean by calling philosophy 'practice for dying'?
Is Socrates like Jesus?
So: what is the examined life, and is it worth living?
sessions.finding: Socrates said philosophy is practice for dying and the care of the soul the only thing that matters; the Church Fathers called him a Christian before Christ, while noting what he did not have: the whole Word, and a death others would die for.

paras: Here are the findings so far. Socrates questioned Athens for a lifetime; his only wisdom was knowing he did not know (sessions 1 and 2). His method stunned the proud and helped the humble (session 3). Condemned, he would obey God rather than the city (session 4), and he would not escape, because he would not return wrong for wrong (session 5). The prosecution had real reasons, and its deepest question remains: does questioning only dissolve, or can it build a life (session 6)?

If you have taken Death and hope, you have read the end of the Phaedo: the poison, the last words and Phaedo's tribute. Here we read the beginning, which that journey left out: how the day began, and why Socrates was not afraid.
background.key: The case so far: Socrates' wisdom, method, defence and refusal to flee, and the prosecution's question, whether questioning can build a life.

paras: The sacred ship returned from Delos, and the day of execution came. Socrates' friends gathered at dawn outside the prison. Athenian executions were by a cup of poison, prepared from hemlock (Plato only calls it 'the poison'), drunk at sunset. The friends spent the whole day with him, talking about whether the soul survives death. Plato, Phaedo tells us, was ill and not there.

The Phaedo is told some time later by Phaedo of Elis, a young man who had been a slave before Socrates' friends freed him, to a philosopher called Echecrates in the town of Phlius in the Peloponnese. Two young men from Thebes, Simmias and Cebes, do most of the questioning; they had studied with followers of Pythagoras, who believed in the soul's rebirth.

timeline.text: Friends gather; Socrates' chains are removed; Xanthippe is sent home
Why a philosopher should not fear death (our reading)
The arguments for the immortality of the soul; the objections of Simmias and Cebes
Socrates bathes, says farewell to his family, drinks the poison and dies (read in Death and hope)

background.key: Socrates spent his last day talking with friends about the soul; Phaedo, who was there, tells the story to Echecrates.

paras: The main reading is the first part of the Phaedo (57a–69e): the last morning and Socrates' 'defence' of why a philosopher welcomes death. It answers the question left by the last session: what positive vision lay behind his questioning? The answer is the care of the soul, pursued to the end.

The comparison is from Justin Martyr, a philosopher who became a Christian and was beheaded in Rome about AD 165. In his Second Apology, a defence of Christians addressed to the Roman Senate, he compares Christ with Socrates: the first serious Christian verdict on the man this journey has followed.
background.key: The Phaedo's opening (57a–69e), and Justin Martyr's verdict comparing Socrates with Christ.

before: What does Phaedo say he felt, being with Socrates on his last day? Why?
What does Socrates mean by saying that true philosophers are 'always occupied in the practice of dying'?
Justin says Socrates knew Christ 'partially'. What, according to Justin, did he lack?
sessions.readWhy: Socrates' last morning, and his reason for meeting death without fear: philosophy as the practice of dying and the care of the soul.

paras: ECHECRATES: Were you yourself, Phaedo, in the prison with Socrates on the day when he drank the poison?
PHAEDO: Yes, Echecrates, I was.

ECHECRATES: I should so like to hear about his death. What did he say in his last hours? We were informed that he died by taking poison, but no one knew anything more; for no Phliasian ever goes to Athens now, and it is a long time since any stranger from Athens has found his way hither; so that we had no clear account.
PHAEDO: Did you not hear of the proceedings at the trial?

ECHECRATES: Yes; some one told us about the trial, and we could not understand why, having been condemned, he should have been put to death, not at the time, but long afterwards. What was the reason of this?
PHAEDO: An accident, Echecrates: the stern of the ship which the Athenians send to Delos happened to have been crowned on the day before he was tried.
ECHECRATES: What is this ship?

PHAEDO: It is the ship in which, according to Athenian tradition, Theseus went to Crete when he took with him the fourteen youths, and was the saviour of them and of himself. And they were said to have vowed to Apollo at the time, that if they were saved they would send a yearly mission to Delos. Now this custom still continues, and the whole period of the voyage to and from Delos, beginning when the priest of Apollo crowns the stern of the ship, is a holy season, during which the city is not allowed to be polluted by public executions; and when the vessel is detained by contrary winds, the time spent in going and returning is very considerable. As I was saying, the ship was crowned on the day before the trial, and this was the reason why Socrates lay in prison and was not put to death until long after he was condemned.

ECHECRATES: What was the manner of his death, Phaedo? What was said or done? And which of his friends were with him? Or did the authorities forbid them to be present--so that he had no friends near him when he died?
PHAEDO: No; there were several of them with him.
ECHECRATES: If you have nothing to do, I wish that you would tell me what passed, as exactly as you can.
PHAEDO: I have nothing at all to do, and will try to gratify your wish. To be reminded of Socrates is always the greatest delight to me, whether I speak myself or hear another speak of him.
ECHECRATES: You will have listeners who are of the same mind with you, and I hope that you will be as exact as you can.

PHAEDO: I had a singular feeling at being in his company. For I could hardly believe that I was present at the death of a friend, and therefore I did not pity him, Echecrates; he died so fearlessly, and his words and bearing were so noble and gracious, that to me he appeared blessed. I thought that in going to the other world he could not be without a divine call, and that he would be happy, if any man ever was, when he arrived there, and therefore I did not pity him as might have seemed natural at such an hour. But I had not the pleasure which I usually feel in philosophical discourse (for philosophy was the theme of which we spoke). I was pleased, but in the pleasure there was also a strange admixture of pain; for I reflected that he was soon to die, and this double feeling was shared by us all; we were laughing and weeping by turns, especially the excitable Apollodorus--you know the sort of man?
ECHECRATES: Who were present?

PHAEDO: Of native Athenians there were, besides Apollodorus, Critobulus and his father Crito, Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines, Antisthenes; likewise Ctesippus of the deme of Paeania, Menexenus, and some others; Plato, if I am not mistaken, was ill.

PHAEDO: I will begin at the beginning, and endeavour to repeat the entire conversation. On the previous days we had been in the habit of assembling early in the morning at the court in which the trial took place, and which is not far from the prison. There we used to wait talking with one another until the opening of the doors (for they were not opened very early); then we went in and generally passed the day with Socrates. On the last morning we assembled sooner than usual, having heard on the day before when we quitted the prison in the evening that the sacred ship had come from Delos, and so we arranged to meet very early at the accustomed place. On our arrival the jailer who answered the door, instead of admitting us, came out and told us to stay until he called us. 'For the Eleven,' he said, 'are now with Socrates; they are taking off his chains, and giving orders that he is to die to-day.' He soon returned and said that we might come in. On entering we found Socrates just released from chains, and Xanthippe, whom you know, sitting by him, and holding his child in her arms.

When she saw us she uttered a cry and said, as women will: 'O Socrates, this is the last time that either you will converse with your friends, or they with you.' Socrates turned to Crito and said: 'Crito, let some one take her home.' Some of Crito's people accordingly led her away, crying out and beating herself. And when she was gone, Socrates, sitting up on the couch, bent and rubbed his leg, saying, as he was rubbing: How singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it; for they are never present to a man at the same instant, and yet he who pursues either is generally compelled to take the other; their bodies are two, but they are joined by a single head. And I cannot help thinking that if Aesop had remembered them, he would have made a fable about God trying to reconcile their strife, and how, when he could not, he fastened their heads together; and this is the reason why when one comes the other follows, as I know by my own experience now, when after the pain in my leg which was caused by the chain pleasure appears to succeed.
Then he, or any man who has the spirit of philosophy, will be willing to die, but he will not take his own life, for that is held to be unlawful.
Here he changed his position, and put his legs off the couch on to the ground, and during the rest of the conversation he remained sitting.
Why do you say, enquired Cebes, that a man ought not to take his own life, but that the philosopher will be ready to follow the dying?
Socrates replied: And have you, Cebes and Simmias, who are the disciples of Philolaus, never heard him speak of this?
Yes, but his language was obscure, Socrates.

My words, too, are only an echo; but there is no reason why I should not repeat what I have heard: and indeed, as I am going to another place, it is very meet for me to be thinking and talking of the nature of the pilgrimage which I am about to make. What can I do better in the interval between this and the setting of the sun?

Then tell me, Socrates, why is suicide held to be unlawful? as I have certainly heard Philolaus, about whom you were just now asking, affirm when he was staying with us at Thebes: and there are others who say the same, although I have never understood what was meant by any of them.

Do not lose heart, replied Socrates, and the day may come when you will understand. I suppose that you wonder why, when other things which are evil may be good at certain times and to certain persons, death is to be the only exception, and why, when a man is better dead, he is not permitted to be his own benefactor, but must wait for the hand of another.
Very true, said Cebes, laughing gently and speaking in his native Boeotian.

I admit the appearance of inconsistency in what I am saying; but there may not be any real inconsistency after all. There is a doctrine whispered in secret that man is a prisoner who has no right to open the door and run away; this is a great mystery which I do not quite understand. Yet I too believe that the gods are our guardians, and that we are a possession of theirs. Do you not agree?
Yes, I quite agree, said Cebes.

And if one of your own possessions, an ox or an ass, for example, took the liberty of putting himself out of the way when you had given no intimation of your wish that he should die, would you not be angry with him, and would you not punish him if you could?
Certainly, replied Cebes.
Then, if we look at the matter thus, there may be reason in saying that a man should wait, and not take his own life until God summons him, as he is now summoning me.

Yes, Socrates, said Cebes, there seems to be truth in what you say. And yet how can you reconcile this seemingly true belief that God is our guardian and we his possessions, with the willingness to die which we were just now attributing to the philosopher? That the wisest of men should be willing to leave a service in which they are ruled by the gods who are the best of rulers, is not reasonable; for surely no wise man thinks that when set at liberty he can take better care of himself than the gods take of him. A fool may perhaps think so--he may argue that he had better run away from his master, not considering that his duty is to remain to the end, and not to run away from the good, and that there would be no sense in his running away. The wise man will want to be ever with him who is better than himself. Now this, Socrates, is the reverse of what was just now said; for upon this view the wise man should sorrow and the fool rejoice at passing out of life.
The earnestness of Cebes seemed to please Socrates. Here, said he, turning to us, is a man who is always inquiring, and is not so easily convinced by the first thing which he hears.

And certainly, added Simmias, the objection which he is now making does appear to me to have some force. For what can be the meaning of a truly wise man wanting to fly away and lightly leave a master who is better than himself? And I rather imagine that Cebes is referring to you; he thinks that you are too ready to leave us, and too ready to leave the gods whom you acknowledge to be our good masters.
Yes, replied Socrates; there is reason in what you say. And so you think that I ought to answer your indictment as if I were in a court?
We should like you to do so, said Simmias.

Then I must try to make a more successful defence before you than I did when before the judges. For I am quite ready to admit, Simmias and Cebes, that I ought to be grieved at death, if I were not persuaded in the first place that I am going to other gods who are wise and good (of which I am as certain as I can be of any such matters), and secondly (though I am not so sure of this last) to men departed, better than those whom I leave behind; and therefore I do not grieve as I might have done, for I have good hope that there is yet something remaining for the dead, and as has been said of old, some far better thing for the good than for the evil.

But do you mean to take away your thoughts with you, Socrates? said Simmias. Will you not impart them to us?--for they are a benefit in which we too are entitled to share. Moreover, if you succeed in convincing us, that will be an answer to the charge against yourself.
I will do my best, replied Socrates. But you must first let me hear what Crito wants; he has long been wishing to say something to me.

Only this, Socrates, replied Crito:--the attendant who is to give you the poison has been telling me, and he wants me to tell you, that you are not to talk much, talking, he says, increases heat, and this is apt to interfere with the action of the poison; persons who excite themselves are sometimes obliged to take a second or even a third dose.
Then, said Socrates, let him mind his business and be prepared to give the poison twice or even thrice if necessary; that is all.
I knew quite well what you would say, replied Crito; but I was obliged to satisfy him.
Never mind him, he said.

And now, O my judges, I desire to prove to you that the real philosopher has reason to be of good cheer when he is about to die, and that after death he may hope to obtain the greatest good in the other world. And how this may be, Simmias and Cebes, I will endeavour to explain. For I deem that the true votary of philosophy is likely to be misunderstood by other men; they do not perceive that he is always pursuing death and dying; and if this be so, and he has had the desire of death all his life long, why when his time comes should he repine at that which he has been always pursuing and desiring?

Simmias said laughingly: Though not in a laughing humour, you have made me laugh, Socrates; for I cannot help thinking that the many when they hear your words will say how truly you have described philosophers, and our people at home will likewise say that the life which philosophers desire is in reality death, and that they have found them out to be deserving of the death which they desire.

And they are right, Simmias, in thinking so, with the exception of the words 'they have found them out'; for they have not found out either what is the nature of that death which the true philosopher deserves, or how he deserves or desires death. But enough of them:--let us discuss the matter among ourselves: Do we believe that there is such a thing as death?
To be sure, replied Simmias.

Is it not the separation of soul and body? And to be dead is the completion of this; when the soul exists in herself, and is released from the body and the body is released from the soul, what is this but death?
Just so, he replied.

There is another question, which will probably throw light on our present inquiry if you and I can agree about it:--Ought the philosopher to care about the pleasures--if they are to be called pleasures--of eating and drinking?
Certainly not, answered Simmias.
And what about the pleasures of love--should he care for them?
By no means.

And will he think much of the other ways of indulging the body, for example, the acquisition of costly raiment, or sandals, or other adornments of the body? Instead of caring about them, does he not rather despise anything more than nature needs? What do you say?
I should say that the true philosopher would despise them.
Would you not say that he is entirely concerned with the soul and not with the body? He would like, as far as he can, to get away from the body and to turn to the soul.
Quite true.
In matters of this sort philosophers, above all other men, may be observed in every sort of way to dissever the soul from the communion of the body.
Very true.

Whereas, Simmias, the rest of the world are of opinion that to him who has no sense of pleasure and no part in bodily pleasure, life is not worth having; and that he who is indifferent about them is as good as dead.
That is also true.

What again shall we say of the actual acquirement of knowledge?--is the body, if invited to share in the enquiry, a hinderer or a helper? I mean to say, have sight and hearing any truth in them? Are they not, as the poets are always telling us, inaccurate witnesses? and yet, if even they are inaccurate and indistinct, what is to be said of the other senses?--for you will allow that they are the best of them?
Certainly, he replied.
Then when does the soul attain truth?--for in attempting to consider anything in company with the body she is obviously deceived.
True.
Then must not true existence be revealed to her in thought, if at all?
Yes.

And thought is best when the mind is gathered into herself and none of these things trouble her--neither sounds nor sights nor pain nor any pleasure,--when she takes leave of the body, and has as little as possible to do with it, when she has no bodily sense or desire, but is aspiring after true being?
Certainly.
And in this the philosopher dishonours the body; his soul runs away from his body and desires to be alone and by herself?
That is true.
Well, but there is another thing, Simmias: Is there or is there not an absolute justice?
Assuredly there is.
And an absolute beauty and absolute good?
Of course.
But did you ever behold any of them with your eyes?
Certainly not.

Or did you ever reach them with any other bodily sense?--and I speak not of these alone, but of absolute greatness, and health, and strength, and of the essence or true nature of everything. Has the reality of them ever been perceived by you through the bodily organs? or rather, is not the nearest approach to the knowledge of their several natures made by him who so orders his intellectual vision as to have the most exact conception of the essence of each thing which he considers?
Certainly.

And he attains to the purest knowledge of them who goes to each with the mind alone, not introducing or intruding in the act of thought sight or any other sense together with reason, but with the very light of the mind in her own clearness searches into the very truth of each; he who has got rid, as far as he can, of eyes and ears and, so to speak, of the whole body, these being in his opinion distracting elements which when they infect the soul hinder her from acquiring truth and knowledge--who, if not he, is likely to attain the knowledge of true being?
What you say has a wonderful truth in it, Socrates, replied Simmias.

And when real philosophers consider all these things, will they not be led to make a reflection which they will express in words something like the following? 'Have we not found,' they will say, 'a path of thought which seems to bring us and our argument to the conclusion, that while we are in the body, and while the soul is infected with the evils of the body, our desire will not be satisfied? and our desire is of the truth. For the body is a source of endless trouble to us by reason of the mere requirement of food; and is liable also to diseases which overtake and impede us in the search after true being: it fills us full of loves, and lusts, and fears, and fancies of all kinds, and endless foolery, and in fact, as men say, takes away from us the power of thinking at all. Whence come wars, and fightings, and factions? whence but from the body and the lusts of the body? wars are occasioned by the love of money, and money has to be acquired for the sake and in the service of the body; and by reason of all these impediments we have no time to give to philosophy; and, last and worst of all, even if we are at leisure and betake ourselves to some speculation, the body is always breaking in upon us, causing turmoil and confusion in our enquiries, and so amazing us that we are prevented from seeing the truth.

It has been proved to us by experience that if we would have pure knowledge of anything we must be quit of the body--the soul in herself must behold things in themselves: and then we shall attain the wisdom which we desire, and of which we say that we are lovers, not while we live, but after death; for if while in company with the body, the soul cannot have pure knowledge, one of two things follows--either knowledge is not to be attained at all, or, if at all, after death. For then, and not till then, the soul will be parted from the body and exist in herself alone. In this present life, I reckon that we make the nearest approach to knowledge when we have the least possible intercourse or communion with the body, and are not surfeited with the bodily nature, but keep ourselves pure until the hour when God himself is pleased to release us. And thus having got rid of the foolishness of the body we shall be pure and hold converse with the pure, and know of ourselves the clear light everywhere, which is no other than the light of truth.' For the impure are not permitted to approach the pure. These are the sort of words, Simmias, which the true lovers of knowledge cannot help saying to one another, and thinking. You would agree; would you not?
Undoubtedly, Socrates.

But, O my friend, if this is true, there is great reason to hope that, going whither I go, when I have come to the end of my journey, I shall attain that which has been the pursuit of my life. And therefore I go on my way rejoicing, and not I only, but every other man who believes that his mind has been made ready and that he is in a manner purified.
Certainly, replied Simmias.

And what is purification but the separation of the soul from the body, as I was saying before; the habit of the soul gathering and collecting herself into herself from all sides out of the body; the dwelling in her own place alone, as in another life, so also in this, as far as she can;--the release of the soul from the chains of the body?
Very true, he said.
And this separation and release of the soul from the body is termed death?
To be sure, he said.
And the true philosophers, and they only, are ever seeking to release the soul. Is not the separation and release of the soul from the body their especial study?
That is true.
And, as I was saying at first, there would be a ridiculous contradiction in men studying to live as nearly as they can in a state of death, and yet repining when it comes upon them.
Clearly.

And the true philosophers, Simmias, are always occupied in the practice of dying, wherefore also to them least of all men is death terrible. Look at the matter thus:--if they have been in every way the enemies of the body, and are wanting to be alone with the soul, when this desire of theirs is granted, how inconsistent would they be if they trembled and repined, instead of rejoicing at their departure to that place where, when they arrive, they hope to gain that which in life they desired--and this was wisdom--and at the same time to be rid of the company of their enemy. Many a man has been willing to go to the world below animated by the hope of seeing there an earthly love, or wife, or son, and conversing with them. And will he who is a true lover of wisdom, and is strongly persuaded in like manner that only in the world below he can worthily enjoy her, still repine at death? Will he not depart with joy? Surely he will, O my friend, if he be a true philosopher. For he will have a firm conviction that there and there only, he can find wisdom in her purity. And if this be true, he would be very absurd, as I was saying, if he were afraid of death.
He would, indeed, replied Simmias.

And when you see a man who is repining at the approach of death, is not his reluctance a sufficient proof that he is not a lover of wisdom, but a lover of the body, and probably at the same time a lover of either money or power, or both?
Quite so, he replied.
And is not courage, Simmias, a quality which is specially characteristic of the philosopher?
Certainly.

There is temperance again, which even by the vulgar is supposed to consist in the control and regulation of the passions, and in the sense of superiority to them--is not temperance a virtue belonging to those only who despise the body, and who pass their lives in philosophy?
Most assuredly.
For the courage and temperance of other men, if you will consider them, are really a contradiction.
How so?
Well, he said, you are aware that death is regarded by men in general as a great evil.
Very true, he said.
And do not courageous men face death because they are afraid of yet greater evils?
That is quite true.
Then all but the philosophers are courageous only from fear, and because they are afraid; and yet that a man should be courageous from fear, and because he is a coward, is surely a strange thing.
Very true.

And are not the temperate exactly in the same case? They are temperate because they are intemperate--which might seem to be a contradiction, but is nevertheless the sort of thing which happens with this foolish temperance. For there are pleasures which they are afraid of losing; and in their desire to keep them, they abstain from some pleasures, because they are overcome by others; and although to be conquered by pleasure is called by men intemperance, to them the conquest of pleasure consists in being conquered by pleasure. And that is what I mean by saying that, in a sense, they are made temperate through intemperance.
Such appears to be the case.

Yet the exchange of one fear or pleasure or pain for another fear or pleasure or pain, and of the greater for the less, as if they were coins, is not the exchange of virtue. O my blessed Simmias, is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged?--and that is wisdom; and only in exchange for this, and in company with this, is anything truly bought or sold, whether courage or temperance or justice. And is not all true virtue the companion of wisdom, no matter what fears or pleasures or other similar goods or evils may or may not attend her? But the virtue which is made up of these goods, when they are severed from wisdom and exchanged with one another, is a shadow of virtue only, nor is there any freedom or health or truth in her; but in the true exchange there is a purging away of all these things, and temperance, and justice, and courage, and wisdom herself are the purgation of them.

The founders of the mysteries would appear to have had a real meaning, and were not talking nonsense when they intimated in a figure long ago that he who passes unsanctified and uninitiated into the world below will lie in a slough, but that he who arrives there after initiation and purification will dwell with the gods. For 'many,' as they say in the mysteries, 'are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the mystics,'--meaning, as I interpret the words, 'the true philosophers.' In the number of whom, during my whole life, I have been seeking, according to my ability, to find a place;--whether I have sought in a right way or not, and whether I have succeeded or not, I shall truly know in a little while, if God will, when I myself arrive in the other world--such is my belief. And therefore I maintain that I am right, Simmias and Cebes, in not grieving or repining at parting from you and my masters in this world, for I believe that I shall equally find good masters and friends in another world. But most men do not believe this saying; if then I succeed in convincing you by my defence better than I did the Athenian judges, it will be well.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was ill and absent that day, and wrote from the accounts of those who were there
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s or 370s BC; the conversation is set in the prison on the day of Socrates' death, 399 BC
parts.title: The ship from Delos
parts.context: The town of Phlius, some weeks or months after the death. Echecrates, a philosopher there, asks Phaedo, who was in the prison, to tell him everything. Cuts in the text are marked '…'. Jowett, 1871.
parts.plain: Echecrates asks how Socrates died. Phaedo explains the delay: the sacred ship to Delos. He says that being there was strange: he could not pity Socrates, who seemed happy and fearless, but he felt pleasure and pain mixed. That morning the friends found Socrates just released from his chains. Xanthippe, his wife, was there with their child, crying; Socrates had her taken home. Then he sat up, rubbed his leg, and remarked how strangely pleasure and pain follow each other.

commentary.on: the ship which the Athenians send to Delos
commentary.text: The delay that gave us the Crito and the Phaedo. Athens' piety towards Apollo, whose oracle had sent Socrates on his mission, kept him alive for a month.

commentary.on: he died so fearlessly, and his words and bearing were so noble and gracious, that to me he appeared blessed
commentary.text: This is the impression Plato wants to leave: not tragedy, but blessedness. Phaedo cannot even pity him.

commentary.on: we were laughing and weeping by turns
commentary.text: A very human detail. The friends are not philosophers in marble; they are people losing a friend.

commentary.on: Plato, if I am not mistaken, was ill.
commentary.text: Plato names himself only three times in all his dialogues: twice in the Apology, as present at the trial, and here, as absent from the death. He tells us honestly that he was not there; the account comes from others.

commentary.on: Socrates turned to Crito and said: 'Crito, let some one take her home.'
commentary.text: Modern readers wince. Xanthippe has been treated harshly by later writers, as a scold. Here she simply grieves. Socrates will see her and the children again at the end of the day, in private, before he dies. Plato's dialogue is about the friends' conversation; it is not the whole of Socrates' last day.

commentary.on: How singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain
commentary.text: Even rubbing a sore leg, Socrates starts to philosophise. The examined life does not stop for the last day.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was ill and absent that day, and wrote from the accounts of those who were there
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s or 370s BC; the conversation is set in the prison on the day of Socrates' death, 399 BC
parts.title: A defence before his friends
parts.context: Socrates has said that any philosopher will be willing to die. This passage also discusses why we must not take our own lives. If you are struggling with thoughts of ending your life, please talk to someone today: in the UK and Ireland, Samaritans on 116 123; elsewhere, a local helpline or a doctor. Philolaus was a Pythagorean philosopher. 'The Eleven' were the officials in charge of the prison.
parts.plain: Socrates says a philosopher will be willing to die, but must not kill himself: we are like possessions of the gods, or soldiers on guard, and must wait until God summons us, as he is summoning Socrates now. Cebes objects: then why would a wise man be glad to leave such good masters? Socrates agrees to make his 'defence' to them, as he did to the jury: he hopes to go to other wise and good gods, and perhaps to good men who have died. The jailer has sent a message not to talk too much, or the poison may need two doses. Socrates says: let him prepare two, or three.

commentary.on: but he will not take his own life, for that is held to be unlawful
commentary.text: Socrates distinguishes accepting death from seeking it. This passage became one of the main ancient arguments against suicide, taken up by Christian writers such as Augustine (City of God I.17–22).

commentary.on: the gods are our guardians, and that we are a possession of theirs
commentary.text: Our lives are not wholly our own. Christians would say something similar: 'you are not your own, for you were bought with a price' (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

commentary.on: Here, said he, turning to us, is a man who is always inquiring
commentary.text: Socrates loves Cebes for objecting. Even on his last day, he wants to be questioned. The examined life welcomes the hardest questions.

commentary.on: I am going to other gods who are wise and good (of which I am as certain as I can be of any such matters)
commentary.text: Notice the careful levels of confidence. Of the good gods he is as sure as he can be; of meeting good men 'I am not so sure'. Even facing death, Socrates will not claim more than he knows.

commentary.on: let him mind his business and be prepared to give the poison twice or even thrice if necessary
commentary.text: A flash of dry humour. He will not stop talking to make dying easier.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was ill and absent that day, and wrote from the accounts of those who were there
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s or 370s BC; the conversation is set in the prison on the day of Socrates' death, 399 BC
parts.title: The practice of dying
parts.context: Now Socrates gives his 'defence': why a philosopher should be of good cheer at death. 'Absolute justice' and 'absolute beauty' are what Plato elsewhere calls the forms: justice itself, beauty itself, as distinct from just acts and beautiful things.
parts.plain: Socrates says: people don't realise that true philosophers spend their lives pursuing death. Death is the separation of soul and body. The philosopher cares little for food, sex or fine clothes, and turns from the body to the soul. The body's senses deceive us; we grasp justice, beauty and goodness themselves only by thought, when the mind is most gathered into itself. The body fills us with desires and fears and wars. So pure knowledge comes, if at all, after death. Therefore philosophers practise dying all their lives, and it would be absurd for them to fear it now.

commentary.on: they do not perceive that he is always pursuing death and dying
commentary.text: The famous claim. Socrates does not mean that philosophers want to die soon; he has just forbidden suicide. He means that the philosopher's whole life is a loosening of the soul from the body's demands, so that death completes what life began.

commentary.on: Is it not the separation of soul and body?
commentary.text: The Greek definition of death that Christians also used for centuries. The difference will be in what happens next: Plato's soul is glad to be free of the body; Christian hope is for the body to be raised and made new.

commentary.on: Is there or is there not an absolute justice?
commentary.text: Here the Socratic question 'What is justice?' meets Plato's answer. Justice itself is never seen with the eyes, only grasped by the mind. If you continue to the Plato journey you will study these forms in depth.

commentary.on: Whence come wars, and fightings, and factions? whence but from the body and the lusts of the body?
commentary.text: Compare James 4:1: 'Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don't they come from your pleasures that war in your members?' Plato and the New Testament agree that disordered desire, not ignorance alone, lies behind violence.

commentary.on: the true philosophers, Simmias, are always occupied in the practice of dying, wherefore also to them least of all men is death terrible
commentary.text: The line this session is named after. Practising death means living now for what does not die: the soul, wisdom, justice. Christian monks and spiritual writers took up the idea; the Rule of Benedict tells monks to keep death daily before their eyes (ch. 4).

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (about 428–348 BC), Socrates' pupil, who was ill and absent that day, and wrote from the accounts of those who were there
parts.when: Athens, probably the 380s or 370s BC; the conversation is set in the prison on the day of Socrates' death, 399 BC
parts.title: The one true coin
parts.context: Socrates now argues that only the philosopher has true courage and self-control. 'The thyrsus-bearers' carried decorated staffs in the processions of the god Dionysus; 'the mystics' were those truly initiated into the sacred rites.
parts.plain: Socrates says: a man who grieves at death loves his body, money or power, not wisdom. Ordinary people are brave out of fear of something worse, and self-controlled because they want other pleasures more: they trade one fear or pleasure for another like coins. But wisdom is the one true coin; without it, virtue is only a shadow. Many carry the staff, few are truly initiated. I have tried all my life to be one of the few. Whether I succeeded I shall know soon, if God wills.

commentary.on: is not his reluctance a sufficient proof that he is not a lover of wisdom, but a lover of the body
commentary.text: A hard saying. Socrates thinks fear of death shows what we really love. Most readers, including many Christians, would add that grief at death is also love for those we leave, and need not be a failure.

commentary.on: Then all but the philosophers are courageous only from fear
commentary.text: A sharp observation that still bites. Much ordinary 'virtue' is self-interest in disguise: honest because we fear being caught, brave because we fear shame.

commentary.on: is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged?--and that is wisdom
commentary.text: Here is Socrates' positive vision, the answer to the charge that he only dissolved. Beneath all the questioning was a conviction: wisdom, the knowledge of the good, is worth everything. The questions cleared the way for it.

commentary.on: 'many,' as they say in the mysteries, 'are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the mystics,'
commentary.text: Compare Jesus: 'many are called, but few chosen' (Matthew 22:14). Both say that outward membership is not the same as the real thing.

commentary.on: whether I have sought in a right way or not, and whether I have succeeded or not, I shall truly know in a little while, if God will
commentary.text: Even here, on the edge of death, Socrates' ignorance is honest. He has hope, not certainty. This is perhaps the most moving sentence in the reading.
