paras: Our doctrines, then, appear to be greater than all human teaching; because Christ, who appeared for our sakes, became the whole rational being, both body, and reason, and soul. For whatever either lawgivers or philosophers uttered well, they elaborated by finding and contemplating some part of the Word. But since they did not know the whole of the Word, which is Christ, they often contradicted themselves. And those who by human birth were more ancient than Christ, when they attempted to consider and prove things by reason, were brought before the tribunals as impious persons and busybodies. And Socrates, who was more zealous in this direction than all of them, was accused of the very same crimes as ourselves. For they said that he was introducing new divinities, and did not consider those to be gods whom the state recognised. But he cast out from the state both Homer and the rest of the poets, and taught men to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things which the poets related;

and he exhorted them to become acquainted with the God who was to them unknown, by means of the investigation of reason, saying, That it is neither easy to find the Father and Maker of all, nor, having found Him, is it safe to declare Him to all. But these things our Christ did through His own power. For no one trusted in Socrates so as to die for this doctrine, but in Christ, who was partially known even by Socrates (for He was and is the Word who is in every man, and who foretold the things that were to come to pass both through the prophets and in His own person when He was made of like passions, and taught these things), not only philosophers and scholars believed, but also artisans and people entirely uneducated, despising both glory, and fear, and death; since He is a power of the ineffable Father, not the mere instrument of human reason.

parts.author: Justin Martyr
parts.title: Partially known even by Socrates
parts.context: Justin writes about AD 150–160, after Christians in Rome had been executed simply for being Christians. Like Socrates, they were accused of atheism, because they refused the gods of the city. 'The Word' translates the Greek logos: reason, word, account. John's Gospel says that the Word was with God and was God, and 'became flesh' in Jesus (John 1:1, 14). Justin uses the idea to explain how pagans could know some truth. The translation is by Marcus Dods, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885).
parts.plain: Justin says: whatever lawgivers and philosophers said well, they found by seeing part of the Word, God's Reason; but they did not know the whole Word, who is Christ, so they contradicted themselves. Socrates, the most zealous of them, was accused of the same crimes as Christians: new gods and denying the city's gods. He told people to reject the poets' wicked stories and seek the unknown God by reason. But no one trusted Socrates so far as to die for his teaching; Christ, whom Socrates partly knew, is trusted to death not only by philosophers but by craftsmen and the uneducated, because he is the power of God, not a human theory.

commentary.on: they elaborated by finding and contemplating some part of the Word
commentary.text: This is Justin's key idea. The Word, God's own Reason, is present in every human mind. So whatever any philosopher saw truly, he saw by the Word's light: truth anywhere belongs to Christ.

commentary.on: And Socrates, who was more zealous in this direction than all of them, was accused of the very same crimes as ourselves
commentary.text: Justin sees Socrates as a forerunner of the Christian martyrs: tried for 'atheism', for refusing the gods everyone else worshipped.

commentary.on: he exhorted them to become acquainted with the God who was to them unknown, by means of the investigation of reason
commentary.text: An echo of Paul at Athens, who spoke of the altar 'to an unknown god' (Acts 17:23). Justin's Socrates is a seeker of the one true God, by reason.

commentary.on: That it is neither easy to find the Father and Maker of all, nor, having found Him, is it safe to declare Him to all
commentary.text: Justin is quoting Plato's Timaeus (28c), a later dialogue in which Plato, through another speaker, says that the maker of the universe is hard to find and impossible to declare to all. Justin attributes it to Socrates' teaching.

commentary.on: For no one trusted in Socrates so as to die for this doctrine
commentary.text: Here is the difference, for Justin. Socrates died for his convictions; no one died for Socrates. Christians, including ordinary working people, were dying for Christ.

commentary.on: who was partially known even by Socrates
commentary.text: Justin's verdict in four words. Socrates knew Christ 'partially': not by name, but as the Reason and Truth he served. This became the Church's most generous way of honouring the best of the pagans.

commentary.on: not the mere instrument of human reason
commentary.text: The last word marks the limit. Socrates' examined life was the best that human reason could do. Christianity claims to be something else: not a better argument, but the power of God.

compare.author: Justin Martyr
compare.why: Justin Martyr was a philosopher from Samaria who searched through the schools, Stoic, Aristotelian, Pythagorean and Platonist, before becoming a Christian. He kept wearing the philosopher's cloak, taught in Rome and was beheaded there about AD 165. Here, in a defence addressed to the Roman Senate, he gives the first Christian verdict on Socrates.
compare.title: Christ and Socrates

paras: On the evidence of this journey, Socrates was not guilty as charged. He honoured the gods as he understood them; he served what he believed was a divine command; he corrupted no one by teaching injustice, and two of his worst companions turned against what he taught. Athens had real fears, and Hegel was right that Socrates' questioning would change the city for ever. But a city that kills its questioner because his questions are uncomfortable destroys its own means of correcting itself, as Athens soon recognised.

What of the examined life? The journey has shown what it was for Socrates: to know the limits of your knowledge; to test your beliefs and other people's, honestly, in conversation; to care for the soul, what kind of person you are, more than for money, reputation or even life; never to do wrong, even in return; and to follow the argument, and conscience, wherever they lead. He showed that it can be lived, and died for. The objection showed that it is not complete in itself: questioning can clear the ground, but it needs something to build.
sections.key: Socrates was not guilty as charged; his examined life, knowing one's limits, testing beliefs, caring for the soul, never doing wrong, is worth living, though questioning alone cannot build everything.

paras: Socrates met death calmly because he hoped the soul would be freed from the body to be with the gods. Christianity agrees that death is not the end, and Christians borrowed much from the Phaedo. But its hope is different. The New Testament does not promise the soul's escape from the body; it promises the resurrection of the body, raised and transformed, as Christ was raised (1 Corinthians 15).

The Swiss scholar Oscar Cullmann made this contrast famous in a lecture of 1955, 'Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead?'. He set Socrates' serene death beside Jesus in Gethsemane, 'greatly troubled and distressed' (Mark 14:33), praying for the cup to pass. For Socrates death was a friend; for the New Testament it is 'the last enemy' (1 Corinthians 15:26), defeated not by philosophy but by God. Many theologians think Cullmann drew the line too sharply, since Christians have also taught that the soul lives on with God until the resurrection. But the difference he saw is real.
sections.key: Socrates hoped for the soul's release from the body; Christianity hopes for the body's resurrection, and treats death as an enemy defeated by God, not a friend.

paras: Socrates' last words, at sunset, after the poison had begun to work, were: 'Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?' (Phaedo 118a). You can learn the whole passage as this session's memory piece. Asclepius was the god of healing; the sick offered him a cockerel when they recovered. What did Socrates mean?

Readers have given at least four answers. Nietzsche, as the last session showed, took it as thanks for being cured of life, the sickness. Others read it as thanks for the healing of his soul by philosophy, or of Plato's illness, mentioned at the start of the dialogue. Some read it as plain piety: a man who kept the city's customs to the end and would not die owing a god anything. The classicist Glenn Most suggested it referred to Plato's recovery; Emily Wilson's book surveys the rest. The words are left open. What they are not is bitter. The last thing Socrates did was to remember a small duty and ask a friend to do it: the examined life, to the end, attending to the next right thing.
sections.key: Socrates' last words asked Crito to pay a cock to Asclepius, god of healing: read as thanks for release from life, for a healed soul, or simple piety; they are not bitter.

paras: People have compared the two since the second century. Both taught by conversation and questions, wrote nothing and are known through followers who disagree in details. Both were tried on religious charges with political undertones, before their own people's authorities. Both could have escaped and did not. Both died with forgiveness rather than revenge.

The differences matter as much. Socrates claimed to know that he did not know; Jesus taught 'with authority' and spoke of God as his Father. Socrates died at seventy, among friends, calmly, by a painless poison; Jesus died in his thirties, abandoned, by torture, crying out to God. Socrates died for his convictions; Christians claim that Jesus died for others, and rose. In the eighteenth century Jean-Jacques Rousseau, no orthodox believer, put the comparison in a famous sentence: if Socrates lived and died like a sage, Jesus lived and died like a God.

Nothing; known through four Gospels and Paul

Did not flee Gethsemane; told Peter to put away his sword

sections.key: Both taught orally, were tried on religious charges and refused escape; Socrates died calm for his convictions, Jesus in anguish, his followers say, for others, and rose.

paras: Justin was not alone. In his First Apology (46) he says that those who lived 'with the Word', such as Socrates and Heraclitus, were Christians, even if they were thought atheists. Clement of Alexandria (about 150–215) called philosophy a schoolmaster that prepared the Greeks for Christ, as the law prepared the Jews. Augustine (City of God VIII.3) praised Socrates for turning philosophy to the purifying of the heart, and noted with approval that he would not claim more than he knew.

In 1522 the Dutch scholar Erasmus, in his dialogue The Godly Feast, has a character say that when he reads such pagans he can hardly stop himself saying, 'Saint Socrates, pray for us' (Sancte Socrates, ora pro nobis). Others in the Church were more cautious. Tertullian asked 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?', and Augustine himself warned that philosophers saw the homeland from afar but not the road to it (Confessions VII.20–21). The Church's mainstream answer, from Justin to Thomas Aquinas, was that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it: Socrates' honest search was real, and pointed beyond itself.
sections.key: Justin, Clement and Augustine honoured Socrates as one who served the Word in part; Erasmus nearly prayed to him; others warned that philosophy sees the goal but not the road.

paras: What would the examined life look like today? Not necessarily a life of argument. Socrates' habits translate into practices anyone can keep: asking what our words mean before we fight over them; admitting what we do not know; listening to the strongest form of the other side; doing a daily review of our actions and motives; refusing to repay a wrong; caring more about what kind of person we are becoming than about what we own or how we look.

Christians have practised several of these for centuries in their own way: the daily examination of conscience, confession, the love of enemies, the 'remembrance of death' as a way of seeing life clearly. The two traditions meet here. Socrates showed how far an honest human being can go by questioning. The Christian claim is that the One he was looking for came looking for us. That claim, too, the examined life must test.
sections.key: The examined life today: question your words, admit ignorance, hear the other side, review your day, refuse revenge, care for the soul; Christians practise much of this, and claim its goal came to meet us.

debate.question: Was Socrates a Christian before Christ?

positions.name: Yes, in part
positions.who: Justin Martyr; Clement of Alexandria; Erasmus; many Christian humanists
positions.view: Socrates served the Word, God's Reason present in every mind, as fully as anyone could without knowing Christ. His honesty, piety, justice and death show the light of Christ at work outside the Church.
positions.evidence: Justin, Second Apology 10 and First Apology 46; Socrates' 'God only is wise', his refusal to return wrong for wrong, his care for the soul.

positions.name: No: a noble pagan, nothing more
positions.who: Tertullian; many Reformation and later Protestant writers; Kierkegaard in his way
positions.view: Socrates was admirable, but his hope rested on human reason and the soul's own immortality. Christianity is not the completion of philosophy but a revelation that judges it. To call him a Christian blurs the difference.
positions.evidence: 1 Corinthians 1:21 ('the world through its wisdom didn't know God'); the contrast between immortality and resurrection; Kierkegaard's insistence that Christ is not a teacher like Socrates but the Saviour.

look.why: There is no painting of the death of Socrates at the National Gallery of Art; Jacques-Louis David's famous one is in New York. Georges de La Tour painted this picture of Mary Magdalene around 1635–1640. It is not Socrates. It is here because it is a painting of exactly what the Phaedo describes: a life spent in the practice of dying. In the Christian tradition such a picture is a meditation on death, a memento mori, 'remember you will die', meant to help the viewer live well.
points: A young woman with long chestnut-brown hair sits at a table in a darkened room.
She rests her chin in her right hand, in thought.
Her left hand reaches for a skull placed on a thick book on the table.
The scene is lit by a single candle, mostly hidden behind the skull.
Shown in profile, she looks into a small mirror beside the skull, which reflects the skull and the book: 'know thyself' and 'remember death' in one image.

music.why: Gabriel Fauré's Requiem (1888) is a requiem without terror: he left out most of the Day of Judgement and ended with 'In Paradisum', the angels leading the soul into paradise. He called death 'a happy deliverance, an aspiration towards happiness above'. It is as close as music comes to the mood of the Phaedo, and it is Christian: listen for the 'Pie Jesu', a prayer for rest addressed to Christ.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What is the examined life, and is it worth dying for? In about 300 words, give your own answer from Socrates' life and death, using at least three of the readings, and answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Read the Apology, the Crito and the death scene at the end of the Phaedo over the next week, one each on three evenings. Each time, stop at one sentence that applies to your own life and copy it out. At the end of the week, read the three sentences together.
synthesis: This journey followed the trial and death of Socrates in 399 BC, step by step, to ask what the examined life is. Here are the short answers to its questions.

Who was Socrates? An Athenian, born about 470 BC, the son of a stonemason and a midwife; a brave infantryman, poor, ugly and barefoot, who spent his life in the market place asking his fellow citizens what they meant by justice, courage and piety. He turned philosophy from the stars to the question of how to live. He married Xanthippe and had three sons. He held no office except, once, a turn on the Council, where he refused to put an illegal vote.

Why didn't he write anything down, and how do we know him? He thought philosophy was a living conversation, and a book cannot answer questions. So we know him through three witnesses who disagree: Aristophanes, who mocked him as a sky-gazing sophist while he lived; Xenophon, who remembered a pious, practical friend; and Plato, his greatest pupil, whose early dialogues most scholars take as closest to the real man. They agree on the public facts.

What did he mean by 'I know that I know nothing'? Not quite that. When the oracle at Delphi said no one was wiser, Socrates tested it by questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen, and found they thought they knew what they did not. His only advantage, he said, was this: 'I neither know nor think that I know.' He did know some things, above all that doing wrong is evil. His wisdom was to know the limits of his knowledge, and that 'God only is wise'.

What is the Socratic method? Questioning that tests a person's beliefs against each other until they see that they do not hang together: the elenchus. It numbs the proud, like a torpedo fish, but it is the first step to learning. In the Meno a slave boy, admitting 'I do not know', goes on to find for himself that the square on the diagonal is double. Plato concluded that learning is remembering; Augustine, that the mind sees truth by the light of God within. Either way, the teacher draws out; he does not pour in.

Why was Socrates put to death? The charge was not recognising the city's gods, bringing in new ones and corrupting the young. Behind it lay real fears: his companions had included Alcibiades, who betrayed Athens, and Critias, who led the Thirty Tyrants; he scorned choosing officials by lot; he spoke of a private divine sign; his questions dissolved the beliefs that held the city together. The amnesty of 403 BC meant the politics could not be named. He refused to plead, told the jury he would 'obey God rather than you', called himself the gadfly God had sent to wake the city, and proposed free meals as his penalty. He was condemned by about 280 votes to 220, and sentenced to death by more.

Why didn't he escape? Because he would not return wrong for wrong. In the Crito he let the Laws of Athens argue that a citizen who had accepted their care for seventy years, and was free to leave, must persuade them or obey them. His defiance in court and his obedience in prison fit together: he would refuse to do wrong at the city's command, but he would suffer wrong rather than escape. Later disobedients, from Thoreau to King, took the lesson: disobey openly, and accept the penalty.

Did Socrates believe in God? Yes, though not in Homer's gods. He sacrificed, obeyed an oracle, spoke of a divine voice and argued that the world shows a caring maker. But he held that the divine must be wholly good and cannot lie, and that only God is wise. That was new, and some Athenians heard it as atheism.

Was he a danger? The case against him is real. Questioning can dissolve beliefs without replacing them; I. F. Stone saw an enemy of democracy, Hegel a tragic collision of two rights, Nietzsche a man who treated life as a disease. But Critias turned against him, he obeyed the democracy's laws to his death, and, as Mill argued, a city that kills its questioners destroys its own means of correcting itself.

Is Socrates like Jesus? In much: both taught orally and wrote nothing, both were tried on religious charges, both refused to escape, both died without revenge. But Socrates claimed not to know, and Jesus taught with authority; Socrates died calmly at seventy among friends, Jesus young, in anguish and abandoned; Socrates hoped for the soul's release from the body, Christians for the body's resurrection. Justin Martyr's verdict has lasted: Socrates knew Christ 'partially', as the Word present to every mind, but no one died for Socrates' teaching as ordinary people died for Christ. Erasmus could hardly keep from praying, 'Saint Socrates, pray for us.'

So, what is the examined life? To know the limits of your knowledge; to test your beliefs, honestly, with others; to care for your soul, what kind of person you are, above money, reputation and even life; never to do wrong, not even in return; and to follow the argument and your conscience wherever they lead. Socrates showed that such a life can be lived, and that it is worth dying for. On his last day he called it 'the practice of dying', and wisdom 'the one true coin'. What it cannot do alone is supply the wisdom it seeks. Socrates knew that; he ended with hope, not certainty: 'I shall truly know in a little while, if God will.' The Christian claim, which this journey leaves you to examine, is that the One he was looking for came looking for us.

title: Epicureans and Stoics
question: How do you find peace?
line: Seven sessions on the two great schools of peace: Epicurus's garden and Lucretius's case against religion; the Stoics' porch, Epictetus on what is up to us, and Seneca at Nero's court; the objection that Stoic calm is cold comfort; and Paul, in prison, content in all things.
why: Almost everyone wants peace of mind. Two schools of Greek philosophy, born in Athens around 300 BC, gave the most famous answers the West has ever had, and both are alive today: the Epicureans, who removed the fear of gods and death and lived simply among friends, and the Stoics, who taught that only virtue is good and that we should want only what is in our power. This journey reads Epicurus, Lucretius, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus Aurelius, tests both answers against the hardest case, grief, with Augustine's objection at full strength, and ends with the apostle Paul, who met both schools in Athens and offered a third peace. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year paper on Hellenistic philosophy (Epicureans and Stoics), with elements of a paper on the reception of ancient philosophy in early Christianity.
before: aristotle
outcomes: Explain what Epicurus meant by pleasure, his sorting of desires, the four-part cure and his argument that death is nothing to us, and assess Cicero's objections.

Explain Epictetus's dichotomy of control and its afterlife in the Serenity Prayer, cognitive therapy and James Stockdale's captivity.
Assess Seneca's life and teaching, the charge of hypocrisy, and the forged correspondence with Paul.
State the objection that Stoic apatheia is incompatible with love at full strength, with Augustine's reply, and compare the three answers to 'how do you find peace?' with Paul in Philippians 4.

sessions.title: The garden
sessions.line: A philosopher buys a garden outside Athens, lives there with his friends on bread and water, and says the goal of life is pleasure.
sessions.plain: Around 306 BC a philosopher called Epicurus bought a garden in Athens and lived there with his friends, men and women, free and slave. He taught that the goal of life is pleasure, and then explained that he meant something surprising: not feasts and sex, but freedom from pain in the body and from fear in the mind. This session reads his own summary of how to live, the Letter to Menoeceus, and a Roman critic who thought he had got pleasure wrong.
sessions.why: This is the first session. The question of this journey is how to find peace. Two schools of ancient philosophy, the Epicureans and the Stoics, gave the most famous answers the West has ever had, and both are alive today. We begin with the one most misunderstood: the man whose name now means a lover of fine food.
answers: What did Epicurus actually teach?
Is Epicureanism just pleasure-seeking?
Why did Epicurus think we should not fear death or the gods?
How did the Epicureans live?
sessions.finding: Epicurus taught that pleasure, understood as freedom from pain and fear, is the goal of life, and that it is reached by friendship, simple living and understanding nature.

paras: Almost everyone wants peace of mind: to stop worrying, to be able to lose things without falling apart, to face death without terror. The Greeks had a word for it, ataraxia, which means 'not being stirred up', like the surface of a calm sea.

In the three centuries after Alexander the Great, two schools of philosophy in Athens offered two different ways to get there. The ancient philosophers liked to call themselves doctors of the soul, and these were two cures for one illness. The Epicureans said: remove the fears that trouble you, the fear of angry gods and the fear of death, want little, and live among friends. The Stoics said: change what you value; want only what is in your power, and accept the rest as the work of a wise order running through the world.
This journey examines each cure in turn, tests both against the hardest case, grief, and then sets beside them the answer of the first Christians, who met both schools in Athens.

background.key: Peace of mind (ataraxia) was the goal of both schools. The Epicureans removed fear; the Stoics changed what we value. We test both, then hear Paul.

paras: Alexander the Great died in 323 BC. His empire broke into kingdoms ruled by his generals, and the free Greek city, where a citizen could hope to shape his own life by speaking in the assembly, lost its power. Historians call the age that followed 'Hellenistic', from Hellen, Greek. Ordinary people felt small and exposed in a world of armies and kings. Philosophy turned from 'how should the city be run?' towards 'how can I live well, whatever happens?'

Athens was still the university of the Greek world. Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum were still teaching. Within a few years of each other two newcomers opened schools there: Epicurus in his garden around 306 BC, and Zeno of Citium in a public colonnade around 300 BC. Their schools were known by those places: the Garden and the Porch.

background.key: After Alexander (d. 323 BC) the free city lost its power, and philosophy turned to how one person can live well. The Garden and the Porch opened in Athens around 300 BC.

paras: Epicurus was born in 341 BC on Samos, an island off the coast of what is now Turkey, to an Athenian family of settlers. He began to study philosophy, he said, at fourteen; one story makes it twelve. He taught first at Mytilene and Lampsacus and then, aged about thirty-five, moved to Athens and bought a house and garden, where his friends came to live with him. He died there in 270 BC, of a kidney stone, after a fortnight of great pain.

He wrote about three hundred books, and almost all are lost. What survives comes mainly from one source: a writer called Diogenes Laertius, who around AD 200 to 250 wrote Lives of the Eminent Philosophers and gave his whole tenth book to Epicurus, copying out three of his letters and a list of his main sayings. We read Diogenes in the translation of R. D. Hicks, published in 1925.
background.key: Epicurus (341–270 BC) taught in his Garden in Athens. Almost all his books are lost; three letters and his main sayings survive in Diogenes Laertius, Book X.

paras: The main reading is the Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus's own short summary of how to live, almost complete. It is the best answer to the question 'what did Epicurus actually teach?', in his own words. Nothing is known of Menoeceus except his name.

The comparison has two parts. First, Diogenes's account of how the Garden actually lived, and Epicurus's last letter, written on the day he died. Then the Roman statesman Cicero, who knew Epicureans well and liked them, attacks the idea that pleasure can be the goal of life. You can judge whether he is fair.
background.key: Epicurus's own summary of his ethics, then how his school lived, then a fair-minded Roman critic.

paras: “Epicurus to Menoeceus, greeting.

122. “Let no one be slow to seek wisdom when he is young nor weary in the search thereof when he is grown old. For no age is too early or too late for the health of the soul. And to say that the season for studying philosophy has not yet come, or that it is past and gone, is like saying that the season for happiness is not yet or that it is now no more. Therefore, both old and young ought to seek wisdom, the former in order that, as age comes over him, he may be young in good things because of the grace of what has been, and the latter in order that, while he is young, he may at the same time be old, because he has no fear of the things which are to come. So we must exercise ourselves in the things which bring happiness, since, if that be present, we have everything, and, if that be absent, all our actions are directed toward attaining it.

123. “Those things which without ceasing I have declared unto thee, those do, and exercise thyself therein, holding them to be the elements of right life. First believe that God is a living being immortal and blessed, according to the notion of a god indicated by the common sense of mankind; and so believing, thou shalt not affirm of him aught that is foreign to his immortality or that agrees not with blessedness, but shalt believe about him whatever may uphold both his blessedness and his immortality. For verily there are gods, and the knowledge of them is manifest; but they are not such as the multitude believe, seeing that men do not steadfastly maintain the notions they form respecting them. Not the man who denies the gods worshipped by the multitude, but he who affirms of the gods what the multitude believes about them is truly impious. 124. For the utterances of the multitude about the gods are not true preconceptions but false assumptions; hence it is that the greatest evils happen to the wicked and the greatest blessings happen to the good from the hand of the gods, seeing that they are always favourable to their own good qualities and take pleasure in men like unto themselves, but reject as alien whatever is not of their kind.

“Accustom thyself to believe that death is nothing to us, for good and evil imply sentience, and death is the privation of all sentience; therefore a right understanding that death is nothing to us makes the mortality of life enjoyable, not by adding to life an illimitable time, but by taking away the yearning after immortality. 125. For life has no terrors for him who has thoroughly apprehended that there are no terrors for him in ceasing to live. Foolish, therefore, is the man who says that he fears death, not because it will pain when it comes, but because it pains in the prospect. Whatsoever causes no annoyance when it is present, causes only a groundless pain in the expectation. Death, therefore, the most awful of evils, is nothing to us, seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not. It is nothing, then, either to the living or to the dead, for with the living it is not and the dead exist no longer.

But in the world, at one time men shun death as the greatest of all evils, and at another time choose it as a respite from the evils in life. 126. The wise man does not deprecate life nor does he fear the cessation of life. The thought of life is no offence to him, nor is the cessation of life regarded as an evil. And even as men choose of food not merely and simply the larger portion, but the more pleasant, so the wise seek to enjoy the time which is most pleasant and not merely that which is longest. And he who admonishes the young to live well and the old to make a good end speaks foolishly, not merely because of the desirableness of life, but because the same exercise at once teaches to live well and to die well. Much worse is he who says that it were good not to be born, but when once one is born to pass with all speed through the gates of Hades. 127. For if he truly believes this, why does he not depart from life? It were easy for him to do so, if once he were firmly convinced. If he speaks only in mockery, his words are foolishness, for those who hear believe him not.
“We must remember that the future is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours, so that neither must we count upon it as quite certain to come nor despair of it as quite certain not to come.

“We must also reflect that of desires some are natural, others are groundless; and that of the natural some are necessary as well as natural, and some natural only. And of the necessary desires some are necessary if we are to be happy, some if the body is to be rid of uneasiness, some if we are even to live. 128. He who has a clear and certain understanding of these things will direct every preference and aversion toward securing health of body and tranquillity of mind, seeing that this is the sum and end of a blessed life. For the end of all our actions is to be free from pain and fear, and, when once we have attained all this, the tempest of the soul is laid; seeing that the living creature has no need to go in search of something that is lacking, nor to look for anything else by which the good of the soul and of the body will be fulfilled. When we are pained because of the absence of pleasure, then, and then only, do we feel the need of pleasure. Wherefore we call pleasure the alpha and omega of a blessed life. Pleasure is our first and kindred good. 129. It is the starting-point of every choice and of every aversion, and to it we come back, inasmuch as we make feeling the rule by which to judge of every good thing. And since pleasure is our first and native good, for that reason we do not choose every pleasure whatsoever, but ofttimes pass over many pleasures when a greater annoyance ensues from them.

And ofttimes we consider pains superior to pleasures when submission to the pains for a long time brings us as a consequence a greater pleasure. While therefore all pleasure because it is naturally akin to us is good, not all pleasure is choiceworthy, just as all pain is an evil and yet not all pain is to be shunned. 130. It is, however, by measuring one against another, and by looking at the conveniences and inconveniences, that all these matters must be judged. Sometimes we treat the good as an evil, and the evil, on the contrary, as a good. Again, we regard independence of outward things as a great good, not so as in all cases to use little, but so as to be contented with little if we have not much, being honestly persuaded that they have the sweetest enjoyment of luxury who stand least in need of it, and that whatever is natural is easily procured and only the vain and worthless hard to win. Plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet, when once the pain of want has been removed, 131. while bread and water confer the highest possible pleasure when they are brought to hungry lips. To habituate one’s self, therefore, to simple and inexpensive diet supplies all that is needful for health, and enables a man to meet the necessary requirements of life without shrinking, and it places us in a better condition when we approach at intervals a costly fare and renders us fearless of fortune.

“When we say, then, that pleasure is the end and aim, we do not mean the pleasures of the prodigal or the pleasures of sensuality, as we are understood to do by some through ignorance, prejudice, or wilful misrepresentation. By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul. 132. It is not an unbroken succession of drinking-bouts and of revelry, not sexual love, not the enjoyment of the fish and other delicacies of a luxurious table, which produce a pleasant life; it is sober reasoning, searching out the grounds of every choice and avoidance, and banishing those beliefs through which the greatest tumults take possession of the soul. Of all this the beginning and the greatest good is prudence. Wherefore prudence is a more precious thing even than philosophy; from it spring all the other virtues, for it teaches that we cannot lead a life of pleasure which is not also a life of prudence, honour, and justice; nor lead a life of prudence, honour, and justice, which is not also a life of pleasure. For the virtues have grown into one with a pleasant life, and a pleasant life is inseparable from them.

133. “Who, then, is superior in thy judgement to such a man? He holds a holy belief concerning the gods, and is altogether free from the fear of death. He has diligently considered the end fixed by nature, and understands how easily the limit of good things can be reached and attained, and how either the duration or the intensity of evils is but slight. Destiny, which some introduce as sovereign over all things, he laughs to scorn, affirming rather that some things happen of necessity, others by chance, others through our own agency. For he sees that necessity destroys responsibility and that chance or fortune is inconstant; whereas our own actions are free, and it is to them that praise and blame naturally attach. 134. It were better, indeed, to accept the legends of the gods than to bow beneath that yoke of destiny which the natural philosophers have imposed. The one holds out some faint hope that we may escape if we honour the gods, while the necessity of the naturalists is deaf to all entreaties. Nor does he hold chance to be a god, as the world in general does, for in the acts of a god there is no disorder; nor to be a cause, though an uncertain one, for he believes that no good or evil is dispensed by chance to men so as to make life blessed, though it supplies the starting-point of great good and great evil. He believes that the misfortune of the wise is better than the prosperity of the fool. 135. It is better, in short, that what is well judged in action should not owe its successful issue to the aid of chance.

“Exercise thyself in these and kindred precepts day and night, both by thyself and with him who is like unto thee; then never, either in waking or in dream, wilt thou be disturbed, but wilt live as a god among men. For man loses all semblance of mortality by living in the midst of immortal blessings.”

parts.author: Epicurus
parts.work: Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X
parts.title: Health of the soul
parts.who: Epicurus, writing from his school in Athens
parts.context: The letter opens like any Greek letter, with a greeting. Diogenes Laertius copied it into his life of Epicurus around AD 200 to 250; the numbers (122, 123 and so on) are the sections of Diogenes's Book X used by scholars. Hicks's English of 1925 deliberately sounds old ('thee', 'thyself').
parts.plain: Epicurus says: it is never too early or too late to study philosophy, because philosophy is the health of the soul. Saying you are too young or too old for it is like saying you are too young or too old to be happy. So everyone should practise the things that bring happiness.

commentary.on: For no age is too early or too late for the health of the soul.
commentary.text: The first idea is the most important: philosophy is medicine. It is not a hobby for clever people, but treatment for a sick soul, and everyone needs it. This is why the ancients called their teachers doctors of the soul.

commentary.on: is like saying that the season for happiness is not yet or that it is now no more
commentary.text: The goal is happiness, here and now. Epicurus does not promise it after death; he thinks there is no after. Happiness must be found in this life or not at all.

commentary.on: So we must exercise ourselves in the things which bring happiness
commentary.text: 'Exercise' is the key word. Epicurus's philosophy is a training, like an athlete's: things to repeat until they become second nature. The letter ends, as you will see, with the same command.

parts.author: Epicurus
parts.work: Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X
parts.title: The gods
parts.context: The first 'element of right life' is a right belief about the gods. Epicurus was not an atheist. He believed the gods existed, but not that they cared about us.
parts.plain: Epicurus says: believe that God is a living being, immortal and perfectly happy, and believe nothing about him that does not fit that. The gods exist, but they are not what most people think. The really irreverent person is not the one who denies the popular gods, but the one who believes the popular stories about them: that they reward and punish us.

commentary.on: First believe that God is a living being immortal and blessed
commentary.text: 'Blessed' means perfectly happy and untroubled. Epicurus reasons from this: a perfectly happy being would never be angry or busy or anxious, so it would never bother with us. The gods live their serene life in the spaces between the worlds.

commentary.on: Not the man who denies the gods worshipped by the multitude, but he who affirms of the gods what the multitude believes about them is truly impious.
commentary.text: A sharp reversal. The popular religion of Greece told of gods who were jealous, lustful and angry, who sent plagues and demanded sacrifices. Epicurus says that to believe such things is the real insult to the gods. Notice that the Hebrew prophets and the early Christians also attacked popular religion, for different reasons.

commentary.on: hence it is that the greatest evils happen to the wicked and the greatest blessings happen to the good from the hand of the gods
commentary.text: This is what 'the multitude' believe: that gods reward and punish. Epicurus thinks this belief causes enormous fear, and he wants to remove it. Hold on to this: it is the whole subject of the next session, still to come, on his Roman follower Lucretius.

parts.author: Epicurus
parts.work: Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X
parts.title: Death is nothing to us
parts.context: The most famous passage in Epicurus. The second great fear, after the fear of the gods, is the fear of death.
parts.plain: Epicurus says: get used to thinking that death is nothing to us. Good and bad are things we feel, and death is the end of all feeling. So death cannot hurt us: while we exist, death is not here; when death is here, we no longer exist. Fearing it in advance is pointless pain. The wise man neither clings to life nor runs from it.

commentary.on: Accustom thyself to believe that death is nothing to us, for good and evil imply sentience, and death is the privation of all sentience
commentary.text: 'Sentience' means the ability to feel. The argument has two steps: only what we can feel can be good or bad for us; when we are dead we feel nothing; so being dead is neither good nor bad for us. Epicurus believed the soul was made of atoms that scatter at death, so there is no one left to suffer.

commentary.on: not by adding to life an illimitable time, but by taking away the yearning after immortality
commentary.text: Here is the cure. Religions promised to defeat death by adding endless time. Epicurus offers the opposite: stop wanting endless time, and mortal life becomes sweet. It is the deepest difference between his answer and the Christian one.

commentary.on: Death, therefore, the most awful of evils, is nothing to us, seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not.
commentary.text: This is the sentence you will learn by heart. It is elegant and hard to answer. Philosophers still argue about it: critics say that death can harm us by taking away the good things we would have had, even if we never feel the loss. Others ask whether it touches the real fear, which for many people is of losing someone they love.

commentary.on: the wise seek to enjoy the time which is most pleasant and not merely that which is longest
commentary.text: Quality, not quantity. A short, good meal is better than a long, bad one; so with life.

commentary.on: Much worse is he who says that it were good not to be born
commentary.text: A jab at a gloomy line of Greek poetry (Hicks's footnote names the poet Theognis): 'best never to be born, and next best to die soon'. Epicurus has no patience with despair. If you really believed that, he says, you would act on it.

parts.author: Epicurus
parts.work: Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X
parts.title: Not the pleasures of the prodigal
parts.context: Now the heart of the ethics: desire and pleasure. Read slowly; this is where Epicurus has been misread for two thousand years.
parts.plain: Epicurus sorts our desires. Some are natural and necessary (food, shelter, friendship); some are natural but not necessary (fine food); some are empty (fame, power, luxury). Pleasure is the starting point of every choice, but we must weigh pleasures against pains, and often choose a pain that leads to a greater good. Simple food gives as much pleasure as rich food once hunger is gone. By pleasure he means freedom from pain in the body and trouble in the soul, not parties and sex. And you cannot live pleasantly without living wisely, honourably and justly.

commentary.on: of desires some are natural, others are groundless
commentary.text: Epicurus's famous sorting of desires. Hicks's 'groundless' translates a word meaning 'empty'. The happy life is mostly a matter of not wanting the empty things, which can never be satisfied.

commentary.on: For the end of all our actions is to be free from pain and fear, and, when once we have attained all this, the tempest of the soul is laid
commentary.text: The calm sea again: the storm in the soul dies down. Pleasure, for Epicurus, is above all this calm. Scholars call it 'static' pleasure, a state of rest, as opposed to the 'moving' pleasure of eating or drinking.

commentary.on: Wherefore we call pleasure the alpha and omega of a blessed life.
commentary.text: Alpha and omega, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet: the beginning and end. It is the boldest claim in the letter. Christians would later use the same phrase for Christ (Revelation 22:13).

commentary.on: not all pleasure is choiceworthy, just as all pain is an evil and yet not all pain is to be shunned
commentary.text: So it is not pleasure-seeking in the ordinary sense. Every pleasure is good in itself, but some lead to greater pains (a hangover, debt, a broken marriage), and some pains lead to greater pleasures (the dentist). Life is a calculation.

commentary.on: bread and water confer the highest possible pleasure when they are brought to hungry lips
commentary.text: One of the most surprising lines in ancient philosophy. The highest pleasure is the removal of pain, and simple things do that perfectly. Learning to be content with little also makes you 'fearless of fortune': you cannot lose much if you need little.

commentary.on: By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul.
commentary.text: The definition. Epicurus complains that he has been misunderstood 'through ignorance, prejudice, or wilful misrepresentation'; he was attacked in his own lifetime, and the attacks never stopped.

commentary.on: we cannot lead a life of pleasure which is not also a life of prudence, honour, and justice
commentary.text: Prudence means practical wisdom. Epicurus holds that the virtues are tools for a pleasant life: an unjust man lives in fear of being found out. Notice what that implies, and keep it for the comparison: the virtues are valued for the sake of pleasure, not for their own sake.

parts.author: Epicurus
parts.work: Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X
parts.title: A god among men
parts.context: The letter ends with a portrait of the wise man, and a command.
parts.plain: Epicurus says: who is better than the wise man? He has a right belief about the gods, no fear of death, and knows that the good is easy to get and the bad is short or slight. He does not believe in fate: some things happen by necessity, some by chance, and some by our own choice, which is free. Practise these things day and night, with a friend, and you will live like a god among men.

commentary.on: understands how easily the limit of good things can be reached and attained, and how either the duration or the intensity of evils is but slight
commentary.text: Here, in one sentence, is what later Epicureans called the 'four-part cure': the gods are not to be feared, death is nothing to fear, the good is easy to get, the terrible is easy to bear. You will meet it in the lecture.

commentary.on: whereas our own actions are free, and it is to them that praise and blame naturally attach
commentary.text: Epicurus insists on free will against fate. If everything is fixed, no one can be praised or blamed. The Stoics, whom you will meet later in this journey, believed in fate; this is one of the great quarrels between the schools.

commentary.on: It were better, indeed, to accept the legends of the gods than to bow beneath that yoke of destiny
commentary.text: A striking admission: even the myths are better than iron fate, because you can at least pray to the gods. The fate of 'the natural philosophers' cannot be moved.

commentary.on: both by thyself and with him who is like unto thee
commentary.text: With a friend. Philosophy in the Garden was never solitary. Epicurus wrote that of all the things wisdom provides for a happy life, by far the greatest is friendship.

commentary.on: wilt live as a god among men
commentary.text: The Epicurean promise: to share, in a mortal life, the untroubled happiness of the gods. It is a high hope, and a lonely one, as the god in question takes no notice of us.

read.author: Epicurus
read.work: Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers X
read.who: Epicurus, writing from his school in Athens

paras: Friends indeed came to him from all parts and lived with him in his garden. 11. This is stated by Apollodorus, who also says that he purchased the garden for eighty minae; and to the same effect Diocles in the third book of his Epitome speaks of them as living a very simple and frugal life; at all events they were content with half a pint of thin wine and were, for the rest, thorough-going water-drinkers. He further says that Epicurus did not think it right that their property should be held in common, as required by the maxim of Pythagoras about the goods of friends; such a practice in his opinion implied mistrust, and without confidence there is no friendship. In his correspondence he himself mentions that he was content with plain bread and water. And again: “Send me a little pot of cheese, that, when I like, I may fare sumptuously.” Such was the man who laid down that pleasure was the end of life.

“On this blissful day, which is also the last of my life, I write this to you. My continual sufferings from strangury and dysentery are so great that nothing could augment them; but over against them all I set gladness of mind at the remembrance of our past conversations. But I would have you, as becomes your life-long attitude to me and to philosophy, watch over the children of Metrodorus.”

But you are for bringing my thoughts over to pleasure. What pleasures? Pleasures of the body, I imagine, or such as are recollected or imagined on account of the body. Is this all? Do I explain your opinion rightly? for your disciples are used to deny that we understand at all what Epicurus means. This is what he says, and what that subtle fellow, old Zeno, who is one of the sharpest of them, used, when I was attending lectures at Athens, to enforce and talk so loudly of; saying that he alone was happy who could enjoy present pleasure, and who was at the same time persuaded that he should enjoy it without pain, either during the whole or the greatest part of his life; or if, should any pain interfere, if it was very sharp, then it must be short; should it be of longer continuance, it would have more of what was sweet than bitter in it; that whosoever reflected on these things would be happy, especially if satisfied with the good things which he had already enjoyed, and if he were without fear of death or of the Gods.

Why, Epicurus, do we use any evasions, and not allow in our own words the same feeling to be pleasure which you are used to boast of with such assurance? Are these your words or not? This is what you say in that book which contains all the doctrine of your school; for I will perform on this occasion the office of a translator, lest any one should imagine that I am inventing anything. Thus you speak: "Nor can I form any notion of the chief good, abstracted from those pleasures which are perceived by taste, or from what depends on hearing music, or abstracted from ideas raised by external objects visible to the eye, or by agreeable motions, or from those other pleasures which are perceived by the whole man by means of any of his senses; nor can it possibly be said that the pleasures of the mind are excited only by what is good, for I have perceived men's minds to be pleased with the hopes of enjoying those things which I mentioned above, and with the idea that it should enjoy them without any interruption from pain." And these are his exact words, so that any one may understand what were the pleasures with which Epicurus was acquainted.

Then he speaks thus, a little lower down: "I have often inquired of those who have been called wise men what would be the remaining good if they should exclude from consideration all these pleasures, unless they meant to give us nothing but words. I could never learn anything from them; and unless they choose that all virtue and wisdom should vanish and come to nothing, they must say with me that the only road to happiness lies through those pleasures which I mentioned above." What follows is much the same, and his whole book on the chief good everywhere abounds with the same opinions. Will you, then, invite Telamon to this kind of life to ease his grief? And should you observe any one of your friends under affliction, would you rather prescribe him a sturgeon than a treatise of Socrates? or advise him to listen to the music of a water organ rather than to Plato? or lay before him the beauty and variety of some garden, put a nosegay to his nose, burn perfumes before him, and bid him crown himself with a garland of roses and woodbines? Should you add one thing more, you would certainly wipe out all his grief.

It may be said, What! do you imagine Epicurus really meant this, and that he maintained anything so sensual? Indeed I do not imagine so, for I am sensible that he has uttered many excellent things and sentiments, and delivered maxims of great weight. Therefore, as I said before, I am speaking of his acuteness, not of his morals. Though he should hold those pleasures in contempt which he just now commended, yet I must remember wherein he places the chief good. For he was not contented with barely saying this, but he has explained what he meant: he says that taste, and embraces, and sports, and music, and those forms which affect the eyes with pleasure, are the chief good. Have I invented this? have I misrepresented him? I should be glad to be confuted; for what am I endeavoring at but to clear up truth in every question? Well, but the same man says that pleasure is at its height where pain ceases, and that to be free from all pain is the very greatest pleasure.

Here are three very great mistakes in a very few words. One is, that he contradicts himself; for, but just now, he could not imagine anything good unless the senses were in a manner tickled with some pleasure; but now he says that to be free from pain is the highest pleasure. Can any one contradict himself more? The next mistake is, that where there is naturally a threefold division--the first, to be pleased; next, to be in pain; the last, to be affected neither by pleasure nor pain--he imagines the first and the last to be the same, and makes no difference between pleasure and a cessation of pain. The last mistake he falls into in common with some others, which is this: that as virtue is the most desirable thing, and as philosophy has been investigated with a view to the attainment of it, he has separated the chief good from virtue.

Epicurus denies that any one can live pleasantly who does not lead a life of virtue; he denies that fortune has any power over a wise man; he prefers a spare diet to great plenty, and maintains that a wise man is always happy. All these things become a philosopher to say, but they are not consistent with pleasure.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.title: Bread, water and a little pot of cheese
parts.context: Diogenes is defending Epicurus against slanders, which he has just listed. A mina was a large sum of silver: eighty minae was the price of a good house. Pythagoras, a philosopher of the 500s BC, had taught that 'friends have all things in common'. Idomeneus was one of Epicurus's oldest friends; Metrodorus, his closest disciple, had died seven years before him.
parts.plain: Diogenes says: friends came from everywhere to live with Epicurus in his garden. They lived very simply, drinking mostly water. Epicurus did not make them share their property, because that would mean they did not trust one another. He wrote that he was content with bread and water, and asked a friend for a little pot of cheese as a treat. On the day he died, in great pain, he wrote that it was a happy day, because he remembered their conversations, and asked his friend to look after a dead disciple's children.

commentary.on: Friends indeed came to him from all parts and lived with him in his garden.
commentary.text: The Garden was a community, unusual for its time: it included women, among them the courtesan Leontion, who wrote philosophy, and slaves, among them a man called Mys, whom Epicurus freed in his will.

commentary.on: such a practice in his opinion implied mistrust, and without confidence there is no friendship
commentary.text: A wise point. A community where everything must be shared is policed; one where friends give freely is trusted. Compare the first Christians in Jerusalem, who 'had all things in common' (Acts 2:44), freely.

commentary.on: “Send me a little pot of cheese, that, when I like, I may fare sumptuously.”
commentary.text: The most charming sentence in Diogenes. It is the opposite of the modern meaning of 'epicure'. To the man who has trained himself to want little, a pot of cheese is a feast.

commentary.on: but over against them all I set gladness of mind at the remembrance of our past conversations
commentary.text: Epicurus dying in agony, and calling it a blissful day. Here is his philosophy tested on himself: the pleasure of the mind, remembering friendship, outweighs the pain of the body. Whatever you think of the theory, it is hard not to admire the man.

parts.author: Cicero
parts.title: Would you prescribe him a sturgeon?
parts.context: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the great Roman orator and statesman, wrote the Tusculan Disputations in 45 BC, at his country house at Tusculum, after the death of his beloved daughter Tullia. Book III asks how to cure grief. He has studied in Athens and heard the Epicurean teacher Zeno of Sidon (not the Stoic Zeno). Telamon is a hero of Greek tragedy, driven into exile. This is C. D. Yonge's translation of 1853; the cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Cicero says: if Epicurus asks me to think of good things in my grief, I will gladly; but he means pleasures. He quotes Epicurus's own words: 'I cannot imagine the good without the pleasures of taste, sex, music and beautiful sights.' So would you comfort a grieving friend with a fine fish, perfume and a garland? Cicero admits Epicurus said many excellent things. But he finds three mistakes: Epicurus contradicts himself (pleasure is the senses, then pleasure is just no pain); he confuses pleasure with the mere absence of pain; and he separates the highest good from virtue. And his praise of virtue and simple living does not fit his theory.

commentary.on: But you are for bringing my thoughts over to pleasure. What pleasures?
commentary.text: Cicero's question is the right one: what does Epicurus mean by pleasure? Everything turns on it.

commentary.on: Nor can I form any notion of the chief good, abstracted from those pleasures which are perceived by taste, or from what depends on hearing music
commentary.text: This is a real quotation from Epicurus's lost book On the End. Diogenes Laertius quotes the same sentence (X.6). It sits awkwardly beside the Letter to Menoeceus, and Epicurus's critics have never let it go.

commentary.on: would you rather prescribe him a sturgeon than a treatise of Socrates?
commentary.text: A sturgeon was a luxury fish. Cicero's point is that pleasure cannot comfort grief. You do not hand a widow a box of chocolates. Remember this when we come to grief again, later in the journey.

commentary.on: I am sensible that he has uttered many excellent things and sentiments, and delivered maxims of great weight
commentary.text: Cicero is fair. He was friends with many Epicureans, among them Atticus, his closest friend. He says he is criticising Epicurus's reasoning, not his morals.

commentary.on: he imagines the first and the last to be the same, and makes no difference between pleasure and a cessation of pain
commentary.text: The philosophical heart of the objection. Is 'not being in pain' really a pleasure? Or is it just a neutral state, like being asleep? If it is neutral, Epicurus's calm happiness is closer to anaesthetic than to joy.

commentary.on: he has separated the chief good from virtue
commentary.text: The deepest objection. For Cicero, as for the Stoics, goodness must be chosen for its own sake. If I am honest only because honesty makes me feel safe, would I lie when I was sure of not being caught?

commentary.on: All these things become a philosopher to say, but they are not consistent with pleasure.
commentary.text: Cicero's final charge: Epicurus lived better than his theory. His simple life, his courage and his friendships are admirable; but they do not follow from 'pleasure is the goal'.

compare.author: Diogenes Laertius and Cicero
compare.why: Did the Epicureans live as they taught? Read how Diogenes describes the Garden, and Epicurus's last letter. Then Cicero, writing in 45 BC, attacks the idea that pleasure can be the goal of life. He is a critic who tries to be fair.
compare.title: The Garden lived, and a Roman critic

paras: Epicurus's school was not a lecture hall but a household. Friends lived together in his house and garden in Athens, sharing simple meals and long conversations. Women belonged to it, which was rare: Leontion wrote a book against the philosopher Theophrastus, and Themista corresponded with Epicurus. So did slaves. Above the gate, according to the Roman writer Seneca, was written: 'Stranger, here you will do well to tarry; here our highest good is pleasure.'

The school kept the master's birthday every year and held a feast for him and Metrodorus on the twentieth of every month, as his will directed. Students learned his sayings by heart. Epicurus wrote: 'Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.' (Principal Doctrines 27, Hicks.) The Garden lasted for centuries, and there were Epicurean communities across the Greek and Roman world.
sections.key: The Garden was a household of friends, including women and slaves, living simply around shared sayings; Epicurus called friendship wisdom's greatest gift.

paras: Why should knowing about nature make you calm? Epicurus took from Democritus, a Greek thinker of the 400s BC, the theory that everything is made of atoms, tiny uncuttable bodies ('atom' means 'uncuttable'), moving in an infinite empty space. Worlds form when atoms collide and cling together, and fall apart again. The soul too is made of fine atoms, which scatter at death.

If that is true, two fears vanish. Thunder and plague are not punishments; they have natural causes. And there is no one left after death to be punished. Epicurus said plainly that if we had never been troubled by fear of the sky and of death, we would have had no need to study nature (Principal Doctrines 11).

But if atoms only fall and collide according to fixed laws, are we free? Epicurus's followers said that atoms sometimes 'swerve' a tiny, unpredictable amount. This swerve, which Lucretius calls the clinamen, makes room for free will. It is not described in Epicurus's surviving letters; we know it from Lucretius and Cicero, and Cicero mocked it as an invention to rescue a theory.
sections.key: Atoms and empty space explain everything, so neither the sky nor death need be feared; a tiny 'swerve' of atoms was meant to leave room for free will.

paras: Later Epicureans boiled the teaching down to four lines, which they called the tetrapharmakos, the 'four-part medicine' (an ointment made from four ingredients). The version that survives comes from Philodemus, an Epicurean teacher of the first century BC whose library was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 at Herculaneum and is still being read today. In plain words: God is nothing to fear; death is nothing to worry about; what is good is easy to get; what is terrible is easy to bear.

Each line answers a fear. The first two are the fears of the gods and death, which the Letter to Menoeceus tackles first. The third answers greed and anxiety about money: the necessary things are cheap. The fourth answers fear of pain: Epicurus held that severe pain is short and long pain is mild (Principal Doctrines 4). You may doubt the fourth; Epicurus, who died of a kidney stone, did not.
sections.key: The four-part cure: God is nothing to fear, death nothing to worry about, the good is easy to get, the terrible easy to bear.

paras: 'Hedonism' comes from hedone, the Greek for pleasure, and in one sense Epicurus is the West's most famous hedonist: he says pleasure is the only thing good in itself. But he is almost the opposite of what the word now suggests. His highest pleasure is a state of rest: no pain in the body and no turmoil in the mind. The best route to it is to want less.

The confusion is ancient. A rival school, the Cyrenaics, did praise the pleasures of the moment, and Epicurus's enemies spread stories that he gorged himself and slept with his pupils. The Roman poet Horace joked that he was 'a pig from Epicurus's herd' (Epistles I.4). The modern 'epicure', a lover of fine food, comes from the slanders, not from the man who asked for a little pot of cheese.
So the fair answer is: yes, Epicurus is a hedonist in theory, because pleasure is the goal; no, he is not a pleasure-seeker in practice, because the pleasure he wants is calm.
sections.key: Epicurus is a hedonist in theory (pleasure is the goal) but not in practice: his pleasure is calm, reached by wanting less.

paras: The Epicureans were the most attacked school of the ancient world. Cicero, as you have read, thought they confused pleasure with the absence of pain and cut goodness loose from virtue. The Stoics agreed. Plutarch, a Greek writer of about AD 100, wrote a whole essay arguing that it is impossible to live pleasantly on Epicurus's principles: without the hope of a life to come, he said, the death of those we love is unbearable.

Jews and Christians had another objection. In the Mishnah, the Jewish law code of about AD 200, 'an Epicurean' (apikoros) is someone who has no share in the world to come (Sanhedrin 10:1), and the word still means a heretic or unbeliever in Hebrew. For Christians, Epicurus's gods, who take no notice of us, are hardly gods at all. And a philosophy that makes friendship the greatest good, but asks nothing of us for strangers, can look small beside a command to love one's neighbour.
Yet the Garden's admirers are many and serious, from Lucretius to Thomas Jefferson, who wrote in 1819, 'I too am an Epicurean'. The next session, still to come, hears its greatest voice.
sections.key: Cicero, the Stoics and Plutarch attacked Epicurus's pleasure; Jews and Christians, his uncaring gods and his denial of a life to come. He has also had serious admirers.

paras: One of Epicurus's most interesting claims is that the virtues and pleasure cannot be separated: 'it is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly' (Principal Doctrines 5). Why should that be? Because the unjust live in fear. Epicurus thought justice was an agreement among people not to harm one another, and that the wrongdoer can never be sure he will not be found out. Even if he escapes, he lives with the dread of discovery, and dread is the opposite of pleasure.

So Epicurus arrives at a fairly ordinary list of virtues (prudence, honesty, justice, courage, moderation) by an unusual road. He values them as a doctor values exercise: for what they do, not for their own sake. Cicero thought this made goodness fragile. A person who is honest only because dishonesty is risky may lie when the risk disappears. Epicurus's defenders answer that a person trained in the Garden would find lying itself disturbing. The argument between them, about whether goodness must be its own reward, runs right through the history of ethics, and you will meet it again in the Stoics.
sections.key: Epicurus held that the virtues are needed for a pleasant life, since the unjust live in fear; critics answered that goodness valued only as a means is fragile.

refs: Diogenes Laertius X.1–28 (life), X.122–135 (Letter to Menoeceus), X.139–154 (Principal Doctrines), tr. R. D. Hicks, Loeb Classical Library (1925).
Cicero, Tusculan Disputations III.17–21 (45 BC), tr. C. D. Yonge (1853); Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods I.69–70 and On Fate 22–23 on the swerve.
Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II.216–293 (the swerve).
Philodemus, Against the Sophists (PHerc. 1005) col. 4.9–14 (the tetrapharmakos).
Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 21.10 (the inscription over the Garden gate); Horace, Epistles I.4.16; Plutarch, That Epicurus Actually Makes a Pleasant Life Impossible (Moralia 1086c–1107c).
Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10:1; Thomas Jefferson to William Short, 31 October 1819.

Modern: Pierre Hadot, What is Ancient Philosophy? (1995, English 2002); Martha Nussbaum, The Therapy of Desire (1994), chapters 4–7; Tim O'Keefe, Epicureanism (2010); James Warren, Facing Death: Epicurus and his Critics (2004).

debate.question: Is Epicurus right that death is nothing to us?

positions.name: Yes: where death is, I am not
positions.who: Epicurus; Lucretius; many modern naturalists
positions.view: Harm must be felt by someone. When I am dead there is no one to feel anything, so being dead cannot harm me. Lucretius added that I do not mind the endless time before I was born, so I should not mind the endless time after I die.
positions.evidence: Letter to Menoeceus 124–125; Principal Doctrines 2; Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III.

positions.name: No: death takes away goods
positions.who: Thomas Nagel, 'Death' (1970), and most modern philosophers who write on it
positions.view: Death harms us not by being felt but by depriving us of the life we would have had. A man betrayed behind his back is harmed though he never finds out. The young person's death is a loss even though they do not experience it.
positions.evidence: The 'deprivation' account; our ordinary sense that an early death is a tragedy for the one who dies.

positions.name: The argument misses what we fear
positions.who: Plutarch; many Christian writers; the Jewish and Christian traditions
positions.view: Even if being dead does not hurt, we love life and people, and death ends love. Epicurus cures fear by teaching us to want less of life. The Bible calls death an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26) and does not ask us to stop minding it.
positions.evidence: Plutarch, That Epicurus Actually Makes a Pleasant Life Impossible; John 11:35; 1 Corinthians 15.

debate.agree: All agree that much fear of death is fear of something imagined, such as punishment after death or the pain of dying, and that facing death clearly can make a life better.

look.why: Louis Le Nain painted this poor family around 1645 in France. It is not a picture of Epicurus, and the people at table are a family, not a school of friends. It is here because it shows the kind of meal Epicurus praised: plain food and drink, a few people, and nothing to spare.
points: An elderly man, a woman and a boy sit around a low barrel, partly covered with a white cloth, used as a makeshift table.
Their clothing, in pale sand-brown and white, has rips and holes.
On the barrel are a pewter plate holding a mound of food, and a spoon; an empty wooden bowl is tucked by the man's elbow.
The boy holds a jug in one hand and a tall, narrow glass of red liquid in the other, and looks at the old man.
In the background a young girl stands at a tall hearth, her face warmed pink by the fire.

music.why: Epicurus put friendship at the centre of the happy life. This old chant, sung while the feet of others are washed, puts love at the centre and God within it: 'Where charity and love are, God is there.' Listen for the difference between a circle of friends and a love that kneels.

think.why: Epicurus says death is nothing to us. See what Christians believe instead.

learn.why: The most famous argument against the fear of death, in one sentence. Know it well enough to weigh it.

check.q: What does Epicurus mean by 'pleasure' when he calls it the goal of life?
options: The pleasures of the table and of love, enjoyed in moderation
Freedom from pain in the body and from trouble in the soul
Whatever each person happens to enjoy
The joy of the gods, which humans reach after death
check.why: 'By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul' (X.131). The first option is the common misreading; the last contradicts his denial of an afterlife.

check.q: Why does Epicurus say the truly irreverent person is the one who believes what most people say about the gods?
options: Because only philosophers are allowed to speak about the gods
Because the popular gods are foreign
Because the popular stories make the gods angry, jealous and busy with us, which does not fit perfectly happy beings
Because he thinks the gods do not exist
check.why: Epicurus believed in gods, but a blessed, immortal being would never be troubled with rewarding and punishing us. The first option is a common mistake: he was not an atheist.

check.q: What follows from Epicurus's argument that 'when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not'?
options: That we should try to live as long as possible
That being dead cannot be bad for us, so fearing it in advance is pointless pain
That the soul survives death in another form
That dying is never painful
check.why: Good and evil need someone to feel them; the dead feel nothing. Note that the argument is about being dead, not about the pain of dying.

check.q: Why does Epicurus praise bread and water?
options: Because once hunger is removed, simple food gives as much pleasure as rich food, and needing little makes you fearless of fortune
Because the gods command a simple diet
Because he was too poor to afford anything else
Because luxury is sinful
check.why: The highest pleasure is the removal of pain, and simple things do that perfectly. The first option sounds right but uses a religious idea Epicurus did not hold.

check.q: Which is Cicero's deepest objection in the Tusculan Disputations?
options: That by making pleasure the goal, Epicurus separates the highest good from virtue
That Epicurus believed in too many gods
That Epicurus wrote too many books
That Epicurus was personally a glutton
check.why: Cicero says explicitly that he is criticising Epicurus's reasoning, not his morals. His charge is that goodness must be valued for its own sake.

check.q: A friend says: 'Epicureanism just means: if it feels good, do it.' What is the best reply?
options: Epicurus said every pleasure is good in itself, but many lead to greater pains, so the wise choose few pleasures and aim at calm
Epicurus thought pleasure was evil
That is right; Epicurus said every pleasure is good
Epicurus only cared about the pleasures of the mind and thought the body was worthless
check.why: 'While therefore all pleasure ... is good, not all pleasure is choiceworthy' (X.129). He valued bodily pleasure too, as the pot of cheese shows.

tutorial.question: Is Epicureanism hedonism?
tutorial.approach: Define hedonism. Show what Epicurus says pleasure is, using the Letter to Menoeceus, and how he sorts desires. Then give Cicero's objections: the quotation from On the End, the confusion of pleasure with no pain, and the separation of good from virtue. End with your own judgement: is calm a pleasure, and is Epicurus's life better than his theory?
strong: Distinguishes hedonism as a theory (pleasure is the only good) from pleasure-seeking.
Quotes Epicurus's definition of pleasure and his sorting of desires.
Explains static pleasure (calm) and why simple things give it.
Gives Cicero's objections fairly, including the awkward quotation from On the End.
Considers whether the virtues can be valued only as means to pleasure.
Reaches a clear judgement.

reading.author: Epicurus
reading.title: The Art of Happiness (tr. George Strodach)
reading.why: All the surviving letters and sayings in a clear modern translation, with an introduction.

reading.author: Tim O'Keefe
reading.title: Epicureanism
reading.why: A short, careful account of the whole system: atoms, the swerve, pleasure and death.

reading.author: Martha Nussbaum
reading.title: The Therapy of Desire
reading.why: The Hellenistic schools as medicine for the soul; chapters 4 to 7 on Epicurus and Lucretius.

reading.author: James Warren
reading.title: Facing Death: Epicurus and his Critics
reading.why: The arguments about death, ancient and modern, weighed with care.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Epicurus's test of desires. Each evening, write down one thing you wanted today. Ask: is this natural and necessary, natural but not necessary, or empty? Go without one 'empty' thing this week, and notice whether you miss it.
sessions.reflect: What do you fear most? Would Epicurus's arguments touch that fear, or miss it?
takeaways: Epicurus taught that pleasure is the goal of life, but by pleasure he meant freedom from pain and fear, reached by wanting little.
He removed two great fears: of gods who punish, and of death, which is 'nothing to us'.
The Garden lived simply among friends; Cicero objected that pleasure cannot comfort grief and that goodness must be loved for its own sake.

sessions.title: The case against religion
sessions.line: A Roman poet turns Epicurus into verse and tells of a king who killed his daughter to get a fair wind: 'Such are the crimes to which Religion leads.'
sessions.plain: Around 55 BC the Roman poet Lucretius wrote a long poem, On the Nature of Things, to carry Epicurus's teaching to Rome. Near its start he tells how the Greek king Agamemnon sacrificed his own daughter to the goddess Diana to win a fair wind for the war against Troy. Religion, he says, breeds terror and crime; knowing how nature works sets us free. This session reads that passage, the West's first great argument against religion, and sets beside it the Bible's own attack on false gods.
