sessions.why: Session 1 showed Epicurus's first step to peace: remove the fear of the gods. His Roman follower Lucretius turned that step into a full attack on religion itself. Before we hear any answer to the question 'how do you find peace?', we should hear the strongest case that religion is the enemy of peace.
answers: Who was Lucretius, and what is his poem about?
Why did he think religion causes evil?
How was the poem lost and found again?
Is Lucretius's critique fair to religion, and does the Bible agree with any of it?
sessions.finding: Lucretius argued that religion breeds terror and crime, and that knowing nature frees us from both: the West's first great argument against religion, which the Bible partly shares, against false gods.

paras: Session 1 read Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus. His first 'element of right life' was a right belief about the gods: they exist, perfectly happy, and take no notice of us. The popular belief that gods reward and punish, he said, causes the greatest fear. His second step was to show that death is nothing to us, because the soul is made of atoms that scatter.
Epicurus wrote in plain prose. Two centuries later, in Rome, a poet set out to make his teaching beautiful.
background.key: Epicurus removed the fear of punishing gods and of death; Lucretius would put his teaching into Latin verse.

paras: Almost nothing is known about Titus Lucretius Carus. He probably lived from about 99 to about 55 BC, in the last troubled years of the Roman Republic, a time of civil wars between Marius and Sulla, and then between Caesar and Pompey. His poem is addressed to Memmius, a Roman politician. Cicero wrote to his brother in February 54 BC that the poem had 'many flashes of genius, yet much art'. Four centuries later, Jerome told a story that Lucretius was driven mad by a love potion and killed himself; most scholars think it a late and hostile invention.

On the Nature of Things has six books, about 7,400 lines of Latin verse: atoms and space (Books I and II), the soul and death (III), the senses and love (IV), the world and the history of humankind (V), and storms, earthquakes and plague (VI). It seems unfinished. It is one of the great poems of Latin literature.

timeline.text: Lucretius probably born
Lucretius probably dies; On the Nature of Things left unfinished
Cicero praises the poem in a letter to his brother
Monks copy the poem: the two oldest manuscripts, now in Leiden
Poggio Bracciolini finds a manuscript in a German monastery
First printed edition, at Brescia
Montaigne's Essays quote Lucretius more than any other poet but Virgil and Horace
William Ellery Leonard's English verse translation, which we read

background.key: Lucretius (c. 99–55 BC) wrote six books of Latin verse to bring Epicurus to Rome. Little is known of his life.

paras: The story at the heart of our reading comes from the myths of the Trojan War. The Greek fleet gathered at Aulis, a harbour in Greece, to sail for Troy, but the goddess Artemis (the Romans called her Diana) held back the winds. A seer declared that she would be satisfied only if the commander, King Agamemnon, sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia. He did. The Athenian playwright Aeschylus told it in the Agamemnon (458 BC); Euripides, in Iphigenia at Aulis, let the goddess snatch the girl away and leave a deer in her place.
Lucretius tells it straight, with no rescue. Leonard's translation does not name her; in the Latin she is Iphianassa, another form of her name.
background.key: Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to win winds for Troy: the story Lucretius tells as the crime of religion.

paras: The main reading is from the opening of Book I: Lucretius's praise of Epicurus as the man who defeated religion, the sacrifice of Iphigenia, the threats of priests, and the promise that knowledge of nature will drive out fear. It is the West's first great written argument that religion itself is harmful. It answers this session's question directly.

The comparison is from the Hebrew Bible. Psalm 14 opens with the famous line 'The fool has said in his heart, "There is no God"', and the prophet Isaiah mocks the man who carves a god from the same log he uses for his fire. They let us ask whether the Bible is on the side of Lucretius's 'Religion' or against it.
background.key: Lucretius's attack on religion, then a psalm and a prophet who also attack false gods.

before: How does Lucretius picture 'Religion'? Notice where she is and what she looks like.
What, according to the poem, gives priests their power over people?
What does Lucretius offer instead of religion?
sessions.readWhy: The opening argument of Lucretius's poem, in four parts: the conqueror, the sacrifice, the threats of the seers, and the cure.

paras:
Whilst human kind
Throughout the lands lay miserably crushed
Before all eyes beneath Religion--who
Would show her head along the region skies,
Glowering on mortals with her hideous face--
A Greek it was who first opposing dared
Raise mortal eyes that terror to withstand,
Whom nor the fame of Gods nor lightning's stroke
Nor threatening thunder of the ominous sky
Abashed; but rather chafed to angry zest
His dauntless heart to be the first to rend
The crossbars at the gates of Nature old.
And thus his will and hardy wisdom won;
And forward thus he fared afar, beyond
The flaming ramparts of the world, until
He wandered the unmeasurable All.
Whence he to us, a conqueror, reports
What things can rise to being, what cannot,
And by what law to each its scope prescribed,
Its boundary stone that clings so deep in Time.
Wherefore Religion now is under foot,
And us his victory now exalts to heaven.

I fear perhaps thou deemest that we fare
An impious road to realms of thought profane;
But 'tis that same religion oftener far
Hath bred the foul impieties of men:
As once at Aulis, the elected chiefs,
Foremost of heroes, Danaan counsellors,
Defiled Diana's altar, virgin queen,
With Agamemnon's daughter, foully slain.
She felt the chaplet round her maiden locks
And fillets, fluttering down on either cheek,
And at the altar marked her grieving sire,
The priests beside him who concealed the knife,
And all the folk in tears at sight of her.
With a dumb terror and a sinking knee
She dropped; nor might avail her now that first
'Twas she who gave the king a father's name.
They raised her up, they bore the trembling girl
On to the altar--hither led not now
With solemn rites and hymeneal choir,
But sinless woman, sinfully foredone,
A parent felled her on her bridal day,
Making his child a sacrificial beast
To give the ships auspicious winds for Troy:
Such are the crimes to which Religion leads.

And there shall come the time when even thou,
Forced by the soothsayer's terror-tales, shalt seek
To break from us. Ah, many a dream even now
Can they concoct to rout thy plans of life,
And trouble all thy fortunes with base fears.
I own with reason: for, if men but knew
Some fixed end to ills, they would be strong
By some device unconquered to withstand
Religions and the menacings of seers.
But now nor skill nor instrument is theirs,
Since men must dread eternal pains in death.
For what the soul may be they do not know,
Whether 'tis born, or enter in at birth,
And whether, snatched by death, it die with us,
Or visit the shadows and the vasty caves
Of Orcus, or by some divine decree
Enter the brute herds, as our Ennius sang,
Who first from lovely Helicon brought down
A laurel wreath of bright perennial leaves,
Renowned forever among the Italian clans.
Yet Ennius too in everlasting verse
Proclaims those vaults of Acheron to be,
Though thence, he said, nor souls nor bodies fare,
But only phantom figures, strangely wan,
And tells how once from out those regions rose
Old Homer's ghost to him and shed salt tears
And with his words unfolded Nature's source.
Then be it ours with steady mind to clasp
The purport of the skies--the law behind
The wandering courses of the sun and moon;
To scan the powers that speed all life below;
But most to see with reasonable eyes
Of what the mind, of what the soul is made,
And what it is so terrible that breaks
On us asleep, or waking in disease,
Until we seem to mark and hear at hand
Dead men whose bones earth bosomed long ago.

This terror, then, this darkness of the mind,
Not sunrise with its flaring spokes of light,
Nor glittering arrows of morning can disperse,
But only Nature's aspect and her law,
Which, teaching us, hath this exordium:
Nothing from nothing ever yet was born.
Fear holds dominion over mortality
Only because, seeing in land and sky
So much the cause whereof no wise they know,
Men think Divinities are working there.
Meantime, when once we know from nothing still
Nothing can be create, we shall divine
More clearly what we seek: those elements
From which alone all things created are,
And how accomplished by no tool of Gods.

parts.author: Lucretius
parts.work: On the Nature of Things, Book I
parts.ref: On the Nature of Things I.62–79
parts.title: A Greek who dared
parts.who: Lucretius, Roman poet
parts.context: The poem opens with a hymn to Venus. Then, at line 62 of the Latin, Lucretius praises Epicurus, without naming him: 'a Greek'. Leonard's 1916 translation is in blank verse, unrhymed lines of ten syllables, so its line numbers differ from the Latin's; we give the Latin numbers. 'Nature old' is Lucretius's word for the whole universe.
parts.plain: Lucretius says: humanity lay crushed under Religion, who glowered down from the sky. Then a Greek, Epicurus, dared to look her in the face. Neither stories of the gods nor thunder frightened him. His mind travelled beyond the walls of the world, through the infinite universe, and brought back the knowledge of what can and cannot happen. Now Religion is under our feet, and his victory raises us to heaven.

commentary.on:
Before all eyes beneath Religion--who
Would show her head along the region skies,
Glowering on mortals with her hideous face--
commentary.text: Religion is a monster in the sky, looking down. The Latin word is religio, which for Lucretius meant fearful scruple about the gods, ritual and taboo, more than belief. Leonard capitalises it, as if it were a goddess. The picture is political as well as spiritual: humanity is 'crushed' by a tyrant.

commentary.on:
A Greek it was who first opposing dared
Raise mortal eyes that terror to withstand,
commentary.text: Epicurus is a hero, almost a god himself, who dares what no one else would. Notice the irony: Lucretius worships the man who abolished worship.

commentary.on: The crossbars at the gates of Nature old.
commentary.text: Nature is pictured as a locked city, and Epicurus as the first to break its gates. Knowledge is a conquest.

commentary.on:
beyond
The flaming ramparts of the world, until
He wandered the unmeasurable All.
commentary.text: The 'flaming ramparts' are the outer sphere of fire that Greeks imagined around the world. Epicurus's mind goes beyond it into the infinite universe of atoms and empty space. Lucretius was among the first to picture an infinite universe with many worlds.

commentary.on:
What things can rise to being, what cannot,
And by what law to each its scope prescribed,
commentary.text: This is what he brings back: the laws of nature. If everything happens by fixed natural law, there is no room for gods who interfere. That is the comfort.

commentary.on:
Wherefore Religion now is under foot,
And us his victory now exalts to heaven.
commentary.text: A triumph. The positions are swapped: Religion, once in the sky, is trampled; humanity, once crushed, is raised to the heavens. It is perhaps the first statement in Western literature that human knowledge can take the place of the gods.

parts.author: Lucretius
parts.work: On the Nature of Things, Book I
parts.ref: On the Nature of Things I.80–101
parts.title: Such are the crimes to which Religion leads
parts.context: Lucretius expects Memmius to object that his philosophy is impious, an offence against the gods. He answers with a story. A passage on the difficulty of putting Greek ideas into Latin, which Leonard (following some editors of his day) prints at this point, is left out; the cut is marked '…'. The 'Danaans' are the Greeks; 'chaplet' and 'fillets' are the wreath and ribbons put on a sacrificial animal, and on a bride.
parts.plain: Lucretius says: you may think my teaching is wicked. But it is religion that has caused wicked deeds. At Aulis the Greek leaders killed Agamemnon's daughter at Diana's altar. She saw her father, the priests hiding the knife, the weeping crowd; she sank to her knees in terror. She was carried to the altar not for her wedding but for her death, killed by her own father, so that the ships could sail to Troy. 'Such are the crimes to which Religion leads.'

commentary.on:
But 'tis that same religion oftener far
Hath bred the foul impieties of men:
commentary.text: The turn of the argument. You call me impious? Religion itself is the great impiety. Lucretius throws the charge back at his accusers, as Epicurus did.

commentary.on:
She felt the chaplet round her maiden locks
And fillets, fluttering down on either cheek,
commentary.text: The details are of a bride and of an animal for sacrifice at once: both wore garlands and ribbons. Lucretius makes us see the girl, and feel her confusion.

commentary.on:
The priests beside him who concealed the knife,
And all the folk in tears at sight of her.
commentary.text: Everyone weeps, and yet it happens. This is Lucretius's point: religion makes decent people do what they know is monstrous, because they fear the gods more than they trust their own pity.

commentary.on:
But sinless woman, sinfully foredone,
A parent felled her on her bridal day,
commentary.text: 'Foredone' means killed. The innocent is destroyed by the guilty, a father kills his child. The Latin plays on the words for pure and impure; Leonard keeps it in 'sinless' and 'sinfully'.

commentary.on:
To give the ships auspicious winds for Troy:
Such are the crimes to which Religion leads.
commentary.text: The line every educated European once knew in Latin: tantum religio potuit suadere malorum, 'so much evil could religion persuade'. Voltaire said it would last as long as the world. Notice what it claims: not that one religion went wrong, but that religion as such leads to crime.

parts.author: Lucretius
parts.work: On the Nature of Things, Book I
parts.ref: On the Nature of Things I.102–135
parts.title: The terror-tales of the seers
parts.context: Lucretius turns from Greek myth to the present. Seers (vates) were prophets and priests who told of punishments after death. Ennius (239–169 BC) was the first great Latin poet, who wrote that Homer's ghost appeared to him in a dream. Orcus and Acheron are names for the underworld.
parts.plain: Lucretius says: you too, Memmius, will be tempted to leave us, frightened by the priests' stories. They have power because people fear eternal punishment after death. And people fear it because they do not know what the soul is: whether it dies with us, goes down to the underworld, or passes into animals. So we must study the sky and, above all, the nature of the soul, and what it is that frightens us in dreams and illness when we seem to see the dead.

commentary.on:
Forced by the soothsayer's terror-tales, shalt seek
To break from us.
commentary.text: Lucretius knows how strong fear is. Even a convinced Epicurean may be pulled back by stories of hell.

commentary.on:
for, if men but knew
Some fixed end to ills, they would be strong
commentary.text: The diagnosis: what makes us vulnerable to priests is uncertainty about death. If we knew suffering ends at death, we would be free.

commentary.on: Since men must dread eternal pains in death.
commentary.text: The heart of the case. For Lucretius, the fear of eternal punishment is the root of religion's power and of human misery. The whole of his Book III argues that the soul dies with the body.

commentary.on:
But most to see with reasonable eyes
Of what the mind, of what the soul is made,
commentary.text: The cure is knowledge: science, as we would say, especially the science of the mind. It is a programme the modern world would recognise.

parts.author: Lucretius
parts.work: On the Nature of Things, Book I
parts.ref: On the Nature of Things I.146–158
parts.title: Nothing from nothing
parts.context: The first law of Lucretius's physics, and his promise.
parts.plain: Lucretius says: this darkness of the mind cannot be chased away by sunlight, only by understanding how nature works. Its first law is that nothing comes from nothing. People are afraid because they see things happen whose causes they do not know, and so they think gods are doing them. Once we know that nothing is made from nothing, we will see how everything comes about without the gods.

commentary.on:
Not sunrise with its flaring spokes of light,
Nor glittering arrows of morning can disperse,
But only Nature's aspect and her law,
commentary.text: These lines appear four times in the poem, like a refrain. The darkness is ignorance, and the light is knowledge of nature.

commentary.on: Nothing from nothing ever yet was born.
commentary.text: The Latin is nil posse creari de nilo, 'nothing can be created from nothing'. It is the first law of Epicurean physics. Notice that Christians would later teach the opposite: that God made the world 'out of nothing' (ex nihilo). The two views of the world part company on the first page.

commentary.on: Men think Divinities are working there.
commentary.text: Lucretius's theory of why people believe in gods: ignorance of causes. It is the ancestor of the modern 'god of the gaps' objection, that religion fills the gaps in our knowledge and retreats as science advances.

commentary.on: And how accomplished by no tool of Gods.
commentary.text: The conclusion: the world runs without gods. Lucretius does not deny that gods exist; like Epicurus, he thinks they live far away in bliss. But they do nothing.

read.author: Lucretius
read.work: On the Nature of Things, Book I
read.ref: On the Nature of Things I.62–79
read.who: Lucretius, Roman poet

paras:
The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.”
They are corrupt.
They have done abominable deeds.
There is no one who does good.

Yahweh looked down from heaven on the children of men,
to see if there were any who understood,
who sought after God.

They have all gone aside.
They have together become corrupt.
There is no one who does good, no, not one.

Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge,
who eat up my people as they eat bread,
and don’t call on Yahweh?

There they were in great fear,
for God is in the generation of the righteous.

You frustrate the plan of the poor,
because Yahweh is his refuge.

Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion!
When Yahweh restores the fortunes of his people,
then Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.

Everyone who makes a carved image is vain.
The things that they delight in will not profit.
Their own witnesses don’t see, nor know, that they may be disappointed.

Who has fashioned a god,
or molds an image that is profitable for nothing?

Behold, all his fellows will be disappointed;
and the workmen are mere men.
Let them all be gathered together.
Let them stand up.
They will fear.
They will be put to shame together.

The blacksmith takes an ax,
works in the coals,
fashions it with hammers,
and works it with his strong arm.
He is hungry,
and his strength fails;
he drinks no water,
and is faint.

The carpenter stretches out a line.
He marks it out with a pencil.
He shapes it with planes.
He marks it out with compasses,
and shapes it like the figure of a man,
with the beauty of a man,
to reside in a house.

He cuts down cedars for himself,
and takes the cypress and the oak,
and strengthens for himself one among the trees of the forest.
He plants a cypress tree,
and the rain nourishes it.

He burns part of it in the fire.
With part of it, he eats meat.
He roasts a roast, and is satisfied.
Yes, he warms himself,
and says, “Aha! I am warm. I have seen the fire.”

The rest of it he makes into a god,
even his engraved image.
He bows down to it and worships,
and prays to it, and says, “Deliver me; for you are my god!”

No one thinks,
neither is there knowledge nor understanding to say,
“I have burned part of it in the fire.
Yes, I have also baked bread on its coals.
I have roasted meat and eaten it.
Shall I make the rest of it into an abomination?
Shall I bow down to a tree trunk?”

He feeds on ashes.
A deceived heart has turned him aside;
and he can’t deliver his soul,
nor say, “Isn’t there a lie in my right hand?”

parts.title: The fool has said in his heart
parts.context: The Psalms are the prayer book of ancient Israel, 150 poems written over several centuries. This one is headed 'For the Chief Musician. By David.' It appears again, almost word for word, as Psalm 53. Like the rest of the World English Bible, it uses God's name, Yahweh.

commentary.on: The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.”
commentary.text: The most quoted line against unbelief. But the Hebrew word for 'fool', nabal, means someone morally foolish, not unintelligent. And 'there is no God' in this psalm probably means 'God does not see or care', as in Psalm 10:4 and 11. It is close to Epicurus's distant gods, not to modern atheism.

commentary.on:
They are corrupt.
They have done abominable deeds.
commentary.text: The psalm connects the denial of God with wrongdoing, the opposite of Lucretius, who connects religion with wrongdoing. Each thinks the other's view lets people do terrible things.

commentary.on: who eat up my people as they eat bread,
commentary.text: The psalm's real target: those who exploit the poor, believing no one will hold them to account. For the psalmist, a God who sees is the protection of the weak.

commentary.on:
You frustrate the plan of the poor,
because Yahweh is his refuge.
commentary.text: Here the fear Lucretius wanted to abolish works the other way: the oppressors, not the poor, should be afraid. God is the refuge of the powerless.

parts.title: Half of it he burns in the fire
parts.context: These chapters of Isaiah were most likely written in the 500s BC, when many of the people of Judah were exiles in Babylon, surrounded by the great statues of the Babylonian gods. The prophet mocks them.

commentary.on: Everyone who makes a carved image is vain.
commentary.text: 'Vain' here means empty, worthless. The prophet's attack on idols is as fierce as Lucretius's attack on religion, and much funnier.

commentary.on:
He is hungry,
and his strength fails;
commentary.text: The god-maker gets tired and hungry. How can a weak man make a strong god?

commentary.on:
Yes, he burns it, and bakes bread.
Yes, he makes a god, and worships it;
commentary.text: The heart of the satire: the same log makes the fire for his supper and the god he prays to. The joke is old and still sharp.

commentary.on: “Deliver me; for you are my god!”
commentary.text: Compare Iphigenia. Isaiah and Lucretius agree that worshipping what we make, and fearing it, is a terrible error. They disagree about what follows: Lucretius says the gods are far away and do nothing; Isaiah says the true God made the cedar and the rain, and does not need us to carve him.

commentary.on: Shall I bow down to a tree trunk?
commentary.text: The early Christians were called 'atheists' by the Romans, because they refused to worship the city's gods. Justin Martyr, around AD 155, accepted the name for those gods (First Apology 6). On idols, Lucretius and the Bible are allies.

compare.why: Is the Bible on the side of Lucretius's 'Religion'? Read a psalm that condemns the person who says there is no God, and a prophet who mocks idols as fiercely as Lucretius mocks the gods.
compare.title: The fool and the idol-maker

paras: Lucretius makes three claims. First, religion is fear: people believe in gods who punish because they do not understand the causes of things. Second, religion is harmful: fear drives people to crimes like Agamemnon's. Third, knowledge cures it: when we understand nature, the fear goes and so does religion's power.

Each claim has had a long life. The first is the ancestor of the 'god of the gaps' objection. The second runs through the Enlightenment to the twenty-first century: the sixteenth-century wars of religion, the Inquisition, terrorism. The third is the hope that science will replace faith. Christopher Hitchens's book God Is Not Great (2007) is, in shape, a modern On the Nature of Things.

It is worth stating the case at its strongest, because it is strong. Religious people have done terrible things in the name of God, and fear of hell has been used to control people. Any honest answer has to begin by admitting that.
sections.key: Lucretius claims that religion is fear, that it causes crime, and that knowledge of nature cures it: claims with a long life down to today.

paras: For a thousand years On the Nature of Things was barely read. Christian writers knew it mostly as the work of an enemy. But it was not destroyed: monks copied it. The two oldest surviving manuscripts were made in the 800s at monasteries in the empire of Charlemagne, and are now in Leiden in the Netherlands.

In 1417 the Italian book-hunter Poggio Bracciolini, a papal secretary, found a copy in a monastery in Germany, probably Fulda, and had it copied. The poem spread through Renaissance Italy and was printed in 1473. Botticelli's Venus, Montaigne's Essays and Shakespeare's age all knew it. In the 1600s the French priest Pierre Gassendi revived Epicurean atomism and made it acceptable to Christians, and atoms passed into modern science.
sections.key: The poem survived in monks' copies, was found again in 1417 by Poggio, and fed the Renaissance and the revival of atomism.

paras: In The Swerve (2011), which won the Pulitzer Prize, the literary scholar Stephen Greenblatt told Poggio's discovery as the moment the modern world began: a lost poem of pleasure and reason escaping from the dark, fearful Middle Ages, with monks as its gaolers. The book was a bestseller, and its story is now widely believed.

Historians of the Middle Ages and Renaissance were sharply critical. They pointed out that monks had preserved the poem in the first place; that medieval scholars were not hostile to nature or to pleasure; that the poem's influence was gradual and mixed; and that the Renaissance was not a sudden escape from religion, since many of its greatest figures were devout. Some reviewers called Greenblatt's picture of the Middle Ages a caricature.
The fair conclusion is that the poem's return mattered, but that the 'dark ages' story is a myth of its own. Lucretius would have said that every age needs to check its stories.
sections.key: Greenblatt's The Swerve (2011) made Poggio's find the birth of modernity; historians answered that monks kept the poem and that his Middle Ages is a caricature.

paras: First, the example. Lucretius's great case is from myth, not history, and the Greeks themselves were horrified by it; Euripides let the goddess save the girl. The Bible tells a parallel story, Abraham and Isaac, and there God stops the knife and forbids child sacrifice. Israel's law condemned it outright (Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31). On this point the Bible is on Lucretius's side.

Second, the cause. Do religions cause crimes, or do people use them? Historians of violence find many causes of war, and the twentieth century's atheist regimes killed on an enormous scale. Third, the cure. Lucretius gave up the gods to escape fear of punishment. But his cure removes hope as well as fear: no justice for Iphigenia, no one who sees the oppressed, as Psalm 14 puts it. For the psalmist, a God who sees is good news for the victim and bad news only for the oppressor.
sections.key: Lucretius's main case is myth; the Bible also condemns child sacrifice and idols. The deeper question is whether removing God removes justice and hope as well as fear.

paras: Epicureanism shaped the modern world more than its size suggests. Its atoms became the atoms of physics. Its picture of a universe running by natural law, with no gods to intervene, became the outlook of much of the Enlightenment. Thomas Jefferson called himself an Epicurean, and David Hume, the Scottish sceptic, set an Epicurean speech at the heart of his Enquiry (1748).

Above all, the idea that the purpose of life is happiness in this world, and that religion is a threat to it, has its first great statement in Lucretius. Many people today hold exactly the view of his poem: a universe of particles, no life after death, and the duty to enjoy life calmly and kindly while it lasts. It is one of the serious answers to our question, and it has its own kind of peace.
sections.key: Lucretius gave the modern world atoms, a universe of natural law, and the idea that religion threatens happiness: a serious, living answer.

paras: Christian writers were among Lucretius's first serious readers. Lactantius, a teacher of rhetoric who became tutor to the emperor Constantine's son, quoted him often in the early 300s in order to answer him. Two of his replies are still made. First, the order and beauty of the world are hard to explain by atoms colliding by chance; a world so fitted for life suggests a mind behind it. Second, a universe without providence leaves the wicked unpunished and the innocent unavenged; Iphigenia, in Lucretius's universe, simply dies.

Later Christians went further and took over what was good in Lucretius. Gassendi, a Catholic priest, kept the atoms and rejected the godless conclusions: God made the atoms, gave them their laws, and gave human beings immortal souls. Isaac Newton, a devout if unorthodox believer, pictured matter as 'solid, massy, hard, impenetrable, movable particles' created by God in the beginning. The atom passed into Christian science; Lucretius's quarrel with providence did not.
sections.key: Lactantius answered Lucretius with order in nature and the need for justice; Gassendi and Newton kept the atoms but made God their maker.

paras: Lucretius's case against religion stands or falls with his case about death, which fills Book III of his poem. If you have taken Death and hope, you have read its climax: the soul is made of atoms and dies with the body, so death is nothing to us; we do not mind the eternity before we were born, so why mind the eternity after? It is the Epicurean argument at its most beautiful.

Notice how the two cases fit together. Religion has power, Lucretius says, because people fear punishment after death. Remove the afterlife and you remove religion's grip. That is why, for Lucretius, physics is liberation. The Christian answer is not to deny that fear of hell has been abused, but to say that the New Testament's last word about death is not threat but promise: 'Death is swallowed up in victory' (1 Corinthians 15:54). Whether that promise is true is a question about evidence, especially about the resurrection, which other journeys take up. Lucretius shows why it matters so much.
sections.key: Lucretius's attack on religion depends on his proof that the soul dies; the Christian reply turns on whether death has been defeated, not on fear.

refs: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things I.1–158; II.216–293; III.830–1094 (tr. W. E. Leonard, 1916; Latin line numbers).
Cicero, Letters to his brother Quintus II.9 (February 54 BC); Jerome, Chronicle, for the year 94 BC.
Aeschylus, Agamemnon 205–247; Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis; Genesis 22; Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31; Psalm 10:4, 11; Justin Martyr, First Apology 6.
The manuscripts: Leiden, Voss. Lat. F. 30 (Oblongus) and Q. 94 (Quadratus), 9th century. Poggio's discovery, 1417; editio princeps, Brescia, about 1473.

debate.question: Does religion do more harm than good?

positions.name: More harm: Lucretius's heirs
positions.who: Lucretius; Voltaire; Christopher Hitchens; Richard Dawkins
positions.view: Religion rests on fear and ignorance, licenses cruelty in the name of God, and stands in the way of knowledge. Remove it and people will be freer and kinder.
positions.evidence: Child sacrifice in the ancient world; wars of religion; persecution of heretics; religious terrorism.

positions.name: More good: the historians' answer
positions.who: Tom Holland, Dominion (2019); Rodney Stark; many historians of charity and of science
positions.view: The Bible itself attacks idols and child sacrifice; Christianity spread care for the poor and the sick, the idea of equal human dignity, and the universities. The worst crimes of the twentieth century were done by atheist regimes.
positions.evidence: Genesis 22; Leviticus 18:21; hospitals and charity in late antiquity; the record of Soviet and Maoist states.

positions.name: It depends on the god
positions.who: Isaiah; Psalm 14; Augustine's City of God; many theologians
positions.view: Lucretius is right about false gods, which are made in our image and demand our children. The question is not religion or no religion, but which God, and whether people worship what they have made.
positions.evidence: Isaiah 44's satire of idols; the early Christians called 'atheists' by Rome.

debate.agree: All agree that religion has been used to justify terrible things, and that fear of the gods can be cruel. They differ over whether that is religion's nature or its corruption.

look.why: No painting for this session: the National Gallery of Art has no painting of the sacrifice of Iphigenia in its open collection, and a stand-in would pretend to be what it is not.

music.why: Mozart's Requiem (1791) contains the Dies irae, 'Day of wrath': the medieval poem of the Last Judgement, the very terror of punishment after death that Lucretius wanted to abolish. Listen to it as he might have, and then as a believer might, for whom judgement means that wrongs will at last be put right.

think.why: The modern debate about God, with the strongest objections stated fairly.

check.q: What does Lucretius mean by 'Religion' in the passage you read?
options: Fearful scruple about gods who punish, with the rituals and priests that feed on that fear
The Christian Church
Belief in any god at all
The study of nature
check.why: Like Epicurus, Lucretius believed gods exist but do nothing. His target is religio: the fear of punishing gods and what it drives people to. Christianity did not yet exist.

check.q: Why, according to Lucretius, do priests and seers have power over people?
options: Because people fear eternal punishment after death, not knowing what the soul is
Because the law requires obedience to them
Because the gods really do speak through them
Because they are rich
check.why: 'Since men must dread eternal pains in death. For what the soul may be they do not know' (I.111–113).

check.q: How does Psalm 14 differ from Lucretius about God and wrongdoing?
options: It links the denial of a God who sees with oppression of the poor, so that God is the refuge of the weak
It says God does not see what people do
It agrees that belief in God causes crime
It says that the poor should fear God more than the rich
check.why: For the psalmist, those who think 'there is no God' feel free to 'eat up my people'; God is the refuge of the poor. Lucretius sees religion as the cause of crime; the psalm sees its absence as the cause.

check.q: On which point do Isaiah 44 and Lucretius agree?
options: That the world was not created
That worshipping and fearing gods made by human hands is a terrible error
That knowledge of atoms frees us from fear
That there are no gods
check.why: Both mock gods that are made by people. They disagree about what follows: Isaiah points to the God who made the forest and the rain.

check.q: What is the strongest historical criticism of the story told in The Swerve?
options: That Lucretius never existed
That the poem was preserved by medieval monks, and that the picture of a fearful, dark Middle Ages is a caricature
That Poggio never found the manuscript
That the poem had no influence at all
check.why: Poggio did find it in 1417, and it was influential; but monks had copied it in the 800s, and historians judge the 'dark ages' picture unfair.

check.q: Lucretius's first law is 'Nothing from nothing ever yet was born.' Why does this matter for the argument with Christianity?
options: It proves that God exists
It is the opposite of the Christian belief that God created the world out of nothing
It shows that Lucretius was a Christian
It has nothing to do with religion
check.why: Lucretius uses it to show the world runs without gods; Christians came to teach creation ex nihilo. The two pictures of reality part on the first principle.

tutorial.question: 'Such are the crimes to which Religion leads.' Is Lucretius's case against religion sound?
tutorial.approach: Set out his three claims: religion is fear, it causes crime, knowledge cures it. Give his evidence, Iphigenia. Then test each claim: is the example typical, and what does the Bible say about child sacrifice and idols? Do religions cause crimes, or do people use them? And what is lost, as well as gained, by Lucretius's cure?
strong: States Lucretius's three claims clearly.
Uses the Iphigenia passage closely, quoting it.
Notes that the Bible also condemns child sacrifice and idols (Genesis 22; Leviticus 18:21; Isaiah 44).
Distinguishes religion as a cause of harm from religion used as an excuse.
Considers what removing God removes: fear, but also hope and justice for victims.
Reaches a balanced judgement.
