sessions.practice: Live it this week: once a day, when you feel afraid or anxious, write the fear down in one line. Then ask Lucretius's question of it: is this fear of something real, or of a story I have been told? Keep the list until the end of the week and read it through.
sessions.reflect: Has religion ever made you afraid? Has it ever made you less afraid? Which do you think is closer to the heart of faith?
takeaways: Lucretius turned Epicurus into great Latin poetry and made the first sustained case that religion itself causes fear and crime.
His cure is knowledge of nature: nothing comes from nothing, the soul dies with the body, and the gods do nothing.
The Bible shares his contempt for idols and child sacrifice, but sees a God who sees as the hope of the oppressed.

sessions.title: The porch
sessions.line: A shipwrecked merchant teaches in a painted colonnade in Athens that the world is ruled by reason, and that being good is the only good.
sessions.plain: Around 300 BC a merchant from Cyprus called Zeno began teaching in a painted colonnade, the Stoa, in the market square of Athens; his followers were called Stoics. They taught that the whole world is ordered by a divine reason, the logos, and that human beings share in it. The only true good is virtue, living in tune with that reason; health, wealth and even life itself are 'indifferent'. This session reads a former slave, Epictetus, on the reason in us and the God who gave it, and an ancient summary of what the Stoics believed.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 and 2 heard the Epicurean answer: peace by removing fear of gods and death, in a world of atoms with no plan. The Stoics gave the opposite picture of the world. Before we can understand their famous advice about what is 'up to us', we need to see the universe they believed in.
answers: What is Stoicism?
Is Stoicism a religion?
What did the Stoics mean by the logos?
Why did they say virtue is the only good?
sessions.finding: The Stoics taught that the world is ordered by divine reason (the logos), that human beings share in it, and that virtue, living by it, is the only good.

paras: Epicurus and Lucretius offered peace through knowledge of a universe of atoms and empty space, with gods who take no notice of us and no life after death. Calm comes from removing fear and wanting little.

The Stoics agreed that peace of mind was the goal. But they thought the Epicurean universe was a mistake. For them the world is not a chance collision of atoms. It is a single living whole, shot through with reason, and guided by providence (pronoia, 'forethought') for the good.
background.key: The Epicureans saw a world of atoms without a plan; the Stoics saw a living whole ruled by reason and providence.

paras: Zeno was born at Citium in Cyprus, around 334 BC. The story goes that he was a merchant, shipwrecked near Athens, who sat down in a bookshop, read about Socrates, and asked where such men could be found; the bookseller pointed at Crates the Cynic, a philosopher who lived rough to show how little a person needs. Zeno later said, 'I made a prosperous voyage when I was wrecked.'

Around 300 BC he began to teach in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch: a long colonnade on the north side of the Agora, the market square of Athens, decorated with famous paintings. Anyone could walk in. His followers were called Stoics, 'porch people'. After him came Cleanthes, a former boxer who wrote a famous Hymn to Zeus, and Chrysippus (about 279 to 206 BC), who wrote over seven hundred books and made Stoicism a complete system. People said, 'If there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Porch.'

timeline.text: Zeno born at Citium in Cyprus
Zeno begins teaching in the Painted Porch, Athens
Death of Zeno; Cleanthes leads the school
Chrysippus leads the school and builds the system
Panaetius and Posidonius bring Stoicism to Rome's ruling class
Epictetus born at Hierapolis in Phrygia
Paul debates with Stoics and Epicureans in Athens (Acts 17:18)
Arrian takes notes of Epictetus's teaching at Nicopolis

background.key: Zeno taught in the Painted Porch from about 300 BC; Cleanthes and Chrysippus completed the system.

paras: Epictetus was born around AD 50 at Hierapolis in Phrygia, in what is now Turkey. The name means simply 'acquired': he was a slave. In Rome he belonged to Epaphroditus, a freedman who served the emperor Nero. He was lame; one story says his master broke his leg. His master let him study with the Stoic teacher Musonius Rufus, and he was later freed.

When the emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome, around AD 93, Epictetus moved to Nicopolis on the west coast of Greece and opened a school. He wrote nothing. A young pupil, Arrian, later a governor and historian, took down his talks, the Discourses, of which four books survive, and made a short summary, the Encheiridion or Manual. We read George Long's translation of 1877. Long gives the talks their old titles, run into the first sentence.
background.key: Epictetus (c. AD 50–135), a slave freed in Rome, taught at Nicopolis; his pupil Arrian recorded his Discourses and the Manual.

paras: The main reading is three of Epictetus's talks: on the one faculty that can examine itself (reason); on being sons of God; and on providence. Together they show the Stoic picture of the world from the inside, from a man who lived by it, and they answer this session's question: is Stoicism a religion?

The comparison is from Diogenes Laertius, the same writer who preserved Epicurus. His Book VII summarises the Stoics' teaching: Zeno's porch, living 'according to nature', the division of things into good, bad and indifferent, and their God.
background.key: Epictetus on reason, God and providence; then an ancient summary of Stoic doctrine.

before: What is the one faculty, according to Epictetus, that can judge both itself and everything else?
What does Epictetus say we share with the animals, and what with the gods?
What are human beings for, according to the talk on providence?
sessions.readWhy: Three talks by Epictetus, in four parts: reason, a free will no one can chain, kinship with God, and providence.

paras: OF THE THINGS WHICH ARE IN OUR POWER AND NOT IN OUR POWER.—Of all the faculties (except that which I shall soon mention), you will find not one which is capable of contemplating itself, and, consequently, not capable either of approving or disapproving. How far does the grammatic art possess the contemplating power? As far as forming a judgment about what is written and spoken. And how far music? As far as judging about melody. Does either of them then contemplate itself? By no means. But when you must write something to your friend, grammar will tell you what words you should write; but whether you should write or not, grammar will not tell you. And so it is with music as to musical sounds; but whether you should sing at the present time and play on the lute, or do neither, music will not tell you. What faculty then will tell you? That which contemplates both itself and all other things. And what is this faculty? The rational faculty; for this is the only faculty that we have received which examines itself, what it is, and what power it has, and what is the value of this gift, and examines all other faculties: for what else is there which tells us that golden things are beautiful, for they do not say so themselves? Evidently it is the faculty which is capable of judging of appearances. What else judges of music, grammar, and the other faculties, proves their uses, and points out the occasions for using them? Nothing else.

What then should a man have in readiness in such circumstances? What else than this? What is mine, and what is not mine; and what is permitted to me, and what is not permitted to me. I must die. Must I then die lamenting? I must be put in chains. Must I then also lament? I must go into exile. Does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness and contentment? Tell me the secret which you possess. I will not, for this is in my power. But I will put you in chains. Man, what are you talking about? Me, in chains? You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower. I will throw you into prison. My poor body, you mean. I will cut your head off. When then have I told you that my head alone cannot be cut off? These are the things which philosophers should meditate on, which they should write daily, in which they should exercise themselves.

What then did Agrippinus say? He said, “I am not a hindrance to myself.” When it was reported to him that his trial was going on in the Senate, he said: “I hope it may turn out well; but it is the fifth hour of the day”—this was the time when he was used to exercise himself and then take the cold bath,—“let us go and take our exercise.” After he had taken his exercise, one comes and tells him, “You have been condemned.” “To banishment,” he replies, “or to death?” “To banishment.” “What about my property?” “It is not taken from you.” “Let us go to Aricia then,” he said, “and dine.”

HOW A MAN SHOULD PROCEED FROM THE PRINCIPLE OF GOD BEING THE FATHER OF ALL MEN TO THE REST.—If a man should be able to assent to this doctrine as he ought, that we are all sprung from God in an especial manner, and that God is the father both of men and of gods, I suppose that he would never have any ignoble or mean thoughts about himself. But if Cæsar (the emperor) should adopt you, no one could endure your arrogance; and if you know that you are the son of Zeus, will you not be elated? Yet we do not so; but since these two things are mingled in the generation of man, body in common with the animals, and reason and intelligence in common with the gods, many incline to this kinship, which is miserable and mortal; and some few to that which is divine and happy. Since then it is of necessity that every man uses everything according to the opinion which he has about it, those, the few, who think that they are formed for fidelity and modesty and a sure use of appearances have no mean or ignoble thoughts about themselves; but with the many it is quite the contrary. For they say, What am I? A poor, miserable man, with my wretched bit of flesh. Wretched, indeed; but you possess something better than your bit of flesh. Why then do you neglect that which is better, and why do you attach yourself to this?

Through this kinship with the flesh, some of us inclining to it become like wolves, faithless and treacherous and mischievous; some become like lions, savage and bestial and untamed; but the greater part of us become foxes, and other worse animals. For what else is a slanderer and malignant man than a fox, or some other more wretched and meaner animal? See then and take care that you do not become some one of these miserable things.

OF PROVIDENCE.—From everything, which is or happens in the world, it is easy to praise Providence, if a man possesses these two qualities: the faculty of seeing what belongs and happens to all persons and things, and a grateful disposition. If he does not possess these two qualities, one man will not see the use of things which are and which happen: another will not be thankful for them, even if he does know them. If God had made colors, but had not made the faculty of seeing them, what would have been their use? None at all. On the other hand, if he had made the faculty of vision, but had not made objects such as to fall under the faculty, what in that case also would have been the use of it? None at all. Well, suppose that he had made both, but had not made light? In that case, also, they would have been of no use. Who is it then who has fitted this to that and that to this?

What, then, are these things done in us only? Many, indeed, in us only, of which the rational animal had peculiar need; but you will find many common to us with irrational animals. Do they then understand what is done? By no means. For use is one thing, and understanding is another; God had need of irrational animals to make use of appearances, but of us to understand the use of appearances. It is therefore enough for them to eat and to drink, and to copulate, and to do all the other things which they severally do. But for us, to whom he has given also the intellectual faculty, these things are not sufficient; for unless we act in a proper and orderly manner, and conformably to the nature and constitution of each thing, we shall never attain our true end. For where the constitutions of living beings are different, there also the acts and the ends are different. In those animals then whose constitution is adapted only to use, use alone is enough;

but in an animal (man), which has also the power of understanding the use, unless there be the due exercise of the understanding, he will never attain his proper end. Well then God constitutes every animal, one to be eaten, another to serve for agriculture, another to supply cheese, and another for some like use; for which purposes what need is there to understand appearances and to be able to distinguish them? But God has introduced man to be a spectator of God and of his works; and not only a spectator of them, but an interpreter. For this reason it is shameful for man to begin and to end where irrational animals do; but rather he ought to begin where they begin, and to end where nature ends in us; and nature ends in contemplation and understanding, and in a way of life conformable to nature. Take care then not to die without having been spectators of these things.

Come, then, do you also having observed these things look to the faculties which you have, and when you have looked at them, say: Bring now, O Zeus, any difficulty that thou pleasest, for I have means given to me by thee and powers for honoring myself through the things which happen. You do not so; but you sit still, trembling for fear that some things will happen, and weeping, and lamenting, and groaning for what does happen; and then you blame the gods. For what is the consequence of such meanness of spirit but impiety? And yet God has not only given us these faculties, by which we shall be able to bear everything that happens without being depressed or broken by it; but, like a good king and a true father, He has given us these faculties free from hindrance, subject to no compulsion, unimpeded, and has put them entirely in our own power, without even having reserved to Himself any power of hindering or impeding. You, who have received these powers free and as your own, use them not; you do not even see what you have received, and from whom; some of you being blinded to the giver, and not even acknowledging your benefactor, and others, through meanness of spirit, betaking yourselves to fault-finding and making charges against God. Yet I will show to you that you have powers and means for greatness of soul and manliness; but what powers you have for finding fault making accusations, do you show me.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: The faculty that examines itself
parts.who: Epictetus, teacher at Nicopolis, recorded by his pupil Arrian
parts.context: The first talk in the collection. Epictetus asks what part of us can judge everything else. 'Appearances' is Long's word for impressions: the way things strike us, before we decide what they mean.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: each skill judges its own subject. Grammar tells you how to spell a letter, but not whether to write it; music tells you how to sing, but not whether to sing now. Only one faculty examines itself and everything else, and decides how to use all the others: reason, the power to judge appearances.

commentary.on: you will find not one which is capable of contemplating itself
commentary.text: Epictetus begins with something you can test: no skill can step outside itself. Your knowledge of grammar cannot tell you whether to send the letter.

commentary.on: The rational faculty; for this is the only faculty that we have received which examines itself
commentary.text: 'Received' is a theological word: our reason is a gift. In the full text of this talk, which Long's selection shortens, Epictetus says the gods gave us this best of all things and kept the rest in their own hands.

commentary.on: it is the faculty which is capable of judging of appearances
commentary.text: The key Stoic idea. Things appear to us (this is a threat, that is a loss), and reason decides whether to agree. Everything in Stoic ethics depends on this moment of judgement.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: Me, in chains?
parts.context: From the same talk. Epictetus imagines a tyrant threatening him. Paconius Agrippinus was a Stoic senator condemned under Nero in AD 66 (Tacitus, Annals XVI.28–33). Aricia was a town on the Appian Way, about sixteen miles from Rome, on the road into exile.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: in trouble, ask what is mine and what is not. I must die; must I die complaining? I may be chained; must I lament? A tyrant can chain my leg, imprison my body, cut off my head, but not even Zeus can overpower my will. Agrippinus, told he was condemned to exile, asked whether his property was safe and said, 'Then let us go to Aricia and dine.'

commentary.on: What is mine, and what is not mine; and what is permitted to me, and what is not permitted to me.
commentary.text: This is the question at the heart of all Stoic practice. It is the subject of the next session, still to come, on what is 'up to us'.

commentary.on: You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower.
commentary.text: From a man who had been a slave and was lame, this is not a classroom exercise. 'Will' translates prohairesis, the power of choice: Epictetus's word for the true self.

commentary.on: When then have I told you that my head alone cannot be cut off?
commentary.text: A grim joke. Stoics did not claim to be invulnerable in body. They claimed that what makes a person good or bad cannot be taken by force.

commentary.on: “Let us go to Aricia then,” he said, “and dine.”
commentary.text: Agrippinus hears his sentence and goes to lunch. It is meant to be admired, and a little funny. You may also find it chilling. Hold that reaction; it will matter later in the journey.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: Sons of Zeus
parts.context: A talk on what follows from believing that God is the father of all. 'Zeus' is the Greek name for the supreme god; for Stoics it meant the divine reason that runs through the world. Caesar is the emperor, who adopted his heirs.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: if we really believed that we are all children of God, we would never think meanly of ourselves. If the emperor adopted you, you would be proud; you are the son of Zeus. We are a mixture: a body like the animals, and reason and intelligence like the gods. Most people think only of the body, call themselves miserable bits of flesh, and become like wolves, lions or foxes.

commentary.on: that we are all sprung from God in an especial manner, and that God is the father both of men and of gods
commentary.text: 'Father of men and gods' is Homer's title for Zeus. Epictetus means it: every human being, slave or emperor, is God's child, because each has reason, a share of the divine reason. The Stoics drew from this the idea of a single human family, citizens of one world.

commentary.on: body in common with the animals, and reason and intelligence in common with the gods
commentary.text: The Stoic picture of a human being: half animal, half divine. Compare Genesis 2:7, dust and breath. The question is which side we live from.

commentary.on: A poor, miserable man, with my wretched bit of flesh.
commentary.text: Epictetus mocks the self-pity of those who see themselves only as bodies. He does not deny the body is weak; he denies that it is all we are.

commentary.on: the greater part of us become foxes
commentary.text: Wolves are treacherous, lions savage, foxes sly. Most of us, he says, are not monsters but small cheats: a fair, unflattering observation.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: A spectator and an interpreter
parts.context: A talk on providence (pronoia), God's care for the world. Phidias was the sculptor of the great gold and ivory statue of Zeus at Olympia, one of the wonders of the world; visitors suffered heat and crowds to see it. A passage on bearing hardship is cut, marked '…'.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: anyone who sees how things fit together, and is grateful, will praise providence. God made colours and the eyes to see them, and light, and fitted them together. Animals use things; we are made to understand them. God brought us into the world to be spectators of his works, and interpreters of them. Do not die without having seen them. So say: 'Bring on any difficulty you like, Zeus; you have given me the powers to bear it.' God, like a good king and father, has given us these powers freely, as our own.

commentary.on: Who is it then who has fitted this to that and that to this?
commentary.text: An argument from design, 1,700 years before William Paley's watch. Eyes, colours and light fit together; something must have fitted them. For a Stoic the answer is the divine reason in nature.

commentary.on: But God has introduced man to be a spectator of God and of his works; and not only a spectator of them, but an interpreter.
commentary.text: The noblest line in the reading. Human beings exist to see the world and understand it, and to say what it means. Science, for a Stoic, is a kind of worship.

commentary.on: Take care then not to die without having been spectators of these things.
commentary.text: People travel far to see a statue of Zeus; the works of Zeus are all around them, and they never look.

commentary.on: Bring now, O Zeus, any difficulty that thou pleasest
commentary.text: A prayer, of a kind: not for help, but in thanks for the strength already given. Epictetus asks God for nothing, because he thinks God has already given everything that matters.

commentary.on: like a good king and a true father, He has given us these faculties free from hindrance
commentary.text: Is Stoicism a religion? Read this, and decide. Epictetus speaks of God as father and king, gives thanks and sings praise. Yet his God is not a person who acts in history or answers prayer; it is the reason of the universe. The Stoics were deeply religious philosophers. Whether that makes Stoicism a religion is the question of the lecture.

read.author: Epictetus
read.who: Epictetus, teacher at Nicopolis, recorded by his pupil Arrian

paras: And he used to walk up and down in the beautiful colonnade which is called the Peisianactium, and which is also called ποικίλη, from the paintings of Polygnotus, and there he delivered his discourses, wishing to make that spot tranquil; for in the time of the thirty, nearly fourteen hundred of the citizens had been murdered there by them.

Accordingly, for the future, men came thither to hear him, and from this his pupils were called Stoics, and so were his successors also, who had been at first called Zenonians, as Epicurus tells us in his Epistles. And before this time, the poets who frequented this colonnade (στοὰ) had been called Stoics, as we are informed by Eratosthenes, in the eighth book of his treatise on the Old Comedy; but now Zeno’s pupils made the name more notorious.

On which account Zeno was the first writer who, in his treatise on the Nature of Man, said, that the chief good was confessedly to live according to nature; which is to live according to virtue, for nature leads us to this point. And in like manner Cleanthes speaks in his treatise on Pleasure, and so do Posidonius and Hecaton in their essays on Ends as the Chief Good. And again, to live according to virtue is the same thing as living according to one’s experience of those things which happen by nature; as Chrysippus explains it in the first book of his treatise on the Chief Good. For our individual natures are all parts of universal nature; on which account the chief good is to live in a manner corresponding to nature, and that means corresponding to one’s own nature and to universal nature; doing none of those things which the common law of mankind is in the habit of forbidding, and that common law is identical with that right reason which pervades everything, being the same with Jupiter, who is the regulator and chief manager of all existing things.

Moreover, they divide all existing things into good, bad, and indifferent. The good are the virtues, prudence, justice, manly courage, temperance, and the rest of the like qualities. The bad are the contraries, folly, injustice, and the like. Those are indifferent which are neither beneficial nor injurious, such as life, health, pleasure, beauty, strength, riches, a good reputation, nobility of birth; and their contraries, death, disease, labour, disgrace, weakness, poverty, a bad reputation, baseness of birth, and the like; as Hecaton lays it down in the seventh book of his treatise on the Chief Good; and he is followed by Apollodorus, in his Ethics, and by Chrysippus. For they affirm that those things are not good but indifferent, though perhaps a little more near to one species than to the other.

For, as it is the property of the hot to warm and not to chill one, so it is the property of the good to benefit and not to injure one. Now, wealth and good health cannot be said to benefit any more than to injure any one: therefore, neither wealth nor good health are goods. Again, they say that that thing is not good which it is possible to use both well and ill. But it is possible to make either a good or a bad use of wealth, or of health; therefore, wealth and good health are not goods. Posidonius, however, affirms that these things do come under the head of goods. But Hecaton, in the nineteenth book of his treatise on Goods, and Chrysippus, in his treatises on Pleasure, both deny that pleasure is a good. For they say that there are disgraceful pleasures, and that nothing disgraceful is good. And that to benefit a person is to move him or to keep him according to virtue, but to injure him is to move him or to keep him according to vice.

They also say that God is an animal immortal, rational, perfect, and intellectual in his happiness, unsusceptible of any kind of evil, having a foreknowledge of the world and of all that is in the world; however, that he has not the figure of a man; and that he is the creator of the universe, and as it were, the Father of all things in common, and that a portion of him pervades everything, which is called by different names, according to its powers; for they call him Δία as being the person (δι’ ὃν) everything is, and Ζῆνα, inasmuch as he is the cause of life, (τοῦ Ζῆν), or because he pervades life. And Ἀθηνᾶ, with reference to the extension of his dominant power over the æther (εἰς αἰθέρα). And Ἥρα, on account of his extension through the air (εἰς ἀέρα). And Ἥφαιστος, on account of his pervading fire, which is the chief instrument of art; and Ποσειδῶν, as pervading moisture, and Δημήτηρ, as pervading the earth (Γῆ). And in the same way, regarding some other of his peculiar attributes, they have given him other names.

But Chrysippus, in his treatise on Fate, and Posidonius, in the second book of his work on Fate, and Zeno, and Boethus, in the eleventh book of his treatise on Fate, say, that all things are produced by fate. And fate, (εἱμαρμένη), is a connected (εἰρομένη) cause of existing things, or the reason according to which the world is regulated.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII (Zeno and the Stoics)
parts.title: The Painted Porch
parts.context: Diogenes describes where Zeno taught. The 'thirty' are the Thirty Tyrants, who ruled Athens by terror in 404–403 BC. Polygnotus was a famous painter of the 400s BC. This is C. D. Yonge's translation of 1853; we have removed his section numbers.
parts.plain: Diogenes says: Zeno taught as he walked up and down the Painted Colonnade, named for its paintings, wishing to make peaceful a place where the Thirty Tyrants had killed many citizens. His pupils were called Stoics, from stoa, colonnade.

commentary.on: wishing to make that spot tranquil
commentary.text: A lovely detail: the place of a massacre becomes a place of calm. The Porch was public; the Garden was private. The Stoics always thought philosophy should serve the city and the world, not retreat from it.

commentary.on: from this his pupils were called Stoics
commentary.text: So 'stoic' first meant simply 'porch people'. The modern meaning, someone who bears pain without complaint, comes later and catches only part of the teaching.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII (Zeno and the Stoics)
parts.title: Live according to nature
parts.context: The Stoic definition of the goal of life. 'Jupiter' is Yonge's Latin name for Zeus.
parts.plain: Zeno said the goal of life is to live according to nature, which means living according to virtue. Our own natures are parts of the nature of the whole. So we should do nothing that the common law of humanity forbids; and that law is the right reason that runs through everything, which is the same as Zeus, the ruler of all.

commentary.on: the chief good was confessedly to live according to nature; which is to live according to virtue
commentary.text: 'Nature' here does not mean the countryside or our instincts. It means the rational order of the universe, and our own nature as rational beings. To live by nature is to live by reason, and that is virtue.

commentary.on: For our individual natures are all parts of universal nature
commentary.text: Each of us is a part of one great whole. This is the root of Stoic calm: a part should accept its place in the whole.

commentary.on: that common law is identical with that right reason which pervades everything, being the same with Jupiter
commentary.text: Here is the logos. The Greek word means word, reason, account. For the Stoics it is the divine reason running through the universe like a law, and it is God. The idea of a 'natural law', binding on all people everywhere, began here and passed through Cicero and the Roman lawyers into Christian thought.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII (Zeno and the Stoics)
parts.title: Good, bad and indifferent
parts.context: The most surprising Stoic doctrine. Hecaton, Apollodorus and Chrysippus were later Stoic teachers.
parts.plain: The Stoics divide everything into good, bad and indifferent. The only goods are the virtues: wisdom, justice, courage, self-control. The only evils are the vices. Everything else, life and death, health and illness, wealth and poverty, fame and disgrace, is 'indifferent'. Why? Because what is good must always do good, and wealth and health can be used badly.

commentary.on: The good are the virtues, prudence, justice, manly courage, temperance
commentary.text: These four, wisdom (prudence), justice, courage and self-control (temperance), had come from Plato. Christians would later call them the cardinal virtues.

commentary.on: Those are indifferent which are neither beneficial nor injurious, such as life, health, pleasure, beauty, strength, riches
commentary.text: Life itself is on the list. So is pleasure: the Stoics flatly deny the Epicurean claim. This is the hardest Stoic teaching. Note that the Stoics did not say we should not care about health at all; elsewhere they call such things 'preferred', worth choosing when we can. They are just not good.

commentary.on: they say that that thing is not good which it is possible to use both well and ill
commentary.text: The argument. A thing that can do harm is not good in itself. Money can buy medicine or poison. Only a good character cannot be misused.

parts.author: Diogenes Laertius
parts.work: Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII (Zeno and the Stoics)
parts.title: The Stoic God
parts.context: The Stoics' theology. The Greek names in Yonge's text are puns: Zeus is called 'Dia', 'because of whom' (di' hon) all things are, and 'Zena', because he is the cause of life (zen, to live).
parts.plain: The Stoics say God is a living being, immortal, rational and perfectly happy, who foresees all things, though not in human shape. He is the maker and father of all, and a part of him runs through everything; the old gods' names are names for his powers. And all things happen by fate, which is the reason by which the world is governed.

commentary.on: having a foreknowledge of the world and of all that is in the world
commentary.text: Unlike Epicurus's gods, the Stoic God knows and cares. Hence providence.

commentary.on: that he is the creator of the universe, and as it were, the Father of all things in common
commentary.text: Language that sounds Christian. But read on.

commentary.on: and that a portion of him pervades everything
commentary.text: The Stoic God is not outside the world, as the Bible's creator is. He is in it, as its soul and reason; many Stoics said the world itself was God. Scholars call this pantheism ('God is all').

commentary.on: or the reason according to which the world is regulated
commentary.text: Fate and reason are one. Everything that happens happens by divine reason, so everything that happens is for the best. That belief is the ground of the Stoic peace, and, as you will see, of its hardest demands.

compare.author: Diogenes Laertius
compare.work: Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII (Zeno and the Stoics)
compare.why: Epictetus speaks from within. Diogenes Laertius, writing about a century later, sets out the Stoic system from outside, as a list of doctrines. Read it for what it adds: the porch, 'live according to nature', the 'indifferents', and the Stoic God.
compare.title: What the Stoics believed

paras: The Stoics divided philosophy into three parts: logic, physics and ethics. They compared it to an egg: logic the shell, physics the white, ethics the yolk; or to a field: logic the fence, physics the soil and trees, ethics the fruit (Diogenes Laertius VII.40).

Logic meant the whole study of thinking clearly: how to test impressions, avoid being fooled, and argue well. Chrysippus was one of the great logicians of antiquity. Physics meant the study of nature, including God. Ethics, the fruit, meant how to live. The parts depend on each other: you cannot know how to live without knowing what the world is, and you cannot know what the world is without thinking clearly. The modern self-help version of Stoicism usually keeps only the fruit.
sections.key: Logic, physics and ethics: shell, white and yolk. Ancient Stoic ethics rested on a picture of the world; modern versions often keep only the ethics.

paras: Stoic physics is the reverse of Epicurus's. There is no empty space inside the world, no chance and no swerve. The universe is one body, held together by a fiery breath (pneuma) that runs through everything, giving stones their shape, plants their growth, animals their life and humans their reason. This breath, intelligent and divine, is the logos: God.

So everything happens by fate, a chain of causes running through all things, and because the chain is reason, it is also providence. The Stoics also taught that the world ends from time to time in fire, and is born again exactly as before. Cleanthes, in his Hymn to Zeus, prays to follow willingly where fate leads; if he refuses, he will be dragged anyway. Seneca later put it in one line: the fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling.
sections.key: One living universe, run through by a divine fiery breath, the logos; everything happens by fate, which is providence. Follow willingly, or be dragged.

paras: If the world is ordered for the best, what is bad? Not illness, not poverty, not death: these are part of the order. The only bad thing is a bad will: to choose against reason. And the only good thing is a good will, virtue. Everything else is 'indifferent'.

This sounds inhuman, and the Stoics softened it. Among indifferents some are 'preferred' (health, wealth, friends) and some 'dispreferred' (illness, poverty). It is natural and right to choose the preferred ones, if you can. But they are not good. You can be perfectly happy without them, as long as you are virtuous. Stoics called this happiness eudaimonia, the same word Aristotle used, but they made it depend on virtue alone.

The result is a kind of invulnerability. Nothing anyone can do to you can make you bad, so nothing anyone can do to you can make you unhappy. This is the Stoic peace. It is costly, and the cost is the question of the session on the objection, still to come.
sections.key: Only virtue is good and only vice is bad; health, wealth and life are 'preferred indifferents'. So no one can take your happiness.

paras: Modern Stoics often present Stoicism as a practical philosophy with no need for God. The ancient Stoics would have been puzzled. Their ethics depended on their theology: we accept what happens because it is the will of a rational, provident God, and we treat every person as a brother because each shares in God's reason. Epictetus praises God, thanks him and calls him father. Cleanthes wrote a hymn.

Yet Stoicism had no temples, priests, sacraments or Scripture of its own, and no God who acts in history. The Stoic God does not speak, choose a people or become anything. So the fairest answer is: Stoicism was a philosophy with a religious heart. You can take the practice without the theology, as many do now, but the Stoics themselves thought the practice made sense only because the world is ruled by reason.
sections.key: Ancient Stoicism was a philosophy with a religious heart: its ethics rested on a provident, rational God, though it had no temples, Scripture or history.

paras: Christians noticed the Stoic logos very early. John's Gospel opens 'In the beginning was the Word', and the Greek for 'Word' is logos. If you have taken In the beginning, you have read that passage. A Greek reader would have heard the Stoic idea: the reason that orders the world. John then says something no Stoic would say: 'The Word became flesh, and lived among us' (John 1:14). The reason of the universe became one particular man.

Paul met Stoics and Epicureans in Athens (Acts 17:18), and in his speech there quoted the Stoic poet Aratus: 'For we are also his offspring' (Acts 17:28). Justin Martyr, in the AD 150s, taught that a 'seed of the logos' was scattered in all people, so that the best of the Greeks had glimpsed part of the truth. The Stoics gave Christianity words; Christians filled them with a story.
sections.key: John's logos and Paul's 'we are his offspring' borrow Stoic words; Christianity's new claim was that the Word became flesh.

paras: If everything happens by fate, are we free? The Stoics said yes, in a special sense, and they had a famous picture for it, reported by the Christian writer Hippolytus around AD 220. A dog is tied to a cart. If it wants to follow, it runs along, pulled and willing at once. If it does not, it is dragged anyway. So it is with us: we cannot change where fate goes, but we can choose to go willingly.

Chrysippus added a subtler answer. Our actions are caused, but partly by our own character, as a cylinder rolls when pushed but rolls because it is round. The push comes from outside; the rolling comes from what it is. So we are responsible for how we respond, even in a world where everything is fated. Philosophers still call views like this 'compatibilism': freedom and causation can live together. Epicurus thought this a trick, and invented the swerve to escape it. Christians took a third path: God's providence governs all things, and human beings are still truly free and responsible, a mystery they did not claim to explain away.
sections.key: Stoics reconciled fate and freedom: the dog tied to the cart may follow willingly, and the cylinder rolls by its own shape. Christians held providence and freedom together as a mystery.

paras: In the 100s BC two Greek Stoics, Panaetius and Posidonius, made Stoicism attractive to Rome's ruling class. They softened its hardest edges, wrote about the duties of ordinary people who are not sages, and stressed public service. Cicero's On Duties (44 BC), drawn largely from Panaetius, became one of the most read books in Europe for 1,800 years.

Roman Stoics included Cato the Younger, who killed himself in 46 BC rather than live under Caesar; senators who opposed bad emperors and were exiled or killed for it; Seneca; the teacher Musonius Rufus, who taught that women should study philosophy; his pupil Epictetus; and the emperor Marcus Aurelius. Stoicism became, in effect, the conscience of the Roman elite: a philosophy for people with power and responsibility, and for the moments when they lost both.
sections.key: Panaetius and Posidonius brought Stoicism to Rome; it became the conscience of the Roman elite, from Cato to Marcus Aurelius.

refs: Diogenes Laertius VII.1–5 (Zeno's life), VII.39–41 (parts of philosophy), VII.87–89 (living according to nature), VII.101–107 (good, bad, indifferent; preferred indifferents), VII.134–149 (God, fate and providence), VII.180 (Chrysippus's books), tr. C. D. Yonge (1853).
Epictetus, Discourses I.1, I.3, I.6, tr. George Long (1877); Arrian's preface to the Discourses.
Cleanthes, Hymn to Zeus (in Stobaeus); Seneca, Letters 107.11 (the fates lead the willing).
Tacitus, Annals XVI.28–33 (Paconius Agrippinus); Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights XV.11 (Domitian's expulsion of philosophers).
John 1:1–14; Acts 17:18, 28; Aratus, Phaenomena 5; Justin Martyr, Second Apology 8 and 13.
Modern: A. A. Long, Hellenistic Philosophy (1974; 2nd ed. 1986); A. A. Long, Epictetus: A Stoic and Socratic Guide to Life (2002); John Sellars, Stoicism (2006).

debate.question: Can you be a Stoic without the Stoic God?

positions.name: Yes: keep the practice
positions.who: Many modern Stoics, e.g. Massimo Pigliucci, How to Be a Stoic (2017), in our words
positions.view: The Stoic method (judge impressions, focus on what is up to you, practise the virtues) works whether or not the universe is rational. Marcus Aurelius himself wrote 'either providence or atoms' and said the practice holds either way.
positions.evidence: Meditations IV.3; the success of Stoic-based therapy; the many atheist and agnostic Stoics today.

positions.name: No: the ethics rests on the physics
positions.who: Chrysippus; most scholars of ancient Stoicism, e.g. A. A. Long and John Cooper
positions.view: Without providence, why accept what happens? Without a shared divine reason, why treat everyone as a brother? Modern Stoicism keeps the advice but loses the reasons, and the advice then becomes a technique for coping.
positions.evidence: Diogenes Laertius VII.87–88; Epictetus, Discourses I.3 and I.6; Cleanthes' hymn.

positions.name: Yes, but with another God
positions.who: Christian readers from Justin Martyr to Justus Lipsius (1584)
positions.view: The Stoics were right that the world is ordered by reason and that virtue matters more than fortune, but wrong to make God the world itself. Take the Stoic practice into a faith in a personal Creator, and it is completed.
positions.evidence: John 1:1–14; Acts 17:28; Ambrose's Christian rewriting of Cicero's Stoic On Duties.

debate.agree: All agree that the ancient Stoics were deeply religious, and that the practice can be taught without the theology; they differ over whether it survives the change.

look.why: Sanford Robinson Gifford, an American landscape painter, painted the ruins on the Acropolis of Athens in 1880. The Painted Porch itself does not survive: only its foundations, found in the Agora below the Acropolis in 1981. This is the city where Zeno taught, as a traveller saw it two thousand years later: temples fallen, and two small figures studying the stones.
points: A wide, brightly lit field scattered with broken pieces of stone is framed to left and right by crumbling stone temples.
The temple on the left has a row of at least nine columns, several broken off, with its roof gone.
In the middle of the field two tiny men inspect the fragments: one kneels and writes or sketches; the other, in a long white pleated tunic and red cap, stands beside him.
To the right, a further building has columns carved in the shape of six robed women.
Beyond the ruins the ground slopes down to a plain and a blue sea, with mountains along the horizon under a pink haze.
The painting is signed and dated 'S.R. Gifford 1880' in the lower left.

music.why: Haydn's The Creation (1798) sets Genesis to music: chaos, then 'and there was light', then a world ordered and full of praise. The Stoics also saw a world shot through with reason and worthy of a hymn; listen for the difference between a world that is God and a world that God made.

think.why: The logos from Heraclitus and the Stoics to John's Gospel.

learn.why: Epictetus's first lesson, which the next session, still to come, reads in full: sort everything into what is in your power and what is not.

check.q: Why did the Stoics say that health and wealth are not 'good'?
options: Because the gods disapprove of the rich
Because what is good must always benefit, and health and wealth can be used well or badly
Because they are sinful pleasures
Because only pleasure is good
check.why: 'That thing is not good which it is possible to use both well and ill' (VII.103). The last option is the Epicurean view the Stoics rejected.

check.q: What did the Stoics mean by 'live according to nature'?
options: Avoid all medicine and technology
Live by reason, which is your own nature and the order of the whole universe
Live simply in the countryside
Follow your instincts and desires
check.why: Nature means the rational order of the world and of human beings; living by it is virtue (VII.87–88).

check.q: How does the Stoic God differ from Epicurus's gods?
options: The Stoic God became a man
The Stoic God is far away and takes no notice of us
The Stoic God knows and orders everything by providence, and runs through the world as its reason
The Stoics had no God
check.why: Epicurus's gods take no notice; the Stoic God foresees all and pervades all. The last option is the Christian claim, not the Stoic one.

check.q: Epictetus says God brought humans into the world to be 'a spectator of God and of his works... but an interpreter'. What follows for how we should live?
options: We should try to change the order of nature
We should withdraw from the world into prayer
We should look at and understand the world with gratitude, using our reason, rather than living only to eat and drink as animals do
We should travel to see the great statues of the gods
check.why: Animals use things; humans are made to understand them and to give thanks. The third option is the mistake he mocks.

check.q: Is ancient Stoicism best described as a religion?
options: It was a philosophy with a religious heart: its ethics rested on a provident, rational God, but it had no temples, Scripture or God acting in history
Yes: it was an early form of Christianity
Yes: it had temples and priests
No: it was purely practical and had no God
check.why: Epictetus thanks and praises God; but there were no rites or Scripture. The second option is the modern picture, not the ancient one.

check.q: What is the most important difference between the Stoic logos and John's 'the Word became flesh'?
options: John did not use the word logos
The Stoics thought the logos was evil
For the Stoics the logos is the reason running through the whole world; John says it became one particular human being
The Stoics thought the logos was a book
check.why: John borrows the word and makes a claim no Stoic could: the universal reason became flesh in Jesus.

tutorial.question: Is Stoicism a religion?
tutorial.approach: Define what you mean by a religion. Set out the Stoic picture of the world: logos, providence, fate, God in all things. Use Epictetus's talks to show how a Stoic spoke of God. Then note what is missing (temples, Scripture, a God who acts in history). End with the modern question: can the practice survive without the theology?
strong: Defines religion before applying it.
Explains the logos, providence and fate, with evidence from Diogenes Laertius.
Quotes Epictetus on God as father and on humans as spectators and interpreters.
Notes Stoic pantheism and how it differs from a creator God.
Considers modern secular Stoicism fairly.
Reaches a clear judgement.

reading.title: Lessons in Stoicism
reading.why: A short, clear introduction by a leading scholar, ancient and modern.

reading.why: The best book on Epictetus, including his theology.

reading.why: The standard account of all three schools.

reading.title: Philosophy as a Way of Life
reading.why: How ancient philosophy was practised as spiritual exercise.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Epictetus says we are made to be spectators and interpreters of the world. Each day, spend five minutes really looking at one ordinary thing (a leaf, a face, the light in a room), and write one sentence of thanks for it.
sessions.reflect: Do you think the world is ordered by reason, or by chance? How would your answer change the way you face a bad day?
takeaways: The Stoics, from Zeno's Painted Porch, taught that the world is one living whole ordered by divine reason, the logos, which is God.
Only virtue is good; health, wealth and even life are 'indifferent', though some are preferred.
Epictetus spoke of God as father and of humans as spectators and interpreters of his works; John's Gospel took the word logos and said it became flesh.

sessions.title: What is up to us
sessions.line: A lame former slave teaches the most famous lesson in ancient philosophy: some things are in our power, and some are not.
sessions.plain: Epictetus's Manual begins with a sentence millions have found life-changing: some things are in our power, and others are not. In our power are our judgements, choices, desires and aversions; not in our power are our bodies, property, reputation and office. Peace comes from wanting only the first. This session reads the opening of the Manual, sets beside it two short passages from the Bible on trust, and follows the lesson into a prison camp in Hanoi and a therapist's consulting room.
sessions.why: Session 3 showed the Stoic universe: a world ordered by divine reason, in which only virtue is good. If that is true, what should we do from moment to moment? Epictetus's answer, the 'dichotomy of control', is the most practical idea in Stoicism, and the reason it is popular today.
answers: What is the dichotomy of control?
Why is Stoicism popular today?
Who was Epictetus, and how did a slave teach freedom?
Does the Bible teach anything like it?
sessions.finding: Epictetus, born a slave, taught that some things are in our power (our judgements and choices) and the rest are not, and that peace comes from wanting only the first.

paras: Session 3 read Epictetus's talks on reason, God and providence, and Diogenes Laertius's summary of the Stoic system. The world is ordered by divine reason; only virtue is good; everything else is 'indifferent'. And Epictetus said: 'What is mine, and what is not mine?'
This session takes that question and turns it into a method. It is the part of Stoicism that people can use on a Monday morning.
background.key: Only virtue is good, and Epictetus asked 'what is mine?'. Now the question becomes a method.

paras: Encheiridion means 'handbook', or more exactly 'something to hold in the hand', like a dagger. Arrian made it from Epictetus's talks: fifty-two short chapters, meant to be carried and used. It became one of the most read books of ancient philosophy. Christian monks adapted it for their own use in the 400s and 500s, changing the gods to God. Soldiers, statesmen and philosophers carried it for centuries.
We read Long's translation of 1877. Long sometimes puts a second English word in brackets to show the range of a Greek word: 'desire (aim at)'. Read them as part of the meaning.

timeline.text: Epictetus born a slave at Hierapolis
Domitian expels philosophers from Rome; Epictetus moves to Nicopolis
Arrian records the Discourses and makes the Manual
Epictetus dies
Christian monks adapt the Manual
The Serenity Prayer appears, credited to Reinhold Niebuhr
Albert Ellis develops Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy, citing Epictetus
James Stockdale a prisoner of war in Hanoi
Aaron Beck's books found cognitive therapy

background.key: The Manual is Arrian's fifty-two-chapter handbook of Epictetus; monks, soldiers and therapists have carried it ever since.

paras: The main reading is the first five chapters of the Manual: the dichotomy of control, desire and aversion, the earthen pot, the bath, and 'men are disturbed not by things but by their opinions about things'. They are the clearest statement of the method there is.

The comparison is from the Bible: Psalm 131, a short prayer of a soul made quiet, and four lines of Proverbs on human plans and God's direction. They let us ask whether the Bible teaches the same lesson, and where it differs. (Jesus's teaching on worry, in Matthew 6, is read in The Sermon on the Mount.)
background.key: The first five chapters of the Manual; then a psalm and proverbs on quiet trust.

before: Make two lists as you read: what Epictetus says is in our power, and what is not.
What does Epictetus say we should tell ourselves when we kiss a child? How do you react?
According to chapter 5, what really disturbs us?
sessions.readWhy: The opening of Epictetus's Manual, in four parts: the two lists, desire, holding things lightly, and opinions.

paras: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion, turning from a thing; and in a word, whatever are our acts. Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices (magisterial power), and in a word, whatever are not our own acts. And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint or hindrance; but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others. Remember then, that if you think the things which are by nature slavish to be free, and the things which are in the power of others to be your own, you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, you will blame both gods and men; but if you think that only which is your own to be your own, and if you think that what is another’s, as it really is, belongs to another, no man will ever compel you, no man will hinder you, you will never blame any man, you will accuse no man, you will do nothing involuntarily (against your will), no man will harm you, you will have no enemy, for you will not suffer any harm.

If then you desire (aim at) such great things remember that you must not (attempt to) lay hold of them with a small effort; but you must leave alone some things entirely, and postpone others for the present. But if you wish for these things also (such great things), and power (office) and wealth, perhaps you will not gain even these very things (power and wealth) because you aim also at those former things (such great things); certainly you will fail in those things through which alone happiness and freedom are secured. Straightway then practise saying to every harsh appearance: You are an appearance, and in no manner what you appear to be. Then examine it by the rules which you possess, and by this first and chiefly, whether it relates to the things which are in our power or to things which are not in our power; and if it relates to anything which is not in our power, be ready to say that it does not concern you.

Remember that desire contains in it the profession (hope) of obtaining that which you desire; and the profession (hope) in aversion (turning from a thing) is that you will not fall into that which you attempt to avoid; and he who fails in his desire is unfortunate; and he who falls into that which he would avoid is unhappy. If then you attempt to avoid only the things contrary to nature which are within your power you will not be involved in any of the things which you would avoid. But if you attempt to avoid disease, or death, or poverty, you will be unhappy. Take away then aversion from all things which are not in our power, and transfer it to the things contrary to nature which are in our power. But destroy desire completely for the present. For if you desire anything which is not in our power, you must be unfortunate; but of the things in our power, and which it would be good to desire, nothing yet is before you. But employ only the power of moving towards an object and retiring from it; and these powers indeed only slightly and with exceptions and with remission.

In everything which pleases the soul, or supplies a want, or is loved, remember to add this to the (description, notion): What is the nature of each thing, beginning from the smallest? If you love an earthen vessel, say it is an earthen vessel which you love; for when it has been broken you will not be disturbed. If you are kissing your child or wife, say that it is a human being whom you are kissing, for when the wife or child dies you will not be disturbed.

When you are going to take in hand any act remind yourself what kind of an act it is. If you are going to bathe, place before yourself what happens in the bath; some splashing the water, others pushing against one another, others abusing one another, and some stealing; and thus with more safety you will undertake the matter, if you say to yourself, I now intend to bathe, and to maintain my will in a manner conformable to nature. And so you will do in every act; for thus if any hindrance to bathing shall happen let this thought be ready. It was not this only that I intended, but I intended also to maintain my will in a way conformable to nature; but I shall not maintain it so if I am vexed at what happens.

Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing. When then we are impeded, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves—that is, our opinions. It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: In our power, and not in our power
parts.who: Epictetus, as summarised by his pupil Arrian
parts.context: The first chapter of the Manual, and the most famous. Long's Greek words, which he printed in brackets after some English ones, are left out here. 'Offices' means public positions.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: some things are in our power and some are not. In our power are our opinions, impulses, desires and aversions: our own acts. Not in our power are our body, property, reputation and position. What is in our power is free; the rest is weak and belongs to others. If you treat what belongs to others as your own, you will be frustrated, unhappy and blame everyone. If you treat only your own as your own, no one can force or harm you. So when anything troubles you, ask: is this in my power? If not, say: it is nothing to me.

commentary.on: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
commentary.text: The 'dichotomy of control', as modern writers call it. A dichotomy is a cut into two. Everything that exists falls on one side or the other.

commentary.on: In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion, turning from a thing; and in a word, whatever are our acts.
commentary.text: Notice how small the first list is. Not our health, our job, our children's safety, or even what happens to our own bodies: only what goes on in our minds. Opinion here means judgement: what we decide things are.

commentary.on: Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices (magisterial power), and in a word, whatever are not our own acts.
commentary.text: The body is on the second list. That surprises modern readers. Epictetus, lame and once a slave, knew that a master or a disease could do what it liked with his body.

commentary.on: you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, you will blame both gods and men
commentary.text: The symptoms of the illness: frustration, grief, anxiety and blame. They all come, he says, from treating what is not ours as ours.

commentary.on: no man will ever compel you, no man will hinder you
commentary.text: The promise. A slave who wants only what is in his power is freer than an emperor who wants everything. Epictetus's whole teaching is a teaching about freedom.

commentary.on: You are an appearance, and in no manner what you appear to be.
commentary.text: A practical tool. When something hits you ('this is a disaster'), stop and say to the impression: 'you are only an appearance'. Then test it. Long's 'harsh appearance' means a painful impression.

commentary.on: be ready to say that it does not concern you
commentary.text: The hardest step. Not 'it does not matter', but 'it is not mine to decide, so my peace will not hang on it'.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: Desire and aversion
parts.context: Aversion means turning away from something, wanting to avoid it.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: if you desire something and do not get it, you are unhappy; if you try to avoid something and it happens, you are unhappy. So try to avoid only what is in your power to avoid, your own wrong choices, and you will never fail. If you try to avoid illness, death or poverty, you will be miserable. As a beginner, stop desiring altogether for now, and move towards and away from things lightly.

commentary.on: But if you attempt to avoid disease, or death, or poverty, you will be unhappy.
commentary.text: Not because these are good, but because you cannot guarantee to avoid them. Every hope that depends on what is not in your power is a hostage to fortune.

commentary.on: But destroy desire completely for the present.
commentary.text: Advice for beginners. Epictetus is a coach: first stop wanting things you cannot control, and only later learn to desire rightly. It is a stern training regime, not a statement that all desire is bad.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: An earthen vessel
parts.context: Two exercises in seeing things as they are. Roman public baths were crowded and rowdy.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: with everything you love, remind yourself what kind of thing it is, beginning with small things. If you love a pot, say 'I love a pot', and when it breaks you will not be upset. If you kiss your child or your wife, say 'I am kissing a human being', and if they die you will not be upset. And before doing anything, picture what it will involve: going to the baths, expect to be splashed and jostled, and decide in advance to keep your calm.

commentary.on: If you love an earthen vessel, say it is an earthen vessel which you love; for when it has been broken you will not be disturbed.
commentary.text: Simple and sensible. Most of our anger at broken things comes from forgetting that pots break.

commentary.on: If you are kissing your child or wife, say that it is a human being whom you are kissing, for when the wife or child dies you will not be disturbed.
commentary.text: And then the shock. Epictetus moves from pots to children in one breath, on purpose: 'beginning with the smallest'. A human being is mortal; remember it, and death will not surprise you. Many readers find this wise; many find it monstrous. We will return to it in the session on the objection, still to come. For now, notice your own reaction.

commentary.on: I now intend to bathe, and to maintain my will in a manner conformable to nature.
commentary.text: Every action has two aims: the outward one (a bath) and the inner one (to keep my character). The first can be spoiled by others; the second only by me.

parts.author: Epictetus
parts.title: Not things, but opinions about things
parts.context: The most quoted sentence in Epictetus. Socrates, executed in 399 BC, faced his death calmly.
parts.plain: Epictetus says: people are disturbed not by what happens but by their opinions about what happens. Death is not terrible, or Socrates would have thought so; the opinion that death is terrible is what is terrible. So when upset, blame your own opinions, not others. The untaught blame others; the beginner blames himself; the wise blame no one.

commentary.on: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things
commentary.text: This sentence is the seed of modern cognitive therapy. Between the event and the feeling there is a judgement; change the judgement and the feeling changes. The psychologist Albert Ellis, who founded one of the first such therapies in the 1950s, cited it.

commentary.on: for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing
commentary.text: Compare Epicurus: both schools try to cure the fear of death by changing what we think about it. Epicurus says death is nothing because we will not be there; Epictetus says it is not evil because it is not a matter of virtue.

commentary.on: It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition
commentary.text: Three stages of growth: blaming others, blaming yourself, blaming no one. The last is not indifference; it is the calm of someone who no longer needs a culprit.

read.author: Epictetus
read.who: Epictetus, as summarised by his pupil Arrian

paras:
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul,
like a weaned child with his mother,
like a weaned child is my soul within me.

Israel, hope in Yahweh,
from this time forward and forever more.

The plans of the heart belong to man,
but the answer of the tongue is from Yahweh.

All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes;
but Yahweh weighs the motives.

Commit your deeds to Yahweh,
and your plans shall succeed.

A man’s heart plans his course,
but Yahweh directs his steps.

parts.title: Like a weaned child
parts.context: One of the 'Songs of Ascents' (Psalms 120–134), probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the festivals. The heading credits David. A weaned child is no longer fed at the breast; it sits with its mother not to be fed but simply to be with her.

commentary.on:
nor do I concern myself with great matters,
or things too wonderful for me.
commentary.text: Close to Epictetus: do not trouble yourself with what is beyond your reach. The psalmist lets go of what is not his to manage.

commentary.on:
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul,
like a weaned child with his mother,
commentary.text: But the picture is very different. Epictetus's calm is the calm of a free man who needs nobody. The psalmist's calm is that of a child with its mother: not independence, but trust.

commentary.on:
Israel, hope in Yahweh,
from this time forward and forever more.
commentary.text: The ground of peace is not a judgement about what is mine, but hope in someone. The Stoic gives up hope in what he cannot control; the psalmist puts his hope in God, who can.

parts.title: A man's heart plans his course
parts.context: Proverbs is a collection of Israel's wisdom sayings, many credited to King Solomon. These lines are about the limits of human control.

commentary.on:
The plans of the heart belong to man,
but the answer of the tongue is from Yahweh.
commentary.text: Like Epictetus, Proverbs draws a line between what is ours (our plans) and what is not (the outcome).

commentary.on:
Commit your deeds to Yahweh,
and your plans shall succeed.
commentary.text: The difference: the outcome is not left to impersonal fate but entrusted to God. 'Commit' is literally 'roll onto': roll your works onto the Lord, as you would roll a heavy load off your back.

commentary.on:
A man’s heart plans his course,
but Yahweh directs his steps.
commentary.text: Both the Bible and the Stoics accept that we do not control outcomes. The Stoics say: so want only your own choices. The Bible says: so trust the one who directs your steps. The first is self-sufficiency; the second, dependence.

compare.why: The Bible also teaches a kind of letting go. Read a psalm of a soul made quiet, and four proverbs on human plans and God's direction. Notice what is the same as Epictetus, and what is different.
compare.title: A quieted soul

paras: Epictetus's first lesson can be put in three steps. Sort: everything is either up to you (your judgements, choices, desires) or not (everything else). Value: only what is up to you can be good or bad for you. Act: put your effort into your choices, and meet everything else with acceptance.

Two misunderstandings are common. First, it is not passivity. A Stoic doctor still treats the sick; a Stoic general still fights the battle. What changes is where their peace lies: in doing their part well, not in the result. The Stoics used the image of an archer, who does everything to aim well but cannot control the wind (Cicero, On Ends III.22). Second, it is not indifference to others. Epictetus taught duties to family, city and the whole human race. But even our care for them is our act; whether they live or die is not.
sections.key: Sort what is up to you, value only that, act on it and accept the rest. It is not passivity: the archer aims well but does not control the wind.

paras: Many people know Epictetus's lesson without knowing his name, through the Serenity Prayer, which asks God for serenity to accept what cannot be changed, courage to change what can, and wisdom to know the difference. It is usually credited to the American theologian Reinhold Niebuhr; the earliest versions appear in the 1930s, and it was taken up by Alcoholics Anonymous in the 1940s. (We describe it in our own words, as its text is still under copyright.)

Notice what the prayer adds. Epictetus thinks the wisdom to tell the difference is ours, and that acceptance follows from a correct judgement. The prayer asks for all three as gifts from God. And it adds courage to change things, which in Epictetus is present but quieter. It is the dichotomy of control turned into a prayer.
sections.key: The Serenity Prayer (1930s, credited to Niebuhr) is Epictetus's lesson turned into a prayer, asking God for what Epictetus thought we must supply ourselves.

sections.h: From the Manual to the consulting room
paras: In the 1950s the American psychologist Albert Ellis broke with Freudian analysis and developed what he called Rational Emotive Therapy. He taught patients that it is not events but their beliefs about events that upset them, and he often quoted Epictetus's fifth chapter. In the 1960s and 70s the psychiatrist Aaron Beck developed cognitive therapy for depression, which teaches people to catch their 'automatic thoughts' and test them against the evidence. Beck and his colleagues wrote in 1979 that the philosophical roots of the approach go back to the Stoics.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which grew from their work, is now one of the most widely used and tested treatments for anxiety and depression. That is a remarkable afterlife for a lame slave's lectures. It is also why Stoicism is popular now: it is a philosophy whose central technique has been tested in clinical trials. CBT, though, keeps the method and drops the Stoic theology and the claim that only virtue is good.
sections.key: Ellis and Beck drew on Epictetus's 'not things but opinions'; CBT keeps his method, without his theology.

paras: On 9 September 1965 an American navy pilot, James Stockdale, was shot down over North Vietnam. As he parachuted down, he later wrote, he said to himself that he was leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus. He had studied the Manual at Stanford. He spent seven and a half years as a prisoner, four of them in solitary confinement, and was tortured many times.

Stockdale said that Epictetus taught him what was within his power: his own will, his honour, his refusal to be used. He organised resistance among the prisoners and once wounded himself rather than be filmed for propaganda. After his release he received the Medal of Honor and wrote and lectured on Epictetus, especially in 'Courage under Fire' (1993). His story is now told in almost every introduction to Stoicism. It shows the teaching at its best: freedom in chains, as Epictetus promised.
sections.key: James Stockdale, a prisoner in Hanoi from 1965 to 1973, held on through Epictetus's teaching that his will was his own.

sections.h: A slave's philosophy, and its limits
paras: It matters who taught this. Epictetus was not a rich man advising people to be calm about their possessions. He was a slave, lame, exiled, who found freedom where no master could reach. That is why his words have meant so much to prisoners, the sick and the powerless.

But his first list can shrink too far. If only my judgements are mine, then injustice done to others, and even to my own body, is 'not my concern'. Epictetus did not mean us to ignore injustice; but his method contains no reason to change the world. The Bible's prophets were less calm and more angry. And the Christian reading in Psalm 131 points to another source of peace: not shrinking what we care about, but trusting someone with it.
sections.key: A slave's philosophy of inner freedom has comforted the powerless; its risk is that it gives no reason to change an unjust world.

paras: The commonest modern criticism of the dichotomy is that very little falls cleanly on either side. Whether I pass an exam, keep a friend or recover from an illness is neither wholly up to me nor wholly outside my control. The American philosopher William Irvine has suggested a 'trichotomy': things we control completely, things we do not control at all, and things we influence. For the third kind, he advises setting inner goals: not 'win the match' but 'play as well as I can'.

Epictetus might reply that this is exactly his point. The outcome of the match is never up to you; your effort and your attitude are. His division is not between kinds of events but between two parts of every event: my choice, and everything else. Read that way, the dichotomy is not a list of topics to stop caring about but a way of looking at any situation. It tells you where to put your effort and where to rest.
sections.key: Critics add a third category, things we influence; Epictetus's reply is that every event has two parts, my choice and the rest.

paras: Christians read the Manual early and kept it. In the 400s and 500s, monks in the Greek East made paraphrases of it for their communities, changing 'the gods' to 'God', adding Bible references, and replacing Socrates with St Paul. One version is credited to the ascetic Nilus of Ancyra. The Manual's training in watching one's thoughts fitted the monks' own practice of examining the heart, which the desert monks called 'watchfulness'.

The Manual remained a Christian text for centuries. The Neoplatonist Simplicius wrote a long commentary on it in the 500s; the first English translation appeared in 1567; and in the 1600s Pascal and others read it closely. What the monks added was the same thing the psalmist adds in this session's comparison: the self is not enough. Watchfulness was practised in prayer, before a God who sees, rather than as a private discipline of the will.
sections.key: Monks adapted the Manual from the 400s, changing 'the gods' to God and setting its watchfulness within prayer.
