debate.question: Is the dichotomy of control the secret of peace?

positions.name: Yes
positions.who: Epictetus; James Stockdale; modern Stoics such as Ryan Holiday and Donald Robertson (in our words)
positions.view: Most suffering comes from wanting what we cannot control. Sort the two, and you gain a freedom no circumstance can take. The evidence from prisons and from therapy shows it works.
positions.evidence: Encheiridion 1 and 5; Stockdale's survival; the evidence for cognitive behavioural therapy.

positions.name: Half true
positions.who: Many philosophers, e.g. William Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009), in our words
positions.view: Very little is wholly in our control or wholly outside it; most things, like our health or a friendship, are partly up to us. The dichotomy needs a third category: things we can influence. And caring about outcomes is part of loving people.
positions.evidence: Ordinary experience: exams, marriages and illnesses are partly up to us.

positions.name: Peace comes from trust, not control
positions.who: The psalmist; Paul; the Christian tradition
positions.view: Epictetus is right that we cannot control outcomes. But the answer is not to care only about our own choices; it is to entrust what we care about to God, who can.
positions.evidence: Psalm 131; Proverbs 16:3, 9; Matthew 6:25–34; 1 Peter 5:7.

debate.agree: All agree that we cannot control outcomes, that much anxiety comes from trying to, and that our own choices are where effort belongs.

look.why: No painting for this session: the National Gallery of Art's open collection has no painting of Epictetus, or of a slave or prisoner that fits without pretending to be what it is not.

music.why: John Greenleaf Whittier's hymn asks God to 'take from our souls the strain and stress' and give 'the beauty of thy peace': the quieted soul of Psalm 131, received as a gift rather than won by training.

think.why: Can daily practice change who we are? The Stoics thought so.

learn.why: Epictetus's hardest lesson in his own words: treat everything as on loan. Learn it, and then ask whether you agree.

check.q: Which of these does Epictetus put on the list of things in our power?
options: Our children's safety
Our health
Our reputation
Our judgements, desires and aversions
check.why: Only 'whatever are our acts': opinion, impulse, desire, aversion. Even the body is not in our power.

check.q: Why, according to Epictetus, do people blame gods and men?
options: Because they have not prayed enough
Because they are slaves
Because they treat what belongs to others, and is not in their power, as their own
Because gods and men really are to blame
check.why: Encheiridion 1: if you think what is in the power of others to be your own, 'you will blame both gods and men'.

check.q: Does the dichotomy of control mean we should not try to change our circumstances?
options: No: a Stoic acts as well as possible, like an archer aiming well, but rests his peace on his own choices, not on the outcome
No: a Stoic should control outcomes by force of will
Yes: a Stoic accepts everything and does nothing
Yes, unless the gods command it
check.why: Stoics acted in the world; what changes is where their peace lies. The first option is the commonest misunderstanding.

check.q: What is the most important link between Epictetus and cognitive behavioural therapy?
options: Both teach that we are disturbed not by events but by our judgements about them, which can be examined and changed
Both teach that the body is not in our power
Both teach that only virtue is good
Both were founded by slaves
check.why: Encheiridion 5 is the seed; Ellis quoted it. CBT does not teach that only virtue is good.

check.q: How does Psalm 131 differ most from Epictetus's teaching?
options: The psalmist finds peace in trust, like a child with its mother, and hope in God, rather than in self-sufficiency
The psalmist wants to control great matters
The psalmist thinks nothing is in our power
There is no difference
check.why: Both let go of what is beyond them; the psalm's ground of peace is a person to trust.

check.q: What is the strongest objection to Epictetus's first list?
options: It contradicts the Epicureans
It shrinks what we care about so far that injustice to others, and even what happens to those we love, becomes 'not our concern'
It was written by a slave
It is too long
check.why: The method protects the self but gives no reason to change an unjust world, and seems to ask us to love less.

tutorial.question: 'Peace comes from wanting only what is in our power.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Explain Epictetus's two lists and why he draws the line where he does. Give the evidence that the method works: Stockdale and cognitive therapy. Then test it: is the line too sharp (things we can influence)? Does it ask us to love less? Compare the Bible's 'commit your deeds to the Lord'. Conclude.
strong: Explains the dichotomy of control accurately, with Encheiridion 1.
Explains 'not things but opinions' (Encheiridion 5) and its link to therapy.
Uses Stockdale or another real case.
Raises the problem of things partly in our control.
Raises the problem of love, using Encheiridion 3.
Compares trust in God (Psalm 131; Proverbs 16) fairly.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each morning, name one thing you are worried about. Draw a line down a page: on the left, what in it is up to you; on the right, what is not. Do one thing from the left column that day. For the right column, either let it go, or, if you pray, hand it over in one sentence.
sessions.reflect: What would you lose if you followed Epictetus's advice about your child or your partner? What would you gain?
takeaways: Epictetus taught that only our judgements, desires and choices are in our power; peace comes from wanting only these.
'Not things, but opinions about things' disturb us: the seed of cognitive therapy, and the lesson that sustained James Stockdale in Hanoi.
The Bible also lets go of outcomes, but grounds peace in trust in God rather than in self-sufficiency.

sessions.title: A Roman Stoic
sessions.line: The richest philosopher in Rome writes to a friend about time, death and slaves, tutors the emperor Nero, and is ordered by him to die.
sessions.plain: Seneca was a Roman statesman, playwright and Stoic philosopher, tutor and then chief adviser to the emperor Nero. In his last years he wrote letters to a friend, Lucilius, about how to live: on not wasting time, on facing death, on treating slaves as fellow human beings. He was also one of the richest men in the empire, and in AD 65 Nero ordered him to kill himself. This session asks what Stoicism looked like in the life of a powerful man, and whether he lived what he taught.
sessions.why: Sessions 3 and 4 heard Stoicism from a former slave, Epictetus, who had nothing to lose. Seneca had everything to lose: wealth, power, the emperor's favour. Can the Stoic teaching survive a life at court? Seneca is the test case, and Christians admired him so much that they forged letters between him and Paul.
answers: Who was Seneca?
What did he teach about time, death and slaves?
Was Seneca a hypocrite?
Did Seneca know Paul?
sessions.finding: Seneca, the rich adviser to Nero, wrote letters on time, death and treating slaves as fellow human beings, was accused even in his lifetime of not living what he taught, and was forced to kill himself by his former pupil.

paras: The Stoics taught that the world is ordered by divine reason and that only virtue is good (session 3). Epictetus turned this into a method: want only what is in your power (session 4). Both lessons came from a man who had been a slave.

Stoicism had reached Rome two centuries before, in the 100s BC, and became the philosophy of many of Rome's ruling class. Its stress on duty, self-control and endurance suited the Roman ideal of a statesman. Seneca is its greatest Roman voice.
background.key: Stoicism came to Rome in the 100s BC and suited its ruling class; Seneca is its great Roman voice.

paras: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born around 4 BC in Corduba, now Córdoba in Spain, to a rich family. He came to Rome as a child, studied philosophy and rhetoric, and became a famous speaker and writer. In AD 41 the emperor Claudius exiled him to Corsica, on a charge of adultery with the emperor's niece. In 49 the empress Agrippina brought him back to tutor her son, Nero.

When Nero became emperor in 54, aged sixteen, Seneca and the soldier Burrus effectively governed the empire, and the first years were remembered as good ones. Seneca wrote On Mercy for the young emperor. But Nero grew cruel: he had his mother murdered in 59, and Seneca seems to have helped write the letter that excused it. In 62 Seneca tried to retire and offered Nero his fortune. In 65, accused of joining a plot against the emperor, he was ordered to die. The historian Tacitus tells how he cut his veins and comforted his friends, and how his wife Paulina tried to die with him (Annals XV.60–64).

timeline.text: Seneca born at Corduba in Spain
Exiled to Corsica by Claudius
Recalled to tutor the young Nero
His brother Gallio, governor in Corinth, dismisses the case against Paul (Acts 18:12–17)
Nero becomes emperor; Seneca his chief adviser
Nero has his mother Agrippina killed
Seneca withdraws from court; writes the Letters to Lucilius

Seneca ordered to kill himself

background.key: Seneca (c. 4 BC–AD 65): exiled, recalled to tutor Nero, chief adviser from 54, retired in 62, forced to die in 65.

paras: Seneca's greatest work is 124 Letters to Lucilius, written in his last years. Lucilius was a younger friend, a Roman official in Sicily. The letters are short essays on how to live, full of examples and sharp sayings. We cannot quote them here at length, because the standard English translation, by Richard Gummere (1917), is still in copyright: Gummere lived until 1969. So we tell them in our own words.

The first letter is about time. Most of our life, Seneca writes, slips away in doing wrong, more in doing nothing, and the most in doing what does not matter. We think death lies ahead, but most of it is already behind us: every hour that has passed belongs to death. Time is the only thing that is truly ours, and we let anyone take it. So, he tells Lucilius, take hold of every hour; start today.

The forty-seventh letter is about slaves. Seneca is glad to hear that Lucilius lives on friendly terms with his slaves. He describes a rich man's dinner where slaves stand silent all night, beaten for a cough. Remember, he says, that the man you call your slave was born of the same seed, enjoys the same sky, breathes, lives and dies as you do. Treat your inferior as you would wish your superior to treat you. 'They are slaves,' people say. In Gummere's translation: "Nay, rather they are men."
background.key: Seneca's Letters to Lucilius: on seizing time, which is all we own (Letter 1), and on slaves as fellow human beings (Letter 47). Told in our own words.

paras: Since Seneca's letters cannot be quoted here, the main reading is Seneca's own words as another writer preserved them. Augustine, in The City of God (written 413–426), quotes at length from a lost book by Seneca, On Superstition, which attacked the cults of Rome; and then he makes the oldest charge against Seneca: that he wrote one thing and did another. It shows both Seneca's freedom of mind and the question of his integrity.

The comparison is from Paul, writing to the church in Corinth in the AD 50s, at the same time as Seneca was governing the empire: what should a Christian who is a slave do, and what is the difference between being a slave and being free?
background.key: Seneca's words on religion as quoted by Augustine, with Augustine's charge of hypocrisy; then Paul on slaves and freedom.

before: What does Seneca think of the Roman gods and their worship?
What does he say a wise man should do about public religion, and why does Augustine object?
In Paul, who is 'free' and who is a 'bondservant'?
sessions.readWhy: Seneca's lost book against superstition, in his own words as Augustine quoted them, and Augustine's verdict on the man, in four parts.

paras: That liberty, in truth, which this man wanted, so that he did not dare to censure that theology of the city, which is very similar to the theatrical, so openly as he did the theatrical itself, was, though not fully, yet in part possessed by Annæus Seneca, whom we have some evidence to show to have flourished in the times of our apostles. It was in part possessed by him, I say, for he possessed it in writing, but not in living. For in that book which he wrote against superstition, he more copiously and vehemently censured that civil and urban theology than Varro the theatrical and fabulous. For, when speaking concerning images, he says, "They dedicate images of the sacred and inviolable immortals in most worthless and motionless matter. They give them the appearance of man, beasts, and fishes, and some make them of mixed sex, and heterogeneous bodies. They call them deities, when they are such that if they should get breath and should suddenly meet them, they would be held to be monsters."

But with what freedom he has written concerning the rites themselves, cruel and shameful! "One," he says, "castrates himself, another cuts his arms. Where will they find room for the fear of these gods when angry, who use such means of gaining their favour when propitious? But gods who wish to be worshipped in this fashion should be worshipped in none.

Whence, with respect to these sacred rites of the civil theology, Seneca preferred, as the best course to be followed by a wise man, to feign respect for them in act, but to have no real regard for them at heart. "All which things," he says, "a wise man will observe as being commanded by the laws, but not as being pleasing to the gods."

But this man, whom philosophy had made, as it were, free, nevertheless, because he was an illustrious senator of the Roman people, worshipped what he censured, did what he condemned, adored what he reproached, because, forsooth, philosophy had taught him something great,--namely, not to be superstitious in the world, but, on account of the laws of cities and the customs of men, to be an actor, not on the stage, but in the temples,--conduct the more to be condemned, that those things which he was deceitfully acting he so acted that the people thought he was acting sincerely. But a stage-actor would rather delight people by acting plays than take them in by false pretences.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo, quoting Seneca
parts.translator: J. J. Smith, in Marcus Dods's edition (1871)
parts.ref: The City of God VI.10 (the opening)
parts.title: A freer man than Varro
parts.who: Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, quoting Seneca's lost On Superstition
parts.context: Augustine has been discussing Varro (116–27 BC), the most learned Roman writer on religion, who criticised the gods of the poets and the theatre but not the official worship of the city. Seneca, says Augustine, was bolder. 'Civil theology' means the state religion of Rome; 'theatrical' or 'fabulous' theology means the myths. The book On Superstition is lost; Augustine's quotations are almost all that survives. Book VI of this edition was translated by J. J. Smith.
parts.plain: Augustine says: Seneca, who lived in the time of the apostles, had the freedom Varro lacked, at least in what he wrote, if not in how he lived. In his book against superstition he attacked the state religion. He mocked statues of the gods made of cheap material in the shapes of men, beasts and fish, which would be called monsters if they came to life.

commentary.on: whom we have some evidence to show to have flourished in the times of our apostles
commentary.text: Augustine reminds his readers that Seneca and Paul were contemporaries. Seneca was at the height of his power when Paul was writing his letters.

commentary.on: for he possessed it in writing, but not in living
commentary.text: The charge, stated at the start: Seneca was free on paper, but not in life. Hold it in mind; Augustine returns to it at the end.

commentary.on: They dedicate images of the sacred and inviolable immortals in most worthless and motionless matter.
commentary.text: Seneca's own words, through Latin into English. Like Isaiah, whom you read in session 2, he mocks the making of gods from dead matter. A Stoic believed in one divine reason, not in statues.

commentary.on: they would be held to be monsters
commentary.text: If the statues breathed, people would run from them. Seneca's wit is sharp and very Roman.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo, quoting Seneca
parts.translator: J. J. Smith, in Marcus Dods's edition (1871)
parts.title: Gods who wish to be worshipped in this fashion
parts.context: Seneca turns to the bloody rites of some cults, especially that of the goddess Cybele, whose priests castrated themselves. The account is brief and not graphic. Part of the quotation, mocking the rites in the Capitol, is cut, marked '…'.
parts.plain: Seneca says: some worshippers castrate themselves, others cut their arms. If this is how people please the gods, how terrible must the gods be when angry? Gods who want worship like this should not be worshipped at all.

commentary.on: Where will they find room for the fear of these gods when angry, who use such means of gaining their favour when propitious?
commentary.text: 'Propitious' means favourable. Seneca's argument is close to Lucretius's: religion of fear makes people cruel, even to themselves.

commentary.on: But gods who wish to be worshipped in this fashion should be worshipped in none.
commentary.text: A memorable sentence. Notice the difference from Lucretius. Seneca is not attacking religion as such; as a Stoic he believed in God and providence. He attacks a religion unworthy of God.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo, quoting Seneca
parts.translator: J. J. Smith, in Marcus Dods's edition (1871)
parts.title: Commanded by the laws
parts.context: After mocking the state cults, what did Seneca advise? Augustine reports his answer.
parts.plain: Augustine says: Seneca thought a wise man should outwardly respect the state religion but inwardly give it no real regard. He quotes Seneca: a wise man will observe all these rites because the laws command them, not because the gods like them.

commentary.on: to feign respect for them in act, but to have no real regard for them at heart
commentary.text: Seneca's advice is outward conformity, inner freedom. It is a very Stoic answer: what is in my power is my judgement; the rites are the city's business.

commentary.on: “All which things,” he says, “a wise man will observe as being commanded by the laws, but not as being pleasing to the gods.”
commentary.text: Many people today would find this sensible: keep the customs, privately disbelieve. Augustine found it unbearable. The early Christians died rather than offer a pinch of incense to the emperor, because they would not do outwardly what they rejected inwardly.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo, quoting Seneca
parts.translator: J. J. Smith, in Marcus Dods's edition (1871)
parts.ref: The City of God VI.10 (the end)
parts.title: An actor in the temples
parts.context: Augustine's verdict on Seneca. He admires him, but cannot forgive him.
parts.plain: Augustine says: philosophy had made Seneca free, yet because he was a senator he worshipped what he criticised and did what he condemned. He was an actor, not on the stage but in the temples, and worse than an actor, because the people thought he meant it.

commentary.on: worshipped what he censured, did what he condemned, adored what he reproached
commentary.text: Three balanced phrases, a Roman orator's style: Augustine had been a professor of rhetoric. The charge is not that Seneca was wicked, but that he was divided.

commentary.on: to be an actor, not on the stage, but in the temples
commentary.text: The Greek word for an actor is hypokrites, from which we get 'hypocrite'. Augustine does not use the word, but that is his charge. It is the charge that has followed Seneca ever since, about his religion and, still more, about his wealth.

commentary.on: But a stage-actor would rather delight people by acting plays than take them in by false pretences.
commentary.text: A sharp ending: the theatre is more honest than the temple, because everyone knows the actor is acting. Ask yourself whether the charge is fair, and whether the same could be said of people today who keep religious customs they do not believe.

read.author: Augustine of Hippo, quoting Seneca
read.ref: The City of God VI.10 (the opening)
read.translator: J. J. Smith, in Marcus Dods's edition (1871)

paras: Only, as the Lord has distributed to each man, as God has called each, so let him walk. So I command in all the assemblies.
Was anyone called having been circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Has anyone been called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.
Let each man stay in that calling in which he was called.
Were you called being a bondservant? Don’t let that bother you, but if you get an opportunity to become free, use it.
For he who was called in the Lord being a bondservant is the Lord’s free man. Likewise he who was called being free is Christ’s bondservant.
You were bought with a price. Don’t become bondservants of men.
Brothers, let each man, in whatever condition he was called, stay in that condition with God.

parts.title: Bought with a price
parts.context: Paul wrote this letter to the church he had founded at Corinth, in Greece, around AD 53–55, from Ephesus. The church included slaves and free people. In the verses before, he has been answering questions about marriage; now he states a general rule: do not think you must change your outward state to belong to God. The World English Bible's 'bondservant' translates the ordinary Greek word for a slave (doulos).

commentary.on: Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.
commentary.text: Paul's first example: being Jewish or Gentile in the flesh does not decide your standing with God. Outward conditions are, in a sense, 'indifferent', as the Stoics would say.

commentary.on: Were you called being a bondservant? Don’t let that bother you, but if you get an opportunity to become free, use it.
commentary.text: Close to Stoicism: your condition does not touch your worth. But then a difference: if you can become free, take it. (The Greek of the last phrase is disputed; some translators read it as 'make use of your present condition instead'. The World English Bible takes it as freedom, as most modern translations do.)

commentary.on: For he who was called in the Lord being a bondservant is the Lord’s free man. Likewise he who was called being free is Christ’s bondservant.
commentary.text: A complete reversal of status. The slave is a freedman of the Lord; the free man is Christ's slave. In the church, both stand on the same ground. Seneca said master and slave share the same nature; Paul says they share the same Lord.

commentary.on: You were bought with a price. Don’t become bondservants of men.
commentary.text: The 'price' is Christ's death. Christians belong to Christ, so no human master owns them in the deepest sense. Paul did not campaign to abolish slavery, and neither did Seneca; but this sentence would later be quoted by Christians who did. If you have taken How we got here, you have read Paul's letter to Philemon about a runaway slave.

compare.why: Seneca told his friend that slaves are fellow human beings, and still owned hundreds of them. At the same moment Paul was writing to a church with slaves among its members. Read what he told them.
compare.title: Slave and free in Christ

paras: Seneca preached that wealth is 'indifferent' while he became one of the richest men in Rome. Tacitus records that in AD 58 a senator, Publius Suillius, attacked him in public: by what wisdom, he asked, had Seneca made three hundred million sesterces in four years of the emperor's friendship, hunting wills and draining Italy with his interest? (Annals XIII.42.) The later historian Cassius Dio, around AD 200, accused him of preaching against tyranny while teaching a tyrant, and of calling in huge loans in Britain so harshly that it helped provoke Boudicca's revolt in AD 60 (Roman History LXI.10; LXII.2).

Seneca answered the charge himself, in On the Happy Life: philosophers, he wrote, speak of how one ought to live, not of how they do; and a wise man may own riches, as long as riches do not own him. Wealth should be in his house, not in his heart.
sections.key: Seneca preached that wealth is indifferent and became immensely rich; he answered that the wise may own riches if riches do not own them.

paras: The case against is strong: the fortune, the years serving a murderer, the help with the letter excusing Nero's matricide, the conformity in the temples that Augustine condemned. The case for is also real. He tried, twice, to give his fortune back and leave court. He wrote that he was not a wise man but a sick man in the same hospital as his readers, sharing their remedies (Letter 27). And his death, as Tacitus tells it, was calm and brave; he left his friends, he said, the only thing he had left, the pattern of his life.

Perhaps the fairest judgement is that Seneca shows the limits of Stoicism in power. Epictetus could want only what was in his power because he had little. Seneca had a great deal, and the Stoic teaching that outward things are 'indifferent' made it easy to keep them while saying they did not matter. A teaching that makes everything outward unimportant can let a man serve a tyrant with a calm mind.
sections.key: Seneca was divided, not wicked: he served a tyrant and kept his fortune, tried to leave, called himself a patient not a sage, and died bravely.

paras: Seneca and Paul lived at the same time, and their paths almost touched. Seneca's elder brother Gallio was governor of Achaia, in Greece, when the Jews of Corinth brought Paul before him around AD 51; Gallio dismissed the case (Acts 18:12–17). Paul was later taken to Rome and wrote of believers in 'Caesar's household' (Philippians 4:22), while Seneca was the emperor's adviser. There is no evidence that they ever met.

But by the 300s Christians were reading a set of fourteen letters said to have passed between Seneca and Paul. Jerome, in 392, included Seneca among the Christian writers for their sake (On Illustrious Men 12), and Augustine mentions them. They are forgeries: their Latin is poor, their content thin, and their style nothing like Seneca's. Erasmus showed this in the 1500s. Yet they show how close the early Church felt to Seneca. Tertullian, around AD 200, called him 'often one of us' (On the Soul 20). In the Middle Ages Seneca was read as almost a Christian moralist, and Dante placed him among the virtuous pagans in Limbo (Inferno IV).
sections.key: Seneca's brother Gallio judged Paul in Corinth, but the fourteen 'letters of Seneca and Paul' are a later forgery; the Church still called Seneca 'often one of us'.

paras: Seneca's letter on slaves draws on one of the Stoics' great ideas: cosmopolitanism, from the Greek kosmopolites, 'citizen of the universe'. Since every human being shares in the divine reason, all are members of one great city, the cosmos. Seneca wrote that each of us belongs to two commonwealths: the city where we happen to be born, and the great one that includes gods and men (On Leisure 4).

This idea passed to Roman law, which spoke of a 'law of nations' common to all peoples, and into Christianity, which preached one human family. It is a root of the modern idea of universal human rights. But it did not end slavery. Seneca told masters to be kind; he did not tell them to free their slaves. Stoicism changed the hearts of some masters, and the law in small ways, but treated the institution itself as one of the 'indifferent' things of the world.
sections.key: Stoic cosmopolitanism made every person a citizen of one world, a root of human rights; but Seneca urged kindness to slaves, not their freedom.

paras: Seneca's most loved teaching is about time. In On the Shortness of Life (about AD 49) he argued that life is not short; we make it short by wasting it. People guard their money but give away their hours to anyone who asks. The cure is to take hold of each day as if it were the last, and to spend time on what matters: wisdom, friends, the good.

And about death: Seneca's letters say again and again that to philosophise is to learn how to die, and that we die daily, as each day passes. This is not gloom; it is the ground of freedom. Someone who has learned to die, he wrote, has unlearned how to be a slave. When Nero's soldiers came, Seneca had been practising for years. Whether his peace was the peace of a good man or only of a well-trained one is the question the next session, still to come, will press hard.
sections.key: Seneca taught that life is long if we use it, that each day is part of our dying, and that whoever has learned to die is free.

paras: In April AD 65 a plot to kill Nero and make the senator Gaius Calpurnius Piso emperor was betrayed. Seneca was named, probably falsely. A tribune came to his villa outside Rome with the order to die. Tacitus, writing about fifty years later, tells the story in detail (Annals XV.60–64). Seneca asked for his will, and was refused; so, turning to his friends, he said he left them the one thing he still had, the pattern of his life. When they wept, he asked where their philosophy was.

His wife Paulina insisted on dying with him, and both cut their veins. Seneca, old and thin, bled slowly; he took hemlock, as Socrates had, and it did not work; at last he was carried into a hot bath and died of the steam. Nero ordered Paulina's wounds bound, and she lived some years more. Tacitus is careful to say that some thought Seneca's last words were staged for posterity. Even so, the scene was one of the most painted and retold in Europe: the philosopher who taught others how to die, dying.
sections.key: Ordered to die in AD 65, Seneca left his friends 'the pattern of his life', cut his veins with his wife Paulina, and died slowly, Socrates-like, as Tacitus tells.

Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 1, 24, 26, 27, 47 (tr. R. M. Gummere, Loeb, 1917–1925: summarised, not quoted beyond one sentence); On the Shortness of Life; On the Happy Life 21–23; On Leisure 4; On Mercy.

debate.question: Was Seneca a hypocrite?

positions.name: Yes
positions.who: Publius Suillius (in Tacitus); Cassius Dio; Augustine, on religion
positions.view: He preached that wealth is indifferent and amassed a vast fortune; he wrote against tyranny and served a tyrant; he mocked the gods and worshipped them in public. His philosophy was a costume.
positions.evidence: Tacitus, Annals XIII.42; Dio LXI.10; City of God VI.10; the letter excusing Agrippina's murder.

positions.name: No: a struggling pupil, honestly
positions.who: Seneca himself; Tacitus, on his death; many modern biographers
positions.view: Seneca never claimed to be a sage. He was trying to restrain Nero, which was better than leaving him to worse advisers; he tried to give up his wealth; and his death showed that the teaching was real in him.
positions.evidence: Letter 27; On the Happy Life 17–18; Tacitus, Annals XIV.53–56 and XV.60–64.

positions.name: The fault lies partly in the teaching
positions.who: Many modern scholars, e.g. James Romm (in our words)
positions.view: Seneca was not simply a bad man. Stoicism's claim that outward things are indifferent let him keep wealth and serve power while telling himself they did not touch his soul. A philosophy of inner freedom can make peace with outward evil.
positions.evidence: The gap between Letter 47's words on slaves and Seneca's continued ownership of them; his service at Nero's court.

debate.agree: All agree that Seneca wrote some of the wisest pages on time, death and human equality in ancient literature, and that his life fell short of them in public ways.

look.why: No painting for this session: the National Gallery of Art has no painting of Seneca or his death in its open collection.

music.why: 'Swift to its close ebbs out life's little day': Henry Francis Lyte wrote this hymn in 1847, weeks before his death. Seneca told his friend that every hour that passes belongs to death; Lyte, facing the same truth, asks for a companion in it.

think.why: Seneca called slaves fellow human beings but did not free them. Who did end slavery, and why?

learn.why: Seneca's first letter teaches that time is all we own and must be used now; Gummere's translation cannot be quoted, so learn the same lesson in the words of another Roman Stoic, Marcus Aurelius.

check.q: Why does this session teach Seneca's Letters in our own words rather than quoting them?
options: Because the standard translation (Gummere, 1917) is still in copyright, as its translator died in 1969
Because Seneca wrote in Greek
Because they are lost
Because they were forgeries
check.why: Translations count as out of copyright here only if the translator died before 1955; Gummere lived until 1969.

check.q: What, according to Augustine, was Seneca's advice about the state religion of Rome?
options: That the gods should be worshipped sincerely
That Christians should be allowed to join it
That a wise man should observe its rites because the law commands them, while regarding them as worthless
That the wise should abolish it
check.why: 'A wise man will observe as being commanded by the laws, but not as being pleasing to the gods' (VI.10). Augustine calls this acting in the temples.

check.q: What was Seneca's teaching about slaves in Letter 47?
options: That slaves have no souls
That slaves should be freed after six years
That slaves are fellow human beings, of the same seed and under the same sky, and should be treated as you would wish your superior to treat you
That slavery should be abolished at once
check.why: He urged kindness and shared humanity, not abolition: the gap between his words and the institution is part of the debate.

check.q: How do Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 7:22 differ from Seneca's argument about slaves?
options: Paul tells slaves to revolt
Paul says slaves are not human
There is no difference
Seneca grounds equality in a shared nature; Paul in a shared Lord, so that the slave is the Lord's free man and the free man Christ's slave
check.why: Both relativise status; Paul reverses it, and adds 'if you can become free, use it'.

check.q: What is the best evidence that the letters between Seneca and Paul are not genuine?
options: Jerome said they were forgeries
Paul could not write
Their Latin is poor and their style unlike Seneca's, and they first appear centuries later
Seneca and Paul lived in different centuries
check.why: They lived at the same time, and Jerome accepted the letters; it was later scholars, Erasmus among them, who showed they are forged.

check.q: Which is the strongest form of the charge that Seneca's failings were partly Stoicism's fault?
options: Stoicism's teaching that outward things are indifferent let him keep wealth and serve a tyrant while telling himself they did not touch his soul
Stoicism taught people to love money
Stoicism forbade philosophers to enter politics
Stoicism taught that slaves should be cruelly treated
check.why: The doctrine of indifferents can make peace with outward evil. The other options misstate Stoic teaching.

tutorial.question: Was Seneca a hypocrite, and does it matter for judging his philosophy?
tutorial.approach: Set out the charges: wealth, service of Nero, conformity in religion (Augustine). Then his defence: his own words, his attempts to retire, his death. Then ask whether the failings come from the man or from the teaching that outward things are indifferent. Finally: can a teaching be true if its teacher fails to live it?
strong: Gives the charges with sources (Tacitus, Dio, Augustine).
Gives Seneca's own defence fairly.
Uses the reading from City of God VI.10 closely.
Asks whether the doctrine of indifferents contributed.
Distinguishes the truth of a teaching from the virtue of its teacher.
Reaches a balanced judgement.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Seneca's first letter. Each evening, note where your time went today: what you chose, what was taken from you, what you let slip. Choose one hour tomorrow to spend deliberately on something that matters, and guard it.
sessions.reflect: Where in your life do you keep outward customs you do not believe, or believe things you do not live? Is that wisdom, or acting?
takeaways: Seneca, tutor and adviser to Nero, wrote letters on using time, facing death and treating slaves as fellow human beings.
He was accused, then and since, of not living his teaching: in his wealth, his service of Nero and, as Augustine charged, his conformity in religion.
Christians admired him enough to forge letters between him and Paul; Paul grounded the equality of slave and free in a shared Lord.

sessions.title: The case against: cold comfort?
sessions.line: An emperor writes that we should pray not to keep our child but not to fear losing him. Is Stoic peace the death of love?
sessions.plain: The Stoics promised a peace nothing could take away. But they bought it at a price: to value nothing that can be lost, including the people we love. Epictetus said to remind yourself, kissing your child, that she is mortal; Marcus Aurelius said to pray not to keep your son, but not to fear losing him. This session first lets Stoicism speak at its best, in the private notebook of a Roman emperor, and then states the objection at full strength: that Stoic peace is cold comfort, and that a good person should grieve.
sessions.why: Sessions 3 to 5 set out Stoicism and showed it at work in a slave and a statesman. Now we test it against the hardest case, the one Cicero raised against Epicurus in session 1: grief. If a philosophy of peace fails at the graveside, does it work at all?
answers: What did Marcus Aurelius write, and why is he loved today?
What is Stoic apatheia, and does it mean feeling nothing?
Can a Christian be a Stoic?
Is it wrong to grieve?
sessions.finding: The Stoic answer to grief, that we should not be disturbed by what we cannot control, can sound like the death of love; Augustine argued that right love must be able to grieve, and that a heart that cannot be moved is not healthy but numb.

paras: The Stoics taught that only virtue is good, that everything else is 'indifferent', and that peace comes from wanting only what is in our power (sessions 3 and 4). Seneca showed the teaching in a powerful man's life, and its gaps (session 5).

In session 4 you read a sentence that many readers find hard to forgive: 'If you are kissing your child or wife, say that it is a human being whom you are kissing, for when the wife or child dies you will not be disturbed.' This session asks whether that sentence is wisdom or a wound.
background.key: Only virtue is good, so the loss of a child is not an evil: this session asks whether that is wisdom or the death of love.

paras: Marcus Aurelius (AD 121–180) was Roman emperor from 161 until his death. He spent much of his reign fighting German tribes on the Danube frontier, while a great plague swept the empire. He was devoted to Stoicism, and had read Epictetus. In camp, in his last decade, he kept a notebook in Greek, which he called simply 'To Himself'. We call it the Meditations. It was never meant to be read by anyone else.

If you have taken A good life, you have read its first book, where Marcus thanks the people who formed him. Today the Meditations is a bestseller, loved for its honesty: an emperor reminding himself, every morning, to be patient, humble and kind. Marcus also had thirteen or fourteen children, of whom only a few outlived him. When he writes about losing a child, he is not writing in the abstract.

Marcus dies on campaign

background.key: Marcus Aurelius, emperor 161–180, wrote the Meditations as a private notebook on campaign; he lost many of his children.

paras: To weigh the objection we need one more piece of Stoic teaching. The Stoics called the emotions that overwhelm us 'passions' (pathe): distress, fear, desire and excessive pleasure. They thought each was a mistaken judgement: grief, for example, is the judgement that something bad has happened to me and that it is right to be crushed by it. Since loss is not truly bad (only vice is), grief is a mistake. The wise person is free of passions: apatheia, 'without passion'. Our word 'apathy' comes from it, but the Stoics did not mean indifference.

They allowed three 'good feelings' (eupatheiai) in the wise: joy, caution and wishing well. And they admitted that even a wise man feels a first shock, a pallor or a tear, before reason can judge. But the wise do not consent to it. You will read Augustine telling a famous story about exactly this.
background.key: Stoics held that passions like grief are mistaken judgements; the wise reach apatheia, keeping 'good feelings' and first shocks but never consenting to grief.

paras: The main reading is from the Meditations: Stoicism at its most attractive and most testing, from the morning resolution of Book II to the prayer about a little son in Book IX and Epictetus's words about kissing a child, which Marcus copied out. It answers the first two questions of this session from the inside.

The comparison is from Augustine's City of God, written over two centuries later. Augustine knew the Stoics through Cicero, admired them, and argued against them that good people rightly fear, desire, grieve and rejoice, and that Jesus himself wept. It is the objection at full strength.
background.key: Marcus at his best, including on losing a child; then Augustine's case that right love grieves.

before: Which of Marcus's thoughts would help you on a bad day?
What does Marcus tell himself to pray for about his little son?
According to Augustine, what is wrong with a heart that cannot be moved?
sessions.readWhy: Stoicism at its best and hardest, in an emperor's private notebook, in four parts.

paras: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil. But I who have seen the nature of the good that it is beautiful, and of the bad that it is ugly, and the nature of him who does wrong, that it is akin to me; not [only] of the same blood or seed, but that it participates in [the same] intelligence and [the same] portion of the divinity, I can neither be injured by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. To act against one another, then, is contrary to nature; and it is acting against one another to be vexed and to turn away.

3. Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul, particularly when he has within him such thoughts that by looking into them he is immediately in perfect tranquillity; and I affirm that tranquillity is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind. Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself; and let thy principles be brief and fundamental, which, as soon as thou shalt recur to them, will be sufficient to cleanse the soul completely, and to send thee back free from all discontent with the things to which thou returnest. For with what art thou discontented? With the badness of men? Recall to thy mind this conclusion, that rational animals exist for one another, and that to endure is a part of justice, and that men do wrong involuntarily; and consider how many already, after mutual enmity, suspicion, hatred, and fighting, have been stretched dead, reduced to ashes;

and be quiet at last.--But perhaps thou art dissatisfied with that which is assigned to thee out of the universe.--Recall to thy recollection this alternative; either there is providence or atoms [fortuitous concurrence of things]; or remember the arguments by which it has been proved that the world is a kind of political community [and be quiet at last].--But perhaps corporeal things will still fasten upon thee.--Consider then further that the mind mingles not with the breath, whether moving gently or violently, when it has once drawn itself apart and discovered its own power, and think also of all that thou hast heard and assented to about pain and pleasure [and be quiet at last].--But perhaps the desire of the thing called fame will torment thee.--See how soon everything is forgotten, and look at the chaos of infinite time on each side of [the present], and the emptiness of applause, and the changeableness and want of judgment in those who pretend to give praise, and the narrowness of the space within which it is circumscribed [and be quiet at last]. For the whole earth is a point, and how small a nook in it is this thy dwelling, and how few are there in it, and what kind of people are they who will praise thee.

This then remains: Remember to retire into this little territory of thy own, and above all do not distract or strain thyself, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal. But among the things readiest to thy hand to which thou shalt turn, let there be these, which are two. One is that things do not touch the soul, for they are external and remain immovable; but our perturbations come only from the opinion which is within. The other is that all these things, which thou seest, change immediately and will no longer be; and constantly bear in mind how many of these changes thou hast already witnessed. The universe is transformation: life is opinion.

13. When we have meat before us and such eatables, we receive the impression that this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or of a pig; and again, that this Falernian is only a little grape-juice, and this purple robe some sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a shell-fish: such then are these impressions, and they reach the things themselves and penetrate them, and so we see what kind of things they are. Just in the same way ought we to act all through life, and where there are things which appear most worthy of our approbation, we ought to lay them bare and look at their worthlessness and strip them of all the words by which they are exalted. For outward show is a wonderful perverter of the reason, and when thou art most sure that thou art employed about things worth thy pains, it is then that it cheats thee most. Consider then what Crates says of Xenocrates himself.

40. Either the gods have no power or they have power. If, then, they have no power, why dost thou pray to them? But if they have power, why dost thou not pray for them to give thee the faculty of not fearing any of the things which thou fearest, or of not desiring any of the things which thou desirest, or not being pained at anything, rather than pray that any of these things should not happen or happen? for certainly if they can co-operate with men, they can co-operate for these purposes. But perhaps thou wilt say the gods have placed them in thy power. Well, then, is it not better to use what is in thy power like a free man than to desire in a slavish and abject way what is not in thy power? And who has told thee that the gods do not aid us, even in the things which are in our power? Begin, then, to pray for such things, and thou wilt see. One man prays thus: How shall I be able to lie with that woman? Do thou pray thus: How shall I not desire to lie with her? Another prays thus: How shall I be released from this? Pray thou: How shall I not desire to be released? Another thus: How shall I not lose my little son? Thou thus: How shall I not be afraid to lose him? In fine, turn thy prayers this way, and see what comes.
33. To look for the fig in winter is a mad-man's act: such is he who looks for his child when it is no longer allowed (Epictetus, iii. 24, 87).

34. When a man kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself, "To-morrow perchance thou wilt die."--But those are words of bad omen.--"No word is a word of bad omen," said Epictetus, "which expresses any work of nature; or if it is so, it is also a word of bad omen to speak of the ears of corn being reaped" (Epictetus, iii. 24, 88).

parts.author: Marcus Aurelius
parts.title: Begin the morning
parts.who: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor, writing to himself
parts.when: On campaign on the Danube, about AD 170–180
parts.context: The first entry of Book II. Marcus, the most powerful man in the world, prepares for a day of difficult people. Long's square brackets mark words he added to make the sense clear. This passage is also in Learn by heart, as 'Begin the morning'.
parts.plain: Marcus tells himself: today I will meet meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, envious and unfriendly people. They are like this because they do not know good from evil. But I know that the person who wrongs me is my kinsman, sharing the same reason and the same portion of the divine. So he cannot harm me, and I cannot be angry with him or hate him. We are made to work together, like hands, feet and eyelids.

commentary.on: I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
commentary.text: Not pessimism but preparation. The Stoics practised imagining the day's troubles in advance (praemeditatio malorum), so as not to be surprised.

commentary.on: the nature of him who does wrong, that it is akin to me
commentary.text: Here is Stoicism at its warmest. The wrongdoer is my relative, because we share the divine reason. You read Epictetus on 'sons of Zeus' in session 3: this is the same idea in practice.

commentary.on: nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him
commentary.text: No anger and no hatred: a remarkable resolution for an emperor with absolute power. It is close to 'love your enemies', though the ground is different: shared reason, not God's love for the sinner.

commentary.on: For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids
commentary.text: An image Paul also uses: the body and its members (1 Corinthians 12). Humanity is one body; to fight one another is a body fighting itself.

parts.author: Marcus Aurelius
parts.title: Retire into thyself
parts.context: Two entries. In IV.3 Marcus reminds himself where peace is found. 'Either there is providence or atoms' sets the Stoic view against the Epicurean, which you met in sessions 1 to 3. In VI.13 Falernian is a famous Italian wine, and the purple robe the emperor's colour. Crates was a Cynic philosopher (Zeno's teacher). Part of IV.3 is in Learn by heart, as 'The retreat within'.
parts.plain: Marcus tells himself: people look for peace in holidays by the sea or in the hills, but you can retire into your own soul at any time. Remember your principles: people do wrong without meaning to, and soon all are dead; whether the world is ruled by providence or by atoms, be quiet; fame is nothing. Two things: things cannot touch the soul, only our opinions disturb us; and everything changes. And look at grand things as they really are: the fine dinner is a dead fish, the wine is grape juice, the purple robe is wool dyed with shellfish blood.

commentary.on: for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself
commentary.text: The 'inner citadel', as the scholar Pierre Hadot called it: a fortress in the soul that no one can storm. It is a real gift. Many people in hospitals and prisons have found it so.

commentary.on: either there is providence or atoms
commentary.text: Marcus admits he cannot be certain the Stoic picture of the world is true. Either way, he tells himself, be calm. This is why modern secular Stoics claim him: the practice, he seems to say, does not depend on the theology.

commentary.on: One is that things do not touch the soul, for they are external and remain immovable; but our perturbations come only from the opinion which is within.
commentary.text: Epictetus's fifth chapter, in Marcus's own words. 'Perturbations' means passions: grief, fear, anger.

commentary.on: The universe is transformation: life is opinion.
commentary.text: Five words of Greek, and the whole Stoic view: everything changes, and how we suffer depends on how we judge.

commentary.on: this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or of a pig
commentary.text: The Stoic exercise of seeing things 'as they are', stripped of glamour. It cures greed and vanity. Hold on to it: the same exercise, applied to a person, is the objection of this session.

parts.author: Marcus Aurelius
parts.title: How shall I not be afraid to lose him?
parts.context: One of the most revealing entries. Marcus writes about prayer.
parts.plain: Marcus tells himself: either the gods have power or they do not. If they do, why not pray for the strength not to fear or desire things, rather than for things to happen or not happen? One man prays to sleep with a woman; pray not to desire her. Another prays to be rid of something; pray not to want to be rid of it. Another prays not to lose his little son; pray not to be afraid of losing him.

commentary.on: why dost thou not pray for them to give thee the faculty of not fearing any of the things which thou fearest
commentary.text: A Stoic account of prayer: ask not for outcomes but for a right mind. Christians would recognise part of this; Jesus in Gethsemane prays 'not what I desire, but what you desire' (Mark 14:36).

commentary.on: How shall I be able to lie with that woman? Do thou pray thus: How shall I not desire to lie with her?
commentary.text: Here the Stoic prayer looks very like Christian teaching on desire (Matthew 5:28).

commentary.on: Another thus: How shall I not lose my little son? Thou thus: How shall I not be afraid to lose him?
commentary.text: And here the two part company. A father prays to keep his child. Marcus tells himself to pray instead not to fear losing him. Is this wisdom, which frees the father from torment? Or does it ask him to love his son less, so as to suffer less? This is the heart of the objection.

parts.author: Marcus Aurelius
parts.title: When a man kisses his child
parts.context: In Book XI Marcus copies out sayings of Epictetus from his Discourses (Long gives the references in brackets). A fig in winter is out of season: there is none.
parts.plain: Marcus copies Epictetus: it is madness to look for a fig in winter, and so is it to long for your child when he is no longer given to you. When you kiss your child, whisper to yourself, 'Tomorrow perhaps you will die.' That is not unlucky to say; it is only nature, like saying the corn will be reaped.

commentary.on: such is he who looks for his child when it is no longer allowed
commentary.text: The longing of a bereaved parent is compared to looking for figs in winter: it wants what nature does not supply. Logically, it fits the system. Humanly, it is very hard to hear.

commentary.on: When a man kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself, "To-morrow perchance thou wilt die."
commentary.text: There is wisdom here: to love someone as mortal is to treasure them now, and not to take them for granted. Many grieving parents say they wish they had. But Epictetus's purpose is also to prepare not to be disturbed when it happens. The question is whether a love that is ready not to be disturbed is still love.

commentary.on: it is also a word of bad omen to speak of the ears of corn being reaped
commentary.text: A child's death is placed beside the harvest: natural, and therefore not evil. The Stoic is consistent. The objector asks whether a philosophy that cannot tell the difference between a child and a crop has understood what a child is.

read.author: Marcus Aurelius
read.who: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor, writing to himself
read.when: On campaign on the Danube, about AD 170–180

paras: Aulus Gellius, a man of extensive erudition, and gifted with an eloquent and graceful style, relates, in his work entitled _Noctes Atticæ_, that he once made a voyage with an eminent Stoic philosopher; and he goes on to relate fully and with gusto what I shall barely state, that when the ship was tossed and in danger from a violent storm, the philosopher grew pale with terror. This was noticed by those on board, who, though themselves threatened with death, were curious to see whether a philosopher would be agitated like other men. When the tempest had passed over, and as soon as their security gave them freedom to resume their talk, one of the passengers, a rich and luxurious Asiatic, begins to banter the philosopher, and rally him because he had even become pale with fear, while he himself had been unmoved by the impending destruction. But the philosopher availed himself of the reply of Aristippus the Socratic, who, on finding himself similarly bantered by a man of the same character, answered, "You had no cause for anxiety for the soul of a profligate debauchee, but I had reason to be alarmed for the soul of Aristippus." The rich man being thus disposed of, Aulus Gellius asked the philosopher, in the interests of science and not to annoy him, what was the reason of his fear? And he, willing to instruct a man so zealous in the pursuit of knowledge, at once took from his wallet a book of Epictetus the Stoic, in which doctrines were advanced which precisely harmonized with those of Zeno and Chrysippus, the founders of the Stoical school.

Aulus Gellius says that he read in this book that the Stoics maintain that there are certain impressions made on the soul by external objects which they call _phantasiæ_, and that it is not in the power of the soul to determine whether or when it shall be invaded by these. When these impressions are made by alarming and formidable objects, it must needs be that they move the soul even of the wise man, so that for a little he trembles with fear, or is depressed by sadness, these impressions anticipating the work of reason and self-control; but this does not imply that the mind accepts these evil impressions, or approves or consents to them. For this consent is, they think, in a man's power; there being this difference between the mind of the wise man and that of the fool, that the fool's mind yields to these passions and consents to them, while that of the wise man, though it cannot help being invaded by them, yet retains with unshaken firmness a true and steady persuasion of those things which it ought rationally to desire or avoid.

If these emotions and affections, arising as they do from the love of what is good and from a holy charity, are to be called vices, then let us allow these emotions which are truly vices to pass under the name of virtues. But since these affections, when they are exercised in a becoming way, follow the guidance of right reason, who will dare to say that they are diseases or vicious passions? Wherefore even the Lord Himself, when He condescended to lead a human life in the form of a slave, had no sin whatever, and yet exercised these emotions where He judged they should be exercised. For as there was in Him a true human body and a true human soul, so was there also a true human emotion. When, therefore, we read in the Gospel that the hard-heartedness of the Jews moved Him to sorrowful indignation, that He said, I am glad for your sakes, to the intent you may believe, that when about to raise Lazarus He even shed tears, that He earnestly desired to eat the passover with His disciples, that as His passion drew near His soul was sorrowful, these emotions are certainly not falsely ascribed to Him. But as He became man when it pleased Him, so, in the grace of His definite purpose, when it pleased Him He experienced those emotions in His human soul.

But we must further make the admission, that even when these affections are well regulated, and according to God's will, they are peculiar to this life, not to that future life we look for, and that often we yield to them against our will. And thus sometimes we weep in spite of ourselves, being carried beyond ourselves, not indeed by culpable desire; but by praiseworthy charity. In us, therefore, these affections arise from human infirmity; but it was not so with the Lord Jesus, for even His infirmity was the consequence of His power. But so long as we wear the infirmity of this life, we are rather worse men than better if we have none of these emotions at all. For the apostle vituperated and abominated some who, as he said, were without natural affection. The sacred Psalmist also found fault with those of whom he said, I looked for some to lament with me, and there was none. For to be quite free from pain while we are in this place of misery is only purchased, as one of this world's literati perceived and remarked, at the price of blunted sensibilities both of mind and body.

And therefore that which the Greeks call ἀπαθεια, and what the Latins would call, if their language would allow them, impassibilitas, if it be taken to mean an impassibility of spirit and not of body, or, in other words, a freedom from those emotions which are contrary to reason and disturb the mind, then it is obviously a good and most desirable quality, but it is not one which is attainable in this life. For the words of the apostle are the confession, not of the common herd, but of the eminently pious, just, and holy men: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. When there shall be no sin in a man, then there shall be this απάθεια . At present it is enough if we live without crime; and he who thinks he lives without sin puts aside not sin, but pardon. And if that is to be called apathy, where the mind is the subject of no emotion, then who would not consider this insensibility to be worse than all vices? It may, indeed, reasonably be maintained that the perfect blessedness we hope for shall be free from all sting of fear or sadness; but who that is not quite lost to truth would say that neither love nor joy shall be experienced there? But if by apathy a condition be meant in which no fear terrifies nor any pain annoys, we must in this life renounce such a state if we would live according to God's will, but may hope to enjoy it in that blessedness which is promised as our eternal condition.

And if some, with a vanity monstrous in proportion to its rarity, have become enamored of themselves because they can be stimulated and excited by no emotion, moved or bent by no affection, such persons rather lose all humanity than obtain true tranquillity. For a thing is not necessarily right because it is inflexible, nor healthy because it is insensible.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.ref: Augustine, The City of God IX.4
parts.title: The Stoic in the storm
parts.context: Augustine wrote The City of God from 413 to 426, in Hippo in North Africa, after the sack of Rome in 410. In Book IX he retells a story from Aulus Gellius, a Roman writer of the 100s, whose Attic Nights describes a sea voyage with a Stoic philosopher. Aristippus was a pupil of Socrates. 'Phantasiae' are impressions, the 'appearances' of Epictetus.
parts.plain: Augustine tells the story: in a violent storm at sea, a famous Stoic went pale with fear. Afterwards a rich passenger mocked him. Gellius asked him why he had been afraid. The Stoic took out a book of Epictetus and showed him: the Stoics teach that frightening impressions strike even the wise man's mind, so that he trembles for a moment; but he does not consent to them. Augustine concludes that the Stoics really agree with the other philosophers: the wise feel these things, but reason rules them.

commentary.on: the philosopher grew pale with terror
commentary.text: The story is funny, and the Stoic is not a fraud. Augustine is fair to him: he explains his teaching.

commentary.on: it is not in the power of the soul to determine whether or when it shall be invaded by these
commentary.text: The Stoics admitted 'first movements': the involuntary shock, the pallor, the tear. These are not passions, because the mind has not yet agreed to them.

commentary.on: the fool's mind yields to these passions and consents to them, while that of the wise man, though it cannot help being invaded by them, yet retains with unshaken firmness a true and steady persuasion
commentary.text: The difference between the wise and the fool is consent. The wise man feels the shock but does not judge that anything truly bad is happening. Augustine thinks this means the Stoics and others differ more in words than in reality. In Book XIV, which you read next, he goes further.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.ref: Augustine, The City of God XIV.9 (shortened)
parts.title: Who will dare to say that they are diseases?
parts.context: Augustine has listed the emotions of Paul and of Christians: fear, desire, grief and joy, rightly directed. Now he turns to Christ, and to the Stoic ideal. New Advent's text, which we use, prints Scripture references in the middle of sentences; we have removed them. The 'one of this world's literati' is most likely the philosopher Crantor, whom Cicero quotes on this point. A cut is marked '…'.
parts.plain: Augustine says: if emotions that come from love of the good are called vices, then vices are virtues. Christ himself, who had no sin, felt grief, anger, joy and longing, and wept at Lazarus's tomb. In this life we often weep in spite of ourselves, out of love. Someone with no such feelings at all is not better but worse. If apatheia means freedom from feelings that go against reason, it is good, but not possible in this life; if it means feeling nothing, it is worse than any vice. A heart that cannot be moved is not healthy because it is unbending, nor well because it feels nothing.

commentary.on: who will dare to say that they are diseases or vicious passions?
commentary.text: The Stoics called passions diseases of the soul. Augustine answers: emotions that come from right love are not diseases; they are love in action.

commentary.on: that when about to raise Lazarus He even shed tears
commentary.text: 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35), the shortest verse in the Bible, is Augustine's decisive evidence. Jesus wept at his friend's tomb even though he was about to raise him. If you have taken Death and hope, you have read the whole chapter. A Stoic sage would not weep; the Son of God did.

commentary.on: we are rather worse men than better if we have none of these emotions at all
commentary.text: The objection in one sentence. A person who felt nothing at a child's death would not be a sage but something less than human.

commentary.on: is only purchased, as one of this world's literati perceived and remarked, at the price of blunted sensibilities both of mind and body
commentary.text: The price of feeling no pain is numbness. Augustine, who wept for his friend and for his mother (Confessions IV and IX), knew what he was talking about.

commentary.on: And if that is to be called apathy, where the mind is the subject of no emotion, then who would not consider this insensibility to be worse than all vices?
commentary.text: Augustine is careful. If apatheia means never being swept away against reason, it is good, and we will have it in heaven. If it means feeling nothing, it is the worst of vices.

commentary.on: For a thing is not necessarily right because it is inflexible, nor healthy because it is insensible.
commentary.text: The closing blow, aimed at those who are proud of their calm: hardness is not strength, and numbness is not health.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.ref: Augustine, The City of God IX.4
compare.why: Augustine (354–430) read the Stoics through Cicero and admired them. In The City of God he takes up their teaching on the passions and argues the opposite: that good people rightly feel, and that Jesus himself wept. Read his two arguments.
compare.title: Jesus wept: Augustine's reply

paras: Before the objection, the case for. Stoicism has given courage to the powerless and restraint to the powerful. It taught an emperor to rise each morning resolved not to hate. It taught a lame slave that no master could own his will, and a prisoner in Hanoi that he could keep his honour under torture. It holds that every person is our kin and that we are made for co-operation.

It is also, in a sense, kind to the grieving. It warns against the long, bitter grief that poisons the rest of a life. It reminds us that everyone we love is mortal, so that we treasure them now. And the Stoics did not forbid all feeling: they allowed joy, care and the first shock of loss. Seneca wrote to a grieving friend that tears are natural, and should be allowed to fall, but not be cultivated for show (Letter 63).
sections.key: Stoicism gives courage, restraint and kinship; even on grief it warns against bitterness and teaches us to treasure the mortal now.

paras: Now the case against, as its best advocates put it. If only virtue is good, then the death of a child is not an evil. The Stoic may feel a first shock, but must not judge that anything bad has happened. Epictetus tells a father to remind himself, as he kisses his child, that she is a mortal like a pot; Marcus tells himself to pray not to fear losing his son. The peace offered is real, but it is bought by valuing nothing that can be lost.

And everything we love can be lost. So the Stoic must, in the end, love no one in a way that could break his heart. That, say the critics, is not a cure for grief but an amputation of love. Augustine put it in one line: a heart that feels nothing is not healthy, it is numb. Martha Nussbaum, in Upheavals of Thought (2001), argues that grief is the measure of love: to grieve is to judge, rightly, that someone outside our control mattered to us more than our own calm.
sections.key: If only virtue is good, a child's death is not an evil; Stoic peace is bought by loving nothing in a way that could break your heart. Critics call that amputation, not cure.

paras: A second objection concerns pride. The Stoic sage needs no one: not friends, not God, not help. The French mathematician and Christian thinker Blaise Pascal, in a conversation recorded in 1655, said that Epictetus understood our duty better than anyone, but not our weakness; he imagined that we can do by our own strength what we ought to do, and so led to pride. (We give it in our own words.)

Friedrich Nietzsche, no Christian, attacked the Stoics from the other side in Beyond Good and Evil (1886, section 9): they claim to live 'according to nature', but nature is wasteful and indifferent; really, he says, they impose their own morality on nature and call it nature's. (Also our own words.) Both critics see the same thing: Stoic calm is a heroic act of will, and few can sustain it.

Stoics have an answer: the Manual is for beginners, and progress is slow; no one is expected to be a sage. Epictetus himself said he was not one. But the objection stands that the goal, a self that needs nothing, is the wrong goal, and that weakness is not only a stage to grow out of but part of being human.
sections.key: Pascal said Epictetus knew our duty but not our weakness, and led to pride; Nietzsche said the Stoics imposed their morality on nature. Both see calm as a heroic act of will.

paras: Since about 2010 Stoicism has had an extraordinary revival. Books by Ryan Holiday, Massimo Pigliucci, Donald Robertson and others sell in millions; an annual 'Stoic Week', begun by academics at the University of Exeter in 2012, invites people to live as Stoics for seven days. Many have found real help in it, especially with anxiety.

Critics, some of them Stoic scholars, warn that a version popular online, sometimes mocked as 'broicism', turns Stoicism into emotional toughness for ambitious young men: hide your feelings, master others, win. That loses the ancient Stoics' kinship with all people, their duty to the city and their God. Pigliucci and others insist that real Stoicism is about virtue and justice, not success. The debate shows that the ancient question is alive: is Stoic peace a way to love well, or a way to stop feeling?
sections.key: Modern Stoicism has helped many; critics warn that a 'tough guy' version drops the virtue, kinship and God of the ancients.

sections.h: Can a Christian be a Stoic?
paras: Christians have borrowed from the Stoics since the beginning: the logos, natural law, the cardinal virtues, the examination of conscience, the brotherhood of all people. Monks adapted Epictetus's Manual; Ambrose rewrote Cicero's Stoic On Duties for his clergy. Many Christians today find Stoic exercises a help.

But at the point of this session, the two part. Christianity does not teach that the death of a child is 'indifferent'. It calls death an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), tells Christians to 'weep with those who weep' (Romans 12:15), and promises not freedom from grief but comfort in it: 'Blessed are those who mourn' (Matthew 5:4). Paul tells the Thessalonians not to grieve 'like the rest, who have no hope' (1 Thessalonians 4:13): not to stop grieving, but to grieve with hope. A Christian can use the Stoics' tools. What he cannot take from them is their peace at the price of love.
sections.key: Christians borrowed much from the Stoics, but part from them at grief: death is an enemy, mourners are blessed, and Christians grieve with hope, not without feeling.

paras: Augustine did not argue about grief from a distance. In his Confessions (about 397–400) he describes the death of a close friend in his twenties, in his home town of Thagaste. 'At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death', he wrote (in E. B. Pusey's translation); he could not bear the places they had shared, and found a bitter sweetness only in tears. Looking back, he judged that his grief was so destroying because he had loved a mortal man as if he would never die, and he concluded that we should love others in God, who is never lost (Confessions IV.4–12).

Years later, when his mother Monica died at Ostia in 387, he tried at first to hold back his tears, because Christians do not grieve as those without hope. He managed it through the funeral. Then, alone, he let himself weep, and confessed it to God without shame (Confessions IX.12). These two scenes are Augustine's real answer to the Stoics. He learned something like their lesson, not to love anyone as if they were God, but he refused their conclusion. Love in God is still love, and it still weeps.
sections.key: Augustine grieved his friend and his mother; he learned not to love anyone as if they were God, but concluded that love in God still weeps.

Augustine, The City of God IX.4 and XIV.8–9, tr. Marcus Dods (1871); Confessions IV.4–12 and IX.12.
Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights XIX.1; Cicero, Tusculan Disputations III.12 (Crantor) and IV; Seneca, Letters 63 and 99.
