debate.question: Is Stoic apatheia compatible with love?

positions.name: Yes: it purifies love
positions.who: Epictetus; Marcus Aurelius; modern Stoics such as Massimo Pigliucci (in our words)
positions.view: Stoics love people deeply but as they really are, mortal and not ours to keep. That frees love from possessiveness and fear, and lets us care for others without being destroyed when we lose them. Stoics allow joy, care and the first shock of grief.
positions.evidence: Meditations II.1; Encheiridion 3 read as a lesson in gratitude; the Stoic 'good feelings'.

positions.name: No: it amputates love
positions.who: Augustine; Martha Nussbaum; many modern philosophers of emotion
positions.view: To love someone is to let your happiness depend on what is outside your control. A teaching that forbids that dependence forbids love. Grief is not an error but the right response to losing what we truly valued.
positions.evidence: City of God XIV.9; John 11:35; Nussbaum, Upheavals of Thought.

positions.name: A third way: grief with hope
positions.who: Paul; the Christian tradition
positions.view: Love rightly grieves, and the Stoics are wrong to call loss indifferent. But grief need not destroy us, because death is not the end and God is with the mourner. Peace comes not from loving less but from trusting more.
positions.evidence: 1 Thessalonians 4:13; Matthew 5:4; 2 Corinthians 1:3–4.

debate.agree: All agree that bitter, endless grief can destroy a life, that every love is of someone mortal, and that we should treasure people while we have them.

look.why: An Italian painter known as the Master of the Franciscan Crucifixes painted this Mourning Madonna around 1270–1275, probably as one end of a painted cross, with Mary grieving beside her crucified son. It is the opposite of Stoic calm: a mother in grief, and the Church set her in gold.
points: A woman in a royal-blue mantle covering her head and body stands against a shining gold background.
She tips her head sharply to rest in one hand, her brow furrowed.
A flush of bright pink marks her cheek, and fine strokes of yellow show wrinkles at the corner of her eye.
A dark violet cloth edged with gold, with tiny tassels, hangs over her shoulders.
A halo is punched and incised into the gold around her head, which is crossed by a network of cracks.

music.why: Brahms's German Requiem (1868) begins with the words of Jesus, 'Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted' (Matthew 5:4). Not freedom from grief, but comfort in it: the Christian answer to the Stoic, in music.

think.why: How the great teachers of the Church thought about suffering and grief.

learn.why: Marcus Aurelius at his best: preparing for difficult people without anger or hatred. Worth carrying, whatever you conclude about Stoic grief.

check.q: What does Marcus Aurelius tell himself to pray for about his little son?
options: That he will not be afraid of losing him
That the boy will live
That the gods will take him quickly
That he will not love him
check.why: 'How shall I not be afraid to lose him?' (IX.40). The third option overstates it; the objection is that the first and second cannot be separated.

check.q: What does Stoic apatheia mean?
options: Freedom from passions, which the Stoics thought were mistaken judgements, while allowing 'good feelings' and the first involuntary shock
Indifference to other people
Feeling nothing at all
Laziness
check.why: The modern word 'apathy' misleads. The Stoic in Gellius's storm grew pale; what he refused was consent.

check.q: What is the strongest form of the objection to Stoic grief?
options: That if only virtue is good, the death of a child is not an evil, so the Stoic must love no one in a way that could break his heart, which is to amputate love
That the Stoics wept too much
That Stoicism is too difficult
That the Stoics were cruel people
check.why: The objection attacks the doctrine, not the people: it follows from 'only virtue is good'.

check.q: Why does Augustine use Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb against the Stoics?
options: Because Lazarus was a Stoic
To prove that Lazarus died
Because Jesus, who had no sin, wept, so grief from love cannot be a vice
To show that Jesus was weak
check.why: 'Even the Lord Himself... when about to raise Lazarus He even shed tears' (XIV.9). If the sinless one grieved, grief is not sin.

check.q: How does Augustine treat apatheia?
options: He accepts it in every sense
If it means not being swept away against reason, it is good but not possible in this life; if it means feeling nothing, it is worse than any vice
He rejects it in every sense
He says it is only for monks
check.why: Augustine distinguishes two senses, and is fair to the first.

check.q: Which best describes the Christian answer to grief, as Paul states it in 1 Thessalonians 4:13?
options: Grief is indifferent
Grieve as much as possible to show love
Grieve, but not like those who have no hope
Do not grieve at all
check.why: Not Stoic absence of grief, nor despair, but grief with hope.

tutorial.question: Is Stoic apatheia compatible with love?
tutorial.approach: Explain what apatheia meant, including first movements and good feelings (Augustine IX.4; Diogenes VII). Set out the Stoic case at its best: Marcus II.1 and the gift of treasuring the mortal. Then the objection at full strength: Encheiridion 3, Meditations IX.40 and XI.34, Augustine XIV.9. Decide, and say what follows for how we should face loss.
strong: Defines apatheia accurately and does not confuse it with apathy.
Presents the Stoic case at its best, with quotations.
States the objection at full strength, from the doctrine that only virtue is good.
Uses Augustine's two senses of apatheia and his appeal to John 11:35.
Considers whether loving people 'as mortal' is wisdom or self-protection.
Reaches a judgement and applies it to real loss.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: take the true part of Epictetus's advice without the cold part. Once a day, when you are with someone you love, remember that they are mortal and will not always be here, and let it make you kinder, not more guarded: say one thing to them that you would want to have said.
sessions.reflect: Think of a loss you have known. Would you have wanted to feel it less? What would that have cost?
takeaways: Marcus Aurelius's Meditations show Stoicism at its best: patience, kinship with all, an inner citadel no one can take.
But Stoic peace rests on treating even the loss of a child as no evil; Marcus tells himself to pray not to fear losing his son.
Augustine replied that right love grieves, that Jesus wept, and that a heart that feels nothing is numb, not healthy.

sessions.title: Content in all things: the verdict
sessions.line: A prisoner writes to his friends that he has learned to be content in every state, and tells them why.
sessions.plain: Paul, the first great Christian missionary, wrote to his friends at Philippi from prison. He tells them not to worry about anything but to pray about everything, and promises 'the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding'. Then he uses a favourite Stoic word: he has learned to be 'content', self-sufficient, in plenty and in hunger. But he gives it a new ground: 'I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.' This session reads that passage, sets it beside Epicurus, and gives the journey's verdict.
sessions.why: Session 6 found the weak point of Stoic peace: it seems to need us to love less. Epicurus's peace, in sessions 1 and 2, needed us to want less and to stop hoping. Now we read the third answer, from a man who had met both schools in Athens and who was writing in chains.
answers: What did the first Christians make of the Stoics and Epicureans?
What does Paul mean by 'I have learned to be content'?
How is Christian peace different from Stoic and Epicurean peace?
So how do you find peace?
sessions.finding: Paul, in prison, used the Stoics' word for contentment and gave it a new ground: 'I can do all things through Christ'. The Epicureans offered peace by removing fear, the Stoics by mastering desire; Christianity offered peace with someone.

paras: Here is where the journey has been going. Both ancient schools were right that peace of mind is precious and that much of our misery comes from fear and from wanting what we cannot have. The Epicureans offered peace by removing fear: of the gods, of death, of want. The Stoics offered peace by changing what we value: wanting only what is in our power. Both are serious and both help. Both ask a price: the Epicurean gives up hope beyond this life; the Stoic gives up loving what can be lost.

Christianity offered a third answer. Its peace is not the absence of fear or desire but the presence of a person: 'the peace of God', given by someone who can be trusted with what we cannot control. You can weigh that answer for yourself in this session.
background.key: Epicureans: peace by removing fear. Stoics: peace by mastering desire. Christians: peace with someone, which keeps love and hope.

paras: Around AD 50 Paul visited Athens. The Acts of the Apostles says that 'some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him' (Acts 17:18), and that in his speech to the council of the Areopagus he quoted a Stoic poet. If you have taken Is there a God?, you have read the whole chapter. Paul was born in Tarsus, a city famous for its Stoic teachers, and some scholars think he knew their ideas well. Others think his language is simply the common speech of the day.
Either way, Paul knew the two schools' answers. A few years later, writing from prison, he gave his own.
background.key: Paul debated with Epicureans and Stoics in Athens (Acts 17:18); he came from Tarsus, a city of Stoic teachers.

paras: Philippi was a Roman colony in northern Greece, where Paul had founded his first church in Europe around AD 49, in the house of a businesswoman called Lydia (Acts 16). The church there loved him and sent him money more than once. Now he is in prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, though some scholars think Ephesus around 54–55. He does not know whether he will be executed. The Philippians have sent a friend, Epaphroditus, with a gift.

The letter is full of joy: the word 'rejoice' and its relatives come again and again. It is also, as scholars have noticed, full of words the philosophers used. In chapter 4 Paul thanks the Philippians for their gift, and explains how he has learned to live with or without it.

background.key: Philippians was written from prison (probably Rome, about AD 60–62) to a church that loved Paul, and is full of joy.

paras: The main reading is Philippians 4:4–7 and 10–13. It answers this session's question in Paul's own words: what peace is, and where it comes from. Verses 8 and 9, Paul's list of 'whatever things are true', are left for another course.
The comparison takes you back to Epicurus: the first five of his Principal Doctrines, the sayings his followers learned by heart. Read them beside Paul, and you have the three answers side by side.
background.key: Paul's peace and contentment in prison, then Epicurus's first five sayings: the answers side by side.

sessions.readWhy: Paul on peace and contentment, written from prison, in two parts.

paras: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
But I rejoice in the Lord greatly, that now at length you have revived your thought for me; in which you did indeed take thought, but you lacked opportunity.
Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.

parts.title: The peace of God
parts.context: Paul is near the end of his letter. Two women in the church, Euodia and Syntyche, have quarrelled (4:2), and he has asked them to agree. Now he speaks to the whole church. 'The Lord is at hand' may mean that Christ will soon return, or that he is near them now; both are possible.

commentary.on: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
commentary.text: A prisoner, who may be executed, commands joy. Not calm, which is what Epicurus and the Stoics sought, but joy. And 'in the Lord': the joy has an object.

commentary.on: Let your gentleness be known to all men.
commentary.text: Gentleness (epieikeia) means a forbearing, reasonable spirit, not insisting on your rights. A Stoic virtue, too.

commentary.on: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
commentary.text: Compare Marcus, who told himself not to pray for his son's life but for the strength not to fear. Paul tells the Philippians to ask God for what they need, anything at all. The Stoic narrows desire; Paul hands it over. You are learning these words by heart.

commentary.on: And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
commentary.text: 'Guard' is a military word: a garrison keeping a city. The Stoics built an inner citadel by their own discipline. Paul says God's peace stands guard over the heart. It 'surpasses all understanding': it is not the product of correct judgement, as in Epictetus, but a gift beyond it.

parts.title: I have learned to be content
parts.context: Paul thanks the Philippians for their gift of money, and is careful to explain that he is grateful, not needy.

commentary.on: But I rejoice in the Lord greatly, that now at length you have revived your thought for me
commentary.text: Paul is moved by their care. This matters: unlike the Stoic sage, he does not pretend not to need friends.

commentary.on: for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
commentary.text: 'Content' translates autarkes, the very word the Stoics and Cynics used for the wise man's self-sufficiency: needing nothing outside himself. Any educated Philippian would have heard it. And 'I have learned', like the Stoics' training.

commentary.on: I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound.
commentary.text: Both, not just poverty. Paul is not against good things, like Epicurus with his pot of cheese; he is free of them.

commentary.on: I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry
commentary.text: 'Learned the secret' is a word from the mystery religions: being initiated. Paul hints that his contentment is not just a technique but a secret revealed. Then he tells it.

commentary.on: I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.
commentary.text: Here is the difference. The Stoic is self-sufficient because he wants only what is his own. Paul is sufficient because someone else strengthens him. His contentment is not autarkeia, self-sufficiency, but, as one scholar has put it, Christ-sufficiency. This verse is often used as a slogan for success in sport or business; in context it means being able to bear hunger and prison.

paras: 1. 139. A blessed and eternal being has no trouble himself and brings no trouble upon any other being; hence he is exempt from movements of anger and partiality, for every such movement implies weakness [Elsewhere he says that the gods are discernible by reason alone, some being numerically distinct, while others result uniformly from the continuous influx of similar images directed to the same spot and in human form.]
2. Death is nothing to us; for the body, when it has been resolved into its elements, has no feeling, and that which has no feeling is nothing to us.
3. The magnitude of pleasure reaches its limit in the removal of all pain. When pleasure is present, so long as it is uninterrupted, there is no pain either of body or of mind or of both together.

4. 140. Continuous pain does not last long in the flesh; on the contrary, pain, if extreme, is present a very short time, and even that degree of pain which barely outweighs pleasure in the flesh does not last for many days together. Illnesses of long duration even permit of an excess of pleasure over pain in the flesh.

5. It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly. Whenever any one of these is lacking, when, for instance, the man is not able to live wisely, though he lives well and justly, it is impossible for him to live a pleasant life.

parts.author: Epicurus
parts.work: Principal Doctrines, in Diogenes Laertius X
parts.title: The first five sayings
parts.context: Diogenes Laertius ends his whole book with these forty sayings, 'to set the seal' on it. The double numbers (1. 139.) give the saying and Diogenes's section. The words in square brackets in the first saying are an ancient note added by a reader, explaining what Epicurus said elsewhere about the gods.
parts.plain: Epicurus says: a blessed, eternal being has no troubles and gives none, so it feels no anger or favour. Death is nothing to us: what has dissolved feels nothing. Pleasure is greatest when all pain is removed. Severe pain is short, and long illnesses allow more pleasure than pain. And you cannot live pleasantly without living wisely, well and justly, or the other way round.

commentary.on: A blessed and eternal being has no trouble himself and brings no trouble upon any other being; hence he is exempt from movements of anger and partiality
commentary.text: The first saying, the first line of the four-part cure: God is nothing to fear. Notice the cost: the God who feels no anger also feels no favour. Paul's God can be asked for anything; Epicurus's gods cannot be asked for anything.

commentary.on: Death is nothing to us; for the body, when it has been resolved into its elements, has no feeling
commentary.text: The second line of the cure. Paul too was unafraid of death, but for the opposite reason: 'to die is gain', he wrote in this letter (Philippians 1:21), because he would be with Christ.

commentary.on: The magnitude of pleasure reaches its limit in the removal of all pain.
commentary.text: The third line: the good is easy to get. Paul's 'I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound' is close to this in practice.

commentary.on: Continuous pain does not last long in the flesh
commentary.text: The fourth line: the terrible is easy to bear. Paul, in chains, would agree that suffering can be borne, but because Christ strengthens, not because pain is brief.

commentary.on: It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly
commentary.text: Epicurus ends with the virtues, as means to pleasure. Paul, in verse 8 of this chapter, tells the Philippians to think about 'whatever things are just'. The schools agree on much of how to live; they differ on why, and on whom we live with.

compare.author: Epicurus
compare.work: Principal Doctrines, in Diogenes Laertius X
compare.why: Epicurus's followers learned his Principal Doctrines by heart. Read the first five beside Paul. They are a creed of peace too, but of a different peace.
compare.title: The Garden's creed

sections.h: The three answers side by side
paras: We can now set the three answers to 'how do you find peace?' side by side. Each has a picture of the world, a diagnosis of our trouble, a cure and a price.

Read the table row by row. The first row decides the rest: what you think the world is shapes what you think is good, what you think has gone wrong and what can cure it. The schools agree in the middle rows more than you might expect: all three warn against greed, fear and empty ambition, and all three call for training. They part at the top, on what the world is, and at the bottom, on what peace costs.

rows: Atoms and empty space; gods far away and uncaring
One living whole ruled by divine reason, the logos
Made by a personal God, out of nothing, and loved
Pleasure: no pain in body, no trouble in soul
God, and his creation; love of God and neighbour
Fear of gods and death; empty desires
False judgements; wanting what is not in our power
Separation from God; fear and grasping that follow
Understand nature; want little; live among friends
Judge rightly; want only what is up to you; accept fate
Trust: bring everything to God in prayer; Christ strengthens
Nothing to us: we will not be there
An enemy defeated: grieve, with hope
No hope beyond this life; gods who do not hear
Loving nothing that could break your heart
Trusting someone you cannot see or control
table.note: A summary for comparison: each school had its own debates, and many Christians have borrowed from both.

sections.key: Three answers: remove fear (Epicureans), master desire (Stoics), trust a person (Christians). Each has a world-picture, a cure and a price.

paras: Scholars have long noticed how much of Paul's language sounds Stoic: 'content' (autarkes), 'whatever things are true... honourable... just', the body and its members, a law written on the heart (Romans 2:15), the call to live by reason. Some, like Troels Engberg-Pedersen in Paul and the Stoics (2000), argue that Paul thought within a Stoic frame. Others think he shared the common moral vocabulary of his day, as anyone would.

What is clear is where he parts from them. The Stoic's peace comes from himself; Paul's from Christ. The Stoic accepts fate; Paul trusts a Father who hears requests. The Stoic sage needs no one; Paul thanks his friends for their gift and loves them 'in the tender mercies of Christ Jesus' (Philippians 1:8). He grieves, too: had his friend Epaphroditus died, he writes, he would have had 'sorrow on sorrow' (2:27). That sentence alone separates him from Epictetus.
sections.key: Paul shares much Stoic vocabulary, but his peace comes from Christ, his God hears requests, and he openly needs and grieves for his friends.

paras: The Church kept borrowing. Ambrose of Milan, around 388, rewrote Cicero's On Duties, a Stoic work, as a handbook for his clergy. Monks adapted Epictetus's Manual. Boethius, condemned to death around 524, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy with much Stoic comfort in it. Thomas Aquinas took over the cardinal virtues and natural law.

At the Reformation, John Calvin's first book (1532) was a commentary on Seneca's On Mercy. In 1584 the Flemish scholar Justus Lipsius wrote On Constancy, launching a 'Neostoicism' that blended Stoic endurance with Christian providence for an age of religious war; it shaped soldiers and statesmen across Europe. Pascal, as you saw, warned that Stoic strength could become pride. The pattern is clear: Christians took the Stoics' discipline, and gave it a different heart.
sections.key: Ambrose, the monks, Boethius, Aquinas, Calvin and Lipsius all borrowed Stoic discipline, setting it within Christian trust.

paras: Epicurus had a later revival too. In the 1600s the French priest and scientist Pierre Gassendi argued that atomism could be Christian, if God made the atoms and the soul was immortal, and that Epicurus's ethics of simple pleasure was far better than its reputation. Through Gassendi, atoms passed into the science of Robert Boyle and Isaac Newton.

In the Enlightenment Epicurus's ethics returned in a secular form. The idea that the goal of life is happiness in this world, that religion breeds fear, and that the wise person lives simply among friends attracted thinkers from Hume to Jefferson, and later the utilitarians, who made pleasure and pain the measure of right and wrong. Many people today are practical Epicureans without knowing it.
sections.key: Gassendi revived Epicurus for Christians and science; the Enlightenment revived his ethics of this-worldly happiness without God.

sections.h: So how do you find peace?
paras: The two schools were right about a great deal. Much of our misery is fear, much of it is wanting what we cannot have, and much of it is our own judgements. Both schools teach real skills: to want less, to look at fear clearly, to prepare for trouble, to put effort where it counts. Christians have used those skills for two thousand years.

But both schools found peace by making us smaller: the Epicurean by giving up hope beyond the grave, the Stoic by giving up love that can be hurt. Paul's answer keeps both hope and love, because it rests not on what we can control but on someone who can be trusted with what we cannot. 'I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.' Whether that someone is real is the question the rest of this course of halls keeps asking. But if he is, Paul's peace is not cold comfort. It is comfort with someone in it.
sections.key: Both schools teach real skills, but find peace by making us smaller; Paul's peace keeps hope and love because it rests on someone, not on control.

paras: Readers have long noticed that one book of the Bible sounds, in places, like Epicurus. Ecclesiastes, written perhaps in the 200s BC, watches generations pass and asks what profit there is in all our labour. Its advice, more than once, is to enjoy simple things: 'Go your way—eat your bread with joy' (Ecclesiastes 9:7), and take pleasure in your work and in the one you love, because this is your portion under the sun. If you have taken Psalms and wisdom, you have read the passage.

Some scholars think the writer knew Greek philosophy; most think the likeness comes from facing the same facts: death comes to all, and much striving is vanity. But the differences are telling. Ecclesiastes enjoys bread and wine as gifts 'from the hand of God' (2:24), not as the absence of pain, and he ends by telling the reader to 'fear God and keep his commandments' (12:13). He shares Epicurus's realism and his simple joys, and he refuses Epicurus's distant gods.
sections.key: Ecclesiastes shares Epicurus's simple joys and realism about death, but receives pleasures as gifts from God's hand.

paras: A fair verdict should say what each answer sees truly. The Epicureans saw that much fear is of things imagined; that desire can be trained; that simple pleasures are real; and that friendship is one of the greatest goods of life. Anyone who has learned to want less knows they were right.

The Stoics saw that our judgements shape our suffering; that our choices are ours in a way that outcomes are not; that every human being is our kin; and that character matters more than fortune. Their method still helps people through anxiety, illness and prison.

The Christian answer, as Paul gives it, claims to keep these truths while setting them on another foundation. It agrees with the Epicureans that fear must go, but it removes fear by trust, not by denying judgement and hope. It agrees with the Stoics that we cannot control outcomes, but it hands them to God in prayer instead of declaring them indifferent. That is why Christians could borrow so freely from both schools: they thought the schools had found true pieces of a picture whose centre they had missed.
sections.key: Epicureans saw the power of fear and simple joys; Stoics, the power of judgement and kinship; Christians kept both on another foundation, trust.

debate.question: Which offers the truest peace: the Garden, the Porch, or the Church?

positions.name: The Garden
positions.who: Epicurus; Lucretius; many modern secular people
positions.view: Peace comes from seeing the world as it is: no angry gods, no afterlife, and simple pleasures enough. It asks nothing beyond the evidence.
positions.evidence: Letter to Menoeceus; Principal Doctrines 1–5; the evidence of science for a natural world.

positions.name: The Porch
positions.who: Epictetus; Marcus Aurelius; modern Stoics
positions.view: Peace comes from governing what is in our power and accepting the rest. It works whatever the world is like, as prisoners and patients have found.
positions.evidence: Encheiridion 1 and 5; Stockdale; the success of cognitive therapy.

positions.name: The Church
positions.who: Paul; Augustine; the Christian tradition
positions.view: Peace comes from trusting God with what we cannot control. It keeps love and hope, which the other two give up, and does not depend on our own strength.
positions.evidence: Philippians 4:4–13; City of God XIV.9; John 11:35; 1 Thessalonians 4:13.

debate.agree: All three agree that peace of mind is worth seeking, that fear and endless wanting destroy it, and that it must be practised, not just understood.

look.why: Rembrandt and his workshop painted the apostle Paul around 1657. It is not a picture of Paul in prison; nothing in the picture shows where he is. But it shows the man who wrote 'I have learned to be content': old, thinking, pen in hand, with the sword that, by tradition, executed him.
points: An older, bearded man sits at a desk in a shadowy room, his head resting in one hand.
He holds a quill in his other hand, which brushes his knee.
A stack of papers or parchment lies on the desk to the right.
The oversized hilt of a long sword leans against the wall behind the desk.
He wears a voluminous brown robe over a rust-red garment, and a cap on the back of his head.

music.why: Horatio Spafford wrote 'It Is Well with My Soul' in 1873, after his four daughters drowned at sea, as his own ship passed the place where they died. It is neither Epicurean calm nor Stoic indifference: it is grief held by trust. 'Whatever my lot, thou hast taught me to say'.

learn.why: Paul's answer to worry, from prison: pray about everything, and peace will stand guard over your heart.

check.q: Why would an educated Philippian have noticed Paul's word 'content' (autarkes)?
options: Because it was a word from the Hebrew Bible
Because it was a legal term
Because Paul invented it
Because it was the Stoics' and Cynics' word for the wise man's self-sufficiency
check.why: It was the philosophers' word; Paul uses it and changes its ground.

check.q: How does Paul's teaching on prayer differ most from Marcus Aurelius's in Meditations IX.40?
options: Marcus tells himself to pray for freedom from fear rather than for outcomes; Paul tells the Philippians to make every request known to God
Paul tells people not to pray
Both say the same thing
Marcus prays to Christ
check.why: The Stoic narrows desire; Paul hands every desire to God, 'with thanksgiving'.

check.q: What does 'I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me' mean in its context?
options: That Paul is self-sufficient
That Christ will free him from prison
That Christians will succeed in sport and business
That Paul can bear plenty and hunger, freedom and prison, because Christ gives him strength
check.why: It follows 'both to be filled and to be hungry'. The first option is the common modern misuse.

check.q: Which detail in Philippians most clearly separates Paul from the Stoic sage?
options: He mentions the peace of God
He openly needs his friends, thanks them for their gift, and says he would have had 'sorrow on sorrow' if Epaphroditus had died
He uses the word 'content'
He tells people to rejoice

check.q: According to the table, what price does each answer ask?

All ask the same price

None of them asks any price
check.why: Each answer is serious, and each has a cost; the Christian cost is trust.

It blended Stoic endurance with Christian providence for an age of religious war, founding Neostoicism

tutorial.question: Paul and the Stoics: how much did Paul borrow, and where did he differ?
tutorial.approach: Show the Stoic words and ideas in Philippians 4 (autarkes, 'I have learned', gentleness) and elsewhere. Weigh whether Paul thought like a Stoic or just used common language. Then show where he differs: the ground of contentment, prayer, friendship and grief. End with your judgement on which peace is truer.

Considers the scholarly debate (Engberg-Pedersen and his critics) fairly.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Philippians 4:6 as a practice. Each evening, write down the things you are anxious about. Turn each into a short request to God, and add one thing you are thankful for. If you do not pray, write each worry as a request anyway, and notice what happens when you hand it over in words.
sessions.reflect: Which peace do you most want: to fear less, to want less, or to trust more? Which do you think is possible?
takeaways: Paul, in prison, used the Stoics' word 'content' and gave it a new ground: 'I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.'
Epicureans sought peace by removing fear, Stoics by mastering desire; Paul offered the peace of God, which guards the heart.
Christians kept borrowing the schools' wisdom, but their peace keeps love and hope because it rests on a person, not on control.

closing.title: Your answer, and make the case
closing.prompt: Make the case (the end of the hall on Athens). Choose one idea you have met in this hall, for example that the examined life is the only one worth living, that a thing's purpose tells you what it is for, that the soul matters more than the body, that democracy needs virtue, or that peace comes from trust rather than control. In about 300 words, defend it from the texts it rests on and answer the strongest objection to it. Then add a few lines: how do you find peace, in your own words, and which of the three answers, the Garden, the Porch or Paul, comes closest to yours?
closing.practice: Read Philippians 4 and Epictetus's Manual, chapters 1 to 5, in one sitting this week, side by side. Then, for seven days, end each day with three lines: one thing that was not in your power and that you let go; one thing that was, and what you did with it; one thing you are thankful for.
synthesis: This journey asked how to find peace. It followed two ancient schools of philosophy that answered that question more famously than any others in the West, tested them against the hardest case, grief, and set beside them the answer of the first Christians. Here are the short answers to the questions people ask, in order.

What did Epicurus actually teach? That the goal of life is pleasure, and that pleasure, properly understood, is freedom from pain in the body and trouble in the soul. We reach it by understanding nature, so as to stop fearing gods and death; by sorting our desires and wanting only the natural and necessary ones; and by living simply among friends. His four-part cure says it all: God is nothing to fear, death nothing to worry about, the good is easy to get, the terrible easy to bear. Is Epicureanism just pleasure-seeking? No. It is hedonism in theory but calm in practice: the man who founded it lived on bread and water and asked a friend for a little pot of cheese as a treat. Cicero's objections still stand, though: is the mere absence of pain really pleasure, and can goodness be valued only as a means to it?

Is it wrong to fear death? Epicurus said yes: when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not. It is a strong argument against the fear of being dead. It does not touch the fear of losing those we love, or the sense that an early death takes away something good.

Lucretius made the Epicurean case into the West's first great argument against religion: religion breeds terror and crime, as when Agamemnon killed his daughter for a fair wind, and knowledge of nature sets us free. It has a long life, from the Renaissance to the new atheists. It is strongest against false gods, and there the Bible agrees with it: Isaiah mocks idols, and Israel's law forbade child sacrifice. It is weakest where it removes hope and justice along with fear. The story that the poem's rediscovery in 1417 freed the world from a dark Middle Ages is, historians say, a myth: monks had copied it.

What is Stoicism? A philosophy, founded by Zeno in the Painted Porch around 300 BC, that sees the world as one living whole ordered by divine reason, the logos, and holds that virtue, living by reason, is the only good. Health, wealth and even life are 'indifferent'. Is Stoicism a religion? It was a philosophy with a religious heart: Epictetus praised God as father and called us spectators and interpreters of his works. But it had no temples, Scripture or God who acts in history; and many modern Stoics keep the practice without the God.

What is the dichotomy of control? Epictetus's first lesson: some things are in our power (our judgements, desires and choices), and the rest are not. Peace comes from wanting only the first. 'Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.' Why is Stoicism popular today? Because this method works. It sustained James Stockdale through seven years as a prisoner in Hanoi, it is the seed of cognitive behavioural therapy, and it is the shape of the Serenity Prayer. Who was Epictetus? A lame former slave, freed in Rome, who taught that no master could own his will.

Who was Seneca? A Roman statesman, tutor and adviser to Nero, one of the richest men in the empire, whose Letters to Lucilius teach that time is all we own, that we die daily, and that slaves are fellow human beings. He was accused in his lifetime of not living his teaching, and Augustine said he was an actor in the temples. He tried to leave court, called himself a patient rather than a sage, and died bravely when Nero ordered it. Did he know Paul? No. His brother Gallio judged Paul at Corinth; the letters between Seneca and Paul are a later forgery, a sign of how much Christians admired him.

Then the objection. If only virtue is good, the death of a child is not an evil. Epictetus told a father, kissing his child, to remember she is mortal so that he will not be disturbed when she dies; Marcus Aurelius told himself to pray not to keep his son but not to fear losing him. Stoic peace is real, but it seems bought by loving nothing in a way that could break the heart. Augustine replied that emotions that flow from right love are not diseases, that Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb, and that a heart that feels nothing is not healthy but numb. Can a Christian be a Stoic? Christians have borrowed Stoic words and disciplines from the beginning: logos, natural law, the virtues, the examination of conscience. What they cannot take is peace at the price of love.

And Paul? In prison, he wrote to his friends: 'In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.' He used the Stoics' own word, content, and gave it a new ground: 'I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.' He thanked his friends for their gift and admitted he would have had 'sorrow on sorrow' had one of them died.

So how do you find peace? The Epicureans offered peace by removing fear; the Stoics by mastering desire. Both teach real skills that anyone can use: to want less, to examine our fears, to prepare for trouble and to put effort where it counts. But both find peace by making us smaller: the one by giving up hope beyond this life, the other by giving up love that can be hurt. Christianity offered peace with someone: not the absence of fear or desire, but the presence of a God who can be trusted with what we cannot control. Whether that God is real is the question of the halls still ahead. But it is worth knowing, as you leave Athens, that the three answers are different, and what each one costs.

title: Aristotle
question: What is a thing for, and what is a person for?
line: Seven sessions with the philosopher who asked of everything 'what is it for?': an acorn, a habit, a wise choice, a city, the soul and the universe. Then his worst answer, about slaves and women, at full strength, and the verdict of Thomas Aquinas, who called him simply 'the Philosopher'.
why: Aristotle taught the West to ask what things are for, and to expect real answers. From him come the four causes, the golden mean, the idea that we become good by habit, practical wisdom, 'man is a political animal', the soul as the life of the body and the unmoved mover. He also taught that some people are slaves by nature. This journey follows his one question outward, reads him beside Paul, Proverbs, Job, Isaiah and Aquinas, faces the case against him, and ends where Aquinas took him: to a happiness that is not only thinking about God but seeing him. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year philosophy paper on Aristotle's ethics and metaphysics (Nicomachean Ethics I–II, VI and X; Politics I; De Anima II; Metaphysics XII), with elements of a paper on the reception of Aristotle in medieval Christian thought.
before: plato
outcomes: Explain the four causes and Aristotle's argument from regularity that nature acts for ends, and assess it in the light of natural selection.
Explain how, for Aristotle, virtue is formed by habit and is a mean relative to us, and answer the main objections.
Explain practical wisdom (phronesis), how it differs from cleverness and knowledge, and why Aristotle held the virtues and practical wisdom need each other.
Explain why Aristotle called human beings political animals, and compare his view with Hobbes's and Augustine's.
Explain Aristotle's account of the soul as the form of the body and his argument for an unmoved mover, and compare his god with the God of the Bible.
State the objection from natural slavery and women's subjection at full strength, and assess the replies; explain Aristotle's view of contemplation and Aquinas's completion of it.

glossary.def: Plato's school in Athens, where Aristotle studied for twenty years.
A thing being fully what it can be, as the full-grown oak is the actuality of the acorn (Greek energeia, entelecheia).
The fifth element of Greek science, from which Aristotle thought the heavens were made, moving always in circles.
In Christian theology, the direct sight of God in heaven, which Aquinas taught is perfect happiness.
The four 'hinge' virtues of the classical and Christian tradition: prudence, justice, courage and temperance.
For Aristotle, someone who shares in judging and ruling in a city; in Athens, free adult men of Athenian parents.
The ability to find the means to any goal, good or bad; Aristotle's contrast with practical wisdom.
The good shared by a whole community, not only by its individual members.
Greek theōria: loving, attentive study of the highest truths for their own sake, which Aristotle called the happiest activity.
Correcting a general law in a particular case the lawmaker did not foresee, as the lawmaker would have wished.
Greek for happiness or flourishing: living well and doing well over a whole life.
What a thing is for, 'that for the sake of which': the fourth of Aristotle's causes.
For Aristotle, the pattern or organisation that makes a thing the kind of thing it is, present in the thing itself.
Aristotle's four kinds of explanation: material (what it is made of), formal (its form), efficient (what brought it about) and final (what it is for).
Greek philia: mutual goodwill; Aristotle distinguished friendships of use, of pleasure and of character.
Aristotle's idea that each virtue is the right amount, relative to us, between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency.
Forming character by repeated action, as builders become builders by building.
Greek for a settled state or habit; Latin habitus. Aristotle's word for what a virtue is; used once in the New Testament (Hebrews 5:14).
Greek oikos: the family unit of husband, wife, children and, in Aristotle's world, slaves; the first community.
The view that living things are matter (hylē) organised by form (morphē), and the soul is the form of the body.
The biblical teaching (Genesis 1:27) that every human being is made in God's image, the basis of equal dignity.
Greek entelecheia, 'having its end within': actuality. Aristotle's word for the soul as the realisation of a living body.
Greek scholē, root of 'school': time free from necessary work, which Aristotle thought was for learning and contemplation.
Aristotle's school in Athens, founded in 335 BC; its members were called Peripatetics, from the covered walk (peripatos) where they taught.
Darwin's theory that living things change over generations because those with useful variations leave more offspring.
Aristotle's claim that some people are by nature fitted only to be ruled and used by others; rejected by later Christian and modern thought.
Greek for practical wisdom: the ability to see what a particular situation calls for and act well in it.
A Greek city-state: a small, self-governing community with its own laws, gods and army.
Aristotle's description of human beings (zōon politikon): made by nature to live in a self-governing community.
The power to become something, as an acorn is potentially an oak (Greek dynamis).
Latin prudentia, the Christian name for phronesis: right reason about what is to be done; the first of the cardinal virtues.
The method of the medieval universities, which used logic, much of it Aristotle's, to explore questions of faith and reason.
Greek psychē: for Aristotle, the form of a living body; plants, animals and humans each have one, with different powers.
From Greek telos, end: explanation by purposes; the view that things act for ends.
The name medieval writers, Aquinas above all, gave to Aristotle.
Aristotle's view that the full virtues come together, because each needs practical wisdom.
Aristotle's first cause of all motion: pure actuality, a mind thinking itself, which moves the heavens by being loved.
Greek aretē, excellence: being good at being what you are; for humans, settled states of good character and mind.

sessions.title: What is it for?
sessions.line: An acorn, a doctor, an archer and a set of teeth: Aristotle asks one question of everything, and it changes how you see the world.
sessions.plain: Aristotle thought you only understand a thing when you know four things about it: what it is made of, what shape or pattern makes it what it is, what brought it about, and what it is for. The last, the 'final cause', mattered most to him. An acorn is for becoming an oak; an eye is for seeing; a doctor's work is for health. 'Nature does nothing in vain,' he liked to say. This session asks whether he was right that the world is full of purposes, and what follows if he was.
sessions.why: This is the first session. If you have taken 'Plato', you met Aristotle's teacher, who looked for the truth of things in eternal Forms beyond this world. Aristotle stayed in this world. He wanted to know what each thing is for, here and now: an acorn, an animal, a person, a city, the universe. This journey follows that one question outwards, and it begins where he began, with nature.
answers: Who was Aristotle, and how did he differ from Plato?
What are the four causes?
What did Aristotle mean by saying that nature does nothing in vain?
Did Aristotle see evolution coming, as Darwin thought?
sessions.finding: Aristotle explained things by four causes, above all the final cause, what a thing is for: in his view nature does nothing in vain.

paras: Ask a child why a giraffe has a long neck, and they will probably say: to reach the leaves. Ask a scientist, and you may be told that is the wrong kind of answer; long-necked giraffes simply left more offspring. The argument between those two answers is about two and a half thousand years old, and Aristotle started it.

Aristotle asked one question of everything he studied: what is it for? This journey follows the question as he did. First nature (this session). Then a person: how we become good, and what wisdom is. Then the city we live in, the soul and the universe. Then we face his worst answer, about slaves and women, at full strength. The last session gives a verdict, and follows Aristotle to the place a Christian thinker, Thomas Aquinas, took him.

background.key: One question, asked of everything: what is it for? We follow it from nature to a person, the city, the soul and the universe, face its worst answer, then give a verdict.

paras: Aristotle was born in 384 BC at Stagira, a small Greek town in the north, near the kingdom of Macedon. His father, Nicomachus, was doctor to the king of Macedon. That may matter: Aristotle grew up among people who examined bodies and asked what each part was for.

At seventeen he went to Athens and joined Plato's school, the Academy, where he stayed for twenty years, until Plato died in 348 or 347 BC. Then he travelled. On the island of Lesbos he spent about two years studying animals in a lagoon. In 343 or 342 BC King Philip II of Macedon asked him to teach his son, the boy who became Alexander the Great. Back in Athens in 335 BC he founded his own school, the Lyceum. When Alexander died in 323 BC, Athens turned against everything Macedonian; Aristotle was charged with impiety and left for Chalcis, on the island of Euboea, where he died in 322 BC.
