background.key: Born in 384 BC, twenty years with Plato, a naturalist on Lesbos, tutor to Alexander, founder of the Lyceum; died in 322 BC.

background.h: What we have, and how to read it
paras: Aristotle wrote polished dialogues for the public, which the Roman orator Cicero admired for their style. Almost all are lost. What survives, about thirty works, are mostly his notes for teaching at the Lyceum, edited in the first century BC by Andronicus of Rhodes. They are dense, compressed and sometimes unfinished. They cover logic, physics, biology, the soul, ethics, politics, rhetoric, poetry and what came to be called metaphysics.

So Aristotle can be hard going, and old translations add to the difficulty. Each passage in this journey comes with a few plain sentences first. Read those, then read Aristotle slowly. He is not trying to dazzle you. He is thinking aloud, testing what people say against what we can see.
background.key: Aristotle's public dialogues are lost; what survives are dense teaching notes on almost every subject, so read the plain words first and then go slowly.

paras: We have no out-of-copyright English translation of Aristotle's Physics, the book where he sets out the four causes, among the texts we can use, so we start with the first page of his Ethics, where the same idea opens his study of human life: everything we do aims at some good. Then we read the key passage of the Physics as Charles Darwin quoted it in The Origin of Species, because Darwin thought Aristotle had glimpsed natural selection. Last comes a short passage from the Politics where Aristotle pushes the idea of purpose further than most of us would.

The comparison is from Paul's letter to the Romans, which says that what God is can be 'clearly seen' in the things he has made. Aristotle and Paul both look at nature and see more than matter. They do not see quite the same thing.
background.key: The opening of the Ethics, Darwin's quotation from the Physics, a passage from the Politics, then Paul on what nature shows.

before: On the first page of the Ethics, how many 'ends' can you count, and how are they arranged?
In the Physics passage, is Aristotle giving his own view or someone else's? Read the words around it carefully.
In the Politics, what does Aristotle conclude from 'nature makes nothing in vain'? Does it follow?
sessions.readWhy: Three short passages on what things are for: human actions (the Ethics), living bodies (the Physics, as Darwin quoted it) and the whole of nature (the Politics).

paras: Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form, and in like manner every action and moral choice, aims, it is thought, at some good: for which reason a common and by no means a bad description of the Chief Good is, “that which all things aim at.”

Now there plainly is a difference in the Ends proposed: for in some cases they are acts of working, and in others certain works or tangible results beyond and beside the acts of working: and where there are certain Ends beyond and beside the actions, the works are in their nature better than the acts of working. Again, since actions and arts and sciences are many, the Ends likewise come to be many: of the healing art, for instance, health; of the ship-building art, a vessel; of the military art, victory; and of domestic management, wealth; are respectively the Ends.

And whatever of such actions, arts, or sciences range under some one faculty (as under that of horsemanship the art of making bridles, and all that are connected with the manufacture of horse-furniture in general; this itself again, and every action connected with war, under the military art; and in the same way others under others), in all such, the Ends of the master-arts are more choice-worthy than those ranging under them, because it is with a view to the former that the latter are pursued.

(And in this comparison it makes no difference whether the acts of working are themselves the Ends of the actions, or something further beside them, as is the case in the arts and sciences we have been just speaking of.)

Since then of all things which may be done there is some one End which we desire for its own sake, and with a view to which we desire everything else; and since we do not choose in all instances with a further End in view (for then men would go on without limit, and so the desire would be unsatisfied and fruitless), this plainly must be the Chief Good, _i.e._ the best thing of all.

Surely then, even with reference to actual life and conduct, the knowledge of it must have great weight; and like archers, with a mark in view, we shall be more likely to hit upon what is right: and if so, we ought to try to describe, in outline at least, what it is and of which of the sciences and faculties it is the End.

Aristotle, in his “Physicæ Auscultationes” (lib.2, cap.8, s.2), after remarking that rain does not fall in order to make the corn grow, any more than it falls to spoil the farmer’s corn when threshed out of doors, applies the same argument to organisation; and adds (as translated by Mr. Clair Grece, who first pointed out the passage to me), “So what hinders the different parts (of the body) from having this merely accidental relation in nature? as the teeth, for example, grow by necessity, the front ones sharp, adapted for dividing, and the grinders flat, and serviceable for masticating the food; since they were not made for the sake of this, but it was the result of accident. And in like manner as to other parts in which there appears to exist an adaptation to an end. Wheresoever, therefore, all things together (that is all the parts of one whole) happened like as if they were made for the sake of something, these were preserved, having been appropriately constituted by an internal spontaneity; and whatsoever things were not thus constituted, perished and still perish.” We here see the principle of natural selection shadowed forth, but how little Aristotle fully comprehended the principle, is shown by his remarks on the formation of the teeth.

It is evident then that we may conclude of those things that are, that plants are created for the sake of animals, and animals for the sake of men; the tame for our use and provision; the wild, at least the greater part, for our provision also, or for some other advantageous purpose, as furnishing us with clothes, and the like. As nature therefore makes nothing either imperfect or in vain, it necessarily follows that she has made all these things for men: for which reason what we gain in war is in a certain degree a natural acquisition; for hunting is a part of it, which it is necessary for us to employ against wild beasts; and those men who being intended by nature for slavery are unwilling to submit to it, on which occasion such a. war is by nature just: that species of acquisition then only which is according to nature is part of economy; and this ought to be at hand, or if not, immediately procured, namely, what is necessary to be kept in store to live upon, and which are useful as well for the state as the family.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: Everything aims at some good
parts.context: These are the opening paragraphs of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle's lectures on how to live, given at the Lyceum in Athens in the 330s or 320s BC and probably named after his son Nicomachus. The translation is by D. P. Chase, an Oxford scholar, first published in 1847. 'Ends' means goals: what something is done for. Chase's notes are removed.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: everything we do, we do for some good. Shipbuilding is for ships, medicine for health, generalship for victory. These goals are stacked: making bridles serves riding, riding serves war, and so on. But the chain cannot go on for ever, or we would want things for no reason at all. So there must be one final goal we want for its own sake. Knowing it would help us live, as a target helps an archer.

commentary.on: Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form, and in like manner every action and moral choice, aims, it is thought, at some good
commentary.text: The first sentence of the Ethics is the whole of Aristotle in miniature. Notice 'it is thought': he starts from what people ordinarily say, and tests it. And notice the claim: every skill and every choice aims at something. Purpose is not added to human action from outside; it is part of what an action is.

commentary.on: of the healing art, for instance, health; of the ship-building art, a vessel; of the military art, victory
commentary.text: These are 'final causes', what each thing is for. Aristotle's examples are ordinary on purpose. You already know that a doctor who does not aim at health is not really practising medicine. He is asking you to notice that you know it.

commentary.on: as under that of horsemanship the art of making bridles
commentary.text: Ends are arranged in a ladder. The bridle-maker works for the rider, the rider for the general, the general for the city's safety. The higher end gives the lower its point.

commentary.on: for then men would go on without limit, and so the desire would be unsatisfied and fruitless
commentary.text: This is the key argument. If everything were wanted only for the sake of something else, nothing would be wanted for itself, and all our wanting would be empty. So there must be a highest good. The rest of the Ethics asks what it is; 'A good life' read his answer in Book I, chapter 7, and this journey's last session returns to it.

commentary.on: like archers, with a mark in view, we shall be more likely to hit upon what is right
commentary.text: One of Aristotle's best images. You can shoot without a target, but you will hit nothing in particular. A life, he thinks, needs a mark too.

parts.author: Charles Darwin, quoting Aristotle
parts.work: The Origin of Species, 6th edition (1872), 'An Historical Sketch', note 1
parts.translator: Aristotle's words translated by Clair James Grece; Darwin's own words original English (1872)
parts.ref: Aristotle, Physics II.8, as quoted by Darwin, The Origin of Species (6th edition, 1872)
parts.title: Rain, corn and teeth
parts.context: From 1861 Darwin added a short history of earlier ideas about evolution to The Origin of Species. In its first footnote he quoted Aristotle's Physics, Book II, chapter 8, in a translation by Clair James Grece, an English lawyer and scholar who had pointed the passage out to him. The words inside the quotation marks are Aristotle's; the rest is Darwin's. The footnote number is removed.
parts.plain: Darwin reports this argument: rain does not fall in order to make the corn grow, any more than it falls in order to spoil the farmer's harvest. It just falls. Perhaps body parts are the same. Front teeth happen to be sharp and back teeth flat; creatures whose parts happened to fit together survived, and the rest died out. Darwin saw natural selection here, but said Aristotle did not really grasp it.

commentary.on: rain does not fall in order to make the corn grow, any more than it falls to spoil the farmer’s corn when threshed out of doors
commentary.text: This is the strongest objection to purpose in nature, and Aristotle states it himself, about 2,300 years before Darwin. Rain falls because water vapour cools. If it helps the farmer, that is luck; if it ruins his harvest, that is bad luck. Why not say the same of eyes and teeth?

commentary.on: since they were not made for the sake of this, but it was the result of accident
commentary.text: The objector says teeth were not made for chewing; they just turned out useful. Aristotle took the idea from Empedocles, an earlier philosopher who imagined random limbs and creatures, some of which fitted together and lasted.

commentary.on: these were preserved, having been appropriately constituted by an internal spontaneity; and whatsoever things were not thus constituted, perished and still perish
commentary.text: Here is why Darwin was excited: survival of what happens to be well put together, and death for the rest. It sounds like natural selection.

commentary.on: how little Aristotle fully comprehended the principle, is shown by his remarks on the formation of the teeth
commentary.text: Darwin is right that Aristotle did not accept the idea, but there is more to it. In the Physics Aristotle states this view only to reject it. His reply, in his own next lines, is that chance gives you rare results, but teeth come out sharp at the front and flat at the back always, or nearly always. What happens regularly is not luck. So nature, he concludes, acts for the sake of something.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: Nature makes nothing in vain
parts.context: The Politics is Aristotle's study of the city and its government, from the same years as the Ethics. In Book I, chapter 8, he is discussing how a household gets what it needs to live. The translation is by William Ellis, first published in 1776. The '…' marks where the passage begins in the middle of a long paragraph; Bekker page numbers are removed.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: nature provides food for every animal. So plants exist for animals, and animals for human beings, the tame ones for work and food and the wild ones for food and clothing. Since nature makes nothing incomplete or pointless, she made all these for people. He adds that war against people 'intended by nature for slavery' who refuse to submit is just.

commentary.on: plants are created for the sake of animals, and animals for the sake of men
commentary.text: Here the idea of purpose runs further than most modern readers can follow. In his biology Aristotle usually means something more modest: an eye is for the good of the animal that has it, not for us. In this passage, about how households live off nature, he turns it into a ladder with human beings at the top.

commentary.on: As nature therefore makes nothing either imperfect or in vain
commentary.text: 'Nature does nothing in vain' is one of Aristotle's favourite sayings, found in his works on the heavens, on animals and on the soul. It is a working rule for a biologist: if an animal has a part, ask what it does. It is a much bigger claim when it is applied to the whole of nature at once.

commentary.on: those men who being intended by nature for slavery are unwilling to submit to it, on which occasion such a. war is by nature just
commentary.text: Notice this line and do not skip it. The same reasoning that says what things are for is here used to say what some people are for. ('a.' is a misprint in the source.) This journey will come back to it later, at full strength, in its own session.

read.author: Aristotle and Charles Darwin, quoting Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great

paras: because that which is known of God is revealed in them, for God revealed it to them.

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.
Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened.
Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools,
and traded the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and creeping things.

parts.title: Clearly seen
parts.context: Paul wrote his letter to the Christians in Rome around AD 57, from Corinth in Greece. In this opening chapter he is explaining why all people, not only Jews, are answerable to God: because God has shown himself in creation.

commentary.on: For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made
commentary.text: Paul says that the order of the world points beyond itself to its maker. Aristotle would agree that the world is ordered and full of purpose. But for Aristotle the purposes are inside things: the acorn aims at the oak by its own nature. He does not say someone designed the acorn. Paul says there is a Creator whose 'everlasting power and divinity' the world reveals.

commentary.on: Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks
commentary.text: Paul's complaint is not that people are ignorant, but ungrateful. Seeing purpose in the world is, for him, the beginning of a relationship, not the end of an argument.

commentary.on: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools
commentary.text: Paul is writing in a world shaped by Greek philosophy, and he is not against thinking. He is against wisdom that stops at the creation and never thanks the Creator.

compare.why: Paul, writing about four hundred years after Aristotle, also thought nature shows more than matter. Compare what each of them sees in it.
compare.title: Seen in the things that are made

paras: Aristotle said we know a thing when we know its 'causes', the answers to the question 'why?'. He found four kinds, set out in Physics II.3. Take a bronze statue. What is it made of? Bronze: the material cause. What makes this bronze a statue and not a lump? Its shape: the formal cause. What brought it about? The sculptor: the efficient cause. What is it for? To honour a god, perhaps: the final cause, 'that for the sake of which'.

Now take an oak. Its material is wood and sap. Its form is the pattern that makes it an oak and not an elm. Its efficient cause is the parent tree that dropped the acorn. And its final cause? To be a full-grown oak, living as oaks live. In living things, Aristotle noticed, the form and the end tend to coincide: what an acorn is for is to become fully what it already is.

rows: Wood, sap, the stuff of the acorn
What makes it this kind of thing?
table.note: Physics II.3 and Metaphysics V.2. 'Cause' translates the Greek aitia, closer to 'explanation' or 'reason why' than to the modern 'cause'.

sections.key: A full explanation names four causes: material, form, maker, and purpose.

sections.h: Why the final cause matters most
paras: Modern science mostly asks about material and efficient causes: what things are made of, and what pushed them. Aristotle thought that left out the most important question. You do not understand a heart until you know it pumps blood; you do not understand a hand until you know it grasps.

His answer to the rain-and-teeth objection, in Physics II.8, rests on regularity. Luck gives rare results. But teeth come out sharp at the front and flat at the back in every healthy animal of a kind, always or for the most part. What happens always or for the most part is not luck. And so, he concludes, nature acts for an end. He adds an image: if the art of shipbuilding were inside the wood, it would make ships by nature. Nature is like a doctor treating himself, an art working from within.

That is the meaning of 'nature does nothing in vain'. It is not a claim that someone planned each thing. It is the claim that living things are organised towards their own good, and that a good explanation must say so.
sections.key: Aristotle argued that what happens regularly is not chance, so nature works towards ends, like a craft working from within.

paras: About a quarter of Aristotle's surviving writing is biology: the History of Animals, the Parts of Animals, the Generation of Animals and shorter works. He describes hundreds of species. He seems to have opened chicks' eggs day by day to watch the embryo develop. He recognised that dolphins breathe air and feed their young on milk. He described the special arm a male octopus uses in mating, a detail many later naturalists dismissed and which was only confirmed in the nineteenth century.

Much of this work was done on Lesbos, at the lagoon of Pyrrha. The biologist Armand Marie Leroi, in The Lagoon (2014), has argued that Aristotle should be called the founder of biology. Darwin, reading a new translation of the Parts of Animals in 1882, wrote to its translator, William Ogle, that his own heroes, Linnaeus and Cuvier, were schoolboys beside old Aristotle. Aristotle also made mistakes, some large: he thought the heart, not the brain, was the seat of thought.
sections.key: Aristotle was a working biologist; Darwin, near the end of his life, ranked him above Linnaeus and Cuvier.

paras: If you have taken 'Plato', you met the Forms: perfect, unchanging patterns such as Justice or Beauty itself, which our world only copies. Aristotle studied under Plato for twenty years and kept much of his thought. But he came to think the Forms explained nothing. If there is a Form of Horse somewhere apart from horses, how does that help us understand the horse in the field?

For Aristotle, the form of a thing is in the thing: the pattern that makes this horse a horse. You find it not by turning away from the world but by looking hard at it, many times, until you see what all horses share. That is why he collected animals and constitutions while Plato wrote about the ideal city. In Raphael's painting The School of Athens (1509–11) in the Vatican, Plato points up to heaven; Aristotle holds his hand out flat, towards the earth.
sections.key: Plato looked for truth in Forms beyond the world; Aristotle found the form in each thing, and studied the world to see it.

paras: Aristotle's final causes are easy to confuse with a later idea: that the world shows design, as a watch shows a watchmaker. William Paley made that argument famous in 1802. It is not Aristotle's. For Aristotle the acorn aims at the oak because of what it is, not because someone intends it to. The world, he thought, had always existed; no one made it.

Christian thinkers later joined the two ideas. Thomas Aquinas, in the 1260s, argued that things without minds act for ends, and that this needs explaining by a mind that directs them; he called that mind God. Whether that step follows is a question for later in this journey, and for later halls. For now, notice the difference: Aristotle sees purpose in nature, Paul sees a Creator through it. Aquinas thought you could have both.
sections.key: Aristotle's purposes are inside things, with no designer; Paley's design argument is different, and Aquinas tried to join them.

paras: Behind the four causes lies a pair of ideas Aristotle used everywhere: potentiality and actuality. An acorn is potentially an oak; a full-grown oak is actually one. A sleeping mathematician is potentially doing mathematics; awake and at work, actually. Change, for Aristotle, is the passage from one to the other.

This lets him answer an old puzzle. Earlier Greek thinkers had argued that change is impossible, because something cannot come from nothing. Aristotle replies that things do not come from nothing; they come from what was already potentially there. The oak was in the acorn, not as a tiny tree but as a power.

The idea will matter at every step of this journey. A child is potentially brave, generous and wise; habit and wisdom make it actual. A city is the actuality towards which families tend. The soul is the actuality of a living body. And the universe, Aristotle will argue, depends on something that is actual through and through, with no unrealised potential at all.
sections.key: Change is the passage from potential to actual: the oak is in the acorn as a power, and this idea runs through all of Aristotle.

paras: Darwin's natural selection explains how parts that look made for a purpose could arise without anyone aiming at them: small differences, a struggle to survive, and time. Most biologists today think it answers Aristotle's argument from regularity. Teeth are regularly sharp at the front because animals with such teeth regularly left more offspring.

But the language of purpose has not gone away. Biologists still say the heart is 'for' pumping blood, and they mean something true. Some call this 'teleonomy', purpose-like order produced by selection. Some philosophers go further: Philippa Foot in Natural Goodness (2001) argued that we judge a plant or an animal good or defective by what its kind needs, and that human goodness can be judged the same way. Thomas Nagel, an atheist, argued in Mind and Cosmos (2012) that nature may contain purpose after all. The question Aristotle asked is still open; this journey's closing returns to it.
sections.key: Natural selection explains apparent purpose without aiming, but biologists still speak of what parts are 'for', and some philosophers defend real purpose in nature.

refs: Aristotle, Physics II.3 (194b–195a), II.8 (198b–199b); Metaphysics V.2; Nicomachean Ethics I.1–2; Politics I.2 (1253a9), I.8 (1256b); De Anima III.9 (432b21); Parts of Animals; History of Animals.
Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers V.1–35 (Aristotle's life and will).
Charles Darwin, The Origin of Species, 6th edition (1872), 'An Historical Sketch', note 1; letter to William Ogle, 22 February 1882 (Darwin Correspondence Project).
Armand Marie Leroi, The Lagoon: How Aristotle Invented Science (2014); Jonathan Barnes, Aristotle: A Very Short Introduction (2000).
William Paley, Natural Theology (1802); Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.3 (the fifth way).
Philippa Foot, Natural Goodness (2001); Thomas Nagel, Mind and Cosmos (2012); Ernst Mayr on 'teleonomy' (1974).

debate.question: Is there real purpose in nature?

positions.name: Yes: nature acts for ends
positions.who: Aristotle; Thomas Aquinas; Philippa Foot (in a modest form); Thomas Nagel
positions.view: Living things are organised towards their own good. You cannot explain an eye, a heart or a seed without saying what it is for. That is not a figure of speech but a fact about them, and a complete account of nature must include it.
positions.evidence: The regularity of living forms (Physics II.8); the way biologists still describe organs by their functions; the difficulty of explaining minds, which plainly do aim at things, by blind causes alone.

positions.name: No: only the appearance of purpose
positions.who: Empedocles, as Aristotle reports him; Darwin's modern followers, such as Richard Dawkins
positions.view: Purpose-talk is shorthand. Natural selection, working on chance variations over vast time, produces parts that look designed. Nothing in nature aims at anything; only minds do.
positions.evidence: Natural selection explains regular adaptation without aims; vestigial organs and poor 'designs' suggest history, not purpose.

positions.name: Purpose, from a Creator
positions.who: Paul (Romans 1); Augustine; Aquinas's fifth way; William Paley
positions.view: Nature is ordered towards ends because a mind orders it. Natural processes, even selection, can be the means a Creator uses. The question is not whether there is purpose but where it comes from.
positions.evidence: The intelligibility of nature, which science assumes; Romans 1:20; the argument that unthinking things acting for ends need a mind to direct them.

debate.agree: All agree that living things look as if they are for something, and that this needs explaining; they differ on whether the explanation is purpose itself, chance and selection, or a Creator.

look.why: No painting of Aristotle at work survives in the gallery. This is the most famous story about his pupil. Plutarch tells how the boy Alexander tamed a horse called Bucephalus that no one else could ride, by noticing that it was afraid of its own shadow and turning it towards the sun. It was soon after this, Plutarch says, that Philip sent for Aristotle to teach him. Degas painted the scene as a young man, around 1861 to 1862.
points: On the left, a pale young man in a white tunic, Alexander, raises his right hand to stroke the head of a reddish-brown horse at his shoulder.
He stands with his feet planted wide and his knees bent, his left hand curled into a fist.
A group of three people under a tree on the right stares back at him: a balding older man, a boy in a white tunic and a woman in a marigold-orange shirt and maroon skirt.
Behind them, a pair of raised arms suggests a fourth person whose head is missing or painted over.
In the distance, horses stand near a river, with white buildings on the far bank and slopes rising beneath a pale blue sky.

music.why: Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Sun calls on sun, wind, water and earth to praise God, each by being what it is. It is Paul's reading of nature, sung: every creature with its own way of pointing beyond itself.

think.why: Aristotle's question, whether nature has purposes, sits underneath the modern argument about science and God.

learn.why: The first sentence of the Ethics: the question behind everything Aristotle wrote.

check.q: A doctor sets a broken leg. Which of Aristotle's four causes is the doctor's aim of a healed, working leg?
options: The final cause
The efficient cause
The formal cause
The material cause
check.why: The final cause is 'that for the sake of which': here, health. The doctor himself is the efficient cause.

check.q: Why, on the first page of the Ethics, does Aristotle think there must be one highest good?
options: Because the gods command it
Because every art has the same end
Because if everything were wanted only for something else, the chain would go on without limit and all wanting would be empty
Because Plato proved it with the Form of the Good
check.why: Without an end wanted for its own sake, 'the desire would be unsatisfied and fruitless'. Note that he says the arts have different ends, so the last option is the opposite of his view.

check.q: In the passage Darwin quoted from the Physics, whose view is Aristotle stating?
options: Plato's
A view he states in order to reject it, which he took from Empedocles
His own considered view
Darwin's
check.why: Aristotle sets out the 'rain and teeth' argument as an objection, then replies that what happens always or for the most part is not chance.

check.q: What is Aristotle's main reply to the claim that teeth only happen to be useful?
options: Chance produces rare results, but teeth are formed this way always or for the most part, so nature acts for an end
God designed them
Teeth are not in fact useful
Only animals with souls have teeth
check.why: His argument rests on regularity, not on a designer.

check.q: How does Aristotle's idea of purpose in nature differ from Paley's argument from design?
options: It doesn't: both say a watchmaker made the world
Aristotle denied there was any purpose in nature
Paley denied that organs have functions
For Aristotle purposes are inside things by their nature, and the world was never made; Paley argues from design to a designer
check.why: Aristotle's acorn aims at the oak because of what it is. He believed the world had always existed.

check.q: Which is the most serious difficulty in the Politics passage that says plants are for animals and animals for men?
options: It turns a biologist's rule into a ladder with humans on top, and the same reasoning is used to call some people 'intended by nature for slavery'
It contradicts the Ethics
It is written by Ellis, not Aristotle
It denies that nature does anything in vain
check.why: Purpose-reasoning stretched to the whole of nature, and then to people, is where Aristotle's method is most open to abuse.

tutorial.question: Can we still say what anything in nature is 'for'?
tutorial.approach: Explain the four causes with your own example. Set out Aristotle's argument from regularity in Physics II.8 and the rain-and-teeth objection. Then explain how natural selection answers the argument. End by asking whether the language of function in biology (the heart is for pumping blood) is only shorthand, or points to something real.

States the rain-and-teeth objection and Aristotle's reply from regularity.
Notes that Darwin read the passage, and that Aristotle stated the objection to reject it.
Distinguishes Aristotle's natural purpose from Paley's design argument.
Explains how natural selection accounts for apparent purpose.
Takes a view on whether function-talk is only shorthand, and gives a reason.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, pick one thing you did that day and ask 'what was that for?', and then 'and what was that for?', until you reach something you want for its own sake. Write down where the chain ended.
sessions.reflect: If someone asked what you are for, what would you say? Does the question feel natural, or strange?
takeaways: Aristotle explained things by four causes: what they are made of, their form, what brought them about, and what they are for.
He argued that what happens regularly in nature is not chance, so nature acts for ends; Darwin's natural selection offers another explanation.
His purposes are inside things, not imposed by a designer; Paul, and later Aquinas, saw a Creator through them.

sessions.title: You become what you repeat
sessions.line: Builders become builders by building. Aristotle's most practical idea: character is made by habit, and virtue is the right amount, at the right time, in the right way.
sessions.plain: Aristotle asked what a person is for, and how we become good at being one. His answer is surprisingly practical. Nobody is born brave or generous, any more than a builder is born knowing how to build; we become brave by doing brave things, again and again, until it is second nature. And each virtue is a 'mean' between too much and too little: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between meanness and waste. This session reads his account of how character is made.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed Aristotle asking of everything in nature: what is it for? Now he turns the question on us. If an acorn is for becoming an oak, what is a human being for, and how do we get there? His answer starts not with rules but with habits.
answers: How do we become good, according to Aristotle?
What is the golden mean, and is it just moderation?
What is a virtue?
Are there things with no 'right amount'?
sessions.finding: We become good as builders become builders, by practice: a virtue is a settled habit of choosing the mean between too much and too little.

paras: Session 1 found that Aristotle explained everything by asking what it is for. The first page of his Ethics applied the question to human action: everything we do aims at some good, and there must be a highest good we want for its own sake. In Book I he gives it a name, eudaimonia, usually translated 'happiness' but closer to 'flourishing' or 'living well'.

If you have taken 'A good life', you read his argument in Book I, chapter 7: a good knife cuts well, a good eye sees well, so a good human being does well what humans are for, which is to live by reason. Happiness is 'a working of the soul in the way of excellence' over a whole life. But how does anyone acquire that excellence? That is Book II.
background.key: The highest good is eudaimonia, flourishing: living well by reason over a whole life. Book II asks how we get the excellence that requires.

paras: The Greek word is aretē, which Chase translates 'excellence' and later writers 'virtue'. It means being good at being what you are. A racehorse has the aretē of a horse when it runs well; a knife, when it cuts well. Human aretē is being good at being human.

Aristotle divides it in two. Intellectual virtues, such as wisdom, are taught. Moral virtues, such as courage, generosity and self-control, are habits of feeling and acting. The word 'ethics' comes from the Greek ēthos, character, which Aristotle links with ethos, habit. Character is what you have become by what you have repeatedly done.
background.key: Virtue (aretē) is excellence at being human; moral virtues are habits of feeling and acting, and 'ethics' itself comes from the Greek for character, linked with habit.

paras: The reading has three parts from Book II of the Ethics: how virtue is made by habit (chapter 1); the warning that talking about goodness is not the same as practising it (from chapter 4); and the famous account of the mean, with Aristotle's definition of virtue (chapters 5–6 in Chase's numbering, chapter 6 in the standard one).

The comparison is a short passage from the Letter to the Hebrews in the New Testament. It uses Aristotle's own word for a settled habit, and it says the same thing about how we learn to tell good from evil.
background.key: Habit, practice not talk, and the mean, from Ethics Book II; then Hebrews, which uses Aristotle's word for habit.

before: What does Aristotle say a stone cannot do, however often you throw it? Why does he bring it up?
What does 'the mean relatively to ourselves' mean? Who is Milo, and why does he need more food?
Which actions does Aristotle say have no mean at all?
sessions.readWhy: Aristotle's account of how character is made, from Book II of the Ethics: habit, practice and the mean.

paras: Well: human Excellence is of two kinds, Intellectual and Moral: now the Intellectual springs originally, and is increased subsequently, from teaching (for the most part that is), and needs therefore experience and time; whereas the Moral comes from custom, and so the Greek term denoting it is but a slight deflection from the term denoting custom in that language.

From this fact it is plain that not one of the Moral Virtues comes to be in us merely by nature: because of such things as exist by nature, none can be changed by custom: a stone, for instance, by nature gravitating downwards, could never by custom be brought to ascend, not even if one were to try and accustom it by throwing it up ten thousand times; nor could file again be brought to descend, nor in fact could anything whose nature is in one way be brought by custom to be in another. The Virtues then come to be in us neither by nature, nor in despite of nature, but we are furnished by nature with a capacity for receiving themu and are perfected in them through custom.

Again, in whatever cases we get things by nature, we get the faculties first and perform the acts of working afterwards; an illustration of which is afforded by the case of our bodily senses, for it was not from having often seen or heard that we got these senses, but just the reverse: we had them and so exercised them, but did not have them because we had exercised them. But the Virtues we get by first performing single acts of working, which, again, is the case of other things, as the arts for instance; for what we have to make when we have learned how, these we learn how to make by making: men come to be builders, for instance, by building; harp-players, by playing on the harp: exactly so, by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave.

And to the truth of this testimony is borne by what takes place in communities: because the law-givers make the individual members good men by habituation, and this is the intention certainly of every law-giver, and all who do not effect it well fail of their intent; and herein consists the difference between a good Constitution and a bad.

Again, every Virtue is either produced or destroyed from and by the very same circumstances: art too in like manner; I mean it is by playing the harp that both the good and the bad harp-players are formed: and similarly builders and all the rest; by building well men will become good builders; by doing it badly bad ones: in fact, if this had not been so, there would have been no need of instructors, but all men would have been at once good or bad in their several arts without them.

So too then is it with the Virtues: for by acting in the various relations in which we are thrown with our fellow men, we come to be, some just, some unjust: and by acting in dangerous positions and being habituated to feel fear or confidence, we come to be, some brave, others cowards.

Similarly is it also with respect to the occasions of lust and anger: for some men come to be perfected in self-mastery and mild, others destitute of all self-control and passionate; the one class by behaving in one way under them, the other by behaving in another. Or, in one word, the habits are produced from the acts of working like to them: and so what we have to do is to give a certain character to these particular acts, because the habits formed correspond to the differences of these.
So then, whether we are accustomed this way or that straight from childhood, makes not a small but an important difference, or rather I would say it makes all the difference.

The facts, it is true, are called by the names of these habits when they are such as the just or perfectly self-mastering man would do; but he is not in possession of the virtues who merely does these facts, but he who also so does them as the just and self-mastering do them.

We are right then in saying, that these virtues are formed in a man by his doing the actions; but no one, if he should leave them undone, would be even in the way to become a good man. Yet people in general do not perform these actions, but taking refuge in talk they flatter themselves they are philosophising, and that they will so be good men: acting in truth very like those sick people who listen to the doctor with great attention but do nothing that he tells them: just as these then cannot be well bodily under such a course of treatment, so neither can those be mentally by such philosophising.
Now what the genus of Virtue is has been said; but we must not merely speak of it thus, that it is a state but say also what kind of a state it is.

We must observe then that all excellence makes that whereof it is the excellence both to be itself in a good state and to perform its work well. The excellence of the eye, for instance, makes both the eye good and its work also: for by the excellence of the eye we see well. So too the excellence of the horse makes a horse good, and good in speed, and in carrying his rider, and standing up against the enemy. If then this is universally the case, the excellence of Man, i.e. Virtue, must be a state whereby Man comes to be good and whereby he will perform well his proper work. Now how this shall be it is true we have said already, but still perhaps it may throw light on the subject to see what is its characteristic nature.

In all quantity then, whether continuous or discrete, one may take the greater part, the less, or the exactly equal, and these either with reference to the thing itself, or relatively to us: and the exactly equal is a mean between excess and defect. Now by the mean of the thing, _i.e._ absolute mean, I denote that which is equidistant from either extreme (which of course is one and the same to all), and by the mean relatively to ourselves, that which is neither too much nor too little for the particular individual. This of course is not one nor the same to all: for instance, suppose ten is too much and two too little, people take six for the absolute mean; because it exceeds the smaller sum by exactly as much as it is itself exceeded by the larger, and this mean is according to arithmetical proportion.

But the mean relatively to ourselves must not be so found ; for it does not follow, supposing ten minæ is too large a quantity to eat and two too small, that the trainer will order his man six; because for the person who is to take it this also may be too much or too little: for Milo it would be too little, but for a man just commencing his athletic exercises too much: similarly too of the exercises themselves, as running or wrestling.
So then it seems every one possessed of skill avoids excess and defect, but seeks for and chooses the mean, not the absolute but the relative.

Now if all skill thus accomplishes well its work by keeping an eye on the mean, and bringing the works to this point (whence it is common enough to say of such works as are in a good state, “one cannot add to or take ought from them,” under the notion of excess or defect destroying goodness but the mean state preserving it), and good artisans, as we say, work with their eye on this, and excellence, like nature, is more exact and better than any art in the world, it must have an aptitude to aim at the mean.

It is moral excellence, _i.e._ Virtue, of course which I mean, because this it is which is concerned with feelings and actions, and in these there can be excess and defect and the mean: it is possible, for instance, to feel the emotions of fear, confidence, lust, anger, compassion, and pleasure and pain generally, too much or too little, and in either case wrongly; but to feel them when we ought, on what occasions, towards whom, why, and as, we should do, is the mean, or in other words the best state, and this is the property of Virtue.

In like manner too with respect to the actions, there may be excess and defect and the mean. Now Virtue is concerned with feelings and actions, in which the excess is wrong and the defect is blamed but the mean is praised and goes right; and both these circumstances belong to Virtue. Virtue then is in a sense a mean state, since it certainly has an aptitude for aiming at the mean.

Again, one may go wrong in many different ways (because, as the Pythagoreans expressed it, evil is of the class of the infinite, good of the finite), but right only in one; and so the former is easy, the latter difficult; easy to miss the mark, but hard to hit it: and for these reasons, therefore, both the excess and defect belong to Vice, and the mean state to Virtue; for, as the poet has it,
“Men may be bad in many ways, But good in one alone.”
Virtue then is “a state apt to exercise deliberate choice, being in the relative mean, determined by reason, and as the man of practical wisdom would determine.”

It is a middle state between too faulty ones, in the way of excess on one side and of defect on the other: and it is so moreover, because the faulty states on one side fall short of, and those on the other exceed, what is right, both in the case of the feelings and the actions; but Virtue finds, and when found adopts, the mean.
And so, viewing it in respect of its essence and definition, Virtue is a mean state; but in reference to the chief good and to excellence it is the highest state possible.

But it must not be supposed that every action or every feeling is capable of subsisting in this mean state, because some there are which are so named as immediately to convey the notion of badness, as malevolence, shamelessness, envy; or, to instance in actions, adultery, theft, homicide; for all these and suchlike are blamed because they are in themselves bad, not the having too much or too little of them.

In these then you never can go right, but must always be wrong: nor in such does the right or wrong depend on the selection of a proper person, time, or manner (take adultery for instance), but simply doing any one soever of those things is being wrong.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: Builders by building
parts.context: Book II of the Ethics opens. Aristotle has said in Book I that happiness is the soul working well, and now asks how we come to have the excellence that requires. The translation is D. P. Chase's (1847). 'Self-mastery' is Chase's word for temperance, self-control with pleasures. Two small errors in the source are left as printed: 'file' for 'fire' and 'themu' for 'them'.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: moral virtue does not come from nature, because nature cannot be changed by habit; you can throw a stone up ten thousand times and it will still fall. But nor is virtue against nature: we are born able to receive it, and habit completes it. We become builders by building and harp-players by playing the harp; in the same way we become just by doing just things and brave by doing brave things. Bad building makes bad builders, and bad habits make bad people. So how we are brought up makes all the difference.

commentary.on: a stone, for instance, by nature gravitating downwards, could never by custom be brought to ascend, not even if one were to try and accustom it by throwing it up ten thousand times
commentary.text: The stone is a comic picture with a serious point. Nature cannot be trained. If virtue were natural, like falling, we could not learn it. Since we plainly can grow in courage or patience, virtue must come from somewhere else.

commentary.on: The Virtues then come to be in us neither by nature, nor in despite of nature
commentary.text: Not by nature, but not against it either. We are born with the capacity, as an acorn has the capacity to be an oak. Habit makes the capacity real. This is session 1's final cause, now applied to character.

commentary.on: men come to be builders, for instance, by building; harp-players, by playing on the harp: exactly so, by doing just actions we come to be just
commentary.text: The most famous sentence in the Ethics, and the one this journey asks you to learn. It reverses a natural assumption. We think we must become good first, then do good things. Aristotle says: do the good things, and you will become good.

commentary.on: the law-givers make the individual members good men by habituation
commentary.text: For Aristotle ethics and politics are one subject. A city's laws and customs train its citizens, for better or worse. This is a theme for later in this journey.

commentary.on: by building well men will become good builders; by doing it badly bad ones
commentary.text: The same practice that makes a good builder makes a bad one, if done badly. Repetition is not good in itself. Repeated cowardice makes a coward.

commentary.on: whether we are accustomed this way or that straight from childhood, makes not a small but an important difference, or rather I would say it makes all the difference
commentary.text: Aristotle has no sentimental view of childhood. Habits are being formed whether anyone intends it or not. This is why he thinks the young are not ready to study ethics: they need to be trained in it first.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: Not by talk
parts.context: A little further on, Aristotle meets an objection: if we must do just acts to become just, aren't we already just when we do them? He answers that a just act done by chance or under orders is not yet the act of a just person. Then he turns on people who think talking about goodness is enough.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: doing a just act does not yet make you a just person; you must do it as a just person does, knowingly, by choice and from a settled character. And that character comes only from doing such acts. Many people avoid doing them and talk philosophy instead, thinking it will make them good. They are like patients who listen carefully to the doctor and then ignore everything he says.

commentary.on: he is not in possession of the virtues who merely does these facts, but he who also so does them as the just and self-mastering do them
commentary.text: A real virtue is not just the outward act. Just before this, Aristotle says the act must be done knowingly, chosen for its own sake, and from a firm and unchanging character. The habit is what turns a good act into a good person.

commentary.on: taking refuge in talk they flatter themselves they are philosophising
commentary.text: A sharp line from a professional philosopher. Reading this journey will not make you good. Only practice will.

commentary.on: acting in truth very like those sick people who listen to the doctor with great attention but do nothing that he tells them
commentary.text: One of Aristotle's many medical images; he was a doctor's son. Ethics, for him, is like medicine: its point is not knowing but getting well.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: The mean
parts.context: Aristotle now asks what kind of thing a virtue is. It is not a feeling (we are not praised for being afraid) nor a capacity (we are born able to feel). It is a 'state', a settled disposition. Then he asks what kind of state. 'Ten minæ' is a weight, about four kilograms; Milo of Croton was the most famous wrestler in Greece. 'Too faulty ones' means 'two faulty ones'.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: every excellence makes a thing good and makes it do its work well, as a good eye sees well. In anything that comes in amounts you can have too much, too little, or the right amount. The right amount for you is not the halfway point: six pounds of meat may be too little for a champion wrestler and too much for a beginner. Virtue aims at the right amount in feelings and actions: to feel fear or anger at the right times, about the right things, towards the right people, for the right reason and in the right way. There are many ways to go wrong and only one way to go right. But some acts, like adultery, theft and murder, have no right amount; they are always wrong.

commentary.on: the excellence of Man, i.e. Virtue, must be a state whereby Man comes to be good and whereby he will perform well his proper work
commentary.text: This links back to session 1. A good eye is one that does what eyes are for. A good person is one who does well what humans are for. Ethics follows from the question 'what is it for?'

commentary.on: for Milo it would be too little, but for a man just commencing his athletic exercises too much
commentary.text: The mean is 'relative to us'. It is not a number you can look up. A trainer judges what this athlete needs today. Courage for a soldier and courage for a nurse will look different.

commentary.on: to feel them when we ought, on what occasions, towards whom, why, and as, we should do, is the mean
commentary.text: This sentence is the heart of the doctrine, and it shows the 'mean' is not about being lukewarm. The right amount of anger at a bully may be a great deal. The mean is about fit: the right feeling, at the right time, for the right reason.

commentary.on: easy to miss the mark, but hard to hit it
commentary.text: The archer again, from session 1. There are countless ways to miss, and one bullseye. That is why virtue is hard and vice is easy.

commentary.on: Virtue then is “a state apt to exercise deliberate choice, being in the relative mean, determined by reason, and as the man of practical wisdom would determine.”
commentary.text: Aristotle's definition of virtue. Each phrase matters: a settled state, not a mood; involving choice; at the mean relative to us; set by reason; as a person of practical wisdom would set it. That last phrase is the subject of the next session.

commentary.on: in reference to the chief good and to excellence it is the highest state possible
commentary.text: Here Aristotle heads off the commonest misunderstanding. The mean is in the middle only as a matter of definition. In goodness it is not middling but the top.

commentary.on: as malevolence, shamelessness, envy; or, to instance in actions, adultery, theft, homicide
commentary.text: Some things have no right amount. There is no right time, or right person, for adultery. So the mean is not a formula that excuses everything in moderation.

read.author: Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great

paras: For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food.
For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby.
But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.

parts.title: Solid food for the mature
parts.context: The Letter to the Hebrews was written in polished Greek, probably before AD 70, to Jewish Christians tempted to give up. Its author is unknown. Here he scolds his readers for not growing up in their faith.

commentary.on: you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God
commentary.text: The readers have heard the teaching but not grown by it: Aristotle's patients who listen to the doctor and do nothing.

commentary.on: who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil
commentary.text: 'By reason of use' translates the Greek dia tēn hexin: because of their settled habit. It is the only time the New Testament uses Aristotle's word for a virtue as a state. 'Exercised' is gegymnasmena, trained like an athlete in the gymnasium. Moral perception, says Hebrews, is a trained skill. Aristotle would agree. The difference is the goal: here it is growing up into Christ, not only into a fine human being.

compare.why: The Letter to the Hebrews in the New Testament uses Aristotle's own word for a settled habit, hexis, to say how Christians learn to tell good from evil.
compare.title: Trained by practice

paras: Most of us assume that we must first understand what is good and then do it. Aristotle reverses the order. We do it first, usually because someone trains us, and understanding follows. A child is made to say thank you long before she feels grateful; with practice the feeling grows into the act.

This is why Aristotle says the young are not fit students of ethics. Not because they are stupid, but because ethics is about experience and character, and argument cannot give you those. His ethics is written for people who already have good habits and want to understand them.

If you have taken 'A good life', you met the psychologist William James's chapter on habit (1890), which says much the same thing in modern terms: we are bundles of habits, and the nervous system can be made our ally. Modern psychology broadly agrees that repeated action shapes character, though it argues about how much and how fast.
sections.key: For Aristotle we act well first, by training, and understand later; character is formed by what we repeatedly do.

paras: In Book II, chapter 7, Aristotle sets out a table of virtues and the vices on either side. Some of his names were invented, he admits, because Greek had no word for the state. The list is not a law code. It is a map of the feelings and situations in which human beings go wrong in two directions.

Read it as a mirror rather than a chart. Most people recognise themselves on one side of some line: too quick to anger, or too slow to stand up for anyone; too tight with money, or unable to keep it. Aristotle also notices that some vices have no name, because almost nobody has them: few people enjoy bodily pleasure too little. And he admits the list is an outline, to be filled in later in the Ethics with greater exactness.

table.note: Nicomachean Ethics II.7, simplified; Chase's names are given in brackets where they differ.

sections.key: Aristotle maps the virtues as means between two vices, in fear, pleasure, money, honour, anger, truthfulness, humour and company.

paras: 'The golden mean' can sound like a recipe for a comfortable, lukewarm life: never too much of anything. That is not what Aristotle means. The mean is relative to the person and the situation. Sometimes the right amount of anger is a great deal; sometimes the right amount of generosity is everything you have.

Nor is the mean always in the middle. Courage is nearer to rashness than to cowardice, Aristotle says later in the chapter, and so we should lean away from the vice we are most drawn to, like straightening a bent stick by bending it the other way. The mean is a target, not an average.

And some things have no mean at all. Adultery, theft and murder are wrong however done. Aristotle's ethics has room for absolute prohibitions, though it does not start with them. That matters when later Christian thinkers built on him.
sections.key: The mean is the right amount for the person and moment, not the middle; and some acts, like murder, have no mean at all.

paras: Aristotle's ethics is unusual in how much it cares about feelings. Virtue concerns 'feelings and actions', he says, and a person who does the right thing while hating it is not yet virtuous. The self-controlled person who longs for the second bottle and refuses it is better than one who drinks it; but the temperate person, who does not much want it, is better still.

This is a high standard, and a hopeful one. It means our feelings can be educated. Fear can be trained to rise at real dangers and stay quiet at false ones; anger can learn to fit its object. Pleasure and pain, Aristotle says, are how we are trained, which is why he quotes Plato: children must be brought up to take pleasure in the right things.

It also explains his test of character. Watch what someone enjoys. The generous person enjoys giving; the brave person, if not enjoying danger, at least does not find it unbearable. When doing good becomes a pleasure, the habit is formed.
sections.key: Virtue governs feelings as well as acts; the test of a formed habit is that doing good has become a pleasure.

sections.h: Why the middle way is hard
paras: Aristotle quotes a line of verse: 'Men may be bad in many ways, but good in one alone.' There are endless ways to miss a target and only one way to hit it. That is why goodness is rare and difficult, and why it cannot be reduced to a checklist.

He offers practical advice in chapter 9. First, avoid the extreme that is more opposed to the mean; better to err towards courage's rashness than its cowardice. Second, know your own tendencies and lean against them, as a carpenter straightens warped wood by bending it back. Third, be most wary of pleasure, because we are not impartial judges of it.

None of this gives a formula. It gives a way of training judgement. Which raises the question Aristotle's own definition points to: who decides where the mean lies? His answer is 'the person of practical wisdom', and that is where the next session begins.
sections.key: There are many ways to miss and one to hit; Aristotle advises leaning away from your own vices, and leaves the final judgement to practical wisdom.

paras: Critics have pressed the doctrine hard. Immanuel Kant, in The Metaphysics of Morals (1797), argued that virtue and vice differ in kind, not degree: lying is not too much truthfulness turned down a little. Others ask where the mean is to be found, if not by a rule. Aristotle's answer, 'as the person of practical wisdom would decide', can sound circular: the good person does what the good person would do.

There is also the question of who is doing the training. Aristotle assumes good parents, good laws and a good city. What of someone raised in cruelty? On his own account they may be almost beyond help, and he says as much in Book X. That is a hard conclusion, and later traditions, the Christian one above all, challenged it with the hope that grace can remake a character habit cannot.
sections.key: Kant said virtue differs from vice in kind, not degree; others call the mean circular, and ask what happens to those badly trained.

paras: Christian writers took up Aristotle's account of habit, but not all at once. The early church knew his ethics mostly at second hand. In the thirteenth century Thomas Aquinas built on it directly: he called a virtue a habitus, the Latin for hexis, and accepted that the moral virtues are acquired by practice.

But he added something Aristotle did not have. Faith, hope and love, the 'theological virtues', cannot be acquired by practice; they are given by God. And God can also give, or 'infuse', moral virtues, which then grow by use, like Hebrews' trained senses. Protestant reformers worried that this made goodness too much our own achievement. The Christian traditions still differ on how far character is something we build and how far something done in us. All agree it is lived out in habits.
sections.key: Aquinas called virtue a habitus and kept Aristotle's habits, but added virtues given by God; the traditions differ on how far goodness is built or given.

refs: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7; II.1–9 (the mean table in II.7, the bent stick in II.9); X.9 (Chase X.VIII).
Hebrews 5:12–14 (Greek dia tēn hexin, gegymnasmena).
William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), chapter IV, 'Habit'.
Immanuel Kant, The Metaphysics of Morals (1797), Doctrine of Virtue, Introduction.
Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II q.49–51 (habits), q.62–63 (theological and infused virtues).

debate.question: Can you become good by practice?

positions.name: Yes: character is made by habit
positions.who: Aristotle; most modern virtue ethicists; much of modern psychology
positions.view: We become what we repeatedly do. Practise courage and you become brave. The task of ethics is to form good habits early and keep them.
positions.evidence: The builder and the harp-player; the observable way practice changes skill and feeling; Hebrews' trained senses.

positions.name: No: duty, not habit, makes an act good
positions.who: Immanuel Kant
positions.view: An act has moral worth when it is done from duty, because reason sees it is right, not because we have been trained to like it. Habit may make good acts easier, but it is not what makes them good.
positions.evidence: Virtue and vice differ in kind, not degree; a well-trained person can still be good only by luck of upbringing.

positions.name: Practice, but grace first
positions.who: Augustine; Aquinas; Luther (more sharply)
positions.view: Habits matter, but the deepest change in a person is a gift. Grace gives love, and love then forms habits. Luther went further: we are not made righteous by doing righteous deeds; we do righteous deeds once we have been made righteous.
positions.evidence: Hebrews 5:14 alongside Ephesians 2:8–10; the experience of people changed suddenly, not slowly; Aristotle's own admission that some cannot be reformed by words.

debate.agree: All agree that habits shape us and that good acts done reluctantly are not yet the whole of goodness; they differ on whether character is made by practice, by duty or by grace.

look.why: Aristotle's favourite examples of how we learn are crafts: building, harp-playing, carving. George de Forest Brush painted this craftsman in the 1880s; the gallery dates it 1887, though the inscription reads 1881. The skill in his hands was learned the way Aristotle says every virtue is: by doing it, many times.
points: We see a person from behind, sitting cross-legged on a blue-green mat with yellow details.
They are carving a large slab of white stone with grey marbling, holding a small chisel and a hammer.
Small lines are being cut into the flat stone.
The top and right edges of the slab already carry intricate patterns: a standing figure in a feathered headdress, vines, animals and geometric shapes.
The carver wears a gold arm band and a leopard-print garment wrapped around the waist.

music.why: The legend says this Mass persuaded the Council of Trent not to ban elaborate church music: a mean between empty plainness and words lost in ornament. True or not, it is music of balance, made by a composer who wrote over a hundred Masses.

think.why: Aristotle's claim that we become what we repeat, set beside what modern research says about practice and character.

learn.why: The heart of Aristotle's ethics in one sentence: we become just by doing just actions.

check.q: Why does Aristotle mention a stone thrown up ten thousand times?
options: To show that what is by nature cannot be changed by habit, so moral virtue cannot be simply natural
To show that virtue is like gravity
To prove that the gods move stones
To show that practice is useless
check.why: Since we can be trained in virtue and a stone cannot be trained to rise, virtue is not by nature, though nature gives us the capacity.

check.q: Someone says: 'I'll start being generous once I feel generous.' What would Aristotle reply?
options: Give generously now; doing generous acts is how you become a generous person, and the feeling follows
Quite right: feelings come first
Generosity is a vice of excess
Generosity is a gift of nature, so wait
check.why: 'By doing just actions we come to be just.' Habit forms the feeling.

check.q: A champion wrestler and a beginner both ask a trainer how much to eat. What does Aristotle's example show?
options: That both should eat the same amount
That six is always the mean between two and ten
That wrestling is a vice
That the mean is relative to us: the right amount depends on the person, not a fixed halfway number
check.why: Six is the arithmetic mean, but 'for Milo it would be too little'.

check.q: Which statement is closest to Aristotle's doctrine of the mean?
options: Do whatever most people do
Always do things in moderation
Feel and act at the right time, about the right things, towards the right people, for the right reason and in the right way
Avoid all strong feelings
check.why: The mean is about fit, not lukewarmness; the right anger may be strong.

check.q: Why does adultery have no mean, according to Aristotle?
options: Because it is wrong in itself, however, whenever and with whomever it is done
Because it is too rare to measure
Because the law forbids it
Because it is a feeling, not an action
check.why: Some acts 'are blamed because they are in themselves bad, not the having too much or too little of them'.

check.q: What does Hebrews 5:14 share with Aristotle?
options: The view that the young should study ethics
The table of the mean
The belief that virtue is a gift of nature
The word hexis, a settled habit, and the idea that discerning good and evil is a trained skill
check.why: 'By reason of use' is dia tēn hexin; 'exercised' is the word for athletic training.

tutorial.question: Is virtue a mean?
tutorial.approach: Explain Aristotle's claim that virtue is formed by habit, and his definition of virtue as a state of choosing the mean relative to us. Use two examples from the table. Then put Kant's objection and the charge of circularity. Decide whether the doctrine is a useful guide, a description of good character, or neither.
strong: Explains habituation with the builder or harp-player.
Explains 'relative to us' with the Milo example.
Shows the mean is not mere moderation, and that some acts have no mean.
States Kant's objection fairly.
Deals with the charge of circularity, perhaps by pointing ahead to practical wisdom.
Comes to a clear view.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose one small virtue you lack, such as punctuality, patience or generosity, and do one act of it every day, whether you feel like it or not. At the end of the week, notice whether it has become any easier.
sessions.reflect: Which of your habits has made you who you are, for good or ill? Which would you most like to change?
takeaways: We become good as builders become builders, by practice: virtue is not natural, but nature gives us the capacity and habit completes it.
A virtue is a settled state of choosing the mean relative to us: the right feeling and act at the right time, in the right way; some acts, like murder, have no mean.
Hebrews uses Aristotle's word for a habit; Aquinas kept his account and added virtues given by God.

sessions.title: Practical wisdom
sessions.line: No rule book can tell you what this moment asks. Aristotle's name for the skill that can: phronesis, practical wisdom.
sessions.plain: Session 2 ended with a question: who decides where the mean lies? Aristotle's answer is the person of practical wisdom, in Greek phronesis. It is the ability to see what a particular situation calls for and to act on it: not cleverness, which can serve any goal, and not book-learning, which the young can have, but a wisdom about life that comes from experience and good character. This session asks what it is, why rules cannot replace it, and why Aristotle thought you cannot be truly good without it, or truly wise without being good.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed that virtue is a habit of hitting the mean, 'as the man of practical wisdom would determine'. That raised a puzzle: the mean depends on the person and the moment, so how is it found? This session gives Aristotle's answer, and it completes his account of what makes a good person.
answers: What is practical wisdom (phronesis)?
How is it different from cleverness and from knowledge?
Why can't rules do its job?
Can you be good without being wise, or wise without being good?
sessions.finding: The virtues need practical wisdom, the trained ability to see what this situation asks, which no rule book can give; and practical wisdom itself needs good character.

paras: Session 1 found Aristotle asking of everything: what is it for? Session 2 applied the question to us. We become good by habit, as builders become builders by building. A virtue is a settled state of choosing the mean between too much and too little: the right feeling, at the right time, towards the right people, in the right way.

But Aristotle's definition of virtue ended with a phrase that needs explaining: the mean is fixed 'as the man of practical wisdom would determine'. If the mean is different for Milo and for the beginner, for the soldier and the nurse, someone has to see what it is here and now. Book VI of the Ethics is about that seeing.
background.key: Virtue is a habit of choosing the mean, as a person of practical wisdom would fix it; Book VI explains that wisdom.

background.h: Five ways of getting things right
paras: In Book VI Aristotle lists the states of mind by which we get at the truth. Scientific knowledge (epistēmē) proves things that cannot be otherwise, like the truths of geometry. Craft (technē) knows how to make things. Intuition (nous) grasps first principles that cannot be proved. Theoretical wisdom (sophia) combines knowledge and intuition about the highest things. And practical wisdom (phronesis) knows how to act well in human affairs.

Practical wisdom differs from all the others because its subject is the particular and the changeable: this person, this decision, today. You cannot prove what to say to a grieving friend the way you prove a theorem. But you can get it right or wrong.

rows: What cannot be otherwise, by proof
The highest truths, known and understood
How to act well, here and now
What to say to a grieving friend
table.note: Nicomachean Ethics VI.3–7.

background.key: Aristotle names five ways of getting at truth; practical wisdom is the one that deals with particular, changeable human situations.

paras: The reading has three parts from Book VI. Aristotle defines practical wisdom (chapter 5). He explains why it needs experience of particulars, and so why the young rarely have it (chapter 8). And he shows how it differs from mere cleverness, and why you cannot be good without it, or have it without being good (chapters 12–13; Chase prints these as one chapter, XII).

The comparison is from the book of Proverbs, part of the Hebrew Bible's 'wisdom' writing. Its word for wisdom, hokmah, is also practical: the skill to live well. Proverbs agrees with Aristotle that wisdom is the most precious thing a person can get. It disagrees about where it starts.
background.key: Book VI on what practical wisdom is, why it needs experience, and why it needs goodness; then Proverbs on getting wisdom.

before: What kind of person does Aristotle point to as an example of practical wisdom?
Why does Aristotle think the young can be good at mathematics but not at practical wisdom?
What is the difference between cleverness and practical wisdom?
sessions.readWhy: Aristotle's account of practical wisdom from Book VI of the Ethics: what it is, why it needs experience, and why it needs goodness.

paras: As for Practical Wisdom, we shall ascertain its nature by examining to what kind of persons we in common language ascribe it.

It is thought then to be the property of the Practically Wise man to be able to deliberate well respecting what is good and expedient for himself, not in any definite line, as what is conducive to health or strength, but what to living well. A proof of this is that we call men Wise in this or that, when they calculate well with a view to some good end in a case where there is no definite rule. And so, in a general way of speaking, the man who is good at deliberation will be Practically Wise. Now no man deliberates respecting things which cannot be otherwise than they are, nor such as lie not within the range of his own action: and so, since Knowledge requires strict demonstrative reasoning, of which Contingent matter does not admit (I say Contingent matter, because all matters of deliberation must be Contingent and deliberation cannot take place with respect to things which are Necessarily), Practical Wisdom cannot be Knowledge nor Art; nor the former, because what falls under the province of Doing must be Contingent; not the latter, because Doing and Making are different in kind.

It remains then that it must be “a state of mind true, conjoined with Reason, and apt to Do, having for its object those things which are good or bad for Man:” because of Making something beyond itself is always the object, but cannot be of Doing because the very well-doing is in itself an End.

For this reason we think Pericles and men of that stamp to be Practically Wise, because they can see what is good for themselves and for men in general, and we also think those to be such who are skilled in domestic management or civil government. In fact, this is the reason why we call the habit of perfected self-mastery by the name which in Greek it bears, etymologically signifying “that which preserves the Practical Wisdom:” for what it does preserve is the Notion I have mentioned, _i.e._ of one’s own true interest.

Nor again does Practical Wisdom consist in a knowledge of general principles only, but it is necessary that one should know also the particular details, because it is apt to act, and action is concerned with details: for which reason sometimes men who have not much knowledge are more practical than others who have; among others, they who derive all they know from actual experience: suppose a man to know, for instance, that light meats are easy of digestion and wholesome, but not what kinds of meat are light, he will not produce a healthy state; that man will have a much better chance of doing so, who knows that the flesh of birds is light and wholesome. Since then Practical Wisdom is apt to act, one ought to have both kinds of knowledge, or, if only one, the knowledge of details rather than of Principles. So there will be in respect of Practical Wisdom the distinction of supreme and subordinate.

A corroboration of what I have said is the fact, that the young come to be geometricians, and mathematicians, and Scientific in such matters, but it is not thought that a young man can come to be possessed of Practical Wisdom: now the reason is, that this Wisdom has for its object particular facts, which come to be known from experience, which a young man has not because it is produced only by length of time.

There is then a certain faculty, commonly named Cleverness, of such a nature as to be able to do and attain whatever conduces to _any_ given purpose: now if that purpose be a good one the faculty is praiseworthy; if otherwise, it goes by a name which, denoting strictly the ability, implies the willingness to do _anything_; we accordingly call the Practically-Wise Clever, and also those who can and will do anything.
