Now Practical Wisdom is not identical with Cleverness, nor is it without this power of adapting means to ends: but this Eye of the Soul (as we may call it) does not attain its proper state without goodness, as we have said before and as is quite plain, because the syllogisms into which Moral Action may be analysed have for their Major Premiss, “since —— is the End and the Chief Good” (fill up the blank with just anything you please, for we merely want to exhibit the Form, so that anything will do), but _how_ this blank should be filled is seen only by the good man: because Vice distorts the moral vision and causes men to be deceived in respect of practical principles.
It is clear, therefore, that a man cannot be a Practically-Wise, without being a good, man.

We must enquire again also about Virtue: for it may be divided into Natural Virtue and Matured, which two bear to each other a relation similar to that which Practical Wisdom bears to Cleverness, one not of identity but resemblance. I speak of Natural Virtue, because men hold that each of the moral dispositions attach to us all somehow by nature: we have dispositions towards justice, self-mastery and courage, for instance, immediately from our birth: but still we seek Goodness in its highest sense as something distinct from these, and that these dispositions should attach to us in a somewhat different fashion. Children and brutes have these natural states, but then they are plainly hurtful unless combined with an intellectual element: at least thus much is matter of actual experience and observation, that as a strong body destitute of sight must, if set in motion, fall violently because it has not sight, so it is also in the case we are considering: but if it can get the intellectual element it then excels in acting. Just so the Natural State of Virtue, being like this strong body, will then be Virtue in the highest sense when it too is combined with the intellectual element.

So that, as in the case of the Opinionative faculty, there are two forms, Cleverness and Practical Wisdom; so also in the case of the Moral there are two, Natural Virtue and Matured; and of these the latter cannot be formed without Practical Wisdom.

This leads some to say that all the Virtues are merely intellectual Practical Wisdom, and Socrates was partly right in his enquiry and partly wrong: wrong in that he thought all the Virtues were merely intellectual Practical Wisdom, right in saying they were not independent of that faculty.

A proof of which is that now all, in defining Virtue, add on the “state” [mentioning also to what standard it has reference, namely that] “which is accordant with Right Reason:” now “right” means in accordance with Practical Wisdom. So then all seem to have an instinctive notion that that state which is in accordance with Practical Wisdom is Virtue; however, we must make a slight change in their statement, because that state is Virtue, not merely which is in accordance with but which implies the possession of Right Reason; which, upon such matters, is Practical Wisdom. The difference between us and Socrates is this: he thought the Virtues were reasoning processes (_i.e._ that they were all instances of Knowledge in its strict sense), but we say they imply the possession of Reason.
From what has been said then it is clear that one cannot be, strictly speaking, good without Practical Wisdom nor Practically-Wise without moral goodness.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: Deliberating well about living well
parts.context: Book VI turns from the moral virtues to the virtues of the mind. Having described scientific knowledge and craft, Aristotle now defines practical wisdom by asking whom people call wise in practical matters. D. P. Chase's translation (1847). 'Contingent' means things that could be otherwise; 'perfected self-mastery' is temperance, which in Greek is sōphrosynē.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: we call someone practically wise when they can think well about what is good for them, not in one area like health, but for living well as a whole. It is not scientific knowledge, because it deals with things that could be otherwise, and not a craft, because acting well is its own goal, while making always aims at a product. It is a true, reasoned habit of acting about what is good and bad for human beings. Pericles, the great Athenian statesman, is an example.

commentary.on: we shall ascertain its nature by examining to what kind of persons we in common language ascribe it
commentary.text: Typical Aristotle: start with the people we already admire. You cannot define practical wisdom from the armchair; you recognise it in the wise friend, the good doctor, the experienced judge.

commentary.on: not in any definite line, as what is conducive to health or strength, but what to living well
commentary.text: Practical wisdom is not expertise in one field. It is the art of the whole of life: knowing what matters, and how much, and when.

commentary.on: Practical Wisdom cannot be Knowledge nor Art
commentary.text: Two contrasts. It is not knowledge in the strict sense, because it deals with what can change; you cannot prove that this is the moment to speak. And it is not a craft, because a craft aims at a product beyond itself, while acting well is its own end.

commentary.on: the very well-doing is in itself an End
commentary.text: A builder builds for the sake of the house. But a kind act is not done for the sake of something else; doing it well is the point. This is why Aristotle separates acting from making, and it echoes session 1's chain of ends.

commentary.on: For this reason we think Pericles and men of that stamp to be Practically Wise
commentary.text: Pericles led Athens in its golden age, in the mid-fifth century BC. Aristotle's example is a statesman, not a philosopher. Practical wisdom is seen in someone who handles real affairs well.

commentary.on: etymologically signifying “that which preserves the Practical Wisdom:”
commentary.text: A pun on the Greek word sōphrosynē, temperance, which Aristotle hears as 'saving phronesis'. His point is serious: uncontrolled pleasure and pain corrupt our judgement about what to do, though they leave our geometry alone. You cannot think straight about your life while ruled by your appetites.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: Particulars and experience
parts.context: A few chapters later. Aristotle explains why practical wisdom needs more than general principles, and why it comes with age. 'Light meats' are foods easy to digest. The '…' marks a cut.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: practical wisdom is not only knowing general rules; it must know particular cases, because action is always about particular things. A person who knows that light meat is healthy but not which meats are light will not make anyone healthy; someone who simply knows that chicken is good for you will. So experience can beat learning. That is why young people can be brilliant mathematicians but are not thought to have practical wisdom: it needs experience, and experience takes time.

commentary.on: it is necessary that one should know also the particular details, because it is apt to act, and action is concerned with details
commentary.text: Nobody acts 'in general'. You act now, with this person, with these words. Rules are general; life is particular. Practical wisdom is the bridge.

commentary.on: sometimes men who have not much knowledge are more practical than others who have
commentary.text: A modest remark from the most learned man of his age. The grandmother who has raised six children may judge a family crisis better than a professor of psychology.

commentary.on: the young come to be geometricians, and mathematicians, and Scientific in such matters, but it is not thought that a young man can come to be possessed of Practical Wisdom
commentary.text: There are child prodigies in mathematics and music, but not in wisdom. Wisdom about life is built from having lived it, which, as Aristotle dryly says, 'is produced only by length of time'.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: Cleverness, goodness and wisdom
parts.context: The end of Book VI. Someone has asked what use practical wisdom is, if good people do the right thing anyway. Aristotle answers by separating practical wisdom from mere cleverness, and natural good temper from real virtue. The blank in the second paragraph is Aristotle's: fill it in with any goal you like. Chase's notes are removed.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: cleverness is the ability to find the means to any goal. If the goal is good, it is admirable; if bad, it is mere cunning. Practical wisdom includes cleverness but needs goodness too, because only a good person sees rightly what the goal should be; vice distorts our vision. In the same way, children and animals have natural tendencies to courage or gentleness, but without wisdom these can do harm, like a strong man who cannot see. So you cannot be fully good without practical wisdom, nor practically wise without being good. Socrates was partly right: the virtues are not mere knowledge, but they cannot exist without reason.

commentary.on: There is then a certain faculty, commonly named Cleverness, of such a nature as to be able to do and attain whatever conduces to _any_ given purpose
commentary.text: Cleverness is the skill of means. The con artist and the surgeon may both have plenty of it. What makes the difference is the goal.

commentary.on: this Eye of the Soul (as we may call it) does not attain its proper state without goodness
commentary.text: Practical wisdom is a way of seeing. And how we see depends on what we are. A greedy person looks at a situation and sees opportunities; a kind person looks at the same situation and sees someone in need.

commentary.on: Vice distorts the moral vision and causes men to be deceived in respect of practical principles
commentary.text: This is a deep claim: wrongdoing is not only a failure of will but a failure of sight. Bad habits make us misperceive what matters. That is why, for Aristotle, ethics cannot be learned by argument alone.

commentary.on: as a strong body destitute of sight must, if set in motion, fall violently because it has not sight
commentary.text: A vivid image. Natural good temper without wisdom is like a strong man who is blind: the stronger he is, the harder he falls. Think of courage without judgement, or kindness that enables harm.

commentary.on: Socrates was partly right in his enquiry and partly wrong
commentary.text: Socrates had taught that virtue is knowledge: no one does wrong knowingly. Aristotle, a generation later, agrees that the virtues cannot exist without reason, but denies that they simply are knowledge. You also need trained desires.

commentary.on: one cannot be, strictly speaking, good without Practical Wisdom nor Practically-Wise without moral goodness
commentary.text: The conclusion, and a famous one: the 'unity of the virtues'. Practical wisdom and good character need each other. That is why sessions 2 and 3 belong together: habit trains our desires, wisdom guides our choices, and neither is complete alone.

read.author: Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great

paras:
Get wisdom.
Get understanding.
Don’t forget, and don’t deviate from the words of my mouth.

Don’t forsake her, and she will preserve you.
Love her, and she will keep you.

Wisdom is supreme.
Get wisdom.
Yes, though it costs all your possessions, get understanding.

Esteem her, and she will exalt you.
She will bring you to honor when you embrace her.

She will give to your head a garland of grace.
She will deliver a crown of splendor to you.”

parts.title: Wisdom is supreme
parts.context: The book of Proverbs is a collection of Israel's wisdom sayings, traditionally linked with King Solomon (tenth century BC) and gathered over several centuries. Chapters 1–9 are speeches of a father to a son. Here the father is passing on what his own father taught him.

commentary.on:
Get wisdom.
Get understanding.
commentary.text: The Hebrew for wisdom, hokmah, is a practical word. It is used of craftsmen's skill (Exodus 31:3) and of a ruler's judgement (1 Kings 3). Like phronesis, it is the skill of living well, learned from others and from experience.

commentary.on:
Wisdom is supreme.
Get wisdom.
Yes, though it costs all your possessions, get understanding.
commentary.text: Aristotle would agree that practical wisdom is worth more than wealth. But notice where Proverbs says wisdom begins: 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom' (Proverbs 9:10). For Aristotle wisdom starts with good habits and experience; for Proverbs it starts with reverence for God, and is a gift to be received as well as a skill to be learned.

commentary.on: Love her, and she will keep you.
commentary.text: Proverbs speaks of wisdom as a woman to be loved. Wisdom is not only a technique; it is something you come to desire. Aristotle would recognise the point: you cannot be wise without wanting the right things.

compare.why: The Hebrew wisdom tradition also prized a practical wisdom for living well. Proverbs urges its readers to get it at any price.
compare.title: Get wisdom

paras: Aristotle warned at the start of the Ethics that we should not expect more precision than the subject allows. Ethics is not geometry. General rules hold 'for the most part': keep your promises, repay your debts. But situations arise that the rule-maker never imagined. Aristotle's own example, in Book V, is the law itself: because laws are general, a good judge sometimes has to correct them in a particular case, as the lawgiver would have done if he had been present. He calls this equity.

So rules need a person to apply them. Two people can know the same rules and act very differently, one tactlessly and one well. That difference is practical wisdom. It is why we trust experienced doctors, judges and teachers to use judgement, and why we worry about systems that try to replace judgement with procedures.
sections.key: Rules hold for the most part; a person of practical wisdom applies them well and, like a good judge, sees when the case is one the rule did not foresee.

paras: Aristotle describes practical reasoning as a kind of syllogism, an argument from premises to a conclusion, but one that ends in an action. The first premise names a good: health is good for people. The second recognises the particular: this is a case where that applies. The conclusion is not a sentence but a deed.

Practical wisdom works at both ends. It must have the right goal, which, Aristotle says, good character supplies. And it must see the particular truly, which needs experience. It also includes deliberation: working out how to reach the goal. Aristotle insists we deliberate about means, not ends; the doctor does not deliberate whether to heal, but how.
This is why practical wisdom cannot be taught as a method. It can be grown: by good habits, by watching wise people, by experience, and by reflecting on what went right and wrong.
sections.key: Practical reasoning moves from a good goal, supplied by character, through a true view of the particular case, to an action.

paras: Can you be brave but unjust, or generous but a coward? In ordinary life we say so. Aristotle agrees that people have natural tendencies, one to boldness, another to gentleness. But he argues that the full virtues come together, because each needs practical wisdom, and practical wisdom, once you have it, governs them all.

The argument has a hard edge. Courage without justice is not quite courage: the brave criminal's daring serves a bad goal, and practical wisdom would have seen that. Scholars still argue whether Aristotle meant a strict unity, all or nothing, or only that the virtues tend to grow together. Most think the second is closer to life. But his point stands: goodness is one thing seen from many sides, not a set of separate skills.
sections.key: Because every virtue needs practical wisdom, and practical wisdom governs all of them, Aristotle held that the full virtues come together.

paras: The Latin for phronesis is prudentia, prudence. In modern English 'prudent' has shrunk to mean cautious, even timid. In the Christian tradition it meant something much larger. Ambrose of Milan in the fourth century, following Plato and Cicero, named four 'cardinal' (hinge) virtues: prudence, justice, courage and temperance. Augustine, Gregory the Great and the medieval church kept the list.

Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, followed Aristotle closely. He defined prudence as 'right reason about things to be done' and made it the guide of all the moral virtues. But he placed it inside a larger whole. Charity, the love of God, directs prudence to its final end, as Proverbs puts the fear of the Lord at wisdom's beginning. A Christian's practical wisdom asks not only what is fitting for a good human life, but what love requires here.
sections.key: Prudentia, prudence, became the first of the four cardinal virtues; Aquinas followed Aristotle and set it under the guidance of charity.

paras: For centuries after the Enlightenment, moral philosophy mostly asked about rules and outcomes. Kant asked which rules reason requires; utilitarians, which acts produce the most happiness. In 1958 the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe argued that we needed to recover the language of virtue. In 1981 Alasdair MacIntyre, a Scottish philosopher who later became a Catholic, published After Virtue.

MacIntyre argued that modern moral argument is in disarray because we use the language of an older tradition, Aristotle's, while having thrown away the idea that gave it sense: that human life has a purpose, a telos. Without that, our moral words become expressions of preference. His remedy was to recover the virtues, learned in shared practices and communities and understood as parts of a life with a story and a goal. The book revived 'virtue ethics', now one of the main schools of moral philosophy. Its critics say MacIntyre's diagnosis is too gloomy, and that a purpose for human life is exactly what modern people cannot agree on.
sections.key: MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981) argued that modern ethics lost its way by abandoning Aristotle's idea of a human purpose, and revived virtue ethics.

paras: If practical wisdom cannot be taught as a method, how does anyone get it? Aristotle's answer is scattered through the Ethics. First, good habits, which keep our desires from distorting our sight. Second, experience, which only time gives. Third, the company of wise people: we should attend to the unproven sayings of the old and experienced, he says in Book VI, because experience has given them an eye to see rightly.

Stories help too. The Bible teaches practical wisdom mostly through narratives and proverbs, not rules: Solomon judging between two mothers, Abigail talking David out of revenge, Jesus answering a lawyer's question about who his neighbour is with the story of a Samaritan. Each trains the reader to see a situation as a wise person would. Jesus's parables often end with a question turned back on the hearer: which of these was a neighbour? That is training in perception, not instruction in rules.

Finally, reflection. Looking back at what went right and wrong, and why, is how experience becomes wisdom rather than mere habit. Christian traditions built practices around this: the examination of conscience, spiritual direction, confession.
sections.key: Practical wisdom grows through good habits, experience, the company of the wise, stories that train perception, and honest reflection.

paras: All the main Christian traditions honour practical wisdom, but they place it differently. Catholic moral theology, following Aquinas, gives prudence a central role and trusts natural reason to see much of the good. Orthodox teaching speaks more of discernment (diakrisis), a gift learned in prayer and under a spiritual father, as the Desert Fathers taught. Protestant traditions, wary of trusting fallen reason, have stressed Scripture and conscience, though many Protestant ethicists, Stanley Hauerwas among them, have returned to the virtues.

rows: The good of a flourishing human life
Habit, and also given by God with grace
Reason, directed by charity to God
Prayer, humility and a spiritual guide
The Spirit, and the tradition of the Fathers
Scripture, and the Spirit's renewing of the mind
table.note: A simplification: each tradition holds all these elements in some measure.

sections.key: Catholics speak of prudence guided by charity, the Orthodox of discernment learned in prayer, Protestants of wisdom under Scripture.

refs: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.3 (precision); V.10 (equity); VI.3–13; VII.3 (practical syllogism); III.3 (deliberation about means).
Proverbs 1–9, esp. 4:5–9; 9:10; Exodus 31:3; 1 Kings 3.
Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy I.24; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II–II q.47 a.2 ('recta ratio agibilium'), I–II q.65 (connection of the virtues).
G. E. M. Anscombe, 'Modern Moral Philosophy', Philosophy 33 (1958); Alasdair MacIntyre, After Virtue (1981).
Stanley Hauerwas, A Community of Character (1981).

debate.question: Can ethics be reduced to rules?

positions.name: No: it needs practical wisdom
positions.who: Aristotle; Aquinas; Alasdair MacIntyre; most virtue ethicists
positions.view: Rules hold for the most part, but life is particular. Only a person of trained character and experience can see what a situation asks. Ethics is more like medicine than geometry.
positions.evidence: Equity correcting general laws; the gap between knowing a rule and applying it well; the young mathematician who is not yet wise.

positions.name: Yes, in principle: good rules can be stated
positions.who: Immanuel Kant; many modern ethicists of rules and outcomes
positions.view: If ethics rests on judgement alone, it is hostage to whoever counts as 'wise'. We need principles anyone can check: act only on maxims you could will as universal laws, or do what produces the greatest good.
positions.evidence: The danger of 'wise men' who are only powerful; the success of clear rights and laws in protecting the weak.

positions.name: Rules and wisdom together
positions.who: Much of the Jewish and Christian tradition
positions.view: There are commandments that hold absolutely, like 'do not murder', and wisdom is needed to apply the rest. Torah and Proverbs sit side by side in the Bible: law and the skill of living.
positions.evidence: Aristotle's own admission that some acts have no mean; Proverbs' practical wisdom alongside the Ten Commandments.

debate.agree: All agree that rules alone cannot foresee every case and that judgement can be corrupted; they differ on whether to trust the wise person or the clear principle more.

look.why: In Jesus's parable of the ten bridesmaids (Matthew 25:1–13), the five 'wise' ones bring oil for their lamps and are ready when the bridegroom comes late at night. Their wisdom is exactly Aristotle's practical kind: seeing ahead what this occasion will need. Sebastiano del Piombo painted a young woman of Venice in this role around 1510.
points: A young woman is shown from the waist up in a shimmering royal-blue dress, against a solid black background.
She holds a metal object at her chest, perhaps a vessel or an incense burner, with a conical top.
Her body is angled to the right; she turns her head to the left and looks back across her body, off to the right, with grey eyes.
Her auburn hair is parted in the middle and loosely braided; a grey pearl earring hangs from her ear.
A full white sleeve is rolled back to her elbow, and her arm stretches nearly across the painting as she holds the vessel.

music.why: Bach's cantata is built on the same parable as the painting: the bridesmaids waiting with their lamps. Listen for the tenors singing the chorale 'Zion hears the watchmen singing' over a dancing melody: wakefulness as readiness, wisdom as being prepared.

think.why: Practical wisdom raises the question MacIntyre pressed: can moral words make sense without a purpose for human life, and without God?

learn.why: Aristotle's reminder that happiness, like wisdom, belongs to a whole life: one swallow does not make a spring.

check.q: Why does Aristotle say practical wisdom is not a craft?
options: Because a craft aims at a product beyond itself, while acting well is its own end
Because crafts are for slaves
Because crafts deal with necessary truths
Because practical wisdom cannot be learned
check.why: 'The very well-doing is in itself an End.' Making aims at the house; acting well aims at nothing beyond itself.

check.q: A brilliant nineteen-year-old wins a mathematics prize. Why would Aristotle hesitate to call her practically wise?
options: Because she is too clever
Because practical wisdom concerns particulars known by experience, which takes time
Because mathematics is a craft
Because women cannot be wise
check.why: The young can master abstract subjects, but practical wisdom 'is produced only by length of time'.

check.q: What distinguishes practical wisdom from cleverness?
options: Cleverness finds the means to any goal; practical wisdom needs a good character to see the right goal
Practical wisdom is slower
There is no difference
Cleverness is a virtue, practical wisdom is not
check.why: 'This Eye of the Soul does not attain its proper state without goodness'.

check.q: Why can't a vicious person be practically wise, on Aristotle's account?
options: Because he has never studied ethics
Because he lacks intelligence
Because the law forbids it
Because vice distorts the moral vision, so he misjudges what is worth aiming at
check.why: Bad habits make us see situations wrongly; the problem is perception, not IQ.

check.q: How does Aristotle correct Socrates?
options: He says only the gods have virtue
He says Socrates was entirely right
He says virtue has nothing to do with reason
He agrees the virtues cannot exist without reason, but denies they simply are knowledge
check.why: 'Wrong in that he thought all the Virtues were merely intellectual Practical Wisdom, right in saying they were not independent of that faculty.'

check.q: Where do Aristotle and Proverbs differ most?
options: On where wisdom begins: for Aristotle in habit and experience, for Proverbs in the fear of the Lord
On whether wisdom is practical
On whether wisdom is valuable
On whether the young need teachers
check.why: Both prize practical wisdom above wealth; Proverbs 9:10 puts its beginning in reverence for God.

tutorial.question: 'You cannot be good without being wise, or wise without being good.' Explain and assess Aristotle's claim.
tutorial.approach: Define practical wisdom, separating it from scientific knowledge, craft and cleverness. Explain why it needs good character (the 'eye of the soul') and why the virtues need it (the strong man without sight). Consider an objection: the clever villain, or the good-hearted fool. Compare the Christian idea of prudence directed by charity.
strong: Defines phronesis and distinguishes it from knowledge, craft and cleverness.
Explains why it deals with particulars and needs experience.
Explains how vice distorts perception.
Explains natural virtue and the image of the strong man without sight.
Tests the claim against a real counter-example.
Brings in Aquinas, MacIntyre or Proverbs.

reading.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
reading.title: After Virtue
reading.why: The book that revived virtue ethics, arguing that modern morality lost its way when it lost Aristotle's idea of purpose.

reading.author: Josef Pieper
reading.title: The Four Cardinal Virtues
reading.why: A short, clear Catholic account of prudence, justice, courage and temperance, in the line of Aristotle and Aquinas.

reading.author: Martha Nussbaum
reading.title: The Fragility of Goodness
reading.why: On practical wisdom, luck and perception in Greek tragedy and Aristotle.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: before one real decision each day, ask three questions: what is the good I am aiming at here, what does this particular situation need, and what would the wisest person I know do? Act on the answer.
sessions.reflect: Who is the wisest person you have known? What did they see that others missed?
takeaways: Practical wisdom (phronesis) is the trained ability to deliberate well about living well: it deals with particulars and needs experience.
It differs from cleverness because it needs good character to see the right goal; vice distorts our moral vision.
So the virtues and practical wisdom need each other; the Christian tradition called it prudence and set it under love.

sessions.title: The political animal
sessions.line: Whoever can live without a city is a beast or a god. Aristotle on why human beings flourish only together.
sessions.plain: Aristotle's most famous saying about human beings is that we are 'political animals': creatures made to live in a polis, a city, a community that governs itself. Families form villages and villages a city, and only in a city can people live not just to survive but to live well. Speech, which only humans have, exists so that we can talk together about what is just. This session reads his argument, and asks what it means for people who live in a society that often treats the individual as complete in himself.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 and 3 showed how a person becomes good: by habit, guided by practical wisdom. But Aristotle kept saying that laws and upbringing shape our habits, and that practical wisdom is shown in a statesman like Pericles. A good person cannot be made alone. So the question 'what is a person for?' leads to another: what is a community for?
answers: What did Aristotle mean by 'man is a political animal'?
Why did he think the city comes before the individual?
What did friendship have to do with politics?
Is Aristotle's view compatible with Christian and modern ideas of the individual?
sessions.finding: For Aristotle a human being can flourish only in a community: the city exists not just for life but for the good life, and whoever lives without it is a beast or a god.

paras: Session 1 found Aristotle asking what each thing is for. Sessions 2 and 3 applied the question to human beings: we flourish by living well according to reason, and we become good by habit, guided by practical wisdom.

But each step pointed beyond the individual. Habits are formed by parents and laws. Practical wisdom is shown at its fullest in running a household or a city. At the very start of the Ethics Aristotle had said that the study of the human good belongs to politics, because the good of a whole community is 'more noble and godlike' than the good of one person. Now we read why.
background.key: Every step so far pointed outward: habits come from parents and laws, and the human good belongs to the study of politics.

paras: The Greek polis is usually translated 'city' or 'city-state', but neither is quite right. It was a small, self-governing community: a town and its farmland, with its own laws, gods, festivals and army. Athens, with perhaps 30,000 adult male citizens in Aristotle's day, was one of the largest. Most had a few thousand.

Our word 'politics' comes from polis, but for Aristotle politics was not mainly about parties and elections. It was the shared life of a community deciding together how to live well. He and his students collected the constitutions of 158 Greek states; one, The Constitution of the Athenians, was rediscovered on papyrus in Egypt and published in 1891. If you have taken 'Democracy and its dangers', you have read part of it.
background.key: A polis was a small self-governing community with its own laws and gods; Aristotle's school studied 158 of their constitutions.

paras: The reading is Politics Book I, chapter 2, one long paragraph in William Ellis's translation. Aristotle traces the city back to its 'seeds': the pairing of man and woman, the household, the village, and finally the city. Then he draws his conclusions about human nature. The passage also contains, almost in passing, his first remarks about slaves, which this journey will look at later, at full strength, in its own session. Notice them, but keep your attention on the main argument.
The comparison is from Ecclesiastes, a book of the Hebrew Bible written by a sceptical sage. It makes a humbler version of the same point: two are better than one.
background.key: Politics I.2: from household to village to city, and what that shows about human nature; then Ecclesiastes on why two are better than one.

before: What are the stages by which, according to Aristotle, the city grows?
What is the difference between the reason a city is founded and the reason it continues?
Why does Aristotle think speech shows we are political animals?
sessions.readWhy: Aristotle's account of how the city grows from the household, and why human beings are political animals by nature.

paras: Now if in this particular science any one would attend to its original seeds, and their first shoot, he would then as in others have the subject perfectly before him; and perceive, in the first place, that it is requisite that those should be joined together whose species cannot exist without each other, as the male and the female, for the business of propagation; and this not through choice, but by that natural impulse which acts both upon plants and animals also, for the purpose of their leaving behind them others like themselves. It is also from natural causes that some beings command and others obey, that each may obtain their mutual safety; for a being who is endowed with a mind capable of reflection and forethought is by nature the superior and governor, whereas he whose excellence is merely corporeal is formect to be a slave; whence it follows that the different state of master and slave is equally advantageous to both. But there is a natural difference between a female and a slave: for nature is not like the artists who make the Delphic swords for the use of the poor, but for every particular purpose she has her separate instruments, and thus her ends are most complete, for whatsoever is employed on one subject only, brings that one to much greater perfection than when employed on many; and yet among the barbarians, a female and a slave are upon a level in the community, the reason for which is, that amongst them there are none qualified by nature to govern, therefore their society can be nothing but between slaves of different sexes. For which reason the poets say, it is proper for the Greeks to govern the barbarians, as if a barbarian and a slave were by nature one.

Now of these two societies the domestic is the first, and Hesiod is right when he says, "First a house, then a wife, then an ox for the plough," for the poor man has always an ox before a household slave. That society then which nature has established for daily support is the domestic, and those who compose it are called by Charondas _homosipuoi_, and by Epimenides the Cretan _homokapnoi_; but the society of many families, which was first instituted for their lasting, mutual advantage, is called a village, and a village is most naturally composed of the descendants of one family, whom some persons call homogalaktes, the children and the children's children thereof: for which reason cities were originally governed by kings, as the barbarian states now are, which are composed of those who had before submitted to kingly government; for every family is governed by the elder, as are the branches thereof, on account of their relationship thereunto, which is what Homer says, "Each one ruled his wife and child;" and in this scattered manner they formerly lived. And the opinion which universally prevails, that the gods themselves are subject to kingly government, arises from hence, that all men formerly were, and many are so now; and as they imagined themselves to be made in the likeness of the gods, so they supposed their manner of life must needs be the same. And when many villages so entirely join themselves together as in every respect to form but one society, that society is a city, and contains in itself, if I may so speak, the end and perfection of government:

first founded that we might live, but continued that we may live happily. For which reason every city must be allowed to be the work of nature, if we admit that the original society between male and female is; for to this as their end all subordinate societies tend, and the end of everything is the nature of it. For what every being is in its most perfect state, that certainly is the nature of that being, whether it be a man, a horse, or a house: besides, whatsoever produces the final cause and the end which we desire, must be best; but a government complete in itself is that final cause and what is best. Hence it is evident that a city is a natural production, and that man is naturally a political animal, and that whosoever is naturally and not accidentally unfit for society, must be either inferior or superior to man: thus the man in Homer, who is reviled for being "without society, without law, without family." Such a one must naturally be of a quarrelsome disposition, and as solitary as the birds. The gift of speech also evidently proves that man is a more social animal than the bees, or any of the herding cattle: for nature, as we say, does nothing in vain, and man is the only animal who enjoys it. Voice indeed, as being the token of pleasure and pain, is imparted to others also, and thus much their nature is capable of, to perceive pleasure and pain, and to impart these sensations to others; but it is by speech that we are enabled to express what is useful for us, and what is hurtful, and of course what is just and what is unjust:

for in this particular man differs from other animals, that he alone has a perception of good and evil, of just and unjust, and it is a participation of these common sentiments which forms a family and a city. Besides, the notion of a city naturally precedes that of a family or an individual, for the whole must necessarily be prior to the parts, for if you take away the whole man, you cannot say a foot or a hand remains, unless by equivocation, as supposing a hand of stone to be made, but that would only be a dead one; but everything is understood to be this or that by its energic qualities and powers, so that when these no longer remain, neither can that be said to be the same, but something of the same name. That a city then precedes an individual is plain, for if an individual is not in himself sufficient to compose a perfect government, he is to a city as other parts are to a whole;

but he that is incapable of society, or so complete in himself as not to want it, makes no part of a city, as a beast or a god. There is then in all persons a natural impetus to associate with each other in this manner, and he who first founded civil society was the cause of the greatest good; for as by the completion of it man is the most excellent of all living beings, so without law and justice he would be the worst of all, for nothing is so difficult to subdue as injustice in arms: but these arms man is born with, namely, prudence and valour, which he may apply to the most opposite purposes, for he who abuses them will be the most wicked, the most cruel, the most lustful, and most gluttonous being imaginable; for justice is a political virtue, by the rules of it the state is regulated, and these rules are the criterion of what is right.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: From the household to the city
parts.context: The Politics opens by saying that every community aims at some good, and the city, the highest community, at the highest good. In chapter 2 Aristotle traces the city back to its origins. The translation is by William Ellis (1776). The Greek words in italics are names for members of a household: 'sharers of the bread-bin' and 'sharers of the hearth'. 'Formect' is a misprint in the source for 'formed'. Bekker page numbers are removed.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: first, man and woman join to have children, by nature, as plants and animals do. Some are fitted by nature to rule and others to obey, master and slave (he says), each for their mutual safety. Households join into villages, and villages into a city. The city is founded so that people can live, but it continues so that they can live well. The city is natural, because it is the goal the earlier communities grow towards, and a thing's nature is what it is when fully grown. So a human being is by nature a political animal; anyone who cannot live in a community, or needs none, is either a beast or a god. Speech, which only humans have, lets us talk about what is useful and harmful, just and unjust. A human being at his best is the best of animals; without law and justice, the worst.

commentary.on: it is requisite that those should be joined together whose species cannot exist without each other, as the male and the female
commentary.text: Aristotle begins with biology: the first community is the couple, joined by the natural drive to leave 'others like themselves'. He builds politics upwards from nature, as a biologist would.

commentary.on: whence it follows that the different state of master and slave is equally advantageous to both
commentary.text: Here, in the second sentence, is the first appearance of the 'natural slave'. Aristotle claims that some people, with bodily strength but little forethought, are made to be ruled, and that this benefits them. It is a terrible claim. Hold it in mind; this journey will return to it later and give the case against it full weight.

commentary.on: first founded that we might live, but continued that we may live happily
commentary.text: Perhaps the most important sentence in the Politics. People come together to survive: for food, safety, trade. But that is not what the city is for. It is for living well, for the flourishing that sessions 2 and 3 described. A city that only keeps people alive has not reached its purpose.

commentary.on: for to this as their end all subordinate societies tend, and the end of everything is the nature of it
commentary.text: Session 1's idea of purpose, now applied to society. An acorn's nature is the oak it grows into. In the same way, the 'nature' of human community is the city it grows into. So the city is not an artificial contract; it is natural.

commentary.on: man is naturally a political animal
commentary.text: The famous phrase, in Greek zōon politikon. 'Political' means 'made for the polis'. Bees and cranes live in groups too, Aristotle says elsewhere, but human beings are political in a fuller sense, as the next lines explain.

commentary.on: for nature, as we say, does nothing in vain, and man is the only animal who enjoys it
commentary.text: The rule from session 1 again. Animals have voice to signal pleasure and pain. Humans have speech, logos, which is for something more: to discuss what is just and unjust. Since nature does nothing in vain, speech shows what we are for: shared reasoning about the good.

commentary.on: for the whole must necessarily be prior to the parts
commentary.text: A hard idea for modern readers. Aristotle does not mean the city exists before its citizens in time. He means that a person cut off from community is like a hand cut off from a body: a hand only in name. We are what we are as members.

commentary.on: makes no part of a city, as a beast or a god
commentary.text: Only two kinds of being need no city: those below humanity and those above it. Nietzsche later quoted this line and added a third: the philosopher. Aristotle would not have agreed.

commentary.on: for as by the completion of it man is the most excellent of all living beings, so without law and justice he would be the worst of all
commentary.text: The double edge of human nature. Our gifts, cleverness and courage, are weapons that can serve justice or cruelty. Law and community turn them to good. Without them we are not noble savages but the most dangerous of animals.

read.author: Aristotle

paras: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

parts.title: A threefold cord
parts.context: Ecclesiastes, in Hebrew Qoheleth ('the Preacher' or 'the Gatherer'), is one of the Bible's wisdom books, probably written between the fifth and third centuries BC. Its author looks hard at life 'under the sun' and finds much of it empty. Just before this passage he describes a man who works endlessly alone, with no one to share his wealth.

commentary.on: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
commentary.text: Where Aristotle builds a theory, the Preacher gives a proverb. If you have taken 'In the beginning', you met an older version: 'It is not good for the man to be alone' (Genesis 2:18). Human beings are made for one another.

commentary.on: woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up
commentary.text: The Preacher's reasons are practical: help when you fall, warmth at night, defence against attack. These are Aristotle's reasons for founding a community, 'that we might live'.

commentary.on: a threefold cord is not quickly broken
commentary.text: Two becomes three at the end. Christian readers have often heard God as the third strand, and the line is read at many weddings. Even read plainly, it says that community grows stronger as it grows.

compare.why: The Hebrew sage called the Preacher reaches a humbler version of Aristotle's conclusion: people are not made to be alone.
compare.title: Two are better than one

paras: Aristotle's account of how the city arose is part history, part logic. The household (oikos) meets daily needs: husband and wife, parents and children, and, in his world, slaves. Several households form a village, which meets more than daily needs and was first ruled by the eldest, like a family. Several villages form a city, which is 'self-sufficient': it has everything needed not just for life but for a good life.

Self-sufficiency is not isolation. Aristotle means that the city has all the parts a full human life needs: friends, laws, education, festivals, courts, a place to take part in deciding the common good. A household cannot provide these; a village only partly. This is why he thought the city, not the family or the tribe, was where human nature came to completion.
sections.key: Households meet daily needs, villages more, and the city, self-sufficient, provides everything needed for a good life.

paras: In Book III Aristotle asks who a citizen is, and answers: someone who shares in judging and in ruling. A citizen takes part, in turn, in the assembly and the courts, ruling and being ruled. The good citizen and the good man are not always the same, he admits; a good citizen is good relative to the constitution, which may be bad. But in the best city they coincide.

This is a demanding idea of citizenship, far beyond voting every few years. It also excluded most people. In Athens citizenship belonged to free adult men with Athenian parents. Women, slaves and resident foreigners, a large majority of the population, had no share. Aristotle thought even manual workers should not be citizens in the best city, because they lacked the leisure for virtue and politics. So his 'political animal' is a noble idea held within narrow limits.
sections.key: A citizen shares in judging and ruling, in turn; but Aristotle's citizenship excluded women, slaves, foreigners and, ideally, manual workers.

paras: Two whole books of the Ethics, VIII and IX, are about friendship, philia. No one would choose to live without friends, Aristotle says, even if he had every other good. Lawgivers care more about friendship than about justice, because when people are friends they have no need of justice, but when they are just they still need friendship.

He distinguishes three kinds: friendships of usefulness, of pleasure, and of character, where each loves the other for who they are. Only the third lasts, and it is rare. But even the looser kinds matter to a city. Fellow citizens share a kind of civic friendship: goodwill, shared purposes, agreement about how to live. A city of strangers who merely avoid harming each other is not, for Aristotle, a city at all, but an alliance.
sections.key: Aristotle thought friendship mattered more to a city than justice, and that a city is held together by shared goodwill and purposes, not just by rules.

paras: Aristotle's view has a rival. In Leviathan (1651) Thomas Hobbes argued that human beings are not naturally political. Bees live together by nature, he said; we do so only by agreement, out of fear of each other. Without a strong government life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. Society is a contract made by individuals for safety, not a natural whole.

Much modern thought followed Hobbes and Locke. The individual comes first, with rights, and society exists to protect them. Aristotle's 'the whole is prior to the parts' sounds dangerous to modern ears; it was abused by twentieth-century regimes that sacrificed persons to the state. Defenders of Aristotle reply that he meant something gentler: that persons are formed in communities and flourish only there, and that a city exists for the good life of its members, not they for it.
sections.key: Hobbes said society is a contract made out of fear; Aristotle that it is natural; modern thought mostly followed Hobbes, though communities still form us.

paras: Christians inherited Aristotle's idea indirectly at first, and changed it. Augustine, writing The City of God after Rome was sacked in 410, said there are two cities, made by two loves: the earthly city by love of self, the heavenly city by love of God. Every human community is a mixture. No city on earth is the place where human nature is finally completed; that is the city of God.

Aquinas, who read the Politics in full, agreed with Aristotle that man is by nature 'a social and political animal', and so that government is natural and good, not merely a punishment for sin. But he placed the person's final end beyond any city: friendship with God. The church, a community open to slaves, women and foreigners, became another 'polis'. For Christians, being a political animal is true, but it is not the whole truth.
sections.key: Augustine's two cities and Aquinas's 'social and political animal' kept Aristotle's insight but placed the final community beyond any earthly city.

paras: In Books VII and VIII of the Politics Aristotle sketches the best city he can imagine. It should be small enough that citizens know one another's characters, and that one herald's voice can reach them all. It should be self-sufficient but not luxurious. Its main task is education: since the city exists for the good life, and the good life needs good habits, bringing up the young in virtue is the city's first business, not a private matter.

For real cities, which are rarely the best, Aristotle preferred a mixture. In Book IV he praises 'polity', a constitution mixing features of rule by the few and rule by the many, held steady by a large middle class neither very rich nor very poor. If you have taken 'Democracy and its dangers', you read that argument there. It had a long future: medieval and early modern thinkers who wanted limited, mixed government, from Aquinas to the American founders, drew on it.
sections.key: Aristotle's best city is small and devoted to educating citizens in virtue; for real cities he preferred a mixed constitution steadied by a middle class.

paras: Modern Catholic social teaching is perhaps Aristotle's most direct heir: it speaks of the 'common good' and of 'subsidiarity', letting families and local communities do what they can before the state steps in. Orthodox Christianity speaks of sobornost, a communion in which persons are most themselves together. Protestant traditions, especially Reformed ones, have stressed covenant communities and the limits of state power under God.

In the late twentieth century, 'communitarian' philosophers, among them MacIntyre, Michael Sandel and Charles Taylor, argued that liberal societies had forgotten Aristotle's point: that we are formed by communities and cannot flourish as isolated choosers. Their critics reply that communities can oppress as easily as they nourish, as Aristotle's own exclusions show. Both sides would agree with the Preacher: woe to him who is alone when he falls.
sections.key: Catholic social teaching, Orthodox sobornost and modern communitarians all echo Aristotle; their critics remind us communities can also oppress.

refs: Aristotle, Politics I.1–2; III.1–5 (the citizen); VII.4 (the size of the city); VII.9 (manual workers); Nicomachean Ethics I.2 (1094b); VIII.1 (1155a); VIII.3–4; IX.6 (concord).
Aristotle, The Constitution of the Athenians, ed. F. G. Kenyon (1891).
Genesis 2:18; Ecclesiastes 4:7–12.
Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), ch. 13 and 17.
Augustine, The City of God XIV.28; XIX.24; Thomas Aquinas, De regno I.1; Summa Theologiae I q.96 a.4.
Michael Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice (1982); Charles Taylor, Sources of the Self (1989).

debate.question: Are human beings political by nature?

positions.name: Yes: we flourish only in community
positions.who: Aristotle; Aquinas; modern communitarians such as MacIntyre and Sandel
positions.view: Human beings are made for shared life. Speech exists for discussing justice; friendship and law form our characters. A person alone is less than fully human, and a society of isolated individuals is not a real community.
positions.evidence: Speech (logos); the need for upbringing and law to form virtue; the misery of isolation; Ecclesiastes 4.

positions.name: No: society is a contract
positions.who: Thomas Hobbes; John Locke (in a gentler form); much modern liberal thought
positions.view: Individuals come first, with their own interests and rights. They agree to form governments for safety and to protect their property and freedom. The state is a tool, not the place where human nature is completed.
positions.evidence: The danger of states that claim to know the good life for everyone; the variety of human goals; history's abuses of 'the whole before the parts'.

positions.name: Yes, but our final community is beyond politics
positions.who: Augustine; Aquinas; most Christian thinkers
positions.view: We are social by nature, and government is good, but no earthly city completes us. Our deepest belonging is in the communion of God's people, which crosses every city and includes those the polis left out.
positions.evidence: The City of God; Galatians 3:28; the early church, which gathered slaves and free, men and women, Jews and Greeks.

debate.agree: All agree that people need others to survive; they differ on whether community is our nature, our contract, or a foretaste of something beyond any state.

look.why: Aristotle's city was smaller than many modern towns: a place where, he said, citizens could know one another's characters. Abel Grimmer's town square in the Low Countries, dated 1590 and 1597, shows shared life of the kind Aristotle meant: trade, talk, worship and defence in one small place.
points: We look down onto a cobbled town square lined with brick, wood and stone buildings, many with stepped roofs.
Men, women and children walk across the square, move goods, or talk with merchants; two women and a child talk to a woman selling wares at a wooden table.
A man with a large drum strapped to his waist raises a drumstick; a man on horseback blows a trumpet near two hooded priests or monks.
Couples gather around a well; a woman peers up out of a cellar door.
Through a gap in the buildings stands a grey stone church with a spire, and on the hill to the right a fortress with towers and battlements.

music.why: 'Where charity and love are, God is there.' The old chant for Maundy Thursday describes the community Christians hoped for: bound not only by civic friendship but by love, gathered around a meal.

think.why: Aristotle's political animal sets up the modern argument about the individual and the community, and how the West came to value both.

learn.why: Donne's meditation says in English prose what Aristotle said of the city: we are parts of a whole, and no one is complete alone.

check.q: According to Aristotle, what is the difference between why a city is founded and why it continues?
options: It is founded for war and continues for trade
There is no difference
It is founded by the gods and continues by human law
It is founded so that people might live, and continues so that they may live well
check.why: 'First founded that we might live, but continued that we may live happily.'

check.q: Why does Aristotle say the city is natural?
options: Because animals also have cities
Because it is very old
Because it is the end towards which households and villages tend, and a thing's nature is what it is when complete
Because it is built of natural materials
check.why: Session 1's teleology applied to society: 'the end of everything is the nature of it'.

check.q: Why does speech show that human beings are political animals?
options: Because speech is needed for trade
Because it is for expressing what is useful and harmful, just and unjust, and sharing these makes a household and a city
Because animals have no voice
Because it lets us give orders
check.why: Animals have voice for pleasure and pain; humans have speech, for discussing justice, and nature does nothing in vain.

check.q: What does Aristotle mean by saying the city is 'prior' to the individual?
options: Cities existed before people
That rulers are more important than citizens
That a person cut off from community is like a hand cut off from the body, only a hand in name
That the state may do anything to its citizens
check.why: He means priority of nature, not time: we are what we are as members of a whole.

check.q: How does Hobbes's view of society differ from Aristotle's?
options: Hobbes thought society was a contract made by individuals out of fear, not a natural whole
Hobbes denied that governments should exist
Hobbes agreed with Aristotle entirely
Hobbes thought society was natural, like bees'
check.why: Hobbes said human beings are not political by nature as bees are; they agree to government for safety.

check.q: What did Augustine and Aquinas add to Aristotle's political animal?
options: They argued that slaves should rule
They said the city should be ruled by philosophers
They agreed people are social by nature, but placed the final human community beyond any earthly city, in God
They rejected the idea that people are social
check.why: Aquinas called man 'a social and political animal'; Augustine described two cities made by two loves.

tutorial.question: 'Whoever is unable to live in society, or has no need of it, is either a beast or a god.' Is Aristotle right?
tutorial.approach: Explain Aristotle's account of the household, village and city, and his argument from speech. Explain what he means by the city being natural and prior to the individual. Put Hobbes's contrary view. Then say how Christian thinkers revised Aristotle, and note the limits of his own city (who was excluded). Reach a judgement.
strong: Explains the growth from household to city and 'living' versus 'living well'.
Explains the argument from speech and 'nature does nothing in vain'.
Explains priority of nature, not time.
States Hobbes's view fairly.
Notes the exclusions in Aristotle's citizenship.
Uses Augustine or Aquinas to assess the claim.

reading.author: Bernard Yack
reading.title: The Problems of a Political Animal
reading.why: A study of community, justice and conflict in Aristotle's political thought.

reading.author: Michael Sandel
reading.title: Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do?
reading.why: A popular book that sets Aristotle beside Kant and the utilitarians on modern questions.

reading.author: Edith Hall
reading.title: Aristotle's Way
reading.why: Its chapters on friendship and community make Aristotle's political animal practical.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: take part in one shared thing you usually leave to others: a local meeting, a church or club event, a neighbour's need, a conversation about something that matters in your street or town. Notice what you receive from it as well as what you give.
sessions.reflect: Which communities have made you who you are? Where do you belong now?
takeaways: Aristotle said the city grows from the household and village, is founded for life and continues for the good life, and so is natural.
Human beings are political animals: speech exists for sharing what is just, and whoever needs no city is a beast or a god.
Hobbes made society a contract; Augustine and Aquinas kept Aristotle's insight but placed our final community beyond any earthly city.

sessions.title: The soul and the unmoved mover
sessions.line: What makes a body alive, and what keeps the heavens turning? Aristotle's answers: the soul is the form of the body, and the universe hangs on a mind that thinks itself.
sessions.plain: Aristotle asked 'what is it for?' of two last things: the living body and the whole universe. His answer about the body was that the soul is not a ghost trapped inside it, as Plato thought, but its 'form': what makes this matter a living, seeing, thinking human being. His answer about the universe was that all motion depends on something that moves without being moved, a perfect, eternal mind, which moves everything as the thing everything longs for. Christians later called this God. This session asks what Aristotle meant, and how close his god is to the God of the Bible.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 to 4 followed Aristotle's question through human life: our habits, our wisdom, our cities. Two things are left: what we are, body and soul, and what the whole world depends on. These are the questions of his De Anima (On the Soul) and Metaphysics, and they take his search for purposes as far as it can go.
answers: What did Aristotle think the soul is?
How is his view different from Plato's?
What is the unmoved mover?
Did Aristotle believe in God, and is his god the God of the Bible?
sessions.finding: The soul is the form of a living body, not a prisoner in it; and the motion of the universe points to an unmoved mover, a mind thinking itself, which Christians later read as God, though it neither creates nor loves the world.

paras: Session 1 found Aristotle explaining everything by four causes, above all the final cause. Sessions 2 and 3 showed how a person becomes good, by habit and practical wisdom; session 4, why we can only do it together, in a city.

Running beneath all this was the pair of ideas from session 1: potential and actual. The acorn is potentially an oak; the oak is that potential realised. Aristotle now uses the same pair for the two deepest questions. A living body is matter whose potential for life is realised: that realisation is its soul. And the universe, full of change from potential to actual, must depend on something that is actual all the way through.
background.key: Potential and actual, from session 1, now answer two last questions: what makes a body alive, and what the universe depends on.

paras: Aristotle's account of the soul is in De Anima (On the Soul), especially Book II, chapter 1. His account of the first mover is in the Physics, Book VIII, and above all the Metaphysics, Book XII (often called Lambda, from its Greek letter), chapters 6 to 10. 'Metaphysics' simply means 'after the Physics': the books that came after the Physics in the ancient edition. They are among the hardest texts in philosophy, terse even by Aristotle's standards.

We have no out-of-copyright English translation of these books among the texts we can use, so this session teaches them in our own words, in the lecture. What we read instead is something rarer: Aristotle's lost early works, quoted by the Roman writer Cicero. They show the same mind thinking about the soul and the heavens, in the polished style that made his name in antiquity.
background.key: The soul is in De Anima II; the unmoved mover in Physics VIII and Metaphysics XII. We read Aristotle's lost early works as Cicero quoted them, and learn the rest in our own words.

paras: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was Rome's greatest orator and a leading statesman of the last years of the Republic. In 45 BC, grieving for his daughter Tullia and shut out of politics by Julius Caesar, he wrote a series of books to bring Greek philosophy to Rome in Latin. Two of them quote Aristotle's dialogues, now lost.

The Tusculan Disputations, named after his country house at Tusculum, discuss death and the soul. On the Nature of the Gods is a debate among an Epicurean, a Stoic called Balbus, and a sceptic; in Book II, Balbus the Stoic argues that the gods exist and govern the world, and calls Aristotle as a witness. Cicero's reports are second-hand and coloured by his own purposes. But they are all we have of the Aristotle the ancient world knew best.
background.key: Cicero (106–43 BC) wrote philosophy in 45 BC and quoted Aristotle's lost dialogues; in On the Nature of the Gods the speaker is Balbus, a Stoic.

paras: The reading has three parts: Cicero's summary of Aristotle on the soul, from the Tusculan Disputations; two arguments from On the Nature of the Gods about why the stars move as they do; and Aristotle's own parable of people who come out from underground and see the sky for the first time, which Cicero quotes almost word for word.
The comparison is from the book of Isaiah. It looks at the same stars and sees a God who names each one, which Aristotle's first mover could not do.
background.key: Cicero on Aristotle's soul, on the stars' motion, and the parable of people from underground; then Isaiah on the God who names the stars.

before: Why, according to Cicero, did Aristotle think the soul needed a 'fifth nature'?
What three kinds of motion does Aristotle distinguish, and which does he think the stars have?
In the parable of people from underground, what would convince them that there are gods?
sessions.readWhy: Aristotle's lost early works, as Cicero quoted them, on the soul, the motion of the stars and what the heavens show.

paras: Aristotle, a man superior to all others, both in genius and industry (I always except Plato), after having embraced these four known sorts of principles, from which all things deduce their origin, imagines that there is a certain fifth nature, from whence comes the soul; for to think, to foresee, to learn, to teach, to invent anything, and many other attributes of the same kind, such as to remember, to love, to hate, to desire, to fear, to be pleased or displeased--these, and others like them, exist, he thinks, in none of those first four kinds: on such account he adds a fifth kind, which has no name, and so by a new name he calls the soul [Greek: endelecheia], as if it were a certain continued and perpetual motion.

As, then, some animals are generated in the earth, some in the water, and some in the air, Aristotle thinks it ridiculous to imagine that no animal is formed in that part of the universe which is the most capable to produce them. But the stars are situated in the ethereal space; and as this is an element the most subtle, whose motion is continual, and whose force does not decay, it follows, of necessity, that every animated being which is produced in it must be endowed with the quickest sense and the swiftest motion. The stars, therefore, being there generated, it is a natural inference to suppose them endued with such a degree of sense and understanding as places them in the rank of Gods.

Aristotle also deserves high commendation for his observation that everything that moves is either put in motion by natural impulse, or by some external force, or of its own accord; and that the sun, and moon, and all the stars move; but that those things which are moved by natural impulse are either borne downward by their weight, or upward by their lightness; neither of which things could be the case with the stars, because they move in a regular circle and orbit. Nor can it be said that there is some superior force which causes the stars to be moved in a manner contrary to nature. For what superior force can there be? It follows, therefore, that their motion must be voluntary. And whoever is convinced of this must discover not only great ignorance, but great impiety likewise, if he denies the existence of the Gods; nor is the difference great whether a man denies their existence, or deprives them of all design and action; for whatever is wholly inactive seems to me not to exist at all. Their existence, therefore, appears so plain that I can scarcely think that man in his senses who denies it.

Well, then, did Aristotle observe: "If there were men whose habitations had been always underground, in great and commodious houses, adorned with statues and pictures, furnished with everything which they who are reputed happy abound with; and if, without stirring from thence, they should be informed of a certain divine power and majesty, and, after some time, the earth should open, and they should quit their dark abode to come to us, where they should immediately behold the earth, the seas, the heavens; should consider the vast extent of the clouds and force of the winds; should see the sun, and observe his grandeur and beauty, and also his generative power, inasmuch as day is occasioned by the diffusion of his light through the sky; and when night has obscured the earth, they should contemplate the heavens bespangled and adorned with stars, the surprising variety of the moon in her increase and wane, the rising and setting of all the stars, and the inviolable regularity of their courses; when," says he, "they should see these things, they would undoubtedly conclude that there are Gods, and that these are their mighty works."

parts.author: Cicero, reporting Aristotle
parts.who: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and philosopher, reporting Aristotle's lost early works
parts.title: A fifth nature
parts.context: In Book I of the Tusculan Disputations Cicero surveys what philosophers have said the soul is: blood, fire, air, a harmony, a number. Then he comes to Aristotle. He is summarising one of Aristotle's early works, not quoting. The 'four known sorts of principles' are the four elements of Greek science: earth, water, air and fire. '[Greek: endelecheia]' is how the Gutenberg edition prints a Greek word.
parts.plain: Cicero says: Aristotle, the greatest genius after Plato, thought the four elements could not explain the soul's powers: to think, plan, learn, teach, remember, love, hate, desire and fear. So he added a fifth kind of nature, which had no name, and called the soul by a new name, endelecheia, meaning something like continuous, unending motion.

commentary.on: Aristotle, a man superior to all others, both in genius and industry (I always except Plato)
commentary.text: Cicero's admiration is telling. For the Romans Aristotle was a great writer and thinker, but always second to Plato. That ranking would last in the West until the thirteenth century.

commentary.on: for to think, to foresee, to learn, to teach, to invent anything
commentary.text: Aristotle's starting point is what the soul does. A soul is known by its activities: thinking, remembering, loving. Earth, water, air and fire do none of these. So whatever the soul is, it is not simply one of the elements.

commentary.on: by a new name he calls the soul [Greek: endelecheia], as if it were a certain continued and perpetual motion
commentary.text: Here Cicero seems to have made a famous slip. Aristotle's word in De Anima is entelecheia, from en (in), telos (end) and echein (to have): 'having its end within', or 'actuality'. Endelecheia, with a d, means 'continuity'. The two sounded alike, and scholars have argued since the Renaissance whether Cicero misread, or whether the early Aristotle really said something different. Either way, the word to remember is entelechy: the soul is the body's actuality, what it is when it is fully at work. The lecture explains.

parts.author: Cicero, reporting Aristotle
parts.who: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and philosopher, reporting Aristotle's lost early works
parts.work: On the Nature of the Gods
parts.translator: An eighteenth-century translation revised for Bohn's Classical Library (1853), edited by C. D. Yonge
parts.ref: Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods II.42–44 (chapters 15–16)
parts.title: Why the stars move
parts.context: Book II of On the Nature of the Gods. Balbus, the Stoic speaker, is arguing that the stars are living and divine, and appeals to Aristotle's lost work On Philosophy. The 'ethereal space' is the region of the heavens, made, Aristotle thought, of a fifth element, aether, which moves in circles. The last three sentences of the second paragraph are Balbus's own conclusion, not Aristotle's.
parts.plain: Balbus says: Aristotle thought it absurd that animals live in earth, water and air, but none in the purest region, the heavens. So the stars must be living beings of the highest intelligence. And Aristotle observed that anything that moves is moved by its nature (heavy things fall, light things rise), by outside force, or by its own will. The stars move in circles, which is neither falling nor rising, and nothing could force them; so they move by their own will. Balbus adds: whoever sees this and still denies the gods is ignorant and impious.

commentary.on: Aristotle thinks it ridiculous to imagine that no animal is formed in that part of the universe which is the most capable to produce them
commentary.text: This is the young Aristotle, still close to Plato, for whom the stars were living gods. It sounds strange to us. But it rests on a principle we met in session 1: nature does nothing in vain, so the best region of the universe should hold the best beings.

commentary.on: everything that moves is either put in motion by natural impulse, or by some external force, or of its own accord
commentary.text: A classification of motion: by nature, by force, or by will. It is the seed of the later argument. Aristotle's mature works ask what moves the movers, and arrive at something that moves without being moved.

commentary.on: because they move in a regular circle and orbit
commentary.text: For Greek science the heavens were perfect because their motion was circular and never ending, unlike the up-and-down motion of earthly things. Aristotle's whole cosmology, overturned by Galileo and Newton, rests on that difference. The argument for a first mover did not depend on it, as Aquinas later showed.

commentary.on: if he denies the existence of the Gods
commentary.text: These are Balbus's words, not Aristotle's. Cicero's Stoic turns Aristotle's observation into a proof of the gods' existence and care for the world. Aristotle's own god, as the lecture explains, did not care for the world in that way.

parts.author: Cicero, reporting Aristotle
parts.who: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and philosopher, reporting Aristotle's lost early works
parts.work: On the Nature of the Gods
parts.translator: An eighteenth-century translation revised for Bohn's Classical Library (1853), edited by C. D. Yonge
parts.ref: Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods II.95 (chapter 37), quoting Aristotle
parts.title: Out of the darkness
parts.context: Later in Book II Balbus quotes Aristotle's lost dialogue, almost word for word. It is one of the longest surviving passages from Aristotle's published works, and a deliberate reply to Plato's allegory of the cave, which you met if you took 'Plato'. Cicero's note in the Bohn edition says the treatise is lost; the note number is removed.
parts.plain: Aristotle imagines people who have always lived underground, in comfortable, beautiful houses, and have only heard rumours of divine power. One day the earth opens and they come up into our world. They see land, sea and sky, clouds and winds, the sun with its beauty and power; then at night the stars, the moon waxing and waning, the regular rising and setting of the heavens. Seeing all this, he says, they would at once conclude that there are gods, and that these are their works.

commentary.on: If there were men whose habitations had been always underground, in great and commodious houses, adorned with statues and pictures
commentary.text: Compare Plato's cave, where prisoners sit in chains watching shadows. Aristotle's underground people are rich and comfortable, surrounded by art. Their problem is not suffering but never having looked up. It is a picture of a busy, comfortable life that has never seen anything bigger than itself.

commentary.on: the inviolable regularity of their courses
commentary.text: What convinces them is order. Not a miracle or a revelation, but the reliable, beautiful regularity of the sky. This is the root of the 'argument from order', one of the oldest arguments for God, and the one behind Aquinas's fifth way.

commentary.on: they would undoubtedly conclude that there are Gods, and that these are their mighty works
commentary.text: 'Mighty works' sounds biblical, and Christian readers loved this passage. But notice what Aristotle's people conclude: that there are gods, plural, and that the heavens are their work in some sense. In his mature thought the first mover does not make the heavens. It moves them as what they love and long for.
