paras:
“To whom then will you liken me?
Who is my equal?” says the Holy One.

Lift up your eyes on high,
and see who has created these,
who brings out their army by number.
He calls them all by name.
by the greatness of his might,
and because he is strong in power,
not one is lacking.

Why do you say, Jacob,
and speak, Israel,
“My way is hidden from Yahweh,
and the justice due me is disregarded by my God?”

Haven’t you known?
Haven’t you heard?
The everlasting God, Yahweh,
the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint.
He isn’t weary.
His understanding is unsearchable.

He gives power to the weak.
He increases the strength of him who has no might.

Even the youths faint and get weary,
and the young men utterly fall;

but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength.
They will mount up with wings like eagles.
They will run, and not be weary.
They will walk, and not faint.

parts.title: Lift up your eyes
parts.context: Isaiah 40 opens the part of the book addressed to the Jewish exiles in Babylon in the sixth century BC, where the stars were worshipped as gods. The prophet tells a defeated people that their God made the stars the Babylonians worshipped.

commentary.on: Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these
commentary.text: Like Aristotle's underground people, the exiles are told to look up. But Isaiah asks 'who created these?', a question Aristotle never asked, because he thought the heavens were eternal and uncreated.

commentary.on: He calls them all by name.
commentary.text: Aristotle's first mover thinks only of itself; it does not know the stars, let alone name them. Isaiah's God knows each star as a shepherd knows each sheep. That is the deepest difference between the two.

commentary.on: The everlasting God, Yahweh, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary.
commentary.text: Aristotle would agree that the first principle is everlasting and never tires; it is pure activity. But Isaiah goes on.

commentary.on: He gives power to the weak.
commentary.text: This is what Aristotle's philosophy had no room for: a perfect God who turns towards the weak and gives them his strength. Aristotle's first mover is loved, but does not love. Isaiah's God is loved because he first gives.

compare.why: Isaiah looks at the same stars as Aristotle and sees a God who made them, numbers them and names them, and who does not forget the weak.
compare.title: He calls them all by name

paras: For Plato, the soul was a separate thing imprisoned in the body, longing to escape; if you took 'Plato', you read the Phaedo, where Socrates welcomes death for that reason. Aristotle disagreed. In De Anima II.1 he defines the soul as the 'first actuality' of a natural body that has organs. In plainer words: the soul is what makes this body a living body, the way it is organised to live.

His examples help. If an axe were a living thing, its soul would be its being able to cut; take that away and it is no longer an axe except in name. If the eye were an animal, its soul would be sight. A dead eye is an eye only as a painted eye is. So we should not ask whether soul and body are one, he says, any more than we ask whether wax and the shape stamped in it are one.
This view is called hylomorphism, from the Greek hylē (matter) and morphē (form). A living thing is matter organised by form, and the soul is that form.
sections.key: Aristotle defined the soul as the form, or first actuality, of a living body: not a prisoner in it, but what makes it alive.

paras: Every living thing has a soul, in Aristotle's sense, because every living thing is organised to live. But souls differ by what they can do. Plants have a nutritive soul: they feed, grow and reproduce. Animals add a sensitive soul: they perceive, desire and, most of them, move. Human beings add a rational soul: they think and choose.

The powers are nested, like shapes inside shapes. A human being does everything a plant does and everything an animal does, and something more. This is why, in session 2, Aristotle said that human excellence is doing well what is distinctively human: living by reason. And it is why he thought a human being is one thing, not a mind riding a body. Your digestion, your eyesight and your thinking are all the work of one soul.

table.note: De Anima II.2–3.

sections.key: Plants have nutritive souls, animals add perception and desire, humans add reason: one soul in each living thing, with nested powers.

paras: If the soul is the form of the body, it seems to die with the body, as the shape of the wax goes when the wax melts. Aristotle mostly accepted this. But in one obscure passage, De Anima III.5, he says that one part of the mind, the 'active intellect', is separable, immortal and eternal. He does not say whether it is personal. Commentators have argued about this for two thousand years.

The Arab philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–98) argued that there is only one intellect for all humankind, so personal immortality is ruled out. Thomas Aquinas wrote a short book against him in 1270. Aquinas argued that the human soul is indeed the form of the body, as Aristotle said, but a form of a unique kind: because it thinks, and thinking does not use a bodily organ, it can survive the body's death, incomplete until the resurrection. Christians had always believed in the resurrection of the body; Aristotle gave Aquinas a way to say why a soul without its body is not a whole human being.
sections.key: Aristotle left it unclear whether any part of us survives; Aquinas argued the thinking soul survives death but is incomplete without the body, awaiting the resurrection.

paras: Everything in the world changes, and every change, Aristotle argued in Physics VIII and Metaphysics XII, is a passage from potential to actual brought about by something already actual. Fire heats wood; the wood does not heat itself. But this chain cannot go back for ever. There must be a first mover that is not itself moved: something wholly actual, with no potential to change.

How does it move things without moving? Not by pushing, Aristotle says in Metaphysics XII.7, but by being loved (the Greek is kinei hōs erōmenon). It moves the heavens the way a beloved moves a lover, or a goal moves the one who seeks it: by being desirable. The outermost heaven turns in its eternal circle in longing for the first mover's perfection, and all other motion follows.

What is it? It cannot be matter, which is always potential. It must be pure activity, and the highest activity is thought. So the first mover is a mind, living a life like our best moments of understanding, but always. On this principle, Aristotle says, the heavens and the whole of nature depend.
sections.key: Change needs a cause already actual; the chain must end in a first, unmoved mover, pure actuality, which moves everything by being loved.

paras: In Metaphysics XII.9 Aristotle asks what this divine mind thinks about. It must think about the best thing, and never change. But anything other than itself would be worse than itself, and thinking about changing things would make it change. So it thinks about itself. Its thinking, he says, is a thinking of thinking (in Greek, noēsis noēseōs).

This is magnificent and strange. Aristotle's god is perfectly happy, perfectly active, eternal. But it does not know the world, does not make it, does not love it, and does not hear prayers. The world loves it; it does not love the world. The universe, in Aristotle's view, had always existed; the first mover is its final cause, not its creator.

Some later readers, Aquinas among them, argued that in knowing itself perfectly the first mover would know everything that depends on it. Most modern scholars think that reading goes beyond what Aristotle wrote. Either way, he also allowed many unmoved movers, one for each heavenly sphere: forty-seven or fifty-five, he calculated in XII.8, depending on the astronomy.
sections.key: Aristotle's god thinks only itself, a thinking of thinking; it neither creates, knows nor loves the world, which loves it.

sections.h: The God of the philosophers and the God of Abraham
paras: Christian thinkers saw at once how much Aristotle's argument gave them: one eternal, perfect, immaterial mind on which everything depends, reached by reason alone. In the 1260s Aquinas made the argument from motion the first of his 'five ways' in the Summa Theologiae and argued it at length in the Summa contra Gentiles I.13; you will read the five ways later, in Hall V. Jewish and Muslim philosophers, Maimonides and Avicenna, had done the same before him.

But they also saw the gap. The God of the Bible creates the world from nothing, knows each creature, and loves it. He speaks, makes covenants, and, Christians say, becomes flesh. Aquinas held that reason can show there is a first mover, but only revelation shows who he is. Blaise Pascal, after a night of religious experience in 1654, wrote a note he kept sewn into his coat: it named the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and set him apart from the god of the philosophers and scholars. The question this session leaves is whether the two are rivals, or the same God seen from two distances.
sections.key: Aquinas and others built on Aristotle's argument, but the God of the Bible creates, knows and loves; Pascal contrasted him with the God of the philosophers.

paras: The argument has faced strong objections. Why must the chain of movers stop? Infinite series are not obviously impossible. Modern physics also says that motion needs no cause to keep it going: a body moves on unless something stops it, as Newton's first law states. David Hume and Immanuel Kant, in the eighteenth century, argued that we cannot reason from the world to anything beyond experience.

Defenders reply that Aristotle and Aquinas were not talking about a chain going back in time, which they thought might be infinite, but about what keeps things existing and acting now, as a hand moves a stick which moves a stone, at the same moment. And 'motion' for them meant any passage from potential to actual, not only movement through space. Whether that answer works is the subject of a whole later hall; for now it is enough to see that Aristotle's first mover came out of his account of nature, not out of piety.
sections.key: Critics say infinite chains are possible and physics needs no first mover; defenders reply that the argument concerns what sustains change now, not the past.

refs: Aristotle, De Anima II.1 (412a–413a), II.2–3, III.5; Physics VIII; Metaphysics XII.6–10 (1071b–1076a), esp. XII.7 (1072b3, kinei hōs erōmenon; 1072b13–14) and XII.9 (1074b34, noēsis noēseōs); XII.8 (the number of movers).
Cicero, Tusculan Disputations I.22; On the Nature of the Gods II.42–44, II.95. The 'endelecheia/entelecheia' question: see, for example, the commentaries on Tusculan Disputations I.22.
Isaiah 40:25–31.
Averroes, Long Commentary on De Anima; Thomas Aquinas, On the Unity of the Intellect against the Averroists (1270); Summa contra Gentiles I.13; Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.3; I q.75–76.
Blaise Pascal, the Memorial (23 November 1654).
Jonathan Barnes, Aristotle: A Very Short Introduction (2000); Lloyd Gerson, God and Greek Philosophy (1990).

debate.question: Is Aristotle's unmoved mover God?

positions.name: Yes: reason reaches the true God, in part
positions.who: Thomas Aquinas; Maimonides; the Catholic tradition (the First Vatican Council, 1870, taught that God can be known by natural reason)
positions.view: Aristotle reasoned truly to one eternal, immaterial, perfect mind on which everything depends. That is God, known dimly. Revelation adds what reason cannot reach: creation, the Trinity, love.
positions.evidence: Metaphysics XII; Romans 1:20; the way Aquinas's first way builds on Physics VIII.

positions.name: No: a different god altogether
positions.who: Pascal; many Protestant theologians, notably Karl Barth; some modern scholars of Aristotle
positions.view: A god who does not create, know or love the world is not the God of Abraham with a few details missing. Starting with the philosophers' god distorts Christian faith.
positions.evidence: XII.9's thinking of thinking; Aristotle's eternal, uncreated world; Isaiah's God who names the stars and strengthens the weak.

positions.name: Neither: the argument fails
positions.who: David Hume; Immanuel Kant; most contemporary philosophers of science
positions.view: The argument rests on outdated physics and on the assumption that causal chains must end. It proves nothing about a first mover, let alone God.
positions.evidence: Newton's first law; the possibility of infinite regress; Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779).

debate.agree: All agree that Aristotle's god is not described in personal terms and that the argument rests on his account of change; they differ on whether that account is sound and what it reaches.

look.why: No painting in the gallery shows Aristotle's spheres. This seascape, painted by Hendrik Willem Mesdag at Scheveningen on the Dutch coast in 1894, shows something close to what Aristotle's underground people saw first: the sea, the sky, the clouds and the sun. It is here for that parable, not as a picture of Aristotle's cosmos.
points: The horizon lies low, in the lower third of the painting, where a calm sea meets the sky.
Several sailing ships float on the water in the distance.
The sun is setting above the water, casting pale yellow and orange light on the sky and sea.
Dark purple clouds cross a pale blue sky.
Cooler blues and muted greys fill the water and the shadows of the clouds.

music.why: Haydn's oratorio sets Genesis 1, and its first part ends with 'The heavens are telling the glory of God', from Psalm 19: the same sky Aristotle's underground people saw, praised as the work of a Creator rather than the longing of the spheres.

think.why: Aristotle's soul as the form of the body is one of the main alternatives to both materialism and the 'ghost in the machine'.

learn.why: The heavens declare the glory of God: the psalmist's version of what Aristotle's underground people would conclude.

check.q: Aristotle says that if an axe were alive, its soul would be its being able to cut. What does the example show?
options: That cutting is the highest activity
That axes have souls
That the soul is a kind of metal
That the soul is what makes a thing able to do its proper work, not a separate object inside it
check.why: The soul is the body's form or actuality: what makes it the living thing it is.

check.q: How does Aristotle's view of the soul differ most from Plato's?
options: Aristotle thought only humans have souls
Aristotle denied the soul exists
Plato thought the soul was made of fire
Plato thought the soul a prisoner in the body; Aristotle thought it the form of the body, making it alive
check.why: Hylomorphism: matter organised by form, not a ghost in a machine.

check.q: Why, according to Aristotle, must there be an unmoved mover?
options: Because Plato proved it
Because the Bible says so
Because every change from potential to actual needs a cause already actual, and the chain cannot go on without end
Because the stars are heavy
check.why: Physics VIII and Metaphysics XII: the series of movers must end in something wholly actual.

check.q: How does the unmoved mover move the heavens?
options: By creating them at the beginning of time
By pushing the outermost sphere
As the object of love, the way a goal moves the one who seeks it
By sending angels
check.why: Metaphysics XII.7: it moves things by being loved.

check.q: Which statement about Aristotle's god would Isaiah 40 most clearly contradict?
options: God is everlasting
God is above the heavens
God thinks only of himself and does not know the stars or care for the weak
God does not grow weary
check.why: Isaiah's God 'calls them all by name' and 'gives power to the weak'.

check.q: In On the Nature of the Gods, who says that denying the gods after seeing the stars is 'great impiety'?
options: Cicero's Stoic speaker, Balbus, drawing his own conclusion
Aristotle
Isaiah
Plato
check.why: The context explains that the last sentences are Balbus's conclusion, not Aristotle's.

tutorial.question: 'Aristotle's god is not the God of Abraham.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Explain the argument for an unmoved mover from change, and what Aristotle says the mover is and does (Metaphysics XII.7 and 9). Set it beside Isaiah 40 and the biblical God who creates, knows and loves. Explain how Aquinas used the argument while holding that revelation adds what reason cannot reach. Weigh Pascal's objection, and decide whether the two are the same God seen differently or different gods.
strong: Explains potential and actual and the argument from change.
Explains how the mover moves by being loved, and why it is a thinking of thinking.
Notes that Aristotle's world is eternal and uncreated.
Uses Isaiah 40 or another biblical text precisely.
Explains Aquinas's view of reason and revelation.
States Pascal's or Barth's objection fairly and reaches a view.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: go outside on a clear night, or watch a sunrise or sunset, and spend ten minutes simply looking, as Aristotle's people did when they first came out of the ground. Then read Isaiah 40:25–31 and ask which picture of God matches what you saw.
sessions.reflect: Do you think of yourself as a mind that has a body, or as a living body that thinks? What difference does it make?
takeaways: Aristotle defined the soul as the form of a living body: plants, animals and humans have nested powers, and a human being is one living whole.
He argued that all change depends on an unmoved mover, pure actuality, which moves the heavens by being loved and thinks only itself.
Aquinas built on this, but the biblical God creates, knows and loves the world; whether these are one God is still debated.

sessions.title: The case against: natural slaves and lesser women
sessions.line: The philosopher of the good life argued that some people are slaves by nature and that women are made to obey. Is his whole method rotten at the root?
sessions.plain: Aristotle, who taught the West to ask what a human being is for, also taught that some human beings are 'slaves by nature', fit only to be used by others, and that women have the power to reason but not to rule. These were not slips. They came from his own method: look at what things are for, and assign each its place. For two thousand years they were used to defend slavery and the subjection of women. This session states the case against Aristotle at full strength, then hears the replies.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 5 followed Aristotle's question 'what is it for?' from the acorn to the unmoved mover, and found much that is true and fruitful. But twice already, in the Politics, we noticed darker lines about slaves. Before we can give a verdict, the case against has to be heard in full: not only that Aristotle was wrong about slaves and women, but that the error grows from the root of his thought.
answers: Did Aristotle really defend slavery, and how?
What did he say about women?
Do these errors come from his whole method?
How did later Christians answer him, and can his ideas be saved?
sessions.finding: Aristotle argued that some people are slaves by nature and that women are made to obey: his greatest errors, reached by his own method, which later Christians had to break.

paras: Session 1 showed Aristotle explaining things by their purpose; sessions 2 and 3, how a person grows good by habit and practical wisdom; session 4, why we flourish only in a city; session 5, the soul as the form of the body and the mover on which the universe depends. Each step used the same question: what is it for?

But in session 1 we read his claim that war against people 'intended by nature for slavery' who refuse to submit is just. In session 4 we read that some people are 'formed to be a slave' and that the state of master and slave benefits both. Now we face this directly.
background.key: Aristotle's question 'what is it for?' has run through every session; twice it has already been turned on people, to call some slaves by nature.

paras: If you have taken 'Human dignity', you read Politics I.4–6, where Aristotle sets out the theory of the natural slave. In brief: a slave is a 'living tool', property that acts. Some people are by nature fitted only for bodily work and lack the capacity to plan their own lives; for them, he says, being ruled is both just and good. Aristotle admits that many actual slaves, captured in war, are not natural slaves, and that enslaving them is unjust. But he never doubts that natural slaves exist.

Slavery was everywhere in the ancient world. In Athens perhaps a third of the people were slaves. Aristotle owned slaves himself; his will, preserved by the biographer Diogenes Laertius, freed some of them. What he added was a theory: not just that slavery is useful, but that for some people it is natural.
background.key: In Politics I.4–6 Aristotle argued that some people are slaves by nature, 'living tools' who benefit from being ruled, while admitting that many actual slaves were enslaved unjustly.

paras: Aristotle thought women were rational, unlike slaves, and that a wife should be ruled 'as a citizen', not as a slave. But he also thought the male 'by nature' fitter to command, permanently. In his biology he called the female a kind of incomplete or defective male: in reproduction, he thought, the male supplies the form and the female only the matter. These ideas, wrong in every particular, were taught as science for nearly two thousand years.
background.key: Aristotle held women rational but made by nature to obey, and in his biology called the female an incomplete male.

paras: The reading is the end of Politics Book I, chapters 12 and 13, where Aristotle sums up how a household should be ruled: wives, children and slaves. It is the clearest statement of how his idea of nature sorts people into rulers and ruled, and the passage where his own reasoning comes closest to contradicting itself.
The comparison is from the book of Job, written perhaps four centuries before Aristotle. Job, a rich man defending his life, says something about his slaves that Aristotle never said.
background.key: Politics I.12–13, where Aristotle sorts the household into rulers and ruled; then Job on his servants.

before: How does Aristotle say a husband should rule his wife, and how a father his children? What is the difference?
What difficulty does Aristotle raise about whether slaves can have virtue? How does he try to solve it?
Look for the place where Aristotle seems to admit that slaves are fully human. What does he do with that admission?
sessions.readWhy: Aristotle's own summary of the household, in which nature is said to make some people rulers and others ruled.

paras: There are then three parts of domestic government, the masters, of which we have already treated, the fathers, and the husbands; now the government of the wife and children should both be that of free persons, but not the same; for the wife should be treated as a citizen of a free state, the children should be under kingly power; for the male is by nature superior to the female, except when something happens contrary to the usual course of nature, as is the elder and perfect to the younger and imperfect. Now in the generality of free states, the governors and the governed alternately change place; for an equality without any preference is what nature chooses; however, when one governs and another is governed, she endeavours that there should be a distinction between them in forms, expressions, and honours; according to what Amasis said of his laver. This then should be the established rule between the man and the woman. The government of children should be kingly; for the power of the father over the child is founded in affection and seniority, which is a species of kingly government; for which reason Homer very properly calls Jupiter "the father of gods and men," who was king of both these; for nature requires that a king should be of the same species with those whom he governs, though superior in some particulars, as is the case between the elder and the younger, the father and the son.

It is evident then that in the due government of a family, greater attention should be paid to the several members of it and their virtues than to the possessions or riches of it; and greater to the freemen than the slaves: but here some one may doubt whether there is any other virtue in a slave than his organic services, and of higher estimation than these, as temperance, fortitude, justice, and such-like habits, or whether they possess only bodily qualities: each side of the question has its difficulties; for if they possess these virtues, wherein do they differ from freemen? and that they do not, since they are men, and partakers of reason, is absurd. Nearly the same inquiry may be made concerning a woman and a child, whether these also have their proper virtues; whether a woman ought to be temperate, brave, and just, and whether a child is temperate or no; and indeed this inquiry ought to be general, whether the virtues of those who, by nature, either govern or are governed, are the same or different; for if it is necessary that both of them should partake of the fair and good, why is it also necessary that, without exception, the one should govern, the other always be governed? for this cannot arise from their possessing these qualities in different degrees;

for to govern, and to be governed, are things different in species, but more or less are not. And yet it is wonderful that one party ought to have them, and the other not; for if he who is to govern should not be temperate and just, how can he govern well? or if he is to be governed, how can he be governed well? for he who is intemperate and a coward will never do what he ought: it is evident then that both parties ought to be virtuous; but there is a difference between them, as there is between those who by nature command and who by nature obey, and this originates in the soul; for in this nature has planted the governing and submitting principle, the virtues of which we say are different, as are those of a rational and an irrational being. It is plain then that the same principle may be extended farther, and that there are in nature a variety of things which govern and are governed; for a freeman is governed in a different manner from a slave, a male from a female, and a man from a child: and all these have parts of mind within them, but in a different manner.

Thus a slave can have no power of determination, a woman but a weak one, a child an imperfect one. Thus also must it necessarily be with respect to moral virtues; all must be supposed to possess them, but not in the same manner, but as is best suited to every one's employment; on which account he who is to govern ought to be perfect in moral virtue, for his business is entirely that of an architect, and reason is the architect; while others want only that portion of it which may be sufficient for their station; from whence it is evident, that although moral virtue is common to all those we have spoken of, yet the temperance of a man and a woman are not the same, nor their courage, nor their justice, though Socrates thought otherwise; for the courage of the man consists in commanding, the woman's in obeying;

In like manner the virtue of a slave is to be referred to his master; for we laid it down as a maxim, that the use of a slave was to employ him in what you wanted; so that it is clear enough that few virtues are wanted in his station, only that he may not neglect his work through idleness or fear:

It is evident then that a slave ought to be trained to those virtues which are proper for his situation by his master; and not by him who has the power of a master, to teach him any particular art. Those therefore are in the wrong who would deprive slaves of reason, and say that they have only to follow their orders; for slaves want more instruction than children, and thus we determine this matter.

Since then every family is part of a city, and each of those individuals is part of a family, and the virtue of the parts ought to correspond to the virtue of the whole; it is necessary, that both the wives and children of the community should be instructed correspondent to the nature thereof, if it is of consequence to the virtue of the state, that the wives and children therein should be virtuous, and of consequence it certainly is, for the wives are one half of the free persons; and of the children the succeeding citizens are to be formed.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: Wife and children
parts.context: The end of Book I of the Politics. Aristotle has discussed the master's rule over slaves and the getting of wealth, and now turns to the other two relations in a household: husband and wife, and father and children. William Ellis's translation (1776). Amasis was a king of Egypt who, Herodotus says, had a gold footbath melted down and made into a statue of a god, which his people then worshipped: the same metal, honoured differently. Bekker page numbers are removed.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: a household has three kinds of rule. A wife should be ruled as a free citizen is ruled, but a child as a king rules. In most free cities citizens take turns to rule, because nature wants equals to be equal; but between man and woman the man always rules, because the male is by nature superior, unless something has gone wrong. A father rules his children like a king, out of love and seniority.

commentary.on: the wife should be treated as a citizen of a free state
commentary.text: This is meant as respect. A wife is not a slave or a child; she is ruled as one free citizen rules another. Compared with many ancient views, it is mild.

commentary.on: for the male is by nature superior to the female, except when something happens contrary to the usual course of nature
commentary.text: Here is the claim, stated without argument. 'By nature' does all the work. Aristotle notices exceptions but treats them as nature going wrong, not as evidence against his rule.

commentary.on: for an equality without any preference is what nature chooses
commentary.text: Notice the tension. Among free citizens, nature 'chooses' equality and taking turns. Between husband and wife, who are both free, the turns never come. Aristotle does not explain why.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: Different virtues for different people
parts.context: Chapter 13. Aristotle asks a question his own theory makes difficult: can slaves, women and children be good, with real virtues? If they can, how do they differ from free men? If they cannot, how are they human? 'Organic services' means work as an instrument. Gorgias (Ellis prints 'Georgias') was a teacher of rhetoric who listed different virtues for different people.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: we may ask whether slaves have virtues like self-control, courage and justice, or only usefulness. If they have virtues, how do they differ from free men? But to say they have none, when they are human and share in reason, is absurd. The same question arises for women and children. His answer: all have some share of virtue, but differently, as nature made some to command and others to obey. A slave has no power of deliberation at all, a woman has it but without authority, a child has it undeveloped. So a man's courage is to command and a woman's to obey.

commentary.on: and that they do not, since they are men, and partakers of reason, is absurd
commentary.text: This is the most important sentence in the passage. Aristotle admits that slaves 'are men, and partakers of reason'. Everything he said about human beings in the Ethics, that we are for living by reason, should apply to them. He sees the problem clearly.

commentary.on: for to govern, and to be governed, are things different in species, but more or less are not
commentary.text: His escape: the difference between ruler and ruled is not one of degree but of kind. Rulers and ruled are made for different purposes, so they have different kinds of virtue. This is where his teleology, the question 'what is it for?', is turned on people.

commentary.on: Thus a slave can have no power of determination, a woman but a weak one, a child an imperfect one
commentary.text: The Greek says the slave lacks the deliberative part of the soul altogether; the woman has it but it is 'without authority' (Ellis translates 'weak'); the child has it but undeveloped. This one sentence sorted human beings into kinds for two thousand years.

commentary.on: for the courage of the man consists in commanding, the woman's in obeying
commentary.text: Aristotle explicitly rejects Socrates here, who had argued that virtue is the same in a man and a woman. It is a rare case of the pupil's pupil being less generous than the teacher's teacher.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.title: The slave's virtue
parts.context: The rest of chapter 13, shortened; the cuts are marked '…'. Aristotle goes on to say how much virtue a slave needs, and ends by saying how the household fits into the city.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: a slave's virtue is measured by his master's needs: he needs only enough virtue not to neglect his work out of laziness or fear. Masters should train their slaves in this virtue. Those who say slaves should only be given orders, without reasons, are wrong: slaves need even more instruction than children. Since the household is part of the city, wives and children must be educated with the city's constitution in view, for wives are half the free population and children are its future citizens.

commentary.on: the virtue of a slave is to be referred to his master
commentary.text: A slave's good is defined entirely by someone else's purpose. This is the logic of the 'living tool': what a tool is for is decided by its user.

commentary.on: Those therefore are in the wrong who would deprive slaves of reason, and say that they have only to follow their orders
commentary.text: Again Aristotle half sees the truth. Slaves must be reasoned with, given explanations, instructed. Yet a being that can be reasoned with is a being that can reason. The theory strains against what he knew from daily life.

commentary.on: for the wives are one half of the free persons
commentary.text: A reminder that Aristotle cared about women's education, within the limits of his view. In the best city, he thought, the virtue of women matters to the virtue of the whole.

read.author: Aristotle

paras:
“If I have despised the cause of my male servant
or of my female servant,
when they contended with me,

what then will I do when God rises up?
When he visits, what will I answer him?

Didn’t he who made me in the womb make him?
Didn’t one fashion us in the womb?

parts.title: My servant's cause
parts.context: The book of Job is a poem about a good man who loses everything; scholars date it anywhere from the seventh to the fourth century BC. In chapter 31 Job, accused by his friends of hidden sin, swears an oath listing what he has not done. Among the sins he denies is despising his servants. The Hebrew word ('ebed') covers both servants and slaves.

commentary.on:
If I have despised the cause of my male servant
or of my female servant,
when they contended with me
commentary.text: Job assumes his slaves have a 'cause', a case, and the right to argue it against their master. Aristotle's natural slave has no power of deliberation; Job's servant can bring a complaint, and his master must answer it.

commentary.on: what then will I do when God rises up?
commentary.text: Job's master is also answerable. How he treats those under him will be judged by God, who stands above both.

commentary.on:
Didn’t he who made me in the womb make him?
Didn’t one fashion us in the womb?
commentary.text: Here is the root of the difference. For Aristotle, nature makes some to rule and others to serve. For Job, the same God made master and slave in the same way. Their difference is a matter of circumstance, not of kind. The Bible did not abolish slavery at once, but this line, with Genesis 1:27, held the seed of its end.

compare.why: Job, defending his life, says his slaves had a right to argue their case against him, because the same God made them both in the womb.
compare.title: Didn't one fashion us?

paras: The case against Aristotle is not only that he held the prejudices of his time. Almost everyone did. It is that he gave those prejudices a philosophy, and the philosophy came from the heart of his method. He asked of everything: what is it for? He then looked at the world as it was in fourth-century Athens, where slaves worked and women stayed at home, and concluded that this was what they were for. The question 'what is it for?' turned the way things are into the way things must be.

Critics such as the political philosopher Susan Moller Okin, in Women in Western Political Thought (1979), have argued that 'functionalist' reasoning of this kind always works this way. Whoever has power decides what others are for, and calls it nature. If that is right, the problem is not a few bad conclusions, but the root. Teleology itself is a tool of domination, and the West was right to abandon it.
sections.key: The charge: Aristotle's question 'what is it for?' turned the way things were into the way they must be; teleology itself serves the powerful.

paras: The theory did not stay in the Politics. In 1550 and 1551 the Spanish crown held a debate at Valladolid on whether the peoples of the Americas could be conquered and enslaved. Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, a scholar who had translated the Politics into Latin, argued that the Indians were natural slaves in Aristotle's sense, and that war against them was just. Aristotle's sentence from Politics I.8, which you read in session 1, was quoted directly.

Defenders of slavery in the American South in the nineteenth century cited Aristotle too. And his biology of women, the female as an incomplete male, passed through medieval medicine and theology into early modern science. For two thousand years 'Aristotle says' was an argument for keeping half of humanity under the other half. Any honest verdict on Aristotle has to begin here.
sections.key: At Valladolid in 1550–51 Sepúlveda used Aristotle to justify enslaving the peoples of the Americas; defenders of slavery and of women's subjection cited him for centuries.

paras: Aristotle's view of women was not only political. In the Generation of Animals he argued that in reproduction the father supplies the form and the mother only the matter, like a carpenter and his wood. A female, on this view, results when the father's form does not fully master the matter; he calls the female something like a deformed or incomplete male. Galen, the great Roman physician, modified the theory, but some version of it was taught in European medicine for nearly two thousand years.

It was overturned by observation, Aristotle's own method. In 1651 William Harvey, who had discovered the circulation of the blood, argued that every animal comes from an egg. In 1827 Karl Ernst von Baer first identified the mammalian egg cell. Nineteenth-century biologists showed that mother and father contribute equally to the new life. The error was built on poor evidence and an assumption of male superiority; better evidence ended it. Here Aristotle the scientist was corrected by scientists who followed his advice to look.
sections.key: Aristotle's biology made the female an incomplete male; Harvey (1651) and von Baer (1827) began the observations that overturned it.

paras: The first reply is that Aristotle's own arguments undermine his conclusions. He admitted that slaves are human and share in reason. He said they should be reasoned with and instructed. He admitted that many slaves were not natural slaves, and that nature often fails to make the bodies and souls of free people and slaves different. In Politics VII he advised that all slaves should be offered freedom as a reward, and in his will he freed some of his own.

His theory of the natural slave required people who completely lack the power to deliberate yet can understand orders, learn virtue and be reasoned with. No such people exist, and he half knew it. Many modern scholars, Bernard Williams among them in Shame and Necessity (1993), conclude that Aristotle's theory of slavery is not a reasoned conclusion at all, but a rationalisation that his own principles could not support.
sections.key: Aristotle admitted slaves share in reason, should be instructed and might be freed; his theory needed people who do not exist, and scholars call it a rationalisation.

paras: The second reply is historical. The tools to break the theory came from the Bible: one God made all human beings in his image (Genesis 1:27); 'Didn't one fashion us in the womb?' (Job 31:15); in Christ 'there is neither slave nor free' (Galatians 3:28). In about AD 379 Gregory of Nyssa, preaching on Ecclesiastes, attacked slave-owning outright: no one can buy a being made in the image of God, he argued, and no price can equal it. Almost no one in the ancient world said anything like it.

At Valladolid, Sepúlveda's opponent was Bartolomé de las Casas, a Dominican friar and former colonist who had freed his own Indian labourers. Las Casas argued that the peoples of the Americas were fully rational, with cities, laws and arts, and that all the peoples of the world are human. Pope Paul III had already declared in 1537 that the Indians were true human beings who must not be deprived of their liberty. Christians did not always live up to this: many owned slaves, and many quoted Aristotle and the Bible to defend it. But the abolitionist movements of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were overwhelmingly driven by Christian conviction.
sections.key: Genesis, Job and Galatians gave the tools to break the theory; Gregory of Nyssa condemned slave-owning, and Las Casas answered Sepúlveda at Valladolid.

paras: Thomas Aquinas, who did more than anyone to bring Aristotle into Christian thought, kept more of him than we might like. He repeated Aristotle's biology of the female as, in a sense, defective, though he added that woman is not defective in God's intention, being made as part of the order of creation. He accepted that some subjection of one person to another is natural, even before the Fall, for the common good.

But he drew a line Aristotle never drew. Slavery, in the sense of owning a person, was for Aquinas not natural but a result of sin, added by human law. Every human being has a rational soul made directly by God and is ordered to the same final end: to know and love God. That one change, that all have the same ultimate purpose, undercuts the heart of the natural slave theory, which depended on some people having a lesser purpose than others.
sections.key: Aquinas kept some of Aristotle's views on women and natural subjection, but held slavery to be a result of sin and every person ordered to the same end in God.

paras: The third reply is philosophical. The fault, its defenders say, was not in asking what human beings are for, but in giving the wrong answer, and giving different answers for different people. Ask it properly, about all human beings, and teleology becomes a weapon against domination, not for it. If every person is made for living by reason, for friendship and for knowing the truth, then slavery, which denies people these, is a crime against nature.

This is the line taken by several modern philosophers. Martha Nussbaum's 'capabilities approach' asks what every human being needs to be able to do and be in order to live a fully human life, and judges societies by whether they provide it. Alasdair MacIntyre, in Dependent Rational Animals (1999), admitted Aristotle's errors and rebuilt his ethics around the dependence of all of us, in childhood, illness and age. On this view the question Aristotle asked was right; his blindness was in not asking it of everyone.
sections.key: Defenders say the error was not asking what humans are for, but answering differently for different people; Nussbaum and MacIntyre rebuild teleology for all.

refs: Aristotle, Politics I.2 (1252a–b), I.4–7, I.8 (1256b), I.12–13 (1259a–1260b), VII.10 (1330a32–33); Generation of Animals II.3 (737a27–28); Diogenes Laertius, Lives V.11–16 (Aristotle's will).
Job 31:13–15; Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28.
Gregory of Nyssa, Homilies on Ecclesiastes IV (on Ecclesiastes 2:7).
Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.92 a.1 ad 1–2; I q.96 a.4; II–II q.57 a.3 ad 2; Supplement q.52 a.1 ad 2 (slavery and sin; sources to be checked).
The debate at Valladolid (1550–51): Sepúlveda, Democrates secundus; Las Casas, Apologia. Paul III, Sublimis Deus (1537).

Susan Moller Okin, Women in Western Political Thought (1979); Bernard Williams, Shame and Necessity (1993), ch. V; Peter Garnsey, Ideas of Slavery from Aristotle to Augustine (1996); Martha Nussbaum, Women and Human Development (2000); Alasdair MacIntyre, Dependent Rational Animals (1999).

debate.question: Is Aristotle's ethics corrupted at the root by his views on slaves and women?

positions.name: Yes: the method serves the powerful
positions.who: Susan Moller Okin; many feminist and critical philosophers
positions.view: Asking 'what is it for?' about human beings lets those in charge define everyone else's purpose and call it nature. Aristotle's slaves and women are not accidents but what his method produces. We should judge people by their rights and choices, not by a supposed nature.
positions.evidence: Politics I.12–13; the use of Aristotle at Valladolid and in the American South; the way 'natural' roles have been used to exclude.

positions.name: No: the method is sound, the answers were wrong
positions.who: Martha Nussbaum; Alasdair MacIntyre; many Thomists
positions.view: Aristotle's errors came from what he saw around him, not from his method. Asked about every human being, 'what are we for?' grounds the claim that all are owed what a human life needs. His own admissions show the theory of natural slavery contradicts his principles.
positions.evidence: 'Since they are men, and partakers of reason'; the capabilities approach; MacIntyre's Dependent Rational Animals.

positions.name: The method needs a Creator to be safe
positions.who: Gregory of Nyssa; Las Casas; much of the Christian tradition
positions.view: If human purposes are read off the world as it is, the strong will always define the weak. If every person is made by God in his image for the same end, then no one can be a natural slave. Teleology without the doctrine of creation is dangerous; with it, it becomes a defence of the weak.
positions.evidence: Job 31:15; Genesis 1:27; Gregory's homily; the debate at Valladolid; Aquinas's view that all are ordered to the same final end.

debate.agree: All agree that Aristotle's views on slaves and women were wrong and did great harm; they differ on whether the fault lies in his method, his blindness, or a world-view without a Creator.

look.why: Aristotle thought those who do the household's manual work have, at best, the small virtue needed 'not to neglect their work'. Jean Siméon Chardin, around 1738, painted a young servant at her work with the same patience and dignity painters gave to saints and kings.
points: A young woman in a white jacket, long white skirt and cap, with a light peach apron, leans over a thigh-high barrel.
She holds a long-handled pot, its handle tucked under her bent left arm, and reaches into it with her right hand.
She faces left in profile, looking off to the left with brown eyes; a gold object like a pendant or bell hangs from a teal-blue ribbon at her neck.
On the floor beside the barrel lie a tall copper-brown container, a brass pot on its side and a brick-red pan with an iron handle; a green-banded clay pot stands behind her.
Light from the upper left glints on the rims of the pots and falls on the woman.

music.why: John Newton, who wrote it, had been the captain of a slave ship. He became a clergyman and, late in life, a public witness against the slave trade, encouraging William Wilberforce. It is the hymn of someone who saw that the people he had treated as cargo were human beings like him.

think.why: How the idea that slavery is wrong took hold, and the part Christians played on both sides.

learn.why: Job's answer to the natural slave: the same God made master and servant in the womb.

check.q: What is the strongest form of the objection in this session?
options: That Aristotle's views on slaves and women grow out of his method itself, which turns the way things are into the way they must be
That Aristotle was not a Christian
That the Politics was badly translated
That Aristotle owned slaves
check.why: The objection is not only that he was wrong, but that his teleology produced the error and served the powerful.

check.q: Where does Aristotle's own reasoning most clearly strain against his theory of natural slaves?
options: When he says slaves are tools
When he discusses Amasis's footbath
When he admits slaves 'are men, and partakers of reason', and says they need more instruction than children
When he says children are ruled like subjects of a king
check.why: A being that can be reasoned with and instructed has the power to deliberate that the theory denies it.

check.q: How does Aristotle try to explain why rulers and ruled have different virtues?
options: By saying it is a matter of degree
By saying ruling and being ruled differ in kind, so nature gave them different kinds of virtue
By appeal to the gods
By saying all virtue is the same

check.q: What does Job 31:15 add that Aristotle lacks?
options: That slaves should be freed at once
That slaves are tools
That the same God made master and servant in the same way, so their difference is not one of kind
That masters need not answer for their treatment of slaves
check.why: 'Didn't one fashion us in the womb?' Master and servant share one origin and one Judge.

check.q: Which change made by Aquinas most undercuts the natural slave theory?
options: He agreed with all of Aristotle's biology
He denied that women have souls
He refused to read the Politics

check.why: The theory needed some people to have a lesser purpose; Aquinas gives all the same end.

check.q: What is the 'repair' that Nussbaum and MacIntyre offer?
options: Return to Aristotle unchanged
Replace ethics with economics
Abandon all talk of human purposes
Ask what every human being needs to flourish, so that teleology protects all instead of ranking some below others
check.why: On this view Aristotle's question was right; his error was not asking it of everyone.

tutorial.question: 'Aristotle's defence of slavery is not an accident but a consequence of his whole philosophy.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Set out the objection at full strength: the theory of the natural slave and women's place, and why critics say they follow from asking what things are for. Use Politics I.12–13 precisely. Then give the replies: Aristotle against himself, the Christian alternatives (Job, Gregory of Nyssa, Las Casas, Aquinas) and the modern repair. Reach a judgement about whether teleology can be saved.
strong: States the objection as its best advocates would, not as a caricature.
Quotes or closely explains Politics I.13 on the deliberative faculty.
Notes the internal tensions in Aristotle's own text.
Uses Job 31 or Genesis 1:27 and at least one historical Christian response.
Considers whether teleology needs a Creator to protect the weak.
Reaches a clear, argued conclusion.
