sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice the people whose work makes your life possible and who are easy to overlook: cleaners, carers, delivery drivers, kitchen staff. Learn the name of one of them, thank them by name, and ask them one question about themselves.
sessions.reflect: Are there people you have quietly decided are 'for' something, rather than people with lives and purposes of their own?
takeaways: Aristotle argued that some people are slaves by nature and that women are made to obey; the theory was used for two thousand years.
The objection at full strength says these errors come from his method; but his own text admits slaves share in reason, and the theory contradicts itself.
Job, Gregory of Nyssa, Las Casas and Aquinas broke it by holding that one God made all for the same end; modern philosophers rebuild teleology for everyone.

sessions.title: Happiness is contemplation: the verdict
sessions.line: Aristotle's last word on the good life: the happiest life is spent contemplating what is highest. Aquinas said he was right, and incomplete.
sessions.plain: The verdict first. Aristotle asked of everything what it is for, and answered: a human being is for living by reason, and its highest activity is contemplation, quiet, loving attention to the highest truths, which makes us most like God. Thomas Aquinas, who took up Aristotle more fully than any Christian before him, said this was true but incomplete. We are made to know God, but in this life we only glimpse him; our happiness is complete only when we see him face to face. This session reads Aristotle's conclusion, then Aquinas's, and tells how Aristotle came back to the West to become simply 'the Philosopher'.
sessions.why: Session 6 heard the case against Aristotle at full strength, and found his teleology most dangerous when it gave some people lesser purposes than others. Now we return to where the Ethics began, in session 1: everything aims at some good, and there must be a highest good. What is it, for every human being? Aristotle's answer, and what Christians made of it, is the verdict of this journey.
answers: What did Aristotle think the happiest life is?
Why did he think contemplation is the highest activity?
How did Aristotle come back to the West, and why did the Church call him 'the Philosopher'?
How is Aristotle different from Plato, and what is the verdict on him?
sessions.finding: Aristotle's highest happiness is contemplation, the most godlike activity; Aquinas said he was right and incomplete, because the end of human life is not only to think about God but to see him.

paras: Aristotle asked of everything: what is it for? His answers were often profound. Nature works towards ends. We become good by habit, guided by practical wisdom. We flourish only together. The soul is the life of the body, and the universe depends on a perfect mind. His worst answers, about slaves and women, came from asking the question of some people and not of all.

His final answer about human beings, in Ethics X, is that our highest happiness is contemplation, the activity in which we are most like God. Christians did not reject this; they completed it. Aquinas argued that the highest happiness is indeed knowing the highest thing, God, but that no human mind can reach it fully in this life. It comes as a gift: the vision of God. Aristotle saw the destination; he could not see how to arrive.
background.key: The verdict: Aristotle's question was the right one and most of his answers profound; his account of happiness was true but incomplete, and Aquinas completed it with the vision of God.

paras: Session 1 found that Aristotle explained things by their purpose, and that the Ethics begins by saying everything aims at some good. Sessions 2 and 3 showed how moral virtue is formed by habit and guided by practical wisdom. Session 4 showed the human being as a political animal. Session 5 described the soul as the form of the body and the first mover as thought thinking itself. Session 6 faced the case against: his natural slaves and lesser women.

In Book I of the Ethics, as you may have read in 'A good life', Aristotle said happiness is the soul's activity in accordance with the best and most complete virtue. In Book X he finally says which virtue that is.
background.key: Book I said happiness is activity in accordance with the best virtue; Book X says which.

paras: The reading is Ethics X.7–8 (chapter VI and the start of VII in Chase's numbering), Aristotle's account of the contemplative life. The comparison has two parts: Aquinas's answer in the Summa Theologiae, written about 1270, to the question whether perfect happiness is the vision of God; and the verses from Paul's first letter to the Corinthians that lie behind it.
background.key: Aristotle on contemplation in Ethics X; then Aquinas on the vision of God, and Paul's 'face to face'.

before: List the reasons Aristotle gives for thinking contemplation is the happiest activity.
Why does Aristotle think the gods cannot be doing just or brave actions? What does he think they do?
Where does Aristotle put the life of moral virtue, and why?
sessions.readWhy: Aristotle's last word on happiness, from Ethics X: the life of contemplation.

paras: Now if Happiness is a Working in the way of Excellence of course that Excellence must be the highest, that is to say, the Excellence of the best Principle. Whether then this best Principle is Intellect or some other which is thought naturally to rule and to lead and to conceive of noble and divine things, whether being in its own nature divine or the most divine of all our internal Principles, the Working of this in accordance with its own proper Excellence must be the perfect Happiness.

That it is Contemplative has been already stated: and this would seem to be consistent with what we said before and with truth: for, in the first place, this Working is of the highest kind, since the Intellect is the highest of our internal Principles and the subjects with which it is conversant the highest of all which fall within the range of our knowledge.
Next, it is also most Continuous: for we are better able to contemplate than to do anything else whatever, continuously.

And the Self-Sufficiency which people speak of will attach chiefly to the Contemplative Working: of course the actual necessaries of life are needed alike by the man of science, and the just man, and all the other characters; but, supposing all sufficiently supplied with these, the just man needs people towards whom, and in concert with whom, to practise his justice; and in like manner the man of perfected self-mastery, and the brave man, and so on of the rest; whereas the man of science can contemplate and speculate even when quite alone, and the more entirely he deserves the appellation the more able is he to do so: it may be he can do better for having fellow-workers but still he is certainly most Self-Sufficient.

Again, this alone would seem to be rested in for its own sake, since nothing results from it beyond the fact of having contemplated; whereas from all things which are objects of moral action we do mean to get something beside the doing them, be the same more or less.

Also, Happiness is thought to stand in perfect rest; for we toil that we may rest, and war that we may be at peace. Now all the Practical Virtues require either society or war for their Working, and the actions regarding these are thought to exclude rest; those of war entirely, because no one chooses war, nor prepares for war, for war’s sake: he would indeed be thought a bloodthirsty villain who should make enemies of his friends to secure the existence of fighting and bloodshed. The Working also of the statesman excludes the idea of rest, and, beside the actual work of government, seeks for power and dignities or at least Happiness for the man himself and his fellow-citizens: a Happiness distinct from the national Happiness, which we evidently seek as being different and distinct.

But such a life will be higher than mere human nature, because a man will live thus, not in so far as he is man but in so far as there is in him a divine Principle: and in proportion as this Principle excels his composite nature so far does the Working thereof excel that in accordance with any other kind of Excellence: and therefore, if pure Intellect, as compared with human nature, is divine, so too will the life in accordance with it be divine compared with man’s ordinary life.

Yet must we not give ear to those who bid one as man to mind only man’s affairs, or as mortal only mortal things; but, so far as we can, make ourselves like immortals and do all with a view to living in accordance with the highest Principle in us, for small as it may be in bulk yet in power and preciousness it far more excels all the others.

In fact this Principle would seem to constitute each man’s “Self,” since it is supreme and above all others in goodness it _would_ be absurd then for a man not to choose his own life but that of some other.

And second in degree of Happiness will be that Life which is in accordance with the other kind of Excellence, for the Workings in accordance with this are proper to Man: I mean, we do actions of justice, courage, and the other virtues, towards one another, in contracts, services of different kinds, and in all kinds of actions and feelings too, by observing what is befitting for each: and all these plainly are proper to man. Further, the Excellence of the Moral character is thought to result in some points from physical circumstances, and to be, in many, very closely connected with the passions.

And that the perfect Happiness must be a kind of Contemplative Working may appear also from the following consideration: our conception of the gods is that they are above all blessed and happy: now what kind of Moral actions are we to attribute to them? those of justice? nay, will they not be set in a ridiculous light if represented as forming contracts, and restoring deposits, and so on? well then, shall we picture them performing brave actions, withstanding objects of fear and meeting dangers, because it is noble to do so? or liberal ones? but to whom shall they be giving? and further, it is absurd to think they have money or anything of the kind. And as for actions of perfected self-mastery, what can theirs be? would it not be a degrading praise that they have no bad desires? In short, if one followed the subject into all details all the circumstances connected with Moral actions would appear trivial and unworthy of Gods.

Still, every one believes that they live, and therefore that they Work because it is not supposed that they sleep their time away like Endymion: now if from a living being you take away Action, still more if Creation, what remains but Contemplation? So then the Working of the Gods, eminent in blessedness, will be one apt for Contemplative Speculation; and of all human Workings that will have the greatest capacity for Happiness which is nearest akin to this.

To the Gods then all their life is blessed; and to men in so far as there is in it some copy of such Working, but of the other animals none is happy because it in no way shares in Contemplative Speculation.

Now he that works in accordance with, and pays observance to, Pure Intellect, and tends this, seems likely to be both in the best frame of mind and dearest to the Gods: because if, as is thought, any care is bestowed on human things by the Gods then it must be reasonable to think that they take pleasure in what is best and most akin to themselves (and this must be the Pure Intellect); and that they requite with kindness those who love and honour this most, as paying observance to what is dear to them, and as acting rightly and nobly. And it is quite obvious that the man of Science chiefly combines all these: he is therefore dearest to the Gods, and it is probable that he is at the same time most Happy.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: The best activity of the best part
parts.context: Near the end of the Ethics. Aristotle has discussed the virtues, friendship and pleasure, and now returns to happiness. D. P. Chase's translation (1847). 'Working' is Chase's word for activity (Greek energeia); 'Contemplative Speculation' and 'Science' here mean theōria, the attentive study of the highest truths, not laboratory science. 'Intellect' is nous.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: if happiness is activity in accordance with virtue, it must be the virtue of the best thing in us, the intellect, which thinks about divine and noble things. Its activity is contemplation. This is the highest activity, because intellect is our highest part and its objects are the highest; the most continuous; the most pleasant; the most self-sufficient, since a just person needs others to be just towards, but a thinker can think alone; loved for its own sake alone; and restful, unlike politics and war, which are always aimed at something further.

commentary.on: the Excellence of the best Principle
commentary.text: The logic of session 1 again. If happiness is doing well what we are for, and we have many powers, then the best happiness must be the best power working at its best. For Aristotle that is the intellect.

commentary.on: for, in the first place, this Working is of the highest kind, since the Intellect is the highest of our internal Principles
commentary.text: Aristotle now gives a series of reasons. Count them as you read: highest, most continuous, most pleasant, most self-sufficient, loved for itself, most at rest.

commentary.on: the just man needs people towards whom, and in concert with whom, to practise his justice
commentary.text: A just person needs someone to be just to; a generous person, money and someone to give it to. The thinker needs very little. Aristotle values this independence; Christians would later ask whether it is a strength or a lack of love.

commentary.on: we toil that we may rest, and war that we may be at peace
commentary.text: One of the most quoted lines in the Ethics. Work is for the sake of leisure, war for the sake of peace. The Greek word for leisure, scholē, gives us 'school': leisure is the time for learning and contemplation, not for doing nothing.

commentary.on: no one chooses war, nor prepares for war, for war’s sake: he would indeed be thought a bloodthirsty villain
commentary.text: Even politics and war, the most honoured activities in Greek life, are for something beyond themselves. A statesman's work aims at the happiness of his people; it is not that happiness itself.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: Make ourselves like immortals
parts.context: The chapter continues, with a short cut marked '…'. Aristotle now admits something startling about the life he has just praised.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: such a life is more than human; we live it not as human beings but because there is something divine in us. Do not listen to those who say that, being human and mortal, we should think only of human and mortal things. As far as we can, we should make ourselves immortal and live by the best thing in us, which, though small, is our truest self. The life of the other virtues, justice and courage and the rest, is happy too, but in second place, because it belongs to our composite, embodied, human nature.

commentary.on: not in so far as he is man but in so far as there is in him a divine Principle
commentary.text: Here Aristotle goes beyond everything he has said so far. Our highest happiness is not strictly human at all. There is something divine in us, and in contemplation it comes alive.

commentary.on: so far as we can, make ourselves like immortals
commentary.text: Some poets had warned: be human, think mortal thoughts, do not reach above your station. Aristotle disagrees. Reach as high as you can. Christian readers heard an echo of their own hope: that human beings are made to share in the life of God.

commentary.on: In fact this Principle would seem to constitute each man’s “Self,”
commentary.text: Your truest self, Aristotle says, is the part of you that can know the highest things. This is a long way from the modern idea of the self as a bundle of preferences.

commentary.on: And second in degree of Happiness will be that Life which is in accordance with the other kind of Excellence
commentary.text: The life of moral virtue is happy, but 'second'. Scholars still argue about how Aristotle fits these together: is the good life contemplation alone, or contemplation crowning a life of virtue and friendship? Most think the second: contemplation is the peak of a whole good life, not a replacement for it.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great
parts.title: The life of the gods
parts.context: Chapter 8, shortened. Aristotle offers one more argument, from what we believe about the gods. Endymion was a figure of Greek myth, granted eternal sleep.
parts.plain: Aristotle says: we think the gods supremely happy. But what could they do? Making contracts and returning deposits, or facing dangers bravely, or giving money away, would be ridiculous for gods. Yet they are alive, so they must be active, and if not in action or making, then in contemplation. So the human activity most like theirs is the happiest. Animals cannot share in it, so they are not happy in this sense. And if the gods care for human beings at all, they will love most those who honour the intellect, which is most like them.

commentary.on: will they not be set in a ridiculous light if represented as forming contracts, and restoring deposits
commentary.text: Aristotle gently mocks the gods of Greek myth, who quarrel, bargain and fight. A perfect being does not need courage or justice, which are virtues for creatures with dangers and debts. This is the god of session 5: pure activity, thought thinking itself.

commentary.on: now if from a living being you take away Action, still more if Creation, what remains but Contemplation?
commentary.text: Note 'Creation', making: Aristotle explicitly denies that God makes anything. The Christian God creates the world and acts in history. That is the deepest point where Aquinas will have to correct him.

commentary.on: To the Gods then all their life is blessed; and to men in so far as there is in it some copy of such Working
commentary.text: Human happiness at its best is a copy of divine life. Christians would agree, and go further: not a copy only, but a share. 'Partakers of the divine nature', the Second Letter of Peter says (1:4).

commentary.on: if, as is thought, any care is bestowed on human things by the Gods
commentary.text: 'If'. Aristotle is unsure whether the gods care for human beings at all. Everything in the Christian answer turns on this 'if'.

read.author: Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great

paras: On the contrary, It is written (1 John 3:2): "When He shall appear, we shall be like to Him; and [Vulgate: 'because'] we shall see Him as He is."

I answer that, Final and perfect happiness can consist in nothing else than the vision of the Divine Essence. To make this clear, two points must be observed. First, that man is not perfectly happy, so long as something remains for him to desire and seek: secondly, that the perfection of any power is determined by the nature of its object. Now the object of the intellect is "what a thing is," i.e. the essence of a thing, according to De Anima iii, 6. Wherefore the intellect attains perfection, in so far as it knows the essence of a thing. If therefore an intellect knows the essence of some effect, whereby it is not possible to know the essence of the cause, i.e. to know of the cause "what it is"; that intellect cannot be said to reach that cause simply, although it may be able to gather from the effect the knowledge of that the cause is. Consequently, when man knows an effect, and knows that it has a cause, there naturally remains in the man the desire to know about the cause, "what it is." And this desire is one of wonder, and causes inquiry, as is stated in the beginning of the Metaphysics (i, 2). For instance, if a man, knowing the eclipse of the sun, consider that it must be due to some cause, and know not what that cause is, he wonders about it, and from wondering proceeds to inquire. Nor does this inquiry cease until he arrive at a knowledge of the essence of the cause.

If therefore the human intellect, knowing the essence of some created effect, knows no more of God than "that He is"; the perfection of that intellect does not yet reach simply the First Cause, but there remains in it the natural desire to seek the cause. Wherefore it is not yet perfectly happy. Consequently, for perfect happiness the intellect needs to reach the very Essence of the First Cause. And thus it will have its perfection through union with God as with that object, in which alone man's happiness consists, as stated above (Articles 1 and 7; I-II:2:8).
For we know in part and we prophesy in part;
but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.

parts.author: Thomas Aquinas
parts.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province, 2nd revised edition (1920)
parts.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II, question 3, article 8
parts.title: Whether happiness is the vision of God
parts.context: Thomas Aquinas (1225–74), an Italian Dominican friar who taught at Paris, wrote the Summa Theologiae from about 1265 until his death. Questions 1–5 of its second part are about happiness, and follow Aristotle closely, calling him 'the Philosopher'. In article 8 he asks whether perfect happiness is the vision of God's essence. The translation is the English Dominicans' (second edition, 1920). Each article gives objections, a text 'on the contrary', then his answer.
parts.plain: Aquinas says: perfect happiness must be the vision of God's very essence. We are not perfectly happy while there is anything left to desire. The mind's natural desire is to know what things are. When we know an effect, we wonder about its cause, as someone seeing an eclipse wonders what causes it, and the wondering does not stop until we know the cause itself. Knowing from the world only that God exists leaves that desire unsatisfied. So perfect happiness requires the mind to reach God himself.

commentary.on: When He shall appear, we shall be like to Him; and [Vulgate: 'because'] we shall see Him as He is.
commentary.text: Aquinas's 'on the contrary' is Scripture (1 John 3:2). The bracket is the translators' note on the Latin. He will argue that reason, following Aristotle, points to the same conclusion.

commentary.on: man is not perfectly happy, so long as something remains for him to desire and seek
commentary.text: This is Aristotle's argument from Ethics I, which you read in session 1: there must be an end wanted for itself, or desire is empty. Aquinas accepts it completely.

commentary.on: And this desire is one of wonder, and causes inquiry, as is stated in the beginning of the Metaphysics
commentary.text: The Metaphysics begins by saying that all human beings by nature desire to know, and that philosophy begins in wonder. Aquinas uses Aristotle to show that the desire to know cannot rest until it reaches the first cause itself.

commentary.on: If therefore the human intellect, knowing the essence of some created effect, knows no more of God than "that He is"; the perfection of that intellect does not yet reach simply the First Cause
commentary.text: Here is Aquinas's correction. Aristotle's contemplation reached a first mover by reasoning from motion. But that is knowing that God is, not what he is. The desire Aristotle himself described can only be satisfied by seeing God directly, which no philosopher can achieve by thinking. It must be given.

parts.title: Now in part, then face to face
parts.context: Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, a Greek city full of people proud of their knowledge, around AD 54. This chapter is his great poem on love. Near its end he contrasts what we know now with what we shall know.

commentary.on: For we know in part and we prophesy in part
commentary.text: Paul agrees with Aristotle that knowing is part of our end, and with Aquinas that in this life it is partial.

commentary.on: For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face.
commentary.text: Ancient mirrors were polished metal, giving a dim, distorted image. Contemplation in this life, even at its best, sees God like that. The promise is sight: face to face, as one person sees another.

commentary.on: but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known
commentary.text: This is what Aristotle could not say. His god knows only itself. Paul's God has known us all along. The happiness Aristotle sought in thinking about God turns out to be a meeting with one who already knows and loves us. In the chapter's next verse, love is the greatest of all.

compare.author: Thomas Aquinas
compare.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II, question 3, article 8
compare.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province, 2nd revised edition (1920)
compare.why: Aquinas agreed that happiness is knowing the highest thing, but argued that only the vision of God himself can complete it, as Paul promised.
compare.title: Face to face

sections.h: Contemplation and the whole good life
paras: Aristotle's conclusion has puzzled readers. Through nine books he described a life of moral virtue, friendship and citizenship. Then in Book X he says the happiest life is contemplation, and the moral life only second. Does that mean the ideal is a philosopher alone in his study?

Most scholars think not. Contemplation is the highest activity, but a human being is not only an intellect. We need food, friends, a city, the virtues. The best human life, on this reading, is a life of virtue and friendship crowned by times of contemplation, which give the rest its point, as leisure gives work its point. Others, such as Richard Kraut, read Aristotle more strictly: everything else is for the sake of contemplation.

Either way, Aristotle's picture is striking. The highest human happiness is not achievement, pleasure or fame. It is understanding: quiet, loving attention to what is true and beautiful, for its own sake.
sections.key: Most read Aristotle's contemplation as the crown of a life of virtue and friendship, not a replacement for it; its highest happiness is understanding, for its own sake.

sections.h: How Aristotle was lost and found
paras: After antiquity most of Aristotle disappeared from the Latin West. In the early sixth century the Roman philosopher Boethius translated some of his logic into Latin, and for six hundred years that was nearly all the West knew. Greek-speaking Byzantium kept the manuscripts. In the Islamic world, from the ninth century, scholars in Baghdad translated Aristotle into Arabic, and philosophers built on him: al-Farabi; Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980–1037); and Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–98) of Córdoba, whose commentaries were so thorough that the Latins called him simply 'the Commentator'. The Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204), also from Córdoba, joined Aristotle to the Hebrew Bible in his Guide for the Perplexed.

In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries translators in Toledo, Sicily and elsewhere put almost all of Aristotle into Latin, from Arabic and from Greek. William of Moerbeke, a Dominican friend of Aquinas, made careful new translations from the Greek.

sections.key: Aristotle survived in Byzantium and in Arabic, was developed by Avicenna, Averroes and Maimonides, and returned to the Latin West in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

paras: Aristotle's return was a shock. Here was a complete account of nature, the soul, ethics and politics, built without the Bible. Some of it contradicted Christian faith: the world is eternal; the god does not create or care; the soul may not survive. The authorities in Paris forbade teaching his natural philosophy in 1210 and 1215. By 1255 the same university required it.

Thomas Aquinas made Aristotle a partner in Christian thought. He wrote commentaries on twelve of his works and called him simply 'the Philosopher'. His principle was that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it; so reason, at its best, cannot contradict faith, and Aristotle, the best of reason, could be corrected and completed rather than thrown away. Where Aristotle was wrong, on the eternity of the world, on creation, Aquinas said so.

Not everyone agreed. In 1277 the bishop of Paris condemned 219 propositions, some of them Aristotelian and a few close to Aquinas's own. Dante, a generation later, placed Aristotle in Limbo, honoured among the great pagans, as the master of those who know.
sections.key: Paris first banned Aristotle's natural philosophy, then required it; Aquinas called him 'the Philosopher' and held that grace perfects nature, correcting him where needed.

paras: Christian traditions have received Aristotle very differently. Their attitudes still shape how they think about faith and reason.

rows: Aquinas; Leo XIII's encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879), which made Thomism central to Catholic teaching
Grace perfects nature; reason can know much of God and the moral law
John of Damascus (8th century) used his logic; Gregory Palamas (14th century) insisted God is known by grace and prayer, not by syllogisms
Theology is the experience of God in prayer, guided by the Fathers, more Platonic than Aristotelian
Luther (1517) called Aristotle an enemy of grace; Melanchthon restored his logic and ethics at Wittenberg; later Reformed and Lutheran universities taught him for two centuries
Luther feared Aristotle's ethics made us righteous by our own habits; Melanchthon saw his value for ordinary moral and civic life

sections.key: Catholics embraced and corrected Aristotle; the Orthodox used him cautiously; Luther attacked him and Melanchthon brought him back.

paras: Raphael's School of Athens shows the two at the centre: Plato pointing upward, holding his Timaeus; Aristotle with his hand flat, holding his Ethics. Ever since, people have described themselves as born Platonists or born Aristotelians. Coleridge said everyone is one or the other.

table.note: A simplification: Aristotle kept much of Plato, and both were read together for most of Christian history.

sections.key: Plato looked up, to Forms beyond the world; Aristotle looked at the world itself. Augustine was Plato's heir, Aquinas Aristotle's.

paras: Aquinas did not say Aristotle's happiness was false. He distinguished two kinds. Imperfect happiness is possible in this life: it consists, he says, first in contemplation and then in the life of practical wisdom and the moral virtues, exactly as Aristotle taught. It is real, but fragile; illness, misfortune and death can cut it off, as Aristotle himself admitted when he said one swallow does not make a spring.

Perfect happiness cannot be lost and leaves nothing to desire. No creature can reach it by its own powers, Aquinas argued, because it is the sight of God himself, infinitely beyond any created mind. It must be given by grace, and Christians believe it is promised in the life to come. So Aquinas keeps Aristotle's whole account, and sets it inside a larger one.

Orthodox theology speaks of the same hope as theosis, 'deification': human beings becoming 'partakers of the divine nature' (2 Peter 1:4), by grace, not by nature. Aristotle had told his hearers to make themselves like immortals as far as they could. The Christian answer is that God does what they could not.
sections.key: Aquinas distinguished imperfect happiness in this life, which is Aristotle's, from perfect happiness, the vision of God, given by grace; the Orthodox call it theosis.

paras: So what is a thing for, and what is a person for? Aristotle's great gift was the question itself, and the conviction that it has real answers. Things have natures; natures have ends; human beings flourish when they live as they are meant to live: by habit and wisdom, with friends, in a community, reaching towards the highest truth. That picture shaped Christian ethics, natural law, the universities and much of Western science.

His failures were real. He gave different purposes to different people, and his theory served the masters of slaves and the rulers of women for two thousand years. Christians broke it not by abandoning his question, but by asking it of everyone, in the light of one Creator who made all alike.

And his final answer was, in Aquinas's word, imperfect. He saw that the human mind is made for the highest truth, and that knowing it would make us most like God. He could not see that the highest truth is a person who knows and loves us first, and who gives himself to be seen. Aquinas's verdict, which this journey adopts, is that Aristotle was right about what we long for, and incomplete about how it is given: not by our thinking alone, but face to face.
sections.key: Aristotle gave the West the question 'what is it for?' and many true answers; he failed by not asking it of everyone, and his happiness is completed, not replaced, by the vision of God.

debate.question: Was Aristotle right that the happiest life is contemplation?

positions.name: Yes, as he said it
positions.who: Aristotle; many philosophers since, including some modern scholars such as Richard Kraut (as an interpretation)
positions.view: Our highest power is understanding, and its full exercise on the highest things is the best and most self-sufficient human activity. The rest of life serves it.
positions.evidence: Ethics X.7–8; the joy of understanding; the restlessness of lives spent only in getting and doing.

positions.name: Yes, but completed by grace
positions.who: Thomas Aquinas; Catholic and much Orthodox and Protestant tradition
positions.view: Aristotle was right that we are made to know the highest truth, but that truth is God, whom no philosopher can see by thinking. Contemplation in this life is a foretaste; perfect happiness is the vision of God, given, not achieved, and inseparable from love.
positions.evidence: Summa Theologiae I–II q.3 a.8; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2.

positions.name: No: the good life is love and action
positions.who: Many modern critics; some Christians, such as those who stress love of neighbour over contemplation
positions.view: Making contemplation the highest good favours the few with leisure, and makes love of others second best. Human beings are fulfilled in relationships and action, not in solitary thought.
positions.evidence: Aristotle's own admission that the contemplative needs others least; the Gospel's command to love God and neighbour; Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42) read as both needed.

debate.agree: All agree that we long for something beyond getting and doing; they differ on whether it is understanding, the vision of God, or love lived out among others.

look.why: The gallery holds no picture of Aristotle. This painting, from Rembrandt's workshop around 1653 and possibly by his pupil Willem Drost, is called simply The Philosopher. It shows what Aristotle meant by contemplation better than a portrait would: a man at rest, attending to something we cannot see. (Rose Window already uses this painting elsewhere; it is reused here because it is exactly the subject.)
points: A gaunt, light-skinned man is shown from the chest up, almost filling the painting.
He wears a large, soft, earth-brown beret over a fringe of dark hair, and his brown beard is trimmed straight.
His chest faces us and leans over his folded hands, at the bottom of the picture, while his head turns to our left and he looks that way.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What is a thing for, and what is a person for? In about 300 words, give your own answer, using at least three of Aristotle's ideas from this journey, and answer the strongest objection to your view: that asking what people are 'for' lets the powerful decide for everyone else.

synthesis: This journey asked one question, as Aristotle did, of everything: what is it for? Here are the short answers to the questions it set out to answer.

Who was Aristotle? A doctor's son from Stagira in northern Greece, born in 384 BC, who spent twenty years in Plato's Academy, studied animals on Lesbos, taught the young Alexander the Great, founded the Lyceum in Athens and died in 322 BC. His public dialogues are lost; his surviving lecture notes cover nearly everything, from logic to biology to politics.

What are the four causes? Four ways of answering 'why?': what a thing is made of, the form that makes it what it is, what brought it about, and what it is for. The last, the final cause, mattered most to Aristotle. Nature does nothing in vain, he said, and he argued that because living things regularly turn out well formed, nature acts for ends. Darwin, who admired him, showed how natural selection can produce that regularity without aims. Whether purpose-talk in biology is only shorthand, or points to something real, is still argued.

How do we become good? As builders become builders: by doing. Virtue is a settled habit, formed by practice from childhood, of feeling and acting well. What is the golden mean? Not moderation, but the right amount for this person at this moment: the right anger, at the right time, towards the right people, for the right reason. Courage lies between cowardice and rashness. Some acts, like murder and adultery, have no mean at all.

What is practical wisdom? Phronesis, the trained ability to see what a particular situation asks and to act on it. It is not cleverness, which serves any goal, nor book-learning, which the young can have. It needs experience and good character, because vice distorts our sight. So, Aristotle concluded, you cannot be fully good without being wise, or wise without being good. Christians called it prudence and set it under love.

What did he mean by 'man is a political animal'? That human beings flourish only in community. Households join into villages and villages into a city, which is founded so that we may live but continues so that we may live well. Speech exists so that we can talk together about what is just. Whoever needs no city is a beast or a god. Hobbes later said society is a contract made out of fear; Augustine and Aquinas kept Aristotle's insight but placed our final community beyond any earthly city.

Did Aristotle believe in God? He believed that all change depends on an unmoved mover: pure actuality, a mind thinking itself, which moves the heavens by being loved. Christians, Jews and Muslims built on his argument. But his god does not create the world, know it or love it. The God of Isaiah names every star and gives strength to the weak. Whether these are one God seen from two distances or two different gods is still debated. Aristotle's soul, meanwhile, is not a prisoner in the body but its life: the form of a living body, one with it as the shape is one with the wax.

Did he defend slavery? Yes, and that is the hardest part of this journey. He argued that some people are slaves by nature and that women are made to obey. These views came from his own method: asking what things are for, and reading the answer off the world as it was. They were used for two thousand years, at Valladolid and in the American South. But his own text admits that slaves 'are men, and partakers of reason'. Job had already said that one God made master and servant in the womb; Gregory of Nyssa condemned slave-owning; Las Casas answered Sepúlveda; Aquinas held that all human beings are made for the same end. The fault, on the best reading, was not asking what human beings are for, but giving different answers for different people.

What is happiness for Aristotle? The activity of our best part in its best way, over a whole life. In Book X he says the highest happiness is contemplation, attending to the highest truths for their own sake, the most godlike thing we do, crowning a life of virtue and friendship.

How did Aristotle come back to the West? His logic survived in Boethius's Latin; the rest was kept in Byzantium and the Islamic world, developed by Avicenna, Averroes and Maimonides, and translated into Latin in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Paris first banned his natural philosophy, then required it. Thomas Aquinas called him 'the Philosopher', and held that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. Luther attacked him; Melanchthon brought him back; the Orthodox used him with caution.

How is Aristotle different from Plato? Plato looked for reality in eternal Forms beyond this world; Aristotle found form in each thing and studied the world to see it. Plato's soul is a prisoner; Aristotle's is the body's life. Plato's best city is ruled by philosophers; Aristotle's is a mixed constitution under law. Augustine was Plato's great Christian heir; Aquinas, Aristotle's.

So, what is a person for? Aristotle's answer was: for living by reason, in virtue and friendship, in a community, reaching towards the highest truth. Aquinas's verdict, which this journey adopts, is that he was right about what we long for and incomplete about how it is given. Our minds are made to know the highest thing, and the highest thing is not a mind thinking only itself but a God who already knows and loves us. Perfect happiness is not only thinking about God but seeing him: 'now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face'.

title: Plato
question: What is real, and what is the soul?
line: Seven sessions climbing Plato's cave: the shadows, the forms, the soul in three parts, the Good like the sun, the return to rule a just city, the case against from Aristotle and Popper, and what Augustine did with it all.
why: Plato asked what is truly real, what a soul is and what makes it just, and whether there is a Good above everything, more sharply than anyone before him, and the West has argued with his answers ever since. This journey follows his most famous picture, the cave, from the prisoners among the shadows to the sun outside and back down into the city, reading the Republic and the Phaedo in Jowett's translation. It gives the case against at full strength, from Aristotle, who said the forms explain nothing, and Karl Popper, who called the Republic a blueprint for tyranny, and ends with Augustine, who found in the Platonists almost everything, and said what was missing. It is written at the depth of a first-year university philosophy paper, for anyone.
follows: A first-year philosophy paper on Plato's metaphysics and psychology: the Republic (the city and soul, the sun, line and cave, the philosopher-kings), the Phaedo on recollection and the forms, Aristotle's criticisms, Popper's political critique, and the reception of Plato by Plotinus and Augustine.

outcomes: Explain the allegory of the cave stage by stage, using Plato's own key, and what he meant by education as the turning of the whole soul.
Set out the theory of forms and the argument from recollection in the Phaedo, and explain the problems Plato himself raised.
Explain the three parts of the soul, the argument for them from the principle of opposites, and Plato's definition of justice as their right order.
Explain the analogy of the sun and the divided line, what 'beyond being' may mean, and whether Plato's Good is God.
Describe Plato's just city, its noble lie and philosopher-kings, and assess Aristotle's and Popper's objections at full strength.
Explain what Augustine and later Christians took from Plato and what they refused.

sessions.title: The cave
sessions.line: Prisoners chained in the dark, watching shadows on a wall and calling them real. One is freed, climbs into the sun, and comes back. Plato's most famous picture, and what he meant by it.
sessions.plain: Plato, a philosopher of ancient Athens, once described people living all their lives chained in a cave, watching shadows and thinking the shadows were all there is. One of them is set free, painfully climbs out into the sunlight, and then goes back down to tell the others, who laugh at him and would kill him if they could. Plato said this is a picture of us: most of what we take for reality is shadow, and real education is not stuffing facts into a head but turning a whole person round towards the light.
sessions.why: This is the first session. You have met Socrates, who spent his life asking questions in the streets of Athens and was put to death for it in 399 BC. His pupil Plato spent the next fifty years trying to answer the questions Socrates asked: what is real, what is good, what is a human soul? The cave is where his answer starts, because it is the picture he drew of the whole of it.
answers: Who was Plato, and how did he write?
What is Plato's cave?

Why does the freed prisoner go back down?
sessions.finding: Plato pictured us as prisoners who take shadows for reality: education is not putting sight into blind eyes but turning the whole soul round towards the light.

paras: Some questions sound abstract until you notice that you live by an answer to them. Is there anything more real than what I can see and touch? Is 'good' just a word for what I happen to like, or is there a goodness that would still be good if nobody liked it? Am I a body, or do I have a soul, and what would that even mean? Plato (about 428 to 348 BC) asked these questions more sharply than anyone before him, and his answers have shaped what the West has thought about them ever since. The philosopher A. N. Whitehead once wrote that the whole European tradition of philosophy is 'a series of footnotes to Plato'. That is an exaggeration, but not by much.

This journey asks Plato's two great questions: what is real, and what is the soul? It follows one picture, the cave, from the bottom to the top and back again. Each session is one step of the climb: the shadows we start among, the forms Plato thought were truly real, the soul that does the climbing, the Good that shines over everything like the sun, the return to the cave to rule a just city, the case that there is no sun at all, and what Christians did with Plato's picture.

background.h: The story so far: Athens after Socrates
paras: In 399 BC an Athenian jury of 501 citizens found Socrates guilty of not believing in the city's gods, bringing in new divine things and corrupting the young. He was seventy. He refused to escape, and drank the poison hemlock in prison. Among the young men who loved him was Plato, then about twenty-eight.

Plato came from one of the richest and best-connected families in Athens. Two of his mother's relatives, Critias and Charmides, had been among the Thirty, a brutal oligarchy that ruled Athens for a few months in 404–403 BC after the city lost its long war with Sparta. Then the restored democracy executed Socrates. Plato had seen the worst of both kinds of government, and both had ended in killing. If you want to understand why he asked what justice really is, and who should rule, start there.

background.key: Plato saw both an oligarchy and a democracy in Athens end in killing, the second in the death of Socrates: that is where his questions about justice began.

paras: Plato did not write treatises. He wrote dialogues: conversations, like short plays, in which Socrates and others argue. About thirty-five survive under his name, more than for any other Greek philosopher, though scholars doubt a few. Plato himself never speaks in them. So when Socrates says something in a dialogue, we cannot always be sure whether it is what the real Socrates thought or what Plato came to think. Most scholars think the early dialogues stay close to the historical Socrates, and that in the 'middle' dialogues, including the Phaedo and the Republic, Socrates becomes the voice of Plato's own ideas.

The Republic is the longest dialogue but one, in ten 'books' (the divisions of an ancient scroll). Socrates tells it himself, the day after a long conversation at a house in the Piraeus, the port of Athens. The question is: what is justice, and is a just person happier than an unjust one, even if nobody ever finds out? To answer it, Socrates imagines building a just city from scratch. The cave comes in Book VII, after two other pictures we will meet later, the sun and the divided line. Keep this table to hand for the speakers.

paras: The reading is the whole of the cave, and the few pages that follow in which Socrates says what it means: about two thousand words of Book VII, from its first line (in the standard numbering used for Plato, 514a) to 519b. It answers the session's question directly, because Plato tells us exactly what the picture is of, and then draws a conclusion about education that he thought followed from it.

The comparison is two short passages from the New Testament that use the same language of light and darkness: Jesus in John's Gospel on people who love darkness rather than light, and Paul on the God who said 'Light will shine out of darkness'. Read them beside Plato and ask where the darkness comes from in each.
