Why does the freed prisoner at first want to turn back?
What does Plato say education is not, and what does he say it is?
sessions.readWhy: Plato's own picture of the human condition and of education, and his explanation of it.

paras: And now, I said, let me show in a figure how far our nature is enlightened or unenlightened:—Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads. Above and behind them a fire is blazing at a distance, and between the fire and the prisoners there is a raised way; and you will see, if you look, a low wall built along the way, like the screen which marionette players have in front of them, over which they show the puppets.
I see.

And do you see, I said, men passing along the wall carrying all sorts of vessels, and statues and figures of animals made of wood and stone and various materials, which appear over the wall? Some of them are talking, others silent.
You have shown me a strange image, and they are strange prisoners.
Like ourselves, I replied; and they see only their own shadows, or the shadows of one another, which the fire throws on the opposite wall of the cave?
True, he said; how could they see anything but the shadows if they were never allowed to move their heads?
And of the objects which are being carried in like manner they would only see the shadows?
Yes, he said.
And if they were able to converse with one another, would they not suppose that they were naming what was actually before them?
Very true.

And suppose further that the prison had an echo which came from the other side, would they not be sure to fancy when one of the passers-by spoke that the voice which they heard came from the passing shadow?
No question, he replied.
To them, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images.
That is certain.

And now look again, and see what will naturally follow if the prisoners are released and disabused of their error. At first, when any of them is liberated and compelled suddenly to stand up and turn his neck round and walk and look towards the light, he will suffer sharp pains; the glare will distress him, and he will be unable to see the realities of which in his former state he had seen the shadows; and then conceive some one saying to him, that what he saw before was an illusion, but that now, when he is approaching nearer to being and his eye is turned towards more real existence, he has a clearer vision,—what will be his reply? And you may further imagine that his instructor is pointing to the objects as they pass and requiring him to name them,—will he not be perplexed? Will he not fancy that the shadows which he formerly saw are truer than the objects which are now shown to him?
Far truer.

And if he is compelled to look straight at the light, will he not have a pain in his eyes which will make him turn away to take refuge in the objects of vision which he can see, and which he will conceive to be in reality clearer than the things which are now being shown to him?
True, he said.

And suppose once more, that he is reluctantly dragged up a steep and rugged ascent, and held fast until he is forced into the presence of the sun himself, is he not likely to be pained and irritated? When he approaches the light his eyes will be dazzled, and he will not be able to see anything at all of what are now called realities.
Not all in a moment, he said.

He will require to grow accustomed to the sight of the upper world. And first he will see the shadows best, next the reflections of men and other objects in the water, and then the objects themselves; then he will gaze upon the light of the moon and the stars and the spangled heaven; and he will see the sky and the stars by night better than the sun or the light of the sun by day?
Certainly.
Last of all he will be able to see the sun, and not mere reflections of him in the water, but he will see him in his own proper place, and not in another; and he will contemplate him as he is.
Certainly.

He will then proceed to argue that this is he who gives the season and the years, and is the guardian of all that is in the visible world, and in a certain way the cause of all things which he and his fellows have been accustomed to behold?
Clearly, he said, he would first see the sun and then reason about him.
And when he remembered his old habitation, and the wisdom of the den and his fellow-prisoners, do you not suppose that he would felicitate himself on the change, and pity them?
Certainly, he would.

And if they were in the habit of conferring honours among themselves on those who were quickest to observe the passing shadows and to remark which of them went before, and which followed after, and which were together; and who were therefore best able to draw conclusions as to the future, do you think that he would care for such honours and glories, or envy the possessors of them? Would he not say with Homer,
‘Better to be the poor servant of a poor master,’
and to endure anything, rather than think as they do and live after their manner?
Yes, he said, I think that he would rather suffer anything than entertain these false notions and live in this miserable manner.
Imagine once more, I said, such an one coming suddenly out of the sun to be replaced in his old situation; would he not be certain to have his eyes full of darkness?
To be sure, he said.

And if there were a contest, and he had to compete in measuring the shadows with the prisoners who had never moved out of the den, while his sight was still weak, and before his eyes had become steady (and the time which would be needed to acquire this new habit of sight might be very considerable), would he not be ridiculous? Men would say of him that up he went and down he came without his eyes; and that it was better not even to think of ascending; and if any one tried to loose another and lead him up to the light, let them only catch the offender, and they would put him to death.
No question, he said.

This entire allegory, I said, you may now append, dear Glaucon, to the previous argument; the prison-house is the world of sight, the light of the fire is the sun, and you will not misapprehend me if you interpret the journey upwards to be the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world according to my poor belief, which, at your desire, I have expressed—whether rightly or wrongly God knows. But, whether true or false, my opinion is that in the world of knowledge the idea of good appears last of all, and is seen only with an effort; and, when seen, is also inferred to be the universal author of all things beautiful and right, parent of light and of the lord of light in this visible world, and the immediate source of reason and truth in the intellectual; and that this is the power upon which he who would act rationally either in public or private life must have his eye fixed.
I agree, he said, as far as I am able to understand you.

Moreover, I said, you must not wonder that those who attain to this beatific vision are unwilling to descend to human affairs; for their souls are ever hastening into the upper world where they desire to dwell; which desire of theirs is very natural, if our allegory may be trusted.
Yes, very natural.

And is there anything surprising in one who passes from divine contemplations to the evil state of man, misbehaving himself in a ridiculous manner; if, while his eyes are blinking and before he has become accustomed to the surrounding darkness, he is compelled to fight in courts of law, or in other places, about the images or the shadows of images of justice, and is endeavouring to meet the conceptions of those who have never yet seen absolute justice?
Anything but surprising, he replied.

Any one who has common sense will remember that the bewilderments of the eyes are of two kinds, and arise from two causes, either from coming out of the light or from going into the light, which is true of the mind’s eye, quite as much as of the bodily eye; and he who remembers this when he sees any one whose vision is perplexed and weak, will not be too ready to laugh; he will first ask whether that soul of man has come out of the brighter life, and is unable to see because unaccustomed to the dark, or having turned from darkness to the day is dazzled by excess of light. And he will count the one happy in his condition and state of being, and he will pity the other; or, if he have a mind to laugh at the soul which comes from below into the light, there will be more reason in this than in the laugh which greets him who returns from above out of the light into the den.
That, he said, is a very just distinction.
But then, if I am right, certain professors of education must be wrong when they say that they can put a knowledge into the soul which was not there before, like sight into blind eyes.
They undoubtedly say this, he replied.

Whereas, our argument shows that the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already; and that just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being, and learn by degrees to endure the sight of being, and of the brightest and best of being, or in other words, of the good.
Very true.

And must there not be some art which will effect conversion in the easiest and quickest manner; not implanting the faculty of sight, for that exists already, but has been turned in the wrong direction, and is looking away from the truth?
Yes, he said, such an art may be presumed.

And whereas the other so-called virtues of the soul seem to be akin to bodily qualities, for even when they are not originally innate they can be implanted later by habit and exercise, the virtue of wisdom more than anything else contains a divine element which always remains, and by this conversion is rendered useful and profitable; or, on the other hand, hurtful and useless. Did you never observe the narrow intelligence flashing from the keen eye of a clever rogue—how eager he is, how clearly his paltry soul sees the way to his end; he is the reverse of blind, but his keen eye-sight is forced into the service of evil, and he is mischievous in proportion to his cleverness?
Very true, he said.

But what if there had been a circumcision of such natures in the days of their youth; and they had been severed from those sensual pleasures, such as eating and drinking, which, like leaden weights, were attached to them at their birth, and which drag them down and turn the vision of their souls upon the things that are below—if, I say, they had been released from these impediments and turned in the opposite direction, the very same faculty in them would have seen the truth as keenly as they see what their eyes are turned to now.
Very likely.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The prisoners
parts.context: Socrates is talking with Glaucon, Plato's brother. They have been discussing what kind of education the rulers of a just city would need, and Socrates has just described two pictures of knowledge, the sun and a line divided into four parts. Now he offers a third, a 'figure' or image. 'The den' is the cave. A 'raised way' is a path or ramp across the cave behind the prisoners.
parts.plain: Imagine people chained since childhood in an underground cave, facing the back wall, unable to turn their heads. Behind them a fire burns, and between the fire and the prisoners people carry objects along a path behind a low wall, like puppeteers. The prisoners see only the shadows of these objects on the wall in front of them, and hear echoes. They would think the shadows were the real things.

commentary.on: let me show in a figure how far our nature is enlightened or unenlightened
commentary.text: Plato tells us at the start what the picture is for. It is about 'our nature', about all of us, and about how far we are 'enlightened', how much light we live by. This is not a fable about other people.

commentary.on: have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them
commentary.text: The prisoners have been like this 'from their childhood'. They did not choose the cave, and they cannot even turn their heads to see that they are in one. That is the point: you cannot notice a prison you have never been outside.

commentary.on: like the screen which marionette players have in front of them, over which they show the puppets
commentary.text: There are four layers here, from the back wall upwards: shadows; the puppets and carved objects that cast them; the fire that makes them visible; and, though the prisoners know nothing of it, the world outside. Notice too that there are people carrying the objects. Someone is making the shadows.

commentary.on: Like ourselves, I replied
commentary.text: Glaucon says these are 'strange prisoners'. Socrates answers in three words. The strangeness is ours. Plato wants us to stop reading and ask what our own shadows are: the pictures of the world we have absorbed from the people around us, from fashion, from what everyone says, and never examined.

commentary.on: would they not suppose that they were naming what was actually before them?
commentary.text: The prisoners talk to one another, and agree. Their whole language is about shadows, so they cannot even say what they are missing. Agreement is not the same as truth, if everyone is looking at the same wall.

commentary.on: the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images
commentary.text: Look at the words: shadows of images. The things carried along the wall are themselves only copies, statues of men and animals. The prisoners see copies of copies. That double distance from the real will matter a great deal when we come to Plato's forms.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The way up, and the way back
parts.context: Socrates now imagines one prisoner being set free and made to climb out. The 'upper world' is the world outside the cave, lit by the sun. The line from Homer is said by the ghost of Achilles in the Odyssey (XI.489–491): he would rather be a poor man's servant on earth than king among the dead.
parts.plain: If one prisoner were freed and turned round, the firelight would hurt his eyes, and he would think the shadows truer than the objects. Dragged up into the sunlight, he would be dazzled and see nothing at first. Slowly he would see shadows, reflections, things themselves, the stars, and at last the sun, and understand that the sun governs everything he sees. He would pity those below. If he went back down, his eyes would be useless in the dark; the prisoners would laugh at him, and would kill anyone who tried to lead them up.

commentary.on: compelled suddenly to stand up and turn his neck round and walk and look towards the light, he will suffer sharp pains
commentary.text: The first thing freedom brings is pain. Plato is honest about this. Learning that what you believed was false does not feel like enlightenment at first. It feels like loss, and the glare hurts.

commentary.on: Will he not fancy that the shadows which he formerly saw are truer than the objects which are now shown to him?
commentary.text: Even when shown the real thing, he prefers the familiar shadow. The answer, 'Far truer', is one of the most honest lines in philosophy. We do not give up our pictures of the world just because someone shows us a better one.

commentary.on: he is reluctantly dragged up a steep and rugged ascent
commentary.text: Nobody in the story climbs out by himself. He is 'liberated', 'compelled', 'dragged'. Someone else does the freeing. Plato never says who. Readers have argued about it ever since: a teacher like Socrates? Philosophy itself? Christians later answered, God.

commentary.on: And first he will see the shadows best, next the reflections of men and other objects in the water, and then the objects themselves
commentary.text: The climb has stages, and they cannot be skipped. The eyes have to get used to each level of light before the next. Real understanding comes in order, slowly, 'by degrees', as Plato will say.

commentary.on: he will contemplate him as he is
commentary.text: The sun 'in his own proper place': not its reflection, but the thing itself. This is the top of the climb. Plato will tell us shortly what the sun stands for.

commentary.on: this is he who gives the season and the years, and is the guardian of all that is in the visible world
commentary.text: Having seen the sun, he can understand what it does: it makes the seasons, it makes things grow, it is 'in a certain way the cause of all things' he used to see. Seeing the source lets you understand everything that comes from it.

commentary.on: Better to be the poor servant of a poor master
commentary.text: Plato quotes Homer, whom he criticised all his life. In the Odyssey these are the words of the dead hero Achilles, who would rather be a servant on earth than a king among the shadows of the dead. Plato turns them round. The cave is the land of the dead; the living are the ones who have seen the sun.

commentary.on: if any one tried to loose another and lead him up to the light, let them only catch the offender, and they would put him to death
commentary.text: No Athenian reader could miss this. Socrates, the man telling the story, had been put to death by his city for trying to lead others out of their certainties. Plato wrote these words years after the execution, and put them in his dead teacher's mouth.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: What the picture means
parts.context: Socrates now explains the image, linking it to what he said just before about the sun and the 'intellectual world', the world that is known by the mind rather than seen by the eyes. Then he draws the lesson for education. 'Professors of education' probably means the Sophists, paid teachers of the day who claimed to teach success.
parts.plain: The cave is the world we see; the fire is the sun; the climb is the soul rising to what is known by the mind. At the top is the 'idea of good', hard to see, and the source of everything right and beautiful. People who have seen it do not want to come back, and look foolish when they do. Education is not putting knowledge into an empty soul. The power to see is already there; it needs the whole soul turned round from the changing world to what truly is.

commentary.on: the prison-house is the world of sight, the light of the fire is the sun
commentary.text: Here is Plato's key. The cave is not some special prison; it is the ordinary world of the senses, the world of sight. Even the sun in our sky is, in the picture, only a fire in the cave. What lies outside is the 'intellectual world', the world of what can only be understood.

commentary.on: according to my poor belief, which, at your desire, I have expressed—whether rightly or wrongly God knows
commentary.text: At the most important moment Socrates becomes modest. This is 'my belief', and 'God knows' if it is right. Plato often does this: his biggest claims are offered as images and hopes, not as proofs.

commentary.on: the idea of good appears last of all, and is seen only with an effort
commentary.text: The sun outside the cave stands for what Plato calls the Good. It is the last thing to be seen, and the hardest. It is 'the universal author of all things beautiful and right' and 'the immediate source of reason and truth'. The fourth session of this journey is about it.

commentary.on: he is compelled to fight in courts of law, or in other places, about the images or the shadows of images of justice
commentary.text: Another reminder of Socrates, who was tried in a court of law by men arguing about 'the shadows of images of justice': about laws and reputations, not about what justice really is. The philosopher looks clumsy there, not because he knows less, but because his eyes are adjusted to a different light.

commentary.on: he who remembers this when he sees any one whose vision is perplexed and weak, will not be too ready to laugh
commentary.text: A gentle and wise remark. People can be confused for two opposite reasons: because they have never seen the light, or because they have just come out of it. Before you laugh at someone who seems lost, ask which.

commentary.on: they can put a knowledge into the soul which was not there before, like sight into blind eyes
commentary.text: Here is the view Plato rejects: that teaching means pouring information into an empty container. Many people still think of education this way.

commentary.on: the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already
commentary.text: This is the heart of the passage, and the memory piece for this session. We are not blind. We are looking the wrong way. The power to see the truth is already in every soul.

commentary.on: can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being
commentary.text: Not the mind alone, but 'the whole soul', as the eye can only turn when the whole body turns. Plato means that you cannot see the truth while your desires and habits face the other way. 'The world of becoming' is everything that changes, grows and dies; 'being' is what simply is. Plato's word for this turning round is periagōgē. Christians later used a similar word, conversion: 'turning round'.

commentary.on: his keen eye-sight is forced into the service of evil, and he is mischievous in proportion to his cleverness
commentary.text: A sharp observation. Cleverness is not the same as wisdom. A clever rogue sees very well; he is simply looking at the wrong things. The more intelligent he is, the more harm he does. Education that only sharpens the mind, without turning it, makes better criminals.

commentary.on: which, like leaden weights, were attached to them at their birth, and which drag them down
commentary.text: What keeps the soul's eye pointing downwards? Not lack of intelligence, but appetites, 'like leaden weights'. Plato is not saying eating and drinking are evil, but that when they rule us they turn our attention away from what matters most.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy

paras: This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil.
For everyone who does evil hates the light, and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed.
But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”
seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

parts.title: Men loved the darkness
parts.context: John's Gospel, probably written about AD 90–100. These are the closing words of a conversation between Jesus and Nicodemus, a teacher of the Jewish law who came to him at night. The 'light' is Jesus himself, sent by God into the world.

commentary.on: the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light
commentary.text: In Plato's cave the light is far away and the prisoners do not know it exists. Here the light 'has come into the world': it comes down to the prisoners. And they are not simply ignorant; they 'loved the darkness'. The problem is not only what we know but what we love.

commentary.on: for their works were evil
commentary.text: Plato blamed appetites that drag the soul's eye downwards. John goes further: people avoid the light because they do not want to be seen. Darkness is a hiding place.

commentary.on: But he who does the truth comes to the light
commentary.text: 'Does' the truth, not just knows it. For Plato the climb is mainly learning. For John, coming to the light begins with how you live.

parts.title: Light will shine out of darkness
parts.context: Paul, writing to the Christians of Corinth in Greece about AD 55. He is defending his preaching, and echoes the first words God speaks in Genesis: 'Let there be light'.

commentary.on: Light will shine out of darkness
commentary.text: Paul remembers the creation story: the God who made light at the beginning now makes light in human hearts. The light does not wait at the top of a climb. It shines into the cave.

commentary.on: in the face of Jesus Christ
commentary.text: Plato's highest light is a principle, the Good, seen 'last of all and with an effort'. Paul says the glory of God is seen in a face. This contrast, between the Good as a principle and God as a person, will come back at the end of this journey.

compare.why: The New Testament also speaks of people who stay in darkness and of a light that frees them. But it gives a different reason why people stay in the dark, and a different account of where the light comes from.
compare.title: Light and darkness in the New Testament

paras: Plato was born in Athens in about 428 or 427 BC, into an old aristocratic family. 'Plato' may have been a nickname, meaning 'broad'; ancient writers said it referred to his shoulders or his forehead. As a young man he expected to go into politics, as men of his class did. He tells us in the Seventh Letter, if it is his (many scholars think it is, some do not), that the cruelty of the Thirty and then the execution of Socrates by the democracy made him despair of politics as it was. He concluded, he says, that cities would never be free of evil until true philosophers came to power, or rulers became philosophers.

After 399 BC he travelled, perhaps to Egypt and certainly to the Greek cities of southern Italy, where he met followers of Pythagoras, and to Sicily. In about 387 BC he founded a school in a grove outside Athens sacred to the hero Academus: the Academy. It lasted, in one form or another, until the sixth century AD, and gave its name to every academy since. Aristotle studied there for twenty years. Plato taught and wrote there until he died, aged about eighty, in 348 or 347 BC.
sections.key: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), an Athenian aristocrat, turned from politics after the death of Socrates and founded the Academy in about 387 BC.

paras: A dialogue is not a lecture with interruptions. Plato chose the form deliberately. In the Phaedrus (275d–e) Socrates complains that written words are like paintings: they look alive, but if you ask them a question they say the same thing over and over. A dialogue tries to get round this by making you a listener in a live argument. Characters make mistakes, change their minds and leave things unfinished.

So read Plato as you would a play. Notice who speaks, what they want and how they react. Glaucon, who hears the cave, is ambitious, clever and eager; earlier in the Republic he put the case for injustice at full strength. Plato is showing us the kind of young man who might become a great ruler or a dangerous one, depending on which way his soul turns.

Scholars usually divide the dialogues into three groups. The early ones (such as the Apology, Crito and Euthyphro) show Socrates questioning people and finding that nobody, himself included, can define courage or piety. The middle ones (Phaedo, Symposium, Republic, Phaedrus) put forward large positive ideas, above all the forms. The late ones (Parmenides, Sophist, Timaeus, Laws) test and revise them. The dating is argued over, but the broad pattern is widely accepted.
sections.key: Read a dialogue like a play: who speaks and why matters. The Republic belongs to Plato's middle period, when he put forward his boldest ideas.

paras: The cave is a story in stages, and each stage stands for a kind of awareness. Plato tells us that the cave is 'the world of sight' and the climb is 'the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world'. Many scholars line the stages up with the four sections of the divided line, which Plato described just before; we will meet the line properly in the fourth session. But the main point is clear without it: there are degrees of reality and degrees of knowing, and most of us live near the bottom.

rows: Living by images and hearsay: what everyone says, never examined
The fire and the carried objects
Seeing the ordinary things behind the images, and being confused by it
Beginning to think about what things really are, by way of models, as in mathematics
Understanding the forms: justice itself, beauty itself
The sun in its own place
Seeing the Good, the source of all being and knowing
Going back to help others, and being mocked or killed
table.note: The table is an interpretation; Plato gives the picture and a brief key, not a chart. Scholars disagree about how exactly the stages match the divided line.

sections.key: The cave has stages, from shadows to the sun and back: degrees of reality, and of knowing, that must be climbed in order.

paras: The lesson Plato draws is about education, and it is radical. The Sophists of his day, paid teachers like Protagoras and Gorgias, claimed to teach young men how to succeed: how to speak persuasively, win in the law courts and get on in politics. Plato thought this was training people to be better at measuring shadows. Real education is not the transfer of information or skills. It is periagōgē, a 'turning round' of the whole soul.

Two ideas sit inside this. First, the power to know is already in us. Plato does not think the soul is empty; it is pointed the wrong way. Second, the turning involves the 'whole soul', not just the intellect. That is why the Republic spends so long on music, gymnastics, habits and desires before it ever gets to philosophy. You cannot see well while your loves pull you elsewhere.

This is why, for Plato, a clever villain is not educated at all, however much he knows. And it is why the turning is also moral. The Greek word Plato uses for the 'conversion' of the soul shares its root with the word Christians would later use for repentance and conversion: a change of direction, not just of opinion.
sections.key: For Plato education is periagōgē, the turning of the whole soul, desires as well as mind, towards the light; cleverness without that turning only makes better rogues.

sections.h: Why the prisoners would kill him
paras: The cave does not end at the top. The freed prisoner goes back down, his eyes are useless in the dark, and he loses the shadow-measuring competitions the prisoners hold. They conclude that going up ruins your eyes, and that anyone who tries to lead them out should be killed. Every reader in Athens would have thought of Socrates.

Plato is making a hard point. Those who see more are not thanked for it. To people comfortable with shadows, someone who questions them looks foolish at best and dangerous at worst. The cave is not only a picture of ignorance; it is a picture of how communities defend their ignorance.

But notice also what Plato says about the one who returns: he should not laugh at the prisoners, and those who see a confused person should ask whether the confusion comes from the dark or from the light. The philosopher's return, which is the subject of the fifth session, is meant to be an act of care, not contempt.
sections.key: The prisoners would kill the one who tries to free them: the cave is a picture of how communities defend their shadows, written with the death of Socrates in mind.

paras: The cave has been retold more often than almost any image in philosophy. The Neoplatonists of late antiquity read it as the soul's ascent to God. Christian writers, from Clement of Alexandria and Origen to Augustine, used its language of darkness, light and turning, though they disagreed with Plato about who does the freeing. In the Renaissance it was painted and preached on.

Modern readers have kept finding new shadows. The German philosopher Martin Heidegger, in an essay on 'Plato's Doctrine of Truth' (1940), argued that the cave marks the moment Western thought began to think of truth as correct seeing, rather than as unconcealment, and he regretted it. Films about simulated worlds, such as The Matrix (1999) and The Truman Show (1998), are often described as versions of the cave. Each age asks what its own shadows are: propaganda, advertising, screens. That is a tribute to Plato. But be careful: Plato's point is not only that our information is unreliable. It is that there is a higher reality, the forms and the Good, and that our souls are made to see it. The next session asks what he meant.
sections.key: The cave has been read as a picture of God's light, of the history of truth and of modern media. Plato's own point is stronger: there is a higher reality our souls are made to see.

refs: Plato, Republic VII.514a–521b (the cave and its interpretation); VI.507b–511e (the sun and the line, just before).
