debate.question: What is the cave really about?

positions.name: Knowledge: a map of the mind's climb
positions.who: Many modern commentators, for example Julia Annas, An Introduction to Plato's Republic (1981), and Nicholas White
positions.view: The cave illustrates Plato's theory of knowledge. Its stages correspond to the kinds of awareness on the divided line, from images to understanding of the forms. It is a picture of how a mind moves from belief to knowledge.
positions.evidence: Plato says the cave should be 'appended' to the previous argument (the sun and the line), and its stages are carefully graded; the lesson he draws is about education.

positions.name: Politics: a picture of the city and of Socrates' death
positions.who: Leo Strauss, The City and Man (1964), and readers in his tradition; also many historians
positions.view: The cave is the political community, held together by shared opinions, laws and stories. The philosopher who sees beyond them is a threat, as Socrates was. The image is about the permanent tension between philosophy and the city.
positions.evidence: The returning prisoner is mocked and threatened with death; he must fight 'in courts of law' about shadows of justice; the passage leads straight into the duty of philosophers to rule.

positions.name: Conversion: a picture of the soul turning to God
positions.who: The Neoplatonists (Plotinus, Proclus) and Christian readers from Augustine to modern scholars such as Werner Jaeger, Paideia (1939–44)
positions.view: The cave describes a turning of the whole person towards a divine source of light and goodness. It is closer to a religious conversion than to a lesson in method.
positions.evidence: The 'beatific vision', the 'divine element' in wisdom, the turning of the 'whole soul', and the Good as 'parent of light' and 'author of all things beautiful and right'.

debate.agree: All agree that the cave joins knowledge, ethics and politics: for Plato, seeing what is real changes how you live and what you owe to others.

look.why: There is no painting of Plato's cave in the National Gallery of Art, but Joseph Wright of Derby painted a shadow on a wall, made by a hidden light. The title refers to an ancient story, told by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, of a young woman of Corinth who traced the shadow of her lover on a wall before he went away, and so invented drawing. It is not the cave; it shows the cave's first stage, a shadow taken for a likeness.
points: A young woman leans forward, one knee on a wooden chair, and reaches out with a stylus to trace a shadow on the brown wall.
The shadow is cast by a young man who sleeps in the chair, in a yellow tunic and a blue cloak, with a spear across his shoulder and a thin dog asleep at his side.
The light falls from over our left shoulder; a deep red curtain bunched in the upper left corner hides where it comes from.
She is barefoot, smiles gently at his face, and looks at him rather than at the shadow she is drawing.
Urns stand and lie in the room; an arched opening leads into a darkened room on the right, with shelves and more urns deep in shadow.

music.why: James MacMillan's short choral setting (2007) of one of the ancient Advent antiphons, which calls on the radiant dawn, the sun of justice, to come and give light to those who sit in darkness. It is the Christian answer to the cave in one prayer: the light is asked to come down.

think.why: Plato is the greatest voice of Athens. See in brief how Greek reason and biblical faith became the two roots of the West.

learn.why: Plato's own conclusion from the cave: education is the turning of the whole soul. You may have learned it already; if so, say it again with the cave in mind.

check.q: Why do the prisoners believe the shadows are real?
options: Because the puppeteers tell them so
Because they have never seen anything else, and they all agree with one another about what they see
Because the shadows are very sharp and clear
Because they are too lazy to turn round
check.why: Chained since childhood, they have no other experience, and their shared language names only shadows. The third option is tempting, but Plato never says the carriers speak to them about the shadows.

check.q: What does Plato say the fire in the cave stands for?
options: The Good
Human reason
Philosophy
The sun in our sky
check.why: 'The light of the fire is the sun': even our sun belongs to the cave, the world of sight. The Good is represented by the sun outside, which is the first option's mistake.

check.q: Plato rejects the idea that education puts knowledge into the soul 'like sight into blind eyes'. What does he think instead, and why does it matter?
options: That only clever people can be educated
That knowledge cannot be taught at all, so teachers are useless
That education should concentrate on useful skills
That the soul already has the power to see, but must be turned round as a whole, desires included, towards what is real
check.why: The power is already there; it is facing the wrong way. Because the whole soul must turn, education involves habits and loves, not just information.

check.q: Why does the freed prisoner, when first shown the real objects, think the shadows are truer?
options: Because the shadows really are truer
Because the objects are only puppets
Because his eyes are hurt by the light and he clings to what is familiar
Because he wants to please the other prisoners
check.why: The glare and the shock make the familiar shadows seem more real. The third option contains a truth (the objects are carved figures), but it is not why he prefers the shadows.

check.q: What is Plato's point about the 'clever rogue'?
options: That rogues cannot be educated
That clever people are usually wicked
That intelligence alone is not wisdom: a mind turned the wrong way is more harmful the sharper it is
That the rogue is really blind
check.why: He is 'the reverse of blind', but his sight serves evil. Plato is not saying cleverness is bad, only that it needs to be turned.

check.q: Which reading best explains why Plato says the prisoners would kill anyone who tried to lead them up?
options: It is a prophecy of the death of Jesus
It recalls the death of Socrates and shows how a community defends its shared opinions against those who question them
It means the freed prisoner had become arrogant
It is a warning that philosophy is too dangerous to try
check.why: Plato wrote years after Athens executed Socrates for questioning it. Christians later saw a likeness to the cross, but that is a later reading, not Plato's meaning.

tutorial.question: 'Education is not what some people say it is.' Using the cave, explain what Plato thought education was, and say whether you agree.
tutorial.approach: Start with the view Plato rejects, knowledge put into the soul like sight into blind eyes. Then explain the cave's stages and what they stand for, using Plato's own key. Explain periagōgē, the turning of the whole soul, and why it involves desires as well as intellect. Use the clever rogue to show that knowing more is not the same as being educated. Then give your own view: is Plato right that we already have the power to see, and that education is mainly about direction rather than content?
strong: States the rejected view precisely and why it might seem natural.
Uses Plato's own key: the cave is the world of sight, the fire is the sun, the climb is the soul's ascent.
Explains that the climb is gradual, painful and has stages.
Explains the turning of the 'whole soul' and why appetites hold the soul's eye down.
Uses the clever rogue to show that intelligence without the right direction is dangerous.
Notices the political edge: the prisoners would kill the one who frees them, as Athens killed Socrates.
Offers a reasoned personal view, with an example from modern education.

reading.author: Plato, tr. Robin Waterfield
reading.title: Republic
reading.why: A clear modern translation with good notes (Oxford World's Classics).

reading.author: Julia Annas
reading.title: Plato: A Very Short Introduction
reading.why: A lively, short way in, by one of the leading scholars of Plato.

reading.author: Julia Annas
reading.title: An Introduction to Plato's Republic
reading.why: The standard guide to the whole Republic, argument by argument.

reading.author: Simon Blackburn
reading.title: Plato's Republic: A Biography
reading.why: The Republic and its readers through the centuries, wittily told.

reading.author: Myles Burnyeat
reading.title: 'Culture and Society in Plato's Republic' (Tanner Lectures)
reading.why: On education, culture and the turning of the soul.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each evening, name one opinion you have held for years simply because everyone around you holds it. Spend five minutes asking where it came from and what the strongest case against it would be. You are not trying to change your mind, only to turn your head.
sessions.reflect: What are the shadows on your own wall: the pictures of life you have taken for reality without ever checking? And who, if anyone, has ever helped you turn round?
takeaways: Plato's cave pictures us as prisoners who take shadows for reality; the freed prisoner climbs painfully to the sun and returns to help the others, who mock and would kill him.
Plato's key: the cave is the world of sight, the climb is the soul's ascent to what is known by the mind, and the sun outside is the Good.
Education, for Plato, is periagōgē: not filling an empty mind but turning the whole soul, desires included, towards the light.

sessions.title: The forms
sessions.line: Two sticks are never exactly equal, yet we all know what 'equal' means. Plato's answer to how: beyond the changing world are unchanging forms, Equality itself, Beauty itself, which the mind remembers.
sessions.plain: Plato noticed something strange. We have never seen two things that are perfectly equal, or a perfect circle, or a perfectly just act; yet we know what those would be, and we use that knowledge to judge everything we see. He concluded that there must be perfect, unchanging realities, which he called 'forms', that the mind knows even though the eyes never see them. In the Phaedo he argues that our souls must have known them before we were born, and that learning is really remembering.
sessions.why: In the cave, the freed prisoner climbed out and saw things in the daylight that were more real than the shadows. Now we ask what those more real things are. Plato's answer is his most famous and most argued-over idea: the forms. Without it nothing else in the journey, the soul, the Good or the just city, makes sense.
answers: What are Plato's forms?
Why did Plato think they must exist?
What does it mean that learning is remembering?
How do beautiful things relate to Beauty itself?
sessions.finding: Plato argued that beyond changing things are unchanging forms, Equality itself, Beauty itself, Justice itself, which the mind knows and the senses only glimpse; the soul that knows them must be akin to them.

paras: In the first session we read the cave. The prisoners see only shadows of carved objects. The freed prisoner, once outside, sees 'the objects themselves' in the sunlight. Plato said the cave is the world of sight, and the world outside is the 'intellectual world', known only by the mind. That is a large claim: that there is a world more real than the one we see. Now we look at his reasons for it.
background.key: In the cave, the things outside are more real than the shadows. This session asks what they are, and why Plato believed in them.

paras: Socrates spent his life asking 'what is it?' questions. What is courage? What is piety? What is justice? When people answered with examples, a brave soldier, a pious sacrifice, he said he did not want examples but the one thing that makes all of them brave or pious. In Plato's early dialogues nobody ever finds it. But the question assumes something: that there is one thing, the same in every case, to be found.

Plato took that assumption seriously. If there really is something that all just acts have in common, it is not itself any one just act. It is not in any one place or time, and it does not change when the examples do. Plato called it the eidos or idea of justice. The Greek words come from a root meaning 'to see', and mean 'look', 'shape' or 'kind'. English uses two translations: 'form' and 'idea'. Jowett often writes 'idea' or 'absolute', as in 'absolute equality'. Do not be misled by the English 'idea': for Plato a form is not a thought in someone's head. It is more real than any head.
background.key: Socrates asked what one thing makes all just acts just. Plato said that thing, the form or idea, really exists, unchanging, and is not in any one place or time.

paras: The main reading comes from the Phaedo, which tells the story of Socrates' last day in prison, and of his death at sunset. His friend Phaedo describes it afterwards to a man called Echecrates. If you have walked the Socrates journey, you have read its opening, where Socrates says philosophy is a practice for dying. Two young men from Thebes, Simmias and Cebes, are not convinced that the soul survives death. Socrates gives them several arguments. The one we read is the argument from recollection.

The comparison passage comes from the Republic, Book V. It is shorter, and puts the same idea another way: people who love beautiful things but cannot see Beauty itself are like dreamers who mistake a likeness for the real thing.
background.key: The Phaedo tells Socrates' last day; the reading is his argument that learning is recollection of forms the soul knew before birth.

paras: Plato never wrote a single treatise called 'the theory of forms'. The idea appears in many dialogues, in different ways. The passage in the Phaedo (72e–77a) is the clearest place where he argues for forms from something anyone can check: our experience of things that are nearly, but never exactly, equal. It answers the session's question directly, and it shows why Plato thought the forms and the soul belong together.
background.key: The Phaedo's argument from recollection is Plato's clearest case for the forms from ordinary experience, and it links the forms to the soul.

before: What example does Socrates use to show that we know something we have never seen?
What do the sticks and stones 'fall short' of?
Why does Socrates conclude that the soul existed before birth?
sessions.readWhy: Plato's clearest argument that the forms exist and that the soul knew them before birth.

paras: Cebes added: Your favorite doctrine, Socrates, that knowledge is simply recollection, if true, also necessarily implies a previous time in which we have learned that which we now recollect. But this would be impossible unless our soul had been in some place before existing in the form of man; here then is another proof of the soul's immortality.
But tell me, Cebes, said Simmias, interposing, what arguments are urged in favour of this doctrine of recollection. I am not very sure at the moment that I remember them.

One excellent proof, said Cebes, is afforded by questions. If you put a question to a person in a right way, he will give a true answer of himself, but how could he do this unless there were knowledge and right reason already in him? And this is most clearly shown when he is taken to a diagram or to anything of that sort. (Compare Meno.)

But if, said Socrates, you are still incredulous, Simmias, I would ask you whether you may not agree with me when you look at the matter in another way;--I mean, if you are still incredulous as to whether knowledge is recollection.

Incredulous, I am not, said Simmias; but I want to have this doctrine of recollection brought to my own recollection, and, from what Cebes has said, I am beginning to recollect and be convinced; but I should still like to hear what you were going to say.
This is what I would say, he replied:--We should agree, if I am not mistaken, that what a man recollects he must have known at some previous time.
Very true.

And what is the nature of this knowledge or recollection? I mean to ask, Whether a person who, having seen or heard or in any way perceived anything, knows not only that, but has a conception of something else which is the subject, not of the same but of some other kind of knowledge, may not be fairly said to recollect that of which he has the conception?
What do you mean?
I mean what I may illustrate by the following instance:--The knowledge of a lyre is not the same as the knowledge of a man?
True.

And yet what is the feeling of lovers when they recognize a lyre, or a garment, or anything else which the beloved has been in the habit of using? Do not they, from knowing the lyre, form in the mind's eye an image of the youth to whom the lyre belongs? And this is recollection. In like manner any one who sees Simmias may remember Cebes; and there are endless examples of the same thing.
Endless, indeed, replied Simmias.
And recollection is most commonly a process of recovering that which has been already forgotten through time and inattention.
Very true, he said.
Well; and may you not also from seeing the picture of a horse or a lyre remember a man? and from the picture of Simmias, you may be led to remember Cebes?
True.
Or you may also be led to the recollection of Simmias himself?
Quite so.
And in all these cases, the recollection may be derived from things either like or unlike?
It may be.
And when the recollection is derived from like things, then another consideration is sure to arise, which is--whether the likeness in any degree falls short or not of that which is recollected?
Very true, he said.

And shall we proceed a step further, and affirm that there is such a thing as equality, not of one piece of wood or stone with another, but that, over and above this, there is absolute equality? Shall we say so?
Say so, yes, replied Simmias, and swear to it, with all the confidence in life.
And do we know the nature of this absolute essence?
To be sure, he said.

And whence did we obtain our knowledge? Did we not see equalities of material things, such as pieces of wood and stones, and gather from them the idea of an equality which is different from them? For you will acknowledge that there is a difference. Or look at the matter in another way:--Do not the same pieces of wood or stone appear at one time equal, and at another time unequal?
That is certain.
But are real equals ever unequal? or is the idea of equality the same as of inequality?
Impossible, Socrates.
Then these (so-called) equals are not the same with the idea of equality?
I should say, clearly not, Socrates.
And yet from these equals, although differing from the idea of equality, you conceived and attained that idea?
Very true, he said.
Which might be like, or might be unlike them?
Yes.
But that makes no difference; whenever from seeing one thing you conceived another, whether like or unlike, there must surely have been an act of recollection?
Very true.

But what would you say of equal portions of wood and stone, or other material equals? and what is the impression produced by them? Are they equals in the same sense in which absolute equality is equal? or do they fall short of this perfect equality in a measure?
Yes, he said, in a very great measure too.

And must we not allow, that when I or any one, looking at any object, observes that the thing which he sees aims at being some other thing, but falls short of, and cannot be, that other thing, but is inferior, he who makes this observation must have had a previous knowledge of that to which the other, although similar, was inferior?
Certainly.
And has not this been our own case in the matter of equals and of absolute equality?
Precisely.
Then we must have known equality previously to the time when we first saw the material equals, and reflected that all these apparent equals strive to attain absolute equality, but fall short of it?
Very true.

And we recognize also that this absolute equality has only been known, and can only be known, through the medium of sight or touch, or of some other of the senses, which are all alike in this respect?
Yes, Socrates, as far as the argument is concerned, one of them is the same as the other.
From the senses then is derived the knowledge that all sensible things aim at an absolute equality of which they fall short?
Yes.

Then before we began to see or hear or perceive in any way, we must have had a knowledge of absolute equality, or we could not have referred to that standard the equals which are derived from the senses?--for to that they all aspire, and of that they fall short.
No other inference can be drawn from the previous statements.
And did we not see and hear and have the use of our other senses as soon as we were born?
Certainly.
Then we must have acquired the knowledge of equality at some previous time?
Yes.
That is to say, before we were born, I suppose?
True.

And if we acquired this knowledge before we were born, and were born having the use of it, then we also knew before we were born and at the instant of birth not only the equal or the greater or the less, but all other ideas; for we are not speaking only of equality, but of beauty, goodness, justice, holiness, and of all which we stamp with the name of essence in the dialectical process, both when we ask and when we answer questions. Of all this we may certainly affirm that we acquired the knowledge before birth?
We may.

But if, after having acquired, we have not forgotten what in each case we acquired, then we must always have come into life having knowledge, and shall always continue to know as long as life lasts--for knowing is the acquiring and retaining knowledge and not forgetting. Is not forgetting, Simmias, just the losing of knowledge?
Quite true, Socrates.

But if the knowledge which we acquired before birth was lost by us at birth, and if afterwards by the use of the senses we recovered what we previously knew, will not the process which we call learning be a recovering of the knowledge which is natural to us, and may not this be rightly termed recollection?
Very true.

So much is clear--that when we perceive something, either by the help of sight, or hearing, or some other sense, from that perception we are able to obtain a notion of some other thing like or unlike which is associated with it but has been forgotten. Whence, as I was saying, one of two alternatives follows:--either we had this knowledge at birth, and continued to know through life; or, after birth, those who are said to learn only remember, and learning is simply recollection.
Yes, that is quite true, Socrates.
And which alternative, Simmias, do you prefer? Had we the knowledge at our birth, or did we recollect the things which we knew previously to our birth?
I cannot decide at the moment.
At any rate you can decide whether he who has knowledge will or will not be able to render an account of his knowledge? What do you say?
Certainly, he will.
But do you think that every man is able to give an account of these very matters about which we are speaking?
Would that they could, Socrates, but I rather fear that to-morrow, at this time, there will no longer be any one alive who is able to give an account of them such as ought to be given.
Then you are not of opinion, Simmias, that all men know these things?
Certainly not.
They are in process of recollecting that which they learned before?
Certainly.
But when did our souls acquire this knowledge?--not since we were born as men?
Certainly not.
And therefore, previously?
Yes.
Then, Simmias, our souls must also have existed without bodies before they were in the form of man, and must have had intelligence.
Unless indeed you suppose, Socrates, that these notions are given us at the very moment of birth; for this is the only time which remains.
Yes, my friend, but if so, when do we lose them? for they are not in us when we are born--that is admitted. Do we lose them at the moment of receiving them, or if not at what other time?
No, Socrates, I perceive that I was unconsciously talking nonsense.

Then may we not say, Simmias, that if, as we are always repeating, there is an absolute beauty, and goodness, and an absolute essence of all things; and if to this, which is now discovered to have existed in our former state, we refer all our sensations, and with this compare them, finding these ideas to be pre-existent and our inborn possession--then our souls must have had a prior existence, but if not, there would be no force in the argument? There is the same proof that these ideas must have existed before we were born, as that our souls existed before we were born; and if not the ideas, then not the souls.

Yes, Socrates; I am convinced that there is precisely the same necessity for the one as for the other; and the argument retreats successfully to the position that the existence of the soul before birth cannot be separated from the existence of the essence of which you speak. For there is nothing which to my mind is so patent as that beauty, goodness, and the other notions of which you were just now speaking, have a most real and absolute existence; and I am satisfied with the proof.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Being reminded
parts.context: Socrates' cell in Athens, on the day he is to die, 399 BC. Cebes reminds the others of 'your favorite doctrine', that knowledge is recollection. '(Compare Meno.)' is Jowett's own note, pointing to another dialogue in which Socrates leads a slave boy, by questions alone, to solve a geometry problem he was never taught. Then Socrates begins with how memory works.
parts.plain: Cebes says that if learning is remembering, our souls must have existed before we were born. Socrates starts with simple examples of being reminded: a lover sees a lyre and thinks of the person who plays it; a picture of Simmias reminds you of Simmias. We can be reminded by things that are like or unlike what we remember. When the reminder is like it, we also notice whether it falls short.

commentary.on: knowledge is simply recollection
commentary.text: The Greek is anamnēsis, 'remembering again'. The claim is that when we learn certain things, we are not taking in something new but recovering what we already knew and had forgotten.

commentary.on: how could he do this unless there were knowledge and right reason already in him?
commentary.text: Cebes refers to an experiment Plato describes in the Meno (82b–85b). A slave boy who has never studied geometry is asked questions, and step by step works out how to double the area of a square. Socrates claims he has told him nothing. Where did the knowledge come from? From inside him, Plato says.

commentary.on: when they recognize a lyre, or a garment, or anything else which the beloved has been in the habit of using
commentary.text: Socrates begins with something everyone knows. You see a coat on a hook and think of the friend who wears it. The coat is not your friend, but it brings your friend to mind. Remembering is being led from one thing to another.

commentary.on: whether the likeness in any degree falls short or not of that which is recollected
commentary.text: This is the hinge of the argument. When a picture reminds you of a person, you can tell whether it is a good likeness. To do that, you must already know the person. Hold on to this.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Equality itself
parts.context: Socrates now turns from pictures and people to something more abstract: things we call equal, like two sticks or two stones of the same length. Jowett's 'absolute equality' translates the Greek 'the equal itself'.
parts.plain: There is equality itself, which is not the same as any two equal sticks. Equal sticks can look equal from one angle and unequal from another, but equality itself is never unequal. When we see equal sticks, they remind us of equality itself, and we notice that they fall short of it. To notice that something falls short of a standard, we must already know the standard. So we knew equality itself before we first used our senses.

commentary.on: over and above this, there is absolute equality
commentary.text: Here is a form. Not this equal pair of sticks, nor that one, but 'the equal itself'. Simmias agrees at once, 'with all the confidence in life'. Plato's readers, used to mathematics, would have found this natural: geometry is about perfect lines and circles, not the ones drawn in sand.

commentary.on: Do not the same pieces of wood or stone appear at one time equal, and at another time unequal?
commentary.text: Two sticks may be equal in length but unequal in thickness, or look equal from here and unequal from there. Visible equal things are never simply and always equal. That is the key difference between them and the form.

commentary.on: But are real equals ever unequal?
commentary.text: 'Real equals', Jowett's rendering of 'the equals themselves', can never be unequal. Equality itself is only and always equal. So it cannot be the same as any pair of sticks.

commentary.on: the thing which he sees aims at being some other thing, but falls short of, and cannot be, that other thing
commentary.text: A beautiful image: visible things 'aim at' or 'strive' to be like the form and never quite manage. The world we see is full of near-misses. That is what made it look, to Plato, like a world of copies.

commentary.on: he who makes this observation must have had a previous knowledge of that to which the other, although similar, was inferior
commentary.text: The heart of the argument. You can only judge that a portrait falls short if you know the face. You can only judge that two sticks fall short of perfect equality if you already know what perfect equality is. And you have never seen it.

commentary.on: we must have had a knowledge of absolute equality, or we could not have referred to that standard the equals which are derived from the senses
commentary.text: So the knowledge of the standard came first. Since we have used our senses since birth, Socrates says, we must have had this knowledge before birth. That is the step most readers find hardest to accept, and we will come back to it.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Before we were born
parts.context: Socrates draws the conclusion, and widens it from equality to all the forms: beauty, goodness, justice, holiness. Simmias' remark about 'to-morrow, at this time' is a reminder that Socrates will be dead by then.
parts.plain: We knew all the forms before birth, lost the knowledge at birth, and recover it through our senses: that is what learning is. Not everyone can give an account of these things, so most people are still in the process of remembering. The knowledge was not given at birth either, since we would have to lose it in the same moment. So our souls existed, and had intelligence, before they were in human bodies. If the forms exist, so did our souls.

commentary.on: not only the equal or the greater or the less, but all other ideas; for we are not speaking only of equality, but of beauty, goodness, justice, holiness
commentary.text: Now the argument widens. The same is true of the forms that matter most for living: Beauty, Goodness, Justice, Holiness. We judge that an act is unjust, or a face beautiful, by a standard we have never seen in any single case.

commentary.on: will not the process which we call learning be a recovering of the knowledge which is natural to us
commentary.text: Learning is recovering, and the knowledge is 'natural to us', our own. Compare the cave: 'the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already'. The two dialogues say the same thing in two pictures.

commentary.on: there will no longer be any one alive who is able to give an account of them such as ought to be given
commentary.text: A quiet, terrible line. Simmias means that after today, when Socrates is dead, nobody will be able to explain these things properly. Plato is showing us what was lost in 399 BC.

commentary.on: Do we lose them at the moment of receiving them
commentary.text: Simmias suggests that we might get the knowledge at the moment of birth. Socrates points out that we are not born knowing it, so we would have to lose it at the very moment we got it, which is absurd. Simmias admits he was 'talking nonsense'.

commentary.on: if not the ideas, then not the souls
commentary.text: The conclusion links the forms and the soul tightly together. If there are forms, the soul existed before birth; if there are no forms, the argument fails. Plato saw that his view of reality and his view of the soul stand or fall together.

commentary.on: beauty, goodness, and the other notions of which you were just now speaking, have a most real and absolute existence
commentary.text: Simmias' last words here are a statement of faith in the forms: nothing seems more obvious to him. Notice that Cebes is still not satisfied that the soul survives after death: the argument shows only that it existed before birth. The Phaedo goes on to other arguments.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy

paras: He said: Who then are the true philosophers?
Those, I said, who are lovers of the vision of truth.
That is also good, he said; but I should like to know what you mean?
To another, I replied, I might have a difficulty in explaining; but I am sure that you will admit a proposition which I am about to make.
What is the proposition?
That since beauty is the opposite of ugliness, they are two?
Certainly.
And inasmuch as they are two, each of them is one?
True again.

And of just and unjust, good and evil, and of every other class, the same remark holds: taken singly, each of them is one; but from the various combinations of them with actions and things and with one another, they are seen in all sorts of lights and appear many?
Very true.
And this is the distinction which I draw between the sight-loving, art-loving, practical class and those of whom I am speaking, and who are alone worthy of the name of philosophers.
How do you distinguish them? he said.

The lovers of sounds and sights, I replied, are, as I conceive, fond of fine tones and colours and forms and all the artificial products that are made out of them, but their mind is incapable of seeing or loving absolute beauty.
True, he replied.
Few are they who are able to attain to the sight of this.
Very true.

And he who, having a sense of beautiful things has no sense of absolute beauty, or who, if another lead him to a knowledge of that beauty is unable to follow—of such an one I ask, Is he awake or in a dream only? Reflect: is not the dreamer, sleeping or waking, one who likens dissimilar things, who puts the copy in the place of the real object?
I should certainly say that such an one was dreaming.

But take the case of the other, who recognises the existence of absolute beauty and is able to distinguish the idea from the objects which participate in the idea, neither putting the objects in the place of the idea nor the idea in the place of the objects—is he a dreamer, or is he awake?
He is wide awake.
And may we not say that the mind of the one who knows has knowledge, and that the mind of the other, who opines only, has opinion?
Certainly.

who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, even as Moses was warned by God when he was about to make the tabernacle, for he said, “See, you shall make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.”
Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.
For by this, the elders obtained testimony.
By faith, we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The lovers of sights
parts.context: Socrates and Glaucon, earlier in the same conversation as the cave. Glaucon has asked who the true philosophers are. 'The sight-loving, art-loving, practical class' were Athenians who went to every festival, play and performance.
parts.plain: Beauty and ugliness are each one thing, but they appear in many things and so seem many. Some people love beautiful sounds, colours and shapes but cannot see Beauty itself. They are like dreamers, who mistake a copy for the real thing. Those who can see Beauty itself, and tell it apart from the things that share in it, are awake.

commentary.on: taken singly, each of them is one; but from the various combinations of them with actions and things and with one another, they are seen in all sorts of lights and appear many
commentary.text: Beauty itself is one; beautiful things are many. A sunset, a face and a melody are all beautiful, in different ways. Plato says the many are beautiful by sharing in the one.

commentary.on: their mind is incapable of seeing or loving absolute beauty
commentary.text: These people are not shallow. They love beauty. But they love it only in its many appearances and cannot see what all of them have in common. They are stuck, as it were, with the shadows of beauty.

commentary.on: who puts the copy in the place of the real object
commentary.text: Plato's definition of dreaming: mistaking a copy for the real thing. In a dream, you think the dream is real. On this view most people spend their waking lives dreaming.

commentary.on: able to distinguish the idea from the objects which participate in the idea
commentary.text: 'Participate' is Plato's word for the relation between things and forms: beautiful things 'share in' or 'participate in' Beauty. This word will cause trouble, as Aristotle will point out.

parts.title: A copy and shadow
parts.context: The Letter to the Hebrews, written in polished Greek by an unknown Christian, probably before AD 70, to Jewish Christians. In chapter 8 the writer says the priests of the Jerusalem temple served 'a copy and shadow' of heavenly things, quoting God's words to Moses about the tent of worship (Exodus 25:40). In chapter 11 he defines faith.

commentary.on: who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things
commentary.text: This sounds very like Plato: the earthly is a shadow, the heavenly is real. The writer of Hebrews probably knew Greek ideas, as did the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC–AD 50), who read the Bible through Plato. But the difference matters: the 'heavenly things' here are not abstract forms but the presence of the living God.

commentary.on: according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain
commentary.text: In Exodus, Moses is shown a 'pattern' of the tabernacle on Mount Sinai, and builds the earthly tent to match it. Jews and Christians later compared this to Plato's forms. But Moses is shown the pattern by God; he does not remember it from before birth.

commentary.on: proof of things not seen
commentary.text: For Plato, the unseen forms are known by reason. For Hebrews, unseen things are grasped by faith, trust in God's word. Both agree that what we see is not all there is.

commentary.on: what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible
commentary.text: The visible world comes from something invisible. Plato would agree. But Hebrews says it was 'framed by the word of God': made by someone, from nothing visible, not copied from eternal forms that stand beside God.

compare.author: Plato
compare.why: In the Republic (V.475e–476d) Plato makes the same point without the argument about birth: some people love beautiful things but cannot see Beauty itself, and they are like people dreaming. Read it beside two passages from the Letter to the Hebrews, which also speak of a visible copy and an unseen reality.
compare.title: Dreaming and waking

paras: Plato never gives a complete list of the features of forms, and he describes them differently in different dialogues. But in the middle dialogues, the Phaedo, Symposium and Republic, a consistent picture appears. A form, such as Beauty itself, Equality itself or Justice itself, is:

rows: There is one Beauty itself, though many beautiful things
It does not come into being or pass away
Beauty itself is only beautiful, in every respect, to everyone
A face is beautiful from one angle, plain from another; beautiful to one person, not to another
It is grasped by thought, not seen or touched
Visible things are known by the senses
Beautiful things are beautiful because they share in Beauty
Things depend on forms; forms do not depend on things
table.note: Key passages: Phaedo 74a–c, 78c–79a, 100b–e; Symposium 211a–b; Republic V.476a–480a. The list is a summary; Plato himself never sets it out like this.

sections.key: A form is one, unchanging, pure, known by the mind, and the cause of the things that share in it.

paras: Plato had several reasons, and they are still discussed. First, the argument from imperfection, which we read in the Phaedo. We judge things by standards that nothing we see perfectly meets; so the standards are not taken from what we see.

Second, the argument from knowledge. Knowledge, Plato thought, must be of what is stable and true. If everything changed all the time, as the earlier philosopher Heraclitus suggested ('you cannot step into the same river twice'), there would be nothing to know. Mathematics seemed to show that there are truths that do not change: the angles of a triangle add up to two right angles, always and everywhere.
Third, the argument from meaning. When we call many different things 'beautiful' or 'just', we seem to mean one thing by the word. What is it? Not any one example. Something they all share.

Fourth, and for Plato perhaps most important, the argument from goodness. If justice were only what the powerful or the majority decide, there would be no way to say that a law or a city is unjust. Earlier in the Republic, Thrasymachus had argued that justice is 'the advantage of the stronger'. The forms are Plato's answer: there is a justice that is not anyone's opinion, by which every city and every person can be judged.
sections.key: Plato believed in forms because we judge by perfect standards we never see, because knowledge needs something stable, because words like 'just' mean one thing, and because justice must be more than power.

sections.h: Recollection, and what to make of it
paras: The Phaedo's argument goes further than the forms. It says our souls knew them before birth. Plato also gives this idea in the Meno, where a slave boy works out a geometry problem by answering questions, and in the Phaedrus, as a myth of souls who once saw the forms in a journey round the heavens.

Few philosophers now accept that we lived before birth. But many accept something nearby. The seventeenth-century philosopher René Descartes and others argued for 'innate ideas', knowledge that does not come from the senses. Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) argued that the mind brings its own structures to experience. Some modern linguists, following Noam Chomsky, have argued that children are born with a grasp of the deep structure of language. And when you solve a problem in mathematics, it can feel less like inventing than discovering something that was always true. Plato's question remains: where does that knowledge come from?

Christian thinkers kept Plato's question and changed his answer. Augustine (354–430) rejected the soul's existence before birth, but argued that we know eternal truths because God, the inner teacher, illuminates the mind. We will see in the last session what he did with Plato.
sections.key: Few now believe the soul lived before birth, but Plato's question, where knowledge not taken from the senses comes from, is still alive; Augustine answered it with God's light in the mind.

paras: If there is a form of Equality and of Beauty, is there a form of everything? Of bed, of horse, of mud? In the Republic (X.596a–b) Socrates speaks of a form of bed, which the carpenter looks to when he makes a bed. In the Parmenides (130c–d), a later dialogue, the young Socrates is asked whether there are forms of hair, mud and dirt, and he is embarrassed: he does not think so, but cannot say why not.

Scholars still argue about how far the forms extend. In the middle dialogues the forms Plato cares about most are the ones that matter for life and for mathematics: Justice, Beauty, Goodness, Holiness, Equality, the Large and the Small, Unity. They are standards, not merely kinds. The form of Justice is not just what all just things have in common; it is what justice ought to be, the perfect pattern.
sections.key: Plato speaks most of forms of values and mathematics, Justice, Beauty, Equality; he was unsure whether there were forms of everything, even mud.

paras: How exactly do beautiful things relate to Beauty itself? Plato uses several words: things 'share in' or 'participate in' forms; things 'resemble' or 'imitate' them, as copies; the form is 'present in' them. None of these is fully explained, and Plato knew it. In the Phaedo (100d) Socrates says he will not insist on the exact relation, only that 'by Beauty all beautiful things become beautiful'.

In the Parmenides Plato puts searching objections into the mouth of the old philosopher Parmenides. If a thing shares in a form, does it get the whole form or a part? If the whole, the form is in many places at once; if a part, a large thing shares in part of Largeness, which is smaller. And if large things and Largeness itself are all large, do we need another form to explain what they have in common, and then another, without end? This last objection was later called the 'third man' argument. Aristotle pressed it hard, and we will hear it at full strength in the sixth session.
It is remarkable that Plato wrote these objections himself. Whether he thought he could answer them, or changed his theory, or left the puzzle for his students, is one of the great debates about him.
sections.key: Plato never fully explained how things 'share in' forms, and in the Parmenides he set out the strongest objections, including what became the 'third man', himself.

paras: The reading ended by tying two things together: 'if not the ideas, then not the souls'. Later in the Phaedo (78b–80b), Socrates makes this explicit. There are two kinds of thing: the visible, which is many, changing and perishable, and the invisible, which is one, unchanging and lasting. The body belongs with the first; the soul, which can know the forms, is most like the second. When the soul uses the body to look at changing things, it 'wanders and is confused'; when it thinks by itself, it reaches what is 'pure and eternal' and is at rest.

This is Plato's view of what a human being is: a soul akin to the eternal, living for a time in a body. It explains why philosophy, in the Phaedo, is a 'practice for dying': loosening the soul's attachment to the changing world. It also raises the question of what the soul itself is like inside, which is the subject of the next session.
sections.key: For Plato, the soul is akin to the forms: unseen and lasting, like what it knows. That is why his view of reality and his view of the soul stand or fall together.

refs: Plato, Phaedo 72e–77a (recollection), 78b–80b (the soul akin to the forms), 100b–e (beautiful things are beautiful by Beauty); Meno 81a–86c (the slave boy); Symposium 210e–211b; Republic V.475e–480a; X.596a–b (the form of bed); Parmenides 130b–135c (objections, including the 'third man' at 132a–b).
Heraclitus, fragments B12 and B91 (Diels–Kranz), the rivers; Plato, Cratylus 402a.
Thrasymachus: Plato, Republic I.338c.
Augustine on illumination: The Teacher (De magistro) 11.38–12.40; Confessions X.10–11; on rejecting pre-existence, Retractations I.4.4 and I.8.2.
Modern: Gail Fine, On Ideas (1993); Richard Kraut (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Plato (1992), essays on the forms; Dominic Scott, Recollection and Experience (1995).

debate.question: Are Plato's forms real?

positions.name: Yes, at least for mathematics and values: Platonism
positions.who: Many mathematicians and philosophers of mathematics (Kurt Gödel; Roger Penrose, The Emperor's New Mind, 1989); in ethics, Iris Murdoch, The Sovereignty of Good (1970), in a modified form
positions.view: Numbers and mathematical truths are discovered, not invented; they would be true if no one existed. Something similar may be true of goodness: we are drawn by a Good we did not make. Plato's language may be poetic, but he saw something real.
positions.evidence: The 'unreasonable effectiveness' of mathematics in physics; the sense of discovery in proof; the way moral standards can judge whole societies.

positions.name: No: forms are words and concepts, not things
positions.who: Aristotle, against separate forms; medieval nominalists such as William of Ockham (d. 1347); most empiricists from Locke and Hume onwards
positions.view: There are only individual things. 'Beauty' and 'equality' are names for resemblances we notice, or concepts in our minds. Putting a separate perfect Beauty in another world explains nothing and doubles the world for no gain.
positions.evidence: We learn general words from examples; the problems of participation and the 'third man'; the success of science without forms.

positions.name: In things, and in the mind of God
positions.who: Augustine (On Eighty-Three Questions 46); Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I.15) and much of the Christian tradition; Aristotle for the first half
positions.view: There are real natures and standards, but they do not float on their own. They exist in things, as their real natures, and in the mind of God, as the patterns by which he made the world. Plato was right that there are standards, wrong to make them independent of God.
positions.evidence: The intelligibility of nature; the objectivity of moral truths; avoiding the problems of separate forms by placing the pattern in a mind.

debate.agree: All agree that Plato raised a real question: how we know what is general, perfect or ideal when every thing we meet is particular and imperfect.

look.why: No painting for this session. The forms, by Plato's own account, cannot be seen, and the gallery holds no painting of a geometric or idealised subject that would show them honestly.

music.why: Arvo Pärt's Spiegel im Spiegel (1978), 'mirror in the mirror': a single, unchanging pattern of notes on the piano, with a violin line moving slowly round it. Listen to it as a picture of Plato's world: a still pattern above, and an image that reaches towards it.

think.why: See how the great teachers, from Plato through Augustine to the medieval builders, thought beautiful things lead the mind to Beauty itself.

learn.why: Plato's other picture of the forms, from the Symposium: the ladder from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself. You may know it already from Why beauty matters; say it now as a description of the forms.

check.q: In the Phaedo, why does Socrates say we must have known 'absolute equality' before we first saw equal things?
options: Because equal sticks are rare
Because the senses always deceive us
Because we were taught it as children
Because to see that equal things fall short of perfect equality, we must already know the standard they fall short of
check.why: Judging a shortfall needs a prior grasp of the standard, as judging a portrait needs knowledge of the face. The third option goes further than Plato does: the senses remind us; they do not always deceive.

check.q: What is the main difference between two equal sticks and 'the equal itself'?
options: The equal itself is larger
Equal sticks can also appear unequal, in some respect or to some observer, but the equal itself is never unequal
Equal sticks are known by the mind, the equal itself by the senses
The sticks are made of wood
check.why: Visible equals are equal in one way and unequal in another; the form is purely and always what it is. The last option has the two the wrong way round.

check.q: Which of these is a form in Plato's sense?
options: A perfect drawing of a circle
The most beautiful person who ever lived
Beauty itself, by which all beautiful things are beautiful
The idea of justice in Plato's head
check.why: A form is not a perfect example, nor a thought in someone's mind; it is the one, unchanging reality that the many share in. The second option is the commonest misreading of the English word 'idea'.

check.q: Why does Plato think the forms and the soul 'stand or fall together'?
options: Because Socrates was about to die
Because both are invisible
Because souls are forms
Because the argument that learning is recollection requires both that the forms exist and that the soul knew them before birth
check.why: 'If not the ideas, then not the souls': the recollection argument depends on both. Plato later says the soul is like the forms, but not that it is one.

check.q: In Republic V, what does Plato mean by calling the lovers of sights 'dreamers'?
options: They have no interest in beauty
They sleep during performances
They love beauty too much
They mistake the many beautiful things, which are copies, for Beauty itself
check.why: Dreaming, for Plato, is putting the copy in place of the real object. These people love beauty but cannot see Beauty itself.

check.q: Hebrews speaks of 'a copy and shadow of the heavenly things'. What is the most important difference from Plato?
options: There is no difference
Hebrews thinks the visible world is evil
Hebrews was written in Hebrew
Hebrews places the reality behind the copy in the living God, who shows the pattern and frames the world by his word, rather than in eternal forms known by remembering
check.why: The language is close, and Greek ideas may lie behind it, but the source is a God who speaks and creates, grasped by faith. The first option is false: neither Plato nor Hebrews says the visible world is evil.

tutorial.question: Explain Plato's argument from recollection in the Phaedo, and assess it.
tutorial.approach: Set out the argument in steps: being reminded by like and unlike things; noticing shortfall; equal things and the equal itself; prior knowledge of the standard; knowledge before birth; the soul's prior existence. Then assess each step. Which do you accept? Is noticing imperfection really evidence of prior knowledge, or could we build the idea of perfect equality from examples? Compare later answers: innate ideas, Kant, Augustine's illumination.
strong: Sets out the steps of the argument clearly and in order.
Explains why equal sticks differ from the equal itself (they can appear unequal).
Identifies the key premise: noticing a shortfall requires knowing the standard.
Distinguishes the claim that we have knowledge not from the senses from the claim that we existed before birth.
Considers the empiricist reply that we form ideals by abstraction from examples.
Brings in at least one later version (innate ideas, Kant, Augustine) and says what it keeps and what it drops.
