sessions.practice: Live it this week: each day, notice one thing you judged as falling short: an unfair decision, a clumsy kindness, a nearly beautiful piece of music. Write down the standard you were measuring it by, and ask where you learned that standard.
sessions.reflect: When you say something is unjust, what are you measuring it against? Could that standard be only your opinion, and if it were, what would happen to the word 'unjust'?
takeaways: Plato's forms are the one, unchanging, perfect realities, such as Equality, Beauty and Justice, in which the many visible things share and which the mind, not the eye, knows.
In the Phaedo he argues that because we judge things as falling short of standards we have never seen, we must have known those standards before birth: learning is recollection.
Plato himself raised strong objections to the forms; Christians later kept his standards but placed them in the mind of God.

sessions.title: The soul in three parts
sessions.line: A man wants to drink and refuses; another stares at corpses and curses his own eyes. Plato's proof that the soul has parts, and his answer to what makes a person just.
sessions.plain: We all know what it is to be at war with ourselves: to want something and at the same time not want it. Plato took this experience seriously and concluded that the soul has three parts: reason, which thinks; spirit, which feels anger and pride; and appetite, which wants food, drink and pleasure. A person is just, he said, when reason rules, spirit backs it up, and appetite is kept in its place, as a city is just when each class does its own work.
sessions.why: In the cave the whole soul must turn towards the light; with the forms we learned what the light shows. But what is this soul that climbs, and why does it so often refuse to turn? The Phaedo spoke of the soul as one simple thing akin to the forms. The Republic looks inside and finds a divided self, and from that division builds an answer to the question the whole Republic asks: what is justice?
answers: What is the soul, for Plato?
What are the three parts of the soul, and how does he prove there are three?
What is justice in the Republic?
Why is a just person happier?
sessions.finding: Justice in the soul is reason ruling, spirit as its ally, and appetite kept in its place, as justice in the city is each class doing its own work: justice is an inner order before it is an outward act.

paras: The cave showed us prisoners who must be turned round, 'the whole soul' at once. The forms showed us what the freed soul sees: unchanging Beauty, Equality, Justice. And the Phaedo argued that the soul, which knows the forms, is like them: invisible and lasting. But if the soul is so akin to the eternal, why does it so often face the wrong way? Why do we know what is right and do what is wrong? Plato's answer is that the soul is not simple. It has parts, and they can fight.
background.key: The soul knows the forms, yet often faces the wrong way. Plato's explanation: it has parts, and they can fight.

background.h: Where we are in the Republic
paras: The Republic began with a challenge. In Book II Glaucon and Adeimantus asked Socrates to prove that justice is good in itself, not just for its rewards. Glaucon told the story of the ring of Gyges, which makes its wearer invisible: who would stay just if they could never be caught? (If you have walked Kings and prophets, you have read it.) Socrates said justice would be easier to see 'written in larger letters', in a city, and set out to build an ideal city in words.

By Book IV the city is built. It has three classes: rulers, called guardians, who are wise; auxiliaries, or soldiers, who are brave; and producers, farmers and craftsmen, who supply the city's needs. The city is wise because its rulers are, brave because its soldiers are, temperate because all agree who should rule, and just because each class does its own work and does not meddle in another's. Now Socrates turns back from the large letters to the small ones: the soul.

timeline.text: What is justice? Thrasymachus: the advantage of the stronger
Glaucon's challenge and the ring of Gyges; the city begins
The guardians' education; the noble lie
The three classes; justice in the city and in the soul
Women guardians; philosopher-kings
The sun, the line and the cave
How cities and souls decline; the tyrant
Poetry banished; the myth of Er

background.key: The Republic looks for justice in the city first, 'written large'. By Book IV the city has three classes; now Socrates looks for the same pattern in the soul.

paras: The reading (Republic IV.434d–444a, shortened) is the argument for the three parts of the soul and the definition of justice that follows. It is the centre of the Republic: the answer to its main question. It is also one of the first serious attempts in history to describe the inner conflicts of a human being.

The comparison is two short passages from the Bible. Proverbs, the collection of Israel's wise sayings, praises the one who rules his spirit. The Letter of James asks where wars and quarrels come from, and answers: from the desires that fight inside us. Both see the same inner war as Plato; neither divides the soul the way he does.
background.key: The reading is the centre of the Republic: the three parts of the soul, and justice as their right order.

before: What rule does Socrates use to prove that the soul has more than one part?
What does the story of Leontius show?
In the end, is justice for Plato mainly about how you treat others, or about something inside you?
sessions.readWhy: Plato's argument that the soul has three parts, and his definition of justice as their right order.

paras: We will not, I said, be over-positive as yet; but if, on trial, this conception of justice be verified in the individual as well as in the State, there will be no longer any room for doubt; if it be not verified, we must have a fresh enquiry. First let us complete the old investigation, which we began, as you remember, under the impression that, if we could previously examine justice on the larger scale, there would be less difficulty in discerning her in the individual. That larger example appeared to be the State, and accordingly we constructed as good a one as we could, knowing well that in the good State justice would be found. Let the discovery which we made be now applied to the individual—if they agree, we shall be satisfied; or, if there be a difference in the individual, we will come back to the State and have another trial of the theory. The friction of the two when rubbed together may possibly strike a light in which justice will shine forth, and the vision which is then revealed we will fix in our souls.
That will be in regular course; let us do as you say.
I proceeded to ask: When two things, a greater and less, are called by the same name, are they like or unlike in so far as they are called the same?
Like, he replied.
The just man then, if we regard the idea of justice only, will be like the just State?
He will.

And a State was thought by us to be just when the three classes in the State severally did their own business; and also thought to be temperate and valiant and wise by reason of certain other affections and qualities of these same classes?
True, he said.

And so of the individual; we may assume that he has the same three principles in his own soul which are found in the State; and he may be rightly described in the same terms, because he is affected in the same manner?
Certainly, he said.

But the question is not quite so easy when we proceed to ask whether these principles are three or one; whether, that is to say, we learn with one part of our nature, are angry with another, and with a third part desire the satisfaction of our natural appetites; or whether the whole soul comes into play in each sort of action—to determine that is the difficulty.
Yes, he said; there lies the difficulty.
Then let us now try and determine whether they are the same or different.
How can we? he asked.

I replied as follows: The same thing clearly cannot act or be acted upon in the same part or in relation to the same thing at the same time, in contrary ways; and therefore whenever this contradiction occurs in things apparently the same, we know that they are really not the same, but different.
Then the soul of the thirsty one, in so far as he is thirsty, desires only drink; for this he yearns and tries to obtain it?
That is plain.

And if you suppose something which pulls a thirsty soul away from drink, that must be different from the thirsty principle which draws him like a beast to drink; for, as we were saying, the same thing cannot at the same time with the same part of itself act in contrary ways about the same.
Impossible.
No more than you can say that the hands of the archer push and pull the bow at the same time, but what you say is that one hand pushes and the other pulls.
Exactly so, he replied.
And might a man be thirsty, and yet unwilling to drink?
Yes, he said, it constantly happens.

And in such a case what is one to say? Would you not say that there was something in the soul bidding a man to drink, and something else forbidding him, which is other and stronger than the principle which bids him?
I should say so.
And the forbidding principle is derived from reason, and that which bids and attracts proceeds from passion and disease?
Clearly.

Then we may fairly assume that they are two, and that they differ from one another; the one with which a man reasons, we may call the rational principle of the soul, the other, with which he loves and hungers and thirsts and feels the flutterings of any other desire, may be termed the irrational or appetitive, the ally of sundry pleasures and satisfactions?
Yes, he said, we may fairly assume them to be different.
Then let us finally determine that there are two principles existing in the soul. And what of passion, or spirit? Is it a third, or akin to one of the preceding?
I should be inclined to say—akin to desire.

Well, I said, there is a story which I remember to have heard, and in which I put faith. The story is, that Leontius, the son of Aglaion, coming up one day from the Piraeus, under the north wall on the outside, observed some dead bodies lying on the ground at the place of execution. He felt a desire to see them, and also a dread and abhorrence of them; for a time he struggled and covered his eyes, but at length the desire got the better of him; and forcing them open, he ran up to the dead bodies, saying, Look, ye wretches, take your fill of the fair sight.
I have heard the story myself, he said.
The moral of the tale is, that anger at times goes to war with desire, as though they were two distinct things.
Yes; that is the meaning, he said.

And are there not many other cases in which we observe that when a man’s desires violently prevail over his reason, he reviles himself, and is angry at the violence within him, and that in this struggle, which is like the struggle of factions in a State, his spirit is on the side of his reason;—but for the passionate or spirited element to take part with the desires when reason decides that she should not be opposed, is a sort of thing which I believe that you never observed occurring in yourself, nor, as I should imagine, in any one else?
Certainly not.

Suppose that a man thinks he has done a wrong to another, the nobler he is the less able is he to feel indignant at any suffering, such as hunger, or cold, or any other pain which the injured person may inflict upon him—these he deems to be just, and, as I say, his anger refuses to be excited by them.
True, he said.

But when he thinks that he is the sufferer of the wrong, then he boils and chafes, and is on the side of what he believes to be justice; and because he suffers hunger or cold or other pain he is only the more determined to persevere and conquer. His noble spirit will not be quelled until he either slays or is slain; or until he hears the voice of the shepherd, that is, reason, bidding his dog bark no more.
The illustration is perfect, he replied; and in our State, as we were saying, the auxiliaries were to be dogs, and to hear the voice of the rulers, who are their shepherds.
I perceive, I said, that you quite understand me; there is, however, a further point which I wish you to consider.
What point?

You remember that passion or spirit appeared at first sight to be a kind of desire, but now we should say quite the contrary; for in the conflict of the soul spirit is arrayed on the side of the rational principle.
Most assuredly.

But a further question arises: Is passion different from reason also, or only a kind of reason; in which latter case, instead of three principles in the soul, there will only be two, the rational and the concupiscent; or rather, as the State was composed of three classes, traders, auxiliaries, counsellors, so may there not be in the individual soul a third element which is passion or spirit, and when not corrupted by bad education is the natural auxiliary of reason?
Yes, he said, there must be a third.
Yes, I replied, if passion, which has already been shown to be different from desire, turn out also to be different from reason.

But that is easily proved:—We may observe even in young children that they are full of spirit almost as soon as they are born, whereas some of them never seem to attain to the use of reason, and most of them late enough.

Excellent, I said, and you may see passion equally in brute animals, which is a further proof of the truth of what you are saying. And we may once more appeal to the words of Homer, which have been already quoted by us,
‘He smote his breast, and thus rebuked his soul,’
for in this verse Homer has clearly supposed the power which reasons about the better and worse to be different from the unreasoning anger which is rebuked by it.
Very true, he said.
And so, after much tossing, we have reached land, and are fairly agreed that the same principles which exist in the State exist also in the individual, and that they are three in number.
Exactly.
We cannot but remember that the justice of the State consisted in each of the three classes doing the work of its own class?
We are not very likely to have forgotten, he said.
We must recollect that the individual in whom the several qualities of his nature do their own work will be just, and will do his own work?
Yes, he said, we must remember that too.
And ought not the rational principle, which is wise, and has the care of the whole soul, to rule, and the passionate or spirited principle to be the subject and ally?
Certainly.

And, as we were saying, the united influence of music and gymnastic will bring them into accord, nerving and sustaining the reason with noble words and lessons, and moderating and soothing and civilizing the wildness of passion by harmony and rhythm?
Quite true, he said.

And these two, thus nurtured and educated, and having learned truly to know their own functions, will rule over the concupiscent, which in each of us is the largest part of the soul and by nature most insatiable of gain; over this they will keep guard, lest, waxing great and strong with the fulness of bodily pleasures, as they are termed, the concupiscent soul, no longer confined to her own sphere, should attempt to enslave and rule those who are not her natural-born subjects, and overturn the whole life of man?
Very true, he said.

Both together will they not be the best defenders of the whole soul and the whole body against attacks from without; the one counselling, and the other fighting under his leader, and courageously executing his commands and counsels?
True.
And he is to be deemed courageous whose spirit retains in pleasure and in pain the commands of reason about what he ought or ought not to fear?
Right, he replied.

And him we call wise who has in him that little part which rules, and which proclaims these commands; that part too being supposed to have a knowledge of what is for the interest of each of the three parts and of the whole?
Assuredly.

And would you not say that he is temperate who has these same elements in friendly harmony, in whom the one ruling principle of reason, and the two subject ones of spirit and desire are equally agreed that reason ought to rule, and do not rebel?
Certainly, he said, that is the true account of temperance whether in the State or individual.

And the division of labour which required the carpenter and the shoemaker and the rest of the citizens to be doing each his own business, and not another’s, was a shadow of justice, and for that reason it was of use?
Clearly.

But in reality justice was such as we were describing, being concerned however, not with the outward man, but with the inward, which is the true self and concernment of man: for the just man does not permit the several elements within him to interfere with one another, or any of them to do the work of others,—he sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself; and when he has bound together the three principles within him, which may be compared to the higher, lower, and middle notes of the scale, and the intermediate intervals—when he has bound all these together, and is no longer many, but has become one entirely temperate and perfectly adjusted nature, then he proceeds to act, if he has to act, whether in a matter of property, or in the treatment of the body, or in some affair of politics or private business; always thinking and calling that which preserves and co-operates with this harmonious condition, just and good action, and the knowledge which presides over it, wisdom, and that which at any time impairs this condition, he will call unjust action, and the opinion which presides over it ignorance.
You have said the exact truth, Socrates.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The large letters and the small
parts.context: Socrates and Glaucon have just found justice in the ideal city: each of the three classes doing its own work. Now Socrates tests whether the same account works for a single person. 'Principles' here means parts or elements of the soul.
parts.plain: We should not be too sure yet. If what we found in the city is also true of the individual, we can be confident; if not, we must look again. A just person will be like a just city. The city was just when its three classes each did their own work, so if a person is just in the same way, the soul must have the same three parts.

commentary.on: The friction of the two when rubbed together may possibly strike a light in which justice will shine forth
commentary.text: Socrates compares the method to rubbing two sticks together to make fire. The city and the soul are to be compared back and forth until justice becomes visible in both. Notice the language of light again.

commentary.on: the three classes in the State severally did their own business
commentary.text: This is the definition of justice in the city: each class doing 'its own business', ta hautou prattein. Not equality, not fairness in the modern sense, but each doing its proper part in a well-ordered whole.

commentary.on: he has the same three principles in his own soul which are found in the State
commentary.text: The great assumption of the Republic: city and soul have the same structure. Plato does not simply assert it; he goes on to argue that the soul really has three parts. Whether the analogy holds is still debated.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: One thing, or three?
parts.context: Socrates admits the question is hard: does the whole soul act in everything we do, or do we learn with one part, get angry with another and desire with a third? He lays down a principle to settle it.
parts.plain: The hard question is whether we do these things with one soul or three parts. The rule is this: one and the same thing cannot do or suffer opposite things, in the same part of itself, in relation to the same thing, at the same time. So if we find the soul doing opposite things at once, there must be more than one part.

commentary.on: we learn with one part of our nature, are angry with another, and with a third part desire the satisfaction of our natural appetites
commentary.text: Here are the three candidates: learning (reason), anger (spirit), desire (appetite). The question is whether these are three activities of one soul or three different parts.

commentary.on: The same thing clearly cannot act or be acted upon in the same part or in relation to the same thing at the same time, in contrary ways
commentary.text: This is sometimes called the principle of opposites, an early version of the law of non-contradiction. If you find a single thing apparently doing two opposite things at once, it is not really a single thing in that respect. Plato then uses it like a surgeon's knife on the soul.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Thirst, Leontius and the angry heart
parts.context: Socrates has spent some pages making the principle precise (cut here, marked '…'). Now he applies it, first to thirst, then to anger. Leontius was a real Athenian; the Piraeus is the harbour of Athens, joined to the city by long walls, and executed criminals were left outside them. 'Concupiscent' means desiring. The line from Homer is Odysseus, in disguise in his own house, holding back his rage at the suitors (Odyssey XX.17).
parts.plain: Thirst, simply as thirst, wants drink. But a man can be thirsty and refuse to drink. Something in him bids him drink and something forbids it, so there are two parts: reason, which forbids, and appetite, which bids. Is anger a third? Leontius wanted to look at corpses and was disgusted with himself, and in the end looked, cursing his own eyes: anger fought desire, on reason's side. Anger is not reason either, since children and animals are full of spirit but have no reason. So there are three parts.

commentary.on: the thirsty principle which draws him like a beast to drink
commentary.text: Thirst on its own simply wants drink, as an animal wants it. It does not want good drink or healthy drink; judging that is someone else's job. Plato is isolating appetite in its pure form.

commentary.on: And might a man be thirsty, and yet unwilling to drink?
commentary.text: Everyone has felt this: the thirsty patient told not to drink before an operation, the person who wants another glass and decides against it. By the principle of opposites, one part wants and another refuses.

commentary.on: the one with which a man reasons, we may call the rational principle of the soul
commentary.text: So the first division is made: reason, which calculates what is best, and appetite, 'the irrational or appetitive', which 'loves and hungers and thirsts'. The 'flutterings' of desire is a vivid phrase.

commentary.on: Look, ye wretches, take your fill of the fair sight
commentary.text: The most famous moment of the argument. Leontius wants to look at the dead bodies and is disgusted with himself for wanting to. At last he gives in, and shouts at his own eyes as if they were someone else. The anger is real, and it is aimed at his own desire. So anger is not just another desire.

commentary.on: his spirit is on the side of his reason
commentary.text: Spirit, thumos, is the part that feels indignation, shame and pride. When desire overpowers reason, spirit takes reason's side and is angry with the self. Plato says he has never seen spirit side with desire against reason, which many readers have doubted.

commentary.on: His noble spirit will not be quelled until he either slays or is slain; or until he hears the voice of the shepherd, that is, reason, bidding his dog bark no more
commentary.text: Spirit is like a good sheepdog: fierce for justice, but it should obey the shepherd. Plato is not against anger. He thinks righteous anger is part of a good soul, so long as reason guides it.

commentary.on: full of spirit almost as soon as they are born, whereas some of them never seem to attain to the use of reason
commentary.text: The proof that spirit is not reason: babies rage long before they reason, and animals have spirit without reason. So spirit is a third thing.

commentary.on: He smote his breast, and thus rebuked his soul
commentary.text: Plato quotes Homer once more. Odysseus, back in his own house in disguise, watches the suitors' outrages and has to stop himself killing them at once. One part of him speaks to another, and that, Plato says, is reason rebuking anger.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Justice within
parts.context: Having found three parts, Socrates now applies the virtues of the city to the soul (some lines are cut, marked '…'). 'Music and gymnastic' was the Greek name for education of the mind and of the body. The 'higher, lower, and middle notes of the scale' are the strings of a lyre, tuned together.
parts.plain: Reason should rule, because it is wise and cares for the whole soul; spirit should be its ally. Education in music and exercise tunes them together, and both guard appetite, which is the largest part and never satisfied. A person is brave when spirit holds to reason's commands, wise when reason knows what is good for all three, temperate when all three agree reason should rule. Justice is each part doing its own work. Real justice is not about outward acts but about the inner self: a person who has made the three parts one, like a tuned lyre.

commentary.on: the rational principle, which is wise, and has the care of the whole soul, to rule
commentary.text: Reason rules not because it is superior in some snobbish sense, but because it alone 'has the care of the whole soul': it alone can think about what is good for all the parts together, as appetite cannot.

commentary.on: the concupiscent, which in each of us is the largest part of the soul and by nature most insatiable of gain
commentary.text: Appetite is the largest part, and it is never full. Give it more and it wants more. Plato's worry is not that we have desires, but that unchecked they 'enslave and rule' the whole person. He will describe exactly that in the tyrant of Book IX.

commentary.on: he is temperate who has these same elements in friendly harmony
commentary.text: Temperance, sōphrosynē, is not grim self-denial. It is 'friendly harmony': all three parts agree that reason should lead, and 'do not rebel'. The temperate person is not at war with himself.

commentary.on: was a shadow of justice
commentary.text: The city's division of labour, each person doing one job, was only 'a shadow of justice', an outward image. We are back in the language of the cave. The real thing is inside.

commentary.on: not with the outward man, but with the inward, which is the true self and concernment of man
commentary.text: This is Plato's great reversal. We usually think of justice as how we treat others: not stealing, keeping promises. Plato says that is the result. Justice itself is the right order of the soul, 'the true self'. Just actions flow from a just soul.

commentary.on: is no longer many, but has become one entirely temperate and perfectly adjusted nature
commentary.text: The just person 'has become one'. The divided self has been made whole, tuned like a lyre. This is why, for Plato, justice is not a cost but a benefit: the unjust person is at war inside, the just person at peace. That is his answer to Glaucon's ring of Gyges.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy

paras:
One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty;
one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.
Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.

parts.title: One who rules his spirit
parts.context: The Book of Proverbs, a collection of Israel's wise sayings, gathered over centuries and traditionally linked with King Solomon (tenth century BC). Most of chapter 16 is single-line sayings about the Lord's guidance and human character.

commentary.on: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty
commentary.text: Proverbs, like Plato, sees anger as a force that must be governed. It does not say anger is evil; it says being slow to it is greater than strength.

commentary.on: one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city
commentary.text: A striking match with the Republic: the soul as a city, and self-rule as a greater victory than conquest. The Hebrew word for 'spirit' here, ruach, is broader than Plato's thumos: it means breath, spirit and temper. But the picture of the self as a city to be ruled is the same.

parts.title: Your pleasures that war in your members
parts.context: The Letter of James, a short, practical letter traditionally ascribed to James the brother of Jesus, leader of the church in Jerusalem until his death in AD 62. He is writing to Christian communities troubled by quarrels.

commentary.on: Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
commentary.text: James traces outward quarrels to an inner war of desires, as Plato traces the just city to the just soul. 'Members' means the parts of the body, and so of the self.

commentary.on: You don’t have, because you don’t ask
commentary.text: Here James parts from Plato. The cure is not only reason ruling desire, but turning to God and asking. For Plato the soul orders itself by reason; for James it needs help from outside itself.

compare.why: The Bible knows the inner war Plato describes. Read two short passages, one from the oldest wisdom of Israel and one from a first-century Christian letter, and ask how they explain it.
compare.title: The war inside, in Israel's wisdom

paras: The Republic's method is an analogy: find justice in a city, where it is 'written large', then read it in the soul, where it is written small. Plato does not simply assume the analogy works. He argues separately that the soul has three parts, using the thirsty man and Leontius. But the analogy shapes the whole book. The three classes of the city match the three parts of the soul, and the four virtues of the city, wisdom, courage, temperance and justice, match four virtues of the soul.

Critics have asked whether the match is too neat. The philosopher Bernard Williams, in a well-known paper of 1973, argued that the analogy creates problems: if a city is just when each citizen is just, then the producers must be ruled by reason in their own souls, but they are defined as the people ruled by appetite. Plato's defenders reply that the analogy is about structure, not about every citizen. The debate shows how much hangs on it.

rows: Thinks, calculates, knows what is good for the whole person
Feels anger at injustice, pride, shame, the will to fight for what is right
Wants food, drink, sex and the money that buys them
table.note: Temperance is the agreement of all three parts that reason should rule; justice is each part doing its own work (Republic IV.441e–443b).

sections.key: The Republic reads justice in the city 'written large', then in the soul: three classes match three parts, and the four virtues of each match. Whether the analogy holds is still argued.

paras: Reason is not just cleverness. It is the part that loves truth and can think about the good of the whole person. In Book IX Plato says each part has its own love: reason loves learning, spirit loves honour and victory, appetite loves gain, because money buys what it wants.

Spirit, thumos, is the most surprising part, and the hardest to translate. It is the part that gets angry at injustice, feels shame and pride, wants to be respected, and will fight. Homer's heroes are full of it; Achilles' wrath is thumos gone wild. Plato thinks it is not bad. Well trained, it becomes courage: holding to what reason says is truly to be feared, 'in pleasure and in pain'. Badly trained, it becomes rage or vanity.

Appetite is the largest part and the least reasonable: it simply wants. Plato later divides its desires into necessary ones, like eating enough, and unnecessary ones that grow wild if fed (Republic VIII.558d–559c). Appetite is not evil, any more than a horse is evil; but it cannot steer.
sections.key: Reason loves truth and cares for the whole; spirit loves honour and can become courage or rage; appetite simply wants, and cannot steer.

paras: Plato gave this same three-part soul its most memorable picture in another dialogue, the Phaedrus (246a–254e). If you have walked Dust that wonders, you have read it. The soul is like a charioteer driving two winged horses. One horse is noble, upright and obedient, moved by a sense of honour and shame: that is spirit. The other is crooked and unruly, deaf to the whip, dragging towards pleasure: that is appetite. The charioteer is reason. Driving is hard, Plato says, and the soul's flight to the heavens, where it once saw the forms, depends on how well he drives.

The picture adds something the Republic's argument leaves out: the parts of the soul have to be trained, and the training is a struggle. The good horse helps the charioteer hold back the bad one. That is exactly Leontius's experience, and ours.
sections.key: In the Phaedrus the soul is a charioteer (reason) driving a noble horse (spirit) and an unruly one (appetite): the same three parts, as a struggle to be won.

paras: From the three parts come four virtues, and Plato is the first to set them out as a group. Wisdom belongs to reason, when it knows what is good for each part and the whole. Courage belongs to spirit, when it holds to reason's judgment under pressure. Temperance is the agreement of all three that reason should rule. Justice is each part doing its own work.

These four had a long life. The Jewish Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek in Alexandria in the first century BC, lists them (8:7). Cicero and the Stoics taught them. Christian writers, from Ambrose of Milan in the fourth century, called them the 'cardinal' virtues, from the Latin cardo, a hinge, because the moral life turns on them, and added the three 'theological' virtues of faith, hope and love. You will meet them again, in full, in the hall of the Good Life.

Notice one thing about Plato's justice. It is not first a rule for how to treat others. It is the health of the soul. A just person does not steal, break promises or betray friends, Plato says, but because each part of him is doing its own work, not because he has learned a list of rules.
sections.key: Plato first set out the four virtues, wisdom, courage, temperance and justice; Christians called them cardinal, 'hinge', virtues. For Plato justice is the soul's health, from which just acts follow.

paras: Now we can see Plato's answer to Glaucon. Glaucon asked: if you had the ring of Gyges, why be just? Plato's answer is that injustice is a disease of the soul. The unjust person is ruled by appetite or by a wild spirit; his reason serves them as a slave. He is at war with himself, 'many', not 'one'. In Book IX Plato describes the tyrant, who has the most power of all and is the most miserable, because he is ruled inside by a single mad desire and can trust no one.

So justice is worth having for its own sake, as health is. No one, Plato says, would choose to live with a ruined body even with all the wealth in the world; why choose to live with a ruined soul? This is perhaps the most important argument in the Republic. It is also the hardest to prove: it depends on accepting that the soul has a health, a right order, given by its nature. That is a claim about what a human being is, not just about behaviour.
sections.key: Plato's answer to the ring of Gyges: injustice is a disease of the soul, disorder and civil war within; justice is its health, worth having for itself.

paras: Plato's division has had many descendants. Aristotle kept a reasoning and a non-reasoning part of the soul, but treated them as capacities of one living thing, not separate agents. Sigmund Freud's id, ego and super-ego (1923) are often compared to Plato's three parts, though Freud's super-ego is not Plato's reason. Modern psychologists such as Daniel Kahneman, in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), distinguish quick, automatic thinking from slow, effortful thinking. None of these is the same as Plato's scheme, but all agree with him that the mind is not one simple voice.

Christian thinkers took the experience but not quite the analysis. Paul writes of 'another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind' (Romans 7:23), a passage read in full in a later hall. Augustine, reading Paul, decided that the deepest division is not between reason and desire but within the will itself: we want and do not want at the same time, and cannot heal ourselves. Plato thought education could order the soul. Augustine thought it needed grace. That disagreement will return at the end of this journey.
sections.key: Aristotle, Freud and modern psychology all keep something of Plato's divided soul; Paul and Augustine kept the inner war but located it in the will, and thought it needed grace to heal.

refs: Plato, Republic II.357a–367e (Glaucon's challenge), II.368c–369a (larger letters), IV.427d–444e (the virtues of city and soul), VIII.558d–559c (necessary and unnecessary desires), IX.571a–592b (the tyrant; the three loves at 580d–581c); Phaedrus 246a–254e (the charioteer).
Homer, Odyssey XX.17–18 (Odysseus rebukes his heart).
Bernard Williams, 'The Analogy of City and Soul in Plato's Republic' (1973), in Exegesis and Argument, ed. Lee, Mourelatos and Rorty.
Wisdom of Solomon 8:7; Cicero, On Duties I.15; Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy I.24 (the cardinal virtues).
Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.13; De Anima III.9–10.
Sigmund Freud, The Ego and the Id (1923); Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).
Romans 7:14–25; Augustine, Confessions VIII.9–10.

debate.question: Does the soul have parts?

positions.name: Yes, three: Plato
positions.who: Plato, Republic IV and Phaedrus; defended in modified form by modern scholars such as John Cooper and Hendrik Lorenz (The Brute Within, 2006)
positions.view: We find in ourselves opposite motions at the same moment, wanting and refusing, desiring and being disgusted at the desire. By the principle of opposites these must belong to different parts. Reason, spirit and appetite each have their own aims and loves.
positions.evidence: The thirsty man who will not drink; Leontius; children and animals with spirit but no reason; the common experience of inner conflict.

positions.name: No: one soul with many powers
positions.who: Aristotle (De Anima II–III; Nicomachean Ethics I.13); later Thomas Aquinas
positions.view: The soul is the form, the life, of a living body. It has many capacities, nourishing, sensing, desiring, thinking, but they are powers of one thing, not little persons inside. To speak of parts fighting is a metaphor; it is the whole person who wants and the whole person who refuses.
positions.evidence: The unity of experience; the way reason and desire shape each other in a trained character, so that a good person comes to want what is good.

positions.name: The division is in the will, and needs healing
positions.who: Paul (Romans 7); Augustine (Confessions VIII); the Christian tradition after them
positions.view: The deepest conflict is not between reason and appetite but within the will itself, which commands and is not obeyed. Knowing the good, as Plato's reason does, is not enough; the will must be healed and re-ordered by love, which is God's gift.
positions.evidence: Augustine's experience that he could order his hand to move but not his will to want; the common failure of good intentions.

debate.agree: All agree that inner conflict is real and that a good life needs the parts or powers of the self brought into harmony; they disagree about what the parts are and how harmony comes.

look.why: Lorenzo Lotto's small panel of 1505, which the gallery calls an Allegory of Virtue and Vice, is not of Plato's soul. But it divides one landscape in two along a broken tree: on one side the instruments of learning and a path climbing to the clouds, on the other a satyr, half man and half goat, with his wine urn and a stormy sea. It is a picture of the same choice Plato describes.
points: In the middle stands a thick tree trunk, broken off abruptly, with one tall shoot of green leaves growing from it.
On the right a satyr with a man's body and goat's legs reclines on green grass, peering with an exaggerated smile into a golden urn; red and white liquids pour out near him.
Behind the satyr a choppy sea stretches into the distance under steel-grey clouds, and a masted ship is being swallowed by the waves.
On the left, on stony ground, a pale, naked child crouches among a compass, small red books, a square, a flute, pan pipes and a scroll.
Beyond the child, a small figure with dark forms on shoulders, arms, hips and ankles, perhaps wings, climbs a path up towards the clouds.
Two shields hang on and lean against the tree, one with an open-mouthed face, one with a white rearing lion on a blue field.

music.why: Hildegard of Bingen's 'O virtus Sapientiae', a twelfth-century chant to Wisdom, which she pictures circling everything and holding it together. Listen to it as the Christian answer to Plato's question of what should rule the soul: not reason alone, but Wisdom, which for Hildegard is God's own.

think.why: Plato's soul, Aristotle's and the Christian soul, and what the great teachers said a person is, set beside today's question about minds and machines.

learn.why: Israel's one-line version of Plato's just soul: the greatest city to rule is yourself.

check.q: Why does a man who is thirsty but refuses to drink show, for Plato, that the soul has at least two parts?
options: Because one and the same thing cannot do opposite things in the same respect at the same time, so what bids and what forbids must be different
Because thirst is a bodily feeling, not part of the soul
Because the man is confused
Because reason is always stronger than appetite
check.why: The principle of opposites: bidding and forbidding at once means two sources. The third option is false: Plato knows appetite often wins.

check.q: What does the story of Leontius show?
options: That reason is weak
That anger can fight against desire on reason's side, so spirit is different from appetite
That the Athenians mistreated criminals
That curiosity is wicked
check.why: Leontius is angry with his own desire to look. So spirit is not just another appetite. The last option is a true fact about the setting, but not the point.

check.q: Why does Plato say reason should rule the soul?
options: Because it alone can think about what is good for the whole soul, as appetite and spirit cannot
Because it is the largest part
Because the gods command it
Because it is the most ancient part
check.why: Reason 'has the care of the whole soul'. Appetite is in fact the largest part, which is the mistake in the first option.

check.q: According to Plato, what is justice, in the end?
options: Doing good to friends and harm to enemies
An inner order of the soul in which each part does its own work; just acts follow from it
Giving everyone exactly the same
Obeying the laws of the city
check.why: Justice concerns 'not the outward man, but the inward'. The last option is an answer considered and rejected in Book I.

check.q: How does Plato's account of the soul answer Glaucon's ring of Gyges?
options: It argues that injustice is a disease and civil war of the soul, so the just person is better off even if never rewarded
It shows that the gods will punish the unjust
It shows that the unjust are always caught
It shows that the ring cannot exist
check.why: Justice is worth having for itself, like health. Plato does add rewards in Book X, but that is not this argument.

check.q: What is the main difference between Plato and James on the inner war?
options: James thinks anger is always good
Plato thinks the war cannot be won
James denies that people have desires
Plato thinks reason, trained by education, can order the soul; James points beyond the self, to asking God
check.why: Both see warring desires; James adds 'you don't have, because you don't ask'. For Plato the soul orders itself by reason.

tutorial.question: 'Justice is not a matter of how we treat others, but of how our soul is ordered.' Explain Plato's view and assess it.
tutorial.approach: Explain the analogy of city and soul and the three classes. Set out the argument for three parts of the soul from the principle of opposites, the thirsty man and Leontius. Explain the four virtues and the definition of justice as each part doing its own work. Then assess: does an inner order guarantee just treatment of others? Could someone be inwardly ordered and still cruel? How does this answer Glaucon? Bring in Aristotle or Augustine as a critic.
strong: Explains the city–soul analogy and the definition of justice in the city.
Sets out the principle of opposites and both arguments (thirst; Leontius) accurately.
Distinguishes the three parts and their loves, and matches the four virtues to them.
Explains why justice is 'inward' for Plato and how just acts follow from it.
Raises the objection that inner order might not guarantee just treatment of others (a gap noted by David Sachs, 1963).
Uses a later critic (Aristotle on one soul; Augustine on the will) to test Plato's view.

reading.author: Plato, tr. Robin Waterfield

reading.author: Hendrik Lorenz

reading.author: David Sachs

sessions.practice: Live it this week: when you notice an inner argument, wanting something and not wanting it, stop for a moment and name the three voices, as Plato would: what does appetite want, what does spirit feel, what does reason say is good for the whole of you? Then let reason decide, and notice how it feels afterwards.
sessions.reflect: Which part of your soul most often takes the reins: appetite, spirit or reason? What would it take for them to be, as Plato says, in 'friendly harmony'?
takeaways: Plato argued from the principle of opposites, the thirsty man and Leontius that the soul has three parts: reason, spirit and appetite.
Justice in the soul, like justice in the city, is each part doing its own work: reason ruling, spirit its ally, appetite kept in place; the four virtues follow from this order.
For Plato justice is the health of the soul and worth having for itself; Christians kept the inner war but placed it in the will, and looked for its healing to grace.

sessions.title: The sun and the Good
sessions.line: Socrates will not say what the Good is. Instead he points to the sun, which lets us see and makes things grow. The highest thing in Plato's world, and whether it is God.
sessions.plain: At the top of the cave is the sun, and Plato says the sun stands for 'the Good'. Just as the sun gives light so that eyes can see and things can be seen, and makes things grow, so the Good makes everything understandable and gives everything its very being, while being 'beyond being' itself. This is Plato's highest idea, and for two thousand years people have asked whether he was describing God.
sessions.why: The cave showed the freed prisoner seeing the sun last of all. The forms gave us what he sees in the daylight; the soul gave us the one who climbs. Now we reach the top: the light that makes all the rest visible. Plato says this is 'the greatest thing to learn', and without it the whole climb has no point.
answers: What is the Good in Plato?
What does the sun stand for in the cave?
What is the divided line?
Did Plato believe in God?
sessions.finding: The highest form, the Good, is like the sun: it makes things knowable and gives them being, and is itself 'beyond being'; later Platonists and Christians read it as a name for God.

paras: In the cave, the last thing the freed prisoner sees is the sun 'in his own proper place'. Plato said the sun outside the cave stands for 'the idea of good', 'seen only with an effort', 'the universal author of all things beautiful and right'. We have met the forms, Beauty, Equality, Justice, and the three-part soul that can rise to know them. But what is the Good, and why is it above all the others?
background.key: In the cave the sun outside stands for the Good, the last and hardest thing to see. This session asks what it is.

background.h: Where we are in the Republic
paras: In Book V Socrates proposed that philosophers should rule the ideal city, because they love and know the forms. In Book VI Adeimantus asks what the philosophers must learn. Socrates says the greatest study of all is the 'idea of good', because only by it do just and beautiful things become useful and good. Glaucon presses him to say what it is. Socrates refuses, and offers three images instead, one after another: the sun, the divided line and the cave. We read the first two now. Plato wrote them before the cave; we have climbed the cave first so that you know where they lead.
background.key: In Republic VI Socrates refuses to define the Good and offers three images instead: the sun, the line and, after them, the cave.

paras: The reading is the sun (Republic VI.506b–509c) and the divided line that follows it (509d–511e). Together they are Plato's most direct statement of what the Good is and how the mind climbs to it. They answer the session's questions as directly as Plato ever did; his reticence is part of the answer.

The comparison is from Psalm 36, a Hebrew psalm of uncertain date, which speaks of God as the spring of life and says 'in your light we will see light'. Set it beside Plato's sun and ask what the two have in common and where they part.
background.key: We read the sun and the divided line from Republic VI, then Psalm 36: 'in your light we will see light'.

before: Why does Socrates refuse to say what the Good is?
What three things does the sun do, in the analogy, and what are their counterparts?
What does it mean that the Good is 'not essence, but far exceeds essence'?
sessions.readWhy: Plato's own images of the highest thing in his philosophy, the Good, and of the mind's climb towards it.

paras: Of course, he replied; but I wish that you would tell me whether you conceive this supreme principle of the good to be knowledge or pleasure, or different from either?
Aye, I said, I knew all along that a fastidious gentleman like you would not be contented with the thoughts of other people about these matters.
True, Socrates; but I must say that one who like you has passed a lifetime in the study of philosophy should not be always repeating the opinions of others, and never telling his own.
Well, but has any one a right to say positively what he does not know?
Not, he said, with the assurance of positive certainty; he has no right to do that: but he may say what he thinks, as a matter of opinion.

And do you not know, I said, that all mere opinions are bad, and the best of them blind? You would not deny that those who have any true notion without intelligence are only like blind men who feel their way along the road?
Very true.
And do you wish to behold what is blind and crooked and base, when others will tell you of brightness and beauty?

Still, I must implore you, Socrates, said Glaucon, not to turn away just as you are reaching the goal; if you will only give such an explanation of the good as you have already given of justice and temperance and the other virtues, we shall be satisfied.

Yes, my friend, and I shall be at least equally satisfied, but I cannot help fearing that I shall fail, and that my indiscreet zeal will bring ridicule upon me. No, sweet sirs, let us not at present ask what is the actual nature of the good, for to reach what is now in my thoughts would be an effort too great for me. But of the child of the good who is likest him, I would fain speak, if I could be sure that you wished to hear—otherwise, not.
By all means, he said, tell us about the child, and you shall remain in our debt for the account of the parent.

I do indeed wish, I replied, that I could pay, and you receive, the account of the parent, and not, as now, of the offspring only; take, however, this latter by way of interest, and at the same time have a care that I do not render a false account, although I have no intention of deceiving you.
Yes, we will take all the care that we can: proceed.
Yes, I said, but I must first come to an understanding with you, and remind you of what I have mentioned in the course of this discussion, and at many other times.
What?
The old story, that there is a many beautiful and a many good, and so of other things which we describe and define; to all of them the term ‘many’ is applied.
True, he said.

And there is an absolute beauty and an absolute good, and of other things to which the term ‘many’ is applied there is an absolute; for they may be brought under a single idea, which is called the essence of each.
Very true.
The many, as we say, are seen but not known, and the ideas are known but not seen.
Exactly.
And what is the organ with which we see the visible things?
The sight, he said.
And with the hearing, I said, we hear, and with the other senses perceive the other objects of sense?
True.
But have you remarked that sight is by far the most costly and complex piece of workmanship which the artificer of the senses ever contrived?
No, I never have, he said.
Then reflect; has the ear or voice need of any third or additional nature in order that the one may be able to hear and the other to be heard?
Nothing of the sort.
No, indeed, I replied; and the same is true of most, if not all, the other senses—you would not say that any of them requires such an addition?
Certainly not.
But you see that without the addition of some other nature there is no seeing or being seen?
How do you mean?

Sight being, as I conceive, in the eyes, and he who has eyes wanting to see; colour being also present in them, still unless there be a third nature specially adapted to the purpose, the owner of the eyes will see nothing and the colours will be invisible.
Of what nature are you speaking?
Of that which you term light, I replied.
True, he said.
Noble, then, is the bond which links together sight and visibility, and great beyond other bonds by no small difference of nature; for light is their bond, and light is no ignoble thing?
Nay, he said, the reverse of ignoble.
And which, I said, of the gods in heaven would you say was the lord of this element? Whose is that light which makes the eye to see perfectly and the visible to appear?
You mean the sun, as you and all mankind say.
May not the relation of sight to this deity be described as follows?
How?
Neither sight nor the eye in which sight resides is the sun?
No.
Yet of all the organs of sense the eye is the most like the sun?
By far the most like.
And the power which the eye possesses is a sort of effluence which is dispensed from the sun?
Exactly.
Then the sun is not sight, but the author of sight who is recognised by sight?
True, he said.

And this is he whom I call the child of the good, whom the good begat in his own likeness, to be in the visible world, in relation to sight and the things of sight, what the good is in the intellectual world in relation to mind and the things of mind:
Will you be a little more explicit? he said.

Why, you know, I said, that the eyes, when a person directs them towards objects on which the light of day is no longer shining, but the moon and stars only, see dimly, and are nearly blind; they seem to have no clearness of vision in them?
Very true.
But when they are directed towards objects on which the sun shines, they see clearly and there is sight in them?
Certainly.

And the soul is like the eye: when resting upon that on which truth and being shine, the soul perceives and understands, and is radiant with intelligence; but when turned towards the twilight of becoming and perishing, then she has opinion only, and goes blinking about, and is first of one opinion and then of another, and seems to have no intelligence?
Just so.

Now, that which imparts truth to the known and the power of knowing to the knower is what I would have you term the idea of good, and this you will deem to be the cause of science, and of truth in so far as the latter becomes the subject of knowledge; beautiful too, as are both truth and knowledge, you will be right in esteeming this other nature as more beautiful than either; and, as in the previous instance, light and sight may be truly said to be like the sun, and yet not to be the sun, so in this other sphere, science and truth may be deemed to be like the good, but not the good; the good has a place of honour yet higher.
What a wonder of beauty that must be, he said, which is the author of science and truth, and yet surpasses them in beauty; for you surely cannot mean to say that pleasure is the good?
God forbid, I replied; but may I ask you to consider the image in another point of view?
In what point of view?
You would say, would you not, that the sun is not only the author of visibility in all visible things, but of generation and nourishment and growth, though he himself is not generation?
Certainly.

In like manner the good may be said to be not only the author of knowledge to all things known, but of their being and essence, and yet the good is not essence, but far exceeds essence in dignity and power.
Glaucon said, with a ludicrous earnestness: By the light of heaven, how amazing!
Yes, I said, and the exaggeration may be set down to you; for you made me utter my fancies.
And pray continue to utter them; at any rate let us hear if there is anything more to be said about the similitude of the sun.
Yes, I said, there is a great deal more.
Then omit nothing, however slight.
I will do my best, I said; but I should think that a great deal will have to be omitted.
I hope not, he said.

You have to imagine, then, that there are two ruling powers, and that one of them is set over the intellectual world, the other over the visible. I do not say heaven, lest you should fancy that I am playing upon the name (‘ourhanoz, orhatoz’). May I suppose that you have this distinction of the visible and intelligible fixed in your mind?
I have.

Now take a line which has been cut into two unequal parts, and divide each of them again in the same proportion, and suppose the two main divisions to answer, one to the visible and the other to the intelligible, and then compare the subdivisions in respect of their clearness and want of clearness, and you will find that the first section in the sphere of the visible consists of images. And by images I mean, in the first place, shadows, and in the second place, reflections in water and in solid, smooth and polished bodies and the like: Do you understand?
Yes, I understand.
Imagine, now, the other section, of which this is only the resemblance, to include the animals which we see, and everything that grows or is made.
Very good.
Would you not admit that both the sections of this division have different degrees of truth, and that the copy is to the original as the sphere of opinion is to the sphere of knowledge?
Most undoubtedly.
Next proceed to consider the manner in which the sphere of the intellectual is to be divided.
In what manner?

Thus:—There are two subdivisions, in the lower of which the soul uses the figures given by the former division as images; the enquiry can only be hypothetical, and instead of going upwards to a principle descends to the other end; in the higher of the two, the soul passes out of hypotheses, and goes up to a principle which is above hypotheses, making no use of images as in the former case, but proceeding only in and through the ideas themselves.
I do not quite understand your meaning, he said.

Then I will try again; you will understand me better when I have made some preliminary remarks. You are aware that students of geometry, arithmetic, and the kindred sciences assume the odd and the even and the figures and three kinds of angles and the like in their several branches of science; these are their hypotheses, which they and every body are supposed to know, and therefore they do not deign to give any account of them either to themselves or others; but they begin with them, and go on until they arrive at last, and in a consistent manner, at their conclusion?
Yes, he said, I know.

And do you not know also that although they make use of the visible forms and reason about them, they are thinking not of these, but of the ideals which they resemble; not of the figures which they draw, but of the absolute square and the absolute diameter, and so on—the forms which they draw or make, and which have shadows and reflections in water of their own, are converted by them into images, but they are really seeking to behold the things themselves, which can only be seen with the eye of the mind?
That is true.

And of this kind I spoke as the intelligible, although in the search after it the soul is compelled to use hypotheses; not ascending to a first principle, because she is unable to rise above the region of hypothesis, but employing the objects of which the shadows below are resemblances in their turn as images, they having in relation to the shadows and reflections of them a greater distinctness, and therefore a higher value.
I understand, he said, that you are speaking of the province of geometry and the sister arts.

And when I speak of the other division of the intelligible, you will understand me to speak of that other sort of knowledge which reason herself attains by the power of dialectic, using the hypotheses not as first principles, but only as hypotheses—that is to say, as steps and points of departure into a world which is above hypotheses, in order that she may soar beyond them to the first principle of the whole; and clinging to this and then to that which depends on this, by successive steps she descends again without the aid of any sensible object, from ideas, through ideas, and in ideas she ends.

I understand you, he replied; not perfectly, for you seem to me to be describing a task which is really tremendous; but, at any rate, I understand you to say that knowledge and being, which the science of dialectic contemplates, are clearer than the notions of the arts, as they are termed, which proceed from hypotheses only: these are also contemplated by the understanding, and not by the senses: yet, because they start from hypotheses and do not ascend to a principle, those who contemplate them appear to you not to exercise the higher reason upon them, although when a first principle is added to them they are cognizable by the higher reason. And the habit which is concerned with geometry and the cognate sciences I suppose that you would term understanding and not reason, as being intermediate between opinion and reason.

You have quite conceived my meaning, I said; and now, corresponding to these four divisions, let there be four faculties in the soul—reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, faith (or conviction) to the third, and perception of shadows to the last—and let there be a scale of them, and let us suppose that the several faculties have clearness in the same degree that their objects have truth.
I understand, he replied, and give my assent, and accept your arrangement.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Glaucon asks
parts.context: Socrates has just said that rulers who do not know the Good will be 'sorry guardians' of justice and beauty. Glaucon wants to know what Socrates himself thinks the Good is: knowledge, pleasure or something else.
parts.plain: Glaucon asks Socrates what he thinks the Good is. Socrates says that opinions without knowledge are blind, and he does not want to give a blind opinion. Glaucon begs him to go on. Socrates says that to say what the Good itself is would be too much for him now; instead he will speak of its 'child', the thing most like it, and Glaucon can take that as interest on a debt.

commentary.on: whether you conceive this supreme principle of the good to be knowledge or pleasure, or different from either?
commentary.text: Glaucon names the two popular answers of the day. Some said the good life was pleasure; the cleverer said it was knowledge. Socrates has just pointed out that both answers break down, because there are bad pleasures, and 'knowledge' must be knowledge of the good, which goes in a circle.

commentary.on: all mere opinions are bad, and the best of them blind
commentary.text: Socrates refuses to offer an opinion about the Good, because an opinion, even a true one, is 'blind': it does not see why it is true. This is a philosopher's honesty about the limits of what he can say.

commentary.on: let us not at present ask what is the actual nature of the good, for to reach what is now in my thoughts would be an effort too great for me
commentary.text: At the climax of the Republic, Plato has Socrates stop short. Some readers think Plato was being modest; some that he thought the Good could not be put into words; some that it was taught only in conversation at the Academy. Aristotle reports that Plato once gave a public lecture 'On the Good' that baffled its audience by being about mathematics.

commentary.on: But of the child of the good who is likest him, I would fain speak
commentary.text: Instead of the father, Socrates offers the child. The Greek word for interest on a loan, tokos, also means 'offspring', so Plato is punning: the child is the interest on the debt.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The sun
parts.context: Socrates first reminds Glaucon of the difference between the many beautiful things and Beauty itself. Then he points out something unusual about sight. 'The artificer of the senses' is whoever made us, a craftsman god.
parts.plain: There are many beautiful things, which we see, and Beauty itself, which we know but do not see. Sight is unlike the other senses: hearing needs only an ear and a sound, but seeing needs a third thing, light, to join eye and object. The sun is the lord of light. It is not sight, but it causes sight, and the eye is the most sun-like of the senses. The sun is the 'child of the good': it is in the visible world what the Good is in the world of the mind.

commentary.on: The many, as we say, are seen but not known, and the ideas are known but not seen
commentary.text: The whole theory of forms in one sentence. The many beautiful things are seen; Beauty itself is known. Two worlds, two ways of grasping them.

commentary.on: without the addition of some other nature there is no seeing or being seen
commentary.text: This is the clever observation the analogy rests on. You can have good eyes and a coloured object in front of you, and still see nothing, in the dark. Sight needs a third thing that is neither the eye nor the object.

commentary.on: for light is their bond, and light is no ignoble thing?
commentary.text: Light 'yokes' or binds sight and the seen together. Keep this in mind: Plato will say the Good does the same for the mind and what it knows.

commentary.on: Then the sun is not sight, but the author of sight who is recognised by sight?
commentary.text: The sun causes sight, and is also seen by it. In the same way, the Good causes knowledge and is also known, though only last of all.

commentary.on: this is he whom I call the child of the good, whom the good begat in his own likeness
commentary.text: A remarkable phrase. The sun is the Good's offspring, made 'in his own likeness', and stands in the visible world as the Good stands in the world of the mind. Christian readers could not help hearing echoes of the Son begotten of the Father, though Plato meant nothing of the kind.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Beyond being
parts.context: Socrates now spells out the analogy. 'Science' in Jowett's English means knowledge, epistēmē. 'Essence' and 'being' translate the Greek ousia, what something is. 'Generation' means coming into being.
parts.plain: When light shines on things, the eyes see clearly; in twilight they see dimly. So with the soul: when it looks at what truth and being shine on, it understands; when it looks at the changing world, it has only opinions. The Good gives truth to what is known and the power of knowing to the knower. It is more beautiful than truth and knowledge. And as the sun makes things grow without being growth, the Good gives things their very being, while it is not being, but beyond it in dignity and power.

commentary.on: when turned towards the twilight of becoming and perishing, then she has opinion only, and goes blinking about
commentary.text: The soul is like the eye. Turned towards the changing world, the 'twilight of becoming', it blinks and shifts from one opinion to another. Turned towards what is lit by truth, it sees. We are back with the turning of the soul in the cave.

commentary.on: that which imparts truth to the known and the power of knowing to the knower is what I would have you term the idea of good
commentary.text: The first thing the Good does: it makes knowledge possible, on both sides. It makes things intelligible, and minds able to understand. Without it there would be facts, perhaps, but nothing would make sense.

commentary.on: the good has a place of honour yet higher
commentary.text: Truth and knowledge are 'like the good, but not the good', as light and sight are like the sun but are not the sun. The Good is above even truth.

commentary.on: the sun is not only the author of visibility in all visible things, but of generation and nourishment and growth, though he himself is not generation
commentary.text: The second thing the sun does: it makes things grow. Plants live by sunlight, but the sun is not a plant.

commentary.on: the good is not essence, but far exceeds essence in dignity and power
commentary.text: The most famous and puzzling sentence in Plato. The Greek is epekeina tēs ousias, 'beyond being'. The Good gives everything else its being, but is not one more thing that exists alongside them. It is the source of being, as the sun is the source of growth. This one phrase shaped the whole later tradition of thinking about God as beyond all our categories.

commentary.on: By the light of heaven, how amazing!
commentary.text: Glaucon's reaction, which Socrates teases as 'ludicrous earnestness', is Plato's own touch of comedy at the highest point. He knows how strange this sounds.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The divided line
parts.context: Socrates' second image. Imagine a line cut into two unequal parts, the visible and the intelligible, and each part cut again in the same proportion, making four sections. Jowett's '(‘ourhanoz, orhatoz’)' is a garbled transliteration of two Greek words, ouranos (heaven) and horatos (visible), on which Socrates says he will not pun. 'Dialectic' is philosophical reasoning by question and answer.
parts.plain: Take a line divided into the visible and the intelligible, each divided again. The lowest section is images: shadows and reflections. Next come the real things they are images of: animals, plants, made things. In the intelligible part, the lower section is mathematics, which uses visible diagrams and starts from assumptions it does not prove. The highest is philosophy, which uses no images and climbs past all assumptions to the first principle of everything, the Good, then comes back down through the forms. Four sections, four states of mind: imagining, belief, thinking and understanding.

commentary.on: the first section in the sphere of the visible consists of images. And by images I mean, in the first place, shadows
commentary.text: The lowest level of the line is exactly where the prisoners in the cave sit: among shadows and reflections. The two images, line and cave, belong together.

commentary.on: the copy is to the original as the sphere of opinion is to the sphere of knowledge
commentary.text: The key proportion. A reflection is to the real thing as all of the visible world is to the world of forms. The visible world is itself a kind of image.

commentary.on: they are thinking not of these, but of the ideals which they resemble; not of the figures which they draw, but of the absolute square and the absolute diameter
commentary.text: A geometer draws a square in the sand, but his proof is about the perfect square, not the wobbly drawing. Mathematics already takes the mind beyond what it sees. That is why Plato thought mathematics the right training for philosophers.

commentary.on: in order that she may soar beyond them to the first principle of the whole
commentary.text: Mathematics starts from assumptions it does not question. Philosophy questions them, climbing to 'the first principle of the whole', which is the Good, the one thing that needs no further explanation. Then it comes back down, understanding everything in its light.

commentary.on: reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, faith (or conviction) to the third, and perception of shadows to the last
commentary.text: Four states of mind for four levels of reality. Scholars use the Greek names: noēsis (understanding or reason), dianoia (thinking, as in mathematics), pistis (belief, here 'faith' or 'conviction', about ordinary things) and eikasia (imagining, about images). Jowett's 'faith' here does not mean religious faith; it means confident belief about the visible world.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy

paras:
Your loving kindness, Yahweh, is in the heavens.
Your faithfulness reaches to the skies.

Your righteousness is like the mountains of God.
Your judgments are like a great deep.
Yahweh, you preserve man and animal.

How precious is your loving kindness, God!
The children of men take refuge under the shadow of your wings.

They shall be abundantly satisfied with the abundance of your house.
You will make them drink of the river of your pleasures.

For with you is the spring of life.
In your light we will see light.

parts.title: The spring of life
parts.context: Psalm 36, one of the psalms headed 'of David', from the hymn book of the Jerusalem temple; its date is uncertain. Its first verses describe a wicked man who flatters himself and plots harm. Then the psalmist turns to God. 'Yahweh' is the personal name of the God of Israel, usually written 'the Lord' in English Bibles.

commentary.on: Your loving kindness, Yahweh, is in the heavens
commentary.text: The psalm begins where Plato does not: with God's 'loving kindness', in Hebrew chesed, faithful love that keeps its promises. Plato's Good is the source of being and knowing; the psalmist's God is that and also faithful, loving and near.

commentary.on: The children of men take refuge under the shadow of your wings
commentary.text: In Plato shadows are what we must escape. Here the 'shadow' of God's wings is a shelter, like a bird protecting its young. The same image, opposite meanings.

commentary.on: For with you is the spring of life
commentary.text: As Plato's sun gives 'generation and nourishment and growth', God here is the 'spring' or fountain of life. Both see the highest reality as the source of all living.

commentary.on: In your light we will see light
commentary.text: Very close to Plato: we do not see the light by our own power, but by the light itself. Augustine and many Christian thinkers quoted this verse to explain how the mind knows truth. The difference is that the psalm says 'your' light: it is spoken to someone.

compare.why: A Hebrew psalm speaks of God in the language Plato used for the Good: the source of life and of light, by whose light we see. Read it beside the sun. (If you have walked Light, stone and glass, you have read 1 John 1:5: 'God is light, and in him is no darkness at all'.)
