sections.h: Why the Good is the highest
paras: Why does Plato put the Good above Beauty, Justice and all the other forms? Because, he says, it is what makes them worth knowing. A guardian who knew what justice was, but not why it was good, would be a 'sorry guardian' of it. Everything we want, we want because we think it good; and unlike justice or beauty, 'no one is satisfied with the appearance of good—the reality is what they seek' (VI.505d). People will settle for seeming just; nobody wants only to seem to be well off.

The Good is also what makes the forms knowable and gives them their being. Each form is a perfect standard: perfect Justice, perfect Equality. What makes them perfect, Plato seems to say, is the Good. It is the principle of order, harmony and value in everything. To understand anything fully is to see how it is good, what it is for and why it is as it should be.
sections.key: The Good is highest because it is what everyone really seeks, and because it makes all the forms knowable, real and worth knowing.

paras: The sun passage is an analogy in three parts, and it helps to set it out side by side. Each thing in the visible world on the left has its counterpart in the intelligible world on the right.

rows: Growth and nourishment, though the sun is not growth
Being and essence, though the Good is 'beyond being'
table.note: Republic VI.507b–509c. The 'child of the good' is the sun itself.

sections.key: As the sun gives light, sight and growth to the visible world, the Good gives truth, knowledge and being to the intelligible world, while being beyond it.

paras: The phrase 'beyond being', epekeina tēs ousias, has been argued over more than almost any other in Plato. On a modest reading, Plato means only that the Good is higher in rank than the other forms, 'in dignity and power'. On a stronger reading, he means that the Good is not a being at all, not one more item in the universe, but the source of all beings, as the sun is not a plant but makes plants grow.

The stronger reading had an enormous future. If the source of everything is beyond being, then nothing we say about ordinary things fits it exactly. We can say what it is not, and speak of it by images and analogies, like the sun. That thought runs from the Neoplatonists through the Christian writer known as Dionysius the Areopagite (around AD 500) to the 'negative theology' of the Middle Ages, which says that God is beyond every name, and to the mystics. It is one reason Socrates refuses to define the Good: perhaps it cannot be defined.
sections.key: 'Beyond being' may mean the Good is only highest in rank, or that it is the source of all being and so beyond our categories; the second reading founded the tradition of negative theology.

paras: The line is Plato's map of reality and of knowing. It has four sections, rising in clarity and truth. Most scholars think the cave is meant to match it, though they disagree about how closely.

rows: The forms, and the Good as first principle
The things outside, and the sun
The carried objects and the fire
table.note: Republic VI.509d–511e; VII.517a–b, 532a–534a. The matching with the cave is an interpretation.

sections.key: The line rises from images through things and mathematics to the forms and the Good, with four states of mind to match; the cave tells the same story as a journey.

paras: Plato never says plainly that the Good is God, and he uses the word 'god' in several ways. The Greeks had many gods, and Plato took part in the city's worship, though he wanted its stories purified: in Republic II he says that God is good and cannot be the cause of evil. In the Timaeus, a late dialogue read in the journey Number and nature, a divine craftsman, the Demiurge, makes the visible world by looking to the forms as a pattern, because he is good and wanted everything to be as like himself as possible. In the Laws (Book X) Plato argues that the gods exist, care for humans and cannot be bribed, and wants atheism punished.

So Plato believed in divine reality, and in a good, ordering mind behind the world. But the Demiurge looks up to the forms; he does not make them. And the Good is not described as a person who knows, loves or acts. Most scholars say Plato's Good is not the God of the Bible: it is the highest principle, not someone who speaks. Others argue that his language of the Good as 'father' of the sun, the cause of all things, comes close to a philosophical idea of God. Both sides agree that Plato pointed further towards one supreme source of all things than any Greek before him.
sections.key: Plato believed in a good divine order: God cannot cause evil; a divine craftsman made the world. But his Good is not clearly a person, and the craftsman looks up to the forms rather than making them.

paras: About six hundred years after Plato, an Egyptian-born Greek philosopher teaching in Rome, Plotinus (about 204–270), built a whole system on the Good beyond being. His pupil Porphyry gathered his writings into six groups of nine, the Enneads. For Plotinus the first principle is the One, or the Good, utterly simple and beyond being and thought. From it, as light streams from the sun without the sun losing anything, flows Mind, which contains the forms; and from Mind flows Soul, which gives life to the world. The human soul's task is to turn back and climb, through virtue and contemplation, to union with the One. Porphyry records that Plotinus reached that union four times in the years he knew him.

This 'Neoplatonism' became the main form of pagan philosophy in late antiquity, and the philosophy Christian thinkers knew best. Augustine read Plotinus in Latin; the Cappadocian Fathers and Dionysius in the East drew on him. Stephen MacKenna's English translation of the Enneads (1917–1930) is how many modern readers first met him.
sections.key: Plotinus (c. 204–270) made Plato's Good into the One beyond being, from which Mind and Soul flow and to which the soul returns: the Platonism Christians knew best.

paras: Not everyone who loves Plato's Good believes in God. The novelist and philosopher Iris Murdoch (1919–1999), in The Sovereignty of Good (1970), argued that Plato was right that goodness is real, a magnetic centre that draws attention away from the self towards what is true, but that we no longer need, or can have, the personal God of Christianity. She thought the Good could do much of the work God had done: moral attention, humility, love of what is outside us. Her book has been widely read by believers and unbelievers alike.

The question she raises runs through the rest of this journey. If the Good is real, is it a principle, or a person? Can a principle be loved, prayed to, trusted? The psalmist speaks to the light: 'in your light we will see light'. Plato looks at it. The last session will show what Christians made of the difference.
sections.key: Iris Murdoch argued that Plato's Good is real without God; the question is whether the highest reality is a principle to look at or a person to speak to.

refs: Plato, Republic VI.504e–511e (the greatest study; the sun; the line); VII.517b–c, 532a–534a; II.379a–c (God is good and not the cause of evil); Timaeus 27c–30c (the Demiurge); Laws X.885b–907d.
Aristoxenus, Elements of Harmony II.30–31, on Plato's lecture 'On the Good'.
Plotinus, Enneads V.1, V.4, VI.9; Porphyry, Life of Plotinus 23 (union four times); tr. Stephen MacKenna (1917–1930; only the volumes up to 1926 are in the public domain under our rule).
Pseudo-Dionysius, Divine Names and Mystical Theology (c. AD 500).
Iris Murdoch, The Sovereignty of Good (1970).
On the Good and God: Lloyd Gerson, God and Greek Philosophy (1990); Julia Annas, An Introduction to Plato's Republic (1981), ch. 10.

debate.question: Is Plato's Good God?

positions.name: Yes, in effect: the Good is the divine source
positions.who: Plotinus and the Neoplatonists; many Christian readers from Augustine to the Cambridge Platonists; modern scholars such as Lloyd Gerson
positions.view: The Good is the cause of all being and knowledge, beyond being, the 'father' of the sun. That is what philosophers mean by God. Plato's reticence is reverence, not doubt.
positions.evidence: 'Beyond being'; the Good as 'universal author of all things beautiful and right'; Plato's theology in Republic II, the Timaeus and the Laws.

positions.name: No: a principle, not a person
positions.who: Many modern scholars, for example Julia Annas and Terence Irwin
positions.view: The Good is the highest form, the principle of order and value that makes the forms what they are. It does not think, choose, love or act; nobody prays to it. Plato's gods are lower beings, and the Demiurge looks up to the forms. To call the Good 'God' reads later religion back into Plato.
positions.evidence: The Good is always called a form or idea; it is known by dialectic, not worshipped; the Timaeus places the forms above the craftsman.

positions.name: Real, but not God: the Good without God
positions.who: Iris Murdoch, The Sovereignty of Good (1970)
positions.view: Plato was right that goodness is real and transcendent, drawing us out of ourselves. But it is not a person and we do not need one. The Good is the proper object of moral attention, as God was for believers.
positions.evidence: The experience of moral attention and humility; the decline of belief in a personal God; Plato's own refusal to describe the Good as personal.

debate.agree: All agree that the Good is Plato's highest principle, the source of the intelligibility and value of everything, and that it shaped later ideas of God.

look.why: There is no painting in the gallery of the sun in its own place, which Plato said can only be seen last of all. David Teniers the Younger painted, in the early 1630s, the view from inside a cave out through its mouth into the light: the moment between the cave and the sun.
points: The round, cavernous mouth of a craggy grotto nearly fills the square painting.
Steep tan and earthy brown rocks rise like cliffs on each side, close to us.
A winding turquoise stream zigzags through the cave and out to a body of vivid blue water beyond the opening, with white caps on the waves.
Beyond, a band of opal-white mountains follows the curve of the opening and almost blends into a pearly white sky and clouds.
A wooden cross, set on a low rocky outcrop in the lower left corner, leans to one side.
Black and white birds fly in the distance, some tiny far away.

music.why: Haydn's oratorio The Creation (1798) begins with music depicting chaos, dark and unresolved, until the chorus sings 'and there was light' and the whole orchestra blazes into C major. In the biblical story light is made by God's word, and the sun only on the fourth day: a different picture from Plato's, but the same astonishment at light.

think.why: How the great teachers, from Plato and Aristotle to Augustine and Aquinas, argued from the order of things to God.

learn.why: The psalm's answer to Plato's sun: the light by which we see light is God's, and it is loving kindness.

check.q: Why does Socrates refuse to say what the Good is?
options: Because Glaucon has not asked
Because it is forbidden to speak of it
Because he thinks an opinion without knowledge would be blind, and the Good is too great for him to state now; he offers an image instead
Because he does not believe in it
check.why: He says 'all mere opinions are bad' and that reaching his thought would be 'an effort too great'. He clearly believes the Good is real, which rules out the first option.

check.q: In the analogy of the sun, what corresponds to light?
options: The forms
The Good
Opinion
Truth, which the Good gives to what is known
check.why: As light binds sight and the visible, truth binds knowledge and the known. The Good corresponds to the sun itself.

check.q: What is most surprising about Plato's claim that the Good gives things their being 'and yet the good is not essence'?
options: That the Good is smaller than the other forms
That being is less important than knowledge
That the source of all being is not itself one more being, but 'beyond being', as the sun makes things grow without being growth
That the Good does not exist
check.why: The sun analogy explains it: the cause of growth is not itself a growing thing. The third option is a common misreading of 'beyond being'.

check.q: Why does Plato place mathematics below philosophy on the divided line?
options: Because mathematics is false
Because philosophers dislike numbers
Because mathematics is about the visible world
Because mathematics uses visible diagrams and starts from assumptions it does not prove, while philosophy climbs past all assumptions to the Good
check.why: Mathematics is about intelligible objects, but it reasons downwards from unexamined starting points. The first option is wrong: geometers think about 'the absolute square', not the drawing.

check.q: What is the strongest reason for saying Plato's Good is not the God of the Bible?
options: Plato's Good is a principle that is known, not a person who speaks, loves or acts; in the Timaeus even the divine craftsman looks up to the forms
Plato lived before Jesus
The Bible never mentions light
Plato did not believe in anything divine
check.why: The difference is between a principle and a person. The third option is false: Plato's works are full of the divine.

check.q: What does Psalm 36 share with Plato's sun, and what does it add?
options: Both say that shadows are evil
Both see the highest reality as the source of life and of the light by which we see; the psalm adds faithful loving kindness and speaks to God as 'you'
The psalm says the sun is God
Nothing: they are unrelated
check.why: 'With you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.' The psalm's shadow of God's wings is a shelter, not a prison.

tutorial.question: What is the Good in Plato's Republic, and is it God?
tutorial.approach: Explain why the Good is the 'greatest study' and why Socrates will not define it. Set out the sun analogy, using a table if it helps, and explain 'beyond being'. Show how the divided line maps the climb. Then weigh the debate: the Neoplatonist and Christian reading, the reading of the Good as an impersonal principle, and Murdoch's Good without God. Give your own judgment with reasons.
strong: Explains why the Good is highest: it is what all seek and what makes the forms knowable and good.
Sets out the three parts of the sun analogy accurately (light/truth, sight/knowledge, growth/being).
Explains 'beyond being' and at least two ways of reading it.
Uses the divided line correctly, including the difference between mathematics and dialectic.
Brings in Plato's other theology (Republic II, Timaeus, Laws) with care.
Weighs at least two positions fairly and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each morning, before you look at a screen, look at the daylight for a minute and say Psalm 36:9 to yourself. Then, once during the day, when you are about to judge something, ask not 'do I like it?' but 'is it good, and how would I know?'
sessions.reflect: Is the highest thing in your life something you look at, or someone you speak to? What difference would it make?
takeaways: Plato's Good is the highest form: like the sun, it gives truth to what is known, knowledge to the knower and being to all things, while being 'beyond being' itself.
The divided line maps the climb from images and belief through mathematics to understanding of the forms and the Good.
Plato believed in a good divine order, but whether his Good is God is disputed; Plotinus made it the One, and Christians read it as a pointer to God.

sessions.title: The just city
sessions.line: A city ruled by philosophers who own nothing and would rather not rule, held together by a 'noble lie'. Plato's ideal state, which has inspired and horrified readers for two thousand years.
sessions.plain: The Republic imagines a perfect city. Its rulers are philosophers, trained for decades, who own no property, have no private families and rule not because they want to but because they must. Everyone is told a story that they were born from the earth with gold, silver or bronze in their souls, to keep each class content. Plato thought only such a city could be just. Many readers have admired its ideals of selfless service and education for women; many have been horrified by its lies, its control and its contempt for ordinary people.
sessions.why: The freed prisoner has climbed to the sun. Now Plato makes him go back down. The Good is not only to be seen; it is to be lived, and the Republic's question was always how a city, not just a soul, can be just. This session reads the return to the cave and the city that the returners are to rule.
answers: Who should rule, according to Plato?
What is the 'noble lie'?
Why must the philosopher go back down into the cave?
Did Plato ever try to put his ideas into practice?
sessions.finding: Plato's Republic imagines a city ruled by philosophers who own nothing and rule from duty, held together by a founding myth: an ideal of selfless, wise government that has inspired and horrified readers, because it puts truth above consent.

paras: We have climbed the whole cave. The prisoners take shadows for reality; the freed soul turns round and climbs. Outside it sees the forms, and last of all the Good, the sun, source of truth and being. On the way we learned that the soul has three parts, and that justice is reason ruling them. The Republic always set the soul beside the city. So now the question is: what would a city look like if it were ruled by those who have seen the Good?
background.key: The soul is just when reason rules; the Republic asks what a city would be like if those who have seen the Good ruled it.

paras: By Book IV Plato's city has three classes: rulers, soldiers (auxiliaries) and producers. The rulers and soldiers together are 'guardians'. In Book V Socrates proposes three things so shocking that he compares them to three great waves that might drown him in laughter. The first wave: women should be guardians alongside men, trained in the same way, since the difference between the sexes is irrelevant to ruling. The second: the guardians should have no private families; partners would be assigned by the rulers and children raised in common, so that no one knows their own child. The third and greatest wave: philosophers must rule.

To see why, remember the soul. The city is ruled by the class that matches reason. Its rulers must be the people who know the Good, and nothing must tempt them to rule for their own advantage: not money, not family, not ambition.

rows: Women may be guardians, with the same education as men
No private families or property for guardians; children raised in common
Philosophers must be kings, or kings philosophers
table.note: The guardians' lack of property is first set out in III.416d–417b.

background.key: Plato's city has rulers, soldiers and producers; its three 'waves' are women guardians, no private families for guardians, and philosopher-kings.

paras: The reading has four short parts, in the order they come in the Republic: the 'noble lie' and the guardians' poverty (Book III), the philosopher-kings (Book V) and the return to the cave (Book VII). Together they show what Plato thought a just city needs, and what he was willing to accept to get it. They answer the session's questions directly, in Plato's own words, which matters, because the Republic is often praised and condemned by people who have not read it.
The comparison is a short passage from Luke's Gospel, in which Jesus' disciples argue about which of them is the greatest. Jesus answers with a different picture of a ruler.
background.key: We read the noble lie, the guardians' poverty, the philosopher-kings and the return to the cave, then Jesus on rulers who serve.

before: What story are the citizens to be told, and why does Socrates hesitate to tell it?
Why must the guardians own nothing?
Why does Plato say the best city is one whose rulers are 'most reluctant to govern'?
sessions.readWhy: Plato's own words on how his just city is to be held together and who is to rule it.

paras: How then may we devise one of those needful falsehoods of which we lately spoke—just one royal lie which may deceive the rulers, if that be possible, and at any rate the rest of the city?
What sort of lie? he said.

Nothing new, I replied; only an old Phoenician tale (Laws) of what has often occurred before now in other places, (as the poets say, and have made the world believe,) though not in our time, and I do not know whether such an event could ever happen again, or could now even be made probable, if it did.
How your words seem to hesitate on your lips!
You will not wonder, I replied, at my hesitation when you have heard.
Speak, he said, and fear not.

Well then, I will speak, although I really know not how to look you in the face, or in what words to utter the audacious fiction, which I propose to communicate gradually, first to the rulers, then to the soldiers, and lastly to the people. They are to be told that their youth was a dream, and the education and training which they received from us, an appearance only; in reality during all that time they were being formed and fed in the womb of the earth, where they themselves and their arms and appurtenances were manufactured; when they were completed, the earth, their mother, sent them up; and so, their country being their mother and also their nurse, they are bound to advise for her good, and to defend her against attacks, and her citizens they are to regard as children of the earth and their own brothers.
You had good reason, he said, to be ashamed of the lie which you were going to tell.

True, I replied, but there is more coming; I have only told you half. Citizens, we shall say to them in our tale, you are brothers, yet God has framed you differently. Some of you have the power of command, and in the composition of these he has mingled gold, wherefore also they have the greatest honour; others he has made of silver, to be auxiliaries; others again who are to be husbandmen and craftsmen he has composed of brass and iron; and the species will generally be preserved in the children. But as all are of the same original stock, a golden parent will sometimes have a silver son, or a silver parent a golden son. And God proclaims as a first principle to the rulers, and above all else, that there is nothing which they should so anxiously guard, or of which they are to be such good guardians, as of the purity of the race. They should observe what elements mingle in their offspring; for if the son of a golden or silver parent has an admixture of brass and iron, then nature orders a transposition of ranks, and the eye of the ruler must not be pitiful towards the child because he has to descend in the scale and become a husbandman or artisan, just as there may be sons of artisans who having an admixture of gold or silver in them are raised to honour, and become guardians or auxiliaries. For an oracle says that when a man of brass or iron guards the State, it will be destroyed. Such is the tale; is there any possibility of making our citizens believe in it?
Not in the present generation, he replied; there is no way of accomplishing this; but their sons may be made to believe in the tale, and their sons’ sons, and posterity after them.

I see the difficulty, I replied; yet the fostering of such a belief will make them care more for the city and for one another. Enough, however, of the fiction, which may now fly abroad upon the wings of rumour, while we arm our earth-born heroes, and lead them forth under the command of their rulers. Let them look round and select a spot whence they can best suppress insurrection, if any prove refractory within, and also defend themselves against enemies, who like wolves may come down on the fold from without; there let them encamp, and when they have encamped, let them sacrifice to the proper Gods and prepare their dwellings.

And not only their education, but their habitations, and all that belongs to them, should be such as will neither impair their virtue as guardians, nor tempt them to prey upon the other citizens. Any man of sense must acknowledge that.
He must.

Then now let us consider what will be their way of life, if they are to realize our idea of them. In the first place, none of them should have any property of his own beyond what is absolutely necessary; neither should they have a private house or store closed against any one who has a mind to enter; their provisions should be only such as are required by trained warriors, who are men of temperance and courage; they should agree to receive from the citizens a fixed rate of pay, enough to meet the expenses of the year and no more; and they will go to mess and live together like soldiers in a camp. Gold and silver we will tell them that they have from God; the diviner metal is within them, and they have therefore no need of the dross which is current among men, and ought not to pollute the divine by any such earthly admixture; for that commoner metal has been the source of many unholy deeds, but their own is undefiled.

And they alone of all the citizens may not touch or handle silver or gold, or be under the same roof with them, or wear them, or drink from them. And this will be their salvation, and they will be the saviours of the State. But should they ever acquire homes or lands or moneys of their own, they will become housekeepers and husbandmen instead of guardians, enemies and tyrants instead of allies of the other citizens; hating and being hated, plotting and being plotted against, they will pass their whole life in much greater terror of internal than of external enemies, and the hour of ruin, both to themselves and to the rest of the State, will be at hand. For all which reasons may we not say that thus shall our State be ordered, and that these shall be the regulations appointed by us for guardians concerning their houses and all other matters?
Yes, said Glaucon.
I think, I said, that there might be a reform of the State if only one change were made, which is not a slight or easy though still a possible one.
What is it? he said.

Now then, I said, I go to meet that which I liken to the greatest of the waves; yet shall the word be spoken, even though the wave break and drown me in laughter and dishonour; and do you mark my words.
Proceed.

I said: ‘Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one, and those commoner natures who pursue either to the exclusion of the other are compelled to stand aside, cities will never have rest from their evils,—nor the human race, as I believe,—and then only will this our State have a possibility of life and behold the light of day.’ Such was the thought, my dear Glaucon, which I would fain have uttered if it had not seemed too extravagant; for to be convinced that in no other State can there be happiness private or public is indeed a hard thing.

Socrates, what do you mean? I would have you consider that the word which you have uttered is one at which numerous persons, and very respectable persons too, in a figure pulling off their coats all in a moment, and seizing any weapon that comes to hand, will run at you might and main, before you know where you are, intending to do heaven knows what; and if you don’t prepare an answer, and put yourself in motion, you will be ‘pared by their fine wits,’ and no mistake.
You got me into the scrape, I said.

And I was quite right; however, I will do all I can to get you out of it; but I can only give you good-will and good advice, and, perhaps, I may be able to fit answers to your questions better than another—that is all. And now, having such an auxiliary, you must do your best to show the unbelievers that you are right.

I ought to try, I said, since you offer me such invaluable assistance. And I think that, if there is to be a chance of our escaping, we must explain to them whom we mean when we say that philosophers are to rule in the State; then we shall be able to defend ourselves: There will be discovered to be some natures who ought to study philosophy and to be leaders in the State; and others who are not born to be philosophers, and are meant to be followers rather than leaders.

Yes, I said; and there is another thing which is likely, or rather a necessary inference from what has preceded, that neither the uneducated and uninformed of the truth, nor yet those who never make an end of their education, will be able ministers of State; not the former, because they have no single aim of duty which is the rule of all their actions, private as well as public; nor the latter, because they will not act at all except upon compulsion, fancying that they are already dwelling apart in the islands of the blest.
Very true, he replied.

Then, I said, the business of us who are the founders of the State will be to compel the best minds to attain that knowledge which we have already shown to be the greatest of all—they must continue to ascend until they arrive at the good; but when they have ascended and seen enough we must not allow them to do as they do now.
What do you mean?

I mean that they remain in the upper world: but this must not be allowed; they must be made to descend again among the prisoners in the den, and partake of their labours and honours, whether they are worth having or not.
But is not this unjust? he said; ought we to give them a worse life, when they might have a better?

You have again forgotten, my friend, I said, the intention of the legislator, who did not aim at making any one class in the State happy above the rest; the happiness was to be in the whole State, and he held the citizens together by persuasion and necessity, making them benefactors of the State, and therefore benefactors of one another; to this end he created them, not to please themselves, but to be his instruments in binding up the State.
True, he said, I had forgotten.

Observe, Glaucon, that there will be no injustice in compelling our philosophers to have a care and providence of others; we shall explain to them that in other States, men of their class are not obliged to share in the toils of politics: and this is reasonable, for they grow up at their own sweet will, and the government would rather not have them. Being self-taught, they cannot be expected to show any gratitude for a culture which they have never received. But we have brought you into the world to be rulers of the hive, kings of yourselves and of the other citizens, and have educated you far better and more perfectly than they have been educated, and you are better able to share in the double duty. Wherefore each of you, when his turn comes, must go down to the general underground abode, and get the habit of seeing in the dark. When you have acquired the habit, you will see ten thousand times better than the inhabitants of the den, and you will know what the several images are, and what they represent, because you have seen the beautiful and just and good in their truth. And thus our State, which is also yours, will be a reality, and not a dream only, and will be administered in a spirit unlike that of other States, in which men fight with one another about shadows only and are distracted in the struggle for power, which in their eyes is a great good. Whereas the truth is that the State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed, and the State in which they are most eager, the worst.
Quite true, he replied.
And will our pupils, when they hear this, refuse to take their turn at the toils of State, when they are allowed to spend the greater part of their time with one another in the heavenly light?

Impossible, he answered; for they are just men, and the commands which we impose upon them are just; there can be no doubt that every one of them will take office as a stern necessity, and not after the fashion of our present rulers of State.

Yes, my friend, I said; and there lies the point. You must contrive for your future rulers another and a better life than that of a ruler, and then you may have a well-ordered State; for only in the State which offers this, will they rule who are truly rich, not in silver and gold, but in virtue and wisdom, which are the true blessings of life. Whereas if they go to the administration of public affairs, poor and hungering after their own private advantage, thinking that hence they are to snatch the chief good, order there can never be; for they will be fighting about office, and the civil and domestic broils which thus arise will be the ruin of the rulers themselves and of the whole State.
Most true, he replied.
And the only life which looks down upon the life of political ambition is that of true philosophy. Do you know of any other?
Indeed, I do not, he said.
And those who govern ought not to be lovers of the task? For, if they are, there will be rival lovers, and they will fight.
No question.

Who then are those whom we shall compel to be guardians? Surely they will be the men who are wisest about affairs of State, and by whom the State is best administered, and who at the same time have other honours and another and a better life than that of politics?
They are the men, and I will choose them, he replied.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The noble lie
parts.context: Socrates and Glaucon have just described how the rulers are to be chosen from among the guardians. Now Socrates asks how to make everyone accept the arrangement. Jowett's '(Laws)' is his own cross-reference to Plato's later dialogue the Laws. The 'Phoenician tale' recalls the legend of Cadmus, a Phoenician, who sowed dragon's teeth from which armed men sprang out of the earth.
parts.plain: Socrates proposes one 'royal lie' to persuade rulers and people alike. Everyone will be told that their upbringing was a dream, and they were really formed inside the earth, their mother, so that they must defend their land and treat each other as brothers. And God mixed gold into rulers, silver into soldiers, and bronze and iron into farmers and craftsmen. Children usually match their parents, but if not, they must be moved up or down. Glaucon thinks this generation will not believe it, but their children might.

commentary.on: one of those needful falsehoods of which we lately spoke—just one royal lie
commentary.text: The Greek phrase is gennaion ti hen pseudomenous, often translated 'noble lie'; 'noble' can also mean 'grand' or 'well-bred'. Earlier (II.382c–d, III.389b) Socrates allowed rulers to lie, like doctors giving medicine, for the city's good. That permission is what modern critics find most chilling.

commentary.on: I really know not how to look you in the face, or in what words to utter the audacious fiction
commentary.text: Socrates is embarrassed, and Glaucon says he has 'good reason' to be ashamed. Plato knows exactly how bad this sounds. Whether he is endorsing it or showing its cost is one of the questions about the Republic.

commentary.on: her citizens they are to regard as children of the earth and their own brothers
commentary.text: The first half of the myth is about unity: everyone is born of the same land, so all are siblings. Many nations have founding stories of this kind. Athenians themselves claimed to be 'autochthonous', sprung from their own soil.

commentary.on: in the composition of these he has mingled gold
commentary.text: The second half is about rank: gold, silver, bronze and iron. It makes the class system seem natural and God-given, so that people accept their place.

commentary.on: a golden parent will sometimes have a silver son, or a silver parent a golden son
commentary.text: This matters, and is often missed. The classes are not hereditary castes. A child of farmers with 'gold' in his soul must be raised to rule, and a ruler's child without it must be moved down. Plato wants rule by merit, not birth, though he wants people to believe merit was set by God.

commentary.on: the fostering of such a belief will make them care more for the city and for one another
commentary.text: Plato's justification: the story makes people care for one another. The question for us is whether a society can be held together by a story its rulers know to be false, and what happens when the people find out.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: No gold for the guardians
parts.context: Socrates explains how the guardians, who have all the power, can be kept from turning on the people like wolves. Some lines are cut, marked '…'.
parts.plain: The guardians must have no property beyond the bare necessities, no private houses or stores, and only a fixed wage from the citizens. They live together like soldiers in a camp. They are told they have divine gold in their souls and need none of the earthly kind; they may not even touch it. If they ever own land, houses or money, they will become tyrants instead of protectors, and the city will be ruined.

commentary.on: nor tempt them to prey upon the other citizens
commentary.text: Plato's great fear, stated just before this (in the lines cut here): that the guardians, the city's watch-dogs, turn into wolves and prey on the sheep. Every political thinker since has had to face it.

commentary.on: none of them should have any property of his own beyond what is absolutely necessary
commentary.text: The guardians live a kind of communism, but only the guardians: the farmers and craftsmen keep private property. The point is not economic equality but keeping power and wealth apart.

commentary.on: the diviner metal is within them, and they have therefore no need of the dross which is current among men
commentary.text: The myth of the metals is now used to keep the rulers honest: their wealth is in their souls. Christian readers thought of Jesus' words about treasure in heaven, and monastic communities later lived something like this.

commentary.on: they will become housekeepers and husbandmen instead of guardians, enemies and tyrants instead of allies of the other citizens
commentary.text: The moment rulers can enrich themselves, Plato says, they rule for themselves. The rest of the sentence describes, with grim accuracy, how such regimes end: in fear, plots and ruin.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Philosopher-kings
parts.context: Glaucon has demanded that Socrates show the ideal city could actually exist. Socrates has just warned that no real city will ever match the ideal exactly. Now he names the one change that would make a real city close to it: the 'third wave'.
parts.plain: One change, not small or easy but possible, would reform a city. Until philosophers become kings, or kings become true philosophers, so that political power and wisdom come together, there will be no end to the troubles of cities or of humanity. Glaucon warns that people will attack him for saying it. Socrates says he must explain who the true philosophers are, those born to lead.

commentary.on: there might be a reform of the State if only one change were made, which is not a slight or easy though still a possible one
commentary.text: Just before this, Socrates has warned that no real city will match the ideal exactly; he is looking for the smallest change that would bring a real city close to it. Remember this when you hear the Republic called a blueprint.

commentary.on: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy
commentary.text: The most famous sentence in the Republic, and the session's memory piece. Notice the two ways in: philosophers can become rulers, or rulers can become philosophers. 'Philosopher' here means a lover of wisdom who has seen the Good, not a professor.

commentary.on: cities will never have rest from their evils,—nor the human race, as I believe
commentary.text: Not only Athens but 'the human race'. Plato thinks the root of political evil is power without wisdom. Remember his life: oligarchs and democrats alike had killed in Athens.

commentary.on: intending to do heaven knows what
commentary.text: Glaucon's comic picture of respectable citizens throwing off their cloaks and grabbing weapons to attack Socrates. Plato knows the idea is outrageous. He still means it.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Back down into the cave
parts.context: These are the pages straight after the cave and the turning of the soul. Socrates turns from education to its purpose: those who have seen the Good must rule. 'The islands of the blest' were where Greek heroes were thought to live after death in happiness.
parts.plain: The best minds must climb to the Good, but they must not be allowed to stay there. They must go back down among the prisoners and share their work and honours. Glaucon objects that this is unfair. Socrates says the law aims at the good of the whole city, not one class. These philosophers owe the city their education. Back in the dark, once their eyes adjust, they will see far better than the prisoners, because they have seen the real things. The best city is ruled by those who least want to rule; those who seek power for gain make it a battlefield.

commentary.on: they must be made to descend again among the prisoners in the den, and partake of their labours and honours
commentary.text: The return is compulsory. The philosopher would rather stay in the light. Plato insists that seeing the Good brings a duty to those still in the dark. Contemplation is not an escape.

commentary.on: the happiness was to be in the whole State
commentary.text: The law does not aim at making one class happy but the whole city. This is the principle by which Plato justifies everything in the Republic, including its harshest parts. It is also the principle his critics attack: whose happiness counts, and who decides?

commentary.on: each of you, when his turn comes, must go down to the general underground abode, and get the habit of seeing in the dark
commentary.text: Now Socrates speaks directly to the future rulers. The philosophers take turns: some time in the light, some in the cave. Their vision of the Good makes them better at seeing the shadows for what they are.

commentary.on: in which men fight with one another about shadows only and are distracted in the struggle for power
commentary.text: Ordinary politics, for Plato, is a fight over shadows: reputations, offices, money. Anyone who has watched a party conference may feel he had a point.

commentary.on: the State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed
commentary.text: Perhaps the most admired sentence in this part of the Republic. Those who want power most are the least fit for it. Plato wants rulers who have something better to do, and rule only from duty.

commentary.on: who are truly rich, not in silver and gold, but in virtue and wisdom
commentary.text: The true wealth of a ruler is in the soul. This links back to the metals: the guardians' gold is inside them. A ruler who is poor inside will try to fill himself with the city's goods.

read.author: Plato
read.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy

paras: A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.
He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
But not so with you. But one who is the greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.
For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.

parts.title: The kings of the nations lord it over them
parts.context: Luke's Gospel, probably written about AD 80–90. The scene is the Last Supper in Jerusalem, the night before Jesus' death. The disciples have just heard him speak of his body and blood given for them, and they start to argue about rank.

commentary.on: The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
commentary.text: 'Benefactor', euergetēs, was a title Greek kings and rich patrons proudly took. Jesus notes the gap between the title and the reality, as Plato did with rulers who fight over shadows.

commentary.on: one who is governing, as one who serves
commentary.text: Plato's rulers serve the city, reluctantly and from duty, but they are still a separate class who know better. Jesus says the one who governs must become like the youngest and like a servant at table.

commentary.on: But I am among you as one who serves
commentary.text: The deepest difference. Plato's philosopher goes down into the cave because the law compels him. Here the one who is greatest has come down willingly, and serves at the table. Christians later read this as the meaning of the incarnation.

compare.why: Jesus' disciples argue about which of them is the greatest. His answer is a different picture of authority from Plato's: not the wisest ruling the rest, but the greatest serving.
compare.title: One who serves

paras: Plato's guardians live a strange life. They own nothing beyond necessities, eat together in common messes, may not touch gold or silver, and have no private families: partners are assigned at festivals by lots the rulers secretly arrange, so that the best breed with the best, and children are raised in common nurseries (V.459d–461e). They are educated from childhood in music, gymnastics and stories carefully censored, then in mathematics for ten years, then in philosophy for five, then sent back into the 'cave' to hold office for fifteen years. Only at fifty do the best see the Good itself and take their turns as rulers (VII.535a–540c).

Plato's reason for abolishing their families is the same as for abolishing their property: private interests divide loyalties. If every guardian thinks of every child as possibly his own, the whole city will be 'one', feeling pleasure and pain together like a single body (V.462a–e). Aristotle, in his Politics (II.1–5), answered that what belongs to everyone is cared for by no one, and a child who is everyone's son is no one's.
sections.key: The guardians own nothing, have no private families, and are educated for decades before ruling; Plato wanted to remove every private interest from power. Aristotle replied that what is everyone's is cared for by no one.

paras: The first 'wave' is often called the most surprising thing in the Republic. In a city where women could not vote, own property in their own name or speak in the assembly, Plato argued that the difference between men and women is no more relevant to ruling than the difference between bald and long-haired men is to shoemaking (V.454c). Women with the right nature should receive the same education, including gymnastics, and serve as guardians and rulers. He adds that women are on the whole weaker, but that does not affect who should rule.

Some scholars have called this the first argument for the equality of women in Western thought; others point out that Plato's motive was the good of the city, not women's rights, and that his 'equality' came with the abolition of the family. Both are true. It was centuries before anyone followed him.
sections.key: Plato argued, against the custom of his day, that women of the right nature should be educated and rule as guardians, though for the city's sake rather than for women's rights.

paras: The myth of the metals is the most troubling thing in the Republic. Plato's rulers are to tell the people, and if possible themselves, a story they know to be false, to make everyone accept their place. Defenders point out that Plato also says the classes are open to talent, that the myth teaches brotherhood, and that every society has founding stories that are not literally true. Some scholars translate gennaion pseudos as 'noble fiction' and compare it to a national myth.

Critics answer that this is the voice of every propaganda ministry. A government that keeps truth for itself and gives stories to the people has made itself the judge of what the people may know. The difficulty is sharp because Plato himself, in the cave, praised the one who leads prisoners to the truth. The Republic gives us the climb to the light and, for the many, a carefully managed shadow. That tension is still at the centre of arguments about Plato.
sections.key: The noble lie makes everyone accept their class by a story the rulers know is false: defenders call it a founding myth; critics call it propaganda, and it sits uneasily with the cave's love of truth.

paras: Why philosophers? Because, Plato argues, only someone who knows the Good knows what is truly good for a city, as only a navigator knows how to steer a ship. In Book VI he compares a democracy to a ship whose sailors fight over the helm, drug the owner and never study navigation (VI.488a–489a; if you have walked Democracy, you have read it).

But Plato's philosopher-king is not a strongman. He has no property, no family interests, and no wish to rule; he would rather be thinking. He goes back into the cave because he owes his education to the city and because justice requires it. That is why Plato says the best rulers are the most reluctant. The ideal has had a long life: in the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, who wrote philosophy in his tent; in medieval 'mirrors for princes', books teaching kings virtue; in the modern civil servant, trained, salaried and supposed to serve whoever governs.
sections.key: Plato's philosopher-king rules because he knows the Good and has nothing to gain; the ideal of the wise, reluctant, incorruptible ruler has had a long life.

paras: Did Plato try it? According to the Seventh Letter and later biographers, he went three times to Syracuse in Sicily, the richest Greek city of the West. In about 388 BC he visited the tyrant Dionysius I and was, the stories say, sent away in disgrace. There he befriended Dion, the tyrant's brother-in-law, who became his devoted follower. When Dionysius II came to power in 367 BC, Dion invited Plato back to educate the young ruler as a philosopher-king. It failed: Dion was exiled, and Plato was kept almost as a prisoner. A third visit, in 361, went no better. Dion later seized Syracuse by force in 357 and was murdered in 354.

The story, if the Seventh Letter is genuine, is a sobering commentary on the Republic. A philosopher tried to make a king into a philosopher and found that power, flattery and fear were stronger than argument. Plato's last and longest work, the Laws, describes a second-best city ruled not by philosopher-kings but by written law, a mixed constitution and elected officials.
sections.key: Plato tried to educate a tyrant of Syracuse into a philosopher-king, and failed; his last work, the Laws, prefers the rule of law and a mixed constitution.

paras: The Republic has been read in both ways for two thousand years. Thomas More's Utopia (1516) borrowed its common property; monastic communities lived something like its guardians' poverty; reformers from the Renaissance to the Victorians read it as a call to educate rulers for public service. Benjamin Jowett, whose translation we read, sent his Oxford students into the Indian Civil Service and Parliament in that spirit.

Others saw in it something darker: rulers who censor art, breed citizens like animals, decide who may know the truth, and justify it all by the good of the whole. When the twentieth century produced states that did exactly these things in the name of history or the nation, some readers looked back at the Republic with horror. The strongest of those critics, the philosopher Karl Popper, is the subject of the next session. First, though, notice the difference Luke shows us: Plato's ruler comes down because he must; the one Christians follow comes down because he loves.
sections.key: The Republic has inspired utopias, monks and public servants, and horrified readers who saw in it censorship, breeding and rule by those who claim to know best.

refs: Plato, Republic III.414b–417b (the noble lie; guardians' property), II.382c–d and III.389b (lies as medicine), V.451c–474c (the three waves), V.459d–462e (breeding and unity), VI.488a–489a (the ship of state), VII.519b–521b (the return), VII.535a–540c (the rulers' education); Laws (esp. III.693d–701b, IV.715b–d).
Aristotle, Politics II.1–5 (against the common family and property).
Seventh Letter 324b–352a; Plutarch, Life of Dion; Diogenes Laertius III.18–23. Authenticity: Burnyeat and Frede, The Pseudo-Platonic Seventh Letter (2015), against; many scholars, for.
On the noble lie: Malcolm Schofield, Plato: Political Philosophy (2006), ch. 8.
On women: Julia Annas, 'Plato's Republic and Feminism', Philosophy 51 (1976).
Thomas More, Utopia (1516); on Jowett and Plato in Victorian Oxford, Frank Turner, The Greek Heritage in Victorian Britain (1981).

debate.question: Should the wisest rule?

positions.name: Yes: rule by those who know
positions.who: Plato, Republic V–VII; in a modern form Jason Brennan, Against Democracy (2016), who argues for 'epistocracy'
positions.view: Ruling is a skill, like medicine or navigation. A city run by the ignorant, or by those who want power for themselves, will be steered onto the rocks. Power should go to those who know the good and have no interest in abusing it.
positions.evidence: The ship of state; the record of Athenian democracy, which executed Socrates and launched the disastrous Sicilian expedition; the failures of uninformed voters.

positions.name: No: the many, under law
positions.who: Pericles' funeral speech (Thucydides II.37–40); Aristotle, Politics III.11 (the wisdom of the many); modern democrats
positions.view: No one is wise enough to be trusted with unchecked power, and the people are better judges of how the shoe pinches than any expert. Wisdom is spread among the many; law and accountability protect against both tyrants and experts.
positions.evidence: The feast to which many contribute is better than one man's (Aristotle); the way rulers with no check become tyrants; the failure of Plato's own Sicilian experiment.

positions.name: Rulers as servants, under God
positions.who: Jesus in Luke 22:24–27; Augustine, City of God XIX; the Christian tradition of limited government
positions.view: Authority is real and needed, but every ruler is under God's law and must serve, not lord it over others. No human being is wise or good enough to deserve absolute power, because all are sinners. That conviction later supported checks and balances.
positions.evidence: 'One who is governing, as one who serves'; the prophets' judgment of Israel's kings; the record of power in every age.

debate.agree: All agree that power without wisdom and virtue is dangerous, and that the great question is how to get good government and keep rulers from becoming wolves.

look.why: Plato's city exists 'in words', nowhere on earth. An unknown American painter of the mid-nineteenth century painted 'A City of Fantasy', a city that exists nowhere either. It is not Plato's city; it is a picture of an imagined, ideal place, and how such dreams mix the old and the new.
points: A collection of buildings and towers stands on rolling green hills around a light grey stretch of water.
In the bottom right corner, ships with billowing sails glide on a wide waterway that divides into three rivers, each crossed by several bridges.
The buildings range from modest to towering: some look like medieval fortresses and towers, others like modern skyscrapers.
The more modern buildings are further away, resting on top of grey and blue clouds under a pale yellow sky.
The colours are muted: earth tones, soft greens, browns, greys, blues and off-whites.

music.why: Handel's coronation anthem Zadok the Priest (1727), sung at every British coronation since George II, retells the anointing of King Solomon. Plato dreamed of a king made wise by philosophy; the Bible's kings were anointed to rule under God. Listen to the great crescendo before the choir enters, and ask what makes a ruler fit to rule.

think.why: Plato's city puts the whole above the person. See in brief why the West came to believe that every single person counts.

learn.why: The most famous and most disputed sentence in the Republic. Learn it, and learn to argue with it.

check.q: What is the main purpose of the noble lie, in Plato's words?
options: To hide the existence of the forms from the people
To deceive enemies in war
To keep the rulers in power for life
To make the citizens care more for the city and one another, and accept their places
check.why: Socrates says the belief 'will make them care more for the city and for one another'. Critics think it also keeps rulers in power, but that is not the reason Plato gives.

check.q: Are Plato's classes hereditary castes?
options: Plato never discusses children
Yes, children always stay in their parents' class
Only the rulers' class is hereditary
No: a child with 'gold' in a farming family must be raised, and a ruler's child without it moved down
check.why: 'A golden parent will sometimes have a silver son'; the eye of the ruler 'must not be pitiful'. Plato wants merit, believed to be God-given.

check.q: Why must the guardians own no property?
options: So that the city saves money
So that power and wealth are kept apart: guardians with homes and money become 'tyrants instead of allies'
Because they are too busy to manage it
Because property is sinful
check.why: Plato's fear is of watch-dogs becoming wolves. The farmers and craftsmen do keep property, so the first option is not his view.

check.q: Glaucon says it is unjust to make the philosophers go back into the cave. What is Socrates' main reply?
options: That the cave is not really dark
That the philosophers will enjoy ruling
That the law aims at the happiness of the whole city, and the philosophers owe the city the education it gave them
That philosophers are naturally ambitious
check.why: Both reasons are in the text. The fourth option is the opposite of Plato's point: the best rulers are 'most reluctant to govern'.

check.q: What does the story of Plato in Sicily suggest about the Republic?
options: That Plato succeeded in creating a just city
That trying to turn a ruler into a philosopher met power, flattery and fear, and failed; Plato's later Laws prefers the rule of law
Nothing, because the story is certainly false
That the Republic was written as a manual for Dionysius
check.why: If the Seventh Letter is genuine, the experiment failed badly. Its authenticity is debated, but 'certainly false' goes too far.

check.q: How does Jesus' answer in Luke 22 differ most from Plato's picture of the ruler?
options: Jesus agrees that philosophers should rule
Plato says rulers should be humble servants of the poor
Jesus says no one should have authority
Plato's ruler comes down because the law compels him and rules as one who knows; Jesus says the greatest must be like a servant, and himself serves
check.why: 'One who is governing, as one who serves'. Jesus does not abolish authority, which rules out the first option, but turns it upside down.

tutorial.question: 'The State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best.' Is Plato's just city an ideal worth pursuing?
tutorial.approach: Describe the city: three classes, the guardians' way of life, the noble lie, the philosopher-kings. Explain Plato's reasons from the soul and the Good. Then weigh what is admirable (rule by the wise and incorruptible, education, women guardians, rulers with nothing to gain) against what is troubling (the lie, the abolition of families, the lack of consent). Use Plato's Sicilian failure and his later Laws, and set Luke 22 beside him.
strong: Describes the city accurately from the text, including the open classes and the guardians' poverty.
Explains why Plato thinks philosophers should rule, linking it to the Good and the return to the cave.
Gives the admirable side fairly: reluctance to rule, no private gain, education, women guardians.
Gives the troubling side fairly: the noble lie, eugenics and abolition of families, no consent.
Notes that Plato himself calls the city a pattern and later preferred the rule of law.
Uses Luke 22 or Aristotle to offer a different picture of authority.

reading.author: Malcolm Schofield
reading.title: Plato: Political Philosophy
reading.why: A clear, balanced guide to Plato's politics, including the noble lie.

reading.author: Plato, tr. Trevor Saunders
reading.title: The Laws
reading.why: Plato's second-best city, in a readable Penguin translation.

reading.author: Simon Blackburn
reading.title: Plato's Republic: A Biography
reading.why: How readers have loved and hated the Republic.

reading.author: Thomas More
reading.title: Utopia
reading.why: The Renaissance's answer to the Republic, with common property and a sting in the tail.

reading.author: Jason Brennan
reading.title: Against Democracy
reading.why: A modern philosopher's case for rule by the knowledgeable.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: in one place where you have some authority, at work, at home or in a group, do one task that serves the people under you and that no one will thank you for. Do it without mentioning it, as one who serves.
sessions.reflect: Who would you trust with power over you, and why? Would you trust yourself?
takeaways: Plato's just city is ruled by philosophers, trained for decades, who own nothing, have no private families and rule from duty; the best rulers are the most reluctant.
It is held together by the noble lie of the metals, which teaches brotherhood and rank; this, and its control of family and art, has horrified many readers.
Plato tried and failed to make a philosopher-king in Sicily, and later preferred the rule of law; Jesus offered another picture of authority: the ruler as one who serves.

sessions.title: The case against: Aristotle and Popper
sessions.line: Plato's greatest pupil said the forms explain nothing. A twentieth-century philosopher said the Republic is a blueprint for tyranny. The case against Plato, at full strength.
sessions.plain: Two famous attacks on Plato are taught in every university. Aristotle, who studied with Plato for twenty years, argued that the forms are useless: they do not explain anything about the world, they lead to absurd conclusions, and a doctor or a carpenter gains nothing from knowing 'the Good itself'. Karl Popper, writing during the Second World War, argued that the Republic is the first blueprint for a totalitarian state: rule by an elite, censorship, lies and the individual sacrificed to the whole. This session gives both charges at full strength, and then the replies.
sessions.why: We have climbed the whole of Plato's cave and come back down to his city. Every step depended on two things: that the forms and the Good are real, and that those who know them should shape the city. Now we test both. If Aristotle is right, there is no sun outside the cave. If Popper is right, the philosopher who returns is the most dangerous prisoner of all.
answers: How is Plato different from Aristotle?
What is the 'third man' argument?
Was Plato a totalitarian?
How do Plato's defenders reply?
sessions.finding: Aristotle argued that a separate Form of the Good explains nothing and helps no one to act; Popper argued that the Republic is a blueprint for a closed, totalitarian society. Both charges hit real weaknesses, and both can be partly answered, but neither can be dismissed.

paras: Here is Plato's case so far. We live among shadows (the cave). Beyond them are the forms, perfect and unchanging, which the mind can know (the forms). The soul has three parts, and is just when reason rules (the soul). Above all the forms is the Good, the sun that makes everything knowable and real (the Good). Those who have seen it must go back down and rule a city ordered by it, held together if need be by a noble lie (the just city). Two great objections strike at the foundation and at the building.
background.key: Plato's case rests on the reality of the forms and the Good, and on the claim that those who know them should rule. Aristotle attacks the first, Popper the second.

paras: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira, in northern Greece, the son of a court doctor. At seventeen he came to Plato's Academy in Athens and stayed twenty years, until Plato died in 347. He then left, tutored the young Alexander the Great, and in 335 founded his own school in Athens, the Lyceum. He wrote on almost everything: logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, poetry. Medieval writers called him simply 'the Philosopher'.

Aristotle admired Plato and kept much of his thought, but he rejected the separate forms. For him the form of a thing is in the thing: the form of a horse is what makes this horse a horse, not a perfect Horse in another world. He attacked Plato's theory in several works: most fully in the Metaphysics (I.9 and XIII–XIV), and in the Nicomachean Ethics (I.6), on the Form of the Good. We read the Ethics passage, because it attacks the very top of Plato's ladder.

background.key: Aristotle studied with Plato for twenty years and kept much of his thought, but placed the forms in things, not in a separate world.

paras: Karl Popper (1902–1994) was born in Vienna to a family of Jewish descent. As Nazism rose he left for New Zealand, where he taught philosophy from 1937 to 1945. When German troops entered Austria in 1938, he began a book he later called his 'war effort': The Open Society and Its Enemies, published in London in 1945. Its first volume, The Spell of Plato, argues that Plato was the first great enemy of the 'open society', a society in which individuals make decisions for themselves and institutions can be criticised and changed. Popper later taught at the London School of Economics and became one of the most influential philosophers of science.

Popper's book is still in copyright, so we give his arguments in our own words. They were not new in every detail; earlier writers such as Richard Crossman, in Plato Today (1937), had compared the Republic to the dictatorships of the 1930s. But Popper's was the fullest and most powerful attack.
background.key: Karl Popper, an Austrian exile in New Zealand, wrote The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945) as his 'war effort', accusing Plato of founding totalitarian thought.

paras: The reading is Aristotle's own attack on the Form of the Good (Nicomachean Ethics I.6), in D. P. Chase's translation of 1847. It is the most direct ancient answer to the sun passage. (His longer attack in the Metaphysics was not available to us in a translation old enough to quote, so we give it in our own words in the lecture.)

The comparison is Plato's own reply to the charge that his city is a blueprint: a short passage at the end of Republic IX, which says the city exists 'in idea only', as 'a pattern laid up in heaven' for anyone who wants to order their own soul.
background.key: We read Aristotle's attack on the Form of the Good, then Plato's own words that his city is a pattern in heaven for ordering the soul.
