paras: Again, the notion of one Universal Good (the same, that is, in all things), it is better perhaps we should examine, and discuss the meaning of it, though such an enquiry is unpleasant, because they are friends of ours who have introduced these εἴδη. Still perhaps it may appear better, nay to be our duty where the safety of the truth is concerned, to upset if need be even our own theories, specially as we are lovers of wisdom: for since both are dear to us, we are bound to prefer the truth. Now they who invented this doctrine of εἴδη, did not apply it to those things in which they spoke of priority and posteriority, and so they never made any ἰδέα of numbers; but good is predicated in the categories of Substance, Quality, and Relation; now that which exists of itself, i.e. Substance, is prior in the nature of things to that which is relative, because this latter is an off-shoot, as it were, and result of that which is; on their own principle then there cannot be a common ἰδέα in the case of these.

In the next place, since good is predicated in as many ways as there are modes of existence [for it is predicated in the category of Substance, as God, Intellect—and in that of Quality, as The Virtues—and in that of Quantity, as The Mean—and in that of Relation, as The Useful—and in that of Time, as Opportunity—and in that of Place, as Abode; and other such like things], it manifestly cannot be something common and universal and one in all: else it would not have been predicated in all the categories, but in one only.

Thirdly, since those things which range under one ἰδέα are also under the cognisance of one science, there would have been, on their theory, only one science taking cognisance of all goods collectively: but in fact there are many even for those which range under one category: for instance, of Opportunity or Seasonableness (which I have before mentioned as being in the category of Time), the science is, in war, generalship; in disease, medical science; and of the Mean (which I quoted before as being in the category of Quantity), in food, the medical science; and in labour or exercise, the gymnastic science. A person might fairly doubt also what in the world they mean by very-this that or the other, since, as they would themselves allow, the account of the humanity is one and the same in the very-Man, and in any individual Man: for so far as the individual and the very-Man are both Man, they will not differ at all: and if so, then very-good and any particular good will not differ, in so far as both are good. Nor will it do to say, that the eternity of the very-good makes it to be more good; for what has lasted white ever so long, is no whiter than what lasts but for a day.

No. The Pythagoreans do seem to give a more credible account of the matter, who place “One” among the goods in their double list of goods and bads: which philosophers, in fact, Speusippus seems to have followed.

But of these matters let us speak at some other time. Now there is plainly a loophole to object to what has been advanced, on the plea that the theory I have attacked is not by its advocates applied to all good: but those goods only are spoken of as being under one ἰδέα, which are pursued, and with which men rest content simply for their own sakes: whereas those things which have a tendency to produce or preserve them in any way, or to hinder their contraries, are called good because of these other goods, and after another fashion. It is manifest then that the goods may be so called in two senses, the one class for their own sakes, the other because of these.

Very well then, let us separate the independent goods from the instrumental, and see whether they are spoken of as under one ἰδέα. But the question next arises, what kind of goods are we to call independent? All such as are pursued even when separated from other goods, as, for instance, being wise, seeing, and certain pleasures and honours (for these, though we do pursue them with some further end in view, one would still place among the independent goods)? or does it come in fact to this, that we can call nothing independent good except the ἰδέα, and so the concrete of it will be nought?

If, on the other hand, these are independent goods, then we shall require that the account of the goodness be the same clearly in all, just as that of the whiteness is in snow and white lead. But how stands the fact? Why of honour and wisdom and pleasure the accounts are distinct and different in so far as they are good. The Chief Good then is not something common, and after one ἰδέα.

But then, how does the name come to be common (for it is not seemingly a case of fortuitous equivocation)? Are different individual things called good by virtue of being from one source, or all conducing to one end, or rather by way of analogy, for that intellect is to the soul as sight to the body, and so on? However, perhaps we ought to leave these questions now, for an accurate investigation of them is more properly the business of a different philosophy. And likewise respecting the ἰδέα: for even if there is some one good predicated in common of all things that are good, or separable and capable of existing independently, manifestly it cannot be the object of human action or attainable by Man; but we are in search now of something that is so.

It may readily occur to any one, that it would be better to attain a knowledge of it with a view to such concrete goods as are attainable and practical, because, with this as a kind of model in our hands, we shall the better know what things are good for us individually, and when we know them, we shall attain them.

Some plausibility, it is true, this argument possesses, but it is contradicted by the facts of the Arts and Sciences; for all these, though aiming at some good, and seeking that which is deficient, yet pretermit the knowledge of it: now it is not exactly probable that all artisans without exception should be ignorant of so great a help as this would be, and not even look after it; neither is it easy to see wherein a weaver or a carpenter will be profited in respect of his craft by knowing the very-good, or how a man will be the more apt to effect cures or to command an army for having seen the ἰδέα itself. For manifestly it is not health after this general and abstract fashion which is the subject of the physician’s investigation, but the health of Man, or rather perhaps of this or that man; for he has to heal individuals.—Thus much on these points.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato's pupil for twenty years, later tutor of Alexander the Great and founder of the Lyceum
parts.title: Friends, but truth first
parts.context: Aristotle's Ethics asks what the chief good for human beings is. Before giving his own answer, he examines Plato's: that there is one Universal Good, the same in all good things. 'They are friends of ours' means Plato and the Academy. Chase keeps the Greek words εἴδη (eidē, 'forms') and ἰδέα (idea, 'form') because, he notes, Aristotle uses both for Plato's theory. 'Categories' are the different kinds of thing that can be said to be: substance, quality, quantity, relation, time, place and so on. 'Very-Man' and 'very-good' are Chase's way of saying 'Man itself' and 'the Good itself'.
parts.plain: It is unpleasant to criticise a theory our friends invented, but lovers of wisdom must put truth before friends. First, the Platonists did not posit a form for things that come in an order, like numbers, yet good is said of things in different categories, one prior to another. Second, 'good' is said in as many ways as 'being': of God, of virtues, of the right amount, of the useful, of the right moment. So it cannot be one common thing. Third, if there were one form of good, there would be one science of all goods, but there are many. And the Good itself adds nothing: 'Man itself' and a man are equally man, and the Good is not more good for being eternal, as a white thing is not whiter for lasting longer.

commentary.on: such an enquiry is unpleasant, because they are friends of ours who have introduced these εἴδη
commentary.text: Aristotle is not a hostile outsider. He spent twenty years in the Academy. He says, with real feeling, that attacking the forms means attacking friends.

commentary.on: for since both are dear to us, we are bound to prefer the truth
commentary.text: This is the session's memory piece, and a fine principle. The Middle Ages turned it into a proverb: 'Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend'. Notice that it is itself a very Platonic idea: truth matters more than anything.

commentary.on: good is predicated in the categories of Substance, Quality, and Relation
commentary.text: The first argument is technical. Plato's followers did not make one form for things that come in a series (first, second, third), because the later depend on the earlier. But good things also come in a series: substances first, qualities and relations depending on them. So by their own rule there should be no single form of Good.

commentary.on: since good is predicated in as many ways as there are modes of existence
commentary.text: The second argument is the most famous. Think how differently we use 'good': God is good, a virtue is good, the right amount is good, a useful tool is good, the right moment is good. These are not one thing shared, as whiteness is shared by snow and chalk. 'Good' has many senses, and so there is no one Good.

commentary.on: there would have been, on their theory, only one science taking cognisance of all goods collectively
commentary.text: The third argument. If there were one Good, one science would know all goods. But a general knows the right moment in war, a doctor the right moment in disease. Knowledge of goodness is spread across many skills.

commentary.on: for what has lasted white ever so long, is no whiter than what lasts but for a day
commentary.text: The fourth argument, with a memorable image. The Good itself is supposed to be better because it is eternal. But a white thing that lasts a thousand years is no whiter than one that lasts a day. Eternity does not add goodness. So 'the Good itself' is just 'good' with the word 'itself' added.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato's pupil for twenty years, later tutor of Alexander the Great and founder of the Lyceum
parts.title: Goods in themselves
parts.context: Aristotle considers a reply a Platonist might make: the form covers only things good in themselves, not things good as means. Speusippus was Plato's nephew and successor as head of the Academy; the Pythagoreans had a famous list of pairs of opposites, with 'One' on the side of the good.
parts.plain: Perhaps the Platonists mean only things good in themselves, not useful things. Very well: take things good in themselves, like wisdom, sight, certain pleasures and honours. If they all fall under one form, the account of their goodness should be the same in each, as whiteness is the same in snow and white lead. But the accounts of the goodness of honour, wisdom and pleasure are different. So the good is not one common thing under one form. Otherwise nothing but the form would be good in itself, and the form would be empty.

commentary.on: The Pythagoreans do seem to give a more credible account of the matter
commentary.text: A sidelong compliment to another school, and to Plato's own successor Speusippus. Aristotle is placing Plato in a wider argument going on in Greek philosophy.

commentary.on: we can call nothing independent good except the ἰδέα, and so the concrete of it will be nought
commentary.text: A sharp dilemma. If only the form is truly good in itself, then nothing in our lives is, and the form is a form of nothing: 'the concrete of it will be nought'. An empty form explains no actual good.

commentary.on: of honour and wisdom and pleasure the accounts are distinct and different in so far as they are good
commentary.text: The core of the argument. Why is wisdom good? Why is honour good? Why is pleasure good? Each has a different answer. They are not good by sharing one thing, as white things share whiteness.

parts.author: Aristotle
parts.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato's pupil for twenty years, later tutor of Alexander the Great and founder of the Lyceum
parts.title: What use is the Good itself?
parts.context: Aristotle asks how the different goods can share the name 'good' at all, then turns to his last and most practical objection. 'The very-good' is the Good itself.
parts.plain: Why then do we call all these things 'good'? Perhaps because they come from one source, or aim at one end, or by analogy, as the mind is to the soul what sight is to the body. But leave that. Even if there were one separate Good, human beings could not do it or get it, and that is what ethics seeks. Someone may say knowing it would help as a model. But no craft uses it: a weaver or carpenter gains nothing by knowing 'the very-good', and a doctor does not study health in general but the health of this patient.

commentary.on: Are different individual things called good by virtue of being from one source, or all conducing to one end, or rather by way of analogy
commentary.text: Aristotle does not say 'good' is just a word with many unrelated meanings. He suggests the meanings are connected: by a common source, a common aim or analogy. This leaves room for a highest good; he will later say the highest human good is a life of excellent activity, and that the universe depends on a divine mind. But it is not a separate form.

commentary.on: manifestly it cannot be the object of human action or attainable by Man
commentary.text: Aristotle's deepest objection. Ethics is about what we can do. A Good in another world, which no one can do or possess, is no help to someone deciding how to live. Chase's footnote calls this 'the capital defect in Aristotle's eyes'.

commentary.on: how a man will be the more apt to effect cures or to command an army for having seen the ἰδέα itself
commentary.text: Plato said rulers must see the Good to rule well. Aristotle answers: show me a doctor who heals better, or a general who commands better, for having seen it. The practical arts work perfectly well without it.

commentary.on: for he has to heal individuals
commentary.text: The last word is the individual. The doctor heals this man. Aristotle's whole philosophy turns towards the particular thing in front of us, where Plato's turns towards the universal above it. Raphael's painting The School of Athens (1509–11) shows the two side by side: Plato pointing up, Aristotle holding his hand flat towards the earth.

read.author: Aristotle
read.who: Aristotle (384–322 BC), Plato's pupil for twenty years, later tutor of Alexander the Great and founder of the Lyceum

paras: To this nobler purpose the man of understanding will devote the energies of his life. And in the first place, he will honour studies which impress these qualities on his soul and will disregard others?
Clearly, he said.

In the next place, he will regulate his bodily habit and training, and so far will he be from yielding to brutal and irrational pleasures, that he will regard even health as quite a secondary matter; his first object will be not that he may be fair or strong or well, unless he is likely thereby to gain temperance, but he will always desire so to attemper the body as to preserve the harmony of the soul?
Certainly he will, if he has true music in him.

And in the acquisition of wealth there is a principle of order and harmony which he will also observe; he will not allow himself to be dazzled by the foolish applause of the world, and heap up riches to his own infinite harm?
Certainly not, he said.

He will look at the city which is within him, and take heed that no disorder occur in it, such as might arise either from superfluity or from want; and upon this principle he will regulate his property and gain or spend according to his means.
Very true.

And, for the same reason, he will gladly accept and enjoy such honours as he deems likely to make him a better man; but those, whether private or public, which are likely to disorder his life, he will avoid?
Then, if that is his motive, he will not be a statesman.
By the dog of Egypt, he will! in the city which is his own he certainly will, though in the land of his birth perhaps not, unless he have a divine call.
I understand; you mean that he will be a ruler in the city of which we are the founders, and which exists in idea only; for I do not believe that there is such an one anywhere on earth?

In heaven, I replied, there is laid up a pattern of it, methinks, which he who desires may behold, and beholding, may set his own house in order. But whether such an one exists, or ever will exist in fact, is no matter; for he will live after the manner of that city, having nothing to do with any other.
I think so, he said.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The city within
parts.context: The end of Book IX. Socrates has finished arguing that the just person is happier than the tyrant. Now he describes how the wise person will live, and Glaucon asks whether such a person would go into politics. 'By the dog of Egypt' is an oath Socrates often uses.
parts.plain: The wise person will spend his life on whatever makes his soul just, temperate and wise, and rule his body and his money to keep the soul in harmony. He will look at 'the city which is within him'. Will he be a statesman? In his own city, yes, though perhaps not in his homeland unless God calls him. Glaucon says this city exists only in words. Socrates says there is a pattern of it in heaven, for anyone who wishes to see it and order himself by it; whether it ever exists on earth does not matter.

commentary.on: He will look at the city which is within him
commentary.text: Here the Republic shows its other face. The city in words has also been a picture of the soul all along. Its first purpose is to help a person order their own life.

commentary.on: in the city which is his own he certainly will, though in the land of his birth perhaps not, unless he have a divine call
commentary.text: The wise man may not take part in the politics of his actual city at all, unless God calls him. This is hardly the voice of a revolutionary planning a seizure of power.

commentary.on: which exists in idea only; for I do not believe that there is such an one anywhere on earth
commentary.text: Glaucon, and Plato through him, admits that the just city exists nowhere. Defenders of Plato quote this against Popper: the Republic is a pattern for the soul, not a plan for a state.

commentary.on: In heaven, I replied, there is laid up a pattern of it, methinks, which he who desires may behold, and beholding, may set his own house in order
commentary.text: The pattern is in heaven, among the forms, and its use is personal: to set your 'own house in order'. Christian readers heard in this the city of God, whose citizens live by its law while on earth.

commentary.on: for he will live after the manner of that city, having nothing to do with any other
commentary.text: A last twist. The wise man lives by the heavenly city's law and no other. Critics can read this too as a dangerous claim: someone who answers only to an ideal city may feel free to ignore the real one.

compare.author: Plato
compare.why: Was Plato's city a blueprint for a real state? At the end of Republic IX, Plato answers in his own words. Read it beside Popper's charge.
compare.title: A pattern laid up in heaven

paras: Put the two charges together and they are formidable. The first says Plato's metaphysics is empty: the forms and the Good are not discoveries but inventions, abstract words turned into things. They double the world without explaining it, and they lead to contradictions Plato himself could not resolve. Nobody acts better for believing in them.

The second says Plato's politics is dangerous, and dangerous because of his metaphysics. If there is one perfect Good, knowable only by a few after decades of training, then those few have a right to rule everyone else, to tell them noble lies, to censor their poetry and arrange their marriages, for their own good. The open society, where anyone may criticise the government and no one claims final knowledge, is impossible on Plato's terms. On this view the cave is not a picture of liberation but of control: the philosopher returns to rule the prisoners, and decides which shadows they may see.
sections.key: Together the charges say Plato's forms are empty inventions, and that believing a few can know the Good leads straight to rule by an elite who lie, censor and control.

paras: Aristotle's attack in the Metaphysics (I.9, repeated in XIII.4–5) goes beyond the Good. Its main charges, in our own words, are these. First, the forms explain nothing about change: they are eternal and unmoving, so they cannot be why anything comes to be, grows or moves. Second, they are just the things themselves with 'itself' added: Man itself is a man made eternal, as the Greeks' gods are humans made immortal. Third, to say things 'participate' in forms, or that forms are 'patterns', is to use empty words and poetic metaphors; Plato never explains what participation is. Fourth, it is impossible for the essence of a thing to exist apart from the thing whose essence it is.

Aristotle's alternative is that forms exist only in things. The form of an oak is the structure and life of each oak, the pattern the acorn grows into. To know it, you study oaks, not a heavenly Oak. That is why Aristotle became the great biologist and observer, and Plato the great mathematician and visionary.
sections.key: Aristotle charged that separate forms explain no change, merely duplicate things with 'itself' added, and rest on empty metaphors; forms exist only in things.

paras: The most famous objection was first made, as far as we know, by Plato himself, in the Parmenides (132a–b), and was pressed by Aristotle, who gave it its name. It runs like this.

Why are Socrates and Plato both men? Because they share in the form, Man itself. But Man itself, on Plato's view, is perfectly a man; Plato speaks as if Beauty itself is beautiful and Largeness itself is large. So now we have three men: Socrates, Plato and Man itself. What do they have in common? By the same reasoning, there must be a further form, a 'third man', in which all three share. And then a fourth, and so on for ever. The theory that was meant to explain why many things share one character produces an endless series and explains nothing.

The argument depends on two assumptions: that a form has the character it explains (Man itself is a man), and that it is different from the things that share in it. Scholars since Gregory Vlastos's famous paper of 1954 have argued about whether Plato was committed to both. If a form is not itself an example of what it is the form of, the regress may not start. Plato may have written the Parmenides precisely to make his students find the answer.
sections.key: The third man: if Man itself is also a man, a further form is needed to explain what it shares with men, and so on for ever; whether Plato is committed to the premises is still debated.

paras: Popper's charges, in our own words, are these. First, Plato's justice is class rule: 'each doing his own work' means each staying in his class and the rulers ruling. That is not justice as most people understand it, equal treatment under law; it is the stability of a hierarchy. Second, Plato puts the state above the individual: the happiness 'of the whole city' justifies anything done to its members. Third, Plato's rulers lie, censor art, control breeding and education, and permit no change. Fourth, Plato's question, 'who should rule?', is the wrong one; it invites the answer 'the best', and then gives them unlimited power. The right question, Popper said, is how to arrange institutions so that bad rulers can be removed without bloodshed.

Behind all this Popper saw what he called 'essentialism' and 'historicism': the belief that there are fixed essences of things, known to experts, and laws of history that experts can see. He thought Plato, Hegel and Marx shared these beliefs, and that the totalitarian states of his day grew from them. Behind Plato's politics, Popper said, was a man frightened by the changes of his time, trying to arrest change for ever.
sections.key: Popper charged that Plato's justice is class rule, his state is above the individual, his rulers lie and censor, and his question 'who should rule?' is the wrong one; the right one is how to remove bad rulers peacefully.

paras: To Aristotle, Plato's defenders reply that the forms are not meant to explain change, but intelligibility and value: why there is anything to know, and why some things are better than others. Aristotle himself needed something like them: his highest being, the unmoved mover, is pure thought, eternal and unchanging, and his ethics needs a human nature that is the same everywhere. Many modern philosophers of mathematics are Platonists of some kind. And Plato, by writing the Parmenides, showed he knew the problems.

To Popper, defenders such as Ronald Levinson, In Defense of Plato (1953), replied that Popper read the Republic as a party manifesto rather than a philosophical dialogue; that Plato calls his city a pattern in heaven, existing nowhere; that his rulers own nothing and rule unwillingly, unlike any dictator; that the classes are open to talent and women; and that his last work, the Laws, prefers law and a mixed constitution. It is also anachronistic to blame a fourth-century Athenian for twentieth-century states.

But the replies do not answer everything. The noble lie is in the text. So are censorship, arranged breeding and the rulers' claim to know what is good for everyone. Plato's best defence is that he showed the dangers himself: in the cave the prisoners kill the one who frees them, and in the Republic the would-be philosopher-king must have nothing to gain. Whether that is enough is for you to judge.
sections.key: Defenders reply that the forms explain value and intelligibility, that Plato saw the problems himself, and that the Republic is a pattern, not a manifesto; but the noble lie and censorship remain in the text.

paras: A very different objection came from Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900). He did not think Plato too political but too otherworldly. In the preface to Beyond Good and Evil (1886) he called Plato's invention of 'pure spirit and the good in itself' the worst of all errors, and Christianity Platonism for the masses. For Nietzsche the 'true world' above the cave was a fiction made by people who could not bear this world of change, struggle and death, and it taught them to despise the body and life itself.

This charge matters for the last session, because it attacks Plato and Christianity together. Christians have answered that the God of the Bible made this world and called it good, became flesh, and will raise the body; that is not a flight from the world but a promise for it. But they have also admitted that some Christian piety, borrowing from Plato, did come to despise the body. The next session asks what Christians took from Plato and what they had to refuse.
sections.key: Nietzsche attacked Plato for inventing a 'true world' that taught people to despise this one, and called Christianity Platonism for the masses: a charge the last session must face.

debate.question: Is Plato's philosophy true, and is it safe?

positions.name: Plato: there is a Good, and it must rule
positions.who: Plato, Republic VI–VII and IX; modern defenders such as Ronald Levinson and Iris Murdoch
positions.view: Without real standards above opinion, there is nothing by which to judge a tyrant or a mob. Knowing the Good does not license tyranny; it forbids it, since the one who knows the Good has nothing to gain from power and everything to lose. The city is a pattern in heaven for ordering the soul.
positions.evidence: The reluctant rulers who own nothing; the city 'in idea only'; the need for standards to condemn injustice; Thrasymachus as the alternative.

positions.name: Aristotle: the forms are in things
positions.who: Aristotle, Metaphysics I.9 and Nicomachean Ethics I.6; the Aristotelian tradition, including Aquinas in part
positions.view: There are real natures and real goods, but they exist in things, not apart from them. A separate Good explains nothing and helps no one to act. Ethics starts from what people actually do and become, and politics from real cities, with their mixed constitutions and laws.
positions.evidence: The many senses of 'good'; the third man; the practical arts, which work without the Good itself; Aristotle's own studies of 158 constitutions.

positions.name: Popper: no one knows enough to rule unchecked
positions.who: Karl Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945); in part Isaiah Berlin and other liberal thinkers
positions.view: Plato's error is not only the forms but the belief that some people can know the good for everyone. All knowledge is fallible. The best society keeps every authority open to criticism and every ruler removable without bloodshed.
positions.evidence: The noble lie, censorship and breeding in the Republic; the record of twentieth-century regimes that claimed to know the course of history or the good of the nation.

debate.agree: All agree that how we answer 'is there a real Good?' shapes how we answer 'who should rule?', and that the Republic must be read whole, with its dangers as well as its vision.

look.why: A painting from Rembrandt's workshop of about 1653, perhaps by his pupil Willem Drost, which the gallery calls The Philosopher. Nothing in it says which philosopher; he could be any thinker weighing an argument. This painting is already in Rose Window's collection.
points: A light-skinned man with a gaunt face, shown from the chest up, almost fills the vertical painting.
He leans over his hands, folded along the bottom of the painting, and turns his head to our left, looking that way.
His deep-set hazel eyes are rimmed in pink under thick, dark brows; his mouth is slightly open.
A soft, oversized, earth-brown beret covers most of his head, and his brown beard is trimmed straight across.
He wears a brocaded robe with bands of rust red and gold over a mustard-yellow garment and a pleated ivory undergarment, with a thick gold chain hanging low across his chest.
The background is mottled honey and tawny brown.

music.why: Thomas Tallis's motet for forty voices (c. 1570), whose Latin text says, 'I have never put my hope in any other but you'. After a session of doubt about the highest thing, listen to forty separate voices, each singing its own line, making one harmony: neither a single ruler nor a crowd.

think.why: The modern debate about whether goodness is real, and the strongest objections to the idea, stated fairly.

learn.why: Aristotle's reason for attacking his teacher's theory: friends are dear, truth dearer. Learn it for every argument with someone you love.

check.q: What is Aristotle's argument from the many senses of 'good'?
options: That only God is good
That pleasure is the only good
That God, a virtue, the right amount, the useful and the right moment are each good in a different way, so goodness cannot be one common form
That 'good' is a meaningless word
check.why: Good is 'predicated in as many ways as there are modes of existence'. Aristotle does not say the word is meaningless: he suggests the senses are linked by source, end or analogy.

check.q: What is the point of Aristotle's remark that a white thing that lasts for ever is no whiter than one that lasts a day?
options: That the Good is white
That colours do not change
That being eternal does not make the Good itself any more good than an ordinary good thing; 'itself' adds nothing
That nothing lasts for ever
check.why: The Platonists praised the Good itself for being eternal; Aristotle replies that duration does not add goodness.

check.q: What is Aristotle's most practical objection to the Form of the Good?
options: That Plato never mentioned it
That it is too difficult to understand
That a separate Good cannot be done or possessed by human beings, and no doctor, weaver or general works better for knowing it
That it is against the gods
check.why: 'It cannot be the object of human action'; the doctor 'has to heal individuals'. The first option may be true, but it is not Aristotle's argument.

check.q: The 'third man' argument depends on assuming that Man itself is also a man. Why does that assumption matter?
options: Because it shows that Socrates was not a man
Because if the form is itself an example of what it explains, a further form is needed for what it shares with ordinary men, and so on for ever
Because Plato denied that men exist
Because it proves that there are exactly three men
check.why: Without that assumption ('self-predication') the regress may not start, which is why scholars argue over whether Plato held it.

check.q: Which of these is the strongest reply to Popper from the text of the Republic itself?
options: That Plato's rulers are rich
That Plato calls his city a pattern 'laid up in heaven' which exists nowhere on earth, to be used for ordering one's own soul
That the noble lie is not in the Republic
That Plato was a democrat
check.why: Republic IX.592a–b. The third option is simply false: the lie is in Book III, which is why Popper's case cannot be dismissed.

check.q: What is Popper's alternative to Plato's question 'Who should rule?'
options: 'How can we arrange institutions so that bad rulers can be removed without bloodshed?'
'How can we abolish government?'
'Who is the wisest?'
'How can philosophers win elections?'
check.why: Popper thought 'who should rule?' invites unlimited power for 'the best'. The open society's question is how to limit and remove rulers.

tutorial.question: 'Plato's forms explain nothing, and his politics is a blueprint for tyranny.' Discuss.
tutorial.approach: Take the two halves separately, then ask whether they are linked. For the forms, set out Aristotle's arguments (the many senses of good, the useless Good, the third man, the empty metaphor of participation) and the replies. For the politics, set out Popper's charges and the replies (the pattern in heaven, the reluctant rulers, the Laws). Then ask whether a belief in a real Good leads to rule by experts, or whether it is the only ground on which tyranny can be condemned.
strong: States Aristotle's arguments accurately from Nicomachean Ethics I.6, and the Metaphysics charges in summary.
Explains the third man argument and the premise of self-predication.
States Popper's charges fairly, including his alternative question.
Uses Republic IX.592 and the reluctant rulers as replies, and notes what they do not answer (the noble lie, censorship).
Considers whether the metaphysics and the politics are connected, as Popper claimed.
Reaches a balanced judgment and does not dismiss either side.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: choose one belief you hold strongly, about politics, faith or how to live, and write down the strongest objection to it in words its best defender would accept. Then write one sentence on what in the objection is true.
sessions.reflect: Plato thought a real Good must rule; Popper thought no one knows enough to rule unchecked. Could both be right?
takeaways: Aristotle argued that a separate Form of the Good is empty: 'good' has many senses, eternity adds nothing, and no doctor or general works better for knowing it; the third man shows a regress in the theory of forms.
Popper argued that the Republic is the first blueprint for a closed, totalitarian society: class rule, lies, censorship and the individual sacrificed to the whole.

Plato's defenders reply that the forms explain value, and that his city is a pattern for the soul whose rulers have nothing to gain; but the noble lie and censorship remain, and both charges must be weighed.

sessions.title: Plato baptised: the verdict
sessions.line: In Milan in 386 a young teacher read 'the books of the Platonists' and found almost everything he was looking for. Almost. What Christians took from Plato, and what they had to refuse.
sessions.plain: The verdict of this journey is Augustine's. He said the Platonists had seen the homeland from far off, from a mountain top, but had not found the way there. Christianity took Plato's picture of a light above the cave, a real Good and a soul made to turn towards it, and gave that light a face: Jesus Christ, who came down into the cave himself. It kept Plato's ladder and refused his contempt for the body, his belief in lives before and after this one, and his trust that knowledge alone can save.
sessions.why: We have climbed Plato's cave, seen the forms, the soul and the Good, watched the return to the city, and heard the case that there is no sun at all, or that its worshippers become tyrants. Now we ask what happened when Plato met the faith that would shape the West. The answer decides how much of this journey a Christian can keep.
answers: What did Christians take from Plato?
What did Augustine find in 'the books of the Platonists', and what did he not find?
What did Christianity reject in Plato?
What is Platonic love?
sessions.finding: Augustine said the Platonists saw the homeland from far off but not the way there: Christianity took Plato's sun and gave it a face, keeping his ladder to the Good and his turning of the soul, and refusing his scorn for the body and his hope of salvation by knowledge.

paras: Here is where the journey ends, so that you can test it as you read. Plato saw that there is a reality above the shadows, a Good that is the source of all truth and being, and that the soul is made to turn towards it. Christians of the first centuries thought he had seen truly, further than any pagan. But they also thought he had not seen the most important thing: that the Good is a person who loves, and who comes down into the cave to bring the prisoners out. In Augustine's words, which we are about to read, the Platonists saw the land of peace 'from the mountain's shaggy top' and found 'no way thither'.
background.key: The verdict: Plato saw the light above the cave; Christianity said the light is a person who comes down into the cave.

paras: This is the whole climb. We live among shadows and must be turned round. Beyond the shadows are the forms, known by the mind. The soul that climbs has three parts, and is just when reason rules. Above all is the Good, like the sun, beyond being. Those who see it must go back down and rule. Aristotle answered that a separate Good explains nothing; Popper, that the Republic is a blueprint for tyranny; Nietzsche, that Plato and Christianity alike invented a 'true world' and despised this one.
background.key: The climb: shadows, forms, soul, Good, return; the objections: no sun (Aristotle), a dangerous return (Popper), a false 'true world' (Nietzsche).

paras: Augustine was born in 354 in Thagaste, a small town in Roman North Africa, to a pagan father and a Christian mother, Monica. He became a brilliant teacher of rhetoric, the art of public speaking, in Carthage, Rome and, from 384, Milan, then the seat of the Western emperor. For nine years he had followed the Manichees, a religion that taught that the world is a battlefield between two equal powers, light and darkness, and that God himself is a kind of shining substance spread through space. By 386 he no longer believed them, but could not imagine anything that was not a physical thing, and could not see where evil came from if God was good.

Then, as he tells us in Confessions Book VII, someone gave him 'certain books of the Platonists', translated into Latin by the scholar Marius Victorinus. They were probably parts of Plotinus's Enneads and perhaps of his pupil Porphyry. They changed everything. A few months later, in a garden in Milan, he became a Christian, and he was baptised by Bishop Ambrose at Easter 387. He wrote the Confessions about ten years later, as bishop of Hippo, as a long prayer to God telling the story of his life.

timeline.text: Augustine born in Thagaste, North Africa
A follower of the Manichees
Teacher of rhetoric in Milan; hears Bishop Ambrose
Reads 'the books of the Platonists'; conversion in a garden in Milan
Baptised by Ambrose at Easter
Ordained priest, then bishop of Hippo
Writes the Confessions
Dies in Hippo as the Vandals besiege it

background.key: Augustine, a North African teacher in Milan who could not imagine anything non-physical, read Plotinus in Latin in 386; months later he became a Christian.

paras: The reading is Augustine's own account of what he found in the Platonists' books and what he did not find (Confessions VII.9–10), and his later judgment on them (VII.20–21). No text answers the question of this session more directly: it is the first and most famous meeting of Plato and the gospel, told by the man in whom it happened. (Augustine's journey of his own, in a later hall, reads other books of the Confessions.)

The comparison is the ending of Plato's Republic: the myth of Er, a soldier who comes back from the dead and describes how souls are judged and choose their next lives. It shows Plato's own hope for the soul beyond death, which Christians both recognised and rejected.
background.key: We read Augustine on the books of the Platonists, then the myth of Er, Plato's own picture of the soul's judgment and choice.
