paras: And Thou, willing first to show me how Thou resistest the proud, but givest grace unto the humble, and by how great an act of Thy mercy Thou hadst traced out to men the way of humility, in that Thy Word was made flesh, and dwelt among men:--Thou procuredst for me, by means of one puffed up with most unnatural pride, certain books of the Platonists, translated from Greek into Latin. And therein I read, not indeed in the very words, but to the very same purpose, enforced by many and divers reasons, that In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: the Same was in the beginning with God: all things were made by Him, and without Him was nothing made: that which was made by Him is life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shineth in the darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not. And that the soul of man, though it bears witness to the light, yet itself is not that light; but the Word of God, being God, is that true light that lighteth every man that cometh into the world. And that He was in the world, and the world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not. But, that He came unto His own, and His own received Him not; but as many as received Him, to them gave He power to become the sons of God, as many as believed in His name; this I read not there.

Again I read there, that God the Word was born not of flesh nor of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. But that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, I read not there. For I traced in those books that it was many and divers ways said, that the Son was in the form of the Father, and thought it not robbery to be equal with God, for that naturally He was the Same Substance. But that He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man, humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death, and that the death of the cross: wherefore God exalted Him from the dead, and gave Him a name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should how, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father; those books have not. For that before all times and above all times Thy Only-Begotten Son remaineth unchangeable, co-eternal with Thee, and that of His fulness souls receive, that they may be blessed;

and that by participation of wisdom abiding in them, they are renewed, so as to be wise, is there. But that in due time He died for the ungodly; and that Thou sparedst not Thine Only Son, but deliveredst Him for us all, is not there. For Thou hiddest these things from the wise, and revealedst them to babes; that they that labour and are heavy laden might come unto Him, and He refresh them, because He is meek and lowly in heart; and the meek He directeth in judgment, and the gentle He teacheth His ways, beholding our lowliness and trouble, and forgiving all our sins. But such as are lifted up in the lofty walk of some would-be sublimer learning, hear not Him, saying, Learn of Me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and ye shall find rest to your souls. Although they knew God, yet they glorify Him not as God, nor are thankful, but wax vain in their thoughts; and their foolish heart is darkened; professing that they were wise, they became fools.

And therefore did I read there also, that they had changed the glory of Thy incorruptible nature into idols and divers shapes, into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and birds, and beasts, and creeping things; namely, into that Egyptian food for which Esau lost his birthright, for that Thy first-born people worshipped the head of a four-footed beast instead of Thee; turning in heart back towards Egypt; and bowing Thy image, their own soul, before the image of a calf that eateth hay. These things found I here, but I fed not on them. For it pleased Thee, O Lord, to take away the reproach of diminution from Jacob, that the elder should serve the younger: and Thou calledst the Gentiles into Thine inheritance. And I had come to Thee from among the Gentiles; and I set my mind upon the gold which Thou willedst Thy people to take from Egypt, seeing Thine it was, wheresoever it were. And to the Athenians Thou saidst by Thy Apostle, that in Thee we live, move, and have our being, as one of their own poets had said. And verily these books came from thence. But I set not my mind on the idols of Egypt, whom they served with Thy gold, who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator.

And being thence admonished to return to myself, I entered even into my inward self, Thou being my Guide: and able I was, for Thou wert become my Helper. And I entered and beheld with the eye of my soul (such as it was), above the same eye of my soul, above my mind, the Light Unchangeable. Not this ordinary light, which all flesh may look upon, nor as it were a greater of the same kind, as though the brightness of this should be manifold brighter, and with its greatness take up all space. Not such was this light, but other, yea, far other from these. Nor was it above my soul, as oil is above water, nor yet as heaven above earth: but above to my soul, because It made me; and I below It, because I was made by It. He that knows the Truth, knows what that Light is; and he that knows It, knows eternity. Love knoweth it. O Truth Who art Eternity! and Love Who art Truth! and Eternity Who art Love! Thou art my God, to Thee do I sigh night and day.

Thee when I first knew, Thou liftedst me up, that I might see there was what I might see, and that I was not yet such as to see. And Thou didst beat back the weakness of my sight, streaming forth Thy beams of light upon me most strongly, and I trembled with love and awe: and I perceived myself to be far off from Thee, in the region of unlikeness, as if I heard this Thy voice from on high: "I am the food of grown men, grow, and thou shalt feed upon Me; nor shalt thou convert Me, like the food of thy flesh into thee, but thou shalt be converted into Me." And I learned, that Thou for iniquity chastenest man, and Thou madest my soul to consume away like a spider. And I said, "Is Truth therefore nothing because it is not diffused through space finite or infinite?" And Thou criedst to me from afar: "Yet verily, I AM that I AM." And I heard, as the heart heareth, nor had I room to doubt, and I should sooner doubt that I live than that Truth is not, which is clearly seen, being understood by those things which are made.

But having then read those books of the Platonists, and thence been taught to search for incorporeal truth, I saw Thy invisible things, understood by those things which are made; and though cast back, I perceived what that was which through the darkness of my mind I was hindered from contemplating, being assured "That Thou wert, and wert infinite, and yet not diffused in space, finite or infinite; and that Thou truly art Who art the same ever, in no part nor motion varying; and that all other things are from Thee, on this most sure ground alone, that they are." Of these things I was assured, yet too unsure to enjoy Thee. I prated as one well skilled; but had I not sought Thy way in Christ our Saviour, I had proved to be, not skilled, but killed. For now I had begun to wish to seem wise, being filled with mine own punishment, yet I did not mourn, but rather scorn, puffed up with knowledge.

For where was that charity building upon the foundation of humility, which is Christ Jesus? or when should these books teach me it? Upon these, I believe, Thou therefore willedst that I should fall, before I studied Thy Scriptures, that it might be imprinted on my memory how I was affected by them; and that afterwards when my spirits were tamed through Thy books, and my wounds touched by Thy healing fingers, I might discern and distinguish between presumption and confession; between those who saw whither they were to go, yet saw not the way, and the way that leadeth not to behold only but to dwell in the beatific country. For had I first been formed in Thy Holy Scriptures, and hadst Thou in the familiar use of them grown sweet unto me, and had I then fallen upon those other volumes, they might perhaps have withdrawn me from the solid ground of piety, or, had I continued in that healthful frame which I had thence imbibed, I might have thought that it might have been obtained by the study of those books alone.

Most eagerly then did I seize that venerable writing of Thy Spirit; and chiefly the Apostle Paul. Whereupon those difficulties vanished away, wherein he once seemed to me to contradict himself, and the text of his discourse not to agree with the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets. And the face of that pure word appeared to me one and the same; and I learned to rejoice with trembling. So I began; and whatsoever truth I had read in those other books, I found here amid the praise of Thy Grace; that whoso sees, may not so glory as if he had not received, not only what he sees, but also that he sees (for what hath he, which he hath not received?), and that he may be not only admonished to behold Thee, who art ever the same, but also healed, to hold Thee; and that he who cannot see afar off, may yet walk on the way, whereby he may arrive, and behold, and hold Thee. For, though a man be delighted with the law of God after the inner man, what shall he do with that other law in his members which warreth against the law of his mind, and bringeth him into captivity to the law of sin which is in his members? For, Thou art righteous, O Lord, but we have sinned and committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and Thy hand is grown heavy upon us, and we are justly delivered over unto that ancient sinner, the king of death; because he persuaded our will to be like his will whereby he abode not in Thy truth.

What shall wretched man do? who shall deliver him from the body of his death, but only Thy Grace, through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom Thou hast begotten co-eternal, and formedst in the beginning of Thy ways, in whom the prince of this world found nothing worthy of death, yet killed he Him; and the handwriting, which was contrary to us, was blotted out? This those writings contain not. Those pages present not the image of this piety, the tears of confession, Thy sacrifice, a troubled spirit, a broken and a contrite heart, the salvation of the people, the Bridal City, the earnest of the Holy Ghost, the Cup of our Redemption. No man sings there, Shall not my soul be submitted unto God? for of Him cometh my salvation. For He is my God and my salvation, my guardian, I shall no more be moved. No one there hears Him call, Come unto Me, all ye that labour. They scorn to learn of Him, because He is meek and lowly in heart; for these things hast Thou hid from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes. For it is one thing, from the mountain's shaggy top to see the land of peace, and to find no way thither; and in vain to essay through ways unpassable, opposed and beset by fugitives and deserters, under their captain the lion and the dragon: and another to keep on the way that leads thither, guarded by the host of the heavenly General; where they spoil not who have deserted the heavenly army; for they avoid it, as very torment. These things did wonderfully sink into my bowels, when I read that least of Thy Apostles, and had meditated upon Thy works, and trembled exceedingly.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.who: Augustine (354–430), North African teacher of rhetoric, later bishop of Hippo
parts.title: What I read there, and what I read not
parts.context: Augustine is speaking to God, as he does throughout the Confessions. 'One puffed up with most unnatural pride' is someone, unnamed, who gave him the books. He sets what he found in them beside the opening of John's Gospel (1:1–14) and Paul's hymn to Christ in Philippians (2:6–11), noting line by line what the Platonists had and lacked. Pusey's text prints 'should how' where 'should bow' is meant; we keep it as printed.
parts.plain: God gave me, through a proud man, some books of the Platonists. In them I found, in other words but the same meaning, the beginning of John's Gospel: the Word was with God and was God, all things were made through him, he is the light of every person. But I did not find there that he came to his own and they did not receive him, nor that the Word became flesh, nor that he emptied himself, became a servant and died on a cross. These truths are hidden from the proud and shown to the humble. I found also how the wise had turned the glory of God into idols; I did not feed on those.

commentary.on: Thou procuredst for me, by means of one puffed up with most unnatural pride, certain books of the Platonists
commentary.text: Augustine's first point is about pride. The books come through a proud man, and they will tempt Augustine to pride. Everything in this chapter turns on the difference between the proud and the humble.

commentary.on: not indeed in the very words, but to the very same purpose
commentary.text: Augustine does not claim the Platonists had read the Bible. He means that Plotinus's teaching, of a divine Mind through which all things are and which is the light of minds, matched the first verses of John in meaning.

commentary.on: the Word of God, being God, is that true light that lighteth every man that cometh into the world
commentary.text: Here is Plato's sun, in John's words. For Plato the Good gives light to minds; for Plotinus, Mind is the light; for John, the Word is 'the true light that enlightens everyone'. Augustine sees them as the same truth seen from two sides.

commentary.on: this I read not there
commentary.text: The refrain of the chapter. What the Platonists did not have is the coming: the Word 'came unto His own'. Plato's freed prisoner must be dragged up; John's light comes down.

commentary.on: But that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, I read not there
commentary.text: The centre of the difference. For Platonists the divine could never take a body; the body was what the soul climbed away from. That the eternal Word became a human being was, to them, absurd. Porphyry wrote a long book against the Christians partly for this reason.

commentary.on: that He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant
commentary.text: From Philippians 2. The Platonist climbs up by his own effort; Christ comes down by his own choice, 'emptying himself'. Compare the philosopher-king, who goes back into the cave because the law compels him.

commentary.on: For Thou hiddest these things from the wise, and revealedst them to babes
commentary.text: Jesus' words (Matthew 11:25). The Platonists were 'the wise'. What they missed was not more knowledge but humility: the way is learned by those who are 'meek and lowly in heart'.

commentary.on: I set my mind upon the gold which Thou willedst Thy people to take from Egypt, seeing Thine it was, wheresoever it were
commentary.text: A famous image. When Israel left Egypt, they took gold with them (Exodus 12:35–36). Augustine says Christians may take the gold of pagan philosophy, because all truth belongs to God wherever it is found. This became the Christian charter for using Plato.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.who: Augustine (354–430), North African teacher of rhetoric, later bishop of Hippo
parts.title: The Light Unchangeable
parts.context: Following the Platonists' advice to turn inwards and upwards, Augustine tries the ascent himself. 'The region of unlikeness' is a phrase from Plato (Statesman 273d) used by Plotinus for the soul's distance from God. 'I AM that I AM' is God's name given to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14).
parts.plain: Warned by those books to return into myself, I went into my inner self with you as my guide, and saw above my mind the unchanging Light: not ordinary light, nor a bigger version of it, but above me because it made me. Whoever knows the truth knows this light; love knows it. I trembled with love and awe and knew I was far from you, 'in the region of unlikeness', and heard: 'I am the food of grown men; you will not change me into you, but you will be changed into me.' And you cried: 'I AM that I AM'.

commentary.on: And being thence admonished to return to myself, I entered even into my inward self, Thou being my Guide
commentary.text: This is Plato's turning of the soul, done by Augustine. But notice the addition: 'Thou being my Guide'. The climb is not his own achievement; someone leads him, as someone frees Plato's prisoner.

commentary.on: the Light Unchangeable. Not this ordinary light, which all flesh may look upon
commentary.text: Augustine sees what Plato called the Good and Plotinus the One: a light that is not physical at all. For a man who had only been able to imagine God as a shining substance in space, this was a revolution.

commentary.on: but above to my soul, because It made me; and I below It, because I was made by It
commentary.text: Augustine explains 'above' not as higher in space but as maker to made. Here the Platonist light becomes the Creator. That is the first step from Plato's Good to the God of the Bible.

commentary.on: O Truth Who art Eternity! and Love Who art Truth! and Eternity Who art Love!
commentary.text: Plato's Good was truth and eternity. Augustine adds love, and addresses it as 'Thou'. The principle has become someone he can speak to.

commentary.on: in the region of unlikeness
commentary.text: A Platonist phrase: the soul has fallen away from the One into a place where it is unlike God. Augustine uses it to describe sin. The vision shows him not only the light but how far he is from it.

commentary.on: nor shalt thou convert Me, like the food of thy flesh into thee, but thou shalt be converted into Me
commentary.text: The Latin is mutabis, 'change', and Pusey translates it 'convert'. The turning of the soul in the cave is now a transformation: not just seeing the light, but being changed into its likeness.

commentary.on: Yet verily, I AM that I AM
commentary.text: Augustine hears God's name from Exodus. Plato's Good was 'beyond being'; the God of the Bible says simply 'I AM': being itself, and a person who speaks. Christian theologians would spend centuries thinking through those two phrases together.

parts.author: Augustine of Hippo
parts.who: Augustine (354–430), North African teacher of rhetoric, later bishop of Hippo
parts.title: Seeing the homeland, and finding the way
parts.context: Augustine has described how his vision did not last; he could not stay in the light (part of the book is cut, marked '…'). Now he looks back on what the Platonists gave him and what they could not. 'The beatific country' is heaven. In the last paragraph he quotes Paul's Romans 7 on the divided self.
parts.plain: The books of the Platonists taught me to look for truth that is not physical, and I saw your invisible things through the things you have made. But I was proud of knowing, not humble. Where was the love built on humility, which is Christ? I think God let me read them before Scripture so that I would learn the difference between those who see where to go but not the way, and the way itself. Then I read Paul, and found there every truth I had found in the Platonists, and also grace: how a man divided against himself can be healed. The Platonists have none of this: no tears of confession, no sacrifice, no cross. It is one thing to see the land of peace from a mountain top and find no way there; another to walk the road that leads there.

commentary.on: I saw Thy invisible things, understood by those things which are made
commentary.text: Paul's words (Romans 1:20). Augustine grants the Platonists real knowledge of God, by reason, from the world. Christians have never said Plato saw nothing.

commentary.on: For where was that charity building upon the foundation of humility, which is Christ Jesus?
commentary.text: Charity, Latin caritas, is love. The Platonists gave Augustine knowledge; they did not give him love or humility. And knowledge without love, he says, made him 'puffed up'.

commentary.on: between those who saw whither they were to go, yet saw not the way, and the way that leadeth not to behold only but to dwell in the beatific country
commentary.text: The verdict of this journey in Augustine's words. Plato saw the destination: the Good, the homeland of the soul. He did not find the way there. And Christianity promises not only to 'behold', as the freed prisoner beholds the sun, but to 'dwell'.

commentary.on: whatsoever truth I had read in those other books, I found here amid the praise of Thy Grace
commentary.text: Nothing true in Plato is lost. Augustine finds it all again in Scripture, but now inside 'the praise of grace': as a gift received, not an achievement. 'What hath he, which he hath not received?' (1 Corinthians 4:7).

commentary.on: what shall he do with that other law in his members which warreth against the law of his mind
commentary.text: Paul's divided self (Romans 7:23). Plato said reason must rule the soul's parts. Augustine says that is right, and impossible on our own: the will itself is divided and must be healed. This is where Plato's psychology and the Christian one part.

commentary.on: This those writings contain not
commentary.text: The second refrain. What the Platonists lack is not an idea but an event: the cross, 'the handwriting, which was contrary to us', blotted out (Colossians 2:14).

commentary.on: For it is one thing, from the mountain's shaggy top to see the land of peace, and to find no way thither
commentary.text: The most famous image in the chapter. The Platonist stands on a mountain and sees the promised land far off, but between him and it are impassable country and enemies. The Christian has not a better view but a road, and companions, and a guide.

read.author: Augustine of Hippo
read.who: Augustine (354–430), North African teacher of rhetoric, later bishop of Hippo

paras: When Er and the spirits arrived, their duty was to go at once to Lachesis; but first of all there came a prophet who arranged them in order; then he took from the knees of Lachesis lots and samples of lives, and having mounted a high pulpit, spoke as follows: ‘Hear the word of Lachesis, the daughter of Necessity. Mortal souls, behold a new cycle of life and mortality. Your genius will not be allotted to you, but you will choose your genius; and let him who draws the first lot have the first choice, and the life which he chooses shall be his destiny. Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified.’ When the Interpreter had thus spoken he scattered lots indifferently among them all, and each of them took up the lot which fell near him, all but Er himself (he was not allowed), and each as he took his lot perceived the number which he had obtained.

Then the Interpreter placed on the ground before them the samples of lives; and there were many more lives than the souls present, and they were of all sorts. There were lives of every animal and of man in every condition. And there were tyrannies among them, some lasting out the tyrant’s life, others which broke off in the middle and came to an end in poverty and exile and beggary; and there were lives of famous men, some who were famous for their form and beauty as well as for their strength and success in games, or, again, for their birth and the qualities of their ancestors; and some who were the reverse of famous for the opposite qualities. And of women likewise; there was not, however, any definite character in them, because the soul, when choosing a new life, must of necessity become different. But there was every other quality, and the all mingled with one another, and also with elements of wealth and poverty, and disease and health;

and there were mean states also. And here, my dear Glaucon, is the supreme peril of our human state; and therefore the utmost care should be taken. Let each one of us leave every other kind of knowledge and seek and follow one thing only, if peradventure he may be able to learn and may find some one who will make him able to learn and discern between good and evil, and so to choose always and everywhere the better life as he has opportunity. He should consider the bearing of all these things which have been mentioned severally and collectively upon virtue; he should know what the effect of beauty is when combined with poverty or wealth in a particular soul, and what are the good and evil consequences of noble and humble birth, of private and public station, of strength and weakness, of cleverness and dullness, and of all the natural and acquired gifts of the soul, and the operation of them when conjoined;

he will then look at the nature of the soul, and from the consideration of all these qualities he will be able to determine which is the better and which is the worse; and so he will choose, giving the name of evil to the life which will make his soul more unjust, and good to the life which will make his soul more just; all else he will disregard. For we have seen and know that this is the best choice both in life and after death. A man must take with him into the world below an adamantine faith in truth and right, that there too he may be undazzled by the desire of wealth or the other allurements of evil, lest, coming upon tyrannies and similar villainies, he do irremediable wrongs to others and suffer yet worse himself; but let him know how to choose the mean and avoid the extremes on either side, as far as possible, not only in this life but in all that which is to come. For this is the way of happiness.

And according to the report of the messenger from the other world this was what the prophet said at the time: ‘Even for the last comer, if he chooses wisely and will live diligently, there is appointed a happy and not undesirable existence. Let not him who chooses first be careless, and let not the last despair.’ And when he had spoken, he who had the first choice came forward and in a moment chose the greatest tyranny; his mind having been darkened by folly and sensuality, he had not thought out the whole matter before he chose, and did not at first sight perceive that he was fated, among other evils, to devour his own children. But when he had time to reflect, and saw what was in the lot, he began to beat his breast and lament over his choice, forgetting the proclamation of the prophet; for, instead of throwing the blame of his misfortune on himself, he accused chance and the gods, and everything rather than himself.

Now he was one of those who came from heaven, and in a former life had dwelt in a well-ordered State, but his virtue was a matter of habit only, and he had no philosophy. And it was true of others who were similarly overtaken, that the greater number of them came from heaven and therefore they had never been schooled by trial, whereas the pilgrims who came from earth having themselves suffered and seen others suffer, were not in a hurry to choose. And owing to this inexperience of theirs, and also because the lot was a chance, many of the souls exchanged a good destiny for an evil or an evil for a good. For if a man had always on his arrival in this world dedicated himself from the first to sound philosophy, and had been moderately fortunate in the number of the lot, he might, as the messenger reported, be happy here, and also his journey to another life and return to this, instead of being rough and underground, would be smooth and heavenly. Most curious, he said, was the spectacle—sad and laughable and strange;

for the choice of the souls was in most cases based on their experience of a previous life. There he saw the soul which had once been Orpheus choosing the life of a swan out of enmity to the race of women, hating to be born of a woman because they had been his murderers; he beheld also the soul of Thamyras choosing the life of a nightingale; birds, on the other hand, like the swan and other musicians, wanting to be men. The soul which obtained the twentieth lot chose the life of a lion, and this was the soul of Ajax the son of Telamon, who would not be a man, remembering the injustice which was done him in the judgment about the arms. The next was Agamemnon, who took the life of an eagle, because, like Ajax, he hated human nature by reason of his sufferings. About the middle came the lot of Atalanta; she, seeing the great fame of an athlete, was unable to resist the temptation:

and after her there followed the soul of Epeus the son of Panopeus passing into the nature of a woman cunning in the arts; and far away among the last who chose, the soul of the jester Thersites was putting on the form of a monkey. There came also the soul of Odysseus having yet to make a choice, and his lot happened to be the last of them all. Now the recollection of former toils had disenchanted him of ambition, and he went about for a considerable time in search of the life of a private man who had no cares; he had some difficulty in finding this, which was lying about and had been neglected by everybody else; and when he saw it, he said that he would have done the same had his lot been first instead of last, and that he was delighted to have it. And not only did men pass into animals, but I must also mention that there were animals tame and wild who changed into one another and into corresponding human natures—the good into the gentle and the evil into the savage, in all sorts of combinations.

And thus, Glaucon, the tale has been saved and has not perished, and will save us if we are obedient to the word spoken; and we shall pass safely over the river of Forgetfulness and our soul will not be defiled. Wherefore my counsel is, that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil. Thus shall we live dear to one another and to the gods, both while remaining here and when, like conquerors in the games who go round to gather gifts, we receive our reward. And it shall be well with us both in this life and in the pilgrimage of a thousand years which we have been describing.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The choice of lives
parts.context: Socrates tells the story of Er, a soldier from Pamphylia (in modern Turkey) who was killed in battle, lay twelve days unburied and came back to life on his funeral pyre. He saw the souls of the dead judged: the just went up to heaven for a thousand years, the unjust down beneath the earth. Now the souls who have finished their thousand years gather to choose their next lives. Lachesis, Clotho and Atropos are the three Fates, daughters of Necessity; a 'genius' is a guardian spirit.
parts.plain: The souls come before Lachesis. A prophet scatters lots to decide the order of choosing and lays out samples of lives of every kind, human and animal, rich and poor, famous and obscure. He proclaims that each soul chooses its own life, and the responsibility is the chooser's; God is not to blame. This, Socrates says, is the great danger of our state: so we must above all learn to tell good from evil, so that we choose the life that makes the soul more just.

commentary.on: Your genius will not be allotted to you, but you will choose your genius
commentary.text: The souls are not assigned their fate; they choose it. Plato's myth is about freedom and responsibility, not destiny.

commentary.on: Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified
commentary.text: The most quoted line of the myth. God is 'justified', not to blame. Plato had said in Book II that God is not the author of evil; here the same conviction is set in a story. Christian thinkers loved this line, and argued over how far it fits with grace.

commentary.on: And here, my dear Glaucon, is the supreme peril of our human state
commentary.text: Socrates breaks into the story to speak directly to Glaucon. Everything depends on choosing well, so everything depends on learning to tell good from evil. That is why the Republic is about education.

commentary.on: giving the name of evil to the life which will make his soul more unjust, and good to the life which will make his soul more just
commentary.text: The measure of a good life is not wealth, fame or beauty, but what it does to the soul. This is the Republic's answer to Glaucon, one last time.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: Choosing badly, and Odysseus' choice
parts.context: Er watches the souls choose. The famous dead appear: Orpheus the singer, Ajax and Agamemnon from the Trojan War, Thersites the mocker, and last of all Odysseus. Odysseus had spent ten years trying to get home after Troy; if you have walked Homer and the heroes, you know his story.
parts.plain: The first soul chooses the greatest tyranny at once, without thinking, and only then sees that it is fated to eat its own children, and blames everyone but itself. It had come from heaven, but had been good only by habit, without philosophy. Souls who had suffered chose more carefully. Many chose lives that answered their old wrongs: Ajax a lion, Agamemnon an eagle. Odysseus, with the last lot, looked for the quiet life of a private man with no cares, found it lying neglected, and chose it gladly.

commentary.on: in a moment chose the greatest tyranny
commentary.text: The first chooser has the best chance and wastes it. He grabs power, the very life the Republic has shown to be the most miserable.

commentary.on: his virtue was a matter of habit only, and he had no philosophy
commentary.text: A searching remark. This soul had lived well in a good city, from habit, without understanding why. Faced with a free choice, it chose disaster. Plato thinks goodness without understanding is fragile.

commentary.on: the pilgrims who came from earth having themselves suffered and seen others suffer, were not in a hurry to choose
commentary.text: Suffering taught what comfort did not. The souls from the place of punishment choose more wisely than those from heaven.

commentary.on: he went about for a considerable time in search of the life of a private man who had no cares
commentary.text: Odysseus, the cleverest and most ambitious of heroes, has learned from his toils, and chooses an ordinary, quiet life. It is a gentle ending to a book about rulers and power.

parts.author: Plato
parts.who: Plato (c. 428–348 BC), Athenian philosopher, pupil of Socrates and founder of the Academy
parts.title: The end of the Republic
parts.context: After choosing, the souls drink from the river of Forgetfulness and are born again (this part is cut, marked '…'). Er wakes on his funeral pyre. These are the last words of the Republic.
parts.plain: So the story was saved, Socrates says, and it will save us if we believe it: we will cross the river of Forgetfulness without defiling our souls. So let us hold to the upward way and follow justice and wisdom always, believing the soul is immortal and can bear every good and evil. Then we will be dear to one another and to the gods, here and in the thousand-year journey.

commentary.on: the tale has been saved and has not perished, and will save us if we are obedient to the word spoken
commentary.text: Plato, who wanted to censor stories, ends with a story, and says it 'will save us'. He knew that the deepest truths may need myths.

commentary.on: that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always
commentary.text: 'The heavenly way', literally 'the upward road': the climb out of the cave, one last time. The Republic ends where the cave began.

commentary.on: considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil
commentary.text: Plato's hope rests on the soul's immortality, by nature. Christianity spoke instead of resurrection, by God's gift: not the soul escaping the body, but the whole person raised. That is the deepest difference between them.

compare.author: Plato
compare.why: Plato ends the Republic with a story about what happens to the soul after death. Read its central scenes beside Augustine: Plato's own hope for the soul, in which choice and responsibility are everything.
compare.title: The myth of Er

paras: Augustine owed Plato, through Plotinus, three gifts that he says changed his life. First, the idea of a reality that is not physical: God is not a bright substance spread through space but Truth itself, above the mind. Second, an answer to the problem of evil: if everything comes from a good source, evil is not a thing at all but a lack, a falling away from the good, as darkness is the absence of light. Third, the way inward and upward: from bodies to the soul, from the soul to the light above it.

In the City of God (VIII.4–11), written twenty years later, Augustine says no philosophers come nearer to Christians than the Platonists, because they saw that God is the cause of existence, the light of knowledge and the good of life. He even wondered whether Plato had met the prophet Jeremiah in Egypt, before deciding the dates did not work. His use of Plato set the pattern for the Latin West for a thousand years.
sections.key: From Plato, through Plotinus, Augustine took a non-physical God, evil as the absence of good, and the way inward and upward; he judged the Platonists the nearest of all philosophers to Christians.

paras: Plato's influence ran through all the great Christian traditions, though differently in each. Set side by side:

rows: Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395); Dionysius the Areopagite (c. 500); Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662)
The soul's endless ascent into God; God beyond being and every name ('negative theology'); the world as a ladder of light
God as Truth above the mind; evil as privation; the 'journey of the mind into God'; Platonist themes kept even after Aquinas made Aristotle central
The Cambridge Platonists, such as Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) and Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688); C. S. Lewis (1898–1963)
Reason as 'the candle of the Lord'; eternal moral truths against Hobbes; the real world as more real than this one
table.note: Many in each tradition also resisted Plato: Tertullian ('What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?'), Luther's attacks on scholastic philosophy, and Orthodox caution about Origen.

sections.key: Platonism shaped the Orthodox East (Gregory of Nyssa, Dionysius), the Catholic West (Augustine, Boethius, Bonaventure) and Protestants such as the Cambridge Platonists and C. S. Lewis.

paras: The best-known modern Christian Platonist is C. S. Lewis. At the end of the last Narnia book, The Last Battle (1956), the children pass through a stable door into a country that is like Narnia but more real, 'deeper' and brighter, and discover that the old Narnia was only a copy of it. The old professor Digory explains it, and says, in one short line, 'It's all in Plato, all in Plato'. Lewis's point, in our words: the world we know is a shadow of a more real world, and death, for those who love the Lion, is going out of the cave into the sun.

Lewis's earlier book The Pilgrim's Regress (1933) and his sermon 'The Weight of Glory' (1941) say similar things. He thought that our longing for beauty, which no beautiful thing satisfies, is a clue that we were made for something beyond this world: a very Platonic thought, which he believed Christianity completed.
sections.key: C. S. Lewis ended Narnia with a Platonist picture: this world is a copy, and death for the faithful is going out of the cave into the real country.

paras: Christians took a great deal from Plato, but they also refused things at the heart of his thought. They refused the idea that the body is the soul's prison or tomb; Plato reports the saying 'the body is a tomb' (Cratylus 400c, Gorgias 493a), and the Phaedo calls philosophy a practice of separation from the body. Christianity says God made the body and called it good, that the Word became flesh, and that the body will be raised.

They refused the soul's existence before birth and its rebirth in other bodies. The theologian Origen (c. 185–254) had taught a form of pre-existence, and it was condemned in the sixth century. They refused the idea that the world is eternal, or made from pre-existing matter by a craftsman looking at forms; God creates from nothing, and the forms, if there are any, are his thoughts. They refused the Good as a principle that does not love. And they refused salvation by knowledge for the few: the gospel was for fishermen and slaves, by grace, through faith.

Nietzsche's charge, that Christianity is Platonism for the people, is half right. Christians did borrow Plato's language of the eternal and the true world. But the incarnation and the resurrection of the body are the opposite of Plato's escape from the body.
sections.key: Christianity refused the body as prison, pre-existence and rebirth, an eternal world, an impersonal Good and salvation by knowledge for the few; the incarnation and resurrection reverse Plato's escape from the body.

paras: One question people often ask about Plato is what 'Platonic love' means. Today it means a friendship without sex. The phrase comes from the Florentine Platonist Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), who spoke of amor platonicus, and Plato's Symposium is its source: love that begins with one beautiful person and climbs, step by step, to Beauty itself. If you have walked Why beauty matters, you have read the ladder.

For Plato the point is not that bodies are bad, but that love of one beautiful body is the first rung of a ladder whose top is the form of Beauty. Christians took the ladder up to God, but changed its direction once again. In the Symposium, love climbs from below; in the Gospel, 'God so loved the world' (John 3:16) that love came down. The Christian word for this, agapē, is love that gives itself rather than love that seeks what it lacks. The Swedish theologian Anders Nygren, in Agape and Eros (1930–36), argued the two are opposites; most later writers think Christianity transformed Plato's eros rather than rejected it.
sections.key: 'Platonic love' comes from Ficino's reading of the Symposium's ladder from one beautiful person to Beauty itself; Christians took the ladder but added love that comes down.

paras: So what is the verdict? Plato asked what is real and what the soul is, and answered: the forms and the Good are most real, and the soul is the part of us made to see them, which must be turned from shadows towards the light. Aristotle doubted the separate forms; Popper feared the rulers who claimed to know them; Nietzsche said the true world was a fable.

Christianity's answer was to keep Plato's question and his direction, and to change the light. In the cave, the prisoner is dragged up by someone unnamed, and the sun stays where it is. In John's Gospel, 'the light has come into the world'. Paul said God has shone in our hearts 'in the face of Jesus Christ'. Augustine said the Platonists saw the homeland from the mountain top, and Christ is the way. Whether you accept that or not, you can now see why so much of the West's thought about truth, the soul and God is, as Whitehead said, a footnote to Plato, and why so much of its faith is an argument with him.
sections.key: Christianity kept Plato's question and his upward direction, and changed the light: the sun came down into the cave, with a face.

refs: Augustine, Confessions VII.9–10, 20–21 (and VIII.2 on Victorinus); City of God VIII.4–11; On Christian Doctrine II.40.60 (the gold of the Egyptians).
Plotinus, Enneads I.6 and V.1; Porphyry, Against the Christians (fragments).
Plato, Republic X.614b–621d (the myth of Er); Cratylus 400c; Gorgias 493a; Phaedo 64a–67e; Statesman 273d ('region of unlikeness'); Symposium 210a–212b.
Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses; Dionysius the Areopagite, Divine Names; Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy; Bonaventure, The Journey of the Mind into God (1259).
Benjamin Whichcote, Moral and Religious Aphorisms (1703); Ralph Cudworth, A Treatise concerning Eternal and Immutable Morality (1731).
C. S. Lewis, The Last Battle (1956), ch. 15; 'The Weight of Glory' (1941).

debate.question: Was Christianity's use of Plato a gift or a corruption?

positions.name: A gift: preparation for the gospel
positions.who: Justin Martyr (d. c. 165); Clement of Alexandria (d. c. 215); Augustine; in our time, Pope Benedict XVI's Regensburg lecture (2006)
positions.view: God prepared the Greeks by philosophy as he prepared the Jews by the law. Plato saw truly that God is good, one, beyond the world and the source of all truth. Christians rightly took the 'gold of the Egyptians'; faith and reason belong together.
positions.evidence: The close match Augustine found between Plotinus and John 1; the Christian use of Platonist ideas to think clearly about God; Clement's report of the saying 'What is Plato but Moses speaking Greek?'

positions.name: A corruption: the gospel Hellenised
positions.who: Adolf von Harnack, History of Dogma (1886–89); in another way Tertullian and some Reformers; from outside, Nietzsche
positions.view: The simple message of Jesus about the kingdom of God was turned into Greek metaphysics: unchangeable substance, the soul's escape from the body, creeds full of philosophical terms. Plato distorted the Hebrew faith in a living, acting God.
positions.evidence: The gap between the language of the Gospels and that of the creeds; Christian suspicion of the body and sexuality; the 'God of the philosophers' who cannot suffer or change.

positions.name: A conversion of Plato
positions.who: Jaroslav Pelikan, Christianity and Classical Culture (1993); many modern historians
positions.view: Christian thinkers did not simply adopt or reject Plato; they transformed him. They used his ideas to say what the Bible meant and changed those ideas in the process: the Good became a person, creation replaced emanation, resurrection replaced escape.
positions.evidence: Augustine's own 'this I read not there'; the Church's rejection of pre-existence and an eternal world; the doctrine of the incarnation, which no Platonist could accept.

debate.agree: All agree that Christianity and Platonism met deeply in the first centuries, and that Western thought about God, the soul and truth cannot be understood without that meeting.

look.why: No painting for this session. The National Gallery of Art holds no painting of Saint Augustine, and none of Augustine reading the Platonists.

music.why: An Irish hymn, from an early medieval Irish poem, asking God to be the singer's vision, wisdom and light. It is Plato's turning of the soul made into a prayer: not to see a light, but to have God himself as the light by which one sees.

think.why: How the great teachers took the Greek idea of reason at the heart of reality and joined it to 'In the beginning was the Word'.

learn.why: The first page of the Confessions, written by the man who read the Platonists and found they could show him the homeland but not the way. You may know it already; say it now as his answer to Plato.

check.q: What did Augustine say he found in 'the books of the Platonists'?
options: Nothing of value
That the body is a prison to escape
In other words but the same meaning, that the Word was with God and was God, the light of every person, through whom all things were made
That the Word became flesh and died on the cross
check.why: He found the meaning of John 1:1–9. The incarnation and the cross are exactly what he says he did not find there.

check.q: What is the main point of Augustine's image of the mountain top?
options: That philosophy is useless
That heaven is a place on earth
That the Platonists lived in the mountains
That the Platonists saw the goal, the land of peace, but did not find the way there, which is Christ, received in humility
check.why: 'It is one thing… to see the land of peace, and to find no way thither.' Augustine does not say philosophy is useless: it showed him the homeland.

check.q: In Confessions VII.10, how does Augustine explain that the Light is 'above' his soul?
options: It is larger than his soul
It is higher in the sky
It is above as maker is above what it makes: 'because It made me'
It is above because it is brighter
check.why: This turns Plato's Good into the Creator. He explicitly denies that it is above as oil is above water or heaven above earth.

check.q: Which of these did Christianity take from Plato, rather than refuse?
options: Evil as a lack or falling away from the good, not a thing in its own right
The soul's existence before birth
The body as the prison of the soul
Rebirth in animal bodies
check.why: Augustine took the idea of evil as privation from the Platonists. The other three were rejected.

check.q: What does the myth of Er's line 'the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified' teach?
options: That the just are always rewarded on earth
That each soul chooses its life and is responsible for it, and God is not the cause of evil
That fate decides everything
That the gods choose for us
check.why: Souls choose their own guardian spirit. Christians welcomed the claim that God is not to blame, while adding that we need grace to choose well.

check.q: Why is Nietzsche's charge that Christianity is 'Platonism for the people' only half right?
options: Because Plato was a Christian
Because Christians did borrow Plato's language of a truer world, but the incarnation and the resurrection of the body are the opposite of escaping the body
Because Christians never read Plato
Because Nietzsche never read Plato
check.why: Christianity borrowed much, and refused Plato's escape from the body at its centre. The first and last options are simply false.

tutorial.question: 'The Platonists saw the homeland from far off, but not the way there.' Using Augustine, assess what Christianity took from Plato and what it refused.
tutorial.approach: Explain Augustine's situation in 386 and what the books of the Platonists did for him. Work through his list of what he found and did not find (Confessions VII.9), his ascent (VII.10) and his verdict (VII.20–21). Then widen it: what other Christians took from Plato (Dionysius, the Cambridge Platonists, Lewis), and what the Church refused (the body as prison, pre-existence, an impersonal Good). Use the myth of Er to show Plato's own hope. End with your judgment: gift, corruption or conversion?
strong: Explains why Augustine needed Platonism (the Manichees; a non-physical God; the problem of evil).
Uses the 'I read there' / 'I read not there' contrast accurately, with the incarnation and the cross.
Explains the ascent in VII.10 and how Augustine turns the Good into the Creator who is love.
Explains the mountain-top image and the difference between seeing and dwelling.
Names what Christianity refused, with reasons, and uses the myth of Er (immortality by nature against resurrection).
Weighs the 'gift', 'corruption' and 'conversion' views and reaches a judgment.

reading.title: The Origins of the Christian Mystical Tradition: From Plato to Denys
reading.why: Plato, Plotinus and the Fathers on the soul's ascent to God.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each night, before sleep, do what Augustine did: turn inward for five minutes, set aside the day's images and noise, and ask for light, not as an idea but as from someone. Use 'Be thou my vision' if you have no words of your own.
sessions.reflect: Augustine said knowledge without love made him proud. Has knowing more ever made you less humble? What would it take for what you have learned on this journey to become love rather than pride?
takeaways: Augustine found in the Platonists that God is incorporeal light, that evil is a lack of good, and the way inward and upward; he did not find the Word made flesh, humility or the cross.
His verdict: the Platonists saw the homeland from the mountain top but not the way; Christ is the way, and Christians may take Plato's gold because all truth is God's.
Christianity kept Plato's ladder and the turning of the soul, and refused the body as prison, pre-existence and an impersonal Good: it took Plato's sun and gave it a face.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: What is real, and what is the soul? In about 300 words, give your own answer, using at least three passages you have read on this journey, and say how far Plato was right. Then answer the strongest objection to your view.
closing.practice: Over the next week, read the whole of Republic VII, the cave and the education of the rulers, a few pages a night, in Jowett or a modern translation. Then read Confessions VII in full. Each night ask one question: what turned me towards the light today, and what turned me away?
synthesis: This journey asked Plato's two questions, what is real and what is the soul, and followed his picture of the cave from the shadows to the sun and back. Here are the short answers to its questions, in order.

Who was Plato? An Athenian aristocrat, born about 428 BC, who saw both an oligarchy and a democracy kill in his city, the second time his teacher Socrates. He turned from politics, founded the Academy in about 387 BC, and wrote some thirty-five dialogues in which Socrates speaks and Plato never does. He died about 348 BC.

What is Plato's cave? Prisoners chained since childhood see only shadows of carved objects thrown by a fire, and take them for reality. One is freed, dragged painfully up into the sunlight, and slowly learns to see real things and at last the sun. He goes back down, and the prisoners mock him and would kill anyone who tried to free them. Plato's key: the cave is the world of sight, the climb is the soul's ascent to what is known by the mind, and the sun is the Good. Education is not putting sight into blind eyes but periagōgē, turning the whole soul round.

What are the forms? The perfect, unchanging realities, Equality itself, Beauty itself, Justice itself, in which the many changing things share, and which the mind knows and the senses only glimpse. In the Phaedo Plato argues that because we judge things as falling short of standards we have never seen, we must have known those standards before birth: learning is recollection. He also raised the hardest objections to the forms himself.

What is the soul? Something akin to the forms, unseen and lasting, and yet divided. In Republic IV, from the thirsty man who will not drink and Leontius cursing his own eyes, Plato argues it has three parts: reason, spirit and appetite. Justice, in the soul as in the city, is each part doing its own work, reason ruling with spirit as its ally. Justice is the soul's health, worth having even if no one ever sees it: Plato's answer to the ring of Gyges.

Did Plato believe in God? He believed in a good divine order: God is good and not the author of evil, a divine craftsman shaped the world, and the gods cannot be bribed. Above all is the Good, which, like the sun, gives truth to what is known, knowledge to the knower and being to everything, while itself 'beyond being'. Whether that Good is God is disputed: it is the source of all, but it is not described as a person who loves. Plotinus made it the One; Christians read it as a pointer to God; Iris Murdoch kept it without God.

Who should rule? Those who have seen the Good, said Plato: philosophers, trained for decades, who own nothing, have no private families and rule from duty. The best city is the one whose rulers least want to rule. But Plato's city is held together by a noble lie of gold, silver and bronze in the soul, and controls its art and its marriages. When he tried to make a philosopher-king in Sicily, he failed, and his last work prefers the rule of law.

Was Plato right? The case against is strong. Aristotle, his pupil, said a separate Good explains nothing and helps no doctor or general; 'good' has many senses; and the forms lead to the endless regress of the 'third man'. Karl Popper said the Republic is the first blueprint for a closed, totalitarian society, and that the question 'who should rule?' should be replaced by 'how can bad rulers be removed without bloodshed?'. Nietzsche said Plato invented a 'true world' that taught people to despise this one. Plato's defenders answer that without a real Good there is nothing by which to condemn a tyrant or a mob, that his city is 'a pattern laid up in heaven' for ordering the soul, and that his rulers have nothing to gain. The noble lie and the censorship remain.

What did Christians take from Plato? Augustine, in Milan in 386, found in the books of the Platonists a God who is not physical, evil as the absence of good, and the way inward and upward to an unchanging Light. He found there the meaning of the first verses of John's Gospel. He did not find that the Word became flesh, that he emptied himself and died on a cross, or the humility and love that the cross teaches. The Platonists, he said, saw the land of peace from the mountain top and found no way there. Christianity kept Plato's ladder, his standards and his turning of the soul, and refused his contempt for the body, the soul's lives before and after this one, an impersonal Good and salvation by knowledge for the few.

What is Platonic love? Not, at first, friendship without sex, but love that climbs from one beautiful person to Beauty itself, as in the Symposium. Christians took the ladder and added a love that comes down.

So here is the verdict. Plato saw that there is more to reality than shadows, that goodness is not just what the strong or the many decide, and that the soul is made to turn towards a light it did not make. That is why the West has never stopped reading him. Christianity's answer was to keep his question and his direction, and to change the light: in the cave the sun stays where it is, and someone unnamed drags the prisoner up; in the Gospel the light has come into the world, and has a face. Whether you accept that or not, you cannot understand what the West has thought about truth, the soul and God without the man who first drew the cave.
exam: Explain the cave. What is Plato's theory of education?
'Learning is recollection.' Explain and assess the argument of Phaedo 72e–77a.
Does Plato show that the soul has three parts?
What is the Good in the Republic, and is it God?
Is Plato's Republic totalitarian?
'The forms explain nothing.' Discuss with reference to Aristotle.
What did Augustine take from Plato, and what did he refuse?
How is Plato different from Aristotle?

next.place: Visit the site of Plato's Academy, now a public park in north-west Athens, or stand before Raphael's School of Athens in the Vatican, with Plato pointing up and Aristotle to the earth.
next.book: Plato's Symposium and Phaedrus, then Iris Murdoch, The Sovereignty of Good (1970), and Augustine, Confessions VII–VIII.
